A compromise.
An account.
A private conversation.
A hidden browser history.
A grudge.
A plan.
An obsession.
Something you would be terrified to hear Jesus ask you to release.
Do not rush past that discomfort.
Sit there for a moment.
Because sometimes we call something a “blessing” simply because we desperately want it.
But desire does not determine holiness.
Opportunity does not equal permission.
Chemistry does not equal covenant.
Profit does not equal God’s approval.
Popularity does not equal anointing.
An open door is not automatically a door God opened.
And getting what you prayed for is not necessarily proof that God endorsed every choice that brought you there.
Scripture refuses to reduce blessing to comfort.
Psalm 1 calls the person who delights in God’s instruction blessed.
Jesus calls the poor in spirit blessed.
He calls those who mourn blessed.
He calls the meek blessed.
He calls those who hunger and thirst after righteousness blessed.
He even calls those persecuted for righteousness’ sake blessed.
Biblical blessing is far deeper than getting your preferred circumstances.
Sometimes the blessing is that God refuses to let your idol satisfy you.
Sometimes mercy feels like disruption.
Sometimes love sounds like conviction.
Sometimes God’s rescue begins when the thing you thought you could never live without starts losing its grip on you.
Think about the rich young ruler.
He came running to Jesus.
He had morality.
Respectability.
Possessions.
Religious seriousness.
Mark tells us something profoundly important before Jesus confronted his deepest attachment:
“Then Jesus beholding him loved him…” (Mark 10:21).
Loved him.
Do not miss that.
Jesus’ hard word came from love.
Christ identified the place where the man’s possessions possessed him.
Then came the invitation:
“…come, take up the cross, and follow me.”
And the man walked away sorrowful.
He came close enough to hear Jesus.
Close enough to be loved by Jesus.
Close enough to receive the invitation.
But something else had his heart.
That story should frighten every comfortable Christian.
Because it is possible to want eternal life while resisting the lordship of Christ.
It is possible to admire Jesus while refusing to follow Him into the one room of your life you keep locked.
We should not twist this passage into a simplistic claim that every Christian must dispose of every possession. Scripture addresses wealth in more nuanced ways than that.
But we should absolutely allow the passage to ask its intended heart-level question:
What possesses you?
What could Jesus ask for that would make you walk away sad?
There.
That may be your altar.
And perhaps you have been asking:
“Why won’t God bless this?”
But another question may be more revealing:
“Why am I so afraid to surrender it?”
Because if losing something would make you abandon Jesus, that thing may already occupy a place in your heart that belongs to Him.
This does not mean every loss is caused by idolatry.
It does not mean suffering automatically proves hidden sin.
Job demolishes that simplistic theology.
The man born blind in John 9 demolishes it too.
We must never look at another suffering person and casually declare, “God took that because you wouldn’t surrender.”
That can be cruel, presumptuous, and biblically irresponsible.
We do not know every purpose of God.
But Scripture does give us permission to examine our own hearts.
“Search me, O God, and know my heart…” (Psalm 139:23).
So this message is not ammunition for judging somebody else.
It is a mirror.
What are you protecting from Jesus?
Maybe you have been saying:
“God, bless my relationship.”
But you know the relationship continually pulls you toward sin.
“God, bless my business.”
But you are cutting ethical corners.
“God, bless my finances.”
But money already determines your identity and security.
“God, bless my ministry.”
But secretly you need applause more than you need holiness.
“God, restore my marriage.”
But you refuse to confess, forgive, seek help, change destructive behavior, or practice costly love.
“God, use me.”
But you refuse to repent privately.
“God, give me peace.”
But you keep feeding the very thing destroying your peace.
There are moments when the prayer must change.
From:
“God, make this work.”
To:
“God, make me Yours.”
From:
“God, give me what I want.”
To:
“God, teach me to want what pleases You.”
From:
“God, remove every consequence.”
To:
“God, transform my heart.”
From:
“God, bless my plans.”
To:
“Jesus, You are Lord. Rewrite them if You must.”
That prayer is terrifying.
Because He might.
But here is what fear forgets:
You are not surrendering to a stranger.
You are surrendering to Jesus.
The One who touched lepers.
The One who welcomed repentant sinners.
The One who wept.
The One who forgave.
The One who restored Peter after Peter publicly denied Him.
Peter’s story is exactly why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to one theme:
Peter had boasted that he would never fall away.
Hours later, he was denying that he even knew Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Imagine that sound.
Imagine Peter realizing that the man who had sworn loyalty had become the man Jesus said he would become.
Luke records that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
Scandal.
Failure.
Shame.
The kind of moment you think should become the final paragraph of your story.
But Jesus was not finished writing.
After the resurrection, John 21 brings Peter back beside a charcoal fire.
That detail matters.
John 18 tells us there had also been a charcoal fire when Peter denied Jesus.
Imagine what the smell might have awakened in him.
Memory.
Failure.
Shame.
And now Jesus brings Peter into another moment beside another charcoal fire.
Not to humiliate him.
To restore him.
“Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?”
Again.
Again.
Again.
Three denials.
Three questions.
Then:
“Feed my sheep.”
Jesus did not pretend Peter’s failure never happened.
Grace did something better.
Grace met Peter inside the wreckage and rewrote what failure had tried to make final.
That is the Gospel.
Not pretending sin does not matter.
Not calling rebellion freedom.
Not renaming darkness so nobody feels uncomfortable.
Grace confronts sin precisely because grace intends to rescue sinners from it.
Jesus does not merely forgive you in your chains.
He begins transforming you so the chains no longer define you.
That is why surrender matters.
You cannot cling to the prison and complain that Jesus has not led you into freedom.
You cannot enthrone the idol and ask Christ to decorate its temple.
You cannot knowingly cherish rebellion and call His conviction rejection.
But neither should you imagine that surrender makes you worthy of love.
Christ loved first.
“We love him, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).
Maybe you failed last night.
Maybe you fell again.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong.
Maybe your Bible has highlights everywhere while your heart has a locked room nobody is allowed to enter.
Maybe you lead others while privately wondering whether God could possibly still want you.
Hear the Gospel clearly:
Stop hiding.
Come to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
There is forgiveness in Jesus Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
Not because sin is small.
Because Christ is sufficient.
The blood of Jesus is not permission to remain comfortably enslaved to sin.
Grace teaches us to turn from ungodliness.
The Jesus who says, “Neither do I condemn thee,” also says, “go, and sin no more” (John 8:11).
Grace and repentance are not enemies.
Grace makes repentance possible.
And perhaps your surrender begins with three words:
“Jesus, take it.”
Not because the words themselves are magical.
Because the heart has finally stopped negotiating.
Take my reputation.
Take my future.
Take this relationship if it dishonors You.
Take this addiction—I cannot defeat it without You.
Take my resentment.
Take my need to be admired.
Take my plans.
Take my money.
Take my sexuality.
Take my success.
Take my failure.
Take the version of myself I have been desperately trying to protect.
Forgive my sin.
Rule my life.
Teach me obedience.
Make me more like You.
And if surrender means I do not receive the outcome I wanted…
be enough for me anyway.
That final sentence separates biblical surrender from prosperity religion.
Jesus is not a vending machine.
Christianity is not inserting obedience until a blessing falls out.
God may give.
God may withhold.
God may redirect.
God may close a door.
God may open one you never imagined.
God may answer immediately.
God may teach you to wait.
And sometimes, like Paul pleading over his thorn, you may hear an answer different from the one you wanted:
“My grace is sufficient for thee…” (2 Corinthians 12:9).
Sometimes the answer is not escape.
Sometimes the answer is sufficient grace.
And grace can carry a surrendered person where comfort never could.
Be real.

And if Christ has already delivered you from something you once thought you could never surrender, tell that testimony. Somebody scrolling through those comments may need evidence that grace still rebuilds lives.
Not because saving a post earns anything from God.
It does not.
Sharing Christian content does not make anyone righteous before God. Supporting a ministry does not purchase blessing, salvation, answered prayer, or a better place in heaven.
Only Christ saves.

But if Gospel-centered truth has helped you, supporting its continued spread can be one practical way of participating in the work of placing biblical encouragement before more people. If you want to glorify God through the resources He has entrusted to you, consider whether supporting and sharing faithful Gospel work is one of the ways you can serve others—not from guilt, not as payment for blessing, but freely, prayerfully, and for His glory.
But before you leave, there is one final question.
Not for the comments.
Not for your friends.
Not for the person you wish had read this.
For you.
What are you still holding?
You have prayed about it.
Protected it.
Explained it.
Excused it.
Cried over it.
Maybe even asked God repeatedly to bless it.
But have you surrendered it?
Jesus asked a devastating question immediately after calling His followers to deny themselves:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?” (Mark 8:36).
The Greek word translated “profit” is ὠφελεῖ — ōphelei.
What does it benefit?
What does it actually gain you?
That question still cuts through every generation.
What does it profit you to win the relationship and lose your obedience?
To build the platform and lose your integrity?
To accumulate the money and lose your worship?
To protect the secret and lose your peace?
To prove them wrong and become bitter?
To gain everybody’s applause while becoming spiritually hollow?
To hold the whole world in your hands while refusing to place your heart in the hands of Christ?
One day, everything you are clutching will leave your hands anyway.
The career.
The house.
The account.
The reputation.
The trophies.
The followers.
The body.
The applause.
The plans.
Everything.
But Jesus Christ remains.
So surrender is not God trying to empty your hands merely for the sake of emptiness.
It is the invitation to stop treating temporary things as though they can carry the eternal weight of your soul.
Open your hands.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Seek forgiveness where you have sinned.
Make restitution where Scripture and wisdom require it.
Get accountable if secrecy has been feeding your bondage.
Walk away from what Christ calls sin.
And where the issue is not sinful but simply precious, hold it with open hands before God.
Then pray without bargaining:

“Father, because of Your mercy, I give this to You. If it should remain, let it remain under Your lordship. If it should go, keep my heart faithful. If You redirect me, teach me to follow. If You make me wait, teach me to trust. Forgive my sins through Jesus Christ. Break every idol I have placed above You. I do not want merely Your gifts while resisting Your rule. I want Christ. Your will be done.”
Maybe your scandal is real.
Maybe the screenshots exist.
Maybe the marriage is wounded.
Maybe the addiction has left scars.
Maybe your children know what happened.
Maybe the church knows.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you destroyed something you cannot rebuild by yourself.
Maybe your greatest shame has already happened.
Peter had his rooster.
Thomas had his doubt.
Paul had his history.
The thief had his cross.
And sinners like us have ours.
Yet none of those stories places human failure above the authority of Jesus Christ to save.
The Gospel does not promise that every earthly consequence disappears.
It promises something infinitely greater:
There is grace for repentant sinners in Jesus.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is resurrection after the tomb.
There is a Savior stronger than your shame.
There is a King worthy of the thing you are terrified to surrender.
So share this with somebody carrying something too heavy to keep pretending about.
Because maybe the thing you are terrified to place in His hands is the very thing keeping your hands too full to cling completely to Him.
The altar is not where your story dies. In the hands of Jesus, it may be where the lie that ruled your story finally does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS SEXUAL REJECTION GROUNDS FOR DIVORCE? THE BIBLICAL ANSWER MAY CONVICT BOTH SIDES OF THE BED
paragraphs: IS SEXUAL REJECTION GROUNDS FOR DIVORCE? THE BIBLICAL ANSWER MAY CONVICT BOTH SIDES OF THE BED

When “not tonight” becomes months or years of rejection, the wound can become almost unbearable. But before you call a lawyer—or condemn the spouse who keeps saying no—you need to hear what Scripture actually says about sex, covenant, abandonment, repentance, and the Jesus who can still enter a marriage that feels dead.
There is a particular kind of loneliness that is difficult to explain to anyone who has never experienced it.
You are married.
But you feel unwanted.
You sleep beside the person who once promised to love you, yet the inches between your bodies sometimes feel like miles.
You remember when they reached for you.
You remember being desired.
You remember affection that did not have to be negotiated.
Now you hesitate even to touch them because you already know the possibility of rejection.
Again.
Maybe tonight you will stare at the ceiling and pretend it doesn't hurt.
Maybe you have stopped asking altogether.
Maybe your spouse is the one lying beside you wondering why every touch seems to carry an expectation they cannot bear.
Maybe sex has become associated with pressure instead of tenderness. Maybe resentment has been accumulating for years. Maybe there are wounds neither of you knows how to name.
And perhaps one terrible question has finally entered the room:
“If my husband or wife continually rejects me sexually, do I have biblical grounds for divorce?”
That question deserves more than a slogan.
It deserves more than somebody shouting, “God hates divorce!”
It also deserves more than somebody saying, “You deserve to be happy. Leave.”
Because a marriage may involve two wounded human beings while still standing beneath the authority of one holy God.
And if you are seriously considering ending your marriage, please hear this before anything else:
Do not use this article as a weapon against your spouse.
Read it first as a mirror.
Because before Scripture asks what your spouse owes you, Scripture has an uncomfortable way of asking what is happening inside you.
Jesus was once confronted with a divorce question.
The Pharisees essentially wanted to know how much justification a person needed to end a marriage.
Jesus took them somewhere deeper.
Back to creation.
Back before divorce certificates.
Back before legal arguments.
Back to God's intention for covenant.
He said that the two become “one flesh,” and then declared:
“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.” — Matthew 19:6, KJV
That is where a Christian conversation about divorce must begin.
Not with, “How miserable am I?”
Not with, “How long has it been since we had sex?”
Not even with, “What can I legally do?”
But with:
What has God joined together, and what does faithfulness to Him require of me now?
That does not make sexual rejection insignificant.
Quite the opposite.
Paul speaks about marital intimacy with startling directness in 1 Corinthians 7.
The Greek of 1 Corinthians 7:3 reads:
Τῇ γυναικὶ ὁ ἀνὴρ τὴν ὀφειλὴν ἀποδιδότω, ὁμοίως δὲ καὶ ἡ γυνὴ τῷ ἀνδρί.
A careful sense of the sentence is:
Let the husband give to his wife what is due, and likewise the wife to her husband.
One important word is ὀφειλή — opheilē.
It means something owed, a debt, an obligation, something due.
Paul is not describing sexual intimacy as an optional bonus for exceptionally happy marriages.
He treats marital intimacy as belonging to the mutual obligations of covenant.
And notice something that ancient and modern selfishness both desperately need to hear.
Paul makes the obligation mutual.
He does not tell wives that their bodies exist for their husbands while husbands remain autonomous.
He immediately applies the same principle in both directions.
Husband toward wife.
Wife toward husband.
Mutuality.
Covenant.
Giving.
Not taking.
This matters enormously, because 1 Corinthians 7 has sometimes been twisted into something ugly.
A husband may quote it to pressure a frightened or hurting wife.
A wife may use it to shame a struggling husband.
Someone may turn “marital duty” into permission to demand another person's body regardless of pain, fear, illness, trauma, exhaustion, or coercion.
That is not a faithful application of Paul's words.
Biblical marital intimacy is not a divine authorization for sexual coercion.
Paul's picture is reciprocal self-giving, not unilateral domination.
In fact, the next words become even stronger.
Μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους — Mē apostereite allēlous.
“Do not deprive one another.”
The verb ἀποστερέω — apostereō can carry the sense of depriving, defrauding, withholding, or robbing someone of what is due.

Then Paul gives an exception: abstinence may occur ἐκ συμφώνου — ek symphōnou, by agreement, and πρὸς καιρόν — pros kairon, for a limited time, in the context he describes of devotion to prayer, followed by coming together again.
Read that slowly.
Mutual agreement.
Limited time.
Spiritual purpose.
Return to one another.
That is radically different from one spouse saying, in effect:
“I don't care about this part of our marriage anymore. Your loneliness is your problem.”

If sexual intimacy is being deliberately withheld for months or years as punishment, manipulation, domination, humiliation, or indifference, Scripture does not require us to pretend nothing serious is happening.
Something serious is happening.
The rejected spouse may experience the wound not simply as sexual frustration but as repeated personal rejection:
I don't want you.
I don't need you.
Your longing does not matter to me.
Over enough time, that can cut deeply.
But now we have to make a distinction that could save someone reading this from making an irreversible decision:
Calling something sinful is not automatically the same thing as calling it biblical grounds for divorce.
That distinction matters.
Lying is sinful.
Bitterness is sinful.
Cruel speech is sinful.
Selfishness is sinful.
Sexual neglect can be sinful.
But Christians cannot simply take every serious marital sin and automatically add it to the biblical grounds for dissolving a marriage.
So what grounds does Scripture actually discuss?
Jesus' words in Matthew 19:9 include the Greek expression:
μὴ ἐπὶ πορνείᾳ — mē epi porneia
The crucial noun is πορνεία — porneia, commonly translated “sexual immorality.”
Jesus is dealing with divorce and remarriage and identifies porneia in the exception clause.
This is one reason many Protestant Christians have historically understood sexual immorality as a legitimate ground upon which divorce may be permissible.
Notice the word permissible.
Not mandatory.
Adultery does not command the innocent spouse to divorce.
The Gospel still leaves room for repentance, forgiveness, reconciliation, rebuilding, and astonishing grace.
Then Paul addresses another catastrophic marital situation in 1 Corinthians 7:15.
εἰ δὲ ὁ ἄπιστος χωρίζεται, χωριζέσθω
“But if the unbelieving [spouse] separates, let him separate.”
Paul then says:
οὐ δεδούλωται ὁ ἀδελφὸς ἢ ἡ ἀδελφὴ ἐν τοῖς τοιούτοις
The believing brother or sister is “not enslaved” or “not under bondage” in such circumstances.
The word translated “is not enslaved” is δεδούλωται — dedoulōtai, from δουλόω — douloō, language associated with bondage or enslavement.

Many Protestant interpreters therefore understand 1 Corinthians 7:15 as recognizing abandonment by an unbelieving spouse as another legitimate ground for divorce, although Christians have disagreed about the precise implications of “not bound,” particularly regarding remarriage.
And now we reach the difficult question.
What if your spouse has not physically walked out the door... but has sexually abandoned the marriage?
This is where sincere Christians begin to disagree.
Some Christians take the narrower position.

They argue that persistent sexual rejection can be genuine, grievous sin and a violation of 1 Corinthians 7, but that Scripture never explicitly calls sexual deprivation itself porneia and never explicitly identifies it as the abandonment described in 1 Corinthians 7:15.
Therefore, on this reading, sexual rejection by itself does not constitute biblical grounds for divorce.
The sin must be confronted.
Repentance should be sought.
Pastoral help may be necessary.
Professional Christian counseling may be wise.
In severe circumstances, temporary separation for safety, clarity, treatment, or intervention may sometimes become necessary.
But divorce cannot simply be inferred because marital intimacy has collapsed.
That position deserves to be represented fairly because it is attempting to avoid adding exceptions that Jesus and Paul did not explicitly state.
Other Christians make a broader covenantal argument.
They point, among other passages, to an intriguing Old Testament text.
Exodus 21:10 speaks of obligations involving a vulnerable wife:
שְׁאֵרָהּ כְּסוּתָהּ וְעֹנָתָהּ לֹא יִגְרָע
Transliterated approximately:
she'erah, kesutah, ve'onatah lo yigra
Her food, her clothing, and her marital rights were not to be diminished.
The final term, עֹנָתָהּ — onatah, has traditionally been understood in this context as referring to marital or conjugal rights.
The following verse says that failure to provide the specified obligations resulted in the woman's freedom.

Some interpreters therefore see a broader biblical covenant principle: persistent, willful deprivation of essential marital obligations can become a form of covenant abandonment even when the abandoning spouse still lives under the same roof.
From there, some Christian thinkers argue that extreme, unrepentant sexual abandonment may eventually constitute constructive or functional desertion.
The spouse has not necessarily abandoned the address.
But, they argue, the spouse may have abandoned the covenant in practice.
That interpretation should not be mocked.
But neither should it be presented as though Scripture simply says, “If your spouse refuses sex long enough, you may divorce.”
It does not say that.
That sentence may be the most important one in this entire article.

Exodus 21 occurs in a particular Old Covenant legal setting concerning a vulnerable woman within an ancient household arrangement. Moving directly from that case to a universal Christian divorce formula requires interpretation. Likewise, moving from Paul's explicit case of an unbeliever physically separating in 1 Corinthians 7:15 to the concept of “constructive abandonment” requires an analogical argument.
Christians who make that argument may believe it faithfully applies biblical covenant principles.
Christians who reject it may believe faithfulness requires remaining with the explicitly stated grounds.
We should be humble enough to acknowledge the difference.
Because people considering divorce do not need us to manufacture certainty where faithful interpreters disagree.
They need truth.
But there is another side to this story.
Perhaps you are the rejected spouse.
And right now you are thinking:
Finally. Someone understands.
Please keep reading.
Because Scripture understanding your pain does not automatically sanctify everything you have done with that pain.
Have you become cruel?
Have you punished your spouse emotionally because they would not satisfy you physically?
Have you been consuming pornography while telling yourself your spouse drove you to it?
Have you begun emotionally attaching yourself to someone else?
Have you been fantasizing about adultery?
Have you humiliated your spouse over their body?
Have you threatened divorce to obtain sex?
Have you treated affection as a transaction?
Have you reduced marriage to access to another person's body?
Your spouse's sin cannot become your permission slip for yours.
Jesus does not merely want to win your argument.
He wants your heart.
And perhaps you are the spouse who has been withdrawing.
Maybe your husband or wife has sent this article to you.
Your defenses are already rising.
You have reasons.
Some may be legitimate.
Perhaps sex hurts.
Perhaps childbirth changed your body.
Perhaps hormones, medication, exhaustion, disability, grief, or illness changed desire.
Perhaps there is unresolved betrayal.
Perhaps you do not feel emotionally safe.
Perhaps your spouse has been harsh outside the bedroom and then cannot understand why tenderness disappears inside it.
Perhaps sex became mechanical.
Perhaps pornography shattered trust.
Perhaps there was infidelity.
Perhaps your spouse does not understand that the body remembers what the mouth tries to forget.
Perhaps there is trauma.
Perhaps there is fear.
Perhaps you are carrying shame you have never told anyone.
If that is you, hear this carefully:
God is not standing over you demanding that you pretend wounds do not exist.
Truth brings wounds into the light.
Love listens.
Repentance changes behavior.
Healing often requires patience.
A Christian spouse should care about why intimacy has disappeared, not merely how quickly it can be restored.
But there is another possibility.
Maybe there is no medical crisis.
No abuse.
No trauma.
No betrayal.
No significant physical barrier.
You simply stopped caring.
You know your spouse is hurting, and you use sexual rejection to control them.
You withhold affection to punish them.
You enjoy watching them beg.
Or you have simply decided that their loneliness is irrelevant because you no longer feel like dealing with that part of marriage.
Then please do not baptize indifference as a “boundary.”
Paul's words remain:
Μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους.
Do not deprive one another.
Your spouse is not merely complaining about sex.
They may be grieving the disappearance of you.
And maybe the bedroom is not the disease anyway.
Maybe it is only where the disease became visible.
Maybe years ago there was a conversation that never finished.
An apology that never came.
A betrayal supposedly forgiven but never healed.
A husband who stopped listening.
A wife who stopped trusting.
Pornography hidden behind a password.
A cruel sentence nobody forgot.
A baby arrived.
Someone's health changed.
Someone gained weight.
Someone lost confidence.
Work swallowed the marriage.
Phones entered the bedroom.
Prayer left it.
Resentment moved in.
And slowly...
touch disappeared.
Then kisses.
Then conversation.
Then sex.
Then hope.
And one night one of you quietly searched:
“Is sexual rejection grounds for divorce?”
But perhaps the question underneath that question was:
“Is there still any hope for us?”
That is the question I desperately want to answer.
Yes.
There can be.
Not because every marriage will be restored.
Not because every spouse will repent.
Not because counseling magically repairs covenant betrayal.

Not because Christians should remain indefinitely in situations involving violence, coercion, or danger. If abuse or immediate danger is present, protecting life and obtaining qualified pastoral, professional, and legal help is not a betrayal of biblical faithfulness.
There is hope because Jesus Christ is still alive.
The Gospel is not merely God's plan for getting sinners into heaven.
The Gospel is God's announcement that dead things do not intimidate the resurrected Christ.
Jesus walked toward tombs.
Toward shame.
Toward adulterers.
Toward failures.
Toward people everyone else had reduced to their worst chapter.
And He still does.
Maybe your marriage has become scandalous.
Maybe nobody at church knows.
You smile together on Sunday.
You sit beside each other.
You say, “We're doing fine.”
Then you go home to separate worlds.
No touching.
No vulnerability.
No prayer together.
No intimacy.
Just two wounded people maintaining the appearance of one marriage.
Jesus is not fooled by appearances.
But neither is He frightened by what He sees.
This is where Christianity becomes more than morality.
Because the answer is not simply:
“Try harder to have sex.”
The answer is Christ.
The husband needs Christ.
The wife needs Christ.
The rejected spouse needs Christ.
The rejecting spouse needs Christ.
The adulterer needs Christ.
The bitter spouse needs Christ.
The wounded spouse needs Christ.
The sexually selfish spouse needs Christ.
The sexually fearful spouse needs Christ.
The spouse who wants to leave needs Christ.
The spouse desperately trying to make them stay needs Christ.
At the cross, Jesus does not flatter either side.
He exposes sin.
And then He offers mercy.
Repentance means more than feeling guilty.
It means turning.
If pornography is destroying intimacy, bring it into the light.
If bitterness is poisoning the bedroom, confess it.
If there is unresolved pain, stop pretending.
If there is a medical problem, seek competent medical care.
If trauma is involved, seek qualified trauma-informed help.
If communication has collapsed, get wise Christian counseling.
If you have manipulated your spouse sexually, repent.
If you have deliberately deprived your spouse as punishment, repent.
If you have demanded intimacy without tenderness, repent.
If you have committed adultery in your imagination, messages, pornography use, or actions, stop defending it and bring your sin to Christ.
And if you are currently preparing to divorce primarily because sexual rejection has convinced you that nothing can ever change...
Please do not make an irreversible decision from the most wounded version of yourself.
Slow down long enough to distinguish several questions that pain tends to collapse into one:
Is my spouse sinning against me?
Is there an underlying cause?
Is there repentance?
Is there danger?
Is this temporary or entrenched?
Have we sought serious help?
Is the marriage being abandoned in a broader covenantal sense?
And finally:
What does faithfulness to Jesus require of me?
Not what Facebook says.
Not what your lonely coworker says.
Not what the person waiting in your private messages hopes you will decide.
Jesus.

If your situation is severe enough that divorce is genuinely being considered, this is not the moment for isolated interpretation. Bring mature, biblically grounded pastors or elders into the situation. Where appropriate, involve a qualified marriage counselor. Where abuse, coercion, threats, or legal concerns exist, seek competent professional and legal assistance as well.
And understand this:
Seeking help does not mean you have promised to remain in every circumstance regardless of what happens.
It means you refuse to make a life-altering decision casually.
There are Christians who will conclude that persistent sexual rejection, though deeply sinful, is not by itself an explicit biblical ground for divorce.
There are Christians who will conclude that extreme, deliberate, prolonged, unrepentant deprivation can eventually become part of a pattern amounting to covenant abandonment.
There are Christian traditions that take an even stricter understanding of marriage's permanence and distinguish civil separation from freedom to remarry.
Those differences matter.
But all faithful interpretations should agree on several things that are too often forgotten:
Sexual intimacy matters.
Marriage is covenant, not convenience.
Neither spouse is biblically authorized to exploit the other.
Neither spouse should weaponize sex.
Neither spouse should weaponize Scripture.
Sexual coercion is not Christian marital love.
Deliberate deprivation is not something Scripture treats casually.
Divorce is not God's cure for every painful marriage.
And Jesus Christ must remain Lord even when obedience hurts.
So perhaps tonight the first step is not filing paperwork.
Perhaps it is turning toward God and finally saying what you have been too angry, embarrassed, or exhausted to say:
“Jesus... my marriage is dying, and I don't know what to do.”
That prayer is not weakness.
It may be the first honest thing you have said in years.
Maybe you need to confess:
“Lord, I have been selfish.”
Maybe:
“Lord, I hate my spouse right now.”
Maybe:
“Lord, I don't want them anymore.”
Maybe:
“Lord, I am tempted to cheat.”
Maybe:
“Lord, I feel disgusting because my spouse keeps rejecting me.”
Maybe:
“Lord, I am terrified of being touched.”
Maybe:
“Lord, I want out.”
Tell Him.
He already knows.
Grace begins where pretending ends.
And if this article exposed something you have been hiding, don't hide behind religious language now.
Not “change my spouse.”
Me.

Somewhere beneath this article may be a husband sitting alone in his car or a wife crying quietly in another room who desperately needs evidence that repentance and restoration are more than Christian vocabulary.
Your testimony might become somebody else's reason not to give up tonight.
Not because sharing a Gospel Warrior article earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
But if this truth could interrupt an affair before it begins...
If it could make a husband examine his heart before blaming his wife...
If it could help a rejected wife realize that her pain matters...
If it could make a withholding spouse recognize the damage being done...
If it could send a collapsing marriage toward wise help instead of silent destruction...
then sharing becomes more than promotion.
It becomes an opportunity to serve someone you may never know was hurting.
Because pain has a way of making us forget what we knew when we were calm.
You may need to read it again before making a decision you cannot easily undo.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing meaningful to say about broken relationships.
But understand why.
You glorify God by loving and obeying Him.
Supporting Gospel work can be one expression of generosity and partnership, but it must never be presented as though purchasing access proves your devotion to Jesus.
They may never comment.
They may never tell you they read every word.
But God knows where truth lands.
Ultimately, the question was:
Is sexual rejection grounds for divorce?
The most biblically responsible short answer is this:

Scripture clearly treats mutual marital intimacy as a real covenant responsibility and condemns deliberate deprivation. Yet Scripture does not explicitly say that sexual rejection, standing by itself, automatically constitutes grounds for divorce. Christians therefore differ over whether extreme, persistent, willful, unrepentant sexual abandonment can become a form of covenant desertion that falls under broader biblical principles of abandonment. Jesus explicitly addresses sexual immorality in the divorce discussion of Matthew 19, while Paul explicitly addresses an unbelieving spouse's departure in 1 Corinthians 7. Anyone considering applying those texts to a situation of prolonged sexual rejection should do so with great caution, wise pastoral counsel, attention to the entire marital situation, and a sincere desire to obey Christ rather than merely escape pain.
But perhaps that is not the final question Jesus is asking you.
Maybe the final question is:
Before you decide whether your marriage is finished, are you willing to let Christ expose what happened to both of your hearts?
Because sometimes the marriage everyone assumes is dead is only waiting for two people to stop defending themselves long enough to kneel.
Sometimes restoration begins with sex.
Sometimes it begins with an apology.
Sometimes with confession.
Sometimes with counseling.
Sometimes with medical treatment.
Sometimes with boundaries.
Sometimes with months of rebuilding trust.
Sometimes reconciliation does not occur because one person refuses repentance.
And sometimes, painfully, a marriage does end.
But whatever happens next, do not let divorce, rejection, betrayal, or sexual failure become the name by which you understand your entire life.
If you belong to Jesus, your deepest identity is not:
Rejected.
Divorced.
Undesirable.
Betrayed.
Abandoned.
Frigid.
Unwanted.
Failure.
Your story ultimately rests in the hands of the Savior who carried sinners' shame to a cross and walked out of a grave.
There is repentance after scandal.
There is forgiveness after failure.
There is healing after rejection.
There is purity after sexual sin.
There is identity after divorce.
There can be reconciliation after betrayal.
And where earthly restoration does not come in the form we begged for, Christ Himself remains faithful.
So before you close this article...
Look at the person beside you if they are still there.
And if they are not, look toward Christ.
The scandal may be real.
The wounds may be real.
The consequences may be real.
But never confuse the chapter that broke your heart with the Author who still holds your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD NEVER SAID YOU WOULDN’T FEEL ABANDONED—THE TERRIFYING TRUTH BEHIND “I WILL NEVER LEAVE YOU”
paragraphs: GOD NEVER SAID YOU WOULDN’T FEEL ABANDONED—THE TERRIFYING TRUTH BEHIND “I WILL NEVER LEAVE YOU”
What if one of Christianity’s most comforting promises does not mean what you thought it meant—and what if its real meaning is far more powerful than the version printed on coffee mugs?
There are nights when “God will never leave you” sounds beautiful.
And then there are nights when it almost hurts to hear it.
Because you prayed.
Nothing happened.
You prayed again.
Still nothing.
The person you begged God to heal died.
The marriage you thought He would rescue collapsed.
The child you raised to know Jesus walked away.
The opportunity you were certain God had opened disappeared.
The person who promised forever left without looking back.
The church wounded you.
The diagnosis came.
The money ran out.
The anxiety returned.
The temptation you thought you had defeated came knocking again.
And somewhere between another unanswered prayer and another sleepless night, you found yourself staring into the darkness with a question you were almost ashamed to say aloud:
“God… where are You?”
Then somebody tells you:
“Don’t worry. God will never leave you.”
You smile because Christians are supposed to smile at sentences like that.
But something inside you whispers:
Then why do I feel so alone?
That question does not necessarily make you faithless.
Some of the most faithful people in Scripture asked questions frighteningly close to it.
David cried:
“How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?”
—Psalm 13:1
Read that slowly.
David did not merely say, “I am having a difficult week.”
He asked God why it seemed as though God had forgotten him.
Yet David was not abandoned.
His feelings were real.
His interpretation of those feelings was not the final truth.
And that distinction may save somebody reading this tonight.
Because perhaps you have been measuring the presence of God by the absence of pain.
Perhaps you assumed that if God remained with you, the relationship would survive.
The disease would disappear.
The temptation would stop.
The doors would open.
The depression of the night would lift.
Your prayers would receive the answer you wanted.
But Scripture never promises that the presence of God means the absence of suffering.
It promises something far more astonishing:
God can remain faithful to you in the middle of suffering that makes you wonder where He is.
That is the truth behind the words:
“I will never leave you.”
And once you see where those words come from, they become much heavier than a Christian slogan.
Hebrews 13:5 says:
“Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.”
The Greek behind that final promise is extraordinarily forceful:
οὐ μή σε ἀνῶ οὐδ’ οὐ μή σε ἐγκαταλίπω
ou mē se anō oud’ ou mē se enkataleipō
The language piles negatives together for emphasis.
A wooden English rendering would sound awkward because English normally does not intensify a statement this way.
But the force is unmistakable:
“I will certainly not leave you; I will certainly not forsake you.”
The word ἐγκαταλίπω — enkataleipō carries the idea of leaving behind, deserting, or abandoning.
God is not merely saying:
“I’ll probably stick around.”
This is covenant language.
Faithfulness language.
The language of a God whose presence does not depend upon whether your circumstances currently feel like evidence of His goodness.
And Hebrews is echoing promises already woven through the Old Testament.
Before Israel entered the Promised Land, Moses told them:
“Be strong and of a good courage, fear not, nor be afraid of them: for the LORD thy God, he it is that doth go with thee; he will not fail thee, nor forsake thee.”
—Deuteronomy 31:6
The Hebrew includes these words:
לֹא יַרְפְּךָ וְלֹא יַעַזְבֶךָ
lo yarpekha velo ya‘azvekha
“He will not fail you, and He will not forsake you.”
Notice something uncomfortable.
God gave Israel the promise because there were enemies ahead.
The promise was not:
“There will be nothing frightening on the other side of this river.”
The promise was:
“You will not face it without Me.”
We often want God’s presence to mean exemption.
God repeatedly reveals His presence as companionship, faithfulness, strength, correction, preservation, and grace in the middle of things from which we desperately wanted exemption.
Joseph had God with him…
and still went into the pit.
God was with Joseph…
and he was still sold.
God was with Joseph…
and he was still falsely accused.
God was with Joseph…
and he still sat inside a prison.
Genesis repeatedly emphasizes that the LORD was with Joseph, not while Joseph was living an easy life, but while his circumstances could have convinced him of precisely the opposite.
That changes the question.
Maybe the question is not:
“If God is with me, why am I in this prison?”
Maybe sometimes the question becomes:
“What is God doing in me while I am here?”
Not every prison is something God sent.
Not every tragedy should be casually labeled “God’s plan” as though evil suddenly becomes good because we attach religious vocabulary to it.
Scripture calls evil evil.
Death is an enemy.
Sin destroys.
People make wicked choices.
Creation groans beneath the consequences of the Fall.
But Christianity makes an audacious claim:
evil does not get the final word over those who belong to Christ.
God can redeem what He does not morally approve.
He can bring holiness from suffering without calling suffering holy.
He can take something intended for destruction and weave redemption through it.
Joseph eventually looked at the brothers who betrayed him and said:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good…”
—Genesis 50:20
Joseph did not pretend their evil was good.
He called their intention evil.
Then he declared that evil had encountered a sovereign God capable of overruling its final purpose.
That is very different.
And perhaps that is where this article becomes painfully personal.
Because some of us are not really angry because we believe God disappeared.
We are angry because God remained…
and still allowed something we desperately wanted Him to stop.
That is harder.
“Where were You?”
“Why didn’t You stop it?”
“Why did You let me lose them?”
“Why did You allow me to be betrayed?”
“Why didn’t You answer when I begged You?”
Those questions have driven some people away from Christianity.
Others never physically left church.
They just learned how to hide.
They still sing.
Still post Bible verses.
Still say, “God is good.”
Still shake hands.
Still serve.
Still smile when somebody asks how they are doing.
But somewhere beneath the worship songs is a wound they are afraid to bring before God.
Maybe that is you.
You did not stop believing that God exists.
You stopped believing He wanted you close.
And there is a difference.
Maybe you failed Him.
Maybe you returned to something you swore you would never touch again.
Pornography.
Alcohol.
Bitterness.
An affair.
Dishonesty.
Pride.
Secret messages.
A hidden addiction.
A private compromise nobody at church knows about.
You remember how close Jesus once felt.
Now prayer feels like talking through concrete.
The Bible feels heavier than it used to.
Worship songs make you uncomfortable.
You avoid silence because silence gives conviction room to speak.
And perhaps “God will never leave you” has slowly mutated into another idea:
“God doesn’t care what you do.”
But that is not the promise either.
God’s faithful presence is not permission to remain comfortably in rebellion.
Grace is not God shrugging at sin.
Jesus did not die so that sin could become harmless.
He died because sin is so devastating that reconciliation required the cross.
The Gospel does not say:
“Your sin doesn’t matter.”
The Gospel says something infinitely better:
Your sin mattered enough for Christ to bleed for it…
and His mercy is great enough to forgive the sinner who comes to Him.
That is why repentance is not the enemy of grace.
Repentance is the turning of the sinner toward the God whose grace has been calling him home.
Jesus began His public proclamation with words including:
μετανοεῖτε
metanoeite
“Repent.”
Turn.
Change your mind in a way that redirects your life.
Come home.
And maybe somebody reading this needs to stop using “God will never leave me” as anesthesia for a life God is commanding you to surrender.
Yes, He is faithful.
But His faithfulness includes loving you too much to bless the chains destroying you.
Hebrews itself does not present God’s presence as an excuse for spiritual laziness.
The same New Testament that celebrates grace calls believers toward holiness, endurance, obedience, confession, love, and faith.
Grace does not merely comfort.
Grace transforms.
And then we reach the darkest place in the entire story.
A hill outside Jerusalem.
A cross.
A bloodied Messiah.
And words so horrifying that Christians have repeated them for two thousand years:
“My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”
—Matthew 27:46
Matthew preserves the cry in a Semitic form:
Ἠλί Ἠλί λεμὰ σαβαχθανί
Ēli Ēli lema sabachthani
Mark records the form:
Ἐλωΐ Ἐλωΐ λαμὰ σαβαχθανί
Elōi Elōi lama sabachthani
And those words point directly back to Psalm 22:1, where the Hebrew reads:
אֵלִי אֵלִי לָמָה עֲזַבְתָּנִי
Eli, Eli, lamah ‘azavtani?
“My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”
Jesus was invoking Psalm 22.
And Psalm 22 begins in apparent abandonment…
but it does not end there.
It moves toward vindication.
Deliverance.
Worship.
The nations remembering the LORD.
Future generations hearing what God has done.
The crucified Christ was not accidentally quoting a random sentence of despair.
The righteous sufferer of Psalm 22 was finding staggering fulfillment before their eyes.
Jesus entered the darkness of the cross willingly.
He bore sin.
He endured judgment.
He experienced the horror of dereliction expressed in the Psalm.
Yet Christians must speak carefully here.
The cross does not mean the eternal Trinity somehow ceased to be Trinity or that the divine nature fractured into pieces.
The Father remained Father.
The Son remained Son.
The eternal unity of God was not destroyed.
Yet the suffering of Christ was no theatrical performance.
Jesus truly suffered.
Truly bore our sins.
Truly entered the judgment our rebellion deserved.
First Peter 2:24 declares that Christ:
“his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree…”
Second Corinthians 5:21 says:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
Think about the scandal of that.
The only truly innocent Man stood where guilty people belonged…
so guilty people could be welcomed where only righteousness belongs.
You want to understand “I will never leave you”?
Look at the cross.
Because Christianity is not fundamentally the story of humanity successfully climbing its way toward God.
It is the story of God coming for humanity.
We wandered.
He pursued.
We rebelled.
He called.
We sinned.
Christ came.
We owed a debt we could not pay.
Christ paid what we could never afford.
We deserved judgment.
Christ offered mercy.
We brought the scandal.
Jesus brought the grace.
This is why the Gospel is offensive to human pride.
You cannot save yourself.
Your morality cannot save you.
Your church attendance cannot save you.
Your baptism certificate cannot save you.
Your Christian family cannot save you.
Your ministry title cannot save you.
Your charitable giving cannot save you.
Only Jesus saves.
That distinction matters.
Supporting a ministry may be meaningful stewardship.
Sharing Gospel truth may help another person encounter Scripture.
Giving may advance worthwhile work.
But none of those things purchase one drop of the blood of Christ.
Salvation is grace.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.”
—Ephesians 2:8
We are not selling access to God.
We cannot sell forgiveness.
We cannot sell salvation.
We cannot sell the Holy Spirit.

But if biblical content like this is helping you return to Scripture, confront hidden sin, understand the Gospel, encourage wounded believers, and point people toward Jesus, then supporting its continued reach can become one practical expression of stewardship.
Not because sharing earns favor with God.
“Has God abandoned me?”
You may never know who reads it at 2:17 in the morning.
You may never know whose finger stops scrolling.
You may never know who is sitting alone in a bedroom trying to decide whether there is any reason left to pray.
You may never know who has sinned so badly they believe Jesus could never want them again.
You may never know who whispers:
“God… if You still want me, show me.”
And perhaps the thing you almost did not share becomes one small instrument God uses to put His Word in front of them.
Send this to the person whose faith has been bruised.
Share it with the believer who stopped going to church because Christians wounded them.
Share it with the prodigal.
Share it with the skeptic.
Share it with the person who believes their scandal is too ugly for grace.
And if this exposed something inside you, do not hide behind religious language.
Someone else may need evidence that dark chapters end.
Not every story resolves the way we want in this lifetime.
That needs to be said too.
Christian hope is not a guarantee that every disease disappears before death.
Not every broken relationship will be restored.
Not every injustice will be corrected before the grave.
Not every prayer receives the answer we wanted.
The Christian hope is ultimately bigger than getting our preferred version of this temporary life.
Our hope is resurrection.
Our hope is Christ.
Our hope is that death itself does not get the last sentence.
Paul writes:
Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
—Romans 8:38–39
Read those words again.
Neither death.
We sometimes speak as though death is proof that God abandoned somebody.
Paul places death on the list of things incapable of separating the believer from God’s love in Christ.
That means the promise “I will never leave you” reaches somewhere prosperity preaching cannot reach.
Into the hospital room.
Into chemotherapy.
Into the funeral home.
Into unemployment.
Into betrayal.
Into persecution.
Into loneliness.
Into aging.
Into the trembling final breaths of a Christian who knows earthly life is ending.
The promise is not merely:
“I will stay with you until life becomes inconvenient.”
It is:
Nothing in creation can separate those who are in Christ from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
And maybe now we can finally confront the question you were afraid to ask.
“What if I don’t feel Him?”
Then do not confuse God's invisibility with God's absence.
Faith is not pretending your feelings do not exist.
Faith is refusing to make your feelings the highest court of truth.
There will be mornings when worship feels effortless.
There may be nights when prayer feels like dragging your wounded soul across broken glass.
Pray anyway.
There will be days when Scripture seems alive in your hands.
There may be days when you read the same verse five times and feel nothing.
Read anyway.
There will be moments when God’s goodness seems obvious.
There may be seasons when you understand almost nothing He is permitting.
Trust His revealed character anyway.
Not because Christians are commanded to become emotionally numb.
But because the cross has already shown us something our circumstances cannot overturn.
God has acted decisively in history for sinners through Jesus Christ.
Your emotions fluctuate.
Calvary does not.
Your circumstances change.
Christ does not.
Your understanding fails.
His character does not.
Your grip weakens.
His grace does not become weak because you do.
And perhaps you are thinking:
“But you don’t know what I did.”
No.
But Jesus does.
Peter denied Him.
Three times.
Peter had heard Jesus preach.
Peter had watched miracles.
Peter had walked with Christ.
Peter boldly insisted he would never abandon Him.
Then fear entered the room.
And Peter collapsed.
“I do not know the man.”
Imagine hearing your own mouth deny the One you love.
Imagine realizing the words cannot be pulled back.
Imagine the shame.
Scripture says Peter went out and wept bitterly.
That could have been the end of his story.
Scandal.
Failure.
Cowardice.
Regret.
But Jesus was not finished writing.
After the resurrection, Christ restored Peter.
“Lovest thou me?”
Then:
“Feed my sheep.”
Jesus did not pretend Peter had never fallen.
He restored a fallen man and gave him work to do.
That is grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace writes something the scandal could never write by itself.
Restoration.
Peter's failure was real.
Jesus' grace was greater.
And maybe that is your story waiting to be rewritten.
Not because consequences always disappear.
Not because repentance erases earthly damage.
Not because everyone you hurt will immediately trust you again.
Biblical restoration is deeper than pretending nothing happened.
It means your worst chapter does not possess the authority to become the final definition of a life surrendered to Jesus.
You are not beyond repentance.
You are not beyond the reach of Christ.
You are not too filthy for His cleansing.
You are not too far away to turn around.
You are not required to repair yourself before approaching the Savior.
Come as the sinner who needs mercy.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice what John does not say.
“If we hide our sins convincingly…”
“If we justify ourselves…”
“If we compare ourselves with worse people…”
“If we promise to become perfect before coming back…”
No.
Confess.
The Greek word is:
ὁμολογῶμεν — homologōmen
It carries the sense of confessing, acknowledging, agreeing.
Stop negotiating with the truth.
Call the sin what God calls it.
Bring it into His light.
Turn toward Christ.
Receive mercy that you could never manufacture for yourself.
And then walk.
One surrendered step after another.
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Not because you needed another inspirational quotation.
Maybe you needed the comforting lie stripped away so you could finally receive the biblical promise.
God never promised Christians an uninterrupted sensation of His presence.
He never promised a painless life.
He never promised that obedience would prevent heartbreak.
He never promised that every prayer would be answered according to our preferred timetable.
He never promised that following Jesus would keep you out of valleys.
Jesus actually told His disciples:
“In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.”
—John 16:33
There it is.
Not denial.
Victory.
Not:
“You will never encounter trouble.”
But:
“I have overcome.”
This is Christianity.
A Savior with scars.
A cross before a crown.
A tomb before resurrection morning.
Friday darkness before Sunday light.
And perhaps your life currently feels like Saturday.
Jesus has been crucified.
The stone has been rolled into place.
The disciples are shattered.
Heaven seems silent.
Nothing appears to be happening.
But the silence between crucifixion and resurrection did not mean God had lost control of the story.
Sunday was already coming.
Be careful here.
That does not mean every earthly tragedy gets a neat “Sunday morning” resolution next week.
Sometimes our resurrection hope reaches beyond the grave itself.
But for the Christian, resurrection means suffering can never truthfully write the final sentence.
Jesus does.
That is why we keep saying:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending your scandal was beautiful.
Not by calling your wounds imaginary.
Not by rewriting history.
He rewrites what the past is permitted to mean about your future.
The adulterer can repent.
The addict can surrender.
The liar can confess.
The bitter heart can forgive.
The wounded can heal.
The prodigal can come home.
The hypocrite can remove the mask.
The lukewarm Christian can awaken.
The skeptic can believe.
The religious person can finally discover that knowing facts about Jesus is not the same as belonging to Jesus.
And the person who feels abandoned can discover that Christ was nearer than their emotions knew.
So before you leave this article, answer one question.
Not publicly at first.
Just you and God.
What are you still hiding from Jesus because you are afraid that bringing it into the light will make Him leave?
Name it.
There.
That thing.
That memory.
That habit.
That resentment.
That secret.
That failure.
That fear.
That question.
Bring it to Him.
You may discover that the Savior you were hiding from is the Savior who has been calling you home.
You may need these words again on a darker night.
It does not purchase blessing.
It does not earn salvation.
It does not make God love you more.
Jesus cannot be bought.
But your voluntary support can help Gospel-centered resources continue being created and shared with people who need them.
Then do something that costs no money at all.
Let your timeline carry something eternal.
Follow so you can continue receiving Scripture-centered encouragement.
Invite somebody else to follow.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because confession, testimony, and encouragement can remind another human being that they are not fighting alone.
And if Christ has already carried you through the valley, tell us what He did.
Your testimony may become someone else's reason to keep praying tonight.
Because the truth behind “God will never leave you” was never that you would always feel Him.
It was never that nothing painful would happen.
It was never that Christians would escape graves, tears, betrayal, temptation, or unanswered questions.
The truth is stronger.
When your feelings collapse, His character remains.
When your plans disappear, His sovereignty remains.
When people leave, Christ remains.
When you stumble, His call to repentance remains.
When you confess, His promise of forgiveness remains.
When death itself comes knocking, resurrection remains.
And when the enemy points at the ugliest chapter of your life and whispers,
“This is how your story ends…”
look toward the empty tomb.
Because sinners do not have to be remembered only for their scandal.
Peter wasn't.
Paul wasn't.
And everyone who comes to Christ discovers the same breathtaking reality:
Jesus specializes in endings sin never saw coming.
The night you thought proved God had abandoned you may become the very place where you discover He was carrying you through a story you could not yet read.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: MARRIAGE WAS NEVER SUPPOSED TO MAKE ATTRACTION DISAPPEAR
paragraphs:
MARRIAGE WAS NEVER SUPPOSED TO MAKE ATTRACTION DISAPPEAR
You can love your spouse, love Jesus, and still notice that someone else is attractive. The question that reveals your heart is not whether your eyes noticed—but what you allowed your heart to do next.
There are some struggles Christians confess easily.
“I’ve been anxious.”
“I’ve been angry.”
“I haven’t prayed like I should.”
But there are other struggles we bury beneath church clothes, wedding rings, family photographs, anniversary posts, and carefully rehearsed smiles.
Because saying them aloud feels dangerous.
So let’s say one of them.
You got married.
You meant your vows.
You love your spouse.
You have no intention of destroying your marriage.
And then one ordinary day, someone walked into the room...
and you noticed.
They were attractive.
Maybe very attractive.
And for one uncomfortable second, something inside you woke up that you thought marriage was supposed to switch off forever.
Then came the guilt.
Why did I notice?
What is wrong with me?
Does this mean I don’t really love my spouse?
Does this mean something is missing in my marriage?
Am I already being unfaithful?
Or perhaps your reaction went in the opposite direction.
I’m married, not blind.
Looking doesn’t hurt anybody.
It’s just attraction.
And somewhere between unnecessary shame and dangerous self-justification is a truth many Christians desperately need to understand:
Marriage was never supposed to make attraction disappear.
Marriage was supposed to teach us what covenant does with desire.
That distinction matters.
Because Scripture does not teach that the wedding ceremony removes your capacity to recognize beauty.
It teaches something far deeper.
Your desires no longer get to be your master.
Jesus does.
And that changes everything.
The Bible begins the story of marriage with breathtaking intimacy.
Genesis 2:24 says that a man leaves his father and mother, clings to his wife, and they become “בָּשָׂר אֶחָד” — basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Not merely two people sharing a house.
Not merely two people legally attached to one another.
One flesh.
Covenant intimacy.
A joining of lives.
Then Scripture gives us one of the most vulnerable descriptions of human intimacy in the entire Bible:
“וַיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עֲרוּמִּים... וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ”
The man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.
That was the original picture.
Desire without exploitation.
Nakedness without manipulation.
Intimacy without comparison.
Love without hiding.
Then sin entered.
And almost immediately...
they hid.
That is worth remembering.
Sin did not invent beauty.
Sin distorted what we do with beauty.
Sin did not invent desire.
Sin corrupted desire.
And the Gospel is not God's plan to turn human beings into emotionless creatures who can no longer recognize attractiveness.
The Gospel transforms what rules us.
That is why marriage cannot be reduced to the expectation that your spouse will become the only physically attractive human being you can perceive.
That expectation may sound spiritual.
It isn't biblical.
Your wedding ring did not rewire your optic nerves.
Your vows did something much more serious.
They established covenant boundaries around what you will pursue.
There is an enormous difference between seeing beauty...
and feeding desire.
Between noticing...
and nurturing.
Between experiencing temptation...
and entertaining it.
Between an involuntary moment of recognition...
and the second look you deliberately take because you want more.
That is where many marriages begin bleeding long before anybody touches anybody.
Jesus went directly to the heart.
In Matthew 5:28, He warned about looking at another person πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι — pros to epithymēsai.
The language matters.
Jesus was not teaching that the mere biological recognition that another human being is attractive automatically constitutes adultery.
His warning penetrates much deeper: the gaze can become intentional, possessive, cultivated desire.
The issue is not simply that your eyes registered beauty.
The issue is what your heart decided to do with what your eyes saw.
That is uncomfortable.
Because adultery does not always begin in a bedroom.
Sometimes it begins in imagination.
Sometimes with a conversation you secretly hope will continue.
Sometimes with a notification that makes your heart beat differently.
Sometimes with deleting messages.
Sometimes with comparing your spouse to somebody who has never had to carry real life with you.
Sometimes with looking at another person's carefully curated photographs while forgetting the exhausted, faithful human being sleeping beside you.
Sometimes nothing “happened.”
But something has already been happening.
Inside you.
And Jesus cares about that hidden room.
Not because He wants to humiliate you.
Because He loves you too much to let secret desire quietly become your master.
James describes temptation with frightening clarity:
“Each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire.”
Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin.
Notice the progression.
Desire can be entertained.
Fed.
Carried.
Conceived.
And eventually something hidden becomes something destructive.
This is why temptation itself must not be confused with surrender to temptation.
Jesus Himself “has been tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).
So experiencing temptation cannot itself automatically equal sin, because our sinless Savior was genuinely tempted.
That truth can free someone reading this from crushing, unnecessary shame.
You noticed someone attractive?
That moment does not automatically mean your marriage is fake.
You experienced temptation?
That does not automatically mean you betrayed your spouse.
But what happens next matters.
A lot.
Because temptation is not permission.
And grace is not permission either.
Maybe nobody has ever explained this to you.
You don't necessarily need to panic because someone caught your attention.
You need to guard what receives your attention afterward.
You don't have to pretend beautiful people suddenly stopped existing when you exchanged vows.
You have to remember that beauty does not give you ownership.
Attraction does not give you permission.
Chemistry does not cancel covenant.
Opportunity does not equal God's approval.
And dissatisfaction at home does not transform temptation into destiny.
Read that again.
Because someone is eventually going to appear who seems easier than your spouse.
They won't carry the history of your arguments.
They won't remind you about bills.
They won't have years of unresolved misunderstandings attached to their voice.
You may only see them when they are dressed well, smiling, attentive, energetic, interested.
Meanwhile, you see your spouse tired.
Stressed.
Sick.
Irritated.
Unshaven.
Without makeup.
Worried about money.
Cleaning up after children.
Recovering from childbirth.
Working overtime.
Growing older.
Carrying grief.
Trying to survive.
And suddenly comparison commits fraud against your marriage.
Because you compare somebody else's presentation...
with your spouse's entire humanity.
You compare a stranger's highlight reel with your covenant partner's behind-the-scenes footage.
Of course fantasy feels lighter.
Fantasy has never had to pay a mortgage with you.
Fantasy has never awakened beside you at 3:17 in the morning because the baby was screaming.
Fantasy has never seen you sick.
Fantasy has never had to forgive your sharp words.
Fantasy has never watched your body change.
Fantasy has never discovered your weaknesses and chosen to remain.
Fantasy has never carried your history.
Your spouse has.
And perhaps the most dangerous attraction is not always physical.
Sometimes what seduces the heart is being understood.
Someone listens.
Someone laughs.
Someone notices you.
Someone says the thing you wish your spouse would say.
And slowly, almost innocently, you begin giving someone else pieces of yourself that should have been protected.
You tell yourself:
We're just friends.
Maybe you are.
But ask yourself the question people usually avoid:
Would you communicate exactly the same way if your spouse were sitting beside you reading every word?
Would you want your husband to hear that conversation?
Would you want your wife to see those messages?
Would you feel the need to explain why you deleted anything?
If secrecy is required to preserve the relationship...
something is already wrong.
Proverbs 4:23 says:
“Above all else, guard your heart.”
The Hebrew word often translated “heart” is לֵב — lev.
In biblical thought, the heart is not merely the emotional part of a person. It reaches into the inner life—the place of thought, intention, desire, and decision.
Guard it.
Not because every person outside your marriage is dangerous.
Because an unguarded heart can make dangerous things out of ordinary encounters.
And please hear this:
Guarding your marriage does not mean treating every attractive person as an enemy.
It means refusing to make them an escape.
It means refusing to secretly rehearse a life with someone God has not given you.
It means refusing to nourish fantasies that slowly make covenant faithfulness feel boring.
It means refusing to use pornography as a substitute for intimacy.
It means refusing to turn social media into a private catalog of bodies.
It means refusing emotional affairs simply because nobody has kissed yet.
It means refusing to call something innocent merely because it has not become physical.
Job expressed radical intentionality when he said:
“I have made a covenant with my eyes.”
A covenant with his eyes.
Imagine that.
Not hatred of beauty.
Not fear of humanity.
Discipline.
Because mature faithfulness is not pretending temptation doesn't exist.
It is deciding beforehand what you will do when it arrives.
Joseph did not stand in Potiphar's house negotiating with temptation.
He ran.
Sometimes the holiest thing you can do is leave.
Close the conversation.
Unfollow the account.
Delete the number.
Change the routine.
Tell your spouse the truth.
Call a mature believer.
Confess.
Get accountability.
Stop going somewhere you know repeatedly weakens you.
Not because running makes you weak.
Sometimes running proves you finally understand how weak you can become.
Paul told Timothy:
“Flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace.”
Notice that Christianity is not merely run away.
It is also run toward.
Run toward righteousness.
Run toward faith.
Run toward love.
Run toward peace.
Run toward Christ.
And if you are married...
run toward your spouse again.
Because sometimes the answer to attraction outside marriage is not merely starving something outside.
It is rebuilding something inside.
When did you stop dating each other?
When did every conversation become logistics?
When did “How was your day?” become the deepest question you asked?
When did affection become something expected instead of something intentionally given?
When did you stop flirting with the person you married?
When did you stop telling them they were beautiful?
When did you stop touching without demanding sex?
When did you stop laughing?
When did the phones become more interesting than the person sitting three feet away?
When did resentment begin sleeping between you?
Maybe attraction did not disappear.
Maybe attention did.
And attention can often be reclaimed.
Song of Songs destroys the idea that biblical marriage must be emotionally sterile or embarrassed by marital desire.
Scripture contains celebration of attraction within covenant.
Husband and wife delight in one another.
They speak beauty.
They express longing.
They enjoy each other.
God is not embarrassed by marital desire.
He designed covenant intimacy.
Christian holiness is not the murder of desire.
It is desire brought under the lordship of Christ and directed according to God's wisdom.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 7 about mutual marital responsibility and intimacy. Ephesians 5 goes deeper still, presenting marriage through the astonishing mystery of Christ and His Church.
Marriage ultimately points beyond itself.
Your spouse was never meant to become your savior.
That burden would crush them.
Your husband cannot complete what only Christ can redeem.
Your wife cannot heal every wound only Christ can reach.
No human being can permanently satisfy the deepest hunger of a soul created for God.
And this is where some marriages quietly go wrong.
We demand from another human being what only Jesus can provide.
Then when they inevitably fail, someone new looks like salvation.
They aren't.
They're human too.
Give fantasy enough time and it eventually becomes ordinary life.
The person who seems flawless from a distance also has wounds, habits, insecurities, selfishness, mornings, moods, weaknesses, and sins.
You are not comparing two realities.
You are comparing reality with imagination.
Reality almost always loses that competition.
So perhaps the question is not:
“Why am I attracted to somebody else?”
Maybe the deeper questions are:
“What am I doing with that attraction?”
“What hunger is this exposing?”
“What boundary needs strengthening?”
“What conversation have I been avoiding?”
“What resentment have I been feeding?”
“What part of my marriage needs attention?”
“What part of my own soul needs repentance?”
And ultimately:
“Is Jesus Lord here too?”
Not just Lord of Sunday.
Not just Lord of theology.
Not just Lord of the Bible verses you post.
Lord of your eyes.
Lord of your imagination.
Lord of your private messages.
Lord of your browser history.
Lord of your loneliness.
Lord of your sexuality.
Lord of the fantasies nobody knows about.
Lord of the part of you that wants to be wanted.
That is where discipleship becomes real.
Maybe this article found you after you already crossed a line.
Maybe yours is not theoretical.
Maybe there is a name attached to this.
A conversation.
A hotel room.
A photograph.
A secret account.
Pornography.
An emotional affair.
An actual affair.
Maybe your spouse still doesn't know.
And you have been carrying the terrifying thought:
If people knew what I did, they would never look at me the same way again.
Perhaps they wouldn't.
Sin has consequences.
Trust can be shattered.
Families can be wounded.
Repentance does not magically remove every earthly consequence of what we have done.
The Gospel never requires us to pretend sin isn't serious.
The cross proves precisely how serious sin is.
But the cross also tells us something else.
Your scandal does not have to become the final sentence of your story.
Look at Jesus.
Look at the woman caught in adultery in John 8.
Dragged into public shame.
Reduced to her worst moment.
Surrounded by people holding stones.
Her sin mattered.
But Jesus refused to let condemnation have the final word.
“Neither do I condemn you,” He told her.
And then:
“Go, and from now on sin no more.”
Grace...
and transformation.
Mercy...
and repentance.
Jesus did not say, “It doesn't matter.”
He essentially gave her something infinitely greater:
Your sin does not have to own your future.
That is Gospel grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not renaming sin.
Not excusing betrayal.
Not hiding consequences.
Grace walks straight into the wreckage and says:
Jesus can still write from here.
Maybe you have been unfaithful.
Jesus can still write from here.
Maybe pornography has hollowed out your intimacy.
Jesus can still write from here.
Maybe you have been emotionally attached to someone who isn't your spouse.
Jesus can still write from here.
Maybe you have compared your husband to another man until resentment poisoned your respect.
Jesus can still write from here.
Maybe you have compared your wife's body to women on a screen until you stopped seeing the woman who has faithfully loved you.
Jesus can still write from here.
Maybe you haven't crossed the physical line...
but you know exactly where your imagination has been living.
Jesus can still write from here.
But grace does not say:
“Keep hiding.”
Grace calls you into the light.
First John 1:9 declares that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
The Greek word translated “confess” is ὁμολογῶμεν — homologōmen, from homologeō—to confess, acknowledge, say the same thing.
Repentance stops negotiating with God about what sin should be called.
It agrees with Him.
No more:
It wasn't technically cheating.
No more:
Everybody does it.
No more:
My spouse drove me to it.
No more:
It was only pornography.
No more:
We were just talking.
No more:
God understands.
Yes.
God understands more completely than anyone.
And because He understands, He knows exactly where the chains are.
Bring them into the light.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia carries the idea of repentance—a decisive change of mind and turning.
Biblical repentance produces movement.
Away from sin.
Toward Christ.
You don't earn forgiveness by becoming clean enough.
You come to Jesus because you cannot clean yourself.
At the cross, Christ carried sin's judgment.
In His resurrection, death did not get the final word.
And when a sinner turns to Christ in faith, forgiveness is not a motivational slogan.
It was purchased at a cost we could never pay.
Maybe that is what someone reading this desperately needed tonight.
Not permission to continue.
Permission to come home.
Come home.
Before the conversation becomes an affair.
Come home.
Before pornography teaches you to despise covenant intimacy.
Come home.
Before secrecy becomes a second life.
Come home.
Before resentment convinces you that betrayal is justified.
And if the damage has already happened...
come home anyway.
Not to easy consequences.
Not necessarily to immediate restoration of trust.
But to Jesus.
Because He still receives repentant sinners.
And if your spouse is the one who betrayed you, please hear this too.
Their sin is not evidence that you were insufficient as a human being.
You do not have to compete with fantasy.
You do not have to transform yourself into every person your spouse might possibly find attractive.
Healing may require truth, boundaries, wise pastoral care, professional counseling, accountability, time, and consequences.
Forgiveness and restored trust are related, but they are not identical.
Reconciliation cannot be built on continuing deception.
Truth matters.
Safety matters.
Repentance bears fruit.
And Jesus does not require wounded people to call darkness light in order to prove they understand grace.
But even betrayal does not have to dictate the rest of your existence.
Christ can meet you in the rubble too.
This is why the Gospel is so much bigger than marriage advice.
We do not simply need stronger willpower.
We need transformed hearts.
We need Jesus.
The One who looked at sinners without exploiting them.
