Pride can say, “God gets all the glory,” while desperately checking whether people noticed who did the work.
Pride can post Bible verses all morning and refuse to apologize by evening.
Pride can cry during worship and still whisper,
“I know I was wrong, but they were more wrong.”
And that is why pride is so dangerous.
The proud person is often the last person in the room to recognize his pride.
There is a reason Jesus told a story about two men praying.
One was a Pharisee.
One was a tax collector.
The Pharisee prayed:
“God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are…” — Luke 18:11, KJV
At first glance, it almost sounds spiritual.
He thanked God.
He mentioned fasting.
He mentioned giving.
He was religious.
Disciplined.
Morally respectable.
But listen carefully.
His prayer was supposedly directed toward God while revolving around himself.
I.
I.
I.
And then he compared himself with the sinner standing nearby.
The tax collector did something very different.
He would not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He struck his chest and cried:
“God be merciful to me a sinner.” — Luke 18:13, KJV
The Greek carries extraordinary weight:
“Ὁ θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ.”
Ho Theos, hilasthēti moi tō hamartōlō.
“God, be merciful to me, the sinner.”
No résumé.
No comparison.
No defense.
No spiritual performance.
Just need.
Just guilt.
Just mercy.
Jesus then delivered the verdict that overturns almost everything human pride expects.
The broken sinner went home justified.
The religious man did not.
“For every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.” — Luke 18:14, KJV
Imagine being the most religious person in the story…
and still being the one who missed grace.
That is the danger.
Pride does not always make you run away from religion.
Sometimes pride learns how to use religion as camouflage.
You can become so good at looking righteous that you stop asking whether your heart is actually surrendered.
You can know how Christians talk.
You can know when to say “Amen.”
You can recognize false teaching.
You can quote theology.
You can tell everyone else what they need to repent of.
And still have an untouched room inside your heart where Jesus is not allowed to enter.
Maybe your room is unforgiveness.
Maybe it is pornography.
Maybe it is bitterness.
Maybe it is your need to control everything.
Maybe it is jealousy disguised as discernment.
Maybe it is the secret pleasure you feel when somebody who hurt you begins suffering.
Maybe it is your inability to say three simple words:
“I was wrong.”
Maybe you have spent years constructing a Christian image strong enough to prevent anyone from discovering how exhausted you really are.
And underneath all of it is the quiet declaration pride has been making since Eden:
I will decide.
I will control.
I will determine what is good for me.
I will protect myself.
I will justify myself.
I will save myself.
That ancient poison is older than your social media account.
Older than your denomination.
Older than your family wounds.
Human rebellion begins with the creature attempting to live independently of the Creator.
And Scripture repeatedly shows what God does with human arrogance.
Proverbs 16:18 warns:
“Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.”
The Hebrew word often translated “pride” there is גָּאוֹן — ga'on, carrying the sense of exaltation, majesty, or pride depending on context.
Human beings were created to reflect God's glory, not compete for it.
That distinction changes everything.
Humility is not pretending you are worthless.
Biblical humility is seeing yourself truthfully before God.
You are created in His image.
You possess dignity because He gave it.
You have gifts because He gave them.
You breathe because He sustains you.
You can accomplish meaningful things because He supplied abilities, opportunities, people, strength, and providence you could never manufacture from nothing.
Paul asks the devastating question:
“And what hast thou that thou didst not receive?” — 1 Corinthians 4:7, KJV
Your intelligence?
Received.
Your opportunities?
Received.
Your voice?
Received.
Your strength?
Received.
Your next heartbeat?
Received.
Your salvation?
Entirely grace.
So what exactly are we boasting about?
This is where Christianity humiliates human pride in the most beautiful possible way.
The Gospel does not tell you to become impressive enough for God.
It announces that you never could.
You could not climb high enough.
So Christ came down.
You could not become righteous enough.
So Christ became your righteousness.
You could not erase your guilt.
So Christ carried it.
You could not defeat death.
So Christ walked out of the grave.
You could not purchase reconciliation.
So the Son of God purchased sinners with His blood.
At the cross, every illusion of self-salvation dies.
You stand before Jesus with empty hands.
Nothing to bargain with.
Nothing to boast about.
Nothing to say except,
“Lord, have mercy on me.”
And here comes the scandal.
He does.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Because the Gospel is not God helping impressive people become slightly better.
The Gospel is God rescuing guilty sinners through the finished work of Jesus Christ.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.” — Ephesians 2:8–9, KJV
Not of yourselves.
There goes pride.
It is the gift of God.
There goes boasting.
Not of works.
There goes the résumé.
Jesus receives the glory because Jesus accomplished the rescue.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been carrying a secret exhaustion caused by constantly trying to prove that you are enough.
Enough for your parents.
Enough for your spouse.
Enough for your church.
Enough for your followers.
Enough for yourself.
Maybe even enough for God.
You are tired.
Because pride is exhausting.
Pride must constantly maintain an image.
Grace lets you tell the truth.
Pride says, “Don't let them see you bleeding.”
Grace says, “Bring the wound to Jesus.”
Pride says, “Explain why it wasn't really your fault.”
Grace says, “Confess your sin.”
Pride says, “Make sure everyone knows what they did to you.”
Grace asks, “What is Christ trying to do in you?”
Pride says, “You deserve better.”
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
Pride says, “Protect your reputation.”
Jesus made Himself of no reputation.
Philippians 2 takes us into one of the most staggering portraits of humility in all Scripture.
Speaking of Christ, Paul writes:
The Greek phrase translated “emptied himself” in many modern translations comes from ἑαυτὸν ἐκένωσεν — heauton ekenōsen.
Christ's humility did not mean He ceased being divine.
Rather, the passage describes the astonishing downward movement of the eternal Son taking the form of a servant, becoming truly human, and walking the path of obedience all the way to death.
“And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.” — Philippians 2:8, KJV
Look at Jesus.
The One who had every right to glory embraced humiliation.
The One before whom angels worship washed feet.
The King wore a crown made of thorns.
The innocent One stood silent before accusers.
The Author of life was nailed to wood by creatures whose lungs continued working only because He sustained them.
And we still struggle to say,
“I'm sorry.”
Do you see the absurdity of human pride beside the cross?
We defend ourselves while worshiping the One who surrendered Himself.
We demand recognition while claiming to follow the One who became a servant.
We obsess over status while following a Savior crucified between criminals.
We cannot cling to the cross and the throne of self at the same time.
Something has to die.
And Christianity has always been very clear about what.
Self-rule.
Not your personality.
Not your God-given dignity.
Not your healthy boundaries.
Not your individuality.
But the rebellious insistence that you belong to yourself.
Jesus said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.” — Luke 9:23, KJV
Daily.
Because yesterday's surrender does not prevent today's pride.
You can humble yourself Monday and become insufferable Tuesday.
You can survive a season that made you desperately dependent on God and then slowly begin believing your own success story.
That is one of prosperity's hidden dangers.
Sometimes adversity drives us toward God.
Success can quietly convince us that we no longer need Him.
Moses warned Israel about exactly this danger in Deuteronomy 8.
They would enter a good land.
Eat.
Build houses.
Multiply possessions.
Prosper.
And then:
“Then thine heart be lifted up, and thou forget the LORD thy God…” — Deuteronomy 8:14, KJV
Notice the progression.
Blessing.
Elevation.
Forgetting.
Then comes the lie:
“My power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth.” — Deuteronomy 8:17, KJV
God warned them not to confuse receiving blessing with becoming self-sufficient.
That warning still speaks.
You prayed desperately when you had nothing.
What happened after God gave you something?
You begged God for the opportunity.
Did you remember Him after the opportunity came?
You prayed for the relationship.
Did you honor Him once you got it?
You prayed for the business.
Did success make you generous or merely more impressed with yourself?
You prayed for the platform.
Now that people listen, are you still listening to God?
You prayed for deliverance.
Now that the chains are gone, do you still love the Deliverer?
Perhaps this article is not reaching you during your collapse.
Perhaps it is reaching you during your success.
And maybe that is precisely why you need it.
Because one of God's greatest mercies may be exposing pride before pride destroys what His grace has built.
The answer is not self-hatred.
The answer is repentance.
James continues:
“Draw nigh to God, and he will draw nigh to you.” — James 4:8, KJV
What an astonishing sentence to place beside such a severe warning.
The God who opposes pride invites the humble sinner near.
That is grace.
He does not say,
“Fix yourself, then approach.”
He calls you to repent.
To cleanse your hands.
To purify your heart.
To stop playing games with sin.
To stop pretending.
To humble yourself before Him.
“Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.” — James 4:10, KJV
You do not have to lift yourself.
That may be exactly what someone needed to hear.
You have spent years lifting yourself.
Promoting yourself.
Defending yourself.
Explaining yourself.
Proving yourself.
Protecting yourself.
God says:
Humble yourself.
Let Me handle the lifting.
Peter echoes the same truth:
“God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.” — 1 Peter 5:5, KJV
Then:
“Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.” — 1 Peter 5:6, KJV
In due time.
Not your time.
His.
And maybe that is where pride has been hiding.
You trust God…
as long as He moves according to your schedule.
You surrender…
as long as He chooses the outcome you wanted.
You obey…
as long as obedience does not cost too much.
But surrender with conditions is still an attempt at control.
Jesus did not call disciples to negotiate ownership.
He called them to follow.
So here is the question that matters more than whether you enjoyed this article.
Where are you still resisting God?
Not your neighbor.
Not your spouse.
Not your pastor.
Not the person whose pride immediately came to mind while you were reading this.
You.
Where is pride still alive in you?
Where can nobody correct you?
Where do you become defensive?
Where are you secretly desperate for applause?
Whose success irritates you?
Whose apology are you demanding while refusing to examine your own heart?
What sin have you renamed so you do not have to repent of it?
What command of Christ have you turned into a suggestion?
Where have you been asking God to surrender to your will while calling it prayer?
Be honest.
Because grace meets us where the truth finally begins.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need impressive language.
Maybe it needs to sound like that tax collector.
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
Maybe it needs to sound like David:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.” — Psalm 51:10, KJV
Maybe it needs to be even simpler.
Jesus…
I have been proud.
Forgive me.
Take the throne again.
And understand this carefully:
Humility does not earn grace.
Grace is not God's paycheck for people who become sufficiently humble.
We are saved because of Christ, not because we performed humility perfectly.
Even our repentance depends upon God's mercy.
The point is not to become proud of how humble you are.
That would be the oldest trap wearing new clothes.
The point is to come empty-handed to Jesus Christ.
To confess.
To believe.
To surrender.
To receive mercy.
And then to walk differently because grace has changed you.
That is the Gospel.
The proud sinner can become the forgiven sinner.
The hypocrite can repent.
The self-righteous can finally drop the mask.
The rebellious can come home.
The broken can be restored.
The guilty can be cleansed.
Not because sin was insignificant.
Not because God lowered His holiness.
But because Jesus Christ took sin seriously enough to carry its judgment at the cross.
And the Christ who was crucified is risen.
Alive.
Lord.
King.
Calling sinners to repentance and faith.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Your pride does not have to write the ending.
Your failure does not have to write the ending.
Your hidden sin does not have to write the ending.
Your shame does not have to write the ending.
Jesus rewrites stories surrendered to Him.
From rebellion to repentance.
From hiding to confession.
From self-rule to surrender.
From death to life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed something you have been hiding from God, do not manufacture a religious response.
Tell Him the truth.
Someone else may read your comment at two in the morning and realize they are not the only Christian still fighting battles nobody sees.
Your testimony might become somebody else's reason to stop hiding.
And if one particular person came to your heart while reading this, do not use this article as a weapon against them.
Pray first.
Not because every sentence is easy to hear.
Because some truths need to be revisited precisely when we least want to hear them.
Not for numbers.
Not for applause.
Not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
For Jesus.
Scripture gives us no right to make either one a spiritual requirement.

But if Gospel Warrior is genuinely helping you know Christ, understand Scripture, repent more deeply, heal biblically, and remain anchored in the Gospel, then supporting and sharing this work can be one practical way of helping these messages reach people who may never walk through a church door but will stop long enough to read something a friend placed in front of them.
There are people scrolling Facebook tonight while silently losing battles their families know nothing about.
People carrying shame.
People questioning whether Jesus could still want them.
People who have mastered smiling while spiritually collapsing.
Sometimes one shared article becomes an unexpected doorway into a conversation about Christ.
They are not purchasing spiritual status.
They are supporting the continued work of producing biblical encouragement, discipleship, Gospel-centered writing, and resources designed to point people toward Jesus Christ.
And there is something deeper than merchandise behind the invitation.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the friend who has grown cold.
Invite the person who does not believe yet.
Invite the Christian who is tired of shallow inspiration and hungry for something that brings them back to Christ.
Come to Jesus.
Because eventually every platform disappears.
Every possession changes hands.
Every accomplishment becomes somebody else's history.
Every human applause grows silent.
Every carefully constructed image dies.
And we stand before God without filters, titles, followers, résumés, excuses, or comparisons.
Only truth remains.
So do not spend your life trying to look taller before men while becoming smaller before God.
Do not protect the pride that Christ died to free you from.
Do not mistake God's patience for His approval.
Do not keep asking Him to bless the throne you refuse to leave.
Get down.
Not because you are worthless.
Because He is worthy.
Repent.
Not because grace has disappeared.
Because grace is still being offered.
Come empty-handed.
Come exposed.
Come tired.
Come ashamed if necessary.
But come.
The frightening truth is that God resists the proud.
The breathtaking truth is what comes next.
He gives grace to the humble.
And there is still grace for you.
The safest place for your shattered pride is at the feet of the Savior whose scarred hands are still strong enough to rewrite your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS MASTURBATION REALLY THE PROBLEM—OR IS YOUR HEART CRYING OUT FOR SOMETHING YOUR BODY CAN NEVER GIVE YOU?
paragraphs: IS MASTURBATION REALLY THE PROBLEM—OR IS YOUR HEART CRYING OUT FOR SOMETHING YOUR BODY CAN NEVER GIVE YOU?

The Bible never directly names masturbation. That does not mean Scripture has nothing to say about what may be happening underneath it—the loneliness, lust, secrecy, wounds, compulsions, fantasies, shame, and desperate search for comfort that can turn a private moment into a spiritual battlefield.
There is a moment after the pleasure disappears that almost nobody talks about.
The room becomes quiet again.
The screen goes dark.
The fantasy ends.
Your breathing settles.
And whatever you were trying not to feel is still there.
Maybe loneliness.
Maybe rejection.
Maybe stress.
Maybe anger.
Maybe boredom.
Maybe memories you wish you could erase.
Maybe a craving to feel wanted.
Maybe a marriage that has become painfully distant.
Maybe years without affection.
Maybe pornography has trained your mind to run toward sexual stimulation whenever life hurts.
Maybe there isn't some dramatic hidden trauma at all. Maybe a habit simply became a pattern, and the pattern became increasingly difficult to control.
But sometimes, beneath the sexual urge, there is another hunger whispering:
Comfort me.
Distract me.
Make me feel something.
Help me escape.
And that is where this conversation becomes much bigger than masturbation.
Because what if the behavior you keep fighting is sometimes only the smoke?
What if somewhere underneath it there is a fire?
Before going any further, we need to say something Christians sometimes fail to say carefully enough.
The Bible does not contain a verse that explicitly says, “You shall not masturbate.”
It does not explicitly identify masturbation by name and then give a direct command concerning the act itself.
That matters.
We must never pretend Scripture says something it does not say.

The often-repeated story of Onan in Genesis 38 is not a legitimate shortcut for proving otherwise. Onan's sin occurs in the context of refusing his covenantal family obligation while exploiting Tamar sexually and deliberately preventing offspring. The passage records God's judgment, but it should not simply be turned into “the Bible verse about masturbation.”
Biblical faithfulness requires more honesty than that.
But there is another mistake we can make.
We can say, “The Bible doesn't mention masturbation explicitly, therefore nothing surrounding masturbation matters spiritually.”
That conclusion does not follow either.

Scripture speaks extensively about the heart, lust, sexual immorality, self-control, holiness, conscience, what masters us, what fills our minds, how we treat other human beings, and what we do with desires that compete for the place belonging to God.
So perhaps the most revealing question is not merely:
“Did I masturbate?”
Perhaps we also need the courage to ask:
What was happening in my heart?
Jesus repeatedly moved conversations in that direction.
In Matthew 5:28, He says:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν…”
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn…
The crucial expression, πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι (pros to epithymēsai), concerns looking at a woman with lustful desire or with the purpose of desiring her.
Jesus continues:
“ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.”
He has already committed adultery with her “ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ”—en tē kardia autou—“in his heart.”
Notice where Jesus takes us.
The heart.
Not because the body is evil.

Christianity does not teach that your body is filthy simply because it experiences sexual desire. God created human beings embodied. Sexuality itself is not an embarrassing accident that slipped past the Creator.
The problem is what sin can do with good desires.
Hunger can become gluttony.
Rest can become laziness.
Money can become greed.
Influence can become pride.
Sexual desire can become lust, exploitation, fantasy, domination, obsession, or escape.
And something does not have to involve another physical person in the room for the heart to become entangled.
That is why reducing the entire struggle to “How many days have I gone without doing it?” can sometimes miss what Jesus wants to heal.
You can restrain your hands while feeding your imagination.
You can delete pornography while continuing to objectify people everywhere you go.
You can count thirty clean days while becoming proud, judgmental, and spiritually cold.
And you can fail after thirty clean days and become so buried beneath shame that you stop praying because you are convinced Jesus no longer wants to hear your voice.
Neither self-righteousness nor despair is freedom.
Jesus wants more than behavior management.
He wants you.
Your mind.
Your desires.
Your wounds.
Your imagination.
Your secret places.
Your exhausted nights.
Your loneliness.
Your body.
Your future.
Your heart.
David understood that transformation had to reach deeper than external appearance.
After devastating sexual sin and the cascading destruction surrounding it, David prayed in Psalm 51:10:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
לֵב — lev.
Heart.
טָהוֹר — tahor.
Clean. Pure.
David did not merely pray, “God, make the consequences disappear.”
He wanted something recreated inside him.
And perhaps that is the prayer some of us have been afraid to pray.
Not:
“Jesus, make me less horny.”
Not merely:
“Jesus, help me reach another streak.”
But:
“Jesus, show me why I keep running here.”
That prayer can be frightening.
Because sometimes sexual release is not merely being pursued for sexual pleasure.
Sometimes it has become anesthesia.
You feel rejected, so you escape.
You feel anxious, so you escape.
You cannot sleep, so you escape.
You feel worthless, so you escape.
You fight with your spouse, so you escape.
You remember something painful, so you escape.
You feel spiritually empty, so you escape.
For a few minutes, the internal noise becomes quieter.
Then it comes back.
And if pornography is involved, another human being can slowly become less of a person made in the image of God and more of an instrument in an internal fantasy.
That should disturb us—not because sex is dirty, but precisely because human beings are sacred.
The man or woman on the screen is not pixels.
The attractive person you noticed today is not raw material for your imagination.
They bear the image of God.
They have a story.
A childhood.
Fears.
Dignity.
A soul.
Jesus died to redeem people, not to teach us more sophisticated ways of consuming them in our minds.
This is why lust matters.
But we also need precision here.

We should not casually declare that every involuntary sexual thought is equivalent to deliberate lust. Temptation is not identical to consenting to temptation. An unwanted thought appearing in your mind is not the same thing as intentionally cultivating it for gratification.
Even Jesus was tempted, yet without sin according to Hebrews 4:15.
The battle often happens in what we choose to welcome, rehearse, feed, pursue, and obey.
And there is another biblical question that may be even more confronting.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:12:
all’ ouk egō exousiasthēsomai hypo tinos.
“But I will not be dominated by anything.”
That word ἐξουσιασθήσομαι — exousiasthēsomai carries the sense of being brought under another's authority or mastery.
Now ask yourself something difficult.
Not because somebody on Facebook needs your answer.
Because God already knows it.
Can you say no?
If you decide not to masturbate tonight, does your mind begin bargaining with you?
If you decide to stop using pornography, do you repeatedly find yourself returning?
When stress rises, does sexual stimulation automatically become your refuge?
Are you arranging your privacy around the habit?
Deleting evidence?
Making promises in the morning and breaking them at night?
Has the behavior begun controlling your time, attention, sleep, relationships, spiritual life, or ability to see others without sexualizing them?
Then regardless of whatever label somebody wants to debate, Paul's question about mastery deserves your attention.
Because Christian freedom is not merely the ability to say:
“I am allowed.”
Freedom also means not being enslaved.
And this is where many believers become trapped in a brutal cycle.
Temptation.
Resistance.
Giving in.
Relief.
Shame.
Promises.
A few good days.
Temptation again.
Giving in again.
More shame.
More promises.
Eventually the promise changes.
Instead of saying, “I will never do this again,” you begin saying:
“Maybe this is just who I am.”
No.
Your struggle may be real.
Your habits may be deeply established.
Your failures may have happened more times than you can count.
But your sin is not your Savior, and your worst night does not possess the authority to write the final chapter of a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα…”
Ouden ara nyn katakrima…
“There is therefore now no condemnation…”
For whom?
For everyone who successfully conquered every sexual temptation?
For everyone who maintained a perfect streak?
For everyone whose browser history has always been spotless?
No.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Κατάκριμα — katakrima.
Condemnation.
The Gospel does not say sin is insignificant.
It says Christ's saving work is sufficient.
There is an enormous difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction says:
“Come into the light.”
Condemnation says:
“Hide from God.”
Conviction says:
“This is destroying something in you.”
Condemnation says:
“You are disgusting.”
Conviction points toward repentance.
Condemnation whispers that repentance is pointless.
Conviction leads you toward Jesus.
Condemnation tells you Jesus is tired of you.
Do you see the ancient lie?
It is the same instinct seen after humanity's first rebellion.
Sin.
Shame.
Hide.
And Jesus keeps calling sinners out of hiding.
Not so He can pretend darkness is light.
So He can bring us into grace and transform us.

First John 1:9 does not tell believers to conceal their sins until they become impressive enough to return to God. It tells us that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
Confession is not informing God.
He already knows.
Confession is agreeing with God and stepping into the light.
And repentance is more than feeling terrible afterward.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance, a changed mind and turning of orientation toward God.
Real repentance therefore asks practical questions.
What feeds this pattern?
What time does it usually happen?
What emotion comes immediately before it?
What access makes falling effortless?
What fantasy keeps returning?
What wound am I trying to medicate?
What relationship needs honesty?
What device needs boundaries?
What account needs deleting?
Who mature and trustworthy needs to know that I am struggling?
What would fleeing temptation actually look like before temptation reaches its strongest point?
Because sometimes Christians keep praying for deliverance while refusing to close the door through which temptation walks every night.
Jesus teaches radical seriousness toward sin.
Paul tells Timothy to flee youthful passions in 2 Timothy 2:22.
Notice that word.
Flee.
Not negotiate.
Not see how close you can stand to the edge.
Not keep the private account “just in case.”
Not continue following the profiles that deliberately stir your imagination and then ask why prayer feels harder afterward.
Flee.
But Paul does not stop with fleeing.
He says to pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace together with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart.
Christian holiness is not simply removing something.
It is pursuing Someone.
That distinction can change the entire battle.
Because if your only spiritual objective is:
“Do not masturbate. Do not masturbate. Do not masturbate.”
then the behavior can become the center of your consciousness even while you are trying to escape it.
But Christianity does not revolve around masturbation.
Christianity revolves around Jesus Christ.
So fill the vacuum.
Pray before the urge arrives.
Open Scripture before you open the app.
Exercise.
Sleep properly.
Get out of isolation.
Serve somebody.
Call a trusted believer.
Cultivate friendships.
Deal honestly with loneliness.
Seek wise pastoral help.

If the pattern feels compulsive or is connected with trauma, anxiety, depression, or other significant emotional distress, receiving help from a qualified mental-health professional can exist alongside prayer, pastoral care, Scripture, and Christian community. Seeking appropriate help is not a betrayal of faith.
And when temptation comes, remember what you are actually pursuing.
Not merely abstinence.
Freedom.
Not merely a clean browser.
A clean heart.
Not merely fewer sexual thoughts.
A mind increasingly shaped by Christ.
Not merely control of your hands.
Surrender of your life.
Galatians 5 speaks about the fruit of the Spirit, including ἐγκράτεια — enkrateia, self-control.
Fruit grows through life connected to its source.
You cannot crucify the flesh through self-hatred.
You cannot shame yourself into sanctification.
You cannot disgust yourself into loving Jesus.
Christian transformation is not accomplished by staring endlessly at yourself and screaming, “Try harder.”

The Holy Spirit changes people as they walk with Christ, put sinful patterns to death, renew their minds, practice obedience, live in community, confess rather than hide, and repeatedly return their attention to the One who loved them enough to die for them.
And yes, sometimes obedience hurts.
Sometimes you will have to sit with loneliness instead of anesthetizing it.
Sometimes you will have to feel the anxiety instead of immediately escaping it.
Sometimes you will discover that underneath the sexual craving is grief.
Or rejection.
Or anger.
Or an aching desire to be held.
Or simply a deeply conditioned habit that now requires patient retraining.
Bring that truth to Jesus too.
You do not have to manufacture a dramatic explanation for every temptation. Not every sexual urge is evidence of a hidden psychological wound.
But neither should you refuse to examine your heart merely because examination is uncomfortable.
Psalm 139 gives us one of the bravest prayers a person can pray:
“Search me, O God, and know my heart…”
Search me.
Not my neighbor.
Not my spouse.
Not the person whose scandal everyone is discussing.
Me.
Know my heart.
Test me.
Show me what I cannot see.
Lead me.
That is dangerous prayer.
Because Jesus may expose things you have spent years protecting.
But exposure in the hands of Christ is not the same thing as humiliation in the hands of a mob.
Jesus exposes to heal.
He confronts to restore.
He calls us to repentance because He loves us too much to make peace with what is destroying us.
And maybe you failed last night.
Maybe you failed ten minutes before reading this.
Maybe you have pornography hidden somewhere nobody knows about.
Maybe you are married and ashamed.
Maybe you are single and exhausted.
Maybe you are a ministry leader carrying a secret you are terrified somebody will discover.
Maybe you are young and confused by a body suddenly full of desires you do not understand.
Maybe you are older and wondering why this battle never completely disappeared.
Maybe you have asked God for forgiveness so many times that saying “I'm sorry” now feels fraudulent.
Listen carefully.
Do not use grace as permission to remain in darkness.
But do not use your failure as permission to run away from grace.
Run toward Christ.
The cross was not designed for respectable sinners with manageable problems.
At Calvary, Jesus carried real guilt.
Real rebellion.
Real sexual sin.
Real shame.
Real wickedness.
Real human brokenness.
He did not bleed because our sin was small.
He bled because His love and saving purpose were greater.
And He rose.
That matters.
Christianity does not end with a guilty man kneeling beneath a cross.
It announces an empty tomb.
Resurrection means sin does not receive the final word over those who belong to Christ.
Your story can move from secrecy to confession.
From slavery to growing freedom.
From objectification to honor.
From shame to grace.
From isolation to community.
From compulsive escape to honest healing.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming sinners in the middle of it.
So tonight, if the familiar urge arrives, perhaps begin with a different question.
Not simply:
“How do I stop myself?”
Ask:
“Jesus, what am I actually hungry for right now?”
Then stay long enough to hear the uncomfortable answer.
Maybe you are lonely.
Tell Him.
Maybe you are angry.
Tell Him.
Maybe you are bored.
Admit it.
Maybe you are lusting.
Confess it.
Maybe you are hurting.
Bring the wound into the light.
Maybe you simply desire sexual release and need wisdom and self-control concerning what you do with that desire.
Bring that to Him too.
Nothing about your humanity surprises the One who created you.
Then remember 1 Corinthians 10:13. Temptation is not uniquely yours, God is faithful, and temptation does not make obedience impossible. Look for the way of escape He provides.
Sometimes the way out will look astonishingly ordinary.
Put the phone outside the bedroom.
Get out of bed.
Take a walk.
Pray aloud.
Message your accountability partner.
Stop following the account.
Block the website.
Leave the room.
Go to sleep.
Open Scripture.
Tell someone the truth tomorrow.
Small acts of obedience can become battlegrounds where allegiance is relearned.
And if you fall?
Do not turn one failure into a week of surrender because you think the streak is already ruined.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive mercy.
Learn what happened.
Stand again.
Follow Christ again.
Micah 7:8 contains the defiant confidence:
“Though I have fallen, I will rise.”
The Christian life is not the story of people who never needed grace again after conversion.
It is the story of people being transformed by the God whose grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness and to live differently.
So if this article uncovered something you have hidden even from yourself, you do not need to publish the details of your private sexual life publicly.
But you also do not have to pretend this battle does not exist.
And when you see somebody else write those words, do not interrogate them.
Pray for them.
There are people behind those comments.
Brothers.
Sisters.
People trying to come home.
Not to announce that you suspect someone. Not to shame anybody.
It offers Jesus.
Salvation cannot be bought, grace cannot be purchased, and the Gospel must never become a sales technique.
One way believers can glorify God is by using what He has entrusted to them to help sound biblical ministry reach others.
And there is much more than merchandise behind the mission.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who has become tired.
Invite the Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the seeker who thinks Christianity is nothing but rules.
Invite the person who thinks their sexual past disqualifies them from ever coming near Jesus.
Invite even the unbeliever who cannot understand why Christians keep talking about grace.
Let them encounter the Gospel.
Because somebody you know is fighting a battle they have never told you about.
Somebody is deleting their history and then deleting their prayers because shame convinced them God does not want either one.
Somebody believes the secret is too ugly.
Somebody believes they have failed too many times.
Somebody believes Jesus receives everyone except people like them.
And perhaps that person is you.
Then hear the Gospel one more time.
You are not saved because you finally mastered your sexuality.
You are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And the grace that forgives you does not abandon you where it found you.
Christ calls you out of darkness.
Christ teaches you holiness.
Christ gives mercy to the repentant.
Christ restores what sin has damaged.
Christ breaks chains.
Christ renews minds.
Christ cleanses hearts.
Christ teaches us to see people as people again.
Christ receives sinners who come to Him.
So stop negotiating with the darkness.
Stop decorating the hiding place.
Bring the whole story into the light.
The lust.
The loneliness.
The pornography.
The fantasies.
The habit.
The pain.
The questions.
The failure.
The shame.
Bring all of it to Jesus.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Seek help where help is needed.
Put boundaries where boundaries are needed.
Make confession where confession is needed.
And receive grace where grace has already been offered.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy was never that you had a secret struggle.
Perhaps the greatest tragedy would be allowing that struggle to convince you that you must stay hidden from the only One capable of transforming you.
The secret you thought would make Jesus walk away may become the very place where you finally discover how far His grace was willing to come looking for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN YOU LOVE JESUS AND SECRETLY LOVE LUST?
paragraphs: CAN YOU LOVE JESUS AND SECRETLY LOVE LUST?

The question is not whether temptation ever enters your mind. The terrifying question is what happens when you invite it to stay—and whether the secret thing you keep feeding is slowly becoming the thing you refuse to surrender to Christ.
There is a version of you that everybody sees.
The version that smiles.
The version that says, “God is good.”
The version that shares the Bible verse.
The version that worships when the song reaches the chorus.
The version that knows when to say “Amen.”
And then there is the version of you that nobody sees.
The version alone with a phone.
The version behind a locked door.
The version scrolling when everyone else is asleep.
The version that knows exactly what to search.
Exactly what account to visit.
Exactly what memory to replay.
Exactly which conversation has crossed a line.
Exactly which fantasy you keep returning to even though something inside you whispers…
You know this is not where Jesus is leading you.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your spouse may not know.
Your parents may not know.
Your pastor may not know.
Your friends may not know.
The people sitting beside you at church may never imagine the war happening behind your eyes.
But Jesus knows.
And before shame convinces you to stop reading, you need to know something else.
Jesus knowing is not the end of your hope.
It may be the beginning of your freedom.
Because the Christ who exposes darkness is also the Christ who walked toward scandalous people when everyone else stepped away.
So stay with me.
Especially if part of you already wants to leave.
Because perhaps the most dangerous question is not, “Have I ever struggled with lust?”
The more penetrating question is:
Have I begun protecting what Jesus is asking me to surrender?
There is a difference.
A massive one.
Temptation can knock on the door without your permission.
A thought can flash through your mind.
Your body can react.
An image can appear.
An attraction can happen.
You can feel temptation intensely and still choose obedience.
Jesus Himself was tempted, yet Scripture says He remained without sin.
Hebrews 4:15 says that Christ was “tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin.”
So temptation itself is not proof that you do not love Jesus.
Please understand that.
A believer may genuinely love Christ and still experience fierce sexual temptation.
A believer may stumble.
A believer may have wounds, habits, memories, and patterns that require serious discipleship and patient sanctification.
A believer may fall and come crawling back to the throne of grace.
The Christian life is not the story of people who never face temptation.
It is the story of sinners who increasingly learn where to run when temptation comes.
But there is another condition entirely.
It is possible not merely to be tempted by lust…
but to feed it.
Schedule it.
Protect it.
Romanticize it.
Return to it.
Hide it.
Make excuses for it.
And eventually become angry whenever Jesus puts His finger on it.
That is where this question becomes uncomfortable:
Can you love Jesus while secretly loving lust?
Listen to Jesus Himself.
In Matthew 5:28, the Greek reads in part:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν…”
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn…
In context, Jesus teaches that whoever looks at a woman with the purpose of lusting after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.

The important word is related to the Greek verb ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō, meaning to desire or long for. The word itself can describe desire in different contexts, but here the construction and context make the sinful direction unmistakable: Jesus is confronting a look cultivated for lustful desire.
Jesus takes the issue deeper than external behavior.
He goes into the heart.
That means you can keep your hands technically “clean” while allowing your imagination to become a private bedroom for sin.
You can never physically touch the person.
Never meet them.
Never sleep with them.
Never get caught.
And still nurture something inside that does not belong to Christ.
That is frightening.
But it is also strangely hopeful.
Because Jesus is not merely interested in making your browser history cleaner.
He wants your heart back.
Pornography promises intimacy without covenant.
Lust promises pleasure without responsibility.
Fantasy promises possession without relationship.
Secret sexual sin whispers that you can take what you want from another human being in your imagination without having to love that person as someone made in the image of God.
And it always asks for another look.
Another video.
Another fantasy.
Another conversation.
Another compromise.
Just one more.
Until “one more” becomes tonight.
Then tomorrow.
Then next week.
Then years.
And eventually you are not simply watching something.
Something is discipling you.
That screen is teaching your eyes what to hunger for.
Your repetition is teaching your brain what to anticipate.
Your secrecy is teaching your conscience when to become quiet.
Your fantasy is teaching your heart to consume instead of covenantally love.
And meanwhile, Jesus stands at the center of Christianity saying something radically different.
Not:
“Manage your lust better.”
Not:
“Hide it more successfully.”
Not:
“Become respectable enough that nobody discovers it.”
Jesus calls you to Himself.
This is why Paul writes in 1 Thessalonians 4:3:
Touto gar estin thelēma tou Theou, ho hagiasmos hymōn…
“For this is the will of God, your sanctification…”
And Paul immediately connects that sanctification with abstaining from sexual immorality.
The Greek word ἁγιασμός — hagiasmos carries the idea of holiness or sanctification—being set apart to God.
Notice what Christianity offers.
Not merely restriction.
Consecration.
Your body is not garbage.
Sexuality is not dirty.
Marriage is not dirty.
God created human beings male and female.
God created covenant.
God created marital union.
The Bible does not oppose sexuality because sexuality is too powerful.

Scripture guards sexuality because sexuality is powerful enough to wound, bind, unite, betray, create life, communicate covenant, and touch places in the human heart that casual consumption can devastate.
Lust takes something sacred and asks:
“How can this satisfy me?”
Love asks:
“How can I honor God and seek the true good of this person?”
Lust consumes.
Love gives.
Lust reduces a person to what their body can make you feel.
Love remembers there is a soul inside that body.
A soul God sees.
A soul Christ calls to repentance and redemption.
A soul that was never created to become raw material for your fantasy.
And perhaps that hurts to read because you know exactly where this reaches into your life.
Maybe it is pornography.
Maybe it is not.
Maybe it is the coworker you keep imagining.
The married person you keep messaging.
The ex whose photographs you still visit.
The account you unfollow and then search for again.
The “innocent” flirting you would never want your spouse to read.
The private folder.
The deleted history.
The second account.
The saved videos.
The explicit fiction.
The emotional affair you refuse to call an affair because nobody has touched anybody.
Maybe it is not even something another human being would easily discover.
But God already has.
Psalm 139 declares that there is nowhere we can flee from His presence.
That should terrify hypocrisy.
But it should comfort the repentant.
Because the God who sees you completely is the God you no longer need to hide from.
Adam sinned and hid.
Human beings have been hiding ever since.
We hide behind bushes.
Behind religion.
Behind ministry.
Behind marriage.
Behind humor.
Behind theological vocabulary.
Behind deleted histories.
Behind “everybody struggles.”
Behind “at least I never actually did anything.”
But grace does not grow in pretending.
First John 1:9 tells believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
The Greek word translated “confess” is ὁμολογέω — homologeō.
At its heart is the idea of acknowledging, admitting, saying what is true.
No more renaming darkness so you can keep it.
No more calling bondage “just how I am.”
No more calling deliberate fantasy “just attraction.”
No more calling secrecy “privacy” when privacy has become the hiding place of rebellion.
Call it what God calls it.
Then bring it to the God who already knows.
Because repentance is not merely feeling disgusting afterward.
Repentance is not crying tonight and arranging another encounter with the same sin tomorrow.
Repentance is a turning.
It is agreeing with God strongly enough that your direction begins to change.
Sometimes dramatically.
Sometimes painfully.
Sometimes with trembling hands deleting what you once protected.
Sometimes with installing accountability systems.
Sometimes with handing another mature believer access to the places where secrecy has been feeding you.
Sometimes with confessing to a trusted, mature Christian who will refuse both to crush you and to flatter your sin.
Sometimes with ending the relationship.
Blocking the account.
Removing the app.
Changing the routine.
Moving the device out of the bedroom.
Refusing to negotiate with yourself at 1:00 in the morning.

Jesus uses shocking language in Matthew 5 when He speaks of tearing out an eye or cutting off a hand if it causes sin. Christians have historically understood this as deliberate hyperbole, not a command for bodily mutilation. Jesus is communicating the radical seriousness with which sin must be treated.
In other words:
Stop petting what is killing you.
You cannot crucify something while simultaneously making sure it remains comfortable.
And this is where someone will ask:
“But if I keep failing, does that mean I never loved Jesus?”
Not necessarily.
Peter loved Jesus and failed catastrophically.
He denied even knowing Him.
Three times.
At the moment when loyalty mattered most.
And after the resurrection, Jesus went looking for Peter.
Not to pretend Peter's denial did not matter.
Not to tell Peter that betrayal was harmless.
Jesus restored him.
Grace did not call Peter's sin acceptable.
Grace made Peter's failure something other than the final chapter.
That is the Gospel.
The Gospel is not that good people learned to control themselves.
The Gospel is that sinners could not save themselves, so the Son of God came for them.
Jesus lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He went to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is offered not because you finally became sexually flawless enough to deserve Jesus…
but because Jesus is sufficient to save sinners who come to Him in repentance and faith.
That distinction changes everything.
You do not clean yourself so Jesus will finally love you.
You come to Jesus because your attempts to save yourself have failed.
Then the grace that forgives you begins teaching you to say no to the things that once mastered you.
Titus 2:11–12 says that the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live self-controlled, upright, godly lives.
Did you catch that?
Grace trains.
Real grace does not merely pardon.
Grace transforms.
Not instant perfection.
Not sinless performance.
But a new allegiance.
A new war.
A new direction.
A new hatred for what separates your heart from obedience.
A new hunger for Christ even when the old appetites scream.
This is why the real warning is not that a Christian experiences temptation.
The warning is when you stop fighting because you have secretly decided the sin deserves a permanent room in your heart.
There is a difference between falling in battle and signing a peace treaty with the enemy.
One says:
“Jesus, I hate that I keep falling. Help me.”
The other eventually says:
“Jesus, You may have everything except this.”
And Christianity gives us no safe category for intentionally crowning Christ as Lord while permanently reserving one protected kingdom where He is forbidden to rule.
Jesus said in John 14:15:
“If you love me, you will keep my commandments.”
That does not mean obedience purchases His love.
It means love for Christ bears fruit.
Imperfectly.
Sometimes slowly.
Sometimes through tears.
Sometimes through repeated battles.
But genuinely.
First John 2:15 says, “Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.”
Scripture does not permit us to make peace with cherished rebellion and then use the language of grace to make ourselves comfortable.
Yet Scripture also does not permit us to tell the struggling believer that every temptation proves he or she is abandoned by God.
Conviction says:
“Come into the light.”
Condemnation whispers:
“Stay hidden because God could never want you now.”
The Gospel says:
Come.
Not because the sin is small.
Because the Savior is greater.
Come while ashamed.
Come while shaking.
Come after the relapse.
Come after the failure you swore would never happen again.
Come honestly.
But come ready to surrender.
Romans 8:1 says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
And Romans 8 does not stop with freedom from condemnation. It speaks of life in the Spirit and putting to death the deeds of the body.
Grace and holiness are not enemies.
The same Jesus who refuses to condemn those who belong to Him refuses to leave them enslaved.
Maybe you have prayed:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
And then failed again.
So you prayed again.
Then failed.
Again.
Again.
Again.
And now you wonder whether your prayers mean anything.
Do not measure the power of Christ by the number of times temptation has knocked you down.
Look instead at what you do when you become conscious of your sin.
Are you running from Christ?
Or running toward Him?
Are you defending the sin?
Or confessing it?
Are you arranging opportunities to fall?
Or beginning to destroy those opportunities?
Are you merely terrified of consequences?
Or increasingly grieved because your sin dishonors the One you love?
Do you want Jesus merely to remove your guilt?
Or do you actually want Him to become Lord over your desires?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Maybe your hands are holding a phone containing something you know needs to disappear.
Maybe somebody's name immediately came into your mind.
Maybe there is a conversation you already know must end.
Maybe your secret has survived because nobody has ever forced you to say it out loud.
You do not need to tell the entire internet the intimate details of your sin.
Wisdom matters.
Privacy matters.
Other people's dignity matters.
But you do need to stop pretending before God.

And for entrenched patterns, bringing the struggle to a trustworthy mature believer, pastor, Christian counselor, or accountability partner may be one of the ways secrecy finally begins losing its oxygen.
James 5:16 speaks about confessing sins to one another and praying for one another.
Sin grows comfortably in darkness.
Healing begins when darkness loses its hiding place.
So perhaps tonight your prayer does not need to be impressive.
Maybe it needs to be brutally simple.
“Jesus, I have been protecting something You died to free me from.”
“Jesus, I don't only want forgiveness for the consequences. Change what I love.”
“Jesus, teach my eyes to belong to You.”
“Jesus, teach my imagination to belong to You.”
“Jesus, teach my body to belong to You.”
“Jesus, expose every excuse I have used to protect this.”
“Jesus, I surrender.”
And if you fail tomorrow?
Get up.
If you fail next week?
Get up.
Not casually.
Not presuming upon grace.
Not saying sin does not matter.
Get up because Christ is still worthy of being pursued.
Proverbs 24:16 says that the righteous falls seven times and rises again.
Your story does not have to end on the floor.
And if you are reading this thinking, “You don't understand what I've watched… what I've imagined… what I've done…”
Maybe I don't.
But the cross does.
The cross is Christianity's declaration that sin is far worse than we wanted to admit and grace is far greater than we dared to hope.
Jesus did not bleed because your sin was insignificant.
He bled because redemption is costly.
First Corinthians 6 speaks with startling clarity about sexual immorality, adultery and other sins, and then Paul says something breathtaking to believers who had come out of sinful lives:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because their histories had vanished.
Not because their past had never happened.
But because Jesus had interrupted the story.
Paul continues:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
That is Christianity.
Not:
“Such were some of you, so remain there forever.”
Not:
“Such were some of you, so God could never use you.”
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Your scandal does not have to receive the final sentence.
Jesus can rewrite what sin tried to finish.
That is why this is bigger than pornography.
Bigger than lust.
Bigger than one hidden tab.
This is about worship.
Who gets your eyes?
Who gets your imagination?
Who gets your body?
Who gets your secret life?
Who gets the version of you nobody else sees?
Jesus does not want merely your Sunday morning.
He wants you.
And what He offers in return is infinitely greater than the temporary satisfaction lust keeps promising and never finally delivers.
If this exposed something hidden, you do not need to describe your private sexual history publicly. But you can draw a line in the sand.
If you need believers to pray for you without knowing every detail, comment, “Pray for me.”

And if Christ has already begun freeing you from a place you once believed would own you forever, tell someone what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the evidence another struggling believer desperately needs that bondage does not have to be permanent.
Not because sharing a Christian article earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
Not because clicking “Share” proves that you are saved.
It doesn't.
Jesus cannot be bought.

But if this truth helped you, sharing it publicly can be one simple way of refusing to be ashamed of Christ and helping biblical truth reach someone whose private battle may be invisible to everybody around them.
There may be a friend on your Facebook list fighting this tonight.
A husband.
A wife.
A teenager.
A church leader.
A lonely believer.
A person who has been silently asking God for help.

Supporting Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity when it is given freely, worshipfully, and without compulsion. Scripture teaches, “God loves a cheerful giver” in 2 Corinthians 9:7. It does not.
But ministry does require people willing to carry the message with their prayers, voices, generosity, sharing, and faithful participation.
You are helping us point more people toward Him.
Jesus remains the treasure.
Jesus remains the message.
Jesus remains the Savior.
Jesus remains the reason.
If you can support the mission, support it freely and joyfully.
If you cannot, pray.
Share.
Save the truth.
Follow along.
Carry the Gospel wherever God has placed you.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is sitting in darkness believing the lie that what they have secretly loved has made them too filthy to come home.
Tell them about Jesus.
Tell them about repentance.
Tell them about the cross.
Tell them about the empty tomb.
Tell them that grace does not give us permission to remain chained.
Grace opens the prison door.
And maybe that “somebody” tonight…
is you.
So put down what has been feeding the darkness.
Open your hands.
Stop bargaining.
Stop hiding.
Come into the light.
Jesus already knows the scandal.
And He is still calling sinners to repentance, forgiveness, cleansing, restoration, and a transformed life in Him.
Your lust does not deserve your worship.
Your secret does not deserve your future.
Your shame does not deserve the final word.
Christ does.
And perhaps years from now, when you remember the night you finally stopped defending what was destroying you, you will realize something beautiful:
The secret you thought would become the end of your story became the very place where you discovered how desperately you needed the Savior.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: EVERY TIME A MAN DIVIDED HIS HOME, SOMETHING BROKE: The Disturbing Pattern Behind Polygamy in the Bible
paragraphs: EVERY TIME A MAN DIVIDED HIS HOME, SOMETHING BROKE: The Disturbing Pattern Behind Polygamy in the Bible

Scripture never needed to say, “Watch what polygamy does to a family” in every story. It simply opened the door and let us watch Abraham’s household fracture, Jacob’s wives compete, Hannah weep, David’s family bleed, and Solomon’s heart wander—until the question becomes impossible to ignore: Why does a practice the Bible records so often leave conflict in its wake?
There is a difference between something being in the Bible and something being endorsed by the Bible.
That distinction matters.
Because some readers encounter Abraham with Sarah and Hagar, Jacob with Leah and Rachel, David with multiple wives, and Solomon with hundreds of wives and conclude:
“If these men belonged to God, maybe God approved of polygamy.”
But Scripture is far more honest than that.
The Bible does not airbrush its heroes.
It exposes them.
It records faith beside failure, obedience beside compromise, courage beside cowardice, worship beside lust, and grace beside scandal.
And when you follow polygamous households through Scripture, something becomes increasingly difficult to overlook.
The Bible may record polygamy...
but it repeatedly makes us live inside its consequences.
Jealousy.
Competition.
Favoritism.
Humiliation.
Manipulation.
Children caught inside adult rivalry.
Inheritance disputes.
Sexual politics.
Resentment.
Division.
And sometimes bloodshed.
The pattern begins long before Abraham.
The first man explicitly described in Scripture as taking two wives is not Adam.
It is Lamech.
Genesis 4:19 says:
“Lamech took two wives.”
The Hebrew is strikingly simple:
וַיִּקַּח־לוֹ לֶמֶךְ שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים
Vayyiqqaḥ-lô Lemeḵ shətê nāšîm.
Literally, in context: “And Lamech took for himself two wives.”
That alone does not prove that every subsequent disaster in Lamech’s life resulted from polygamy. We should never force Scripture to say what it does not say.
But Genesis has already established another pattern.
Before humanity fractured...
before Cain murdered Abel...
before violence spread...
before Lamech boasted about killing a man...
God had shown us marriage.
Not through a philosophical essay.
Through creation.
God formed Adam.
God formed Eve.
Then Genesis 2:24 gives the pattern:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
‘Al-kēn ya‘ăzāḇ-’îš ’eṯ-’āḇîw wə’eṯ-’immô, wəḏāḇaq bə’ištô, wəhāyû ləḇāśār ’eḥāḏ.
A man leaves his father and mother, clings to his wife...
and they become בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad — “one flesh.”
One flesh.
And centuries later, when Jesus was questioned about marriage, He did something enormously important.
He went backward.
Past Moses.
Past Israel’s kings.
Past patriarchal customs.
Past fallen human arrangements.
Back to creation.
Jesus quotes Genesis and says:
οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
hoi dýo eis sárka mían
“the two [shall become] one flesh.”
Notice the language Jesus emphasizes:
οἱ δύο — hoi dýo — “the two.”
Then:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Jesus’ argument in Matthew 19:4–6 is about divorce, so we should not pretend He was answering a direct question about polygamy.
He wasn’t.
But the marital pattern to which Christ appeals is unmistakable.
Male and female.
The two.
One flesh.
God’s design is established at creation before human sin begins distorting everything it touches.
And perhaps that explains why the biblical stories become so painful.
Because every attempt to divide something designed for covenantal union introduces tensions that human hearts are poorly equipped to carry.
Look at Abraham.
God had promised him descendants.
But time passed.
Sarah remained barren.
And waiting became painful.
You know what that feels like, don’t you?
Maybe not infertility.
Maybe you are waiting for healing.
Waiting for marriage.
Waiting for reconciliation.
Waiting for money.
Waiting for a door to open.
Waiting for your child to come back to God.
Waiting for a prayer you have whispered so many times that even praying it now hurts.
Waiting has a strange way of exposing what we believe about God.
Because eventually the temptation comes:
“If God is not doing it quickly enough...
maybe I need to help Him.”
That is where Genesis 16 becomes painfully human.
Sarai gives Hagar, her Egyptian servant, to Abram as a wife in an attempt to obtain children through her.
Hagar conceives.
And almost immediately...
the household changes.
Genesis 16:4 says that when Hagar realized she had conceived, her mistress became diminished in her eyes.
Sarah becomes angry.
Abraham refuses meaningful responsibility and tells Sarah that Hagar is in her hand.
Sarah deals harshly with Hagar.
Hagar runs away.
Think about what happened.
A promise from God.
Human impatience.
A culturally understandable solution.
A pregnancy.
Jealousy.
Humiliation.
Abuse.
Flight.
And a woman alone in the wilderness.
Yet that wilderness contains one of Scripture’s breathtaking moments.
God sees Hagar.
The discarded servant.
The outsider.
The woman caught in somebody else’s attempt to manufacture a promise.
She calls the LORD:
אֵל רֳאִי — El Ro’i
commonly understood as “God who sees me” or “God of seeing.”
That matters.
Because the Bible is not merely exposing broken family structures.
It is revealing the God who walks into the wreckage human beings create.
God sees the person everyone else reduced to a problem.
Maybe that is already touching something you buried.
Maybe you know what it is like to feel second.
Second choice.
Second favorite.
The child compared with another child.
The spouse who wonders whether someone else owns a part of the heart that was promised to you.
The person quietly asking:
“Am I actually enough?”
Then Jacob’s household takes the emotional devastation even further.
Jacob loves Rachel.
But through Laban’s deception he receives Leah first, then Rachel.
Genesis does not hide the inequality.
Jacob loves Rachel more than Leah.
God sees Leah is unloved.
Leah bears children.
Rachel is barren.
Rachel becomes jealous of her sister.
Then servants are brought into the reproductive struggle.
Bilhah.
Zilpah.
Children become entangled in the rivalry between women desperate for love, security, dignity, and motherhood.
At one point Rachel tells Jacob:
“Give me children, or I shall die!”
Later Leah and Rachel negotiate access to Jacob through mandrakes.
Read those chapters slowly.
These are not sterile genealogical details.
This is a wounded household.
One woman desperately wants children.
Another desperately wants love.
Each possesses something the other aches for.
Rachel has Jacob’s affection.
Leah has children.
And neither woman feels whole.
That is what comparison does.
It can make you stare so intensely at what another person possesses that you become unable to see the mercy already present in your own life.
Leah keeps naming sons out of her pain.
Reuben.
Simeon.
Levi.
Again and again you can hear a woman hoping:
“Maybe now my husband will love me.”
That sentence could have been written yesterday.
Maybe now he will notice me.
Maybe now she will choose me.
Maybe if I become prettier.
More successful.
More spiritual.
More useful.
More sexually desirable.
More accomplished.
Maybe then I will finally be enough.
But human approval is a cruel god.
It always demands another sacrifice.
Then something changes.
Leah gives birth again.
And Genesis 29:35 records:
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
She names him Judah.
יְהוּדָה — Yehudah.
And suddenly the story is pointing somewhere larger than Leah understands.
Because from Judah’s line...
Jesus Christ will come.
Do you see the grace buried inside the scandal?
A rejected woman.
A fractured marriage.
A household poisoned by comparison.
And through that wounded story, God moves redemptive history toward Christ.
That does not make the dysfunction good.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace demonstrates that evil does not get the final word.
That distinction is everything.
God can redeem what He never commanded.
God can work through what He never designed.
God can bring Christ-centered purpose from circumstances human sin has mangled without endorsing the mangling.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Then Scripture brings us to another household.
Elkanah has two wives:
Hannah and Peninnah.
First Samuel 1 tells us Peninnah has children.
Hannah does not.
Elkanah loves Hannah.
And Peninnah becomes her rival.
Scripture says her rival provoked her grievously because the LORD had closed her womb.
Year after year.
Not once.
Year after year.
Imagine Hannah preparing for worship knowing the person traveling beside her knew exactly where her deepest wound was...
and knew exactly how to press it.
Have you ever been wounded by somebody who understood precisely where you were fragile?
That pain is different.
Because they did not accidentally find the wound.
They knew the address.
Hannah weeps.
She cannot eat.
Even her husband does not fully understand the depth of her grief.
Then Hannah goes before God.
She pours out her soul.
Her lips move while her voice cannot be heard.
Eli initially assumes she is drunk.
Even the priest misunderstands her.
Her rival torments her.
Her husband cannot fix her.
The priest misreads her.
But God hears her.
Somebody reading this needs that sentence.
God hears what people misunderstand.
Hannah eventually gives birth to Samuel.
But again, notice the biblical honesty.
The story does not make rivalry beautiful.
It shows God meeting Hannah inside it.
Then comes David.
The warrior.
The poet.
The king.
The man after God’s own heart.
And also...
a deeply flawed man whose household becomes a warning.
David accumulated wives and concubines.
Second Samuel 5:13 explicitly says David took more concubines and wives in Jerusalem.
Yet Deuteronomy 17:17 had already warned Israel’s future king:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים
Wəlō’ yarbeh-lô nāšîm.
“He shall not multiply wives for himself.”
Why?
The verse continues:
וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
Wəlō’ yāsûr ləḇāḇô.
“So that his heart may not turn aside.”
That warning becomes terrifying when you reach Solomon.
But before Solomon, David’s household itself fractures.
Amnon violates Tamar.
Absalom murders Amnon.
Absalom rebels against David.
Political ambition and family trauma intertwine.
Eventually Absalom publicly takes David’s concubines as part of his rebellion.

We should be precise here: Scripture does not say every tragedy in David’s family happened simply because David had multiple wives. David’s sins, failures as a father, Amnon’s wickedness, Absalom’s vengeance and ambition, and the consequences announced after David’s sin with Bathsheba all matter.
Biblical interpretation must not become simplistic.
But neither should we ignore the larger picture.
David’s multiplied household is not presented as an Edenic paradise.
It becomes extraordinarily complicated, politically vulnerable, sexually fractured, and violent.
Then Solomon takes the pattern to its extreme.
First Kings 11 says Solomon loved many foreign women.
He had seven hundred wives who were princesses and three hundred concubines.
Then Scripture says something devastating:
וַיַּטּוּ נָשָׁיו אֶת־לִבּוֹ
Vayyattû nāšāw ’eṯ-libbô.
“His wives turned away his heart.”
The warning in Deuteronomy becomes biography.
“He shall not multiply wives... lest his heart turn away.”
Solomon multiplies wives.
His heart turns away.
This is one of the Bible’s most sobering demonstrations that wisdom in your head cannot protect a heart unwilling to obey God.
Solomon could write wisdom...
and still violate wisdom.
He could understand truth...
and still compromise with desire.
He could possess extraordinary discernment...
and still slowly give pieces of his allegiance away.
And that should terrify every Christian who thinks biblical knowledge automatically equals spiritual faithfulness.
You can know verses and still be drifting.
You can preach truth and secretly negotiate with sin.
You can sing worship songs while protecting an idol.
You can explain theology while your heart quietly belongs to something Jesus told you to surrender.
The greatest danger may not be that you reject God loudly.
It may be that you divide your heart gradually.
A little for Jesus.
A little for lust.
A little for Jesus.
A little for money.
A little for Jesus.
A little for approval.
A little for Jesus.
A little for resentment.
Until one day you realize the King has been given a room in a house He purchased with His blood.
But Jesus did not die to become one love among many.
He is Lord.
And suddenly the ancient stories about divided households become a mirror.
Because perhaps you have never practiced polygamy.
But your heart knows what divided loyalty feels like.
James 1:8 describes the δίψυχος — dipsychos, the “double-minded” or literally “two-souled” person, unstable in all his ways.
Two directions.
Two allegiances.
Two competing loves.
Jesus said no one can serve two masters.
And now the question becomes uncomfortable.
What has been competing with Christ for you?
Not publicly.
Privately.
What do you refuse to surrender?
What relationship matters more than obedience?
What hidden browser history has become another master?
What resentment do you protect because forgiveness feels too expensive?
What ambition receives more emotional energy than the Kingdom of God?
What secret sin keeps hearing:
“Just one more time.”
This article was never ultimately about ancient men with multiple wives.
It was about the human heart trying to possess God while keeping competing lovers.
And Jesus wants the whole heart.
Not because He is insecure.
Because He is worthy.
This is where we must return to marriage.
When the New Testament describes marriage, its deepest theological meaning is not merely romance.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5:31–32:
Then he says:
“This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.”
Marriage becomes a sign pointing beyond itself.
Christ.
And His Bride.
Jesus does not maintain a collection of competing covenant brides.
There is one Bride.
The Church.
He loves her.
He gives Himself for her.
He sanctifies her.
He cleanses her.
And He is preparing her for Himself.
That is why biblical marriage cannot finally be understood merely through what fallen cultures tolerated.
Its deepest meaning is revealed through Christ.
Marriage points toward covenant.
Faithfulness.
Exclusive devotion.
Sacrificial love.
One flesh.
Christ and His Church.
This is also why we must be careful with people whose lives are already complicated.
Maybe someone reading this entered Christ while already living inside circumstances formed before understanding biblical truth.
Maybe your family history is messy.
Divorce.
Remarriage.
Infidelity.
Abandonment.
Sexual sin.
Children from different relationships.
Maybe you read biblical teaching about marriage and immediately feel shame rather than hope.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not permission to pretend sin never mattered.
But neither is the Gospel a message that your past has permanently disqualified you from grace.
Jesus came for sinners.
Real ones.
People with histories.
People with consequences.
People who cannot travel backward and rewrite yesterday.
That is precisely why Christ came.
The scandal of Christianity is not that Christians have spotless histories.
The scandal is that the spotless Son of God willingly took the place of guilty people.
At the cross, Jesus did not merely offer advice for improving dysfunctional lives.
He carried sin.
Isaiah had prophesied of the suffering Servant.
The New Testament announces that Christ died for our sins.
Jesus bore judgment.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now forgiveness is offered not because we successfully repair our past but because Christ accomplished redemption.
Repentance does not mean pretending consequences disappear.
Repentance means turning toward God.
Grace does not say:
“Nothing was wrong.”
Grace says:
“Your wrong does not have to own your future.”
Maybe you broke covenant.
Maybe covenant was broken against you.
Maybe you were Leah, begging someone to love you.
Maybe you were Rachel, consumed by what somebody else had.
Maybe you were Hagar, caught in somebody else’s bad decision.
Maybe you were Hannah, tormented in the place where you were already hurting.
Maybe you were David, blessed beyond measure and still capable of catastrophic choices.
Maybe you were Solomon, knowing better while slowly drifting anyway.
There is room at the cross for every one of those people.
But nobody comes to the cross carrying a résumé.
We come carrying need.
And Jesus meets sinners there.
This is why the repeated conflict surrounding polygamous families in Scripture matters.
The biblical authors do not give us a simplistic slogan saying that every argument in every such household has one single cause.
Scripture is more sophisticated than that.
Human sin produces jealousy, favoritism, pride, lust, manipulation, cruelty, impatience, and rivalry in many kinds of relationships.

But when marriage itself becomes multiplied, Scripture repeatedly shows those sinful impulses finding additional opportunities for comparison, competition, unequal affection, inheritance tension, and divided loyalty.
Meanwhile, the canonical trajectory keeps pulling us backward to Genesis and forward to Christ.
One man.
One woman.
One flesh.
And ultimately:
One Christ.
One Bride.
One covenant love.
This is not merely an argument about marriage.
It is an invitation to recover covenant in an age addicted to options.
We live in a world terrified of permanence.
Keep another option.
Keep another person in the messages.
Keep the backup relationship.
Keep the secret account.
Keep one foot outside the covenant.
Never surrender completely.
Never become vulnerable enough to belong.
But covenant says:
I am here.
Faithfulness says:
I remain.
And the Gospel says something infinitely greater:
Christ loved His people enough to give Himself for them.
He did not merely speak love.
He bled it.
He carried the cross.
He entered death.
And He rose victorious.
So maybe the deepest question is not:
“Why did biblical polygamous families experience so much conflict?”
Maybe the deeper question is:
Why do human beings keep dividing what God calls into faithfulness?
And even deeper:
What happens when our divided lives finally meet the undivided love of Christ?
Grace happens.
Repentance happens.
Forgiveness happens.
Restoration begins.
Jesus starts rewriting what sin tried to make permanent.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
We want people rooted in Scripture.
Convicted where conviction is necessary.
Comforted where wounds are bleeding.
Corrected where culture has distorted truth.
And continually brought back to Jesus Christ.
If this article exposed a divided place in your own heart, do not hide behind religious language.
Be honest before God.
And if you are willing, be honest with this community.
There may be another believer reading your three words tonight who realizes they are not the only person fighting.
Come back to it when divided loyalty starts disguising itself as harmless compromise.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works.

But if Gospel Warrior is helping you know Christ, understand Scripture, confront sin, and grow in truth, supporting and sharing this ministry can be one practical way you help put Christ-centered biblical teaching in front of people who may never walk through a church door.

If your desire is to glorify God, glorify Him first through faith, obedience, holiness, love, generosity, and faithfulness to Christ. And when you find Gospel-centered work worth supporting, helping that work reach others can become part of that stewardship.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend quietly losing faith.
Invite the believer who has become spiritually numb.
Invite the person who does not believe yet.
Invite the Christian who is hungry for something deeper than motivational Christianity.
But remember what matters most.
Not the merchandise.
Not the algorithm.
Not the page.
Jesus.
If this ministry ever becomes bigger in your heart than the Christ it exists to proclaim, we have failed.
The goal is not merely another follower.
It is another person following Jesus.
The goal is not merely another comment.
It is confession becoming repentance.
The goal is not merely another share.
It is truth reaching another wounded human being.
It is another disciple being nourished, sharpened, encouraged, corrected, and continually pointed toward Christ.
So share this if it carries truth worth carrying.
Follow if you want to stay close to Scripture-centered truth.
But above everything...
follow Jesus.
Because Abraham could not engineer the promise.
Jacob could not manufacture peace through divided affection.
David could not escape the consequences of compromise.
Solomon could not outthink disobedience.
And none of us can save ourselves.
Only Christ can.
The Bible contains scandal because humanity contains scandal.
But Scripture does not end with our scandal.
It moves toward a cross.
An empty tomb.
A risen King.
A Bride being made ready.
