“Could I find someone more attractive?”
ask:
“What would happen if I invested that energy into becoming intimate with my spouse again?”
Instead of scrolling through bodies engineered to awaken dissatisfaction, put the phone down.
Look across the room.
There is a human being there.
Not an algorithm.
Not pornography.
Not a fantasy.
Not a profile picture.
A human being.
Perhaps wounded.
Perhaps imperfect.
Perhaps aging.
Perhaps difficult.
Perhaps lonely.
Perhaps waiting to know whether the person who once promised “for better or worse” still means it when “worse” becomes ordinary Tuesday night.
And maybe your spouse needs to hear something they have not heard from you in a painfully long time:
“I still choose us.”
Not because feelings never matter.
But because feelings were never meant to be your lord.
Jesus is.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't turn the conviction into shame and disappear.
Bring it into the light.

And if sharing those words publicly would put you in danger or expose private circumstances that should remain confidential, you do not owe the internet your private pain. Bring it to God and to trustworthy people who can actually walk beside you.
But don't keep this article only for yourself.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be sitting beside their spouse tonight asking the exact question they are ashamed to say aloud.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God. It does not.

But if this ministry is helping people encounter biblical truth, supporting and sharing Gospel-centered work can become one voluntary way of participating in getting that truth in front of someone who needs it.
Send it privately to someone who needs grace more than public attention.
It cannot purchase blessing.
It cannot prove your faith.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.

But financially supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one practical expression of generosity when it is given freely, wisely, and cheerfully. Your support helps us keep creating and sharing Christ-centered resources intended to call people toward repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through the Gospel.
Come back to Jesus.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you have wandered, return.
If you have wounded your spouse, seek forgiveness.
If you have been wounded, seek wise help and bring the wound into the light.
If your marriage is dry, don't immediately assume dry means dead.
If attraction has faded, don't automatically translate that feeling into a verdict that God gave you the wrong person.
You may be staring at the end of one kind of love…
only to discover that Christ is teaching you a deeper one.
Because someday, if God gives you enough years together, neither of you will look like the people standing in your wedding photographs.
Your hands may shake.
Your hair may thin.
Your faces may carry lines.
Your bodies may become fragile.
And perhaps one day one of you will sit beside a hospital bed holding the hand of the person who no longer resembles the young man or woman you married.
At that moment, beauty may look entirely different.
Beauty may be fifty years of forgiveness.
Beauty may be staying.
Beauty may be repentance after failure.
Beauty may be learning how to laugh again after almost losing everything.
Beauty may be wrinkled hands still reaching for each other.
Beauty may be two sinners who discovered that marriage was never about finding somebody perfect enough to worship.
It was about two imperfect people continually needing the perfect Savior.
And maybe that is the answer to the question you were afraid to ask.
“What if I married someone I'm no longer attracted to?”
Then don't worship attraction.
Tell the truth.
Guard your heart.
Deal honestly with what has damaged desire.
Seek wise help.
Reject fantasy.
Pursue intimacy.
Practice tenderness.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where biblical forgiveness is possible.
Remember your covenant.
And above everything else…
look to Christ.
Because the deepest hope for your marriage is not that your spouse somehow becomes twenty-five again.
It is that both of you become more like Jesus.

You may no longer recognize the people in your wedding photograph—but by the grace of Christ, you may someday discover that what grew between you became more beautiful than what first drew you together.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: When Romantic Desire Becomes the Center of Your Entire Future
paragraphs: When Romantic Desire Becomes the Center of Your Entire Future

The relationship you keep asking God to give you may not be the deepest thing your heart is actually asking for—and sometimes the most dangerous idol is not something evil, but something beautiful you have asked to do what only Jesus can do.
There is a version of your future that you may have rehearsed so many times it almost feels like a memory.
Someone finally chooses you.
Not temporarily. Not ambiguously. Not with mixed signals and disappearing messages. They choose you clearly.

There is a wedding. A home. Maybe children. Morning coffee beside someone who stayed. Someone notices when you are quiet. Someone reaches for your hand without being asked. Someone knows the wounds behind your jokes and does not leave when they see them.
And somewhere inside that picture is a sentence you may never say aloud:
Then I will finally be okay.
That sentence is where we need to stop.
Because wanting marriage is not the problem.
Wanting companionship is not the problem.

Wanting to be known, desired, held, pursued, and loved is not automatically sinful. Scripture does not require Christians to become emotionally numb before they become spiritually mature. Marriage is God's creation, not Satan's invention. Scripture can describe the finding of a wife as receiving something good from the Lord (Proverbs 18:22), and the Bible can celebrate marital desire without embarrassment.
So this is not an article telling you to stop wanting love.
It is asking something much more uncomfortable:
What happens when romantic love stops being one beautiful possibility within your future and becomes the thing that gives your entire future permission to matter?
Because you can desire marriage...
and quietly worship what you imagine marriage will give you.
You can pray for a spouse...
and slowly make a spouse your functional savior.
You can say, “God, I trust You,” while internally adding, as long as Your plan eventually includes the person I want.
And that is where a beautiful desire can become a brutal master.
Maybe you know exactly what that feels like.
Another engagement announcement appears on your screen.
You smile.
You tap the heart.
“Congratulations!”
And you mean it.
Mostly.
Then something aches.
You put the phone down, and suddenly your room feels quieter than it did thirty seconds ago.
Another person found someone.
Another wedding.
Another anniversary.
Another pregnancy announcement.
Another smiling photograph beneath words about answered prayers.
And somewhere beneath your genuine happiness for them comes the question you are almost ashamed to ask:
Jesus... what about me?
You have prayed.
You have tried to surrender.
You have deleted the app and downloaded it again.
You have promised yourself you would stop checking their profile.
You have wondered whether you were too picky, not attractive enough, too damaged, too late, too intimidating, too ordinary, too spiritual, not spiritual enough.
Maybe somebody left.
Maybe somebody almost chose you.
Maybe the person you imagined standing beside you in your future is now standing beside somebody else.
That kind of grief is real.
God does not need you to pretend it isn't.
But pain becomes spiritually dangerous when disappointment begins rewriting your theology.
If God loved me, He would give me this.
If I were enough, someone would have chosen me.
If I remain single, my life will somehow be less complete.
Once I find the right person, then my real life can begin.
Read that last sentence again.
Because there is a graveyard filled with years that people accidentally buried beneath the word someday.
Someday, when I'm married.
Someday, when someone chooses me.
Someday, when I have the family.
Someday, when I am finally wanted.
Someday...
I will live.
But Jesus never told you to postpone obedience until romance arrives.
He never said, “Seek first a relationship, and when you finally feel secure enough, pursue My kingdom.”
He said:
ζητεῖτε δὲ πρῶτον τὴν βασιλείαν... καὶ τὴν δικαιοσύνην αὐτοῦ
Zēteite de prōton tēn basileian... kai tēn dikaiosynēn autou.
“Seek first His kingdom and His righteousness...” (Matthew 6:33).
The Greek matters.
ζητεῖτε — zēteite — “seek.”
Not casually notice.
Not occasionally remember.
Seek.
Pursue.
Make this the governing direction of your life.
And then comes the word that exposes us:
πρῶτον — prōton — “first.”
First.

Jesus is talking in context about anxiety over life's necessities, not specifically giving a teaching about dating. We should not rip His words from their setting and pretend Matthew 6:33 is secretly a romance verse. But the kingdom priority He commands reaches straight into this struggle: the Father's kingdom and righteousness belong at the center, while everything else must take its rightful place beneath Him.
Not first until someone attractive notices you.
Not first until you turn thirty.
Not first because God will reward you with a spouse.
First.
Period.
And perhaps that exposes something.
Some of us have turned Christianity into a transaction without realizing it.
God, I stayed pure. Where is my spouse?
God, I prayed. Where is my spouse?
God, I stopped dating the wrong people. Where is my spouse?
God, I served You. Where is my spouse?
As though obedience were currency placed into a heavenly vending machine and marriage were the product we were promised.
But Jesus is not a strategy for getting the life you really want.
Jesus is the treasure.
That changes everything.
Because if Jesus is merely the bridge between you and your dream life, then your dream life—not Jesus—is actually sitting on the throne.
And idols are cruel.
Especially beautiful idols.
An idol does not have to look demonic.
Sometimes an idol wears a wedding dress.
Sometimes it has the face of the person who left you.
Sometimes it is the imaginary husband you have not met.
Sometimes it is the imaginary wife you believe will heal your loneliness.
Sometimes it is the family photograph you desperately want to take five years from now.
The problem is not that those things are ugly.
The problem is that they are not God.
And whatever you ask to carry the weight of God will eventually collapse underneath you.
Marriage cannot bear the weight of your identity.
A husband cannot carry the responsibility of proving your worth.
A wife cannot become your permanent source of peace.
Romance cannot cleanse your guilt.
Sex cannot reconcile you to God.
Being desired cannot erase your sin.
A wedding ring cannot resurrect your soul.
Only Christ can.
And perhaps that is why this hurts so much.
Because sometimes God is not merely confronting what we want.
He is revealing what we expected that desire to save us from.
Maybe you do not simply want marriage.
Maybe you want marriage to prove you are lovable.
Maybe you want someone attractive to choose you because rejection convinced you that your value must be externally verified.
Maybe you want a relationship because silence feels unbearable.
Maybe you want a spouse because you are frightened that nobody will be there when you grow old.
Maybe romance has become your imagined escape from insecurity, sexual temptation, family dysfunction, loneliness, boredom, shame, or the terrifying possibility of being forgotten.
And then Jesus comes near—not to mock the desire, but to ask for the throne beneath it.
This is where surrender becomes painful.
Because surrender does not mean pretending you no longer care.
Surrender sounds more like:
Jesus, I still want this.
I still hope for marriage.
I still feel lonely sometimes.
I still wonder whom I might meet.
I still want to love someone deeply and be loved faithfully.
But You may not have to give me my preferred future in order to remain good.
That sentence can cost tears.
Because surrender is not telling God that your desire is meaningless.
It is telling your desire that God is greater.
Paul speaks into this with words modern Christian culture sometimes struggles to hear.
In 1 Corinthians 7:32, the Greek text begins:
Θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀμερίμνους εἶναι. ὁ ἄγαμος μεριμνᾷ τὰ τοῦ κυρίου...
Thelō de hymas amerimnous einai. Ho agamos merimna ta tou Kyriou...

Paul's concern is that believers be free from distracting concern, and he describes the unmarried person as able to concern himself with “the things of the Lord”—with how to please the Lord. He later explains that his aim is not to put a restraint upon believers, but to promote devotion to the Lord without distraction.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not describe singleness as God's waiting room.
He does not speak as though unmarried Christians are unfinished humans waiting for their “real” lives to arrive.
And in the same chapter, Paul does not condemn marriage. He explicitly allows and honors marriage while also showing that marriage brings legitimate earthly responsibilities.
That destroys two errors at once.
Marriage is not inferior spirituality.
Singleness is not inferior humanity.
Your marital status is not the measurement of your completeness in Christ.
This matters because Christian culture can accidentally communicate something Scripture does not.
We ask single adults, “So, are you seeing anyone?”
Again.
And again.
And again.
As if this were the primary plotline of their existence.
We celebrate engagements loudly and sometimes barely notice years of quiet faithfulness.
We can make twenty-three-year-olds panic because they have not “found someone.”
We can make thirty-five-year-olds feel as though something went wrong.
We can make divorced people feel permanently branded.
We can make widows and widowers feel as though the greatest chapter of their lives has already closed.
But the Gospel tells a radically different story.
The most complete human being who ever walked this earth was unmarried.
Jesus Christ did not need romantic love to validate His humanity.
He did not need marriage to make His life meaningful.
He did not need another human being to complete Him.
And yet He knew love more deeply than we can comprehend.
He knew friendship.
He knew betrayal.
He knew affection.
He knew grief.
He knew rejection.
He knew what it was to have people leave.
He knew what it was to love people who would fail Him.
Then He went to a cross.
And there, Jesus answered a question deeper than:
Will anybody ever choose me romantically?
He answered:
Can someone like me ever be reconciled to God?
Yes.
But not cheaply.
At Calvary, the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Your greatest problem was never singleness.
It was sin.
Your deepest need was never a soulmate.
It was reconciliation with the holy God you had sinned against.
And your greatest rescue is not somebody finally saying, “I choose you.”
It is Christ crucified and risen, calling sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
That is where romantic idolatry begins losing its grip.
Not when you convince yourself relationships are unnecessary.
But when something infinitely greater fills the center.
Jesus.
Jesus when the messages stop.
Jesus when everybody around you seems to be getting married.
Jesus when someone rejects you.
Jesus when desire burns and obedience hurts.
Jesus when you are forty and the story did not unfold according to the timeline you wrote at twenty-two.
Jesus if marriage comes.
Jesus if marriage does not come soon.
Jesus if your heart gets broken.
Jesus if God rebuilds it.
Jesus in the longing.
Jesus above the longing.
Jesus at the center.
And if God gives you marriage someday, this surrender will not make you love your spouse less.
It may finally teach you how to love them properly.
Because when another human being no longer has to be your god, they are finally free to be human.
They can disappoint you without destroying your identity.
They can have weaknesses without collapsing your universe.
They can fail to read your mind.
They can have difficult days.
They can grow old.
They can need forgiveness.
They can need grace.
And you can love them not as your savior...
but as your neighbor, your covenant companion, and—if both of you belong to Christ—a fellow redeemed sinner walking toward Jesus.
That kind of love is freer.
Healthier.
Holier.
Because two people desperately demanding, Complete me, will eventually exhaust each other.
But two people learning to say, Christ is Lord; let us follow Him together, have discovered a foundation deeper than romance.
So perhaps the question is not merely:
Do you want to get married?
The better question is:
What have you made marriage mean?
Does it mean you finally matter?
Does it mean you finally won?
Does it mean you are finally attractive enough?
Does it mean God finally proved He loves you?
Does it mean your life finally begins?
Does it mean the loneliness finally disappears forever?
If so, do not merely ask God for the relationship.
Ask Him to expose the altar.
Because there may be something underneath your romantic desire that needs to die before it destroys your ability to love.
And that is not cruelty.
That is grace.
Grace sometimes feels like God pulling your fingers away from something you were clutching so tightly that you could no longer receive Him with open hands.
Maybe you have already compromised because romance became too important.
You ignored convictions.
You accepted breadcrumbs.
You stayed in a relationship you knew was dragging you from Christ.
You crossed sexual boundaries and then learned to rename conviction as “being too religious.”
You tolerated manipulation because being mistreated seemed less frightening than being alone.
You kept returning to someone God was using circumstances and wisdom to remove from your life.
You became emotionally dependent on attention.
You flirted because silence made you feel invisible.
You entertained people you knew you should not build a future with because at least somebody wanted you.
Maybe you know exactly where you compromised.
Then hear this carefully:
The Gospel does not say, “You ruined everything.”
The Gospel says there is forgiveness for sinners who come to Christ.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the One whose mercy is greater than your scandal.
Peter denied Jesus.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left with which to impress God.
The Samaritan woman in John 4 carried a complicated relational history into a conversation with Jesus.
Again and again, Scripture refuses to let human failure write the final sentence when grace enters the story.
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes Christ glorious.
Maybe your romantic history is messy.
Maybe you gave yourself to someone who promised forever and disappeared.
Maybe you became someone you barely recognized just to keep another person interested.
Maybe you have regrets you cannot undo.
Maybe you are reading this while secretly involved with someone you know is pulling your heart farther from Christ.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Not tomorrow.
Not after one final conversation.
Not after one final night.
Jesus did not shed His blood so you could decorate your chains with Christian vocabulary.
He came to save.
And grace does not merely forgive the person you were.
Grace begins transforming the person you are becoming.
You are not required to drag yesterday's scandal into tomorrow as your identity.
At the cross, guilty people meet a Savior whose mercy is stronger than their worst chapter.
This is why we keep returning to these words:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin righteousness.
Not by giving everybody the romantic ending they requested.
He rewrites everything by redeeming sinners.
By forgiving.
By cleansing.
By restoring.
By becoming the center again.
Maybe God will bring someone into your life.
Maybe one day you will look across a room and realize that an ordinary conversation became the beginning of something extraordinary.
Maybe there will be vows.
Maybe there will be children.
Maybe there will be decades together.
If God gives you that gift, receive it with gratitude.
But do not worship it.
And do not build your theology around the assumption that God owes it to you.
Scripture gives Christians hope in Christ; it does not give every believer an individual guarantee of marriage.
That distinction matters.
Because false promises create unnecessary spiritual wreckage.
“Just wait—God has someone for you” sounds comforting.
But unless God has specifically revealed something, we should not promise what Scripture does not promise.
What we can promise is infinitely stronger.
Christ is enough to obey today.
Christ will not become less glorious if your timeline changes.
Christ will not cease being Lord because somebody left.
Christ's cross will not become less sufficient because you are sleeping alone tonight.
Christ's resurrection does not depend upon your relationship status.
And if you belong to Him, your future is ultimately not moving toward a wedding altar on earth.
It is moving toward Christ.
So dream.
Hope.
Pray for marriage if that desire is in you.
Meet people.
Seek wise counsel.
Become emotionally mature.
Learn how to communicate.
Heal where you need healing.
Reject pornography.
Practice sexual holiness.
Develop friendships.
Serve your church.
Build a meaningful life.
Learn generosity.
Become someone capable of covenant faithfulness.
But please...
do not wait to become alive.
You are alive now.
There are people you can love now.
There are lonely people you can notice now.
There are prayers you can pray now.
There is Scripture you can learn now.
There are wounds Christ can address now.
There is holiness to pursue now.
There is Gospel work to do now.
There are people walking toward eternity who need to hear about Jesus now.
Do not sacrifice the life God actually gave you on the altar of the life you imagined He would give you.
And maybe that is the sentence you needed tonight.
Not “stop wanting marriage.”
Not “someone will definitely come.”
But:
Stop making your future wait for a human being before you give it completely to Jesus.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, be honest.
And if Christ has already carried you through heartbreak, comment your testimony. Somebody scrolling through those comments may need proof that heartbreak did not get the final word.
God is glorified by faith, obedience, generosity, love, and lives surrendered to Christ.

Invite your family. Invite the friend who is struggling. Invite the believer who feels spiritually cold. Invite the seeker with difficult questions. Even invite the unbeliever who is willing to listen.
Come back to Jesus.
If romance has become your god, repent.
If rejection became your identity, bring it to Christ.
If loneliness made you compromise, come into the light.
If shame tells you that you are too dirty to return, look again at the cross.
If your imagined future has become more precious than the One who holds your future, open your hands.
You may still desire the wedding.
You may still pray for the person.
You may still cry when the room gets quiet.
Faith does not require pretending.
It requires knowing where to bring the ache.
Bring it to Jesus.
Because one day, whether your earthly story contains the romance you imagined or takes a road you never expected, the deepest question will never have been:
Did somebody finally choose me?
The deepest question is:
Did I belong to Christ?
And if you are His, then your life is not an unfinished love story desperately waiting for another human character to arrive.
Your story already has a center.
His name is Jesus.
Never let the absence of a human hand make you forget the nail-scarred hands that already reached for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU’VE QUOTED “LEAN NOT ON YOUR OWN UNDERSTANDING” — BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN MISSING THE MOST IMPORTANT PART?
paragraphs:
YOU’VE QUOTED “LEAN NOT ON YOUR OWN UNDERSTANDING” — BUT WHAT IF YOU’VE BEEN MISSING THE MOST IMPORTANT PART?
Proverbs 3:5–6 Is Not Telling You to Stop Thinking. It Is Calling You to Stop Treating Your Limited Understanding as if It Were God.
There are moments when trusting God sounds beautiful.
And then there are moments when trusting God feels terrifying.
When the prayer is answered, the door opens, the diagnosis is good, the relationship survives, the money arrives, and everything seems to be falling into place, it is easy to say, “God, I trust You.”
But what happens when heaven seems silent?
What happens when you prayed…and the person still left?
When you obeyed…and things became harder?
When you tried to do what was right…and watched someone dishonest get ahead?
When you begged God to restore something…and instead He allowed it to end?
What happens when the God you believe is good allows a chapter you cannot understand?
That is where Proverbs 3:5–6 stops being a decorative Bible verse and becomes a battlefield.
Because perhaps the hardest place to trust God is not when you have nothing.
It is when you have enough information to create your own explanation…but not enough information to know whether your explanation is true.
And somewhere in that painful distance between what God knows and what you can see, Scripture says:
“Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding.
In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.”
—Proverbs 3:5–6, KJV
Read it again.
Slowly.
Because these words do not tell you to become irrational.
They do not command Christians to reject knowledge.
They do not mean you should ignore wise counsel, refuse medical advice, avoid planning, dismiss evidence, or make reckless decisions and call it “faith.”
In fact, Proverbs repeatedly praises wisdom, knowledge, understanding, instruction, prudence, and discernment.
So when Scripture says, “lean not unto thine own understanding,” it cannot mean, “Stop using the mind God gave you.”
Something much deeper is happening.
And the original Hebrew makes it difficult to miss.
Proverbs 3:5 begins:
בְּטַח אֶל־יְהוָה בְּכָל־לִבֶּךָ
Bəṭaḥ el-YHWH bəḵāl-libbeḵā.
“Trust in the LORD with all your heart.”
That opening word, בְּטַח (bəṭaḥ), comes from the Hebrew verb בָּטַח (bāṭaḥ), carrying the idea of trusting, being confident, placing one’s security in something.
Then comes the contrast:
וְאֶל־בִּינָתְךָ אַל־תִּשָּׁעֵן
Wə’el-bînāṯəḵā ’al-tiššāʿên.
“And do not lean on your own understanding.”
The verb behind “lean,” שָׁעַן (shāʿan), means to lean upon, support oneself upon, or rely upon.
That changes the picture.
God is not saying:
“Do not have understanding.”
He is saying:
“Do not make your understanding the thing holding you up.”
There is an enormous difference.
Imagine someone leaning their entire weight against a wall.
If the wall fails, they fall with it.
That is the image hiding inside this famous verse.
Your understanding may be useful.
Your reasoning may be valuable.
Your experience may teach you something.
Your plans may even be wise.
But none of them were designed to carry the full weight of your soul.
Only God can do that.
And this is where the verse becomes painfully personal.
Because many of us say we trust God while secretly leaning against something else.
We lean on money.
We lean on relationships.
We lean on careers.
We lean on our ability to control outcomes.
We lean on our reputation.
We lean on our intelligence.
We lean on our plans.
We lean on what somebody promised us.
And sometimes we even lean on our interpretation of what God “must” be doing.
Then one of those supports moves.
And suddenly we discover what we were really trusting.
Sometimes the collapse is not evidence that God abandoned you.
Sometimes the collapse reveals that something other than God had quietly become your wall.
That hurts.
Because there are seasons when you can love Jesus sincerely and still find yourself asking:
“Lord…why?”
Why this person?
Why this loss?
Why this delay?
Why this closed door?
Why did You let me hope for it?
Why did You allow me to get this far only for everything to change?
Why does obedience sometimes hurt more than compromise seemed to?
And perhaps you have felt ashamed for asking.
But Scripture is filled with people bringing painful questions before God.
The danger is not simply having questions.
The danger begins when our unanswered questions become evidence in a courtroom where we place God on trial and appoint our limited perspective as judge.
That is what Proverbs confronts.
The Hebrew word translated “understanding” is בִּינָה (bînāh), a word associated with understanding and discernment.
Again, Proverbs does not despise bînāh. It celebrates understanding elsewhere.
The warning is against your own understanding becoming ultimate.
Because human understanding has a horizon.
God's does not.
You see the moment.
God sees the entire road.
You see what disappeared.
God sees what would have happened if it stayed.
You see the door that closed.
God sees what was behind it.
You see the prayer that seems unanswered.
God sees yesterday, today, tomorrow, every consequence, every hidden motive, every unseen danger, every person involved, and every thread of providence simultaneously.
You are looking at one frame.
God sees the entire film.
And one frame can look like tragedy while the finished story reveals redemption.
Joseph knew something about that.
Imagine being betrayed by your own brothers.
Sold.
Taken from home.
Falsely accused.
Imprisoned.
Forgotten.
If Joseph had interpreted God solely through the circumstances surrounding him, what conclusion would have seemed reasonable?
“God has forgotten me.”
But God had not forgotten Joseph.
The pit was not the end of the story.
The prison was not the end of the story.
The betrayal was not the end of the story.
Years later Joseph could look at the brothers who had wounded him and say:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good…”
—Genesis 50:20
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not call the brothers’ evil good.
Their sin remained evil.
But their evil did not outrun God's sovereignty.
That matters.
Christian faith does not require pretending that betrayal does not hurt.
It does not require calling abuse good.
It does not require smiling at tragedy and pretending everything feels fine.
Biblical trust looks evil in the face and still declares:
Evil does not get the final sentence.
God does.
The cross proves it.
Think about Calvary.
If you had stood near the cross on Friday without knowing Sunday was coming, what would your understanding have told you?
Jesus is bleeding.
His disciples have scattered.
Judas betrayed Him.
Peter denied Him.
Religious leaders condemned Him.
Rome crucified Him.
The Messiah appears defeated.
Hope appears buried.
The stone rolls over the tomb.
Finished.
At least, that is what human understanding might conclude.
But heaven knew something Friday could not yet see.
The cross that looked like defeat was accomplishing redemption.
The blood that looked like evidence of Rome's victory was the blood of the Lamb poured out for sinners.
The grave that looked like the ending was about to become the scene of resurrection.
This is why Christianity does not ultimately ask you to trust an idea.
It calls you to trust a Person.
Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen Lord.
And that changes Proverbs 3:5–6 for the Christian.
We do not trust God because every circumstance makes sense.
We trust Him because He has revealed His character supremely in Christ.
At Calvary, God did not watch human suffering from an unreachable distance.
The Son of God entered our broken world.
Jesus knew rejection.
Jesus knew betrayal.
Jesus knew grief.
Jesus knew injustice.
Jesus knew agony.
And He willingly bore sin at the cross so guilty people could be reconciled to God.
Our greatest problem was never merely that life confused us.
Our greatest problem was sin.
We did not simply need better circumstances.
We needed reconciliation.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed rescue.
We needed a Savior.
And Jesus came.
He lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He gave Himself for sinners.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the Gospel announces something astonishing:
Your sin does not have to write your ending.
Your shame does not have to name you forever.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Your scandal does not have the last word.
Jesus does.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But notice what comes immediately after “lean not unto thine own understanding.”
בְּכָל־דְּרָכֶיךָ דָעֵהוּ
Bəḵāl-dərāḵeḵā ḏāʿêhū.
“In all your ways acknowledge Him.”
The word translated “acknowledge” comes from יָדַע (yādaʿ)—“to know.”
That is stronger than merely giving God a polite nod before continuing with the life you already planned.
This is not:
“Remember that God exists.”
This is a life oriented toward knowing Him and recognizing Him in all your ways.
Not just Sunday.
Not just church.
Not just your devotional time.
Not just when the worship music is playing.
“In all your ways.”
Your relationship.
Your private messages.
Your browser history.
Your finances.
Your ambitions.
Your sexuality.
Your anger.
Your business.
Your marriage.
Your parenting.
Your loneliness.
Your secret habits.
Your plans.
Your disappointments.
Your future.
Your wounds.
Your dreams.
All your ways.
There are no locked rooms in a surrendered life.
And perhaps that is why this verse can become uncomfortable.
We love:
“He shall direct thy paths.”
But we often want God to direct a path we have refused to surrender.
We want divine guidance without divine authority.
“Lord, show me which relationship to choose.”
But will you obey Him if His Word says neither relationship is honoring Him?
“Lord, bless my business.”
But will you surrender the dishonest practice making the business profitable?
“Lord, restore my marriage.”
But will you repent of the pride poisoning it?
“Lord, give me peace.”
But will you release the sin you keep protecting?
“Lord, guide me.”
But what if His guidance contradicts what you desperately want?
That is where trust becomes worship.
Because surrender means God remains God even when His answer is not the answer you hoped for.
And then comes the promise:
וְהוּא יְיַשֵּׁר אֹרְחֹתֶיךָ
Wəhūʾ yəyaššēr ʾōrəḥōṯeḵā.
“And He will make your paths straight.”
The Hebrew verb יָשַׁר (yāshar) carries the sense of making straight or right.
Notice what God does not promise.
He does not say every path will be painless.
He does not say every path will be short.
He does not say every path will make immediate sense.
He does not say faithful Christians will never experience cancer, grief, betrayal, unemployment, persecution, heartbreak, or unanswered questions.
“Straight” does not mean “comfortable.”
And it certainly does not mean that trusting God guarantees wealth, ease, or every desired outcome.
Look one verse further:
“Be not wise in thine own eyes: fear the LORD, and depart from evil.”
—Proverbs 3:7
There is the context.
“Lean not on your own understanding” is connected to refusing to become wise in your own eyes, fearing the LORD, and turning away from evil.
This is not permission for foolishness.
It is a confrontation with self-sufficiency.
You can study.
You can investigate.
You can ask questions.
You can seek wise counsel.
You can make careful plans.
You can think deeply.
You can consult qualified professionals.
You can weigh evidence.
You can use every ounce of the intelligence God has given you.
And after doing all of that, you still bow.
You say:
“Father, this is what I see.
This is what I understand.
This is what seems wise to me.
But You are God.
I am not.
If my understanding conflicts with Your revealed truth, Your Word wins.
If my desire conflicts with Your will, Your will wins.
If the road ahead makes no sense but obedience requires another step, give me grace to take it.”
That is not intellectual suicide.
That is humility.
And maybe somebody reading this is standing at exactly that place tonight.
You cannot understand what God is doing.
You have replayed the situation a hundred times.
You have prayed.
You have cried.
You have asked friends.
You have searched Scripture.
You have stared into the darkness asking God for one explanation that would make the pain easier to carry.
And you still do not have it.
Maybe the answer you need tonight is not an explanation.
Maybe it is Him.
Because sometimes God gives answers.
Sometimes God gives deliverance.
Sometimes God changes circumstances.
And sometimes, before anything around you changes, He teaches you that His presence is enough to keep walking without seeing the entire road.
Trust is not saying:
“I understand everything.”
Trust is saying:
“I know enough about the One holding me that I do not need to understand everything before I obey Him.”
Perhaps your marriage did not unfold the way you imagined.
Perhaps your child walked away from the faith.
Perhaps the ministry opportunity disappeared.
Perhaps somebody you loved died while you were still praying for healing.
Perhaps the person you trusted betrayed you.
Perhaps you are looking at your life thinking:
“This was not how the story was supposed to go.”
And that sentence may be exactly where Proverbs 3:5 meets you.
Because you have been leaning so hard against your picture of how the story was “supposed” to go that when the picture broke, you thought God had broken His promise.
But God never promised to obey your script.
He promised to be God.
And sometimes grace looks like God refusing to become the supporting character in the story we wrote for ourselves.
Sometimes He closes something we were begging Him to bless.
Sometimes He exposes something we wanted hidden.
Sometimes He allows consequences that finally bring us to repentance.
Sometimes He removes the illusion that we are in control.
And sometimes the collapse we called destruction becomes the place where surrender finally begins.
Peter knew something about scandal.
He promised Jesus loyalty.
Then pressure came.
And Peter denied Him.
Not once.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine hearing the rooster.
Imagine remembering the words of Jesus.
Imagine realizing that the version of yourself you believed in was not as strong as you thought.
Peter had leaned on his own confidence.
It collapsed.
But Jesus was not finished with Peter.
After the resurrection, Christ restored the disciple who had failed Him.
Failure became restoration.
Shame met grace.
The man who denied Christ would later publicly proclaim Him.
That is what Jesus does.
He does not merely improve respectable people.
He redeems sinners.
Maybe your scandal is different.
Nobody knows about it.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe it happened years ago and you still hear it accusing you.
Maybe you caused the wreckage.
Maybe somebody else did.
Maybe you cannot change what happened.
But hear this carefully:
The Gospel does not promise you the power to rewrite history.
It gives you something better.
A Redeemer who can transform what your history means for your future.
Repentance does not erase earthly consequences.
Grace does not call sin harmless.
Forgiveness does not make evil imaginary.
But because of Christ, sin does not have to remain your master, shame does not have to remain your identity, and condemnation does not have to remain your destiny.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
—Romans 8:1
So maybe “lean not on your own understanding” needs to become more than something printed on your wall.
Maybe tonight it becomes your confession.
“Jesus, I have been leaning on myself.”
“I have trusted my plans more than Your wisdom.”
“I have demanded explanations before obedience.”
“I have called You unfaithful because You did not follow the future I imagined.”
“I have been wise in my own eyes.”
“I have wanted Your direction without surrendering my ways.”
“I have tried to control what belongs to You.”
And perhaps the most honest prayer you can pray is simply:
“Lord, I don't understand.
But I surrender.”
Not because pain is good.
Not because confusion is holy.
Not because Christians should stop thinking.
But because Jesus Christ is more trustworthy than your ability to see the ending.
And if you have never surrendered your life to Christ, do not confuse Christianity with merely trying to become more positive, spiritual, disciplined, or religious.
You need more than inspirational advice.
You need forgiveness.
Turn from sin.
Come to Christ.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
Bring Him the guilt.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the life you cannot repair.
You may have written pages you are ashamed to read again.
But Jesus is still the Redeemer.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Be honest.
No performance.
No pretending.
Sometimes three honest words are the beginning of coming out of hiding.
And somewhere on your Facebook friends list is probably someone quietly fighting a battle you know nothing about.

Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it does not. We are saved by grace through faith, not by social-media activity—but because proclaiming and passing on biblical truth can be one practical way of serving others and glorifying God.
Send it to the person grieving.
Send it to the believer questioning God's direction.
Send it to the prodigal.
Send it to the exhausted Christian.

Send it even to the person who does not yet believe but needs to know that Christianity is not built upon pretending suffering does not exist. It is built around a crucified and risen Savior who entered suffering and conquered sin and death.
There may come a night when Proverbs 3:5–6 no longer feels like a verse you are studying.
It may become the verse you are surviving.
Supporting Gospel ministry is not a substitute for worship, generosity to your local church, caring for your family, or helping people in need.

But if God has used this ministry to strengthen you, supporting the work can be one voluntary and practical way to help that same truth reach another exhausted believer, another searching soul, another person scrolling alone at midnight wondering whether God has forgotten them.
But above everything else…
Trust Christ.
Because one day you may look backward at the road that makes no sense to you tonight.
You may finally see dangers from which God protected you.
You may understand why certain doors could not remain open.
You may recognize how suffering stripped away idols you did not know you had.
You may see how God used tears you thought were wasted.
Or perhaps some questions will remain unanswered in this life.
Christian hope does not depend upon receiving every explanation before we die.
It rests upon Jesus Christ.
The One who entered the grave and walked out.
The One who takes sinners and calls them forgiven.
The One who takes rebels and makes them children.
The One who takes shame and meets it with grace.
The One who takes graves and promises resurrection.
So when you cannot trace His hand…
when the road disappears into darkness…
when your understanding reaches its limit…
when everything inside you wants an explanation before taking another step…
remember:
Your understanding was never meant to carry the weight of your soul.
Jesus was.
And sometimes the chapter you cannot understand is the very chapter in which you discover whom you truly trust.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: FLIRTING WITH WHAT CAN DESTROY YOU
paragraphs:
FLIRTING WITH WHAT CAN DESTROY YOU
You keep calling it harmless because it hasn’t destroyed you yet. But some things don’t enter your life like an executioner. They enter like a conversation.
There is a terrifying distance between the moment something first catches your eye and the moment it finally owns your heart.
And most people never notice themselves crossing it.
Nobody wakes up one morning and calmly announces, “Today I’m going to wreck my marriage.”
Nobody plans to become addicted.
Nobody dreams of becoming spiritually cold.
Nobody deliberately schedules the night they will betray someone who trusted them.
Nobody who once trembled at the presence of God imagines becoming the person who can sin without trembling anymore.
Usually, destruction begins much quieter than that.
A glance.
A message.
A private search.
A little resentment you keep feeding.
A conversation you know you should end.
A fantasy you keep revisiting.
A relationship you refuse to surrender.
A compromise nobody knows about.
A secret account.
A hidden appetite.
A second look.
A justification.
A sentence whispered inside your own mind:
“It’s not that serious.”
And perhaps that is why this article found you.
Not because you have already fallen off the cliff.
Maybe you are simply standing dangerously close to the edge...
telling yourself you are only enjoying the view.
Please keep reading.
Because the most dangerous thing in your life may not be the sin you hate.
It may be the sin you are slowly learning to tolerate.
Scripture gives us one of the clearest descriptions of this progression in the letter of James.
“ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος.”
James 1:14.
The language is uncomfortable because it is supposed to be.
The Greek word often translated “desire” is ἐπιθυμία — epithymia. Depending on context, it can refer to desire, craving, or lust. James is describing desire operating in a corrupted direction.
Then comes δελεαζόμενος — deleazomenos.
It carries the imagery of being enticed, lured, baited.
Think about that.
Bait never advertises the hook.
The fish sees the meal.
The fisherman sees the death hidden inside it.
That is how temptation works.
Satan does not need to convince you that destruction is beautiful.
He only needs to make the bait beautiful enough that you stop thinking about the hook.
James continues:
“εἶτα ἡ ἐπιθυμία συλλαβοῦσα τίκτει ἁμαρτίαν, ἡ δὲ ἁμαρτία ἀποτελεσθεῖσα ἀποκύει θάνατον.”
“Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death.”
James 1:15.
Notice the progression.
Desire.
Enticement.
Conception.
Sin.
Growth.
Death.
Death rarely introduces itself as death.
Sometimes it introduces itself as relief.
Sometimes as romance.
Sometimes as curiosity.
Sometimes as “I deserve this.”
Sometimes as “Nobody will ever know.”
Sometimes as “Just one more time.”
Sometimes as a person who makes you feel understood while slowly pulling you away from everything God has told you is holy.
Sometimes it looks like pornography behind a locked door.
Sometimes it is emotional intimacy with someone who is not your spouse.
Sometimes it is money you know you obtained dishonestly.
Sometimes it is bitterness you have rehearsed so many times that hatred now feels like justice.
Sometimes it is alcohol, gambling, approval, status, revenge, attention, lust, pride, envy, or an obsession you would rather defend than surrender.
And sometimes it looks completely respectable.
That is the frightening part.
Not every idol is ugly.
Some idols are beautiful enough to make you argue with God.
Go back to Eden.
Genesis tells us that the woman saw that the forbidden tree was “good for food,” “pleasant to the eyes,” and desirable for gaining wisdom.
The forbidden thing looked desirable before its consequences became visible.
That pattern has never really changed.
The serpent still sells rebellion by showing you what you might gain while hiding what disobedience will cost.
And maybe you know exactly what that feels like.
There is something you have been circling.
Something your conscience has already confronted.
Something you keep asking God to bless when deep inside you know He has been asking you to release it.
You have deleted it...
then downloaded it again.
Blocked them...
then unblocked them.
Repented...
then returned.
Cried...
then repeated it.
Promised God you were finished...
then found yourself standing at the same door.
And now shame is whispering something even more dangerous:
“You might as well stop fighting.”
No.
That voice is lying to you.
But you also need to hear something Christianity sometimes explains poorly.
Being tempted does not mean you have already sinned.
Jesus Himself was tempted.
Hebrews 4:15 says that Christ was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin.
Temptation is not proof that Christ has abandoned you.
A thought arriving at the door is not the same thing as inviting it inside, feeding it dinner, making it comfortable, and handing it a key.
The battle becomes dangerous when we stop resisting and begin negotiating.
That is where many of us get trapped.
We want to know exactly how close we can get without technically crossing the line.
“How far is too far?”
“How much can I watch?”
“How much can I drink?”
“How flirtatious is too flirtatious?”
“How emotionally involved can I become?”
“How long can I entertain this fantasy?”
“How much compromise can I keep while still calling myself faithful?”
But love asks a different question.
Not:
“How close can I get to sin?”
But:
“How close can I stay to Christ?”
Joseph understood this.
When Potiphar’s wife repeatedly attempted to seduce him, Joseph did not begin a theology seminar in the bedroom.
He ran.
Genesis 39:12 says he left his garment in her hand and fled.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is run.
Not analyze.
Not negotiate.
Not prove how strong you are.
Run.
Block the number.
End the conversation.
Cancel the meeting.
Leave the room.
Delete the account.
Install the accountability software.
Tell your spouse the truth.
Call the mature believer you trust.
Confess what secrecy has been protecting.
Stop returning to the environment where you repeatedly collapse.
Jesus used deliberately severe imagery when speaking about sin in Matthew 5:29–30, describing the radical removal of what causes a person to stumble.
He was not commanding self-mutilation.
He was teaching the seriousness with which His disciples should deal with sin.
We tend to pet what Jesus tells us to put to death.
We rename it.
Manage it.
Excuse it.
Hide it.
Christianize it.
And sometimes we even pray about something God has already told us to flee.
Paul’s instruction is wonderfully uncomplicated:
“φεῦγε δὲ τὰς νεωτερικὰς ἐπιθυμίας.”
“Flee youthful passions.”
2 Timothy 2:22.
The Greek imperative φεῦγε — pheuge — means flee.
Get away.
Escape.
Do not stand there admiring your ability to resist the fire while your clothes begin smelling like smoke.
But Paul does not merely say what to flee.
He says what to pursue:
“δίωκε δὲ δικαιοσύνην πίστιν ἀγάπην εἰρήνην...”
“Pursue righteousness, faith, love, peace...”
Christian holiness is not merely running away from something.
It is running toward Someone.
Jesus Christ.
That distinction matters.
Because if Christianity becomes nothing more than “stop doing bad things,” eventually your exhausted willpower will collapse.
You need something greater than prohibition.
You need affection.
You need to see Christ as more beautiful than the thing trying to replace Him.
Sin says:
“I can satisfy you.”
Jesus says:
“I am the bread of life.”
Sin says:
“I can quench you.”
Jesus says:
“If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.”
Sin says:
“I can make you free.”
Jesus says:
“If the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.”
Sin offers anesthesia.
Christ offers resurrection.
Sin gives moments and takes years.
Christ can take shattered years and redeem them for eternity.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because perhaps while reading this, you have not been thinking about something you are merely flirting with.
Maybe you are thinking about something that has already devastated you.
Maybe the affair already happened.
Maybe the addiction has lasted years.
Maybe your family already discovered the secret.
Maybe you have already lied.
Already crossed the boundary.
Already broken the promise.
Already returned to the screen.
Already compromised your body.
Already betrayed someone.
Already become someone your younger self would hardly recognize.
And now you are reading an article about fleeing temptation while thinking:
“Too late.”
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is for people for whom “too late” appears to have become their biography.
The Bible does not give us a Savior who only rescues people before their scandal.
It gives us a Savior who walks directly into the wreckage.
David committed adultery and arranged the death of Uriah.
Peter denied Jesus.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
The Corinthian church contained people whose former lives included serious sexual and moral sin.
Paul himself had persecuted the church.
Scripture does not sanitize human failure.
But neither does Scripture permit human failure to have the final word.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:11:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
There may be no more beautiful grammatical doorway in the chapter.
Your sin can describe what you did without being permitted to define who Christ is making you.
Paul continues:
“ἀλλὰ ἀπελούσασθε, ἀλλὰ ἡγιάσθητε, ἀλλὰ ἐδικαιώθητε...”
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified...”
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Not because they successfully repaired their reputations.
Not because they accumulated enough religious points.
Not because they bought anything.
Not because they donated enough.
Because salvation is grace.
Jesus paid.
Jesus saves.
Jesus cleanses.
Jesus justifies.
Jesus transforms.
That distinction must never be blurred.
You cannot purchase the favor of God.
You cannot share enough Christian articles to cancel your sin.
You cannot buy enough Christian merchandise to make God owe you mercy.
“For by grace you have been saved through faith,” Ephesians 2:8 teaches, “and this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God.”
The cross destroys both despair and pride.
You cannot say, “I am too terrible to be saved,” because that makes your sin greater than Christ’s sufficiency.
And you cannot say, “I am good enough not to need saving,” because the cross declares that your condition required the death of the Son of God.
We all come empty-handed.
Repentance is not payment for grace.
It is the turning of a heart that has finally stopped defending the thing that is killing it.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia — speaks of repentance, a changed mind and turning that bears fruit in a changed direction.
Real repentance does not mean you will never experience another temptation.
It means you stop making peace with the enemy.
You stop calling darkness your roommate.
You stop keeping emergency access to the thing you supposedly surrendered.
You bring it into the light.
This is why 1 John 1:9 remains precious:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Not some.
All.
The cross is not God pretending your sin did not matter.
The cross is the terrifying proof that it mattered so much that redemption required blood.
And then came Sunday.
The tomb is empty.
Jesus Christ is alive.
Therefore the Christian message is not merely that guilty people can receive a cleaner record.
Dead people can receive life.
Slaves can become free.
Enemies can become children.
The ashamed can come home.
The hidden can step into light.
The ruined can become testimonies.
Scandal can meet grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But grace does not mean returning affectionately to the chains Christ broke.
Paul asks in Romans 6:
“Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound?”
His answer is emphatic:
“By no means!”
Grace is not permission to flirt more confidently with destruction.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace does not merely forgive the prisoner.
Grace opens the cell.
So why are you still sleeping beside the chains?
Maybe that is the question God is pressing into your heart right now.
What are you protecting that is quietly destroying you?
Whose name immediately appeared in your mind?
What application?
What website?
What relationship?
What habit?
What fantasy?
What resentment?
What secret?
What conversation?
What compromise?
What do you keep hiding because somewhere inside you know that bringing it into the light might require you to give it up?
Do not answer me.
Answer God.
And please do not confuse conviction with condemnation.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Condemnation says:
“Hide from God. You are finished.”
Conviction draws you into the light:
“Come home. Stop running.”
Remember what happened after Adam and Eve sinned.
They hid.
Humanity has been sewing fig leaves ever since.
We hide behind humor.
Success.
Ministry.
Church attendance.
Busyness.
Relationships.
Social media.
Religious vocabulary.
Sometimes the person posting Bible verses is privately begging God to break an addiction nobody knows exists.
Sometimes the marriage everyone admires is bleeding behind a locked door.
Sometimes the believer singing with both hands raised on Sunday is fighting thoughts at midnight that would shock everyone standing beside them.
Maybe that person is you.
Then hear this without religious performance:
Come into the light.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you feel stronger.
Now.
Tell Jesus the truth He already knows.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Trust Him.
And where your struggle requires accountability, bring a trustworthy, mature Christian into the battle.

If another person is being harmed, endangered, manipulated, or abused, seeking appropriate professional or legal help may also be necessary. “Keeping it private” is not a biblical excuse for allowing harm to continue.
Repentance can be painful because sometimes obedience costs you access to something your flesh still wants.
But there are things worth losing in order to stop losing yourself.
There are numbers worth deleting.
There are relationships worth ending.
There are environments worth leaving.
There are confessions worth making.
There are boundaries worth building.
There are nights of withdrawal worth surviving.
There are uncomfortable conversations worth having.
There are tears worth crying.
There is freedom worth fighting for.
And above all, there is a Christ worth following.
Maybe you fail again.
Then do not turn failure into permission.
Run back to Christ.
Repent again.
Get back up.
Strengthen the boundaries.
Expose the pattern.
Seek help.
Keep fighting.
Micah 7:8 carries the defiant hope:
“When I fall, I shall rise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD will be a light to me.”
Do not build a house where you fell.
Do not decorate the pit.
Do not introduce yourself by the name of your wound.
Rise.
Not because you are powerful enough to rescue yourself.
Because Christ is still Christ.
There is something else I want you to do.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not manufacture a polished Christian response.
Be honest.
If you are exhausted but still refusing to surrender your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need believers to stand with you in prayer, simply comment, “pray for me.”
And if Christ has already begun healing something you once thought would destroy you, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Someone reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only person fighting.
Your honesty might become somebody else’s courage.
And think of one person right now who needs this article.
Not the person you want to embarrass.
The person you love enough to warn.
Or send this privately if public tagging would expose something that is not yours to expose.
Not as proof that you are spiritually superior.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
Somebody may be one message away from destroying a marriage.
One click away from reopening an addiction.
One secret meeting away from a decision they will spend years wishing they could reverse.
One hopeless night away from believing that Jesus no longer wants them.
Your share could place truth in front of them at the exact moment they were preparing to believe a lie.

If you genuinely want your life to glorify God, one practical way to do that is to use what He has placed in your hands—including your voice, your influence, your resources, and your social reach—to point people toward Christ.
Supporting Gospel-centered work can be part of that stewardship.
But hear this clearly:
God cannot be purchased.
And you should never be manipulated into thinking that clicking a button proves your devotion to Jesus.
But the deepest value is not merchandise.
It is growth.
It is staying close to truth.
It is having another voice in your week reminding you that temptation is not your master, shame is not your identity, and Jesus Christ has not surrendered His throne.
Because temptation has a strange way of making tomorrow’s version of you forget what tonight’s version of you finally understood.
Save it so you can remember:
Bait is never worth the hook.
Let your timeline become more than entertainment.
Let it become territory where truth travels.
And before you leave this article, there is one final thing you need to understand.
You may have spent years thinking Christianity is mainly the story of you trying hard enough not to ruin your life.
It is not.
Christianity is the announcement that humanity already ruined itself through sin...
and God came looking for us anyway.
Jesus did not stand at a safe distance shouting instructions toward drowning people.
The eternal Son took on flesh.
He entered our world.
He lived without sin.
He carried our guilt.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
The scandal of your sin met the greater scandal of grace:
the Holy One taking the place of the guilty.
So stop flirting with what crucified your Savior.
Stop petting what wants to devour you.
Stop calling bondage freedom.
Stop calling poison medicine.
Stop standing at the grave wondering how much death you can touch without becoming cold.
There is something better.
There is Someone better.
Jesus.
And perhaps tonight the bravest prayer you can pray is not eloquent at all.
“Jesus, I want You more.”
More than the screen.
More than the affair.
More than the attention.
More than the resentment.
More than the secret.
More than the fantasy.
More than the addiction.
More than the applause.
More than the person you know you need to surrender.
More than the temporary pleasure that keeps leaving permanent wounds.
Jesus...
I want You more.
If that prayer is becoming yours, comment it:
Let that comment become a marker.
Not a magical formula.
Not public performance.
A marker.
A moment when you stopped pretending the hook was harmless because the bait tasted good.
Then send this to somebody who is still standing near the edge.
Tag wisely.
Because somewhere tonight...
someone is flirting with what almost destroyed you.
And perhaps your testimony will be the warning that helps them finally run.
Remember this when temptation becomes beautiful again:
The devil only needs you to admire the bait long enough to forget there is a hook—but Jesus was pierced so you would never have to remain chained to what caught you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE SECRET JESUS HID IN A SEED
paragraphs:
THE SECRET JESUS HID IN A SEED
Why Christ Kept Talking About Seeds—and Why Understanding What He Meant May Change the Way You See Your Pain, Your Waiting, Your Faith, and the Story God Is Still Writing
There is something almost unsettling about a seed.
Hold one between your fingers and it looks insignificant.
Small enough to lose.
Ordinary enough to ignore.
You could walk past a thousand of them and never stop to wonder what is happening beneath their shells.
But Jesus noticed seeds.

He noticed them so often that when He wanted people to understand the Kingdom of God, He repeatedly pointed toward fields, farmers, soil, harvests, mustard seeds, wheat, weeds, fruit, death, burial, and growth.
Why?

Why would the Son of God—who could have reached for the language of kings, armies, palaces, thunder, stars, oceans, or empires—keep returning to something so small that it could disappear into the palm of a farmer?
Maybe because a seed carries one of the most uncomfortable truths about following Jesus:
Some of God's deepest work begins where human eyes can no longer see anything happening.
And perhaps that is exactly where you are right now.
You prayed.
Nothing seemed to happen.
You tried to obey.
Nothing changed overnight.
You repented, but you still remember who you used to be.
You opened your Bible, but some mornings your heart still felt dry.
You planted something in faith and expected a harvest, yet all you can see is dirt.
And somewhere inside you, a question has been growing:
“God, are You doing anything at all?”
Jesus understood that question long before you asked it.
That is why He gave us the seed.

In Mark 4, Jesus tells the famous parable of the sower. A farmer goes out scattering seed. Some falls beside the road. Some lands on rocky ground. Some falls among thorns. Some reaches good soil and eventually produces an extraordinary crop.
Then Jesus explains what the seed represents.
The Greek is beautifully direct:
“Ὁ σπείρων τὸν λόγον σπείρει.”
Ho speirōn ton logon speirei.
“The sower sows the word.”
That is Mark 4:14.
The word translated “sows” comes from σπείρω (speirō), meaning to sow or scatter seed. And λόγος (logos) here refers to the message—the word being proclaimed.
Jesus is not giving agricultural advice.
He is revealing something about the way God's truth enters human lives.
The Word is sown.
Think about that.
God's Word does not always arrive like an explosion.
Sometimes it arrives like a seed.
Quietly.
Small enough to dismiss.
Powerful enough to change everything.
A verse you heard as a child.
A sermon you barely paid attention to.
A Bible your grandmother kept beside her bed.
A conversation with a believer you thought you had forgotten.
A Scripture that irritated you because it confronted something you did not want to surrender.
A sentence about Jesus that somehow followed you home.
Seed.
And seed can remain in places people assume are dead.
That is part of the mystery.
But Jesus' parable also destroys a comforting misconception: hearing God's Word is not the same thing as allowing God's Word to transform us.
The same seed is scattered.
The soils respond differently.
One heart is hardened.
Another receives quickly but has no depth.
Another allows competing desires and anxieties to choke what was heard.
Another receives the Word and bears fruit.
The problem in the parable is not a defective seed.
The question is the soil.
And suddenly the story becomes painfully personal.
Because Jesus is no longer merely describing ancient farmers.
He is describing us.
It is possible to sit near Scripture without surrendering to Scripture.
It is possible to enjoy Christian content while resisting Christ.
It is possible to become emotionally moved without becoming spiritually rooted.
It is possible to know worship songs, quote verses, share Christian posts, wear Christian shirts, own several Bibles, and still protect areas of the heart where Jesus is not allowed to rule.
That is why the seed imagery is so piercing.
Seeds expose soil.
And the Word of God exposes hearts.
Hebrews 4:12 says that God's Word is living and active, penetrating deeply and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart.
It does not merely inform us.
It confronts us.
It reveals us.
It shows us the stones we have hidden beneath the surface.
Pride.
Bitterness.
Secret lust.
Unforgiveness.
Self-righteousness.
Envy.
Greed.
Fear.
Religious performance.
The desperate need to appear spiritually healthy while something inside us is starving.
And grace begins when we stop pretending the soil is better than it really is.
Maybe that is why this hurts.
Because you know exactly where the thorns are.
You know what keeps competing with Jesus.
You know the compromise nobody sees.
You know the resentment you keep watering.
You know the habit you keep renaming so you do not have to call it sin.
You know how exhausting it is to look alive while slowly becoming dry inside.
But the Gospel does not expose us merely to humiliate us.
Jesus reveals what is killing us because He came to save us.
That distinction matters.
Conviction says, “Bring this into the light.”
Condemnation says, “Hide because there is no hope for you.”
The Gospel says something radically different.
Come into the light because Christ has already carried the shame of sinners to the cross.
Repentance is not God demanding that you clean yourself before approaching Him.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can cleanse you.
The Greek New Testament often uses μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance, carrying the sense of a change of mind that results in a changed direction.
Not cosmetic Christianity.
Not image management.
Not “I am sorry I got caught.”
A turning.
A surrender.
A return.
And then Jesus tells another seed story.
In Mark 4:26–27, He compares the Kingdom of God to a man scattering seed on the ground. The man sleeps and wakes, night after night and day after day, and the seed sprouts and grows.
Jesus adds something fascinating:
The man does not know how.
There it is.
The sentence exhausted believers need to hear.
He does not know how.
The farmer has responsibility. He sows.
But he does not manufacture life inside the seed.
He cannot stand over the field screaming, “Grow!”
He cannot dig everything up every morning to check whether growth has begun.
He sows.
He waits.
God gives what human effort cannot manufacture.
Paul uses similar imagery in 1 Corinthians 3:6:
“I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.”
That should humble us.
And it should relieve us.
You are called to faithfulness.
You are not God.
There are things obedience can plant that only God can bring to maturity.
Somebody needs that truth tonight.
Because you have been digging up everything you planted.
You prayed for your child and became discouraged because you did not see immediate change.
You shared Christ with somebody and assumed your words accomplished nothing.
You started rebuilding your life after failure and became frustrated because restoration was slower than destruction.
You repented and expected every temptation to disappear.
You began reading Scripture and expected instant spiritual maturity.
But seeds do not become trees by sunset.
And slowness is not the same as absence.
Hidden is not the same as dead.

That does not mean every disappointment is secretly a promise that God will give us whatever outcome we want. Scripture never gives us permission to turn seed imagery into a blank check for our personal ambitions.
Jesus is not teaching a Christian version of manifestation.
He is teaching us about God's Kingdom, God's Word, spiritual receptivity, growth, fruitfulness, judgment, faith, and ultimately His sovereign work.
Sometimes we misuse biblical language about sowing and reaping as though God were a vending machine.
Give this and God owes you that.
Plant money and demand wealth.
Perform enough spiritual activity and demand the life you imagined.
That is not the Gospel.
God owes us nothing.
Everything we receive in Christ is grace.
And grace becomes even more astonishing when we realize that Jesus did not merely teach about seeds.
Eventually, He described Himself with one.
In John 12:24, shortly before His crucifixion, Jesus says:
“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.”
The Greek begins:
“ἐὰν μὴ ὁ κόκκος τοῦ σίτου…”
ean mē ho kokkos tou sitou…
“Unless the grain of wheat…”
Now the seed imagery becomes darker.
Because the Teacher who spoke about sowing was walking toward His own burial.
The One who spoke about seed entering soil would soon enter a tomb.
The hands that scattered truth would be pierced.
The voice that commanded storms would cry from a cross.
The King would wear thorns.
The innocent One would be numbered among transgressors.
Jesus was not murdered because He lacked power to escape. According to the New Testament, He willingly laid down His life.
He bore sin.
He suffered.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
Christianity stands or falls here.
Not on motivational language.
Not on religious aesthetics.
Not on whether Christianity makes your week easier.
Paul says in 1 Corinthians 15 that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, and was raised on the third day.
Death.
Burial.
Resurrection.
Suddenly the seed becomes more than an illustration of patience.
It points us toward the shape of redemption itself.
Down before up.
Burial before emergence.
Death before resurrection.
Not because every painful circumstance guarantees the earthly outcome we desire, but because the center of Christianity is a crucified and risen Savior.
And this is where scandal becomes grace.
The cross looked like scandal.
The Messiah rejected.
The Holy One mocked.
The Creator treated like a criminal by creatures whose breath He sustained.
Yet God turned the place of apparent defeat into the place where redemption was accomplished.
The cross did not become good because cruelty was good.
Sin remained sin.
Betrayal remained betrayal.
Injustice remained injustice.
But evil did not get the final word.
Jesus did.
And maybe that is why you cannot stop thinking about your own story.
Your scandal.
Your failure.
Your divorce.
Your addiction.
Your betrayal.
Your years away from God.
Your secret.
Your regret.
The person you hurt.
The season you wasted.
The version of yourself you wish nobody had ever met.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not teach that your sin was secretly good.
It teaches something far greater:
Your sin does not have to write your final chapter.
Jesus can forgive sinners.
Jesus can restore what shame convinced you was beyond redemption.
Jesus can take a person with a past and give that person a future rooted in grace.
Peter denied Him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to build a respectable religious résumé.
Again and again, Scripture gives us people whose stories should have ended in shame.
Then grace entered the story.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by removing repentance.
He rewrites everything by doing what we could never do for ourselves.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He reconciles.
He redeems.
He makes new.
“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation,” Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 5:17.
That is not self-improvement.
That is resurrection language.
And now another teaching of Jesus about seeds begins to shine.
The mustard seed.
Jesus says the Kingdom is like a mustard seed—something proverbially tiny in His teaching context that grows far beyond what its beginning seems to predict.
Do not miss the point by turning the parable into a botany contest.
Jesus is emphasizing the astonishing contrast between an unimpressive beginning and remarkable growth.
The Kingdom arrived in ways many people did not expect.
A child born in Bethlehem.
Raised in Nazareth.
A carpenter.
A small group of disciples.
No earthly palace.
No Roman army.
No political machine.
Then a cross.
Then an empty tomb.
Then frightened disciples proclaiming that Jesus Christ is Lord.
And the message kept spreading.
Seed.
That is how the Kingdom often moves.
Person to person.
Heart to heart.
Home to home.
Generation to generation.
Someone tells someone about Jesus.
A mother teaches her child to pray.
A man finally opens the Bible somebody gave him years ago.
A prisoner hears the Gospel.
A skeptic asks one more question.
A broken Christian returns to church.
A prodigal remembers the Father's house.
Someone scrolling through Facebook at 2:13 in the morning reads one sentence about Christ and cannot shake it.
Seed.
You may never know what one faithful act becomes in the hands of God.
That is why sharing the Gospel matters.
Not because clicking “share” earns favor with God.
Not because an algorithm determines your spirituality.
And certainly not because Christians purchase salvation through religious activity.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 makes unmistakably clear.
But people who have received good news naturally want others to hear it.
Someone who would never tell you they have been crying.
Someone whose marriage is collapsing.
Someone who secretly wonders whether God could forgive what they have done.
Someone who appears strong online and feels completely hollow offline.
Someone who has been one terrible night away from abandoning their faith.
Not to prove you love God.
Not to bargain with Him.
Hidden does not mean dead.
Failure does not have to become identity.
And Jesus still saves sinners.
Send this to the prodigal you are still praying for—with gentleness, not condemnation.
Because there may come a night when the soil of your own heart feels dry again, and you will need to remember what Jesus taught you through something as ordinary as a seed.
No religious performance.
No pretending.
Your comment might become somebody else's courage to stop pretending.
That is another strange thing about seeds.
One seed can eventually produce more seed.
Grace received becomes grace proclaimed.
Truth received becomes truth shared.
A testimony becomes another person's invitation to investigate Jesus.
A disciple helps make disciples.
This is why Gospel-centered ministry matters.
There is already enough noise in the world.
Enough outrage.
Enough empty motivation.
Enough Christianity reduced to inspirational slogans.
We need Scripture.
We need truth.
We need repentance without self-righteousness.
Grace without compromise.
Compassion without abandoning holiness.
Conviction without hopeless condemnation.
And above everything, we need Jesus Christ.

Supporting Christian ministry can be an expression of voluntary generosity when it is done freely, wisely, and for God's glory. Scripture teaches cheerful rather than coerced giving in 2 Corinthians 9:7.
So support because you want truth to travel.
Share because somebody needs the seed.
Follow because you want to keep Scripture and Christ-centered encouragement close in a world constantly competing for your attention.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with purchasing God's approval.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot share enough posts to erase your sins.
You cannot donate enough money to make God owe you salvation.
The price of redemption was not paid by you.
It was paid by Christ.
That is precisely why Christian generosity should flow from grace rather than fear.
We give because He first gave.
We serve because He served.
We love because He first loved us.
We proclaim because somebody once proclaimed the Gospel to us.
We scatter because somebody once scattered a seed that reached our soil.
And somewhere beneath all of this is perhaps the question Jesus has been quietly asking you from the beginning:
What kind of soil have you become?
Not your spouse.
Not your pastor.
Not the hypocrite who hurt you.
Not the Christian who disappointed you.
You.
Has disappointment hardened you?
Have shallow roots made you dependent on emotional highs?
Have worries, money, ambition, entertainment, resentment, lust, or the approval of people slowly grown around the Word until you can barely hear Christ anymore?
Or are you willing to become good soil?
Because there is still time to repent.
