There is still grace.
There is still a Savior.
And perhaps the most beautiful truth hidden inside Jesus' seed imagery is this:
The seed disappears before the harvest appears.
There are moments when faithfulness feels invisible.
Moments when obedience feels buried.
Moments when repentance hurts.
Moments when following Jesus costs you something.
Moments when you cannot yet see what God is producing through His Word.
Do not build your theology merely from what you can see today.
Return to Scripture.
Remain in Christ.
Pray.
Repent when you sin.
Forgive because you have been forgiven.
Love your neighbor.
Serve faithfully.
Stay rooted in a faithful Christian community.
Keep hearing the Word.
Keep obeying Christ.
Keep scattering Gospel seed.
And leave the growth to God.
One day the farmer who thought he was staring at empty dirt sees green breaking through the ground.
What appeared empty was not necessarily inactive.
What appeared insignificant contained more possibility than the eye could measure.
And what looked like the end at a sealed tomb outside Jerusalem became the announcement that death itself would not have the final word over those who belong to Jesus.
That is why Christ's followers can have hope without pretending pain is painless.
Our hope is not that every earthly story ends exactly the way we wanted.
Our hope has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Buried.
Risen.
Lord.
So if your heart feels buried right now, do not worship the darkness.
Look to Christ.
If you have sinned, do not decorate the sin.
Repent.
If shame keeps replaying your past, bring your past beneath the authority of the cross.
If you have wandered, come home.
If you have become hard, ask God to break the ground.
If the thorns have grown high, stop protecting what is choking your soul.
And if you have never truly surrendered yourself to Jesus, understand what the seed has been pointing toward all along.
The Kingdom of God is not an accessory to the life you already planned.
The King calls you to Himself.
Jesus did not come merely to make bad people behave slightly better.
He came to save sinners.
He died for sins.
He rose from the dead.
He calls people everywhere to repent, believe the Gospel, follow Him, and receive the life that only He can give.
Maybe this article was simply another seed.
What happens next is not ultimately about whether you admired the writing.
It is about what you do with the Word.
And comment something real.
“I’m still fighting.”
“Pray for me.”
“No more hiding.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
Or write your testimony.
Tell someone what Jesus rescued you from.
Because perhaps another frightened person will read your words and realize that grace is still possible for people with complicated stories.
Not because God can be purchased.
But because when Christ has given us everything, we begin asking a different question:
“How can what God has entrusted to me help somebody else encounter Jesus?”
A seed looks insignificant until you realize you are holding tomorrow's harvest in your hand.
And sometimes what feels like a burial is the very place where God teaches us that the tomb does not get the last word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY IS LUST HARDER TO DEFEAT THAN ANGER?
paragraphs: WHY IS LUST HARDER TO DEFEAT THAN ANGER?
Because anger usually tells you what hurt you. Lust can make you love what is hurting you—and Jesus did not come merely to make you behave better. He came to make you free.
There is a reason you can walk away from an argument and know immediately that something went wrong.
Your chest is tight. Your words replay in your head. You remember the look on their face. Maybe conviction comes quickly.
“I shouldn’t have said that.”
Anger often leaves fingerprints.
Lust is different.
Lust can leave perfume.

It can disguise itself as comfort when you are lonely. Relief when you are stressed. Curiosity when you are bored. Fantasy when reality disappoints you. Validation when you feel unwanted. Escape when life becomes painfully ordinary.
And sometimes the most dangerous thing about lust is not that it feels evil.
It is that, for a moment, it feels like medicine.
That is why someone can genuinely love Jesus, genuinely hate what sin is doing to them, genuinely repent with tears—and still find themselves fighting the same temptation again.
Maybe that sentence already made you uncomfortable.
Good.
Not because shame is the goal.
Because hiding has never healed anyone.
You can confess anger after exploding because everybody saw it.
But lust?
Lust often grows where nobody is watching.
Behind locked doors.
Inside deleted histories.
Under blankets illuminated by a phone screen.
Inside private fantasies no spouse knows about.
Inside glances that linger slightly too long.
Inside conversations you keep calling “innocent.”
Inside memories you deliberately replay.
Inside the secret version of yourself that knows exactly what to search for, exactly when to search for it, and exactly how to erase the evidence afterward.
Then Sunday comes.
You worship.
You smile.
You shake hands.
You say, “God is good.”
And somewhere beneath all of that, you wonder:
“If God is really changing me, why am I still fighting this?”
Here is where we need Scripture more than slogans.
Jesus said:
“Everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Matthew 5:28
The Greek is painfully precise.
The expression includes:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn
The key verb, ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō, carries the idea of desiring, longing for, craving, or setting desire upon something.
Jesus was not declaring that merely noticing another person's beauty is identical to adultery.
He was going deeper.
He was exposing cultivated desire.
The look that becomes feeding.
The noticing that becomes possessing in the imagination.
The moment another human being stops being someone made in the image of God and becomes material for private consumption.
That is one reason lust can become so difficult to defeat.
Anger often erupts because something happened to you.
Lust often survives because something happens for you.
At least temporarily.
It rewards you.
That distinction matters.
When someone insults you, anger can flare because you feel threatened, dishonored, frustrated, wounded, or powerless.
But lust frequently offers something immediately pleasurable in return.
A rush.
An escape.
A fantasy.
A feeling of control.
A few minutes in which loneliness disappears.
A few minutes in which rejection cannot reach you.
A few minutes in which the imaginary person never says no, never disappoints you, never demands vulnerability, never exposes your insecurity.
And then the moment ends.
The screen goes dark.
The fantasy dissolves.
Reality returns.
And what promised intimacy leaves you more alone.
What promised satisfaction leaves you wanting another dose.
What promised freedom begins creating rituals.
That is the cruelty of lust.
It keeps making promises that require another payment.
James describes the movement of temptation with frightening accuracy:
“But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin…”
James 1:14–15
The Greek word translated “desire” is ἐπιθυμία — epithymia.
Desire itself must be understood carefully because Scripture does not teach that every human desire is inherently sinful. The New Testament can use this word in different contexts.
The problem is desire turned away from God's design.
Desire becomes a tyrant when it begins telling God:
“I know what You said, but I want this more.”
And perhaps that is where this article becomes personal.
Because lust is rarely defeated simply by saying:
“I need to stop being horny.”
That may not even be the deepest battle.
Sometimes underneath sexual temptation is loneliness.
Sometimes rejection.
Sometimes resentment toward your spouse.
Sometimes boredom.
Sometimes insecurity.
Sometimes the craving to feel desirable.
Sometimes an unwillingness to suffer discomfort.
Sometimes years of conditioning.
Sometimes the habit of reaching for stimulation whenever silence becomes unbearable.
And sometimes it is simply sinful desire that needs to be denied rather than endlessly explained.
Biblical honesty requires both truths.
You are more complicated than your temptation.
But your complexity does not make sin holy.
God understands your wounds.
He also calls you to repentance.
Those truths are not enemies.
They meet at the cross.
And this is where many people misunderstand Christianity.
Jesus did not die so that we could rename bondage as authenticity.
But neither did He die so that broken sinners would spend the rest of their lives terrified to approach Him.
The Gospel says something far more astonishing.
You can come into the light.
Completely.
John writes:
1 John 1:9
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say:
“If we become impressive enough…”
“If we successfully hide it long enough…”
“If we punish ourselves enough…”
“If we promise God dramatically enough…”
It says:
ἐὰν ὁμολογῶμεν τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν — ean homologōmen tas hamartias hēmōn
“If we confess our sins…”
The verb ὁμολογέω — homologeō carries the sense of acknowledging, confessing, agreeing, admitting.
In other words, freedom begins when you stop negotiating with God about what He already called sin.
No more euphemisms.
No more “I was just looking.”
No more “We’re only talking.”
No more “Everybody does it.”
No more “At least I didn’t physically cheat.”
No more “God knows my heart” used as camouflage for refusing to surrender your heart.
Yes.
God knows your heart.
That is precisely why grace is such astonishing news.
He knows.
And Christ still calls you.
He knows.
And Christ still receives repentant sinners.
He knows.
And Christ still cleanses.
He knows.
And Christ still transforms.
This is not permission to remain in bondage.
This is the reason you can finally stop hiding.
Think about King David.
One glance became desire.
Desire became inquiry.
Inquiry became adultery.
Adultery became deception.
Deception became manipulation.
Manipulation became bloodshed.
That progression should terrify anyone who thinks private lust is harmless.
Sin rarely introduces itself by showing you the final invoice.
David saw Bathsheba.
But he did not initially see Nathan confronting him.
He did not see the wreckage.
He did not see how desperately he would later cry:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים — lev tahor bera-li Elohim
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Psalm 51:10
The Hebrew word בְּרָא — bara, “create,” is striking.
David needed more than image management.
More than damage control.
More than a cleaner browser history.
More than stronger embarrassment.
He needed God to do something deep within him.
“Create in me a clean heart.”
That prayer still belongs in bedrooms.
It belongs in hotel rooms.
It belongs in marriages.
It belongs in dormitories.
It belongs in offices after everybody else leaves.
It belongs in the mouth of the teenager who discovered pornography before understanding what sexuality even meant.
It belongs in the mouth of the husband whose wife thinks everything is fine.
It belongs in the mouth of the wife emotionally fantasizing about someone who listens to her differently.
It belongs in the mouth of the single Christian who is tired of pretending sexual temptation disappeared at baptism.
It belongs in the mouth of the pastor.
The worship leader.
The ministry volunteer.
The person reading this while simultaneously hoping nobody ever discovers what they have been fighting.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Not merely:
“Make me afraid of getting caught.”
Make me clean.
Because there is a tremendous difference between wanting freedom and wanting secrecy.
Some people do not actually want lust gone.
They want the consequences gone.
They want the marriage without surrendering the fantasy.
They want ministry without surrendering the secret.
They want peace without repentance.
They want Jesus as Savior while repeatedly protecting the room where He is not allowed to be Lord.
And Christ loves us too deeply to cooperate with that arrangement.
Jesus said something radical immediately after His warning concerning lust:
“If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away…”
Matthew 5:29
Jesus is using deliberately shocking language to communicate radical action against sin—not commanding routine physical mutilation. The heart itself is the deeper battlefield.
But notice what He refuses to give us.
Casual Christianity.
Jesus does not say:
“Manage the temptation comfortably.”
He teaches us to treat sin seriously.
That may mean deleting something.
Ending a conversation.
Blocking someone.
Removing an app.
Moving the computer.
Changing where you take your phone at night.
Stopping the secret emotional relationship you keep defending because nothing physical has happened “yet.”
Speaking honestly with your spouse where appropriate.
Confessing to a mature believer who will not flatter your excuses.
Seeking wise pastoral care.

And when compulsive sexual behavior has become deeply entrenched, getting qualified professional help can be an act of wisdom rather than an admission that Christ is insufficient. God routinely works through His people, wise counsel, accountability, disciplined habits, and truthful community.
Paul did not tell Timothy to negotiate with youthful passions.
He said:
“Flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace…”
2 Timothy 2:22
There are two movements.
Flee.
Pursue.
This is where many attempts at purity collapse.
People try to remove lust while leaving an empty throne.
But Christianity is not fundamentally about becoming a person who wants nothing.
It is about becoming a person whose deepest desires are being reordered around Someone.
Jesus Christ.
You do not merely flee pornography.
You pursue Christ.
You do not merely stop fantasizing.
You learn to see people as image-bearers rather than consumable bodies.
You do not merely remove secret messages.
You pursue honesty.
You do not merely say no to adultery.
You learn covenant faithfulness.
You do not merely avoid impurity.
You pursue holiness.
You do not merely starve lust.
You feed your soul.
This is why lust can sometimes feel harder to defeat than anger.
Because lust can become attached to reward, secrecy, imagination, habit, loneliness, bodily appetite, emotional escape, and repeated patterns all at once.
But harder does not mean undefeatable.
And repeated temptation does not mean Jesus has abandoned you.
Listen carefully.
Temptation is not identical to surrender.
Even Jesus “in every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin.”
Hebrews 4:15
The presence of temptation does not prove the absence of faith.
What matters is what you do with it.
Do you feed it?
Hide it?
Romanticize it?
Arrange opportunities for it?
Or bring it into the light and run toward Christ?
Paul writes:
1 Corinthians 6:18
And the surrounding context gives us something far more beautiful than prohibition:
“You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.”
1 Corinthians 6:19–20
That changes everything.
Your body is not garbage.
Your sexuality is not garbage.
Biblical Christianity is not embarrassed that God created sexuality.
The same Bible that condemns sexual immorality celebrates covenant intimacy.
The problem is not that desire exists.
The problem is when desire refuses God's boundaries and begins ruling the person who was supposed to offer their whole life to Christ.
You were bought with a price.
Not silver.
Not gold.
Blood.
Christ's blood.
So when temptation whispers:
“This body belongs to you. Do whatever feels good.”
The Gospel answers:
“I was bought with a price.”
When lust whispers:
“Nobody will know.”
The Gospel answers:
“Christ is here.”
When shame whispers:
“After what you have done, Jesus wants nothing to do with you.”
The Gospel answers:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Romans 8:1
And when your flesh whispers:
“You will never change.”
The Gospel points toward a Savior who specializes in resurrection.
Maybe you have failed hundreds of times.
Come back.
Maybe you promised God you would never do it again and then did it again three days later.
Come back.
Maybe you are reading this immediately after falling.
Come back.
Maybe your sin has consequences that repentance cannot magically erase.
Come back anyway.
Repentance is not pretending consequences do not exist.
Repentance is turning toward God in truth.
The New Testament word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō.
It speaks of repentance, a changed mind and turning of one's orientation. Biblical repentance is more than feeling terrible after sin.
Judas felt terrible.
Repentance moves toward God.
That means you stop asking only:
“How can I stop doing this?”
And eventually begin asking:
“What do I believe this sin gives me that I am refusing to seek rightly under God?”
Comfort?
Validation?
Escape?
Power?
Pleasure?
Intimacy?
Control?
Then bring that hunger to Jesus without pretending the counterfeit can satisfy it.
Because lust's greatest lie may not be “this is pleasurable.”
Sin can indeed produce temporary pleasure.
Hebrews 11:25 itself speaks of “the fleeting pleasures of sin.”
The greater lie is:
“This will satisfy you.”
It will not.
That is why it needs you to return.
Again.
Again.
Again.
Jesus offers something fundamentally different.
He told the woman at the well:
“Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never be thirsty again.”
And consider who heard those words.
A woman whose relational history was complicated enough that Jesus named it directly.
Five husbands.
And the man she was currently with was not her husband.
Yet Jesus did not approach her merely as a scandal.
He approached her as a soul.
He exposed truth without removing dignity.
He named her reality without declaring her irredeemable.
Then the woman who arrived carrying an empty water jar became someone running toward others with testimony.
“Come, see a man who told me all that I ever did.”
John 4:29
Do you see it?
Jesus knew the story.
And stayed.
Jesus exposed the story.
And offered living water.
Jesus confronted the truth.
And the truth did not become the end of her story.
That is Gospel Warrior territory.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your scandal has never become public.
Maybe your greatest fear is that it will.
But Christ does not need your scandal to become public before He can begin transforming you privately.
Bring it into His light.
Confess.
Repent.
Cut off what keeps feeding it.
Find trustworthy accountability.
Fill your mind with Scripture.
Learn to pray before temptation becomes an emergency.
Stop carrying your phone into the place where you most frequently fall.
Stop following accounts that train your eyes to consume bodies.
Stop calling flirtation harmless when you know exactly why you enjoy it.
Stop testing how close you can stand to the fire while still calling yourself obedient.
And when you fall, do not convert failure into an excuse for another week of sin.
Run to Jesus immediately.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you feel spiritual again.
Immediately.
Because shame says:
“Hide until you become worthy.”
Grace says:
“Come because Christ is worthy.”
There is a world of difference between grace and permission.
Grace does not whisper:
“Keep sinning. It doesn't matter.”
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 makes that unmistakable.
The grace that forgives you is also training you.
The Christ who receives you also transforms you.
The Savior who says, “Come,” also says, “Follow Me.”
And perhaps tonight, your greatest act of warfare will not look dramatic.
Maybe nobody will applaud.
Maybe there will be no music.
No altar.
No audience.
Just you.
A phone.
A temptation.
And the name of Jesus.
And for once…
you put the phone down.
You walk away.
You pray.
You message someone trustworthy.
You choose obedience while every conditioned impulse in you screams for another taste.
Nobody sees the battle.
But heaven is not confused about what happened.
You chose whom you wanted to obey.
Then tomorrow you fight again.
Not to earn salvation.
Because salvation has given you Someone worth fighting for.
And if you fail tomorrow?
Repent.
Get up.
Learn where the door was left open.
Close it.
Return to Christ.
Keep walking.
Sanctification is not pretending Christians never struggle.
It is refusing to make peace with the sin Christ died to save us from.
If this exposed something hidden, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly. But you can stop pretending you are the only one fighting.
And if Christ has already brought you out of sexual bondage, consider leaving a wise, non-graphic testimony. Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that transformation is possible.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget everything we believed while we were strong.
Send it privately to the believer who has been disappearing into shame.
Send it to the husband trying to become faithful again.
Send it to the wife carrying secret temptation.
Send it to the teenager who needs to learn that pornography is not preparation for love.
Send it even to the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is merely a collection of people pretending they never struggle.
Let them see the Gospel.
Not perfect people climbing toward God.
A holy God coming down to rescue sinners through Jesus Christ.
If your desire is to glorify God, do that first and ultimately through loving Christ, obeying His Word, loving people, serving faithfully, giving generously, and making the Gospel known.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with purchasing God's favor.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Forgiveness does not arrive in a package.
Christ already paid the price sinners could never pay.
And that is exactly why those who have received freely should want others to hear freely.
So tonight, when lust knocks again…
remember this:
You are not merely saying no to an image.
You are saying yes to a Person.
You are not merely deleting a fantasy.
You are protecting your capacity to love real people.
You are not merely resisting pleasure.
You are refusing to worship a pleasure that cannot keep its promises.
You are not merely fighting your body.
You are learning to glorify God with it.
And you are not fighting so Jesus will finally love you.
If you belong to Christ, you fight because the One who loved you unto death has already called you out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
The scandal may explain a chapter.
It does not get to write the ending.
Because when a sinner finally stops hiding, sometimes the sound they feared would be judgment is actually the sound of Christ calling them home.
The secret that keeps whispering, “This is who you are,” has never had more authority than the blood of Jesus saying, “You were bought with a price.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HOW DO YOU KNOW THE HOLY SPIRIT REALLY LIVES IN YOU?
paragraphs:
HOW DO YOU KNOW THE HOLY SPIRIT REALLY LIVES IN YOU?
You can attend church, cry during worship, know Bible verses, and feel spiritual emotions—but none of those things, by themselves, answer the terrifying question: “Does the Spirit of God actually dwell in me?”
There is a question some Christians are almost afraid to ask.
Not because they do not care about God.
Because they care so much that the possible answer frightens them.
It usually comes when everything becomes quiet.
The worship music has stopped.
The sermon is over.
Nobody is watching.
The Bible is sitting beside you, your phone is glowing in the darkness, and somewhere beneath all the Christian language you have learned to speak is a question you cannot silence:
“How do I actually know the Holy Spirit lives in me?”
Maybe you have watched other Christians worship with tears streaming down their faces while you felt almost nothing.
Maybe someone told you that if the Holy Spirit really lived in you, you would have experienced something dramatic by now.
Maybe you have sinned again after promising God you were finished with that sin.
Again.
And now the enemy has turned your failure into an accusation:
“If God really lived inside you, would you still struggle like this?”
That question can become brutal.
Because perhaps you remember who you used to be.

Or perhaps you are painfully aware of what you are still capable of becoming when anger takes over, temptation arrives, loneliness gets loud, lust starts negotiating, bitterness starts growing, or nobody is around to see what you do.
So how do you know?
Not how do you feel.
Not what did somebody tell you at a conference.
Not whether you once had goosebumps during worship.
What does Scripture actually say?
Jesus gave His disciples an extraordinary promise before the cross.
Speaking about the Holy Spirit, He said:
“τὸ πνεῦμα τῆς ἀληθείας”
to pneuma tēs alētheias.
“The Spirit of truth.”
And then Jesus said something breathtaking:
“παρ’ ὑμῖν μένει καὶ ἐν ὑμῖν ἔσται”
par’ hymin menei kai en hymin estai.
“He dwells with you and will be in you.”
John 14:17.
Do not rush past those final words.
In you.
Christianity is not merely God giving sinful people better rules.
It is not merely human beings trying harder to imitate Jesus from a distance.
The Gospel announces something far more radical.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose from the dead.
Christ saves those who trust in Him.
And God gives His Spirit to His people.
Paul therefore writes with astonishing clarity in Romans 8:9 that anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to Christ.
That means the Holy Spirit is not an optional upgrade for unusually spiritual Christians.
There are not ordinary Christians over here and Holy-Spirit Christians somewhere over there.
If you belong to Christ, the Spirit of Christ dwells in you.
Paul tells believers that after hearing the Gospel and believing in Christ, they were “sealed with the promised Holy Spirit,” who is the guarantee of their inheritance (Ephesians 1:13–14).
The Greek language is beautiful here.
Paul uses the word ἐσφραγίσθητε — esphragisthēte, from sphragizō, carrying the idea of being sealed or marked.
Then he describes the Spirit as ἀρραβών — arrabōn—a pledge, deposit, down payment, guarantee.
In other words, salvation is not God reluctantly tolerating you until He decides whether He wants you.
The Spirit is God's pledge that those who are truly Christ's belong to Him.
But this brings us back to the question keeping someone awake tonight.
How do I know?
Here is where we must be careful.
Because many people search for evidence of the Holy Spirit in places Scripture never tells us to make the foundation of our assurance.
They search their emotions.
Did I feel enough?
They search dramatic experiences.
Did something supernatural happen?
They compare themselves with other Christians.
Why do they worship differently?
Why do they seem more passionate?
Why does God seem closer to them?
But Scripture repeatedly directs our attention somewhere deeper.
The evidence of the Spirit is not sinless perfection.
It is a life increasingly being brought under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And sometimes the first evidence is something you almost hate experiencing:
conviction.
You sin...
and something inside you refuses to let you make peace with it.
The sin you once defended begins disturbing you.
The lie that once felt harmless starts feeling filthy.
The bitterness you once justified begins exhausting you.
The pornography you once consumed without resistance begins producing grief.
The pride you once called confidence begins looking ugly.
The gossip you once called “just telling the truth” starts sounding cruel.
The relationship you know dishonors Christ becomes harder to rationalize.
And suddenly there is a war inside you.
Listen carefully.
The existence of a battle does not automatically mean the Spirit is absent.
Sometimes the battle exists precisely because something has changed.
Before Christ, sin can feel like home.
But when God begins transforming a heart, the old home starts becoming uncomfortable.
Paul describes the conflict between flesh and Spirit in Galatians 5.

That does not mean every guilty feeling comes from the Holy Spirit. Human conscience, fear, shame, psychological distress, consequences, and even unhealthy religious environments can produce powerful feelings of guilt.
Biblical conviction has a direction.
The Holy Spirit does not merely whisper, “You are disgusting. Hide from God.”
He exposes sin truthfully and drives us toward repentance, toward the Gospel, toward Christ.
Condemnation says:
“Run away from God.”
Grace says:
“Stop hiding and come home.”
That distinction matters because some of you reading this have confused relentless self-hatred with holiness.
You keep punishing yourself for sins Jesus died to forgive.
You think repeatedly calling yourself worthless proves you are repentant.
It does not.
Repentance agrees with God about sin, turns from it, and runs toward Christ.
The Gospel does not minimize your sin.
It reveals something even greater than your sin:
the sufficiency of Jesus.
At Calvary, Christ did not die for an imaginary, cleaned-up version of you.
He died for sinners.
And resurrection means your scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
That is why our message will always be:
Long before Pentecost, God had promised something astonishing through Ezekiel.
The Hebrew text of Ezekiel 36:26 says:
וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב חָדָשׁ וְרוּחַ חֲדָשָׁה אֶתֵּן בְּקִרְבְּכֶם
Venatatti lakhem lev chadash, veruach chadashah etten bekirbekhem.
God promises a לֵב חָדָשׁ — lev chadash, a “new heart,” and a רוּחַ חֲדָשָׁה — ruach chadashah, a “new spirit.”
Then comes Ezekiel 36:27:
וְאֶת־רוּחִי אֶתֵּן בְּקִרְבְּכֶם
Ve'et-ruchi etten bekirbekhem.
“I will put My Spirit within you.”
Notice what follows.
God says His Spirit will move His people toward walking according to His ways.
That changes the question.
Instead of merely asking,
“Have I experienced something spiritual?”
ask:
“What is happening to my relationship with Jesus?”
Do you find yourself being drawn toward Christ?
Does truth about Him matter to you differently than it once did?
When you fall, is there something inside you that wants to return?
When Scripture confronts you, do you merely want the Bible to approve your lifestyle—or is there a growing willingness for God to change your lifestyle?
Because Jesus said the Spirit would glorify Him.
That is crucial.
The Holy Spirit does not arrive to make the Holy Spirit the center of Christianity.
He glorifies Christ.
Jesus said:
“ἐκεῖνος ἐμὲ δοξάσει”
ekeinos eme doxasei.
“He will glorify Me.”
John 16:14.
So one of the deepest evidences of the Spirit's work is not an obsession with spiritual experiences.
It is an increasingly unavoidable obsession with Jesus Christ.
Jesus becomes more beautiful.
His cross becomes more personal.
His mercy becomes more astonishing.
His Word becomes more authoritative.
His holiness becomes more desirable.
His absence becomes more painful.
His forgiveness becomes more precious.
His glory begins mattering more than yours.
You start wanting Jesus—not merely what Jesus can give you.
There is another sign.
Fruit begins growing.
Not overnight.
Not perfectly.
Sometimes painfully slowly.
But something starts changing.
Paul says:
“ὁ δὲ καρπὸς τοῦ πνεύματός ἐστιν...”
ho de karpos tou pneumatos estin...
“But the fruit of the Spirit is...”
Then Galatians 5:22–23 names love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.
Notice Paul says fruit.
Fruit grows.
A tree does not scream itself into producing apples.
Life inside eventually becomes visible outside.
That means one of the questions is not:
“Have I become perfect?”
Ask instead:
“Is Christ changing what grows from my life?”
Maybe you are still impatient.
But five years ago you never apologized.
Now conviction will not let you sleep until you make it right.
Maybe anger still rises.
But now you hate what your anger does to people you love.
Maybe temptation still comes.
But something in you has stopped calling bondage freedom.
Maybe forgiveness is still difficult.
But you find yourself praying for the strength to release someone you once wanted to destroy.
Maybe you still fall.
But you cannot comfortably stay down anymore.
Something keeps calling you back to Jesus.
Do not mistake slow fruit for no fruit.
At the same time, do not use grace as permission to remain unchanged.
That would also contradict Scripture.
The Holy Spirit comforts us, but He does not negotiate peace treaties with the sin that crucified Christ.
Grace is not God saying sin no longer matters.
Grace is God saving sinners who could never save themselves and transforming them into the likeness of His Son.
So if someone says,
“I have the Holy Spirit,”

while deliberately cherishing sin, rejecting Christ's authority, refusing repentance, and having no desire whatsoever for holiness, Scripture gives no basis for casual assurance simply because that person once prayed a prayer, attended church, was baptized, had an emotional experience, or knows Christian vocabulary.
Jesus did not come merely to make bad people feel spiritually secure.
He came to save.
And salvation transforms.
But please hear the other side of this.
Some sincere Christians are torturing themselves because they think real Christians never struggle.
That is not biblical either.
Read Romans 7.
Read Galatians 5.
Read the Psalms.
Read Peter's story.
The Christian life is not the absence of warfare.
It is warfare with a new allegiance.
You may stumble while following Jesus.
Peter did.
You may have moments of terrible weakness.
Peter did.
You may even do something that makes you wonder how you could possibly belong to Christ.
Peter publicly denied that he even knew Jesus.
Imagine that moment.
A charcoal fire.
Questions.
Fear.
One denial.
Another.
Then another.
And somewhere in the darkness, a rooster crowed.
Peter looked toward Jesus.
Jesus looked toward Peter.
And Peter broke.
The man who had promised loyalty suddenly discovered how weak he really was.
But that courtyard was not the final chapter of Peter's story.
There would be another charcoal fire.
John 21.
A risen Jesus.
Breakfast beside the sea.
And the Savior Peter denied did not discard him.
Jesus restored him.
“Do you love Me?”
Three denials.
Three opportunities to confess love.
Failure met grace.
Shame met restoration.
A broken disciple met the resurrected Christ.
Then Peter, the man who collapsed under pressure before a servant girl, would eventually stand publicly and proclaim Jesus.
What changed?
Peter had encountered the risen Christ.
And at Pentecost, the promised Spirit came upon the disciples with power for witness.
This is what grace does.
It does not pretend the scandal never happened.
It refuses to let the scandal have the final word.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Because there is a scandal somewhere in your story.
Something you did.
Something you became.
Something nobody knows.
Something everybody knows.
A secret browser history.
An affair.
An addiction.
A betrayal.
A season when you walked away from God.
A marriage you damaged.
Children you disappointed.
Years you wasted.
Words you cannot take back.
A version of yourself you desperately wish you could erase.
And perhaps you have been asking the wrong question.
“Could God still want someone like me?”
Look at the cross.
Jesus already knew.
Before the nails pierced His hands, He knew.
Before the blood ran down the wood, He knew.
Before the stone rolled away, He knew every chapter you would someday wish you could tear from your story.
And still He went to Calvary.
Not because your sin was small.
Because His grace is greater.
The Spirit's presence does not mean you never grieve over who you have been.
Sometimes it means you finally see who you have been clearly enough to stop defending it.
But conviction is not the destination.
Jesus is.
The Holy Spirit reveals truth, glorifies Christ, leads God's children, produces His fruit, helps believers in weakness, and conforms God's people toward holiness.
And there is another extraordinarily tender evidence Scripture gives us.
Romans 8 describes believers crying:
“Ἀββᾶ ὁ πατήρ”
Abba ho Patēr.
“Abba, Father.”
“Abba” is Aramaic.
It is an intimate address to a father—not childish sentimentality, but the language of relationship.
The Spirit does not merely teach you facts about God.
Through Christ, you are brought into the family of God.
You stop seeing God merely as a distant Judge you must somehow impress.
Through Jesus, you begin approaching Him as Father.
Sometimes confidently.
Sometimes crying.
Sometimes crawling.
Sometimes barely able to pray.
And Romans 8 even speaks into those moments when words disappear.
When grief becomes too heavy.
When you kneel beside your bed and nothing comes out.
When your prayer is barely more than:
Scripture says the Spirit helps us in our weakness.
So no, the evidence of the Spirit is not that you always feel spiritually powerful.
Sometimes His presence is revealed in your weakness.
You are still praying when part of you wanted to quit.
Still returning to Scripture.
Still confessing.
Still fighting.
Still reaching toward Jesus.
Still whispering His name through tears.
Still refusing to make permanent peace with the sin trying to reclaim you.
Still here.
And maybe you need to hear this:
Your struggle does not save you. Jesus does.
Your tears do not save you.
Your church attendance does not save you.
Your ministry does not save you.
Your baptism does not purchase salvation.
Your good behavior does not purchase salvation.
Your ability to feel the Holy Spirit does not purchase salvation.
Christ saves.
The question is ultimately not:
“Am I impressive enough to prove the Spirit lives in me?”
It is:
“Have I truly come to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith?”
Because when Paul describes believers being sealed with the Spirit in Ephesians 1:13, he connects it with hearing the word of truth—the Gospel of salvation—and believing in Christ.
The center is Jesus.
Always Jesus.
Crucified.
Risen.
Lord.
Savior.
King.
So examine yourself, but do not spend your entire Christian life staring at yourself.
A person looking constantly at his own spiritual pulse can eventually become as self-absorbed as someone living openly for sin.
Look to Christ.
Ask Him to expose what needs exposing.
Ask Him to kill what needs killing.
Ask Him to heal what needs healing.
Ask Him to teach you obedience.

Ask Him to make the fruit of His Spirit increasingly visible in your relationships, your marriage, your private habits, your finances, your sexuality, your speech, your temper, your ambitions, your wounds, your phone, your thoughts, and your treatment of people who can do absolutely nothing for you.
And if something inside you is saying right now,
“I want Jesus. I am tired of pretending. I am tired of hiding. I want to repent. I want Him to change me”...
do not bury that moment beneath another scroll.
Come to Christ.
Tell Him the truth.
No performance.
No religious speech.
No pretending.
Confess the sin.
Trust the Savior.
Ask God to search you.
Open His Word.
And follow Jesus.
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not the only person fighting.
Your honesty may become somebody else's courage.
Then think of one person who needs this message.
Not fifty random people.
One.
The friend quietly drifting from God.
The believer who keeps questioning their salvation.
The person trapped in shame.
The Christian who thinks temptation means God abandoned them.
The person who stopped attending church because they believe their scandal made them permanently disqualified.
Send this to them.
Not because sharing a Christian article earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Christ alone saves, and grace cannot be bought.
But if this biblical message can help another person look toward Jesus, sharing it is one practical way you can use the platform God has placed in your hands to serve others and glorify Him.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite the Christian who has grown cold.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who has questions about Jesus.
Because there may come another night when you fail.
Another night when accusation gets loud.
Another night when you wonder whether God has abandoned you.
Come back and remember what Scripture actually says.
The Spirit's presence is not proven by your ability to manufacture a spiritual feeling.
Look for His fingerprints.
Christ becoming precious.
Sin becoming grievous.
Truth becoming desirable.
Repentance becoming necessary.
Holiness becoming beautiful.
Love beginning to grow.
Forgiveness becoming possible.
Self-control slowly strengthening.
Prayer becoming instinctive.
Scripture becoming food.
Pride being exposed.
Compassion deepening.
Your heart crying, “Abba, Father.”
And after falling...
again...
your soul somehow turning toward Jesus.
Do not worship the evidence.
Worship Christ.
Do not trust the fruit instead of the Savior.
Trust Christ—and recognize that the Spirit who unites believers to Christ does not leave them untouched.
Perhaps you are not where you want to be.
Perhaps you are embarrassed by how far you still have to go.
Perhaps your life does not look dramatic enough to become somebody's viral testimony.
But maybe the miracle is quieter.
You used to love darkness.
Now you hate what darkness does to you.
You used to run from Jesus.
Now even when you stumble, you keep running back.
You used to protect your sin.
Now you are asking God to destroy its power over you.
You used to want Christianity without surrender.
Now, trembling, you are beginning to whisper:
“Jesus... You can have all of me.”
That whisper may not impress the internet.
But heaven is not measuring you by internet applause.
Keep looking to Christ.
Keep repenting.
Keep believing the Gospel.
Keep walking by the Spirit.
Keep returning when you fall.
Keep opening Scripture.
Keep praying when prayer feels dry.
Keep allowing God to expose the rooms of your heart you would rather keep locked.
Because the Holy Spirit did not come merely to make you feel something.
He came to glorify Jesus Christ and transform God's people.
And one day the war with sin will end.
Faith will become sight.
The believer who spent years whispering “Jesus, help me” will finally see the face of the One who never stopped holding them.
Until then...
keep fighting.
Keep trusting.
Keep coming home.
And never forget this:
The clearest evidence that grace has entered your story may not be that you never fall again—but that you can no longer make a home on the ground when Jesus keeps calling you to rise and follow Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT THE BIBLE’S BROKEN MARRIAGES REVEAL THAT HAPPY COUPLES CAN EASILY MISS
paragraphs: WHAT THE BIBLE’S BROKEN MARRIAGES REVEAL THAT HAPPY COUPLES CAN EASILY MISS
The Greatest Lesson Is Not How to Find the Perfect Spouse—It Is What Happens When Sin Enters a Covenant, Grace Meets the Wreckage, and Jesus Christ Becomes Our Only Perfect Bridegroom
Some of the most uncomfortable marriage stories in the Bible were never cleaned up for church.
God could have given us a Bible filled only with faithful husbands, devoted wives, peaceful homes, restored relationships, and marriages that ended exactly the way everyone prayed they would.
He didn’t.
Instead, Scripture lets us walk into homes where jealousy is growing.
Into bedrooms where betrayal has happened.
Into marriages distorted by lust, manipulation, favoritism, bitterness, hardness of heart, abandonment, infertility, cultural corruption, selfish ambition, and sin.
Abraham and Sarah knew marital tension complicated by fear, impatience, and Hagar.
Isaac and Rebekah’s household became divided by parental favoritism.
Jacob entered a family arrangement poisoned by deception and spent years inside a home fractured by rivalry between Leah and Rachel.
David’s marriage to Michal deteriorated tragically.
Hosea was commanded into a marriage that would become a living prophetic sign of Israel’s unfaithfulness toward God.
And when Jesus was questioned about divorce, He did something remarkable.
He did not pretend broken marriages were imaginary.
He went deeper.
He went after the heart.
That may be the greatest lesson hidden inside the Bible’s broken marriages:
Marriage problems are rarely only marriage problems.

Eventually, Scripture takes us beneath the argument, beneath the betrayal, beneath the silence, beneath the resentment, beneath the slammed door, beneath the separate beds, beneath the tears nobody sees...
and confronts the human heart.
Maybe that is why this subject hurts.
Because some people reading this are married but lonely.
Some are divorced and still wondering what they could have done differently.
Some were betrayed.
Some did the betraying.
Some begged another person to stay.
Some stayed far longer than anyone knows.
Some destroyed something beautiful through choices they would give almost anything to undo.
Some came from homes where “marriage” meant screaming, manipulation, fear, infidelity, or watching two people slowly become strangers.
And some are smiling publicly while privately wondering:
“How did we become this?”
If that question has ever lived inside you, keep reading.
Because the Bible does not tell these broken stories merely so we can stare at other people’s failures.
It tells them because, sooner or later, we recognize ourselves.
Go back to the beginning.
Before divorce lawyers.
Before adultery.
Before pornography.
Before emotional affairs.
Before resentment.
Before “irreconcilable differences.”
Before sin itself entered human experience, Scripture describes marriage with extraordinary language:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
Genesis 2:24.
The Hebrew says:
וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ
“vedavaq be’ishto” — “and he shall cling to his wife.”
That word דָּבַק, davaq, carries the idea of clinging, adhering, holding fast.
Then Scripture says:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
“vehayu levasar echad” — “and they shall become one flesh.”
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד.
Basar echad.
One flesh.
Not merely two people sharing an address.
Not merely two people wearing rings.
Not merely romance sustained by chemistry.
Something covenantal and profoundly unitive has happened.
This is so foundational that when Jesus speaks about marriage in Matthew 19, He reaches back beyond the dysfunction of His listeners, beyond later disputes, all the way to creation.
He quotes Genesis and declares:
“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
Then comes the painful question.
If this is God’s design, why are marriages shattered?
Jesus answers with words that should make every married and unmarried person examine themselves.
“Because of the hardness of your hearts...”
Matthew 19:8.
The Greek expression is:
σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν
sklērokardian hymōn.
“The hardness of your hearts.”
σκληροκαρδία—sklērokardia—is where we get the image of a hardened heart.
Suddenly, the conversation is no longer merely about legal paperwork.
Jesus has exposed something deeper.
The heart can become hard.
A husband can stop listening.
A wife can stop forgiving.
Desire can become entitlement.
Hurt can become resentment.
Resentment can become contempt.
Attention can wander.
Truth can become inconvenient.
Secret messages can become emotional dependency.
A private fantasy can become an addiction.
An apology can be delayed until pride becomes stronger than tenderness.
Two people who once could not imagine life apart can eventually sit three feet from each other and feel three thousand miles away.
And here is where we must be careful.
The Bible does not teach that every broken marriage has two equally guilty people.
That would be cruel, simplistic, and biblically irresponsible.

Scripture recognizes serious covenant-breaking sins. Jesus explicitly addresses sexual immorality in Matthew 19:9. Paul addresses abandonment by an unbelieving spouse in 1 Corinthians 7:15. Scripture repeatedly condemns violence, oppression, treachery, exploitation, and abuse of power.
So this article must never be weaponized against someone experiencing abuse.
“Submit harder” is not a biblical excuse for someone else to terrorize you.
“Forgive” does not mean pretending evil is good.

Reconciliation and forgiveness are related, but they are not identical. Genuine reconciliation requires truth, repentance, and the rebuilding of trust; forgiveness does not magically erase consequences.
And repentance is not saying, “Sorry you got hurt.”
Repentance turns.
The New Testament word μετάνοια—metanoia—speaks of repentance, a changed mind and turning that produces a changed direction.
Biblical grace does not make sin less serious.
Grace is astonishing precisely because sin is serious.
Look at Hosea.
Few biblical marriages have been preached about more dramatically, and few should be handled more carefully.

God commands Hosea’s family life to function as a prophetic sign exposing Israel’s covenant unfaithfulness. Hosea’s painful domestic imagery becomes a window through which God reveals the horror of His people abandoning Him for other gods.
But Hosea should never be reduced to the message, “If your spouse continually betrays or abuses you, God requires you to stay no matter what.”
That is not the point of the book.
The central scandal is larger.
Israel has been unfaithful to God.
Yet God’s covenant love remains breathtaking.
In Hosea 2:19, God says of His people:
“I will betroth thee unto me for ever...”
The Hebrew verb is אָרַשׂ—’aras—to betroth.
The betrayed God speaks the language of restoration.
That should stop us.
Because eventually Hosea’s story stops being merely about “those unfaithful Israelites.”
It becomes a mirror.
We are the wanderers.
Humanity has betrayed its Creator.
We have loved created things more than the Creator.
We have demanded God’s gifts while resisting God Himself.
We have hidden sins.
Protected idols.
Excused lust.
Fed pride.
Nursed bitterness.
Broken promises.
Worshiped approval.
Chased money.
Desired people and things we had no right to possess.
We have wanted the blessings of God while sometimes wishing God would stay out of the rooms we keep locked.
That is spiritual adultery.
And still...
God pursued sinners.
This is where the broken marriages of Scripture ultimately push us beyond marriage.
They push us toward the Gospel.
Because if you read the Bible looking only for marriage advice, you can miss the Bridegroom standing at the center of redemption.
Jesus Christ.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5 that the mystery of marriage ultimately points beyond husband and wife:
“This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.”
The Greek word translated “mystery” is μυστήριον—mystērion.
Paul is telling us that marriage carries a meaning greater than itself.
Christian marriage is meant to point toward Christ and His Church.
And suddenly the deepest tragedy of human unfaithfulness meets the greatest faithfulness imaginable.
We failed.
Christ remained faithful.
We sinned.
Christ came for sinners.
We accumulated guilt.
Christ went to the cross.
We deserved judgment.
Christ bore judgment for His people.
We wandered.
The Shepherd came searching.
We could not cleanse ourselves.
His blood cleanses.
We could not resurrect ourselves.
He rose.
This is Christianity.
Not broken people pretending to be whole.
Broken sinners being reconciled to a holy God through the crucified and risen Son.
The Gospel is not that Jesus helps respectable people maintain respectable lives.
The Gospel is that Jesus saves sinners.
And that changes the way we understand broken marriages.
Maybe your marriage survived infidelity.
Maybe it didn’t.
Maybe you were the faithful spouse.
Maybe you were the one who detonated everything.
Maybe both of you spent years wounding each other.
Maybe you are remarried and still carry memories you wish you could erase.
Maybe you are single but terrified that your future will resemble your parents’ marriage.
Maybe your spouse walked away from Christ.
Maybe you prayed for restoration and did not receive the ending you desperately wanted.
Hear this carefully:
Jesus Christ is not merely the repairman for your preferred ending.
He is Lord.
And redemption does not always mean God recreates the exact life you lost.
Sometimes relationships can be genuinely restored, and praise God when repentance, forgiveness, wisdom, safety, and patient rebuilding make that possible.
Sometimes consequences remain.
Sometimes trust takes years to rebuild.
Sometimes a marriage does not survive.
Sometimes a person sincerely repents after damage that cannot simply be reversed.
But no repentant sinner is beyond the reach of Christ.
That distinction matters.
The Bible never promises that every broken marriage will be restored if someone prays hard enough.
It promises something greater than a guaranteed earthly outcome.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
Romans 8:1.
There is a sentence someone reading this desperately needs.
No condemnation does not mean no accountability.
No condemnation does not mean your choices did not hurt anyone.
No condemnation does not mean consequences disappear.
It means that for the person who belongs to Christ, the verdict of eternal condemnation has been answered at the cross.
Your worst chapter does not possess greater authority than the blood of Jesus.
That does not give you permission to minimize what happened.
It gives you courage to finally tell the truth about it.
Maybe the first miracle your marriage needs is not your spouse changing.
Maybe it is you standing before God without your rehearsed defense.
No blaming.
No “but she...”
No “but he...”
No “you don’t understand what they did first.”
Just truth.
“Lord, this is what I became.”
“Lord, this is what I did.”
“Lord, this is what I have been hiding.”
“Lord, I have become cold.”
“Lord, I have lusted.”
“Lord, I have lied.”
“Lord, I have manipulated.”
“Lord, I have withheld affection to punish.”
“Lord, I have worshiped being right more than I have loved.”
“Lord, have mercy on me.”
That prayer is dangerous to pride.
But beautiful to grace.
Because the Gospel does not begin where excuses survive.
It begins where sinners realize they need a Savior.
And perhaps you were the one sinned against.
Your confession may sound different.
“Jesus, I cannot carry this bitterness anymore.”
“I cannot make what happened unhappen.”
“I cannot force another human being to repent.”
“I cannot manufacture reconciliation.”
“I cannot keep allowing someone else’s sin to become the center of my identity.”
“Teach me what obedience, wisdom, forgiveness, justice, truth, and healing look like now.”
That too can be surrender.
Jesus does not ask you to call darkness light.
He calls you to come to Him in the darkness.
This is why the greatest lesson from the Bible’s broken marriages is not simply “choose your spouse carefully,” although wisdom matters.
It is not simply “communicate better,” although communication matters.
It is not “never get divorced,” spoken without biblical context, compassion, or attention to what Scripture actually teaches.
The deeper lesson is this:
Sin destroys what God designed for love, covenant, and faithfulness—but human failure does not exhaust the redemptive power of Jesus Christ.
Marriage needs more than romance.
It needs hearts continually brought under the lordship of Christ.
A wedding can change your legal status in a day.
Only God can keep transforming your heart for a lifetime.
The greatest threat to marriage is not that two imperfect people discover each other’s imperfections.
That was inevitable.
The danger comes when imperfect people stop bringing those imperfections into the light of Christ.
When pride stops confession.
When shame stops honesty.
When lust demands secrecy.
When resentment becomes identity.
When winning becomes more important than loving.
When the marriage becomes an idol.
Or when the spouse becomes an enemy.
Jesus said:
“Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.”
Matthew 12:34.
Eventually, what fills the heart leaks into the home.
So before asking, “How do I fix my marriage?” there may be another question worth asking:
“What is happening inside my heart before God?”
Not your spouse’s heart.
Yours.
Because you cannot repent for your spouse.
You cannot believe for your spouse.
You cannot surrender for your spouse.
You cannot force another person to become faithful.
But you can stand before Jesus yourself.
And that is where transformation begins.
Perhaps you are reading this while lying beside someone who no longer feels close.
Put the phone down when you finish and pray.
Perhaps you are reading this after a divorce.
Do not turn your divorce into your permanent name.
Perhaps you committed adultery and have genuinely repented.
Do not confuse endless self-hatred with holiness. Make restitution where appropriate. Accept consequences. Walk transparently. Seek pastoral accountability. Become faithful now.
Perhaps somebody cheated on you.
Their betrayal does not make you worthless.
Perhaps you are single.

Learn from these stories before you make a covenant. Do not marry merely because someone gives you butterflies. Ask whether both of you are learning to bow before Jesus when obedience costs something.
Perhaps your marriage is healthy.
Do not become arrogant.
Protect it.
Pray.
Confess quickly.
Forgive biblically.
Guard your eyes.
Guard your private conversations.
Guard your thought life.
Refuse to nurture secret versions of yourself.
Keep dating your spouse.
Keep listening.
Keep learning.
Keep Christ at the center—not as Christian decoration hanging on the wall, but as Lord.
Because marriages usually do not collapse in a single dramatic second.
There are often small compromises before public catastrophes.
One hidden conversation.
One unresolved wound.
One secret search.
One lie that required another lie.
One apology never spoken.
One flirtation entertained.
One bitterness rehearsed until it felt righteous.
One spiritual compromise nobody else could see.
And then one day people look at the ruins and ask:
“How did we get here?”
Slowly.
And sometimes healing happens the same way.
Slowly.
One confession.
One boundary.
One counseling appointment.
One act of obedience.
One difficult conversation.
One deleted contact.
One night of honest prayer.
One decision to stop lying.
One decision to ask forgiveness without demanding immediate trust.
One morning choosing faithfulness again.
One day.
Then another.
Then another.
Grace is not permission to keep destroying.
Grace teaches us to live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 says the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live self-controlled, upright, godly lives.
Real grace has muscle.
It confronts.
Corrects.
Forgives.
Trains.
Transforms.
This is why “From Scandal to Grace” is more than a beautiful phrase.
It is the shape of the Gospel.
Scandal says, “Look what you did.”
Grace says, “Look what Christ has done.”
Scandal exposes the wound.
Grace does not deny the wound; it brings it to the Physician.
Scandal remembers your failure as your identity.
Grace tells the repentant believer that identity is now found in Christ.
Scandal whispers, “Hide.”
Jesus says, “Come.”
Scandal says, “You ruined everything, so there is nothing left.”
The Gospel says the crucified Savior walked out of a grave.
And Christians should be the last people on earth to believe resurrection is impossible.
That does not mean every dead relationship will resurrect.
It means no sinner should measure the power of God by the condition of one earthly relationship.
Jesus is greater than your marriage.
Jesus is greater than your divorce.
Jesus is greater than your betrayal.
Jesus is greater than your loneliness.
Jesus is greater than the family you came from.
Jesus is greater than the mistake you cannot undo.
Jesus is greater than the shame that still wakes you at 2:00 in the morning.
And if you are His, your story does not end at the scene where everything broke.
The cross looked like the end too.
Then came Sunday.
Talk to Jesus.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Seek wise, biblically grounded pastoral care or professional help where necessary.

If there is abuse, coercion, violence, or immediate danger, pursue safety and appropriate outside help. Do not use this article—or anyone’s misuse of Scripture—as a reason to remain silently endangered.
And if your heart is simply exhausted, you do not need an impressive prayer.
“Jesus, help me” is still a prayer.
Maybe someone you know needs these words.
Not so you can indirectly shame them.
Not so you can post it with, “Somebody needs to read this.”
And maybe even send it privately to someone who would never admit publicly that their home is hurting.
If this exposed something you have been hiding from God, comment, “Jesus forgive me.”
If you are exhausted but still fighting for faithfulness, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If your heart has been carrying wounds nobody around you understands, simply comment, “pray for me.”
If Christ has been restoring you after failure, betrayal, divorce, shame, or years of regret, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Your comment may become the sentence another wounded person reads and realizes they are not the only one desperately reaching for Jesus.
Because conviction can feel painfully clear tonight and strangely distant tomorrow.
Come back when pride returns.
Come back when resentment whispers.
Come back when temptation tells you secrecy will cost nothing.
Come back when shame tells you Christ could forgive everyone except you.
It does not.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
God is not glorified by financial pressure, manipulation, or giving motivated by guilt.
God is glorified when His people respond to grace with willing obedience, generosity, love, and a desire to see truth carried to others.
Come to Christ.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot save your marriage.
A pastor cannot save your soul.
A Christian book cannot wash away your sins.
Jesus saves.
If you have never truly surrendered to Him, do not mistake Christian content for Christianity.
Turn from sin.
Believe the Gospel.
Trust the One who died for sinners and rose again.
And if you already belong to Christ, stop protecting the parts of your heart you know He is confronting.
Bring Him the marriage.
Bring Him the divorce.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the resentment.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the loneliness.
Bring Him the guilt.
Bring Him the shattered photograph of the life you thought you were going to have.
Bring Him the scandal.
Because the final lesson of the Bible’s broken marriages is not that human beings became exceptionally good at keeping covenants.
It is that we desperately needed Someone who would never break His.
Jesus Christ is that faithful One.
And perhaps the most beautiful thing God will rewrite is not the marriage you desperately want Him to change.
Perhaps He will begin with the heart reading these words.
Because sometimes the place where your story looks most irreparably broken becomes the very place where you finally discover that grace was never afraid of the ruins.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: God’s Battle Plan Was to Walk Around a City for Seven Days. Then the Walls Collapsed.
paragraphs: God’s Battle Plan Was to Walk Around a City for Seven Days. Then the Walls Collapsed.

Jericho looked impossible. God’s instructions looked unreasonable. Israel’s weapons were not enough. And before a single stone fell, God was teaching His people a truth we still struggle to believe: sometimes the wall in front of you is not merely something God intends to remove. Sometimes it is the place where He exposes what you actually trust.
There is something almost uncomfortable about the battle plan.
Walk.
That was part of it.
Not charge.
Not build siege ramps.
Not spend the night calculating where the defenses were weakest.
Walk around the city.
Then go back to camp.
Wake up the next day.
Walk around it again.
And again.
And again.
For six days.
Then, on the seventh day, circle Jericho seven times.
Priests would carry trumpets. The ark of the covenant would go with them. The people would remain under Joshua’s command concerning when to shout.
And after all of that strange obedience…
the walls would fall.
If you already know the story, familiarity can make it sound almost easy.
It was not.
Imagine being there.
You have crossed the Jordan. The promise is in front of you. But standing between you and the next step is a fortified city.
Jericho.
Joshua 6:1 describes the situation with striking Hebrew:
וִירִיחוֹ סֹגֶרֶת וּמְסֻגֶּרֶת
Vîrîḥô sōgeret ûmesuggeret.
The sense is that Jericho was tightly shut up—closed and secured.
The verse continues:
אֵין יוֹצֵא וְאֵין בָּא
’Ên yōṣē’ we’ên bā’.
“No one went out, and no one came in.”
Jericho was not casually waiting for Israel.
It was sealed.
Defensive.
Inaccessible.
And perhaps that is why this story still reaches into places we would rather keep hidden.
Because some of us know exactly what it feels like to stand in front of something that will not move.
You prayed.
Still there.
You cried.
Still there.
You tried to change.
Still there.
You promised God that this time would be different.
Still there.
The addiction still whispers.
The resentment still burns.
The shame still remembers your name.
The marriage still hurts.
The prodigal still has not come home.
The grief still wakes up before you do.
The temptation still knows where to find you.
The consequences of yesterday are still standing in the middle of today.
And somewhere inside your exhausted heart, you have begun asking the question faithful people sometimes feel guilty for asking:
“God… if You brought me this far, why is there still a wall?”
Then God speaks to Joshua.
And notice something astonishing.
The wall is still standing when God says:
רְאֵה נָתַתִּי בְיָדְךָ אֶת־יְרִיחוֹ
Re’eh, nātattî beyādekha ’et-Yerîḥô.

“See, I have given Jericho into your hand.”
—Joshua 6:2
Look carefully at the wording.
Jericho has not fallen yet.
Israel has not marched around it yet.
The trumpet has not sounded.
The people have not shouted.
Dust has not begun falling from the walls.
Yet God speaks of the victory as something He has given.
The Hebrew נָתַתִּי — nātattî comes from the verb natan, “to give.”
God does not begin by congratulating Israel on its military strength.
He begins with His gift.
That changes the center of the story.
Jericho is not primarily a monument to Israelite ingenuity.
It is a testimony to the God who keeps His word.
But here is where the story becomes painfully personal.
God promised the victory…
and then required Israel to obey Him while the wall still looked exactly like a wall.
That is where many of us struggle.
We want obedience after explanation.
God often calls us to obedience because He is trustworthy.
We want to understand the entire route before taking the next step.
God sometimes gives enough light for the next faithful step and asks us to trust Him with what we cannot yet see.

Israel was told to march around Jericho once each day for six days. Seven priests were to carry seven trumpets before the ark. On the seventh day, they were to circle the city seven times. Then, at Joshua’s command, the people were to shout.
Imagine the first day.
Footsteps.
Trumpets.
A fortified city towering above them.
Then they return to camp.
Nothing.
Second day.
Walk.
Return.
The wall is still there.
Third day.
Still there.
Fourth day.
Still there.
Fifth day.
Still there.
Sixth day.
Still standing.
Have you ever obeyed God and watched absolutely nothing seem to happen?
That can be one of the loneliest places in faith.
You forgave, but the wound still aches.
You stopped going back to the sin, but temptation did not stop coming back to you.
You opened your Bible again, but heaven did not suddenly feel close.
You started praying for your family, but they still seem far from Christ.
You chose integrity and lost an opportunity because of it.
You repented, but now you must live through consequences repentance does not instantly erase.
You have been walking…
and walking…
and walking…
and the wall has had the audacity to remain standing.
Maybe the miracle of Jericho did not begin when stones started falling.
Maybe, from the human side of the story, one of the first miracles was that Israel kept walking when the stones had not moved.
Faith is not pretending the wall is imaginary.
Biblical faith looks at the wall, hears the Word of God, and decides that the wall does not get the final word.
But Jericho must never be reduced to a motivational slogan.
This is not Scripture telling you to “manifest your breakthrough.”
It is not a divine formula promising that if you repeat something seven times, every financial problem, illness, relationship crisis, or personal dream will resolve exactly as you want.
Joshua 6 records a specific moment in God’s redemptive history, connected to His covenant purposes and His judgment upon Canaan.

The number seven is unmistakably repeated throughout the chapter—seven priests, seven trumpets, seven days, seven circuits on the seventh day—but the passage does not authorize Christians to turn seven into a magical technique.
The power was never in the number.
The power was never in Israel’s footsteps.
The power was never in the volume of their shout.
The power belonged to God.
And that matters because we are always tempted to turn gifts from God into formulas for controlling God.
“Maybe if I pray exactly like this…”
“Maybe if I give enough…”
“Maybe if I say the right words…”
“Maybe if I become spiritual enough…”
Then God will owe me my Jericho.
No.
Grace does not put God in our debt.
Faith does not manipulate Him.
God is God.
We are not.
And sometimes faithfulness ends with a wall collapsing.
Sometimes faithfulness looks like Paul pleading three times for the thorn to leave and hearing Christ say, “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:8–9).
Sometimes faithfulness looks like Jesus in Gethsemane praying, “Not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42).
The Christian hope is not that God must make every earthly circumstance obey our preferred ending.
Our hope is that because of Jesus Christ, even suffering, waiting, weakness, persecution, loss, and death cannot separate God’s children from His love.
That is a much stronger Gospel than “God will give you whatever breakthrough you imagine.”
Then comes the seventh day.
They rise early.
Once around Jericho.
Twice.
Three times.
Four.
Five.
Six.
Imagine the exhaustion.
Imagine staring at the same stones you saw yesterday.
Then…
seven.
Joshua tells the people to shout.
The trumpets sound.
And Joshua 6:20 records:
וַתִּפֹּל הַחוֹמָה תַּחְתֶּיהָ
Vattippōl haḥômāh taḥtehā.
“And the wall fell down in its place,” commonly rendered along the sense of the wall falling down flat.
The wall that had announced, “You cannot enter,” was suddenly on the ground.
But if we stop there, we risk turning Jericho into nothing more than an inspirational victory story.
Joshua 6 is also a chapter of judgment.
That part should not be hidden because it makes modern readers uncomfortable.
The city was placed under חֵרֶם — ḥērem, a Hebrew term used in this context for something devoted to destruction under divine judgment.
This is difficult Scripture.
It should be treated with sobriety, not celebrated with bloodthirsty triumphalism.

According to the biblical storyline, Israel was not given a universal permission slip for religious violence. The conquest belongs to a particular covenantal and historical setting in which God acts as Judge. Deuteronomy had already made clear that Israel's possession of the land was not because Israel was inherently righteous (Deuteronomy 9:4–6), and the same covenant later warned Israel that persistent rebellion would bring judgment upon them too.
God is not tribal property.
He cannot be recruited to baptize our hatred.
Jericho should make us tremble before divine holiness as much as it makes us marvel at divine power.
And then, inside a city marked for judgment, Scripture gives us a scandal.
Rahab.
A woman with a past.
A Canaanite.
An outsider.
A woman Scripture identifies as a prostitute.
If human beings were writing a respectable religious story designed to impress respectable religious people, Rahab might have been edited out.
God did not edit her out.
Earlier, in Joshua 2, Rahab had hidden Israel’s spies and confessed what she had come to believe about Israel’s God:
“The LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.”
When Jericho fell, Rahab and those with her were spared according to the promise made to her.
Read that slowly.
Judgment was falling.
Walls were collapsing.
A city was being conquered.
And grace knew Rahab’s address.
That is where Jericho begins pointing beyond Jericho.
Because Rahab does not disappear after Joshua.
Her name appears again.
And again.
Then centuries later, Matthew begins telling the story of Jesus Christ.
There, in the genealogy of the Messiah, stands a name some people might have preferred to hide.
Rahab.
Matthew 1:5 names her in the ancestry that leads to Jesus.
Hebrews 11:31 remembers her faith.
James 2:25 remembers the action that demonstrated it.
The woman who once lived inside the doomed city became part of the human family line through which the Messiah entered the world.
Tell me grace is not scandalous.
Her past did not become good.
Her sin did not become holy.
But her past was no longer powerful enough to cancel what God, in grace, was doing with her future.
That is the difference between biblical grace and cheap affirmation.
Jesus does not call darkness light.
He rescues sinners from darkness.
He does not rewrite our story by pretending our sin never mattered.
At the cross, He shows us exactly how much sin matters.
And then He shows us how much mercy costs.
Jericho had walls made of stone.
We build different kinds.
Pornography behind a locked screen.
Bitterness behind a smile.
Pride behind ministry.
Greed behind ambition.
Loneliness behind jokes.
Envy behind congratulations.
Lust behind secrecy.
Unforgiveness behind “I’m fine.”
Fear behind control.
Religious performance behind church attendance.
Some walls are built to keep other people out.
Others are built because we are terrified someone will discover what is inside.
And perhaps the most dangerous wall is the one we construct between our public Christianity and our private life.
People know the worship version of us.
God knows what happens when the music stops.
People see the verse we posted.
God sees the message we deleted.
People hear the testimony.
God remembers the compromise we are still protecting.
People call us strong.
God hears us crying at 2:13 in the morning.
And still…
He calls us.
Not into better hiding.
Into repentance.
The Gospel is not Jesus standing outside your carefully fortified life shouting, “Pretend harder.”
The Gospel is Christ calling sinners out of hiding.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia for repentance, carrying the sense of a change of mind that turns a person toward God.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Judas felt terrible.
Repentance turns.
It stops negotiating with the sin Jesus died to save us from.
It stops calling bondage “just who I am.”
It stops protecting what God is exposing.
It stops decorating the wall.
And it comes to Christ.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Not because you needed another article about an ancient city.
Because there is a wall in you.
Something you have been defending.
Something exhausting you.
Something nobody knows.
Something you keep promising to surrender “eventually.”
And perhaps the Holy Spirit has been putting His finger on it for longer than you want to admit.
Be careful here.
Do not turn Jericho into permission to name another person as “your wall” and imagine God exists to destroy everyone standing in your way.
Before asking God to bring down the walls around you, ask Him what must come down within you.
Your pride.
Your secret sin.
Your self-righteousness.
Your refusal to forgive.
Your need to control everything.
Your obsession with human approval.
Your belief that your worst chapter has made redemption impossible.
Because the deepest Christian victory is not getting everything we want.
It is belonging completely to Jesus.
And Jesus takes us somewhere even more astonishing than Jericho.
Jericho tells us about a city under judgment where one household receives mercy.
Calvary tells us about the sinless Son of God willingly bearing judgment so sinners could receive mercy.
At Jericho, a shout accompanied the fall of a wall.
At Calvary, Jesus cried out and gave up His spirit.
At Jericho, Rahab was brought out of a condemned city.
At Calvary, Christ opened the way for condemned sinners to be reconciled to God.
And on the third day, the stone meant to seal a grave could not imprison the risen King.
That is our center.
Not Jericho.
Jesus.
Not your breakthrough.
Jesus.
Not your success.
Jesus.
Not a better version of your old self.
Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
The scandal of Christianity is not that good people can become slightly better.
The scandal is that guilty people can be forgiven because the righteous Christ gave Himself for sinners.
Paul writes in Romans 5:8 that God demonstrates His love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
While.
We.
Were.
Still.
Sinners.
Rahab had a history.
Peter had a denial.
Paul had blood on his résumé.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Yet grace reached where human respectability could not.
This does not make sin small.
It makes the Savior magnificent.
Maybe you thought Christianity was about becoming clean enough for Jesus to tolerate you.
It is the opposite.
You come because you cannot cleanse yourself.
You repent.
You believe.
You entrust yourself to Christ.
You stop defending the ruins.
You stop hiding behind the wall.
You stop trying to become your own savior.
And you discover that the hands strong enough to judge sin are the hands that were pierced to save sinners.
That is why our theme will always be:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by changing history.
Not by pretending your wounds never happened.
Not by renaming evil as good.
Not by erasing every earthly consequence.

He rewrites everything by taking a story headed toward judgment and, through repentance and faith, bringing a sinner into grace, forgiveness, reconciliation, holiness, purpose, and ultimately resurrection life.
Look at Rahab.
Jericho was part of her biography.
It was not the final definition of her identity.
Maybe you need that sentence today.
Your worst chapter may be part of your biography.
It does not have to be the final definition of your identity.
Jesus still saves sinners.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still breaks chains.
Jesus still receives people who finally stop pretending they do not need Him.
Talk to God.
Confess it.
Name it.
Repent.
Ask Christ for mercy.
If you do not know what to pray, begin without impressive religious language.

“Jesus, have mercy on me. Forgive me. I have sinned. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Turn my heart toward You. Teach me to follow You. I surrender what I have been hiding.”
Then do not confuse emotion with completion.
Take the next obedient step.
Open Scripture.
Pray.
Turn away from the sin.
Make restitution where biblical wisdom requires it.
Seek mature Christian accountability.
