Become rooted in a faithful local church where Scripture is taught and Christ is exalted.
Keep walking.
Even when the wall still looks like a wall.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, be brave enough to say it.
Or tell your testimony.
Someone reading the comments may be standing where you once stood.
Your honesty may remind them that grace can reach their Jericho too.
Supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way to help biblical encouragement reach more people. Christ cannot be bought, grace cannot be purchased, and salvation is not merchandise.

Your support helps us keep putting Scripture, conviction, encouragement, discipleship, and the message of Jesus before believers, seekers, struggling Christians, the spiritually exhausted, and people who may never walk through the doors of a church but will stop long enough to read something a friend shared.
Invite your family. Invite the friend whose faith is fading. Invite the believer quietly fighting temptation. Invite the seeker with questions. Invite even the person who says they do not believe.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody behind a screen may be staring at a wall tonight.
Somebody is ashamed.
Somebody is thinking they have gone too far.
Somebody believes Jesus would never want them after what they did.
Somebody has been walking around the same Jericho for years.
Maybe your share becomes the moment they hear:
“Rahab had a past too.”
Maybe they read far enough to hear:
“Christ receives repentant sinners.”
Maybe they open a Bible.
Maybe they pray.
Maybe they come home.
But before you leave, look once more at Jericho.
A sealed city.
An impossible wall.
A strange command.
Days of obedience with no visible result.
Then the trumpet.
The shout.
The collapse.
And walking out from the ruins…
Rahab.
The woman whose past should have made her forgettable became a woman Scripture refused to forget.
Eventually her name would appear in the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ.
That may be the detail your heart needed most.
Because perhaps you have spent years staring at the ruins and assuming ruins are all God can see.
But Jesus sees the repentant sinner who can be redeemed.
You see scandal.
Grace sees a place where redemption can write another ending.
You see the wall.
God sees beyond it.
You see what you were.
Christ calls His people toward what His grace is making them.
So keep walking when obedience feels quiet.
Keep trusting when you cannot see movement.
Keep repenting when pride tells you to hide.
Keep coming to Jesus when shame tells you to run.
And never mistake the silence before the wall falls for the absence of God.
Because one day you may discover that the wall you thought marked the end of your story was standing at the beginning of a testimony.
Jericho remembers the wall that fell. Heaven’s story remembers the woman grace brought out of the ruins.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Does the Devil Attack New Believers?
paragraphs: Why Does the Devil Attack New Believers?

You thought coming to Jesus would end the battle. Then temptation got louder, old wounds reopened, doubts appeared from nowhere, and the person you thought you had left behind started knocking on the door again. What if the battle is not proof that Christ abandoned you—but evidence that you have entered a war you could not see before?
There is a moment many new believers are afraid to admit.
Nobody posts it with the baptism pictures.
Nobody puts it underneath the smiling testimony.
You came to Jesus.
You repented.
You believed.
Maybe you cried when you finally understood that the cross was not merely something Jesus did for humanity in general.
He died for sinners.
For you.
And for the first time in a long time, perhaps the first time ever, you felt clean.
Forgiven.
Wanted.
Alive.
Then something strange happened.
The temptation you expected to disappear came back.
Sometimes harder.
The thoughts became darker.
The doubts became louder.
Old habits started calling your name with a familiarity that frightened you.
People you thought you had outgrown suddenly reappeared.
Memories you buried resurfaced.
Your emotions became unpredictable.
Prayer felt powerful one day and painfully empty the next.
Then came the question you were almost ashamed to ask:
“If Jesus really saved me, why does it feel like I am being attacked more now than before?”
Read this carefully.
Your struggle does not automatically mean your conversion was false.
Temptation does not mean Jesus has rejected you.
Spiritual warfare does not mean Satan owns you.
And the presence of a battle does not mean the absence of God.
In fact, Scripture prepares believers for exactly the opposite expectation.
The Christian life is not Jesus rescuing you so that you never face another battle.
It is Jesus rescuing you from the kingdom of darkness, making you His own, teaching you to stand, and promising that the enemy who accuses you will not have the final word.
That distinction matters.
Because if Satan can convince a new believer that temptation equals abandonment, he does not have to destroy that believer.
He only has to make that believer despair.
And despair whispers:
“You haven't changed.”
“You're still disgusting.”
“God is tired of forgiving you.”
“Look what you thought during prayer.”
“Look what you did again.”
“You might as well go back.”
That voice sounds devastating because it mixes accusation with things you genuinely regret.
But the Gospel does something accusation never does.
The Gospel tells the truth about your sin without lying about your Savior.
Scripture describes the devil as an adversary. Peter warned Christians:
“Your adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour.” — 1 Peter 5:8
The Greek word translated “adversary” is ἀντίδικος — antidikos.
It carries the sense of an opponent, an adversary, even one standing against another in a legal dispute.
Peter does not tell believers to pretend the enemy is imaginary.
But notice what comes next.
“Resist him, steadfast in the faith.” — 1 Peter 5:9
Not worship him.
Not obsess over him.
Not fear him as though he were equal to God.
Resist him.
Christianity is not cosmic dualism in which God and Satan are two equal powers fighting to see who wins.
Satan is a creature.
God is Creator.
The devil is dangerous, but he is not sovereign.
He is not omnipotent.
He is not omniscient.
He is not omnipresent.
And at the cross, Jesus did not negotiate with darkness.
He triumphed.
Paul writes that God “delivered us from the power of darkness and conveyed us into the kingdom of the Son of His love.” — Colossians 1:13
The Greek verb translated “delivered” is ἐρρύσατο — errysato, from ῥύομαι — rhyomai, carrying the idea of rescue or deliverance.
That is the identity of the Christian.
Rescued.
Transferred.
Belonging to Christ.
So why would a new believer experience spiritual resistance?
Because salvation changes allegiance.

Before Christ, Scripture describes humanity not as spiritually neutral, but as dead in trespasses and sins, following the course of this world and living under the influence of “the prince of the power of the air” (Ephesians 2:1–3).
Then comes one of the most beautiful interruptions in Scripture:
“But God…”
“But God, who is rich in mercy, because of His great love with which He loved us…” — Ephesians 2:4
That is Christianity in two words.
But God.
You were guilty.
But God.
You were wandering.
But God.
You were spiritually dead.
But God.
Your past had written an ugly story.
But God.
Grace entered the scandal.
Jesus stepped into the wreckage.
And the Author began rewriting everything.
This is why the enemy's attacks so often aim at identity.
Think about the temptation of Jesus.
After His baptism, the Father declared:
“This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” — Matthew 3:17
Then Jesus entered the wilderness.
The tempter came and said:
“If You are the Son of God…” — Matthew 4:3
Do you see the pattern?
The Father had spoken identity.
Then the tempter challenged it.

Of course, Jesus' sonship is unique; He is the eternal Son of God, and Christians do not share His divine identity. But the temptation account reveals something important about Satan's strategy: he challenges truth with distortion.
And new believers are especially vulnerable when they do not yet know Scripture well enough to recognize the counterfeit.
God says forgiven.
Accusation says filthy.
God says adopted.
Accusation says unwanted.
God says come boldly to the throne of grace.
Accusation says hide until you fix yourself.
God says confess.
Accusation says conceal.
God says repent and return.
Accusation says run and disappear.
This is why learning Scripture is not optional decoration for the Christian life.
It is survival.
When Jesus was tempted, He repeatedly answered:
γέγραπται — gegraptai.
“It is written.”
Not “I feel.”
Not “I suppose.”
Not “Someone online told Me.”
It is written.
Jesus answered deception with the revealed Word of God.
And this is where many new believers unknowingly enter danger.
They have experienced grace emotionally, but they have not yet developed deep roots doctrinally.
They know Jesus loves them.
But they may not yet know Romans.
They know their sins are forgiven.
But they may not yet understand justification.
They know they want to follow Christ.

But they have not yet learned how Scripture distinguishes temptation from sin, conviction from condemnation, discipline from rejection, or spiritual warfare from the ordinary consequences of poor decisions.
So every difficult feeling becomes “an attack.”
Every inconvenience becomes “the devil.”
Every conflict becomes “warfare.”
That is not biblical maturity.
Yes, Scripture teaches spiritual warfare.
But Scripture also teaches the flesh.
The world.
Our own foolish choices.
Consequences.
Suffering.
Trials.
Persecution.
Discipline.
And ordinary life in a fallen creation.
Not everything painful was personally arranged by Satan.
Sometimes we are tempted by our own desires. James writes that “each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own desires and enticed” (James 1:14).
That truth protects us from two dangerous mistakes.
The first is denying the devil.
The second is blaming him for everything.
Biblical Christianity does neither.
It takes Satan seriously without making him the center of the story.
Jesus is the center.
And perhaps one of the cruelest attacks against a new believer is not temptation itself.
It is what happens after temptation becomes failure.
You fall.
Again.
And suddenly the room feels different.
You cannot believe what you just did.
You had promised God.
You meant it.
You said you would never go back.
But you did.
Now shame enters.
And shame rarely knocks politely.
It kicks the door open.
“You hypocrite.”
“Fake Christian.”
“After everything Jesus did for you?”
“You think God wants to hear another apology?”
“Don't pray.”
“Don't open the Bible.”
“Don't go to church.”
“Hide.”
That last word should sound familiar.
Human beings have been hiding since Eden.
After Adam and Eve sinned, they hid themselves from the presence of God.
Sin still makes people hide.
But the Gospel calls sinners out of hiding.
There is a difference between the Holy Spirit's conviction and satanic condemnation.
Conviction exposes sin so that you run toward Christ in repentance.
Condemnation weaponizes sin so that you run away from Christ in despair.
Conviction says:
“This is sin. Bring it into the light.”
Condemnation says:
“You are beyond grace. Stay in the dark.”
Conviction leads toward confession.
Condemnation feeds concealment.
And Scripture gives believers one of the strongest answers imaginable:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.” — Romans 8:1
The Greek word is κατάκριμα — katakrima.
Condemnation.
A judicial sentence.
Paul does not say there are no consequences.
He does not say Christians never need correction.
He does not say sin no longer matters.
He says that for those who are in Christ Jesus, the condemning verdict has been answered.
Why?
Because Jesus bore judgment at the cross.
The Christian's confidence is not:
“I have behaved well enough today, therefore God may love me.”
It is:
“Christ is enough, therefore I can repent honestly instead of hiding.”
That does not make grace cheap.
It makes grace astonishing.
Cheap grace says sin does not matter.
Biblical grace says sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and His blood is so sufficient that repentant sinners do not have to pretend anymore.
Maybe that is exactly where you are.
You love Jesus.
But there is something you keep hiding.
An addiction.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Pride.
A secret relationship.
Envy.
Alcohol.
A private compromise.
An unforgiving heart.
A habit nobody at church knows about.
And every time you fail, you wonder whether Jesus has finally reached the point where He says:
“Enough.”
Listen to the Gospel.
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9
Notice John does not say God is merely emotional enough to forgive.
He says He is faithful and just.
The cross matters here.
Christian forgiveness is not God pretending evil was harmless.
Jesus bore sin.
Justice and mercy meet at Calvary.
So when the believer confesses, he does not come begging an unwilling Savior to become merciful.
He comes because mercy has already been revealed in Jesus Christ.
This is why Satan's accusations are so spiritually destructive.
They attempt to make your sin look bigger than Christ's sufficiency.
Revelation calls Satan “the accuser of our brethren” (Revelation 12:10).
The Greek word is κατήγωρ — katēgōr, meaning accuser.
But an accusation is not the final verdict.
Christ has the final word over those who belong to Him.
Paul asks:
“Who shall bring a charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is he who condemns? It is Christ who died, and furthermore is also risen…” — Romans 8:33–34
Read that again when shame tells you there is no road home.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Your defense against accusation is not your perfect record.
It is His finished work.
But there is another reason new believers often experience intense conflict.
They are learning to say no to masters they once obeyed automatically.
Before Christ, certain sins may not have felt like warfare because there was little resistance.
Now something inside you grieves what once entertained you.
You notice the lust.
You notice the pride.
You notice how cruel your words can be.
You notice what you consume.
You notice the idols you used to call ambitions.
You notice that resentment you have protected for years.
And sometimes you think:
“I'm getting worse.”
Perhaps not.
Perhaps the light has simply been turned on.
Imagine entering a dark room.
It looks clean.
Then morning sunlight pours through the window and suddenly you see dust everywhere.
Did the sunlight create the dust?
No.
The light revealed what darkness concealed.
The closer you walk with Christ, the more clearly you may see sin that previously did not bother you.
That discovery can hurt.
But it can also be evidence of sanctification beginning.
Paul describes the conflict between flesh and Spirit in Galatians 5:17.
The Christian life contains a real struggle.
Yet the command is not merely:
“Try harder.”
It is:
“Walk in the Spirit.” — Galatians 5:16
Christian transformation is not self-improvement wearing a cross necklace.
It is life under the power and leadership of the Holy Spirit.
That means when temptation comes, you do not merely grit your teeth.
You pray.
You flee situations that feed sin.
You confess to mature believers.
You immerse yourself in Scripture.
You participate in the life of the church.
You cut off access to what repeatedly destroys you.
You forgive.
You worship.
You learn obedience.
You get back up.
And when you fall, you run to Jesus again.
Not because sin is trivial.
Because Jesus is merciful.
Peter knew something about this.
Jesus warned him:
“Simon, Simon! Indeed, Satan has asked for you, that he may sift you as wheat.” — Luke 22:31
Imagine hearing that from Jesus.
Satan wants to sift you.
But the next sentence changes everything.
“But I have prayed for you, that your faith should not fail; and when you have returned to Me, strengthen your brethren.” — Luke 22:32
Jesus knew Peter would fall.
Peter would deny Him.
Not once.
Three times.
The man who had confidently said he would go with Jesus to prison and death would soon insist that he did not even know Him.
That is scandal.
A disciple denying his Lord while Jesus is being taken toward suffering.
Then the rooster crowed.
Peter remembered.
And he wept bitterly.
Maybe you understand those tears.
The tears that come when you finally see yourself without excuses.
When you realize you were capable of the thing you swore you would never do.
When you disappointed yourself.
When your confidence collapsed.
When all you have left is:
“Jesus, have mercy.”
But Peter's story did not end beside that fire.
After the resurrection, another fire appears.
John 21 tells us Jesus met His disciples by the Sea of Galilee.
And there, beside a charcoal fire, the risen Christ restored the disciple who had denied Him.
“Simon, son of Jonah, do you love Me?”
Three denials.
Then a wounded conversation of restoration.
Jesus did not pretend Peter's failure never happened.
He rewrote what failure would mean.
Peter's scandal would not become his tomb.
Grace would turn a broken disciple into a shepherd.
Later, Peter—the man once intimidated by a servant girl's question—would publicly proclaim the risen Christ.
That is what Jesus does.
He does not merely erase embarrassing chapters.
He redeems people.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you are reading this shortly after giving your life to Christ.
And perhaps nobody warned you that following Jesus would expose things.
Friendships may change.
Desires may collide.
Old identities may fight to survive.
Your past may attempt to reclaim you.
The enemy may accuse you.
The world may mock you.
Your flesh may resist you.
You may sometimes feel exhausted.
But hear the words of Scripture:
“Therefore submit to God. Resist the devil and he will flee from you. Draw near to God and He will draw near to you.” — James 4:7–8
Notice the order.
Submit to God.
Then resist.
The center of spiritual warfare is not shouting louder at Satan.
It is belonging more deeply to God.
Paul gives believers the armor of God in Ephesians 6.
Truth.
Righteousness.
The Gospel of peace.
Faith.
Salvation.
The Word of God.
Prayer.
The armor is profoundly God-centered.
Stand in what God has given.
And there is one Greek word in that passage worth remembering:
στῆτε — stēte.
“Stand.”
Sometimes victory looks dramatic.
Sometimes victory looks like a trembling Christian whispering:
“No. I belong to Jesus.”
Sometimes it is deleting the number.
Sometimes closing the browser.
Sometimes confessing the secret.
Sometimes calling a mature Christian at midnight.
Sometimes returning to church after shame told you everyone would judge you.
Sometimes opening the Bible when you feel nothing.
Sometimes praying through tears.
Sometimes saying:
“Jesus, I don't even know how to fight this. Please help me.”
That is not weakness disqualifying you from Christianity.
Christianity begins with the admission that you need a Savior.
And the Savior's name is Jesus.
So, new believer, do not build your faith on whether today feels spiritually powerful.
Build upon Christ.
Feelings change.
Christ does not.
Do not measure God's love by the intensity of today's battle.
Look at the cross.
Do not interpret every temptation as proof you secretly belong to Satan.
Look at whom you are learning to resist.
Do not make your failure your identity.
Repent.
Confess.
Return.
Do not isolate yourself.
Find a biblically faithful local church.
Learn from mature Christians whose lives demonstrate godliness.
Read Scripture in context.
Pray even when prayer feels dry.
Take sin seriously.
Take grace even more seriously.
And never confuse grace with permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus receives sinners exactly as sinners.
But He loves us too much to leave us enslaved to the things that are destroying us.
This is discipleship.
Not instant perfection.
Transformation.
Day after day.
Repentance after repentance.
Grace after grace.
Until the believer increasingly resembles the One who saved him.
If this article exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn this moment into another scroll.
Bring it to Jesus.
And if you need words, let them be simple.
Not because typing a phrase saves you.
Only Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when someone finally stops pretending.
And perhaps another believer reading your comment needs to discover that he is not the only Christian fighting.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It does not. We are saved by grace through faith, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And if Gospel Warrior helps you know Christ, understand Scripture, resist deception, heal through biblical truth, and grow into a more mature disciple of Jesus, stay close and follow.

Supporting a ministry is not a condition of salvation, proof of devotion, or a way to purchase God's favor; Scripture forbids us from turning grace into a transaction. But generosity and willing partnership can glorify God when they arise freely from love for Christ and a desire to advance faithful ministry (2 Corinthians 9:7; Philippians 4:14–18).
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
You cannot merchandise your way into God's favor.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Our response is worship.
Our message is Christ.
Our hope is the cross.
Our victory is the risen Savior.
So when the enemy whispers tonight:
“You're finished…”
Remember Peter.
When he says:
“You failed again…”
Remember the cross.
When he says:
“God doesn't want you anymore…”
Remember Romans 8.
When he says:
“Go back to who you were…”
Remember Colossians 1.
You have been rescued from darkness and brought into the kingdom of the beloved Son.
And when shame tells you to hide…
Step into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Stand.
Come home.
Jesus Christ is not intimidated by the chapter you are ashamed to let anyone read.
The enemy may keep quoting your scandal, but Jesus is still writing your story in grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHEN LOYALTY TO THE ORGANIZATION MATTERS MORE THAN LOYALTY TO SCRIPTURE
paragraphs:
WHEN LOYALTY TO THE ORGANIZATION MATTERS MORE THAN LOYALTY TO SCRIPTURE
The most dangerous betrayal of Christ may not begin when someone leaves the church—but when protecting the church’s system becomes more sacred than obeying the Lord of the Church.
There is a kind of silence that looks like loyalty.
It sits quietly in meetings.
It nods when everyone else nods.
It knows something is wrong but tells itself, This is not the right time.

It sees Scripture being bent around personalities, traditions, reputations, denominational expectations, ministries, movements, leadership structures, family loyalties, or institutional survival—and still whispers:
Don't cause trouble.
Don't question leadership.
Don't embarrass the ministry.
Think about what people will say.
Protect the organization.
And sometimes the sentence that finally silences the conscience sounds almost spiritual:
Don't touch the Lord's anointed.
So the believer goes home carrying something heavy.
Not rebellion.
Not hatred.
Not bitterness.
A question.
What happens when being loyal to the organization requires me to become disloyal to what God has actually said?
Stay with that question.
Because Jesus once stood before deeply religious people who were convinced that preserving their established tradition was an act of faithfulness to God.
And Christ said something terrifying.
In Mark 7:8, the Greek text reads:
Ἀφέντες τὴν ἐντολὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ κρατεῖτε τὴν παράδοσιν τῶν ἀνθρώπων.
“Having left the commandment of God, you hold to the tradition of men.”
Look closely at the contrast.
ἐντολὴν τοῦ Θεοῦ — entolēn tou Theou
The commandment of God.
Then:
παράδοσιν τῶν ἀνθρώπων — paradosin tōn anthrōpōn
The tradition of human beings.
And the verb κρατεῖτε — krateite carries the sense of holding firmly, retaining, grasping.
Jesus was exposing something frighteningly possible in religious life: people can loosen their grip on what God commanded while tightening their grip on what human beings handed down.
That should make every Christian uncomfortable.
Including me.
Including you.
Because this article is not ammunition for attacking churches we dislike.
It is a mirror.

Jesus was not condemning every tradition simply because it was a tradition. Scripture itself can speak positively about apostolic teaching being handed down. The problem in Mark 7 was that human tradition had been elevated until it functionally displaced divine command.
That distinction matters.
An organization is not automatically evil.
A denomination is not automatically evil.
Church policies are not automatically evil.
Leadership structures are not automatically evil.
Statements of faith, ministry procedures, accountability systems, customs, committees, boards, networks, and traditions can serve genuinely good purposes.
But none of them are Scripture.
And none of them were crucified for you.
That distinction becomes painfully important when someone says:
“You must choose.”
Choose between what the Bible plainly teaches and what the institution expects.
Choose between truth and reputation.
Choose between conscience and acceptance.
Choose between obedience and belonging.
Choose between asking the uncomfortable question and keeping your position.
Choose between exposing what is wrong and protecting the name on the building.
Choose between Christ and the machinery built in Christ's name.
That is where loyalty is tested.
And sometimes the most heartbreaking part is that the organization you are afraid to disappoint may be an organization you genuinely love.
You were saved there.
You were baptized there.
Your children grew up there.
Someone there prayed with you when your marriage was collapsing.
They brought food when somebody died.
They helped pay a bill when you had nothing.
Your pastor visited the hospital.
Your friends worship beside you.
You have photographs, memories, tears, testimonies, funerals, weddings, Christmas services, Bible studies, prayer meetings, and years of your life wrapped around that community.
So questioning something feels almost like betrayal.
That is why this subject hurts.
Loyalty itself is beautiful.
Faithfulness is biblical.
Gratitude is biblical.
Honoring godly leaders is biblical.
Submission to legitimate spiritual leadership is biblical.
Unity is biblical.
And reckless accusation, gossip, slander, divisiveness, pride, and rebellion are sins too.
But biblical submission was never intended to become the burial place of biblical discernment.
A Christian is never commanded to surrender his or her conscience to another human being as though that person were Christ.
There is only one Head of the Church.
Jesus.
There is only one sinless Shepherd.
Jesus.
There is only one King whose authority is absolute.
Jesus.
This is why Acts 5 contains one of Christianity's clearest boundaries.
The apostles had been commanded by legitimate authorities to stop teaching in the name of Jesus.
Peter and the apostles answered:
“We ought to obey God rather than men.”
That was not an anthem for rebellious personalities.
It was the recognition of a hierarchy.
Human authority is real.
God's authority is higher.
And when the two genuinely collide, the Christian's ultimate allegiance has already been decided.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
Not your denomination.
Not your pastor.
Not your bishop.
Not your elder board.
Not your ministry founder.
Not your favorite theologian.
Not your movement.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not me.
Not you.
Christ.
And because Christ is Lord, Scripture cannot become a prop we use to defend whatever our group has already decided must be true.
That is precisely where religious loyalty can become spiritually dangerous.
Because organizations naturally develop survival instincts.
Organizations have reputations.
Organizations have donors.
Organizations have buildings.
Organizations have leaders.
Organizations have histories.
Organizations have internal cultures.
Organizations have people whose livelihoods may depend upon them.
And none of those realities automatically makes an organization corrupt.
But they create temptation.
When truth threatens reputation, reputation can become an idol.
When repentance threatens influence, influence can become an idol.
When accountability threatens leadership, leadership can become an idol.
When biblical correction threatens institutional stability, stability can become an idol.
And idols rarely introduce themselves by saying:
Hello. I am your new god.
Sometimes they sound like:
We have to protect the ministry.
That sentence can describe genuine wisdom.
It can also conceal terrible compromise.
The question is:
Protect it from what?
From false accusations?
Yes. Truth matters.
From malicious gossip?
Yes. Justice matters.
From needless division?
Yes. Unity matters.
But protect an organization from truthful accountability?
Protect a leader from legitimate biblical correction?
Protect a reputation by hiding wrongdoing?
Protect a theological system by forcing Scripture to say what the system requires?
Protect unity by punishing sincere questions?
Now something has changed.
We are no longer merely protecting ministry.
We may be protecting ourselves from the light.
And Jesus does not need darkness to protect His Church.
Think again about Mark 7.

Jesus gave a concrete example involving Corban—something declared as devoted to God. A religious mechanism was being used in a way that allowed people to evade the obligation of honoring their parents. Christ's accusation reaches its climax when He says their tradition was effectively making God's Word void.
Imagine the horror of that.
Something wearing religious clothing was being used to obstruct obedience to God.
That danger did not die in the first century.
We can still put Christian vocabulary around disobedience.
We can call fear “wisdom.”
We can call secrecy “protection.”
We can call unquestioning compliance “submission.”
We can call institutional preservation “unity.”
We can call cowardice “peace.”
We can call loyalty to personalities “honor.”
We can even call silence “grace.”
But changing the label does not change the substance.
God sees beneath vocabulary.
Maybe that is why this is hitting somewhere uncomfortable.
Maybe you have sat in a room where everybody knew something was wrong.
Nobody said it.
Maybe you watched someone get treated unfairly and stayed silent because speaking might cost you relationships.
Maybe you repeated an interpretation you had never seriously examined because everyone around you believed it.
Maybe you discovered that a cherished teaching did not survive careful reading of Scripture, and the realization terrified you.
Maybe someone asked an honest biblical question and you immediately labeled them rebellious because questioning the system felt like questioning God.
Or perhaps you are on the other side.
Maybe you were the person who asked.
And suddenly conversations stopped when you entered the room.
Friends became distant.
People questioned your motives instead of answering your Scripture.
You discovered how lonely conviction can become when belonging has a price.
If that is your story, hear this carefully:
Do not allow mistreatment by Christians to turn into hatred of Christ.
Do not confuse Jesus with every person who has misrepresented Him.
Do not let institutional failure become your excuse for abandoning the Savior.
People can fail you.
Churches can fail you.
Leaders can fail you.
Organizations can fail you.
And you can fail them too.
But Christ remains Christ.
This article is not permission to become cynical.
It is not permission to become unteachable.
It is not permission to appoint yourself judge of every pastor on Facebook.
It is not permission to call every disagreement “heresy” or every leadership decision “spiritual abuse.”
Sometimes you are wrong.
Sometimes I am wrong.
Sometimes the leader you suspect is actually right.
Sometimes the tradition you dislike is perfectly compatible with Scripture.
Sometimes what feels like persecution is correction.
Humility demands that possibility remain on the table.
Biblical discernment asks something harder than “Who offended me?”
It asks:
“What has God actually said?”
Then it opens the Bible.
Context matters.
Genre matters.
Original language matters.
Historical setting matters.
The whole counsel of Scripture matters.
Christ matters.
And our interpretation must be humble enough to be corrected by the text.
There is another ancient scene that cuts deeply into this conversation.
King Saul had been given a command from God, but afterward he presented Samuel with something that sounded religious.
Sacrifice.
Worship.
Something supposedly being offered to the Lord.
Samuel answered with words that have survived for centuries because religious activity cannot substitute for obedience:
“To obey is better than sacrifice.”
That is 1 Samuel 15:22.
The Hebrew word commonly rendered “to obey” is connected with שָׁמַע — shāmaʿ, a word whose semantic range includes hearing, listening, and obeying.
Biblical obedience is not merely sound entering the ear.
It is hearing that bends the life.
And this is where the knife turns toward us.
Because it is easy to condemn an institution for refusing to listen to Scripture while refusing to listen to Scripture ourselves.
You can leave a controlling organization and still carry a controlling heart.
You can expose hypocrisy and become proud.
You can defend sound doctrine without love.
You can win an argument and lose tenderness.
You can identify everybody else's idol while protecting your own.
Jesus does not merely want to rescue us from bad systems.
He came to rescue sinners.
Us.
The deepest scandal is not merely that institutions sometimes become corrupt.
The deepest scandal is that sin runs through the human heart.
Mine.
Yours.
The pastor's.
The critic's.
The whistleblower's.
The congregation's.
The victim's wounds do not make every conclusion infallible.
The leader's office does not make every decision infallible.
We all desperately need grace.
And this is where Christianity becomes something infinitely greater than institutional reform.
Because Jesus did not come merely to improve religious organizations.
Jesus came to reconcile sinners to God.
The Son of God entered our rebellion.
He confronted hypocrisy without becoming hateful.
He exposed religious corruption without abandoning holiness.
He touched people respectable society avoided.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He called the proud to repentance.
He spoke truth when truth cost Him.
And eventually the machinery of religious and political power converged around Him.
Accusations.
Mockery.
Violence.
A cross.
And there hangs Jesus.
Not as the victim of an unfortunate misunderstanding outside God's sovereign purpose, but as the Lamb who willingly gives Himself for sinners.
Our sin.
Our pride.
Our cowardice.
Our tribalism.
Our idolatry.
Our obsession with reputation.
Our fear of people.
Our hunger for approval.
Our secret compromises.
Our rebellion.
The scandal of the cross is that the innocent Christ suffers for the guilty.
Then grace does what nobody standing near that tomb could manufacture.
Jesus rises.
And suddenly Christianity's center is not an organization desperately preserving itself.
It is a living King.
That changes everything.
Because if Jesus is alive, you do not need to manipulate truth to protect Him.
You do not need to bury sin to protect Him.
You do not need to destroy questioners to protect Him.
You do not need to rewrite Scripture to protect Him.
Truth does not threaten Christ.
Repentance does not weaken His Church.
Biblical accountability does not embarrass heaven.
What dishonors Christ is when we use His holy name to protect what He calls us to bring into the light.
But there is another side we cannot ignore.
If you have used “I follow Jesus, not organizations” as an excuse to reject all accountability, you need repentance too.
Christ loves His Church.
The New Testament does not envision Christianity as isolated individuals answering to nobody, belonging nowhere, refusing correction, and calling independence spiritual maturity.
God gives teachers and shepherds to His people.
Believers are commanded to love one another, serve one another, forgive one another, bear with one another, gather together, pursue unity, and submit appropriately to godly leadership.
The answer to institutional idolatry is not spiritual isolation.
The answer is rightly ordered allegiance.
Christ first.
And because Christ is first, we can love His Church without worshiping its institutions.
We can honor leaders without idolizing them.
We can receive correction without surrendering discernment.
We can defend people against false accusations while refusing to cover genuine sin.
We can pursue unity without purchasing it with truth.
We can ask questions without becoming quarrelsome.
We can confront error while trembling over our own capacity for error.
We can say, “I love you,” and still say, “I cannot call this biblical.”
Sometimes that sentence will cost you.
Maybe a position.
Maybe an invitation.
Maybe a platform.
Maybe friends.
Maybe the comfortable identity you built around belonging to the right group.
That loss can feel like death.
But there is something worse than losing your place at someone's table.
It is slowly training your conscience to stop trembling at God's Word.
One compromise becomes easier after another.
At first your conscience screams.
Then whispers.
Then eventually you learn the vocabulary necessary to silence it.
And one day you may discover that you became extraordinarily loyal to something carrying the name of Jesus while becoming strangely unfamiliar with the voice of Jesus.
That is the tragedy I want you to remember.
Not because I want you suspicious of everyone.
Because I want you anchored so deeply in Christ that neither charisma nor pressure nor fear nor tribal loyalty can easily move you away from Him.
Read Scripture.
Study it carefully.
Pray.
Test what you hear.
Listen to mature believers.
Invite correction.
Refuse gossip.
Demand evidence before accepting serious accusations.
Distinguish disagreement from abuse.
Distinguish preference from doctrine.
Distinguish tradition from commandment.
Distinguish your interpretation from the actual text.
And when you discover that you are wrong...
repent.
Quickly.
Beautifully.
Without excuses.
Because repentance is not humiliation for the Christian.
Repentance is coming home.
Maybe you spent years defending something you now realize was wrong.
Grace is still available.
Maybe you stayed silent when you should have spoken.
Grace is still available.
Maybe you hurt somebody because you thought protecting the organization meant protecting God.
Grace is still available.
Maybe you became bitter after being hurt.
Grace is still available.
Maybe you stopped trusting Christians.
Maybe you stopped opening your Bible.
Maybe you still believe in God but somewhere inside you have been keeping Jesus at arm's length because people bearing His name wounded you.
Come back.
Not necessarily to the same institution.
Not automatically to the same leader.
But come back to Christ.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the confusion.
Bring Him the questions.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the years you wish you could rewrite.
Because this is the Gospel:
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
Jesus can redeem what yesterday did to you.
This is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to one truth:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing consequences.
Grace is far more powerful than denial.
Jesus enters the wreckage, tells the truth about sin, calls us to repentance, forgives those who come to Him in faith, and begins transforming people who thought their story was already ruined.
So ask yourself the question you may have avoided throughout this entire article:
If Scripture contradicted something precious to my tribe, which one would I protect?
Don't answer quickly.
Would you protect your position?
Your denomination?
Your favorite preacher?
Your reputation?
Your friendships?
Your theology because admitting error would be embarrassing?
Or could you place everything before Christ and say:

“Lord Jesus, if I am wrong, correct me. If I am afraid, strengthen me. If I am proud, humble me. If I have made an idol out of belonging, tear it down. I want You more than I want to be right in front of people.”
That prayer can rearrange a life.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs to make it public—not because comments save anyone, but because sometimes confession breaks the power of hiding.
And if you once defended a system more fiercely than you defended truth, you do not need to pretend anymore.
Christ already knows.
Repentance can begin right here.
It does not.
It isn't.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ.
But one practical way you can help this ministry continue spreading Christ-centered, Scripture-rooted content is by supporting the work that produces and distributes it.
Check what we teach against Scripture too.
Test it.
Open your Bible.
Our goal must never be to create people loyal to a brand.
Our prayer must be to help form disciples loyal to Christ.
Because ministries will come and go.
Organizations will rise and fall.
Buildings will eventually crumble.
Platforms disappear.
Famous names are forgotten.
But the Word of our God stands.
And Jesus Christ will still be King when the last human institution has become a paragraph in a history book.
So when the choice becomes painful...
when obedience becomes expensive...
when belonging demands silence...
when tradition begins competing with revelation...
when everybody around you says, Just go along with it...
remember who carried the cross for you.
The organization didn't.
Jesus did.
Remember who conquered the grave for you.
The institution didn't.
Jesus did.
Remember whose blood purchased your redemption.
No denomination shed it.
No ministry founder shed it.
No religious system shed it.
Jesus did.
Give honor where honor is due.
Love the Church.
Serve faithfully.
Walk humbly.
Reject gossip.
Seek truth carefully.
Forgive freely.
Repent quickly.
Honor godly leadership.
But reserve the throne for Christ.
And if loyalty ever demands that you place human authority above the clear authority of God's Word, remember Peter's ancient confession:
We must obey God rather than men.
Because sometimes the most faithful thing you can do for an organization you love is refuse to help it become an idol.
And sometimes the moment you think your story is collapsing is the very place where Christ begins rewriting it.
You were never saved to become loyal enough to a religious system that you could no longer hear the voice of the Savior who died to make you His.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY THREW THEIR BROTHER INTO A PIT — YEARS LATER, THEY BOWED BEFORE HIM BEGGING FOR FOOD
paragraphs: THEY THREW THEIR BROTHER INTO A PIT — YEARS LATER, THEY BOWED BEFORE HIM BEGGING FOR FOOD
They thought they were burying Joseph’s future. They had no idea God was writing a rescue story through the very man they betrayed.
There are wounds caused by strangers.
And then there are wounds that know your name.
Wounds that sat at your table.
Wounds that grew up in the same house.
Wounds with familiar faces.
Joseph knew the difference.
The men who stripped him, threw him into a pit, and eventually sold him were not foreign enemies.
They were his brothers.
His own blood.

And years later, when famine emptied their fields and hunger drove them into Egypt, those same brothers would stand before Joseph needing something from the man they once decided they could live without.
Food.
But before we rush to that extraordinary reversal, we need to stand beside the pit.
Because somebody reading this knows what it feels like to be there.
Not literally.
But emotionally.
You know what it is to discover that someone you trusted could hurt you.
You know what it is to replay a betrayal at two in the morning and wonder how someone who knew your heart could treat it so carelessly.
You know what it is to watch people continue living normally after what they did nearly destroyed you.
And perhaps the hardest question has not been, “Why did they do this?”
Perhaps it has been:
“God… where were You?”
Joseph's story does not insult that question with an easy answer.
It takes us into the pit first.
Genesis 37:24 records the moment in stark Hebrew:
וַיִּקָּחֻהוּ וַיַּשְׁלִכוּ אֹתוֹ הַבֹּרָה וְהַבּוֹר רֵק אֵין בּוֹ מָיִם
Vayyiqqachuhu vayashlikhu oto habborah; vehabbor req, ein bo mayim.
“They took him and threw him into the pit. The pit was empty; there was no water in it.”
The Hebrew word בּוֹר — bor means a pit or cistern.
Notice how brutally simple Scripture is.
They took him.
They threw him.
The pit was empty.
No water.
No inspirational speech appears from heaven.
No angel immediately lifts Joseph out.
No explanation arrives telling him how everything will eventually work.
Just darkness.
And that matters.
Because sometimes we retell Joseph's story so quickly that we accidentally remove its pain.
We know the ending.
Joseph didn't.
We know Egypt is coming.
Joseph didn't.
We know Pharaoh is coming.
Joseph didn't.
We know the palace is coming.
Joseph didn't.
We know his brothers will one day bow before him.
Joseph didn't.
Inside the pit, Joseph had only the pit.
And faith becomes painfully real when you cannot see the next chapter.

His brothers had already hated him because of his father's favoritism and because of the dreams Joseph reported. They saw him coming and conspired against him. They stripped away the special robe his father had given him.
Imagine that moment.
The hands pulling the robe from Joseph's body belonged to men he had called brothers.
Then they threw him down.
And while Joseph was trapped, something almost unbearable happened.
They sat down to eat.
The people responsible for his terror could still swallow their lunch.

Later, when famine brought those brothers before Joseph, they remembered what happened far more vividly than Genesis 37 initially tells us. Genesis 42:21 records their confession: they remembered seeing the distress of Joseph's soul and hearing him plead with them.
Joseph had begged.
They had heard him.
And they refused to listen.
That changes the emotional temperature of the pit.
This was not a silent teenager stoically accepting his destiny.
This was a brother crying out to brothers.
Please.
Help me.
Don't do this.
And they did it anyway.
Maybe that is why this story reaches places inside us that polished Christianity sometimes cannot.
Because some of you prayed while somebody was hurting you.
You asked God to change the situation.
You begged someone to reconsider.
You hoped the marriage would heal.
You hoped the friendship would survive.
You hoped the family member would finally acknowledge what happened.
You hoped the person who betrayed you would come back and make it right.
But the footsteps disappeared.
And you were left wondering whether God had disappeared with them.
He hadn't.
That is one of the great truths of Joseph's story.
God's silence is not God's absence.
Joseph was taken from the pit and sold into slavery. He eventually entered the household of Potiphar in Egypt. Scripture repeatedly emphasizes that the LORD was with Joseph.
Not merely after Joseph became successful.
With him there.
In slavery.
Then came another injustice.

Potiphar's wife attempted to seduce Joseph. Joseph refused, grounding that refusal not merely in loyalty to Potiphar but in loyalty to God. He asked how he could commit such wickedness and sin against God.
Joseph chose integrity.
And his immediate reward was prison.
Read that again slowly.
He did the right thing…
and his circumstances became worse.
That destroys one of the most dangerous counterfeit versions of Christianity: the idea that obedience guarantees immediate comfort.
Sometimes obedience costs you.
Sometimes telling the truth costs you.
Sometimes refusing temptation costs you.
Sometimes doing what honors Christ does not immediately open a door.
Sometimes it appears to slam one shut.
Joseph went from pit…
to slavery…
to false accusation…
to prison.
If you stopped reading there, you might conclude that Joseph had been abandoned.
But heaven was still writing.
Even in prison, God was with him.
Eventually Joseph interpreted dreams for Pharaoh's officials. One of those men, the cupbearer, was restored to his position.
Joseph asked to be remembered.
But he was forgotten.
Again.
Have you ever survived betrayal only to be wounded by being forgotten?
You helped people who disappeared when you needed help.
You poured into people who stopped checking on you.
You celebrated people who never celebrated you.
You thought, “Maybe this person is the answer God sent.”
Then nothing.
Joseph waited.
Until Pharaoh dreamed.
And suddenly the gift that seemed useless inside a prison became necessary inside a palace.
Joseph was summoned.
God enabled Joseph to explain that Egypt was approaching seven years of extraordinary abundance followed by seven devastating years of famine. Joseph proposed wise preparation.
Pharaoh recognized something extraordinary in him and elevated the former Hebrew slave to enormous authority over Egypt.
Think about the reversal.
The boy stripped of his robe was clothed in authority.
The brother thrown into a pit was lifted beside Pharaoh.
The slave became an administrator.
The prisoner became the man entrusted with grain.
But do not reduce Joseph's story to “suffer now and God will make you rich later.”
That is not the Gospel.
The deepest miracle is not that Joseph received a position.
It is what God did through Joseph's suffering to preserve life—and what God did inside Joseph's heart.
Because then the famine came.
And eventually…
so did his brothers.
The men who once looked down into a pit at Joseph now bowed down before him.
They did not recognize him.
Joseph recognized them.
Imagine the emotional collision.
One glance…
and suddenly the pit is back.
The voices.
The robe.
The pleading.
The merchants.
The journey away from home.
Years of separation from his father.
Joseph now possessed something his younger self never had.
Power.
He could punish them.
He could expose them.
He could make them experience a fraction of what he had experienced.
And nobody in Egypt would have stopped him.
This is where we discover whether Joseph merely escaped the pit…
or whether God had begun removing the pit from Joseph.

The story unfolds carefully. Joseph tests his brothers, and Scripture shows that they are no longer the same men who sold him. Judah, who had once participated in Joseph's sale, eventually offers himself in place of Benjamin rather than allow their father to suffer the loss of another beloved son.
Something has changed.
Then Joseph can no longer contain himself.
Genesis 45 says he ordered everyone else out of the room.
And Joseph wept.
Not a dignified little tear.
He wept so loudly that Egyptians heard him and Pharaoh's household heard about it.
Years of history erupted through one man's chest.
Then came the words his brothers could never have expected.
“I am Joseph.”
Imagine their faces.
The brother they sold.
Alive.
Standing before them.
Powerful.
Their survival now resting in the hands of the man whose cries they had once ignored.
They were terrified.
And then Joseph did something astonishing.
He invited them closer.
“Come near to me.”
Then he identified the wound without pretending it never happened:
“I am your brother Joseph, whom you sold into Egypt.”
That sentence matters.
Forgiveness did not require Joseph to rewrite evil as good.
He named what they did.
You sold me.
Biblical forgiveness is not pretending betrayal was harmless.
It is not calling abuse love.
It is not denying consequences.
It is not automatically restoring trust without repentance, wisdom, or boundaries.
Joseph could acknowledge human evil while simultaneously recognizing divine providence.
He continued by explaining that God had sent him ahead to preserve life.
Later, after Jacob died and Joseph's brothers again feared retaliation, Joseph gave one of Scripture's clearest statements about God's providence over human evil.
Genesis 50:20 says:
וְאַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה
Ve'attem chashavtem alai ra'ah; Elohim chashavah letovah.
“You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”
The repeated Hebrew verb comes from חָשַׁב — chashav, carrying the sense of thinking, planning, reckoning, or intending.
Do not miss the force of the sentence.
Joseph did not say:
“What you did wasn't evil.”
He said it was evil.
Human responsibility remained real.
But human evil did not become sovereign.
They intended one thing.
God intended another.
Same history.
Different intentions.
They were not secretly doing God's righteous work when they betrayed Joseph. Their motives were sinful.
Yet their sin was incapable of overthrowing God's purpose.
That is biblical providence.
God does not need evil to become good in order to defeat it.
He is so sovereign that evil cannot ultimately force Him to surrender His purposes.
The pit did not become good.
The betrayal did not become good.
Slavery did not become good.
False accusation did not become good.
Prison did not become good.
God remained good.
And He brought saving purposes through circumstances other people intended for destruction.
That distinction matters enormously, especially for wounded people.
Christianity never requires you to look at what destroyed pieces of your life and call darkness light.
You can say:
“That was wrong.”
“That hurt me.”
“They betrayed me.”
“I still have scars.”
And at the same time say:
“But Jesus will not allow my wound to become my god.”
Maybe this is where Joseph's story stops being ancient history and starts reading your mail.
Because perhaps someone threw you into a pit years ago, and although your body climbed out, your heart still lives there.
Every new relationship gets interrogated for the crimes of the old one.
Every disagreement feels like abandonment.
Every silence sounds like rejection.
Every memory reopens court.
You survived what happened…
but what happened is still governing you.
And Jesus wants more for you than survival.
He wants freedom.
Forgiveness does not mean the offender was right.
Forgiveness means you refuse to let their sin become the permanent owner of your soul.
And here the road from Joseph leads us toward Someone greater than Joseph.
Jesus Christ.
Joseph is not Jesus, and we should not force every detail of Joseph's life into an allegory. But Scripture's great redemptive story ultimately moves toward Christ, and there are striking resonances.
Joseph was rejected by his brothers.
Jesus “came to His own,” and His own did not receive Him.
Joseph was handed over and sold.
Jesus was betrayed for silver.
Joseph suffered despite innocence.
Jesus was perfectly sinless and nevertheless condemned.
Joseph descended into humiliation and later was exalted.
Christ humbled Himself to death—even death on a cross—and God highly exalted Him.
Joseph's suffering became part of God's means of preserving lives during famine.
But Jesus went infinitely further.
He did not merely preserve starving people with grain.
He gives eternal life to sinners who deserve judgment.
At the cross, humanity's deepest scandal collided with God's astonishing grace.
Men crucified the Son of God.
And through that very cross, according to God's sovereign redemptive purpose, Christ bore sin and opened the way of forgiveness for everyone who repents and believes.
This is why Christianity is not ultimately a message about becoming powerful enough that your enemies someday need you.
It is about Christ being merciful enough to save His enemies.
That includes us.
Before pointing at Joseph's brothers, remember:
Sin makes rebels of all of us.
We have lied.
Lusted.
Envied.
Hated.
Hidden.
Manipulated.
Worshiped ourselves.
Ignored God.
Excused what He calls sin.
Some sins are public.
Others wear church clothes.
But every one of us needs grace.
The most shocking part of the Gospel is not merely that Jesus was betrayed.
It is that Jesus willingly died for sinners.
Romans tells us that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
You may have spent years asking, “How could they do that to me?”
There is another question that eventually brings every human heart to its knees:
“How can a holy God show mercy to me?”
The answer is Jesus.
Not your religious résumé.
Not your charitable deeds.
Not the image you maintain online.
Not the verses you repost while hiding the sins you refuse to surrender.
Jesus.
Crucified.
Risen.
King.
The Gospel does not tell you to decorate your pit.
It calls you out of it.
Repent.
Stop making peace with the sin Christ died to save you from.
Stop confusing conviction with condemnation. Conviction points you toward the Savior.
Bring the secret thing into the light.
Bring the bitterness.
Bring the pornography.
Bring the pride.
Bring the affair.
Bring the envy.
Bring the unforgiveness.
Bring the religious performance.
Bring the anger you have fed for years.
Bring the wound you turned into an identity.
Jesus already knows.
And still He calls sinners to come near.
That may be the most beautiful echo in Joseph's story.
When the guilty brothers were terrified, Joseph said:
Come near.
And the Gospel announces something even greater to repentant sinners.
Come to Christ.
Not because your sin is small.
Because His grace is greater.
Not because justice does not matter.
Because at Calvary, justice and mercy meet in the crucified Savior.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying something nobody around you knows.
Maybe you are Joseph, wounded by people you trusted.
Maybe you are one of the brothers, haunted by something you did years ago.
Maybe you are both.
Wounded…
and guilty.
Betrayed…
and betrayer.
That is where grace becomes more than a Christian vocabulary word.
Grace means your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming people inside the scandal.
Joseph's brothers could not undo the pit.
Joseph could not recover the stolen years.
But God could still write redemption into a family stained by jealousy, deception, betrayal, and grief.
And from that deeply imperfect family line, God's covenant purposes continued until, generations later, the promised Messiah came.
Jesus Christ.
So maybe the question is no longer:
“Why did God let me enter the pit?”
Maybe tonight the question is:
“What if the pit does not get the final word?”
What if the betrayal that changed you does not have to define you?
What if the person who abandoned you does not get to decide your capacity to love?
What if the failure you are ashamed of does not have to become the name you answer to forever?
What if repentance is still possible?
What if forgiveness is still possible?
What if restoration is still possible?
What if God has been present in chapters where you were certain He had left?
Joseph looked backward and saw something his younger self could never have seen from inside that empty cistern.
God had not surrendered the story.
Neither had He excused the evil.
He had overruled it.
That is why Genesis 50:20 is not a motivational slogan promising that every Christian will become wealthy, influential, famous, or publicly vindicated.
It is far better than that.
It tells us that evil is not sovereign.
God is.
And for those who belong to Christ, suffering cannot separate us from the love of God.
Sometimes God changes circumstances.
Sometimes He changes us while the circumstances remain painful.
Sometimes earthly reconciliation happens.
Sometimes wisdom requires distance.
Sometimes justice comes quickly.
Sometimes we wait for the final judgment of the perfectly righteous King.
But Christians never have to pretend evil wins.
The empty tomb has already announced otherwise.
Jesus Christ walked into death itself…
and walked out alive.
So if you are in a pit right now, do not worship the darkness.
If you are waiting, do not assume waiting means abandonment.
If you have been betrayed, do not let another person's sin teach your heart to become sinful.
If you have betrayed someone, stop hiding behind excuses. Repent. Confess where appropriate. Make restitution where possible. Seek forgiveness.
And if you are exhausted from carrying bitterness, place judgment into the hands of the only Judge who sees every detail perfectly.
You do not have to become what hurt you.
Joseph didn't.
And by the transforming grace of Jesus Christ, neither do you.
If this exposed something hidden in you, don't perform for anybody.
Be honest.
Not because typing a phrase saves anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession is the moment somebody finally stops hiding, and another believer realizes they are not fighting alone.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
Not because sharing proves your faith.
Not because an algorithm glorifies God.
But because the Gospel is worth carrying beyond ourselves.
Someone may believe betrayal has destroyed their future.
Someone may be drowning in guilt over what they did years ago.
Someone may be one sentence away from remembering that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Send it to them.
Because Joseph's story leaves us with an image difficult to forget:
The brothers who once stood above Joseph while he lay helpless in a pit eventually stood helpless before Joseph.
But the greatest reversal was not that Joseph finally had power over them.
It was that when revenge became possible…
mercy was still alive inside him.
And that points our eyes beyond Joseph.
Toward Jesus.
The King before whom every knee will ultimately bow is the same Savior who stretched His hands upon a cross and offers forgiveness to repentant sinners today.
So bring Him the pit.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the years.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the guilt.
Bring Him the scandal.
And bring Him the pieces of yourself you thought could never become anything beautiful again.
Because the hands of Christ still bear scars.
And scarred hands know how to hold broken stories.
They thought the pit would become Joseph's grave—but God turned the place of his rejection into a road toward the preservation of the very people who rejected him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Bible Begins With Water—and Ends With a River: The Hidden Significance of Water From Genesis to Revelation
paragraphs: The Bible Begins With Water—and Ends With a River: The Hidden Significance of Water From Genesis to Revelation

Before Scripture closes, God shows John a river flowing from the throne. But thousands of years earlier, before Eden, before Abraham, before Israel, before Bethlehem, before Calvary, water was already there. Follow that river through the Bible and you begin to see something breathtaking: judgment, rescue, cleansing, thirst, the Holy Spirit, the cross, and finally the restoration of all things converge in Jesus Christ.
There is water in the first chapter of your Bible.
And there is water in the last.
That is not permission to turn every mention of water into a secret code. Scripture deserves better than that. Biblical symbols must be allowed to mean what their context says they mean.
But once you begin following water through the biblical story, something becomes impossible to ignore.
Water keeps appearing at moments when worlds change.
Creation.
Judgment.
Deliverance.
Covenant.
Cleansing.
Thirst.
New life.
The Holy Spirit.
And finally...
a river flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb.
Maybe that is why this story feels so personal.
Because you know what thirst feels like.
Not merely the thirst that sends you reaching for a glass.
The other kind.
The thirst nobody sees.
The thirst beneath the promotion.
Beneath the relationship.
Beneath the scrolling.
Beneath the church attendance.
Beneath the smile you learned to wear when somebody asks, “How are you?”
You can have a full refrigerator and a thirsty soul.
You can know worship songs and still feel spiritually dry.
You can sit inside a church while secretly wondering why God feels so far away.
You can drink from success, approval, sex, entertainment, money, romance, achievement, attention, religion, and even ministry—and discover that some wells make you thirstier the more you drink.
So perhaps the question running through Scripture is not simply, What does water symbolize?
Perhaps the more terrifying question is:
What have you been drinking from because you were afraid Jesus would not satisfy you?
Go back to the beginning.
Genesis 1:2 opens with words that sound almost frightening in Hebrew:
“וְהָאָרֶץ הָיְתָה תֹהוּ וָבֹהוּ... וְרוּחַ אֱלֹהִים מְרַחֶפֶת עַל־פְּנֵי הַמָּיִם”
Veha’aretz hayetah tohu vavohu... veruach Elohim merachefet al-penei hammayim.

The earth is tohu vavohu—formless and empty. Darkness lies over the tehom, the deep. And the ruach Elohim, the Spirit of God, hovers over the mayim, the waters. Genesis 1:2 really does place the Spirit of God over the waters at the threshold of the creation account.
Before the garden blooms, there is the deep.
Before human voices speak, the Spirit hovers.
Before the world takes the ordered form in which humanity will inhabit it, God is already present.
Do not miss that.
God is not frightened by the place that has no shape yet.
He does not panic in the darkness.
He does not abandon the unfinished.
And somebody reading this needs that truth more than another motivational sentence.
Your life may feel like tohu vavohu right now.
Formless.
Empty.
A marriage you cannot repair.
A child you cannot reach.
A temptation you promised God you would never return to.
A grief you cannot explain.
A secret you are terrified somebody will discover.
A prayer that seems to have disappeared into silence.
And perhaps you have mistaken disorder for divine absence.
Genesis refuses that conclusion.
The darkness was real.
The deep was real.
The unfinished world was real.
But God was there.
Then God speaks.
And what appears hopeless begins receiving order from the voice of its Creator.
That pattern matters because the Bible will repeatedly show us a God who enters what humans cannot repair and does what human strength cannot accomplish.
But water in Scripture is not sentimental.
Sometimes it carries life.
Sometimes it carries judgment.
That becomes terrifyingly clear in Noah's generation.
Human wickedness fills the earth, and the flood comes.
The waters that appeared near the beginning of creation now become part of a scene of catastrophic judgment. Yet through that judgment God preserves Noah and his family in the ark.
Water, therefore, cannot simply be reduced to “blessing.”
The Bible will not let us flatten it.
The flood reminds us that the God who gives life is also holy.
Sin is not cute.
Rebellion is not freedom.
God's patience should never be confused with moral indifference.
Yet even there, judgment is not the final word of the biblical story.
The waters eventually recede.
The ark rests.
Noah emerges.
God establishes His covenant sign.
And humanity continues.
Then generations later, another body of water stands between God's people and freedom.
Israel has left Egypt, but Pharaoh's army is behind them.
The sea is ahead.
There is nowhere to go.
You know that feeling, don't you?
The past chasing you.
The future blocked.
No visible escape.
You obeyed God, and somehow obedience brought you to a shoreline you cannot cross.
Then God makes a road where there was no road.
Israel passes through the sea.
The oppressor does not.
The same waters become deliverance for God's people and judgment upon their pursuers.
Later Scripture looks back on this event as foundational to Israel's identity. The God of Israel is the God who rescues slaves.
And already a greater Exodus is beginning to cast its shadow.
Because Egypt was not humanity's deepest slavery.
Pharaoh was not humanity's greatest master.
The ultimate tyrants are sin and death.
And Moses was never going to be the final Deliverer.
Keep following the water.
Israel enters the wilderness.
Now the people who watched God divide a sea become thirsty.
That may be one of the most painfully human scenes in Scripture.
Yesterday's miracle does not automatically eliminate today's fear.
People who have seen God move can still panic.
People who have testimonies can still doubt.
People who worship on Sunday can unravel on Tuesday.
Israel needs water.
At one point, God brings water from the rock.
Centuries later, Paul makes a startling Christ-centered connection while warning the Corinthian church from Israel's wilderness history: “that Rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4).
Paul is not inviting us to invent secret meanings everywhere. He is teaching us to read Israel's story in light of Christ.
And the picture becomes unforgettable.
A thirsty people.
No ability to produce what they need.
God provides.
That is the Gospel before the Gospel arrives in its fullest historical revelation.
You cannot manufacture living water for your own soul.
Religion cannot produce it.
Self-improvement cannot produce it.
Your reputation cannot produce it.
You need what only God can give.
Then water appears again and again throughout Israel's worship and prophetic imagination.
There are washings associated with ritual cleansing.
There are prophetic promises of purification.
Isaiah calls the thirsty to come to the waters.
Ezekiel sees cleansing and renewal intertwined with God's promise of a new heart and Spirit.
Then Ezekiel sees something astonishing: water flowing from the temple, becoming deeper and deeper until it is a river bringing life wherever it goes.
Dead places live.
Fruit appears.
Healing follows the river.
Remember that image.
You will see the river again.
But first, we need to walk into Samaria.
It is midday.
A woman comes to a well.
And Jesus is waiting.
John tells us that she is a Samaritan woman, and the conversation quickly crosses social, ethnic, religious, and moral boundaries.
She came for ordinary water.
Jesus begins speaking about another kind.
In John 4:14 the Greek text says:
“τὸ ὕδωρ ὃ δώσω αὐτῷ γενήσεται ἐν αὐτῷ πηγὴ ὕδατος ἁλλομένου εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον.”
The water Christ gives becomes within a person a spring of water welling up into eternal life.
Notice the verbs.
Jesus does not merely point toward the water.
He gives it.
This is where Christianity separates itself from every attempt to save ourselves by climbing toward God.
The Gospel is not primarily humanity climbing.
It is God coming.
The Samaritan woman has come carrying a water jar.
But the deeper thirst is standing beside the well.
Jesus begins exposing her story.
Five husbands.
The man she now has is not her husband.
And this is where careless preaching can turn her into a caricature.
Scripture tells us the facts Jesus names, but it does not give us enough information to reconstruct every cause behind her marital history. We should not pretend to know what God did not tell us.
What we do know is enough.
Jesus knows her.
Completely.
And He stays.
That may be one of the most beautiful truths in the chapter.
The One who knows what everybody else does not know...
does not walk away.
Think about that slowly.
What if Jesus opened the folder you keep hidden?
What if He replayed every conversation?
Every browser history.
Every private compromise.
Every jealous thought.
Every betrayal.
Every night you became somebody you swore you would never become.
Every time you used Christianity to hide from Christ.
Would He discover something He did not already know?
No.
The scandal of grace is not that Jesus saves people after accidentally overlooking their sin.
He knows.
And He calls sinners anyway.
Not so that they can remain unchanged.
Grace is not God's permission to continue destroying yourself.
Jesus brings truth into the woman's life precisely because His mercy is not superficial.
He exposes without exploiting.
He confronts without discarding.
He reveals Himself.
And eventually she leaves her water jar behind and goes toward the people.
The woman who arrived alone becomes a witness.
Do you see what Jesus does?
He does not merely give thirsty people a drink.
He turns thirsty people into witnesses.
That is grace.
Your past may explain some things about you.
It does not have the authority to name your future when Christ enters the story.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But the water imagery becomes even more explicit in John 7.

Jesus stands and cries out that anyone who thirsts should come to Him and drink. He speaks of rivers of living water, and John immediately explains that Jesus was speaking about the Spirit whom believers would receive.
There is no need for speculation.
John gives us the interpretation.
Living water is directly connected there with the Holy Spirit.
Jesus is not offering spiritual decoration.
He is offering life from God.
And this is where the article stops being something you merely read.
Because you have to answer Him.
Are you thirsty?
Not, “Are you religious?”
Not, “Were you baptized?”
Not, “Do you believe God exists?”
Not, “Do you post Bible verses?”
Are you thirsty enough to admit that what you have been drinking is not working?
Some people never come to Christ because they are still protecting the well that is killing them.
We keep lowering the bucket.
Another relationship.
Another purchase.
Another fantasy.
Another achievement.
Another secret habit.
Another round of applause.
Another promise that this time the created thing will do what only the Creator can do.
The bucket comes back up.
We drink.
For a moment, the ache becomes quieter.
Then midnight comes.
And the thirst returns.
Jesus says, in effect:
Come to Me.
Not merely to Christian culture.
Not merely to religious information.
Not merely to an inspirational version of yourself.
To Me.
Then we arrive at another scene involving water.
A basin.
A towel.
A room full of disciples.
Jesus kneels.
The Lord takes the posture of a servant and washes His disciples' feet.
Peter resists.
Of course he does.
Grace can be humiliating when you are accustomed to proving yourself.
We like serving Jesus when serving makes us feel strong.
It is harder to let Jesus expose how deeply we need to receive.
Peter has to learn that discipleship is not built on his heroic adequacy.
Soon he will prove just how inadequate he is.
He will deny Jesus.
Three times.
And still Christ will restore him.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Then comes the cross.
And here we have to be careful.
The Gospel is not a collection of symbols floating free from history.
Jesus truly suffered.
Jesus truly died.
The crucifixion is not merely poetic imagery about washing.
It is the historical, saving death of the Son of God.
At the cross, Christ bears sin. The New Testament presents His death as sacrificial, substitutionary, redemptive, reconciling, and victorious.
John records that when Jesus' side was pierced, blood and water came out.

Christians throughout history have reflected deeply on that detail, sometimes connecting it with cleansing, sacramental imagery, or the birth of the church. Some theological connections may be fruitful, but we should distinguish explicit biblical statements from later interpretation.
What John makes unmistakably clear is that Jesus truly died—and that the eyewitness testimony matters.
The Gospel rests on what God has done in history.
And Jesus does not remain dead.
The tomb empties.
The crucified Christ rises.
The Gospel is not “become a better person.”
It is news.
Christ died for our sins.
Christ was buried.
Christ was raised.
The sinner's hope is not that we can clean ourselves thoroughly enough for God to tolerate us.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
This is why biblical cleansing reaches its fulfillment not in human effort but in the saving work of Christ.
You do not wash yourself into sonship.
You do not scrub your history until God forgets it.
You come to Christ in repentance and faith.
Repentance is not paying Jesus back.
You cannot.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior.
Faith is not pretending you have never failed.
It is entrusting yourself to the One who saves failures.
And grace is not cheap because forgiveness cost nothing.
Grace is free to the sinner because Christ bore the cost.
Now follow the water one final time.
Genesis began with waters and the Spirit hovering over them.
Revelation brings us to the consummation of God's redemptive story.
John sees:
“ποταμὸν ὕδατος ζωῆς λαμπρὸν ὡς κρύσταλλον, ἐκπορευόμενον ἐκ τοῦ θρόνου τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τοῦ ἀρνίου”
A river of the water of life, bright as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb.
That is Revelation 22:1.
There is the river again.
But now look where it comes from.
The throne of God...
and of the Lamb.
The Lamb.
The One Revelation has already presented as slain and victorious.
The Bible's final river does not flow from human achievement.
It flows from God's throne.
Life has always come from God.
And at the center of this final vision stands the Lamb.
The biblical story has moved from creation...
through fall...
through judgment...
through covenant...
through Exodus...
through wilderness...
through prophets...
through incarnation...
through cross...
through resurrection...
toward new creation.
And the final chapters of Scripture do not end with God's people escaping creation forever.
They end with God making all things new.
The curse is gone.
God dwells with His people.
The tree of life appears again.
The river of life flows.
The servants of God see His face.
The Bible that opened with a world waiting for God's ordering word closes with a world fully restored under God's reign.
And suddenly the question becomes painfully personal.
Where are you in this story?
Maybe you are still standing at the well.
Still pretending you only came for ordinary water.
Maybe you have spent years keeping people from discovering how thirsty you really are.
Maybe you know Christian vocabulary but have been drinking from secret wells.
Maybe you are exhausted from performing.
Maybe you have fallen again.
Maybe your prayer life has become almost nonexistent.
Maybe shame whispers that you have wandered too far.
Maybe you are the prodigal rehearsing speeches while the Father is calling you home.
Hear this carefully:
The Gospel does not tell you that your sin does not matter.
The cross proves that it matters more terribly than we like to admit.
But the cross also tells you that God's mercy is greater than you dared to imagine.
Jesus did not come to make respectable sinners feel slightly more religious.
He came to seek and save the lost.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He reconciles.
He gives His Spirit.
He makes people new.
And He does what your favorite counterfeit well never could.
He gives life.
So stop calling your chains freedom.
Stop calling your numbness peace.
Stop decorating the well that cannot satisfy you.
Come thirsty.
Come guilty.
Come without pretending.
Come repentant.
Come believing.
Come to Christ.
If something in you is saying, I have gone too far, remember the woman at the well.
Remember Peter after his denial.
Remember the thief beside Jesus.
Remember Paul, once a persecutor of the church.
The Gospel is filled with ruined résumés that grace refused to make the final chapter.
That does not make sin small.
It makes Christ magnificent.
