So when somebody wounds you again—and somebody eventually will—remember:
You do not have to become weak.
You do not have to become a doormat.
You do not have to pretend evil is good.
You do not have to abandon truth.
But neither do you have to become cruel.
You belong to another King.
A King strong enough to confront evil.
Tender enough to touch the broken.
Holy enough to expose sin.
Merciful enough to forgive sinners.
Powerful enough to conquer death.
And meek enough to wear a crown of thorns on His way to a throne.
So unclench your fist.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the wound.
Bring Him the humiliation.
Bring Him the person you cannot forgive.
Bring Him the part of yourself you are ashamed to admit exists.
Repent where you must repent.
Forgive because you have been forgiven.
Stand for truth without surrendering your soul to hatred.
And follow the meek King.
Because the person who hurt you may have written one terrible chapter of your life…
but they do not get to write your ending. Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: FIRE FROM GENESIS TO ACTS: THE TERRIFYING, BEAUTIFUL SIGN WE KEEP MISUNDERSTANDING
paragraphs:
FIRE FROM GENESIS TO ACTS: THE TERRIFYING, BEAUTIFUL SIGN WE KEEP MISUNDERSTANDING
When Fire Appears in Scripture, Something Is Often Being Revealed—God’s Presence, His Holiness, His Judgment, His Purifying Work, or His Power. And Eventually, the Fire Leads Us to Jesus.
There is something about fire that makes human beings stop.
You can ignore a flickering light.
You can walk past a shadow.
But when you see fire, you look.
Maybe that is part of the reason Scripture keeps bringing us back to it.
A flaming torch moving through the darkness.
A bush burning without being consumed.
A pillar glowing against the wilderness night.
A mountain wrapped in smoke.
Fire falling upon an altar.
A prophet watching flames consume a sacrifice.
A warning of judgment.
A refiner purifying precious metal.
And then, centuries later, frightened followers of a crucified and risen Messiah sitting together in Jerusalem...
when suddenly something resembling fire appears over them.
From Genesis to Acts, fire repeatedly appears near moments that demand attention.
But we have to be careful here.
The Bible does not give us permission to turn every occurrence of fire into one simplistic formula.
Sometimes fire is ordinary fire.
Sometimes it accompanies divine presence.
Sometimes it communicates holiness.
Sometimes judgment.
Sometimes purification.
Sometimes acceptance of sacrifice.
Sometimes it becomes an image for God's Word.
And sometimes what appears is not described as literal fire at all, but “as of fire.”
That distinction matters.
Because Scripture is more powerful when we allow Scripture to say what it actually says.
The Hebrew word frequently translated “fire” is אֵשׁ — ’esh.
The Greek word is πῦρ — pyr.
Simple words.
But across the biblical story, fire can become an unforgettable sign that something holy, dangerous, purifying, covenantal, or divinely powerful is happening.
And perhaps the uncomfortable question is not merely:
“What does biblical fire symbolize?”
Perhaps the question underneath it is:
What happens when the holiness represented by that fire gets close to someone like me?
Because we like the fire when it means power.
We sing about the fire when it means revival.
We pray for the fire when we imagine spiritual excitement.
But biblical fire should make us slower before it makes us louder.
Because the God who reveals Himself through these terrifying and beautiful scenes is not a spiritual accessory.
He is holy.
And holiness exposes things.
Hidden things.
The resentment you learned to call discernment.
The pride you renamed confidence.
The lust you keep deleting from your history but not surrendering from your heart.
The unforgiveness you have justified for years.
The secret habit nobody at church knows about.
The version of Christianity that wants Jesus as Savior but quietly resists Jesus as Lord.
Fire has a way of making hiding difficult.
Go back near the beginning.
Genesis 15.
Abram is waiting on a promise from God.
God has promised descendants, yet Abram's circumstances seem to contradict the promise.
Then comes one of Scripture's strangest and most breathtaking covenant scenes.
Animals are divided.
Darkness falls.
And Genesis 15:17 describes a smoking firepot and a flaming torch passing between the pieces.
The Hebrew includes the expression לַפִּיד אֵשׁ — lappid ’esh, a torch of fire, or flaming torch.
This is not random religious theater.
The passage is about covenant.
God is binding Himself to His promise.
The scene is solemn, bloody, dark—and blazing with divine significance.
Abram's future ultimately depends not upon Abram being strong enough to manufacture God's promise, but upon God being faithful to what He has spoken.
That matters when your life feels dark.
Because sometimes we assume darkness means God has abandoned the story.
Genesis 15 gives us another picture.
Abram sees the fire in the darkness.
Read that again.
The darkness did not cancel the promise.
The darkness became the backdrop against which God's covenant faithfulness was displayed.
Maybe somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You prayed.
Nothing moved.
You obeyed.
Nothing changed.
You waited.
Nothing happened.
And somewhere between the promise and the fulfillment, you started wondering whether God had forgotten your address.
But biblical faith is not confidence that God will obey our preferred timetable.
Biblical faith rests upon the character of God.
Then Exodus takes us deeper.
Moses is no celebrated deliverer when God confronts him in the wilderness.
He is a man with history.
A man who once killed an Egyptian.
A man who fled.
A man living far from the palace where he had been raised.
Then Exodus 3 says the angel of the LORD appeared to him “in a flame of fire” from the midst of a bush.
The Hebrew expression contains those same unforgettable words:
בְּלַבַּת־אֵשׁ — belabbat-’esh
“In a flame of fire.”
The bush burns.
Yet it is not consumed.
Moses turns aside.
And God calls his name.
“Moses, Moses.”
Think about that.
God knew the name of the fugitive.
He knew his history.
He knew the blood in his past.
He knew his fear.
He knew every excuse Moses was about to make.
And still God called him.
That does not mean God approved of Moses' sin.
Grace never requires God to pretend sin is harmless.
It means failure did not possess greater authority over Moses' future than God's sovereign purpose.
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not “God doesn't care how I live” grace.
Transforming grace.
The kind that meets a broken man in the wilderness and sends him back different.
Maybe your wilderness is not geographical.
Maybe you are smiling in photographs while living in one internally.
Maybe nobody knows how far you feel from the person you thought you would become.
You still say “God is good.”
You still share verses.
You still know how Christians are supposed to answer.
But somewhere underneath all that polished faith is a tired sentence:
“God... can You still use me?”
Look at the bush.
Then look at Moses.
God has always been able to call people from places they thought were the end of their story.
But Moses has to learn something immediately.
“Do not come any closer.”
“Take off your sandals.”
Why?
Holy ground.
That is the tension modern Christianity can easily lose.
God's presence is comforting.
But God's presence is not casual.
The fire attracts Moses, but holiness establishes the terms of approach.
God is near.
God is merciful.
God hears suffering.
God intends deliverance.
And God is still God.
Soon the imagery grows larger.
Israel leaves Egypt.
The LORD goes before His people, with a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night.
Fire now accompanies guidance.
Imagine being surrounded by wilderness darkness and seeing that fiery sign ahead.
You do not know everything about tomorrow.
But you know where to look.
Somebody needs that distinction.
God rarely gives us the entire map.
He gives enough light for obedience.
We want a ten-year explanation.
He often gives today's step.
We want certainty about every bend in the road.
He says, in effect, follow Me.
Then Sinai.
Exodus 19:18 describes Mount Sinai covered in smoke because the LORD descended upon it in fire.
The mountain trembles.
Smoke rises.
The scene is deliberately overwhelming.
This is not the domesticated deity human beings create when we want spirituality without surrender.
This is the holy God.
The One before whom sinners cannot swagger.
And that creates the central problem of the Bible.
How can sinful people dwell with a holy God?
How can guilty humanity approach the One whose holiness exposes our rebellion?
How can people who have broken God's law survive the presence of the Lawgiver?
Religion often answers:
“Try harder.”
“Clean yourself up.”
“Become impressive.”
“Hide the scandal.”
Jesus gives a radically different answer.
Come through Me.
And now the biblical story begins pulling us toward the cross.
But before we arrive there, fire continues appearing in different contexts.
Leviticus 9 records fire coming out from before the LORD and consuming the burnt offering.
The people shout and fall facedown.
Later, in Leviticus 10, Nadab and Abihu offer unauthorized fire before the LORD, contrary to His command, and judgment follows.
That contrast should destroy any shallow idea that biblical fire simply means “spiritual excitement.”
The same biblical canon that gives us fire associated with God's accepted sacrifice also gives us fire associated with judgment.
God is not ours to manipulate.
His holiness is not a toy.
His presence is not a performance.
You cannot manufacture God with atmosphere.
You cannot substitute emotional intensity for obedience.
You cannot turn worship into theater and assume volume equals holiness.
Then Elijah stands on Carmel.
A nation is divided in loyalty.
False prophets cry out.
Nothing.
Elijah repairs the LORD's altar.
The sacrifice is prepared.
Water is poured over it.
And Elijah prays.
Then the fire of the LORD falls and consumes the offering.
The people fall facedown and confess that the LORD is God.
Notice where the biblical emphasis lands.
Not:
“Elijah is amazing.”
But:
The LORD—He is God.
That is the test of genuine spiritual awakening.
Does it make celebrities bigger...
or Christ greater?
Does it produce fascination with personalities...
or repentance before God?
Does it leave people saying, “What an experience”...
or, “The Lord—He is God”?
Then the prophets give fire another dimension.
Jeremiah 23:29 records God asking:
“Is not My word like fire?”
The point in context is the devastating difference between God's true word and false prophetic dreams.
God's Word is not empty religious noise.
It exposes.
Breaks.
Judges.
Burns through deception.
And that may explain why some passages make us uncomfortable.
We do not always dislike the Bible because it is unclear.
Sometimes we dislike it because it is painfully clear.
We want Scripture to affirm the life we already chose.
Instead, Scripture reads us.
It reaches the room we locked.
It touches the wound we hid.
It names the idol we defended.
It asks questions we hoped God would never ask.
Then Malachi speaks of the coming Lord with the imagery of a refiner's fire.
A refiner does not apply heat because the silver is worthless.
The heat is applied in the process of purification.
And here is where this becomes painfully personal.
We frequently ask God to remove the heat.

Sometimes God is using hardship—not necessarily as direct punishment, and never as an excuse for us to interpret every tragedy simplistically—but as part of the larger work through which He disciplines, matures, exposes, and sanctifies His people.
Not every painful thing is something we should label “God's refining fire.”
Scripture deserves more care than that.
But Scripture absolutely does teach that God is committed to the holiness of His people.
He loves us too deeply to make peace with the sin destroying us.
And then...
Jesus comes.
John the Baptist stands in the wilderness announcing someone greater.
In Luke 3:16 he says of Christ:
βαπτίσει ὑμᾶς ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ καὶ πυρί
“He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire.”
But context matters enormously.
The next verse speaks about the winnowing fork, wheat gathered into the barn, and chaff burned with unquenchable fire.

Christians have debated the precise relationship between “Holy Spirit and fire” here—whether the fire language should be read primarily with purification, judgment, or in relation to both ideas in the larger biblical picture.
We should not pretend the debate does not exist.
But Luke's immediate context unquestionably contains judgment.
That means we should be cautious about turning “fire” into nothing more than a slogan for emotional revival.
Jesus is not merely coming to give humanity an interesting spiritual sensation.
The King is coming.
And every person must reckon with Him.
Then comes Calvary.
There are no “tongues as of fire” hovering over Jesus at Golgotha.
We should not force imagery onto the text that the Gospel writers did not put there.
Something greater is happening.
The sinless Son of God is crucified.
Christ bears our sins in His body on the tree.
He suffers for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring us to God.
The scandal is almost unbearable.
The Holy One stands in the place of the guilty.
The Judge provides the sacrifice.
The Shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.
The One who never sinned receives what sinners deserved so that those who trust in Him may receive what they could never earn.
This is where every cheap version of grace dies.
Forgiveness was not cheap.
Grace is free to us because Christ paid what we could never pay.
Your salvation is not God shrugging at your sin.
It is God dealing with sin through the cross of His Son.
And if you have spent years hiding...
listen carefully.
Jesus already knows.
The affair.
The addiction.
The pornography.
The rage.
The jealousy.
The lie.
The secret account.
The double life.
The years you wasted.
The prayerlessness.
The religious pride.
The bitterness you feed when nobody is watching.
The fact that you sometimes sing worship songs while your heart feels a thousand kilometers from God.
He knows.
And the Gospel does not say, “Make yourself clean enough, then approach Jesus.”
The Gospel calls sinners to repent and believe in Christ.
Bring the scandal into His light.
Stop defending it.
Stop renaming it.
Stop blaming everybody else for it.
Confess.
Repent.
Trust Him.
Because Jesus did not rise from the dead to help you become better at hiding.
He rose to make sinners new.
And He did rise.
Death could not keep Him.
The tomb did not become the ending.
The crucified Christ became the risen Lord.
Then we arrive at Acts.
The disciples are together at Pentecost.
Suddenly there comes a sound from heaven like a mighty rushing wind.
It fills the house.
Acts 2:3 in Greek says:
καὶ ὤφθησαν αὐτοῖς διαμεριζόμεναι γλῶσσαι ὡσεὶ πυρός
“And there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire...”
Pay attention to ὡσεὶ πυρός — hōsei pyros.
“As of fire.”
Luke uses comparison language.
We should say what he says rather than exaggerating it into something else.
These tongues resembling fire are distributed and rest upon them, and they are filled with the Holy Spirit.
Then they speak in other tongues as the Spirit gives them utterance.
And what follows?
Mission.
Witness.
The mighty works of God are proclaimed.
Peter stands and preaches Jesus.
Not fire.
Jesus.
Jesus crucified.
Jesus raised.
Jesus exalted.
Jesus as Lord and Christ.
And the listeners are cut to the heart.
“What shall we do?”
Peter answers with repentance.
Do you see where the fire imagery has carried us?
From covenant...
to presence...
to holiness...
to guidance...
to sacrifice...
to judgment...
to purification...
and ultimately into a New Testament scene where something like fire accompanies the Spirit's empowering presence and the Gospel begins exploding outward to the nations.
The point is not to become obsessed with fire.
The point is to become consumed with Christ.
Because Pentecost is not an invitation to chase manifestations while ignoring the Messiah.
The Holy Spirit glorifies Christ.
The Spirit empowers witness to Christ.
The Gospel announces Christ.
Repentance turns sinners toward Christ.
Faith rests in Christ.
The Church belongs to Christ.
And salvation is found in Christ.
Maybe this article found you while your spiritual life feels cold.
You remember when prayer felt alive.
You remember when Scripture could stop you mid-sentence.
You remember when sin bothered you quickly.
Now you can compromise and barely flinch.
You can scroll for two hours and struggle to pray for ten minutes.
You can consume endless entertainment while saying you have no time for Scripture.
You know Christian language.
You know the songs.
But privately...
something is dying.
If that is you, do not manufacture emotion.
Do not fake fire.
Return to Jesus.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Confess what needs confessing.
Open His Word again.
Pray when you feel something.
Pray when you feel nothing.
Obey when it is exciting.
Obey when nobody applauds.
Christian maturity is not measured by how intensely you can look spiritual.
It is measured by increasingly faithful allegiance to Christ flowing from His grace.
And perhaps the fire you should fear most is not the absence of an emotional spiritual experience.
Perhaps it is becoming so comfortable with sin that you no longer care that Christ died to free you from its dominion.
Be honest.
Did this expose something?
Then don't rush to another post.
Sit there for a moment.
Talk to God.
Not with church language.
With truth.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, I have become cold.”
“Jesus, I believe; help my unbelief.”
“Jesus, I need You.”
Somebody scrolling beneath this article may need evidence that grace still reaches people in dark places.
Do not share this merely because it was emotional.
Send it to the family member you have been praying for.
Even send it, gently and respectfully, to the unbelieving friend who has misunderstood Christianity as nothing more than religious people pretending to be good.
Let them see the center of Christianity:
Not good people bragging about goodness.
Guilty people pointing toward a perfect Savior.
There may come a night when you need to remember that the God who revealed His covenant faithfulness in darkness has not stopped being faithful.
It does not.
Not because giving money purchases blessing.
It does not.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Supporting a Christian ministry is not a condition of salvation, and Christians glorify God in countless acts of faithful obedience, generosity, worship, service, love, and witness.
Your support helps us keep producing and distributing content designed to point people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through Jesus Christ.
If you have been consuming these messages quietly for months, perhaps this is your opportunity not merely to read but to help carry them farther.
Not as a transaction with God.
As mission.
And eternity is too serious for us to keep the Gospel safely inside our own feed.
From Genesis to Acts, fire repeatedly arrests human attention.
But Scripture never calls us to worship the fire.
The burning bush points beyond itself.
Sinai points beyond itself.
The altar points beyond itself.
The prophets point beyond themselves.
John points beyond himself.
Pentecost points beyond itself.
Again and again, the story drives us toward the One who stands at the center of God's saving purposes:
Jesus Christ.
The Savior of sinners.
The friend of the broken.
The Lord who commands repentance.
The Lamb who bears sin.
The risen King who conquers death.
The One who takes people whose stories look irredeemable and writes grace where everyone else expected the final chapter.
So if your life feels like ashes tonight...
do not worship the ashes.
And do not pretend they are not there.
Bring them to Christ.
Because the most unforgettable truth in your story will never be how badly you burned your life down.
It will be what Jesus did when you finally stopped hiding in the smoke and surrendered everything to Him.
Your scandal may explain the ashes behind you—but only Jesus gets to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Joseph: They Threw Him Into a Pit to Bury the Dream—But God Was Already Writing the Ending
paragraphs: Joseph: They Threw Him Into a Pit to Bury the Dream—But God Was Already Writing the Ending

His brothers stripped him, sold him, lied about his death, and went home believing the dream was finished. Years later, they bowed before the brother they had betrayed—because what people mean for evil, God can sovereignly weave toward good.
There is a particular kind of pain that does not come from enemies.
It comes from people who know your name.
People who have eaten beside you.
People who know your weaknesses, your history, your family, your hopes.
People close enough to know exactly where betrayal will hurt.
Joseph knew that pain.

Long before he stood dressed in the authority of Egypt, long before Pharaoh placed his signet ring on Joseph's hand, long before starving nations came looking for grain, there was a teenage boy standing in front of his own brothers.
And they hated what God had shown him.

Joseph was seventeen when Genesis introduces him in the story that would define generations. He was the son Jacob loved deeply, born to Rachel, and Jacob's favoritism was painfully obvious. Genesis does not sanitize this family. Scripture does not pretend Joseph grew up in some flawless biblical household where everyone prayed together and handled conflict perfectly.
This family was complicated.
There was favoritism.
Jealousy.
Competition.
Old wounds.
Bad decisions.
And resentment growing quietly until resentment became hatred.

Jacob gave Joseph the famous garment described in Genesis 37:3. The Hebrew expression is כְּתֹנֶת פַּסִּים — ketonet passim. Traditionally rendered a “coat of many colors,” its precise appearance is debated; translations such as “ornate robe” or “long robe” reflect that uncertainty.
But the emotional meaning in the narrative is unmistakable.
Joseph had been singled out.
His brothers saw it.
And every time they looked at Joseph, they were reminded of their father's unequal affection.
Then Joseph dreamed.
In one dream, Joseph and his brothers were binding sheaves in a field. Joseph's sheaf stood upright, while the others gathered around and bowed to it.
His brothers immediately understood the implication.
“Are you indeed to reign over us?”
Then another dream came.
The sun, moon, and eleven stars bowed before him.
Even Jacob rebuked him.
Joseph could not yet see the road between revelation and fulfillment.
He saw the dream.
He did not see the pit.
He saw people bowing.
He did not see himself begging.
He saw elevation.
He did not see slavery.
He saw what God would eventually accomplish.
He did not see how much suffering would stand between the promise and its fulfillment.
And maybe that is where Joseph's story begins touching yours.
Because sometimes God allows you to see enough to keep walking without showing you everything walking will cost.
You thought obedience would make the road easier.
Instead, people misunderstood you.
You thought doing what was right would protect you from betrayal.
It didn't.
You prayed.
And something still collapsed.
You tried to remain faithful.
And someone else appeared to prosper while you were hurting.
Maybe you have wondered in the darkness:
“God, did I misunderstand You?”
Joseph's brothers saw him approaching from a distance one day.
Before Joseph ever reached them, they were already plotting.
Genesis 37:19 records their contempt:
בַּעַל הַחֲלֹמוֹת הַלָּזֶה בָּא — ba'al haḥalomot hallazeh ba'
Loosely and naturally:
“Here comes this dreamer.”
Then came words that expose the heart of their conspiracy:
“Come now, let us kill him…”
And then:
“we shall see what will become of his dreams.”
Think about that.
They were not merely attacking Joseph.
They believed that by destroying the dreamer, they could determine the destiny of the dream.
They stripped Joseph of his robe.
They threw him into a pit.
Genesis tells us the pit was empty and contained no water.
Then comes one of the coldest details in the entire account.
They sat down to eat.
Joseph was in the pit.
His brothers were having a meal.
Years later, Genesis 42:21 reveals something Genesis 37 does not initially emphasize: Joseph had been in distress and had pleaded with them.
Imagine hearing your own brother begging while you continue eating.
That is betrayal.
Not merely being wounded by strangers.
Being wounded by people who can hear you crying and still choose themselves.
Eventually, instead of killing Joseph, they sold him to passing traders, and Joseph was taken into Egypt.
Then the brothers dipped his robe in the blood of a goat and allowed their father to conclude that Joseph had been torn apart by a wild animal.
One lie devastated an entire household.
Jacob mourned his son.
Joseph disappeared into slavery.
And the brothers carried a secret home.
If the story ended there, Joseph would simply be another victim of human cruelty.
But Genesis contains a sentence more powerful than the pit.
וַיְהִי יְהוָה אֶת־יוֹסֵף — vayhi YHWH et-Yosef.
“And the LORD was with Joseph.”
That truth appears in Genesis 39.
Do not rush past it.
Joseph had been betrayed…
and the LORD was with Joseph.
Joseph had been sold…
and the LORD was with Joseph.
Joseph was living far from home…
and the LORD was with Joseph.
God's presence did not mean Joseph avoided suffering.
God's presence meant suffering did not have ultimate ownership of Joseph's story.
That distinction matters.
Because some believers quietly assume that if God is truly with them, nothing devastating should happen.
Joseph's life destroys that theology.
You can be loved by God and misunderstood by people.
You can walk faithfully and still be falsely accused.
You can obey God and still spend nights wondering when deliverance will come.
God's presence is not proven by the absence of trouble.
Sometimes His presence becomes most precious in the middle of it.
Joseph entered the household of Potiphar, an Egyptian official, and God caused his work to prosper. Eventually Potiphar entrusted his household to Joseph.
For a moment, perhaps life seemed to be rebuilding.
Then another scandal came.
Potiphar's wife repeatedly tried to seduce Joseph.
Joseph refused.
His response reveals the center of his integrity:
“How then can I do this great wickedness and sin against God?”
Joseph understood something our generation desperately needs to recover.
Sin is not merely breaking a rule.
Sin is ultimately against God.
So Joseph ran.
He left his garment behind rather than leave his integrity behind.
And what did righteousness get him?
A false accusation.
Potiphar's wife used the garment Joseph abandoned while escaping to construct a lie against him.
There is almost painful irony here.
A garment had once been used by Joseph's brothers to deceive their father.
Now another garment was being used to falsely accuse Joseph.
Joseph did the right thing…
and went to prison.
Somebody reading this knows exactly why that sentence hurts.
You apologized and they still left.
You told the truth and people believed the lie.
You refused the compromise and lost the opportunity.
You remained faithful and watched someone dishonest move ahead.
You prayed for restoration and received another disappointment.
And somewhere inside you, perhaps you have whispered:
“What is the point of doing right if doing right still hurts?”
Joseph's story answers—not with cheap optimism, but with providence.
The prison was not proof that God had forgotten Joseph.
Genesis again emphasizes that the LORD was with him.
In prison Joseph interpreted the dreams of Pharaoh's cupbearer and baker. The cupbearer would be restored to his position, and Joseph asked him to remember him.
The interpretation came true.
The cupbearer was restored.
And then Scripture says he forgot Joseph.
Imagine surviving betrayal by your brothers.
Surviving slavery.
Surviving false accusation.
Then finally believing somebody might speak your name in the right room…
only to be forgotten.
Days passed.
Weeks.
Months.
Then years.
Genesis 41 tells us two full years passed before Pharaoh dreamed dreams that Egypt's wise men could not interpret.
Suddenly the cupbearer remembered.
Joseph was brought from the dungeon.
And the forgotten prisoner stood before the most powerful man in Egypt.
Pharaoh told Joseph that he had heard Joseph could interpret dreams.
Joseph could have seized the moment and marketed himself.
Instead he answered:
“It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer.”
That is spiritual maturity forged in darkness.
The seventeen-year-old Joseph had once told people his dreams.
The older Joseph standing before Pharaoh pointed immediately to God.
Suffering had not destroyed the gift.
It had deepened the man carrying it.
Joseph interpreted Pharaoh's dreams: seven years of extraordinary abundance would be followed by seven years of devastating famine.
Joseph then recommended wise preparation.
Pharaoh recognized unusual wisdom in him.
And in one breathtaking reversal, the prisoner became Egypt's governor.
The pit had not canceled the dream.
The prison had not canceled the dream.
The lie had not canceled the dream.
Being forgotten had not canceled the dream.
Because ultimately Joseph's future was never sitting in his brothers' hands.
And neither is God's sovereign purpose for your life sitting in the hands of the person who rejected you.
But be careful here.
Joseph's story is not a promise that every Christian who suffers will become wealthy, famous, politically powerful, or publicly vindicated.
That would distort Scripture.
The point is greater than that.
God is sovereign.
God is faithful.
God can work through circumstances human beings intended for destruction.
And sometimes His purposes are much larger than the comfort of one individual.
The famine eventually came.
Joseph's brothers traveled to Egypt looking for food.
They entered the presence of Egypt's governor without recognizing him.
And then…
they bowed.
The brothers who had mocked the dream were standing inside its fulfillment.
Can you imagine Joseph's heartbeat?
These were the faces from the pit.
The voices from the nightmare.
The men whose choices had changed the course of his life.
Now they were vulnerable before him.
Joseph possessed what wounded people often fantasize about possessing:
power over the people who hurt him.
He could punish them.
Humiliate them.
Starve them.
Make them feel helpless.
He could finally make them hurt the way he had hurt.

And the story becomes profoundly revealing because Joseph does test his brothers, particularly regarding Benjamin, and the narrative shows evidence of their changed hearts—especially when Judah offers himself in Benjamin's place.
Then Joseph can no longer contain himself.
He sends the Egyptians from the room.
And he weeps.
Not a polished little tear for religious effect.
Genesis describes such loud weeping that the Egyptians heard it.
Then Joseph says words his brothers never expected:
“I am Joseph.”
Imagine the terror.
The brother you sold is alive.
The boy you threw away has authority.
The secret you buried is standing in front of you.
Then Joseph says:
“Come near to me, please.”
Read that again.
Come near.
The men who once rejected Joseph were invited closer.
Joseph did not pretend their evil was good.
Biblical forgiveness does not require calling wickedness righteous.
Joseph explicitly acknowledges what they did.
“You sold me here.”
But he also recognizes something greater than their sin operating through history.
Later, after Jacob dies, the brothers fear Joseph may finally seek revenge.
Joseph weeps again.
And then comes the sentence that has echoed through generations.
Genesis 50:20:
וְאַתֶּם חֲשַׁבְתֶּם עָלַי רָעָה אֱלֹהִים חֲשָׁבָהּ לְטֹבָה
Ve'atem ḥashavtem 'alai ra'ah; Elohim ḥashavah letovah.
A faithful rendering is:
“As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good…”
The Hebrew is striking because the verb חָשַׁב — ḥashav, carrying the sense of planning, reckoning, or intending, appears on both sides.
They intended.
God intended.
Same event.
Different intention.
Joseph does not say:
“What you did wasn't really evil.”
He calls it רָעָה — ra'ah.
Evil.
The Bible does not need to minimize human evil in order to magnify God's sovereignty.
They meant evil.
God meant good.
Not because evil magically became righteous, but because human wickedness could not overthrow divine providence.
And the “good” was bigger than Joseph receiving a promotion.
Joseph explains the purpose:
“to bring it about that many people should be kept alive.”
God was preserving lives.
God was preserving Jacob's family.
And through that family, the biblical story would continue toward Israel, Judah, David…
and ultimately Jesus Christ.
This is where Joseph's story becomes larger than Joseph.
Joseph is not Jesus, and we should not flatten the differences between them. Yet Joseph's story contains patterns that prepare Christian readers to recognize something even greater in Christ.
A beloved son rejected by his own.
Humiliated.
Handed over.
Suffering despite innocence.
Then exalted.
And through what looked like catastrophic defeat, God brought deliverance to others.
Then we reach Jesus.
Jesus was not merely a dreamer thrown into a pit.
He is the Son of God who willingly gave Himself for sinners.
He was rejected.
Betrayed.
Mocked.
Condemned.
Crucified.
Human beings meant the cross as an instrument of shame, suffering, and death.
Yet God accomplished redemption through the very cross intended to destroy Him.
Peter would later proclaim concerning Jesus that He was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, while lawless men crucified and killed Him.
Human responsibility.
Divine sovereignty.
At the same cross.
Then resurrection.
What looked like the end became the announcement that death itself had been defeated.
That is the Gospel.
And this is where the story stops being safely about Joseph's brothers.
Because we like identifying with Joseph.
We like imagining ourselves as the misunderstood dreamer.
The betrayed one.
The falsely accused one.
The forgotten one who eventually gets vindicated.
But what if sometimes…
we are the brothers?
What if jealousy has lived inside us?
What if we have secretly resented someone else's blessing?
What if we smiled publicly while bitterness grew privately?
What if we damaged someone with our words?
What if we betrayed trust?
What if there are things in our past we desperately hope never walk through the door and say:
“I am Joseph”?
We do not only need a God who can rescue Joseph from a pit.
We need a Savior who can forgive Joseph's brothers.
We need Jesus.
Because the deepest scandal in Scripture is not merely that innocent people suffer.
It is that guilty people like us can be offered grace because the truly innocent Christ suffered in the place of sinners.
This is why Christianity is not self-improvement wearing a cross necklace.
The Gospel is not:
“Become impressive enough for God to accept you.”
It is that sinners who could never save themselves are called to repent and trust in Jesus Christ—the crucified and risen Lord.
Grace does not pretend your sin never mattered.
Grace says it mattered so much that Christ bore sin's judgment at the cross.
Forgiveness is not God shrugging at evil.
Forgiveness was purchased at terrible cost.
And resurrection announces that sin and death do not get the final word.
Maybe your scandal is known.
Maybe yours is hidden.
Maybe nobody knows what you did.
Maybe everybody knows what was done to you.
Maybe your pit was betrayal.
Maybe your prison has been shame.
Maybe you have spent years trying to outrun a chapter you cannot rewrite.
You cannot change yesterday.
But Jesus Christ can redeem a life you thought yesterday had permanently defined.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
It does not mean every broken relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
It does not mean repentance is unnecessary.
Real grace calls us out of hiding.
Real grace produces repentance.
Real grace teaches us to confess rather than perform.
Real grace does not merely make guilty people feel better.
It begins transforming them.
That is why our theme is not “From Scandal to Pretending Nothing Happened.”
It is:
He rewrites the meaning of the chapter without pretending the chapter never happened.
Joseph still had a pit in his history.
But the pit no longer possessed his future.
The betrayal remained part of his testimony.
But betrayal did not become his identity.
His brothers' sin was real.
But their sin was not stronger than God's providence.
And your darkest chapter does not have greater authority than Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have been carrying hatred toward the person who threw you into your pit.
Joseph's forgiveness does not teach that abuse should be tolerated, that boundaries are sinful, that justice never matters, or that trust must instantly be restored.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are related, but they are not identical. Trust can require truth, repentance, wisdom, time, and evidence of change.
But Christian forgiveness does mean surrendering personal vengeance to God.
You cannot keep drinking bitterness and expect your soul to remain untouched.
Maybe the person you need to bring before Christ tonight is not the person who betrayed you.
Maybe it is you.
Maybe you became hard.
Maybe disappointment slowly turned into unbelief.
Maybe church hurt became an excuse to run from Jesus.
Maybe secret sin became your anesthesia.
Maybe you have been smiling online while spiritually bleeding behind the screen.
No more hiding.
Bring it to Christ.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Seek help where wisdom requires help.
Make restitution where possible.
Tell the truth.
Come into the light.
Jesus already knows the chapter you are afraid to show Him.
And He is still calling sinners to Himself.
Somebody reading silently may need evidence that grace still reaches people in pits.
Do not underestimate what happens when believers stop pretending.
Someone else's confession can become another person's courage.
Someone else's testimony can become another person's reason to seek Christ.
There may come a night when betrayal starts talking again.
A night when the old accusation comes back.
A night when you wonder whether God has forgotten where you are.
Come back and remember:
וַיְהִי יְהוָה אֶת־יוֹסֵף.
The LORD was with Joseph.
Let your feed become one more place where people encounter biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and the Gospel of Jesus Christ.

It does not buy God's blessing, prove your faith, or make you more pleasing to Him—Christ alone is our righteousness. But generous support can be one genuine way to participate in spreading resources that point people toward Jesus.
And there is much more waiting for believers who are serious about growing deeper.
If this ministry has strengthened you, consider helping strengthen the person who has not discovered it yet.
Follow.
Save these words for the night you need them again.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because confession, testimony, prayer, and encouragement can turn a comment section into a place where people stop hiding.
Because somewhere tonight, another Joseph is staring at the walls of a pit.
Another betrayed believer thinks the betrayal was the ending.
Another forgotten person believes silence means God has left.
Another guilty brother is wondering whether grace could possibly still have his name on it.
And another wounded heart is about to discover the truth the enemy desperately wants buried:
What they threw into the pit was not beyond the reach of God—and what you surrender to Jesus is never beyond the reach of redemption.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY WERE FALSE PROPHETS SO COMMON?
paragraphs:
WHY WERE FALSE PROPHETS SO COMMON?
The Terrifying Reason Their Voices Were Easier to Love Than God’s—and Why Jesus Warned They Would Still Be Among Us
There is something disturbing buried inside the pages of Scripture.
Something so familiar that we can read past it without feeling the weight of it.
Again and again, God sends His people a true prophet.
And again and again…
there are already other voices waiting.
Confident voices.
Religious voices.
Voices invoking the name of God.
Voices announcing dreams.
Voices promising peace.
Voices telling frightened people exactly what frightened people desperately want to hear.
And sometimes the false prophet appears to have everything the true prophet does.
Religious vocabulary.
An audience.
Confidence.
A claim of divine authority.
Maybe even a sign.
That raises an uncomfortable question:
Why were false prophets so common in the Bible?
Why did Israel repeatedly encounter them?
Why did Jeremiah have to confront them?
Why did Jesus warn about them?
Why did the apostles continue warning the Church after Christ's resurrection?
And perhaps the most unsettling question of all:
Why are human beings so vulnerable to them?
The answer is more personal than we might want it to be.
False prophets flourish because there has always been a market for a god who tells fallen human beings what they already wanted to believe.
That sentence should bother us.
Because the story of false prophecy is not merely the story of wicked people deceiving innocent people.
Sometimes it is the story of people desperately searching for someone who will make rebellion feel righteous.
Someone who will call compromise "peace."
Someone who will rename greed "blessing."
Someone who will baptize ambition as "destiny."
Someone who will reassure us that we can keep our idols…
and keep God too.
That is why this subject cannot remain ancient history.
Because while the costumes change, the human heart does not.
And Jesus knew it.
Long before social media gave every voice a microphone, Christ warned:
“Beware of false prophets.”

The Greek expression in Matthew 7:15 is τῶν ψευδοπροφητῶν — tōn pseudoprophētōn, from ψευδοπροφήτης — pseudoprophētēs, literally a false prophet. The New Testament uses this term repeatedly, including in Jesus' warnings about deceptive religious figures.
But notice what Jesus says next.
They do not necessarily arrive looking dangerous.
They come in sheep's clothing.
That changes everything.
Jesus is warning us that spiritual deception often succeeds precisely because it does not initially look like deception.
A wolf that looks like a wolf is relatively easy to avoid.
The terrifying wolf is the one you invite into the flock because you mistook him for a sheep.
And this problem did not begin in the New Testament.
Centuries earlier, Moses had already established something fundamental: no human being had the right to attach God's name to words God had never spoken.
Deuteronomy 18:20 records:
אַךְ הַנָּבִיא אֲשֶׁר יָזִיד לְדַבֵּר דָּבָר בִּשְׁמִי אֵת אֲשֶׁר לֹא־צִוִּיתִיו לְדַבֵּר
'Akh hannavi asher yazid ledabber davar bishmi et asher lo-tsivvitiv ledabber…'

The sense is devastatingly clear: the prophet who presumes to speak a word in God's name that God did not command has crossed a line of enormous seriousness. Deuteronomy goes on to give Israel a test concerning predictions that fail to occur.
Think about what that means.
The problem was not merely saying something incorrect.
The scandal was saying:
“God said…”
when God had not said it.
It was identity theft at the highest possible level.
Taking human imagination…
human ambition…
human fear…
human desire…
and signing God's name underneath it.
That is why false prophecy was so serious.
The false prophet did not merely deceive people about tomorrow.
He distorted their understanding of God.
And once you distort someone's understanding of God, you can distort almost everything else in that person's life.
You can make disobedience feel obedient.
You can make greed feel spiritual.
You can make pride feel anointed.
You can make cowardice feel like wisdom.
You can make judgment sound like blessing.
You can even make people believe they are walking toward God while quietly leading them away from Him.
Jeremiah saw this nightmare firsthand.
He lived in a generation approaching catastrophe. Judah's sin was serious. Judgment was coming. Babylon would become God's instrument of discipline.
Jeremiah's message was not what the nation wanted.
Repent.
Turn back.
Stop pretending.
Stop trusting religious appearances while your hearts remain rebellious.
Then other prophets appeared with something far more attractive.
Reassurance.
Hope without repentance.
Peace without surrender.
Deliverance without transformation.
Jeremiah 23 records God saying of such prophets:
הַנְּבִאִים הַנִּבְּאִים בִּשְׁמִי שֶׁקֶר
Prophets who were prophesying falsely in His name.
Their message even sounded spiritual.
“I had a dream, I had a dream.”
Yet God identifies them as prophets speaking from the deception of their own hearts, and later declares that He had neither sent nor commanded them.
Do not miss that.
They had experiences.
They had stories.
They had dreams.
They had words.
They had confidence.
What they did not have…
was God's authorization.
That distinction may be one of the most desperately needed distinctions in modern Christianity.
An experience is not automatically revelation.
A dream is not automatically a message from God.
Confidence is not confirmation.
Popularity is not proof.
Emotional intensity is not inspiration.
A large audience is not divine endorsement.
And repeatedly saying “God told me” does not obligate God to take responsibility for something He never said.
Jeremiah 29 makes the matter painfully explicit. God warns the exiles not to let the prophets and diviners among them deceive them, then says:
בְשֶׁקֶר הֵם נִבְּאִים לָכֶם בִּשְׁמִי לֹא שְׁלַחְתִּים
They were prophesying falsely in His name.
Then comes the crushing declaration:
“I did not send them.”
Imagine hearing those words from God.
You built a ministry around His name.
You gathered listeners around His name.
You spoke confidently in His name.
People admired you because they believed you represented His name.
And heaven's verdict is:
I never sent you.
There may be few sentences more frightening for anyone who teaches Scripture.
Including us.
Including me.
Including your favorite preacher.
Including the person whose sermons you watch every week.
Including the viral Christian creator with millions of views.
Including anyone who opens a Bible and claims to explain what God means.
That is why biblical discernment must never become a weapon we use exclusively against teachers we already dislike.
It begins with humility.
“Lord, do not let me put words in Your mouth either.”
Because false prophecy was common for another reason.
Truth can be expensive.
Falsehood often offers discounts.
Truth may tell you to repent.
Falsehood tells you that everybody else is the problem.
Truth may expose your idol.
Falsehood may promise God will give you more of it.
Truth may tell you to forgive.
Falsehood can make bitterness feel justified.
Truth may call you to holiness.
Falsehood can redefine holiness until your favorite sin fits comfortably inside it.
Truth may tell you that following Jesus includes a cross.
Falsehood sells Christianity without crucifixion.
And that is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because perhaps false prophets were common not simply because false prophets loved speaking…
but because people loved listening.
There is a chilling transaction that can happen between a deceiver and an audience.
Tell me the lie I want to believe, and I will reward you for telling it.
Give me certainty without Scripture.
Give me blessing without obedience.
Give me heaven without repentance.
Give me Jesus without lordship.
Give me resurrection without crucifixion.
Give me Christianity without a cross.
And I will call you prophetic.
This is why Scripture's warnings cannot be reduced to “avoid obviously crazy religious people.”
Jesus takes us deeper.
He says we recognize false prophets by their fruits.
Not merely charisma.
Not presentation.
Not eloquence.
Not dramatic stories.
Fruit.
What grows from the tree?
What does the teaching ultimately produce?
Does it exalt Christ or build a personality cult?
Does it lead toward holiness or excuse sin?
Does it produce humility or spiritual superiority?
Does it submit to Scripture or constantly require Scripture to submit to someone's private revelations?
Does it produce repentance, love, truth, endurance, obedience and Christlike character?
Or does it create addiction to the messenger?
That last question matters.
Because a faithful Christian teacher should ultimately make you more dependent upon Christ, not more dependent upon the teacher.
A faithful teacher should make you hungry for Scripture.
A manipulator makes you hungry for the next secret.
The faithful teacher says, in effect, “Look at Christ.”
The false teacher eventually whispers, “Look at me.”
And sometimes the difference is almost invisible at first.
That is why the New Testament refuses to treat discernment as optional.
John writes:
Why?
Because many false prophets had gone out into the world.

The ancient Syriac Peshitta preserves the thought with the words נביאי דגלא — nbiye daggala, false/deceitful prophets, in 1 John 4:1, while the passage immediately anchors discernment in the confession of Jesus the Messiah come in the flesh.
There it is again.
Christ at the center.
Not our fascination with prophecy.
Not our obsession with identifying villains.
Not endless conspiracy hunting.
Jesus Christ.
Biblical discernment is not paranoia.
It is fidelity.
There is a difference.
The paranoid Christian suspects everybody.
The discerning Christian tests everything against God's revealed truth and remains humble enough to be corrected.
And here is where we must be extremely careful.
A teacher is not automatically a false prophet because they make a mistake.
Christians can misunderstand a passage.
Pastors can misspeak.
Teachers can reach conclusions that need correction.
Faithful believers can disagree on secondary theological questions.
The biblical category is more serious than ordinary human fallibility.

Scripture repeatedly connects false teachers and false prophets with deception, presumptuous claims of divine authority, corrupt fruit, departure from apostolic truth, exploitation, and leading people away from faithfulness to God.
So discernment requires both courage and restraint.
We should not call everything prophecy.
But neither should we call everyone we disagree with a false prophet.
Both errors abuse the authority of God.
And now we arrive at perhaps the hardest moment in this entire conversation.
Before asking…
“Who is the false prophet?”
ask:
“What kind of message am I secretly hoping God will tell me?”
Because deception becomes especially powerful when it finds an unrepented desire already waiting inside us.
Maybe you desperately want someone to tell you that the relationship God has been convicting you about is fine.
Maybe you want someone to tell you your obsession with money is really “kingdom ambition.”
Maybe you want someone to assure you that unforgiveness is merely having boundaries.
Maybe you want Christianity to validate every political instinct, cultural preference, personal ambition, or emotional impulse you already possess.
Maybe you have been asking God for guidance…
when what you actually wanted was permission.
Read that again.
Sometimes we ask God for guidance when what we really want is permission.
Permission to keep the idol.
Permission to avoid repentance.
Permission to remain angry.
Permission to stay comfortable.
Permission to continue pretending.
And somewhere in the world, there will almost always be a voice willing to give us that permission in Jesus' name.
That is why knowing Scripture matters.
That is why context matters.
That is why doctrine matters.
That is why a Christianity built exclusively on inspirational clips is dangerously undernourished.
You need more than somebody else's revelation.
You need the Word.
You need prayer.
You need the historic Gospel.
You need mature believers who are willing to tell you the truth when the truth hurts.
Above everything…
you need Christ.
Because the ultimate answer to false prophets is not merely becoming better at detecting counterfeit voices.
It is becoming deeply acquainted with the true Shepherd.
Jesus says His sheep hear His voice.
And the voice of Jesus will never contradict the truth He has revealed.
He will never lead you into a holiness He Himself rejects.
He will never tell you sin does not matter when His own blood demonstrates how devastating sin truly is.
The cross destroys cheap spirituality.
Look at Calvary.
If sin were insignificant, why the cross?
If repentance were unnecessary, why did Jesus preach repentance?
If holiness were irrelevant, why are His followers repeatedly called to holiness?
If every road eventually reached God, why did the Son of God come seeking the lost?
At the cross, every false gospel is exposed.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the message:
“God wants to make all your dreams come true.”
The Gospel is infinitely greater.
You were a sinner who could not rescue yourself.
The holy God did not owe you salvation.
Yet in love, the Father sent His Son.
Jesus Christ lived in perfect obedience.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now forgiveness is proclaimed in His name.
The guilty can be pardoned.
The rebellious can come home.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
The ashamed can stop hiding.
The sinner can repent and believe.
That is not motivational speaking.
That is rescue.
And maybe that is why false prophecy remains so seductive.
The counterfeit gospel usually tells us that we need improved circumstances.
The true Gospel tells us we needed resurrection.
The counterfeit tells us God exists to help us accomplish our plans.
Jesus calls us to follow Him.
The counterfeit puts us at the center and asks God to orbit our desires.
The Gospel puts Christ on the throne and invites us to die to ourselves…
and discover that surrender to Jesus is where life actually begins.
Perhaps you have been deceived before.
Maybe you trusted someone because they sounded certain.
Maybe you gave money because you were promised something God never promised.
Maybe someone weaponized “God told me” against you.
Maybe you followed a personality so closely that when that person fell, your faith nearly collapsed with them.
Hear this carefully.
Do not confuse the failure of someone who used Christ's name with the character of Christ Himself.
Jesus is not exposed as false because somebody falsely represented Jesus.
Come back to Him.
Open the Scriptures again.
Test what you hear.
Ask questions.
Read passages in context.
Do not be intimidated by someone simply because they claim supernatural authority.
Deuteronomy itself gave God's people permission to test prophetic claims.
Truth does not fear examination.
And if you discover that you were the one who followed error?
There is grace for that too.
If you discover that you have preferred comforting lies over uncomfortable truth?
Grace.
If you have twisted Scripture to justify something you did not want to surrender?
Grace.
If pride made you spiritually gullible?
Grace.
But biblical grace does not say:
“Stay there.”
Grace says:
“Come home.”
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you out of the darkness that was destroying you.
This is the scandal of Christianity.
The people who got it wrong can be forgiven.
The deceived can return.
The compromised can repent.
The ashamed can come out of hiding.
The prodigal can walk home.
The sinner can kneel at the cross…
and rise belonging to Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And maybe right now, the Holy Spirit is not bringing somebody else's face to your mind.
Maybe He is dealing with you.
Not the preacher you distrust.
Not the denomination you dislike.
Not the Christian influencer who annoys you.
You.
Your appetite.
Your compromises.
Your secret desire to hear only what comforts you.
Your willingness to follow Christ only when Christ agrees with you.
Be honest.
Somebody quietly reading may desperately need to know that being deceived does not have to be the end of their story.
Not because every sentence here deserves unquestioned acceptance—it does not.
Open your Bible.
Read Deuteronomy 13 and 18.
Read Jeremiah 23 and 28–29.
Read Matthew 7 and 24.
Read 1 John 4.
Read 2 Peter 2.
Read Jude.
Test what you have read here too.
That is what serious disciples do.
Send it privately to the believer who has been confused by competing voices.
Send it even to the seeker who thinks Christianity is merely a marketplace of preachers making competing claims.
Let them discover that Scripture itself warned us this would happen.

Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as purchasing God's favor. You cannot buy blessing, salvation, answered prayer, or a higher place in God's heart. Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.

Not from guilt. But because voluntarily supporting faithful Christian content can help put Scripture, discipleship, encouragement, conviction, and the Gospel in front of another person who might desperately need it.
If these messages are feeding your faith, stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the person asking hard questions.
Invite the unbeliever who thinks Jesus has nothing to say to people like them.
Never make Gospel Warrior your foundation.
Never make a preacher your foundation.
Never make an influencer your foundation.
Never make a denomination your foundation.
Christ is the foundation.
Follow us only insofar as we follow Him.
Test what we teach against Scripture.
Correct us when correction is biblically warranted.
And never surrender to any human voice the authority that belongs to Jesus Christ.
Because perhaps that is the deepest answer to the question we started with.
Why were false prophets so common?
Because counterfeit voices have always found an audience wherever human beings wanted God's authority without God's truth.
But there is another voice.
The voice of the Shepherd who does not flatter us into destruction.
The Shepherd who tells us the truth because He loves us.
The Shepherd who calls sinners to repentance and then receives repentant sinners with mercy.
The Shepherd who did not exploit His sheep…
but laid down His life for them.
So when a thousand voices are shouting…
when prophecy becomes entertainment…
when charisma becomes confused with anointing…
when personalities become larger than Scripture…
when somebody promises everything your flesh desperately wants to hear…
remember the Shepherd.
Return to His Word.
Return to the cross.
Return to repentance.
Return to grace.
Return to Jesus.
Because the most dangerous lie may not be the one that sounds obviously evil.
It may be the one that sounds exactly like what you wanted God to say.
And when that realization breaks your heart, do not run away from Christ.
Run toward Him.
The final answer to spiritual deception is not fear.
It is knowing, loving, obeying, and remaining in the One who said:
“I am the truth.”
And when Truth Himself finds you tangled in lies, His purpose is not merely to expose your scandal.
He can redeem your story.
He can forgive your sin.
He can restore what deception damaged.
He can teach you to recognize His voice again.
He can take the chapter you wish had never been written…
and cover it with grace.
The lie may have written part of your past—but it does not get to write your ending when Jesus holds the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SOME CHRISTIAN MARRIAGES ARE LIVING IN THE PALACE OF VASHTI—AND THEY DON’T EVEN KNOW IT
paragraphs:
SOME CHRISTIAN MARRIAGES ARE LIVING IN THE PALACE OF VASHTI—AND THEY DON’T EVEN KNOW IT
When love becomes a battle over respect, when wounded pride starts making decisions, and when husband and wife would rather prove a point than protect the marriage, the story of Vashti and King Ahasuerus becomes frighteningly familiar.
There are marriages that have not ended.
But something inside them has.

The wedding pictures are still hanging on the wall. The rings are still being worn. They still sit beside each other in church. They may still post anniversary pictures with Bible verses underneath them.
But at home?
The conversations have become shorter.
The silence has become longer.
Affection has been replaced by tension.
One spouse feels disrespected.
The other feels unseen.
One is waiting for an apology.
The other is waiting to be understood.
Neither wants the marriage to die.
But both are exhausted from being the first one expected to surrender.
And somewhere between “You never listen to me” and “I’m tired of explaining myself,” something dangerous enters the room.
Pride.
Not always loud pride.
Sometimes wounded pride.
Sometimes embarrassed pride.
Sometimes pride wearing the clothes of self-protection.
Sometimes pride that says:
“If I soften first, they win.”
“If I apologize first, they’ll think I was wrong about everything.”
“If I forgive too quickly, they’ll do it again.”
“If I reach for them after what they did, I’ll look weak.”
And that is where an ancient palace suddenly begins to look disturbingly modern.
Because thousands of years ago, before Esther ever walked into the king’s court, another woman occupied that palace.
Her name was Vashti.

And before we turn her into either a villain or a feminist heroine, before we turn Ahasuerus into either a helpless husband or a cartoon tyrant, we need to slow down and let Scripture say what Scripture actually says.
The Hebrew text calls the king אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ — Aḥašwērôš, commonly rendered Ahasuerus and widely identified historically with Xerxes I of Persia.
Vashti is וַשְׁתִּי — Waštî.
Esther 1 opens not with romance, but with power.
The king reigns over an enormous empire stretching from India toward Ethiopia. He displays the wealth and glory of his kingdom for 180 days, and afterward holds a seven-day feast.
The language of the chapter drips with magnificence.
Gold.
Silver.
Royal wine.
Marble.
Purple fabric.
Wealth.
Power.
Excess.
Image.
Status.
And alcohol.
Esther 1:10 says the king's heart was “merry with wine.” The Hebrew expression includes the words:
טוֹב לֵב־הַמֶּלֶךְ בַּיָּיִן
ṭôḇ lēḇ-hammeleḵ bayyāyin
The king's heart was merry with wine.
Then comes the command that changes everything.
Ahasuerus orders that Queen Vashti be brought before him wearing her royal crown so that he can display her beauty before the people and officials.
And Vashti refuses.
The Hebrew is stark:
וַתְּמָאֵן הַמַּלְכָּה וַשְׁתִּי
Wattəmāʾēn hammalkâ Waštî.
“Queen Vashti refused.”
Esther 1:12.
A few words.
An enormous consequence.
But here is where responsible Bible reading matters.
Scripture does not tell us exactly why Vashti refused.
That matters.

People have filled that silence with speculation for centuries. Some explanations may be interesting. Some may come from later traditions. But we should never preach speculation as though God placed it in the biblical text.
The Bible tells us she refused.
The Bible tells us the king became furious.
The Bible tells us advisers became involved.
The Bible tells us the conflict expanded from one royal marriage into an empire-wide political issue.
And the Bible tells us Vashti lost her royal position.
But Scripture does not give us enough information to declare every hidden motive in Vashti's heart.
That restraint is important because this story was never given to Christians as permission for husbands to dominate their wives.
Nor was it given as permission for wives to despise their husbands.
Esther 1 is narrative. It tells us what happened in a Persian royal court. It is not a New Testament marriage manual commanding Christian husbands to behave like Ahasuerus.
And perhaps that is precisely why this chapter can expose us so deeply.
Because some Christian homes are becoming little Persian palaces.
Not because there is a literal king sitting on a throne.
But because somebody always has to win.
Somebody has to be obeyed.
Somebody has to have the final word.
Somebody has to be proven right.
Somebody has to lose face.
And slowly the marriage stops becoming a covenant to protect and becomes a courtroom in which both spouses are collecting evidence.
You remember what they said three years ago.
They remember what you did six months ago.
You know exactly which sentence will wound them.
They know exactly which insecurity will silence you.
You don't argue to understand anymore.
You argue to win.
And winning is expensive when the person you defeat is the person you promised to love.
Look carefully at what happens after Vashti refuses.
The king becomes furious.
Then, instead of the conflict remaining between husband and wife, other voices enter it.
Officials advise him.
Memucan interprets Vashti's refusal not merely as a personal marital conflict but as a threat to husbands throughout the empire.
Suddenly one painful moment between two people becomes a national crisis.
Does that sound completely ancient?
Or have you watched marriages deteriorate the same way?
A husband tells his friends only his version.
A wife tells her friends only hers.
A parent gets involved.
A sibling gets involved.
A group chat gets involved.
Social media gets involved.
People who will not have to live with the consequences begin supplying advice.
“Don't let her disrespect you.”
“Show him you're not going to tolerate that.”
“Make her learn.”
“Leave him on read.”
“Give him the same treatment.”
“Don't apologize.”
“Make her come to you.”
And two wounded people begin receiving counsel from people who are emotionally invested in helping them win instead of helping their covenant heal.
This does not mean wise counsel is wrong.
Scripture celebrates godly counsel.

But there is an enormous difference between counsel that moves you toward truth, repentance, safety, wisdom, reconciliation where possible, and obedience to Christ—and counsel that simply feeds your anger.
Not everybody who agrees with you is helping you.
Read that again.
Not everybody who validates your anger is protecting your marriage.
Sometimes the voice telling you exactly what your wounded ego wants to hear is the voice you most desperately need to question.
Ahasuerus was angry.
Then other voices helped turn anger into policy.
And what began with one refusal ended with a decree that could not simply recreate what had existed before.
That should sober every married person reading this.
Because there are sentences you can apologize for but never make unheard.
There are humiliations you can regret but never make unseen.
There are screenshots that cannot be unsent.
There are secrets publicly exposed that cannot be made private again.
There are children who hear arguments their parents assume they will forget.
There are wounds created in ten seconds that may require ten years of tenderness to heal.
This is why Scripture repeatedly treats uncontrolled anger so seriously.
James 1:19–20 tells believers to be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger because human anger does not produce the righteousness of God.
Ephesians 4:26–27 warns us not to allow anger to become an opportunity for the devil.
Think about that.
The enemy does not always need adultery to attack a marriage.
Sometimes he only needs two wounded Christians who refuse to humble themselves.
He does not always need somebody to walk out.
Sometimes he only needs them to stop reaching toward each other.
He does not always need hatred.
Sometimes resentment will do.
Sometimes contempt will do.
Sometimes comparison will do.
Sometimes silent punishment will do.
Sometimes the sentence “I don't care anymore” will do.
And sometimes the most dangerous moment in a Christian marriage is not when somebody screams.
It is when somebody stops caring enough to fight for healing.
But there is another mistake we must avoid.
We must not use Vashti's story to tell abused spouses that godliness means silently accepting violence, coercion, degradation, threats, or danger.
Biblical submission is never a license for abuse.
A Christian husband's model is not Ahasuerus displaying royal power.
His model is Jesus Christ.
That changes everything.
Ephesians 5:25 does not tell husbands, “Make sure she knows who's king.”
It says:
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
The Greek contains the devastating standard:
καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν
kathōs kai ho Christos ēgapēsen tēn ekklēsian
“As Christ also loved the church.”
How did Christ love?
By protecting His ego?
By demanding to be pampered?
By humiliating His bride?
No.
He gave Himself.
The cross destroys our cheap definitions of marital leadership.
Jesus shows us authority kneeling with a towel.
Strength carrying a cross.
Greatness serving.
Love sacrificing.
Holiness telling the truth.
Grace paying a cost.
And Christian wives are likewise called into a life shaped by Christ—marked by respect, faithfulness, wisdom, truth, holiness, and love, not contempt and retaliation.
Christian marriage is not supposed to be a competition over who possesses more power.
It is supposed to become a living witness to covenant love under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Which means sometimes the most spiritually powerful sentence in your marriage will not be:
“I was right.”
It will be:
“I was wrong.”
Sometimes revival begins at home with:
“Please forgive me.”
Sometimes spiritual warfare sounds like:
“I will not punish you for what I already said I forgave.”
Sometimes victory looks like turning off your phone, sitting beside your spouse, and finally listening without preparing your defense.
Sometimes courage means saying:
“We cannot keep living like this. We need help.”
And sometimes repentance means realizing that you have been praying for God to change your spouse while resisting every attempt of the Holy Spirit to change you.
That one hurts.
Because it is easier to see Vashti in someone else.
It is easier to see Ahasuerus in someone else.
It is harder to look into the palace of our own heart.
Where have I allowed pride to rule?
Where have I demanded respect while behaving disrespectfully?
Where have I used silence as punishment?
Where have I spoken about my spouse in ways I would never tolerate them speaking about me?
Where have I allowed friends to feed resentment instead of directing me toward Christ?
Where have I confused control with leadership?
Where have I confused retaliation with strength?
Where have I kept an emotional record of wrongs that I pull out whenever I need ammunition?
Where have I demanded repentance while refusing to repent?
And maybe the question that frightens us most:
What if the greatest threat to my marriage right now is not merely what my spouse needs to change...
but what I refuse to surrender?
There is something else extraordinary about Esther.
The book does not end in chapter one.
Thank God.
The palace disaster is not the conclusion.

Vashti's removal creates the circumstances in which Esther eventually enters the royal court. Later, when Haman's murderous plot threatens the Jewish people, Esther is positioned where her courageous intervention becomes central to their deliverance.
This does not mean every action in chapter one was morally right.
God's providence does not make human sin righteous.
That distinction is essential.
The God of Scripture is so sovereign that human pride, political dysfunction, broken decisions, and frightening circumstances cannot ultimately overthrow His purposes.
And that is where this ancient story whispers something powerful to the broken marriage.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Maybe terrible words have already been spoken.
Maybe trust has been damaged.
Maybe affection has grown cold.
Maybe one of you crossed boundaries.
Maybe both of you became versions of yourselves you hardly recognize.
Maybe you are reading this beside the person you once prayed God would give you, wondering how the answer to your prayer became the source of so many tears.
There is no guarantee that every damaged marriage will be restored exactly as we desire. Scripture never gives us permission to manufacture promises God has not made.
But Scripture gives us something greater than sentimental optimism.
It gives us Christ.
And wherever Christ truly rules, repentance is possible.
Forgiveness is possible.
Transformation is possible.
Wisdom is possible.
Truth is possible.
Help is possible.
Grace is possible.
And where reconciliation is biblically and safely possible, healing may begin with something painfully small.
One confession.
One honest conversation.
One boundary established in wisdom.
One counseling appointment.
One prayer prayed without pretending.
One decision to stop recruiting allies and start seeking godly help.
One moment when somebody finally says:
“I love you more than I love winning this argument.”
Because marriage does not need another Ahasuerus.
And it does not need another throne.
There is already a King.
His name is Jesus.
This is where the Gospel enters the room.
Jesus did not come merely to make difficult husbands nicer and frustrated wives calmer.
He came to save sinners.
That includes husbands.
That includes wives.
That includes the person reading this article who already knows exactly which paragraphs were about them.
Romans 3:23 levels the room: all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
The problem beneath our marriage problems is ultimately deeper than communication techniques.
The human heart is fallen.
Self-centered.
Proud.
Afraid.
Hungry to justify itself.
We do not merely need better arguments.
We need new hearts.
And Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
The answer to your deepest brokenness is not simply “try harder.”
It is repentance and faith in Christ.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the secret messages.
Bring Him the emotional affair.
Bring Him the coldness.
Bring Him the controlling behavior.
Bring Him the manipulation.
Bring Him the unforgiveness.
Bring Him the words you wish you could pull back into your mouth.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the marriage you have been pretending is fine.
Grace does not mean pretending sin did not happen.
Grace means sin does not have to have the final word.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
And when sinners truly encounter Jesus, repentance stops sounding like humiliation and starts looking like freedom.
Maybe you have spent years asking:
“Who is wrong?”
Tonight, perhaps the Holy Spirit is asking something more personal:
“What will you surrender?”
Not your dignity.
Not truth.
Not necessary safety.
Not biblical boundaries.
Your pride.
Your revenge.
Your secret sin.
Your demand to control another human heart.
Your insistence on being innocent in every story.
Your refusal to forgive what Christ is calling you to forgive.
Your refusal to confess what Christ is calling you to confess.
There are marriages where both people are waiting for the other person to move first.
Imagine what could happen if one person decided:
Jesus moved toward me first.
So I can take the first faithful step.
Not because your spouse deserves unlimited access to hurt you.
Not because reconciliation eliminates consequences.
Not because trust magically returns overnight.
But because Christians are not called to imitate the palace of Persia.
We are called to imitate Christ.
Put the phone down.
Go find your husband.
Go find your wife.
And say what pride has kept trapped in your throat.
“I am sorry.”
“I need help.”
“I have been hiding something.”
“I forgive you.”
“I want us to get counseling.”
“I don't want to keep hurting each other.”
“Can we pray?”
“I still want to fight for us.”

And if your marriage involves abuse, violence, coercive control, credible threats, or immediate danger, seeking safety and qualified help is not spiritual failure. Do not use this article—or anyone's misuse of Scripture—as a reason to remain in immediate danger. Truth and wisdom matter.
But for the husband and wife whose greatest battlefield has become pride...
How much longer?
How many more nights will you sleep inches apart physically and miles apart emotionally?
How many Sundays will you worship Jesus publicly while refusing to humble yourself privately?
How many times will you ask God for revival while maintaining a cold war in the room where you sleep?
You can know Greek.
You can quote Hebrew.
You can share sermons.
You can carry the biggest Bible in church.
And still refuse to say two words:
“Forgive me.”
That is not maturity.
The Gospel does not merely change what we believe about eternity.
The Gospel changes how we speak when we're angry.
How we apologize.
How we forgive.
How we handle authority.
How we treat the person who knows our weaknesses.
How we behave when nobody from church is watching.
Jesus rewrites people.
And rewritten people can begin writing different endings.
Be honest.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that repentance, patience, wise help, forgiveness, and grace can still produce beautiful things.
And if you know a husband, wife, fiancé, struggling believer, or friend who needs this truth, don't use this article as a weapon against them.
Don't send it with, “See? This is you.”
Send it with humility.
Maybe say:
“This made me examine myself too.”
Not because every sentence will be comfortable when you read it again.
Because some truths need to remain nearby precisely because they are uncomfortable.
Supporting Gospel work is not a substitute for giving to your local church, serving others, obeying Scripture, or living faithfully before God.
Jesus Christ.
Come to Christ.
A ministry cannot save your soul.
A Facebook page cannot forgive your sins.
Jesus can.
Maybe Vashti and Ahasuerus are not merely characters in an ancient royal scandal.
Maybe their palace has become a mirror.
A warning about anger.
A warning about pride.
A warning about public humiliation.
A warning about listening to voices that amplify conflict.
A warning about making enormous decisions while emotions are burning.

And perhaps tonight, before another door closes, another sentence is spoken, another secret grows, or another night passes in silence, someone needs to walk away from the throne of pride and kneel before the cross.
You don't need to win against your spouse.
You need Christ to win in you.
And comment before you leave.
Not for an algorithm alone.
For honesty.
For accountability.
For the exhausted husband who thinks he is the only one struggling.
For the wife crying where nobody sees her.
For the couple sitting in church tomorrow pretending everything is okay.
For the person who needs enough courage to finally ask for help.
“Jesus, change me first.”
Because perhaps the greatest miracle God wants to begin in your marriage is not making the other person finally surrender.
Perhaps it begins when you surrender to Christ.
And remember this when pride tells you the damage has already written the ending:
A ruined chapter may carry consequences, but surrendered to Christ, it does not have the authority to write the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE VERSE WE LOVE TO QUOTE—UNTIL JESUS STARTS TAKING AWAY THE SPOTLIGHT
