Your companion and your wife by covenant.
Covenant.
That word changes everything.
Marriage in Scripture is not merely sustained by the emotion of being in love.
Feelings rise.
Feelings fall.
Attraction fluctuates.
Bodies age.
Stress arrives.
Children change schedules.
Grief enters homes.
Money gets tight.
Illness comes.
Misunderstandings happen.
And sometimes two people who once could not stop talking suddenly realize they have become very good at discussing groceries and very bad at discussing their souls.
But covenant says:
I am still here.
Not because every day feels romantic.
Because I promised myself to you before God.

That does not mean enduring abuse, concealing violence, or refusing necessary outside help. Biblical covenant must never be weaponized to trap someone in danger. Seeking pastors, mature believers, counselors, authorities, physicians, or other appropriate help can be necessary and wise.
But in an ordinary struggling marriage, covenant calls us back from the fantasy that somebody new will effortlessly heal what two wounded sinners stopped tending together.
Sometimes the answer is not another person.
Sometimes the answer is repentance.
A conversation.
A confession.
A boundary.
A phone placed on the table.
An apology without excuses.
A marriage counselor.
A pastor.
A night when the television finally stays off and two people look at each other again.
And somebody whispers:
“I miss us.”
Maybe that is you.
Maybe your marriage is not collapsing dramatically.
Maybe it is disappearing quietly.
You still sleep in the same room.
Still take family pictures.
Still attend church.
Still say “love you.”
Still celebrate anniversaries.
But neither of you knows what is happening inside the other anymore.
Your bodies share an address while your hearts live miles apart.
If that describes your marriage, hear this carefully:
Do not use an article about emotional faithfulness as ammunition against your spouse.
Do not shove this into their face and say, “See? This is what you’re doing to me.”
Start with your own heart.
Where have I withdrawn?
Where have I become harsh?
Where have I stopped listening?
Where have I entertained attention I should have redirected?
Where have I compared my spouse unfairly?
Where have I allowed resentment to become a wall?
Where have I demanded intimacy while refusing vulnerability?
Where have I expected my spouse to read a heart I refuse to open?
And where have I asked another person to meet needs in ways that are beginning to compete with my marriage covenant?
Marriage is not supposed to make your spouse your god.
No husband can carry that weight.
No wife can carry that weight.
The deepest hunger of the human soul cannot finally be satisfied by romantic intimacy.
That place belongs to Christ.

If you demand that your spouse heal every wound, erase every insecurity, satisfy every emotional need, understand every thought, and make you feel permanently whole, you have placed a human being on an altar that belongs to Jesus.
Your spouse is your covenant companion.
Jesus is your Savior.
Those roles must never be confused.
And strangely, marriage becomes healthier when Christ occupies the throne that neither spouse was designed to occupy.
Paul takes marriage somewhere astonishing in Ephesians 5.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
The Greek word for love there is ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate — from ἀγαπάω, agapaō.
The command is not merely:
“Feel butterflies.”
It calls a husband toward a love patterned after Christ’s self-giving love for His church.
Then Paul quotes Genesis:
ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
“the two shall become one flesh.”
And immediately afterward he writes:
τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν
“to mystērion touto mega estin”
“This mystery is great.”
Then:
ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω εἰς Χριστὸν καὶ εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν
“But I speak concerning Christ and the church.”
Do you see what Paul just did?
He looked at marriage…
and pointed beyond marriage.
Toward Jesus.
Christian marriage is not merely about two people trying to remain attracted to one another until death.
It is meant to reflect something of Christ’s covenant love for His people.
Faithful.
Sacrificial.
Truthful.
Holy.
Forgiving.
Enduring.
That is why the Gospel must stand at the center of this conversation.
Because some people reading this have already crossed the line.
You know it.
Your heart started pounding paragraphs ago.
Maybe there are messages you deleted.
Maybe there is someone you need to stop contacting.
Maybe you have emotionally abandoned your spouse while physically remaining home.
Maybe it became physical.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse knows everything.
Maybe your marriage is bleeding because of what you did.
And now shame is telling you:
“It’s over.”
“You ruined everything.”
“God is finished with you.”
“You might as well keep going.”
Listen carefully.
That is not the Gospel.
The Gospel does not say sin is harmless.
The Gospel says sin was so serious that the Son of God went to the cross.
But the cross also declares that sinners are not beyond redemption.
Jesus Christ came for guilty people.
Not imaginary people who never failed.
Real sinners.
Adulterers.
Liars.
Lustful people.
Proud people.
Secretive people.
Broken husbands.
Wounded wives.
People who crossed lines they swore they never would cross.
At the cross, grace does not rename darkness as light.
Grace brings us out of darkness.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible because you were exposed.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia — speaks of repentance, a turning of mind and direction.
Biblical repentance comes home.
It stops defending.
Stops blaming.
Stops negotiating with the thing that is destroying us.
It brings hidden things into the light.
And then it turns toward Christ.
First John 1:9 gives hope to believers who confess their sins: God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because Jesus does.
Maybe the most spiritual thing you can do after reading this is not type an emotional comment.
Maybe it is walk into the other room.
Sit beside your husband.
Sit beside your wife.
Put the phone down.
And tell the truth.
“I have been distant.”
“I have been hiding.”
“I have been talking to someone in a way that I know is becoming dangerous.”
“I have compared you to somebody else.”
“I have neglected you.”
“I am sorry.”
“I need help.”
“I want Christ to rebuild what I helped tear down.”
For some couples, restoration will be painfully slow.
Forgiveness does not magically erase consequences.
Trust that took years to build can be damaged in minutes and may require considerable time, accountability, patience, wise pastoral care, and professional counseling to rebuild.
Do not demand instant trust from the person you wounded.
Repentance does not say:
“I apologized, so get over it.”
Repentance accepts the painful work of becoming trustworthy again.
And wounded spouse, forgiveness does not mean pretending evil never happened.
Christian forgiveness is not denial.
Reconciliation and restored trust involve truth, repentance, wisdom, safety, and time.
Jesus does not heal marriages through pretending.
He works in truth.
But perhaps you have not crossed that line yet.
Perhaps this reached you while the door is only beginning to open.
Then close it while it is still easy to close.
Do not wait until you are emotionally addicted to another person before establishing boundaries.
Do not cultivate privately what you would be ashamed to reveal publicly.
Do not feed a connection and then pray that God prevents it from becoming something more.
Wisdom sometimes looks terribly unromantic.
Delete the unnecessary conversation.
Change the pattern.
Stop creating private opportunities.
Bring your spouse into the friendship where appropriate.
Talk openly about the attraction instead of secretly feeding it.
Seek mature Christian accountability.
Get counseling before you are discussing divorce papers.
Pray together even when it feels awkward.
Learn your spouse again.
Ask questions.
Listen without preparing a defense.
Court the person you already married.
And remember something the world constantly forgets:
The grass often looks greener where somebody has been secretly watering it.
Water your covenant.
There may be people reading this who are single.
This matters for you too.
Do not train your heart now to normalize relationships with married people that require secrecy from their spouses.
Honor somebody else’s covenant before you have one of your own.
Do not become the person another husband or wife has to fear.
And do not accept the excuse:
“My marriage is basically over anyway.”
If it is over, let it be dealt with truthfully and rightly.
Do not build your future on somebody else’s deception.
And if you are married, never forget:
Your spouse does not need to become your only friend.
Healthy marriages need Christian community.
Men and women need wise friendships, family relationships, church fellowship, mentors, and appropriate counsel.
The biblical goal is not possessiveness.
It is faithfulness.
The issue is not whether you care deeply about another human being.
The issue is whether a relationship is becoming romantic, secretive, sexually charged, emotionally dependent, deceptive, or competitive with the covenant you made before God.
There is a difference.
And mature believers should be able to recognize it before catastrophe teaches it to them.
Maybe this article exposed something.
Do not run from that feeling.
Bring it to Jesus.
If you need repentance, repent.
If you need help, ask for help.
If you need boundaries, establish them.
If your marriage needs counseling, seek it.
If your spouse needs an apology, stop rehearsing one and give it.
Not because strangers on the internet can replace pastoral care, counseling, or your local church.
But because sometimes one small confession is the first crack in a wall of isolation.

And if Jesus has already restored your marriage from betrayal, distance, addiction, secrecy, or emotional infidelity, consider sharing part of your testimony. Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that repentance and restoration are more than Christian vocabulary.
Not because every sentence will apply to every marriage, but because temptation has a strange way of making us forget convictions we once considered obvious.
Not as an accusation aimed at somebody.
Send it privately to someone who needs truth without humiliation.
And when you share it, pray before you press the button.
“Jesus, let this reach whoever needs it.”
Supporting Gospel-centered work can also be one practical way of helping biblical encouragement reach more people. We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives surrendered to Him.
And even if you never purchase anything, keep growing.
The most important response happens after the screen goes dark.
When nobody is watching.
When that message arrives.
When that old connection reaches out.
When loneliness whispers that you deserve somebody who “understands you.”
When temptation tells you that secrecy is harmless because nothing physical happened.
When you have to decide whether your covenant is worth protecting before anybody applauds you for protecting it.
That is where faithfulness lives.
Perhaps tonight the most beautiful love story is not beginning with two strangers meeting.
Perhaps it is beginning with two married people finding their way back to each other.
Not because they suddenly became perfect.
But because somebody finally stopped hiding.
Somebody confessed.
Somebody forgave.
Somebody established the boundary.
Somebody reached for the other person’s hand.
Somebody prayed:
“Jesus, teach us how to love again.”
And the Savior who specializes in bringing dead things to life began writing where everybody else thought the story had ended.
Because sometimes the greatest scandal is what sin almost destroyed…
and the greatest grace is watching Jesus redeem what surrender finally placed back into His hands.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES TEMPTATION FEEL STRONGER AFTER I FOLLOW JESUS?
paragraphs: WHY DOES TEMPTATION FEEL STRONGER AFTER I FOLLOW JESUS?
You Thought Following Jesus Would Silence the Battle. Instead, You Started Hearing the War.
There is a frightening moment in the life of some believers that almost nobody prepares them for.
You finally surrender.
You repent.

You begin praying again. You open your Bible with hunger instead of obligation. You delete what keeps dragging you backward. You distance yourself from relationships that keep feeding your old life. You decide that this time you are serious about Jesus.
And then something confusing happens.
The temptation gets louder.

Thoughts you thought would disappear suddenly seem more aggressive. Old desires knock on doors you thought you had permanently closed. Memories return. Anger resurfaces. Lust whispers. Pride finds new disguises. Envy slips into your prayers. Your phone becomes a battlefield. Your loneliness becomes vulnerable territory.
And somewhere in the middle of all of it, a terrifying question enters your mind:
“If I really belong to Jesus… why am I still fighting this?”
Maybe you have never said that aloud.
Maybe you are ashamed even reading it.
Because everyone else at church seems fine.
They raise their hands.
They post Bible verses.
They say, “God is good.”
Meanwhile, you are sitting there wondering why the person who supposedly “gave everything to Jesus” is still capable of wanting things that would break His heart.
Listen carefully.
The presence of temptation is not proof that Jesus has abandoned you.
Jesus Himself was tempted.
Hebrews 4:15 says that Christ was “tempted in all things as we are, yet without sin.”
The Greek language makes this even more striking.
The word translated “tempted” comes from πειράζω — peirazō — a word that can carry the sense of testing, trying, or tempting depending on its context.
Jesus entered the reality of human testing without entering into sin.
Temptation touched His human experience.
Sin never conquered Him.
That distinction matters enormously because many believers condemn themselves merely because temptation appeared.
They think, “If that thought came into my mind, something must be wrong with me.”
Not necessarily.
A temptation knocking on your door is not the same thing as inviting it inside.
A battlefield is not evidence that the enemy owns the territory.
Sometimes the battle is evidence that the territory is being contested.
And there is something else Scripture shows us that may completely change how you understand what is happening.
Look at Jesus.
Matthew 3 records His baptism.
The Father declares, “This is My beloved Son.”
Then Matthew 4 begins.
“Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.”
Do not miss the sequence.
Baptism.
Affirmation.
Then wilderness.
The wilderness did not mean the Father’s declaration had been revoked.
The temptation did not mean Jesus had wandered outside the Father’s will.
And Satan’s attack did not change Jesus’ identity.
In fact, Satan immediately attacked that identity:
“If You are the Son of God…”
That strategy is ancient.
The enemy loves turning temptation into an identity crisis.
You experience temptation, and the accusation follows:
“If you were really saved…”
“If you actually loved Jesus…”
“If the Holy Spirit were really in you…”
“If your repentance were genuine…”
“If you were really a Christian…”
And before you know it, you are no longer merely fighting temptation.
You are fighting despair.
That is where many believers become vulnerable.
They confuse being tempted with being defeated.
But Scripture does not.
James 1:14 says:
“But each one is tempted when he is carried away and enticed by his own lust.”
The Greek word commonly translated “desire” or “lust” there is ἐπιθυμία — epithymia.
At its basic level, the word speaks of strong desire or craving; its moral character depends on its object and context. In James 1, the context is clearly sinful desire drawing a person toward sin.
Then James describes a progression.
Desire conceives.
Sin is born.
Sin matures.
Death follows.
In other words, Scripture distinguishes temptation from surrender.
The temptation is real.
The desire may be disturbingly real.
But temptation does not have to become obedience.
You can feel the pull without giving it your allegiance.
That may explain part of what has been confusing you.
Before you began seriously following Jesus, you may not have recognized some battles as battles.
You simply followed the desire.
You did what anger wanted.
You watched what lust wanted.
You said what pride wanted.
You held the grudge.
You fed the fantasy.
You entertained the bitterness.
You justified the compromise.
There was less internal resistance because you were not fighting the current.
But when Christ begins changing the direction of your life, you become increasingly conscious of currents you once floated with.
Suddenly you notice things you previously excused.
That joke bothers you now.
That browser history bothers you now.
The way you speak to your spouse bothers you now.
The resentment you have carried for years bothers you now.
The secret flirting bothers you now.
The greed bothers you now.
The need for everybody’s approval bothers you now.
The private pride beneath your public Christianity bothers you now.
And you wonder why everything suddenly feels so intense.
Perhaps some temptations have intensified.
But sometimes what has intensified is your awareness of them.
The light has been turned on.
And light exposes what darkness allowed you to ignore.
Paul describes a real conflict in Galatians 5:17:
“For the flesh sets its desire against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these are in opposition to one another…”
The Greek word translated “flesh” is σάρξ — sarx.

In passages like this, Paul is not teaching that the physical human body is inherently evil. He is describing fallen human existence oriented away from God—the rebellious impulses and desires of the old way of life.
And notice what Paul says.
There is opposition.
Conflict.
Resistance.
Christianity is not Jesus decorating your old life.
Christianity is Jesus becoming Lord of it.
That means there will be things inside you that have to die.
Some quietly.
Some painfully.
Some repeatedly.
And this is where grace becomes more beautiful than you ever imagined.
Because perhaps you thought grace meant you would never struggle again.
But biblical grace is even stronger than that.
Grace meets you in the struggle and teaches you to say no.
Titus 2:11–12 says the grace of God trains us to deny ungodliness and worldly desires and to live sensible, righteous, godly lives.
Grace does not merely forgive the repentant sinner.
Grace begins retraining the forgiven sinner.
And retraining can hurt.
Ask anyone who has ever recovered from years of destructive habits.
The old reflex does not always disappear simply because the heart has changed direction.
This is why you must stop measuring your relationship with Jesus exclusively by the intensity of your temptation.
Measure it also by where you run when temptation comes.
There was a time you ran toward the sin.
Now maybe you fall to your knees.
There was a time you defended it.
Now you confess it.
There was a time you hid because you wanted to keep it.
Now you hide because you are ashamed you still want it.
But Jesus is calling you out of both kinds of hiding.
Not into condemnation.
Into the light.
Remember what happened in Eden?
After Adam and Eve sinned, they hid.
Sin has been teaching humanity to hide ever since.
Hide the browser.
Hide the messages.
Hide the addiction.
Hide the resentment.
Hide the fantasies.
Hide the marriage problems.
Hide the doubt.
Hide the jealousy.
Hide the secret second life.
Then polish the outside.
Go to church.
Smile.
Post the verse.
Tell everyone you are “blessed.”
But somewhere beneath the Christian vocabulary is a terrified person whispering:
“If people knew what I was fighting, would they still think I belonged here?”
Jesus already knows.
And He still calls sinners to come.
That does not mean He approves of the sin.
Grace is not divine permission to remain enslaved.
Jesus does something infinitely better.
He forgives, cleanses, restores, disciplines, transforms, and teaches His people to walk differently.
The Gospel does not say, “Your sin does not matter.”
The Gospel says your sin mattered enough that Christ went to the cross—and His mercy is powerful enough that your sin does not have to write the final chapter of your life.
That is why Hebrews 4 does not tell tempted believers to run away from God.
It tells them to approach Him.
After telling us that Jesus was tempted yet without sin, Scripture says:
“Therefore let us draw near with confidence to the throne of grace…”
Think about that.
You are tempted.
And God says, “Come closer.”
You are weak.
“Come closer.”
You are ashamed.
“Come closer.”
You almost fell.
“Come closer.”
You did fall and are genuinely repenting.
Come back.
Not because sin is trivial.
Because Christ is sufficient.
The throne you approach is called the throne of grace.
And Hebrews says there we “receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need.”
The time of temptation is not the time to stop praying because you feel unworthy to pray.
That may be the moment you desperately need to pray.
“Jesus, help me.”
Sometimes that prayer is all you can manage.
Pray it anyway.
There is another image in Scripture that reaches all the way back to Genesis.
Before Cain murdered Abel, God warned him:
“Sin is crouching at the door; and its desire is for you, but you must master it.”
The Hebrew contains this haunting picture:
חַטָּאת לַפֶּתַח רֹבֵץ
ḥaṭṭā’t la-petaḥ rōvēṣ
“Sin is crouching at the door.”
Crouching.
Waiting.
Close.
Sin rarely introduces itself by announcing the funeral it intends to create.
It introduces itself as relief.
“One look.”
“One message.”
“One drink.”
“One lie.”
“One night.”
“One little compromise.”
“Nobody will know.”
“You deserve this.”
“You can repent afterward.”
That is how temptation talks.
It advertises pleasure and hides the chains.
It shows you the moment and hides the morning after.
It shows you the secret conversation but not the broken marriage.
It shows you revenge but not the person bitterness will turn you into.
It shows you the pornography but not the distortion of intimacy.
It shows you the applause but not the slavery of needing human approval.
It shows you money but not what greed can do to your soul.
It shows you escape but never tells you the price of coming back.
This is why temptation can feel so powerful.
It speaks to something you actually desire while concealing where that desire will take you.
And Satan is not always creative.
Sometimes he simply watches what repeatedly works.
First Peter 5:8 warns believers to be sober and watchful because their adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour.
Peter does not write that warning to unbelievers.
He writes to believers.
So spiritual vigilance is not evidence of weak Christianity.
It is part of faithful Christianity.
But do not become so fascinated with the devil that you forget your own responsibility.
James does not allow us to blame every temptation on Satan.
Our own desires matter.
The world matters.
The flesh matters.
Spiritual opposition matters.
Biblical Christianity does not permit us to say, “The devil made me do it.”
You still choose.
You still need repentance.
You still need boundaries.
You still need wisdom.
You may need to delete the number.
You may need to cancel the account.
You may need to stop going to that place.
You may need to confess to a mature Christian you trust.
You may need to stop calling something a “struggle” when you have deliberately built an environment that keeps feeding it.
Jesus spoke radically about dealing with sin.
Not because He wanted His followers mutilating themselves—His language in Matthew 5 emphasizes the seriousness of removing what causes us to stumble—but because sin should never be treated casually.
Some of us keep asking Jesus for victory while preserving easy access to defeat.
We pray, “Lead me not into temptation,” and then carry temptation around in our pocket.
At 1:13 a.m.
Door closed.
Lights off.
Nobody watching.
Just you, your screen, your loneliness, and a decision.
That is where theology becomes painfully practical.
What do you do then?
Remember that Jesus is better.
Not merely stronger.
Better.
Because sin cannot ultimately be defeated merely by telling yourself, “I am not allowed to want this.”
Your heart needs a greater treasure.
The Christian life is not simply learning to hate bad things.
It is learning to see Christ as more beautiful than the things competing for your worship.
You were created for Him.
Your deepest hunger cannot finally be satisfied by pornography, romance, money, attention, achievement, revenge, substances, status, applause, entertainment, or another secret escape.
They may anesthetize.
They cannot resurrect.
Jesus can.
And maybe that is exactly where this article found you.
Not during your strongest week.
During your weakest night.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been fighting.
Maybe you fell again yesterday.
Maybe you promised God you would never do it again, and then you did.
Maybe you are disgusted with yourself.
Maybe you are tempted to abandon Christianity because you think a real Christian could never struggle this much.
Do not use grace as permission to continue sinning.
But do not use your failure as permission to run away from the only Savior who can rescue you.
Confess.
Repent.
Bring it into the light.
Receive Christ’s mercy.
Get back up.
Fight again.
First John 1:9 says that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and righteous to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Your confidence is not that you have become impossible to tempt.
Your confidence is Jesus Christ.
The One who resisted temptation.
The One who obeyed where humanity failed.
The One who carried sin to the cross.
The One who shed His blood for sinners.
The One who was buried.
The One who rose.
The One who intercedes for His people.
The One who will finish what He began.
Christianity is not the story of impressive people becoming slightly better.
It is the story of spiritually helpless sinners being reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ and transformed by His grace.
From scandal…
to grace.
Peter denied Him.
Grace restored him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Grace transformed him.
The thief was dying beside Jesus with no religious résumé left to present.
Grace met him there.
Again and again Scripture refuses to let human scandal have the last word when genuine repentance meets the mercy of God.
That does not make scandal beautiful.
Jesus is beautiful.
That does not make sin harmless.
Grace is costly.
The cross proves both.
Sin is worse than we want to admit.
Jesus is more merciful than we dare to imagine.
So why does temptation sometimes feel stronger after you begin following Jesus?
Because following Jesus does not mean you have entered a life without conflict.
You have entered a life in which your allegiance has changed.
You now recognize enemies you once entertained.
You notice desires you once obeyed without question.
The Spirit produces new desires that oppose the old patterns of the flesh.
And you are learning that sanctification is not performed by pretending temptation does not exist.
It happens as you abide in Christ, walk by the Spirit, renew your mind through Scripture, pray, flee sin, pursue holiness, remain in Christian fellowship, confess honestly, and depend on grace.
You will not always feel victorious.
Sometimes victory will look dramatic.
Sometimes victory will simply look like closing the tab.
Walking out of the room.
Not sending the message.
Calling someone.
Opening your Bible.
Getting on your knees.
Whispering the name of Jesus while everything inside you wants to go backward.
Do not despise those moments.
A quiet “no” offered to temptation because Christ is Lord can be an act of worship nobody on earth applauds.
Heaven does not need your sin to become public before obedience becomes meaningful.
Fight where nobody sees.
And when you fail, repent where necessary, make things right where possible, and return to Christ.
Maybe you need to do that right now.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
No performance.
No Christian vocabulary.
Just honesty.
“Jesus, I have sinned.”
“Jesus, I still want things I should not want.”
“Jesus, I cannot overcome this without You.”
“Forgive me.”
“Cleanse me.”
“Change what I love.”
“Teach me to walk by Your Spirit.”
“I surrender again.”
Or simply comment, “I’m still fighting.”
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing a struggle into the light begins with refusing to pretend anymore.
Better yet, send this to them privately and remind them that temptation does not have to become surrender.
There may be a night when the battle comes back.
And on that night, you may need to remember:
Temptation is not your master.
Your past is not your master.
Your appetite is not your master.
Your shame is not your master.
Jesus Christ is Lord.

If Gospel Warrior has been helping you stay near Scripture, consider following and supporting this ministry so more Christ-centered biblical encouragement can continue reaching people who are struggling quietly.
It does not purchase blessing, salvation, answered prayer, or a higher spiritual status. Those things cannot be bought. Salvation is the gift of God through Jesus Christ.
Leave it fighting differently.
Leave it looking toward Christ.
Leave knowing that the goal is not to become a person who boasts, “I am too strong to fall.”
Become the person who knows:
“I am weak enough to need Jesus every single day.”
Because perhaps the greatest danger was never discovering that you could be tempted.
Perhaps the greater danger was believing you could defeat temptation without Him.
So tonight, when the old voice returns…
when the old appetite wakes up…
when the secret door starts looking attractive again…
when shame tells you to hide…
when Satan whispers that a person like you could never really belong to Jesus…
remember the wilderness.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember the throne of grace.
And run toward Christ.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Because the strongest evidence that grace is rewriting your story may not be that you never hear temptation knocking again.
It may be that, by the grace of God, you no longer have to open the door.
And before you go, remember this:
Your temptation may know your weakness—but your Savior knows your name, carried your sin to a cross, walked out of a grave, and is still rewriting stories the enemy thought were already finished.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Bible’s Hardest Sexual Stories Were Never Written to Entertain You—They Were Written to Expose You
paragraphs: The Bible’s Hardest Sexual Stories Were Never Written to Entertain You—They Were Written to Expose You

David took another man’s wife. Judah slept with a woman he thought was a prostitute. Tamar entered a desperate sexual scandal. Samson repeatedly confused desire with love. A woman caught in adultery was dragged before Jesus and publicly shamed. Scripture refuses to sanitize any of it. But if you think these stories are mainly about “those terrible people back then,” you may have missed the most frightening—and beautiful—reason God allowed them to remain in the Bible.
There are passages in the Bible we love to underline.
And then there are passages we quietly hope nobody asks us about.
The Psalms make their way onto coffee mugs.
Philippians becomes wall art.
John 3:16 appears on signs and shirts.
But nobody decorates the living room with Genesis 38.
Nobody sends newlyweds a greeting card featuring David, Bathsheba, and Uriah.
Nobody casually says, “For tonight’s family devotional, let’s talk about Judah and Tamar.”
Some biblical stories are uncomfortable because Scripture is brutally unwilling to pretend that human beings are cleaner than we really are.
Sexual desire.
Adultery.
Exploitation.
Deception.
Lust.
Power.
Shame.
Broken marriages.
Secret fantasies.
Public humiliation.
And consequences that sometimes ripple through generations.
The Bible does not blush.
We do.
And perhaps that is precisely why we need these stories.

Because God did not give us a Bible filled exclusively with polished saints standing heroically beneath heavenly spotlights. He gave us a Bible populated by human beings whose lives sometimes look disturbingly familiar.
Not because God celebrates their sin.
Because God tells the truth about it.
And underneath some of Scripture's darkest sexual stories is a question that eventually stops being about David, Judah, Tamar, Samson, or the woman standing terrified before an angry crowd.
The question becomes personal.
What does God see when He looks into the rooms of my life that nobody else enters?
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because sexual sin rarely begins where everybody can see it.
Jesus took His listeners somewhere much deeper.

“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:27–28).
The Greek construction matters.
Matthew uses:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn

The idea is not merely noticing that another human being is physically attractive. The construction points toward looking in order to desire—the intentional cultivation of lust. The gaze becomes more than sight; it becomes the deliberate feeding of desire.
Jesus moves the battlefield from the bedroom to the heart.
That destroys one of our favorite hiding places.
“I never actually did anything.”
Jesus asks what you wanted.
“I never touched anybody.”
Jesus asks what you entertained.
“Nobody knows.”
Jesus does.
And suddenly the Bible's scandalous stories are no longer ancient gossip.
They are mirrors.
Think about David.
This was not some pagan king who had never encountered God.
This was David.
Shepherd.
Psalmist.
Warrior.
King.
The man who had stood before Goliath when almost everyone else was terrified.
And then Scripture gives us one of the most chilling sentences in David's biography:
“But David remained in Jerusalem.”
His army went to war.
David stayed home.
One evening he walked onto the roof of his palace and saw a woman bathing.
Then the verbs begin moving.
David saw.
David inquired.
David sent.
David took.
The text identifies her clearly: Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam, wife of Uriah the Hittite. David therefore receives a boundary before he crosses it. She belongs within another man's marriage covenant.
Yet David sends for her anyway.
That matters because sin often gives us exits before it gives us consequences.
A warning.
A conviction.
A Scripture suddenly remembered.
A spouse's face flashing through your mind.
A strange heaviness in your spirit.
A moment when you could close the browser.
Delete the conversation.
Walk away.
Tell somebody.
Confess.
Run.
David had an exit.
He kept walking.
Then Bathsheba became pregnant.
Now David had another decision.
Repent?
Or manage the scandal?
He chose management.
David summoned Uriah home, apparently hoping Uriah would sleep with Bathsheba and later assume the child was his.
But Uriah refused the comforts of home while his fellow soldiers remained in battle.
So David's cover-up became darker.
He arranged Uriah's death.
Pause there.
David did not wake up one morning planning to become the kind of man who would arrange a loyal soldier's death.
That is one of sin's terrifying characteristics.
It rarely shows you the final destination when it offers you the first compromise.
Pornography says, “Just look.”
The emotional affair says, “We're only talking.”
Adultery says, “Nobody will know.”
Secret messaging says, “Delete it afterward.”
Fantasy says, “It's only happening in your head.”
Sin almost never introduces itself by saying:
“Hello. I am here to hollow out your integrity, wound the people you love, numb your conscience, damage your communion with God, and possibly destroy things you spent decades building.”
It simply says:
“One more time.”
Then Nathan arrives.
He tells David about a wealthy man with many sheep who steals the one beloved lamb belonging to a poor man.
David is furious.
The king demands justice.
And Nathan turns the entire story around with four devastating words:
“You are the man.”
The Hebrew is even more stark:
אַתָּה הָאִישׁ — attah ha’ish
You are the man.
Not your enemy.
Not the culture.
Not the woman.
Not your childhood.
Not your loneliness.
Not your hormones.
Not the algorithm.
Not your spouse's failures.
You.
David finally says:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
No elaborate defense.
No public-relations statement.
No blame shifting.
Just confession.
And Nathan answers with something almost shocking:
“The LORD also has put away your sin.”
David is forgiven.
But the story does not pretend his choices were harmless. Serious consequences remain.
That distinction is essential to biblical grace.
Grace is not God calling evil good.
Grace is not pretending nobody was wounded.
Grace is not removing accountability from abusers, adulterers, predators, exploiters, or manipulators.
Biblical forgiveness does not mean victims must deny reality, abandon wise boundaries, refuse lawful justice, or immediately restore broken trust.
God names David's evil before announcing forgiveness.
That is grace.
Truth first.
Confession.
Mercy.
And transformation.
Some people want forgiveness without repentance.
Others believe their sin is too ugly for forgiveness.
The Gospel destroys both lies.
And then there is Judah and Tamar.
Genesis 38 may be one of the most awkward chapters in Scripture.
Tamar had married Judah's son Er. After Er died, the family obligation passed to Onan, but Onan exploited the arrangement while deliberately refusing the responsibility attached to it.
After Onan died under God's judgment, Judah promised Tamar his younger son Shelah when he grew older.
Then Judah failed to fulfill his promise.
Tamar was left vulnerable.
Eventually she disguised herself, and Judah—believing her to be a prostitute—slept with her.
When Tamar's pregnancy became known, Judah reacted with horrifying hypocrisy and demanded severe punishment.
Then Tamar produced evidence identifying the father.
Judah recognized it.
And confessed:
צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי — tsadqah mimmenni
Often translated:
“She is more righteous than I.”
Do not misunderstand the point.
The Bible is not turning deception or prostitution into virtues.
The story exposes Judah's failure, Tamar's vulnerability, the hypocrisy of sexual double standards, and the tangled consequences of covenant faithlessness.
Judah was ready to condemn publicly the very sexual scandal in which he was secretly implicated.
Does that sound ancient?
We still do it.
We condemn the person whose scandal became visible while protecting the version of ourselves nobody discovered.
We rage against somebody else's adultery while feeding pornography privately.
We criticize another person's divorce while emotionally abandoning our own spouse.
We mock someone's sexual brokenness while carefully clearing our browser history.
We demand that fallen Christians be exposed while praying nobody ever screenshots our private messages.
But Scripture keeps turning the mirror around.
“You are the man.”
And maybe that sentence hurts because somewhere inside you there is something you desperately do not want exposed.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you have become incredibly skilled at appearing spiritually healthy.
You worship.
You post Scripture.
You say “Amen.”
You serve.
You encourage others.
And then night comes.
The door closes.
The phone lights up.
And another version of you appears.
If that sentence made your stomach tighten, do not run from Jesus.
Run to Him.
Because conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Conviction says, “Come into the light.”
Condemnation whispers, “Hide because God could never want you now.”
The Gospel says something entirely different.
Christ already knows.
And still He calls sinners to Himself.
Consider the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She is caught in adultery and placed before Him publicly.
Notice the obvious unanswered question.
Where is the man?
Adultery requires more than one participant, yet only the woman is dragged into the spectacle.
Jesus refuses to become another instrument in their hypocrisy.
After the accusers leave, He speaks to her.
“Neither do I condemn you.”
But Jesus does not stop there.
“Go, and sin no more.”
Grace.
And truth.
No condemnation from Christ.
No permission from Christ to remain enslaved.
That combination is breathtaking.

A textual note is important here for readers who care about biblical accuracy: the account commonly called the woman caught in adultery, John 7:53–8:11, is absent from some of the earliest and strongest Greek manuscript witnesses and appears in different locations in parts of the manuscript tradition. Christians should therefore be careful about building a doctrine uniquely upon this passage. Its central picture of Jesus extending mercy while calling sinners away from sin, however, is abundantly established elsewhere in the New Testament.
And that brings us to something Christianity understands that our culture desperately needs.
You are more than your sexual history.
You are also responsible for what you do with your sexuality.
Both are true.
Christianity refuses two opposite lies.
One says:
“Sexual desire defines you.”
The other says:
“Sexual choices don't matter.”
Jesus rejects both.
Your desires are not your god.
Your body is not meaningless.
Other people's bodies are not products.
Marriage is not disposable.
Sex is not merely recreational chemistry.
Pornography does not become harmless because nobody physically entered the room.
And sexual holiness is not God trying to keep pleasure away from humanity.
God created human sexuality.
The biblical story begins with embodied human beings created male and female and a marriage union described with the Hebrew expression:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad
“one flesh.”
Sexuality therefore enters Scripture not as something dirty but as something powerful enough to require covenant faithfulness.
The enemy's strategy has always been to take gifts from God and detach them from the God who gave them.
Desire without covenant.
Pleasure without responsibility.
Bodies without dignity.
Intimacy without faithfulness.
Freedom without holiness.
And eventually people discover that getting everything they wanted did not cure the ache underneath what they wanted.
Because sometimes what we call lust is carrying another hunger beneath it.
To be wanted.
To be chosen.
To escape.
To feel powerful.
To stop feeling lonely.
To numb pain.
To feel alive again.
That does not excuse sin.
But it may explain why simply saying “try harder” has failed so many people.
You do not merely need stronger willpower.
You need a greater love.
This is where Jesus becomes more than a religious teacher telling sexually broken people to behave.
He becomes Savior.
Jesus did not come merely to improve your habits.
He came to give you a new heart.
At the cross, Christ carries guilt without pretending guilt does not exist.
He absorbs judgment without calling sin harmless.
He offers mercy without rewriting evil as virtue.
The scandal of Christianity is not that God discovered humanity was better than expected.
The scandal is that God knew exactly what humanity was—and Christ came anyway.
David's adultery did not surprise Him.
Judah's hypocrisy did not surprise Him.
Samson's appetites did not surprise Him.
Peter's denial did not surprise Him.
Your browser history does not surprise Him.
Your affair does not surprise Him.
Your secret fantasies do not surprise Him.
Your sexual past does not surprise Him.
What happened to you does not surprise Him either.
And hear this carefully, especially if someone else's sexual sin was committed against you:
Another person's evil is not your moral stain.
Scripture's sexual stories contain sinners who need repentance, but they also contain people who were exploited, betrayed, objectified, abandoned, or violated.
Those categories must never be confused.
The wounded do not need to repent for having been wounded.
The guilty must not use “grace” to silence the wounded.
Jesus is full of compassion toward the broken, and biblical repentance requires sinners to stop hiding behind spiritual language.
Maybe that is why these difficult stories survived thousands of years.
God knew we would need them.
We would need David because some believers would fall terribly after years of walking with God.
We would need Judah because religious people would become experts at seeing everybody else's sexual failure.
We would need Tamar because vulnerable people would need to know Scripture does not simply erase them from the story.
We would need Samson because gifted people would mistake gifting for godliness.
And we would need Jesus because eventually every honest person would realize:
I cannot save myself.
That is the moment the Gospel stops being theology you agree with and becomes oxygen.
You stop saying, “Jesus died for sinners.”
And whisper:
“Jesus died for me.”
You stop talking about grace like a doctrine.
You fall into it like someone who has finally stopped pretending he can swim.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Repentance is turning.
The New Testament word is μετάνοια — metanoia: repentance, a decisive change of mind and direction that bears fruit in a changed life.
It means bringing darkness into light.
Ending what needs to end.
Deleting what needs to disappear.
Confessing what needs to be confessed.
Seeking accountability where secrecy has become your hiding place.
Making restitution where appropriate.
Accepting consequences where necessary.
Getting pastoral and professional help where patterns have become deeply entrenched.
And refusing to call bondage “freedom” merely because culture gave it a softer name.
Jesus does not expose you because He enjoys humiliating you.
He exposes what is killing you because He intends to make you free.
That is why His words about lust are severe.
Jesus says:
ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
The one intentionally looking toward lust.
He goes after the gaze because He loves the person behind the eyes.
He goes after fantasy because He wants the heart.
He goes after secret sin because He wants the whole human being.
Christ does not merely want your Sunday.
He wants the midnight version of you.
The lonely version.
The aroused version.
The wounded version.
The ashamed version.
The version holding the phone.
The version nobody else meets.
That person needs Jesus too.
Maybe especially that person.
And if something inside you has been whispering while you read this—
This is me.
Then stop running.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you clean yourself up.
Not when you become worthy.
Come now.
Tell Jesus the truth.
No performance.
No religious vocabulary necessary.
“Jesus, I sinned.”
“Jesus, I am trapped.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, I need You.”
David's confession was painfully simple:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
Sometimes freedom begins with one honest sentence.
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
It does not.
Christ alone saves.
But sometimes publicly acknowledging our need for mercy is the first crack in a wall of pretending.

And if Christ has already rescued you from a sexual past you once believed would define you forever, tell your testimony. Somebody scrolling beneath this article may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores people.
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Not because it is comfortable.
Because there may come a night when you need to read it again.
Not as a badge proving that you are holy, but as a doorway through which someone hiding in shame may encounter biblical truth and the mercy of Christ.

If you know someone whose marriage is struggling, someone fighting pornography, someone drowning in shame over their past, someone who believes Christianity has nothing to say except “you are disgusting,” or even an unbelieving friend who has never understood what Christians actually mean by grace—send this to them.
That is one simple way to glorify God: not by promoting us for our sake, but by helping His truth travel farther than it would have traveled without you.
More importantly, stay because you want to grow.
But before you leave, remember the strangest thing about the Bible's hardest sexual stories.
God could have edited them out.
He didn't.
David's scandal remained in Scripture.
Judah's scandal remained.
Tamar's pain remained.
Samson's collapse remained.
Humanity's shame remained.
Because the Bible was never written to convince you that God's people were flawless.
It was written to reveal a faithful God who enters the wreckage of sinful humanity and accomplishes redemption that sinners could never manufacture for themselves.
And Matthew's genealogy makes the point almost impossible to miss.
Judah appears.
Tamar appears.
David appears.
“Uriah's wife” appears.
And eventually—
Jesus appears.
The genealogy walks through human scandal until it arrives at the Savior.
That does not make the scandals good.
It makes grace astonishing.
God does not need to pretend your past never happened in order to redeem your future.
He does not call adultery faithfulness.
He does not call lust purity.
He does not call exploitation love.
He does not call darkness light.
He does something far greater.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He forgives those who come to Him through Christ.
He cleanses.
He restores.
He transforms.
He teaches wounded people that what happened to them is not the end of their story.
And He teaches guilty people that repentance is not the funeral of hope.
It may be where hope finally begins.
So perhaps the question is no longer:
“Why did God put such scandalous sexual stories in the Bible?”
Perhaps the question is:
“What if God left them there so people with scandalous stories would know they could still come home?”
The Bible's darkest stories are not permission to remain in darkness.
They are evidence that darkness does not get the final word when Jesus enters the story.
Your worst chapter may tell the truth about what happened—but only Jesus gets to write the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Israel’s Greatest Leader Was Dead. Then God Told Joshua, “Arise.”
paragraphs: Israel’s Greatest Leader Was Dead. Then God Told Joshua, “Arise.”

The man who had led Israel for forty years was gone. The Jordan was still in front of them. The enemies were still waiting on the other side. And into the terrifying silence after Moses’ death, God spoke one word that every grieving, frightened, stuck believer eventually has to hear: Arise.
There are moments when life divides itself into two pieces.
Before the phone call.
After the diagnosis.
Before the betrayal.
After the funeral.
Before the marriage collapsed.
After the person you trusted walked away.
Before you lost the job.
After the dream died.
Before you discovered what they had been hiding.
After you realized you could never return to the person you used to be.
Joshua knew something about that kind of dividing line.
He was standing at one.
Behind him was a wilderness filled with memories.
In front of him was a river.

Beyond the river were fortified cities, hostile armies, giants, uncertainty, responsibility, and a promise that suddenly felt much heavier now that Moses was no longer there to carry the burden of leadership.
And Moses was dead.
Not missing.
Not recovering.
Not temporarily absent.
Dead.
Scripture refuses to soften the moment.
The Hebrew text opens Joshua with words that almost sound like the closing scene of one story crashing into the beginning of another:
וַיְהִי אַחֲרֵי מוֹת מֹשֶׁה עֶבֶד יְהוָה
Vayehi acharei mot Moshe eved YHWH.
“And it came to pass after the death of Moses the servant of the LORD…”
Then God speaks to Joshua.
And His first words do not pretend the loss did not happen.
מֹשֶׁה עַבְדִּי מֵת
Moshe avdi met.
“Moses My servant is dead.”
Then comes the turn:
וְעַתָּה קוּם עֲבֹר
Ve‘attah qum, ‘avor.
“And now, arise, cross over.”
That is Joshua 1:2.
Read those words slowly.
Moses My servant is dead. And now… arise.
God acknowledges the grave before He commands the movement.
That matters.
Biblical faith is not pretending something did not hurt.
Faith is not painting a smile over grief.
Faith is not calling devastation “nothing.”
God Himself named Joshua’s reality.
Moses was dead.
Something precious really had ended.
The wilderness generation really had buried its leader.
Joshua really was stepping into a role previously occupied by one of the most extraordinary servants of God in biblical history.
But there is something almost frighteningly beautiful about what God says next.
And now.
There are two words somebody reading this desperately needs.
And now.
What happened matters.
But it does not have to become the final chapter.
What they did to you matters.
But it does not own every page still unwritten.
What you lost matters.
But loss does not automatically mean God has lost His purpose for your life.
Your failure was real.
Your sin may have been real.
Your consequences may be real.
Your tears are certainly real.
But there can still be an “and now” after everything you thought was the end.
Maybe that is where you are.
You keep visiting something God is calling you to walk beyond.
You keep replaying a conversation that cannot be rewritten.
You keep imagining how life would have turned out if somebody had stayed.
You keep punishing yourself over a version of yourself that Jesus is calling to repentance, forgiveness, and transformation.
You are physically living in today while emotionally sleeping beside yesterday's grave.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part is this:
Yesterday has become familiar.
The Jordan has not.
Grief can become familiar.
Fear can become familiar.
Shame can become familiar.
Even spiritual paralysis can become familiar.
Sometimes we become so accustomed to surviving that obedience begins to feel dangerous.
Then God says:
קוּם
Qum.
Arise.
Not because Moses did not matter.
Precisely because God's purpose did.
God was not asking Joshua to dishonor Moses by moving forward. Joshua's obedience would honor everything God had already done through Moses.
That distinction matters for anyone who feels guilty about moving forward.
You can remember without remaining.
You can grieve without building your permanent address inside grief.
You can honor what God did yesterday without demanding that He repeat yesterday exactly.
You can cry…
and still arise.
You can tremble…
and still arise.
You can miss someone…
and still arise.
You can admit, “I don't know whether I can do this”…
and still arise.
Because biblical courage is not the absence of trembling.
It is obedience in the presence of fear.
And Joshua had reasons to fear.
Moses had confronted Pharaoh.
Moses had stretched out his hand over the sea.
Moses had stood before Israel.
Moses had received the Law.
Moses had interceded for a rebellious nation.
And now Joshua was supposed to lead the people forward.
Imagine the comparisons.
“You're not Moses.”
“Moses wouldn't have done it like that.”
“When Moses was here…”
“Remember how Moses used to lead us?”
Anyone who has ever inherited responsibility understands the suffocating pressure of following somebody admired.
But notice what God never tells Joshua.
God never says, “Become Moses.”
Instead He gives Joshua something infinitely better than imitation:
“As I was with Moses, so I will be with thee; I will not fail thee, nor forsake thee.”
Joshua did not need Moses' personality.
He needed Moses' God.
And so do you.
You do not need somebody else's calling.
You do not need somebody else's testimony.
You do not need somebody else's platform, marriage, ministry, personality, gifts, audience, income, appearance, story, or spiritual vocabulary.
You need the presence of God.
Because the secret of Moses was never merely Moses.
It was God with Moses.
And the hope of Joshua would never merely be Joshua.
It would be God with Joshua.
This is where the story begins reaching beyond Joshua toward something greater.
Because Joshua's story is not ultimately permission for us to turn every personal ambition into our own private “Promised Land.”

Joshua 1 is about God's covenant purposes for Israel. The land promise in this chapter was given to Israel; we should not rip it from its biblical setting and make it mean, “God guarantees me the promotion, house, business, relationship, money, or dream I want.” God specifically commands Joshua to lead Israel across the Jordan into the land He had promised.
The deeper Christian hope is even greater than getting everything we want.
It is getting Christ.
Joshua would lead Israel into Canaan.
But Joshua could not conquer humanity's deepest enemies.
He could not cleanse the guilty conscience.
He could not bear the sins of the world.
He could not defeat death itself.
Another Savior would come.
And His name carries an astonishing connection.
The Hebrew name Joshua, יְהוֹשֻׁעַ — Yehoshua, belongs to the same biblical name-family from which the name Jesus comes to us through Greek.
Joshua led God's people across a river.
Jesus came to rescue sinners from something far deeper than geography.
Joshua confronted armies.
Jesus confronted sin, Satan, judgment, and death.
Joshua brought Israel into an earthly inheritance.
Jesus brings those who trust Him into reconciliation with God and an inheritance that death cannot finally steal.
And here is where the Gospel becomes painfully personal.
Maybe the Jordan in front of you is not your greatest problem.
Maybe the deepest problem is inside you.
We like stories about courage because courage makes us feel heroic.
The Gospel first tells us something far less flattering:
We need mercy.
We have sinned.
We have wanted God's gifts without God's rule.
We have defended what should have been confessed.
We have hidden what should have been brought into the light.
We have blamed others while quietly protecting our own idols.
We have called compromise “complicated.”
We have called disobedience “being human.”
We have called pride “boundaries.”
We have called greed “ambition.”
We have called lust “a private struggle.”
We have called bitterness “discernment.”
And sometimes we have called religious activity “knowing God.”
Then Jesus walks into the scandal.
Not to tell us sin does not matter.
The cross proves it matters more terribly than we imagined.
Christ comes to do what we could never do for ourselves.
The sinless Son of God bears sin.
The condemned sinner is offered mercy.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The rebel can be reconciled.
The ashamed can stop hiding.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
That is grace.
Not God pretending the scandal never happened.
God rewriting what the scandal gets to become through Jesus Christ.
Repentance is therefore not God humiliating you for entertainment.
It is the mercy of God calling you out of the grave you have mistaken for home.
There may be somebody reading this who has been saying:
“When I become stronger, I'll come back to God.”
“When I clean myself up, I'll pray again.”
“When I stop struggling, I'll open my Bible again.”
“When I feel worthy, I'll return.”
But if you could make yourself worthy, you would not need a Savior.
Come broken.
Come ashamed.
Come exposed.
Come tired.
Come with the secret.
Come with the relapse.
Come with the questions.
Come confessing the sin instead of negotiating with it.
But come to Christ.
Because Jesus did not die for the imaginary version of you that finally gets everything together.
He died for sinners.
And He rose.
That changes everything.
There is a fascinating rhythm in Joshua 1.
God tells Joshua to be strong and courageous repeatedly, but He does not disconnect courage from obedience.
חֲזַק וֶאֱמָץ
Chazaq ve’ematz.
“Be strong and courageous.”
Then God anchors that courage in His Word.

Joshua is commanded not to turn aside from God's instruction, and the “book of the law” is not to depart from his mouth; he is to meditate on it “day and night” so that he may carefully do what is written.
That destroys one of our culture's favorite definitions of courage.
Biblical courage is not “believe in yourself.”
Joshua's confidence was not supposed to rest in Joshua.
It was rooted in God's presence, God's promise, and obedience to God's Word.
That is why some of the most courageous words you will ever speak are not:
“I can do anything.”
Sometimes they are:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“I was wrong.”
“I need help.”
“I need to repent.”
“I cannot keep living like this.”
“I forgive them.”
“I surrender.”
“Your will, not mine.”
“I will obey even though I am afraid.”
Maybe your qum moment is not launching something impressive.
Maybe it is deleting the secret conversation.
Maybe it is confessing what you have hidden.
Maybe it is returning money that was never yours.
Maybe it is asking forgiveness without defending yourself.
Maybe it is finally opening Scripture before opening social media.
Maybe it is walking away from a relationship that continually pulls you into sin.
Maybe it is forgiving somebody while still maintaining wise boundaries.
Maybe it is admitting that the image everyone applauds is not the person you have become behind closed doors.
Maybe it is kneeling beside your bed tonight and whispering:
“Jesus… I don't want to hide anymore.”
Be honest.
Maybe this hit harder than you expected.
Not because typing three words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when pride finally stops controlling the sentence.
There is no shame in needing prayer.
Joshua himself was never commissioned into solitary self-sufficiency.
He was called to lead a people under the authority and presence of God.
And then something remarkable happens.
Joshua moves.
God speaks in verses 1–9.
Then verse 10 begins:
“Then Joshua commanded the officers of the people…”
Do you see it?
God said arise.
Joshua did not form a committee to determine whether arising felt comfortable.
He moved toward obedience.
That may be the line separating the life you keep praying about from the obedience God has already made clear.
Not another emotional moment.
Not another saved sermon.
Not another inspirational quote.
Obedience.
There are moments when you have prayed enough to know what the next faithful step is.
Now take it.
The river will not become less of a river because you stare at it.
And eventually, Israel would have to put feet beneath faith.

Later, when they came to the Jordan in Joshua 3, the waters were overflowing their banks, and the priests carrying the ark stepped toward the water. The passage emphasizes God's presence through the ark and God's miraculous action as the people crossed.
God was teaching Israel something they would repeatedly need to remember:
The future did not belong to the strongest people.
It belonged to God.
And that truth reaches its blazing fulfillment in the Gospel.
At the cross, Jesus looked defeated.
The Messiah was mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
Buried.
There was a stone.
There was grief.
There was silence.
There was a Saturday when the disciples could see nothing except the wreckage of what they thought would happen.
Then came Sunday.
The grave that looked like punctuation became a doorway.
Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead.
And because He lives, Christianity is not ultimately a philosophy about coping with yesterday.
It is the announcement that death does not get the last word.
Sin does not get the last word.
Shame does not get the last word.
Your worst chapter does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
This does not mean every earthly tragedy will be reversed the way we want during this life.
Some wounds leave scars.
Some people never return.
Some consequences remain.
Some prayers are answered differently than we begged.
Some Jordans lead into battles rather than immediate comfort.
Following Christ is not a guarantee of an easy life.
Joshua crossed the Jordan and found Jericho waiting.
Sometimes obedience does not remove the battle.
It brings you to the place where the battle must finally be fought.
But the believer does not walk there abandoned.
God's words to Joshua were:
כִּי עִמְּךָ יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ בְּכֹל אֲשֶׁר תֵּלֵךְ
Ki ‘immekha YHWH Elohekha bekhol asher telekh.
“For the LORD thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.”

For Christians, that theme of divine presence reaches a breathtaking climax in Jesus Christ—Immanuel, “God with us”—and in His promise to His disciples that He is with them as they carry out His commission.
So perhaps courage is not waking tomorrow without fear.
Perhaps courage is waking afraid and saying:
“Jesus, I am Yours.”
Perhaps courage is walking toward the Jordan while your knees still shake.
Perhaps courage is discovering that faith was never about your grip on God being perfect.
It was about the faithfulness of the God who refuses to abandon His people.
And perhaps somebody you know is standing beside their own Jordan right now.
They have not told anyone.
Their pictures look normal.
Their jokes sound normal.
But at night they are barely holding themselves together.
Not as a performance.
Not to prove you are spiritual.
Arise.
Send this to the believer who thinks failure permanently disqualified them.
Send it to the grieving parent.
The exhausted pastor.
The ashamed Christian.
The person trying to return to Jesus.
The friend who has not prayed in months.
Even the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is merely religion for people who have everything together.
Let them discover the scandalous center of Christianity:
We did not save ourselves.
Jesus came for sinners.

There will probably be another Jordan. There may be another night when yesterday starts calling your name, and you will need to remember that God's faithfulness did not expire when your circumstances changed.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite the Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Invite even the person who does not yet believe.
Not because Gospel Warrior is the destination.
Jesus is.
Any ministry worth supporting should keep pointing beyond itself to Christ.
Supporting Gospel work financially does not purchase God's favor. We are saved by grace through faith, not by purchasing access to God.
But Christians are called to generosity, partnership in Gospel work, and stewardship of what God has entrusted to them.

Your support helps us keep creating Christ-centered material, expanding resources, encouraging wounded believers, confronting comfortable Christianity with Scripture, and placing the Gospel in front of people who might never walk through a church door.
It should never be a shirt.
It should never even be a discount.
Pray.
Share.
Follow.
Save the message.
Speak about Jesus.
Carry the Gospel farther than this page.
And comment.
Somebody else's trembling faith may need evidence that Christians still walk through fire and discover Christ waiting with them there.
Moses was dead.
Joshua could not change that.
The Jordan was ahead.
Joshua could not pretend it wasn't.
Enemies were waiting.
Joshua could not wish them away.
But God was still God.
And that was enough to take the next step.
Maybe you cannot rewrite what happened yesterday.
Maybe you cannot resurrect the relationship.
Maybe you cannot recover the years.
Maybe you cannot undo the sentence you spoke.
Maybe you cannot remove every consequence of what you did.
Maybe you cannot return to who you were before everything shattered.
But the Gospel offers something infinitely greater than pretending the past never happened.
It offers a Redeemer.
Jesus Christ takes guilty people and makes them forgiven.
He takes rebels and makes them sons and daughters.
He takes shame into the light.
He takes sinners to a cross.
He takes death to an empty tomb.
He does not merely decorate ruined lives.
He makes people new.
So when the enemy whispers,
“Your best days died back there…”
remember Joshua.
When shame says,
“You can never move beyond this…”
remember the cross.
When fear says,
“You are not strong enough…”
remember that Joshua was not commanded to trust his own greatness.
He was commanded to trust and obey the God who would be with him.
And when yesterday tries to become your identity, look toward Jesus.
There is life after the chapter you thought would finish you.
There is repentance after rebellion.
There is forgiveness after confession.
There is restoration after ruin.
There is purpose after loss.
There is grace after scandal.
And there is resurrection after a cross.
Moses was dead.
Then God said:
וְעַתָּה קוּם
Ve‘attah qum.
And now… arise.
Maybe that is the word you came here to hear.
Not “forget.”
Not “pretend.”
Not “become invincible.”
Arise.
Arise forgiven because of Christ.
Arise surrendered to Christ.
Arise dependent upon Christ.
Arise obedient to His Word.
Arise knowing that the God who writes redemption is not frightened by the page you wish you could tear out.
The grave may explain why you cried yesterday, but it does not have authority to write tomorrow when Jesus Christ holds the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY SOME CHRISTIAN MARRIAGES BECOME SEXLESS
paragraphs:
WHY SOME CHRISTIAN MARRIAGES BECOME SEXLESS
They Still Sleep in the Same Bed. They Still Say “I Love You.” They May Even Go to Church Together. But Somewhere Between the Wedding Vows and the Quiet Resentment, They Stopped Reaching for Each Other.
There is a particular kind of loneliness that almost nobody talks about in church.
It is the loneliness of lying inches away from the person you promised your life to...
and feeling miles apart.
The house may still look like a Christian home.
There may be a Bible on the nightstand.
Worship music may play in the car.
The children may see Mom and Dad sitting beside each other on Sunday.
There may still be anniversary photographs on Facebook.
There may still be “I love you” at the end of a phone call.
But when night comes...
one turns toward the wall.
The other stares into the darkness.
And neither knows how to say what has been dying between them.
Sometimes the husband feels rejected so many times that eventually he stops asking.
Sometimes the wife feels emotionally abandoned so deeply that physical intimacy begins to feel disconnected from everything her heart has been begging for.
Sometimes the roles are reversed.
Sometimes exhaustion has swallowed desire.

Sometimes childbirth, aging, grief, medication, hormonal changes, disability, chronic illness, depression, anxiety, trauma, pain, infertility, betrayal, pornography, unresolved conflict, financial pressure, caregiving, or years of accumulated disappointment have entered the bedroom with them.
Sometimes sex disappeared suddenly.
Sometimes it died one disappointed night at a time.
And sometimes two sincere Christians who genuinely love Jesus discover something frightening:
They have become excellent roommates...
but wounded lovers.
Before anyone turns this into ammunition against a spouse, hear this carefully.
This article is not permission to demand sex.
It is not permission to manipulate someone with Scripture.
It is not permission to shame a husband or wife whose body is suffering.
It is certainly not permission for coercion, intimidation, violence, or abuse.

The Bible's vision of marital intimacy cannot be separated from the Bible's commands concerning sacrificial love, honor, tenderness, faithfulness, truth, forgiveness, and concern for another person's good.
Marriage was never meant to become a courtroom where Scripture verses are presented as evidence against the person sleeping beside you.
It was meant to become a covenant in which two people increasingly learn how to love one another under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And that is exactly why sexlessness can sometimes reveal something deeper than the absence of sex.
Sometimes the bedroom is where wounds from everywhere else in the marriage finally become visible.
Long before Paul wrote about marital intimacy, Scripture gave us an astonishing description of marriage.
Genesis 2:24 says that a man leaves his father and mother, clings to his wife, and they become “one flesh.”
The Hebrew expression is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad
“One flesh.”
Not merely two people occupying one address.
Not merely two incomes paying one mortgage.
Not merely two Christians raising children under one roof.
One flesh.

Marriage is a profound covenant union, and sexual intimacy belongs within that larger reality. Sex is not the whole marriage, but neither does Scripture treat the physical union of husband and wife as meaningless.
Then Paul writes words that become uncomfortable precisely because they are so direct.

In 1 Corinthians 7:3–5, he teaches husbands and wives to give one another the marital affection that is due, and he warns them against depriving one another except temporarily by mutual agreement for prayer, after which they are to come together again.
Notice what is often missed.
Paul addresses both husband and wife.
This is not a weapon handed to husbands.
It is not a weapon handed to wives.
The passage contains a startling reciprocity. Husband and wife are called away from selfish possession and toward mutual self-giving.
And the Greek phrase connected with abstaining is deeply important:
ἐκ συμφώνου — ek symphōnou
It carries the idea of agreement, consent, being of one accord.
That matters.
Biblical marital intimacy is not supposed to look like one spouse winning while the other surrenders under pressure.
Christian marriage is not sanctified selfishness.
Sex is not a debt collector pounding on the bedroom door.
It is meant to exist within covenant love.
And perhaps that exposes one reason some Christian marriages become sexless.
Because somewhere along the journey...
intimacy stopped feeling like love.
Maybe every touch began to carry an expectation.
Maybe affection disappeared unless sex was likely.
Maybe conversations became transactional.
Maybe tenderness became rare.
Maybe one spouse started feeling that their body mattered more than their heart.
Maybe another began feeling unwanted, undesirable, and chronically rejected.
Maybe neither knew how to describe the pain without accusing the other.
So silence became safer.
Then silence became normal.
Then normal became years.
This is where Ephesians 5 becomes impossible to ignore.
Paul tells husbands:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας...
Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas...
“Husbands, love your wives...”
But Paul does not stop there.
The standard is devastatingly high:
καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν
“...as Christ loved the church.”
Think about that.
The model for a Christian husband's love is not cultural masculinity.
Not entitlement.
Not domination.
Not “I provide the money, therefore you owe me.”
Not “The Bible says your body belongs to me.”
Christ.
The crucified Christ.
The Savior who gives Himself.
The King who washes feet.
The Bridegroom who sacrifices Himself for His bride.
A husband cannot invoke 1 Corinthians 7 while conveniently forgetting Ephesians 5.
And a wife cannot use intimacy as a weapon of punishment, manipulation, contempt, or control while claiming that the rest of the marriage remains untouched.
Both husband and wife stand beneath the authority of Christ.
Both must ask the terrifying question:
“Lord, where have I stopped loving?”
Because sometimes a sexless marriage is not primarily suffering from a sex problem.
It is suffering from a tenderness problem.
A trust problem.
A forgiveness problem.
A listening problem.
A pornography problem.
A resentment problem.
A secrecy problem.
A medical problem.
A trauma problem.
An exhaustion problem.
A selfishness problem.
A communication problem.
A spiritual problem.
Or several of these at once.
And merely telling a hurting couple to “have more sex” may be like telling someone with a fractured leg to run faster.
You have not healed the fracture.
You have only increased the pain.
There is another Scripture husbands especially should sit with before blaming their wives.
Peter tells husbands to live with their wives κατὰ γνῶσιν — kata gnōsin, “according to knowledge” or with understanding, and to give them τιμήν — timēn, honor.
Then comes the sobering warning:
εἰς τὸ μὴ ἐγκόπτεσθαι τὰς προσευχὰς ὑμῶν
“So that your prayers may not be hindered.”
—1 Peter 3:7
That should stop a Christian man cold.
God cares about how you treat your wife.
Your spirituality at church cannot be neatly separated from your behavior at home.
You cannot become cruel at 8:00 p.m. and imagine that religious language at 8:00 a.m. makes cruelty disappear.
You cannot humiliate your wife, ignore her pain, treat her as an object, and then consider yourself spiritually healthy simply because you know theology.
Peter connects a husband's treatment of his wife with his prayers.
That is serious.
And wives should not read that paragraph merely thinking, “I hope my husband sees this.”
The Gospel does not merely expose the person beside us.
It exposes us.
What have I done with my spouse's vulnerability?
Have I listened?
Have I mocked?
Have I punished?
Have I compared?
Have I withdrawn affection to gain power?
Have I made confession dangerous?
Have I made rejection habitual?
Have I become harsh?
Have I become contemptuous?
Have I carried secret fantasies into our covenant?
Have I expected my spouse to heal wounds I refuse to acknowledge?
Have I prayed for my marriage while refusing to repent inside my marriage?
Those questions hurt.
They are supposed to.
Because repentance often begins where excuses end.
And this is where pornography deserves to be named.
Pornography trains desire away from covenant and toward consumption.
It teaches the eyes to demand novelty while a real spouse grows older beside you.
It offers fantasy without responsibility, bodies without covenant, stimulation without sacrifice.
Then the person consuming it may wonder why ordinary marital intimacy no longer produces the same excitement.
Jesus takes lust seriously.
In Matthew 5:28, He brings the battle into the heart.
The answer, however, is not merely shame.
It is repentance.
Bring darkness into light.
Confess.
Remove access.
Seek accountability.
Stop protecting the thing destroying your ability to see another human being with holy love.
And if pornography has wounded your marriage, do not demand that trust regenerate overnight.
Broken trust may be forgiven before it is fully rebuilt.
Forgiveness and restored trust are related, but they are not identical processes.
Trust often returns through truth consistently practiced over time.
But pornography is not the explanation for every sexless marriage.
Sometimes there is no secret scandal.
There is simply pain.
A woman may experience painful intercourse and remain silent because she thinks a “good Christian wife” is supposed to endure it.
A husband may experience sexual dysfunction and drown in shame because he believes admitting it makes him less masculine.
A new mother may be physically exhausted, touched-out, hormonally changed, and emotionally overwhelmed.
A spouse taking necessary medication may experience changes in desire or sexual functioning.
Illness can change bodies.
Menopause can change bodies.
Pregnancy can change bodies.
Grief can change bodies.
Trauma can change bodies.
Age changes bodies.
And Christian compassion must be large enough to acknowledge bodies without treating every difficulty as rebellion against God.
Sometimes the faithful next step is prayer.
Sometimes it is repentance.
Sometimes it is a difficult conversation.
Sometimes it is a physician.
