“Maybe your suffering will change them.”
“Hosea stayed faithful.”
“Marriage is for life.”
“God hates divorce.”
So you stayed.
You prayed harder.
You became quieter.
You learned which words would trigger the explosion.
You learned how to read footsteps.
You learned how to recognize the sound of anger before anger entered the room.
You learned to hide bruises beneath sleeves, humiliation beneath smiles, fear beneath worship songs, and exhaustion beneath the sentence Christians are expected to say:
“God is good.”
And God is good.
But the evil being done to you is not.
Please hear that distinction.
Because confusing those two things has kept too many people imprisoned.
Maybe there were never bruises on your body.
Maybe the wounds were harder to photograph.
The threats.
The sexual coercion.
The financial control.
The isolation.
The monitoring.
The intimidation.
The screaming.
The destruction of property.
The constant degradation.
The manipulation disguised as spirituality.
The apologies that sounded like repentance until the same nightmare returned.
Maybe Scripture itself was weaponized against you.
“Submit.”
“Forgive.”
“Seventy times seven.”
“God hates divorce.”
“Hosea took Gomer back.”
And perhaps the most terrifying part was that eventually you stopped asking, “Is this abuse?”
You started asking:
“Would leaving make me a bad Christian?”
That question deserves a biblical answer.
And Gomer’s story is not permission to stay in abuse.
Read Hosea carefully.
God tells the prophet:
“Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms…”
—Hosea 1:2, KJV
The Hebrew contains the striking expression אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים — ’eshet zenunim — commonly rendered “a wife of whoredom” or “a wife of promiscuity.”
The language is deliberately shocking because Hosea’s marriage becomes a prophetic sign.
God explains the symbolism in the same verse:
“…for the land hath committed great whoredom, departing from the LORD.”
That is the interpretive key.
Hosea is not primarily a handbook teaching abused spouses how long they must endure mistreatment.
Hosea is a prophetic book exposing Israel’s covenant unfaithfulness to God.
Gomer’s unfaithfulness becomes a living picture of Israel’s spiritual unfaithfulness.
Hosea’s wounded love points beyond Hosea.
It points toward the astonishing covenant love of God.
Later God tells Hosea:
“Go yet, love a woman beloved of her friend, yet an adulteress, according to the love of the LORD toward the children of Israel…”
—Hosea 3:1, KJV
Do not miss the words “according to the love of the LORD.”
The center of the story is God.
His holiness.
His grief over sin.
His judgment.
His covenant faithfulness.
His pursuing mercy.
His willingness to restore the repentant and undeserving.
That is why one of Hosea’s most beautiful Hebrew words matters so deeply.
חֶסֶד — ḥesed.
It carries the rich biblical idea of steadfast love, covenant loyalty, mercy, and faithfulness.
God declares:
“For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.”
—Hosea 6:6, KJV
The word translated “mercy” there is חֶסֶד.
And centuries later, Jesus Himself quotes Hosea 6:6.
“I will have mercy, and not sacrifice…”
—Matthew 9:13, KJV
Jesus did not build His kingdom around protecting religious appearances while wounded human beings were crushed underneath them.
He repeatedly exposed hypocrisy.
He confronted those who exploited the vulnerable.
He defended the dignity of people religious culture preferred to condemn.
And He never taught that another person’s sin becomes holy merely because you endure it quietly.
That distinction matters enormously.
Forgiveness is Christian.
Reconciliation is beautiful when genuine repentance and restoration make it possible.
But forgiveness and immediate restoration of access are not identical.
You can forgive someone and still recognize danger.
You can refuse revenge without volunteering for another beating.
You can desire someone’s repentance without pretending they have already repented.
You can pray for someone while maintaining distance.
You can love an enemy without giving that enemy unrestricted access to harm you.
Jesus Himself said:
“Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.”
—Matthew 10:16, KJV
Wise.
Not vindictive.
Not cruel.
Not consumed by revenge.
But wise.
Scripture does not define love as enabling evil.
First Corinthians 13 says love “rejoiceth not in iniquity, but rejoiceth in the truth.”
Love and truth belong together.
Biblical love does not require calling darkness light.
And biblical forgiveness does not require calling an unsafe person safe.
This becomes especially important when people invoke Jesus’ teaching about forgiveness.
When Peter asked how often he should forgive, Jesus answered:
“I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.”
—Matthew 18:22, KJV
That is a devastating command against bitterness, vengeance, and the human desire to keep a ledger of offenses.
But notice something.
Jesus does not say:
“Give an unrepentant violent person seventy times seven opportunities to injure you.”
Those are not the same statement.
The New Testament can command radical forgiveness while also condemning violence and commanding believers to walk wisely.
Paul writes:
—Colossians 3:19, KJV
And:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
—Ephesians 5:25, KJV
Read that again.
“As Christ also loved the church.”
Christlike headship is cruciform.
Self-giving.
Protective.
Holy.
Tender.
It is not domination baptized with Bible vocabulary.
It is not terror with a wedding ring.
It is not coercion followed by a Scripture quotation.
It is not demanding submission while refusing Christlike sacrifice.
And this matters because Ephesians 5:22 is sometimes ripped from its context and turned into a weapon:
“Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord.”
But immediately before the household instructions, Paul writes:
—Ephesians 5:21, KJV
The Greek verb behind “submitting” is ὑποτάσσω — hypotassō.

Whatever debates Christians may have about the precise structure of authority within marriage, nothing in Ephesians transforms cruelty, battery, rape, threats, coercive control, or terror into a husband’s biblical privilege.
Nothing.
Jesus never handed an abuser a theological license.
And submission to God can never mean participating in another person's rebellion against God.
Perhaps someone told you, “But God hates divorce.”
They may be referencing Malachi 2.
But read the surrounding passage.
Malachi is not giving abusive husbands ammunition against wounded wives.
He is confronting covenant treachery.
The passage condemns faithlessness toward “the wife of thy covenant” and speaks severely about violence.
The God who cares about covenant also cares about how covenant partners are treated.
Marriage is sacred.
That is precisely why abuse is so serious.
Abuse does not honor the marriage covenant.
It desecrates it.
A marriage certificate does not magically turn cruelty into righteousness.
And staying physically accessible to danger is not the definition of covenant faithfulness.

There may be situations in which immediate separation for safety is necessary even while complicated questions about reconciliation, divorce, church discipline, legal protection, children, finances, and future decisions are worked through carefully.
Those questions deserve serious pastoral, legal, and practical wisdom.
But immediate safety does not need to wait until every theological question about the future has been solved.
If you or your children are in immediate danger, get to a safe place and contact appropriate emergency services or trusted local help.
That is not a failure of faith.
The Bible repeatedly treats protection from violent people as wisdom.
David fled Saul.
Think about that.
David had been anointed by God.
Saul was still king.
David refused to murder Saul when opportunities arose.
He would not take vengeance into his own hands.
Yet David also did not stand beside Saul indefinitely saying:
“If I were more spiritual, perhaps I would let him throw another spear.”
David fled.
He maintained boundaries.
He recognized danger.
He refused personal vengeance.
Those truths existed simultaneously.
That is incredibly important.
You do not have to hate someone to get away from them.
You do not have to seek revenge to seek protection.
You do not have to deny forgiveness to establish a boundary.
And you do not have to surrender your body to somebody’s violence to prove that Jesus lives inside you.
Sometimes leaving the room is wisdom.
Sometimes leaving the house is wisdom.
Sometimes calling authorities is wisdom.
Sometimes telling the truth to trusted people is wisdom.
Sometimes refusing secrecy is the first moment darkness begins losing its power.
Romans 13 describes civil authority as having a legitimate role in restraining wrongdoing.
Reporting criminal violence is not automatically an act of unforgiveness.
There are sins that require more than a private apology.
And there are crimes that remain crimes even when the offender knows Bible verses.
This is where Christian communities must examine themselves.
We should never become so desperate to save the appearance of a marriage that we sacrifice the person trapped inside it.
A church should not become an abuser’s hiding place.
A pastor should not become the public-relations department for someone’s violence.
A Bible study should not become a courtroom where the wounded person is interrogated while the perpetrator receives endless benefit of the doubt.
And “keep this between us” should never become a spiritualized gag over the mouth of someone who needs protection.
Sin thrives in darkness.
Jesus brings things into light.
Yet another truth must be spoken carefully.
Not every painful marriage is abusive.
Not every argument is abuse.
Not every insensitive spouse is an abuser.
Not every marital failure requires separation.
Human beings can behave selfishly, communicate terribly, wound each other, repent, mature, receive counseling, rebuild trust, and experience extraordinary restoration through Christ.
We should not casually weaponize the word “abuse.”
But neither should we minimize genuine abuse because the word makes us uncomfortable.
Discernment matters.
Truth matters.
Evidence matters.
Safety matters.
And repentance matters.
Real repentance is more than crying after consequences arrive.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia — speaks of repentance, a genuine turning of mind and direction.
Biblical repentance bears fruit.
John the Baptist said:
“Bring forth therefore fruits meet for repentance.”
—Matthew 3:8, KJV
Fruit.
Not merely promises.
Not “I’m sorry” followed by intimidation three days later.
Not flowers followed by another assault.
Not tears followed by another threat.
Not Bible verses followed by another cycle of control.

Where repentance is genuine, there should increasingly be truthfulness, accountability, humility, changed behavior, acceptance of consequences, respect for boundaries, and a willingness to seek serious help.
Forgiveness can be offered from a heart surrendered to Christ.
Trust, however, is rebuilt through demonstrated faithfulness.
Reconciliation requires more than one person wanting peace.
And restoration should never be manufactured by pressuring a victim back into danger.
This is where Gomer’s story becomes even more beautiful when we stop forcing it to say something it was never intended to say.
Because ultimately, you are not Hosea.
And your abusive spouse is not Gomer in some simplistic one-to-one reenactment.
Hosea’s prophetic marriage belongs to a specific prophetic calling within Israel’s covenant history.
Its great theological horizon is the scandal of divine grace toward a people who betrayed God.
And that story reaches toward something even greater.
Jesus Christ.
Because eventually Scripture reveals a Bridegroom whose love surpasses Hosea’s.
A Bridegroom who does not abuse His bride.
He gives Himself for her.
Christ does not terrorize His people into submission.
He lays down His life.
He does not exploit weakness.
He enters human weakness.
He does not crush bruised reeds.
He heals.
He does not excuse sin.
He bears sin’s judgment at the cross so sinners can be forgiven and transformed.
This is the Gospel.
We were not innocent lovers abandoned by God.
We were the unfaithful ones.
We wandered.
We worshiped other things.
We loved creation more than Creator.
We sinned in thought, desire, word, and deed.
And still Christ came.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8, KJV
There is the scandal.
And there is the grace.
The scandal is our sin.
The grace is His cross.
The scandal is that humanity rejected its Creator.
The grace is that the Creator came looking for rebels.
The scandal is that our debt was real.
The grace is that Jesus paid what we could never pay.
The scandal is that sin deserves judgment.
The grace is that Christ bore judgment for everyone who comes to Him in repentant faith.
But grace does not make sin harmless.
Grace confronts sin.
Grace forgives sin.
Grace breaks sin’s dominion.
Grace teaches us to renounce ungodliness.
Grace transforms.
So if someone repeatedly abuses another person and then demands “grace” as protection from consequences, they have misunderstood grace.
Grace is not permission to continue destroying people.
The grace that forgives also calls sinners to repentance.
The Jesus who said, “Neither do I condemn thee,” also said, “go, and sin no more.”
Maybe this article is exposing something you have never said aloud.
Maybe you have been defending someone publicly who terrifies you privately.
Maybe you know someone whose smile changes the moment their spouse enters the room.
Maybe someone you love keeps making excuses for injuries, disappearing from friendships, becoming increasingly isolated, or apologizing constantly for things that are not their fault.
Do not immediately become judge and jury.
But do not look away.
Listen.
Take credible danger seriously.
Help them reach qualified local support.
If children are endangered, act responsibly according to applicable safeguarding and reporting requirements.
If immediate danger exists, prioritize immediate safety.
And if you are the person living this story, please understand:
You do not need to prove your Christianity by keeping abuse secret.
Bring darkness into the light.
Tell someone trustworthy.
Seek wise pastoral care from leaders who understand abuse rather than merely demanding appearances.
Seek qualified professional help.
Seek appropriate legal protection where necessary.
Make a safety plan if leaving could increase danger.
And if you are in immediate danger, contact emergency services or an appropriate domestic-violence service where you live.
Your next step does not have to answer every question about the rest of your life.
It may simply need to get you through tonight safely.
Then tomorrow.
Then the next faithful step.
And perhaps one day, when the fear has stopped screaming loudly enough for you to hear your own thoughts again, you will realize something:
Jesus was never standing with your abuser demanding that you endure another blow to prove your devotion to Him.
Christ is holy.
Christ opposes evil.
Christ calls sinners to repentance.
Christ receives the broken.
Christ gives grace to the guilty who repent and believe.
And Christ is capable of writing redemption into places human sin has devastated.
That does not mean every marriage will be restored.
It does not mean every relationship should resume.
It does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
Sometimes redemption looks like reconciliation after profound repentance, accountability, safety, and long-term transformation.
Sometimes redemption looks like God carrying a wounded person through consequences they never wanted.
Sometimes it looks like finally telling the truth.
Sometimes it looks like discovering that the end of one chapter was not the end of your usefulness to God.
Because Jesus does not need your story to remain pretty in order to redeem it.
He specializes in graves.
Crosses.
Failures.
Shame.
Ruins.
Places everybody else thinks are finished.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to produce comfortable Christianity that helps us pretend everything is fine.
But to keep bringing wounded, wandering, ashamed, exhausted, hungry people back to Scripture—and ultimately back to Jesus Christ.
If this article uncovered something you have been afraid to name, you do not have to tell strangers every detail. But you also do not have to keep carrying everything alone.
And if you have survived something God has carried you through, consider leaving a word of hope for the person reading the comments at 2:13 in the morning wondering whether anybody understands.
Your testimony may become someone else’s reason to seek help.
Not as a religious performance.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
But if you genuinely believe biblical truth should reach people trapped behind closed doors, sharing it is one practical way to serve them.
You may never know who reads it silently.
Send it privately to someone who may need it.
And invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—even the person who does not yet believe—to follow too.
It doesn't.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Him.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership when it is done freely, cheerfully, and for Christ rather than human recognition.
The believer sitting silently in a frightening house.
The Christian wondering whether getting somewhere safe means betraying Jesus.
The woman staring at Hosea and thinking Gomer’s story means she must endure one more night.
The man ashamed to admit that he is being abused because he thinks nobody will believe him.
The child listening from another room while adults call chaos “marriage.”
Hear this clearly:
Hosea reveals a God whose covenant love pursues the unfaithful.
It does not reveal a God who delights in watching the vulnerable remain available to violence.
The cross proves something even deeper.
Jesus entered suffering to rescue sinners.
He did not sanctify our cruelty.
He died to save us from sin—and to make us new.
So forgive without pretending evil is good.
Seek peace without surrendering truth.
Pray for repentance without manufacturing reconciliation.
Protect life without feeling ashamed of wisdom.
Bring darkness into the light.
And wherever genuine repentance becomes possible, remember that no sinner is beyond the reach of Christ.
Not the wounded.
Not the ashamed.
Not even the perpetrator who truly repents, submits to accountability, accepts consequences, and turns toward Jesus.
That is the scandal of grace.
Nobody gets to use grace as permission to keep sinning.
And nobody who truly comes to Jesus has sinned beyond His power to save.
You were never commanded to keep the darkness hidden just so everyone else could keep believing the house was full of light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE HAD EVERYTHING… UNTIL GOD ALLOWED HIM TO LOSE IT ALL
paragraphs: HE HAD EVERYTHING… UNTIL GOD ALLOWED HIM TO LOSE IT ALL

Job lost his wealth. His children died. His body broke. His wife despaired. Heaven seemed silent. But buried beneath the ashes was a truth Satan could not destroy: when everything God has given you disappears, God Himself is still there.
There is a kind of faith that is easy to talk about when the children are healthy.
When the bills are paid.
When your body still obeys you.
When the people you love are still one phone call away.
When the prayer was answered the way you hoped.
When you can look around your life and quietly conclude, God has been good to me.
But what happens when the phone rings…
and everything changes?
What happens when the doctor says the sentence you never wanted to hear?
When the person you thought would stay walks away?
When the business collapses?
When the funeral ends, everyone goes home, and you are left staring at a room that suddenly feels too quiet?
What happens when you pray…
and heaven does not immediately explain itself?
There is a terrifying question hiding inside the book of Job.
It is not merely, “Why do good people suffer?”
It is deeper.
More personal.
More uncomfortable.
If God stopped giving you the things you thank Him for… would God Himself still be enough?
That question is why Job is dangerous.
Because Job does not allow us to hide behind comfortable Christianity.
He had almost everything human beings spend their lives trying to obtain.
Family.
Wealth.
Influence.
Respect.
Security.
And Scripture introduces him not as a fraud secretly deserving his collapse, but as a man who was “blameless and upright,” one who feared God and turned away from evil.
Then the curtain is pulled back.
Job does not know what the reader knows.

There is a heavenly scene beyond his sight. Satan challenges the sincerity of Job's devotion. The accusation is essentially this: Job does not love God for God. Job loves God because God has made his life comfortable.
Take away the blessing, the accusation goes, and Job will curse the Blesser.
And suddenly the book becomes painfully relevant.
Because the accusation is no longer merely about Job.
It reaches toward us.
Would I still worship if the blessing disappeared?
Would I still call Jesus Lord if following Him cost me instead of benefiting me?
Do I love the hand of God…
or the God whose hand gives?

God permits Satan to strike what Job possesses, but Scripture is equally clear that Satan operates under boundaries established by God. Evil is not God's equal. Satan does not become sovereign for a chapter. He remains a creature under divine limitation.
Then Job's world begins collapsing.
A messenger arrives.
Before he can finish, another arrives.
Then another.
Then another.
It is almost cinematic in its cruelty.
Livestock gone.
Servants killed.
Resources destroyed.
And then comes the sentence no parent should ever have to hear.
His sons and daughters were together when catastrophe struck the house.
They were dead.
All of them.
Imagine the silence after that message.
Not the polished Job from a children's Bible illustration.
Imagine the father.
Ten children.
Ten voices he knew.
Ten histories.
Ten sets of memories.
Gone.
Job stands.
Tears his robe.
Shaves his head.
Falls to the ground.
And then he does something Satan said he would never do.
He worships.
Not because losing children does not hurt.
Not because righteous people are forbidden to grieve.
Not because Job somehow understood what had happened.
He worships while shattered.
The Hebrew of Job 1:21 preserves the terrible beauty of that moment:
יְהוָה נָתַן וַיהוָה לָקָח יְהִי שֵׁם יְהוָה מְבֹרָךְ
YHWH natan, wa-YHWH laqach; yehi shem YHWH mevorakh.
“The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.”
Look carefully at the order.
יְהוָה נָתַן — YHWH natan.
The LORD gave.
Job begins by remembering that what he possessed had first been gift.
His children were gifts.
His wealth was gift.
His breath was gift.
His years were gift.
And this is one of suffering's most painful revelations:
We eventually have to release everything we were never truly able to keep forever.
Job arrived naked.
Job knew he would leave naked.
Yet between those two moments he had been loved, blessed, entrusted, surrounded.
Now he is standing in the wreckage saying, in effect:
I do not understand You.
I am devastated.
I would never have chosen this.
But You are still God.
That is not denial.
That is worship with blood on it.
And maybe somebody reading this knows exactly what it means to worship wounded.
You still go to church, but there is an empty chair in your heart.
You still say “God is good,” but sometimes your voice trembles when you say it.
You still pray, but your prayers no longer sound impressive.
Some nights they are only:
“Jesus…”
“Help me.”
“I don't understand.”
“Please don't leave me here.”
Listen carefully.
Job teaches us that lament is not the opposite of faith.
Sometimes lament is what faith sounds like when it has been dragged through fire.
Job would ask questions.
He would grieve.
He would protest.
He would say things that reveal how deeply wounded and confused he had become.
The Bible does not airbrush him.
And that matters.
Biblical faith is not pretending pain does not hurt.
Faith does not require you to smile at the grave.
Jesus Himself wept.
Jesus Himself knew anguish.
Christianity does not offer us a Savior standing far away from suffering shouting instructions.
It gives us Jesus Christ crucified.
God the Son entered our suffering.
He was rejected.
Betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Pierced.
Crucified.
And here the story of Job begins pointing beyond Job.
Job was a righteous sufferer, but he was not sinless.
Jesus was.
Job suffered without knowing the heavenly conversation behind his trial.
Jesus went knowingly toward the cross.
Job longed for someone who could stand between himself and God.
The Gospel announces the Mediator.
Jesus Christ.
Job's agony gives voice to one of Scripture's great longings when he speaks of a living Redeemer:
וַאֲנִי יָדַעְתִּי גֹּאֲלִי חָי
Va'ani yadati go'ali chai.
“I know that my redeemer lives.”
That Hebrew word גֹּאֵל — go'el carries the idea of a redeemer, one who acts on behalf of another.

Within Job's own ancient context, we should not carelessly force every later theological detail into every syllable. But Christians cannot read the whole canon without hearing the breathtaking resonance.
Because the New Testament reveals the Redeemer Job could only long toward with limited sight.
Jesus.
The One who did not merely restore possessions.
The One who came to redeem people.
And He did it through what looked, for several horrifying hours, like absolute defeat.
Think about that.
On Friday, Jesus' followers watched their hope nailed to wood.
The Messiah appeared defeated.
His body was placed inside a tomb.
A stone was rolled into place.
To human eyes, the story looked finished.
But heaven was not finished writing.
Sunday came.
The stone moved.
The tomb opened.
Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead.
And suddenly the cross—the place of shame, violence, rejection and apparent catastrophe—became the place where God's redemptive purpose blazed before the world.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
God does not merely decorate our scandals.
In Christ, He redeems sinners.
He forgives the guilty.
He restores the repentant.
He gives new life to the spiritually dead.
He takes people whose histories seem irredeemable and writes grace where condemnation once appeared to have the final word.
But be careful.
That does not mean every Christian who loses money will become richer.
It does not mean every illness will be healed in this life.
It does not mean every marriage will be restored, every business resurrected, or every earthly tragedy reversed before we die.
Job cannot honestly be preached as a formula:
Suffer faithfully now and God will make you wealthy later.
That would cheapen the book.
Yes, Job's earthly fortunes were restored. Scripture tells us the LORD blessed Job's latter days greatly.
But his restoration does not turn his dead children into disposable numbers in an accounting equation.
New blessings do not make old grief unreal.
And the ultimate Christian hope is not “God will replace your stuff.”
Our hope is Christ.
Resurrection.
A kingdom that cannot be shaken.
Life with God beyond death.
A Redeemer who lives.
James later reaches back to Job and reminds suffering believers that they have heard of Job's endurance and have seen the Lord's outcome, because the Lord is compassionate and merciful.
Notice what Scripture remembers.
Not Job's bank account.
His endurance.
And God's compassion.
Maybe that is what you needed tonight.
Not another promise that everything will become easy by next Tuesday.
Not another motivational sentence pretending your wound is small.
Maybe you needed permission to say:
This hurts.
I don't understand God.
I have questions.
But I am still here.
Maybe your greatest act of worship right now is simply refusing to walk away.

There is another line associated with Job that is often quoted as though the Hebrew textual question behind it were simple. Job 13:15 has a well-known textual complexity involving לֹא (“not”) and the traditional reading לוֹ (“in Him/to Him”). That is precisely why we should resist building sentimental theology on an English slogan while ignoring the text's difficulty.
Job's faith is not powerful because he never wrestles.
It is powerful because he brings his wrestling before God.
He argues toward God.
Cries toward God.
Questions toward God.
Bleeds toward God.
And somehow keeps turning toward the One he cannot understand.
That may be one of the most honest descriptions of battered faith you will ever hear:
I don't understand You, God… but I have nowhere better to go.
Peter would one day say something similar to Jesus:
“Lord, to whom shall we go?”
There are seasons when mature faith sounds less like shouting victory from a mountaintop and more like whispering the name of Jesus from the floor.
And perhaps you are on that floor now.
You lost something.
Someone.
Maybe nobody knows.
You learned how to laugh in public while grieving privately.
Your Facebook photos look normal.
Your coworkers think you're okay.
Your family stopped asking.
But there are moments when one smell, one photograph, one song, one date on the calendar opens the wound again.
You wonder whether God saw what happened.
Job says:
Yes.
You wonder whether questions automatically make you faithless.
Job says:
No.
You wonder whether God can handle your grief.
The entire book of Job says:
Bring it.
But Job also warns us about something.
His friends arrive.
At first, they do something remarkably wise.
They sit with him.
Then they start talking.
And much of the trouble begins.
They want a clean explanation.
Surely Job did something.
Surely suffering can be reduced to a formula.
Surely if something terrible happened, somebody must be spiritually responsible in a way they can diagnose.
They defend their tidy theology while wounding the suffering man sitting in front of them.
Be careful when explaining another person's ashes.
Not every tragedy is God's punishment for a particular personal sin.
Jesus Himself rejected simplistic equations between individual tragedy and individual guilt.
Sometimes the holiest thing you can do beside a devastated person is not explain the mystery.
It is stay.
Cry.
Listen.
Pray.
Carry food.
Answer the phone at 2:13 in the morning.
Remind them that Christ has not abandoned them.
Job's friends wanted answers.
Job needed presence.
And eventually God speaks.
But fascinatingly, God does not hand Job the tidy explanation modern readers often want.
God reveals Himself.
Job wanted an answer.
He encountered the Answerer.
That distinction can change your life.
Because there will be questions you may carry for years.
Why that child?
Why that accident?
Why that betrayal?
Why that diagnosis?
Why did God permit it?
Why did the door close?
Why did I pray and still bury someone?
Christianity does not require us to invent explanations God has not revealed.
There is humility in saying:
I don't know.
But there is something we do know.
We know what God has revealed about Himself supremely in Jesus Christ.
At Calvary, we discover that God is not indifferent to suffering.
At Calvary, we discover the seriousness of sin.
At Calvary, we discover grace.
At the empty tomb, we discover that death does not receive the final sentence.
And suddenly Job's story becomes more than an ancient tragedy.
It becomes a mirror.
Maybe Satan's old accusation still exposes something in us:
Does this person love God… or only what God gives?
That question hurts.
Because sometimes we do not realize how much of our identity is built on gifts until a gift disappears.
A title.
A relationship.
A ministry.
Money.
Beauty.
Health.
Approval.
Followers.
A reputation.
Even religious usefulness.
Then God permits the scaffolding to shake, and underneath it we discover how much we were leaning on something other than Him.
Loss can expose idols we never knew had altars.
That does not mean every loss is God punishing idolatry.
It means suffering can reveal what comfort concealed.
And perhaps the deepest miracle in Job is not that his possessions eventually increased.
Perhaps the deeper miracle is that Satan tried to prove Job only loved God's gifts…
and suffering drove Job into an encounter with God Himself.
What if the enemy expected your pain to make you abandon Christ…
but your pain eventually drove your roots deeper into Him?
What if the season you would never choose becomes the season in which superficial Christianity finally dies?
What if your prayer changes from:
“God, give me what I need so I can trust You,”
to:
“God, even when I cannot understand what You are doing, keep me near Jesus.”
That is not passive resignation.
That is surrender.
And surrender is frightening because it removes our illusion of control.
But the Gospel was never:
Give Jesus enough obedience and He will guarantee you a painless life.
The Gospel is that sinners separated from God can be reconciled to Him through the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ.
We deserve judgment because of sin.
Christ bore sin's penalty for His people.
It is grace.
Received through faith in Christ.
So if suffering has exposed you…
come to Jesus.
If success made you forget Him…
come to Jesus.
If you have been pretending…
come to Jesus.
If you have sinned privately while performing Christianity publicly…
repent and come to Jesus.
If bitterness has been growing inside you…
bring it into His light.
You do not need to clean the ashes off before approaching Christ.
Come covered in them.
Come confused.
Come grieving.
Come ashamed.
Come exhausted.
But come.
Because the greatest thing Job ultimately needed was not twice as many possessions.
And the greatest thing you need is not the restoration of everything you lost.
You need God.
You need forgiveness.
You need reconciliation.
You need Christ.
Maybe you have spent years asking God to rewrite your circumstances while Jesus has been reaching for your heart.
Do not miss Him while staring at what disappeared.
Be honest.
Somebody reading beneath you may desperately need evidence that a wounded believer can keep walking with Jesus.
Do not turn vulnerability into performance.
Make it testimony.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The friend who stopped attending church.
The mother grieving quietly.
The father carrying financial pressure nobody sees.
The believer angry with God.
The person smiling online while falling apart offline.
You don't have to carry this alone.
There may come a night when the words “God is good” become much harder to say than they are today.
Keep Job close for that night.

Sharing biblical truth can be a meaningful way to glorify God when the motive is love rather than attention. You never know who is silently scrolling at midnight asking God for one reason not to walk away.
It doesn't.
Not because supporting a ministry purchases blessing.
It cannot.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel is free.
Use them.
Share them.
Put truth in front of people.
But never confuse the resource with the Source.
The library cannot save you.
This article cannot save you.
A ministry cannot save you.
Jesus Christ saves.
And that brings us back to the man sitting in ashes.
Job did not know chapter 42 was coming while he was living chapter 2.
Think about that.
We read Job knowing there is an ending.
Job suffered without turning the page.
He had to live inside the chapter where God had not explained Himself yet.
And maybe that is where you are.
You cannot see chapter 42.
You cannot see what God will do next.
You cannot see how this wound will be used.
You cannot see which prayers will be answered differently than expected.
You cannot see how Christ will sustain you tomorrow.
You only know that today hurts.
So do what Job did before he understood.
Fall before God.
Not because the loss was good.
Not because evil suddenly became beautiful.
Not because grief stopped hurting.
But because God remains God when life stops making sense.
And unlike Job at the beginning of his suffering, you stand on this side of a cross and an empty tomb.
You know something Job could not yet see with New Testament clarity.
Your Redeemer has come.
Your Redeemer was crucified.
Your Redeemer rose.
Your Redeemer lives.
And if you belong to Jesus Christ, your final chapter is not the grave.
So cry.
Ask questions.
Grieve honestly.
Repent where you need to repent.
Let people carry you when you cannot carry yourself.
But do not confuse God's silence with God's absence.
Do not mistake an unfinished chapter for the end of the story.
And do not let what you lost convince you that you have lost Christ.
Because sometimes faith does not look like standing triumphantly above the ashes.
Sometimes faith is sitting inside them…
tears running down your face…
with almost nothing left to say…
except His name.
Jesus.
And sometimes that is enough to begin again.
The enemy may touch what was placed in your hands, but he cannot erase the name of the Redeemer written across your eternity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY WAS JACOB’S HOUSEHOLD FILLED WITH RIVALRY?
paragraphs: WHY WAS JACOB’S HOUSEHOLD FILLED WITH RIVALRY?
The Family God Chose Was Messier Than You Remember—and the Scandal Reveals Something Stunning About Grace
There was tension at the dinner table long before Joseph ever received his famous coat.
Long before the pit.
Long before the blood on the garment.
Long before the brothers stood before their father and watched grief consume him.
Something had already gone terribly wrong inside Jacob’s home.

Two sisters were competing for the affection of the same husband. Children were being born into an emotional battlefield. One woman had the husband’s affection but desperately wanted children. The other had children but desperately wanted the husband’s affection. Servants became part of the struggle. Sons inherited tensions they did not create. Favoritism hardened into resentment.
And eventually resentment became hatred.
This was the household through which God chose to build the twelve tribes of Israel.
That should make us uncomfortable.
It should also give some of us hope.

Because if you have ever looked at your family and wondered, “How could God possibly bring anything holy out of this?” Jacob’s household answers with a story far more complicated—and far more beautiful—than a polished religious family portrait.
The Bible does not hide the scandal.
And that matters.
Scripture begins Jacob’s marriage story with one of the most painful deceptions in Genesis.
Jacob loved Rachel.
He agreed to work seven years for her, and Genesis says those years “seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her” (Genesis 29:20).
Then came the wedding.
The celebration.
The night.
And the morning.
“And it came to pass, that in the morning, behold, it was Leah” (Genesis 29:25).
You can almost feel Jacob’s shock in that word:
Behold.
Leah.
Jacob, the man who had once participated in deceiving his father Isaac and obtaining the blessing while disguised as Esau, now found himself deceived by Laban.
But Leah was not merely a plot device in Jacob’s consequences.
She was a woman.
A human being.
A daughter.
A sister.
And now a wife trapped inside a marriage where she knew another woman possessed the affection she wanted.
Jacob eventually married Rachel as well, and Genesis states the emotional reality without sanitizing it:
“And he loved also Rachel more than Leah” (Genesis 29:30).
Then comes one of the most heartbreaking sentences in the story:
“And when the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren” (Genesis 29:31).
The Hebrew deserves careful attention.
The text describes Leah with the word שְׂנוּאָה, senu’ah, from the Hebrew root שָׂנֵא, sane’, commonly associated with being hated.
But context matters.
Genesis has just told us Jacob loved Rachel “more than Leah.” The language therefore communicates Leah’s devastating position as the less-loved, rejected, or comparatively unloved wife.
God saw her.
That may be the first sentence someone reading this desperately needs today.
God saw her.
Not merely Jacob.
Not merely Rachel.
Not merely the woman who would bear children.
God saw the rejected woman behind the family drama.
And listen to what Leah named her first son.
Reuben.
רְאוּבֵן — Re’uven.
Leah said:
“Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me” (Genesis 29:32).
Read those final words again.
“Now therefore my husband will love me.”
There is the wound.
She had a baby in her arms, but her heart was still reaching for Jacob.
Then another son came.
Simeon.
And Leah said:
“Because the LORD hath heard that I was hated, he hath therefore given me this son also” (Genesis 29:33).
Another child.
Another hope.
Another attempt to interpret motherhood through the ache of rejection.
Then Levi was born.
“This time will my husband be joined unto me, because I have born him three sons” (Genesis 29:34).
Do you hear the progression?
Now he will love me.
Now maybe he will see me.
Now perhaps he will attach himself to me.
Some people spend years doing exactly this.
Maybe if I become successful, they will love me.
Maybe if I lose the weight.
Maybe if I earn more money.
Maybe if I become useful enough.
Maybe if I stop disappointing everyone.
Maybe if I become the perfect spouse.
Maybe if I serve harder at church.
Maybe if I never say no.
Maybe if I become impressive enough, spiritual enough, attractive enough, productive enough…
someone will finally choose me.
Leah’s story is ancient.
Her wound is not.
But then something happens when her fourth son is born.
She calls him Judah.
יְהוּדָה — Yehudah.
And this time she says:
“Now will I praise the LORD” (Genesis 29:35).
Something has shifted.
For three births, Jacob dominates the emotional horizon.
Will he love me?
Will he hear me?
Will he become attached to me?
Then Judah arrives.
And Leah looks upward.
“I will praise the LORD.”
Not because every problem disappeared.
Not because Jacob suddenly loved her the way she desired.
Not because Rachel ceased being Rachel.
But somewhere in the pain, Leah’s attention turned from desperately trying to earn the affection of a man toward praising the God who had seen her all along.
And through Judah…
Christ would come.
Do not rush past that.
The Messiah’s human genealogy would run through Judah.
Through Leah.
Through the woman who knew what it felt like to be less loved.
Matthew opens the New Testament by identifying Jesus as “the son of David, the son of Abraham” and traces the royal line through Judah (Matthew 1:1–3).
Revelation calls Christ “the Lion of the tribe of Juda” (Revelation 5:5).
The woman crying, “Maybe now my husband will love me,” could not see the generations ahead.
She could not see Bethlehem.
She could not see David.
She could not see the promised King.
She could not see the cross.
But God could.
This is grace working through a family that did not look graceful.
And the rivalry was far from over.
Rachel watched Leah bear children while she remained barren.
Genesis 30:1 says:
“And when Rachel saw that she bare Jacob no children, Rachel envied her sister.”
Then she cried to Jacob:
“Give me children, or else I die.”
Pain had become competition.
Her sister’s blessing felt like evidence of her own deprivation.
That is what comparison can do.
It can make someone else’s blessing feel like your punishment.
Their marriage becomes evidence against your singleness.
Their child becomes evidence against your infertility.
Their ministry becomes evidence against your calling.
Their promotion becomes evidence against your worth.
Their healing becomes evidence against your unanswered prayer.
Their happiness becomes something you quietly resent because you cannot understand why God has not given you the same thing.
Rachel had Jacob’s love.
Leah had children.
And each woman was staring at what the other possessed.
Neither rivalry nor manipulation could heal the deeper ache.

The household became increasingly complicated. Rachel gave her servant Bilhah to Jacob. Leah later gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob. Children became entangled with the sisters’ competition, and Genesis 30 even records an argument involving mandrakes.
The Bible does not present this household as a model for healthy marriage.
It records what happened.
That distinction matters.

The presence of polygamy in biblical narratives is not the same thing as divine endorsement of everything those narratives describe. Scripture repeatedly shows the grief and disorder surrounding rival wives and divided households.
The creation pattern reaches further back.
Genesis 2:24 declares that a man shall leave father and mother, cleave to his wife, and “they shall be one flesh.”
Jesus Himself returned to that creation text when teaching about marriage:
“For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh” (Matthew 19:5).
The Greek expression is:
σάρκα μίαν — sarka mian.
“One flesh.”
Jesus then says:
“Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh” (Matthew 19:6).
Jacob’s divided household shows us in narrative form how devastating divided affection can become.
But another wound was developing.
Favoritism.
Jacob, who grew up in a household where Isaac favored Esau while Rebekah favored Jacob (Genesis 25:28), eventually reproduced favoritism in his own family.
That is one of the frightening realities of generational dysfunction.
What wounded us can become what we repeat.
Not inevitably.
Not because change is impossible.
But because unexamined wounds have a way of becoming inherited patterns.
Genesis 37:3 says:
“Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children.”
There it is again.
More.
Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.
Then Jacob loved Joseph more than his other children.
And the consequences were immediate:
“And when his brethren saw that their father loved him more than all his brethren, they hated him, and could not speak peaceably unto him” (Genesis 37:4).
Favoritism became resentment.
Resentment became hatred.
Hatred eventually stood beside a pit while Joseph cried for mercy.
Years later, the brothers remembered his anguish:
“We saw the anguish of his soul, when he besought us, and we would not hear” (Genesis 42:21).
Imagine that scene.
Your brother is begging.
You hear him.
And you walk away.
They sold Joseph.
Then they took his garment, dipped it in blood, and allowed their father to believe his beloved son had been killed.
The deceiver had been deceived again.
The family was bleeding internally.
And if Genesis ended there, Jacob’s household would simply be another tragedy about what happens when jealousy, favoritism, deception, and unresolved wounds are allowed to grow.
But God was not finished.
That sentence belongs over more lives than we realize.
God was not finished.
Joseph went from the pit to slavery.
From slavery to Potiphar’s house.
From false accusation to prison.
From prison to Pharaoh’s court.
From humiliation to authority.
And then famine came.
The same brothers who had sold him eventually stood before him needing food.
Joseph recognized them.
They did not recognize him.
Think about the power of that moment.
The people responsible for one of the deepest wounds of his life were standing within his reach.
Joseph possessed authority now.
He could make them hurt.
He could make them afraid.
He could finally settle the account.
And after a long, emotionally complex process in which the character of the brothers—especially Judah—was tested, Joseph revealed himself.
Genesis 45:3 records the words:
“I am Joseph.”
Imagine the silence.
The brother you betrayed is alive.
The slave became ruler.
The victim now has power.
And you are standing before him.
But Joseph does something astonishing.
He tells them to come near.
“Come near to me, I pray you” (Genesis 45:4).
Near.
Not because their sin was imaginary.
Not because selling him was acceptable.
Not because betrayal no longer mattered.
Joseph names what they did:
“I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt.”
Grace does not require pretending evil was good.
Forgiveness does not rewrite sin into innocence.
But God can write redemption through what human beings intended for destruction.
Joseph eventually tells them:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good” (Genesis 50:20).
That verse is sometimes used too casually.
Joseph was not saying evil is good.
He called their intention evil.
The breathtaking truth is that their evil intention was not powerful enough to overthrow God’s providential purpose.
They meant evil.
God meant good.
The wound was real.
God was greater.
And that brings us to Jesus.
Because Joseph’s story can remind Christians of a much greater pattern that reaches its fulfillment not in Joseph, but in Christ.
Jesus was rejected.
Betrayed.
Sold.
Condemned.
Humiliated.
Crucified.
Human beings intended evil against the sinless Son of God.
Yet the cross became the place where God accomplished redemption.
Peter preached that Jesus was delivered according to “the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God,” while also holding His killers morally responsible for crucifying Him (Acts 2:23).
Human wickedness did not defeat God’s saving purpose.
At Calvary, what looked like catastrophe became the stage upon which Christ bore sin and accomplished redemption.
This is not merely the story of Jacob’s dysfunctional family.
It is the story of a God whose purposes are not defeated by dysfunctional people.
And maybe that is why this story is reaching you right now.
Maybe your family has names nobody mentions anymore.
Maybe your childhood taught you to compete for affection.
Maybe your father had a favorite.
Maybe your mother compared you with your sibling.
Maybe somebody else always seemed more loved, more celebrated, more beautiful, more successful.
Maybe you became the responsible one.
The invisible one.
The angry one.
The achiever.
The peacemaker.
The runaway.
Maybe you are still trying to earn today what somebody failed to give you years ago.
And perhaps, without realizing it, you have started repeating some of the very patterns that hurt you.
Jacob did.
But inherited dysfunction does not have to become your destiny.
The Gospel announces something stronger than your family history.
In Christ, repentance is possible.
Forgiveness is possible.
A new identity is possible.
Reconciliation, where truth and wisdom allow it, is possible.
Transformation is possible.
You are not saved because you came from the right family.
You are not disqualified because you came from the wrong one.
The family line through which Jesus entered the world was filled with complicated people and painful stories.
Yet Christ came.
And He did not come merely to make dysfunctional people slightly more functional.
He came to save sinners.
At the cross, Jesus bore the judgment sin deserves.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith receives something no human family can manufacture:
grace.
Maybe you have spent your entire life saying what Leah’s heart was saying:
Now they will love me.
Maybe after this achievement.
After this relationship.
After this promotion.
After this transformation.
After I prove myself.
But Jesus does not stand at the end of an exhausting performance ladder waiting for you to become impressive enough.
The Gospel confronts our sin, strips away our self-salvation projects, and calls us to come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Then let His grace begin changing the places where pain taught you to sin.
Maybe you became controlling because chaos terrified you.
Maybe jealousy has quietly poisoned relationships.
Maybe you punish people for wounds they did not create.
Maybe you show favoritism.
Maybe you manipulate affection.
Maybe you keep score.
Maybe bitterness has become so familiar that you call it discernment.
Bring it into the light.
Jesus does not merely expose wounds to humiliate us.
He exposes sin so that we can repent, and He meets repentant sinners with grace.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
No more hiding.
No more pretending your family history gives sin permission to rule your future.
You do not owe strangers the details.
But sometimes three honest words can become the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.

And if someone came to mind while you were reading this—not someone you want to shame, but someone who desperately needs to know that family dysfunction is not stronger than the grace of Christ—send this to them.
Save it too.
Because family wounds have a way of returning on difficult days, and you may need to remember again that the Gospel gives you something stronger than the patterns you inherited.
Salvation and God’s grace cannot be bought.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical way believers freely participate in helping biblical truth reach more people.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who stopped going to church.
Invite the believer who is barely holding on.
Invite the person who thinks they have sinned too much.
Invite the skeptic who has only ever seen Christianity represented by polished people pretending they have never bled.
Because Jacob’s family was not polished.
Leah was hurting.
Rachel was jealous.
Jacob played favorites.
Brothers became enemies.
Joseph was betrayed.
Judah had his own scandals.
And still…
God kept writing.
Generation after generation.
Until another Son from the line of Judah appeared.
Jesus Christ.
The One Jacob’s family could never produce by moral perfection.
The One Leah could never earn through rejection.
The One Judah’s descendants desperately needed.
The One Joseph’s story could only faintly anticipate.
Jesus.
And this is where every broken family must ultimately look.
Not toward pretending the past never happened.
Not toward calling evil good.
Not toward endlessly blaming our parents.
Not toward becoming prisoners of what was done to us.
Toward Christ.
The crucified and risen King.
The Savior who forgives sinners and makes them new.
The Lord who can teach a rejected person to stop begging human beings for an identity.
The Lord who can teach a jealous heart to rejoice when somebody else is blessed.
The Lord who can teach parents to repent of favoritism.
The Lord who can teach siblings to put down weapons they have carried since childhood.
The Lord who can interrupt patterns that have survived for generations.
Maybe your family gave you wounds.
Do not let those wounds become instructions.
Maybe somebody taught you rivalry.
Jesus can teach you love.
Maybe somebody taught you rejection.
Jesus can anchor your identity in Him.
Maybe somebody taught you deception.
Jesus calls you into truth.
Maybe somebody taught you bitterness.
Jesus calls you toward forgiveness.
Maybe somebody taught you to hide.
Jesus calls you into the light.
Jacob’s household tells us something uncomfortable about human beings:
Broken people can create broken homes.
But the Gospel tells us something infinitely greater about God:
Brokenness does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
And if you cannot find any other words:
“Pray for me.”
Someone reading your comment may realize they are not fighting alone.
And never forget the strange, beautiful lesson hidden inside Jacob’s troubled household:
Leah thought she needed Jacob to choose her before her story could matter.
Joseph’s brothers thought a pit could erase his future.
Jacob thought blood on a garment meant the story was over.
They were all looking at one chapter.
God was still holding the pen.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the final sentence when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE PATTERN BEHIND LOSING YOUR PASSION FOR GOD: You Rarely Wake Up One Morning and Stop Loving Jesus—It Usually Dies One Small Compromise at a Time
paragraphs:
THE PATTERN BEHIND LOSING YOUR PASSION FOR GOD: You Rarely Wake Up One Morning and Stop Loving Jesus—It Usually Dies One Small Compromise at a Time
You still believe. You still know the verses. You may even still go to church. But somewhere between the person who once couldn't get enough of God and the person staring back at you today… something went cold. And Jesus warned us this could happen.
There was a time when you didn't have to force yourself to pray.
Remember?
You actually wanted to.
There was a time when opening your Bible didn't feel like another responsibility waiting to be completed.
You were hungry.
One verse could wreck you.
One worship song could bring tears to your eyes.
One reminder of the cross could make everything else in your life suddenly seem small.
You talked to Jesus in the car.
You whispered His name before falling asleep.
You thought about Him when nobody was watching.
You wanted your friends to know Him.
You hated the thought of disappointing Him—not because you were terrified He would stop loving you, but because you were beginning to understand just how much He had loved you first.
Then something changed.
Not necessarily dramatically.
That's what makes this frightening.
There may have been no announcement.
No moment when you stood before God and said, "I don't want You anymore."
Maybe you never rejected Jesus at all.
You simply became busy.
Then distracted.
Then spiritually tired.
Prayer became shorter.
Scripture became occasional.
Conviction became inconvenient.
Things that once bothered your conscience slowly became easier to tolerate.
You still loved God…
at least you kept telling yourself you did.
But somehow you could spend two hours consuming entertainment and feel irritated after ten minutes alone with Him.
You could scroll when exhausted.
Watch another episode when exhausted.
Talk for an hour about something that excited you when exhausted.
But when it came time to pray?
Suddenly you were too tired.
And perhaps the most dangerous part was that your Christian life continued functioning well enough that almost nobody noticed.
Maybe even you didn't.
Jesus said something terrifyingly precise:
“Because lawlessness will be increased, the love of many will grow cold.” — Matthew 24:12
The Greek is striking:
“διὰ τὸ πληθυνθῆναι τὴν ἀνομίαν, ψυγήσεται ἡ ἀγάπη τῶν πολλῶν.”
The crucial word is ψυγήσεται—psychēsetai.
“Will grow cold.”
Not necessarily disappear overnight.
Grow cold.
And ἀγάπη—agapē—is love.
Jesus was describing a world in which increasing ἀνομία—anomia, lawlessness—would be accompanied by the chilling of love.
Read that again slowly.
Love can grow cold.
A heart that once burned can cool.
And perhaps that explains something you have been unable to put into words.
You didn't necessarily stop believing in God.
You stopped burning for Him.
And spiritual coldness usually has a pattern.
It begins when something else starts receiving what once belonged to God.
Your attention.
Your affection.
Your obedience.
Your wonder.
Your time.
Your secret thoughts.
Your hunger.
At first, the replacement doesn't have to look evil.
That's important.
Sometimes what steals your passion for God isn't obvious wickedness.
Sometimes it's endless distraction.
Ambition.
Comfort.
Entertainment.
Romance.
Work.
Approval.
Money.
Success.
Ministry itself.
Even good things become dangerous when they begin occupying the throne reserved for the Giver.
And slowly, almost invisibly, your soul becomes accustomed to living on crumbs while sitting feet away from the Bread of Life.
You tell yourself you're just busy.
But days become weeks.
Weeks become months.
And eventually you can remember the person you used to be with God more clearly than you recognize the person you've become.
That should disturb us.
But it should not make us despair.
Because Scripture shows us that God has confronted this pattern before.
Through Jeremiah, God spoke to a people who had wandered:
“I remember the devotion of your youth, your love as a bride, how you followed Me in the wilderness…”
Jeremiah 2:2.
The Hebrew contains this beautiful expression:
אַהֲבַת כְּלוּלֹתָיִךְ
ahavat kelulotayikh—
the love associated with your betrothal, your bridal love.
God remembered when His people followed Him into the wilderness.
But they wandered.
They exchanged the glory of God for substitutes that could never satisfy them.
And that is still the anatomy of spiritual drift.
We exchange.
We rarely decide, “Today I will destroy my relationship with God.”
We trade pieces of it.
Five minutes here.
One compromise there.
One conviction ignored.
One prayer postponed.
One sin defended.
One warning dismissed.
One appetite continually fed.
One resentment protected.
One secret nobody knows about.
And every trade seems too small to matter.
Until one day you realize you traded a fire for ashes.
Maybe you're reading this and thinking:
That's me.
I remember who I was.
I remember wanting Jesus.
I remember praying because I couldn't imagine not praying.
I remember worshipping when nobody was watching.
I remember conviction.
I remember tenderness.
I remember tears.
Now?
You feel numb.
And because you feel numb, perhaps you've concluded that God must be far away.
But before you accuse God of moving, ask yourself a painful question:
Who moved?
There is a moment in Revelation 2 that every serious Christian should wrestle with.
Jesus speaks to the church in Ephesus.
These weren't people who had abandoned Christian activity.
They had works.
Endurance.
Discernment.
They had resisted false teachers.
From the outside, this could look like a strong church.
And yet Jesus says:
“But I have this against you, that you have abandoned the love you had at first.”
Then comes the remedy:
“Remember therefore from where you have fallen; repent, and do the works you did at first.”
Notice the movement.
Remember.
Repent.
Return.
Jesus doesn't tell them to manufacture goosebumps.
He doesn't tell them to wait for a worship song powerful enough to make them emotional again.
He calls them to remember where they have fallen from, repent, and return to faithful action.
That changes everything.
Because maybe you've been waiting to feel passionate before you start pursuing God again.
What if obedience comes first?
What if you open the Bible while your emotions are still cold?
What if you kneel while prayer still feels difficult?
What if you confess the sin before you feel sufficiently sorry?
What if you delete what keeps pulling you back?
What if you forgive?
What if you return to church?
What if you tell another believer the truth about what has been happening inside you?
What if instead of waiting for the fire…
you start bringing God the wood?
Because passion for God isn't sustained by chasing spiritual emotion.
It grows from seeing Christ clearly, abiding in Him, believing His Gospel, obeying His Word, walking by His Spirit, and continually returning to the astonishing reality of what Jesus has done.
Look at the cross again.
Not the decorative cross around someone's neck.
Not the polished cross hanging inside a sanctuary.
Look at that cross.
The Son of God.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
Bearing sin.
The innocent One dying for the guilty.
Jesus did not go to Calvary because humanity was impressive.
He went because humanity was lost.
Your salvation was never the story of a decent person becoming slightly better.
The Gospel is far more scandalous than that.
We sinned.
We rebelled.
We wandered.
We loved darkness.
We could not rescue ourselves.
And God came after us.
Jesus Christ lived the righteous life we failed to live, gave Himself for sinners, died, was buried, and rose victorious.
Grace is not God pretending sin doesn't matter.
The cross proves how terribly sin matters.
Grace is God doing for sinners what sinners could never do for themselves.
That is why repentance isn't punishment.
It's an invitation home.
And maybe that's what you need right now.
Not another motivational Christian quote.
Home.
Maybe your prayer life has collapsed.
Come home.
Maybe pornography has quietly hollowed out your spiritual appetite.
Come home.
Maybe bitterness has been sitting in your chest so long that you have started calling it discernment.
Come home.
Maybe success became your god.
Come home.
Maybe you've been sleeping with someone you know you shouldn't.
Come home.
Maybe money owns more of your heart than Jesus does.
Come home.
Maybe nobody knows what you're doing behind closed doors.
Come home.
Maybe you're not living in obvious scandal at all.
Maybe you're simply spiritually exhausted and distracted and you've forgotten how to sit quietly in the presence of God.
Come home.
But don't confuse “come home” with “God doesn't care how you live.”
Jesus did not die merely to make us comfortable while we remain enslaved to what destroys us.
Grace forgives.
Grace also transforms.
The Christ who receives sinners calls sinners to follow Him.
And this is where the enemy has deceived many people.
He tells the rebellious person, “God doesn't care.”
Then when the rebellious person finally wakes up, he changes the message:
“God could never want you now.”
Same liar.
Different lie.
The Gospel destroys both.
Your sin matters.
And Christ's blood is sufficient.
Repentance matters.
And mercy is real.
Holiness matters.
And you are not saved by earning God's affection.
Jesus is not waiting for you to become impressive enough to approach Him.
Remember the prodigal son.
The son rehearsed his confession and headed home.
But while he was still far away, his father saw him.
Then one of the most breathtaking pictures of grace in Scripture unfolds.
The father was moved with compassion.
He ran.
He embraced him.
He kissed him.
The Greek text of Luke 15:20 intensifies the scene with κατεφίλησεν—katephilēsen—he kissed him affectionately.
The son came home carrying the smell of his rebellion.
The father ran toward him anyway.
That doesn't make rebellion beautiful.
It makes mercy breathtaking.
And if you have wandered from God, please understand this:
Satan wants you staring at the pigpen until you forget there is a Father to run home to.
Get up.
Go home.
Confess what happened.
Stop negotiating with the thing that's killing your love for Christ.
Stop calling bondage “just something I'm struggling with” if you've secretly decided to protect it forever.
Bring it into the light.
Repent.
And if you've fallen again?
Repent again.
Not casually.
Not presuming upon grace.
But genuinely.
Come back to Jesus.
Again.
Again.
Again.
Not because sin is insignificant, but because Christ is a greater Savior than you imagined.
David knew what it meant for sin to devastate the inner life.
After the horror of his sin was exposed, Psalm 51 records one of Scripture's most desperate prayers of repentance.
And listen to what David asks:
הָשִׁיבָה לִּי שְׂשׂוֹן יִשְׁעֶךָ
Hashivah li seson yishecha.
“Restore to me the joy of Your salvation.”
That first word matters.
הָשִׁיבָה — hashivah.
Restore.
Bring back.
David did not ask God to help him fake enthusiasm.
He asked for restoration.
And notice whose salvation it is.
“Your salvation.”
Not David's achievement.
God's salvation.
That means if your heart has grown cold, the answer isn't pretending you're still on fire.
It's admitting you're cold enough to need God to rekindle what you cannot manufacture.
Maybe your most honest prayer tonight isn't impressive.
Maybe it's simply:
“Jesus, I miss You.”
Maybe:
“Jesus, I don't even know when I changed.”
Maybe:
“Lord, I have wanted Your gifts more than You.”
Maybe:
“I've been pretending.”
Maybe:
“I don't feel what I used to feel, but I want to want You again.”
Pray it.
God is not intimidated by an honest prayer.
But don't stop at emotion.
Ask Him to expose what has been cooling your love.
Then be willing to surrender it.
Because we cannot repeatedly feed what numbs us and then wonder why we're spiritually numb.
We cannot continually rehearse bitterness and wonder why worship feels empty.
We cannot feast on lust all week and wonder why holiness feels tasteless.
We cannot give every spare second to noise and wonder why we cannot hear the whisper of Scripture in our minds.
We cannot treat Jesus like an emergency contact and expect intimacy to flourish.
A relationship starved of attention will feel distant.
Jesus said in John 15:
“Abide in Me.”
Not visit occasionally.
Abide.
Remain.
Stay.
Make your home in Christ.
The Christian life isn't primarily about having one dramatic encounter with Jesus twenty years ago.
It's about continuing with Him today.
And tomorrow.
And when life hurts.
And when prayer feels glorious.
And when prayer feels ordinary.
And when you're celebrated.
And when you're forgotten.
And when you understand what God is doing.
And when heaven seems silent.
Faithfulness is not proved only by how loudly you worship when you feel God.
Sometimes faithfulness looks like opening Scripture with tears in your eyes and saying:
“Jesus, I'm still here.”
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear something else.
Your loss of emotional intensity does not automatically mean you've abandoned God.
Human beings get tired.
We grieve.
We suffer.
We pass through seasons where emotions change.
Christian maturity should not be measured solely by whether every prayer gives you chills.
There is a difference between emotional dryness and deliberate spiritual drift.
Sometimes deep faith is quiet.
Sometimes mature love feels less like fireworks and more like staying.
The question isn't merely:
“Do I feel what I used to feel?”
Ask:
“Am I still following Jesus?”
“Am I abiding in His Word?”
“Am I obeying what He has shown me?”
“Am I confessing sin rather than protecting it?”
“Do I still desire Christ Himself?”
“Am I becoming more like Him?”
And when the answer exposes something painful…
don't hide.
That's where grace begins doing surgery.
You don't need to impress Jesus.
You need Jesus.
That is the pattern behind losing passion for God.
Attention drifts.
Compromise enters.
Conviction gets negotiated.
Sin becomes familiar.
Prayer becomes optional.
Scripture becomes distant.
Jesus becomes peripheral.
And eventually the heart grows cold.
But there is another pattern.
Remember.
Repent.
Return.
Abide.
Obey.
Receive grace.
Walk with Jesus again.
The way back isn't mysterious.
It may be painful.
But it isn't hidden.
Talk to God now.
Not later.
Now.
Tell Him the truth.
And then tell someone else if you need accountability.
And if God has been restoring you already, tell us what He has done. Your testimony may become the exact thing another wounded believer needs to read tonight.
Don't underestimate that comment.
Somebody else may see it and realize they're not the only one fighting.
Somebody may pray for you.
Somebody may finally confess what they've been hiding because you were brave enough to go first.
This is what Christian community should look like—not a museum full of people pretending they never struggled, but redeemed sinners pointing one another toward Jesus.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
Not because clicking “share” proves you're a better Christian. It doesn't.
But if this message is biblically faithful and you believe someone in your circle needs to return to Jesus, sharing it can be one simple act of witness.
Think about the person who has stopped going to church.
The friend whose faith has quietly gone cold.
The teenager drowning in distractions.
The father carrying secret shame.
The mother spiritually exhausted from holding everybody together.
The Christian who looks perfectly fine online but cries when nobody is looking.
Send it privately if publicly tagging them would embarrass them.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite the lukewarm.
Invite seekers.
Even invite the person who doesn't believe yet.
Let them encounter the Gospel.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel is free.

But supporting Gospel-centered work can help that work continue reaching people, creating biblical resources, strengthening believers, and putting Christ-centered truth in front of people who desperately need it.
If you want to glorify God through your resources, Scripture gives us a far bigger vision than merely clicking a button: steward what He has entrusted to you for His purposes.
And there is something else we want you to know.
Because we don't simply want you inspired for five minutes.
We want you discipled.
Grounded.
Sharpened.
Healed by truth.
Corrected by Scripture.
Strengthened in prayer.
Anchored in the Gospel.
And increasingly transformed into the likeness of Jesus Christ.
Come back to Jesus.
Not to a page.
Not to a brand.
Not to merchandise.
Not to religious performance.
To Jesus.
The One who was crucified for sinners.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who still receives repentant people.
The One who knows exactly how cold your heart has become and is not shocked by what He finds.
The One who can restore the joy you've lost.
Maybe that's why you kept reading.
Maybe beneath all the distractions, compromises, disappointment, exhaustion, shame, and spiritual numbness…
there is still a tiny ache.
A memory.
A whisper inside you saying:
“I want Him again.”
Don't despise that ache.
Take it to Christ.
The story does not have to end with the fire going out.
Peter failed spectacularly and Jesus restored him.
Thomas doubted and Jesus met him.
The prodigal wandered and came home.
David fell into devastating sin and cried out for a clean heart.
The cross itself looked like the darkest scandal imaginable until resurrection morning revealed that God was writing redemption through what looked like defeat.
And maybe your chapter right now is ugly.
Maybe there are paragraphs you wish you could erase.
Maybe there are pages you are ashamed anybody could ever read.
But the Gospel has never been about pretending the scandal didn't happen.
It is about what Jesus does with sinners who surrender their stories to Him.
Repent.
Come home.
Let Him restore what sin damaged.
Let Him expose what distraction buried.
Let Him become precious to you again.
Then tomorrow…
come back again.
Open His Word.
Pray.
Obey.
Abide.
And the day after that?
Again.
Not chasing yesterday's spiritual emotion.
Following today's living Christ.
If this pierced you, comment before you leave.
Share it before the urgency fades.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy isn't discovering that your heart has grown cold.
Perhaps the greater tragedy would be discovering it…
hearing Jesus call you home…
and choosing to remain where you are.
You may remember the moment your fire started dying—but by the grace of Jesus Christ, that does not have to be the final sentence of your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN CHRISTIANS HAVE ANXIETY? YES—AND WHAT JESUS SAYS NEXT MAY CHANGE THE WAY YOU SEE YOURSELF
paragraphs: CAN CHRISTIANS HAVE ANXIETY? YES—AND WHAT JESUS SAYS NEXT MAY CHANGE THE WAY YOU SEE YOURSELF

You can love Jesus deeply and still feel your chest tighten at 2:17 in the morning. Anxiety does not automatically mean your faith is fake. But Jesus loves you too much to leave fear sitting on the throne of your heart.
There is a particular kind of loneliness that happens when everyone thinks you are strong.
You know how to smile at church.
You know when to say, “God is good.”
You know the verses.
You know the worship songs.
You know how to encourage somebody else when their world is collapsing.
And yet there are nights when you lie in bed staring into the darkness while your mind rehearses disasters that have not happened.
What if I lose my job?
What if the test result is bad?
What if my marriage never heals?
What if my child walks away from God?
What if I cannot pay this?
What if they leave?
What if I fail?
What if tomorrow destroys everything I am trying to hold together today?
Your body is exhausted, but your mind refuses to sleep.
Your heart beats harder.
You pray.
You try to surrender it.
Five minutes later, you are carrying it again.
Then something even heavier enters the room.
Shame.
Because now you are not merely anxious.
You are anxious about being anxious.

You remember Jesus telling His disciples not to worry. You remember Paul saying not to be anxious about anything. And suddenly the frightened believer begins conducting a spiritual trial against himself.
“If I really trusted God, would I feel this way?”
“If my faith were stronger, would I still be struggling?”
“Is God disappointed in me?”
“Can a real Christian even have anxiety?”
Please stay with me.
Because the answer matters.
And before this is over, we need to confront not only what anxiety whispers about tomorrow, but what shame has been whispering about your relationship with God.
Yes.
Christians can experience anxiety.
Deeply committed Christians can experience anxiety.

People who genuinely love Jesus can experience fear, distress, overwhelming circumstances, sleepless nights, physical symptoms, and seasons when their thoughts feel frighteningly difficult to control.
But Scripture does not therefore tell us that anxiety should become our master, identity, theology, or permanent residence.
There is a difference between experiencing anxiety and enthroning anxiety.
There is a difference between being attacked by fear and surrendering your life to fear.
There is a difference between a frightened nervous system and a faithless heart.
And there is a difference between Jesus correcting our anxious thinking and Jesus condemning an anxious person.
That distinction changes everything.
When Jesus speaks about worry in Matthew 6, the Greek text says:
“μὴ μεριμνᾶτε τῇ ψυχῇ ὑμῶν…”
Mē merimnate tē psychē hymōn…
“Do not be anxious/worried about your life…”
The key word is related to μεριμνάω — merimnaō, a verb used for being anxious, concerned, or occupied with care.
Jesus is speaking about the consuming worry surrounding ordinary human needs—food, drink, clothing, tomorrow.
But notice what Jesus does next.
He does not humiliate frightened people.
He redirects their vision.
He tells them to look at birds.
Imagine that.

The Son of God is addressing people living in a world without modern insurance systems, refrigerators, retirement accounts, instant banking, modern medicine, or guaranteed salaries—and He points toward the sky.
Look.
The birds do not control tomorrow.
Yet your heavenly Father feeds them.
Then comes the question that anxiety desperately needs to hear:
Are you not worth much more than they are?
Jesus moves the discussion from circumstances to Fatherhood.
That is crucial.
Because anxiety says, “Everything depends on you.”
Jesus says, “You have a Father.”
Anxiety says, “Predict everything.”
Jesus says, “Look at your Father.”
Anxiety says, “Control tomorrow.”
Jesus says, “Seek first the kingdom of God.”
Anxiety says, “What if?”
Jesus keeps bringing us back to “Who?”
Who feeds the birds?
Who clothes the grass?
Who knows what you need?
Who holds tomorrow?
Who calls you His own?
The biblical answer to anxiety is not pretending frightening circumstances do not exist.
It is learning that frightening circumstances do not have the final word.
And perhaps that is why your anxiety has been so exhausting.
You have been trying to carry a tomorrow that God never gave you permission to carry today.
You keep mentally traveling into a future where God has not abandoned you—but in your imagination, you arrive there without Him.
