Before the sons of Jacob became names remembered for generations, their mothers were living through rivalry, infertility, jealousy, sexual competition, unequal affection, servitude, and an aching hunger to be seen.
Genesis does not hide any of it.
And that may be one of the reasons this story can speak so powerfully to people whose own families do not resemble stained-glass windows.
Maybe your family has secrets.
Maybe somebody cheated.
Maybe your parents played favorites.
Maybe children became weapons in adult conflict.
Maybe affection was withheld.
Maybe you spent years trying to earn the love someone freely gave to somebody else.
Maybe your family photographs look peaceful while the memories behind them are anything but peaceful.
Then Jacob's household may feel disturbingly familiar.
And here is the truth that should keep you reading:
God does not call the dysfunction good.
But He is so sovereign, so faithful, and so overflowing with redemptive mercy that human sin cannot force Him to surrender His promises.
Jacob himself entered this chapter carrying a complicated history.
He had deceived his father Isaac and obtained the blessing associated with Esau. Then, after fleeing, Jacob arrived among his mother's relatives and encountered Rachel. Genesis 29:18 says simply:
“Jacob loved Rachel.”
The Hebrew is direct:

וַיֶּאֱהַב יַעֲקֹב אֶת־רָחֵל
Vayye'ehav Ya'aqov et-Rachel.
Jacob loved Rachel.

He agreed to serve Laban seven years for her, and Genesis gives us one of Scripture's most beautiful descriptions of romantic devotion: those years seemed like only a few days to Jacob because of his love for Rachel.
It sounds like the beginning of a love story.
Then comes the wedding.
The feast.
The night.
And the morning.
Genesis 29:25 records Jacob's shock:
וַיְהִי בַבֹּקֶר וְהִנֵּה־הִוא לֵאָה
Vayehi vabboqer vehinneh-hi Le'ah.
“And it came to pass in the morning, behold, it was Leah.”
Leah.
Jacob, the man whose story had already been marked by deception, had now been deceived by Laban.
But do not become so fascinated with the irony that you forget the woman standing inside it.
Leah was not merely a plot twist.
She was a woman.

Whatever responsibility the surrounding culture and Laban's scheme placed upon her, the biblical narrative leaves us staring at a devastating reality: she entered a marriage in which her husband loved her sister more.
Jacob subsequently received Rachel as his wife as well and served Laban another seven years.
Now two sisters were married to the same man.
This is where we need biblical honesty.
The Bible's description of polygamy is not the same thing as God's endorsement of polygamy.

Genesis has already presented the foundational marriage pattern in Genesis 2:24: a man is joined to his wife and the two become “one flesh.” Jesus Himself returns to that creation pattern in Matthew 19:4–6.
And whenever Scripture shows us polygamous households, the consequences are frequently painful.
Jacob's household is no exception.
Genesis 29:30 tells us Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.
Then Scripture says something breathtaking:
וַיַּרְא יְהוָה כִּי־שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה
Vayyar YHWH ki-senu'ah Le'ah.
“The LORD saw that Leah was hated/unloved.”
The Hebrew word שְׂנוּאָה — senu'ah can carry the sense of being hated, but within a comparison of affection it can also communicate being less loved or unloved.
Either way, do not miss the first words.
The LORD saw.
Jacob's eyes were fixed on Rachel.
God's eyes were on Leah.
That sentence belongs to every person who has ever wondered whether heaven noticed what rejection was doing to them.
God saw Leah.
He saw the woman waking beside a husband whose heart belonged elsewhere.
He saw the comparisons.
He saw the humiliation.
He saw what nobody could repair for her.
And He opened her womb.
Then Leah gave birth to Reuben.
Listen to what she said:
“Because the LORD has looked upon my affliction; for now my husband will love me.”
There it is.
The cry beneath the child.
Maybe now he will love me.
She named another son Simeon because the LORD had heard that she was unloved.
Then came Levi.
And Leah said, in effect, Now this time my husband will become attached to me, because I have borne him three sons.
Can you hear the heartbreak?
One son.
Maybe now.
Another son.
Maybe now.
Another son.
Surely now.
How many people are still living like Leah?
If I become prettier, maybe he will love me.
If I earn more, maybe they will respect me.
If I become indispensable, maybe they will stop leaving.
If I serve harder at church, maybe God will finally be pleased with me.
If I get enough followers, enough money, enough accomplishments, enough applause, enough attention...
Maybe then I will finally feel chosen.
That is an exhausting way to live.
Then something changes when Judah is born.
Leah says:
הַפַּעַם אוֹדֶה אֶת־יְהוָה
Happa'am odeh et-YHWH.
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
This time.
For three births, Jacob's affection dominates the language.
Then Judah comes, and Leah's eyes rise higher.
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
Jacob may still prefer Rachel.
The marriage has not suddenly become uncomplicated.
But Leah's words have shifted from perhaps my husband will love me to I will praise the LORD.
And then history moves in a direction Leah could never have imagined.
Judah's line ultimately leads to David.
And ultimately, according to the New Testament genealogies and the messianic story of Scripture, to Jesus Christ.
The rejected woman's son becomes part of the human ancestry through which the Messiah enters history.
Think about that.
Leah was trying to become valuable enough for Jacob to love her.
God was weaving her into a story that would ultimately point toward the One whose love cannot be purchased by human performance.
But Rachel was hurting too.
Being loved did not eliminate her pain.
Genesis 30 opens with Rachel seeing that she had borne Jacob no children. Envy takes hold of her, and she cries to Jacob:
“Give me children, or else I die.”
Jacob becomes angry and answers that he is not God, the One who has withheld the fruit of the womb.
The loved woman is miserable.
The unloved woman is miserable.
Leah has children and wants Jacob's love.
Rachel has Jacob's love and wants children.
Read that again.
Leah possesses what Rachel desperately wants.
Rachel possesses what Leah desperately wants.
And neither woman is content.
That is envy.
It teaches you to stare at another person's blessing until you become blind to the grace already present in your own life.
Someone is looking at your marriage while you are looking at their career.
Someone wants your children while you want their freedom.
Someone wants your ministry while you want their platform.
Someone wants your home while you want somebody else's income.
Someone is praying for something you barely notice anymore.
Comparison can turn blessings into evidence that God supposedly loves somebody else more.
Then the family conflict becomes even darker.
Rachel gives her servant Bilhah to Jacob so that children might be borne through her according to an ancient surrogate-like household arrangement. Bilhah bears Dan and Naphtali.
Leah, after she stops bearing for a time, gives her servant Zilpah to Jacob. Zilpah bears Gad and Asher.
We should not romanticize this.

These women were servants operating inside an ancient patriarchal household with radically different power dynamics from modern individual freedom. Scripture reports what happened; it does not require us to pretend the arrangement was emotionally healthy or God's ideal for marriage.
Bilhah and Zilpah were not reproductive props.
They were human beings.
Their bodies became entangled in a rivalry that began between two sisters.
And the competition continued.
Then comes one of the strangest episodes in Genesis.
Reuben finds mandrakes and brings them to Leah. Rachel wants some. Leah responds with the bitterness that has clearly been simmering:
“Is it a small matter that you have taken my husband? Would you take away my son's mandrakes also?”
Rachel then bargains for the night.
Jacob comes home.
Leah goes out to meet him and essentially tells him that he must sleep with her because she has “hired” him with her son's mandrakes.
Read Genesis 30 slowly and the polished Sunday-school family portrait collapses.
Sex has become entangled with bargaining.
Marriage has become competition.
Children have become connected to status.
Servants have been drawn into reproductive conflict.
Sisters are rivals.
A husband is being negotiated over.
And somehow...
this is the family through which God continues His covenant purposes.
Not because dysfunction is holy.
Not because sexual disorder does not matter.
Not because jealousy is harmless.
Not because manipulation is acceptable.
Grace never requires us to rename sin as righteousness.
Grace means sin does not get the final word when God intervenes.
Eventually Scripture says:
וַיִּזְכֹּר אֱלֹהִים אֶת־רָחֵל
Vayyizkor Elohim et-Rachel.
“Then God remembered Rachel.”
Biblically, when Scripture says God “remembered,” it does not mean God had previously forgotten her. It is covenantal language describing God turning toward someone in purposeful action.
God remembered Rachel.
He listened.
He opened her womb.
Joseph was born.
The rivalry did not create God's faithfulness.
The mandrakes did not control God's faithfulness.
Human schemes did not manufacture God's faithfulness.
God remained God through all of it.
And perhaps that is where this ancient household reaches into ours.
Some of us have spent years trying to control outcomes only God can give.
We manipulate because we are afraid.
We compete because we feel unseen.
We perform because we fear rejection.
We cling because we fear abandonment.
We compare because somebody else's blessing feels like evidence against God's goodness toward us.
We use people because pain has convinced us that getting what we want will finally heal what is broken.
But it never does.
Jacob eventually had sons through Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah. From this turbulent household came the family that would become Israel.
Yet Genesis does not conclude by telling us these people finally became perfect.
Far from it.
More scandal was coming.
Jealousy.
Violence.
Sexual sin.
Deception.
Joseph sold by his own brothers.
Judah's shameful encounter with Tamar.
Years of grief.
A family nearly destroyed by what its members did to one another.
Yet God kept moving His promise forward.
This is not a story about impressive people building God's kingdom.
It is a story about a faithful God working through profoundly imperfect people without ever becoming the author or approver of their sin.
And that distinction matters.
Because otherwise “grace” becomes an excuse.
Biblical grace is something far greater.
Grace confronts us.
Grace exposes us.
Grace calls us to repentance.
Grace forgives the repentant sinner.
Grace begins transforming what sin has deformed.
And ultimately, grace has a name.
Jesus.
John tells us that the eternal Word became flesh and dwelt among us, “full of grace and truth.”
The Greek of John 1:14 says:
πλήρης χάριτος καὶ ἀληθείας
plērēs charitos kai alētheias.
“Full of grace and truth.”
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Jesus brings both.
That matters when reading Jacob's family because Christianity does not ask us to pretend the scandal never happened.
The Gospel is powerful precisely because God tells the truth about human sin.
Scripture's family histories contain embarrassing chapters because redemption is not reputation management.
God is not editing the Bible to make His people look impressive.
He is revealing why sinners need a Savior.
And Jesus does not descend into human history through a sterilized family tree.
Matthew's genealogy itself recalls complicated people and painful stories: Judah and Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, David and “the wife of Uriah.”
Then comes Jesus.
The Messiah.
The Son of David.
The Son of Abraham.
The One who enters the wreckage of humanity without sharing humanity's sin.
This is where Jacob's household stops being merely ancient family drama and becomes a mirror.
Maybe you are Leah.
You keep trying to earn someone's love.
Maybe you are Rachel.
You have something another person desperately wants, yet your heart remains consumed by what you do not have.
Maybe you recognize Jacob in yourself.
You have wounded people while chasing what you wanted.
Maybe you recognize the ugliness of comparison, manipulation, lust, favoritism, bitterness, jealousy, or control.
Maybe your family's history contains chapters you hope nobody ever discovers.
The answer is not to call darkness light.
The answer is to bring the darkness to Jesus.
The Greek New Testament announces the invitation with a word that refuses to leave us comfortable:
μετανοεῖτε — metanoeite.
“Repent.”
Jesus begins His public proclamation in Matthew 4:17 with that call because the Gospel is not merely an invitation to feel better about ourselves.
It is a summons to turn.
To come out of hiding.
To stop defending what Christ died to forgive.
To stop building identities around wounds He wants to redeem.
To stop demanding from human beings what only God can ultimately provide.
Repentance does not purchase grace.
It receives God's mercy with empty hands.
And at the center of Christianity is not Jacob's ladder, Leah's children, Rachel's longing, Judah's lineage, or our ability to repair ourselves.
At the center stands a cross.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, was crucified for sinners and raised from the dead.
The Gospel does not say, “Fix your family history and then come.”
It says come to Christ.
Come guilty.
Come exhausted.
Come ashamed.
Come with the secret.
Come with the addiction.
Come with the jealousy.
Come with the bitterness.
Come with the years you cannot recover.
Come with the wounds other people caused.
Come also with the wounds you caused.
But come willing to surrender.
Because Jesus does not merely offer better optics for broken people.
He offers forgiveness and new life.
That is why the theme is not “scandal does not matter.”
It is From Scandal to Grace.
Scandal is real.
Sin destroys.
People get hurt.
Consequences remain.
But Jesus Christ can write redemption into places where sin appeared to have written the ending.
Maybe that is what somebody reading this needs to hear tonight:
Your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write the final sentence when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
Not because every earthly consequence disappears.
Not because every relationship will automatically be restored.
Not because faith guarantees the exact family, spouse, child, healing, or future you want.
But because the person who belongs to Christ is no longer defined ultimately by condemnation.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).
That is bigger than motivational optimism.
That is Gospel.
So be honest before God.
What are you still trying to earn?
Whose approval has become your idol?
Whose life are you secretly envying?
Who have you been using to medicate your loneliness?
What family wound have you allowed to become permission for your own sin?
What are you hiding because you are terrified that if people knew the whole story, they would never look at you the same way?
Jesus already knows the whole story.
And still the Gospel invitation stands.
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.
Someone scrolling beneath this article may desperately need evidence that Christ still restores people.
Do not keep this article trapped on this page either.
Not as a performance of spirituality. Not because clicking “share” somehow earns favor with God.
But if this truth can reach somebody who is hiding behind a smiling profile picture while their family is collapsing, sharing it can become a simple act of witness.
Send it privately to the friend whose family is complicated.

Supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one practical way of helping biblical content reach more people, alongside prayer, sharing, service, generosity, and faithful witness. We would never tell you that giving us money is required to glorify God. It isn't. Christ purchased salvation; we do not sell it.
Because somewhere tonight there is a Leah still whispering, Maybe now they will love me.
There is a Rachel staring at somebody else's blessing.
There is a Jacob discovering that manipulation cannot produce peace.
There is a family embarrassed by its history.
There is a Christian convinced their past has disqualified them.
And there is still a Savior whose grace is greater than the scandal.
Jacob's family became Israel not because every relationship in that household was righteous, but because the covenant God remained faithful.
And generations later, from the unfolding biblical story connected to that broken family came Jesus Christ—the Lion of the tribe of Judah.
Leah once held Judah and said:
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
She could not have seen everything that would follow.
David.
Kings.
Exile.
Return.
Bethlehem.
A manger.
A cross.
An empty tomb.
A Gospel proclaimed to the nations.
She only knew that, this time, she would praise God.
Maybe that is where your next chapter begins too.
Not with pretending the scandal never happened.
Not with calling evil good.
Not with finally convincing everyone to love you.

But with turning your face toward the One who saw Leah, remembered Rachel, disciplined Jacob, preserved His promise, sent His Son, received the nails, conquered the grave, and still calls sinners home.
The people who failed you may appear in your history, but they do not have to become the authors of your identity. Jesus still holds the pen of redemption.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID GOD ALLOW POLYGAMY IN THE OLD TESTAMENT? THE ANSWER MAY CHANGE THE WAY YOU READ THE ENTIRE BIBLE
paragraphs:
WHY DID GOD ALLOW POLYGAMY IN THE OLD TESTAMENT? THE ANSWER MAY CHANGE THE WAY YOU READ THE ENTIRE BIBLE
God permitted something He never presented as Eden’s ideal—and the broken marriages of Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon reveal a truth far more uncomfortable, and far more beautiful, than most people expect.
There is a question Christians sometimes hope nobody asks.
Because when someone finally does, the room can get uncomfortable.
“If marriage is supposed to be between one man and one woman, why did God allow men in the Old Testament to have multiple wives?”
Abraham had Sarah and Hagar.
Jacob married Leah and Rachel and also fathered children through Bilhah and Zilpah.
David had multiple wives.
Solomon had hundreds of wives and concubines.
And these are not obscure villains hiding in forgotten corners of Scripture.
These are some of the most recognizable names in the Bible.
So what are we supposed to do with that?
Pretend those passages are not there?
Explain them away?
Say, “Well, that was the Old Testament,” and quickly change the subject?
No.
Christian faith does not require us to be frightened by difficult passages.
We need to read them more carefully.
Because once you see what Scripture is actually doing, something remarkable happens.
The scandal does not disappear.
It becomes part of the story of grace.
And the answer begins somewhere many people never think to look.
Not with Abraham.
Not with Jacob.
Not with David.
Not with Solomon.
Before there was a king with a harem…
before there was a patriarch caught between two women…
before jealousy entered a tent…
before one household became divided between competing mothers and wounded children…
there was a garden.
And in that garden, God showed us the pattern before human sin complicated it.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
Look closely at the Hebrew ending:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
wehayu lebasar echad
“And they shall become one flesh.”
That final word, אֶחָד — ʾeḥāḏ, means “one.”
One flesh.
The biblical story does not begin with one man surrounded by wives.
It begins with Adam and Eve.
A man.
His wife.
A covenantal union expressed as one flesh.
That matters enormously, because one of the biggest mistakes we can make while reading Scripture is assuming that everything the Bible describes is something God prescribes.
The Bible describes murder.
That does not mean God approves of murder.
It describes adultery.
It does not bless adultery.
It describes drunkenness, deception, slavery, betrayal, incest, idolatry, war, abuse of power, and spectacular moral failure.
The Bible is brutally honest about humanity because the Bible is not propaganda for human goodness.
It is the story of a holy God dealing with fallen people.
And that distinction helps us understand polygamy.
More precisely, most of the biblical examples involve polygyny—one man having multiple wives—rather than the broader category of polygamy.
Scripture records it.
The Mosaic Law regulates circumstances arising within it.
But regulation is not the same thing as declaring something God’s original ideal.
That difference is enormous.
Imagine finding guardrails beside a dangerous mountain road.
The existence of the guardrails does not mean the government designed the cliff.
The guardrails exist because the cliff is already there and human lives need protection.
In a fallen world, biblical law sometimes restrains damage inside situations that are already far removed from Eden.
Consider Exodus 21:10, where a man who takes another wife is forbidden to deprive the first woman of essential marital provision.
Or consider Deuteronomy 21:15–17, which addresses inheritance when a man has two wives and favors one over the other.
The law is dealing with an existing human reality and limiting injustice within it.
It does not follow that God is saying, “This is My beautiful design for marriage.”
In fact, Scripture gives us another extraordinary clue in its instructions for Israel’s future kings.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
welōʾ yarbeh-lô nāšîm welōʾ yāsûr leḇāḇô
In essence:
“He shall not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.”
Notice that.
God does not tell Israel’s king to build the largest harem in the nation.
He warns him against multiplying wives.
And then centuries later Solomon practically becomes a living illustration of why the warning existed.
The tragedy is breathtaking.
The king famous for wisdom becomes foolish precisely where God had warned kings to be careful.
Solomon accumulates wives.
His affections become divided.
And eventually his heart turns.
What Deuteronomy warned about, Solomon’s life dramatized.
That should make us rethink the claim that the Old Testament casually celebrates polygamy.
Because when you actually follow these households through the story, the picture is often painful.
Look at Abraham.
God promised Abraham descendants.
Years passed.
Sarah remained barren.
The waiting became unbearable.
So Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham.
Genesis does not hide what happened next.
Pregnancy produced contempt.
Contempt produced jealousy.
Jealousy produced mistreatment.
Mistreatment drove Hagar into the wilderness.
Eventually Ishmael and Hagar were sent away.
What looked like a human solution to an impossible promise became a household soaked in tears.
Then look at Jacob.
He loved Rachel.
He was deceived into marrying Leah.
He then married Rachel too.
And suddenly we are watching two sisters competing for the affection of the same husband.
Leah desperately wants to be loved.
Rachel desperately wants children.
Children begin to carry the emotional weight of their mothers’ rivalry.
Servant women are brought into the reproductive struggle.
Names given to babies become windows into heartbreak, competition, vindication, and longing.
Read those chapters slowly and you stop seeing a glamorous ancient household.
You start hearing wounded people.
One woman whispering, in effect, “Maybe now my husband will love me.”
Another crying because she cannot conceive.
A husband trapped inside the consequences of deception and favoritism.
Children growing up inside a fractured family system.
The Bible does not need to interrupt every paragraph and say, “Polygyny creates problems.”
The story is showing you.
Then comes David.
A man after God’s own heart—and also a man capable of terrible sin.
David accumulated wives.
Then he saw Bathsheba.
She belonged to another man.
David already possessed what Uriah did not: multiple wives and royal power.
Yet power whispered the same ancient lie sin always whispers:
“You deserve more.”
David took Bathsheba.
Then he arranged Uriah’s death.
And when Nathan confronted him, the prophet exposed the ugliness of David’s entitlement.
This was never simply about sexual desire.
It was about a heart that stopped recognizing boundaries.
Then Solomon takes the pattern to catastrophic proportions.
Women become part of royal accumulation.
Political alliances become marriages.
Desire and power merge.
And eventually the king’s heart is pulled toward other gods.
The story moves from Eden’s “one flesh” toward a palace filled with divided affection.
And perhaps that is the deepest issue.
Because marriage in Scripture is not merely about sexuality.
It is about covenant.
Faithfulness.
Union.
Belonging.
Exclusive devotion.
And those themes eventually point beyond human marriage altogether.
But before we reach that point, we need to face the hardest part of the question.
Why would God tolerate arrangements that fell short of His original design?
Jesus gives us a principle that helps enormously.
When religious leaders questioned Him about divorce in Matthew 19, Jesus did something revealing.
He went backward.
Past Moses.
Past Israel.
Back to creation.
He quoted the Genesis pattern of male and female becoming one flesh.
When they objected by pointing to Moses’ allowance concerning divorce, Jesus answered with words that unlock far more than the divorce debate:
πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν
pros tēn sklērokardian hymōn
“Because of your hardness of heart…”
Then comes the crucial statement:
ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δὲ οὐ γέγονεν οὕτως
ap’ archēs de ou gegonen houtōs
“But from the beginning it was not so.”
Do not miss that sentence.
Jesus teaches us that something can exist within Mosaic regulation without representing God’s creational ideal.
Why?
Because God was dealing with hard-hearted human beings.

That does not mean every Old Testament concession can automatically be treated identically. We should not force Jesus’ specific teaching about divorce into passages where He was not directly speaking about polygyny.
But the interpretive principle is unmistakable:
To understand God’s design, Jesus takes us back to the beginning.
And what do we find at the beginning?
Not Adam, Eve, Rachel, Leah, Bilhah, and Zilpah.
Adam and Eve.
One flesh.
God enters history not by waiting until humanity becomes morally perfect, but by meeting sinners inside the wreckage they have created and progressively moving His redemptive purposes forward.
That is what makes the Bible so painfully believable.
If human beings were inventing a religious propaganda book designed to make their heroes look magnificent, the Old Testament would be an extraordinarily strange way to do it.
Noah gets drunk.
Abraham lies.
Jacob deceives.
Moses loses his temper.
David commits adultery and orchestrates a killing.
Solomon’s wisdom does not save him from catastrophic compromise.
Peter denies Jesus.
The disciples argue about greatness.
The Bible refuses to airbrush its heroes.
Because they were never the Hero.
Jesus is.
That is where this question becomes much more personal than an argument about ancient marriage customs.
Because it is easy to stare at Solomon’s household and think:
“How could he let his heart become so divided?”
But perhaps the more uncomfortable question is:
How divided is yours?
Solomon multiplied wives.
Maybe you multiply secret identities.
One version of you worships on Sunday.
Another version lives online after midnight.
One version speaks about Jesus.
Another quietly feeds an addiction.
One version tells everyone the marriage is fine.
Another knows resentment has been poisoning the home for years.
One version posts Scripture.
Another cannot forgive.
One version says, “God is first.”
But money gets the first anxiety.
Sex gets the strongest appetite.
Approval gets the deepest craving.
Politics gets the loudest passion.
Entertainment gets the most time.
And Jesus gets whatever remains.
Different century.
Same divided heart.
That is why this cannot remain merely an article about “those polygamous people in the Old Testament.”
Scripture is holding up a mirror.
God warned the king not to multiply wives because his heart could turn away.
The issue underneath the visible behavior was the heart.
לְבָבוֹ — leḇāḇô.
His heart.
And perhaps somebody reading this has just realized:
“My heart has been turning too.”
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your pastor does not know.
Maybe your children think you are stronger than you are.
And maybe you have become so good at carrying two versions of yourself that you almost forgot which one was real.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not God pretending your sin does not matter.
The Gospel is God doing something infinitely more costly.
He exposes sin…
and then provides a Savior.
The answer to human brokenness was never Abraham.
Never Jacob.
Never David.
Never Solomon.
Every one of them needed mercy.
Every one of them pointed beyond himself.
Then Jesus came.
And unlike every compromised king before Him, Christ remained faithful.
Where Adam failed, Christ obeyed.
Where Israel wandered, Christ remained faithful.
Where kings accumulated power for themselves, Jesus emptied Himself and took the form of a servant.
Where David took another man’s bride and sent the husband toward death, Jesus moves in the opposite direction:
Christ gives Himself to death to rescue His Bride.
Do you see how beautiful the reversal is?
Sin says:
“Take.”
Jesus says:
“I give Myself.”
Sin consumes.
Jesus sacrifices.
Sin uses people.
Jesus lays down His life for people.
Sin divides.
Jesus reconciles.
Sin stains.
Jesus cleanses.
And suddenly marriage becomes even larger than Genesis.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5 about husband and wife, then unveils the mystery:
marriage ultimately points toward Christ and the Church.
Jesus is the faithful Bridegroom.
And His covenant faithfulness is not fragile.
He does not abandon His people because another bride catches His attention.
He does not become bored with His covenant.
He does not wake up one morning and decide His Bride has become inconvenient.
He loves.
He gives Himself.
He sanctifies.
He cleanses.
He keeps His promises.
That is why biblical faithfulness matters.
Human marriage was always meant to tell a larger story.
And this is also why the Bible’s record of polygyny should never become ammunition for mocking people who lived within those broken arrangements.
Especially women.
Hagar was not a theological problem to God.
She was a suffering woman whom God saw in the wilderness.
Leah was not merely “the unwanted wife.”
God saw that she was unloved.
Bathsheba was not merely a footnote in David’s biography.
The biblical story ultimately places her within the genealogy leading toward Christ.
Again and again, God walks into stories human beings have complicated beyond recognition…
and grace starts rewriting them.
That does not make the sin good.
Grace never needs evil to become good in order to redeem people from it.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
The crucifixion of Jesus was an act of horrifying human injustice.
And God turned humanity’s darkest act into the place where redemption was accomplished.
That is what God does.
He does not call darkness light.
He enters darkness carrying resurrection.
Maybe that is why this subject matters more than you thought.
You came here asking:
“Why did God allow polygamy?”
But perhaps underneath that question is another one.
“Why does God tolerate broken people at all?”
Why Abraham?
Why Jacob?
Why David?
Why Solomon?
Why Peter?
Why me?
And there it is.
The question has finally reached your own front door.
Because if God only worked through people whose lives perfectly reflected His design, the Bible would become very short.
And so would the Church.
We are all people standing somewhere between what God designed and what sin has damaged.
Some damage is visible.
Some is hidden behind church clothes and carefully selected photographs.
Some people have broken marriages.
Some have broken sexuality.
Some have broken trust.
Some have broken families.
Some have addictions they promised God they would quit a hundred times.
Some are carrying consequences that cannot simply be reversed.
And Christianity does not announce:
“Fix your history, and then Jesus might accept you.”
Christianity announces:
Christ came for sinners.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come into the light.
Receive mercy.
And then follow Him.
Grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace is the power and pardon that meet us in our guilt and begin transforming us.
That is why Jesus’ words are so powerful:
“From the beginning it was not so.”
Jesus does not merely expose how far humanity wandered.
He points us toward restoration.
Toward God’s intention.
Toward faithfulness.
Toward holiness.
Toward hearts no longer divided between God and idols.
And ultimately toward the new creation, where everything sin fractured will finally be placed beneath the reign of Christ.
So did God “allow” polygyny in the Old Testament?
Yes, in the sense that He dealt with people living within societies where it existed and gave laws addressing and restraining circumstances created by it.
But do not confuse divine toleration and regulation in a fallen world with the declaration of a creational ideal.
Scripture begins with one man and one woman becoming one flesh.
It warns Israel’s king against multiplying wives.
It repeatedly shows the jealousy, rivalry, exploitation, favoritism, family conflict, and spiritual danger surrounding plural marriages.
And when Jesus is asked about marriage and divorce, He directs His hearers back beyond later concessions:
to the beginning.
That is the biblical trajectory.
Creation.
Fall.
Human hardness.
Divine restraint.
Promise.
Redemption.
Christ.
Restoration.
And maybe now you understand why the Bible leaves the scandals in.
God could have given us sanitized heroes.
Instead, He gave us Abraham’s household.
Jacob’s rivalry.
David’s collapse.
Solomon’s divided heart.
Why?
Because Scripture is not telling us how impressive humanity is.
Scripture is telling us how desperately humanity needs Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is exactly what somebody you know needs to hear today.
Not another polished Christian pretending the Bible has no difficult passages.
Not another believer frightened by hard questions.
But someone willing to open Scripture, face the scandal honestly, and still discover that Christ stands at the center of the story.
Not merely because you agree with it.
Be honest.
Somebody reading your three words may realize they are not the only person fighting their way back toward the light.
Because difficult questions return.
And when they do, you need more than a slogan.
You need Scripture.
It does not.
Not because giving money purchases blessing, salvation, forgiveness, or spiritual status.
It cannot.
Jesus purchased our redemption—not us.
But one genuine way believers can glorify God is by willingly using what He has entrusted to them to support faithful Gospel work and help truth reach other people.
And there is more.
Come to Jesus.
Not to a brand.
Not to merchandise.
Not to a page.
To Christ.
Repent of sin.
Trust the crucified and risen Savior.
Bring Him the divided heart.
Bring Him the secret chapter.
Bring Him the marriage wounds.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the questions you were afraid Christians would not let you ask.
The Bible is filled with scandal because humanity is filled with sinners.
But the Bible does not end with scandal.
It moves toward a wedding.
Toward Christ and His redeemed people.
Toward a Bridegroom who never betrays His Bride.
Toward a King whose heart never turns away.
Toward the Lamb who was slain.
Toward resurrection.
Toward restoration.
Toward grace.
And perhaps the most unforgettable truth hiding inside all those broken Old Testament households is this:
God did not preserve their scandals so you would imitate their brokenness; He preserved them so you would recognize your need for the faithful Savior they could never be.
Share that truth.
Because the names change.
The centuries change.
The scandals change.
But humanity still needs the same Savior.
And when sin has written a chapter that looks impossible to redeem, never forget who is holding the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN CHURCH MINISTRY CREATE UNEXPECTED TEMPTATION?
paragraphs:
CAN CHURCH MINISTRY CREATE UNEXPECTED TEMPTATION?
You Thought Serving God Would Make You Safer. But What Happens When the Place Where You Serve Jesus Becomes the Place Where Your Heart Is Most Vulnerable?
Nobody warned you that temptation could find you while you were carrying a Bible.
You expected it in the obvious places.
In secrecy.
In loneliness.
In the old life you thought you had buried.
You expected temptation to knock when you were spiritually cold, disconnected from church, running from God, or deliberately wandering somewhere you knew you should never be.
But ministry?
Surely not there.
Not while praying with someone.
Not while leading worship.
Not while counseling a hurting person.
Not while organizing an outreach.
Not while answering messages from someone who “just needs spiritual encouragement.”
Not while serving beside another believer whose passion for Jesus seems to mirror your own.
And perhaps that is precisely why certain temptations can become so dangerous.
Because when temptation arrives wearing obvious darkness, Christians recognize it.
But when it arrives wrapped in ministry, compassion, spiritual intimacy, admiration, exhaustion, affirmation, or the feeling that someone finally understands you...
we may not recognize what is happening until something inside us has already begun moving.
This article is not an accusation against pastors, ministry leaders, worship teams, volunteers, counselors, missionaries, or Christians who serve faithfully.
Ministry itself is not the enemy.
Serving Christ is beautiful.
The danger is forgetting that serving Christ does not make us incapable of being tempted.
Jesus Himself taught His disciples to pray:
“Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.”
The Greek word translated “temptation” is πειρασμός — peirasmos — a word that can refer, depending on context, to testing, trial, or temptation.
Jesus did not teach that prayer only to people outside ministry.
He taught it to disciples.
People following Him.
People serving Him.
People who would eventually preach Him.
That should humble every one of us.
Because sometimes the most dangerous sentence a Christian can say is:
“That could never happen to me.”
Peter once sounded remarkably confident too.
When Jesus warned His disciples that they would stumble, Peter insisted that even if everyone else fell away, he would not.
Yet before morning came, Peter denied Jesus three times.
The lesson is not that Peter never loved Christ.
He did.
The lesson is that sincere love for Jesus does not make human weakness disappear.
And if you serve in ministry, you need to hear this without shame and without pretending:
You are not beyond temptation simply because you are being used by God.
Sometimes ministry creates unusual circumstances in which ordinary human vulnerabilities become spiritually dangerous.
Think about it.
People trust you.
People open their wounds to you.
People tell you things they may not tell anyone else.
You pray together.
You cry together.
You celebrate breakthroughs together.
You walk through grief together.
Someone may admire your faith.
Someone may tell you that your preaching changed their life.
Someone may say your worship brought them back to God.
Someone may tell you that nobody has ever understood their pain the way you do.
And admiration can feel innocent.
Until you begin needing it.
Compassion can be holy.
Until boundaries disappear.
Spiritual friendship can be beautiful.
Until emotional dependence quietly replaces healthy fellowship.
Private conversations can begin with Scripture...
and slowly become something else.
You tell yourself you are helping.
You tell yourself they need you.
You tell yourself nobody else understands the situation.
You tell yourself there is nothing inappropriate happening.
And perhaps physically, nothing has happened.
Yet.
But Jesus never reduced faithfulness merely to what our bodies eventually do.
He went after the heart.
In Matthew 5:28, Jesus warned about looking at another person “to lust after” them.
The Greek expression includes the verb ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō — to desire, long for, or covet, with the moral meaning determined by context.
Jesus was exposing something terrifyingly important:
Sin can begin long before anyone else can see it.
That is why some spiritual disasters begin with things that look almost harmless.
One message you are strangely excited to receive.
One conversation you keep replaying.
One compliment that feeds something starving inside you.
One person whose approval begins mattering too much.
One private connection you would feel uncomfortable explaining fully to your spouse.
One emotional dependency you continue calling “ministry.”
One boundary you keep moving because nothing terrible has happened...
yet.
And this is where Scripture becomes painfully practical.
James writes:
The Greek behind “desire” or “lust” is ἐπιθυμία — epithymia.
James continues by describing desire conceiving and eventually giving birth to sin, and sin reaching maturity and producing death.
Notice where James places responsibility.
He does not tell us merely to blame the environment.
He forces us to confront what temptation finds inside us.
Ministry can create circumstances.
Opportunity can create circumstances.
Exhaustion can create circumstances.
Admiration can create circumstances.
Loneliness can create circumstances.
But circumstances often reveal desires we have not surrendered.
That is uncomfortable.
And necessary.
Because sometimes the problem is not simply that somebody became attracted to you.
The deeper question is:
Why did their attention begin feeding you?
Sometimes the problem is not merely that somebody crossed an emotional boundary.
The deeper question is:
Why were you secretly relieved when they did?
Sometimes the problem is not merely that ministry became demanding.
The deeper question is:
Why did being needed become your identity?
Sometimes we become so accustomed to being the person who helps everyone else that we forget how desperately our own hearts need shepherding.
You preach grace while secretly starving for affirmation.
You counsel marriages while yours is becoming emotionally distant.
You tell people Jesus is enough while quietly building your identity around applause.
You teach others about confession while hiding your own battle because you are terrified of what people will think.
You become the strong one.
The spiritual one.
The dependable one.
The one everyone calls.
And somewhere along the way, you stop allowing anyone to ask whether your own soul is okay.
That is dangerous territory.
Paul understood the necessity of vigilance.
After describing the spiritual history of Israel and warning the Corinthian believers from those examples, he wrote:
“Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.”
The Greek verb behind “take heed” is βλέπω — blepō — literally connected with seeing, watching, paying attention.
Watch yourself.
Not because Christ is weak.
Because you are human.
Then comes one of Scripture's most frequently quoted promises:
“There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful…”
That phrase matters enormously.
God is faithful.
The Christian answer to temptation is not confidence in our spiritual résumé.
It is confidence in the faithfulness of God accompanied by obedient dependence upon Him.
Paul continues:
God “will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.”
The Greek word translated “way to escape” is ἔκβασις — ekbasis — an exit, outcome, or way out.
Sometimes that escape looks deeply spiritual.
Sometimes it looks painfully ordinary.
End the conversation.
Move the meeting into a public place.
Invite another leader into the situation.
Tell your spouse.
Tell your pastor.
Tell an elder.
Tell a mature Christian who loves Jesus more than they love protecting your reputation.
Stop counseling someone you are emotionally attracted to.
Hand the responsibility to somebody else.
Delete the secret communication channel.
Do not travel alone together.
Do not manufacture reasons to spend time together.
Stop calling secrecy “privacy.”
Stop calling emotional dependency “discipleship.”
Stop asking how close you can stand to the cliff while remaining technically innocent.
Run.
Joseph did.
When Potiphar's wife repeatedly pursued him sexually, Joseph did not stay in the room to demonstrate how spiritually mature he was.
Genesis records his refusal:
“How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?”
Then, when she physically grabbed him, Joseph left his garment and fled.
There are moments when running is not cowardice.
Running is worship.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is leave the room.
Sometimes blocking the number is obedience.
Sometimes resigning from a particular counseling relationship is integrity.
Sometimes telling another leader what has been happening is courage.
Sometimes admitting, “I am attracted to this person and I need boundaries immediately,” may prevent months or years of destruction.
Because temptation grows remarkably well in secrecy.
Sin whispers:
Don't tell anyone.
They'll misunderstand.
You can handle this.
Nothing has happened.
You're still in control.
But Scripture says:
“Flee also youthful lusts.”
Paul's word is φεῦγε — pheuge.
Flee.
Not negotiate.
Not study how close you can get.
Not prove your maturity.
Flee.
And pursue “righteousness, faith, charity, peace” with those who call upon the Lord from a pure heart.
Notice something beautiful there.
Biblical fleeing is not merely running away.
It is running toward something.
Toward righteousness.
Toward faith.
Toward love.
Toward peace.
Toward healthy Christian community.
Toward Christ.
Because Christianity is not primarily behavior modification.
The Gospel is not Jesus standing over dirty people shouting, “Try harder.”
The Gospel is that the holy Son of God entered our broken world to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
Jesus Christ lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He resisted temptation.
He remained without sin.
He went willingly to the cross.
There He bore sin's judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The answer to hidden temptation is not simply better reputation management.
It is Jesus.
And perhaps someone reading this has already crossed the boundary.
Perhaps this did not reach you before the message.
Before the emotional affair.
Before the pornography.
Before the secret relationship.
Before the adultery.
Before the lie.
Before the ministry collapse.
Perhaps you are reading this afterward.
And now you feel dirty.
Exposed.
Terrified.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe your name became the conversation you once feared having about somebody else.
And you wonder whether grace still has your address.
Listen carefully.
Grace does not mean consequences disappear.
Repentance does not mean trust must instantly be restored.
Forgiveness does not erase the need for accountability.
A fallen leader may need to step away from ministry, perhaps for a significant period, and restoration to fellowship with God should never be confused with automatic restoration to leadership.
Some consequences of sin remain painfully real.
But consequences are not the same thing as condemnation for the person who truly belongs to Christ.
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
Romans 8:1.
The Greek word translated “condemnation” is κατάκριμα — katakrima.
The verdict of condemnation.
And Paul says that for those who are in Christ Jesus, there is now no condemnation.
Why?
Not because the sin was small.
Not because God pretended it never happened.
Not because holiness suddenly stopped mattering.
Because Jesus carried judgment at the cross.
This is where scandal can become grace.
Not because Jesus rewrites history by pretending the scandal never happened.
Jesus does something far greater.
He rewrites what sin believed would be the final chapter.
Peter denied Him.
Jesus restored Peter.
David committed horrifying sin and suffered severe consequences, yet when confronted, he confessed:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
Psalm 51 gives us the language of a shattered man:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.”
The Hebrew word translated “create” is בְּרָא — bera, from the verb ברא (baraʾ), a word Scripture famously uses for God's creative action.
David did not merely ask God to polish his public image.
He asked for a clean heart.
That is repentance.
Not:
“God, make sure nobody finds out.”
But:
“God, change me.”
Not:
“Protect my platform.”
But:
“Purify my heart.”
Not:
“Restore everyone's opinion of me.”
But:
“Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation.”
There is an enormous difference between being sorry that sin became expensive and grieving because sin offended the God you love.
Paul describes “godly sorrow” as producing repentance leading toward salvation.
That is the kind of sorrow grace invites.
Not despair.
Not self-destruction.
Not endless self-hatred.
Repentance.
Turning.
Coming home.
Bringing what was hidden into the light.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe somewhere between the first paragraph and this sentence, a face appeared in your mind.
A conversation.
A relationship.
A message thread.
A fantasy.
A ministry connection.
Something you keep defending because admitting what it has become would require you to change it.
Do not wait for catastrophe to give you permission to obey God.
You do not need to commit adultery before establishing boundaries.
You do not need to destroy your marriage before seeking accountability.
You do not need to lose your ministry before admitting you are spiritually exhausted.
You do not need a public scandal before choosing private repentance.
Jesus is offering you the exit before the wreckage.
Take it.
And if you have already created wreckage...
take His hand anyway.
Repent.
Confess.
Accept necessary consequences.
Seek biblical accountability.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Stop protecting the image.
Start pursuing holiness.
Because your platform was never your Savior.
Your reputation was never your Savior.
Your ministry was never your Savior.
Jesus is.
This is something the Church desperately needs to recover:
Ministers need ministry too.
Pastors need pastors.
Counselors need accountability.
Worship leaders need shepherding.
Teachers need correction.
Strong Christians need places where they can stop performing strength.
Married ministry workers need to guard their marriages intentionally.
Single ministry workers need wise relational boundaries too.
Every Christian needs brothers and sisters who are allowed to ask difficult questions.
Not because we expect everyone to fail.
Because we understand the human heart and believe God's warnings are mercy.
Guardrails are not evidence that your marriage is weak.
Accountability is not evidence that your faith is weak.
Boundaries are not evidence that you cannot control yourself.
They are often evidence that you take holiness seriously enough not to gamble with what God has entrusted to you.
And please hear this:
The goal is not paranoia.
Men and women can serve Christ together with purity, wisdom, dignity, and genuine Christian love.
The answer is not treating every person as a threat.
The answer is refusing to treat yourself as invulnerable.
Paul told Timothy:
“Keep thyself pure.”
That calling still matters.
Your private life matters.
Your thought life matters.
Your marriage matters.
Your integrity matters.
The person you become when nobody is applauding matters.
And Christ matters infinitely more than the ministry you perform in His name.
You can preach Jesus publicly and still desperately need Jesus privately.
You can lead people toward living water while dying of thirst yourself.
So drink.
Return.
Come back to the secret place where nobody knows your title.
Where nobody applauds your sermon.
Where nobody calls you pastor, prophet, teacher, leader, worshipper, mentor, counselor, missionary, or minister.
Just you...
and Jesus.
Maybe your prayer tonight needs to become very simple:
“Search me, O God, and know my heart.”
Those words come from Psalm 139.
The Hebrew plea begins:
חָקְרֵנִי אֵל וְדַע לְבָבִי
ḥoqreni El, veda levavi.
“Search me, O God, and know my heart.”
Then:
“Try me, and know my thoughts: And see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.”
That is a terrifying prayer when you mean it.
Because God may show you something.
But it is also a beautiful prayer.
Because the God searching you is the God who loved sinners enough to give His Son.
He exposes in order to heal.
He convicts in order to call us home.
And if this article exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn the conviction into entertainment.
Respond.
If necessary, put the phone down and pray before reading another sentence.
Tell Jesus the truth.
He already knows it.
If appropriate and safe, bring it to a trustworthy mature believer who can help you walk faithfully.
And if your heart is saying, “This is me,” you do not need to describe your private situation publicly. But you can leave one simple confession of dependence:
Maybe somebody else needs to see that they are not the only Christian fighting to remain faithful.
If you are already rebuilding after failure, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Not as performance.
As testimony.
If you need prayer, simply comment, “Pray for me.”
There is no shame in admitting you need Jesus.
And think about one person who needs this warning before their hidden struggle becomes a public disaster.
Or send this privately if that would protect their dignity.
You may not need every sentence tonight.
You might need it six months from now.
Come to Christ.
Because eventually every platform disappears.
Every microphone goes silent.
Every title is surrendered.
Every audience leaves.
Every ministry assignment ends.
And what remains is not how many people knew your name.
The question is whether you knew Him.
So guard your heart.
Protect your marriage.
Honor your brothers and sisters.
Establish boundaries before you need them.
Confess temptation before temptation becomes captivity.
Run when Scripture tells you to run.
Repent when you fall.
Receive grace when you return.
And never confuse being useful to God with being spiritually invulnerable.
The hands holding the Bible can still tremble.
The mouth preaching grace can still need forgiveness.
The person leading others home can still become lost along the road.
But Jesus is still standing there.
Not approving our sin.
Not minimizing its damage.
Not protecting our illusions.
Calling us out of darkness.
Calling us into truth.
Calling us toward repentance.
Calling us home.
Because your worst chapter does not have authority to write your final sentence when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
That is the Gospel.
That is the hope beyond the scandal.
That is grace.
And maybe the sentence you need to carry with you tonight is this:
Do not wait until temptation becomes your scandal to discover that Jesus had already provided a door back into the light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DO SOME CHRISTIANS NEVER GROW?
paragraphs:
WHY DO SOME CHRISTIANS NEVER GROW?
The frightening possibility is not that you stopped believing in God. It is that you became comfortable knowing about Jesus without allowing Him to change the parts of you that still refuse to surrender.
There is a kind of Christianity that can survive for years without ever becoming mature.
It knows the songs.
It knows when to say “Amen.”
It knows which Bible verses to post when life becomes painful.
It knows how to look faithful in public.
It may attend church, listen to sermons, own several Bibles, follow Christian pages, defend Christian beliefs, and speak fluently about grace.
And yet...
year after year, the same bitterness remains.
The same secret sin keeps returning.
The same unforgiveness controls the heart.
The same pride refuses correction.
The same prayerlessness continues.
The same spiritual excuses survive.
The same wounds become permission to hurt other people.
The same person keeps saying, “God is working on me,” while quietly resisting almost everything through which God intends to change them.
And eventually a terrifying question has to be asked:
Why do some people spend years around Christianity and still seem spiritually unchanged?
Maybe an even harder question is this:
Could that person be me?
Before you answer too quickly, stay here.
Because Scripture gives us something far more uncomfortable than another motivational message about “becoming your best self.”
The Gospel is not self-improvement.
Jesus did not die so that the old you could become slightly more religious.
He died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God, forgive the guilty, give His people new life, and progressively transform those who belong to Him.
And sometimes the greatest obstacle to spiritual growth is not that God has stopped working.
It is that we have learned how to live close enough to Christian truth to feel safe while remaining far enough from surrender that the truth never reaches the rooms we keep locked.
Peter wrote:
“As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby.”
—1 Peter 2:2, KJV
The Greek text contains this striking expression:
ὡς ἀρτιγέννητα βρέφη... τὸ λογικὸν ἄδολον γάλα ἐπιποθήσατε
Hōs artigennēta brephē... to logikon adolon gala epipothēsate.
The picture is intensely physical.
Newborn babies longing for milk.
Peter's word ἐπιποθήσατε — epipothēsate carries the sense of earnestly longing for or craving something.
Not casually appreciating it.
Not occasionally remembering it.
Craving it.
And ἄδολον — adolon means pure, genuine, unadulterated, without deceit.
Peter's point is beautiful and devastating: believers are to hunger for the nourishment God provides because through it they grow toward maturity in the salvation they have received.
A newborn does not need to be convinced that milk matters.
Hunger tells him.
So perhaps one diagnostic question for the spiritually stagnant Christian is not merely, “How much Scripture do I know?”
It is:
What am I actually hungry for?
Because eventually your appetite reveals what has captured your heart.
You can carry a Bible and hunger for applause.
You can attend church and hunger for status.
You can post Scripture and hunger for validation.
You can sing worship songs and hunger for someone's attention.
You can speak about holiness while secretly feeding lust.
You can talk about forgiveness while replaying someone's offense every night.
You can say that Jesus is enough while spending your entire emotional life trying to prove to strangers that you are enough.
And then Sunday arrives.
You dress the wound.
You hide the addiction.
You silence the questions.
You smile.
Someone asks, “How are you?”
And almost automatically you answer...
“Blessed.”
But inside?
Exhausted.
Dry.
Angry.
Jealous.
Numb.
Secretly ashamed.
Still wrestling with something you promised God six months ago you would surrender.
And perhaps you have begun wondering why Christianity seems alive for everybody else while your own soul feels like it has been standing in the same place for years.
Listen carefully.
Spiritual growth is not measured by how emotional you become during worship.
It is not measured by how many Christian posts you share.
It is not measured by how impressive your theological vocabulary becomes.
It is not measured by how long you have attended church.
Time alone does not produce maturity.
A person can be around Christian things for decades and still require what Hebrews calls “milk” rather than solid food because he has remained immature in understanding and practice.
Paul encountered a similar tragedy in Corinth.
He told believers that he could not address them as spiritually mature but as infants in Christ. Jealousy and strife among them exposed their immaturity.
Think about that.
Their spiritual condition became visible through their relationships.
That means one of the places your spiritual maturity is tested is not merely inside a church building.
It is in your home.
In your marriage.
In the way you speak when angry.
In what happens when somebody corrects you.
In what you do when nobody can see your screen.
In how you treat the person who cannot advance your career.
In whether you secretly celebrate when somebody you envy fails.
In whether you apologize without adding, “but you also...”
In whether you forgive.
In whether you tell the truth when lying would protect your reputation.
In whether Jesus is still Lord when obedience becomes expensive.
That is where theology becomes discipleship.
And this is precisely why spiritual growth can hurt.
Because Jesus loves us too much to merely decorate the person we used to be.
He confronts.
He exposes.
He prunes.
Jesus said:
“I am the vine, ye are the branches.”
Then comes the sentence our self-sufficient hearts hate:
“Without me ye can do nothing.”
—John 15:5, KJV
Nothing.
Christian maturity is not produced by gritting your teeth hard enough.
You cannot manufacture the fruit of the Spirit through personality.
You cannot defeat the flesh through inspirational quotes.
You cannot heal your soul through religious performance.
You cannot become holy while remaining independent of Christ.
The branch lives because it remains connected to the Vine.
This means spiritual growth begins with something our culture deeply dislikes:
dependence.
Jesus, I need You.
Not just when somebody dies.
Not just when money disappears.
Not just when the diagnosis arrives.
Not just when the relationship collapses.
Not just when panic wakes me at 2:17 in the morning.
I need You when everything is going well.
I need You when temptation whispers.
I need You when pride tells me I am right.
I need You when somebody wounds me.
I need You when nobody applauds my obedience.
I need You when Scripture contradicts what I want.
I need You when repentance costs me something.
That is where growth begins to become real.
Paul tells Christians in Romans 12:2:
“Be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind...”
The Greek is breathtaking:
μεταμορφοῦσθε τῇ ἀνακαινώσει τοῦ νοός
metamorphousthe tē anakainōsei tou noos.
Μεταμορφοῦσθε — metamorphousthe.
Be transformed.
The word describes transformation, a change of form.
And then:
ἀνακαίνωσις — anakainōsis.
Renewal.
Renovation.
A making new.
Christianity is not primarily about teaching an old heart religious manners.
God changes people.
He renews minds.
He reshapes desires.
He teaches His children to hate what destroys them and love what reflects Him.
Yet this transformation does not mean Christians instantly become flawless.
Look carefully at the New Testament and you will never find mature Christianity described as sinless swagger.
Quite the opposite.
Growth often makes a Christian increasingly aware of how desperately he needs grace.
The closer you walk with Christ, the harder it becomes to romanticize the darkness inside yourself.
Things you once excused begin bothering you.
Words you once spoke without conviction begin grieving you.
Pride you once called “confidence” becomes easier to recognize.
Gossip you called “venting” starts looking different.
Lust you called “normal” becomes something you want crucified.
Bitterness you called “protecting my peace” begins revealing its chains.
You start noticing the difference between being sorry that sin produced consequences and being grieved because sin dishonors the God who loves you.
That is growth.
Not perfection.
Direction.
Not pretending you never fall.
Learning where to run when you do.
And the mature Christian increasingly runs toward Jesus instead of away from Him.
This is where shame has deceived countless believers.
You sinned.
Again.
You knew better.
Again.
You prayed about it.
Again.
You promised it was over.
Again.
Then you failed.
Again.
And shame whispered:
“Don't pray now.”
“You're fake.”
“God is tired of you.”
“Hide.”
“Wait until you become better before coming back.”
But that voice does not understand the Gospel.
The Gospel says you were never rescued because you were impressive.
Christ came for sinners.
Jesus carried sin to the cross.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Your hope has never been the strength of your performance.
Your hope is the sufficiency of Jesus Christ.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace does exactly the opposite.
Grace teaches us that sin is so serious Christ had to die—and that God's mercy is so astonishing Christ willingly came to save sinners.
So repentance is not paying God back.
Repentance is turning from the poison toward the Physician.
It is finally saying:
Jesus, I cannot keep defending the thing that is destroying me.
I cannot keep calling bondage freedom.
I cannot keep asking You to bless the life I refuse to surrender.
I cannot keep polishing my Christian image while starving my actual soul.
No more hiding.
And maybe that sentence just landed somewhere uncomfortable.
Maybe nobody knows what you are fighting.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Your pastor does not know.
Your family does not know.
Your Christian friends would never imagine it.
Maybe people look at you and think you are strong.
But God sees the browser history.
God sees the resentment.
God sees the private tears.
God sees the secret relationship.
God sees the jealousy.
God sees the compromises.
God sees what happened.
God sees what was done to you.
God sees what you did.
And still the Gospel announces something scandalously beautiful:
Jesus receives repentant sinners.
This has always been the heartbeat of grace.
Peter denied Him.
David collapsed morally and discovered the agony of repentance.
Thomas doubted.
Paul once persecuted the church.
The woman caught in adultery was publicly humiliated.
The thief beside Jesus was dying under judgment with no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Again and again Scripture refuses to hide human wreckage.
Why?
Because the Bible is not the story of impressive people climbing their way toward God.
It is the story of the holy God pursuing, redeeming, correcting, forgiving, restoring, and transforming people who desperately need Him.
That is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming sin.
Not by calling evil good.
Jesus does something infinitely greater.
He enters the wreckage and redeems people from it.
The cross does not say your sin did not matter.
The cross reveals how much it mattered.
And the resurrection declares that sin and death do not get the final word over those who belong to Christ.
So why do some Christians never seem to grow?
Sometimes because they consume sermons but rarely obey what they hear.
Sometimes because they want encouragement without correction.
Sometimes because they confuse conviction with condemnation and run from God whenever He exposes something.
Sometimes because they have isolated themselves from meaningful Christian community.
Sometimes because they feed their minds for hours on everything except the things of God.
Sometimes because they have made peace with a sin Jesus is calling them to forsake.
Sometimes because bitterness has become part of their identity.
Sometimes because pride makes correction almost impossible.
Sometimes because they are trying to produce through human effort what can only grow through abiding in Christ and walking by the Holy Spirit.
And sometimes the deepest issue is more fundamental.
Scripture tells us to examine ourselves to see whether we are in the faith.
That should never be weaponized to torment tender believers who genuinely trust Christ and struggle with assurance.
But neither should it be ignored.
Christianity is not merely agreeing that Jesus existed.
It is not inheriting your parents' religion.
It is not baptism without faith.
It is not church attendance without Christ.
It is not Christian vocabulary without conversion.
Jesus calls people to Himself.
To repent.
To believe.
To follow.
And genuine saving faith produces fruit—not flawless fruit, not instant maturity, not identical growth rates, but a life in which God's transforming work becomes increasingly evident.
Maybe your growth feels painfully slow.
Do not confuse slow growth with no growth.
Maybe you still struggle with anger, but now you repent instead of celebrating it.
Growth.
Maybe temptation still comes, but now you fight instead of comfortably feeding it.
Growth.
Maybe forgiveness still hurts, but you are bringing your bitterness to Jesus instead of building your identity around it.
Growth.
Maybe you missed prayer yesterday, but today your heart aches to return.
Growth.
Maybe you still cry over what happened to you, but you no longer believe your wound has the authority to define your future.
Growth.
Maybe you fell again—but this time you stopped making excuses.
Growth.
Fruit grows slowly.
Roots grow where nobody applauds.
And some of God's deepest work happens underground long before anyone else sees the evidence.
So do not despise what Christ is doing merely because it is not dramatic enough for social media.
Stay near Jesus.
Open Scripture when you feel nothing.
Pray when the words come out broken.
Confess sin quickly.
Seek mature believers who will tell you truth instead of merely protecting your feelings.
Belong to a faithful local church where Scripture is taught and Christ is honored.
Receive correction.
Forgive.
Serve when nobody notices.
Give without needing applause.
Turn off what keeps poisoning your mind.
Run from temptation before you feel strong enough to resist it.
Stop negotiating with what Jesus has already told you to surrender.
And when you fail...
run back to Christ.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Not because sin is trivial.
Because His grace is greater than your ability to rescue yourself.
There is another danger we rarely discuss.
You can become addicted to Christian content without becoming devoted to Christ.
Another sermon.
Another reel.
Another devotional.
Another podcast.
Another quote.
Another article.
Another theological argument.
Another emotional worship video.
Consume.
Scroll.
Feel convicted.
Forget it.
Repeat.
Information enters the mind but never reaches the feet.
James warns against hearing the Word without doing it.
Imagine standing in front of a mirror, seeing exactly what needs attention, walking away, and immediately forgetting what you saw.
That is the tragedy of conviction without response.
You can be moved and remain unchanged.
You can cry and remain unchanged.
You can shout “Amen” and remain unchanged.
The question is not whether this article made you feel something.
The question is:
What will you do with what God has shown you?
Maybe tonight the next step is not dramatic.
Maybe it is deleting the number.
Maybe it is confessing the lie.
Maybe it is opening the Bible again.
Maybe it is finally forgiving.
Maybe it is asking someone for help.
Maybe it is returning to church.
Maybe it is admitting that your secret sin has become slavery.
Maybe it is getting on your knees beside your bed and saying the most honest prayer you have prayed in years:
“Jesus, I need You.”
Not eloquent.
Not impressive.
Just true.
If that is you, understand this carefully.
You do not clean yourself up so Jesus will finally want you.
Come to Him.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive His mercy.
And let the One who saved you begin changing what you could never change alone.

And if Christ has already been transforming wounds, habits, relationships, desires, or places in your life that once seemed impossible to change, tell somebody what Jesus has done. Your testimony may become the reason another wounded believer realizes there is still hope.
Someone may be one honest encounter with the Gospel away from finally asking for help.
Send this privately to the friend who disappeared from church.
Share it with the believer who thinks struggling means God has abandoned them.
Because there may come a night when the person who needs to read these words again is you.
It does not purchase blessing.
It does not make you more righteous.
It does not earn salvation.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
But voluntary generosity can help Gospel ministry reach people.
Supporting this particular ministry is an invitation, never a biblical requirement; Scripture calls Christian giving willing rather than coerced.
Come closer to Jesus.
Because someday your books will remain on a shelf.
Your shirts will fade.
Your mugs will break.
Your followers will forget your posts.
Your achievements will belong to history.
Your body will return to dust.
And none of us will stand before God boasting about how polished our Christian image looked online.
We need Christ.
We need His righteousness.
His mercy.
His blood.
His resurrection.
His grace.
And if you have been spiritually asleep, wake up.
If you have wandered, come home.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you are exhausted, abide in Christ.
If you are ashamed, stop hiding from the Savior who already knows the truth.
If you are growing slowly, keep going.
If you fell yesterday, turn toward Jesus today.
And if you suddenly realized that you have spent years looking Christian while your heart has remained untouched...
do not waste that realization.
Run to Jesus.
Because perhaps the most frightening Christian life is not the visibly scandalous one.
Perhaps it is the life that becomes so comfortable around holy things that it no longer notices it has stopped growing.
And perhaps the greatest scandal of grace is this:
The moment you finally stop pretending you do not need rescuing may become the moment you discover just how far Jesus was willing to go to rescue you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Samson Could Defeat an Army… But He Couldn’t Defeat the Desire Destroying Him
paragraphs: Samson Could Defeat an Army… But He Couldn’t Defeat the Desire Destroying Him

He could tear apart a lion, carry away a city gate, and leave armies broken behind him. But the enemy that finally brought Samson to his knees was not standing in front of him. It was a desire he kept allowing to live inside him.
There is a terrifying kind of strength that can make everyone around you believe you are winning while something inside you is quietly killing you.
Samson knew that kind of strength.
He was the man people feared.
The man enemies planned around.
The man whose name could make Philistines nervous.

He could tear a lion apart with his bare hands. He could strike down enemies in astonishing numbers. He could rip ropes from his arms. He could take the doors of Gaza's city gate, along with their posts, put them on his shoulders, and carry them away.
Imagine seeing that man walking toward you.
You would probably assume nothing could destroy him.
But you would be wrong.
Because sometimes the most dangerous enemy in your life is not the one strong enough to overpower you.
It is the one you keep inviting back.
And that is why Samson's story is not merely an ancient story about a strong man and a seductive woman.
It is a mirror.
Maybe an uncomfortable one.
Samson's story begins before Samson was even born. His birth was announced by the angel of the LORD, and he was set apart for a divine purpose. Judges 13:5 describes him with the Hebrew expression:
נְזִיר אֱלֹהִים — nezir Elohim
A Nazirite, one consecrated or set apart to God.
The angel said that Samson would begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines.
Before Samson had muscles, he had a calling.
Before anyone knew his name, God had placed purpose over his life.
That matters because Samson's tragedy was not that he had no purpose.
It was that extraordinary gifting did not automatically produce extraordinary character.
And Christians desperately need to understand the difference.
You can be gifted and still be vulnerable.
You can know Scripture and still entertain temptation.
You can serve in ministry and still have a secret life.
You can encourage everybody else while privately starving.
You can sing worship songs while feeding something God has been asking you to surrender.
You can look spiritually powerful in public while becoming spiritually careless in private.

Samson's supernatural strength came from God. Judges repeatedly connects his extraordinary acts with the Spirit of the LORD coming powerfully upon him. His hair was not a magical battery. The uncut hair belonged to the sign of his consecration as one set apart to God.
And that distinction changes everything.
Samson's deepest problem was never simply a haircut.
His downfall was the culmination of a life increasingly careless with consecration.
Watch the pattern.
Samson goes down to Timnah and sees a Philistine woman.
His response is revealing.
He wants what he sees.
Later he goes to Gaza and sleeps with a prostitute.
Then comes Delilah.
Again and again, Samson walks dangerously close to what can destroy him because he has learned something incredibly dangerous:
He has survived before.
That may be one of the most frightening conditions a believer can enter.
When God's mercy yesterday becomes your excuse for disobedience today.
You compromised before and nothing immediately collapsed.
You went back to the website.
Nothing happened.
You reopened the conversation.
Nothing happened.
You entertained the fantasy.
Nothing happened.
You lied and covered it.
Nothing happened.
You returned to the relationship God had already exposed.
Nothing happened.
You drank again.
You gambled again.
You fed the bitterness again.
You flirted with the attention again.
You kept the secret again.
And because judgment did not arrive immediately, you started confusing God's patience with God's permission.
Samson kept escaping.
Until one day he didn't.
That is how many strong people fall.
Not suddenly.
Gradually.
One tolerated compromise at a time.
One boundary moved.
One warning ignored.
One secret protected.
One prayer postponed.
One conviction silenced.
One more night telling yourself:
"I can handle this."
Then Delilah enters the story.
Judges 16 says Samson loved her.
The Philistine rulers recognized an opportunity and offered her money to discover the source of his strength.
She began pressing him.
Samson lied to her.
She tried what he told her.
He escaped.
Then he lied again.
She tried again.
He escaped again.
Then again.
Stop there.
Because this is where the story becomes painfully modern.
Samson now had evidence that this relationship was dangerous.
He did not need another sign.
He did not need another confirmation.
He did not need another prophetic word.
The warning was happening directly in front of him.
Yet he stayed.
Why?
Scripture does not give us a psychological diagnosis, and we should not invent one.
But Scripture does show us his behavior.
He continued placing himself near the thing threatening his calling.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You already know.
That relationship keeps dragging you away from Christ.
You know.
