He was beaten, imprisoned, rejected, shipwrecked, hungry, endangered and persecuted.
And Jesus?
Jesus was perfectly righteous.
Perfectly obedient.
Perfectly faithful.
And He was crucified.
If material prosperity were the reliable evidence of God's favor, Calvary would become one of the hardest scenes in the Bible to explain.
But Calvary is not evidence that the Gospel failed.
Calvary is the Gospel.
This is where Christianity becomes scandalous.
The prosperity gospel says blessing looks like climbing.
Jesus reveals glory through descending.
The world says greatness means being served.
Jesus washes feet.
The world says winning means preserving yourself.
Jesus gives Himself away.
The world says power means avoiding weakness.
Christ displays divine power through what looked, for a moment, like catastrophic defeat.
And Paul captures something astonishing about this in 2 Corinthians 8:9.
The Greek text reads:
γινώσκετε γὰρ τὴν χάριν τοῦ κυρίου ἡμῶν Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ὅτι δι’ ὑμᾶς ἐπτώχευσεν πλούσιος ὤν, ἵνα ὑμεῖς τῇ ἐκείνου πτωχείᾳ πλουτήσητε.
“For you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, for your sake He became poor, so that through His poverty you might become rich.”
Pay attention to the movement.
ἐπτώχευσεν — eptōcheusen — “He became poor.”
And then:
πλουτήσητε — ploutēsēte — “you might become rich.”
Those words are real.
But context matters.

Paul is not writing a secret formula teaching the Corinthians how to transform donations into personal luxury. Second Corinthians 8 is saturated with grace, generosity, sacrifice and concern for others. Paul points to Christ's self-emptying generosity as the supreme pattern for Christian giving.
Jesus does not become the mascot of accumulation.
Jesus becomes the model of self-giving love.
The riches of Christ cannot honestly be reduced to a larger bank account.
Forgiveness is wealth.
Reconciliation with God is wealth.
Adoption is wealth.
The Holy Spirit is wealth.
Eternal life is wealth.
Freedom from condemnation is wealth.
Knowing Christ is wealth.
Being able to lose what the world calls everything and still possess a kingdom that cannot be shaken...
that is wealth the stock market cannot measure.
And here is where one of the most frequently quoted prosperity-adjacent verses becomes almost painfully beautiful when we stop ripping it from its surroundings.
“I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.”
Philippians 4:13.
You have seen it on shirts.
Athletes quote it.
Entrepreneurs post it.
People attach it to winning championships, getting promotions, achieving dreams and overcoming impossible goals.
But listen to Paul immediately around that famous sentence.
He says he knows how to live with plenty.
And he knows how to live with hunger.
He knows abundance.
And he knows need.
Before that, Philippians 4:11 says:
οὐχ ὅτι καθ’ ὑστέρησιν λέγω, ἐγὼ γὰρ ἔμαθον ἐν οἷς εἰμι αὐτάρκης εἶναι.
Paul says he has learned to be content in whatever circumstances he is in.
The word αὐτάρκης — autarkēs carries the idea of being content or sufficient.
Do you see what happened?
The verse so often turned into a slogan for achievement was spoken by a man explaining Christ-given strength for both abundance and deprivation.
“I can do all things through Christ” does not merely mean, “Jesus will help me reach the top.”
It includes something far more dangerous to our idols:
“Jesus can hold me together even when I don't.”
Even when the money disappears.
Even when the opportunity closes.
Even when obedience costs me.
Even when the prayer is not answered the way I begged.
Even when following Jesus leads through a valley instead of around it.
Christ is enough there too.
That is a Gospel worth dying for.
And some did.
This does not mean money is evil.
Scripture does not teach that.
This does not mean every wealthy Christian is compromised.
Scripture does not teach that either.
Abraham possessed wealth. Job possessed tremendous resources. There were people of means who supported Jesus' ministry. Wealthy believers existed in the early church.
The problem is not possessing possessions.
The danger begins when possessions possess us.

Paul does not command wealthy Christians in 1 Timothy 6 simply to throw everything away. He tells them not to become arrogant or put their hope in uncertain riches, but in God. Then comes a remarkable line.
ἀγαθοεργεῖν, πλουτεῖν ἐν ἔργοις καλοῖς...
Do good.
πλουτεῖν ἐν ἔργοις καλοῖς — ploutein en ergois kalois — “be rich in good works.”
Then Paul speaks of generosity and willingness to share.
God is not ashamed of the word “rich.”
He simply has a radically different definition of what deserves to make you rich.
Imagine that.
Rich in mercy.
Rich in generosity.
Rich in good works.
Rich in love.
Rich toward God.
A person can have millions in the bank and be spiritually bankrupt.
Another person can have almost nothing the world envies and go to sleep possessing Christ.
Which one is truly rich?
Jesus Himself warned that life does not consist in the abundance of possessions.
He told the rich fool about a man who accumulated more and more for himself, built bigger barns, and believed his stored wealth guaranteed years of comfort.
Then came the sentence no investment portfolio could prevent:
His life was required of him.
The man's tragedy was not simply that he had possessions.
His tragedy was that he had prepared for retirement but not eternity.
He had full barns and an empty soul.
And there are people reading this right now who understand that more personally than they want to admit.
You finally got something you prayed for...
and discovered you were still empty.
You earned more...
but worried more.
You bought the thing...
and the excitement died faster than expected.
You received the promotion...
then immediately needed another achievement to feel important.
You got noticed...
then became terrified of being forgotten.
You accumulated...
but never arrived.
And perhaps nobody knows.
Your Facebook pictures look fine.
Your family thinks you're doing well.
Your friends assume you're blessed.
You know the language.
“God is good.”
“Highly favored.”
“Blessed beyond measure.”
But somewhere underneath the Christian vocabulary is an exhausted soul whispering:
Why isn't any of this enough?
Because it was never designed to be.
Money makes a terrible messiah.
Success makes a terrible savior.
Comfort makes a terrible god.
They demand everything and cannot forgive a single sin.
Jesus can.
And perhaps the most damaging part of prosperity theology is not merely what it says about money.
It is what it can make suffering Christians believe about God.
Imagine the mother who prayed for healing and still stood beside a grave.
Imagine the faithful father who lost his job.
Imagine the missionary who obeyed God and became sick.
Imagine the believer who tithed faithfully and still faced foreclosure.
Imagine the Christian persecuted because he refused to deny Jesus.
Then imagine telling them that enough faith should have guaranteed the outcome they wanted.
That is not merely bad theology.
It can become cruelty wearing Bible verses.
The New Testament never promises Christians immunity from suffering.
Jesus warned His disciples about tribulation.
Paul suffered repeatedly.
Peter wrote to believers enduring fiery trials.
James taught believers how to endure trials.
Revelation honors saints who remained faithful even unto death.
Christianity does not promise that nothing painful will happen to you.
Christianity announces that nothing—not even death—can ultimately separate those in Christ from the love of God.
That promise is better.
Because the prosperity gospel works beautifully...
until the diagnosis.
Until the funeral.
Until bankruptcy.
Until betrayal.
Until persecution.
Until the miracle does not happen.
Until you have prayed the same prayer for five years and heaven seems silent.
Then you need more than a formula.
You need Someone.
You need Jesus.
The Jesus who wept.
The Jesus who was rejected.
The Jesus who knew anguish.
The Jesus who prayed in Gethsemane.
The Jesus who was betrayed by a friend.
The Jesus who carried a cross.
The Jesus who entered death itself.
And the Jesus who walked out of the grave.
That is why biblical Christianity can stare suffering directly in the face without pretending suffering is good.
Our hope is not that Christians never enter graves.
Our hope is that Jesus Christ conquered one.
And suddenly the scandal becomes grace.
Because maybe you came to Jesus thinking He would make your life easier.
Then somewhere along the road you discovered something greater:
He came to make you His.
Maybe you wanted His gifts.
And through heartbreak you learned to want the Giver.
Maybe you wanted Him to change your circumstances.
And while you were begging Him to change everything around you, He began changing something inside you.
Maybe you prayed, “Jesus, get me out.”
And sometimes He did.
But sometimes He whispered through His Word:
“I will walk with you through.”
There are miracles where God removes the furnace.
And there are miracles where God meets His people in the fire.
Do not confuse the second with abandonment.
The cross proves that apparent defeat is not evidence that God has lost control.
And resurrection proves suffering does not get the final word.
This is where the Gospel reaches deeper than prosperity ever could.
You have sinned.
So have I.
Not merely mistakes.
Sin.
Pride.
Lust.
Greed.
Bitterness.
Selfishness.
Secret compromises.
Things we would delete before handing someone our phone.
Thoughts we would never project onto a church screen.
Moments hidden beneath respectable Christian appearances.
And no financial breakthrough can repair our greatest problem.
We don't primarily need God to make us comfortable.
We need God to make us alive.
We need forgiveness.
We need reconciliation.
We need a righteousness we cannot manufacture.
We need a Savior.
Jesus Christ lived the righteousness we failed to live, went willingly to the cross, bore sin, died, and rose again.
The Gospel is not:
“Believe in Jesus and become rich.”
The Gospel is infinitely greater:
Repent and believe in Jesus Christ, and the sinner who deserves judgment can receive mercy, forgiveness, reconciliation with God and eternal life through Him.
That is prosperity no recession can touch.
That is treasure thieves cannot steal.
That is inheritance death cannot cancel.
That is why repentance is not God's attempt to ruin your life.
Repentance is turning from the lies that are ruining you and returning to the One who gives life.
Maybe one of those lies has been this:
If God really loves me, He will give me what I want.
Look again at the cross.
God's love is not ultimately measured by the size of your house.
God's love was displayed at Golgotha.
The Son of God stretched out His hands.
Nails went through them.
And grace answered a question money never could:
“What can wash away my sin?”
Not success.
Not positive thinking.
Not a seed offering.
Not religious performance.
Jesus.
Only Jesus.
So if this article has made you uncomfortable, don't immediately think about somebody else's preacher.
Ask the harder question.
What do I actually love Jesus for?
Would I still call Him good if the promotion never came?
Would I still worship if the business failed?
Would I still follow if obedience cost me popularity?
Would I still believe if my prayer received an answer I did not want?
If everything temporary were stripped away...
would Christ still be enough?
That question frightens me too.
Because discipleship is easier when Jesus and our desires are traveling in the same direction.
The test comes when they separate.
And somewhere in that painful intersection, faith stops being transactional.
You stop saying:
“God, I will follow You so that You will give me this.”
And eventually your trembling heart learns another prayer:
“Jesus, even if I lose this...
don't let me lose You.”
That is freedom.
Maybe your bank account will grow.
Maybe it won't.
Maybe God will entrust enormous resources to you, and if He does, use them with humility and radical generosity for His glory and the good of others.
Maybe He will call you into a simpler life.
Maybe doors will open.
Maybe obedience will close doors you desperately wanted.
Christianity cannot be reduced to promising which circumstance will happen.
But it can tell you who will remain faithful in every circumstance.
Christ.
Always Christ.
And if this exposed something hidden in you—some place where you have quietly treated God like a transaction—don't hide behind religious language.
Not because typing words earns a blessing.
It doesn't.
But because Christians were never meant to suffer anonymously while pretending everything is fine.
Someone reading may desperately need your testimony tonight.

Not because saving a post makes you more spiritual, but because there may come a day when disappointment tries to convince you God abandoned you—and you may need to remember that Christianity never promised an easy road.
It promised a risen Savior.
And there is another way you can help.
It cannot.
Not because giving forces God to prosper you.
It doesn't.
And not because anyone can purchase a blessing from Jesus.
Grace cannot be bought.
Support should flow from gratitude, stewardship and a willing heart—not spiritual coercion.
But ministry does require people who willingly stand behind the work.
Not to glorify Gospel Warrior.
Not to glorify yourself.
Let it point to Jesus.
Because perhaps someone you know has spent years believing that their empty wallet meant God rejected them...
that their illness meant they failed...
that their unanswered prayer meant they lacked faith...
that their suffering meant Jesus had walked away.
Maybe your share is how that person encounters a truth they should have heard long ago:
The Gospel was never “Come to Jesus and you will never suffer.”
The Gospel is that the Holy One came for sinners.
The King wore thorns.
The Rich One became poor.
The Innocent One was condemned.
The Crucified One rose.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The wandering can come home.
The spiritually dead can live.
And the person whose earthly life looks shattered can still possess an eternal treasure beyond calculation because Jesus Christ is not merely the giver of treasure.
Jesus Christ is the treasure.
So no...
the New Testament does not promise you your best life now.
It announces something infinitely greater.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ saves sinners.
Christ remains faithful in abundance and in need.
Christ is worth following when the miracle comes.
Christ is worth following when it doesn't.

And when every house is eventually left behind, every possession passes into someone else's hands, every trophy gathers dust, every account belongs to another generation, and every earthly empire becomes history...
the person who has Christ will discover that the only Treasure death could not take was the Treasure grace had already given.
If Jesus is only precious to you when His hands are full of gifts, you may not yet understand why His nail-scarred hands are enough.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE SIN THE BIBLE NEVER ROMANTICIZED: What Polygamy Reveals About the Human Heart—and the One-Flesh Love God Intended
paragraphs: THE SIN THE BIBLE NEVER ROMANTICIZED: What Polygamy Reveals About the Human Heart—and the One-Flesh Love God Intended

Scripture records men with multiple wives. That does not mean Scripture celebrates what they did. Follow the story carefully enough, and something painful begins to emerge: divided beds so often became divided homes, divided loyalties, wounded hearts—and sometimes hearts divided from God Himself.
There is a dangerous way to read the Bible.
You can mistake description for approval.

You can read that Abraham had Hagar, Jacob had Leah and Rachel, David had multiple wives, and Solomon had hundreds of wives and concubines—and conclude, “If these men belonged to God, perhaps polygamy was acceptable to God.”
But the Bible is far more honest than that.
Scripture does not airbrush its heroes.
It exposes them.

It lets you walk into their tents after the wedding celebrations are over. It lets you hear jealousy between women who wanted to be loved. It lets you see children growing up inside rivalry. It lets you watch powerful men take what they wanted and then live with consequences they could not control.
And perhaps that is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because this article is not ultimately about how many wives ancient men had.
It is about what happens whenever human desire tries to rewrite what God designed.
Go back before Abraham.
Before Jacob.
Before David.
Before Solomon.
Before Israel had kings, palaces, wars, concubines, political marriages, or complicated family trees.
Go back to Eden.
God creates the man. God creates the woman. And Genesis 2:24 gives the foundational pattern:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” — Genesis 2:24, KJV
The Hebrew is striking:
וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ … וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
vedaḇaq be’ishto … vehayu levasar eḥad
The thought is: he clings, holds fast, to his wife, and they become one flesh.
Basar eḥad.
One flesh.
Not merely shared property.
Not merely sexual access.
Not merely an arrangement for producing heirs.
A covenantal union in which two lives are joined.
And centuries later, when religious leaders questioned Jesus about marriage, Christ did something enormously important.
He did not point them to Abraham's household.
He did not use Jacob's marriages as the standard.
He did not appeal to David's royal household.
He went back to creation.
Jesus quoted Genesis and said:
“They twain shall be one flesh.” — Matthew 19:5, KJV
The Greek says:
οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
hoi dýo eis sárka mían
“The two into one flesh.”
Then Jesus continued:
“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.” — Matthew 19:6, KJV
That matters.
The Christian vision of marriage must begin where Jesus began—not with every marital arrangement Scripture records in a fallen world, but with God's creational design.
And this is where we need biblical precision.

It would be careless to claim that every Old Testament instance of plural marriage is explicitly labeled with the sentence, “This is the sin of polygamy.” The Mosaic Law contains regulations addressing situations where plural marriages existed, including protections concerning inheritance and treatment of wives (see Exodus 21:10–11; Deuteronomy 21:15–17). Regulation of a fallen social reality, however, is not the same thing as establishing that reality as God's creation ideal.
The Bible sometimes regulates broken situations without presenting the brokenness as the pattern to pursue.

Jesus Himself gives us the interpretive principle when discussing another marital distortion—divorce. Moses permitted certain things, Jesus explained, “because of the hardness of your hearts,” but then He said:
“from the beginning it was not so.” — Matthew 19:8, KJV
Those words should make us tremble whenever we try to build God's ideal from human behavior rather than God's design.
From the beginning.
Look there.
And when we do, polygamy begins to reveal something larger than marital arithmetic.
It reveals the tragedy of the divided heart.
Consider the first man Scripture explicitly identifies as taking two wives.
It was not Abraham.
It was Lamech, in the violent line of Cain.
Genesis 4:19 says:
“And Lamech took unto him two wives.”

The text does not stop to preach a sermon against him at that moment, but its literary setting is sobering. Lamech appears in a genealogy increasingly marked by humanity's rebellion, and soon he is boasting of violence and vengeance.

That does not mean having two wives is presented as the cause of all Lamech's wickedness. It means we should be careful before treating the Bible's first explicit plural marriage as though Scripture introduced it as an ideal family portrait.
Then comes Abraham.
God had promised him descendants.
But waiting hurt.
Time passed.
Sarah remained barren.
And eventually human beings did what human beings still do when God's promise seems too slow:
they tried to help God fulfill His word.
Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham.
A child was conceived.
And almost immediately, the household fractured.
Genesis 16 describes contempt, jealousy, harsh treatment, and Hagar fleeing into the wilderness.
Think about that.
A decision intended to solve pain multiplied pain.
One woman's infertility became another woman's exploitation and suffering.
One man's attempt to secure an heir produced a home filled with tension.
Yet even there, God saw Hagar.
That detail should not be missed.
The Lord met the woman who fled into the wilderness.
The human family had become complicated.
God's mercy had not.
Then Jacob.
Here is where the story becomes almost unbearable if you stop reading it as an ancient genealogy and start reading it as a household.
Jacob loved Rachel.
But through Laban's deception he received Leah first, then Rachel, and eventually children were borne through Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah.
And Genesis does not give us a glamorous portrait of a man surrounded by women.
It gives us Leah.
A woman who knew she was less loved.
Imagine carrying that into bed.
Imagine waking beside a husband knowing his heart is longing for your sister.
Leah bears Reuben and says, in effect, perhaps now my husband will love me.
Then another son.
And another.
Again and again, childbirth becomes entangled with the aching hope that maybe this time she will finally be cherished.
Meanwhile Rachel envies her sister because Rachel cannot conceive.
One woman has the husband's affection and aches for children.
The other bears children and aches for the husband's affection.
Everyone possesses something someone else desperately wants.
Almost nobody is whole.
That is not romantic.
That is heartbreak.

And this is where the sins surrounding polygamous relationships become painfully visible: jealousy, favoritism, rivalry, envy, manipulation, sexual competition, bitterness, neglect, exploitation, and the temptation to treat another human being as a means of satisfying desire, securing status, producing heirs, or increasing power.
Not every one of those sins occurred identically in every plural marriage recorded in Scripture. We should not accuse biblical characters of sins the text itself does not establish.
But the recurring pattern is impossible to ignore.
A divided household creates opportunities for divided affection.
And divided affection creates wounds.
Then comes David.
David loved God.
David wrote psalms.
David defeated Goliath.
David was called a man after God's own heart.
And David also sinned catastrophically.
Those truths exist in the same Bible because Scripture refuses to turn its servants into idols.
God had already given Israel's future kings a warning:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away.” — Deuteronomy 17:17, KJV
Notice the danger God identifies.
The heart.
This is not merely about how many names appear on a marriage certificate.
It is about what multiplication can do to allegiance.
David accumulated wives, and later his lust for Bathsheba crossed into unmistakable adultery, deception, abuse of royal power, and the arranged death of Uriah.

Polygamy and David's adultery with Bathsheba should not simply be collapsed into the same offense; Scripture treats the Bathsheba episode with particular severity. But David's life destroys the fantasy that spiritual greatness makes a person immune to sexual compromise.
You can worship deeply and still need boundaries.
You can know Scripture and still rationalize desire.
You can have a history with God and still make decisions that devastate other people.
Then Solomon takes the warning to its terrifying conclusion.
Solomon had wisdom almost beyond imagination.
But wisdom possessed is not always wisdom obeyed.
First Kings 11 tells us Solomon had seven hundred wives who were princesses and three hundred concubines.
Then comes the sentence that should haunt every person who thinks compromise can remain contained:
“and his wives turned away his heart.” — 1 Kings 11:3, KJV
There it is.
Exactly what Deuteronomy warned about.
The heart turned.

Solomon's problem was not merely that his household was enormous. His marriages, including alliances with foreign women who worshiped other gods, became entangled with idolatry. First Kings 11 says that when Solomon was old, his wives turned his heart after other gods.
The man who built the temple began accommodating idols.
The man famous for wisdom acted foolishly.
The king who had almost everything slowly surrendered the one thing he could never afford to divide:
his heart.
And perhaps you are reading this thinking, I am not polygamous. What does this have to do with me?
Maybe more than you think.
Because you can have only one spouse and still possess a divided heart.
You can be married and secretly maintain an emotional relationship with someone else.
You can never physically commit adultery and still feed lust through pornography.
You can tell your spouse, “I love you,” while privately comparing them with somebody on your screen.
You can preserve the appearance of faithfulness while fantasizing about another life.
Jesus did not merely confront behavior.
He went after the heart.
He taught that lustful looking itself can become adultery of the heart (Matthew 5:27–28).
That destroys our hiding places.
Suddenly this is no longer an article about Solomon.
It is about us.
The hidden messages.
The deleted conversations.
The fantasy nobody knows about.
The second relationship we have been calling “just friendship.”
The pornography history we clear.
The emotional affair we refuse to name.
The hunger for attention from someone who is not our spouse.
The secret belief that one covenant is not enough because one person cannot satisfy every craving inside us.
And beneath so much sexual sin is an ancient lie:
God's boundaries are keeping something good from me.
That lie is older than polygamy.
It was whispered in Eden.
Take.
Reach.
You deserve more.
God is withholding.
And humanity has been reaching ever since.
But there is another danger here.
Somebody may read an article like this and immediately think about someone else's sin.
“My husband needs this.”
“My wife needs this.”
“My father needs this.”
“That pastor needs this.”
“That man with two women needs this.”
Maybe.
But before you send it to them, let Scripture search you.
Where is your heart divided?
Where have you demanded from created things what only Christ can give?
Where have you justified something because culture permits it?
Where have you confused God's patience with God's approval?
Where have you used biblical characters to excuse behavior instead of allowing the whole counsel of Scripture to correct you?
And if your past is sexually complicated, hear this carefully.
The Gospel is not good news because your history can be edited.
The Gospel is good news because your history can be redeemed.
Jesus Christ did not come for people with immaculate relationship histories.
He came for sinners.
Adulterers need Him.
The sexually broken need Him.
The betrayed need Him.
The betrayer needs Him.
People carrying shame from relationships they wish they could erase need Him.
People living with consequences that cannot simply be undone need Him.
People who knew better and did it anyway need Him.
And people who were wounded by somebody else's selfishness need Him too.
At the cross, Jesus does not call evil good.
He does something infinitely better.
He bears the judgment sinners deserve so that those who repent and believe can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed.
That is why grace is not permission to continue sinning.
Grace teaches us to leave darkness.
Grace says you do not have to keep becoming the person your appetite has been creating.
Grace says confession does not have to be the final chapter.
Grace says repentance is not God humiliating you—it is God calling you out of the grave.
First Corinthians 6 names forms of sexual immorality among sins incompatible with inheriting God's kingdom when they characterize unrepentant life. But Paul does not stop with condemnation.
He turns to believers whose pasts were stained and says:
“And such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified…” — 1 Corinthians 6:11, KJV.
Were.
One of the most beautiful words a sinner can hear.
That was you.
That does not have to remain you.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin righteousness.
Not by erasing consequences with religious clichés.
He rewrites everything by meeting guilty people with truth, calling them to repentance, cleansing those who trust Him, and beginning a transformation no human being could manufacture.
That is From Scandal to Grace.
Maybe your scandal was adultery.
Maybe it was lust.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe manipulation.
Maybe serial relationships.
Maybe you betrayed someone.
Maybe someone betrayed you.
Maybe your family was fractured by another person's choices.
Maybe you grew up watching adults compete for affection and you still carry wounds you cannot explain.
Maybe your story is so complicated that when Christians speak about marriage, you quietly feel disqualified from the conversation.
Look at Jesus.
Not at your résumé.
Not at your worst night.
Not at the whispers.
Not at the screenshots.
Not at the relationship you destroyed.
Not at the years you cannot recover.
Look at Christ.

Repentance does not mean pretending consequences disappear. Some wrongs require confession, accountability, restitution where appropriate, wise pastoral counsel, and difficult decisions made according to Scripture. If multiple marriages or complex family obligations already exist, simplistic commands can create further injustice; such situations deserve faithful, case-specific pastoral guidance rather than reckless abandonment of responsibilities.
But nobody is beyond the reach of Christ because their family story became complicated.
Nobody.

The biblical trajectory is clear: creation presents the one-flesh union of man and woman; Jesus deliberately returns marriage ethics to that beginning; Scripture warns against multiplying wives; biblical narratives repeatedly expose the fractures accompanying divided households; and the New Testament describes church overseers and deacons with the expression μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα (mias gynaikos andra), commonly rendered “the husband of one wife” or understood as a “one-woman man” (1 Timothy 3:2, 12; Titus 1:6).
The emphasis is beautiful.
Faithfulness.
Undivided covenant loyalty.
Because Christian marriage ultimately points beyond itself.
Ephesians 5 takes us somewhere astonishing.
Marriage becomes a living picture of Christ and His church.
Jesus does not casually flirt with His bride.
He does not abandon her when she becomes difficult.
He does not exploit her weakness.
He gives Himself for her.
Christ loves sacrificially.
Christ cleanses.
Christ remains faithful.
Christ gives Himself for His bride.
So Christian marriage cannot ultimately be defined by how much desire a person can satisfy.
It must be shaped by the character of Christ.
And that means the deepest question is no longer merely:
“Can I find an argument that permits what I want?”
The deeper question is:
“Does my life tell the truth about Jesus?”
That question reaches beyond marriage.
Into your phone.
Your bedroom.
Your private browser.
Your friendships.
Your fantasies.
Your ambitions.
Your money.
Your secrets.
Your heart.
Perhaps that is why this subject hurts.
We began talking about men with many wives thousands of years ago.
And somehow Scripture walked into our own room.
If this exposed something hidden, do not run from Jesus.
Run to Him.
And if you know someone quietly drifting toward a decision that could fracture a marriage, wound children, or turn a heart away from God, share this with them privately.
Not to prove you are righteous.
Not to shame somebody.
Not to build Gospel Warrior's name.

Supporting Christian ministry should never be treated as a way to purchase God's favor, prove that you glorify God, or manipulate Him into blessing you. We glorify God through Christ-centered obedience, generosity, worship, love, and faithful stewardship. But when you freely choose to support sound Gospel ministry, your generosity can help that ministry reach more people.
More importantly, stay because you want to grow.
But whatever you do after reading this, do not reduce the message to a debate about ancient marriage customs.
Remember the heart.
Lamech's world warns us what human rebellion can normalize.
Abraham's household reminds us what happens when human solutions try to outrun God's timing.
Jacob's family lets us hear the cries of people competing to be loved.
David warns us that yesterday's devotion does not make today's compromise safe.
Solomon proves that extraordinary wisdom cannot protect a heart that refuses to obey what it knows.
And Jesus takes us back before all the excuses.
Back before the brokenness.
Back to God's intention.
One covenant.
One flesh.
Faithfulness.
And beyond marriage, one heart belonging wholly to God.
Maybe you have already crossed lines you promised yourself you never would.
Maybe your scandal is already written.
Then hear the Gospel one more time.
Your scandal may explain how you arrived here, but surrendered to Christ, it does not get to write your final sentence.
Jesus does.
Because when Jesus enters the story, repentance can replace rebellion, forgiveness can answer guilt, faithfulness can replace divided desire, and grace can begin rebuilding what sin tried to destroy.
The heart that once kept reaching for “more” can finally discover that its deepest need was never another person—it was Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “YOUR MONEY PERISH WITH YOU”—THE TERRIFYING MOMENT A MAN TRIED TO PUT A PRICE ON THE POWER OF GOD
paragraphs: “YOUR MONEY PERISH WITH YOU”—THE TERRIFYING MOMENT A MAN TRIED TO PUT A PRICE ON THE POWER OF GOD

Simon saw something extraordinary in Samaria. He had money in his hands, apostles standing before him, and the power of God unfolding before his eyes. Then Peter spoke words severe enough to expose a temptation that still walks through churches, ministries, platforms, and human hearts today: What happens when we begin wanting what comes from God more than we want God Himself?
There are sentences in Scripture that comfort you.
There are sentences that carry you when grief has emptied the room and you no longer know how to pray.
And then there are sentences that stop you cold.
This is one of them.
“Your money perish with you.”
Imagine hearing those words from the apostle Peter.
Not from an enemy.
Not from someone mocking your faith.
From a man who had walked with Jesus.
A man who had watched Christ touch lepers, forgive sinners, confront religious hypocrisy, carry a cross, die under Roman execution, and rise again.
And Peter was not talking to a pagan who had never heard the Gospel.
He was talking to Simon.
A man who had believed Philip’s preaching and had been baptized.
That should make every Christian read more slowly.
Because Acts 8 is not merely a story about one strange man in ancient Samaria who made one terrible offer.
It holds up a mirror.
And if we are courageous enough to stand in front of it, we may discover that Simon’s temptation did not die with Simon.
It simply learned how to dress differently.
The story begins with a man accustomed to attention.

Acts 8 describes Simon as someone who had previously practiced magic in Samaria and astonished the people. He presented himself as someone great, and people paid attention to him. They were so impressed that they associated him with extraordinary power.
Then Philip arrived.
And suddenly Simon encountered something he could not manufacture.
Philip did not come preaching Philip.
He preached Christ.
Acts 8:5 says Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed Christ to them.
That changes everything.
The center of genuine Christian ministry is never the charisma of the messenger.
Never the size of the platform.
Never the personality.
Never the brand.
Never the merchandise.
Never the bank account.
Never the applause.
Jesus Christ is the center.

Philip preached the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ. Men and women believed and were baptized. Simon himself believed, was baptized, and continued with Philip, astonished by the signs and great miracles taking place.
Think about that.
The man who had once astonished everyone was now astonished himself.
The performer had found a power he could not perform.
The man accustomed to impressing others was now watching works that left him speechless.
Then Peter and John came from Jerusalem.
They prayed for the Samaritan believers, laid hands on them, and the Holy Spirit was given.
Simon saw what happened.
And something inside him moved.
But what moved inside him was precisely the problem.
Scripture says:
“Ἰδὼν δὲ ὁ Σίμων ὅτι διὰ τῆς ἐπιθέσεως τῶν χειρῶν τῶν ἀποστόλων δίδοται τὸ πνεῦμα, προσήνεγκεν αὐτοῖς χρήματα.”
In context, Acts 8:18 means:
“When Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money.”
Money.
Simon looked at the work of the Holy Spirit…
and reached for his wallet.
He said, in essence, “Give me this authority too.”
Do not rush past that.
Simon was not merely asking for prayer.
He wanted the ability associated with what he had witnessed.
He saw spiritual power and apparently imagined that money could obtain it.
Perhaps the old Simon was still breathing underneath the newly baptized Simon.
The old hunger to be somebody.
The old fascination with power.
The old attraction to influence.
The old desire to possess what made crowds look in his direction.
And suddenly Peter answered.
The Greek of Acts 8:20 is devastating:
“Τὸ ἀργύριόν σου σὺν σοὶ εἴη εἰς ἀπώλειαν, ὅτι τὴν δωρεὰν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐνόμισας διὰ χρημάτων κτᾶσθαι.”
A direct rendering is:
“May your silver be with you unto destruction, because you thought the gift of God could be acquired through money.”
The familiar English force of it is unforgettable:
“Your money perish with you.”
But Peter was not declaring that money itself is inherently evil.
Scripture does not teach that.
The problem was Simon’s heart and what he believed money could do.
Peter tells him why.
“You thought the gift of God could be acquired through money.”
There it is.
The scandal.
Simon had encountered grace…
and instinctively tried to turn it into a transaction.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because human beings still try to negotiate with God.
We just use different currency.
“God, if I give enough, will You finally love me?”
“If I serve enough, will You overlook what I did?”
“If I attend church enough, will You owe me a blessing?”
“If I become successful enough, will that prove You approve of me?”
“If I donate enough, will You make my prayer happen?”
“If I look spiritual enough, can I avoid confronting what is actually inside me?”
“If people admire my ministry, does that mean my heart must be right?”
And sometimes the currency is not money at all.
Sometimes we pay with performance.
Reputation.
Religious activity.
Followers.
Titles.
Connections.
Public generosity.
Bible knowledge.
Even ministry.
We place our achievements on the counter and quietly ask heaven:
“Is this enough to buy what I need?”
And the cross answers:
You cannot buy it.
Because Jesus already paid.
That is the difference between the Gospel and every human attempt to save ourselves.
The Gospel does not announce that spiritually impressive people can purchase their way upward.
The Gospel announces that God came down.
We were sinners unable to purchase reconciliation with God, so Christ did what our morality, reputation, religious activity, and money could never accomplish.
He gave Himself.
Peter knew this better than most.
Years earlier, Peter himself had failed spectacularly.
He had promised loyalty to Jesus.
Then came the courtyard.
Questions.
Fear.
Denial.
“I do not know the man.”
Again.
Again.
Again.
Then the rooster.
Imagine Peter’s shame.
Imagine remembering the face of the Christ you swore you would never abandon.
Peter could not purchase his way out of that courtyard.
He could not donate enough to erase three denials.
He could not perform enough miracles to rewrite what he had done.
Peter needed grace.
And after the resurrection, Jesus came for him.
That is why Peter’s warning to Simon must never be separated from the Gospel Peter himself had received.
Peter was not a flawless man looking down upon a dirty sinner.
He was a restored sinner confronting another man whose heart desperately needed God.
Peter continued:
“You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God.”
Then came the command Simon desperately needed.
“Repent.”
Not:
Pay more.
Not:
Build your reputation.
Not:
Prove yourself.
Not:
Purchase another opportunity.
Repent.
Acts 8:22 records Peter telling Simon to repent of his wickedness and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intention of his heart might be forgiven.
That is a hard word.
But it is also mercy.
Because exposure is not always rejection.
Sometimes exposure is the mercy that interrupts us before our hidden desires destroy us.
There are moments when God loves us too deeply to let us remain comfortable with the thing killing our souls.
The Holy Spirit may put His finger on the secret ambition.
The hidden greed.
The obsession with recognition.
The addiction nobody knows about.
The bitterness we have baptized as “discernment.”
The pride disguised as standards.
The envy disguised as concern.
The hunger for spiritual power without the willingness to surrender.
And it hurts.
Of course it hurts.
Surgery hurts too.
But the Surgeon cuts because something precious is worth saving.
Peter tells Simon, “I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity.”
Bondage.
That is what sin eventually does.
It promises control and becomes your master.
It promises pleasure and demands another payment.
It promises significance and makes you terrified of becoming insignificant.
It promises freedom and slowly builds a prison around the heart.
Maybe your prison does not look like Simon’s.
Maybe nobody suspects yours exists.
You still smile.
Still post the verse.
Still say, “God is good.”
Still show up.
Still know when to lift your hands.
Still know Christian vocabulary.
But privately?
You are exhausted.
There is something between you and God, and you know its name.
Perhaps money has become your security.
Perhaps success has become your identity.
Perhaps ministry has become the place where you secretly need applause.
Perhaps you are following Jesus partly because you hope He will give you the life you actually worship.
Perhaps you want His gifts more than His presence.
Perhaps you want His power without His holiness.
His promises without His lordship.
His heaven without His cross.
His forgiveness without repentance.
And perhaps the frightening part is that you can live around Christian things long enough to stop noticing the difference.
Simon had been baptized.
Simon stayed near Philip.
Simon watched miracles.
Simon witnessed apostolic ministry.
Yet Peter still went directly to the condition of his heart.
That should humble us.
Proximity to holy things is not the same as surrender to a holy God.
A Bible in your hand cannot substitute for Christ ruling your heart.
A church seat cannot repent for you.
A Christian family cannot believe for you.
A ministry position cannot sanctify secret sin.
A donation cannot purchase forgiveness.
And no Christian ministry worthy of the Gospel should ever tell you otherwise.
You cannot buy the Holy Spirit.
You cannot buy salvation.
You cannot purchase an answered prayer.
You cannot buy a miracle.
You cannot pay your way into heaven.
You cannot make God owe you because you financially supported His work.
Grace ceases to be grace the moment we imagine it can be purchased.
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
And neither is His blood.
The apostle Peter later wrote that believers were redeemed not with corruptible things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
There is the answer to Simon’s silver.
Silver could not redeem Simon.
Gold cannot redeem you.
Christ can.
The currency at Calvary was not your money.
It was His blood.
The price was not paid by the sinner climbing toward God.
It was paid by the Son of God giving Himself for sinners.
This is why the Gospel can reach the person who thinks he has ruined everything.
Maybe that person is you.
Maybe there are chapters in your life you would burn if memories could be destroyed.
Maybe you have manipulated people.
Maybe greed got into your heart.
Maybe pornography hollowed out your secret life.
Maybe adultery shattered what you promised to protect.
Maybe pride made you cruel.
Maybe religion made you self-righteous.
Maybe money became the god you would never call a god.
Maybe you have spent years presenting a version of yourself that does not exist when the door closes.
And somewhere beneath all the pretending is one terrifying question:
“If Jesus knew everything, would He still want me?”
He already knows.
That is what makes grace so scandalous.
Christ did not go to the cross because humanity was secretly better than it appeared.
He went because our condition was worse than we wanted to admit—and His mercy was greater than we dared imagine.
The cross tells the truth about both.
Your sin was serious enough that Christ had to die.
His love was great enough that He willingly did.
And the resurrection announces that sin, shame, death, and the grave do not get the final sentence over everyone who comes to Christ.
Jesus does.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Peter knew the scandal of denial.
Christ wrote restoration.
Paul knew the scandal of persecuting believers.
Christ wrote apostleship and mission.
The thief beside Jesus knew the scandal of a condemned life.
Christ spoke hope to a dying man who could no longer build a respectable religious résumé.
Again and again, Scripture refuses to pretend sin is harmless.
But Scripture also refuses to pretend sin is stronger than the Savior.
That is why repentance is not God saying, “Clean yourself up so perhaps I will tolerate you.”
Repentance is the sinner turning from sin toward the God whose mercy is found in Jesus Christ.
You stop defending what Christ died to save you from.
You stop calling darkness light.
You stop negotiating.
You stop hiding.
You come empty-handed.
No spiritual résumé.
No bargaining chips.
No silver.
Just:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
And He is not a reluctant Savior.
First John 1:9 teaches that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Jesus said in John 6:37 that the one who comes to Him He will never cast out.
Read that again if shame has been telling you to stay away.
Come.
Not because your sin is small.
Come because Christ is sufficient.
Come because the blood shed at Calvary is greater than the stain you cannot remove yourself.
Come because the tomb is empty.
Come because Jesus still saves sinners.
Come because grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace breaks chains.
Maybe Simon’s story disturbed you because you recognized something.
Sit with it.
Ask the question most of us avoid:
“What do I actually want from Jesus?”
Do I want Him…
or merely what I believe He can give me?
If God removed the applause, would I still worship?
If the promotion never came, would He still be worthy?
If the healing took longer than I hoped, would Christ still be Lord?
If nobody knew my name, would knowing His be enough?
If following Jesus cost me instead of advancing me, would I follow?
Those questions expose things.
Mine too.
Because Simon’s story is not ammunition for pointing at prosperity preachers, corrupt ministries, wealthy Christians, poor Christians, famous pastors, or somebody else we already dislike.
The safest way to read Acts 8 is not:
“Thank God I am not Simon.”
It is:
“Lord, search me.”
Search my motives.
Search my giving.
Search my ministry.
Search my ambition.
Search what I secretly want people to think about me.
Search what I believe money can secure.
Search what I want from You.
And where You find Simon hiding in me…
bring me to repentance.
That prayer is dangerous.
It is also freeing.
Because the Christian life was never supposed to be an exhausting project of protecting an image.
At the foot of the cross, there is finally nowhere left to perform.
You are known.
You are exposed.
You are invited to repent.
And in Christ, there is grace.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail. But you also do not have to pretend conviction never happened.
Someone reading silently may need to discover that repentance is not the end of the story.
It can be where restoration begins.
Not because sharing a Gospel Warrior article earns favor with God.
It does not.
Not because an algorithm can measure your devotion.
It cannot.
Share because somebody you love may be quietly becoming Simon.
Someone may be trying to purchase with performance what can only be received through Christ.
Someone may be surrounded by Christianity while privately drifting from Jesus.
Someone may need to hear tonight that repentance is still possible.
There may come a night when ambition starts whispering again.
A night when money begins feeling more trustworthy than God.
A night when shame tells you to hide.
Come back and remember Simon.
Come back and remember Peter.
Come back and remember the cross.

We want this community to be a place where people encounter daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered not on personalities, but on Jesus Christ.
It does not purchase God’s favor.
It does not purchase the Holy Spirit.
It does not make God owe you a blessing.
Jesus purchased redemption. We never could.

Sharing this article publicly is another. Prayer is another. Telling someone about Jesus is another. Faithful generosity should flow from love for God, not pressure, fear, or an attempt to purchase spiritual reward.
But never confuse supporting the messenger with purchasing the Message.
The Gospel was bought at a price you could never afford…
and then offered to repentant sinners as grace.
Simon reached for silver.
Peter pointed toward repentance.
And Jesus still stands at the center of the story.
So perhaps the most important question is no longer what Simon wanted to buy.
Perhaps it is what you have been trying to buy from God.
Approval?
Security?
Influence?
Forgiveness?
A clean conscience?
A second chance?
Put the silver down.
Put the performance down.
Put the religious résumé down.
Put the secret bargaining down.
You cannot purchase resurrection.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot purchase the love of God.
Come to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive what money could never buy.
And then, because you have received grace, live generously—not to purchase God, but because in Christ you have discovered a treasure money could never contain.
“Jesus, search my heart.”
Sometimes the most dangerous thing in your hand is not the money you are holding—it is the secret belief that there is something Jesus will give you only after you prove you deserve Him.
But at Calvary, empty hands were always the only hands capable of receiving grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ISRAEL’S FIRST KING DIED ON THE BATTLEFIELD—BUT HIS REAL FALL BEGAN YEARS BEFORE THE SWORD
paragraphs: ISRAEL’S FIRST KING DIED ON THE BATTLEFIELD—BUT HIS REAL FALL BEGAN YEARS BEFORE THE SWORD

Saul was chosen, anointed, celebrated, and given a kingdom. Then, little by little, he began protecting the one thing God was asking him to surrender: himself. His death on Mount Gilboa is more than the tragic ending of Israel’s first king. It is a warning about what can happen when a person keeps hearing God while slowly learning how not to obey Him.
There is something terrifying about the final battlefield of King Saul.
Not because swords were flashing.
Not because arrows were falling.
Not because Israel was losing.
The terrifying part is that when Saul finally collapsed on Mount Gilboa, the man dying beneath the weight of his armor was not some pagan king who had never known God.
He had been chosen.
He had been anointed.
He had felt the Spirit of God move upon him.
He had heard the prophet Samuel speak the word of the LORD.
He had been given opportunities many men could only dream of receiving.
And now he was dying.

The Philistines were pressing hard against Israel. Saul watched his sons fall in battle. Among them was Jonathan—the son whose friendship with David became one of Scripture’s most beautiful portraits of covenant loyalty.
Then the archers found Saul.
First Samuel 31:3 describes the horror with painful simplicity: the battle became heavy against him, the archers found him, and he was badly wounded.
The king who had spent years hunting David was now the hunted man.
The king who once commanded armies could not command what happened next.
The king who had desperately tried to preserve his throne was watching his kingdom disappear in blood.
And Saul knew what capture could mean.
So he turned to his armor-bearer and commanded him to draw his sword and kill him, fearing what the Philistines would do if they captured him.
His armor-bearer was terrified and refused.
Then comes one of the darkest sentences in the story of Israel’s monarchy:
וַיִּקַּח שָׁאוּל אֶת־הַחֶרֶב וַיִּפֹּל עָלֶיהָ
Vayyiqqaḥ Sha’ul et-haḥerev vayippol ‘aleha.
“Saul took the sword and fell upon it.”
That is 1 Samuel 31:4.
Read it again slowly.
Saul took the sword.
And fell upon it.
The first king of Israel—the man who once stood above the people physically, the man Samuel had anointed, the man crowds once celebrated—ended his reign bleeding on a mountain.
But Saul’s tragedy did not begin on Mount Gilboa.
Gilboa was where the collapse became visible.
The fall had been happening inside him for years.
And that is what makes Saul’s story so frighteningly relatable.
Because most spiritual disasters do not begin with a battlefield.
They begin with a compromise.
A justification.
A delayed obedience.
A wounded ego.
A jealousy we refuse to kill.
A command from God that we edit until it becomes easier to live with.
A sin we rename because repentance would cost us too much.
Saul did not wake up one morning and decide, “I am going to destroy everything God has given me.”
Almost nobody does.
He drifted.
And perhaps that is why his story should make us examine ourselves before we judge him.

Earlier in Saul’s reign, Samuel confronted him after Saul failed to wait as instructed and offered the sacrifice himself. First Samuel 13 records Samuel telling Saul that he had acted foolishly and that his kingdom would not continue as it otherwise might have.
Yet God still gave Saul more opportunities.
Then came the command concerning Amalek in 1 Samuel 15.
Saul was commanded to carry out judgment, but he spared Agag and preserved the best livestock.
And when Samuel confronted him, Saul initially defended himself.
That moment matters.
Because rebellion becomes especially dangerous when we become skilled at explaining why our disobedience should count as obedience.
Saul told Samuel:
“I have obeyed the voice of the LORD.”
But Samuel could hear sheep.
Imagine that scene.
Saul is claiming obedience while the evidence of his disobedience is making noise behind him.
How many of us have done the same thing?
Maybe not with sheep.
But with browser histories.
Secret conversations.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Pornography.
Dishonest business practices.
An affair we keep calling “a connection.”
Gossip we disguise as concern.
Greed we rename ambition.
Unforgiveness we call boundaries when what we really mean is revenge.
A relationship we know is dragging us from Christ.
A private addiction nobody at church knows exists.
We say, “God, I obey You.”
And somewhere behind us...
the sheep are still making noise.
Samuel answered Saul with words that have echoed for generations:
הִנֵּה שְׁמֹעַ מִזֶּבַח טוֹב
Hinneh shemoa‘ mizzevaḥ tov.
“Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice.”
The Hebrew verb שָׁמַע — shama‘ carries the sense of hearing, listening, and—depending on context—heeding or obeying.
Biblical hearing is not merely sound entering the ear.
God was not looking for Saul merely to acknowledge His command.
He was looking for a heart that would heed Him.
That is where this story comes painfully close.
Because you can hear sermons and still refuse God.
You can highlight your Bible and still refuse God.
You can post verses and still refuse God.
You can sing worship songs with tears running down your face and still protect the very thing Christ is confronting.
Religious activity cannot substitute for surrender.
Samuel eventually told Saul:
יַעַן מָאַסְתָּ אֶת־דְּבַר יְהוָה וַיִּמְאָסְךָ מִמֶּלֶךְ
“Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, He has rejected you from being king.”
That is the terrible irony of Saul.
He spent years desperately trying to keep what his disobedience had already forfeited.
Then David appeared.
Young.
Anointed.
Victorious.
Loved by the people.
And Saul’s insecurity began consuming him.
When the women celebrated David’s victories and sang that Saul had slain his thousands and David his ten thousands, Saul did not simply hear a song.
He heard a threat.
First Samuel 18:9 says that from that day forward Saul watched David suspiciously.
Jealousy changed the way Saul interpreted another person’s blessing.
David’s victory should have benefited Saul’s kingdom.
Instead, Saul experienced David’s success as a personal attack.
That is what insecurity can do.
It can make you resent the person God never asked you to compete with.
It can make another person’s testimony feel like evidence of your failure.
Their ministry grows.
Their marriage heals.
Their prayer is answered.
Their opportunity arrives.
Their business succeeds.
Their family celebrates.
And suddenly something ugly whispers inside you:
“Why them?”
Saul listened to that voice until jealousy became hostility.
Hostility became obsession.
Obsession became pursuit.
Again and again Saul hunted David.
And again and again, remarkably, David refused to seize the throne by murdering Saul.
In 1 Samuel 24, David could have killed Saul in the cave.
He did not.
In 1 Samuel 26, David again had an opportunity to kill him.
He refused.
Saul was chasing the man who repeatedly spared his life.
Think about that.
Saul was treating mercy like an enemy.
And some people reading this are doing something painfully similar with God.
Christ has been calling you.
Convicting you.
Interrupting you.
Exposing things.
Giving you another morning.
Another sermon.
Another warning.
Another opportunity to repent.
Another moment when your conscience suddenly becomes loud.
Another night when you cannot escape the question:
“What am I becoming?”
And because conviction hurts, you have started treating mercy like an enemy.
But conviction is not God delighting in your pain.
Conviction can be mercy knocking before consequences kick the door down.
Saul kept running.
Not geographically from God—as though anyone could escape His presence—but relationally and morally from the God whose word he repeatedly resisted.
Eventually Saul reached one of the darkest nights of his life.
The Philistine army gathered.
Saul was afraid.
Samuel was dead.
And 1 Samuel 28 says Saul inquired of the LORD, but the LORD did not answer him through the means Saul sought.
Then Saul did something staggering.
The king who had removed mediums and spiritists from the land disguised himself and went to a medium at Endor.
The man who desperately wanted guidance from God sought forbidden spiritual counsel.
This is what persistent rebellion can do.
When we repeatedly refuse the truth God has already spoken, desperation can make counterfeit voices increasingly attractive.
Saul wanted an answer.
But throughout his life, his deeper problem had often been what he did when God gave him one.

The scene at Endor is chilling, and Christians should not romanticize it as biblical permission for necromancy. Scripture explicitly condemns occult practices. Whatever questions interpreters discuss concerning the precise mechanics of the extraordinary event in 1 Samuel 28, the narrative itself presents Saul’s consultation of the medium as part of his catastrophic unfaithfulness.
The message Saul received was devastating.
The next day Israel would fall.
Saul and his sons would die.
And now we return to Mount Gilboa.
Arrows.
Blood.
Defeat.
Jonathan dead.
Saul wounded.
A sword.
A final fall.
Yet Scripture gives us something even more important than the battlefield report.
First Chronicles interprets Saul’s death theologically.
It says:
וַיָּמָת שָׁאוּל בְּמַעֲלוֹ אֲשֶׁר מָעַל בַּיהוָה
Vayyamot Sha’ul bema‘alo asher ma‘al baYHWH.
“So Saul died for his unfaithfulness which he committed against the LORD.”
First Chronicles 10:13 continues by identifying his unfaithfulness in relation to the word of the LORD that he did not keep and his consultation with a medium.
Then verse 14 says:
וְלֹא־דָרַשׁ בַּיהוָה
Velo-darash baYHWH.
“And he did not seek the LORD.”
At first that can sound puzzling.
Didn’t 1 Samuel 28:6 say Saul inquired of the LORD?
Yes.
And the distinction is sobering.
First Samuel 28 uses language describing Saul’s inquiry, while Chronicles gives the inspired theological verdict on the direction of Saul’s life: he did not truly דָּרַשׁ — darash, seek the LORD.
Saul wanted answers from God.
But wanting an answer from God is not necessarily the same as wanting God.
There is a difference between seeking God because you love Him and seeking God because your life is collapsing.
There is a difference between asking, “God, get me out of this,” and praying, “God, even if this costs me everything, make me Yours.”
There is a difference between wanting divine assistance and wanting divine authority.
And suddenly Saul is no longer merely an ancient king.
Saul is standing uncomfortably close to us.
Because maybe you have wanted Jesus to fix your marriage without letting Him confront your pride.
Maybe you want Him to remove your anxiety while refusing to surrender the secret life feeding your chaos.
Maybe you want God to bless the relationship He has repeatedly convicted you about.
Maybe you want peace without repentance.
Resurrection without crucifixion.
A crown without surrender.
Grace without Lordship.
You want Jesus near enough to rescue you...
but not near enough to rule you.
Saul’s story warns us where that road can lead.
But this is where the Gospel changes everything.
Because Saul is not the final King.
There is another King.
Jesus Christ.
Saul clung to a throne that was slipping away.
Jesus possessed all authority and humbled Himself.
Saul became consumed with protecting himself from a perceived rival.
Jesus willingly laid down His life for His enemies.
Saul pursued an innocent man.
Jesus allowed sinful men to pursue, arrest, mock, scourge, and crucify Him.
Saul fell upon his own sword on a battlefield of judgment and defeat.
Jesus went willingly to a Roman cross and bore judgment on behalf of sinners.
Saul’s kingship exposes what happens when the human heart rules itself.
Christ’s kingship reveals the beauty of the perfectly obedient Son.
The New Testament describes Jesus’ obedience reaching even unto death—death on a cross.
Where sinful humanity fails, Christ is faithful.
Where we rebel, Christ obeyed.
Where we deserve judgment, Christ offers mercy through His atoning death and victorious resurrection.
This is why Christianity is not ultimately the message:
“Try harder so you don’t become Saul.”
It is:
“Run to Christ because you already need a Savior.”
That distinction is everything.
Saul’s story should produce warning.
But the Gospel produces hope.
Because perhaps you recognize yourself somewhere in this story.
Maybe you have been running.
Maybe your compromise has lasted years.
Maybe you know Christian language so well that you can explain away almost anything.
Maybe nobody knows what you have become in private.
Maybe jealousy is eating you alive.
Maybe lust owns parts of your imagination.
Maybe bitterness has become part of your personality.
Maybe you are exhausted from pretending.
Maybe you have spent years asking God for help while refusing the surrender He has been asking from you.
Hear this carefully.
Do not use Saul’s story to conclude that you are beyond grace.
Use Saul’s story to understand why delayed repentance is dangerous—and then look to Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not tell repentant sinners to clean the blood off themselves before approaching the cross.
Jesus came for sinners.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ rose from the dead.
And the call of the Gospel is not to hide more effectively.
Repent.
Believe.
Come into the light.
Stop defending what Christ died to forgive.
Stop negotiating with what is destroying you.
Stop confusing shame with repentance.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Biblical repentance turns.
It comes home.
It stops arguing with God and begins agreeing with Him about sin.
And faith looks away from our ability to save ourselves and rests in Jesus Christ.
There is forgiveness in Him.
Not cheap forgiveness.
Blood-bought forgiveness.
There is grace.
Not grace that celebrates rebellion, but grace powerful enough to forgive rebels and begin transforming them.
There is restoration.
There is a new Master.
There is a better King.
Jesus.
Maybe this article found you while the sheep are still making noise behind you.
You know what that means.
There is something you have been defending.
Something you need to confess.
Something you need to surrender.
Do not wait for your Mount Gilboa.
Do not wait until consequences finally become louder than conviction.
You do not know how many tomorrows you have.
Today, while your heart can still hear the call, turn to Jesus Christ.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to write the details publicly. But you can take one small step out of isolation.
Or if God has been restoring you after years of running, leave your testimony. Somebody reading the comments may desperately need evidence that Christ still receives prodigals.
And please understand why sharing matters.
You probably know a Saul.
Not a wicked caricature.
A real person.
A brother who used to burn for God.
A daughter quietly drifting.
A friend trapped in compromise.
A churchgoer who knows Scripture but is losing the private war.
A believer who thinks one more hidden sin will not matter.
A seeker who believes his past has already disqualified him from mercy.
Maybe even someone who does not believe in Jesus at all but needs to understand what Christianity actually says about sin, judgment, grace, and redemption.
Not because every sentence is easy to read.
Because some truths need to be revisited when temptation starts rewriting the story.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ.
Your support can help this message travel beyond your screen.
Beyond your church circle.
Beyond people who already agree.
Toward the exhausted believer.
The secret addict.
The wandering son.
The skeptical friend.
The person sitting alone at midnight wondering whether Jesus could possibly want someone like them.
Do it because you want to stay close to Scripture.
Do it because you want biblical nourishment in a world constantly discipling you in another direction.
Do it because spiritual growth requires more than occasional inspiration.
Do it because you want Christ-centered encouragement, conviction, healing, accountability, discipleship, and spiritual sharpening continually pointing you back to Jesus.

And if God has blessed you through this ministry, supporting its work can be one practical expression of gratitude—not a payment to God, not a purchase of His favor, but voluntary support for the continued spread of Gospel-centered truth.
Invite your family.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly.
Because Saul’s grave leaves us with a question far more important than how Israel’s first king died.
What are you doing with the voice of God while you are still alive?
Saul had an anointing.
Saul had opportunities.
Saul had warnings.
Saul had a prophet.
Saul had victories.
Saul had a throne.
But none of those things could replace a surrendered heart.
So do not merely admire Jesus.
Do not merely quote Jesus.
Do not merely post about Jesus.
Do not merely ask Jesus to rescue the parts of your life that hurt.
Bow to the King.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Bring the hidden thing into His light.
Receive the mercy you could never earn.
And follow Christ while today is still called today.
Because the most haunting thing about Saul’s final battlefield is not simply that a king died there.
It is that for years before his body fell on Gilboa, his heart had been teaching itself how to resist the God who had called him.
And the most beautiful thing about the Gospel is that your story does not have to end where your rebellion has taken you.
Jesus Christ still receives repentant sinners.
The cross still announces that sin is more serious than we wanted to believe—and grace is more costly, more astonishing, and more beautiful than we dared to imagine.
The empty tomb still declares that death does not get the final word.
So if you have been running...
turn around.
The King you need is not Saul.
And it is not you.
It is Jesus.
Do not wait until the battlefield takes everything to surrender what Jesus is asking for today.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Rachel Said, “Give Me Children, or I’ll Die”—When Desire Becomes Desperation
paragraphs: Rachel Said, “Give Me Children, or I’ll Die”—When Desire Becomes Desperation

She wanted something good so badly that life without it began to feel unbearable. And somewhere between prayer and comparison, longing became an ultimatum. Rachel’s story is ancient—but if we are brave enough to admit it, her cry still sounds frighteningly familiar.
There are sentences in Scripture that feel less like ancient history and more like someone accidentally opened the door to a private room in the human heart.
Rachel spoke one of them.
“Give me children, or I shall die.”
That is how Genesis 30:1 records her anguish.
The Hebrew is even more arresting:
הָבָה־לִּי בָנִים וְאִם־אַיִן מֵתָה אָנֹכִי
Havah-li vanim, ve’im-ayin, metah anokhi.
“Give me children, and if not, I am dying.”
The Hebrew text really is that stark. Rachel sees that she has not borne children to Jacob, becomes envious of her sister, and cries out to her husband.
Read it slowly, because this is not merely a story about infertility.
It is a story about what happens when a legitimate desire becomes so enormous that we begin asking it to give us what only God can ultimately give.
Rachel wanted a child.
Not money.
Not fame.
Not an empire.
A child.
Something beautiful.
Something deeply human.
Something Scripture itself treats as a blessing.
And that is precisely why her story can reach places in us that warnings about obviously sinful desires sometimes cannot.
Because some of the most dangerous idols in our hearts do not begin as evil things.
They begin as good things we slowly decide we cannot live without.
Maybe yours is marriage.
“God, I’ve waited long enough.”
Maybe it is a baby.
Maybe healing.
Maybe reconciliation.
Maybe financial stability.
Maybe the ministry you thought God promised would grow.
Maybe the person who walked away.
Maybe the apology that never came.
Maybe recognition.
Maybe the career.
Maybe the house.
Maybe the answered prayer you have whispered for so many years that you no longer know whether you are praying from faith or bleeding from disappointment.
You still attend church.
You still say, “God is good.”
You still know the verses.
But somewhere inside you is a sentence you are almost afraid to say aloud:
God, if You don’t give me this, I don’t know how I can be okay.
That is where Rachel meets us.
And before we condemn her, we need to sit beside her.
Because Rachel's pain was real.
Genesis does not introduce her desperation in a vacuum. The family into which she had entered was already fractured by rivalry, favoritism, rejection, competition, and longing.
Jacob loved Rachel, while Leah lived with the agony of being less loved. God saw Leah's suffering and opened her womb, while Rachel remained barren. Leah then bore children while Rachel watched.
Imagine the emotional geography of that house.
One woman had the husband's affection and wanted children.
The other had children and desperately wanted the husband's affection.
Leah was saying, in effect, “Maybe now he will love me.”
Rachel was saying, “Give me children, or I’ll die.”
Two wounded women.
Two different emptinesses.
Same trap.
If I can only get the thing I lack, then I will finally be whole.
That lie is still alive.
We just dress it differently.
We scroll through photographs of engagements while wondering why everyone seems to have found someone except us.
We watch pregnancy announcements while privately grieving another negative test.
We congratulate someone on the promotion we prayed would be ours.
We watch another ministry explode in growth while ours seems invisible.
We see someone our age buying a home, traveling, building a family, succeeding, smiling—and suddenly gratitude evaporates.
Not because their blessing harmed us.
But because their blessing reminded us of our absence.
That is the poison hidden inside comparison.
Rachel did not merely see her empty arms.
She saw Leah's full ones.
Genesis says Rachel envied her sister.
And envy has a cruel way of turning another person's blessing into evidence that God has forgotten you.
Someone else's wedding becomes your rejection.
Someone else's pregnancy becomes your abandonment.
Someone else's breakthrough becomes your accusation against heaven.
Someone else's success becomes proof that you are behind.
But their blessing is not God's verdict against you.
Read that again.
Their blessing is not God's verdict against you.
The person receiving what you desperately want is not proof that God loves them more.
Yet desperation can make the heart interpret life that way.
And eventually desire starts changing its vocabulary.
“I would love this” becomes “I need this.”
“I am praying for this” becomes “God owes me this.”
“This would bring me joy” becomes “I cannot have joy without this.”
Then, almost without noticing, the gift climbs onto the throne.
That is the frightening part.
You can worship an answered prayer before it has even been answered.
You can build your identity around a future spouse you have never met.
You can build your peace around money you do not yet possess.
You can build your worth around a child you are still praying for.
You can build your significance around a ministry God never promised would become famous.
You can make an idol out of something beautiful.
And idols always make terrible saviors.
Rachel turns toward Jacob:
Give me children.
Jacob's response is angry, but underneath it he identifies something Rachel's desperation has obscured: he is not God. Genesis 30:2 has Jacob asking whether he stands “in the place of God.”
In other words:
Rachel, you are asking a human being to do what only God can do.
And suddenly the story stops being only Rachel's story.
How many times have we done the same thing?
We look at a spouse and silently say:
Make me feel valuable.
We look at our children:
Make my life meaningful.
We look at our career:
Tell me I matter.
We look at money:
Make me safe.
We look at followers:
Tell me I am seen.
We look at romance:
Make me whole.
We look at ministry:
Prove God is using me.
We look at another human being and hand them a job description no human being was created to fulfill.
Save me.
Complete me.
Secure me.
Validate me.
Never disappoint me.
Never leave me.
Make the ache disappear.
And then we are devastated when finite people fail under infinite expectations.
There is only one Savior.
His name is Jesus Christ.
That truth does not make legitimate desires illegitimate. Christianity does not require pretending that painful things do not hurt.
Infertility hurts.
Loneliness hurts.
Rejection hurts.
Bereavement hurts.
Waiting hurts.
Watching other people receive what you have begged God for can hurt in places nobody sees.
Biblical faith does not demand that you smile while your heart is breaking.
The Psalms destroy that caricature.
God permits His people to lament.
To weep.
To ask why.
To ask how long.
To bring Him confusion, sorrow, disappointment, and longing.
The problem is not that Rachel desired children.
The warning comes when desire becomes desperation, and desperation begins telling us:
Without this, life has no meaning.
Because the Gospel confronts that sentence.
Not cruelly.
Not dismissively.
But radically.
The Gospel says your deepest life is not located in what you are waiting to receive.
It is located in Christ.
Jesus does not promise that every earthly longing will be fulfilled according to our preferred timetable—or even in the form we desire.
He promises something greater.
Himself.
And this is where Christianity becomes far more than motivational religion.
Jesus did not come merely to help you acquire the life you have designed.
He came to rescue you from sin, reconcile you to God, make you His own, and teach your heart that the Creator is greater than every created gift.
The cross demolishes the lie that God has to give us everything we desire before we can know that He loves us.
Look at Calvary.
The Son of God was pierced for sinners.
Christ bore sin.
Christ endured judgment.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Grace was purchased at a cost we could never pay.
So when your circumstances whisper, “God has forgotten you,” the cross answers:
Look at what He has already done to bring you home.
That does not eliminate grief.
It anchors grief.
There is a difference.
You may cry and still trust.
You may ache and still worship.
You may ask and still surrender.
You may deeply desire something while refusing to make that thing your god.
And perhaps the most astonishing words in Rachel's story arrive later.
After the rivalry.
After the envy.
After Bilhah.
After the household competition.
After years of longing.
Genesis 30:22 says:
“Then God remembered Rachel.”
The Hebrew begins:
וַיִּזְכֹּר אֱלֹהִים אֶת־רָחֵל
Vayizkor Elohim et-Rachel.
“Then God remembered Rachel.”
Scripture then says God listened to her and opened her womb.
Do not misunderstand the word “remembered.”
It does not mean God had misplaced Rachel somewhere in the universe and suddenly thought, “Oh yes—Rachel.”

When Scripture speaks this way of God's remembering, it signals God's purposeful attention and action within His covenant dealings; the same kind of language appears when God “remembered” Noah in Genesis 8:1.
Rachel felt empty.
But she was not invisible.
Rachel was waiting.
But she was not outside God's sight.
Rachel was hurting.
But heaven had not lost her address.
And somebody reading this needs that distinction desperately.
God's silence is not proof of God's absence.
The unanswered prayer is not proof that He stopped listening.
The delay is not automatically punishment.
Someone else's blessing is not evidence of your rejection.

And you must be especially careful not to turn Rachel's eventual pregnancy into a formula promising that every Christian who waits long enough will eventually receive the exact earthly outcome desired.
That would not be faithful to Scripture.
