Some prayers receive the answer we hoped for.
Others receive a different answer.
Some wounds are healed here.
Others await resurrection.
Some doors open.
Others remain closed despite sincere prayer.
Faith is not a technique for controlling God.
Faith says:
Even here, You are God.
That is where desperation begins becoming surrender.
And surrender is not giving up.
Surrender is giving God back His throne.
It sounds like:
“Father, I still want this.”
“I still ache.”
“I still hope.”
“I will still ask.”
“But I refuse to make this desire my master.”
“If You give it, I will worship You.”
“If You make me wait, teach me to worship You.”
“If Your answer looks different from mine, hold me while I learn to trust You.”
“Jesus, I want You more than I want the life I imagined.”
That prayer can hurt.
Because sometimes we do not realize how tightly we are holding something until Christ asks us to open our hands.
And maybe that is why this story found you.
Not so you will stop wanting good things.
But so you can ask yourself a terrifying question:
Has something I desire become something I believe I need in order for God to be enough?
Be honest.
If God gave you Christ but delayed the relationship, would Christ still be worthy?
If God gave you Christ but your career unfolded differently, would Christ still be worthy?
If God gave you Christ but your timeline shattered, would Christ still be worthy?
If God gave you Christ but people misunderstood you, would Christ still be worthy?
If God gave you Christ while you carried unanswered questions, would Christ still be worthy?
The Christian answer cannot merely be theological.
Eventually it must become personal.
Because Jesus is not an accessory added to the life of your dreams.
Jesus is Lord.
And sometimes grace begins by exposing how desperately we have tried to make something else our savior.
That exposure may feel like scandal.
The envy.
The bitterness.
The jealousy you hide behind congratulations.
The resentment toward God.
The silent rage when someone receives what you wanted.
The secret thought that your life would finally matter if only one thing changed.
Bring that scandal into the light.
Jesus already knows.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Christ does not wait for desperate sinners to make themselves presentable before calling them to Himself.
We come with our envy.
Our disordered desires.
Our comparisons.
Our demands.
Our shame.
Our failed attempts to control outcomes.
Our broken worship.
And at the cross we discover that grace is not God pretending our sin does not matter.
Grace is God dealing with our sin through Jesus Christ.
Repentance therefore is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
It is coming home.
It is saying:
Jesus, I have wanted Your gifts more than I wanted You.
Forgive me.
Jesus, I have measured Your goodness by whether You gave me what I demanded.
Forgive me.
Jesus, I have envied people You called me to love.
Forgive me.
Jesus, I have asked people to carry expectations only You can carry.
Forgive me.
Jesus, take the throne again.
And He is a far better Savior than the thing you have been chasing.
Your dream cannot forgive your sins.
Your spouse cannot resurrect you.
Your bank account cannot reconcile you to God.
Your children cannot carry your soul into eternity.
Your popularity cannot wash away guilt.
Your accomplishments cannot defeat death.
But Jesus can save.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus redeems.
Jesus restores.
Jesus makes sinners new.
That is why the ultimate answer to desperate desire is not “stop wanting.”
It is start worshiping rightly.
Desire the gift.
Love the Giver more.
Pray for the blessing.
Trust the Blesser more.
Ask boldly.
Surrender completely.
Cry when it hurts.
But never confuse God's hand with God's heart.
And never mistake delay for abandonment.
Rachel eventually conceived and bore Joseph, saying that God had taken away her disgrace.
Yet even Joseph was not the end of the biblical story.
Generation after generation would pass.
Broken families.
Failures.
Scandals.
Promises.
Waiting.
Until eventually the story of Scripture leads us to the One in whom God's saving purposes reach their fulfillment:
Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is the deepest lesson hiding underneath Rachel's desperate sentence.
We spend so much of our lives saying:
“Give me this, or I’ll die.”
Then Jesus comes and teaches us something completely different:
Without Him, even possessing everything cannot save us. With Him, even in our deepest lack, we are not abandoned.
So what is your “Give me this”?
Do not answer quickly.
What would devastate you so completely to lose that you secretly wonder whether life would still be worth living?
What unanswered prayer has slowly become an accusation against God?
Whose blessing has become painful for you to watch?
What person are you asking to be your functional savior?
What dream has become your identity?
What good thing has quietly become an ultimate thing?
Bring it to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
You do not have to pretend the desire disappeared.
Just stop allowing it to sit on the throne.
Open your hands.
“Lord Jesus, this is what I want.
But You are who I need.
If my desire has become an idol, expose it.
If comparison has poisoned my gratitude, cleanse me.
If disappointment has hardened my heart, soften me.
If I have accused You because Your timing did not match mine, forgive me.
Teach me to ask without demanding, wait without worshiping the outcome, grieve without abandoning faith, and hope without making the gift my god.
I surrender this desire to You.
And above everything else...
give me more of Christ.”
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn the moment into another scroll.
Someone else may be living tonight inside the chapter God already brought you through.
Not because every sentence will feel easy tomorrow, but because desperation has a way of returning when the room gets quiet.

Not as a performance of spirituality, and not because clicking “share” earns favor with God. We glorify God through lives of faith, obedience, love, generosity, witness, and worship—not through an algorithm. But sharing biblical truth can be one simple act of witness.
The woman quietly grieving.
The man whose plans collapsed.
The believer fighting comparison.
The person angry with God but afraid to admit it.
The Christian who needs to remember that an unanswered prayer does not mean an absent Christ.
Financial support does not make anyone more faithful, more saved, or more loved by God.

Invite your family. Invite struggling believers. Invite seekers. Invite lukewarm Christians. Even invite the friend who does not yet believe. Let them encounter Scripture. Let them ask questions. Let them see that Christianity is not about pretending broken people are spotless.
It is about sinners meeting a spotless Savior.
Jesus Christ is not for sale. Grace is not merchandise. The Gospel is not a product.
Christ calls sinners freely to repent and believe.
So share because someone needs truth.
Tag because somebody you love may be suffering silently.
Save because you may need these words again.
Follow because your soul needs more than endless noise.
But above all...
Come to Jesus.
Rachel cried, “Give me children, or I’ll die.”
Maybe your sentence has different words.
“Give me love.”
“Give me healing.”
“Give me success.”
“Give me my family back.”
“Give me the answer.”
“Give me the breakthrough.”
“Give me what everyone else seems to have.”
Jesus meets us underneath all those sentences and exposes the deeper hunger.
Because sometimes the thing you thought you could not live without has to loosen its grip before you discover the One you were created to live for.
And when your desperate hands finally open, you may discover they were never opening into emptiness.
They were opening toward Christ.
The gift you are begging God for may change your circumstances—but only Jesus can redeem your soul.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Betrayed Jesus for 30 Pieces of Silver — But Judas’ Real Tragedy Came After the Betrayal
paragraphs: He Betrayed Jesus for 30 Pieces of Silver — But Judas’ Real Tragedy Came After the Betrayal
The most terrifying part of Judas’ story is not that a man betrayed Jesus. It is that a man could be close enough to Jesus to kiss His face—and still run away from the only One who could save him.
Thirty pieces of silver.
Not a throne.
Not an empire.
Not a fortune that could make generations wealthy.
Thirty pieces.
That was the price attached to one of the darkest transactions in human history.
But if you think the silver is the most disturbing part of Judas Iscariot’s story, keep reading.
Because Judas’ greatest tragedy was not simply what he did in the darkness of Gethsemane.
It was what happened when the darkness finally broke inside him.
There is a moment in his story that should make every Christian uncomfortable.
Judas realized what he had done.
He felt the weight of it.
He confessed that he had sinned.
He returned the money.
And yet his story still ended in death.
That should stop us.
Because it means there is a kind of sorrow that can recognize sin without yet running into the arms of the Savior.
And somewhere reading this right now is a person who knows exactly what that feels like.
Maybe you have never sold Jesus for silver.
But perhaps you have traded obedience for pleasure.
Truth for approval.
Purity for a secret habit.
Your family for ambition.
Prayer for distraction.
Conviction for convenience.
Perhaps nobody knows.
Perhaps everybody at church thinks you are doing fine.
Perhaps you still post the verses.
Still say, “God is good.”
Still know when to raise your hands.
Still know Christian vocabulary.
Still know the songs.
And yet somewhere inside you there is a sound you cannot silence.
The sound of silver hitting the floor.
Matthew tells us that Judas was not an outsider who accidentally stumbled into the story. He was “one of the twelve” (Matthew 26:14).
Think about the weight of those words.
One of the Twelve.
He traveled with Jesus.
He heard teachings from the mouth of Christ Himself.
He saw miracles.
He watched blind eyes open.
He watched broken people restored.
He watched demons flee.
He witnessed compassion that religious leaders could not understand.
He sat near the One whom generations of prophets had anticipated.
And still, according to Matthew 26:15, Judas approached the chief priests and essentially asked what they would give him to hand Jesus over.
Their answer was thirty pieces of silver. Matthew deliberately connects the sum with the prophetic imagery surrounding thirty pieces of silver in Zechariah 11:12–13.
The Hebrew of Zechariah describes the payment as:
שְׁלֹשִׁים כָּסֶף — sheloshim kesef
“Thirty [pieces of] silver.”

The amount carries an additional disturbing biblical echo. Exodus 21:32 names thirty shekels of silver as compensation in a case involving a slave killed by an ox. We should be careful not to flatten every passage into exactly the same situation, but Matthew himself directs his readers back toward Zechariah's thirty pieces of silver. The Gospel wants us to feel the grotesque irony of the valuation: the Messiah is handed over for silver.
Imagine the coins in Judas’ hand.
One.
Two.
Three.
Perhaps they felt heavier than he expected.
Thirty.
Then Matthew says something chilling:
“From then on Judas watched for an opportunity to hand him over.”
Sin often works that way.
Before the public collapse comes the private negotiation.
Before somebody sees what happened, something has already been bargaining inside the heart.
“How close can I get without destroying everything?”
“Nobody will know.”
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“Just this once.”
“I deserve this.”
“I'll repent later.”
That is how compromise speaks.
It rarely introduces itself by saying, “I am here to destroy you.”
It offers relief.
Pleasure.
Money.
Attention.
Validation.
Control.
Revenge.
Escape.
And somewhere underneath the offer is always another question:
What would you take in exchange for faithfulness to Jesus?
That question is uncomfortable because Judas’ thirty pieces of silver can look very different in our hands.
For one person, it is pornography hidden behind a locked screen.
For another, an affair disguised as “just talking.”
For another, money acquired dishonestly.
For another, resentment that has become too precious to surrender.
For another, applause.
For another, a relationship God has repeatedly convicted them about.
For another, the desperate need to be admired.
For another, a private life completely different from the public Christian image.
The currency changes.
The transaction does not.
We exchange something eternal for something that cannot keep its promise.
Then came Gethsemane.
Judas arrived with the arresting crowd.
And the signal he chose was horrifyingly intimate.
A kiss.
The betrayal did not look like hatred.
It looked like affection.
That may be one of the most frightening pictures of religious hypocrisy in Scripture: lips can approach Jesus while a heart has already negotiated against Him.
You can know Christian language and still need repentance.
You can carry a Bible and still hide something from God.
You can sing worship songs while protecting an idol.
You can appear near Jesus without actually surrendering to Jesus.
But Judas’ story becomes even more devastating after the betrayal.
Jesus is condemned.
And suddenly the money cannot anesthetize Judas anymore.
Matthew 27:3 tells us that when Judas saw what had happened, he was overcome with remorse and returned the thirty pieces of silver.
The Greek word used there deserves attention:
μεταμεληθεὶς — metamelētheis

It comes from μεταμέλομαι — metamelomai and can express regret, remorse, or a change of mind or feeling. The word itself should not be simplistically defined as “fake repentance”; its usage is broader than that. But Matthew's narrative makes the decisive issue painfully clear: Judas experienced terrible remorse, yet the story does not show him returning to Christ in trusting repentance.
That distinction matters.
Because feeling horrible about your sin is not the same thing as entrusting yourself to the mercy of Jesus.
Crying is not automatically repentance.
Shame is not automatically repentance.
Being exposed is not automatically repentance.
Hating the consequences is not automatically repentance.
Even admitting wrongdoing, by itself, is not the whole Gospel response.
Judas actually said:
“I have sinned...”
He acknowledged that he had betrayed innocent blood.
Those words are haunting.
He knew.
He knew the blood was innocent.
He knew what he had done was sin.
He knew the money was contaminated by betrayal.
So he tried to return it.
But money can be returned without the past being undone.
You cannot buy yesterday back.
You cannot throw enough silver onto a temple floor to reverse a kiss in Gethsemane.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Have you ever wished you could undo something?
One conversation.
One night.
One decision.
One click.
One affair.
One lie.
One explosion of anger.
One season of rebellion.
One person you wounded.
One relationship you destroyed.
One moment when you knew better and did it anyway.
If only you could go back.
If only you could become the person you were five minutes before it happened.
But you cannot.
Neither could Judas.
The coins fell.
The religious leaders who had been happy to use Judas suddenly had no comfort for him.
His guilt had served their purpose. His soul apparently did not concern them.
“What is that to us?”
The same people willing to participate in his sin offered no rescue when the sin began crushing him.
There is a warning there too.
Sin will introduce you to companions who celebrate your compromise but disappear when the consequences arrive.
The world can help you rebel.
It cannot cleanse your conscience.
Money can purchase distraction.
It cannot purchase forgiveness.
Pleasure can numb pain temporarily.
It cannot reconcile you to God.
Human approval can make you feel important.
It cannot remove guilt.
Religion without Christ can tell you what you did wrong.
It cannot wash you clean.
Only Jesus can do that.
And here lies the unbearable tragedy of Judas.
The innocent blood Judas betrayed was the very blood being poured out for sinners.
Read that again.
The blood that terrified his conscience was the blood through which forgiveness would be proclaimed.
The cross was not evidence that mercy had disappeared.
The cross was God's great declaration that mercy had come at immeasurable cost.
Judas looked at his sin and apparently saw an ending.
The Gospel tells sinners to look at Christ and see a door.
This is why Judas must be read beside another disciple who failed Jesus catastrophically.
Peter.
Peter did not sell Jesus for silver.
But Peter promised loyalty and then denied even knowing Him.
Not once.
Three times.
Peter failed publicly.
Shamefully.
Cowardly.
Jesus had warned him, and Peter still did it.
Then the rooster crowed.
Peter remembered.
And Peter wept bitterly.
Now notice something extraordinary.
Both Judas and Peter failed Jesus.
Both experienced anguish afterward.
But their stories moved in radically different directions.
Judas moved deeper into despair and died.
Peter lived long enough to encounter the risen Christ.
On the shore in John 21, Jesus did not pretend Peter's denial never happened.
He restored him.
“Do you love me?”
Again.
“Do you love me?”
Again.
“Do you love me?”
The man who denied Jesus three times was given a threefold opportunity to affirm his love and was recommissioned to care for Christ's flock.
That is grace.
Grace does not call betrayal righteousness.
Grace does not pretend sin is harmless.
Grace tells the truth about the wound and then reveals a Savior greater than the wound.
Somebody needs that sentence tonight:
Your sin may be greater than you ever wanted to admit, but Jesus is greater than your sin.
Do not misunderstand this.
Scripture never gives us permission to presume upon grace.
Grace is not God's permission slip for continuing rebellion.
The Gospel calls us to repent and believe.
Jesus did not die so we could become comfortable with the chains He came to break.
He died and rose so sinners could be forgiven, reconciled to God, given new life, and transformed.
Real grace does not merely soothe the conscience.
Grace changes allegiance.
And perhaps the enemy has been telling you the opposite.
“You've gone too far.”
“You knew better.”
“After everything God gave you, look what you did.”
“You're disgusting.”
“You can never pray again.”
“God might forgive other people, but not you.”
So you hide.
You stop opening Scripture.
You avoid prayer because prayer feels like walking into a courtroom.
You avoid Christians who might ask real questions.
You punish yourself emotionally because part of you thinks suffering long enough might somehow pay the debt.
But hear the Gospel clearly:
You cannot punish yourself into forgiveness.
That is not repentance.
That is attempting to become your own savior.
The Christian Gospel is not that sinners eventually suffer enough to make themselves worthy of God.
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ bore sin at the cross, died, was buried, rose again, and now calls sinners to turn to Him in repentance and faith.
You do not cleanse yourself and then approach Christ.
You approach Christ because you cannot cleanse yourself.
This is why one of the most beautiful promises in Scripture is 1 John 1:9: when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Because Christ is sufficient.
There is a world of difference between conviction and condemnation.
Godly conviction exposes the wound so you will run toward the Physician.
Condemnation whispers that the wound makes you unworthy to approach Him.
Conviction says, “Come into the light.”
Condemnation says, “Hide.”
Conviction says, “Confess it.”
Condemnation says, “You are what you did.”
Conviction leads toward Christ.
Despair tells you there is nowhere left to go.
Judas' story warns us never to confuse despair with repentance.
And we should speak carefully here.
Matthew tells us that Judas threw the silver into the temple, departed, and hanged himself.

His death should never be romanticized, sensationalized, or used to shame people who struggle with despair. The theological warning in Judas' story is not that hurting people are beyond grace. It is precisely the opposite:
Do not let shame persuade you to run away from the only Savior who can carry your shame.
When your sin is exposed, run to Jesus.
When your hypocrisy is exposed, run to Jesus.
When the consequences cannot be reversed, run to Jesus.
When you cannot forgive yourself, run to Jesus.
When you are ashamed to say what you did aloud, run to Jesus.
Not because repentance is cheap.
Because His blood was not.
There is another chilling detail in the silver.
Centuries before Judas, Zechariah wrote of thirty pieces of silver being thrown in the house of the Lord, imagery Matthew later draws into his account of Judas' money and the potter's field.
The coins Judas thought would profit him became testimony against the entire transaction.
He wanted the silver.
Then he could not bear to keep it.
Isn't that how sin behaves?
First:
“You need this.”
Then:
“How could you have done this?”
First temptation minimizes the cost.
Then accusation magnifies the guilt.
The enemy does not need you merely to sin.
He wants you to believe afterward that grace cannot reach you.
That second lie can be even deadlier than the first.
The first says Jesus is not worth obeying.
The second says Jesus is not willing to forgive.
Both are lies about Jesus.
This is why the answer to Judas' story is not merely, “Don't betray Jesus.”
Of course, do not betray Him.
But the deeper warning is this:
If you fall, do not run from Him.
Peter's failure was terrible.
But Peter's failure was not the final sentence of Peter's life.
Jesus rewrote what failure seemed destined to become.
The denier became a preacher.
The frightened disciple stood publicly and proclaimed Christ.
The man who collapsed under pressure became a witness of the resurrection.
That does not make Peter impressive.
It makes Jesus magnificent.
And that is our theme because it is the heartbeat of the Gospel:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By taking sinners whose stories should have ended in ruin and redeeming them for His glory.
Look through Scripture.
David had adultery and bloodshed in his story.
The Samaritan woman carried relational wreckage.
The woman caught in adultery was dragged into public shame.
Zacchaeus had exploitation attached to his name.
Paul had persecution and violence behind him.
Peter had denial.
And yet Christ's grace kept interrupting stories that looked finished.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
Forgiveness does not always erase consequences.
Restoration does not mean history becomes imaginary.
The scars may remain.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Confession may be necessary.
Restitution may be appropriate.
Relationships may take time.
Some consequences may follow us for years.
But in Jesus Christ, consequence does not have to become identity.
Your worst chapter does not have the authority to name the whole book.
Jesus does.
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Maybe there is silver on the floor of your heart.
Something you regret.
Something you would give almost anything to undo.
Something nobody knows.
Something everybody knows.
Maybe you have spent months replaying it.
Maybe years.
You keep revisiting the scene as though staring at it long enough could rewrite it.
It cannot.
But Jesus can write what comes next.
So stop trying to negotiate with yesterday.
Bring yesterday to Christ.
Confess without excuses.
Repent without bargaining.
Believe without pretending you deserve it.
You do not need to convince Jesus that your sin is small.
You need to believe that His cross is enough.
There is room at the feet of Jesus for people with terrible histories.
There is room for betrayers.
Deniers.
Addicts.
Liars.
Adulterers.
Proud people.
Religious hypocrites.
People who knew better.
People who promised God they would never do it again—and did.
The invitation is not to remain what you were.
The invitation is to come and be made new.
Be honest.

And if Christ has already carried you through a season you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what He did. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded believer desperately needs to read tonight.
Not as a religious decoration.
Send it privately to the person who has been disappearing.
We never want to manipulate something sacred.
And there is more waiting for believers who are hungry to grow.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who has become lukewarm.
Invite the person quietly struggling with sin.
Invite the seeker who is not sure what they believe.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is only a religion for people who have their lives together.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that good people finally earned their way to God.
It is the announcement that while sinners could not rescue themselves, God acted in Christ.
Thirty pieces of silver fell onto a temple floor.
But silver was never going to have the final word.
Neither was Judas.
Neither was Peter's denial.
Neither is your failure.
Jesus Christ was crucified.
Jesus Christ was buried.
Jesus Christ rose.
And the risen Christ is still calling sinners out of hiding.
So when your past whispers, “Look what you did,” look toward the cross and remember what He did.
When shame says, “Run,” run—but run toward Jesus.
When guilt says, “There is no way back,” remember that Christ Himself is the Way.
And when you hear the silver hitting the floor in your memory again...
remember this:
The sound of your failure does not have to be the last sound in your story—the empty tomb is louder.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DID GOD EVER COMMAND POLYGAMY? The Bible’s Answer Is More Uncomfortable—and More Beautiful—Than You Think
paragraphs: DID GOD EVER COMMAND POLYGAMY? The Bible’s Answer Is More Uncomfortable—and More Beautiful—Than You Think

Abraham had more than one woman. Jacob had two wives and two concubines. David had multiple wives. Solomon had hundreds. So why would a Bible that records polygamy also present marriage as two becoming one flesh? And did God ever actually command a man to take multiple wives?
There is a dangerous way to read the Bible.
You can open its pages, find something one of its characters did, and quietly assume that because Scripture records it, God approves it.
But the Bible is far more honest than that.
It does not airbrush its heroes.
It lets Abraham stumble.
It lets Jacob deceive.
It lets David fall.
It lets Peter deny Jesus.
It records jealousy, lust, murder, betrayal, cowardice, broken homes, shattered promises, and consequences that sometimes echo across generations.
The Bible does not protect the reputations of its human characters.
It reveals the faithfulness of God in spite of them.
And that matters enormously when someone asks:
“Did God ever command anyone to practice polygamy?”
The careful biblical answer is no—not as God's creational design or moral command for marriage.

There are passages where Scripture recognizes, regulates, or describes situations involving multiple wives. There are difficult texts that deserve careful treatment rather than convenient avoidance. But regulation is not the same thing as institution, description is not prescription, and God's working through broken human arrangements is not the same thing as God declaring those arrangements His original design.
And if you want to know what that design is, there is one voice that should settle the matter for a Christian.
Jesus.
When religious leaders came to Christ with a difficult marriage question, Jesus did something extraordinary.
He went backward.
Past their arguments.
Past their customs.
Past Moses.
Past centuries of human failure.
Back to Eden.
Back to the beginning.
Back before sin had fractured anything.
Genesis 2:24 gives us the foundational language:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
ʿAl-kēn yaʿăzov-ʾîš ʾet-ʾāvîw wəʾet-ʾimmô, wədāvaq bəʾištô, wəhāyû ləbāśār ʾeḥād.
In straightforward English:
Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother, holds fast to his wife, and they become one flesh.
The Hebrew is beautiful.
Dāvaq carries the idea of clinging, adhering, holding fast.
And then comes:
בָשָׂר אֶחָד — bāśār ʾeḥād.
One flesh.
Not merely two people sharing a roof.
Not merely a sexual arrangement.
A covenantal joining.
And centuries later, Jesus reaches directly back to this text.
Matthew records His words in Greek:
ἕνεκα τούτου καταλείψει ἄνθρωπος τὸν πατέρα καὶ τὴν μητέρα καὶ κολληθήσεται τῇ γυναικὶ αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
“For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.”
Then Jesus presses the truth home:
ὥστε οὐκέτι εἰσὶν δύο ἀλλὰ σὰρξ μία
“So they are no longer two, but one flesh.”
Do not race past those words.
The two.
οἱ δύο — hoi duo.
Jesus is not merely commenting on an ancient social convention. He is answering a marriage controversy by appealing to God's order “from the beginning.”
That is crucial.
Human beings want to begin with what fallen humanity has practiced.
Jesus begins with what the Creator intended.
And those are not always the same thing.
This is where so many arguments about polygamy become confused.
Someone says, “But Abraham had Hagar.”
Yes.
Read what happened afterward.
Sarah was barren. God had made Abraham a promise. Time passed. Waiting became painful. Sarah proposed that Abraham obtain a child through Hagar.
And Abraham agreed.
Then Hagar conceived.
And almost immediately the household began bleeding.
Contempt.
Jealousy.
Anger.
Mistreatment.
Running away.
Family fracture.
Later, Ishmael and Hagar were sent away, and Abraham was deeply distressed.
God was merciful to Hagar.
God saw her.
God heard Ishmael.
God cared for the people trapped inside that broken situation.
But God's mercy toward people in a broken arrangement does not transform the arrangement into His original design.
That distinction matters.
Because maybe you have confused God's mercy in your own life with God's approval of everything that brought you there.
Maybe God rescued you from consequences you created.
Maybe He fed you while you were wandering.
Maybe He answered you while you were broken.
Maybe He stayed near when you had made a mess of everything.
That does not mean the mess was His will.
It means His mercy was greater than your mess.
Then there is Jacob.
Jacob loved Rachel.
But through Laban's deception, he first received Leah, then also married Rachel. The household expanded through their servants Bilhah and Zilpah.
And what followed?
Read Genesis slowly.
Competition.
Jealousy.
Women aching to be loved.
Children becoming part of a struggle for affection.
One sister saying, in effect, perhaps now my husband will love me.
Another tormented by infertility.
Servants brought into the reproductive rivalry.
Mandrakes negotiated.
Children born into a household where affection and status were painfully unequal.
The Bible does not need to stop and place a warning label over every paragraph saying:
“This is broken.”
The consequences are screaming it.
Then comes David.
David had multiple wives.
Does that prove God commanded polygamy?
No.
It proves that David, like every other biblical hero except Christ, was a sinner in need of grace.
In fact, Israel's kings had already been warned in Deuteronomy 17:17 not to multiply wives, lest their hearts turn away.
And then Solomon practically becomes the living demonstration of that warning.
Solomon accumulated wives and concubines on an enormous scale.
And what happened?
His wives turned his heart toward other gods.
The king famous for wisdom became living evidence that knowing wisdom is not the same as obeying it.
That should frighten every Christian just a little.
Because biblical knowledge alone does not make you holy.
You can know verses and still feed the thing destroying you.
You can explain theology and still hide a secret life.
You can post Christian content and still refuse to surrender the room in your heart where Jesus has been knocking for years.
Solomon's tragedy was not that nobody had warned him.
His tragedy was that wisdom heard but not obeyed eventually becomes judgment against the one who knows better.
But someone may object:
“What about Old Testament laws concerning multiple wives?”
That is where we have to read carefully.
Exodus 21:10 speaks about obligations in a situation where another wife is taken. Deuteronomy 21:15–17 addresses inheritance when a man has two wives and favors one over the other.
These passages matter.
But notice what they do.
They place protections and obligations inside situations that existed in ancient Israelite society.
They do not read like Genesis 2.
They do not say, “This is why God created marriage.”
They do not command Israelite men generally to acquire additional wives.
They regulate circumstances in a fallen world.
That difference between regulation and endorsement appears elsewhere in Scripture too.
Jesus Himself teaches us to recognize it.
When discussing divorce in Matthew 19, He says Moses permitted divorce because of the hardness of human hearts.
And then Jesus says something devastatingly important:
“But from the beginning it was not so.”
There it is.
The interpretive key.
There are realities Scripture regulates because God is dealing with sinful people in a broken world.
But when Jesus wants to expose God's design, He takes us back to creation.
From the beginning.
That is where the Christian must ultimately stand.
Not, “What did ancient people manage to normalize?”
Not, “What did famous biblical men get away with?”
Not, “What arrangement existed in a fallen culture?”
But:
What did God establish from the beginning, and how did Jesus interpret it?
There is another difficult passage people sometimes raise: Deuteronomy 25 and levirate marriage.

If a married man died childless, his brother had an obligation connected with preserving the dead brother's family line. People sometimes argue that this could potentially place an already-married brother in a complicated marital situation.
But even granting the difficulty, the passage still does not establish a general divine command to practice polygamy.

Its purpose concerns the preservation of the deceased brother's name and family line within Israel's covenant society. It is a specific legal institution addressing a specific tragedy, not a universal command that men should collect wives.
And there is an even more emotionally charged text.
Nathan's rebuke of David in 2 Samuel 12.
Speaking for God, Nathan reminds David of all God had given him, including the “wives” associated with his master's house, and says that if this had been too little, God would have added more.
Some read that and conclude, “There. God gave David multiple wives.”
But we need precision.

The passage is not a creation ordinance commanding polygamy. It occurs in a prophetic courtroom speech exposing David's monstrous ingratitude after his adultery with Bathsheba and the arranged death of Uriah.
Its point is not, “Go practice polygamy.”
Its point is:
David, God had already given you abundance, and still you coveted what was not yours.
David's sin was not excused because his life already contained complicated marital arrangements.
He saw another man's wife.
He wanted her.
He took her.
Then he tried to hide what he had done.
And when deception failed, a faithful man died.
That is where this subject suddenly stops being an ancient debate.
Because David's real disease still lives in human hearts.
I want what God has not given me.
That sentence has destroyed marriages.
Families.
Ministries.
Friendships.
Churches.
Reputations.
Lives.
“I want what God has not given me.”
Maybe the object is different.
Another person.
Another relationship.
Another body.
Another life.
Another experience.
Another secret tab on your phone.
Another conversation your spouse would be devastated to read.
Another emotional connection you keep calling “innocent.”
Another compromise.
Another fantasy.
Sin has always been good at renaming itself.
Lust becomes “chemistry.”
Adultery becomes “following my heart.”
Greed becomes “ambition.”
Bitterness becomes “boundaries.”
Pride becomes “knowing my worth.”
And rebellion becomes “God just wants me happy.”
But the Gospel does not come merely to improve the vocabulary of our bondage.
Jesus comes to set captives free.
And this is why the biblical teaching on marriage cannot end with winning an argument about polygamy.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about proving that those ancient people were broken.
It is about discovering that we are too.
You may never have practiced polygamy.
But have you divided a heart that God called to faithfulness?
Have you committed adultery in imagination?
Have you used pornography while telling yourself nobody is being hurt?
Have you emotionally belonged to someone who is not your spouse?
Have you treated another human being as something to consume rather than someone bearing God's image?
Have you demanded from marriage what only Christ can give?
Have you looked righteous in public while something secret has been eating your soul alive?
This is where Jesus becomes more than the answer to a theological controversy.
He becomes the only hope for the person reading this with trembling hands.
Because Scripture's story is not:
Good people obeyed God's marriage plan, bad people did not, and God loved the good people.
No.
The story is far more scandalous.
Abraham failed.
Jacob failed.
Judah failed.
David failed spectacularly.
Solomon failed despite extraordinary wisdom.
Israel failed.
Humanity failed.
We failed.
And then came Jesus.
Not another compromised patriarch.
Not another king collecting women.
Not another man using power to satisfy appetite.
The true Bridegroom came to rescue His bride.
Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.
Do you see the reversal?
Sin says:
“Give yourself to me so I can consume you.”
Jesus says:
“I give Myself for you so I can save you.”
Sin takes.
Christ gives.
Sin uses.
Christ serves.
Sin hides.
Christ exposes darkness so He can heal what darkness has imprisoned.
Sin produces shame.
Christ carries shame to a cross.
This is why Christian marriage finds its deepest meaning not merely in social stability, romance, sexuality, companionship, or reproduction.
Paul takes us somewhere astonishing in Ephesians 5.
He quotes Genesis again.
A man leaves father and mother.
He is joined to his wife.
The two become one flesh.
Then Paul says the mystery is profound—and he is speaking about Christ and the church.
Marriage points beyond itself.
Toward Jesus.
Toward covenant faithfulness.
Toward a Bridegroom who does not abandon His people when loving them becomes costly.
Toward a Savior who does not exploit His bride but bleeds for her.
Toward the Lamb whose covenant is sealed not by human perfection but by His own blood.
Suddenly the question “Did God command polygamy?” opens into something much bigger.
What kind of love does God ultimately reveal?
Look at Jesus.
The cross answers.
And perhaps this article has reached someone who is not merely curious about ancient marriage customs.
Perhaps you are reading because your own story is complicated.
Divorce.
Adultery.
Sexual sin.
A second marriage.
A broken engagement.
Pornography.
Betrayal.
A child born outside marriage.
A relationship you regret.
A spouse who left.
A secret nobody at church knows.
Maybe biblical discussions about marriage make your stomach tighten because your life does not resemble Eden.
Then hear this carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that only people with clean histories may come to Jesus.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners may come.
Not by pretending sin is righteousness.
Not by rewriting God's Word until repentance becomes unnecessary.
But by bringing the truth into the light and discovering that the blood of Christ is sufficient for people whose stories cannot be undone.
Jesus did not die for imaginary people with imaginary sins.
He died for sinners.
Real ones.
Guilty ones.
Ashamed ones.
People with histories.
People who crossed lines.
People who knew better.
People who ruined things they cannot rebuild by themselves.
The cross does not tell you your sin was insignificant.
The cross tells you your sin was so serious that redemption required the blood of the Son of God—
and that His love was so astonishing that He gave it.
That is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that winks at rebellion.
Grace that finds you in rebellion, calls you to repentance, washes you, forgives you, and begins making you new.
Maybe you cannot rewrite yesterday.
Jesus can redeem what yesterday did to you.
Maybe you cannot restore every relationship.
Jesus can restore your soul.
Maybe consequences remain.
Grace does not always erase consequences.
But consequences do not get the final word over someone who belongs to Christ.
Jesus does.
So did God ever command humanity to practice polygamy as His ideal for marriage?
No.
Scripture records polygamous relationships.
The Mosaic law regulates realities involving them.
God sovereignly works through deeply imperfect families.
But none of those facts overturns the creation pattern to which Jesus Himself deliberately returns:
A man.
His wife.
The two.
One flesh.
And the New Testament continues in that direction, describing church leaders as the husband of one wife and portraying covenant marriage as a living picture of Christ's relationship with His church.
Yet do not finish this article merely saying:
“Good. Now I know the correct position on polygamy.”
That would be the easiest way to miss the point.
Ask the harder question.
Is Jesus Lord over the way I love?
Over your marriage?
Your sexuality?
Your private messages?
Your browser history?
Your imagination?
Your loneliness?
Your desires?
Your wounds?
Your secret relationships?
Your past?
Your future?
Your body?
Your heart?
Because you can win the argument about biblical marriage and still lose your soul to hidden sin.
You can defend Eden publicly while feeding Babylon privately.
You can quote “one flesh” while your heart belongs to everything except Christ.
And maybe that is the question God is pressing into you right now.
Not:
“Can you prove somebody else wrong?”
But:
“Will you let Jesus make you faithful?”
If something hidden was exposed while you read this, do not hide behind theology. Bring it to Christ. Confess it. Repent. Ask for help. If appropriate, seek wise pastoral accountability.
Not because typing a sentence saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when someone finally stops protecting the darkness.
Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to keep another wounded believer from giving up tonight.
Not merely because you agree with it.
God's standard has not changed.
And neither has the power of His grace.
We glorify God through Christ by faithful obedience, generosity, truth, love, and worship.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical expression of that generosity.
Not to earn God's love.
Not to prove you are spiritual.
Not because clicking “share” somehow makes you righteous.
Christ alone is our righteousness.
We receive grace—
then we carry the news of grace.

And after all the Hebrew, all the Greek, all the difficult laws, all the broken marriages, all the patriarchs, kings, failures, warnings, consequences, and questions, perhaps the deepest truth is astonishingly simple:
God did not give us the Bible so we could admire flawless human beings.
There aren't any.
He gave us Scripture so that through the wreckage of human sin we would finally recognize the One who never failed.
Jesus Christ.
The faithful Bridegroom.
The crucified Savior.
The risen King.
The One who receives repentant sinners without calling their sin good.
The One who tells the truth without withdrawing His mercy.
The One who can take stories stained by lust, betrayal, foolishness, divorce, shame, regret, and years we wish we could erase—and write redemption where we thought only ruins remained.
Your worst chapter may explain your scars, but when your life is surrendered to Christ, it does not get to write your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE PAYCHECK YOU NEVER WANTED: Why “The Wages of Sin Is Death” Still Applies Today
paragraphs:
THE PAYCHECK YOU NEVER WANTED: Why “The Wages of Sin Is Death” Still Applies Today
We modernized our language for sin. We renamed it, normalized it, excused it, monetized it, laughed about it, and sometimes even celebrated it. But changing the name of the poison never changed what the poison does. And the most terrifying part of Romans 6:23 may not be the word “death.” It may be the word “wages.”
There are Bible verses people love putting on coffee mugs.
Romans 6:23 usually isn’t one of them.
Because it refuses to flatter us.

It does not tell us that everything inside us should be trusted. It does not say that every desire deserves expression. It does not tell us that sin becomes harmless when culture approves of it, when enough people practice it, when celebrities celebrate it, when algorithms promote it, or when we find a softer word to describe it.
It says:
“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
That sentence was written nearly two thousand years ago.
And somehow...
it still knows us.
It knows the man deleting his browser history before his wife walks into the room.
It knows the woman smiling in church while bitterness has been quietly consuming her for years.
It knows the teenager who learned how to perform Christianity before learning how to surrender to Christ.
It knows the pastor who can preach repentance while secretly needing to repent.
It knows the person posting Bible verses publicly while privately feeding an addiction.
It knows the respectable sinner.
The religious sinner.
The wounded sinner.
The successful sinner.
The ashamed sinner.
The sinner who does not even call it sin anymore.
And it knows something we desperately need to remember:
Sin always sends an invoice.
Maybe not tonight.
Maybe not publicly.
Maybe not in the way you expected.
But sin has wages.
Paul's Greek is painfully precise:
Τὰ γὰρ ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας θάνατος
Ta gar opsōnia tēs hamartias thanatos.
“For the wages of sin [is] death.”
The word translated “wages” is ὀψώνια — opsōnia.
It refers to pay, compensation, wages—what is received for service rendered. The word had associations with a soldier’s pay or provisions.
Paul does not merely describe death as an unfortunate possibility surrounding sin.
He describes death as sin’s wage.
Something earned.
Something paid.
Something sin produces according to its terrible economy.
And then Paul does something breathtaking.
He changes the vocabulary.
He does not say:
“The wages of sin is death, but the wages of righteousness are eternal life.”
No.
Because if eternal life were something fallen human beings could earn, the Gospel would cease to be good news.
Instead Paul writes:
τὸ δὲ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιος
to de charisma tou theou zōē aiōnios
“but the gift of God [is] eternal life.”
Did you see it?
Wages.
Then...
Gift.
Sin pays.
God gives.
Death is what sin earns.
Life is what grace gives.
And that difference is the heartbeat of Christianity.
You cannot put God into your debt.
You cannot accumulate enough religious points to purchase eternal life.
You cannot undo yesterday’s rebellion by behaving better tomorrow.
You cannot save yourself by becoming slightly more moral than the person sitting next to you.
Eternal life is χάρισμα — charisma.
A gracious gift.
And Paul refuses to leave that gift floating in vague spirituality.
He tells us exactly where it is found:
ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν
en Christō Iēsou tō kyriō hēmōn
“in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
Not in self-improvement.
Not in religious performance.
Not in being “a good person.”
Not in comparing yourself with worse sinners.
Not in spirituality without surrender.
Not in Christianity without Christ.
In Christ Jesus our Lord.
That is why Romans 6:23 still applies today.
Human technology changed.
Human clothing changed.
Our vocabulary changed.
Our entertainment changed.
Our economies changed.
Our methods of communication changed.
Human rebellion did not.
We simply became better at decorating it.
We call greed ambition when it benefits us.
We call lust harmless entertainment when nobody knows.
We call gossip “venting.”
We call envy motivation.
We call pride self-confidence even when it makes repentance almost impossible.
We call unforgiveness boundaries when what we really mean is that we secretly enjoy replaying another person's offense.
We call compromise nuance.
We call idolatry priorities.
And sometimes we use legitimate psychological, cultural, or therapeutic language as camouflage for something Scripture is asking us to confront spiritually.
Not every struggle is sin.
Not every wound is rebellion.
Not every painful emotion is evidence that someone has disobeyed God.
Jesus showed profound compassion toward suffering people.
But neither does compassion require us to pretend sin is harmless.
Christ did not come merely to make sinners feel more comfortable while remaining enslaved.
He came to save.
The angel's announcement concerning Jesus in Matthew 1:21 was astonishingly specific:
“He shall save his people from their sins.”
Not merely from uncomfortable consequences.
From their sins.
Because sin is deeper than bad habits.
Sin alienates.
Sin enslaves.
Sin deceives.
Sin corrupts.
Sin destroys.
And ultimately, apart from God's saving grace in Christ, sin ends in death.
Paul had already written in Romans 3:23:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
All.
That word destroys our favorite escape route.
Comparison.
We love finding someone whose darkness looks darker than ours.
“At least I never cheated.”
“At least I don't drink.”
“At least I go to church.”
“At least I provide for my family.”
“At least I'm not like them.”
But heaven's courtroom does not operate on a curve.
The question is not whether you have sinned less spectacularly than somebody else.
The question is whether you have sinned.
And Scripture answers for us:
All have.
That includes me.
That includes you.
That includes the person preaching.
The person reading.
The person judging.
The person hiding.
Every one of us stands in desperate need of grace.
And this is where Christianity becomes scandalous.
Because the Gospel does not say good people go to heaven while bad people go to hell.
The Gospel announces something far more humbling:
Sinners need a Savior.
And there is only One.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe this is where the article becomes uncomfortable.
Because perhaps there is something you have been negotiating with God about.
Something you keep renaming because calling it what Scripture calls it would require you to confront it.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your spouse doesn't know.
Your parents don't know.
Your children don't know.
Your church doesn't know.
Your friends don't know.
Your followers certainly don't know.
But God does.
That sentence can sound terrifying.
Until you remember the cross.
Because the God who knows completely is also the God who calls sinners to repentance and offers mercy through His Son.
Jesus did not accidentally die.
The cross was not merely an inspirational example of sacrificial love.
Scripture presents Christ's death as God's saving work for sinners.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
Read those words again.
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we conquered every addiction.
Not after our thoughts became pure.
Not after we repaired our reputation.
Not after we finally became worthy.
Christ died for sinners.
The Gospel is not:
“Fix yourself and perhaps Jesus will accept you.”
The Gospel announces that the Son of God entered our ruin to accomplish what we could never accomplish for ourselves.
Jesus lived without sin.
He went willingly to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The wages of sin is death...
and Christ walked directly into death.
First Peter 2:24 says that Christ “his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree.”
Second Corinthians 5:21 declares:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
This is substitution.
This is grace.
This is the scandal at the center of Christianity.
The guilty cannot purchase acquittal.
So Christ pays what we cannot.
The dead cannot manufacture resurrection.
So Christ gives life.
The lost cannot invent a road home.
So Jesus says:
“I am the way, the truth, and the life.”
Sin says:
Earn your wages.
Jesus says:
Receive My gift.
Sin says:
Hide.
Jesus calls:
Come.
Sin whispers:
You've gone too far.
The cross declares that Christ's mercy is greater than the sinner who truly comes to Him.
But grace must never be confused with permission.
Romans 6 itself destroys that misunderstanding.
Paul begins the chapter:
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.”
Grace is not God's permission slip for continuing comfortably in rebellion.
Grace breaks sin's claim over us.
Grace teaches us to say no.
Grace calls us out of hiding.
Grace produces repentance.
Grace does not merely pardon the rebel and then leave the rebel unchanged.
Grace begins transformation.
That transformation may involve battles.
Sometimes long ones.
Sometimes humiliating ones.
A Christian can stumble.
A Christian can struggle.
A Christian can need accountability.
A Christian can find himself crying over the same temptation he thought he had defeated.
But there is an enormous difference between fighting sin and making peace with it.
Maybe you needed that sentence.
Because perhaps you have been fighting something for months.
Years.
You fell again and thought, “Maybe God is finished with me.”
Listen carefully.
Do not use grace to excuse your sin.
But do not use your sin to deny the sufficiency of Christ either.
Run toward Jesus.
Confess.
Repent.
Seek help.
Bring darkness into the light.
Cut off what continually feeds the temptation.
Open Scripture.
Pray when you don't feel spiritual.
Get accountable to mature believers.
If you fall, do not build a house where you fell.
Get up and return to Christ.
First John 1:9 gives struggling believers extraordinary hope:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
There is cleansing.
There is forgiveness.
There is restoration.
There is a Savior.
Maybe you've carried shame so long that it has started feeling like your identity.
You don't merely think:
“I committed something terrible.”
You think:
“I am what I did.”
And that is exactly where the Gospel reaches into the graveyard of identity.
Peter denied Jesus.
David committed grievous sin.
Paul had persecuted the church.
The Bible does not sanitize their failures.
That matters.
Scripture refuses to protect its heroes by editing away their scandals.
Why?
Because the glory belongs to God.
Grace does not pretend the scandal never happened.
Grace reveals that the scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
That is the Gospel Warrior heartbeat:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting history as though sin never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing responsibility.
Jesus rewrites everything by redeeming people who could never redeem themselves.
The cross does not tell you your sin was insignificant.
The cross shows you just how serious sin is.
And then it shows you something else.
How astonishing God's love is.
If sin were trivial, Calvary would make no sense.
If humans could save themselves, the cross would be unnecessary.
But if the wages of sin truly are death...
then suddenly the empty tomb becomes the greatest announcement the universe has ever heard.
Death did not win.
Jesus rose.
And because He lives, those who belong to Him have hope beyond the grave.
This is why Christianity cannot be reduced to “be nicer.”
Jesus did not endure the cross merely to turn rude people into polite people.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
To forgive.
To redeem.
To make new.
To give eternal life.
And perhaps the most dangerous person reading this article is not the person who knows he is broken.
Maybe it is the person convinced he isn't.
The person who has mastered religious appearances.
The person who can quote Scripture while resisting surrender.
The person who knows Christian vocabulary but has never truly come to Christ.
The person who knows how to lift hands in worship but refuses to release the secret idol in his heart.
You can know church culture without knowing Christ.
You can own five Bibles and still refuse the One they reveal.
You can sing about surrender while protecting the one room in your life where Jesus is not welcome.
You can have a Christian family.
A Christian playlist.
A Christian profile.
A Christian reputation.
And still need to repent.
Jesus did not say merely, “Admire Me.”
He said:
“Follow me.”
And following Jesus eventually leads us to places where something has to die.
Pride.
Lust.
Self-rule.
Bitterness.
The obsession with approval.
The addiction to being right.
The secret relationship.
The hidden habit.
The idol we keep asking God to bless rather than remove.
That is where Romans 6:23 stops being a verse on a page.
It becomes a mirror.
What is sin paying you right now?
Maybe it promised pleasure but pays shame.
Promised freedom but pays bondage.
Promised revenge but pays bitterness.
Promised status but pays anxiety.
Promised intimacy but pays emptiness.
Promised control but pays isolation.
Not every hardship in life is a direct payment for a particular personal sin; Scripture itself rejects such simplistic thinking.
But sin as a master still leads toward death.
That remains true whether the year is AD 60 or 2026.
Culture cannot repeal spiritual reality.
A vote cannot repeal it.
An algorithm cannot repeal it.
A trend cannot repeal it.
Your feelings cannot repeal it.
My feelings cannot repeal it.
“The wages of sin is death.”
But thank God Paul didn't put the period there.
There is another side of the sentence.
BUT.
Sometimes the Gospel can hide inside a three-letter word.
“The wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
You sinned...
but Jesus.
You wandered...
but Jesus.
You hid...
but Jesus.
You failed...
but Jesus.
Your past testifies against you...
but Jesus.
The grave waits for every human body...
but Jesus.
That does not mean everyone is automatically saved regardless of their response to Christ.
Jesus calls us to repent and believe.
Mark 1:15 records His proclamation:
“Repent ye, and believe the gospel.”
Repentance is not purchasing salvation with remorse.
It is the turning of a heart toward God.
Faith is not merely agreeing that Jesus existed.
It is trusting in Christ.
And perhaps that is exactly what needs to happen right now.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you become more religious.
Not after you fix everything.
Now.
Tell Him the truth.
He already knows.
Confess the sin you've been defending.
Stop negotiating with what is destroying you.
Turn toward Christ.
Trust Him.
Ask for mercy.
Surrender.
And if this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not need to give strangers the private details of your life.
But you can stop pretending.
Or simply write:
Someone else reading the comments may realize they are not the only person fighting their way back toward the light.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, don't merely think about them.
Send this privately if that would be wiser.
You never know which friend is smiling publicly while collapsing privately.
Because temptation has a strange ability to make us forget truths we were absolutely certain about yesterday.
Come back when sin starts advertising itself as freedom again.
Come back when shame tells you there is no road home.
Come back and remember:
Sin pays wages. God gives a gift. And that gift is found in Jesus Christ.

Supporting Christian ministry does not purchase God's favor, earn salvation, or make someone more righteous before Him. We glorify God by trusting and obeying Him, and Scripture teaches generosity as a willing response to grace rather than spiritual coercion.
But one practical way you can participate in spreading Gospel-centered resources is by helping support the work that produces and distributes them.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Eternal life is not merchandise.
It is the gift of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.
That distinction matters because this entire article began with two words that belong to two completely different kingdoms:
Wages.
And...
Gift.
One is earned.
One is given.
One reveals what sin produces.
The other reveals what God provides through Christ.
And eventually every one of us must decide which master we will serve.
So share the Gospel.
Support faithful Gospel work when you are able.
Encourage someone who is struggling.
Confess what needs confessing.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Seek accountability where secrecy has become dangerous.
Open the Bible again.
Pray again.
Come back to church if you've been hiding.
Come back to the feet of Jesus.
And above everything else...
Do not walk away from Christ because you are ashamed of the very wounds you need Him to heal.
The Gospel was never written for people who successfully avoided having a scandal.
It was written for sinners who need grace.
And when the accuser points toward everything you have done and whispers, “Look at your record,” the Christian does not have to pretend the record is clean.
We point somewhere else.
To a cross.
To an empty tomb.
To Jesus Christ.
Because the final hope of the Christian is not:
“Look how good I became.”
It is:
“Look how merciful my Savior is.”
Remember this when temptation whispers tonight:
Sin will always demand its wages—but Jesus still holds out the gift that death could never keep buried.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Buried Stolen Treasure Under His Tent. God Already Knew Where It Was.
paragraphs: He Buried Stolen Treasure Under His Tent. God Already Knew Where It Was.
The terrifying story of Achan’s hidden sin—and the Gospel hope for everyone who has ever buried something beneath the surface and prayed nobody would find it.
There was treasure beneath the tent.
Nobody walking past could see it.
Nobody looking Achan in the eyes could see it.
The robe was hidden.
The silver was hidden.
The gold was hidden.
But Achan had made one catastrophic mistake.
He had confused hidden from people with hidden from God.

And somewhere beneath the ordinary movements of family life, beneath conversations and meals and sleep, beneath a tent that probably looked no different from hundreds of other Israelite tents, stolen treasure sat in the dirt.
Silent.
Buried.
Waiting.
That may be why Joshua 7 is so uncomfortable.
Because most of us have never stolen a Babylonian robe from Jericho.
But we know something about tents.
We know what it means to have a public life above the ground and something we desperately do not want exposed underneath it.
The browser history.
The secret messages.
The money nobody knows about.
The resentment dressed up as discernment.
The relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
The private addiction followed by public worship.
The bitterness you keep feeding while telling everybody you have forgiven.
The compromise you renamed so you could keep it.
The image you protect.
The lie you maintain.
The thing you keep promising God you will surrender—just not today.
And perhaps the most frightening sentence in Achan’s story is not something Achan said at all.
It is what the narrator tells us before almost everybody else knows what happened:
God knew.

Joshua 7 opens immediately after one of Israel’s greatest victories. Jericho had fallen in a way that made human boasting almost ridiculous. Israel marched. Priests blew trumpets. The people shouted. The walls came down.
God had given the victory.
But Jericho was not Israel’s personal shopping opportunity.

Certain things had been placed under what the Hebrew text calls חֵרֶם — ḥērem, a word referring in this context to that which had been irrevocably devoted to the LORD and therefore was not Israel’s to take for private possession. Joshua had explicitly warned the people concerning these devoted things. The Hebrew terminology matters because Achan was not merely picking up abandoned battlefield property. He was taking what God had forbidden him to appropriate.
Then Joshua 7:1 drops a sentence like thunder:
וַיִּמְעֲלוּ בְנֵי־יִשְׂרָאֵל מַעַל בַּחֵרֶם
Vayyimʿalu vene-Yisra’el maʿal baḥerem.
The central Hebrew idea is מַעַל — maʿal: an act of unfaithfulness, a breach of trust, a trespass against what is sacred.
This is bigger than “Achan took something.”
Something relational has been violated.
God had spoken.
Achan knew.
And Achan took anyway.

Scripture tells us that Achan, from the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things, and the LORD’s anger burned against Israel. The chapter deliberately presents Achan’s private act as covenant unfaithfulness with consequences extending beyond the secrecy of his own tent.
That is the first lie hidden sin tells us.
This only affects me.
It whispers, Nobody else needs to know.
I can control this.
This is private.
I’m not hurting anybody.
Achan probably did not imagine thirty-six funerals when he looked at the treasure.
He saw a robe.
Silver.
Gold.
He saw something desirable.
That is how temptation often works.
It shows you the object.
It hides the invoice.
Israel moved against the small city of Ai with confidence. The spies had assessed it and concluded that only a few thousand soldiers would be needed.
Then everything went wrong.
Israel fled.
Approximately thirty-six men were killed.
The courage of the people collapsed.
Joshua tore his clothes and fell before the LORD.
Imagine the confusion.
They had just watched Jericho fall.
Now they could not handle Ai.
Joshua is on his face asking God what happened.
And God’s answer cuts through the confusion:
Israel has sinned.
Something forbidden has been taken.
Something has been stolen.
Something has been concealed among their possessions.
Joshua was looking at the battlefield.
God was looking beneath the tent.
Read that again.
Joshua was trying to understand what went wrong out there.
God identified what was wrong in here.
How many times have we done the same thing?
“Lord, why is everything falling apart?”
“Why am I spiritually numb?”
“Why can’t I find peace?”
“Why does worship feel empty?”
“Why am I constantly hiding?”
“Why am I becoming someone I never thought I would become?”

Not every hardship is punishment for a particular hidden sin. Scripture absolutely does not permit us to look at every tragedy, sickness, financial problem, or defeat and conclude that somebody secretly sinned. Job alone should destroy that cruel theology, and Jesus rejected simplistic attempts to connect particular suffering automatically with particular personal guilt.
So Joshua 7 must never become a weapon for accusing suffering people.
But neither should we miss what Joshua 7 actually says.
In this story, there really was something beneath the tent.
And God knew exactly where it was.
Then comes the moment that should make every reader uncomfortable.
The search begins.
Tribe.
Clan.
Household.
Man.
Closer.
Closer.
Closer.
Until Achan stands exposed.
Imagine his heartbeat.
Judah.
Still silent.
The clan of Zerah.
Still silent.
The household.
Still silent.
Achan.
There are moments when silence stops protecting you and starts carrying you toward exposure.
Joshua tells him to acknowledge what he has done.
And finally Achan speaks.
His confession in Joshua 7:20–21 reveals the anatomy of temptation with frightening simplicity.
He saw.
He coveted.
He took.
He hid.
There it is.
The progression is ancient because the human heart has not changed nearly as much as our technology has.
We see.
Desire begins negotiating.
We take.
Then we hide.

Achan says he saw a beautiful garment from Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver, and a gold bar weighing fifty shekels. The text places the silver at roughly 2.3 kilograms and the gold at roughly 575 grams.
It was enough to awaken desire.
Not enough to save him.
That is sin’s cruel economy.
It can make something temporary look worth something eternal.
Achan looked at what God had forbidden and apparently decided that possession was worth disobedience.
Then he buried it.
And perhaps this is where the story stops being ancient history and starts reading us.
Because human beings are still astonishingly talented at burial.
We bury lust under deleted histories.
We bury greed under the word “ambition.”
We bury envy under criticism.
We bury unforgiveness under distance.
We bury pride under ministry.
We bury spiritual emptiness under Christian vocabulary.
We bury pornography beneath passwords.
We bury emotional affairs beneath “we’re only friends.”
We bury dishonesty inside technically true sentences.
We bury obsession with money beneath “providing for my family.”
We bury our desperate need for human approval beneath carefully curated spirituality.
Sometimes we even bury sin underneath religious activity.
And then Sunday comes.
We shower.
Dress.
Smile.
Sing.
Lift our hands.
Say “Amen.”
Maybe even tell someone else how to live.
All while there is treasure beneath the tent.
But Scripture will not allow us to make Achan’s story merely a psychological metaphor.
His sin was real.
God’s holiness was real.
Judgment was real.
Achan’s story ends terribly.

The stolen objects were retrieved and placed before the LORD. Achan and all connected with his household and possessions were brought to the Valley of Achor. Judgment followed, a great heap of stones was raised, and the text says that the LORD turned from His burning anger. The name Achor is associated with “trouble,” deliberately echoing Joshua’s words that Achan had brought trouble upon Israel.
We should not sanitize that because modern ears find judgment uncomfortable.
God is holy.
Sin is not harmless.
God does not owe sinners indifference toward rebellion.

Yet we must also refuse a careless leap from Israel’s unique covenant setting and the conquest judgment of Joshua directly into the church as though Christians were authorized to reproduce Achan’s punishment.
We are not.
Joshua 7 describes a particular moment in Israel’s history under the old covenant and the divine judgment connected with the conquest. The church is never commissioned to stone sinners.
And this is exactly where the road from scandal to grace begins to open.
Because if Joshua 7 leaves you thinking, Then what hope is there for someone with something buried beneath the tent?—the Bible does not leave that question unanswered.
It leads us to Jesus.
And Jesus does something far greater than teaching sinners how to hide better.
He brings sinners into the light and gives them something Achan desperately needed:
a Savior.
The Gospel does not say God stopped seeing sin.
The Gospel says God dealt with sin.
At the cross.
This is what makes grace so staggering.
Christianity is not the announcement that sin stopped mattering.
It is the announcement that sin mattered so much that the Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Jesus did not die because God decided holiness was unnecessary.
Jesus died because our guilt was real.
The cross is where divine holiness and astonishing mercy meet without either becoming pretend.
The New Testament says:
Χριστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀπέθανεν
Christos hyper hēmōn apethanen.
“Christ died for us.”
Paul’s words in Romans 5:8 place that truth inside one of the Gospel’s most beautiful declarations: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not after we cleaned the tent.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we successfully buried the evidence.
While we were sinners.
Christ died for us.
And that changes how a Christian responds when the Spirit exposes hidden sin.
The instinct of Adam says, hide.
The invitation of the Gospel says, come into the light.
First John 1:9 does not tell believers to become experts at concealment. It calls us to confession, with the promise that God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
The Greek verb used for confessing is ὁμολογῶμεν — homologōmen, from homologeō: to confess, acknowledge, agree.
Confession is not informing an ignorant God.
God already knows.
Confession is finally agreeing with God about what He already sees.
That is why repentance is not God discovering your secret.
It is you stopping the exhausting attempt to hide from the One who already knows it.
Think about that.
The pornography.
He knows.
The affair.
He knows.
The hatred.
He knows.
The secret drinking.
He knows.
The stolen money.
He knows.
The dishonest business practice.
He knows.
The messages.
He knows.
The jealousy.
He knows.
The manipulation.
He knows.
The secret life that would terrify you if everyone saw it.
He knows.
And if you belong to Christ, His answer is not, “Become better at hiding.”
It is:
Come into the light.
Repent.
Turn.
Confess.
Forsake what is destroying you.
Run to Christ.

There is a difference between Achan’s eventual admission after exposure and the Gospel call to repentance flowing from a heart that turns toward God. We must not reduce repentance to saying, “Fine, you caught me.”
Biblical repentance is deeper.
It is not merely being sorry that consequences arrived.
It is turning from sin toward God.
And maybe somebody reading this has been waiting for consequences before taking repentance seriously.
Please do not wait.
Do not wait for the marriage to collapse.
Do not wait for the screenshots to surface.
Do not wait for the addiction to own another year.
Do not wait until your children discover the person you became in secret.
Do not wait until bitterness has hardened into identity.
Do not wait until the thing beneath the tent becomes the thing that defines the tent.
Bring it into the light now.
Not because confession earns salvation.
Jesus does.
Not because tears purchase forgiveness.
Jesus paid.
Not because you can punish yourself enough to become clean.
You cannot.
Come because Christ receives repentant sinners.
Come because the blood of Jesus cleanses from sin.
Come because grace is not permission to keep treasure buried.
Grace is power to stop digging holes.
And there is another beautiful biblical thread running beyond Joshua 7.
The Valley of Achor does not disappear from Scripture.
Centuries later, through Hosea, God speaks about restoration and describes the Valley of Achor—the valley associated with trouble—as a “door of hope” (Hosea 2:15).
Do not miss the beauty of that.
A place remembered for trouble becomes imagery for hope.
A place marked by judgment becomes part of the vocabulary of restoration.
That does not erase what happened to Achan.
It reveals something magnificent about the larger biblical story.
God can write hope into places associated with our deepest trouble.
And ultimately our hope is not a valley.
Our hope has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe your life has an Achor.
A place of trouble.
A chapter you wish you could tear out.
A failure you cannot believe belongs to your biography.
A season when you betrayed what you claimed to believe.
A decision that cost more than you imagined.
A secret that finally came into the light.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not require you to pretend the scandal never happened.
The Gospel announces that scandal does not have to write the final sentence.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul had persecuted the church.
The Corinthian believers carried histories filled with serious sin, yet Paul could speak of washing, sanctification, and justification in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
That is Christianity.
Not good people congratulating themselves for having clean tents.
Sinners washed by Christ.
Sinners forgiven by Christ.
Sinners being transformed by Christ.
Sinners learning to stop hiding because the One who knows everything is also the One who went to the cross to save.
Maybe you have spent years believing that if people really knew you, they would leave.
Perhaps some would.
Jesus already knows.
That is the part that should break something open inside you.
You have never surprised Him.
There has never been a morning when Christ discovered a hidden chapter of your history and said, “I did not know that.”
There is no dirt deep enough to hide something from omniscience.
There is no password strong enough.
No deleted message deleted enough.
No locked room locked enough.
No carefully maintained reputation polished enough.
God knows.
And still the Gospel invitation goes out:
Repent and believe.
Come to Christ.
Stop defending what is killing you.
Stop calling darkness complicated.
Stop demanding that God bless what He has told you to bury forever.
Open your hands.
You do not need the stolen treasure.
You need Jesus.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn this moment into another emotional experience that disappears when you scroll.
Pray.
Confess your sin to God.

Where appropriate, make things right with people you have wronged. Seek mature, biblically faithful pastoral help and accountability when the struggle requires it. If your hidden actions involve abuse, exploitation, criminal wrongdoing, or danger to another person, repentance does not mean merely feeling guilty in private; protecting those harmed, telling the truth, and accepting rightful consequences matter.
Grace does not teach us to escape responsibility.
Grace teaches us to stop running from God.
And maybe your first honest step is only three words.
“Jesus, forgive me.”

And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once thought would own you forever, tell your testimony. Somebody scrolling in silence may need to discover that repentance is not the funeral of hope.
It may be where hope finally begins.
Not because every sentence is comfortable.
What sin promises to give you is never worth what sin demands from you.
Not as a performance.
Not so people think you are spiritual.
Send this to the person who thinks they have sinned beyond the reach of Christ.

Supporting Gospel-centered work matters, but it should never be confused with buying God’s favor. Scripture calls believers to glorify God freely in all of life, including generous support of faithful ministry when they are able.
Your support helps us keep creating and distributing Christ-centered resources designed to call people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through Jesus.
You can support a ministry and still hide from God.
You can share Christian articles and still hide from God.
You can own Christian books, wear Christian shirts, drink from Christian mugs, fill Christian journals, quote Christian posts, and still have treasure beneath the tent.
Jesus wants more than your engagement.
He wants you.
Your heart.
Your surrender.
Your repentance.
Your trust.
Your whole life.
So before you leave this article, ask the question Achan’s story forces upon every honest heart:
What am I still trying to bury that God is asking me to bring into the light?
Do not answer quickly.
Sit there.
Let the silence become honest.
Then remember the cross.
The God who sees beneath the tent is the God who sent His Son.
