And for the single Christian, this matters enormously.
Song of Songs is not telling you that you are half a human being until somebody desires you romantically.
Jesus Himself lived the perfect human life without marriage.
Paul could speak positively of singleness in 1 Corinthians 7.
Your marital status does not determine your spiritual completeness.
Christ does.
Human marriage is temporary.
The marriage toward which history itself is moving is eternal.
Revelation does not end with humanity finally discovering better dating.
It ends with a wedding.
The Bridegroom.
Christ.
His redeemed people.
The marriage supper of the Lamb.
And here the beauty of Song of Songs begins opening toward something greater than itself.
Every faithful marriage whispers that covenant matters.
Every husband who sacrifices instead of exploiting whispers something about Christ.
Every wife cherished rather than consumed reminds us that biblical love recognizes dignity.
Every act of forgiveness inside a wounded marriage whispers that grace can enter places pride wanted to bury.
Every couple choosing fidelity when temptation says “Nobody will know” declares that love is more than appetite.
Yet every human marriage eventually confronts its limits.
Bodies age.
Beauty changes.
Hands wrinkle.
Desire passes through seasons.
Illness comes.
Death separates.
The lovers of Song of Songs can say love is strong as death.
The Gospel goes further.
Jesus Christ entered death…
and came back.
That changes everything.
The greatest love story in Scripture is ultimately not humanity climbing toward God.
It is God coming after rebels.
Christ did not wait for His Bride to make herself worthy before loving her.
He gave Himself for her.
He cleanses.
He sanctifies.
He restores.
He makes beautiful what sin had stained.
And that means your story does not have to end where your worst chapter happened.
Maybe your scandal was sexual.
Maybe it was adultery.
Pornography.
Secret messages.
Emotional infidelity.
Sex outside marriage.
A relationship you knew dishonored God.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe your scandal was not something you chose but something another person did to you, leaving you with wounds you still struggle to name.
Jesus does not confuse what was done against you with what you willingly did.
And neither should the Church.
But whether you need forgiveness for sin you committed or healing from evil committed against you, the invitation leads toward the same Savior.
Jesus Christ.
There is grace here.
Not cheap grace that tells you to continue destroying yourself.
Transforming grace.
Grace that forgives and then teaches you to walk differently.
Grace that can teach a husband to look at his wife again with tenderness instead of entitlement.
Grace that can teach a wife that her worth was never dependent upon comparison.
Grace that can teach a teenager that waiting is not weakness.
Grace that can teach the lonely that loneliness does not justify disobedience.
Grace that can lead the addicted into confession.
Grace that can lead the adulterer into repentance.
Grace that can lead a wounded marriage toward truth.
Grace that can teach a generation raised on pornography how to see human beings as image-bearers again.
This is what Song of Songs really celebrates.
Not lust.
Not promiscuity.
Not bodies detached from souls.
Not desire without boundaries.
It celebrates the astonishing goodness of embodied, faithful, exclusive human love under the wisdom of God.
It tells us desire is powerful enough that we should not awaken it carelessly.
It tells us genuine love cannot be bought.
It tells us the body can be spoken about without shame and admired without degradation.
It reminds married believers that delight in one's spouse is not spiritually inferior simply because it is physical.
And within the full story of Scripture, marriage itself becomes a signpost pointing beyond every earthly lover toward Christ and His redeemed Bride.
So perhaps the question is no longer merely, “What does Song of Songs mean?”
Perhaps the more dangerous question is:
What has been teaching you how to love?
Pornography?
TikTok?
Movies?
Your wounds?
Your hormones?
Your loneliness?
Your parents' broken marriage?
The person who abandoned you?
The culture?
Or the God who invented love before the world learned how to counterfeit it?
Be honest.
Some of us do not need another relationship.
We need repentance.
Some do not need another dating app.
We need healing.
Some married couples do not need a newer partner.
They need renewed covenant faithfulness.
Some singles do not need to lower their standards because the waiting hurts.
They need to remember that awakening love before its proper time can create wounds desperation never warned them about.
And some of you need to stop believing your past has disqualified you from ever becoming clean.
If Christ has forgiven you, stop digging through the graveyard looking for the person He buried.
Walk in repentance.
Walk in purity.
Walk in grace.
And when you fall, do not run deeper into darkness.
Run toward Jesus.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to describe your private sin publicly. But you can comment, “Jesus, make my heart clean.”
If you are fighting to honor Christ with your body and relationships, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If your marriage needs prayer, simply comment, “Pray for us.”

And if Christ is restoring an area of your life you once thought was beyond redemption, comment, “Christ is still healing me.” Your testimony may become the reason another ashamed believer finally realizes that repentance is not the end of the story.
Not because every sentence will be easy to hear, but because there may come a night when desire becomes louder than wisdom and you need to remember:
Do not awaken love before its time.

Supporting Gospel work should never be presented as purchasing God's favor or proving that you glorify Him—salvation is by grace, not payment. But generous support can genuinely help biblical teaching reach people who may never walk into a church.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the person who walked away from church.
Invite the Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the seeker.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity only knows how to shame human desire.
Let them encounter the Bible for themselves.
Because Song of Songs does not reveal a God embarrassed by love.
It reveals a God wise enough to know that something this powerful must never be treated cheaply.

And maybe tonight, after all the Hebrew words, ancient poetry, gardens, kisses, warnings, fire, longing, covenant, failure, repentance, and grace, only one sentence needs to remain burning in your memory:
Your desires do not get to write the ending—Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD IS NOT MOCKED: The Terrifying Verse We Quote at Sinners but Forget to Read to Ourselves
paragraphs:
GOD IS NOT MOCKED: The Terrifying Verse We Quote at Sinners but Forget to Read to Ourselves
And strangely, that terrifying truth may be the doorway to the grace you desperately need.
There are some verses we love putting on other people.
“God is not mocked.”
We say it when somebody openly rebels against God.
We post it when culture celebrates something Scripture condemns.
We remember it when an arrogant person seems to be getting away with evil.
And yes, the warning is real.
But there is something uncomfortable about Galatians 6:7 that we sometimes miss.
Paul was not standing in a pagan marketplace shouting this sentence at unbelievers.
He was writing to people inside the church.
People who knew the language of faith.
People who had heard the Gospel.
People who could say the right things about God.
People disturbingly similar to us.
And before you keep reading, understand where this is going.
This is not an article about “those terrible people out there.”
This is about the seed in your hand.
The seed in mine.
The secret decisions nobody applauds and nobody sees.
The compromises we keep watering.
The repentance we keep postponing.
The habits we excuse because judgment has not arrived yet.
The private things we assume will somehow never become a harvest.
Paul writes:
—Galatians 6:7
The Greek makes the warning even more piercing:
“Μὴ πλανᾶσθε, Θεὸς οὐ μυκτηρίζεται· ὃ γὰρ ἐὰν σπείρῃ ἄνθρωπος, τοῦτο καὶ θερίσει.”
Mē planasthe, Theos ou myktērizetai; ho gar ean speirē anthrōpos, touto kai therisei.
“Do not be deceived. God is not mocked; for whatever a person sows, this also he will reap.”
Notice how Paul begins.
“Μὴ πλανᾶσθε.”
Mē planasthe.
Do not be deceived.
Before Paul speaks about mocking God, he speaks about deception.
Because one of sin’s greatest powers is not merely making evil attractive.
It makes consequences look impossible.
Sin whispers:
Nothing happened last time.
Nobody knows.
You can stop whenever you want.
God understands.
It isn't really hurting anyone.
You still pray.
You still go to church.
You still post Bible verses.
You still believe in Jesus.
So surely everything is fine.
That is the deception.
Then Paul says:
“Θεὸς οὐ μυκτηρίζεται.”
Theos ou myktērizetai.
God is not mocked.
The verb translated “mocked” is μυκτηρίζω (myktērizō). It carries the sense of treating someone with contempt or derision—of sneering at someone as though they can be dismissed.
Paul's point is far deeper than “Don't make jokes about God.”
This is about attempting to treat the living God as though His moral order can be ignored.
As though we can plant one thing and demand that He give us another.
Plant lust and demand purity.
Plant bitterness and demand peace.
Plant dishonesty and demand trust.
Plant pride and demand spiritual intimacy.
Plant neglect and demand a flourishing marriage.
Plant cruelty and demand healthy relationships.
Plant secret sin and demand public anointing.
Plant spiritual laziness and wonder why our souls feel empty.
Plant years into the flesh and then become angry with God when the harvest does not resemble heaven.
That is the insanity Paul exposes.
We want to choose the seed and command God to change the harvest.
But God is not mocked.
And perhaps the most frightening thing about sowing is that harvests do not normally appear immediately.
You can sow today and still smile tonight.
You can compromise today and still sing worship songs on Sunday.
You can betray someone's trust and still receive compliments.
You can feed an addiction and still function at work.
You can carry bitterness for years and still call yourself forgiving.
You can maintain a hidden life while everybody thinks you are spiritually strong.
That delay can become its own form of deception.
Because when consequences are delayed, we begin confusing God's patience with God's approval.
But Scripture warns us against precisely that mistake.
Romans 2:4 asks whether we presume upon the riches of God's kindness, patience, and forbearance, failing to recognize that God's kindness is meant to lead us to repentance.
Read that carefully.
His patience is not permission.
His kindness is an invitation.
His delay is mercy.
The fact that God has not exposed you does not mean He endorses what you are hiding.
The fact that you woke up this morning is not evidence that sin does not matter.
It may be evidence that mercy has given you another morning to repent.
And that changes everything.
Because “God is not mocked” is not merely a threat hanging over a sinner.
In Christ, it can become an alarm clock.
Wake up.
Come home.
Stop pretending.
Put down the shovel.
Stop planting what is destroying you.
There is still time to surrender the field.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been fighting.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Your pastor does not know.
Your parents do not know.
Your children do not know.
Your friends see your smile but not what happens when the room gets quiet.
Maybe your browser history tells a different story from your Sunday worship.
Maybe your bank statement exposes priorities your mouth would never admit.
Maybe there is a conversation you keep deleting.
A resentment you keep feeding.
An affair of the heart you keep calling harmless.
A secret addiction.
An obsession.
A lie you have repeated so many times that you almost believe it.
A person you refuse to forgive.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
A private compromise you have renamed so you no longer have to call it sin.
And somewhere inside, you keep thinking:
I will deal with it later.
That sentence has buried more spiritual lives than we realize.
Later.
Later I will repent.
Later I will forgive.
Later I will confess.
Later I will return to Scripture.
Later I will become serious about Jesus.
Later I will repair what I damaged.
Later I will stop.
But every “later” plants another seed.
Paul continues:
“For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.”
—Galatians 6:8
This is the context we cannot remove from “God is not mocked.”
Paul is describing two directions of life.
The flesh.
The Spirit.
And the question becomes painfully personal:
What are you feeding?
Not what do you claim to believe.
Not what Christian label do you use.
Not what verse is written in your bio.
What are you actually feeding?
Because eventually, what we repeatedly feed begins feeding on us.
That secret anger changes the way you speak.
That pornography changes the way you see people.
That envy makes another person's blessing feel like your punishment.
That greed teaches you that “enough” is always one purchase away.
That pride makes correction feel like persecution.
That unforgiveness allows someone who wounded you years ago to continue occupying your heart today.
That constant hunger for human approval slowly makes obedience to God feel dangerous.
Seeds become habits.
Habits become patterns.
Patterns shape character.
And character has consequences.
This is why biblical grace must never be reduced to God shrugging at sin.
Grace is far more beautiful than that.
Grace does not merely tell guilty people, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
The cross tells us sin mattered so profoundly that the Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Jesus did not die because rebellion was insignificant.
He died because we could not save ourselves from it.
“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree.”
—1 Peter 2:24
At Calvary, God did not pretend sin was harmless.
Justice and mercy met at the cross.
Christ bore sin.
Christ endured the cross.
Christ rose from the dead.
And now forgiveness is offered not because we have successfully cleaned ourselves up, but because Jesus Christ is a sufficient Savior.
That is where this warning becomes breathtaking.
The God who cannot be mocked is also the God who receives repentant sinners.
The God who sees everything is the God from whom you no longer need to hide.
The God who knows the scandal is the God who offers grace.
Think about Peter.
He promised loyalty.
Then fear entered the room.
One accusation.
Another.
Then another.
And the man who said he would die with Jesus denied even knowing Him.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine hearing your own voice say the words you swore you would never say.
Imagine realizing that Jesus had already told you this would happen.
Peter's failure was real.
His tears were real.
His scandal was real.
But his scandal was not the final chapter.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him.
Not because denial suddenly became acceptable.
Not because holiness stopped mattering.
But because grace can restore what sin has shattered.
Peter's story did not end beside a charcoal fire of denial.
Jesus met him again beside another charcoal fire in John 21.
Failure met mercy.
Shame met restoration.
The fallen disciple heard Christ call him forward again.
“Follow me.”
That is the Gospel.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not rewriting evil as good.
Not calling darkness light.
Jesus does something infinitely greater.
He redeems sinners.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you need that sentence more than you expected.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
But grace is not permission to keep writing the same rebellion forever.
Jesus does not merely offer you a prettier version of your old life.
He calls you to Himself.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Repentance is not earning forgiveness.
You cannot.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior because the Holy Spirit has opened your eyes to see that the thing you were embracing is killing you and Christ is better.
This is why the Gospel destroys both despair and presumption.
Despair says:
“I have gone too far. Jesus could never forgive someone like me.”
The cross answers:
Christ saves sinners.
Presumption says:
“I can continue deliberately embracing sin because Jesus will forgive me anyway.”
The cross answers:
You were purchased at an immeasurable price. Do not treat grace as permission to cherish the very rebellion from which Christ came to redeem you.
Grace neither tells the broken sinner to stay away nor tells the comfortable sinner to stay asleep.
Grace says:
Come to Jesus.
Come honestly.
Come guilty.
Come exhausted.
Come exposed.
Come without excuses.
Come without pretending.
But come ready to surrender.
Perhaps that is why this verse feels so sharp.
“God is not mocked.”
There is nowhere to hide.
And maybe that is good news.
Because hiding is exhausting.
Maintaining two versions of yourself is exhausting.
Pretending you are okay is exhausting.
Managing appearances while your soul is bleeding is exhausting.
Explaining away conviction is exhausting.
Running from God is exhausting.
Adam discovered that in Eden.
After sin came hiding.
But God called:
“Where are you?”
Not because an omniscient God had misplaced Adam.
The question brought the hiding man into the open.
And perhaps, through these words, God is asking something similar of you.
Where are you?
Not your Facebook version.
Not your church version.
Not the version everybody congratulates.
You.
Where are you?
What have you been sowing?
What are you becoming?
What are you hiding?
What are you refusing to surrender?
What would happen if Jesus touched the one room in your life you keep locked?
This is the moment when some people close the article.
Don't.
Because conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
For those who belong to Christ, conviction is not God gleefully crushing you.
The Holy Spirit exposes darkness to lead us toward truth, repentance, restoration, and deeper fellowship with Christ.
The enemy wants exposure to end in hopelessness.
Jesus brings sinners into the light so healing and transformation can begin.
So stop negotiating with the seed.
Stop asking how close you can live to sin without consequences.
Ask a better question:
How completely can I belong to Jesus?
And if you have failed again?
Run toward Christ.
If you have fallen?
Run toward Christ.
If yesterday was ugly?
Run toward Christ.
If your secret finally came into the light?
Run toward Christ.
If consequences remain even after forgiveness?
Walk through them with Christ.
If repentance requires an apology, make it.
If integrity requires confession, seek wise and biblically appropriate help and tell the truth.
If temptation requires boundaries, build them.
If a relationship continually leads you into rebellion, stop pretending proximity to sin is strength.
If you need mature Christian accountability, seek it.
If something keeps feeding your flesh, stop feeding it.
Then begin sowing differently.
Open Scripture when you would normally scroll.
Pray when anxiety tells you to panic.
Forgive when your flesh demands revenge.
Give when greed says hoard.
Tell the truth when lying would be easier.
Turn your eyes away when lust tells you to stare.
Serve when pride demands attention.
Worship when despair says God has abandoned you.
Return when shame tells you to disappear.
These things do not purchase salvation.
Jesus purchased redemption.
We obey because grace has changed the direction of our lives.
And don't miss what comes immediately after Paul's warning.
Galatians 6:9 says:
“And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up.”
There is another harvest.
Maybe you needed to hear that too.
Not every seed you planted was evil.
Some of you have been praying for years.
Keep sowing.
Some of you have been resisting a temptation nobody knows exists.
Keep sowing.
Some of you are raising children and wondering whether anything you teach them is reaching their hearts.
Keep sowing.
Some of you chose forgiveness even though the wound still hurts.
Keep sowing.
Some of you returned to Jesus after years away and are frustrated because transformation feels slower than you expected.
Keep sowing.
Some of you are serving while nobody notices.
Keep sowing.
Some of you are fighting to rebuild a marriage, restore integrity, renew your mind, break destructive patterns, and learn obedience one difficult day at a time.
Do not grow weary.
The God who is not mocked is also the God who sees faithfulness nobody else sees.
And that makes Galatians 6:7 more than frightening.
It makes it hopeful.
Seeds matter.
Your choices matter.
Faithfulness matters.
Repentance matters.
What you do when nobody watches matters.
And above all, Jesus matters.
Maybe this article found you while you are standing between two fields.
One contains what you have been sowing.
The other contains what, by God's grace, you could begin sowing today.
You cannot return to yesterday and remove every seed.
Some earthly consequences may remain.
Some apologies may still need to be made.
Some trust may require time to rebuild.
Some wounds need patient healing.
But you can bring your life to Jesus Christ.
And He is still in the business of redeeming people whose stories looked ruined.
That is why Gospel Warrior will never preach behavior modification without Christ.
We do not need motivational Christianity.
We need Jesus.
Crucified.
Risen.
Reigning.
Calling sinners to repentance.
Offering forgiveness.
Breaking chains.
Restoring the fallen.
Transforming hearts.
Making old things new.
Be honest.

And if Christ has already begun restoring a chapter you thought was beyond redemption, tell your testimony. Someone reading the comments may desperately need evidence that failure does not have to be final.
Then think of one person who needs this message.
Not somebody you want to embarrass.
Not somebody you want to “teach a lesson.”
Someone you love.
Someone drifting.
Someone hiding.
Someone exhausted from maintaining appearances.
Someone who believes his or her scandal is too ugly for grace.
Your share might put the truth in front of them at the exact moment they were preparing to give up.
Not because every sentence will be comfortable tomorrow, but because some truths need to confront us more than once.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, confront sin honestly, understand biblical truth, heal through the Gospel, and grow deeper in Jesus Christ, stay close.
Supporting a ministry is not what saves you.
We are saved by God's grace through faith, not by purchasing access to religious content.

But Scripture does teach willing generosity and partnership in Gospel work. If God has blessed you with the ability and you genuinely believe this ministry is bearing biblical fruit, supporting it can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership—freely given, never coerced.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Give freely where God leads you to give.
Serve.
Pray.
Love people.
Support faithful Gospel work according to your ability.
And never turn money into the measure of someone's devotion to Jesus.
Christ already paid the price that matters most.
So tonight, before you close this article, forget everybody else for a moment.
Forget the person you thought needed to read this.
Look at your own field.
What have you been planting?
What seed is in your hand right now?
Because tomorrow's harvest is being touched by today's surrender.
God is not mocked.
But neither is His grace exhausted by the repentant sinner who comes home through Jesus Christ.
The God who sees the seed also sees the tears.
The God who sees the scandal also sees what Christ can redeem.
And perhaps the chapter you are most ashamed of is not where your story ends.
The seed may explain your yesterday—but surrendered to Jesus, your yesterday does not have to own your tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN SATAN USE GOOD THINGS TO DISTRACT YOU?
paragraphs:
CAN SATAN USE GOOD THINGS TO DISTRACT YOU?
The Most Dangerous Distractions May Be the Ones You Thank God For
What if the thing pulling you away from Jesus does not look sinful?
What if it looks responsible?
Productive.
Necessary.
Even blessed.
What if you are not running from God at all?
What if you are simply becoming so busy with good things that you no longer notice how little room remains for the One who gave them to you?

That question is uncomfortable because most Christians know how to watch for obvious temptation. We know to be cautious around lust, greed, bitterness, drunkenness, pornography, dishonesty, hatred, pride, and rebellion.
But what do you do when the distraction looks like a promotion?
A relationship you prayed for.
A growing business.
A ministry opportunity.
A child you adore.
A dream finally coming true.
A phone filled with messages from people who need you.
A schedule filled with things that genuinely matter.
There are sins that drag a person away from God screaming.
And then there are distractions that carry them away quietly.
No scandal.
No dramatic rebellion.
No moment when you consciously announce, “Jesus, I do not want You anymore.”
Just a hundred small decisions in which everything else keeps getting your attention first.
Until one night you realize something frightening.
You still believe in Jesus.
You still call yourself a Christian.
You may still attend church.
You may still share Bible verses.
You may even be serving people in His name.
But somewhere between the deadlines, notifications, responsibilities, ambitions, entertainment, relationships, ministry, and exhaustion...
your heart stopped sitting at His feet.
And perhaps that is why this question matters so much:
Can Satan use good things to distract you?
Scripture gives us a more careful answer than a sensational yes.

Satan does not become the author of God's good gifts. James tells us that every good and perfect gift is from above (James 1:17). Marriage is not evil because someone idolizes a spouse. Work is not evil because someone worships success. Family is not evil because someone places family above Christ. Ministry is not evil because a minister becomes consumed by ministry.
The gift can remain good while our relationship to the gift becomes disordered.
And Scripture absolutely warns that spiritual deception does not always arrive wearing darkness.
Paul wrote:
“καὶ οὐ θαῦμα· αὐτὸς γὰρ ὁ Σατανᾶς μετασχηματίζεται εἰς ἄγγελον φωτός.”
“And no wonder, for Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light.” — 2 Corinthians 11:14
The Greek verb μετασχηματίζεται — metaschēmatizetai carries the idea of changing outward appearance or disguising oneself.
But context matters enormously.

Paul is specifically warning the Corinthians about false apostles and deceitful workers presenting themselves as apostles of Christ. So we should not abuse this verse by claiming that every pleasant circumstance, every opportunity, or every busy season is secretly satanic.
The biblical principle is subtler and more sobering:
Appearance alone is not enough to determine whether something is spiritually healthy.
Something can look bright and still lead you away from truth.
Something can look religious and still distort Christ.
Something can appear successful while slowly starving your soul.
The enemy does not need to convince a believer that Jesus is worthless if he can tempt that believer to live as though everything else is more urgent.
Read that again.
Because perhaps your greatest spiritual battle right now is not between something obviously evil and something obviously good.
Perhaps it is between what is good and the One who is greatest.
Jesus once entered a home where two sisters loved Him.
One of them, Martha, began serving.
Notice that.
She was not committing adultery.
She was not stealing.
She was not worshiping an idol.
She was serving Jesus.
Preparing.
Working.
Doing something useful.
Something hospitable.
Something good.
Yet Luke tells us she became distracted with much serving, while Mary sat at Jesus' feet listening to Him. Martha eventually became frustrated enough to ask Jesus to make Mary help her.
Then came Christ's tender correction:
“Martha, Martha...”
You can almost hear the affection before the correction.
She was worried and troubled about many things, but Jesus told her that one thing was necessary, and Mary had chosen the good portion (Luke 10:38–42).
Martha's problem was not simply that she was doing something evil.
That is precisely what makes the scene so penetrating.
She was doing something for Jesus while becoming distracted from Jesus.
And that sentence should frighten every person involved in Christian ministry.
You can preach about Him and neglect Him.
You can design graphics about Him and stop listening to Him.
You can sing worship songs while your private prayer life disappears.
You can moderate Christian communities, write devotionals, answer theological questions, volunteer at church, lead Bible studies, feed the poor, raise money, build ministries...
and slowly begin loving the work of the Lord more than the Lord of the work.
Sometimes the most dangerous sentence a Christian can say is:
“But I'm doing this for God.”
Because even something done for God must never become a substitute for being with God.
Jesus gives another disturbing picture in the parable of the soils.
Some seed falls among thorns. The Word is genuinely heard, but then something happens.
The Greek of Mark 4:19 says:
“αἱ μέριμναι τοῦ αἰῶνος... εἰσπορευόμεναι συμπνίγουσιν τὸν λόγον.”
The concerns or anxieties of the age enter in and “choke” the Word.
The verb is συμπνίγουσιν — sympnigousin.
Choke.
Crowd.
Suffocate.
And Jesus does not mention only obviously wicked things. He speaks about the cares of the age, the deceitfulness of riches, and desires for other things entering in until the Word becomes unfruitful.
That is one of the Bible's most terrifying pictures of distraction.
The seed is there.
The Word is there.
But so are the thorns.
And thorns do not need to destroy the seed in one dramatic attack.
They simply have to keep growing around it.
Perhaps that describes somebody reading this.
You did not wake up one morning and reject Christ.
The thorns just grew.
Work grew.
Bills grew.
Netflix grew.
Scrolling grew.
Your ambitions grew.
Your relationship grew.
Your children's schedules grew.
Your hobbies grew.
Your worries grew.
Your notifications grew.
Your plans grew.
Even your ministry grew.
And somewhere underneath everything growing...
your attention to Jesus became smaller.
Five minutes of Scripture while checking notifications.
A hurried prayer while walking out the door.
“I'll spend time with God tonight.”
Then tonight becomes tomorrow.
Tomorrow becomes next week.
Next week becomes, “I've just been really busy lately.”
And eventually you become accustomed to surviving on spiritual crumbs while sitting at a table Jesus has already invited you to feast from.
That is how distraction can become spiritually devastating.
Not necessarily because the things filling your life are inherently sinful.
But because anything can become spiritually dangerous when it consistently occupies the place of obedience, affection, trust, identity, or worship that belongs to Christ.
Your career can be a gift.
But your career cannot be your god.
Your marriage can be a gift.
But your spouse cannot be your savior.
Your children can be precious gifts.
But they cannot sit on Christ's throne.
Money can feed your family and fund the Gospel.
But money makes a terrible master.
Rest is biblical.
Entertainment can be morally permissible.
Technology can spread Scripture across continents.
Social media can put the Gospel before someone at 2:00 in the morning who would never voluntarily enter a church.
The question is not merely:
“Is this thing bad?”
Sometimes the better question is:
“What is this thing doing to my hunger for Christ?”
Does it make obedience easier or continually postpone it?
Does it help you love people or make you increasingly self-absorbed?
Can you put it down when God calls you away from it?
Can you lose it without losing yourself?
Can you thank God for it without needing it to feel whole?
Can Christ say “give this to Me” without your heart immediately constructing ten arguments for why He should leave it alone?
That last question exposes idols quickly.
Because an idol is not always a statue.
Sometimes it has a salary.
Sometimes it has a screen.
Sometimes it has someone's name in your contacts.
Sometimes it is your reputation.
Sometimes it is your dream.
Sometimes it is even the version of your future you have been asking God to bless.
And this is where we must be careful not to blame Satan for every weakness of our own flesh.

Scripture speaks about the world, the flesh, and the devil. Not every distraction is a direct demonic attack. Sometimes we simply lack discipline. Sometimes our desires are disordered. Sometimes we have trained ourselves to need constant stimulation.
But Scripture also tells believers not to be ignorant of Satan's schemes, to resist the devil, and to remain sober and watchful.
So yes, the enemy can exploit good things.
He can tempt us to turn gifts into gods.
He can encourage distorted priorities.
He can exploit anxiety.
He can counterfeit light.
He can whisper half-truths.
He can tempt you toward tomorrow's obedience instead of today's obedience.
Because delayed obedience can eventually become comfortable disobedience.
And Satan has been twisting good things since Genesis.
When Jesus Himself was tempted in the wilderness, Satan even quoted Scripture.
Think about that.
The devil can quote Bible verses.
Matthew 4 records Satan taking words from Psalm 91 and placing them inside a temptation.
Jesus answered with Scripture rightly understood and rightly applied.
That means the existence of a Bible verse attached to an idea does not automatically make the idea biblical.
Context matters.
Truth matters.
Christ matters.
And discernment matters.
The enemy's question in Eden was essentially:
“Did God really say...?”
His strategy was not merely to make evil attractive.
It was to make God's goodness questionable.
That strategy has not become obsolete.
“Surely God understands why you're too busy to pray.”
“You deserve this.”
“You can repent later.”
“Everybody does it.”
“Your career needs you more right now.”
“Once life settles down, you'll get serious about Jesus.”
“You don't need fellowship.”
“You already know the Bible.”
“You're doing enough Christian things.”
“You've suffered. God won't mind this compromise.”
And perhaps the most dangerous:
“It's not technically a sin.”
Maybe not.
But Christian maturity asks a deeper question than merely, “How close to sin can I walk without technically crossing the line?”
It asks:
“Will this help me run toward Jesus?”
Paul described Christian freedom with wisdom: not everything permissible is beneficial, and he refused to be mastered by anything (1 Corinthians 6:12).
That word mastered matters.
Because some things begin as tools and end as masters.
You picked up the phone.
Then eventually the phone began picking the direction of your attention.
You started building the career.
Then the career began building your identity.
You wanted financial security.
Then security quietly became the thing you trusted more than Providence.
You wanted someone to love you.
Then their approval became oxygen.
You wanted ministry growth.
Then numbers began determining whether you felt valuable.
And one day God touches the thing you once called a blessing...
and you discover you cannot surrender it.
That is when the gift reveals the throne you built beneath it.
Maybe this article is not asking you to throw away your phone, quit your job, abandon your ambitions, stop enjoying recreation, or become suspicious of every blessing.
Maybe Jesus is asking something much more personal.
“Do you still love Me more?”
Not in your theology.
In your Tuesday.
In your calendar.
In your browser history.
In your bank statement.
In the first thoughts of your morning.
In the last thirty minutes before sleep.
In what you reach for when loneliness arrives.
In what you daydream about.
In what you fear losing.
In what you refuse to surrender.
Peter once believed he loved Jesus more than he actually understood.
Then came the courtyard.
A charcoal fire.
Questions.
Fear.
Three denials.
“I don't know Him.”
Imagine hearing yourself say those words after promising you would die for Him.
Imagine seeing Jesus afterward.
Imagine the shame.
Peter had failed publicly and personally.
But that was not the end of Peter's story.
After the resurrection, Jesus met him again beside another charcoal fire.
And Jesus asked him the question beneath every other question:
“Do you love Me?”
Not, “Peter, can you erase your scandal?”
Not, “Peter, can you undo your failure?”
Not, “Peter, can you prove you deserve another chance?”
“Do you love Me?”
And then Jesus recommissioned the man who had denied Him.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely expose our distractions.
He calls distracted hearts home.
He does not reveal idols because He enjoys humiliating sinners.
He reveals what is killing us because He loves us.
The answer is not to become obsessed with Satan.
The answer is to become captivated again by Christ.
The Christian life is not primarily about staring into darkness trying to identify every demonic strategy.
It is about walking in the Light.
Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners.
He bore sin.
He endured judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day He rose.
Our hope is not superior time management.
Our hope is not digital minimalism.
Our hope is not greater productivity.
Our hope is not becoming disciplined enough to impress God.
Our hope has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have been distracted for months.
Maybe years.
Maybe nobody knows.
Your Christianity still looks intact from the outside.
But inside...
you know.
The fire has become an ember.
Prayer feels foreign.
Scripture feels distant.
Worship feels mechanical.
Sin feels easier to excuse.
You miss the person you were when hearing the name Jesus could bring tears to your eyes.
Listen carefully.
Do not turn this conviction into another promise you forget tomorrow.
Come home now.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It is a turning.
Turn from whatever has taken Christ's rightful place.
Confess what needs confessing.
Remove what needs removing.
Restore what needs restoring.
Ask forgiveness where forgiveness is needed.
Open the Scriptures again.
Pray badly if you cannot pray beautifully.
Whisper His name if that is all you can manage.
Jesus.
The Savior who restored Peter is not intimidated by the wreckage you bring Him.
There is grace for distracted people.
Grace for compromised people.
Grace for people who wasted years.
Grace for people who loved gifts more than the Giver.
Grace for people whose priorities became upside down.
But grace is not permission to remain asleep.
Grace calls you home.
And perhaps your first act of repentance tonight is astonishingly small.
Turn the screen off.
Close the door.
Open the Bible.
And say:
“Jesus, show me what has been taking Your place.”
Then do not rush to answer for Him.
Stay.
Listen.
Let Scripture search you.
Maybe the thing He reveals will surprise you.
Maybe it is not pornography.
Maybe it is productivity.
Maybe it is not drunkenness.
Maybe it is success.
Maybe it is not hatred.
Maybe it is hurry.
Maybe it is not some secret scandal.
Maybe it is something everybody congratulates you for.
That is why discernment matters.
Good things make wonderful servants.
They make terrible gods.
And when a blessing begins competing with the Blesser, surrender is not losing the blessing.
Surrender is putting it back where it belongs.
Be real.
Or tell your story. Someone else reading may discover they are not the only believer fighting to find their way back to undistracted devotion to Christ.
Not because an article deserves a place in your saved folder, but because there may come a night when the thorns start growing again and you need the question waiting for you:
“Do you still love Me more?”
But do it for the right reason.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
It cannot.
Christ's grace cannot be bought.

If Gospel Warrior helps you grow in Christ, however, supporting and sharing this ministry can be one practical way to help biblical encouragement reach another person. Giving, sharing, and supporting Christian work can glorify God when they flow freely from love, gratitude, generosity, and a desire to advance truth—not guilt or spiritual coercion.

Think of it not as purchasing God's favor—never that—but as voluntarily standing behind a ministry you want to see reach more souls while receiving deeper biblical nourishment, encouragement, accountability, and spiritual sharpening.
Share because someone may need the message.
Follow because your soul needs truth more often than your feed gives it to you.
Save because distraction has a way of returning.
And comment because your confession may become someone else's permission to stop pretending.
But above all...
return to Jesus.
Because eventually every notification will stop.
Every career will end.
Every possession will belong to someone else.
Every applause will become silent.
Every trend will disappear.
Every achievement will become history.
And when everything that competed for your attention is finally gone...
Christ will still be Christ.
So perhaps the question was never merely:
“Can Satan use good things to distract you?”
Perhaps the question that has been waiting underneath this entire article is much closer to the heart:
What good thing have you allowed to become more precious than Jesus?
Whatever your answer is, bring it into the light.
The scandal may be that you wandered while carrying His blessings in your hands.
The grace is that Jesus is still calling your name.
Do not spend your whole life protecting the gifts and wake up one day realizing you neglected the Giver.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Porn Doesn’t Just Change What You See—It Can Change How You See Scripture
paragraphs: Porn Doesn’t Just Change What You See—It Can Change How You See Scripture

What happens when eyes repeatedly trained to consume bodies are opened to a Bible that calls those same eyes to behold Christ? This is not merely an article about pornography. It is about what repeated lust can teach the heart to do with people, with truth, with shame—and even with the Word of God.
There is a strange moment that many Christians caught in pornography know but almost never talk about.
The screen goes dark.
The room becomes quiet again.
Whatever excitement was there collapses almost instantly, and in its place comes something heavier.
Maybe disgust.
Maybe numbness.
Maybe shame.
Maybe that familiar promise whispered for the hundredth time:
That was the last time.
Then your eyes move across the room.
And there it is.
Your Bible.
Perhaps it is sitting on your nightstand.
Perhaps the Bible app is still on the same phone you just used to watch what you know you should not have watched.
And suddenly Scripture feels different.
You know the words have not changed.
But something inside you has.
You open the Bible hoping to hear God, yet part of you is terrified that God is going to speak.
You read about holiness and feel accused.
You read about judgment and feel exposed.
You read about grace and wonder whether it could possibly still include you.
You read about God's love and secretly think, Yes, but He doesn't know what I just did.
Except He does.
That is where this conversation must begin.
Not with pretending.
Not with religious performance.
Not with another promise that sheer willpower will finally make you clean.
But with Jesus Christ meeting sinners in the place where they have stopped believing they can be honestly known and still invited home.

Pornography can affect the way you approach Scripture because sin does not merely involve what we do with our bodies. Sin reaches into desire, attention, imagination, conscience, relationships, and worship.
But be careful here.
The Bible does not contain the modern word pornography in the technological sense in which we use it today.
So biblical faithfulness requires us not to pretend that a verse says something it does not say.

What Scripture does address unmistakably is lust, sexual immorality, impurity, covetous desire, self-control, the stewardship of the body, and what a person intentionally does with his or her eyes and heart.
Jesus goes directly beneath outward behavior.
In Matthew 5:28, the Greek text reads:
πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν...
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn...
In context, Jesus teaches that the one who looks at a woman with the purpose of lusting after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
That matters.

Jesus is not teaching that noticing another person's beauty is automatically adultery. He is confronting the intentional cultivation of lust—the gaze that does not merely notice but continues in order to desire sexually what has not been given to it.
The Greek verb connected with desire here is ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō, meaning to desire, long for, or covet depending upon context.
The problem is not simply that eyes receive an image.
The problem is what the heart chooses to do with what the eyes have seen.
And pornography is built around something dangerously close to the very pattern Jesus exposes.
Look longer.
Desire more.
Consume another person visually.
Return.
Search.
Scroll.
Choose.
Enlarge.
Replay.
Want again.
Then Scripture opens and says something completely different.
See people as image-bearers.
Love instead of consume.
Serve instead of use.
Give instead of take.
Flee instead of linger.
Worship the Creator instead of turning His creation into fuel for appetite.
Do you see the collision?
Pornography is not simply competing with your Bible for ten minutes of your evening.
It can be training your attention in the opposite direction from discipleship.
Porn says, What can this person give me?
Jesus says, Love your neighbor.
Porn trains the eyes to evaluate bodies.
Jesus teaches us to recognize persons.
Porn encourages appetite without covenant.
Scripture calls sexuality into holiness, faithfulness, love, responsibility, and God's purposes.
Porn invites you into secrecy.
Jesus calls you into the light.
Porn promises satisfaction without sacrifice.
Jesus says:
“Follow Me.”
And this is one reason pornography can make reading Scripture so uncomfortable.
The Bible refuses to become pornography for the religious mind.
Pornography says, Give me stimulation.
Scripture says, Give Me your heart.
Pornography asks, What can I get from this?
Scripture eventually confronts us with another question:
What if God wants to change me through this?
That difference is enormous.
Because repeated consumption can teach us to approach experiences according to immediate payoff.
Is this exciting?
Is this satisfying?
Does this make me feel something right now?
Give me more.
Give me something stronger.
Give me another image.
Another scene.
Another rush.
But Scripture frequently refuses instant gratification.
Sometimes God gives you Leviticus.
Sometimes genealogies.
Sometimes lament.
Sometimes a command you would rather not obey.
Sometimes a promise that requires waiting.
Sometimes a passage exposes something you desperately wanted to keep hidden.
Sometimes the Word comforts you.
Sometimes it wounds before it heals.
Sometimes you close the Bible exhilarated.
Sometimes you close it convicted.
Christian discipleship cannot survive if God is valued only according to how quickly He stimulates us.
The psalmist understood something profound about the relationship between eyes and spiritual life.
Psalm 119:37 pleads with God to turn the eyes away from worthless things and preserve life according to His way.
That prayer is thousands of years older than the internet.
Yet it sounds almost frighteningly contemporary.
Turn my eyes.
Because sometimes the battle begins before the hands move.
Before the browser opens.
Before the search is typed.
Before the video plays.
There was an eye.
Then attention.
Then desire.
Then consent.
Then action.
Then shame.
Then hiding.
And hiding changes how you read the Bible.
When Adam and Eve sinned in Genesis 3, one of their immediate responses was concealment.
They hid.
Human beings have been hiding ever since.
We hide behind jokes.
We hide behind ministry.
We hide behind theology.
We hide behind church attendance.
We hide behind marriages that look healthy in photographs.
We hide behind worship songs.
We hide behind deleted histories.
We hide behind “I'm doing okay.”
And sometimes we even hide behind Bible reading.
You can read Scripture without allowing Scripture to read you.
That may be one of pornography's most subtle spiritual consequences.
You begin developing defensive ways of encountering God's Word.
You rush through passages about purity.
You soften verses about lust.
You become unusually fascinated with arguments about what technically “counts” as sexual sin.
You compare yourself with someone worse.
You search for loopholes instead of holiness.
Or you go in the opposite direction.
Every verse becomes condemnation.
Every warning becomes proof that God despises you.
Every sermon feels aimed directly at your secret.
Every call to holiness becomes another courtroom.
Then eventually you stop opening the Bible altogether.
Not necessarily because you stopped believing in God.
Sometimes because you still believe enough to be afraid of what He will say.
But listen carefully.
Conviction and condemnation are not the same thing.
Biblical conviction says:
Come into the light.
Condemnation whispers:
Stay hidden because there is no hope for someone like you.
Conviction identifies the wound because God intends healing.
Despair tells you the wound has become your identity.
The Gospel does something astonishing with both lies.
It refuses to tell you that your sin is harmless.
And it refuses to tell you that your sin is greater than Christ.
That is Christianity.
Not denial.
Not despair.
A cross.
Paul's language to the Corinthians is breathtakingly direct.
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
The verb φεύγετε — pheugete carries the sense of fleeing, escaping, running away, shunning.
Not negotiate.
Not see how close you can stand.
Not keep the account because maybe you are strong enough now.
Not keep the secret folder.
Not continue following the accounts that repeatedly pull your imagination toward lust.
Flee.
But Paul does not stop there.
And this is where the Gospel becomes far more beautiful than another purity lecture.
A few lines later he tells believers why their bodies matter.
They belong to God.
Their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit.
They were bought with a price.
Therefore, Paul says, glorify God with your body.
Read that again.
Bought with a price.
Paul does not motivate holiness by saying:
Make yourself valuable enough for God.
He reminds Christians that a price has already been paid.
The Gospel order matters.
You do not become valuable because you finally conquered every sexual temptation.
Christ's blood is not the trophy God gives people who successfully cleaned themselves.
Jesus came for sinners.
At the cross, Christ bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Forgiveness is not purchased by your streak of good behavior.
It was purchased by Christ.
And that changes how a struggling Christian reads Scripture.
Imagine two people opening the same Bible after falling into the same sexual sin.
One reads:
“Flee sexual immorality.”
And hears:
God hates me.
The other reads:
“Flee sexual immorality.”
And eventually hears:
My Father loves me too much to leave me chained to something that is destroying me.
Same command.
Different understanding of the Gospel.
Grace does not make the command weaker.
Grace finally gives you a reason to obey that is deeper than terror.
You are not fleeing pornography so Jesus might someday love you.
You flee because in Christ you have discovered a love more holy than lust and a Savior more satisfying than secrecy.
That does not mean recovery is effortless.
Some people need radical changes.
Confession.
Accountability.
Removing access.
Changing routines.
Ending secret accounts.
Putting devices outside bedrooms.
Seeking mature pastoral help.

In some cases, professional counseling can also be valuable, particularly when compulsive sexual behavior has become deeply entrenched or is connected with trauma, anxiety, loneliness, or other struggles.
None of those actions earn salvation.
They are ways of refusing to make peace with what you are asking Christ to help you put to death.
Repentance is not merely feeling disgusting after sin.
Feeling terrible is not necessarily repentance.
Repentance turns.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance, a change of mind that expresses itself in turning toward God.
And perhaps that is what needs to happen with your Bible too.
You may need to relearn how to read it.
Not as a defendant desperately searching the pages to discover whether God has finally had enough of you.
Not as a consumer hunting for a quick spiritual sensation.
Not as a lawyer searching for loopholes.
Not as a hypocrite collecting verses you have no intention of obeying.
But as someone standing hungry before the living God saying:
“Lord, tell me the truth—even when it hurts. And then give me grace to obey.”
Something remarkable begins happening when grace enters that room.
The Bible you were afraid to open becomes the place where hiding begins to die.
Psalm 51 stops sounding like someone else's prayer.
“Create in me a clean heart” becomes personal.
Romans 8 stops being decorative theology.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” becomes oxygen.
First John 1:9 stops being a memory verse from childhood and becomes a doorway back into honest fellowship: if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
And suddenly you realize something.
God knew.
He knew before you confessed.
He knew before you deleted the history.
He knew while you were promising everyone you were fine.
He knew when you worshiped Sunday morning after falling Saturday night.
He knew every search.
Every return.
Every rationalization.
Every tear.
Every promise.
Every failure.
And the invitation of Christ was never:
Hide better.
It was:
Come.
This is where pornography's distortion of Scripture begins to lose its grip.
Because pornography teaches you to separate bodies from persons.
The Gospel reunites what sin fragments.
Pornography says bodies exist for consumption.
Scripture says the body matters to God.
Pornography teaches secrecy.
Scripture calls us to walk in light.
Pornography trains appetite.
The Spirit produces self-control.
Pornography whispers that desire must be obeyed.
Jesus demonstrates that obedience to the Father is greater than appetite.
Pornography tells you, You need this.
Jesus asks whether you will trust Him when your flesh screams otherwise.
Pornography says, Again.
Grace says, Come home.
And perhaps you have been asking the wrong question.
Maybe you keep asking:
“How can I stop wanting pornography?”
But perhaps underneath it is another question:
“How can I begin wanting Christ more?”
Because Christianity is not ultimately a story about emptying the human heart until nothing remains.
It is about a greater affection taking the throne.
Paul tells believers in Romans 12:2 to be transformed by the renewing of the mind.
Transformation.
Renewal.
Not merely suppression.
The Gospel does not only address your browser history.
Jesus wants your imagination.
Your loneliness.
Your wounds.
Your desires.
Your eyes.
Your sexuality.
Your memories.
Your body.
Your worship.
Your future.
All of you.
And maybe that scares you because you have spent years compartmentalizing.
Jesus can have Sunday.
Jesus can have my theology.
Jesus can have my public life.
Jesus can have my ministry.
But this room stays locked.
Except the room you refuse to surrender eventually becomes the room from which chains are dragged through the rest of your life.
So open it.
Not to the internet.
To Christ.
Bring Him the thing you have been editing out of your testimony.
Bring Him the relapse.
Bring Him the loneliness beneath the relapse.
Bring Him the marriage pain.
Bring Him the curiosity that became a habit.
Bring Him the habit that became bondage.
Bring Him the shame that convinced you bondage had become identity.
You are not being invited to rename darkness as light.
You are being invited out of darkness.
There is a difference.
And if you fall again?
Do not turn grace into permission.
But do not turn failure into a new religion either.
Confess.
Repent.
Get up.
Run toward Christ.
Bring the sin into appropriate, trustworthy Christian accountability.
Strengthen the boundaries.
Return to Scripture.
Pray when you feel nothing.
Obey while your emotions catch up.
Keep walking.
Sanctification can involve a long war.
A war is not won by pretending there are no battles.
And one failure does not give you permission to surrender the battlefield.
Maybe you need to hear this tonight:
Your pornography history should not become the most important story about you.
Jesus Christ must be.
There were sexually broken people in the first-century church.
Paul could speak with startling bluntness about sexual immorality and then remind believers of what God's grace had done.
The scandal of Christianity is not that Christians never had filthy histories.
The scandal is that Christ takes sinners who could never cleanse themselves, washes them, sanctifies them, justifies them, and gives them a new name.
That is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By refusing to let the scandal have the final word.
Maybe this article exposed something you have hidden for years.
Then don't perform here.
Be honest.
Someone else reading the comments may realize for the first time that they are not the only Christian fighting this war.
And if somebody came into your mind while reading this, don't weaponize this article against them.
Love them.
Pray for them.
Then send it privately if that is wiser.
There may be someone quietly scrolling tonight who will never tell you what they have been watching.
Someone whose spouse does not know.
Someone serving in church while secretly collapsing.
Someone young who has already begun believing that what pornography teaches about sex is what intimacy actually is.
Someone convinced God wants nothing more to do with them.
Let the Gospel interrupt their scrolling.

If this ministry helps you see Christ more clearly, then supporting it can be one practical way of participating in the spread of biblical truth. Scripture teaches that we glorify God through lives of faith, love, holiness, obedience, generosity, worship, and service.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend drifting from God.
Invite the Christian secretly struggling.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the lukewarm believer.
Invite even the person who does not yet believe.
Not because you need another saved post you'll never open again.
Read it before you open that other window.
Then open Scripture.
But before you leave, remember the scene where we started.
The screen has gone dark.
The room is quiet.
Your Bible is still sitting there.
And perhaps for years you thought that Bible was waiting to prosecute you.
Open it again.
Read the warnings honestly.
Do not domesticate God's holiness.
Do not rename lust.
Do not negotiate with what Christ commands you to flee.
But keep reading.
Read until you reach the cross.
Read until you see the blood.
Read until the empty tomb interrupts your shame.
Read until you understand that Jesus did not come merely to make dirty people feel guilty.
He came to save sinners.

Read until holiness stops looking like God taking something wonderful away from you and begins looking like Christ leading you out of something that was slowly teaching your heart to live without Him.
Then shut off the other screen.
And come into the light.
Because the eyes pornography trained to consume can become eyes grace teaches to behold Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHEN HEAVEN DOESN’T ANSWER: What If God’s Silence Is Not God’s Absence?
paragraphs: WHEN HEAVEN DOESN’T ANSWER: What If God’s Silence Is Not God’s Absence?
You prayed. You waited. You prayed again. Nothing changed. And somewhere between “Amen” and another unanswered morning, a frightening question entered your heart: “God… are You even listening?”
There is a kind of pain that comes from suffering.
And then there is another kind of pain entirely.
Suffering while praying for God to stop it.
You know what that feels like.

You prayed before you went to sleep. You prayed when you woke up. You whispered the same request while driving, washing dishes, working, crying in the bathroom, staring at the ceiling at 2:17 in the morning.
“Lord, please.”
Not an eloquent prayer.
Not something you would say behind a pulpit.
Just…
“Please.”
Please heal them.
Please bring my child back.
Please restore my marriage.
Please open the door.
Please give me work.
Please deliver me from this temptation.
Please save the person I love.
Please take this anxiety away.
Please let the test results be good.
Please show me what to do.
Please answer me.
And then…
silence.
No dramatic breakthrough.
No unmistakable sign.
No sudden phone call.
No door swinging open.
Sometimes the situation actually gets worse.
That is when unanswered prayer stops being merely disappointing and becomes spiritually dangerous, because the enemy begins interpreting God's silence for you.
“See?”
“He doesn't care.”
“You must not have enough faith.”
“Maybe God answers everybody except you.”
“Maybe you have disappointed Him too many times.”
“Maybe prayer doesn't work.”
And the most frightening thought of all:
“Maybe nobody is there.”
But before you walk away from God because heaven feels silent, you need to know something Scripture refuses to hide from us:
Some of the most faithful people in the Bible knew exactly what it felt like to pray into what seemed like silence.
David cried:

“My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring? O my God, I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent.”
— Psalm 22:1–2, KJV
The Hebrew opening is devastating:
אֵלִי אֵלִי לָמָה עֲזַבְתָּנִי
’Eli, ’Eli, lamah ‘azavtani?
“My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?”
Notice what David does not say.
He does not say, “There is no God.”
He says, “My God.”
That changes everything.
His confusion is enormous.
His pain is real.
His perception of abandonment is terrifying.
But somehow, buried underneath the anguish, relationship remains.
My God.
Perhaps that is where you are.
You do not understand Him anymore.
But somewhere beneath your disappointment, you still want Him.
You are angry because you expected Him to care.
You are hurt because you believed He could intervene.
You are confused precisely because you once trusted Him.
And perhaps you have been ashamed to admit that.
You sit in church while everyone sings about God's faithfulness, and something inside you whispers:
“Then why hasn't He answered me?”
You hear someone testify that they prayed for three days and God opened a door.
You have been praying for three years.
Someone says, “God came through!”
You clap for them.
You smile.
You genuinely want to celebrate.
But somewhere behind that smile is a wounded question:
“Lord… when is it my turn?”
That question does not automatically make you faithless.
The Bible contains prayers of lament precisely because biblical faith is strong enough to tell God the truth.
Psalm 13 begins:
“How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?”
— Psalm 13:1, KJV
How long?
That question belongs in the Bible.
Which means God is not frightened by it.
There is a difference between abandoning God and bringing your anguish to God.
Lament still turns toward Him.
Even wounded faith is still faith when it crawls toward Christ instead of running away from Him.
And then Scripture takes us somewhere even more astonishing.
Centuries after David wrote Psalm 22, Jesus Christ was hanging on a Roman cross.
Beaten.
Mocked.
Bleeding.
Crucified.
And from the darkness came words that echoed David's ancient lament:
“Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?”
— Matthew 27:46, KJV
Matthew preserves the cry in a Semitic form and then gives its meaning:
“My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?”
Think about that.
Christianity does not give you a Savior who watches human anguish from a comfortable distance.
Jesus entered suffering.
He entered rejection.
He entered betrayal.
He entered grief.
He entered death.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God bore our sins, fulfilling the saving purpose for which He came. As Peter writes, Christ “his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).
So when you cry in the darkness, you are not praying to a Savior unfamiliar with darkness.
Jesus knows.
And the cross also warns us against one of our greatest mistakes:
We often interpret God by what we can see in the moment.
Imagine standing near Calvary without knowing Sunday was coming.
What would Friday look like?
Failure.
Jesus is arrested.
Failure.
The disciples scatter.
Failure.
Peter denies Him.
Failure.
Jesus is condemned.
Failure.
Nails.
Blood.
Mockery.
Darkness.
A sealed tomb.
If you judged God's plan only by what was visible on Friday evening, you might conclude that evil had won.
But Friday was not the end of the story.
The resurrection changed the meaning of everything that appeared to have happened.
The tomb was not God's defeat.
It became the stage upon which Christ's victory over death was revealed.
And perhaps this is one of the hardest truths about unanswered prayer:
You are trying to understand the Author while you are still inside the chapter.
You see this page.
God sees the story.
That does not mean every tragedy will receive a neat explanation in this life. Christianity does not require us to pretend that every wound suddenly makes sense.
Some things hurt because this world is fallen.
Some losses remain losses.
Some prayers will not be answered in the way we desperately wanted.
The Bible never promises Christians a painless life.
Jesus actually told His disciples:
“In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.”
— John 16:33, KJV
Notice what He promises.
Not escape from every tribulation.
His presence and His victory in the middle of it.
This is where we must correct something Christians sometimes say too casually.
“God always answers prayer with yes, no, or wait.”
That phrase can be helpful, but Scripture gives us something richer than a slogan.
God calls us to ask.
Jesus teaches persistence in prayer.
James tells believers to ask God.
Paul tells Christians to pray continually.
But biblical prayer is never a technique for controlling God.
Prayer is not a spiritual vending machine where enough faith guarantees the outcome we selected.
Even the apostle Paul learned this painfully.
He pleaded with the Lord three times concerning his “thorn in the flesh.”
God did not remove it.
Instead, the answer came:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
— 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
Paul asked for removal.
Christ gave sustaining grace.
That was still an answer.
Just not the answer Paul originally requested.
And then there is Gethsemane.
If you ever begin believing that genuine faith means receiving whatever you ask for, look at Jesus.
Facing the cross, He prayed:
“O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.”
— Matthew 26:39, KJV
There is no unbelief in that prayer.
There is perfect trust.
Jesus asks honestly and submits completely.
“Not as I will, but as thou wilt.”
That is not weak prayer.
That is surrendered prayer.
And surrender may be the place where some of us discover what prayer was meant to become.
Because perhaps we approached God saying:
“Give me what I need.”
And through prayer He begins teaching us to say:
“Give me Yourself.”
We wanted His hand.
He was drawing us toward His heart.
We wanted an immediate solution.
He was forming endurance.
We wanted circumstances to change.
Sometimes He begins by changing us.
But be careful here.
Do not turn this into another simplistic explanation.
You cannot look at another suffering person and confidently announce, “God hasn't answered because He's teaching you patience.”
You do not know that.
Neither do I.
Scripture gives us categories for understanding suffering, but it does not authorize us to invent God's secret reasons for somebody else's pain.
Sometimes we simply do not know why.
Job did not know.
And much of the book bearing his name is the story of human beings trying to explain what they did not understand.
Faith sometimes has to say:
“I don't know why this is happening. But I know who God has revealed Himself to be.”
That distinction can keep your soul alive.
Because God's apparent silence is not proof of God's absence.
Consider Lazarus.
The message reached Jesus:
“Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick.”
— John 11:3, KJV
They did not even need a long explanation.
Jesus loved Lazarus.
Surely He would come immediately.
But John tells us something shocking:
“Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus. When he had heard therefore that he was sick, he abode two days still in the same place where he was.”
— John 11:5–6, KJV
Read that carefully.
Jesus loved them.
Therefore, He waited.
From the sisters' perspective, the delay must have felt unbearable.
By the time Jesus arrived, Lazarus had died.
Martha met Him with words that sound painfully familiar:
“Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died.”
— John 11:21, KJV
In other words:
“You could have stopped this.”
Maybe that is the sentence you have never dared say aloud.
“Jesus, You could have stopped this.”
“You could have healed them.”
“You could have prevented that betrayal.”
“You could have opened the door.”
“You could have changed their heart.”
“You could have answered sooner.”
And what does Jesus do in that story?
Before Lazarus walks out of the tomb, Scripture gives us one of its shortest and most profound verses:
“Jesus wept.”
— John 11:35, KJV
He knew resurrection was moments away.
And He still wept.
Never let anyone convince you that trusting God's sovereignty means becoming emotionally numb.
Jesus knew the ending and still entered the grief.
Your tears are not necessarily evidence that your faith has failed.
Sometimes tears are what faith looks like when it has no words left.
But there is another side to unanswered prayer we must face.
Sometimes the obstacle is not mysterious.
Sometimes Scripture calls us to examine ourselves.
Psalm 66:18 says:
“If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear me.”
James warns about asking with corrupt motives (James 4:3).
Peter even connects a husband's treatment of his wife with his prayers being hindered (1 Peter 3:7).
That means there are moments when the right response is not merely, “God, why are You silent?”
Sometimes it is:
“God, search me.”
Is there sin I am defending?
Bitterness I refuse to surrender?
Someone I refuse to forgive?
A relationship I know dishonors Christ?
Pride disguised as discernment?
Greed disguised as ambition?
Lust disguised as loneliness?
Disobedience followed by prayers asking God to bless the consequences?
This is not about earning answers from God.
The Gospel destroys that idea.
We come to God through Christ and His grace, not because we have performed well enough to deserve divine favors.
But grace never means making peace with sin.
Grace brings us home.
Grace teaches us repentance.
Grace exposes what is killing us and then points us toward the One who can forgive us.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia, commonly translated “repentance.”
Biblically, repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It involves a genuine turning—a changed mind and direction toward God.
And maybe the prayer you came here wanting God to answer has exposed another prayer your soul desperately needs:
“Jesus, change me.”
Maybe your greatest need tonight is not an explanation.
Maybe it is reconciliation with God.
Because there is a deeper silence than waiting for a job, relationship, healing, opportunity, or breakthrough.
It is living far from the God who made you while pretending everything is fine.
Sin has touched every one of us.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
— Romans 3:23, KJV
But scandal is not where the Gospel ends.
The cross stands in the middle of human rebellion and announces that sinners can be forgiven.
Jesus died for sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Grace is not God pretending your sin never mattered.
Grace is God providing in Christ what you could never provide for yourself.
You do not clean yourself up enough to become worthy of Jesus.
You come to Jesus because you aren't.
That is the scandal of grace.
Peter denied Him.
Jesus restored him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Christ transformed him into a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
He turned to Christ.
And Jesus gave him hope beyond the grave.
Again and again, Scripture tells stories of ruined people meeting a redeeming God.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe even you.
Maybe especially you.
But what about your unanswered prayer?
Should you stop asking?
No.
Unless Scripture has shown that what you are asking is contrary to God's will, keep bringing your heart to Him.
Jesus told a parable specifically teaching that people “ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luke 18:1).
Ask.
Seek.
Knock.
Cry if you need to.
Tell God you are confused.
Tell Him you are disappointed.
Tell Him you are exhausted.
God does not need your polished religious performance.
Come through Christ.
Come honestly.
And when you cannot understand His hand, anchor yourself in what He has already revealed about His character.
The cross is the permanent answer to the accusation that God does not care.
“He that spared not his own Son, but delivered him up for us all…”
— Romans 8:32, KJV
Christian hope does not say, “Everything I want will happen.”
Christian hope says something far stronger:
Whatever happens, I belong to Jesus Christ.
And if you belong to Christ, unanswered prayer does not get the final word.
Cancer does not get the final word.
Betrayal does not get the final word.
Grief does not get the final word.
The grave does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
There is coming a day when God's people will no longer pray beside hospital beds.
No more funeral processions.
No more midnight panic.
No more watching someone you love disappear.
No more unanswered questions tormenting exhausted minds.
Revelation says:
“And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain.”
— Revelation 21:4, KJV
Until then, we pray.
We trust.
We lament.
We repent.
We wait.
We obey.
We hold onto Christ.
Sometimes with strong hands.
Sometimes with trembling hands.
Sometimes with barely enough strength to whisper His name.
And if all you can pray tonight is…
“Jesus…”
then pray that.
If all you can say is…
“Help me…”
say it.
If you have been pretending your faith is fine while privately falling apart, perhaps tonight is the night the pretending ends.
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
If something hidden in your life needs to be brought into Christ's light, you can simply write “no more hiding.”
Someone reading beneath this article may be living through the chapter you already survived.
Do not underestimate what God can do with an honest testimony.
And think of one person who has stopped talking about their pain.
One person whose prayers seem unanswered.
One person who still attends church but has quietly become tired of hoping.
Because there may be another night when the answer still has not come.
And on that night, you may need to remember:
Silence is not necessarily absence.
If Gospel Warrior is helping you remain close to Scripture, consider following and supporting this ministry.

Supporting Gospel work financially is not a way to purchase God's blessing, prove your salvation, or force God to answer a prayer. The New Testament calls Christian giving willing rather than coerced: “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7).
Return to Jesus.
Return to Scripture.
Return to prayer.
And when your emotions tell you God has disappeared, remember Calvary.
There was once a Friday when everything looked silent, defeated, sealed, and finished.
Then came resurrection morning.
So perhaps tonight your prayer should become:

“Father, I still want the answer. You know how desperately I want it. But more than an answer, keep me near Jesus. Search me. Correct me. Forgive me. Teach me. Give me strength to obey while I wait. And if Your answer looks different from mine, give me grace to trust You without pretending it doesn't hurt.”
Because faith is not always shouting confidently on a mountaintop.
Sometimes faith is crying in the dark…
and still calling Him,
“My God.”
Remember this when heaven feels unbearably quiet:
The silence you hear today does not have authority to write the ending—Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BLOOD WAS REAL: Why “The Blood of Jesus” Is Not Just Symbolic
paragraphs: THE BLOOD WAS REAL: Why “The Blood of Jesus” Is Not Just Symbolic

Christianity does not rest on a beautiful metaphor about sacrifice. It rests on Jesus Christ—the Son of God who truly entered our humanity, truly suffered, truly shed His blood, truly died, and truly rose again. And once you understand what Scripture means by “the blood of Jesus,” you may never hear those words casually again.
There are Christian phrases we can hear so often that they stop startling us.
“The blood of Jesus.”
“Washed in the blood.”
“Redeemed by His blood.”
“We plead the blood.”
Words repeated in sermons. Sung in churches. Printed on shirts. Whispered in hospital rooms. Spoken through tears beside graves.
And familiarity can do something dangerous.
It can make something breathtaking feel ordinary.
So imagine, for a moment, that you had never heard the phrase “the blood of Jesus” before.
No church vocabulary.
No hymn playing in your memory.
No religious assumptions.
Just you standing outside Jerusalem nearly two thousand years ago, watching a condemned Man being led toward execution.
His back has been torn.
His face has been struck.
A crown of thorns has wounded His head.
His hands will be pierced.
His body will be lifted onto Roman timber.
And blood will actually fall.
Not metaphorical blood.
Not imaginary blood.
Not a poetic device invented centuries later.
Blood.
