He came to give eternal life death cannot take away.
And maybe that is the scandal prosperity-centered religion cannot understand.
The King became poor.
The innocent One was condemned.
The Holy One carried sinners' shame.
The One who owned everything was stripped of everything.
The Son of God wore thorns instead of gold.
And through His wounds, guilty people are offered grace.
That is our treasure.
That is our wealth.
That is our Gospel.
So give.
Give generously.
Give wisely.
Give joyfully.
Give sacrificially when God leads.
Support faithful churches and Gospel ministry.
Care for the poor.
Provide for your household.
Practice stewardship.
Refuse greed.
Refuse manipulation.
And never reduce the Almighty God to a vending machine where money goes in and prosperity comes out.
Your tithe cannot purchase God's love.
Your offering cannot purchase salvation.
Your generosity cannot purchase heaven.
Jesus already purchased redemption for sinners with His blood.
And when that Gospel captures you, you stop asking only, “How much must I give?”
You begin whispering:
“Jesus... after everything You have given me, how could anything I possess not belong to You?”
That is where generosity becomes worship.
That is where money loses its throne.
That is where grace rewrites the story.
Because the greatest evidence that God has blessed you is not that your hands are finally full—but that even when they are empty, your heart has discovered that Christ is still enough.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES PRAYER FRIGHTEN THE ENEMY?
paragraphs:
WHY DOES PRAYER FRIGHTEN THE ENEMY?
Because Hell Knows What Happens When a Broken Person Falls to Their Knees
There is something the enemy would rather have you do than pray.
Almost anything.
He would rather have you scroll for another hour.
He would rather have you rehearse the argument again.
He would rather have you stare at the ceiling at 2:17 in the morning, imagining everything that could go wrong.
He would rather have you obsess over what they said about you, what you lost, what you did, what you cannot fix, what you wish you could undo.
He would even rather have you talk endlessly about God than actually get alone with God.
Because something happens when a human being finally closes the door, puts the phone down, stops pretending, and whispers:
“Jesus… I need You.”
Not because those words are a magic formula.
Not because prayer makes you spiritually impressive.
And certainly not because Christians possess some secret incantation that forces God to obey them.
Prayer frightens the enemy for a far more biblical reason.
Prayer brings a helpless human being into conscious dependence upon the sovereign God whom Satan cannot defeat.
And perhaps that is why prayer has been such a battle for you.
You thought you were simply distracted.
Maybe sometimes you are.
You thought you were simply tired.
Maybe sometimes you are.
You thought you had become spiritually weak because you could spend forty minutes watching videos but struggled to spend ten minutes praying.
And perhaps there is ordinary human weakness involved.
But Scripture also refuses to let Christians pretend that the spiritual life contains no spiritual conflict.
Paul writes:
Hoti ouk estin hēmin hē palē pros haima kai sarka…
“For our struggle is not against flesh and blood…”
Then Paul speaks of rulers, authorities, the powers of darkness, and spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms.
That word translated “struggle” or “wrestling” is πάλη — palē.
This is not the language of spectatorship.
Christianity is not Jesus added decoratively to an otherwise self-governed life.
There is a battle.
But we need to be careful here, because Christians can become fascinated with darkness in ways Scripture never encourages.
The Bible does not tell you to spend your life studying demons.
It tells you to fix your eyes on Jesus.
It does not present Satan as God's equal opposite.
There are not two eternal gods fighting for control of the universe.
Satan is a creature.
God is Creator.
Satan is limited.
God is sovereign.
Satan can be resisted.
Christ has already triumphed.
At the cross, what looked like the greatest scandal in history became the place of victory.
Jesus Christ was betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Nailed to wood.
His enemies thought they were watching the destruction of His mission.
Instead, they were watching redemption unfold.
The innocent Son of God was bearing sin.
The Lamb was giving Himself for sinners.
And then came the morning darkness could not prevent.
The tomb was empty.
Jesus was alive.
That matters when we talk about prayer, because Christian prayer is not an attempt to persuade an uncertain God to defeat an equally powerful devil.
Christian prayer begins on the other side of Christ's victory.
And that changes everything.
Think about the night before the cross.
Gethsemane.
Darkness.
Olive trees.
Sleeping disciples.
A Savior in anguish.
Jesus knew what was coming.
And what did He tell His disciples?
“Watch and pray.”
Why?
Because temptation was coming.
The spirit might be willing, but human flesh was weak.
Peter was confident in himself.
Soon he would be terrified by the questions of a servant girl.
Hours earlier he had essentially declared that even if everyone else abandoned Jesus, he would remain.
That confidence collapsed spectacularly.
“I don't know Him.”
Again.
“I don't know Him.”
Again.
And then the rooster crowed.
Imagine that moment.
Peter's stomach dropping.
Jesus turning.
Their eyes meeting.
The memory returning.
The shame arriving all at once.
Perhaps you know something about that feeling.
Not Peter's exact story.
Yours.
The promise you made to God and broke.
The temptation you swore you had conquered.
The website you returned to.
The bitterness you fed.
The lie you told.
The person you used.
The marriage you wounded.
The secret nobody knows.
The prayer life that quietly disappeared.
The version of yourself everyone sees on Sunday…
and the version only God sees at midnight.
There are moments when the most terrifying sound in the world is not an accusation from another person.
It is your own conscience saying:
You knew better.
And this is where the enemy loves to distort the story.
Conviction says, “Come back.”
Condemnation whispers, “Stay away.”
Conviction exposes sin so that you will run toward Christ.
Condemnation weaponizes your sin so that you hide from Him.
“You prayed yesterday and still failed.”
“So why pray tonight?”
“You've asked forgiveness before.”
“God must be tired of hearing you.”
“Look at you.”
“Hypocrite.”
And slowly, almost imperceptibly, shame begins doing what temptation alone could not accomplish.
It keeps you away from the One who can restore you.
That is one reason prayer matters so deeply.
Prayer interrupts hiding.
Prayer says:
“Father, here I am.”
Not the edited me.
Not the church me.
Not the Facebook me.
Not the me who knows exactly what Christian words to use.
Me.
The frightened me.
The angry me.
The tempted me.
The exhausted me.
The ashamed me.
The me who failed again.
The me who cannot repair myself.
Here I am.
And Scripture gives us one of the clearest pictures of spiritual resistance in James 4:7:
“Ὑποτάγητε οὖν τῷ Θεῷ· ἀντίστητε δὲ τῷ διαβόλῳ, καὶ φεύξεται ἀφ’ ὑμῶν.”
Hypotagēte oun tō Theō; antistēte de tō diabolō, kai pheuxetai aph’ hymōn.
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”
Notice the order.
This matters enormously.
James does not begin:
“Resist the devil.”
He begins:
Submit to God.
The Greek ὑποτάγητε — hypotagēte carries the sense of subjecting or submitting oneself.
Then comes ἀντίστητε — antistēte:
Resist.
Stand against.
The devil flees not because Christians discover how powerful they are independently of God.
The entire sentence destroys that interpretation.
Submission comes first.
Our resistance is Godward dependence.
That is the opposite of spiritual swagger.
The strongest Christian in the room may be the one quietly saying:
“Lord, I cannot do this without You.”
That sentence humiliates human pride.
And it destroys one of the enemy's favorite lies:
You can handle this yourself.
That lie is ancient.
You don't need God's wisdom.
You don't need God's boundaries.
You don't need God's Word.
You don't need God's strength.
You don't need God's forgiveness.
You don't need God's presence.
You can be your own master.
Prayer is an act of rebellion against that lie.
Every genuine prayer says, whether explicitly or implicitly:
“I am not God.”
And then:
“But I know the One who is.”
That is why prayer changes the atmosphere of a human heart.
Fear says, “Everything depends on me.”
Prayer says, “Father, I belong to You.”
Anxiety says, “I must control tomorrow.”
Prayer says, “Give us this day our daily bread.”
Bitterness says, “I will make them pay.”
Prayer remembers, “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive…”
Temptation says, “Just this once.”
Prayer cries, “Lead us not into temptation.”
Spiritual evil says, “You are mine.”
Prayer answers, “Deliver us from evil.”
And beneath all of it stands the name Jesus taught His people to approach:
Father.
This is what makes Christian prayer astonishing.
Through Christ, forgiven sinners are invited near.
Hebrews does not tell believers to crawl toward the throne of grace wondering whether God might tolerate them.
Because of our great High Priest, Jesus Christ, believers are invited to approach God's throne of grace with confidence so that they may receive mercy and find grace in time of need.
Mercy.
Grace.
In time of need.
Read that again if you have been avoiding prayer because you failed.
In time of need.
Not after you have successfully repaired yourself.
Not after seven consecutive spiritually impressive days.
Not after you feel worthy.
You come because Christ is worthy.
That is the Gospel.
And perhaps this is the part someone reading this desperately needs tonight.
You keep waiting to become good enough to come back.
You think repentance means cleaning yourself before entering the Father's house.
But the prodigal son came home smelling like the country where he had wasted everything.
He rehearsed his speech.
He knew his scandal.
He knew what he deserved.
But while he was still far away, his father saw him.
Ran.
Embraced him.
The son returned repentant, but restoration was flowing from the father's mercy.
That does not make sin trivial.
Grace never calls evil good.
Grace is costly precisely because sin is deadly.
At Calvary, forgiveness was not God pretending your sin didn't matter.
It mattered enough for the Son of God to bleed.
And you mattered enough that He willingly did.
This is where prayer becomes dangerous to everything that wants to keep you chained.
Because when a pornography addict begins genuinely praying, “Jesus, expose what I am becoming and teach me to love holiness,” secrecy has been breached.
When a bitter wife whispers, “Father, I don't know how to forgive, but I surrender my right to revenge,” bitterness has been challenged.
When a proud husband admits, “Lord, I was wrong. Give me courage to apologize,” pride begins losing oxygen.
When an exhausted mother cries in the bathroom because it is the only quiet room in the house and says, “God, I cannot carry everyone today,” she has stopped pretending she is omnipotent.
When a teenager surrounded by pressure whispers, “Jesus, help me choose You even if they laugh,” allegiance is being declared.
When the believer who relapsed falls to the floor instead of running farther from God and cries, “Have mercy on me,” shame has failed to achieve its ultimate objective.
When the dying saint can barely speak but whispers the name “Jesus”…
that is not weakness heaven despises.
That is dependence.
And dependence upon Christ is not defeat.
It is where Christian strength begins.
But prayer does something else the enemy hates.
It changes what you want.
Sometimes we approach prayer almost like a vending machine.
Insert request.
Press button.
Receive desired outcome.
But Jesus did not teach prayer as a mechanism for controlling God.
Gethsemane destroys that theology.
Jesus prayed in anguish, yet surrendered Himself to the Father's will.
“Not my will, but Yours.”
Prayer is not merely asking God to change circumstances.
Sometimes prayer is where God changes us in the circumstances.
Sometimes the miracle is the door opening.
Sometimes the miracle is receiving strength while the door remains closed.
Sometimes God removes the storm.
Sometimes He teaches His child to trust Him in the boat.
Sometimes He heals immediately.
Sometimes believers continue praying through suffering while trusting the God whose final promise is resurrection.
This distinction matters because careless teaching about prayer has wounded people.
Someone prayed for a loved one who still died.
Someone prayed for the marriage and was still abandoned.
Someone prayed for the child and is still waiting.
Someone prayed through tears and did not receive the answer they imagined.
Please hear this carefully:
Unanswered prayer is not proof that God did not hear you.
And suffering is not proof that you lacked enough faith.
Paul prayed about his thorn.
Jesus prayed in Gethsemane.
The early church prayed while persecution continued.
Christian prayer does not promise exemption from suffering.
It promises communion with God within a world awaiting final restoration.
That is stronger than a slogan.
Because eventually every shallow theology collapses beside a hospital bed.
But Jesus remains.

This is why prayer frightens the enemy—not because every prayer immediately changes your circumstances, but because prayer keeps bringing you back into fellowship, truth, dependence, repentance, worship, and obedience before the God who saves.
The enemy wants isolation.
Prayer brings you near.
The enemy wants accusation.
Prayer brings confession into grace.
The enemy wants self-sufficiency.
Prayer produces dependence.
The enemy wants panic.
Prayer remembers sovereignty.
The enemy wants resentment.
Prayer makes room for forgiveness.
The enemy wants temptation hidden.
Prayer drags it into God's light.
The enemy wants your eyes fixed upon darkness.
Prayer lifts them toward Christ.
And perhaps most threatening of all…
prayer can turn your greatest scandal into the place where grace becomes undeniable.
Ask Peter.
The man who denied Jesus did not remain forever beside that charcoal fire of failure.
After the resurrection, Jesus came for him.
There would be another charcoal fire.
Another conversation.
Another opportunity.
“Do you love Me?”
Jesus did not pretend Peter had never fallen.
He restored the man who had.
That is grace.
Not erasure of history.
Redemption of history.
Peter's worst chapter did not get the final sentence.
Jesus did.
And years later, Peter would become a man of courageous witness.
The mouth that once said, “I don't know Him,” would publicly proclaim Christ.
Do you see it?
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By refusing to let the scandal have the last word.
Maybe you have been thinking your story is already decided.
Divorce.
Addiction.
Betrayal.
Failure.
Abortion.
Pride.
Sexual sin.
Anger.
Years wasted.
Faith abandoned.
Secret compromises.
A cold marriage.
A child who no longer speaks to you.
A Bible gathering dust.
Prayer reduced to emergencies.
And somewhere inside you is the sentence:
“Maybe God can forgive other people, but after everything I've done…”
Stop.
Look at the cross.
If salvation depended upon your record, you would have reason to despair.
But Christianity is not the announcement that good people can save themselves.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Repentance does not mean you are beyond grace.
Repentance is the turning of a heart toward the One whose grace you desperately need.
So pray.
Not theatrically.
Not impressively.
Not for Facebook.
Not to sound spiritual.
Close the door.
Put the phone down.
Tell God the truth.
“Father, I am angry.”
“Jesus, I am tempted.”
“Lord, I am jealous.”
“God, I don't understand.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Help me.”
“I believe; help my unbelief.”
“Teach me to obey.”
“Change what I love.”
“Break what needs breaking.”
“Heal what I cannot heal.”
“Lead me.”
“Keep me.”
“Jesus… don't let me run from You again.”
Maybe that is the prayer.
Maybe tonight does not need another complicated spiritual strategy.
Maybe it needs surrender.
Be honest.
Someone reading your comment may realize they are not the only believer struggling.
Someone may pray for you.
Someone may finally confess what they have been hiding because your honesty gave them courage.
And please don't keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Jesus cannot be bought, salvation cannot be purchased, and grace is not merchandise.
But if this message points people toward Christ, then sharing it can become a simple act of witness.
Someone awake at 2 a.m.
Someone ashamed to enter a church.
Someone considering giving up.
Someone who has convinced themselves that Jesus could never want them back.
It is where desperate people meet a gracious God.
Because the day may come when you are that person again.
When temptation gets loud.
When prayer feels dry.
When shame says, “Don't go back.”
Come back and remember:
Submit to God. Resist the devil. He will flee. Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you.
Not to glorify Gospel Warrior.
To help Gospel Warrior keep glorifying God.
Supporting Gospel-centered work is not a condition of salvation, and we will never tell you that money purchases God's favor.
Let them encounter Scripture.
Let them encounter conviction.
Let them encounter grace.
Let them discover that Christianity is not about pretending broken people are whole.
It is about broken people meeting the Savior whose wounds purchased their redemption.
And before you leave this page, there is one more thing you need to know.
The enemy may remind you of the night you fell.
Jesus can remind you of the morning He rose.
The enemy may point at your chains.
Jesus points at an empty tomb.
The enemy may whisper your accusation.
The Gospel announces your Advocate.
The enemy may know your past.
But he does not own your future.
If you belong to Christ, your story is held by scarred hands.
So tonight…
pray.
Even if your voice shakes.
Pray.
Even if all you have are tears.
Pray.
Even if you don't know how to finish the sentence.
Pray.
Even if yesterday you failed miserably.
Pray.
Not because prayer proves how strong you are.
Because prayer admits how desperately you need the One who is.
And maybe that is what darkness fears most about a Christian on their knees:
The person who finally realizes, “I cannot save myself”… is now looking directly toward the Savior who can.
Follow so truth remains close when the noise gets loud.
And comment something honest before you leave.
Maybe only three words:
“Jesus, keep me.”
Because sometimes the prayer that terrifies darkness begins with the confession that you were never strong enough without Christ.
Your knees may touch the floor in the chapter where you thought your story ended—and discover that grace was already writing the next sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Had Money, Morality, and Influence. He Still Walked Away From Jesus Sad.
paragraphs: He Had Money, Morality, and Influence. He Still Walked Away From Jesus Sad.
The Rich Young Ruler did almost everything religious people admire—and still discovered that being close to Jesus is not the same as belonging completely to Jesus.
There is something terrifying about a man running toward Jesus… only to eventually walk away from Him.
Not cursing Him.
Not mocking Him.
Not denying that He was good.
Just walking away.
Sad.
That may be one of the most uncomfortable scenes in the Gospels because the man does not look like someone we would expect to be spiritually lost.
He is not presented as a public scandal.
He is not the thief hanging on a cross.
He is not the woman whose reputation entered the room before she did.
He is not the tax collector everyone despised.
By the standards of respectable society, this man appears to have almost everything right.
He is young.
He has wealth.
Luke calls him a ruler.
He appears morally serious.
And when Jesus comes near, Mark tells us something remarkable:
“καὶ προσδραμὼν εἷς καὶ γονυπετήσας αὐτόν…”
A man came running and knelt before Him.
That matters.
This was not casual curiosity.
Imagine the scene.
A wealthy, influential man sees Jesus leaving. Something inside him refuses to let the moment pass. Dignity gives way to desperation. He runs. He drops to his knees.
Then comes the question:
“Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
It sounds like the beginning of a beautiful conversion story.
But before this conversation is finished, the same man who ran toward Jesus will walk away from Jesus.
And perhaps the most haunting question in the story is not simply why he walked away.
It is this:
What could Jesus ask you to surrender that would make you do the same?
Because it is possible to run toward Jesus while still carrying something you have already decided He cannot have.
That is where this story stops being ancient history.
That is where it finds us.

The account appears in Matthew 19:16–30, Mark 10:17–31, and Luke 18:18–30. The familiar description “rich young ruler” comes from reading those accounts together: Matthew identifies him as young, Luke calls him a ruler, and all three emphasize his wealth.
He comes asking about eternal life, and Jesus brings the conversation into the territory of God’s commandments.
The man answers with astonishing confidence.
“Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth.”
Think about that.
He has morality.
He has discipline.
He has religious knowledge.
He has social standing.
He has money.
And apparently he still knows that something is missing.
There are people reading this who understand that feeling more than they want to admit.
You learned how to behave.
You learned Christian language.
You know when to say “God is good.”
You know which verses to post.
You may attend church, give money, avoid obvious scandals, take care of your family, work hard, and try to be a decent person.
People may even look at your life and think,
That person is blessed.
But late at night, when there is nobody left to impress, a quieter question sometimes rises:
Why does my soul still feel like it is negotiating with God?
That is the danger of respectable Christianity.
A person can clean the outside of life so thoroughly that nobody notices there is still a throne inside the heart occupied by something other than Christ.
And Jesus knows exactly where that throne is.
Mark gives us a detail so beautiful that it changes the emotional temperature of the entire encounter.
“ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς ἐμβλέψας αὐτῷ ἠγάπησεν αὐτόν.”
Jesus looked at him and loved him.
Do not rush past that.
Jesus is about to say the sentence that exposes the man’s deepest attachment.
And Mark tells us first that Jesus loved him.
The confrontation came from love.
The exposure came from love.
The demand came from love.
Jesus was not trying to humiliate a wealthy man.
He was uncovering the rival that owned him.
Then Jesus said:
“ἕν σε ὑστερεῖ…”
“You lack one thing.”
One thing.
The man had accumulated so much, yet Jesus could see the poverty hidden underneath the abundance.
Then came the command:
“Go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow Me.”
This passage must be handled carefully.

Jesus is not teaching that people purchase eternal life by donating enough money. Scripture does not teach salvation by charitable achievement. Salvation is by God’s grace, received through faith, not earned by works.

Nor does Scripture give a universal command requiring every Christian in every circumstance to dispose of every possession. The New Testament includes believers who possessed homes and resources, and it repeatedly teaches generosity, stewardship, freedom from greed, and care for those in need.
But none of that makes Jesus’ command to this particular man less radical.
Jesus placed His finger precisely where this man’s allegiance was divided.
The man asked what he needed.
Jesus showed him what owned him.
His wealth was not merely something sitting in his hands.
It had reached his heart.
This is why the story is bigger than money.
For one person, the rival may be wealth.
For another, it is a relationship they know is pulling them away from Christ.
For another, pornography hidden behind a password.
For another, applause.
A career.
A reputation.
Bitterness.
Control.
Sexual sin.
Comfort.
Pride.
A secret habit.
A public image.
Even ministry can become an idol when being seen serving Jesus becomes more precious than Jesus Himself.
An idol is not merely a statue someone bows before.
It is anything we refuse to place beneath the lordship of Christ.
And sometimes we discover what we worship only when God touches it.
We sing, “I surrender all,” until Jesus points toward the thing we mentally excluded from the word all.
That is what happened on the road.
Jesus did not merely discuss the man’s possessions.
He revealed his master.
Then Mark uses a word that almost lets you see the man’s face change:
“στυγνάσας.”
His expression fell.
He became gloomy, shocked, disheartened.
Then:
“ἀπῆλθεν λυπούμενος.”
He went away grieving.
Why?
“ἦν γὰρ ἔχων κτήματα πολλά.”
Because he had many possessions.
He arrived running.
He left grieving.
He arrived kneeling.
He left unwilling to surrender.
He wanted eternal life.
He wanted Jesus’ answer.
But when the answer threatened his treasure, he chose the treasure.
And this is where the story becomes frighteningly personal.
He did not walk away because Jesus failed to love him.
Jesus loved him.
He walked away because the love of Jesus confronted another love he was unwilling to release.
Read that again slowly.
Jesus loved him enough to tell him the truth that could cost Jesus the man’s approval.
That is real love.
Modern Christianity can be tempted to imagine love as affirmation without confrontation.
Jesus refuses that definition.
Sometimes Christ loves us by comforting us.
Sometimes Christ loves us by exposing us.
Sometimes His mercy feels like arms around the wounded.
Sometimes His mercy feels like light entering a locked room.
Both are love.
The Rich Young Ruler wanted assurance.
Jesus offered discipleship.
He wanted to know what could be added to his life.
Jesus exposed what needed to lose its throne.
He seems to have approached eternal life as another possession to acquire.
He already had status.
He already had morality.
He already had wealth.
Perhaps eternal life could become one more treasure in an impressive collection.
But Jesus cannot simply be added to a life whose throne remains occupied.
Christ does not come merely to become another item in our collection.
He comes as Lord.
That word matters.
Lord.
κύριος.
The Christian confession is not merely that Jesus is useful, inspiring, therapeutic, or spiritually comforting.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
And lordship reaches into bank accounts.
Bedrooms.
Phones.
Relationships.
Ambitions.
Private thoughts.
Public reputations.
The parts of us nobody else sees.
This does not mean Christians become perfect overnight.
It means we stop defending our rebellion as though Jesus has no right to touch it.
There is an enormous difference between struggling against sin and protecting it.
Between falling and refusing to get up.
Between weakness that cries for grace and rebellion that demands permission.
The Gospel does not say, “Fix yourself so Jesus will accept you.”
The Gospel says something infinitely better.
You cannot save yourself.
And Jesus came for sinners who cannot.
After the wealthy man leaves, Jesus tells His disciples how difficult it is for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom of God. The disciples are astonished.
Then they ask the question underneath every human attempt at salvation:
“Who then can be saved?”
Jesus looks at them and answers:
“With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.”
There is the Gospel breaking through the story.
Impossible with man.
Possible with God.
You cannot purchase salvation.
You cannot behave your way into resurrection.
You cannot build a résumé impressive enough to make God owe you heaven.
You cannot give enough money, attend enough services, perform enough religious acts, or accumulate enough moral accomplishments to erase your guilt.
You need something you cannot manufacture.
Grace.
You need Someone you cannot replace.
Jesus.
The Rich Young Ruler had asked, in effect, “What can I do?”
Jesus eventually brings the conversation to the terrifying and liberating reality:
Human beings cannot save themselves.
That is why the cross matters.
Jesus did not come merely to make morally impressive people slightly better.
He came to save sinners.
The scandal of Christianity is that the respectable moralist and the publicly disgraced sinner ultimately stand in need of the same Savior.
Different histories.
Different wounds.
Different temptations.
Same need for grace.
At the cross, Jesus bears sin.
In His resurrection, death is defeated.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not to purchase mercy but to repent and believe.
Repentance is not payment for grace.
It is the turning of the heart toward the God who gives grace.
Faith is not another achievement we wave before God.
It is the empty hand receiving Christ.
And perhaps this is why the story hurts so much.
The man was standing in front of the Treasure he could never purchase.
Yet he walked away because he could not imagine releasing the treasures he already possessed.
He had money.
But Jesus offered treasure in heaven.
He had status.
But Jesus offered discipleship.
He had moral accomplishments.
But Jesus offered grace.
He had possessions.
But Jesus said:
“Follow Me.”
And he walked away.
We are not told that Jesus chased him down and renegotiated the terms.
Jesus did not shout after him:
“Wait! Keep the idol. Just add Me to it.”
He let the man feel the weight of his choice.
That silence should disturb us.
Because there are moments when the most dangerous thing God can allow is for us to keep choosing what we demanded.
Some people want Jesus as Savior from hell while resisting Jesus as Lord of life.
They want forgiveness without repentance.
Comfort without surrender.
Heaven without holiness.
A cross that saves them, but never crosses out anything they worship.
But biblical grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace forgives us and begins transforming us.
Titus says the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness.
Paul says that anyone in Christ is a new creation.
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
The Gospel does not merely change our destination after death.
It begins changing our allegiance now.
And here is where our theme becomes more than a slogan:
Some scandals are visible.
Everybody knows.
The affair.
The addiction.
The arrest.
The divorce.
The collapse.
The betrayal.
The public failure.
But some scandals wear expensive clothes.
Some scandals have excellent reputations.
Some scandals sit quietly in church.
Some scandals know Bible verses.
Some scandals give to charity.
Some scandals look morally admirable while privately telling Jesus:
“You can have everything except this.”
The Rich Young Ruler’s scandal was not that he possessed wealth.
The deeper scandal was that when Jesus exposed the competing loyalty of his heart, he preferred what he possessed to the One standing before him.
Yet even here, grace remains breathtakingly close.
Remember the sentence Mark refused to leave out:
Jesus looked at him and loved him.
Before the man surrendered, Jesus loved him.
While exposing him, Jesus loved him.
Knowing what he would choose, Jesus loved him.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible without pretending.
You can stop hiding because Christ already knows what is behind the door.
He knows the browser history.
He knows the bank statement.
He knows the resentment.
He knows the secret relationship.
He knows why you need everybody to admire you.
He knows what you are afraid to lose.
He knows the thing you hope He never mentions.
And still the crucified and risen Christ calls sinners to Himself.
So ask the question you may have avoided for years:
What is my “one thing”?
What makes your heart tense when surrender is mentioned?
What do you repeatedly justify even though Scripture keeps confronting it?
What loss seems more unbearable than distance from Jesus?
What are you afraid Christ might ask you to put down?
Your answer may reveal more about your worship than a hundred songs ever could.
Maybe you have already walked away emotionally.
Your body still goes to church, but your heart has been drifting.
You pray less.
You hide more.
You have learned how to look spiritually alive while becoming exhausted inside.
Maybe shame convinced you that after everything you have done, Jesus would not want you back.
Look again at the Gospel.
Peter failed.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
The Gospel is filled with people whose stories should have ended in ruin.
Then grace entered the sentence.
That is what Jesus does.
He does not pretend sin is harmless.
He pays its terrible price.
He does not call darkness light.
He enters the darkness and saves.
He does not merely improve scandals.
He redeems sinners.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe today the story of the Rich Young Ruler is not asking whether you are wealthy.
Maybe it is asking whether Jesus is worth more to you than whatever you are terrified of losing.
Bring it to Christ.
Tell Him the truth.
Repent.
Ask for mercy.
Ask Him to break the grip of whatever has become your functional god.
If you need words, let them be simple:

“Jesus, I have loved something more than You. Forgive me. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Teach me to surrender what I keep protecting. Be Lord over the places I have kept locked. I want You more than the thing that owns me.”
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
It does not.
But because sometimes bringing a struggle into the light is the first public refusal to keep pretending.
Someone reading silently may need evidence that grace still walks into ruined stories.
Not because every sentence is comfortable.
Not as a religious performance. Not to prove that you love God.
But if this biblical message helped you see Christ more clearly, sharing it can become a simple act of witness.

Supporting Gospel work is one practical way believers can participate in spreading biblical teaching, but it should always flow from willing generosity and love for Christ—not guilt, pressure, or an attempt to earn anything from God.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with following Jesus.
You can buy every Christian book in the store and still need Jesus.
You can wear the shirt and still need Jesus.
You can share the article and still need Jesus.
The Rich Young Ruler teaches us something far too important to bury beneath marketing:
Jesus Himself must remain the treasure.
Everything else is secondary.
Everything.
Because one day your money will belong to somebody else.
Your title will belong to somebody else.
Your house will belong to somebody else.
Your possessions will scatter.
Your photographs will fade.
People who once knew your voice will eventually be gone.
And the question will no longer be what you managed to accumulate.
The question will be whether all those temporary treasures kept you from the eternal Treasure standing in front of you saying:
“Follow Me.”
The Rich Young Ruler ran to Jesus.
Knelt before Jesus.
Spoke respectfully to Jesus.
Asked Jesus about eternal life.
Received a loving answer from Jesus.
And still walked away.
Sad.
Do not let familiarity with Jesus become a substitute for surrender to Jesus.
Do not settle for being almost persuaded.
Do not protect the very chain Christ is offering to break.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the idol.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the grief.
Bring Him the reputation.
Bring Him the money.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the thing you cannot imagine surrendering.
And discover that the hands asking you to release it are the same hands that were pierced to redeem sinners.
Do not spend your life clutching something that will eventually leave your hands while walking away from the One who was willing to stretch out His hands on a cross for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: PHARAOH KEPT SAYING NO TO GOD—UNTIL ONE NIGHT, EGYPT HEARD A CRY IT COULD NEVER FORGET
paragraphs: PHARAOH KEPT SAYING NO TO GOD—UNTIL ONE NIGHT, EGYPT HEARD A CRY IT COULD NEVER FORGET

The Ten Plagues were not merely a story about an ancient king who refused to listen. They are a terrifying warning about what happens when a human heart keeps resisting the God who has already spoken—and a breathtaking preview of the greater Exodus Jesus Christ would accomplish for sinners who could never free themselves.
There is a frightening kind of silence that comes after you have told God “no” so many times that saying no no longer frightens you.
The first refusal may trouble your conscience.
The second may require an excuse.
The third becomes easier.
Eventually, you can sit beneath the weight of God's Word and feel almost nothing.
That may be one of the most terrifying conditions a human being can reach—not because God has become silent, but because the heart has become practiced at resisting Him.
And that is why the story of Pharaoh is not safely buried beneath Egyptian sand.
It can happen inside us.
Not with a golden throne.
Not with pyramids outside our windows.
Not with Moses standing in our palace.
But whenever God confronts our pride, our secret sin, our bitterness, our unforgiveness, our sexual immorality, our greed, our self-righteousness, our obsession with control—and we keep answering:
Not yet.
Not this.
Not now.
Pharaoh's tragedy began with a question that sounded powerful but revealed how blind he really was:
“Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice…?”
That is Exodus 5:2.
In Hebrew, the challenge is devastating:
מִי יְהוָה אֲשֶׁר אֶשְׁמַע בְּקֹלוֹ
Mi YHWH asher eshma beqolo?
“Who is YHWH, that I should listen to His voice?”
That question becomes the heartbeat of the confrontation.
Who is the LORD?
Pharaoh was about to find out.
But understand what was happening before the Nile ever turned to blood.
Israel had been enslaved.
Human beings made in God's image were being crushed beneath an empire. Exodus describes bitter forced labor. Earlier, Pharaoh had commanded that Hebrew sons be killed.
So the plagues are not the tantrums of an unpredictable deity.
They unfold in the context of oppression, covenant, judgment, deliverance, and God's determination to make Himself known.
God tells Moses:
“I am the LORD.”
Again and again, Exodus returns to that purpose: Egypt will know that He is the LORD.
Pharaoh believed he occupied the highest seat.
Then God entered the courtroom.
And suddenly the man who believed he controlled everything discovered that he could not command a river, frogs, insects, livestock, disease, weather, locusts, darkness—or death.
The Nile turned to blood.
Imagine it.
Egypt's great river—the artery of the nation—struck before Pharaoh's eyes.
Water became undrinkable.
Fish died.
The river stank.
And Pharaoh?
He went home.
That detail should disturb us.
A nation is watching catastrophe unfold, and the king walks back into his house.
Because a hard heart can witness consequences and still refuse surrender.
Then came frogs.
Not one amusing frog hopping through a royal courtyard.
Frogs everywhere.
Bedrooms.
Houses.
Beds.
Ovens.
Kneading bowls.
The nation that Pharaoh believed he controlled became uncontrollable.
And now something fascinating happened.
Pharaoh asked Moses to pray.
He wanted relief.
But relief is not the same thing as repentance.
That distinction could expose somebody reading this.
How many times have we wanted God to remove the consequences without removing the sin?
“God, fix my marriage.”
But don't touch my pride.
“God, restore my peace.”
But don't ask me to forgive.
“God, rescue my finances.”
But don't confront what I worship.
“God, heal what is breaking.”
But leave the secret room of my life locked.
Pharaoh wanted the frogs gone.
He did not yet want Pharaoh gone from the throne of Pharaoh's heart.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because repentance is not merely wanting pain to stop.
Repentance turns toward God.

The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly describe Pharaoh's heart with language connected to hardness, heaviness, and strengthening. One important word is כָּבֵד — kaved/kabed, carrying the sense of being heavy. Exodus 7:14 describes Pharaoh's heart as heavy or unyielding.
Another verb appearing in the hardening narrative is חָזַק — chazaq, meaning to be strong, firm, or strengthened.

The text is deliberately sobering because Exodus does not describe the hardening in only one way. At points Pharaoh hardens his own heart or his heart becomes hard; elsewhere God hardens or strengthens Pharaoh's heart.
We should not flatten that tension just to make the passage easier.
Pharaoh is not presented as an innocent man desperately trying to repent while God prevents him.

Before several explicit statements that the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart, Pharaoh had repeatedly resisted God's command. He saw signs. He received warnings. He experienced relief. Then he returned to rebellion.
Later, Scripture is equally clear that God's sovereign judgment is operating through Pharaoh's hardness.

By Exodus 10:1, God explicitly says He has hardened Pharaoh's heart so that His signs may be displayed. Paul later takes Pharaoh seriously in Romans 9, declaring God's sovereign freedom in mercy and hardening and quoting God's purpose concerning Pharaoh. Scripture refuses to make God helpless, and it refuses to make Pharaoh innocent.
That should make us tremble before playing games with repentance.
Because one of God's judgments upon persistent rebellion can be giving the rebel over to the path he insists on walking.
Pharaoh kept saying no.
Then the consequences of his no became bigger than Pharaoh.
Gnats or mosquitoes came.
Flies swarmed.
Livestock suffered.
Boils broke out.
Hail devastated the land.
Locusts consumed what remained.
Darkness swallowed Egypt.
And something extraordinary becomes increasingly clear:
Pharaoh's rebellion was never merely private.
Neither is ours.
We live in a culture that loves the sentence, “It's my life.”
But sin rarely stays inside the boundaries we assign to it.
A father's hidden addiction enters his children's home.
A mother's bitterness can become the emotional atmosphere her family breathes.
A leader's pride can wound thousands.
A husband's secret life can shatter a wife who never consented to participate in it.
A person's refusal to forgive can poison relationships years after the original wound.
Pharaoh kept saying no to God.
Egypt kept paying for Pharaoh's no.
Maybe someone needs to hear this before another year disappears:
Your private rebellion may already have public consequences.
This is not permission to assume every hardship is punishment for a particular personal sin. Jesus Himself rejected simplistic equations between individual suffering and individual guilt.
But Scripture absolutely teaches that sin has consequences—and Pharaoh demonstrates how devastating those consequences can become when power and hardness join hands.
Then came darkness.
Exodus says darkness covered Egypt for three days.
People could not see one another.
They did not move from where they were.
Yet the Israelites had light where they lived.
Think about that image.
Darkness over Egypt.
Light among God's people.
And Pharaoh was still negotiating.
That is another symptom of the unsurrendered heart.
We negotiate with God about things over which God has already declared His authority.
“I'll follow You, but not there.”
“I'll obey You, but not with that relationship.”
“I'll give You Sunday, but not Monday night.”
“I'll surrender my future, but not my money.”
“I'll forgive, but I won't release my hatred.”
“I want Jesus as Savior, but I still want to be lord.”
Pharaoh tried bargaining with Moses.
Go—but not too far.
Go—but leave certain people.
Go—but leave the livestock.
Partial surrender kept masquerading as obedience.
But God was not negotiating Israel's freedom.
And Jesus does not call us into carefully managed discipleship where He receives the rooms we are comfortable unlocking.
Christ is Lord.
Then came the final night.
The night Egypt would never forget.
The death of the firstborn.

This is one of the most severe scenes in Scripture, and it should never be turned into entertainment. The text presents it as divine judgment after repeated warnings and Pharaoh's prolonged refusal to release an oppressed people.
But right there—in the darkness of judgment—appears one of Scripture's most powerful signs pointing forward toward Christ.
God instructed Israel to take a lamb without blemish.
The lamb would die.
Its blood would be placed on the doorway.
And when judgment passed through the land, the blood marked the household.
Exodus 12 calls it the LORD's Passover.
Do not miss what protected the Israelites.
It was not their ethnic superiority.
It was not their moral perfection.
It was not because every Israelite household contained better human beings than every Egyptian household.
They stood beneath blood God had provided as the sign of covenant protection.
A lamb died.
A household lived.
Centuries later, John the Baptist would see Jesus approaching and cry:
“Behold, the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.”
Paul would write:
Suddenly Exodus becomes bigger than Egypt.
Because there is another slavery.
Sin.
There is another tyrant.
Death.
There is another judgment from which human strength cannot rescue us.
And there is another Lamb.
Jesus Christ.
This is where the story reaches us.
The Gospel does not say that basically good people need religious improvement.
It says sinners need rescue.
We have all sinned.
We have all fallen short of God's glory.
And the frightening truth about Pharaoh is that something of his rebellion echoes in every fallen human heart.
“Who is the LORD that I should obey Him?”
We may never say those exact words.
We simply live them.
God says forgive.
We say no.
God says flee sexual immorality.
We say later.
God says confess.
We hide.
God says humble yourself.
We defend ourselves.
God says come.
We run.
God says surrender.
We negotiate.
And every time we treat God's patience as permission to continue rebelling, we make the same catastrophic mistake Pharaoh made.
God's patience is mercy.
It is not approval.
The apostle Paul asks whether we presume upon the riches of God's kindness, not realizing that God's kindness is meant to lead us to repentance.
Read that slowly.
His kindness is calling you home.
Maybe the fact that you are reading this is itself another mercy.
Another knock.
Another warning.
Another invitation.
Because unlike Pharaoh's story, yours is not finished while Christ is still calling you to repent and believe.
And here is the Gospel:
The judgment we deserved did not disappear because God decided sin no longer mattered.
At the cross, Jesus bore sin.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
The blood of animals in Exodus pointed beyond itself toward something infinitely greater—the once-for-all saving work of Jesus Christ.
Peter says believers were redeemed with the precious blood of Christ, “as of a lamb without blemish and without spot.”
The Lamb was slain.
The guilty can go free.
Not because God compromised justice.
Because Jesus satisfied what sinners could never satisfy for themselves.
That is grace.
Scandalous grace.
Grace for adulterers.
Grace for addicts.
Grace for liars.
Grace for hypocrites.
Grace for religious people who have perfected the appearance of holiness while hiding a private Egypt inside.
Grace for the person who has promised God “never again” and then did it again.
Grace for the ashamed.
Grace for the exhausted.
Grace for people who have wasted years.
Grace for people reading through tears because somewhere inside they know God has been putting His finger on something they keep refusing to surrender.
But grace is not permission to remain Pharaoh.
Grace brings us to Jesus and changes us.
Repentance is not purchasing forgiveness with good behavior. Forgiveness is God's gift through Christ.
Repentance is the turning of the heart toward the Savior.
It is laying down your crown.
It is finally admitting:
“Jesus, You are Lord. I am not.”
And perhaps that is the real question behind the Ten Plagues.
Not merely:
Why was Pharaoh's heart hard?
But:
What has God been asking you to surrender that you keep hardening your heart against?
Don't answer quickly.
Stay there.
What is it?
The relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ?
The secret messages?
The pornography nobody knows about?
The resentment you have baptized as “boundaries” when deep inside you know it has become hatred?
The money you worship?
The applause you need?
The pride that will not apologize?
The church wound you have allowed to become an excuse for abandoning Jesus?
The hidden compromise?
The double life?
The fear?
The control?
What is your “no”?
Because Pharaoh teaches us something terrifying:
A heart does not usually become stone overnight.
It becomes stone one refusal at a time.
One excuse.
One compromise.
One delayed repentance.
One ignored conviction.
One more tomorrow.
Until tomorrow becomes years.
But Jesus Christ is still in the business of rewriting stories.
Peter denied Him.
Jesus restored Peter.
Thomas doubted.
Jesus met Thomas.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Jesus transformed Paul into an apostle.
The thief beside Christ had nothing left to offer—no lifetime of religious achievement, no opportunity to repair his reputation—and he turned toward Jesus.
Grace found him at the edge of death.
This is the scandal of the Gospel.
Your worst chapter does not have to be your final chapter when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
It means sin no longer gets to write the ending.
Jesus does.
From scandal...
to grace.
From slavery...
to freedom.
From condemnation...
to forgiveness.
From death...
to life.
The Exodus was not ultimately a celebration of Moses' greatness.
It revealed God's greatness.
God told Pharaoh that He had allowed him to stand so that God's power would be shown and His name proclaimed throughout the earth—a declaration Paul later quotes in Romans 9:17.
And thousands of years later, here we are.
Still talking about His name.
Pharaoh had monuments.
God has the final word.
Pharaoh had armies.
God divided the sea.
Pharaoh had a throne.
God had eternity.
Pharaoh wanted everyone to know his greatness.
Yet generations remember Pharaoh primarily because his resistance became the stage upon which the greatness of the LORD was displayed.
That is a warning to every proud heart:
God does not need our permission to be God.
The question is whether we will bow before Him in repentance and mercy or continue resisting the One before whom every knee will ultimately bow.
And this is where I want to speak to the person who has been hiding.
Not the audience.
You.
Maybe everybody thinks you are fine.
Maybe you post Scripture.
Maybe you attend church.
Maybe you know Christian language so well that nobody notices how exhausted your soul has become.
But God knows.
And you know.
Stop running.
You do not have to clean yourself before coming to Christ.
Come because you cannot clean yourself.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Ask for mercy.
Not because typing words saves you, but because Jesus Christ saves sinners who come to Him in faith.
Not as a performance.
Not as superstition.
Let it be an honest public marker of what your heart is praying privately.
Someone reading the comments may need to discover that they are not the only believer fighting tears behind a smiling profile picture.
If Christ has already brought you out of something you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what He did.
Your testimony might become another person's reason to believe that their story is not over.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to preach at them.
But believers can freely choose to support Gospel-centered work so more Scripture, discipleship, encouragement, and evangelistic content can continue reaching people.
Invite your family. Invite the friend drifting from church. Invite the believer secretly struggling. Invite the skeptic. Invite the person who thinks they have gone too far for Jesus.
Because someday temptation may whisper, “One more no won't matter.”
Come back and remember Pharaoh.
One more no mattered.
Then another.
Then another.
Until an entire nation heard the consequences of a heart that would not bow.
But do not leave this story merely afraid of becoming Pharaoh.
Leave looking at Jesus.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of frightened people trying hard enough to soften themselves.
It is the story of a holy God pursuing sinners with mercy.
The Father sent the Son.
The Son willingly went to the cross.
The Lamb shed His blood.
The tomb was sealed.
Then death discovered that it had imprisoned Someone it could not hold.
Jesus rose.
And because He lives, the enslaved can become free.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The ashamed can come home.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
The hardened can cry out for mercy.
The ruined can be redeemed.
The scandal can become a testimony of grace.
So if God is confronting something in you right now, do not say tomorrow.
Pharaoh had tomorrows.
Until he didn't.
Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your heart.
Turn to Jesus.
There is mercy in Him.
There is forgiveness in Him.
There is freedom in Him.
There is a new beginning in Him.
And there is enough grace in the crucified and risen Christ to rewrite a story you thought had already reached its final page.
The most terrifying thing about Pharaoh was not that God never spoke to him—it was that God spoke again and again, and Pharaoh kept believing there would always be another tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IF BIBLICAL HEROES PRACTICED POLYGAMY, WHY CAN’T CHRISTIANS?
paragraphs:
IF BIBLICAL HEROES PRACTICED POLYGAMY, WHY CAN’T CHRISTIANS?
Abraham had more than one woman. Jacob had two wives and two concubines. David had several wives. Solomon had hundreds. So why does Christianity insist on one man and one woman? The answer is hiding in a distinction that could change the way you read the entire Bible.
There is a question Christians sometimes become uncomfortable answering.
Not because Scripture has nothing to say.
But because Scripture says more than the comfortable answer.
“If men in the Bible had multiple wives, why can’t Christians?”
It sounds like a devastating objection.
Abraham had Sarah and Hagar.
Jacob married Leah and Rachel and fathered children through Bilhah and Zilpah.
David had multiple wives.
Solomon took the practice to an almost unimaginable extreme.
These are not obscure villains hiding in forgotten corners of Scripture.
Abraham is called the father of all who believe.
Jacob became Israel.
David was the king whose royal line eventually led to Christ.
Solomon built the temple.
So the question deserves more than an embarrassed answer.
If they did it...
why can’t we?
But there is something you must understand before reading another sentence.
The Bible is not a carefully edited advertisement for religious people.
It is a rescue story filled with damaged people.
And if you confuse everything the Bible records with everything God approves, you will eventually make sin look holy simply because a biblical character committed it.
Scripture records murder.
That does not make murder righteous.
Scripture records adultery.
That does not sanctify adultery.
Scripture records deception, drunkenness, incest, betrayal, cowardice, idolatry, violence, jealousy, greed, and catastrophic failures by people God nevertheless chose to pursue with grace.
And yes...
Scripture records polygamy.
The question is not merely:
“What did biblical men do?”
The deeper question is:
“What did God establish?”
Those are not the same thing.
And the difference takes us all the way back before Abraham.
Before Jacob.
Before David.
Before Solomon.
Before Israel had kings.
Before sin had entered the human story.
Back to a garden.
Back to a man.
Back to a woman.
Back to God.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
Look carefully at the Hebrew behind that sentence.
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew verb often transliterated dabaq—דָּבַק—carries the idea of clinging, adhering, holding fast.
And then comes the phrase:
בָשָׂר אֶחָד
basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Not merely two people occupying the same house.
Not merely a sexual arrangement.
Not merely a social contract.
A covenantal union.
One flesh.
And notice something even more important.
God did not begin humanity by giving Adam a collection of wives and then explaining how to manage them.
He created Adam.
He created Eve.
And Scripture presents their union as the foundational pattern from which marriage is described.
But perhaps someone says:
“That was Genesis. Later men had multiple wives.”
True.
And this is where the argument becomes fascinating.
Because when Jesus Himself was asked about marriage, He did not point His listeners to Abraham’s household.
He did not point them to Jacob.
He did not point them to David.
He did not point them to Solomon.
Jesus went behind all of them.
He went back to creation.
In Matthew 19, Jesus says:
“Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female...?”
Then Jesus quotes Genesis.
“For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife...”
And then Matthew’s Greek makes something especially significant explicit:
καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
kai esontai hoi duo eis sarka mian.
“And the two shall become one flesh.”
οἱ δύο.
hoi duo.
“The two.”
Then Jesus continues:
“Wherefore they are no more twain, but one flesh.”
There is the interpretive center.
When Christ explains marriage, He takes His hearers back to God’s creational design and speaks of “the two” becoming one flesh.
Jesus does not use the complicated marriages of fallen human beings to redefine creation.
He uses creation to evaluate fallen human beings.
That changes everything.
Because the existence of polygamy in biblical history does not automatically establish polygamy as the biblical ideal.
In fact, read the stories.
Don't sanitize them.
Don't turn Sunday-school heroes into marble statues.
Walk into their homes.
Listen to the crying.
Feel the rivalry.
Watch what happens when human desire collides with covenant.
Abraham received a promise from God.
But years passed.
Sarah remained barren.
Waiting became painful.
Hope became exhausting.
And eventually Sarah proposed a human solution to a divine promise.
Hagar.
Genesis does not present what follows like a romantic expansion of Abraham's family.
It becomes heartbreak.
Hagar conceives.
Sarah feels despised.
Conflict erupts.
Hagar suffers.
Later Ishmael and Isaac become caught inside consequences they did not create.
Eventually Hagar and her son are sent away.
Read that scene slowly.
A mother wandering in the wilderness.
Water gone.
Her son nearby.
Her heart breaking.
She cannot bear to watch him die.
And God hears the boy.
Grace enters the wilderness.
But grace rescuing people from the consequences of human decisions does not mean God endorsed every decision that put them there.
That distinction matters.
God's mercy toward broken families should never be twisted into God's approval of everything that broke them.
Then comes Jacob.
He loves Rachel.
But through Laban's deception, he receives Leah.
Then Rachel.
Then Bilhah.
Then Zilpah.
And suddenly the household becomes an emotional battlefield.
One woman is loved.
Another feels rejected.
One bears children.
Another is barren.
Jealousy grows.
Competition intensifies.
Children become entangled in the rivalry of adults.
Names are given to sons in the language of longing, pain, vindication, hope, and desperation.
This is not Scripture saying:
“Look how beautifully polygamy works.”
This is Scripture refusing to hide how fractured human hearts actually are.
And somehow...
God still works through that family.
That is grace.
Not endorsement.
Grace.
Then David.
A man capable of extraordinary faith.
A shepherd who faced Goliath.
A worshiper.
A warrior.
A king.
A man who knew what it meant to cry before God.
And yet David's household became filled with devastating sexual and relational disorder.
His multiplication of wives did not produce a peaceful dynasty.
His lust for Bathsheba eventually led him into adultery, deception, and the arranged death of Uriah.
The sword entered his house.
His family experienced violation, vengeance, rebellion, grief, and death.
The Bible does not airbrush David.
That is precisely why David's story can reach people like us.
Because perhaps you have loved God...
and still made choices you deeply regret.
Perhaps you have worshiped with tears...
and later surrendered to something you knew was wrong.
Perhaps there are chapters of your life you wish could be ripped from the book.
David reminds us that being used by God does not mean every decision we make is approved by God.
Then Solomon.
If multiplying wives were proof of divine blessing, Solomon should have become the greatest advertisement for it.
Instead, Scripture gives us a warning.
Solomon accumulated wives and concubines on a massive scale, and his wives turned his heart toward other gods.
Think about the tragedy.
The man who asked God for wisdom became foolish enough to allow divided loves to divide his worship.
That should terrify every Christian who says:
“But a biblical hero did it.”
Yes.
And sometimes the reason Scripture tells you what a biblical hero did is so that you will not do it.
There had already been a warning for Israel's kings.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says concerning the king:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away...”
Solomon's life eventually became a living demonstration of that warning.
The Bible is brutally honest about its heroes because the Bible ultimately does not have human heroes.
It has a Savior.
Abraham cannot save you.
Jacob cannot save you.
David cannot save you.
Solomon cannot save you.
Peter cannot save you.
Paul cannot save you.
Every human being in Scripture eventually forces your eyes beyond human greatness toward the One who does not fail.
Jesus Christ.
And this is where the discussion becomes much bigger than polygamy.
Because the Bible's teaching about marriage is not ultimately about winning an argument over relationship structures.
Marriage becomes a window into the Gospel itself.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5 and again reaches back to Genesis:
“For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh.”
And then Paul says something breathtaking:
“This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.”
There it is.
Marriage is not merely about human companionship.
At its deepest theological level, Christian marriage is designed to point beyond itself.
Toward Christ.
Toward covenant.
Toward faithful love.
Toward the Bridegroom and His people.
Jesus does not collect disposable lovers.
He gives Himself for His bride.
Christ loves the church.
Christ sacrifices Himself for her.
Christ cleanses.
Christ sanctifies.
Christ remains faithful.
The Gospel is not the story of a Savior shopping for something better when His bride disappoints Him.
It is the story of a Savior who goes to a cross for people who betrayed Him.
And suddenly marriage becomes holy ground.
Because Christian marriage is supposed to whisper something about Jesus.
This does not mean every Christian marriage does that perfectly.
Far from it.
Christian husbands fail.
Christian wives fail.
Some marriages become deeply wounded.
Some collapse.
Some involve betrayal.
Some people reading this have been abandoned.
Some have been cheated on.
Some carry memories they almost never discuss.
Some were raised inside chaotic homes and promised themselves they would never repeat what they witnessed...
only to discover years later that brokenness has a strange way of traveling through generations.
And perhaps that is why this subject hurts more than we admit.
Because sometimes theological questions are hiding personal questions.
“If biblical heroes practiced polygamy, why can't Christians?”
Maybe underneath that question is another one.
“How much of what I desire must actually surrender to Jesus?”
Now we are getting close.
Because following Christ means we do not begin with:
“What can I justify?”
We begin with:
“Lord, what do You desire?”
Christian discipleship is not the art of searching Scripture for the maximum amount of permission we can extract from it.
It is surrender.
Jesus does not call us merely to believe facts about Him.
He says:
“Follow me.”
And following Him means there will be moments when Christ confronts something we want.
Sexual desire.
Pride.
Money.
Ambition.
Bitterness.
Revenge.
Relationships.
Identity.
Control.
Our preferred version of happiness.
And suddenly the question is no longer whether Abraham did something.
The question becomes whether Jesus is Lord.
That is much harder.
Because we love loopholes.
We love asking how close we can stand to the edge without technically falling.
“How far is too far?”
“Does the Bible explicitly forbid this exact scenario?”
“Didn't somebody in Scripture do something similar?”
But love does not ask:
“How little obedience can I give and still call Him Lord?”
Love says:
“Jesus, even here...
You can have me.”
And before anyone turns this article into a weapon against people with complicated marital histories, remember the Gospel.
Christianity is not a museum for people with flawless relationship histories.

The church is filled with people whose stories contain divorce, adultery, sexual sin, abandonment, betrayal, abuse, foolish decisions, broken vows, blended families, painful consequences, and memories soaked in regret.
The answer is not pretending those things never happened.
The answer is Jesus.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is cleansing at the cross.
There is restoration at the cross.
There is wisdom for complicated situations.
There is grace for people who cannot travel backward and rewrite yesterday.
And there is power to obey Christ today.
Maybe you cannot change the first half of your story.
But Jesus can change what the broken chapters mean.
That is the scandal of grace.
God does not wait until sinners become impressive enough to deserve redemption.
Christ dies for sinners.
He walks into stories we would rather hide.
He exposes what must be exposed.
He forgives what we confess.
He teaches us to repent.
He begins rebuilding what sin shattered.
This does not mean consequences magically disappear.
Grace is not a time machine.
But grace can make the place of your greatest shame become the place where God's mercy becomes impossible to deny.
Maybe your scandal was sexual.
Maybe it was adultery.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe emotional infidelity.
Maybe divorce.
Maybe relationships built on lies.
Maybe you hurt someone who trusted you.
Maybe someone who promised to love you destroyed your trust instead.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Hear this carefully:
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve respectable people.
He came to save sinners.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you out of the grave.
Grace does not say sin does not matter.
Grace says sin mattered so much that Christ carried it to Calvary...
and you are loved too deeply to be left enslaved to it.
That is why biblical heroes can be so messy.
Their failures are not embarrassing interruptions in God's story.
Their failures help expose why humanity needs Christ.
Abraham needed grace.
Jacob needed grace.
David needed grace.
Solomon needed grace.
Peter needed grace.
You need grace.
I need grace.
And none of us gets to rewrite God's design merely because broken people in Scripture departed from it.
Jesus points us backward to creation...
and then forward to redemption.
One man.
One woman.
One-flesh covenant.
And beyond every imperfect marriage stands the greater Bridegroom...
Jesus Christ...
whose covenant faithfulness never fails.
So if somebody asks you:
“If biblical heroes practiced polygamy, why can't Christians?”
Don't panic.
Don't hide the difficult passages.
Open them.
Read them.
Let Scripture tell the whole story.
The Bible does not need us to protect it from its own honesty.
The presence of polygamy in biblical narratives demonstrates that God worked through profoundly imperfect cultures and profoundly imperfect people.
But description is not automatically prescription.
Tolerance within fallen history is not identical to creational design.
And when Jesus was confronted with questions about marriage, His compass pointed back toward “the beginning.”
That should matter enormously to anyone who calls Him Lord.
But perhaps the most important question is not whether you won the argument.
Perhaps the most important question is whether Jesus has won your heart.
Because you can defend biblical marriage while destroying your own marriage with pride.
You can condemn polygamy while secretly feeding pornography.
You can quote Genesis while emotionally abandoning your spouse.
You can preach fidelity while flirting privately.
You can defend God's design publicly while violating God's heart secretly.
And maybe that sentence just found someone.
If it did...
don't hide.
Run toward Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Get accountable.
Ask forgiveness where appropriate.
Seek wise biblical counsel.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Jesus is still rewriting stories.
You do not have to perform here.
Sometimes two honest words are the beginning of coming out of hiding.
Save it too.

Because the next time somebody says, “But Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon did it,” you may need to remember the difference between what Scripture honestly records and what Christ calls His disciples to follow.

We want Gospel Warrior to remain a place where difficult questions are not feared, broken people are not discarded, Scripture is not diluted, sin is not celebrated, and Jesus Christ remains at the center.
It doesn't.
It isn't.
Jesus alone saves.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can help that work continue reaching people with Scripture, discipleship, conviction, encouragement, and the message of Christ.
do not miss Jesus.
Because that is the tragedy greater than losing an argument about marriage.
You can study Abraham and miss Abraham's God.
You can analyze David and miss David's greater Son.
You can possess Solomon's writings and still lack wisdom.
You can debate marriage while never surrendering your own heart.
The Bible was never given so we could become experts at finding loopholes around obedience.
It was given to lead us into truth...
and ultimately to the One who said:
“Follow me.”
So bring Him the complicated relationship.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the failure.
Bring Him the desire you have been trying to justify.
Bring Him the marriage hanging by a thread.
Bring Him the loneliness.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the chapter you wish had never happened.
Jesus already knows.
And the hands reaching toward repentant sinners still carry scars.
Because the greatest hero of Scripture was never Abraham.
Never Jacob.
Never David.
Never Solomon.
It was always Jesus.
And when every human hero's record becomes stained...
His remains spotless.
When their houses fracture...
He builds His church.
When their desires wander...
His love remains faithful.
When our sin writes a chapter called “ruined”...
the crucified and risen Christ can write another word over the life that turns to Him:
“Redeemed.”
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter when it is surrendered to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Fear That Makes You Run Toward God, Not Away From Him
paragraphs: The Fear That Makes You Run Toward God, Not Away From Him
Understanding “The Fear of the Lord” Correctly—and why the God who should leave us trembling is the very God who invites sinners to come home.
There is a kind of fear that makes you hide.
And there is a kind of fear that makes you kneel.
Confuse the two, and you can spend years calling anxiety “holiness,” distance “reverence,” and terror “the fear of the Lord.”
Maybe that has been your story.
You heard someone say, “Fear God,” and somewhere deep inside, you translated it into something Scripture never actually said:
God is waiting for you to mess up.
So you became careful.
Not surrendered. Careful.

You prayed carefully. Worshiped carefully. Confessed carefully. You tried to keep your failures out of sight—as though the God who formed your inward parts could somehow be kept from seeing the rooms you refused to open.
Then you failed again.
And suddenly you were Adam among the trees.
“I was afraid… so I hid.”
That sentence from Genesis 3:10 still describes millions of people.
Afraid.
So hiding.
But what if the biblical “fear of the Lord” was never supposed to drive a repentant sinner deeper into hiding?
What if understanding it correctly could completely change the way you see holiness, grace, obedience, worship—and even your own failures?
Stay with this, because Scripture contains a sentence so startling that, at first glance, it almost sounds contradictory.
The Bible tells us to fear God.
Then the Bible tells us that with God there is forgiveness… so that He may be feared.
Yes.
Forgiveness produces fear.
That changes everything.
Psalm 130:3–4 says:
“If You, LORD, should mark iniquities, O Lord, who could stand? But there is forgiveness with You, that You may be feared.”
The Hebrew phrase translated “that You may be feared” is לְמַעַן תִּוָּרֵא — lemaʿan tivvareʾ, from the Hebrew root ירא — y-r-ʾ, associated with fear, reverence, and awe.
Notice the movement of the Psalm.
Sin.
Judgment.
Human helplessness.
Then forgiveness.
Then fear.
The psalmist does not say, “There is forgiveness with You, therefore nobody needs to take You seriously.”
He says almost the opposite.
There is forgiveness with You…
therefore You are feared.
Why?
Because biblical fear is far deeper than being frightened that God might hurt you.
It is the soul awakening to the unbearable weight of who God actually is.
Holy.
Sovereign.
Righteous.
Creator.
Judge.
Merciful.
Near.
The One against whom you have sinned is also the One who forgives you.
And when that truth finally gets beneath your religious vocabulary, something happens.
You stop treating grace cheaply.
Imagine standing guilty before a perfectly righteous Judge.
There is no excuse left.
No defense.
No comparison with someone worse than you.
No religious performance you can slide across the table.
The evidence is already there.
And the Judge is not corrupt.
He cannot simply pretend evil is good.
Then imagine discovering that the Judge Himself has provided the satisfaction of justice at unimaginable cost.
That is where Christianity becomes scandalous.
Because at the center of our faith is not humanity climbing toward God.
It is God coming toward sinners in Jesus Christ.
The cross does not tell us that sin was insignificant.
The cross tells us sin was so serious that redemption required the blood of Christ.
And simultaneously, the cross tells us that God's love toward sinners is so astonishing that Christ willingly gave Himself for us.
Romans 5:8 says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we became respectable.
Not once our secret history became presentable.
While we were sinners.
This is where fear and grace meet.
The person who understands neither holiness nor grace can casually say, “God will forgive me.”
The person beginning to understand both falls silent and thinks:
He forgave even me?
That trembling is closer to the fear of the Lord.
Proverbs 1:7 declares:
יִרְאַת יְהוָה רֵאשִׁית דָּעַת
Yirʾat YHWH reʾshit daʿat.
“The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge.”
The expression יִרְאַת יְהוָה — yirʾat YHWH means “the fear of the LORD.”
This is not presented as an embarrassing stage of spiritual immaturity.
It is the beginning of knowledge.
Why?
Because wisdom begins when God becomes God in your understanding again.
Not your assistant.
Not your cosmic vending machine.
Not a motivational accessory attached to your ambitions.
Not a grandfatherly figure whose primary purpose is approving whatever you already wanted to do.
God.
When you begin seeing Him as He reveals Himself, your entire life is rearranged.
Your pride looks different.
Your secret sin looks different.
Your money looks different.
Your sexuality looks different.
Your grudges look different.
Your entertainment looks different.
Your ambitions look different.
Your words look different.
Your worship looks different.
And grace looks infinitely more beautiful.
This is why Proverbs 8:13 can say:
“The fear of the LORD is to hate evil.”
Real fear of God does not merely create religious feelings.
It changes allegiance.
You begin hating what destroys communion with the God you have come to treasure.
That does not mean a Christian instantly becomes sinless.
It means sin can no longer comfortably remain your unquestioned master.
There is a difference between falling into sin and building a home there.
There is a difference between struggling and surrendering.
There is a difference between temptation and making peace with rebellion.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly why those sentences hurt.
There is something you have been excusing.
Something hidden.
Something repeatedly renamed so you would not have to call it what Scripture calls it.
Maybe nobody knows.
But God does.
And strangely, that should not only terrify you.
For the person willing to repent, it should also give you hope.
Because the God who sees everything is the God before whom hiding is finally unnecessary.
You can confess what He already knows.
You can bring into the light what has been poisoning you in darkness.
You do not need to impress Jesus into saving you.
You need Jesus because you cannot save yourself.
This is why the fear of the Lord and the Gospel belong together.
At Sinai, God's holiness was not casual.
At Calvary, God's holiness did not disappear.
The cross is not God abandoning justice so He can become nice.
At the cross, we see both the horror of sin and the magnitude of divine mercy.
Jesus Christ, truly righteous, bore sin on behalf of sinners.
As 2 Corinthians 5:21 declares, God made the One who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
That is grace.
Costly grace.
Blood-bought grace.
Grace that does not wink at rebellion but rescues rebels.
Grace that does not say, “Remain exactly as you are.”
Grace says, “Come exactly as you are—and follow Christ.”
There is a difference.
Jesus receives sinners.
And Jesus transforms sinners.
That is why our theme will always be:
But notice who does the rewriting.
Jesus.
Not positive thinking.
Not religious image management.
Not self-improvement.
Jesus Christ.
Perhaps this is where you misunderstood fear.
