You thought fearing God meant spending every waking moment wondering whether He was about to crush you.
Scripture gives us something richer.
Psalm 103:13 says:
“As a father pities his children, so the LORD pities those who fear Him.”
Read that again.
Those who fear Him receive fatherly compassion.
Psalm 147:11 likewise says that the LORD takes pleasure in those who fear Him, in those who hope in His mercy.
Fear.
Hope.
Mercy.
Together.
Biblical fear is not the opposite of trusting God.
Properly understood, it belongs alongside trust.
It recognizes God's terrifying majesty while resting in His covenant mercy.
It refuses to make God small enough to manage.
It refuses to make grace cheap enough to exploit.
It bows.
It listens.
It obeys.
It worships.
It repents.
And yet it draws near.
The New Testament preserves this same reality.
Hebrews 12:28–29 tells believers to serve God acceptably “with reverence and godly fear,” because “our God is a consuming fire.”
The Greek expression includes εὐλάβεια — eulabeia, carrying the sense of reverence or godly awe.
God did not stop being holy when Jesus came.
Jesus did not arrive to rescue humanity from an embarrassing Old Testament version of God.
The Father and the Son are not opponents.
The Gospel reveals the saving purpose of the triune God.
And here is where Hebrews becomes breathtaking.
The same letter that speaks about reverence and consuming fire also tells believers to approach God's throne boldly because of Christ.
Hebrews 4:16 invites us to come boldly to the throne of grace to receive mercy and find grace in time of need.
Do you see the beautiful tension?
He is a consuming fire.
Come near.
He is holy.
Come near.
He knows you completely.
Come near.
You need mercy.
Come near.
How?
Not arrogantly.
Not because sin does not matter.
Not because God lowered His standards.
We come through Jesus Christ.
The fear of the Lord does not make the redeemed person casually stroll into God's presence.
But neither does it leave that person outside the door.
It makes you enter with wonder.
There is another passage that helps protect us from misunderstanding.
First John 4:18 says:
“There is no fear in love; but perfect love casts out fear, because fear involves torment.”
The Greek word commonly translated “fear” there is φόβος — phobos, while the passage specifically connects this fear with κόλασις — kolasis, punishment.
John is addressing fear connected with judgment and punishment.
So Scripture can tell believers both to fear God and that perfect love drives out fear because it is not using “fear” in a simplistic, identical sense in every context.
The child of God does not need to live as though Christ's finished work were meaningless and condemnation were still hanging over every forgiven failure.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.”
No condemnation.
That is not permission to sin.
That is permission to stop pretending.
There are people who continue hiding because they think shame will make them holy.
It won't.
There are people punishing themselves for sins they have confessed because suffering somehow feels more spiritual than receiving forgiveness.
But your self-punishment cannot improve the blood of Jesus.
Repentance is necessary.
Obedience matters.
Holiness matters.
But salvation is not Christ plus your ability to hate yourself sufficiently.
The Gospel calls you away from both presumption and despair.
Presumption says, “God is loving, so my sin doesn't matter.”
Despair says, “My sin is so terrible that God's grace cannot reach me.”
The cross destroys both lies.
At Calvary, God says sin matters more than you imagined.
And grace reaches farther than you imagined.
That is the scandal.
Peter denied Jesus.
David committed grievous sin.
Paul had persecuted the church.
The woman caught in adultery was publicly humiliated.
The thief beside Jesus was dying under condemnation.
Scripture never sanitizes human failure to make its heroes marketable.
Because Scripture is ultimately not the story of impressive people rescuing themselves.
It is the story of a holy God redeeming sinners.
And perhaps that is why you are still reading.
Because somewhere underneath everything people see, you know there is a chapter of your story you wish you could tear out.
Maybe it happened years ago.
Maybe it happened yesterday.
Maybe it is happening right now.
Listen carefully.
Grace does not mean pretending the chapter was beautiful.
Grace means Jesus is capable of writing beyond it.
Repentance does not erase historical consequences.
Forgiveness does not always remove earthly consequences.
But your worst chapter does not have authority to become the final sentence when Christ takes hold of your life.
That is what fearing God correctly eventually does.
It makes sin frightening…
but God irresistible.
It makes rebellion bitter…
and mercy sweet.
It makes obedience something deeper than avoiding punishment.
You begin wanting to please the One who rescued you.
Think of Joseph when tempted by Potiphar's wife.
His question was not merely, “What happens if somebody catches me?”
He said, in Genesis 39:9:
“How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?”
That is fear of the Lord operating when nobody important is watching.
Human fear asks:
Will I get caught?
Fear of God asks:
How could I do this against Him?
Human fear protects reputation.
Fear of God protects communion.
Human fear performs when people are watching.
Fear of God remains when the door closes.
That distinction exposes us.
What do you watch when nobody knows?
What conversation would embarrass you if it became public?
What bitterness have you protected because forgiveness feels unfair?
What compromise have you renamed “weakness” even though you have stopped fighting it?
What does your private life say about how large God is in your heart?
Do not answer for somebody else.
This is between you and God.
And if something just surfaced in your conscience, do not run from Him.
Run toward Him.
Confess it.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Notice the language.
Faithful.
Just.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
The Gospel is not merely about being forgiven from something.
Christ is also transforming His people for something.
Holiness.
Love.
Truth.
Good works.
Worship.
Mission.
A life increasingly shaped by Jesus.
And that means the fear of the Lord is not meant to paralyze you.
It frees you from lesser fears.
When God becomes enormous in your sight, human approval begins shrinking.
You do not need everybody to clap.
You do not need everybody to understand.
You do not need everybody to approve your obedience.
Jesus said in Matthew 10:28 not to fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul, but rather to fear the One who has authority over both soul and body in hell.
Those are serious words.
Jesus Himself taught the judgment of God.
A Christ-centered message cannot erase judgment without erasing part of Christ's own teaching.
Hell is not a marketing device.
Judgment is not a preacher's prop.
Scripture treats final judgment as reality.
And precisely because eternity matters, the Gospel is extraordinarily urgent.
If you have never surrendered yourself to Jesus Christ, do not reduce this article to interesting Hebrew and Greek words.
You do not merely need a better definition of fear.
You need reconciliation with God.
Jesus calls sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
Repentance is more than feeling bad.
It is a turning—a change of mind and direction that bears fruit in life.
Faith is more than admitting that Jesus existed.
It is entrusting yourself to Him.
His death.
His resurrection.
His lordship.
His mercy.
His righteousness rather than yours.
You may have spent years running because you were afraid of God.
But perhaps today you need to discover the fear that finally makes you stop running away.
The fear that whispers:
He is God.
I am not.
I have sinned.
He is holy.
Christ is merciful.
So I will come home.
And Christian, if you already belong to Christ but have grown casual with Him, perhaps you need this reminder too.
Grace should never make Jesus ordinary to you.
The more deeply you understand forgiveness, the more astonishing the Forgiver should become.
The hands pierced for you should never become boring.
The empty tomb should never become background decoration.
The name of Jesus should never become merely branding.
We are talking about the King.
The Lamb.
The Savior.
The One before whom every knee will ultimately bow.
And somehow, through His Gospel, sinners like us are invited near.
You do not have to publish the details of your private struggle. Wisdom matters, and some confessions belong in private before God and with trustworthy mature believers rather than on a public page.
But you do not have to pretend anymore.

And if Christ has already delivered you from a season where shame once controlled you, tell someone what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer desperately needed tonight.
Not because saving a post makes anyone holy, but because there will probably be a day when shame tries to convince you to hide again.
Come back and remember:
The fear of the Lord does not make grace smaller.
It makes grace astonishing.
We want people receiving daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
Your support can participate in the work of putting biblical encouragement in front of people who may never walk through the doors of a church.
Know Christ.
Fear God.
Turn from sin.
Receive grace.
Walk in obedience.
Love Him.
And never confuse being terrified of rejection with biblical reverence for the Father who receives His children through Christ.
Because perhaps the greatest surprise hidden inside “the fear of the Lord” is this:
When you finally understand how holy God is, you realize you should never have been able to approach Him.
Then you look at the cross…
and discover that Jesus opened the way.
The God before whom you should tremble is the God who, through Christ, tells the repentant sinner to come near.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: BEFORE GOD GAVE ISRAEL A KING, HE KEPT FINDING SHEPHERDS
paragraphs:
BEFORE GOD GAVE ISRAEL A KING, HE KEPT FINDING SHEPHERDS
Abel carried a lamb. Moses carried a staff. David walked out of a pasture. Then Jesus said something that made the entire pattern impossible to ignore: “I am the Good Shepherd.”
There is blood in the grass.
A brother is lying dead.
Another brother is walking away from the presence of God with innocent blood crying from the ground behind him.
And strangely, one of the first occupations Scripture ever pauses to identify is this:
Abel was a shepherd.
Not a warrior.
Not a king.
Not a priest standing inside a temple.
A shepherd.
Genesis 4:2 describes him in Hebrew as:
וַיְהִי־הֶבֶל רֹעֵה צֹאן
Vayehi-Hevel ro'eh tzon.
“And Abel was a keeper of sheep.”
The expression רֹעֵה צֹאן (ro'eh tzon) means one who tends, feeds, or shepherds a flock.
It seems like an ordinary detail.
Until you keep reading the Bible.
Because generations later, another man will be standing among sheep when God begins preparing him to confront Pharaoh.
Later still, a forgotten son will be called in from watching sheep and anointed king.
And centuries after that, outside Jerusalem, the Son of God will look into a world filled with wandering, wounded, hunted, spiritually dying people and declare:
ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός.
Egō eimi ho poimēn ho kalos.
“I am the good shepherd.”
John 10:11.
And suddenly the pasture begins to feel much bigger.
Abel.
Moses.
David.
Jesus.
Different generations. Different circumstances. Different roles in redemptive history.
But there is a thread running through the fields.
And if you follow it far enough, it leads to a cross.
Maybe that is why this story matters so much to people like us.
Because some of us know exactly what it feels like to be sheep without admitting that we are lost.
We know how to smile while wandering.
We know how to post Bible verses while privately starving.
We know how to say, “God is good,” while secretly wondering whether He still wants anything to do with us.
We know how to sit in church with our hands raised while carrying something inside that we hope nobody ever discovers.
A secret.
A relapse.
A resentment.
An affair.
A hidden browser history.
A collapsing marriage.
A prayer life that disappeared months ago.
A heart that has become colder than we are willing to admit.
And perhaps the most dangerous sentence a wandering sheep can ever believe is:
“I can find my own way back.”
Because sheep need a shepherd.
And Scripture keeps bringing us back to that image.
Abel appears near the beginning.

Genesis tells us that Abel brought “the firstborn of his flock and of their fat portions,” and the LORD regarded Abel and his offering. His brother Cain became angry. God warned Cain about sin crouching at the door, but Cain eventually rose against Abel and killed him.
The shepherd became a victim of violence.
His blood entered the ground.
God said to Cain:
“The voice of your brother’s blood is crying to me from the ground.”
Abel is not Jesus.
We should never force Scripture to say something it does not say.
But the New Testament itself places Abel's blood into a remarkable theological contrast with Christ.
Hebrews 12:24 speaks of Jesus, the mediator of the new covenant, and “the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.”
Think about that.
Abel's blood cries out from the ground after an act of injustice.
Then, at the center of history, another innocent man is murdered.
Jesus Christ.
But His blood speaks a better word.
Abel's blood exposes guilt.
Christ's blood provides atonement for the guilty.
Abel's death demands that evil be taken seriously.
Christ's death shows us both how seriously God takes evil and how astonishingly far His mercy goes to redeem sinners.
At Calvary, God does not pretend sin does not matter.
He reveals exactly how terrible it is.
And exactly how great His grace is.
That matters when you have done something you cannot undo.
Some people reading this have memories that still make their stomach turn.
You would give anything to go backward.
You wish you could unsend it.
Unsee it.
Undo it.
Unbetray them.
Unsay those words.
You have asked yourself whether God could possibly look at the person you became and still call you home.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you that your sin was insignificant.
It tells you that the blood of Jesus is sufficient.
There is a difference.
Grace is not God pretending there was never a scandal.
Grace is God entering the scandal, bearing sin's judgment in the person of His Son, and writing redemption where we deserved condemnation.
Then the biblical story moves forward.
And eventually we find Moses.
Not in Pharaoh's palace.
Not commanding an army.
Not standing before the Red Sea.
We meet the future deliverer in Midian doing something surprisingly familiar.
Exodus 3:1 says:
וּמֹשֶׁה הָיָה רֹעֶה אֶת־צֹאן יִתְרוֹ
Umosheh hayah ro'eh et-tzon Yitro.
“Now Moses was keeping the flock of Jethro…”
There is that Hebrew idea again.
רֹעֶה.
Ro'eh.
Shepherding.
Moses had once lived inside Pharaoh's world.
Then everything collapsed.
He killed an Egyptian.
His action became known.
Pharaoh sought to kill him.
Moses fled.
The man who had lived among royalty became a fugitive in the wilderness.
And there, far from the life he once knew, Moses tended somebody else's sheep.
Imagine the humiliation.
Yesterday, Egypt.
Today, sheep.
Yesterday, proximity to power.
Today, dust.
Perhaps Moses thought the important part of his life was over.
But Exodus 3 tells us that while Moses was shepherding the flock, he came to Horeb, the mountain of God.
And a bush burned without being consumed.
The wilderness Moses may have interpreted as exile became the location of divine encounter.
God called his name.
“Moses, Moses.”
And the runaway discovered something many wounded believers desperately need to remember:
Your wilderness is not proof that God has lost your address.
Moses had a past.
God knew it.
Moses had fears.
God heard them.
Moses had objections.
God answered them.
Moses felt inadequate.
God did not respond by telling Moses how extraordinary Moses was.
He gave Moses something infinitely better.
“I will be with you.”
That is where so much modern spirituality gets the story backward.
We keep trying to convince broken people that they are powerful enough.
Scripture gives us something better than self-confidence.
The presence of God.
Moses did not rescue Israel because he finally discovered his inner greatness.
God delivered Israel through an inadequate man who had to learn dependence upon the One who said, “I AM WHO I AM.”
And perhaps somebody reading this has been standing in Midian for years.
You thought you ruined your calling.
You thought your worst chapter became the title of your entire life.
You thought the failure was final.
You thought the wilderness meant abandonment.
But God has always known how to find people in wilderness places.
Then comes David.
When Samuel arrived at Bethlehem to anoint the king God had chosen, Jesse brought his sons before the prophet.
One after another.
Strong-looking men.
Impressive men.
Men who apparently looked kingly enough that Samuel himself initially assumed Eliab must be God's anointed.
But God said:
“Do not look on his appearance or on the height of his stature…”
Then came the devastatingly beautiful truth:
“For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.”
Eventually Samuel asked whether Jesse had any sons left.
There was one.
The youngest.
But he was not standing in the room.
He was keeping the sheep.
David was in the field while everyone else was at the ceremony.
Do not miss the ache inside that scene.
They gathered the family.
And apparently nobody thought David needed to be there.
Some people know that feeling.
Overlooked.
Uninvited.
Underestimated.
The person nobody expects much from.
The sibling who does not measure up.
The believer whose past follows them into every room.
The person doing unseen work while somebody else receives the applause.
But God knew where David was.
The pasture did not hide him from God.
Samuel said, in effect, send for him.
David came.
And the LORD said:
“Arise, anoint him, for this is he.”
The shepherd boy was anointed king.
Later David would write one of the most beloved opening lines in all Scripture:
יְהוָה רֹעִי לֹא אֶחְסָר
YHWH ro'i, lo echsar.
“The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.”
Psalm 23:1.
David understood shepherding from both sides.
He knew what it meant to guide sheep.
And he knew what it meant to desperately need God to guide him.
That second lesson would become painfully important.
Because David's story does not remain clean.
The shepherd becomes king.
The king becomes powerful.
And the powerful king eventually sees Bathsheba.
Desire becomes action.
Action becomes deception.
Deception becomes manipulation.
And manipulation ends with Uriah dead.
One of Scripture's great heroes becomes the center of a horrifying moral scandal.
The man who wrote about the Shepherd wandered.
Badly.
And Scripture does not airbrush him.
That is one reason you can trust the Bible's honesty.
It does not turn its heroes into plastic saints.
No amount of poetic language can make David's sin harmless. What he did was evil. Nathan confronted him. Consequences followed.
Yet when David was confronted, he did not ultimately save himself with public relations.
He confessed:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
Psalm 51 gives us the language of a shattered man returning to God:
“Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love.”
Then:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
David had once defended sheep from predators.
Now David needed to be rescued from the predator that had risen inside his own heart.
And maybe that is where this article stopped being ancient history for you.
Because the greatest threat to your soul is not always outside you.
Sometimes it has your name.
Sometimes it knows your password.
Sometimes it uses your voice.
Sometimes the wolf is the desire you keep feeding while asking God to make it harmless.
Sin promises freedom and slowly teaches us how to wear chains.
And this is exactly why we need more than Abel.
More than Moses.
More than David.
We need the Shepherd none of them could ever fully be.
Then Jesus comes.
And in John 10 He does not merely say that He knows something about shepherding.
He says:
ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός.
Egō eimi ho poimēn ho kalos.
“I am the good shepherd.”
The Greek word ποιμήν (poimēn) means shepherd.
But Jesus does not stop with His identity.
He tells us what the Good Shepherd does.
ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλὸς τὴν ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ τίθησιν ὑπὲρ τῶν προβάτων.
Ho poimēn ho kalos tēn psychēn autou tithēsin hyper tōn probatōn.
“The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
John 10:11.
There it is.
The road out of the pasture leads to Calvary.
Jesus is not merely a motivational shepherd helping decent people become slightly better.
He lays down His life.
Why?
Because our problem is deeper than low self-esteem.
We have sinned.
We have wandered.
Isaiah had said centuries earlier:
“All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way.”
But Isaiah continues with the shocking announcement that the LORD laid upon the suffering servant “the iniquity of us all.”
This is the Gospel.
The sheep wandered.
The Shepherd came.
The sheep deserved judgment.
The Shepherd laid down His life.
Jesus bore sin on the cross.
Then He rose from the dead.
The Shepherd who lays down His life is also the Shepherd who takes it up again.
Jesus says in John 10:18:
“I have authority to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again.”
Christianity does not end at a sealed tomb.
The Shepherd lives.
And because He lives, repentance is not a walk toward hopelessness.
It is a return to Someone.
Maybe you have wandered farther than you ever intended.
Come home.
Not because your sin does not matter.
Because Christ matters more.
Repentance is not saying, “I made a few mistakes.”
It is turning from sin toward God, trusting the crucified and risen Christ.
You cannot wash yourself clean enough to deserve Him.
You cannot perform enough religious acts to purchase forgiveness.
Salvation is by God's grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
That distinction must remain absolutely clear.
We do not support Gospel work so God will love us.
In Christ, we love and serve because He loved us first.
And when grace grips a person deeply enough, it does something to our hands.
We begin asking:
“How can I help someone else hear?”
Maybe that is why you found this today.
A Moses convinced his failure disqualified him.
A Cain standing dangerously close to a decision that will destroy something precious.
A wounded believer wandering quietly.
A skeptic who thinks Christianity is merely about religious people pretending to be better than everyone else.
Or a sheep who simply cannot remember the way home.
Not as a performance.
Not to prove how spiritual you are.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but desperately needs to know the Shepherd still calls wandering people home.
Someone scrolling beneath this article may need evidence that grace still reaches real people in real ruins.
Because wandering rarely announces itself.
There may come a night when you need to read these words again and remember:
The Shepherd has not changed.
We want this community to be a place of daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered unapologetically on Jesus Christ.
It does not make anyone a better Christian.
And it certainly does not buy salvation.
But supporting Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership when it is done freely, gratefully, and for God's glory.
Because the point is not merely to build an audience.
It is to point people toward Jesus.
The algorithm cannot save anybody.
A ministry cannot save anybody.
A pastor cannot save anybody.
Jesus saves.
And that brings us back to the field.
Abel was a shepherd, and his blood cried from the ground.
Moses was shepherding when God called him from the wilderness to participate in Israel's deliverance.
David was called from the sheepfold to become king, only to discover that even a shepherd-king desperately needed the mercy and shepherding of God.
Then Jesus came.
Not merely another shepherd in the sequence.
Not merely another flawed man God would use.
Not merely another leader who would eventually need rescuing himself.
Jesus Christ is the sinless Son of God, the Good Shepherd who voluntarily laid down His life for His sheep and rose again.
And the New Testament gives Him another breathtaking shepherd title.
Hebrews 13:20 calls Jesus:
τὸν ποιμένα τῶν προβάτων τὸν μέγαν
ton poimena tōn probatōn ton megan.
“The great shepherd of the sheep.”
First Peter 5:4 calls Him:
ἀρχιποίμενος
archipoimēn.
The “Chief Shepherd.”
The pattern has reached the One who towers over every human shepherd.
And now the question is no longer merely whether you understand the pattern.
The question is:
Who is shepherding you?
Your appetite?
Your trauma?
Your ambition?
Your sexuality?
Your bitterness?
Your money?
Your need to be admired?
Your political tribe?
Your secret sin?
Your fear?
Your past?
Your own understanding?
Everyone follows something.
Jesus does not merely offer lost sheep directions.
He offers Himself.
He knows His sheep.
He calls them.
He leads them.
He lays down His life for them.
And He lives.
So if you have wandered, stop pretending the wilderness is home.
If you have sinned, stop decorating the chains.
If you have fallen, stop confusing your failure with God's final sentence.
If you are exhausted, stop believing you have to impress the Shepherd before He will hear your cry.
Turn to Christ.
Confess your sin.
Trust Him.
Follow Him.
Let His Word expose what needs exposing.
Let His grace heal what shame keeps reopening.
Let His truth confront what culture taught you to excuse.
Let His Spirit produce what willpower never could.
And when you look backward at the wreckage of your story, remember that Christianity never asks you to call darkness light.
David's sin was still sin.
Moses' past was still real.
Abel's blood still cried from the ground.
The cross itself proves that evil is more serious than we want to believe.
But the empty tomb announces something scandalously beautiful:
Sin does not get the last word for the one who belongs to Christ.
Shame does not get the last word.
Your worst chapter does not get the last word.
The grave does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
So share this with somebody who has forgotten the Shepherd's voice.
Leave the honest comment you almost decided not to leave.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is standing in a field they never planned to enter, carrying a past they cannot repair, wondering whether God could possibly still know their name.
He does.
And perhaps the most unforgettable truth running through all these fields is this:
The sheep may have forgotten the way home, but the Shepherd has never forgotten the sheep.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY THE NUMBER 1 ALWAYS POINTS BACK TO GOD ALONE
paragraphs: WHY THE NUMBER 1 ALWAYS POINTS BACK TO GOD ALONE
Before there was a second thing to compare Him with, God was. And when everything you have built your life around finally disappears, He will still be God.
There is something strangely uncomfortable about the number one.
Not because the number itself possesses mystical power. It does not.

The Bible never tells Christians to hunt for secret messages in license plates, clocks, receipts, dates, repeating digits, or “angel numbers.” Biblical faith is not numerology. We do not need 1:11 on a clock to know God is speaking when He has already given us His Word.
But Scripture does repeatedly confront us with a truth expressed through the language of one.
One God.
One Lord.
One faith.
One body.
One hope.
One Mediator.
One name through whom salvation comes.
And once you understand what Scripture is actually saying, “one” stops being merely something you count.
It becomes a confrontation with everything competing for the throne of your heart.
Because the biblical message is not that the numeral 1 has supernatural power.
The message is infinitely greater:
God has no rival.
Before your career existed, God was.
Before anyone knew your name, God was.
Before your first heartbreak, God was.
Before your greatest failure, God was.
Before the secret you are terrified somebody will discover, God was.
Before the universe had a sunrise, an ocean, a human heartbeat, or a single voice capable of whispering His name…
God was.
And this is where the story becomes personal.
Because most of us would never say, “I worship another god.”
We know better than that.
We know the vocabulary.
We know the songs.
We know when to say “Amen.”
We know how to share the verse.
We know how to look faithful in photographs.
But an idol does not need a temple anymore.
Sometimes it has your password.
Sometimes it appears in your bank balance.
Sometimes it is the relationship you cannot surrender.
Sometimes it is the opinion of people whose approval controls your emotions.
Sometimes it is success.
Sometimes it is ministry.
Sometimes it is your reputation.
Sometimes the idol staring back at you from the throne is…
you.
That is why one of the most important declarations in all Scripture begins with a command to listen.
שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ יְהוָה אֶחָד
Shema Yisrael, YHWH Eloheinu, YHWH echad.

“Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is one.”
—Deuteronomy 6:4
The Hebrew word אֶחָד — ’eḥad (echad) means “one.” In its context, this confession calls Israel away from the gods of the nations and toward exclusive covenant loyalty to YHWH.
Notice the first word.
Shema.
Hear.
Listen.
Pay attention.
This is not trivia for theologians.
This is truth demanding a human response.

Israel lived surrounded by nations filled with gods. Gods for fertility. Gods for storms. Gods for harvest. Gods for war. Gods carved from wood and stone and carried into temples by the very human beings who supposedly depended upon them.
Then into that world came this thunderous confession:
YHWH echad.
The LORD is one.
You do not need another god for another part of your life.
You do not need God for Sunday and something else for Monday.
You do not need God for eternity but money for identity.
You do not need Jesus for forgiveness but human applause for worth.
You do not need Christ for heaven while keeping control as lord of earth.
He is not one option sitting among your other loyalties.
He is God.
And Jesus did not abandon this confession.
When asked about the greatest commandment, Christ began by repeating Israel's confession that the Lord is one, and then called us to love God with the totality of our being.
Not with the religious portion.
Not with whatever remains after ambition has taken its share.
Not with the leftovers after entertainment, relationships, money, ego, lust, resentment, and anxiety have eaten first.
All.
Heart.
Soul.
Mind.
Strength.
That word “one” eventually becomes frightening because it forces a question few of us want to answer:
If God is truly God alone, why does He receive so little of me?
Read that again without rushing.
Why does the One who gave you breath sometimes receive only the moments when you cannot breathe?
Why does the One who gave you life sometimes hear from you only when your life is falling apart?
Why does the One who gave His Son receive whatever time remains after you have given hours to things you will not remember ten years from now?
Why are we capable of scrolling until 2:00 a.m. but suddenly exhausted after six minutes of prayer?
Why can someone's rejection ruin an entire week while Christ's acceptance barely changes our afternoon?
Why can a number in a bank account determine whether we feel secure when Jesus told us our Father knows what we need?
Perhaps our greatest idols are not the things we kneel before.
Perhaps they are the things we cannot imagine living without.
And now the knife reaches deeper.
Because you can remove an idol from your hands while secretly keeping it in your heart.
You can delete the number and still worship the memory.
You can leave the relationship and still live for their approval.
You can give away the money and still crave status.
You can preach Christ and secretly worship being recognized as someone who preaches Christ.
You can serve God while becoming addicted to people noticing that you serve God.
You can build a ministry supposedly for Jesus and slowly begin needing the ministry more than Jesus.
That is how subtle idolatry becomes.
It does not always say, “Reject God.”
Sometimes it whispers:
“God can stay. Just don't let Him be first.”
But biblical Christianity will not permit Jesus to become a decorative addition to a life still ruled by self.
Paul writes:
ἀλλ’ ἡμῖν εἷς θεὸς ὁ πατήρ
all’ hēmin heis theos ho patēr
“For us there is one God, the Father…”
and then:
καὶ εἷς κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστός
kai heis kyrios Iēsous Christos
“…and one Lord, Jesus Christ.”
—1 Corinthians 8:6
The Greek word εἷς — heis means “one.”

Paul writes those words in a discussion about idols. His point is not mystical arithmetic. He is drawing a dividing line between the many supposed “gods” and “lords” of the surrounding culture and the Christian confession of the one God and the one Lord, Jesus Christ. Paul says that all things are from the Father and that all things are through Jesus Christ.
That changes everything.
Jesus is not your motivational accessory.
Jesus is not merely someone who helps you become a more successful version of yourself.
Jesus did not endure the cross so that you could sprinkle Christianity over a life whose true center remains you.
He is Lord.
And suddenly the scandal of grace appears.
Because if God alone deserves the throne, every one of us has committed treason.
Every time I chose my sin over His command.
Every time I knew what Scripture said and deliberately walked the other direction.
Every time I wanted His blessings without His authority.
Every time I wanted forgiveness without repentance.
Every time I wanted heaven without holiness.
Every time I wanted Jesus as Savior while resisting Jesus as Lord.
I was not merely “making mistakes.”
I was taking what belonged to God and placing something else there.
Sometimes myself.
And perhaps you know exactly what that feels like.
Maybe nobody knows what happened last night.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe your parents do not know.
Maybe your church does not know.
Maybe the people who admire your faith would be stunned if they could see your private history.
Maybe you have learned how to lift your hands while hiding chains.
Maybe you have become exceptionally good at appearing spiritually alive while something inside you is starving.
And somewhere beneath all that Christian language is the fear you almost never admit:
If people really knew me, would they still love me?
There is an even more important question.
Does Jesus know?
Yes.
Every chapter.
Every deleted message.
Every compromise.
Every hidden appetite.
Every night you promised God it would be the last time.
Every prayer you prayed and then violated.
Every mask.
Every wound.
Every ugly thought you wish you could erase.
He knows.
And He went to the cross knowing.
That is the scandal.
The holy God you displaced from the center came looking for rebels.
The King we dishonored came wearing flesh.
The Lord we resisted walked toward a cross.
Jesus did not die because sin was insignificant.
He died because sin was so devastating that reconciliation required a price we could never pay.
At Calvary, grace does not pretend your rebellion was beautiful.
Grace exposes how terrible sin really is…
and then shows you how much greater Christ is.
This is where “one” becomes breathtaking again.
Scripture says:
“For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.”
—1 Timothy 2:5
One Mediator.
Not your goodness.
Not your religious résumé.
Not your pastor.
Not your church attendance.
Not your generosity.
Not your suffering.
Not your morality.
Not your family name.
Not your ability to promise that you will “do better next time.”
Jesus Christ.
The sinner does not climb his way toward God.
God came down.
The guilty do not negotiate their acquittal.
Christ bears the judgment.
The dead do not resuscitate themselves.
Christ gives life.
The lost do not become their own road home.
Jesus says He is the way.
That is why the Gospel is simultaneously offensive and magnificent.
It destroys our pride before it heals our shame.
It tells the moral person, “You cannot save yourself.”
It tells the broken person, “Your sin does not have to be the final chapter.”
It tells the proud, “Bow.”
It tells the ashamed, “Come.”
It tells the sinner, “Repent.”
It tells the forgiven, “Rise.”
It tells the wounded, “Your scars do not get to name you.”
And it tells every human heart:
There is one throne. Stop trying to sit on it.
Maybe that is the sentence you needed tonight.
Because you are tired.
Tired of controlling everything.
Tired of maintaining the image.
Tired of pretending the addiction is manageable.
Tired of telling everybody “I'm okay.”
Tired of trying to be your own savior.
Tired of carrying tomorrow before tomorrow arrives.
Tired of fighting battles in your imagination that God never commanded you to fight.
There is only one God.
And perhaps one of the greatest freedoms you will ever experience is finally admitting:
I am not Him.
You do not have to control the universe tonight.
You do not have to know how every chapter ends.
You do not have to force every person to understand you.
You do not have to make everyone stay.
You do not have to manufacture your own redemption.
You need Christ.
Jesus prayed to the Father:
“And this is life eternal, that they might know thee the only true God, and Jesus Christ, whom thou hast sent.”
—John 17:3, KJV
Notice what eternal life is described as.
Knowing God.
Not merely knowing about God.
You can know Bible stories and not surrender.
You can memorize verses and remain proud.
You can understand theology and still secretly cherish sin.
You can know church culture without knowing the Shepherd's voice.
Christianity is not fundamentally an information transfer.
It is reconciliation with God through Christ that transforms the human being.
And that transformation has consequences.
If God is one, your life cannot remain divided forever.
You cannot continually say, “Jesus owns this room, but He cannot enter that one.”
My worship belongs to You, Lord…
but not my relationship.
My Sunday belongs to You…
but not my sexuality.
My songs belong to You…
but not my money.
My public life belongs to You…
but not my private browser history.
My future belongs to You…
as long as You choose the future I already wanted.
Eventually Christ reaches the locked door.
And He does not expose it because He delights in humiliating you.
He exposes what is killing you because He loves you too much to call bondage freedom.
Repentance is not God saying, “Clean yourself up enough and perhaps I will love you.”
Repentance is the sinner turning from sin toward the God whose mercy is offered in Christ.
Grace is not permission to keep your idols.
Grace brings you home to the One your idols could never replace.
So what sits in the center of your life right now?
Do not answer quickly.
What are you most afraid to lose?
Whose opinion controls you?
What do you run toward when you are empty?
What do you protect even when obedience requires surrender?
What makes you say, “God can have everything except that”?
There it is.
Perhaps that is the door.
And Christ is standing on the other side of your excuses.
Not calling you toward destruction.
Calling you home.
This is why our theme at Gospel Warrior keeps returning to the same impossible beauty:
Because Scripture is filled with people whose stories should have ended differently.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted believers.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Again and again, human scandal collided with divine mercy.
Grace did not rewrite their past by pretending it never happened.
Grace rewrote what their past was allowed to become.
And Jesus still does that.
Your worst chapter does not intimidate the Author.
Your shame does not shock the Savior.
Your sin must be confessed, not romanticized. Your rebellion must be repented of, not renamed. But when a sinner comes to Christ in faith, the answer is not self-redemption.
The answer is Jesus.
Maybe you have spent years trying to turn yourself into somebody worthy of being loved by God.
Stop negotiating with grace.
Come empty-handed.
One God.
One Lord.
One Mediator.
One Savior.
And one sinner reading these words who may finally be tired enough to stop running.
Maybe that sinner is you.
Sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
And somebody reading your comment may realize they are not fighting alone.
Not because sharing a Facebook article earns favor with God. It does not. Christ alone saves.
Send this to the believer who is exhausted from pretending.
There is only one God—and you were never required to become Him.

If you genuinely want to glorify God, let that desire become more than a slogan. Glorifying God includes faithful stewardship, generosity, encouragement, sharing truth, serving others, and supporting sound Gospel work as the Lord enables you.
And there is something else worth knowing.
Bring your family.
Bring the friend asking difficult questions.
Bring the Christian who has gone cold.
Bring the person who does not believe yet.
Bring the person quietly wondering whether Jesus could possibly want them after everything they have done.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting God Himself.
God does not need our money to remain God.
God was God before Gospel Warrior existed.
God will remain God when every platform disappears.
We give because He first gave.
We serve because Christ served.
We share because someone shared the Gospel with us.
We support Gospel work because the Gospel is worth carrying.
And we worship because there is only One worthy of the throne.
So tonight, before you close this article, imagine your heart as a room.
One throne stands in the center.
Look carefully at who—or what—is sitting there.
Your career?
Your fear?
Your relationship?
Your reputation?
Your wounds?
Your money?
Your lust?
Your need to be admired?
Your need to control everything?
Your own reflection?
Now look beyond the throne.
There is a cross.
And on that cross is the One who did what none of your idols could ever do.
Money could not bleed for you.
Approval could not forgive you.
Pleasure could not reconcile you to God.
Success could not carry your guilt.
Control could not conquer death.
Your reputation could not rise from the grave.
Jesus did.
And the risen Christ does not merely offer to become another important part of your crowded life.
He calls you to Himself.
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.
Let the idols fall.
Let the masks fall.
Let the excuses fall.
There is one God.
There is one Lord.
And there is grace for the sinner who finally stops running.
Follow because your soul needs truth more often than your feed gives it.
remember the One Name we are trying to point toward.
Jesus Christ.
Because someday the applause will stop.
The numbers will disappear.
The possessions will change hands.
The body will return to dust.
The kingdoms we spent our lives building will belong to someone else.
And all the little gods we were terrified to surrender will finally reveal how powerless they always were.
But God will still be God.
Christ will still be Lord.
Grace will still have been grace.
And the question will never have been whether you managed to become important enough.
The question is whether you belonged to the One who is.
When everything you thought you needed finally becomes nothing, may you discover that the One you surrendered everything to was always enough.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Did God Give Israel Judges Instead of Kings? — Because Israel’s Greatest Danger Was Never the Throne. It Was the Heart.
paragraphs: Why Did God Give Israel Judges Instead of Kings? — Because Israel’s Greatest Danger Was Never the Throne. It Was the Heart.

Before Israel demanded a man they could see on a throne, God was teaching them to trust the King they could not see—and the scandal of what happened next points straight to humanity’s desperate need for Jesus Christ.
There is something unsettling about the book of Judges.
Not because God failed.
Because Israel kept forgetting.

Again and again, people who had witnessed the faithfulness of God drifted toward idols. They compromised. They rebelled. Their enemies oppressed them. They cried out. God raised a deliverer. They experienced relief.
Then they wandered again.
It is one of Scripture’s most painful cycles because, if we are willing to admit it, it does not feel ancient.
It feels familiar.

You can delete the names of the Canaanite gods, replace the swords with smartphones, replace the carved idols with money, approval, pleasure, relationships, influence, careers, politics, addictions, secret habits, and self-worship...
…and suddenly Judges becomes uncomfortable.
Because the question is no longer merely, “Why did God give Israel judges instead of kings?”
The deeper question becomes:
Why do human beings keep looking for someone or something to rule them when God Himself has already spoken?
And once that question gets inside you, the entire story changes.

Israel’s judges were not kings in the later dynastic sense. They were not supposed to establish royal bloodlines and sit permanently above God’s covenant people. The Hebrew word commonly translated “judge” is שֹׁפֵט — shofet, from the root שפט — shafat, carrying the sense of judging, governing, administering justice, or exercising leadership.
But when Scripture describes what God actually did through these figures, another word becomes incredibly important.
Judges 2:16 says:
וַיָּקֶם יְהוָה שֹׁפְטִים וַיּוֹשִׁיעוּם
Vayyaqem YHWH shofetim vayyoshi'um.
In context: “Then the LORD raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them.”
Notice who raised them.
The LORD.
Notice why they appeared.
Israel needed deliverance.
And notice the Hebrew verb connected with what the judges did:
וַיּוֹשִׁיעוּם — vayyoshi'um
It comes from ישע — yashaʿ, “to save” or “deliver.”
That matters.
The judges were never meant to become Israel’s replacement gods.
They were instruments in the hand of Israel’s true King.
God would raise them.
God would empower them.
God would deliver through them.
Then the human instrument would eventually disappear, forcing Israel to confront the question they repeatedly tried to escape:
Will you trust God when there is no impressive human figure standing in front of you?
That question is still alive.
Some of us trust God until the relationship disappears.
Until the pastor disappoints us.
Until the money gets tight.
Until the diagnosis comes.
Until the person we depended upon walks away.
Until prayer seems unanswered.
Until the thing we could see is removed and all that remains is the God we claim to believe.
Then our hearts start searching for another king.
Something tangible.
Something controllable.
Something we can point to and say:
“That will save me.”
Israel eventually did exactly that.
But before we reach their demand for a king, we have to understand something easily missed.
God was not fundamentally opposed to kingship.
That would contradict the broader biblical story.

Long before Saul, Deuteronomy 17 anticipated Israel eventually having a king. But that king was to remain under God’s law rather than becoming a law unto himself. He was not to multiply horses, wives, and wealth in the manner of surrounding rulers. He was to write for himself a copy of God’s instruction and read it continually.
Why?
Deuteronomy 17:20 gives the heart of the matter:
“that his heart may not be lifted up above his brothers.”
There it is.
The problem was never merely whether Israel had a throne.
The problem was what happened when a human heart sat on it.
God was preparing Israel for kingship under His authority.
Israel wanted something different.
By the time we reach 1 Samuel 8, Samuel is old. His sons do not walk faithfully in his ways. Israel’s elders come to him with a demand that initially sounds almost reasonable:
“Now appoint for us a king to judge us like all the nations.”
Do not rush past those last words.
Like all the nations.
That was the poison hidden inside the request.
They were God's covenant people, yet they wanted their security to look like everybody else's security.
They had the LORD.
They wanted what the nations had.
They had divine covenant.
They wanted visible political certainty.
They had the God who brought their ancestors out of Egypt.
They wanted a man on a throne.
And God told Samuel something heartbreaking:

“They have not rejected you, but they have rejected me from being king over them.”
—1 Samuel 8:7
The Hebrew makes the wound unmistakable:
כִּי אֹתִי מָאֲסוּ מִמְּלֹךְ עֲלֵיהֶם
Ki oti ma'asu mimlokh aleihem.
“For they have rejected Me from reigning over them.”
The verb מָאַס — ma'as means to reject, refuse, despise, or treat something as unwanted.
Think about that.
The God who rescued them was being treated as insufficient.
The God who fed their ancestors in the wilderness was insufficient.
The God who gave them His covenant was insufficient.
The God who repeatedly heard their cries was insufficient.
Why?
Because everybody else had something they could see.
And perhaps that is where this stops being Israel’s scandal and becomes ours.
How many times have we effectively told God:
“I know You are there... but I need this person.”
“I know Your Word says this... but everyone else is doing that.”
“I know Jesus should be enough... but I need their approval.”
“I know You promised never to leave me... but I cannot live without this relationship.”
“I know money cannot save me... but if I had enough of it, I would finally feel safe.”
“I know this habit is destroying me... but it comforts me.”
Different century.
Different idols.
Same heart.
The book of Judges repeatedly shows what happens when people abandon God's rule.
Its famous closing sentence is devastating:

“In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.”
—Judges 21:25
The Hebrew says:
אִישׁ הַיָּשָׁר בְּעֵינָיו יַעֲשֶׂה
Ish hayashar be'enav ya'aseh.
Literally, the idea is that each person did what was right in his own eyes.
Not necessarily what he openly called evil.
What looked right to him.
That may be one of the most frightening descriptions of sin in Scripture.
Because sin does not always introduce itself by saying:
“I am evil.”
Sometimes it whispers:
“This feels right.”
“You deserve this.”
“Everybody does it.”
“God understands.”
“You can repent later.”
“This is your life.”
“Follow your heart.”
And suddenly the human heart has climbed onto the throne.
That is why the period of the judges becomes increasingly dark.
The judges themselves are also increasingly complicated.
God truly used flawed people, but Scripture does not ask us to imitate every action of every judge. The Bible is often brutally honest about the failures of the people through whom God works.
Gideon begins trembling and ends with troubling compromises.
Jephthah's story becomes tragic.
Samson is empowered by God while repeatedly demonstrating how destructive uncontrolled appetite can become.
The point is not:
“Look how wonderful human heroes are.”
The point increasingly becomes:
We need a better Deliverer.
Someone who will not be corrupted by power.
Someone whose appetites will not enslave Him.
Someone who will not betray God's covenant.
Someone who can rescue us from an enemy deeper than Midianites, Philistines, armies, governments, poverty, sickness, or circumstances.
Someone who can save us from sin.
And this is where the road through Judges, Samuel, and the kings eventually leads us toward Jesus Christ.
Israel would receive Saul.
Saul would fail.
David would come.
David would be a man after God's heart, yet David would also sin terribly.
Solomon would possess extraordinary wisdom, yet his heart would turn after other gods.
The kingdom would divide.
Kings would rise.
Kings would fall.
Some would seek God.
Many would rebel.
Eventually Israel and Judah would experience devastating judgment and exile.
Human kingship could not cure the human heart.
Even the best earthly king could not permanently save sinful people.
David himself needed mercy.
The king needed a Savior too.
But God had made David a promise.
His throne would ultimately point beyond him.
The prophets began speaking of a coming righteous King.
Isaiah spoke of a child upon whose shoulder the government would rest.
Micah pointed toward a ruler coming from Bethlehem.
Jeremiah spoke of a righteous Branch from David's line.
Zechariah pictured Zion's King coming humble and riding on a donkey.
Then...
Jesus came.
Not with Saul's armor.
Not with Solomon's wealth.
Not surrounded by the military spectacle Israel might have expected.
He came as a child.
He walked among ordinary people.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed sinners who repented.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He proclaimed God's kingdom.
He forgave sins.
He healed the broken.
He called people away from darkness.
And when the King finally received a crown...
humanity gave Him thorns.
Do not miss the scandal.
Israel once demanded a king they could see.
Centuries later, when the true King stood visibly before humanity, He was rejected.
John's Gospel captures the horrifying irony surrounding the crucifixion.
Pilate asked:
“Shall I crucify your King?”
And the chief priests answered:
“We have no king but Caesar.”
The human disease exposed in Israel had reached its terrible climax.
Reject God's reign.
Choose another ruler.
Except this time...
the rejected King did something no judge could do.
No Saul could do.
No David could do.
No Solomon could do.
Jesus carried our sin to the cross.
The King became the sacrifice.
The Judge took the judgment borne for His people.
The righteous One died for the unrighteous.
The sinless Christ shed His blood for sinners.
And the cross looked like the greatest scandal in history.
The Messiah mocked.
The King stripped.
The Holy One condemned.
The Author of life dying.
But God was writing grace into the scandal.
Because the tomb did not keep Him.
Jesus Christ rose.
And suddenly the entire biblical hunger for righteous rule finds its answer not merely in a political system but in a Person.
The New Testament gives Jesus a title loaded with royal meaning:
Χριστός — Christos
“Christ,” the Anointed One—the Greek equivalent corresponding to the Hebrew concept of מָשִׁיחַ — Mashiach, Messiah.
And Revelation calls Him:
βασιλεὺς βασιλέων καὶ κύριος κυρίων
Basileus basileōn kai kyrios kyriōn.
“King of kings and Lord of lords.”
There is the King Israel could never manufacture.
There is the King Saul could never become.
There is the King David could only foreshadow.
There is the King Solomon's glory could never equal.
Jesus.
And perhaps now you understand why the question “Why did God give Israel judges instead of kings?” cannot remain an academic Bible question.
God's dealings with Israel reveal a pattern that exposes us.
We keep wanting deliverance without surrender.
We want Jesus to rescue us while something else rules us.
We want Him as Savior but become uncomfortable when He speaks as Lord.
We want forgiveness without repentance.
Peace without obedience.
Heaven without holiness.
Grace without transformation.
A cross that comforts us without a cross that calls us to die to ourselves.
But Jesus did not die merely to become one more influence competing for space inside your life.
He is King.
And maybe the throne He is confronting tonight is not in Jerusalem.
Maybe it is inside you.
Who sits there?
Your ambition?
Your wounds?
Your sexual desires?
Your bitterness?
Your political identity?
Your money?
Your reputation?
Your relationship?
Your fear?
Your addiction?
Your need to be admired?
Your determination to control everything because trusting God feels terrifying?
You can sing about Jesus while another king quietly governs your decisions.
Israel did religious things while wandering from God too.
That is what makes this dangerous.
You can know Christian vocabulary and still resist Christ's rule.
You can share Bible verses while hiding a secret life.
You can attend church while nursing hatred.
You can call Him Lord publicly while privately telling Him there are rooms in your heart He cannot enter.
And maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you have become extraordinarily good at looking okay.
But Jesus knows.
And astonishingly...
He still calls you.
Not because sin does not matter.
It matters so much that Christ went to the cross.
Not because repentance is optional.
Jesus Himself called sinners to repent.
But because grace means your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
This is the Gospel.
Not God pretending the scandal never happened.
God redeeming sinners through Jesus Christ.
Peter denied Jesus and was restored.
Paul persecuted the church and became a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left to repair his reputation, yet he turned toward Jesus and heard words of paradise.
Grace does not tell sin, “You were never serious.”
Grace tells the repentant sinner:
Christ is greater.
That is why our heartbeat is:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting history as though your sin never mattered.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by congratulating rebellion.

Jesus rewrites everything by doing what you could never do for yourself—bearing sin, offering forgiveness, reconciling sinners to God, giving new life, and transforming those who come to Him in faith.
Maybe your scandal is known by thousands.
Maybe it is known by five people.
Maybe nobody knows except you and God.
Maybe your greatest battle is not something you did but the person you became while trying to survive what was done to you.
Maybe you have spent years running.
Maybe you are exhausted from pretending.
Maybe you keep promising God, “This is the last time,” only to discover yourself kneeling in the wreckage again.
Hear this carefully:
Do not make another promise to become your own savior.
You need a King.
Turn to Jesus.
Confess your sin.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Stop negotiating with the thing Christ is calling you to surrender.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the broken marriage.
Bring Him the failure.
Bring Him the doubt.
Bring Him the part of your story you wish could be erased.
The Gospel does not promise that every earthly consequence disappears.
It promises something infinitely deeper:
In Christ, sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, made new, and brought under the reign of the King who died and rose for them.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not turn the moment into empty emotion.
Respond to Christ.

And if Christ has already taken part of your own story from scandal to grace, tell us what He has done. Someone reading your testimony may be sitting tonight in the same darkness God brought you through.
Do not underestimate what happens when redeemed people stop hiding God's faithfulness.
And if this article made you think of one specific person, do not merely think about them.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to preach at them.
Because someday the person tempted to choose another king may be you.
Someday fear may get loud again.
Someday the visible thing may look more trustworthy than the invisible God.
And you may need to remember:
The throne was never empty.
But the deeper reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is staying close to Scripture.
It is being reminded of truth when the world becomes deafening.
It is helping carry the Gospel into another exhausted person's midnight.
But before you leave this page, remember why Israel's story matters.
God gave Israel judges who could deliver them temporarily from oppressors.
Israel eventually demanded a human king.
God gave them kings.
And history demonstrated something painfully clear:
No merely human ruler could cure the rebellion inside the human heart.
So God did something infinitely greater than giving humanity another Samson.
Another Gideon.
Another Saul.
Another David.
Another Solomon.
He gave us His Son.
And when humanity rejected its rightful King, God turned the darkest scandal into the doorway of redemption through the cross and resurrection.
So the question is no longer simply:
“Why did God give Israel judges instead of kings?”
The question following you out of this article is much more personal:
Who is king of you?
Because sooner or later, every false king asks for more than it promised.
Money asks for your peace.
Lust asks for your purity.
Pride asks for your relationships.
Bitterness asks for your joy.
Approval asks for your identity.
Fear asks for your obedience.
Sin eventually asks for everything.
But Jesus gave everything to rescue sinners.
The Judge became our Deliverer.
The promised Messiah became the crucified and risen King.
And the sinner who comes to Him does not discover a throne occupied by another broken human being.
He discovers Jesus Christ.
So surrender.
Come home.
Repent.
Believe.
And let the King have the throne.
Because perhaps the greatest scandal was never that Israel asked for another king—it is that our hearts still do, while the scarred and risen King is standing at the door.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU WERE NEVER PROMISED YOU WOULD SEE THE WAY: The Deeper Meaning of “Walk by Faith, Not by Sight”
paragraphs:
YOU WERE NEVER PROMISED YOU WOULD SEE THE WAY: The Deeper Meaning of “Walk by Faith, Not by Sight”
What if the verse you quote when life makes no sense was never meant to promise that everything would eventually make sense—but to teach you how to keep following Jesus when it doesn’t?
There comes a moment in almost every believer’s life when the words become harder to say.
“For we walk by faith, not by sight.”
They looked beautiful when you first underlined them.
They sounded powerful when somebody preached them.
They fit perfectly beneath the photograph, inside the devotional, across the T-shirt, on the wall.
Then life happened.
The prayer remained unanswered.
The person you loved still walked away.
The diagnosis came.
The opportunity disappeared.
The money became tighter.
The marriage became colder.
The child you prayed for wandered farther.
The ministry you believed God gave you became painfully quiet.
You obeyed…and somehow obedience seemed to cost you more than compromise ever did.
And suddenly “walk by faith, not by sight” stopped sounding like inspirational Christian language.
It became survival.
Because there are seasons when everything your eyes can see seems to argue against everything your heart has believed about God.
And that is precisely where we need to hear what Paul actually wrote.
Not the slogan.
Not the motivational version.
The Scripture.
In 2 Corinthians 5:7, the Greek reads:
“διὰ πίστεως γὰρ περιπατοῦμεν, οὐ διὰ εἴδους”
dia pisteōs gar peripatoumen, ou dia eidous.
“For we walk by faith, not by sight.”
Every word matters.
Pisteōs comes from pistis—faith, trust, belief, confidence.
Peripatoumen means “we walk,” but in biblical usage walking can describe the course or conduct of one’s life.
And then comes the word that makes Paul’s statement especially striking:
eidous.
It can refer to visible form, appearance, or what is seen.
Paul is describing two radically different ways of navigating existence.
One life is governed by what can presently be seen.
The other is governed by trust in the God who cannot presently be seen.
But here is where this verse becomes deeper—and perhaps more uncomfortable—than the way we often use it.
Paul was not sitting comfortably somewhere telling struggling Christians, “Just believe and your dreams will happen.”
Read the surrounding passage.
He is talking about mortality.
Groaning.
The weakness of our earthly bodies.
Being away from the Lord while we remain in the body.
Longing to be with Christ.
Living in such a way that we please Him.
And ultimately standing before the judgment seat of Christ.
That is the atmosphere surrounding:
“For we walk by faith, not by sight.”
This is not positive thinking wearing a Christian shirt.
This is resurrection confidence staring mortality in the face.
Paul’s point is not, “Ignore reality.”
His point is that visible reality is not the whole reality.
That difference can change your life.
Faith does not tell you that the hospital report does not exist.
Faith tells you the hospital report does not have authority to redefine who God is.
Faith does not pretend the grave is imaginary.
Faith declares that because Jesus Christ rose from the dead, the grave does not get the final word.
Faith does not require you to call pain pleasure, darkness light, or disappointment victory.
Biblical faith can cry.
Biblical faith can groan.
Biblical faith can admit, “I do not understand.”
And still whisper…
“But I know whom I have believed.”
Somebody reading this needs that distinction desperately.
You thought strong faith meant never feeling afraid.
So when fear came, you assumed something was wrong with you.
You thought faith meant never asking questions.
So when questions came, you hid them behind church language.
You thought walking by faith meant possessing absolute certainty about what God was going to do next.
But perhaps you have been trying to possess something God never promised you.
God did not promise to give you tomorrow’s map.
He gave you Himself.
Think about Abraham.
God called him to leave his country and go toward a land God would show him.
Think about Israel approaching the Red Sea.
Think about David hiding from Saul despite having already been anointed.
Think about the disciples watching the One they believed was Messiah being nailed to a Roman cross.
At Calvary, sight screamed:
“It is finished.”
Faith would eventually discover that Jesus meant something entirely different when He said those words.
Sight saw nails.
God was accomplishing redemption.
Sight saw humiliation.
Heaven saw the Lamb of God bearing sin.
Sight saw blood.
God saw atonement.
Sight saw a sealed tomb.
God saw Sunday coming.
That is why Christianity ultimately cannot be reduced to “believe hard enough and things will work out the way you want.”
Christian faith has something infinitely stronger than that.
It has a crucified and risen Christ.
Our confidence is not that every chapter will end the way we wrote it.
Our confidence is that the Author is faithful.
And perhaps this is where the verse reaches into the place you have been trying to keep hidden.
Because maybe what you see right now really does look terrible.
Maybe you have prayed until you are tired of hearing your own prayer.
Maybe everybody thinks you are strong because you know exactly what to say at church.
“God is good.”
“I’m trusting Him.”
“It’s all in His hands.”
And those things are true.
But nobody sees you afterward.
Nobody sees the drive home.
Nobody sees you staring at the ceiling.
Nobody sees the tears you wipe away before walking into another room.
Nobody knows how many times you have asked God quietly:
“Lord…where are You?”
Walking by faith does not mean that question disqualifies you.
It means you keep walking toward Christ even while carrying the question.
That is faith.
Sometimes faith looks triumphant.
Sometimes faith looks like worship with both hands raised.
Sometimes faith looks like courage in front of thousands.
But sometimes faith looks like getting out of bed.
Sometimes it looks like refusing to return to the sin Jesus delivered you from.
Sometimes it looks like forgiving somebody when your emotions are still catching up with your obedience.
Sometimes it looks like opening Scripture when heaven feels silent.
Sometimes it looks like praying one more prayer after yesterday’s prayer seemed unanswered.
Sometimes it looks like saying:
“Jesus, I cannot see what You are doing…but I will not leave You.”
That may be one of the purest expressions of faith a human heart can offer.
Because biblical faith is not ultimately faith in an outcome.
It is faith in God.
There is an enormous difference.
If your faith is anchored primarily in a particular outcome, then when that outcome collapses, your faith may collapse with it.
“I believed God would give me that relationship.”
“I believed God would give me that job.”
“I believed God would heal this exactly the way I expected.”
“I believed God would open that door.”
Perhaps He will.
We should pray boldly.
We should ask.
We should hope.
We should believe that God is able to do immeasurably beyond what we can accomplish ourselves.
But God Himself—not the answer we prefer—must remain the foundation.
Otherwise we can accidentally turn faith into an attempt to control God with religious expectations.
Jesus showed us something better in Gethsemane.
He prayed concerning the cup before Him, yet surrendered Himself perfectly to the Father’s will.
Faith asks boldly…and still bows deeply.
“Your will be done.”
Those words are not weak faith.
They may require stronger faith than demanding the outcome we want.
Because surrender says:
“Father, I trust Your wisdom when it contradicts mine.”
And now we begin to understand why walking by faith can hurt.
Faith requires surrendering the illusion that seeing everything would make us secure.
We want explanations.
God repeatedly calls us to trust.
We want certainty about circumstances.
God gives certainty about His character.
We want to know where the road goes.
Jesus says, in effect:
Follow Me.
There is something almost frighteningly intimate about that.
Because if God showed you the entire road, you might trust the map.
When He gives you enough light for the next obedient step, you must trust Him.
And that changes the question.
Instead of asking only:
“God, what are You going to do?”
Faith begins asking:
“Jesus, how can I please You here?”
That question takes us directly back into Paul’s context.
Immediately after speaking about walking by faith rather than sight, Paul says that whether at home or away, “we make it our aim to please him.”
That means walking by faith is not passive.
It is not sitting still while calling inactivity “trust.”
Faith moves.
Faith obeys.
Faith repents.
Faith forgives.
Faith gives.
Faith loves.
Faith endures.
Faith tells the truth.
Faith follows Jesus when obedience is expensive.
And faith remembers that our lives are headed somewhere.
Paul continues by reminding believers that we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.
Suddenly the verse becomes far more serious than inspirational wall décor.
You are walking toward an encounter with Jesus.
So am I.
Every heartbeat moves us closer.
And when you understand that, the things sight tells you are enormously important begin shrinking.
Approval.
Applause.
Status.
Possessions.
Followers.
Recognition.
Being admired.
Winning every argument.
Having everybody understand you.
Having everybody like you.
Sight says:
“Protect your image.”
Faith says:
“Please Christ.”
Sight says:
“Everybody else is doing it.”
Faith says:
“What does Jesus say?”
Sight says:
“You deserve revenge.”
Faith remembers the mercy of the cross.
Sight says:
“Hide your sin.”
Faith runs toward confession and grace.
Sight says:
“You have ruined everything.”
The Gospel says:
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
And that is where “walk by faith, not by sight” becomes inseparable from grace.
Because perhaps the ugliest thing you can see right now is not your circumstances.
Perhaps it is your past.
Maybe when you look backward you see decisions you wish you could erase.
People you hurt.
Years you wasted.
Promises you broke.
Purity you surrendered.
A marriage you damaged.
Children you failed.
An addiction nobody knows about.
A secret browser history.
A private compromise.
A version of yourself you cannot believe you became.
Sight looks at the evidence and says:
“This is who you are.”
Then Jesus enters the scandal.
The Gospel does not tell us our sin was insignificant.
The cross proves exactly the opposite.
Our sin is so serious that reconciliation with a holy God required something we could never provide for ourselves.
Christ provided it.
The sinless Son of God died for sinners and rose again.
And later in the very same chapter containing “walk by faith, not by sight,” Paul announces the staggering result:
“If any man be in Christ, he is a new creature.”
Then Paul speaks of God reconciling us to Himself through Christ.
Do you see the movement?
Mortality.
Faith.
Judgment.
Christ.
Reconciliation.
New creation.
Grace.
This is not a motivational speech.
It is the Gospel.
You do not need stronger positive thoughts.
You need Jesus.
You do not need to manifest a better future.
You need reconciliation with God.
You do not need to pretend your sin never happened.
You need the Savior whose blood can forgive it.
You do not need to edit your scandal until respectable Christians approve of you.
Bring the scandal to Jesus.
Repent.
Stop hiding.
Confess the sin.
Turn from it.
Come into the light.
Trust Christ.
Grace does not mean God looks at rebellion and shrugs.
Grace means the holy God has made a way for guilty sinners to be reconciled to Him through Jesus Christ.
And when Christ takes hold of a life, grace does not leave that person comfortably chained to what Jesus came to destroy.
He changes us.
Sometimes slowly.
Sometimes painfully.
Often through battles nobody else sees.
But genuinely.
This is why your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Peter denied Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine the sight of that failure.
Imagine hearing your own voice swear that you did not know the Man you had promised never to abandon.
Then the rooster.
Then the eyes of Jesus.
Then bitter weeping.
If Peter had allowed his visible failure to write the ending, his story would have ended in shame.
But Jesus was not finished.
There was resurrection.
There was restoration.
There was a charcoal fire.
There was a question:
“Do you love me?”
There was a commission:
“Feed my sheep.”
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending Peter never failed.
By redeeming a broken man and transforming what came afterward.
Maybe that is why you found this article today.
Not because God is promising that by tomorrow everything around you will look different.
Perhaps the deeper invitation is that Christ wants to change the one doing the looking.
Maybe you have spent months begging God for a different landscape while He has been forming a different walker.
More surrendered.
Less dependent on applause.
More prayerful.
Less impressed by appearances.
More compassionate toward broken people.
Less confident in yourself.
More anchored in Christ.
What if the waiting has not been empty?
What if the darkness has exposed where your confidence actually lived?
What if the closed door protected you from something you could not see?
What if the season that made you feel forgotten became the season in which Jesus became more precious than the blessing you originally asked Him to provide?
We must be careful here.
We cannot claim to know the hidden reason behind every tragedy.
Scripture does not authorize us to manufacture explanations God has not revealed.
Sometimes we simply do not know why something happened.
Faith does not invent answers.
Faith trusts God without possessing all of them.
That is part of its beauty.
And part of its agony.
You may never receive an explanation for every tear on this side of eternity.
But Christians have been given something greater than an explanation.
We have been given a Person.
Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Reigning.
Coming again.
And because He lives, the Christian can stand in a cemetery and grieve without grieving as one who has no hope.
We can lose something precious without losing Christ.
We can be misunderstood without being abandoned by God.
We can walk through darkness without concluding there is no Light.
We can confess our sin without believing condemnation is our only future.
We can die knowing death itself has been defeated.
That is walking by faith.
Not blindness.
Not denial.
Not fantasy.
Trust.
Trust built upon the character of God and the finished work of Jesus Christ.
So perhaps tonight your prayer does not need to be complicated.
“Jesus, I cannot see very far.”
That is okay.
“Jesus, I am afraid.”
Tell Him.
“Jesus, I don't understand why You allowed this.”
Tell Him that too.
“Jesus, part of me wants to run.”
Be honest.
“But Lord…where else would I go?”
There it is.
Faith.
Not the polished kind.
The bleeding kind.
The kind that crawls toward Jesus when it cannot confidently walk.
The kind that says through tears:
“I still choose You.”
And if someone came into your mind while reading this, do not merely think about them.
Send this to them.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God—it absolutely does not. We are saved by grace, not by social-media activity, financial support, purchases, or religious performance.
Supporting Gospel work can be one practical expression of stewardship when it is done freely, prayerfully, and cheerfully for Christ’s glory—not from guilt or as a way of purchasing God’s blessing.
But the deeper reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is keeping biblical truth in front of us in a world constantly discipling our eyes to believe that what we see is all there is.
Invite your family. Invite the friend who is questioning everything. Invite the believer who has grown cold. Invite the person who has never followed Jesus.
But please remember this clearly:
Sharing cannot save you.
A Christian library cannot save you.
Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
Jesus Christ saves.
Am I actually following Him?
Not merely quoting Him.
Not merely posting about Him.
Not merely attending church around Him.
Following Him.
Because one day faith will become sight.
One day the Christian will no longer speak of an unseen Christ.
One day every temporary thing that looked enormous will be exposed as temporary.
One day every hidden act of faithfulness will be known by the One whose approval mattered all along.
Until then…
Walk.
When you understand, walk.
When you do not understand, walk.
When the answer comes, walk.
When heaven seems silent, walk.
When you feel strong, walk.
When you can barely whisper His name, keep moving toward Jesus.
Repent when you fall.
Receive His grace.
Get back up.
Forgive.
Obey.
Pray.
Love.
Tell somebody about Christ.
And keep walking.
Not because your eyes have finally seen enough to guarantee the road ahead.
But because the One leading you has already walked through death itself…and walked out of the grave alive.
Your eyes may not be able to see what Jesus is doing with this chapter yet.
But the empty tomb is proof that God can be working most powerfully in the very place where sight tells you the story is over.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE VERSE ABOUT “TREASURES IN HEAVEN” WE KEEP READING—BUT MAY HAVE NEVER REALLY HEARD
paragraphs:
THE VERSE ABOUT “TREASURES IN HEAVEN” WE KEEP READING—BUT MAY HAVE NEVER REALLY HEARD
