What if you are giving another woman the version of yourself your wife has been begging to see again?
That one lands differently.
Because maybe the problem is not simply that another woman became interesting.
Maybe you stopped being intentional at home.
And now you are spending outside the marriage what belongs inside it.
Your attention.
Your imagination.
Your tenderness.
Your curiosity.
Your romantic energy.
Your words.
Your emotional vulnerability.
Your pursuit.
Your wife may be receiving whatever is left after another woman has already received the excitement.
That is why Hebrews treats marriage with tremendous seriousness:
“Marriage should be honored by all, and the marriage bed kept pure.”
Marriage is not merely paperwork.
It is covenant.
And covenant faithfulness matters to God.
But now we need to speak to the man who has already crossed lines.
Maybe this isn't theoretical anymore.
Maybe you already flirted.
Maybe the messages became explicit.
Maybe you've been emotionally involved for months.
Maybe you've kissed her.
Maybe you've slept with her.
Maybe your wife doesn't know.
Maybe she does.
Maybe your marriage is hanging by a thread because of what you did.
And perhaps right now shame is whispering:
You hypocrite.
You ruined everything.
God is finished with you.
There is no coming back from this.
Listen carefully.
The Bible never makes adultery small.
But the Gospel never makes Christ's mercy small either.
Those two truths must remain together.
Grace is not God pretending your sin didn't matter.
Grace is God providing in Christ what sinners could never provide for themselves.
At the cross, Jesus did not die because humanity's sin was insignificant.
He died because sin was deadly.
The cross simultaneously destroys our excuses and destroys our despair.
You cannot stand beneath the cross saying, “My sin isn't serious.”
Look at what redemption cost.
But neither can the repentant sinner stand beneath the cross saying, “My sin is too great for Jesus.”
Look at who is hanging there.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that says, “Keep the other woman and keep Jesus too.”
Not grace that baptizes secrecy.
Not grace that protects your image while your wife bleeds.
Biblical grace teaches us to leave darkness.
Repentance is not feeling terrible because you were caught.
Repentance is a turning.

It means bringing sin into the light before God, ending what must be ended, refusing to continue feeding the relationship, accepting accountability, pursuing truth, and seeking wise biblical and professional help where necessary.
It may mean blocking a number.
Ending private meetings.
Changing routines.
Removing access.
Giving up secrecy.
Confessing without blaming your wife for your choices.
Getting pastoral accountability.
Seeking qualified marriage counseling.
Allowing trust to be rebuilt on your wife's timetable rather than demanding immediate forgiveness because you apologized.
There may be consequences.
Grace does not always erase consequences.
But consequences are not proof that Christ has abandoned the repentant sinner.
Sometimes restoration begins with the terrifying sound of truth finally being spoken.
And if you have not crossed the physical line yet, don't congratulate yourself while continuing to walk toward the cliff.
Jesus' language in Matthew 5:29–30 is deliberately severe: if something causes you to stumble into sin, deal with it radically.
The point is not casual self-mutilation.
The point is ruthless repentance.
Stop negotiating with what is killing your faithfulness.
Don't ask how close you can stand to adultery without technically becoming an adulterer.
Ask how fiercely you can protect what God has entrusted to you.
Maybe that means tonight you stop messaging her.
Maybe you unfollow the account.
Maybe you tell another mature Christian man the truth.
Maybe you hand over the secret you have been protecting.
Maybe you stop telling yourself, “We're only friends,” when you know perfectly well you would be devastated if your wife had the same relationship with another man.
And perhaps the deepest repentance is not simply saying goodbye to another woman.
Perhaps it is learning to turn your face toward your wife again.
Look at her.
Not as furniture in your familiar life.
Not merely as the mother of your children.
Not as the woman who knows your flaws.
Look at the person who stood before God and entrusted part of her future to you.
Remember her laughter.
Remember the nervous excitement.
Remember the first conversations.
Remember what made you choose her.
Then understand something even deeper:
Biblical marriage cannot survive forever on nostalgia.
You must choose faithfulness today.
Love eventually becomes more than something you feel.
It becomes something you practice when feelings fluctuate.
That doesn't make love less beautiful.
It can make love deeper.
The world says the great romance is finding someone who continually gives you butterflies.
Covenant teaches a harder beauty:
Sometimes the great romance is choosing the same person after the butterflies have gone quiet... and discovering that roots can grow deeper than wings ever flew.
And if your marriage is deeply damaged, faithfulness does not mean pretending everything is fine.
Get help.
Have difficult conversations.
Seek wise pastoral counsel.
Seek competent marriage counseling.
Address abuse, betrayal, addiction, contempt, sexual dysfunction, emotional abandonment, or whatever is actually happening rather than covering it with Christian clichés.
And where there is abuse or danger, faithfulness does not require silently remaining unsafe; seek appropriate professional, pastoral, and legal support.
But do not use a broken marriage as permission to build a secret romance.
Bring the brokenness into the light.
Bring your loneliness into the light.
Bring your sexual frustration into the light.
Bring your disappointment into the light.
Bring the other woman's name into the light.
Bring your fantasies into the light.
Bring your phone into the light.
Bring yourself into the light.
Because Jesus Christ does some of His most astonishing rewriting with stories people thought were already ruined.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples fled.
Paul carried a violent past.
The early church was filled not with people who had never needed mercy, but with sinners transformed by Christ.
That doesn't excuse what you have done.
It means what you have done does not have to become the final author of who you are.
Sin may have written a terrible chapter.
Jesus Christ still holds the pen of redemption.
This is From Scandal to Grace.
Not scandal denied.
Scandal confessed.
Not consequences avoided.
Grace encountered.
Not lust renamed “connection.”
Lust surrendered.
Not another secret relationship hidden behind a Christian profile.
A heart finally exposed before Jesus.
Maybe you came into this article defending yourself.
Maybe somewhere halfway through, you stopped.
Maybe one woman's name has been sitting in your mind throughout every paragraph.
You know exactly who she is.
And maybe you know exactly what Christ is asking you to surrender.
Conviction is a mercy when it drives us toward Christ.
Go to Jesus.
Not after you have cleaned yourself enough to become presentable.
Now.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Ask Him for the courage to make what is crooked straight.
Ask Him to teach you how to become faithful in private, not merely respectable in public.
And then take concrete action.
Because there may be a wife somewhere in your house who does not need to compete with every woman who makes you feel admired.
She needs a husband whose heart is learning to come home.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to publish the details of another person's life. But you can stop pretending.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that repentance is possible and Jesus still restores broken people.
Not because saving a post changes a heart, but because there may be a night when temptation starts rewriting the story again and you need to remember what you decided in the light.

Supporting Gospel work financially does not purchase God's blessing, prove your salvation, or make you more spiritual. We glorify God through Christ-centered obedience, generosity, truth, worship, love, and faithful stewardship.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends who are willing to listen.
Go home in your heart.
Close the door that should never have been opened.
Turn toward your covenant.
And above everything else, turn toward Christ.
Because your greatest hope is not becoming a man strong enough never to be tempted.

Your greatest hope is Jesus Christ—the Savior strong enough to forgive the repentant, expose darkness, break chains, transform desires, teach faithfulness, heal what sin has wounded, and make sinners new.
Maybe the story became scandalous.
Maybe you helped write the scandal.
But if you will bring the truth into the light and surrender yourself to Christ, the scandal does not have to write the final sentence.
The woman you need to stop pursuing may not be the end of your story; surrendering her may be the moment Jesus begins teaching your heart how to come home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU CALL HIM “LORD”—BUT WHAT IF JESUS ACTUALLY TOOK YOU AT YOUR WORD?
paragraphs:
YOU CALL HIM “LORD”—BUT WHAT IF JESUS ACTUALLY TOOK YOU AT YOUR WORD?
“Jesus Is Lord” may be the most familiar Christian confession on earth—and one of the most dangerous sentences to say without understanding what you have just confessed.
There is a sentence Christians sing.
We print it on shirts.
We put it in captions.
We whisper it when life falls apart.
We shout it when prayers are answered.
We write it beneath photographs of sunsets, Bibles, baptisms, hospital recoveries, weddings, funerals, and testimonies.
“Jesus is Lord.”
Three words.
Simple enough for a child to remember.
Powerful enough to rearrange an entire human life.
But somewhere between our lips and our living, something can go terribly wrong.
Because it is possible to call Jesus “Lord” while quietly reserving certain rooms of your life where He is not allowed to enter.
Your money.
Your sexuality.
Your bitterness.
Your ambition.
Your secret browser history.
Your relationship.
Your unforgiveness.
Your pride.
Your plans.
Your reputation.
Your private habits.
Your Sunday Christianity and your Monday decisions.
And suddenly the question becomes painfully personal:
What do you actually mean when you say, “Jesus is Lord”?
Because the earliest Christian confession was not merely, “Jesus helps me.”
It was not, “Jesus inspires me.”
It was not even merely, “Jesus saved me.”
Paul writes in Romans 10:9:
Transliterated:
hoti ean homologēsēs en tō stomati sou kyrion Iēsoun…
“If you confess with your mouth Jesus as Lord…”
The crucial words are κύριον Ἰησοῦν — kyrion Iēsoun — Jesus as Lord.

Paul joins that confession immediately to believing in your heart that God raised Jesus from the dead, promising salvation to the one who believes and confesses. Romans 10 does not present salvation as a reward for religious performance. It presents Christ as the One in whom righteousness is received by faith, and the confession of Jesus as Lord flows from that faith.
That distinction matters.
Because Christianity is not:
“Make Jesus Lord enough, obey well enough, clean yourself up enough, give enough, serve enough, and perhaps God will finally save you.”
No.
The Gospel is far more shocking.
You were the sinner.
Christ came for sinners.
You had the debt.
Christ paid it.
You deserved judgment.
Christ bore judgment for His people.
You could not resurrect yourself spiritually any more than a corpse can perform CPR on itself.
Salvation is grace.
And grace does something astonishing.
It does not merely forgive rebels.
It brings rebels home.
It does not merely cancel the record of sin.
It gives the sinner a new King.
That is where “Jesus is Lord” becomes uncomfortable.
Because everyone wants a Savior when the boat is sinking.
Far fewer people want a Lord when He begins telling them where the boat must go.
We love Jesus when He says, “Come to Me.”
But what happens when He says, “Follow Me”?
We love forgiveness.
But what happens when forgiveness leads into repentance?
We love grace.
But what happens when grace begins dismantling the life we built without God?
We love the cross when Jesus is hanging on it.
But Jesus also told His followers to take up theirs.
That is the part modern Christianity can sometimes soften until discipleship becomes almost unrecognizable.
Jesus Himself asked a terrifyingly simple question:
“Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?”
Luke 6:46.
There it is.
No complicated theological vocabulary.
No escape hatch.
Just Jesus confronting the distance between confession and obedience.
Why call Me Lord…
if My words never get the final word?
That question follows us into rooms nobody else sees.
Imagine the phone glowing against your face at 1:17 in the morning.
Nobody knows what you are looking at.
Nobody knows what conversation you deleted.
Nobody knows what fantasy you keep feeding.
Nobody knows what resentment you rehearse when you are alone.
Nobody knows how jealous you have become.
Nobody knows that you smile at church and quietly hate someone three rows away.
Nobody knows how exhausted you are from pretending.
Then, somewhere inside that darkness, comes the confession you have made a thousand times:
Jesus is Lord.
And suddenly it is no longer a slogan.
It is a confrontation.
Lord over this too?
Yes.
This addiction?
Yes.
This relationship?
Yes.
This wound?
Yes.
This money?
Yes.
This future?
Yes.
This body?
Yes.
This resentment?
Yes.
This secret?
Yes.
This dream?
Yes.
Even this?
Especially this.
That is why repentance hurts before it heals.
Repentance forces us to stop negotiating with the God we claim to worship.
Some of us have spent years trying to make Jesus the constitutional monarch of our lives.
Beautiful ceremonies.
Beautiful songs.
Beautiful titles.
But practically no governing authority.
We want Jesus on the throne for photographs while we continue signing the laws.
But κύριος — kyrios — Lord is not decorative language.
It identifies authority.
And the New Testament pushes the confession even higher.
Paul writes of Christ in Philippians 2 that after His humiliation and obedience unto death, God highly exalted Him, so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess:
“κύριος Ἰησοῦς Χριστός”
Kyrios Iēsous Christos.
“Jesus Christ is Lord.”
And Paul says this confession is “to the glory of God the Father.”
Notice where the road leads.
Every knee.
Every tongue.
Jesus is not campaigning for Lordship.
He is Lord.
The question is not ultimately whether humanity will acknowledge Him.
Philippians says the day is coming when His Lordship will be universally confessed.
The question is whether you will bow before Him now in repentant faith and joyful surrender.
Because there is an enormous difference between surrendering to the King who saves you and finally facing the King you spent your life rejecting.
And perhaps that exposes something uncomfortable.
Maybe you do believe in Jesus.
But you have been fighting Him.
You pray…
but you keep one hand wrapped around the thing He told you to release.
You worship…
but there is someone you refuse even to begin forgiving.
You read Scripture…
until Scripture disagrees with you.
You ask God to guide your future…
provided His answer resembles the future you already selected.
You say, “Your will be done”…
while secretly meaning, “as long as Your will does not cost me mine.”
And then grace interrupts the story.
Because Jesus already knew.
Before you confessed the hidden thing, He knew.
Before anybody discovered your double life, He knew.
Before your marriage cracked.
Before the addiction returned.
Before the affair.
Before the angry words.
Before the compromise.
Before the years you wasted.
Before the night you became someone you promised yourself you would never become.
He knew.
And still the Gospel came looking for sinners.
This is why Christianity is not the story of respectable people impressing God.
It is the story of a holy God rescuing guilty people through the crucified and risen Christ.
Peter denied Jesus.
Three times.
Think about that.
The man who had said he would die with Christ eventually insisted that he did not even know Him.
Imagine Peter after the rooster crowed.
Imagine remembering the sound of your own voice denying the One who loved you.
Imagine looking across that courtyard and realizing Jesus had been right about you.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Scandal.
Failure.
Cowardice.
Shame.
The kind of moment a human being would delete from his biography.
Yet Jesus was not finished writing Peter's story.
After the resurrection, Christ restored the disciple who had denied Him.
Not because Peter's betrayal did not matter.
It mattered terribly.
But Peter's sin was not greater than Christ's grace.
Jesus did not call evil good.
He redeemed the man who had committed it.
That is the difference between cheap grace and biblical grace.
Cheap grace says:
“It doesn't matter.”
Jesus says:
“It mattered enough for Me to bleed.”
Cheap grace says:
“Stay exactly where you are.”
Jesus says:
“Follow Me.”
Cheap grace excuses bondage.
Jesus breaks chains.
Cheap grace protects our idols.
Jesus confronts them.
Cheap grace makes peace with sin.
The Gospel makes peace with God through the blood of Christ—and then begins transforming the person who has been reconciled.
So when you confess, “Jesus is Lord,” you are not announcing that you have become perfect.
Read that again.
You are not saying you never struggle.
You are not saying temptation disappeared.
You are not saying you will never stumble again.
You are saying something deeper:
My struggle no longer gets to rename evil as good.
Jesus does.
My culture does not have final authority.
Jesus does.
My feelings do not have final authority.
Jesus does.
My trauma does not have final authority.
Jesus does.
My desires do not have final authority.
Jesus does.
My political tribe does not have final authority.
Jesus does.
My pastor does not have final authority.
Jesus does.
Gospel Warrior does not have final authority.
Jesus does.
No ministry does.
No influencer does.
No denomination does.
No algorithm does.
No crowd does.
Christ does.
That is Lordship.
And this is where some frightened believer needs to hear something equally important.
Do not turn Lordship into another ladder by which you attempt to climb into God's acceptance.
You cannot obey yourself into the cross.
The cross came down to you.

Ephesians 2:8–10 holds together what we are constantly tempted to tear apart: salvation is by grace through faith, not the result of our works so that no one can boast, yet those who are saved are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace is the root.
A transformed life is fruit.
Never reverse them.
You do not obey Jesus so that His blood will finally become sufficient.
You obey because His blood is sufficient.
You do not repent to persuade God to become merciful.
You repent because in Christ you have encountered mercy.
You do not surrender so Jesus will finally love you.
You discover in the Gospel a love so costly that surrender becomes the only sane response.
This also means Christian obedience is not a commercial transaction.
You cannot buy God's favor.
You cannot purchase salvation.
You cannot share a Christian article and call that surrender.
You cannot donate enough money to erase one sin.
Christ alone saves.
Christ alone deserves the throne.
And perhaps that is exactly why genuine Christian generosity becomes beautiful.
Because when grace grips you, you stop asking only:
“What must I do to get something from God?”
You begin asking:
“What has God entrusted to me that I can use for His glory?”
Your time.
Your voice.
Your home.
Your gifts.
Your money.
Your platform.
Your testimony.
Your influence.
Even the little blue “share” button sitting underneath a Gospel message.
None of those things purchase heaven.
But all of them can become instruments placed in the hands of the King.
Maybe someone on your Facebook friends list has been silently drowning.
Maybe the person who jokes the loudest has been thinking about eternity.
Maybe somebody who has not entered a church in fifteen years will read an article because you shared it.
Maybe your cousin.
Your old classmate.
Your brother.
Your daughter.
The friend you stopped talking to.
The believer who has slowly gone cold.
The skeptic who thinks Christians have nothing to offer except condemnation.
You do not know where a seed will land.
So if this article has confronted you, do not share it because sharing earns favor with God.
Send it privately to someone who would never admit publicly that they are struggling.
If spreading biblical truth is one practical way you want to glorify God with the influence He has given you, then use that influence deliberately.
Not polished.
Not religious.
Honest.
Maybe your comment becomes permission for another person to stop pretending.
Maybe someone replies, “Me too.”
Maybe someone prays for you.
Maybe confession becomes community.
Maybe community becomes accountability.
Maybe accountability becomes restoration.
There is no shame in needing prayer.
There is danger in becoming comfortable with hiding.
Not because saving a post makes you spiritual, but because tomorrow the emotions may fade.
The conviction may become quieter.
The old excuses may return.
And you may need to read again the question Jesus asked:
“Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?”
Then ask Him something dangerous.
“Jesus, where am I calling You Lord but refusing Your authority?”
Do not rush the answer.
Let Scripture search you.
Maybe He exposes pride.
Repent.
Maybe pornography.
Repent.
Maybe bitterness.
Repent.
Maybe greed.
Repent.
Maybe gossip.
Repent.
Maybe dishonesty.
Repent.
Maybe spiritual laziness.
Repent.
Maybe self-righteousness.
Repent.
Maybe an obsession with being admired.
Repent.
Maybe you have turned Christianity into content while your prayer life quietly died.
Repent.
And when repentance makes you feel like running away from God…
run toward Christ.
Because repentance is not merely turning away from sin.
Christian repentance turns toward the Savior.
Toward the One whose hands still bear the testimony of what your forgiveness cost.
Toward the One who was crucified.
Toward the One who was buried.
Toward the One whom God raised from the dead.
Toward the One Romans tells us to confess as Lord.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Not because the scandal disappears from history.
Peter still denied Him.
Paul really persecuted Christians.
The thief really was a criminal.
The prodigal really wasted what he had been given.
David really sinned grievously.
Human beings really fall.
And you really have sinned.
So have I.
The Gospel does not require us to rewrite the past until we become the hero.
The Gospel announces that Jesus Christ entered the story.
And suddenly your worst chapter does not have the authority to write your final sentence.
Christ does.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build another personality cult.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to make people dependent upon a page.

But to keep placing Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, Gospel-centered discipleship, healing, repentance, restoration, and spiritual nourishment in front of people who desperately need Jesus.

If that mission has strengthened your walk with Christ, consider following Gospel Warrior and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too.
Not to purchase God's blessing.
Not to prove your salvation.
But because Christian generosity can help Gospel-centered resources reach people who need them.
Jesus is still Lord.
Your agreement does not make Him Lord.
Your obedience does not crown Him Lord.
Your surrender does not elect Him Lord.
He is Lord.
The question is what you will do with the King who stands before you.
One day, Paul says, every knee will bow and every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
Every knee.
The successful.
The forgotten.
The famous.
The anonymous.
The skeptic.
The preacher.
The billionaire.
The prisoner.
The king.
The beggar.
The person reading these words.
Me.
You.
Every knee.
And suddenly so much of what consumes us becomes painfully small.
The followers.
The money.
The house.
The applause.
The argument you needed to win.
The person whose approval controlled you.
The secret sin you thought you could never surrender.
The image you spent decades maintaining.
One day none of it will compete with the sight of Christ.
So why wait until eternity to acknowledge what is already true?
Bow now.
Not merely with your knees.
With your plans.
With your wounds.
With your appetites.
With your relationships.
With your finances.
With your phone.
With your sexuality.
With your bitterness.
With your gifts.
With your reputation.
With your future.
With the part of yourself you are terrified to surrender because you are afraid Jesus will destroy you if you finally give it to Him.
Look at the cross.
That is not the face of a Savior trying to destroy repentant sinners.
That is the King who died to redeem them.
Come out of hiding.
Confess the sin.
Ask forgiveness.
Make restitution where biblical repentance requires it.
Seek accountability where you need it.
Forgive because you have been forgiven.
Obey what Christ has clearly commanded.
Return when you fall.
Keep walking when obedience hurts.
Trust grace when shame tells you that your story is finished.
And never confuse struggling against sin with surrendering to it.
A believer may stumble.
A believer may weep.
A believer may have nights when the battle feels unbearable.
But something inside the redeemed heart keeps returning to the throne:
“Jesus, You are Lord.
Not my sin.
Not my past.
Not my fear.
Not my shame.
Not my appetite.
Not the voices in my head.
Not the crowd.
You.”
That is the confession.
That is the surrender.
That is the beginning of freedom.
And comment something real.
“Jesus, be Lord of all of me.”
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But perhaps typing those words will become the moment you stop hiding from the question you already know He has been asking.
Because maybe the part of your life you are most afraid to place in His hands is the very place where grace is waiting to rewrite the story.
And when your shame whispers, “This chapter proves you are finished,” remember the nail-scarred King still holds the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “THE TRUTH WILL SET YOU FREE” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MOST PEOPLE THINK IT MEANS
paragraphs:
“THE TRUTH WILL SET YOU FREE” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MOST PEOPLE THINK IT MEANS
Jesus Wasn’t Giving You a Motivational Quote. He Was Exposing the Invisible Master You May Still Be Serving—and Revealing the Only One Who Can Actually Break the Chains.
There are Bible verses we love because they comfort us.
And then there are Bible verses we love because we have never allowed them to finish speaking.
“The truth will set you free.”
You have seen those words on walls.
Graduation speeches.
Captions.
Posters.
Books.
Maybe even tattoos.
They sound beautiful because they seem to confirm something almost everyone wants to believe:
Find the truth about yourself.
Speak your truth.
Discover enough truth.
Accept enough truth.
And eventually…
you will become free.
But there is a problem.
That is not what Jesus was talking about.
And when you put His famous words back into the conversation from which we so often remove them, they become far more uncomfortable…
and infinitely more beautiful.
Because Jesus was not standing before wounded people merely offering better information.
He was standing before people who believed they were already free…
and telling them they were slaves.
Read that again.
They thought they were free.
Jesus knew they were bound.
And perhaps that is where this story stops being about people who lived two thousand years ago.
Perhaps it becomes about us.
Because some chains make noise.
Others learn your name.
Some prisons have bars.
Others have passwords, private histories, secret habits, respectable appearances, religious vocabulary, applause, careers, relationships, church attendance, and smiling profile pictures.
You can look free while something inside you owns you.
You can tell everybody, “I can stop whenever I want,” while quietly arranging your life around the thing you supposedly control.
You can sing worship songs on Sunday and return to the same hidden compromise on Monday.
You can preach forgiveness while feeding bitterness.
You can talk about purity while protecting a secret browser history.
You can post Scripture while starving your soul.
You can know Christian language and still be terrified of what would happen if somebody discovered the unedited version of you.
That is what makes the words of Jesus so dangerous.
He does not merely address the chains people can see.
He walks directly toward the chains we have renamed.
Jesus says in John 8:31–32:
“Ἐὰν ὑμεῖς μείνητε ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τῷ ἐμῷ…”
“If you abide in My word…”
Then:
“καὶ γνώσεσθε τὴν ἀλήθειαν…”
“and you will know the truth…”
And then comes the famous declaration:
“καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια ἐλευθερώσει ὑμᾶς.”
“and the truth will set you free.”
Notice what we usually leave out.
Jesus does not begin with freedom.
He begins with remaining.
The Greek verb behind “abide” or “remain” is related to μένω—menō.
Remain.
Stay.
Continue.
Do not merely visit My word when life collapses.
Do not merely quote My word when it supports something you already want.
Remain in it.
Live under it.
Allow it to confront you.
Allow it to correct you.
Allow it to expose you.
Allow it to contradict you.
Allow it to become more authoritative than your impulses, your culture, your wounds, your desires, your excuses, and even your own interpretation of yourself.
That changes everything.
Jesus is not describing truth as an inspirational slogan detached from discipleship.
He connects knowing truth with continuing in His word as His disciple.
And then His listeners react.
“We are offspring of Abraham and have never been enslaved to anyone. How is it that you say, ‘You will become free’?”
There it is.
The reflex of the human heart.
Free?
What do You mean I need freedom?
I’m fine.
I have this under control.
I can leave whenever I want.
I’m not addicted.
I’m just stressed.
I’m not bitter.
I just remember what they did.
I’m not proud.
I just know my worth.
I’m not hiding.
It’s private.
I’m not compromising.
God understands.
I’m not far from God.
I still believe in Him.
And Jesus does not flatter their self-assessment.
He goes deeper.
“Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν…”
“Truly, truly, I say to you…”
Then comes the diagnosis:
“πᾶς ὁ ποιῶν τὴν ἁμαρτίαν δοῦλός ἐστιν τῆς ἁμαρτίας.”
Everyone practicing sin is a slave of sin.
That word is devastating.
δοῦλος.
Doulos.
Slave.
Jesus is not merely describing somebody who occasionally makes an unfortunate mistake.
He is exposing sin as a master.
That is why sin always lies to you about freedom.
It tells you:
Do this and you will finally feel alive.
Then after you obey it, it demands another payment.
One more look.
One more lie.
One more drink.
One more secret.
One more compromise.
One more revenge fantasy.
One more purchase.
One more person’s approval.
One more night pretending you are okay.
One more promise that tomorrow will be different.
Sin advertises itself as liberation and slowly becomes occupation.
At first you choose it.
Eventually you begin discovering how much it has been choosing for you.
Your schedule.
Your thoughts.
Your relationships.
Your reactions.
Your money.
Your body.
Your attention.
Your conscience.
Your worship.
Your ability to sit alone in silence without reaching for something to numb what is happening inside you.
That is slavery.
And this is precisely why “the truth will set you free” cannot honestly be reduced to “learning facts will improve your life.”
Because Jesus continues.
He does not leave freedom floating in the air as an abstract philosophical principle.
He brings freedom directly back to Himself.
John 8:36 says:
“ἐὰν οὖν ὁ υἱὸς ὑμᾶς ἐλευθερώσῃ, ὄντως ἐλεύθεροι ἔσεσθε.”
“If therefore the Son sets you free, you will truly be free.”
Did you see it?
Verse 32:
The truth will set you free.
Verse 36:
The Son sets you free.
This is where the popular quotation becomes unmistakably Christ-centered.
Christian freedom is not merely discovering an idea.
Freedom comes through Jesus Christ.
And later in John’s Gospel, Jesus does not merely say that He teaches truth.
He says:
“I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”
The Gospel does not ultimately hand you a self-improvement philosophy and tell you to repair yourself.
The Gospel brings you to a Person.
Jesus Christ.
And that matters because your deepest problem was never simply that you lacked information.
We have known things were wrong and done them anyway.
We have promised ourselves we would stop and returned.
We have known we should forgive and kept rehearsing the wound.
We have known comparison was poisoning us and kept scrolling.
We have known lust was hollowing us out and kept feeding it.
We have known pride was destroying relationships and still needed to win.
We have known God was calling us back and whispered…
later.
Information alone cannot resurrect a dead heart.
A prisoner does not merely need somebody to explain the architecture of his prison.
He needs the door opened.
And Jesus did not come merely to describe your chains.
He came to break their claim over you.
This is where the cross becomes breathtaking.
Because the truth about us is actually worse than the motivational version of Christianity wants to admit.
We have sinned.
Not merely “made mistakes.”
Sinned.
Against a holy God.
We have loved created things more than the Creator.
We have wanted God’s gifts without God’s rule.
We have justified ourselves.
Hidden ourselves.
Excused ourselves.
Compared ourselves with people worse than us so we could feel righteous.
And if Christianity ended with the truth about us…
we would have reason to despair.
But the truth about you is not the whole Gospel.
There is also the truth about Him.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
He lived without sin.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore judgment.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Grace does not mean your sin was insignificant.
Grace means your sin was so serious that Christ went to the cross—and His love was so extraordinary that He went willingly.
This is why repentance is not God standing over you saying, “Clean yourself up before I love you.”
Repentance is the King calling a slave away from the master who has been destroying him.
Turn around.
Come home.
Stop defending the chains I died to break.
There may be someone reading this who has spent years believing freedom means finally becoming strong enough not to struggle.
So every relapse became proof that God was finished with you.
Every temptation became proof that you were fake.
Every failure sent you deeper underground.
You became skilled at hiding.
And perhaps nobody knows.
They know your Christian version.
They know the version that says, “God is good.”
They know the version that serves.
Smiles.
Prays.
Encourages everybody else.
But they do not know what happens when the room gets quiet.
They do not know what you keep returning to.
They do not know what you deleted.
They do not know whom you still hate.
They do not know how exhausted you are from trying to appear spiritually alive.
Jesus does.
And He still says:
Come.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because it matters so much that He refuses to leave you enslaved to it.
Grace is not permission to decorate your chains.
Grace brings you out of the cell.
This is where Christianity separates itself from cheap inspiration.
Jesus does not say freedom means you can finally do whatever you want.
Biblical freedom means sin no longer has the right to be your master.

Paul develops this same reality in Romans 6: those united to Christ are not to continue presenting themselves to sin as obedient slaves. Having been set free from sin, they become servants of righteousness.
That does not mean Christians instantly become incapable of sin.
Scripture does not teach sinless perfection the moment someone believes.
Believers still battle the flesh.
They still need confession.
They still need repentance.
They still stumble.
But something fundamental has changed.
The throne has changed.
The ownership has changed.
The direction has changed.
The Christian may still fight sin…
but no longer has to call slavery home.
There is an enormous difference between struggling against chains and peacefully decorating them.
If you hate the sin that once owned you…
if you keep crawling back toward Christ when you fall…
if conviction still hurts…
if you are tired of pretending…
do not mistake the battlefield for abandonment.
Bring the battle into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Ask for help.
Cut off what continually feeds the temptation.
Open Scripture again.
Pray when you do not feel spiritual.
Find mature believers who will tell you the truth and still walk beside you.
And above everything…
look again at Jesus.
Because the final answer in John 8 is not:
“If your discipline sets you free…”
Not:
“If religion sets you free…”
Not:
“If your reputation sets you free…”
Not:
“If your church attendance sets you free…”
Not:
“If your willpower sets you free…”
Jesus says:
“If the Son sets you free…”
The Son.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe that is the sentence someone needs tonight.
Your past does not have greater authority than Jesus.
Your addiction does not have greater authority than Jesus.
Your shame does not have greater authority than Jesus.
The person who wounded you does not have greater authority than Jesus.
The secret you are terrified to confess does not have greater authority than Jesus.
The worst thing you have ever done does not possess greater saving power than the blood of Christ.
Do not misunderstand that.
Consequences can remain.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Wounds may require time.
Some battles require serious pastoral, relational, and professional support.
Forgiveness does not magically erase every earthly consequence.
But the Gospel announces something greater than pretending the scandal never happened.
Jesus can write grace into a story sin tried to finish.
That is the heartbeat behind these words:
Not because scandal becomes good.
Not because sin becomes harmless.
Not because truth is softened.
But because Jesus Christ can enter the ugliest chapter of a repentant sinner’s story and refuse to let that chapter have the final word.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul had persecuted His church.
The woman at the well carried a tangled relational history.
The thief beside Jesus was running out of minutes.
Again and again Scripture introduces us to people whose stories looked disqualified…
until grace entered the sentence.
That is the Gospel.
Not good people becoming slightly better.
The guilty forgiven.
The lost found.
The dead made alive.
The enslaved liberated.
The ashamed brought near.
The sinner reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
And perhaps now you understand why the truth sometimes hurts before freedom feels like freedom.
Truth turns on the light.
And when you have lived in darkness long enough, light hurts your eyes.
Truth tells you the relationship is destroying you.
Truth tells you your secret habit is not harmless.
Truth tells you unforgiveness has become a prison.
Truth tells you pride is wearing religious clothing.
Truth tells you that you cannot simultaneously surrender to Jesus and keep negotiating permanent ownership of the thing He is commanding you to release.
Truth wounds the lie.
Grace heals the person.
And Jesus does both because He loves you too much to leave your chains unnamed.
So ask yourself something you may not want to answer.
What is the one thing in your life you hope Jesus never asks you to surrender?
There.
That thing.
Sit with it.
What are you protecting?
What are you hiding?
What has repeatedly whispered, “You need me,” even though it keeps taking more than it gives?
What would happen if today, instead of defending it…
you brought it to Christ?
Maybe your prayer does not need impressive language.
Maybe tonight it simply needs honesty:
Jesus, I have been calling slavery freedom.
Forgive me.
Expose what I keep hiding.
I cannot save myself.
I believe You died for sinners and rose again.
Teach me to remain in Your Word.
Break what has mastered me.
Give me strength to repent.
Make me Yours.
Set me free.
And if those words exposed something you have kept hidden, do not turn this moment into another emotional experience you forget tomorrow.
Not because typing three words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing a battle into the light begins with refusing to keep pretending.
Someone else reading the comments may need to discover that they are not the only believer in a battle.
If your spirit has been exhausted lately, you can simply write:
Let the body of Christ do what the body of Christ is supposed to do.
Pray.
Carry burdens.
Speak truth.
Point one another back to Jesus.
And if Christ has already begun breaking chains you once believed would own you forever, tell somebody.
Your testimony may become someone else’s reason to believe that grace can reach their address too.
“Christ is still healing me.”
Not because sharing an article earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Salvation is the gift of God’s grace, not a transaction we can buy.
But if you genuinely want your Facebook presence to glorify God, one practical way to use what He has placed in your hands is to put Christ-centered truth where other people can encounter it.
Someone you know may be smiling while secretly enslaved.
Someone may be one night away from giving up.
Someone may have mistaken Christianity for moral performance and never understood grace.
Someone may desperately need to hear that Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Because there may come a night when the old chains start whispering again, and you need to remember:
the prison is not your home.

Stay close to Gospel Warrior and invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even the unbeliever who is willing to listen—to follow for daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
But remember this clearly:
You do not glorify God by purchasing salvation.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot purchase God’s love.
Christ has already paid the price sinners could never pay.
We glorify God because we have been redeemed, and from that grace we can freely choose to give, serve, share, encourage, support faithful ministry, and help carry the Gospel farther.
Not as a religious performance.
As a mission.
Because somebody in your circle may recognize their chains in these words before they recognize the Savior standing at the door.
And after everything you have read, never forget the sentence Jesus Himself uses to finish the argument:
It is the Son who makes you free.
Not your image.
Not your willpower.
Not your secrets staying buried.
Not the approval of people.
Jesus.
The One who knows the scandal.
The One who speaks the truth.
The One who carried the cross.
The One who walked out of the grave.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who still breaks chains.
And maybe the freedom you have been begging God to give you begins when you finally stop asking Him to bless the chain you refuse to release.
The truth does not merely expose your prison—the Truth has a name, and the Son still opens doors slaves could never open for themselves.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: BIBLICAL SUBMISSION: What Christians Actually Owe Their Leaders—and What They Never Owe Them
paragraphs: BIBLICAL SUBMISSION: What Christians Actually Owe Their Leaders—and What They Never Owe Them

You were told, “Touch not God’s anointed.” You were told questioning a leader meant questioning God. You may even have been taught that submission means silence. But when Scripture itself is allowed to speak, something far more beautiful—and far more demanding—emerges: biblical submission is real, Christian leadership is real, obedience matters, and yet Jesus Christ alone remains Lord.
There is a sentence that has kept wounded Christians awake at night.
“Maybe I’m the rebellious one.”
Sometimes it comes after a pastor has been questioned.
Sometimes after a church member says no.
Sometimes after someone notices that what is happening behind the pulpit does not resemble the Jesus being preached from it.
And sometimes it comes after years of being taught that a faithful Christian never challenges spiritual authority.
So you sit there with the Bible open and your heart pounding.
You love Jesus.
You do not want to rebel against God.
You do not want bitterness growing inside you.
You do not want to dishonor someone whom God has called to shepherd His people.
But something is wrong.
And now the question becomes terrifying:
What does God actually require me to give my spiritual leaders?
The answer matters because there are two cliffs on either side of this road.

On one side is rebellion disguised as discernment—the arrogant spirit that refuses correction, despises authority, church-hops whenever confronted, and calls every uncomfortable truth “spiritual abuse.”

On the other side is unquestioning allegiance disguised as submission—the belief that a pastor, elder, ministry leader, husband, parent, politician, or Christian celebrity can demand what belongs only to Christ.
Scripture permits neither.
And somewhere between those cliffs stands Jesus.
Not weak.
Not confused.
Not intimidated by authority.
Not contemptuous of legitimate authority.
Jesus—the King who washed feet.
The Lord who submitted Himself to the Father.
The Shepherd who laid His life down for sheep instead of using sheep to build His kingdom.
That changes everything.
Hebrews 13:17 is one of the passages Christians most often encounter in conversations about spiritual authority. The Greek contains two especially important words:
πείθεσθε — peithesthe
and
ὑπείκετε — hypeikete

The verse calls believers to respond appropriately to their leaders and yield to them because those leaders “keep watch” over souls and will themselves have to give an account. The Mounce interlinear renders the first term in the sense of continuing to obey and the second as submitting or yielding. The verse therefore gives genuine weight to spiritual leadership; it is not permission to treat pastors and elders as irrelevant.
But notice what is sitting inside the very verse sometimes used to demand unquestioning loyalty.
Accountability.
Leaders watch over souls “as those who must give an account.”
That sentence should make every Christian leader tremble before it makes any congregation member tremble.
The sheep belong to God.
The church belongs to Christ.
The pulpit belongs to Christ.
The ministry belongs to Christ.
The reputation belongs to Christ.
The money belongs to Christ.
The wounded person sitting in the back row belongs to Christ.
The pastor does not own the flock.
He will answer for how he treated it.
That is why biblical submission can never mean surrendering your conscience to another human being.
There is only one throne at the center of Christianity.
And your pastor is not sitting on it.
Neither am I.
Neither are you.
Jesus is.
This is where some people become uncomfortable, because abuses of authority have made the word submission itself sound dangerous.
But throwing away biblical submission because somebody corrupted it would be another tragedy.
Scripture really does teach submission.
Ephesians 5:21 uses the Greek:
ὑποτασσόμενοι ἀλλήλοις ἐν φόβῳ Χριστοῦ
“being subject to one another out of reverence for Christ.”

The key word ὑποτάσσω — hypotassō carries the idea of being subject or placing oneself in an ordered relationship. Yet notice the atmosphere surrounding Christian submission: it is rooted in reverence for Christ.
Christ remains the gravitational center.
Biblical submission is not personality worship.
It is not intellectual suicide.
It is not pretending sin is holiness because the sinner owns a microphone.
It is not protecting a ministry brand while victims bleed quietly.
It is not allowing someone to manipulate you with “God told me” when what follows contradicts what God has already said.
And it certainly is not giving another human being the obedience that belongs uniquely to Jesus Christ.
The apostles themselves demonstrated the boundary.
When the authorities commanded them to stop proclaiming Christ, Peter and the apostles answered with one of the clearest principles in the New Testament:
“We must obey God rather than men.” — Acts 5:29
There it is.
Not rebellion for rebellion’s sake.
Not disrespect.
Not anarchy.
A hierarchy of allegiance.
When human authority and divine authority collide, God wins.
Every time.
And this becomes even clearer when Scripture turns from the responsibilities of the flock to the responsibilities of the shepherd.
Peter does not tell elders, “Make sure everybody knows who is in charge.”
He tells them to shepherd God’s flock willingly and eagerly, then explicitly warns them against domineering over those entrusted to their care. Instead, leaders are to become examples to the flock.
Read that again slowly.
Not domineering.
Examples.
The New Testament model of leadership is therefore not:
“Look how many people obey me.”
It is:
“Look how faithfully I imitate Christ.”
Jesus Himself destroyed the worldly definition of greatness.
The rulers of the nations “lord it over” people.
Christ tells His disciples that it must not be that way among them.
The greatest becomes a servant.
Then Jesus does something almost unbearable in its beauty.
The One who could command angels kneels.
God the Son takes a towel.
The hands through whom creation came wash dirty feet.
And suddenly Christian authority has a permanent shape.
A cross.
This is the scandal.
The highest King became the lowest servant.
The Lord did not need to crush people to prove He was Lord.
He loved.
He served.
He corrected.
He confronted.
He commanded.
He forgave.
And finally He stretched out His hands and allowed sinners to nail Him to wood.

So when someone uses “submission” to justify domination, coercion, concealment, exploitation, sexual misconduct, financial manipulation, retaliation against legitimate questions, or unquestioning loyalty to a personality, the problem is not that Christianity takes authority too seriously.
The problem is that such leadership does not take Christ’s authority seriously enough.
Maybe this is where your story enters.
Maybe somebody wounded you in church.
And perhaps what makes the wound so confusing is that they used Scripture while doing it.
Maybe you asked a sincere question and were labeled rebellious.
Maybe you reported something troubling and suddenly became “divisive.”
Maybe you watched everyone protect the influential person while the wounded person disappeared.
Maybe you left.
And perhaps you have carried shame ever since.
But there is another possibility we must have enough humility to confront.
Maybe nobody abused you.
Maybe you simply hated being corrected.
Maybe a faithful pastor told you something your flesh did not want to hear.

Maybe Scripture exposed your relationship, your pride, your sexual sin, your greed, your bitterness, your unforgiveness, your gossip, or your compromise—and instead of repenting, you renamed conviction “control.”
That happens too.
We must tell the whole truth.
Not every confrontation is abuse.
Not every boundary is manipulation.
Not every pastor who disagrees with you is controlling.
Not every uncomfortable sermon is toxic.
Sometimes the shepherd is warning you because the cliff is real.
Sometimes you are not being persecuted.
Sometimes you are being corrected.
And sometimes the most loving thing a Christian leader can say is:
No. This is sin. Come back.
Biblical discernment cuts both directions.
It protects sheep from wolves.
And it protects sheep from becoming stubborn enough to wander away from the Shepherd.
That is why the mature Christian does not begin with, “Do I like what my leader said?”
The mature Christian asks:
“Is it faithful to Christ and His Word?”
That question changes everything.
If your pastor faithfully teaches Scripture, pray for him.
Encourage him.
Receive correction humbly.
Make his work a joy rather than manufacturing unnecessary conflict.
Refuse gossip.
Refuse the consumer mentality that treats churches like restaurants and pastors like customer-service representatives.
Honor faithful elders.

Give thanks for shepherds who study while everyone else sleeps, answer calls when families are collapsing, visit hospitals, bury loved ones, counsel marriages, preach when exhausted, carry secrets they cannot repeat, and quietly wonder whether they are making any difference.
Hebrews 13:17 says leaders are watching over souls knowing that they must answer for that stewardship. That is a staggering burden.
Pray for them.
But do not worship them.
Listen to them.
But keep your Bible open.
Honor them.
But never hand them Christ’s throne.
Receive biblical correction.
But test teaching by Scripture.
Follow godly examples.
But remember whose footsteps ultimately matter.
Jesus Christ.
There is something deeply freeing about this.
Healthy biblical submission does not require you to become less devoted to Jesus.
It makes you more devoted to Jesus.
Healthy leadership does not fear Scripture being opened.
It welcomes it.
Healthy shepherds are not terrified when sheep know the Shepherd’s voice.
They desperately want them to.
Because faithful pastors understand something celebrity Christianity can make us forget:
The goal of Christian leadership is not to make people dependent upon the leader.
The goal is to help people mature in Christ.
Paul could say, in effect, imitate me as I imitate Christ.
That qualification matters.
Christ is the standard.
Christ is the destination.
Christ is the Head of the Church.
Christ purchased His people with blood.
And when a human leader forgets that, the Gospel brings him back to reality.
Pastors need grace too.
Leaders sin too.
Leaders need repentance too.
Leaders need accountability too.
Leaders need brothers who can look them in the eyes and say, “No.”
A leader who cannot be corrected is not demonstrating strength.
He is standing somewhere spiritually dangerous.
Peter—the apostle who wrote about shepherding—knew what correction felt like.
He had failed spectacularly.
He had denied Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine the scandal.
A leading apostle publicly collapsing at the exact moment courage was required.
If Christianity were merely a public-relations campaign, Peter's story would have been buried.
Instead, Scripture preserved it.
Why?
Because Christianity is not the story of impressive people protecting impressive reputations.
It is the story of sinners being redeemed by an impressive Savior.
Peter failed.
Peter wept.
Peter was restored.
And Jesus still used him.
That is grace.
Perhaps that is what somebody reading this desperately needs to hear.
Maybe you were a leader who failed.
Maybe pride entered your ministry slowly.
Maybe applause became addictive.
Maybe criticism started feeling like betrayal.
Maybe somewhere along the road, “Jesus’ ministry” quietly became “my ministry.”
Repent.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
The cross is not only for the people sitting in your congregation.
It is for you.
There is forgiveness for pastors.
There is restoration where biblical restoration is appropriate.
There is mercy for elders.
There is cleansing for leaders who stop defending darkness and drag it into the light.
Jesus is still rewriting stories.
And perhaps you are not the leader.
Perhaps you are the wounded sheep.
Then hear this carefully:
Do not allow what a human shepherd did to convince you that the Good Shepherd is like him.
Jesus is not the pastor who betrayed you.
Jesus is not the ministry that manipulated you.
Jesus is not the Christian who exploited your trust.
Jesus is not the person who covered darkness while quoting Bible verses.
Look at Christ Himself.
The Shepherd in John 10 does not devour the sheep.
He lays down His life for them.
That is your Jesus.
And maybe your next act of faith is not pretending nothing happened.
Maybe it is bringing what happened into truth.
Seeking wise, biblically grounded counsel.
Reporting criminal conduct to the appropriate civil authorities when necessary.
Rejecting vengeance while refusing concealment.
Forgiving without calling evil good.
Remembering that forgiveness and restored trust are not identical things.
And refusing to let another person's sin become the graveyard of your faith.
Because Satan would love a double victory.
First, let someone wound you in the name of Christianity.
Then convince you to abandon Christ because of what that person did.
Do not give darkness the second victory.
Run past the failed representative.
Run to Jesus.
And if you are the Christian who has spent years refusing every authority because someone once abused authority, Christ can heal that too.
You do not have to live permanently suspicious.
You can learn discernment without becoming cynical.
You can honor without idolizing.
You can submit without surrendering your conscience.
You can ask questions without becoming rebellious.
You can receive correction without becoming controlled.
You can forgive without pretending.
You can love the Church while acknowledging where churches have failed.
You can believe in biblical leadership without building idols out of leaders.
This is the narrow road.
And Jesus walks it with us.
So what do Christians actually owe their leaders?

Biblically, we owe faithful leaders honor, prayer, appropriate cooperation and submission, teachability, love, encouragement, and a willingness to receive leadership consistent with Christ and His Word.
What do we never owe them?
Worship.
Blind allegiance.
The surrender of conscience.
Participation in sin.
Silence about criminal wrongdoing.
Permission to contradict Scripture.
Or the obedience that belongs to God alone.
There is one Chief Shepherd.

First Peter 5 ultimately points earthly shepherds beyond themselves to the Chief Shepherd who will appear. Earthly leaders are under-shepherds. Their authority is borrowed, accountable, temporary, and answerable to Him.
Jesus owns the Church.
That truth protects both pastors and congregations.
It protects pastors from the unbearable delusion that everything depends on them.
And it protects congregations from the equally dangerous delusion that their pastor is their mediator before God.
There is already a Mediator.
His name is Jesus.
There is already a spotless High Priest.
Jesus.
There is already a King.
Jesus.
There is already a Savior.
Jesus.
And He did not save you by demanding that you climb high enough to reach Him.
He came down for you.
That is the Gospel.
You sinned against a holy God.
So did I.
Our deepest problem is not bad leadership, bad churches, bad institutions, or bad experiences—terrible as those things can be.
Our deepest problem is sin.
And Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, took the judgment sinners deserved upon Himself at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
Grace walked out of a tomb.
And now the invitation is not, “Find a perfect pastor.”
You never will.
The invitation is:
Come to the perfect Savior.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Jesus.
And then learn, inside His redeemed community, how imperfect Christians can honor imperfect leaders who are themselves bowing before the perfect King.
That is biblical submission.
Not slavery to men.
Freedom under Christ.
Not silence in darkness.
Walking in light.
Not leader worship.
Christ worship.
Not rebellion masquerading as independence.
Humility anchored in truth.
And maybe this article found you because you have been wrestling with this for years.
If it exposed rebellion in you, do not defend it.
Repent.
If it exposed unhealthy allegiance to a human personality, do not hide from that either.
Return your worship to Jesus.
If it reopened a church wound, bring that wound to the Good Shepherd instead of allowing it to rot beneath Christian language.
And if your heart is exhausted and all you can manage today is honesty, then be honest.
Your honesty may become permission for another wounded believer to stop hiding.
And please do not keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing earns God's favor. It does not.
It cannot.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift, received through faith in Christ.
But if you sincerely want to glorify God with what He has entrusted to you, one practical response is to help sound biblical truth travel farther.

Your support helps us keep producing and distributing Christ-centered biblical content and expanding resources intended to point people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through Jesus Christ. But Christians can glorify God through willing generosity and by helping faithful Gospel work reach people who need it.
Your leader may help shepherd your soul—but only Jesus purchased it with His blood.
So honor faithful leaders.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Receive biblical correction.
Refuse arrogant rebellion.
Expose darkness rather than protecting it.
Forgive.
Discern.
Keep your Bible open.
Keep your knees bent.
Keep your eyes on Christ.

Because when every platform disappears, every title is surrendered, every congregation is scattered, every ministry brand is forgotten, and every human shepherd stands before the One to whom he must give an account, there will still be only one name above every name.
Jesus.
And perhaps the most dangerous spiritual mistake is not merely refusing to submit to a leader.
Perhaps it is submitting to anyone so completely that you forget who died for you.
Human shepherds may carry the staff for a season. The nail-scarred Shepherd carries you into eternity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Wasted His Father’s Money on Wild Living — Then He Came Home Expecting Rejection
paragraphs: He Wasted His Father’s Money on Wild Living — Then He Came Home Expecting Rejection

He had already rehearsed the speech that would reduce him from son to servant. But before he could finish it, his father was running toward him. And if you have ever wondered whether you have sinned too badly, wandered too far, wasted too much, or disappointed God too deeply to come home, Jesus told this story for people exactly like you.
He could probably see the house before anyone in the house could see him.
And that may have been the hardest part.
Every step toward home carried another memory.
The road he once walked with money in his pocket, dreams in his head, and freedom burning in his chest was now the road of his humiliation.
He had left as somebody.
He was returning with nothing.
No inheritance.
No impressive story.
No evidence that his rebellion had somehow worked out.
Nothing to show his father except the wreckage of everything his father had entrusted to him.
Maybe you know that road.
Maybe your "far country" never appeared on a map.
Maybe you never disappeared geographically. You still went to work. Still answered messages. Still smiled in photographs. Still said, "I'm fine."
But somewhere inside, you left home.
Maybe your far country was pornography nobody knew about.
Maybe it was an affair.
Maybe it was alcohol.
Maybe it was bitterness you kept feeding while pretending you had forgiven.
Maybe it was money.
Attention.
Pride.
A relationship you knew was pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe you didn't run from God dramatically.
You simply stopped listening.
Stopped praying.
Stopped opening Scripture.
Stopped feeling bothered by what once convicted you.
And eventually you learned one of sin's oldest lessons:
The far country always advertises freedom before revealing the bill.
Jesus tells this story in Luke 15, and the setting matters.

Tax collectors and people publicly regarded as sinners were gathering around Jesus, while Pharisees and scribes complained that He welcomed sinners and ate with them. Jesus answered their grumbling with three stories about what was lost and what was found: a sheep, a coin, and finally a son.
Then Jesus begins:
Ἄνθρωπός τις εἶχεν δύο υἱούς.
Anthrōpos tis eichen dyo huious.
Literally: "A certain man had two sons."
Two sons.
Remember that.
Because this is not merely a story about one reckless young man.
Jesus is going after the hearts of sinners and religious people.
One son becomes lost far away.
The other will eventually reveal that a person can be lost while standing frighteningly close to the father's house.
But first comes the scandal everyone remembers.
The younger son asks for his share of the property.
He wants what belongs to him without remaining under his father's roof.
He wants the father's possessions more than the father's presence.
And that is where this ancient story suddenly becomes painfully modern.
Because isn't that one of the deepest forms of human rebellion?
"God, give me life—but don't govern it."
"Give me love—but don't tell me whom to love."
"Give me a body—but don't tell me what holiness looks like."
"Give me money—but don't tell me what to do with it."
"Give me success—but don't ask for the glory."
"Give me another morning—but don't ask me to surrender the day."
We want the Father's gifts while resisting the Father's authority.
The younger son receives his portion, gathers everything together, travels into a distant country, and wastes what he has.
Luke describes his manner of living with a devastating Greek word:
ἀσώτως — asōtōs.
It carries the sense of reckless, wasteful, dissolute living.
This was not merely a young man who made a poor investment.
He was unraveling.
He took what had been given in love and burned through it in rebellion.
And sin still works like that.
Sin rarely announces itself by saying, "I have come to destroy you."
It says:
"You deserve this."
"Just once."
"Nobody will know."
"You can stop whenever you want."
"God understands."
"You've been good long enough."
"This will finally make you happy."
Then one day you discover that what promised to serve you has become your master.
The money disappeared.
Then the circumstances changed.
A severe famine came.
And suddenly the people, pleasures, and possibilities surrounding the young man could not save him.
Jesus brings him lower and lower until this Jewish son is feeding pigs and longing for their food.
Think about the humiliation.
The boy who demanded his inheritance is now hungry beside swine.
The hands that once held his father's wealth are now surrounded by pig food.
The freedom he demanded has become bondage.
And there, somewhere beneath the shame, something happens.
Luke 15:17 contains one of the most beautiful descriptions of awakening in Scripture:
εἰς ἑαυτὸν δὲ ἐλθὼν
eis heauton de elthōn
In a very literal sense:
"But having come to himself..."
He came to himself.
Sin had taken him so far from the man he was created to be that repentance began to feel like waking up.
This is one reason biblical repentance is so much more beautiful than mere religious shame.
Shame says, "Hide."
Pride says, "Excuse it."
Culture may say, "Redefine it."
Despair says, "It's too late."
Repentance says, "I will arise and go to my father."
The son finally tells the truth.
No excuses.
No blaming his friends.
No blaming the famine.
No blaming his upbringing.
No carefully edited explanation designed to make rebellion sound respectable.
He knows he has sinned.
So he prepares his confession.
He will tell his father that he has sinned against heaven and before him and is no longer worthy to be called his son.
Then he develops a survival plan.
Make me like one of your hired servants.
That part matters.
Because he is returning home, but he still doesn't understand the father's heart.
He believes the best possible ending is employment.
He expects consequences without intimacy.
Survival without sonship.
Bread without belonging.
Perhaps that is where some people reading this are living right now.
You believe Jesus can forgive other people.
You believe grace theoretically.
You sing about mercy.
You share Bible verses.
But when your own secret failure comes to mind, something inside whispers:
"Not you."
"You knew better."
"You've done this too many times."
"After everything God gave you?"
"After all your promises?"
"Maybe God will tolerate you, but He could never delight in you again."
So you start negotiating like the younger son.
"I'll work harder."
"I'll prove myself."
"I'll punish myself."
"I'll become religious enough to compensate for what I did."
But then Jesus changes the entire emotional direction of the story.
The son is still far away when his father sees him.
That detail should stop you.
While he was still far away.
The father sees him.
Then Luke uses an extraordinary word:
ἐσπλαγχνίσθη — esplagchnisthē.
He was moved with deep compassion.
This is not the picture of a cold father reluctantly agreeing to process a sinner's application for reinstatement. The language communicates profound, visceral compassion.
And then—
the father runs.
The son had rehearsed a speech.
The father had compassion.
The son expected distance.
The father closed it.
The son expected anger.
The father embraced him.
The son expected to negotiate.
The father kissed him.
Can you see him?
Dirty.
Hungry.
Ashamed.
Probably smelling like the life he had just escaped.
And his father does not stand on the porch shouting:
"Clean yourself up first!"
He runs toward him.
This does not mean the son's rebellion did not matter.
It mattered enough to bring him to ruin.
Grace never requires us to pretend sin is harmless.
The son confesses that he has sinned.
Jesus Himself frames Luke 15 around repentance; earlier in the chapter He speaks of heaven rejoicing over one sinner who repents.
Grace is not God calling evil good.
Grace is God receiving the repentant sinner who has finally stopped calling evil good.
That distinction matters.
Christianity is not:
"Live however you want because God forgives."
The Gospel is infinitely more glorious:

You have sinned against a holy God. You cannot save yourself. Yet God has acted in mercy through Jesus Christ. Christ bore sin, died, and rose again; forgiveness is offered to sinners who turn to Him in repentant faith.
The Father's house is not reached by pretending the far country was beautiful.
You come home by admitting it was killing you.
And look at what happens next.
The son begins his confession.
But before he can turn his return into a plan for earning his place, the father starts giving orders.
Bring the best robe.
Put a ring on his hand.
Put shoes on his feet.
Prepare the feast.
Why?
Because, in the father's words, his son was dead and is alive again.
He was lost and has been found.
Notice the language.
Not:
"My employee has returned."
Not:
"The disappointment is back."
Not:
"Let's keep him outside for six months and see whether he deserves another chance."
My son.
The boy came home carrying a servant's speech.
The father answered with signs of restoration.
That is grace.
And grace is scandalous precisely because it cannot be purchased by the person who desperately needs it.
The prodigal had no money left to buy his restoration.
He had already wasted his resources.
All he could bring home was repentance.
The father supplied the celebration.
And here the story points beyond itself toward the heart of the Gospel.
We do not reconcile ourselves to God by accumulating enough religious merit to cancel our sins.
Our hope is Jesus Christ.
At the cross, grace does not ignore justice.
Christ bears judgment.
At the empty tomb, death does not get the final word.
Christ rises.
The Gospel is not God shrugging at your sin.
It is God providing in His Son what sinners could never provide for themselves.
You do not clean yourself up enough to make Christ willing to receive you.
You come because you need Christ to save you.
Maybe you have wasted years.
Come home.
Maybe you destroyed trust.
Come home—and be willing to walk through the costly work of repentance and rebuilding.
Maybe you have been hiding an addiction.
Bring it into the light and come home.
Maybe your marriage bears scars from your selfishness.
Repent and come home.
Maybe you have money but no peace.
Come home.
Maybe everyone at church thinks you are strong, while privately you feel spiritually numb.
Come home.
Maybe you returned to the same sin after swearing before God that you never would.
Do not turn repeated failure into permission to keep sinning.
Repent.
Seek help.
Cut off what feeds the sin.
Confess where confession is biblically appropriate.
And run to Christ.
Come home.
But Jesus isn't finished.
There is another son.
The older brother hears the celebration and becomes angry.
He has remained near the house.
He has worked.
He has obeyed outwardly.
Yet when grace is poured over his broken brother, his heart exposes itself.
He cannot celebrate mercy because he thinks relationship with his father operates like wages.
He essentially argues from his record.
Look how long I served.
Look what I did.
Look what I never did.
And suddenly we realize:
There are two ways to be far from the Father's heart.
You can rebel against Him by breaking every rule.
Or you can try to put Him in your debt by keeping them.
One says:
"I don't need the Father because I have pleasure."
The other says:
"I don't need grace because I have performance."
Both hearts need rescue.

This is why reducing Luke 15 to a sentimental story about a rebellious teenager misses part of Jesus' confrontation. The story responds to religious leaders who resented Jesus for welcoming sinners, and the father's response to both sons is central to the parable.
Jesus is confronting the person in the nightclub.
And the person in the pew.
The obvious sinner.
And the polished sinner.
The person ashamed of everything he has done.
And the person secretly proud of everything he hasn't done.
Both need grace.
Both need repentance.
Both need Jesus.
Maybe you never had a dramatic far-country season.
Maybe your danger is subtler.
You read the story and think, "At least I never became like him."
Be careful.
That sentence sounds frighteningly similar to the older brother.
If another person's restoration irritates you...
If someone's testimony makes you compare rather than celebrate...
If you secretly believe certain sinners should have to crawl farther before Christians welcome their repentance...
If you love being known as righteous more than you love seeing sinners rescued...
Jesus may be exposing a far country located inside a religious heart.
And still the father goes out.
That is another breathtaking detail.
He runs toward the rebellious younger son.
He also goes out and appeals to the angry older son.
One was lost through rebellion.
One was endangered by self-righteousness.
The father moves toward both.
This is why Luke 15 refuses to let any of us stand safely outside the story.
Some of us wasted the inheritance.
Some of us resented the party.
Some of us have done both.
But the center of the story is not ultimately the impressive repentance of a son.
It is the astonishing mercy of the father.
That is why some commentators have noted that "the prodigal son" can be an inadequate title; the father's response occupies the theological center of the story.
And that changes how you hear it.
Because perhaps tonight you are sitting somewhere with a secret you have carried for years.
You think your worst chapter became your permanent name.
Adulterer.
Addict.
Failure.
Hypocrite.
Backslider.
Liar.
Unclean.
Unworthy.
But Jesus Christ is not asking you to pretend that chapter never happened.
He is calling you to repent and surrender the pen.
That is the difference between cheap inspiration and the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely improve the ending of the old life.
He saves sinners and makes them new.
The scars may remain.
Consequences may remain.
Restitution may be necessary.
Relationships may require time to rebuild.
Forgiveness does not magically erase every earthly consequence of sin.
But your sin does not have greater saving power than Christ has redeeming power.
The cross is stronger than the accusation that says you can never return.
So stop rehearsing the speech that says you must earn your way into mercy.
You cannot purchase grace.
That is why it is grace.
Come to Christ honestly.
Come repentant.
Come empty-handed.
Come without pretending.
Come because Jesus still receives sinners.
And perhaps there is someone on your Facebook friends list who needs to hear that before they go to sleep tonight.
Someone smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
Someone convinced God is finished with them.
Someone standing emotionally in a far country, wondering whether the road home is still open.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Christ alone saves.
Not as a formula.
Not as public theater.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
But because sometimes honesty begins when somebody finally stops protecting the mask.
And if someone confesses struggle beneath this article, don't crush them.
Pray.
Encourage.
Point them toward Christ.
Remember the older brother.
The Church should never become a porch where restored prodigals are forced to explain why the Father let them inside.

Supporting Gospel Warrior is not a payment to God, and it does not buy spiritual favor. But financial support can be an act of Christian generosity and partnership when it helps biblical teaching reach more people.
And don't overlook the free resources.
But before you leave, go back to that road one more time.
See the boy.
No money.
No reputation.
No leverage.
No speech powerful enough to undo what he had done.
Just dust on his feet and repentance in his heart.
Now look farther down the road.
Someone is running.
That is the image Jesus wanted sinners—and religious people—to confront.
The son thought the defining fact about his life was what he had wasted.
The father believed the defining fact was that his son had come home.
And the Gospel takes us deeper still.
Our hope is not that we can somehow walk far enough back toward God to rescue ourselves.

Our hope is Jesus Christ—the One who came to seek and save the lost, who gave Himself for sinners, who rose victorious, and who calls us to repent, believe, follow Him, and live as people transformed by grace.
So if you are still in the far country...
Come home.
If you are halfway down the road...
Keep coming.
If you are standing outside the celebration angry that grace reached somebody you thought deserved rejection...
Come inside.
There is no trophy for being the prodigal.
There is no trophy for being the older brother.
There is only grace for sinners who finally understand how desperately they need the Father.
Follow because we need truth more often than our algorithms naturally give it to us.
And remember this when shame whispers your old name:
You may remember yourself by the road you wasted your life on—but grace remembers there is still a road home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Were Told to Love God—So Why Does the Bible Tell You to Fear Him?
paragraphs: You Were Told to Love God—So Why Does the Bible Tell You to Fear Him?
Understanding “The Fear of the Lord” Correctly—and why losing it may explain why we can sing about a holy God on Sunday while casually negotiating with sin on Monday.
