Think about the moments before you fall.
Were you lonely?
Rejected?
Angry?
Overwhelmed?
Restless?
Ashamed?
Tired?
Discouraged?
Feeling unwanted?
Feeling powerless?
Pornography can become a counterfeit refuge.
For a few minutes, you do not have to feel what hurts.
Then the escape ends.
And now you have the original pain plus shame.
So you feel worse.
And because you feel worse, you become more vulnerable to the same escape that helped create the shame.
The trap begins feeding itself.
This does not make pornography innocent.
It helps explain why simply shouting “STOP!” at yourself has sometimes failed.
You are trying to remove a counterfeit refuge without discovering why you keep running there.
God wants more than behavior management.
He wants the wounded rooms of your heart too.
The loneliness.
The rejection.
The insecurity.
The anger.
The memories.
The fear that nobody will ever truly know you and still love you.
Pornography whispers:
Come here. I can make the ache disappear.
Jesus says:
Come to Me.
And those invitations are not remotely equal.
Porn promises relief and leaves chains.
Jesus may lead you through painful truth, confession, discipline and surrender—but He leads toward freedom.
Listen to His words in John 8.
Jesus says that the one practicing sin becomes a slave to sin.
The Greek word is:
δοῦλος — doulos
A slave.
Then comes one of the most magnificent promises in this entire battle:
ἐὰν οὖν ὁ υἱὸς ὑμᾶς ἐλευθερώσῃ, ὄντως ἐλεύθεροι ἔσεσθε
Ean oun ho huios hymas eleutherōsē, ontōs eleutheroi esesthe.
“If therefore the Son sets you free, you will be truly free.”
John 8:36.
Notice who stands at the center of freedom.
Not your streak.
Not your browser filter.
Not your discipline.
Not your accountability partner.
Not this article.
The Son.
Jesus Christ.
Filters matter.
Accountability matters.
Boundaries matter.
Wise habits matter.
Confession matters.
But none of them died for you.
Jesus did.
None of them can justify you before God.
Jesus can.
None of them can wash away guilt.
The blood of Christ can.
Christian freedom is therefore not merely learning how to stop opening a website.
It is learning to belong completely to Jesus.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because the Gospel is not:
“Clean yourself up so Jesus will finally love you.”
The Gospel is that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
Romans 5:8.
Jesus did not wait for humanity to become sexually pure, morally impressive and spiritually disciplined before going to the cross.
He went to the cross for sinners.
But do not misunderstand grace.
Jesus does not rescue you so that sin can keep ruling you comfortably.
Grace does not merely pardon.
Grace begins transformation.
At the cross, your sin is not called harmless.
It is shown to be so serious that redemption required the blood of the Son of God.
And at that same cross, your sin is shown not to be beyond forgiveness, because Jesus willingly paid for sinners who come to Him.
That means you do not need to minimize pornography.
And you do not need to believe pornography is more powerful than Christ.
Both are lies.
Your sin is serious.
Your Savior is greater.
Maybe you fell last night.
Maybe ten minutes ago.
Maybe you are reading this because afterward you searched for some indication that God has not abandoned you.
Hear this carefully.
Do not turn conviction into hiding.
Adam sinned and hid.
Pornography thrives in hiding too.
The Gospel calls you into the light.
1 John 1:9 says that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
Confession does not inform God of something He failed to notice.
Confession stops pretending.
It says:
“Lord, this is what I did.”
“No excuses.”
“No softer vocabulary.”
“No blaming stress.”
“No blaming my spouse.”
“No blaming loneliness.”
“No pretending everyone does it.”
“I sinned.”
“Have mercy on me because of Jesus Christ.”
That is not weakness.
That is where warfare becomes honest.
And if you belong to Christ, do not confuse the voice of conviction with the voice of hopeless condemnation.
Conviction says:
Come into the light.
Condemnation says:
Hide because there is no hope for you.
Conviction says:
This must die.
Condemnation says:
You might as well die with it.
Conviction points you toward Christ.
Hopeless shame keeps you staring at yourself.
Romans 8:1 announces that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
That does not make pornography less serious.
It makes Christ more precious.
The Christian response after falling is therefore not:
“I already ruined everything. I might as well keep going.”
No.
Get up.
Confess.
Run back to Christ.
Bring the failure into the light.
Study what opened the door.
Strengthen the boundary.
Ask for help.
Keep fighting.
You do not honor Jesus by pretending you never fell.
You honor Him by refusing to make peace with the ground.
And please hear this:
Your longest pornography-free streak cannot become your savior either.
Imagine reaching 30 days.
Then 90.
Then a year.
Wonderful.
Praise God.
But if somewhere along the way your heart begins saying, Now God must be pleased with me because I finally became clean enough, you have simply constructed another throne.
Your righteousness before God is Jesus Christ.
Your obedience matters deeply—but obedience is the fruit of salvation, not the price you pay to purchase it.
Freedom is not earning the Father's love.
Freedom grows from learning to live as someone who has been loved in Christ.
That changes the battle.
You are no longer merely saying:
“I cannot watch this because Christians aren't supposed to.”
You begin saying:
“I do not want to train my heart to consume people Jesus commands me to love.”
“I do not want fantasy discipling my desires.”
“I do not want secrecy becoming normal.”
“I do not want pixels teaching me what intimacy means.”
“I belong to Jesus.”
“My eyes belong to Jesus.”
“My sexuality belongs to Jesus.”
“My loneliness belongs to Jesus.”
“My body belongs to Jesus.”
“My future marriage—or my present marriage—belongs to Jesus.”
“My singleness belongs to Jesus.”
“My imagination belongs to Jesus.”
“Even this broken part of me belongs to Jesus.”
That is surrender.
And surrender goes deeper than deleting history.
It changes ownership.
Maybe this is the moment you finally need to tell somebody.
Not everybody.
Somebody trustworthy.
A mature Christian friend.
A pastor.
A mentor.
An accountability partner.

If the behavior has become compulsive or is entangled with trauma, severe anxiety, depression, relationship breakdown or other serious struggles, getting help from a qualified professional alongside faithful Christian community can also be wise.
You were never designed to defeat every secret battle in secret.
James 5:16 tells believers to confess sins to one another and pray for one another.
Pornography tells you:
If people knew, they would leave.
The Gospel creates a people who can say:
“We know sinners need grace because every one of us came to Jesus needing grace.”
That does not remove accountability.
It makes genuine accountability possible.
So what happens tonight?
Because inspirational words are easy at noon.
Temptation may arrive at 12:43 a.m.
When it comes, remember this moment.
Before you touch the screen, name what is happening.
I am being tempted.
Then ask another question:
What am I actually looking for right now?
Comfort?
Escape?
Control?
Affection?
Excitement?
Relief?
Then take that hunger to Jesus instead of feeding it a counterfeit.
Pray—even if the prayer feels embarrassingly simple.
“Jesus, I want this right now, but I want You more. Help me.”
Then move.
Do not lie there negotiating.
Stand up.
Put the phone somewhere else.
Message the person who knows your struggle.
Open Scripture.
Walk.
Pray aloud.
Change the environment.
Make temptation fight uphill.
And if you fall again?
Do not interpret another fall as permission to surrender the entire war.
Confess again.
Learn again.
Strengthen the weak place again.
Return to Christ again.
But never use grace as an excuse to schedule the next fall.
Repentance means turning.
Sometimes trembling.
Sometimes crying.
Sometimes after crawling farther into darkness than you ever imagined.
But turning.
Back toward Jesus.
Perhaps you have spent years thinking your story would always be:
Christian by day. Secret slave by night.
But Jesus Christ is still writing.
Peter had a scandal.
David had a scandal.
The Corinthian church had sexual brokenness in its past.
The Bible is filled with human beings whose stories would have been devastating if their worst chapter had been their final chapter.
The Gospel does not say your scandal never happened.
Grace does something better.
Grace refuses to let your scandal have the final word.
That is not permission to romanticize sin.
It is permission to believe Jesus can rewrite what sin tried to destroy.
Maybe one day someone will sit across from you, unable to make eye contact, whispering:
“I keep going back to porn. I think God is finished with me.”
And perhaps your eyes will fill with tears.
Not because you read a clever article once.
But because you remember the nights when that sentence belonged to you.
And you will be able to say:
“Listen to me. Do not hide. Run to Jesus. Bring it into the light. Fight seriously. Get help. Keep walking. Christ is greater than the thing telling you that you will never change.”
Your wound may become somebody else's doorway toward hope.
Your confession may become the beginning of somebody else's courage.
Your testimony may someday sound like:
“I thought pornography had written the ending.
Jesus hadn't finished the story.”
Be honest.
Someone silently reading the comments may desperately need to discover that Christians actually fight battles like this—and that they do not have to fight alone.
And if somebody came to mind while you were reading, send this to them privately.
Do it with compassion, not accusation.
Do not send it saying, “This is obviously about you.”
Say, “I thought this might encourage you.”
Someone may never walk into a church and admit it.
Not because God needs your money.
Jesus alone saves.
But Christians can voluntarily use what God has entrusted to them to help Gospel ministry reach others.
Do something with the conviction.
Confess what needs confessing.
Remove what needs removing.
Tell the person who needs telling.
Seek help where help is needed.
Open the Word.
Pray.
Run from temptation.
Run toward Christ.
They are not.
And more importantly—
Jesus Christ is not standing at the end of the road waiting for cleaned-up sinners to impress Him.
He is calling sinners out of darkness.
Into truth.
Into repentance.
Into grace.
Into holiness.
Into freedom.
Into Himself.
Pornography may have occupied chapters of your story.
It does not get to be your savior.
It does not get to name you.
And it does not get to write the ending.
The screen may know your history. The enemy may know your weakness. But Jesus still holds the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “MY PASTOR SAID NO.” BUT DID GOD?
paragraphs:
“MY PASTOR SAID NO.” BUT DID GOD?
Does the Bible Really Teach That You Need a Pastor’s Permission for Major Life Decisions—or Have We Confused Godly Shepherding With Control?
There is a sentence some Christians are terrified to say out loud.
“My pastor told me not to do it… but I don’t know if God actually said no.”
Maybe it was marriage.
A career.
Moving to another city.
Leaving a ministry position.
Starting a business.
Changing churches.
Going to Bible school.
Accepting an opportunity.
Or making some other decision that could alter the direction of your life.
You prayed. You searched Scripture. You tried to examine your motives. You sought counsel.
Then someone asked the question that suddenly made you feel spiritually guilty:
“But did your pastor give you permission?”
And now something inside you is trembling.
Because you love God.
You respect spiritual leadership.
You do not want to become rebellious.

You have heard stories about people who “went against their pastor” and supposedly destroyed their lives. You have heard Hebrews 13:17 quoted: “Obey your leaders and submit to them.” You have been warned about “touching God’s anointed.” Perhaps you were even taught that moving forward without pastoral approval means moving outside God’s covering.
So now you are not merely asking whether your decision is wise.
You are wondering whether disagreeing with your pastor means disagreeing with God.
That is a much heavier burden.
And before we go any further, hear this carefully:
This article is not an attack on pastors.

Faithful pastors are gifts to Christ’s church. They teach, counsel, protect, correct, encourage, pray, warn, suffer quietly, carry burdens nobody sees, and sometimes lie awake thinking about people who barely realize how deeply their shepherd loves them.
Scripture commands Christians to respect godly leadership.
Scripture commands Christians to receive correction.
Scripture praises wisdom that seeks counsel.
Scripture condemns arrogance, stubbornness, divisiveness, and rebellion.
So this is not permission to become unteachable.
But Scripture also does something else.
It places every shepherd beneath the Chief Shepherd.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
That distinction changes everything.
The question is not, “Should Christians listen to their pastors?”
Absolutely.
The deeper question is:
Does the Bible give a pastor universal veto authority over the ordinary personal decisions of another adult Christian?
When we examine Scripture carefully, the answer requires more nuance than either extreme allows.
Hebrews 13:17 is usually where the conversation begins:
“Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they are keeping watch over your souls…”
The Greek begins:
Πείθεσθε τοῖς ἡγουμένοις ὑμῶν καὶ ὑπείκετε
Peithesthe tois hēgoumenois hymōn kai hypeikete.
The words are significant.

Πείθεσθε — peithesthe comes from peithō, a word associated with persuading, being convinced, trusting, or yielding in response to persuasion. In Hebrews 13:17 it functions as an imperative and is commonly and legitimately translated “obey.” ὑπείκετε — hypeikete carries the idea of yielding or submitting.
So we should not weaken the verse until submission means nothing.
There really is biblical authority in the church.
There really is a responsibility to follow faithful spiritual leadership.
But notice what the verse says immediately afterward.
These leaders “keep watch over your souls” and will “give an account.”
The authority described here is therefore not the authority of an owner.
It is the responsibility of a steward.
The shepherd watches because the sheep belong to Someone Else.
And that Someone Else is Christ.
The New Testament never tells pastors, “These people belong to you.”
Peter says almost the opposite.
Writing to elders, he tells them to shepherd God’s flock, exercising oversight willingly and eagerly, but “not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:2–3).
Then Peter identifies the One above every earthly shepherd:
“the Chief Shepherd” (1 Peter 5:4).
That title belongs to Jesus.
Your pastor may be your shepherd.
But your pastor has a Shepherd.
Your pastor may exercise authority.
But your pastor remains under authority.
Your pastor may give counsel.
But your pastor does not become your conscience.
Your pastor may warn you.
He may correct you.
He may tell you that he believes you are making a terrible mistake.
And sometimes—please hear this—he may be right.
Sometimes the thing we call “control” is actually correction we do not want to hear.
Sometimes the pastor is not manipulating us at all.
Sometimes we are simply angry because someone loved us enough to confront our sin.
If Scripture clearly calls something sin, “God told me” cannot make it holy.

If you are committing adultery, stealing, lying, abandoning biblical responsibilities, practicing sexual immorality, pursuing greed, cultivating hatred, or deliberately violating the commands of Christ, you do not get to hide behind “personal conviction.”
God will never lead you contrary to what He has already revealed in His Word.
That matters enormously.
But there is another danger.
It is possible to turn legitimate spiritual authority into something Scripture never authorized.
Paul himself wrote something astonishing to the Corinthians:
οὐχ ὅτι κυριεύομεν ὑμῶν τῆς πίστεως
ouch hoti kyrieuomen hymōn tēs pisteōs
In 2 Corinthians 1:24, Paul says, in essence:
“Not that we lord it over your faith.”
The verb κυριεύομεν — kyrieuomen comes from kyrieuō, carrying the sense of exercising lordship or dominion.
Think about who is saying this.
Paul.
An apostle.
A man personally commissioned by the risen Christ.
A man through whom the Holy Spirit gave inspired Scripture to the church.
And yet Paul deliberately distinguishes apostolic ministry from lording over another believer’s faith.
Instead, he says they are “fellow workers” for the believers’ joy.
That should stop us.
If Paul could describe ministry that way, pastors should be very careful about language that effectively communicates:
“You cannot make this decision unless I authorize it.”
And Christians should be equally careful before handing another human being authority Christ never commanded them to surrender.
Jesus Himself established the pattern.
When the disciples became fascinated with power, Jesus pointed toward Gentile rulers who “lord it over” others.
Then He said:
“It shall not be so among you.”
Christian leadership was supposed to look different.
Greatness in Christ’s kingdom bends downward.
It serves.
It sacrifices.
It washes feet.
It carries burdens.
And ultimately it looks like Jesus Christ, who said that the Son of Man came “not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:25–28).
That is the shape of Christian authority.
Not domination.
Cruciform service.
A faithful pastor should increasingly help you depend upon Jesus—not increasingly make you incapable of functioning without the pastor’s personal approval.
That does not mean spiritual independence.
Biblical Christianity knows nothing of the arrogant believer who says, “Nobody can tell me anything. It’s just me and Jesus.”
That attitude is dangerous too.
Proverbs repeatedly praises counsel:
“Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety” (Proverbs 11:14).
And:
“Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed” (Proverbs 15:22).
Notice something beautiful.
Scripture says counselors.
Advisers.
Plural.
Wisdom welcomes voices.
Wisdom listens.
Wisdom does not surround itself exclusively with people who say what it wants to hear.
A mature believer should be able to sit before a pastor and say:
“Please tell me if you see something I am missing.”
That is not weakness.
That is wisdom.
A mature believer should be able to hear:
“I love you, but I think you are making a mistake.”

And instead of immediately shouting, “You’re controlling me!” the believer should go home, pray, open Scripture, examine motives, seek additional mature counsel, and ask God whether pride is making correction difficult to receive.
But counsel and permission are not identical.
That distinction may save someone reading this from two completely different disasters.
One disaster is rebellion disguised as freedom.
The other is control disguised as submission.
Neither resembles Jesus.
Consider the Bereans.
Paul preached to them, and Acts 17:11 says they received the message eagerly while “examining the Scriptures daily to see if these things were so.”
They tested the teaching of an apostle against Scripture.
And Luke calls them noble for doing it.
Think about that.
They did not dishonor Paul by opening their Bibles.
They honored truth.
Biblical submission does not require you to turn off discernment.
Biblical authority does not fear an open Bible.
A healthy pastor should be able to say:
“Do not believe something merely because I said it. Search the Scriptures. Follow Christ.”
That kind of pastor is not losing authority.
He is demonstrating it properly.
And this becomes especially important when Christians make major decisions.
Should you seek pastoral counsel before marriage?
Often, yes. Strongly.
Marriage is enormous. A wise pastor may see character issues romantic emotion has blinded you to.
But Scripture does not establish a universal rule saying every adult Christian marriage requires a pastor’s personal authorization to become morally legitimate before God.
Should you seek counsel before moving?
Certainly it can be wise.
A pastor may see spiritual, family, financial, or relational consequences you have overlooked.
But there is no New Testament command saying an adult believer may not relocate without pastoral permission.
Should you seek counsel before changing churches?
Absolutely.
Leaving in anger, bitterness, unresolved conflict, or resistance to legitimate discipline can reveal serious spiritual problems.
But no pastor owns a Christian.
Christ does.
Should you seek counsel before starting a ministry, changing careers, accepting a job, entering school, launching a business, or making another life-altering decision?
Wisdom says:
Do not despise godly counsel.
Humility says:
Listen carefully.
Love says:
Honor faithful shepherds.
Discernment says:
Test everything by Scripture.
Responsibility says:
You will ultimately answer to God for your obedience.
That last sentence can be terrifying.
Because sometimes we secretly want someone else to make every decision for us.
If the pastor chooses, then perhaps the pastor can carry the blame if everything collapses.
But spiritual maturity does not mean outsourcing your conscience.
There are matters where Scripture gives direct commands.
Obey them.
There are matters where Scripture gives principles.
Apply them prayerfully.
There are matters of wisdom where multiple choices may be morally permissible.
Seek counsel.
Examine your motives.
Count the cost.
Consider your responsibilities.
Listen to mature believers.
Pray.
Search Scripture.
And then walk before God with a clear conscience.
Romans 14 is especially illuminating because Paul addresses disputed matters among believers. His answer is not to appoint one Christian as the conscience of every other Christian.
He repeatedly brings the believer back before the Lord.
“Each of us will give an account of himself to God” (Romans 14:12).
That sentence destroys both pride and unhealthy dependence.
You belong to Jesus.
Which means you are not free to do whatever you want.
But it also means no human being becomes Jesus for you.
There is only one Lord of the conscience.
Christ.
There is only one Head of the church.
Christ.
There is only one Savior whose blood purchased you.
Christ.
There is only one Mediator between God and humanity.
Christ Jesus.
Your pastor did not die for your sins.
Jesus did.
Your pastor did not rise from the grave.
Jesus did.
Your pastor will not sit upon the throne at the final judgment.
Jesus will.
And any faithful pastor reading those words should be able to say:
Amen.
Because healthy shepherds do not want Christ’s throne.
They want people at Christ’s feet.
This is where the subject becomes painfully personal.
Maybe someone used spiritual authority to frighten you.
Maybe every disagreement was called rebellion.
Maybe questions were treated as betrayal.
Maybe leaving was described as abandoning God.
Maybe “submission” meant never saying no.
Maybe you learned to distrust your own ability to read Scripture because you were told only the leader could properly hear from God.
If that happened, do not respond by running into the opposite ditch.
Do not let abusive authority make you hate biblical authority.
Do not let a controlling shepherd make you suspicious of every shepherd.
Do not let wounds turn into permanent rebellion.
Jesus can heal what people misrepresented.
And perhaps the harder possibility is this:
Maybe your pastor was not controlling you.
Maybe he was warning you.
Maybe you called it manipulation because the truth hurt.
Maybe mature believers have repeatedly told you the relationship is unhealthy.
Maybe everyone who loves Jesus and genuinely knows you sees danger, but you have decided that anyone who disagrees with you “doesn’t understand what God told me.”
That should frighten you too.
Because refusing every warning is not spiritual maturity.
Sometimes God protects us through counsel.
Sometimes the answer to prayer arrives through an uncomfortable conversation.
Sometimes the shepherd sees the cliff before the sheep does.
The solution, therefore, is not:
“Ignore your pastor.”
Nor is it:
“Your pastor must approve everything.”
The biblical road is harder because it demands maturity.
Honor your leaders.
Receive correction.
Seek counsel.
Test teaching by Scripture.
Reject manipulation.
Reject rebellion.
Follow Jesus.
And never confuse the voice of a human shepherd with the voice of the Chief Shepherd.
There are times when a pastor may rightly say, “Scripture forbids what you are planning.”
In that case, the authority does not ultimately rest in the pastor’s preference.
It rests in God’s Word.
There are other times when a pastor may say, “Scripture does not explicitly forbid this, but based on what I know, I believe this is unwise.”
Take that seriously.
Very seriously.
You may discover later that the warning saved you years of pain.
But there is a difference between:
“I believe this would be unwise, and here is why.”
and
“God will punish you because you made a morally permissible personal decision without my permission.”
The first can be shepherding.
The second requires biblical evidence.
Whenever someone claims authority from God, Christians have every right—and responsibility—to ask:
Where does Scripture say that?
Not arrogantly.
Not mockingly.
Not rebelliously.
Humbly.
With an open Bible.
Because Scripture is not threatened by examination.
Neither is truth.
And neither should faithful Christian leadership be.
Maybe this article exposed something uncomfortable in you.
Perhaps you have been controlled.
Perhaps you have been rebellious.
Perhaps you have been afraid to make any decision without another person validating it.
Perhaps you have been calling stubbornness “discernment.”
Perhaps you are a leader and suddenly realize that somewhere along the way, shepherding quietly became controlling.
There is grace for that too.
This is the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely expose us.
He calls us home.
The controlling pastor can repent.
The rebellious Christian can repent.
The wounded believer can heal.
The frightened believer can learn to walk in wisdom.
The proud believer can become teachable.
The abused believer can rediscover healthy Christian community.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of people who got church leadership perfectly right.
It is the story of sinners rescued by a perfect Shepherd.
Jesus said:
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11).
There He is.
The Shepherd who does not exploit His sheep.
The Shepherd who bleeds for them.
The Shepherd who does not manipulate people into protecting His position.
The Shepherd who surrendered Himself at Calvary.
The Shepherd who bore our scandal.
Our pride.
Our rebellion.
Our fear.
Our religious hypocrisy.
Our lust for control.
Our desperate need for human approval.
He carried it into death.
And then the stone moved.
The Shepherd lives.
So perhaps the question underneath this entire article was never merely:
“Do I need my pastor’s permission?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
“Who truly owns my life?”
If the answer is Jesus, then you cannot use Christian freedom as permission for rebellion.
And nobody else can use Christian leadership as permission to possess you.
You are Christ’s.
That means you should become more humble, not less.
More teachable, not less.
More discerning, not less.
More accountable, not less.
More saturated in Scripture.
More willing to listen.
More willing to repent.
And more courageous when obedience to Christ costs you human approval.
Not because every disagreement with a pastor is abuse—it is not.
Both need Jesus.

One meaningful way believers can glorify God is through generous, voluntary support of sound Gospel work and by sharing truth with others; Scripture calls Christian giving willing rather than coerced (see 2 Corinthians 9:7).
But whatever you do after reading this, remember the truth beneath all of it:
A good pastor can counsel you.
A faithful pastor can warn you.
A biblical pastor can correct you.
A loving pastor can sometimes tell you something you desperately do not want to hear.
Honor that gift.
But the best pastors will eventually point beyond themselves and say:
“Follow Jesus.”
Because your pastor is a shepherd.
Jesus is the Shepherd.

And when every human voice has faded, every title has disappeared, every platform has fallen silent, and every earthly shepherd stands before God to give account, there will still be One with scars in His hands who purchased His people with His own blood.
Never give a human shepherd the throne that belongs to the Shepherd who died for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN THE HOLY SPIRIT LEAVE A BELIEVER? The Answer May Change the Way You Understand Every Dark Season of Your Faith
paragraphs: CAN THE HOLY SPIRIT LEAVE A BELIEVER? The Answer May Change the Way You Understand Every Dark Season of Your Faith

If you have ever sinned after coming to Christ, felt God become painfully quiet, watched your fire disappear, or secretly wondered whether the Holy Spirit finally became tired of you… please don’t leave this article halfway. Because the difference between grieving the Holy Spirit and losing the Holy Spirit may be the difference between running back to Jesus tonight… and spending years hiding from the One who was calling you home.
There is a particular kind of fear that Christians rarely admit out loud.
It usually comes after the fall.
After the temptation you promised God you would never return to.
After the angry words.
After the secret browser history.
After the relationship you knew was pulling you away from Christ.
After weeks without prayer.
After opening your Bible and realizing the words that once made your heart burn now seem strangely distant.
You remember how alive you once felt.
You remember worship when tears came without effort.
You remember conviction that felt almost immediate.
You remember wanting Jesus more than you wanted the world.
And now?
Silence.
So somewhere in that silence, a terrifying question begins whispering:
“Did the Holy Spirit leave me?”
Maybe you have never said it to anyone.
Maybe you still attend church.
Maybe you still raise your hands during worship.
Maybe your family thinks you are doing fine.
But privately, you are afraid that something happened between you and God that cannot be repaired.
And perhaps you have even found a Bible verse that seems to confirm your worst fear.
David cried:
“Cast me not away from thy presence; and take not thy holy spirit from me.”
Psalm 51:11, KJV.
There it is.
So does that settle it?
Can God give His Spirit to someone…and later take Him away?
Not so fast.

Because if we are going to answer this question faithfully, we cannot build an entire doctrine from one frightened sentence torn from its covenantal setting. We have to allow the whole counsel of Scripture to speak.
And when we do, something breathtaking begins to emerge.
Something terrifying to casual Christianity…
but deeply comforting to the repentant believer.
David’s prayer was real.
His fear was real.
His sin was horrifying.
Psalm 51 comes from the wreckage surrounding David’s sin with Bathsheba and the death of Uriah. David was not minimizing what he had done. He was shattered before God.
But David also lived under the Old Covenant and before Pentecost.
That matters.

In the Old Testament, the Spirit of God could come upon particular people for particular purposes and ministries. Saul provides one of Scripture’s sobering examples. First Samuel 16:14 tells us that the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul.
David knew Saul’s story.
He had watched what happened to a king whom God had rejected.

So when David pleaded, “take not thy holy spirit from me,” he was not writing a systematic New Testament explanation of regeneration. He was crying from inside an Old Covenant reality that preceded the finished work of Christ, His resurrection, ascension, and the outpouring of the Spirit at Pentecost.
Then Jesus came.
And Jesus said something extraordinary.
Speaking about the coming Helper, He promised that the Father would give His disciples “another Comforter” who would abide with them “for ever” (John 14:16, KJV).
The Greek expression is:
εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα — eis ton aiōna
Literally carrying the sense of continuing into the age — enduring, abiding.
Not until your next terrible week.
Not until you disappoint God.
Not until your emotions collapse.
Jesus pointed toward an abiding New Covenant presence.
Then Paul goes even further.
Ephesians 1:13 describes believers as having been:
ἐσφραγίσθητε — esphragisthēte
“sealed.”
The verb comes from σφραγίζω — sphragizō, associated with sealing, marking, authenticating, or identifying ownership.
Paul says believers were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit.
Then he describes the Spirit as:
ἀρραβών — arrabōn
a pledge, deposit, down payment, or guarantee of the inheritance to come.
Think about what Paul is communicating.
God does not merely give the believer a temporary spiritual sensation.
The Holy Spirit is God’s mark upon those who belong to Christ and the pledge of the inheritance God has promised.
Then comes a verse every terrified Christian needs to read slowly.
“And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption.”
Ephesians 4:30, KJV.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say, “Do not grieve the Spirit, or He will immediately abandon you.”
He warns Christians that they can grieve Him while simultaneously reminding them that they have been sealed unto the day of redemption.
The Greek word translated “grieve” is:
λυπεῖτε — lypeite
from λυπέω — lypeō: to cause sorrow, distress, or grief.
That word should destroy one dangerous misconception immediately.
The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal spiritual electricity.
He is not a religious atmosphere.
He is not goosebumps during worship.
He is not merely “the feeling” in the room when the music becomes emotional.
The Holy Spirit is personal and divine.
And sin matters because sin grieves Him.
So if you are asking, “Can I sin and nothing happens because I am sealed?”
You have misunderstood grace.
Grace is not God handing us permission to love what crucified Christ.
Grace teaches us to renounce ungodliness.
The believer should never hear assurance and translate it into permission for rebellion.
Paul anticipated that distortion centuries ago:
“Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.”
Romans 6:1–2, KJV.
This means we must hold two biblical truths together without sacrificing either one.
There is profound security in Christ.
And there are profound warnings against persistent, hardened, unrepentant rebellion.
Scripture refuses both cheap assurance and hopeless despair.
A person should not conclude, “I prayed a prayer twenty years ago, therefore I can reject Christ, embrace darkness, live without repentance, and Scripture gives me nothing to fear.”

The New Testament contains severe warnings about apostasy, false profession, hardening the heart, fruitless faith, and people who appear to belong to the covenant community but ultimately reveal something devastating about themselves.
First John 2:19 describes people who went out from the Christian community because, John says, they were not truly “of us.”
Jesus warned that not everyone who calls Him “Lord” actually belongs to Him.
Hebrews repeatedly warns against hardened unbelief and falling away.
Those warnings should never be erased.
But neither should frightened, repentant Christians take passages aimed at hardened rejection of Christ and use them to torture themselves because they stumbled and now desperately want Jesus again.
Those are not necessarily the same spiritual condition.
There is an enormous difference between fighting sin and making peace with sin.
Between falling and refusing to rise.
Between grieving the Spirit and despising Christ.
Between struggling against darkness and deciding darkness is your home.
Romans 8:9 gives us another crucial piece:
“If any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his.”
The Spirit’s indwelling is bound up with belonging to Christ.
And Romans 8 does not end by teaching frightened Christians to stare endlessly at themselves.
It lifts their eyes toward the faithfulness of God.
Nothing in creation, Paul declares, can separate those in Christ Jesus from the love of God.
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes grace astonishing.
Perhaps this is where the question becomes personal.
Maybe what you are experiencing is not abandonment.
Maybe it is conviction.
Maybe the reason your sin bothers you is not because God has disappeared but because the Spirit of God refuses to let you become comfortable in what is destroying you.
Think about that.
The numbness frightens you.
The distance hurts you.
You miss prayer.
You miss Scripture.
You miss who you were becoming.
Something inside you keeps whispering:
“Come back.”
And you interpreted that ache as proof God had abandoned you.
What if the ache itself is part of His mercy?
What if conviction is not God slamming the door?
What if conviction is God exposing what must die because He loves you too much to let sin quietly consume you?
There is a reason Scripture distinguishes grieving the Spirit from quenching the Spirit.
First Thessalonians 5:19 says:
“Quench not the Spirit.”
The Greek is striking:
τὸ πνεῦμα μὴ σβέννυτε — to pneuma mē sbennute
The verb σβέννυμι — sbennymi means to extinguish or quench.
The picture is fire.
You can resist His work.
Ignore conviction.
Feed the flesh.
Starve prayer.
Neglect Scripture.
Become spiritually dull.
You can repeatedly say “no” where God is calling you to obedience.
And eventually you may become so numb that yesterday’s conviction becomes tomorrow’s rationalization.
That is dangerous.
But spiritual dullness must not automatically be confused with the Spirit permanently departing from every genuine believer who falls.
Otherwise Peter’s story would become impossible to explain.
Peter did not merely have a bad afternoon.
He denied Jesus.
Three times.
At the moment when loyalty mattered most.
Imagine Peter hearing the rooster.
Imagine the eyes of Jesus.
Imagine remembering his own confident declaration that everybody else might fall away, but he never would.
Then watching himself become exactly the man he swore he could never become.
The Gospel says Peter went out and wept bitterly.
And if Christianity were merely the story of strong people proving their loyalty to God, Peter’s story should have ended there.
Failure.
Disqualified.
Finished.
But Jesus was not finished.
After the resurrection, Christ came back for the disciple who had collapsed.
Not to tell Peter his denial was insignificant.
Not to pretend sin did not matter.
Jesus brought Peter directly back to the wound.
“Lovest thou me?”
Again.
“Lovest thou me?”
Again.
“Lovest thou me?”
Three denials.
Three questions.
And then:
“Feed my sheep.”
Do you see the Gospel?
Jesus did not rewrite Peter’s past by pretending it never happened.
He rewrote Peter’s future by redeeming the man who had failed.
That is grace.
And maybe somebody reading this needs to stop believing the lie that your worst chapter gets to write your final chapter.
Maybe you betrayed your convictions.
Maybe you became addicted again.
Maybe you slept with someone you knew you should not.
Maybe anger poisoned your home.
Maybe pride destroyed relationships.
Maybe pornography quietly hollowed out your prayer life.
Maybe you became successful and stopped needing God.
Maybe church hurt turned into bitterness, and bitterness turned into distance, and distance turned into years.
Maybe nobody knows.
But Jesus does.
And the Gospel is not:
“Clean yourself up enough so God might tolerate your return.”
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ entered our scandal.
He bore our guilt.
He carried our judgment.
He died for sinners.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose victorious.
Your hope is not the strength of your grip on Christ.
Your hope is Christ.
Your righteousness is not your spiritual résumé.
Your righteousness is found in Him.
Your forgiveness was purchased with blood.
So come home.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you feel spiritual again.
Not after you manage seven perfect days.
Come while your hands are still shaking.
Come while your prayer feels awkward.
Come while your Bible feels unfamiliar.
Come while shame is screaming.
Confess what you did.
Call sin what God calls it.
Do not rename rebellion “a season.”
Do not call bondage “just who I am.”
Do not hide behind grace while protecting the thing Christ is commanding you to surrender.
First John 1:9 tells believers that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse.
Repentance does not purchase forgiveness.
Christ purchased forgiveness.
Repentance is the turning of the heart away from sin and toward the Savior.
And maybe the question that brought you here was:
“Can the Holy Spirit leave a believer?”

Within historic Christian theology, traditions differ over questions surrounding final apostasy and perseverance. Some emphasize that truly regenerated believers will ultimately persevere because God preserves them; others understand the New Testament’s apostasy warnings as indicating that a genuine believer must continue abiding in Christ and can ultimately fall away through decisive rejection.
We should be honest about that disagreement rather than pretending sincere Christians have never debated these passages.
But several things are unmistakably clear in Scripture.
Those who belong to Christ have His Spirit.
The Holy Spirit is not presented as a disposable guest who vanishes every time a Christian stumbles.
Jesus promised His Helper’s abiding presence.
Believers are described as sealed with the Spirit.
The Spirit is called the pledge of our inheritance.
Christians can grieve Him.
Christians are commanded not to quench His work.
Christians are commanded to walk by the Spirit.
And persistent, hardened unbelief must never be treated casually.
So if you have fallen into sin, the biblical response is not to sit in a dark room endlessly asking whether God has finally stopped wanting you.
Repent.
Run to Christ.
Confess.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Open Scripture again.
Ask mature believers to walk with you.
If necessary, seek pastoral help and accountability.
Stop negotiating with the thing that is killing your fellowship with God.
But do not confuse the voice of condemnation with the voice of conviction.
Condemnation says:
“Hide from Jesus.”
Conviction says:
“Run to Jesus.”
Condemnation says:
“You sinned, therefore there is no way home.”
The Gospel says:
“You sinned. Stop hiding. The way home was opened by the blood of Christ.”
Remember Adam.
After sin entered the garden, humanity’s instinct was hiding.
We have been hiding ever since.
Behind religion.
Behind ministry.
Behind jokes.
Behind church attendance.
Behind theology.
Behind “I’m blessed.”
Behind “God is good.”
While privately bleeding.
But Jesus came looking for sinners.
That is the scandal of grace.
The Holy One moved toward the unholy.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
The King wore thorns.
The Judge received judgment.
The Author entered the ruined story.
And the cross became the place where justice and mercy met.
So no…
your sin is not small.
But neither is His cross.
Your failure is not imaginary.
But neither is His blood.
Your rebellion matters.
But resurrection matters more.
And if you belong to Christ, your story is not fundamentally the story of how perfectly you held yourself together.
It is the story of a Savior powerful enough to rescue, sanctify, restore, discipline, transform, and finish what He began.
Maybe you need to say something publicly today that breaks the secrecy.
There are moments when three words are enough to open a door someone has kept locked for years.
And if someone came into your mind while reading this, do not ignore that.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to preach at them.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
We glorify God through Christ-centered faith, worship, obedience, love, generosity, and faithful witness—not through a financial transaction.
But if this ministry is helping people encounter biblical truth, then supporting and sharing the work can become one practical way of participating in spreading that truth.
They may never open a Christian book.
But tonight they might stop at this question:
“Can the Holy Spirit leave a believer?”
And underneath that theological question may be a human being desperately wondering:
“Does Jesus still want me?”
Let your share become the doorway.

Because the enemy loves attacking believers with old accusations when they are tired, ashamed, isolated, and spiritually weak. Come back to these Scriptures. Test every emotional accusation against the Word of God.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend drifting from church.
Invite the believer secretly struggling.
Invite the skeptic.
Invite the person everyone assumes is spiritually strong.
Sometimes the person posting Bible verses is fighting a war nobody can see.
Not to buy God’s favor.
Not to purchase salvation.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior somehow proves that you love Jesus.
Salvation is by grace.
Christ cannot be purchased.
But believers can freely choose to support Gospel work they believe is faithfully serving others.

More importantly, your support helps this ministry continue producing Scripture-centered content designed to call people away from hiding, compromise, despair, and spiritual numbness—and toward repentance, grace, forgiveness, discipleship, and transformation through Jesus Christ.
But before you leave, hear this.
If you came to this article terrified that the Holy Spirit had abandoned you because you failed…
do not spend tonight staring at your failure.
Look at Christ.
Look at the cross.
Look at the empty tomb.
Confess what needs confessing.
Surrender what needs surrendering.
Destroy what needs destroying.
Forgive whom you need to forgive.
Ask for help where you need help.
And come home.
Because perhaps the most heartbreaking possibility is not that God stopped calling…
but that shame convinced you to stop listening.
The rooster that announced Peter’s greatest failure did not announce the end of Peter’s story.
Jesus was already writing the next page.
And He is still the Savior who turns denial into devotion, shame into testimony, brokenness into surrender, and scandal into grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT IS THE ONE SIN GOD WILL NEVER FORGIVE?
paragraphs: WHAT IS THE ONE SIN GOD WILL NEVER FORGIVE?
The Terrifying Warning of Jesus—and Why the Person Afraid They’ve Committed It May Be Missing the Most Important Part of the Story
There is a sentence from the mouth of Jesus that has kept people awake at night.
Not because they hate God.
Because they desperately want Him.

They remember something they said years ago. A season when they mocked Christianity. A terrible thought that entered their mind during prayer. A moment of anger when they cursed God. A period when they walked away from church, resisted conviction, laughed at something holy, lived rebelliously, or deliberately did something they knew was wrong.
Then one day they encounter the words of Jesus:
“Blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.”
And suddenly their stomach drops.
What if that was me?
What if I crossed a line?
What if I came back too late?
What if everyone keeps telling me about grace…but there is no grace left for me?
That fear becomes even more terrifying when you realize Jesus really did speak about a sin that would not be forgiven.
This is not a theological myth designed by medieval preachers to frighten people.
Jesus said it.
So we should not soften His warning.
But we should not distort it either.
Because when you read His words in their actual biblical setting, something startling happens.
The warning becomes even more serious than many people realize…
and, at the same time, it becomes profoundly hopeful for the trembling person who fears they are beyond the mercy of Christ.
Listen carefully to Jesus:
“Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.”
Matthew 12:31
The Greek is striking:
πᾶσα ἁμαρτία καὶ βλασφημία ἀφεθήσεται τοῖς ἀνθρώποις, ἡ δὲ τοῦ πνεύματος βλασφημία οὐκ ἀφεθήσεται.
“Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people, but the blasphemy of the Spirit will not be forgiven.”
Before your eyes race toward the terrifying second half, notice what Jesus said first.
“Every sin and blasphemy…”
Every.
That word matters.
Jesus begins this terrifying warning by declaring something astonishing about the reach of forgiveness.
Human beings have committed atrocities.
People have betrayed those they loved.
People have destroyed marriages.
People have stolen.
People have lied.
People have worshiped idols.
People have lived sexually immoral lives.
People have hated God.
People have mocked Christ.
People have persecuted Christians.
People have ruined years of their lives through addictions and secret sins.
People have carried things into church that nobody sitting beside them knew existed.
And yet the Gospel announces that the blood of Jesus Christ is powerful enough to cleanse sinners who repent and come to Him in faith.
Paul himself had once been a persecutor of Christians.
He approved while Stephen was killed.
He hunted followers of Jesus.
Yet Paul later wrote:
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.”
1 Timothy 1:15
That sentence should destroy one of Satan’s favorite lies.
The lie that says:
“You have done too much.”
Paul did not build his hope on the smallness of his sin.
He built his hope on the greatness of Christ.
That distinction changes everything.
Christianity does not say your sin is insignificant.
Christianity says your Savior is greater.
But Jesus nevertheless gives one terrifying exception.
What is it?
To understand it, we cannot rip Matthew 12:31 out of the story surrounding it.
Something had just happened.
A demon-oppressed man who was blind and mute was brought to Jesus. Christ healed him.
The crowd was astonished.
They began asking whether Jesus might actually be the promised Son of David—the Messiah.
The Pharisees saw what was happening.
They saw the evidence.
And instead of bowing before Christ, they made an accusation.
“This man casts out demons only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons.”
Matthew 12:24
Think about what they were doing.
They were looking at the liberating work of God taking place through Jesus Christ and deliberately identifying it with Satan.
Mark’s Gospel makes the connection even more explicit.
Jesus warns:
“Whoever blasphemes against the Holy Spirit never has forgiveness, but is guilty of an eternal sin.”
Mark 3:29
Then Mark immediately tells us why Jesus said this:
“for they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit.’”
Mark 3:30
That sentence is crucial.
The warning did not appear in a vacuum.
Jesus was responding to people who were witnessing His works and perversely calling the work of the Holy Spirit demonic.
The Greek expression in Mark is:
βλασφημήσῃ εἰς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον
“blasphemes against the Holy Spirit.”
And Jesus says such a person:
οὐκ ἔχει ἄφεσιν εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα
“does not have forgiveness forever.”
These are severe words.
We do Christianity no favors by pretending Jesus did not mean them.
But neither should we turn His warning into something He never said.
Jesus did not say:
“Whoever has an intrusive blasphemous thought cannot be forgiven.”
He did not say:
“Whoever once became angry with God cannot be forgiven.”
He did not say:
“Whoever doubts cannot be forgiven.”
He did not say:
“Whoever falls badly into sin cannot be forgiven.”
He did not say:
“Whoever once speaks foolishly about spiritual things cannot be forgiven.”
Peter denied Jesus three times.
And Jesus restored Peter.
Paul persecuted Christ’s church.
And Jesus saved Paul.
Thomas doubted.
Jesus met Thomas in his doubt.
The Corinthian church had people whose former lives included devastating patterns of sin, yet Paul could write:
1 Corinthians 6:11
That is the scandal of grace.
“Such were some of you.”
Were.
The Gospel can put your darkest identity into the past tense.
Not because you became good enough to erase your history.
Because Jesus entered history carrying a cross.
The unforgivable sin, understood in the setting of Jesus’ warning, is not a frightened believer accidentally arranging the wrong words inside their head.

It is connected with a profound, hardened rejection and slander of the Holy Spirit’s testimony to Christ—seeing the light and calling it darkness, encountering the work of God and perversely identifying it with evil.
This is why the warning should make every hardened heart tremble.
Not because God is reluctant to forgive repentant sinners.
But because a heart can become so committed to rejecting the truth that it refuses the very One to whom the Spirit is pointing.
Jesus.
And here is the frightening paradox:
The problem is not that a repentant sinner runs desperately toward Jesus and discovers that Jesus refuses to forgive him.
The problem is the heart that becomes so hardened against the Spirit’s testimony concerning Christ that it refuses to run to Jesus at all.
Imagine a physician standing beside a dying patient holding the only medicine that can save him.
The horror is not that the medicine lacks power.
The horror is that the patient calls the medicine poison and refuses the hand offering it.
That is why this subject cannot merely become theological trivia.
This is about your heart.
Right now.
Because there is another question hiding underneath the question, “What is the unforgivable sin?”
The deeper question is:
What are you doing with Jesus?
You can spend hours researching whether you crossed an invisible theological line while avoiding the Savior standing in front of you.
Maybe that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Perhaps you did not open this article because you were curious.
Perhaps you opened it because you are afraid.
You remember the night.
The relationship.
The betrayal.
The pornography.
The affair.
The abortion.
The lie.
The hatred.
The addiction.
The years of pretending.
The private messages.
The secret habit.
The person you hurt.
The prayers you stopped praying.
The church you walked away from.
The promises you made to God and broke three days later.
Maybe people look at you and see someone functioning normally.
You go to work.
You laugh.
You scroll.
You answer messages.
You post photographs.
You tell people you are fine.
But when the room becomes quiet, another voice starts talking.
“You knew better.”
“You failed again.”
“God is tired of you.”
“You had your chance.”
“You cannot come back after that.”
And perhaps the most painful one:
“Maybe God would forgive other people…but not you.”
Listen to the Gospel.
That voice is not the final authority over your soul.
Jesus Christ is.
The apostle John wrote:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
1 John 1:9
Notice that forgiveness rests upon God’s character.
“He is faithful and just…”
The cross means Christian forgiveness is not God casually pretending evil never happened.
Sin is serious.
So serious that the Son of God went to the cross.
At Calvary, Jesus did not minimize sin.
He bore sin.
“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree…”
1 Peter 2:24
This is why grace is scandalous.
Grace does not look at a guilty person and say, “You were never guilty.”
Grace looks directly at guilt and points toward a crucified Savior.
Jesus was betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
And on the third day, He rose.
The Christian hope is not that humanity eventually learns to repair itself.
The Christian hope is that Jesus saves sinners.

And if your heart is grieving over sin, longing for Christ, wanting forgiveness, and terrified that you have somehow placed yourself beyond His mercy, do not confuse that grief with the hardened hostility Jesus confronted in Matthew 12 and Mark 3.
Run toward Christ.
Do not turn your fear into another hiding place.
Confess your sin.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Repentance is more than feeling terrible about yourself.
Biblical repentance turns.
It stops defending darkness and turns toward the Light.
It stops saying, “I need to make myself clean enough to approach Jesus.”
It says, “Jesus, I cannot cleanse myself. Have mercy on me.”
Remember the tax collector in Jesus’ parable.
He would not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He simply cried:
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner!”
Luke 18:13
Jesus said that man went home justified.
Maybe somebody needs to read that twice.
The man did not walk home justified because he gave God an impressive speech.
He walked home justified because he came empty-handed for mercy.
This is where Christianity is radically different from the religion we instinctively build inside ourselves.
We want ladders.
Jesus gives us a cross.
We want to prove ourselves.
Jesus tells us to come.
We want to pay.
Jesus says the debt has been dealt with through Him.
We want to rewrite our past.
Jesus gives us a new future.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming the sinner caught inside it.
But there is another side to Jesus’ warning that we dare not ignore.
If you hear the Gospel today, do not use grace as an excuse to keep resisting God.
Do not say, “I can repent later.”
You do not know how many tomorrows you have.
And repeated resistance to truth does something dangerous to the human heart.
Sin rarely walks into your life announcing:
“I have come to destroy you.”
It whispers:
“Just once.”
Then:
“One more time.”
Then:
“You can stop whenever you want.”
Then:
“This is simply who you are.”
Eventually the thing that once disturbed your conscience can begin to feel normal.
That is why Scripture says:
“Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”
Hebrews 3:15
Today.
Not because Jesus is unwilling to receive tomorrow’s repentant sinner.
But because Scripture never teaches us to gamble with tomorrow.
If the Spirit is exposing something in you now, respond now.
If there is sin to confess, confess it.
If there is someone you must forgive, begin dealing with it.
If you have been hiding, step into the light.
If you have been living two lives, stop negotiating with the darkness.
If you walked away from Jesus, turn toward Him.
You do not need a polished prayer.
You need honesty.
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
Sometimes that is where resurrection begins.
And maybe the fact that this article has unsettled you is not something to run from.
Maybe conviction is mercy knocking.
There is a difference between condemnation that drives you hopelessly away from Christ and godly conviction that exposes sin and calls you toward repentance and life.
The Gospel does not say:
“Clean yourself up and perhaps Jesus will accept you.”
Jesus says:
“Come to me…”
Matthew 11:28
Come.
With the wreckage.
With the questions.
With the shame.
With the history you wish you could delete.
Come.
But come ready to surrender.
Grace is free, but grace is not permission to remain comfortably enslaved to the thing Christ died to save us from.
The Jesus who forgives also transforms.
The Jesus who receives sinners calls sinners to follow Him.
The Jesus who said, “Neither do I condemn you” also said, “go, and from now on sin no more” (John 8:11).
Forgiveness and transformation belong together.
And maybe someone reading this has been waiting for permission to come home.
Here it is:
Do not wait until you feel worthy.
You never will.
Come because Christ is worthy.
Come because His blood is sufficient.
Come because the tomb is empty.
Come because the Gospel is still good news for sinners.
Come because the prodigal did not wash the pigsty off himself before beginning the journey home.
He arose and went to his father.
And while he was still a long way off, his father saw him.
That image from Luke 15 has broken hard hearts for generations.
The son had rehearsed his shame.
The father was already moving toward him.
That does not make rebellion beautiful.
It makes mercy breathtaking.
Maybe you are still rehearsing your speech.
Maybe Jesus is calling you to stop rehearsing and come.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to tell strangers every detail. But you can stop pretending.

Or tell your testimony. Someone scrolling beneath this article may believe they are too far gone, and the story of what Christ has done in your life may be exactly what reminds them that grace still reaches sinners.
And please do not keep a message like this trapped on your screen.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who will never tell you what they are fighting.
Not as a religious performance.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
It does not.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by social-media engagement.
“Can Jesus still forgive me?”
Send it privately to the person who needs hope.
Share it with the believer drowning in shame.
Share it with the skeptic who thinks Christianity is only for respectable people.
Share it with the person who thinks their scandal has already written the final chapter.
Because shame has a habit of returning at 2:00 in the morning and trying to make you forget everything grace told you in the daylight.
Come back and remember:
Peter failed.
Paul persecuted.
The prodigal ran.
Sinners came.
Christ received.
Grace rewrote stories.
If you genuinely want to glorify God, glorify Him first through trusting Christ, obeying His Word, loving people, serving faithfully, giving generously as He leads, and making the Gospel known.
Then invite someone else to come with you.
Family.
Friends.
Struggling believers.
Seekers.
People who have grown lukewarm.
Even the person who says they do not believe any of this.
Because eternity matters more than algorithms.
And people matter more than numbers.
And now return to the question that brought you here.
What is the one sin God will never forgive?
Jesus warned about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.

In its immediate Gospel context, this involved hardened opposition to the Spirit’s testimony displayed through Christ—so hardened that people looked upon the liberating work of God and attributed it to Satan.
That warning is real.
Do not mock it.
Do not dilute it.
Do not play games with persistent resistance to God.
But neither should a broken, repentant person take Jesus’ warning and use it as evidence that Christ refuses everyone who comes trembling for mercy.
The same Jesus who issued that terrifying warning stretched His arms upon a cross for sinners.
So if your heart is asking:
“Is there mercy for me?”
Do not spend the rest of your life staring at your sin trying to determine whether it is stronger than the blood of Christ.
Look at Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Come.
The question is not whether your past is ugly enough to need a Savior.
It is.
The question is whether Jesus is mighty enough to save sinners.
He is.
Your scandal may explain yesterday.
It does not have authority to write tomorrow.
Jesus does.
And perhaps that is the sentence you need to carry with you when this article is over:
Your darkest chapter does not get the final sentence when the Author of redemption is still holding the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What God Sees in Secret Should Terrify Your Hypocrisy—and Heal Your Hidden Heart
paragraphs: What God Sees in Secret Should Terrify Your Hypocrisy—and Heal Your Hidden Heart

You have a life people can see. Then you have the life behind the closed door, beneath the smile, underneath the worship song, beyond the carefully chosen words. Jesus says the Father sees that life too—and what He does with what He sees may completely change the way you understand secrecy, repentance, prayer, grace, and yourself.
There is a version of you that people know.
They know the version that answers, “I’m good.”
The version that walks into church.
The version that posts the verse.
The version that says the right thing when somebody asks how your relationship with God is going.
They see your clothes.
Your smile.
Your ministry.
Your family pictures.
Your comments.
Your Christian posts.
Maybe even your Bible highlighted on the table.
But there is another room.
And almost nobody gets invited there.
It is the room where the phone screen glows after everyone else has gone to sleep.
The room where resentment gets rehearsed.
Where temptation negotiates.
Where jealousy whispers.
Where loneliness becomes unbearable.
Where you replay what somebody did to you and imagine saying everything you were too afraid to say.
Where prayers sometimes sound less like sermons and more like:
“God… I don’t know how much longer I can do this.”
There are tears nobody has photographed.
Questions you would never post.
Desires you would be ashamed to admit.
Battles your friends do not know you are fighting.
And perhaps sins you have become very skilled at hiding.
Then Jesus says something that destroys the illusion that any of that room is actually empty.
In Matthew 6, while confronting religious performance, Jesus repeatedly speaks about “your Father who sees in secret.”
The Greek is striking:
ὁ πατήρ σου ὁ βλέπων ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ
ho patēr sou ho blepōn en tō kryptō
Literally, the thought is: your Father—the One seeing in the secret place.
That last word matters.
κρυπτός — kryptos carries the sense of what is hidden, concealed, inward, secret.
Jesus is talking about the place beyond the audience.
And notice something beautiful before you notice something frightening.
He does not merely say:
“God sees.”
He says:
“your Father… sees.”
That changes everything.
Because the eyes looking into your secret place are not merely the eyes of a cosmic investigator searching for enough evidence to destroy you.
For those who belong to Christ, these are the eyes of the Father.
But do not make that sentimental.
The Father who loves you is holy.
And holy love refuses to make peace with the thing destroying the person it loves.
That is why what God sees in secret should change you.
Because secrecy does something dangerous to the human heart.
It makes us believe that unseen means insignificant.
Nobody found out.
Nobody confronted me.
Nothing happened.
So maybe it is okay.
But Scripture demolishes that illusion.
Psalm 139 says:
“O LORD, thou hast searched me, and known me.”
The Hebrew verb translated “searched” is חָקַר — ḥāqar, carrying the idea of searching out, examining, investigating.
David continues:
“Thou knowest my downsitting and mine uprising, thou understandest my thought afar off.”
And then comes the sentence from which there is nowhere left to hide:
“For there is not a word in my tongue, but, lo, O LORD, thou knowest it altogether.”
God does not merely know what you eventually did.
He knows what you almost did.
He knows why you wanted to do it.
He knows the wound underneath the anger.
The pride underneath the argument.
The insecurity underneath the boasting.
The hunger underneath the addiction.
The envy underneath the criticism.
The fear underneath the control.
The unbelief underneath the anxiety.
He sees beneath behavior into motive.
And that means Christianity cannot ultimately be sustained as reputation management.
Jesus makes that painfully clear in Matthew 6.
He talks about giving.
Prayer.
Fasting.
These are good things.
Holy things.
Things religious people are supposed to do.
Yet Jesus warns that even holy activities can become spiritually corrupted when the hidden motive is human applause.
He warns against practicing righteousness “before men, to be seen of them.”
The Greek verb behind “to be seen” is related to θεάομαι — theaomai, to be observed or noticed.
In other words, Jesus is exposing something uncomfortable:
You can do something that looks like worship while secretly worshiping the attention it brings you.
You can pray to God while performing for people.
You can give money while feeding your ego.
You can speak about humility while secretly craving recognition.
You can post Scripture because you love Christ.
And you can post the same Scripture because you love being perceived as someone who loves Christ.
Same verse.
Same post.
Different altar.
That is why the secret place matters.
Because the crowd sees the action.
God sees the reason.
And eventually you have to ask yourself a terrifying question:
If nobody ever knew I did this, would I still do it for Jesus?
Would you still pray if nobody called you a prayer warrior?
Would you still give if your name disappeared from the donor list?
Would you still serve if somebody else received the credit?
Would you still worship if nobody could hear your voice?
Would you still obey if obedience cost you the image you spent years building?
Would you still follow Christ if following Him made you less impressive instead of more impressive?
Because one of the most dangerous spiritual conditions is learning how to appear alive while becoming hollow inside.
Jesus confronted precisely this kind of religion.
But perhaps your secret place contains something different.
Maybe you are not hiding spiritual pride.
Maybe you are hiding pain.
You love Jesus.
But you are exhausted.
You have encouraged everybody else while wondering who will encourage you.
You have prayed for other marriages while yours feels cold.
You have told other people God provides while quietly calculating whether you can survive another month.
You have smiled in church while grief sat beside you like an invisible stranger.
Nobody noticed.
God did.
That changes the meaning of “God sees in secret.”
Because those words are not only a warning to hypocrites.
They are comfort for the forgotten.
The Father saw the prayer nobody applauded.
He saw you close the browser when temptation was screaming.
He saw you delete the message you knew you should not send.
He saw you forgive somebody who never apologized.
He saw you open your Bible with shaking hands when you barely had enough faith to read another promise.
He saw you whisper the name “Jesus” because it was the only prayer you had left.
People may never know how close you came to giving up.
Your Father does.
People may congratulate you for strength you never felt.
Your Father knows how much it cost simply to remain standing.
And suddenly the secret place is no longer merely frightening.
It becomes sacred.
Jesus says in Matthew 6:6:
“But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret…”
Think about that.
Shut the door.
The world is addicted to being seen.
Jesus tells you to disappear.
Not forever.
Not because public worship is wrong.
Not because every public expression of faith is hypocrisy.
But because there must be somewhere in your life where God is enough of an audience.
Somewhere there is no applause.
No analytics.
No comments.
No likes.
No reputation to protect.
Just you.
And God.
That room will tell the truth about you.
But here is where this message can be terribly misunderstood.
Someone will read “God sees everything you do in secret” and immediately imagine Christianity as surveillance.
God caught you.
God saw the pornography.
God heard the lie.
God knows about the affair.
God saw what you stole.
God heard what you said about them.
God knows the secret addiction.
God knows what you did years ago.
Therefore:
Run.
Hide.
Pretend.
Clean yourself up.
Then perhaps God will tolerate you.
But that is not the Gospel.
Yes, God sees the sin.
Scripture gives us no permission to soften that reality.
Hebrews 4:13 says that no creature is hidden from His sight; everything is exposed before the One to whom we must give account.
Sin is not made harmless because it is private.
Secret sin still damages.
Secret bitterness still poisons.
Secret lust still trains the heart.
Secret pride still corrupts worship.
Secret dishonesty still bends the soul away from truth.
And repentance cannot mean merely becoming better at hiding consequences.
The Greek word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō.
Biblical repentance involves a genuine turning of mind and heart toward God that bears fruit in a changed direction.
Not perfection purchased by human effort.
Not theatrical remorse.
Not crying because you got caught.
Turning.
Coming into the light.
Agreeing with God about what sin actually is.
And then something astonishing happens.
The Gospel tells us that the God who completely knows the sinner is the God who sent His Son to save sinners.
Jesus did not die for the polished version of you.
He died knowing the truth.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after the rehabilitation.
Not after the deleted history.
Not after the addiction disappeared.
Not after the apology.
Not after you finally became impressive enough for heaven.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible without despair.
Because the cross tells you that exposure does not have to be the end of your story.
Peter knew something about that.
He had promised Jesus loyalty.
Then came the courtyard.
Pressure.
Fear.
A question.
Then denial.
Again.
Again.
Luke tells us that after Peter's third denial:
“the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter.”
Imagine that moment.
The eyes of Jesus.
The man who had said he would never abandon Him.
The disciple who had boasted about his loyalty.
Now exposed.
Peter remembered the words of Jesus.
Then Scripture says:
“Peter went out, and wept bitterly.”
The look broke him.
But Jesus was not finished with Peter.
After the resurrection, John 21 records Jesus restoring him.
“Lovest thou me?”
“Feed my sheep.”
The failure was real.
The grief was real.
The restoration was real.
Peter's worst moment did not receive permission to become his final identity.
That is grace.
Grace does not rewrite history by pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace rewrites what the scandal gets to become.
Peter's denial became part of the testimony of a man restored by Christ.
The cross itself looked like scandal.
The Messiah mocked.
Stripped.
Rejected.
Crucified between criminals.
His followers scattered.
His body placed in a tomb.
It looked finished.
Then Sunday came.
And this is why our theme is not merely a slogan.
He rewrites shame into testimony.
Bondage into freedom.
Rebellion into repentance.
Enemies into sons and daughters.
The condemned into the justified.
The lost into the found.
The spiritually dead into the alive.
But notice the wording carefully:
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not us.
Christianity is not self-reinvention.
It is resurrection.
And maybe this is where the article stops being about “people” and becomes about you.
Because you know what your secret is.
I don't.
Your spouse might not.
Your pastor might not.
Your parents might not.
Your children might not.
Your followers certainly might not.
But while reading this, something came to mind.
A name.
A habit.
A memory.
A browser.
A conversation.
A relationship.
A resentment.
A compromise.
Something.
And your instinct may be to close this before the discomfort gets any deeper.
But what if conviction is not God pushing you away?
What if it is God refusing to let you comfortably continue walking toward something that will destroy you?
First John 1:9 gives sinners one of Scripture's great promises:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
The Greek verb translated “confess” is ὁμολογέω — homologeō, literally carrying the sense of acknowledging, admitting, saying the same thing.
Confession stops negotiating with darkness.
“This is sin.”
“I did it.”
“I cannot justify it.”
“I need mercy.”
And Christianity gives you somewhere to take that confession.
Not into a spiritual void.
To Jesus Christ.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One about whom 1 Peter 2:24 says:
“Who his own self bare our sins in his own body on the tree…”
This is where secret shame loses its ultimate weapon.
Shame says:
“If the truth becomes known, you are finished.”
The Gospel says:
“God already knows the truth—and Christ is able to save.”
That is not permission to keep sinning secretly.
It is the strongest reason to stop hiding.
You cannot shock an omniscient God with information He already possesses.
You can only continue resisting the mercy to which He is calling you.
So tonight, perhaps your prayer does not need sophisticated language.
Maybe it needs truth.
“Jesus, You see it.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I cannot keep living two lives.”
“Jesus, change what I secretly love.”
“Jesus, teach me to desire You more than this sin.”
“Jesus, heal what I keep hiding.”
“Jesus, make me the same person when the door closes.”
That last prayer is dangerous.
Because God may answer it.
He may expose idols.
He may require an apology.
He may lead you to make restitution.
He may tell you to end a sinful relationship.
He may move you to seek mature Christian accountability.
He may force you to confront the bitterness you have renamed “boundaries.”
He may show you that the person you have been blaming is not the only person who needs repentance.
He may dismantle the public version of Christianity you have been using to protect the private version of yourself.
But freedom is worth losing the mask.
And for somebody else reading this, the issue is not hidden rebellion.
It is hidden faithfulness.
You have been doing the right thing without recognition for so long that you are beginning to wonder whether it matters.
Listen carefully.
Your Father sees in secret.
Do not trade His gaze for the applause of people.
The world may never celebrate the night you resisted temptation.
He saw it.
Nobody may understand the sacrifice required for you to remain faithful.
He knows.
Nobody may repost your obedience.
He sees.
Nobody may congratulate you for refusing to retaliate.
He sees.
Nobody may know that you gave when money was tight.
He sees.
Nobody may know you prayed for the person who wounded you.
He sees.
There is something extraordinarily freeing about becoming convinced that the most important Person in the universe already sees you.
You no longer have to advertise every good thing.
You no longer have to construct an image of holiness.
You can simply pursue holiness.
You can stop performing intimacy with God and actually become intimate with God.
And perhaps that is what “God sees in secret” should ultimately change in us.
It should make hypocrisy frightening.
It should make hidden faithfulness meaningful.
It should make prayer intimate.
It should make repentance urgent.
It should make grace astonishing.
And it should make Jesus precious.
Because there is only One who knew the complete truth about humanity and still willingly walked toward the cross.
So do not leave this article merely thinking:
“I need to hide better.”
Leave saying:
“I want Christ to change me deeper.”
Not image management.
Transformation.
Not religious performance.
Communion.
Not pretending.
Repentance.
Not despair.
Grace.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to describe your private sin publicly. But you can mark this moment honestly.
