Stop feeding yourself media that deliberately awakens what you are asking God to help you govern.
Do not repeatedly walk toward the cliff and then pray for supernatural brakes.
Paul does not say negotiate with sexual immorality.
He says:
φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν — pheugete tēn porneian
“Flee sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18).
Flee.
Sometimes holiness looks incredibly spiritual.
Sometimes holiness looks like leaving.
Closing the tab.
Ending the conversation.
Going home.
Changing seats.
Blocking the account.
Calling someone.
Turning on the light.
Getting out of bed.
Opening the door.
Running.
Joseph did not remain beside Potiphar's wife to demonstrate how mature he was.
He fled (Genesis 39:12).
There are moments when running away is not cowardice.
It is worship.
But there is another danger here.
Some Christians begin to believe marriage will solve everything.
“If I could just get married…”
Then the fantasies would stop.
The pornography would disappear.
The loneliness would vanish.
The battle would finally be over.
Scripture never promises that.

Marriage is holy, beautiful, and honorable. Paul even acknowledges the reality of sexual passion when discussing marriage in 1 Corinthians 7:9. But marriage is not a rehabilitation program for an undiscipled heart.
A wedding ring cannot do the work of the Holy Spirit.
If you have trained your mind for years to consume bodies, marriage does not magically teach you covenant love.
If you have learned to use sexual release as medication for stress, marriage does not automatically create self-control.
If you expect another human being to satisfy every lonely place inside you, you are placing a weight on your future spouse that no human being was created to carry.
Your spouse cannot be your savior.
Only Jesus can occupy that throne.
And yes, this means there may be nights when obedience hurts.
We need to say that because shallow Christian advice can become cruel.
Sometimes you will pray and still feel desire.
Sometimes you will worship and still feel lonely.
Sometimes you will quote Scripture and your body will not instantly become quiet.
Sometimes you will watch friends get engaged while you go home alone.
Again.
Sometimes someone will tell you, “Just be content in Jesus,” and although the statement contains truth, the way they say it will make you feel guilty for ever wanting marriage.
But the Bible does not require you to pretend that good desires do not hurt when they remain unmet.
Jesus Himself experienced sorrow without sin.
Biblical faith does not mean emotional anesthesia.
You can say:
“Lord, I want marriage.”
“Lord, I want intimacy.”
“Lord, I am tired of sleeping alone.”
“Lord, this desire is strong tonight.”
“Lord, I don't understand why You have not answered this prayer.”
And then you can say the sentence that turns longing into worship:
“But I still belong to You.”
That is costly worship.
When nobody applauds.
When nobody sees.
When there is no romantic ending yet.
When obedience gives you no immediate emotional reward.
When your body says now…
and your faith says:
Jesus is worth waiting for.
But what if you already failed?
That may be why you are still reading.
Maybe this stopped being theoretical paragraphs ago.
You slept with someone.
You went farther than you intended.
You have watched things you wish you could erase from your memory.
Maybe masturbation, fantasy, sexting, pornography, hookups, or an emotionally tangled relationship has become part of your hidden life.
Maybe you have repented so many times that even saying “I'm sorry, Jesus” makes you feel like a hypocrite.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that clean people can come to Jesus.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can.
Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners.
He shed His blood for sinners.
He rose from the grave for sinners.
And when sinners repent and trust in Him, forgiveness is not imaginary.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
All.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It makes the cross magnificent.
Grace is not God's permission to remain enslaved.
Grace is God's answer to people who could never scrub themselves clean enough to deserve Him.
Repentance therefore means more than feeling terrible after orgasm.
More than deleting something and reinstalling it three days later.
More than crying because you were caught.
Biblical repentance turns toward God.
It brings the sin into His light.
It stops defending what Christ died to deliver us from.
And sometimes genuine repentance must become painfully practical.
Delete the number.
End the sexually compromising arrangement.
Stop calling fornication “basically married.”
Stop calling pornography “stress relief.”
Stop calling deliberate fantasy “just thoughts.”
Stop constructing softer vocabulary for what God is asking you to surrender.
But then—equally important—stop calling yourself something Jesus has already died to redeem.
If you belong to Christ, your deepest identity is not:
Porn addict.
Damaged goods.
Used.
Dirty.
Unwanted.
Too far gone.
Your story does not end at the scandal.
This is where grace walks onto the page.
Paul reminded the Corinthians of people whose former lives included serious sexual sin, and then he wrote three astonishing words:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Then:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11).
Do you see it?
Christianity does not merely say:
“Behave better.”
It announces:
Christ can make sinners new.
You may have history.
Jesus has blood.
You may have scars.
Jesus has resurrection.
You may have fallen.
Jesus still calls sinners to repent, rise, and follow Him.
That is our heartbeat:
Not because your past never happened.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
But because the worst chapter does not have authority to write the final sentence when Jesus Christ becomes Lord of the story.
So how does a single Christian handle sexual desire?
Not by pretending it does not exist.
Not by worshiping it.
Not by letting culture define it.
Not by drowning in shame because temptation came knocking.
Not by repeatedly feeding lust and calling the resulting fire uncontrollable.
You bring your sexuality under the lordship of Jesus.
You refuse sexual immorality.
You guard what enters your mind.
You flee when fleeing is necessary.
You cultivate prayer before temptation, not merely after failure.
You stay close to Scripture.
You build honest Christian community.
You learn your patterns.
You establish boundaries while your mind is clear.
You confess sin rather than protecting secrecy.
You repent when you fall.
You receive the forgiveness Christ actually purchased.
And then you get up and keep following Him.
Again.
Again.
Again.
Not because repeated sin does not matter.
But because the answer to failure is not running away from the only Savior who can restore you.
And perhaps tonight, victory will not look dramatic.
Maybe nobody will know it happened.
Maybe victory is simply this:
You put down the phone.
You walk away.
You whisper the name of Jesus.
You cry because you still want what you decided not to take.
And you choose Christ anyway.
He sees that.
The world may never applaud the sins you refused to commit.
There will be no trophy for the message you never sent.
No celebration for the website you closed.
No human audience for the night you trembled, prayed, and stayed obedient.
But your Father sees what happens in secret.
And one day you may discover that those hidden decisions were building something inside you.
Integrity.
Freedom.
Endurance.
A deeper hunger for God.
A capacity to love another human being instead of merely consuming them.
Holiness.
Not perfection manufactured overnight.
Sanctification.
ἁγιασμός.
A life increasingly set apart for God.
And if this article exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not have to tell strangers the details. But you also do not have to pretend.
Someone reading your comment may realize they are not the only Christian fighting this battle.
But before you leave this page, remember this:
The desire screaming inside you does not get the final word, the sin behind you does not get the final word, the shame accusing you does not get the final word—Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: MOSES SPENT 40 YEARS IN A PALACE—AND 40 YEARS IN A WILDERNESS. THEN GOD CALLED HIS NAME FROM THE FIRE.
paragraphs:
MOSES SPENT 40 YEARS IN A PALACE—AND 40 YEARS IN A WILDERNESS. THEN GOD CALLED HIS NAME FROM THE FIRE.
He thought exile meant his story was over. God knew the wilderness was where the man Egypt had shaped would finally become the servant Heaven could send back.
There is a kind of silence that makes you wonder whether God has forgotten your address.
Moses knew that silence.
Before the Red Sea opened…
before Pharaoh heard the terrifying words, “Thus says the LORD”…
before manna fell from heaven…
before Sinai trembled beneath the presence of God…
before Moses became the man whose name would forever be connected with deliverance…
he ran.
And for forty years, the man who had once belonged to Pharaoh’s world lived far from Egypt, tending somebody else’s sheep.
Think about that.
One chapter of his life smelled like royalty.
The next smelled like sheep.
One season placed him near the machinery of Egyptian power.
The next placed him in Midian, far from the place where he apparently thought his destiny would unfold.
One season gave him status.
The next gave him obscurity.
And somewhere between Egypt and the wilderness, Moses had to learn something many of us spend our entire lives resisting:
God is not finished with you simply because the life you imagined has fallen apart.
Maybe that is why you are reading this.
Maybe you know what it feels like to look backward and wonder where everything went wrong.
You thought you would be farther along by now.
Stronger by now.
More useful to God by now.
You thought the marriage would survive.
You thought the ministry would grow.
You thought the addiction would already be behind you.
You thought your children would be walking with God.
You thought that prayer would have been answered.
You thought you would never become the person you became.
And perhaps there is a part of you quietly asking:
“Did I ruin what God wanted to do with my life?”
Moses gives us a breathtaking answer.
But we need to tell his story carefully, because Scripture deserves more than a catchy slogan.

The Bible does not explicitly tell us that Moses literally spent every moment of his first forty years living inside Pharaoh’s palace. Exodus tells us that Pharaoh’s daughter took him as her son, and Stephen later explains that Moses “was instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians” and became powerful in words and deeds (Exodus 2:10; Acts 7:22).
Then Acts 7:23 tells us:
“Ὡς δὲ ἐπληροῦτο αὐτῷ τεσσαρακονταετὴς χρόνος…”
The sense is:
“When he was approaching forty years of age…”
Moses went to visit his Israelite brothers.

So the familiar description of his life as “forty years in the palace and forty years in the wilderness” is a useful summary of two radically different eras, but we should not force Scripture to say more than it says.
What Scripture does tell us is powerful enough.
At approximately forty years old, Moses made a catastrophic decision.
He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew.
Exodus says Moses “looked this way and that,” saw no one, struck the Egyptian, killed him, and hid the body in the sand.
Read that again.
He hid him in the sand.
The future deliverer became a fugitive.
The man who would eventually confront Pharaoh could not even remain in Egypt.
The man God would use in one of the greatest liberation events in biblical history had blood in his past.
And the sand could not keep the secret.
The next day Moses discovered that his killing was known.
Pharaoh sought to kill him.
So Moses fled.
There are moments when one decision seems capable of dividing your entire existence into two lives:
who you were before…
and who you became afterward.
Before the affair.
After the affair.
Before the relapse.
After the relapse.
Before the lie was exposed.
After everyone knew.
Before the divorce.
After the papers were signed.
Before you walked away from God.
After you realized how far you had wandered.
Before you hurt them.
After you realized an apology could not rewind time.
Moses fled into Midian carrying something heavier than anything he could pack.
A past.
And perhaps you know how heavy a past can become.
You can change cities and still carry it.
Change relationships and still carry it.
Change churches and still carry it.
Delete the photographs and still remember.
Smile for everybody and still hear the accusations when the room becomes quiet.
You can bury something in the sand…
and discover that you buried the evidence without burying the memory.
Then Moses became a shepherd.
The prince became obscure.
The man educated in Egyptian wisdom started walking behind sheep.
Days became months.
Months became years.
Years became decades.
Acts 7:30 says:
“Καὶ πληρωθέντων ἐτῶν τεσσαράκοντα…”
“When forty years had passed…”
Forty.
Years.
Do not read those words too quickly.
We read Moses’ story in minutes.
Moses lived the waiting for decades.
There was no little caption appearing over Midian saying:
“Don’t worry, Moses. Only 14,597 days until the burning bush.”
He did not know when the silence would end.
He simply lived inside it.
And that may be where this story stops being ancient history and starts becoming painfully personal.
Because waiting is easier when you know the expiration date.
It is harder when heaven seems silent.
You pray.
Nothing changes.
You obey.
Nothing changes.
You repent.
Nothing changes immediately.
You keep showing up.
Still nothing.
And eventually the question changes from:
“When will God do something?”
to:
“Will God ever do anything?”
But Exodus 3 opens with Moses doing something spectacularly ordinary.
He is tending the flock of Jethro, his father-in-law.
Not commanding armies.
Not addressing nations.
Not performing miracles.
Watching sheep.
Then he sees it.
A bush burning without being consumed.
Moses turns aside.
And God speaks.
“Moses, Moses.”
Imagine hearing your name after forty years in the wilderness.
Not “murderer.”
Not “failure.”
Not “fugitive.”
“Moses.”
God knew exactly where he was.
All along.
The wilderness had never placed Moses beyond the reach of God.
And neither has yours.
Then comes one of the most beautiful assurances in the passage.
When Moses asks who he is that he should go to Pharaoh, God does not begin by inflating Moses’ self-esteem.
God says:
כִּי־אֶהְיֶה עִמָּךְ
ki ’ehyeh ‘immakh

“Certainly, I will be with you.”
(Exodus 3:12)
That changes everything.
Moses essentially asks, “Who am I?”
God answers with His presence.
That is the Gospel-shaped heartbeat we desperately need.
Christianity is not ultimately the story of damaged people discovering that they were secretly powerful all along.
It is the story of helpless sinners discovering that God is gracious.
Moses’ sufficiency was never Moses.
And yours is not you.
The wilderness exposes that.
Egypt can teach you to trust what you possess.
The wilderness teaches you how quickly possessions, reputation, influence, strength, plans, and self-confidence can disappear.
And sometimes what feels like God stripping your life is actually God exposing the things you were asking to function as gods.
Moses had objections.
“Who am I?”
“What shall I say?”
“What if they do not believe me?”
“I am slow of speech and tongue.”
“Please send someone else.”
Does that sound like a superhero?
No.
It sounds like a human being.
A frightened one.
A hesitant one.
A man who had once acted impulsively and now seemed terrified to act at all.
Forty years earlier, Moses apparently believed he could intervene.
Now he is asking God to choose somebody else.
Failure can do that to a person.
Sometimes failure does not merely humble you.
It convinces you that you should never try again.
Sometimes shame disguises itself as humility.
“I’m not worthy.”
“I’m not capable.”
“God could never use someone like me.”
There is truth buried inside that—we are not worthy in ourselves.
But when God calls, “I am unworthy” cannot become an excuse for unbelief.
Because the ultimate question is not whether Moses is impressive enough.
The question is whether the God sending Moses is faithful enough.
And God says:
“I will be with you.”
Maybe somebody reading this has spent years staring at what happened in Egypt while God is trying to get your attention in Midian.
You keep replaying the failure.
God is calling you toward obedience.
You keep rehearsing your shame.
God is calling you toward repentance and faith.
You keep saying, “Look what I did.”
The Gospel says, “Look what Christ has done.”
And here we must go beyond Moses.
Because Moses is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
Moses was a deliverer, but he needed grace himself.
Moses led enslaved people out of Egypt.
Jesus delivers sinners from a deeper slavery—the dominion of sin.
Moses mediated the covenant at Sinai.
Jesus is the mediator of the new covenant.

Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness so that those who looked upon it might live; Jesus Himself used that event to point toward His own being lifted up, so that whoever believes in Him may have eternal life (Numbers 21:8–9; John 3:14–16).
Moses could lead Israel toward the Promised Land.
Jesus brings His people home.
That is why your hope cannot ultimately be:
“I will become another Moses.”
Your hope must be:
“I belong to Jesus Christ.”
There is an enormous difference.
The Gospel does not say your past does not matter.
It says Jesus Christ is greater than your past.
It does not rename sin as a “mistake” merely to make us comfortable.
Sin is real.
Guilt is real.
Judgment is real.
Repentance is necessary.
But grace is also real.
The cross is real.
The empty tomb is real.
Forgiveness is real.
And for everyone who turns to Christ in repentance and faith, condemnation does not get the final word.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
Moses could not resurrect the Egyptian he killed.
Grace does not turn history into fiction.
It does something even more astonishing.
God redeems sinners without pretending their sin was righteous.
That is scandalous grace.
At the cross, God does not sweep evil underneath the rug.
Christ bears judgment.
The sinless Son of God takes upon Himself what sinners could never remove by self-improvement.
Jesus dies.
Jesus rises.
Jesus saves.
So perhaps the question is not:
“Can I somehow repair everything I have broken?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
“Will I surrender what remains of my life to Jesus?”
You may not be able to rewrite yesterday.
But Christ can redeem the person who lived it.
You may carry scars.
Christ carried scars after the resurrection.
You may have consequences.
Grace can meet you inside consequences.
You may have wasted years.
God is not intimidated by calendars.
Moses was around eighty years old when he stood before Pharaoh. Exodus 7:7 explicitly tells us, “Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three years old, when they spoke to Pharaoh.”
Eighty.
Some people would have called his greatest years finished.
God was about to open the sea.
Never confuse a late chapter with the last chapter.
Never assume obscurity means abandonment.
Never interpret waiting as proof that God has forgotten you.
And never use Moses’ story as permission to remain in sin while expecting God to use you anyway.
Grace is not God giving us permission to cherish what crucified Christ.
Grace teaches us to leave sin.
Titus 2:11–12 says the grace of God trains us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions and to live self-controlled, upright, godly lives.
Real grace transforms.
Real forgiveness produces gratitude.
Real encounters with Christ change direction.
So if something hidden is eating you alive, bring it into the light.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you have wandered, come home.
If you need forgiveness, run to Christ.
If restitution is biblically and wisely possible, stop hiding behind religious language and make things right.
If you have been pretending to be spiritually healthy while dying privately, tell the truth.
Jesus did not shed His blood so you could become better at hiding.
He came to save sinners.
Maybe your Midian has lasted longer than you expected.
Maybe you feel forgotten.
Maybe everybody who once knew your name seems to have moved on.
But remember the bush.
Moses was doing an ordinary job on an ordinary day after decades of ordinary wilderness life…
and God knew his name.
“Moses, Moses.”
The God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob had not misplaced him.
And if you belong to Christ, God has not misplaced you either.
Your wilderness is not your savior.
Pain itself does not sanctify anyone.
Time itself does not heal sin.
Suffering does not automatically make us holy.
God does the transforming.
And He calls us to respond in faith and obedience.
That distinction matters.
Because some people spend years romanticizing suffering instead of surrendering to God.
Do not worship the wilderness.
Meet God there.
Do not build your identity around what happened to you.
Build your life on Christ.
Do not make your scandal your permanent name.
Let Jesus have the final word.
Maybe that is why this story has survived generation after generation.
Because somewhere inside Moses’ eighty-year journey to that moment of calling, we recognize ourselves.
The confidence.
The collapse.
The running.
The hiding.
The waiting.
The excuses.
The fear.
And then…
God.
That may be the most beautiful interruption in Scripture and in a human life.
You failed…
and then God.
You wandered…
and then God.
You hid…
and then God.
You thought your usefulness was over…
and then God.
Not because failure earns a calling.
Not because sin qualifies us.
Not because every shattered dream will be restored exactly as we imagined.
But because God remains sovereign, holy, merciful, and astonishingly capable of redeeming people who surrender themselves to Him.
And all of it ultimately leads us beyond Moses to Jesus Christ.
The greater Deliverer.
The spotless Lamb.
The crucified Savior.
The risen King.
The One who does not merely improve scandalous people but makes those who are in Him new creations.
“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17).
That is our message at Gospel Warrior.
Not self-help with Bible verses attached.
Not motivational Christianity.
Not “believe in yourself.”
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Sinners forgiven.
Prodigals coming home.
Broken lives surrendered.
Disciples being formed.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that another believer survived the season they are currently walking through.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
It does not.
It cannot.
Jesus Christ cannot be bought, and salvation is the gift of God received by grace through faith, not a reward for financially supporting a page (Ephesians 2:8–9).

But glorifying God includes making His truth known, encouraging His people, supporting faithful Gospel work as God enables us, and refusing to be ashamed of Christ. If this message points people toward Jesus, sharing it is one simple way you can help put that truth in front of someone who may never have searched for it themselves.
There may come a night when Midian feels endless and you need to remember:
God knew Moses’ location.
God knew Moses’ history.
God knew Moses’ weakness.
God knew Moses’ name.
And God was not finished.
Your support helps sustain and expand this Gospel work. It helps us keep writing, teaching, creating, sharing, and building resources designed to point people toward Jesus Christ.
But remember this clearly:
You do not purchase salvation.
You do not earn grace.
Christ already paid the price sinners could never pay.

Support the work because you believe the Gospel should travel farther. Share because somebody in your circle may be standing in their own Midian right now. Follow because your soul needs more than an occasional inspirational sentence. Stay close to Scripture. Stay close to biblical community. Stay close to truth.
And above everything else…
stay close to Jesus.
Moses spent decades becoming somebody in Egypt.
Then decades becoming nobody in the wilderness.
And when God finally called him, the answer to Moses’ weakness was never, “Moses, discover how powerful you really are.”
It was:
“I will be with you.”
Perhaps that is the sentence you needed today.
Your palace may be gone.
Your Egypt may be behind you.
Your wilderness may have lasted far longer than you ever imagined.
Your hands may not be clean enough to boast.
Your story may contain pages you would burn if you could.
But if Jesus Christ is calling you to repent, believe, rise, and obey…
do not let your yesterday speak louder than His voice.
Because the most important thing about Moses was never where Moses had been.
It was the God who went with him.
The wilderness may look like the place where your story disappeared—but in the hands of God, it can become the place where you finally hear Him call your name.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WOMAN AT HIS FEET AT MIDNIGHT: The Ruth and Boaz Encounter We Read Too Quickly
paragraphs:
THE WOMAN AT HIS FEET AT MIDNIGHT: The Ruth and Boaz Encounter We Read Too Quickly
Ruth walked onto a dark threshing floor carrying widowhood, poverty, foreign blood, and an uncertain future. What happened before sunrise was not the secret affair some modern readers imagine—and it was not the sanitized romance we sometimes make it either. It was a dangerous midnight appeal for redemption. And hidden inside Ruth’s Hebrew words is a breathtaking picture of what every desperate sinner ultimately needs: someone with the right to redeem who is also willing to do it.
There is a moment in the book of Ruth that becomes uncomfortable if you read it slowly.
Perhaps that is why we often do not.
We rush from Ruth gleaning in Boaz’s field to Ruth becoming Boaz’s wife. We know the beautiful ending. We know the genealogy. We know David is coming.
But between the field and the wedding...
there is midnight.
A threshing floor.
A sleeping man.
A vulnerable widow.
An uncovered place at his feet.
And one sentence whispered in the darkness that changes everything.
This scene deserves careful reading because Scripture itself does not tell it casually.
Naomi tells Ruth that Boaz will be at the threshing floor winnowing barley. Then she gives her daughter-in-law instructions that would make almost any careful reader feel the tension.
Wash.
Anoint yourself.
Put on your clothes.
Go down to the threshing floor.
Wait until Boaz has finished eating and drinking.
Watch where he lies down.
Then approach quietly.
Uncover the place at his feet.
Lie down.
And wait.
Ruth does it.
Boaz eats and drinks, his heart is described as good or merry, and he lies beside the grain. Ruth comes quietly, uncovers the place at his feet, and lies down.
Then Scripture gives us the hour.
Not afternoon.
Not sunset.
Not morning.
Midnight.
The Hebrew says:
וַיְהִי בַּחֲצִי הַלַּיְלָה
Vayehi ba-chatzi ha-laylah.
“And it happened in the middle of the night...” — Ruth 3:8.
Boaz suddenly wakes.
There is a woman lying at his feet.
Imagine the silence.
Imagine Ruth’s heartbeat.
She is a Moabite widow in a society where her security is fragile. She has no husband beside her. No wealth protecting her. No powerful family standing around her.
And now the man wakes.
“Who are you?”
Ruth answers.
But this is where we need to slow down, because her answer is far more significant than a woman simply telling a man her name.
The Hebrew of Ruth 3:9 reads:
אָנֹכִי רוּת אֲמָתֶךָ וּפָרַשְׂתָּ כְנָפֶךָ עַל־אֲמָתְךָ כִּי גֹאֵל אָתָּה
Anokhi Rut amatecha, ufarasta kenafekha al-amatekha, ki go’el attah.
“I am Ruth, your servant. Spread your wing over your servant, for you are a redeemer.”
There it is.
The heart of the midnight encounter.
כָּנָף — kanaf.
Wing.
Edge.
Extremity.
The word can refer to a wing or to the edge of a garment, which explains why translations may render Ruth’s request as spreading a “wing,” “garment,” “skirt,” or “cloak” over her.
But there is something astonishing happening here.
Earlier, Boaz had spoken this same imagery over Ruth.
He had heard what she did for Naomi. He knew she had left her homeland. He knew she had walked away from what was familiar and attached herself to Naomi’s people and Naomi’s God.
So in Ruth 2:12 Boaz blesses her for coming to seek refuge under the “wings” of the LORD.
Then, one chapter later, Ruth effectively takes Boaz’s own language and places it back before him.
You told me I came under His wings.
Now spread your wing over me.
Boaz had prayed for Ruth to find refuge under God.
Ruth is now asking Boaz to become part of God’s answer.
That changes the entire scene.
This is not merely, “Boaz, I find you attractive.”
Ruth explicitly tells us why she has come:
כִּי גֹאֵל אָתָּה
Ki go’el attah.
“For you are a go’el.”
A redeemer.
A kinsman with a role in restoring what has been lost.

The language of redemption is essential to the story. Ruth and Naomi are not merely looking for romance. Naomi’s family has been shattered by death. Ruth is a widow. Their future and family inheritance are at stake.
And Ruth is appealing to Boaz to act.
This is one reason we should neither sterilize Ruth 3 nor sensationalize it.
Yes, the scene contains extraordinary intimacy and social vulnerability.

Yes, interpreters have long discussed the suggestive potential of its language, including the expression translated “uncover his feet.” Biblical Hebrew can sometimes use language concerning “feet” euphemistically in other contexts, which helps explain why scholars debate the undertones of this scene.
But we must not make Scripture say what Scripture does not say.
Ruth 3 never states that Ruth and Boaz had sexual intercourse that night.
What the narrative explicitly emphasizes is Ruth’s appeal for redemption and Boaz’s response of integrity.
And Boaz’s response matters enormously.
Because he could have exploited the darkness.
Instead, he speaks blessing.
He calls her “my daughter.”
He praises her חֶסֶד — hesed: her covenantal kindness, loyal love, steadfast devotion.
He tells her not to fear.
Then comes a detail that destroys the simplistic version of the story where Boaz impulsively takes what he wants.
Boaz tells Ruth there is another redeemer who is nearer than he is.
Think about that.
He wants to help her.
He appears willing to marry her.
She has placed herself vulnerably before him.
It is dark.
Almost nobody knows she is there.
Yet Boaz refuses to bypass what is right simply because doing wrong would be convenient.
That is character.
Anybody can appear righteous when the sanctuary lights are on.
Character is what remains when nobody appears to be watching.
Boaz could have used secrecy as permission.
Instead, he treats secrecy as responsibility.
And someone reading this knows exactly why that hurts.
Because perhaps somebody once used your vulnerability against you.
Maybe somebody discovered you were lonely and exploited it.
Maybe somebody heard your wounds and learned where to manipulate you.
Maybe somebody called it love when what they really wanted was access.
Maybe you gave someone your trust and they turned your trust into leverage.
Ruth walks into one of the most vulnerable situations imaginable.
And Boaz does not consume her vulnerability.
He covers it.
There is a lesson here for Christian men that desperately needs recovering.
Strength is not proven by how much access you can obtain from a vulnerable woman.
Godly strength knows how to protect what could have been exploited.
And there is a lesson here for Christian women too.
Ruth's courage does not make her cheap.
Her poverty does not make her worthless.
Her widowhood does not erase her dignity.
Her foreign origin does not place her outside God's ability to write redemption into her future.
Boaz says something remarkable about her:
אֵשֶׁת חַיִל — eshet chayil.
A woman of strength.
A woman of noble character.
A worthy woman.
That phrase should stop us.
Because Ruth arrived in Bethlehem as “Ruth the Moabite.”
The outsider.
The widow.
The foreigner.
The woman gleaning behind harvesters because she needed food.
Yet Boaz says the community knows she is an eshet chayil.
A woman of worth.
Do you see what grace has been quietly doing?
Her history still exists.
But her history is no longer the only sentence describing her.
Some of you have spent years believing the worst chapter of your life is your name.
Divorced.
Addicted.
Rejected.
Abandoned.
Abused.
Bankrupt.
Unwanted.
Impure.
Failure.
Backslider.
The one who ruined everything.
You think everybody sees the label before they see you.
And sometimes people do.
But God has never needed a spotless human résumé before beginning a redemption story.
Ruth came from Moab.
That fact is not hidden.
Scripture repeatedly calls attention to it.
Yet Ruth will eventually stand inside the family line through which King David comes.
And centuries later Matthew deliberately places her name in the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ.
Ruth.
The Moabite widow.
The outsider who once followed harvesters gathering leftover grain becomes an ancestor in the earthly lineage of the Messiah.
Tell me grace cannot rewrite a story.
Tell me God cannot walk into family histories filled with death, scandal, shame, poverty, complicated decisions and broken expectations and bring something holy out of them.
But notice something crucial.
Biblical grace does not pretend sin does not matter.
Grace is not God looking at evil and shrugging.
Grace cost blood.
That is why Ruth's story becomes even more beautiful when read from this side of the cross.
Boaz is not Jesus, and we should not flatten every historical detail into an allegory. Ruth is a real woman. Boaz is a real man. Their story has its own historical and literary meaning.
But the theme of redemption that runs through their story prepares Christian hearts to understand something far greater.
We needed a Redeemer too.
Not because we lacked romance.
Because we were sinners.
We needed someone able to redeem us who was also willing.
And unlike Ruth, we could not simply walk across a threshing floor and solve the problem ourselves.
Our deepest problem was not loneliness.
Not finances.
Not reputation.
Not relationship status.
Sin had separated humanity from God.
And no amount of religious performance could purchase our innocence.
Then Jesus came.
Not merely as an inspirational teacher.
Not merely to make damaged people feel better.
Christ came to save sinners.
At the cross, the innocent Son of God bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Redemption became more than something humanity desperately wished for.
The Redeemer had come.
That is why the Gospel is not “clean yourself up so God might tolerate you.”
The Gospel announces what God has done in Christ and calls sinners to repent and believe.
Maybe that is why Ruth at Boaz’s feet feels so personal.
There comes a moment when pride has to stop negotiating.
Ruth does not stand over Boaz boasting about what she deserves.
She comes needing redemption.
And perhaps the hardest sentence some of us will ever speak before God is not a theological sentence.
It is simply:
Jesus, I need You.
Not...
Jesus, improve my image.
Not...
Jesus, make everybody who hurt me regret it.
Not...
Jesus, give me enough success that I never feel insecure again.
Jesus...
redeem me.
Forgive me.
Change me.
Take the parts of my life I keep hiding and bring them underneath Your lordship.
Because some people reading this are living their own midnight right now.
Nobody knows.
Your Facebook photos look fine.
You still say “God bless.”
You still know the worship songs.
You can quote verses.
But midnight comes and the distractions stop working.
And there you are.
Alone with the thing you have been avoiding.
The secret habit.
The resentment.
The pornography.
The affair nobody knows about.
The bitterness you keep baptizing as discernment.
The unforgiveness.
The prayerlessness.
The compromise.
The exhaustion.
The fear.
The shame.
The memory you cannot erase.
The version of yourself you are terrified someone will discover.
And suddenly Ruth’s story is no longer ancient history.
Because midnight has a way of asking:
Who are you when nobody is watching?
Boaz answered that question with integrity.
Ruth answered it with courage.
How will you answer it?
There is another detail we cannot miss.
Boaz does not merely promise.
He acts.
He goes to the city gate.
He handles the matter publicly and lawfully.
He speaks with the nearer redeemer.
He accepts the cost and responsibility.
Then Ruth becomes his wife.
Their union produces Obed.
Obed fathers Jesse.
Jesse fathers David.
And the story keeps moving.
Generation after generation.
Until eventually Matthew opens his Gospel and traces the line toward Jesus Christ.
Ruth could not see all of that while lying at Boaz’s feet.
That may be the sentence someone needs today.
She could not see the genealogy from the threshing floor.
She only knew it was dark.
She only knew she needed redemption.
She only knew tomorrow was uncertain.
But God was already writing generations beyond what Ruth could see.
You may be judging God's entire story by your current midnight.
Don't.
You cannot see the genealogy from the threshing floor.
You cannot see everything God may do with surrendered obedience.
You cannot see how repentance today might change your children's tomorrow.
You cannot see how breaking one sinful cycle may echo through generations.
You cannot see who may eventually find courage because you finally told the truth about what Jesus rescued you from.
And perhaps this is where Ruth's story becomes dangerous to our shame.
Because shame says:
Hide.
Jesus says:
Come.
Shame says:
Your past disqualifies you.
The Gospel says:
Christ receives repentant sinners.
Shame says:
If people knew everything, your story would be over.
Grace says:
Bring everything into the light and let Jesus begin transforming what darkness kept chained.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
It does not mean every broken relationship will be restored exactly as we desire.
It does not mean Christianity promises an earthly Boaz, marriage, wealth, children, or a comfortable ending to every faithful person.
Ruth is not a formula for getting a spouse.
Jesus is the treasure.
Redemption in Christ is the greater ending.
Maybe you are still single.
Maybe the person you prayed would return never returned.
Maybe your marriage ended.
Maybe the diagnosis did not change.
Maybe the grave is still occupied by somebody you begged God not to take.
Ruth herself knows something about graves.
She buried a husband before she ever met Boaz.
The book does not begin with romance.
It begins with famine, migration and funerals.
Grace does not require pretending those graves never happened.
Grace means the grave does not get the final word.
And Christianity takes that truth farther than Ruth could have imagined.
Because our Redeemer entered a grave Himself.
And on the third day...
the grave lost.
That is why Jesus Christ is not merely a supporting character in your self-improvement story.
He is Lord.
He calls you to repentance.
He offers forgiveness.
He breaks chains.
He gives new life.
He does not merely edit your public image.
He transforms people from the inside out.
Maybe your midnight encounter happens tonight.
Not on a threshing floor.
On the edge of your bed.
In a parked car.
In a hospital corridor.
In a bathroom where nobody can hear you crying.
With your phone screen glowing against your face after everyone else has gone to sleep.
And maybe the prayer does not need to sound impressive.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, I cannot save myself.”
“Jesus, I believe You died and rose again.”
“Jesus, teach me to follow You.”
“Jesus, redeem what I have surrendered to sin.”
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to describe your private sin publicly. But you can draw a line in the sand.
Someone else reading the comments may need to discover that they are not the only person still fighting.
And please do not let this article die quietly on your screen.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because clicking “share” proves you are a better Christian. It does not.
There are truths you understand differently when midnight eventually becomes your own.

Supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one practical way to steward what God has entrusted to you, alongside prayer, sharing truth, serving your local church, caring for people in need, and faithfully using your gifts. Salvation is God's gift in Christ.
And stay close to Gospel Warrior even if you cannot financially support us.
But before you leave, return one final time to the threshing floor.
It is still dark.
Ruth still cannot see David.
She cannot see Bethlehem generations later.
She cannot see shepherds looking into the night sky.
She cannot hear angels announcing good news.
She cannot see a carpenter carrying a cross.
She cannot see nails.
She cannot see an empty tomb.
All Ruth can see is midnight.
Yet God is already writing beyond midnight.
Maybe that is exactly where you are.
You cannot see what comes next.
You only see what died.
What failed.
What you lost.
What you did.
What was done to you.
You see the scandal.
God sees farther.
So repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive because Christ has forgiven you.
Come into the light.
Stop protecting the secret that is destroying you.
Stop believing shame deserves the final paragraph.
Run to Jesus.
Because Ruth’s story reminds us that redemption can begin in places that look nothing like redemption.
And the cross proves it forever.
The place that looked like ultimate defeat became the place where Christ declared that sin, shame and death would not have the last word over everyone who belongs to Him.
You may only be able to see the midnight—but Jesus already knows what redemption looks like in the morning.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Is the Dead Sea Called Dead?
paragraphs: Why Is the Dead Sea Called Dead?

The Bible calls it the “Sea of Salt.” Science explains why ordinary aquatic life struggles to survive there. But centuries before anyone measured its salinity, Scripture placed this strange body of water inside a story of judgment, promise, restoration—and a God who can bring life where death seems to have won.
There is something unsettling about standing before water that looks alive.
The sunlight dances on it.
Waves move across it.
The horizon stretches beyond it.
You can step into it. Float upon it. Watch the sky reflected across its surface.
And yet we call it dead.
Why?
That question sounds geographical.
It isn't only geographical.
Because somewhere between the salt, the silence, the ancient Hebrew words, and one astonishing vision from the prophet Ezekiel, the Dead Sea begins to feel uncomfortably familiar.
Maybe because some people know exactly what it is like to look alive while something inside them is dying.
You still wake up.
Still work.
Still answer messages.
Still smile when someone takes the picture.
Still say, “I'm okay.”
Still go to church.
Still know the songs.
Still know when to say “Amen.”
But beneath the surface...
something has become painfully quiet.
Prayer became difficult.
The Bible became something you meant to read.
The sin you once fought became the sin you learned to manage.
The wound you never surrendered became an identity.
The disappointment you never processed became bitterness.
And slowly, almost invisibly, what once flowed became stagnant.
So stay with me.
Because the answer to why the Dead Sea is called dead becomes far more powerful when you discover what the Bible actually calls it—and what Ezekiel saw happening to its waters.

The modern name “Dead Sea” describes its extraordinary environment. The lake has no natural outlet; water primarily leaves through evaporation, leaving dissolved minerals behind. NASA has reported salt concentrations above 30 percent, compared with roughly 3.5 percent for ordinary ocean water. Such extreme salinity makes survival extraordinarily difficult for ordinary plants, fish, and animals, which explains the name “Dead Sea.” This does not mean the water is absolutely sterile; specialized microorganisms can exist in extreme environments like this. So “dead” is descriptive, not scientifically absolute.
The U.S. Geological Survey puts the basic mechanism simply: the Dead Sea has no outlet. Water evaporates, while dissolved minerals remain behind and become increasingly concentrated.
But open the Hebrew Bible and something interesting happens.
You do not first encounter the familiar English expression “Dead Sea.”
In Genesis 14:3, the Hebrew text identifies it as:
יָם הַמֶּלַח — Yām haMelaḥ
Literally:
“the Sea of Salt.”
The Hebrew noun יָם — yām means “sea,” while מֶלַח — melaḥ means “salt.” Genesis 14:3 places the expression in the sentence:
הוּא יָם הַמֶּלַח
hu yam ha-melaḥ
“That is the Salt Sea.”
That is not a clever modern reinterpretation. It is what the Hebrew text actually says.
And that distinction matters.
The Bible is not trying to give the lake a dramatic nickname.
It is describing what it is.
Salt.
Concentration.
A place where normal aquatic life cannot flourish.
And here is where we must be careful.
The Bible never says, “The Dead Sea represents your spiritual condition.”
That would be forcing an allegory onto the text.

But Scripture does repeatedly use physical realities—water, thirst, wilderness, fruitfulness, barrenness, life and death—to communicate spiritual truths. And most importantly for our subject, Ezekiel himself receives a prophetic vision in which waters flowing from God's sanctuary transform deadly waters into a place overflowing with life.
That connection is actually in the biblical text.
And it is breathtaking.
Ezekiel sees water coming from the temple.
At first it is small.
Then deeper.
Ankle deep.
Knee deep.
Waist deep.
Until eventually it becomes a river too deep to cross.
Then the prophet is shown trees.
Life.
Fruitfulness.
Abundance.
And the river travels toward the Arabah, the great depression in which the Dead Sea lies.
Then Ezekiel is told that when these waters enter the sea, its waters will be healed.
And suddenly...
fish.
A great multitude of fish.
Fishermen standing along shores associated with this region.
Nets spread out.
Life where the landscape had been associated with salt and barrenness.
Ezekiel 47:9 says that wherever the river goes, living creatures will live. The vision specifically describes the waters being healed and fish becoming exceedingly numerous.
Read that again slowly.
The prophet sees life entering a place characterized by death...
and death cannot keep its name.
That is where geography begins sounding like Gospel.
Not because Ezekiel 47 is secretly an allegory about your bad week.
Not because every mineral in the Dead Sea has a hidden spiritual meaning.
But because the God revealed throughout Scripture is the God whose redemptive purpose moves toward restoration, life, resurrection, and ultimately the reign of Jesus Christ.
The biblical story does not end with death winning.
And neither does the Gospel.
Maybe that is why this hits so deeply.
Because we know what spiritual accumulation feels like.
The Dead Sea receives water but has no natural outlet. Evaporation removes water while minerals remain and accumulate.
And while we should not confuse hydrology with theology, there is still an illustration worth hearing.
What happens when everything keeps coming in...
but nothing healthy flows out?
Sermons come in.
Podcasts come in.
Bible verses come in.
Christian videos come in.
Worship music comes in.
Devotionals come in.
But obedience doesn't flow out.
Forgiveness doesn't flow out.
Generosity doesn't flow out.
Repentance doesn't flow out.
Mercy doesn't flow out.
Love doesn't flow out.
Service doesn't flow out.
You can consume Christian content every day and still become spiritually dry.
You can know theology and hide pornography.
You can quote Scripture and refuse to forgive.
You can sing about surrender while privately negotiating with sin.
You can defend Christianity online while treating people cruelly offline.
You can look spiritually alive from a distance while carrying enormous dead places beneath the surface.
That is the frightening thing about spiritual death.
It does not always look dead immediately.
Sometimes it looks religious.
Sometimes it knows vocabulary.
Sometimes it has a ministry.
Sometimes it posts Bible verses.
Sometimes it says all the correct things.
Jesus confronted precisely this kind of contradiction.
He spoke of people who honored God with their lips while their hearts remained far from Him.
He confronted religious leaders who appeared righteous outwardly while corruption remained within.
And that means the most dangerous question may not be:
“Do people think I am close to God?”
It may be:
“What does Jesus see beneath the surface?”
There are sins nobody knows about.
Search histories nobody sees.
Messages already deleted.
Jealousies hidden beneath compliments.
Bitterness disguised as discernment.
Pride disguised as standards.
Lust disguised as loneliness.
Greed disguised as ambition.
Unforgiveness disguised as boundaries.
Spiritual laziness disguised as being busy.
And sometimes we become so skilled at maintaining the appearance of Christianity that we forget Christianity was never primarily about maintaining appearances.
Jesus did not come to improve your disguise.
He came to raise the dead.
That is the scandal.
And that is the grace.
The Gospel begins with news far more offensive to human pride than “try harder.”
Scripture says we are sinners.
Not merely imperfect people needing inspiration.
Not fundamentally righteous people who occasionally make unfortunate choices.
Sinners.
Separated from a holy God.
Unable to purchase our own forgiveness.
Unable to scrub ourselves clean enough.
Unable to accumulate enough religious activity to erase guilt.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
That includes the addict.
The pastor.
The skeptic.
The worship leader.
The person reading this secretly.
The person sharing it publicly.
Me.
You.
Everybody comes to the cross empty-handed.
And then comes the scandalous part.
God did not wait for sinners to make themselves worthy of rescue.
Christ came for them.
Jesus lived the righteous life we failed to live.
He bore sin upon the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day...
the tomb became the most important empty place in human history.
Christianity does not announce that humanity discovered a technique for climbing upward to God.
It announces that God came down to rescue sinners.
Jesus Christ crucified.
Jesus Christ buried.
Jesus Christ risen.
Jesus Christ reigning.
Jesus Christ calling sinners to repent and believe.
That is why grace is not permission to remain dead.
Grace is God's undeserved favor toward sinners that brings us to the One who gives life.
Repentance is not God demanding that you clean yourself before approaching Jesus.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior because you finally recognize that the thing you have been protecting is killing you.
Somebody reading this has been protecting the very thing you keep asking God to heal.
You want peace without surrender.
Freedom without confession.
Restoration without repentance.
Jesus without the cross.
Resurrection without burial.
But Christ does not merely decorate graves.
He calls people out of them.
Think of Lazarus.
Four days.
A sealed tomb.
Grief everywhere.
Martha hurting.
Mary weeping.
People mourning.
Then Jesus stands before a place everyone else has accepted as final.
And He cries:
“Lazarus, come forth.”
The dead man comes out.
That is Jesus.
He walks toward what everyone else has given up on.
He approaches what smells hopeless.
He speaks where death seems to have the final word.
And death discovers that it has met Someone with greater authority.
This does not mean every earthly tragedy disappears immediately when someone becomes a Christian.
Christians still grieve.
Christians still suffer.
Christians still become sick.
Christians still struggle.
Faith is not denial.
But Christianity declares something infinitely greater:
death is no longer ultimate.
Sin does not have to remain master.
Guilt does not have to remain your identity.
Your past does not have to become your prophecy.
The cross can forgive what shame keeps replaying.
The Spirit can transform what sin has corrupted.
And resurrection means the grave itself does not get the final sentence.
Maybe you have called yourself something for years.
Dirty.
Ruined.
Addicted.
Rejected.
Divorced.
Abandoned.
Failure.
Hypocrite.
Unworthy.
Too far gone.
Maybe somebody else gave you the name.
Maybe you gave it to yourself.
Maybe your worst decision became the headline over your entire life.
But hear this carefully:
Jesus knows your sin more completely than you do...
and still calls you to Himself.
Not so you can pretend the sin never happened.
Not so evil becomes acceptable.
Not so repentance becomes optional.
But so the sinner can be forgiven, cleansed, reconciled, and transformed.
That is what grace does.
Grace does not rewrite history by pretending the scandal never existed.
Grace rewrites what the scandal gets to become.
Peter denied Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine carrying that memory.
The charcoal fire.
The accusation.
The denial.
The rooster.
Then the eyes of Jesus.
Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
If Peter's failure had been the final chapter, his story would have ended in shame.
But Jesus rose.
And after the resurrection, Christ restored Peter and entrusted him with responsibility among His people.
Failure was real.
Sin was real.
The tears were real.
But they were not final.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps this is why Ezekiel's vision is so unforgettable.
A place associated with salt and inhospitable waters becomes, in the prophet's vision, a place where living creatures flourish.
Not because the dead waters repair themselves.
The river comes to them.
Life comes from God's presence.
That distinction matters.
Christianity is not primarily about dead people learning better self-improvement techniques.
Life comes from God.
Jesus said:
“I am the resurrection, and the life” (John 11:25).
Not:
“I have several useful resurrection principles.”
I am.
Christianity ultimately offers you Christ Himself.
And maybe you have spent months trying to repair yourself without surrendering yourself.
Maybe nobody around you knows how tired you are.
You know how to smile.
You know how to function.
You know how to say “God is good.”
But late at night...
when there is no audience...
you wonder where the fire went.
You remember when prayer felt real.
You remember when conviction came quickly.
You remember when worship broke something open inside you.
Now?
Numb.
And the numbness scares you more than the pain used to.
If that is you, do not confuse numbness with hopelessness.
Run to Christ.
Confess the sin.
Stop feeding what is starving your soul.
Open Scripture again.
Pray even when the prayer sounds broken.
Ask another mature believer for help.
Return to Christian fellowship.
Make restitution where Scripture requires it and where doing so is wise and safe.
Forgive.
Repent.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
You do not need a better religious performance.
You need Jesus.
And if you have never truly trusted Him, understand this:
the Gospel is not “become religious enough and perhaps God will accept you.”
The Gospel is that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again, and God calls you to repent and believe in Him.
You cannot purchase salvation.
You cannot donate your way into heaven.
You cannot share enough Christian articles to earn forgiveness.
Salvation is God's gift, received through faith in Christ—not a transaction with Gospel Warrior or any ministry.
That needs to be unmistakably clear.
But once grace has reached us, grace does change what we do with what God has entrusted to us.
We begin wanting other people to hear.
We support Gospel work.
We give.
We serve.
We share truth.
We help put biblical resources into somebody else's hands.
Not to buy God's love...
but because in Christ we have already encountered a love we could never buy.

So if this article brought you closer to Jesus, convicted something you have been hiding, or reminded you that God can still bring life into places you had written off as dead, don't let it simply disappear beneath another hundred posts.
There may come a night when you need these words again.
You may never know who reads it at 2:13 in the morning.
You may never know whose secret prayer was, “God, if You're still there, please speak to me.”

Sharing biblical truth can be one simple way of glorifying God by making Christ known. Support should flow from gratitude and willing stewardship, never fear, guilt, or an attempt to purchase God's blessing.
Not to embarrass them.
Not because you know their secrets.
Just because sometimes love says:
I thought you might need this.

And if God has already rescued you from a season you once believed would destroy you, tell somebody what Jesus did. Your testimony may become another person's reason to believe that their present chapter is not necessarily their final chapter.
It is mission.
It is helping sustain the creation and distribution of biblical content designed to point people toward Christ.
But before you leave, remember the water.
The Dead Sea is real.
Its extraordinary salinity is real.
Its name has a physical explanation.
The Hebrew Bible calls it יָם הַמֶּלַח — Yām haMelaḥ, the Sea of Salt.

And Ezekiel really did see a prophetic vision in which waters flowing from God's sanctuary entered the region's waters, healing them so that living creatures and abundant fish appeared where such life could not normally flourish.
We should not turn geography into a doctrine Scripture never teaches.
But we should not miss what Scripture actually reveals either.
God is a God of life.
The Bible moves toward restoration.
The Gospel centers upon a crucified Savior who walked out of His grave.
And everyone united to Christ shares in a hope death cannot finally extinguish.
So perhaps the question you should carry away from this article is no longer merely:
“Why is the Dead Sea called dead?”
Maybe the question is:
What have you already called dead that Jesus is asking you to surrender to Him?
Your marriage?
Your faith?
Your calling?
Your capacity to forgive?
Your relationship with your child?
Your prayer life?
Your future?
Your hope?
Yourself?
I cannot promise you that God will restore every situation exactly the way you imagine.
Scripture does not give us permission to promise that.
But I can tell you what Christianity unapologetically proclaims:
Jesus Christ is alive.
Forgiveness is available.
Repentance is possible.
Grace is real.
The Holy Spirit still transforms people.
And for everyone who belongs to Christ, even physical death itself will not have the final word.
The Dead Sea received a name because of what could scarcely live within it.
But Christian...
never give your darkest chapter the authority to name your whole story when the risen Jesus is still holding the pen.
One more family.
One more prodigal.
One more skeptic.
One more exhausted believer.
One more person sitting alone behind a glowing screen thinking their story is already over.
Because sometimes the place everybody calls dead...
is exactly where God chooses to make the possibility of life impossible to ignore.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Your Desire Is Not Your Master: What the Bible Really Says About Self-Control, Sexual Desire, and the Grace That Meets You in the Dark
paragraphs: Your Desire Is Not Your Master: What the Bible Really Says About Self-Control, Sexual Desire, and the Grace That Meets You in the Dark

The Bible does not pretend sexual desire is weak. It reveals something stronger: a Savior who can redeem what desire has wounded, teach you holiness without teaching you shame, and prove that your most secret struggle does not have to become your final story.
There is a moment nobody posts on Facebook.
Nobody takes a selfie of it.
Nobody announces it at church.

It happens when the room is quiet, the phone is in your hand, your spouse is asleep, your loneliness is screaming, your memories are awake, or somebody you know you should not be thinking about suddenly occupies your mind.
Maybe it begins with an image.
A message.
A memory.
A fantasy.
A profile you promised yourself you would stop checking.
Maybe nobody else knows.
And that is precisely why the battle feels so powerful.
Because some of the most dangerous spiritual wars are fought in rooms where nobody is watching.
You love Jesus.
At least, you believe you do.
You pray. You worship. You know the verses. Maybe you serve in church. Maybe people actually come to you for spiritual advice.
And yet there is this appetite inside you that sometimes seems louder than everything you believe.
Then comes the question many Christians are terrified to ask out loud:
“If I really belonged to Jesus, why do I still feel this?”
Read carefully, because misunderstanding the answer has driven countless people either into shame or into compromise.
Sexual desire itself is not proof that you are dirty.
But sexual desire is also not automatically holy simply because it feels natural.
And self-control is not pretending you have no desires.
Biblical self-control is learning, by the power of the Holy Spirit, that your desires are not your god.
That distinction changes everything.

From the beginning, Scripture does not present human sexuality as an embarrassing accident God reluctantly tolerates. God created humanity male and female and established the one-flesh covenant of marriage in Genesis 2:24. Before sin entered the world, embodiment, intimacy, marriage, and sexuality already existed within God's good design.
So Christianity is not fundamentally anti-sex.
It is anti-slavery.
And there is an enormous difference.

The Bible does not teach that every sexual impulse is sinful. Scripture instead places sexual expression within God's covenantal boundaries and repeatedly warns against allowing desire to become lust, impurity, exploitation, adultery, or sexual immorality.
That is where many modern messages become uncomfortable.
Our culture often tells us that if we strongly desire something, denying ourselves must somehow mean denying our authentic identity.
Jesus says something radically different.
He teaches that discipleship itself involves self-denial: “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me” (Matthew 16:24).
Jesus never promised that every desire you experience deserves obedience.
Some desires must be surrendered precisely because He is Lord.
And perhaps this is where the battle becomes personal.
Because sexual temptation rarely introduces itself by saying, “I want to destroy you.”
It usually whispers something much softer.
You deserve this.
Just look.
Just imagine.
Just answer the message.
Nobody will know.
You're lonely.
Your marriage isn't satisfying you.
You're single. What are you supposed to do?
You've already failed before, so what difference does one more time make?
And perhaps the most dangerous whisper of all:
You can repent afterward.
That is how bondage often works.
It asks for five minutes and slowly demands your life.

Jesus goes beneath outward behavior and exposes the battlefield of the heart. In Matthew 5:28 He warns about looking with lustful intent. The Greek verb connected with desire there is ἐπιθυμέω — epithymeō, meaning to desire, long for, or covet depending on context. The word itself can describe desire in different contexts; therefore Scripture's concern is not the mere existence of desire but desire directed toward what God forbids and cultivated in the heart.
That matters.
Noticing that someone is attractive is not identical to deliberately turning that person into material for fantasy.
Experiencing temptation is not identical to consenting to temptation.
Jesus Himself “has been tempted as we are, yet without sin” (Hebrews 4:15).
So do not confuse being tempted with already having committed the sin.
But do not use that distinction to play games with temptation either.
There is a moment when noticing becomes staring.
When attraction becomes cultivation.
When the thought you could have rejected becomes the fantasy you choose to feed.
And Jesus cares about that hidden moment.
Not because He wants to humiliate you.
Because He wants your heart.
Paul becomes startlingly direct in 1 Corinthians 6:18:
“Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν” — Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
The opening word, φεύγετε — pheugete, is an imperative: flee. Run. Get away.
Paul does not say negotiate with it.
He does not say prove your spiritual maturity by standing as close to temptation as possible.
He says flee.

And πορνεία — porneia is the Greek term commonly translated “sexual immorality,” referring broadly in the New Testament to sexual conduct outside God's moral boundaries. In the same passage Paul grounds his command not merely in prohibition but in Christian identity: the believer's body belongs to God, is a temple of the Holy Spirit, and has been “bought with a price”; therefore the Christian is commanded to glorify God in the body.
Think about how radically different that is from shame.
Shame says:
Your body is disgusting.
The Gospel says:
Your body was purchased at an unimaginable price.
Shame says:
God wants nothing to do with you because of what you have done.
The Gospel points toward a crucified Savior and says:
Look at what God was willing to do to redeem sinners.
Christian sexual holiness is therefore not primarily about hating your body.
It is about recognizing to whom your body belongs.
“You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.”
That price was not silver.
Not gold.
Not religious performance.
Not years of perfect behavior.
Christ gave Himself.
Suddenly self-control becomes something far greater than trying not to click something.
It becomes worship.
The Greek word commonly translated “self-control” in Galatians 5:23 is ἐγκράτεια — enkrateia. Paul includes it among the fruit of the Spirit.
Notice that.
Fruit of the Spirit.
Christian self-control is not merely clenched-teeth willpower.
It is not, “I am strong enough to save myself.”
It is the Spirit of God increasingly producing in a surrendered believer the ability not to be ruled by appetite.
That means when temptation says, You need this, the Spirit can teach your heart to answer:
No. I need Christ more.
When lust says, You cannot live without satisfying me, the believer can answer:
You are a desire. You are not my master.
When your body says now, holiness teaches you to remember eternity.
This is especially important because the Bible's vision of holiness is not merely avoidance.

Paul tells believers in 1 Thessalonians 4 that God's will includes their sanctification, abstaining from sexual immorality, and learning to conduct themselves in holiness and honor rather than lustful passion. The passage even warns against wronging or exploiting another person sexually.
Sexual sin is therefore never merely about private pleasure.
There is another human being involved somewhere, even when reduced to an image.
A person made in God's image.
Someone's daughter.
Someone's son.
Someone with a soul.
Someone Christ commands you to see as more than a body designed for your consumption.
Pornography trains the eyes to consume.
Lust trains the imagination to possess.
The Gospel trains the heart to love.
And love asks a completely different question.
Lust asks:
“What can I get from this person?”
Christlike love asks:
“How can I honor this person before God?”
That is why self-control is not punishment.
It is liberation from the tyranny of appetite.
Yet somebody reading this has already stopped believing liberation is possible.
Because you have tried.
You deleted it.
Then downloaded it again.
You confessed.
Then returned.
You cried.
Then returned.
You promised God, “Never again.”
And three days later you were staring at the ceiling wondering whether your repentance had ever been real.
Perhaps pornography has become your secret anesthetic.
Perhaps masturbation and fantasy have become the place you run whenever loneliness hurts.
Perhaps you are emotionally attached to somebody who is not your spouse.
Perhaps you keep reopening a relationship God has repeatedly convicted you to surrender.
Perhaps you are single and exhausted from being told simply to “wait,” while nobody seems willing to acknowledge how physically and emotionally difficult waiting can actually become.
Perhaps you are married and discovered that marriage did not magically erase lust.
Perhaps somebody sexually wounded you, and desire, fear, shame, intimacy, and memory have become tangled together in ways you struggle even to explain.
Hear this carefully.
The Gospel does not require you to lie about the intensity of the battle.
It requires you to stop making peace with what Christ calls you to surrender.
There is a difference between struggling against sin and settling into sin.
A struggling believer may fall and hate the fall.
A compromised heart eventually begins decorating the pit.
One says, “Lord, rescue me.”
The other says, “Lord, stop interfering.”
And if you are still fighting, still grieving your sin, still returning to Christ, do not allow Satan to turn conviction into hopelessness.
Because Scripture contains another sentence you desperately need.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).
No condemnation does not mean no conviction.
Conviction and condemnation are not the same thing.
Condemnation says, Run away from God because you are filthy.
Godly conviction says, Come back to God because Christ is merciful.
Condemnation says, Hide.
Grace says, Confess.
Condemnation says, This is who you are.
The Gospel says, This is what Christ came to redeem.
And this is where the scandal becomes grace.
Because Christianity's answer to sexual sin is not merely “control yourself.”
If that were the entire Gospel, we would all be doomed.
Christianity announces something infinitely greater:
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
Not imaginary sinners.
Real ones.
Adulterers.
The sexually immoral.
The lustful.
The hypocritical.
The secretive.
The ashamed.
The religious person with a hidden browser history.
The person carrying memories they wish they could erase.
The person who has crossed boundaries and now wonders whether purity can ever mean anything again.

Paul wrote to Corinth—a church living within a sexually permissive environment—and reminded believers that some among them had formerly lived in serious sin. Then comes one of Scripture's most beautiful reversals:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11).
Were.
That word carries thunder.
Your past may explain some of your scars.
It does not possess the authority to name your future.
Jesus does.
The cross means your sin is serious enough that Christ had to die.
And grace means His blood is sufficient enough that repentant sinners can be forgiven.
That keeps us from two deadly extremes.
We cannot say sexual sin does not matter.
The cross proves sin matters terribly.
But neither can we say sexual sinners are beyond redemption.
The cross proves God's mercy reaches sinners we would have written off.
Maybe even you.
Repentance, however, is more than feeling terrible after gratification.
Biblical repentance turns.
It brings darkness into light.
It stops protecting access to the thing that keeps destroying you.
Sometimes repentance looks surprisingly practical.
It looks like removing an app.
Moving the phone out of the bedroom.
Ending the private conversation.
Installing accountability software.
Giving a mature Christian permission to ask uncomfortable questions.
Refusing to be alone in environments where you repeatedly fall.
Ending the relationship you keep trying to rename so you do not have to admit what it has become.
Seeking wise pastoral care and, where appropriate, professional counseling when trauma, compulsive behavior, or deeper wounds are involved.

Jesus' language about tearing out an eye or cutting off a hand in Matthew 5:29–30 is deliberate hyperbole, not a command to mutilate yourself. His point is the seriousness with which disciples should deal with sin.
In modern language:
Stop giving your temptation VIP access to your life.
You cannot repeatedly feed what you are praying God will starve.
And perhaps this is the sentence somebody needed tonight:
You do not defeat temptation by proving how close you can stand to it.
Joseph did not hold a Bible study in Potiphar's wife's bedroom.
He ran.
Paul says flee.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is leave the room.
Turn off the screen.
Block the number.
Go outside.
Call somebody.
Pray before the craving becomes a decision.
And keep replacing, not merely removing.
Because an empty heart is vulnerable.
Fill your imagination with Scripture.
Fill your loneliness with Christian community.
Fill your time with meaningful work and service.
Learn what circumstances precede your recurring falls.
Are you usually lonely?
Angry?
Rejected?
Bored?
Tired?
Anxious?
Looking for comfort?
Sometimes what presents itself as overwhelming sexual hunger has learned to function as medication for another wound.
Identifying that wound does not make sin righteous.
It helps you fight more wisely.
And above everything else, pursue Christ.
Not merely purity.
Christ.
Because purity without Christ can become pride.
Rules without Christ can become legalism.
Failure without Christ becomes despair.
But holiness flowing from communion with Christ becomes worship.
There will be nights when you do not feel powerful.
There will be moments when obedience feels costly.
There may be seasons when your body seems to be shouting while heaven seems silent.
But self-control does not mean never feeling the pull.
Sometimes self-control looks like trembling while saying no.
Sometimes victory is not dramatic.
Sometimes victory is simply closing the tab.
Not sending the message.
Getting out of bed.
Calling your brother in Christ.
Walking away.
Praying through tears.
Going to sleep lonely rather than waking up compromised.
And heaven sees those quiet obediences.
Your sexuality does not need to be destroyed.
It needs to be discipled.
Your desires do not need to become your identity.
They need to come under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Your body is not your enemy.
Your body belongs to the Lord.
Your singleness is not permission for impurity.
Your marriage is not permission for selfishness.
Your attraction is not automatically a command.
Your temptation is not your identity.
Your failure is not beyond the reach of the cross.
And your repeated struggle does not give you permission to stop fighting.
Run to Jesus again.
Confess again.
Get accountable again.
Remove access again.
Open Scripture again.
Ask the Holy Spirit for strength again.
And when you fall, do not turn one failure into seven days of rebellion because you think the week is already ruined.
Return immediately.
There is no spiritual wisdom in staying in the mud because you already slipped.
Get up.
Come home.
Christ is still worthy.
Grace is still grace.
Repentance is still possible.
And Jesus is still rewriting stories.
If this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not have to publish the details of your struggle. But you can stop pretending you do not need prayer.
Let shame discover that it cannot survive forever when believers stop performing perfection and start carrying one another toward Jesus.

It does not. We are saved by grace, not by financially supporting a ministry. But generosity and sharing can genuinely become ways believers choose to serve others and help biblical resources travel farther.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who has grown cold.
Invite the Christian who is struggling privately.
Invite the seeker.
Invite even the person who does not yet believe.
Following Gospel Warrior costs them nothing, but the Scripture they encounter might become part of the road God uses to bring them face-to-face with Christ.
But before you leave this article, remember why any of this matters.
The goal is not to become a person who can boast, “Look how disciplined I am.”
The goal is to become a person whose life whispers:
“Look how worthy Jesus is.”
You are not fighting sexual sin so God will finally decide you are worth loving.
If you belong to Christ, you fight because at Calvary you discovered how costly His love already was.
You were bought with a price.
So when temptation comes again—and it may—remember that your body has a King.
Your eyes have a King.
Your imagination has a King.
Your sexuality has a King.
Your loneliness has a King.
Your wounds have a King.
Your future has a King.
And even your scandal does not get the final sentence.
The desire may knock on the door again—but it does not own the house anymore. Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHEN ONE HOME HAS TOO MANY HEARTS
paragraphs: WHEN ONE HOME HAS TOO MANY HEARTS

The Bible records men with multiple wives without pretending their homes were peaceful. Behind the marriages came rivalry, jealousy, wounded children, divided loyalties, and generational pain. But the deepest message of Scripture is not that broken families are beyond hope. It is that Jesus Christ enters what sin has fractured—and grace can begin rewriting what we thought could never change.
There is a kind of pain that does not leave bruises where people can see them.
It sits at the dinner table.
It sleeps in the next room.
It smiles for family photographs.
It learns to say, “Everything is fine,” because telling the truth might tear open a wound everyone has agreed not to touch.
Sometimes that wound is the knowledge that the person who promised to belong to you also belongs matrimonially to someone else.
Sometimes it is a child wondering why another household receives more attention.
Sometimes it is one wife quietly measuring herself against another.
Sometimes it is a husband discovering that what looked like an expansion of love has instead multiplied responsibility, rivalry, insecurity, and pain.
And sometimes the deepest tragedy is that everybody has become so accustomed to the arrangement that nobody remembers what peace was supposed to feel like.
This is where a careful reading of Scripture becomes uncomfortable.
Because the Bible does contain polygamy.

Abraham had Sarah and Hagar. Jacob married Leah and Rachel and also fathered children through Bilhah and Zilpah. Elkanah had Hannah and Peninnah. David accumulated wives. Solomon multiplied wives on an extraordinary scale.
But here is the distinction we must never lose:
The Bible recording something is not the same thing as God recommending it.
Scripture is remarkably honest about human beings. It does not airbrush its heroes.
It shows Abraham afraid.
Jacob deceptive.
David adulterous.
Peter denying Christ.
Thomas doubting.
