Pharaoh feared Israel's growing population, oppressed the Hebrews, and eventually commanded that their sons be cast into the Nile. Moses' mother hid him for three months, but eventually hiding him became impossible.
So Exodus 2:3 tells us that she made something for him.
The Hebrew word is startling:
תֵּבָה — tevah
An ark.
The same uncommon Hebrew noun is famously used for Noah's ark in Genesis.
Moses' mother coated this little tevah with bitumen and pitch, placed her son inside, and set it among the reeds beside the Nile.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not tell us that Jochebed stopped loving him.
It does not tell us that she stopped caring.
It tells us that she reached a moment when she could no longer hide him.
There are moments when faith does not look like confidently holding everything together.
Sometimes faith looks like trembling hands doing the only faithful thing left to do.
Perhaps you know something about that.
You prayed.
You fought.
You protected.
You tried to control every possible outcome.
And eventually you reached the terrible edge of your own ability.
The marriage.
The child.
The diagnosis.
The debt.
The addiction in someone you love.
The future you cannot guarantee.
The person you cannot change.
The prayer you cannot force God to answer according to your preferred timetable.
There comes a point when human hands discover their limits.
But God's sovereignty does not begin where your strength ends.
He was already sovereign.
Moses' sister stood at a distance.
Exodus 2:4 preserves the moment in Hebrew:
וַתֵּתַצַּב אֲחֹתוֹ מֵרָחֹק לְדֵעָה מַה־יֵּעָשֶׂה לוֹ
His sister stationed herself at a distance to know what would happen to him.
Later Scripture identifies Moses' sister as Miriam.
Picture her there.
Watching.
Waiting.
Unable to know the ending.
That matters.
We know Moses becomes Moses.
She didn't.
We know about the burning bush.
She didn't.
We know about Pharaoh being confronted.
She didn't.
We know about Passover.
She didn't.
We know about the Red Sea.
She didn't.
We read Exodus 2 knowing Exodus 14 is coming.
Miriam stood beside the river with no Exodus 14 in her hands.
She only had the moment in front of her.
That may be where some of you are living right now.
You are standing somewhere between the basket and the Red Sea.
You believe God has written promises, but you cannot yet see how the chapter you are living could possibly connect to them.
You know what God has done for others.
You know what Scripture says.
But your own situation still looks like reeds, water, uncertainty, and waiting.
Then Pharaoh's daughter came down to the Nile.
She noticed the basket.
It was brought to her.
She opened it.
And Scripture gives us one of those tiny scenes capable of carrying enormous emotional weight:
וְהִנֵּה־נַעַר בֹּכֶה
"Behold, a boy crying."
Then:
וַתַּחְמֹל עָלָיו — vataḥmol alav
She had compassion on him.
She recognized him as one of the Hebrew children.
Do not rush past that.
She knew.
This was not merely an unidentified abandoned infant.
She recognized that he belonged to the people her father's regime had oppressed.
The baby lying before her was part of the population Pharaoh had targeted.
And she had compassion.
There is an astonishing irony here.
Pharaoh commands Hebrew boys to be destroyed.
Pharaoh's own daughter becomes the means by which one is preserved.
And not just any Hebrew boy.
Moses.
The future instrument God would use to confront Pharaoh himself.
Human evil is real.
Human decisions have consequences.
Scripture never asks us to pretend otherwise.
But human rulers are not sovereign over God's redemptive purposes.
Pharaoh could issue decrees.
He could not dethrone God.
He could command the Nile to become an instrument of death.
God could preserve His chosen servant beside that very river.
And then Miriam moved.
Imagine the courage required.
She is a Hebrew girl approaching the daughter of Pharaoh while the life of her baby brother hangs in the balance.
One wrong word could expose everything.
Yet Miriam speaks.
הַאֵלֵךְ וְקָרָאתִי לָךְ אִשָּׁה מֵינֶקֶת מִן הָעִבְרִיֹּת
"Shall I go and call for you a nursing woman from the Hebrew women...?"
The princess answers with one word:
לֵכִי — lekhi
"Go."
And Miriam goes.
Where?
To get the baby's mother.
Think about what happens next.
The mother who placed her son among the reeds because she could no longer safely keep him is summoned back.
Pharaoh's daughter essentially tells her:
Take this child.
Nurse him for me.
And...
וַאֲנִי אֶתֵּן אֶת־שְׂכָרֵךְ
"I will give your wages."
Read that again slowly.
The Hebrew mother had been forced by Pharaoh's murderous policy into a situation where she could no longer safely hide her own son.
Then, through an astonishing turn of providence, Pharaoh's own household becomes involved in preserving him, and his own mother is paid to nurse him.
You could not invent the irony without someone accusing you of making the story too dramatic.
But Scripture records it.
The empire that threatened the child unwittingly helps provide for the child's preservation.
The river associated with Pharaoh's decree becomes the setting of Moses' rescue.
The mother who feared losing him receives him back for a season.
The sister who appeared to be merely watching becomes the person whose courageous question reconnects mother and child.
And the baby Pharaoh wanted eliminated eventually becomes the man through whom God announces:
Let My people go.
This is providence.
But we need to be careful here.
Biblical providence does not mean every painful situation will reverse tomorrow.
It does not mean every Christian who loses something will receive that exact thing back in the same form.
It does not mean faithful people never suffer.
The Bible itself will not allow us to make those promises.
What it does mean is that God's purposes cannot finally be defeated by circumstances that terrify us.
Joseph can be sold and still arrive where God intends.
David can be hunted and still receive what God promised.
Daniel can enter Babylon without Babylon becoming his god.
The cross can look like the triumph of darkness while becoming the very place where Christ accomplishes redemption.
And a Hebrew baby can float beside the Nile while heaven remains completely unpanicked.
Maybe that is what you needed to remember.
God is not panicking about the chapter that is panicking you.
You may not understand it.
You may grieve inside it.
You may pray until your voice shakes.
You may have no idea how God will act.
But the throne of heaven has not become vacant.
And there is another detail we cannot ignore.
Miriam spoke.
She could have remained hidden.
She could have watched the princess carry Moses away and concluded, "There is nothing I can do."
Instead she recognized a moment and stepped into it.
Her question seems small compared with the plagues, Passover, Sinai, and the Red Sea.
But history often turns on acts of faithfulness that seem small while they are happening.
One conversation.
One prayer.
One refusal to compromise.
One act of compassion.
One Gospel shared.
One apology.
One decision to forgive.
One invitation to church.
One Scripture sent to someone at midnight.
One moment when you stop watching from a distance and say what faith requires you to say.
You may never know what God does downstream from one obedient act.
Miriam could not part the Red Sea.
That was not her assignment.
She could speak beside the Nile.
That was.
And somebody reading this needs freedom from the exhausting belief that you must accomplish everything.
You don't.
You are not the Savior.
Jesus is.
Your responsibility is faithfulness with whatever God has placed before you.
Miriam did not need tomorrow's power.
She needed today's courage.
But even Moses is not ultimately the Hero of the Bible.
Jesus Christ is.
If we turn Moses into nothing more than motivational material about "believing in yourself," we have missed the greater movement of Scripture.
Moses becomes a deliverer used by God.
But Moses himself points beyond himself.
Israel needed liberation from Pharaoh.
Humanity needs liberation from something deeper: sin and death.
Moses would stand before an earthly ruler.
Jesus would conquer the powers of sin, death, and the grave.
Through Moses, God led Israel out of physical bondage.
Through Christ, sinners are reconciled to God and brought from slavery to sin into new life.
Jesus said in John 8:36:
"If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed."
And this is where the story stops being safely ancient.
Because you can admire Miriam's courage and still be hiding from God.
You can celebrate Moses' rescue and still need rescue yourself.
You can know every detail of Exodus and remain enslaved to bitterness, lust, pride, greed, unforgiveness, secret sin, self-righteousness, or unbelief.
The Gospel is not God helping reasonably good people become slightly better.
The Gospel announces that sinners who cannot rescue themselves can be forgiven and reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
At the cross, Jesus bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
Grace does not pretend your sin was harmless.
Grace reveals how serious sin is while revealing something even more astonishing:
Christ willingly came to save sinners.
That is why repentance matters.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior.
It is the collapse of the performance.
The end of pretending.
The moment you stop defending what Christ died to free you from.
Maybe your "Pharaoh" is not another person.
Maybe it is the sin you keep protecting.
Maybe the chains are hidden behind a Christian vocabulary.
You know how to say "God is good" while secretly becoming cold toward Him.
You know how to post Scripture while privately feeding something destroying your soul.
You know how to appear strong while your prayer life has almost disappeared.
You know how to encourage everybody else while wondering whether God could possibly still want you after what you have done.
Listen carefully.
Your scandal does not have to be your final sentence.
Peter denied Jesus.
Grace restored him.
Paul persecuted believers.
Grace transformed him.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
He had a dying Savior beside him who was about to rise.
Christianity is filled with people whose histories should have disqualified them if salvation depended upon spotless histories.
It doesn't.
Salvation rests upon Christ.
"For by grace are ye saved through faith...not of works" (Ephesians 2:8–9).
And that grace does not leave us unchanged.
The next verse says we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
Grace forgives.
Grace also transforms.
Grace does not tell you to become comfortable in the chains.
Grace brings you to Jesus so the chains no longer own you.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior keeps returning to the same heartbeat:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by erasing repentance.
Jesus rewrites the story by taking guilty people who come to Him in faith, forgiving them by grace, giving them a new identity in Him, and beginning the lifelong work of transforming them.
The scars may remain.
Consequences may remain.
Memories may remain.
But condemnation does not have the final word for those who are in Christ Jesus.
Maybe you feel like Moses in the basket.
Helpless.
Maybe you feel like Jochebed.
You have done everything you know to do and now must entrust what you love to God.
Maybe you feel like Miriam.
Watching.
Waiting.
Wondering when to speak.
Or perhaps you feel like Pharaoh's daughter.
God has placed something in front of you that requires compassion and courage even when the surrounding culture points in another direction.
Wherever you see yourself, do not make yourself the center of Scripture.
Look higher.
God is the One working through Exodus.
And the God who revealed His saving power in Israel's history has given us the fullest revelation of His saving grace in His Son.
What are you still trying to rescue without surrendering it to Christ?
What are you hiding?
What are you defending?
What are you afraid Jesus will uncover if you finally become completely honest with Him?
You do not need another religious mask.
You need Christ.
Come to Him.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Receive the mercy you cannot earn.
And if you already belong to Jesus but your spirit has been exhausted lately, stop pretending with God.
He already knows.
Return.
Pray.
Open His Word again.
Ask another believer to walk with you.
There is no spiritual maturity in hiding wounds until they become infections.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person needed to read tonight.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
Someone whose life feels like a basket surrounded by dark water right now.
Not for numbers.
Not for applause.
Because truth is meant to travel.
If an article centered on Christ can put Scripture in front of someone who would never walk into a church today, sharing becomes more than clicking a button. It can become a simple act of witness.
There may come a night when you need to remember that Miriam did not know the Red Sea was coming while she stood beside the Nile.
We want this community to remain a place of daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.

Supporting Gospel work does not purchase God's favor, earn salvation, or make anyone more spiritual. Salvation is by grace through faith in Christ, not by financial support. But Christians are called to use their resources willingly and cheerfully for God's purposes, and supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one practical way to participate in spreading biblical truth.
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
A ministry cannot save you.
Moses cannot save you.
Only Christ can reconcile sinners to God.
The baby in the basket grew into Israel's great deliverer, but even Moses belonged to a story reaching toward a greater Deliverer.
And perhaps that is why this scene beside the Nile still reaches into the human heart thousands of years later.
A mother thought she was releasing her son.
A sister thought she was only watching.
A princess thought she was rescuing one crying child.
None of them could yet see everything that would follow.
Egypt.
Passover.
Deliverance.
The sea opening.
A nation walking toward freedom.
Sometimes you are standing so close to the river that all you can see is the basket.
God sees farther than you do.
So surrender what you cannot control.
Speak when faithfulness requires courage.
Show compassion when the world teaches indifference.
Repent where sin has taken root.
Run toward Jesus instead of hiding from Him.
And when your life looks like a scandal too tangled, a failure too public, a wound too deep, or a history too broken to redeem, remember the Gospel:
Christ specializes in raising hope where sinners thought the story had already ended.
Because sometimes what looks like a helpless basket drifting beside the reeds is already sitting inside a story God has not finished writing.
The river only knew the baby was crying. Heaven knew a deliverer was coming.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Does God Care What You Post Online? The Question Most Christians Never Ask Before They Hit “Post”
paragraphs: Does God Care What You Post Online? The Question Most Christians Never Ask Before They Hit “Post”

Your timeline may disappear in a scroll. Your story may expire in twenty-four hours. But the heart behind what you publish matters to the God who sees what no follower, friend, critic, or algorithm can see.
There is a moment almost nobody talks about.
Your thumb is hovering over the button.
Post.
Maybe you are angry.
Maybe somebody embarrassed you, and this is your chance to answer without mentioning their name.
Maybe the photograph has been edited until even you barely look like you.
Maybe the caption sounds spiritual, but somewhere underneath it you desperately want someone to notice you.
Maybe what you are about to share is true.
Or maybe you never actually checked.
Maybe it is funny.
Maybe it will get reactions.
Maybe it will make people furious.
Maybe it will make somebody jealous.
Maybe it will make you feel important for five minutes.
Your thumb is still hovering there.
And then comes the question that could change the way a Christian uses the internet:
If Jesus were visibly standing beside me, would I still post this?
Not because Jesus is frightened by social media.
Not because Christianity requires believers to become humorless, silent people afraid of technology.
Not because every photograph needs a Bible verse underneath it.
But because Jesus Christ is already Lord when you unlock your phone.
He does not become Lord when you enter church and temporarily stop being Lord when you open Facebook.
There is no “offline Jesus” and “online me.”
That division does not exist in biblical discipleship.
The frightening—and strangely beautiful—truth is that God cares about the person holding the phone before He cares about the performance happening on the screen.
Your timeline can reveal something about your heart.
So can your comments.
Your private messages.
The jokes you share.
The rumors you repeat.
The people you humiliate.
The arguments you cannot walk away from.
The compliments you secretly live for.
The photographs designed to provoke envy.
The spiritual posts written more to impress Christians than to honor Christ.
And yes...
even the comment you typed, deleted, typed again, stared at for thirty seconds...
and finally sent.
Jesus said something long before smartphones existed that reaches uncomfortably into the digital age:
“For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.”
—Matthew 12:34
The principle is devastatingly simple.
What comes out eventually reveals something about what is happening within.
Today, what comes out of us does not travel only through our mouths.
Sometimes it travels through our thumbs.
Sometimes the modern tongue has a touchscreen.
And that means the deeper question is not merely, “Was my post inappropriate?”
The deeper question may be:
“What did I want this post to do for my heart?”
Did I want revenge?
Attention?
Approval?
Validation?
Control?
Did I want someone to envy me?
Did I want my enemy to hurt?
Did I want strangers to think I possessed a life I do not actually possess?
Did I want to appear holy instead of becoming holy?
That question hurts because social media gives us something previous generations never possessed at this scale:
a stage we can carry in our pockets.
And stages are dangerous places for hearts that hunger to be worshiped.

Jesus warned His disciples about practicing righteousness “to be seen” by others in Matthew 6:1. He was not discussing Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, or any modern platform. We should not pretend He was.
He was exposing something far older than technology.
The human appetite to be noticed.
That appetite simply found better equipment.
Now we can measure attention.
Likes.
Views.
Shares.
Comments.
Followers.
Numbers moving upward.
Numbers moving downward.
Refresh.
Refresh again.
Someone reacted.
Someone did not.
Someone else is doing better.
Someone else's family looks happier.
Someone else's ministry looks larger.
Someone else's body looks better.
Someone else's marriage looks perfect.
Someone else's life appears blessed.
And somewhere between comparison and performance, a person can slowly begin asking the internet a question that only God was meant to answer:
“Am I worth something?”
The Gospel answers before the algorithm ever can.
Your deepest worth is not established by how many people notice you.
For the Christian, identity is rooted in belonging to Christ.
You were not redeemed by engagement.
You were not purchased by applause.
You were not reconciled to God because people approved of you.
Jesus Christ went to the cross for sinners.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Grace does not arrive because your image is impressive.
Grace arrives because Christ is sufficient.
And perhaps that is exactly why this subject cuts so deeply.
Because sometimes we are trying to receive from strangers what Jesus already offers in Himself.
But there is another side to this.
Social media is not merely a place where Christians can sin.
It is also a place where Christians can love.
A screen can carry cruelty.
It can also carry hope.
A comment can humiliate someone.
A comment can also stop a hurting person from believing nobody sees them.
A post can spread a lie.
A post can proclaim truth.
A message can seduce.
A message can encourage.
A timeline can become an altar to self.
Or it can become one small place where the character of Christ becomes visible.
Paul wrote:
“Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up...”
—Ephesians 4:29
The Greek word often translated “corrupting” is σαπρός — sapros.
It carries the sense of something rotten, spoiled, bad, or unfit.
Imagine applying that test before posting.
Not merely:
Is this technically allowed?
But:
Is this rotten?
Will it decay something?
Will it unnecessarily tear someone apart?
Will it spread suspicion I cannot prove?
Will it feed lust?
Will it cultivate hatred?
Will it make cruelty entertaining?
Will it wound somebody merely because wounding them feels satisfying?
Then Paul gives the alternative.
Words that build.
Words appropriate to the need.
Words capable of giving grace to those who hear.
That is not weakness.
Sometimes grace tells the truth people do not want to hear.
Jesus Himself spoke hard truth.
The apostles confronted sin.
Biblical love is not sentimental silence.
But there is an enormous difference between speaking truth because you desire someone's restoration and weaponizing truth because you enjoy someone's destruction.
You can be factually correct and spiritually ugly.
You can win the comment section and dishonor Christ in the process.
You can defend Christianity with a manner completely unlike Christ.
And Christians especially need to hear this:
Not every argument deserves your presence.

Proverbs repeatedly warns about foolish speech and needless quarrels. James tells believers to be “quick to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger” because human anger does not produce God's righteousness.
Imagine if Christians became known online for that kind of restraint.
Not cowardice.
Not compromise.
Restraint.
The ability to know truth without needing to humiliate everyone who disagrees.
The ability to defend the faith without treating another human being as garbage.
The ability to say, “That is wrong,” without secretly meaning, “And I would enjoy watching you suffer.”
Because behind the profile picture is a soul.
Behind the political opinion is a soul.
Behind the atheist comment is a soul.
Behind the offensive joke is a soul.
Behind the person mocking Christianity is a soul.
Behind the person who wounded you...
is a soul.
A soul Jesus commands you to treat differently from the way the world teaches people to treat enemies.
That does not mean tolerating abuse.
It does not mean refusing boundaries.
It does not mean remaining in dangerous conversations.
It does not mean calling evil good.
It means remembering that Christians do not receive permission to abandon Christlike character simply because someone else behaved badly first.
Then there is another category.
The post is not hateful.
It is not obscene.
It is not even obviously sinful.
But something about it still needs examination.
Paul told the Philippians:
“whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is commendable...think about these things.”
—Philippians 4:8
Look at part of the Greek:
ὅσα ἐστὶν ἀληθῆ... ὅσα δίκαια, ὅσα ἁγνά...
hosa estin alēthē... hosa dikaia, hosa hagna...
Whatever is true...
whatever is right...
whatever is pure.

Paul was instructing believers about the orientation of Christian thought and life, not giving a social-media policy. But the principle reaches straight into what we consume, celebrate, meditate upon, and circulate.
Because before you share something, you have often already allowed it into your mind.
And then you potentially place it into hundreds of other minds.
That should make us tremble a little.
Is it true?
Not: Does it agree with me?
Not: Did someone I trust share it?
Not: Does the headline make the people I dislike look terrible?
Is it true?
Christians worship the One who called Himself “the truth.”
We therefore have no spiritual permission to become enthusiastic distributors of falsehood merely because the falsehood benefits our side.
Before sharing the accusation, check it.
Before destroying somebody's reputation, check it.
Before forwarding the screenshot, ask whether you know its context.
Before announcing another person's failure, ask whether the world genuinely needs you to become its broadcaster.
Before turning someone's worst moment into entertainment, remember how desperately you would want mercy if the worst thing you ever did became tomorrow's viral content.
And suddenly...
we arrive at grace.
Because maybe while reading this, you remembered something.
A post.
A photograph.
A conversation.
A cruel reply.
A lie.
A flirtation.
A private message.
A public humiliation.
Something you shared while angry.
Something you posted because you needed people to admire you.
Something you would desperately erase if Jesus projected your motives onto the wall.
And now shame starts talking.
Look at you.
Hypocrite.
Fake Christian.
You knew better.
This is where Christianity becomes radically different from mere moral improvement.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean up your timeline so God might finally love you.”
The Gospel says sinners need a Savior.
Jesus Christ.
The answer to digital sin is ultimately the same answer as every other sin:
repentance and faith in Christ.
Repentance does not mean feeling embarrassed because somebody caught you.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance, a turning of mind and direction toward God.
Real repentance can have practical consequences.
Delete what needs deleting.
Correct what was false.
Apologize where you wounded someone.
Stop visiting what is feeding secret sin.
Block what repeatedly pulls you toward temptation if necessary.
Leave the argument.
Tell the truth.
Ask forgiveness.
Make restitution where appropriate.
But do not confuse repentance with self-salvation.
You cannot delete enough posts to erase your guilt before a holy God.
You need Christ.
The scandal of the Gospel is that Jesus receives people whose histories are worse than their carefully edited profiles reveal.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul had persecuted believers.
The woman of Samaria carried a complicated relational history.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime remaining to rebuild his reputation.
Again and again, Scripture introduces us to people whose stories looked ruined...
until grace entered the story.
That is why our message remains:
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because grace pretends sin never mattered.
Grace is costly precisely because sin mattered enough for Christ to go to the cross.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years curating a version of themselves online because they are terrified that the real person underneath would not be loved.
Listen carefully.
Jesus already knows.
The browser history.
The deleted messages.
The jealousy.
The insecurity.
The private pride.
The secret bitterness.
The craving for attention.
The spiritual performance.
The nights you posted something cheerful while crying after you put your phone down.
He knows.
And His invitation is not:
“Improve your brand.”
It is:
“Follow Me.”
Come out of hiding.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Receive mercy.
Walk differently.
Not perfectly overnight.
But genuinely.
Maybe the most Christlike thing you can post today is not another verse graphic.
Maybe it is an apology.
Maybe it is silence.
Maybe it is encouragement.
Maybe it is refusing to share gossip.
Maybe it is celebrating someone without secretly competing with them.
Maybe it is telling the truth about what Jesus rescued you from without making yourself the hero of the testimony.
Maybe it is using the platform God has allowed you to have—even if only thirty people see it—to make one exhausted person remember that Christ has not abandoned them.
And maybe before your next post, you need five seconds of holy hesitation.
Is it true?
Is it loving?
Is it necessary?
Does it build rather than merely destroy?
Can I post this with a clear conscience before Jesus Christ?
Not everything difficult must remain unsaid.
Not everything controversial dishonors God.
Not every joke is sinful.
Not every selfie is vanity.
Not every disagreement is hatred.
Not every successful Christian is showing off.
We should be careful not to create commandments God never created.
But Scripture gives us something far more demanding than a list of forbidden posts.
It gives us a Lord.
And when Christ owns the heart, eventually He begins reaching the fingers too.
That includes what they type.
What they share.
What they delete.
What they refuse to watch.
What they refuse to spread.
What they write when angry.
And what they do when nobody knows who is behind the account.
So yes...
God cares about what you post online.
But not because heaven is running a social-media department counting how many Christian graphics you upload.
God cares because He cares about you.
Your words matter because hearts matter.
Truth matters.
Purity matters.
Love matters.
Your neighbor matters.
Your witness matters.
And above everything...
Christ matters.
If this article exposed something you have been hiding behind a screen, do not merely feel guilty and keep scrolling.
Take it to Jesus.
If necessary, put the phone down and pray.
Confess specifically.
Repent honestly.
Receive the mercy Christ purchased.
Then come back differently.
And if you need words for that moment, make them simple:
“Jesus, forgive me. Make even my online life belong to You.”
Not as a performance.
Not because typing a comment saves you.
Christ alone saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that God is dealing with us becomes the moment we stop pretending.
Someone else reading the comments may discover they are not fighting alone.
Not because saving an article makes someone spiritual, but because there may come a night when anger is burning through your fingers and you need to read these words again before pressing “Post.”
Do not share it merely to grow a page.
“Does what you're posting look like the Jesus you're following?”

There are many ways to glorify God. Generosity, encouragement, sharing biblical truth, serving others, supporting faithful ministry, and using whatever influence God has entrusted to us can all become acts of worship when they flow from faith and love rather than spiritual pressure.
Jesus is not asking you to purchase your way into His love.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Salvation is God's gift in Christ.
But if this ministry is feeding your faith and you are able and willing to help carry that message farther, your support can help Gospel truth reach another screen...
another home...
another exhausted believer...
another skeptic...
another person hiding behind a perfect profile while privately falling apart.
Not theirs.
Yours.
Imagine Jesus beside you.
Not angry with crossed arms.
Not impressed by follower counts.
Not fooled by filters.
Just Christ...
looking beyond the screen...
into the heart of the person holding it.
And ask Him:
“Lord, if there is anything on my screen that does not belong to You, show me. If there is anything in my heart that does not belong to You, change me.”
Then have the courage to obey whatever Scripture makes clear.
Because someday your final post will be posted.
Your account will eventually go silent.
The notifications will stop.
The followers will move on.
The algorithm will forget your name.
But Christ will still be King.
And perhaps the question was never merely whether God cares what you post.
Perhaps the question underneath everything has always been:
Does Jesus have the person doing the posting?
And invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to come with you.
Because the goal was never to create better religious profiles.
The goal is surrendered people who belong completely to Jesus Christ.
And remember this when the screen goes dark:
Jesus does not merely want control of what appears on your timeline—He wants to redeem the heart that writes it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Secret Friendships Damage Marriages
paragraphs: Why Secret Friendships Damage Marriages

The relationship you keep saying is “just a friendship” may never have crossed a bedroom door—and still may have crossed a covenant boundary. Before a marriage collapses publicly, something sacred is often surrendered privately.
It usually does not begin with a kiss.
That is what makes it dangerous.
It begins with a conversation.
A message that feels harmless.
A joke your spouse never hears.
A person who seems to understand you when home has become complicated.
A notification you instinctively turn away from your husband or wife.
A conversation you delete—not because anything “happened,” but because explaining it would be uncomfortable.
And then comes the sentence that has protected countless dangerous relationships from necessary examination:
“We’re just friends.”
Maybe you are.
But here is the question that reaches deeper than the label:
Why does the friendship need secrecy to survive?
Read that again.

Because this article is not arguing that every friendship outside marriage is sinful. Scripture does not teach that married people must never have meaningful friendships with others, including people of the opposite sex. We should never manufacture a command God did not give.
But Scripture says a great deal about covenant faithfulness, guarding the heart, truthfulness, temptation, sexual purity, wisdom, and refusing to make provision for sin.
And that changes the conversation.
The danger is not merely that a secret friendship might someday become sexual.

The danger is that someone who is not your spouse may already be receiving pieces of your emotional intimacy, vulnerability, anticipation, affection, secrecy, loyalty, or romantic energy that should have been guarded within your marriage.
Nothing physical may have happened.
Yet something may already be moving.
Your heart.
And Scripture takes the movement of the heart seriously.
“Guard your heart with all diligence, for from it flow springs of life” is the sense of Proverbs 4:23. The Hebrew is striking:
מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ
Mi-kol mishmar, netzor libbekha.
“Above all guarding, guard your heart.”
The imperative נְצֹר — netzor means to guard, watch, preserve, keep.
Not because every human connection is evil.
Because your heart is powerful.
And your heart can travel somewhere long before your body follows.
That is why the most dangerous question may not be, “Have I committed adultery?”
It may be:
“What am I allowing my heart to rehearse?”
Maybe you have not touched them.
But you wait for their messages.
Maybe you have never kissed them.
But you think about them after an argument with your spouse.
Maybe you have never said, “I love you.”
But they are becoming the first person you want to tell when something wonderful—or terrible—happens.
Maybe you insist there is no affair.
But you protect that relationship more fiercely than you protect your spouse’s peace.
Maybe your spouse has said, “Something about this friendship makes me uncomfortable,” and instead of becoming curious about their pain, you became furious about your freedom.
That should make us stop.

Not because a spouse's jealousy automatically makes every friendship wrong. Jealousy can itself become unhealthy or controlling, and biblical marriage does not give either spouse permission to isolate or dominate the other.
But neither does “you’re just jealous” give us permission to dismiss legitimate covenant concerns.
Marriage was never designed to be a courtroom where you search for the technical definition of adultery so you can determine how close to the boundary you are permitted to walk.
Marriage is covenant.
And covenant asks a different question:
“How can I love this person faithfully before God?”
Go back to the beginning.
Genesis 2:24 says:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
Al-ken ya'azov-ish et-aviv ve'et-immo, vedavaq be'ishto, vehayu levasar echad.
Therefore a man leaves his father and mother, clings to his wife, and they become one flesh.
That word is enormous:
וְדָבַק — vedavaq.
From the Hebrew root דבק — dabaq.
To cling.
To cleave.
To adhere.
To stay close.
To hold fast.
Genesis does not describe marriage as two independent lives that happen to share an address.
There is a covenantal holding-fast.
Jesus Himself returned to this creation text when teaching about marriage, declaring that the two become one flesh and that what God has joined together should not be separated (Matthew 19:4–6).
Paul returns to the same text in Ephesians 5:31 and places marriage inside an even greater mystery—the relationship between Christ and His Church.
Marriage, then, is bigger than romance.
It is bigger than chemistry.
It is bigger than the wedding photographs.
Christian marriage is meant to bear witness to covenant love.
And this is where secret friendships become spiritually serious.
Because secrecy creates a room inside your marriage where your spouse is not allowed to enter.
At first, that room may contain almost nothing.
A few messages.
An inside joke.
A complaint about your marriage.
A little validation.
A little flirting that everybody pretends is humor.
A confession.
A late-night conversation.
Then another.
And another.
Until one day you realize this person knows things about your marriage that your spouse does not know about the friendship.
Think about that sentence.
They know your spouse’s weaknesses.
Your spouse does not even know the depth of their access to you.
That is not a small thing.
You may say, “But they listen to me.”
Perhaps they do.
“They understand me.”
Perhaps they do.
“My spouse doesn't talk to me anymore.”
That may even be painfully true.
And this is where Christians must resist shallow answers.
Some marriages are lonely.
Some husbands feel invisible.
Some wives have spent years begging to be heard.
Some couples live under the same roof while emotionally existing on different planets.

There are marriages where tenderness has disappeared beneath work, parenting, disappointment, resentment, exhaustion, unresolved wounds, sexual frustration, financial pressure, or years of things nobody had the courage to say.
Then somebody appears.
They notice you.
They laugh at your jokes.
They ask how you are doing—and actually wait for the answer.
Suddenly you remember what it feels like to be interesting.
Wanted.
Seen.
Alive.
That feeling is powerful.
And that is precisely why wisdom is necessary.
Because something can feel like rescue while quietly becoming temptation.
The other person usually gets the edited version of you.
Your spouse gets the exhausted you.
The stressed you.
The morning-breath you.
The bills.
The children.
The laundry.
The disappointments.
The history.
The arguments that never quite got resolved.
The friend gets twenty beautiful minutes of conversation.
No mortgage.
No screaming toddler.
No years of accumulated misunderstanding.
No discussion about whose turn it is to clean the kitchen.
And then the comparison begins.
“My spouse never listens like this.”
“My spouse doesn't appreciate me like this.”
“I can tell this person anything.”
Be careful.
You may be comparing the hardest reality of covenant with the easiest moments of an escape.
And fantasy almost always wins that comparison because fantasy never has to wash dishes with you.
This is one reason secrecy changes everything.
Healthy friendships can normally survive appropriate boundaries.
Dangerous ones often require exceptions.
“Don't tell your husband I said this.”
“Your wife wouldn't understand.”
“Delete that.”
“Let's keep this between us.”
“I wish I had met you before…”
“We're not doing anything wrong.”
When people repeatedly need to announce that nothing is wrong, sometimes the heart already knows there is something worth examining.
Jesus does not allow us to reduce faithfulness to physical technicalities.

In Matthew 5:27–28, He takes the command against adultery and drives it into the interior life. He speaks of looking with lustful intent and says adultery can already be committed ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ — en tē kardia — “in the heart.”
Jesus is not saying an inward temptation and a completed physical affair produce identical earthly consequences. They do not.
He is doing something even more searching.
He is exposing the lie that holiness is merely external behavior.
God cares about what happens in the hidden room.
The imagination.
The desire.
The intention.
The heart.
That means you can be technically faithful while becoming emotionally unfaithful.
You can keep your clothes on while slowly giving your heart away.
You can never meet in a hotel and still cultivate a relationship you desperately hope your spouse never fully discovers.
And maybe that is where these words found you.
Maybe there is already a name in your mind.
A face.
A conversation.
A notification.
Maybe you immediately became defensive.
“They don't understand our friendship.”
Perhaps.
But answer this before God:
Would you communicate exactly the same way if your spouse were sitting beside you reading every message?
Would the tone change?
Would certain jokes disappear?
Would certain confessions suddenly feel inappropriate?
Would you be comfortable handing your spouse your phone and saying, “Read the entire conversation. I have nothing I need to hide”?

This is not an argument for marital surveillance, obsessive phone checking, coercive control, or the destruction of legitimate privacy. Healthy marriages require trust, dignity, wisdom, and appropriate personal space.
But privacy and secrecy are not always the same thing.
Privacy says, “I am still a person.”
Secrecy says, “There is something here I need you not to know because your knowledge could threaten what I want to continue.”
That difference matters.
Especially when emotional intimacy is involved.
Hebrews 13:4 says marriage should be held in honor and the marriage bed kept undefiled.
Notice the posture.
Honor.
You do not merely avoid destroying what you honor.
You protect it.
You do not ask, “How close can I get to betrayal before God calls it betrayal?”
You ask, “How can I honor what God entrusted to me?”
Romans 13:14 tells believers to put on the Lord Jesus Christ and make no provision for the flesh.
That is mature Christianity.
Not merely resisting sin after it becomes overwhelming.
Refusing to prepare a room for it.
Some affairs explode.
Others are furnished slowly.
One private conversation at a time.
One complaint about your spouse at a time.
One “good morning” text at a time.
One emotional dependency at a time.
One deleted message at a time.
One boundary moved two inches at a time.
Until two inches becomes two miles and both people wonder how they arrived there.
You arrived there gradually.
That is how many compromises work.
And yet…
If you are reading this with a knot in your stomach, I do not want the story to end with your shame.
Because the Gospel does not merely expose.
The Gospel restores.
Jesus Christ did not go to the cross so sinners could become better at hiding.
He went to the cross to save sinners.
The scandal of Christianity is not that righteous people finally became impressive enough for God.
The scandal is grace.
Christ died for sinners.
Christ receives the repentant.
Christ forgives.
Christ cleanses.
Christ transforms.
Christ teaches us to walk in the light.
So if there is a secret friendship in your life that has crossed emotional, romantic, sexual, or covenant boundaries, the answer is not to rename darkness until it feels innocent.
Bring it into the light.
Do not wait until the relationship becomes physical to admit that your heart has moved.
Do not wait for discovery.
Do not wait until screenshots appear.
Do not wait until your spouse is standing in front of you asking, “How long has this been happening?”
Repentance does not mean merely feeling guilty.
Biblical repentance turns.
It tells the truth.
It stops feeding what needs to die.
It establishes boundaries.
It seeks wisdom.
It accepts accountability.
And where appropriate and safe, it begins the difficult work of rebuilding honesty with the spouse whose trust has been wounded.
Sometimes that will require pastoral care.
Sometimes wise Christian counseling.
Sometimes long conversations.
Sometimes tears.
Sometimes consequences.
Sometimes the person you hurt will not trust you immediately simply because you apologized.
Forgiveness and rebuilt trust are related, but they are not identical.
Trust can require time.
Do not demand instant healing from the person your secrecy injured.
Stay faithful in the rebuilding.
And if your marriage is deeply distressed, do not use another person as anesthesia.
Get help.
Fight for truth.
Invite mature, trustworthy believers into the struggle.
Pray together if you can.
Seek qualified counseling when needed.
Return again and again to Christ.
Because your spouse cannot be your Savior either.
Marriage is sacred, but marriage is not God.
Your deepest hunger cannot finally be satisfied by a husband, wife, friend, or secret admirer.
It was always meant to lead you deeper than all of them.
To Jesus.
Perhaps that is the hidden ache underneath some emotional affairs.
We demand from another human being the affirmation, identity, security, excitement, or unconditional acceptance that our souls ultimately need to receive from Christ.
Then we become spiritually hungry and start eating wherever someone offers us attention.
Jesus offers something deeper.
Not secret excitement.
New life.
Not temporary validation.
Identity.
Not an escape from truth.
Freedom through truth.
Not permission to continue hiding.
Grace strong enough to bring you into the light.
And maybe today the bravest thing you can do is stop saying, “Nothing happened.”
Maybe something did happen.
Maybe your heart wandered.
Maybe boundaries blurred.
Maybe you enjoyed attention you knew was becoming dangerous.
Maybe you said things you would never have said with your spouse standing there.
Maybe you have been emotionally feeding a relationship that should have been starving.
Then do not waste this conviction.
Run toward Christ.
Not away from Him.
First John 1:9 teaches that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
There is blood for this.
There is mercy for this.
There is grace for this.
There is no secret so dark that Jesus needs you to hide it from Him.
He already knows.
The question is whether you will surrender it.
And for the spouse who has discovered something like this—your pain matters too.
You are not required to pretend betrayal did not hurt in order to prove that you are spiritual.
Grief is not unbelief.
Questions are not automatically bitterness.
Reconciliation, where possible, is not pretending nothing happened.
Christian restoration is built on truth.
Jesus does not heal marriages by asking people to worship appearances.
He works in the light.
Maybe your marriage looks nothing like the wedding photographs now.
Maybe both of you are carrying scars.
Maybe conversations are awkward.
Maybe trust feels fragile.
Maybe you wonder whether tenderness can ever return.
Do not confuse wounded with worthless.
God has rebuilt people from ruins before.
The Gospel itself is the announcement that what looked irredeemably lost can be touched by resurrection power.
That does not guarantee every marriage will unfold exactly as we hope. Scripture never gives us permission to promise outcomes God has not promised.
But it does mean no repentant sinner is beyond the reach of Christ.
No wounded heart is outside His sight.
No confession surprises Him.
No darkness intimidates Him.
And no human scandal gets the final word over a life surrendered to Jesus.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to create perfect-looking Christians.
To keep pointing broken, tempted, exhausted, ashamed, wounded, wandering people back to Jesus Christ.
Someone scrolling beneath this article may need evidence that grace still walks into wreckage.
You may need to read it again when your heart begins negotiating with a boundary you already know should not move.
Sharing biblical truth can be an act of ministry.

Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ, not by financial support for a ministry. Supporting Gospel work can be one voluntary way of stewarding what God has given you, but it must never replace obedience, generosity to your local church and those in need, prayer, repentance, or faithful service.
Sharing places it in front of someone we may never be able to reach ourselves.
Is there a relationship in your life that can survive only because somebody you made a covenant with does not know the whole truth?
Do not protect the secret and sacrifice the covenant.
Do not trade something sacred for the temporary intoxication of being understood by someone new.
Do not wait for adultery to become physical before you begin fighting for faithfulness.
Guard your heart.
Honor your covenant.
Tell the truth.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive as Christ teaches you to forgive.
Seek help where healing requires help.

And cling first to Jesus Christ, because only He can teach two imperfect people what covenant love looks like when feelings fluctuate, wounds ache, temptation whispers, and grace has to become more than a word printed on a church wall.
The world may remember your worst chapter.
Jesus is still capable of writing what comes next.
Some doors save a marriage when they are finally closed—and some hearts begin healing the moment the hiding ends.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: MANY ARE CALLED. FEW ARE CHOSEN. AND THAT SHOULD TERRIFY THE PERSON WHO ONLY LOOKS CHRISTIAN.
paragraphs:
MANY ARE CALLED. FEW ARE CHOSEN. AND THAT SHOULD TERRIFY THE PERSON WHO ONLY LOOKS CHRISTIAN.
The Warning Jesus Hid in Plain Sight—and Why the Wedding Garment Changes Everything
There are words of Jesus that comfort you.
And then there are words of Jesus that refuse to let you sleep comfortably.
“Many are called, but few are chosen.”
We print verses about grace on coffee mugs. We underline promises of peace. We share Scriptures about blessing when life becomes unbearable.
But this sentence?
This sentence follows you into the quiet.
Because Jesus did not say it to atheists mocking Him from a distance.
He said it at the end of a story about people who had been invited to a wedding.
People who had heard the call.
People who were close enough to the celebration to know that something important was happening.
And one man even made it inside.
That is where the warning becomes frightening.
You can be near holy things and still not belong to Christ.
You can know Christian vocabulary.
You can sing worship songs.
You can repost Bible verses.
You can sit in church until the preacher recognizes your face.
You can know when to say “Amen.”
You can look spiritually alive to everybody watching you...
and still have a heart that has never truly surrendered to the King.
Jesus ends His parable in Matthew 22:14 with these Greek words:
Πολλοὶ γάρ εἰσιν κλητοί, ὀλίγοι δὲ ἐκλεκτοί.
Polloi gar eisin klētoi, oligoi de eklektoi.
“For many are called, but few are chosen.”
The word κλητοί — klētoi carries the idea of those who are called or invited.
The word ἐκλεκτοί — eklektoi means chosen, selected, elect.
But if we isolate that sentence from the story Jesus just told, we can easily turn a terrifyingly beautiful Gospel warning into something Jesus was not saying.
So go back to the banquet.
Jesus describes a king who prepared a wedding feast for his son.
Already, the picture matters.
A king.
A son.
A wedding.
An invitation.
A feast prepared at tremendous cost.
And messengers sent to tell the invited guests:
Come.
Everything is ready.
But they would not come.
Think about the insanity of that.
The king was not asking starving people to provide the meal.
The feast had already been prepared.
They simply had to respond to the invitation.
Yet some were indifferent.
One went to his farm.
Another went to his business.
Others became violently hostile toward the king’s servants.
Different reactions.
Same rejection.
Some hated the invitation.
Others were simply too busy for it.
And perhaps that second group should frighten modern Christians even more.
Because not everybody rejects Christ by shaking a fist toward heaven.
Some reject Him by being perpetually distracted.
Work.
Money.
Relationships.
Entertainment.
Ambition.
Notifications.
Pleasure.
Another episode.
Another purchase.
Another promotion.
Another tomorrow.
Nothing necessarily looks dramatic.
Nobody announces, “I reject Jesus Christ.”
They simply keep living as though the King’s invitation can wait.
And one day they discover that eternity did not wait with them.
Jesus said elsewhere:
“What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul?”
You can succeed at almost everything people applaud...
and fail at the one thing eternity exposes.
But then the parable takes an astonishing turn.
The original invitees reject the king, so the servants are sent out into the roads.
Bring whoever you find.
Matthew deliberately tells us that they gathered “both bad and good.”
Do not rush past those words.
Bad and good.
Suddenly the wedding hall begins filling with people who may never have imagined themselves sitting at the king’s table.
This is where scandal begins turning into grace.
The unwanted can come.
The morally disgraced can come.
The person with a past can come.
The person whose family knows exactly what he did can come.
The woman carrying memories she wishes she could erase can come.
The addict can come.
The hypocrite who finally admits his hypocrisy can come.
The religious person who discovers that religion cannot save him can come.
The ashamed can come.
The broken can come.
The guilty can come.
The person reading this article while secretly wondering, “After everything I have done, could Jesus possibly still want me?” can come.
The invitation goes into the streets.
Grace goes looking where respectable people sometimes refuse to go.
This is Christianity.
Not bad people pretending they became good enough for God.
It is guilty people being summoned to a feast they could never have earned.
But then Jesus introduces one guest who should make every reader examine his own heart.
The king enters.
He sees a man without a wedding garment.
“Friend,” the king asks, “how did you get in here without a wedding garment?”
And Scripture says:
ὁ δὲ ἐφιμώθη.
Ho de ephimōthē.
“But he was speechless.”
The verb carries the force of being silenced—muzzled, left without an answer.
No excuse.
No argument.
No defense.
He had entered the celebration, but he was unprepared for the king.
And here we must be careful.

Christians have interpreted the wedding garment in several related ways across the history of the Church. Some emphasize the righteousness God provides; others emphasize the transformed life appropriate to those who genuinely respond to God’s invitation. We should not force one small detail of a parable beyond what Scripture permits.
But the central warning is unmistakable:
Being around the kingdom is not the same as belonging to the King.
An outward response without inward reality will not survive divine examination.
That truth appears repeatedly in the teaching of Jesus.
“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven.”
Notice what those people call Him.
Lord.
They possess religious language.
They even point toward impressive spiritual works.
Yet Jesus warns that outward profession by itself is not saving faith.
This should destroy one of the most dangerous lies in modern Christianity:
“I’m probably okay.”
Probably?
Your soul is too valuable for probably.
“I believe in God.”
James reminds us that even demons believe that God is one—and shudder.
“I grew up Christian.”
Jesus never said, “You must grow up Christian.”
He said:
“You must be born again.”
“I go to church.”
Wonderful.
But entering a church building cannot reconcile a sinner to God any more than entering a hospital lobby makes someone a physician.
“I’m a good person.”
Compared with whom?
Your neighbor?
Your ex?
The criminal on television?
The standard is not the worst person you know.
The standard is the holiness of God.
And that is exactly why the Gospel is such spectacular news.
Because Christianity does not announce that you can climb high enough to reach God.
It announces that God came down to rescue sinners.
Jesus Christ did not enter history merely to make decent people slightly nicer.
The eternal Son of God took on flesh.
He lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He went willingly toward a Roman cross.
And there, the sinless One suffered for sinners.
Isaiah had written centuries earlier:
כֻּלָּנוּ כַּצֹּאן תָּעִינוּ
Kullānu ka-tzon ta‘inu.
“All we like sheep have gone astray.”
Then comes the breathtaking turn:
וַיהוָה הִפְגִּיעַ בּוֹ אֵת עֲוֹן כֻּלָּנוּ
The LORD laid upon Him the iniquity of us all.
Our sin.
His suffering.
Our guilt.
His sacrifice.
Our rebellion.
His wounds.
And the cross was not the end.
Jesus rose from the dead.
The tomb could not keep Him.
Death could not defeat Him.
Sin did not have the final word.
And your scandal does not have to have the final word either.
That is why the Gospel is not self-improvement.
It is rescue.
It is not Jesus helping you decorate your old life with religious language.
It is Christ calling you to repent, believe, die to the old master, and walk in newness of life.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia, repentance.
Biblical repentance is deeper than feeling embarrassed because consequences finally arrived.
It is a Spirit-awakened turning of the heart toward God.
It says:
I have sinned.
I cannot save myself.
I will stop defending what Christ died to forgive.
Jesus, have mercy on me.
And this is where “many are called, but few are chosen” must not be twisted into despair.
Jesus is not telling broken sinners, “Become worthy enough and perhaps God will let you into the banquet.”
Look again at the story.
The banquet was prepared by the king.
The invitation originated with the king.
The servants were sent by the king.
The undeserving were gathered because the king commanded that they be brought in.
Grace starts with God.
Salvation is not your trophy for becoming impressive.
Paul writes that by grace you have been saved through faith, and that this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so nobody can boast.
But the grace that saves us is not permission to remain comfortably married to the sin from which Christ came to rescue us.
Grace does not say, “Keep your idols. Keep your secret rebellion. Keep Christ as an accessory.”
Grace says:
Come home.
The door is open because Someone paid the price.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe behind the version of you everybody sees is another version nobody knows.
You know exactly which browser history you keep deleting.
You know the bitterness you keep feeding.
You know the relationship you know dishonors God.
You know the money you worship.
You know how carefully you manufacture your Christian appearance.
You know the unforgiveness.
The secret messages.
The hidden addiction.
The pride.
The envy.
The lust.
The compromise.
The prayerlessness.
The spiritual exhaustion.
The strange emptiness that arrives when everybody else has gone to bed and there is nobody left to impress.
And perhaps your greatest fear is not that God does not see it.
Your greatest fear is that He does.
He does.
And here is what might break you:
He is still calling you.
Not because your sin is insignificant.
The cross proves that sin is devastatingly serious.
But the same cross proves that the mercy of God is greater than anything repentance brings into the light.
Peter denied Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine the shame when the rooster crowed.
Peter had insisted that even if everyone else abandoned Christ, he would remain.
Then fear exposed him.
“I do not know the man.”
Imagine having that sentence trapped inside your memory after Jesus is crucified.
Peter could have believed his worst moment had become his permanent name.
Failure.
Coward.
Denier.
Scandal.
But resurrection morning changed the vocabulary.
Jesus restored Peter.
Grace did not pretend the denial never happened.
Grace rewrote what the denial would ultimately mean.
Peter's failure was real.
Christ's mercy was greater.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel Warrior message:
Not because consequences always disappear.
Not because repentance makes history imaginary.
Not because Christianity teaches us to call evil good.
Jesus rewrites everything because the sinner who comes to Him in repentant faith is no longer required to be defined by the darkest chapter of his past.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ — en Christō Iēsou.
In Christ Jesus.
Those three words change everything.
The question is not whether you have scandal in your story.
We all carry the stain of sin.
The question is:
Are you in Christ?
Not merely around Christians.
Not merely familiar with Christianity.
Not merely emotionally moved by Jesus.
Not merely following Christian pages.
Not merely baptized while living as your own god.
Not merely wearing the vocabulary.
Are you His?
Because eventually the King enters the room.
That is the uncomfortable part of Matthew 22 we cannot remove to make Christianity easier to market.
There is judgment.
There is accountability.
There is an eternity beyond the grave.
Jesus Himself speaks of outer darkness and weeping and gnashing of teeth.
The same Jesus who welcomed children warned adults about judgment.
The same Jesus who touched lepers called sinners to repentance.
The same Jesus who forgave the guilty warned religious hypocrites.
The same Jesus who went to the cross will also return as King.
Biblical love does not erase His warnings.
Biblical love believes Him.
So do not turn this article into another emotional moment you forget by dinner.
Examine yourself.
Not obsessively staring at whether you have performed enough good works to purchase salvation.
Look to Christ.
Ask whether your hope rests in Him.
Ask whether your profession of faith is accompanied by the evidence of a heart being transformed by His grace.
When you fall, do you run toward Christ in repentance or hide from Him while protecting the sin?
Do you want Jesus Himself—or merely the benefits you hope He will give you?
Would you still want Christ if following Him cost you the approval of people you desperately want to impress?
Those questions are uncomfortable.
Let them be.
Eternity is too important for comfortable lies.
And if something inside you is whispering, “It is too late for me,” remember the thief beside Jesus.
He had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
No decades available for religious achievement.
No opportunity to build an impressive Christian résumé.
He had a dying body, a guilty history, and Christ beside him.
He turned toward Jesus.
“Remember me.”
And Jesus answered with paradise.
That is grace.
But notice something else.
The thief did not say, “My sin does not matter.”
He acknowledged his guilt.
He recognized Christ.
He entrusted himself to the King.
That is the difference between cheap religious comfort and saving grace.
Saving grace brings sinners home to Jesus.
So if this has exposed something you have been hiding, do not perform for the comments.
But do not hide from God either.
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray for you, simply write:
Pray.
We need fewer audiences and more brothers and sisters.
It cannot.
But if Christ has given us good news, we should not be ashamed to carry it.
Someone connected to you may never enter a church this week.
They may never open a Bible today.
But they might stop because you shared this.
Send it privately to the friend whose faith has grown cold.
Share it with the believer who thinks one terrible chapter means Jesus has abandoned the entire story.
Not so we can build a crowd around a page.
So we can keep pointing the crowd toward Christ.
It does not.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
before you share...
before you comment...
before you tag anybody...
before you save this...
settle the question that matters infinitely more than all of them:
What have you done with the invitation of the King?
Because one day your follower count will not matter.
Your bank balance will not matter.
The house will belong to someone else.
The trophies will collect dust.
The clothes will be discarded.
The notifications will stop.
Someone else will eventually sit at your desk.
And the world that seemed incapable of continuing without you...
will continue.
But you will meet God.
On that day, Christianity will no longer be content.
Jesus will no longer be a subject for debate.
Eternity will no longer be theoretical.
And “many are called, but few are chosen” will no longer be merely a verse you once read on Facebook.
So hear the invitation while you can hear it.
Come to Christ.
Come honestly.
Come guilty.
Come ashamed.
Come tired.
Come without pretending.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
Do not wait until you become worthy.
You cannot make yourself worthy of grace—that is why it is grace.
Bring Christ the chapter you thought destroyed your story.
Bring Him the failure.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the religious mask.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the heart you cannot repair.
And trust the crucified and risen Savior who receives sinners.
The warning is real.
Judgment is real.
Sin is real.
But so is the cross.
So is the empty tomb.
So is forgiveness.
So is grace.
And so is Jesus.
But never confuse supporting the messenger with responding to the Message.
A share cannot save you.
A comment cannot save you.
A church membership cannot save you.
Your reputation cannot save you.
Your good works cannot erase your guilt.
Jesus saves.
And perhaps the most terrifying tragedy is not that the invitation was never sent...
but that it arrived again and again, while someone kept assuming there would always be another tomorrow.
Do not merely admire the invitation to the wedding feast—make sure your heart has truly bowed before the King.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Moses Murdered a Man and Ran Away — God Still Wasn’t Finished With His Story
paragraphs: Moses Murdered a Man and Ran Away — God Still Wasn’t Finished With His Story

He buried a man in the sand, fled the life he knew, and disappeared into the wilderness. Then, decades later, God called his name from a fire that refused to go out. If you think your worst chapter has already written the ending of your life, Moses has something to tell you.
There was a body beneath the sand.
And Moses knew exactly how it got there.
Before the Red Sea.
Before the plagues.
Before Pharaoh heard the words, “Let my people go.”
Before Sinai trembled.
Before the tablets of stone.
Before generations would speak his name as one of the defining figures of Scripture...
there was an Egyptian lying dead.
And Moses had killed him.
That detail matters because sometimes we remember biblical heroes after grace has finished telling their story.
We remember Moses with the staff in his hand.
God remembers the entire man.
The frightened baby hidden among the reeds.
The adopted son raised in Pharaoh’s household.
The Hebrew who saw the suffering of his people.
The man who became violent.
The fugitive who ran.
The shepherd who disappeared into obscurity.
The trembling man standing barefoot before a burning bush.
The reluctant servant.
The leader.
The intercessor.
The sinner who needed grace.
And if you have ever looked backward at something you did and wondered whether God could possibly do anything meaningful with the person who did it...
do not leave this story too quickly.
Because there is something buried in the sand.
And eventually, Moses discovered that sand cannot bury what God already knows.
Exodus 2 tells the story with uncomfortable simplicity. Moses went out to his Hebrew brothers and witnessed their forced labor. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew. Then Scripture says:
“וַיַּךְ אֶת־הַמִּצְרִי וַיִּטְמְנֵהוּ בַּחוֹל”
Vayyakh et-hammitzri vayitmenehu bachol.
In straightforward English:
“He struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.”
That is the force of Exodus 2:12.

The Hebrew does not allow us to turn this into a harmless misunderstanding. The verb נכה (nakah), appearing here in the form וַיַּךְ (vayyakh), carries the idea of striking or striking down. What follows makes the outcome unmistakable: Moses hides the Egyptian in the sand, and the next day another Hebrew confronts him about killing the Egyptian.

Acts 7 later retells the event explicitly: Moses saw an Israelite being mistreated, defended him, and struck down the Egyptian. Stephen also tells us something important about Moses' thinking: Moses apparently believed his own people would understand that God was giving them deliverance through him.
They did not understand.
That makes the tragedy deeper.
Moses seems to have sensed something real about his connection to Israel and perhaps even about his role in their deliverance.
But sensing a calling is not the same thing as being ready to fulfill it.
He saw oppression.
He cared.
He acted.
But he acted disastrously.
And there is a warning here for every passionate believer.
You can care about something God cares about and still respond to it in a way God has not commanded.
A right burden does not automatically sanctify a wrong method.
Moses could not manufacture God's deliverance through human violence.
God would indeed use Moses to confront Egypt—but God's deliverance would unfold according to God's command, God's timing, and God's power.
There is a difference between being used by God and trying to play God.
Moses had not learned that difference yet.
Look at the scene.
Before striking the Egyptian, Moses looked around.
He looked this way.
Then that way.
No one.
Or so he thought.
There is something painfully human about that moment.
Have you ever done something you would never have done if the right person had been watching?
Have you ever checked the room?
Deleted the message?
Cleared the history?
Closed the tab?
Changed the story?
Hidden the receipt?
Covered the tracks?
Practiced the explanation?
Smiled in church while carrying something inside you that you desperately hoped nobody would discover?
Moses looked around.
But he did not look up.
And by the next day, his secret was already talking.
Two Hebrews were fighting. Moses confronted the one in the wrong.
The man's answer must have hit like a knife:
“Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you plan to kill me, as you killed the Egyptian?”
Then Scripture gives us four terrifying words:
“Moses was afraid.”
The secret was out.
Pharaoh heard about it.
Pharaoh wanted Moses dead.
And Moses ran. Exodus records his flight to Midian, while Acts likewise recounts that after the killing became known, Moses fled and lived as a foreigner there.
Imagine that journey.
Behind him was Egypt.
Behind him was privilege.
Behind him was the palace.
Behind him was a dead man.
Behind him was a warrant for his life.
Ahead of him?
Desert.
Silence.
Uncertainty.
Moses went from Pharaoh's household to the wilderness.
From somebody to nobody.
From proximity to power to tending another man's sheep.
And perhaps you understand that kind of wilderness better than you wish you did.
Maybe nobody is chasing you across a desert.
But you know what it is to run mentally from yesterday.
You know what it is to replay a decision at 2:17 in the morning.
You know what it is to wonder what your life would look like if you had chosen differently.
If you had not slept with that person.
If you had not betrayed that trust.
If you had controlled your anger.
If you had not walked away.
If you had told the truth.
If you had stayed sober.
If you had listened.
If you had not wasted those years.
If you had not wounded the people you loved.
Some consequences cannot simply be undone.
Christianity does not require us to pretend otherwise.
Grace is not calling evil good.
Forgiveness is not God developing amnesia.
Redemption does not mean sin was secretly harmless.
A man was dead.
Moses had fled.
Nothing about God's later use of Moses makes that death insignificant.
And that is precisely why this story is so powerful.
The Bible does not need to airbrush its servants to prove the power of God.
It tells us the scandal...
because the glory belongs to God.
Then something astonishing happens.
Years pass.
Not hours.
Not a weekend.
Not one emotional worship service followed by an instant comeback.
Years.
Acts 7 places Moses' life in striking stages and says that forty years passed before the burning-bush encounter.
Forty years.
Think about that.
Long enough for Egypt to become a memory.
Long enough for the fugitive to become a husband and father.
Long enough for royal rhythms to be replaced by sheep.
Long enough, perhaps, for Moses to assume that whatever his life might once have become was over.
And then...
fire.
A bush was burning.
But it was not consumed.
Moses turned aside.
And from the place where he expected nothing extraordinary, God spoke his name:
“Moses, Moses.”
What must it have felt like to discover that heaven still knew your name?
Moses had changed addresses.
God had not lost him.
Moses had disappeared into Midian.
God had not misplaced him.
Moses had a history.
God already knew it.
Moses had become a shepherd.
God was preparing to send him to shepherd a nation.
The wilderness that looked like the burial ground of Moses' calling became the landscape where God summoned him.
But notice what Scripture does not teach.
God did not say, “Moses, murder doesn't matter.”
God did not celebrate Moses' sin.
God did not tell him his choices were irrelevant because everything eventually worked out.
Biblical grace never requires God to lower His holiness.
Instead, the story reveals something far greater:
Human sin does not make God less sovereign.
Moses' failure was real.
God's purpose was greater.
And when God called Moses, He did not call him because murder had somehow become acceptable.
He called him according to His covenant purposes and mercy.
Stephen later describes the stunning reversal: the Moses who had been rejected with the question, “Who made you ruler and judge?” became the very Moses God sent as ruler and deliverer.
Do you see it?
The accusation from Moses' past did not become the final sentence over Moses' future.
And maybe that is where this story has finally reached you.
Because somewhere inside you there may be a sentence you have been repeating for years.
“God could never use someone like me.”
“I knew better.”
“I went too far.”
“I ruined everything.”
“People would look at me differently if they knew.”
“I wasted my opportunity.”
“My family will never forgive me.”
“I cannot become the person I should have been.”
Maybe you have spent years hiding your own Egypt beneath emotional sand.
Listen carefully.
Moses' story does not give you permission to minimize your sin.
It gives you permission to stop believing that your sin is more powerful than God's ability to redeem a repentant sinner.
Those are very different things.
And this is where Moses' story must lead us beyond Moses.
Because Moses is not the Savior of this article.
Jesus is.
Moses was a deliverer, but he himself was a sinful man in need of God.
Jesus Christ is the greater Deliverer.
Moses fled after the death of another man.
Jesus willingly walked toward His own death.
Moses could lead Israel out of physical slavery, but he could not cleanse the human heart from sin.
Jesus came to deal with the slavery beneath every other slavery.
Sin.
Guilt.
Condemnation.
Death.
At the cross, God did not sweep sin beneath cosmic sand.
He dealt with it.
This is why grace can never mean, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
The cross declares the opposite.
Sin matters so terribly that reconciliation with a holy God required something we could never provide for ourselves.
Christ bore sin and judgment, and He rose again.
That is why the Gospel is infinitely better than self-improvement.
Jesus did not come merely to help guilty people become slightly nicer guilty people.
He came to save.
Forgive.
Reconcile.
Redeem.
Make new.
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel:
Your salvation is not purchased by becoming impressive enough to erase yesterday.
You cannot.
Neither can I.
The Christian hope is that Christ has done what sinners could never do for themselves.
So repentance is not pretending the body beneath the sand never existed.
Repentance brings the truth into the light.
It stops defending.
Stops hiding.
Stops renaming sin.
Stops blaming everybody else.
And turns toward God.
Grace meets us there—not as permission to continue living in rebellion, but as God's undeserved favor that leads us into a transformed life.
Maybe your Egypt is calling you right now.
Maybe there is something you need to confess to God.
Maybe there is someone you need to ask forgiveness from.
Maybe restitution is possible and appropriate.
Maybe accountability needs to begin.
Maybe the secret has been eating you alive because you have spent more energy hiding than healing.
Do not confuse hiding with repentance.
Moses buried something in sand.
God eventually brought Moses onto holy ground.
Sand is where humans hide things.
Holy ground is where we stop pretending before God.
And perhaps that is why the burning bush feels so breathtaking.
The same Moses who once looked around to make sure nobody saw him eventually stood before the God who sees everything.
And God still spoke his name.
Not because Moses deserved a second chapter.
Grace, by definition, is not wages.
God spoke.
“Moses.”
The fugitive heard his name.
“Moses.”
The shepherd heard his name.
“Moses.”
The failed would-be deliverer heard his name.
And the man who once ran from Egypt would eventually be commanded to walk back toward it.
God did not merely give Moses something to do.
He dismantled Moses' confidence in himself.
When Moses first acted in Egypt, he seemed ready to take matters into his own hands.
At the burning bush, he sounded profoundly different.
“Who am I?”
That question matters.
The man who once behaved as though strength were enough had learned weakness.
And God's answer was not a motivational speech about Moses discovering how extraordinary Moses really was.
God's answer was better:
“I will be with you.”
That is the center.
Not Moses.
God.
Not your greatness.
Christ.
Not the heroic reconstruction of your personal brand.
Grace.
The Gospel does not tell broken sinners to stare into mirrors until they become convinced they are powerful.
It tells sinners to look to Jesus Christ.
Your hope is not that you can rewrite everything.
Jesus Christ is the One who saves, redeems, restores, and transforms.
And no, that does not mean every consequence disappears.
