He knows the bitterness behind the smile.
He knows what happened in the hotel room.
He knows what you did with the money.
He knows why you stopped praying.
He knows what you secretly envy.
He knows the resentment you rehearse at night.
He knows the habit you promised would never happen again.
He knows the part of your testimony you conveniently leave out.
And still He calls sinners out of hiding.
That is what makes Eden so devastating and so beautiful.
Adam had sinned.
God came looking.
Adam hid.
God called.
Adam confessed only partially.
Then Adam blamed.
“The woman whom You gave to be with me...”
Listen carefully to that sentence.
Sin rarely remains content simply to disobey God.
It starts rewriting responsibility.
Adam effectively points toward Eve—and ultimately toward God who gave Eve to him.
Eve then points toward the serpent.
Human beings have been pointing ever since.
My parents.
My spouse.
My childhood.
My church.
My boss.
My loneliness.
My trauma.
My friends.
My circumstances.
Those things can genuinely wound us, influence us, tempt us, and help explain our struggles. Compassion requires acknowledging that.
But explanation cannot become absolution for our own sin.
The Gospel does not heal us by teaching us to blame better.
It heals us by bringing us into truth.
There is an enormous difference between shame and biblical conviction.
Shame says, “Hide.”
Conviction says, “Come into the light.”
Condemnation says, “There is no hope for someone like you.”
The Gospel says that for those who are in Christ Jesus there is no condemnation.
Shame wants your sin concealed.
Grace brings your sin to a Savior.
And this is where “Who told you?” becomes dangerously personal.
Because some of us have allowed voices other than God’s Word to become interpreters of our identity.
Someone abandoned you, and somewhere inside you a sentence formed:
I am unlovable.
Someone abused you, and shame whispered:
I am dirty.
You failed publicly:
I am finished.
You fell into the same temptation again:
God must be tired of me.
Someone chose somebody else:
I was never enough.
Your prayers seem unanswered:
God has forgotten me.
You look at somebody else’s life:
God loves them more.
You remember what you did ten years ago:
That is who I really am.
And God’s question cuts through the noise:
Who told you?
Not every thought that speaks in your own voice tells the truth.
Not every feeling deserves authority.
Not every accusation deserves agreement.
Not every label deserves residence in your soul.
But neither should we answer God’s question with cheap positive thinking.
The biblical answer to shame is not standing in front of a mirror repeating, “I’m amazing.”
The biblical answer is much stronger.
We really have sinned.
We really are guilty.
We really cannot save ourselves.
And God really has provided a Savior.
Christianity does not rescue you by pretending the scandal never happened.
It announces that grace can rewrite what sin tried to make final.
Look again at Eden.
Judgment is pronounced. Sin has consequences. Death enters the human story.
But in the middle of judgment comes a promise.
Genesis 3:15 speaks of the offspring of the woman who will ultimately crush the serpent’s head while Himself being wounded.

Christians have long recognized here the earliest biblical anticipation of the Gospel—the first glimmer of the coming victory that unfolds across Scripture and reaches its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Before Adam and Eve leave Eden, something else happens.
Genesis 3:21 says:
וַיַּעַשׂ יְהוָה אֱלֹהִים לְאָדָם וּלְאִשְׁתּוֹ כָּתְנוֹת עוֹר וַיַּלְבִּשֵׁם
The LORD God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife...
וַיַּלְבִּשֵׁם — wayyalbishem
“And He clothed them.”
Do not rush past that.
They made coverings.
God clothed them.
Their coverings were inadequate.
God provided what they could not provide for themselves.

We should be careful not to claim more than Genesis explicitly states. The text does not directly explain how the skins were obtained or explicitly call this an atoning sacrifice. But within the larger biblical story, the scene powerfully anticipates a recurring reality: sinful humanity cannot ultimately solve guilt and shame through self-made coverings. God must provide what sinners cannot.
And eventually, He does so fully in Christ.
Not fig leaves.
Not reputation.
Not religious performance.
Not pretending.
Jesus.
At the cross, the scandal becomes almost unbearable.
The sinless Son of God is publicly humiliated.
Stripped.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Wounded.
Crucified.
He bears sin, though He Himself is without sin.
And here the Gospel becomes more than inspirational language.
Paul writes that God made Christ, who knew no sin, to be sin for us so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.
Peter says Christ Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree.
Isaiah, centuries earlier, speaks of the Servant wounded for our transgressions.
Jesus does not merely tell ashamed sinners to feel better about themselves.
He deals with the reason sinners should fear judgment.
He deals with sin.
The cross says your sin is more serious than your excuses have admitted...
and God’s grace is greater than your shame has imagined.
That is Christianity.
Not denial.
Redemption.
Not “You never did anything wrong.”
Forgiveness.
Not “Sin does not matter.”
A cross demonstrating exactly how much it matters.
Not “Stay as you are.”
Repent, believe, receive mercy, and follow Jesus.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe beneath everything people know about you, there is something they do not know.
A room in your heart you keep locked.
A memory you cannot erase.
A habit you cannot seem to kill.
A wound that distorted how you see yourself.
A sin you have renamed because calling it sin would require repentance.
A version of yourself you work very hard to keep everyone from meeting.
And perhaps you have spent years sewing leaves.
Jesus is not asking you to sew faster.
Come into the light.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repent of what needs abandoning.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Seek reconciliation where it is biblically possible and wise.
Ask for help when you cannot fight alone.
Stop calling bondage “just who I am.”
Stop calling compromise “complicated.”
Stop calling hiding “privacy” when what you really fear is exposure.
But also stop calling yourself something Jesus has not called the repentant sinner who belongs to Him.
If you are in Christ, your sin may be part of your history.
It does not get to be your lord.
Your wound may explain part of your story.
It does not get to write the ending.
Your failure may have consequences.
It does not possess greater authority than the blood of Jesus.
This is the Gospel’s breathtaking reversal:
We hide because we are ashamed.
God calls us out.
We expect only judgment.
God points toward redemption.
We try to cover ourselves.
God provides the covering.
We run from Him.
Christ comes for sinners.
We deserve death.
Christ dies.
Christ rises.
And everyone who repents and trusts in Him receives something Adam’s fig leaves could never manufacture:
reconciliation with God.
That is why the question still matters.
Who told you?
Who told you Jesus cannot forgive that?
Who told you repentance means God will reject you?
Who told you confession is the end of your story?
Who told you the prodigal cannot come home?
Who told you the sexually broken cannot become holy?
Who told you the addict cannot become free?
Who told you the bitter cannot learn forgiveness?
Who told you the lukewarm cannot wake up?
Who told you the wounded cannot heal?
Who told you the fallen believer should simply stay on the ground?
Scripture does not promise that every earthly consequence disappears when we repent.
It promises something infinitely better.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is reconciliation with God through Christ.
There is new life in Christ.
There is transformation by the Spirit of Christ.
There is resurrection hope because Christ walked out of His grave.
Your answer to shame is not a better opinion of yourself.
Your answer is Jesus Christ.
Maybe you know someone hiding right now.
You can see it in them.
The smile is there, but something behind their eyes is exhausted.
They still say, “God is good,” but privately they wonder whether He could still be good to them.
And if this exposed something in you, do not disappear quietly.
Your comment may become the sentence another ashamed believer reads and realizes, I am not the only person fighting.
Not because every sentence is easy.
There may be a night when shame remembers your address.
When that happens, come back—not merely to these words, but to the Scriptures behind them.
Supporting Gospel work should never be treated as a way to purchase God’s favor, prove that you love God, or earn spiritual blessing. Salvation is by grace, and generosity must never be manipulated.

But if you genuinely desire to glorify God with the resources He has entrusted to you, supporting faithful Gospel work is one practical way your generosity can help truth travel farther. Pray for the ministry because nothing of eternal value happens apart from God.
If you are ready to support the mission and go deeper:
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
The Gospel is not merchandise.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Christ paid the price sinners could never pay.
So before you leave, return once more to the garden.
See Adam hiding.
See the leaves.
Hear God walking toward the fugitive.
Listen.
“Where are you?”
Then hear Adam confess his fear.
And finally...
“Who told you that you were naked?”
Thousands of years later, humanity is still hiding.
Different gardens.
Different leaves.
Different scandals.
Same desperate need.
But now we know where the story was going.
From Eden to Bethlehem.
From Bethlehem to Golgotha.
From Golgotha to an empty tomb.
From our scandal...
to His grace.
So when shame whispers your old name tonight, do not answer it with another fig leaf.
Answer by running to Jesus.

Because the voice that exposed Adam’s hiding in the garden became the Gospel invitation calling sinners out of darkness—and the hands that sinners could never cleanse themselves were answered by nail-scarred hands strong enough to bring them home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “TOUCH NOT MY ANOINTED”: THE BIBLE VERSE THAT WAS NEVER MEANT TO MAKE A MAN UNTOUCHABLE
paragraphs: “TOUCH NOT MY ANOINTED”: THE BIBLE VERSE THAT WAS NEVER MEANT TO MAKE A MAN UNTOUCHABLE

What Psalm 105:15 really means—and why the same Bible that commands honor never commands you to surrender discernment, excuse sin, silence truth, or give any human being the place that belongs to Jesus Christ alone.
There are Bible verses people run to when they are afraid.
There are Bible verses people cling to when they are hurting.
And then there are Bible verses people sometimes use to make other people afraid.
“Touch not mine anointed.”
Five words from the King James Bible.
Five words that have comforted believers.
Five words that have also been whispered from pulpits, thrown across arguments, posted beneath accusations, and used as a spiritual warning:
Be careful what you say about me.
Don't question the pastor.
Don't challenge the prophet.
Don't expose the leader.
Don't criticize the man of God.
Touch not God's anointed.
And suddenly, a frightened believer begins wondering whether asking an honest question might put them in rebellion against God.
Maybe you have been there.
Maybe something didn't look right, but you were afraid to say it.
Maybe someone with a title wounded you, manipulated you, embarrassed you, or behaved in a way that contradicted Scripture—and when questions began rising inside you, another voice rose even louder:
Don't touch God's anointed.
So you stayed quiet.
But what if the verse is being asked to carry a meaning its original context never gave it?
What if honoring God's servants and testing what they teach are not enemies?
What if biblical submission never required spiritual blindness?
And what if the most dangerous thing about misusing “Touch not My anointed” is that it can slowly move our eyes away from the One Anointed King whom Scripture ultimately calls us to worship?
Before you defend the phrase…
before you reject it…
before you use it against somebody…
open the Bible.
Because context changes everything.

Psalm 105 remembers God's covenant faithfulness to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and their descendants. The psalmist describes a vulnerable people—few in number, strangers moving from nation to nation—whom God sovereignly protected. Psalm 105:14 says that God permitted no one to oppress them and even rebuked kings for their sake. Then comes the famous declaration:
“Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.”

That same wording appears in 1 Chronicles 16:22 in David's song of thanksgiving. The surrounding passage likewise remembers God's covenant and His protection of His people before calling the earth to proclaim His salvation and glory.
Now look closer.
The Hebrew of Psalm 105:15 reads:
אַל־תִּגְּעוּ בִמְשִׁיחָי וְלִנְבִיאַי אַל־תָּרֵעוּ
’Al-tigge‘u vimshichai, velinvi’ai ’al-tare‘u.
The important expression is בִמְשִׁיחָי — bimshichai, commonly rendered “My anointed ones.”
Notice something that can disappear when people quote the familiar English phrase casually:
It is plural.
“My anointed ones.”

The Hebrew mashiach is associated with someone anointed or set apart, and the form in Psalm 105:15 refers to God's “anointed ones.” The accompanying phrase speaks of “My prophets.” The verb translated “touch” comes from naga‘, a word that can mean to touch, reach, or strike, while the final expression forbids doing evil or harm to God's prophets.
That matters enormously.
Psalm 105 is not originally presenting a modern pastor standing behind a pulpit and declaring himself immune from examination.
Read backward.
The psalm remembers Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
The covenant.
A small wandering people living among nations more powerful than themselves.
“They went from one nation to another,” the psalm recalls, while God protected them and rebuked kings on their behalf. Then comes the declaration not to touch His anointed ones or harm His prophets.
The picture is not primarily an influential religious leader protecting his reputation from criticism.
It is the powerful God protecting vulnerable covenant people.
That turns the emotional direction of the verse almost completely around.
The text so often used by powerful people to warn vulnerable people was originally spoken in the context of God defending vulnerable people from powerful people.
Read that again.
God is the Protector in Psalm 105.
His covenant faithfulness is the story.
His sovereignty is the security.
His glory is the point.

That doesn't mean Christians should become disrespectful toward pastors, elders, teachers, or other believers. Scripture repeatedly calls Christians toward honor, love, humility, peace, and proper respect for faithful spiritual leadership.
Nor does this mean slander suddenly becomes acceptable.
It doesn't.
False accusations are still sinful.
Gossip is still destructive.
Maliciously trying to ruin someone is not Christian discernment.
Celebrating another person's downfall is not holiness.
You can be correct about someone's failure and still be sinful in the way you talk about it.
But there is a canyon between slander and biblical discernment.
There is a difference between attacking someone and testing someone's teaching.
There is a difference between rebellion and refusing to participate in wrongdoing.
There is a difference between dishonoring faithful leadership and holding leadership accountable to the Word of God.
And Scripture itself proves it.
Think about David and Saul.

David famously refused to kill Saul because Saul was “the LORD's anointed.” When David had opportunities to take Saul's life, he would not stretch out his hand to destroy the king. That demonstrates a profound fear of God and refusal to seize vengeance for himself.
But notice what David did not do.
He did not pretend Saul was behaving righteously.
He did not call Saul's murderous pursuit holy because Saul had been anointed.
He did not conclude that anointing transformed evil behavior into good behavior.
He could respect the office, refuse personal vengeance, entrust judgment to God—and still recognize that Saul was trying to kill him.
Biblical honor did not require biblical amnesia.
And that distinction could set somebody free.
You do not need to hate someone to tell the truth.
You do not need to destroy someone to establish boundaries.
You do not need to become bitter to recognize wrongdoing.
You do not need to appoint yourself judge, jury, and executioner.
And you certainly do not need to pretend darkness is light because the person responsible carries a Bible.
Jesus never asked you to surrender truth in order to protect someone's religious image.
In fact, the New Testament repeatedly assumes that claims and teachings must be tested.
The Bereans were praised because they examined the Scriptures to determine whether what Paul preached was true (Acts 17:11).
Think about how extraordinary that is.
Paul was an apostle.
Yet Scripture does not rebuke the Bereans for checking his message against Scripture.
It commends them.
Paul himself later tells believers, “Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1 Thessalonians 5:21).
John warns Christians not to believe every spirit but to test the spirits (1 John 4:1).
Paul publicly confronted Peter when Peter's behavior compromised the truth of the gospel (Galatians 2:11–14).
And the pastoral qualifications of 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 would make little sense if Christian leaders were never allowed to have their character examined.
Biblical authority therefore cannot mean:
Never question me.
It means authority itself remains underneath the authority of God.
Every pastor is underneath Christ.
Every teacher is underneath Christ.
Every prophet is underneath Christ.
Every ministry is underneath Christ.
Every church is underneath Christ.
Every Christian platform is underneath Christ.
Every person writing an article like this is underneath Christ.
Including us.
Do not believe something merely because Gospel Warrior published it.
Open your Bible.
Examine the context.
Test what you read.
Search the Scriptures.
Because the goal of Christian ministry should never be to make people dependent upon the personality delivering the message.
The goal is to bring people nearer to Jesus.
And this is where the phrase becomes even more beautiful.
Because the Bible's language of “anointed” ultimately draws our attention toward the supreme Anointed One.
Jesus Christ.
The Greek word Χριστός — Christos, “Christ,” means the Anointed One and corresponds to the messianic concept expressed by Hebrew mashiach.
“Christ” is not Jesus' surname.
It is a royal, messianic declaration.
Jesus is the Christ.
The Anointed King.
The promised Messiah.
The One before whom every earthly title eventually becomes small.
And look at what happened to God's ultimate Anointed One.
He was touched.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Struck.
Falsely accused.
Scourged.
Nailed to a cross.
A crown of thorns was pressed onto His head.
Blood ran down His face.
People mocked His kingship while the true King stood before them.
The hands that had healed the sick were pierced.
The feet that carried good news were nailed down.
The voice that commanded storms was mocked by men whose lungs were being sustained by His power.
And He could have ended it.
Yet He stayed.
Not because evil had won.
Because redemption was being accomplished.
This is where “Touch not My anointed” collides with the scandal of the Gospel.
The Anointed One allowed wicked hands to seize Him so guilty people like us could be reconciled to God.
He bore sin.
He endured shame.
He died.
And then…
the grave discovered it had swallowed Someone it could not keep.
Jesus rose.
That is Christianity.
Not celebrity Christianity.
Not personality Christianity.
Not untouchable-leader Christianity.
Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Reigning.
Coming again.
And when you see Him clearly, something begins changing inside you.
You stop asking, “Which Christian personality am I supposed to defend at all costs?”
And you begin asking:
“Is Jesus being honored?”
“Is Scripture being handled faithfully?”
“Is sin being confronted with truth and grace?”
“Are wounded people being shepherded or silenced?”
“Is repentance expected from everyone—or only from people without titles?”
Because repentance has no VIP section.
The pastor needs grace.
The congregation needs grace.
The preacher needs forgiveness.
The listener needs forgiveness.
The famous Christian needs Jesus.
The anonymous Christian needs Jesus.
The person who wounded you needs Jesus.
And you need Jesus too.
That last part matters.
Because an article about abusive authority can easily become an excuse to examine everybody except ourselves.
We can become experts at identifying someone else's manipulation while remaining blind to our own pride.
We can expose hypocrisy while secretly feeding hatred.
We can demand another person's repentance while refusing to forgive.
We can correctly identify a leader's sin and then allow bitterness to become ours.
Jesus does not merely want to rescue you from someone else's darkness.
He wants to rescue you from yours.
Maybe your wound is real.
Maybe the betrayal happened.
Maybe the spiritual intimidation was devastating.
Maybe someone used God's name to control you.
If so, calling evil “evil” is not the same thing as abandoning Christ.
But do not allow what a flawed Christian did to you to convince you that Jesus is like them.
People can misuse His name.
They cannot change His character.
A shepherd may fail you.
The Good Shepherd remains good.
A father may abandon you.
Your heavenly Father has not changed.
A Christian may lie to you.
Jesus remains the Truth.
A church may wound you.
Christ still bears scars Himself.
And perhaps that is the sentence somebody needed tonight:
Do not confuse the person who wounded you in Jesus' name with Jesus Himself.
Come back to Christ.
Not necessarily back to an unsafe situation.
Not back to manipulation.
Not back to pretending.
Back to Christ.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the questions.
Bring Him the disappointment.
Bring Him the memories you keep replaying at 2:13 in the morning.
Bring Him the church hurt you don't know how to explain without crying.
Bring Him your cynicism.
Bring Him your shame.
And bring Him your own sin too.
Because the Gospel is not merely God exposing bad leaders.
The Gospel is God rescuing sinners.
All kinds of sinners.
People in pews.
People behind pulpits.
People holding microphones.
People hiding behind screens.
You.
Me.
All of us stand in desperate need of the mercy purchased by Jesus Christ.
That is why accountability should never thrill us because someone is falling.
It should break our hearts because sin destroys.
Truth without love can become a weapon.
Love without truth can become permission.
Jesus gives us neither counterfeit.
He is full of grace and truth.
So honor faithful leaders.
Pray for them.
Encourage them.
Protect them from malicious lies.
Do not participate in gossip disguised as discernment.
Do not treat pastors as disposable simply because they are imperfect human beings.
But never turn honor into idolatry.
Never give a spiritual leader the authority to rewrite Scripture.
Never allow charisma to outrank character.
Never let someone's “anointing” become an excuse for unrepentant sin.
And never surrender the throne of your conscience to a human being.
That throne belongs to God.
If you are a Christian leader reading this, there is something here for you too.
The safest response to criticism is not always:
“Touch not God's anointed.”
Sometimes the holiest response is:
“Lord, search me.”
Maybe the accusation is false.
Then walk faithfully and trust God with your name.
But maybe part of it is true.
Maybe somebody saw what you refused to see.
Maybe success made correction increasingly difficult.
Maybe the ministry became so important that protecting the organization began feeling more urgent than protecting people.
Maybe “God told me” started ending conversations Scripture should have been allowed to examine.
If conviction is knocking, don't barricade the door with Psalm 105:15.
Open it.
Repentance is not the destruction of a ministry.
Sometimes repentance is the first evidence that the ministry still belongs to Jesus.
Peter failed terribly.
Jesus restored him.
David sinned grievously.
When confronted, he confessed.
The Gospel does not require flawless servants.
It produces repentant ones.
There is no shame in falling before Christ and saying:
“I was wrong.”
There is danger in becoming too important to say it.

Maybe this article exposed something you have carried silently for years. If it did, you don't have to tell strangers every detail of your pain. But you also don't have to keep pretending nothing happened.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only person struggling.
That matters.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the unbeliever who quietly reads your posts to follow too.
We will not put words in God's mouth.
But hear this clearly:
It doesn't.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Support ministry because you freely want the Gospel proclaimed, believers strengthened, biblical resources created, and more wounded and wandering people pointed toward Christ.
Give freely.
Share freely.
Serve freely.
And glorify God above every ministry—including this one.
Because one day there will be no famous pastors.
No follower counts.
No verified badges.
No platforms.
No bestselling books.
No impressive ministry statistics.
No Christian celebrities.
There will be a King.
And every one of us will stand before Him.
So perhaps the question was never merely:
“Who is God's anointed?”
Perhaps the question beneath the question is:
What have you done with God's Anointed One?
Jesus Christ.
Have you admired Him without surrendering?
Quoted Him without obeying?
Defended Christianity without actually knowing Christ?
Protected religious appearances while hiding sin?
Then stop hiding.
Repent.
Come to Jesus.
The cross is proof that your sin is more serious than you wanted to believe—and God's mercy is greater than you dared to hope.
You don't need an untouchable preacher.
You need an unstoppable Savior.
You don't need a religious celebrity who can never be questioned.
You need the Christ who already knows every question, every wound, every secret, every failure—and still calls sinners to come, repent, believe, and be made new.
And maybe that is why this verse needed to be rescued from the slogan it became.
Because Psalm 105:15 was never permission to make a human being untouchable.
It was a testimony that God's covenant people were never beyond His protection.
And the Gospel takes us further still.
Our ultimate hope is not that nobody will ever touch us.
Our hope is that even when this broken world wounds us, nothing can tear Christ's redeemed people from the hands of their Savior.
So test everything.
Reject slander.
Honor what is honorable.
Expose darkness truthfully and responsibly.
Forgive without calling evil good.
Seek justice without worshiping vengeance.
Repent when you are wrong.
Protect the vulnerable.
Pray for faithful shepherds.
And keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because pastors do not rewrite everything.
Prophets do not rewrite everything.
Churches do not rewrite everything.
Influencers do not rewrite everything.
Jesus does.

And when human hands have written shame across your story, when spiritual wounds have written distrust across your heart, when your own sins have written chapters you desperately wish you could erase…
remember this:
The hands they pierced are still the hands capable of rewriting your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY PSALM 23 HITS DIFFERENTLY WHEN YOU UNDERSTAND ANCIENT SHEPHERDING
paragraphs:
WHY PSALM 23 HITS DIFFERENTLY WHEN YOU UNDERSTAND ANCIENT SHEPHERDING
You Thought David Was Writing About Peaceful Sheep in a Green Field. He Was Actually Writing About What It Feels Like to Be Completely Helpless—and Completely Kept.
There is something about Psalm 23 that changes after life has hurt you.
You can memorize it as a child.
You can frame it on a wall.
You can hear it read at funerals and whisper it beside hospital beds.
You can recite every familiar line and still miss the terrifying beauty hiding underneath it.
Because David was not describing a decorative countryside scene.
He knew sheep.

Before there was a crown on his head, there had been sheep under his care. Before royal courts, battles, political betrayal, family scandal, grief, and power, David had known the lonely work of watching a vulnerable flock.
He knew what happened when something defenseless depended completely upon a shepherd.
And that changes Psalm 23.
Because suddenly the Psalm is not mainly about sheep.
It is about dependence.
It is about danger.
It is about being led somewhere you cannot survive by yourself.
And perhaps that is why you need to read it again.
Slowly.
Not as the person who has everything together.
As the sheep.
The Hebrew opens with words almost too simple for the weight they carry:
יְהוָה רֹעִי לֹא אֶחְסָר
YHWH ro‘i, lo echsar.
“The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.”
Notice what David does not say.
“The LORD is a shepherd.”
He says:
“My shepherd.”
Ro‘i.
Mine.
That is personal language.
David is not merely making a theological statement about what God does somewhere in heaven. He is confessing a relationship.
The God who created everything has chosen to shepherd people who cannot shepherd themselves.
And that sounds comforting until you realize what being the sheep means.
It means admitting that you do not always know where you are going.
That you can mistake danger for freedom.
That you can wander.
That fear can control you.
That what looks harmless can lead somewhere deadly.
That sometimes you desperately need someone wiser than you to lead you.
Our culture tells us to become our own masters.
Follow your heart.
Trust yourself.
Create your own truth.
Find your own path.
David says something far more humbling:
I need a Shepherd.
Maybe that is where Psalm 23 begins working on us.
Not when we admire the Shepherd.
When we finally admit we are the sheep.

“I shall not want” does not mean the believer will receive everything the believer desires. David's confidence is not that God will satisfy every appetite. His confidence is that under the Shepherd's care, he will not ultimately lack what the Shepherd knows he needs.
There is a difference.
And some of us have spent years angry with God because He did not give us something that, looking backward, might have destroyed us.
You called the closed door rejection.
Perhaps the Shepherd called it protection.
You called the delay abandonment.
Perhaps the Shepherd was still leading.
You called the loss the end of your story.
God had not finished writing.
Then David says:
בִּנְאוֹת דֶּשֶׁא יַרְבִּיצֵנִי
Bin’ot deshe yarbitzeni.
“He makes me lie down in green pastures.”
And:
עַל־מֵי מְנֻחוֹת יְנַהֲלֵנִי
Al-mei menuchot yenahaleni.
“He leads me beside waters of rest.”
Do not turn this into a fantasy painting too quickly.
Biblical shepherding belonged to a world where finding nourishment, water, safe routes, and protection mattered. The shepherd's care was not sentimental decoration.
It was survival.
The sheep does not create the pasture.
The shepherd finds it.
The sheep does not need to understand the entire route.
It needs to stay near the shepherd.
And maybe somebody reading this is exhausted because you have been trying to be both sheep and shepherd.
You are trying to control tomorrow.
Control your children.
Control the relationship.
Control your reputation.
Control the outcome.
Control what people think.
Control whether you will ever be hurt again.
Your body lies down at night, but your mind keeps walking.
Planning.
Replaying.
Predicting.
Fearing.
And Psalm 23 whispers something almost offensive to an anxious heart:
You were never meant to carry the shepherd's job.
There are things obedience requires you to do.
There are responsibilities God has genuinely given you.
But being God is not one of them.
Then comes one of the most beautiful lines in the Psalm:
נַפְשִׁי יְשׁוֹבֵב
Nafshi yeshovev.
Traditionally:
“He restores my soul.”
The Hebrew word nefesh can carry the sense of one's life, self, or living being—not merely the modern idea of an invisible spiritual compartment inside you.
And the verb translated “restores” carries the beautiful idea of bringing back, returning, restoring.
He brings me back.
Read that again.
He brings me back.
Back from wandering.
Back from exhaustion.
Back from places I should never have gone.
Back from the version of myself I became while trying to survive without Him.
Somebody needs those four words tonight:
He brings me back.
Maybe you wandered deliberately.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your browser history tells a different story than your Sunday clothes.
Maybe bitterness has been living inside you so long that you have started calling it discernment.
Maybe you compromised slowly.
One message.
One lie.
One secret.
One drink.
One affair.
One hidden habit.
One rationalization at a time.
Maybe you still know the worship songs.
Still post the verses.
Still say “God bless.”
Still know exactly when to lift your hands.
But somewhere inside, you know.
You wandered.
And shame has been telling you that the Shepherd wants nothing more to do with you.
But David knew something about scandal.
He knew catastrophic moral failure.
Scripture does not airbrush David's adultery with Bathsheba or his orchestration of Uriah's death. The Bible refuses to turn its heroes into plastic saints.
David sinned terribly.
David needed repentance.
David needed mercy.
And when confronted, he could not save himself with a crown.
That is why grace is so shocking.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace tells the truth about evil—and then reveals a Savior greater than our sin.
Repentance is not pretending you never wandered.
Repentance is turning back to the One who can restore you.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting sin into innocence.
Not by pretending rebellion never happened.
But by taking guilty sinners, cleansing them, forgiving them, reconciling them to God, and beginning something new.
Then the landscape darkens.
גַּם כִּי־אֵלֵךְ בְּגֵיא צַלְמָוֶת
Gam ki-elekh begei tsalmavet.
“Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death…”
That famous Hebrew expression, tsalmavet, has traditionally been rendered “shadow of death,” while many scholars understand it more broadly as “deep darkness.”
Either way, the poetry suddenly loses its sunlight.
Pasture disappears.
Darkness arrives.
And here is what prosperity-shaped Christianity sometimes struggles to explain:
The Shepherd led him there.
David does not say, “If God is my Shepherd, valleys will cease to exist.”
He says, essentially:
Even there…
You are with me.
That distinction could save somebody's faith.
Because perhaps you thought suffering meant God had abandoned you.
The diagnosis came.
The marriage broke.
Someone died.
The business collapsed.
Your child walked away.
Your prayers seemed to hit the ceiling.
Depression darkened the room.
People you trusted betrayed you.
You obeyed God and still ended up somewhere painful.
And you began asking:
“If God really loves me, why am I here?”
Psalm 23 does not give us the cheap answer that God's people never enter dark valleys.
It gives us something better.
The Shepherd enters them with us.
And notice something intimate in David's language.
Earlier David speaks about God:
“He makes me lie down.”
“He leads me.”
“He restores me.”
“He guides me.”
But inside the valley, David speaks to God:
“For You are with me.”
Pain turned theology into conversation.
The Shepherd was no longer merely someone David described.
He became the One David addressed in the darkness.
Some of the deepest encounters with God happen when all you have left is:
“You are with me.”
Not, “I understand.”
Not, “I like this.”
Not, “I know exactly what happens tomorrow.”
Just:
“You are with me.”
And sometimes that is enough to take the next step.
David continues:
שִׁבְטְךָ וּמִשְׁעַנְתֶּךָ הֵמָּה יְנַחֲמֻנִי
Shivtekha u-mishantekha, hemah yenachamuni.
“Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me.”
Ancient shepherd imagery makes those words stronger.
The shevet, the rod, could represent the shepherd's authority and protection; it could function as an implement capable of striking against danger.
The mish‘enet, the staff, is associated with support.
David looks at what is in the Shepherd's hands and says:
I am comforted.
Why?
Because comfort is not merely the absence of enemies.
Sometimes comfort is knowing your enemy will have to get through your Shepherd to finally destroy you.
That does not mean Christians cannot suffer.
They can.
It does not mean believers cannot be killed.
Throughout Scripture, faithful people suffer terribly.
It means something infinitely deeper:
Nothing can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
Then something unexpected happens.
The Psalm seems to move from the open country into the imagery of hospitality.
“You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies.”
Not after the enemies disappear.
In their presence.
We often pray:
“God, remove them.”
God sometimes answers by demonstrating:
“They cannot cancel what I have prepared for you.”
The enemies are watching.
The table is still there.
The opposition exists.
God is still faithful.
The accusation is loud.
Grace is louder.
The wound is real.
The Shepherd is still present.
And then:
“You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows.”
Here we should be careful.

You may have heard sermons claiming that shepherds routinely poured oil over sheep's heads specifically to stop insects from crawling into their ears and killing them. Versions of that illustration circulate widely, but we should not build biblical interpretation on details we cannot confidently establish from the text or strong historical evidence.
Psalm 23 does not need embellishment to become powerful.
Its own imagery is enough.
In the world of biblical hospitality, oil could signify welcome, refreshment, honor, and abundance.
The picture has changed.
The frightened traveler has become an honored guest.
The one walking through darkness now sits at a table.
The cup is not empty.
It overflows.
And then David reaches the ending:
אַךְ טוֹב וָחֶסֶד יִרְדְּפוּנִי
Akh tov va-chesed yirdefuni.
“Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me…”
But “follow” can sound almost passive in English.
The Hebrew verb radaph can mean to pursue.
Think about that.
David spent parts of his life being pursued by enemies.
Now he says something else is pursuing him.
Goodness.
And chesed.
That magnificent Hebrew covenant word often translated “mercy,” “lovingkindness,” or “steadfast love.”
David has enemies behind him.
But they are not the only things chasing him.
God's steadfast love is pursuing him too.
Maybe you have spent your life running.
Running from your past.
Running from what your father did.
Running from what your mother said.
Running from the mistake you cannot undo.
Running from the addiction nobody knows about.
Running from church because somebody representing God wounded you.
Running from conviction because surrender feels terrifying.
Running from Jesus because you assume He is chasing you only to condemn you.
But what if the sound behind you is mercy?
What if you have mistaken the footsteps of grace for the footsteps of judgment?
What if the Shepherd has been pursuing you through every chapter you thought disqualified you?
And this is where Psalm 23 becomes unmistakably Christ-centered.
Centuries after David wrote about the Shepherd, Jesus stood before people and declared:
“I am the good shepherd.”
And then He explained what kind of Shepherd He is.
“The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.”
There is the Gospel.
Psalm 23 ultimately finds breathtaking fulfillment not merely in a shepherd carrying a staff…
but in the Shepherd carrying a cross.
Jesus did not come merely to make stressed people calmer.
He came to save sinners.
Our deepest problem is not anxiety, poverty, loneliness, trauma, disappointment, or even death itself.
Our deepest problem is sin and separation from a holy God.
We wandered.
“All we like sheep have gone astray.”
Every one of us.
Religious and rebellious.
Successful and broken.
The preacher and the prisoner.
The respectable sinner and the public scandal.
We wandered.
And the Good Shepherd came looking for the lost.
Jesus lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
And He rose again.
The Shepherd became the Lamb sacrificed for His sheep.
Think about that until it hurts.
The One you wandered away from is the One who came after you.
The One whose commands you broke is the One who bore judgment for sinners.
The hands capable of holding the rod opened themselves to nails.
The Shepherd walked into death itself…
and came out alive.
So when the Christian says, “I will fear no evil,” that is not positive thinking.
We have a resurrected Shepherd.
When we say, “You are with me,” that is not sentimental optimism.
Christ has conquered the grave.
When we say, “I will dwell in the house of the LORD,” our hope rests not in our ability to keep ourselves alive but in the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
Perhaps now Psalm 23 sounds different.
Maybe you are not reading it anymore.
Maybe it is reading you.
Where have you wandered?
What valley are you walking through?
What are you desperately trying to control?
What secret are you exhausted from hiding?
What would happen if you stopped pretending you were the shepherd and finally surrendered to Jesus as the sheep?
You do not need to clean yourself up before coming to Christ.
Come honestly.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Bring Him the scandal.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the failure.
Bring Him the exhausted version of you that everybody else never sees.
Grace is not permission to remain in sin.
Grace is God's invitation out of it.
And Jesus still restores wandering people.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not write an impressive comment.
Write an honest one.
There are moments when three honest words before God are worth more than three paragraphs of religious performance.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
We are saved by grace, not by transactions.

But if something points people toward Jesus and you genuinely believe another soul needs to encounter it, sharing becomes a simple opportunity to serve. You never know who is scrolling at 2:13 in the morning asking God for one reason not to give up.
Your share could place truth in front of them.
Because valleys have a strange way of making us forget what we knew in the pasture.
Come back when the night gets heavy.
Come back when anxiety starts preaching.
Come back when shame tells you the Shepherd has abandoned you.
Read the Hebrew again:
יְהוָה רֹעִי
YHWH ro‘i.
The LORD is my Shepherd.
Supporting Gospel work is not a way to purchase God's approval, and no Christian should ever be manipulated into believing that giving money proves salvation or guarantees blessing.
But believers who value a ministry can freely help sustain and spread its work.

If your desire is to glorify God, glorify Him first through faith in Christ, obedience, holiness, love, generosity, and a life surrendered to Him. And if Gospel Warrior is genuinely bearing good fruit in your life, consider supporting that work rather than merely consuming it.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has questions.
Invite the believer who is exhausted.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who needs awakening.
Invite the person who does not yet believe.
And before you leave, remember the part of Psalm 23 we so easily forget.
The valley was never the destination.
David said:
“Though I walk through…”
Through.
Not buried there.
Not abandoned there.
Not forgotten there.
Through.
The Shepherd knows where the path ends.
So if today you can barely see beyond the next step, stay close to Jesus.
If you wandered, return.
If you sinned, repent.
If you are ashamed, stop hiding.
If you are exhausted, let Him lead.
If you are afraid, remember who walks beside you.
If your past looks like a scandal, remember that the Gospel specializes in stories human beings would have thrown away.
And if you hear footsteps behind you tonight…
perhaps you should stop running long enough to discover what has been pursuing you.
You thought your past was chasing you. Maybe all this time, mercy was closer.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES THE BIBLE RECORD POLYGAMY WITHOUT ALWAYS CONDEMNING IT?
paragraphs:
WHY DOES THE BIBLE RECORD POLYGAMY WITHOUT ALWAYS CONDEMNING IT?
Abraham had more than one woman. Jacob had two wives and two concubines. David had multiple wives. Solomon had hundreds. So why does the Bible sometimes tell us these things without immediately saying, “And this was evil”? The answer may completely change the way you read some of Scripture’s most disturbing stories.
There is a question many Christians are afraid to ask out loud.
Maybe because they fear what the answer might be.
Maybe because someone hostile to Christianity has already asked them and they did not know what to say.
Maybe because they were reading Genesis one night, reached the stories of Abraham, Jacob, Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah, and suddenly thought:
Wait.
Why is nobody stopping this?
Why does Scripture record men having multiple wives without attaching a condemnation to every occurrence?
And if God intended marriage to be between one man and one woman, why does the Old Testament contain so much polygamy?
That question deserves more than a nervous Christian cliché.
It deserves the Bible.
And once we allow the whole story of Scripture to answer it, something extraordinary happens.
What initially looks like an embarrassing problem begins revealing one of the Bible’s most powerful characteristics:
Scripture refuses to sanitize its heroes.
The Bible records many things it does not endorse.
That distinction is absolutely essential.
Description is not necessarily prescription.
Narrative is not automatically command.
And silence at the moment an action occurs is not necessarily divine approval.
The Bible tells us that Cain murdered Abel. It does not need to interrupt every sentence of the narrative to remind us that murder is wrong.
It records Noah becoming drunk.
It records Abraham lying.
It records Jacob deceiving.
It records Judah sleeping with a woman he believed was a prostitute.
It records David committing adultery and arranging the death of Uriah.
It records Peter denying Christ.
Scripture is often brutally descriptive because God apparently has no interest in protecting the reputations of fallen human beings.
Even the people God uses are exposed.
Their faith.
Their fear.
Their obedience.
Their stupidity.
Their courage.
Their lust.
Their compromises.
Their consequences.
Their repentance.
Their need for grace.
And polygamy belongs inside that larger biblical story.
To understand it, we have to go farther back than Abraham.
Farther back than Jacob.
Farther back than David.
Farther back than Moses.
We have to return to a garden.
Before kings accumulated wives...
before cultures normalized harems...
before powerful men treated marriage as political strategy...
before sin twisted human relationships...
there was one man.
And one woman.
Genesis 2:24 gives us the foundational pattern:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew contains language worth slowing down for:
וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ
vedavaq be’ishto
“and he shall cling to his wife.”
The verb דָּבַק (dāvaq) carries the sense of clinging, adhering, holding fast.
Then comes:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
vehayu levasar echad
“and they shall become one flesh.”
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
One flesh.
Not merely two people sharing property.
Not merely a sexual transaction.
A profound covenantal union is being described.
And thousands of years later, when religious leaders questioned Jesus about marriage and divorce, Christ did something incredibly important.
He went back to creation.
Jesus did not establish His definition of marriage by appealing to Abraham’s household.
He did not point to Jacob.
He did not point to David.
He did not point to Solomon.
He pointed behind all of them.
Back to the beginning.
In Matthew 19:4–6 Jesus recalls Genesis and says that the Creator made them male and female and that “the two shall become one flesh.”
The Greek emphasizes:
οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
hoi dyo eis sarka mian
“the two into one flesh.”
Then Jesus says:
ὥστε οὐκέτι εἰσὶν δύο ἀλλὰ σὰρξ μία
hōste ouketi eisin dyo alla sarx mia
“So they are no longer two, but one flesh.”
Two.
One flesh.
Jesus reaches through centuries of human brokenness and points back toward creation.
That matters enormously.
Because one of the most important principles for understanding difficult Old Testament passages is this:
God sometimes regulates human brokenness without presenting that brokenness as His original ideal.
Jesus Himself gives us a striking example.
When discussing divorce, He explains that Moses permitted divorce because of the hardness of human hearts, but then says:
“from the beginning it was not so.”
Those words are devastating to the assumption that everything permitted or regulated within Israel’s civil life automatically represents the highest expression of God’s creational intention.
“From the beginning it was not so.”
Human beings fell.
Cultures became corrupted.
Power became abusive.
Women could become extraordinarily vulnerable economically and socially.
Families fractured.
Wars happened.
Men died.
Widows remained.
Inheritance mattered.
Survival mattered.
And God gave laws to an actual ancient people living inside an already fallen world.
This is where many readers make a serious interpretive mistake.
They encounter laws regulating an existing practice and conclude that God must therefore be celebrating the practice.
But regulation and endorsement are not identical.
Consider Exodus 21:10. In a society where a man could take another wife, the law explicitly protected the first woman from being deprived of food, clothing, and marital rights.
That is not Scripture saying, “Go collect wives.”
It is legislation confronting what men were already doing and placing obligations upon them.
Likewise, Deuteronomy 21:15–17 addresses inheritance when a man has two wives, preventing favoritism from robbing the rightful firstborn son.
Again, the existence of legislation concerning a broken situation does not automatically transform that situation into the creational ideal.
In fact, the Old Testament eventually gives us an astonishing warning concerning Israel’s kings.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says that the king must not “multiply wives” for himself, lest his heart turn away.
And then Solomon arrives.
A king famous for wisdom.
A king blessed beyond imagination.
A king who eventually possesses seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines according to 1 Kings 11:3.
And what happens?
Exactly what the warning anticipated.
His wives turn his heart toward other gods.
The Bible does not need to place a flashing red sign above every chapter saying:
POLYGAMY IS CAUSING PROBLEMS.
The story itself is screaming.
Look at Abraham’s household.
Sarah cannot conceive.
Hagar enters the situation.
A child is born.
Then jealousy erupts.
Conflict erupts.
Humiliation erupts.
Hagar flees.
Eventually Hagar and Ishmael are sent away.
Read the story slowly enough and you stop seeing some romantic patriarchal fantasy.
You see tears in the wilderness.
Then look at Jacob.
He loves Rachel.
He is deceived into marrying Leah.
Then marries Rachel.
Then the sisters compete.
Children become part of that competition.
Handmaids are brought into the struggle.
Listen to Leah naming her children and hoping desperately that perhaps now her husband will love her.
That is not a commercial for polygamy.
That is heartbreak preserved in Scripture.
Imagine Leah lying beside a man whose heart belongs to her sister.
Imagine Rachel watching Leah give Jacob children while her own womb remains closed.
Imagine two sisters slowly becoming rivals inside the same home.
The Bible doesn't merely give us a theological argument.
It gives us bedrooms full of jealousy.
Dinner tables full of tension.
Women wondering whether they are enough.
Children growing inside rivalries they did not create.
And generations inheriting wounds created by adults.
Then David.
Multiple wives.
Multiple sons.
Multiple households.
Sexual sin.
Rivalries.
Violation.
Murder.
Absalom.
Rebellion.
A palace becoming a house of grief.
And then Solomon takes multiplication to grotesque proportions.
The biblical trajectory is not difficult to see when these stories are read together.
Something can be historically recorded without being morally recommended.
And perhaps that explains something even deeper about why these stories bother us.
We sometimes approach Scripture expecting every biblical character to behave like a polished church leader in a devotional book.
God gives us something much more uncomfortable.
Human beings.
Real ones.
Broken ones.
People capable of trusting God one chapter and making catastrophic decisions the next.
Abraham can believe God and still try to manufacture the promise through human strategy.
Jacob can encounter God and still carry a disastrously complicated household.
David can write breathtaking psalms and still destroy lives through sexual sin and abuse of power.
Solomon can write about wisdom while gradually becoming a monument to the danger of ignoring it.
That should frighten us.
Because spiritual knowledge does not make someone immune to compromise.
Yesterday's encounter with God does not automatically guarantee tomorrow's obedience.
A person can know Scripture and still rationalize desire.
A person can worship and still hide sin.
A person can preach truth publicly while negotiating with temptation privately.
And suddenly this article is no longer about ancient men with multiple wives.
It is about us.
Because perhaps your compromise has a different name.
Maybe nobody knows about the messages you delete.
Maybe your spouse thinks everything is okay.
Maybe pornography has quietly become your secret refuge.
Maybe emotional intimacy with someone who isn't your husband or wife has already crossed boundaries your body has not crossed yet.
Maybe you keep telling yourself:
“Nothing actually happened.”
Maybe you have normalized something because everyone around you normalizes it.
Maybe you found enough Christian-sounding excuses to keep doing what your conscience has been begging you to stop.
That is precisely why we need to understand these Old Testament stories correctly.
Human beings have always been extraordinarily gifted at turning tolerated brokenness into celebrated normality.
But Jesus keeps calling us back.
Back beyond culture.
Back beyond excuses.
Back beyond what everyone else is doing.
Back to the heart of God.
“From the beginning...”
And there is something even more beautiful here.
Marriage does not ultimately terminate on marriage itself.
Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 in Ephesians 5 and then unveils something astonishing.
The mystery points toward Christ and the church.
Suddenly “one flesh” becomes part of a much larger Gospel picture.
Jesus Christ is the faithful Bridegroom.
And His church is His bride.
This Bridegroom does not collect women for His ego.
He does not exploit His bride.
He does not abandon her when she becomes inconvenient.
He does not use power to satisfy Himself at her expense.
He gives Himself for her.
The cross completely overturns the world's understanding of power.
Jesus does not say:
“Die for Me while I protect Myself.”
He dies for His bride.
The King bleeds.
The Bridegroom wears thorns.
The Holy One absorbs shame.
The innocent Christ carries the guilt of sinners.
And this is where every scandalous biblical story ultimately makes us confront our own need.
The Bible is not a museum filled with flawless saints.
It is the history of a rescue mission.
Again and again, human beings take God's gifts and distort them.
Marriage.
Sex.
Power.
Family.
Kingship.
Freedom.
Desire.
Religion itself.
We corrupt what God creates.
And God keeps moving history toward Christ.
That does not mean every Old Testament failure is a direct allegory of Jesus. We should never force Scripture into symbolism it does not claim.
It means the entire biblical story exposes humanity's desperate need for the Savior who finally comes.
Jesus is not another Abraham.
Not another Jacob.
Not another David.
Not another Solomon.
He is the sinless Son.
Where humanity fails, Christ remains faithful.
Where kings use people, Christ serves.
Where sinners take, Christ gives.
Where shame tells you to run from God, Christ stretches His arms upon a cross.
And maybe that is the part somebody reading this desperately needs tonight.
You have made decisions you cannot undo.
Perhaps your marriage is broken.
Perhaps you were unfaithful.
Perhaps someone was unfaithful to you.
Perhaps your family story is complicated enough that reading biblical family scandals feels painfully familiar.
Perhaps there are children from different relationships.
Divorce papers.
Custody battles.
Betrayal.
Regret.
Years you wish you could erase.
Names you still cannot hear without feeling something twist inside your chest.
Listen carefully.
Biblical truth does not require pretending sin has no consequences.
Grace does not rename darkness as light.
Repentance does not mean saying, “It didn't matter.”
The Gospel is far more powerful than denial.
The Gospel says:
It mattered so much that Christ died.
And Christ loved sinners enough to die anyway.
At the cross, God neither trivializes sin nor abandons sinners.
Justice and mercy meet.
Your past may explain your scars.
It does not have to become your master.
Your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write your final sentence.
Jesus does.
Repentance is not God demanding that you repair yourself before approaching Him.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior because you finally realize the far country is killing you.
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace opens the prison door.
And Jesus still says:
Come.
Come out of hiding.
Come with the wreckage.
Come with the shame.
Come with the consequences.
Come with the marriage that needs healing.
Come with the secret that needs confessing.
Come with the habit you keep defending.
Come with the tears nobody sees.
Come with the question you were afraid Christians would punish you for asking.
Christ is not intimidated by complicated stories.
Look at the genealogy through which He entered the world.
Human scandal is everywhere.
And yet God keeps writing redemption through ruined pages.
That is why the Bible's honesty about polygamy should not weaken our confidence in Scripture.
In a strange way, it should deepen it.
The Bible doesn't airbrush Abraham.
It doesn't clean up Jacob.
It doesn't protect David's public image.
It doesn't hide Solomon's catastrophic contradictions.
Scripture lets its heroes bleed on the page.
Because they were never the Hero.
Jesus is.
Maybe you came here asking:
“Why doesn't the Bible condemn polygamy every time it appears?”
Perhaps the better question by the end is:
“Why does God keep dealing with people whose lives are this broken?”
And then comes the uncomfortable answer.
Because otherwise He could never deal with people like us.
We want biblical characters separated neatly into heroes and villains.
God shows us sinners who need mercy.
We want stories where righteous people never stumble.
God gives us stories where grace must become real.
We want spotless human heroes.
God gives us Jesus.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, don't turn conviction into another five minutes of scrolling.
Talk to Christ.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Seek forgiveness where forgiveness is needed.

Get trustworthy pastoral or Christian counsel if your family situation is complicated. Do not use an article on the internet as a substitute for careful, personal biblical counsel where real marriages, children, abuse, legal obligations, or serious relational wounds are involved.
But don't hide.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that grace still reaches broken homes.
The Bible's recording of human behavior is not automatically God's endorsement of human behavior.
Send it privately to the believer whose family story has become so complicated that they wonder whether God still wants them.
And send it even to the skeptic who believes the Bible has nothing intelligent to say about its own disturbing stories.
Not to win an argument.
To open a conversation.

If Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, confront sin, return to Christ, or grow stronger in the Gospel, one tangible way you can help this ministry glorify God is by supporting the work rather than simply consuming it.
Salvation cannot be purchased, and financially supporting a Christian ministry is never a condition of glorifying God.
Your share may place this message in front of someone Gospel Warrior could never reach otherwise.
Because difficult questions do not frighten the Gospel.
Broken families do not frighten Jesus.
Scandal does not surprise Him.
Your past does not overpower Him.
And the same Bible courageous enough to show us Abraham's failure, Jacob's chaos, David's sin, and Solomon's collapse is courageous enough to tell us where our only lasting hope has always been.
Not Abraham.
Not Jacob.
Not David.
Not Solomon.
Jesus.
The Bridegroom who remained faithful.
The King who gave Himself for His people.
The Savior who carried sinners' shame.
The Lamb who died.
The Lord who rose.
The Christ who still receives repentant sinners.
So when you encounter the scandal in Scripture, don't stop reading when the humans fail.
Keep reading until you reach Jesus.
Because the deepest message running through the Bible was never that God found perfect people.
It was that a perfect Savior came looking for sinners.
And remember this when your own story feels too stained to redeem:
The ink of your scandal may already be dry—but the nail-scarred hands of Jesus still hold the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES THE HOLY SPIRIT STILL GIVE SPIRITUAL GIFTS TODAY?
paragraphs:
DOES THE HOLY SPIRIT STILL GIVE SPIRITUAL GIFTS TODAY?
Tongues. Prophecy. Healing. Miracles. Discernment. Have They Ceased—or Have We Become So Afraid of Counterfeits That We No Longer Expect the Spirit to Move?
There is a strange tension in the modern church.
Some Christians seem willing to believe almost anything as long as someone says, “The Holy Spirit told me.”
Others become uncomfortable the moment someone mentions prophecy, healing, tongues, miracles, or supernatural gifts.
One side can become so hungry for manifestations that discernment disappears.
The other can become so frightened of deception that expectation disappears.
And somewhere between the sensationalism and the skepticism stands an uncomfortable question:
Does the Holy Spirit still give spiritual gifts today?
Not...
“Have I seen something convincing?”
Not...
“What does my denomination teach?”
Not even...
“What happened at that conference?”
The deeper question is:
What does Scripture actually give us permission to believe?
Because your experience is not the final authority.
Neither is mine.
A preacher is not.
A church tradition is not.
A viral testimony is not.
A spectacular miracle video is not.
And neither is a disappointing experience in which you prayed desperately and nothing seemed to happen.
The Word of God must judge our experiences rather than our experiences rewriting the Word of God.
And when Paul writes to the Corinthians about spiritual gifts, he uses a word that should immediately humble all of us:
χαρίσματα — charismata.
It comes from the same family of words associated with χάρις — charis — grace.
Gifts of grace.
That matters.
Because spiritual gifts were never supposed to become spiritual trophies.
They were never given so Christians could build celebrity identities around themselves.
They were never intended to create a hierarchy in which one believer says, “God uses me more than He uses you.”
They are gifts.
Grace given.
Grace distributed.
Grace that leaves no room for boasting.
Paul writes:
Then comes the sentence that destroys spiritual pride:
“But all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will.”
—1 Corinthians 12:8–11
The Greek behind that final thought is striking:
καθὼς βούλεται — kathōs bouletai
“As He wills.”
Not as the preacher wills.
Not as the congregation demands.
Not as the person seeking a platform decides.
As the Spirit wills.
And perhaps that is where this conversation needs to begin.
The Holy Spirit is not a force Christians learn to control.
He is God.
He is sovereign.

Jesus spoke of the Holy Spirit personally, not as an impersonal spiritual electricity. The Spirit teaches, testifies, guides, glorifies Christ, convicts, distributes gifts, intercedes, and can be grieved.
And if our fascination with spiritual gifts becomes greater than our fascination with Jesus Christ, something has already gone terribly wrong.
Jesus said of the Spirit:
“He shall glorify me.”
—John 16:14
That may be one of the most important tests in this entire discussion.
Does what we are calling a movement of the Holy Spirit magnify Jesus—or magnify the person claiming to possess the gift?
Because the Spirit who inspired Scripture will never contradict the Scripture He inspired.
The Spirit who glorifies Christ will never lead us away from Christ.
The Spirit of truth will never require us to abandon truth in order to experience Him.
And yet...
We must be equally careful about making the opposite mistake.
The existence of counterfeit money does not prove real money does not exist.
False prophecy does not logically prove that God can never graciously work through spiritual gifts.
Fraudulent healers do not prove God cannot heal.
Emotional manipulation does not prove every powerful spiritual experience is manipulation.
Paul knew churches could mishandle spiritual gifts.
The Corinthian church certainly did.
And his solution is fascinating.
He does not simply tell them:
“Stop everything supernatural.”
Instead, he corrects them.
Orders them.
Centers them on love.
Demands intelligibility.
Requires discernment.
And repeatedly redirects attention away from personal exhibition and toward the building up of Christ’s church.
Paul says:
“Now concerning spiritual gifts, brethren, I would not have you ignorant.”
—1 Corinthians 12:1
Then later:
“Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy.”
—1 Corinthians 14:1
The Greek is even more forceful:
ζηλοῦτε δὲ τὰ πνευματικά — zēloute de ta pneumatika
Earnestly desire spiritual things or spiritual gifts.
And near the end of the chapter Paul says:
“Wherefore, brethren, covet to prophesy, and forbid not to speak with tongues. Let all things be done decently and in order.”
—1 Corinthians 14:39–40
Notice the balance.
Do not forbid.
But also:
Decently and in order.
That is uncomfortable for extremists on both sides.
The Christian who accepts every supernatural claim without examination must deal with Scripture's commands concerning discernment.
The Christian who dismisses every claim automatically must deal with Scripture's warning not to despise prophecy.
Paul tells the Thessalonians:
“Quench not the Spirit. Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.”
—1 Thessalonians 5:19–21
That is astonishingly balanced Christianity.
Do not quench.
Do not despise.
But test.
The Greek verb translated “prove” or “test” is:
δοκιμάζετε — dokimazete
Test.
Examine.
Discern what is genuine.
Biblical faith is not gullibility.
You do not have to switch off your discernment to believe in the supernatural.
In fact, Scripture commands the opposite.
John writes:
—1 John 4:1
That single verse destroys the idea that questioning a claimed supernatural revelation is somehow resisting God.
God Himself commands examination.
If someone tells you, “Don't question me; I am anointed,” you have already been given biblical reason to become cautious.
If someone claims God told them something that contradicts Scripture, Scripture wins.
Every time.

If someone uses supposed spiritual authority to manipulate people, enrich themselves, excuse sexual immorality, control relationships, predict things falsely, or make themselves functionally unquestionable, their charisma should never override biblical truth.
The Holy Spirit does not need deception to accomplish the work of God.
But this brings us to the difficult part.
Some sincere, Bible-believing Christians argue that certain miraculous gifts were uniquely associated with the apostolic era and ceased after their foundational purpose had been fulfilled.
This position is commonly called cessationism.

Other sincere, Bible-believing Christians argue that Scripture never explicitly teaches that all such gifts cease before Christ's return and therefore believe God may continue distributing them according to His sovereign will.
This is commonly called continuationism.
Christians on both sides have attempted to ground their conclusions in Scripture.
And we should represent each other honestly.

Cessationists frequently point to the unique foundational role of the apostles, the signs associated with apostolic ministry, the foundational language of Ephesians 2:20, and passages such as Hebrews 2:3–4. Some also understand 1 Corinthians 13 as compatible with the eventual cessation of revelatory or sign gifts.

Continuationists respond that no New Testament passage unambiguously says all miraculous gifts will disappear with the death of the apostles or the completion of the biblical canon. They point especially to Paul's instructions concerning gifts, Peter's Pentecost sermon, and the language of 1 Corinthians 13.
That passage deserves careful attention.
Paul writes:
Someone might stop there and say:
“There it is. They cease.”
Yes.
Paul absolutely says they cease.
The question is when.
He continues:
“For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away.”
—1 Corinthians 13:8–10
Then Paul describes the present condition:
“For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.”
—1 Corinthians 13:12
The Greek phrase translated “face to face” is:
πρόσωπον πρὸς πρόσωπον — prosōpon pros prosōpon
Face to face.
Continuationists commonly understand Paul's language as pointing toward the consummation when believers encounter Christ in fullness rather than toward the closing of the biblical canon.
Cessationists offer different readings and emphasize the temporary and partial nature of these gifts together with the unique foundational period of the apostles.
We should therefore resist pretending the debate can be settled by shouting one isolated verse louder than everyone else.
But there is something both sides desperately need to hear.
You can win an argument about spiritual gifts...
and still grieve the Holy Spirit.
You can have flawless cessationist theology and be proud, loveless, prayerless, cold, bitter, and spiritually asleep.
You can have passionate continuationist theology and be undiscerning, manipulative, disorderly, obsessed with experiences, and hungry for manifestations instead of holiness.
And Paul places something right in the middle of his teaching on gifts that should terrify both camps.
First Corinthians 12 discusses gifts.
First Corinthians 14 discusses gifts.
And sitting between them is First Corinthians 13.
Love.
That is not an accident we should rush past.
Paul says you could speak with extraordinary tongues...
and without love become noise.
You could prophesy.
Understand mysteries.
Possess remarkable knowledge.
Exercise astonishing faith.
And still be...
nothing.
Think about that.
A person could appear spiritually spectacular and still be spiritually hollow.
Because the greatest evidence of God's work in your life is not how impressive you appear in a church service.
Paul also speaks of something far less glamorous:
“The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance.”
—Galatians 5:22–23
Maybe someone needs to hear this.
You have been asking God for a gift people can see...
while He has been trying to produce fruit nobody applauds.
Patience when you are provoked.
Purity when nobody is watching.
Forgiveness toward the person who wounded you.
Self-control when temptation whispers.
Kindness toward someone who cannot repay you.
Faithfulness when serving feels invisible.
Love when bitterness would be easier.
Those things will probably never make you famous.
But heaven notices.
And there is an even deeper danger.
We can become so fascinated with the gifts of the Spirit that we neglect the greatest gift God has given us:
Jesus Christ Himself.
Before you argue about whether someone can speak in tongues...
Have you spoken honestly to Jesus about your sin?
Before you chase prophecy...
Are you obeying what God has already revealed in Scripture?
Before you search for signs...
Have you looked at the cross?
Before you ask whether God still heals bodies...
Have you allowed the Gospel to expose the disease of sin in your own heart?
Because Christianity is not ultimately about obtaining supernatural abilities.
Christianity is about reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
We were not separated from God because we lacked spiritual gifts.
We were separated because of sin.
And Christ did not come primarily to turn ordinary people into impressive religious performers.
He came to save sinners.
The scandal of Christianity is not that broken people can become powerful.
The scandal is that a holy God would show mercy to rebels.
That the innocent Son of God would stand where the guilty belonged.
That Christ would bear sin.
That the King would wear thorns.
That the hands through which creation came would be pierced by His creation.
That Jesus would die...
and rise again.
This is where every spiritual gift must eventually kneel.
At the cross.
Because you can pursue supernatural experiences and still miss the Savior.
Jesus Himself gave one of Scripture's most sobering warnings:
“Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name?... and in thy name done many wonderful works?”
Yet He warns that miraculous claims are not, by themselves, proof that someone belongs to Him.
—Matthew 7:22–23
That should shake us.
The question is not merely:
“What gifts do you have?”
The deeper question is:
“Does Jesus have you?”
Maybe you have spent years arguing about the Holy Spirit while quietly resisting Him.
Maybe nobody knows about the pornography.
The bitterness.
The secret relationship.
The pride.
The jealousy.
The resentment.
The religious performance.
The hidden compromise.
You can debate Greek words and still hide from God.
You can know every theological argument and still need repentance.
And perhaps the most supernatural thing that could happen in your life tonight is not falling to the floor.
Maybe it is finally falling to your knees.
Maybe it is whispering:
“Jesus... I have been pretending.”
Maybe the miracle you desperately need begins with repentance.
Because the Holy Spirit does not merely distribute gifts.
He glorifies Christ.
He convicts concerning sin.
He produces fruit.
He empowers witness.
He sanctifies God's people.
He leads believers toward truth.
And genuine spiritual life will ultimately make Jesus larger in your vision and self smaller.
So, does the Holy Spirit still give spiritual gifts today?

Christians who affirm the continuing operation of the gifts have substantial biblical reasons for believing the Spirit remains free to distribute gifts according to His will, and Scripture contains no universally agreed-upon verse explicitly stating that every miraculous gift must cease with the death of the apostles.

Christians who believe some gifts ceased rightly remind the church that the apostles occupied a unique foundational role and that extraordinary claims must never be allowed to compete with the final authority of Scripture.
Wherever you land, several truths should remain immovable:
Christ is Lord.
Scripture is authoritative.
The Gospel cannot be altered.
The Holy Spirit glorifies Jesus.
Spiritual claims must be tested.
Gifts must never become grounds for pride.
Everything in gathered worship should seek the edification of Christ's body.
Love is indispensable.
Holiness matters.
And salvation comes through Jesus Christ—not through possessing any particular spiritual gift.
You are not saved because you speak in tongues.
You are not saved because you do not speak in tongues.
You are not saved because you have experienced healing.
You are not saved because your theology of healing is perfectly formulated.
You are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
And if God gives gifts, they belong to Him.
If He heals, the glory belongs to Him.
If He gives wisdom, the glory belongs to Him.
If He empowers someone to serve, teach, encourage, give, lead, show mercy, discern, or minister in extraordinary ways...
the glory belongs to Him.
Always.
Perhaps the better prayer is therefore not:
“Holy Spirit, make me impressive.”
But:
“Holy Spirit, make me useful to Jesus.”
Use my mouth.
Use my hands.
Use my weakness.
Use my testimony.
Use the parts of my story I wish had never happened.
Use the scars.
Use the failures You redeemed.
Use everything.
Just let Jesus be seen.
Because this is what grace does.
Grace walks into stories we thought were ruined and writes redemption across pages covered in shame.
Peter denied Christ...
and was restored.
Paul persecuted Christians...
and became a preacher of the Christ he once opposed.
The Corinthians were confused, divided, immature, and disorderly...
yet Paul still called them toward holiness, love, truth, and the proper use of what God had given.
Maybe your story feels equally disqualified.
It isn't beyond Christ's reach.
Your worst chapter does not possess authority over the Author.
Jesus does.
So whether you have spent your life in a charismatic church, a cessationist church, no church at all, or somewhere painfully between belief and doubt...
come back to Jesus.
Not hype.
Not personalities.
Not denominations.
Not experiences.
Not cynicism.
Jesus.

And if God has brought you through confusion, church hurt, spiritual deception, or seasons of doubt, consider sharing a little of your testimony. Someone reading beneath this article may desperately need to discover that struggling with questions does not mean they have to run away from Christ.
Send it privately to the believer who is afraid to ask.
Save it so you can return to the Scriptures and examine them carefully for yourself.

But if these resources genuinely strengthen your walk with Jesus and you want to help us reach more people with biblical content, your support can become an act of generosity and stewardship offered for God's glory.
Do not leave Jesus outside the locked rooms of your life.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ is calling you to forgive.
Test what claims to be spiritual.
Return to Scripture.
Pursue love.
Seek holiness.
