But grace does something deeper than merely making Peter feel better.
John 21 takes us to another fire.
That detail matters.
John uses the Greek word ἀνθρακιά — anthrakia, a charcoal fire, in the courtyard scene and again beside the Sea of Galilee.
Peter had denied Jesus near a charcoal fire.
Now the risen Jesus meets Peter beside another.
Christ is not afraid of the place associated with Peter’s shame.
Jesus can walk directly into the memory you have spent years avoiding.
There, after breakfast, Jesus asks:
“Simon, son of John, do you love Me?”
Peter answers.
Jesus tells him:
“Feed My lambs.”
Again:
“Do you love Me?”
Again Peter answers.
“Tend My sheep.”
Then a third time.
“Do you love Me?”
Peter is grieved.
Three denials.
Three questions.

We should be cautious about forcing every detail into a mechanical formula, but the narrative connection is difficult to miss: the risen Christ is publicly recommissioning the disciple who publicly denied Him.
Jesus does not pretend the failure never happened.
He restores Peter through it.
And then He gives Peter words that sound astonishing after everything that happened:
“Follow Me.”
Again.
Follow Me.
Peter had failed.
Follow Me.
Peter had denied Him.
Follow Me.
Peter had overestimated himself.
Follow Me.
Peter had cried bitter tears.
Follow Me.
Peter had discovered that he was weaker than he imagined.
Follow Me.
Because Christianity has never been about proving that you were strong enough to deserve Jesus.
It is about discovering that Jesus is sufficient to save sinners who cannot save themselves.
This is where some people misunderstand grace.
Grace is not Jesus saying, “Your denial does not matter.”

Grace is Jesus taking sin seriously enough to die for it, defeating death through His resurrection, calling the sinner to repentance, forgiving the repentant, restoring the fallen, and transforming people who once ran from Him into people willing to suffer for His name.
Look at Peter later.
The frightened man in the courtyard does not remain the frightened man in the courtyard.
In Acts, Peter stands publicly and proclaims the crucified and risen Christ.
The mouth that said, “I do not know Him,” becomes a mouth announcing Him.
The man who crumbled under questioning becomes a witness.
What changed?
Peter finally knew something he could not learn through self-confidence.
He needed grace.
He needed the Holy Spirit.
He needed Christ more than Christ needed Peter’s heroic promises.
And perhaps that is what God wants to expose in us.
We often want Jesus to make us impressive.
Jesus wants to make us dependent.
We want a testimony that says, “Look how strong I became.”
The Gospel creates a testimony that says, “Look how merciful Christ has been.”
Maybe your rooster has already crowed.
Maybe you did the thing you promised God you would never do again.
Maybe you went back.
Maybe you compromised.
Maybe you denied Him not with your lips but with your lifestyle.
Maybe you became ashamed of Jesus around people whose approval felt more immediate than His.
Maybe you know exactly what it is like to hear your own heart whisper:
After what I did, surely Jesus is finished with me.
Peter’s story answers that lie without minimizing sin.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Stop defending what Christ died to forgive.
Stop confusing shame with repentance.
Shame says, “Hide from Jesus because you failed.”
Repentance says, “Run to Jesus because you failed.”
Judas and Peter both failed Jesus grievously, but Peter’s tears were not the end of Peter’s story. The risen Christ restored him and called him forward.
There is a difference between stumbling into sin and making peace with sin.
There is a difference between weakness that drives you back to Christ and rebellion that insists Christ has no right to rule you.
Biblical grace never gives us permission to comfortably remain in what nailed our Savior to the cross.
Paul asked whether believers should continue in sin so grace might increase.
His answer was emphatic:
μὴ γένοιτο — mē genoito.
“By no means.”
Grace does not merely pardon.
Grace changes allegiance.
Tell Jesus the truth.
He already knows it.
Confess the sin.
Turn from it.
Ask for mercy.
If necessary, seek help from mature, trustworthy believers who can walk with you in truth and accountability.
And remember the promise of 1 John 1:9: when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Not because our tears purchase forgiveness.
Not because we punish ourselves long enough.
Not because we promise we will never fail again.
Because Jesus Christ is enough.
His blood is enough.
His cross is enough.
His resurrection is enough.
His grace is enough.
Peter’s confidence said:
“I will never deny You.”
Grace eventually taught Peter a better confession:
“Lord, You know.”
You know me.
You know my weakness.
You know my love.
You know my failure.
You know what I did beside that fire.
You know what I wish I could erase.
And still You call me:
Follow Me.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.

Not to build an audience around religious entertainment, but to keep placing biblical truth in front of people living through real battles—people fighting temptation, shame, spiritual exhaustion, lukewarmness, grief, secret wounds, questions, failure, and the desperate need to know Jesus more deeply.
Be honest.

And if Christ has already restored you from something you thought would destroy your story, share your testimony if it is wise and appropriate. Someone reading it may be standing in the same darkness you once survived by grace.

Not because Peter’s failure deserves preservation, but because there may come another night when yours feels unbearable and you need to remember that repentance can lead a broken disciple back to the feet of Jesus.
Not as a religious performance. Not to earn favor with God. We are saved by grace through faith, not by works.

But if you genuinely believe this Gospel-centered work helps proclaim Christ and strengthen believers, supporting it can be one practical way of stewarding your resources for ministry. Scripture calls believers to glorify God with what He has entrusted to them and to participate generously in Gospel work. Let that support come from gratitude and conviction—not guilt or spiritual coercion.
So share this publicly if you believe someone in your circle needs it.
The friend who failed and disappeared.
The believer who thinks God cannot use them anymore.
The husband trying to come home spiritually.
The wife carrying private shame.
The young Christian terrified that one terrible decision has erased their future.
The lukewarm believer who needs awakening.
Even the unbelieving friend who has always assumed Christianity was only for people who somehow managed to keep themselves clean.
Let them meet Peter.
Then let them meet Peter’s Jesus.
Because perhaps tonight someone is hearing their rooster crow.
Perhaps they believe they have gone too far.
Perhaps they are sitting alone thinking their worst chapter has become the title of their entire life.
They need to know what Peter discovered.
Failure can be real.
Consequences can be real.
Repentance is necessary.
But for the one who turns to Christ, failure does not have to have the final word.
The final word belongs to Jesus.
The same Peter who once stood beside a fire saying, “I do not know Him,” would eventually spend his life making Him known.
That is grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not rewriting evil as good.
But taking a shattered sinner, forgiving him through Christ, transforming him, and writing redemption where shame expected only an ending.
So when the rooster crows in your memory again, do not only remember the courtyard.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember the second fire.
Remember the risen Christ.
Remember the words:
“Follow Me.”
And remember this:
The rooster may remind you of the night you failed Jesus—but the empty tomb reminds you that Jesus is still writing after the night you thought your story ended.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: BILHAH SHARED RACHEL’S HUSBAND—BUT DID ANYONE ASK WHAT BILHAH WANTED?
paragraphs: BILHAH SHARED RACHEL’S HUSBAND—BUT DID ANYONE ASK WHAT BILHAH WANTED?

She entered Scripture as somebody’s servant, somebody’s solution, somebody’s mother, and somebody’s concubine. The Bible records what Rachel wanted. It records what Jacob did. It records the sons Bilhah bore. But there is one thing the text never records: Bilhah being asked what she wanted. And that silence should make us read more carefully—not rewrite the Bible, but finally notice the person standing quietly inside it.
There are Bible stories we remember because somebody killed a giant.
Others because a sea opened.
Others because fire fell from heaven.
And then there are stories that disturb you precisely because almost nothing is said.
Bilhah is one of them.

Her name appears in the story of Jacob, Rachel, and Leah, but she rarely becomes the person readers stop to see. She is introduced in relation to someone else. Genesis 29:29 tells us that Laban gave Bilhah to Rachel as her servant. Later, Rachel is unable to conceive while her sister Leah bears children, and the household becomes consumed with fertility, rivalry, jealousy, longing, and the desperate human desire to matter.
Rachel cries to Jacob:
“Give me children, or I shall die.”
Jacob becomes angry.
Then Rachel proposes a solution.
And suddenly Bilhah's body stands in the middle of somebody else's heartbreak.
Listen carefully to the Hebrew of Genesis 30:3:
וַתֹּאמֶר הִנֵּה אֲמָתִי בִלְהָה בֹּא אֵלֶיהָ וְתֵלֵד עַל־בִּרְכַּי וְאִבָּנֶה גַם־אָנֹכִי מִמֶּנָּה
Vattomer, hinneh amati Bilhah, bo eleha; veteled al-birkai, ve'ibbaneh gam-anokhi mimmennah.
In a close rendering:
“Then she said, ‘Here is my maidservant Bilhah. Go in to her, and she will bear upon my knees, so that I too may be built up through her.’”

The Hebrew noun Rachel uses is אֲמָתִי — amati, “my female servant/maidservant,” from amah. The text identifies Bilhah according to her subordinate position in Rachel's household. Genesis 30:4 then says Rachel gave Bilhah to Jacob לְאִשָּׁה — le'ishshah, “as a wife,” and Jacob went in to her. The terminology matters because Scripture does not flatten Bilhah into a modern category; it presents the complicated social reality of an ancient household in which she is simultaneously Rachel's servant and a woman joined to Jacob.
And here is where we must be extremely careful.
The Bible tells us what Rachel said.
It tells us what Rachel did.
It tells us what Jacob did.
It tells us that Bilhah conceived.
But Scripture does not tell us what Bilhah said when this arrangement was made.
There is no recorded “yes.”
There is also no recorded “no.”
There is no recorded conversation in which Bilhah explains how she felt about Jacob, Rachel's proposal, pregnancy, motherhood, or the household arrangement.
That means responsible interpretation must resist two opposite mistakes.
We should not pretend the text explicitly tells us Bilhah consented freely when it does not.
But neither should we invent a scene and claim Scripture explicitly says she resisted when it does not.
The silence is real.
And sometimes biblical faithfulness means refusing to fill a silence with whatever answer makes us most comfortable.
That may be what makes Bilhah's story so haunting.
Everyone around her has something they desperately want.
Rachel wants children.
Leah wants Jacob's love.
Jacob wants a household and descendants.
Laban has already treated marriages and family relationships as pieces in his own negotiations.
And Bilhah?
We hear almost nothing from her.
Yet her body bears part of the cost.
Maybe that sentence touched something in you.
Because perhaps you know what it feels like to become useful to everyone while becoming invisible yourself.
Maybe you became the dependable daughter.
The strong son.
The spouse who keeps forgiving.
The church volunteer who never says no.
The mother who carries everybody's problems.
The father who is expected to provide while quietly collapsing inside.
The friend everybody calls at midnight who has nobody to call when the darkness comes for you.
People know what you can do for them.
They know what you provide.
They know what you solve.
They know what you carry.
But sometimes you wonder...
Does anybody know me?
Not my usefulness.
Not my position.
Not what I can produce.
Me.
Bilhah bore Dan.
Then she bore Naphtali.
And even the naming scene centers Rachel's interpretation of what has happened. Rachel declares that God has judged her cause and later speaks of wrestling with her sister.
Two children have emerged from Bilhah's womb, yet the narrative foregrounds Rachel's struggle.
Read that slowly.
A woman can carry something in her body while somebody else makes the story about themselves.
That is ancient Genesis.
And somehow...
it still happens.
People can use your sacrifice to build their reputation.
They can benefit from your loyalty without asking what it costs you.
They can celebrate what came through you while barely acknowledging what happened to you.
They can love your gift while neglecting the person carrying it.
And sometimes religious people can make this worse.
We can quote “serve.”
“Submit.”
“Forgive.”
“Sacrifice.”
“Carry your cross.”
All biblical words in their proper contexts.
But biblical truth must never become camouflage for selfishness, exploitation, coercion, or abuse.
Jesus never gave us permission to use another human being merely as an instrument for our ambitions.
The Christ who said the greatest must become a servant also warned against rulers who “lord it over” others. His kingdom does not baptize domination; it overturns it.
And Bilhah's story becomes even darker.
Years later, after Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin, Genesis records one devastating sentence:
Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, slept with Bilhah, his father's concubine.
The Hebrew designation later associated with Bilhah is פִּילֶגֶשׁ — pilegesh, commonly rendered “concubine.” Genesis 35:22 records the act with astonishing brevity and then adds:
“and Israel heard of it.”
That is almost all the narrative gives us there.
No recorded words from Bilhah.
No description of her emotional response.
No explanation of what happened from her perspective.
The text simply moves forward.

Later, Genesis 49:3–4 shows that Jacob had not forgotten Reuben's action. On his deathbed, Jacob condemns Reuben's instability and specifically recalls that he went up to his father's bed. The act cost Reuben the privilege associated with his firstborn status. The biblical narrative therefore does not treat what happened as morally insignificant.
But again...
what did Bilhah feel?
Scripture doesn't tell us.
And we must not pretend it does.

That restraint matters especially here. Genesis 35:22 tells us Reuben “went and lay with” Bilhah, but it does not narrate enough details to reconstruct Bilhah's agency, resistance, or consent in that encounter. We can recognize the enormous power dynamics surrounding her without claiming knowledge God has not given us.
Sometimes respecting a silenced person means refusing to put invented words into her mouth.
Yet we can still notice her.
And perhaps that is where this ancient story starts looking uncomfortably modern.
Somebody reading this knows the feeling of having decisions made around you.
Maybe even decisions made for you.
Somebody remembers being young and powerless while adults controlled the room.
Somebody learned early that keeping everyone happy was safer than speaking.
Somebody has smiled through things they never wanted.
Somebody has confused silence with peace because speaking felt too expensive.
Somebody became so accustomed to surviving that you stopped asking yourself the question nobody else seemed interested in asking:
What do I actually feel?
And perhaps even more frightening:
Does God care?
This is where Bilhah's story must eventually take us beyond Bilhah.
Because Christianity does not ultimately offer us a sentimental promise that every human being will finally understand us.
It offers us Jesus Christ.
And Jesus has a strange habit throughout the Gospels.
He notices people crowds have turned into categories.
A bleeding woman touches His garment while everyone else is pressing against Him, and Jesus stops.
A blind beggar cries from the roadside while people tell him to be quiet, and Jesus stops.
A Samaritan woman comes to a well carrying a history complicated enough to make respectable people whisper, and Jesus speaks to her.
A woman caught in adultery becomes the center of a public religious spectacle, and Jesus refuses to treat her merely as somebody else's object lesson.
A dying criminal hangs beside Him with nothing left to offer, and Jesus hears him.
Jesus sees people.
Not resources.
Not statistics.
Not bodies to be used.
Not scandals to exploit.
People.
That matters because the Gospel begins with something both terrifying and beautiful:
God sees the whole truth about us.
Not only what others did to us.
What we have done too.
Our sins.
Our jealousies.
Our manipulation.
Our lust.
Our pride.
Our selfish ambition.
Our hidden compromises.
Our desire to control people.
The ways we have treated others as tools for our happiness.
The times we became Rachel—so consumed by our own pain that another person's humanity became secondary.
The times we became Jacob—participating in a broken arrangement because it benefited us.
The times we became Reuben—crossing boundaries God never gave us permission to cross.
And the times we have felt like Bilhah—present in the story, carrying consequences, barely heard.
The Gospel refuses to let us choose only the role that makes us innocent.
It exposes us.
Then it offers us Christ.
That is grace.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not renaming sin so nobody feels uncomfortable.
Not rewriting history.
Grace is God entering the wreckage and doing what human beings cannot do for themselves.
Jesus came for sinners.
Jesus died for sinners.
Jesus bore sin at the cross.
Jesus rose from the grave.
And everyone who turns from sin and trusts Him receives something no human arrangement can manufacture:
forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
A new identity.
A new heart.
A new future.
The cross tells every wounded person, “God does not overlook evil.”
And the cross tells every guilty person, “Your evil does not have to be the final word.”
That is why repentance is not humiliation.
Repentance is coming out of hiding.
It is finally telling God the truth He already knows.
“Lord, I have been used.”
“Lord, I have used people.”
“Lord, I am angry.”
“Lord, I am ashamed.”
“Lord, I crossed boundaries.”
“Lord, I let bitterness become my identity.”
“Lord, I kept pretending.”
“Lord Jesus... have mercy on me.”
And He does not save us because we constructed the perfect explanation of ourselves.
He saves by grace through faith.
Maybe your greatest fear has been that the ugliest chapter of your life has already determined the ending.
It hasn't.
Ask Peter.
His scandal included denying Jesus.
Ask Paul.
His past included persecuting Christ's people.
Look at the genealogy leading to Jesus in Matthew 1—a family history containing broken relationships, sexual scandal, outsiders, kings, failures, and unexpected grace.
God does not need a spotless human history to accomplish a holy purpose.
He is the Redeemer.
That does not mean evil becomes good because God can redeem its aftermath.
It means evil does not get sovereignty over the ending.
There is a difference.
Joseph eventually said that what human beings intended for evil, God intended for good.
He did not call the evil good.
He declared God greater than it.
And maybe somebody desperately needs that distinction tonight.
What happened was not necessarily good.
What they did was not necessarily right.
What you did may require repentance.
What you lost may actually have been precious.
Some consequences may remain.
Some scars may stay.
Some unanswered questions may never receive satisfying answers in this life.
But Jesus Christ is still Lord over the ending.
Bilhah's story did not disappear from Israel's history.
Dan and Naphtali became two of the tribes of Israel. Centuries passed. Kingdoms rose and fell.
Then Matthew opens the New Testament by identifying Jesus as the Messiah, the son of David, the son of Abraham.
The Bible's grand story keeps moving toward Christ.
Toward the One in whom the promises of God find their fulfillment.
Toward the One who came not to be served but to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many.
Toward the One who touched the unclean, welcomed the rejected, confronted hypocrisy, forgave repentant sinners, and laid down His own life willingly.
That last word matters.
Willingly.
Jesus says in John 10:18 concerning His life:
“No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord.”
The cross was not Jesus becoming a helpless victim of someone else's plan.
The Son willingly gave Himself in obedience to the Father for our redemption.
And resurrection morning announced that sin, shame, violence, death, and the grave would not have the final word.
So what do we do with Bilhah?
We don't invent a speech Scripture never gave her.
We don't force twenty-first-century assumptions into every detail of an ancient text.
We don't turn her into a political slogan.
And we certainly don't pretend that every custom recorded in Genesis represents God's ideal for human relationships.
Narrative is not automatically endorsement.
Genesis repeatedly shows us families distorted by favoritism, rivalry, deception, polygamy, sexual sin, jealousy, and human attempts to force outcomes.
The Bible is remarkably honest about the mess.
And through that mess runs the relentless faithfulness of God.
Maybe that is why Bilhah matters so much.
She reminds us to notice the people standing quietly at the edges of the stories we tell about ourselves.
Who pays for your ambition?
Who absorbs your anger?
Whose kindness have you mistaken for unlimited availability?
Whose silence have you interpreted as permission?
Whose service have you enjoyed without stopping to ask whether that person is exhausted?
Whom have you reduced to what they can provide?
Your spouse?
Your employee?
Your child?
Your parent?
Your pastor?
Your friend?
That person online whose face you forgot represents an actual soul?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all:
Have you ever used God Himself as justification for getting what you wanted?
Those questions hurt.
Good.
Not because shame saves us.
It doesn't.
But conviction can drive us toward the One who does.
Talk to Jesus.
Not as an algorithm trick.
As a confession.
You may discover that someone reading the same words thought they were alone too.
Not to embarrass them.
To remind them:
God still sees people others overlook.
Save this too.
Because there may come a night when the person who needs to reread it is you.
It does not.
Not because Christians must pay us in order to glorify God.
They do not.
Jesus cannot be purchased, grace cannot be bought, and salvation is not merchandise.
If you have been consuming these messages quietly and thinking, I want to help this reach more people, this is one way to stand with the work.
Share because someone you know may be fighting silently.
Save the truth because emotions forget what Scripture teaches.
Follow because your soul needs more than endless scrolling.
But above everything else...
follow Jesus.
Because Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
A Christian library cannot save you.
A viral article cannot save you.
Only Christ saves.
And perhaps that is the final lesson hidden in Bilhah's silence.
Human beings may fail to ask what you wanted.
They may remember what you produced and forget what it cost.
They may call you by your position instead of seeing your personhood.
They may move on while you are still trying to understand what happened.
But the God revealed fully in Jesus Christ does not lose people in the margins.
He sees.
He knows.
He judges rightly.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He gives grace to the undeserving.
He receives the brokenhearted.
And He is able to take a human story filled with things that should never have happened and refuse to let those things write the final sentence.
So if you have spent years believing you are merely the thing somebody did to you...
or the terrible thing you once did...
or the role people assigned you...
or the body somebody wanted...
or the mistake everybody remembers...
or the scandal everybody whispers about...
look toward the cross.
Then look at the empty tomb.
Your past is real.
Sin is real.
Wounds are real.
Consequences are real.
But for the person who belongs to Jesus Christ, none of them is more final than resurrection.
Some people may remember you by the chapter where you were used, wounded, or ashamed—but Jesus is still holding the pen where they thought your story ended.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY “DO NOT FEAR MAN” IS HARDER THAN IT SOUNDS
paragraphs:
WHY “DO NOT FEAR MAN” IS HARDER THAN IT SOUNDS
You may never deny Jesus with your mouth. But every time you edit your obedience because you are afraid of someone’s reaction, you discover why Scripture calls the fear of man a trap.
There is a version of you that loves Jesus boldly when nobody is threatening anything.
When the worship music is playing.
When you are surrounded by believers.
When the verse you post gets hearts instead of angry comments.

When obedience does not cost a friendship, disturb a relationship, threaten your reputation, make the room uncomfortable, or force you to choose between being accepted by people and being faithful to Christ.
It is easy to say, “I don’t fear anyone but God.”
Until obedience has a face.
Until the person whose approval you desperately want looks disappointed in you.
Until your family thinks you have become “too serious” about Jesus.
Until your friends begin treating your convictions like an inconvenience.
Until speaking truth could cost you an opportunity.
Until refusing compromise makes you the difficult person in the room.
Until somebody you love says, “If you really cared about me, you wouldn’t believe that.”
Until following Jesus means someone may no longer understand you.
Then suddenly three simple words become painfully expensive:
Do not fear.
And this is where Scripture becomes frighteningly personal.
Proverbs 29:25 says:
“חֶרְדַּת אָדָם יִתֵּן מוֹקֵשׁ וּבוֹטֵחַ בַּיהוָה יְשֻׂגָּב׃”
Ḥerdat ’adam yitten moqesh, u-voteaḥ ba-YHWH yesuggav.

The Hebrew is vivid. חֶרְדַּת אָדָם (ḥerdat adam) speaks of the fear or anxiety of man, and מוֹקֵשׁ (moqesh) is a snare—a trap, a lure, something that catches its victim. The second half turns in the opposite direction: the one trusting in YHWH “will be set on high,” carrying the picture of being placed securely beyond the reach of what threatened to capture him.
Read that again.
The Bible does not merely say the fear of man is unpleasant.
It calls it a snare.
A trap.
And traps rarely announce themselves.
A trap does not stand in the forest screaming, “I am here to destroy you.”
It disguises itself.
So does the fear of man.
Sometimes it calls itself politeness.
Sometimes wisdom.
Sometimes keeping the peace.
Sometimes protecting your reputation.
Sometimes avoiding drama.
Sometimes being “open-minded.”
Sometimes not wanting to offend anybody.

And certainly, Christians are not commanded to become rude, combative, arrogant, reckless, or needlessly offensive. Jesus calls His people to love. Scripture calls us to gentleness. Christian courage is not permission to become cruel.
But there is a difference between gentleness and surrender.
There is a difference between being gracious and being ashamed.
There is a difference between choosing the right moment to speak and spending your entire life waiting for a moment when obedience will cost nothing.
That moment may never come.
Maybe that is why this subject hurts.
Because some of us are not being persecuted into silence.
We are being liked into silence.
We have become so accustomed to approval that disapproval feels like persecution.
One unfollow.
One mocking comment.
One uncomfortable dinner.
One disappointed relative.
One colleague raising an eyebrow.
One friend calling you judgmental.
One person asking, “You actually believe that?”
And suddenly we discover how much power another human being's opinion has been holding over us.
Jesus spoke about fear with words far stronger than most inspirational Christian posts would dare to use.
In Matthew 10:28, the Greek text reads:
“καὶ μὴ φοβεῖσθε ἀπὸ τῶν ἀποκτεννόντων τὸ σῶμα…”
Kai mē phobeisthe apo tōn apoktennontōn to sōma…
“Do not fear those who kill the body…”

Jesus continues by contrasting those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul with the One whose authority extends beyond physical death. The verb φοβεῖσθε (phobeisthe) comes from the language of fear. Jesus is deliberately rearranging the disciples’ hierarchy of fear. Human beings may possess frightening earthly power, but they do not possess ultimate authority.
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not tell His disciples that people cannot hurt them.
They can.
That is precisely why His command is so staggering.

Jesus was sending disciples into a world where confessing Him could produce real consequences. Matthew 10 is not motivational advice for becoming more confident around difficult personalities. Christ is preparing His followers for hostility because of their allegiance to Him.
Christian courage, therefore, is not believing, “Nothing bad will happen to me.”
Christian courage says:
“Even if obedience costs me something, Jesus is still Lord.”
That changes everything.
Because perhaps you have misunderstood courage.
Courage is not the absence of trembling.
Sometimes courage is trembling while obeying anyway.
Peter knows something about that.
Hours before the crucifixion, Peter sounded fearless.
Even if everybody else abandoned Jesus, Peter insisted that he would remain.
Then came the courtyard.
The questions.
The accusations.
The pressure.
“You also were with Jesus.”
Suddenly the man who had spoken so confidently discovered something terrifying about himself.
There are things we believe about our courage before the test that the test itself exposes.
Peter denied knowing Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
And Luke records one of the most devastating moments in the Gospel narrative: Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Peter remembered.
And Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
Imagine those tears.
Not merely tears because he had been caught.
Tears because he finally saw himself.
“I said I would die for Him.
I could not even admit that I knew Him.”
Maybe you have never stood in Peter’s courtyard.
But perhaps you have lived your own version of it.
You laughed at something you knew dishonored Christ because you wanted to belong.
You stayed silent when someone asked what you really believed.
You changed your convictions depending on who entered the room.
You removed the Christian post because you worried what people would think.
You compromised because losing that relationship frightened you more than grieving God.
You knew what Scripture said, but you desperately wanted somebody else to approve of you.
You prayed afterward.
You felt sick afterward.
You wondered:
“How could I love Jesus and still be this afraid?”
Peter could answer you.
Because fear of man does not always mean you do not love Jesus.
Sometimes it reveals that there are places inside you where the approval of people is still competing with obedience to Jesus.
And Jesus loves us too much to leave those places hidden.
There is another passage that cuts even deeper.
Paul asks in Galatians 1:10:
“Ἄρτι γὰρ ἀνθρώπους πείθω ἢ τὸν θεόν; ἢ ζητῶ ἀνθρώποις ἀρέσκειν;”
In context, Paul asks whether he is seeking human approval or God's, and whether he is trying to please people. Then comes the devastating conclusion:
“εἰ ἔτι ἀνθρώποις ἤρεσκον, Χριστοῦ δοῦλος οὐκ ἂν ἤμην.”
“If I were still trying to please people, I would not be a servant of Christ.”
Paul is not condemning ordinary kindness.
He is not saying Christians should deliberately make everyone angry.
He is exposing a deeper allegiance.
Who gets the final vote over your obedience?
That is the question.
Because there is a kind of people-pleasing that looks compassionate while quietly enthroning human approval.
And if you need everybody to approve of your obedience before you obey God, they have become more than people whose opinions you value.
They have become people whose permission you require.
That is the snare.
You begin checking faces before checking Scripture.
You measure truth by applause.
You calculate obedience by consequences.
You become one person around believers and another around unbelievers.
You tell yourself that you are protecting relationships when, deep inside, you know you are protecting yourself.
And perhaps the most terrifying part is that you can do this while still appearing deeply religious.
You can sing loudly and fear man.
You can quote Scripture and fear man.
You can preach and fear man.
You can run a Christian page and fear man.
You can have thousands of Christian followers and secretly become addicted to their approval.
You can even tell people not to fear man while refreshing the screen to see whether they approved of the way you said it.
That is how deep the trap goes.
Fear of man is not only a problem “out there.”
It can stand behind a pulpit.
It can hold a microphone.
It can carry a Bible.
It can write this article.
Which means nobody reading this gets to point outward first.
Neither do I.
The Gospel forces us inward before it sends us outward.
“Lord… where am I still afraid of people?”
That question requires courage.
Maybe you fear your parents.
Your spouse.
Your children.
Your employer.
Your pastor.
Your congregation.
Your customers.
Your followers.
Your old friends.
Your new friends.
Maybe there is one person whose disappointment can rearrange your entire emotional world.
You know the person.
You can almost see the face right now.
And if following Jesus brought you into conflict with that person's expectations, you are not completely sure which voice would win.
Do not rush past that.
That may be exactly where Jesus wants to meet you.
Because freedom from the fear of man does not begin with pretending people cannot hurt you.
It begins when Christ becomes more precious than the approval you are terrified of losing.
And this is where the story turns.
Because Peter's courtyard was not the end of Peter.
Thank God.
The man who denied Jesus was not discarded by Jesus.
After the resurrection, Christ came for him.
Jesus restored Peter.
He did not pretend Peter's denial had never happened.
Grace is not amnesia.
Jesus confronted the place of failure and restored the man who had failed.
“Do you love Me?”
Again.
“Do you love Me?”
Again.
“Do you love Me?”

The threefold questioning in John 21 has long been noticed beside Peter's threefold denial. Whatever conclusions we draw about every detail of that correspondence, the narrative itself unmistakably shows the risen Christ restoring Peter and recommissioning him to care for His sheep.
The coward in the courtyard did not write the final chapter.
Jesus did.
And there it is.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming the sinner caught inside it.
Peter's story is not, “A coward finally became impressive enough for God.”
Peter's story is grace.
The cross stands between Peter's shame and Peter's future.
And it stands between yours.
The Gospel is not that courageous people save themselves by becoming fearless.
The Gospel is that sinners—including fearful, compromised, approval-addicted sinners—are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Christ lived in perfect obedience where we have compromised.
Christ remained faithful where we have been ashamed.
Christ went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He rose.
And those who turn from sin and trust in Him are not merely given a better motivational strategy.
They are given Christ.
Forgiveness.
Grace.
A new allegiance.
A new identity.
A new Lord.
This is why repentance matters.
Repentance is not saying, “I need to become more confident.”
It is saying:

“Jesus, forgive me. I have sometimes wanted their approval more than Yours. I have obeyed my fear. I have protected my image. I have hidden when I should have stood. I have made people too large in my heart and treated You as though You were small. Have mercy on me.”
And He is merciful.
The answer to the fear of man is not self-worship disguised as confidence.
It is not, “Stop caring what everybody thinks because you are amazing.”
That is simply replacing one idol with another.
Biblical freedom comes when God becomes weightier in your heart than human applause.
People can misunderstand you.
Christ knows you.
People can reject you.
Christ remains Lord.
People can mock you.
Christ is not dethroned.
People can unfollow you.
Christ has not moved.
People can remove your seat from their table.
They cannot erase your name from the hands of the Savior who purchased His people with His blood.
And perhaps this is the sentence somebody needs tonight:
You do not have to hate people to stop worshiping their approval.
Love them.
Serve them.
Listen to them.
Honor them where honor is due.
Apologize when you are wrong.
Be gentle.
Be teachable.
Do not confuse stubbornness with holiness.
Do not call every criticism persecution.
Sometimes the person correcting you is right.
Sometimes your behavior—not your Christianity—is what offended them.
Humility must remain beside courage.
But when Scripture is clear, Christ is Lord.
When obedience becomes costly, Christ is Lord.
When your reputation trembles, Christ is Lord.
When your voice trembles, Christ is Lord.
When you lose applause, Christ is Lord.
When following Him makes you misunderstood, Christ is Lord.
And when you fail again?
Run toward Christ, not away from Him.
Peter wept.
Peter was restored.
Peter was changed.
The same disciple once intimidated by questions in a courtyard later stood publicly identifying himself with the crucified and risen Jesus.
That transformation should give frightened believers hope.
Not confidence in themselves.
Confidence in the grace of God.
Maybe you are reading this because you have spent years editing yourself to remain acceptable.
Maybe everybody knows the version of you that causes the least trouble.
Your family gets one version.
Church gets another.
Work gets another.
Social media gets another.
And somewhere underneath all those carefully managed versions is a tired soul whispering:
“I don't even know who I am anymore.”
Come back to Jesus.
You were never meant to carry the impossible burden of being approved by everyone.
You cannot.
Even Jesus was rejected.
So why have we made universal approval the evidence that we are doing Christianity correctly?
The goal is not to become hated.
The goal is faithfulness.
The goal is not controversy.
The goal is Christ.
The goal is not winning arguments.
The goal is obedience flowing from love for the One who first loved us.
And sometimes that obedience will be welcomed.
Sometimes mocked.
Sometimes misunderstood.
Sometimes costly.
But the fear of man is still a snare.
And trust in the Lord is still freedom.
So here is the question I want following you after this article closes:
Whose reaction are you currently allowing to negotiate your obedience to Jesus?
Do not answer quickly.
Name the face.
Name the fear.
Name what you think you could lose.
Then put it before Christ.
Maybe your prayer tonight needs only a few words:
“Jesus, I am afraid.
But I want You more.”
That is not weakness.
That can become the beginning of courage.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, do not hide behind a polished Christian answer.
Pray.
We need Christian spaces where people can admit that following Jesus is sometimes frightening without being treated as spiritual failures.
Supporting Gospel work matters.
But hear this carefully: you cannot purchase God's favor.
Sharing a post does not earn salvation.
No product can purchase grace.
Jesus Christ alone saves.
We support Gospel ministry not to buy God's approval, but because grace has already taught us that the Gospel is worth carrying to others.
If this ministry feeds you spiritually, stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who walked away from church.
Invite the believer who is exhausted.
Invite the person who is becoming lukewarm.
Invite the person who does not believe yet.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is deciding whether being accepted by people is worth becoming silent about Jesus.
Maybe that person is reading these words.
Maybe that person is you.
Remember Peter.
The courtyard was real.
The denial was real.
The tears were real.
But so was the empty tomb.
So was restoration.
So was grace.
Your worst moment of cowardice does not have to become the final sentence of your story.
Repent.
Come back.
Receive mercy.
Stand again.
And the next time fear whispers, “What will they think of you?”
Remember the better question:
“What has Jesus done for me?”
He was mocked.
Rejected.
Wounded.
Crucified.
Buried.
And He rose.
Your Savior did not remain in the grave.
So do not build your prison from other people's opinions.
The snare is real.
But Christ is greater.
And perhaps the freedom you have been begging God to give you begins the moment you stop asking everyone else for permission to belong completely to Jesus.
The rooster may remind you where you failed—but the empty tomb reminds you Who gets to write what happens next.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY GOD MAY REMOVE PEOPLE BEFORE HE BLESSES YOU
paragraphs:
WHY GOD MAY REMOVE PEOPLE BEFORE HE BLESSES YOU
Sometimes the goodbye you begged God to reverse becomes the doorway through which He teaches you that Jesus was the One you could never afford to lose.
There is a particular kind of pain that doesn’t bleed where anyone can see it.
It happens when someone who once knew your favorite song becomes a stranger.
When the person you prayed with stops answering.
When someone who promised, “I’m not going anywhere,” somehow goes anyway.
When the friendship changes.
The relationship ends.
The invitation stops coming.
The messages become shorter.
Then silence.
And you sit there staring at a phone that isn’t ringing, asking God a question you are almost afraid to say aloud:
“Lord… why did You let them leave?”
Maybe you have asked an even more painful question.
“Was I not worth staying for?”
Read this carefully.
Because there is a dangerous Christian cliché that sounds comforting but can become biblically careless:
“God removed them because He is about to bless you.”
Sometimes that may describe what God is doing.
But Scripture never gives us permission to turn every broken relationship into a prophecy of an approaching promotion.
Sometimes people leave because of sin.
Sometimes relationships fracture because we were wrong.
Sometimes reconciliation should be pursued.
Sometimes forgiveness is required even when restoration is impossible.
Sometimes another person makes a decision God never commanded them to make.
Sometimes God calls us to walk away from what is sinful or destructive.
Sometimes He permits a separation we would never have chosen.
And sometimes God really does lead His people out of familiar relationships, places, patterns, and dependencies because obedience to Him requires letting go.
The biblical truth is better than the cliché.
God does not have to destroy everyone around you in order to bless you.
But He loves you too much to allow anyone—including the person you cannot imagine living without—to occupy the throne that belongs to Jesus Christ alone.
That changes everything.

Long before Abraham became the father of a nation, long before generations would speak his name, long before he could see the fulfillment of what God had promised, God spoke words that required departure.
Genesis 12:1 records:
“לֶךְ־לְךָ” — lekh-lekha.
“Go forth.”
The Hebrew begins with an imperative. Abram is being commanded to leave his land, his kindred, and his father’s household and go toward a land God would show him.
Notice what God did not give him first.
A map.
A photograph of the destination.
A five-year plan.
An explanation for every mile.
God gave him a command attached to a promise.
Leave.
Then walk with Me.
And perhaps that is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Because we often want God to reveal the destination before we surrender the departure.
“Lord, show me what replaces this relationship, and then I’ll release it.”
“Show me who will love me next.”
“Show me why they betrayed me.”
“Show me what You are going to give me.”
“Show me how this ends.”
Then I will trust You.
But faith says something different.
Faith says:
“If Christ is calling me forward, I do not need tomorrow’s entire map to obey Him today.”
Maybe your deepest grief is not simply that someone left.
Maybe it is that when they left, they carried away the version of your future you had already rehearsed in your imagination.
You saw the wedding.
The friendship lasting forever.
The ministry together.
The business.
The family gatherings.
The old age.
The answered prayer.
You did not merely lose a person.
You buried a future that existed inside your head.
And nobody held a funeral for it.
So you kept functioning.
Kept smiling.
Kept posting.
Kept saying, “God is good.”
But privately?
You were shattered.
And perhaps the most frightening discovery was how much of your peace had become attached to somebody else staying.
That is where God sometimes performs surgery on the human heart.
Not because human relationships are evil.
They are gifts.
Scripture celebrates friendship, marriage, family, fellowship, reconciliation, loyalty, and sacrificial love.
But a gift becomes dangerous when we ask it to become God.
No human being was designed to carry the weight of being your savior.
No spouse can do it.
No pastor can do it.
No best friend can do it.
No parent can do it.
No child can do it.
No audience can do it.
No relationship can do it.
Eventually every human shoulder collapses beneath the weight of expectations only Christ was meant to carry.
And this is why some losses expose us before they heal us.
You thought you were grieving only the person.
Then God showed you the dependency.
You thought you missed their presence.
Then God exposed how desperately you needed their approval.
You thought you were afraid of loneliness.
Then the Spirit revealed that somewhere along the journey you had started measuring your worth by whether another human being chose you.
And Jesus comes into that wreckage not merely to make you feel better.
He comes to reclaim His throne.
This is where John 15 becomes breathtaking.
Jesus describes Himself as the true vine and His Father as the vinedresser. Speaking about the fruitful branch, the Greek text of John 15:2 says:
“καθαίρει αὐτὸ ἵνα καρπὸν πλείονα φέρῃ”
kathairei auto hina karpon pleiona pherē.
The central word καθαίρει — kathairei carries the idea of cleansing or pruning.
Why?
So that the branch may bear more fruit.
Do not misunderstand the metaphor.
Jesus is not specifically saying, “Every painful breakup means God removed that person.”
That would force the text to say something it does not say.
The point is deeper.
The Father is committed to the fruitfulness of those who abide in Christ.
And pruning hurts precisely because the branch is alive.
There are seasons when God confronts attachments, habits, ambitions, environments, dependencies, and yes, sometimes relationships that interfere with faithful obedience.
Pruning can feel like punishment when you do not understand the Gardener.
But the hands doing the pruning belong to the Father.
And the Vine is still Jesus.
That matters.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of God removing people so you can become successful.
It is the story of God reconciling sinners to Himself through Jesus Christ.
The greatest blessing is not the replacement relationship.
It is Christ.
The greatest breakthrough is not finally becoming admired by the people who rejected you.
It is belonging to Christ.
The greatest revenge is not becoming so successful that somebody regrets losing you.
That is wounded pride wearing Christian clothing.
The Gospel offers something infinitely better.
Freedom.
You no longer have to spend your life proving to somebody that they made a mistake by leaving.
Jesus Christ already settled the question of your value at a bloody Roman cross.
You were not purchased with somebody’s apology.
You were purchased by the blood of Christ.
And perhaps somebody reading this desperately needs to hear that.
Stop building your future around making somebody regret your past.
Stop fantasizing about the day they see you blessed.
Stop checking whether they viewed your profile.
Stop secretly hoping your healing makes them jealous.
That is not freedom.
You are still chained to them—you simply decorated the chain with Bible verses.
Jesus offers you something better.
Forgive.
Release.
Repent where you were wrong.
Make peace where peace can biblically be made.
Set boundaries where wisdom requires them.
Then follow Christ.
Paul knew what abandonment felt like.
Near the end of his life, he wrote about his first defense that no one came to stand with him.
People deserted him.
Imagine that sentence.
After the churches.
After the preaching.
After the beatings.
After the imprisonments.
After pouring himself out for others.
When he needed people beside him, they were absent.
Yet 2 Timothy 4:17 gives us one of Scripture’s most beautiful answers to human abandonment:
“But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me.”
There it is.
Not:
“Everyone came back.”
Not:
“Paul immediately found better friends.”
Not:
“God made everybody who abandoned him suffer.”
The Lord stood with him.
Maybe that is the miracle you have been overlooking.
You keep asking God to restore the person while God is revealing the presence of Christ.
You keep staring at the empty chair.
God keeps pointing toward the occupied throne.
You keep saying:
“Look who left.”
He keeps reminding you:
“Look Who remained.”
Jesus.
Still here.
When they misunderstood you.
Jesus.
When they stopped calling.
Jesus.
When your own failures contributed to the wreckage and repentance became necessary.
Jesus.
When you discovered things you wish you had never discovered.
Jesus.
When you cried in a bathroom because you did not want anybody to hear.
Jesus.
When you deleted the message, rewrote it, deleted it again, and finally realized there was nothing left to say.
Jesus.
When loneliness climbed into bed beside you.
Jesus.
When Sunday worship sounded different because your heart was breaking.
Jesus.
And there is something else we must say because biblical truth matters more than a viral slogan:
Sometimes the person who needs to be removed is not “them.”
Sometimes the thing God wants removed is in us.
Our pride.
Our jealousy.
Our manipulation.
Our lust.
Our bitterness.
Our obsession with being chosen.
Our fear of being alone.
Our hunger for human applause.
Our refusal to forgive.
Our insistence that God bless our plans instead of surrendering ourselves to His will.
It is easy to make yourself the hero of every breakup.
It is harder to kneel before Jesus and pray:
“Search me.”
That prayer is dangerous.
Because grace does not merely comfort us.
Grace transforms us.
The Gospel does not tell you that everybody else was toxic and you were always innocent.
The Gospel says something far more humbling and far more liberating:
All of us are sinners who need a Savior.
You do not stand before God because you successfully identified everybody else’s dysfunction.
You stand because Jesus Christ took the judgment sinners deserved, died, was buried, and rose again.
At the cross, excuses die.
Pride dies.
Self-righteousness dies.
And mercy speaks.
Maybe that relationship ended because somebody sinned against you.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending evil was acceptable.
Maybe you sinned against them.
Then repentance may require an apology without demanding reconciliation as payment.
Maybe neither of you was prepared for what you tried to build.
Maybe distance became necessary.
Maybe God is calling you away from something that continually pulls you toward sin.
Whatever the details, do not waste your pain by turning it into bitterness.
Bring it to Jesus.
Let Him expose what needs exposing.
Let Him heal what needs healing.
Let Him forgive what needs forgiving.
Let Him teach you how to forgive.
Let Him become more precious than the answer you were demanding.
Because sometimes we ask:
“God, why did You let me lose them?”
And years later, after the tears have dried and wisdom has grown where desperation once lived, the question changes.
“Lord… what were You teaching me when I thought I couldn’t survive without them?”
Maybe you learned discernment.
Maybe you learned boundaries.
Maybe you learned repentance.
Maybe you learned that chemistry is not covenant.
Maybe you learned that attention is not love.
Maybe you learned that being needed is not the same as being cherished.
Maybe you learned that loneliness cannot kill the person whose life is hidden in Christ.
Maybe you learned to pray again.
Maybe you opened your Bible because there was nobody left to text at 2:00 a.m.
Maybe heartbreak drove you into the presence of God.
And one night, somewhere between “Why did You allow this?” and “Jesus, I surrender,” something happened.
You stopped asking God merely to give the person back.
You started asking Him to give you Himself.
That is a different prayer.
And that prayer changes people.
Do not hear me saying loss is automatically good.
Death hurts.
Betrayal hurts.
Divorce hurts.
Friendships ending hurt.
Family fractures hurt.
Rejection hurts.
Scripture never requires you to pretend otherwise.
Jesus Himself wept.
Christian maturity is not learning how to become emotionally numb.
It is learning where to carry the pain.
Bring it to Christ.
Bring the confusion.
Bring the anger you are embarrassed to admit.
Bring the questions.
Bring the screenshots you keep rereading.
Bring the memories.
Bring the plans that never happened.
Bring the apology you never received.
Bring your own sin too.
Especially your own sin.
Put everything at the feet of Jesus.
Then leave the throne empty for Him alone.
And if God eventually brings new people into your life, love them deeply.
Just do not worship them.
If God restores an old relationship through genuine repentance, wisdom, truth, and reconciliation, receive that restoration humbly.
If He does not, keep following Christ.
If God gives you marriage, thank Him.
If you are waiting, follow Him.
If friends surround you, thank Him.
If you are walking through a lonely wilderness, follow Him.
Because the promise of Christianity was never that everybody you love will remain.
The promise is that Christ will never cease to be enough.
That is why your story does not have to end at the scandal.
The betrayal is not the final chapter.
The rejection is not the final chapter.
Your mistake is not the final chapter.
Your divorce is not the final chapter.
Your loneliness is not the final chapter.
Your shame is not the final chapter.
Even your sin does not have to write the ending.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By bringing grace into the middle of it.
The cross itself looked like scandal before resurrection morning revealed victory.
The Messiah rejected.
Mocked.
Abandoned.
Crucified between criminals.
Then the stone moved.
Death lost.
Christ rose.
And suddenly the darkest chapter in human history became the doorway through which redemption was proclaimed to the world.
That is the Gospel.
And that is why your broken chapter does not intimidate Jesus.
He specializes in resurrection.
So perhaps the question is no longer:
“Why did they leave?”
Perhaps tonight the better question is:
“Jesus, what are You asking me to surrender so I can follow You without divided loyalty?”
Be honest.
Do not comment because an algorithm needs engagement.
Your honesty may become another believer’s permission to stop pretending.
And if one person came to mind while reading this, send this to them.
Save it too.
Heartbreak has a strange way of making us forget tomorrow what God showed us tonight.
Come back when the memories return.
Come back when loneliness starts rewriting history and convincing you to run back toward something Christ called you to surrender.
And stay connected to Gospel Warrior if you want daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
It does not.
Not because giving money purchases a blessing.
It cannot.
The Gospel of Jesus Christ is not for sale.
But supporting faithful Christian work can be one practical way to glorify God when it is done freely, gratefully, wisely, and from a heart that wants biblical truth to reach more people.
If you believe this work should continue reaching wounded believers, struggling Christians, seekers, families, and even unbelievers who desperately need to hear about Jesus, you can support it here:
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
We are not trying to build a crowd around Gospel Warrior.
We want to point a crowd toward Christ.
So share the Gospel.
Share Scripture.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the Christian who has grown cold.
Invite the person who stopped attending church.
Invite the believer whose faith is hanging by a thread.
Invite the skeptic who thinks their scandal disqualified them from grace.
Tell them there is still a cross.
There is still an empty tomb.
There is still forgiveness.
There is still repentance.
There is still mercy.
There is still a Savior.
His name is Jesus.
And perhaps someday you will look back at the season when you thought losing them meant losing everything and realize something that brings tears to your eyes all over again:
The empty space they left became the place where you finally discovered that Christ had never left you.
Some people may disappear from your story, but when Jesus holds the pen, your wound never gets the privilege of writing the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DID GOD APPROVE OF SOLOMON’S 700 WIVES? THE ANSWER IS MORE DISTURBING—AND MORE PERSONAL—THAN YOU THINK
paragraphs:
DID GOD APPROVE OF SOLOMON’S 700 WIVES? THE ANSWER IS MORE DISTURBING—AND MORE PERSONAL—THAN YOU THINK
The Bible never says God approved Solomon’s many wives. It says almost the exact opposite. But buried beneath Solomon’s scandal is a warning about the human heart—and a trail of grace that eventually leads us to Jesus Christ.
Imagine standing inside Solomon’s palace.

Gold catches the light everywhere. Servants move through enormous halls. Foreign dignitaries wait for an audience with the man whose wisdom has become legendary. Kings know his name. Nations have heard of his wealth. The Queen of Sheba herself will marvel at what God has allowed him to possess.
And somewhere behind those palace doors is something almost impossible to comprehend.
Hundreds of women.
Wives.
Concubines.
Political alliances.
Relationships multiplied beyond anything resembling the marriage covenant we see established at creation.
Then comes the uncomfortable question Christians sometimes hesitate to ask:
If Solomon was blessed by God…
if Solomon was given extraordinary wisdom by God…
if Solomon built the Temple…
if Solomon was king over God’s covenant people…
did God approve of all those wives?
No.
And Scripture is remarkably clear about it.
The tragedy is that Solomon possessed enough wisdom to recognize the danger while apparently becoming unable—or unwilling—to escape it himself.
That should frighten us a little.
Because Solomon’s story is not merely about ancient polygamy.
It is about what happens when a person can recognize truth intellectually while slowly negotiating with it personally.
And perhaps that is why his story can feel uncomfortably familiar.
You can know Scripture…
and still compromise.
You can teach truth…
and still hide something.
You can have influence…
and still have idols.
You can appear tremendously blessed…
while something inside your heart is quietly drifting away from the One who blessed you.
Long before Solomon was born, God had already given Israel instructions concerning its future kings.
Deuteronomy 17:17 says in Hebrew:
“וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים, וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ”
Ve-lo yarbeh-lo nashim, ve-lo yasur levavo.
A careful sense of the words is:
“He shall not multiply wives for himself, so that his heart does not turn aside.”
Read that again.
God did not merely warn Israel’s king about pagan worship after the fact.
God warned him about the road that could take his heart there.
Do not multiply wives.
Why?
“וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ”
So that his heart will not turn aside.
The Hebrew word levavo refers to his heart—his inner person, his will, his allegiance.
God was protecting something deeper than Solomon’s reputation.
God was guarding his heart.
And then, generations later, Solomon did almost exactly what the Torah had warned Israel’s king not to do.
First Kings 11 records the devastating result.

Solomon loved many foreign women. The issue in that chapter is not ethnicity, as though Scripture were teaching racial superiority. The text itself identifies the spiritual danger: these relationships involved peoples whose gods could draw Israel into idolatry, and Solomon eventually participated in that idolatry.
The king who should have guarded covenant faithfulness accumulated seven hundred royal wives and three hundred concubines.
One thousand women.
But the number is not even the darkest sentence in the story.
The darkest sentence concerns what happened to his heart.
The Hebrew text of 1 Kings 11:3 says:
“וַיַּטּוּ נָשָׁיו, אֶת־לִבּוֹ”
Vayyattu nashav et-libbo.
His wives turned—or inclined—his heart.
The warning of Deuteronomy had become Solomon’s biography.
God had said that multiplying wives could turn the king’s heart.
Solomon multiplied wives.
And his heart turned.
That is not divine approval.
That is divine warning followed by human disobedience followed by devastating consequences.
We need to understand something important when reading Scripture.
The Bible records many things it does not endorse.
Description is not automatically prescription.

When Scripture tells us that Abraham, Jacob, David, Solomon, and others had multiple wives or concubines, the existence of those relationships in the narrative does not mean God was presenting them as His ideal.
The Bible is brutally honest about its heroes.
That honesty is actually one reason Scripture feels so unlike religious propaganda.
Its greatest human figures are not airbrushed.
Noah becomes drunk.
Abraham acts out of fear.
Jacob deceives.
Moses disobeys.
David commits adultery and orchestrates a man's death.
Peter denies Jesus.
Solomon becomes entangled in idolatry.
The Bible does not need flawless human heroes because the Bible is moving toward a flawless Savior.
And when we return to the beginning, before kings, kingdoms, political marriages, concubines, harems, and royal compromises, the pattern of marriage is strikingly simple.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ, וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד”
Ve-davaq be-ishto, ve-hayu le-vasar echad.
A man is joined to his wife, and they become “one flesh.”
One covenant union.
And centuries later, when Jesus is questioned about marriage, He does something profoundly important.
He goes backward.
Not merely to Israel’s kings.
Not merely to Moses.
Back to creation.
In Matthew 19, Jesus recalls that the Creator made humanity male and female and speaks of the two becoming one flesh.
The Greek expression is:
“οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν”
hoi dyo eis sarka mian—
“the two into one flesh.”
Then Christ says they are no longer two, but one flesh.
Jesus points His listeners toward God’s creational design.
So no, Solomon’s thousand relationships do not overturn Genesis.
Solomon is not the standard.
Creation is the pattern, and Christ Himself directs us back toward it.
But there is another question hiding underneath all this.
Why would the wisest man alive do something so foolish?
Maybe because wisdom possessed is not necessarily wisdom obeyed.
And now Solomon stops being merely an ancient king.
Now he becomes a mirror.
Because some of us know exactly what God says too.
We know that relationship is pulling us away from Christ.
We know that habit is poisoning us.
We know what happens every time we open that private browser.
We know that bitterness is becoming hatred.
We know that secret conversation with someone who is not our spouse has crossed emotional boundaries.
We know that money has become more than provision—it has become identity.
We know applause has become addictive.
We know pride is controlling us.
We know the Holy Spirit has been pressing the same conviction into our conscience again and again.
Yet somewhere inside ourselves we whisper:
Just one more time.
It isn't that serious.
I can control it.
God understands.
Nobody knows.
I still pray.
I still go to church.
I still post Bible verses.
I still believe.
So did Solomon.
That is what makes his fall terrifying.
This was not a man who had never encountered God.
According to 1 Kings 11, God had appeared to Solomon twice.
Think about that.
Solomon did not fall because he lacked evidence that God existed.
He fell while possessing extraordinary revelation.
And perhaps one of the most dangerous lies a believer can embrace is the idea that yesterday’s encounter with God guarantees tomorrow’s obedience to God.
It does not.
A powerful testimony cannot replace present surrender.
Yesterday’s tears cannot substitute for today’s repentance.
Yesterday’s obedience cannot sanctify today’s compromise.
Solomon’s decline also appears to have happened over time.
That is usually how hearts drift.
Few people wake up and announce, “Today I will destroy my spiritual life.”
It begins smaller.
A boundary moved.
A warning rationalized.
A conviction delayed.
A secret protected.
An appetite fed.
Another compromise.
Then another.
Until eventually the thing you once controlled begins controlling you.
Sin rarely introduces itself by saying, “I have come to ruin you.”
It usually whispers, “You deserve this.”
Solomon “clung” to these women in love.
That detail matters.
Because something can feel deeply emotional and still be spiritually destructive.
Something can feel like love while competing with your love for God.
Something can feel impossible to surrender while becoming the very thing Christ is asking you to place in His hands.
And here is where this story becomes painful.
Maybe your “many wives” are not people.
Maybe they are the many little loyalties competing for your heart.
The approval you cannot live without.
The money you cannot stop chasing.
The lust nobody sees.
The resentment you secretly rehearse.
The relationship you know is pulling you from Christ.
The status you worship.
The ministry platform that quietly became more important than the God you were supposedly serving through it.
The image of yourself you are terrified to lose.
Your heart has only one throne.
And anything we love more than Christ eventually becomes a cruel master.
That is why Solomon’s story cannot simply end with us shaking our heads at Solomon.
We need to ask the question we would rather avoid:
What is turning my heart?
Not what turned Solomon’s.
Mine.
What have I been calling harmless that God has been calling dangerous?
What have I been defending because surrender would hurt?
What warning have I repeatedly heard but quietly ignored?
Be honest.
This may be hitting harder than you expected.
Maybe you look completely fine to everyone around you.
Maybe people come to you for encouragement.
Maybe you can explain doctrine.
Maybe you know verses by memory.
Maybe you have spent years serving God.
And still there is a locked room in your heart you hope Jesus will never ask you to open.
He already knows what is inside.
And remarkably…
He has not stopped calling you.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not come merely to expose people like Solomon.
Jesus came to save sinners like Solomon.
And sinners like us.
The Bible ultimately refuses to let Solomon become our final king.
Israel needed someone greater.
Jesus Himself spoke of “something greater than Solomon.”
Solomon possessed wisdom.
Jesus Christ is the One in whom the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are found.
Solomon’s heart turned away.
Jesus perfectly obeyed His Father.
Solomon’s kingdom fractured.
Christ establishes a kingdom that will never finally be destroyed.
Solomon accumulated glory.
Jesus laid His glory aside, took the form of a servant, humbled Himself, and went obediently toward a cross.
Solomon’s disobedience helped tear a kingdom apart.
Christ allowed His own body to be torn so rebels could be reconciled to God.
Look at the scandal of the cross.
The innocent One condemned.
The Holy One surrounded by sinners.
Nails through hands that healed.
Blood running from the brow of the King of kings.
Jesus was not dying because He had lost control.
He was laying down His life.
For adulterers.
For idolaters.
For hypocrites.
For the sexually broken.
For religious pretenders.
For secret addicts.
For proud people.
For people whose hearts have wandered.
For people who knew better.
For people who promised God they would never do it again…
and did it again.
For us.
That is grace.
But biblical grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
The cross proves precisely how serious sin is.
Grace is God doing for sinners what sinners could never do for themselves.
Christ bears sin.
Christ satisfies divine justice.
Christ offers forgiveness.
Christ calls sinners to repentance.
Christ gives new life.
So if Solomon’s story is exposing something inside you right now, do not waste the conviction by merely feeling emotional.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Name the thing.
Stop decorating what Jesus died to deliver you from.
Stop calling bondage freedom.
Stop protecting the idol that is slowly eating your heart.
You do not need another hiding place.
You need a Savior.
And His name is Jesus.
Maybe you have wandered farther than you ever imagined you would.
Maybe you once burned for God.
Maybe worship once made you weep.
Maybe Scripture once felt alive.
Then something happened.
Pain.
Success.
Disappointment.
Lust.
Money.
A relationship.
Church hurt.
Pride.
Exhaustion.
Secret sin.
Slowly, almost invisibly, Jesus moved from the center of your attention toward the edge.
Come home.
Not because you can repair yourself.
Because Christ receives repentant sinners.
The Gospel is not “clean yourself up and perhaps Jesus will accept you.”
The Gospel announces that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
Repentance is not purchasing His mercy.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior whose mercy you desperately need.
Perhaps your scandal is different from Solomon’s.
Grace still knows your address.
If conviction is exposing something you need to surrender, you can simply write “Jesus, forgive me.”
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that we need Him becomes the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And if you need prayer, say it without shame:
“Pray for me.”
There are people reading this who may understand your battle more than you realize.
And if Christ has already brought you through something you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody.
Your testimony may become another person’s reason to believe that restoration is possible.
Someone else may desperately need to see those words tonight.
Then think about one person whose heart has been drifting.
Not ten people.
One.
The friend who stopped going to church.
The husband quietly struggling.
The wife carrying wounds nobody notices.
The son or daughter questioning everything.
The believer living two lives.
The person who thinks his or her sin has gone too far for Jesus.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It does not.
It does not.
But if biblical truth has strengthened you, sharing it can become a simple act of stewardship.
Your share may put Scripture in front of them at exactly the moment they are wondering whether God still wants them.
There may come a day when Solomon’s warning is no longer something you are reading about.
It may become something you desperately need to remember:
Guard your heart before the thing you love begins pulling your heart away from the One who loves you.
We want this community to be more than another stream of religious content.

We want people continually brought back to Jesus Christ—to Scripture, conviction, repentance, grace, forgiveness, healing, discipleship, spiritual nourishment, and the transforming power of the Gospel.
It does not purchase blessing.
It does not make someone a better Christian.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of stewarding resources for something you believe is helping people encounter biblical truth.
Pray.
Share.
Save the article.
Invite others into the community.
Because the goal was never simply to build an audience.
The goal is that Christ would be known.
That Scripture would be opened.
That wandering hearts would return.
That sinners would repent.
That wounded believers would discover they have not outrun the reach of Christ’s mercy.
That people trapped in darkness would hear the Gospel clearly.
That Jesus—not Solomon, not Gospel Warrior, not any preacher, ministry, author, platform, or personality—would receive the glory.
Solomon had wisdom, wealth, influence, women, palaces, servants, international recognition, and almost everything the human heart imagines will finally make it satisfied.
Yet none of it could safely occupy the place belonging to God.
Neither can your idol.
Neither can mine.
The question was:
Did God approve of Solomon’s many wives?
Scripture’s answer is no.
God had warned Israel’s king not to multiply wives precisely because his heart could turn away.
Solomon multiplied them anyway.
His heart turned.
His idolatry brought judgment.
But even that is not the final word of the Bible.
Because beyond Solomon stands another King.
A better King.
A faithful King.
A sinless King.
A crucified King.
A risen King.
Jesus Christ.
And perhaps the most beautiful difference between Solomon’s story and yours is this:
Your story is not finished simply because you wandered.
You can repent today.
You can come into the light today.
You can surrender the idol today.
You can confess the secret today.
You can return to Christ today.
You can stop defending the thing that is destroying you.
You can fall before the King who already knows the worst chapter and still calls sinners to Himself.
Maybe that is why this story survived for thousands of years.
Not so we could gossip about Solomon’s scandal.
So we could recognize our own hearts.
And then look beyond ourselves toward Jesus.
Solomon teaches us that extraordinary wisdom cannot save the human heart.
Only Christ can.
And when grace reaches the place you thought had ruined your story forever, the scandal no longer gets to write the ending.
The thing that turned your heart away from God does not have to have the final word—Jesus is still calling your heart home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Was Eli Weak, Wicked, or Both? The Terrifying Story of a Good Man Who Wouldn’t Stop What He Knew Was Wrong
paragraphs: Was Eli Weak, Wicked, or Both? The Terrifying Story of a Good Man Who Wouldn’t Stop What He Knew Was Wrong
Eli’s sons were openly corrupt. Eli knew. God warned him. Judgment came anyway. But the most disturbing part of the story is not what Eli’s sons did—it is what Eli loved too much to confront.
There is a kind of sin almost everyone recognizes.
Hophni and Phinehas committed that kind.

They were priests, but Scripture calls them “sons of Belial”—worthless, wicked men who “knew not the LORD” (1 Samuel 2:12, KJV). They abused their priestly position, treated the LORD’s offering with contempt, and slept with women who served at the entrance of the tabernacle.
Their corruption was not difficult to identify.
It was public.
Predatory.
Sacrilegious.
Ugly.
Then there was Eli.
And Eli is more frightening.
Because Eli did not look like Hophni and Phinehas.
He was an old priest. He could recognize the voice of God. When young Samuel kept hearing his name in the night, Eli eventually understood what was happening and told him how to respond:
“Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth.”
Eli could still give someone else good spiritual advice.
That is what makes his story so uncomfortable.
You can know what another person should do with God while refusing to do what God is demanding from you.
You can understand Scripture.
You can recognize God’s activity.
You can occupy a respected spiritual position.
You can even say true things.
And still protect something God has told you to confront.
So was Eli merely weak?
Was he wicked?
Or had weakness, tolerated long enough, become participation in wickedness?
That question reaches much farther than ancient Shiloh.
It reaches the father who knows what is happening in his home but refuses to intervene because confrontation might cost him the relationship.
It reaches the Christian who condemns darkness in society while quietly protecting darkness in private.
It reaches the leader who knows someone under his authority is hurting people but keeps choosing reputation over righteousness.
It reaches the person who keeps calling compromise “love” because obedience would be painful.
And perhaps most painfully...
it reaches the part of us that knows.
Knows what needs to stop.
Knows what God has already said.
Knows what obedience would require.
Yet keeps postponing it.
Eli knew.
That is one of the central facts of the story.
First Samuel tells us that Eli was “very old” when he heard “all that his sons did unto all Israel” (1 Samuel 2:22).
He confronted them verbally:
“Why do ye such things? for I hear of your evil dealings by all this people.”
He even warned them that they were sinning against the LORD.
So Eli was not ignorant.
He was not fooled.
He was not completely morally indifferent.
He knew his sons were wrong, and he said they were wrong.
But apparently saying it was where his courage ended.
And Scripture refuses to let him hide behind the fact that he had spoken to them.
God sent a man of God to Eli with a devastating accusation:
“Wherefore kick ye at my sacrifice and at mine offering... and honourest thy sons above me...?” (1 Samuel 2:29).
Read those words carefully.
God did not merely accuse Eli’s sons.
God confronted Eli.
“Honourest thy sons above me.”
That is the wound at the center of the story.
The Hebrew verb translated “honourest” is כָּבַד — kāḇaḏ, from a root carrying the idea of being heavy, weighty, honored, or given significance.
Eli had given his sons a weight in his heart that belonged to God.
This was not simply a parenting mistake.
It was disordered worship.

When the approval, comfort, protection, relationship, reputation, ambition, appetite, or affection you cannot surrender becomes heavier to you than obedience to God, that thing has begun occupying sacred territory.
And suddenly Eli does not feel ancient anymore.
He feels painfully modern.
How many times have we known something was wrong but whispered:
“I don't want to lose them.”
“I don't want trouble.”
“I don't want people angry with me.”
“I don't want anyone finding out.”
“I'll deal with it later.”
“God understands.”
Sometimes He certainly understands our weakness.
But understanding weakness does not transform disobedience into obedience.
Grace is not God pretending rebellion is harmless.
