Because somewhere tonight, a person is smiling publicly while privately drowning in bitterness.
Somebody is destroying a marriage one sentence at a time.
Somebody is teaching a child to hate themselves without realizing it.
Somebody is gossiping while calling it discernment.
Somebody is preaching grace while refusing to apologize.
And somebody else is sitting alone, believing one cruel sentence spoken twenty years ago is still the truest thing about them.
It isn't.
If you belong to Christ, the ugliest sentence spoken over you does not have final authority.
Jesus does.
And if you were the one who spoke the ugly sentence, your failure does not have to become the final chapter either.
Repent.
Make it right where you can.
Come into the light.
Run to Christ.
There is forgiveness for the liar.
Grace for the gossip.
Mercy for the angry.
Cleansing for the hypocrite.
Restoration for the person whose mouth has burned bridges they now desperately wish they could rebuild.
The warning remains:
Words matter.
Judgment is real.
The heart will be exposed.
But so is the Gospel.
Christ receives repentant sinners.
Christ forgives.
Christ cleanses.
Christ changes hearts.
And when Christ changes the treasure...
eventually the mouth begins telling the story.
Maybe not perfectly.
Maybe with painful failures along the way.
But increasingly, the person who once used words to destroy begins using them to heal.
The mouth that once cursed begins blessing.
The person who lied begins loving truth.
The gossip learns silence.
The arrogant learn gentleness.
The wounded stop bleeding on everybody around them.
And the sinner who once used the name of Jesus carelessly begins whispering that Name with tears because now they understand:
He saved me.
So before you speak today, remember Matthew 12.
Before you post, remember Matthew 12.
Before you forward the screenshot, remember Matthew 12.
Before you answer in anger, remember Matthew 12.
Before you turn someone's weakness into entertainment, remember Matthew 12.
But when you fail...
remember Calvary.
The same Jesus who warned that careless words will be brought into judgment is the Jesus who went willingly to the cross for sinners.
That is why conviction does not have to end in despair.
It can end at the feet of Christ.
"Jesus, forgive me."
"Pray for me."
"No more hiding."
"Christ is still changing me."
Whatever is true.
Let somebody else know they are not the only Christian still learning how deeply the Gospel must reach.
Your words have weight.
So let one of your next words be the name above every name.
Jesus.
And never forget this:
The mouth may reveal the scandal hidden in the heart—but when that heart is surrendered to Christ, grace can rewrite what comes out next.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Can Christians Get Tattoos? The Question Is Deeper Than the Ink
paragraphs: Can Christians Get Tattoos? The Question Is Deeper Than the Ink
Before you put something permanent on your skin, Scripture asks a question far more permanent: Who owns the body beneath it?
The needle touches the skin.
Buzz.
A line appears.
Buzz.
Another line.
Maybe it is a cross.
Maybe the name of someone you loved and buried.
Maybe a verse that carried you through the darkest season of your life.
Maybe it is simply art.
Maybe you already have tattoos, and you clicked this article wondering whether God is disappointed with you.
Or maybe you have been considering one for months while Christians around you seem divided into two camps.
One says, “The Bible clearly forbids tattoos.”
The other laughs and says, “That was Old Testament law. It doesn't matter anymore.”
But what if both answers are too quick?

Because Scripture actually does mention something remarkably close to tattooing. Yet understanding what that passage means for a Christian requires more than pulling one sentence from Leviticus and dropping it into the twenty-first century.
And before this article ends, we are going to arrive at a question much more uncomfortable than:
“Can Christians get tattoos?”
The deeper question is:
Can I honestly place this decision before Jesus Christ and say, “Lord, this belongs completely to You”?
That question changes everything.
The passage almost everyone knows is Leviticus 19:28.
The Hebrew reads:
וְשֶׂרֶט לָנֶפֶשׁ לֹא תִתְּנוּ בִּבְשַׂרְכֶם וּכְתֹבֶת קַעֲקַע לֹא תִתְּנוּ בָּכֶם אֲנִי יְהוָה
Weseret la-nephesh lo tittenu bivsarkhem, ukhetovet qa'aqa lo tittenu bakhem; ani YHWH.
In straightforward English:
“You shall not make gashes in your flesh for the dead, or incise any marks on yourselves: I am the LORD.”

The Hebrew expression כְתֹבֶת קַעֲקַע — ketovet qa'aqa refers to an inscribed or tattoo-like permanent mark. The expression is unusual—qa'aqa occurs only here in the Hebrew Bible—but ancient Jewish interpretation also understood the command as involving a permanent mark made in the flesh with pigment.
So we should not play word games and claim, “Leviticus isn't talking about anything resembling tattoos.”
It is.
But we also shouldn't pretend the surrounding context doesn't exist.
Immediately before the marking prohibition comes this:
וְשֶׂרֶט לָנֶפֶשׁ
A cutting “for the dead.”

Leviticus 19 is calling Israel to holiness—to be distinct as the covenant people belonging to YHWH. The chapter warns against idolatry and incorporates commands concerning worship, sexuality, occult practices, justice, treatment of neighbors, and Israel's separation from pagan practices. Traditional Jewish commentary also connects the cutting mentioned in verse 28 with pagan mourning customs.
That context matters.
But here is where we must be careful.
Some Christians conclude that because pagan mourning and idolatrous customs form part of the historical setting, therefore every modern tattoo is automatically permissible.
That conclusion goes beyond what the text proves.
Others conclude that Leviticus 19:28 can simply be transferred unchanged into the new covenant as an absolute command forbidding every Christian tattoo.
That requires an argument too.
Christians do not approach the Mosaic covenant as though Christ never came.

Jesus fulfilled the Law. The apostles wrestled directly with what obedience looks like for Gentile believers. The New Testament does not simply place Gentile Christians under Israel's entire covenantal law code.
And interestingly, the New Testament never gives the church a command saying, “You shall never receive a tattoo.”
That is important.
But please don't stop reading there.
Because “the New Testament doesn't explicitly forbid it” is not the same thing as “Jesus therefore approves of whatever I want.”
Christian freedom was never intended to become Christian self-rule.
The Gospel does something far more radical.
It changes the question from:
“Is this technically allowed?”
to:
“Does this body belong to me?”
Paul writes to the Corinthians:
ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίου πνεύματός ἐστιν...
“Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you...?”
Then comes the devastating conclusion:
“You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.”
—1 Corinthians 6:19–20
Now context matters here too.
Paul is addressing sexual immorality. We should not dishonestly turn this passage into “Paul's tattoo verse.” It isn't.
But the theological reality underneath his argument is enormous:
The Christian's body belongs to Christ.
You were bought.
There is Calvary language hiding inside that sentence.
Bought with what price?
Not silver.
Not gold.
Not religious performance.
Blood.
The body you are thinking about marking belongs to the Savior whose body was pierced to redeem you.
Suddenly the conversation feels different, doesn't it?
This is no longer merely:
“Can I?”
It becomes:
“Jesus, what do You want?”
And that is where some of us become uncomfortable.
Because sometimes we are not looking for God's will.
We are looking for biblical permission for a decision we already made.
We ask ten friends until the eleventh finally tells us what we wanted to hear.
We search sermons.
Scroll videos.
Read comment sections.
Find the most permissive interpretation possible.
Then call the result “peace.”
But peace and permission are not always the same thing.
And conviction is not legalism merely because it tells us “no.”
There may be Christians who, after prayer, Scripture, wise counsel, examination of motive, and a clear conscience, conclude that receiving a particular tattoo is not inherently sinful.
There may be other Christians whose conscience will not permit it.
Romans 14 gives us an important principle for disputed matters.
Paul writes:
πᾶν δὲ ὃ οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως ἁμαρτία ἐστίν
pan de ho ouk ek pisteōs hamartia estin.
“Whatever is not from faith is sin.”

In Romans 14, Paul is specifically discussing disputed questions concerning food and observance—not tattoos. We should respect that context. Yet his principle concerning acting against conscience before God is deeply relevant: if you cannot proceed in faith before the Lord, bulldozing your conscience is spiritually dangerous.
So if something inside you keeps whispering,
“Don't do this,”
don't silence that voice merely because another Christian says you are free.
Your brother's conscience cannot replace yours.
Your pastor's body isn't yours.
A Christian influencer will not stand before Christ for your motives.
You will.
But there is another side to this conversation that the church desperately needs to hear.
Maybe you already have tattoos.
Maybe some were done before you knew Christ.
Maybe your arms carry evidence of a life you would never choose again.
A gang symbol.
An occult symbol.
An ex-lover's name.
Something obscene.
Something violent.
Something connected to addiction.
Something from the person you were before Jesus found you.
And perhaps every time you enter church, you pull your sleeves down.
Because Christians stare.
And you wonder whether Jesus does too.
Listen carefully.
Ink is not stronger than blood.
The blood of Jesus Christ does not cleanse only unmarked skin.
The Gospel is not cosmetic restoration.
It is resurrection.
When Christ saves a sinner, He does not merely improve the appearance of the old life. Scripture says that anyone in Christ is a new creation. The old has passed away; the new has come.
Your tattoos may tell where you have been.
They do not have the authority to determine where Christ is taking you.
Maybe there are scars underneath them.
Maybe somebody hurt you.
Maybe you hurt yourself.
Maybe you tattooed something because you desperately needed your pain to become visible.
Maybe the ink was your way of saying:
“I survived.”
Jesus sees deeper than the ink.
He sees the night nobody knows about.
He sees the bathroom floor.
The funeral.
The betrayal.
The addiction.
The father who left.
The marriage that collapsed.
The secret shame.
The prayers you thought Heaven ignored.
And He does not stand at a distance asking you to make yourself presentable before approaching Him.
Christ came for sinners.
He touched lepers.
He ate with people respectable religion despised.
He welcomed the broken.
And then He carried sin to a Roman cross.
That is Christianity.
Not good people becoming slightly better.
Dead people being made alive through Jesus Christ.
So no—having tattoos does not put you beyond God's grace.
A tattoo cannot separate a repentant sinner from the saving mercy of Christ.
But grace also does not mean that everything we desire should automatically receive God's blessing.
Jesus loves us too much to merely endorse us.
He transforms us.
That means the Christian considering a tattoo should ask questions that reach much deeper than whether a needle is involved.
Why do I want this?
What am I trying to communicate?
Am I trying to provoke someone?
Am I chasing approval?
Am I building an identity around appearance?
Is the imagery consistent with holiness?
Could this unnecessarily wound another believer's conscience?
Could it damage my witness in the particular culture or ministry where God has placed me?
Am I honoring legitimate responsibilities and stewardship?
Have I prayed about this honestly—or only prayed that God would agree with me?
Could I thank Jesus while doing it?
And perhaps most revealing of all:
If Jesus told me no, would I still want Jesus more than I want the tattoo?
There it is.
That is the question beneath the question.
Because the greatest idol in this discussion may not be ink.
It may be self.
“My body.”
“My choice.”
“My expression.”
“My identity.”
“My freedom.”
But Christianity begins with another sentence:
Jesus is Lord.
Paul gives believers an astonishingly comprehensive rule:
εἴτε οὖν ἐσθίετε εἴτε πίνετε εἴτε τι ποιεῖτε, πάντα εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ ποιεῖτε.
Eite oun esthiete eite pinete eite ti poieite, panta eis doxan Theou poieite.
“So whether you eat or drink or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.”
—1 Corinthians 10:31
Notice how ordinary Paul's examples are.
Eating.
Drinking.
Whatever you do.
The Greek πάντα εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ — panta eis doxan Theou drives everything toward one destination:
the glory of God.

And the surrounding discussion again concerns disputed practices—particularly food associated with idols, conscience, freedom, and concern for others. Paul refuses both legalistic simplification and selfish freedom. Christian liberty is exercised under God's glory and love for one's neighbor.
That gives us a better Christian framework for tattoos.
Not panic.
Not condemnation.
Not rebellion disguised as freedom.
Not legalism disguised as holiness.
Surrender.
Can Christians get tattoos?

Scripture explicitly prohibited Israel from receiving the kind of permanent bodily marking described in Leviticus 19:28, within a chapter calling God's covenant people away from pagan practices and toward holiness. Christians must take that passage seriously rather than pretending it doesn't exist.

At the same time, the New Testament does not explicitly repeat a universal prohibition against tattoos for the church, and Christians disagree about precisely how Leviticus 19:28 applies under the new covenant.
Therefore we should be cautious about declaring every modern tattoo automatically sinful when the New Testament does not explicitly make that declaration.
But we should be equally cautious about declaring every tattoo harmless merely because we cannot find a New Testament verse containing the English word tattoo.
A tattoo honoring Satan is obviously incompatible with allegiance to Christ.
An obscene tattoo is not sanctified by calling it artistic expression.
A tattoo obtained specifically to glorify sin, hatred, sexual immorality, occultism, violence, or rebellion cannot be defended merely by shouting “Christian liberty.”
And even something morally neutral may become wrong for a particular believer when pursued against conscience, from sinful motives, irresponsibly, or without love.
So perhaps you came here wanting a yes or no.
Instead, Scripture places something heavier in your hands.
A mirror.
Not:
“How close can I get to sin without technically crossing the line?”
But:
“How completely can my life belong to Jesus?”
That changes what holiness feels like.
Holiness stops being God stealing your freedom.
Holiness becomes Christ freeing you from the exhausting need to belong to yourself.
You belong to Someone better.
And maybe that is the word somebody with old tattoos desperately needed today.
You belong to Jesus now.
Your past may still be visible.
Grace can make it testify.
Imagine someone noticing an old tattoo and asking what it means.
You could hide.
Or perhaps one day you will say:
“That belonged to an older chapter of my life.”
Then tell them about Jesus.
Tell them who you were.
Tell them what He rescued you from.
Tell them about the addiction He broke.
The shame He forgave.
The pride He confronted.
The wounds He is still healing.
The person you used to be.
The Savior you now belong to.
Suddenly the mark that once represented rebellion becomes the doorway through which someone hears about redemption.
That does not make the old sin good.
It makes grace astonishing.
Joseph could look at what his brothers meant for evil and recognize that God brought good through it.
Paul could remember persecuting Christians while spending the rest of his life proclaiming the Christ he once opposed.
Peter could remember denying Jesus beside a charcoal fire and later spend his life preaching His name.
The Gospel does not need a spotless history to write a holy future.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to this truth:
Maybe your scandal is visible on your arm.
Maybe yours is hidden where nobody can see it.
Do not become proud because your skin is clean if your heart is filthy.
And do not believe you are disqualified because your skin tells a story of the person you used to be.
Jesus confronted religious people who looked clean outside while corruption remained within.
God has always been after something deeper than appearances.
The heart.
So before asking what should be written on your skin, ask what God is writing upon your heart.
Before displaying a Bible verse on your arm, ask whether that Bible verse is ruling your life.
Before tattooing a cross across your chest, ask whether you have taken up your cross to follow Christ.

Before permanently writing the name Jesus on your body, ask whether Jesus has authority over your money, sexuality, relationships, entertainment, bitterness, ambitions, habits, phone, secret life, and future.
Because Christianity is not branding.
It is surrender.
And if you are reading this with conviction tightening around your heart, maybe the Holy Spirit isn't primarily talking to you about tattoos at all.
Maybe He is touching something deeper.
Something hidden.
Something you keep defending.
Something you already know needs to be surrendered.
Don't run.
The hands calling you home still carry scars.
Jesus was pierced too.
Not with decorative ink.
With nails.
For you.
He carried our sins in His body on the tree so that sinners could die to sin and live to righteousness.
That is the center of this entire conversation.
Not tattoos.
Christ.
Not skin.
The heart.
Not merely rules.
Redemption.
If you have never truly surrendered yourself to Jesus Christ, this is bigger than deciding whether to get tattooed.
You need reconciliation with God.

Sin has separated humanity from Him. Religious appearance cannot repair that separation. Good behavior cannot erase guilt. Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, died for sinners and rose again. Forgiveness is received through repentance and faith in Him.
Come to Christ.
Not when you have cleaned yourself up.
Now.
Bring Him the rebellion.
The shame.
The secrets.
The regrets.
The body.
The soul.
Everything.
And if you already follow Jesus but this exposed an area you have been refusing to surrender, be honest before Him.
You don't need to perform for the comment section.
But you also don't have to hide.
Come back to the Scriptures. Pray through them slowly.

Someone in your circle may have spent years believing their appearance made them unwelcome to Jesus. Someone else may be using “freedom” to silence genuine conviction. Either person may need this today.
God's glory cannot be purchased.
What you can do is turn your resources, influence, and opportunities toward serving Christ.
Because eventually every tattoo fades.
Every body ages.
Every mirror changes.
Every trend disappears.
But there is one question that reaches beyond the grave:
Did I belong to Jesus?
So whether you have untouched skin or a body covered in ink, don't spend your life obsessing over the canvas while neglecting the soul.
Give Christ both.
Your skin may carry yesterday's story, but only Jesus has the authority to write your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A Servant Prayed for a Sign Beside a Well. Before He Finished Praying, She Appeared.
paragraphs: A Servant Prayed for a Sign Beside a Well. Before He Finished Praying, She Appeared.
Isaac and Rebekah, the prayer God was already answering, and the terrifying beauty of trusting Him when you cannot see what He is arranging.
He was still praying.
That is the detail I cannot get past.
Not the camels.
Not the jewelry.
Not even the young woman walking toward the well with a jar resting on her shoulder.
The prayer.
Because Genesis does not say Abraham's servant prayed, went home, waited three months, and eventually discovered that God had heard him.
It says something far more breathtaking.
The Hebrew of Genesis 24:15 reads:
וַיְהִי־הוּא טֶרֶם כִּלָּה לְדַבֵּר וְהִנֵּה רִבְקָה יֹצֵאת
Vayehi-hu terem killah ledabber, vehinneh Rivqah yotzet...
“And it came to pass, before he had finished speaking, behold, Rebekah came out...”
Before he finished.
Read that again slowly.
Before he finished.
The servant was still forming words while the answer to those words was already walking toward him.
He did not know her name.
He did not know her family.
He did not know whether she would stop.
He could not see what God had been arranging beyond the horizon of his understanding.
All he knew was that Abraham had sent him on what must have felt like an enormous assignment: travel back toward Abraham's relatives and find a wife for Isaac.
Not just anybody.
The woman who would become Isaac's wife would enter the covenant family through which God's promises to Abraham would continue.
And the servant understood something that many of us learn only after exhausting ourselves:
Some assignments are too large for human cleverness.
So beside a well, far from home, he prayed.
“LORD, God of my master Abraham...”

He asked God to show chesed—חֶסֶד—steadfast kindness toward Abraham. Then he proposed an extraordinary test of character: when he asked a young woman for water, the right woman would not merely give him a drink. She would voluntarily offer water to his camels as well. Genesis explicitly presents this as the servant's requested confirmation concerning the woman God had appointed for Isaac.
Then...
before he finished praying...
a woman appeared.
Her name was Rebekah.
And perhaps you already know this story so well that you are tempted to hurry through it.
Don't.
Because somewhere reading this is a person who has been praying for something that still has no visible answer.
You have prayed until your vocabulary became smaller.
At first your prayers were long.
Detailed.
Confident.
Then months passed.
Maybe years.
And now sometimes all you can manage is:
“Lord... please.”
Maybe you are praying for your marriage.
Your child.
Your family.
Direction.
Provision.
Restoration.
A prodigal who seems determined to keep running.
Freedom from something you are ashamed to admit still has a grip on you.
Maybe you are asking God whether the door should open or close.
Maybe everyone around you thinks you are doing fine, while privately you have whispered:
“God, I need You to show me that You still see me.”
Genesis 24 does not promise that every prayer will receive an immediate answer.
It does not teach us to manufacture signs, manipulate God, or turn circumstances into a superstitious code.
God is sovereign. His wisdom is higher than ours. Biblical prayer is not a technique for forcing heaven to obey our preferences.
But Genesis 24 does reveal something precious:
God can be working beyond your sight long before His answer enters your field of vision.
Think about it.
For Rebekah to appear while the servant was still speaking, she had to begin moving before he finished praying.
Her steps were already happening while his words were still happening.
The jar was already on her shoulder.
She was already approaching the place where his prayer and her ordinary day would collide.
The servant experienced the answer suddenly.
God did not begin being sovereign suddenly.
There is a difference.
And somebody needs that difference tonight.
Because you have mistaken “I cannot see God working” for “God is not working.”
Those are not the same sentence.
Faith does not mean pretending you know what God has not revealed. Faith means trusting the God who has revealed Himself even when you do not know what He is doing.
Rebekah arrives.
The servant runs toward her and asks for a little water.
She answers:
“Drink, my lord.”
And then she does exactly what he had prayed about.

She offers to draw water for the camels too. Genesis emphasizes her haste: she quickly empties her jar, runs back to the well, and keeps drawing until the camels have finished. The narrative itself highlights her generosity and hospitality.
Do not miss this.
Rebekah did not wake up that morning knowing she was walking into Genesis 24.
To her, this may have looked like another trip for water.
Another ordinary responsibility.
Another jar.
Another walk.
Another evening.
But heaven can hide enormous purposes inside ordinary obedience.
She did not need a platform.
She needed a pitcher.
She did not need to know the entire plan.
She simply needed to be the kind of woman who saw a thirsty stranger and served generously.
We spend so much time asking God for the spectacular that sometimes we underestimate the holiness of the ordinary.
The phone call you felt prompted to make.
The person you forgave.
The temptation you refused.
The meal you brought.
The truth you told when lying would have been easier.
The stranger you treated with dignity.
The prayer nobody heard.
The small obedience nobody applauded.
What if some of the most important moments of your life will not announce themselves as important?
Rebekah was carrying water.
God was carrying history.
And while she served, the servant watched her silently.

Genesis 24:21 says he observed her, waiting to learn whether the LORD had made his journey successful. Even after an astonishing apparent answer, he did not immediately explode into presumptuous certainty. He watched. He waited. More had to become clear.
There is wisdom there too.
Not everything that resembles an answer is automatically God's answer.
Discernment matters.
Scripture matters.
Character matters.
Truth matters.
God's providence will never give you permission to contradict God's revealed Word.
We should never use “God told me” as spiritual camouflage for something Scripture calls sin.
And this story is especially dangerous if we reduce it to a formula for finding a spouse.
“Ask God for a sign and the next attractive person who appears is your soulmate.”
No.
Genesis 24 is narrative, not a romantic fortune-telling technique.

This is a specific moment within the unfolding history of God's covenant promise to Abraham. The servant's prayer occurs within an assignment Abraham had already given him, and the eventual confirmation includes Rebekah's family connection, her character, her willingness, and the recognition by her household that the matter had come from the LORD.
And that makes what happens next even more beautiful.
The servant discovers who Rebekah is.
Then he bows.
Before the romance reaches Isaac, worship reaches God.
Genesis 24:26 says:
וַיִּקֹּד הָאִישׁ וַיִּשְׁתַּחוּ לַיהוָה
The man bowed and worshiped the LORD.
Then he declares that God has not abandoned His חַסְדּוֹ וַאֲמִתּוֹ — chasdo va'amitto, His steadfast kindness and faithfulness toward Abraham.
Notice what the servant does when the door opens.
He does not worship the door.
He worships God.
That will preach to a generation obsessed with blessings.
We pray for the relationship.
The promotion.
The healing.
The opportunity.
The breakthrough.
The provision.
Then when it arrives, there is a subtle temptation to become more fascinated with the gift than the Giver.
But the servant's knees hit the ground.
Because answered prayer should produce worship, not entitlement.
Maybe the greatest danger is not that God never gives us what we ask for.
Maybe sometimes the danger is receiving it...
and forgetting Him.
Rebekah eventually faces a decision of her own.
Her family asks whether she will go with this man.
Genesis preserves her answer with almost shocking simplicity:
אֵלֵךְ — Elekh.
“I will go.”
Two words in English.
One Hebrew word.
A life surrendered into uncertainty.
She had not built a life with Isaac.
She had not even met him.
She was being asked to leave what was familiar and travel toward a future she could not yet see.
And she said:
Elekh.
I will go.
There are moments when faith sounds like a sermon.
And there are moments when faith is only one trembling sentence.
“I will go.”
“I forgive.”
“I surrender.”
“I confess.”
“I'll obey.”
“Jesus, save me.”
Maybe your next act of faith does not need to sound impressive.
Maybe it just needs to be real.
Because following God has always involved trusting Him beyond the edge of what we can see.
But there is something else in this story that hurts before it heals.
Isaac.
While the servant has been traveling...
while Rebekah has been drawing water...
while families have been talking...
Isaac has his own story.
His mother Sarah has died.
Genesis 23 records her death before this journey begins.
Then, at the end of Genesis 24, Isaac walks in the field toward evening and sees camels approaching.
Rebekah sees him.
He receives her as his wife.
And Scripture says:
וַיֶּאֱהָבֶהָ — vayye'ehaveha
“and he loved her.”
Then comes the line people rush past:
וַיִּנָּחֵם יִצְחָק אַחֲרֵי אִמּוֹ
Isaac was comforted after his mother.
There was grief in the love story.
An empty tent before a bride entered it.
A son carrying the absence of his mother.
A family moving forward while still remembering what had been lost.
The Bible is painfully human like that.
It does not pretend that a new blessing erases an old wound.
Rebekah did not make Sarah unimportant.
Love did not rewrite history by pretending grief never happened.
But God brought comfort into a place that had known loss.
And perhaps that is where this story finally reaches into your chest.
Because maybe you are not waiting beside the well.
Maybe you are Isaac in the field.
You lost something.
Someone.
A relationship.
A season.
A dream.
A version of yourself you thought would survive.
You have learned how to function around an empty space.
And you wonder whether joy would somehow betray what you lost.
Listen carefully:
God's comfort does not require you to pretend the wound never existed.
The God of Scripture meets real people inside real grief.
And the greater story of Scripture tells us that grief, sin, death, and brokenness do not receive the final word.
That is where Isaac and Rebekah's story must ultimately push the Christian reader beyond Isaac and Rebekah.
Because Genesis is moving somewhere.
The covenant promise is moving somewhere.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Israel.
And ultimately, through the unfolding biblical story, toward Jesus Christ.
The greatest love story in Scripture is not ultimately a man finding a woman beside a well.
It is the holy God pursuing sinners who could never rescue themselves.
We were not Rebekah impressing heaven with our generosity.
We were sinners in need of mercy.
We had rebelled.
Hidden.
Compromised.
Lusted.
Lied.
Hated.
Envied.
Worshiped ourselves.
Promised God we would stop and then returned to the same chains.
Some of us became skilled at looking Christian while secretly dying.
We knew the songs.
We knew when to say “Amen.”
We knew what verse to post.
But behind the screen...
behind the smile...
behind the Sunday clothes...
there were things we hoped nobody would ever discover.
And God already knew.
That is the scandal.
The Gospel does not begin with good people needing inspiration.
It begins with sinners needing salvation.
And God did not answer that need by sending advice.
He sent His Son.
Jesus Christ lived without sin, went willingly to the cross, bore sin, died, was buried, and rose again.
Grace is not God pretending your sin does not matter.
The cross proves it matters more terribly than we want to admit.
Grace is God providing in Christ what guilty people could never provide for themselves.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new heart.
A new life.
Not because sin was cheap.
Because Christ paid dearly.
This is why repentance is not religious self-hatred.
It is coming out of hiding.
It is agreeing with God about our sin and turning toward the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
Maybe you clicked this because the title sounded romantic.
Maybe God used a love story to bring you somewhere much more personal.
What are you hiding?
What keeps returning when nobody is watching?
What have you renamed so you would not have to repent of it?
What relationship has become an idol?
What bitterness have you protected?
What secret appetite has slowly become your master?
What if the prayer you most desperately need tonight is not:
“Lord, send me my Rebekah.”
What if it is:
“Jesus, take all of me.”
Because the greatest answer God can give you is not another human being.
It is Himself.
A spouse cannot carry the weight of being your savior.
Marriage cannot forgive your sins.
Romance cannot resurrect your soul.
Only Christ saves.
Be honest before God.
You do not owe strangers the private details of your struggle. But sometimes three honest words are the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.
And if someone comes to mind while reading this, do not just think about them.
Send this to them.
And there is more than content behind this mission.
Because there may come a night when heaven feels silent and you will need to remember the servant standing beside that well.
He was praying.
Rebekah was walking.
He was speaking.
God was already working.
But remember this carefully: Genesis 24 is not a promise that every unanswered prayer has the exact answer you desire already walking toward you.
Sometimes God's answer is yes.
Sometimes no.
Sometimes wait.
Sometimes His providence takes us somewhere we never would have chosen.
Christian hope is not confidence that God will obey our script.
Christian hope is confidence that God remains faithful when we cannot read His script.
The servant could not see Rebekah until she appeared.
Rebekah could not see Isaac when she said, “I will go.”
Isaac could not see the journey taking place while he carried his grief.
Each person saw only part of the road.
God saw the whole road.
And centuries later, we can read the chapter they had to live one sentence at a time.
That may be your life right now.
You are living a sentence and demanding to understand the chapter.
You are standing beside a well asking why.
You are carrying a jar without realizing what ordinary obedience may mean.
You are crossing unfamiliar country wondering whether surrender was a mistake.
You are walking through a field carrying grief.
You see one sentence.
God sees more than you do.
So pray.
Obey what Scripture has made clear.
Refuse to manufacture signs.
Refuse to call sin “God's will.”
Refuse to make an idol out of the answer you want.
Keep walking faithfully.
Keep serving when nobody applauds.
Keep repenting when you fall.
Keep bringing your grief to Christ.
Keep your eyes on Jesus.
And when God answers differently from what you imagined, remember that the purpose of faith was never to make God the servant of your dreams.
The purpose is to know Him.
To trust Him.
To become like Christ.
To glorify Him.
Not because sharing saves you. Jesus saves.
Do it because somebody else may need the truth you almost scrolled past.
And comment something real—not something impressive.
“Jesus, I trust You while I wait.”
Maybe that is your prayer tonight.

Because somewhere between the prayer at the well, the woman carrying the jar, the grieving man in the field, and the God who saw all of them at once, Genesis leaves us with a truth difficult to forget:
You may still be speaking while God is already writing a story you cannot yet see.
And above every lesser story stands the greater one: the Savior who receives sinners, forgives the repentant, restores the broken, and turns histories marked by shame into testimonies of grace.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final sentence when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES THE BIBLE TEACH SOULMATES?
paragraphs:
DOES THE BIBLE TEACH SOULMATES?
The Truth That Could Save You From Waiting for Someone God Never Promised—and Help You Recognize the Love He Actually Designed
Maybe the hardest person to let go of is not the person who left.
Maybe it is the person you were convinced was “the one.”
The one you prayed about.
The one whose arrival felt too perfectly timed to be accidental.
The one who seemed to understand wounds you never explained.
The one whose name somehow found its way into your prayers, your plans, your imagined wedding, your future children, your private conversations with God.
And then…
it ended.
Or perhaps you are still waiting.
Still wondering whether somewhere on this earth there is one specific human being carrying the missing piece of your soul.
Maybe you have whispered the question Christians sometimes feel embarrassed to ask:
“God, where is my soulmate?”
But there is another question we rarely ask.
A more dangerous one.
What if the Bible never promised you a soulmate in the way our culture taught you to believe in one?
And what if discovering that does not make biblical love less romantic…
but infinitely more beautiful?
Because Scripture tells a love story far greater than “two incomplete souls finally finding each other.”
It tells the story of a God who finds sinners.
A Savior who pursues the undeserving.
A Bridegroom who gives Himself for His bride.
And men and women who can love one another deeply—not because another human being becomes their savior, but because Jesus already is.
That distinction can change everything.
The Bible begins the human marriage story with loneliness.
God forms the man from the dust and breathes life into him. Creation unfolds beneath God's declaration of goodness.
Light—good.
Land—good.
Vegetation—good.
Living creatures—good.
Humanity bearing God's image—very good.
Then Genesis 2:18 interrupts the rhythm:
“It is not good that the man should be alone.”
The Hebrew deserves our attention.
God says:
אֶעֱשֶׂה־לּוֹ עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ
'e'eseh-lo ezer kenegdo.
The crucial expression is:
עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ — ezer kenegdo.
It is commonly translated along the lines of “a helper suitable for him” or “a helper corresponding to him.”
But “helper” can sound weaker in modern English than the Hebrew requires.

The noun עֵזֶר (ezer) does not inherently mean servant, assistant, or inferior. Scripture can even use ezer when speaking of God as the help of His people. And כְּנֶגְדּוֹ (kenegdo) carries the sense of one corresponding to him—one matching or suitable to him, standing in meaningful correspondence with him.
Then God creates the woman.
When Adam sees her, Scripture gives us poetry:
“This at last is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”
There is recognition.
Wonder.
Correspondence.
Then Genesis gives us the foundational statement that Jesus Himself would later appeal to when teaching about marriage:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
One flesh.
There is your biblical language.
But notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say, “Every person has one predetermined romantic soulmate somewhere in the world, and your primary task is discovering who that person is.”
The Bible teaches marriage.
The Bible teaches covenant.
The Bible teaches faithfulness.
The Bible teaches wisdom in choosing whom to marry.
The Bible teaches sexual holiness.
The Bible teaches sacrificial love.
The Bible teaches that marriage creates a profound one-flesh union.
But the popular idea that there is exactly one mysteriously predetermined romantic person whom you must locate or else forever miss God's true plan is not a doctrine Scripture explicitly teaches.
That matters.
Because sometimes we take a beautiful biblical truth—marriage—and quietly attach an unbiblical burden to it:
“If I choose the wrong person, I will miss the one person God created for me.”
And suddenly dating becomes terror.
Every coincidence becomes prophecy.
Every feeling becomes revelation.
Every attraction becomes a “sign.”
Every breakup becomes an existential crisis.
And every lonely season starts feeling like evidence that God forgot your address.
But listen carefully.
God is sovereign.
God can providentially bring two people together.
God can answer prayers concerning marriage.
God can guide His children through Scripture, wisdom, prayer, circumstances, and godly counsel.
There are relationships whose stories make you stand back and marvel at Providence.
But God's sovereignty is not permission to invent promises He never made.
Consider something Paul says that is almost startlingly ordinary.
Speaking about a widow, he writes in 1 Corinthians 7:39:
ἐλευθέρα ἐστὶν ᾧ θέλει γαμηθῆναι, μόνον ἐν Κυρίῳ
eleuthera estin hō thelei gamēthēnai, monon en Kyriō.
In straightforward terms, she is free to marry whom she wishes—only in the Lord.
The Greek text really does contain ᾧ θέλει—“whom she wishes”—followed by the decisive Christian qualification μόνον ἐν Κυρίῳ, “only in the Lord.”
Think about what that does to the panic.
Paul does not say:
“Find the one hidden person heaven assigned to you before it is too late.”
He gives meaningful freedom under the lordship of Christ.
That does not mean every Christian is automatically a wise marriage partner.
Far from it.
Character matters.
Doctrine matters.
Wisdom matters.
Spiritual maturity matters.
How someone handles anger matters.
How someone treats people who cannot benefit them matters.
Whether they repent matters.
Whether they tell the truth when lying would be easier matters.
Whether their profession of Christianity is producing recognizable fruit matters.
Whether the two of you can pursue Christ faithfully together matters.
Marriage is too serious to reduce to butterflies.
And perhaps somebody reading this desperately needed that sentence.
Butterflies cannot carry a covenant.
Chemistry cannot repent for you.
Attraction cannot forgive for you.
Compatibility cannot crucify selfishness.
A spectacular first date cannot guarantee faithfulness twenty years later.
And saying “God told me you're my soulmate” cannot transform an unhealthy relationship into a holy one.
Sometimes Christians spiritualize obsession.
Sometimes we call anxiety “discernment.”
Sometimes we call chemistry “confirmation.”
Sometimes we call possessiveness “fighting for love.”
Sometimes we call an inability to let somebody go “God won't let me forget them.”
And sometimes the person we are begging God to return is the very person we need to surrender to Him.
That hurts.
Because when a relationship ends, you are not merely grieving what happened.
You may be grieving what could have happened.
The wedding that existed only in your imagination.
The house you mentally furnished.
The children whose names you discussed.
The Christmas mornings you pictured.
The prayers you thought were being answered.
The future version of yourself who was supposed to be standing beside that person.
That grief is real.
But grief is not proof that you lost your “one chance” at love.
And losing someone does not mean you have lost God's ability to lead your life.
Maybe you were betrayed.
Maybe you were abandoned.
Maybe you ignored warning signs because you were terrified that walking away meant throwing away your soulmate.
Maybe someone used spiritual language to keep you attached:
“God told me we're supposed to be together.”
“We're meant for each other.”
“You can't walk away from what God ordained.”
Be careful.
Invoking God's name does not turn manipulation into prophecy.
No romantic partner gets to occupy the throne belonging to Christ.
And no human relationship deserves unquestioning allegiance simply because someone stamped the words “God told me” across it.
Biblical marriage is extraordinarily sacred precisely because it points beyond itself.
When Jesus speaks about marriage in Matthew 19, He returns to Genesis and the one-flesh reality. Marriage is covenantal, serious, and not something to treat casually.
And when Paul speaks of marriage in Ephesians 5, the horizon becomes even larger.
A husband is called to love his wife as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
Then Paul reaches back to Genesis:
“The two shall become one flesh.”
And immediately says:
“This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.”
There it is.
The deepest Christian meaning of marriage does not terminate on romance.
Marriage points beyond husband and wife.
It points toward Jesus Christ.
Human marriage is a sign.
Christ is the destination.
And this is where the soulmate fantasy can quietly become spiritually dangerous.
If you believe another person exists to complete you, you may eventually demand from them what only Christ can provide.
You will need them to make you secure.
Need them to make you whole.
Need them to erase your loneliness.
Need them to validate your worth.
Need them never to disappoint you.
Need them to heal wounds they did not create.
Need them to become emotionally omnipresent.
But no husband can bear the weight of being God.
No wife can bear the weight of being God.
No boyfriend.
No girlfriend.
No fiancé.
No future spouse.
Put a human being on the throne of your heart and eventually either you will crush them beneath your expectations…
or their humanity will crush your illusion.
Jesus does something better.
He does not send another broken human being to become your Messiah.
He becomes your Messiah Himself.
This is why singleness is not Christianity's waiting room.
Read 1 Corinthians 7 carefully and you discover something astonishing: Paul can speak positively about singleness precisely because a person's ultimate completeness is not dependent upon marriage.
That would make little sense if every human being were spiritually incomplete until finding a romantic counterpart.
Jesus Himself lived the fullest human life ever lived without marrying.
That fact alone should destroy the cruel idea that an unmarried Christian is somehow only half alive.
You are not half a person waiting for your other half.
If you belong to Christ, your identity does not begin on your wedding day.
Your purpose does not begin when somebody chooses you.
Your worth does not rise when somebody puts a ring on your finger.
Your calling does not remain suspended until your relationship status changes.
Before anyone ever calls you husband or wife, the Gospel invites you to be able to say:
I belong to Jesus.
And perhaps this is where someone reading needs to stop pretending.
You have been asking God for a relationship when your deepest hunger is actually for reassurance that you are lovable.
You have been scrolling through engagement announcements wondering why everybody else's life seems to be moving while yours feels frozen.
You smile.
You congratulate them.
You type the heart emoji.
Then the screen goes dark…
and something inside you whispers:
“What is wrong with me?”
Nothing about another person's wedding is evidence that God has abandoned you.
Your singleness is not proof of divine rejection.
Your breakup is not proof that your story is ruined.
Your divorce does not place you beyond redemption.
Your widowhood does not mean your usefulness ended at a graveside.
Your romantic history does not outrank the blood of Jesus.
And your worst relationship decision does not get the final sentence.
That belongs to Christ.
This is the Gospel.
Not that God guarantees everyone a fairytale romance.
But that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
The scandal of Christianity is not that good people eventually find their perfect match.
The scandal is that guilty people can be reconciled to a holy God because the sinless Son of God bore their sin.
We betrayed.
Christ remained faithful.
We wandered.
Christ came looking.
We sinned.
Christ carried the cross.
We deserved judgment.
Christ offered mercy.
We brought shame.
He brought grace.
We brought graves.
He walked out of one.
That is the love story beneath every Christian love story.
And if God gives you marriage, receive it as a gift—not as a god.
Love your spouse fiercely.
Honor your covenant.
Be faithful when feelings fluctuate.
Repent quickly.
Forgive biblically.
Pray together.
Laugh together.
Carry burdens together.
Grow old together if God gives you those years.
Let your marriage become a small earthly window through which people catch a glimpse of Christ's covenant faithfulness.
But never ask your spouse to become Jesus.
And if you are single, do not surrender your discernment because you are tired of waiting.
Loneliness can make red flags look pink.
Desperation can make attention feel like love.
Chemistry can make compromise feel reasonable.
And the fear of being alone can make almost anyone look like an answered prayer.
You do not need somebody who merely gives you goosebumps when they text.
Look for character.
Look for humility.
Look for repentance.
Look for faithfulness.
Look for someone whose life makes following Jesus easier rather than continually dragging your conscience into negotiations.
And become that kind of person yourself.
Stop asking only:
“Are they the one?”
Start asking:
“Can we faithfully follow the One together?”
That question changes everything.
Because Christianity's great romance is not ultimately about finding a soulmate.
It is about being found by Christ.

Perhaps someday God will place someone beside you and years later you will look across a kitchen table—past bills, wrinkles, arguments survived, prayers answered, funerals attended, children raised, disappointments endured, forgiveness given—and realize something far more beautiful than the fantasy of effortless soulmates happened.
You became faithful.
You chose one another again and again under Christ.
You learned to repent.
You learned to forgive.
You discovered that covenant love can become deeper than the emotional fireworks with which it began.
And perhaps that is more romantic than destiny.
Because biblical love is not powerful merely because two people “were meant to be.”
Biblical love becomes powerful when two imperfect people kneel before a perfect Savior and repeatedly say:
“Jesus, teach us how to love.”
And maybe your story has already gone terribly wrong.
Maybe there was scandal.
Adultery.
Divorce.
Sexual sin.
Manipulation.
An engagement that collapsed.
Years spent with someone you should never have dated.
Perhaps you compromised convictions because you feared losing them.
Perhaps you wounded someone.
Perhaps you were the one who was unfaithful.
Then hear the Gospel clearly.
Grace does not mean sin did not matter.
Grace means sin does not have to write the ending.
Repentance is real.
Forgiveness is real.
Transformation is real.
The cross is real.
The resurrection is real.
Jesus Christ still receives sinners who come to Him.
Your past may explain some of your scars.
It does not have authority to become your savior, your identity, or your final chapter.
From scandal to grace—that is what Jesus does. He rewrites everything.
Not always by restoring the relationship you wanted.
Sometimes His rewriting begins by removing an idol.
Sometimes by exposing deception.
Sometimes through repentance.
Sometimes through reconciliation where reconciliation is biblically possible and wise.
Sometimes through learning to walk faithfully after something cannot be restored to what it once was.
But always by drawing sinners away from self-rule and toward Himself.
So does the Bible teach soulmates?
Not in the popular sense of one uniquely predetermined romantic person whom you must somehow discover in order to become complete.
Scripture gives us something sturdier.
God's providence.
Human responsibility.
Biblical wisdom.
Marriage covenant.
One-flesh union.
Faithfulness.
Holiness.
Sacrificial love.
And above all…
Christ.
So perhaps the prayer should change.
Instead of only:
“Lord, show me my soulmate…”
maybe pray:

“Lord Jesus, make me Yours. Give me wisdom. Guard me from relationships that pull me away from You. If marriage is Your gift for my life, help me choose faithfully and love sacrificially. If I am waiting, keep loneliness from becoming my master. If my heart has been broken, heal me without letting bitterness own me. If I have sinned, lead me into genuine repentance. And whether married or single, let my life belong completely to You.”
That is a prayer worth praying.
Your honesty may become permission for somebody else to stop pretending too.
If Christ has used these words to expose a lie and point you back toward Him, allowing someone else to encounter that truth can become a simple act of witness.
If you want to support the work and go deeper:
And remember this when your heart starts telling you that your life cannot begin until somebody chooses you:
You were never created to spend your whole life searching for the human being who could complete your soul—you were created to belong to the Christ who gave His life to redeem it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE WAS CAUGHT IN ADULTERY… THEN JESUS SAID SOMETHING NOBODY EXPECTED
paragraphs:
SHE WAS CAUGHT IN ADULTERY… THEN JESUS SAID SOMETHING NOBODY EXPECTED
They dragged her sin into the light expecting Jesus to condemn her. Instead, He exposed an entire crowd—and then spoke words that still confront every person hiding behind shame, religion, secret sin, or a carefully managed reputation.
Imagine hearing your worst sin announced in public.
Not whispered.
Not discovered privately by someone who loves you.
Exposed.
People staring. Religious leaders watching. No opportunity to explain yourself. No time to repair your reputation before everybody decides who you are.
And somewhere in the crowd, someone is already holding a stone.
That is where this story begins.
But before it ends, the woman standing in shame will hear words from Jesus Christ that neither excuse her sin nor leave her imprisoned by it.
And if you have ever done something you desperately wish you could erase…
if you have ever smiled at church while hiding something you hoped nobody would discover…
if you have ever wondered whether Jesus would still want you if everything about you became public…
then don't rush through this story.
Because perhaps the most frightening person in this scene is not the adulterous woman.
Perhaps it is the person who thinks he doesn't need mercy.
John records that Jesus was teaching when the scribes and Pharisees brought before Him a woman caught in adultery.
They did not quietly ask for pastoral counsel.
They put her in the middle.
ἐν μέσῳ.
En mesō.
“In the midst.”
Right there where everybody could see her.
That detail hurts when you allow yourself to feel it.
She wasn't merely confronted.
She was displayed.
Her failure had become a spectacle.
Her shame had become someone else's argument.
They said to Jesus:
“Teacher, this woman has been caught in the act of adultery.”
Then they appealed to Moses and asked what Jesus thought should happen to her.
But John tells us what was really happening:
“This they said to test him, that they might have some charge to bring against him.”
The woman was guilty, but she was also being used.
She was not a soul to them.
She was evidence.
A trap.
A theological weapon with a heartbeat.
And there is another uncomfortable question hanging over the scene.
Adultery requires two people.
Where was the man?
The Mosaic law addressed both parties in adultery; Leviticus 20:10 and Deuteronomy 22:22 speak of judgment involving both the adulterer and the adulteress.
Yet somehow only the woman is standing in the dust.
Only her shame has been dragged into public view.
Only her body has become evidence.
Only her reputation is bleeding in front of the crowd.
Something is wrong with this picture.
And Jesus knows it.
The religious leaders are talking.
The accusation is serious.
The crowd is waiting.
And Jesus…
bends down.
He writes on the ground with His finger.
People have proposed countless explanations for what Jesus wrote, but Scripture does not tell us.
That matters.
We should not pretend certainty where God has not given certainty.
Perhaps that silence itself forces us to keep our attention where John places it—not on deciphering mysterious words in the dust, but on the words Jesus finally speaks aloud.
They keep questioning Him.
They want an answer.
They want judgment.
They want Jesus trapped between mercy and righteousness.
Then Jesus stands.
And says:
“Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her.”
The Greek is piercing:
Ὁ ἀναμάρτητος ὑμῶν πρῶτος ἐπ’ αὐτὴν βαλέτω λίθον.
Ho anamartētos hymōn prōtos ep’ autēn baletō lithon.
The crucial word is ἀναμάρτητος — anamartētos.
“Without sin.”
Jesus is not declaring adultery acceptable.
He is not rewriting God's holiness into sentimental tolerance.
He is exposing the hearts of people eager to execute judgment while standing in need of mercy themselves.
And suddenly the courtroom changes.
The accused woman is no longer the only person being examined.
Everybody is.
That is what happens when Jesus enters the room.
We bring Him someone else's sin.
He reaches ours.
We point.
He sees the hand doing the pointing.
We rehearse someone else's failure.
He sees what happened last night when nobody was watching.
We know the Bible verses that expose them.
Jesus knows the hidden rooms inside us.
The secret messages.
The resentment.
The pornography.
The affair nobody discovered.
The pride disguised as discernment.
The unforgiveness disguised as boundaries.
The greed disguised as ambition.
The gossip disguised as concern.
The spiritual coldness hidden underneath Christian vocabulary.
The private compromise.
The public performance.
The thing you deleted.
The thing you never confessed.
The thing you promised God you would stop.
The thing you hope never becomes your “caught in adultery” moment.
And suddenly the stone feels heavier.
One by one, the accusers leave.
The text says they went away.
And eventually Jesus is left with the woman.
Picture that moment.
The crowd has thinned.
The accusations have gone quiet.
The stones never came.
She is still standing there.
And Jesus asks:
“Woman, where are they? Has no one condemned you?”
She answers:
“No one, Lord.”
Then come the words that have survived centuries because they reveal something breathtaking about the heart of Christ:
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.”
In Greek:
Οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω· πορεύου, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε.
Oude egō se katakrinō; poreuou, kai apo tou nyn mēketi hamartane.
“Neither do I condemn you.”
But Jesus does not stop there.
“From now on sin no more.”
There it is.
Grace and truth in the same breath.
Mercy without pretending sin is harmless.
Holiness without crushing the sinner who needs redemption.
Jesus does not say, “Adultery isn't really a big deal.”
He does not say, “Follow your heart.”
He does not say, “Your truth is all that matters.”
He also does not say, “You are disgusting. You are permanently ruined. You will always be what you did.”
He refuses both lies.
He does not redefine sin.
He calls her out of it.
And He does not reduce her identity to her sin.
He sends her toward a different life.
That is the scandal of grace.
Grace is not God looking at sin and shrugging.
Grace is God doing what sinners could never do for themselves.
And the reason Christians can read the words “Neither do I condemn you” with hope is not because God stopped caring about justice.
It is because the Gospel eventually leads us to a hill outside Jerusalem where justice and mercy meet.
There, Jesus will not merely stand between a guilty person and a stone.
He will stand in the place of sinners beneath judgment.
The sinless One will be condemned.
The innocent One will suffer.
The One who deserved no cross will carry one.
Isaiah had spoken centuries earlier of the suffering servant who would be “pierced for our transgressions” and “crushed for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5).
And the New Testament announces the astonishing exchange:
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” — 2 Corinthians 5:21
This is why grace is not cheap.
Someone paid for it.
This is why forgiveness is not God ignoring evil.
Christ bore judgment for sinners.
This is why repentance is not punishment for receiving grace.
Repentance is the turning of a heart that has encountered grace.
Jesus does not save us so we can comfortably return to the chains from which He came to free us.
He forgives.
Then He transforms.
“Go.”
“Sin no more.”
In other words:
You don't have to die where they exposed you.
You don't have to build your identity around what you did.
You don't have to spend the rest of your life introducing yourself by your worst chapter.
But neither should you call the chains freedom and walk back into the prison.
Come to Christ.
Receive mercy.
Leave the darkness.
That is repentance.
And maybe this is where the story stops being about a woman from long ago and starts becoming painfully personal.
Because some people reading this are carrying stones.
And some are standing in the middle.
Some know exactly what it feels like to be exposed.
Others have become experts at exposing everyone except themselves.
Some have been wounded by Christians who seemed more interested in proving them guilty than helping them find Christ.
Others have used “truth” as permission to be cruel.
Some have used “grace” as permission to remain unchanged.
Jesus permits neither.
Truth without love can become a weapon in sinful hands.
Grace stripped of repentance becomes a counterfeit.
But in Jesus Christ, grace reaches the guilty and truth calls the guilty into freedom.
Maybe you are the one hiding today.
Your family doesn't know.
Your spouse doesn't know.
Your pastor doesn't know.
Your friends see the edited version.
Your Sunday face looks fine.
But when the room gets quiet, you know.
And you have wondered:
If Jesus knew everything, would He still let me come near Him?
He already knows.
That is the part we keep forgetting.
You cannot shock an omniscient Savior with information He already possesses.
You cannot confess something to God and watch Him suddenly discover who you really are.
Psalm 139 describes a God who knows us intimately.
Hebrews 4:13 says that no creature is hidden from His sight.
Yet the Gospel invitation still stands.
Jesus knew what sinners were when He went to the cross.
Romans 5:8 does not say Christ died for us after we successfully cleaned ourselves up.
It says:
“While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
While.
Still.
Sinners.
That word “while” can break a person open.
Not after your perfect streak.
Not after you repaired your image.
Not after you became impressive enough for church people.
Christ died for sinners.
But do not mistake His welcome for permission to remain enslaved.
The same Savior who receives you says:
Come out.
Leave it.
Repent.
Follow Me.
There is something better than hiding.
There is confession.
There is something better than pretending.
There is forgiveness.
There is something better than repeatedly returning to the sin that keeps hollowing you out.
There is freedom in Christ.
First John 1:9 tells believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Read those words carefully.
Not “no consequences.”
Not “sin doesn't matter.”
Not “every lifestyle choice receives God's approval.”
No condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
Your hope is not that you were innocent all along.
Your hope is that Jesus saves guilty people.
That changes everything.
It means Christianity is not fundamentally the story of respectable people congratulating themselves for being better than everybody else.
Christianity is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
The proud need Him.
The sexually broken need Him.
The religious need Him.
The addicted need Him.
The hypocrite needs Him.
The betrayed need Him.
The betrayer needs Him.
The person holding the stone needs Him.
The person trembling in the dirt needs Him.
We all need Him.
And there is an important textual detail serious Bible readers should know.

The account traditionally called the woman caught in adultery, John 7:53–8:11, has a complicated manuscript history. Many of the earliest and most important Greek manuscripts of John do not contain this passage, and some later manuscripts place the account elsewhere. That is why many modern Bible translations mark the passage with brackets or a textual note.
Christians should not be frightened by that fact.
We should be honest about it.
Faith does not require pretending manuscript evidence doesn't exist.

The account was preserved in the Christian textual tradition, but responsible interpretation should acknowledge its disputed location and early manuscript absence rather than claiming a certainty the evidence does not provide.
And crucially, the theological truths illustrated in this beloved account do not stand or fall on this passage alone.
Jesus' mercy toward sinners is everywhere in the Gospels.
His call to repentance is everywhere.
His refusal to approve sin is everywhere.
His compassion toward the disgraced is everywhere.
His death for sinners is central to apostolic preaching.
His resurrection is central to Christianity.
Justification in Christ is taught explicitly elsewhere.
The Gospel does not depend upon hiding a textual footnote.
Truth has nothing to fear from careful reading.
And perhaps that makes the scene even more challenging.
Because whether you identify with the woman or with the crowd, the rest of Scripture leaves you nowhere to hide.
You need grace.
I need grace.
We need Jesus.
So what are you carrying today?
A stone?
Or shame?
If you are carrying a stone, put it down long enough to remember the cross.
If you are carrying shame, bring it to Christ.
Not to a vague spirituality.
Not to self-affirmation.
Not to another attempt at hiding better.
To Jesus.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Seek reconciliation where appropriate.
Accept responsibility where necessary.
Get trustworthy Christian help when you need it.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
And follow Christ.
Maybe your scandal is known by everybody.
Maybe nobody knows yet.
Maybe your deepest wound is something somebody did to you.
Maybe your deepest shame is something you did to somebody else.
The Gospel does not tell us those things are identical.
It tells us Jesus Christ is sufficient for sinners who come to Him and powerful enough to begin making broken people new.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to turn shame into entertainment.
Not to build a community of stone-throwers.
But to keep pointing people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, healing, discipleship, and above all, Jesus Christ.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to write the details publicly.
But you can make a small act of honesty.
And when you see somebody else write those words, don't interrogate them.
Don't speculate.
Don't pick up a stone.
Pray.
There are real people behind those comments.
Real marriages.
Real temptations.
Real wounds.
Real nights of crying.
Real battles nobody sees.
Let this become more than another article people read and forget.
Send it privately to the person who thinks church has no place for somebody with their past.
Send it to the believer drifting back toward an old bondage.
Send it to the person who has been standing spiritually in the dirt, convinced everybody else is holding stones.
But understand this clearly:
You do not glorify God only by financially supporting a ministry. Salvation cannot be bought, and grace is not merchandise.
We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives surrendered to Him. Yet Scripture also teaches cheerful generosity and partnership in Gospel work.
Not to prove your faith.
Not to earn a blessing.
Not because an algorithm is sacred.
Let them encounter Jesus before they encounter another stone.
Because perhaps that is the question this ancient scene leaves trembling in our own generation:
What if the person everyone has reduced to a scandal is standing one encounter with Christ away from a testimony of grace?
The woman entered the scene known by what she had done.
She encountered Jesus.
And the last recorded command she receives points toward a life no longer ruled by the sin that brought her there.
That is the Gospel pattern we must never reverse.
Jesus does not say sin doesn't matter.
Jesus says sin doesn't get the final word over the person who belongs to Him.
The cross tells us sin was serious enough for Christ to die.
The empty tomb tells us death was not powerful enough to keep Him.
And grace tells every repentant sinner:
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
So put down the stone.
Step out of hiding.
Come to Christ.
And when He calls you out of the darkness…
don't crawl back into the grave He came to bring you out of.
Your scandal may explain yesterday—but when Jesus takes hold of your story, your scandal does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT JESUS MEANT BY “DENY YOURSELF” — AND WHY THIS ONE HURTS
paragraphs:
WHAT JESUS MEANT BY “DENY YOURSELF” — AND WHY THIS ONE HURTS
You can sing about Jesus, post about Jesus, defend Jesus, and still spend your entire life protecting the one thing He told you to surrender: yourself.
There is a version of Christianity that almost everyone can tolerate.
Jesus comforts me.
Jesus protects me.
Jesus forgives me.
Jesus blesses me.
Jesus understands me.
And every one of those things can be gloriously true.
But then Jesus says something that feels like a blade passing through every comfortable version of Christianity we have constructed:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.” — Luke 9:23, KJV
Read it again.
Slowly.
Because Jesus did not say, “Improve yourself.”
He did not say, “Discover yourself.”
He did not say, “Protect yourself at all costs.”
He did not even say, “Add Me to your life.”
He said:
Deny yourself.
And this one hurts.
The Greek of Luke 9:23 preserves the force of His words:
“εἴ τις θέλει ὀπίσω μου ἔρχεσθαι ἀρνησάσθω ἑαυτὸν καὶ ἀράτω τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ καθ’ ἡμέραν καὶ ἀκολουθείτω μοι.”
In plain sense:
If anyone desires to come after Me, let him deny himself, take up his cross every day, and follow Me.
That expression translated “deny himself” is ἀρνησάσθω ἑαυτόν — arnēsasthō heauton.
The language carries the idea of denying, disowning, refusing the claim of self.
And suddenly Jesus' words become painfully personal.
Because Christianity is not merely asking whether you believe Jesus exists.
It eventually confronts you with a much more uncomfortable question:
Who gets the final word over your life?
Jesus?
Or you?
That is where discipleship begins to hurt.
You can want Jesus to save you while still desperately wanting yourself to remain king.
You can want forgiveness without surrender.
Heaven without holiness.
Grace without repentance.
Resurrection without crucifixion.
A Savior who rescues you, but never a Lord who contradicts you.
And then Jesus stands in the road.
Not cruelly.
Not angrily.
Not because He hates you.
But because He loves you too much to leave you enslaved to a god who cannot save you.
That god is you.
Think about how deeply self-rule reaches.
“I know what God says, but I want this.”
“I know I should forgive, but they don't deserve it.”
“I know this relationship is pulling me away from Christ, but I can't let it go.”
“I know nobody sees what I'm doing on this screen.”
“I know pride is destroying my marriage, but I'm not apologizing first.”
“I know I should repent, but what will people think?”
“I know Jesus is calling me deeper, but I don't want Christianity to cost me anything.”
That is precisely where these words stop being inspirational.
“Deny yourself.”
Jesus reaches into the throne room of the human heart and touches the chair we have spent our entire lives defending.
Mine.
My body.
My desires.
My reputation.
My plans.
My sexuality.
My money.
My future.
My comfort.
My dreams.
My revenge.
My truth.
My life.
And Jesus does not negotiate for half the throne.
He is Lord.
But there is something essential we must understand, because “deny yourself” has sometimes been twisted into something Jesus never taught.
Jesus was not commanding self-hatred.
He was not telling abused people that abuse is acceptable.
He was not saying your personality must disappear.
He was not commanding you to believe you are worthless.
He was not saying suffering itself makes someone holy.
Biblical self-denial is not believing that you have no value.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
You mattered enough that the Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
The scandal of the Gospel is not that human beings are worthless.
It is that sinners who could never rescue themselves were loved at an unimaginable cost.
Self-denial means surrendering your claim to autonomous lordship.
It means that when your desires collide with Christ, Christ wins.
When your pride collides with Christ, Christ wins.
When culture collides with Christ, Christ wins.
When your plans collide with Christ, Christ wins.
Even when obedience costs something.
Especially then.
And notice what comes next.
“Take up his cross.”
We hear the word cross through two thousand years of Christian imagery.
The first hearers did not.
The Greek word is σταυρός — stauros.
To them, a cross was not jewelry.
It was not wall decoration.
It was not a sentimental metaphor for having a difficult week.
Rome used crucifixion as a brutal instrument of execution and public humiliation.
So imagine standing in that crowd.
Jesus essentially tells people who want to follow Him that discipleship involves such radical allegiance that they must be prepared to lose even their lives.
Then Luke adds two words that make escape nearly impossible:
καθ’ ἡμέραν — kath’ hēmeran.
Daily.
Not once at an emotional altar call.
Not only when worship music makes you cry.
Not only when tragedy scares you back into prayer.
Daily.
That means there may be a cross waiting for you tomorrow morning.
Maybe it looks like deleting the secret conversation.
Maybe telling the truth when lying would protect your reputation.
Maybe forgiving someone while still maintaining wise boundaries.
Maybe admitting:
“I was wrong.”
Maybe walking away from something everyone around you calls normal because Christ calls you somewhere else.
Maybe opening Scripture when your soul would rather scroll.
Maybe praying when heaven feels silent.
Maybe refusing the temptation nobody else would ever discover.
Maybe choosing faithfulness when obedience brings absolutely no applause.
Nobody sees.
Nobody claps.
Nobody posts about it.
But Jesus knows.
And perhaps that is where some of the holiest moments of your life happen.
In rooms where nobody is watching.
When temptation whispers:
Nobody will know.
And your surrendered heart answers:
Jesus will.
That is denying yourself.
But here comes the part that changes everything.
Jesus does not merely say:
“Deny yourself.”
He says:
“Deny yourself... and follow Me.”
There is a Person on the other side of surrender.
Christianity is not self-destruction for self-destruction's sake.
You are relinquishing the throne because Someone infinitely better belongs there.
Jesus Christ.
This is why the Gospel is not fundamentally a program of behavior modification.
The Christian message is not:
Become impressive enough for God to accept you.
It is that sinners cannot save themselves, yet God acts in grace through Jesus Christ.
Christ lived in perfect obedience.
Christ went willingly to the cross.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose.
And salvation is received by grace through faith, producing a life increasingly surrendered to the Lord who saved us.
Paul describes the astonishing reality of union with Christ:
“I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me...” — Galatians 2:20, KJV
The Greek begins:
“Χριστῷ συνεσταύρωμαι...”
Christō synestaurōmai.
“I have been crucified with Christ.”
Then comes one of the most beautiful reversals in Scripture.
The old center is displaced.
Christ lives in me.
This is what self-denial eventually reveals.
Jesus is not trying to make you less alive.
He is rescuing you from the counterfeit life you were destroying yourself trying to preserve.
Remember what Jesus says immediately after His command:
“For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: but whosoever will lose his life for my sake, the same shall save it.” — Luke 9:24, KJV
There is the paradox.
Clench your fists around your life...
and eventually you lose everything.
Open them to Christ...
and discover life you could never manufacture for yourself.
Somebody reading this has been exhausted because you have been trying to keep one hand around Jesus and the other around the thing He keeps asking you to surrender.
And you know exactly what it is.
I don't.
The people around you may not.
But while reading this, something came immediately into your mind.
That habit.
That relationship.
That resentment.
That hidden browser history.
That pride.
That secret compromise.
That obsession with people's approval.
That dream you have decided God must fulfill before you will trust Him.
That identity you refuse to place beneath the authority of Christ.
You keep praying:
“Jesus, why don't I have peace?”
And perhaps the question underneath the question is:
What are you still gripping?
There is a strange misery in trying to follow Jesus while continuously negotiating with His lordship.
You become divided.
One part of you wants holiness.
Another wants the secret.
One part wants Scripture.
Another wants validation.
One part wants Christ.
Another wants control.
You worship on Sunday and resurrect the old throne on Monday.
Then guilt comes.
Then promises.
Then failure.
Then shame.
Then hiding.
Then another Sunday.
And somewhere inside that cycle you begin wondering whether Jesus is tired of you.
Look at the cross before you answer that.
The Christian's hope has never rested on the strength of his grip on Christ.
It rests upon Christ.
The One commanding surrender is also the One who gave Himself for sinners.
Galatians 2:20 does not end with our sacrifice.
Paul speaks of “the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.”
Do you see it?
Before Christ asks you to carry a cross behind Him, He goes to His.
Before your surrender ever became part of the story, His sacrifice stood at the center of salvation.
Jesus does not stand safely at a distance pointing toward suffering.
He walks toward Calvary.
He is betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
And there, the sinless Christ gives Himself for sinners.
Then the grave receives Him.
And the grave cannot keep Him.
That changes the sound of “follow Me.”
Jesus is not leading you into meaningless death.
He is the crucified and risen Lord leading His people through death into life.
Maybe you have fallen badly.
Maybe your Christian story contains chapters you wish could be ripped from the book.
Sexual sin.
Addiction.
Pride.
Hypocrisy.
Anger.
Years wasted.
Promises broken.
Faith neglected.
People wounded.
Maybe you knew better.
That makes the memory hurt even more.
You have whispered:
How could Jesus possibly want me now?
But the Gospel has never been the story of impressive people earning their way toward Jesus.
It is the announcement of grace for sinners.
Repentance means you stop defending what Christ died to save you from.
You bring the darkness into His light.
You confess.
You turn.
You trust Christ.
You stop calling your chains freedom.
And grace does something scandalous.
Grace does not pretend your sin wasn't serious.
Grace reveals how serious it was...
