and then points toward a cross where mercy became unimaginably costly.
This is our story.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Peter knew something about that.
Only moments before Jesus' teaching about self-denial in Mark's account, Peter confessed Jesus as the Christ.
Then Jesus began explaining that He would suffer, be rejected, die, and rise again.
Peter rebuked Him.
Peter wanted Jesus.
But apparently not this road.
Not suffering.
Not a cross.
And isn't that frighteningly relatable?
We want Jesus.
Just not always His road.
We want resurrection power.
But not dying to pride.
We want freedom.
But not confession.
We want restored marriages.
But not humility.
We want holiness.
But not separation from cherished sin.
We want purpose.
But not obedience when purpose becomes painful.
Then Jesus gathers the crowd and disciples and says:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.” — Mark 8:34, KJV
The Greek text reads in part:
“ἀπαρνησάσθω ἑαυτὸν καὶ ἀράτω τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀκολουθείτω μοι.”
Deny himself.
Take up his cross.
Follow Me.
Not admire Me.
Not merely quote Me.
Follow Me.
And Peter would later discover something beautiful.
Failure did not get the final word over him.
The man who once resisted the language of the cross would eventually become a bold witness to the risen Christ.
The disciple who failed spectacularly was restored.
That is what Jesus does.
He does not rewrite our stories by pretending the scandal never happened.
He rewrites them with grace.
Maybe that is why you needed this today.
Not because you need another religious article.
Because somewhere beneath the polished photographs, responsibilities, jokes, church attendance, family obligations, and “I'm okay” answers...
you are tired.
Tired of carrying two masters.
Tired of protecting the very thing killing your peace.
Tired of hiding.
Tired of promising God “tomorrow.”
Tomorrow I'll forgive.
Tomorrow I'll stop.
Tomorrow I'll confess.
Tomorrow I'll come back.
Tomorrow I'll pray.
Tomorrow I'll surrender.
But Jesus said daily.
And today is one of those days.
So perhaps your prayer does not need impressive language.
Maybe it sounds like:
Jesus, I have been trying to follow You without surrendering me.
Forgive me.
I cannot save myself.
I cannot cleanse myself.
I cannot be my own lord and call You Lord at the same time.
Expose what I have protected.
Break what needs breaking.
Heal what needs healing.
Teach me to obey You.
Teach me to take up my cross.
Teach me to follow You when nobody applauds.
I belong to You.
And if you cannot honestly pray all of that yet, start with honesty.
“Jesus, I want to want You more.”
Bring Him the truth.
Christian repentance is not theater.
You don't have to impress the One who already knows everything.
Come into the light.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to describe your private sin publicly.
And if you are exhausted but still fighting to follow Christ:
“I'M STILL FIGHTING.”
Someone else may read your comment tonight and realize they are not the only believer struggling to surrender.
That matters.
Not because every word here is equally important, but because the words of Jesus are.
There may come a morning when the thing you surrendered comes knocking again.
Come back.
Read Luke 9:23–25.
Remember who sits on the throne.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to announce that you think they are sinful.
Not as proof that you are spiritual.
Not to earn favor from God.
Not because clicking “share” makes someone a disciple.
Someone may need to hear that surrender is not the end of their story.
Someone may need to meet the Christ who receives repentant sinners.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has drifted.
Invite the believer who is quietly exhausted.
Invite the person asking questions about Jesus.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who needs truth more than another motivational quote.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who is willing to listen.
And if you want to go deeper while helping this Gospel work continue:
But before you leave this page, there is still one question.
Not for your pastor.
Not for your spouse.
Not for the person you tagged.
For you.
What is Jesus asking you to surrender?
Because eventually every disciple discovers that following Christ costs something.
Pride.
Control.
Approval.
Comfort.
Sin.
Sometimes relationships.
Sometimes plans.
Sometimes dreams we thought God was obligated to fulfill.
But Christianity contains an even greater scandal.
The One asking for your life already gave His for you.
So when Jesus says,
“Deny yourself.”
He is not calling you toward emptiness.
He is calling you away from a throne that was killing you.
When He says,
“Take up your cross.”
He is not promising an easy Christianity.
He is calling you to identify yourself with the crucified King.
And when He says,
“Follow Me,”
He is not sending you into darkness alone.
He is walking ahead.
There are nail scars in the hands of the One leading you.
And beyond the cross stands an empty tomb.
So loosen your grip.
Come out of hiding.
Repent.
Receive grace.
Follow Jesus.
And tomorrow...
do it again.
Because perhaps the most painful funeral you will ever attend is the daily burial of the person you thought you had to remain.
And perhaps the greatest freedom you will ever discover begins when you finally stop trying to save the life Jesus told you to surrender.
Because the cross does not merely ask what you are willing to give up—it reveals the Savior who gave Himself to bring you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE LAST TIME SAMUEL SPOKE TO SAUL
paragraphs:
THE LAST TIME SAMUEL SPOKE TO SAUL
The terrifying tragedy of a man who kept asking God for direction after repeatedly refusing what God had already said—and the breathtaking difference between Saul’s darkness and the grace waiting for sinners in Jesus Christ.
There is something more frightening than hearing a hard word from God.
It is reaching the day when you desperately want another word...
and discovering that the real problem was never that God had failed to speak.
You had simply refused to obey what He had already said.
That is where Saul’s story becomes painfully personal.
Because Saul did not begin his story hiding in darkness, consulting a forbidden medium, terrified of tomorrow.
He began as Israel’s king.
Chosen.
Anointed.
Given opportunity.
Given responsibility.
Given the word of God.
And yet, by the time we reach one of the darkest nights recorded in Scripture, the king who once stood among God's people is walking through the night disguised as someone else.
That detail should haunt us.
Because sin rarely begins by making you look like the person you will eventually become.
It begins with one compromise you can explain.
One command you partially obey.
One conviction you postpone.
One excuse that sounds reasonable.
One moment when protecting your reputation matters more than surrendering your heart.
Then another.
Then another.

Until eventually you are hiding in clothes that are not yours, walking toward something you once knew was wrong, desperately searching for a voice because you would not listen when truth was standing directly in front of you.
Saul's collapse did not begin at Endor.
It began much earlier.
In 1 Samuel 15, God commanded Saul concerning Amalek. Saul went into battle, but instead of carrying out the command as given, he spared King Agag and kept the best livestock.
Then Samuel confronted him.
Saul initially insisted:
“I have performed the commandment of the LORD.”
But Samuel could hear the evidence of Saul's disobedience.
The sheep were still bleating.
The cattle were still making noise.
Imagine the scene.
Saul is declaring obedience while the evidence of his compromise is making noise behind him.
And perhaps that is where this story stops being ancient history.
What is bleating behind your confession?
What have you renamed so you do not have to repent of it?
What are you defending that God has been asking you to surrender?
We can become astonishingly skilled at calling partial obedience faithfulness.
We can worship publicly while resisting God privately.
We can post Scripture and still protect secret sin.
We can know Christian vocabulary, attend church, pray emotional prayers, sing with tears in our eyes—and still negotiate with commands God never invited us to negotiate.
Samuel tells Saul something devastating:
“Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice.”
The Hebrew places enormous weight on hearing.
שְׁמֹעַ — shemōaʿ

It comes from שָׁמַע — shamaʿ, a Hebrew verb meaning to hear, listen, or heed. In biblical thought, genuinely hearing God is not merely receiving sound. It carries the idea of responding to what has been heard.
That is exactly where Saul kept collapsing.
He could hear Samuel.
He could speak about the LORD.
He could offer religious explanations.
But hearing that never becomes obedience is spiritually dangerous.
Samuel continued:
כִּי חַטַּאת־קֶסֶם מֶרִי
“For rebellion is as the sin of divination…”
The irony becomes almost unbearable when you know where Saul's story is going.
Samuel warns him that rebellion is like divination.
Later, Saul literally seeks forbidden divination.
The thing Samuel used as a comparison eventually became Saul's behavior.
Sin has a terrifying way of taking us farther than the first compromise seemed capable of going.
Saul eventually admits:
“I have sinned.”
But even there, Scripture exposes something deeper.
He tells Samuel that he feared the people and obeyed their voice.
Then, after admitting his sin, Saul asks Samuel to honor him before the elders and before Israel.
Do you see the tragedy?
He is losing a kingdom...
and he is still thinking about appearances.
He needs repentance.
But reputation remains in the room.
That is one of the most dangerous conditions of the religious heart: being more devastated that people might discover what you did than devastated that your sin offended God.
There is a kind of sorrow that wants consequences removed without wanting the heart transformed.
There is confession that says, “I was wrong.”
And there is repentance that says, “Jesus, I cannot keep protecting the thing that is destroying me.”
They are not always the same.
Samuel turns away.
Saul grabs the edge of Samuel's robe.
It tears.
And Samuel tells him that the LORD has torn the kingdom from him and given it to another.
Then comes one of the saddest sentences in Saul's story.
Samuel went to Ramah.
Saul went home.
And 1 Samuel 15:35 tells us that Samuel did not see Saul again until the day of Samuel's death. Samuel nevertheless mourned for Saul.
Think about that.
The prophet grieved for the king who would not listen.
Samuel was not celebrating Saul's destruction.
Truth can pronounce judgment and still grieve.
Biblical confrontation is not cruelty.
Sometimes the person warning you most seriously is the person refusing to pretend that the cliff in front of you is a harmless road.
Then Samuel dies.
Israel mourns him.
And time moves forward.
Until the night comes.
The Philistines gather for war.
Saul sees their army.
Scripture says he is afraid and that his heart trembles greatly.
He asks the LORD what to do.
But no answer comes through dreams.
No answer through the Urim.
No answer through the prophets.
And Saul says something in 1 Samuel 28:15 that may be among the loneliest confessions in Scripture:
צַר־לִי מְאֹד
Tsar-li me'od.
“I am greatly distressed.”
Then:
וֵאלֹהִים סָר מֵעָלַי
“God has departed from me.”
Read that slowly.
God has departed from me.
This is a man who once had Samuel speaking into his life.
A man who had been anointed.
A man who had received divine instruction.
Now he is terrified, desperate, and looking for guidance.
And here is the terrible irony:
Saul wants a new answer from God while standing under judgment for refusing God's previous answer.
Sometimes we ask, “God, why aren't You telling me what to do?”
when perhaps another question deserves to be asked:
“What was the last thing God clearly told me in Scripture that I have been refusing to obey?”
Not every season of divine silence means judgment. Scripture gives us faithful sufferers who cried to God through seasons when He seemed silent.
So we must not turn Saul's experience into a cruel formula and tell every hurting Christian that God's apparent silence proves secret rebellion.
It does not.
But Saul's particular silence cannot be separated from Saul's persistent rejection of God's revealed command.
And instead of allowing that silence to drive him toward humble repentance, Saul reaches for another source.
He asks his servants to find a בַּעֲלַת־אוֹב — baʿalat-ʾov, a woman associated with consulting the dead or a spirit-medium.
This is especially disturbing because Saul himself had previously removed mediums and spiritists from the land. Scripture explicitly reminds us of that fact before describing what happens next.
The king who enforced the prohibition is now secretly breaking it.
And then Scripture gives us a cinematic detail that almost preaches by itself:
וַיִּתְחַפֵּשׂ שָׁאוּל
“Saul disguised himself.”
He changed his clothes.
And went out at night.
There are moments when the outward action becomes a picture of the inward condition.
Saul has spent so long protecting appearances that now the king himself disappears underneath a disguise.
That is what hidden sin does.
Eventually you are not only hiding what you do.
You start hiding who you are.
There is the church version of you.
The Facebook version.
The family version.
The private version.
The version everybody praises.
And then the version sitting alone after midnight with the thoughts nobody knows about.
Maybe your darkness is not a medium at Endor.
Maybe it is pornography you keep deleting from your history but not from your life.
Maybe bitterness.
An affair.
A secret conversation.
A dishonest business practice.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Maybe pride wearing ministry clothing.
Maybe resentment toward God.
Maybe an addiction to approval.
Maybe you have learned how to look spiritually alive while privately becoming exhausted from maintaining the disguise.
Saul arrives at the woman's house at night and asks her to bring up Samuel.

The narrative then identifies the figure as Samuel. The woman sees Samuel and cries out; Saul himself does not initially see the figure but asks what she sees. Whatever questions readers may debate about the precise mechanics of this extraordinary event, Scripture never presents Saul's occult consultation as acceptable or as a technique believers may imitate. The entire episode is part of his tragic rebellion.
Then comes the voice Saul once had access to while Samuel was alive.
Samuel speaks.
But there is no new strategy.
No secret escape route.
No loophole.
Samuel essentially repeats what Saul had already been told.
“Why then do you ask me, since the LORD has departed from you…?”
Samuel reminds him that the kingdom has been taken and given to David.
And then Samuel reaches backward into Saul's history:
“Because you did not obey the voice of the LORD…”
There it is again.
The issue was not lack of information.
It was disobedience.
Saul crossed into forbidden darkness looking for a new answer...
only to hear the old answer again.

And this time, Samuel tells him that tomorrow Saul and his sons will die and Israel will fall into Philistine hands. The Hebrew narrative records Saul immediately collapsing full-length on the ground, terrified by Samuel's words.
Imagine the silence after that sentence.
A king on the floor.
A crown that suddenly means nothing.
Tomorrow is coming.
And Saul cannot command it to stop.
This is the last recorded conversation between Samuel and Saul.
No triumphant reconciliation.
No restored throne.
No second coronation.
Only the terrible harvest of years spent resisting the voice of God.
And if this article ended here, it would leave us in the darkness with Saul.
But the Bible does not end in 1 Samuel 28.
And your story does not have to end where Saul's did.
Because another King came.
Saul was Israel's failed king.
Jesus Christ is the faithful King.
Saul grasped at a kingdom he was losing.
Jesus possessed all authority and yet humbled Himself.
Saul repeatedly protected himself.
Jesus gave Himself.
Saul feared people.
Jesus perfectly obeyed His Father.
Saul's disobedience brought judgment.
Christ's obedience carried Him all the way to the cross, where He bore judgment for sinners.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Because Christianity does not announce that decent people can improve themselves enough for God to accept them.
The Gospel announces something infinitely better:
Christ came for sinners.
For rebels.
For hypocrites.
For people with histories.
For people who have worn disguises.
For people who knew better and still did it.
For people ashamed of what they became.
For people who cannot go backward and undo yesterday.
Jesus does not call your darkness light.
Grace never requires God to lie about your sin.
The cross proves how serious sin actually is.
But the cross also proves how far God's mercy was willing to go to save sinners.
Jesus died for sins and rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith is not merely offered better religious advice.
There is forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new heart.
A new identity.
A new Lord.
A new future.
The scandal is what sin made of us.
The grace is what Jesus can make of a surrendered sinner.
Maybe you have been reading Saul's story and recognizing pieces of yourself.
Do not make the mistake of merely feeling emotional.
Conviction is mercy when it drives you to Christ.
You are reading this now.
You can confess now.
You can stop defending it now.
You can bring the secret into God's light now.
You can turn from the sin you have been feeding.
You can call upon Jesus Christ.
Do not wait until consequences force you to care about what conviction has been whispering for years.
Do not confuse God's patience with God's approval.
Do not keep asking Him to bless what His Word tells you to abandon.
And do not tell yourself you need to become clean enough before approaching Christ.
You come because you cannot cleanse yourself.
Come honestly.
“Jesus, I sinned.”
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I surrender.”
“Jesus, save me and change me.”
That prayer is not a magic formula. Salvation rests in Jesus Christ, not in perfectly arranged sentences.
But call upon Him sincerely.
Turn to Him.
Trust Him.
Because the answer to Saul's tragedy is not “try harder to be Saul on his best day.”
The answer is Christ.
Maybe that is why this story hurts so deeply.
Some people will read it and remember the first conviction they ignored.
Some will remember the relationship God told them to leave.
Some will remember the apology they still have not made.
Some will remember the secret they promised God they would surrender.
Some will realize that they have been sacrificing religious activity while withholding obedience.
And someone reading this may finally realize:
“I have been asking God for another word while resisting the Word He has already given me.”
But if you are ready to stop hiding, you can simply write:
And if grace has been rebuilding places in you that sin once destroyed, leave a testimony:
“Christ is still healing me.”
Someone reading beneath you may need to know they are not the only person fighting their way back toward the light.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedience, love, generosity, truth, worship, and lives surrendered to Him—not through transactions with a ministry.
But if this message is faithful to Scripture and helped you see Christ more clearly, sharing it can become one simple act of helping truth reach someone else.
Send it privately to the person you have been praying for.
One share can place the Gospel in front of someone you may never know was struggling.
There may come a night when you need to remember Saul's tragedy before making a decision that could become your own.

Supporting Gospel ministry financially is not a substitute for worship, obedience, generosity to your local church, or care for those in need. But voluntary support of faithful Christian teaching can be a meaningful form of partnership in spreading the Gospel.
Come to Jesus.
Because merchandise cannot redeem you.
A ministry cannot save you.
Only Christ can.
Saul's story leaves us with a question much more important than whether we found the story fascinating.
What will you do with the voice of God while you can still respond?
When Scripture exposes your pride—listen.
When Scripture confronts your sexual sin—listen.
When Christ commands forgiveness—listen.
When He calls you away from idolatry—listen.
When He exposes hypocrisy—listen.
When the Gospel tells you to repent and believe—listen.
Not because obedience purchases grace.
Because grace changes the people it saves.
Saul teaches us the horror of wanting God's guidance without wanting God's government.
Jesus offers something greater than guidance.
He offers Himself.
So stop protecting the disguise.
Stop negotiating with the conviction.
Stop rehearsing excuses.
Bring the scandal into the light.
Bring the failure.
Bring the secret.
Bring the shame.
Bring the years you wasted.
Bring the obedience you delayed.
Bring the pieces you cannot put back together.
Bring them to the crucified and risen Christ.
Because when Jesus takes hold of a surrendered life, your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
And perhaps that is the line worth carrying with you long after you close this article:

Do not wait until you are desperate to hear God's voice before valuing the truth He has already spoken—and when your past tells you it is too late for redemption, run to Jesus while grace is calling your name.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Sin That Doesn't Stay in the Bedroom
paragraphs:
The Sin That Doesn't Stay in the Bedroom
How Sexual Sin Destroys Trust—and Why the Gospel Says Your Worst Betrayal Does Not Have to Become Your Final Chapter
There are betrayals that make noise.
A slammed door. A screaming argument. A wedding ring dropped onto a table.
And then there are betrayals that happen almost silently.
A phone turned facedown.
A browser history erased.
A conversation renamed.
A message deleted before walking through the front door.
A second account nobody knows exists.
A friendship that has quietly crossed a line.
A pornography habit defended with the words, “It isn't like I'm actually sleeping with somebody.”
A private fantasy repeatedly fed until the person lying beside you no longer knows that part of your heart has been living somewhere else.
And sometimes the most devastating sentence in a relationship is not shouted.
It is whispered through tears:
“Was any of it real?”
That is what sexual sin can do.
It does not merely violate a rule about sex. It can fracture the very thing intimacy requires in order to breathe:
trust.
And perhaps you are reading this from one side of that fracture.
Maybe you were betrayed.
Maybe you were the one who betrayed.
Maybe nobody knows yet.
Maybe your spouse thinks everything is fine while you carry a secret that makes your stomach tighten whenever your phone leaves your hand.
Maybe you have confessed, repented, and changed—but the person you wounded still looks at you differently.
Or maybe you are single and telling yourself this subject does not apply to you.
Stay with me.
Because Jesus did not begin His teaching about sexual faithfulness at the bedroom door.
He went deeper.
He went to the heart.
In Matthew 5:28, Jesus says:
“ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν… πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν… ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.”

In context, Christ warns that looking at another person in order to lust has already brought adultery into the heart. The Greek verb epithymeō carries the idea of desire or craving; context determines whether that desire is good or sinful. Here the context is unmistakably sexual coveting. Jesus is exposing something uncomfortable: adultery does not suddenly begin when bodies touch. Sin can be cultivated internally long before it becomes externally visible.
That means faithfulness is bigger than technically avoiding intercourse.
Faithfulness has a heart.
This matters because trust is built on the confidence that what you see in someone is substantially consistent with who that person is when you cannot see them.
Think about that.
Trust says:
I believe your private life and your public promises belong to the same person.
Sexual deception tears those two identities apart.
“I love you.”
Delete.
“You're the only one.”
Clear history.
“You can trust me.”
Close the app.
“Nothing is going on.”
Hide the conversation.
Eventually the greatest damage may no longer be only what happened sexually.
It becomes the terrifying discovery that reality itself was being edited.
That is why sexual betrayal can make someone question months—or even years—of memories.
Were you thinking about someone else when we were together?
Was that trip really what you said it was?
Why were you distant that month?
When you told me you loved me, were you lying?
How many times did you look directly into my eyes while hiding this?
Suddenly the wounded person is not merely grieving an act.
They are reconstructing history.
And Scripture never treats sexual sin casually.
Paul's language in 1 Corinthians 6:18 is startlingly direct:
“Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.”
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not negotiate with it.
Not see how close you can get.
Not keep it bookmarked because you intend to quit eventually.
Not maintain the emotionally charged friendship while insisting that technically nothing physical has happened.
Pheugete.
Flee.
There is urgency in that command because Paul understands something our culture repeatedly tries to forget: your body is not spiritually meaningless.
The surrounding passage grounds sexual holiness in union with Christ and in the reality that the believer's body belongs to God.
Christian sexual ethics are therefore not built on the idea that sex is filthy.
Quite the opposite.
Sex matters because the body matters.
Covenant matters.
People matter.
What we do with another human being matters.
And what we train our hearts to desire matters.
Hebrews 13:4 makes the seriousness even clearer:
“Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος…”
Timios ho gamos en pasin kai hē koitē amiantos.
Marriage is to be honored, and the marriage bed kept undefiled.
The word timios carries the sense of something precious, valuable, honored. Amiantos means undefiled, unstained, uncontaminated. The verse then warns that God judges sexual immorality and adultery.
Notice what Scripture is doing.
God is not degrading marital sexuality.
He is protecting its sacredness.
The marriage bed is not presented as dirty.
It is presented as something worth guarding.
Sexual holiness, then, is not God standing outside human happiness shouting, “No.”
It is the Creator saying:
“This is precious. Do not destroy what it was designed to carry.”
Because sex can carry vulnerability.
Knowledge.
Attachment.
Promise.
Nakedness without shame.
The extraordinary human experience of allowing yourself to be fully seen while trusting that the person seeing you will not exploit what you have entrusted to them.
That is why sexual betrayal can cut so deeply.
The betrayed person may not simply think:
“You broke a rule.”
They may feel:
“You gave away something I believed was ours.”
And Scripture anticipated the destructive character of adultery thousands of years ago.

Proverbs 6:32 says that the person committing adultery lacks sense and brings destruction upon himself. The Hebrew text uses the language of nō'ēph—one committing adultery—and speaks of destruction reaching one's own nephesh, a word with a range involving the self, life, or person.
Sexual sin promises expansion.
Then it shrinks your world.
It promises freedom.
Then you need passwords.
It promises excitement.
Then you live afraid of discovery.
It promises intimacy.
Then it teaches you secrecy.
It promises that nobody will get hurt.
Then somebody discovers the messages.
It promises, “Just once.”
Then once needs another once.
It promises, “You deserve this.”
Then you wake up becoming someone you never planned to become.
This is one of sin's oldest tricks.
Sin rarely introduces itself by showing you the funeral.
It shows you the pleasure.
It does not show David the dead child, the murdered Uriah, the violated household, and the public consequences when he first sees Bathsheba.
It shows him Bathsheba.
Read 2 Samuel 11.
David sees.
David desires.
David inquires.
David sends.
David takes.
Then David hides.
And when hiding becomes difficult, manipulation follows.
Then death.
One concealed sin begins demanding additional sins to protect it.
That is how darkness works.
It asks for a room.
Then demands the house.
But David's story does not end in 2 Samuel 11.
Psalm 51 exists.
And that changes everything.
When confronted, David eventually stops managing appearances and begins confessing reality.
“Against You, You only, have I sinned…”
“Create in me a clean heart, O God…”
David does not call adultery a mistake.
He does not blame Bathsheba.
He does not say his marriage was difficult.
He does not say powerful men have complicated needs.
He calls for mercy.
That is repentance.
And this distinction matters enormously because regret and repentance are not the same thing.
Regret says:
“I hate what this cost me.”
Repentance says:
“I hate what my sin is before God.”
Regret wants consequences removed.
Repentance wants the heart changed.
Regret can cry because it was caught.
Repentance eventually becomes willing to tell the truth even when truth is expensive.
If you are hiding sexual sin right now, please hear this without mistaking grace for softness:
You cannot heal what you are committed to hiding.
You cannot rebuild trust while protecting the machinery that destroyed it.
You cannot ask someone to trust you while demanding that they remain blind.
And you cannot meaningfully repent while continually arranging secret opportunities to return to the same sin.
Jesus receives sinners.
But Jesus does not make peace with the sin destroying them.
The Gospel is not:
“Jesus understands, so continue.”
The Gospel is:
Jesus died and rose to save sinners, reconcile them to God, and give them new life.
Grace does not rename darkness as light.
Grace walks into darkness carrying a cross.
That cross destroys both pride and despair.
Pride says:
“My sin isn't that serious.”
The cross answers:
It was serious enough that Christ died for sinners.
Despair says:
“My sin is too terrible for forgiveness.”
The cross answers:
Christ's blood is sufficient for repentant sinners who come to Him.
This is where the person carrying sexual shame needs to listen carefully.
You are not being invited to minimize what happened.
You are being invited to bring what happened into the presence of the One who already knows.
There is a difference.
Biblical grace never requires pretending the wound is small.
Grace is powerful precisely because the wound is real.
First John 1:9 promises forgiveness and cleansing when we confess our sins.
First Corinthians 6 contains an extraordinary Gospel movement. After naming serious sins, including sexual immorality and adultery, Paul tells the Corinthian believers, in essence:
Some of you were this.
Were.
Then comes washing.
Sanctification.
Justification in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
Christianity does not say sexual sinners are beyond redemption.
Christianity says redemption is exactly what sinners need.
But if you betrayed someone, understand this:
Forgiveness and restored trust are related, but they are not identical.
You may confess tonight.
Trust may take much longer.
You cannot reasonably spend months or years constructing deception and then demand that another person reconstruct trust by Tuesday.
Repentance does not say:
“I apologized. Why aren't you over it?”
Repentance says:
“I understand why my words are difficult to believe now. I will keep becoming trustworthy whether or not I receive immediate emotional relief from the consequences.”
There may need to be transparency.
Boundaries.
Accountability.
Pastoral care.
Wise Christian counseling.
Removal of access to the circumstances feeding the sin.
Ending inappropriate relationships.

And when there is coercion, abuse, exploitation, threats, or danger, simplistic pressure to “just forgive and stay” can itself become harmful. Biblical forgiveness should never be weaponized to force someone to remain exposed to ongoing abuse or deception. Safety, truth, justice, and wise pastoral or professional help matter.
Trust is rebuilt through truth practiced repeatedly over time.
Not dramatic promises.
Not flowers.
Not tears alone.
Not another vow made at 2:00 a.m.
Truth.
Consistency.
Humility.
Time.
Repentance with fruit.
And if you are the betrayed person, your pain does not make you spiritually immature.
You may love Jesus and still shake when the phone vibrates.
You may forgive and still have questions.
You may want restoration and simultaneously be terrified of being fooled again.
You may worship on Sunday and cry in the parking lot afterward.
Healing is not always dramatic.
Sometimes healing looks like getting through one evening without checking.
Sometimes it looks like finally telling a trusted mature believer what happened.
Sometimes it looks like admitting:
“I am angry.”
Sometimes:
“I still love them.”
Sometimes:
“I don't know what I feel.”
And sometimes healing begins with realizing that another person's betrayal does not determine your worth.
The cross has already said something stronger about your value than someone's lust ever could.
You were never valuable merely because somebody remained faithful to you.
You are a human being made in God's image, and for those who belong to Christ, your deepest identity is anchored in Him.
But there is another reader here.
The one nobody suspects.
You have not been discovered.
Yet.
And perhaps every paragraph has made your chest tighter.
You know the name.
You know the account.
You know the website.
You know the conversations.
You know what happens after everyone goes to sleep.
You know what you delete.
You know what you would panic to see projected onto the wall at church.
And somewhere inside you is a sentence you keep postponing:
“I need to stop.”
Please understand something.
The fact that you have not been exposed does not mean you have escaped damage.
Secrecy itself is already changing you.
Every lie trains you to lie more easily.
Every hidden compromise makes the next compromise easier to explain.
Every repeated act of lust can teach you to look at human beings as consumable experiences rather than neighbors bearing God's image.
Every time you protect the secret instead of the relationship, the secret becomes another relationship.
And eventually you may discover something horrifying:
You were protecting the thing that was destroying you.
So stop calling chains freedom.
Come into the light.
Not because exposure is painless.
Because darkness is killing what exposure might finally allow Christ to heal.
And if you have fallen again after promising God you never would, do not turn this article into another emotional moment that disappears tomorrow morning.
Repent.
Bring the sin into the light before God.
Seek mature Christian accountability.
Remove access.
Stop romanticizing the temptation.
Stop feeding the fantasy.
Stop arranging your environment around the assumption that next time your willpower will magically become stronger.
Run.
Pheugete.
Flee.
And run toward Christ.
Because Christianity's answer to sexual sin is not merely stronger self-control.
Ultimately, it is a greater Savior.
Jesus Christ was not crucified for an imaginary population of respectable people who needed minor adjustments.
He died for sinners.
Liars.
Adulterers.
The sexually immoral.
The proud.
The lustful.
The broken.
The people whose search histories would humiliate them.
The people whose marriages are hanging by a thread.
The people sitting in church terrified that somebody will discover what they did.
And the people who were betrayed and now wonder whether they will ever feel safe again.
The scandal of Christianity is not that sin does not matter.
It is that sin matters so much that the Son of God went to the cross—and grace is so powerful that the cross can become the beginning of a story sin thought it had already finished.
This is our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming sinners inside the wreckage.
Peter still denied Him.
David still committed adultery.
Paul still persecuted the church.
The past does not become fiction when grace arrives.
Grace does something greater.
It refuses to let the past have the final word.
That is why maybe the question tonight is not simply:
“Can my relationship survive?”
Maybe the deeper question is:
“Will I finally surrender the part of me I keep protecting from Jesus?”
Because you can save your reputation and lose your soul in secrecy.
You can keep everyone convinced and become increasingly hollow.
You can win every argument about why your behavior “technically isn't cheating” while your heart moves farther and farther away from covenant faithfulness.
Or you can surrender.
No performance.
No excuses.
No more hiding.
Jesus already knows.
And He is still calling sinners to repentance.
Someone reading beneath you may need proof that repentance is possible.
Someone may need to see that a Christian can fall without deciding to live on the ground.
Someone may need the courage your honesty gives them.
Not as a badge announcing that you have everything together.
Send it privately to the friend whose secret is slowly consuming him.
Share it with the believer who fell.
Share it with the person who was betrayed.
Share it with the person who has quietly drifted from Jesus.
Stay close to truth.
Stay nourished.
Stay challenged.
Stay around messages that keep pointing you away from hiding and back toward Jesus.
Not because you expect to need it tonight.
What are you protecting that is slowly destroying your ability to be trusted?
Do not answer me first.
Answer Jesus.
Because one day you may realize the most dangerous thing about your secret was never that somebody might discover it.
It was that you were becoming willing to lose everything just to keep it hidden.
Come into the light.
The scandal may be part of your history.
It does not have to be the author of your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “WHERE TWO OR THREE ARE GATHERED” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MOST CHRISTIANS THINK IT MEANS
paragraphs: “WHERE TWO OR THREE ARE GATHERED” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MOST CHRISTIANS THINK IT MEANS

Matthew 18:20 is often quoted when a church service feels small. But when you read the words surrounding it, you discover something far more serious, uncomfortable, beautiful—and deeply revealing about the kind of Jesus who refuses to abandon His people when sin, confrontation, repentance, forgiveness, and restoration get painfully real.
You have probably heard the verse in a nearly empty prayer meeting.
Only three people came.
Someone looks around at all those empty chairs and smiles.
“Well… where two or three are gathered, Jesus is here.”
And everybody nods.
Because that is what Matthew 18:20 means.
Right?
Not exactly.

The comforting conclusion—that Christ is present with even the smallest gathering of believers—is certainly consistent with the wider testimony of Scripture. Christians do not need a packed auditorium, a famous preacher, a worship band, or thousands of people in a room before Jesus cares about them.
But that is not the primary point Jesus is making in Matthew 18:20.
And once you see the verse inside its actual context, those familiar words become heavier.
More demanding.
More beautiful.
And perhaps more frightening.
Because Matthew 18:20 was not originally spoken into the atmosphere of a disappointing church attendance report.
It was spoken into the mess of human sin.
Listen to Jesus’ words:
“For where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I among them.”
Matthew 18:20, ESV
The Greek reads:
“οὗ γάρ εἰσιν δύο ἢ τρεῖς συνηγμένοι εἰς τὸ ἐμὸν ὄνομα, ἐκεῖ εἰμι ἐν μέσῳ αὐτῶν.”
Hou gar eisin dyo ē treis synēgmenoi eis to emon onoma, ekei eimi en mesō autōn.
A close rendering is:
“For where two or three have been gathered into My name, there I am in their midst.”
Those words are breathtaking.
But before turning them into a slogan, we have to ask the question that responsible Bible reading always asks:
Why did Jesus say them?
Go backward.
Matthew 18:15 begins:
“If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone.”
Suddenly the atmosphere changes.
This is not primarily a prayer meeting.
This is confrontation.
Someone has sinned.
Someone has been wounded.
Something has happened inside the community of believers that cannot simply be covered with religious smiles and Sunday-morning handshakes.
And Jesus tells His disciple what to do.
Go to the person.
Privately.
Not Facebook first.
Not the group chat first.
Not the prayer circle that mysteriously becomes a gossip circle.
Not fifteen people who were never involved.
Go to your brother.
Why?
Jesus says:
“If he listens to you, you have gained your brother.”
That sentence reveals the heart behind the entire process.
The goal is not humiliation.
The goal is not revenge.
The goal is not winning an argument.
The goal is gaining your brother.
Restoration.
Reconciliation.
Truth serving love.
But Jesus knows something about us.
Sometimes people refuse to listen.
So He continues:
“But if he does not listen, take one or two others along with you, that every charge may be established by the evidence of two or three witnesses.”
Matthew 18:16.
There they are.
The two or three.
Before Jesus ever says, “where two or three are gathered,” He has already mentioned “two or three witnesses.”
And that language did not appear from nowhere.
It reaches backward into Israel’s Scriptures.
Deuteronomy 19:15 says:

“A single witness shall not suffice against a person for any crime or for any wrong in connection with any offense that he has committed. Only on the evidence of two witnesses or of three witnesses shall a charge be established.”
The Hebrew contains the same numerical pattern:
עַל־פִּי שְׁנֵי עֵדִים אוֹ עַל־פִּי שְׁלֹשָׁה עֵדִים
‘al-pi shenei ‘edim ’o ‘al-pi sheloshah ‘edim
“On the testimony of two witnesses or on the testimony of three witnesses…”
Now Matthew 18 begins to come into focus.

Jesus is addressing sin among His people and describing a process designed to pursue truth without recklessness, correction without gossip, accountability without mob justice, and restoration wherever restoration is possible.
First, go privately.
If the person will not listen, involve one or two others.
If the person still refuses to listen, Jesus says:
“tell it to the church.”
And if the person persistently refuses even the church’s correction, Jesus gives the sobering final instruction of Matthew 18:17.
Then come the words about binding and loosing.
Then agreement.
Then two or three gathered in His name.
This is the neighborhood in which Matthew 18:20 lives.
And that changes everything.
Because Jesus is not merely saying:
“Don’t worry if attendance is low.”
He is assuring His disciples that when His people must carry out the painful work of accountability according to His will and under His authority, He has not abandoned them.
He is in their midst.
That little phrase “in my name” matters enormously.
The Greek is:
εἰς τὸ ἐμὸν ὄνομα
eis to emon onoma
This is not a magical formula.
Saying “in Jesus’ name” does not automatically sanctify whatever Christians have already decided to do.
People can gather around bitterness.
People can gather around gossip.
People can gather around revenge.
People can gather around theological pride.
People can even use the Bible while satisfying the flesh.
The promise is attached to gathering in His name—to His identity, His authority, His purposes.
That means Matthew 18:20 should never become permission for two angry Christians to agree that a third Christian deserves destruction.
Jesus is not a stamp we place on our grudges.
His name is not a weapon for baptizing our vengeance.
And maybe that is where this verse stops being merely interesting and starts becoming personal.
Because some of us love Matthew 18:20…
but we avoid Matthew 18:15.
We want His presence.
We do not want His process.
We want Jesus “in the midst.”
But we do not want to walk across the room and have the conversation.
We would rather tell eleven people how somebody hurt us than tell the one person who actually hurt us.
We call it “venting.”
Sometimes it is gossip wearing the perfume of pain.
We call it “asking for prayer.”
Sometimes we have already decided who the villain is before the prayer request ever leaves our mouth.
We say we want reconciliation.
Sometimes what we really want is vindication.
And Jesus sees through all of it.
He sees the wound.
He sees the offender.
He sees the offended.
He sees the conversation nobody wants to have.
He sees the screenshots.
The resentment.
The carefully edited version of the story we told our friends.
The apology we refused to make.
The forgiveness we pretended to give.
The sin we hoped nobody would confront.
And still…
He moves toward His people.
This is what makes Matthew 18 so stunning.
Jesus does not build His church by pretending Christians never hurt each other.
He teaches His church what to do when they do.
That is a very different Christianity from the polished version many people try to display.
Real churches contain people who still need sanctification.
Real Christians sometimes fail.
Real relationships sometimes fracture.
Real brothers and sisters sometimes need correction.
And biblical love is not pretending evil is harmless.
Grace does not require us to rename darkness as light.
Forgiveness does not mean truth becomes irrelevant.
Restoration does not mean every consequence instantly disappears.
And accountability is not the enemy of grace.
Sometimes accountability is one of grace’s instruments.
But there is another danger hiding on the opposite side.
Some Christians discover the church-discipline context of Matthew 18 and become almost excited about confrontation.
That misses Jesus too.
Look again at His purpose:
“You have gained your brother.”
Not crushed him.
Not embarrassed her.
Not exposed them for entertainment.
Gained.
Your.
Brother.
The heart of biblical correction is not:
“How can I prove that I am right?”
It is:
“How can this person be restored to truth?”
And that becomes even clearer when you refuse to stop reading at verse 20.
Immediately after Jesus speaks about the two or three, Peter approaches Him with another uncomfortable question:
“Lord, how often will my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? As many as seven times?”
Jesus answers:
“I do not say to you seven times, but seventy-seven times.”
Matthew 18:21–22.
Do you see the breathtaking movement?
A brother sins.
Go to him.
Seek restoration.
Take witnesses when necessary.
Take sin seriously.
Exercise responsibility carefully.
Christ promises His presence.
And then Peter asks about forgiveness.
This chapter refuses to let us choose between truth and grace.
It will not allow sentimental grace that refuses to confront sin.
And it will not allow cold orthodoxy that enjoys condemning sinners.
Jesus holds truth and mercy together perfectly.
That is because the One speaking in Matthew 18 is the same Jesus who would go to the cross.
The Judge would be judged in the place of sinners.
The sinless One would bear sin.
The innocent One would suffer for the guilty.
Christ did not save us by pretending our rebellion was insignificant.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
And grace is so astonishing that He willingly did.
That is the Gospel.
Not:
“You were basically good, so Jesus helped you become better.”
Not:
“God lowered His standards because He loves you.”
Not:
“Your sin does not matter.”
The Gospel announces that our sin is real, our guilt is real, judgment is real—and the mercy of God in Jesus Christ is greater than we could ever deserve.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He was raised.
And sinners who repent and trust in Him are not merely given religious advice.
They are reconciled to God.
Forgiven.
Redeemed.
Made new.
That is why Christian restoration can exist at all.
We forgive because we are people who desperately needed forgiveness.
We confront humbly because we know we ourselves stand only by grace.
We pursue wandering brothers and sisters because Jesus pursued us.
We refuse gossip because the person who failed is not entertainment.
We refuse self-righteousness because there is no room for boasting at the foot of the cross.
Maybe you started reading because you thought this article was going to correct a commonly misunderstood Bible verse.
Maybe the verse has been correcting you instead.
Maybe there is someone you have been talking about when Jesus has been telling you to talk to them.
Maybe you wounded somebody and have spent months defending yourself because repentance would cost your pride.
Maybe somebody confronted you in love, and you rejected them because you confused correction with hatred.
Maybe you are the wounded one.
And what happened to you really was wrong.
Matthew 18 does not require you to call evil good.
But perhaps bitterness has slowly begun owning a room in your heart that belongs to Christ.
Or maybe you are hiding sin and terrified somebody will finally see it.
Hear this carefully.
Being exposed before God does not have to become the end of your story.
For the repentant sinner, exposure can become the doorway to healing.
Peter failed publicly.
David fell catastrophically and was confronted.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples abandoned Jesus in His darkest earthly hour.
The New Testament is not a museum filled with flawless people.
It is the testimony of a flawless Savior rescuing sinners.
And if you belong to Jesus, your worst chapter does not have authority to write your final sentence.
Christ does.
That is our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by editing sin out of the story.
But by bringing sinners through repentance to the mercy found in Christ.
So the next time you hear someone say, “Where two or three are gathered…”
remember the empty chairs if you want.
Yes, Christ cares about the tiny prayer gathering.
Yes, you can pray when only two believers are in the room.
Yes, the risen Christ is not impressed by crowd size.
But remember something deeper too.
Remember the difficult room.
The trembling conversation.
The wounded brother.
The stubborn heart.
The witnesses.
The church trying desperately to remain faithful to Christ.
The offender being called to repentance.
The offended believer being called away from vengeance.
The possibility of restoration hanging painfully between them.
And Jesus saying, in effect:
When you gather under My authority to do this faithfully…
I am not absent.
I am there.
That changes the way we confront.
Because Jesus is in the room.
It changes the way we speak.
Because Jesus is in the room.
It changes the way we listen.
Because Jesus is in the room.
It changes the way we discipline.
Because Jesus is in the room.
It changes the way we forgive.
Because Jesus is in the room.
And perhaps most importantly, it reminds us whose church this actually is.
Not ours.
His.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to confess private details publicly.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only believer struggling to follow Jesus through the mess.
And please do not let this truth stop with you.
Even send it privately to someone who would never call themselves a Christian.
Not to win an argument.
To point them toward Jesus.
Because eventually almost every Christian will need Matthew 18.
Eventually somebody will hurt you.
Eventually you will hurt somebody.
Eventually truth and grace will have to meet somewhere painfully close to home.
And when that day arrives, you may need these words again.
Supporting a ministry is not a condition for glorifying God, and nobody purchases spiritual favor from Him.
But if God has genuinely used this work to strengthen you, you can choose to help carry it farther.

Your support helps us keep creating Scripture-centered content designed to call people toward Jesus Christ, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, healing, discipleship, and transformed lives. And when you share these articles publicly, you help place biblical truth in front of people we may never be able to reach ourselves.
Because this was never ultimately about building an audience.
It is about pointing people to Jesus.
And maybe the most haunting truth in Matthew 18 is not merely that Jesus is present when two or three gather.
It is that the Jesus standing in the middle is the same Savior who went looking for the one who wandered.
Earlier in this very chapter, Jesus spoke about the shepherd and the wandering sheep.
Then He spoke about pursuing a sinning brother.
Then about two or three.
Then about forgiveness.
Do not miss the heartbeat.
The Shepherd is still seeking people.
Still confronting what destroys them.
Still calling sinners home.
Still teaching His church to pursue restoration.
Still extending mercy to the repentant.
Still standing in the middle of situations we thought were too broken to redeem.
Maybe you are one of those situations.
Maybe your marriage has a chapter you wish could disappear.
Maybe your family knows a version of you that your church friends have never met.
Maybe your faith has scars.
Maybe your past has receipts.
Maybe your reputation has a stain.
Maybe you have done things you cannot undo.
The Gospel does not offer you a time machine.
It offers you something infinitely greater.
A Redeemer.
Jesus does not need an unbroken past to create a redeemed future.
He takes sinners seriously enough to call them to repentance…
and loves sinners deeply enough to have died to save them.
So when the room gets uncomfortable…
when truth finally gets spoken…
when sin loses its hiding place…
when repentance breaks through pride…
when forgiveness costs more than anyone expected…
when wounded people begin learning how to walk toward the light again…
remember who promised to be in the midst.
Jesus.
And when Jesus stands in the middle of a ruined story, ruin does not necessarily get the final word.
Grace does.
The chapter you are most ashamed of may become the very place where people someday see most clearly that Jesus Christ still restores what sin tried to destroy.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Jacob Loved Rachel—So Why Did He Keep Sleeping With Leah?
paragraphs: Jacob Loved Rachel—So Why Did He Keep Sleeping With Leah?

The disturbing question inside Genesis 29–30 is not really about sex. It is about what happens when wounded people try to get from another human being what only God can ultimately give—and how, from one painfully broken family, God carried the bloodline that would lead to Jesus Christ.
Jacob loved Rachel.
Scripture does not leave us guessing.
Genesis 29:18 says:

וַיֶּאֱהַב יַעֲקֹב אֶת־רָחֵל
Vayye’ehav Ya‘aqov et-Rachel
“And Jacob loved Rachel.”
He loved her enough to work seven years for her. Genesis says those years seemed to him “but a few days” because of his love for her.
That sounds like the beginning of one of the Bible’s great romances.
Then comes the wedding.
The darkness.
The deception.
And the morning after.
Jacob wakes up beside the wrong woman.
“Behold, it was Leah” (Genesis 29:25).

It is one of Scripture’s most brutal reversals. The deceiver has been deceived. Jacob, who once exploited the blindness of his father Isaac and participated in deception surrounding the blessing, has now been deceived under the cover of darkness by Laban.
But that creates a question many readers quietly think and few people want to say aloud:
If Jacob loved Rachel so much, why did he keep sleeping with Leah?
Because Leah did not have just one child by Jacob.
She had Reuben.
Then Simeon.
Then Levi.
Then Judah.
Later Issachar.
Then Zebulun.
And Dinah.
So this was not simply one disastrous wedding night.
Jacob continued having marital relations with a woman Scripture explicitly tells us he loved less than Rachel.
And suddenly this ancient family stops feeling so ancient.
Because underneath the tents, livestock, marriages, servants, pregnancies, and rivalries is something painfully modern:
A woman desperately wanting to be chosen.
Another woman desperately wanting what her sister has.
A husband whose heart is divided.
A father manipulating his children.
Two sisters turning motherhood into a battlefield.
Servants being pulled into somebody else’s family conflict.
Children being born into emotional warfare they did not create.
And God somehow refusing to abandon any of them.
Before we answer the question, we need to correct something important.
The Bible records Jacob’s polygamous household.
It does not present that household as God’s beautiful ideal for marriage.
There is an enormous difference between biblical description and biblical prescription.

Genesis begins with a different picture: one man and one woman joined together as “one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). Jesus Himself later reaches back to that creation pattern when teaching about marriage (Matthew 19:4–6).
So when Genesis shows us Jacob with Leah, Rachel, Bilhah, and Zilpah, Scripture is not saying, “Copy this.”
Look at the fruit.
Jealousy.
Competition.
Favoritism.
Bitterness.
Manipulation.
Desperation.
Children becoming emotional trophies.
Women measuring their worth through fertility and through a man’s affection.
The household itself becomes evidence of how destructive divided love can become.
Jacob did not originally choose Leah.
Laban engineered the marriage.

According to Genesis 29, Jacob agreed to work seven years for Rachel. But on the wedding night Laban secretly substituted Leah. When Jacob confronted him, Laban appealed to the local custom that the older daughter should be married first. Jacob completed Leah’s bridal week and was then given Rachel, in exchange for another seven years of service.
That means Leah became Jacob’s wife within the social and legal world of the narrative, even though Jacob had been deceived into the marriage.
Genesis 29:30 then gives us the painful reality:
Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.
The next verse becomes even sharper.

וַיַּרְא יְהוָה כִּי־שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה
Vayyar YHWH ki-senu’ah Leah.
Literally, the Hebrew can carry the force:
“YHWH saw that Leah was hated.”

Many English translations render the idea “unloved” or understand it comparatively—loved less than Rachel. That comparative sense fits the immediate context because verse 30 has just told us Rachel was loved more. But we should not soften the emotional force until Leah’s pain disappears.
She was the unwanted wife.
And God saw her.
That may be the sentence somebody reading this needed more than the answer to the title.
God saw Leah.
Jacob may have entered her tent without giving her the love she desperately wanted.
But God entered her suffering with His eyes open.
“When the LORD saw…”
Those words change the story.
Because Leah begins having children, and through the names she gives them, Genesis lets us hear the private ache of a woman trying to turn childbirth into affection.
She gives birth to Reuben and essentially says:
God has seen my misery.
Now my husband will love me.
There it is.
Not theology in a classroom.
A wounded woman whispering the sentence millions of people have whispered in different forms:
Maybe now I’ll be enough.
Maybe if I give him this…
Maybe if I become prettier…
Maybe if I lose the weight…
Maybe if I earn more money…
Maybe if I become successful…
Maybe if I stop complaining…
Maybe if I become more sexual…
Maybe if I become more spiritual…
Maybe if I serve everybody…
Maybe if I never say no…
Maybe if I give them everything they want…
Maybe then they will love me.
Reuben arrives.
But the wound remains.
Then Simeon.
Leah says the LORD has heard that she is unloved.
Notice the progression.
God has seen me.
God has heard me.
But she is still looking toward Jacob.
Then Levi is born.
And Leah says:
“Now this time my husband will be joined to me.”
Can you hear the heartbreak?
One son.
Surely now.
Two sons.
Maybe now.
Three sons.
Now he will finally attach himself to me.
This is what idolatry of human approval does.
It keeps moving the finish line.
One more achievement.
One more sacrifice.
One more compromise.
One more child.
One more promotion.
One more surgery.
One more sexual encounter.
One more attempt to become impossible to abandon.
And perhaps the most devastating thing about Leah’s story is that she was receiving genuine blessings from God while still trying to use those blessings to purchase something from Jacob.
Some of us do the same thing.
God gives us gifts, and instead of enjoying them in Him, we turn them into advertisements for our worth.
“Look at me.”
“Choose me.”
“Notice me.”
“Tell me I matter.”
Then something changes.
Leah conceives again.
A fourth son.
But this time she does not name him around what she hopes Jacob will finally do.
Genesis 29:35 records her words:

הַפַּעַם אוֹדֶה אֶת־יְהוָה
Happa‘am odeh et-YHWH.
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
And she calls him Judah—Yehudah—a name connected in the narrative with praise or thanksgiving.
Read that slowly.
Reuben: Maybe my husband will love me.
Simeon: God heard I was unloved.
Levi: Maybe my husband will finally attach himself to me.
Judah:
This time I will praise the LORD.
Something has shifted.
The circumstances have not suddenly become romantic.
Rachel has not disappeared.
Jacob has not suddenly become the husband Leah dreamed about.
But for one breathtaking moment, Leah’s eyes rise above Jacob.
She stops making her husband the center of the sentence.
And she praises God.
And here the story becomes far bigger than Leah could possibly have understood.
Because Judah would become part of the line through which Israel’s kings would come.
And ultimately, from the tribe of Judah, Jesus Christ would come according to the flesh.

The New Testament deliberately identifies Jesus with Judah. Matthew’s genealogy traces the messianic line through “Judah and his brothers” (Matthew 1:2–3). Hebrews calls Jesus “our Lord” who “was descended from Judah” (Hebrews 7:14). Revelation announces Him as “the Lion of the tribe of Judah” (Revelation 5:5).
Do you see the scandal?
Rachel was Jacob’s chosen love.
But Leah—the woman who spent years wondering whether she was enough—became the mother of Judah.
And through Judah’s line came the Messiah.
Jesus.
The rejected Stone.
The suffering Servant.
The King.
The Savior.
The Bridegroom who does not love His people because they finally performed well enough to deserve Him.
This does not mean Leah earned the Messiah by suffering.
It does not mean every painful marriage will receive the earthly outcome Leah wanted.
It does not mean God approved every decision in Jacob’s household.
It means something far more beautiful:
Human sin, rejection, favoritism, deception, and dysfunction could not derail God’s redemptive purpose.
God did not need a spotless family tree to bring a spotless Savior into the world.
That is the Gospel hiding in plain sight throughout Scripture.
God does not sanitize the ancestry of Jesus.
Judah himself would later become involved in the scandalous story of Tamar.
Rahab would enter the messianic genealogy.
Ruth, the Moabite, would enter it.
David and the terrible story surrounding “the wife of Uriah” would appear in Matthew 1.
Again and again, the genealogy moves through human wreckage until it reaches Jesus Christ.
Not because sin does not matter.
Sin matters so much that Christ had to die.
But grace is so powerful that sin does not get the final word for those whom God redeems.
Now return to the uncomfortable question.
Why did Jacob keep sleeping with Leah?

Because after Laban’s deception, Leah remained Jacob’s wife within the marriage arrangement narrated in Genesis. Jacob continued marital relations with her while also loving Rachel more deeply. Genesis does not portray this as a healthy romantic triangle. It exposes a broken household operating inside an ancient polygamous structure, and the consequences become increasingly painful.
And Leah was not the only wounded person.
Rachel had Jacob’s affection.
But Rachel could not conceive.
Leah looked across the family and thought:
If only I had Rachel’s love.
Rachel looked back and thought:
If only I had Leah’s children.
That is comparison.
It convinces you that the person you envy possesses the missing piece that would finally make your life whole.
Leah had children and wanted love.
Rachel had love and wanted children.
Neither woman felt complete.
Genesis 30 says Rachel envied her sister.
Eventually Rachel gives her servant Bilhah to Jacob so children might be produced through her according to the customs reflected in the ancient story.
Leah later gives Zilpah.
The rivalry escalates.
Even mandrakes become bargaining material.
At one point Leah effectively negotiates for a night with her own husband.
Think about how emotionally broken that sentence is.
A wife bargaining for access to the man whose children she has already borne.
This is not Scripture glamorizing polygamy.
This is Scripture refusing to airbrush what broken human desire can do.
And yet God is still there.
That distinction matters.
God’s presence in a story does not mean God approves everything happening in the story.
If we forget that, we will misunderstand enormous portions of the Bible.
Scripture frequently shows God accomplishing His purposes despite human sin rather than endorsing human sin.
Jacob’s family becomes Israel.
The twelve sons become patriarchs of the tribes.
And yet read their family story.
Jealousy.
Sexual sin.
Violence.
Favoritism.
Betrayal.
Joseph sold by his own brothers.
Judah’s failure.
Years of grief.
This family is not a trophy case displaying human goodness.
It is evidence of divine mercy.
And perhaps that is why this story can reach people who think their lives are too messy for Jesus.
Maybe your family looks nothing like the Christian photographs people post online.
Maybe your parents failed you.
Maybe your marriage broke.
Maybe somebody chose someone else.
Maybe you became jealous.
Maybe you compromised because you were terrified of being alone.
Maybe you have slept beside somebody while feeling completely unseen.
Maybe you have spent years trying to earn affection.
Maybe your children know there is tension in the house even when nobody talks about it.
Maybe you are Rachel, holding what somebody else envies while secretly grieving what you do not have.
Maybe you are Leah, wondering why being useful never made you feel loved.
Maybe you are Jacob, realizing your choices have wounded people around you.
Maybe you are carrying consequences that cannot simply be erased.
Then hear what Christianity actually announces.
Not:
“Try harder until your past becomes respectable.”
Not:
“Pretend it never happened.”
Not:
“Call sin acceptable so nobody feels uncomfortable.”
The Gospel says something infinitely more costly and infinitely more hopeful.
Repent. Come to Christ. Receive mercy. Become new.
At the cross, Jesus does not pretend sin is harmless.
He bears its judgment.
“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).
The scandal of grace is not that God shrugs at sin.
The scandal is that the holy Son of God willingly stood in the place of sinners.
Jesus was rejected so rejected people could be received by God.
Jesus was wounded so sinners could be reconciled.
Jesus died and rose again so our worst chapter does not have authority to write our final chapter.
And that brings us back to Leah.
The woman who kept saying,
Maybe now my husband will love me…
became the mother of the tribe associated with the Messiah.
She wanted Jacob to look at her.
God had already seen her.
She wanted Jacob to hear the cry beneath her motherhood.
God had already heard her.
She wanted Jacob to attach himself to her.
But eventually her lips found a better sentence:
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
Somebody reading this has been living between Reuben and Judah.
You are still trying to make somebody love you.
Still measuring your worth by who texts you.
Who leaves.
Who stays.
Who desires you.
Who applauds you.
Who follows you.
Who chooses somebody else.
You keep saying:
Maybe now.
Maybe after this achievement.
Maybe after this relationship.
Maybe after this body transformation.
Maybe after this amount of money.
Maybe after this ministry succeeds.
Maybe after everybody sees that I mattered.
But what if freedom begins when your sentence changes?
From:
“Maybe now they will love me.”
To:
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
That does not make rejection painless.
It means rejection no longer gets to name you.
Your deepest identity cannot safely rest in another fallen human being.
It rests in Christ.
If you belong to Jesus, you are not saved because somebody finally chose you romantically.
You are saved because the Father gave His Son, Christ died for sinners, Christ rose from the dead, and everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith receives forgiveness and eternal life.
That is why this story cannot end with Jacob.
It cannot even end with Leah.
It has to end with Jesus.
Because Leah can show us the ache.
Judah can show us the line.
But only Christ can give us redemption.
And maybe this article exposed something you have hidden even from yourself.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when we finally stop pretending.
And somebody reading your comment may realize they are not the only person still fighting their way back toward Christ.
“What do I have to do to finally be loved?”
It does not.
Scripture drags the dysfunction into the light—and then shows us a Redeemer greater than it.
Because perhaps the most unforgettable detail in Leah’s story is not that Jacob kept coming into her tent.
It is that God saw the woman whose husband did not love her the way she wanted to be loved—and God was already weaving redemption through the very life she thought was evidence that she was unwanted.
The child named Judah emerged from that wounded home.
And generations later, from Judah’s line came Jesus Christ.
So when your life looks too tangled, too embarrassing, too fractured, too late, remember:
The Bible is filled with people whose stories would have looked disastrous halfway through.
But halfway through is not where God stopped writing.
The wound that made Leah ask, “When will I finally be loved?” became part of a story that ultimately pointed toward the Savior whose cross declares how far God was willing to go to redeem sinners.
Don’t forget that.
And when the old voice whispers, “Nobody chose you,” remember the greater truth:
Your rejection does not get to write the ending when your life has been surrendered to the Redeemer.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “NO. NOT UNTIL YOU SUFFER LIKE I DID.” — CAN YOU WITHHOLD SEX TO PUNISH YOUR SPOUSE?
paragraphs:
“NO. NOT UNTIL YOU SUFFER LIKE I DID.” — CAN YOU WITHHOLD SEX TO PUNISH YOUR SPOUSE?
When the Marriage Bed Becomes a Battlefield, Scripture Asks a Question More Dangerous Than “Who Started It?”: Are You Still Loving Your Spouse Like Someone Jesus Died to Redeem?
The bedroom was quiet.
Not peaceful.
Quiet.
There is a difference.
Peace can sleep.
Bitterness stays awake.

Two people can lie inches apart beneath the same blanket while emotionally living in different countries. They can share a mortgage, children, meals, photographs, a church pew, even prayers before dinner...
and still use silence as a knife.
Maybe you know that silence.
Maybe the argument happened hours ago.
Maybe it happened three years ago and never really ended.
He reaches toward her.
She pulls away.
Or she reaches toward him.
He turns toward the wall.
And somewhere beneath the rejection is a sentence nobody says aloud:
Now you know how it feels.
That is where this conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because there are legitimate reasons a husband or wife may not be ready or able to have sex.
Illness is real.
Exhaustion is real.
Childbirth recovery is real.
Pain is real.
Medication effects are real.
Grief is real.
Trauma is real.
Marital conflict can deeply affect emotional and physical intimacy.

And where there is abuse, intimidation, coercion, threats, or fear, the biblical response is never to pressure the endangered spouse into sexual activity. Sexual intimacy within Christian marriage is meant to express covenant love—not domination. No verse of Scripture should ever be twisted into permission to force, threaten, manipulate, or sexually coerce another human being.
So this article is not asking:
“Must a spouse say yes every time?”
No.
The question is far more specific.
Can a Christian deliberately withhold sexual intimacy for the purpose of punishing, controlling, humiliating, manipulating, or getting revenge on a spouse?
And on that question, Scripture refuses to let us hide behind excuses.
Paul writes to married believers in Corinth:
The sense is:
Let the husband give his wife what is due within the marriage relationship, and likewise the wife to her husband.
Then Paul becomes even more direct:
“Μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους...”
Μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε — Mē apostereite.
“Do not deprive one another.”
Notice the words Paul did not use.
He did not say:
“Wives, do not deprive your husbands.”
He did not say:
“Husbands, your wives owe you whatever you demand.”
He said:
ἀλλήλους — allēlous.
One another.
That one word destroys a mountain of selfish interpretations.
This is mutual.
Reciprocal.
Covenantal.
Husband toward wife.
Wife toward husband.
Neither spouse is handed a biblical weapon.
Both are handed a biblical responsibility.
Paul continues by describing even temporary abstinence as something undertaken “ἐκ συμφώνου” — ek symphōnou — by mutual agreement, for a time, in connection with prayer, followed by reunion.
Mutual agreement.
Not revenge.
Not manipulation.
Not “I’ll make you pay.”
Not “You disappointed me, so now I control whether you feel loved.”
Not “I know exactly where you are vulnerable, and I am going to use that vulnerability against you.”
That is not intimacy.
That is punishment wearing the clothes of intimacy.
And sometimes Christians become extremely creative at baptizing revenge.
We do not scream.
We withdraw.
We do not strike.
We freeze.
We do not say, “I want to hurt you.”
We simply discover what matters most to our spouse...
and quietly remove it.
Affection.
Conversation.
Kindness.
Attention.
Touch.
Sex.
Respect.
Encouragement.
Tenderness.
Until the marriage becomes a courtroom where both spouses are simultaneously prosecutor, defendant, judge, and executioner.
But marriage was never designed to become a courtroom.
It was designed to become a covenant.
And covenant love does something our flesh hates.
It refuses to make revenge its god.
Maybe your spouse wounded you.
Maybe deeply.
Maybe there was an argument and no apology.
Maybe you feel invisible.
Maybe you have been carrying responsibilities nobody notices.
Maybe every affectionate touch now feels suspicious because you think, You ignore me all day and suddenly remember I exist when you want sex.
That pain should not be mocked.
It should be heard.
Because sometimes what looks like “withholding sex” from one side feels like “I cannot emotionally connect with someone who refuses to listen to me” from the other.
Those are not necessarily the same thing.
Motives matter.
Circumstances matter.
Safety matters.
Love listens before it accuses.
So before quoting 1 Corinthians 7 at your spouse, perhaps you should allow 1 Corinthians 7 to interrogate you.
Are you demanding intimacy while refusing tenderness?
Are you asking for your spouse’s body while neglecting your spouse’s heart?
Are you treating sex as an entitlement instead of a gift shared within covenant love?
Are you attentive to exhaustion?
Pain?
Fear?
Unresolved wounds?
Do you become angry when your spouse says no?
Do you pout?
Threaten?
Quote Scripture as leverage?
Pressure until resistance collapses?
If so, you are not defending biblical marriage.
You are violating the spirit of Christlike love.
Because the Bible that says, “Do not deprive one another,” also tells husbands:
“Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν...”
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church...”
And how did Christ love His church?
He gave Himself for her.
Read that again.
He did not exploit her.
He gave Himself for her.
He did not ask, “How much can I take?”
His love demonstrated, “I give Myself.”
That is why Christian marital intimacy can never be reduced to:
“You owe me.”
The cross changes the vocabulary.
The question becomes:
“How can I love you?”
“How can I understand you?”
“How can I serve you?”
“How can I protect what God has entrusted to us?”
“How can we heal what resentment has damaged?”
“How can we become one again instead of winning another argument?”
Peter tells husbands to live with their wives “κατὰ γνῶσιν” — kata gnōsin — according to knowledge, with understanding, giving honor, recognizing them as fellow heirs of the grace of life.
Honor.
Understanding.
Grace.
Those words belong in the bedroom too.
Imagine what would happen if Christian husbands stopped asking only, “Why doesn’t she want me?” and sometimes asked, “What is happening inside the woman I promised to cherish?”

Imagine what would happen if Christian wives stopped asking only, “How can I make him understand how angry I am?” and sometimes asked, “Am I using rejection specifically because I know it will hurt him?”
Imagine if both stopped keeping score.
Because that is where punishment begins.
A ledger.
You embarrassed me Tuesday.
You ignored me Thursday.
You forgot something important Saturday.
You rejected me last week.
You hurt me last month.
You said something six years ago that I technically forgave but emotionally preserved in a glass case.
So now...
you owe me.
And the debt keeps growing.
This is how marriages become cold without anybody filing for divorce.
Nobody leaves.
They simply stop giving themselves.
The house remains.
The covenant remains legally intact.
The wedding photographs remain on the wall.
But tenderness slowly bleeds out.
One sarcastic comment.
One withheld apology.
One night of calculated rejection.
One retaliatory silence.
One act of selfishness.
One more score added to the ledger.
Until two people who once could not wait to touch each other cannot remember how to talk without defending themselves.
And somewhere the enemy whispers:
Good.
Because Satan does not necessarily need to destroy every Christian marriage through adultery.
Sometimes resentment will do.
Sometimes pride will do.
Sometimes years of unresolved rejection will do.
Sometimes pornography will do.
Sometimes selfishness will do.
Sometimes emotional neglect will do.
Sometimes the refusal to repent will do.
Sometimes two Christians can destroy intimacy while both remain convinced the other person is the problem.
That is why Paul’s warning in 1 Corinthians 7 is so sobering.
He understands that sexual intimacy is not spiritually irrelevant.
Marriage has vulnerabilities.
Temptation exists.
The enemy exploits fractures.
