The Bible repeats this warning because the most dangerous lie is not always the one you know is false—it is the one you have believed so deeply that you no longer think to question it.
There is a frightening possibility most of us would rather not consider.
You can be sincere… and sincerely wrong.
You can feel peaceful about something that is destroying you.
You can call bondage “freedom.”
You can rename compromise “growth.”
You can mistake applause for confirmation, emotion for revelation, popularity for truth, and religious activity for actually knowing Jesus.
You can even hold a Bible in your hands while resisting what the Bible is trying to tell you.
That is why three words keep appearing like warning lights throughout the New Testament:
Do not be deceived.
In Greek, Paul repeatedly writes:
μὴ πλανᾶσθε — mē planasthe.
“Do not be deceived.” “Do not be led astray.”

The expression appears in passages such as 1 Corinthians 6:9, 1 Corinthians 15:33, and Galatians 6:7. The verb belongs to the family of πλανάω — planaō, carrying the idea of wandering, straying, misleading, or being led away from the right path. In 1 Corinthians 6:9 the Greek text explicitly reads μὴ πλανᾶσθε.
That image matters.
Deception is not always someone grabbing you by the shoulders and announcing, “I am about to ruin your life.”
Sometimes deception simply gets you walking.
One step.
Then another.
Just a few degrees away from truth.
Nothing dramatic happens at first.
You still pray.
You still attend church.
You still post verses.
You still know Christian vocabulary.
You still say, “God knows my heart.”
But somewhere along the road, something changed.
The question stopped being, “Lord, is this true?”
It became, “How can I make this feel acceptable?”
The question stopped being, “What does Scripture say?”
It became, “What interpretation will let me keep what I do not want to surrender?”
And that is precisely why biblical warnings against deception are acts of mercy.
God warns us because deception, by definition, rarely announces itself as deception.
A deceived person normally does not wake up thinking, I am deceived.
They wake up thinking they can see clearly.
That is what makes the subject so terrifying.
And so personal.
Because this article is not primarily about “those people.”
It is about me.
It is about you.
It is about the uncomfortable possibility that there may be something we desperately want to believe because the truth would require something from us.
Jesus Himself warned His disciples this way.
When they asked Him about the signs surrounding His coming and the end of the age, His response begins:
Βλέπετε μή τις ὑμᾶς πλανήσῃ.
Blepete mē tis hymas planēsē.
The sense is: “See to it that no one leads you astray.”
That is Matthew 24:4, and the Greek text confirms the force of the warning: Βλέπετε carries the command to watch or take heed, while πλανήσῃ speaks of misleading or leading astray.
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not say deception would only threaten foolish people.
He was speaking to His disciples.
People who followed Him.
People who heard His teaching.
People who had seen His works.
Apparently, proximity to religious truth does not make vigilance unnecessary.
It makes vigilance essential.
And suddenly Scripture's repeated warnings begin making sense.
The Bible warns us about deception because human beings have an extraordinary capacity to believe what protects their desires.
We do it in relationships.
“They'll change.”
We do it with secret sin.
“I can stop whenever I want.”
We do it with bitterness.
“I've forgiven them. I just never want anything good to happen to them.”
We do it with pride.
“I'm not arrogant. I simply know I'm right.”
We do it with greed.
“I just want security.”
We do it with compromise.
“Everybody does it.”
We do it spiritually.
“God understands.”
Yes.
God understands perfectly.
And because He understands perfectly, He loves us enough to tell us the truth.
That is the part our generation desperately needs to recover.
Love and warning are not enemies.
Sometimes warning is love.
A physician who sees something dangerous on a scan does not prove compassion by hiding the diagnosis.
A father who sees his child walking toward traffic does not whisper, “I affirm your journey.”
He shouts.
Not because the child is hated.
Because the child is loved.
Scripture's “Do not be deceived” passages are the voice of divine love refusing to watch human beings walk peacefully toward destruction.
Consider Galatians 6:7.
Paul again begins with the warning:
Μὴ πλανᾶσθε — Mē planasthe.
Then comes the reality we spend much of our lives trying to negotiate:
God is not mocked. A person reaps what he sows.
There is something painfully ordinary about sowing.
Seeds are small.
That is why we underestimate them.
A private click.
A secret conversation.
A little dishonesty.
One more drink when you already know where this road goes.
One flirtation you insist is harmless.
One resentment rehearsed before bed.
One compromise nobody else knows about.
One morning without prayer becomes several.
One week without opening Scripture becomes months.
One excuse becomes a lifestyle.
Seeds.
Tiny things.
Then harvest comes.
And harvest always looks disproportionate until you remember how long the seeds were growing underground.
That is why “Do not be deceived” is not God trying to ruin your pleasure.
It is God standing at the edge of the field saying:
Please understand what these seeds become.
The same pattern appears with remarkable severity in 1 Corinthians 6.
Paul asks whether the Corinthians understand that the unrighteous will not inherit God's kingdom, and then says:
μὴ πλανᾶσθε — do not be deceived.
The warning is serious because sin is serious.
But stopping at verse 10 would mutilate Paul's message.
Because then comes verse 11.
And there, suddenly, the thunderstorm breaks open and grace comes pouring through.

Paul reminds these believers that some of them had been characterized by the very sins he had just named—but they had been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God.
Do you see it?
The Gospel does not say sin is imaginary.
The Gospel says sin does not have to have the final word.
Christianity does not save us by changing the definition of darkness.
Christ saves us by bringing us into the light.
Paul's message is not:
“Those terrible people over there should be ashamed.”
It is:
That was some of you.
Were.
There may not be a more beautiful past-tense word in the Christian life.
Were.
You were enslaved.
You were guilty.
You were wandering.
You were hiding.
You were living for yourself.
You were trying to satisfy a hunger with things that only made the hunger deeper.
You were carrying shame into rooms where nobody knew your name for it.
You were smiling in photographs while something inside you was collapsing.
You were pretending.
You were running.
You were lost.
But Jesus Christ entered the sentence.
And when Jesus enters the sentence, were becomes possible.
That is Christianity.
Not self-improvement.
Not religious cosmetics.
Not learning how to hide your wounds underneath church clothes.
Death and resurrection.
Guilt and justification.
Defilement and washing.
Slavery and freedom.
Scandal and grace.
Maybe that is why this subject hurts.
Because somewhere beneath our theological discussions, many of us already know where we have been deceiving ourselves.
You know the conversation you need to end.
You know the habit you keep deleting from your history but not from your life.
You know the resentment you have baptized as “discernment.”
You know whether your public Christianity resembles your private Christianity.
You know the thing you hope nobody ever asks about.
You know the prayer you are afraid to pray because you suspect obedience may cost you something.
Maybe your greatest deception is not that you stopped believing in God.
Maybe it is that you learned how to keep believing in God without allowing Him to contradict you.
Read that again.
Because deception does not always make an atheist.
Sometimes it makes a religious person who has placed himself on God's throne.
That is why Scripture must remain above us rather than beneath us.
If I only accept biblical truth when it agrees with me, Scripture is not my authority.
I am.
If Jesus is Lord only when His commands match my preferences, my preferences are actually lord.
The Gospel confronts that illusion.
Jesus did not come merely to decorate our existing identities with Christian vocabulary.
He calls us to Himself.
“Follow Me.”
Those words contain both death and life.
Death to self-rule.
Life in Christ.
Death to the illusion that I belong to myself.
Life under the King who loved me enough to give Himself for me.
This is why biblical repentance is so beautiful when properly understood.
Repentance is not purchasing forgiveness by becoming miserable enough.
Repentance is turning.
Coming home.
Dropping the weapon.
Opening the locked room.
Agreeing with God about the darkness because you have finally seen the Light standing in front of you.
And the Light has a name.
Jesus.
The Christian answer to deception is therefore not paranoia.
It is not spending your life obsessed with identifying everybody else's errors.
There is a strange irony in becoming an expert on everyone else's deception while remaining blind to your own pride.
The answer is Christ-centered vigilance.
Scripture.
Prayer.
Humility.
A teachable heart.
The fellowship of believers.
Testing what we hear rather than swallowing every spiritual-sounding claim.
And above everything else, abiding in Jesus Christ.
Because deception thrives wherever truth becomes negotiable.
This matters especially now.
We live in an age where algorithms learn what keeps our attention and repeatedly place similar material before us. Eventually, familiarity can begin to feel like confirmation.
But repetition does not make something true.
Virality does not make something true.
A million likes cannot turn falsehood into truth.
A preacher's confidence cannot make an interpretation biblical.
A Christian label cannot sanctify an idea.
Your feelings cannot rewrite God's character.
And this article should not receive a free pass either.
Check what you read here against Scripture.
Open the Bible.
Read the surrounding chapters.
Look at context.
Ask what the author actually intended to communicate.
Let Scripture correct the writer, the preacher, the influencer, the tradition, the culture—and you.
And me.
Especially me.
Because one of the safest prayers a Christian can pray may also be one of the most frightening:
“Jesus, show me where I am wrong.”
Not where they are wrong.
Where I am wrong.
Show me what I have excused.
Show me what I have renamed.
Show me where pride has disguised itself as conviction.
Show me where fear has disguised itself as wisdom.
Show me where bitterness has disguised itself as justice.
Show me where lust has disguised itself as love.
Show me where greed has disguised itself as ambition.
Show me where cowardice has disguised itself as peace.
Show me where religion has become a substitute for knowing You.
And then, Lord…
lead me home.
Perhaps you are reading this with something already rising inside you.
A memory.
A name.
A habit.
A compromise.
Something hidden.
Do not run from conviction.
But do not confuse conviction with hopeless condemnation either.
Look again at 1 Corinthians 6.
The warning is real.
The sin is real.
The consequences are real.
And then:
“Such were some of you.”
Grace does not deny the scandal.
Grace rewrites what happens after it.
Peter denied Jesus.
The thief beside Christ reached the final hours of a ruined life.
Paul had persecuted the church.
The Corinthians carried histories Paul could describe without pretending those histories were harmless.
Yet the center of Christianity has never been the impressive moral résumé of redeemed people.
The center is the crucified and risen Christ.
At Calvary, God did not shrug at sin.
Jesus bore judgment.
At the empty tomb, death did not receive the last word.
Christ rose.
And now forgiveness is not offered because sin does not matter.
Forgiveness is offered because Jesus Christ has done what sinners could never do for themselves.
That means you do not need to hide in order to come to Him.
You need to come honestly.
No performance.
No carefully edited testimony.
No spiritual résumé.
No pretending.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
Bring the real thing into the light.
The addiction.
The pride.
The sexual sin.
The secret messages.
The envy.
The unbelief.
The rage.
The greed.
The religious hypocrisy.
The years you wasted.
The thing you swore you would never do again and then did again.
Bring that person to Jesus.
Because that is the person who needs grace.
And grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace is the undeserved mercy of God that receives sinners and begins transforming them.
This is where “Do not be deceived” becomes unexpectedly beautiful.
God exposes the lie because He wants you free.
He tells you the road is wrong because there is still time to turn around.
He names the poison because He is offering life.
He turns the lights on because He is not afraid of what they reveal.
Jesus already knew the worst thing about you when He went to the cross.
You are not going to shock Him with your confession.
But you cannot experience the freedom of bringing something into His light while continually insisting that darkness is light.
So perhaps the question is no longer, “Why does Scripture say ‘Do not be deceived’ so often?”
Perhaps the question is:
What does God love us enough to keep warning us about?
The answer is devastating and beautiful.
He knows how easily we wander.
And He still calls wanderers home.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to explain the details publicly.
There is no shame in admitting you need prayer.
Someone reading silently may desperately need to discover that “such were some of you” can become their story too.
Send it privately to the believer who has been drifting.
Send it to the person asking hard questions.
Send it to the Christian who feels too ashamed to come home.
We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives of worship, obedience, love, generosity, and faithful stewardship.
Not because an algorithm is our savior.
Jesus is.
But because behind screens are real human beings.
Real marriages breaking.
Real teenagers confused.
Real Christians secretly drowning.
Real skeptics searching.
Real prodigals wondering whether God would still receive them.
Let that possibility make sharing feel less like promotion and more like mission.
We cannot force anybody to believe.
We cannot manipulate anybody into repentance.
We cannot save a soul.
But we can refuse to hide the light we have been given.
We can tell the truth.
We can point toward Christ.
We can say, “I was wandering too.”
We can say, “Jesus found me.”
We can say, “There is still mercy.”
We can say, “Come home.”
And when Scripture says “Do not be deceived,” perhaps we should finally hear the heart behind the warning.
Not the voice of a God searching for an excuse to reject sinners.
The voice of the Shepherd calling wandering sheep away from the cliff.
Truth is not always comfortable.
But neither is a surgeon's knife.
Some wounds heal because somebody loved us enough to cut away what was killing us.
So when God's Word exposes you, do not immediately silence the discomfort.
Ask what the discomfort is revealing.
Open Scripture.
Look at Jesus.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive the grace you cannot earn.
Then get up and follow Him.
Because the most frightening deception may be believing you are safe while wandering away from Christ.
And one of the sweetest moments of grace is discovering that when the truth finally exposes where you have wandered…
the Shepherd is already calling your name.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Do Some Christians Act Worse Than Unbelievers?
paragraphs: Why Do Some Christians Act Worse Than Unbelievers?

The scandal is not that sinners sin. The scandal is when people carry the name of Christ while refusing the transforming rule of Christ—and Jesus warned us not to confuse religious language with a surrendered life.
There is a particular kind of wound that is difficult to explain to someone who has never experienced it.
It is the wound of being hurt by someone who prayed before they hurt you.
Someone who quoted Scripture before they lied about you.
Someone who lifted their hands in worship on Sunday and used those same hands to destroy someone's reputation on Monday.
Someone who knows exactly when to say, “God bless you,” but somehow never learned how to say, “I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
Maybe that person was a pastor.
Maybe a ministry leader.
Maybe a parent who knew the Bible but made home feel like a battlefield.
Maybe a Christian spouse who demanded forgiveness while refusing repentance.
Maybe a church member who could identify false doctrine faster than they could identify pride in their own heart.
Or perhaps the most uncomfortable possibility is this:
Maybe sometimes...
that person has been you.
That is where this question becomes dangerous.
Because it is easy to ask, “Why do some Christians act worse than unbelievers?” while quietly imagining somebody else.
Jesus has a way of turning the mirror around.
And suddenly the question is no longer:
“What is wrong with those Christians?”
It becomes:
“Jesus... is there anything in me that carries Your name but does not resemble Your heart?”
That prayer can change a life.
Because Scripture never teaches that merely adopting the Christian label automatically makes someone spiritually mature.
Jesus said something far more frightening.
“Not everyone who says to Me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven...” — Matthew 7:21.
The Greek begins:
Οὐ πᾶς ὁ λέγων μοι, Κύριε κύριε...
Ou pas ho legōn moi, Kyrie kyrie...
Literally, the force is unmistakable: not everyone saying to Me, “Lord, Lord...” will enter.
The repeated Κύριε, κύριε — Kyrie, kyrie — “Lord, Lord” is especially sobering.
These are not people presented as atheists mocking Jesus.
They are addressing Him as Lord.
Religious vocabulary is present.
Recognition is present.
Yet Jesus continues by contrasting merely saying with ποιῶν — poiōn, “doing,” the will of His Father.

That does not mean we earn salvation by accumulating enough good behavior. Scripture is clear that salvation is by grace through faith, not our works (Ephesians 2:8–9). But the very next verse says we are created in Christ Jesus for good works (Ephesians 2:10).
Works are not the price paid to purchase salvation.
A transformed life is the fruit expected from union with the Savior.
That distinction matters enormously.
A tree is not alive because somebody taped fruit onto its branches.
Fruit appears because life exists inside it.
And Christianity without Christ's transforming life eventually becomes exactly that—
plastic fruit hanging from a dying tree.
It can look convincing from a distance.
Come closer.
There is no fragrance.
No softness.
No life.
And this helps answer the question.
Some people identify as Christians culturally but have never truly surrendered themselves to Christ.
Some may possess genuine faith yet remain painfully immature, inconsistent, undisciplined, or trapped in patterns they have not brought fully under the lordship of Jesus.
Some know theology while resisting obedience.
Some have learned Christian performance without Christian character.
And some may genuinely belong to Christ while going through seasons of serious failure from which God is calling them to repentance.
Those categories must not be carelessly confused.
A Christian committing a terrible sin does not automatically prove that person was never saved.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
David committed horrifying sins involving adultery, deception, and bloodshed.
The Corinthian church contained jealousy, division, sexual immorality, lawsuits, selfishness and disorder.
The Bible does not airbrush God's people.
That is one reason Scripture is so painfully believable.
Its heroes bleed.
Its leaders collapse.
Its saints sometimes make decisions that leave you wondering how someone who knew God could wander so far.
But Scripture also refuses to rename darkness just because a believer committed it.
Sin remains sin.
And grace never becomes permission to protect it.
David's story did not end with God saying, “Nobody is perfect.”
Nathan confronted him:
“You are the man.”
Peter's denial was not excused.
Peter wept bitterly.
The Corinthians were not told that grace meant continuing comfortably in their corruption.
Paul confronted them because Christ had called them into something radically different.
This is where one of the most beautiful sentences in the New Testament appears.
After describing lifestyles incompatible with God's kingdom, Paul turns toward the Corinthian believers and writes:
καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε...
Kai tauta tines ēte...
“And such were some of you.”
Notice the word that carries enormous Gospel weight:
ἦτε — ēte.
“Were.”
Not “this is your permanent identity.”
Not “Jesus found you there, so remain there.”
Were.
Then Paul unleashes three enormous declarations:
ἀπελούσασθε... ἡγιάσθητε... ἐδικαιώθητε...
You were washed.
You were sanctified.
You were justified.

“In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.” — 1 Corinthians 6:11. The Greek grammatical forms reinforce Paul's backward-looking declaration: something decisive has happened to these believers because of Christ.
That is Christianity.
Not “I found religion.”
Not “I started posting Bible verses.”
Not “I joined the correct denomination.”
Not “I learned Christian vocabulary.”
Not “I became better at hiding my sins.”
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
Jesus does not merely give sinners a religious costume.
He gives sinners a new relationship with God.
And by His Spirit, He begins making them new.
That transformation is often progressive, messy and painful. Christians still stumble. Christians still need confession. Christians still battle the flesh. Christians still need correction.
But there is a difference between fighting sin and making peace with sin.
There is a difference between falling into mud and building your house there.
There is a difference between crying, “Jesus, rescue me from this,” and saying, “Jesus, stop interfering with this.”
The Christian life is not sinless perfection.
But neither is it comfortable surrender to sin.
That may explain something you have seen.
You met an unbeliever who was generous, patient and compassionate.
Then you met a professing Christian who was arrogant, dishonest and cruel.
And something inside you whispered:
“If Christianity is true, why is that unbeliever behaving better than the Christian?”

First, Christianity never teaches that unbelievers are incapable of admirable moral actions, natural affection, generosity, courage or civic virtue. Human beings remain God's image-bearers, even though humanity is fallen.
Second, Christianity does not claim that every person using the word “Christian” is therefore regenerated, mature, obedient or even genuinely Christ's.
Jesus Himself warned against false profession.
Third—and this may be the part Christians most desperately need to hear—the hypocrisy of God's people can do catastrophic damage to God's reputation among those watching.
Paul writes in Romans 2:24:
τὸ γὰρ ὄνομα τοῦ Θεοῦ δι’ ὑμᾶς βλασφημεῖται ἐν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν...
To gar onoma tou Theou di’ hymas blasphēmeitai en tois ethnesin...
“For the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.”

The key word βλασφημεῖται — blasphēmeitai means “is blasphemed,” “spoken against,” or “reviled.” Paul was confronting people who possessed religious knowledge while violating the very truth they claimed to teach.
Read that again slowly.
People were looking at religious hypocrisy...
and God's name was being dishonored.
That should terrify every Christian with a platform.
Including this one.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody may be deciding what they think about Christianity by watching somebody who claims to follow Christ.
A child is watching how Dad treats Mom after church.
A waitress is watching the table that prayed loudly before the meal.
An employee is watching the manager with the Bible verse on the office wall.
An unbelieving husband is watching whether his newly converted wife has become more gracious or merely more judgmental.
A teenager is watching whether Mom's Christianity produces humility when Mom is wrong.
Your family is watching.
Your coworkers are watching.
Your Facebook friends are watching.
Not because Christians must perform perfection for an audience.
But because the Gospel we proclaim with our mouths should increasingly become visible through our lives.
And when we fail?
We repent.
Quickly.
Honestly.
Without public-relations language.
Without blaming the victim.
Without saying, “I'm sorry you felt hurt.”
Without hiding behind “God knows my heart.”
Yes.
God knows your heart.
That is precisely why repentance matters.
Sometimes the most powerful Christian witness is not pretending you never failed.
Sometimes it is looking someone in the eyes and saying:
“I sinned against you. What I did was wrong. There is no excuse. Will you forgive me?”
Imagine what would happen if Christians became famous for that.
Not perfection.
Repentance.
Not pretending.
Confession.
Not defending every failure.
Running back to Jesus.
Because repentance is not humiliation designed to destroy you.
Repentance is the doorway through which grace brings you home.
And perhaps you are reading this from the other side of the wound.
A Christian hurt you.
Badly.
Maybe they manipulated you using Scripture.
Maybe church became the place where you learned to hide pain instead of heal from it.
Maybe someone preached grace publicly and became merciless privately.
Maybe you walked away thinking:
“If this is Christianity, I don't want it.”
Please hear something that may separate Jesus from the people who misrepresented Him:
Jesus was never impressed by religious hypocrisy either.
Some of His strongest words were directed not toward visibly broken sinners begging for mercy, but toward religious people who polished the outside while corruption remained within.
So do not confuse the person who wounded you with the Christ whose name they carried.
Judge Jesus by Jesus.
Look at Him.
Watch Him kneel beside the condemned.
Watch Him touch the unclean.
Watch Him confront hypocrites.
Watch Him welcome children.
Watch Him weep.
Watch Him wash feet.
Watch Him forgive His executioners.
Then watch Him walk toward a cross carrying sins He never committed.
There hangs the answer to both self-righteous religion and hopeless rebellion.
Jesus.
Bloodied.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Crucified.
Not because human beings were already good enough.
Because we weren't.
Christianity begins with an offensive confession:
I need saving too.
The cross leaves no room for Christian superiority.
How could I look down on another sinner while kneeling before a Savior who had to bleed for mine?
The ground beneath the cross destroys boasting.
The respectable church member needs Jesus.
The addict needs Jesus.
The preacher needs Jesus.
The prostitute needs Jesus.
The skeptic needs Jesus.
The person reading this secretly ashamed of last night's sin needs Jesus.
And the person thinking, “Thankfully this article describes somebody else”...
needs Jesus.
All of us come empty-handed.
That is why the Gospel is simultaneously devastating and beautiful.
It tells you the truth about your sin without telling you that your sin must have the final word.
Maybe your scandal is pride.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe adultery.
Maybe gossip dressed as “concern.”
Maybe greed dressed as ambition.
Maybe unforgiveness disguised as boundaries.
Maybe cruelty disguised as discernment.
Maybe you know how to expose everybody else's false doctrine while your own heart has become cold.
Maybe you have mastered looking Christian while privately drifting miles from Christ.
Jesus already knows.
There is nothing hidden in your browser history, your bedroom, your bank account, your conversations, your imagination or your heart that will surprise Him.
And still the invitation of the Gospel remains:
Repent.
Come home.
Not because your sin is small.
Because His grace is greater.
Repentance does not mean merely feeling terrible about yourself.
Biblically, repentance involves a genuine turning—a changed mind and direction toward God that bears fruit in life.
You stop negotiating with the thing Jesus died to free you from.
You bring it into the light.
You confess.
You ask forgiveness where appropriate.
You make restitution where possible.
You seek accountability.
You cut off what feeds the darkness.
And when you fall, you do not run away from Christ because you are ashamed.
You run toward Him because He is your only hope.
That is the difference grace makes.
Grace is not God lowering holiness until our rebellion becomes acceptable.
Grace is God meeting guilty people in Christ, forgiving them through Christ, giving them His Spirit, and beginning the lifelong work of making them increasingly like Christ.
From scandal...
to grace.
That is our story.
Not because Christians never make scandals.
History proves otherwise.
Our churches prove otherwise.
Our own hearts prove otherwise.
But Jesus specializes in taking people whose stories appear ruined and writing something no human being could have predicted.
Peter became more than the night he denied Jesus.
The Corinthians became more than what they had been.
Paul became more than the persecutor he once was.
And if you belong to Christ, your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter either.
But you must stop handing the pen back to your sin.
Maybe this article made you think of a hypocritical Christian.
Before you send it to them, sit with it yourself.
Ask:
“Jesus, where am I pretending?”
“Where have my words and my life separated?”
“Whom have I wounded?”
“What am I defending that You are asking me to surrender?”
“What would repentance actually cost me?”
Then become quiet enough to hear the answer.
No performance.
No elaborate explanation required.
Just honesty.
Someone reading the comments may realize they are not fighting alone.
There may be a night when you need these words again.
Send it privately to someone who needs to know that Jesus is still worth following even when His followers fail to represent Him well.
It does not.
It cannot.
We glorify God through Christ-centered obedience, worship, generosity and love—not by purchasing access to a page.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical expression of stewardship when you prayerfully believe that work is helping people encounter Scripture, repentance, grace and Jesus Christ.
Because maybe they do not need another Christian pretending Christians never fail.
Maybe they need to encounter Christians who know exactly what to do when they do.
Confess.
Repent.
Return.
Forgive.
Make things right.
And cling desperately to Jesus.
It deserves to see Christians becoming like Christ.
And before you leave, remember the question we started with:
Why do some Christians act worse than unbelievers?
Sometimes because the Christian label is not the same thing as conversion.
Sometimes because genuine Christians can become immature, compromised and grievously sinful when they stop walking faithfully with Christ.
Sometimes because sanctification is unfinished.
Sometimes because religious knowledge can coexist with astonishing hypocrisy.
But none of those realities overturn the Gospel.
They demonstrate why every one of us desperately needs it.
Christianity was never the announcement that Christians are better people.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God because Jesus Christ died for sins and rose again—and that those who belong to Him are called into a new life under His lordship.
So when Christians fail, do not lower Christ to the level of our failure.
Call Christians upward to Christ.
And when you fail, do not rewrite Scripture to protect your sin.
Let Jesus rewrite you.
Because the greatest evidence for Christianity is not a Christian who claims, “Look how perfect I have become.”
It is a sinner who can say:
“Look what Jesus is doing with someone like me.”
And perhaps that is the sentence somebody desperately needs tonight.
Your failure may explain yesterday.
Your wound may explain why you ran.
Your hypocrisy may need confession.
Your sin may require painful repentance.
Your consequences may not disappear overnight.
But if you will bring the truth into the light and come to Jesus, the scandal does not have to write the ending.
The hands that were pierced for your sin are still capable of turning your ugliest chapter into a testimony of grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “ONLY GOD CAN JUDGE ME”—BUT WHAT IF GOD SENT SOMEONE TO WARN YOU?
paragraphs:
“ONLY GOD CAN JUDGE ME”—BUT WHAT IF GOD SENT SOMEONE TO WARN YOU?
The sentence that sounds like spiritual confidence can become one of the most dangerous hiding places for a heart that no longer wants to be corrected.
There is a sentence people say when the truth gets too close.
Sometimes it comes with anger.
Sometimes with a laugh.
Sometimes with a Bible verse attached to it.
Sometimes with tears in the eyes and years of church hurt underneath it.
“Only God can judge me.”
And there is something absolutely true inside those words.

God alone knows the whole heart. God alone possesses perfect knowledge. God alone is the final Judge. No pastor, parent, friend, stranger, church member, or social-media commentator sits on the throne of God.
Scripture says plainly:
“So then every one of us shall give account of himself to God.” — Romans 14:12
Yes.
You will answer to God.
So will I.
But there is a frightening question hiding behind that truth:
What if the God you say is the only One allowed to judge you is the very God using Scripture—and perhaps another believer—to correct you before your choices destroy something precious?
What if you keep asking God to speak...
while rejecting every voice that tells you something you do not want to hear?
That changes the conversation.
Because sometimes “Only God can judge me” does not mean, “I humbly recognize God's authority.”
Sometimes it means:
“Nobody gets to tell me I'm wrong.”
And those are not the same thing.
Not even close.
Jesus did say:

Μὴ κρίνετε, ἵνα μὴ κριθῆτε.
Mē krinete, hina mē krithēte.
“Judge not, that you be not judged.” — Matthew 7:1
Those words are real. They are sacred. They must never be explained away merely because they make religious people uncomfortable.
The Greek verb translated “judge” is κρίνω (krinō), a word that can carry the ideas of judging, deciding, distinguishing, or condemning depending upon context.
And context matters enormously.
Jesus was not handing humanity a divine commandment that says, “Never recognize anything as sinful.”
How could He?
Only a few verses later, Jesus warns about false prophets and says:
“Ye shall know them by their fruits.” — Matthew 7:16
Recognizing fruit requires discernment.
Jesus also taught:
“Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.” — John 7:24
So Christ cannot mean, “Never make a moral evaluation of anything anyone does.”
Matthew 7 is attacking something uglier.
Hypocritical judgment.
The person examining the speck in someone else's eye while ignoring the beam in his own.
Jesus continues:
“And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?” — Matthew 7:3
Then notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not say the speck should remain there forever because removing it would be “judgmental.”
He says:
“Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye.” — Matthew 7:5
Read that slowly.
First your eye. Then your brother's.
Repentance before correction.
Humility before confrontation.
Self-examination before intervention.
Jesus does not abolish loving correction.
He abolishes the arrogance that makes correction cruel.
That distinction could save relationships.
It could save churches.
It could save marriages.
And for somebody reading this, it might expose the excuse that has kept you running from God.
Because maybe somebody confronted you.
About the affair.
The secret messages.
The bitterness.
The addiction.
The dishonesty.
The gossip.
The relationship pulling you away from Christ.
The pride nobody is allowed to mention.
The habit you keep defending because surrender would cost too much.
The version of Christianity where Jesus is Savior but apparently never Lord.
And something inside you immediately became defensive.
“Don't judge me.”
Maybe the person correcting you really was arrogant.
That happens.
Christians can mishandle truth terribly.
Some people do not correct because they love you; they correct because exposing your weakness makes them feel stronger.
Some weaponize Scripture.
Some gossip and call it “discernment.”
Some humiliate and call it “accountability.”
Some seem almost excited when another believer falls.
That is not the spirit of Christ.
Biblical correction was never intended to become spiritual target practice.
Paul gives us one of Scripture's clearest pictures of what correction should look like:
“Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.” — Galatians 6:1
The Greek becomes especially beautiful here.
καταρτίζετε τὸν τοιοῦτον ἐν πνεύματι πραΰτητος
katartizete ton toiouton en pneumati prautētos
At the heart of the command is καταρτίζετε (katartizete), from katartizō—to restore, repair, put into proper condition, mend.
That changes the atmosphere completely.
The goal is not:
“Destroy the sinner.”
It is:
“Restore the person who has fallen.”
The objective of biblical correction is not humiliation.
It is restoration.
Not superiority.
Restoration.
Not public entertainment.
Restoration.
Not winning an argument.
Restoration.
And Paul immediately places that restoration inside πνεύματι πραΰτητος — pneumati prautētos:
a spirit of gentleness.
Then comes the warning to the corrector: watch yourself, because you can be tempted too.
In other words, the person confronting sin should approach another believer almost trembling with awareness:
“Without the grace of Jesus, I am capable of falling too.”
That is biblical correction.
It has tears in its eyes.
It remembers the cross.
It does not stand above the fallen person.
It kneels beside them and points toward home.
But here is where this becomes uncomfortable.
The fact that someone corrected you badly does not automatically mean what they said was false.
Sometimes we focus on the messenger's tone because we do not want to face the message.
“They shouldn't have said it like that.”
Maybe.
“They don't know everything I've been through.”
Probably.
“They've made mistakes too.”
Certainly.
“They're not God.”
Absolutely.
But...
Was what they said true?
That is the question pride desperately wants to avoid.
Because a flawed messenger can still deliver a true warning.
If somebody screams that your house is burning, you do not stay inside because you dislike their tone.
You check for smoke.
And sometimes grace sounds like an alarm.
Proverbs says:
“Open rebuke is better than secret love. Faithful are the wounds of a friend...” — Proverbs 27:5–6
Faithful wounds.
What an uncomfortable phrase.
Because we have been trained to assume love should always feel pleasant.
Scripture refuses to reduce love to comfort.
Sometimes love embraces you.
Sometimes love feeds you.
Sometimes love sits beside you while you cry.
And sometimes love looks directly into your eyes and says:
“You cannot keep doing this to yourself.”
The wound is not the destination.
Healing is.
A surgeon cuts because something must be removed.
A loving friend confronts because something precious is being endangered.
And Jesus Himself demonstrated a kind of grace far deeper than the modern counterfeit that says grace means nobody ever confronts sin.
Think of the woman caught in adultery in John 8.
She was dragged into public shame.
Her sin became somebody else's spectacle.
Religious men surrounded her with accusations.
Then Jesus intervened.
“He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her.” — John 8:7
One by one, the accusers disappeared.
Then Jesus spoke to her.
No stone.
No mob.
No humiliation.
No denial of her humanity.
But also...
no celebration of her sin.
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” — John 8:11
There is the Gospel rhythm.
“Neither do I condemn thee.”
Grace.
“Go, and sin no more.”
Transformation.
Jesus did not say, “Your choices do not matter.”
He did not say, “Live your truth.”
He did not say, “Anyone who calls this sin is toxic.”
He rescued her from condemnation and called her away from sin.
Because Jesus loves too deeply to leave people chained to what He came to free them from.
That is where “Only God can judge me” becomes terrifying.
Because yes...
God judges.
And God has already spoken about sin.
If I use “Only God can judge me” to silence every biblical correction, I may actually be saying:
“I only want God to speak when He agrees with me.”
But Jesus is not a supporting character in the story of our self-expression.
He is Lord.
He does not exist to validate everything we desire.
He came to save us from sin, reconcile us to God, give us new life, and transform us into His likeness.
And transformation requires the death of something.
Pride.
Self-rule.
Secret sin.
Excuses.
Sometimes even the identity we constructed around our wounds.
This is why correction hurts so badly.
It threatens the version of ourselves we have worked hardest to protect.
Maybe your anger became your armor.
Maybe promiscuity became proof that somebody still desired you.
Maybe alcohol became the only place your mind became quiet.
Maybe pornography became the room where loneliness temporarily disappeared.
Maybe money became your security.
Maybe bitterness became the last connection you had to the person who hurt you.
Maybe religious performance became the mask hiding how spiritually exhausted you really are.
Then somebody touched that wound.
And you called it judgment.
But somewhere beneath the defensiveness...
you knew.
You knew God had been dealing with you already.
That is why the words hurt so much.
Not every accusation deserves your agreement.
Not every critic deserves access to your life.
Not every opinion is biblical correction.
But when correction agrees with Scripture, is offered toward restoration, and exposes something the Holy Spirit has already been pressing upon your conscience...
do not reject medicine simply because it tastes bitter.
David understood this posture.
“Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness: and let him reprove me; it shall be an excellent oil...” — Psalm 141:5
Imagine becoming spiritually mature enough to say:
“If I am wrong, love me enough to tell me.”
That prayer is dangerous.
Because God may answer it.
He may use your spouse.
Your pastor.
Your child.
Your closest friend.
A sermon.
A verse you have read fifty times.
A conversation you wish had never happened.
Or perhaps even these words on your screen right now.
Not because God hates you.
Because He refuses to abandon you to the thing destroying you.
Hebrews says:
“For whom the Lord loveth he chasteneth...” — Hebrews 12:6
Correction is not proof that grace has disappeared.
Sometimes correction is proof that grace is pursuing you.
And perhaps this is where your story turns.
Not when everybody finally approves of you.
Not when your critics disappear.
Not when you become perfect.
But when you finally become honest.
“I have sinned.”
Three words pride hates.
Three words grace welcomes.
Because Christianity does not begin with pretending you are innocent.
It begins with recognizing you need a Savior.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
All.
The person being corrected.
The person doing the correcting.
The pastor.
The addict.
The betrayed spouse.
The betrayer.
The religious person.
The rebel.
You.
Me.
That levels the room.
And then the Gospel does something scandalous.
Christ enters it.
Jesus did not die for imaginary sinners.
He died for guilty ones.
He did not wait for humanity to become respectable enough to deserve salvation.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8
At the cross, sin is taken more seriously than we ever wanted...
and sinners are loved more deeply than we ever imagined.
The cross tells you your sin is so serious that the Son of God went to Calvary.
The cross also tells you His mercy is so astonishing that He went willingly.
That is why repentance is not humiliation.
Repentance is coming home.
The Greek New Testament uses μετάνοια (metanoia) for repentance—the idea of a changed mind that issues in a changed direction.
Repentance says:
“I was defending what Jesus wanted to deliver me from.”
“I called conviction judgment.”
“I called rebellion freedom.”
“I called accountability control.”
“I demanded grace while refusing surrender.”
“But Jesus...
I am done running.”
And perhaps somebody reading this has been running for years.
You still attend church.
Still post verses.
Still know worship songs.
Still say you love God.
But there is one room in your heart with a locked door.
Jesus can have everything except that.
And whenever someone gets close to it...
“Don't judge me.”
What if Jesus is standing at that door tonight?
Not with a stone.
With scars.
Not saying, “You are beyond redemption.”
Saying:
“Give Me the key.”
This is the scandal of grace.
Jesus already knows what is behind the door.
You cannot shock the One who carried your sin to Calvary.
You cannot confess something He did not know when He chose the cross.
The question is not whether Jesus knows.
The question is whether you will finally stop hiding.
Be honest.
Maybe that becomes your prayer.
Not “God, prove everybody wrong.”
Not “God, remove everyone who challenges me.”
But:
“Jesus, correct me wherever I am wrong. Give me enough humility to receive truth and enough discernment to reject condemnation. Search me. Restore me. Change me.”
And if you know someone who keeps confusing correction with condemnation, share this with them—but share it carefully.
Do not send it as a weapon.
Send it as an invitation.
“I need this too.”
That kind of sharing glorifies God far more than spiritual finger-pointing ever could.

Salvation cannot be purchased, and generosity does not make God owe us anything. We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ. But believers can freely choose to support Gospel-centered work so more people can be reached, discipled, encouraged, and pointed toward Christ.
Someone scrolling tonight may be one sentence away from finally surrendering something that has been destroying them quietly.
Invite your family. Invite struggling believers. Invite seekers. Invite lukewarm Christians. Invite the friend who does not even believe yet.
Because the mission was never to build an audience that applauds us.
It is to point people toward Christ.
And perhaps that begins with one final distinction.
When someone condemns you, they are effectively saying:
“There is no hope for you.”
But biblical correction says:
“This cannot continue because, in Christ, there is something better for you.”
Condemnation pushes you away from the cross.
Conviction pulls you toward it.
Condemnation says, “Hide.”
Jesus says, “Come.”
Condemnation says, “You are finished.”
Jesus says, “Repent and follow Me.”
And that is why the Christian response cannot simply be:
“Only God can judge me.”
A more humble response is:
“God will judge me—so while there is still time, Lord, teach me to receive the correction that leads me closer to You.”
Because one day there will be no Facebook arguments.
No carefully curated image.
No defensive captions.
No crowd to impress.
No reputation to protect.
No “they don't understand me.”
Every one of us will stand before God.
And on that day, your greatest hope will not be that nobody ever corrected you.
Your only hope will be Jesus Christ.
The One who was pierced for sinners.
The One who receives the repentant.
The One whose blood cleanses.
The One who forgives.
The One who restores.
The One who can take the ugliest chapter you thought would define your entire life and write something you never believed could come afterward.
Grace.
Redemption.
Restoration.
A new beginning.
So if God sends truth into your life today...
do not shoot the messenger before checking your heart.
Maybe the correction you wanted to reject is not God trying to shame you.
Maybe it is mercy knocking before consequences kick the door down.
And if Jesus is knocking...
please...
open.
Because sometimes the sentence that hurts your pride today becomes the warning you thank God for the rest of your life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WATER WAS NEVER THE END: Noah’s Flood, the Red Sea, Baptism—and the God Who Brings New Life Through What Should Have Buried You
paragraphs: THE WATER WAS NEVER THE END: Noah’s Flood, the Red Sea, Baptism—and the God Who Brings New Life Through What Should Have Buried You

From Noah stepping into a world washed clean, to slaves walking out of the sea as a liberated people, to the waters of baptism pointing us to the death and resurrection of Jesus—Scripture keeps bringing us back to water. Not because water itself is the Savior, but because God keeps using it to tell the same breathtaking story: judgment is real, bondage is real, death is real… but in Jesus Christ, death does not get the final word.
There is something terrifying about deep water.
You cannot negotiate with it.

You cannot breathe beneath it indefinitely. You cannot command it to move because you have plans tomorrow. When it rises above your head, all the strength you thought you possessed suddenly feels very small.
Maybe that is one reason water appears at some of the most dramatic turning points in Scripture.
Noah saw water erase the world he knew.
Israel saw water blocking the only escape from Pharaoh.
And centuries later, followers of Jesus willingly stepped into water and came back out confessing that their old allegiance was finished and that their life now belonged to Christ.
Different moments.
Different covenants and circumstances.
And we must not flatten their distinctions or pretend every appearance of water in Scripture means exactly the same thing.
Yet the biblical writers themselves connect these events in remarkable ways.
The apostle Paul looks back at Israel passing through the sea and says they were “baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:1–2).
Peter looks back at Noah, the ark, and the Flood and deliberately connects that event with baptism (1 Peter 3:20–21).
Then Paul explains Christian baptism through an even greater reality: union with Jesus Christ in His death and resurrection.
Suddenly, the pattern becomes difficult to ignore.
Water.
Judgment.
Deliverance.
An old existence left behind.
A new beginning on the other side.
And standing at the center of the entire story is not Noah.
Not Moses.
Not even the water.
Jesus Christ.
Because the deepest Christian hope has never been that God will help us become slightly improved versions of ourselves.
The Gospel announces something far more radical:
the sinner can die with Christ…
and rise with Christ into new life.
But before we reach the baptismal waters, go backward.
Far backward.
Back to a world drowning morally before it ever drowned physically.

Genesis describes humanity before the Flood in devastating terms. Human wickedness had become great, and the inclination of the human heart was continually evil (Genesis 6:5). Violence filled the earth. Corruption spread through humanity.
Then Scripture introduces a Hebrew word that carries enormous weight in Noah’s story:
מַבּוּל — mabbûl
Flood.
Not a sentimental rainstorm.
Not a children's nursery scene with smiling giraffes peeking through an ark window.
Judgment.
Genesis refuses to romanticize human rebellion. The Flood narrative confronts us with something modern people often desperately want Christianity to stop saying:
Sin matters.
Evil matters.
What human beings do with the life God gives them matters.
A holy God does not look at violence, corruption, cruelty and rebellion and shrug.
Yet right inside this terrifying account comes one of Scripture's great interruptions:
“But Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD” (Genesis 6:8).
The Hebrew word translated “favor” or “grace” is חֵן — ḥēn.
Grace appears in a story of judgment.
Hold onto that.
Because that tension will eventually take us all the way to Calvary.
Noah did not survive because humanity had suddenly become innocent. God provided a means of preservation.
An ark.
And after the waters receded, Noah eventually stepped onto ground beneath a sky carrying the sign of God's covenant.
The world Noah entered was not the world he had left.
Water had become a boundary between what was before and what came afterward.
But Noah's new beginning was not yet humanity's final answer.
Because something survived the Flood that water could never wash from the human heart.
Sin.
Noah's descendants would demonstrate it.
So would Israel.
So would David.
So would Peter.
So would you.
So would I.
That is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
We often want God to change our circumstances when the deeper problem lives inside us.
We imagine, “If God would just get me out of this situation, everything would finally be different.”
A different marriage.
A different job.
A different city.
More money.
Less pressure.
Better health.
A second chance.
And sometimes God does change circumstances.
But you can walk into a completely new environment carrying the same old heart.
Noah's Flood demonstrates that judgment alone cannot transform the human heart.
Humanity needed something greater than another restart.
We needed redemption.
Now move forward.
Night.
Egypt.
A terrified nation trapped between Pharaoh's army and the sea.
Imagine being an Israelite parent.
You hear horses.
Chariot wheels.
Shouting.
Your children are beside you.
Behind you is the empire that enslaved your people.
In front of you is water.
There is nowhere to go.
Maybe you know that feeling.
Not literally standing before a sea, but trapped between something you cannot return to and something you cannot cross.
You prayed.
Nothing moved.
You obeyed as best you knew how.
Nothing opened.
You thought following God would make the road clearer, but somehow obedience brought you to a place where there appears to be no road at all.
Then Moses stretches out his hand.
Exodus says:
וַיִּבָּקְעוּ הַמָּיִם — vayyibbāqəʿû hammāyim
“The waters were divided.”
And Israel walks through the sea on יַבָּשָׁה — yabbāšâ—dry ground.
Think about that.
God did not merely show Israel a philosophical argument explaining why they should trust Him.
He made a road where there wasn't one.
They entered the sea as slaves being hunted by Pharaoh.
They emerged on the other side as a people whom God had delivered.
The water that appeared to be their grave became the boundary of their liberation.
And what chased them could not follow them into their future.

That does not mean every painful situation in your life will end the way you want. Scripture never promises believers a life without suffering. Some faithful Christians have suffered terribly and died without seeing earthly circumstances reversed.
Christian hope is deeper than “everything will work out exactly as I imagined.”
Christian hope says that if you belong to Christ, even death itself cannot prevent God from bringing you home.
That is stronger.
Because eventually every earthly rescue ends at another shoreline called death.
And that is precisely why we need Jesus.
Paul later reaches back toward the Exodus and writes that Israel was “baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:2).
Then Peter makes an equally startling connection with Noah.
After speaking of those preserved through the Flood, he writes in Greek:
ὃ καὶ ὑμᾶς ἀντίτυπον νῦν σῴζει βάπτισμα
The crucial word is ἀντίτυπον — antitypon.
A corresponding reality.
A counterpart.
Peter deliberately connects the Flood waters with baptism.
But then he immediately guards his meaning.
Baptism is “not the removal of dirt from the body,” but an appeal or pledge of a good conscience toward God, and Peter anchors the entire statement in one decisive reality:
δι’ ἀναστάσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ — di’ anastaseōs Iēsou Christou
“through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.”
That final phrase matters enormously.
Christian baptism is not magic water.
The water does not possess independent saving power.
Peter refuses to let us reduce baptism to an external bath. Its saving significance cannot be separated from Jesus Christ and His resurrection.

And here Christians from different traditions sometimes explain the precise sacramental relationship between baptism and salvation differently. We should acknowledge that rather than pretending centuries of theological discussion do not exist.
But every faithful reading must preserve what Peter himself preserves:
the center is Jesus Christ.
The resurrection is the power.
The Gospel is the reality.
Baptism points beyond itself to what God has done in Christ.
Paul makes that Christ-centered meaning breathtakingly clear in Romans 6.
When believers are baptized into Christ Jesus, Paul connects baptism with His death. He speaks of being buried with Christ and then walking in καινότης ζωῆς — kainotēs zōēs:
“newness of life.”
There it is again.
A boundary.
Before.
After.
Death.
Life.
But this time we have reached the heart of what all those earlier deliverances could only anticipate.
Noah needed an ark.
Israel needed a path through the sea.
You need a Savior.
And His name is Jesus.
The Gospel is not that decent people can clean themselves up enough for God to accept them.
The Gospel begins with much worse news.
We have sinned.
Not merely “made mistakes.”
Sinned.

We have loved things God hates and resisted things God loves. We have hidden pride beneath religion, lust beneath secrecy, bitterness beneath smiles, greed beneath ambition, unbelief beneath sophistication and self-righteousness beneath morality.
Some of us became experts at looking dry while drowning inside.
Nobody knew about the browser history.
Nobody knew about the messages.
Nobody knew how much you drank when nobody was watching.
Nobody knew about the resentment.
Nobody knew how jealous you became.
Nobody knew you had begun questioning whether God even wanted you anymore.
You still posted the verse.
Still went to church.
Still said, “I'm blessed.”
Still smiled when somebody asked how you were doing.
But underneath?
Water rising.
And perhaps the most exhausting part wasn't the sin itself anymore.
It was maintaining the version of you that nobody was allowed to discover was struggling.
Listen carefully.
Jesus did not come for the fictional version of you.
He came for sinners.
Real ones.
The scandalous ones.
The ashamed ones.
The religious ones.
The sexually broken ones.
The angry ones.
The addicted ones.
The proud ones.
The hypocritical ones.
The ones whose hands look clean while their hearts are hiding bodies.
Christ did not go to the cross because humanity needed motivational improvement.
He went because sin brings death.
At Calvary, something infinitely greater than the Flood and infinitely greater than the Red Sea took place.
The judgment our sin deserved fell upon the sinless Son who willingly gave Himself for sinners.
“He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).
Jesus died.
Really died.
The stone was rolled across the tomb.
His disciples watched their hopes collapse.
And then came the morning Christianity stands or falls upon.
The tomb was empty.
Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead.
That is why Peter can speak of baptism and immediately say:
“through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.”
Because Christianity is not ultimately about water.
It is about resurrection.
Baptism is a visible confession that the person I was cannot be my lord anymore because Jesus is Lord.
Down into the water.
Buried with Christ.
Up from the water.
Newness of life.
Not sinless perfection.
Not instant emotional healing.
Not the disappearance of every temptation.
New ownership.
New allegiance.
New identity.
A new direction.
Grace does not merely say, “Your past doesn't matter.”
Grace says something far more beautiful:
“Your past does not get to be your master because Jesus paid for your sin and calls you to follow Him.”
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Perhaps there is something you desperately want washed away.
A decision.
An affair.
An addiction.
An abortion.
A betrayal.
Years of rebellion.
Years of pretending.
Something somebody did to you.
Something you did to somebody else.
Something nobody knows.
And you've wondered whether people like you can actually begin again.
The answer of Christianity is not that your sin was insignificant.
The answer is that Christ is sufficient.
Repentance does not mean pretending the past never happened.
It means turning from sin toward the One who died and rose to redeem sinners.
Grace does not rewrite history by calling evil good.
Jesus rewrites the sinner's future by forgiving, reconciling and transforming those who come to Him.
That distinction matters.
Because “From Scandal to Grace” does not mean scandal becomes acceptable.
It means scandal does not have to become your final chapter.
Peter denied Jesus.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Yet grace reached sinners exactly where their histories said hope should have ended.
This is why Jesus is better than another chance.
If all God gave us were another chance, eventually we would ruin that one too.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed reconciliation.
We needed a new heart.
We needed the Holy Spirit.
We needed resurrection life.
We needed Christ.
So perhaps the question isn't merely why water keeps marking new beginnings in Scripture.
Perhaps the question is:
What are you still trying to drag across the water that Jesus is telling you to leave behind?
Pharaoh cannot own Israel forever.
The grave cannot own Jesus.
And if you are united to Christ, sin must no longer reign as your master.
Maybe you fell again.
Come back.
Maybe you've been hiding.
Come into the light.
Maybe your faith feels exhausted.
Call upon Christ.
Maybe you've never truly surrendered to Jesus at all.
Do not confuse familiarity with Christianity for belonging to Christ.
You can know worship songs and not know the Savior.
You can own a Bible and resist its Author.
You can be baptized and still spend your life running from the One baptism proclaims.
The water is not a substitute for repentance and faith.
Come to Jesus.
Confess your sin.
Trust the crucified and risen Christ.
Follow Him.
And if you have believed but have never been baptized, do not treat Jesus' command casually. Speak with faithful church leaders, learn what Scripture teaches, and obey Christ publicly.
There is no shame in admitting you need grace.
The tragedy is insisting on drowning while refusing the rescue God has provided in His Son.
Be honest.

And if God has already carried you through something that once looked like it would destroy you, tell your testimony. Someone reading silently tonight may need evidence that Christians struggle, stumble, repent, heal and keep walking because Christ has not abandoned His people.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
Someone trapped between Pharaoh and the sea.
Someone whose private life is collapsing.
Someone ashamed of their past.
Someone who believes God could forgive almost anyone except them.
Not for an algorithm.
For the night when the water rises again.
Read it when shame tells you that your worst chapter is your final chapter.
Read Romans 6.
Read Exodus 14.
Read Genesis 6–9.
Read 1 Peter 3.
Then look again toward the empty tomb.
Salvation cannot be purchased. Grace cannot be bought.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can help that work continue.
Let your support become an act of generosity and mission—not a transaction with God.
If this ministry is feeding you spiritually, stay close.
Jesus is calling sinners to Himself.
Noah walked out after the Flood into a new beginning.
Israel walked through the sea into freedom.
The Christian rises from baptism confessing a greater deliverance—the crucified Jesus lives, and those who belong to Him are called to walk in newness of life.
The water was never the Savior.
God was.
The ark was never the ultimate refuge.
Christ is.
The Red Sea was never the final liberation.
The cross broke a deeper slavery.
And baptism is not the end of the Christian story.
It announces the beginning of a life surrendered to the One who died, was buried, rose again, reigns, and is coming again.
So when your past whispers your old name…
when shame recites everything you have done…
when temptation tells you nothing has really changed…
remember the shoreline.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember whose name you now bear.
Because sometimes God does not erase the chapter that broke you.
He does something greater.
He refuses to let that chapter write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN EVERY CHRISTIAN BE FILLED WITH THE HOLY SPIRIT?
paragraphs: CAN EVERY CHRISTIAN BE FILLED WITH THE HOLY SPIRIT?
You Were Never Meant to Spend Your Christian Life Trying to Survive on Yesterday’s Strength
What if one of the greatest tragedies in the Church is not that Christians do not believe in the Holy Spirit…
…but that many Christians have quietly learned how to live as though they can manage without His filling?
They believe in the Father.
They confess Jesus Christ as Lord.
They believe the Bible.
They attend church. They worship. They pray. They serve. They try to resist temptation.
And yet, somewhere beneath the Christian vocabulary and Sunday smiles, there is an exhausted confession they are almost afraid to say aloud:
“I know what I’m supposed to be… but I don’t have the strength to keep being it.”
Maybe you know that feeling.
You love Jesus, but your prayer life has become dry.
You know the Scriptures, but temptation still seems louder than truth.
You worship publicly while privately wondering why your heart feels so empty.
You keep promising God, “This time I’ll change.”
Then the same anger returns.
The same lust.
The same bitterness.
The same fear.
The same secret compromise.
The same spiritual exhaustion.
And eventually a terrifying thought enters your mind:
Maybe this is all Christianity is.
Trying harder.
Failing.
Feeling guilty.
Asking forgiveness.
Trying harder again.
But what if Jesus never intended you to live the Christian life by squeezing spiritual strength out of your own exhausted soul?
What if God has already answered the question of whether ordinary believers may be filled with His Spirit?
And what if the answer is far more hopeful than you imagined?
Listen carefully to the words of Paul:
“And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit.”
—Ephesians 5:18
The Greek is striking:
ἀλλὰ πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι
alla plērousthe en pneumati
“But be filled with the Spirit.”
The word πληροῦσθε—plērousthe—comes from πληρόω, plēroō, meaning to fill, make full, or bring to fullness.
And there is something important about the grammar.
Paul is addressing believers collectively. This is not presented as an invitation reserved for apostles, pastors, missionaries, unusually emotional Christians, or some spiritual elite.
It is a command to the Christian community.
And the present imperative carries the sense of an ongoing reality: keep being filled. Continue living under the Spirit’s influence and fullness.
That changes everything.
Because Paul is not telling Christians merely to remember an experience they had years ago.
He is describing a life continually yielded to the Holy Spirit.
Notice the contrast.
“Do not get drunk with wine…”
Why compare drunkenness with being filled with the Spirit?
Because Paul is contrasting controlling influences.
Wine can dominate behavior, judgment, speech, and conduct.
The Christian, however, is not to surrender control to intoxication. We are to live under the holy influence and direction of God’s Spirit.
And what follows in Ephesians is revealing.
Spirit-filled believers speak to one another with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. They sing to the Lord. They give thanks to God. They walk in relationships shaped by reverence for Christ.
In other words, biblical Spirit-filling is not merely about having a dramatic moment.
It produces a transformed life.
This matters because Christians sometimes fall into opposite errors.
Some become suspicious of virtually anything associated with the Holy Spirit because they have witnessed manipulation, emotionalism, counterfeit spirituality, or abuses committed in His name.
Others become fascinated with manifestations while paying far less attention to holiness, truth, love, obedience, humility, and Christ.
Scripture gives us permission to reject both extremes.
You do not have to choose between biblical truth and the Holy Spirit.
The Holy Spirit inspired the Scriptures.
You do not have to choose between Jesus and the Spirit.
The Spirit glorifies Jesus.
Christ Himself said:
“When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth…”
And then:
“He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you.”
That is one of the safest biblical tests of anything claiming to be a work of the Holy Spirit:
Does it glorify Jesus Christ?
Does it agree with God’s truth?
Does it lead toward holiness rather than excuse sin?
Does it produce the fruit Scripture associates with the Spirit?
Because the Holy Spirit does not come to make Jesus peripheral.
He magnifies Christ.
The Spirit does not whisper, “Look how spiritual you are.”
He turns the heart toward Jesus.
Look at Pentecost.
Acts 2 records something extraordinary.

The disciples were gathered when suddenly there came from heaven a sound like a mighty rushing wind. They were filled with the Holy Spirit, spoke in other tongues as the Spirit gave utterance, and Peter—the same Peter who had denied Jesus before a servant girl—stood publicly and proclaimed Christ.
Think about that man for a moment.
Peter had promised loyalty.
Then pressure came.
And Peter collapsed.
“I do not know the man.”
Three denials.
Then the rooster.
Then the unbearable realization of what he had done.
Scripture says Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Scandal.
Failure.
Shame.
But Jesus was not finished writing Peter’s story.
The risen Christ restored him.
Then the Holy Spirit empowered him.
The frightened disciple became a courageous witness.
That is not motivational psychology.
That is grace.
That is what Jesus does.
He takes people whose stories appear permanently stained and writes redemption where shame thought it had written the final sentence.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps that is exactly why you needed to read this today.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your battlefield exists behind a locked bedroom door.
Maybe your greatest spiritual failure is stored in browser history.
Maybe it lives inside resentment toward someone you still pretend to forgive.
Maybe it is pride hidden beneath ministry.
Maybe you have mastered the language of Christianity while slowly losing intimacy with Christ.
People call you strong.
But God knows how tired you are.
And perhaps you have been trying to defeat spiritual battles with nothing but human determination.
You keep saying:
“I need more discipline.”
Sometimes you do.
“I need stronger boundaries.”
Maybe you do.
“I need to try harder.”
There is a place for effort and obedience.
But Christianity is not self-improvement with Bible verses attached.
Jesus did not merely die so that bad people could become slightly better behaved.
He died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God, forgive sin, give new life, and make His people a dwelling place of His Spirit.
Paul asks the Corinthians:
“Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?”
—1 Corinthians 3:16
And Romans declares:
“Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.”
—Romans 8:9
That means we must distinguish carefully between the Spirit’s indwelling and the repeated biblical language of believers being filled with the Spirit.
Every true Christian belongs to Christ through faith and has the Spirit of God dwelling within.
Yet Christians are repeatedly commanded and described as being filled with the Spirit.
Peter was filled with the Holy Spirit at Pentecost in Acts 2.
Then Acts 4:8 says Peter was again “filled with the Holy Spirit.”
Later, after believers prayed together, Acts 4:31 says:
“And when they had prayed, the place in which they were gathered together was shaken, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit and continued to speak the word of God with boldness.”
Notice those words:
“They were all filled.”
Not merely Peter.
Not merely John.
Not merely the apostles.
The gathered believers.
So can every Christian be filled with the Holy Spirit?

Biblically, Christians are commanded to be filled with the Spirit, and Scripture presents Spirit-filled life as normal Christian discipleship rather than an exclusive privilege for a spiritual aristocracy.
But that raises another question.
How?
And this is where we must resist turning the Holy Spirit into a formula.
The Holy Spirit is not an impersonal force.
He is not spiritual electricity.
He is not a technique.
He is God.
Throughout Scripture He speaks, teaches, leads, gives gifts, can be grieved, and acts according to divine wisdom and will.
So being filled with the Holy Spirit is not learning how to manipulate God into producing an experience.
It is surrender.
It is dependence.
It is obedience.
It is asking.
It is yielding.
Jesus gave this remarkable promise:
“If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!”
—Luke 11:13
Look at the tenderness of that statement.
Father.
Children.
Gift.
Ask.
Some Christians are afraid to ask God for more of His Spirit because they fear deception.
Yet Jesus places the invitation inside the goodness of the Father.
That does not mean abandoning biblical discernment.
Quite the opposite.
The Spirit of truth will never lead us contrary to the truth He inspired.
But we should not allow fear of counterfeit spirituality to make us afraid of authentic dependence upon God.
Perhaps the more uncomfortable question is not:
“Will God fill me?”
Perhaps it is:
“Am I willing to surrender what I keep asking Him to fill?”
Because we sometimes want the power of the Holy Spirit without the surrender of our hidden rooms.
We want boldness without obedience.
Anointing without repentance.
Gifts without character.
Power without the cross.
Comfort without conviction.
We want God to fill the house while certain rooms remain locked.
But the Holy Spirit loves us too much to become an accessory to our rebellion.
Paul writes:
—Ephesians 4:30
Look at the surrounding context and you find practical sins: falsehood, corrupt speech, bitterness, wrath, anger, clamor, slander, malice.
Spirit-filled Christianity becomes painfully practical.
How do you speak to your spouse?
What do you watch when nobody is looking?
What happens inside your mind when someone else succeeds?
What do you secretly refuse to forgive?
How do you treat people who cannot advance your career, platform, ministry, or reputation?
What happens when conviction comes?
Do you repent?
Or do you negotiate?
There are moments when we ask God for revival while protecting the very sins His Spirit is confronting.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly what that means.
You have been asking God to change your circumstances.
Meanwhile the Holy Spirit has been touching the wound beneath them.
You have been asking Him to remove the pressure.
He has been exposing your pride.
You have been asking Him to restore your joy.
He has been confronting your compromise.
You have been asking for power.
He has been asking for surrender.
And you know what it is.
That thing you hoped this article would never mention because the moment you started reading, it came into your mind.
You know.
God knows.
There is grace there too.
Do not confuse conviction with condemnation.
Romans 8:1 says:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Conviction says, “Come into the light.”
Condemnation says, “Hide because there is no hope for you.”
The Gospel says something entirely different.
Come into the light because Someone already carried your shame to the cross.
Jesus was crucified for sinners.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Your hope is not that you can clean yourself enough to become worthy of the Holy Spirit.
Your hope is Christ.
Your righteousness is Christ.
Your forgiveness is purchased by Christ.
Your reconciliation with God comes through Christ.
Your new life is found in Christ.
The Holy Spirit does not fill us so that we can become impressed with ourselves.
He transforms us so that our lives increasingly testify:
Jesus Christ is Lord.
This is why Galatians describes something more enduring than spiritual excitement:
“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control…”
—Galatians 5:22–23
Fruit grows.
Sometimes slowly.
Sometimes painfully.
But genuinely.
Maybe you were expecting being filled with the Spirit to mean you would never struggle again.
Scripture never promises that.
Galatians speaks directly about conflict between the flesh and the Spirit.
The presence of battle does not necessarily mean the Spirit has abandoned you.
Sometimes the battle itself becomes evidence that you no longer want to make peace with what once enslaved you.
Before Christ, sin could feel like home.
Now something within you cries:
“This cannot be my home anymore.”
So if you fell yesterday, repent today.
If you failed this morning, run toward Christ rather than away from Him.
If you are spiritually exhausted, stop pretending.
Ask.
Seek.
Surrender.
Open the Scriptures.
Pray.
Confess your sin.
Walk with mature believers.
Obey what God has already made clear.
Do not chase experiences while ignoring Jesus.
And do not settle for lifeless religious routine when Scripture commands:
“Be filled with the Spirit.”
Maybe your prayer does not need impressive vocabulary tonight.
Maybe it needs honesty.
“Father, I cannot live this Christian life in my own strength.
Forgive my sin.
Expose what I have hidden.
Break what I keep protecting.
Jesus, You are Lord.
Holy Spirit, fill me and lead me according to Your truth.
Make me holy.
Make me obedient.
Make me love what Christ loves.
Give me courage to witness.
Produce Your fruit in me.
Glorify Jesus through my life.
I surrender again.
Amen.”
And when you finish praying, do not measure God’s faithfulness merely by whether you felt goosebumps.
Walk.
Obey.
Trust.
Keep asking.
Keep surrendering.
Keep returning to Christ.
Keep being filled.
There may be someone reading this whose greatest miracle will not be falling to the floor.
It will be getting back up after years of secret defeat.
Someone will forgive.
Someone will confess.
Someone will delete what has been poisoning their soul.
Someone will finally ask another believer for help.
Someone will reopen a Bible covered in dust.
