The Judge provides the rescue.
The Holy One provides the Lamb.
The God before whom sinners cannot boast provides salvation that sinners cannot earn.
That is grace.
And perhaps now we can understand why Scripture's fire imagery is not always merely about destruction.
Fire also reveals.
Tests.
Purifies.
First Peter speaks of tested faith as more precious than gold tested by fire.
Paul uses fire imagery in 1 Corinthians 3 concerning the testing of a person's work.
Malachi speaks of the Lord in imagery of a refiner's fire.
But we must be careful here.
We should not flatten every biblical reference to fire into exactly the same meaning.
Context matters.
Sometimes biblical fire signifies judgment.
Sometimes divine presence.
Sometimes testing or purification.
Sometimes imagery associated with God's holiness.
The faithful reader does not make every flame say the same thing.
Yet across Scripture one truth refuses to disappear:
The living God is not casual about holiness.
And neither is Jesus.
The Jesus who welcomed sinners also told them to repent.
The Jesus who touched lepers also warned about judgment.
The Jesus who forgave also commanded transformed living.
The Jesus who said, “Come to me,” also said, “Follow me.”
Grace is free.
But grace was never cheap.
It cost the blood of Christ.
And when grace truly takes hold of someone, it does not merely change where that person expects to go after death.
It begins changing whom that person belongs to right now.
Maybe this article is touching something you hoped nobody would touch.
Good.
Not because shame is the goal.
Jesus is.
Maybe you need to close the secret browser window.
Maybe you need to forgive someone.
Maybe you need to confess the lie.
Maybe you need to end the affair.
Maybe you need to surrender the bitterness you have justified for years.
Maybe you need to return what does not belong to you.
Maybe you need to admit that your Christianity has become performance.
Maybe you need to stop asking God to bless the life you refuse to surrender.
Or maybe your greatest struggle is not scandalous at all.
Maybe you are simply tired.
Your prayers feel empty.
Your Bible has stayed closed.
You love Jesus, but something inside you feels numb.
Even then, do not run from Him.
Run toward Him.
You do not need a prettier mask.
You need Christ.
And if you are reading this thinking, “But you don't know what I've done…”
You're right.
I don't.
But the power of the Gospel does not depend upon the writer knowing your history.
It depends upon Jesus Christ being sufficient.
Peter denied Him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The thief beside Christ reached the end of a ruined life with nothing left to offer but faith in the King dying beside him.
Scripture is filled with people whose stories would have looked irredeemable if human failure had been allowed to write the final chapter.
But God specializes in endings human beings could never manufacture.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Because grace is astonishing.
That is the heartbeat behind these words:
Not scandal ignored.
Not scandal celebrated.
Not scandal renamed so nobody has to repent.
Scandal confronted by truth.
Scandal brought into the light.
Scandal carried to the Cross.
Scandal met by mercy.
Scandal no longer permitted to define the person Christ redeems.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the old pages never happened.
But by refusing to let them determine the ending.
Be honest.
Someone reading your words may realize they are not the only person fighting to come home.
And if one particular person came into your mind while reading this, don't ignore that.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Salvation cannot be bought, and God's grace is never merchandise.
But if Christ has given us truth worth proclaiming, sharing biblical truth can be one simple way of helping place that truth before someone who desperately needs it.
Because there may come a night when temptation returns.
A night when shame tells you to hide.
A night when you start confusing God's patience with permission to compromise.
Come back and remember:
Our God is a consuming fire.
And the same Scriptures that tell us to worship Him with reverence and awe point us toward Jesus, the Mediator of the new covenant.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to manufacture emotional Christianity.
Not to replace your local church.
Not to replace Scripture.
But to keep pointing wounded, wandering, hungry people toward biblical truth and ultimately toward Jesus Christ.
But never confuse the benefit with the reason.
A mug cannot transform you.
A shirt cannot forgive you.
A journal cannot redeem you.
Jesus Christ can.
Not as spiritual advertising.
As an invitation.
Someone ashamed to pray.
Someone trapped in secret sin.
Someone convinced God wants nothing to do with them.
Someone who needs to discover that the consuming holiness of God does not make the Cross irrelevant.
It makes the Cross breathtaking.
The fire tells us God is holy.
The Cross tells us grace is costly.
The empty tomb tells us Jesus conquered death.
And the Gospel tells sinners:
Come out of hiding.
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
You may have arrived at this article afraid of the words:
“Our God is a consuming fire.”
Perhaps now you understand why Christians should never erase them.
We need the God who is actually there.
Not the God our culture invents.
Not the God our preferences edit.
Not a grandfather in the sky who smiles indifferently at everything.
Not an angry caricature waiting eagerly for someone to fail.
The God revealed in Scripture.
Holy.
Righteous.
Jealous for His glory.
Merciful.
Patient.
Just.
Gracious.
And revealed supremely to us in Jesus Christ.
So stop running from the light.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the religious performance.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the heart you thought was too ruined.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
You do not need to make yourself worthy enough to need a Savior.
Your need is precisely why you need Him.
And perhaps this is the sentence you should remember long after you close this article:
The fire of God's holiness exposes what cannot save you, so that grace can lead you to the One who can.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHEN DOES FITNESS BECOME VANITY?
paragraphs: WHEN DOES FITNESS BECOME VANITY?
The dangerous moment when discipline stops being stewardship, your reflection becomes your judge, and a good gift quietly begins asking for the worship that belongs to Jesus.
There is a moment nobody photographs.
Nobody uploads it.
Nobody turns the camera toward it.
You are standing in front of the mirror after the workout. Your muscles are fuller. Your waist is smaller. The number on the scale finally moved. The clothes fit differently. Maybe somebody noticed.
“You look amazing.”
And for a few seconds, something inside you comes alive.
Then you walk away.
An hour later, you look again.
Another angle.
Another check.
Another photograph.
Another comparison.
Another quiet question:
Do I look good enough yet?
And somewhere between wanting to become healthier and desperately needing to become impressive, something changed.
Maybe nobody else noticed.
Maybe you didn't notice.
But God did.
Because the most dangerous idols are not always ugly things.
Sometimes they have abs.
Sometimes they count calories.
Sometimes they wake up at five in the morning.
Sometimes they call themselves discipline.
And sometimes they can quote the verse about your body being God's temple while slowly turning that temple into a monument to themselves.
So when does fitness become vanity?
Not when you lift the weight.
Not when you lose the fat.
Not when you build muscle.
Not when you run farther than you could last month.
Not when you enjoy becoming stronger.
Fitness begins crossing into vanity when caring for the body God entrusted to you quietly becomes needing that body to give you what only Christ can give you:
worth.
identity.
approval.
security.
superiority.
love.
And if that sentence made you uncomfortable, don't run from the discomfort yet.
Because this is not an article telling Christians that exercise is sinful.
Scripture does not say that.

Paul actually acknowledges the value of physical training. In 1 Timothy 4:8, he contrasts bodily training with something infinitely greater: godliness. Many English translations render the first part along the lines of physical training having some or limited value.
The Greek behind the idea is striking:
ἡ γὰρ σωματικὴ γυμνασία πρὸς ὀλίγον ἐστὶν ὠφέλιμος
Hē gar sōmatikē gymnasia pros oligon estin ōphelimos.
The important point is not that bodily training is worthless.
It isn't.
Paul's contrast is about proportion.
Physical training has real value, but godliness reaches somewhere muscle never can. It reaches beyond appearance. Beyond aging. Beyond sickness. Beyond the grave.
Your strength will eventually decline.
Your skin will change.
Your metabolism will change.
The body you worked so hard to sculpt will not remain twenty-five, thirty-five, or forty-five forever.
But what Christ is forming in you has eternal consequence.
That changes the question.
The question is no longer merely, “Is working out good?”
The deeper question becomes:
“What am I asking my body to do for my soul?”
Because your body was never designed to carry the unbearable weight of your identity.
Some people exercise because they enjoy movement.
Some train because their occupation requires physical capacity.
Some want energy to play with their children.
Some are rebuilding healthy habits.
Some enjoy competition.
Some simply like feeling strong.
None of those motives automatically equal vanity.
But another person can perform the exact same workout while worshiping an entirely different god.
Two people can stand beside each other in the same gym.
Same dumbbells.
Same repetitions.
Same sweat.
Same discipline.
One is saying in the heart, “Lord, thank You for this body. Help me steward it faithfully.”
The other is silently saying, “Please let this finally make me enough.”
Outwardly, almost identical.
Spiritually, worlds apart.
That is why Christianity cannot be reduced to appearance management.
God has always gone deeper.
When Samuel was impressed by outward appearance while searching for Israel's next king, God corrected the human instinct to evaluate the outside while He sees the heart (1 Samuel 16:7).
That truth still walks into every gym.
Every locker room.
Every bathroom mirror.
Every progress picture.
Every social-media feed.
Every fitting room.
Every moment when you pinch the skin around your stomach and quietly hate yourself.
God sees deeper.
And perhaps that is frightening.
But if you belong to Jesus, it is also extraordinarily freeing.
Because the God who sees what the mirror cannot see is the God who loved you enough to send His Son for sinners.
Your mirror knows nothing about your redemption.
The scale cannot measure justification.
A measuring tape cannot calculate grace.
Your body-fat percentage cannot determine whether God welcomes you.
The algorithm cannot measure holiness.
And your reflection has absolutely no authority to pronounce your worth.
The cross has already exposed the terrible truth and the beautiful truth at the same time.
You were more sinful than cosmetic self-improvement could ever repair.
And you were loved at a cost no physique could ever earn.
That is the scandal of grace.
We keep trying to renovate the outside while Jesus came to resurrect the dead.
And this is where one of the most frequently quoted fitness verses needs to be handled carefully.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:19–20:
τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίου πνεύματός ἐστιν
To sōma hymōn naos tou en hymin hagiou pneumatos estin.
Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you.
Then comes the sentence our self-focused culture desperately needs:
καὶ οὐκ ἐστὲ ἑαυτῶν
Kai ouk este heautōn.
You are not your own.
And then:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς
Ēgorasthēte gar timēs.
You were bought with a price.
Therefore:
δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν
Doxasate dē ton Theon en tō sōmati hymōn.

Glorify God in your body. The Greek text and the central sense of the passage support exactly that movement: your body belongs to God, you were purchased at a price, therefore God is to be glorified through your embodied life.
Notice what Paul does not say.
“Your body is a temple, therefore make everybody jealous of the temple.”
He doesn't say:
“Your body is a temple, therefore obsess over the temple.”
Or:
“Your body is a temple, therefore your appearance determines your spiritual maturity.”
The center of the passage isn't self-admiration.
It is ownership.
You are not your own.
Those words destroy both neglect and narcissism.
If my body belongs to God, I have no right to recklessly mistreat it.
But if my body belongs to God, I also have no right to turn it into an idol devoted to my own glory.
Christian stewardship says:
“This body belongs to Jesus.”
Vanity whispers:
“This body exists to make people admire me.”
And the difference can become painfully subtle.
You can say, “I'm just being disciplined,” while checking repeatedly whether people noticed the results.
You can call it “motivation” while secretly needing strangers to envy you.
You can post a progress picture supposedly to “inspire people” and then spend the next hour refreshing the notifications because their reactions have become emotional oxygen.
You can become physically stronger while becoming spiritually enslaved.
You can conquer sugar and still be conquered by pride.
You can control every gram of food entering your mouth and have almost no control over the arrogance leaving it.
You can count macros while refusing to count the cost of following Jesus.
You can spend ninety minutes training your body and tell yourself you cannot find ten quiet minutes to pray.
And eventually the question is unavoidable:
Am I training my body… or training myself to worship my body?
That question cuts because vanity rarely introduces itself as vanity.
It calls itself standards.
It calls itself self-improvement.
It calls itself “the grind.”
Sometimes it even calls itself health.
But there is a revealing test.
What happens emotionally when the results disappear?
An injury comes.
The scale rises.
Pregnancy changes the body.
Medication affects weight.
Age changes muscle and skin.
Stress interrupts your routine.
You miss workouts.
Someone more attractive enters the room.
Someone stronger stands beside you.
Someone younger receives the attention you wanted.
What happens inside you then?
Disappointment is human.
But devastation can reveal something deeper.
When losing the physique feels like losing yourself, perhaps the physique had become more than a physique.
It had become an identity.
And idols are cruel masters because they always demand maintenance.
Jesus says, in effect, Come to Me.
Vanity says, Improve yourself enough and perhaps you'll finally deserve to be seen.
Jesus gives grace.
Vanity gives a treadmill with no finish line.
Five pounds becomes ten.
Ten becomes twenty.
Visible abs become sharper abs.
Healthy becomes impressive.
Impressive becomes exceptional.
Exceptional becomes still-not-enough.
Because vanity does not actually want beauty.
Vanity wants assurance.
And physical perfection cannot provide it.
Ask the person whose body everyone envies but who cannot stop criticizing the reflection.
Ask the person with thousands of compliments who still needs one more.
Ask the person terrified of gaining three pounds because somewhere along the way thinness became synonymous with worth.
Ask the man who built the physique he dreamed about only to discover that insecurity can grow muscles too.
That is the tragedy.
You can transform your body without transforming your heart.
Only Jesus can do the deeper work.
And Christ does not merely walk into our vanity and say, “Try harder not to be vain.”
He goes to the root.
Why do you need their approval so badly?
Why does being overlooked hurt so much?
Why does another person's beauty feel like a threat?
Why do you need the room to notice you?
Why are you punishing your body for failing to resemble somebody else's?
Why does a photograph determine whether you have a good day?
Why are you terrified of aging?
Why is being ordinary unbearable?
Maybe beneath the vanity is fear.
Maybe beneath the obsession is rejection.
Maybe somebody mocked your body when you were younger.
Maybe a spouse compared you with someone else.
Maybe your father never affirmed you.
Maybe your mother constantly criticized your appearance.
Maybe social media trained you to believe that love belongs to beautiful people.
Maybe you changed your body and suddenly people treated you differently.
And you quietly made a vow:
I will never become invisible again.
Jesus sees that wound too.
He does not excuse idolatry.
But neither does He heal us by merely humiliating wounded people.
He calls us to repentance and then offers something vanity never could:
a new identity.
The Gospel doesn't tell you that you were secretly perfect all along.
It tells something far more glorious.
You were a sinner who needed reconciliation with God, and Christ came for sinners.
Jesus lived the righteous life you could not live.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And everyone who turns from sin and trusts in Him receives something no mirror can grant and no aging body can remove:
forgiveness.
reconciliation.
adoption.
new life.
Christ.
Suddenly fitness can return to its proper place.
A gift.
A tool.
A stewardship.
Not a savior.
You can lift weights without asking the weights to tell you who you are.
You can lose weight without believing thinner means holier.
You can build muscle without building an altar to yourself.
You can enjoy looking good without living to be looked at.
You can receive a compliment without feeding on compliments.
You can pursue discipline without despising people whose bodies look different from yours.
You can train hard and still stop when wisdom says rest.
You can eat nourishing food without turning food into a system of righteousness.
You can become stronger while remembering that weakness does not make someone less valuable before God.
And perhaps one of the clearest questions you can ask before the mirror is this:
If nobody could ever see the results, would I still want to care for this body?
Then another:
If God allowed my appearance to change tomorrow, would Jesus still be enough for me?
Don't answer too quickly.
Sit there.
Because one day the mirror will change whether you give it permission or not.
One day every person reading these words will have an older face.
If the Lord gives you many years, the body you are desperately trying to preserve will bear those years.
And that isn't failure.
There is something profoundly Christian about being able to watch youth leave without watching your identity leave with it.
Imagine growing older without panic because your treasure was never your reflection.
Imagine wrinkles arriving while your faith deepens.
Imagine muscles weakening while compassion strengthens.
Imagine your pace slowing while your worship becomes richer.
Imagine becoming less impressive to a culture obsessed with youth while becoming increasingly beautiful in the things heaven calls precious.
That is freedom.
So exercise.
Walk.
Run.
Lift.
Stretch.
Train.
Rest.
Eat wisely.
Enjoy the body God has entrusted to you.
But do not kneel before it.
The body is a servant.
A terrible god.
And a temporary home awaiting resurrection.
Christianity does not end with contempt for the body. Our hope includes bodily resurrection. Jesus Christ rose bodily, and Christian hope looks toward resurrection and restoration.
So stewardship matters.
But stewardship and worship are not the same thing.
Maybe today your repentance needs to happen somewhere you never expected.
Maybe your altar is a mirror.
Maybe your incense is attention.
Maybe your congregation is a follower count.
Maybe your offering is every hour sacrificed trying to become physically worthy of admiration.
And maybe Jesus is calling you away from an exhausting god that has never once loved you back.
You do not need to smash your mirror.
You need to dethrone it.
You do not necessarily need to cancel the gym membership.
You may need to surrender the heart that walks through the gym doors.
You don't have to stop becoming strong.
You need to remember where your strength comes from and whom your strength is for.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, don't perform spirituality now either.
Be honest.
Not because typing a phrase saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when we finally stop pretending.
And somebody reading the comments may discover they weren't the only Christian fighting this battle.
You cannot. Christ's grace is not merchandise.
But if you genuinely want to glorify God by helping Gospel-centered teaching reach more people, voluntary support and sharing are practical ways you can participate in that mission.

And stay close to Gospel Warrior by following and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even the unbeliever who has questions about Jesus—to follow along for daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment.
But whatever you do after reading this, remember what matters most.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not your physique.
Not your followers.
Not your reflection.
Jesus.
If fitness makes you healthier, thank God.
If discipline makes you stronger, use that strength for God.
If your appearance changes, receive it humbly.
But the moment the mirror begins telling you who you are, take it back to the cross.
Because at Calvary, the question of your deepest worth was never answered by how beautiful you could become.
It was answered by how costly your redemption was.
You were bought with a price.
So glorify God in your body.
Train it if you can.
Care for it wisely.
Enjoy it gratefully.
Age in it faithfully.
And surrender it completely.
Because someday you will take your final photograph.
Someday you will perform your final repetition.
Someday you will look into a mirror for the last time.
And when that day comes, your greatest victory will not be that you managed to preserve a body everyone admired.
It will be that, by grace through faith, your life belonged to Jesus.
The mirror will eventually forget the face you fought so hard to perfect—but the hands scarred for your redemption will never forget your name.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY SATAN HATES A HUMBLE CHRISTIAN
paragraphs:
WHY SATAN HATES A HUMBLE CHRISTIAN
The Enemy Knows How to Fight Your Strength. What Terrifies Him Is the Moment You Stop Trusting It.
There is a kind of Christian Satan knows how to manipulate.
Talented.
Passionate.
Knowledgeable.
Gifted.
The kind who can quote Scripture, defend doctrine, recognize false teaching, speak confidently about Jesus, and still carry something dangerous beneath the surface...
the quiet belief that they are stronger than they really are.
But there is another kind of believer the enemy encounters differently.
A believer on their knees.
Not pretending.
Not performing.
Not telling God how impressive they have become.
Not comparing themselves with everybody else.
Not hiding their weakness behind Christian vocabulary.
Just a trembling human being who has finally realized:
“I cannot win without Jesus.”
And strangely...
that person may be far more dangerous to the kingdom of darkness than the person who appears powerful.
Because biblical humility is not weakness.
It is surrender to the right King.
And Scripture places an extraordinary statement beside that surrender:
“Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”
James 4:7.
Read it again, because we often rush straight toward the exciting part.
Resist the devil.
He will flee.
But James begins somewhere else.
Submit to God.
The Greek reads:
“Ὑποτάγητε οὖν τῷ θεῷ· ἀντίστητε δὲ τῷ διαβόλῳ, καὶ φεύξεται ἀφ’ ὑμῶν.”
Hypotagēte oun tō Theō; antistēte de tō diabolō, kai pheuxetai aph’ hymōn.
“Therefore submit yourselves to God; resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”
The order matters.
Submission comes before resistance.
And immediately before this, James writes:
James 4:6.
The language is startling.
God opposes the proud.
The Greek word translated “opposes” or “resists” is ἀντιτάσσεται — antitassetai.
It carries the sense of setting oneself against someone.
Then James tells believers to ἀντίστητε — antistēte — resist the devil.
Do you see the terrifying contrast?
Pride puts you in a posture Scripture says God opposes.
Humility puts you beneath the grace of God, from which you can stand against the devil.
That changes the entire conversation about spiritual warfare.
Sometimes we imagine warfare only as shouting louder, praying longer, recognizing demons, rebuking darkness, or declaring powerful words.
Yet James brings us somewhere painfully ordinary.
Your pride.
Your desires.
Your quarrels.
Your divided loyalty.
Your unwillingness to surrender.
And then he says, essentially:
Humble yourself.
Submit to God.
Resist the devil.
Come near to God.
That is warfare too.
Maybe some of your greatest spiritual battles are being fought in places nobody sees.
The apology you do not want to give.
The sin you keep defending.
The correction you resent.
The person you secretly believe you are better than.
The ministry success you have started calling yours.
The compliment you desperately need.
The argument you cannot bear to lose.
The hidden addiction you keep telling yourself you can control.
The prayer you stopped praying because somewhere along the way you began believing you could handle life yourself.
Pride does not always walk into church announcing,
“I think I am greater than God.”
Sometimes pride worships with both hands raised.
Sometimes pride serves.
Sometimes pride preaches.
Sometimes pride posts Bible verses.
Sometimes pride gives advice to everyone while refusing correction from anyone.
Sometimes pride sounds like:
“I already know.”
“I don’t need help.”
“They need to apologize first.”
“Nobody can teach me anything.”
“I would never fall like that.”
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“I deserve better.”
“God should have done this differently.”
And sometimes the most dangerous form of pride is not thinking highly of yourself.
It is being so consumed with yourself that even your shame becomes self-centered.
You fail, and instead of running to Christ, you spend days staring at yourself.
You sin, and instead of confessing, you hide because you cannot tolerate anyone discovering that you are not who you pretended to be.
You fall, and instead of receiving mercy, you punish yourself as though your suffering could somehow add something to the blood of Jesus.
Even shame can whisper:
“Keep looking at yourself.”
Grace says:
“Look at Christ.”
That is why humility is so powerful.
Humility stops negotiating with reality.
It says:
“Yes, Lord. I sinned.”
“Yes, Lord. I need mercy.”
“Yes, Lord. I was wrong.”
“Yes, Lord. I need help.”
“Yes, Lord. Your Word is right even when it exposes me.”
“Yes, Lord. Without You, I can do nothing.”
That is not spiritual defeat.
That is the beginning of freedom.
Peter gives us a remarkably similar picture.
“God resisteth the proud, and giveth grace to the humble.”
Then:
“Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.”
1 Peter 5:5–6.
And only a few verses later:
“Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour: whom resist stedfast in the faith.”
1 Peter 5:8–9.
Again...
humility.
Dependence.
Watchfulness.
Resistance.
Peter does not portray humility as becoming passive before evil.
He portrays humble believers as sober, vigilant, steadfast people.
That matters.
Biblical humility does not mean allowing people to abuse you.
It does not mean pretending your gifts do not exist.
It does not mean becoming timid.
It does not mean refusing leadership.
It does not mean thinking you are worthless.
And it certainly does not mean calling yourself garbage when Jesus purchased you with His blood.
Humility is agreeing with God about who He is and who you are.
He is Creator.
You are creature.
He is holy.
You need mercy.
He is Savior.
You need saving.
He is Lord.
You are not.
And yet through Christ, the humbled sinner is not discarded.
The sinner is welcomed.
Forgiven.
Adopted.
Restored.
Loved.
That is the scandal of grace.
You come before God with nothing to brag about...
and Jesus gives you everything you could never earn.
This is why the Christian does not defeat pride merely by thinking less of himself.
He defeats pride by becoming captivated with Someone infinitely greater.
Jesus Christ.
Look at Him.
The eternal Son entered our world not wrapped in earthly prestige but in human flesh.
He touched lepers.
Welcomed children.
Ate with sinners.
Washed His disciples’ feet.
Endured mockery.
Allowed His creatures to spit upon Him.
And walked toward a Roman cross.
Philippians 2 says of Christ:
“ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτὸν”
etapeinōsen heauton.
“He humbled himself.”
Philippians 2:8.
How far?
“...becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.”
The humility of Jesus was not helplessness.
It was obedient strength.
He could have pursued status.
Instead He took the form of a servant.
He could have demanded earthly recognition.
Instead He obeyed the Father.
He could have abandoned the road to Calvary.
Instead He went willingly.
And at the cross, something happened Satan could never undo.
Our debt was answered.
Our sin was borne.
Our condemnation fell upon the spotless Lamb.
Jesus died.
Jesus was buried.
And Jesus rose again.
The devil's accusations do not become powerless because Christians develop impressive self-esteem.
They lose their ultimate claim against the believer because Christ has accomplished redemption.
Revelation calls Satan “the accuser.”
But the Gospel points us away from our résumé and toward Christ.
When accusation says,
“Look what you did,”
humility does not need to lie.
It can say,
“Yes. I have sinned. And my hope has never been that I was innocent. My hope is that Jesus Christ is merciful.”
That is devastating to accusation.
Because Satan can weaponize a secret you are desperately trying to protect.
But what happens when you bring that secret into the light before God?
What happens when the alcoholic says, “I need help”?
When the husband says, “I have been selfish”?
When the wife says, “I have been bitter”?
When the pastor says, “I was wrong”?
When the teenager says, “I have been hiding this”?
When the successful Christian finally whispers,
“I am exhausted from pretending”?
The mask falls.
And suddenly there is nothing left to defend except the mercy of Jesus.
Maybe that is where this article found you.
Not in rebellion everyone can see.
But in exhaustion.
You have been trying so hard to appear strong.
You tell everyone, “God is good.”
And He is.
But behind closed doors you are tired.
Your prayer life has become thin.
Your Bible stays closed longer than you want anyone to know.
Temptation has been getting louder.
Your heart has become harder.
You are offended more easily.
Correction feels like an attack.
You are comparing.
Resenting.
Hiding.
Maybe there is a sin you promised God you would never touch again...
and you went back.
Now shame is telling you to hide from the only One who can cleanse you.
Listen carefully.
Do not let pride keep you from grace.
You do not have to impress Jesus before approaching Jesus.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people successfully climbed their way to God.
The Gospel is the announcement that God came down to rescue sinners.
Jesus said:
“Without me ye can do nothing.”
John 15:5.
Nothing.
Our culture hates that sentence.
Our ego hates that sentence.
But exhausted souls eventually discover how beautiful it is.
You were never supposed to be your own savior.
You were never supposed to carry your eternity on your shoulders.
You were never supposed to conquer sin through raw willpower.
You were never supposed to manufacture righteousness impressive enough to make God owe you heaven.
Christ is Savior.
You are not.
And that is good news.
So why can humility function as a weapon against Satan?
Not because humility is a magical technique.
Not because saying humble things frightens demons.
Not because Christians earn supernatural power by degrading themselves.

Humility is powerful because it puts the believer in the posture Scripture commands: submitted to God, dependent upon grace, receptive to truth, ready to repent, watchful against temptation, and able to resist the devil through faith.
Pride says, “I can handle this.”
Humility prays, “Lead us not into temptation.”
Pride hides sin.
Humility confesses it.
Pride resents correction.
Humility listens.
Pride needs recognition.
Humility can serve when nobody applauds.
Pride asks, “How do I look?”
Humility asks, “Is Christ being honored?”
Pride compares.
Humility worships.
Pride tries to become indispensable.
Humility remembers that Jesus was Lord before we arrived and will still be Lord after we are gone.
And pride is extraordinarily dangerous precisely because it can survive inside religious success.
This is where Scripture requires us to be careful.

Christians sometimes state that the Bible explicitly gives one simple sentence saying Satan originally fell because of pride. Scripture's treatment of Satan, evil, and passages traditionally connected with his fall requires more care than that. Isaiah 14 directly addresses the king of Babylon, and Ezekiel 28 directly addresses the ruler or king of Tyre, even though Christians throughout history have debated whether those passages also echo realities beyond those earthly rulers.
We do not need to force those texts to make humility important.
The New Testament already gives us more than enough.
Paul warns that a church overseer must not be a recent convert, “lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil” in 1 Timothy 3:6.
James explicitly connects God's grace with humility and immediately commands submission to God and resistance to the devil.
Peter does the same while warning believers about their adversary.
And Jesus Himself is the supreme pattern of self-humbling obedience.
The biblical case is already powerful.
We do not need exaggeration when truth is this sharp.
Perhaps the real question, then, is not:
“Why is humility a weapon against Satan?”
Perhaps the question is:
Where is pride giving the enemy room to work in me?
That question hurts more.
Because now this is not an article about somebody else.
It is about the conversation you replay because you need to win.
The grudge you call discernment.
The jealousy you call concern.
The arrogance you call confidence.
The stubbornness you call strength.
The prayerlessness you call busyness.
The hidden sin you call manageable.
The refusal to apologize you call principle.
The spiritual coldness you keep covering with Christian activity.
Be honest.
Did this expose something you were hoping nobody would touch?
Then do not waste the conviction.
You do not need to confess private details publicly, but you can stop pretending before God.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that grace still rebuilds people.
Then take the harder step.
Go somewhere quiet.
Put the phone down.
Open your hands.
And pray without performing.
“Jesus, I need You.
Search me.
Expose what I have defended.
Forgive what I have hidden.
Break my pride without hardening my heart.
Teach me to submit to You.
Teach me to resist the devil.
Teach me to receive correction.
Teach me to forgive.
Teach me to repent quickly.
Teach me to depend on Your grace.
I cannot save myself.
Thank You for the cross.
Thank You for mercy.
Thank You that my failures do not have the final word when I belong to You.
You do.
Amen.”
And if someone came into your mind while reading this, do not merely think about them.
Send it privately to the believer who feels ashamed to return to God.
Share it with the person who has become spiritually cold.
Share it with the Christian who is succeeding publicly but may be starving privately.
Share it even with the person who is not yet sure what they believe about Jesus.
If this truth matters, allow it to travel farther than your screen.
Because pride does not disappear after one emotional moment.
There will be another argument.
Another temptation.
Another success.
Another wound.
Another opportunity to make everything about yourself.
You may need these Scriptures again.

Supporting Gospel ministry can glorify God when it is done freely, faithfully, wisely, and from love for Christ—not from guilt or pressure. Scripture teaches willing generosity, not manipulation. So pray about it.
Come back to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you fix yourself.
Not after you become impressive again.
Now.
The Christian life was never about becoming strong enough to stop needing Christ.
Maturity is discovering how completely you need Him—and learning to rejoice that He is completely sufficient.
The world may teach you to build an image.
Jesus calls you to surrender.
The world may tell you never to admit weakness.
Jesus meets people who know they need mercy.
The enemy would gladly watch you spend your life protecting a version of yourself that does not exist.
But grace invites the real you into the light.
The ashamed you.
The exhausted you.
The proud you.
The wounded you.
The secretly struggling you.
The you who promised never again...
and did it again.
Come.
Not because sin does not matter.
It mattered enough for Christ to bleed.
Come because the cross proves both how terrible sin is and how astonishing God's mercy is.
Repentance is not God humiliating you for entertainment.
Repentance is surrendering the lie so grace can lead you into truth.
And perhaps that is why hell has so little to work with when a Christian finally kneels and says:
“I was wrong.
Jesus is right.
I cannot save myself.
Christ, have mercy on me.”
No résumé.
No mask.
No boasting.
Just a sinner...
and an all-sufficient Savior.
And comment something honest—not something impressive.
“Jesus, humble me.”
“Pray for me.”
“No more hiding.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
Because maybe the most dangerous moment for your enemy is not when everybody finally sees how strong you are.
Maybe it is the moment you stop pretending you are strong without Christ.
And remember this when pride comes knocking again:
Satan can do much with the Christian determined to prove he needs nobody—but the Christian on his knees has placed himself beneath the mighty hand of God.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Can Christians Date Without Marriage in Mind?
paragraphs: Can Christians Date Without Marriage in Mind?
Dating is not marriage. A first date is not a proposal. But if you already know you would never build a Christ-centered future with someone, why are you training your heart to ache when they leave?
There is a kind of heartbreak nobody warns Christians about.
It does not begin when somebody cheats.
It does not begin when somebody walks away.
Sometimes it begins much earlier...
when two people start giving each other pieces of their hearts without ever asking where the relationship is supposed to go.
You text every morning.
You talk until midnight.

You know how they take their coffee. You know what makes them laugh. You know what happened in their childhood that they rarely tell anyone. You know when something is wrong from the way they type “I’m fine.”
You pray together sometimes.
You hold hands.
You call each other “babe.”
You become emotionally attached enough to feel married...
while remaining undefined enough to leave whenever things become uncomfortable.
Then somebody finally asks the terrifying question:
“Where is this going?”
And suddenly the relationship that felt so intimate becomes strangely vague.
“I don’t know.”
“Why do we need to label everything?”
“Can’t we just enjoy what we have?”
“I’m not thinking about marriage right now.”
And perhaps the most painful one:
“I never promised you anything.”
Technically, maybe they didn’t.
But hearts do not require contracts before they start attaching themselves.
That is why the question is bigger than whether Christians are “allowed” to date without knowing they will marry the person.
Of course you do not know.

Dating is partly a process of discernment. Christians do not need to approach a first cup of coffee already choosing wedding colors and naming future children. Scripture gives us no command saying every date must end in marriage. Sometimes faithful discernment concludes, peacefully and honestly, that two people should not marry.
But there is a profound difference between dating to discern marriage and dating while deliberately excluding marriage from consideration.
One says:
“I don't know whether I should marry you, so I want to know you truthfully, honor Christ faithfully, guard both of our hearts wisely, and discover whether we could walk toward covenant together.”
The other says:

“I already know I do not intend to build a life with you, but I would still like the affection, attention, emotional intimacy, physical closeness, companionship, validation, and comfort you can give me right now.”
Those are not the same thing.
And Scripture gives us a vision of human love far deeper than “just enjoy each other until it stops being fun.”
Go all the way back to the garden.
Before dating apps.
Before relationship statuses.
Before engagement photos.
Before broken marriages.
Before sin fractured human relationships.
God said:
עַל־כֵּן֙ יַֽעֲזׇב־אִ֔ישׁ אֶת־אָבִ֖יו וְאֶת־אִמּ֑וֹ וְדָבַ֣ק בְּאִשְׁתּ֔וֹ וְהָי֖וּ לְבָשָׂ֥ר אֶחָֽד׃
‘Al-kēn ya‘ăzov-’îsh ’eth-’āvîw we’eth-’immô, wedhāvaq be’ishtô; wehāyû lebhāsār ’eḥād.
Genesis 2:24.
The central movement is breathtaking: a man leaves father and mother, clings to his wife, and they become one flesh.
The Hebrew verb דָּבַק — dabaq carries the sense of clinging, adhering, holding fast.
Notice the direction of biblical intimacy.
It moves toward faithful union.
Toward covenant.
Toward belonging.
Toward permanence.
Toward “one flesh.”

And Jesus Himself reaches back to this passage when questioned about marriage. In Matthew 19:4–6, Christ cites Genesis and then declares that the two are no longer merely two but one flesh, concluding that what God has joined together, humans must not tear apart.
Jesus did not treat marriage as a disposable social arrangement.
He rooted it in creation.
That matters.
Because Christianity does not begin its understanding of relationships by asking, “How close can I get without technically sinning?”
It asks:
“How can I love this person in a way that tells the truth about God?”
That question changes dating.
Maybe you are thinking, “But the Bible never mentions dating.”
Correct.
Modern dating as we know it is not directly described in Scripture. That means we should be careful not to manufacture commandments God did not give.
There is no biblical verse saying, “Thou shalt know on the third date whether this is your spouse.”
There is no command requiring every romantic relationship to become a marriage.
And there is no sin in discovering through honest courtship that you are incompatible.
Sometimes ending a relationship is the godliest decision two people can make.
But Scripture does give principles governing how Christians treat one another.
People are not recreational experiences.
Bodies are not entertainment.
Affection is not currency.
Loneliness does not give us permission to borrow someone else's heart.
And another human being is not something God created for us to use until somebody “better” appears.
Paul writes in Philippians 2:3–4 that Christians should reject selfish ambition and look not merely to their own interests but also to the interests of others.
Apply that to dating.
Not just:
“What does this relationship give me?”
But:
“What is my presence doing to this person's heart?”
That question can hurt.
Because sometimes what we call “dating” is really mutual anesthesia.
Two lonely people soothing wounds neither intends to heal.
Two people terrified of being alone.
Two people enjoying relationship benefits while avoiding relationship responsibility.
Two people saying “I love you” while silently meaning:
“I love what you do for my loneliness.”
And eventually reality arrives.
It always does.
One person becomes serious.
The other retreats.
One begins imagining a future.
The other says, “I thought we were just having fun.”
One has been building a home in their imagination.
The other was renting the room.
And somebody gets evicted from a future that never actually existed.
That is why Christian dating requires something culture increasingly treats as optional:
intentionality.
Intentionality does not mean desperation.
It does not mean interviewing someone for marriage during dinner.
It does not mean every relationship needs to move quickly.
It does not mean staying with somebody merely because you have invested time.
And it certainly does not mean marrying somebody despite serious incompatibility, ungodliness, abuse, manipulation, or danger.
Intentionality simply means refusing to play games with something as powerful as romantic attachment.
It means being honest.
“I am dating because marriage is something I could genuinely desire if God leads us there.”
“I don't know whether you are the person.”
“I want time to discern that.”
“But I refuse to pretend this relationship is meaningless while asking you to give me increasingly meaningful pieces of yourself.”
That is maturity.
And Christian singleness matters here too.
Marriage is not the ultimate destination of the Christian life.
Jesus is.
Paul could speak positively about remaining unmarried for undistracted devotion to the Lord in 1 Corinthians 7. A Christian is not incomplete because he or she is single.
Your salvation does not wear a wedding ring.
Your identity is not “someone's future spouse.”
Your deepest identity is found in Christ.
So the biblical alternative to marriage is not careless romantic consumption.
It can be joyful, purposeful, holy singleness.
That means you do not need a boyfriend or girlfriend simply because loneliness is loud.
You do not need to manufacture intimacy because everyone around you is getting engaged.
You do not need somebody's attention to prove you are desirable.
And you certainly do not need to remain in a relationship that continually drags you away from Jesus simply because being alone scares you.
Maybe that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because perhaps you already know.
You have been trying not to know...
but you know.
You know this person does not want Christ the way you want Christ.
You know every conversation about spiritual growth becomes awkward.
You know boundaries keep collapsing.
You know conviction keeps arriving afterward.
You know you keep explaining away things you once said you would never tolerate.
You know you are becoming spiritually colder.
You know you are praying less.
Compromising more.
Hiding more.
Defending more.
And somewhere beneath all your explanations is one terrifying possibility:
You may be asking God to bless something you are afraid to surrender to Him.
Read that again.
Because sometimes the most dangerous relationship is not the obviously terrible one.
It is the relationship that is almost right.
Kind enough to keep you.
Wrong enough to slowly reshape you.
Romantic enough to make leaving painful.
Spiritual enough to silence your alarm bells.
But not surrendered enough to lead you toward Christ.
The Christian question is therefore not merely:
“Do I want to marry this person?”
It is also:
“Who am I becoming while I love this person?”
Am I becoming more truthful?
More patient?
More pure?
More prayerful?
More obedient?
More compassionate?
More courageous?
More like Jesus?
Or am I slowly negotiating away convictions because losing them feels easier than losing this person?
That question exposes us.
And perhaps you already crossed boundaries.
Perhaps the relationship became sexual.
Perhaps you slept beside somebody you knew was not your spouse.
Perhaps you ignored conviction so many times that conviction became quieter.
Perhaps you stayed because starting over terrified you.
Perhaps you used someone.
Perhaps someone used you.
Perhaps you promised forever and disappeared.
Perhaps you carry memories that still make you ashamed when you pray.
Then hear the Gospel before you hear anything else.
Your story does not end at your worst relationship decision.
Jesus Christ did not come for people who successfully kept themselves spotless.
He came to save sinners.
The cross is where our excuses die...
and where our condemnation can die too.
Repentance does not mean pretending sin was harmless.
Repentance means turning from sin toward the Savior who actually has authority to forgive it.
The apostle John writes that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us from unrighteousness (1 John 1:9).
Not some unrighteousness.
Not merely respectable failures.
There is cleansing in Christ.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is a new beginning in Christ.
There is no romantic history so messy that the blood of Jesus suddenly becomes insufficient.
But grace is not permission to return happily to the chains Christ broke.
Grace teaches us to walk differently.
So maybe repentance means ending a relationship.
Maybe it means establishing boundaries.
Maybe it means confessing what you have hidden.
Maybe it means apologizing to somebody whose heart you treated casually.
Maybe it means admitting that you were not dating because you were ready to love someone—you were dating because you could not stand being alone.
Maybe it means remaining single for a season and discovering that solitude with Jesus is infinitely safer than intimacy that requires disobedience.
And maybe it means something gentler.
Maybe the person beside you really does love Christ.
Maybe neither of you knows whether marriage is right yet.
Good.
You are allowed to discern.
Ask difficult questions.
Watch character over time.
Seek wise counsel.
Pray separately and together.
Learn how the other person handles disappointment, temptation, money, conflict, family, service, correction, forgiveness, church, Scripture, and suffering.
Chemistry can introduce you.
Character tells you whether you should stay.
Because butterflies cannot carry a covenant.
Eventually the excitement settles.
Bodies age.
Circumstances change.
Bills arrive.
Children may arrive.
Sickness may arrive.
Grief arrives.
Disagreements arrive.
And then you discover whether you merely found somebody attractive...
or whether, by God's grace, you found someone willing to keep walking toward Jesus beside you.
So can Christians date without marriage in mind?
If by that you mean, “Must Christians know before dating that they will marry this particular person?”
No.
Dating can be honest discernment precisely because you do not yet know.

But if you mean, “Can Christians deliberately pursue romantic attachment while having no openness to covenant, no concern about where escalating intimacy leads, and no responsibility for the other person's heart?”
That vision is extraordinarily difficult to reconcile with the self-giving, truthful, neighbor-loving ethic Jesus calls His people to embody.
Christian dating should not demand certainty before discernment begins.
But it should have direction.
Not obsession with marriage.
Not desperation for marriage.
Not worship of marriage.
Direction.
Toward truth.
Toward holiness.
Toward sacrificial love.
Toward wise discernment.
Toward covenant if God leads two people there.
And above everything else...
toward Christ.
Maybe the person you are dating will become your spouse.
Maybe they won't.

But even if the relationship ends, you should desire to leave that person closer to Jesus than when you met them—not spiritually confused, emotionally exploited, sexually wounded, or wondering whether any of your words were real.
Imagine dating like that.
Not:
“How much can I get?”
But:
“How faithfully can I love?”
Not:
“How close to the line can we go?”
But:
“How clearly can our relationship honor Christ?”
Not:
“How do I keep this person from leaving?”
But:
“Jesus, if holding onto them requires letting go of You, give me the courage to open my hands.”
That prayer is terrifying.
Because Jesus may expose what you have been protecting.
But He may also rescue you from spending years trying to turn temporary chemistry into permanent covenant.
Be honest.
You do not owe strangers the details.
Sometimes three words are enough to tell another struggling believer:
You are not the only one fighting.
And if somebody came into your mind while reading this, send this to them.
Not as an accusation.
As an invitation.
Save it too.
Because loneliness has a strange ability to make us forget convictions we were certain about when we felt strong.
Come back when your heart starts negotiating.
Come back before you confuse attention with love.
Come back before chemistry convinces you that compromise is destiny.

Supporting Gospel work can be one meaningful way to glorify God when it flows from worship, generosity, and a sincere desire to help biblical truth reach more people. It is about helping sustain and spread Christ-centered resources if you believe this ministry is worth supporting.
Because somewhere on your Facebook friends list may be a person begging God for an answer while pretending everything in their relationship is fine.
Your share might place this message in front of them before another compromise.
Your tag might begin a conversation they were afraid to start.
Your comment might remind somebody else that Christians still struggle—and still run toward grace.
And your support can help Gospel truth travel farther.
But never forget what all of this is ultimately about.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not dating.
Not marriage.
Jesus.
The One who loved you before anyone swiped right.
The One who knew every chapter you would regret and still went to the cross.
The Bridegroom who does not exploit His bride.
The Savior who does not disappear when loving you becomes costly.
The King who does not ask for your heart because He needs validation...
but because He knows exactly what destroys it.
So before you ask whether someone is marriage material, ask whether Jesus truly has your heart.
Before asking God to send “the one,” surrender yourself again to the One who died and rose for you.
And if your romantic story has already become a scandal of broken boundaries, broken promises, broken trust, or broken hearts...
do not hand the pen to shame.
Bring the pages to Jesus.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where forgiveness is commanded.
Leave what must be left.
Repair what can righteously be repaired.
Receive grace.
Then walk forward differently.
Because perhaps the most important question was never merely:
“Will I marry the person I'm dating?”
Perhaps it has always been:
“When this chapter is over, will the way I loved them prove that Jesus was Lord of my heart?”
And remember this when loneliness whispers that you must hold onto someone at any cost:
Never cling so tightly to a temporary relationship that you loosen your grip on the Christ who died to give you eternity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS CALLING SOMEONE “BABE” WHILE YOU’RE MARRIED CHEATING? THE ANSWER MAY EXPOSE MORE THAN YOUR TEXT MESSAGES
paragraphs: IS CALLING SOMEONE “BABE” WHILE YOU’RE MARRIED CHEATING? THE ANSWER MAY EXPOSE MORE THAN YOUR TEXT MESSAGES

The Bible never says the word “babe” is adultery. But Jesus goes much deeper than vocabulary—and what He says about the heart, secrecy, desire, and covenant faithfulness may make this question far more uncomfortable than we expected.
Maybe it was nothing.
That is usually where the story begins.
“It’s just how I talk.”
“She knows I’m married.”
“He’s only a friend.”
“You’re making too much out of one word.”
“It doesn’t mean anything.”
And perhaps, in some situations, that is genuinely true.

“Babe” is not a forbidden biblical word. Scripture contains no verse saying, “Thou shalt not call another person babe.” Depending on culture, family, personality, and context, affectionate terms can sometimes be used casually without romantic intention.
So we need to be careful.
Christians should never manufacture sins God did not call sins.
But we should be equally careful about doing the opposite:
using the absence of an explicit rule to excuse a heart that already knows it is crossing a line.
Because sometimes the real question is not…
“Is the word ‘babe’ cheating?”
Sometimes the real question is…
Why do I need this person to feel special to me in a way I would be uncomfortable letting my spouse see?
And suddenly this is no longer an article about one little word.
It is about the heart.
The phone lights up.
Your spouse is sitting nearby.
A message appears.
“Goodnight, babe ❤️”
And almost instinctively, the screen turns downward.
That tiny movement may say more than a thousand explanations.
Not always.
But sometimes.
Because secrecy has a language of its own.
Deleting.
Archiving.
Changing contact names.
Turning notifications off.
Moving conversations to disappearing messages.
Explaining things differently depending on who is asking.
Saying, “You wouldn’t understand.”
Calling someone “just a friend” while feeding an emotional connection you know would wound the person wearing your wedding ring.
That is where Christians must stop asking only, “How far can I go before this technically becomes cheating?”
That question is already aimed in the wrong direction.
The Gospel does not train us to walk as close to betrayal as possible without receiving the label.
Jesus calls us toward faithfulness.
Toward truth.
Toward holiness.
Toward love.
Toward Him.
And when Jesus addressed sexual sin, He refused to let people hide behind merely external definitions.
Matthew 5:27–28 records His words:
“Ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἐρρέθη· Οὐ μοιχεύσεις. ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.”
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Jesus was not saying that every friendly interaction between a married person and someone else is adultery.
He was doing something far more penetrating.
He brought the issue into the heart.
The Greek expression translated “to lust after her” includes πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn, pointing toward desire directed at another person.
Jesus exposes something we desperately try to conceal:
A person can maintain an externally respectable image while internally cultivating unfaithfulness.
That changes the conversation.
Calling somebody “babe” does not automatically prove adultery.

But if “babe” is the verbal fruit of romantic desire, flirtation, secret intimacy, emotional dependency, or an attachment deliberately being cultivated outside your marriage, then arguing about the dictionary definition of “babe” may simply be a convenient way of avoiding the condition of your heart.
Imagine your spouse standing behind you while you type it.
Would the message change?
Would the emoji disappear?
Would your tone become different?
Would you suddenly need to explain context?
Would you feel exposed?
That discomfort is not an infallible test of sin. Some spouses can be unreasonably suspicious, and some innocent interactions can be misunderstood.
But it is still worth asking:
Why am I comfortable doing privately what I am afraid to do transparently?
Proverbs 4:23 says:
“מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ כִּי־מִמֶּנּוּ תּוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים”
Mi-kol mishmar netzor libbekha, ki-mimmennu totze'ot chayyim.
“Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life.”
Guard your heart.
Not because affection is evil.
Not because friendship is evil.
Not because every conversation with someone other than your spouse is dangerous.
But because hearts drift.
Usually quietly.
Almost nobody wakes up one morning planning to destroy a marriage.
It begins smaller.
A conversation you start looking forward to.
A compliment that feels a little too good.
A joke you would not make if your husband were beside you.
A pet name you would not use if your wife could hear it.
A problem in your marriage that you begin discussing intimately with somebody you are attracted to.
Then comes the comparison.
“They actually listen to me.”
“She appreciates me.”
“He notices things my husband doesn't.”
“She makes me feel alive again.”
And somewhere along the way, another person begins receiving emotional territory that should have been guarded.
This is why the biblical picture of marriage matters.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד”
Al-ken ya'azov ish et-aviv ve'et-immo, vedavaq be'ishto, vehayu levasar echad.
A man leaves his father and mother, holds fast to his wife, and they become one flesh.
The Hebrew verb דָּבַק — davaq carries the sense of clinging, holding fast, sticking closely.
Marriage in Scripture is not presented merely as legal permission for sexual activity.
It is covenantal union.
And the New Testament makes marriage even more breathtaking.
Ephesians 5 points beyond husband and wife toward Christ and His Church.
Marriage therefore carries a sacred signpost.
Faithfulness says something.
Sacrifice says something.
Forgiveness says something.
Covenant says something.
And betrayal says something too.
So perhaps the better question is not:
“Can married people call somebody else babe?”
Ask:
What am I building with this person?
Is this ordinary kindness?
Or cultivated intimacy?
Is this cultural vocabulary?
Or flirtation disguised as personality?
Would my spouse reasonably understand the context?
Or have I intentionally kept the context hidden?
Am I treating another person affectionately because that is genuinely how I speak to everyone?
Or because I enjoy knowing that this particular person feels desired by me?
Do I secretly enjoy being desired back?
Would I delete the conversation before handing my phone to my spouse?
Would I be comfortable if my spouse communicated with someone else exactly the way I am communicating with this person?
That last question can hurt.
Because sometimes we demand boundaries from our spouse that we quietly resent having applied to ourselves.
If your wife called another man “babe,” sent him heart emojis, confided in him late at night, hid their conversations, and insisted that you were insecure for being uncomfortable…
would you genuinely call it harmless?
If your husband called another woman “babe,” constantly complimented her appearance, waited for her messages, erased their conversations, and became emotionally defensive whenever you mentioned her…
would “nothing physical happened” completely settle your heart?
Maybe the deepest betrayal began before bodies ever touched.
Scripture recognizes that sin can be conceived inwardly before its outward consequences become visible.
James 1:14–15 describes desire conceiving and eventually giving birth to sin.
That does not mean every temptation is itself identical to committing the outward act. Temptation must not be confused with surrender.
Jesus Himself was tempted and yet without sin.
That distinction matters tremendously.
You can notice someone attractive without committing adultery.
You can experience an unwanted temptation without betraying your spouse.
You can have friends of the opposite sex without living in sin.
You can even make a foolish relational mistake and repent without being permanently defined by that failure.
But feeding desire is different from experiencing temptation.
Protecting secret intimacy is different from encountering attraction.
Choosing flirtation is different from noticing beauty.
Returning repeatedly to a relationship because it gives you romantic or emotional gratification outside your marriage deserves serious spiritual examination.
And Jesus does not expose these things because He delights in humiliating people.
He exposes darkness because He came to rescue people from it.
That distinction changes everything.
Perhaps you are reading this and feeling conviction.
Not theoretical conviction.
Specific conviction.
A name entered your mind.
A conversation.
A deleted thread.
A coworker.
An ex.
A “friend.”
A person you keep saying means nothing…
yet somehow you cannot bear the thought of losing their attention.
Maybe nothing sexual has happened.
Maybe you have never kissed.
Never touched.
Never met privately.
But deep down, you know something has begun taking root.
Please do not wait for the seed to become a forest before admitting you planted something.
And please do not mistake conviction for condemnation.
Conviction says, “Come into the light.”
Condemnation says, “Hide because there is no hope for you.”
The Gospel says something radically different.
There is a Savior standing in the light.
His name is Jesus.
First John 1:9 tells believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
Not excuse us.
Not teach us to rename sin.
Forgive us.
Cleanse us.
Restore us.
This is why Christianity is not ultimately a religion of people pretending they never crossed boundaries.
Christianity is the announcement that sinners can come home because Christ died and rose again.
At the cross, Jesus did not minimize sin.
He demonstrated how serious it truly is.
And at the same cross, He demonstrated how astonishing grace truly is.
Maybe your marriage is already bleeding because of emotional infidelity.
Maybe you were betrayed.
Maybe you were the one who betrayed.
Maybe screenshots were discovered.
Maybe trust collapsed.
Maybe “babe” was only one word in thousands of messages you wish you could take back.
Maybe your spouse looks at you differently now.
Maybe you look at yourself differently.
Listen carefully:
Your sin can have real consequences and still not be greater than the mercy of Christ.
Grace does not erase accountability.
Grace gives us courage to face it.
Repentance is not merely feeling horrible because you got caught.
The New Testament word often translated “repentance,” μετάνοια — metanoia, speaks of a change of mind, a turning that produces a changed direction.
Biblical repentance does not ask:
“How can I convince my spouse that this wasn't technically cheating?”
It asks:
“Jesus, what in me needs to change?”
That may mean ending an inappropriate relationship.
It may mean confessing what you have concealed.
It may mean stopping flirtatious communication.
It may mean creating wise boundaries.
It may mean seeking mature pastoral counsel and, where appropriate, qualified marriage counseling.
It may mean giving your wounded spouse time instead of demanding instant trust because you apologized.
Forgiveness and restored trust are related, but they are not identical.
Trust can require rebuilding.
Slowly.
Painfully.
Honestly.
One truthful day at a time.
And if you are the spouse who discovered the messages, your pain should not be mocked as “insecurity.”
Neither should every ambiguous word automatically be treated as proof of an affair.
Truth matters in both directions.
Do not exaggerate evidence.
Do not minimize evidence.
Bring everything into the light.
Because Christian marriage cannot survive indefinitely on surveillance, suspicion, secrecy, and technicalities.
It needs truth.
It needs grace.
It needs repentance.
It needs Christ.
Ephesians 4:25 tells believers to put away falsehood and speak truth.
Ephesians 5:25 tells husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the Church and gave Himself for her.
First Corinthians 13 teaches that love does not rejoice in wrongdoing but rejoices with the truth.
Do you see the pattern?
Biblical love does not ask how much darkness it can preserve.
Love moves toward truth.
So, is calling somebody “babe” while married cheating?
Not automatically.
There is no biblically responsible basis for declaring that a particular English pet name, by itself and regardless of context, constitutes adultery.
But that does not make every use innocent.
Context matters.
Intent matters.
Desire matters.
Secrecy matters.
The nature of the relationship matters.
Your pattern of behavior matters.
And above all, your heart before God matters.
A grandmother calling everybody “babe” is not equivalent to a married man secretly calling a woman he desires “babe” at 1:00 a.m.
A culturally normal term of endearment is not automatically equivalent to cultivating a hidden romantic attachment.
Biblical wisdom refuses both extremes.
It refuses legalism that invents sins Scripture never names.
And it refuses loophole Christianity that searches Scripture for technical permission to keep playing with fire.
Maybe that is why this question became uncomfortable.
We began with one word.
We ended up standing before our own hearts.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every private detail. But you do need to stop running from Jesus.
And if you have lived through emotional betrayal and Jesus has been restoring you, your testimony may become someone else's reason not to give up.
Share what wisdom you can without exposing private information that belongs to your spouse.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God. We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
Send it privately to the married couple who has been fighting to rebuild trust.
We never want to turn devotion to Jesus into a sales technique.
But before you leave this article, return to the question you may have hoped we would answer with a simple yes or no.
Is calling someone “babe” cheating?
Sometimes the word is innocent.
Sometimes the word is merely the smoke.
And if there is fire beneath it, changing the vocabulary will never heal the heart.
Jesus did not die merely to make adulterers use cleaner language.
He died and rose again to make sinners new.
So bring Him the message you deleted.
Bring Him the attraction you keep rationalizing.
Bring Him the marriage that feels numb.
Bring Him the betrayal you committed.
Bring Him the betrayal you survived.
Bring Him your shame.
Bring Him your anger.
Bring Him your excuses.
Bring Him the part of your heart nobody else can see.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive as Christ teaches you to forgive.
Seek reconciliation where it is safe, truthful, wise, and possible.
Rebuild what can be rebuilt.
And when consequences remain, remember that consequences do not mean Christ has abandoned the repentant sinner.
Peter failed.
David fell catastrophically.
The Scriptures are filled with people whose darkest chapters were real.
The Bible does not airbrush scandal.
Neither does it allow scandal to have the final word when grace enters the story.
That is the Gospel Warrior message.
Not that sin does not matter.
That Jesus matters more.
Not that betrayal does not wound.
That Christ still heals.
Not that broken trust magically returns overnight.
That redemption can begin even among the ruins.
And perhaps somebody reading this right now is staring at a conversation they already know they need to end.
You know.
God knows.
And maybe this article arrived before the affair did.
Before the hotel room.
Before the confession.
Before the children discovered it.
Before two families shattered.
Before “we're only friends” became “I don't know how this happened.”
Close the door now.
Not merely the chat window.
The door in your heart.
Then turn around.
Jesus is still calling you home.
And comment before you go.
Not for an algorithm alone.
For honesty.
“No more hiding.”
Three words.
Maybe the first three words of a restored marriage.
Maybe the first three words of genuine repentance.
Maybe the first three words of a completely rewritten story.

Because the message you are hiding may feel like the end of your story—but placed honestly into the hands of Jesus, even the chapter you are most ashamed of does not have to write your final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SAUL WAS DESPERATE FOR AN ANSWER FROM GOD. SO HE WENT TO A MEDIUM IN THE DARK.
paragraphs:
SAUL WAS DESPERATE FOR AN ANSWER FROM GOD. SO HE WENT TO A MEDIUM IN THE DARK.
The terrifying story of the woman at Endor is not really about how to contact the dead. It is about what can happen when a heart wants an answer from God more than it wants God Himself.
There is something almost unbearable about the sentence.
God did not answer him.
Not because Saul had never known God.
That would make the story easier.
Saul knew what it was to be chosen.
He knew what it was to have Samuel speak the word of the LORD over his life. He knew what it was to stand among ordinary men and suddenly discover that God had placed a kingdom on his shoulders.
He had experienced victory.
Anointing.
Prophetic confirmation.
The Spirit of God had come upon him.
Once, Saul looked like the beginning of something beautiful.
And now...
he was standing in the dark.
Terrified.
Desperate.
Disguised.
Looking for a woman he himself had once driven out of the land.
A medium.
Because heaven seemed silent.
And if you have ever prayed until your throat felt empty...
if you have ever begged God for direction and received no immediate explanation...

if you have ever watched the deadline approach, the relationship collapse, the diagnosis arrive, the money disappear, the opportunity close, the person walk away, or the future become terrifyingly unclear...
then be careful before you look down on Saul.
You may have never walked to Endor.
But desperation has its own Endors.
And some of them are only one frightened decision away.
The Philistines had gathered for war.
Saul saw their army, and Scripture does not soften what happened inside him.
The Hebrew says:
וַיִּרָא וַיֶּחֱרַד לִבּוֹ מְאֹד
Vayyira, vayyecherad libbo me’od.
He was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly.
This was not mild anxiety.
The king was unraveling.
Then comes one of the darkest sentences in Saul’s life:
וַיִּשְׁאַל שָׁאוּל בַּיהוָה וְלֹא עָנָהוּ יְהוָה
Vayyish’al Sha’ul ba-YHWH, velo ‘anahu YHWH.
“Saul inquired of the LORD, but the LORD did not answer him.”
Not by dreams.
Not by the Urim.
Not by the prophets.
Nothing.
Silence.
And this is where the story becomes frighteningly personal.
Because silence reveals things.
When God does not give us the answer we want when we want it, we discover whether we were seeking God...
or merely seeking relief.
There is an enormous difference between wanting God’s will and wanting God to approve ours.

Saul had spent years resisting the voice of God, rationalizing disobedience, preserving what God told him to destroy, fearing people, protecting his position, hunting David, and repeatedly moving farther from surrendered obedience.
Now he wanted guidance.
But guidance cannot be separated from surrender.
Saul wanted another word while his life was still haunted by the words he had already refused to obey.
That should make every believer uncomfortable.
Because sometimes we cry,
“God, speak to me!”
while an old command is still lying ignored at our feet.
Forgive them.
No.
End the secret sin.
Not yet.
Tell the truth.
That would cost too much.
Repent.
Maybe tomorrow.
Stop returning to what is destroying you.
But Lord, just give me a sign...
We can become obsessed with receiving new revelation while resisting old obedience.
Saul’s tragedy did not begin at Endor.
Endor was simply where years of compromise finally became visible.
Long before Saul walked into that night, Samuel had confronted him with words that still pierce the conscience:
“To obey is better than sacrifice.”
Saul wanted the kingdom without surrender.
He wanted God’s power without God’s government.
He wanted divine confirmation without complete obedience.
Eventually desperation exposed him.
And that is when Saul said something astonishing:
בַּקְּשׁוּ־לִי אֵשֶׁת בַּעֲלַת־אוֹב
Baqqeshu-li ’eshet ba‘alat-’ov.
“Find me a woman who is a medium.”

The Hebrew expression בַּעֲלַת־אוֹב — ba‘alat-’ov describes a woman associated with or possessing an ’ov, a term used in the Old Testament in connection with forbidden attempts to consult the dead or spirits.
And Saul knew it was forbidden.
That makes the scene even darker.
Earlier in the very chapter, Scripture tells us that Saul himself had removed the mediums and spiritists from the land.
He knew.
He had enforced the prohibition.
God’s Law was not unclear about occult consultation. Israel had been explicitly forbidden from turning to mediums, spiritists, divination, and attempts to consult the dead.
Yet fear can make a person seek privately what he once condemned publicly.
Read that again.
Because that is not merely Saul’s problem.
A person can preach against something and secretly hunger for it.
A person can warn others about sin while slowly negotiating with the same sin behind closed doors.
A person can look spiritually strong in daylight and become someone completely different when night falls.
And Saul literally went at night.
He removed his royal clothing.
He disguised himself.
He took two men with him.
And Scripture says:
וַיָּבֹאוּ אֶל־הָאִשָּׁה לָיְלָה
They came to the woman by night.
What a picture.
Israel’s king...
hiding his identity...
walking through darkness...
looking for forbidden guidance...
because he could no longer bear the silence.
There are sins that love darkness because darkness makes us believe nobody can see the contradiction.
The hidden browser.
The deleted conversation.
The second account.
The secret relationship.
The private addiction.
The horoscope you insist is “just entertainment.”
The psychic reading you call curiosity.
The spiritual practice you know does not belong to Christ.
The compromise nobody at church knows about.
The bitterness you have learned to hide beneath Christian vocabulary.
The sin you keep renaming because calling it what Scripture calls it would require repentance.
You may change clothes.
You may delete history.
You may fool your family.
You may fool your pastor.
You may even fool yourself.
But you cannot disguise yourself before God.
Saul entered that house pretending not to be Saul.
But heaven knew exactly who had walked through the door.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been doing the same thing.
Not consulting a medium.
Something subtler.
You still post Bible verses.
Still say “God is good.”
Still know when to raise your hands.
Still know Christian language.
Still look normal.
But somewhere inside, you know you have been walking farther into the night.
And the most dangerous part is that you still want God to answer you without touching the thing you refuse to surrender.
Saul asked the woman to bring up Samuel.
What follows has generated centuries of discussion.

The narrative itself repeatedly calls the figure Samuel, and the message given to Saul is consistent with judgment previously announced through Samuel: the kingdom had been torn from Saul, David would receive it, and Saul and his sons were facing death.

Christians have proposed different explanations for exactly what occurred—whether God sovereignly permitted Samuel himself to appear despite the forbidden ritual, or whether the event should be understood differently.
We should not pretend Scripture tells us more than it does.
But we must not miss what Scripture makes unmistakably clear:
Saul’s action was rebellion, not a model for spiritual guidance.
The Bible never presents necromancy as an acceptable way to seek God.
