“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:27–28).
The Greek expression translated “to lust after” includes πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn.
Jesus is not declaring that noticing beauty, experiencing attraction, or involuntarily feeling sexual desire is identical to adultery.
He goes deeper.
He confronts the deliberate cultivation of lust.
The lingering look that becomes possession in the imagination.
The person on the screen who stops being somebody made in God's image and becomes material for consumption.
The fantasy you repeatedly return to because reality has disappointed you.
The secret relationship you justify because your marriage is painful.
The pornography you excuse because you are lonely.
The bitterness you baptize as “needs.”
The entitlement that whispers:
“I deserve this.”
And eventually:
“Therefore I am allowed to disobey God to get it.”
That is where sexual frustration becomes spiritually dangerous.
Not because wanting intimacy makes you evil.
But because an unmet desire can quietly become an idol.
And idols always make promises they cannot keep.
Sex says, “I can make you whole.”
Jesus says, “Come to Me.”
Pornography says, “Nobody will know.”
Jesus says that darkness never heals what it teaches you to hide.
Fantasy says, “Escape.”
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
Resentment says, “You have the right to punish the person withholding what you want.”
Jesus calls you to love.
Entitlement says, “Your desire is your authority.”
Jesus says:
“Deny yourself and take up your cross daily and follow me” (Luke 9:23).
And this is where Christianity becomes painfully different from the message of the culture around us.
The Gospel does not say every powerful desire must be satisfied.
It says every part of us must come under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Including sexuality.
Especially sexuality.

The New Testament repeatedly calls believers to sexual holiness. Paul writes that God's will includes our sanctification and that believers should “abstain from sexual immorality” (1 Thessalonians 4:3).
The Greek word translated sexual immorality is πορνεία — porneia.
Within New Testament moral teaching, it refers broadly to sexual conduct outside God's design for sexual holiness.
But Christian holiness is not merely saying “no” to forbidden sex.
It is saying “yes” to belonging completely to Christ.
Paul asks:
“Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you... You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).
Read that again.
Your body is not disgusting.
Your body belongs to God.
There is a massive difference.
Christian sexual ethics are not built upon hatred of the body.
They are built upon the sacredness of the body.
You were bought with a price.
Christ did not shed His blood merely to rescue the religious-looking parts of you.
He purchased all of you.
Your thoughts.
Your loneliness.
Your sexuality.
Your memories.
Your wounds.
Your desires.
Your disappointments.
Even the parts of your life you are embarrassed to bring into prayer.
And perhaps that is exactly where somebody reading this needs to stop hiding.
You have been trying to defeat sexual frustration by pretending you do not experience it.
But secrecy is fertile soil for temptation.
Bring it into the light.
Tell God the truth.
Not the polished prayer.
The real prayer.
“Lord, I am lonely.”
“Lord, I feel rejected.”
“Lord, I am angry.”
“Lord, I want intimacy.”
“Lord, I am tempted.”
“Lord, I keep fantasizing.”
“Lord, part of me wants to disobey You.”
“Jesus, I need You more than I need another promise that I will somehow become strong enough tomorrow.”
That is not weak Christianity.
That is dependence.
Hebrews does not tell struggling believers to run away from God until they have cleaned themselves up.
It says:
“Let us then with confidence draw near to the throne of grace, that we may receive mercy and find grace to help in time of need” (Hebrews 4:16).
The word translated “grace” is χάρις — charis.
Grace.
Not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace that meets sinners where sin has wounded them and begins transforming them into people who increasingly resemble Christ.
That means if sexual frustration has already taken you somewhere you know you should never have gone, this article is not finished.
Maybe it became pornography.
Maybe masturbation has become entangled with pornography, lustful fantasy, compulsion, or a pattern you can no longer honestly describe as self-controlled.
Maybe it became sexting.
Maybe you crossed physical boundaries.
Maybe you are emotionally involved with someone who is not your spouse.
Maybe resentment toward your husband or wife has hardened your heart.
Maybe you have been using another person's body in your imagination for years.
Maybe you crossed a line last night.
And now you feel filthy.
The Gospel has something stronger than pretending it did not happen.
Repentance.
The biblical word commonly translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō: to repent, to undergo a change of mind that expresses itself in turning.
Biblical repentance is more than feeling horrible about yourself.
Judas felt remorse.
Repentance turns toward God.
It agrees with Him about sin.
It stops defending what Christ died to redeem us from.
It brings darkness into the light.
It receives mercy.
And then it begins walking in another direction.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
Do you see the scandal?
God already knows what you did.
And still He invites confession.
God already knows what you watched.
God already knows what you imagined.
God already knows how many times you promised Him, “Never again.”
And the cross still stands.
Not because your sin is small.
Because Christ is sufficient.
Christianity does not minimize sexual sin.
It announces that Jesus Christ is greater than sexual sin.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die for an imaginary version of you who never struggled.
“For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6).
Weak.
Not impressive.
Not victorious-looking.
Weak.
And if you have fallen, Christ does not call you to make peace with the mud.
He calls you out of it.
Grace does not whisper, “Stay there.”
Grace says, “Come home.”
That is the difference between condemnation and conviction.
Condemnation says, “Hide from God.”
Conviction says, “Run to God.”
Condemnation says, “You are beyond mercy.”
The Gospel says there is “now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).
Condemnation says, “This is who you will always be.”
Jesus says, in effect, “Follow Me.”
And following Him may require decisions that hurt.
Delete the hidden account.
Install accountability.
Stop messaging that person.
Tell a mature Christian you trust what is actually happening.
If you are married, stop allowing resentment to replace honest, compassionate conversation.
If serious relational, medical, psychological, or trauma-related issues are affecting intimacy, seek appropriate pastoral and professional help rather than turning suffering into accusation.
And married Christians should remember something equally important.
Scripture does speak seriously about mutual marital intimacy.

Paul tells husbands and wives not to deprive one another except by mutual agreement for a limited time for prayer, after which they should come together again because temptation is real (1 Corinthians 7:3–5).
That passage should never be weaponized to demand sex, ignore consent, dismiss illness, pressure a traumatized spouse, or excuse coercion.
Biblical marriage is not ownership of another person's body for selfish gratification.
Paul's language is strikingly mutual.
Husband and wife are called away from selfishness toward covenantal giving.
Christian intimacy should reflect love, tenderness, faithfulness, patience, sacrifice, and honor—not manipulation.
So if you are sexually frustrated in marriage, your pain may be real.
Do not pretend otherwise.
But your pain does not give you permission to sin against your spouse.

And if your spouse is hurting, frightened, exhausted, physically unwell, emotionally wounded, or carrying unresolved trauma, winning an argument about your “rights” while crushing the person you vowed to love is not Christlike victory.
Talk.
Listen.
Pray.
Seek help.
Be patient.
Pursue healing rather than leverage.
And if you are single, please hear this:
You are not spiritually defective because you desire marriage and sexual intimacy.
Paul acknowledges both celibacy and marriage within Christian discipleship and says that if people cannot exercise self-control, “they should marry” (1 Corinthians 7:9).
Scripture does not mock sexual desire.
But neither does it promise every Christian marriage on the timetable they want.
That hurts.
There are faithful believers who have carried unwanted singleness much longer than they expected.
There are widows and widowers who know exactly what intimacy felt like and now sleep alone.
There are divorced believers trying to obey Christ while navigating wounds and complicated questions.
There are spouses living through seasons when intimacy is difficult or impossible.
There are Christians who experience powerful desires that obedience to Jesus does not permit them to fulfill.
Christian discipleship sometimes means bringing a real desire before Jesus and saying:
“I want this.
But I want You more.”
That sentence is easy to print.
It can be agonizing to live.
Jesus understands costly obedience.
In Gethsemane, facing suffering beyond anything we can adequately comprehend, He prayed:
“Not my will, but yours, be done” (Luke 22:42).
This does not mean sexual frustration is comparable to Christ's atoning suffering.
It means the Christian pattern is unmistakable:
Desire is brought beneath obedience to the Father.
There will be moments when holiness feels like loss.
There will be nights when obedience feels less dramatic than temptation and much lonelier.
Nobody applauds the browser you closed.
Nobody sees the message you decided not to send.
Nobody knows you got out of bed and prayed because staying there with your imagination felt dangerous.
Nobody sees the tears after you chose faithfulness again.
But God sees.
Your hidden obedience is not wasted.
And self-control is not merely a personality trait possessed by unusually disciplined Christians.
It is named among the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22–23.
The Greek word is ἐγκράτεια — enkrateia: self-control, mastery over one's impulses.
Notice whose fruit it is.
The Spirit's.
This battle was never meant to be fought by gritting your teeth while secretly feeding the very things you are begging God to remove.
You need the Holy Spirit.
You need Scripture.
You need prayer.
You need wise Christian community.
You may need accountability.
You may need counseling.
You may need an honest conversation with your spouse.
You may need to grieve an expectation that God never promised to fulfill according to your schedule.
And you may need to discover something deeper:
The ultimate answer to sexual frustration is not the extinction of sexuality.
It is the enthronement of Christ.
Because even fulfilled sexual desire cannot carry the weight of being your god.
Marriage cannot save you.
Sex cannot save you.
Romance cannot save you.
A spouse cannot heal every wound in your soul.
Only Jesus can reconcile you to God.
Only Jesus carried our sins to the cross.
Only Jesus rose from the grave.
Only Jesus can take the person hiding behind shame and write a different ending.
That is why we keep returning to these words:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By meeting sinners inside the wreckage and doing what sinners could never do for themselves.
Forgiving.
Cleansing.
Restoring.
Transforming.
Making dead hearts alive.
If you have never surrendered your life to Jesus Christ, sexual frustration may be the question that brought you here, but Jesus wants more than management of your sexuality.
He wants you.
Turn from sin.
Trust in Christ.
Believe the Gospel.
Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
Stop negotiating with the darkness that keeps promising satisfaction and leaving you emptier.
Come to Christ.
Confess it.
Bring it into the light.
Ask for help.

Following Gospel Warrior also helps you stay connected to daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment—and you can invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelievers to follow with you.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with earning God's favor.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot share enough Christian posts to erase one sin.
Salvation is God's gift in Jesus Christ.
We support Gospel ministry because we love the One who saved us—not because our support saves us.
And perhaps tonight, when nobody sees the battle except God, remember this:
The desire screaming inside you does not get the final word. The temptation does not get the final word. Your worst failure does not get the final word. Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD NEVER TOLD YOU TO FOLLOW A LEADER BLINDLY
paragraphs: GOD NEVER TOLD YOU TO FOLLOW A LEADER BLINDLY

The most dangerous spiritual deception may not begin when you stop listening to godly leaders. It may begin when you become so loyal to a human voice that you stop checking whether that voice still agrees with Jesus.
There is a sentence many Christians are terrified to say out loud:
“My pastor might be wrong.”
Not evil.
Not necessarily dishonest.
Not necessarily a false teacher.
Just... wrong.
And somehow, for some believers, even admitting that possibility feels like rebellion against God.
Maybe you were taught that questioning a spiritual leader means questioning God's authority.
Maybe someone quoted, “Touch not mine anointed,” whenever uncomfortable questions surfaced.
Maybe you learned to stay quiet because you did not want to become “divisive.”
Maybe the leader was there when your marriage was collapsing.
Maybe he prayed for you when nobody else knew you were drowning.
Maybe she discipled you when your faith was barely alive.
Maybe that ministry introduced you to Scripture.
So when something eventually felt wrong, you fought the feeling.
You told yourself, Who am I to question them?
And that is exactly where this conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because gratitude is biblical.
Honor is biblical.
Submission is biblical.
Pastoral authority is biblical.
But blind allegiance to a human being is not.
There is only One Shepherd who has never needed correction.
Only One Teacher who has never mishandled Scripture.
Only One King whose motives have never been contaminated by pride.
Only One Savior whose authority is absolute.
His name is Jesus Christ.

And if your loyalty to a Christian leader ever requires you to silence Scripture, excuse sin, suppress truth, surrender your conscience, or protect someone's reputation at the expense of righteousness...
something has gone terribly wrong.
This is not an article teaching rebellion.
It is an article pleading for biblical discernment.
Because there is another side to this that must be said immediately.
Some Christians use “discernment” as camouflage for pride. They refuse accountability, reject correction, church-hop whenever confronted, and call every pastor who challenges them “controlling.”
That is not spiritual maturity either.

Scripture genuinely commands believers to respect faithful leaders. Hebrews 13:17 speaks seriously about responding to those who watch over souls. First Thessalonians 5:12–13 calls believers to recognize and esteem those who labor among them. First Timothy 5:17 speaks of elders who rule well as worthy of honor.
So this is not permission to become cynical.
It is permission to remember that your pastor is not your Christ.
Your denomination is not your Christ.
Your favorite preacher is not your Christ.
Your ministry founder is not your Christ.
Your spiritual mentor is not your Christ.
Jesus is.
And Scripture gives us one of the clearest pictures of healthy discernment in Acts 17.
Paul arrives preaching Christ, and the Bereans listen.
But they do something remarkable.
They examine the Scriptures to determine whether what Paul is teaching is true.
Think about that.
This is Paul.
An apostle.
The man whose Spirit-inspired letters would become part of the New Testament.
And yet Acts 17:11 praises the Bereans because they received the message eagerly while examining the Scriptures daily to see whether these things were so.
They were teachable...
without becoming gullible.
Hungry...
without becoming blind.
Respectful...
without surrendering discernment.
That combination is desperately needed again.
Paul himself gives us another astonishing safeguard.

In Galatians 1:8 he essentially places even his own preaching beneath the authority of the Gospel already proclaimed. He says that even if we—or even an angel from heaven—should proclaim a gospel contrary to the one already preached, that messenger is to be rejected.
Do you see how radical that is?
Paul does not say, “Believe it because I said it.”
He effectively says:
If even I contradict the Gospel, do not let my identity override the truth.
The messenger does not own the message.
The messenger stands underneath it.
And this principle becomes even sharper in 1 Thessalonians 5:21:
πάντα δὲ δοκιμάζετε, τὸ καλὸν κατέχετε
Panta de dokimazete, to kalon katechete.
“Test everything; hold fast what is good.”

The Greek verb δοκιμάζετε — dokimazete, from dokimazō, carries the sense of testing, examining, or evaluating something to determine its genuineness or worth. It is an imperative. Paul is not teaching believers to swallow everything labeled “spiritual.” He commands discernment.
Notice what Scripture does not say.
Test everything except your favorite preacher.
Test everything except the sermon that made you cry.
Test everything except the prophecy spoken over you.
Test everything except the ministry with millions of followers.
Test everything except the leader who helped you.
No.
πάντα — panta.
Everything.
And that means something can sound powerful and still need testing.
A preacher can make you cry and still mishandle a passage.
A leader can be charismatic and still lack character.
A ministry can grow numerically while becoming spiritually unhealthy.
Someone can speak confidently without speaking accurately.
Someone can have a gift without possessing infallibility.
And sometimes the most difficult deception to recognize is the one wrapped in vocabulary you already trust.
“God told me.”
“Submit to authority.”
“Don't question the anointed.”
“You're touching God's servant.”
“You just need to obey.”
Those sentences can sometimes appear in legitimate contexts.
But put them in the hands of an unhealthy leader, and suddenly spiritual language becomes a cage.
Jesus warned His disciples about leadership that imitates worldly domination.

In Mark 10:42–45, He contrasts Gentile rulers who “lord it over” people with leadership among His disciples. Greatness in Christ's kingdom is expressed through service, and Jesus Himself provides the supreme pattern: the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many.
That means Christian leadership should increasingly resemble a towel and a basin...
not a throne.
A shepherd is not called to consume sheep.
A shepherd protects them.
A teacher is not called to make disciples dependent upon his personality.
He points them toward Christ.
John the Baptist understood this beautifully:
“He must increase, but I must decrease.”
That is healthy ministry.
The closer people get to Jesus, the less indispensable the human messenger should need to feel.
But unhealthy spiritual systems reverse the equation.
Eventually everything becomes about protecting the leader.
Protect the platform.
Protect the reputation.
Protect the organization.
Protect the brand.
Protect the numbers.
Protect the image.
And somewhere beneath all that protecting is a wounded believer asking:
“But what about the truth?”
Maybe that believer is you.
Maybe you noticed something years ago.
A manipulation.
A contradiction.
A pattern of favoritism.
Money that nobody was allowed to question.
Sin that was condemned publicly but protected privately.
A leader demanding standards from others that somehow never applied to himself.
Maybe you asked respectfully.
And instead of receiving an answer, you received a label.
Rebellious.
Bitter.
Disloyal.
Unsubmissive.
Dangerous.
So you learned silence.
And perhaps the deepest wound was not merely what a leader did.
It was what happened to your picture of God afterward.
You started wondering whether Jesus was like them.
Controlling.
Temperamental.
Impossible to please.
Demanding unquestioning loyalty.
Ready to punish questions.
And that is where spiritual disappointment becomes spiritually dangerous.
Because when a human representative of Christ wounds us, the temptation is to project that person's character onto Christ Himself.
But hear this carefully:
Jesus is not embarrassed by your questions.
Jesus is not threatened by truth.
Jesus does not need lies to defend His reputation.
Jesus never needs abuse hidden to preserve His kingdom.
Jesus never asks you to call darkness light because a respected Christian created the darkness.
Christ is truth.
And truth does not fear examination.
Yet there is something else you must hear.
Discernment is not vengeance.
If a leader disappointed you, Jesus is not giving you permission to hate.
If someone sinned against you, bitterness is not healing.
If a church wounded you, abandoning Christ because Christians failed you gives broken human beings an authority over your soul they were never supposed to possess.
Maybe this is the moment you separate the face of Jesus from the face of the person who hurt you.
Look at Christ again.
Not the celebrity preacher.
Not the scandal.
Not the institution.
Christ.
See Him touching lepers nobody wanted near them.
See Him receiving sinners religious people despised.
See Him confronting hypocritical religious leadership.
See Him washing feet.
See Him weeping.
See Him forgiving.
Then see Him walking toward Calvary.
No security detail.
No luxury throne.
No demand that sinful humanity protect His reputation.
The King carries a cross.
Nails tear through His flesh.
Blood runs down the wood.
And the One with all authority gives Himself for people who rebelled against Him.
That is your Shepherd.
Leadership in the kingdom is ultimately measured against Him.
This is why the Gospel protects us from both spiritual rebellion and spiritual idolatry.
At the cross, nobody gets to pretend he is God.
Not the pastor.
Not the prophet.
Not the apostle.
Not the teacher.
Not you.
Not me.
We stand together beneath the same blood.
We need the same grace.
We need the same Savior.
The ground beneath the cross destroys celebrity Christianity because every redeemed person arrives there as a sinner needing mercy.
And maybe that is what someone reading this desperately needs to hear tonight:
You do not have to abandon Jesus because someone who preached Jesus failed you.
Peter failed.
David failed.
Moses failed.
The disciples failed.
Christian leaders can fail.
But Christ remains Christ.
Hebrews calls Jesus the author and perfecter of our faith.
Your faith was never supposed to terminate in the person holding the microphone.
Look beyond the microphone.
Look beyond the stage.
Look beyond the personality.
Look beyond the scandal.
There He is.
Jesus.
Still holy.
Still merciful.
Still calling sinners home.
Still forgiving repentant people.
Still restoring the broken.
Still exposing darkness.
Still cleansing shame.
Still rewriting stories everybody else thought were finished.
And perhaps there is another person reading this who has not been wounded by bad leadership.
Perhaps you have become blindly loyal to good leadership.
That can become dangerous too.
Because even godly leaders remain human.
Paul confronted Peter publicly in Galatians 2 when Peter's conduct compromised the truth of the Gospel.
Think about that.
Peter walked with Jesus.
Peter witnessed miracles.
Peter heard the Sermon on the Mount.
Peter saw the risen Christ.
Peter preached at Pentecost.
And Peter could still be wrong.
If Peter could require correction, your favorite preacher can require correction.
So can mine.
The question is not:
“Do I like this preacher?”
The question is:
“Is this faithful to Christ and His Word?”
Not:
“How large is the ministry?”
But:
“Is Christ being honored?”
Not:
“How convincing did it sound?”
But:
“Is it true?”
Not:
“Everyone in my church believes this.”
But:
“What does Scripture actually teach in context?”
This is not distrust.
This is discipleship.
Open your Bible.
Read entire passages.
Learn context.
Pray.
Ask questions.
Listen humbly.
Receive correction.
Respect faithful shepherds.
Submit where Scripture calls you to submit.
Refuse gossip.
Reject slander.
Do not make accusations without evidence.
Do not confuse disagreement with abuse.
Do not call every doctrinal difference heresy.
But never surrender to a human being what belongs only to Christ.
Worship.
Ultimate allegiance.
Absolute authority over conscience.
Those belong to Jesus.
And if you are a Christian leader reading this, perhaps the question cuts differently.
Are you creating disciples of Jesus...
or dependents of yourself?
Can people disagree with you without being humiliated?
Can someone ask where your teaching is found in Scripture without becoming your enemy?
Can you say, “I was wrong”?
Can you repent publicly when the sin was public?
Do people around you feel increasingly free to follow Jesus faithfully, or increasingly afraid of disappointing you?
Because one of the most Christlike sentences a leader can speak may sometimes be:
“I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
That does not necessarily destroy spiritual authority.
Sometimes it reveals genuine spiritual authority.
Pride protects an image.
Grace tells the truth.
And this is why our message remains:
Not because scandal does not matter.
It matters.
Sin matters.
Truth matters.
Justice matters.
Repentance matters.
But scandal does not have to write the final chapter.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Imagine the scandal.
“I do not know the man.”
The disciple who promised loyalty collapses beside a charcoal fire.
Then the rooster cries.
And Peter weeps.
If social media existed that morning, Peter might have been finished before sunrise.
Screenshots.
Clips.
Commentary.
Hashtags.
Former followers explaining how they “always knew.”
But Jesus was not finished writing Peter's story.
After the resurrection, beside another charcoal fire, Jesus meets the man who denied Him.
Not to pretend the denial never happened.
Not to redefine betrayal as faithfulness.
Not to erase repentance.
Jesus confronts Peter with love.
“Do you love me?”
And then:
“Feed my sheep.”
That is grace.
Grace does not call the scandal righteous.
Grace takes the repentant sinner through the scandal and refuses to let the scandal become his final identity.
That is what Jesus does.
Maybe your story contains spiritual disappointment.
Maybe it contains manipulation.
Maybe you were the leader who failed.
Maybe you defended someone you should have questioned.
Maybe you attacked someone who was telling the truth.
Maybe you became cynical and walked away.
Maybe you have spent years pretending your faith was fine while privately wondering whether you could ever trust the church again.
Whatever brought you here, do not stop at human failure.
Come to Christ.
Repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ is calling you to forgive.
Seek wise help where serious wrongdoing occurred.
Tell the truth.
Reject bitterness.
Reject idolatry.
Reject blind allegiance.
Reject arrogant rebellion too.
And follow Jesus.
If this exposed something you have been afraid to admit, you do not need to tell strangers every detail. But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Someone reading the comments may realize tonight that they are not the only believer trying to find their way back to Jesus.
Not because every pastor is dangerous.
Most faithful shepherds need prayer, encouragement, patience, and honor—not suspicion.
Someday disappointment may tempt you to abandon Christ because a Christian failed.
Come back and remember:
Jesus is the Shepherd.
Not to start a witch hunt.
Not to create suspicion.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Support Christian work because you freely believe the work is worth supporting.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has stopped attending church.
Invite the believer struggling with doubt.
Invite the Christian who has become too dependent on personalities.
Invite the seeker who thinks Christianity is merely another institution protecting powerful people.
Invite even the unbeliever who needs to discover that the center of Christianity is not a flawless Christian celebrity.
It is a crucified and risen Christ.
Read your Bible.
Test what you hear.
Love faithful leaders.
Pray for them.
Honor them.
Learn from them.
Correct with humility where correction is biblically warranted.
Never idolize them.
And when human voices become so loud that you can barely hear the Shepherd anymore...
go back to the Scriptures.
Go back to the cross.
Go back to the empty tomb.
Go back to Jesus.
Because your pastor did not bleed for your sins.
Your denomination did not walk out of the grave.
Your favorite preacher is not seated at the right hand of the Father.
Jesus is.
And perhaps that is the sentence you need to carry with you long after this article disappears from your screen:
Never let the failure—or fame—of a human messenger make you lose sight of the nail-scarred hands of the One who actually saved you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “BUT IT’S BIBLICAL!” — THE POLYGAMY ARGUMENT THAT COLLAPSES WHEN YOU READ THE WHOLE BIBLE
paragraphs:
“BUT IT’S BIBLICAL!” — THE POLYGAMY ARGUMENT THAT COLLAPSES WHEN YOU READ THE WHOLE BIBLE
Abraham had more than one woman. Jacob had multiple wives. David had multiple wives. Solomon had hundreds. So if the Bible records polygamy—and sometimes even regulates it—how can Christians say monogamy is God’s design? The answer is more uncomfortable, more beautiful, and far more Christ-centered than either side usually admits.
There is an argument spreading through conversations, comment sections, religious groups, and even Christian circles.
It sounds devastatingly simple.
“Polygamy is biblical.”
Then come the names.
Abraham.
Jacob.
David.
Solomon.
Then come the verses.
Exodus 21.
Deuteronomy 21.
2 Samuel 12.
And suddenly the Christian defending monogamy can feel trapped.
Because the verses are real.
The men are real.
The marriages are real.
And pretending those passages do not exist does nothing to defend the truth.
So we are not going to hide from them.
We are going straight into them.
Because Christians should never be afraid of a Bible verse.
But there is one question we must ask before allowing anyone to build a theology from a biblical story:
Does the Bible recording something mean the Bible is recommending it?
That question changes everything.
Scripture records murder.
Scripture records incest.
Scripture records deception.
Scripture records adultery.
Scripture records drunkenness.
Scripture records slavery.
Scripture records kings who rebel against God and disciples who abandon Jesus.
Nobody reasonably concludes that because an event occurs inside the Bible, the event therefore represents God’s ideal.
The Bible is brutally honest about humanity.
That is part of its power.
It does not airbrush its heroes.
It shows Abraham afraid.
Jacob deceptive.
David adulterous.
Solomon compromised.
Peter denying Christ.
The Bible is not a collection of flawless people demonstrating flawless behavior.
It is the story of a holy God pursuing deeply flawed people.
And that distinction matters enormously when discussing polygamy.
To be precise, the Old Testament contains polygyny—the marriage of one man to multiple women. Mosaic legislation also addresses circumstances in which a man has more than one wife.

That means Christians should not make a careless claim such as, “Polygamy never existed among God’s people,” or, “The Old Testament contains an explicit universal law saying every Israelite man may have only one wife.”
Those claims would go beyond the text.
The stronger biblical argument is different.
Scripture can regulate a fallen human practice without presenting that practice as the creational ideal.
Jesus Himself gives us the interpretive key.
When religious leaders questioned Him about marriage and divorce, Jesus did something remarkable.
He did not begin with Abraham.
He did not begin with Jacob.
He did not begin with David.
He did not begin with Solomon.
He went behind all of them.
Back before Israel.
Back before Moses.
Back before kings.
Back before human culture had accumulated centuries of brokenness.
Jesus went to Eden.
He said:
“Have you not read that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female?”
Then Jesus cited Genesis:
“For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh.”
And then Christ declared:
“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
Matthew 19:4–6.
Do not rush past what Jesus just did.
When asked about the boundaries of marriage, Christ appealed to the beginning.
The Greek text of Matthew 19:5 contains a small phrase with enormous significance:
οἱ δύο — hoi dýo
“The two.”
καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
“And the two shall become one flesh.”
Jesus points His hearers toward God’s creation pattern: male and female, husband and wife, the two becoming one flesh.
And the Hebrew beneath the Genesis passage is equally beautiful:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
ve-hayu levasar echad
“And they shall become one flesh.”
Genesis 2:24.
One flesh.
Not because marriage is merely a contract for sexual access.
Not because a woman is an addition to a man’s collection.
Not because marriage exists to maximize one person’s desires.
Biblical marriage is covenantal union.
And when Jesus wanted His audience to understand marriage, He deliberately took them back to the architecture of creation.
This becomes crucial because someone may immediately object:
“But Abraham had Hagar.”
Yes.
And what happened?
God had promised Abraham descendants through whom blessing would come. But Abraham and Sarah became impatient with the timing of that promise.
Sarah gave Hagar to Abraham.
Genesis 16 does not read like an advertisement for expanding the household.
It reads like a warning about what happens when frightened human beings attempt to manufacture with their own hands what God has promised by His power.
Abraham went in to Hagar.
She conceived.
And almost immediately the house fractured.

Genesis says that when Hagar realized she had conceived, her mistress became contemptible in her eyes. Sarah became furious. Abraham withdrew responsibility into Sarah’s hands. Hagar was treated harshly and fled.
A child would eventually stand in the middle of an agonizing household division.
Yes, God cared for Hagar.
Yes, God heard Ishmael.
That matters tremendously.
God's compassion toward Hagar and Ishmael should never be twisted into contempt for either of them.
But God showing mercy inside human brokenness is not the same thing as God declaring the brokenness His original design.
That distinction appears repeatedly throughout Scripture.
Then there is Jacob.
Jacob loved Rachel.
But through Laban’s deception, he first received Leah.
Then Rachel.
Then Bilhah.
Then Zilpah.
And what follows?
Read Genesis 29 and 30 slowly.
Do not merely count the wives.
Count the tears.
Count the jealousy.
Count the competition.
Count the desperation.
Leah longs to be loved.
Rachel envies her sister.
Children become entangled in a painful struggle for affection and status.
Even mandrakes become bargaining currency in the competition for Jacob’s attention.
This is one of the great mistakes people make when reading Scripture.
They see multiple wives and stop reading.
Keep reading.
The consequences are part of the story.
The Bible does not need to place a warning label after every dysfunctional relationship when the narrative itself is showing you the devastation.
Then there is Elkanah.
First Samuel 1 introduces Hannah and Peninnah.
Again, two women attached to one man.
Again, rivalry.
Again, anguish.
Peninnah provokes Hannah because Hannah has no children.
Hannah weeps.
She cannot eat.
Her soul is bitter with grief.
Elkanah loves her, but his affection cannot erase the structure of rivalry surrounding the household.
Once again:
Do not just count wives.
Count tears.
Then comes David.
This is where defenders of biblical polygamy sometimes point to 2 Samuel 12:8, where God, speaking through Nathan, describes what had been given into David’s hands, including Saul’s house and wives.
That passage deserves serious treatment rather than evasion.

The language occurs in Nathan’s indictment after David has taken Bathsheba and arranged Uriah’s death. The point is that David had already received abundance and nevertheless coveted and seized what was not his.
But the existence of royal wives in David’s household does not erase another command already written into Israel’s Torah.
Long before David sat on a throne, God warned Israel concerning its future king:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים
ve-lo yarbeh-lo nashim
“He shall not multiply wives for himself.”
Deuteronomy 17:17.
And why?
“that his heart turn not away.”
Then Solomon arrives.
And suddenly the warning becomes almost terrifying.
First Kings 11 says Solomon loved many foreign women and eventually possessed seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines.
If quantity were proof of divine approval, Solomon would become the champion of the argument.
Instead, Scripture makes him the warning.
His wives turned his heart after other gods.
The king famous for wisdom became living evidence that knowing truth does not make a person immune to disobedience.
That should frighten every one of us.
Because this article is no longer merely about polygamists.
It is about us.
It is about the frightening human ability to find religious language for something our hearts already want.
We can search Scripture not because we want Scripture to correct us, but because we desperately want a verse that will protect us from correction.
And if we search long enough without respecting context, covenant, genre, redemptive history, and the whole counsel of God, almost anything can begin to sound “biblical.”
That is why the statement “The Bible regulates polygamy” requires careful thinking.
Yes, Mosaic law contains regulations involving plural marriages.
Exodus 21:10, for example, protects a woman’s rights if another wife is taken.
Deuteronomy 21:15–17 addresses inheritance where a man has two wives.
Those texts are there.
We should not erase them.
But regulation does not automatically equal idealization.
The Torah governed real Israelites living in a fallen social world. Some laws restrained injustice and protected vulnerable people within circumstances that were already less than Eden.
And Jesus gives us a powerful example of this distinction with divorce.
In Matthew 19, His opponents appeal to Moses.
Jesus answers:
“Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.”
Matthew 19:8.
Read those final words again.
“From the beginning it was not so.”
That sentence teaches us something profound about biblical interpretation.
Something may be tolerated or regulated within fallen human conditions without representing the pattern established at creation.
So when we ask what marriage is supposed to be, Jesus does not tell us merely to catalogue every marriage practiced by every Old Testament figure.
He points backward:
Beginning.
Male and female.
Man and wife.
Two.
One flesh.
And then the New Testament continues speaking of marriage in strikingly singular terms.
Paul writes:
1 Corinthians 7:2.
He tells husbands:
“love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
Ephesians 5:25.
Then Paul reaches back to Genesis 2:24:
“For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh.”
Ephesians 5:31.
And suddenly marriage becomes even bigger than marriage.
Paul says:
“This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.”
Ephesians 5:32.
There it is.
The center is Jesus.
Christian marriage is not ultimately about maximizing romantic possession.
It is meant to testify to covenant faithfulness.
Christ and His Church.
Sacrificial love.
Faithfulness.
Union.
A husband is not called to imitate Solomon collecting women.
He is called to imitate Jesus giving Himself.
That changes the question from:
“How many women can I biblically justify having?”
to:
“How can my marriage tell the truth about Christ?”
Those are radically different questions.
And perhaps that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Because polygamy is not the only subject on which people ask, “How far can I go and still call myself biblical?”
We do it with lust.
We do it with money.
We do it with unforgiveness.
We do it with pride.
We do it with sexual sin.
We do it with bitterness.
We do it with relationships.
We do it with ambition.
Sometimes we are not asking God, “What is Your heart?”
We are asking, “Where is the technical boundary beyond which You can finally tell me no?”
There is a dangerous way to hold a Bible.
You can hold it open while keeping your heart closed.
You can know verses while resisting their Author.
You can win an argument and lose the very thing Scripture was trying to expose inside you.
So to the polygamist who says, “But Abraham did it,” the Christian response should never be mockery.
It should be:
Abraham needed grace too.
To the person who says, “Jacob did it”:
Jacob needed grace too.
“David did it.”
David desperately needed grace too.
“Solomon did it.”
And Solomon discovered that extraordinary wisdom does not make rebellion safe.
That is the scandal running through Scripture.
God works through broken people without calling their brokenness good.
And that is incredibly good news.
Because if God only worked through people whose histories were spotless, none of us would have hope.
The Bible's heroes are not the Savior.
Jesus is.
Abraham cannot save you.
Jacob cannot save you.
David cannot save you.
Solomon cannot save you.
And your ability to defend your lifestyle with carefully selected verses cannot save you either.
Only Christ can.
Maybe you have used Scripture to defend something God has been trying to confront.
Maybe your issue has nothing to do with polygamy.
Maybe nobody knows what your issue is.
Maybe you have become extraordinarily skilled at giving spiritual names to things that are slowly destroying you.
God is not asking you to become better at hiding.
He is calling you into the light.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is God calling you away from the cliff.
Grace does not say sin does not matter.
Grace says sin mattered so much that Christ carried it to a cross.
At Calvary, Jesus did not die merely to make our chosen lifestyles more comfortable.
He died to forgive sinners, reconcile us to God, and transform people who could never rescue themselves.
He was crucified.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the same Jesus who forgives also says:
“Follow me.”
That means sometimes following Him requires surrendering an argument we desperately wanted to win.
It may require saying:
“Lord, I used Your Word to defend myself instead of allowing Your Word to search me.”
That confession is not the end of your story.
It might be where your real story finally begins.
This is why our theme remains:
Not because scandal is insignificant.
Not because sin should be romanticized.
Not because every choice is equally biblical.
But because Jesus Christ specializes in meeting sinners inside stories that look irredeemable and writing something grace alone could write.
If this exposed something you have been defending, do not turn the comment section into a battlefield.
Turn it into an altar.

If you are wrestling with this teaching, say so honestly. Ask your question. Bring the verse you believe challenges this conclusion. We should be willing to examine Scripture together rather than fear difficult passages.
Somebody may need to discover that surrender did not destroy you.
Jesus met you there.
It does not.
Context matters.
Creation matters.
The whole counsel of Scripture matters.
And above everything else, Jesus matters.
Let them see that serious Christianity does not require pretending difficult passages do not exist.
But hear this carefully:
You do not earn salvation by supporting a Christian ministry.
You do not glorify God merely by clicking a button.
Jesus Christ purchased redemption—not us.

But if this ministry genuinely helps you glorify God, supporting it is one practical way you can help put more Christ-centered teaching, Scripture, discipleship resources, and Gospel truth in front of people who desperately need it.
Sharing costs nothing.
Following helps you stay connected.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not to prove that you are righteous.
Not because Gospel Warrior is the Gospel.
But because if truth has helped you, passing truth forward can become an act of love toward someone who has not encountered it yet.
Invite your family.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite Christians who have become spiritually tired.
Invite even the person who does not believe any of this yet.
Let them investigate Jesus for themselves.
Because at the end of this argument, the greatest danger is not simply misunderstanding polygamy.
It is learning how to quote the Bible without ever surrendering to the Christ the Bible reveals.
And perhaps that is the sentence that should follow you after you close this article:
The most dangerous Bible verse may be the one you use as a shield when Jesus intended it to become a mirror.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DINAH WAS VIOLATED—THEN EVERYONE ELSE TOOK OVER HER STORY
paragraphs: DINAH WAS VIOLATED—THEN EVERYONE ELSE TOOK OVER HER STORY
What Dinah’s story teaches us about violated dignity, dangerous silence, revenge disguised as justice, and the God who refuses to let human scandal have the final word.
There is a detail in Genesis 34 that should make us uncomfortable.
Dinah goes out.
She is seen.
She is taken.
She is violated.
And then, for most of the chapter, everybody talks except Dinah.
Her father speaks.
Her brothers speak.
Shechem speaks.
Hamor speaks.
Men negotiate.
Men become angry.
Men make promises.
Men deceive.
Men bleed.
Men die.
But the young woman at the center of the catastrophe almost disappears beneath the noise everybody else makes about what happened to her.
And perhaps that is the first reason Dinah’s story still feels frighteningly modern.
Because sometimes the person who was wounded becomes the quietest person in the room while everybody else decides what her pain means.
Genesis introduces her simply as “Dinah the daughter of Leah, whom she had borne to Jacob” (Genesis 34:1). She goes out “to see the daughters of the land.”
Then Scripture turns brutally dark.
Genesis 34:2 says Shechem saw her, took her, lay with her, and—
וַיְעַנֶּהָ — vay‘anneha

The word comes from the Hebrew root ענה — ‘anah, a word that in this context carries the sense of humiliating, afflicting, violating, or treating someone by force in a degrading way. English translations render the verse with language such as “violated her,” “humiliated her,” or explicitly “raped her.”
Whatever softened version someone may be tempted to place over the story, the Hebrew refuses to turn what happened into romance.
Dinah was wronged.
And this matters because the next verses contain language that, read carelessly, could make the episode sound like a tragic love story.
After violating her, Shechem’s soul is drawn to Dinah. Genesis says he “loved the young woman” and spoke tenderly to her. He then asks his father to obtain her as his wife.
But affection after violation does not erase violation.
Desire does not retroactively manufacture consent.
Tender words do not make an evil act righteous.
The Bible does not ask us to call darkness light simply because the person who caused the wound later expresses strong feelings.
That truth reaches far beyond Dinah.
Some people reading this know what it feels like to have someone hurt you and then expect their apology, affection, tears, gifts, religious language, or promises to make the wound disappear.
Maybe your story was not Dinah’s story.
But you know what it means to have a boundary crossed.
To have trust broken.
To discover that someone who claimed to love you was capable of using you.
To have people discuss your suffering as though you were an issue to solve instead of a person to love.
And sometimes the deepest confusion comes when the person who hurt you also says, “But I love you.”
Genesis 34 gives us permission to reject that confusion.
Love cannot make evil good.
And then another danger enters the story.
Dinah’s brothers hear what happened.
Genesis 34:7 says they were grieved and very angry because Shechem had committed a disgraceful thing in Israel.
Their anger at the violation of their sister was understandable.
What follows was not.

Hamor and Shechem attempt to negotiate a marriage and broader intermarriage between their peoples. Dinah’s brothers respond deceitfully. They demand that every male in the city be circumcised. Shechem and Hamor agree and persuade the men of their city to submit to circumcision.
On the third day, while the men are in pain, Simeon and Levi take their swords.
They enter the city.
They kill every male.
They kill Hamor and Shechem.
They take Dinah from Shechem’s house.
Then Jacob’s sons plunder the city.
The story has moved from one terrible violation to an eruption of collective bloodshed.
That is another lesson Dinah’s story refuses to let us escape:
Being genuinely wounded does not make every response to the wound righteous.
You can be right about the evil that happened to you and still become wrong in what you choose to do because of it.
You can call something sin and then sin while answering it.
You can demand justice and quietly begin craving vengeance.
You can carry legitimate anger until anger starts carrying you.
Simeon and Levi could point to something horrifying that had happened to their sister.
But another person’s sin did not give them permission to become lawless themselves.
And Scripture does not eventually romanticize their violence.
Years later, when Jacob gives his final words concerning his sons, he returns to Simeon and Levi.
“Simeon and Levi are brothers; weapons of violence are their swords” (Genesis 49:5).
Then comes the devastating judgment:
“Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel!” (Genesis 49:7).
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not say Dinah’s violation was insignificant.
It does not vindicate Shechem.
But neither does it sanctify cruelty simply because cruelty was committed by wounded people.
That distinction is desperately needed.
Because pain can whisper dangerous theology into the human heart.
After what they did to me, I deserve to destroy them.
After what I survived, nobody gets to tell me how angry I should be.
God understands why I hate them.
Perhaps He understands your pain more completely than anyone ever could.
But understanding the wound is not the same as blessing everything the wound produces.
Jesus does not heal us by teaching us to pretend evil never happened.
Neither does He heal us by turning us into the thing that wounded us.
This is where Dinah’s story becomes painfully personal.
Some people have become prisons for crimes committed against them years ago.
The offender may no longer be in the room.
But the anger is.
The betrayal is.
The memory is.
The imagined conversations are.
The questions are.
The shame is.
And sometimes revenge never looks like a sword.
Sometimes revenge is replaying someone’s failure every morning.
Sometimes it is destroying their reputation long after truth has become secondary to retaliation.
Sometimes it is refusing to release hatred because hatred feels like the last remaining evidence that what happened mattered.
But forgiveness does not mean evil did not matter.
Biblical forgiveness does not require calling abuse acceptable, abandoning appropriate boundaries, preventing lawful justice, or returning yourself to an unsafe situation.
Forgiveness means vengeance no longer belongs to you.
“Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord” (Romans 12:19).
There is freedom hidden inside that command.
God is not saying, “What happened to you does not matter.”
He is saying, in effect, You do not have to become executioner in order for Me to remain Judge.
And there is another uncomfortable part of Genesis 34.
Jacob’s immediate response after the massacre centers on the consequences for his household.
“You have brought trouble on me by making me stink to the inhabitants of the land,” he tells Simeon and Levi (Genesis 34:30).
His sons answer:
“Should he treat our sister like a prostitute?” (Genesis 34:31).
Then the chapter ends.
No neat resolution.
No recorded speech from Dinah.
No paragraph describing how she processed what happened.
No sentimental sentence assuring us that everything immediately became okay.
Scripture does something more honest.
It leaves the ugliness ugly.
That matters.
We should never manufacture details about Dinah that God did not reveal.
We cannot honestly claim Scripture tells us what she thought afterward, how she emotionally recovered, or exactly what the rest of her life felt like.
The Bible does not tell us.
But the silence of the text is not evidence that God considered her insignificant.
Dinah appears again among Jacob’s family in Genesis 46:15.
She had a name.
She belonged to the covenant family.

And most importantly, the Bible containing her painful story continues moving toward Someone who would enter a world filled with violated people, violent people, frightened people, ashamed people, guilty people, grieving people, and sinners who desperately needed something greater than human revenge.
Jesus Christ.
And here the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Christianity is not the announcement that good people can repair themselves.
It is the announcement that God entered our scandal.
Jesus did not observe human brokenness from a safe distance.
“The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).
Christ entered a world of betrayal, exploitation, violence, hypocrisy, injustice, shame, and death.
He was betrayed by someone close to Him.
He was falsely accused.
He was mocked.
He was stripped and publicly humiliated.
He was beaten.
He was crucified.
And yet Jesus was not merely another helpless casualty of human evil.
He willingly gave Himself.
“No one takes it from me,” Jesus says concerning His life, “but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18).
At the cross, something happened that neither denial nor revenge could ever accomplish.
Justice and mercy met.
Sin was not excused.
It was judged.
Grace was not cheap.
It was purchased at unimaginable cost.
The innocent Christ bore the judgment deserved by sinners so that guilty people who repent and trust in Him could receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life.
That means the Gospel has something to say to every side of human brokenness.
To the wounded, Jesus does not say your wound was imaginary.
To the guilty, Jesus does not say your sin was harmless.
To the angry, Jesus does not say vengeance will heal you.
To the ashamed, Jesus does not say you must spend the rest of your life wearing what happened as your identity.
To the sinner, Jesus does not say clean yourself up and then come.
He says:
“Come to me” (Matthew 11:28).
This is grace.
Not God pretending there was never a scandal.
God writing redemption where sin tried to write the ending.
Maybe that is why Dinah’s story hurts so much.
We want the chapter to give her a speech.
We want someone to sit beside her.
We want every wrong immediately corrected.
We want justice without collateral destruction.
We want the wounded restored before the chapter closes.
But Genesis 34 does not give us that kind of ending.
And neither does life always give us one by Friday afternoon.
Some prayers remain unanswered longer than we expected.
Some apologies never arrive.
Some people never admit what they did.
Some wounds leave consequences.
Some chapters end while we are still asking God why.
But the Bible does not end at Genesis 34.
And if you belong to Christ, neither does your story end at the worst chapter somebody else helped write.
That is the difference between pretending and hope.
Christian hope does not say, “It never happened.”
Christian hope says, “It happened, but Jesus Christ will have the final word.”
Perhaps someone labeled you according to what happened to you.
Perhaps someone remembers your worst decision more clearly than your repentance.
Perhaps you are not Dinah in this story.
Perhaps you recognize something of Simeon and Levi in yourself.
You were hurt.
Then you hurt people.
You were betrayed.
Then bitterness became your permission slip.
You were humiliated.
Then you learned how to humiliate others.
You were wounded by sin, and somewhere along the road you started using your wound to justify your own.
Jesus came for you too.
That is the scandal of grace.
The cross does not divide humanity into respectable people who need a little encouragement and terrible people who need salvation.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
All.
The abused need a Savior.
The angry need a Savior.
The self-righteous need a Savior.
The sexually immoral need a Savior.
The religious need a Savior.
The respectable need a Savior.
The person reading this while secretly carrying something nobody knows needs a Savior.
And there is only one.
Jesus.
Repentance means we stop negotiating with our sin.
Faith means we stop trying to become our own savior.
Grace means Christ receives people who could never purchase their way back to God.
And transformation means He loves us too much to leave us enslaved to the person we were.
Bring it into the light before Christ.
If you need forgiveness, ask Him.
If you have been living in hatred, surrender it.
If you have wounded someone, stop hiding behind what was done to you and repent of what you have done.

If you have been violated or abused, understand this clearly: another person's sin against you is not your moral guilt. Seek wise, safe support and appropriate help. Forgiveness never requires pretending criminal or abusive behavior is acceptable.
And if your spirit has been exhausted from carrying a chapter you cannot rewrite yourself, you can simply comment, “pray for me.”
No performance.
No explanation required.
If Christ is working in places you thought would remain broken forever, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
If you have been hiding behind anger, shame, religion, pride, or appearances, comment, “no more hiding.”
And if you are still wrestling but refuse to abandon Jesus, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
Someone else reading those words may discover that they are not the only person in the battle.
That is why stories like Dinah’s should not merely be consumed.
They should travel.
You may need these truths again when an old memory becomes loud.

Scripture gives us no right to manipulate anyone into believing otherwise. But generosity, sharing truth, encouraging others, and helping Gospel-centered work reach more people can certainly be sincere ways of honoring God when they are done freely, faithfully, and from the heart.
Come to Christ.
A ministry cannot save you.
A church attendance record cannot save you.
A Christian T-shirt cannot save you.
Your good intentions cannot save you.
Your suffering cannot save you.
And your ability to appear okay cannot save you.
Jesus Christ saves.

Dinah's story teaches us that sin damages real people. It teaches us that human desire does not redefine evil as love. It teaches us that righteous anger can mutate into sinful vengeance. It teaches us not to use someone else's wickedness as permission for our own. It teaches us how painfully incomplete human justice can become.
And the larger story of Scripture teaches us where all those unfinished cries ultimately point.
To Jesus.
The One who does not need us to rename darkness before He can redeem sinners from it.
The One who can forgive what you have done without calling it good.
The One who can meet you in what was done to you without making it your identity.
The One who can take the chapter you wish had never existed and refuse to let it become the title of your entire life.
So be honest before God tonight.
What are you still carrying?
Whom are you still trying to punish in your imagination?
What wound became your excuse?
What shame became your name?
What secret are you terrified Jesus will uncover?
Bring it to Him.
Repent where you have sinned.
Seek safety and wise help where you have been harmed.
Forgive without pretending evil was good.
Pursue justice without becoming consumed by vengeance.
Receive grace without turning grace into permission to continue in sin.
And follow Jesus.
And comment something real.
Not something impressive.
Real.
“Jesus forgive me.”
“Pray for me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
“No more hiding.”
Sometimes the first crack in a prison wall is simply telling the truth in the presence of grace.
And remember this when the chapter you never wanted threatens to name the rest of your life:
What happened may explain one chapter of your story—but it does not get to sit on the throne. Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: David Saw Her Bathing From His Rooftop — One Look Became a Chain of Devastating Choices
paragraphs: David Saw Her Bathing From His Rooftop — One Look Became a Chain of Devastating Choices

He had survived lions, giants, battlefields, betrayal, and a murderous king. But one evening on a rooftop, David discovered that some of the most dangerous battles are fought where nobody else can see—and one unchecked desire can become a chain strong enough to drag a worshiper into darkness.
There is something terrifying about the first sentence of David's greatest moral collapse.
Not because it begins with adultery.
It doesn't.
Not because it begins with murder.
It doesn't.
It begins with a man being somewhere he should not have been.
“In the spring, at the time when kings go off to war…”
David sent somebody else.
Joab went.
The army went.
Israel's fighting men went.
“But David remained in Jerusalem.”
Then evening came.
The battlefield was miles away. The palace was quiet. David rose from his bed and walked across the rooftop of the king's house.
And then he saw her.
Scripture says:
וַיַּרְא אִשָּׁה רֹחֶצֶת
Vayyar ishah rochetzet.
“And he saw a woman bathing.”
Then comes the detail that turned observation into temptation:
וְהָאִשָּׁה טוֹבַת מַרְאֶה מְאֹד
Veha'ishah tovat mar'eh me'od.
The woman was very beautiful in appearance.
That is where many people stop telling the story correctly.
They say David saw Bathsheba, as though the sight itself was the entirety of his sin.
But read the passage slowly.
David saw.
Then David sent.
Then David inquired.
Then David learned who she was.
And what he learned should have stopped everything.
“Bathsheba… the wife of Uriah the Hittite.”
Wife.
That word was the boundary.
That was the warning.
That was the moment to turn around.

Bathsheba was not an unnamed fantasy standing on a rooftop below him. She was a person. A daughter. A wife. And Uriah was not merely some inconvenient husband standing between David and what David desired. He was one of David's own fighting men, later named among David's mighty warriors.
David had been given enough information to walk away.
Instead, he sent again.
That is what makes this story so frighteningly personal.
Sin often gives you an exit before it gives you consequences.
There was an exit between seeing and asking.
There was another between asking and sending.
Another between sending and taking.
Another between adultery and deception.
Another between deception and murder.
David kept walking past them.
And maybe that is why this ancient rooftop can feel disturbingly modern.
Because you probably don't live in an ancient palace.
But you have a rooftop in your pocket.
A screen nobody else is watching.
A conversation nobody knows about.
A browser history you erase.
A message you know you should not answer.
A relationship you keep calling “innocent” because admitting what it is would require you to end it.
A bitterness you feed privately.
A fantasy you revisit.
A compromise you have carefully renamed so you can continue carrying it without calling it sin.
It was “just a look.”
Until David wanted another look.
Then information.
Then access.
Then possession.
Then concealment.
Then control.
Then blood.
One look did not murder Uriah.
But an unchecked desire became a series of deliberate choices, and those choices eventually put a faithful man in the path of enemy weapons.
That distinction matters.

Because Scripture is not teaching that noticing beauty automatically makes someone guilty of everything that follows. Nor does the biblical text invite us to make Bathsheba the convenient villain of David's story.
The narrative places responsibility relentlessly on the king.
David saw.
David sent.
David inquired.
David sent messengers.
David took.
David tried to cover what he had done.
And when the cover-up failed, David escalated.
Bathsheba became pregnant and sent David a devastatingly short message:
“I am pregnant.”
Four words in English.
A kingdom suddenly felt very small.
David could command armies.
He could summon servants.
He could write orders.
He could move soldiers across battlefields.
But he could not command reality to stop being true.
So the man who once ran toward Goliath began running from the truth.
David summoned Uriah from the battlefield.
The plan was simple: get Uriah home. Let him sleep with his wife. Make the pregnancy appear to be his.
But Uriah would not cooperate.
And the irony is almost unbearable.
Uriah displayed the integrity David had abandoned.
His brothers were sleeping in the field. The ark and Israel's forces were in temporary shelters. How could he go home, eat, drink, and lie with his wife while his fellow soldiers remained at war?
The king was trying to hide sin.
The soldier was refusing comfort because of loyalty.
David even got him drunk.
Still, Uriah did not go home.
So the scandal became darker.
David wrote a letter to Joab.
Place Uriah where the fighting is fiercest.
Then withdraw from him.
Let him die.
And David placed that death sentence into Uriah's own hands.
Imagine that walk.
Uriah carrying the sealed orders of his king, unaware that he was carrying instructions for his own death.
He had been loyal to David.
David used that loyalty to kill him.
The battlefield swallowed Uriah.
A messenger eventually returned.
Uriah was dead.
Perhaps David thought the nightmare was finally contained.
The husband was gone.
The evidence could be absorbed into a royal marriage.
The scandal could disappear beneath palace walls.
Bathsheba mourned her husband. When the mourning period ended, David brought her into his house and she became his wife.
From the outside, perhaps the king had managed the crisis.
Then Scripture gives us one sentence that tears the roof off the palace:
וַיֵּרַע הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂה דָוִד בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה
Vayyera haddavar asher-asah David be'einei YHWH.
“The thing David had done was evil in the eyes of the LORD.”
David could hide Uriah's blood from the public.
He could not hide it from God.
And neither can we.
That is uncomfortable because we have become extremely skilled at managing appearances.
We know how to worship while hiding.
How to post Scripture while hiding.
How to say “God is good” while hiding.
How to serve in ministry while hiding.
How to smile at church while something secret is slowly hollowing out our souls.
People may know your public version.
God knows the room you lock.
And yet—this is where the Gospel begins cutting deeper than mere condemnation.
Because God did not leave David alone with his deception.
וַיִּשְׁלַח יְהוָה אֶת־נָתָן אֶל־דָּוִד
Vayyishlach YHWH et-Natan el-David.
“The LORD sent Nathan to David.”
Notice that.
David had been sending people throughout the entire scandal.
David sent Joab.
David sent inquiries.
David sent messengers for Bathsheba.
David sent for Uriah.
David sent instructions that resulted in Uriah's death.
Now God sends someone.
Nathan.
Grace sometimes arrives looking like confrontation.
Nathan tells David about a rich man with many sheep who steals the single beloved lamb belonging to a poor man.
David is furious.
The king demands justice.
How fascinating that we can sometimes recognize evil immediately when we believe someone else committed it.
Then Nathan stops speaking in parables.
אַתָּה הָאִישׁ
Attah ha'ish.
“You are the man.”
Imagine the silence after those words.
No army could protect him from that sentence.
No crown could silence it.
No palace wall could hide him.
“You are the man.”
David finally saw himself.
Not Goliath's conqueror.
Not Israel's songwriter.
Not the celebrated king.
Not the man after God's own heart as though that description were permission to live without accountability.
A sinner.
Guilty.
Exposed.
And David said:
חָטָאתִי לַיהוָה
Chatati laYHWH.
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
No excuse.
No blaming Bathsheba.
No blaming loneliness.
No blaming pressure.
No blaming the responsibilities of kingship.
No public-relations statement.
“I have sinned.”
That is repentance beginning to breathe.
But we must not turn this into sentimental Christianity.
David was forgiven, but his actions still carried devastating consequences.
Forgiveness is not God pretending evil never happened.
Grace is not God calling darkness light.
The sword entered David's household. His family suffered terribly. The child born from the union died. Later chapters record horrifying fractures within David's house.
Sin can be forgiven while consequences remain.
That truth should make us tremble before treating grace cheaply.
Yet David's story did not end beneath Nathan's accusing finger.
And yours does not have to end beneath your worst chapter either.
Psalm 51 lets us hear what happened inside David after exposure.
He cries:
חָנֵּנִי אֱלֹהִים כְּחַסְדֶּךָ
Chonneni Elohim kechasdecha.
“Be gracious to me, O God, according to Your steadfast love.”
Then comes one of the most desperate prayers in Scripture:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create for me a clean heart, O God.”
David does not merely ask God to repair his reputation.
He asks God to remake his heart.
The Hebrew verb בְּרָא — bara, “create,” is striking. David knows cosmetic religion will not save him.
He needs creation.
He needs something only God can do.
Maybe you do too.
Maybe beneath all the religious language, what you really need tonight is not another technique for hiding better.
You need a clean heart.
Maybe somebody reading this has crossed a boundary.
Maybe your marriage is quietly bleeding.
Maybe pornography has become a room you keep returning to.
Maybe emotional intimacy with someone who is not your spouse has already become something you would panic to have exposed.
Maybe greed owns you.
Maybe bitterness has become your private religion.
Maybe pride has made repentance almost impossible because everyone thinks you are spiritually strong.
Maybe you have become so good at hiding that people ask you for prayer while you secretly wonder who could ever pray for you.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin does not matter.
The cross proves that it matters more than you imagined.
But the cross also proves God's mercy reaches farther than you imagined.
David could repent.
But David could not die for David.
David needed a greater King.
And generations later, from David's own royal line, Jesus Christ came.
Matthew does something astonishing when introducing Him. In the genealogy of Jesus, he deliberately reminds us of this scandal, referring to Solomon's mother in relation to Uriah.
The stain is not airbrushed out of the family history.
Why?
Because Jesus did not enter a sanitized human story.
He entered ours.
Into adultery.
Into violence.
Into shame.
Into dysfunctional families.
Into guilty bloodlines.
Into ruined reputations.
Into a world filled with people who desperately needed more than inspiration.
They needed redemption.
Jesus is not merely another David.
He is the greater Son of David.
David took another man's wife and arranged another man's death to protect himself.
Jesus gives Himself for His Bride and willingly goes to death to save sinners.
David sacrificed Uriah to preserve his throne.
Jesus left heavenly glory and surrendered Himself to rescue His enemies.
David tried to cover his own sin.
Jesus came to bear ours.
At Calvary, Christ did not minimize sin.
He carried judgment.
And when He rose from the grave, He announced that sin, shame, death, and condemnation would not have the final word over everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith.
That is why your scandal does not have to become your identity.
But hear this carefully:
Grace is not permission to stay on the rooftop.
Grace calls you down.
Delete the conversation.
Confess the secret.
End the affair.
Install the accountability.
Tell the truth.
Return what you stole.
Ask forgiveness.
Get help.
Run from what keeps pulling you away from Christ.
Stop protecting the thing Jesus died to free you from.
Repentance is not simply feeling terrible because you got caught.
Repentance turns toward God.
David's first look became inquiry.
Inquiry became taking.
Taking became adultery.
Adultery became pregnancy.
Pregnancy became deception.
Deception became manipulation.
Manipulation became murder.
Murder became mourning.
And concealed sin eventually stood exposed before God.
That is the chain.
But Jesus breaks chains.
Not by pretending they never existed.
By calling sinners out of darkness, forgiving those who come to Him, giving His Spirit, and beginning the painful, beautiful work of transformation.
And perhaps the most astonishing detail comes after judgment and grief.
Bathsheba later gave birth to Solomon.
Scripture says the LORD loved him.
Think about that.
The same biblical story that refuses to hide David's wickedness also refuses to let David's wickedness have the last sentence.
Eventually, through Solomon's royal line recorded in Matthew's genealogy, the story moves toward Christ.
Scandal did not become good.
Adultery did not become acceptable.
Uriah's death did not become insignificant.
God remained holy.
Sin remained sin.
Consequences remained real.
But grace kept writing.
That is the difference between biblical grace and cheap grace.
Cheap grace says, “It doesn't matter.”
Biblical grace says, “It mattered enough for Christ to bleed—and His mercy is powerful enough to transform the sinner who comes home.”
So perhaps this article is not really about David staring from a rooftop.
Perhaps it is about you standing at your own turning point.
There is still an exit.
Before the next message.
Before the next search.
Before the next lie.
Before the next secret meeting.
Before resentment becomes hatred.
Before temptation becomes habit.
Before habit becomes bondage.
Before the thing you control begins controlling you.
Turn around.
Come down from the rooftop.
Run toward Christ.
And if you have already gone farther than you ever thought you would, do not mistake conviction for an announcement that mercy is unavailable.
Nathan's “You are the man” eventually led David to “Create in me a clean heart.”
Exposure became confession.
Confession met mercy.
And the shattered king discovered that God desired something deeper than religious performance: “a broken and contrite heart.”
Maybe that is what God is asking from you.
Not performance.
Not another Christian caption.
Not pretending.
Truth.
Not because typing words into a comment saves anyone—only Christ saves—but because perhaps you are tired of pretending you do not need His mercy.
Your testimony may become the sentence another ashamed person needs to read tonight.
Supporting Gospel work is one meaningful way believers can steward resources for God's glory when it is done freely, cheerfully, and from love—not pressure.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot share enough Christian posts to erase your guilt.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
Salvation is God's gift received through faith in Him.
And that may be the deepest lesson hiding beneath David's rooftop.
The Bible did not preserve David's scandal so Christians could stare at someone else's failure.
It preserved it so we would recognize how quickly our own hearts can wander—and how desperately every one of us needs the greater Son of David.
David's story warns us:
Guard the first look.
Take the first exit.
Listen to the warning.
Confess before concealment grows roots.
Repent before desire builds a kingdom inside you.
And when you have fallen, do not run farther into darkness because shame tells you God would never want you back.
Run toward Jesus.
Bring Him the truth.
Bring Him the shattered pieces.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the consequences.
Bring Him the heart you cannot clean yourself.
And pray David's prayer:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Because the most dangerous thing about the rooftop was never merely what David saw.
It was what he refused to surrender after seeing it.
And the most beautiful thing about grace is not that God rewrites history as though our sins never mattered.
It is that through Jesus Christ, our sins no longer have to write the ending.
The rooftop may explain where you fell—but the cross can determine where your story goes next.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She Was a Prostitute in a Doomed City. One Decision Changed Her Bloodline Forever.
paragraphs:
She Was a Prostitute in a Doomed City. One Decision Changed Her Bloodline Forever.
Rahab had a reputation nobody would forget, lived behind walls that were about to fall, and belonged to a city marked for judgment. Then faith made her choose a side—and generations later, her name appeared in the earthly genealogy of Jesus Christ. If you think your past has already decided how your story ends, you need to read this to the final line.
Everybody in Jericho probably knew what kind of woman lived in that house.
They knew where her door was.
They knew what happened behind it.
They knew her reputation.
And Scripture doesn't sanitize it.
It doesn't introduce her as Rahab the respectable.
Rahab the religious.
Rahab the woman who had always made good decisions.
The Hebrew text of Joshua 2:1 calls her:
אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה — ishah zonah.
A woman who was a prostitute.
That matters.
Because when God tells stories of grace, He does not need to rewrite the past to redeem the person.
And maybe that is where this story finds you.
Because perhaps there are things in your life you desperately wish could be erased.
Things you did.
Things done to you.
Years you wasted.
Relationships you destroyed.
Rooms you should never have entered.
Secrets you hope nobody discovers.
A reputation you cannot seem to outrun.
