Maybe people still remember the version of you that you're begging God to change.
Rahab understands what it feels like to have a name attached to a past.
But there was another problem.
Rahab wasn't merely a broken woman.
She was a broken woman living in a doomed city.
Jericho stood in Israel's path as Israel entered the land God had promised. Joshua sent two spies into the city, and they came to Rahab's house.
Suddenly, this woman's private little world collided with the purposes of God.
And Rahab had a decision to make.
She could protect the world she knew...
or trust the God she had only heard about.
That distinction is enormous.
Because Rahab had heard.
She told the spies that Jericho had heard what the LORD had done—how He dried up the Red Sea and what had happened to Israel's enemies. The city was terrified.
But hearing the same truth did not produce the same response in everyone.
Jericho heard and hardened itself.
Rahab heard and believed.
Then she said something astonishing.
יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם הוּא אֱלֹהִים בַּשָּׁמַיִם מִמַּעַל וְעַל־הָאָרֶץ מִתָּחַת
YHWH Eloheikhem hu Elohim bashamayim mimma'al ve'al-ha'aretz mittachat.
In context, her confession means:
“The LORD your God, He is God in heaven above and on earth beneath.”
Stop there.
A Canaanite woman.
A prostitute.
Inside a condemned city.
And she is confessing the supremacy of Israel's God.
She did not have generations of covenant upbringing behind her.
She didn't grow up hearing Moses read.
She wasn't standing in Israel's camp.
Yet from inside Jericho, Rahab looked at the evidence she had been given and essentially declared:
Your God is the true God.
And then her faith moved.
That is why the New Testament refuses to let us dismiss her as merely a frightened woman who made a clever political decision.
Hebrews reaches backward into this scandalous story and gives us heaven's interpretation:
Πίστει Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη...
Pistei Rhaab hē pornē...
“By faith Rahab the prostitute...”
By faith.
Those two words change how we read everything that follows.
Hebrews 11:31 says Rahab did not perish with the disobedient because she received the spies in peace.
James goes even further. James 2:25 points to Rahab as an example of faith demonstrated by action when she received the messengers and sent them away by another route.
She wasn't saved because prostitution somehow didn't matter.
She wasn't rescued because sin had become irrelevant.
Grace is not God pretending darkness is light.
Rahab was rescued because she turned in faith toward the living God—and that faith became visible in what she did.
Real faith moved her feet.
Real faith changed her allegiance.
Real faith made obedience costly.
And this is where Rahab stops being an ancient character and starts becoming painfully personal.
Because many people want Jesus as an addition without Jesus becoming Lord.
We want forgiveness without surrender.
Rescue without repentance.
Grace without a changed allegiance.
We want Christ to save us from the consequences of the old kingdom while we keep living comfortably inside its walls.
Rahab couldn't do that.
A line had been drawn through Jericho.
And eventually she had to decide which side of that line she belonged on.
So do we.
Jesus did not come merely to improve the old you.
He came to save sinners and make them His own.
The Gospel is not:
“Become respectable enough and maybe God will accept you.”
The Gospel is that sinners who could never cleanse themselves are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ saves.
And the response of genuine faith is not casual admiration.
It is surrender.
Repentance means the old kingdom no longer gets your loyalty.
And maybe that's the decision you've been avoiding.
Not because you don't know about Jesus.
Rahab knew something about Israel's God before the spies ever entered her house.
The issue was what she would do with what she knew.
You may know Bible verses.
Know worship songs.
Know Christian vocabulary.
Know how to look spiritually alive online.
Know exactly when to say “Amen.”
And still be hiding behind Jericho's walls.
Then came the scarlet cord.
The spies promised protection for Rahab and those gathered in her house under the agreed conditions. They told her to bind a particular crimson cord in the window.
The Hebrew of Joshua 2:18 is striking:
תִּקְוַת חוּט הַשָּׁנִי
tiqvat chut hashani
The expression refers to the cord/thread of scarlet or crimson.
And there is a beautiful detail in the Hebrew.
תִּקְוָה — tiqvah can carry the sense of a cord in this context, while elsewhere the same Hebrew word is associated with hope.
A scarlet cord hanging from the window of a doomed city.
Outside that house: judgment approaching.
Inside: people waiting on a promise.
We should be careful here. Joshua itself does not explicitly say, “This scarlet cord represents the future blood of Christ.”
We should never force Scripture to say what it does not say.

But standing on this side of the cross, Christians cannot read a story of judgment, promised rescue, faith, and scarlet without remembering the greater rescue toward which the whole biblical story ultimately moves.
Not salvation through a piece of rope.
Salvation through Jesus Christ.
Not because red fabric possesses power.
Because Christ's blood does.
Not because Rahab earned mercy.
Because the God of mercy received a sinner who trusted Him.
And one day the walls fell.
Imagine the sound.
Stone crashing.
Dust filling the air.
Screaming.
Everything that had looked permanent suddenly collapsing.
Jericho had walls.
Rahab had a promise.
And the walls lost.
Joshua 6 tells us that Rahab, her father, her mother, her brothers, and those belonging to her were brought out.
Think about that.
Her decision didn't touch only her.
People she loved were standing inside that house.
People who might have died in Jericho were brought out with her.
You may never know how many people are watching what you do with Jesus.
Your children.
Your spouse.
Your brother.
Your sister.
Your friend.
The person who silently reads what you share but never comments.
Your faith cannot automatically save someone else—each person must respond to God personally—but your witness can point people toward the One who can.
That is why sharing the Gospel matters.
You do not know whose Jericho is already shaking.
You do not know who looks fine publicly and is terrified privately.
You do not know who has been asking God for one final sign that He has not abandoned them.
Sometimes sharing truth is not social media activity.
Sometimes it is mission.
But Rahab's story still isn't finished.
Because if Scripture stopped after Joshua 6, this would already be breathtaking.
The prostitute survived.
The outsider was welcomed among Israel.
The condemned woman received mercy.
But centuries pass.
Generations come and go.
Then Matthew begins his Gospel.
And before Jesus preaches a sermon...
before He heals a leper...
before He raises the dead...
before nails pierce His hands...
Matthew gives us a genealogy.
Most people rush through genealogies.
Don't rush through this one.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
Generations.
Names.
History.
Then suddenly...
Rahab.
Matthew 1:5 identifies Rahab in the family line leading through Boaz, Obed, Jesse, and David—and ultimately Matthew's genealogy leads us to Jesus Christ.
Read that again.
The woman whose name had been associated with prostitution became part of the family line through which, generations later, the Messiah entered history according to His humanity.
Jericho may have called her prostitute.
Hebrews remembered her as a woman of faith.
James remembered her faith as active.
Matthew put her name in the genealogy of Jesus.
This does not mean Rahab became sinless.
It means her sin did not have the final word.
And that is the Gospel-shaped thunder inside this story.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write your final chapter when Jesus Christ becomes Lord of your story.
Maybe people remember what you were.
Jesus knows what grace can make you.
Maybe shame keeps replaying your history.
The cross announces that forgiveness is real for those who come to Christ.
Maybe your family has repeated the same destruction for generations.
Addiction.
Abandonment.
Infidelity.
Anger.
Abuse.
Bitterness.
Idolatry.
Secrets.
Maybe you've quietly wondered:
Is this simply who we are?
No family name is stronger than the grace of God.
But hear this carefully: Christianity is not a promise that one emotional decision magically guarantees easy circumstances for every descendant.
Rahab's story teaches something deeper.
God can take a life marked by shame and weave it into purposes that person could never have imagined.
Your past can explain where you've been.
It does not have to become the god that determines where you go.
Jesus can rewrite everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By bringing grace into the middle of it.
That is why we say:
Rahab is scandal and grace standing in the same genealogy.
And ultimately, her story points beyond Rahab.
Because the greatest story isn't that Rahab entered the genealogy.
The greatest story is Who eventually came through that genealogy.
Jesus.
The Son of David.
The promised King.
The sinless Savior.
The friend of sinners.
The Lamb of God.
The One who touched the unclean.
The One who welcomed the rejected.
The One who confronted self-righteous religious people and called sinners to repentance.
The One who carried our sins to a Roman cross.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who still saves.
Rahab does not prove that sin doesn't matter.
Rahab proves that sin does not intimidate grace.
The cross proves what sin costs.
The resurrection proves death doesn't get the last word.
And Jesus proves that your identity does not have to remain chained to the ugliest thing you've ever done.
Maybe you've been reading this with someone else's face in mind.
Now remove their face.
Put yours there.
What wall are you hiding behind?
What secret keeps following you?
What sin have you renamed because repentance would cost too much?
What part of your life have you kept locked away from Christ?
What reputation have you started believing is your identity?
What if the thing you are most ashamed of is exactly the place where you need to stop hiding and finally surrender to Jesus?
Rahab heard.
Rahab believed.
Rahab acted.
And when Jericho fell, she discovered that trusting God was worth losing the world she had known.
Maybe somebody reading this is standing at that window right now.
Not physically.
Spiritually.
Your old life behind you.
Christ calling you forward.
And you're afraid.
Afraid of what repentance will cost.
Afraid of what people will say.
Afraid you have gone too far.
Afraid God could forgive everyone except you.
Look at Rahab.
Then look beyond Rahab to the cross.
You are not being invited to clean yourself up so Jesus will finally tolerate you.
You are being called to repent and trust the Savior who receives sinners.
Bring Him the truth.
Not the edited version.
Not the church version.
Not the Facebook version.
The truth.
“Jesus, I have sinned.”
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
“Jesus, I cannot save myself.”
“Jesus, I believe You died and rose again.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, be Lord of my life.”
And if this exposed something you've been hiding, don't manufacture a polished response.
Be honest.
And if God has already brought you through your own Jericho, tell somebody what He did. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person needed to read tonight.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
Not because an algorithm can advance God's Kingdom by itself.
It can't.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that they're drowning.
Rahab's past was real.
God's grace was greater.
We want this community to remain a place of daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
There is another practical way to stand with this work.

Supporting Gospel work can itself become an act offered for God's glory when it is done freely, prayerfully, cheerfully, and for the sake of helping truth reach people—not as a payment for God's favor and never as a substitute for obedience, generosity to your local church, or caring for people in need.
Not out of guilt.
Out of mission.

Because glorifying God is bigger than supporting any ministry. We glorify Him through faith in Christ, worship, holiness, love, generosity, obedience, serving others, proclaiming the Gospel, and lives transformed by grace. But when a Christ-centered ministry is genuinely helping people encounter biblical truth, supporting and sharing that work can be one meaningful way to participate in getting that truth in front of another soul.
Maybe Rahab never imagined that strangers thousands of years later would speak her name when talking about faith.
Maybe she thought she was simply trying to survive the destruction of Jericho.
But grace was writing farther than she could see.
And perhaps that is what you need to remember tonight.
You cannot see every generation your surrender may touch.
You cannot see every person your testimony may strengthen.
You cannot see who might find Jesus because you stopped hiding what His grace has done in you.
Rahab had a past.
She also had faith.
Jericho had walls.
God had a promise.
And when the dust settled, the walls were gone...
but Rahab was still standing.
Then centuries later, her name was still there.
Not erased from the story.
Redeemed inside it.
So when your past whispers, “This is who you will always be,” remember the woman in the window.
Remember the scarlet cord.
Remember the falling walls.
Remember the genealogy.
And above everything else...
remember Jesus.
Because the most unforgettable thing about Rahab's story is not that a prostitute somehow became respectable.

It is that the grace of God reached into a condemned city, called an unlikely sinner to faith, brought her out alive, welcomed her among His people, and placed her name inside a story that ultimately leads the reader to Christ.
Maybe your story began in scandal.
Maybe entire chapters still make you cry.
But if you belong to Jesus, scandal does not get the final sentence.
The walls that witnessed your shame do not get to write the ending that Jesus purchased with His blood.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: For Seven Years, Jacob Loved Rachel—But What Was Leah Feeling While She Watched?
paragraphs: For Seven Years, Jacob Loved Rachel—But What Was Leah Feeling While She Watched?

The Bible never tells us what Leah felt during those seven years. What it tells us afterward may be even more heartbreaking—and it leads to one of Scripture’s most astonishing reversals: the woman who longed to be chosen became part of the bloodline through which Jesus Christ came.
There is a sentence in Genesis that sounds breathtakingly romantic when you read it from Jacob’s side.
But read it again from Leah’s side.
Suddenly, it hurts.
Jacob had arrived in Haran and fallen in love with Rachel. When Laban asked what wages Jacob wanted for his labor, Jacob answered with remarkable specificity:
“I will serve you seven years for Rachel your younger daughter.” — Genesis 29:18
The Hebrew is equally direct:

וַיֶּאֱהַב יַעֲקֹב אֶת־רָחֵל
Vayye’ehav Ya‘aqov et-Rachel.
“And Jacob loved Rachel.”
Not merely “a daughter.”
Not “one of your daughters.”
Rachel.
Scripture names the woman he wanted.
And then comes one of the most famous descriptions of romantic love in the Old Testament:
“So Jacob served seven years for Rachel and they seemed to him but a few days because of his love for her.” — Genesis 29:20
Beautiful.
Unless you are Leah.
Because while seven years felt like days to Jacob because he loved Rachel...
what might those same seven years have felt like to Rachel’s older sister?
We need to be careful here.

The Bible does not tell us what Leah was thinking during those seven years. It does not record seven years of secret tears. It does not say Leah was jealous every night. It does not give us permission to manufacture conversations, motives, or emotions and then call them Scripture.
So we won't.
But Scripture does tell us enough about what happened afterward to let us see something painfully real about Leah's life.
Before Jacob's declaration of love, Genesis introduces the sisters side by side:
“Now Laban had two daughters; the name of the older one was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel.”
Then:

וְעֵינֵי לֵאָה רַכּוֹת
Ve‘einei Leah rakkot.
Leah's eyes were rakkot.

The Hebrew word rak can carry the sense of tender, delicate, soft, or weak, and translations differ in how they render the expression. Ancient interpretation was not completely uniform either: the Aramaic Targum Onkelos renders Leah's eyes positively as tender or beautiful. We should therefore resist building an entire portrait of Leah as physically unattractive from one debated phrase.
What Scripture makes unmistakably clear is the contrast that follows:
Rachel was beautiful in form and appearance.
And Jacob loved Rachel.
Imagine living beside a person everyone seems to notice.
Maybe you don't have to imagine it.
Maybe you know what it is to be the sibling who wasn't praised as much.
The friend standing beside the friend everybody noticed first.
The person watching someone else receive the relationship you prayed for.
The employee watching someone else get chosen.
The believer scrolling through engagement announcements, pregnancy announcements, promotions, ministries growing, prayers apparently being answered...
while quietly wondering:
“Lord, when will somebody choose me?”
That question can become dangerous.
Because eventually the desire to be loved can become the desire to prove that you deserve love.
And Leah's story will expose just how exhausting that prison can become.
Seven years pass.
Jacob works.
Rachel waits.
And Leah is there.
Again, Scripture does not tell us what Leah felt throughout those years, so we must not pretend to know.
But then the wedding arrives.
Laban prepares a feast.
Night falls.
And Genesis says:
“When evening came, he took his daughter Leah and brought her to him.”
Whatever questions modern readers have about precisely how the deception was carried out, the biblical emphasis is unmistakable: Laban deceived Jacob by substituting Leah for Rachel.
Then morning came.
And Scripture records one of the most devastatingly abrupt revelations in Genesis.
Jacob wakes.
And realizes the woman beside him is Leah.
He confronts Laban:
“What is this you have done to me? I was in your service for Rachel! Why did you deceive me?”
Think carefully about Leah's position in this story.
Her father has used her in a deception.
Her husband discovers that she is not the woman he expected.
And the entire conflict erupting around her exists because Jacob wanted her sister.
Then Laban gives Rachel to Jacob after Leah's bridal week, with Jacob obligated to serve another seven years.
And Scripture does not romanticize what happens next.
Genesis 29:30 says Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah.
Then comes the verse that changes the emotional center of the entire chapter:
וַיַּרְא יְהוָה כִּי־שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה
Vayyar YHWH ki-senu’ah Leah.
“And the LORD saw that Leah was unloved...”

The Hebrew word translated by many versions as “unloved” is שְׂנוּאָה — senu’ah, literally associated with being hated. In this context, Genesis 29:30 has already established the relational comparison: Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah. So translations that render the idea as “unloved” or less loved are capturing the painful relational reality without requiring us to conclude that Jacob felt nothing but active hostility toward her.
But don't miss the first words.
The LORD saw.
Jacob saw Rachel.
God saw Leah.
People saw the woman who was preferred.
God saw the woman who was hurting.
Jacob's eyes were fixed on the woman he loved.
God's eyes were fixed on the woman who knew what it was like not to be loved as she desperately wanted to be.
And maybe that is why Leah's story has survived thousands of years.
Because somewhere reading this right now is a Leah.
Someone who knows the humiliation of being tolerated when you wanted to be treasured.
Someone who keeps wondering why you weren't enough.
Someone who gave more, served more, forgave more, stayed longer, tried harder...
and still watched someone's heart turn somewhere else.
Maybe they chose another person.
Maybe your father never gave you the affirmation you spent childhood trying to earn.
Maybe your mother compared you with your sibling until comparison became the voice inside your own head.
Maybe a spouse stopped seeing you.
Maybe the person who promised forever walked away.
Maybe social media has become a daily parade of everybody else's Rachel moments while you sit privately inside Leah's pain.
And perhaps you have begun doing what Leah did next.
Trying to earn through performance what your soul is starving to receive through love.
Leah becomes pregnant.
She gives birth to a son.
She names him Reuben.
And listen to her explanation:
“The LORD has seen my affliction; now my husband will love me.”
There it is.
The wound speaks.
Now he will love me.
I gave him a son.
Now maybe I will matter.
Now maybe he'll look at me differently.
Now maybe I'll finally become enough.
Some people have been living inside that sentence their entire lives.
If I become prettier, maybe they'll love me.
If I lose the weight...
If I earn more money...
If my ministry grows...
If I become successful...
If I become indispensable...
If I never disappoint anybody...
If I keep giving...
If I keep proving myself...
then maybe somebody will finally choose me.
But Leah bears another son.
And this time she says:
“The LORD heard that I was unloved...”
She names him Simeon, connected with the Hebrew verb for hearing.
First:
God saw.
Now:
God heard.
Do you see what Scripture is quietly doing?
The husband Leah desperately wants to notice her may still not be giving her the love she longs for.
But heaven is neither blind nor deaf.
God sees.
God hears.
Then another son comes.
Leah names him Levi and says:
“This time my husband will become attached to me.”
Again.
Still hoping.
Still reaching.
Still attaching her heart to the possibility that one more blessing might finally make someone love her.
Reuben:
Maybe now he'll love me.
Simeon:
God heard that I was unloved.
Levi:
Maybe now he'll become attached to me.
Can you hear the exhaustion?
This isn't merely an ancient family drama.
This is the human heart.
We turn careers into Reubens.
Relationships into Simeons.
Bodies into Levis.
Achievements.
Followers.
Money.
Sex.
Approval.
Children.
Ministry.
Even religious performance.
We keep giving birth to another reason someone should finally tell us:
You are enough.
And then Leah conceives again.
A fourth son.
Something changes.
Not necessarily everything in her circumstances.
Something changes in what she says.
Genesis 29:35 records:
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
In Hebrew:
הַפַּעַם אוֹדֶה אֶת־יְהוָה
Happa‘am odeh et-YHWH.
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
And she names the child Judah — יְהוּדָה, Yehudah, a name connected in the narrative with praise or thanksgiving.
Notice what disappears from her recorded explanation.
Jacob.
“Now my husband will love me” is gone.
“My husband will become attached to me” is gone.
This time...
I will praise the LORD.
That does not mean Leah never hurt again.
It does not mean she suddenly stopped wanting her husband's affection.
Genesis will show that this family remains deeply complicated.
But at this moment, the direction of Leah's words changes.
From chasing Jacob's affection...
toward praising Yahweh.
And then the biblical story does something so breathtaking that you can miss it if you read Genesis too quickly.
Leah wanted Jacob to choose her.
Jacob preferred Rachel.
But when God begins unfolding the royal line through which Israel's kings—and ultimately the Messiah according to the flesh—would come...
the line runs through Judah.
Leah's son.
Matthew opens the New Testament by tracing Jesus Christ's genealogy through Judah.
“Judah the father of Perez...”
Generation after generation follows.
Until the genealogy reaches:
“Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom Jesus was born, who is called Christ.”
The woman who knew the ache of not being preferred became an ancestor in the messianic line.
Not because Leah earned God's grace by suffering.
Not because rejection automatically guarantees earthly greatness.
And certainly not because God owed Leah compensation.
Grace does not work like wages.
The point is more beautiful.
Human preference never controls God's redemptive purposes.
The person people overlook is not invisible to God.
The person people reject is not beyond God's purpose.
And your value before God is not decided by whether another human being finally recognizes it.
But the story goes deeper still.
Because Judah's line does not lead merely to another human success story.
It leads eventually to Jesus.
And Jesus knows rejection.
Isaiah foretold the Servant as one who would be despised and rejected.
John tells us that Christ came to His own and His own did not receive Him.
The Gospels lead us to a cross where the sinless Son of God is mocked, abandoned, pierced, and crucified.
Yet He was not merely another rejected victim in a tragic story.
He willingly gave Himself for sinners.
Jesus entered our shame to bear our sin.
He endured the cross.
He rose from the dead.
And now the Gospel does something no amount of human approval can do:
It reconciles guilty sinners to God through Christ.
That means Christianity's answer to your rejection is not:
“You are amazing, so forget everyone who didn't recognize it.”
The Gospel goes much deeper.
It says you and I are sinners who cannot save ourselves.
We have chased idols.
We have looked to people for what only God can ultimately give.
We have sinned in our rejection, and we have sinned while responding to rejection.
We need more than improved self-esteem.
We need forgiveness.
We need reconciliation.
We need a Savior.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
At the cross, grace meets scandal.
Sin meets mercy.
Guilt meets forgiveness.
Death meets the risen Christ.
You do not have to spend your entire life manufacturing another Reuben, another Simeon, another Levi, hoping that finally somebody will love you enough to heal what is broken inside you.
Turn to Christ.
Repent of your sin.
Stop asking created things to carry the weight only the Creator can bear.
Trust the One who died and rose again.
There is a freedom that begins when your deepest question changes from:
“What must I do so they will finally choose me?”
to:
“How can my life praise the God who has shown mercy to me in Christ?”
Maybe that is the sentence someone reading this needed tonight.
You have spent years trying to become somebody's Rachel.
And all the while...
God saw you.
Not because you were secretly superior to everyone who overlooked you.
Not because every desire you have will eventually be granted.
Not because following Jesus guarantees that the person who rejected you will return.
But because the God of Scripture sees His people in their affliction, hears their cries, and has given sinners something infinitely greater than human validation:
His Son.
If this exposed the place where you have been begging people to give you what you should be bringing before Christ, don't hide behind a polished Christian answer.
Be honest.
There is no shame in admitting that being overlooked hurt.
And if Christ has already been teaching you to stop living for human approval, tell somebody what He has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person needs to survive tonight.
Not because every sentence will be easy to remember, but because there may come another night when rejection starts preaching to you again.
And rejection is a terrible theologian.
It will tell you that being unwanted by one person means being worthless.
It will tell you another person's beauty diminishes yours.
It will tell you someone else's blessing proves God's absence from your life.
It will tell you being passed over means your story is over.
Genesis refuses that lie.
“Now maybe he will love me.”
Send it to the woman rebuilding after abandonment.
Send it to the man who has spent years trying to prove his worth.
Send it to the believer whose faith has become exhausted from comparison.
Send it even to the person who doesn't yet know Christ but desperately needs to discover that Christianity is not an invitation to become impressive enough for God.
It is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God by grace through Jesus Christ.
It doesn't.
Not because giving money proves you love Jesus.
It doesn't.
The Gospel cannot be purchased, and salvation is not for sale.

But if you genuinely want to glorify God through supporting the spread of Christ-centered biblical teaching, one practical way you can participate is by supporting ministries and resources that faithfully proclaim His Word—and by sharing that truth so someone beyond your own screen encounters it.
But before you leave this page, remember Leah.
Remember the woman whose first recorded longing after childbirth was essentially:
Maybe now my husband will love me.
Remember the woman who later said:
This time I will praise the LORD.
Remember Judah.
Remember that generations later, from Judah's line came Jesus Christ.
And remember this whenever rejection whispers that another human being's inability to treasure you has written the final sentence over your life:
The eyes that overlooked Leah were never the eyes that determined her place in God's redemptive story.
And they do not determine yours.
Jesus does not promise to rewrite every circumstance into the ending you would have chosen.
He does something greater.
He forgives sinners.
He redeems what sin has shattered.
He transforms those who come to Him.
And He is still writing stories in places where wounded people thought only rejection remained.
You may have spent years asking, “When will someone choose me?”—while grace was calling you to look at the Christ who chose the cross to save sinners like us.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU THOUGHT GOD FORGOT YOU: THE HEARTBREAKING TRUTH BEHIND ISAIAH 40:31
paragraphs: YOU THOUGHT GOD FORGOT YOU: THE HEARTBREAKING TRUTH BEHIND ISAIAH 40:31
What “Wait Upon the Lord” Really Means When You Have Prayed, Cried, Believed—and Nothing Seems to Be Changing
There is a kind of waiting that feels almost cruel.
Not waiting for your coffee.
Not waiting for traffic to move.
Not waiting for someone to answer a message.
I mean the kind of waiting where you have prayed until you no longer know what to say.
The kind where you wake up and the situation is still there.
The diagnosis has not changed.
The marriage is still strained.
The child is still far from God.
The door is still closed.
The loneliness is still sitting beside you.
The temptation you thought you would have conquered by now still knows your name.
The grief still ambushes you in ordinary places.
The financial pressure still follows you to bed.
And perhaps the hardest part is this:
God could change it.
You know He could.
So why hasn't He?
That is where Isaiah 40:31 is often quoted.
“But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength…”
Beautiful words.
But when your heart is exhausted, beautiful words can become painful words if nobody explains what they actually mean.
Because maybe you have waited.
And waited.
And waited.
And instead of feeling stronger, you feel tired.
So tired that you have quietly wondered whether this promise works for everybody except you.
If that is where you are, Isaiah 40 was written for people who understood that feeling far more deeply than we sometimes realize.
And the verse becomes even more powerful when we stop treating it like an inspirational slogan and listen to what God was actually saying.
Isaiah 40:31 reads in Hebrew:

וְקוֹיֵי יְהוָה יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ
יַעֲלוּ אֵבֶר כַּנְּשָׁרִים
יָרוּצוּ וְלֹא יִיגָעוּ
יֵלְכוּ וְלֹא יִיעָפוּ
Wəqōwê YHWH yaḥălîp̄û kōaḥ; yaʿălû ʾēḇer kannəšārîm; yārûṣû wəlō yîgāʿû; yēlḵû wəlō yîʿāp̄û.
The familiar King James rendering says:
“But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.”
But here is what changes everything.
Biblical waiting is not doing nothing.
And waiting upon the Lord does not mean pretending you are not hurting while you passively sit around hoping something eventually happens.
The Hebrew expression translated “they that wait upon the LORD” comes from the verb קָוָה — qāvâ.
In this context, it carries the sense of waiting with hope, looking expectantly toward someone, trusting and hoping in the one upon whom your expectation rests.
That distinction matters.
You are not merely waiting for something.
You are waiting upon Someone.
That means Isaiah 40:31 is not primarily a promise about God giving impatient people faster circumstances.
It is about God becoming the inexhaustible source of strength for people whose own strength has reached its end.
And maybe that is exactly where God has found you.
At the end of yourself.
You thought reaching the end of yourself meant you had failed.
God may be showing you that you have finally discovered where His strength begins to become unmistakable.
Look at the heartbreaking question immediately before the famous promise.
Isaiah 40:27 says:
“Why sayest thou, O Jacob, and speakest, O Israel, My way is hid from the LORD, and my judgment is passed over from my God?”
There it is.
The Bible does not sanitize the feeling.
God's people were essentially saying:
God doesn't see me.
My situation has escaped His attention.
My cause has been overlooked.
Sound familiar?
You prayed.
Nothing happened.
You obeyed.
The door remained closed.
You tried to live faithfully while someone who seemingly cared nothing about God appeared to prosper.
You watched other people announce the engagement, the pregnancy, the healing, the breakthrough, the ministry opportunity, the restored relationship.
You congratulated them.
You smiled.
You even thanked God for blessing them.
Then you put your phone down.
And something inside you whispered:
“Lord… what about me?”
That whisper is closer to Isaiah 40 than many polished sermons ever get.
God does not answer Israel by humiliating them for being tired.
He answers by reminding exhausted people who He is.
“Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?”
Isaiah 40:28.
Read that slowly.
You become weary.
God does not.
You lose perspective.
God does not.
You cannot see tomorrow.
God already stands sovereign over it.
Your emotional resources can collapse.
His character cannot.
Your body can become exhausted.
His power cannot.
Your plans can fall apart.
His throne does not.
That is why verse 29 says:
“He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.”
Notice who receives strength.
The faint.
The powerless.
The person who finally has to admit:
“I cannot carry this anymore.”
Christianity was never the story of impressive people proving how strong they are for God.
The Gospel is the story of helpless sinners being rescued by a mighty Savior.
That pattern reaches its blazing center in Jesus Christ.
Humanity could not climb its way back to God.
Religion could not erase our guilt.
Good intentions could not remove sin.
Self-improvement could not reconcile rebels to a holy God.
So Christ came to us.
Jesus lived the righteousness we could not produce.
He bore sin at the cross.
He entered death.
And He rose victorious.
The scandal of human sin met the greater scandal of divine grace.
The guilty could be forgiven.
The condemned could be justified.
The runaway could come home.
The ashamed could be clothed in Christ's righteousness.
The spiritually dead could receive life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And that changes how Christians wait.
We do not wait wondering whether God loves us.
The cross has already answered that question.
We do not wait wondering whether sin gets the final word.
The empty tomb has already answered that question.
We do not wait because God has abandoned His throne.
We wait because the God who cannot become weary is still God when we are completely exhausted.
Then Isaiah says something remarkable:
“Even the youths shall faint and be weary, and the young men shall utterly fall.”
Even youth fails.
Even natural strength fails.
Even the person everyone assumes can handle everything eventually discovers a limit.
Your limit is not God's limit.
Then comes the promise:
וְקוֹיֵי יְהוָה יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ
Wəqōwê YHWH yaḥălîp̄û kōaḥ.
Those who wait for—hope in—the LORD “shall renew their strength.”
The verb translated “renew” is related to חָלַף — ḥālap̄, carrying ideas such as changing, passing on, replacing, or renewing depending on context.
The picture is not that exhausted believers somehow manufacture another reserve of human determination.
Their hope rests in the God who “giveth power to the faint.”
That destroys one of the most dangerous lies exhausted Christians believe:
“I just need to try harder.”
Sometimes you don't.
Sometimes you need to stop pretending your strength is infinite.
You need God.
Not merely another productivity system.
Not another motivational speech.
Not another mask.
God.
Maybe your waiting season has exposed things you did not know were inside you.
Control.
Fear.
Bitterness.
Jealousy.
Secret sin.
An addiction to people's approval.
Anger toward God.
A relationship you made into an idol.
A dream you began loving more than the One who gave you the ability to dream.
Waiting has a strange way of revealing what comfort allowed us to hide.
When God does not immediately give us what we want, we sometimes discover whether we wanted God—or merely wanted God to give us something.
That realization can hurt.
But conviction is not the same thing as rejection.
Jesus exposes wounds in order to heal.
He confronts sin in order to call sinners into repentance and grace.
So perhaps the deepest question of your waiting season is not merely:
“When will God change this?”
Perhaps another question needs to be asked:
“What is God doing in me while I am waiting?”
Because sometimes we become so obsessed with escaping the waiting room that we miss the Savior sitting with us inside it.
Isaiah continues:
“They shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary…”
Those are the lines everybody remembers.
Flying.
Running.
Strength.
Victory.
But then comes the final phrase.
“And they shall walk, and not faint.”
Walk?
After soaring?
After running?
Why end there?
Perhaps because much of faithfulness does not look like soaring.
It looks like walking.
Getting out of bed when your heart is heavy.
Opening Scripture when you feel spiritually dry.
Praying when you cannot feel anything spectacular.
Refusing the temptation you secretly want.
Forgiving again.
Repenting again.
Showing up again.
Choosing truth again.
Taking another ordinary step with Jesus.
We love testimonies about soaring because soaring looks miraculous.
But sometimes the miracle is that you are still walking.
Nobody applauded.
Nobody posted about it.
Nobody knew how close you came to giving up.
But you woke up.
And somehow whispered:
“Jesus, I still trust You.”
Then you took another step.
That is not insignificant faith.
Sometimes that is faith stripped down to its purest form.
Maybe you expected God to make you fly over the valley.
Instead, He is giving you enough grace to walk through it.
Do not despise that grace.
The Lord who gives strength for soaring is also the Lord who gives strength for the next step.
And Scripture never promises that waiting upon God means every earthly story will resolve exactly as we demand.
Some prayers are answered differently than we hoped.
Some doors remain closed.
Some losses are not reversed in this life.
Some faithful believers die still waiting for things they longed to see.
Christian hope therefore cannot ultimately rest in getting the earthly ending we wrote for ourselves.
Our hope rests in Christ.
Romans 8 points believers beyond present suffering toward coming glory.
Revelation 21 points toward the day when God will wipe away every tear and death will be no more.
The Christian does not merely believe:
“Eventually everything will happen exactly the way I want.”
The Christian believes something far stronger:
“Whatever happens, Jesus Christ will remain faithful, and because I belong to Him, suffering, sin, death, and the grave will not have the final word.”
That is hope sturdy enough for a hospital room.
A cemetery.
A divorce court.
A rejection letter.
An empty bank account.
A prodigal child's bedroom.
A sleepless night.
A season where heaven seems silent.
Maybe God has not forgotten you.
Maybe silence is not absence.
Maybe waiting is not rejection.
Maybe the chapter you called “God abandoned me” will someday look completely different from the other side of eternity.
But there is also something you must not miss.
Waiting upon the Lord is not permission to continue comfortably in sin.
If the thing exhausting your soul is rebellion against God, the biblical response is not merely to “wait for strength.”
Repent.
Come into the light.
Bring the hidden thing to Jesus.
Stop negotiating with what Christ died to free you from.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter.
Grace cost the blood of Christ.
And the same Savior who forgives also calls us to follow Him.
If you have wandered far from God, you do not need to clean yourself up enough to earn your journey home.
Come home.
If you have fallen again, confess it.
If shame tells you to hide, remember what happened in Eden: sin drove humanity into hiding.
But the Gospel announces that God came looking for sinners.
Jesus still saves sinners.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still transforms.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years believing that what happened in your worst chapter permanently became your identity.
It didn't.
Your scandal does not outrank His grace.
Your failure is not more powerful than His cross.
Your past is not sovereign.
Jesus is.
Peter had denial in his story.
Paul had persecution in his story.
The woman at the well had brokenness in hers.
The thief beside Jesus was running out of minutes.
Yet grace entered their stories.
That does not make sin beautiful.
It makes the Savior magnificent.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So what does it mean to wait upon the Lord?
It means your expectation shifts from your own strength to His faithfulness.
It means you keep trusting when immediate evidence does not give you everything you want.
It means praying without treating God like a vending machine.
It means obeying when obedience costs you.
It means repenting when waiting exposes sin.
It means remembering who God is when circumstances tempt you to rewrite His character.
It means believing that the everlasting Creator has not become exhausted by your need.
It means allowing your weakness to drive you toward Christ instead of deeper into hiding.
And sometimes…
it simply means walking.
One more prayer.
One more act of obedience.
One more confession.
One more morning.
One more “Jesus, help me.”
One more step.
If you are reading this while spiritually exhausted, you do not have to pretend here.
Be honest.
Not because a comment is a magic formula.
Not because typing words earns God's favor.
But because sometimes bringing the struggle into the light is the first time we stop pretending we are okay.
And if God has used this to expose something you need to surrender, you can simply write:
Let somebody else reading the comments discover they are not the only Christian who has struggled.
Let testimony become community.
Let honesty point people toward grace.
Not as a religious performance.
Not to prove you are spiritual.
Send it privately to the family member whose faith has been bruised.

Following Gospel Warrior is another simple way to stay close to daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment—and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow may place Gospel truth in front of someone at exactly the moment they need to hear about Jesus.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
But supporting faithful Christian ministry can be one practical way of helping biblical teaching and Gospel-centered encouragement reach more people.
Do not leave Jesus outside your waiting.
Bring Him your exhaustion.
Bring Him the prayer you stopped praying.
Bring Him the anger you were afraid to admit.
Bring Him your secret sin.
Bring Him the disappointment.
Bring Him the dream.
Bring Him the diagnosis.
Bring Him the relationship.
Bring Him the future you cannot control.
Bring Him the part of your story you are convinced cannot possibly be redeemed.
And wait upon the Lord.
Not because waiting guarantees that tomorrow will look exactly the way you wanted.
But because the One you are waiting upon is everlasting.
He does not faint.
He does not grow weary.
His understanding is unsearchable.
He gives power to the faint.
And in Jesus Christ, even death itself does not get the final sentence.
Perhaps you are not soaring today.
Perhaps you are not running.
Perhaps all you can do is walk.
Then walk.
And if all you can manage right now is one trembling step toward Jesus…
take it.
Because one day you may discover that the season in which you thought God was doing nothing was the very season in which He was teaching your exhausted heart where strength had always come from.
You thought you were waiting for God to change your circumstances—but perhaps, in the silence, Christ was refusing to let your circumstances become your god.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: A Criminal Was Dying Beside Jesus — His Final Conversation Changed His Eternity
paragraphs: A Criminal Was Dying Beside Jesus — His Final Conversation Changed His Eternity

He had no time left to repair his reputation, repay his debts, prove his sincerity, or rebuild his life. He had only a dying breath, a guilty past, and Jesus beside him. And what happened next destroys one of the most dangerous lies we tell ourselves about grace.
There are moments when a human being can no longer pretend.
A hospital room can do that.
A courtroom can do that.
A grave can do that.
And a cross certainly can.
Imagine knowing the exact instrument on which you are going to die because you are already hanging from it.
No tomorrow.
No second career.
No opportunity to go home and become a better man.
No chance to return what you stole.
No years remaining in which to convince everyone that you have changed.
Your hands cannot reach anyone to make restitution.
Your feet cannot walk toward a new beginning.
Your reputation is already destroyed.
Your sentence has already been handed down.
And death is getting closer with every breath.
That was the condition of the criminal beside Jesus.

Luke does not romanticize him. Scripture does not introduce him as a misunderstood hero who simply made a few unfortunate decisions. Luke calls the crucified men beside Jesus κακοῦργοι — kakourgoi, criminals or evildoers.
They were being executed.
One was on one side of Christ.
One was on the other.
And between guilty men hung the innocent Son of God.
That picture alone is almost the entire Gospel.
The Holy One among the guilty.
The righteous One numbered with transgressors.
The sinless Christ suffering in the company of sinners.
Luke tells us that one criminal joined the mockery surrounding Jesus:
Εἷς δὲ τῶν κρεμασθέντων κακούργων ἐβλασφήμει αὐτόν…
One of the criminals hanging there was reviling Him.
His demand was essentially this:
If You are really the Christ, save Yourself.
And save us.
It sounds like faith until you listen carefully.
He did not necessarily want Jesus.
He wanted escape.
He wanted the consequences removed.
He wanted the nails gone.
He wanted another chance at earthly life.
And that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
Because sometimes we do the same thing.
“Jesus, fix my marriage.”
“Jesus, get me out of this debt.”
“Jesus, heal my body.”
“Jesus, restore what I lost.”
“Jesus, make this pain stop.”
“Jesus, save me from what my choices have produced.”
None of those requests is automatically wrong. Christ invites us to bring our needs to Him.
But there is a frightening difference between wanting Jesus and merely wanting Jesus to remove something painful.
One criminal wanted Christ to get him off the cross.
The other began to realize that his deepest problem was not the cross.
It was his guilt before God.
And suddenly, from another dying man, came words nobody expected.
He rebuked the first criminal.
“Do you not fear God?”
Then came something astonishingly rare in a world addicted to excuses.
He admitted that his punishment was deserved.
No blaming his childhood.
No blaming Rome.
No blaming his friends.
No rewriting his history.
No carefully edited version of himself.
He effectively said:
We are receiving what our deeds deserve.
But this Man has done nothing wrong.
That is where grace begins to become visible.
Not because admitting guilt earns salvation.
It does not.
But because repentance stops arguing with God about the truth.
The criminal had nothing left with which to impress Jesus.
And maybe that is exactly what somebody reading this needs to understand.
You do not come to Christ by presenting your résumé.
You come with your need.
You do not negotiate your way into mercy by explaining why your sins were understandable.
You confess that you need mercy.
The criminal could not climb down and perform years of good works.
He could not get baptized before dying.
He could not join a church.
He could not build a ministry.
He could not feed a thousand poor families.
He could not spend the next twenty years proving that his conversion was genuine.
His hands were occupied by a cross.
His remaining life could apparently be measured in hours.
He had nothing to offer Jesus except a guilty man turning toward a King.
And then he said words that have traveled through history:
μνήσθητί μου…
mnēsthēti mou…
“Remember me.”
Then:
ὅταν ἔλθῃς ἐν τῇ βασιλείᾳ σου
“When You come into Your kingdom.”
Do not rush past what he just confessed.
Look at Jesus.
Really look.
Jesus did not look like a king at that moment.
He looked defeated.
His body had been brutalized.
His clothes had been taken.
His hands were pierced.
His enemies were mocking Him.
An inscription identifying Him as King hung above a crucified body.
Yet somehow this dying criminal looked at a condemned Jesus and spoke of His coming kingdom.
Others saw a dying man.
He saw a King.
Others mocked Christ's kingship.
He appealed to it.
And perhaps the most heartbreaking part is how small his request was.
He did not say:
“Give me a throne.”
He did not say:
“Make people forget what I did.”
He did not say:
“Let history remember me as a good man.”
He simply asked Jesus to remember him.
Almost as if a man who knew exactly what he deserved was afraid to ask for anything more.
“Jesus… remember me.”
Maybe you understand that prayer more than you would like to admit.
Maybe you have looked at your own life and wondered whether you have gone too far.
Maybe nobody knows what you did.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe the thing haunting you happened twenty years ago.
Maybe it happened last night.
Maybe you still sit in church.
Maybe you still post Bible verses.
Maybe people call you strong while privately you are exhausted from carrying a secret version of yourself.
Maybe you know how to worship publicly while avoiding God privately.
And somewhere underneath all the religious language is one terrified question:
Would Jesus still want me if everything came into the light?
Listen carefully to what Jesus said to a guilty dying man.
The Greek of Luke 23:43 reads:
Ἀμήν σοι λέγω, σήμερον μετ’ ἐμοῦ ἔσῃ ἐν τῷ παραδείσῳ.
Amēn soi legō, sēmeron met’ emou esē en tō paradeisō.
“Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise.”
Read it again.
The criminal asked to be remembered.
Jesus promised him presence.
He asked about some future moment when Christ came into His kingdom.
Jesus answered:
σήμερον — sēmeron — today.
Not after you somehow repair your past.
Today.
Not after centuries of wondering whether mercy was enough.
Today.
And then perhaps the most beautiful words in the sentence:
μετ’ ἐμοῦ — met’ emou — with Me.
That is the heart of salvation.
Not merely escaping punishment.
Not merely receiving something pleasant after death.
Christ Himself.
“With Me.”
Jesus did not tell the criminal that his crimes were insignificant.
The man himself had already acknowledged his guilt.
Grace did not rewrite evil into goodness.
Grace did something infinitely greater.
It gave a guilty man what he could never earn.
That is why cheap grace and biblical grace must never be confused.
Biblical grace does not say sin does not matter.
The cross says precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that redemption required the sacrifice of the Son of God.
But the cross simultaneously declares something almost unbearable in its beauty:
God's mercy toward repentant sinners is greater than the record they bring to Christ.
The criminal's salvation was not purchased by the eloquence of his prayer.
Jesus was purchasing it beside him.
That is the scandal.
The guilty man was dying because of his crimes.
Jesus was dying though He was innocent.
One deserved condemnation.
The other did not.
Yet the innocent Christ was accomplishing the salvation of sinners.
This is why Christianity is not ultimately the story of bad people becoming respectable.
It is the proclamation that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
The criminal could contribute nothing to Calvary.
Christ did the saving.
And this is where his story reaches through the centuries and puts its hand on your shoulder.
Because you may not be hanging from a Roman cross, but you are dying.
So am I.
Every person reading these words is moving toward an appointment we cannot cancel.
The thief simply knew his deadline.
Most of us do not.
That is why this passage should never become an excuse to postpone repentance.
Some people look at the criminal and think, “See? I can come to Jesus at the end.”
But you have been promised no such ending.
The thief had a deathbed conversion.
You have not been promised a deathbed.
The miracle of Luke 23 is not permission to delay.
It is proof that while life remains, no sinner should conclude that Christ's mercy is beyond reach.
There is another sobering detail.
There were two criminals.
Both were near Jesus.
Both saw Him suffering.
Both heard what was happening around that cross.
Both were dying.
Both needed mercy.
Yet proximity to Jesus did not automatically save either man.
One hardened himself.
The other turned toward Christ.
You can be close to Christian things and still resist Christ.
You can know worship songs.
You can own several Bibles.
You can have Christian parents.
You can attend church every Sunday.
You can share inspirational Scripture online.
You can know exactly how Christians speak.
And still remain spiritually untouched by the King hanging at the center of the Gospel.
The question is not merely whether Jesus is near your life.
The question is whether you have entrusted yourself to Jesus.
And notice something else.
Jesus never climbed down from the cross to prove Himself to the mocking criminal.
The demand was essentially, “Save Yourself and us.”
Jesus could have come down.
But if He abandoned the cross merely to silence His mockers, He would not accomplish the saving work for which He had come.
The irony is staggering.
They mocked Him because He would not save Himself.
But He would not save Himself because He was giving Himself to save sinners.
He remained.
The nails remained.
The suffering continued.
The King stayed on the cross.
And because He stayed, sinners could be forgiven.
Soon darkness covered the land. Luke records that the temple curtain was torn, and Jesus ultimately entrusted His spirit to the Father and died.
But death would not have the final word.
Luke's Gospel continues.
Jesus rose.
The crucified King was vindicated.

And after His resurrection, Christ explained that His suffering and resurrection stood at the center of God's saving plan, and that repentance for the forgiveness of sins would be proclaimed in His name to the nations.
That means the criminal's story is not a sentimental loophole in Christianity.
It is a breathtaking demonstration of the Gospel.
Repentance.
Faith.
Christ.
Grace.
Forgiveness.
A guilty sinner.
A sufficient Savior.
And a promise stronger than death.
So perhaps the question is no longer what happened to the criminal.
Perhaps the question is what you will do with the Christ who answered him.
Because eventually every excuse becomes useless.
You can spend years telling yourself you will get serious about God when life settles down.
After the promotion.
After the wedding.
After the children grow up.
After the addiction is under control.
After you stop feeling like a hypocrite.
After you become worthy.
But worthy is never going to happen.
That is why you need grace.
Christianity does not say, “Clean yourself enough so Jesus will receive you.”
The Gospel announces that Jesus receives repentant sinners who trust Him, and the grace that saves also begins transforming the life surrendered to Him.
Come as you are does not mean remain as you are.
Grace receives us where we are and brings us under the lordship of Christ.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior.
Faith is not pretending you have never failed.
It is placing your hope in the One who did not fail.
And if you are reading this with something heavy inside you, stop hiding behind polished Christian language for a moment.
What are you afraid Jesus will uncover?
What have you been defending that you should be confessing?
What sin have you renamed because repentance would hurt your pride?
What secret has convinced you that everyone else may receive grace, but somehow you are the exception?
Look again at the cross.
A criminal is dying beside Jesus.
He has no future achievements to present.
No religious performance.
No impressive spiritual history.
He brings Christ the truth about himself and a desperate appeal of faith:
Remember me.
And Jesus gives him more than he dared request.
“With Me.”
That does not mean every person who casually whispers Jesus' name is automatically converted. Scripture does not teach salvation by magic words.
The criminal's words reveal something deeper.
He acknowledged his guilt.
He feared God.
He recognized Jesus' innocence.
He looked beyond Christ's apparent defeat and trusted Him as the coming King.
And he entrusted his eternity to Jesus.
His faith was simple.
But the Savior receiving it was infinitely sufficient.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need to be impressive either.
Maybe it needs to be honest.
“Jesus, I have sinned.”
“Jesus, I cannot save myself.”
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
“Jesus, I trust You.”
“Jesus, make me Yours.”
Not because those exact sentences function like a formula.
But because the heart of the Gospel is not learning the correct password.
It is turning in repentance and faith to the living Christ.
Be honest before God.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need to know that grace is not merely theology you discuss—it is mercy that reaches real sinners.
And if somebody came into your mind while you were reading this, do not dismiss that name.
Send this to them personally.

Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not. We glorify God because of His grace, not to purchase it. But if this Gospel is true—and it is—then making Christ known is worth more than protecting ourselves from what people may think of us.
Someone may be carrying guilt they have never confessed aloud.
Someone may look perfectly fine in photographs while privately wondering whether God could forgive them.
Let your share become an open door.
Let your profile carry something more eternal than another argument, another advertisement, another photograph, another passing trend.
Carry the Gospel there.
There may come a night when shame tries to preach another gospel to you.
Come back and remember the criminal.
But before you leave, look one final time at Calvary.
Three crosses.
Two criminals.
One Savior.
One criminal wanted Jesus to change his circumstances.
The other entrusted Jesus with his eternity.
And the man who had almost no life left discovered that grace did not need years to reach him.
His past was real.
His guilt was real.
His sentence was real.
But Jesus was more real still.
He could not undo yesterday.
He could not create a better résumé.
He could not climb down and become the man he should have been.
But beside him was the One who could do what he could never do for himself.
Jesus could save.
That is the scandal of grace.
And that is why your worst chapter does not have to be the final sentence.
The criminal had only enough breath left to ask Jesus to remember him—and discovered that Jesus had enough grace to give him eternity.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Screen Goes Dark, but the Secret Stays: What Practical Steps Actually Help Break Porn Habits?
paragraphs: The Screen Goes Dark, but the Secret Stays: What Practical Steps Actually Help Break Porn Habits?

You deleted the history. You promised God it was the last time. Then the temptation came back. Jesus does not merely want to help you survive another night—He wants to bring the hidden war into the light and teach you how to fight for freedom.
There is a particular kind of silence after pornography.
The screen goes dark.
The room looks exactly the same.
Nobody knows.

Maybe your spouse is asleep nearby. Maybe your parents think you are studying. Maybe tomorrow morning you will walk into church, lift your hands during worship, answer messages, post a Bible verse, encourage somebody else, smile at everyone...
and carry a secret nobody can see.
Then comes the familiar conversation with God.
“Lord, forgive me.”
“I hate this.”
“I don't understand why I keep coming back.”
“This was the last time.”
You mean it.
That is what makes the next fall hurt so much.

Because perhaps you have prayed sincerely. Perhaps you have deleted files, cleared histories, unfollowed accounts, cried during worship, made promises at 2:00 in the morning and wondered why someone who genuinely loves Jesus can still feel dragged toward something he or she genuinely hates.
If that is where you are, hear this carefully:
Pornography is not stronger than Jesus Christ.
But freedom usually requires more than feeling ashamed enough to promise you will never do it again.
It requires repentance that becomes action.
It requires grace that teaches you to fight.
It requires bringing darkness into light.
And sometimes it requires doing something painfully practical.
Jesus said something startling in Matthew 5 while speaking about sexual lust:

“...everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.” Then He speaks of the offending eye and hand with deliberately severe imagery—remove what causes you to stumble rather than peacefully allowing sin to rule you.
The Greek behind part of this passage is worth slowing down for.
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn

In context, Jesus is not condemning the involuntary recognition that another human being is attractive. He is confronting the intentional look directed toward lust—the gaze that welcomes and cultivates sexual desire for someone who is not yours to possess.
That distinction matters.
Temptation arriving at your door is not identical to inviting temptation inside, feeding it, replaying it, searching for more of it, and giving it a room in your imagination.
Jesus goes beneath outward behavior and exposes the heart.

And then He uses shocking language about the eye and the hand. Scripture does not present self-mutilation as the cure for lust. The point is the ruthless seriousness with which disciples should remove occasions of sin. Jesus' imagery refuses our favorite compromise:
“I'll keep the doorway open. I'll just become strong enough not to walk through it.”
No.
Sometimes obedience sounds like:
Delete it.
Block it.
Move the phone.
Cancel the account.
Leave the room.
Tell somebody.
Stop pretending you need unrestricted access to the very environment in which you repeatedly collapse.
If an app consistently becomes your doorway, why is it still on your phone?
If being alone with a device after midnight repeatedly becomes the battlefield where you surrender, why is the device still beside your bed?
If a particular social-media feed continually awakens lust, why are you protecting your access to it more fiercely than you are protecting your soul?
We sometimes ask God for miraculous deliverance while refusing ordinary obedience.
“Jesus, take this temptation away.”
And perhaps one part of His answer is:
“Stop carrying the temptation into bed with you.”
That isn't legalism.
That is wisdom.
You don't prove spiritual maturity by seeing how close you can stand to the fire without burning.
You flee.
Paul's language in 1 Corinthians 6 is not “negotiate with sexual immorality,” “study it,” or “see how long you can resist it.”
It is φεύγετε — pheugete.
Flee.
Run.
Get away.
And this is where breaking a pornography habit becomes painfully practical.
You need to identify your doors.
Not merely the pornography itself—the road that keeps taking you there.
What happens twenty minutes before you fall?
Loneliness?
Rejection?
Stress?
Boredom?
Anger?
Exhaustion?
An argument with your spouse?
Scrolling in bed?
Being home alone?
Alcohol lowering your restraint?
A suggestive video that becomes another video, which becomes a search, which becomes the same place you swore you would never visit again?
Learn the geography of your temptation.
Because many people keep fighting the final click while ignoring the twenty decisions that preceded it.
The battle may begin long before explicit material appears.
It begins when you know you are vulnerable but keep scrolling.
When you isolate.
When you refuse sleep.
When you entertain fantasy.
When you revisit an account you know triggers you.
When you tell yourself, “I'm only looking.”
That sentence has buried a thousand promises.
So build friction between temptation and access.

Use filtering and accountability tools. Remove private browsers if possible. Restrict app installation. Unfollow triggering accounts. Keep devices out of bedrooms or bathrooms if those places have repeatedly become part of the pattern. Charge your phone somewhere inconvenient. Use your device in shared spaces. Establish a cutoff time at night. Give a trustworthy mature Christian access to accountability reports or restrictions where appropriate.
Not because software can sanctify your heart.
It cannot.
A filter cannot give you a new heart.
A password cannot crucify the flesh.
An accountability report cannot replace the Holy Spirit.
But if you know a particular bridge repeatedly leads you toward destruction, wisdom does not require you to leave the bridge standing.
And then comes one of the hardest steps.
Tell someone.
Not Facebook.
Not everybody at church.
Someone safe, spiritually mature, trustworthy, and capable of telling you the truth without exploiting your vulnerability.
Sin grows comfortably in secrecy.

James 5:16 connects confession to one another, prayer, and healing. That does not mean broadcasting every sin publicly. It means Christianity was never designed as an anonymous battle in which nobody is allowed to know you are bleeding.
You need somebody who can ask you questions you cannot escape with “I'm doing fine.”
“When did you last fall?”
“What triggered it?”
“What did you do immediately afterward?”
“Are you hiding anything from me?”
“Where is your phone tonight?”
“How is your prayer life?”
“How is your marriage?”
“What are you running from?”
And perhaps the most terrifying question:
“Are you telling me the whole truth?”
Because pornography frequently develops an ecosystem of deception around itself.
Deleted histories.
Second accounts.
Hidden folders.
Secret passwords.
Carefully positioned screens.
Half-truths.
And eventually you are not merely hiding pornography.
You are hiding yourself.
This is why confession can feel terrifying and strangely liberating at the same time.
Darkness says, “If they know, you're finished.”
Grace says, “Bring it into the light.”
But understand something essential: accountability is not merely having someone who receives a confession after every collapse.
Biblical accountability should help interrupt the collapse before it happens.
Your message should not always be:
“I failed again.”
Sometimes it needs to be:
“I'm alone. I'm tempted. Call me.”
That message can feel humiliating.
Send it anyway.
You are not trying to preserve an image.
You are fighting for freedom.
And when temptation arrives, do not sit there arguing with it.
Move.
Stand up.
Leave the room.
Put the device somewhere else.
Call somebody.
Pray aloud.
Open Scripture.
Take a walk.
Do something incompatible with the secrecy the temptation requires.
There is an enormous difference between praying, “God, please make pornography unattractive while I continue staring at it,” and praying while physically removing yourself from access to it.
Flee.
Sometimes victory looks remarkably uncinematic.
It looks like a man leaving his phone in the kitchen.
A teenager telling his father, “I need help.”
A woman unfollowing accounts nobody knew were feeding fantasies.
A husband confessing instead of deleting evidence.
A believer texting an accountability partner before the fall rather than afterward.
A laptop moved from behind a locked bedroom door to a common room.
A password surrendered.
An app deleted.
A late-night routine changed.
A door closed.
And then tomorrow...
you do it again.
Because freedom is not always one dramatic altar moment.
Sometimes God transforms us through thousands of small acts of obedience.
But there is something even deeper that must change.
You cannot merely remove pornography.
You must learn what sexuality is for.
Pornography trains the imagination to consume people.
The Gospel teaches us to love them.
Pornography turns bodies into products and intimacy into consumption.
Jesus teaches us to see human beings as image-bearers, not instruments for fantasy.
So when temptation tells you, “Look,” learn to remember:
That is a person.
Someone God sees.
Someone with dignity.
Someone whose body was never created to become merchandise for my imagination.
This changes the battle from merely “I must not look” to something much more Christlike:
“I refuse to practice consuming another human being in my heart.”
And if you are married, pornography is not harmless simply because no physical affair occurred.
Bring your sexuality back toward covenant, tenderness, patience, truth, service, and genuine intimacy rather than secrecy and comparison.
If your pornography use has wounded your spouse, do not demand instant trust because you finally confessed.
Repentance accepts consequences.
Trust may need to be rebuilt slowly.
Transparency may feel inconvenient.
Questions may feel painful.
Healing may take longer than your apology.
Stay faithful anyway.

And if your pornography use has become compulsive, severe, escalating, connected to trauma, or resistant despite sincere efforts, seek qualified professional help alongside mature pastoral care. Getting help is not evidence that Christ has failed you. God often works through wise people, responsible structures, counseling, community, and patient discipleship.
But there is another danger.
You can become so obsessed with defeating pornography that pornography remains the center of your spiritual life.
Every prayer becomes about porn.
Every journal entry becomes about porn.
Every spiritual victory becomes measured by how many days you avoided porn.
Eventually your Christianity becomes pornography management.
Jesus offers something greater.
Christ Himself.

Paul does not merely give Christians a list of forbidden behaviors. Again and again, he grounds holiness in identity, union with Christ, the indwelling Spirit, the ownership of God, and the reality that believers were bought at a price.
You were not redeemed merely so you could maintain an impressive streak.
You were redeemed for God.
That means replacing, not merely removing.
Fill your eyes with better things.
Fill your mind with Scripture.
Fill your schedule with meaningful work.
Exercise.
Sleep properly.
Serve people.
Worship.
Pray before temptation arrives.
Build friendships that don't require pretending.
Spend time with believers who sharpen your affection for Christ.
Learn Scripture well enough that God's truth becomes available when your imagination starts lying to you.
And when you fall?
This may be the paragraph somebody desperately needs tonight.
Do not turn one fall into a weekend of surrender.
Do not say, “I've already ruined my streak, so it doesn't matter anymore.”
That is another lie.
Run to Christ immediately.
Confess specifically.
Tell your accountability person.
Identify what happened.
Strengthen the weak boundary.
Receive God's forgiveness in Christ.
Get back up.
Repentance is not minimizing sin.
Grace is not pretending pornography doesn't matter.
Grace is the astonishing announcement that sinners do not have to clean themselves sufficiently before coming home.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
Notice where your hope rests.
Not in the strength of your promise.
In the faithfulness of God.
This is where shame loses its throne.
Shame says:
“Hide until you're worthy.”
Jesus says:
“Come.”
Shame says:
“You did it again. You obviously belong to this.”
The Gospel says:
Sin may describe what you did. It does not have the authority to become your savior, your master, or your final identity.
Shame says:
“God must be disgusted with you.”
The cross says something far more devastating and far more beautiful.
Your sin really is serious.
So serious that Christ went to Calvary.
And God's mercy really is that astonishing.
Christ died for sinners.
Jesus did not shed His blood for the imaginary version of you who finally gets everything right.
He died for sinners.
The hidden ones.
The ashamed ones.
The repeat offenders.
The people who knew better.
The people who promised God and broke the promise.
And resurrection means your worst chapter does not get to write the ending.
This is our message:
Not because scandal isn't scandalous.
Not because sin doesn't matter.
Not because repentance is optional.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
He takes Peter's denial and writes restoration.
He takes Paul's persecution and writes apostleship.
He takes the sexually broken, greedy, idolatrous, drunken, dishonest people described in 1 Corinthians 6 and then announces one of the most beautiful reversals in Scripture:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
That word is thunder.
The Gospel does not merely forgive a person's history.
Jesus begins making a person new.
So perhaps tonight you need to stop saying, “Tomorrow I'll become serious.”
Start tonight.
Put the phone outside the bedroom.
Delete what needs deleting.
Block what needs blocking.
Write down your triggers.
Choose the person you are going to tell.
Send the message.
Open your Bible.
Pray without performing.
Tell Jesus the truth He already knows.

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned. I cannot rescue myself. Forgive me. Cleanse me. Teach me to hate what destroys intimacy with You and to love what is holy. Give me courage to bring this into the light. Show me what must be removed. Give me strength to flee instead of negotiate. Restore what my sin has damaged. Make my body, mind, imagination, and sexuality instruments of worship rather than consumption. I belong to You. Teach me to live like it. Amen.”
And tomorrow, fight again.
Not to convince Jesus to love you.
Fight because in Christ you have discovered a love worth protecting.
If this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not have to describe your private struggle publicly. But you can make one small declaration that darkness does not own you.
And if you know somebody fighting quietly, don't embarrass them by tagging them publicly in a way that exposes something they never disclosed. Send this article privately instead.
Not as a badge announcing that you have mastered sexual purity.

Salvation cannot be purchased. Grace cannot be bought. But Christians can glorify God through generous, willing support of faithful Gospel work, just as they can through prayer, service, encouragement, and sharing truth with others.
It is an invitation to stay close to Scripture, discipleship, encouragement, conviction, healing, accountability, and Christ-centered spiritual nourishment.
Only Jesus saves.
But perhaps one ordinary share places an extraordinary truth in front of someone on the exact night they were about to surrender.
Perhaps the person reading this at 2:17 in the morning needs to know something before closing the screen.
Your secret does not have to become your future.
Bring it into the light.
Cut off the road that keeps carrying you backward.
Find someone trustworthy.
Flee when temptation comes.
Return quickly when you fall.
Fill your life with Christ.
And keep walking.
Because one day you may look back at the room where you once whispered, “God, I don't think I'll ever change,” and realize Jesus had already begun writing a chapter you could not yet imagine.
The screen can go dark tonight—but this time, let the secret come into the light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “BE WATCHFUL” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MOST CHRISTIANS THINK—AND ONE DAY, YOU MAY WISH YOU HAD UNDERSTOOD IT SOONER
paragraphs: “BE WATCHFUL” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MOST CHRISTIANS THINK—AND ONE DAY, YOU MAY WISH YOU HAD UNDERSTOOD IT SOONER

Jesus was not teaching His followers to live terrified of tomorrow. He was warning them about something far more dangerous: a heart that can slowly fall asleep while the body is still sitting in church.
There is a frightening kind of sleep that has nothing to do with closing your eyes.
You can wake up every morning.
Go to work.
Pay the bills.
Laugh with friends.
Scroll through Facebook.
Sing worship songs.
Say grace before dinner.
Open a Bible occasionally.
Even sit beneath preaching every Sunday...
and still be asleep.
Spiritually asleep.
Not because you stopped believing God exists.
Not necessarily because you openly rejected Jesus.
But because somewhere between yesterday’s conviction and today’s distractions, eternity stopped feeling urgent.
Sin stopped frightening you.
Prayer became optional.
Repentance became something other people needed.
The Bible became familiar enough to quote but not powerful enough to interrupt you.
And Jesus became Someone you believed in without necessarily being Someone you were actively watching for.
That is why some of Christ’s most unsettling words were not spoken only to atheists, pagans, or people openly hostile to God.
They were spoken to people who were supposed to be waiting for Him.
Jesus said:
“Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come.”
—Matthew 24:42, KJV
That little word “watch” can sound harmless in English.
Almost passive.
Like standing beside a window and looking into the distance.
