And when you fail, run toward Christ instead of hiding from Him.
Repent.
Receive grace.
Get up.
Follow Jesus again.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy would not be having little.
Perhaps it would be despising the little so much that you never discovered what Christ wanted to form in you through it.
One day every platform will disappear.
Every statistic will stop moving.
Every possession will leave your hands.
Every human applause will become silent.
And the Christian will stand before the Lord whose opinion mattered all along.
May we discover that what seemed like a thousand insignificant acts of obedience were never insignificant to Him.
May we discover that the greatest thing the “little” was leading toward was not merely more possessions, more influence, or more authority...
but deeper faithfulness to Jesus.
And when the world has forgotten your name, may the words you spent your life longing for still remain:
“Well done.”
Because sometimes the little thing nobody sees is where Jesus is writing the part of your story eternity will remember.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE DOOR YOU KEEP BEGGING GOD TO OPEN MAY NOT BE THE DOOR JESUS WAS TALKING ABOUT
paragraphs:
THE DOOR YOU KEEP BEGGING GOD TO OPEN MAY NOT BE THE DOOR JESUS WAS TALKING ABOUT
The deeper meaning of “Knock, and it will be opened to you” is far more beautiful—and far more confronting—than “keep praying until God gives you what you want.”
There is a particular kind of silence that hurts more when you have been praying.
You prayed when you still had confidence.
You prayed when you were scared.
You prayed when you could barely get the words out.
You asked God to save the relationship.
You asked Him to heal what was breaking.
You asked Him for the opportunity.
You asked Him to bring your child home.
You asked Him to change your circumstances.
You asked Him to remove the temptation that keeps dragging you backward.
You asked Him for an answer.
Then you waited.
And waited.
And somewhere between another unanswered prayer and another sleepless night, a verse you had heard a hundred times began to hurt:
“Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.”
Matthew 7:7, KJV.
So you knocked.
At least, you thought you did.
And when the thing you desperately wanted did not happen, a terrible question began whispering inside you:
What if God isn't listening?
Maybe you have never said that aloud.
Maybe you would never dare.
You still go to church. You still post the verse. You still tell other people that God is faithful.
But privately?
There is a door in your life that still looks closed.
And you cannot understand why.
But what if Jesus' words have been turned into something He never intended them to be?
What if “knock, and it will be opened” is not a blank check from heaven promising that sufficient persistence will eventually force God to give us whatever stands behind the door we have chosen?
What if this promise is actually better than that?
The Gospel of Matthew was written in Greek, and Matthew 7:7 reads:
“Αἰτεῖτε, καὶ δοθήσεται ὑμῖν· ζητεῖτε, καὶ εὑρήσετε· κρούετε, καὶ ἀνοιγήσεται ὑμῖν.”
Aiteite, kai dothēsetai hymin; zēteite, kai heurēsete; krouete, kai anoigēsetai hymin.
A straightforward rendering is:
“Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.”
Three movements.
Ask.
Seek.
Knock.
Three verbs of dependence.
Three pictures of a human being who does not possess what he needs within himself.

The Greek verbs αἰτεῖτε (aiteite), ζητεῖτε (zēteite), and κρούετε (krouete) are present imperatives. They carry the force of ongoing action in this setting: ask, seek, knock—and continue in that posture.
But notice something equally important.
Jesus does not say:
“Demand.”
He says:
Ask.
He does not say:
“Control.”
He says:
Seek.
He does not say:
“Break the door down.”
He says:
Knock.
That changes everything.
Because knocking acknowledges that somebody else owns the house.
You do not knock on a door you believe belongs to you.
You simply walk inside.
Knocking is simultaneously bold and humble.
It says:
“I have come.”
But it also says:
“I cannot open this on my own.”
And perhaps that is where some of us have misunderstood prayer.
We thought faith meant telling God which door He had to open.
Jesus teaches us to trust the Father standing on the other side.
Read what comes immediately after the famous promise.
Jesus speaks of a son asking his father for bread.
Would a good father hand his child a stone?
The child asks for a fish.
Would his father give him a serpent?
Then Jesus brings the lesson home: if flawed human parents know how to give good things to their children, “how much more” will the heavenly Father give good things to those who ask Him?
That context matters enormously.
Matthew 7:7 is not primarily presenting God as a celestial vending machine.
Jesus presents Him as Father.
And a good father does not prove his love by saying yes to everything his child requests.
He proves his love by giving what is good.
Sometimes that includes what the child requested.
Sometimes it doesn't.
And that second possibility can hurt terribly.
Because there are moments when the stone and the bread look remarkably similar from our side of eternity.
We see the relationship.
God sees where it leads.
We see the promotion.
God sees what it could do to our soul.
We see the person we cannot imagine living without.
God sees everything we cannot see.
We see Friday.
God already sees Sunday.
That does not mean every disappointment should casually be explained with, “God closed the door.”
Scripture does not authorize us to invent God's secret reasons for every tragedy, loss, rejection, illness, or unanswered request.
Sometimes we simply do not know.
Faith is not pretending to know what God has not revealed.
Faith is trusting the character God has revealed when the explanation has not been revealed.
And Jesus reveals Him here as Father.
That is the center of the promise.
You may have approached Matthew 7:7 thinking the greatest miracle would be getting your door opened.
But perhaps the deeper miracle is discovering Who is listening while you knock.
A Father.
Not an algorithm.
Not fate.
Not positive energy.
Not “the universe.”
Not a cosmic servant waiting for sufficiently confident Christians to issue instructions.
Your Father.
And suddenly asking becomes more than requesting things.
Seeking becomes more than hunting for solutions.
Knocking becomes more than attempting to obtain an outcome.
It becomes relationship.
It becomes dependence.
It becomes the surrender of someone who can finally pray:
“Father, I know what I want. But I trust You with what is good.”
That prayer sounds suspiciously like Jesus.
Because there was another night when a prayer seemed to stand before a terrible door.
Gethsemane.
Jesus knew what was coming.
Betrayal.
Humiliation.
Scourging.
Nails.
A cross.
He prayed concerning the cup before Him.
Yet His surrender remained: the Father's will, not His own.
And the Father did not spare the Son from Calvary.
Think about that before someone tells you that unanswered prayer automatically means insufficient faith.
Jesus Christ Himself walked through suffering in perfect obedience.
The cross destroys the shallow theology that says God's love can always be measured by whether today's painful circumstance disappears.
Sometimes faith receives deliverance from suffering.
Sometimes faith is carried through suffering.
And Christianity rests upon the greatest example imaginable:
Friday looked like the door had slammed shut on every promise of God.
The Messiah was bleeding.
The disciples were scattering.
Hope was being lowered into a borrowed grave.
If someone had frozen history on Saturday, Christianity would have looked like a scandalous failure.
But God was not finished writing.
Sunday came.
The stone moved.
Christ rose.
Death lost its claim.
And suddenly what looked like the ending became the doorway through which redemption exploded into history.
That is why the Gospel is not the story of human beings becoming strong enough to open heaven.
It is the story of Jesus Christ doing for sinners what sinners could never do for themselves.
Our deepest problem was never that we had not discovered the correct technique for getting our preferred doors opened.
Our deepest problem was sin.
We had rebelled against God.
We needed forgiveness.
We needed reconciliation.
We needed rescue.
We needed a righteousness we could never manufacture.
We needed Jesus.
And at the cross, the innocent Son of God bore sin and judgment, giving Himself for sinners.
Then He rose.
Grace opened what human effort never could.
This is where “ask, seek, knock” becomes painfully personal.
Because perhaps you have spent years knocking on doors of success while ignoring the condition of your soul.
Perhaps you have asked God to fix your circumstances while refusing to surrender your sin.
Perhaps you have sought blessing while avoiding the One who blesses.
Perhaps you have wanted Jesus to improve your life without permitting Him to rule it.
Maybe nobody knows.
They see your Sunday version.
They do not see what happens after midnight.
They don't know about the messages.
The bitterness.
The pornography.
The secret relationship.
The addiction.
The pride.
The jealousy.
The private compromises.
The resentment you keep feeding.
The guilt you learned to disguise with Christian vocabulary.
You have become extraordinarily skilled at looking spiritually alive while something inside you is starving.
And Jesus is not inviting you to become better at pretending.
He calls sinners to repentance and faith.
Grace does not say your sin does not matter.
Grace says your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and His mercy is so astonishing that repentant sinners can be forgiven.
Maybe the door you most desperately need opened tonight is not the door to another opportunity.
Maybe it is the prison door of the life you have been hiding.
Ask.
Seek.
Knock.
Not because repetition earns God's attention.
Not because persistence manipulates Him.
Not because enough faith forces His hand.
But because Jesus teaches needy people to keep coming to their Father.
Keep asking when you do not understand.
Keep seeking when everything feels dark.
Keep knocking when heaven feels quiet.
And while you are knocking, surrender the right to dictate what must be waiting behind the door.
There is something terrifyingly beautiful about that kind of faith.
“Father, if this relationship will destroy what You are forming in me, I surrender it.”
Knock.
“If this opportunity will feed my ego but starve my soul, I surrender it.”
Knock.
“If what I desperately want is not what You call good, teach me to want You more.”
Knock.
“If I have been using prayer to chase blessings while running from obedience, forgive me.”
Knock.
“If there is sin hidden behind my Christian image, bring it into Your light.”
Knock.
“If You open the door, I will worship You.”
Knock.
“If You keep it closed, help me trust You.”
Knock.
“And if the answer comes differently than I imagined, keep me close enough to Jesus that disappointment does not become unbelief.”
That is not weak faith.
That is surrendered faith.
And surrender is not giving up on God.
It is giving up the illusion that you are God.
Somebody reading this has been interpreting a closed door as proof that God abandoned you.
Please hear what Matthew 7 actually points you toward.
Look at the Father.
The argument Jesus makes is not, “You are so powerful that every request must become reality.”
His argument moves from earthly fathers to the infinitely better heavenly Father.
“How much more…”
Those words are an anchor.
Your confidence ultimately rests not in the perfection of your asking but in the goodness of the One you ask.
And that means you can come honestly.
You can tell Him you're angry.
Tell Him you're confused.
Tell Him the waiting hurts.
Tell Him you wanted another answer.
Tell Him you are frightened that nothing will change.
Tell Him you are tired of knocking.
Biblical faith does not require theatrical confidence.
Read the Psalms.
God's people cried.
Questioned.
Lamented.
Waited.
Hoped.
And kept turning toward God.
That last part matters.
They kept turning toward Him.
The enemy would love to use one unanswered prayer to convince you to stop knocking altogether.
Because if disappointment can become distance, eventually distance can become indifference.
Don't let the door you wanted become the reason you walk away from the Father you need.
Come back.
Even if your prayer tonight is only:
“Jesus, I don't understand.”
Come back.
“Jesus, I'm angry.”
Come back.
“Jesus, I failed again.”
Come back.
“Jesus, forgive me.”
Come back.
“Jesus, I don't know whether I have enough faith left.”
Come back.
Your hope was never supposed to rest in the strength of your fingers against the door.
Your hope rests in Christ.
This is the scandal of grace.
People with dirty hands can knock.
Prodigals can come home.
Failures can repent.
The ashamed can step into the light.
The sexually broken can be made new.
The proud can bow.
The addicted can cry for mercy.
The religious hypocrite can finally stop pretending.
The exhausted believer can whisper one more prayer.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Because Jesus is sufficient.
And perhaps this is the moment you stop asking only:
“God, when will You open my door?”
And begin asking:
“God, what are You doing in me while I wait?”
Maybe He is exposing an idol.
Maybe He is teaching dependence.
Maybe He is calling you to repentance.
Maybe He is redirecting you.
Maybe He is strengthening endurance.
Or maybe you simply do not yet know.
Do not claim certainty where Scripture gives none.
But know what Scripture does give you:
a Father to whom Jesus tells you to come.
So knock.
And while you knock, look at the nail-scarred Savior who made reconciliation with God possible.
The cross is where your confidence must ultimately land.
Not on getting the job.
Not on recovering the relationship.
Not on receiving the money.
Not even on getting the earthly healing for which you are praying.
Those things matter. Bring them to God.
But none of them is the Gospel.
Jesus is.
Christ crucified.
Christ risen.
Christ reigning.
Christ forgiving sinners who turn to Him.
Christ receiving those who come.
Christ transforming people who thought their story was already ruined.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And don't keep this article trapped on your screen.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who has been praying behind a closed door for months and quietly assuming God's silence means God's absence.
We glorify God by loving Him, obeying Him, bearing fruit, and making Christ known—not by making a payment.
And there is something bigger than merchandise behind the invitation.
So if these messages keep meeting you in places ordinary posts cannot reach, stay close.
Invite the friend who is drifting.
Invite the Christian who has become spiritually numb.
Invite the person who doesn't believe yet.
Jesus alone saves.
Not because supporting a ministry earns God's blessing.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Support it because, if Christ-centered truth has strengthened you, helping that truth reach another wounded person can become an act of generosity and Gospel mission.
Somewhere tonight, another person is sitting in front of a door that will not open.
They may be one unanswered prayer away from giving up.
Your share might put this message in front of them.
Your tag might tell them, “I remembered you.”
Your comment might give another struggling believer courage to admit, “Me too.”
Your support might help another piece of Gospel truth travel farther than you ever personally could.
Jesus Christ.
If you have been seeking everything except Him, come home.
If sin has separated your public image from your private life, repent.
If shame tells you that you are too dirty to return, look at the cross.
If pride tells you that you do not need mercy, look again.
Ask.
Seek.
Knock.
And when you cannot understand what God is doing behind the doors of your life, remember the door that seemed most hopeless of all:
a sealed tomb.
For one dark Sabbath, it looked as though death had spoken the final word.
Then came morning.
Jesus walked out.
So never confuse a chapter you cannot understand with the end of the story God has revealed in Christ.
The door you wanted may remain closed—but because the tomb is empty, the heart that belongs to Jesus never waits without hope.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE KILLED A MAN, RAN AWAY, AND THOUGHT HIS STORY WAS OVER. THEN GOD CALLED HIS NAME.
paragraphs: HE KILLED A MAN, RAN AWAY, AND THOUGHT HIS STORY WAS OVER. THEN GOD CALLED HIS NAME.

Before Moses stood before Pharaoh, before the sea opened, before a nation followed him into freedom, there was blood in the sand, a frightened fugitive in the wilderness, and forty years of silence. If you have ever wondered whether the worst thing you have done has permanently disqualified you from being used by God, do not leave this story too quickly.
There was a body in the sand.
And Moses knew exactly who put it there.

Before we turn him into stained glass, before we picture the staff raised over the Red Sea, before we remember the plagues, the Passover, Sinai, and the Ten Commandments, Scripture forces us to meet Moses somewhere far less comfortable.
At the scene of his failure.
Egypt.
A Hebrew man is being beaten by an Egyptian.
Moses sees it.
Something inside him erupts.
Exodus 2:12 records the terrifying sequence with almost cinematic simplicity:
“וַיַּךְ אֶת־הַמִּצְרִי וַיִּטְמְנֵהוּ בַּחוֹל”
Vayyakh et-haMitzri vayitmenehu bachol.
He struck the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.
There is something especially revealing about what happens immediately before the killing.
Scripture says Moses “looked this way and that way.”
Then he acted.
Then he hid the body.
The man who would one day stand publicly before Pharaoh was, at this moment, looking around to see who might be watching.
And perhaps that is where this story stops being merely Moses' story.
Because some of us know what it means to look this way and that way.
Not necessarily before committing murder.
But before opening the browser.
Before sending the message.
Before returning to the addiction.
Before lying.
Before crossing the boundary.
Before feeding the bitterness.
Before doing something we would desperately prefer nobody ever discover.
We look this way.
We look that way.
And somewhere inside us, we begin behaving as though the absence of human witnesses means the absence of God.
But there is always Someone we forget to look toward.
Up.
Moses buried the Egyptian beneath the sand.
And human beings have been burying things ever since.
Different sand.
Same instinct.
We bury memories beneath achievement.
We bury addictions beneath respectable appearances.
We bury wounds beneath jokes.
We bury resentment beneath church attendance.
We bury secret compromises beneath Bible verses posted publicly.
We bury shame beneath productivity.
We bury loneliness beneath scrolling.
We bury spiritual exhaustion beneath “I’m blessed.”
We learn how to smile while standing over graves nobody else knows exist.
And perhaps nobody knows yours.
Perhaps there is something in your past that still makes your stomach tighten when you remember it.
Perhaps your failure is not ancient history.
Perhaps it happened last night.
Perhaps you have asked God for forgiveness and still cannot imagine how He could ever use someone who did what you did.
Keep reading.
Because the sand did not finish Moses' story.
The next day Moses discovers that his secret is not secret.
Two Hebrews are fighting. Moses intervenes, and one of them fires a sentence directly into the place Moses hoped nobody could see:
“Who made you ruler and judge over us? Are you thinking of killing me as you killed the Egyptian?”
The blood beneath the sand suddenly has a voice.
Moses is afraid.
Pharaoh hears about the killing and seeks to kill him.
So Moses runs.

Acts 7 later confirms the event plainly: Moses killed the Egyptian, and after his deed became known, he fled to Midian. Stephen's speech also gives us an important detail about Moses' thinking: Moses apparently believed his fellow Israelites would understand that God was giving them deliverance through him, but they did not.
That detail matters.
Moses appears to have had some awareness that his life was connected to Israel's deliverance.
But calling and timing are not the same thing.
A God-given concern does not justify a flesh-driven method.
Moses wanted liberation.
God wanted liberation too.
But God did not need Moses to become a murderer to accomplish it.
That distinction protects us from a dangerous distortion of this story.
The Bible is not saying, “Moses murdered somebody, so apparently sin does not matter.”
No.
The killing was wrong.
The hiding was real.
The consequences were real.
The fear was real.
The exile was real.
Grace does not require us to rename evil as good.
Grace is infinitely more beautiful than that.
Grace says God can confront what was evil without surrendering the person who committed it to hopelessness.
That is different.
And that is Gospel.
Moses runs from Egypt into Midian.
Imagine the contrast.
He had known Pharaoh's household.
Now wilderness.
He had known influence.
Now obscurity.
He had known Egypt's power.
Now sheep.
Day after day.
Dust.
Heat.
Animals.
Silence.
Morning.
Evening.
Again.
Again.
Again.
And again.
Acts 7 tells us something staggering.
Forty years passed.
Forty.
Years.
We read those words in seconds.
Moses lived them one sunrise at a time.
There are people reading this who understand that wilderness more than they wish they did.
You thought God was going to use you by now.
You thought the marriage would be healed by now.
You thought the prayer would have been answered by now.
You thought you would have overcome that struggle by now.
You thought your children would have returned to God by now.
You thought the door would have opened.
You thought the grief would hurt less.
You thought your life would look different.
Instead, you are feeding sheep in a chapter you never planned to enter.
And the frightening thought begins whispering:
Maybe this is all my life will ever be.
Maybe I missed God.
Maybe I ruined it.
Maybe my best years disappeared.
Maybe the thing I did disqualified me.
Maybe heaven has moved on.
Maybe God uses people like Moses...
just not people like me.
Then one ordinary day, a bush burns.
And does not burn up.
Moses turns aside.
And from inside the fire comes something he may never have expected to hear again.
His name.
Not “murderer.”
Not “failure.”
Not “fugitive.”
Not “disappointment.”
Not “washed-up old man.”
“Moses! Moses!”
The Hebrew of Exodus 3:4 is breathtakingly personal:
“מֹשֶׁה מֹשֶׁה”
Mosheh, Mosheh.
Moses.
Moses.
God knew exactly who He was calling.
Do not miss that.
God did not discover Moses' history after calling him.
There was no embarrassing file heaven forgot to check.
God knew Egypt.
God knew the Egyptian.
God knew the sand.
God knew the fear.
God knew Midian.
God knew every wilderness year.
And God called his name anyway.
That does not make Moses innocent.
It makes grace astonishing.
There is a difference between God excusing a person's past and God redeeming a person's life.
Biblical grace never says sin is insignificant.

Biblical grace says sin is so serious that redemption ultimately requires blood—and the blood that finally answers humanity's guilt is not the blood Moses spilled in Egypt, but the blood Jesus Christ willingly shed at Calvary.
That is where Moses' story begins pointing beyond Moses.
Because Moses can inspire us.
But Moses cannot save us.
Moses needed grace too.
The deliverer of Israel needed a greater Deliverer.

Hebrews makes the Christ-centered dimension of Moses' faith explicit. It says that Moses chose suffering with God's people over the temporary pleasures associated with Egypt and regarded the reproach connected with Christ—the Messiah—as greater treasure than Egypt's riches.
Moses points forward.
Jesus fulfills.
Moses confronted an earthly Pharaoh.
Jesus conquered sin and death.
Moses led slaves out of Egypt.
Jesus liberates sinners from slavery to sin.
Moses stretched out his hand and Israel passed through the sea.
Jesus stretched out His hands on a cross and opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
Through Moses came the law.
In Jesus Christ we behold the One who perfectly fulfills God's righteous purpose and bears the curse sinners could never remove from themselves.
And here is where this story becomes painfully personal.
You may be trying to bury what Jesus came to redeem.
You may have spent years running from a God who already knows where you are.
You may think repentance means approaching Christ with information He has not heard yet.
It doesn't.
He already knows.
Repentance is not informing God.
It is surrendering to God.
It is coming into the light and saying:
“Lord, no more hiding.”
No more defending it.
No more renaming it.
No more blaming everybody else.
No more pretending.
No more sand.
This is what I did.
This is who I became.
This is where I am.
Have mercy on me.
And the Gospel does not answer the repentant sinner with self-improvement.
It answers with a Person.
Jesus Christ.
At the cross, God does not pretend sin never happened.
He demonstrates exactly how serious sin is.
Christ, the sinless Son of God, gives Himself for sinners.
Justice is not brushed aside.
Grace is not cheapened.
Forgiveness is purchased at terrible cost.
And because Jesus rose from the dead, failure does not have to write the final sentence over anyone who comes to Him in repentant faith.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
Moses' story certainly does not teach that.
Grace is not a time machine.
You may not be able to undo what happened.
You may need to apologize.
You may need to confess.
You may need to make restitution where appropriate.
You may need accountability.
You may need to accept consequences.
Some relationships may require years to rebuild.
Some scars may remain.
But hear this carefully:
Consequences are not the same thing as condemnation.
For those who are in Christ Jesus, condemnation does not own the final word.
Jesus does.
And perhaps the most extraordinary thing about Moses is that God did not merely forgive a broken man and leave him hidden in Midian.
God sent him back.
Back toward Egypt.
Back toward Pharaoh.
Back toward the geography of his fear.
Imagine Moses walking toward the place from which he once fled.
Same Egypt.
Different Moses.
Years earlier, Moses had acted in his own strength and buried one Egyptian.
Now God would display His power and lead an enslaved nation toward freedom.
Moses once looked this way and that way before acting.
Later, Hebrews remembers him as a man who endured by looking toward the One who is invisible.
Do you see the transformation?
His first question was essentially:
Who is watching me?
Faith taught him to live by a greater reality:
God is.
The man who ran from Pharaoh would return to confront Pharaoh.
The man who hid a body would stand openly before a king.
The man who believed his usefulness had collapsed would become an instrument through whom God displayed extraordinary deliverance.
But do not turn this into the shallow slogan, “Your mess automatically becomes your ministry.”
Scripture promises nothing so mechanical.
Not every failure leads to a platform.
Not every redeemed person becomes famous.
Not every wilderness ends with public prominence.
Sometimes grace leads you into a quiet life of faithful obedience that nobody applauds.
And that is enough.
The treasure is not becoming another Moses.
The treasure is belonging to Christ.
The greatest miracle in this story is not that Moses eventually became important.
The greatest miracle is that the Holy God speaks to sinful human beings at all.
And this is why somebody reading this needs to stop saying:
“God could never want me after what I've done.”
Be careful about finishing a sentence God has not finished writing.
Peter denied Jesus.
Paul persecuted Christians.
David's history contains adultery, deception, and bloodshed.
Moses killed a man.
None of their sins became virtues.
None should be romanticized.
Yet none proved stronger than God's redemptive purpose.
And your sin is not made harmless by grace either.
It must be brought to Christ.
Confessed.
Forsaken.
Placed beneath the mercy of the crucified and risen Savior.
Maybe you have been in Midian emotionally for years.
You still attend church.
Still smile.
Still answer, “I'm okay.”
But somewhere deep inside, you have quietly sentenced yourself.
You believe Jesus forgives other people.
You preach grace to everyone except the person in your mirror.
Then perhaps the question is no longer whether your past is ugly.
Perhaps it is whether you believe Christ's cross is sufficient.
Your shame says:
Hide.
Jesus says:
Come.
Your shame says:
Run.
Jesus says:
Follow Me.
Your shame says:
You are what you did.
The Gospel says that those who belong to Christ receive a new identity rooted not in their worst moment but in Him.
Your shame keeps pointing toward the sand.
Grace points toward the cross.
And the cross is not permission to continue sinning.
It is the place where the sinner dies to the fantasy that sin can save, satisfy, or define him and begins learning to walk in newness of life.
So repent.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you clean yourself up.
Not when you feel worthy enough to pray.
Come to Jesus Christ now.
Tell Him the truth.
The entire truth.
The truth He already knows.
Ask for mercy.
Trust His finished work rather than your ability to compensate for your past.
And then walk where obedience leads.
Maybe somebody reading this is thinking:
“But you don't know what I did.”
You're right.
I don't.
But Jesus does.
That is precisely the point.
The One inviting sinners to repentance is not working with incomplete information.
Christ knew the cost when He went to the cross.
Be honest.
Someone else may be sitting in their own Midian believing restoration is impossible, and God may use your testimony to remind them that grace is real.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It does not. We are saved by grace through faith, and every act of Christian service must flow from grace rather than attempt to purchase it.
Put it where the person who would never walk into your church might still read it at 1:17 in the morning.
Send it privately to the believer who disappeared because shame convinced him he could never come home.
Gospel Warrior cannot save you.
Moses cannot save you.
A church cannot save you.
Your good deeds cannot save you.
Jesus Christ saves.
So after the comments stop...
after the shares slow down...
after the screen goes dark...
after everyone else goes home...
remember the wilderness.
Remember the fugitive.
Remember the fire.
Remember the voice.
“Moses, Moses.”
God knew the whole story before He spoke the name.
And He knows yours.
Maybe there are chapters you wish could be torn from the book.
Maybe there is blood beneath your sand.
Maybe there are decades you call wasted.
Maybe you ran farther than you ever intended.
Maybe you no longer recognize the person staring back from the mirror.
Do not make peace with sin.
Do not romanticize your failure.
Do not hide what needs to be confessed.
But do not declare yourself beyond the reach of the Savior whose blood cleanses sinners and whose resurrection announces that death itself does not get the final word.
Bring the scandal into the light.
Bring the shame to the cross.
Bring the ruins to Jesus.
Because Moses' greatest moment was not when everybody finally knew his name.
It was when, after all those years of running, he discovered that God still did.
You may have buried your past in the sand, but Jesus was already preparing a road through the sea.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Lazarus Was Already Dead — Jesus Still Told Them to Move the Stone
paragraphs: Lazarus Was Already Dead — Jesus Still Told Them to Move the Stone
What if the thing you buried is not the thing Jesus has abandoned—and the stone you are protecting is standing between your surrender and what He wants you to see?
There are some prayers you stop praying because eventually the silence becomes too painful.
At first, you prayed with expectation.
Then you prayed with tears.
Then you prayed because you were terrified not to.
And somewhere between another unanswered morning and another sleepless night, your prayer quietly changed from, “Jesus, please save this,” to, “Jesus, help me survive this.”
Maybe it was your marriage.
Your child.
Your faith.
Your calling.
Your purity.
Your family.
The person you used to be before disappointment hollowed something out inside you.
Maybe nobody even knows it died.
You still go to church.
You still know when to say amen.
You still share verses.
You still tell people, “God is good.”
But there is a tomb somewhere inside your heart that you stopped taking people near.
Because some things hurt differently after you have buried them.
Martha understood.
By the time Jesus stood outside Lazarus’s tomb, there was no medical emergency left.
There was no sickbed.
No final treatment to attempt.
No pulse to recover.
No desperate message left to send.
Lazarus was dead.
John makes that painfully clear. Jesus Himself had already told His disciples plainly, “Lazarus died.” Then, when He finally arrived near Bethany, Lazarus had already been in the tomb four days.
Four days.
And Martha had already spoken the sentence so many wounded believers have whispered in different words:
“Lord, if You had been here...”
That sentence is not atheism.
It is wounded faith.
Martha still calls Him Lord.
She still believes He possesses extraordinary authority.
But she cannot reconcile His love with His timing.
And perhaps that is where this story finds you.
You believe Jesus could have done something.
You just cannot understand why He did not do it when you begged Him.
That distinction matters.
Because some of the deepest crises of faith do not begin when people stop believing God exists.
They begin when people know He exists and cannot understand why the God who loves them allowed something to die.
John tells us something almost unbearable before Lazarus dies: Jesus loved Martha, Mary, and Lazarus.
And then Jesus delayed.
Those truths stand beside each other in the text.
Love.
Delay.
That destroys one of our most dangerous assumptions—that if Jesus loves us, He must always operate according to the timetable we would choose.
Scripture does not permit that conclusion.
His delay was not evidence of indifference.
And when Jesus finally reached the grieving sisters, He did not stand at a safe theological distance from their sorrow.
Jesus wept.
The One who knew resurrection was minutes away still entered their grief.
Think about that.
Jesus knew Lazarus was coming out...
and Jesus still cried.
Christian hope does not require pretending death does not hurt.
Faith is not emotional anesthesia.
Jesus Christ does not shame Mary for weeping at His feet. He does not tell the mourners that their tears prove insufficient faith.
He weeps.
But then He walks toward the tomb.
And everything becomes uncomfortable.
Because Jesus does not merely comfort them beside the place of death.
He tells them to open it.
The Greek of John 11:39 is strikingly direct:
“Ἄρατε τὸν λίθον.”
Arate ton lithon.
“Take away the stone.”
The verb ἄρατε is an imperative. Jesus is giving a command. The people standing there cannot give Lazarus life—but they can move what is blocking the tomb.
And Martha immediately objects.
Of course she does.
“Lord, by this time there will be an odor, for he has been dead four days.”
In the Greek text, her words include:
“Κύριε, ἤδη ὄζει...”
Kyrie, ēdē ozei...
“Lord, already he smells...”
This is not a polished church scene anymore.
This is death.
Real death.
A sealed grave.
Decomposition.
Grief with an odor.
Jesus is asking Martha to expose the very thing she has already accepted as irreversible.
And suddenly this ancient tomb feels frighteningly modern.
Because we have stones too.
We put them over places we never want opened again.
The addiction nobody knows about.
The resentment we learned to justify.
The pornography history we keep deleting.
The affair we insist is finished but never confessed.
The bitterness toward the person who wounded us.
The shame from something done to us.
The shame from something done by us.
The secret compromise hidden underneath Christian vocabulary.
The prayer life that quietly died.
The Bible collecting dust while our phone receives hours of our attention.
The marriage that still exists legally but feels buried emotionally.
The child whose rebellion has exhausted every prayer you know how to pray.
The ministry wound that made you suspicious of everyone.
The sin you renamed “struggle” because repentance sounded too expensive.
Stone after stone.
And eventually we become skilled at decorating tombs.
That is the terrifying possibility.
You can become so accustomed to protecting dead places that when Jesus says, “Move the stone,” your first instinct is not hope.
It is embarrassment.
“Lord... it smells in there.”
Lord, You do not understand what You will uncover.
Lord, people will see.
Lord, I buried that for a reason.
Lord, I cannot reopen that memory.
Lord, I cannot confess that.
Lord, I cannot forgive them.
Lord, I cannot admit how far I have fallen.
Lord, what if nothing happens after I move it?
And here we need to be biblically careful.

John 11 is first and foremost a revelation of Jesus Christ. It is not a formula promising that every broken relationship will be restored, every illness healed in this life, every lost opportunity returned, or every earthly tragedy reversed exactly as we desire.
Lazarus’s resurrection is a sign.
It points beyond Lazarus.
Jesus had already told Martha:
“I am the resurrection and the life.”
Not merely, I perform resurrection.
“I am.”
Christian hope ultimately rests not in getting every earthly circumstance resurrected according to our preferences, but in Christ Himself—the Son of God who has authority over sin and death.
That distinction protects this beautiful passage from becoming a prosperity slogan.
Jesus is not promising you that every dream you buried is coming back.
Some things need to remain buried.
Some relationships should not be restored to their former form.
Some doors God closes should stay closed.
Some versions of ourselves should never be resurrected.
The Gospel is far greater than “Jesus will give me my old life back.”
The Gospel announces that sinners who were spiritually dead can receive new life in Christ.
And that is where Lazarus’s tomb begins pointing toward something infinitely greater.
Jesus stands before a dead man and commands life where human beings possess no power to produce it.
After the stone is removed, Jesus prays.
Then comes one of the most breathtaking commands in the Gospel of John:
“Λάζαρε, δεῦρο ἔξω.”
Lazare, deuro exō.
“Lazarus, come out.”
Notice what Jesus does not say.
“Lazarus, heal yourself.”
“Lazarus, try harder.”
“Lazarus, become worthy.”
“Lazarus, prove you deserve another chance.”
The dead man contributes no power to his resurrection.
Jesus speaks.
Lazarus comes out.
That is why Christianity is not fundamentally a self-improvement project.
The Gospel is not Jesus standing outside the tomb shouting motivational advice to corpses.
We need grace.
We need forgiveness.
We need life.

Sin is more serious than bad habits needing adjustment. Scripture describes humanity apart from Christ as dead in trespasses and sins. We cannot boast our way into salvation, perform our way into reconciliation with God, or clean ourselves enough to make the cross unnecessary.
Jesus came because we could not save ourselves.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
The sinless Christ bore judgment for sinners.
He was buried.
And on the third day, the tomb that should have held Him could not.
Lazarus came out of his grave still wrapped in grave clothes and would one day physically die again.
Jesus Christ rose never to die again.
That is the greater glory toward which this sign points.
And there is another detail in John 11 that should stop us.
Jesus could raise Lazarus.
Yet He told other people to move the stone.
Then, after Lazarus emerged, Jesus told them:
“Unbind him, and let him go.”
Jesus alone supplied the resurrection power.
Yet people were commanded to participate obediently in what they actually could do.
That matters.
Moving the stone did not resurrect Lazarus.
Jesus did.
Their obedience did not manufacture the miracle.
Jesus did.
So never turn this passage into “If you just work hard enough, God will perform your miracle.”
That is not the Gospel.
But neither should we use the sovereignty of Christ as an excuse for disobedience.
There are stones Jesus has already told us to move through the clear teaching of Scripture.
Repent.
Confess.
Forgive.
Flee sexual immorality.
Put away deceit.
Love one another.
Care for the vulnerable.
Pray.
Abide in Christ.
Take up your cross.
Follow Him.
You cannot resurrect yourself.
But you can stop defending the stone.
Maybe that is the sentence somebody reading this needed.
Stop defending the stone.
Stop explaining why your secret sin deserves one more month.
Stop waiting to feel repentant enough before you repent.
Stop confusing conviction with condemnation.
Stop telling Jesus, “It has been four days,” as though the length of your failure determines the reach of His grace.
Maybe it has been four days.
Maybe four years.
Maybe forty.
Jesus is not intimidated by how long you have been hiding.
But grace is not permission to remain inside the tomb.
Grace calls you out.
There is a counterfeit Christianity that wants Jesus to forgive the old life without ever commanding the old life to surrender.
But the Jesus of Scripture says, “Follow Me.”
The Gospel does not merely change your eternal destination while leaving your allegiance untouched.
Christ saves by grace, and the grace that saves begins transforming the person it saves.
Not perfectly overnight.
Not without battles.
Not without stumbling.
But genuinely.
This is where “From Scandal to Grace” becomes more than a beautiful phrase.
Because Scripture is filled with people whose stories should have ended differently.
Peter denied Jesus.
Grace found him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Grace transformed him.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Grace met him at a cross.
And the cross itself looked like the greatest scandal, defeat, and ending imaginable.
The Messiah crucified.
The disciples scattered.
Hope apparently sealed behind stone.
Then came Sunday.
That is what Jesus does.
He takes stories sin has vandalized and writes redemption across them.
He does not call evil good.
He does not pretend wounds never happened.
He does not erase justice.
He does something far more glorious.
He redeems.
Maybe your scandal is public.
Maybe yours has never left your bedroom.
Maybe nobody knows what you have become.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe you are carrying consequences that repentance will not magically remove.
Hear this carefully:
The grace of Jesus Christ is not reserved for people with respectable histories.
The cross exists precisely because sinners need mercy.
Repentance means you stop negotiating with the tomb and turn toward Christ.
You bring Him the truth.
All of it.
The ugly part.
The embarrassing part.
The part you wish you could edit out of your testimony.
And you discover that Jesus already knew what was behind the stone when He called you.
He knew.
That may be the most frightening and beautiful truth in this entire article.
Jesus knew what was inside Lazarus’s tomb before anyone moved the stone.
And Jesus knows what is inside yours.
You are not informing an ignorant Savior when you confess.
You are surrendering to a Savior who already knows.
So perhaps today your prayer does not need impressive language.
Perhaps it sounds like this:
Jesus, I have been hiding.
Jesus, forgive me.
Jesus, I cannot save myself.
Jesus, I believe You died for sinners and rose again.
Jesus, expose what must be exposed.
Remove what must be removed.
Kill what must die.
Heal what You desire to heal.
Teach me to obey You.
Make me Yours.
And if those words exposed something you have kept behind a stone, do not turn this into another emotional article you read, feel, and forget.
Be honest.
Somebody scrolling beneath this article may need evidence that Christians do not have to pretend they have never been in tombs.
Not to embarrass them.
To remind them that Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
You do not know who is scrolling at 2:17 in the morning.
You do not know whose marriage is collapsing.
Whose secret addiction is winning.
Whose shame has convinced them God could never want them.
Whose finger might stop on the words:
Jesus already knows what is behind your stone.

Not because the post itself possesses power, but because there may come a night when disappointment whispers that God has forgotten you, and you will need to return to John 11 and remember what Scripture actually says.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the unbeliever you have been praying for to follow too.
It does not.
Not because supporting a ministry contributes anything to your salvation.
It cannot.
Jesus purchased salvation. Grace cannot be bought.
But generosity, Gospel partnership, and helping biblical teaching reach more people can be sincere ways believers choose to glorify God with resources He has entrusted to them.
It is discipleship.
It is staying close to Scripture.

It is helping build a place where conviction does not end in despair, where broken people are pointed toward Christ rather than personalities, and where the answer to human scandal is never self-righteousness but repentance, the cross, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through Jesus.
And before you leave, go back in your mind to Bethany one final time.
See Martha standing there.
See the mourners.
See the stone.
Smell the reality nobody wanted exposed.
Hear the scraping as human hands begin moving what had sealed the grave.
Then silence.
Jesus lifts His eyes.
He prays.
And the voice that spoke creation into existence addresses a man who cannot possibly answer.
“Lazarus, come out.”
Then...
movement.
The impossible sound of life inside a place built for death.
A man walks out wearing the evidence of where he has been.
And Jesus says to unbind him.
That is grace.
Not pretending there was never a tomb.
Not pretending Lazarus had never died.
Not rewriting history by denying what happened.
Grace is Jesus Christ entering a story everyone else has already pronounced finished and demonstrating that death itself does not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
So move whatever stone Scripture is calling you to move.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repent of what needs abandoning.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Ask for help where you cannot fight alone.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
And leave resurrection power where it belongs:
in the hands of Jesus.
Because perhaps the stone you are most afraid to move is covering the very place where you most desperately need to encounter the authority, mercy, and glory of Christ.
The tomb may explain where you have been—but when Jesus calls your name, it does not get to decide where your story ends.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY JOSHUA MADE THEM CARRY 12 HEAVY STONES OUT OF THE JORDAN
paragraphs: WHY JOSHUA MADE THEM CARRY 12 HEAVY STONES OUT OF THE JORDAN

They had already crossed the river. They were already safe. God had already performed the miracle. So why did Joshua send twelve men back into the place they had just escaped… and tell each one to put a heavy stone on his shoulder? Because God knew something about the human heart Israel was about to discover: sometimes surviving the miracle is easier than remembering the God who performed it.
The river was behind them.
Imagine the scene.
Children who had grown up hearing stories about the Red Sea were suddenly standing on the other side of their own impossible water.
Parents were gathering their families.
Feet that had walked through the Jordan were finally touching the soil of Canaan.
For forty years, Israel had wandered.
Forty years of funerals.
Forty years of dust.
Forty years of consequences.
Forty years of hearing about a land that always seemed to exist somewhere beyond tomorrow.
And now…
they were standing in it.
But before Israel could rush toward Jericho, before the walls fell, before battles were fought and territories were possessed, God gave Joshua a strange command.
Go back to the river.
Choose twelve men.
One from every tribe.
And tell each man to pick up a stone.
Not a pebble.
Not a souvenir small enough to slip unnoticed into his pocket.
Joshua 4:5 says:
“Take you up every man of you a stone upon his shoulder…”
Upon his shoulder.
Something with weight.
Something he would feel while carrying it.
Something that would make forgetting inconvenient.
The Hebrew word translated “stone” is אֶבֶן — ʾeven.
And the command appears in a story saturated with another Hebrew idea:
זָכַר — zākar.
To remember.
Not merely to recall information.
Biblical remembrance is often active. It brings the past into the present so that what God has done shapes how His people live now.
And God knew Israel would need that.
Because the greatest danger after a miracle is sometimes not another river.
It is forgetting who brought you through the first one.
That may be where this story stops being ancient history and starts becoming painfully personal.
Because you have crossed some Jordans too.
There were nights you thought would destroy you.
There were prayers you whispered because you did not have enough strength to pray loudly.
There were seasons when you could not understand what God was doing.
There were doors that looked permanently closed.
There were losses you thought you would never survive.
There were moments when fear told you, “This is where your story ends.”
Yet somehow…
you are still here.
Maybe wounded.
Maybe rebuilding.
Maybe still carrying questions.
But here.
And the frightening thing about the human heart is that yesterday's miracle can become today's forgotten memory.
Israel knew this pattern.
God provided, and they complained.
God rescued, and they doubted.
God remained faithful, and they wandered.
Before we judge them too quickly, look at us.
How many prayers did we desperately beg God to answer that eventually became blessings we barely notice?
How many things surrounding us today were once things we prayed for?
How quickly can rescue become routine?
How quickly can grace become familiar?
How quickly can a person cry desperately for God in the river and then become spiritually sleepy once standing safely on the shore?
That is why the stones mattered.
Joshua 4:6–7 explains their purpose:
“That this may be a sign among you, that when your children ask their fathers in time to come, saying, What mean ye by these stones? Then ye shall answer them…”
Do not miss that.
God was not merely creating a monument.
He was creating a conversation.
The stones were supposed to make children ask questions.
“Dad…
why are those stones there?”
And suddenly a father would have to remember.
“We didn't put those there because we were strong.”
“We didn't put those there because we defeated the river.”
“We didn't put those there because we figured everything out.”
“Those stones are there because the Jordan stood between us and God's promise…
and God made a way.”
The Hebrew of Joshua 4:7 says the stones would become:
לְזִכָּרוֹן לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל עַד־עוֹלָם
ləzikkārôn livnê Yiśrāʾēl ʿad-ʿôlām
In context, this means they were to serve as a memorial for the children of Israel enduringly—generation after generation.
A memory with stones attached to it.
Because God did not want His faithfulness buried with the generation that experienced it.
He wanted children who had never stood inside the Jordan to know the God who stopped it.
That should confront every Christian parent.
Every grandfather.
Every grandmother.
Every believer.
Your testimony was never meant to die inside you.
Your children need more than your possessions.
They need to hear what God has done.
They need to know where Jesus found you.
They need to know what He forgave.
They need to know what He restored.
They need to know about the prayers nobody else heard.
They need to know there were moments when you almost surrendered to despair…
but grace kept calling your name.
Tell them.
Tell them about the Jordan.
Tell them about the stones.
But there is something even deeper happening in Joshua 3–4.
The miracle did not begin when Israel became brave enough to conquer the water.
God went before them.
The priests carrying the ark entered first.
Joshua 3:13 says the waters would be cut off when the feet of the priests bearing the ark rested in the Jordan.
The ark represented God's covenant presence among His people.
Israel crossed because God made passage possible.
That distinction matters.
Biblical salvation has always exposed the bankruptcy of human boasting.
We want to tell stories in which we saved ourselves.
“I became stronger.”
“I fixed my life.”
“I found my way.”
“I overcame.”
But the Gospel destroys that illusion.
You did not need a motivational speech.
You needed a Savior.
You did not merely need improvement.
You needed reconciliation with God.
Sin is not simply the collection of unfortunate mistakes we wish we had handled differently.
Sin is rebellion against the holy God who made us.
Scripture says:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.” — Romans 3:23
The Greek word commonly translated “sin” in that verse is ἥμαρτον — hēmarton, from ἁμαρτάνω (hamartanō).
We have sinned.
All of us.
The respectable.
The religious.
The addicted.
The successful.
The ashamed.
The person reading this with a Bible nearby.
The person reading this while hiding something nobody knows.
All.
That is the scandal.
We cannot carry enough stones, perform enough religious acts, give enough money, attend enough services, or clean ourselves up enough to erase our guilt before God.
But then comes grace.
Romans 3 continues by pointing us toward justification as God's gift through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
That changes everything.
Christianity is not the story of bad people becoming impressive.
It is the announcement that sinners can be forgiven and reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Jesus entered the place we could never escape ourselves.
He carried what we could never carry away.
Our guilt.
Our judgment.
Our shame.
At the cross, the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
And He did not remain in the grave.
Jesus Christ rose.
That is why grace is not positive thinking.
Grace has scars.
Grace has a cross.
Grace has an empty tomb.
Grace has a name.
Jesus.
And perhaps you have spent years carrying stones God never commanded you to carry.
The stone of what you did.
The stone of what they did to you.
The stone of the marriage that collapsed.
The stone of the addiction you keep hiding.
The stone of the secret browser history.
The stone of bitterness.
The stone of hypocrisy.
The stone of the child who walked away.
The stone of the prayer that seems unanswered.
The stone of your past.
You have carried it so long that you started thinking its weight was your identity.
But the twelve stones of Joshua were not monuments to Israel's shame.
They were witnesses to God's faithfulness.
The stone did not say:
“Look how powerful Israel was.”
The stone said:
“Look what God did.”
And that is what Jesus does with surrendered lives.
He does not pretend the past never happened.
He redeems people from it.
Peter's denial remained part of Peter's story.
But denial did not get the final sentence.
Paul's persecution of Christians remained part of Paul's history.
But persecution did not get the final sentence.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Yet when he turned to Christ, grace reached him even there.
This is why the Gospel is so devastatingly beautiful.
Jesus does not need your edited résumé.
He wants the truth.
The real truth.
The part you crop out before anybody sees it.
The part you bury beneath church language.
The part that still wakes you up sometimes.
Bring that to Christ.
Repentance is not pretending sin does not matter.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who died and rose again.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia — for repentance, carrying the idea of a changed mind and turning that results in a changed direction.
Grace does not say sin is harmless.
Grace says sin was so serious that Christ went to the cross—and God's love is so astonishing that Christ willingly came for sinners.
Maybe that is why you needed this article today.
Not because you needed another inspirational quote.
Because somewhere along the road, you forgot your stones.
You forgot the hospital room God carried you through.
You forgot the night you begged Jesus for mercy.
You forgot the addiction that once owned you.
You forgot the door God closed that later protected you.
You forgot the people He sent.
You forgot the prayers He answered differently than you expected.
You forgot that there was once a Jordan in front of you…
and somehow God brought you across.
Go back in your memory.
Not to worship the past.
To worship the God who was faithful there.
Because the God of the Jordan was preparing Israel for Jericho.
And sometimes remembering yesterday's faithfulness is how God strengthens His people to face tomorrow's walls.
There is another reason the twelve stones matter.
They represented everybody.
Twelve tribes.
One people.
One testimony.
Nobody could say, “That miracle belongs only to them.”
The memorial belonged to Israel.
And in Christ, something even greater happens.
People who would otherwise have little reason to belong together become one family around one Savior.
Different histories.
Different wounds.
Different languages.
Different nations.
Different failures.
One cross.
One risen Lord.
One Gospel.
That means your testimony may become someone else's stone.
When you say, “Jesus met me there,” somebody drowning in the place you survived realizes the river may not be the end.
When you say, “I had to repent too,” somebody ashamed of their failure realizes Christians are not people who never needed mercy.
When you say, “Christ is still healing me,” somebody who thought healing had to happen instantly realizes sanctification can be a journey of continued dependence on Jesus.
This is why you should not hide every scar.
Some scars become signposts.
Not every detail belongs publicly online, and wisdom still matters.
But never be ashamed of giving Christ glory for what He has redeemed.
Someone in your family may need your testimony.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be silently falling apart.
Someone who looks completely fine may be one night away from abandoning faith.
Someone may have stopped praying.
Someone may think Jesus would never receive someone like them.
And your willingness to share the Gospel may put a stone beside their Jordan.
Send it privately to the believer who has grown tired.
Send it to the person who does not believe yet.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor. It does not.
It cannot.
Christ's saving grace cannot be bought.
We support Gospel work because we have received grace, not because we are trying to purchase it.
But please hear this clearly.
Do not share because you think God will forgive you faster.
Do not buy something because you think generosity purchases salvation.
It does not.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Support should flow from gratitude, worship, stewardship, and a desire to help truth travel farther—not spiritual pressure.
And maybe the most important thing you can do right now costs absolutely nothing.
Be honest.
And if there is something hidden that needs to come into the light before Christ, you do not have to publicly describe your sin.
Let those words become your first small act of honesty.
Then take the deeper step where nobody online can do it for you.
Go to Jesus.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Ask Him for mercy.
If you already belong to Christ but have wandered, come home.
If your spirit has become cold, ask Him to awaken you.
If shame has kept you hiding, remember the promise of 1 John 1:9: God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse those who confess their sins.
And if you have never truly trusted Christ, understand what the twelve stones ultimately cannot do.
Stones can remind you of a miracle.
They cannot save you.
Religious memories cannot save you.
Christian parents cannot save you.
Church attendance cannot save you.
Only Jesus saves.
The Jordan eventually began flowing again.
The generation that crossed it eventually died.
Even the stones themselves belonged to a world that was passing away.
But Jesus Christ lives.
The One crucified for sinners rose from the dead.
The Gospel does not promise that Christians will never face another river.
It gives us something infinitely greater:
Christ Himself.
So perhaps tonight you need to build a memorial—not necessarily from literal stones, but from remembered grace.
Write down what God has done.
Tell your children.
Tell your spouse.
Call somebody.
Open your Bible.
Remember the prayers.
Remember the rescue.
Remember the correction.
Remember the mercy.
Remember the cross.
And when the enemy points toward everything behind you and whispers,
“Look what you were…”
look toward Jesus and remember what grace has done.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because testimony should have a voice.
Tell us what God brought you through.
Maybe somebody reading your comment is standing exactly where you once stood.
Perhaps that is the hidden beauty of Joshua's stones.
One generation carried them…
so another generation could ask about them.
One generation remembered…
so another could believe that the God who had been faithful before was still worthy of trust.
Your scars do not need to become your throne.
Your shame does not need to become your name.
Your worst chapter does not possess the authority to write your ending.
Jesus does.
And someday, someone may look at the evidence of grace in your life and ask:
“What does this mean?”
May you be able to answer:
“This is where I should have drowned.
This is where I thought everything was over.
This is where I discovered I could not save myself.
And this…
this is where God brought me through.”
Never be ashamed of the stones that remind you where the river should have swallowed you—because they may become the very place where somebody else learns to trust the God who brought you across.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Do Guardian Angels Really Exist? The Biblical Truth Is Stranger—and More Beautiful—Than the Stories We Were Told
paragraphs: Do Guardian Angels Really Exist? The Biblical Truth Is Stranger—and More Beautiful—Than the Stories We Were Told
What Scripture actually says about angels watching over God’s people—and why the greatest comfort in your darkest night is not the angel beside you, but the Savior who will never leave you.
Maybe you have wondered about it after surviving something you should not have survived.
The car missed you by seconds.
The diagnosis could have been worse.
Something woke you in the middle of the night and you still cannot explain why.
You walked away from an accident staring at the wreckage, wondering how you were still standing.
Or perhaps your story is painfully different.
Perhaps you prayed for protection...
and the tragedy happened anyway.
Someone died.
The marriage collapsed.
The child suffered.
The prayer seemed to disappear into a silent heaven.
And somewhere between the miracle stories people tell and the wounds nobody sees, you have wondered:
Do guardian angels actually exist?
Not the tiny winged babies painted on greeting cards.
Not sentimental folklore.
Not the mystical stories passed around social media until nobody remembers where they came from.
What does the Bible actually say?

The answer is more careful than some Christians expect, more supernatural than skeptics may expect, and ultimately far more beautiful than merely imagining an invisible bodyguard following you around.
Yes, angels are real.
Scripture leaves virtually no room for a Christian to dismiss them as metaphors.
But whether Scripture teaches that every individual human being is permanently assigned one specific personal “guardian angel” from birth to death is another question.
The Bible never plainly says that.
And that distinction matters.
Because biblical faith does not need exaggeration to become exciting.
Truth is already breathtaking.
The Hebrew word commonly translated “angel” is מַלְאָךְ — malʾākh, meaning a messenger. The corresponding Greek word is ἄγγελος — angelos, likewise meaning messenger.
That immediately corrects one of our assumptions.
“Angel” primarily describes what these beings do, not what popular culture has made them look like.
They are God's messengers.
God's servants.
Created spiritual beings operating beneath the absolute authority of the Creator.
And Scripture repeatedly describes God using angels in the lives of His people.
Psalm 91:11 declares:
כִּי מַלְאָכָיו יְצַוֶּה־לָּךְ
Ki mal'akhav yetzavveh-lakh...
“For he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways.”
Notice what the text does not say.
It does not tell you to command the angels.
It does not tell you to discover your angel's name.
It does not tell you to pray to your angel.
It points to God.
“He shall give His angels charge...”
The protection originates with God.
The command belongs to God.
The angels belong to God.
The glory belongs to God.
That distinction becomes even clearer in Hebrews.
The New Testament asks concerning angels:
οὐχὶ πάντες εἰσὶν λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα
Ouchi pantes eisin leitourgika pneumata...
“Are they not all ministering spirits, sent forth to minister for them who shall be heirs of salvation?” — Hebrews 1:14, KJV.
The expression λειτουργικὰ πνεύματα — leitourgika pneumata means, in context, ministering or serving spirits.
And then comes an extraordinary expression:
ἀποστελλόμενα εἰς διακονίαν
spirits “being sent” for service.
Sent.
That word matters.
Angels are not independent supernatural freelancers roaming heaven looking for humans to adopt.
They are sent.
There is a Sender.
Hebrews explicitly describes angels as ministering spirits sent to serve for the sake of those who will inherit salvation.
Think about that for a moment.
If you belong to Christ, there may have been moments in your life when God exercised providential care over you through angelic servants and you never knew it.
No flash of light.
No visible wings.
No supernatural announcement.
You simply kept walking.
That is entirely compatible with the biblical picture.
But then Jesus says something that has caused Christians to ask about guardian angels for centuries.
Speaking about the “little ones,” Jesus warns:
“Take heed that ye despise not one of these little ones; for I say unto you, That in heaven their angels do always behold the face of my Father which is in heaven.” — Matthew 18:10, KJV.
The Greek contains the striking expression:
οἱ ἄγγελοι αὐτῶν
hoi angeloi autōn
“their angels.”
That language should not be brushed aside.

Jesus clearly connects angels in heaven with these “little ones,” and those angels stand in privileged relation to the Father's presence. Matthew 18:10 therefore gives genuine biblical grounding for believing that angels have a special ministry concerning God's vulnerable people.
But we should also refuse to make Jesus say more than He said.
The verse does not explicitly establish a one-human-to-one-angel assignment system.
It does not explain whether one angel accompanies one person throughout life.
It does not tell us that everyone has exactly one.
It does not give instructions for communicating with them.
So can Christians believe in “guardian angels”?
If by guardian angels we mean angels whom God sends to watch over, assist, protect, or minister for His people according to His sovereign purposes, there is strong biblical support for that reality.
If we mean the dogmatic claim that Scripture guarantees every person one individually assigned angel who remains constantly beside that person for life, we should be more cautious.
Scripture gives us angels.
It gives us angelic ministry.
It gives us angelic protection.
It even gives us Jesus' remarkable phrase “their angels.”
But Scripture does not give us permission to construct an elaborate doctrine beyond what God actually revealed.
And perhaps that restraint protects us from something spiritually dangerous.
Because there is a moment when fascination with angels can quietly steal our eyes from Jesus.
That has happened before.
The early church had to confront improper fascination with spiritual beings. Paul warned the Colossians against the “worshipping of angels” in Colossians 2:18.
And Revelation gives us an unforgettable scene.
John falls before an angel.
The angel immediately refuses his worship.
“See thou do it not... worship God.” — Revelation 22:9.
That is the biblical posture.
If a true angel of God stood visibly in front of you tonight, he would not want to become the center of your Christianity.
He would point beyond himself.
Because angels are servants.
Jesus is Lord.
And this is where the guardian-angel question suddenly becomes something much deeper.
Perhaps what your heart has really been asking is not:
“Do I have an angel?”
Perhaps it is:
“Am I really being watched over?”
Does heaven know where I am?
Does God see what happened to me?
Was anyone there during the night nobody knew I cried?
Did heaven notice when I almost gave up?
Does God know how tired I have become?
And Scripture's answer is infinitely greater than merely saying, “There might be an angel nearby.”
Jesus said:
“Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father.”
Then He says:
“But the very hairs of your head are all numbered.”
And finally:
“Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows.” — Matthew 10:29–31.
You were never valuable because an angel might be watching you.
Angels may watch over you because God values you.
Do you see the difference?
The angel is not the source of your security.
God is.
And even angelic protection does not mean Christians will never suffer.
That needs to be said because shallow teaching can become cruel when tragedy arrives.
Stephen loved Christ.
Stephen was murdered.
James followed Christ.
James was killed.
Peter was imprisoned—and in Acts 12 an angel miraculously delivered him.
James was executed.
Peter was delivered.
Same God.
Same Gospel.
Different providence.
So biblical angelic protection cannot mean, “Nothing painful will ever happen to believers.”

Psalm 91 itself must never be turned into a magical contract promising immunity from every accident, disease, persecution, or death. Satan himself quoted Psalm 91 during the temptation of Jesus, attempting to manipulate its promise of angelic protection into a demand that Jesus test God.
Jesus refused.
Faith trusts God.
Presumption tries to control Him.
And some of you reading this know exactly why that distinction hurts.
You prayed.
You believed.
And God did not stop the thing you begged Him to stop.
So somebody telling you, “Your guardian angel will never let anything happen to you,” does not comfort you.
It confuses you.
Because something already happened.
Something terrible.
Something you still carry.
Here is the truth Christianity offers instead:
God never promised that His people would escape every valley.
He promised something greater.
We would never enter one without Him.
The Christian's ultimate hope is not that angels prevent death.
It is that Jesus defeated death.
Our deepest protection is not immunity from suffering.
It is belonging to a Savior from whom suffering, demons, angels, rulers, powers, life, and even death itself cannot separate us.
Romans 8 reaches its climax with that staggering assurance.
Nothing in creation can separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
Not even angels.
And suddenly the question changes.
You started reading wondering whether there might be an angel watching over you.
But the Gospel confronts you with something infinitely more important:
Do you belong to Jesus Christ?
Because you can become fascinated with angels and still remain separated from God.
You can collect stories about miracles while refusing repentance.
You can believe supernatural beings exist while keeping Christ outside the locked rooms of your heart.
You can talk about “protection” while the greatest danger facing the human soul is not an accident on the highway.
It is sin.
That is the scandal.
We have all sinned.
We have hidden things.
Wanted things.
Done things.
Repeated things.
Defended things God called evil.
Some sins were visible.
Others lived behind respectable smiles, church attendance, successful careers, carefully filtered photographs, and Sunday worship songs.
Angels cannot erase that guilt.
An angel did not die for you.
Gabriel did not carry your cross.
Michael did not shed his blood for your sins.
Jesus did.
The eternal Son of God entered our broken world.
He took flesh.
He walked among sinners.
He touched the rejected.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He welcomed the repentant.
He carried the cross.
And at Calvary, the One through whom the angels were created allowed sinful men to nail Him to wood.
Think about the reversal.
The King of heaven...
bleeding.
The Lord whom angels serve...
mocked by men.
The Holy One...
treated like a criminal.
The innocent Christ...
bearing the judgment deserved by the guilty.
Why?
Because your greatest need was never an angel to keep you from temporary danger.
Your greatest need was a Savior who could rescue you from eternal separation from God.
And Jesus did what no angel could ever do.
He took our scandal...
and opened the door to grace.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now forgiveness is offered not to people who successfully hide their mess, but to sinners who come to Him in repentance and faith.
That is why the Gospel is not “become good enough and perhaps God will accept you.”
The Gospel is that Christ has accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves, and those who turn to Him receive mercy they could never earn.
Maybe your scandal has a name.
Addiction.
Adultery.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Greed.
Secret messages.
A double life.
Religious hypocrisy.
Years wasted running from God.
Or perhaps your scandal is quieter.
Nobody knows.
Nobody suspects.
You have become remarkably skilled at appearing okay.
But tonight you know.
God knows too.
And strangely, that is not the worst news.
Because the God who completely knows you is the God who still calls sinners to come home through Jesus Christ.
You do not need an angel to carry your confession to God.
Scripture says there is “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” — 1 Timothy 2:5.
One Mediator.
Jesus.
Come directly to Him.
Repent.
Stop negotiating with the sin that is destroying you.
Stop calling chains “freedom.”
Stop postponing surrender because you think tomorrow belongs to you.
Bring the hidden thing into the light before God.
Christ's invitation is not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace forgives...
and grace transforms.
Maybe heaven has protected you in ways you will never discover in this life.
Maybe one day, in God's presence, you will understand providences that currently make no sense.
Maybe you will discover how many dangers you never even knew existed.
But do not become so fascinated by an unseen angel that you miss the Savior Scripture has plainly revealed.
You do not need to know your angel's name.
You need to know the name of Jesus.

And if grace has already carried you through places you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what Jesus has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Christ's grace cannot be bought.

But if you genuinely want your life, resources, influence, and online presence to glorify God, one practical way to serve the spread of biblical truth is to support Gospel-centered work you believe is faithful.
but in Christ.
There may come a night when fear returns and you need these Scriptures again.
And please remember this distinction because it matters:
You do not glorify God by paying for grace. Grace is free in Christ.

You glorify God when, because grace has captured you, your time, testimony, resources, influence, generosity, sharing, and service increasingly become instruments through which others encounter the truth.
So share what points people to Christ.
Support what faithfully proclaims Christ.
But worship Christ alone.
Perhaps angels have stood nearer to some moments of your life than you will ever know.
Perhaps heaven intervened when you thought you were simply “lucky.”
Perhaps there are stories God will explain only in eternity.
But there is one rescue you do not have to speculate about.
Two thousand years ago, outside Jerusalem, Jesus Christ went willingly to a cross for sinners.
And the empty tomb announced that death did not get the final word.
So yes...
Angels exist.
God sends them.
Scripture says they minister.
Scripture gives us real reasons to believe God uses angels in His providential care for His people.
But never let your fascination with the servants eclipse your worship of the King.
When darkness comes, you do not have to whisper into the darkness hoping your angel hears you.
Call upon the Lord.
When guilt crushes you, do not search for a supernatural intermediary.
Run to Jesus.
When your past screams your name, remember the cross.
When shame says your story is finished, remember the empty tomb.
When you cannot understand why God allowed the valley, remember that the Shepherd entered suffering Himself and conquered the grave.
And when you wonder whether heaven has forgotten you...
look again at Calvary.

Because the greatest evidence that heaven has not forgotten you is not an angel you might never see—it is a Savior who allowed Himself to be seen bleeding for sinners, then walked out of His grave alive.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Your shame does not have to write the ending.
Your sin does not have to own your name.
Because when Jesus enters a surrendered story, the grave itself loses the authority to write the final sentence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU KEEP ASKING GOD TO BREAK THE CHAINS—BUT ROMANS 6 SAYS SOMETHING SHOCKING ALREADY HAPPENED
paragraphs: YOU KEEP ASKING GOD TO BREAK THE CHAINS—BUT ROMANS 6 SAYS SOMETHING SHOCKING ALREADY HAPPENED
What Romans 6 Really Teaches About Freedom From Sin—and Why Grace Was Never Permission to Stay in the Prison Jesus Died to Open
There is a terrifying kind of prison where the door is already open...
but the prisoner keeps sleeping inside.
Not because the chains are still locked.
Not because the jailer still owns him.
Not because freedom was never purchased.
But because after living in bondage for so long, the cell has started to feel like home.
Maybe that is why Romans 6 can feel so uncomfortable.
