Three moments of divine mercy filtered through the same desperate question:
Will he love me now?
That is what makes Leah painfully relatable.
You can receive blessings from God while still trying to use those blessings to fill a wound they were never meant to fill.
You can have children and still feel empty.
You can have a relationship and still feel unwanted.
You can have money and still feel insignificant.
You can have thousands of followers and still obsess over the one person who refuses to notice you.
You can even serve God while secretly hoping your usefulness will prove your worth.
Then another child comes.
Judah.
And something changes.
Genesis 29:35 says:
“And she conceived again, and bare a son: and she said, Now will I praise the LORD: therefore she called his name Judah.”
In Hebrew, Leah’s declaration is:
הַפַּעַם אוֹדֶה אֶת־יְהוָה
ha-pa'am odeh et-YHWH
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
The verb אוֹדֶה — odeh comes from the Hebrew root ידה — y-d-h, associated with giving thanks, confessing, acknowledging, or praising.
And Judah’s Hebrew name, יְהוּדָה — Yehudah, is intentionally connected to that declaration of praise.
Something enormous has happened.
Look at what Leah does not say.
She does not say:
“Now Jacob will love me.”
She does not say:
“Now my husband will become attached to me.”
She does not say:
“Now Rachel will finally envy me enough.”
She does not say:
“Now everybody will understand my value.”
For the first time in the naming sequence, Jacob disappears from Leah’s recorded explanation.
And Yahweh fills the sentence.
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
That is the breakthrough.
Not that Jacob finally became everything Leah wanted.
Scripture never gives us that romantic ending.
The breakthrough was that, for one breathtaking moment, Leah’s worship was no longer being narrated around Jacob’s approval.
Her eyes moved higher.
Her heart turned Godward.
Her language changed.
The woman who kept saying, in effect, “Maybe now he will love me,” finally said:
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
Please understand what this does not mean.
It does not mean rejection stops hurting when you worship.
It does not mean Christians should pretend emotional wounds do not exist.
It does not mean mistreatment becomes acceptable.
And it does not mean Leah never struggled again. Genesis continues to portray a complicated, wounded household marked by rivalry and longing.
Biblical transformation is often messier than the inspirational version we wish Scripture gave us.
But Genesis 29:35 gives us a genuine turning point.
Leah praised God without making Jacob’s affection the conclusion of the sentence.
And then comes one of the most astonishing reversals in Scripture.
She named that boy Judah.
Judah.
The son born when a rejected woman said, “I will praise the LORD.”
Generations passed.
Kings came through Judah.
David came through Judah.
And eventually...
Jesus Christ came according to the flesh through this line.
Matthew’s genealogy traces Jesus through Judah.
Hebrews calls Christ:
“the Lion of the tribe of Juda.” — Revelation 5:5
Think about the scandal of grace.
Leah thought the great question of her life was whether Jacob would choose her.
God was writing something infinitely larger.
She was staring at one man’s affection.
God was moving redemptive history toward the Messiah.
She wanted Jacob.
God would bring Jesus through Judah’s line.
She wanted to be chosen.
God incorporated this rejected woman into the human ancestry through which the promised Christ entered the world.
That does not make Leah’s suffering good.
It reveals that suffering does not have the authority to stop God’s redemptive purposes.
This is where Leah’s story stops being merely Leah’s story.
Because some of us are still standing emotionally beside Reuben.
“Maybe now they’ll love me.”
Some are beside Simeon.
“Maybe now they’ll hear me.”
Some are beside Levi.
“Maybe now they’ll stay.”
And God is calling us toward Judah.
Not toward denial.
Not toward pretending we never wanted human love.
But toward a deeper freedom:
Even if another person refuses to become the source of my identity, I can still praise the LORD.
That freedom becomes even clearer in Jesus Christ.
Because the Gospel does not tell you that you become valuable after enough people choose you.
The Gospel tells you about the Son of God who came for sinners.
Jesus was rejected.
Isaiah prophetically describes the suffering Servant as:
“despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.” — Isaiah 53:3
John writes:
And at the cross, Christ bore sin and shame, giving Himself for people who could never earn salvation.
This is where Christianity becomes radically different from the exhausting religion of proving yourself.
You do not clean yourself up enough to force God to love you.
You do not manufacture enough spiritual Reubens, Simeons, and Levis until heaven finally says, “Fine. You have proven yourself.”
Salvation is grace.
Paul writes:
While we were sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we became religious enough.
Not after we collected enough good works.
Christ died for sinners.
And He rose again.
The answer to the deepest wound of rejection is therefore not merely positive thinking.
It is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
Because another human being was never designed to carry the weight of being your god.
Jacob could not save Leah.
Rachel could not complete Jacob.
Marriage cannot save you.
Popularity cannot save you.
Success cannot save you.
Money cannot save you.
A ministry cannot save you.
A relationship cannot save you.
Even the affection you desperately want cannot cleanse your conscience, forgive your sins, defeat death, reconcile you to God, or give you eternal life.
Jesus can.
Maybe that is why this story hurts so much.
We recognize ourselves in Leah.
We have been naming our lives after people who will never have the power to heal them.
Maybe your “Jacob” is not a person.
Maybe it is applause.
Recognition.
Money.
Marriage.
Beauty.
Achievement.
A platform.
A title.
A parent whose approval you have chased for thirty years.
Someone who left.
Someone who betrayed you.
Someone who never apologized.
Someone you keep checking online even though every visit reopens the wound.
You keep whispering:
“Maybe now.”
Maybe now they will notice.
Maybe now they will regret losing me.
Maybe now they will see what I became.
Maybe now I will finally be enough.
But freedom may begin with a different sentence.
הַפַּעַם אוֹדֶה אֶת־יְהוָה
This time I will praise the LORD.
Not because everything turned out the way you wanted.
Not because rejection suddenly stopped hurting.
Not because Jacob finally became your reward.
But because God is God even when Jacob does not choose you.
Because Christ is enough even when somebody walks away.
Because your sin can be forgiven.
Because grace is available.
Because the tomb is empty.
Because your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Because Jesus still saves sinners.
This is the heartbeat of From Scandal to Grace.
The Bible is filled with people whose stories would never survive our polished religious image management.
Deception.
Jealousy.
Sexual sin.
Family dysfunction.
Betrayal.
Murder.
Failure.
Rejection.
Shame.
And yet the Gospel does not pretend the scandal never happened.
Grace enters the scandal.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by calling evil good.
He rewrites everything by redeeming sinners, forgiving the repentant, transforming lives, and accomplishing purposes human brokenness cannot overthrow.
Maybe your breakthrough is not getting the person you have been begging God to give you.
Maybe it is finally realizing that person was never supposed to sit on the throne of your heart.
Maybe your breakthrough is not hearing them say, “I choose you.”
Maybe it is finally hearing the Gospel clearly enough to surrender your identity to Christ.
Maybe your breakthrough is not revenge.
Maybe it is repentance.
Maybe it is forgiveness.
Maybe it is freedom.
Maybe it is finally admitting:

“Jesus, I have made another person’s approval too important. I have chased validation harder than I have chased You. I have tried to make human love answer questions only Your Gospel can answer. Forgive me. Take the throne again.”
If that exposed something hidden in you, do not perform spirituality here.
Be honest.

There are believers reading beside you who know what it means to cry over someone who never chose them. Your honesty may become the doorway through which another wounded person finally realizes they are not fighting alone.
And please do not keep this article trapped on this page.
Not as a superstition. Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
“Maybe now they will love me.”
Send this to the person recovering from heartbreak.
Share it with the spouse who feels invisible.
Share it with the believer who has forgotten who sits on the throne.
If this truth helped you, save it too. There are days when old wounds become loud again, and you may need to return to four words:
I will praise the LORD.
But keep the order right.
We do not give to purchase His blessing.
We do not share articles to prove that we glorify God.
Christ alone saves.
We support Gospel ministry because grace has already moved our hearts toward generosity, discipleship, and the desire to help biblical truth reach other people.
If you are ready to support the mission and go deeper:
Maybe God will use your share to interrupt their despair with the Gospel.
Maybe they need to discover what Leah began discovering thousands of years ago.
Your Jacob was never your Savior.
Your rejection is not your identity.
Your wound is not your name.
And the person who refused to choose you does not get to write the final sentence of your life.
Jesus does.
So when your heart whispers again...
“Maybe now they will love me...”
remember Leah.
Remember Judah.
Remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
And answer the wound:
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
Because sometimes the greatest breakthrough is not finally getting what you spent years begging for—it is discovering that Jesus was greater than the thing you thought you could never live without.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE HIDDEN REASON ELIJAH CHOSE ELISHA
paragraphs: THE HIDDEN REASON ELIJAH CHOSE ELISHA
He Wasn’t Looking for a Celebrity, a Warrior, or a Man Chasing a Platform—He Found Someone Working a Field, and What Happened Next Reveals the Kind of Heart God Can Entrust With a Mantle
There is something almost unsettling about the way Elijah found Elisha.
No sanctuary.
No theological academy.
No crowd waiting for the announcement of Israel’s next great prophet.
No young man standing on a mountain begging God for influence.
There was dirt.
Oxen.
Sweat.
A field.
And a man working behind a plow.
That detail is easy to read past.
But maybe we shouldn’t.
Because immediately before this moment, Elijah himself had been shattered.

He had stood on Mount Carmel and watched fire fall from heaven. He had confronted the prophets of Baal. He had witnessed one of the most dramatic demonstrations of God’s power recorded in the Old Testament.
Then Jezebel threatened his life.
And the prophet who had just stood before a nation ran.
He went into the wilderness, sat beneath a broom tree, and asked to die.
“Enough.”
That was essentially Elijah’s cry.
He was exhausted.
Afraid.
Disappointed.
And painfully human.
Some people know that place.
You can love God and still become exhausted.
You can remember what God did yesterday and still struggle to understand what He is doing today.
You can survive the mountain and nearly collapse in the wilderness afterward.
Elijah discovered something there that generations of believers would need to remember: God does not abandon His servants when their strength disappears.
The Lord fed him.
Let him rest.
Spoke to him.
Corrected his distorted sense of isolation.
And then gave him another assignment.
Among God’s instructions was this:
“…Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abel-meholah shalt thou anoint to be prophet in thy room.”
—1 Kings 19:16, KJV
That changes the question.
Strictly speaking, Elijah did not independently “choose” Elisha as though he interviewed several candidates and decided Elisha was the best applicant.
God chose Elisha.
Elijah was commanded to call him.
That distinction matters.
The hidden reason Elijah chose Elisha begins with the fact that Elijah was obeying a choice God had already made.
And that should humble every person who has ever wanted to be “chosen” by God.
Elisha did not campaign for the mantle.
God knew his name while he was still behind the plow.
Read that again.
God knew his name before the public knew his name.
There are people reading this who feel invisible because nobody seems to recognize what is inside them.
You are serving quietly.
Working.
Raising children.
Cleaning.
Building.
Driving.
Studying.
Praying when nobody hears.
Fighting temptations nobody knows about.
Trying to remain faithful while other people appear to be moving faster than you.
And somewhere inside you is the fear that obscurity means God has forgotten you.
Elisha’s field says otherwise.
When Elijah arrived, Scripture says:
“So he departed thence, and found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he with the twelfth…”
—1 Kings 19:19, KJV
The Hebrew describes Elisha as חֹרֵשׁ — ḥōrēš — “plowing.”
Not waiting.
Not performing.
Plowing.
He was already doing something with what was in his hands.
And then Elijah did something extraordinary.
“…and Elijah passed by him, and cast his mantle upon him.”
The Hebrew word used for Elijah’s mantle is אַדֶּרֶת — ’adderet.
It can refer to a mantle, cloak, or garment of distinction. In Elijah’s story, that garment becomes inseparably associated with his prophetic ministry.
Elijah throws it over Elisha.
Imagine that moment.
The oxen are still there.
The field is still there.
The dirt beneath Elisha’s feet has not changed.
But suddenly the ordinary afternoon is carrying the weight of eternity.
One moment he is plowing his father’s field.
The next moment the prophet of God has walked past him and placed the mantle over his shoulders.
Sometimes God interrupts ordinary life without warning.
Moses had sheep.
Gideon was threshing wheat.
David was tending sheep.
Peter and Andrew had fishing nets.
Matthew had a tax booth.
Elisha had a plow.
God has never needed a glamorous location to begin a holy calling.
But here is where Elisha’s response becomes impossible to ignore.
“And he left the oxen, and ran after Elijah…”
He ran.
There is urgency in that sentence.
Yet Elisha first asks permission to kiss his father and mother goodbye.
Then comes the moment that exposes how seriously he understood what had happened.
Scripture says:
“And he returned back from him, and took a yoke of oxen, and slew them, and boiled their flesh with the instruments of the oxen…”
—1 Kings 19:21, KJV
Do you see it?
Elisha did not merely leave the plow.
He destroyed his easy road back to it.
The animals that had powered his former occupation became the sacrifice.
The wooden equipment associated with that former life became fuel.
Then he gave the food to the people.
They ate.
And Elisha arose and followed Elijah.
The Hebrew conclusion is striking:
וַיָּקָם וַיֵּלֶךְ אַחֲרֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ וַיְשָׁרְתֵהוּ
Vayyāqām vayyelekh ’aḥărê ’Ēliyyāhû wayšārĕtēhû.
In context:
“He arose, and went after Elijah, and ministered unto him.”
That last word matters.
וַיְשָׁרְתֵהוּ — wayšārĕtēhû.
He served him.
Before Elisha became famous for miracles, he became known for service.
Before the Jordan divided for him, he served.
Before poisoned food was purified, he served.
Before Naaman was healed, he served.
Before kings sought his prophetic counsel, he served.
Before anybody spoke about Elisha’s mantle, Elisha learned what it meant to minister.
And years later, when people identified him, they remembered something surprisingly ordinary about him.
In 2 Kings 3:11, Elisha is described as the one “which poured water on the hands of Elijah.”
Think about that.
The man who would eventually carry an extraordinary prophetic ministry was remembered as the man who poured water over another man’s hands.
That is devastating to our modern obsession with visibility.
We want mantles.
God teaches service.
We want platforms.
God forms character.
We want people to recognize the anointing.
God watches what we do when recognition never comes.
We want the double portion.
But sometimes we do not want the years of pouring water.
And maybe that is one of the deepest lessons hidden inside Elijah and Elisha.
God had already designated Elisha, but the narrative also reveals the character of the man God called.
He was working when the call arrived.
He responded decisively.
He honored his family.
He surrendered his former security.
He followed.
And then he served.
The mantle was not permission for Elisha to become important.
It was an invitation to become surrendered.
That distinction can expose us.
Because some of us want Jesus to improve the life we have already designed.
We want Him to bless the plow.
Protect the oxen.
Increase the field.
Make us successful.
Give us influence.
Remove the pain.
Open doors.
Fix relationships.
And occasionally Jesus comes near enough to confront the deeper question:
What if following Me costs you the version of yourself you were determined to preserve?
Elisha’s story points toward something even greater than Elijah’s mantle.
It points toward the radical nature of discipleship that reaches its fullness in Jesus Christ.
Centuries later, Jesus would walk up to ordinary people and say:
“Follow me.”
Fishermen would leave nets.
Matthew would rise from his tax booth.
People would discover that encountering Christ creates a decision no comfortable middle ground can permanently contain.
Jesus said:
“If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me.”
—Matthew 16:24, KJV
The Greek behind “deny himself” is:
ἀπαρνησάσθω ἑαυτόν
aparnēsasthō heauton.
The idea is far stronger than simply giving up a few conveniences.
It is self-denial—a refusal to allow the old self to remain the supreme authority.
Then comes:
ἀράτω τὸν σταυρὸν αὐτοῦ
aratō ton stauron autou
“let him take up his cross.”
And then:
ἀκολουθείτω μοι
akoloutheitō moi
“let him follow Me.”
Christianity is not Jesus becoming an accessory to our ambitions.
It is Christ becoming Lord.
And this is where Elisha’s burned plow begins to feel uncomfortable.
Because everybody has a plow.
Maybe yours is not made of wood.
Maybe it is the relationship you know keeps pulling you away from God.
Maybe it is secret pornography.
Maybe resentment has become so familiar that you cannot imagine yourself without it.
Maybe your plow is pride.
Money.
Approval.
An addiction.
A hidden conversation.
A private compromise.
A reputation you have spent years protecting.
Maybe you want Jesus desperately…
but you also keep one hand wrapped around the handle of the life He is calling you to surrender.
You pray.
You worship.
You quote Scripture.
You tell people God is good.
But somewhere behind your spiritual language is an ox you refuse to sacrifice.
And you know exactly what it is.
That is why this story hurts.
Elisha did not burn the plow because wood was sinful.
He did not slaughter the oxen because farming was evil.
His former occupation was legitimate.
The point is not that every believer must literally abandon employment, possessions, family responsibilities, or ordinary work.
The point is surrender.
Elisha’s actions made his response tangible.
He was going with Elijah.
No pretending.
No sentimental farewell followed by a secret return.
He stepped into the call.
And perhaps someone reading this has spent years trying to follow Jesus while repeatedly rebuilding the same plow.
You surrender Sunday.
Rebuild Monday.
Repent after midnight.
Return by Thursday.
Delete it.
Download it again.
Walk away.
Text them again.
Confess it.
Hide it again.
Promise God.
Break the promise.
Cry.
Repeat.
And eventually shame begins whispering:
“God must be finished with you.”
But this is where the Gospel becomes infinitely greater than the story of human determination.
Because your salvation does not depend upon how spectacularly you can burn your plow.
Your salvation depends upon Jesus Christ.
Elisha sacrificed oxen.
Jesus gave Himself.
Elisha followed a prophet.
We are called to follow the Son of God.
And at the cross, Christ did what no prophet, priest, king, sacrifice, resolution, religious performance, or human act of repentance could accomplish.
He bore sin.
“He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities…”
—Isaiah 53:5, KJV
The scandal of the Gospel is that guilty people can be forgiven.
Adulterers.
Liars.
Addicts.
Hypocrites.
The proud.
The sexually broken.
The religious pretender.
The bitter.
The greedy.
The person who promised God a hundred times and failed a hundred and one.
Not because sin does not matter.
The cross proves exactly how seriously sin matters.
But the cross also proves how astonishing grace is.
Jesus did not come merely to polish respectable sinners.
He came to save the lost.
He came to call sinners to repentance.
He came to forgive.
Redeem.
Restore.
Transform.
This is scandalous grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not permission to remain unchanged.
Grace that meets you in the field…
calls you away from the old master…
and begins rewriting everything.
That is our heartbeat:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe the most important question is no longer, “Why did Elijah choose Elisha?”
Maybe it is:
What did God see happening in that field that He wants happening inside you?
Availability.
Surrender.
Faithfulness.
Service.
A willingness to follow when following becomes expensive.
And above all, a life that ultimately points beyond Elijah and Elisha to Jesus Christ.
Elisha eventually witnessed Elijah being taken away.
Then came another unforgettable scene.
Elijah’s mantle fell.
Elisha picked it up.
He returned to the Jordan and cried:
“Where is the LORD God of Elijah?”
—2 Kings 2:14, KJV
Then he struck the waters.
They divided.
And Elisha crossed.
But understand this carefully.
The power was never inside a magical piece of fabric.
The God of Elijah was still God.
Elijah could leave.
The mantle could change shoulders.
Generations could rise and disappear.
But God remained.
And perhaps that is what somebody desperately needs tonight.
People leave.
Mentors die.
Parents grow old.
Churches disappoint.
Friends disappear.
Relationships collapse.
Bodies weaken.
Careers end.
Platforms vanish.
Everything you thought would remain can eventually fall from your hands.
But Jesus Christ remains.
“Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.”
—Hebrews 13:8, KJV
So stop building your identity around the temporary.
The field will change.
The oxen will disappear.
The applause will stop.
Your name will eventually become a memory on earth.
But Christ remains.
And if you belong to Him, your deepest story is not the scandal behind you.
It is the grace that found you.
Maybe your past is ugly.
Maybe you have chapters you would burn if you could.
Maybe there are things you hope nobody discovers.
Maybe you are reading this while privately fighting something that would shock people who think they know you.
Jesus already knows.
And still the Gospel calls you.
Not into hiding.
Into repentance.
Not into pretending.
Into grace.
Not into religious performance.
Into reconciliation with God through Christ.
So be honest.
What plow keeps calling you back?
What are you afraid to surrender?
What secret compromise keeps surviving every emotional promise you make to God?
Pray.
Confess.
Repent.
Bring darkness into the light.
Ask a mature believer to walk with you if necessary.
Return to Scripture.
Return to prayer.
Return to Christ.
If you need believers to pray for you, simply write:

And if Christ has already begun rewriting chapters you thought could never be redeemed, tell somebody what He has done. Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to keep another wounded believer from giving up.
Send it to the believer who feels forgotten.
Send it to the person who walked away.
Send it even to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is only about respectable people pretending they have never been broken.
Those cannot be bought. Salvation is the gift of God through Jesus Christ.
But generosity can become an act of stewardship when it flows from a willing heart.

Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, sharing the Gospel, encouraging struggling believers, reaching seekers, and building resources designed to lead people deeper into Scripture and closer to Christ.
Follow Jesus.
No share can replace surrender.
No comment can replace confession.
No Christian merchandise can replace the cross.
And no ministry deserves the place that belongs to Christ alone.
Support Gospel work because you love Him, if you are able.
Share truth because someone needs it.
Give because your heart is willing.
But worship Jesus because He alone is worthy.
Elisha left a field behind.
One day you will leave everything behind.
The question is not whether your hands will eventually release this world.
They will.
The question is whether your heart has surrendered to Christ before that day comes.

Maybe God brought you this far into these words because beneath all the noise, all the scrolling, all the religious language, and all the excuses, there is still one handle your fingers have refused to release.
You already know its name.
And perhaps tonight is the night you finally stop asking God to bless the plow…
and start following Jesus without it.
The field remembers who you were.
Grace is calling you toward who Christ is making you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Understanding “Endure to the End” — The Words of Jesus That Were Never Meant to Make You Save Yourself
paragraphs: Understanding “Endure to the End” — The Words of Jesus That Were Never Meant to Make You Save Yourself

What Jesus really meant when He said, “The one who endures to the end will be saved”—and why these words are not a command to earn salvation, but a terrifyingly beautiful call to keep clinging to Christ when everything around you is trying to make your love grow cold.
There is a kind of tiredness nobody sees.
You still go to church.
You still know when to say “Amen.”
You still share the verse.
You still tell people, “God is good.”
But somewhere underneath the Christian vocabulary, the worship songs, the smiling profile picture, and the carefully composed answer when someone asks how you are doing...
you are tired.
Not sleepy.
Soul tired.
Tired of fighting the same temptation.
Tired of praying about something that has not changed.
Tired of watching people who once seemed on fire for Jesus slowly disappear from Him.
Tired of hypocrisy.
Tired of disappointment.
Maybe even tired of yourself.
And somewhere in that exhaustion, you remember something Jesus said:
“But the one who endures to the end will be saved.”
Matthew 24:13.
And instead of comforting you, the verse frightens you.
What if I don't endure?
What if I fail again?
What if my faith becomes weak?
What if I am not strong enough?
Does Jesus mean I have to survive every spiritual battle perfectly before He will finally save me?
Those questions deserve more than a motivational quote.
They deserve Scripture.
Because Jesus did not speak Matthew 24:13 as an isolated slogan.
Before we interpret what He meant, listen to what He actually said in Greek:
ὁ δὲ ὑπομείνας εἰς τέλος οὗτος σωθήσεται.
ho de hypomeinas eis telos, houtos sōthēsetai.
A straightforward translation is:
“But the one who has endured to the end, this one will be saved.”
The key word is ὑπομείνας — hypomeinas, from ὑπομένω — hypomenō.
It carries the sense of remaining, staying, persevering, bearing up under pressure.
This is not the vocabulary of somebody casually agreeing with Christianity.
It is the language of someone who stays when staying becomes costly.
And that matters because the sentence immediately before Matthew 24:13 is devastating.
Jesus says that because lawlessness increases, “the love of many will grow cold.”
That is the danger.
Not merely pain.
Coldness.

Jesus describes persecution, betrayal, hatred, deception, false prophets, increasing lawlessness, and people falling away. Then, standing in the middle of that collapsing landscape, He speaks of the person who endures.
Suddenly Matthew 24:13 sounds different.
Jesus is not describing someone purchasing salvation by accumulating enough suffering points.
He is describing persevering allegiance to Himself in a world relentlessly pressuring His followers to abandon Him.
That distinction matters.
Christianity is not:
Jesus did most of the saving, and now you must endure well enough to finish His unfinished work.
The Gospel is infinitely better.
Jesus saves.
Jesus redeems.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus reconciles sinners to God.
And the faith that truly belongs to Christ is called to continue trusting Christ.
Endurance does not make the cross sufficient.
The cross makes endurance possible.
Think about Peter.
On the night Jesus was arrested, Peter looked like anything but an enduring saint.
He had promised loyalty.
Then pressure arrived.
A servant girl recognized him.
Fear entered the room.
And the man who had said he would die with Jesus began denying that he even knew Him.
Once.
Twice.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Imagine Peter's face.
Imagine the shame.
The man who had walked on water with Jesus was now drowning in his own cowardice.
If “endure to the end” meant “never stumble, never collapse, never fail terribly,” Peter's story would have ended beside that charcoal fire.
But it didn't.
Because failure is not always the end of the story when Jesus is writing it.
Peter wept.
Peter was broken.
And after the resurrection, Jesus came looking for him.
That is grace.
Not grace that pretends denial did not matter.
Grace that confronts, restores, recommissions, and transforms.
The Gospel does not say your sin is small.
It says your Savior is greater.
And somebody reading this needs that distinction desperately.
Maybe you have fallen.
Maybe badly.
Maybe there are things in your browser history you hope nobody discovers.
Maybe bitterness has been eating you alive.
Maybe you secretly resent God because the prayer you begged Him to answer seemed to disappear into silence.
Maybe you promised Him, “Never again,” and then did it again.
Maybe everyone around you thinks you are spiritually strong, while privately you are wondering whether you have anything left.
Listen carefully.
Endurance is not pretending you never bleed.
It is continuing to return to Christ because you know there is nowhere else salvation can be found.
It is Peter saying elsewhere, when many abandoned Jesus:
“Lord, to whom shall we go?”
That is the heartbeat of endurance.
Not:
“Look how strong I am.”
But:
“Jesus, where else could I go?”
There is a profound difference between stumbling while following Christ and deciding you no longer want Christ.
A wounded disciple may limp.
A frightened disciple may cry.
A confused disciple may wrestle.
A convicted disciple may fall on his face again and again in repentance.
Endurance does not require emotional invincibility.
It requires that our hope remain ultimately anchored in the One who saves.
This is why another New Testament passage uses the related noun ὑπομονή — hypomonē, “endurance” or “perseverance.”
Hebrews 10:36 says:
ὑπομονῆς γὰρ ἔχετε χρείαν
“For you have need of endurance...”
Why?
So that, having done God's will, they might receive what was promised.
The original readers of Hebrews were not being coached toward comfortable Christianity.
They were being warned not to throw away their confidence.
They needed endurance.
So do we.
Because sometimes the greatest threat to your faith is not somebody putting a weapon against your head and demanding that you deny Jesus.
Sometimes it is much quieter.
Disappointment.
Comfort.
Pornography.
Success.
Bitterness.
Busyness.
Secret compromise.
A prayer that seemed unanswered.
A church wound you never processed.
A relationship that slowly became more important than obedience.
A career that consumed everything.
A private sin that stopped making you feel guilty.
A thousand tiny compromises whispering:
You don't really need Jesus that much anymore.
That may be one of the most frightening ways love grows cold.
Not dramatically.
Gradually.
Nobody wakes up one morning planning to become spiritually cold.
Usually there is no funeral for the fire.
It simply gets fed less.
Prayer becomes occasional.
Scripture becomes optional.
Repentance becomes embarrassing.
Sin becomes manageable.
Conviction becomes annoying.
Jesus becomes familiar.
And eventually the Savior who once brought tears to your eyes becomes merely part of your religious vocabulary.
That is why Christ's warning is mercy.
He loves us enough to wake us up.
“But the one who endures to the end will be saved.”
Jesus is telling His disciples that following Him is not merely an emotional beginning.
There is an end.
There is a finish line.
There is a Kingdom.
There is resurrection.
There is judgment.
There is eternity.
And there is a Savior worth holding onto through every mile between here and there.
But we must be careful.
A verse about endurance can easily be twisted into spiritual pride.
Someone reads it and thinks:
Fine. I will become strong enough.
No.
That is not Christianity either.
Your confidence is not ultimately that your grip on Jesus is impressive.
Your confidence is Jesus.
The same Christ who commands perseverance is the Christ who went to the cross for sinners who could never rescue themselves.
He did not die for people who had successfully endured their way into worthiness.
He died for the ungodly.
He bore sin.
He took judgment.
He rose from the dead.
Salvation is not the trophy God hands to people who prove they never needed grace.
Salvation is grace from beginning to end.
Yet grace does not teach us to abandon Christ.
Grace teaches us to cling to Him.
This is why biblical endurance and biblical grace are not enemies.
They belong together.
We endure because Christ is worthy.
We endure through dependence upon Him.
We repent because we belong to Him.
We get back up because mercy has not become meaningless.
We fight sin not to convince Jesus to love us, but because the Jesus who loved us gave Himself to rescue us from sin's dominion.
And when we stumble, we do not make peace with the mud.
We return to the Shepherd.
Revelation gives us another stunning picture.
In Revelation 14:12 we read:
Ὧδε ἡ ὑπομονὴ τῶν ἁγίων ἐστίν
“Here is the endurance of the saints...”
And who are these enduring saints?

The text continues by describing those who keep God's commandments and hold to πίστιν Ἰησοῦ — pistin Iēsou, a phrase translated in English versions along the lines of faith in Jesus, faithfulness to Jesus, or “the faith of Jesus,” depending on how the construction is understood. The central picture remains unmistakable: God's people endure while remaining identified with Jesus.
Notice what Scripture keeps bringing us back to.
Jesus.
Not endurance for endurance's sake.
Jesus.
You are not being asked merely to survive life.
You are being called to remain faithful to Christ.
And maybe this is where the verse stops being a theological debate and becomes painfully personal.
Because there may be something trying to make you quit right now.
You know what it is.
Maybe nobody else does.
But you do.
And God does.
There is a difference between being exhausted and being finished.
You may be exhausted.
You may be wounded.
You may have questions.
You may have walked into church last Sunday smiling while silently falling apart.
But if there is still something inside you crying,
Jesus, don't let me go...
then bring that cry to Him.
Do not hide it beneath religious performance.
Bring Him the real thing.
The fear.
The addiction.
The anger.
The doubt.
The shame.
The disappointment.
The secret.
The relapse.
The resentment.
Bring it into His light.
Christian endurance is not learning to hide your wounds better.
It is learning where to take them.
And the answer is Christ.
Always Christ.
Perhaps that is why some of the strongest Christians you will ever meet do not look impressive.
They simply kept coming back to Jesus.
They buried people they loved...
and came back.
They were betrayed...
and came back.
They sinned, were convicted, repented...
and came back.
They prayed through silence...
and came back.
They were mocked...
and came back.
They were confused...
and came back.
They walked through seasons when worship felt effortless and seasons when worship felt like dragging a broken heart toward the throne...
and they kept coming back.
Not because they were superheroes.
Because they learned something.
There is nowhere better to go.
Jesus has the words of eternal life.
So what does “endure to the end” mean?
It means Christianity cannot be reduced to one emotional moment in your past while Christ has no claim upon your present.
It means Jesus warned that deception, persecution, lawlessness, betrayal, and spiritual coldness would test professing disciples.
It means genuine discipleship perseveres.
It means perseverance does not purchase the blood of Christ.
It means we dare not use grace as permission to abandon the One who gave Himself for us.
It means the Christian life is not “I once raised my hand.”
It is:
Jesus Christ is my hope.
Today.
Tomorrow.
When I understand.
When I don't.
When following Him is celebrated.
When following Him costs me.
When I feel strong.
When I crawl back in repentance.
Until my final breath...
Christ.
And if this article exposed something you have been hiding, don't manufacture a polished Christian response.
Be honest.
Somebody scrolling beneath this article may need proof that a terrible chapter does not have to become the final chapter.
Because that is the scandal of grace.
Peter denied Him.
Jesus restored him.
Thomas doubted.
Jesus met him.
The disciples scattered.
Jesus gathered them again.
Paul persecuted the church.
Jesus turned the persecutor into a preacher.
Again and again Scripture introduces us to people whose worst moment looked capable of becoming their final identity.
Then Jesus entered the story.
That is what He does.
If this truth strengthened you, do not treat it merely as content you consumed.
Pass it on.
Send it privately to the believer who disappeared.

Supporting Gospel work financially does not purchase God's favor, earn salvation, or make someone more righteous than another believer. We glorify God through lives of faith, worship, obedience, love, generosity, and service—not through a commercial transaction.
But voluntary generosity can be one practical way of participating in Gospel-centered work.
The free resources matter because the Gospel must never become a product reserved for people who can afford it.
It is helping support a mission that wants to keep pointing people toward the One whose grace cannot be bought.
Jesus is the treasure.
Jesus is the message.
Jesus is the Savior.
Your money cannot purchase what His blood already accomplished.
But your life can become an offering of gratitude.
Your voice can tell somebody about Him.
Your share can put truth in front of somebody you may never know was desperate for it.
Your testimony can remind a collapsing believer that Christ still restores.
Your generosity can help send biblical encouragement farther.
So glorify God with whatever He has entrusted to you—your time, your words, your resources, your influence, your compassion, your obedience.
And keep going.
Not because the road will become painless.
Not because Christians never fall.
Not because you will eventually become strong enough to stop needing grace.
Keep going because the Jesus who called you is worth following all the way home.
When temptation whispers, “Quit,” look toward Christ.
When shame whispers, “Hide,” run toward Christ.
When suffering whispers, “God abandoned you,” remember the cross.
When the world whispers, “Compromise,” remember the empty tomb.
When your heart whispers, “I can't do this anymore,” stop trying to prove how powerful you are and confess how desperately you need Him.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Ask forgiveness where forgiveness is needed.
Cut off what is dragging you away.
Return to prayer.
Open the Scriptures again.
Ask another believer for help.
Come out of hiding.
And fix your eyes on Jesus.
Because endurance was never the story of how tightly a flawless person held onto God.
It is the story of sinners who discovered that Jesus Christ was worth returning to again...
and again...
and again...
until one day faith becomes sight.
One day there will be no more temptation to endure.
No more funeral.
No more relapse.
No more persecution.
No more night when you wonder whether you can keep going.
No more love growing cold.
The race will be finished.
And the Savior you trusted through tears will be standing before you.
Until then...
endure.
Not to become your own savior.
Because you already know His name.
And when everything else is trying to become the final sentence of your life, remember this:
Your darkest chapter does not get to write the ending when the nail-scarred hands of Jesus are still holding the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Before you call it harmless—or condemn everyone who participates—there is a harder, more biblical question every follower of Jesus needs to face.
paragraphs: Before you call it harmless—or condemn everyone who participates—there is a harder, more biblical question every follower of Jesus needs to face.
There is a moment every October when the argument begins again.
One Christian posts, “Halloween is demonic. Christians should have nothing to do with it.”
Another replies, “Relax. My children are dressing like superheroes and collecting candy. We aren’t worshiping Satan.”
Someone posts a video about pagan origins.
Someone else points out that October 31 became associated with the eve of All Saints’ Day.

Parents become defensive. Churches divide into camps. One family attends a harvest festival. Another turns off the porch light. Another lets the children trick-or-treat but refuses frightening costumes. Another believes participating at all compromises their witness.
And somewhere underneath all the shouting is a sincere believer whispering a much quieter question:
“Jesus… what do You actually want from me?”
That is the question worth answering.
Not, “What will make other Christians approve of me?”
Not, “What does my culture consider normal?”
Not even merely, “Where did Halloween come from?”
But this:
Can I place what I am doing before Jesus Christ with a clean conscience and say, “Lord, this belongs to You”?
Because the most dangerous thing about Halloween may not be the costume hanging in your child’s bedroom.
It may be how easily Christians can spend hours arguing about darkness while ignoring the darkness hiding inside their own hearts.
Read that again.
A person can refuse Halloween and still secretly entertain pornography.
A person can throw away every plastic skeleton in the house and still harbor unforgiveness.
A person can condemn witches in October while practicing greed, gossip, lust, bitterness, pride, drunkenness, hatred, manipulation, envy, or hypocrisy the rest of the year.
And a person can also make the opposite mistake—using “Christian freedom” as an excuse to become comfortable with things Scripture explicitly tells believers to reject.
So this article is not going to give either side an easy escape.
Because Jesus did not die merely to make us culturally conservative.
And He did not die to make us culturally comfortable.
He died to make us His.
That changes the question completely.

Historically, what people today call “Halloween” is not reducible to one simple origin story. The name itself is connected with “All Hallows’ Eve,” the evening before All Saints’ Day, while customs associated with the modern holiday developed through a mixture of Christian observances, European folk traditions, and customs often connected by historians with Samhain and later cultural developments. That history is worth understanding, but history alone cannot settle the Christian’s moral responsibility.
Why?
Because Scripture does not contain the sentence, “Thou shalt not celebrate Halloween.”

But Scripture does give us principles strong enough to examine what we are doing, why we are doing it, what it communicates, what it awakens in us, how it affects others, and whether Christ can truly be glorified through it.
Paul dealt with a surprisingly relevant problem in Corinth.

Christians there lived in a culture saturated with pagan religion. One controversy involved food associated with idols. Paul did not respond with the simplistic principle that previous pagan association automatically made every subsequent ordinary use of an object sinful.

He could tell believers to eat food sold in the marketplace without conducting an investigation into its history for conscience’s sake (1 Corinthians 10:25–26). Yet in the very same chapter, he drew an uncompromising boundary against actual participation in idolatrous fellowship (1 Corinthians 10:20–21).
That distinction matters enormously.
Something having a complicated cultural history is not identical to a Christian personally participating in idolatry.
But neither does Christian liberty mean Christians may knowingly participate in occultism, divination, sorcery, spiritism, or the celebration of evil.
Scripture is unmistakably serious about those things.

Deuteronomy 18:10–12 condemns practices such as divination, sorcery, interpreting omens, witchcraft, mediums, spiritists, and attempts to consult the dead. Whatever debates Christians may have about costumes, candy, pumpkins, neighborhood gatherings, or October 31 itself, there should be no ambiguity here:
The follower of Jesus does not play with the occult.
We do not seek supernatural power apart from God.
We do not consult spirits.
We do not romanticize demonic powers.
We do not treat witchcraft as spiritually harmless merely because culture packages it as entertainment.
We belong to Jesus Christ.
Paul writes in Ephesians 5:11:
A careful sense of the Greek is:
“Do not participate with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather expose them.”

That word συγκοινωνεῖτε carries the idea of sharing in or participating together with something. Paul is not telling Christians to become terrified of the existence of darkness. He is telling them not to become participants in its works.
And that changes how we approach Halloween.
The biblical question cannot merely be, “Is October 31 pagan?”
The deeper questions are:
What exactly am I participating in?
What am I celebrating?
What am I teaching my children to admire?
What am I normalizing?
What is happening in my conscience?
What does my participation communicate to people around me?
And can I sincerely do this for the glory of God?
Paul gives us one of the most devastatingly simple tests in the New Testament:
“Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.” — 1 Corinthians 10:31
Notice the reach of that sentence.
Whatever you do.
That reaches the costume.
The decorations.
The movie.
The party.
The social-media post.
The joke.
The haunted attraction.
The church event.
The decision to participate.
The decision not to participate.
Even the way you speak about Christians whose conscience differs from yours.
Can you bring it underneath the lordship of Christ?
That is where this becomes uncomfortable.
Or perhaps you came wanting me to say, “Halloween is completely harmless,” so your conscience would stop bothering you.
Scripture refuses to serve either agenda so cheaply.
Romans 14 speaks directly to disagreements among believers over disputable matters.
Paul writes:
“One person regards one day above another; another regards every day alike…”
Then comes the principle:
“Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.” — Romans 14:5

The Greek verb κρίνει, krinei, can carry the sense of judging, evaluating, or regarding. Paul’s concern in Romans 14 is not that truth becomes subjective. Murder does not become righteous because somebody feels peaceful about it. Idolatry does not become acceptable because someone has “liberty.” Sexual immorality does not become holy because someone’s conscience has stopped protesting.
Romans 14 concerns matters in which believers can differ without overturning explicit commands of God.
That distinction protects us from two opposite errors.
Legalism says, “My personal conviction must become God’s command for everyone.”
License says, “My personal freedom allows me to ignore God’s commands.”
The Gospel gives us neither.
Jesus gives us freedom under His lordship.
So should Christians celebrate Halloween?
The most biblically responsible answer requires more maturity than a meme.

A Christian should never participate in actual occult practice, glorification of evil, divination, spiritism, witchcraft, satanic worship, or anything that requires fellowship with what Scripture calls darkness.
That boundary should not be blurry.

But whether every non-occult cultural activity associated with October 31—such as children receiving candy, wearing an innocent costume, visiting neighbors, sharing a meal, or attending a Christ-centered alternative event—is inherently sinful is much harder to establish from Scripture.
The Bible does not give us permission to manufacture commandments God did not give.
And it does not give us permission to ignore commandments He did give.
This means one Christian family may prayerfully decide, “We will not participate at all. Our conscience before Christ will not allow it.”
That family should not be mocked.
Another Christian family may say, “Our children will wear innocent costumes, visit neighbors, receive candy, and we will deliberately avoid occult imagery and anything celebrating evil.”
That family should not automatically be accused of worshiping demons merely because another believer has a stricter conviction.
But both families must answer to the same Lord.
And both need humility.
Romans 14:6 says that the person who observes a day should do so unto the Lord.
That phrase destroys superficial Christianity.
“Unto the Lord.”
Can you say that?
Not “because everyone does it.”
Not “because my children begged me.”
Not “because my church forbids it.”
Not “because Christians on Facebook told me what to think.”
Unto the Lord.
Jesus, this decision is Yours.
Jesus, these children are Yours.
Jesus, this home is Yours.
Jesus, my entertainment is Yours.
Jesus, my conscience is Yours.
Jesus, my freedom is Yours.
Jesus, even my October 31 is Yours.
And perhaps that is the confrontation some of us desperately need.
Because we have spent so much time asking how close Christians can stand to darkness without technically sinning that we have forgotten how breathtaking it is to walk in the Light.
The Christian life is not supposed to be a lifelong investigation into how much darkness we can safely tolerate.
We have something infinitely better.
Jesus said:
“I am the light of the world: he that followeth me shall not walk in darkness, but shall have the light of life.” — John 8:12
That is Christianity.
Not fear of darkness.
Not fascination with darkness.
Not legalistic obsession with darkness.
Christ.
The Light.
And maybe October 31 presents believers with an opportunity we have overlooked.
While houses around you are opening their doors…
open yours with love.
While neighbors who rarely speak to each other are walking the same streets…
learn their names.
While children knock at your door…
be kind.
While culture talks about death…
tell people about the One who conquered it.
Because Christianity possesses a message far more terrifying to hell than Christians hiding behind locked doors.
The tomb is empty.
Death lost.
Sin can be forgiven.
Satan has not won.
Jesus Christ was crucified, buried, and raised.
The King lives.
And the Gospel does not tell frightened sinners to clean themselves up enough to approach Him.
It announces that the holy Son of God entered our darkness to rescue us from it.
Think about that.
Jesus did not merely shout instructions into the darkness.
He came for people trapped inside it.
“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.” — Luke 19:10
Maybe you are reading an article about Halloween, but something much more personal has started happening.
Because you know there is darkness in your life that has nothing to do with October.
Something nobody sees.
A secret relationship.
An addiction.
A browser history.
Bitterness toward someone who hurt you.
A habit you keep promising God you will quit.
A fascination with occult material that went farther than entertainment.
A private compromise.
A double life.
A wound you disguised as anger.
A prayer life that slowly disappeared.
A Bible gathering dust while your soul starves.
And suddenly the question is no longer:
“Should Christians celebrate Halloween?”
It is:
“What have I allowed into my heart?”
That question hurts.
But conviction is not the same thing as hopeless condemnation.
The Gospel does not expose your darkness so Jesus can stand at a distance and humiliate you.
The Gospel exposes darkness because Christ came to rescue sinners.
At the cross, Jesus carried sin.
Real sin.
Ugly sin.
Embarrassing sin.
The kind we confess publicly.
The kind we hope nobody ever discovers.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
Grace does not mean darkness was harmless.
Grace means darkness does not have to have the final word.
Repentance is not God demanding that you save yourself.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who can.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Come home.
Maybe you compromised.
Come home.
Maybe you knew better.
Come home.
Maybe your conscience has been whispering for months and you kept drowning it out.
Come home.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
That is why our message will always be:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrites the story of the addict.
The hypocrite.
The prodigal.
The religious person secretly dying inside.
The skeptic who thought Christianity had nothing left to say.
The believer who wandered farther than anyone knows.
He does not rewrite evil by pretending it was good.
He rewrites sinners by forgiving, cleansing, redeeming, and transforming those who come to Him in repentance and faith.
So before deciding what your family will do this Halloween, do something more important than searching for another argument online.
Pray.
Open Scripture.
Ask whether the activity itself violates God’s Word.
Ask what it celebrates.
Ask what it communicates.
Ask whether it could wound another believer’s conscience.
Ask what it is teaching your children.
Ask whether your own conscience is clear.
And finally ask:
“Jesus, can I genuinely do this for Your glory?”
If the answer is no, walk away.
You do not need what you cannot offer to Christ.
If your conscience remains troubled, do not violate it merely because other Christians tell you to relax. Romans 14:23 gives a sobering principle: whatever does not proceed from faith is sin.
And if your conscience permits something Scripture does not prohibit, do not turn your freedom into arrogance.
Love is more important than proving how free you are.
Likewise, if you abstain, do not turn abstinence into spiritual pride.
Holiness is not measured by how many people you can condemn.
It is possible to avoid Halloween and still miss Jesus.
It is possible to win the argument and lose tenderness.
It is possible to expose darkness everywhere except the place God wanted to expose first:
inside us.
So whether your porch light is on or off this October, make certain another Light is burning.
Christ in you.
Let your children remember that Jesus was more beautiful to you than fear.
Let your neighbors discover that Christians are not merely people famous for what they oppose, but people transformed by the Savior they adore.
Let darkness remind you of the Light.
Let death remind you of resurrection.
Let costumes remind you how exhausting it is to spend your life pretending to be someone you are not.
Take off the spiritual mask.
Jesus already knows.
And He is still calling.

And if you disagree with parts of this article, you are welcome here too. Open your Bible. Test what was written. Speak with grace. We do not need another Christian shouting match. We need believers learning to search Scripture, love one another, repent quickly, and submit everything to Jesus.
Supporting Gospel ministry should never be presented as a requirement for earning God’s favor or proving that you glorify Him—salvation and grace cannot be purchased.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the struggling Christian.
Invite the person who walked away from church.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the lukewarm believer.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Jesus could never want someone with their history.
Because perhaps the greatest answer Christians can give to a culture fascinated with darkness is not panic.
It is a life so surrendered to Jesus that the darkness cannot explain the light coming from it.
And when October 31 finally arrives, remember this:
The question is not merely whether you walked past the darkness—the question is whether the world could see Christ’s Light walking through you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SAUL HUNTED CHRISTIANS—THEN JESUS STOPPED HIM ON THE ROAD
paragraphs: SAUL HUNTED CHRISTIANS—THEN JESUS STOPPED HIM ON THE ROAD

He left for Damascus carrying authority to arrest followers of Jesus. Before he reached the city, the risen Christ confronted him—and the man who came to silence the Gospel would spend the rest of his life proclaiming it.
There are some people you quietly assume will never change.
You may never say it aloud.
But somewhere inside you have already written their ending.
Too angry.
Too addicted.
Too proud.
Too religious.
Too cruel.
Too far gone.
Maybe that person is someone who wounded you so deeply that even imagining their repentance feels impossible.
Maybe it is the son who stopped believing.
The husband who hardened his heart.
The friend who mocks Jesus.
The woman whose secret life is slowly destroying her.
Maybe it is the person staring back at you from the mirror.
Because there are nights when your greatest fear is not that God cannot forgive sinners.
Your greatest fear is that what you have done somehow placed you beyond the reach of His mercy.
Then you meet Saul.
And suddenly that argument becomes very difficult to defend.
Because Saul was not wandering toward Jesus when Jesus found him.
He was hunting Jesus' people.

Acts does not introduce Saul as a harmless skeptic searching for spiritual answers. When Stephen was killed, Saul approved of his death. Soon afterward, he was ravaging the church, entering homes and dragging away men and women to prison. Later, Paul himself would openly admit that he had intensely persecuted the church of God and tried to destroy it.
Then Acts 9 opens with language so severe that we should not sanitize it.
Saul was still “breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord” (Acts 9:1, KJV).
The Greek behind the scene is chilling.
Ἐμπνέων ἀπειλῆς καὶ φόνου — empneōn apeilēs kai phonou.
Breathing threat and murder.
Luke does not merely describe something Saul occasionally said. The imagery makes violence feel like the atmosphere coming from his lungs.
He breathed it.
And he was heading toward Damascus with authorization to seize followers of “the Way,” bind them, and bring them back to Jerusalem.
Imagine being a Christian in Damascus and hearing that Saul was coming.
Imagine the conversation around a dinner table.
Doors locked.
Voices lowered.
Children pulled closer.
Someone whispering, “He knows where believers are gathering.”
Perhaps someone prayed for Saul to be stopped.
But who would have imagined how Jesus would stop him?
Saul approached Damascus.
Then heaven interrupted the journey.
A light suddenly flashed around him.
He fell to the ground.
And then came a voice.
“Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?”
Not merely:
Why are you persecuting them?
Why are you attacking My followers?
Jesus made Saul's assault upon His people profoundly personal.
“Why persecutest thou me?”
That should change the way suffering Christians understand the heart of Christ.
Jesus is not indifferent to what happens to His people.
The risen Lord identifies Himself with them so intimately that Saul's persecution of believers is addressed as persecution of Christ Himself.
And then Saul asked the question that shattered the world he thought he understood:
“Who art thou, Lord?”
The answer came.
“I am Jesus whom thou persecutest.”
Jesus.
The name Saul wanted suppressed.
Jesus.
The name attached to the movement he intended to crush.
Jesus.
Alive.
Speaking.
Lord.
Think about the terror of that realization.
Saul believed he was defending God.
Then God confronted him.
Saul believed he could see clearly.
Soon he could see nothing.
Saul believed the followers of Jesus were the problem.
Then he discovered that he himself was standing against the risen Christ.
There is a warning here for religious people that should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Sincerity does not automatically equal truth.
Passion does not automatically equal obedience.
Religious zeal does not automatically mean we are pleasing God.
A person can be extraordinarily convinced...
and extraordinarily wrong.
Paul would later describe his former life as intensely zealous for the traditions of his fathers. Yet that zeal had driven him into persecution.
That means one of the most dangerous prayers you can pray may also be one of the most necessary:
Jesus, show me where I am wrong.
Not where they are wrong.
Me.
Expose the pride I renamed conviction.
Expose the bitterness I renamed discernment.
Expose the compromise I renamed freedom.
Expose the secret sin I renamed weakness.
Expose the religious performance I renamed faithfulness.
Because sometimes grace begins with being knocked off the throne we built for ourselves.
Saul rose from the ground.
But the man who had been confidently marching toward Damascus now had to be led by the hand.
The hunter entered the city helpless.
For three days he could not see.
He did not eat.
He did not drink.
Imagine those hours.
Darkness.
Silence.
Memory.
Stephen.
The homes.
The arrests.
The terrified faces.
The screams.
And now the voice:
Saul, Saul...
There are moments when God allows the noise around us to disappear long enough for us to finally hear what our souls have spent years avoiding.
Perhaps you know that darkness.
Not Saul's physical blindness—but the moment when everything you used to justify yourself stops working.
The relationship collapses.
The addiction stops feeling harmless.
The secret gets exposed.
The applause disappears.
The money cannot quiet you.
The religious routine cannot numb you.
And suddenly you are alone with God and the truth.
That place can feel terrifying.
But sometimes the collapse of an illusion becomes the doorway to mercy.
Because Jesus did not stop Saul on the Damascus road merely to destroy him.
Jesus stopped him to claim him.
That distinction is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Saul deserved judgment.
Instead, Jesus confronted him, humbled him, and redirected his life.
Then God did something astonishing.
He sent a Christian named Ananias to Saul.
Ananias knew Saul's reputation.
He had heard what this man had done to believers in Jerusalem.
You can almost feel the hesitation in his response.
Lord...
that man?
The dangerous one?
The persecutor?
The one everybody fears?
Yes.
That one.
Because Jesus had already declared something about Saul that nobody looking at Saul's past would have predicted.
He was a chosen instrument.
Think about that.
The church saw a persecutor coming.
Jesus saw a future preacher going.
People saw Saul's record.
Jesus knew what grace would make of him.
People knew whom Saul had hurt.
Jesus knew whom Saul would eventually reach.
And Ananias went.
Perhaps one of the most beautiful moments in the entire story comes in the first words this frightened Christian spoke to the notorious persecutor.
“Brother Saul...”
Brother.
Not monster Saul.
Not murderer Saul.
Not enemy Saul.
Not “you are the reason our people have been terrified.”
Brother Saul.
Grace had entered the room before Saul had done anything impressive enough to earn the title.
Ananias laid his hands on him.
Saul regained his sight.
He was baptized.
And then Scripture gives us one of the most stunning reversals imaginable.
The man who traveled toward Damascus intending to arrest people for confessing Jesus began proclaiming Jesus.
Acts says he preached that Jesus is the Son of God.
People were astonished.
Of course they were.
They essentially asked:
Isn't this the man who was destroying those who called on this name?
Yes.
Same man.
Different master.
Same history.
Different direction.
Same Saul.
Encountered by Jesus.
This is what grace does.
Grace does not pretend Saul never persecuted anybody.
Grace does not rewrite evil into goodness.
Grace does not call sin acceptable.
Biblical grace tells the truth about sin while revealing that Jesus Christ can redeem the sinner.
That distinction matters.
Christianity is not the message that your past does not matter.
It is the message that your past does not have to be your master when Christ becomes your Lord.
Paul never needed to invent a sanitized testimony.
Years later, he could say plainly that he had been a blasphemer, persecutor, and violent man.
Then come some of the most beautiful words a guilty human being can hear:
“But I obtained mercy.”

Paul continued by declaring that the grace of the Lord was exceedingly abundant and that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners. He even described himself as chief—or foremost—among sinners, and explained that the mercy shown to him displayed Christ's extraordinary patience as an example for future believers.
Do you understand what that means for the person reading this while secretly believing Jesus could save everyone except you?
Paul's testimony was never meant to make Paul look impressive.
It was meant to make the patience of Jesus look enormous.
Paul essentially became living evidence that grace can reach horrifying places.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace without repentance.
Not grace that leaves a person comfortably chained to the same rebellion.
Transforming grace.
Grace that confronts.
Grace that humbles.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that redirects.
Grace that gives the former enemy of Christ a new allegiance.
And this is where Saul's road becomes uncomfortably close to ours.
Most of us have never carried official letters authorizing the arrest of Christians.
But we know what rebellion looks like in smaller rooms.
We know the browser history nobody sees.
The conversation we deleted.
The resentment we feed.
The person we refuse to forgive.
The secret habit we keep promising to surrender.
The Sunday worship followed by Monday compromise.
The smile that convinces everybody we are fine.
The private exhaustion.
The pride.
The envy.
The lust.
The anger.
The hypocrisy.
The years wasted running from the One who already knows where we are going.
And sometimes we think salvation means becoming slightly more respectable.
Saul's story destroys that idea.
Saul did not need polishing.
He needed Jesus.
So do we.
The Gospel is not God helping reasonably good people become nicer.
The Gospel announces that sinners who cannot rescue themselves can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.

The Son of God entered history, died for sins, was buried, rose again, and reigns. Forgiveness is not God pretending sin never mattered. At the cross we see exactly how serious sin is—and how astonishing God's love is.
Jesus does not merely offer you a better reputation.
He offers reconciliation with God.
Forgiveness.
New life.
A new Lord.
A new direction.
And repentance is not payment for mercy.
Repentance is the turning of a heart that has finally realized the road it was traveling leads away from God.
Maybe this article found you while you are on your own Damascus road.
Everything still looks normal around you.
Nobody knows what is happening inside.
But Jesus has been disturbing the comfortable lies.
You know something needs to change.
Do not confuse conviction with rejection.
The Christ who confronted Saul was the Christ who would commission Saul.
The hands of Jesus can expose what is killing you without abandoning you in the wreckage.
Maybe you have been hiding because you think Christians would be horrified if they knew everything.
Jesus already knows.
Maybe you think you need to clean yourself up before approaching Him.
Saul did not clean himself up on the road to Damascus.
Jesus interrupted him there.
Come honestly.
Come guilty.
Come exhausted.
Come without the performance.
Confess your sin.
Turn toward Christ.
Trust Him.
There is no virtue in pretending you do not need mercy.
The miracle of Saul's testimony is not that a terrible man discovered hidden goodness inside himself.
The miracle is that a guilty man encountered an overwhelmingly merciful Savior.
That is why Paul could later look backward without allowing his past to become his identity.
He remembered what he had been.
But he knew whose he had become.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this desperately needs tonight.
Your worst chapter does not outrank the authority of Jesus Christ.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
Paul's conversion did not erase the suffering he had caused from history.
Grace is not amnesia.
Forgiveness is not permission to avoid accountability.
Restoration does not mean every damaged relationship instantly returns to what it was.
But the Gospel makes an audacious declaration:
Your sin does not possess a greater saving power than Christ possesses forgiving power when you turn to Him in faith.
Saul hunted Christians.
Jesus stopped him.
Saul tried to silence the name.
Then he proclaimed the name.
Saul entered Damascus blind.
Then he began seeing everything differently.
The persecutor became a preacher.
The enemy received mercy.
The man who helped spread fear among believers became a man willing to suffer for the Christ he once opposed.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps the most astonishing detail is that Jesus is still doing this.
Somewhere, an addict is surrendering.
Somewhere, a bitter heart is finally forgiving.
Somewhere, a prodigal is coming home.
Somewhere, a religious person is discovering that knowing Christian language is not the same as knowing Christ.
Somewhere, somebody who mocked Jesus is whispering His name differently for the first time.
And somewhere, perhaps right now, someone is reading these words while realizing:
This is about me.
Bring it to Jesus.
If something hidden has been exposed, you can simply comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
If you are exhausted but refusing to abandon your faith, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with you, comment, “pray for me.”
And if your testimony is still unfinished, maybe your words are simply, “Christ is still healing me.”
Not because a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing what was hidden into the light begins with refusing to pretend anymore.
Not as a performance of spirituality. Not to collect approval. Share it because somebody in your circle may be quietly losing a war you know nothing about.
Supporting Gospel work matters, but it should never be manipulated into a test of someone's love for God. Scripture teaches willing, purposeful generosity rather than giving under compulsion.
Jesus is worth following.
The Gospel is worth sharing.
People are worth reaching.
And the man walking toward Damascus reminds us never to decide that somebody is beyond the reach of Christ.
Not your rebellious child.
Not your unbelieving friend.
Not the person who wounded you.
Not the hardened skeptic.
Not the prisoner.
Not the addict.
Not the hypocrite.
Not the person whose past makes everyone whisper.
And not you.
You may be carrying chapters you wish could be burned from your story.
Jesus does not need a spotless past before He can call you.
Saul's testimony proves something far better.
Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Paul himself became evidence of the patience of Christ toward those who would later believe and receive eternal life.
So tonight, remember the road.
Remember the light.
Remember the voice.
Remember the blind man being led into Damascus.
Remember Ananias saying, “Brother Saul.”
Remember the former persecutor opening his mouth and proclaiming the Jesus he once tried to silence.
And when your past whispers, “After everything you've done, there is no story left for God to write...”
remember Saul.
Sometimes the person everyone has written off is standing only one encounter with Jesus away from becoming living evidence that grace had the final word.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN SATAN EXPLOIT YOUR SEXUAL TEMPTATION? THE BIBLE’S ANSWER IS MORE TERRIFYING—AND MORE HOPEFUL—THAN YOU THINK
paragraphs:
CAN SATAN EXPLOIT YOUR SEXUAL TEMPTATION? THE BIBLE’S ANSWER IS MORE TERRIFYING—AND MORE HOPEFUL—THAN YOU THINK
The enemy may study the door, your desires may reach for the handle, but Jesus Christ did not shed His blood so you would spend the rest of your life chained behind it.
There is a moment almost nobody sees.
The screen is glowing.
The house is quiet.
Your spouse is asleep. Or maybe you are single and painfully aware that nobody is beside you.
Maybe you have been lonely for months.
Maybe your marriage has grown cold.
Maybe somebody at work has started giving you the attention you stopped receiving at home.
Maybe you told yourself you were only going to look.
Only going to answer the message.
Only going to scroll.
Only going to fantasize for a few seconds.
Only going to see whether that person replied.
And somewhere between “only this once” and the thing you promised God you would never do again, something inside you begins negotiating.
That is where this question becomes painfully real:
Can Satan exploit sexual temptation?
Scripture gives an answer that is both sobering and strangely liberating.
Yes.
But probably not in the simplistic way people sometimes imagine.
Satan does not need to manufacture sexuality. God created human sexuality.
He does not need to create desire from nothing.
He looks for something he can exploit.
And the apostle Paul was startlingly direct about it.
Writing about sexual intimacy within marriage, Paul warned husbands and wives against unnecessarily depriving one another and then said:
“ἵνα μὴ πειράζῃ ὑμᾶς ὁ Σατανᾶς διὰ τὴν ἀκρασίαν ὑμῶν.”
Hina mē peirazē hymas ho Satanas dia tēn akrasian hymōn.
“…so that Satan may not tempt you because of your lack of self-control.”
—1 Corinthians 7:5
Read those words carefully.
Paul actually names Satan.

The Greek verb πειράζῃ (peirazē) comes from peirazō, carrying the idea of testing or tempting. Then Paul identifies the vulnerability through which that temptation can operate: ἀκρασίαν (akrasian)—lack of self-control, lack of restraint.
That distinction matters.
Paul does not say sexual desire itself is Satanic.
He does not say marriage is dirty.
He does not tell married Christians that spirituality requires permanent sexual deprivation.

Quite the opposite. In its immediate context, 1 Corinthians 7:5 concerns husband and wife, mutual agreement, temporary abstinence for prayer, and then coming together again so that unnecessary vulnerability to temptation is not created.
God created sex.
Satan corrupts what God creates.
God designed sexuality for covenant faithfulness.
Sin tears desire away from God’s boundaries and whispers, “You deserve this on your terms.”
And sometimes Satan does not have to create a new appetite.
He only has to notice the appetite you refuse to surrender.
But here is where Christians must be careful.
Because blaming Satan for every sexual failure can become another hiding place.
James refuses to let us do that.
He writes:
Hekastos de peirazetai hypo tēs idias epithymias exelkomenos kai deleazomenos.
“But each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire.”
—James 1:14
There is a devastating little word in that Greek sentence:
ἰδίας.
Idias.
His own.
His own desire.
James uses ἐπιθυμία (epithymia) for desire or passionate longing. In this context it is desire operating as the lure toward sin.
So Scripture will not allow you to say, “The devil made me do it.”
Satan can tempt.
Satan can exploit.
Satan can deceive.
Satan can take advantage of vulnerabilities.
But your desires matter too.
Your choices matter.
Your habits matter.
What you repeatedly feed matters.
What you secretly protect matters.
What you refuse to confess matters.
The browser history matters.
The private conversation matters.
The emotional affair you insist is “just friendship” matters.
The fantasy you keep rehearsing matters.
The account you keep revisiting matters.
The person you know you should stop messaging matters.
Not because Jesus is waiting to humiliate you.
Because He loves you too much to let you rename chains as freedom.
And perhaps that is why sexual temptation can become so spiritually destructive.
It rarely introduces itself by saying, “I am here to destroy something you love.”
It says:
“You need this.”
“Nobody will know.”
“You've been deprived.”
“You deserve to feel wanted.”
“Your marriage is already broken.”
“You're single. What else are you supposed to do?”
“It isn't physical, so it isn't adultery.”
“Everybody watches this.”
“You can repent afterward.”
“One more time.”
And sometimes the most dangerous lie of all:
“You have already gone too far, so you might as well keep going.”
That last lie smells like hell.
Because temptation wants the act.
Shame wants everything after the act.
Temptation says, “Come closer.”
Then condemnation says, “How could someone like you call yourself a Christian?”
First the bait.
Then the accusation.
First the fantasy.
Then the disgust.
First the secret.
Then the fear of being discovered.
First, “Nobody needs to know.”
Then, “If anybody knew, nobody could love you.”
And suddenly a believer who should be running toward Christ is hiding from the only One who can cleanse him.
A woman who should be crying at the feet of Jesus is avoiding prayer because she feels filthy.
A husband becomes distant.
A wife becomes divided inside.
A teenager believes years of pornography have permanently destroyed him.
A single Christian begins wondering whether holiness is even possible anymore.
A pastor preaches freedom while secretly terrified that somebody will discover his bondage.
A believer worships on Sunday while fighting fantasies on Monday and quietly wondering:
“Does Jesus still want me?”
Listen carefully.
Yes.
Not because your sin is insignificant.
Because His grace is greater.
The Gospel does not minimize sexual sin.
It does something infinitely better.
It offers forgiveness to sexual sinners.
Jesus Christ did not come for people who successfully constructed an image of purity.
He came to save sinners.
The scandal of grace is not that God eventually decided sin did not matter.
The scandal is that sin mattered so much that the Son of God went to the cross—and love was so great that He went willingly.
Jesus never had to sin in order to understand temptation.
Hebrews describes our High Priest as:
“πεπειρασμένον … χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας”
pepeirasmenon … chōris hamartias
tempted/tested…yet without sin.
—Hebrews 4:15
Think about that.
Jesus understands temptation without sharing our guilt.
