This is why the cross simultaneously humiliates human pride and resurrects human hope.
You cannot stand at Golgotha and say, “I was good enough.”
But neither must the repentant believer stand there saying, “I am too filthy to be forgiven.”
The cross destroys both lies.
You were not good enough to save yourself.
But Christ is sufficient to save those who come to God through Him.
Maybe that is why “outside” hurts so beautifully.
Human beings pushed Jesus outside.
But outside, Jesus was accomplishing salvation for people who had made themselves outsiders through sin.
He entered shame.
He endured reproach.
He bore the curse.
Galatians 3:13 says:
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.”
The cross looked like defeat.
Heaven called it redemption.
It looked like humiliation.
God was accomplishing reconciliation.
It looked like the end of Jesus.
It became the death of death's claim over everyone united to Him.
And then came the morning the powers of darkness could not prevent.
The tomb was empty.
Jesus Christ rose bodily from the dead.
The rejected Stone became the cornerstone.
The crucified Messiah became the proclaimed Lord.
The One taken outside in disgrace now calls sinners into a kingdom that cannot be shaken.
But Hebrews does something uncomfortable with this truth.
It does not merely invite us to admire Jesus outside the gate.
It says:
“Therefore let us go to him outside the camp and bear the reproach he endured.”
Do you see it?
We often ask Jesus to come into the respectable little kingdoms we have built.
Jesus, bless my plans.
Jesus, protect my reputation.
Jesus, make people approve of me.
Jesus, give me success without embarrassment.
Jesus, give me Christianity without a cross.
But Hebrews says:
Go to Him.
Where?
Outside.
There comes a moment when following Christ may cost something.
Approval.
Popularity.
Convenience.
A sinful relationship.
A secret habit.
An identity you built apart from Him.
The applause of people who loved the version of you that never challenged their darkness.
Jesus never promised that discipleship would preserve every comfortable attachment.
He said:
“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.”
—Matthew 16:24
That does not mean Christians should deliberately become obnoxious, persecuted, or socially rejected and then call the consequences holiness.
We do not manufacture reproach.
We follow Christ faithfully when obedience is celebrated and when obedience costs us.
There is a difference.
And maybe tonight, the “outside” for you is simply honesty.
Finally admitting you need help.
Finally confessing the sin.
Finally ending the compromise.
Finally forgiving.
Finally saying, “Jesus, I have spent years protecting an image while my soul has been starving.”
You do not need to clean yourself enough to make Christ willing to receive you.
Come repentant.
Come believing.
Come empty-handed.
Jesus said:
“Whoever comes to me I will never cast out.”
—John 6:37
Did you catch the staggering reversal?
The One who was cast outside says He will not cast away the one who comes to Him.
That is the Gospel.
Maybe you have spent years afraid of being exposed.
But repentance is not running away from Jesus because the truth has been exposed.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the One who already knows the truth and still calls sinners to Himself.
Peter failed publicly.
David's sin became Scripture.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Paul carried memories of persecuting the church.
Their sins were not made beautiful.
Grace was.
Christianity is not the celebration of scandal.
It is the announcement that scandal does not have to write the final chapter when a sinner is brought to repentance and faith in Jesus Christ.
That is why our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior is:
Not scandal to self-improvement.
Not scandal to religious performance.
Not scandal to pretending nothing happened.
Scandal to repentance.
Scandal to the cross.
Scandal to forgiveness.
Scandal to restoration.
Scandal to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And if this article has exposed something you have been hiding, do not rush past that conviction.
Be honest before God.
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need to discover that they are not the only one fighting.
Your testimony does not have to be polished.
It only has to be honest.
And please don't keep this message trapped on this page.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list smiling through a private war.
Send it to the person who stopped going to church because shame convinced them they could never return.
Share it with the believer who is tired.
The skeptic who still has questions.
The lukewarm Christian who needs awakening.
The person whose life looks so messy that everyone else has quietly decided there is no hope.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by financially supporting a ministry.
If Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, consider staying close to this mission.
There will probably come a day when “outside” means more to you than it does today.
If you want to support the work and continue walking with this community:
A ministry cannot save you.
A church membership cannot save you.
A Christian bookshelf cannot save you.
Your reputation cannot save you.
Your tears cannot save you.
Your promise to “do better next time” cannot save you.
Jesus saves.
The Jesus who suffered outside the gate.
The Jesus who bore sin.
The Jesus who shed His blood.
The Jesus who rose from the grave.
The Jesus who receives repentant sinners.
The Jesus who takes people whose stories look permanently ruined and writes something grace alone could have written.
So when shame whispers, “You belong outside,” remember where your Savior went.
He went outside.
And He did not remain in the grave.
He walked through rejection, suffering, blood, death, and burial—and emerged victorious.
Now He calls sinners to leave their hiding places and come to Him.
Maybe your story has chapters you wish you could tear out.
Maybe there are sentences you wish had never been written.
Maybe your past contains names, nights, decisions, betrayals, failures, wounds, and secrets you would give anything to erase.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus Christ can redeem the person who lived it.
So repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come to Christ.
Then stand up and follow Him—even if following Him means walking outside the comfortable gate.
And when the world reminds you of the scandal, point to the cross.
When shame reminds you who you were, remember whose you are in Christ.
When the enemy tells you your story is finished, remember the empty tomb.
Save these words for the night your past tries to become your identity again.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is standing outside believing God has forgotten them.
And perhaps the message they need most is the one the cross has been preaching for two thousand years:
The Savior went outside the gate so sinners would know that no place of shame is beyond the reach of His redeeming grace.
Your worst chapter may explain the scars—but it does not get to write the ending when the pen belongs to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Was Rich, Religious, and Respected — Then Jesus Told Him the One Thing He Didn’t Want to Hear
paragraphs: He Was Rich, Religious, and Respected — Then Jesus Told Him the One Thing He Didn’t Want to Hear
He ran to Jesus. He knelt before Jesus. He wanted eternal life. And yet he walked away grieving—because Jesus touched the one thing he loved too much to surrender.
There is something terrifying about a man kneeling before Jesus while his heart is still standing.
Read that again.
Because this story is not really about some wealthy stranger who lived two thousand years ago.
It is about the frightening possibility of being sincere about God... interested in eternity... morally respectable... outwardly obedient... even willing to kneel before Christ—
and still having one locked room in your heart where Jesus is not allowed to enter.
The man comes running.
Mark tells us that as Jesus was setting out on His journey, a man ran toward Him and knelt before Him.
Imagine the scene.
Dust beneath his knees.
People watching.
A respected man lowering himself publicly before an itinerant Teacher from Galilee.
Matthew tells us he was young. Luke describes him as a ruler. The Gospel accounts tell us he possessed great wealth.
Young.
Influential.
Religious.
Rich.
Respectable.
By almost every measurement people use to determine whether someone has "made it," this man had won.
Yet something inside him was still restless.
So he ran to Jesus.
“Good Teacher,” he asked, “what must I do to inherit eternal life?”
There is almost an ache hidden inside the question.
What am I still missing?
He had possessions.
He had morality.
He had status.
He had religion.
But apparently, when the noise disappeared and he was alone with his soul, none of it could silence eternity.
Maybe you understand him more than you would like to admit.
You can have money in the bank and anxiety in your chest.
You can have people respecting you while secretly wondering whether God really knows you.

You can attend church, quote Scripture, share Christian posts, worship with your hands raised, give offerings, avoid obvious scandals, and still sense something uncomfortable when the room becomes quiet:
There is something I have never completely surrendered.
Jesus begins mentioning commandments.
Do not murder.
Do not commit adultery.
Do not steal.
Do not bear false witness.
Do not defraud.
Honor your father and mother.
And the young man answers with extraordinary confidence:
“Teacher, all these I have kept from my youth.”
Then comes one of the most beautiful—and devastating—sentences in the entire encounter.
Mark 10:21 records:
“Jesus looked at him and loved him.”
The Greek is striking:
Ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς ἐμβλέψας αὐτῷ ἠγάπησεν αὐτόν
Ho de Iēsous emblepsas autō ēgapēsen auton.
Jesus, having looked intently at him, loved him.
Mark does not say Jesus looked at him and became disgusted.
He does not say Jesus looked at him and mocked his spiritual blindness.
He does not say Jesus exposed him because He enjoyed humiliating him.
He loved him.
And what Jesus says next comes from that love.
That matters enormously.
Because biblical conviction is not Christ trying to destroy you.
Sometimes the most painful thing Jesus exposes is precisely the place His love refuses to leave enslaved.
Then Christ speaks:
Ἕν σε ὑστερεῖ
Hen se hysterei.
“One thing you lack.”
One thing.
The sentence must have landed like thunder.
The man who seemed to have everything...
lacked one thing.
And that one thing exposed everything.
Jesus tells him to sell what he has, give to the poor, receive treasure in heaven, and then:
ἀκολούθει μοι
akolouthei moi.
“Follow Me.”
That is the center of the story.
Not merely:
Sell.
Not merely:
Give.
But:
Follow Me.

Jesus was not offering this man a financial transaction by which eternal life could be purchased through charitable giving. Scripture does not teach salvation by liquidating enough assets or donating enough money. Salvation is by God's grace, not human achievement.
Jesus was exposing the throne.
The man's wealth was not merely in his hands.
It had captured his heart.
His possessions had become something more than possessions.
They had become security.
Identity.
Control.
Perhaps significance.
And Jesus put His finger directly on the rival king.
That is why this passage must never be reduced to, “Being wealthy is sinful.”

Scripture does not teach that every believer must possess exactly the same amount of material wealth. Scripture does repeatedly warn, however, about loving money, trusting riches, greed, and allowing possessions to become masters of the heart.
The issue was not merely what the man possessed.
The issue was what possessed the man.
And suddenly this ancient story becomes painfully modern.
Because maybe your “great possessions” are not money.
Maybe Jesus could remove every dollar from your account and still not touch your real idol.
Maybe yours is approval.
Your reputation.
Your relationship.
Your career.
Your secret habit.
Your bitterness.
Your sexuality.
Your ambition.
Your comfort.
Your image.
Your political identity.
Your need to control everything.
Your dream for your future.
Your resentment toward someone who hurt you.
Your determination to be admired.
Even your religious reputation.
Anything can become dangerous when your heart whispers:
Jesus can have everything except this.
And perhaps that is the sentence this entire article has been leading you toward:
What is the one thing you desperately hope Jesus never asks you to surrender?
Don't answer quickly.
Sit with it.
Because the rich man probably believed he was ready for Jesus' answer too.
Until Jesus answered.
There is a Christianity that wants forgiveness without surrender.
Heaven without holiness.
Jesus as Savior without Jesus as Lord.
A cross that comforts us but never crucifies our idols.
Grace that excuses us but never transforms us.
We want Christ close enough to rescue us...
but sometimes not close enough to rearrange us.
The rich man wanted eternal life.
Jesus offered him something greater than another possession.
Jesus offered him Jesus.
And the tragedy is almost unbearable.
Mark tells us the man's face fell.
He went away grieving.
Think about that.
He came running.
He left walking.
He arrived kneeling.
He departed grieving.
He came asking about eternal life.
And when Eternal Life stood in front of him and said, essentially, Come with Me...
the price of surrender felt greater than the beauty of Christ.
He walked away.
Not because Jesus hated him.
The text specifically says Jesus loved him.
Not because Jesus refused him.
Jesus invited him.
Not because he wasn't religious enough.
He was extraordinarily religious.
He walked away because when Christ confronted the deepest allegiance of his heart, he discovered that there was something he wanted more than following Jesus.
And that is where this story stops being comfortable.
Because there are ways to walk away from Jesus without physically leaving a church.
You can walk away while sitting in a pew.
You can walk away while singing worship songs.
You can walk away while posting Bible verses.
You can walk away while everyone around you assumes you are spiritually healthy.
Every time Christ says, “Follow Me,” and our heart answers, “Except there,” we are standing dangerously close to this man's road.
Jesus then tells His disciples how difficult it is for those who have riches to enter God's kingdom.
The disciples are astonished.
Eventually they ask the question underneath every human attempt at self-salvation:
“Then who can be saved?”
And Jesus gives the answer that rescues this passage from despair.
“With man it is impossible, but not with God. For all things are possible with God.”
There is the Gospel.
Humanly impossible.
Divinely possible.
You cannot purchase salvation.
You cannot perform your way into salvation.
You cannot impress God into saving you.
You cannot become moral enough to make the cross unnecessary.
You cannot empty your bank account and purchase heaven.
You cannot repair your sinful heart through religious determination.
You need rescue.
And this is where the rich young ruler's story collides with the scandal of grace.
The rich man was asked to release his treasure.
But the Gospel tells us that God gave His Treasure for sinners.
Jesus did not merely stand at a distance and demand sacrifice.
Christ Himself walked toward a cross.
The eternal Son humbled Himself.
The sinless One was rejected.
The innocent One was condemned.
Jesus bore sin's judgment and died, and He rose again.
The One calling you to surrender is the One who gave Himself to redeem sinners.
Christianity is not fundamentally the story of people climbing their way toward God.
It is the breathtaking announcement that in Jesus Christ, God came down to rescue people who could never save themselves.
That means repentance is not paying Jesus back.
You cannot.
Obedience is not purchasing His love.
You cannot.
Surrender is the response of someone whose eyes are finally opening to the reality that Christ is worth more than whatever sits on the throne of the heart.
This is grace with teeth.
Grace that forgives the adulterer and tells them to leave sin.
Grace that welcomes the greedy and teaches generosity.
Grace that receives the proud and begins dismantling pride.
Grace that finds the broken and does not merely make them comfortable in their chains.
Grace loves us too deeply to call bondage freedom.
And notice again the order in Mark's account.
Jesus looked at him.
Jesus loved him.
Then Jesus confronted him.
Love came before the wound.
Maybe that changes how you hear conviction.
Perhaps Jesus has been touching something in your life lately.
Something uncomfortable.
Something you keep defending.
Something you keep renaming so you do not have to repent of it.
Something you pray around instead of surrendering.
And perhaps you have interpreted His conviction as rejection.
But what if the reason Christ keeps touching that wound is because He loves you too much to let an idol quietly consume you?
The question is not whether you own anything.
The question is whether anything owns you.
Can Jesus have your plans?
Can Jesus have your money?
Can Jesus have your reputation?
Can Jesus have the relationship you know is pulling you away from Him?
Can Jesus have your private browser history?
Can Jesus have the grudge?
Can Jesus have the applause?
Can Jesus have the dream?
Can Jesus have the version of yourself you worked years to build?
Can Jesus have the hidden thing nobody knows about?
And before this becomes legalism, remember carefully:
We are not saved because we surrender perfectly.
We surrender because Christ saves sinners by grace and calls those He saves to follow Him.
Even disciples stumble.
Peter would fail spectacularly.
The Gospel is not “surrender flawlessly or Jesus will never love you.”
The Gospel is that sinners are called to repent and trust in the crucified and risen Christ—and His grace begins making new people out of those who belong to Him.
There is forgiveness for the person who suddenly realizes:
I have loved something more than Jesus.
There is mercy for the person who has compromised.
There is restoration for the person who wandered.
There is hope for the person reading this with tears forming because God just put a name on something you have spent years hiding.
Your scandal does not have to be the final chapter.
Your greed does not have to be the final chapter.
Your secret does not have to be the final chapter.
Your failure does not have to be the final chapter.
Your hypocrisy does not have to be the final chapter.
Your shame does not get authorship rights over the rest of your life.
Jesus does.
That is why we keep saying it:
But rewritten lives begin when we stop handing Jesus an edited version of ourselves.
Bring Him the real thing.
The greed.
The lust.
The fear.
The pride.
The addiction.
The anger.
The hunger for attention.
The spiritual exhaustion.
The hidden compromise.
Bring Him the thing you are ashamed to say aloud.
Repentance begins where pretending ends.
Maybe you have been trying to look respectable while your soul is starving.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong.
Maybe everyone thinks your marriage is perfect.
Maybe everyone thinks your faith is unshakable.
Maybe your social media looks blessed while your private life feels spiritually hollow.
Jesus is not asking you to impress Him.
He already sees you.
The same Christ who looked into that young ruler's heart sees beyond your public version too.
And still the Gospel invitation stands:
Come.
Follow Me.
Be honest.

And if Christ has already brought you through a season where you once chose an idol over Him but His grace restored you, tell your testimony. Someone reading your words may desperately need evidence that failure does not have to be the end when repentance brings us back to Christ.
Then think of one person.
Not fifty.
One.
The successful friend who has everything except peace.
The Christian who has slowly grown cold.
The person trapped in materialism.
The believer protecting a secret compromise.
The family member who thinks being a “good person” is the same as being reconciled to God through Christ.
Because there may come a day when the thing you surrendered starts whispering your name again.
Come back and remember the rich young ruler.
Remember the dust.
Remember the knees.
Remember the invitation.
Remember the sorrow of a man who discovered that wanting Jesus and surrendering to Jesus were not necessarily the same thing.

Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even the person who does not yet believe—to follow too. The point is not building an audience around us. The point is helping more people encounter the Word of God and the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Your support helps strengthen the work and helps us keep putting biblical content and resources into people's hands.
Jesus already paid the price we never could.
The real question this story leaves burning in the room is far more personal.
If Jesus looked directly into your heart tonight...
past the Christian vocabulary...
past the reputation...
past the achievements...
past the money...
past the church attendance...
past the posts people see...
and lovingly placed His finger on the one thing competing with Him—
would you surrender it...
or would you walk away grieving?
The young ruler's footsteps disappear from Mark's scene.
We are not told in that passage that he turned around.
But your story is still being written.
You are still here.
The invitation is still before you.
Christ is still worthy.
Grace is still astonishing.
Repentance is still possible.
The cross is still sufficient.
The tomb is still empty.
And Jesus still calls sinners out of slavery and into life:
Follow Me.
Don't walk away carrying the very thing that is keeping your heart from freedom.
Because sometimes the saddest person in the story is not the one who lost everything.
It is the one who stood before Jesus, was loved by Jesus, was invited by Jesus—and decided that what he was holding was worth more than the One standing in front of him.
When Jesus asks for the thing you cannot imagine losing, He may be exposing the thing that has been quietly keeping you from realizing that He is the Treasure you were searching for all along.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THEY COULD THROW DANIEL TO THE LIONS, BUT THEY COULDN’T TAKE HIS FAITH
paragraphs:
THEY COULD THROW DANIEL TO THE LIONS, BUT THEY COULDN’T TAKE HIS FAITH
They could control the law. They could seal the stone. They could surround him with lions. But there was one thing Babylon could never reach: the part of Daniel that already belonged to God.
There comes a moment when faith stops being something you say you have…
and becomes something you may have to suffer for.
Daniel knew that moment.

He was no longer the young exile first dragged into Babylon. By Daniel 6, kingdoms had shifted, rulers had changed, and Daniel had grown older. Yet something inside him had remained remarkably untouched.
His loyalty to God.
That is what makes his story uncomfortable.
Because Daniel did not suddenly become faithful when the lions appeared.
The lions merely revealed the faith he had been quietly practicing for years.
And perhaps that is where this story reaches through the centuries and finds us.
Because most of us will never be lowered into a literal den of lions.
But we know what it feels like when obedience costs something.
When telling the truth threatens a relationship.
When refusing compromise makes you unpopular.
When everybody else seems comfortable doing what your conscience will not allow.
When you are exhausted, frightened, misunderstood, tempted, disappointed with God, and still somehow expected to pray.
There are lions that have never grown fur.
Some have names like rejection.
Pressure.
Loneliness.
Addiction.
Shame.
Fear.
Compromise.
The approval of people.
And sometimes the most dangerous lion is the quiet voice inside you whispering:
Would it really matter if you compromised just this once?
Daniel had every human reason to do exactly that.
King Darius had appointed officials throughout his kingdom, and Daniel distinguished himself so dramatically that the king planned to place him over the whole realm.
Scripture says an “excellent spirit” was in him.
His enemies noticed.
They searched for corruption.
They searched for negligence.
They searched for scandal.
Imagine people examining your life because they desperately want something they can use against you.
Daniel 6:4 says they could find no corruption because he was trustworthy.
So his enemies reached a chilling conclusion.
If they could not destroy Daniel through his failures…
they would try to destroy him through his faithfulness.
They persuaded Darius to establish a decree forbidding anyone for thirty days from making a petition to any god or man except the king. Anyone who violated it would be thrown into the lions’ den.
Then came the sentence that exposes what Daniel actually believed.
“Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed…”
He knew.
Daniel was not ignorant of the consequences.
He did not accidentally pray.
He knew the decree existed.
He knew people were watching.
He knew the punishment.
And he went home anyway.
The Aramaic text of Daniel 6:10 describes him going to his house, where the windows of his upper room were open toward Jerusalem. The verse says:
וְזִמְנִין תְּלָתָה בְיוֹמָא הוּא בָּרֵךְ עַל־בִּרְכוֹהִי וּמְצַלֵּא וּמוֹדֵא קֳדָם אֱלָהֵהּ
At its heart, the picture is painfully simple: three times a day Daniel got down upon his knees, prayed, and gave thanks before his God.
But then Scripture adds the words that make the scene unforgettable:
כָּל־קֳבֵל דִּי־הֲוָא עָבֵד מִן־קַדְמַת דְּנָה
In context: just as he had been doing before.
That may be the most convicting part of the entire lions’ den story.
Daniel did not manufacture dramatic faith for a crisis.
He continued an existing relationship with God.
Before there was a decree, there was prayer.
Before there was persecution, there was prayer.
Before there was a lions’ den, there was prayer.
And when obedience became dangerous…
there was still prayer.
Daniel did not suddenly discover God when his life fell apart.
He already knew Him.
Maybe that is the question this story quietly asks us:
If tomorrow’s crisis exposes today’s spiritual habits, what will it reveal?
We often want lions’-den faith while living a prayerless life.
We want courage without communion.
Conviction without Scripture.
Power without surrender.
We want God to become overwhelmingly real when disaster strikes while treating Him as optional when life is comfortable.
Daniel shows us another way.
His public courage grew out of private faithfulness.
Notice something else.
Daniel prayed…
and gave thanks.
Think about that.
The decree had already been signed.
People were trying to kill him.
His career was threatened.
His life was threatened.
And Daniel was giving thanks.
Not because death was good.
Not because persecution was pleasant.
Not because lions were harmless.
Daniel could give thanks because circumstances had changed without changing the identity of his God.
That distinction matters.
Biblical faith is not pretending the lions do not have teeth.
Faith is knowing the lions do not have the final word.
Daniel's enemies caught him praying and brought the accusation before Darius.
The king realized what had happened.
He wanted to rescue Daniel, but the law trapped even the ruler who had signed it.
Eventually Daniel was brought to the den.
Imagine the walk.
The stone.
The darkness.
The sounds below.
Daniel had served God faithfully, and faithfulness had apparently brought him here.
That destroys one of the most dangerous distortions of Christianity:
the idea that obedience guarantees an easy life.
Sometimes obedience makes life harder.
Sometimes integrity costs opportunities.
Sometimes holiness costs relationships.
Sometimes following Jesus means refusing what everybody around you calls normal.
Sometimes faithfulness leads directly toward a den.
Jesus never hid this from His disciples.
He told them that following Him involved denying themselves and taking up their cross.
The Christian Gospel is not, “Come to Jesus and nothing painful will ever happen to you.”
The Gospel is far better:
Come to Jesus, and even suffering cannot separate you from the love of God.
Darius spoke to Daniel before he was lowered into the den:
“Your God whom you continually serve, He will deliver you.”
Then Daniel disappeared beneath the stone.
And the stone was sealed.
There is something haunting about sealed stones in Scripture.
A sealed stone says:
Finished.
Impossible.
Nobody is coming out.
Daniel had one placed over his den.
Centuries later, another stone would stand before another place of death.
But hold that thought.
Because first Daniel had to spend the night with lions.
Scripture does not tell us everything Daniel felt.
That silence is important.
We should not turn him into something less than human.
Courage does not necessarily mean the absence of fear.
Faith means fear does not become your god.
The king spent the night fasting and unable to sleep.
Then at dawn he rushed toward the den.
“Daniel, servant of the living God…”
Imagine the silence before the answer.
“Has your God, whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?”
Then a voice came out of the place that was supposed to contain a corpse.
Daniel was alive.
He told the king:
אֱלָהִי שְׁלַח מַלְאֲכֵהּ וּסֲגַר פֻּם אַרְיָוָתָא
“My God sent His angel and shut the lions’ mouths.”
Daniel 6:23 then says no injury was found on him because he had trusted in his God.
The lions were real.
The den was real.
The danger was real.
But so was God.
Yet we need to read Daniel carefully.
The lesson cannot be reduced to:
Trust God and nothing bad will happen to you.
Hebrews 11 refuses to let us preach that shallow message.
That chapter remembers people who through faith conquered kingdoms and escaped the edge of the sword.
But it also remembers faithful people who were imprisoned, tortured, mistreated, and killed.
Same faith.
Same God.
Different earthly outcomes.
Daniel was not faithful because he had been guaranteed survival.
He was faithful because God was worthy of faithfulness whether Daniel survived or not.
That is the kind of Christianity darkness cannot negotiate with.
A faith that says:
“If God gives me what I want, I will worship Him” can be purchased.
But a surrendered heart says:
“Even if obedience costs me something, Christ is still Lord.”
And this is where Daniel’s story becomes much larger than Daniel.
Because Daniel was a faithful servant unjustly condemned.
But Jesus Christ is the perfectly faithful Son.
Daniel’s enemies searched for something against him and struggled to find grounds for accusation.
Jesus’ enemies also sought testimony against Him.
Daniel was condemned through the machinery of human power.
Jesus was delivered into the hands of sinful men.
Daniel entered a place from which death was expected.
Jesus actually entered death.
A stone was placed over Daniel’s den.
A stone was rolled before Christ’s tomb.
Daniel came out alive because God preserved him from death.
Jesus did something infinitely greater.
He passed through death…
and rose victorious over it.
Daniel points our eyes beyond heroic human courage toward the God who saves.
And the Gospel tells us exactly where that saving God has ultimately revealed Himself:
Jesus Christ.
This matters because your deepest problem is not the lion outside you.
It is sin within you.
You can escape rejection and still be separated from God.
You can overcome adversity and still carry guilt.
You can become successful, respected, admired, religious, disciplined, and still desperately need grace.
The Gospel does not merely teach us how to survive lions.
It announces that Jesus came to save sinners.
He lived the righteousness we have failed to live.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is offered not because we have been Daniel-like enough…
but because Christ is enough.
Maybe you have not been Daniel.
Maybe you compromised.
Maybe pressure got to you.
Maybe you stopped praying.
Maybe you hid your faith because you wanted approval.
Maybe you promised God you would never return to that sin…
and returned anyway.
Maybe the scandal is not what somebody did to you.
Maybe the scandal is what you know about yourself.
The secret browser history.
The bitterness.
The affair nobody knows about.
The addiction beneath the worship songs.
The jealousy behind the smile.
The anger.
The double life.
The prayerlessness.
The religious appearance covering spiritual emptiness.
And somewhere inside, you wonder whether God could possibly want you after everything you have done.
Listen carefully.
This is where scandal can meet grace.
Not cheap grace that pretends sin does not matter.
The cross proves sin matters terribly.
But the same cross proves something else:
God's mercy toward repentant sinners is greater than the shame they bring to Him.
Jesus does not call you to decorate your chains.
He calls you to repent.
To come into the light.
To surrender.
To believe.
To stop negotiating with the sin that is consuming you.
The same Christ who forgives also transforms.
Grace does not merely say, “Your past does not matter.”
Grace says, “Your past does not have to remain your master.”
From scandal to grace… because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by removing repentance from Christianity.
Jesus rewrites lives by forgiving sinners, reconciling them to God, giving them new life, and teaching them to walk differently.
Maybe your lions’ den right now is not persecution.
Maybe it is Tuesday night when nobody knows you are falling apart.
Maybe it is the marriage you keep praying for.
The child who walked away from God.
The temptation you are ashamed to admit still tempts you.
The grief that has made prayer difficult.
The financial pressure making compromise look reasonable.
The workplace where integrity feels expensive.
The loneliness that keeps whispering that holiness is not worth it.
The unanswered prayer that has slowly turned into disappointment.
And perhaps you have been asking:
“God, where are You?”
Daniel’s story does not promise that God will always remove the den.
Sometimes He meets His people inside it.
And Christianity's greatest proof of that truth is not Daniel.
It is Jesus.
At the cross, Christ entered suffering more deeply than Daniel ever did.
Therefore when a Christian suffers, we are not crying toward a Savior who observes pain from a safe distance.
We are calling upon the crucified and risen Christ.
He knows betrayal.
He knows false accusation.
He knows rejection.
He knows agony.
He knows death.
And because He rose, suffering is no longer the final chapter for those who belong to Him.
Maybe God will shut the mouth of the lion you are facing.
Maybe He will lead you through a road you would never have chosen.
Either way, Christian hope is ultimately anchored somewhere stronger than immediate circumstances.
It is anchored in Christ.
That means the question is no longer merely:
“Will God get me out of this?”
Sometimes the deeper prayer becomes:
“Jesus, whether You deliver me from this, through this, or ultimately beyond this, do not let this take my heart away from You.”
That is dangerous faith.
Not dangerous to people.
Dangerous to darkness.
Because what can temptation offer someone whose greatest treasure is Christ?
What can shame permanently do to someone who has truly received forgiveness?
What can rejection ultimately steal from someone adopted by God?
What can death finally threaten when resurrection stands on the other side?
They could throw Daniel among lions.
They could not make Daniel stop belonging to God.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to stop asking God for a life without lions and begin asking Him for a faith the lions cannot eat.
If that is you, be honest.
Someone reading beneath this article may desperately need evidence that another believer has walked through darkness and kept trusting Jesus.
Do not make the comments a performance.
Make them a place of honesty.
There may come a night when your emotions tell you everything you believe is collapsing. Come back and remember Daniel.
More importantly, come back and remember Jesus.
Not because paying for something earns favor with God.
It does not.
It does not.
Salvation is God's gift of grace received through faith in Christ, not something purchased through financial support.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one voluntary way of helping that work continue and reach others.

Invite your family. Invite the friend quietly struggling with faith. Invite the believer who has grown cold. Invite the seeker with questions. Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing meaningful to say to broken people.
But before you leave, remember the detail that changes everything.
Daniel's greatest testimony was not that he never entered the lions’ den.
It was that when the den opened, he still belonged to God.
Your faith may be tested.
Your reputation may be attacked.
Your prayers may seem unanswered.
People may misunderstand you.
You may walk through seasons that feel brutally unfair.
You may even discover painful things about your own heart that drive you toward repentance.
But if you are in Christ, your story is not finally held by lions, enemies, failures, shame, or graves.
It is held by the Savior who walked out of His own sealed tomb.
So when the night becomes dark enough that you can hear the lions breathing…
remember:
The lions may enter your story, but they do not get to write the ending. Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE MOST DANGEROUS WALK NEBUCHADNEZZAR EVER TOOK WAS ON HIS OWN ROOF
paragraphs:
THE MOST DANGEROUS WALK NEBUCHADNEZZAR EVER TOOK WAS ON HIS OWN ROOF
He thought he was admiring everything he had built. Heaven knew he was standing only moments away from losing everything he thought made him great.
There are walks that change your life.
A walk down an aisle.
A walk out of a hospital.
A walk away from a grave.
A walk back home after realizing you have nowhere else to go.
And then there was the walk of King Nebuchadnezzar.
No battlefield.
No assassin waiting behind a curtain.
No invading army surrounding Babylon.
Just a king...
walking on the roof of his royal palace.
That is what makes the story so terrifying.
Because sometimes the most dangerous moments of your spiritual life do not feel dangerous at all.
Sometimes temptation does not arrive looking like temptation.
Sometimes destruction does not announce itself with screaming alarms.

Sometimes judgment approaches while the evening is quiet, the bills are paid, the career is going well, people respect you, your plans are working, and you are standing on the metaphorical rooftop of everything you have accomplished thinking:
Look what I have built.
Daniel tells us that twelve months had passed since Nebuchadnezzar received a terrifying warning from God.
Twelve months.
That detail matters.

God had given the king a dream of an enormous tree reaching toward heaven. It was visible across the earth. Animals found shelter beneath it. Birds lived in its branches. Everything about the tree communicated greatness, influence, provision, power.
Then a heavenly watcher commanded that the tree be cut down.
Daniel explained the meaning.
The tree was Nebuchadnezzar.
His greatness had grown enormously, but the king was about to be humbled until he learned that “the Most High rules the kingdom of men.”
Daniel did not merely interpret the dream.
He pleaded with the king.
Break away from your sins.
Practice righteousness.
Show mercy to the oppressed.
In other words:
Repent while mercy is still calling.
And then...
nothing happened.
Not immediately.
One month passed.
Perhaps Nebuchadnezzar remembered the dream.
Three months.
Still king.
Six months.
Still powerful.
Nine months.
Still living in the palace.
Twelve months.
Still no judgment.
And this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because delayed consequences can deceive us into thinking there will be no consequences.
We prayed after the affair almost happened.
We cried after getting caught.
We promised God we would change.
We deleted something.
Then downloaded it again.
We apologized.
Then slowly returned to the same behavior.
We felt conviction during worship.
Then Monday arrived.
Nothing collapsed.
Nobody found out.
Our marriage survived another week.
Our reputation remained intact.
The secret remained secret.
The money kept coming.
The followers kept increasing.
The ministry kept growing.
And somewhere inside us, something dangerous whispered:
Maybe God wasn't that serious.
Nebuchadnezzar had twelve months of mercy.
But he treated mercy like permission.
Then one day the king walked on the roof of the royal palace of Babylon.
And he spoke.
Daniel preserves his words in Aramaic.
“הֲלָא דָא־הִיא בָבֶל רַבְּתָא דִּי־אֲנָה בֱנַיְתַהּ”
Transliterated:
Hălā dā-hî Bāḇel rabbəṯā dî-ʾănāh ḇənayṯah?
The sense is devastatingly simple:
“Is not this great Babylon that I have built...?”
Listen carefully to the center of that sentence.
I.
“I have built.”
Nebuchadnezzar continues by describing Babylon as something built by his mighty power for the glory of his majesty.
There it is.
The ancient disease wearing royal clothing.
My strength.
My achievement.
My kingdom.
My glory.
And before we condemn him too quickly...
How different are we?
My business.
My house.
My degree.
My children.
My ministry.
My platform.
My followers.
My money.
My discipline.
My intelligence.
My sacrifice.
My reputation.
My success.
We may never stand on the roof of Babylon.
But almost everyone eventually finds a rooftop.
A place where you can look down at what has happened in your life and quietly forget Who gave you breath while you were building it.
Pride is not merely thinking you are wonderful.
Biblical pride can be far more subtle.
It is living as though God is unnecessary.
It is receiving gifts while forgetting the Giver.
It is enjoying mercy without bowing before the One who gave it.
It is confusing stewardship with ownership.
It is looking at what grace allowed you to hold and eventually convincing yourself your own hands created everything.
Nebuchadnezzar's problem was not that Babylon was impressive.
It was.
His problem was that he interpreted greatness without God.
And Scripture gives us one of its most chilling transitions:
While the words were still in the king's mouth, a voice came from heaven.
Not tomorrow.
Not after another warning.
While the words were still there.
The kingdom was taken from him.

The mighty king who had commanded nations was driven away from human society. Daniel describes him living like the beasts of the field, eating grass like cattle, his body wet with the dew of heaven, his hair growing like feathers and his nails like claws.
The man who wanted to elevate himself above everyone was brought lower than almost everyone.
But do not miss what God was doing.
This was judgment.
Yes.
But it was not meaningless cruelty.
God was destroying an illusion that was destroying Nebuchadnezzar.
The king believed he was sovereign.
God humbled him until he recognized the Sovereign.
And that is where this story becomes more than a warning.
It becomes hope.
Because Nebuchadnezzar's story did not end in the field.
After the appointed period, the king says something extraordinary:
He lifted his eyes toward heaven.
Think about that.
The man who had spent his life looking down...
finally looked up.
And his reason returned.
His first response was worship.
The king who once praised himself began blessing the Most High.
The mouth that had said, “I built this,” began confessing that God's dominion is everlasting.
Nebuchadnezzar learned something on the ground that he could not understand from the roof.
God was God before Nebuchadnezzar became king.
God was God while Nebuchadnezzar ruled Babylon.
God was God when Nebuchadnezzar lost his sanity.
And God would still be God long after Babylon became dust.
Maybe that is the warning hidden in the king's walk on the roof.
The greatest danger is not always losing everything.
Sometimes the greater danger is gaining enough that you begin believing you no longer need God.
Success can test the soul differently than suffering.
Pain often makes us look toward heaven.
Success can tempt us to look into the mirror.
Suffering says, “God, I need You.”
Pride says, “Look what I did.”
And there may be somebody reading this who has been walking on a rooftop without realizing it.
God answered the prayer.
You survived the season you thought would destroy you.
You got the job.
Your business grew.
Your family recovered.
The door opened.
People finally noticed you.
The ministry expanded.
The money became more comfortable.
The addiction loosened its grip.
The relationship was restored.
And slowly...
gratitude became familiarity.
Familiarity became entitlement.
Entitlement became independence.
And independence started sounding suspiciously like:
I built this.
Maybe your rooftop looks completely different.
Maybe you have very little outward success, yet pride has found another entrance.
You cannot apologize.
You cannot forgive.
You cannot receive correction.
You always need to be right.
You compare your spirituality with someone else's failures.
You secretly believe your morality makes God more willing to love you.
You judge another person's scandal because yours has not become public.
That is still a rooftop.
Religious pride is still pride.
And this is exactly why we need Jesus Christ.
Christianity is not the story of morally impressive people climbing high enough to reach God.
The Gospel is the announcement that the Son of God came down to rescue people who could never save themselves.
Nebuchadnezzar boasted in his glory.
Jesus surrendered His.
Nebuchadnezzar exalted himself.
Jesus humbled Himself.
Nebuchadnezzar looked at a kingdom and said, in effect, “Look what I built for my glory.”
Jesus Christ, though truly Lord, walked the road toward a cross.
Philippians 2 tells us that Christ humbled Himself and became obedient unto death—even death on a cross.
And because of His obedience, God highly exalted Him.
Do you see the collision?
Human pride climbs upward.
Jesus willingly came downward.
Human pride says, “Notice me.”
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
Human pride wants a throne without surrender.
Jesus wore a crown of thorns before resurrection glory.
At Calvary, our boasting dies.
You cannot stand beneath the cross and brag about saving yourself.
You cannot stare at the crucified Christ and say, “I earned this.”
You cannot look at His wounds and congratulate yourself.
The cross leaves us with empty hands.
And empty hands are exactly what grace fills.
That is why repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
Repentance is coming home to reality.
God is God.
We are not.
We have sinned.
Christ is sufficient.
Grace is available.
Forgiveness was purchased.
The tomb is empty.
Jesus is alive.
And the person who finally stops defending himself can finally discover what it means to be rescued.
Maybe God has been warning you about something.
Not through Nebuchadnezzar's dream...
but through conviction.
A Scripture you cannot forget.
A sermon that disturbed you.
A conversation that exposed you.
A relationship that keeps revealing your selfishness.
A secret sin you keep promising to abandon.
An arrogance nobody else sees.
A bitterness you have renamed “discernment.”
An obsession with being admired.
A hunger for applause.
A private compromise hidden beneath a public Christian identity.
And perhaps because twelve metaphorical months have passed and your life has not collapsed, you have assumed everything must be fine.
Do not mistake God's patience for God's approval.
Romans 2 teaches that God's kindness is intended to lead us toward repentance.
Mercy is not heaven ignoring your sin.
Mercy is heaven giving you another opportunity to come home.
Nebuchadnezzar received a warning before judgment.
And today, perhaps this story is functioning as a warning for someone else.
Not because God delights in destroying sinners.
The cross proves otherwise.
Christ came to save sinners.
But grace does not tell us to make peace with the chains Jesus died to break.
Grace calls us out.
Grace washes us.
Grace forgives us.
Grace teaches us to say no to ungodliness.
Grace takes people with scandalous histories and begins writing something different.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
It means your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Maybe you have spent years building your own Babylon.
Your identity.
Your reputation.
Your secret kingdom.
Your carefully managed image.
And perhaps the Holy Spirit is putting His finger on the one sentence you desperately do not want to surrender:
“I did this.”
Then surrender it.
The abilities were gifts.
The opportunities were gifts.
The breath was a gift.
The years were gifts.
The people who helped you were gifts.
The doors were gifts.
Even your ability to work hard exists because God permitted your heart to keep beating while you worked.
There is nothing wrong with working faithfully.
There is nothing wrong with building something beautiful.
There is nothing wrong with achievement.
The danger begins when the gift becomes a monument to ourselves.
Nebuchadnezzar's rooftop asks every one of us a question:
If everything God allowed you to build disappeared tomorrow, would Jesus still be enough?
Do not answer too quickly.
If the audience disappeared...
If the title disappeared...
If the money disappeared...
If the applause disappeared...
If the beauty faded...
If the influence vanished...
If people stopped recognizing your name...
Would Christ still be your treasure?
Because eventually every earthly Babylon falls.
Empires become ruins.
Names become history.
Possessions change hands.
Bodies return to dust.
The applause stops.
But Jesus Christ remains.
And there is something incredibly beautiful about Nebuchadnezzar finally lifting his eyes toward heaven.
He had been brought low.
But low was not the end.
He looked up.
Maybe that is what you need to do today.
Look up.
Not at your achievements.
Not at your failures.
Not at your reputation.
Not even at your scandal.
Look to Christ.
If you have sinned, repent.
If you have wandered, return.
If you have become proud, humble yourself.
If you have been pretending, stop hiding.
If you have fallen, call upon Jesus.
If you are exhausted from trying to maintain an image of yourself that was never real in the first place, bring the truth into the light.
You do not need another rooftop.
You need grace.
And grace has a name.
Jesus.
Someone reading the same words may need to know they are not the only person being brought back to humility.
That is what Christian community should look like.
Not perfect people performing for one another.
Redeemed people continually pointing one another toward Jesus.
And please do not keep this article trapped on this page.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because clicking a button proves your faith. It does not.
Someone succeeding.
Someone hiding.
Someone compromising.
Someone slowly drifting from God while everything outwardly still looks fine.
Someone may need the warning before they experience the fall.
It is that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
There will probably come a day when you find yourself standing on another rooftop, tempted to forget how much of your life has always depended upon grace.
Come back and read it again.
Supporting faithful Gospel work can become one way we steward what God has entrusted to us when it is done freely, cheerfully, prayerfully, and for His glory rather than ours.
But the greater purpose is discipleship.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling Christian.
Invite the person who has become lukewarm.
Invite the believer rebuilding after failure.
Invite the seeker asking whether Jesus could possibly forgive what they have done.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is merely religion for people pretending to have perfect lives.
Because it isn't.
The Gospel begins with the devastating admission that none of us can boast before God.
And then comes the astonishing news:
Jesus saves.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus restores.
Jesus transforms.
Nebuchadnezzar walked onto his roof believing the greatest story in Babylon was what he had built.
He eventually discovered that the greater story was the God who humbled him enough to make him look toward heaven.
Maybe years from now you will realize the same thing.
Maybe the moment you thought God was stripping something away was actually the moment He was rescuing you from worshiping it.
Maybe the exposure was mercy.
Maybe the broken pride was mercy.
Maybe the unanswered prayer was mercy.
Maybe being brought low was not God abandoning you.
Maybe it was God refusing to leave you on the rooftop believing you were your own king.
And maybe your story does not have to end where your pride, your sin, your failure, or your scandal says it should.
Because when Jesus Christ enters the story, ruins are not always endings.
Sometimes they are where resurrection begins.
Never forget this: Nebuchadnezzar had to lose sight of his own greatness before he finally lifted his eyes and saw God's.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Jesus Washed Feet. Why Do Some Leaders Demand Thrones?
paragraphs: Jesus Washed Feet. Why Do Some Leaders Demand Thrones?

The night before the cross, the One who possessed all authority did something terrifying to human pride: He knelt. And if our Christianity keeps making us more entitled to honor instead of more willing to serve, we may need to ask whether we are actually becoming like the Christ whose name we carry.
There was a towel on His waist.
Water in a basin.
Dust on the feet in front of Him.
And within hours, nails would be driven through His flesh.
Do not rush past that scene.
Because the hands holding those dirty feet were the hands of the One through whom all things were made.
Jesus knew exactly who He was.
John makes that detail impossible to miss.
The Father had given all things into His hands. Jesus knew that He had come from God and was returning to God.
And what did the Son of God do with that knowledge?
He got down.
That may be one of the most devastating pictures of leadership in the entire Bible.
Because we often imagine that the more important someone becomes, the more people should serve them.
Jesus reveals something radically different.
The more clearly He knows His authority...
the lower He bends.
John describes the moment in the Greek text:
“ἤρξατο νίπτειν τοὺς πόδας τῶν μαθητῶν”
ērxato niptein tous podas tōn mathētōn
“He began to wash the feet of the disciples.”
John 13:5.
Not metaphorically.
Not from a platform.
Not through an assistant.
Jesus physically took their feet into His hands.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable detail is not merely that He washed feet.
It is whose feet were in that room.
Peter was there.
The man who would soon swear that he did not know Him.
The other disciples were there.
Men who would scatter when Jesus was arrested.
And Judas was there.
John explicitly places Judas's coming betrayal inside the setting of the meal before describing Jesus rising, taking the towel, and washing the disciples' feet.
Think about that.
Jesus knew betrayal was already moving toward Him...
and still reached for the basin.
Some of us struggle to speak kindly to someone who embarrassed us.
Some cannot forgive the family member who wounded us.
Some leaders become cold when their loyalty is questioned.

Some Christians can worship with raised hands on Sunday and spend Monday demanding recognition, defending status, collecting titles, protecting reputations, and punishing anyone who fails to honor them sufficiently.
Then Jesus kneels in front of people who are about to fail Him.
Suddenly our excuses become very small.
This article is not an attack on leadership.
Scripture recognizes leadership, elders, shepherds, teachers, authority, order, honor, responsibility, and accountability. Biblical humility does not mean pretending leadership does not exist.
The issue is not whether Christians should lead.
The issue is what Christian leadership is supposed to look like.
And Jesus did not leave that question unanswered.
After washing their feet, He said:
“ὑπόδειγμα γὰρ ἔδωκα ὑμῖν”
hypodeigma gar dedōka hymin
“For I have given you an example.”
John 13:15.
An example.
Not a publicity stunt.
Not a sentimental moment inserted into Holy Week.
An example.
Christ was showing His disciples the shape His authority must take in those who belong to Him.
And this is where the towel begins confronting the throne hidden inside us.
Because wanting a throne is not only a pastor's temptation.
It can happen to anyone.
You can demand a throne without ever standing behind a pulpit.
A father can demand one in his home.
A mother can demand one from her children.
A ministry volunteer can demand one through recognition.
A worship leader can demand one through applause.
A Christian creator can demand one through numbers.
A church member can demand one through influence.
A husband can call control “headship.”
A spiritual leader can call unquestioning loyalty “submission.”
A believer can call wounded pride “discernment.”
Sometimes the throne is not made of gold.
Sometimes it is simply the desperate need to be noticed.
To be thanked.
To be consulted.
To be praised.
To win every disagreement.
To have the final word.
To make people feel guilty when they leave.
To remind everyone how much we sacrificed.
To make ourselves indispensable.
And this is where Scripture stops being something we examine and becomes something that examines us.
Because before asking, “Why do some leaders demand thrones?”
perhaps we should whisper:
“Jesus... where am I demanding one?”
That question hurts differently.
James and John once came to Jesus wanting prominent seats in His glory.
They wanted proximity to the throne.
Jesus answered by redefining greatness itself.
In Mark 10, He contrasted the domination practiced by Gentile rulers with life among His disciples. The Greek becomes especially sharp:
“οὐχ οὕτως δέ ἐστιν ἐν ὑμῖν”
ouch houtōs de estin en hymin
“But it is not so among you.”
Then He says the one who wants to become great must become a διάκονος — diakonos, a servant, and whoever wants to be first must become πάντων δοῦλος — pantōn doulos, “slave of all.”
Then comes the reason:
Even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many. Mark 10:45.
There is the Christian revolution.
Jesus does not merely tell ambitious people to stop being great.
He tells them what greatness looks like in His kingdom.
Serve.
Give.
Lower yourself.
Spend yourself for others.
Not because you are worthless.
Because you belong to the King who did exactly that.
Christian humility is not insecurity.
Jesus was not washing feet because He had forgotten His identity.
John tells us the opposite.
He knew where He came from.
He knew where He was going.
He knew what the Father had placed into His hands.
And because His identity was secure, He did not need other people's submission to prove His significance.
That is worth reading twice.
When you know who you are before the Father, you do not have to turn everyone around you into evidence that you matter.
You can serve without being photographed.
You can apologize without losing your identity.
You can listen without surrendering truth.
You can celebrate another person's success without feeling diminished.
You can correct someone without humiliating them.
You can carry authority without becoming addicted to control.
You can hold a title without needing everyone to bow emotionally before it.
Jesus had nothing to prove.
So He could kneel.

And perhaps some of our obsession with thrones comes from the fact that somewhere beneath the religious vocabulary, we are terrified that if people stop applauding us, we will discover how insecure we really are.
So we collect recognition.
Followers.
Positions.
Honorifics.
Influence.
Access.
Platforms.
And none of those things are automatically sinful.
A platform can preach Christ.
Money can feed people.
Influence can defend the vulnerable.
Leadership can protect a congregation.
A large ministry can accomplish enormous good.
The problem begins when the platform stops being an altar and becomes a throne.
When ministry becomes identity.
When disagreement becomes disloyalty.
When accountability becomes “rebellion.”
When questions become threats.
When wounded people are treated as liabilities to the brand.
When the shepherd begins needing the sheep to feed his ego.
That is not the pattern Jesus gave us.
Jesus said:
“οὐκ ἔστιν δοῦλος μείζων τοῦ κυρίου αὐτοῦ”
ouk estin doulos meizōn tou kyriou autou
“A servant is not greater than his master.”
John 13:16.
So here is the uncomfortable question.
If our Master carried a towel...
why are His servants fighting over thrones?
But there is another danger here.
It would be easy to finish this article angry at pastors, bishops, ministry leaders, Christian celebrities, or someone who hurt you.
Please do not miss Jesus that way.
The Gospel is not primarily a weapon for exposing everyone else's pride.
It is first a mirror.
Maybe nobody knows about your throne.
Maybe yours sits inside your marriage.
Maybe you punish people with silence until they apologize.
Maybe you secretly resent people who receive the opportunities you wanted.
Maybe you serve faithfully but become bitter when nobody notices.
Maybe you post Scripture partly because you love Christ and partly because you desperately want people to admire your spirituality.
Maybe you give...
but need your name remembered.
Maybe you forgive...
but make sure the person never forgets what they did.
Maybe you call yourself a servant...
until someone actually treats you like one.
That last one exposes us.
It is easy to love the title “servant of God.”
It is much harder when serving costs something.
When nobody applauds.
When somebody misunderstands you.
When another person receives the credit.
When you wash feet and the feet walk away without saying thank you.
And suddenly we understand why we need more than leadership principles.
We need a Savior.
Because Christianity is not the story of morally superior people learning better management techniques.
It is the story of sinners who cannot cleanse themselves being rescued by the Son of God.
Peter initially resisted Jesus washing him.
“Lord, are You washing my feet?”
Then he protested.
Jesus answered with words far deeper than etiquette:
“If I do not wash you, you have no part with Me.”
Before Peter could imitate the washing...
Peter had to receive it.
Do you see the Gospel hiding in plain sight?
Before you become useful, you must admit that you need cleansing.
Before you serve Christ, Christ must save you.
Before your hands carry the towel, your heart must surrender to the One carrying it.
And the basin points forward.

John opens the scene by saying Jesus loved His own εἰς τέλος — eis telos: “to the end,” with the expression carrying the sense of His love reaching its full extent. The foot washing anticipates the sacrificial love soon to be displayed at the cross.
The towel was not the end of His descent.
There was a cross coming.
The One kneeling before dirty feet would soon be stripped.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
The hands washing dust away would be pierced.
The knees bending beside the basin would carry Him toward Calvary.
And Jesus would do something infinitely greater than wash dirt from skin.
He would give His life as a ransom for many.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Our scandal is deeper than corrupt leadership.
It is deeper than celebrity Christianity.
It is deeper than hypocritical ministers.
The scandal lives inside every human heart that wants God's throne while resisting God's rule.
We have all wanted to be our own king.
We have all sinned.
We have all needed cleansing we could never accomplish ourselves.
And Jesus came anyway.
He did not climb onto a human throne and demand that sinners crawl toward Him.
The King came down.
He served.
He suffered.
He carried sin to the cross.
He died.
And He rose.
That is why repentance is not humiliation for humiliation's sake.
Repentance is coming down from a throne that was killing you and discovering that the rightful King is merciful.
Maybe you have been hurt by spiritual leadership.
Maybe someone used the name of Jesus while behaving nothing like Him.
Maybe Scripture was twisted to control you.
Maybe “honor” became a weapon.
Maybe your questions were treated as rebellion.
Maybe you were made to believe that protecting a leader's reputation mattered more than telling the truth.
Do not confuse someone's misuse of Christ's name with Christ Himself.
Look at Jesus.
Look at the towel.
Look at the basin.
Look at the cross.
Human leaders can fail you.
Jesus remains Lord.
And if you are a leader reading this, do not read these words merely thinking about someone worse than you.
Ask the dangerous prayer:
“Jesus, show me where I have loved the throne more than the towel.”
Show me where I demand what You never demanded.
Show me where my ego has disguised itself as authority.
Show me whether people around me are becoming more like Christ—or simply more afraid of disappointing me.
Show me whether I am building Your kingdom or quietly building a monument to myself.
And give me enough grace to repent when You answer.
That prayer can save a ministry from becoming a machine.
It can save a marriage.
A family.
A friendship.
Perhaps even a church.
Because repentance is not the death of Christian leadership.
Repentance is often where Christian leadership finally begins.
The greatest Leader who ever walked this earth knelt.
The highest King became the servant.
The sinless One died for sinners.
And the grave could not hold Him.
So no, the answer is not that Christians should despise leadership.
The answer is that Christian leadership must keep returning to Jesus.
Authority under His authority.
Strength shaped by His character.
Truth spoken with His love.
Courage without cruelty.
Conviction without vanity.
Leadership without idolatry.
A crown surrendered beneath the cross.
A towel within reach.
And perhaps tonight, the person who needs to surrender the throne is not “that pastor.”
Not that famous preacher.
Not your spouse.
Not your father.
Not your boss.
Maybe it is you.
Maybe it is me.
That is the uncomfortable beauty of grace.
Jesus does not expose our pride merely to shame us.
He calls us down because He loves us too much to leave us worshiping ourselves.

And if Christ has already been teaching you that leadership means serving rather than being worshiped, share part of your testimony. Someone reading the comments may need the hope God has already written into your story.
Then do something beyond commenting.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Salvation is God's gift of grace, received through faith—not a transaction we can buy.
But if this message is proclaiming truth that you believe another person needs, sharing it can become one small act of service.
Someone may be becoming the very kind of leader Jesus warned against.
Someone may be sitting quietly in a church wondering whether Jesus Himself is really like the people who wounded them.
Let them see the towel.
Send this to the Christian who is becoming influential before influence becomes their identity.
Save it too, because pride rarely dies after reading one article. We need to return again and again to the Christ who kneels.
Jesus has already paid the price we never could.
Go back to the room.
Hear the water.
See the basin.
Watch the King kneel.
Then ask yourself whether the Christianity you are living looks anything like the Christ you claim to follow.
Because someday every earthly platform will disappear.
Every title will become irrelevant.
Every follower count will reach zero.
Every stage light will go dark.
Every human throne will become dust.
But Jesus Christ will still be King.
And astonishingly, the King who deserves every throne is the King who took the towel, went to the cross, conquered the grave, and still calls proud, broken, scandal-covered people into grace.
When everyone else is fighting for the highest seat, never forget the sound of your King pouring water into a basin.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Philippians 4:13 Does NOT Mean What Many People Think It Means — And the Truth Is Far More Powerful
paragraphs: Philippians 4:13 Does NOT Mean What Many People Think It Means — And the Truth Is Far More Powerful
“I can do all things through Christ” was never a promise that you would always win. It was the testimony of a man who discovered that even when everything else was taken away, Jesus was still enough.
There is a version of Philippians 4:13 that looks beautiful on a coffee mug.
Then there is the version you need when you are crying where nobody can see you.
Those are not always the same thing.
“I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.”

For generations, Philippians 4:13 has been written beneath championship photographs, printed across shirts, quoted before examinations, whispered before interviews, posted before business launches, and repeated whenever someone needs courage to accomplish something difficult.
And there is nothing wrong with asking Christ for strength.
But what if the verse is saying something deeper than, “Jesus will help me achieve what I want”?
What if we have sometimes turned a declaration of radical dependence into a slogan about personal achievement?
Because Paul was not standing on a winner's podium when the words of Philippians 4:13 were born.
He was writing as a man intimately acquainted with suffering.
And immediately before the famous verse, Paul speaks about something our success-obsessed world rarely puts on motivational posters:
Need.
Hunger.
Having little.
Having plenty.
Contentment.
Listen to the flow of his thought:
“I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.”
Then Paul explains that he knows what it is to be brought low and what it is to abound. He knows fullness, and he knows hunger. He knows abundance, and he knows need.
Then comes the sentence we love:
“I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me.”
That context changes everything.
Paul's “all things” includes the mountain.
But it also includes the valley.
It includes abundance.
But it also includes emptiness.
It includes the days when provision arrives.
And it includes the nights when you have to trust God while the answer still has not come.
Paul's declaration is not merely, “Christ gives me strength to accomplish extraordinary things.”
It is closer to this:
Whatever circumstance obedience to Christ requires me to walk through, I have strength in the One who strengthens me.

That understanding follows directly from Philippians 4:11–13, where Paul says he has learned contentment in need and abundance, hunger and fullness. The Greek places πάντα—panta, “all things”—prominently at the beginning of verse 13, while the surrounding sentences define the circumstances Paul has in view.
And suddenly this verse becomes much more dangerous to despair.
Because maybe you are reading this after something did not work out.
Maybe you prayed.
Believed.
Waited.
Quoted Scripture.
And the door still closed.
Maybe somebody else got the opportunity.
Maybe the relationship still ended.
Maybe the money became tighter.
Maybe the person you loved still walked away.
Maybe you did everything you knew to do, and instead of standing on a mountain shouting, “I can do all things,” you found yourself sitting in the wreckage asking:
Jesus… where are You?
Philippians 4:13 was written for that moment too.
Especially that moment.
The Greek text reads:
πάντα ἰσχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμοῦντί με
Panta ischyō en tō endynamounti me.

The verb ἰσχύω — ischyō carries the sense of having strength, being able, prevailing, or possessing the strength required. ἐνδυναμοῦντί — endynamounti comes from a verb meaning to strengthen or empower. So Paul's confidence is not rooted in some hidden reservoir of extraordinary human willpower. His adequacy comes from outside himself—from the One continually supplying strength.
Notice something else important.
Several early and highly regarded Greek manuscripts read simply:
πάντα ἰσχύω ἐν τῷ ἐνδυναμοῦντί με
“I have strength for all things in/through the One strengthening me.”

Other manuscript traditions explicitly include Χριστῷ — Christō, “Christ,” which is why familiar translations such as the KJV read, “through Christ which strengtheneth me.” This textual difference does not turn the passage away from Christ: Paul's letter repeatedly locates his life, joy, confidence, and sufficiency in the Lord, and the immediate passage begins with his rejoicing “in the Lord.” But accuracy matters, especially when claiming to examine the original wording.
And perhaps that textual detail makes the sentence feel even more intimate:
the One strengthening me.
Not merely the One who strengthened Paul once.
The One strengthening him.
In the hunger.
In the abundance.
In the humiliation.
In the uncertainty.
In the prison.
In the waiting.
God did not always strengthen Paul by removing the circumstance.
Sometimes God strengthened Paul inside it.
That distinction may change the way you understand some of your unanswered prayers.
We often pray:
“Jesus, get me out.”
And sometimes He does.
But sometimes His answer is:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).
We ask Him to stop the storm.
Sometimes He does.
Other times He teaches us that the presence of a storm does not mean the absence of Christ.
We ask for the burden to disappear.
Sometimes it disappears.
Sometimes our shoulders become stronger because we discover they were never carrying it alone.
This is where Philippians 4:13 stops being merchandise and becomes medicine.
You can lose something and still belong to Christ.
You can be disappointed and still worship.
You can be exhausted and still obey.
You can have questions and still trust Him.
You can be overlooked and still be loved by God.
You can walk through a season you never would have chosen without surrendering your soul to bitterness.
You can have little and remain spiritually rich.
You can have much without allowing possessions to possess you.
You can survive the chapter you thought would destroy you.
Not because Christians are invincible.
Because Christ is faithful.
There is an enormous difference.
Biblical Christianity does not teach that believers can accomplish anything whatsoever simply by attaching Jesus' name to their ambition.
If that were Paul's meaning, “all things” would become permission for desires God never promised to fulfill.
Christ does not exist to baptize our ego.
He came to crucify the old self and raise us into new life.
Jesus said, “without me ye can do nothing” (John 15:5).
Paul says, in effect, that through the One strengthening him, he can face all these circumstances.
Those truths belong together.
Without Christ: nothing.
In Christ: strength for whatever faithful obedience requires.
And that means Philippians 4:13 may actually confront us before it comforts us.
Because some of us do not merely want Christ's strength.
We want Christ to strengthen our plan.
We want Jesus as fuel for our ambition.
Jesus as insurance for our dreams.
Jesus as the divine signature beneath the future we already designed.
But following Jesus begins with surrender.
Christ did not say, “Come after Me, and I will guarantee every version of success you imagine.”
He said:
“Follow me.”
That road eventually led to a cross.
And then to resurrection.
That is the pattern of the Gospel.
Death before resurrection.
Surrender before transformation.
Grace where scandal once lived.
A cross before an empty tomb.
Maybe that is why this verse becomes most beautiful when your own strength finally runs out.
Because as long as you believe you can save yourself, you will keep trying.
You will perform.
Pretend.
Hide.
Smile when you are collapsing.
Tell everyone you are blessed while privately wondering why your soul feels empty.
You will compare your life with somebody else's highlight reel and quietly conclude that perhaps God loves them more.
Then one day the illusion breaks.
You cannot fix everything.
You cannot control everybody.
You cannot undo yesterday.
You cannot earn forgiveness.
You cannot make yourself righteous before a holy God.
You cannot carry your sin into eternity and somehow convince God that being “better than most people” should be enough.
And right there—in the place human pride calls failure—the Gospel announces astonishing news.
Jesus Christ did what you could never do.
He lived the righteousness you could never perfectly live.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He rose again.
And salvation is not the trophy handed to people strong enough to reach God.
It is grace given to sinners who come to God through Christ in repentance and faith.
That is why Philippians 4:13 is not ultimately a monument to Paul's confidence in Paul.
It is a confession of dependence.
Paul is essentially saying:
My circumstances are not my source.
Read that again.
My circumstances are not my source.
If I have abundance, Christ remains my strength.
If I have little, Christ remains my strength.
If people applaud me, Christ remains my strength.
If they forget my name, Christ remains my strength.
If tomorrow looks promising, Christ remains my strength.
If tomorrow terrifies me, Christ remains my strength.
Jesus does not become more faithful when your bank account is full.
He does not become less sovereign when the diagnosis frightens you.
He does not become more present because people celebrate you.
He does not abandon His throne because somebody abandoned you.
Your circumstances change.
Christ does not.
And somebody desperately needed to remember that tonight.
Perhaps you have been secretly measuring God's goodness by whether He gives you what you asked for.
Perhaps you have been thinking:
“If God loved me, this would have happened.”
“If I had enough faith, this door would have opened.”
“If Jesus were really with me, I would not be hurting this badly.”
But Paul dismantles that theology with his own testimony.
He had Christ when he had plenty.
He had Christ when he was hungry.
He had Christ when he abounded.
He had Christ when he suffered need.
The miracle was not that Paul never experienced lack.
The miracle was that lack could no longer determine whether Christ was enough.
That is contentment.
Not pretending pain does not hurt.
Not calling evil good.
Not refusing to grieve.
Not becoming emotionally numb.
Biblical contentment is a learned confidence that your deepest sufficiency rests in Christ rather than circumstances.
Paul explicitly says, “I have learned” contentment.
Learned.
Meaning Paul did not simply wake up one morning spiritually immune to hardship.
There was a process.
Perhaps there is one happening in you too.
The disappointment may be teaching you.
The waiting may be exposing you.
The loneliness may be showing you where you have been looking for identity.
The closed door may be revealing how deeply your peace depended on getting your way.
