Share because somewhere behind another glowing screen may be a husband telling himself, “We're only friends.”
A wife deleting a conversation she knows she should not need to delete.
A lonely believer drifting toward someone else's arms emotionally before their body ever follows.
A betrayed spouse wondering whether their pain counts.
A ashamed Christian convinced Jesus could forgive everyone except them.
Send it to that person.
Because sometimes God uses a truth somebody almost did not share to interrupt a decision somebody almost could not undo.
And if that person is you...
Put the phone down for a moment.
Look at your heart.
Say the name you have been avoiding.
Tell Jesus the truth.
Then do the next faithful thing.
The secret conversation may have begun quietly.
The attachment may have grown slowly.
The boundary may already have moved farther than you intended.
But while you still have breath, repentance can begin.
Grace is still calling.
Christ is still able to forgive.
Truth can still enter the room.
What has been wounded can still be brought to the Great Physician.
And your worst hidden chapter does not have to become the sentence that defines the rest of your life.
The relationship you are afraid to surrender may be the very thing standing between you and the healing you keep asking God to give.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “COME TO ME”—THE THREE WORDS EXHAUSTED CHRISTIANS KEEP READING TOO FAST
paragraphs:
“COME TO ME”—THE THREE WORDS EXHAUSTED CHRISTIANS KEEP READING TOO FAST
What Jesus Really Meant by “Come to Me, All Who Are Weary”—and Why His Invitation May Be Speaking to the Part of You That Is Tired of Pretending You’re Fine
There is a kind of tiredness sleep cannot cure.
You can sleep eight hours and wake up carrying it.
You can take a vacation and pack it in your suitcase.
You can sit in church, raise your hands during worship, smile when somebody asks how you are doing, whisper “God is good” at exactly the right moment...
and still go home exhausted.
Not merely physically tired.
Soul tired.
Tired of fighting the same temptation.
Tired of wondering why the prayer still seems unanswered.
Tired of carrying everybody while quietly wondering who would carry you if you finally collapsed.
Tired of trying to be the strong Christian.
Tired of disappointing yourself.
Tired of promising God, “This is the last time,” only to find yourself kneeling beside the wreckage of another failure.
Tired of hiding.
Tired of performing.
Tired of being needed.
Tired of being afraid.
Tired of knowing Bible verses your heart seems too wounded to feel.
And somewhere inside all that exhaustion, there may be a question you are almost afraid to say aloud:
“Jesus... what if I don’t have much left?”
That is exactly why three words spoken by Christ deserve to be heard again.
Not as Christian wall art.
Not as a comforting caption beneath a photograph of a sunset.
Not as religious anesthesia.
Listen to them as though you were standing in the crowd when they first left His mouth.
“Come to Me.”
The Gospel of Matthew preserves the saying in Greek:
“Δεῦτε πρός με πάντες οἱ κοπιῶντες καὶ πεφορτισμένοι, κἀγὼ ἀναπαύσω ὑμᾶς.”
“Come to Me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest.”
Matthew 11:28.
Slow down.
Because the most astonishing part of that sentence may not be “rest.”
It may be “Me.”
Jesus does not merely say, “Come learn a better coping mechanism.”
He does not say, “Come discover the hidden strength already inside yourself.”
He does not say, “Come fix yourself, clean yourself, prove yourself, and then perhaps I will receive you.”
He says:
“Come to Me.”
That changes everything.
The Greek expression begins, “Δεῦτε πρός με”—deute pros me.
“Come to Me.”
It is an invitation toward a Person.
Christianity, at its center, is not exhausted people being handed another religious checklist.
It is sinners being summoned to Christ.
And the context makes this even more breathtaking.
Immediately before this invitation, Jesus speaks about His unique relationship with the Father and declares that the Father is known through the Son. Then comes the invitation.
Come to Me.
In other words, Jesus is not standing on the roadside merely offering inspirational advice to stressed people.
He is placing Himself at the center of the invitation.
The exhausted are summoned to Him.
The burdened are summoned to Him.
And that means your deepest need is not merely a lighter schedule.
You need Jesus.
Maybe that is difficult to hear because we have become experts at treating symptoms.
We think, “If I could just make more money, I would finally breathe.”
“If my marriage changed, I would finally have peace.”
“If this anxiety disappeared...”
“If my children came back...”
“If the diagnosis changed...”
“If people understood me...”
“If I could undo what I did...”
“If I could stop thinking about what they did to me...”
“If God would finally answer this one prayer...”
Then I could rest.
Some of those desires are completely understandable. Some are things worth praying about.
But Jesus goes beneath them.
Because you can have money and still have no rest.
You can have applause and still hate the silence.
You can have thousands of followers and feel completely unseen.
You can escape one difficult season and discover that your own heart traveled with you.
Jesus does not merely offer changed circumstances.
He offers Himself.
And notice who receives the invitation.
“πάντες οἱ κοπιῶντες καὶ πεφορτισμένοι.”
All who are laboring and burdened.
The word translated “weary” or “laboring” comes from κοπιάω, carrying the sense of laboring, working to the point of weariness.
Then Matthew gives us πεφορτισμένοι—a form describing those who have been loaded or burdened.
Do you see the picture?
People exhausted from carrying.
And perhaps that describes somebody reading this right now.
You have become frighteningly good at carrying things nobody knows about.
You carry childhood wounds into adult relationships.
You carry rejection into every room and call it independence.
You carry shame underneath ministry.
You carry pornography underneath worship songs.
You carry resentment underneath politeness.
You carry fear underneath ambition.
You carry loneliness underneath jokes.
You carry disappointment with God underneath theological answers.
You carry secret sin underneath public Christianity.
Nobody sees the weight because you learned how to smile while lifting it.
But Jesus sees.
And He says:
Come.
Not when you have conquered everything.
Come.
Not when you have become impressive.
Come.
Not after you have hidden the evidence.
Come.
There is something scandalous about grace because grace destroys our favorite illusion—that somehow we can make ourselves worthy enough to need less mercy.
The Gospel says something far more humbling and far more beautiful.
You cannot save yourself.

Sin is not merely a collection of unfortunate habits requiring self-improvement. Scripture describes humanity as guilty before God and unable to establish its own righteousness. We have sinned. We need reconciliation. We need forgiveness. We need a Savior.
And Christianity announces that God did not wait for sinners to climb their way back to Him.
Jesus Christ came for sinners.
He lived in righteousness.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the One saying “Come to Me” is not offering cheap comfort that pretends your sin does not matter.
He is the Savior who dealt with sin at the cost of His own blood.
That is why grace is not God saying your rebellion was insignificant.
Grace is God demonstrating just how serious sin is—and how astonishing His mercy is—at the cross.
Maybe you have spent years thinking Jesus is waiting for the improved version of you.
Read His invitation again.
“Come to Me.”
But now we must keep reading, because this is where one of the most beautiful sayings of Jesus is sometimes misunderstood.
Christ does not say:
“Come to Me, and you will never carry anything again.”
He says:
“Take My yoke upon you.”
That sounds almost shocking.
You came carrying a burden...
and Jesus mentions a yoke?
The Greek reads:
“ἄρατε τὸν ζυγόν μου ἐφ’ ὑμᾶς καὶ μάθετε ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ...”
“Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me...”
Matthew 11:29.
Jesus is not inviting you into autonomous comfort.
He is inviting you into discipleship.
This is not “Jesus will make sure nothing difficult ever happens to you.”
He Himself tells His followers elsewhere that discipleship includes self-denial and a cross.
The apostles suffered.
The early church suffered.
Faithfulness has never meant exemption from pain.
So what kind of rest is this?
Listen to Jesus finish the sentence:
“...καὶ εὑρήσετε ἀνάπαυσιν ταῖς ψυχαῖς ὑμῶν.”
“And you will find rest for your souls.”
Your souls.
This goes deeper than circumstances.
The word ἀνάπαυσις carries the idea of rest, repose, refreshment.
Jesus is speaking to something beneath your calendar.
Beneath your workload.
Beneath your public image.
The soul.
And there is another detail we cannot miss.
Jesus describes Himself.
“πραΰς εἰμι καὶ ταπεινὸς τῇ καρδίᾳ.”
“I am gentle and humble in heart.”
Think about who is saying this.
The One through whom we come to know the Father.
The Lord who commands repentance.
The King before whom every knee will ultimately bow.
And when burdened sinners approach Him, He tells them something about His heart:
Gentle.
Humble.
Some people are afraid to come to Jesus because they have confused Him with the people who misrepresented Him.
Perhaps somebody used Scripture to humiliate you.
Perhaps religion became a place where everybody performed holiness while wounds were pushed underground.
Perhaps you were taught to fear everybody discovering who you really were.
Perhaps you started believing God tolerates you from a distance but secretly wishes you were somebody else.
But listen to Christ describe His own heart.
Gentle.
Humble.
This does not mean indifferent toward sin.
The Jesus who says “Come” also calls people to repentance.
Grace never requires God to pretend darkness is light.
Jesus loves sinners too much to bless the chains destroying them.
He receives us as we come, but His grace does not leave us where sin has taken us.
That is why coming to Christ is both comfort and surrender.
You bring Him the burden.
And you take His yoke.
You stop pretending you are your own savior.
You stop negotiating with the sin you were commanded to forsake.
You stop using grace as permission to remain unchanged.
You stop trying to earn what only mercy can give.
You come.
You repent.
You believe.
You learn from Him.
You follow Him.
And slowly, sometimes painfully, sometimes through tears nobody sees, Christ begins rewriting what sin tried to make the final chapter.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
That would not be redemption.
He enters the wreckage.
Peter denied Him.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
The man who insisted he would remain faithful crumbled when faithfulness became dangerous.
Then came the rooster.
Sometimes one sound can carry an entire lifetime of regret.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
But failure did not get Peter’s final sentence.
The risen Christ restored him.
Not because denial suddenly became acceptable.
Not because Peter deserved another chance.
Grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Think of the woman in John 4.
Complicated history.
Broken relationships.
A life Jesus knew before she explained it.
Yet Christ deliberately met her beside a well and offered living water.
Her history was real.
But her history was not more powerful than the One sitting beside her.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Think about the criminal dying beside Jesus.
No lifetime left to repair his reputation.
No decades available to accumulate religious achievements.
He could not climb down from his cross and build an impressive testimony.
He could only turn toward Christ.
And Christ was enough.
Maybe that is why this invitation frightens us.
Because “Come to Me” means surrendering the fantasy that someday we will save ourselves.
There is a strange exhaustion produced by self-salvation.
Always proving.
Always comparing.
Always hiding.
Always wondering whether you have prayed enough, accomplished enough, suffered enough, given enough, impressed enough people, cleaned yourself thoroughly enough for God to finally want you.
But you cannot outperform your need for grace.
The Gospel does not say, “Try harder until God owes you.”
The Gospel says Christ has done what sinners could never do for themselves.
This does not produce laziness.
Grace produces worship.
Obedience stops being a desperate attempt to purchase God's love and becomes the grateful response of someone who has been loved in Christ.
And maybe tonight, that is the burden beneath all your other burdens.
You are exhausted from trying to be enough.
Enough for your parents.
Enough for your spouse.
Enough for your church.
Enough for the internet.
Enough for yourself.
Maybe even enough for God.
Jesus says:
Come to Me.
You do not need to impress the One who already knows everything.
He knows the thought you never told anyone.
He knows what happened behind that closed door.
He knows the relapse.
He knows the bitterness.
He knows the questions.
He knows the night you nearly gave up.
He knows why you became cold.
He knows why you stopped trusting people.
He knows the prayer you are embarrassed to pray.
He knows.
And still the invitation stands.
Come to Me.
But do not confuse coming with merely feeling emotional while reading Christian words.
Come means come.
Turn toward Christ.
Bring the sin into the light.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Ask for help where secrecy has become your prison.
Open Scripture again.
Pray even when your prayer comes out broken.
Return to fellowship if isolation has been feeding your darkness.
Stop waiting to become worthy of mercy.
You never will.
That is why mercy is mercy.
Perhaps somebody reading this has been away from Jesus for years.
You still know the songs.
You still know when to say “Amen.”
You know enough Christian vocabulary to make everybody believe you are spiritually alive.
But inside?
Dry.
Far away.
Secretly compromised.
Exhausted from pretending.
Maybe you have wondered whether you have gone too far.
Hear the invitation again.
Come to Me.
Not to an internet personality.
Not to Gospel Warrior.
Not to a denomination.
Not to a personality cult.
To Jesus Christ.
Everything we write should ultimately become a finger pointing beyond ourselves toward Him.
Jesus saves.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus restores.
Jesus transforms.
Jesus is Lord.
And if these words have exposed something you have been hiding, do not rush past that moment.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need impressive language.
Maybe it is simply:
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
There is no trophy for pretending.
And somebody else reading your comment may finally find the courage to stop pretending too.
Because there may come a night when the strong version of you disappears again.
A night when the old accusation returns.
A night when the burden feels heavier.
Come back and remember:
Jesus never said you had to become invulnerable.
He said you had to come.
Financial support is not what makes someone faithful to Christ, but generous believers have always been able to use their resources to help Gospel ministry go farther.
It is discipleship.
Truth.
Encouragement.
Conviction.
Accountability.
Biblical nourishment.
And helping put the Gospel before another weary human being.
Then invite someone with you.
A struggling believer.
A family member who has drifted.
A friend who quietly stopped praying.
A lukewarm Christian.
A seeker.
Even someone who does not yet believe.
Because somewhere tonight, a person is lying awake believing exhaustion is proof that God has abandoned them.
Somebody is scrolling through Facebook because silence makes the pain louder.
Somebody is hiding a failure.
Somebody is considering giving up.
Somebody thinks their scandal became their identity.
And perhaps God can use something as ordinary as your share to put an extraordinary invitation in front of them:
Come to Me.
Not “fix yourself.”
Come.
Not “pretend harder.”
Come.
Not “hide until you become respectable.”
Come.
To Christ.
And when you come, you discover that the hands receiving weary sinners are the same hands that were pierced for them.
That is where the burden finally meets grace.
At the feet of Jesus.
So if you remember nothing else from these words, remember this:
You were never meant to carry the weight of being your own savior when the Savior Himself is still saying, “Come to Me.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “BUT WHAT IF MY WIFE KEEPS NAGGING ME?”
paragraphs:
“BUT WHAT IF MY WIFE KEEPS NAGGING ME?”
When Her Words Feel Like Disrespect, Your Heart Starts Closing, and You Wonder How Long God Expects You to Keep Loving Like This
There is a moment some husbands never talk about.
Not with their pastor.
Not with their friends.
Sometimes not even with God.
It happens after another argument.
Another correction.
Another sigh from across the room.
Another sentence that somehow makes you feel as though nothing you do is enough.
You worked.
You came home tired.
You tried to provide.
You tried to keep your mouth shut because you knew where the conversation might go.
And then it starts again.
“Why haven't you done this?”
“How many times do I have to tell you?”
“You never listen.”
“Why can't you just...?”
Something inside you tightens.
You don't necessarily yell.
Sometimes you just become quiet.
Cold.
Distant.
You pick up your phone.
You walk into another room.
You stay at work a little longer the next day.
And eventually a dangerous sentence begins forming in your heart:
“What if my wife just won't stop nagging me?”
Maybe you've even found Bible verses that seem to validate how miserable you feel.
Proverbs certainly doesn't pretend that destructive conflict inside a home is harmless.
“...the contentions of a wife are a continual dropping.”
— Proverbs 19:13, KJV
Proverbs 21:9 even says:
“It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman in a wide house.”
Those are uncomfortable verses.
But before you turn them into ammunition...
before you screenshot them and send them to your wife...
before you use Scripture to put her on trial...
there is something Jesus may want to confront first.
What if the greatest danger to your marriage isn't merely what keeps coming out of her mouth—but what is slowly happening inside your heart?
That question hurts.
Because when you feel disrespected long enough, withdrawal starts feeling justified.
You tell yourself you're keeping the peace.
But sometimes you're actually withholding yourself.
You stop asking questions.
Stop touching her affectionately.
Stop listening with curiosity.
Stop praying for her tenderly.
Stop noticing what is underneath the words.
You remain married physically while slowly filing for divorce emotionally.
And perhaps nobody notices.
There was no affair.
No suitcase by the door.
No dramatic announcement.
Just two people sleeping inches apart...
while their hearts move miles away.
And this is where the Gospel becomes painfully personal.
Because Christianity does not merely teach us how to respond when people treat us the way we think they should.
It reveals who we become when they don't.
Husband, Scripture gives you a command that is far more demanding than winning an argument.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
— Ephesians 5:25, KJV
The Greek is devastatingly beautiful:
Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας
Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas.
“Husbands, love your wives.”
That word ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate is a present imperative form of agapaō.
In other words, Paul isn't merely describing a feeling you hopefully maintain when marriage is pleasant.
He is commanding a continuing posture of love.
And then Paul destroys every convenient definition of love by giving husbands the standard:
καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν
“as Christ also loved the church.”
Think about that before reading another sentence.
Christ loved the Church.
Not because the Church had never failed Him.
Not because His bride had never disappointed Him.
Not because we had perfectly honored Him.
He loved sinners.
He moved toward the undeserving.
He gave Himself.

That does not mean sin, cruelty, manipulation, contempt, or abuse should be ignored. Biblical love is not pretending evil is good. Serious or unsafe behavior requires truth, wise pastoral counsel, professional help where appropriate, boundaries, and—in situations involving danger—immediate attention to safety.
But ordinary marital conflict presents another uncomfortable question:
What if you have been asking, “Does she deserve my tenderness?” when Jesus has been asking, “Will you love her as someone who belongs to Me?”
And wife, if you're reading over his shoulder, there is a word for you too.
The Bible does not give you permission to repeatedly humiliate, belittle, mock, or contemptuously tear down your husband and then call it “communication.”
“Death and life are in the power of the tongue...”
— Proverbs 18:21, KJV
Your husband's failures may need to be addressed.
His irresponsibility may need to be confronted.
His habits may genuinely frustrate you.
But there is a difference between addressing a problem and attacking a person.
Between:
“We need to talk about what happened.”
and:
“You always ruin everything.”
Between:
“I need you to hear me.”
and:
“You're useless.”
Words can expose a wound.
Words can also deepen one.
But husband...
there is another possibility you may not want to consider.
What you call “nagging” may sometimes be a woman who has been trying desperately to tell you something you keep refusing to hear.
Not always.
But sometimes.
Maybe she has repeated herself because the first ten times disappeared into your phone.
Maybe what sounds like criticism to you began months ago as a gentle request.
Maybe she isn't really angry about the dishes.
Or the laundry.
Or the money.
Or the thing you forgot.
Maybe underneath the anger is:
“Do I matter to you?”
Maybe underneath the repeated reminders is:
“Can I depend on you?”
Maybe underneath the sharp tone is:
“Are we still a team?”
Maybe underneath “You never listen” is a woman wondering whether the man who once studied every detail of her heart has stopped being curious about it.
That doesn't justify sinful communication.
But wisdom listens beneath the volume.
Because sometimes the argument isn't really about what the argument is about.
You think you're fighting over a dirty kitchen.
She's grieving partnership.
You think you're fighting over money.
She's afraid.
You think you're fighting over how late you came home.
She's lonely.
You think you're fighting because she “doesn't respect you.”
Meanwhile she may be wondering:
“Does he still cherish me?”
And suddenly there are two wounded people in the same house, each waiting for the other person to become Christlike first.
That's how marriages freeze.
“I'll respect you when you love me properly.”
“I'll love you when you respect me properly.”
“I'll apologize when you apologize.”
“I'll change when you change.”
And Satan doesn't always need to destroy a Christian marriage with one spectacular scandal.
Sometimes all he needs is two proud people keeping score.
Then Jesus walks into the scorekeeping.
And the cross ruins the game.
Because at Calvary, Christ did not wait for sinners to clean themselves up before He moved toward them.
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
— Romans 5:8, KJV
While we were yet sinners.
Not afterward.
While.
That is grace.
And grace does not mean becoming a doormat.
Grace does not mean refusing necessary confrontation.
Grace does not mean allowing another person to continually sin against you without truth.
Grace means you no longer need revenge to feel whole.
You can speak truth without trying to wound.
You can establish boundaries without hatred.
You can confront without contempt.
You can listen without surrendering truth.
You can apologize without adding, “but you...”
And sometimes one of the most Christlike sentences a husband can say is:
“Help me understand what you're actually trying to tell me.”
Not sarcastically.
Not while scrolling.
Not as a technique to make her stop talking.
Look at her.
Listen.
Then perhaps say:

“I feel disrespected when we speak to each other this way. But I don't want to shut you out. If there's something I've been failing to hear, tell me. I want us to fight for our marriage, not against each other.”
Imagine what might happen if she hears humility instead of defensiveness.
And wife...
imagine what might happen if his vulnerability isn't punished.
If instead of immediately presenting Exhibit A through Exhibit Z of everything he has done wrong, you say:
“I don't want to tear you down either. I'm hurting. I want you to understand why.”
Now something holy can happen.
Not because the disagreement disappeared.
But because the enemy standing across the room suddenly stops looking like your spouse.
The problem becomes the problem again.
Your wife is not the enemy.
Your husband is not the enemy.
And marriage was never supposed to become a courtroom where two wounded sinners spend forty years building cases against one another.
It was meant to become one of the places where two imperfect people repeatedly discover how desperately they both need Jesus.
Maybe that is what your marriage needs tonight.
Not another marriage hack.
Not another viral relationship quote.
Not another friend telling you that you “deserve better” without knowing the whole story.
Maybe you need to sit somewhere quiet together.
Put the phones down.
Stop prosecuting.
Stop rehearsing.
And confess.
“Jesus, I have become hard.”
“Jesus, my words have become cruel.”
“Jesus, I stopped listening.”
“Jesus, I wanted to punish her with silence.”
“Jesus, I wanted to hurt him because I felt hurt.”
“Jesus, forgive us.”
There is something incredibly powerful about hearing your spouse repent without being forced to.
No excuses.
No counterattack.
Just truth.
Because repentance can do something pride never can:
it opens a door.
And through that door comes grace.
John writes:
— 1 John 1:9, KJV
The Greek word translated “confess” is ὁμολογῶμεν — homologōmen, from homologeō, carrying the sense of acknowledging or confessing.
Christian restoration begins when we stop editing our guilt.
When we stop saying:
“I'm sorry you felt that way.”
And start saying:
“I was wrong.”
“I sinned in how I spoke.”
“I ignored you.”
“I became bitter.”
“I wanted to punish you.”
“Please forgive me.”
That is where scandal starts becoming grace.
Because perhaps the scandal in your marriage isn't something Facebook would gossip about.
Maybe it's quieter.
A husband who hasn't lovingly touched his wife in months.
A wife who has forgotten how to speak to her husband without contempt.
Two Christians who worship together on Sunday but barely speak tenderly on Monday.
Two people posting anniversary pictures while privately wondering what happened to them.
But Jesus specializes in entering stories people think are too damaged to rewrite.
The Gospel is not the story of good people improving themselves.
It is the announcement that sinful people can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
Forgiveness is real.
Grace is real.
New life is real.
And the same Jesus who raises spiritually dead sinners is not intimidated by a marriage that feels emotionally exhausted.
Your restoration may not happen tonight.
Trust may need rebuilding.
Communication patterns may need serious work.
You may need mature Christian counseling.
You may have years of wounds that cannot responsibly be reduced to one conversation.
But somebody has to stop feeding the fire.
Somebody has to put down the weapon.
Somebody has to say:
“This cycle will not own us forever.”
Why not you?
Not because you're admitting everything is your fault.
Because Jesus is Lord of you.
There is a difference.
You cannot repent for your spouse.
You cannot force your spouse to change.
You cannot control whether your wife speaks gently tomorrow.
But through the Spirit of God, you can bring your own heart before Christ today.
And perhaps instead of praying only:
“Lord, change my wife...”
you could dare to pray:
“Lord, show me where I need to change too.”
That prayer is frightening.
Because God may answer it.
He may show you defensiveness you called strength.
Neglect you called exhaustion.
Pride you called leadership.
Withdrawal you called peacekeeping.
Bitterness you called discernment.
And wife, He may show you contempt you called honesty.
Control you called concern.
Cruel words you called “just telling the truth.”
Scorekeeping you called accountability.
But conviction is not God abandoning you.
For those who are in Christ, conviction calls us out of darkness and toward restoration.
Jesus exposes what is killing us because He loves us too much to leave us there.
So tonight, before you call her a nag again...
look deeper.
And before you call him uncaring again...
look deeper.
Maybe behind the anger is fear.
Behind the criticism is loneliness.
Behind the silence is hurt.
Behind the defensiveness is shame.
And behind two exhausted sinners...
there may still be a Savior standing with enough grace for both.

If there is genuine abuse, coercion, threats, violence, or fear for someone's safety, do not use this message as a reason to remain silently endangered. Seek immediate safety and qualified help. Biblical reconciliation never requires pretending abuse is acceptable.
But if what has overtaken your home is resentment, poor communication, unresolved wounds, selfishness, contempt, defensiveness, emotional withdrawal, and accumulated disappointment...
don't pronounce dead what Jesus may still be calling you to surrender.
Go to Christ.
Then go to your spouse differently.
Listen before defending.
Confess before accusing.
Speak truth without contempt.
Forgive as someone who has been forgiven.
Seek wise help before pride convinces you that asking for help means failure.
And remember Paul's words:
“And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.”
— Ephesians 4:32, KJV
Maybe somebody reading this is sitting beside the person they once couldn't imagine living without...
and now they don't know how to live together.
Maybe that's you.
If it is, don't hide behind appearances.
Not because a comment magically fixes anything.
It doesn't.
But sometimes bringing the struggle into the light is the first honest admission that you don't want pride to have the final word.
Salvation cannot be purchased, and glorifying God cannot be reduced to financially supporting a ministry.

But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical way of helping biblical encouragement reach another exhausted husband, another wounded wife, another struggling believer, another seeker, and another family that desperately needs to hear about Jesus.
Because maybe the next marriage God touches begins with one person refusing to keep score.
Maybe the next apology begins with this article.
Maybe tonight a husband finally listens.
Maybe a wife finally lowers the weapon of contempt.
Maybe two people who thought they were finished kneel beside the same bed and whisper the same name:
Jesus.
And maybe years from now, when somebody asks how your marriage survived the season when you could barely stand being in the same room...
you won't say,
“Because she finally stopped nagging.”
You won't say,
“Because he finally became perfect.”
You'll look at the person whose weaknesses once drove you crazy, remember the weaknesses Christ had to expose in you too, and realize that neither one of you was the hero of the story.
Jesus was.
The marriage you are tempted to bury today may someday become the place where your children learn what repentance, forgiveness, and grace actually look like.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “JUDGE NOT” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT YOU THINK IT MEANS
paragraphs: “JUDGE NOT” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT YOU THINK IT MEANS
The Verse We Use to Silence Truth May Actually Be Judging Us
There are two words people love to quote from Jesus when they desperately want Jesus to stop talking.
“Judge not.”
They appear in arguments.
In comment sections.
Between family members.
Inside churches.
After someone confronts adultery, dishonesty, bitterness, sexual sin, drunkenness, greed, gossip, compromise, hypocrisy, or some secret life nobody is supposed to mention.
“Who are you to judge me?”
“Jesus said judge not.”
And just like that, Matthew 7:1 becomes a spiritual emergency exit.
A way to escape conviction.
A shield held up against anyone who dares to say, “Brother… sister… this road is destroying you.”
But what if the verse we keep using to protect ourselves from judgment was actually spoken by Jesus to expose something far more uncomfortable?
What if Jesus was not forbidding us from recognizing sin at all?
What if He was forbidding us from confronting another person’s sin while remaining comfortably blind to our own?
Because Jesus did say:
“Judge not, that ye be not judged.” — Matthew 7:1
But He did not stop talking there.
And when we stop where Jesus did not stop, we can make Jesus sound like He said something He never meant.
The Greek is striking:
Μὴ κρίνετε, ἵνα μὴ κριθῆτε.
Mē krinete, hina mē krithēte.
In straightforward English:
“Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.”
The key word is κρίνετε — krinete, from κρίνω — krinō.
Depending on context, the word can carry the idea of judging, deciding, evaluating, distinguishing, or condemning.
And context is everything.
Because if Matthew 7:1 meant, “A Christian must never make a moral judgment about anybody or anything,” the rest of the New Testament would become impossible to obey.
Jesus Himself says later:
“Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.” — John 7:24
Think about that.
The same Jesus who said, “Judge not,” also commanded people to judge rightly.
So Jesus cannot be condemning every act of moral discernment.
He is condemning a certain kind of judgment.
And Matthew 7 tells us exactly what kind.
Keep reading.
Jesus says that with the judgment we use, we will be judged, and with the measure we use, it will be measured back to us.
Then comes one of the most unforgettable images in the Sermon on the Mount.
A man sees a tiny speck in his brother’s eye…
while there is a beam sticking out of his own.
Picture it.
It is almost absurd.
A man with a wooden beam protruding from his face is leaning toward another person saying:
“Hold still. I see something wrong with you.”
And Jesus gives that man a name.
Hypocrite.
That changes everything.
Jesus does not say the speck is imaginary.
He does not call evil good.
He does not tell the man, “Your brother’s eye is none of your business.”
He says, in essence:
Deal with your own eye first.
Matthew 7:5 says:
“Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye.”
Did you catch it?
Then shalt thou see clearly.
Jesus does not end with both people remaining blind.
The goal is not, “Ignore the speck.”
The goal is restored vision.
First repentance.
Then clarity.
Then loving help.
That is worlds apart from the judgment Jesus condemns.
There is a kind of judgment that stands over another human being with pride.
It enjoys exposure.
It whispers about someone instead of weeping for them.
It points at another person’s chains while secretly polishing its own.
It knows everybody else’s failures but has somehow misplaced the mirror.
It says, “Look what they did.”
Grace says, “Lord, search me too.”
That is where this verse becomes frightening.
Because some of us have used Matthew 7:1 against people who were trying to wound us.
But some of us have also used Matthew 7:1 against people who were trying to rescue us.
And those are not the same thing.
Sometimes the person who tells you the truth is not your enemy.
Sometimes they love you enough to risk becoming unpopular with you.
Imagine seeing someone you love walking toward the edge of a cliff.
Would love say:
“I don't want to judge.”
Or would love scream:
“Stop!”
If a physician discovers cancer, compassion does not require the physician to call it health.
If your house is burning, the neighbor who wakes you is not condemning you by shouting, “Fire!”
Truth can hurt without being hatred.
Correction can sting without being condemnation.
And love can confront without becoming self-righteous.
This is why the Bible refuses to fit inside the comfortable slogan our culture has sometimes made from “judge not.”
Paul asks the Corinthian believers:
τί γάρ μοι τοὺς ἔξω κρίνειν; οὐχὶ τοὺς ἔσω ὑμεῖς κρίνετε;
In 1 Corinthians 5:12, the sense is:
“What have I to do with judging those outside? Is it not those inside whom you judge?”
There is that word-family again.
κρίνειν… κρίνετε.
Paul is dealing with serious, unrepentant sin among professing believers. His answer is not, “Nobody can ever evaluate anybody’s conduct because Jesus said judge not.”
Quite the opposite.
The church has a responsibility to take holiness seriously.
But notice something equally important.
Paul distinguishes between those inside and those outside.
Christians are not commissioned to wander around treating unbelievers like church members who have violated church discipline.
Lost people need Christ.
The broken need the Gospel.
The spiritually dead need life.
We should not expect someone who does not follow Jesus to behave as though Jesus is already Lord of his life.
The Gospel does not begin with:
“Clean yourself up enough for Jesus.”
It begins with:
Come to Jesus because you cannot save yourself.
And this is where judgment becomes deeply personal.
Because Christianity gives us neither permission to become moral cowards nor permission to become religious executioners.
We cannot call darkness light merely because someone might call us judgmental.
But neither can we use truth as a weapon to make ourselves feel superior.
We speak truth.
But we speak it remembering the cross.
We confront sin.
But we confront it as people who needed mercy ourselves.
We call people to repentance.
But we do it knowing that our own salvation exists only because the Son of God had mercy on sinners.
The Christian does not stand above the sinner saying:
“Look how disgusting you are.”
The Christian stands beside the cross saying:
“There is room here for sinners like us.”
That difference changes everything.
Maybe you know what religious judgment feels like.
Maybe people found out what you did.
The affair.
The addiction.
The divorce.
The pregnancy.
The relapse.
The pornography.
The lie.
The arrest.
The failure.
The years you wasted.
The person you hurt.
The secret you thought would remain buried.
And suddenly you were no longer a person.
You became your scandal.
People stopped saying your name and started saying what you did.
They discussed you.
Analyzed you.
Reduced you.
Maybe people who never asked how badly you were bleeding somehow knew exactly how guilty you were.
And perhaps that wounded your view of Christianity itself.
If that happened, hear this carefully:
The hypocrisy of religious people does not erase the holiness of Jesus.
And neither does human cruelty make sin harmless.
Jesus does something far more beautiful than either pretending sin does not matter or crushing sinners beneath it.
Jesus tells the truth about sin…
and then gives His life for sinners.
That is the Gospel.
At the cross, God did not announce that sin was insignificant.
The cross announces exactly the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation with a holy God required what we could never provide for ourselves.
And grace is so astonishing that God provided it Himself in His Son.
Jesus Christ bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And now forgiveness is not offered because you successfully convinced God that you were innocent.
Forgiveness is offered because Christ is sufficient.
That means Christianity is not the story of good people looking down on bad people.
It is the story of guilty people discovering that the Judge stepped into history to become their Savior.
And that should destroy our arrogance.
How can I stand at the foot of a bloodstained cross, knowing Christ died for my sin, and then boast over another sinner?
How can I receive mercy with one hand and throw stones with the other?
Yet how can I claim to love someone while celebrating the very sin Christ died to rescue us from?
Grace does not say sin does not matter.
Grace says sin does not get the final word.
That is the difference between scandal and grace.
Maybe your scandal is public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your church thinks you're strong.
Your spouse thinks you're fine.
Your children think you're fine.
Your Facebook friends think you're fine.
You post Scripture.
You say “Amen.”
You encourage everybody else.
And yet there is something behind the screen.
Something you keep deleting.
Something you keep returning to.
Something you have renamed because calling it what Scripture calls it would hurt too much.
Maybe you have spent years examining specks because you are terrified someone might notice the beam.
And now Jesus is standing in front of you.
Not the version of Jesus created by angry religious people.
Not the version created by a culture that wants a Savior who never contradicts us.
The real Jesus.
Full of grace.
Full of truth.
And perhaps His words to you today are not:
“Look how terrible everybody else has become.”
Perhaps they are:
“Give Me the beam.”
The pride.
The secret lust.
The unforgiveness.
The envy.
The gossip disguised as concern.
The bitterness you have baptized as discernment.
The compromise you keep calling freedom.
The superiority you keep calling holiness.
The silence you keep calling love.
Give it to Him.
Because repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the One who can actually save you from it.
And maybe this is where someone needs to stop reading for a moment.
Not because this article exposed somebody you know.
Because it exposed you.
Be honest.
Did you spend the first half of this article thinking about somebody else?
Their hypocrisy.
Their sin.
Their compromise.
Their Facebook post.
Their marriage.
Their theology.
Their lifestyle.
Their failure.
And somewhere along the way…
the mirror turned around.
That is the dangerous beauty of Matthew 7.
Jesus takes the finger we were pointing outward and gently brings it back toward our own heart.
Not to destroy us.
To free us.
Because the Gospel does not end with exposure.
Peter denied Jesus.
Grace found him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Grace found him.
The thief beside Christ had nothing left to offer.
Grace found him.
And if you come to Jesus in repentance and faith, your worst chapter does not have authority to write your ending.
Christ does.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to these words:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming darkness.
Not by abolishing truth.
He rewrites everything by taking sinners who deserve judgment, cleansing them through His saving work, making them His own, and teaching them to walk in newness of life.
This is not cheap grace.
It cost blood.
And the grace that forgives also transforms.
So the next time someone says, “Judge not,” do not turn Matthew 7 into ammunition for another argument.
Remember the beam.
Remember the speck.
Remember the cross.
Ask yourself:
Am I trying to restore this person… or defeat them?
Am I grieving over their sin… or enjoying exposing it?
Have I examined myself before correcting them?
Am I speaking because I love their soul… or because being right makes me feel powerful?
And if somebody lovingly confronts you, do not automatically assume they hate you.
Take their words before God.
Search the Scriptures.
Examine your heart.
Reject false accusations, yes.
But never become so afraid of “judgment” that you make yourself unreachable by correction.
Proverbs repeatedly presents wise correction as something the wise receive rather than despise.
Sometimes one of God's mercies is a person courageous enough to tell you what everyone else is afraid to say.

And when correction is necessary, Galatians 6:1 gives us the spirit in which restoration should happen: those who are spiritual should restore someone caught in transgression gently, while watching themselves lest they too be tempted.
There it is again.
Truth.
Restoration.
Gentleness.
Self-examination.
Biblical correction should smell less like a courtroom full of spectators…
and more like a rescue.
So no, “Judge not” does not mean morality disappears.
It does not mean truth becomes subjective.
It does not mean Christians must pretend they cannot recognize destructive behavior.
And it certainly does not mean nobody can ever call us to repentance.
It means we have no permission to climb onto God's throne.
Final judgment belongs to Him.
We are not omniscient.
We cannot perfectly see motives.
We are not the Savior.
We are not the standard.
Jesus is.
And before you attempt to remove the speck from someone else's eye, Christ commands you to deal honestly with what is obstructing your own vision.
Maybe that is the word somebody needed tonight.
Not “judge them.”
Not “ignore them.”
But:
Look at Jesus first.
Then look in the mirror.
Then, when love requires it, reach toward your brother or sister with clean hands, trembling humility, biblical truth, and the heart of someone attempting restoration rather than destruction.
Be honest.
And if you need prayer because conviction has found a place you have been hiding, you do not have to write your entire story publicly.
Someone reading may know exactly how to pray.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ.

Invite your family. Invite your friends. Invite struggling believers. Invite the lukewarm Christian who has almost stopped listening. Invite the seeker with questions. Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is nothing more than religious people judging everybody else.
Leave different.
Put down the stone.
Pick up the mirror.
Bring the beam to Jesus.
And when He has humbled you, forgiven you, cleansed you, and taught you to see more clearly…
help your brother with the speck.
Not as his executioner.
As someone who knows what it feels like to need mercy.

Because one day, when every opinion has gone silent, every comment section has disappeared, every defense has collapsed, and every human verdict has become irrelevant, there will remain only one Judge whose verdict ultimately matters.
And for everyone who belongs to Jesus Christ, the Judge is also the Savior who bore our condemnation and opened the way home.
You were never saved so you could become better at throwing stones; you were saved so your life could become evidence that grace can still resurrect what judgment said was finished.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Told Jairus, “Your Daughter Is Dead.” Jesus Kept Walking Toward His House.
paragraphs: They Told Jairus, “Your Daughter Is Dead.” Jesus Kept Walking Toward His House.
When the message arrived, everyone thought the story was over. Jesus treated it as the moment faith had to keep walking.
There are sentences that divide a life into before and after.
“The results came back.”
“We need to talk.”
“I don’t love you anymore.”
“We couldn’t save him.”
“The company is letting you go.”
“There’s nothing more we can do.”
And then there was the sentence Jairus heard.
“Your daughter is dead.”
Try not to read that like someone who already knows how the story ends.
Stand there with him.
Feel the air leave his lungs.
Because Jairus did not know what would happen next.
He only knew that somewhere behind him was a house containing the little girl he loved more than his own comfort—and somewhere in front of him stood Jesus.
And Jesus had not reached her in time.
Or so it seemed.
That may be one of the most painful places faith can ever stand: when you prayed, believed, waited, and watched the situation become worse anyway.
Jairus had already humbled himself publicly.
Mark tells us that he was “one of the rulers of the synagogue” (Mark 5:22). He was not introduced as an anonymous man wandering through the crowd. He carried position. Recognition. Responsibility.
But desperation has a way of making reputation feel very small.
When Jairus saw Jesus, Scripture says he fell at His feet and pleaded earnestly:
“My little daughter lies at the point of death. Come and lay Your hands on her, that she may be healed, and she will live” (Mark 5:23, NKJV).
The Greek is painfully tender.
Mark uses the expression τὸ θυγάτριόν μου — to thygatrion mou.
“My little daughter.”
Not merely a case.
Not merely a theological problem.
Not merely another sick person.
His little girl.
If you have ever loved someone so deeply that you would have traded places with them if God allowed it, you understand something of Jairus walking through that crowd.
And then comes one of the most hopeful sentences in the passage:
“So Jesus went with him” (Mark 5:24, NKJV).
Jesus went with him.
Imagine what those words meant to that father.
The Teacher was coming.
Hope was coming down the road.
Jairus had found Jesus, Jesus had listened, and now Jesus was heading toward his house.
Just keep moving.
Just get Him there.
But then Jesus stopped.
A woman in the crowd had been suffering from bleeding for twelve years. She touched Jesus’ garment in faith and was healed. Jesus stopped to address her.
And somewhere nearby, a desperate father was waiting.
Every moment mattered to Jairus.
His daughter was dying.
Yet Jesus stopped.
This is where the story becomes painfully familiar.
Because sometimes God appears to be doing something beautiful for somebody else while you are begging Him to hurry toward you.
You watch someone else receive the breakthrough.
Someone else announces the pregnancy.
Someone else gets married.
Someone else finds work.
Someone else tells the testimony.
Someone else receives the answer you have been begging God for.
And you are trying to celebrate with them while something inside you whispers:
“Jesus… what about my house?”
The woman had suffered twelve years.
Jairus’ daughter was twelve years old (Mark 5:42).
One life had spent twelve years suffering.
Another had spent twelve years growing.
And in one crowded road, both stories collided with Jesus Christ.
The delay was not meaningless.
But Jairus could not see that yet.
Neither can we, many times.
Then the messengers arrived.
Mark records:
“While He was still speaking, some came from the ruler of the synagogue’s house who said, ‘Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the Teacher any further?’” (Mark 5:35, NKJV).
There it is.
The sentence that seemed to cancel everything.
Your daughter is dead.
Why trouble Jesus anymore?
Notice the logic.
As long as she was sick, Jesus was useful.
As long as there was still a pulse, prayer made sense.
As long as human possibility remained, hope remained respectable.
But now?
Stop bothering Him.
It is over.
And that voice still speaks.

Maybe not through messengers from Jairus’ house, but through shame, disappointment, statistics, memories, failures, funerals, addictions, broken relationships, unanswered prayers, and years you cannot recover.
Why keep praying?
Why repent again?
Why return to church?
Why believe God could restore you?
Why bring that ruined part of your life back to Jesus?
Why trouble the Teacher anymore?
Because the Gospel begins precisely where human self-rescue ends.
Mark 5:36 contains one of the most important moments in the story.
The Greek text reads:
Ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς παρακούσας τὸν λόγον λαλούμενον λέγει τῷ ἀρχισυναγώγῳ· Μὴ φοβοῦ, μόνον πίστευε.
A faithful rendering is:
“But Jesus, overhearing what was spoken, said to the ruler of the synagogue, ‘Do not fear; only believe.’”
Μὴ φοβοῦ, μόνον πίστευε.
Mē phobou, monon pisteue.
“Do not fear; only believe.”
Jesus did not tell Jairus that death was imaginary.
He did not tell him grief was weakness.
He did not pretend the report had not arrived.
Christian faith is not pretending terrible things are pleasant.
Biblical faith looks directly at what is terrifying and then looks at Christ.
The command πίστευε — pisteue carries the sense of continuing to believe, continuing to trust.
The circumstances had changed.
Jesus had not.
The report had changed.
Jesus had not.
What Jairus could see had changed.
Jesus had not.
And perhaps someone reading this has been living as though a terrible report has greater authority over your soul than Jesus Christ.
Maybe something really did die.
A dream.
A marriage.
A friendship.
A reputation.
A season.
Maybe someone you loved actually died, and no sentimental Christian phrase can make the grief small.

This passage should never be abused to promise that every earthly tragedy will be reversed immediately if we simply believe hard enough. Scripture does not teach that Christians are exempt from suffering or physical death. Even people whom Jesus raised during His earthly ministry eventually died physically again.
The Christian hope is deeper than denial.
Jesus Himself declared, “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25).
The final Christian hope is not that believers somehow avoid every grave.
It is that the grave does not get the final word over those who belong to Christ.
Jairus was about to receive an extraordinary foretaste of that truth.
Jesus kept walking toward his house.
Think about that.
The messengers said there was no reason to continue.
Jesus continued.
The mourners believed death had finished the story.
Jesus continued.
Fear had every reason to tell Jairus to collapse.
Jesus continued.
Sometimes one of the greatest mercies in your life is that Christ does not surrender to the conclusions you have made about yourself.
You may call yourself ruined.
He calls sinners to repentance.
You may call yourself unforgivable.
His blood says forgiveness is available to those who come to Him.
You may say you have wandered too far.
He still commands sinners everywhere to repent and come home.
You may think your scandal is the final chapter.
Then Jesus walks into the room.
When they arrived, there was commotion. People were weeping and wailing loudly.
Jesus said:
“Why make this commotion and weep? The child is not dead, but sleeping” (Mark 5:39, NKJV).
They laughed at Him.
That detail matters.
They went from mourning to mockery.
Because resurrection language sounds ridiculous when death appears absolute.
Jesus removed the crowd and entered where the child was lying.
Then Mark preserves something extraordinary.
He records Jesus’ actual Aramaic words:
Ταλιθὰ κούμ — Talitha koum.
Mark immediately translates them:
“Little girl, I say to you, arise” (Mark 5:41).
Talitha is an affectionate Aramaic address for a young girl.
Koum means “arise,” or “get up.”
The scene is almost shockingly gentle.
Jesus does not perform for the crowd.
He takes her by the hand.
The hand of a dead child.
Then He speaks to her as though a father were waking his daughter from sleep.
Little girl.
Get up.
And she did.
Mark says:
“Immediately the girl arose and walked, for she was twelve years of age” (Mark 5:42, NKJV).
Immediately.
The same house that had received the message of death was now watching a twelve-year-old girl walk.
The mourners had arrived for a funeral.
Jesus turned the room into a testimony.
But do not miss what this miracle reveals about Jesus.
This is not primarily a story telling you to “believe in yourself.”
Jairus was powerless.
The girl was powerless.
The mourners were powerless.
The miracle happened because Jesus possesses an authority no human being possesses.
Christ is the center of this story.
And that changes how we understand our own scandals.
Because some of us have spent years trying to resurrect ourselves.
We try to repair guilt with achievement.
We cover shame with appearances.
We rename sin instead of confessing it.
We curate the photograph.
We polish the testimony.
We learn Christian vocabulary.
We know when to lift our hands.
We know what verse to post.
We know how to answer, “How are you?”
“Blessed.”
But underneath the religious language, something may still be bleeding.
Something may still be hiding.
Something may still need repentance.
And Jesus did not come merely to improve the image we present to people.
He came to save sinners.
The Bible's diagnosis of humanity is more severe than “you need encouragement.”
Scripture says we are dead in trespasses and sins apart from God's saving work (Ephesians 2:1).
Dead.
That word destroys our pride.
But keep reading.
“But God…”
Those may be two of the sweetest words ever placed beside human ruin.
“But God, who is rich in mercy, because of His great love with which He loved us… made us alive together with Christ” (Ephesians 2:4–5, NKJV).
That is Christianity.
Not dead people learning better religious behavior.
Grace making sinners alive in Christ.
That is why the cross matters.
At Calvary, Jesus was not giving humanity motivational content.
He was bearing sin.
Isaiah had foretold the suffering Servant who would be wounded for our transgressions (Isaiah 53:5).
Peter writes that Christ “suffered once for sins, the just for the unjust, that He might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18, NKJV).
Paul declares that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
Christianity stands or falls on this Gospel.
Jesus Christ was crucified.
Jesus Christ was buried.
Jesus Christ rose.
And because He lives, repentance is not walking toward humiliation without hope.
It is turning from sin toward a living Savior.
Grace does not say your sin does not matter.
The cross proves how seriously God takes sin.
Grace says your sin does not have to be your master because Jesus paid what sinners could never pay for themselves.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Not because God edits the ugly parts out of your history.
Because Jesus can redeem a life that history seemed to disqualify.
Maybe people remember who you were.
Jesus knows everything they do not.
Maybe you have secret chapters nobody knows.
Jesus already knows.
Maybe your greatest fear is that if people knew the entire story, they would never look at you the same way again.
Christ already sees the entire story.
And still the Gospel invitation stands:
Repent.
Believe.
Come.
Not because you deserve mercy.
Because He is merciful.
There is a strange tenderness near the end of Jairus’ story that is easy to overlook.
After raising the girl, Jesus told them to give her something to eat (Mark 5:43).
Think about that.
The One who had just demonstrated authority over death cared about her next meal.
Majesty and tenderness in the same room.
The King who commands death notices hunger.
This is Jesus.
Not a distant religious symbol.
Not an accessory for your biography.
Not a spiritual emergency contact you use only when life collapses.
Lord.
Savior.
King.
The One before whom death itself must eventually surrender.
And perhaps the most dangerous thing you could do after reading this is admire the story without responding to the Christ at its center.
Do not merely say, “Beautiful.”
Ask yourself what Jairus had to confront:
When everything I trusted collapses, do I still trust Jesus?
And then ask something even deeper:
Have I actually surrendered my life to Him?
Not, “Do I believe God exists?”
Not, “Did I grow up Christian?”
Not, “Do I occasionally pray?”
Have I repented of my sin and trusted Jesus Christ?
Because the greatest miracle you need is not a better week.
It is reconciliation with God.
If something hidden has been exposed while reading this, do not run from Jesus.
Run toward Him.
Somebody may be reading from the place you survived.
Do not turn vulnerability into performance. Let it become community.
And think of one person whose house has received terrible news.
Someone grieving.
Someone ashamed.
Someone who believes they have ruined everything.
Someone who has quietly stopped believing that Jesus could still want them.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not by financial support (Ephesians 2:8–9). We never want to manipulate something holy into a transaction.
Come to Jesus.
The merchandise is not the Gospel.
Gospel Warrior is not the Gospel.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
So share because someone needs the truth.
Tag because someone you love may be losing hope.
Save because one day you may need these words again.
Follow because your soul needs more than endless noise.
Support Gospel work if God has given you the desire and means to do so.
But above everything else, repent, believe the Gospel, follow Jesus, and make Him known.
Jairus began that journey believing Jesus could stop his daughter from dying.
He ended it discovering that even when death arrived first, Jesus was still Lord when He walked through the door.
Maybe that is what you needed to remember.
The message may have arrived.
The tears may already be falling.
People may have declared the story finished.
You may even hear the laughter of those who think hope has become foolish.
But never confuse the end of your ability with the end of Christ's authority.
There is a Savior who entered our death, carried our sin to the cross, walked out of His own grave, and promises resurrection life to everyone who belongs to Him.
So when fear whispers, “It is over,” remember the words spoken on that road:
Μὴ φοβοῦ, μόνον πίστευε.
Do not fear.
Only believe.
And when your shame whispers that your scandal has written the final sentence, remember the hand reaching toward a silent little girl and the voice that death itself could not refuse:
Talitha koum.
Little girl.
Arise.
Because sometimes what looks like the final page is only the place where we discover that Jesus still holds the pen.
The world may remember the moment everything died; grace remembers the moment Jesus walked into the room.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHAT IF I DON’T FEEL GUILTY ANYMORE?
paragraphs:
WHAT IF I DON’T FEEL GUILTY ANYMORE?
The Most Terrifying Part of Sin May Not Be That You Fell Again… but That This Time, It Barely Hurt
There was a time when it bothered you.
You remember that, don’t you?
The first time, your heart pounded.
You knew.
You didn’t need a preacher screaming at you. You didn’t need somebody quoting ten Bible verses. You didn’t need your church to find out.
Something inside you already knew.
You had crossed a line.
So you prayed.
Maybe you cried.
Maybe you whispered, “Jesus, forgive me.”
Maybe you promised God you would never do it again.
Then it happened again.
And again.
And somewhere between the first compromise and the hundredth excuse, something changed.
Not necessarily the temptation.
Not necessarily the sin.
You.
The thing that once kept you awake at night barely interrupts your sleep now.
The words you once hated hearing yourself say come naturally.
The browser history gets deleted without much thought.
The bitterness feels justified.
The secret relationship feels normal.
The dishonesty feels necessary.
The pride feels like confidence.
The unforgiveness feels like wisdom.
The gossip feels like concern.
The greed feels like ambition.
The lust feels like loneliness.
The compromise feels like survival.
And perhaps the most frightening sentence you have whispered lately is not, “God, I sinned.”
It is…
“Why don’t I feel guilty anymore?”
Stay with that question.
Because there are at least two very different reasons a person may no longer live under guilt, and confusing them can be spiritually devastating.
One is breathtakingly beautiful.
The other is terrifying.

A person may be free from condemnation because he has come honestly to Jesus Christ, confessed his sin, trusted the sufficiency of Christ’s sacrifice, and discovered that the Gospel really does cleanse guilty people.
Or a person may have become so accustomed to resisting truth that sin no longer produces the alarm it once did.
Those are not the same thing.
One is a conscience finding rest at the cross.
The other may be a conscience becoming numb away from it.

And Christianity was never meant to keep forgiven people psychologically chained to sins Jesus has actually forgiven. Romans 8:1 declares that there is “no condemnation” for those who are in Christ Jesus. First John 1:9 teaches that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
So if you have genuinely repented and trusted Christ, repeatedly punishing yourself is not greater holiness.
Jesus does not need your self-hatred added to His blood.
The cross was enough.
But Scripture also gives another warning, and this is where the question becomes uncomfortable.
Hebrews 3:13 warns believers to encourage one another continually so that none becomes hardened through what the Greek text calls the “ἀπάτῃ τῆς ἁμαρτίας” — the deceitfulness of sin.
The word behind “hardened” is connected with σκληρύνω, sklērynō: to make hard, to become stubborn.
And notice what Scripture says does the hardening.
Sin’s deceitfulness.
Sin lies.
That is one of its oldest weapons.
It rarely walks into your life announcing:
“I am here to destroy your intimacy with God.”
It whispers instead.
Just once.
Nobody knows.
You deserve this.
Everybody does it.
God understands.
You can repent later.
This isn’t really hurting anyone.
At least you’re not as bad as that person.
You still believe in Jesus.
You still go to church.
You still post Scripture.
You still pray sometimes.
You’re fine.
That is the deceitfulness of sin.
And repetition has a frightening ability to make what once shocked us begin to feel ordinary.
Think about walking into a dark room.
At first, you can barely see.
Then your eyes adjust.
The room did not become brighter.
You simply became accustomed to the darkness.
That picture should make some of us uncomfortable.
Because perhaps the question is not merely:
“Why doesn’t this bother me anymore?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
“When did I begin calling darkness normal because my eyes adjusted to it?”

Paul uses another severe image in 1 Timothy 4:2 when he describes people whose consciences have been “seared.” The Greek word is κεκαυτηριασμένων, kekautēriasmenōn, language associated with branding or cauterizing. The image can carry the chilling idea of tissue that has become insensitive after being burned.
Touch healthy skin with something hot and the nerves scream.
Burn it badly enough and eventually the damaged place may stop feeling what it should.
Now hear this carefully.
If you are frightened because you are afraid your heart has become hard, your fear itself is not proof that God has abandoned you.
Do not turn this article into a weapon against yourself.
Do not diagnose your eternal condition from the intensity of one emotion.
Feelings fluctuate.
Exhaustion can affect feelings.
Habit can affect feelings.
Personality can affect feelings.
Trauma can affect feelings.
Spiritual maturity can even change how repentance feels.
Sometimes repentance comes with tears.
Sometimes it comes with trembling.
Sometimes it comes quietly, with a sober decision:
“Jesus, this is sin. You are right. I have been wrong. I am turning back.”
The Bible does not command you to manufacture a particular emotional sensation before God will receive you.
Repentance is deeper than feeling terrible.

The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia — speaks of repentance, a changed mind and direction toward God. Romans 2:4 says something extraordinarily beautiful: God’s kindness leads us toward repentance.
Read that again.
His kindness.
Not merely terror.
Not humiliation.
Not emotional manipulation.
His kindness.
God is not standing at the doorway of repentance saying, “Cry harder and perhaps I will consider you.”
He is calling sinners to come home.
But grace must never be confused with permission.
The kindness of God leads toward repentance, not deeper rebellion.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could make peace with the thing that crucified Him.
Grace does not say sin does not matter.
Grace says sin mattered so much that the Son of God bore judgment for sinners, and grace is so powerful that sinners no longer have to remain slaves to it.
That is why the cross is simultaneously horrifying and beautiful.
At Calvary, God did not pretend sin was harmless.
Look at Jesus.
Betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Rejected.
Crucified.
The sin we casually rename “a mistake” required something infinitely more costly than our excuses could ever pay.
Yet the same cross that exposes the seriousness of sin announces the unimaginable mercy of God.
Christ died for sinners.
Not cleaned-up sinners.
Not impressive sinners.
Not sinners who successfully repaired themselves before approaching Him.
Sinners.
Romans 5:8 says Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
That means your numbness does not have to become the final chapter.
Your compromise does not have to become your identity.
Your secret does not have to become your master.
Your past does not have to become your name.
Jesus Christ still saves.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still calls wandering people home.
And maybe that is why you are reading this.
Perhaps you expected condemnation.
Instead, God is putting a mirror in front of you.
Not because He delights in crushing repentant people…
but because sometimes mercy looks like finally allowing us to see what we have been refusing to see.
David understood this.
After his devastating sin, Psalm 51 records the prayer of a man who finally stopped hiding behind power, excuses, and secrecy.
The Hebrew of Psalm 51:17 says:
זִבְחֵי אֱלֹהִים רוּחַ נִשְׁבָּרָה לֵב־נִשְׁבָּר וְנִדְכֶּה אֱלֹהִים לֹא תִבְזֶה
The heart of the verse is devastatingly beautiful: the sacrifices acceptable to God include a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart God will not despise.
The Hebrew נִשְׁבָּר, nishbar, carries the idea of being broken, while וְנִדְכֶּה, ve-nidkeh, carries the sense of being crushed or contrite.
David finally had nothing left to perform.
No royal image to protect.
No clever explanation.
No public relations strategy.
Just truth.
“I sinned.”
And maybe that is where somebody reading this needs to arrive.
Not:
“I made some questionable choices.”
Not:
“I was going through something.”
Not:
“They pushed me into it.”
Not:
“Nobody is perfect.”
Not:
“God knows my heart.”
Yes.
God does know your heart.
That is precisely why pretending is useless.
He sees what your followers cannot see.
He sees what your spouse cannot see.
He sees what your pastor cannot see.
He sees what your children cannot see.
He sees what your parents cannot see.
He sees the message you deleted.
He sees the resentment you feed.
He sees the fantasy you revisit.
He sees the money.
He sees the pride.
He sees the envy.
He sees the private version of you.
And somehow…
He still calls sinners to Himself.
That is scandalous grace.
Not grace that tells you to remain where you are.
Grace that finds you where you are and refuses to leave you there.
Maybe you are thinking:
“But I don’t feel broken.”
Then begin with honesty.
“Jesus, I don’t even hate this sin the way I know I should.”
That is a prayer.
“Jesus, my conscience feels numb.”
That is a prayer.
“Jesus, I keep defending something Your Word calls sin.”
That is a prayer.
“Jesus, I want to want You again.”
That is a prayer.
“Jesus, soften what I have hardened.”
That is a prayer.
You do not have to manufacture tears to impress the One who already knows your heart.
Bring Him the numbness too.
Bring Him the absence of guilt.
Bring Him the excuses.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the hypocrisy.
Bring Him the double life.
Bring Him the part of you that does not even know whether it wants to change.
Tell Him the truth.
Then turn.
Because biblical repentance is not merely feeling bad about where you are standing.
It is turning toward Christ.
You may stumble during that turning.
You may need accountability.
You may need to confess something to a trustworthy mature believer.
You may need to remove access to something.
You may need to end a relationship that continually pulls you into sin.
You may need to apologize.
You may need to make restitution where appropriate.
You may need to stop calling temptation “who I am.”
But none of those actions purchase forgiveness.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
We repent because Christ is worthy.
We obey because He is Lord.
We fight sin because grace has given us something better than slavery.
And when we fall, we do not run away from the cross in shame.
We run toward Christ in repentance and faith.
There is another danger here too.
Some Christians feel guilty about sins God has already forgiven.
They have confessed.
They have repented.
They have turned.
Yet years later they are still standing emotionally inside the courtroom after the Judge has already declared the debt paid through Christ.
If that is you, your problem may not be that you feel too little guilt.
You may be carrying guilt Jesus never commanded you to continue carrying.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Godly conviction exposes sin and calls you toward Christ.
Condemnation whispers that because you sinned, there is no road home.
The Gospel says otherwise.
Peter denied Jesus.
David committed horrifying sin.
Paul once persecuted Christians.
The Bible does not sanitize its heroes because Scripture is not ultimately the story of impressive human beings.
It is the story of a holy God redeeming sinful people.
Scandal after scandal.
Failure after failure.
Mercy after mercy.
Until everything converges on a bloodstained cross and an empty tomb.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By doing something greater.
He redeems the sinner.
So perhaps you do not need to ask only:
“Do I feel guilty?”
Ask:
“Do I agree with God about my sin?”
“Am I defending what Christ calls me to surrender?”
“Am I willing to turn?”
“Do I want Jesus more than I want the right to keep hiding?”
Those questions go deeper than emotion.
And if something inside you is saying, “Come home”…
come home.
Not tomorrow.
Hebrews says, “Today.”
There are people who spend years waiting to feel sufficiently sorry before surrendering.
Do not make an idol out of the feeling.
Come to Jesus.
Confess honestly.
Repent genuinely.
Trust completely.
Obey courageously.
And when your feelings lag behind, anchor yourself in what Christ has done rather than in your ability to produce the perfect emotional response.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes one honest sentence is the moment somebody stops performing Christianity and admits, “I need Christ.”
And somebody else reading your words may realize they are not the only person fighting their way back toward the light.
Not because every word is easy to hear, but because there may come another night when sin starts whispering that compromise is normal.
Read it again then.
Not as a performance. Not to prove that you are spiritual. Share it because someone scrolling silently through your feed may be asking the exact same frightening question:
“Why don’t I feel guilty anymore?”
Send this privately to the believer who has disappeared behind “I’m fine.”
Send it to the person who thinks they have sinned too much to come home.
Send it to the lukewarm Christian.
Send it to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is only about making guilty people feel worse.
Let them discover what the Gospel actually says:
Sin is worse than we wanted to admit.
Grace is greater than we dared to imagine.
And Jesus is better than both our rebellion and our religious pretending.
Supporting Gospel ministry should never be treated as purchasing God’s favor. Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership.
But before you leave, remember the question that brought you here.
“What if I don’t feel guilty anymore?”
Do not panic merely because an emotion is absent.
But do not make peace with sin merely because the alarm has grown quiet.
Take your heart to Jesus.
Ask Him to search you.
Ask Him to expose what you excuse.
Ask Him to soften what has hardened.
Ask Him to forgive what you confess.
Then believe the Gospel when it tells you that the blood of Christ is sufficient for repentant sinners.
The goal is not to become a person who walks around drowning in guilt.
The goal is to become a person who walks closely enough with Jesus that sin can no longer convince you it is home.
Because conviction is not God gleefully pushing you into darkness.
Sometimes conviction is mercy standing in the doorway, calling your name before you wander any farther.
And if you can still hear Him calling…
answer.

The most frightening heart is not the one that breaks when it sees its sin—it is the one that learns to live comfortably without needing the Savior; but even a hardened wanderer can turn toward Christ while He is calling today.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Man Who Killed Goliath Nearly Lost Everything Because He Couldn't Control His Desire
paragraphs: The Man Who Killed Goliath Nearly Lost Everything Because He Couldn't Control His Desire
David knew how to defeat a giant in public. He almost destroyed his own house because he failed to defeat desire in private.
The stone was not David’s most dangerous weapon.
And Goliath was not David’s most dangerous enemy.
Years after the shepherd boy walked into a valley carrying a sling and faith in the living God, another battle came looking for him.
There was no giant shouting across a battlefield.
No Philistine army watching.
No frightened soldiers.
No sword raised against his throat.
Just a rooftop.
A woman.
A look.
And a king who had enough power to turn desire into action.
That should frighten every one of us who has ever assumed that yesterday’s spiritual victory guarantees tomorrow’s faithfulness.
Because the man who stood before Goliath without trembling would eventually stand before temptation and fall.
And Scripture introduces the tragedy with a detail that is painfully easy to overlook.
It was the season “when kings go out to battle,” yet David remained in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 11:1).
His army went.
Joab went.
His servants went.
David stayed.
Then one evening he rose from his bed and walked on the roof of the palace.
From there, he saw a woman bathing.
Scripture says she was very beautiful.
David asked who she was.
The answer should have ended everything.
“This is Bathsheba… the wife of Uriah.”
Wife.
That word was the boundary.
That word was the warning.
That word told David, She belongs to a covenant you have no right to violate.
But desire has a terrifying ability to make boundaries feel negotiable when the heart has already decided what it wants.
David sent messengers.
He took her.
He slept with her.
Then came four words that shattered whatever illusion of secrecy remained:
“I am pregnant.”
Suddenly the rooftop had consequences.
The private moment had become a public threat.
And David had a decision to make.
Confess…
or conceal.
He chose concealment.
That is where this story becomes uncomfortable, because David’s fall was not merely about uncontrolled sexual desire. It became a horrifying progression of sin attempting to protect sin.
First came desire.
Then taking.
Then adultery.
Then deception.
Then manipulation.
Then death.
David summoned Uriah from the battlefield and tried to send him home, apparently hoping Uriah would sleep with Bathsheba and believe the child was his.
But Uriah refused the comforts of home while Israel’s soldiers remained in battle.
