Be careful with that sentence.
“God knows my heart” is not always comforting.
Sometimes it is terrifying.
Saul's deeper problem eventually surfaces in his own confession:

“I have sinned: for I have transgressed the commandment of the LORD, and thy words: because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.”
—1 Samuel 15:24, KJV
There it is.
Another voice had become louder than God's.
The people.
Their approval.
Their expectations.
Their reaction.
And suddenly this ancient king feels uncomfortably modern.
How much disobedience begins because we fear losing something?
A relationship.
A following.
A reputation.
A paycheck.
A friendship.
Acceptance.
Comfort.
Control.
We tell ourselves we are making complicated decisions when sometimes the truth is brutally simple:
God spoke through His Word, but another voice mattered more.
Samuel then gives Saul an even harder diagnosis:

“For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry.”
—1 Samuel 15:23, KJV
Why compare stubborn rebellion with idolatry?
Because persistent disobedience eventually reveals a throne problem.
Someone gets the final word.
If God says one thing and I knowingly insist upon another, the deepest question is not merely which rule I violated.
The question is who is king.
That is why “obedience is better than sacrifice” still stands.
Not because Christians earn salvation by performing well.
Not because God loves obedient people and refuses grace to struggling people.
Not because one failure means you are beyond restoration.
And certainly not because human beings can obey perfectly enough to save themselves.
The Gospel destroys that illusion.
If our hope were perfect obedience, every one of us would be finished.
“All have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
There has only ever been one perfectly obedient Son.
Jesus Christ.
Where Saul failed as an anointed king, Christ—the true King—obeyed the Father completely.
Jesus said:

“I do always those things that please him.”
—John 8:29, KJV
And when obedience led Him toward suffering, He did not search for a religious substitute.
In Gethsemane, with the cross approaching, Jesus prayed:

“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.”
—Luke 22:42, KJV
Feel the difference.
Saul effectively said, “I changed what You commanded, but look at what I brought You.”
Jesus said, “Not My will, but Yours.”
And He went to the cross.
Philippians 2:8 says Christ “humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.”
This is where the story moves from scandal to grace.
Because the answer to our rebellion is not merely, “Try harder.”
The answer is Jesus.
The Gospel is not that good people finally became obedient enough for God to accept them.

The Gospel is that sinners who could never repair their guilt were met by the obedient Son of God, who bore sin and conquered death, so that those who repent and trust in Him can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed.
Jesus does not merely expose the scandal.
He rewrites the story with grace.
But grace must never be twisted into permission to continue embracing rebellion.
The same Jesus who forgives sinners calls sinners to follow Him.
“If ye love me, keep my commandments,” He says in John 14:15.
Notice the order.
Love.
Then obedience flowing from love.
Christian obedience is not payment for Calvary.
It is a response to Calvary.
We do not obey so that Christ will finally love us enough to die for us.
Christ already went to the cross.
We obey because the crucified and risen Christ is Lord.
This is also why repentance is beautiful rather than merely humiliating.
Repentance is the moment you stop defending what is destroying you.
It is the moment the excuses run out.
The sheep are still making noise.
God already knows.
And instead of constructing another explanation, you finally say:
“Jesus, I was wrong.”
No performance.
No religious bargaining.
No blaming your childhood, your spouse, your church, your friends, your stress, your loneliness, your temptations, or your circumstances as though those things can erase personal responsibility.
Just truth.
“I sinned.”
And then grace meets truth.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).
Read that again.
Not merely forgive.
Cleanse.
Jesus is not interested only in changing your eternal destination while leaving every idol comfortably seated on the throne of your present life.
He saves.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He transforms.
He teaches His people to walk differently.
Maybe that is why this message hurts.
You may already know what God has been confronting.
You did not need another sermon to identify it.
You needed courage to stop renaming it.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe people see your worship but not your compromise.
Your Bible is highlighted.
Your private history is hidden.
You know Christian vocabulary well enough to sound healthy while quietly starving.
You know how to lift your hands while protecting the thing you refuse to place in God's hands.
And perhaps the most exhausting part is not even the sin anymore.
It is maintaining two versions of yourself.
The visible one.
And the hidden one.
How long are you going to live divided?
Jesus already knows what is behind you.
He hears the sheep.
And still He calls sinners to come into the light.
Not so they can impress Him.
So they can surrender.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need to be impressive.
Maybe it needs to be honest.

“Jesus, forgive me. I have been giving You sacrifices while withholding obedience. Show me what I have excused. Give me grace to repent. Teach me to love what You love, reject what You call sin, obey Your Word, and follow You even when obedience costs me something. I cannot save myself. My hope is in Your death and resurrection. Be Lord over the places I have tried to keep for myself. Amen.”
If something in you tightened while reading this, do not rush past it.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes public honesty is the first crack in a carefully maintained wall, and another believer reading your comment may realize they are not the only person being called back to surrender.
Not as a badge proving that you are spiritual.
Not as a substitute for obeying what God is telling you.
Somebody may be one honest encounter with Scripture away from repentance. Somebody may be quietly drowning behind a convincing Christian smile.
There may come a day when the temptation to negotiate with God returns, and you need to remember the sound of Saul's sheep.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well. Truth is worth passing on.
But there is an important distinction we should never corrupt.
Supporting a Christian ministry does not purchase God's favor.
Buying a book cannot make God owe you a blessing.
Sharing an article is not a substitute for repentance.
Giving money is not proof that your heart belongs to Christ.
If this article taught anything, it would contradict itself if it told you otherwise.

You glorify God by belonging to Christ and living for Him in faith, love, truth, worship, generosity, and obedience. Let that support be an expression of willing generosity and Gospel partnership—not guilt, superstition, or an attempt to buy God's approval.

Not because sharing earns heaven. Not because supporting Gospel Warrior is a condition of glorifying God. But because if biblical truth has helped you, passing that truth to someone else can itself become an act of love. Your share may travel somewhere you never could. Your tag may reach someone who would never search for a sermon. Your comment may give another struggling Christian the courage to stop hiding.
Support what faithfully points people to Christ.
Share what may awaken someone who is sleeping spiritually.
Save what you may need when compromise begins sounding reasonable again.
Follow so you can keep growing.
But above everything else—
obey Jesus.
Because Saul's tragedy was not that he sacrificed too little.
It was that he thought sacrifice could replace surrender.
And perhaps the most dangerous altar you will ever build is the one where you offer God everything except yourself.
The sheep are still making noise.
The excuses are getting tired.
The King already knows.
But for the repentant sinner, the story does not have to end where the scandal happened.
There is still a cross.
There is still an empty tomb.
There is still forgiveness.
There is still grace.
There is still a Savior who receives sinners and transforms those who come to Him.
So stop negotiating with the One who died to redeem you.
Bring Him the truth.
Bring Him your repentance.
Bring Him the hidden room.
Bring Him the relationship.
Bring Him the habit.
Bring Him the resentment.
Bring Him the fear.
Bring Him the reputation you have been desperately protecting.
And when obedience costs you something, remember the Savior who became “obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.”
You do not need another sacrifice to hide behind; you need the grace of Jesus to bring you out of hiding.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Bought Back the Woman Who Broke His Heart — And That Is Why Hosea Should Terrify and Heal Every Christian
paragraphs: He Bought Back the Woman Who Broke His Heart — And That Is Why Hosea Should Terrify and Heal Every Christian
How Hosea reveals the scandal of our spiritual unfaithfulness, the relentless redeeming love of God, and the Gospel truth that your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
There is a sentence in the Bible that becomes almost unbearable when you understand who God was talking about.
Not because it is complicated.
Because it is painfully simple.
God told Hosea:
“Go again, love…”
In Hebrew, the words begin:

לֵךְ עֹד אֱהַב־אִשָּׁה
Lekh ‘od, ’ehav-ishah…
“Go again. Love a woman…”
Again.
That one word changes everything.
Because loving someone once can be romantic.
Loving someone after betrayal is something else entirely.
Loving after you know what they did…
after trust has been shattered…
after promises have been violated…
after the person who belonged beside you went looking for satisfaction somewhere else…
that kind of love costs something.
And Hosea is not merely a strange Old Testament marriage story.
It is a mirror.
Before you finish reading this, you may realize that you have spent years identifying with Hosea when God intended you to recognize yourself in the unfaithful one.
That is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
And that is where grace becomes breathtaking.
The book opens with words we would probably remove if we were trying to make Christianity more marketable.

God commands Hosea to enter a marriage that will become a living prophetic picture of Israel's covenant unfaithfulness. Hosea 1:2 uses the striking Hebrew expression אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים — ’eshet zenunim, commonly rendered along the lines of “a wife of whoredom” or “a promiscuous woman.”
The language is intentionally disturbing.
Israel belonged to Yahweh, yet Israel repeatedly ran after other gods.
God had rescued them.
Fed them.
Protected them.
Covenanted with them.
Loved them.
And still they wandered.
So God made Hosea's home into a sermon Israel could not easily ignore.
Imagine Hosea walking through town knowing people were whispering.
Imagine hearing the rumors.
Imagine wondering where your wife is tonight.
Imagine loving someone who keeps treating your love as though it were disposable.
Then imagine God saying:
Now you are beginning to understand what idolatry does to Me.
That changes how we think about sin.
We often reduce sin to rule-breaking.
God reveals something deeper.
Sin is relational treason against the God who made us.
Idolatry is not merely bowing before a carved statue.
Anything we demand to give us what only God should ultimately give us can become an idol.
Approval.
Money.
Sex.
Success.
Romance.
Status.
Career.
Pleasure.
A relationship.
A following.
Even ministry.
Even religion.
We can sing worship songs while secretly worshiping applause.
We can post Bible verses while starving for validation.
We can know Christian vocabulary while our private lives belong to another master.
We can say, “Jesus is Lord,” while quietly negotiating which rooms of our lives He is actually allowed to enter.
And perhaps that is why Hosea still hurts.
Gomer's wandering is easier to condemn when we imagine her scandal occurring somewhere outside ourselves.
But then the Holy Spirit turns the mirror around.
How many times has God been faithful while you wandered?
How many prayers did you pray only after everything else failed?
How many blessings did you enjoy without thanking the One who gave them?
How many times did God become important only when you were frightened?
How often have we wanted God's gifts more than God Himself?
Suddenly Gomer does not feel so distant.
Suddenly her footsteps sound disturbingly familiar.
But Hosea contains something even more shocking than betrayal.
God does not merely expose Israel's unfaithfulness.
He announces His intention to restore.
In Hosea 2, judgment is real. Sin has consequences. God does not pretend adultery is faithfulness or rebellion is harmless.
Biblical love never requires God to lie about evil.
Yet judgment is not the only word God speaks.
After exposing Israel's sin, the language changes.
God speaks of alluring her, bringing her into the wilderness, and speaking tenderly to her.
Then comes one of Scripture's extraordinary covenant promises:

וְאֵרַשְׂתִּיךְ לִי לְעוֹלָם
Ve’erastikh li le‘olam.
“I will betroth you to Me forever.”
And God continues:
בְּצֶדֶק וּבְמִשְׁפָּט וּבְחֶסֶד וּבְרַחֲמִים
betzedeq uvmishpat uvechesed uverachamim
“In righteousness and in justice, in steadfast love and in mercy.”
Do not rush past חֶסֶד — chesed.

English translations often render it “steadfast love,” “lovingkindness,” or “faithful love.” No single English expression captures every shade of the Hebrew word in every context. Here it belongs to the language of committed, covenantal faithfulness.
God is not saying sin never mattered.
He is saying sin will not have the final word over His redemptive purpose.
Then Hosea 3 arrives.
And Scripture gives us that devastating command:
לֵךְ עֹד אֱהַב־אִשָּׁה
Go again.
Love again.

Hosea 3:1 describes the woman as an adulteress and deliberately compares Hosea's love with Yahweh's love for Israel even while Israel turns toward other gods. The precise relationship implied by some wording in the Hebrew has been debated and translated differently, so we should resist pretending every detail is more certain than the text allows.
But the theological point is unmistakable.
God loves an unfaithful people.
Hosea goes.
And then he pays.
Fifteen shekels of silver together with barley.
Pause there.
He pays for the woman who had betrayed him.

The text does not invite us to turn every detail of Hosea's payment into a simplistic one-to-one prediction of the cross. Hosea first speaks directly about Yahweh's covenant relationship with Israel. Responsible interpretation should allow Hosea to say what Hosea says.
But once we read Hosea within the whole biblical story, something magnificent comes into view.
The God who reveals Himself as the One who loves and restores His unfaithful covenant people ultimately reveals the staggering cost of redemption in Jesus Christ.
Hosea bought the woman back.
At Calvary, redemption reaches its climactic Gospel revelation.
Peter writes that believers were redeemed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
And suddenly the scandal becomes personal.
You were not redeemed because God discovered that you were secretly worth saving because of your righteousness.
You were redeemed because God is rich in mercy.
Christianity does not announce that basically good people need spiritual improvement.
The Gospel announces that sinners need reconciliation with a holy God.
We did not climb our way back.
God came for sinners.
Jesus did not die for an imaginary, cleaned-up version of you.
Scripture says:

“God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8
While we were still sinners.
Not once we became impressive.
Not once the addiction disappeared.
Not once the shame was gone.
Not once our theology became perfect.
Not once we had prayed enough.
Not once we had cried enough.
Christ died for sinners.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible.
Grace is not God's permission to remain enslaved to the thing destroying you.
Grace opens the prison door.
Jesus did not shed His blood merely so we could decorate our chains with Christian vocabulary.
He came to save.
Forgive.
Cleanse.
Reconcile.
Transform.
Make alive.
This is why Hosea's message should never be reduced to, “God loves you no matter what, so everything is fine.”
Everything was not fine.
Israel's idolatry mattered.
Gomer's unfaithfulness mattered.
Your sin matters.
My sin matters.
The cross itself proves how seriously God takes sin.
If sin were trivial, Calvary would be incomprehensible.
But the cross simultaneously tells us something else.
Your sin may be greater than you have admitted…
but Christ is a greater Savior than you have imagined.
Maybe you are reading this with a secret.
Something nobody at church knows.
Something your spouse does not know.
Something your family would never expect.
Maybe you have learned how to smile while spiritually bleeding.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know which worship songs to raise your hands to.
You know how to look strong.
But somewhere beneath the Christian appearance is a room you have kept locked.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
An affair.
Alcohol.
Pride.
Jealousy.
Greed.
Secret messages.
Resentment.
Compromise.
A double life.
Or perhaps nothing outwardly dramatic at all.
Perhaps you simply do not love Jesus the way you once did.
Your Bible remains closed longer.
Prayer feels mechanical.
Worship became background noise.
Sin stopped frightening you.
Conviction became easier to silence.
And you have wondered whether you wandered too far.
Listen carefully.
Hosea is not permission to keep wandering.
It is an invitation to come home.
Repentance is not God humiliating you before He reluctantly allows you back.
Repentance is turning away from the false lover that cannot save you and returning to the God who can.
Hosea 14 eventually gives Israel words for that return:
“Take away all iniquity…”
And then God answers with one of the most beautiful promises in the book:
“I will heal their apostasy; I will love them freely.”
That is the heart of redemption.
God does not merely cover the evidence and leave the disease untouched.
He heals.
And this is where Hosea points our eyes beyond Hosea.
Jesus Christ is not Hosea wearing a New Testament costume. The biblical connections must be handled carefully.
Hosea was a prophet whose marriage dramatized Yahweh's covenant relationship with unfaithful Israel.
Jesus is the incarnate Son of God, the promised Messiah, the Bridegroom who gives Himself for His people.
The New Testament describes Christ's sacrificial love for His church with astonishing marital imagery: Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.
Hosea therefore contributes to a biblical pattern that becomes breathtaking when viewed from the cross.
A holy God pursues covenant breakers.
A faithful God confronts unfaithfulness.
A merciful God calls sinners home.
And in Jesus Christ, God provides the redemption sinners could never purchase for themselves.
Gomer had a price she could not apparently escape without someone paying.
We had a debt we could never erase by religious performance.
Then Jesus came.
Not carrying fifteen pieces of silver.
Carrying a cross.
Not bargaining with sin.
Bearing judgment.
Not pretending we were innocent.
Giving His life for the guilty.
Not standing far away shouting instructions about how to return.
Entering our world to rescue sinners.
The nails did not mean sin was small.
The nails meant love was costly.
And resurrection means death did not win.
That is why your scandal does not have to become your identity.
Maybe people remember what you did.
Jesus knows everything you did.
There is an enormous difference.
People may know the rumor.
Christ knows the heart.
People may know the failure.
Christ knows every hidden motive, every secret thought, every compromised night, every tear, every excuse, every lie.
And still the Gospel invitation stands:
Repent.
Believe.
Come home.
Not because you deserve another chance.
Because Jesus is enough.
There are people who will read these words convinced that Christianity belongs to cleaner people.
People with better marriages.
Better histories.
Better habits.
Better childhoods.
Better reputations.
But look at the Bible.
God's redemptive story repeatedly moves through human wreckage.
Liars.
Adulterers.
Murderers.
Cowards.
Idolaters.
Persecutors.
Broken families.
Public failures.
And repentant sinners transformed by grace.
Christianity is not the museum of people who never fell.
It is the proclamation of a crucified and risen Savior who rescues sinners.
So stop trying to edit your past before bringing it to Jesus.
You cannot shock the One who already knows.
You cannot cleanse yourself enough to make the cross unnecessary.
You cannot outperform your guilt.
You cannot heal spiritual adultery by pretending it never happened.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Run to Christ.
There is forgiveness in Jesus.
There is cleansing in Jesus.
There is a new life in Jesus.
And maybe that is what somebody reading this needed tonight.
Not another motivational quote.
Not another religious performance.
Not another promise that tomorrow you will try harder.
You need Christ.
Be honest before God.
And believers who see those words—pray.
Do not interrogate.
Do not shame.
Pray.
Someone's comment section can become a small place where masks finally come off.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
But if Christ has given you truth that could help another person, sharing that truth can become a simple act of witness.
Send it privately to the person whose name came into your mind while reading.

And stay close to Gospel Warrior if you want Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment that keeps pointing beyond personalities and back to Jesus Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who is drifting.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the person who thinks Christianity is only for respectable people.
Invite even the unbelieving friend who cannot understand why Christians keep talking about grace.
Let them meet Hosea.
Then let Hosea point them toward Christ.
Not to buy God's approval.
Not to prove your salvation.
Not because giving money automatically glorifies God.
It is not a shirt.
It is not a discount.
It is the opportunity to help keep biblical truth moving.

If Gospel Warrior has fed your faith, challenged your compromise, strengthened your family, helped you return to Scripture, or reminded you that Jesus Christ is still worthy of everything, you can help sustain that mission.
Not as payment to God.
As witness.
Someone thinks their adultery is the ending.
Someone thinks their addiction is the ending.
Someone thinks their divorce is the ending.
Someone thinks their relapse is the ending.
Someone thinks their shame is the ending.
Someone thinks the night they ruined everything became the final sentence of their life.
Tell them about Jesus.
Tell them repentance is real.
Tell them forgiveness is real.
Tell them grace is not imaginary.
Tell them the cross was sufficient.
Tell them the tomb is empty.
Tell them sinners can come home.
Maybe somebody else needs to see that testimony and realize God has not finished with them either.
Hosea's story begins in scandal.
But scandal is not where God's message ends.
Betrayal does not speak the final word.
Shame does not speak the final word.
Failure does not speak the final word.
Your past does not speak the final word.
Jesus does.
And for everyone who repents and trusts Him, His word is not merely exposure.
It is redemption.
So when your past whispers your old name…
when shame shows you the chapters you wish you could tear out…
when the enemy points toward the road where you wandered…
remember the God revealed in Scripture.
The God who says:
Go again.
Love again.
Restore.
Redeem.
Come home.
And remember the Savior who went farther than Hosea ever could.
All the way to a cross.
All the way into death.
And out of an empty tomb.
Your scandal may explain where grace found you—but it does not get to decide where Jesus is taking you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Is Porn an Addiction—or a Choice? The Question That Could Be Keeping You in Chains
paragraphs: Is Porn an Addiction—or a Choice? The Question That Could Be Keeping You in Chains
What if the argument over whether pornography is an addiction or a choice is distracting us from the deeper question Jesus is asking: “Do you want to be free?”
It usually happens when nobody is watching.
The room is quiet. The door is closed. Your family thinks you are asleep. Your spouse may be lying only a few feet away. Your Bible may even be sitting on the nightstand.
And there is that screen.
That search bar.
That familiar pull.
You tell yourself you are only going to look for a moment.
Then the moment becomes another click.
Another image.
Another video.
Another promise you swore you would never break again.
And afterward comes the silence.
Not pleasure anymore.
Silence.
You close the browser. Delete the history. Put the phone down.
Maybe you whisper, “God, I'm sorry.”
Maybe you cannot even bring yourself to pray because you prayed the same prayer last week.
And somewhere inside that exhausted cycle, a question begins haunting you:
If I keep choosing this, do I actually want Jesus?
Or perhaps another question:
If I desperately want to stop but keep going back, am I addicted?
That distinction matters. But it can also become a hiding place.

Because pornography can involve genuine patterns of compulsion, and yet calling something compulsive does not magically make moral responsibility disappear. Likewise, calling it “just a choice” can badly underestimate how entrenched repeated sexual behavior can become.
Modern clinical language is actually more careful than much of the internet.

The World Health Organization's ICD-11 recognizes compulsive sexual behaviour disorder, or CSBD, and classifies it as an impulse-control disorder. Clinical descriptions include persistent difficulty controlling intense, repetitive sexual impulses or behaviors, repeated unsuccessful attempts to reduce them, neglect of responsibilities or other interests, and continuation despite adverse consequences. Problematic pornography use can be one expression of this pattern.
That is important because Christians should not have to distort science in order to defend Scripture.
But science cannot answer the whole question either.

A diagnostic category can describe patterns of behavior. It cannot tell you what humanity was created for, why lust ultimately violates love, what holiness means, why the human body possesses dignity, or how sinners are reconciled to God.
For that, we have to listen to Jesus.
And Jesus takes the conversation somewhere painfully deeper than the browser history.
In Matthew 5:28, He says:
“But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
The Greek text contains a phrase worth slowing down for:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν — pros to epithymēsai autēn

The construction carries the sense of looking in order to desire/lust after her. This is why translations such as the ESV render the idea as looking with “lustful intent.” Jesus is not teaching that accidentally noticing an attractive person is identical to adultery. He is exposing something deliberate happening in the heart—the gaze that becomes cultivated desire, the person mentally consumed for sexual gratification.
That distinction matters enormously.
Temptation is not identical to surrender.
Seeing is not automatically lusting.
An unwanted sexual thought entering your mind is not the same thing as welcoming it, feeding it, replaying it, searching for more of it, and turning another human being into material for fantasy.
Jesus goes after the heart because sin does not begin when somebody catches you.
It begins much earlier.
Pornography therefore cannot be reduced merely to pixels.
There is a person on that screen.
A human being bearing the dignity of being made in the image of God.
Porn trains the eyes to ask, What can I take from this body?
Jesus teaches the heart to ask, How do I love my neighbor?
Porn says, Consume.
Christ says, Love.
Porn says, Take.
Christ says, Give.
Porn says, Hide.
Christ says, Come into the light.
And perhaps that is why this battle hurts so deeply for believers.
You know the difference.
You may genuinely love Jesus.
You may worship on Sunday.
You may serve at church.
You may know Scripture.
You may have a spouse who trusts you.
You may have children who think you are the strongest Christian in the house.
And still, at 1:17 in the morning, there you are.
Again.
That is where shame begins preaching its own gospel.
Fraud.
Hypocrite.
Disgusting.
God must be tired of you.
You have repented too many times.
You might as well stop pretending.
Listen carefully.
That voice is not the Gospel.
The Gospel never calls darkness light. Jesus does not minimize sexual sin. Matthew 5 makes that impossible. But the same Christ who exposes sin is the Christ who came to save sinners.
Christianity does not say, “Porn isn't serious.”
Christianity says something infinitely more hopeful:
Your sin is serious enough that Christ had to die—and His grace is powerful enough that He willingly did.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction says, Come out.
Condemnation says, Stay hidden.
Conviction says, Confess.
Condemnation says, You're disgusting.
Conviction leads toward Christ.
Shame tells you to run from Him.
And hiding is where pornography becomes strongest.
You sin.
You feel ashamed.
Because you feel ashamed, you isolate yourself.
Because you isolate yourself, emotional pressure grows.
Because pressure grows, you seek escape.
Because pornography has become an established escape, you return to it.
Then you feel even more ashamed.
And the prison builds another wall.
So is porn an addiction or a choice?

For some people, compulsive behavior has become severe enough that professional assessment may be appropriate. Repeated failure to control sexual behavior despite harmful consequences is a recognized clinical concern, and seeking qualified mental-health care is not spiritual failure.
But Scripture refuses to let any diagnosis become an excuse for surrender.
And Scripture also refuses to let moral responsibility become an excuse for mercilessness.
The better Christian answer is not simply addiction or choice.
It can involve both entrenched compulsion and morally meaningful choices.

Repeated choices can become powerful patterns. Powerful patterns can make future resistance profoundly difficult. Difficulty does not make holiness irrelevant, and responsibility does not mean a struggling person should simply “try harder” in secrecy.
The Gospel gives us a better path.
Truth without cruelty.
Responsibility without hopelessness.
Grace without permission.
Repentance without despair.
You are not being invited merely to stop watching porn.
You are being invited to rediscover what your sexuality was created for.
Because pornography does something subtle over time.
It teaches you to separate bodies from souls.
It teaches you to consume intimacy without covenant.
To experience stimulation without sacrifice.
To desire without serving.
To take without knowing.
To watch without loving.
And eventually, something frightening can happen.
You stop seeing people.
You see bodies.
Categories.
Fantasies.
Thumbnails.
But Jesus restores sight.
He teaches you to see a woman not as an object created for your gratification, but as someone's daughter, someone's sister, perhaps someone's wife—and above all, a human being made in God's image.
He teaches you to see a man not as an object either, but as a person bearing that same God-given dignity.
Pornography asks, How can this person satisfy me?
The Gospel asks, How can I honor this person before God?
That is transformation.
Not merely cleaner browser history.
A different heart.
And that is why merely blocking websites, while often wise, cannot by itself save you.
You can install every filter available and still carry an unfiltered imagination.
You can throw away your phone and still remember the images.
You can make yourself externally inaccessible to pornography while internally remaining devoted to lust.
You need more than restriction.
You need renewal.
Yet renewal does not mean abandoning practical wisdom.
If certain apps repeatedly lead you into sin, remove them.
If your phone in the bedroom has become the doorway, stop bringing it there.
If secrecy is feeding the pattern, bring it into appropriate, trustworthy Christian accountability.
If you repeatedly lose the battle at midnight, stop designing your life as though midnight-you possesses unlimited strength.
Do not keep placing yourself five inches from the cliff and asking God why you keep falling.
There is no spiritual maturity in making temptation unnecessarily convenient.

Jesus' language immediately following His warning about lust is deliberately severe: if your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out; if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off. Christians have historically understood this as forceful imagery demanding radical action against sin, not as a command to physically mutilate ourselves.
The point is unmistakable:
Stop negotiating with what is destroying you.
Somebody reading this already knows exactly what needs to go.
The secret account.
The hidden folder.
The private browser.
The second phone.
The saved videos.
The social-media feed you pretend is innocent.
The conversation that keeps drifting sexual.
The nighttime routine that has become a ritual of temptation.
You keep asking God for freedom while keeping the prison key under your pillow.
Maybe tonight repentance needs to become tangible.
Delete it.
Confess it.
Bring it into the light.
Not tomorrow.
Not after “one last time.”
There is almost always another last time when sin is allowed to schedule the farewell.
And if you fall again?
Do not turn failure into permission.
Run back to Christ.
Confess specifically.
Learn what happened.
Strengthen the weak place.
Get up.
Keep fighting.
Grace is not God's permission to make peace with chains.
Grace is God's declaration that chains do not have to have the final word.
The cross destroys two lies at once.
The first lie says, “My sin isn't that serious.”
Look at Calvary.
It is.
The second says, “My sin is too serious for Jesus.”
Look again.
It isn't.
Christ knew what He was purchasing when He shed His blood.
There were no hidden browser tabs at the cross.
No secret searches He somehow failed to anticipate.
No midnight relapse outside the knowledge of the Savior who came for sinners.
That does not make your next click harmless.
It makes your next act of repentance hopeful.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Not because God pretends the scandal never happened.
Because Jesus enters the scandal and begins rewriting the person inside it.
Peter had denial.
David had sexual sin and bloodguilt.
The Corinthian church had a past filled with sexual immorality and other sins, yet Paul could speak of people who had been washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of Jesus Christ.
The Gospel does not edit the past.
It redeems people from its dominion.
Maybe you have been watching pornography for twenty years.
Maybe twenty minutes.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your spouse discovered it and your marriage is bleeding.
Maybe you are single and terrified that these patterns will follow you into marriage.
Maybe you are a pastor, ministry worker, father, mother, teenager, widow, professional, student, or someone who never imagined this would become your secret.
Your title does not frighten Jesus.
Your history does not confuse Him.
Your hypocrisy cannot be healed by deeper hypocrisy.
Come into the light.
Not because exposure is painless.
Because darkness is killing you.

And if your pornography use feels uncontrollable, if repeated attempts to stop have failed, if it is damaging your relationships, responsibilities, mental health, or daily functioning, seek appropriate professional help as well as mature spiritual support. Needing serious help does not make repentance less real. Sometimes humility looks like finally admitting, I cannot keep fighting this alone.
But never confuse getting help with getting a substitute Savior.
A therapist cannot forgive sin.
An accountability partner cannot regenerate your heart.
A filter cannot crucify the flesh.
A pastor cannot become your mediator.
Only Jesus saves.
All those other forms of help can become instruments of wisdom and grace, but Christ remains the center.
And perhaps the most important question is no longer:
Am I addicted?
Maybe the question is:
What am I willing to surrender to follow Jesus?
Because you can spend years debating terminology while continuing the behavior.
You can study dopamine.
Read books.
Watch testimonies.
Install blockers.
Promise yourself.
Count streaks.
Reset counters.
Cry.
Relapse.
Repeat.
And still avoid the terrifyingly simple words:
Jesus, I surrender this to You.
Not because surrender makes temptation disappear overnight.
But because freedom begins when secrecy stops being your refuge and Christ becomes your refuge instead.
Be honest.
And if Christ has already brought you through this battle, tell someone that freedom is possible. Your testimony may become the rope God uses to remind another believer that the pit has an exit.
Not because saving a post changes you, but because there may be a night when temptation starts rewriting your memory and you need to remember what you decided while you could see clearly.
Not as proof that you have everything together.
Send it privately to the brother who disappeared.
The husband who is struggling.
The teenager who needs a better vision of sexuality.
The believer drowning in shame.
Even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing to say except “stop.”
Show them that the Gospel says far more.
It says come home.
But before you leave this article, remember something.
The goal is not for you to become the person who can proudly say, “I haven't watched porn in 500 days.”
The goal is to become the person who increasingly looks like Jesus.
Freedom is bigger than abstinence.
It is learning to love what is holy.
Learning to see people instead of bodies.
Learning to choose truth when nobody is watching.
Learning to confess instead of conceal.
Learning to run toward Christ instead of hiding from Him.
And one day you may realize the screen that once seemed impossible to resist has lost some of its power.
Not because you became invincible.
Because something better became more beautiful.
Christ.
His presence.
His holiness.
His mercy.
His cross.
His empty tomb.
His promise that sin will not write the final chapter of everyone who belongs to Him.
So tonight, when the room gets quiet and the old voice whispers again, remember:
You do not have to answer every knock at the door of your mind.
You do not have to feed every desire that asks to be fed.
You do not have to obey every urge simply because it feels powerful.
And you certainly do not have to hide from the Savior who already knows why you are crying.
Bring Him the truth.
Bring Him the craving.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the relapse.
Bring Him the wounded marriage.
Bring Him the secret account.
Bring Him the years you wish you could erase.
Bring Him all of it.
Then follow Him into the light.
Because perhaps the greatest tragedy was never simply that pornography captured your eyes.
It was that shame convinced you to stop lifting them toward Jesus.
The screen may know your history. But it does not get to write your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SAMSON KILLED A LION WITH HIS BARE HANDS. WHEN HE RETURNED, SOMETHING IMPOSSIBLE WAS WAITING INSIDE THE CORPSE.
paragraphs: SAMSON KILLED A LION WITH HIS BARE HANDS. WHEN HE RETURNED, SOMETHING IMPOSSIBLE WAS WAITING INSIDE THE CORPSE.
The disturbing riddle of Samson, the honey hidden inside death, and the Gospel truth for anyone who thinks the ugliest chapter of their life is too ruined for God to redeem.
There was something inside the dead lion.
Something that should make you stop.
Something Samson could not have seen coming when the animal came roaring toward him.
Honey.
But before there was honey, there was a roar.
Before there was sweetness, there was violence.

Before there was a riddle told at a wedding feast, there was a private battle in a vineyard where a young man discovered that the Spirit of God could empower him to do what human strength alone could never explain.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes uncomfortable for us.
Because most of us want the honey.
We just don't want the lion.

We want resurrection without death. Restoration without devastation. Testimony without testing. A healed marriage without the night somebody almost walked away. Freedom without admitting what enslaved us. Grace without confronting sin. A new life without the death of the old one.
But Judges 14 gives us one of Scripture's strangest images.
A lion.
A carcass.
Bees.
Honey.
And a riddle nobody could solve unless they knew what Samson had survived.
The story begins with a man who was extraordinarily gifted by God and yet painfully capable of making reckless choices.
That matters.
Samson was not the sanitized hero we sometimes turn him into.
He was a judge raised up during a dark period in Israel's history. His birth had been announced before he was conceived. He was set apart from the womb. God's calling rested upon his life.
And yet Samson could be impulsive, angry, secretive, driven by appetite, and dangerously confident in his own strength.
That tension is part of the point.
God's power working through Samson never meant that everything Samson desired was righteous.
Spiritual gifting is not the same thing as spiritual maturity.
You can be strong in one place and frighteningly weak in another.
You can know Scripture and still have an appetite you refuse to surrender.
You can worship publicly and struggle privately.
You can have people admire what God has placed upon you while almost nobody knows what is slowly destroying you.
Maybe that sentence found you.
Samson went down toward Timnah because he had seen a Philistine woman he wanted to marry. His parents objected, asking why he would seek a wife among the uncircumcised Philistines.
Samson's response was essentially: get her for me, because she is right in my eyes.
That phrase should bother us.
Because Judges repeatedly describes an age in which people did what was right in their own eyes.
And Samson's eyes would become one of the recurring battlegrounds of his life.
He saw.
He wanted.
He pursued.
How many disasters still begin that way?
Not because something was right before God.
Because it looked right to us.
Then, somewhere near the vineyards of Timnah, everything changed.
Scripture says a young lion came roaring toward Samson.
No sword.
No spear.
No weapon in his hand.
Just Samson...
and the lion.
Then Judges 14:6 says:
“וַתִּצְלַח עָלָיו רוּחַ יְהוָה”
Vattitzlach alav Ruach YHWH.
The sense is that the Spirit of the LORD rushed powerfully upon him.
That detail cannot be removed from the story.
Samson's victory is not presented merely as the achievement of an unusually muscular man.
The text points us toward the empowering presence of God.
Samson tore the lion apart with his bare hands.
And then he kept walking.
He did not even tell his father and mother what had happened.
Imagine carrying a victory nobody knows about.
Imagine surviving something privately that would have terrified everyone who knows you.
Some of you understand that better than you wish you did.
People see you smiling now.
They did not hear the roar.
They see you worshipping.
They never saw the night you nearly quit.
They see the marriage that survived.
They don't know how close it came to dying.
They see the person who serves Jesus today.
They don't know who you used to be when nobody was watching.
They see honey.
They never met the lion.
Time passed.
Then Samson returned along that road.
And this time, he deliberately turned aside to look at what remained of the animal he had killed.
Judges 14:8 records the strange discovery:
“וְהִנֵּה עֲדַת דְּבוֹרִים בִּגְוִיַּת הָאַרְיֵה וּדְבָשׁ”
Vehinneh adat devorim bigviyyat ha'aryeh udevash.
In plain sense:
Behold, a swarm of bees was in the body of the lion—and honey.
Honey.
Inside the remains of what once tried to kill him.
Read that again slowly.
The place associated with terror now contained sweetness.
The thing that once came roaring against him had become the location of something he could eat.
The predator was dead.
And inside its remains was honey.
Now we must be careful here.
Judges does not explicitly tell us, “The lion symbolizes your trials,” nor does it say, “The honey symbolizes salvation.” We should never force Scripture to say what Scripture does not say.
The immediate story explains Samson's coming riddle.
But the image is so striking that it can legitimately remind Christians of a truth proclaimed throughout the rest of Scripture:
God is astonishingly capable of bringing good out of places marked by suffering, evil, weakness, judgment, and death without ever calling evil good.
Joseph could tell the brothers who betrayed him that they intended evil against him, while God intended it for good.
Paul could write that God works all things together for good for those who love Him and are called according to His purpose.
And at the very center of Christianity stands an even greater scandal:
a cross.
Rome meant it for execution.
Human wickedness nailed the innocent Son of God there.
Yet through that very death, according to God's redemptive purpose, came forgiveness and reconciliation for sinners.
That does not mean your suffering was good.
It means suffering does not get the final word when your life belongs to God.
That betrayal was not good.
The abuse was not good.
The addiction was not good.
Your sin was not good.
The funeral was not good.
The divorce papers were not good.
The diagnosis was not good.
The night you broke down on the bathroom floor was not good.
The years you wasted running from God were not good.
Christianity does not require us to rename darkness and call it light.
It announces something far more breathtaking:
darkness cannot defeat the redemptive purposes of God.
Samson reached into the remains and took honey.
Later, at his wedding feast, he turned what had happened into a riddle.
The Hebrew of Judges 14:14 is compact and unforgettable:

“מֵהָאֹכֵל יָצָא מַאֲכָל
וּמֵעַז יָצָא מָתוֹק”

Meha'okhel yatza ma'akhal,
ume'az yatza matok.

“Out of the eater came something to eat,
and out of the strong came something sweet.”
The eater became the source of food.
The strong became the place of sweetness.
Nobody could solve it.
Of course they couldn't.
They had not seen what Samson had seen.
They didn't know about the lion.
They didn't know about the battle.
They didn't know about the carcass.
They didn't know where the honey came from.
And there are people looking at your life right now who cannot understand your worship because they don't know what God brought you through.
They don't understand why you cry when you sing about grace.
They don't know what you were forgiven of.
They don't know how close you came to destroying everything.
They don't know the secret prayer God answered.
They don't know the temptation you fought at 2:00 in the morning.
They don't know the hospital corridor.
They don't know the betrayal.
They don't know the grave you stood beside.
They don't know how far you wandered.
They don't know the lion.
So they cannot understand why the honey tastes so sweet.
But you know.
And God knows.
Yet there is another side to Samson's story that we cannot romanticize.
The same man who killed a lion could not consistently master his own appetites.
That may be the most frightening part.
He could defeat something outside himself while slowly losing battles inside himself.
He could tear apart a lion but repeatedly allow desire, anger, pride, secrecy, and compromised relationships to pull him toward destruction.
And if we're courageous enough to admit it, Samson can look painfully familiar.
Some of us are incredibly good at fighting visible lions.
We work.
Provide.
Lead.
Preach.
Serve.
Protect.
Build.
Survive.
Everybody calls us strong.
But there is another battle.
The browser history.
The bitterness.
The secret messages.
The bottle.
The jealousy.
The obsession.
The pride.
The relationship you know is pulling you away from God.
The habit you keep renaming so you don't have to call it sin.
The wound you have turned into permission to hurt everybody around you.
The applause you secretly need.
The anger your family has learned to walk around.
You can kill lions in public and still be dying in private.
Samson's strength never made Samson his own savior.
And yours won't either.

Eventually the riddle itself became entangled in manipulation, threats, betrayal, rage, and bloodshed. Samson's life continued spiraling through extraordinary victories and devastating compromises until the man famous for his eyes eventually lost them.
The hero became a prisoner.
The strong man became entertainment for his enemies.
The man who once tore apart a lion was eventually led by the hand.
That is where cheap motivational Christianity would abandon Samson.
God didn't.
Near the end of Samson's story, blind and humiliated, he prayed again.
And God heard him.
Samson's story is messy enough that Hebrews 11 later mentioning him among people associated with faith can surprise us.
Because grace has always been scandalous.
Not cheap.
Not permissive.
Not indifferent to sin.
Scandalous.
Grace does not tell Samson that his choices did not matter.
They mattered terribly.
Grace does not erase consequences.
Grace means human failure does not possess greater authority than the mercy and purposes of God.
And this is where Samson's strange riddle can turn our eyes toward Someone infinitely greater than Samson.
Jesus Christ.
Samson killed a lion and later found sweetness associated with its death.
Jesus did something incomparably greater.
He entered death itself.
Not because death overpowered Him as an unwilling victim, but because He willingly laid down His life for sinners.
At Calvary, humanity's darkest crime became the stage upon which God's saving purpose was accomplished.
The cross looked like defeat.
Then came Sunday.
The tomb looked final.
Then the stone was rolled away.
Death swallowed countless generations.
Then Christ rose.
The eater was defeated.
The grave did not get the final word.
And because Jesus lives, repentance is not the funeral of your hope.
It is where resurrection life begins.
You may have done things you cannot undo.
You may carry consequences you cannot erase.
You may have wasted years.
You may have betrayed people.
You may have compromised.
You may have been the victim in one chapter and the villain in another.
You may be reading this while hiding something from everybody who loves you.
But listen carefully:
Jesus Christ did not come merely to make respectable people slightly better.
He came to save sinners.
Real ones.
Guilty ones.
Ashamed ones.
Addicted ones.
Religious ones.
Broken ones.
Proud ones.
People with carcasses in their past.
People who still hear lions roaring in their memories.
People like Samson.
People like us.
The Gospel is not God pretending your sin never mattered.

The Gospel is that your sin mattered so much that Christ bore judgment for sinners upon the cross, and God's grace is so astonishing that everyone who turns to Christ in repentance and faith can receive forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life.
Maybe the lion in your story has already fallen.
Maybe you're still fighting it.
Maybe, if you're honest, you have discovered that the most dangerous lion was never outside you.
It was the sin within.
Either way, your answer is not Samson's strength.
Your answer is Samson's God.
Your answer is Jesus.
So stop pretending.
Stop polishing the testimony while hiding the wound.
Stop calling bondage a personality trait.
Stop defending what Christ is asking you to surrender.
Bring it into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Return.
Ask for help.
Open the Bible again.
Pray again.
Walk into church again.
Tell a mature believer the truth.
Come back to Christ.
There is grace for the prodigal who turns home.
And maybe one day you will stand in a place you once thought would destroy you and realize:
the lion did not write the ending.
Jesus did.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, don't write an impressive comment.
Write an honest one.
You don't have to tell strangers every detail.
God already knows the whole story.
But sometimes one honest sentence is the moment hiding begins to lose its power.
And if somebody came into your mind while reading this, don't ignore that.
Send it privately to the person who thinks their worst chapter disqualified them from God's mercy.
Send it to the believer who wandered.
Send it to the person who doesn't believe yet but needs to understand what Christians actually mean by grace.
Not because every day will feel spiritual, but because there may come a night when the lion starts roaring again and you need to remember that the roar is not the same thing as the ending.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you open Scripture, confront sin, return to prayer, understand grace, or look toward Jesus again, stay close.
It does not.
Not because giving money proves someone is a better Christian.
It doesn't.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Salvation is the gift of God through Christ.
But generosity can be one practical way believers choose to glorify God by helping sound biblical encouragement reach more people.
It is mission.
It is helping another exhausted believer encounter Scripture.
Helping another prodigal remember the road home.
Helping another person discover that Christianity is not about pretending to be strong enough.
It is about discovering that Christ is enough.
Tell somebody what Jesus has done.
Forgive someone.
Confess something.
Return somewhere.
Repent of something.
Pray for someone.
Because Samson's riddle was never merely interesting because honey appeared inside a dead lion.
It was unforgettable because nobody looking at the sweetness could understand it without knowing the story of the battle.
Maybe people won't understand your worship either.
Let them wonder.
You know where Jesus found you.
You know what should have destroyed you.
You know what you deserved.
You know the roar.
You know the scars.
And if Christ has redeemed you...
you know why grace tastes so sweet.
The lion may explain your scars. But it does not get to write your ending. Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Can Demons Influence Your Dreams? The Biblical Truth About the Darkness That Visits When You Sleep
paragraphs: Can Demons Influence Your Dreams? The Biblical Truth About the Darkness That Visits When You Sleep

You woke up shaken. The room was quiet, but your heart was racing. The dream felt darker than a dream should feel. Was it only your mind… or was something spiritual happening while you slept? Scripture gives us an answer—but perhaps not the sensational answer you have heard.
There are dreams you forget before your feet touch the floor.
Then there are dreams that follow you into breakfast.
Into the shower.
Into the car.
Into prayer.
You wake up with your heart pounding, your body covered in sweat, and one disturbing question circling your mind:
“Was that just a dream… or was something evil trying to reach me?”
Maybe you saw someone you lost.
Maybe you were being chased.
Maybe something spoke to you.
Maybe you experienced temptation so vivid that you woke up ashamed.
Maybe you saw a figure standing in the darkness.
Maybe you dreamed something so horrifying that even after opening your eyes, you were afraid to close them again.
And if you are a Christian, another fear can quietly appear.
What if a demon was influencing my dream?
We need to answer that carefully.
Not with superstition.
Not with viral horror stories.
Not with somebody's frightening testimony treated as though it were another book of the Bible.
And not by pretending spiritual warfare does not exist.
We need Scripture.
Because fear becomes dangerous when imagination starts speaking louder than the Word of God.

The Bible absolutely teaches that a spiritual world exists. Angels are real. Satan is real. Demonic powers are real. Spiritual warfare is real. Paul writes that our struggle is not merely against “flesh and blood” but against spiritual forces of evil (Ephesians 6:12). Peter warns believers to remain sober and watchful because the devil prowls like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour (1 Peter 5:8–9).
So Christianity is not permitted to dismiss the supernatural simply because modern culture finds it uncomfortable.
But Christianity is equally forbidden from inventing supernatural doctrines that Scripture never actually teaches.
And here is where this question becomes important.
The Bible never explicitly teaches that demons routinely enter, manufacture, or control a Christian's dreams.
Read that again.

That does not mean we can prove demonic influence upon dreams is impossible. Scripture gives us abundant evidence that Satan deceives, tempts, accuses, opposes, and seeks to influence human beings. Yet Scripture does not give us permission to declare every nightmare, disturbing dream, sexual dream, frightening image, or strange nighttime experience a demonic attack.
That distinction matters.
Because sometimes Christians become so obsessed with discovering the demon behind everything that they stop looking at Jesus.
And anything that keeps your eyes permanently fascinated with darkness has already distracted you from the Light.
The Bible gives us a much richer theology of dreams than many people realize.
The Hebrew word commonly associated with “dream” is חֲלוֹם — ḥălôm.
Ecclesiastes 5:3 says:
כִּי בָא הַחֲלוֹם בְּרֹב עִנְיָן
Ki va haḥalom berov inyan…
In context, the writer connects dreams with an abundance of activity, occupation, or cares.
That is enormously important.
Scripture itself leaves room for dreams arising amid the ordinary pressures and activities of human life.
In other words, not every dream requires a supernatural explanation.
Sometimes you dreamed about the argument because you spent six hours thinking about the argument.
Sometimes you dreamed about losing someone because you are terrified of losing them.
Sometimes yesterday's anxiety followed you into tonight's sleep.
Sometimes grief has pictures.
Sometimes stress has a nighttime voice.
Sometimes memories you buried during daylight become impossible to ignore when the room goes dark.
And sometimes a nightmare is exactly that—a nightmare.
This does not make your experience meaningless. It simply means Christians should resist the temptation to turn every disturbing experience into a revelation.
Yet the opposite error is also wrong.
Because Scripture unquestionably records occasions when God used dreams.
Jacob dreamed of the stairway reaching toward heaven in Genesis 28.
Joseph received significant dreams in Genesis 37.
Pharaoh dreamed in Genesis 41, and God gave Joseph the interpretation.
Nebuchadnezzar was troubled by dreams in Daniel 2.
Joseph, the husband of Mary, received divine direction through dreams.
Matthew 1:20 records:
ἄγγελος Κυρίου κατ’ ὄναρ ἐφάνη αὐτῷ
angelos Kyriou kat’ onar ephanē autō
An angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream.
The Greek word ὄναρ — onar means “dream.”
So biblical Christianity cannot say, “God never communicates through dreams.”
He clearly did.
But notice something critical.
When God gave revelatory dreams in Scripture, their authority did not come from the emotional intensity of the dream.
They came from God.
And Scripture also warns about false dreams.

Jeremiah confronted people claiming divine authority for their dreams while speaking falsely in God's name. Jeremiah 23 repeatedly exposes prophets saying, in effect, “I dreamed! I dreamed!” while leading God's people away from truth.
That means the biblical question is not merely:
Did I have a supernatural experience?
The biblical question is:
Does what I experienced agree with what God has already revealed?
That changes everything.
Because something can feel spiritual and still be false.
Something can feel peaceful and still be deceptive.
Something can feel terrifying and still be nothing more than a dream.
Something can feel prophetic and still originate in your own fears, desires, memories, imagination, or expectations.
Intensity is not authority.
Emotion is not revelation.
A dream does not become Scripture because it made you cry.
And this is precisely where spiritual deception becomes dangerous.
Paul warns in 2 Corinthians 11:14 that Satan can disguise himself as an angel of light.
Think about the implication.
Deception does not always arrive looking demonic.
Sometimes deception looks beautiful.
Spiritual.
Comforting.
Even religious.
That is why John tells believers:

“Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God.”
—1 John 4:1
The Christian response to a strange dream, therefore, should not be panic.
It should be discernment.
Suppose you dream that someone tells you to abandon your spouse because “God has someone better.”
Scripture has already given you moral boundaries. Your dream does not outrank them.
Suppose someone appears in a dream claiming to be Jesus but gives you a message contradicting the Gospel.
Reject the message.
Suppose a deceased loved one appears and tells you something contrary to God's Word.
Your emotional attachment does not transform the message into truth.
Suppose you have a dream telling you that you are beyond forgiveness.
That is not the Gospel.
Suppose you dream that because of your past sins, God could never receive you again.
That accusation collapses at the cross.
Suppose the voice says:
“Jesus doesn't want you anymore.”
Then answer it with Scripture.

“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
—Romans 8:1
Suppose the darkness whispers:
“Your sin is too disgusting.”
Look toward Calvary.
The cross was built for sinners.
Suppose it says:
“God is finished with you.”
Remember Peter.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Not privately.
Not accidentally.
He denied knowing the Lord he had sworn he would never abandon.
Imagine the shame.
Imagine Peter remembering the sound of his own voice saying, in effect, I don't know Him.
Then the rooster crowed.
Jesus looked at him.
Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
If anyone could have gone to sleep haunted by yesterday, it was Peter.
But Peter's scandal was not the final chapter.
Jesus met him again.
Jesus restored him.
Jesus recommissioned him.
Jesus took the man who had denied Him beside a fire and transformed him into a man who would publicly proclaim Him.
That is the Gospel.
Not pretending your darkness never happened.
Not pretending your sin was harmless.
Not pretending spiritual warfare is imaginary.
But declaring that darkness does not get the final sentence when Jesus Christ holds the pen.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps that is why this question about dreams reaches deeper than dreams.
Maybe you are not really frightened by what happened last night.
Maybe you are frightened by what it reminded you of.
Something you did.
Something done to you.
Someone you lost.
Something you secretly desire.
Something you desperately regret.
A temptation you thought you defeated.
A memory you thought you buried.
A version of yourself you hoped was dead.
And then you dreamed about it.
Suddenly the past was standing in your bedroom again.
Listen carefully.
A dream revealing that you are still wounded does not mean Jesus has abandoned you.
A dream exposing temptation does not mean temptation owns you.
A nightmare about your past does not mean your past has authority over your future.
And an unwanted dream is not automatically an act of conscious sin.
You are responsible for what you willingly embrace, cultivate, believe, and do—not for every involuntary image produced while you are unconscious.
Somebody reading this has been carrying shame over something you did not consciously choose.
You woke up disgusted with yourself.
You wondered whether God was angry.
You were afraid even to pray.
But the answer to shame is not hiding from Christ.
Run toward Him.
Confess actual sin where actual sin exists.
Repent where repentance is necessary.
Reject what contradicts Scripture.
Forgive where Christ commands forgiveness.
Seek wise pastoral help when you need it.

And if nightmares are frequent, severe, or connected with trauma, medication, sleep disruption, anxiety, or another health concern, seeking appropriate professional help is not evidence of weak faith. God's common grace is not God's competition.
But whatever you do, do not build your theology around your nightmares.
Build it around Jesus Christ.
Before you sleep, you do not need a magical formula.
You need your Father.
You do not need to spend forty minutes screaming threats into the darkness to prove you have faith.
You can pray.
You can fill your mind with Scripture.
You can confess sin.
You can forgive.
You can surrender your fears.
You can ask God for protection.
You can rest knowing that your security is not based upon how intensely you prayed tonight but upon the faithfulness of the One to whom you belong.
Jesus taught His disciples to pray:
“Deliver us from evil.”
Simple.
Dependent.
God-centered.
The power was never in producing the perfect sentence.
The power belongs to God.
And Christian spiritual warfare is never meant to become an obsession with Satan.
Read Ephesians 6 carefully.
Truth.
Righteousness.
The Gospel of peace.
Faith.
Salvation.
The Word of God.
Prayer.
Paul's answer to spiritual warfare is not fascination with demons.
It is a life anchored in God.
So, can demons influence your dreams?
The most biblically responsible answer is:

Scripture clearly teaches demonic influence and spiritual deception are real, but Scripture does not explicitly establish that demons routinely control or insert themselves into our dreams. Therefore, Christians should neither declare such influence impossible nor confidently label particular dreams demonic without biblical warrant.
That answer may be less sensational.
But it is safer because it refuses to say more than Scripture says.
And perhaps the more important question is not:
“Was there a demon in my dream?”
Perhaps the question is:
“Who has authority over me when I wake up?”
If you belong to Jesus Christ, your nightmare is not your lord.
Your trauma is not your lord.
Your temptation is not your lord.
Your past is not your lord.
Satan is not your lord.
Fear is not your lord.
Jesus is Lord.
That does not mean Christians never suffer.
It does not mean believers never experience terror.
It does not mean every night will be peaceful.
It means darkness is no longer sovereign over your story.
Colossians 1:13 says God has delivered believers from the domain of darkness and transferred them into the kingdom of His beloved Son.
Do you understand how beautiful that is?
Christianity is not ultimately the story of frightened people desperately trying to keep demons away.
It is the story of sinners rescued by a King.
Jesus entered our darkness.
Carried our sin.
Absorbed judgment.
Died our death.
Was buried.
And rose again.
The tomb opened.
Death lost its claim.
And the risen Christ now calls sinners out of hiding.
Maybe you have spent years trying to rebuke darkness while secretly refusing to surrender the one thing Christ keeps touching.
Your bitterness.
Your pornography.
Your affair.
Your pride.
Your secret messages.
Your unforgiveness.
Your addiction.
Your dishonesty.
Your religious performance.
Your hidden life.
You want protection from demons.
But do you want deliverance from sin?
That question hurts.
It is supposed to.
Because the greatest need of your soul is not merely a peaceful night's sleep.
It is reconciliation with God.
And reconciliation has a name.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe tonight your prayer does not need to sound impressive.
Maybe it needs to become honest.
Jesus, I have been hiding.
Jesus, forgive me.
Jesus, expose what needs to die in me.
Jesus, heal what I cannot heal.
Jesus, teach me to discern truth from fear.
Jesus, I surrender my mind, my body, my past, my future, my waking hours, and my sleeping hours to You.
I belong to You.
Someone reading beneath this article may desperately need evidence that another believer has walked through darkness and discovered that Jesus was still there.
Not because every nightmare is demonic.
They may need someone to point them back to Christ.
And yes—even send it to the skeptic, the lukewarm Christian, or the person who has not followed Jesus in years.
Truth was never given to us merely to collect.
It was given to be lived and shared.
Supporting Gospel work does not purchase God's favor, earn salvation, or make someone more spiritual—grace cannot be bought.
Because someday the article you almost didn't share may appear on the screen of someone who was one night away from giving up.
And sometimes evangelism begins with something as small as pressing Share.
So tonight, when the lights go out…
when the room becomes quiet…
when your mind remembers things you wish it would forget…
when fear tries to interpret every shadow…
when yesterday comes knocking again…
remember this:
You do not have to understand every dream to know whom you belong to.
You do not have to decode every nightmare to trust your Shepherd.
You do not need secret knowledge to defeat darkness.
You need Jesus.
The crucified Jesus.
The risen Jesus.
The reigning Jesus.
The Jesus who forgives sinners.
The Jesus who restores failures.
The Jesus who receives prodigals.
The Jesus who breaks chains.
The Jesus who walks into stories filled with shame, wreckage, secrets, wounds, and scandal—and refuses to leave them where He found them.
So if darkness visits your dreams tonight, do not give darkness the throne when morning comes.
Open your eyes.
Call upon Christ.
Stand upon His Word.
And remember who gets the final sentence.
Your darkest night may know your name—but it does not own your story. Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Sin Nobody Wants to Talk About
paragraphs: The Sin Nobody Wants to Talk About
The Bible never uses the English word “masturbation.” So can Christians really call it sin? The answer requires more honesty—and more grace—than many people have been given.
There is a particular kind of silence that happens after temptation.
The screen goes dark.
The fantasy ends.
The body settles.
And suddenly the noise inside you becomes louder than everything else.
Maybe you have whispered, “God, I’m sorry.”
Maybe you promised Him it was the last time.
Maybe it was the tenth “last time.”
Maybe the hundredth.
Maybe you have wondered whether God is disgusted with you.
Or maybe you have gone in the opposite direction.
“It’s natural.”
“Nobody gets hurt.”
“The Bible never even mentions masturbation.”
And that last statement is technically important.

There is no biblical passage that explicitly says, “You shall not masturbate.” The Bible does not use a Hebrew or Greek term corresponding neatly to the modern English word masturbation. Christians should never pretend a verse exists when it does not.
But that does not end the conversation.
It begins it.
Because Scripture often addresses human behavior by going beneath the behavior to the desires, intentions, fantasies, habits, and loyalties of the heart.
And Jesus goes straight there.
He said:
“But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
—Matthew 5:28, ESV
The Greek is devastatingly precise:
πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn
The crucial word is ἐπιθυμῆσαι — epithymēsai, from epithymeō: to desire, long for, covet, or lust after.
Jesus was not condemning the mere recognition that another human being is attractive. Nor was He teaching that involuntary temptation itself is identical to committing physical adultery.
He was confronting the deliberate cultivation of sexual desire toward someone who is not yours to possess.
That distinction matters.
And suddenly the real Christian question concerning masturbation becomes much harder than, “Where does the Bible mention the physical act?”
The deeper question is:
What is happening in my heart while I do it?
What am I imagining?
Whom am I mentally undressing?
What images am I consuming?
What fantasies am I rehearsing?
Am I training my body toward holiness—or teaching it that whenever desire demands satisfaction, desire must be obeyed?
That is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because for many people masturbation does not exist in some morally sterile laboratory.
It comes attached to pornography.
Fantasy.
Coveting.
Objectification.
Memories of someone else's body.
Imagined sexual encounters.
Secret browsing.
Deleted histories.
Private accounts.
The person on the screen becomes a collection of body parts instead of someone bearing the image of God.
And Jesus refuses to let us call something harmless merely because nobody else can see it.
He sees the heart.
That is frightening.
But keep reading.
Because it is also the beginning of hope.
Paul wrote:
“For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality.”
—1 Thessalonians 4:3, ESV
The Greek word translated “sexual immorality” is πορνεία — porneia.

It refers broadly to sexual immorality rather than functioning as a technical Greek word for masturbation. That distinction is important. We should not force the text to say something more specific than Paul actually wrote.
But Paul continues:
“that each one of you know how to control his own body in holiness and honor, not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God.”
—1 Thessalonians 4:4–5, ESV
Notice the biblical vision.
Holiness. Honor. Self-control.
Not merely, “How close can I get to sin without technically crossing the line?”
Christian discipleship asks something far greater:
“Does this desire rule me, or does Christ?”
That question reaches beyond masturbation.
It reaches alcohol.
Money.
Food.
Anger.
Attention.
Approval.
Sex.
Screens.
Anything that begins whispering, You need me. You cannot say no to me. Obey me and I will make you feel better.
Paul wrote:
“I will not be dominated by anything.”
—1 Corinthians 6:12, ESV
Read that again.
I will not be dominated by anything.
Some people know exactly what domination feels like.
You did not plan to do it tonight.
Then loneliness arrived.
Stress arrived.
The argument happened.
You felt rejected.
You couldn't sleep.
You saw one image.
You opened one page.
One thought became another.
And suddenly your hand was moving almost before your conscience had finished protesting.
Afterward came shame.
Then repentance.
Then several clean days.
Then temptation.
Then failure.
Then shame again.
And eventually you stopped believing your own prayers.
“I’m sorry, Jesus.”
But somewhere inside, another voice answered:
Are you really? You said that last time.
That is where Satan loves to turn conviction into condemnation.
Biblical conviction says, Come into the light.
Condemnation says, Hide from God.
Conviction says, This is killing something in you.
Condemnation says, You are beyond saving.
Those are not the same voice.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Not less condemnation.
Not delayed condemnation.
No condemnation.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It makes the cross magnificent.
Jesus did not endure crucifixion because sin was trivial.

He endured crucifixion because our sin was so serious that reconciliation with God required something we could never accomplish for ourselves—and because His love was so astonishing that He willingly gave Himself for sinners.
This is where many Christian discussions about sexual sin fail.
They tell you what to stop doing without telling you whom to run toward.
They give you shame without a Savior.
Rules without resurrection.
Disgust without discipleship.
But Christianity is not ultimately the story of sexually pure people congratulating themselves for behaving better than sexually broken people.
Christianity is the story of sinners who desperately needed Jesus Christ.
All of us.
The sexually immoral need Him.
The proud need Him.
The hypocrite needs Him.
The gossip needs Him.
The religious performer needs Him.
The porn-addicted churchgoer needs Him.
The pastor needs Him.
The person reading this at 2:00 in the morning with tears in their eyes needs Him.
And His invitation remains:
Come.
Not, “Clean yourself perfectly and then come.”
Come.
Repentance does not mean pretending your sin never happened. The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia speaks of repentance—a profound turning of mind and direction toward God.
Grace does not teach us to make peace with bondage.
Grace teaches us to leave the prison.
Paul says our bodies are not meaningless biological machinery.
“You are not your own, for you were bought with a price. So glorify God in your body.”
—1 Corinthians 6:19–20, ESV
δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν
Doxasate dē ton Theon en tō sōmati hymōn.
Glorify God in your body.
That changes the question completely.
Instead of asking only:
“Can I get away with this?”
Ask:
“Can I glorify Christ through this?”
Instead of:
“Does the Bible explicitly name this exact act?”
Ask:
“Does what I am doing require lust, fantasy, pornography, objectification, lack of self-control, or surrender to an appetite that is beginning to master me?”
This is why a careful Christian answer should avoid an unsupported claim that Scripture explicitly names every instance of masturbation as a distinct offense. It does not.

Yet masturbation as it is commonly practiced becomes sinful when it involves what Scripture clearly condemns—lust, pornography, coveting another person sexually, degrading another image-bearer into an object, or being mastered by sexual appetite.
And for the believer who cannot separate the act from those things, the question is no longer theoretical.
You already know where the door leads.
Perhaps you have discovered something else too.
Sometimes what you thought was a sex problem was partly a pain problem.
You were lonely.
You wanted comfort.
You wanted to feel wanted.
You were anxious.
You were bored.
You were carrying rejection you never processed.
Sexual release became anesthesia.
For a few minutes, you did not have to feel what hurt.
Then the relief disappeared.
The wound remained.
So you returned.
Again.
Again.
Again.
But Jesus wants more for you than improved behavior.
He wants your heart.
The lonely part.
The rejected part.
The traumatized part.
The restless part.
The part that keeps reaching for counterfeit intimacy because real intimacy feels terrifying.
Bring that person to Christ.
