It means your story belongs to Someone who already walked through death and came out alive.
And when you cannot hold yourself together anymore, perhaps the most beautiful truth is not how tightly you are holding onto Jesus.
It is that your salvation rests on Jesus Christ, whose grace is stronger than your weakness and whose faithfulness is not measured by the weather of your emotions.
So cry if you need to.
Repent where you need to.
Ask questions.
Ask for prayer.
Come home.
But do not confuse the darkness of the chapter with the absence of the Author.
Because sometimes the chapter where you were certain God had disappeared becomes the chapter where you finally discover He was carrying you through what you could never have survived alone.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE OFFER THAT MADE AN APOSTLE TREMBLE: THE WARNING HIDDEN IN SIMON THE SORCERER’S MONEY
paragraphs: THE OFFER THAT MADE AN APOSTLE TREMBLE: THE WARNING HIDDEN IN SIMON THE SORCERER’S MONEY

He thought the power of God could be obtained through a transaction. Peter’s answer exposes something far more frightening than ancient sorcery: the hidden desire to possess what was only meant to be received by grace.

There is a sentence in the book of Acts that should make every Christian who has ever wanted influence, recognition, spiritual authority, ministry success, a platform, a title, a following—or even the appearance of being close to God—stop and examine the heart.
It begins with money in a man’s hand.
But the real scandal was happening somewhere much deeper.
Simon had seen something extraordinary.

He had watched the apostles lay their hands upon believers, and he witnessed the manifestation of the Holy Spirit’s work. Whatever Simon saw was powerful enough that the former magician immediately wanted access to it.
And then he made the offer.
Acts 8:18–19 records:

“Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given through the laying on of the apostles’ hands, he offered them money, saying, ‘Give me this power also, so that anyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit.’”
At first glance, someone might almost misunderstand him.
Perhaps Simon simply wanted to serve.
Perhaps he wanted to help people.
Perhaps he wanted to participate in what God was doing.
Perhaps he was merely enthusiastic.
But Peter did not respond to the appearance of Simon’s request.
Peter went after the heart underneath it.
And what Peter said was terrifying.
The Greek text of Acts 8:20 begins:
“Τὸ ἀργύριόν σου σὺν σοὶ εἴη εἰς ἀπώλειαν…”
To argyrion sou syn soi eiē eis apōleian…
“May your silver perish with you…”
Why?
“ὅτι τὴν δωρεὰν τοῦ θεοῦ ἐνόμισας διὰ χρημάτων κτᾶσθαι.”
Hoti tēn dōrean tou Theou enomisas dia chrēmatōn ktasthai.
“…because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money.”
There it is.
The warning hidden inside Simon’s offer.
Simon saw a gift…
and imagined a transaction.
God was giving.
Simon was thinking about acquiring.
God was pouring out grace.
Simon was calculating access.
The apostles were servants through whom God was working.
Simon wanted the power associated with their hands.
And suddenly this story stops feeling ancient.
Because Simon may be dead…
but Simon’s temptation is not.
It can walk into churches.
It can stand behind pulpits.
It can sit behind microphones.
It can open ministry pages.
It can publish books.
It can build Christian brands.
It can chase titles.
It can count followers.
It can obsess over engagement.
It can envy another believer’s influence.
It can secretly dream about being called “anointed.”
And sometimes it can kneel during worship while quietly asking a question the mouth would never dare say aloud:
“What can Christianity give me?”
That is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because you do not need to practice sorcery to share Simon’s temptation.
You only need to want the things of God more than you want God Himself.
Simon’s story begins earlier in Acts 8.
Before Philip arrived in Samaria preaching Christ, Simon had practiced magic and astonished the people. Acts tells us that he presented himself as someone great, and people paid attention to him.
That detail matters.
Simon knew what it felt like to have people watching.
He knew influence.
He knew attention.
He knew what it was like when a crowd associated his name with extraordinary power.
Then Philip arrived.
And everything changed.
Philip did not preach Philip.
Acts 8:5 says:
“Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ.”
Christ.
Not personal greatness.
Not celebrity.
Not spiritual branding.
Christ.
The crowds who had been amazed by Simon began paying attention to the Gospel.
People believed.
People were baptized.
Lives were changing.
And remarkably, Acts 8:13 says that Simon himself believed and was baptized, continuing with Philip and being amazed at the signs and great miracles he witnessed.
Then Peter and John arrived.
And Simon saw something he had never possessed.
Something money could not manufacture.
Something technique could not reproduce.
Something reputation could not create.
Something sorcery could not imitate into existence.
The work of the living God.
And the old instinct surfaced.
Acquire it.
Possess it.
Get access to it.
“Give me this power also…”
Those words expose one of the oldest corruptions of religion:
wanting God’s power without surrendering to God’s ownership.
And Peter refuses to entertain it.
He tells Simon:
“You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God.”
Notice where Peter points.
Not Simon’s wallet.
His heart.
“ἡ γὰρ καρδία σου οὐκ ἔστιν εὐθεῖα ἔναντι τοῦ θεοῦ.”
Hē gar kardia sou ouk estin eutheia enanti tou Theou.
“For your heart is not right before God.”
That is the diagnosis.
Simon’s money merely revealed what his heart believed.
And money still does that.
Influence still does that.
Ambition still does that.
Success still does that.
The desire to be noticed still does that.
They expose us.
There is nothing inherently sinful about money. Scripture does not teach that possessing money is itself evil. Paul says in 1 Timothy 6:10 that “the love of money” is a root of all kinds of evils.
There is nothing inherently sinful about having influence either. God gave influence to Joseph, Daniel, Esther, Peter, Paul, and many others.
The question is what happens inside us when influence becomes available.
Do we want people to see Jesus?
Or do we secretly need them to see us standing near Jesus?
There is a difference.
A devastating one.
You can speak about Christ while building yourself.
You can serve people while craving their admiration.
You can give generously while secretly wanting recognition.
You can know biblical vocabulary while your heart is negotiating with God.
You can even want spiritual gifts for selfish reasons.
And perhaps one of the most frightening possibilities is that other people may never notice.
But Jesus does.
This is why Simon’s story should not primarily become ammunition for accusing somebody else.
It should become a mirror.
Before you think about the preacher you distrust…
the ministry you criticize…
the Christian influencer you suspect…
the wealthy religious leader who irritates you…
look inward.
Ask the harder question.
“Lord, is Simon hiding anywhere in me?”
Would I still serve if nobody applauded?
Would I still give if nobody knew?
Would I still pray if nobody heard me?
Would I still worship if there were no emotional reward?
Would I still obey if obedience cost me followers?
Would I still preach Christ if somebody else received the recognition?
Would I still love Jesus if He never made me impressive?
That last question hurts.
Because there is a version of Christianity that can quietly turn Jesus into a means of obtaining something else.
Jesus for success.
Jesus for money.
Jesus for influence.
Jesus for relationships.
Jesus for healing.
Jesus for status.
Jesus for an audience.
Jesus for a better life.
And yes, God gives good gifts.
He provides.
He heals according to His will.
He restores.
He opens doors.
He blesses His children in countless ways.
But Christianity is not ultimately about using Jesus to obtain the treasure.
Jesus is the treasure.
Paul could say in Philippians 3:8 that he counted everything as loss because of “the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord.”
Not merely knowing what Jesus could provide.
Knowing Jesus.
Simon wanted power.
Peter called him to repentance.
Acts 8:22:
“Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord that, if possible, the intent of your heart may be forgiven you.”
The Greek begins:
“μετανόησον οὖν…”
Metanoēson oun…
“Repent, therefore…”
That word matters.
Repentance is not image management.
It is not learning how to hide your sin more effectively.
It is not changing vocabulary while protecting the idol.
Biblical repentance involves turning from sin toward God.
Peter does not tell Simon to improve his personal brand.
He does not tell him to make a larger donation.
He does not offer Simon a premium level of apostolic power.
He tells him to repent.
That destroys every attempt to turn the Gospel into merchandise.
Grace cannot be purchased because grace, by definition, is gift.
The Greek word Peter uses in Acts 8:20 is dōrea—gift.
“The gift of God.”
Simon’s fundamental mistake was trying to place a price tag on what God called gift.
And here is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Because Christianity really does involve a transaction—but not the transaction Simon imagined.
You do not purchase salvation from God.
You could never afford it.
Your morality cannot purchase it.
Your church attendance cannot purchase it.
Your donations cannot purchase it.
Your tears cannot purchase it.
Your ministry cannot purchase it.
Your suffering cannot purchase it.
Your reputation cannot purchase it.
Your followers cannot purchase it.
Your religious achievements cannot purchase it.
Someone else paid.
Jesus Christ.
Peter himself would later write:
Not silver.
Not gold.
Blood.
His blood.
The Son of God did what Simon’s money could never do.
Christ stepped into the place of sinners.
He bore sin.
He suffered.
He died.
And He rose again.
The Gospel does not say, “Bring enough and God might accept you.”
The Gospel announces that Christ has accomplished what sinners could never accomplish for themselves, and calls us to repent and believe.
That is why grace humiliates human pride before it heals the human heart.
You arrive empty-handed.
The rich arrive empty-handed.
The poor arrive empty-handed.
The famous arrive empty-handed.
The forgotten arrive empty-handed.
The pastor arrives empty-handed.
The addict arrives empty-handed.
The successful businessman arrives empty-handed.
The broken mother arrives empty-handed.
The ashamed teenager arrives empty-handed.
The prisoner arrives empty-handed.
The religious person arrives empty-handed.
The person who ruined everything arrives empty-handed.
And at the foot of the cross there is no VIP line.
Only sinners who need mercy.
Maybe that is why this story found you.
Maybe you have been performing.
Maybe you have spent years trying to make God impressed with you.
Maybe nobody knows how exhausted you are from trying to appear spiritually strong.
Maybe your prayers have quietly become negotiations.
“God, if I do this, will You give me that?”
“God, if I serve You, will You make my life easier?”
“God, if I give, will You owe me?”
“God, if I obey, will You make people recognize me?”
And when God did not follow the script…
you became angry.
Because somewhere along the way, surrender became a contract.
Simon’s story whispers across the centuries:
God cannot be bought.
But the Gospel shouts something even better:
You do not need to buy Him.
Christ invites sinners to come.
Maybe you have failed badly.
Maybe your motives have been polluted.
Maybe pride has been hiding underneath ministry.
Maybe greed has been hiding underneath ambition.
Maybe you wanted the platform more than the presence of God.
Maybe you wanted people impressed with your Christianity more than you wanted Christ transforming your character.
Do not run from Jesus because the truth exposed you.
Run toward Him.
Conviction is not an invitation to pretend harder.
It is an invitation to repent.
There is grace for the exposed.
There is forgiveness for the repentant.
There is cleansing for sinners.
There is restoration for people who finally stop defending what God is trying to remove.
That is the scandal of grace.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending sin was never serious.
He rewrites everything because He took sin so seriously that He carried its judgment at the cross.
Grace is not God saying sin does not matter.
Grace is God doing for sinners what sinners could never do for themselves.
So examine your heart.
Not your image.
Not your profile.
Not your reputation.
Your heart.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to manufacture a spiritual answer. Tell Christ the truth.
Someone reading those words may realize they are not the only believer fighting that battle.
Your confession may become somebody else’s courage.
And do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Let them discover Jesus.
Because Simon’s temptation does not disappear after one reading.
Success can resurrect it.
Recognition can resurrect it.
Money can resurrect it.
Ministry growth can resurrect it.
Even answered prayer can reveal motives we did not know were hiding inside us.
Come back and read this when your heart begins confusing being used by God with being admired by people.
It does not.
Not because supporting this ministry earns salvation.
It cannot.
Not because God needs your money before He can work.
He does not.
Simon’s story should make us extremely careful never to communicate anything like that.
If you want to glorify God through your resources, do so first by surrendering those resources to His lordship and using them faithfully, generously, and without compulsion.
Simon reached for his money because he misunderstood the gift.
Do not repeat his mistake in another form.
You cannot purchase the Holy Spirit.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
You cannot purchase the favor of God.
You cannot purchase spiritual authority.
You cannot purchase a place at the cross.
You cannot purchase the blood of Jesus.
You come empty-handed.
You repent.
You believe.
You receive grace.
And then, because grace has changed you, you begin living differently.
Giving differently.
Serving differently.
Leading differently.
Loving differently.
You stop asking, “How can I use God to become somebody?”
And begin praying:
“Jesus, even if nobody remembers my name, let my life make them remember Yours.”
That is freedom.
Simon wanted power in his hands.
Jesus wants surrender in your heart.
Simon offered silver.
Jesus offered Himself.
Simon wanted something he could possess.
The Gospel gives us a Savior before whom we gladly surrender possession of ourselves.
So the next time ambition whispers that you need a platform…
the next time comparison tells you someone else has more spiritual influence…
the next time money tempts you to believe everything has a price…
the next time you secretly crave the appearance of anointing more than the holiness produced through abiding in Christ…
remember the silver in Simon’s hand.
Remember Peter’s warning.
Remember the cross.
And remember that the greatest gift God gives sinners cannot be bought because the price has already been paid by Someone else.
If this article exposed you, comment.
Because someday, every platform disappears.
Every follower count becomes irrelevant.
Every title is laid down.
Every bank account is left behind.
Every human name eventually fades from somebody’s memory.
And when all the silver finally slips from our hands, only one question will matter:
Did we want what Jesus could give us…
or did we finally realize that Jesus Himself was everything?
You were never meant to purchase the fire of God—you were meant to lay your life on the altar and belong completely to Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Can Generational Curses Affect Christians? The Truth That Could End a Fear Your Family Has Carried for Years
paragraphs: Can Generational Curses Affect Christians? The Truth That Could End a Fear Your Family Has Carried for Years

You may have inherited a broken story. You may still be living with its consequences. But if you belong to Jesus Christ, Scripture gives you something far stronger than fear of your bloodline: a new identity, a new kingdom, and a Redeemer who has already borne the curse.
Maybe you have looked at your family and quietly wondered whether something is following you.
Your grandfather struggled with alcohol.
Your father did too.
Now you feel the same pull.
Your grandmother lived through a destructive marriage. Your mother repeated the pattern. Now your own relationship seems frighteningly familiar.
Anger keeps appearing.
Addiction keeps appearing.
Abandonment keeps appearing.
Sexual sin. Divorce. Abuse. Debt. Bitterness. Occult involvement. Fear. Fatherlessness. Secret shame.
Different faces.
Different decades.
Same wounds.
And somewhere along the way, perhaps someone gave those patterns a terrifying name:
“Generational curse.”
Suddenly every struggle became evidence.
Every nightmare became confirmation.
Every family resemblance became spiritual suspicion.
You started wondering whether repentance was enough. Whether faith in Christ was enough. Whether the cross was enough.
Maybe you love Jesus and still secretly fear something your ancestors did before you were even born.
So the question is not merely theological.
It is painfully personal:
Can a Christian still be under a generational curse?
And we need to answer carefully, because there are two dangerous mistakes we can make.
One is pretending that the sins of previous generations have no effect on us.
The other is telling blood-bought believers that Jesus saved them—but somehow their ancestral curse still owns them.
Scripture allows neither.
The Bible absolutely teaches that sin can produce consequences that travel through families.
But Scripture also teaches personal responsibility before God, and the New Testament places those who are in Christ under the saving lordship of Jesus—not under some competing ancestral ownership.
That distinction changes everything.
When God gave Israel the commandments, He warned them about idolatry:

“You shall not bow down to them or serve them; for I the LORD your God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation of them that hate me.” — Exodus 20:5, KJV
This is one of the passages commonly used to support the idea of generational curses.
And it is real Scripture. We must not explain it away.

The Hebrew wording includes the idea expressed by פֹּקֵד עֲוֹן — poqed avon, commonly rendered “visiting the iniquity.” The language concerns God dealing with iniquity and its outworking; and notice the crucial qualification at the end of the verse: “of them that hate me.” The warning appears in the context of idolatry and covenant rebellion, not as a declaration that every descendant is automatically condemned for an ancestor's sin regardless of that descendant's relationship with God.
Sin travels farther than the sinner imagines.
A father may repent of alcoholism, yet his children can still carry memories of drunken rage.
A mother may escape an abusive relationship, yet her daughter may have learned distorted ideas about love.

A family can normalize greed, adultery, racism, violence, superstition, manipulation, unforgiveness, or addiction until children absorb those patterns before they are old enough to understand what they are learning.
In that sense, you can inherit a battlefield you did not create.
But inheriting a battlefield is not the same thing as inheriting another person's guilt before God.
That distinction matters enormously.
God says through Ezekiel:
הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַחֹטֵאת הִיא תָמוּת — ha-nephesh ha-chote't hi tamut
“The soul that sinneth, it shall die.”
And then:
בֵּן לֹא־יִשָּׂא בַּעֲוֹן הָאָב — ben lo-yissa ba'avon ha'av
“The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.”
Ezekiel 18:20 explicitly distinguishes the moral accountability of father and son: the son does not bear the father's iniquity, nor the father the son's.
Read that again if you have spent years afraid of your family tree.
The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.
You may experience consequences created by somebody else's sin.
You may have learned patterns from somebody else's sin.
You may have wounds because of somebody else's sin.
You may even face temptations that have been normalized and reinforced through generations.
But Scripture does not permit us to tell a repentant believer in Jesus, “God still holds you guilty for what your grandfather did.”
And then we arrive at the cross.
This is where fear begins losing its vocabulary.
Paul writes:
Χριστὸς ἡμᾶς ἐξηγόρασεν ἐκ τῆς κατάρας τοῦ νόμου γενόμενος ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν κατάρα
Christos hēmas exēgorasen ek tēs kataras tou nomou genomenos hyper hēmōn katara.
“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.” — Galatians 3:13.
There is a word in that Greek sentence you should remember:
ἐξηγόρασεν — exēgorasen.
Redeemed.
Christ did not merely sympathize with condemned sinners.
He redeemed them.

Paul's immediate subject in Galatians 3 is specifically “the curse of the law.” We should therefore resist turning this verse into a slogan that says Christians will never experience consequences, temptation, spiritual warfare, suffering, discipline, or the fallout of previous generations.
That is not what Paul says.
What he does say is magnificent enough without exaggeration:
Christ became a curse for us.
At Calvary, Jesus did not make a down payment and leave your redemption unfinished.
He bore sin's judgment.
He gave Himself for sinners.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
And everyone who truly repents and trusts in Him belongs to Him.
So the Christian's confidence is not:
“My ancestors were good enough.”
It is:
“Jesus Christ is enough.”
Your genealogy is not your savior.
But neither is your genealogy your lord.
Jesus is.
Paul gives another astonishing description of conversion:
ὥστε εἴ τις ἐν Χριστῷ, καινὴ κτίσις
Hōste ei tis en Christō, kainē ktisis.
“If anyone is in Christ, [there is] a new creation.”
The Greek expression καινὴ κτίσις — kainē ktisis means “new creation.” The old has passed away; the new has come.
Notice where the power is.
ἐν Χριστῷ — en Christō.
“In Christ.”
That is the center.
Not “in a perfect family.”
Not “in a family with no occult history.”
Not “in a family without addiction.”
Not “in a family whose parents never divorced.”
In Christ.
This does not mean that becoming a Christian instantly erases every learned behavior, traumatic memory, temptation, financial consequence, damaged relationship, or sinful habit.
Conversion is not amnesia.
Grace does not pretend your past never happened.
Grace gives your past a new master.
Some Christians need to repent of patterns they learned from their parents.
Some need counseling and wise pastoral care because wounds from childhood are still affecting their relationships.
Some need to confess hidden sin.
Some need to destroy occult objects or abandon practices that contradict allegiance to Christ.
Some need accountability for addiction.
Some need to forgive—not because what happened was acceptable, but because bitterness must no longer control them.
Some need years of sanctification before a pattern that took decades to form finally loses its grip.
But there is a massive difference between saying,
“My family history influences the battles I face,”
and saying,
“My family history has greater authority over me than Jesus Christ.”
Christian, do not confuse a recurring temptation with an unbreakable curse.
Do not confuse learned dysfunction with spiritual ownership.
Do not confuse consequences with condemnation.
Do not confuse spiritual warfare with Christ somehow failing to redeem you.
And do not turn every difficult thing in your life into evidence of an ancestral curse.
Sometimes the reason anger keeps returning is because anger has been practiced for twenty years.
Sometimes debt keeps returning because financial habits have not changed.
Sometimes destructive relationships repeat because dysfunctional behavior became familiar.
Sometimes lust persists because it is repeatedly fed.
Sometimes bitterness survives because forgiveness keeps being postponed.
And yes, Scripture takes the spiritual realm seriously. Christians really do face spiritual opposition. We should neither mock spiritual warfare nor become obsessed with it.
But our attention must remain fixed on Christ.
Paul says that God “has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son,” in whom believers have redemption and forgiveness.
Transferred.
Think about that word.
There has been a change of kingdom.
A change of allegiance.
A change of ownership.
You may still hear echoes from the house you came from.
But echoes are not ownership.
Maybe your father was absent.
That wounded you.
But absence does not get to become your identity.
Maybe your mother was bitter.
That shaped you.
But bitterness does not have to become your inheritance.
Maybe generations before you practiced occultism.
Do not imitate it. Do not romanticize it. Renounce every practice contrary to Christ and worship God alone.
But do not spend the rest of your Christian life staring backward in terror as though Jesus is standing helplessly beside your family tree.
Look at the cross.
The question is no longer merely, “What did my ancestors do?”
The deeper question is:
“Whom do I belong to now?”
And for the Christian, the answer is Jesus Christ.
This is where the story becomes intensely uncomfortable, because “generational curse” language can sometimes become a hiding place.
If everything is the curse, I never have to call anything my sin.
“My father was angry.”
Yes.
But now you are screaming at your children.
“My mother never forgave.”
Yes.
But now you are nurturing bitterness.
“Men in our family always cheat.”
Maybe they did.
But their adultery cannot repent for yours.
At some point grace looks you directly in the eyes and says:
The pattern may not have started with you, but by the power of Christ it does not have to continue through you.
That is both terrifying and beautiful.
Because now you cannot blame everything on your ancestors.
But you also do not have to surrender your future to them.
You can repent.
You can confess.
You can forgive.
You can seek help.
You can learn obedience.
You can walk by the Spirit.
You can teach your children what nobody taught you.
You can become the father you never had.
You can become the mother you desperately needed.
You can build a marriage different from the one you watched collapse.
You can become generous after generations of greed.
Faithful after generations of adultery.
Sober after generations of addiction.
Tender after generations of violence.
Truthful after generations of secrets.
Not because you possess some heroic power within yourself.
Because Jesus Christ saves sinners and the Holy Spirit transforms people.
Maybe this is why you needed to read this today.
You have spent years asking:
“What curse is following me?”
Perhaps there is another question Scripture wants you to ask:
“What sin must I repent of, what lie must I stop believing, what wound needs healing, what pattern must I stop feeding, and what truth about Jesus must I finally trust?”
Because freedom is not found by becoming fascinated with darkness.
Freedom is found in Christ.
And perhaps somebody reading this has never actually surrendered to Him.
You know Christian vocabulary.
You share Christian posts.
You know worship songs.
Maybe you even attend church.
But deep inside, Jesus is something you admire rather than Someone you obey.
Then your greatest problem is not your grandmother's sin.
It is yours.
Your greatest need is not discovering what happened four generations ago.
Your greatest need is reconciliation with God.
Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose from the dead. Turn from sin. Stop hiding. Stop negotiating. Stop pretending religious familiarity is the same thing as saving faith.
Come to Christ.
Not when you become clean enough.
Come because you cannot clean yourself.
Bring the addiction.
Bring the shame.
Bring the family secrets.
Bring the sexual sin.
Bring the resentment.
Bring the occult past.
Bring the anger.
Bring the memories.
Bring the thing you desperately hope nobody discovers.
Repent and trust Him.
Grace is not God saying your sin does not matter.
Grace is God revealing just how much sin matters—and then showing you the cross where Christ paid what you could never pay.
That is the scandal.
The guilty are offered forgiveness.
The ashamed are invited home.
The rebellious can become sons and daughters.
The spiritually dead can be made alive.
The family story everyone thought was destined to repeat itself can suddenly encounter Jesus Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Be honest.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that another story is possible.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not. We are saved by God's grace, not by supporting a page.
But if you sincerely want your online life to glorify God, one practical way to do that is to help biblical truth travel farther than fear.
Your history may explain part of your battle, but Jesus Christ determines the identity of those who belong to Him.
There may come a night when an old pattern returns and fear whispers, See? Nothing changed.
Come back and remember:
A battle is not proof that Christ abandoned you.
Temptation is not ownership.
Sanctification can be difficult without redemption being defective.
And following Jesus does not mean pretending your family wounds never happened. It means those wounds no longer have permission to write the ending.
Invite struggling believers. Invite seekers. Invite the person who stopped going to church. Invite the one who thinks Jesus would never want them back.
Because the Gospel was never meant to become another chain around frightened people.
It is the announcement that the King has come.
Christ has died.
Christ has risen.
Sinners can be forgiven.
Captives can belong to another Kingdom.
Families can learn another way.
And the person who thought, “This is simply who we are,” can kneel before Jesus and discover that inherited brokenness does not have to become inherited rebellion.
Maybe the darkness really did run through your family for generations.
Maybe nobody before you knew how to stop it.
Maybe you inherited wounds you never asked for.
But hear this carefully:
You do not honor Jesus by pretending those wounds are imaginary. You honor Him by refusing to give them a throne.
Your grandfather does not get the final sentence.
Your father does not get the final sentence.
Your trauma does not get the final sentence.
Your worst failure does not get the final sentence.
Your family scandal does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
And perhaps the most beautiful inheritance you will ever leave your children will be the moment your family's old story reached you...
and by the grace of Jesus Christ,
it did not leave you the same way it found you.
The pattern may have your family's fingerprints all over it—but the ending can still bear the scars of the hands that were pierced for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Devil Doesn’t Need the Whole House—Just One Room You Refuse to Surrender
paragraphs: The Devil Doesn’t Need the Whole House—Just One Room You Refuse to Surrender
What “Give No Place to the Devil” Really Means—and Why the Door You Keep Calling a Small Compromise May Be Costing You More Than You Realize
There is a frightening possibility in the Christian life that almost nobody wants to talk about.
You can love Jesus… and still nurse resentment.
You can worship on Sunday… and spend Monday replaying the wound.
You can know Scripture… and secretly enjoy imagining the person who hurt you finally getting what they deserve.
You can pray, serve, give, smile, post Bible verses, encourage other people—and still keep one locked room inside your heart where you have quietly decided:
“God can have everything except this.”
This anger.
This bitterness.
This secret habit.
This relationship.
This private fantasy.
This unforgiveness.
This pride.
This wound I keep touching because somehow the pain has become part of who I am.
And then Paul writes one sentence so short that we can read over it in seconds, yet so serious that it should make every believer examine the doors of the heart:
“Neither give place to the devil.”
Ephesians 4:27, KJV.
The Greek is even more arresting:
μηδὲ δίδοτε τόπον τῷ διαβόλῳ
Mēde didote topon tō diabolō.
Literally, the words carry the sense: and do not give place, room, opportunity, or ground to the devil.

The word τόπον — topon, from topos, refers fundamentally to a place or location and can extend figuratively to an opportunity. That is why faithful English translations render Paul's warning in slightly different but complementary ways: “give no opportunity to the devil,” “do not give the devil an opportunity,” or “do not give the devil a foothold.” The Greek verb δίδοτε — didote is an imperative: Paul is issuing a command.
But here is where we need to be careful.
Paul is not teaching frightened Christians to obsess over whether Satan is hiding behind every inconvenience.
He is not telling us that every bad day is demonic.
He is not giving us permission to blame the devil for choices we willingly make.
And he certainly is not teaching that Satan becomes the owner of a Christian every time that Christian struggles with temptation.
Read the sentence where Paul actually put it.
“Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath: Neither give place to the devil.”
Ephesians 4:26–27, KJV.
Do you see it?
The warning about the devil appears in the middle of instructions about ordinary human behavior.
Anger.
Words.
Stealing.
Work.
Bitterness.
Forgiveness.
Relationships.
Paul takes spiritual warfare out of the realm of theatrical imagination and brings it painfully close to home.
Sometimes the battlefield is your kitchen.
Sometimes it is the message you are about to send.
Sometimes it is what you whisper about somebody after they leave the room.
Sometimes it is what happens when your spouse falls asleep and you lie awake rehearsing every offense from the last ten years.
Sometimes it is the secret browser window.
Sometimes it is jealousy dressed up as discernment.
Sometimes it is gossip disguised as a prayer request.
Sometimes it is a wound you have transformed into an identity.
Sometimes the devil does not need you to renounce Jesus publicly.
He would be delighted if you simply refuse to obey Jesus privately.
That is what makes this verse so uncomfortable.
Because Paul does not merely say, “Watch out for the devil.”
He says, in effect, do not give him room.
Which means there are responses we can choose that serve his destructive purposes.
Look at the surrounding passage.

Paul tells believers to put away falsehood and speak truth. He tells the thief to stop stealing and begin honest labor so that he can actually become generous. He commands believers to reject corrupt speech and instead speak words that build people up and give grace. He tells them not to grieve the Holy Spirit. Then he names bitterness, wrath, anger, clamor, slander, and malice—and commands that these things be put away.
And where does the passage land?
Not with paranoia.
Not with obsession over Satan.
Not with elaborate techniques for identifying demons.
It lands here:
“Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.”
That is the direction of Paul's argument.
And suddenly the verse becomes painfully personal.
Because perhaps you have been asking God to remove the devil's influence from an area where God has already told you what obedience looks like.
You keep praying for peace while feeding bitterness.
You keep praying for freedom while protecting the secret.
You keep asking God to restore the marriage while sharpening the words you use against your spouse.
You keep rebuking darkness while refusing to apologize.
You keep asking Jesus to heal what happened to you while insisting upon the right to hate the person who did it.
And yes…
What happened to you may have been genuinely evil.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending abuse was acceptable.
It does not mean remaining in danger.
It does not mean refusing appropriate justice or consequences.
It does not require calling evil good.
Christian forgiveness is not pretending the wound never happened.
It is refusing to become a permanent servant of the wound.
There is a difference.
Somebody reading this has carried an offense so long that you no longer remember who you were before it happened.
They betrayed you.
They lied about you.
They abandoned you.
They embarrassed you.
They used you.
They broke something inside you and walked away while you were left gathering pieces they never even apologized for shattering.
So you built a room for the pain.
At first, you only visited it.
Then you furnished it.
Then you began sleeping there.
You replayed conversations.
Invented arguments.
Imagined apologies.
Imagined revenge.
Checked their profile.
Compared their life with yours.
Watched to see whether God would finally punish them.
And somewhere along the way, what wounded you began discipling you.
Read that again.
What wounded you began discipling you.
It began teaching you how to think.
How to trust.
How to love.
How to interpret people's motives.
How quickly to become defensive.
How deeply to expect abandonment.
How aggressively to protect yourself.
And the enemy did not have to create the original wound to exploit what happened afterward.
That distinction matters.
Scripture does not teach us to attribute every trauma, conflict, temptation, or sinful choice directly to Satan. Human sin is real. Our own sinful desires are real. A broken world is real.
But Scripture absolutely warns believers that the devil seeks opportunities for destruction.
Peter describes him as an adversary prowling like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour (1 Peter 5:8).
James tells believers:
“Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”
But notice what comes immediately before that:
“Submit yourselves therefore to God.”
James 4:7, KJV.
Submission first.
Resistance follows.
Because biblical spiritual warfare is not principally about shouting louder than darkness.
It is about belonging obediently to Christ.
There are doors that close when repentance enters the room.
There are lies that lose their grip when truth is confessed.
There are patterns that begin starving when secrecy ends.
There are grudges that lose oxygen when forgiveness begins.
There are temptations whose power diminishes when you stop negotiating with them.
Paul's language in Ephesians is especially important because διάβολος — diabolos, translated “devil,” carries the idea of a slanderer or accuser.
Think about that.
Then look again at the passage.
Falsehood.
Corrupt speech.
Bitterness.
Wrath.
Anger.
Clamor.
Slander.
Malice.
Division.
And right in the middle:
Do not give the devil a place.
The enemy loves whatever fractures what God is building.
He loves a marriage where neither person will humble themselves.
He loves churches where suspicion becomes normal.
He loves Christian families where everybody quotes Scripture but nobody says, “I was wrong. Please forgive me.”
He loves friendships destroyed over offenses nobody had the courage to discuss.
He loves Christians who know how to identify everybody else's sin but have become experts at renaming their own.
“My bitterness is discernment.”
“My pride is confidence.”
“My gossip is concern.”
“My lust is loneliness.”
“My greed is ambition.”
“My cruelty is honesty.”
“My unforgiveness is boundaries.”
“My compromise is freedom.”
Be careful.
A renamed sin is still a sin.
And the Gospel does not invite us to become better at explaining our chains.
Jesus came to break them.
This is where the story changes.
Because if Ephesians 4:27 were merely a warning, some of us would finish reading terrified.
We know the rooms.
We know where the compromises are.
We know what we deleted.
We know what we hid.
We know whose name instantly changes our heartbeat.
We know what happens after midnight.
We know the conversation nobody else knows about.
We know the version of ourselves that appears when nobody is watching.
And if Christianity were simply the announcement that you have failed to keep every door closed, there would be no good news here.
But Christianity is not ultimately the story of how successfully you kept darkness away.
It is the story of the Light coming for people sitting in darkness.
Jesus Christ did not come for people who had perfectly guarded every room.
He came for sinners.
Scandalous sinners.
Ashamed sinners.
Religious sinners.
Sexual sinners.
Angry sinners.
Self-righteous sinners.
Secretly addicted sinners.
Publicly disgraced sinners.
People whose lives looked clean.
People whose lives had completely collapsed.
People like Peter, who swore he would never abandon Jesus—and then denied knowing Him.
People like the thief dying beside Christ, who had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
People like Paul himself, who had persecuted the church before becoming an apostle of the Gospel he once tried to destroy.
And people like us.
That is grace.
Not God pretending sin doesn't matter.
Grace is God dealing with sin at a cost we could never pay.
At the cross, Jesus did not negotiate with our guilt.
He bore it.
He did not excuse our rebellion.
He suffered for sinners.
He did not tell humanity to climb its way back to God.
The Son of God came down.
Christ was crucified.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
And now forgiveness is not a sentimental religious idea.
It has a name.
Jesus.
So when Scripture says, “give no place to the devil,” the answer is not to become obsessed with the devil.
The answer is to become radically surrendered to Christ.
Bring Jesus the room.
Not the cleaned-up version.
The actual room.
Open the door you have been guarding.
“Jesus, this is my anger.”
“This is my pornography.”
“This is my jealousy.”
“This is my pride.”
“This is the relationship I know dishonors You.”
“This is my hunger for people's approval.”
“This is my hatred.”
“This is the person I cannot forgive.”
“This is the lie I keep telling.”
“This is what I do when nobody sees.”
“This is the thing I am terrified people would discover.”
No more religious performance.
No more negotiating.
No more decorating what Christ is commanding you to surrender.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
Confession brings what darkness wants hidden into the light of God's truth.
And perhaps the most beautiful sentence in the entire surrounding passage is the reason Christians can forgive at all:
“…as God in Christ forgave you.”
Ephesians 4:32.
There it is.
Not:
Forgive because they deserve it.
Forgive because what happened wasn't serious.
Forgive because Christians aren't allowed to hurt.
Forgive because justice doesn't matter.
No.
Forgive because you have been forgiven in Christ.
The cross becomes the reference point.
You look at what somebody owes you…
and then you remember Calvary.
You remember your own debt.
Your rebellion.
Your pride.
Your hidden sins.
Your repeated failures.
Your promises to God that lasted three days.
Your wandering heart.
And then you remember that Jesus knew every chapter before He called your name.
He knew the scandal.
He knew the relapse.
He knew the hypocrisy.
He knew the shame.
He knew what you would become.
And still He went to the cross.
That does not make sin smaller.
It makes grace astonishing.
Maybe this article found you at the exact moment you were preparing to keep the door open.
Maybe you were about to message them again.
Maybe you were about to return to the habit.
Maybe you were planning another night of bitterness.
Maybe you have been saying, “I can stop whenever I want,” while quietly discovering that you cannot.
Maybe everyone thinks your spiritual life is strong.
But you know.
God knows.
And right now, you know exactly which room we are talking about.
Do not run from Christ because you are ashamed of what is inside it.
Run to Christ because He already knows.
There is mercy for the repentant.
There is cleansing for the sinner.
There is restoration after failure.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is resurrection after what looked like the end.
There is still grace.
This is the heartbeat behind Gospel Warrior:
Not because your past magically disappears.
Not because consequences always disappear.
Not because every broken relationship will automatically return to what it was.
But because your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending when your life belongs to Jesus Christ.
Be honest before God.
Your comment may become the sentence another ashamed believer reads and realizes, I'm not the only person who needs Jesus this desperately.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns God's favor. It doesn't.
Not because clicking “share” proves your salvation. It doesn't.
We are saved by God's grace, not by social-media activity.
Send it privately to the person who has been drifting.
But the greater reason to stay connected is not merchandise. It is discipleship.
And please don't keep this article inside your own screen.
Invite somebody who has stopped going to church.
Invite somebody who thinks God could never want them again.
Invite the Christian who is quietly becoming cold.
Invite the person whose life currently looks like a scandal.
Because you never know which shared article God may use to interrupt somebody's darkest night.
And tonight, before you sleep, ask yourself one question:
What have I been asking Jesus to protect me from while still refusing to surrender the place where it enters?
Then take the key.
Walk to the room.
Open the door.
And give it to Christ.
Because the devil does not deserve one room in a life purchased by the blood of Jesus.
And whatever you discover behind that door, remember this:
The room you are most ashamed to open may become the very place where you discover just how deep the grace of Jesus really goes.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “JUDGE NOT.” THE VERSE EVERYONE QUOTES—UNTIL YOU READ WHAT JESUS SAID NEXT
paragraphs: “JUDGE NOT.” THE VERSE EVERYONE QUOTES—UNTIL YOU READ WHAT JESUS SAID NEXT
Matthew 7:1 was never permission to call darkness light. It was a warning that before you reach for someone else’s speck, you had better let Jesus deal with the plank in your own eye.
There is a sentence people love to throw at Christians.
Sometimes it comes from a friend.
Sometimes from a comment section.
Sometimes from someone who has been wounded by religious hypocrisy.
Sometimes from a person who simply does not want anyone questioning the direction of their life.
“Judge not.”
Two words.
Conversation over.
Or so it seems.
Because Jesus did say something very close to those words.
In Matthew 7:1, the Greek text reads:
Μὴ κρίνετε, ἵνα μὴ κριθῆτε.
Mē krinete, hina mē krithēte.
“Do not judge, so that you may not be judged.”
And if we stop there, it can sound absolute.
Never evaluate.
Never confront.
Never identify sin.
Never warn someone.
Never distinguish truth from error.
Never say that something is morally wrong.
Just love everybody, affirm everything, and keep your mouth closed.
There is only one problem.
Jesus did not stop speaking at verse 1.
And sometimes the most dangerous way to misunderstand Jesus is to quote His words accurately while cutting Him off before He finishes the sentence.
That is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because Matthew 7:1 is not merely a verse about how you look at other people.
It is a mirror.
And before this article is finished, you may discover that the person Jesus is asking you to examine first is not the sinner you have been criticizing.
It is you.

The Greek verb translated “judge” comes from κρίνω — krinō. Depending on context, the word can carry senses such as judging, deciding, evaluating, or passing judgment. That matters because Scripture itself shows that not every act of moral discernment is forbidden.
Jesus is not commanding His disciples to become morally blind.
He is confronting something far more sinister.
The kind of judgment that can see everybody else’s sin while remaining strangely blind to its own.
Listen to what He says next:
“For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you.”
Then Jesus paints an almost ridiculous picture.
Why do you notice the tiny speck in your brother’s eye while ignoring the massive beam sticking out of your own?
Imagine it.
A man walking toward his brother saying, “Hold still. There is something in your eye.”
Meanwhile, a wooden beam is protruding from his own face.
He cannot see properly.
He cannot approach properly.
He may even injure the person he claims he is trying to help.
Then Jesus uses a word we should not rush past:
ὑποκριτά — hypokrita.
“Hypocrite.”
That is the heart of the warning.
Jesus is exposing hypocrisy.
He is confronting the terrifying human ability to become intensely sensitive to another person’s failure while becoming remarkably tolerant of our own.
Their anger is sinful.
Our anger is justified.
Their gossip is wicked.
We were only “telling somebody so they could pray.”
Their pride is disgusting.
Ours is confidence.
Their greed is materialism.
Ours is ambition.
Their sexual sin deserves confrontation.
Our secret lust apparently deserves another excuse.
Their marriage problems prove they need God.
Ours are complicated.
Their children are rebellious because the parents failed.
Our children are simply “going through a season.”
Their church hurt has made them bitter.
Our church hurt gives us permission to speak poison.
Their compromise is evidence that they are lukewarm.
Our compromise?
We have a reason.
And suddenly Matthew 7 is no longer ammunition for an argument.
It is surgery.
Because Jesus does not merely expose the sin of judging.
He exposes the scandal of unequal scales.
We can become prosecutors when examining another person's life and defense attorneys when examining our own.
That is what Christ destroys here.
But notice something extremely important.
Jesus does not say:
“You have a plank in your eye, therefore you can never help your brother with his speck.”
Read what He actually says:
“First take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye.”
First.
That word changes everything.
Repentance comes first.
Self-examination comes first.
Humility comes first.
Grace comes first.
Then, with clearer vision, you may actually be able to help your brother.
Jesus is not abolishing discernment.
He is purifying the discerner.
He is not saying sin should never be confronted.
He is saying the person confronting it must first stand beneath the same holy light of God.
Before you expose someone, ask God to expose you.
Before you correct someone, ask whether Scripture has corrected you.
Before you talk about their marriage, examine yours.
Before you condemn their parenting, examine your heart toward your own children.
Before you post about another Christian’s failure, ask whether you secretly enjoy being the one who knows.
Before you call somebody a hypocrite...
make sure you have heard Jesus whisper the word toward your own heart.
That changes the tone of Christian correction completely.
And the rest of Scripture confirms that Christians are not commanded to abandon moral discernment.
Later in Matthew 7, Jesus warns about false prophets and says they will be recognized “by their fruits.” Recognition requires discernment.
In John 7:24, Jesus says:
“Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment.”

Paul tells believers in Galatians 6:1 that if someone is caught in transgression, those who are spiritual should restore that person in a spirit of gentleness, while watching themselves lest they also be tempted.
That is almost the heartbeat of Matthew 7 in another form.
See the sin.
Do not pretend it is righteousness.
But approach the sinner remembering that you are made of the same fallen dust.
Restore.
Do not enjoy destroying.
Speak truth.
Do not weaponize truth.
Correct.
Do not humiliate.
Discern.
Do not play God.
There is an enormous difference between saying, “What you are doing contradicts Scripture,” and saying, “You are beyond the mercy of God.”
One may be biblical discernment.
The other attempts to sit in a chair that belongs to God alone.

Christians are called to recognize good and evil. We are commanded to test teaching. We are commanded to pursue holiness. There are even circumstances in which church discipline is biblically required.
But nowhere are Christians given permission to become self-righteous executioners of people Christ may still be pursuing.
Remember the woman caught in adultery.
Her sin was real.
Jesus did not rename adultery as authenticity.
He did not tell everyone that moral truth was subjective.
He showed astonishing mercy, and then He called her away from sin.
Grace and truth were not enemies in Jesus.
They met perfectly in Him.
That matters because our generation often offers us two counterfeit choices.
Condemn people without mercy.
Or affirm people without truth.
Jesus does neither.
He can look directly at sin without looking away from the sinner.
He can expose darkness without extinguishing the bruised soul standing in front of Him.
He can say, in effect:
This is sin.
And I am still calling you.
This must die.
And I am offering you life.
Repent.
And come home.
That is the Gospel.
And perhaps that is why Matthew 7:1 becomes so dangerous when ripped from its context.
“Judge not” can be abused to silence legitimate biblical correction.
But biblical correction can also be abused to disguise cruelty as courage.
Both distort Jesus.
Some people use Matthew 7:1 because they do not want repentance.
Others ignore Matthew 7:1 because they do not want humility.
Christ confronts both.
Maybe you have been on the receiving end of religious judgment.
Maybe somebody discovered your worst chapter and treated it like the title of your entire life.
Maybe Christians discussed you before anyone prayed with you.
Maybe your divorce became gossip.
Your addiction became entertainment.
Your pregnancy became scandal.
Your failure became a screenshot.
Your past became your name.
People who had never carried your wounds confidently announced what was wrong with you.
And maybe somewhere along the way you began to believe that God looked at you the same way they did.
Please hear this carefully.
Human hypocrisy does not change the character of Jesus Christ.
People may have handled truth without love.
Jesus did not.
People may have exposed you because they enjoyed your humiliation.
Jesus exposes darkness because He calls sinners into light.
People may have wanted your scandal remembered forever.
Jesus went to a cross to accomplish something scandal could never accomplish.
Redemption.
At Calvary, the only truly righteous Judge stepped into the place of the guilty.
He did not pretend sin was harmless.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so devastating that reconciliation with a holy God required something we could never provide for ourselves.
Yet the cross simultaneously announces the staggering depth of divine grace.
Jesus Christ bore sin and judgment so that those who repent and trust in Him can receive forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life.
That means Christianity is not a community of people who never needed mercy.
Christianity is supposed to be a community of people who know exactly why mercy matters.
We do not stand above the sinner.
We stand beside the sinner pointing to the Savior.
And sometimes the sinner standing beside us is a brother or sister who needs correction.
Sometimes it is someone who has wandered.
Sometimes it is someone deceived by false teaching.
Sometimes it is somebody trapped in a destructive pattern.
Love does not always remain silent.
If someone you loved were walking toward a cliff in darkness, you would not whisper, “I don't want to judge their journey.”
You would warn them.
But you would warn them because you wanted them alive.
That is the question.
When you confront someone...
do you want restoration, or do you want victory?
When you point out their sin...
do you want them closer to Jesus, or do you want everyone to know you were right?
When someone falls...
does your heart break?
Or does something inside you secretly enjoy watching someone else become smaller?
Be honest.
Because you can defend biblical truth with an unbiblical heart.
You can win an argument while misrepresenting Christ.
You can quote Scripture while feeding pride.
You can identify another person's speck while carrying lumber in your own eye.
And maybe that is the sentence somebody reading this needed today.
Not because you should abandon truth.
Because truth should first conquer you.
There is another side to this.
Maybe you are using “judge not” as a shield.
You know what Scripture says.
You know the relationship is dragging you away from Christ.
You know the secret habit is consuming you.
You know your bitterness has become an identity.
You know the compromise is no longer accidental.
But whenever somebody lovingly challenges you, your heart immediately says:
“Who are they to judge me?”
Maybe they are imperfect.
They certainly are.
But an imperfect messenger can still deliver a biblical warning.
The fact that another Christian has flaws does not automatically make every correction false.
So instead of immediately asking, “Who are you to judge me?” perhaps there is a harder question:
Is what they are saying actually true?
Not pleasant.
Not perfectly delivered.
Not convenient.
True.
If it agrees with Scripture, do not let pride make you reject medicine because you dislike the hand holding the cup.
And if someone has confronted you harshly, remember that their harshness does not transform your sin into righteousness.
Take the truth to Jesus.
Open Scripture.
Pray.
Examine yourself.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Reject accusations that contradict God’s Word.
But never let another person’s hypocrisy become permission for your own rebellion.
That is freedom.
Not freedom from moral truth.
Freedom from pretending.
Freedom from constantly needing to prove that you are better than somebody else.
Freedom from hiding.
Freedom from condemnation for those who are in Christ.
Freedom to repent because your identity no longer depends upon pretending you have never fallen.
That is where scandal meets grace.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Corinthian church was a mess of serious problems.
The Bible does not airbrush human failure.
Yet Scripture repeatedly shows God redeeming people who could never rewrite themselves.
This does not make sin beautiful.
It makes grace astonishing.
And somebody reading this may desperately need to understand the difference.
Your scandal is not your savior.
Your shame is not your savior.
Your church attendance is not your savior.
Your morality is not your savior.
Your ability to identify everybody else’s sin is certainly not your savior.
Jesus Christ is.
The answer to hypocrisy is Jesus.
The answer to self-righteousness is Jesus.
The answer to hidden sin is Jesus.
The answer to condemnation is Jesus.
The answer to the plank and the speck is Jesus.
Come into His light.
Let Him search what you keep defending.
Let Him touch what you keep hiding.
Let Him confront the resentment you renamed discernment.
Let Him confront the compromise you renamed freedom.
Let Him confront the pride you renamed conviction.
And when He exposes something, do not run.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
In Christ, repentance is the road home.
Maybe your prayer today needs to become painfully simple:
“Jesus, show me my plank before I obsess over their speck.”
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only Christian still being rebuilt.

Not because every sentence will be comfortable tomorrow, but because eventually you may need Matthew 7 again—perhaps when someone judges you, perhaps when you are tempted to judge someone else, and perhaps when someone loves you enough to tell you something you desperately do not want to hear.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not as a way to purchase His favor.
Not because giving money somehow makes someone more spiritual.
We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, and one practical way believers can support Gospel-centered work they believe is bearing good fruit is to help sustain it and share it with others.
And before you leave, remember the verse everybody quotes.
“Judge not.”
Now remember what Jesus said next.
Before staring at their speck...
bring your plank to Christ.

Then, when grace has humbled your heart and truth has cleared your vision, you may finally be able to reach toward another wounded sinner—not as their executioner, but as another person who knows where mercy can be found.
Because someday you may discover that the hand you almost raised to condemn someone was the very hand Jesus wanted you to extend to help them home.
Your worst chapter may explain the scars—but Jesus still gets the final word over the story surrendered to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN A CHRISTIAN BE DEMON-POSSESSED? THE ANSWER MAY DESTROY ONE OF THE MOST DANGEROUS LIES YOU HAVE EVER BELIEVED
paragraphs: CAN A CHRISTIAN BE DEMON-POSSESSED? THE ANSWER MAY DESTROY ONE OF THE MOST DANGEROUS LIES YOU HAVE EVER BELIEVED
What Scripture actually says about demons, believers, spiritual warfare, the indwelling Holy Spirit—and why your darkest battle does not necessarily mean the devil owns you.
There is a particular kind of fear Christians rarely admit out loud.
You love Jesus.
You believe the Gospel.
You pray.
You worship.
You have confessed Christ as Lord.
And yet there are moments when something inside your life feels frighteningly dark.
Thoughts you hate keep returning.
Temptations you thought you defeated suddenly come screaming back.
Your prayer life becomes dry.
Your mind becomes a battlefield.
You feel accused.
Condemned.
Tormented.
Perhaps you wake in the middle of the night terrified for reasons you cannot explain.
Perhaps an old addiction suddenly begins calling your name again.
Perhaps anger erupts from somewhere you thought had already been healed.
And eventually a terrifying question whispers through your mind:
“What if there is a demon inside me?”
That question has frightened countless Christians.
And depending on whom you ask, you may receive two radically different answers.
One person will tell you, “Absolutely not. Christians have nothing whatsoever to fear from demons.”
Another will tell you, “Absolutely. Christians can have demons living inside them and may need those demons cast out.”
But neither slogan is sufficient.
Because Scripture presents something more careful.
More sobering.
And ultimately far more hopeful.
The New Testament unquestionably teaches that demons are real.
Jesus did not treat them as metaphors.
He confronted them.
He commanded them.
They recognized Him.
They feared Him.
They obeyed Him.
When Jesus encountered two demonized men in Matthew 8, the Greek text uses a form of the verb δαιμονίζομαι (daimonizomai), a word associated with being under demonic influence or affliction.
The demons cried out:
“Τί ἡμῖν καὶ σοί, υἱὲ τοῦ θεοῦ;”
Literally:
“What [is there] to us and to You, Son of God?”
They knew exactly who stood before them.
And notice something Christianity must never forget.
Jesus did not struggle with them.
He did not negotiate with them.
He did not discover that Satan was almost His equal.
Christ spoke.
Demons obeyed.
That matters because biblical spiritual warfare never begins with how powerful demons are.
It begins with how absolutely supreme Jesus Christ is.
The Christian faith does not present Jesus and Satan as two equal supernatural forces wrestling over the universe.
Satan is a creature.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
Paul says of Christ that all things were created through Him and for Him, including rulers and authorities, and that Christ is before all things.
The darkness is real.
But darkness has never been equal to the King.
Now comes the difficult question.
Can someone who genuinely belongs to Jesus Christ actually be possessed by a demon?
Here we need humility because the Bible never gives us a verse saying in precisely those modern words, “A Christian cannot be demon-possessed.”
But neither does the New Testament give us a clear example of a regenerate, Spirit-indwelt Christian being presented as demon-possessed and then having a demon exorcised from within him or her.
That distinction matters.
We should never build certainty where Scripture itself has not spoken with equal specificity.
What Scripture does tell believers is extraordinary.
Paul writes that the Christian's body is “ναὸς τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίου πνεύματος” — naos tou en hymin hagiou pneumatos — a temple or sanctuary of the Holy Spirit who is “in you.”
Not merely near you.
Not occasionally visiting you.
In you.
The believer belongs to God.
You were bought with a price.
And John tells Christians:
“μείζων ἐστὶν ὁ ἐν ὑμῖν ἢ ὁ ἐν τῷ κόσμῳ.”
Meizōn estin ho en hymin ē ho en tō kosmō.
“Greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world.”
Read that slowly.
Greater is He who is in you.
This does not mean Christians become untouchable.
It does not mean Satan suddenly loses interest in believers.
In fact, the New Testament repeatedly warns Christians precisely because spiritual warfare continues after conversion.
Peter warns believers that the devil prowls around like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour.
James tells believers to resist the devil.
Paul tells Christians to put on the whole armor of God because their struggle involves spiritual forces of evil.
Paul even warns believers not to give the devil an opportunity or foothold.
So Christianity does not teach:
“You belong to Jesus, therefore spiritual warfare is over.”
It teaches something closer to this:
“You belong to Jesus, therefore learn how to stand.”
That is a massive difference.
A Christian can be tempted.
A Christian can be deceived.
A Christian can be harassed.
A Christian can fall into serious sin.
A Christian can believe lies.
A Christian can become spiritually exhausted.
A Christian can give Satan opportunities through persistent disobedience.
A Christian can experience intense spiritual warfare.
But none of those things automatically proves that a demon possesses that Christian.
And this is where some believers have been deeply wounded.
They struggled with depression and someone told them it was a demon.
They experienced trauma and someone told them it was possession.
They developed intrusive thoughts and someone told them an evil spirit was speaking through them.
They suffered panic attacks and someone attempted deliverance instead of helping them obtain appropriate care.
They battled addiction and were taught to search endlessly for a demon instead of also confronting patterns of sin, wounds, habits, accountability, discipleship, and the renewing of their minds.
We must be extremely careful here.
Not every dark thought is a demon.
Not every sickness is demonic.
Not every emotional wound is demonic.
Not every psychological disorder is demonic.
Not every temptation requires an exorcism.
Scripture itself refuses simplistic explanations for human suffering.

Jesus could distinguish sickness from demonic affliction. The biblical writers could distinguish temptation arising from our own desires from satanic activity. Paul could speak about the flesh, the world, and spiritual enemies without collapsing all three into one category.
Sometimes the enemy attacking you is temptation.
Sometimes the problem is sinful desire.
Sometimes it is trauma.
Sometimes it is exhaustion.
Sometimes it is illness.
Sometimes it is consequences from decisions.
Sometimes spiritual warfare may indeed be involved.
And sometimes several realities may overlap.
Wisdom does not panic.
Wisdom tests.
Wisdom prays.
Wisdom searches Scripture.
Wisdom seeks mature pastoral counsel.
And when psychological or medical symptoms are present, wisdom is not afraid of qualified professional care.
God is not threatened by truth.
But perhaps you are reading this because you have done things that terrify you.
Maybe you opened doors you should never have opened.
Occult practices.
Pornography.
Drugs.
Hatred.
Sexual sin.
Manipulation.
Bitterness.
Witchcraft.
New Age spirituality.
Spiritism.
An obsession with darkness.
Maybe your history is ugly enough that you wonder whether Jesus could possibly want you now.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not the story of clean people being rewarded for staying clean.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners.
Your history does not frighten Him.
Your chains do not surprise Him.
Your shame does not disqualify you from coming to Him.
Look at the people Jesus encountered.
Some were scandalous.
Some were sexually broken.
Some were religious hypocrites.
Some were thieves.
Some were violent.
Some were demonized.
Some were despised by respectable society.
And Jesus walked directly into their darkness.
Not because darkness was harmless.
But because He came to destroy its claim.
This is where deliverance becomes bigger than an argument about terminology.
The deepest human problem is not merely whether a demon can inhabit someone.
The deepest human problem is sin.
We have rebelled against the God who created us.
And no ritual can reconcile sinful humanity to a holy God.
We needed a Savior.
So Christ came.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
Paul describes what happened at the cross with breathtaking language: Christ disarmed the rulers and authorities and triumphed over them.
The cross looked like Satan's victory.
It became the announcement of his defeat.
The nails looked like humiliation.
They became instruments in redemption.
The tomb looked like the final chapter.
Then Sunday morning came.
This is why Christians should never become more fascinated with demons than with Jesus.
Some believers know endless classifications of demons but barely know the Sermon on the Mount.
They know supposed names of spirits but cannot explain justification.
They chase manifestations but neglect holiness.
They search every family history for curses while barely opening the New Testament.
That is not spiritual maturity.
The goal of Christianity is not becoming an expert in darkness.
The goal is knowing Christ.
If you belong to Jesus, spiritual warfare should drive you toward Jesus.
When temptation comes, run toward Christ.
When accusation comes, remember the Gospel.
When shame says, “Look at what you did,” remember the blood of Christ.
When Satan whispers, “You will always be this person,” remember that anyone in Christ is a new creation.
When your past says, “This is your identity,” answer with the cross.
You are not saved because you became powerful enough to defeat Satan.
You are saved because Jesus defeated what you could never defeat yourself.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this desperately needed to hear.
Maybe your greatest fear has not actually been demons.
Maybe your greatest fear has been that God abandoned you because you are still struggling.
You thought genuine Christians never wrestled like this.
So every temptation became evidence against your salvation.
Every intrusive thought became an indictment.
Every relapse whispered:
“See? Nothing changed.”
Every spiritually dry morning whispered:
“God left.”
Every failure whispered:
“You were never His.”
But struggle is not the same thing as ownership.
Being attacked is not the same thing as belonging to the attacker.
A battlefield is not proof that the enemy owns the territory.
Sometimes a battlefield exists precisely because territory has changed hands.
Read that again.
You may be fighting because you no longer belong willingly to what once enslaved you.
The Christian life is not sinless perfection after conversion.
It is a life of repentance, faith, sanctification, warfare, grace, discipline, falling, getting back up, confessing, resisting, learning, surrendering, and becoming increasingly like Jesus.
Your confidence must never rest in how strongly you feel saved today.
It rests in Christ.
And if there is sin in your life right now, do not use grace as permission to keep it.
Repent.
Bring it into the light.
Confess it.
Cut off what feeds it.
Ask mature believers for help.
Seek biblical pastoral care.
If you have deliberately involved yourself with occult practices, renounce those practices and turn completely to Jesus Christ.
Destroy the bridge back to the darkness.
But do not spend your life staring over your shoulder wondering whether Satan is stronger than your Savior.
He is not.
John did not say:
“Greater is your willpower.”
He did not say:
“Greater is your religious discipline.”
He did not say:
“Greater is your pastor.”
He said:
Greater is He who is in you.
Jesus.
That changes everything.
So can Christians be demon-possessed?

If by “possessed” we mean owned and inhabited in the fullest sense as the property and dwelling place of a demon, Scripture gives us strong reasons not to describe a genuine Spirit-indwelt believer that way. Christians belong to Christ, have been bought with a price, are described as temples of the Holy Spirit, and are told that the One in them is greater than the one in the world.
At the same time, Christians should never turn that conclusion into careless denial of spiritual warfare.
Believers can be attacked.
Tempted.
Deceived.
Oppressed or harassed in the ordinary sense of those words.
Entrapped through sin.
And deeply wounded.

That is why Scripture tells Christians—not unbelievers—to resist the devil, stand firm, remain sober-minded, put on God's armor, pray, pursue holiness, forgive, reject lies, and remain anchored in truth.
The answer is neither paranoia nor denial.
It is Christ.
Maybe you came to this article terrified of what might be inside you.
But perhaps the question God wants you asking is different.
Who owns you?
Because Christianity is ultimately about lordship.
If you have never truly surrendered to Jesus Christ, stop playing with Christianity around the edges.
You cannot save yourself.
Religious activity cannot wash away sin.
Church attendance cannot resurrect a dead heart.
Christian content cannot substitute for knowing Christ.
Turn to Him.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Come to the crucified and risen Savior.
And if you already belong to Jesus but have wandered into compromise, come home.
No more hiding.
No more secret agreement with the thing destroying you.
No more pretending.
Grace does not say your sin does not matter.
Grace says your sin mattered so much that Christ bled for it—and His blood is sufficient to forgive the repentant sinner.
Maybe your story has become scandalous.
Good.
Not because scandal is good.
But because scandal does not get the final word when Jesus enters the story.
Peter denied Him.
Christ restored him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Christ turned him into an apostle.
The thief was dying beside Jesus with no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Grace still found him.
That is the Gospel Warrior message.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Be honest.
And if Christ has already delivered you from a dark season, tell part of your testimony. Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that restoration is possible.
There may be a night when accusation returns and you need to remember that being attacked does not mean you belong to the attacker.
Not as a purchase of God's favor.
Not because giving money earns spiritual blessing.
We do not buy grace.
We receive grace through Christ.

But when biblical ministry strengthens us, voluntary financial support can help that ministry continue reaching others. If you want to glorify God through your resources, one legitimate way is to prayerfully support faithful Gospel work and help sound biblical teaching reach people who may never enter a church building.
If this ministry is helping you follow Jesus, stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling Christian.
Invite the person who walked away from church.
Invite the lukewarm believer.
Invite the seeker.
Even invite the unbeliever who keeps asking difficult questions.
Jesus is the Savior.
Gospel Warrior is not.
A ministry cannot forgive your sins.
A pastor cannot become your mediator.
Only Jesus Christ saves.
And perhaps years from now you will forget almost everything you read here.
Forget the Greek words.
Forget the arguments.
Forget the controversy.
But do not forget this:
The darkness may have touched your story, but if your life belongs to Jesus Christ, darkness does not get to write the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “LOVE YOUR ENEMIES” SOUNDS BEAUTIFUL—UNTIL JESUS ASKS YOU TO LOVE YOURS
paragraphs:
“LOVE YOUR ENEMIES” SOUNDS BEAUTIFUL—UNTIL JESUS ASKS YOU TO LOVE YOURS
The command we quote when the enemy is imaginary becomes painfully different when the enemy has a name, a face, a history with you—and wounds you still carry.
“Love your enemies.”
Four words.
Beautiful enough for a church wall. Gentle enough for a Christian caption. Familiar enough that some of us can repeat them without even thinking.
But then Jesus allows a face to appear in your mind.
And suddenly the verse is not beautiful anymore.
It hurts.
Because your enemy is not an abstract theological category.
Your enemy may be the person who humiliated you when nobody defended you.
The friend who knew your secrets and weaponized them.
The spouse who betrayed promises made before God.
The relative who keeps reopening wounds and then acts as though nothing happened.
The person who lied about you.
The person who damaged your reputation.
The person who never apologized.
The person who apologized—and somehow did it again.
Maybe even the person who sits in church, raises their hands during worship, speaks about Jesus publicly, and still knows exactly what they did to you.
Now read Christ’s words again.
“But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you…”
—Matthew 5:44, KJV
In the Greek text, the heart of the command is startlingly direct:
ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν, ἀγαπᾶτε τοὺς ἐχθροὺς ὑμῶν
egō de legō hymin, agapate tous echthrous hymōn
“But I say to you, love your enemies.”
That word ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate comes from ἀγαπάω — agapaō, the verb commonly translated “to love.”
And notice something important.
Jesus did not say, “Pretend they never hurt you.”
He did not say, “Call evil good.”
He did not say, “Trust everyone who betrayed you.”
He did not say, “Remain where someone can continue abusing you.”
He did not say forgiveness eliminates wisdom, justice, consequences, boundaries, or accountability.
He said:
Love them.
And perhaps that is harder.
Because biblical enemy-love does not require you to manufacture warm feelings toward evil.
It requires something deeper.
It requires surrendering your supposed right to become evil because evil was done to you.
That is where this command finds us.
Not in sentiment.
In the war happening inside the wounded heart.
There is a version of revenge that never throws a punch.
It simply keeps the courtroom open.
Every morning.
Every night.
Every time their name appears.
