And while staring at someone else's life, you slowly stop stewarding your own.
Saul became obsessed with David.
David remained occupied with God.
And there came a moment when the roles were reversed.
David had the opportunity to kill Saul.
Saul entered a cave where David and his men were hiding.
David's men essentially told him, This is your chance.
Imagine the temptation.
The man hunting you is suddenly vulnerable.
The person who threw spears at you is within reach.
The king who forced you from your home is defenseless.
David could have called revenge justice.
He could have called murder destiny.
He could have interpreted opportunity as permission.
Instead, David refused.
He said:
“The LORD forbid that I should do this thing to my lord, the LORD's anointed.”
—1 Samuel 24:6
David understood something many wounded people forget:
Someone else's sin does not give you permission to become sinful.
Saul's spear did not justify David's knife.
That sentence may be for someone reading this with tears behind their eyes.
You were betrayed.
You were lied about.
You were humiliated.
Someone became jealous of you and tried to destroy your name.
Someone you helped turned against you.
Someone you defended became the person attacking you.
Someone took your kindness and answered it with cruelty.
Your pain is real.
But Jesus is not calling you to become the person who wounded you.
Do not let another person's bitterness reproduce itself inside you.
Do not carry Saul's spear simply because Saul threw it first.
David's restraint was not weakness.
It was evidence that David trusted God with justice.
And eventually the contrast between Saul and David becomes heartbreaking.
One man was desperately trying to keep a kingdom.
The other was learning how to surrender his future to God.
One grasped.
One waited.
One hunted.
One trusted.
One became consumed with another man's calling.
The other learned to survive caves without abandoning his God.
But we must be careful here.
David was not the perfect hero.
If we stop the story at David's noblest moments, we miss the Gospel.
Because David himself would later fall catastrophically.
The man who refused to murder Saul would eventually arrange circumstances leading to Uriah's death after committing adultery with Bathsheba.
David needed mercy too.
That is why the Bible is not ultimately a collection of stories about good people defeating bad people.
It is the story of sinful humanity desperately needing a perfect King.
Saul cannot save us.
David cannot save us.
Only Jesus can.
And this is where the story moves from scandal to grace.
Because generations after David, another King came.
Jesus Christ.
The Son of David.
The King David could only foreshadow.
He had no sinful jealousy.
No selfish ambition.
No corrupt throne to protect.
No insecurity.
No hidden rebellion against the Father.
Jesus was betrayed by someone close to Him.
Accused falsely.
Mocked.
Rejected.
Beaten.
Spat upon.
Stripped.
Crucified.
And unlike David, Jesus did not merely spare the life of an enemy.
Jesus gave His life for His enemies.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
And Romans 5:10 says that we were reconciled to God through the death of His Son while we were enemies.
There is the Gospel.
We were not merely Davids being hunted by Sauls.
In our sin, we were rebels against God.
We have envied.
Compared.
Resented.
Gossiped.
Hated.
Coveted.
Judged.
Competed.
Wounded.
Hidden.
And Christ went to the cross for sinners like us.
The answer to jealousy is therefore deeper than telling yourself, Stop comparing.
You need a new heart.
You need repentance.
You need grace.
You need Jesus.
Because when your identity becomes rooted in Christ, another person's blessing no longer has to feel like God's rejection of you.
Their calling does not cancel yours.
Their testimony does not erase yours.
Their opportunity does not prove God forgot you.
Their beauty does not diminish your worth.
Their ministry does not make yours meaningless.
Their success does not mean heaven has run out of grace.
You do not have to throw spears at people because God placed something beautiful in their hands.
You can celebrate them.
You can pray for them.
You can bless them.
You can say, “Father, thank You for what You are doing in their life. Keep my heart clean.”
And perhaps that prayer is exactly what someone reading this needs tonight.
Because there is a name in your mind right now.
You know it.
The person whose success stings.
The person whose posts you sometimes cannot stand seeing.
The person you secretly compare yourself with.
The person whose failure would give a dark corner of your heart a little satisfaction.
Do not excuse it.
Bring it into the light.
Jesus already knows.
Repentance does not begin when you become impressive.
Repentance begins when you stop hiding.
Tell Him:

“Jesus, forgive me. I have been comparing. I have been jealous. I have allowed someone else's blessing to become bitterness in me. Clean my heart. Teach me to love what You are doing in other people without believing You have forgotten me.”
Not because typing a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes confession begins when we finally stop pretending the struggle is not there.

And maybe somebody else reading your comment needs to discover that Christians do not have to pretend they never struggle—we bring our darkness to Jesus because His grace is greater than what we have hidden.
Not because what happened was acceptable.
Not because forgiveness means pretending there was no wound.
But because you refuse to let their spear become your identity.
Jesus can heal what they damaged without turning you into what damaged you.
Not as a performance.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.

But if this truth can interrupt one person's jealousy before it destroys a friendship, one marriage, one family, one church, or one calling, sharing it becomes a simple opportunity to put biblical truth in front of someone who may desperately need it.
Send this privately to the person exhausted from comparison.
Your support can help this ministry place more Gospel-centered material before believers, struggling Christians, seekers, and people who may not yet know Christ.
Come to Jesus.
A ministry cannot cleanse your heart.
A Christian product cannot reconcile you to God.
Jesus Christ can.
The same Gospel that confronts the Saul hiding in us also offers mercy to the Saul hiding in us.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Lay down the spear.
Stop treating God's children as competitors.
Stop measuring your worth against somebody else's calling.
Stop letting comparison rob you of gratitude.
Stop demanding somebody else's light become dimmer before you believe God can still use yours.
There is room in the kingdom for obedience without rivalry.
There is grace enough to celebrate another person's victory.
There is healing for the person who has been hunted.
There is forgiveness for the person who has done the hunting.
And there is a King greater than Saul, greater than David, greater than every throne we have ever fought to protect.
His name is Jesus.
Maybe the greatest victory in your life will not be proving your enemies wrong.
Maybe it will be discovering that some of the people you were fighting were never your enemies at all.
And maybe tonight, Jesus is asking you to finally put the spear down.
Because when grace takes hold of the hand that once held the spear, the story does not have to end in scandal.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU WILL EAT WHAT YOU PLANT
paragraphs: YOU WILL EAT WHAT YOU PLANT

“You reap what you sow” is not karma, not a threat that every tragedy is punishment, and not a cute motivational quote. In the hands of the apostle Paul, it is a warning about something frighteningly ordinary: the life you keep feeding is quietly becoming the life you will eventually have to live.
There are seeds in your life that nobody can see yet.
That is what should make you pause.

Not because God is waiting behind a corner to destroy you the moment you fail. Not because every painful thing happening to you is proof that you secretly deserved it. And certainly not because Christianity teaches some baptized version of karma.
It doesn’t.
But Scripture does teach something uncomfortable.
What you repeatedly plant matters.
The private compromise matters.
The resentment you keep watering matters.
The pornography you keep returning to matters.
The lie you have repeated so many times that it barely feels like lying anymore matters.
The unforgiveness you rehearse when nobody is listening matters.
The secret generosity matters too.
The prayer nobody applauds matters.
The temptation you resisted while your flesh screamed for satisfaction matters.
The apology that cost your pride matters.
The Scripture you opened when you wanted to scroll instead matters.
The quiet obedience nobody will ever post about matters.
Seeds are small.
Harvests are not.
And perhaps that is why these words from Paul should make every one of us stop:
“Μὴ πλανᾶσθε, Θεὸς οὐ μυκτηρίζεται· ὃ γὰρ ἐὰν σπείρῃ ἄνθρωπος, τοῦτο καὶ θερίσει.”
Μὴ πλανᾶσθε — Mē planasthe.
“Do not be deceived.”
Then:
Θεὸς οὐ μυκτηρίζεται — Theos ou myktērizetai.
“God is not mocked.”
And then the principle:
ὃ γὰρ ἐὰν σπείρῃ ἄνθρωπος, τοῦτο καὶ θερίσει.
“For whatever a person sows, this also he will reap.”
That is Galatians 6:7.
Notice where Paul begins.
Not with “reaping.”
With deception.
“Do not be deceived.”
Because one of sin’s greatest powers is not merely making evil attractive.
It is making consequences seem impossible.
Just once.
Nobody knows.
I can stop whenever I want.
God understands.
It isn't hurting anyone.
I'll repent later.
This is just who I am.
Everybody does it.
And little by little, what once disturbed your conscience becomes familiar enough to live with.
A seed disappears beneath the soil.
Nothing happens.
So you plant another.
Still nothing.
Another.
Nothing.
And because there is no immediate harvest, you begin to believe there never will be one.
That is the deception.
We often imagine consequences should arrive like lightning.
But seeds don't work like lightning.
They work underground.
Paul continues:
“For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life” (Galatians 6:8).
The Greek word translated “flesh” is σάρξ — sarx.

In this context, Paul is not saying that the physical human body is inherently evil. He is speaking about human life oriented away from God—the fallen self with its desires enthroned, the life that keeps saying, “My will. My appetite. My glory. My way.”
And there is something terrifying about feeding that life.
Whatever you feed grows stronger.
You don't usually wake up one morning and suddenly become bitter.
You rehearse offenses.
You replay conversations.
You assume motives.
You keep watering the wound.
Eventually bitterness stops feeling like something you carry.
It starts feeling like who you are.
You don't usually destroy a marriage in one afternoon.
You sow neglect.
You stop listening.
You hide things.
You entertain fantasies.
You make small compromises.
You protect your pride.
You keep planting.
Then one day everyone stares at the harvest and asks:
“How did we get here?”
Seeds.
You don't usually abandon your faith with one dramatic announcement.
Sometimes it happens one almost invisible decision at a time.
One prayer skipped.
Then another.
One compromise excused.
One conviction ignored.
One Sunday where Jesus can wait.
One month where Scripture stays closed.
One relationship that keeps pulling you away from Christ.
One secret you refuse to bring into the light.
Until eventually you look around and realize you have traveled much farther from Jesus than you ever intended.
Seeds.
But now we have to be very careful.
Because “you reap what you sow” has also been used cruelly.
Someone gets cancer: “You must have sown something.”
Someone loses a child: “You're reaping what you planted.”
Someone experiences abuse: “Maybe this is the consequence of your choices.”
No.
That is not faithful biblical interpretation.

Jesus Himself rejected simplistic equations between personal tragedy and personal guilt. In John 9, when His disciples encountered a man blind from birth, they asked whose sin caused his blindness—his or his parents'. Jesus refused their assumption.
And in Luke 13, when people told Jesus about Galileans whom Pilate had killed, Jesus did not tell the survivors, “They suffered because they were worse sinners.”
Scripture teaches sowing and reaping.
Scripture does not give you permission to stand over every suffering person and pretend you know why they are bleeding.
We live in a fallen world.
People suffer because of their own decisions.
People suffer because of other people's sins.
People suffer because creation itself is groaning under the curse of the Fall.
And sometimes we simply do not know why a particular tragedy happened.
So Galatians 6:7 is not a weapon for diagnosing somebody else's pain.
It is a mirror for examining your own life.
That changes everything.
Because suddenly the question isn't:
“What are they going to reap?”
It is:
“What am I planting?”
And that question can become painfully personal.
What are you planting in your marriage?
What are you planting in your children?
What are you planting into your mind at midnight when nobody else is watching?
What are you planting every time someone succeeds and jealousy rises inside you?
What are you planting through the words you speak about people who aren't in the room?
What are you planting with your money?
Your eyes?
Your time?
Your anger?
Your phone?
Your habits?
Your secret life?
If everything you repeatedly planted during the last year suddenly became visible as a harvest tomorrow morning...
would you want to eat it?
That question hurts.
It hurts me too.
Because none of us gets through Galatians 6 by pointing at everybody else.
We have all planted things we regret.
Some of us are living among the weeds right now.
Maybe you ignored the warnings.
Maybe you knew better.
Maybe God convicted you and you kept going.
Maybe the relationship collapsed.
Maybe trust disappeared.
Maybe addiction dug its roots deeper.
Maybe anger cost you people you loved.
Maybe years disappeared while you kept promising yourself that tomorrow would be different.
And now you are staring at consequences you cannot simply pray backward.
This is where people sometimes misunderstand grace.
We imagine grace means consequences magically disappear.
Sometimes God does mercifully remove consequences.
Sometimes He doesn't.
David was forgiven after his grievous sins, but forgiveness did not mean every earthly consequence vanished.
A thief can meet Jesus and still need to return what was stolen.
An adulterer can genuinely repent and still face shattered trust.
An addict can be forgiven completely and still need years of healing, accountability, and restoration.
Forgiveness is not God pretending the seed was never planted.
The Gospel is something even more astonishing.
God can meet you in the field you ruined.
Read that again.
God can meet you in the field you ruined.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of good farmers congratulating themselves on producing perfect crops.
It is the story of sinners who desperately needed a Savior.
And His name is Jesus.
This is where “you reap what you sow” becomes far more profound than karma.
Karma says, in simplified popular usage, that your deeds return to you.
The Gospel announces that guilty people can receive mercy they did not earn because Jesus Christ bore judgment for sinners.
Scripture says:
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
All.
The religious.
The rebellious.
The preacher.
The addict.
The person reading this with tears in their eyes.
The person reading this while hiding something nobody else knows.
If our hope were simply receiving exactly what our sins deserve, none of us could boast.
But the center of Christianity is a cross.
Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, was crucified.
Not because He needed forgiveness.
We did.
Peter writes that Christ “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18).
Paul says that God made Christ, who knew no sin, “to be sin for us, that we might become the righteousness of God in him” (2 Corinthians 5:21).
This is scandalous grace.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The unclean can be washed.
The wandering can come home.
The spiritually dead can be made alive.
Not because sin didn't matter.
Look at the cross and try saying sin doesn't matter.
It mattered enough that redemption cost blood.
But look at the empty tomb before saying your story cannot change.
Jesus rose.
And because Christ lives, your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
That doesn't mean you can sow rebellion all week and casually sprinkle “grace” over it on Sunday.
Paul destroys that idea elsewhere:
“Are we to continue in sin that grace may abound? By no means!” (Romans 6:1–2).
Grace is not permission to keep planting poison.
Grace takes the shovel out of your hand, calls you out of the field, forgives you, changes you, and teaches you to plant differently.
That is repentance.
Repentance is not merely feeling horrible about yesterday.
It is turning toward Christ today.
It is bringing the hidden thing into the light.
It is confessing.
It is surrendering.
It is saying:
“Jesus, I cannot keep living like this.”
And maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needs to say tonight.
Not tomorrow.
Tonight.
Maybe nobody knows what you're fighting.
Maybe everybody thinks you're strong.
Maybe your Facebook photos look happy.
Maybe you know how to say “God is good” while quietly wondering how much longer you can keep pretending.
Maybe you have become frighteningly skilled at appearing spiritually alive while starving inside.
Jesus already knows.
There is no room in your heart so dark that Christ has to discover it.
He knows.
And still He calls sinners to come.
Not to perform.
Not to hide.
To repent and believe.
So come.
Come ashamed.
Come exhausted.
Come with the consequences.
Come with the memories.
Come with the habit you swore you would never return to.
Come with the marriage you damaged.
Come with the pride you protected.
Come with the years you wasted.
Come with the field full of things you wish you had never planted.
But come to Jesus.
Because your past sowing may explain part of your present harvest, but in Christ it does not have sovereign authority over your eternal future.
Jesus does.
And now, by the Spirit, begin planting differently.
Paul does not end his teaching with despair.
Immediately after speaking about sowing to the Spirit, he says:
“And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up” (Galatians 6:9).
Did you catch that?
Don't give up.
Perhaps you've been praying and seeing nothing.
Keep planting.
You've been trying to rebuild trust and it feels painfully slow.
Keep planting faithfulness.
You've been fighting temptation and nobody knows how difficult the battle has been.
Keep planting obedience.
You've been opening Scripture even though your emotions feel numb.
Keep planting truth.
You've been forgiving again and again.
Keep planting mercy.
You've been serving without recognition.
Keep planting love.
You've been praying for your child who seems farther from God than ever.
Keep praying.
You do not control the harvest.
God does.
Your calling is faithfulness.
Some seeds take time.
That truth cuts both ways.
It warns the person secretly sowing destruction:
Don't confuse delayed consequences with divine approval.
But it also comforts the exhausted believer sowing faithfulness:
Don't confuse delayed fruit with divine absence.
God sees what is underground.
So perhaps today is not merely another day.
Perhaps today is planting season.
You cannot crawl back into yesterday and remove every seed.
But because of Jesus, you can repent today.
You can confess today.
You can forgive today.
You can delete it today.
You can make the call today.
You can ask for help today.
You can open your Bible today.
You can return to church today.
You can tell the truth today.
You can kneel beside your bed tonight and finally stop negotiating with the sin that is destroying you.
Be honest.
If you're exhausted but still refusing to abandon Christ, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray with you, simply comment, “pray for me.”
And if God has been rebuilding what sin, pain, or years of wandering damaged, comment, “Christ is still healing me.”
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing the struggle into the light is the first time we stop pretending there isn't a struggle.
And please don't keep this article trapped on your screen.
Save it too.
There may be a night when temptation becomes louder than conviction, and you need to remember what kind of seed is sitting in your hand.
Christ alone is Lord, salvation is by grace, and Christians glorify God through lives surrendered to Him.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has been drifting.
Invite the believer who is tired.
Invite the person who thinks they have gone too far.
Invite even the person who doesn't yet believe.
Because somebody scrolling through your shared post may be holding a seed tonight.
A decision.
A temptation.
A secret.
A surrender.
And God may use one truth-filled article to make them stop before they plant something they will spend years wishing they could uproot.
Or perhaps the person holding that seed is you.
Then hear the warning.
But hear the Gospel too.
You will reap what you sow.
So stop planting what is killing you.
Run to Jesus.
Receive the mercy you could never earn.
And by the power of His Spirit, start planting what you will someday thank God you did.
Because the most breathtaking part of your story may not be the field you ruined...
but the Savior who walked into it and refused to leave you there.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD WARNED THE KING ABOUT HIS WIVES—THEN SOLOMON DID THE VERY THING GOD SAID WOULD DESTROY HIM
paragraphs:
GOD WARNED THE KING ABOUT HIS WIVES—THEN SOLOMON DID THE VERY THING GOD SAID WOULD DESTROY HIM
Deuteronomy’s forgotten warning about power, women, wealth, and the human heart is not merely an ancient command for kings. It exposes something frightening about us all: you can possess wisdom, influence, success, and even a history with God—and still slowly give your heart to something that takes you away from Him.
There is a sentence buried in Deuteronomy that becomes almost unbearable when you know what happens later.
God was preparing Israel for a future they had not yet reached.
There was no magnificent royal palace in Jerusalem.
No golden throne.
No famous son of David surrounded by international dignitaries.
No temple glittering beneath the sun.
No Solomon.
Not yet.
But God already knew what power could do to a human heart.
And so, long before Israel's kings began collecting horses, treasures, political alliances, and wives, the Lord gave them a warning.
In Deuteronomy 17:17, speaking specifically about Israel's future king, the Hebrew says:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
V'lo yarbeh-lo nashim, v'lo yasur levavo.
In context, the sense is:
He must not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn aside.
Read those final words again.
Lest his heart turn aside.
That is the center of the warning.
God was not merely regulating the size of a royal household.
He was guarding the heart of the king.
And centuries later, one of the wisest men who ever lived would become a living tragedy of that very sentence.
Solomon.
The man who had wisdom.
The man who built the temple.
The man who experienced extraordinary blessing.
The man whose fame crossed borders.
The man kings and queens wanted to hear.
The man who seemingly had everything.
And yet there came a point when everything was not enough.
That should frighten us more than it does.
Because some people imagine spiritual collapse begins when someone suddenly wakes up and decides, “Today I am going to abandon God.”
Usually it does not.
It begins smaller.
Another compromise.
Another appetite excused.
Another boundary moved.
Another affection allowed to become too powerful.
Another warning rationalized because nothing terrible happened yesterday.
Then another.
Then another.
Until something you once controlled begins controlling you.
Deuteronomy's warning about wives sits beside two other warnings for Israel's king.
He was not to multiply horses.
He was not to multiply wives.
He was not to excessively accumulate silver and gold.
Power.
Pleasure.
Possessions.
God knew the temptations surrounding the throne before Israel ever had a throne.
The king could begin thinking his security came from military strength.
His satisfaction from multiplying relationships.
His significance from accumulating wealth.
And underneath all three temptations was essentially the same lie:
God is not enough.
That lie is ancient.
And it is still destroying people.
You may never sit on a throne.
You may never command an army.
You may never possess Solomon's treasury.
You may never have hundreds of wives.
But you can still multiply the thing God warned you about.
Another drink.
Another purchase.
Another flirtation.
Another private conversation.
Another secret account.
Another fantasy.
Another achievement.
Another relationship you know is pulling your heart somewhere Jesus never asked it to go.
Another little kingdom where you are king and God is expected to remain silent.
And slowly...
וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
The heart turns aside.
That Hebrew word לְבָבוֹ — levavo refers to his heart, his inner person—the center of desire, allegiance, thought, and will.
That matters because the biblical problem is deeper than counting wives.
God was concerned about allegiance.
Who owns the heart?
Who sits at its center?
Who receives its deepest loyalty?
This also keeps us from twisting the passage into something it never says.
Deuteronomy 17:17 is not a license to despise women.
Women are not presented as some inherently corrupting class of people.
The command confronts the king.
He must not multiply wives.
His heart must not turn aside.
The responsibility rests on the ruler who refuses God's boundary.
And Scripture gives us another crucial piece of context when Solomon's story arrives.

First Kings 11 tells us that Solomon loved many foreign women and entered relationships with women from nations concerning whom Israel had been warned because of the danger of being drawn into the worship of their gods.
The central issue was not ethnicity as though God despised foreigners.
The Old Testament itself destroys that interpretation.
Ruth was a Moabite woman, yet through faithfulness to Israel's God she became part of the covenant community and even entered the genealogy leading to David—and ultimately to Jesus Christ.
Rahab was not born an Israelite either.
The biblical concern was covenant faithfulness and idolatry.
The danger was being drawn away from the living God.
And then Solomon's story becomes heartbreaking.
First Kings 11 records that Solomon eventually had seven hundred wives who were princesses and three hundred concubines.
One thousand women.
But the most terrifying number in the chapter is not one thousand.
The most terrifying thing is what happened to one heart.
His wives turned his heart away.
Exactly what God had warned about.
Long before Solomon's palace existed, God had effectively said:
Do not multiply wives...
lest your heart turn aside.
Then Solomon multiplied wives...
and his heart turned aside.
The warning became biography.
The command became tragedy.
And perhaps the most unsettling thing about Solomon's collapse is that wisdom did not make him immune.
You can know truth and still disobey truth.
You can explain Scripture and still resist Scripture.
You can recognize temptation in somebody else's life while quietly negotiating with it in your own.
You can have yesterday's testimony and today's compromise living under the same roof.
Knowing what God said is not the same as surrendering to what God said.
Solomon knew much.
But somewhere along the road, knowledge stopped governing desire.
And somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You know the verse.
You know the warning.
You know what the Holy Spirit has been pressing on your conscience.
You know that relationship is compromising you.
You know that secret habit is getting stronger.
You know that bitterness has lived inside you too long.
You know that what began as entertainment has become bondage.
You know that you keep telling yourself you can stop whenever you want.
You know.
And that is what makes this uncomfortable.
Sometimes our greatest spiritual danger is not ignorance.
Sometimes it is becoming comfortable disobeying something we already understand.
There are people who have not verbally rejected Jesus.
They simply keep adding competitors to Him.
Jesus...
plus my secret sin.
Jesus...
plus the approval I cannot live without.
Jesus...
plus the relationship I refuse to surrender.
Jesus...
plus money.
Jesus...
plus pornography.
Jesus...
plus status.
Jesus...
plus revenge.
Jesus...
plus the private version of me nobody at church knows exists.
Eventually the heart becomes divided.
And divided hearts do not usually announce their departure.
They drift.
Quietly.
Gradually.
Respectably.
Until one day the person looks back and realizes they have traveled miles from the place where they first compromised.
But Deuteronomy does not only tell the king what not to do.
It tells him what must keep him near God.

The king was instructed to possess a copy of God's law, keep it with him, and read it throughout his life so that he would learn to fear the LORD, carefully obey God's words, and prevent his heart from being lifted above his fellow Israelites.
Do you see the contrast?
The king could surround himself with possessions...
or surround his heart with God's Word.
He could multiply whatever fed his appetite...
or repeatedly return himself to the voice of God.
He could exalt himself...
or live underneath the authority of the LORD.
God's answer to royal arrogance was not more applause.
It was Scripture.
Read it.
Keep it near.
Remember who you are.
Remember who God is.
Remember that although people may call you king, you are still under the King.
And now the story reaches us.
Because the Bible's kings leave us longing for another King.
A King who would not be corrupted by power.
A King who could be offered the kingdoms of the world and refuse Satan's shortcut.
A King who would possess ultimate authority yet humble Himself.
A King who would not exploit people for pleasure but give Himself to rescue sinners.
A King who would not accumulate earthly treasure for Himself but become poor for our sake.
A King whose heart never turned away from His Father.
Jesus Christ.
Solomon possessed extraordinary wisdom and still failed.
Jesus is greater than Solomon.
Solomon built a temple.
Jesus spoke of the temple of His body and rose again.
Solomon sat on an earthly throne.
Jesus reigns as Lord.
Solomon's divided heart contributed to disaster in the kingdom.
Jesus came to rescue people with divided hearts and make rebels children of God.
This is where the story becomes more than a warning.
It becomes Gospel.
Because perhaps your heart has already wandered.
Perhaps this article did not catch you before the compromise.
Perhaps it found you afterward.
After the affair.
After the addiction.
After the lie.
After the divorce.
After the secret.
After the night you wish you could erase.
After the years you cannot recover.
After you ignored God's warning and discovered that sin always charges more than its advertisement promised.
Then hear this carefully.
The Gospel is not the announcement that your sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more terribly than we like to admit.
The Gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ came for sinners.
He lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is offered not because we can rewrite our past, but because Christ can redeem sinners who cannot repair themselves.
Repentance does not mean pretending the scandal never happened.
It means turning from sin toward the Savior.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Grace enters the darkness and brings the guilty person to Jesus.
Maybe you multiplied the wrong things.
Maybe your heart turned aside.
Maybe everyone sees the Christian version of you while God sees the exhausted person underneath it.
You do not need another performance.
You need Christ.
Bring Him the truth.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the lust.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the greed.
Bring Him the relationship.
Bring Him the secret messages.
Bring Him the hidden browser history.
Bring Him the resentment.
Bring Him the part of your life you desperately hope nobody discovers.
Repent.
Not because Jesus is waiting to humiliate you.
Because sin is already destroying what Christ came to redeem.
There is mercy for the repentant sinner.
There is forgiveness through Christ.
There is no scandal so powerful that it can somehow make the blood of Jesus insufficient for the person who truly comes to Him.
That does not make sin small.
It makes Christ glorious.
So ask yourself the question Deuteronomy quietly forces upon every generation:
What am I multiplying that is slowly turning my heart away from God?
Do not answer quickly.
Sit with it.
Maybe it is not obviously sinful.
Maybe it is something good that became ultimate.
Career.
Money.
Romance.
Recognition.
Ministry.
Followers.
Comfort.
Success.
Even good things become dangerous when they demand the place belonging to God.
Maybe the Holy Spirit has already put something in your mind.
Be honest.
Not as a magic phrase.
Not as a public performance.
Let it be the beginning of honesty.
Someone else reading the comments may desperately need to discover that they are not the only person struggling to remain faithful.
Sometimes three words are enough to stop pretending.
And if Christ has already been restoring areas of your life you thought were permanently ruined, tell somebody.
Your testimony might become another person's reason not to surrender to despair tonight.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. We are saved by God's grace through faith in Christ.
They know the warnings.
They love God with part of themselves.
But something else is slowly taking the throne.
They may never tell you.
There may come a night when the temptation you thought you defeated comes knocking again, and you need to remember:
Do not keep multiplying what is turning your heart away from God.
Not because God can be bought.
Not because financial support earns salvation or blessing.
But because when believers freely support Gospel-centered work they genuinely value, they help that work keep reaching people.

If you want to glorify God through your support, do it with the right heart: not purchasing favor from Him, but freely helping biblical content reach another exhausted believer, another wandering heart, another curious unbeliever, another person hiding behind a smile.
Not to prove your faith.
Not to manipulate God into blessing you.
Share because truth travels when somebody is willing to carry it.
There could be someone in your circle standing one compromise away from a disaster they cannot yet see.
Let the warning reach them before the consequences do.
Because that is ultimately what Deuteronomy's warning about kings and wives reveals.
God saw the danger before Solomon did.
God gave the warning before Solomon broke it.
And God was right.
The horses could not save him.
The gold could not satisfy him.
The women could not complete him.
The wisdom could not excuse him.
The throne could not protect his heart.
And none of the things you are tempted to put in God's place can save you either.
There is only one King who can carry the full weight of your worship.
Jesus.
So whatever has been multiplying...
whatever has been quietly competing...
whatever has been pulling...
whatever has been sitting on the throne of your heart pretending it belongs there...
bring it down.
Return to Christ.
Because the most dangerous thing Solomon multiplied was not ultimately horses, gold, or wives.
It was distance between his heart and God.
And perhaps the greatest mercy God can give you today is allowing you to recognize that distance before it becomes your story.
Come home while you can still hear His voice calling.
Come home with the scandal.
Come home with the shame.
Come home with the consequences.
Come home without excuses.
Come to Jesus.
Because your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
The heart that wandered does not need a better hiding place—it needs to come home to its King.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Warning Hidden in David’s Census: When the King Who Trusted God Began Counting What He Could Control
paragraphs: The Warning Hidden in David’s Census: When the King Who Trusted God Began Counting What He Could Control

David survived lions, giants, betrayal, caves, war, grief, and scandal. But near the end of his story, one of his most devastating failures began with something that looked almost harmless: he wanted a number. And hidden inside that census is a warning for every Christian who has ever been tempted to measure what only God can sustain.
There is a frightening kind of spiritual danger that does not look like rebellion.
It looks responsible.
It looks organized.
It looks strategic.
Sometimes it even looks wise.
Nobody sees you bowing before an idol. Nobody catches you abandoning the faith. You still pray. You still know the Scriptures. You still talk about God.
But somewhere beneath the surface, almost without noticing it, you begin asking a different question.
“How much do I have?”
How much money?
How much influence?
How many followers?
How many customers?
How many people are with me?
How much security have I built?
How strong am I if tomorrow becomes difficult?
And slowly, almost imperceptibly, the heart can move from trusting the God who provides the numbers to trusting the numbers God has provided.
David knew that temptation.
That is what makes his story terrifying.
This was not young David trembling before Goliath.
This was experienced David.
Battle-tested David.
Psalm-writing David.
King David.
A man who had watched God rescue him when human calculations said he should have died.
And then came the census.
Second Samuel 24 opens with one of the most difficult sentences in David's story. The Hebrew begins:
וַיֹּסֶף אַף־יְהוָה לַחֲרוֹת בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
Vayyosef af-YHWH lacharot b'Yisrael.
The sense is: “Again the anger of the LORD burned against Israel.”
Then the narrative says David was moved toward the disastrous command:
לֵךְ מְנֵה אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֶת־יְהוּדָה
Lekh meneh et-Yisrael ve'et-Yehudah.
“Go, number Israel and Judah.”
But Chronicles gives us another angle on the same event:
וַיַּעֲמֹד שָׂטָן עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵל וַיָּסֶת אֶת־דָּוִיד לִמְנוֹת אֶת־יִשְׂרָאֵל
Vayya'amod satan al-Yisrael, vayyaset et-David limnot et-Yisrael.
“Satan arose against Israel and incited David to number Israel.”

The Hebrew שָׂטָן — satan carries the idea of an adversary or accuser. Scripture therefore presents the event from two theological perspectives rather than requiring us to imagine God as morally tempting David to evil. Samuel begins with God's judicial anger against Israel; Chronicles identifies the adversarial agency involved in David's temptation. Scripture elsewhere explicitly says that God Himself does not tempt anyone with evil: “God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one” (James 1:13).
God remained sovereign.
The adversary acted.
David chose.
And David was accountable.

That distinction matters because the Bible refuses to let us solve the mystery of divine sovereignty by turning God into the author of sin, and it refuses to let us solve human responsibility by pretending David was merely a helpless puppet.
David made the decision.
And what is remarkable is that even Joab could see something was wrong.
Joab was hardly the moral hero of David's story. Yet when David ordered the census, Joab protested:
“Why should my lord require this? Why should it be a cause of guilt for Israel?”
Imagine that.
When Joab is warning you that your decision may be spiritually dangerous, perhaps you should listen.
But David's command prevailed.
So they counted.
Month after month, the machinery of the kingdom moved.
Names.
Tribes.
Soldiers.
Totals.
Statistics.
Strength.
And finally the numbers came back.
David got exactly what he requested.
Then something happened inside him.
Second Samuel 24:10 says:
וַיַּךְ לֵב־דָּוִד אֹתוֹ
Vayyakh lev-David oto.
Literally, David's heart “struck” him.
What an image.
No prophet had yet arrived to expose him.
No public scandal had erupted.
His own heart struck him.
Suddenly the number that had promised reassurance became evidence against him.
And David said:
חָטָאתִי מְאֹד בַּאֲשֶׁר עָשִׂיתִי
Chatati me'od ba'asher asiti.
“I have sinned greatly in what I have done.”
That is where this ancient story gets painfully close to us.
Because perhaps you have had that moment too.
You got what you thought you wanted...
and afterward your heart hurt.
You won the argument, but lost peace.
You got attention, but compromised something to obtain it.
You accumulated enough money to feel safe, then discovered that fear simply invented a larger number.
You built an image people admired while privately becoming someone you barely recognized.
You kept checking the views.
The likes.
The account balance.
The sales.
The applause.
The attendance.
The achievements.
The comparison.
The statistics.
And none of those things is automatically sinful.
That is precisely why David's census deserves careful handling.
The Bible does not teach that counting people is inherently evil.

God Himself commanded censuses in Israel. The book of Numbers contains them. Exodus 30 even gives instructions connected with census-taking, including the ransom payment associated with enrollment so that no plague would come upon the people.
So David's sin cannot responsibly be reduced to, “Counting is always wrong.”
Something deeper was happening.

Chronicles explicitly calls the census sinful, and Joab asks why David would bring guilt upon Israel. The text does not give us one neat sentence explaining every dimension of David's motive, so we should not pretend Scripture tells us more than it does. Various interpreters have connected the offense with improper census procedure, pride, military self-reliance, or David's desire to measure the strength available to him.
But the spiritual warning running through the episode is unmistakable:
A gift from God can become a rival to God when our confidence shifts from the Giver to the gift.
David had once stood before a giant with almost nothing measurable in his favor.
Goliath had the numbers.
Height.
Armor.
Experience.
Weaponry.
David had God.
And David understood then what older David was in danger of forgetting:
“The battle is the LORD's.”
Young David looked at an army and trusted God.
Older David looked at an army and wanted it counted.
That should make every mature believer uncomfortable.
Because yesterday's faithfulness does not make today's heart untouchable.
You can have testimonies and still be tempted.
You can know Scripture and still drift.
You can have been rescued dramatically by God and later begin quietly trusting what His rescue produced.
You can start a ministry desperate for Jesus and eventually become desperate for metrics.
You can pray for provision when you have nothing and then, once God provides, begin believing your savings are your savior.
You can beg God for influence and then become enslaved to maintaining it.
You can ask God for a family and eventually love the family more than the One who gave it.
You can ask for success and eventually need success to tell you who you are.
The danger is not merely having something countable.
The danger is needing what you can count to tell your soul that you are safe.
And then judgment came.
David was given terrible alternatives, and his response reveals that underneath his failure, he still knew God's character:
“Let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for his mercy is great.”
A plague struck Israel.
People died.
David's private decision became public devastation.
That is another warning we desperately need.
Sin loves telling us that our choices belong only to us.
They rarely do.
A father's hidden compromise can bleed into a home.
A leader's pride can wound people who trusted him.
A pastor's secret ambition can reshape a church.
A spouse's hidden sin can fracture a family.
Our culture says, “It's my life.”
Scripture repeatedly asks, “Who else will bleed from what you choose?”
David finally saw the cost.
And when he saw the destroying angel, he cried out that he had sinned and done wickedly.
Then the story moves somewhere extraordinary.
A threshing floor.
A sacrifice.
An altar.
David is instructed to build an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah, called Ornan in Chronicles.
Araunah offers David what he needs.
Take the property.
Take the oxen.
Take what is necessary.
But David refuses to turn repentance into cheap religion.
He says:
“I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing.”
David purchases the site.
An altar rises.
Sacrifice is offered.
Judgment is halted.
And suddenly the scandal of the census is standing on holy ground.

Because according to 1 Chronicles 22:1, David recognizes this location as the place associated with the future house of the LORD. Later, 2 Chronicles 3:1 identifies Solomon's temple site on Mount Moriah at the threshing floor of Ornan.
Do not rush past that.
The place associated with David's catastrophic failure becomes connected with the place of worship.
The place where judgment confronted sin becomes associated with sacrifice.
The ground stained by the consequences of human pride becomes ground on which generations would approach God.
That does not make the sin good.
God does not need evil in order to accomplish good.
It means evil does not get the final word when God redeems.
And now the road leads beyond David.
Beyond Araunah.
Beyond Solomon.
Beyond the temple.
To Jesus.
Because David could purchase a threshing floor.
He could build an altar.
He could offer sacrifices.
But David could not permanently solve humanity's deepest problem.
Neither can we.
Our deepest problem is not that we have occasionally trusted the wrong numbers.
Our deepest problem is sin.
Pride.
Self-rule.
Idolatry.
The ancient instinct to find life somewhere other than God.
We do not merely need better habits.
We need reconciliation.
We need forgiveness.
We need a Savior.
And the Gospel announces something far greater than David's altar.
Jesus Christ, the Son of God, came not merely to point toward a sacrifice.
He became the sacrifice.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21).
Christ bore sin.
Christ endured judgment.
Christ shed His blood.
Christ died.
And Christ rose.
The gospel is not God pretending your sin never mattered.
The Cross proves it mattered more than we can comprehend.
The gospel is that Jesus paid what sinners could never pay and offers forgiveness that sinners could never earn.
That means you can stop hiding.
Maybe your census is not an army.
Maybe it is your bank account.
Maybe it is your followers.
Maybe it is your reputation.
Maybe it is your career.
Maybe it is your children's accomplishments.
Maybe it is your ministry.
Maybe it is the number on a scale, the letters after your name, the title before it, the possessions in your house, or the applause underneath your post.
Perhaps you keep counting because counting gives you the illusion that tomorrow can be controlled.
But there will always be something you cannot count.
One diagnosis.
One phone call.
One betrayal.
One economic collapse.
One accident.
One funeral.
One unexpected door opening.
One unexpected door closing.
One ordinary Tuesday on which everything changes.
Eventually every human being discovers that control was never as complete as it felt.
So perhaps the question hidden inside David's census is not simply:
“What are you counting?”
Perhaps it is:
What are you trusting because you counted it?
That question hurts.
Let it.
Conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
For the person who belongs to Christ, conviction is often mercy knocking before destruction kicks the door down.
David's heart struck him.
Maybe yours is striking you now.
Do not silence it.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Tell Jesus the truth.
Not the polished Christian version.
The truth.
“Lord, I trusted money more than You.”
“I needed people's approval.”
“I made ministry about myself.”
“I wanted everyone to think I was strong.”
“I have been terrified of losing control.”
“I have been counting everything except Your faithfulness.”
“I have been pretending.”
This is repentance.
Not theatrical shame.
Not religious self-hatred.
Turning.
Returning.
Coming home to the God we abandoned while still using His name.
Someone reading your comment may discover they are not the only Christian still fighting battles nobody sees.
That matters.
Because testimony breaks isolation.
And maybe you know exactly who needs this article.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Someone you love.
There may come a night when the numbers stop comforting you.
Come back then.
Remember David.
Remember the altar.
Remember the Cross.
Remember that your security was never hiding inside a statistic.

And stay close to Gospel Warrior if you want daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, and discipleship centered on Jesus Christ. Invite your family, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow too.
Grace cannot be bought. Salvation cannot be purchased. God's approval is not for sale.
But ministry does require people willing to help carry the message.
Your support helps extend the reach of biblical teaching to people you may never personally meet.
But before you leave, remember what happened to David.
The man who defeated Goliath still had something to learn about where strength comes from.
The king counted his soldiers.
God counted the cost.
David sinned.
David confessed.
An altar rose from the wreckage.
And generations later, another Son of David would come.
Jesus.
The King who did not exploit His power to save Himself.
The Shepherd who gave His life for His sheep.
The Savior whose kingdom cannot be measured by the fragile arithmetic of human greatness.
So stop asking your numbers to promise what only Jesus can give you.
Your bank balance cannot say, “I will never leave you.”
Your followers cannot say, “Your sins are forgiven.”
Your career cannot resurrect you.
Your reputation cannot cleanse your conscience.
Your achievements cannot conquer death.
Only Christ can save.
And perhaps that is the warning hidden in David's census:
The moment you begin counting what God gave you to prove you no longer need to depend on the God who gave it, the blessing has begun becoming an idol.
But even there...
grace is calling.
Even after pride.
Even after failure.
Even after consequences.
Even after scandal.
There is an altar.
And beyond every altar in David's story stands the Cross of Jesus Christ, where guilty people discover that repentance is not the end of their story.
Grace is.
So comment if God exposed you.
Share if someone you love needs awakening.
And then put down the calculator in your soul.
You were never held together by the number anyway.
When everything you counted disappears, you will finally discover whether you were trusting the gifts in God's hand—or God Himself.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What If a Couple Cannot Have Children?
paragraphs: What If a Couple Cannot Have Children?

When the nursery stays empty, the pregnancy test stays negative, and heaven seems painfully quiet—does Scripture say your marriage is incomplete, your faith is defective, or your story has somehow failed? The answer may heal something you have been afraid to say out loud.
There is a particular kind of silence that exists in a house where someone desperately wanted to hear a baby cry.
It is difficult to explain to people who have never lived inside it.
The silence is not always dramatic.
Sometimes it sounds like a husband saying, “Maybe next month,” while trying to hide how disappointed he is.
Sometimes it sounds like a wife locking the bathroom door because she cannot bear for him to watch her stare at another negative pregnancy test.
Sometimes it sounds like relatives asking an innocent question that no longer feels innocent:
“So... when are you two having children?”
You smile.
You change the subject.
You laugh because crying would require an explanation.
Then another pregnancy announcement appears on Facebook.
Another baby shower invitation arrives.
Another friend posts an ultrasound.
And you are genuinely happy for them.
You really are.
But somewhere beneath that happiness is an ache you immediately feel guilty for having.
“Lord... why them?”
Then comes the question Christians sometimes become frightened even to whisper:
“Why not us?”
If you have ever asked that question, Scripture does not require you to pretend it doesn't hurt.
The Bible is astonishingly honest about childlessness.
Before Sarah became the laughing mother holding Isaac, Scripture introduced her with a sentence so painfully direct that it almost feels cruel:
“וַתְּהִי שָׂרַי עֲקָרָה אֵין לָהּ וָלָד”
Vattehi Sarai ‘aqarah; ein lah walad.

In Genesis 11:30, the Hebrew says, essentially, “Sarai was barren; she had no child.” The important word is עֲקָרָה (‘aqarah)—barren, unable to bear children. Scripture does not sanitize Sarah's condition. It names it.
And that matters.
Because sometimes Christians rush so quickly toward Sarah eventually having Isaac that we accidentally erase the decades when Sarah did not have Isaac.
We remember the miracle.
God remembers the waiting too.
Sarah knew childlessness.
Rebekah knew it before Isaac prayed for her.
Rachel knew it.
Hannah knew it.
Elizabeth knew it.
These were not women forgotten outside the biblical story.
Their tears became part of the biblical story.
But we must be careful here, because there is a dangerous mistake Christians can make with these accounts.
Sarah eventually conceived.
Rebekah eventually conceived.
Rachel eventually conceived.
Hannah eventually conceived.
Elizabeth eventually conceived.
Therefore, someone may tell the childless Christian couple:
“Just keep believing. Your baby is coming.”
But Scripture does not give us permission to make that promise to every couple.
God can perform miracles.
We should absolutely believe that.
We may pray boldly for conception. We may seek wise medical help. We may grieve honestly. We may ask God for healing. We may continue hoping when circumstances seem impossible.
But faith is not the ability to force God into the ending we selected.
Faith ultimately says:
“Jesus, I still trust You even when I cannot write the ending.”
That distinction matters enormously.
Otherwise we can turn beautiful biblical miracles into weapons against hurting people.
A woman begins wondering whether she simply has insufficient faith.
A husband secretly wonders whether God is punishing him.
A couple wonders whether some hidden sin has closed the womb.
Someone tells them, “Maybe you haven't prayed hard enough.”
Someone else tells them, “You need to claim your miracle.”
And slowly grief acquires another companion:
shame.
Please hear this carefully.
The Bible does not teach that infertility automatically means God is punishing a couple for personal sin.

We live in a creation that Scripture describes as groaning under the effects of the Fall. Bodies become sick. Bodies age. Bodies malfunction. People experience losses they did not choose. Romans 8 describes creation itself as groaning while believers await the redemption of our bodies.
Not every broken thing in your body is God's personal verdict against you.
And perhaps one of the most important biblical corrections comes from a passage Christians rarely mention when discussing childlessness.
Isaiah speaks to the eunuch—a person for whom biological descendants could be impossible—and records this devastating self-description:
“Behold, I am a dry tree.”
A tree without fruit.
No descendants.
No continuation of the family name.
No little face carrying your eyes.
No child calling you father.
No daughter calling you mother.
But God answers that despair with something extraordinary.
To the faithful eunuchs who hold fast to His covenant, God promises “a monument and a name better than sons and daughters” and “an everlasting name” that will not be cut off.
Do not rush past that.
God does not say biological children are meaningless.
Throughout Scripture, children are repeatedly presented as blessings.
But Isaiah destroys the idea that a human being without biological descendants is therefore spiritually worthless, forgotten, fruitless, or without legacy.
God looks at the person saying,
“I am a dry tree,”
and essentially answers,
“Your story is larger than what your body could produce.”
That changes everything.
Because maybe somewhere along the way you began believing that motherhood was the ultimate proof of a woman's fruitfulness.
It isn't.
Maybe you began believing fatherhood was the ultimate proof of a man's legacy.
It isn't.
Maybe you believed marriage without children was merely an unfinished version of marriage.
It isn't.
The center of Christianity is not fertility.
The center of Christianity is Jesus Christ.
And Jesus Himself never married and never fathered biological children.
Yet no human life has ever been more fruitful.
That alone should make us reconsider some of the careless things Christian culture can say about childlessness.
Your value before God is not measured by the number of chairs surrounding your dinner table.
Your salvation does not live inside your reproductive system.
Your identity is not “the infertile woman.”
Your identity is not “the man who couldn't give his wife children.”
If you belong to Christ, your deepest identity is found in Him.
And that does not make the longing disappear.
Christian hope is not emotional anesthesia.
You may still want a child desperately.
You may still cry when your period comes.
You may still feel something inside you collapse when someone announces another pregnancy.
You may need to excuse yourself from a baby shower because the grief is simply too fresh.
You may love children and simultaneously find being around them painful.
You may pray for your friend's pregnancy while crying afterward because you want what she has.
Those emotions need to be brought under Christ, yes.
Envy must not be allowed to become bitterness.
Bitterness must not become hatred.
But grief itself is not unbelief.
Jesus wept.
The Psalms are filled with “How long?”
Hannah poured out her soul before the Lord.
Biblical faith has room for tears.
What it does not have room for is making the gift greater than the Giver.
And infertility can expose that line in terrifying ways.
There comes a moment when the prayer can quietly change from:
“Lord, please give us a child,”
to:
“Lord, I cannot believe You are good unless You give us a child.”
Those sentences sound similar.
Spiritually, they are worlds apart.
One is petition.
The other can become an ultimatum.
This is where Jesus comes near—not to mock your longing, but to rescue your heart from being destroyed by it.
Because sometimes the thing we desperately want from God slowly becomes the thing we believe we need instead of God.
That is when even something beautiful can become an idol.
A baby is beautiful.
Motherhood is beautiful.
Fatherhood is beautiful.
Family is beautiful.
But none of them can bear the weight of being your savior.
Only Jesus can.
And perhaps this is where someone reading needs to stop pretending.
Maybe infertility has made you angry with God.
Tell Him.
Maybe you have been jealous.
Confess it.
Maybe you secretly resent your spouse because you believe the infertility is “their fault.”
Repent.
Your husband is not your enemy.
Your wife is not your enemy.
Do not allow a diagnosis to turn covenant partners into opposing sides.
When infertility enters a marriage, there is a temptation to reduce one another to medical results.
His numbers.
Her condition.
His problem.
Her problem.
But Christian marriage says something radically different.
This is our sorrow.
These are our tears.
This is our marriage.
And Christ is still our Lord.
Your spouse needs your arms more than your accusations.
Sometimes the most Christlike sentence spoken in an infertility journey may simply be:
“I married you—not your ability to give me children.”
Read that again.
“I married you.”
Not your fertility.
Not your uterus.
Not your sperm count.
Not the imaginary children we once pictured running through our house.
You.
And if God grants biological children, receive them with trembling gratitude.

If God leads toward adoption or fostering, pursue that calling prayerfully, wisely, ethically, and lovingly—not as though an adopted child were a consolation prize for infertility. Adoption is not second-class parenthood, and a child should never be expected to function as medicine for unresolved grief.
And if God does not give you children biologically or through adoption?
Your life is not over.
Your marriage is not pointless.
Your home is not useless.
Your legacy has not vanished.
The New Testament radically expands our understanding of family around Jesus Christ.
The household of God becomes filled with brothers and sisters joined not primarily by blood but by faith.
Paul could call Timothy his true child in the faith.
Spiritual fathers and mothers can leave fingerprints on generations they never biologically produced.
A couple without children can disciple teenagers.
Mentor young believers.
Feed families.
Support missionaries.
Open their home.
Strengthen marriages.
Care for the lonely.
Serve vulnerable children without attempting to possess them.
Teach Scripture.
Evangelize.
Pray.
Give.
Build.
Encourage.
Become the safe older couple a struggling young Christian desperately needed.
There are people you may meet in eternity whose lives were changed because you poured into them.
People who never carried your surname.
People who never shared your DNA.
People who nevertheless encountered Jesus because you refused to believe the lie:
“We have no children, therefore we have nothing to give.”
Isaiah 56 will not allow that lie to stand.
God promised the one who thought himself a “dry tree” something “better than sons and daughters.”
And ultimately, Christianity points us toward an inheritance even deeper than earthly lineage.
Jesus went to a cross.
There He bore sin.
There He endured shame.
There the perfectly righteous Son of God suffered for sinners.
And there He purchased a family no human biology could create.
You do not enter God's family because somebody conceived you.
You enter God's redeemed family through Christ.
You are saved by grace through faith in Him.
Your greatest need was never ultimately a child.
Your greatest need was reconciliation with God.
And Jesus came for that.
This is why infertility, devastating as it can be, does not get the final word over the Christian.
Cancer doesn't.
Miscarriage doesn't.
Childlessness doesn't.
Age doesn't.
Death itself doesn't.
Jesus does.
Perhaps you prayed for a nursery and instead discovered wounds inside yourself you never knew existed.
Perhaps your marriage nearly broke beneath the pressure.
Perhaps you became angry.
Perhaps you stopped praying.
Perhaps you avoided church because Mother's Day became unbearable.
Perhaps you grew tired of smiling when people asked questions they did not know were knives.
Perhaps you have carried shame for years.
Come back to Christ.
Not because He guarantees that you will eventually hold the child you imagined.
Come because Christ Himself is worthy.
Come because grace still has your name on it.
Come because the cross is still sufficient.
Come because repentance is still available.
Come because forgiveness is still offered.
Come because resurrection means no suffering surrendered to Christ is ultimately meaningless.
Maybe your miracle will be conception.
Maybe your story will include adoption.
Maybe it will include spiritual sons and daughters.
Maybe your earthly home will remain quieter than you once dreamed.
I cannot promise which road God will choose for you.
Scripture does not authorize me to.
But I can tell you something Scripture gives us far greater confidence to say:
Childlessness cannot make a Christian Christless.
And if you still have Christ, your story is not empty.
There is something else we need to say because someone reading this may desperately need permission to believe it:
You are allowed to seek help.
Prayer and medicine are not enemies.

Seeking appropriate medical evaluation does not automatically demonstrate weak faith. Both husband and wife may need evaluation, and neither should carry unnecessary blame or humiliation. Wise pastoral care, Christian counseling, and qualified medical guidance can help couples walk through complicated emotional, relational, ethical, and medical decisions.
There may be difficult questions ahead.
Treatments.
Money.
Waiting.
Ethical concerns.
Disappointment.
Perhaps doors opening.
Perhaps doors closing.
Do not walk those roads merely asking, “Can this give us a baby?”
Ask something even deeper:
“Can we do this faithfully before Jesus Christ?”
Because the Christian's highest goal is not getting everything we desperately want.
It is glorifying God.
And glorifying God sometimes looks like receiving a miracle with gratitude.
Sometimes it looks like continuing to pray.
Sometimes it looks like accepting a door God has closed.
Sometimes it looks like grieving without abandoning Him.
Sometimes it looks like two people sitting together in a silent house, holding each other's hands, whispering through tears:
“Jesus is still enough.”
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to pretend here.
Someone silently reading may need evidence that grief does not have to destroy faith.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in love, obedience, generosity, truth, and service—not through a transaction.
Let your feed become more than entertainment. Let it become somewhere truth keeps interrupting despair.
But before you leave, remember this.
The empty bedroom does not mean God has abandoned the house.
The unanswered prayer does not mean Jesus stopped listening.
The diagnosis does not become your identity.
And whether your arms someday hold the child you prayed for or your story takes a road you never imagined, the Gospel announces something infertility can never take away:
In Christ, you can have a name that will never be cut off.
Your body may have written a sentence you never wanted to read.
But Jesus still holds the pen over the meaning of your life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE NIGHT A KING KNOCKED ON THE WRONG DOOR
paragraphs: THE NIGHT A KING KNOCKED ON THE WRONG DOOR

Saul had once heard the voice of God. On the eve of his final battle, terrified and desperate for an answer, Israel’s first king disguised himself, entered the darkness, and sought a forbidden medium. His tragedy was not that God’s grace had been too small—but that a heart hardened by repeated disobedience kept reaching for guidance without surrendering to God.
There is something terrifying about watching a man walk into darkness when he once stood in the light.
Not because he never knew God.
Because he did.
Saul had known what it was to be chosen.

He had felt the prophet’s oil poured over his head. He had experienced the Spirit of God coming powerfully upon him. He had been lifted from obscurity and placed on Israel’s throne. He had heard Samuel speak the word of the LORD.
He had everything many people imagine would guarantee a strong spiritual life.
Calling.
Opportunity.
Anointing.
Authority.
Victory.
Yet on one of the final nights of his life, King Saul was not standing before the LORD in humble repentance.
He was walking through the darkness in disguise.
Looking for a medium.
The scene in 1 Samuel 28 is one of Scripture’s darkest and most unsettling portraits of spiritual collapse.
The Philistine armies had gathered for war. Saul looked across the battlefield and became terrified. Scripture says:

“When Saul saw the army of the Philistines, he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly.”
—1 Samuel 28:5
The Hebrew intensifies the picture.
וַיִּרָא שָׁאוּל אֶת־מַחֲנֵה פְלִשְׁתִּים וַיִּרָא וַיֶּחֱרַד לִבּוֹ מְאֹד
Vayyar Sha’ul et-machaneh P’lishtim, vayira, vayyecherad libbo me’od.
The language communicates more than mild nervousness. Saul sees the Philistine camp, becomes afraid, and his heart trembles greatly.
The king who once towered physically above the people is now collapsing inwardly.
And then comes the sentence that makes the darkness even heavier:

“And when Saul inquired of the LORD, the LORD did not answer him, either by dreams, or by Urim, or by prophets.”
—1 Samuel 28:6
God’s silence frightened Saul.
But to understand that silence correctly, we must remember the story that came before it.
Saul’s downfall did not begin at Endor.
It began much earlier.
It happened through compromises.
Impatience.
Self-will.
Partial obedience dressed up as obedience.
Excuses disguised as explanations.
Fear of people.
Resistance to correction.
When Samuel confronted Saul after his disobedience concerning Amalek, Saul initially defended himself. He insisted that he had obeyed.
Samuel answered with words that still cut through religious excuses:

“To obey is better than sacrifice.”
—1 Samuel 15:22
Then Saul eventually admitted something revealing:

“I have sinned: for I have transgressed the commandment of the LORD, and thy words: because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice.”
—1 Samuel 15:24
There was the fracture.
Saul feared people more than he feared God.
And eventually a person who continually chooses other voices over God’s voice can become desperate when those other voices cannot save him.
That is what makes Saul’s story painfully modern.
You do not need a crown to understand him.
You only need to know what it feels like to want God’s help while resisting God’s authority.
We can want direction without surrender.
Comfort without repentance.
Deliverance without obedience.
God to remove consequences without God touching the thing that created them.
We can pray, “Lord, tell me what to do,” while quietly hoping He will not say, “Give that up.”
We can want an answer more than we want God Himself.
And that is dangerous.

Saul had previously removed mediums and spiritists from the land, in keeping with Israel’s law against occult practices. Deuteronomy 18:10–12 explicitly condemns divination, sorcery, mediums, spiritists, and seeking the dead.
Yet when Saul became desperate enough, he commanded his servants:

“Seek me a woman that hath a familiar spirit, that I may go to her, and enquire of her.”
—1 Samuel 28:7
Think about that.
The king who had expelled mediums now wanted one.
Conviction had become inconvenience.
The boundary he once enforced became the boundary he crossed.
That is how compromise often works.
Yesterday, “I would never.”
Today, “Just this once.”
Tomorrow, “I had no choice.”
His servants told him there was a woman at Endor.
Saul removed his royal clothing and put on other garments.
Then he went to her at night.
The symbolism is almost unbearable.
A king stripping away the clothing that identified him.
A king hiding his face.
A king traveling under darkness.
A king searching for forbidden knowledge because he was terrified of tomorrow.
How many people are living some version of that scene?
Not necessarily visiting a medium.
But hiding.
Deleting history.
Maintaining secret accounts.
Returning to pornography after promising God they were finished.
Opening the bottle again.
Texting the person they know keeps pulling them away from Christ.
Consulting horoscopes, tarot cards, psychics, manifestation practices, spirit guides, or occult spirituality because they desperately want certainty.
Standing in church on Sunday while secretly feeding something in darkness Monday through Saturday.
Saul wore a disguise before the medium.
We have learned to wear ours everywhere.
“I’m okay.”
“I’m just tired.”
“It’s under control.”
“Nobody needs to know.”
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“God understands.”
But disguises may fool people.
They do not fool God.
At Endor, Saul asked the woman to bring up Samuel.

What follows has generated centuries of theological discussion, but the text itself presents the appearance as Samuel. The woman reacts with alarm, and the figure delivers a message entirely consistent with the judgment Samuel had previously announced against Saul.
Scripture gives us no permission to turn this event into an endorsement of necromancy.
Quite the opposite.
Saul’s action was rebellion.
Later Scripture interprets his death explicitly:

“So Saul died for his transgression which he committed against the LORD… and also for asking counsel of one that had a familiar spirit, to enquire of it.”
—1 Chronicles 10:13
Whatever questions readers debate about precisely how God sovereignly permitted the extraordinary event at Endor, the moral conclusion Scripture gives us is unmistakable.
Do not seek the dead.
Do not pursue mediums.
Do not seek supernatural guidance through practices God has forbidden.
The Christian response to spiritual darkness is not curiosity.
It is Christ.
Saul finally heard the message he had been desperate to obtain.
But it was not the message he wanted.
Samuel told him that the kingdom had been torn from him and given to David, and that Israel would fall before the Philistines. Saul and his sons would die.
Then the king fell.
Scripture says:

“Then Saul fell straightway all along on the earth, and was sore afraid.”
—1 Samuel 28:20
Imagine the room.
The disguise.
The darkness.
The frightened medium.
The fallen king.
The knowledge that morning was coming.
And somewhere beyond those walls, an army was waiting.
This is where Saul’s story stops being ancient history and begins looking through the window of our own souls.
Because some people reading this are terrified too.
Not of Philistines.
Of consequences.
Of exposure.
Of losing the marriage.
Of what the doctor might say.
Of the debt nobody knows about.
Of the addiction getting stronger.
Of the children discovering who you have secretly become.
Of judgment.
Of death.
Of eternity.
And fear makes people reach for strange doors.
But there is a door Saul’s story should make us run toward.
Not Endor.
Christ.
Because there is another King in Scripture.
And He could not be more different from Saul.
Saul began as a king and descended into humiliation.
Jesus willingly humbled Himself and was exalted.
Saul grasped desperately for control.
Jesus prayed in Gethsemane:

“Nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done.”
—Luke 22:42
Saul disobeyed and tried to preserve his kingdom.
Christ obeyed His Father even unto death.
Saul approached his final battle terrified about dying.
Jesus walked deliberately toward the cross knowing exactly what awaited Him.
Saul went into darkness searching for an answer from the dead.
Jesus entered death itself and rose victorious from the grave.
This is the Gospel.
Christianity is not the announcement that good people can improve themselves enough to deserve God.
It is the announcement that sinners who cannot rescue themselves can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Paul writes:
—Romans 5:8
The Greek words behind “Christ died for us” are breathtakingly simple:
Χριστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀπέθανεν
Christos hyper hēmōn apethanen.
Christ died for us.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we defeated every secret sin.
While we were sinners.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible.
The Gospel does not say, “Hide better.”
It says, “Come into the light.”
It does not say, “Pretend the sin was harmless.”
It says, “Confess it.”
It does not say, “Save yourself.”
It says there is a Savior.
And perhaps this is where Saul’s tragedy should become deeply personal.
Saul repeatedly said words of confession, yet his life reveals the terrible difference between being distressed by consequences and genuinely surrendering to God.
You can regret where sin has taken you while still refusing to release the sin.
You can cry because you were caught without grieving that you rebelled against God.
You can want relief without wanting holiness.
You can even use religious language while protecting the throne of self.
Real repentance is deeper.
The New Testament word μετάνοια—metanoia—carries the sense of repentance, a changed mind and turning.
Repentance is not purchasing forgiveness with enough tears.
Christ purchased redemption.
Repentance is turning from sin toward God in faith.
It is bringing the hidden thing into His light and saying:
Jesus, I cannot keep ruling my own life.
Have mercy on me.
Forgive me.
Change me.
I belong to You.
And hear this carefully: Saul’s story is a warning, but if you are alive and hearing Christ’s call today, do not turn that warning into an excuse for despair.
Do not say, “I have gone too far.”
Look at Peter.
He denied Jesus three times.
Yet Christ restored him.
Look at the thief crucified beside Jesus.
He had no lifetime left in which to repair his reputation, build a ministry, or prove himself.
He turned toward Jesus.
And Jesus gave him hope beyond the grave.
Look at Paul.
He persecuted Christians.
Grace found him.
The Gospel is filled with people whose stories should have ended in scandal.
Then Jesus entered the story.
Scandal became testimony.
Shame met mercy.
Rebellion met forgiveness.
Broken people became witnesses.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
Grace is not pretending sin did not matter.
The cross proves precisely how seriously God takes sin.
Grace means sin does not get the final word over everyone who belongs to Christ.
Jesus does.
Maybe your greatest spiritual danger tonight is not that you have never heard God’s truth.
Maybe you have heard it so many times that you have learned how to postpone obeying it.
“Tomorrow.”
“When life settles down.”
“When I’m older.”
“After one more time.”
“Eventually.”
Saul eventually ran out of tomorrows.
So will we.
The question is not whether you have a scandal in your story.
Every sinner does.
The question is what you will do with it.
Hide it?
Feed it?
Defend it?
Rename it?
Blame someone else for it?
Or carry it into the light of the crucified and risen Christ?
There is no medium who can reconcile you to God.
No horoscope can cleanse your conscience.
No tarot card can bear your sin.
No algorithm can tell you what your soul is worth.
No manifestation can conquer the grave.
No dead prophet can become your Savior.
Jesus Christ died and rose again.
And He is enough.
Respond to God.
Pray.
Confess.
Turn.
Seek trustworthy Christian help where you need accountability.
Open Scripture again.
Return to fellowship with believers.
And if you need words because your heart feels too heavy to explain itself, comment, “Jesus, forgive me.”
Not as a performance.
Not because typing a comment saves anyone.
Only Jesus saves.
