Even your desires must eventually bow before Christ.
And suddenly the battle becomes intensely personal.
Because pornography often promises something deeper than sexual stimulation.
Sometimes it promises escape.
You were rejected.
Click.
You feel lonely.
Click.
Your marriage feels distant.
Click.
You're stressed.
Click.
You feel unwanted.
Click.
You are angry.
Click.
You cannot sleep.
Click.
You hate yourself.
Click.
For a few minutes, the ache disappears beneath sensation.
Then the sensation disappears.
And the ache is still there.
Only now shame has joined it.
Pornography keeps promising intimacy while training you to avoid it.
It promises satisfaction while teaching the appetite to demand another image.
It offers bodies without covenant, exposure without knowing, stimulation without sacrificial love.
Then Jesus walks into that darkness and offers something radically different.
Not fantasy.
Himself.
This is why simply shouting “STOP WATCHING PORN” is not enough.
The human heart was made for more than behavior modification.
You need a greater affection.
A greater beauty.
A greater treasure.
A greater King.
You need Jesus.
And perhaps the most dangerous moment after sexual sin is not the sin itself.
Perhaps it is the moment shame tells you:
Don't pray now.
God doesn't want to hear from you.
You've apologized too many times.
Clean yourself up first.
That voice does not understand the Gospel.
You do not wash yourself before coming to the fountain.
You come because you need washing.
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9.
Confession does not mean casually saying, “Sorry, God,” while protecting every pathway back to the same sin.
Biblical repentance involves a turning.
Sometimes that turning becomes painfully practical.
Delete the secret account.
Remove the app.
Move the computer.
Stop taking the phone into the place where you repeatedly fall.
Use accountability tools.
Tell a mature believer who will actually ask you difficult questions.
Talk honestly with your spouse where appropriate and wise.
Seek faithful pastoral help.
If the behavior has become deeply compulsive, professional counseling from someone whose approach respects your Christian convictions may also be valuable.
Stop constructing an environment where you repeatedly ask God to deliver you from something for which you keep leaving the door unlocked.
Paul does not say, “Study sexual immorality until you can safely coexist with it.”
He says:
Φεύγετε.
Flee.
There is no shame in running from something that wants to enslave you.
Joseph ran.
Paul told Timothy to flee youthful passions.
Jesus taught radical seriousness toward sin.
Sometimes victory looks surprisingly unimpressive.
Sometimes holiness looks like leaving your phone outside the bedroom.
Sometimes worship looks like turning the screen off.
Sometimes spiritual warfare looks like sending one humiliating message to a trusted brother:
“I'm struggling tonight. Please call me.”
Sometimes repentance sounds like a grown man crying because he is finally tired of lying.
Sometimes freedom begins with four terrifying words:
I need some help.
And if you fall again?
Do not rename sin as freedom.
Do not excuse it.
Do not make peace with it.
But do not make an idol out of your failure either.
Get up.
Confess.
Run to Christ.
Bring the sin into the light.
Strengthen the boundaries.
Continue fighting.
Because your confidence is ultimately not that you have become impressive at resisting temptation.
Your confidence is Christ crucified and risen.
Peter failed Jesus terribly.
David's sexual sin produced devastating consequences.
The Corinthian church contained people with deeply sinful histories.
Yet after naming patterns of sexual immorality and other sins, Paul writes something breathtaking:
Were.
That word carries hope.
Your history can explain your wounds without becoming your identity.
Your worst night does not possess greater authority than the blood of Jesus.
Your browser history does not get the final word over a life surrendered to Christ.
Your shame does not get to rename someone Jesus has redeemed.
This is exactly where scandal meets grace.
Not grace that says sin does not matter.
Grace that says sin mattered enough for Christ to bleed—and His blood is powerful enough to cleanse the sinner who comes to Him.
At the cross, Jesus did not pretend darkness was light.
He entered our darkness.
He carried sin.
He endured judgment.
He died.
And He rose.
So Christianity is not the story of dirty people becoming skilled at pretending they are clean.
It is the story of dead people receiving life in Christ.
Guilty people receiving pardon.
Captives learning to walk free.
Ashamed people discovering that they can finally stop hiding.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe you are reading this immediately after falling again.
Then do something different this time.
Don't just delete the history.
Bring the history to Jesus.
Don't merely close the tab.
Open your heart.
Don't promise God another dramatic thirty-day streak.
Give Him tonight.
Give Him the next decision.
Give Him the password.
Give Him the secret account.
Give Him the loneliness beneath the lust.
Give Him the rejection beneath the fantasy.
Give Him the marriage pain.
Give Him the memories.
Give Him the shame.
Give Him the body He already purchased.
And tomorrow morning, give Him tomorrow too.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly. But you can refuse to keep pretending.
Not because saving a post changes a heart, but because temptation has a strange way of making us forget what conviction sounded like yesterday.
Come back when the night gets quiet.
Come back before the click.
Come back when your mind begins negotiating.
Then pray.
Send it privately to the brother who has been disappearing.
Send it to the husband fighting alone.
Send it to the young believer who thinks temptation means God has abandoned him.
Send it to the Christian who has mastered looking holy while slowly dying behind a locked screen.
Christ alone is Lord, and the Gospel must never be turned into a sales technique.

But if Gospel Warrior is genuinely helping you know Christ, understand Scripture, confront sin, and walk toward holiness, you can help this ministry place more Christ-centered truth in front of people who may never walk through a church door.
But remember what matters most.
Not the comment.
Not the share.
Not the merchandise.
Jesus.
If you do anything after reading this, let it begin there.
Repent.
Believe.
Come into the light.
Pray when temptation screams.
Pray when you are strong.
Pray when you are weak.
Pray when you have won.
Pray when you have fallen.
And keep bringing your eyes back to Christ until the secret thing that once seemed irresistible begins losing its throne before the One who is infinitely more beautiful.
Because pornography asks you to hide in darkness with a screen.
Jesus stepped into the darkness carrying a cross so you could finally walk into the light.
You do not have to spend the rest of your life deleting the evidence of the person Jesus is calling you to stop being.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE QUEEN WHO SAID “NO”… AND LOST HER CROWN: What Really Happened to Vashti When King Xerxes Removed His Own Wife?
paragraphs: THE QUEEN WHO SAID “NO”… AND LOST HER CROWN: What Really Happened to Vashti When King Xerxes Removed His Own Wife?

She refused one command. The king exploded in anger. An empire became involved. Her crown went to another woman. Then Vashti disappeared from the biblical story almost as suddenly as she entered it. But before we turn her into either a villain or a feminist hero, there is a disturbing truth in Esther that Christians cannot afford to miss: sometimes we become so fascinated by the person who lost the crown that we fail to see the invisible hand of God preparing the way for the woman who would risk hers.
There was wine everywhere.
Gold vessels. Marble pillars. Royal colors. Powerful men. An empire stretching across 127 provinces.
For 180 days King Ahasuerus displayed the wealth and glory of his kingdom. Then came another feast lasting seven days.
This was not an ordinary dinner.
This was power performing for power.
And on the seventh day, Scripture tells us something important about the king before it tells us what happened to his queen.
His heart was “merry with wine.”
Then he gave the command that would change two women’s lives and eventually become part of the chain of events through which an entire people would be delivered.
Bring Vashti.
Not privately.
Bring the queen before the gathered people and officials wearing her royal crown.
Why?
The Hebrew text of Esther 1:11 says:
לְהַרְאוֹת הָעַמִּים וְהַשָּׂרִים אֶת־יָפְיָהּ כִּי־טוֹבַת מַרְאֶה הִיא
Lehar'ot ha'amim vehassarim et-yofyah, ki-tovat mar'eh hi.
In context: he wanted “to display her beauty to the peoples and the officials; for she was a beautiful woman.”
That detail matters.
The biblical text does not say Vashti was summoned to preach, advise the king, participate in government, or receive an honor.
Her beauty was to be displayed.
Then comes one of the shortest sentences in Esther—and one of the most consequential.
וַתְּמָאֵן הַמַּלְכָּה וַשְׁתִּי לָבוֹא
Vatte'ma'en hammalkah Vashti lavo.
“But Queen Vashti refused to come.”
She refused.
And suddenly the party stopped being about wine, wealth and royal magnificence.
Now it was about wounded authority.
Scripture says the king became extremely angry and that his fury burned within him.
But here we need to be careful.
Christians sometimes repeat details about Vashti that Scripture itself never gives us.
The Bible does not tell us why she refused.
It does not explicitly say she refused because she was protecting her modesty.
It does not explicitly say she was staging a political rebellion.
It does not explicitly tell us that the king commanded her to appear naked.
Those explanations appear in later interpretations and traditions, but they should not be presented as though Esther itself says them.
The inspired text gives us the fact.
She refused to come.
And perhaps that silence should humble us.
Because human beings love filling biblical silence with whatever makes our preferred interpretation easier.
Some want Vashti to be the villain.
Others want Vashti to be the hero.
Scripture does neither for us.
It simply lets the moment happen.
The king calls.
Vashti refuses.
The king burns with anger.
And powerful men begin talking.
That is where the situation becomes even more revealing.
King Ahasuerus asks his advisers what should legally be done to Queen Vashti because she refused his command.
Memucan answers.
And his response escalates what happened between a husband and wife into an empire-wide crisis.
According to his argument, Vashti had not merely wronged the king. Her refusal could become known among women throughout Persia and Media, causing wives to despise their husbands.
One woman said no…
and frightened men began imagining an empire filled with women doing the same.
Then Memucan proposed the judgment.
Listen carefully to the Hebrew of Esther 1:19:
אֲשֶׁר לֹא־תָבוֹא וַשְׁתִּי לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ וּמַלְכוּתָהּ יִתֵּן הַמֶּלֶךְ לִרְעוּתָהּ הַטּוֹבָה מִמֶּנָּה
The decree was that Vashti would no longer come before King Ahasuerus, and that the king would give her royal position to another woman considered better than she.
The king approved it.
So was Vashti “disposed of” by her husband?
If by “disposed” we mean deposed, removed as queen and permanently excluded from the king’s presence, then yes.
If by “disposed” we mean killed, Scripture does not say that.
If we mean a divorce exactly equivalent to a modern civil divorce, the biblical text does not describe the event in those terms either.
What Scripture clearly tells us is devastating enough:
Vashti lost her queenship.
Her royal position would belong to someone else.
And then…
she disappears.
No farewell speech.
No description of her packing belongings.
No final conversation between husband and wife.
No account of her death.
No explanation of where she lived afterward.
The curtain simply closes.
And somewhere outside that curtain was a young Jewish woman who had absolutely no idea that a vacancy in the palace was about to collide with her life.
Her name was Esther.
That is where this story becomes bigger than Vashti.
Because the book is not ultimately about the humiliation of one queen or the elevation of another.
It is about providence.
Strangely, the Hebrew book of Esther never explicitly mentions the name of God.
Yet His providential fingerprints appear everywhere.
A queen refuses.
A king becomes furious.
Advisers speak.
A decree is issued.
A crown becomes vacant.
A Jewish orphan eventually enters the palace.
A genocidal conspiracy later emerges.
A sleepless king asks for royal records.
A forgotten act of loyalty is remembered.
Haman falls.
Mordecai rises.
Esther intercedes.
The threatened people survive.
Coincidence after coincidence after coincidence…
until coincidence begins looking suspiciously like providence.
And this is where Esther stops being ancient Persian history and starts walking into your life.
Because maybe you are living in the chapter where nothing makes sense yet.
Something ended.
Someone rejected you.
A relationship collapsed.
A door slammed.
A position disappeared.
Something you thought would remain forever suddenly became inaccessible.
And you have been asking:
“God… where are You?”
Esther whispers something uncomfortable and beautiful:
You may not recognize God's providence while you are standing inside the unfinished chapter.
Esther could not see chapter 8 while she was living chapter 2.
Mordecai could not see Haman's downfall while the gallows were being constructed.
The Jewish people could not see deliverance while the decree of destruction was circulating.
And you cannot always see what God is doing from the chapter you are currently surviving.
But we must be equally careful here.
The message of Esther is not that every painful event automatically means God is preparing you for earthly promotion.
Christianity is not “lose something today, receive something bigger tomorrow.”
Sometimes faithful people lose things and do not receive them back in this life.
Sometimes the miracle is not a palace.
Sometimes the miracle is Christ holding you together when the palace never comes.
Because Esther itself points us toward a greater reality.
Esther approached a throne knowing she could die.
She would eventually say:
“If I perish, I perish.”
She risked herself to plead for condemned people.
But centuries later, another Deliverer came.
Not a queen approaching an earthly king…
but the eternal Son of God entering our fallen world.
Not risking the possibility of death…
but deliberately walking toward it.
Jesus Christ did not merely enter a palace.
He went to a cross.
We were not innocent people needing better circumstances.
We were sinners needing reconciliation with God.
We had rebelled.
We had lied.
Lusted.
Hated.
Hidden.
Worshiped created things instead of the Creator.
Protected secret sins while maintaining public appearances.
Some of us learned how to look Christian while becoming spiritually numb inside.
And still Christ came.
This is where the scandal becomes grace.
Because the Gospel does not say, “Make yourself worthy enough and Jesus might receive you.”
The Gospel announces that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
He carried sin.
He endured judgment.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
The King we deserved to face as guilty rebels became the Savior who bore judgment for everyone who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
Vashti's story contains a terrifying picture of exclusion from a king's presence.
But the Gospel announces something infinitely greater about entrance into the presence of God.
Through Christ, sinners can be reconciled.
Forgiven.
Cleansed.
Adopted.
Restored.
Not because we possessed enough beauty to impress the King.
Not because we performed perfectly.
Not because we earned a crown.
Because Jesus wore thorns.
Think about that.
Human kingdoms obsess over crowns.
Jesus accepted thorns.
Human rulers display their glory.
Jesus laid aside privilege and took the form of a servant.
Human pride says, “Look at what belongs to me.”
Jesus stretched His arms across a cross and gave Himself for people who had nothing worthy to offer Him.
Maybe that is the part somebody reading this needed.
You have spent years trying to become impressive enough to deserve love.
Even with God.
You pray harder when you feel guilty.
You promise to change after falling into the same sin.
You hide when you fail.
You come back when you feel cleaner.
Then you fall again.
Hide again.
Promise again.
Cry again.
And somewhere along the way you began treating Jesus like an earthly king whose presence you could enter only when you looked acceptable.
But the cross destroys that illusion.
You do not clean yourself so Christ will save you.
You come to Christ because you cannot save yourself.
Repentance does not mean pretending your sin was small.
It means finally agreeing with God about how serious it is, turning from it, and throwing yourself upon the mercy found in Jesus Christ.
Grace is not permission to continue loving the chains Christ died to break.
Grace brings us home…
and begins changing us.
Maybe your scandal is known by everybody.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your family thinks you are strong.
Maybe people at church think you have everything together.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Adultery.
Jealousy.
Pride.
Alcohol.
Secret messages.
Unforgiveness.
A prayer life that quietly disappeared.
A Bible collecting dust.
A marriage barely breathing.
A faith surviving on memories of who you used to be.
Listen.
Jesus already knows.
There is no locked room in your soul into which Christ cannot see.
And yet the invitation of the Gospel remains:
Come.
Repent.
Believe.
Stop hiding.
The story of Esther reminds us that earthly crowns can disappear.
Positions change.
Beauty fades.
Power changes hands.
People who seem untouchable become footnotes.
But Jesus Christ is the King whose throne does not become vacant.
He does not need advisers to protect His ego.
He cannot be manipulated by wine.
He does not panic when His authority is challenged.
He is holy.
Righteous.
Merciful.
Sovereign.
And His kingdom has no expiration date.
So perhaps the deepest question is no longer:
“What happened to Vashti?”
Perhaps the question is:
What is happening to you while you are reading about her?
Are you merely collecting biblical information…
or is Scripture exposing something?
Is there something Christ has been confronting that you keep defending?
Something you need to confess?
Someone you need to forgive?
A hidden sin you need to bring into the light?
A relationship with God that has become performance instead of surrender?
Conviction can be mercy knocking.
And believers reading those comments—do not become spectators to somebody else's vulnerability.
Pray.
Encourage.
Point them toward Christ.
This is what the Church should look like.
Not perfect people protecting religious reputations.
Redeemed sinners helping wounded sinners find the Savior.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Salvation is God's gift through Christ, not a transaction with Gospel Warrior.
But if biblical truth has strengthened you, sharing it can place that truth in front of someone you may never realize needed it.

If you genuinely want to glorify God through what you have received here, one practical response is to help Gospel-centered truth travel farther. Share it. Speak about Christ. Support ministries that faithfully proclaim Him. Let your profile become more than a record of your life; let it occasionally become a doorway through which someone encounters Scripture.

There may come a night when you need to read it again—not because Vashti's crown matters to your salvation, but because you need to remember that an unfinished chapter is not proof that God has abandoned the story.
It is not a shortcut to blessing.
It is simply a practical way of standing behind the continued creation and distribution of Christ-centered resources, biblical encouragement and digital discipleship.
Someone in your circle may be smiling publicly while privately wondering whether God has forgotten them.
Someone may be one night away from giving up on prayer.
Someone may believe their scandal has written the final sentence of their life.
Someone may need the truth you almost scrolled past.
Because that may ultimately be what makes Vashti's disappearance so haunting.
She leaves the narrative…
but God's providential story keeps moving.
And eventually Esther enters.
Eventually Haman's plot is exposed.
Eventually mourning becomes celebration.
Eventually the gallows intended for Mordecai become Haman's end.
Eventually what looked like impending destruction becomes deliverance.
But even Esther's deliverance was temporary.
Those people eventually died.
Persia eventually fell.
Every earthly crown eventually passed away.
Humanity still needed a greater rescue.
And then came Jesus.
The greater Deliverer.
The sinless King.
The crucified Savior.
The risen Christ.
The One who does not merely rewrite circumstances but transforms sinners.
So bring Him the chapter you are ashamed of.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the betrayal.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the marriage.
Bring Him the grief.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the version of yourself you are exhausted from pretending to be.
Repent.
Believe.
Surrender.
Because your greatest hope is not that God will turn you into another Esther.
Your greatest hope is that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
And when Christ takes hold of a life, shame does not have to write the ending.
Failure does not have to write the ending.
Your worst night does not have to write the ending.
Your scandal does not get the final word.
The crown Vashti lost reminds us how quickly earthly glory can disappear; the thorns Jesus wore remind us how far eternal Love was willing to go to bring sinners home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS OVERTURNED TABLES—WOULD HE RECOGNIZE TODAY’S RELIGIOUS MARKETPLACE?
paragraphs: JESUS OVERTURNED TABLES—WOULD HE RECOGNIZE TODAY’S RELIGIOUS MARKETPLACE?
What if the table Jesus wants to overturn today is not in somebody else’s ministry—but somewhere inside our own hearts?
There is a version of Jesus that almost nobody finds threatening.
The gentle Jesus.
The Jesus holding children.
The Jesus touching lepers.
The Jesus forgiving sinners.
The Jesus carrying lambs in paintings.
And every one of those pictures points toward something beautifully true about Him.
But then there is this scene.
Coins are rolling across stone.
Animals are moving through the temple courts.
Merchants are scrambling.
Tables are crashing.
And standing in the middle of the disruption is not an angry atheist protesting religion.
It is Jesus Christ.

John tells us that when Passover approached, Jesus entered the temple and found cattle, sheep, doves, and money changers there. He made a whip from cords, drove the animals out, scattered the coins, and overturned the tables. Then He confronted those selling doves: “Take these things out of here! Stop making my Father’s house a marketplace!”
Read that slowly.
My Father’s house.
That changes everything.
Jesus was not throwing a tantrum because commerce existed.
He was defending what belonged to His Father.

And before we use this passage as a weapon against every pastor who ever sold a book, every church that ever charged for a conference, every Christian author who earned royalties, or every ministry that ever offered a product, we need enough humility to allow Scripture to say what Scripture actually says.
Because the Bible does not teach that receiving material support for genuine ministry is inherently sinful.

Jesus taught that “the worker deserves his wages” (Luke 10:7). Paul defended the legitimacy of material support for those who labor spiritually, even while sometimes surrendering that right for the Gospel’s sake (1 Corinthians 9:3–18). Paul also wrote that elders who labor in preaching and teaching are worthy of honor, again appealing to the principle that the worker deserves wages (1 Timothy 5:17–18).
So the scandal in the temple cannot honestly be reduced to:
Money = evil.
The question is much more uncomfortable.
What happens when something intended to serve worship begins competing with worship?
What happens when ministry becomes merchandise, people become metrics, generosity becomes leverage, desperation becomes opportunity, and Jesus becomes branding?
That question does not merely belong to “those ministries.”
It belongs to us.
It belongs to me.
It belongs to you.
Because it is incredibly easy to condemn someone else's table while quietly protecting our own.
John’s Greek makes the confrontation especially striking. Jesus says, μὴ ποιεῖτε τὸν οἶκον τοῦ πατρός μου οἶκον ἐμπορίου—mē poieite ton oikon tou patros mou oikon emporiou.
In straightforward English:
“Do not make My Father’s house a house of commerce.”
The important word is ἐμπορίου — emporiou, from emporion: commerce, trade, a marketplace.
John's account therefore confronts us with a terrifying possibility:
Something can begin around legitimate religious activity and still become spiritually disordered when commerce takes possession of sacred purpose.
But Mark takes us deeper.
Jesus overturns the tables there too, but then He teaches:
“My house will be called a house of prayer for all nations.”
And then comes the indictment:
“But you have made it a den of robbers.”
The Greek expression behind “den of robbers” is σπήλαιον λῃστῶν — spēlaion lēstōn.
A cave.
A den.
A hideout of robbers.
And Jesus did not invent those images on the spot.
He was pulling together Israel's Scriptures.
“My house will be called a house of prayer for all nations” reaches back to Isaiah 56:7. “Den of robbers” reaches back to Jeremiah 7:11. Mark itself identifies those scriptural connections.
And Jeremiah's context makes the warning even sharper.
The people had begun treating the temple almost like spiritual shelter from judgment while continuing in disobedience. Religious confidence had become a hiding place for unrepentant hearts.
That means Jesus was confronting something larger than overpriced livestock.
He was confronting corrupted worship.
Religious exploitation.
Spiritual hypocrisy.
A sacred place being used in ways that contradicted the character and purposes of God.
And now we arrive at the question nobody wants to ask.
If Jesus walked through today's Christian world...
would He recognize His Father's house?
Or would He recognize a marketplace?
Would He condemn every one of them?
Scripture gives us no basis for saying that.
Money itself is not the villain.
Selling a Christian book is not automatically corruption.
A ministry receiving support is not automatically greed.
A preacher being paid is not automatically compromise.
A Christian business is not automatically Babylon.
But perhaps Jesus would ask questions more devastating than our simplistic accusations.
Where is My Father in all of this?
Who is being glorified?
Who is being served?
Who is being exploited?
What happens to the poor person who cannot pay?
Do you still preach the same Gospel when there is nothing to sell afterward?
Would you still serve if nobody applauded?
Would you still preach if the algorithm buried you?
Would you still write if nobody knew your name?
Would you still give if there were no camera?
Would you still worship if there were no platform?
Would you still follow Me if following Me cost you the audience you spent years building?
That is where the tables begin shaking.
Because this passage is remarkably easy to preach at somebody else.
The prosperity preacher.
The celebrity pastor.
The televangelist.
The Christian influencer.
The megachurch.
The denomination.
The ministry organization.
Them.
Them.
Them.
Until Jesus turns around...
and looks at us.
Because you do not need a television ministry to commercialize God.
You can do it privately.
You can treat prayer like a transaction.
“God, I did this. Now You owe me that.”
You can treat obedience like an investment strategy.
“Lord, I gave. Where is my blessing?”
You can treat church like a spiritual supermarket.
“What am I getting out of this?”
You can treat Jesus like a product whose purpose is improving your life instead of the Lord before whom your life is surrendered.
You can even turn repentance into performance.
You can cry publicly and remain unchanged privately.
You can post Scripture you refuse to obey.
You can sing about surrender while protecting the one room of your heart where Christ is not allowed to enter.
And suddenly...
the temple story stops being about money changers.
It becomes about us.
There is something else John refuses to let us miss.
After the tables fall, the story moves toward a far greater temple.
Jesus says:
“Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”
His listeners think He means the building.
John tells us He was speaking about His body.
There is the Gospel hiding in plain sight.
Jesus did not merely come to clean up religion.
He came to give Himself.
The One overturning tables would soon allow wicked men to lay hands upon Him.
The hands scattering coins would be pierced.
The body standing in the temple courts would be broken.
The voice defending His Father's house would cry from a cross.
And the Temple they thought they had destroyed would rise on the third day.
This is why Christianity cannot ultimately be reduced to a religious marketplace.
At its center is not a product.
Not a personality.
Not a conference.
Not a building.
Not a brand.
At its center is a crucified and risen King.
Jesus Christ.
And He cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Forgiveness cannot be purchased.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
The blood of Christ is not merchandise.
Peter later confronted the idea that God's gift could be acquired with money (Acts 8:18–23). The Gospel destroys the illusion that eternal life is available to the highest bidder.
You come empty-handed.
Guilty.
Unable to save yourself.
And Christ offers what money could never buy.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new heart.
A new identity.
A new life.
Not because you paid enough.
Not because you donated enough.
Not because you became religious enough.
But because Jesus paid what you could never pay.
That distinction matters enormously.
Supporting Gospel work can be an act of worship.
Buying salvation never can be.
Giving can glorify God.
Manipulating people into giving dishonors Him.
Selling useful resources can legitimately support ministry.
Turning people's fear, grief, guilt, poverty, sickness, or desperation into spiritual leverage is another matter entirely.
And any ministry—including ours—should be willing to live underneath that examination.
If Gospel Warrior ever points you toward supporting this work, hear this clearly:
Your money cannot purchase God's favor.
Buying a book cannot erase one sin.
Sharing an article cannot earn heaven.
Only Jesus saves.
Only His blood cleanses.
Only His grace reconciles sinners to God.
Only the risen Christ gives eternal life.
That truth must remain sacred.
And strangely enough, once money is removed from the throne, generosity becomes beautiful again.
Then giving is no longer payment to God.
It becomes gratitude toward God.
Then sharing Christian truth is no longer merely helping an algorithm.
It can become mission.
Then supporting faithful Gospel work is not buying divine favor.
It can become partnership in helping truth travel farther.
Not to purchase blessing.
Not to impress God.
Not because we promise you prosperity.
But because generosity offered freely for Christ's glory can help Gospel work continue.
If you want to support the mission and go deeper with us:
Free.
Because some truths need to reach the person who has nothing.
And perhaps that is part of the test of every Christian ministry:
Can we still give when there is nothing coming back?
Can we still serve the person who cannot support us?
Can we preach Christ without turning Christ into bait?
Because the moment Jesus becomes merely the hook for the sale, something sacred has gone terribly wrong.
Jesus is not the hook.
Jesus is the treasure.
Maybe you have been wounded by religious commercialization.
Maybe somebody made you feel that God would answer if you gave enough.
Maybe you watched leaders live extravagantly while desperate people emptied their pockets.
Maybe hypocrisy made you suspicious of every church, every preacher, every Christian organization.
If that happened, do not confuse Jesus with the people who misrepresented Him.
Look again at the temple.
Jesus is not standing beside exploitation.
He is confronting it.
He is not protecting corrupted religion.
He is overturning it.
But there is another person reading this.
You are not angry at religious hypocrisy.
You are hiding behind religion.
You know the songs.
You know the vocabulary.
You post the verses.
You say “God is good.”
You know when to lift your hands.
Everybody thinks your faith is strong.
But somewhere underneath the Christian appearance is a table you desperately hope Jesus never touches.
Secret pornography.
Bitterness.
An affair nobody knows about.
Greed.
Pride.
Envy.
A private addiction.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
A business practice you would never want exposed.
A hunger to be admired.
A wound you turned into hatred.
A public ministry covering a private collapse.
And perhaps you have spent years decorating the table.
Jesus did not come to decorate it.
He came to overturn it.
That sounds terrifying until you remember who is overturning the table.
The same Jesus who touched lepers.
The same Jesus who welcomed repentant sinners.
The same Jesus who restored Peter after failure.
The same Jesus who carried a cross.
The same Jesus whose blood was poured out for sinners.
His holiness is not cruelty.
His confrontation is not hatred.
Sometimes grace sounds like:
“Get this out of My Father's house.”
Because Christ loves you too much to peacefully coexist with what is destroying you.
The Gospel is not Jesus walking into your mess and saying, “Everything here is fine.”
The Gospel is Jesus entering our ruined condition, bearing our judgment, conquering death, forgiving repentant sinners, and beginning the work of making us new.
Grace does not mean the tables never fall.
Sometimes grace is the reason they fall.
And maybe this article found you because there is something that needs to fall tonight.
Not somebody else's table.
Yours.
Mine.
Ours.
So be honest before God.
What have you turned into an idol?
What have you monetized that should have remained ministry?
What have you called ministry that was secretly ego?
What have you called blessing that was actually greed?
What have you called wisdom that was actually fear?
What have you called freedom that Scripture calls sin?
What have you been protecting from Jesus?
Do not run from Him.
Repentance is not the door out of grace.
It is the turning of a sinner toward the Savior who is gracious.
Bring the hidden thing into His light.
Confess it.
Turn from it.
Trust Christ.
Your testimony might become the sentence another exhausted believer needed tonight.
Not because sharing earns favor with God.
It does not.
Christ has already demonstrated God's love at the cross.
Come back when ministry starts becoming performance.
Come back when numbers begin whispering that they determine your worth.
Come back when success tempts you to soften truth.
Come back when you are tempted to judge everybody else's tables while ignoring your own.
Invite your family.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite seekers.
Invite lukewarm Christians.
Invite even the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is nothing more than another religious business.
Let them encounter the Christ who overturned the tables.
Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, publishing, building resources and placing Christ-centered truth before people who may never walk through the doors of a church.
But whether you ever spend a single cent here or not...
hear the most important invitation in this entire article.
Come to Jesus.
Not the merchandise.
Not the personality.
Not the platform.
Not the religious machine.
Jesus.
The One who overturned tables.
The One who exposed hypocrisy.
The One who defended His Father's house.
The One who was crucified for sinners.
The One who rose again.
The One who still receives those who repent and believe.
Maybe the most frightening question is not whether Jesus would recognize today's religious marketplace.
Maybe it is whether, beneath all our Christianity, Jesus would recognize Himself in us.
And maybe the greatest mercy of all is that when Christ overturns the table you thought you could never live without, He is not necessarily destroying your life.
He may be clearing the room for something only grace can rebuild.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY GOD WON’T COMPETE FOR YOUR ATTENTION
paragraphs: WHY GOD WON’T COMPETE FOR YOUR ATTENTION
The frightening thing may not be that you stopped believing in God. It may be that you still believe in Him while giving everything else the attention that belongs to Him.
There is a kind of distance from God that does not look like rebellion.
It looks like a normal day.
You wake up.
Before your feet touch the floor, your hand reaches for your phone.
Notifications.
Messages.
News.
A quick scroll that becomes twenty minutes.
Someone else's vacation. Someone else's marriage. Someone else's success. Someone else's body. Someone else's opinion. Someone else's crisis.
Your mind has barely awakened, and already a hundred voices have entered the room.
But the One who gave you another morning has not heard your voice.
You tell yourself you will pray later.
Later comes.
Work needs you.
Children need you.
Bills need paying.
Messages need answering.
Deadlines are waiting.
Something is always vibrating, ringing, refreshing, playing, demanding, reminding, advertising, entertaining.
Then night arrives.
You are exhausted.
You climb into bed and perhaps whisper a tired prayer because somewhere inside you, you still love Jesus.
And that is what makes this uncomfortable.
Because this article is not primarily about atheists.
It is about people who love God...
but have slowly trained their attention to live somewhere else.
People who would never bow before a carved idol, yet surrender hours to things they cannot stop checking.
People who would never say, "Jesus doesn't matter to me," yet repeatedly give Him whatever fragments remain after everything else has eaten.
And perhaps the most unsettling question is not:
Do you believe in Jesus?
Perhaps it is:
What receives the first, deepest, and most dependable attention of your heart?
Because whatever continually captures your attention eventually begins discipling your desires.
And whatever disciples your desires will begin shaping your life.
This is why the title of this article needs one important clarification.
When we say God won't compete for your attention, we do not mean God is incapable of defeating His competitors.
God has no equal.
He is not anxiously standing beside your phone hoping you choose Him.
He is not threatened by entertainment, success, relationships, money, ambition, algorithms, celebrities, careers, or possessions.
Scripture does not present Yahweh as one needy deity among competing gods.
It presents Him as Lord.
The issue is not God's insecurity.
The issue is God's rightful exclusivity.
After Israel's catastrophic betrayal with the golden calf, God renewed His covenant with His people. And in Exodus 34:14 we encounter startling Hebrew language:
כִּי לֹא תִשְׁתַּחֲוֶה לְאֵל אַחֵר ... יְהוָה קַנָּא שְׁמוֹ אֵל קַנָּא הוּא
The central word is קַנָּא — qannāʾ, commonly translated "jealous."
God declares that His people must not worship another god because Yahweh is qannāʾ.
Jealous.
But do not import the ugliest form of human jealousy into that word.
Human jealousy can say, "I want what belongs to you."
God's covenant jealousy says, in effect, "I will not treat your idolatry as harmless because you were made to belong to Me."
The Hebrew term in these passages is used of God's demand for exclusive covenant loyalty.
This is holy jealousy.
Covenant jealousy.
The fierce love of the God who refuses to call spiritual adultery harmless.
And notice when Exodus 34 happens.
After the golden calf.
Israel had witnessed wonders.
They had watched Egypt tremble under God's judgments.
They had walked through the sea.
They had eaten God's provision.
They had seen His power.
And still...
they made something they could see, then gave it the devotion that belonged to the God who had saved them.
That should frighten every religious person reading this.
Because apparently it is possible to experience God's goodness and still manufacture substitutes for God.
Our calves are simply better designed now.
Some fit inside our pockets.
Some are called careers.
Some are called relationships.
Some are called followers.
Some are called success.
Some are called comfort.
Some are even called ministry.
An idol does not have to be something evil.
It can be something good that has quietly received what belongs ultimately to God.
Your child can become an idol.
Your spouse can become an idol.
Your dream can become an idol.
Your ministry can become an idol.
Your reputation can become an idol.
Your political obsession can become an idol.
Your need to be admired can become an idol.
Your pain can even become the center around which your entire identity begins revolving.
And yes...
your phone can become an altar without ever looking like one.
Not because smartphones are inherently sinful.
They aren't.
Neither are careers, hobbies, entertainment, possessions, or social media inherently sinful.
The deeper question is whether something has begun commanding your heart.
What can you not imagine losing?
What determines whether you feel valuable?
Where does your mind instinctively run when silence arrives?
What gets your first attention?
What receives your best energy?
What makes you feel alive?
What are you willing to disobey God to keep?
There.
That last question hurts.
Because idolatry is eventually exposed not merely by what we enjoy...
but by what we refuse to surrender.
Jesus once entered a home where two sisters responded very differently to His presence.
Martha was serving.
That matters.
She was not committing some obvious scandal.
She was doing something useful.
Something hospitable.
Something respectable.
Yet Luke tells us she was distracted by her serving.
Jesus answered her tenderly:
"Martha, Martha..."
Then He exposed the condition underneath the activity.
She was anxious and troubled about many things, while Mary had chosen the good portion.
Don't miss this.
Martha's problem was not that she was serving Jesus.
Her problem was that serving Jesus had somehow distracted her from Jesus.
Read that again.
Because some Christians are doing exactly this.
You can sing about Jesus while your heart is elsewhere.
You can post Scripture while your private life starves.
You can defend Christianity online while barely speaking to Christ.
You can serve at church while secretly becoming spiritually hollow.
You can build a ministry around Jesus while gradually losing intimacy with Jesus.
You can spend your life discussing Him...
and stop sitting at His feet.
That is one of the most terrifying possibilities in Christianity.
Being busy around Jesus while becoming distant from Jesus.
And the world is extraordinarily good at keeping you busy.
Not necessarily wicked.
Just busy.
Distracted.
Fragmented.
Overstimulated.
Always consuming.
Always reacting.
Always moving.
Never still long enough to notice what is happening inside your soul.
Maybe that is you.
Maybe you haven't abandoned God.
You are simply distracted.
And distraction feels innocent because there was never a dramatic moment when you decided to walk away.
There was no declaration.
No slammed Bible.
No conscious renunciation of Christ.
Just...
tomorrow.
"I'll pray tomorrow."
"I'll read Scripture tomorrow."
"I'll deal with that sin tomorrow."
"I'll forgive them tomorrow."
"I'll repent tomorrow."
"I'll return to church tomorrow."
"I'll get serious about Jesus tomorrow."
And tomorrow became months.
Maybe years.
Until one day you realized you could remember when your heart used to burn for God.
You remember worship that once broke you.
You remember opening Scripture hungry.
You remember conviction arriving quickly.
You remember wanting holiness more than applause.
You remember when prayer was not merely something you did when your life fell apart.
But now...
you scroll.
You consume.
You laugh.
You work.
You perform.
You survive.
And somewhere underneath all the noise is a frightening ache:
What happened to me?
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not answer that question by telling you to become impressive enough for God to take you back.
Christianity is not the story of distracted sinners finally becoming disciplined enough to climb their way to God.
It is the story of God coming for sinners.
Jesus Christ entered our world.
The eternal Son took on flesh.
He lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He resisted temptation.
He loved the Father perfectly.
He obeyed where we rebelled.
Then He went to a cross.
And there the scandal becomes grace.
Because the cross reveals something devastating about sin:
Sin is worse than we wanted to admit.
And the cross simultaneously reveals something breathtaking about God's mercy:
His grace is greater than we dared hope.
Jesus endured the cross and its shame. Hebrews 12:2 places before us this extraordinary Greek expression:
ἀφορῶντες εἰς ... Ἰησοῦν
aphorōntes eis ... Iēsoun
Looking to Jesus.

The verb carries the sense of directing one's gaze toward Him. Hebrews calls Christ the pioneer and perfecter of faith and points to His endurance of the cross before His exaltation at God's right hand.
Do you see the beauty?
The answer to a distracted soul is ultimately not merely:
Look at your screen less.
It is:
Look to Jesus.
Because Christianity cannot be reduced to digital minimalism.
You could throw your phone into the ocean and still worship yourself.
You could delete every social-media account and still idolize money.
You could live alone in the mountains and still be consumed by pride.
The deepest problem is not the device in your hand.
It is the throne in your heart.
And only one King belongs there.
Jesus.
This is where repentance becomes beautiful.
Repentance is not God screaming, "Do better!"
Repentance is the gracious summons to turn.
Come home.
Bring Him the divided heart.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the secret compromise.
Bring Him the prayerlessness.
Bring Him the nights you wasted.
Bring Him the hidden browser history.
Bring Him the ambition you worshiped.
Bring Him the relationship you made ultimate.
Bring Him the image you have spent years protecting.
Bring Him the part of yourself you are terrified anyone will discover.
Bring Him your scandal.
Because Jesus has always been in the business of rewriting stories people thought were finished.
Peter denied Him.
Christ restored Peter.
Thomas doubted.
Christ met Thomas.
A thief was dying beside Him with nothing left to offer.
Christ gave him hope.
Paul had persecuted the church.
Christ turned the persecutor into a preacher of the Gospel.
Again and again Scripture tells the same impossible story:
Sin does not get the final sentence when Jesus enters the story.
Failure does not get the final sentence.
Shame does not get the final sentence.
Your past does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible.
Grace is not permission to continue worshiping your idols.
Grace breaks their claim over you and calls you back to the living God.
So perhaps the question tonight is not whether God can get your attention.
Perhaps He already has.
Perhaps that strange discomfort you feel while reading this is the moment when the noise has finally become quiet enough for you to recognize what your soul has been missing.
Jesus.
Not merely Christian content.
Jesus.
Not religious motivation.
Jesus.
Not another inspirational quotation.
Jesus.
Not an emotional experience that disappears tomorrow morning.
Jesus Christ crucified, risen, reigning, forgiving sinners, receiving the repentant, transforming lives.
Maybe you need to put the phone down after this.
Maybe you need to open your Bible.
Maybe you need to kneel beside your bed.
Maybe you need to confess something you have spent months defending.
Maybe there is an app you need to delete because you know exactly what it keeps doing to you.
Maybe there is a relationship you have elevated above obedience to Christ.
Maybe success has become your functional savior.
Maybe people's approval has become your oxygen.
Maybe you have been feeding everyone else's perception of you while starving your soul.
Whatever it is, do not turn this into vague guilt.
Take it to Christ.
Name it.
Confess it.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
And look again to Jesus.
You do not need to earn His cross.
You cannot.
You need the mercy purchased there.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, don't pretend it didn't.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that we need prayer is the first crack in the wall we have spent years building around ourselves.
Not to embarrass them.
Send this to the friend whose faith has become tired.
There is also something important I want to say about supporting this work.
Supporting Gospel ministry is a worthy act when it flows from love for Christ, generosity, and a desire to help biblical truth reach people.
It doesn't.
You do not glorify God by being pressured into paying for something.
You glorify God by belonging to Christ and faithfully obeying Him.
Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, encouraging, and putting Gospel-centered material in front of people who may desperately need it.
The goal is not to create consumers.
It is to help cultivate disciples.
People who know Scripture.
People who pray.
People who repent.
People who forgive.
People who endure.
People who refuse to make peace with hidden sin.
People whose eyes keep returning to Christ.
And comment.
Be honest.
What has been competing for your attention lately?
You don't have to tell your entire story.
Maybe your answer is "work."
"Money."
"My phone."
"A relationship."
"Pornography."
"Approval."
"Success."
"Fear."
"Myself."
Or simply:
"Jesus, take back my attention."
There may be another believer reading the comments who thought they were the only one fighting the same battle.
Your honesty may become somebody else's courage.
Because somewhere tonight, another person is staring into the glow of a screen while carrying a soul that is starving for eternity.
Maybe they will see what you shared.
Maybe they will remember Jesus.
Maybe they will come home.
And perhaps that is worth one share.
Because eventually every notification will disappear.
Every trend will die.
Every possession will belong to somebody else.
Every applause will become silent.
Every follower count will become meaningless.
Every screen will go dark.
And the question will never have been whether God was worthy of your attention.
He always was.
The question is what you did with the brief life in which He gave you the opportunity to know Him.
So come back.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Look away from the thousand things begging to become your master...
and look again to Jesus.
Because the tragedy is not merely that the world stole your attention—it is that Christ was worthy of your whole heart while you were giving Him the leftovers.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE GOD WHO REFUSED TO STAY DISTANT
paragraphs: THE GOD WHO REFUSED TO STAY DISTANT
Why four words in John’s Gospel destroy our picture of a distant God—and reveal the staggering truth that Jesus Christ entered our wounded world to bring sinners from scandal to grace.
There are moments when God feels impossibly far away.
You pray, but the ceiling seems silent.
You open your Bible, but your mind keeps wandering back to the thing you regret.
You sit in church surrounded by people singing about victory while quietly wondering whether anyone would still look at you the same way if they knew everything.
The addiction you promised God you would stop.
The marriage nobody knows is barely surviving.
The resentment you disguise as discernment.
The private messages.
The secret browser history.
The loneliness.
The shame.
The prayer you have almost stopped praying because disappointment hurts less when you expect nothing.
And somewhere inside all of that, a terrifying question begins forming:
Does God really understand what it is like to be human?
John answers that question with one of the most breathtaking sentences ever written.
Not with philosophy alone.
Not with sentimental religion.
Not with advice about becoming a better person.
He gives us Jesus.
The Greek text of John 1:14 begins:
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο.
“And the Word became flesh.”
Those words are so familiar that Christians can read them without feeling their weight anymore.
But John did not write something safe.
He wrote something staggering.
The λόγος — Logos — the Word whom John has already identified at the beginning of his Gospel as existing “in the beginning,” as being “with God,” and as being God, became flesh.
Not merely appeared human.
Not merely visited humanity wearing a convincing disguise.
Not merely sent another prophet to tell suffering people how to find Him.
The Word became flesh.

The Greek word John chooses is σάρξ — sarx — “flesh.” And the verb ἐγένετο — egeneto — means “became.” The language presents a real historical incarnation: the eternal Word truly entered human existence. Christian confession therefore does not mean that the Son stopped being divine and changed into something non-divine. It means that the One who eternally was the Word truly assumed humanity. John presents Jesus as genuinely divine and genuinely human.
Think about what John could have written.
He could have chosen language that kept everything polished and distant.
Instead:
σὰρξ.
Flesh.
Human vulnerability.
A body capable of hunger.
Skin capable of bleeding.
Eyes capable of tears.
A body capable of exhaustion.
Hands that could be pierced.
A heart that could experience anguish.
The Creator entered His creation.
The One through whom John says everything came into existence stepped into the world that existed through Him.
The eternal entered history.
The invisible God made Himself known in the Son.
And suddenly Christianity becomes something far more astonishing than humanity climbing upward toward God.
It is the story of God coming down to us.
Maybe that is exactly what someone reading this needs to understand tonight.
You have spent years trying to climb.
Trying to become worthy enough.
Clean enough.
Religious enough.
Disciplined enough.
Successful enough.
Trying to repair yourself before approaching God.
You have thought, Once I defeat this sin, then I can really come back.
Once I fix my marriage.
Once I stop drinking.
Once I become disciplined.
Once I stop looking at those things.
Once I stop being angry.
Once I become the Christian everyone thinks I already am.
Then God will want me.
But the Gospel begins by destroying the ladder.
God came down.
That does not make repentance unnecessary.
It makes repentance possible.
Grace is not God pretending sin does not matter. The incarnation ultimately moves toward the cross precisely because sin matters terribly.
The Child of Bethlehem came to become the crucified Savior.
John will eventually bring us from:
“The Word became flesh”
to:
“It is finished.”
And those sentences belong together.
The flesh He assumed could be wounded.
The hands that touched lepers could be nailed.
The feet that walked toward sinners could be pierced.
The head that knew every human thought could wear thorns.
The body through which divine compassion embraced the unwanted could hang upon a Roman cross.
Christianity does not proclaim a God watching human suffering through the safety of heaven.
It proclaims Jesus Christ.

And Hebrews makes the implications breathtaking: because Christ truly shared our humanity and was tempted yet without sin, believers do not approach a High Priest incapable of sympathizing with human weakness. We are invited to draw near to the throne of grace for mercy and help.
That changes prayer.
You are not explaining human pain to someone unfamiliar with humanity.
Jesus knew hunger.
Jesus knew weariness.
Jesus knew rejection.
Jesus knew grief.
Jesus wept.
Jesus was betrayed.
Jesus was falsely accused.
Jesus experienced physical agony.
Jesus knew what it was to have people abandon Him.
Yet Scripture is equally clear about something our culture desperately needs to hear:
Jesus entered our broken world without participating in our sin.
Compassion is not compromise.
Grace is not approval.
Love does not require God to rename darkness as light.
Christ comes near enough to touch sinners while remaining holy enough to save them.
And this is where John 1:14 becomes even more beautiful.
John continues:
καὶ ἐσκήνωσεν ἐν ἡμῖν
Usually translated:
“and dwelt among us.”

But ἐσκήνωσεν — eskēnōsen carries the sense of dwelling or pitching one's tent. This is why commentators often render the thought as “tabernacled among us.” The wording naturally recalls the biblical tabernacle—the dwelling associated with God's presence among His people.
That matters.
Long before Bethlehem, Israel knew the imagery of God's presence dwelling among His people.
The tabernacle declared something extraordinary:
God desires to dwell among His people.
Then John looks at Jesus and effectively tells us:
Look again.
God's presence has come among us in a way the tent in the wilderness anticipated but could never accomplish.
The Word tabernacled among us.
And then John says:
“we beheld His glory.”
Do you see the movement?
Word.
Flesh.
Dwelling.
Glory.
And then:
grace and truth.
Not grace without truth.
Not truth without grace.
Grace and truth.
That combination confronts both kinds of people hiding from God.
Some hide because they think their sin is too terrible for grace.
Others hide because they refuse to admit that their sin actually is sin.
Jesus confronts both illusions.
Truth says:
Yes. It really is sin.
Grace says:
Come.
Truth says:
You cannot save yourself.
Grace says:
Christ can save completely.
Truth tears the mask from our faces.
Grace refuses to throw the exposed sinner away.
Truth brings us to confession.
Grace meets the repentant sinner there.
This is why Jesus is dangerous to hypocrisy and irresistible to the brokenhearted.
You cannot stand before Christ indefinitely pretending.
Eventually the mask becomes too heavy.
And perhaps yours is heavy now.
Maybe everyone calls you strong.
But you are exhausted.
Maybe people come to you for prayer while your own prayer life has almost disappeared.
Maybe you know Christian vocabulary so well that nobody realizes how far your heart has wandered.
Maybe you still post Scripture.
Still say “Amen.”
Still attend church.
Still encourage everybody else.
But something between you and Jesus has become cold.
And you know it.
Here is the scandalous beauty of John 1:14:
He came near anyway.
Not because sin was insignificant.
Because love was determined to rescue sinners from it.
Jesus did not enter the world merely to make bad people slightly nicer.
He came to save.
He came for people whose histories could embarrass them.
People with sexual sin.
Religious pride.
Greed.
Bitterness.
Fear.
Self-righteousness.
Broken families.
Failed promises.
Hidden wounds.
People who had made themselves scandals.
People other people had turned into scandals.
And ultimately, people who discovered that underneath all the carefully managed appearances was the same desperate human condition:
We need a Savior.
That is why the incarnation cannot be reduced to a Christmas decoration.
Bethlehem is an invasion.
The kingdom of darkness is being confronted.
The rescue has begun.
God's promise is taking on flesh.
And the road from the manger leads eventually toward Golgotha.
Paul captures the descent in Philippians 2: Christ, existing in the form of God, humbled Himself, taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient to the point of death—even death on a cross.
The One above us came among us.
The Holy One came for sinners.
The King became the Servant.
The Author entered His own story.
And humanity did what fallen humanity does.
We crucified Him.
But even that became the stage upon which grace displayed its unimaginable depth.
Because the cross was not Jesus losing control of the story.
The cross was central to the saving mission for which He came.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, Jesus Christ rose.
The grave could not write His ending.
Your sin does not have to write yours either.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
It does not mean repentance magically restores every relationship.
It does not mean Christians never suffer again.
Biblical grace is far deeper than motivational optimism.
It means the repentant sinner can be forgiven.
The condemned can be justified through faith in Christ.
The estranged can be reconciled to God.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
The ashamed can stop hiding.
The enslaved can begin walking in freedom.
The sinner can become a child of God—not because the sinner rewrote the record, but because Jesus Christ became flesh, went to the cross, and rose again.
This is where the Gospel becomes personal.
Not:
Jesus came for humanity.
But:
Jesus came for sinners like me.
Not:
The world needed redemption.
But:
I need redemption.
Not:
People should repent.
But:
Lord, I repent.
Maybe you have spent your entire life around Christianity without surrendering yourself to Christ.
You know the songs.
You know the verses.
You know when to say amen.
But knowing Christian things is not the same as knowing Christ.
John's Gospel will later tell us why it was written: so that people may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing they may have life in His name.
Life.
Not religious performance.
Not reputation management.
Not pretending.
Life.
And perhaps this is the moment you finally stop negotiating with Jesus.
You do not need another year of hiding.
You do not need another carefully constructed version of yourself.
Bring Him the real person.
The guilty person.
The wounded person.
The angry person.
The addicted person.
The disappointed person.
The religious person who secretly knows religion has become a substitute for intimacy with Christ.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Trust Christ.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace opens the prison door and calls you to follow Jesus out.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not manufacture a polished response. Be honest.
Or simply write:

Not because typing words saves anyone. Christ saves. But sometimes a public sentence becomes the moment somebody stops protecting the mask and begins admitting what God has already been showing the heart.
Someone reading the same comments may realize they are not the only believer fighting through a dark season.
That matters.
The Gospel was never meant to terminate with us.
If Christ has given you truth, carry truth.
If grace found you, point someone else toward grace.
So think of one person.
Not your entire friends list.
One.
The brother who has stopped attending church.
The daughter quietly questioning whether God cares.
The friend drowning behind jokes.
The believer who failed and assumes Christians will never let him forget it.
The person who does not believe in Jesus but might finally read something because you shared it.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedience and love—not through financial transactions.
But supporting faithful Gospel work can be one practical way believers participate in helping biblical truth reach more people.
Not because clicking a button proves your faith.
But because Gospel ministry requires people willing to pray, participate, share, give, encourage, and help truth travel farther than it otherwise would.
If you want to support that mission and go deeper with us:
Use them.
Share them.
Send them to someone struggling.
Invite your family.
Invite the believer who is drifting.
Invite the seeker.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Invite the person who thinks Christianity has nothing left to say to their pain.
Because perhaps they have heard plenty about Christians.
Perhaps they have heard plenty about churches.
Perhaps they have heard plenty about religion.
But maybe they have never truly encountered the staggering announcement John placed before the world:
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο.
The Word became flesh.
God did not save us by shouting instructions from a safe distance.
The Son came near.
Near enough to be touched.
Near enough to be rejected.
Near enough to bleed.
Near enough to carry a cross.
Near enough to die.
And powerful enough to rise again.
So when shame tells you God would never come near someone like you, remember Bethlehem.
When suffering tells you God cannot understand, remember the incarnation.
When sin tells you there is no road home, remember the cross.
When death tells you every story eventually belongs to the grave, remember the empty tomb.
And when your past whispers that the scandal is the final chapter, remember Jesus.
Because perhaps the most astonishing truth of “the Word became flesh” is not merely that God entered human history.
It is that in Jesus Christ, God entered a world filled with sinners to rescue them—and He is still calling sinners out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
Your scandal may be part of your history.
It does not have to become your identity.
Your failure may explain some of your wounds.
It does not have authority to become your savior or your master.
Your worst chapter may tell the truth about what you did.
But the cross tells the greater truth about what Christ has done.
And the empty tomb tells you that Jesus still specializes in endings everyone else thought were already written.
The Word became flesh because God was not willing to leave redemption as a distant promise—He came personally to bring sinners home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE BIBLE TALKS ABOUT ADULTERY MORE HONESTLY THAN MANY CHURCHES DO
paragraphs: THE BIBLE TALKS ABOUT ADULTERY MORE HONESTLY THAN MANY CHURCHES DO
Scripture does not sanitize betrayal, excuse secret desire, or pretend shattered marriages do not bleed. But neither does Jesus leave repentant sinners buried beneath their worst chapter.
There are sins people confess in church without lowering their voices.
“I’ve been impatient.”
“I’ve struggled with anger.”
“I haven’t been praying enough.”
Then there are sins that change the temperature of the room.
Adultery is one of them.
Say the word, and suddenly somebody remembers a deleted conversation.
Somebody remembers discovering a second phone.
Somebody remembers the hotel receipt.
Somebody remembers the night their spouse finally asked the question they had been terrified to answer.
Somebody remembers being the betrayed one.
Somebody remembers being the betrayer.
And somebody reading this right now has never physically crossed the line...
but knows exactly which message thread they would panic to see opened in front of their husband or wife.
The Bible does not look away from any of this.
We sometimes do.
Scripture doesn't.
That may be one reason the Bible can feel more painfully honest about adultery than some Christian conversations surrounding it.
The Bible gives us David.
Not sanitized David.
Not merely giant-killing David.
Not harp-playing David.
Not Psalm-writing David.
It gives us David standing on a rooftop while another man's wife is bathing.
It gives us desire.
Abuse of royal power.
Sexual sin.
Pregnancy.
Manipulation.
A desperate cover-up.
And eventually a dead husband.
Second Samuel 11 does not airbrush the king because he is one of Israel's heroes.

David sees Bathsheba, inquires about her, sends messengers for her, sleeps with her, and when she becomes pregnant, attempts to conceal what happened. When his plan fails, David arranges for Uriah to be placed where he will die in battle.
Then Scripture delivers one devastating verdict:
“But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.”
No celebrity exemption.
No ministry exemption.
No “but look how much God has used him.”
No rewriting evil into a “mistake.”
God loved David enough to tell the truth about David.
That is something the church must never lose.
Because grace without truth becomes sentimentality.
And truth without grace becomes a firing squad.
Jesus gives us neither.
He gives us truth that cuts...
and grace that heals what the truth exposes.
The Hebrew Scriptures use the verb נָאַף — na’aph — for committing adultery. The commandment in Exodus 20:14 is startlingly brief:
לֹא תִנְאָף
Lo tin’af.
“You shall not commit adultery.”
God does not need twenty paragraphs to explain whether covenant betrayal matters.
It matters because marriage matters.
Covenant matters.
Faithfulness matters.
People matter.
The wounded spouse matters.
The children caught in the wreckage matter.
And the soul becoming comfortable with deception matters too.
But then Jesus walks into the conversation and makes it even more uncomfortable.
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Matthew 5:27–28.
The Greek phrase reaches beneath outward behavior:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
pros to epithymēsai autēn — looking with the purpose or desire of lusting after her.
Jesus moves the courtroom into the heart.
Suddenly adultery is not merely about beds.
It is also about desires we cultivate.
Fantasies we feed.
People we mentally possess.
Conversations deliberately hidden.
Emotional intimacy deliberately transferred away from a spouse.
The secret life we protect because exposure would cost us something.

Jesus is not saying every passing temptation is identical to physically committing adultery. Temptation itself is not the same thing as choosing and cultivating lust. His words confront the intentional gaze—the heart that welcomes, nourishes, and uses another person as an object of desire.
That distinction matters.

Otherwise wounded consciences can be crushed by a standard Jesus was not teaching, while deliberately lustful hearts escape by pretending that because “nothing physical happened,” nothing happened at all.
Jesus refuses both distortions.
He goes after the heart because adultery usually has a history before it has an address.
Before the hotel room, there may have been permission.
Before the touch, a fantasy.
Before the kiss, a conversation.
Before the conversation, a dissatisfaction quietly fed instead of honestly confronted.
Before the affair became visible, something hidden had already begun asking:
“How close can I get without technically crossing the line?”
But holiness asks a different question:
“How faithfully can I love?”
That question changes everything.
Maybe that is where this becomes personal.
Maybe you are reading this with tears forming because you were betrayed.
You didn't commit the adultery.
You discovered it.
You remember how your body reacted before your mind could understand what you had just seen.
The shaking.
The nausea.
The disbelief.
The strange instinct to reread the evidence as though the words might rearrange themselves if you stared long enough.
They didn't.
Maybe you asked questions whose answers injured you even more.
“How long?”
“How many times?”
“Did you love them?”
“Were you thinking about them when you were with me?”
“Was any of our life real?”
Adultery is not merely a sexual event.
It can become an earthquake beneath someone's understanding of reality.
That is why Christians should never rush betrayed spouses through grief with shallow phrases.
“Just forgive.”
“Don't be bitter.”
“God hates divorce.”
“Think about the family.”
Biblical forgiveness is real.
So is biblical repentance.
So are consequences.
So is wisdom.
So is justice.
So is the need for safety.
So is the long, painful work of rebuilding trust when reconciliation is possible.
Forgiveness and trust are not identical.
Forgiveness does not require pretending betrayal was insignificant.
Reconciliation cannot be manufactured by demanding that the wounded person act as though nothing happened.
The Bible takes covenant too seriously for that.
But perhaps you are not reading this as the betrayed spouse.
Perhaps you are David.
Perhaps you're the person who did it.
And nobody knows.
Or everybody knows.
Maybe your marriage survived, but something inside you still hasn't.
Maybe years have passed and you still introduce yourself internally by the ugliest thing you ever did.
Adulterer.
Cheater.
Liar.
Hypocrite.
Failure.
Maybe people stopped calling you those names years ago.
But you didn't.
And this is where the Gospel becomes almost scandalously beautiful.
David's story does not end in 2 Samuel 11.
Nathan confronts him in chapter 12.
David finally stops hiding.
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
There is no elaborate defense.
No blaming Bathsheba.
No blaming pressure.
No blaming loneliness.
No blaming his marriage.
No blaming opportunity.
“I have sinned.”
That is repentance beginning to breathe.
Psalm 51 gives us an even deeper window into David's brokenness:
“Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love.”
Later he pleads:
לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Notice what David asks for.
Not merely:
“Repair my reputation.”
Not:
“Make everybody forget.”
Not:
“Keep me from consequences.”
He asks for a clean heart.
That is repentance.
Repentance is not being embarrassed that you were caught.
Repentance is coming into agreement with God about your sin and turning toward Him.
The New Testament word μετάνοια — metanoia — carries the sense of repentance, a change of mind that turns the person in a new direction.
Real repentance bears fruit.
It stops hiding.
It stops blaming.
It tells the truth.
It accepts consequences.
It abandons the secret relationship.
It seeks accountability.
It becomes willing to lose the image in order to save the soul from continuing in deception.
And then comes the part religious shame sometimes struggles to believe:
God actually forgives repentant sinners.
Not pretend sinners.
Not theoretical sinners.
Real ones.
Sexually broken ones.
Unfaithful ones.
Liars.
Adulterers.
People whose screenshots would destroy their reputation.
People whose past could become tomorrow's gossip.
People who have sinned grievously and finally come trembling into the light.
Paul wrote to believers in Corinth after listing patterns of serious sin, including adultery and sexual immorality:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
That word is thunder.
Not because their histories vanished.
Not because consequences magically disappeared.
But because their histories no longer possessed the authority to define their identity before God.
Paul continues:
“But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
First Corinthians 6:11.
Washed.
Sanctified.
Justified.
This is not permission to continue cheating.
It is the announcement that through Jesus Christ, sinners do not have to remain what sin made them.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus did not die so we could become more sophisticated at hiding.
He died and rose again to save sinners.
At the cross, grace does not call adultery harmless.
Grace agrees that sin is so serious that redemption cost the blood of Christ.
And then grace announces that Christ's sacrifice is sufficient for everyone who genuinely turns to Him in faith.
That means there is hope for the betrayed.
And there is hope for the betrayer who truly repents.
There is hope for the marriage being rebuilt one painfully honest conversation at a time.
There is hope even when reconciliation does not happen and life now looks nothing like the future you once imagined.
There is hope for the person fighting lust before it becomes an affair.
There is hope for the person deleting a secret conversation tonight—not merely deleting evidence, but ending the deception.
There is hope for the husband finally willing to confess.
There is hope for the wife finally willing to tell the truth.
There is hope for the single person who became involved with someone else's spouse and now realizes how much destruction has been rationalized as “love.”
There is hope.
But biblical hope never asks darkness to remain hidden.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
First John 1:9.
The Greek verb ὁμολογῶμεν — homologōmen, “we confess” — carries the idea of acknowledging, admitting, saying the same thing about our sin rather than disguising it.
Grace begins to feel terrifying when you have survived by hiding.
Because grace opens the curtains.
But grace does not open them merely to humiliate you.
Grace brings you into the light so darkness no longer owns you.
And maybe that is the sentence somebody needed tonight:
You do not defeat darkness by becoming better at hiding it.
You bring it to Jesus.
If you are currently committing adultery, the loving message is not “God understands, so continue.”
Stop.
Tell the truth.
End the affair.
Seek wise pastoral and professional counsel where appropriate.
Accept that repentance may be costly.
Do not manipulate Scripture to force your spouse into immediate trust or reconciliation.
Do not call consequences persecution.
Do not use tears as a substitute for transformation.
Run toward Christ.
If you are being tempted, do not wait until temptation has a hotel reservation.
Cut off what feeds it.
Jesus' language about tearing out an eye and cutting off a hand in Matthew 5 is deliberate hyperbole communicating radical action against sin, not a command to physically harm yourself.
Take sin seriously before sin takes something precious from you.
Delete the number.
End the private flirting.
Stop revisiting the profile.
Move the conversation into the light.
Tell a mature believer who will not flatter your compromise.
Fight for your covenant before you are standing in the ashes asking why nobody warned you that fire burns.
And if you are the betrayed one, hear this carefully:
Someone else's adultery is not evidence that you were worthless.
You may need time.
You may need boundaries.
You may need wise pastoral counsel, professional counseling, legal advice, or protection depending on the circumstances.
Do not let anybody weaponize “Christian forgiveness” to silence legitimate grief, erase accountability, or pressure you into pretending trust has been restored when it has not.
Jesus is close to brokenhearted people.
He is not intimidated by your questions.
Bring Him the anger.
Bring Him the confusion.
Bring Him the nights you cannot sleep.
Bring Him the future you thought you had.
Christ knows betrayal.
He was betrayed with a kiss.
He understands wounds inflicted by people who were close enough to touch Him.
And still...
the story moves toward resurrection.
That is what we believe here at Gospel Warrior.
Not because scandal is insignificant.
