Not the tears you wipe away before anyone enters the room.
Not the doubt you are terrified to admit.
Not the sin you promised God you would never repeat.
He sees beneath the costume.
And strangely enough, that should not only terrify us.
For the repentant sinner, it can become one of the most comforting truths imaginable.
Because the God who sees everything is the same God who calls sinners to come into the light.
Jacob's life eventually brought him to a night when there would be nowhere left to run.
Years had passed.
He had wives.
Children.
Servants.
Livestock.
Possessions.
He had survived Laban.
Now he was returning home.
And Esau was coming toward him with four hundred men.
Suddenly the past had a face again.
Jacob was terrified.
He divided his family and possessions.
He prepared gifts.
He strategized.
He prayed.
And then night fell.
Genesis 32 says:
“Jacob was left alone.”
Sometimes God allows everything else to grow quiet because there is finally a conversation we can no longer escape.
That night, a mysterious Man wrestled with Jacob until daybreak.
Jacob clung to Him.
Then came a question that echoes backward through Jacob's entire life:
“What is your name?”
Think about that.
Years earlier, an old father effectively asked Jacob who he was.
Jacob answered with another man's identity.
Now, in the darkness, the question comes again.
“What is your name?”
This time there are no goat skins.
No brother's clothing.
No mother whispering instructions.
No performance.
No disguise.
He answers:
יַעֲקֹב — Ya‘aqov.
Jacob.
His own name.
His real identity.
Then comes the astonishing response:
לֹא יַעֲקֹב יֵאָמֵר עוֹד שִׁמְךָ כִּי אִם־יִשְׂרָאֵל
“Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel…”
Genesis 32:28.
Do you see the beauty?
Years earlier, Jacob lied about his identity to obtain a blessing.
Now he confesses his own name…
and God gives him a new one.
That is not a formula suggesting that confession earns salvation.
It is a picture within Jacob's story that points us toward something much greater.
God does not merely expose.
God transforms.
But Jacob's story is still not the Gospel itself.
It points beyond Jacob.
Because generations later, from the covenant family associated with the name Israel, another Son would come.
Jesus Christ.
And here the contrast becomes breathtaking.
Jacob approached his father wearing another son's clothing to receive a blessing.
Jesus, the true and beloved Son, willingly entered our world so that guilty people could be clothed in a righteousness that is not their own.
Jacob's deception fractured a family.
Christ's obedience creates a redeemed family.
Jacob fled because his brother wanted him dead.
Jesus deliberately went toward Jerusalem knowing death awaited Him.
Jacob wrestled through the night and walked away wounded.
Jesus entered the darkness of Gethsemane, submitted Himself to the Father's will, and went all the way to the cross.
Jacob desperately sought blessing.
Jesus became the One through whom the blessing promised to Abraham reaches the nations.
And at the cross, the scandal becomes grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls evil good.
Not grace that tells us sin does not matter.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that reconciliation with a holy God required something we could never provide for ourselves.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
And sinners are called not to perfect their disguises but to repent and believe.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia, “repentance,” carrying the sense of a changed mind that turns toward God.
Jesus did not come to teach us how to become more convincing Jacobs.
He came to save sinners.
That means you can stop pretending.
You do not need Esau's clothes.
You do not need somebody else's testimony.
You do not need somebody else's spiritual vocabulary.
You do not need to convince Jesus that you are cleaner than you are.
Come as the sinner who needs mercy.
Confess what God already sees.
Turn from what is destroying you.
Trust the crucified and risen Christ.
Because Christianity is not God rewarding people who become talented enough at looking righteous.
It is the Gospel announcing that salvation is by grace through faith, not our own achievement, so that no one can boast.
That is why Ephesians 2:8–9 remains so devastating to human pride and so beautiful to exhausted sinners.
Grace means your worst chapter does not have authority to become your final chapter when Christ becomes Lord of your story.
Jacob's story still carried consequences.
His family would continue experiencing pain.
Grace did not erase history.
But God remained faithful.
And then something happened that Jacob had probably replayed in his imagination a thousand different ways.
He finally saw Esau.
The brother he had wronged.
The brother whose blessing he had taken through deception.
The brother whose murderous anger had driven him away.
Jacob approached.
He bowed repeatedly.
Perhaps he expected judgment.
Perhaps revenge.
Perhaps the consequences he had feared for years.
But Genesis 33:4 says:
“Esau ran to meet him.”
Then Esau embraced him.
Fell on his neck.
Kissed him.
And they wept.
Two brothers.
Years of pain between them.
And tears falling where hatred once lived.
The text does not pretend their history never happened.
Reconciliation is not amnesia.
But something once shattered had been met with unexpected mercy.
And perhaps this is where your heart needs to stop reading like a spectator.
Who are you in this story?
Are you Jacob, carrying something you desperately hope nobody discovers?
Are you Esau, still bleeding from what someone did to you?
Are you Isaac, wounded because someone you trusted deceived you?
Are you Rebekah, realizing that manipulating circumstances produced consequences you never imagined?
Or perhaps you recognize pieces of yourself in all of them.
That is one reason Scripture feels so painfully human.
Its heroes are not polished statues.
Abraham failed.
Jacob deceived.
Moses sinned.
David fell catastrophically.
Peter denied Jesus.
Paul had persecuted the church.
And none of their failures made sin acceptable.
They made grace astonishing.
The Bible is not primarily the story of impressive humans reaching God.
It is the unfolding story of the holy God pursuing, judging, redeeming, covenanting, rescuing, and ultimately revealing salvation in Jesus Christ.
So perhaps tonight your prayer does not need to sound impressive.
Maybe it simply needs to be true.
“Jesus, this is who I really am.”
No costume.
No performance.
No pretending.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when we finally stop protecting the image we have built.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
Not because clicking a button proves your faith. It doesn't.
But because if Christ has given us truth worth receiving, it is truth worth carrying to others.
Send it to the brother who disappeared from church.
Share it with the Christian who has become exhausted from pretending.
Send it even to the person who does not believe yet but needs to understand what Christians mean when we speak about grace.

If you want your digital life to glorify God, don't measure support merely by whether you enjoyed something. Ask whether you can help put Christ-centered truth in front of another human being who needs it.
Sharing can become mission when the motive is love.
Supporting Gospel-centered work can also be stewardship when it is freely, wisely, and cheerfully given—not spiritual coercion and never an attempt to purchase God's favor.
And there is something else we want people to know.
Because there may come a night when the costume feels heavy again.
A night when the old name whispers.
A night when shame reminds you who you were.
A night when Satan tempts you to believe that your worst failure is the truest thing about you.
Come back then and remember Jacob.
Remember the tent.
Remember the disguise.
Remember the running.
Remember the wrestling.
Remember the confession.
Remember the new name.
And above everything else…
remember Jesus.
Jacob's story ultimately matters because God's covenant purposes moved through generations of deeply imperfect people toward Christ.
And Christ is greater than Jacob.
He does not merely improve your disguise.
He calls you out of hiding.
He does not ask you to manufacture righteousness.
He is the Savior sinners need.
He does not tell you to rewrite yesterday.
He calls you to repent, believe, follow Him, and entrust your tomorrow to His grace.
So bring Him the truth.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the fractured family.
Bring Him the consequences.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the resentment.
Bring Him the years you cannot recover.
Bring Him the identity you constructed because you were afraid the real you could never be loved.
And come to Christ.
Because the most astonishing part of Jacob's story was never that a deceiver managed to steal a blessing.
It was that the sovereign God remained faithful enough to transform a deceiver, preserve His covenant purposes, and continue a story that would ultimately lead to the Savior.
You may have walked into your darkest chapter wearing a disguise—but Jesus is still calling sinners out of hiding and into grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Can Christians Play the Lottery? The Ticket in Your Hand May Reveal More Than You Think
paragraphs: Can Christians Play the Lottery? The Ticket in Your Hand May Reveal More Than You Think
The Bible never says, “Thou shalt not buy a lottery ticket.” But Jesus asks a far more uncomfortable question: What has your heart begun trusting to save you?
It is only a little piece of paper.
A few numbers.
A few coins or dollars.
A tiny purchase made at a convenience store, on an app, or at a counter while telling yourself, What if?
What if this is the one?
What if tomorrow I wake up and the debt is gone?
What if I can finally buy my mother a house?
What if I can stop worrying about tuition, rent, medicine, groceries, retirement?
What if I win enough to help the church?
What if I give millions to missions?
What if God lets me win?
And suddenly the lottery ticket is no longer just a lottery ticket.
It has become a tiny paper doorway into another life.
That is where this conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because the deepest Christian question is not simply, “Is buying a lottery ticket a sin?”
The deeper question is:
What is happening inside my heart when I buy it?
There is an important distinction we must make immediately if we want to handle Scripture honestly.

The Bible does not contain a verse explicitly saying, “Christians must never participate in a modern lottery.” Modern state-sponsored lotteries did not exist in the biblical world in precisely the form we know them today.
So we should not manufacture a commandment God did not write.
But neither should we make the opposite mistake.
Silence about the modern mechanism does not mean Scripture is silent about the desires surrounding it.
The Bible speaks relentlessly about money.
It speaks about greed.
Contentment.
Covetousness.
Stewardship.
Work.
Generosity.
Sudden riches.
Trust.
The poor.
The heart.
And perhaps most importantly, it speaks about the terrifying ability of money to begin functioning like a god.
Jesus said something in Matthew 6:24 that cuts through almost every excuse we can make about wealth:
“οὐ δύνασθε θεῷ δουλεύειν καὶ μαμωνᾷ.”
Ou dynasthe Theō douleuein kai mamōna.
“You cannot serve God and mammon.”
The Greek verb δουλεύειν — douleuein is stronger than casually “liking” or “using.” It comes from the language of serving as a slave.
Jesus is not teaching that possessing money is automatically sinful.
He is warning that money can become a master.
And masters demand allegiance.
That means the most dangerous lottery ticket may not be the one that loses.
It may be the one your heart secretly believes can rescue you.
Imagine someone sitting alone at a kitchen table late at night.
Bills are scattered everywhere.
The refrigerator is almost empty.
There is another message from the bank.
The children are sleeping down the hallway.
The person whispers something he would be embarrassed to say at church:
“God... I just need a miracle.”
Then he checks the lottery numbers.
Nothing.
His heart sinks.
Tomorrow he buys another ticket.
Then another.
Not because he thinks of himself as greedy.
He is scared.
That distinction matters.
Some people fantasize about wealth because they worship luxury.
Others fantasize about wealth because they are exhausted.
And Jesus sees both.
He sees the millionaire terrified of losing what he possesses.
He sees the struggling father dreaming of finally breathing again.
He sees the widow counting coins.
He sees the young worker imagining financial freedom.
He sees the believer saying, “Lord, if You let me win, I promise I’ll give some of it away.”
Jesus sees deeper than the ticket.
He sees the heart holding it.
That is why Scripture's warnings about wealth deserve more attention than the question, “Can I technically get away with this?”
Proverbs 13:11 contains a striking principle:
הוֹן מֵהֶבֶל יִמְעָט וְקֹבֵץ עַל־יָד יַרְבֶּה
Hon mehevel yim'at, veqovetz al-yad yarbeh.

The Hebrew begins with the idea of wealth associated with הֶבֶל — hevel, a word carrying the sense of vapor, breath, emptiness, or transience. English translations render the proverb somewhat differently, but its contrast is unmistakable: wealth obtained through empty, hasty, or dubious means diminishes, while wealth gathered gradually increases. Proverbs repeatedly commends patient, diligent acquisition rather than fantasies of instant abundance.
That does not mean every person who receives unexpected money has sinned.
Inheritance can arrive suddenly.
A gift can arrive suddenly.
A business can unexpectedly become valuable.
God can provide in ways nobody anticipated.
The issue is not simply speed.
The issue is what kind of heart and way of life we are cultivating.
And then someone inevitably says:
“But didn't people cast lots in the Bible?”
Yes.
They did.
Proverbs 16:33 says that the lot is cast into the lap, while its decision belongs to the Lord, and Acts 1:26 records the apostles casting lots when Matthias was selected to join the Eleven.
But biblical casting of lots should not casually be equated with purchasing a lottery ticket for financial gain.
In those biblical contexts, lots could function as a means of making or discerning a decision. The participants were not purchasing chances at a jackpot in the hope of becoming wealthy.
Same concept of randomness?
Perhaps superficially.
Same moral purpose?
No.
That distinction matters enormously.
Otherwise we could take virtually any ancient practice involving chance and use it to baptize modern gambling.
The better question is not, “Did anybody in the Bible ever cast lots?”
The better question is, “What does Scripture teach me about the desires that make gambling attractive to me?”
And that brings us to one of the most misquoted verses about money.
Paul writes in 1 Timothy 6 about people who desire to become rich and warns of temptation, snares, and destructive desires. Then comes the famous phrase:
ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία
The crucial word is φιλαργυρία — philargyria.
It means love of money.
Paul does not say money itself is evil.
A bank account cannot repent.
A coin cannot become greedy.
A paycheck cannot worship.
A lottery ticket cannot love money.
You can.
So can I.
And suddenly the conversation becomes personal.
Because perhaps you have never gambled irresponsibly.

Perhaps you occasionally buy a ticket for entertainment, expect to lose the money, never chase losses, never neglect your responsibilities, never conceal it from your spouse, and never place your hope in winning.
It would be careless to pretend that your situation is automatically identical to the person spending grocery money every week while desperately chasing a jackpot.
Christian moral discernment should be more serious than slogans.
But there is another possibility.
Maybe this article is hurting a little.
Maybe you know exactly what it feels like to say:
“One more.”
Maybe you have spent money that belonged somewhere else.
Maybe you have hidden purchases.
Maybe you have calculated jackpots more eagerly than you have considered generosity.
Maybe losing makes you desperate to recover what disappeared.
Maybe winning does not satisfy you—it simply makes you want to win again.
Maybe the fantasy has quietly become emotional oxygen.
Maybe when life becomes frightening, you reach for chance before you reach for Christ.
Then this is no longer an abstract theological debate.
Something is mastering you.
And the Gospel does not tell you to hide.
It tells you there is a Savior.
This is where Christianity becomes radically different from moralism.
Religion without the Gospel says:
“Look what you did. Clean yourself up so God might tolerate you.”
The Gospel says:
“Look what Christ has done. Come out of hiding and bring your chains to Him.”
Jesus did not go to the cross merely to make respectable people slightly more respectable.
He came for sinners.
Greedy sinners.
Fearful sinners.
Secretive sinners.
Religious sinners.
Financially irresponsible sinners.
Self-righteous sinners.
People who keep telling themselves, “I can stop whenever I want.”
People who cannot.
People who have wasted money.
People who have wasted years.
People who wonder whether God could possibly want them after everything they have done.
That is the scandal.
And then comes grace.
At the cross, Christ bore the judgment sinners deserve. He rose again, and everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith receives something infinitely greater than a jackpot:
forgiveness.
Reconciliation with God.
A new identity.
A new Master.
A new heart being taught to treasure what cannot be bought.
Jesus does not merely want the ticket out of your hand.
He wants the throne of your heart.
That is why the Christian response to gambling cannot simply be a legalistic universal formula of “one ticket equals one sin” where Scripture itself does not phrase the command that way.
But neither can we shrug and say, “The Bible doesn't explicitly mention lotteries, so anything goes.”
Ask harder questions.
Can I genuinely thank God for this?
Am I being a faithful steward of money entrusted to me?
Does this encourage contentment or feed covetousness?
Am I hoping for provision—or fantasizing about escape from faithful responsibility?
Could this money better serve my household, someone in need, or something eternally meaningful?
Can I walk away without agitation?
Am I hiding it?
Would I be comfortable if my spouse knew exactly how much I spent?
Has gambling become my emotional refuge?
Do I secretly believe that one winning number could give me the peace Jesus apparently has not?
And perhaps the hardest question:
If God never makes me rich, will Jesus still be enough?
Do not answer that quickly.
Sit with it.
If the jackpot never comes...
If the house remains ordinary...
If you never drive the dream car...
If your name never appears beside millions...
If you have to work patiently, budget carefully, give sacrificially, live modestly, and trust God one ordinary day at a time...
Is Christ still enough?
Because Christianity's greatest treasure was never financial independence.
It was Christ Himself.
There is something tragically revealing about spending years dreaming about winning enough money to finally start living while missing the life God has already placed in front of us.
Your children are growing.
Your parents are aging.
Your spouse needs your presence.
Someone needs your forgiveness.
Someone needs to hear the Gospel.
There is Scripture you have not opened.
There are prayers you have postponed.
There are people you could serve.
There is generosity you could practice now.
There is a Savior worth knowing now.
And we keep whispering...
“When my numbers come in.”
Maybe they never will.
But Christ already came.
Maybe the breakthrough you desperately need is not a jackpot.
Maybe it is contentment.
Maybe it is repentance.
Maybe it is financial discipline.
Maybe it is asking for help.
Maybe it is finally admitting that gambling stopped being entertainment months or years ago.
Maybe it is deleting the app.
Maybe it is telling your spouse the truth.
Maybe it is allowing trusted believers to hold you accountable.
Maybe it is looking at the money you would normally gamble and saying:
“Jesus, teach me to steward this differently.”
Not because giving money purchases God's favor.
It never does.
Grace cannot be bought.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
Christ already paid the price sinners could never pay.
And that distinction matters even here.
Supporting Christian ministry does not make God owe you blessing. Sharing an article does not make you more righteous before God.
But when something genuinely strengthens your faith and helps proclaim Christ, supporting it can become one voluntary expression of stewardship and partnership.

So if Gospel Warrior has confronted you, encouraged you, brought you back to Scripture, helped you speak about Jesus, or placed biblical truth in front of someone who desperately needed it, you can help keep that work moving.
If this article exposed something you have been hiding, do not pretend it did not.
No performance.
No pretending.
Just truth.
Because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday's convictions disappear tomorrow.
And remember this before you buy another ticket:
God is not asking you to pretend money does not matter.
He knows the rent matters.
He knows groceries matter.
He knows debt hurts.
He knows financial pressure can make sleep difficult.
He knows why the possibility of suddenly having enough feels intoxicating.
But He loves you too much to let money impersonate a savior.
A jackpot might change your bank balance.
It cannot cleanse your conscience.
It cannot reconcile you to God.
It cannot conquer death.
It cannot guarantee peace.
It cannot resurrect your soul.
Jesus can.
And perhaps that is the answer underneath the question, “Can Christians play the lottery?”

The Bible does not give us a verse explicitly naming the modern lottery and declaring that every ticket purchased under every circumstance is automatically sinful. We should be honest enough to say that.
But Scripture gives us something more demanding than a loophole.

It commands us to flee the love of money, reject covetousness, practice faithful stewardship, pursue contentment, care for others, work faithfully, refuse enslavement, and treasure Christ above wealth.
So before asking whether a Christian can buy the ticket, ask whether buying it is helping you become the person Christ is calling you to be.
And if the answer exposes something ugly...
good.
Not because shame gets the final word.
Because grace does.
Peter had a scandal.
The woman caught in adultery had a scandal.
The thief beside Jesus had a scandal.
Paul had blood on his history.
The Corinthians had histories they probably wished nobody remembered.
And the Gospel kept doing what the Gospel does.
Jesus took sinners who could not rewrite yesterday...
and began writing something new.
Your worst financial decision does not have to become your final chapter.
Your gambling losses do not have to become your identity.
Your greed does not have to own you.
Your secret does not have to remain secret.
Your shame does not have to have the last sentence.
Repent.
Come to Christ.
Receive grace.
Tell the truth.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Seek accountability where necessary.
Walk away from whatever has begun mastering you.
And learn the strange freedom of being able to hold money without letting money hold you.
Because in the end, the greatest tragedy would not be spending your whole life buying losing tickets.
It would be winning everything you ever wanted—and discovering that somewhere along the way, you traded your heart for something that could never save it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Would God Put a Fence Around Something He Created So Beautiful?
paragraphs: Why Would God Put a Fence Around Something He Created So Beautiful?

Sex was never God’s dirty secret. It was His gift. And understanding why Scripture places it inside marriage may completely change the way you see desire, purity, your body, your past—and the grace of Jesus Christ.
There is something strange about the way Christians sometimes talk about sex.
We whisper about it.
We blush around it.
We warn teenagers about it.
We preach against its misuse.
And somewhere along the way, people can walk away with the impression that God created human sexuality and then immediately became embarrassed by His own invention.
But that cannot be the biblical story.

Before pornography existed, before adultery shattered homes, before lust became an industry, before dating apps, secret messages, casual hookups, broken vows, hidden browser histories, and lonely people learned to use another human body as temporary medicine for an aching soul...
there was Eden.
And before there was sexual sin, there was sexual goodness.
God created the human body.
God created attraction.
God created marriage.
God created the possibility of a husband and wife knowing one another with an intimacy so profound that Scripture reaches for language stronger than merely saying they became physically close.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew is breathtaking:
וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ ... וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
ve-davaq be-ishto ... ve-hayu le-vasar echad.
He clings to his wife...
and they become בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad — “one flesh.”

That word davaq carries the idea of clinging, holding fast, adhering. Even the translation tradition preserves that force: Genesis 2:24 is rendered “hold fast,” “be joined,” or “be united” across major English translations.
Notice the order.
Leave.
Hold fast.
Become one flesh.
Sex does not create the whole marriage covenant, but biblically it belongs inside that covenantal union. It is bodily language expressing something much larger than bodily pleasure.
And suddenly the Christian sexual ethic begins to make more sense.
God did not reserve sex for marriage because sex is filthy.
He reserved sexual union for marriage because it is profoundly significant.
We often protect worthless things carelessly and valuable things carefully.
You don't put a diamond in the driveway and complain that the jewelry box is restricting it.
You protect what is precious precisely because it is precious.
And perhaps this is where somebody reading needs to stop.
Because maybe nobody ever taught you this.
Maybe you were only told:
“Don't.”
Don't have sex.
Don't lust.
Don't cross the line.
Don't sleep together before marriage.
But nobody explained the beauty behind the boundary.
So eventually the boundary looked arbitrary.
Maybe even cruel.
“If we love each other, why would God care?”
“We're committed.”
“We're practically married.”
“Nobody is getting hurt.”
“Times have changed.”
And underneath those questions is often another one:
Why would a loving God care what consenting adults do with their bodies?
Jesus gives us an important answer.
When questioned about marriage, Christ did something remarkable.
He went backward.
Back beyond contemporary culture.
Back beyond human preference.
Back to creation.
Jesus quoted Genesis and said that a man leaves father and mother, is joined to his wife, and “the two shall become one flesh.” Then He added:
“What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Jesus did not treat marriage as an arbitrary social invention.
He rooted it in God's creative intention.
And the New Testament keeps doing the same thing.
Hebrews says marriage is to be honored and the marriage bed kept pure.
Paul tells believers to flee sexual immorality because their bodies belong to God, have become temples of the Holy Spirit, and were “bought at a price.” His conclusion is intensely physical:
“Therefore honor God with your bodies.”
That changes everything.
Christianity does not say your body is meaningless.
It says almost the opposite.
Your body matters so much that Jesus purchased you at the cost of His blood.
Your sexuality matters.
What you do with another person's body matters.
What you allow another person to do with yours matters.
Your private life matters.
Your desires matter.
Not because God hates pleasure.
Because God loves people.
The biblical vision refuses to reduce another human being to an experience.
Sex says something with the body.
It says closeness.
Nakedness.
Knowledge.
Trust.
Giving.
Receiving.
Vulnerability.
Union.
“One flesh.”
That is why Scripture refuses to pretend sex is merely recreation involving two bodies.
Paul makes this almost startlingly clear in 1 Corinthians 6.
Speaking about prostitution—not marriage—he warns that sexual intercourse creates a real “one flesh” involvement, quoting Genesis itself: “The two will become one flesh.”
Think about what that means.
Paul's argument only works because sex is not meaningless.
The modern world often tells us that sex can simply be physical.
Scripture says the body cannot be separated so neatly from the person.
You are not a soul temporarily renting some disposable biological machinery.
Your body is part of you.
So God cares about sexual holiness because God cares about you.
And He cares about the person you desire.
This is also why biblical sexuality can never be reduced to “wait until the wedding and then anything goes.”
Marriage does not turn selfishness into holiness.
A marriage certificate is not permission to exploit another person's body.
Biblical marital intimacy must exist within the wider commands of Christlike love, faithfulness, mutual care, honor, and self-giving.

Paul tells husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her. Then, astonishingly, he quotes Genesis 2:24 again and connects the mystery of marriage with Christ and His church.
So Christian marriage is not merely two people finally receiving religious permission to have sex.
It is covenant.
Faithfulness.
Sacrifice.
Belonging.
Service.
A lifelong union in which sexuality finds its intended covenantal home.
Sex is not the foundation of marriage.
Christlike covenant love is.
And sexual intimacy becomes one beautiful expression within it.
But now we have to enter the room most Christian articles quietly avoid.
The room where somebody is reading this with tears beginning to form.
Because theology is easy until it collides with memory.
Maybe you already crossed the line.
Maybe many times.
Maybe you knew better.
Maybe you didn't.
Maybe somebody introduced you to sexuality before you were old enough to understand what was happening—and what happened to you was not your sin.
Maybe pornography became your secret anesthesia.
Maybe you slept with someone because you desperately wanted to feel chosen.
Maybe you gave your body because you were terrified they would leave.
Maybe you were told, “If you really love me...”
Maybe you convinced yourself you were basically married.
Then the relationship ended.
And they walked away carrying memories of a version of you that you wish you could retrieve.
Maybe you are married now, but pornography followed you into the marriage.
Maybe there is an affair nobody knows about.
Maybe there are messages on your phone that would devastate your spouse.
Maybe you keep promising God:
“This is the last time.”
And then comes another night.
Another search.
Another compromise.
Another morning staring at the ceiling wondering how somebody who loves Jesus can keep returning to something that leaves them feeling so divided inside.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not begin by pretending sin isn't sin.
But neither does it end by leaving sinners where they fell.
One of the most beautiful sentences in Paul's discussion of serious sin comes immediately after a devastating list.
After naming sexual immorality alongside other sins, Paul turns toward redeemed believers and says:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Then comes the Gospel thunder:
“You were washed... you were sanctified... you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.”
Read that again.
Not because your past doesn't matter.
Because Jesus can change what your past gets to mean.
Christian purity is not the boast of people who never became dirty.
Christian purity ultimately rests upon Christ cleansing sinners.
The cross destroys two lies at once.
The first says:
“My sexual choices don't matter.”
The cross answers:
Sin matters enough that Christ died.
The second says:
“My sexual past has ruined me beyond redemption.”
The cross answers:
Grace is powerful enough that Christ rose.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by calling darkness light.
He rewrites everything by entering our darkness, bearing sin at Calvary, conquering death, forgiving repentant sinners, and beginning the work of making them new.
Maybe you cannot become someone who never committed that sin.
But in Christ you can become someone no longer ruled by it.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
Jesus can redeem tomorrow.
You cannot make yourself innocent by pretending nothing happened.
But Christ can justify the guilty.
You cannot cleanse your conscience by collecting enough good behavior to outweigh your failures.
But the blood of Jesus Christ cleanses sinners who come to Him in repentance and faith.
And this is why God's design for sex is ultimately not about deprivation.
It is about worship.
Paul's conclusion is not merely:
“Stop having immoral sex.”
It is:
Glorify God in your body.
Your body can become an altar of obedience.
That means the unmarried Christian who says no when desire screams yes can worship God with that no.
The boyfriend who refuses to pressure his girlfriend can worship God with restraint.
The girlfriend who refuses to trade her convictions for someone's affection can worship God with courage.
The engaged couple who establish boundaries because they want Christ more than immediate gratification can worship God while waiting.
The husband who shuts down the secret account can worship God through repentance.
The wife or husband who confesses hidden sexual sin rather than continuing a double life can begin walking toward truth.
The person who closes pornography and reaches for accountability can worship God in the battle.
The Christian who has fallen and comes crawling back to Jesus can worship through repentance.
And married couples can worship God by cultivating an intimate life marked by faithfulness, tenderness, mutual honor, patience, generosity, and love.
God's command is not:
“Desire nothing.”
It is:
Let Me teach your desires where home is.
And that is harder.
Because sometimes obedience hurts.
Singleness can hurt.
Waiting can hurt.
Being thirty, forty, fifty, or older and still unmarried can hurt.
Watching friends build families while your prayers seem unanswered can hurt.
Wanting touch does not make someone spiritually defective.
Wanting companionship is not automatically idolatry.
Loneliness is real.
Sexual desire can be powerful.
Scripture does not need us to pretend otherwise.
But Christianity makes an audacious claim:
Jesus Christ is worthy of obedience even when obedience costs us something.
We do not obey God because every command immediately feels comfortable.
We obey because He is Lord.
And because the One giving the command is also the One who gave Himself for us.
The hands asking you to surrender are scarred hands.
That matters.
Purity without Jesus becomes pride for those succeeding and despair for those failing.
But holiness centered on Jesus produces something different.
Humility.
Repentance.
Dependence.
Grace.
You stop asking merely:
“How close can I get to sin without technically sinning?”
And begin asking:
“How completely can this part of my life belong to Christ?”
That question changes dating.
It changes marriage.
It changes what you watch.
It changes what you send.
It changes what you fantasize about.
It changes what happens when nobody is watching.
It changes how you see another person's body.
It changes how you see your own.
And maybe tonight the greatest battle is not whether you understand the theology.
Maybe you understand it perfectly.
Maybe the real battle is whether you believe Jesus is better than the thing you keep running toward.
That is where surrender begins.
Not:
“Jesus, make me less human.”
But:
“Jesus, make every part of my humanity Yours.”
Your eyes.
Your hands.
Your imagination.
Your loneliness.
Your hormones.
Your memories.
Your wounds.
Your relationships.
Your sexuality.
Your future marriage, if He gives you one.
Your singleness, for however long He asks you to carry it.
All of it.
His.
And if you've fallen, don't confuse repentance with self-hatred.
Repentance means turning.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Break secret patterns.
Seek wise pastoral accountability where needed.
End relationships that continually pull you away from Christ.
Put practical boundaries around devices, conversations, places, and circumstances where you repeatedly fall.
And when you stumble, do not turn your failure into permission to surrender completely.
Run back to Christ.
Again.
Not because sin is small.
Because His mercy is great.
There may be consequences from yesterday that grace does not instantly erase.
There may be trust that takes time to rebuild.
There may be wounds requiring patient healing.
Forgiveness does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
But your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps this article found you because somebody shared it.
Think about that.
Someone else's small act of pressing “share” may have carried biblical truth into the exact moment you needed it.
So don't let this stop with you.
Someone's teenager may need this.
Someone's unmarried friend may need it.
Someone's marriage may need it.
Someone trapped in pornography may need it.
Someone convinced their sexual past has disqualified them from Jesus may desperately need to hear that the Gospel still says:
“Such were some of you... but you were washed.”
Not because typing words saves anybody.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing the battle into the light is the first crack in the wall secrecy built around you.
Scripture calls believers to generosity and Gospel partnership; it does not give any ministry permission to turn support for itself into a test of devotion to Christ.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because people need Jesus.
The person who reads what you shared tomorrow may never tell you what they almost did tonight.
And perhaps that's the thought worth carrying with you:
Your body is not too dirty for Christ to redeem, your desire is not too strong for Christ to rule, and your story is not too scandalous for grace to write another ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What Is the Battle Between Flesh and Spirit?
paragraphs:
What Is the Battle Between Flesh and Spirit?
The war inside you may be fiercer than anyone knows—but the fact that there is a battle does not mean Christ has abandoned you. It may mean you are finally learning what it means to stop surrendering to the enemy within.
There is a version of you that wants to pray.
And there is a version of you that keeps reaching for the phone.
There is a version of you that wants holiness, honesty, purity, forgiveness, patience, and a life completely surrendered to Jesus Christ.
And then there is that other pull.
The thought you promised yourself you would stop entertaining.
The bitterness you keep replaying.
The temptation that seems to know exactly when you are weakest.
The anger that erupts before wisdom gets a chance to speak.
The appetite that keeps whispering, Just once more.
The secret habit nobody at church knows about.
The pride that wants to win the argument even when love is losing.
The jealousy you would never admit publicly.
The craving to be noticed.
The urge to retaliate.
The desire to obey God tomorrow while satisfying yourself today.
And sometimes the most frightening part is not merely that these desires exist.
It is that they can exist inside someone who genuinely loves Jesus.
So you begin asking questions you are almost afraid to say aloud.
If I really belong to Christ, why is this battle still happening?
If the Holy Spirit lives in me, why can temptation still feel so powerful?
Why can I worship God on Sunday and wrestle with ugly thoughts on Monday?
Why does part of me hunger for righteousness while another part keeps pulling toward what Christ died to rescue me from?
Maybe you have mistaken the battlefield for evidence that God has abandoned you.
Scripture tells a different story.
Paul describes the conflict with startling clarity:

“For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other...”
— Galatians 5:17, KJV
The Greek is even more revealing.
ἡ γὰρ σὰρξ ἐπιθυμεῖ κατὰ τοῦ πνεύματος, τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα κατὰ τῆς σαρκός
Hē gar sarx epithymei kata tou pneumatos, to de pneuma kata tēs sarkos.
“For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh.”
Two words matter enormously here.
σάρξ — sarx.
Flesh.
And πνεῦμα — pneuma.
Spirit.

When Paul speaks of sarx in this context, he is not teaching that the physical human body is inherently evil. Christianity does not teach that matter itself is wicked. God created human beings bodily. Jesus truly came in the flesh. Christ was bodily raised from the dead, and Christian hope includes the resurrection of the body.
Paul is describing something deeper than skin, muscles, hormones, and bones.

“Flesh” in this moral sense is fallen human existence oriented away from God—the self attempting to rule itself, desires corrupted by sin, humanity operating independently of the rightful reign of its Creator.
It is the old instinct that says:
I want what I want.
I will decide what is good.
I will satisfy this desire regardless of what God has said.
I will sit on the throne.
That is why the works of the flesh extend far beyond sexual temptation.
Paul continues:

“Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are these; Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness, Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies, Envyings, murders, drunkenness, revellings, and such like...”
— Galatians 5:19–21, KJV
Notice what is standing beside sexual sin.
Hatred.
Jealousy.
Anger.
Rivalry.
Division.
Envy.
The flesh can wear expensive clothes.
The flesh can quote Bible verses.
The flesh can sing worship songs.
The flesh can want recognition for ministry.
The flesh can secretly enjoy another person's failure.
The flesh can demand an apology while refusing to forgive.
The flesh can even perform religious acts when the real hunger underneath them is human applause.
This battle is far more serious than “good habits versus bad habits.”
It is a battle over lordship.
Who rules here?
Me?
Or Christ?
That question reaches places nobody else can see.
Imagine a man sitting alone late at night.
His family believes he is sleeping.
His Bible is a few feet away.
His phone is in his hand.
Nobody would know.
One click.
One message.
One compromise.
One secret.
His flesh begins negotiating.
You have been stressed.
You deserve an escape.
God understands.
You can repent afterward.
And somewhere beneath all that noise comes another conviction:
Run.
Not because salvation is earned by surviving temptation.
Not because Jesus loves perfect people.
But because sin is trying to drag him back toward chains Christ came to break.
That moment—the trembling space between temptation and obedience—is where many believers discover that Christianity is not merely something they believe.
It is Someone to whom they belong.
Paul writes:
— Galatians 5:24, KJV
Crucified.
Not entertained.
Not renamed.
Not excused.
Not decorated with Christian vocabulary.
Crucified.
And crucifixion is violent language because sin is not a harmless pet.
Sin destroys.
Sin promises pleasure and sends invoices afterward.
It offers freedom while manufacturing chains.
It tells you secrecy will protect you and then uses secrecy to imprison you.
It tells you bitterness makes you strong while slowly turning someone else's sin against you into poison inside you.
It tells you pride protects your dignity while separating you from repentance.
It tells you lust is intimacy.
Greed is security.
Revenge is justice.
Drunkenness is relief.
Applause is identity.
Control is peace.
And then Jesus enters the wreckage.
Not carrying a motivational slogan.
Carrying a cross.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Christianity is not the story of decent people learning to behave better.
It is the announcement that sinners who could not rescue themselves were pursued by a holy and merciful God.
We sinned.
We rebelled.
We exchanged God's authority for our own desires.
And Scripture does not minimize the consequence:

“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
— Romans 6:23, KJV
There is the scandal.
We earned death.
Then comes grace.
God gives life.
How?
Through Jesus Christ our Lord.

At the cross, Jesus did not merely provide inspiration for struggling people. He bore sin. The innocent One suffered for the guilty. Christ died and rose again, defeating death and opening the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself up until Jesus accepts you.”
The Gospel announces that salvation is found in Christ, and the person who comes to Him in repentance and faith is forgiven, reconciled, and brought into a new life.
That changes the battle.
Before Christ, sin was not merely something outside us tempting us. Sin had dominion.
But Paul tells believers:

“For sin shall not have dominion over you: for ye are not under the law, but under grace.”
— Romans 6:14, KJV
Read that carefully.
It does not say sin will never tempt you again.
It says sin shall not have dominion over you.
There is a profound difference between the presence of temptation and the reign of sin.
A temptation can knock without being given the keys.
An impulse can scream without becoming your king.
A sinful thought can appear without receiving your allegiance.
The Christian life is not sinless perfection achieved by human determination. Neither is grace permission to make peace with sin.
Grace forgives us—and grace transforms us.
The Holy Spirit begins producing something the flesh cannot manufacture:

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance...”
— Galatians 5:22–23, KJV
Paul says fruit, not costume.
Real transformation grows from the life of God at work within His people.
Slowly, sometimes painfully, the person who once needed the final word learns silence.
The person consumed by resentment begins forgiving.
The person ruled by lust learns to flee.
The person addicted to approval becomes increasingly content to be known by God.
The greedy hand begins opening.
The proud heart begins confessing.
The angry mouth begins stopping before speaking.
Not perfectly.
Not instantly.
But genuinely.
This is sanctification.
And this is where some Christians become discouraged because they expected transformation to mean the disappearance of struggle.
Sometimes transformation means that what you once embraced, you now fight.
What once entertained you now grieves you.
What you once justified, you now confess.
What once controlled you, you are learning—through the Spirit—to put to death.
Paul writes:
— Romans 8:13, KJV
Notice the phrase:
through the Spirit.
Christian warfare is not self-salvation.
You do not defeat the flesh so Jesus will finally love you.
You fight because Christ loved you, gave Himself for you, calls you His own, and gives His Spirit to His people.
This keeps us away from two deadly cliffs.
One is legalism:
God will accept me because I performed well enough.
The other is lawlessness:
Because God is gracious, my sin does not matter.
The Gospel destroys both.
You cannot boast because salvation is grace.
And you cannot comfortably enthrone sin because grace has brought you under a new King.
Maybe that is exactly where this becomes personal.
Perhaps you have been hiding.
Everybody sees your Christian posts.
Nobody sees your private browser history.
Everybody hears you say, “God is good.”
Nobody knows how bitter you have become.
Everybody thinks your marriage is fine.
Nobody knows how emotionally distant you are.
Everybody thinks you are strong.
Nobody knows you are exhausted from fighting the same temptation.
Everybody sees the ministry.
Jesus sees the motive.
Everybody sees the smile.
God sees the war.
And here is the question:
What are you feeding?
Paul writes:
— Galatians 5:16, KJV
Walk.
That word matters.
Christian maturity is ordinarily lived step by step.
Today you pray when you would rather scroll.
Today you confess instead of hiding.
Today you close the page.
Today you refuse the message.
Today you forgive again.
Today you open Scripture before opening the noise of the world.
Today you tell a mature believer the truth about the thing secrecy has protected.
Today you stop calling bondage “just who I am.”
Today you refuse to use grace as camouflage for rebellion.
And when you fall?
You do not make peace with the mud.
You run back to Christ.
John writes:
— 1 John 1:9, KJV
The enemy wants failure to become identity.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance, forgiveness, restoration, and transformation.
Peter denied Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
He had promised loyalty.
Then pressure came.
Fear took over.
And the man who said he would die with Christ denied even knowing Him.
What a scandal.
But denial was not the final chapter of Peter's story.
The risen Jesus restored him and called him forward.
That does not make Peter's sin insignificant.
It makes Christ's grace astonishing.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by eliminating repentance.
Jesus rewrites ruined stories by meeting sinners with truth and mercy, forgiving those who come to Him, and transforming lives that surrender to His lordship.
Maybe your story contains pages you desperately wish you could tear out.
Jesus already knows what is written there.
The pornography.
The affair.
The hatred.
The addiction.
The lies.
The spiritual laziness.
The pride.
The envy.
The secret messages.
The hypocrisy.
The years you wasted.
The person you wounded.
The promise you broke.
The prayer life you abandoned.
The compromise you keep rationalizing.
Christ does not need you to deceive Him before you approach Him.
Bring the truth.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.

The New Testament word commonly translated “repentance,” μετάνοια — metanoia, carries the idea of a changed mind, a turning of one's orientation. Biblical repentance involves turning from sin toward God.
Not:
Jesus, forgive me while I protect the thing destroying me.
But:
Jesus, this is sin. I have no defense. Have mercy on me. Change me. I belong to You.
And perhaps tonight that prayer is the beginning of a war you finally stop pretending does not exist.
You may have to delete something.
End something.
Confess something.
Forgive someone.
Ask forgiveness from someone.
Install boundaries.
Walk away from an environment that continually feeds temptation.
Seek accountable Christian community.
Open your Bible again.
Get on your knees again.
Not to purchase God's grace.
Because grace has awakened you to the seriousness of what was killing you.
And when the flesh whispers tomorrow, You haven't changed...
remember:
Your confidence is not that your flesh became trustworthy.
Your confidence is Jesus Christ.
The One who died.
The One who rose.
The One who saves.
The One who intercedes.
The One who gives His Spirit.
The One who finishes what He begins.
So stop measuring God's faithfulness by how loud today's temptation feels.
A loud enemy is not necessarily a victorious enemy.
Keep walking.
Keep confessing.
Keep resisting.
Keep returning to Scripture.
Keep praying.
Keep depending upon the Spirit.
Keep your eyes on Christ.
And when you stumble, do not turn a stumble into surrender.
Get up and run toward Jesus.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly. But you can make one small declaration that secrecy will not have the final word.
Not because every sentence will feel urgent today, but because there may come a night when the flesh starts negotiating again and you need to remember who your King is.
Not as religious decoration.

We should never confuse supporting a ministry with earning God's favor—salvation cannot be purchased, and giving money does not make anyone more loved by God. We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, and one expression of stewardship can be freely choosing to support Gospel-centered work that you believe is bearing good fruit.
But the deeper reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
It is staying close to Scripture.
It is refusing to let your soul survive on whatever the algorithm happens to feed you.
Truth shared can reach the person you never knew was one temptation away from surrendering.
And never forget this:
The battle inside you does not get the final sentence—Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: David Had the Perfect Opportunity to Kill Saul — But Refused to Take Revenge
paragraphs: David Had the Perfect Opportunity to Kill Saul — But Refused to Take Revenge

The man who tried to destroy David walked defenseless into David’s hiding place. One blade could have ended the nightmare. One moment could have settled the score. But in the darkness of that cave, David discovered something every wounded believer eventually has to learn: just because you have the opportunity to hurt the person who hurt you does not mean God has given you permission.
Imagine hearing the footsteps before you see the man.
You are hiding deep inside a cave.
Your breathing becomes shallow.
The men around you stop moving.
Outside, sunlight burns across the wilderness of En-gedi, but where you are sitting there is darkness, stone, sweat, fear, and the exhaustion of living like a fugitive.
Then he walks in.
Saul.
The king.
The man who has been hunting you.
The man who threw a spear at you.
The man whose jealousy turned your life upside down.
The man who mobilized thousands of soldiers to find you.
And now...
he is alone.
Vulnerable.
Unaware that the man he wants dead is only a few steps away.
David does not have to chase Saul.
He does not have to manufacture an opportunity.
He does not have to arrange revenge.
The opportunity walks directly into the cave.
And David's men immediately recognize what appears to be an unmistakable act of providence.
They essentially tell him, This is it.
This must be God.
This must be your moment.
This must be the answer.
Saul has been delivered into your hand.
Do what you want with him.

The biblical scene is astonishingly tense. First Samuel 24 tells us that Saul took three thousand chosen men to search for David near the Rocks of the Wild Goats. Saul entered a cave, apparently unaware that David and his men were concealed in its deepest recesses. David's men interpreted the situation as permission to act.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes frighteningly personal.
Because sometimes temptation does not arrive looking evil.
Sometimes it looks like an opportunity.
Sometimes revenge looks like justice.
Sometimes bitterness sounds like discernment.
Sometimes the people around you can even give spiritual language to something God never commanded you to do.
"This must be God."
"Look how perfectly everything lined up."
"After everything they did to you, they deserve this."
"Maybe God finally gave you the opportunity to expose them."
But an open door is not automatically God's permission.
Read that again.
An open door is not automatically God's permission.

David had been anointed to become king. Saul was actively persecuting him. David was innocent of the rebellion Saul imagined. Yet none of those truths gave David permission to seize God's promise through sinful vengeance.
That distinction matters.
David moved toward Saul.
Close enough to touch the royal garment.
Close enough that the difference between mercy and bloodshed may have been only a movement of his hand.
Then David cut off a corner of Saul's robe.
And stopped.
No assassination.
No triumphant revenge.
No corpse on the cave floor.
Only a piece of cloth in David's hand.
Then Scripture records something remarkable.

David's heart troubled him even for cutting the robe. The Hebrew wording behind the expression is vivid: וַיַּךְ לֵב־דָּוִד אֹתוֹ — vayyakh lev-David oto, literally carrying the sense that David's heart struck him.
His conscience was pierced.
Not because he had murdered Saul.
He hadn't.
His heart was troubled over what he had done.
David then declared:
חָלִילָה לִּי מֵיהוָה — chalilah li me-YHWH.
The thought is essentially, "Far be it from me because of the LORD."
He refused to stretch out his hand against Saul, whom he repeatedly called מְשִׁיחַ יְהוָה — meshiach YHWH, "the LORD's anointed."

The Hebrew word mashiach means "anointed one." In this immediate historical context, David is speaking about Saul's status as Israel's anointed king; this phrase should not be carelessly treated as though Saul himself were the Messiah. The larger biblical story ultimately brings the hope of God's Anointed King to its fulfillment in Jesus Christ, but 1 Samuel 24 first demands that we hear David's words in their own setting.
David was not pretending Saul was righteous.
He was not denying Saul's abuse.
He was not saying evil did not matter.

And this passage should never be weaponized to tell someone that honoring God means remaining trapped in abuse, refusing legitimate protection, hiding criminal behavior, or never seeking lawful justice.
David himself was physically separated from Saul.
He had fled.
He confronted Saul truthfully.
He appealed for judgment.
He maintained boundaries.
Mercy did not require David to walk back into Saul's palace and stand within spear-throwing distance again.
That matters for anyone reading this who has confused forgiveness with becoming available for repeated destruction.
Biblical forgiveness does not call evil good.
Biblical mercy does not erase wisdom.
Refusing revenge does not mean refusing boundaries.
You can forgive someone and still recognize that trust has been shattered.
You can release vengeance to God without giving an unsafe person unrestricted access to your life.
You can pray for someone from a distance.
You can refuse hatred without pretending nothing happened.
David's response is extraordinary precisely because Saul really had wronged him.
This was not imaginary pain.
David had reasons to be angry.
And maybe you do too.
Maybe someone lied about you.
Maybe someone embarrassed you publicly.
Maybe someone abandoned you when you desperately needed them.
Maybe someone used your kindness and then disappeared.
Maybe someone betrayed your confidence.
Maybe somebody damaged your reputation and continued living as though nothing happened while you were left trying to rebuild yourself from pieces.
And somewhere inside you, perhaps you have rehearsed the moment when the tables finally turn.
The message you could screenshot.
The secret you could expose.
The story you could tell.
The humiliation you could return.
The sentence you could say that you know would wound them exactly where they wounded you.
You have the corner of the robe in your hand.
And nobody else may know.
But God does.
That is where revenge becomes more than an action.
It becomes a battle over lordship.
Who gets to determine justice?
Who gets the final word?
Who owns your wounded heart?
David eventually stepped out of the cave and called after Saul.
He could have killed him from the darkness.
Instead, he confronted him in the light.
He bowed before the king and showed him the piece of the robe.
David essentially said: Look at what is in my hand. I could have harmed you. I didn't. There is no rebellion in me, even though you are hunting me.
Then David said something that reveals the foundation beneath his restraint:
יִשְׁפֹּט יְהוָה בֵּינִי וּבֵינֶךָ — yishpot YHWH beini uveinekha.
"May the LORD judge between me and you."
That is the heartbeat of the story.
David did not say there would be no judgment.
He changed the judge.
He refused to make himself the final court.
He placed Saul into God's hands.
That is not weakness.
That takes a terrifying kind of faith.
Revenge says, "I need to make you pay."
Faith says, "God saw it."
Revenge says, "I cannot rest until you hurt."
Faith says, "I will not become what wounded me."
Revenge keeps your enemy living inside your heart long after they have left your life.
Forgiveness hands the case to God.
And here the story begins pointing beyond David.
Because David's mercy in the cave was beautiful...
but David was not the sinless Savior.
The Bible refuses to turn its heroes into flawless legends. David himself would later commit terrible sins. The man who showed mercy would himself desperately need mercy.
And so do we.
That is why Christianity cannot ultimately end with, "Be more like David."
We need Someone greater than David.
We need Jesus.
Centuries later, another King would be surrounded by enemies.
Not because He had sinned.
Not because He deserved punishment.
Jesus Christ was mocked, falsely accused, beaten, humiliated, and crucified.
And unlike David, who had Saul at his mercy, Jesus possessed authority beyond anything David could have imagined.
Yet Christ did not use His power to rescue Himself through vengeance.
At the cross, while His enemies mocked Him, Jesus prayed:
Πάτερ, ἄφες αὐτοῖς — Pater, aphes autois.
"Father, forgive them."
Luke 23:34.
Think about that.
The hands capable of judgment were stretched onto wood.
The King wore thorns.
The innocent One bled for the guilty.
And this is where the Gospel becomes painfully personal, because we naturally want to imagine ourselves standing beside David as the wounded innocent person.
But before the holiness of God, we must also recognize ourselves among the guilty.
We have sinned.
We have wounded others.
We have harbored hatred.
We have spoken words we cannot retrieve.
We have wanted people to suffer.
We have secretly celebrated someone's downfall.
We have demanded justice for everybody else's sin while pleading for mercy over our own.
Yet at Calvary, Jesus did something infinitely greater than David sparing Saul.
Christ gave Himself for sinners.
The scandal of the Gospel is not that God decided sin did not matter.
Sin mattered so much that the Son of God went to the cross.
And grace is not God pretending we are innocent.
Grace is God offering guilty people forgiveness because Christ bore sin and conquered death.
This is where revenge loses its throne.
You do not forgive because what happened was acceptable.
You forgive because Jesus Christ is Lord.
You do not release vengeance because justice is meaningless.
You release vengeance because judgment belongs to God.
You do not forgive because you feel nothing.
Sometimes forgiveness happens while tears are still falling.
Sometimes your emotions need time to catch up with your obedience.
Sometimes you must surrender the same wound to Christ again tomorrow.
And again next week.
And again when the memory suddenly comes back.
Forgiveness can be a decision you repeatedly bring beneath the lordship of Jesus while God heals what hatred could never heal.
Paul later writes in Romans 12:19:
That is not God's way of saying evil does not matter.
It is God's way of telling you that you were never meant to carry the unbearable weight of being judge, jury, and executioner over every person who wounded you.
There is freedom in finally admitting:
"Jesus, I cannot change what they did."
"I cannot force them to apologize."
"I cannot make them understand how badly they hurt me."
"I cannot control whether they ever repent."
"But I can give You my right to revenge."
That prayer may hurt.
Because sometimes hatred has been living inside us so long that releasing it feels like losing the only evidence that the wound mattered.
But Jesus does not ask you to say the wound did not matter.
He asks you to give the wound to Him.
There is a difference.
Maybe your Saul will never apologize.
Maybe the person who wounded you will never understand.
Maybe there will never be the conversation you rehearsed a thousand times in your head.
Maybe they will never give you closure.
But Christ can still give you freedom.
Your healing does not have to wait for your enemy's apology.
Your obedience does not have to wait for their repentance.
Your future does not have to remain chained to their past behavior.
And perhaps the deepest miracle in that cave was not that Saul survived.
Perhaps it was that David refused to let Saul's sin decide what kind of man David would become.
Do not miss that.
The person who hurt you has already taken enough.
Do not give them your character too.
Do not give them your worship.
Do not give them your peace.
Do not let what somebody did to you become permission for what sin wants to do inside you.
Bring it to Jesus.
All of it.
The rage.
The fantasies of revenge.
The screenshots.
The resentment.
The questions.
The tears nobody saw.
The prayer you stopped praying because you became tired of hurting.
Bring the entire ugly, bleeding truth into the presence of Christ.
Repent where bitterness has become sin.
Receive forgiveness where you have failed.
Ask Jesus to create in you what you cannot manufacture yourself.
Mercy.
Freedom.
A clean heart.
Maybe while reading this, one person's face has been in your mind the entire time.
You know who it is.
And maybe the Holy Spirit is touching something you have hidden beneath "I'm over it."
Be honest.
Are you?
You do not have to perform spirituality here.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that Jesus still heals wounded hearts.
Then think of one person who needs this story.
Not twenty strangers.
One person.
The friend who was betrayed.
The husband carrying anger.
The wife quietly breaking.
The believer who stopped attending church because someone wounded them.
The person who loves Jesus but cannot release what happened.
And if Gospel Warrior is helping you stay near Scripture, follow so we can continue walking through the difficult places in the Bible where conviction, grace, healing, repentance, and real life meet.
Come to Jesus.
Not to a page.
Not to a brand.
Not to merchandise.
To Christ.
If you have been hiding sin, repent.
If you have been feeding bitterness, surrender it.
If you have been wounded, bring the wound to Him.
If you have failed like David would later fail, remember that your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.

The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can be forgiven, captives can become free, enemies can become family, shattered people can be restored, and dead hearts can receive life through Jesus Christ.
That is why our story will always be...
from scandal...
to grace.
Because the cave was never merely about whether Saul deserved to die.
It was about whether David would trust God enough to put down the blade.
And perhaps tonight, the most powerful thing you can place at the feet of Jesus is not the person who wounded you...
but the weapon you have been keeping in your heart.
You may never be able to rewrite what they did to you—but when you surrender the pen, Jesus can still rewrite what happens inside you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE PROPHET GOD TOLD NOT TO MOURN HIS WIFE
paragraphs:
THE PROPHET GOD TOLD NOT TO MOURN HIS WIFE
God told Ezekiel the woman he loved would die—and then gave him a command that sounds almost unbearable. But behind this disturbing moment is a warning about losing what is precious, the holiness of God, and the scandalous grace that would ultimately lead us to Jesus.
There are Bible passages we underline because they comfort us.
There are passages we quote because they strengthen us.
And then there are passages that make us stop.
Read them again.
Sit silently.
And whisper...
“God... why?”
Ezekiel 24 is one of those passages.
Because one morning, a prophet woke up with a wife he loved.
And before the day was over, she was gone.
But the part that makes this story almost impossible to forget is what God told Ezekiel before it happened.
The Lord said:
“Son of man, behold, I am about to take from you the desire of your eyes with a blow; but you shall not mourn and you shall not weep, and your tears shall not come.”
That expression—“the desire of your eyes”—comes from the Hebrew:
מַחְמַד עֵינֶיךָ — maḥmad ʿeineikha
It carries the sense of something precious, desirable, treasured by your eyes.
God did not speak about Ezekiel's wife as though she were disposable.
The language itself tells us she was precious to him.
She was the delight of his eyes.
Someone he loved.
Someone whose presence had become woven into the ordinary rhythm of his life.
And God told him she was going to die.
Then came the command:
“Sigh in silence; make no mourning for the dead.”
And suddenly this is no longer one of those Bible stories we can read comfortably from a distance.
Because some of us know what it means to lose the desire of our eyes.
A spouse.
A parent.
A child.
A friendship.
A home.
A future we were certain would happen.
A marriage we thought would survive.
A person whose phone number is still saved even though we know they will never call again.
Sometimes grief leaves an empty chair.
Sometimes it leaves an empty side of the bed.
Sometimes nobody died at all...
but something inside you still went to a funeral.
And perhaps that is why Ezekiel's story can hit so deeply.
But we must be careful here.
Because if we pull these verses away from their biblical context, we can accidentally make God appear cruel.
This passage is not teaching that grief is sinful.
It is not teaching Christians to suppress emotion.
It is not teaching husbands not to mourn their wives.
Scripture repeatedly shows genuine grief.
Abraham mourned Sarah.
David grieved.
The Psalms are filled with tears.
Paul described believers as “sorrowful, yet always rejoicing.”
And Jesus Himself stood outside Lazarus's tomb and wept.
The shortest verse many Christians memorized as children remains one of the most revealing:
“Jesus wept.”
So Ezekiel's silence was not God's universal command for grieving people.
It was a prophetic sign.
And that changes everything.
Ezekiel was not simply living through a private tragedy.
His life had become part of God's prophetic message to a rebellious people.
The historical setting matters.
Jerusalem was approaching catastrophe.

The people of Judah had repeatedly rebelled against God. Ezekiel's ministry confronted idolatry, violence, corruption, covenant unfaithfulness, and the false confidence that judgment would somehow never reach them.
They possessed something unimaginably precious:
the sanctuary.
The temple.
The place associated with God's presence among His covenant people.
And many apparently assumed that what they treasured could never be taken away.
Then God described the sanctuary using language hauntingly similar to the language used for Ezekiel's wife.
In Ezekiel 24:21, God speaks of:
“My sanctuary, the pride of your power, the desire of your eyes, and the delight of your soul.”
There it is again.
The desire of your eyes.
Suddenly the terrible sign begins to make sense.
What Ezekiel's wife was to Ezekiel personally...
the sanctuary had become to the people nationally.
Something beloved was about to be taken away.
And when the catastrophe came, the devastation would be so overwhelming that ordinary mourning rituals would be disrupted by the scale of judgment.
Ezekiel's private heartbreak became a living prophecy.
Imagine the scene.
The prophet has delivered God's message.
People have heard him.
Maybe some dismissed him.
Maybe some thought he was extreme.
Then evening came.
Scripture records the moment with devastating simplicity:
“So I spoke to the people in the morning, and in the evening my wife died.”
No dramatic paragraph.
No sentimental description.
One sentence.
Morning...
he preached.
Evening...
she died.
Then Scripture says:
“And in the morning I did as I was commanded.”
That sentence may be one of the quietest pictures of costly obedience in the Old Testament.
Ezekiel obeyed while hurting.
He obeyed without pretending the loss was insignificant.
He obeyed when obedience itself became part of the message.
And perhaps someone reading this understands that kind of morning.
The morning after the diagnosis.
The morning after the funeral.
The morning after the betrayal.
The morning after you discovered that the prayer you desperately wanted answered had not been answered the way you hoped.
You still had to get up.
Still had responsibilities.
Still had people depending on you.
Still had to decide whether God was worthy of trust when your emotions were screaming questions you could not answer.
There is a dangerous version of Christianity that tells people faith means never asking why.
The Bible is far more honest.
Biblical faith can cry.
Biblical faith can lament.
Biblical faith can tremble.
Biblical faith can say with the psalmists, “How long, O LORD?”
Faith is not the absence of anguish.
Sometimes faith is refusing to abandon God while anguished.
And Ezekiel's story confronts another uncomfortable truth.
We can treasure God's gifts while slowly forgetting God Himself.
That is where this ancient prophecy becomes painfully modern.
We can love the marriage more than the One who gave marriage.
Love ministry more than Christ.
Love reputation more than holiness.
Love Christian culture more than Christ Himself.
Love the church building while resisting the Lord of the Church.
Love blessings while resenting the God who calls us to repentance.
We can even turn religious things into hiding places from God.
Judah had the temple.
They had history.
They had religious identity.
But possessing sacred things did not excuse rebellion against the Sacred One.
That should disturb us.
Because you can own a Bible and avoid its Author.
You can sing worship songs while protecting secret sin.
You can post verses while refusing forgiveness.
You can say “God knows my heart” while knowing your heart is desperately trying to negotiate with something God has already told you to surrender.
You can appear spiritually alive while slowly becoming numb inside.
And eventually grace confronts what religious appearance tries to conceal.
So ask yourself something that may hurt.
If God touched the thing you treasure most, would you discover that you loved His gifts more than Him?
Do not answer quickly.
Sit with it.
What is the desire of your eyes?
What could you not imagine living without?
Whose approval controls you?
What possession defines you?
What relationship has become your functional savior?
What secret would you rather protect than confess?
What are you asking Jesus to bless that He may actually be asking you to surrender?
This is where Ezekiel's story stops being merely ancient history.
It becomes a mirror.
And mirrors are uncomfortable when we have spent years learning how to hide.
Maybe your hidden thing is pornography.
Maybe bitterness.
Maybe pride.
Maybe an affair nobody knows about.
Maybe greed dressed as ambition.
Maybe resentment toward God because He allowed something you still cannot understand.
Maybe you have mastered Christian language while your prayer life has almost disappeared.
Maybe everyone thinks you are strong.
But you know.
You know how tired your soul has become.
You know the compromise.
You know the secret.
You know what you delete.
You know what you replay.
You know the name you cannot forgive.
You know the prayer you stopped praying.
You know how far your heart has wandered.
And somehow...
Jesus knows too.
Every room.
Every motive.
Every hidden search.
Every bitter thought.
Every compromise.
Every wound.
Every failure.
And still the Gospel says:
Come.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because it matters so much that Christ went to the cross.
This is where the story moves from scandal toward grace.
Ezekiel's prophetic sign pointed toward judgment on Jerusalem because God's holiness cannot simply call rebellion harmless.
The Gospel does not erase that holiness.
The Gospel reveals the astonishing way God's holiness and mercy meet.
Centuries after Ezekiel stood grieving in silence, another Son would approach Jerusalem.
Jesus Christ.
He looked upon the city destined again for judgment...
and He did something Ezekiel had been specifically commanded not to do in his prophetic sign.
Jesus wept.
Luke records Him seeing Jerusalem and weeping over it.
Think about that.
The God whom sinners rebelled against was not emotionally indifferent toward their destruction.
Christ grieved.
And then He kept walking toward the cross.
The Gospel is not God deciding that sin was never serious.
The Gospel is God demonstrating exactly how serious sin is...
and how astonishing His love is.
At Calvary, Jesus willingly bore the curse for sinners.
Isaiah had foretold the suffering Servant.
“He was wounded for our transgressions.”
The New Testament announces that Christ “suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God.”
Paul writes:
And from the cross comes one of Christianity's most breathtaking declarations.
In Greek:
Τετέλεσται — Tetelestai.
“It is finished.”
Not “try harder.”
Not “hide better.”
Not “make yourself worthy first.”
Finished.
Christ's saving work was accomplished.
The scandal of human sin met the grace of God at a Roman cross.
But grace is not permission to remain unchanged.
The Jesus who forgives sinners also calls sinners to repent.
The Greek New Testament uses the word:
μετάνοια — metanoia
Repentance.
A turning of mind and heart that bears fruit in a changed direction.
Jesus did not die merely to make us comfortable with the chains destroying us.
He came to save us.
Forgive us.
Reconcile us to God.
Make us new.
The Gospel does not say, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
It says something far more powerful:
Your sin mattered enough for Christ to die, and His grace is powerful enough that your sin does not have to write your final chapter.
That is why your scandal does not have to become your identity.
Your divorce is not your name.
Your addiction is not your name.
Your betrayal is not your name.
Your shame is not your name.
Your worst night is not your name.
Your failure is not your name.
Your grief is not your name.
If you belong to Jesus Christ, your story is now held by Someone who specializes in resurrection.
Peter denied Him...
Jesus restored Peter.
Paul persecuted Christians...
Jesus transformed him into a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The thief was dying beside Christ with no lifetime left to repair his reputation...
and Jesus promised him paradise.
Again and again Scripture shows us the same breathtaking truth.
Sin destroys.
Judgment is real.
Repentance matters.
But grace gets the final word for everyone who comes to Christ.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that sentence is why you found this article.
Maybe nobody knows what you have been carrying.
Maybe you have been smiling publicly and collapsing privately.
Maybe you have spent years believing that if people knew everything about you, they would never look at you the same way again.
Listen carefully.
Jesus already knows everything.
