Because somewhere between Leah's tears, Rachel's jealousy, Jacob's preference, Joseph's robe, and the brothers' hatred...
you recognized your house.
Or maybe you recognized yourself.
Don't run from that recognition.
Bring it to Jesus.
Not because typing a comment saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing something into the light begins with refusing to pretend anymore.
Let somebody else reading know they are not the only person trying to build a healthier home than the one they inherited.
And send this to someone personally.
Not as an accusation.
Not “You need to read this.”
Send it with compassion.
“I read this and thought maybe we both needed it.”
Saving an article might seem small, but save this one for the day an old family wound suddenly starts speaking again.
Then return to the truth.
Your wound is not your identity.
Your family pattern is not your destiny.
Christ is not asking you to pretend the past never happened.
He is calling you to stop letting the past become your master.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you open Scripture, confront sin, heal through biblical truth, and grow deeper in Jesus, stay close.
Not because giving money earns God's favor.
It does not.
It does not.
Your support helps us keep creating and distributing Christ-centered resources while pointing people back to Scripture, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and Jesus.
If you want to support the mission and go deeper:
Come to Christ.
Because the greatest tragedy would be reading about Jacob's broken family, recognizing your own wounds, feeling deeply moved...
and still refusing the Savior who came to redeem sinners.
Rachel was favored.
Leah was wounded.
Rachel was wounded too.
Jacob repeated what had once wounded his own family.
Joseph became favored.
The brothers became bitter.
The family fractured.
And still...
God was not finished.
That is grace.
Not the denial of scandal.
The redemption of people inside it.
Maybe your family tree has names you do not like discussing.
Maybe there are divorces.
Affairs.
Addictions.
Abandonment.
Favoritism.
Abuse.
Jealousy.
Estrangement.
Secrets.
Years nobody can recover.
You cannot rewrite yesterday.
But Jesus Christ can redeem what yesterday tried to destroy.
So stop asking whether your family history is too messy for God.
Look at Genesis.
Then look at the cross.
God has always been extraordinarily good at bringing redemption into stories humans thought they had ruined beyond repair.
Because perhaps the child who spent years asking, “Why wasn't I the favorite?” needs to hear something infinitely greater:
At the cross, Jesus did not offer you favoritism. He offered you grace—and grace is better, because it was never something you had to defeat somebody else to receive.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Satan Quoted Scripture Too—Knowing Verses Is Not the Same as Teaching Truth
paragraphs: Satan Quoted Scripture Too—Knowing Verses Is Not the Same as Teaching Truth
The most dangerous lie may not sound like a lie at all. Sometimes it comes carrying a Bible, quoting a verse correctly, and asking you to believe something God never actually said.
There is a moment in the wilderness that should make every Christian who teaches, posts, preaches, shares devotionals, quotes Bible verses, or says, “God told me…” tremble.
Jesus is standing at the highest point of the temple.
And Satan begins quoting Scripture.
Not pagan philosophy.
Not atheism.
Not some obviously demonic sentence that any believer could recognize from a mile away.
Scripture.
That should bother us.
Because apparently, having Bible verses in your mouth is not proof that biblical truth is governing your heart.
Matthew records the devil saying:
“γέγραπται γὰρ…”
Gegraptai gar.
“For it is written…”
Then Satan quotes from Psalm 91.
The Greek wording in Matthew 4:6 includes:
“Τοῖς ἀγγέλοις αὐτοῦ ἐντελεῖται περὶ σοῦ…”
“He will command His angels concerning You…”
And:
“ἐπὶ χειρῶν ἀροῦσίν σε…”
“They will lift You up in their hands…”
Those words come from Scripture.
That is what makes this scene so disturbing.
Satan did not need to invent a fake Bible verse.
He needed only to take a true one and use it wrongly.
Read that again.
Because some of the most spiritually destructive teaching you will ever encounter may contain words that are completely biblical while communicating a message that is not.
A verse can be authentic while its application is false.
A quotation can be accurate while its conclusion is corrupt.
Someone can say something the Bible says without teaching what the Bible means.
And that distinction may save your faith from manipulation.
Psalm 91:11 in Hebrew reads:
“כִּי מַלְאָכָיו יְצַוֶּה־לָּךְ לִשְׁמָרְךָ בְּכָל־דְּרָכֶיךָ”
Ki mal'akhav yetsavveh-lakh, lishmorkha bekhol-derakhekha.
The sense is:
“For He will command His angels concerning you, to guard you in all your ways.”
Then verse 12 continues:
“עַל־כַּפַּיִם יִשָּׂאוּנְךָ פֶּן־תִּגֹּף בָּאֶבֶן רַגְלֶךָ”
Al-kappayim yissa'unekha, pen-tiggof ba'even raglekha.
“They will bear you upon their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone.”
Beautiful words.
True words.
God-breathed words.
And in Matthew 4, the devil weaponizes them.
He essentially tells Jesus:
If You really are the Son of God, prove it.
Jump.
God promised protection.
Make Him demonstrate it.
Turn trust into a stunt.
Turn faith into presumption.
Turn the Father's promise into a test the Father must pass.
And suddenly you begin to understand something frightening about deception.
The enemy does not always need to convince you to reject Scripture.
Sometimes he only needs to convince you to misuse it.
He does not always whisper, “The Bible is false.”
Sometimes the temptation is much subtler:
“Here is a verse. Ignore everything around it.”
And Jesus refuses.
His answer is devastatingly simple:
“Πάλιν γέγραπται…”
Palin gegraptai.
“Again, it is written…”
Then:
“Οὐκ ἐκπειράσεις κύριον τὸν θεόν σου.”
“You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.”
Jesus answers from Deuteronomy 6:16.
Do you see what happened?
Satan quoted Scripture.
Jesus interpreted Scripture with Scripture.
The issue was never whether Psalm 91 was true.
Of course it was true.
The issue was what Psalm 91 meant and whether Satan had the right to make it mean something God never intended.
Jesus did not reject the promise.
He rejected the manipulation of the promise.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because we live in an age of cropped Bible verses.
A verse over beautiful music.
A verse printed over a sunrise.
A verse in a thirty-second video.
A verse beneath somebody's opinion.
A verse attached to a political argument.
A verse used to promise money.
A verse used to excuse sin.
A verse used to control frightened people.
A verse used to tell suffering Christians that if they had enough faith, their pain would disappear.
A verse used to baptize ambition.
A verse used to make personal desires sound like divine decrees.
And because there is a Bible reference underneath it, we assume God signed His name to the entire message.
But Satan quoted Scripture too.
That does not mean everyone who misinterprets Scripture is satanic. Christians can make sincere mistakes, and faithful believers should correct one another with humility.
But Matthew 4 destroys the idea that quotation alone proves interpretation.
It doesn't.
The question is not merely:
“Did they quote a verse?”
The deeper question is:
“Is that what the verse actually means?”
What comes before it?
What comes after it?
Who is speaking?
Who is being addressed?
What is happening historically?
How does this passage fit within the book?
How does it fit within the whole counsel of Scripture?
And above everything else...
Where does this lead us concerning Jesus Christ?
Because the Bible was never given to become ammunition for our egos.
It was given to reveal God, expose sin, proclaim redemption, make us wise for salvation, train God's people in righteousness, and ultimately bear witness to the saving work fulfilled in Jesus Christ.
You can memorize hundreds of verses and still resist the Lord those verses reveal.
That sentence hurts.
Especially if you grew up around Christianity.
Maybe you know the language.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know the songs.
You know how Christians talk.
You know Romans 8:28.
You know Philippians 4:13.
You know Jeremiah 29:11.
You know Psalm 23.
Maybe you can explain doctrine.
Maybe people come to you for spiritual advice.
Maybe your social media profile is covered with Scripture.
Maybe you have taught others.
Maybe you are reading this thinking about all the false teachers who need to see it.
But before you send this to them...
What if the Holy Spirit wants to search you?
And me.
Because there is a quieter way to misuse Scripture that happens inside ordinary Christian hearts.
We search for verses that agree with decisions we already made.
We ask God for guidance after deciding what answer we want.
We highlight promises and quietly walk past commands.
We love “God will provide,” but struggle with “seek first His kingdom.”
We love grace when we need forgiveness but sometimes forget that the grace that forgives us also trains us to renounce ungodliness.
We want Scripture to comfort us...
but not confront us.
To reassure us...
but not correct us.
To validate our dreams...
but not crucify our pride.
And if we are not careful, the Bible stops becoming the voice that examines us and becomes a collection of sentences we recruit to defend ourselves.
That is not discipleship.
That is using God.
There is an enormous difference between asking, “What verse supports what I believe?” and asking, “Lord, what must I believe because You have spoken?”
One puts us over Scripture.
The other places us underneath it.
And somewhere reading this is a person who has been wounded by someone holding a Bible.
Maybe Scripture was used to silence you when you asked legitimate questions.
Maybe someone quoted “submission” while refusing accountability.
Maybe someone used forgiveness to pressure you into pretending consequences no longer mattered.
Maybe someone promised prosperity God never guaranteed.
Maybe you were told every tragedy happened because you lacked faith.
Maybe someone confidently said, “God told me,” and you were terrified that questioning them meant questioning God.
Listen carefully.
Jesus is not threatened by honest examination of what people claim in His name.
In Acts 17, the Bereans were commended for examining the Scriptures to see whether Paul's teaching was true.
Think about that.
They checked the teaching of an apostle against Scripture.
Biblical discernment is not rebellion.
But discernment must also never become an excuse for arrogance.
There is another ditch waiting for us.
You can become so obsessed with detecting false teaching that you become proud of your own correctness.
You can win arguments about theology while your heart becomes cold.
You can expose everybody else's error while refusing to repent of your own sin.
You can know Greek words, Hebrew grammar, historical backgrounds, theological systems, creeds, commentaries, and doctrines...
and still desperately need Jesus.
Knowledge matters.
Doctrine matters.
Truth matters enormously.
But truth was never meant to inflate the disciple.
It was meant to transform the disciple.
Paul warned that knowledge can puff up while love builds up.
James warned teachers that they will be judged with greater strictness.
Jesus repeatedly confronted people who possessed extraordinary familiarity with Scripture while failing to recognize the One standing before them.
That is the tragedy.
Imagine knowing the verses...
and missing the Word made flesh.
Imagine studying messianic expectation...
and rejecting Messiah.
Imagine defending Scripture...
while resisting the Lord of Scripture.
That is why this cannot merely be an article about “those false teachers.”
It has to become a mirror.
What are you doing with God's Word?
When Scripture contradicts your lifestyle, which one moves?
When Jesus confronts your bitterness, do you repent or find another verse?
When Scripture confronts your sexual sin, your greed, your dishonesty, your pride, your unforgiveness, your secret addiction, your hatred, your envy, your self-righteousness...
do you surrender?
Or do you negotiate?
Because the final evidence that you understand Scripture is not that you can quote more of it than everyone else.
The question is whether the truth is bringing you to Jesus in repentance, faith, obedience, love, holiness, humility, and dependence upon grace.
And here is where this wilderness story becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did what Adam failed to do.
Israel was tested in the wilderness and failed repeatedly.
Christ entered the wilderness and remained faithful.
He would not turn stones into bread at Satan's command.
He would not force the Father's hand by jumping from the temple.
He would not bow for the kingdoms of the world.
The Son obeyed.
Where humanity failed...
Jesus remained faithful.
And He continued walking toward the cross.
That matters because Christianity is not ultimately the story of good people becoming better at Bible interpretation.
It is the story of sinners who desperately need a Savior.
All of us have twisted things.
All of us have justified ourselves.
All of us have wanted God's blessing more than God's rule.
All of us have sinned.
And none of us can rescue ourselves by becoming religious enough.
So Jesus went to the cross.
Not merely to improve us.
To redeem us.
The righteous One for the unrighteous.
The innocent for the guilty.
The obedient Son bearing the judgment deserved by rebels.
He was crucified.
Buried.
And He rose again.
That means your worst misuse of truth does not have to be the final chapter of your story.
Your hypocrisy does not have to be the final chapter.
Your secret sin does not have to be the final chapter.
Your years of pretending do not have to be the final chapter.
Your spiritual pride does not have to be the final chapter.
Your religious performance does not have to be the final chapter.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Stop hiding behind verses and surrender to the Savior those verses reveal.
Grace does not mean God pretends your sin never mattered.
Grace means Christ paid a price you could never pay so that sinners who turn to Him can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and transformed.
That is the scandal.
The guilty are offered mercy because the Innocent One took their place.
The rebels are invited home.
The ashamed are clothed in Christ.
The broken are not discarded.
The sinner who finally stops defending himself can discover something astonishing:
Jesus already knew the whole story.
And He still went to Calvary.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So perhaps today you need to stop asking whether you know enough Bible verses.
Maybe the question is whether the Bible you know has brought you to your knees before Christ.
Not, “Can I quote Scripture?”
But:
“Does Scripture rule me?”
Not:
“Can I identify everybody else's error?”
But:
“Lord Jesus, where am I wrong?”
Not:
“Can I defend Christianity?”
But:
“Have I surrendered to Christ?”
If something inside you has been exposed while reading this, don't rush past it.
Be honest.
Not because typing words saves you.
Only Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when pride finally stops pretending.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
But if biblical truth has strengthened you, sharing it can become one simple way of placing that truth where someone else may encounter it.
Maybe the person who needs this will never walk into your church.
Maybe they will never open the Bible someone gave them.

Come back to it whenever a viral sermon, prophetic claim, inspirational quotation, theological argument, or thirty-second clip sounds biblical but leaves you wondering whether it actually represents Scripture faithfully.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend drifting from God.
Invite the believer who is discouraged.
Invite the seeker with difficult questions.
Invite the lukewarm Christian.
Even invite the person who does not yet believe.
Let them encounter Christ.
We want your support to come freely, not through spiritual pressure.
keep following Jesus.
Keep opening your Bible.
Keep reading verses in their context.
Keep testing teaching.
Keep praying for wisdom.
Keep receiving correction.
Keep repenting when Scripture exposes you.
Keep returning to grace.
Because Satan's ability to quote Scripture was never evidence that he belonged to God.
And your ability to quote Scripture is not the foundation of your salvation either.
Jesus is.
The Word of God is not a costume we wear to look holy.
It is truth that leads us to the Holy One.
So the next time someone says...
“It is written…”
don't stop listening because they quoted a verse.
Open the Bible.
Read what surrounds it.
Test the interpretation.
Look at the fruit.
Consider the whole counsel of God.
And above all, keep your eyes fixed on Jesus.
Because you can have a verse in your mouth while your heart runs from its Author.
But when the Author captures your heart...
the verses stop becoming weapons for proving yourself right.
They become bread.
Light.
Correction.
Hope.
Truth.
And a road leading a sinner home.
Never become so impressed that someone can quote the Bible that you forget to ask whether they are faithfully leading you to the Jesus the Bible reveals.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Can One Man Truly Be “One Flesh” With Multiple Wives?
paragraphs: Can One Man Truly Be “One Flesh” With Multiple Wives?

The Bible records men with many wives. God even regulated life in polygamous households. But when Jesus was asked what marriage truly is, He did something striking: He did not point to Abraham, Jacob, David, or Solomon. He went back before the scandal—back to Eden.
There is a question hiding inside Genesis that becomes uncomfortable the moment you refuse to answer it too quickly.
If a man can become “one flesh” with a woman…
what happens when there is another woman?
And another?
Can one husband be “one flesh” with several wives at the same time?
Or have we confused something the Bible records with something God designed?
That distinction matters.

Because Scripture contains stories that are brutally honest about human beings. It records murder without blessing murder. It records adultery without sanctifying adultery. It records deception, drunkenness, slavery, betrayal, violence, idolatry, and catastrophic family failure without presenting those things as the Creator's ideal.
And yes—the Bible records polygamy.
Abraham had Sarah and Hagar.
Jacob had Leah and Rachel, along with Bilhah and Zilpah.
David had multiple wives.
Solomon multiplied wives on a scale that eventually became spiritually catastrophic.
So someone can open the Old Testament and reasonably ask:
“If God intended one man and one woman, why are all these men walking around with multiple wives?”
That question deserves more than a slogan.
It deserves Scripture.
And perhaps the most revealing place to begin is not with Solomon's palace, David's household, Jacob's tents, or Abraham's family.
It is with a garden.
Before kings.
Before Israel.
Before Moses.
Before human civilization had accumulated centuries of broken customs.
Before adultery.
Before divorce.
Before jealousy.
Before lust had ever shattered a household.
Before sin entered the world, Scripture gives us the pattern:
one man, one woman, one covenantal union.
Genesis 2:24 reads in Hebrew:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִּמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
ʿAl-kēn yaʿăzov-ʾîš ʾet-ʾāvîw wəʾet-ʾimmô, wədāvaq bəʾištô, wəhāyû ləbāśār ʾeḥād.
In straightforward English:
“Therefore a man leaves his father and his mother and clings to his wife, and they become one flesh.”
The final words are unforgettable:
לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד — ləbasar echad — “one flesh.”
Notice the movement.
A man.
His wife.
They become one flesh.

The Hebrew verb דָּבַק — davaq carries the sense of clinging, adhering, holding fast. Marriage is not pictured merely as two people sharing an address or obtaining social permission for sexual relations. Something profound happens: two lives are joined in a new covenantal reality.
And אֶחָד — echad means “one.”

We should be careful here, because Christians sometimes make linguistic claims that Hebrew itself cannot support. Echad does not secretly mean “compound unity” in every occurrence, nor does the word by itself prove monogamy. Its ordinary meaning is simply one.
The argument is stronger when we allow the text to speak naturally rather than forcing more into a Hebrew word than it actually says.
One man leaves.
He clings to his wife.
They become one flesh.
And centuries later, when religious leaders questioned Jesus about marriage and divorce, Jesus reached directly back to this creation account.
That is where the discussion becomes difficult to escape.
Jesus said:
“Have you not read that He who created them from the beginning made them male and female…?”
Then He quoted Genesis:
“The two shall become one flesh.”
And concluded:
“So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Matthew preserves the Greek expression:
οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
hoi dyo eis sarka mian
“the two into one flesh.”
Two.
One flesh.
Jesus could have grounded marriage in the later practices of Israel's patriarchs or kings.
He didn't.
He went to “the beginning.”
That matters enormously.
Because Jesus distinguishes between what entered human society in its brokenness and what God intended in creation.

In the same discussion, when His opponents appealed to Moses' provision for divorce, Jesus answered that Moses permitted divorce because of the hardness of human hearts, and then He uttered the words that should govern how Christians approach many difficult Old Testament marriage texts:
“But from the beginning it was not so.”
There is a world of theology in that sentence.
From the beginning it was not so.
In other words, the existence of a regulated practice within fallen human society does not automatically establish that practice as God's creational ideal.
That principle helps us understand polygamy.

Scripture undeniably contains legal provisions dealing with households in which more than one wife exists. Exodus 21:10, for example, protects a wife's provision if another wife is taken. Deuteronomy 21:15–17 addresses inheritance in a household containing two wives.
Those passages matter.
But regulation is not necessarily endorsement.
A law can restrain injustice inside an already broken social arrangement without declaring the arrangement itself to be the Creator's original design.
And Scripture does something else remarkable.
It repeatedly allows us to watch what happens inside polygamous households.
The pictures are rarely romantic.
Abraham's household becomes torn by Sarah and Hagar's conflict.
Jacob loves Rachel more than Leah.
Leah lives with the agony of being the less-loved wife.
Rachel envies her sister.
The sisters compete for Jacob's affection and children.
The household becomes emotionally fractured.
Then comes David.
Multiple marriages become intertwined with political power, family rivalries, sexual catastrophe, and eventually a household marked by devastating dysfunction.
Then Solomon.
And Scripture does not whisper about what happened.
The king who accumulated wives eventually allowed those relationships to pull his heart toward other gods.
Deuteronomy had already warned Israel's future king:
“He shall not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.”
Solomon multiplied them anyway.
His heart turned.
The pattern is difficult to miss.
Yet we should make an important distinction if we want to remain faithful to everything Scripture says.
The Bible's theological case is not simply, “Every man who ever had multiple wives was therefore incapable of any genuine marital or sexual union with those women.”
Paul prevents us from making “one flesh” so narrow that it describes only an ideal marriage ceremony.
In 1 Corinthians 6:16, warning Christians against sexual immorality, Paul writes that the one joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her, and then quotes Genesis:
“The two will become one flesh.”
The Greek text says:
ὁ κολλώμενος τῇ πόρνῃ ἓν σῶμά ἐστιν … Οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
Paul's warning is startling precisely because sexual union is not spiritually or bodily trivial. Even an immoral sexual joining invokes the profound bodily reality for which sexuality was created.
So the careful answer to our question requires nuance.
Can a man have real sexual and marital bonds with more than one woman?
Biblically, yes, Scripture recognizes that such relationships existed and treats the women involved as wives rather than pretending the relationships were imaginary.
But can multiplying those unions reproduce the exclusive creational pattern Jesus identifies when He defines marriage from Genesis?
That is where the answer changes.
The pattern Jesus gives is not one man endlessly adding separate “one-flesh” relationships.
It is the two becoming one.
And this becomes even more beautiful when Paul carries Genesis 2 into Ephesians 5.
Marriage suddenly becomes bigger than marriage.
Paul quotes the ancient words about leaving, cleaving, and becoming one flesh—and then says:
“This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.”
Now we are standing on holy ground.
Christian marriage is not merely about companionship.
Not merely romance.
Not merely sex.
Not merely children.
Not merely legal status.
Marriage has been drawn into a Gospel-shaped mystery.
A husband is commanded to love his wife as Christ loved the church and gave Himself for her.
Think about that.
Christ does not casually consume His bride.
He gives Himself for her.
Christ does not collect brides as trophies of His power.
He lays down His life for His bride.
Christ does not exploit covenant.
He bleeds for covenant.
The Gospel transforms the question from:
“How many wives can a man technically possess?”
into something far more searching:
“What kind of marriage tells the truth about Jesus?”
Suddenly the argument is no longer merely about numbers.
It is about covenant.
Faithfulness.
Sacrifice.
Exclusive devotion.
Holy love.
And perhaps that is why this subject reaches much farther than polygamy.
Because most people reading this will never have multiple spouses.
But many of us know exactly what it feels like to have a divided heart.
You can have one spouse and still give pornography the intimacy that belongs to your marriage.
You can have one spouse and secretly cultivate another emotional relationship.
You can have one spouse while your heart belongs to ambition.
You can sleep beside someone every night while emotionally abandoning them.
You can wear a wedding ring while hiding messages.
You can preach covenant while feeding lust.
You can publicly defend biblical marriage while privately destroying your own.
And suddenly this article is not about Solomon anymore.
It is about us.
That is where Scripture becomes uncomfortable.
We love discussing someone else's scandal because it allows us to avoid confronting our own.
We can debate Abraham.
Analyze Jacob.
Condemn David.
Shake our heads at Solomon.
And never ask what Jesus sees when He looks at our hidden lives.
Maybe nobody knows what is on your phone.
Maybe nobody knows about the conversations you delete.
Maybe nobody knows why your marriage feels cold.
Maybe nobody knows about the fantasy you keep feeding.
Maybe nobody knows how lonely you are.
Maybe nobody knows that you are reading Christian content while quietly wondering whether God could possibly still want you after what you have done.
But Jesus knows.
And here is the part religion sometimes gets terribly wrong:
Jesus knowing your scandal is not the same thing as Jesus being finished with you.
The Gospel does not say sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more terribly than we want to admit.
But the cross also proves that God's grace reaches farther than sinners dare to hope.
Jesus Christ did not come because humanity had maintained Eden perfectly.
He came because we hadn't.
We broke covenant.
We distorted desire.
We wounded people.
We worshiped created things.
We betrayed.
We hid.
We blamed.
We lusted.
We hardened our hearts.
And the Son of God stepped directly into the wreckage.
Not to rename darkness as light.
Not to call adultery faithfulness.
Not to pretend sexual sin is harmless.
Not to congratulate us for rewriting His commands.
He came to save sinners.
There is an enormous difference between grace and permission.
Permission says, “Stay as you are.”
Grace says, “Come as you are—and Jesus will not leave you as you are.”
That is Christianity.
Repentance is not God demanding that you clean yourself before approaching Christ.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Christ whose mercy you desperately need.
The adulterer can repent.
The sexually broken can repent.
The pornography addict can repent.
The husband who has failed his wife can repent.
The wife who has betrayed her husband can repent.
The person carrying years of sexual shame can come into the light.
The person whose family history looks more like Genesis' scandals than Eden's beauty is not beyond redemption.
And no, restoration does not always erase earthly consequences.
Some wounds take years to heal.
Some relationships require difficult truth, pastoral wisdom, accountability, boundaries, counseling, and patient rebuilding.
Grace is not pretending nothing happened.
Grace is discovering that what happened does not have to write the final sentence.
That is why the Gospel Warrior theme matters so deeply:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by rewriting God's definition of holiness.
By rewriting the sinner's destiny.
The cross does not change sin into righteousness.
The cross takes guilty sinners and, through faith in Christ, clothes them in a righteousness they could never manufacture for themselves.
And perhaps you came here asking whether one man can truly be “one flesh” with multiple wives.
But somewhere along the way, another question found you:
Is my heart actually one with Christ—or have I divided it among a hundred other lovers?
Money.
Pornography.
Approval.
Status.
Resentment.
Secret relationships.
Pride.
Religion without surrender.
A public Christianity protecting a private rebellion.
Jesus does not merely want a corner of you.
He is Lord.
And the astonishing news of the Gospel is that the One who has every right to condemn repentant sinners is the very One who stretched out His hands to save them.
So stop hiding.
Bring the secret into His light.
Confess.
Repent.
Ask forgiveness where forgiveness must be asked.
Seek help where help is needed.
Return to Scripture.
Return to prayer.
Return to covenant faithfulness.
Return to Christ.
Not because your repentance purchases mercy.
Because mercy has already come looking for sinners in the person of Jesus.
If this exposed something you have kept hidden, you do not need to tell strangers the details. But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Let other believers pray instead of letting shame convince you that you have to fight alone.
Not to win an argument.
To bring someone closer to truth.

Some truths are not meant to be consumed once between two pieces of entertainment and forgotten. Come back to the Scriptures. Check the claims. Read Genesis 2, Matthew 19, 1 Corinthians 6, Ephesians 5, Deuteronomy 17, and the complicated household stories for yourself.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.

If this ministry is feeding you spiritually, stay close. Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians—and even the unbeliever who keeps asking hard questions—to follow too.
Follow because discipleship is not a moment of emotion. It is a life of continually returning to Christ.
Because beneath all the arguments about marriage is an even greater marriage story.
A Bridegroom came looking for a broken people.
We were not spotless.
He is making us spotless.
We were not faithful.
He remained faithful.
We could not rescue ourselves.
So He gave Himself.
That is the Gospel.
And when Jesus gets hold of a scandal, He does not call the scandal good.
He writes grace where sin thought it had already written the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Boaz Was Closer to David Than Most People Realize — And His Family Story Points Straight to Jesus
paragraphs: Boaz Was Closer to David Than Most People Realize — And His Family Story Points Straight to Jesus

He was not merely a distant ancestor in an old genealogy. Boaz was King David’s great-grandfather—and when you follow the bloodline through Ruth, Rahab, David, and ultimately Jesus Christ, you discover something breathtaking about the kind of families God is willing to redeem.
There is a detail hidden near the end of Ruth that is easy to read too quickly.
A wedding happens.
A child is born.
Names are recorded.
The story appears to be ending.
But then Scripture quietly drops a name that changes the meaning of everything that came before it.
David.
Not just any David.
The David.
The shepherd boy.
The giant killer.
The psalmist.
The fugitive.
The warrior.
The sinner who would fall catastrophically.
The repentant king.
The man whose royal line would eventually lead the Gospel writer Matthew to Jesus Christ.
And suddenly you realize that the little love story between a grieving Moabite widow and an honorable man from Bethlehem was never merely about two lonely people finding each other.
God was building a royal family while almost everyone involved was simply trying to survive.
That should make some of us stop reading for a moment.
Because perhaps you have looked at the broken pieces of your own family and wondered whether anything beautiful could possibly come from them.
Perhaps there are names in your family history you would rather not discuss.
Divorce.
Addiction.
Abandonment.
Betrayal.
Infidelity.
Poverty.
Abuse.
Prison.
Failure.
Secrets.
Maybe your family tree does not look like something God would use.
Neither did this one.
And that is exactly why you need to understand who Boaz was to David.
The Hebrew text at the end of Ruth gives the genealogy with almost startling simplicity:
וְשַׂלְמוֹן֙ הוֹלִ֣יד אֶת־בֹּ֔עַז וּבֹ֖עַז הוֹלִ֥יד אֶת־עוֹבֵֽד׃ וְעֹבֵד֙ הוֹלִ֣יד אֶת־יִשָׁ֔י וְיִשַׁ֖י הוֹלִ֥יד אֶת־דָּוִֽד׃
Ve-Salmon holid et-Bo'az, u-Vo'az holid et-Oved; ve-Oved holid et-Yishai, ve-Yishai holid et-David.
In straightforward English:
Salmon fathered Boaz. Boaz fathered Obed. Obed fathered Jesse. Jesse fathered David.
That genealogy is explicitly preserved in Ruth 4:21–22.
So how exactly was Boaz related to David?
Boaz was David's great-grandfather.
Boaz and Ruth became the parents of Obed.
Obed became the father of Jesse.
Jesse became the father of David.
Boaz → Obed → Jesse → David.
There is no need to speculate. Scripture gives us the relationship directly.
But knowing the answer is only the beginning.
Because once you know who Boaz was to David, another question becomes far more interesting:
Why did God make sure we knew?
Ruth begins nowhere near a throne.
It begins with famine.
A man named Elimelech leaves Bethlehem with his wife Naomi and their sons. They settle in Moab. Then Elimelech dies. Naomi's sons marry Moabite women, Ruth and Orpah.
Then both sons die too.
Three widows.
Three funerals.
No obvious future.
No king.
No palace.
No heroic music playing in the background.
Just grief.
Naomi eventually returns to Bethlehem so devastated that she tells the women there not to call her Naomi—associated with pleasantness—but Mara, meaning bitter.
She had left full, she said, and returned empty.
And somewhere reading this is a person who understands that sentence without needing it explained.
You left one season believing life was going somewhere.
Then the phone rang.
The relationship ended.
The person died.
The money disappeared.
The betrayal surfaced.
The prayer seemed unanswered.
The future you had pictured collapsed.
You came back carrying a version of yourself you barely recognized.
Naomi believed she had returned empty.
But walking beside her was Ruth.
And Naomi could not yet see what God was going to do through the woman walking beside her.
That is one of the brutal limitations of pain:
grief can make emptiness feel more visible than grace.
Ruth was a Moabite outsider. Humanly speaking, she did not arrive in Bethlehem looking like the beginning of a royal dynasty.
She arrived as a widow gathering leftover grain.
Think about that.
The great-grandmother of King David entered this part of the biblical story picking up what harvesters left behind.
And then she walked into the field of Boaz.
Boaz is introduced as a man of standing from Elimelech's family. As Ruth's story unfolds, he becomes the willing family redeemer who acts lawfully and compassionately toward Ruth and Naomi.
This matters because the biblical idea surrounding redemption in Ruth is not sentimental romance.
It involves costly covenant responsibility.
The Hebrew root associated with the redeemer is גאל — ga'al, and the related noun גֹּאֵל — go'el refers to one who acts as a redeemer within the obligations of kinship.
Boaz does not merely tell Ruth that he cares.
He acts.
He protects.
He provides.
He assumes responsibility.
He publicly settles the matter at the city gate.
He pays the cost associated with taking up the family obligation.
And then he marries Ruth.
Scripture says that the LORD enabled Ruth to conceive, and she gave birth to a son.
They called him Obed.
Then Scripture pulls the camera backward.
Obed becomes the father of Jesse.
Jesse becomes the father of David.
The grieving widow gathering grain in a Bethlehem field becomes the great-grandmother of Israel's most famous king.
And Boaz becomes David's great-grandfather.
But centuries later, another genealogy opens.
Matthew begins tracing the ancestry of Jesus Christ.
Genealogies are the part many readers are tempted to skim.
Do not skim this one.
Because suddenly familiar names appear.
Matthew records that Salmon fathered Boaz by Rahab, Boaz fathered Obed by Ruth, Obed fathered Jesse, and Jesse fathered David the king.
Read that again slowly.
Rahab.
Ruth.
Boaz.
Obed.
Jesse.
David.
And Matthew keeps going.
Toward Jesus.

This does not mean every detail people sometimes attach to these characters is equally certain. We should be careful not to turn speculation into Scripture. But Matthew explicitly names Rahab in connection with Boaz and Ruth in connection with Obed. That claim is in the biblical text itself.
And now the family tree becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
Rahab's story begins for us in Jericho, where she is identified as a prostitute.
Ruth is a Moabite widow.
David becomes Israel's celebrated king—but later commits adultery with Bathsheba and orchestrates Uriah's death.
Yet the genealogy keeps moving.
Not because sin does not matter.
It matters so much that Christ had to die.
Not because repentance is optional.
Jesus' message calls sinners to turn to God.
Not because grace pretends evil never happened.
Grace is not denial.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy toward guilty and broken people, ultimately displayed at the cross where Christ bore sin and opened the way of reconciliation to God.
That distinction matters.
The message of this genealogy is not, “Your past doesn't matter.”
The message is far more powerful:
Your past does not have greater authority than the redeeming purposes of God.
There are consequences God does not erase.
There are wounds that leave scars.
There are choices that cannot simply be undone.
David himself would learn that painfully.
Christian redemption is not God calling darkness light.
It is God entering our darkness with a Savior.
And this is where Boaz becomes more than an interesting answer to a Bible trivia question.
Boaz was a real redeemer within the historical and covenant setting of Ruth.
But Christians should not confuse Boaz with Jesus or force every detail of his life into an allegory. Boaz is not Christ.
Jesus is infinitely greater.
Yet the biblical theme of redemption that shines through Ruth prepares our hearts to understand something central to the Gospel:
redemption costs the redeemer something.
Boaz was willing to act for Ruth.
Jesus came to save sinners at the cost of His own blood.
Peter writes that believers were redeemed not with perishable things such as silver or gold, but with the precious blood of Christ.
That is the center.
Not Boaz.
Not David.
Not Ruth.
Not Rahab.
Jesus.
Boaz's story moves toward David.
David's royal line moves toward Christ.

Matthew intentionally presents Jesus as the Messiah, the son of David, the son of Abraham, and organizes the genealogy around the movement from Abraham to David, David to the exile, and the exile to the Christ.
And there is something especially moving about Bethlehem.
Ruth gathered grain around Bethlehem.
Boaz lived there.
Obed entered the family story there.
David would come from Bethlehem.
And generations later, according to the Gospel accounts, Jesus would be born in Bethlehem.
The field that looked ordinary was standing inside a story far larger than anyone could see.
Maybe your life feels like that field right now.
Ordinary.
Unnoticed.
Hard.
You are simply trying to make it through another day.
Trying to raise your children.
Trying to rebuild your marriage.
Trying to resist the temptation nobody knows about.
Trying to forgive someone who wounded you.
Trying to pray when heaven feels silent.
Trying to come back to Jesus after wandering farther than you ever intended.
You may think nothing significant is happening.
Ruth probably did not wake up every morning thinking, “I am becoming the great-grandmother of a king.”
She needed food.
Naomi needed hope.
Boaz needed to decide whether he would live honorably before God.
They lived faithfully inside the day they had been given.
God could see generations they could not.
That does not mean every Christian will become famous, wealthy, influential, or historically remembered. Scripture never promises that.
Something better is true.
No act of faithfulness offered to Christ is meaningless simply because nobody applauds it.
You do not know what God may accomplish through an obedient decision made when nobody is watching.
The prayer you pray with your child.
The temptation you finally confess.
The relationship you refuse to compromise.
The person you forgive.
The Bible you open again after months away.
The church you return to.
The apology you finally make.
The secret sin you drag into the light.
The Gospel you share with one frightened person.
The decision to follow Jesus when your emotions are screaming for you to walk away.
You see today.
God sees generations.
And maybe that is why this genealogy hurts in the best possible way.
Because some of us have spent years believing our family history disqualified us.
“My father wasn't there.”
“My mother failed me.”
“My marriage collapsed.”
“I destroyed years of my life.”
“My children have seen things I wish they had never seen.”
“I have sexual sin in my past.”
“I've been addicted.”
“I've lied.”
“I've cheated.”
“I've walked away from God.”
“I knew better and still did it.”
Listen carefully.
The genealogy of Jesus does not give us permission to romanticize sin.
It gives sinners permission to run toward the Savior.
The cross does not say sin was insignificant.
The cross shows exactly how serious sin is.
The Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
And the resurrection announces that sin and death do not get the final word over those who belong to Christ.
This is why Christianity is not self-improvement.
You do not need a slightly cleaner version of yourself.
You need redemption.
You need forgiveness.
You need reconciliation with God.
You need the righteousness you cannot manufacture.
You need Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have been trying to edit your reputation while Jesus is calling you to surrender your heart.
Stop hiding.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the failure.
Bring Him the years you cannot recover.
Bring Him the family history you cannot rewrite.
You cannot change yesterday.
But Jesus can redeem the person who lived it.
That is grace.
And grace changes what happens next.
That is why the journey from Boaz to David matters.
Boaz did not live long enough to see everything God would accomplish through his descendants.
He never saw David standing before Goliath.
He never heard David's psalms echo through generations.
He never watched kings rise from that family line.
He never stood in Bethlehem centuries later and saw Mary holding the infant Jesus.
Boaz simply lived faithfully in his generation.
And God wrote his faithfulness into a story that reached far beyond his lifetime.
What if obedience is more important than visibility?
What if faithfulness matters more than applause?
What if the decision you make with Jesus tonight matters beyond what you can presently measure?
That is worth sitting with.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding from God, do not turn this into another article you read, felt, and forgot.
Talk to Him.
Be honest.
Someone reading beneath you may desperately need evidence that Jesus still restores people.

That is a meaningful way to support Gospel-centered work and glorify God: not because clicking a button earns God's favor—it absolutely does not—but because willingly helping biblical truth reach another person can be an act of Christian generosity and witness.
It does not make God love you more.
It does not earn salvation.
Salvation is by God's grace, received through faith in Christ.
But supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one practical way of participating in work you believe is helping people hear biblical truth.
Because now you know the answer.
How was Boaz related to David?
He was David's great-grandfather.
Boaz fathered Obed.
Obed fathered Jesse.
Jesse fathered David.
But beneath that simple genealogy is something far harder to forget.
A widow thought her future was finished.
A grieving woman thought she had returned empty.
A foreigner gathered leftovers from a field.
A man quietly chose integrity.
A child named Obed was born.
Then Jesse.
Then David.
And generations later, the genealogy leads us to Jesus Christ.
The people inside the story could see only the page they were living.
God could see where the genealogy was going.
Maybe tonight you can only see your page too.
Do not confuse an unfinished chapter with a finished story.
Repent where you have sinned.
Trust Christ where you are afraid.
Obey Him where the next step is clear.
And leave the pages you cannot see in the hands of the God who already sees them.
Because sometimes the place you thought your story ended is exactly where grace begins writing a name you never expected.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHEN THE PERSON YOU LOVE WANTS YOU MORE THAN YOU WANT SEX
paragraphs:
WHEN THE PERSON YOU LOVE WANTS YOU MORE THAN YOU WANT SEX
What If Your Spouse Has a Much Higher Sex Drive? The Christian Marriage Conversation We Keep Avoiding—Until Rejection, Resentment, Shame, and Silence Start Sleeping Between Us
There is a particular kind of loneliness that can happen in a marriage nobody else thinks is lonely.
You still sleep in the same bed.
You still say, “Love you.”

You still pay bills together, raise children together, pray before meals, attend church, laugh at old memories, and perhaps even post anniversary pictures that make everyone think your marriage is beautiful.
But somewhere between turning off the lamp and facing opposite sides of the mattress, something hurts.
One spouse is thinking:
Why don’t you want me anymore?
And the other is thinking:
Why does everything have to become about sex?
One feels rejected.
The other feels pressured.
One begins counting how long it has been.
The other begins dreading the moment affection might become expectation.
One wonders, Am I unattractive?
The other wonders, Am I failing as a spouse?
And sometimes neither one says any of it.
That is where the danger begins.
Because what started as a difference in sexual desire can slowly become something much larger.
Rejection.
Resentment.
Shame.
Suspicion.
Anger.
Withdrawal.
Pornography.
Fantasy.
Emotional distance.
Temptation.
And eventually two people who once could not wait to touch each other can become frightened to talk honestly about why they no longer know how.
If this is your marriage, hear this before anything else:
Your spouse is not the enemy.
And neither is sexual desire.
Scripture is far less embarrassed about marital sexuality than many Christians are.

The Song of Songs contains language that would make some church people uncomfortable precisely because Scripture refuses to pretend that married lovers are merely roommates who occasionally hold hands.
Listen to the Hebrew declaration of the bride:
אֲנִי לְדוֹדִי וְעָלַי תְּשׁוּקָתוֹ
Ani le-dodi, ve'alai teshuqato.
“I am my beloved’s, and his desire is for me.”
That is Song of Songs 7:10.

The word תְּשׁוּקָה — teshuqah carries the sense of desire or longing. The Song places that desire inside a larger picture of mutual romantic love and committed belonging. The woman is not describing herself as property. She is rejoicing in being desired by the one to whom she has lovingly given herself.
There is no shame in that.
Desire between husband and wife is not an embarrassing theological accident.
God created bodies.
God created marriage.
God created the possibility of marital delight.
But here is where many marriages become wounded:
God did not create two spouses as identical machines.
You can deeply love the same Jesus, faithfully honor the same covenant, and still experience desire differently.
Perhaps your husband desires sexual intimacy far more frequently than you do.
Perhaps it is your wife.
Yes, wives can be the higher-desire spouse too.
And that woman may suffer silently because she has absorbed the stereotype that “men always want sex.” So when her husband repeatedly does not, she begins wondering what is wrong with her.
Or with him.
Perhaps nothing is “wrong” in the simplistic sense.
Human desire is complicated.
Stress matters.
Sleep matters.
Conflict matters.
Parenthood matters.
Emotional closeness matters.
Age and life seasons can matter.
Physical wellbeing can matter.
Medication can matter.
Past experiences can matter.
And sometimes two people simply experience sexual desire at different frequencies.
The problem is not automatically that your spouse wants sex more often than you.
The deeper question is what the two of you do with that difference.
Because mismatched desire can become either a battlefield where two sinners punish one another...
or a place where two disciples learn how to love one another.
And Scripture says something remarkably radical about the marriage bed.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 7:3–4 that husband and wife owe one another marital affection and that, astonishingly in his ancient context, the authority language is reciprocal.
Not merely wife toward husband.
Husband toward wife too.
Then comes verse 5:
μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους
Mē apostereite allēlous.
In context: do not deprive or defraud one another.
That last idea matters enormously.
ἀλλήλους — allēlous — “one another.”
Paul's vision is mutual.
Christian marriage is not one spouse standing over the other shouting, “The Bible says you owe me.”
It is two people standing beneath the lordship of Jesus asking:
How can I faithfully love you?
That changes everything.
The higher-desire spouse must hear something difficult:
Your longing matters.
But your spouse is not an object God assigned to satisfy every sexual impulse whenever you experience it.
And the lower-desire spouse must hear something difficult too:

Your spouse's repeated experience of rejection may be hurting more deeply than you realize, and treating that pain as shallow, ridiculous, dirty, immature, or “just hormones” can wound the person you promised to cherish.
Both truths can exist at once.
That is why 1 Corinthians 7 must never become ammunition.
The passage calls spouses toward mutual care; it does not sanctify coercion.
Sex extracted through fear, threats, intimidation, manipulation, humiliation, spiritual blackmail, or disregard for another person's condition is not a beautiful fulfillment of biblical intimacy.
Jesus does not teach us to use Scripture to dominate people.
Look at the pattern Paul gives husbands elsewhere:
οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας
“Husbands, love your wives...”
And how?
“As Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”
Ephesians 5:25 does not point a husband toward selfish consumption.
It points him toward cruciform love.
Christ gives Himself.
Christ does not exploit His bride.
Christ's love is self-giving.
Imagine what would happen if that shaped the bedroom.
Instead of:
Why won't you give me what I need?
What if the question became:
What has your heart been carrying lately?
Instead of:
You never want me.
Perhaps:
When we go a long time without intimacy, I start feeling unwanted. I know that may not be what you mean, but I need you to understand what happens inside me.
Instead of:
All you care about is sex.
Perhaps:
Sometimes I become anxious about affection because I worry it must always lead somewhere. I want closeness with you, but I need to feel safe enough to tell you when I'm overwhelmed.
Do you hear the difference?
Accusation produces defense.
Vulnerability creates the possibility of understanding.
Sometimes the higher-desire spouse isn't merely saying, “I want sex.”
Sometimes underneath those words is:
I want to know that you still choose me.
I want to feel desired.
I miss us.
I don't know how to ask for tenderness without feeling weak.
And sometimes the lower-desire spouse isn't saying, “I don't love you.”
Sometimes underneath the hesitation is:
I'm exhausted.
I don't feel emotionally connected.
I feel pressure every time you touch me.
Something has changed in me and I don't understand it either.
I'm afraid you will take my “not tonight” as “I don't want you anymore.”
Two people can misinterpret each other for years.
That is the tragedy.
The husband thinks she is rejecting him when she may be struggling with exhaustion, unresolved hurt, fear, or simply a different pattern of desire.
The wife thinks he only wants her body when sexual intimacy may be one of the places where he most strongly experiences closeness and reassurance.
Reverse the genders and the pain can be just as real.
And suddenly you realize:
You haven't been fighting over sex.
You've been fighting over what sex means to each of you.
That conversation requires extraordinary tenderness.
Ask questions when you are not standing beside the bed waiting for an answer.
Talk when neither spouse is trying to initiate.
Ask:
When do you feel most desired by me?
When do you feel pressured by me?
What makes intimacy easier for you?
What makes you withdraw?
Have I made rejection feel dangerous?
Have I made desire feel shameful?
Are there hurts between us we keep carrying into the bedroom?
What does loving you faithfully in this season actually look like?
And then...
listen.
Do not listen like a lawyer waiting to cross-examine.
Listen like someone who made a covenant.
There may also be situations where wise help is needed.

Persistent or dramatic changes in sexual desire can have physical, emotional, relational, or medication-related dimensions worth discussing with an appropriate qualified professional. Serious unresolved marital conflict may warrant a wise Christian marriage counselor who respects both biblical conviction and personal dignity.

And where there has been sexual coercion, violence, threats, or abuse, this is no longer merely a “different sex drive” problem. Safety and qualified pastoral, professional, and where appropriate legal help matter.
But for many couples, healing may begin with something painfully ordinary.
Truth.
“I miss you.”
“I feel rejected.”
“I feel pressured.”
“I didn't know you felt that way.”
“I'm sorry.”
“Can we start again?”
Those sentences do not look spectacular.
Neither did a manger.
Neither did twelve ordinary disciples.
Neither did a bloodied Savior hanging between criminals.
God has always been extraordinarily good at beginning redemption in places human beings would overlook.
And this is where the Gospel reaches farther than bedroom advice ever could.
Because ultimately your marriage cannot be saved by achieving a perfectly synchronized libido.
You could solve the frequency problem and still have selfish hearts.
Marriage needs something deeper.
It needs grace.
The higher-desire spouse needs grace to reject entitlement.
The lower-desire spouse needs grace to reject contempt and indifference.
Both need grace to forgive.
Both need grace to repent.
Both need grace to speak truth without cruelty.
Both need grace to serve without keeping score.
Both need Jesus.
Because at the center of Christianity is not a technique for getting another person to meet your needs.
At the center is a Savior who gave Himself for sinners.
Christ did not wait until His bride was attractive enough.
Faithful enough.
Responsive enough.
Clean enough.
He loved.
He pursued.
He gave Himself.
The cross exposes the selfishness in all of us.
The cross also announces that selfish people can be forgiven.
That means the husband who has pressured can repent.
The wife who has weaponized rejection can repent.
The husband who withdrew can repent.
The wife who mocked can repent.
The spouse who escaped into pornography can repent.
The spouse carrying bitterness can bring it into the light.
Repentance does not mean pretending the damage never happened.
It means refusing to keep defending what Christ is calling you to surrender.
Maybe this article exposed something nobody knows.
Maybe you have been punishing your spouse with rejection.
Maybe you have been demanding intimacy instead of cultivating it.
Maybe pornography has become your secret substitute.
Maybe you have stopped touching because every touch became loaded with expectation.
Maybe your spouse lies inches away from you every night...
and you have never felt farther apart.
Then perhaps tonight does not need to begin with sex.
Perhaps it needs to begin with truth.
Put the phone down.
Turn toward the person you married.
And say what pride has kept buried.
“I don't want us to keep living like strangers.”
There are marriages that do not need another argument.
They need confession.
There are bedrooms that do not need another performance.
They need tenderness.
There are spouses who do not need to “win.”
They need to be seen.
And there are Christians reading this who need to remember that Jesus Christ is still in the resurrection business.
He resurrects what sin buries.
He restores what pride fractures.
He forgives what repentance brings into the light.
No, restoration is not always instant.
Some wounds require time.
Trust can require rebuilding.
Some conversations need help.
But never confuse “difficult” with “impossible for God.”
Be honest.

If you have walked through a season of mismatched desire and Christ taught you how to love your spouse more patiently, share part of your testimony. Someone silently reading may desperately need to discover that they are not the only married Christian who has struggled here.
Some conversations belong in private. Send this privately to a husband or wife who needs encouragement.
Save it too.
Not because every paragraph is comfortable.
Because difficult nights have a way of making us forget what we knew in peaceful ones.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, consider following and inviting your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends who are open to hearing about Jesus. We want this community to remain a place where Scripture confronts us, grace meets us, and Christ—not personalities, outrage, or algorithms—remains at the center.
You cannot purchase grace, and supporting a ministry does not make someone more righteous before God. Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
But willing generosity can become one practical way believers support Gospel-centered work they genuinely believe is bearing good fruit.
Share because somebody else's marriage may be silently bleeding.
Follow because we all need truth repeatedly, not occasionally.
Save what you may need to remember later.
Tag with wisdom.
And comment because sometimes bringing a struggle into the light begins with three humble words:
“Pray for us.”
But after everything written here, remember this most:
Your spouse's body was never meant to become the battlefield where two wounded hearts fight for proof that they are loved.
Bring the deeper hunger to Jesus.
Then turn toward each other again.
Not as enemies.
Not as competitors.
Not as debtor and collector.
As two sinners standing beneath the same cross, learning how to become one flesh without losing tenderness, dignity, patience, repentance, or grace.
Maybe your marriage has a chapter you are ashamed to read aloud.
Jesus has never been frightened by ugly chapters.
The woman caught in scandal met mercy.
Peter's denial met restoration.
Thomas's doubt met wounded hands.
The thief's dying confession met paradise.
And sinners like us still meet a Savior whose blood speaks a better word than our worst failure.
So perhaps the most important question tonight isn't:
Which one of us has the higher sex drive?
Perhaps it is:
Will we let Jesus teach us how to love each other here too?
Because the bedroom may reveal the wound...
but grace can rewrite what shame convinced you was already the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SHE THOUGHT NOBODY SAW HER CRYING IN THE WILDERNESS. GOD DID.
paragraphs:
SHE THOUGHT NOBODY SAW HER CRYING IN THE WILDERNESS. GOD DID.
Hagar ran into the desert carrying a wound nobody seemed to care about. Then God called her by name—and what happened beside a forgotten spring still speaks to every person who has ever cried where nobody could see.
There are tears you wipe away quickly because somebody is watching.
And then there are tears you let fall because nobody is.
Those are different tears.
They come when the bedroom door is locked.
When the bathroom fan is running so nobody hears you.
When you sit inside a parked car a few minutes longer because you cannot walk into the house pretending to be okay yet.
When everybody thinks you are strong.
When you answered, “I’m fine.”
When you even went to church.
But somewhere underneath the worship songs, the smiles, the responsibilities, and the Christian vocabulary, something inside you whispered:
Does anybody actually see what this is doing to me?
Hagar would have understood.

Her story in Genesis 16 is not sentimental. Scripture does not introduce her as a powerful woman with choices and influence. It identifies her as an Egyptian servant belonging to Sarai. Sarai was barren. Abram had received promises from God concerning descendants, but the waiting became unbearable, and human beings did what human beings still do when God seems slow:
They tried to manufacture what only God could fulfill.
Sarai gave Hagar to Abram.
Hagar conceived.
Relationships fractured.
Pride entered the wound.
Jealousy entered the house.
Bitterness followed.
Then Scripture says Sarai treated Hagar harshly, and Hagar fled.
Do not sanitize that sentence.
She fled.
Whatever was happening had become painful enough that the wilderness looked better than staying.
So picture her.
Pregnant.
Egyptian.
A servant.
Away from home.
Running.
No carefully packed suitcase.
No five-year plan.
No inspirational soundtrack playing behind the scene.
Just a woman carrying an unborn child and enough pain to make a desert look like freedom.
And perhaps that is why her story still reaches through thousands of years and grabs people by the heart.
Because sometimes you do not run with your feet.
Sometimes you run emotionally.
You stop trusting.
You stop talking.
You stop praying honestly.
You disappear behind work.
You bury yourself in entertainment.
You laugh louder.
You scroll longer.
You become everybody’s encourager because encouraging other people keeps them from asking what is happening inside you.
You can sit in the same house with your family and still be in a wilderness.
You can sleep beside somebody and still feel abandoned.
You can sing about God on Sunday and wonder where He is on Monday night.
And here is where Hagar’s story becomes breathtaking.
Genesis does not merely say that Hagar found God.
It says:
God found Hagar.
“The angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness” (Genesis 16:7).
Found her.
That word matters.
She was running away from people.
She was not beyond the sight of God.
She had left Abram’s household.
She had not left God’s attention.
She had entered the wilderness.
She had not entered a place where God could not find her.
Then comes one of the most tender moments in the chapter.
God addresses her:
“Hagar…”
Her name.
Before addressing where she was going, God addressed who she was.
Think about that.
In a world where Hagar could easily have felt like property, an instrument in somebody else’s plan, a womb being used to solve another family’s problem, heaven spoke her name.
Hagar.
God knew exactly who was sitting beside that spring.
And He knows exactly who is reading this.
Not your username.
Not your job title.
Not the version of yourself you present publicly.
Not simply “somebody struggling.”
You.
The person underneath all of it.
The one carrying memories nobody knows about.
The one who sometimes wonders whether God notices the prayers that never make it past your throat.
The one who has apologized but still struggles to forgive yourself.
The one who keeps encouraging everybody else while secretly wondering how much longer you can carry your own heart.
God sees you.
But Scripture gives us something even deeper.
The Hebrew text of Genesis 16:13 reads:
אַתָּה אֵל רֳאִי
Attah El Ro'i.

The expression אֵל רֳאִי — El Ro'i is commonly rendered “God who sees me” or “God of seeing.” The exact nuance of Hagar’s following statement is difficult Hebrew and has been translated in several ways, so we should resist building theology on an overly confident rendering of every syllable. But the central reality of the passage is unmistakable:
Hagar realizes that the God who encountered her in the wilderness is the living God who sees.
She names the place of encounter accordingly.
Genesis 16:14 gives us:
בְּאֵר לַחַי רֹאִי
Be'er Lahai Ro'i—
associated with “the well of the Living One who sees me.”
And there is another name buried in this story that wounded people need to hear.
God tells Hagar that her son will be called יִשְׁמָעֵאל — Yishma'el, Ishmael.
Why?
Because the LORD had heard her affliction.
The name is connected with the Hebrew root שׁמע — shama, “to hear.”
Do you see what is happening?
She is in a wilderness believing herself abandoned, and heaven answers her pain with two realities:
God sees.
God hears.
The tears nobody noticed?
Seen.
The pain nobody understood?
Heard.
The nights nobody knew you were barely holding yourself together?
Seen.
The prayer that sounded less like a prayer and more like, “Jesus, please help me”?
Heard.
The betrayal you never posted about?
Seen.
The temptation you are ashamed to admit you are fighting?
Seen.
The grief you thought you should have gotten over by now?
Seen.
The repentance you whispered after failing God again?
Heard.
And perhaps somebody needs this sentence tonight:
Being unseen by people has never meant being unseen by God.
But we need to be careful here.
Because biblical encouragement becomes dangerous when we turn it into sentimental promises God never made.
God seeing Hagar did not mean God told her that every decision she had made was right.
God hearing her did not mean God endorsed every attitude in the conflict.
God's compassion did not erase truth, responsibility, obedience, or the complicated consequences surrounding Abram, Sarai, Hagar, and Ishmael.
The God who sees us is also the God who speaks to us.
And sometimes being truly seen by God is uncomfortable because His gaze does not merely notice our wounds.
It exposes our sin.
He sees what they did to you.
And He sees what bitterness has done inside you.
He sees who abandoned you.
And He sees whom you refuse to forgive.
He sees the wound.
And He sees the idol you built to survive the wound.
He sees the loneliness.
And He sees the secret relationship you entered because loneliness convinced you holiness was too expensive.
He sees your exhaustion.
And He sees your compromise.
He sees your tears.
And He sees your rebellion.
That is what makes the Gospel so astonishing.
We do not have a God who sees only the edited version of us.
He sees everything.
And still He calls sinners to come.
This is where Hagar's wilderness points our eyes beyond Hagar.
Toward Jesus Christ.
Centuries later, another weary person would encounter God beside water.
A Samaritan woman came to Jacob’s well.
Her life was complicated.
Her relationships carried history.
Her soul was thirsty for something water could never satisfy.
And Jesus knew.
Before she could explain herself, He knew.
He knew her past.
He knew her relationships.
He knew the places where she had tried to satisfy a thirst only God could reach.
Yet Jesus did not walk away.
He spoke to her.
He exposed truth without stripping away dignity.
He confronted her life while offering living water.
That is Jesus.
He does not heal us by pretending sin is harmless.
He heals us by bringing sin into the light and offering something we could never earn:
grace.
Then there was Zacchaeus.
Jesus looked up into a tree and called him by name.
There was Peter.
Jesus knew Peter would deny Him before Peter knew how weak he really was.
There was Mary Magdalene.
There was Thomas.
There was the thief dying beside Him.
Again and again, the Gospel shows us a Savior who sees people everybody else has categorized.
Sinner.
Outcast.
Failure.
Unclean.
Traitor.
Doubter.
Hopeless.
Jesus sees deeper.
And eventually the One who sees us allowed Himself to be rejected before the eyes of the world.
Jesus Christ went to the cross.
Not because humanity was basically good and needed encouragement.
Because we were sinners who needed rescue.
The cross is not God telling you that your sin does not matter.
The cross is God showing you how much it mattered.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God bore judgment for sinners.
Grace is so astonishing that He willingly did.
Jesus was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day He rose.
This is Christianity.
Not “believe in yourself.”
Not “follow your heart.”
Not “God will approve whatever makes you happy.”
Christ died for our sins and rose again, and He calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
That means your wilderness does not have to become your identity.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Your shame does not get the last word.
Your addiction does not get the last word.
Your betrayal does not get the last word.
Your divorce does not get the last word.
Your failure does not get the last word.
Your secret does not get the last word.
Your past does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
Maybe that is why Hagar's story hurts so beautifully.
Because many of us have spent years asking God to change our circumstances while God has been trying to reveal Himself in the middle of them.
We wanted an exit.
He wanted an encounter.
We wanted explanations.
He gave us His presence.
We wanted everybody who hurt us to finally understand what they did.
But perhaps tonight the deepest healing begins somewhere else:
Knowing that God already knows.
You do not have to exaggerate your pain for Him to notice it.
You do not have to minimize your pain to appear spiritual.
You do not have to perform strength for Jesus.
You can tell Him the truth.
“I’m angry.”
“I’m tired.”
“I’m jealous.”
“I’m scared.”
“I feel forgotten.”
“I sinned.”
“I went back to something You delivered me from.”
“I don't know how to forgive them.”
“I don't know how to forgive myself.”
“I don't even know how to pray anymore.”
Tell Him.
Then listen when the Gospel answers:
You are not saved because you finally became impressive.
You are saved by grace through faith in Christ.
Bring the sin into the light.
Repent.
Stop defending what Jesus died to forgive.
Stop calling bondage freedom.
Stop running from the Savior whose hands were pierced to bring sinners home.
There is mercy at the cross.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is cleansing at the cross.
There is a new beginning at the cross.
And resurrection means Jesus is not standing beside the grave of your past wondering whether redemption is possible.
He has already defeated death.
Maybe you have been asking:
“Does God see me?”
Yes.
But there is an even more piercing question.
What will you do now that you know He does?
Because you cannot hide forever from the God who sees.
And strangely, wonderfully, terrifyingly—
you do not need to.
The eyes that see your sin belong to the Savior whose blood can cleanse it.
The God who knows the ugliest truth about you is the God calling you toward repentance, forgiveness, restoration, and life.
So stop performing.
Come home.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Do not make the comment section a place for religious performance.
Make it a place where people remember that grace still finds human beings in wildernesses.
And think of one person who has been unusually quiet lately.
One person who keeps saying, “I'm okay.”
One person going through divorce, grief, rejection, depression, loneliness, temptation, shame, disappointment, or a crisis of faith.
I thought of you. Please remember that God sees you.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
We are saved by grace, not by social-media activity, money, merchandise, or religious works.

But if Christ has given us truth, sharing that truth can become an act of love. Supporting Gospel-centered ministry can be one practical expression of stewardship. Someone scrolling tonight may be sitting in a wilderness you know nothing about, and the article you almost did not share may put Scripture in front of them at exactly the moment they were ready to give up.
If Gospel Warrior has strengthened your faith, consider helping us keep putting Christ-centered biblical content in front of people who desperately need it.
More importantly, stay because you want to grow.
Stay because conviction is better than comfortable deception.
Stay because your soul needs more than motivational quotes.
Stay because following Jesus requires daily nourishment from His Word.
Because another wilderness may come.
And when it does, you may need to remember the woman sitting beside a spring thousands of years ago.
Hagar.
Pregnant.
Hurting.
Running.
Probably uncertain about tomorrow.
And nevertheless—
seen.
Heard.
Found.
But before you leave, remember what Hagar's wilderness teaches us.
People may misunderstand your story.
Some may never apologize.
Some wounds may leave scars.
Following God does not mean you will never enter another desert.
But no wilderness is remote enough to escape the eyes of God.
No crying is quiet enough to escape His hearing.
No past is scandalous enough to overpower the grace available in Jesus Christ to the repentant sinner.
And no surrendered life is too shattered for Christ to begin rewriting.
Maybe you thought the wilderness was where your story disappeared. It may become the place where you finally discover that God never took His eyes off you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Can Christians Have a High Sex Drive and Still Be Holy?
paragraphs: Can Christians Have a High Sex Drive and Still Be Holy?
What if the desire you keep asking God to remove is not the sin—and the real battle is over who gets to rule it?
There is a prayer some Christians are almost too embarrassed to pray.
“God… why am I like this?”
They love Jesus.
They read Scripture. They worship. They want a clean heart. They genuinely want to honor Christ with their bodies.
And yet sexual desire can feel incredibly strong.
Sometimes painfully strong.
So they begin wondering whether something must be spiritually wrong with them.
Maybe I’m not holy enough.
Maybe a mature Christian wouldn’t feel this much.
Maybe if I really loved Jesus, these desires would disappear.
Maybe God is disappointed that my body still wants what it wants.
And because churches sometimes speak extensively about sexual sin while saying comparatively little about sexual desire, believers can quietly begin treating the two as though they were identical.
They are not.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because Scripture does not teach that holiness means becoming a person incapable of sexual desire.
Scripture teaches something far more demanding—and far more beautiful.
Your desires must come under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
That means the answer to the question, “Can Christians have a high sex drive and still be holy?” is yes.
But that “yes” needs the rest of the Bible wrapped around it.

A strong sexual appetite is not automatically sexual immorality. Neither is it automatically evidence of spiritual health. Desire is powerful, and like every powerful part of human life, it must be governed by God rather than enthroned as god.
Paul was not naïve about this.
Writing to believers in Corinth, he said:
“εἰ δὲ οὐκ ἐγκρατεύονται, γαμησάτωσαν· κρεῖττον γάρ ἐστιν γαμεῖν ἢ πυροῦσθαι.”
“If they do not exercise self-control, let them marry; for it is better to marry than to burn.”

The final Greek word is πυροῦσθαι (pyrousthai), from a verb meaning to burn or be set on fire. In context, Paul recognizes the reality of intense sexual passion rather than pretending mature believers never experience it.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say, “If you experience strong sexual desire, you obviously do not love God.”
He does not tell believers that possessing sexual passion itself makes them filthy.
He takes desire seriously enough to insist that it be handled within God's design.
And that changes the conversation.
Because perhaps you have spent years fighting the wrong enemy.
Perhaps you thought your sexuality itself was the monster when Scripture was calling you to confront something different: sexuality severed from obedience to God.

The Bible can speak positively about marital desire with a frankness that sometimes surprises modern Christians. Song of Songs describes physical attraction and marital longing without treating embodied desire itself as shameful. The woman can say of her beloved, “I am my beloved's, and his desire is toward me.”
That sentence belongs in the same Bible that commands sexual holiness.
Think about that.
God does not need to choose between holiness and marital passion.
We do.
We are the ones who sometimes imagine that “holy” must mean emotionally sterile, physically indifferent, embarrassed by sexuality and frightened of desire.
Scripture presents a richer picture.
Hebrews 13:4 reads in Greek:
“Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος…”
Marriage is to be honored, and the marriage bed ἀμίαντος (amiantos)—undefiled, unpolluted, unstained. The verse then warns that God will judge sexual immorality and adultery.
Do not miss the contrast.
The marriage bed is not presented as inherently dirty.
It is presented as capable of being undefiled.
Christian holiness does not require married couples to apologize for enjoying the covenant intimacy God permits them to share.
But neither does the goodness of sexuality give us permission to redraw God's boundaries around it.
