After what they did?
We need to be careful here.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending abuse never happened.
Mercy does not mean removing wise boundaries.
Reconciliation and forgiveness are related, but they are not identical; restored trust ordinarily requires truth, repentance, and fruit.
Justice matters to God.
Evil matters to God.
Victims matter to God.
But Jonah exposes another danger—the possibility that our desire for justice quietly mutates into a desire for damnation.
There is a difference between wanting evil stopped and wanting a human soul to remain forever beyond mercy.
Jonah crossed that line.
He essentially tells God:
I knew You would do this.
I knew You would be merciful.
And then comes the sentence that makes the story almost unbearable:
כִּי טוֹב מוֹתִי מֵחַיָּי
Ki tov moti me-ḥayyay.
“For it is better for me to die than to live.”
Jonah would rather die than live in a world where God forgives people Jonah believes deserve destruction.
And God answers him with a question.
Not lightning.
Not immediate rejection.
A question.
הַהֵיטֵב חָרָה לָךְ
Haheitev ḥarah lakh?
In essence:
“Is it right for you to be angry?”
God begins exposing the heart of the prophet while the prophet is furious about the hearts of the pagans.
That may be where this story turns toward us.
Because sometimes we are so busy asking God to deal with them that we never notice God is dealing with us.
Jonah walks outside Nineveh and sits east of the city.
He builds himself a shelter.
Then he waits.
Why?
The text says he wanted to see what would happen to the city.
You can almost see him staring at the skyline.
Waiting.
Maybe hoping.
Perhaps judgment will still fall.
Perhaps fire will still come.
Perhaps mercy will expire.
Then God appoints a plant to shade Jonah, and Jonah becomes exceedingly glad about it.
Think about the contrast.
A city is spared.
Jonah is angry.
A plant gives him shade.
Jonah is delighted.
More than 120,000 human beings are before God's compassionate gaze, and Jonah is emotionally captivated by vegetation that improves his afternoon.
Then God appoints a worm.
The plant withers.
The sun rises.
A scorching east wind comes.
Jonah grows faint.
And again he wants to die.
God asks whether Jonah is right to be angry about the plant.
Jonah answers, essentially:
Yes.
Angry enough to die.
Then God opens the prophet's heart with one devastating comparison.
Jonah cared about a plant he did not labor over and did not cause to grow. It appeared quickly and disappeared quickly.
Then God asks:
וַאֲנִי לֹא אָחוּס עַל־נִינְוֵה הָעִיר הַגְּדוֹלָה
Va'ani lo aḥus ʿal-Nineveh, haʿir ha-gedolah...
“And should not I care about Nineveh, that great city...?”
And then the book ends.
No neat resolution.
No paragraph telling us Jonah finally understood.
No emotional embrace.
No report that Jonah went back into Nineveh and celebrated.
Just God's question hanging in the air.
Because perhaps the question was never meant only for Jonah.
Perhaps God wanted it to reach you.
Should I not care about them?
That relative you stopped praying for.
That person whose name changes your breathing.
That politician you despise.
That former spouse.
That betrayer.
That addict.
That criminal.
That arrogant unbeliever.
That hypocritical Christian.
That person whose repentance you secretly do not trust because part of you does not want it to be real.
Should God not care about them?
Be careful how you answer.
Because Christianity begins with the humiliating admission that you were somebody's Nineveh too.
Scripture does not describe salvation as God discovering decent people and rewarding them.
Paul says that “while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we cleaned ourselves enough to deserve the cross.
While we were sinners.
The scandal of grace is that nobody enters the kingdom carrying a receipt proving they paid for admission.
Jesus paid.
At Calvary, mercy did not defeat justice by pretending sin was insignificant.
Justice and mercy met at the cross.
Sin was so serious that the Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Grace is free to us precisely because it was unimaginably costly to Christ.
Jesus took upon Himself the judgment sinners deserve so that those who repent and believe can receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and eternal life.
That is why the cross destroys both despair and pride.
Despair says, “I have sinned too badly for God to forgive me.”
The cross answers, “Christ is sufficient.”
Pride says, “They have sinned too badly for God to forgive them.”
The cross answers again:
“Christ is sufficient.”
And this is where Jonah becomes more than a children's story about a reluctant missionary.
Jesus Himself points to Jonah.

In Matthew 12:40–41, Christ speaks of Jonah's three days and three nights in the great fish as a sign pointing toward His own death and resurrection, and He says that the people of Nineveh repented at Jonah's preaching while One greater than Jonah had come.
Greater than Jonah.
Jonah was sent toward enemies and ran away.
Jesus was sent for sinners and came willingly.
Jonah descended into the sea because of his own disobedience.
Jesus descended into death in perfect obedience to the Father.
Jonah wanted guilty people condemned.
Jesus prayed from the cross, “Father, forgive them.”
Jonah sat outside the city hoping judgment might fall.
Jesus went outside Jerusalem and allowed judgment to fall upon Him.
Jonah was furious that his enemies might live.
Jesus died so His enemies could become His family.
That is the Gospel.
And perhaps that is why grace can feel scandalous.
Because we love grace when it rescues us from our past.
We become suspicious of grace when it reaches someone we have sentenced in our heart.
But you cannot worship the crucified Christ while secretly demanding that His blood be sufficient for your sins and insufficient for somebody else's.
Maybe there is someone you need to forgive.
Maybe there is someone you need to start praying for again.
Maybe the person is not safe to contact, and wisdom means maintaining distance. You can still surrender vengeance to God.
Maybe your prayer cannot yet honestly be, “God, bless them.”
Then begin smaller.
“Jesus, make me willing to want what You want.”
That is a prayer God can work with.
And perhaps the person you have been refusing mercy is yourself.
You believe Jesus forgives other people's scandals.
Just not yours.
You remember what you did.
The secret.
The addiction.
The betrayal.
The abortion.
The affair.
The years wasted.
The person you became.
The prayer you stopped praying because shame convinced you that God was tired of hearing your voice.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not tell you that your sin was small.
It tells you the Savior is greater.
Repentance is not pretending the past did not happen.
Repentance turns from sin toward God.
Faith does not argue that you deserve another chance.
Faith throws itself upon Jesus Christ.
“If we confess our sins,” 1 John 1:9 says, “he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Your scandal does not surprise Jesus.
Your failure does not exhaust Calvary.
Your shame does not get the final sentence.
Jesus does.
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes grace astonishing.
This is From Scandal to Grace.
Not scandal erased by pretending.
Scandal confronted by truth.
Sin exposed.
Repentance awakened.
Mercy offered.
The guilty forgiven.
The broken restored.
The dead made alive.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Who is your Nineveh?
Whose salvation would make you uncomfortable?
Whose repentance would force you to surrender a grudge you have carried so long that it now feels like part of your identity?
And perhaps the harder question:
Have you become so familiar with receiving God's mercy that you resent Him for giving it to someone else?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
You can simply write, “Jesus, change my heart.”
If you are exhausted from fighting bitterness, comment, “pray for me.”
If grace is teaching you to release someone into God's hands, comment, “I choose mercy.”
And if Christ has forgiven a past you thought could never be redeemed, tell somebody what He has done. Your testimony may become the crack through which hope enters another person's darkness.

Supporting Gospel work is one practical way believers can participate in helping biblical teaching reach more people. We glorify God first through trusting and obeying Christ; generosity and sharing can then become grateful expressions of that devotion.
Let his story search you.
Because somewhere tonight, there is a person praying for the mercy you think they do not deserve.
And somewhere else, there is a person convinced they are too dirty to receive the mercy you already know.
Both need the same answer.
Jesus Christ.
The One greater than Jonah.
The Savior who does not excuse sin but carries the sinner's judgment.
The King who calls enemies to repentance and turns forgiven enemies into sons and daughters.
The Lamb who was slain.
The Lord who rose.
The Christ who still saves.
Maybe the greatest scandal in Jonah was never that God loved Nineveh.
Maybe the greatest scandal was that He loved Jonah too.
The angry prophet.
The runaway servant.
The man who knew Scripture but struggled with mercy.
God kept speaking to him.
Kept pursuing him.
Kept teaching him.
Kept asking questions.
Grace was not only inside Nineveh.
Grace was sitting beneath the withered plant, confronting a bitter prophet without abandoning him.
And that means there is hope for the Nineveh in your life.
There is hope for the Jonah in your heart.
There is hope for the scandal in your past.
There is hope because the final word over a repentant sinner does not belong to shame, hatred, failure, or yesterday.
It belongs to Jesus.
The mercy you struggle to see God give another person may be the same mercy keeping you alive before Him today.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Should Christians Become Influencers? The Question Isn’t Whether People See You—It’s Who They See Through You
paragraphs: Should Christians Become Influencers? The Question Isn’t Whether People See You—It’s Who They See Through You

The internet tells you to build a name, grow an audience, protect your image, and make people remember you. Jesus calls you to something far more dangerous: become visible enough for people to see the light—and surrendered enough that they forget you and remember Him.
There is a strange moment that happens when a post begins to take off.
The notifications keep coming.
Someone shared it.
Someone tagged a friend.
Ten comments become a hundred. A hundred followers become a thousand. Suddenly people are listening to what you say.
And somewhere between the first notification and the thousandth follower, a question begins whispering inside the heart:
What if I could become somebody?
That question isn't automatically sinful.
But it can become spiritually dangerous very quickly.
Because there is another question hiding beneath it.
Do I want people to encounter Jesus…or do I secretly need them to notice me?
That is where the conversation about Christian influencers must begin.
Not with algorithms.
Not with follower counts.
Not with whether Christians should use Facebook, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, podcasts, books, livestreams, or whatever platform comes next.
The issue is the heart.
And Scripture refuses to let us hide from it.
Jesus looked at His disciples and said something astonishing:
“Ὑμεῖς ἐστε τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου.”
Hymeis este to phōs tou kosmou.
“You are the light of the world.” — Matthew 5:14.
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not tell His followers to become invisible.
He did not command them to withdraw from every public square.

In the verses that follow, He speaks about a city that cannot be hidden and a lamp that is not placed under a basket. Then comes the purpose: people are to see the believers' good works and glorify their Father in heaven.
There is visibility in Christianity.
There is public witness.
There is influence.
But there is a massive difference between being seen so God is glorified and using God so we can be seen.
And that difference may be one of the most important spiritual battles facing Christians in the age of social media.
Because only a chapter later, Jesus gives what initially sounds like the opposite warning.
He warns His disciples not to practice righteousness before people in order to be seen by them. — Matthew 6:1.
Read those truths together.
Matthew 5: let them see.
Matthew 6: don't do it to be seen.
That is not a contradiction.
That is heart surgery.
Jesus is exposing the motive.
The same outward action can come from radically different hearts.
One person can speak publicly about Christ because they desperately want Christ known.
Another can speak publicly about Christ because they desperately want themselves known.
Sometimes nobody watching can tell the difference.
Sometimes even the person posting cannot tell anymore.
That is why the most dangerous thing about Christian influence may not be becoming famous.
It may be becoming addicted to being noticed while convincing yourself that everything is “for God's glory.”
That sentence should make every Christian creator uncomfortable.
Including us.
Especially us.
Because the moment ministry becomes immune to self-examination, ministry becomes vulnerable to self-worship.
Paul gives perhaps the clearest biblical sentence for anyone who wants influence in the name of Jesus:
“For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake.” — 2 Corinthians 4:5, KJV.
The heart of the sentence is devastatingly simple.
Not ourselves. Christ Jesus as Lord.

The Greek behind Paul's language makes the contrast unmistakable. The apostolic proclamation is not centered upon the messengers themselves; Christ Jesus is proclaimed as Lord, while the messengers take the posture of servants. That is also how major English translations consistently render the verse.
There is the biblical theology of Christian influence.
You may have a platform.
You may have reach.
You may have a microphone.
You may have a million followers.
But the microphone is not a throne.
The platform is not an altar to your personality.
And followers are not disciples who belong to you.
Jesus is Lord.
You are a servant.
That changes everything.
So, should Christians become influencers?
Perhaps we need to stop asking whether Christians should become “influencers” and start asking whether Christians are willing to become faithful witnesses who happen to have influence.
Because influence itself is morally neutral.
A mother influences her children.
A pastor influences a congregation.
A teacher influences students.
A teenager influences friends.
A businessman influences employees.
A woman sharing what Christ carried her through may influence someone she will never meet.
A man opening Scripture on camera from his bedroom may reach a lonely believer thousands of miles away.
The question is not whether you influence people.
You already do.
The question is:
Where are you influencing them to go?
Toward admiration of you?
Toward envy of your life?
Toward dependency on your personality?
Toward endless controversy?
Toward consumerism disguised as Christianity?
Or toward repentance, grace, truth, holiness, forgiveness, Scripture, the cross, the empty tomb, and Jesus Christ?
Because eventually every platform becomes a signpost.
And every signpost points somewhere.
Imagine standing before Christ one day and discovering that thousands knew your face but barely knew His Word.
Imagine people remembering your catchphrases but not His commands.
Imagine building an audience around Christianity while quietly building your identity around applause.
Imagine defending biblical truth publicly while neglecting prayer privately.
Imagine gaining followers while losing tenderness toward God.
Imagine becoming known for Jesus while slowly forgetting how to sit alone with Jesus when nobody is watching.
That is the scandal hiding beneath Christian celebrity.
And none of us should assume we are above it.
James gives another sobering warning:
“Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness.” — James 3:1.
Influence increases responsibility.
More reach does not simply mean more opportunity.
It means more accountability.
Every person teaching Scripture publicly should feel some weight when pressing “Post.”
Is this true?
Did Scripture actually say this?
Am I forcing the Bible to support something I already wanted to say?
Am I stirring fear because fear gets engagement?
Am I manufacturing outrage because outrage gets shares?
Am I turning someone's pain into content?
Am I making promises God never made?
Am I preaching Christ—or performing Christianity?
Those questions matter because human souls are not analytics.
A view count has a person behind it.
A comment has a story behind it.
A share may land on the screen of someone sitting alone at 2:13 in the morning wondering whether God could possibly forgive what they have done.
That person does not need a Christian celebrity.
They need Christ.
They need to know that sin is real, judgment is real, repentance matters—and grace is more glorious than the scandal they thought disqualified them forever.
They need to know there is a Savior who did not merely give motivational advice from heaven.
He came.
He entered our broken world.
He touched people respectable religion avoided.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He called sinners to repentance.
He carried the cross.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
The Gospel is not “believe in yourself.”
The Gospel is that sinful human beings can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
That is why Christian influence must ultimately become smaller at the foot of the cross.
Because the cross destroys our obsession with image.
At Calvary, there are no impressive influencers.
There are sinners who need mercy.
There are no follower counts impressive enough to purchase forgiveness.
There are no verified badges that open heaven.
There are no algorithms that can resurrect a dead heart.
There is Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Lord.
And grace.
This is where something beautiful can happen to the Christian who has been chasing recognition.
Jesus does not merely expose our vanity to humiliate us.
He calls us out of slavery to it.
Maybe you started posting because you loved Jesus.
Then somewhere along the way, numbers began determining your mood.
A successful post made you feel valuable.
A failed post made you question yourself.
Someone else's growth made you jealous.
Someone else's ministry began feeling like competition.
You refreshed the analytics again.
And again.
And again.
You told yourself you were checking “the reach.”
But underneath it, perhaps you were checking whether you still mattered.
Jesus offers something better.
Your identity was never supposed to live inside a dashboard.
You were not redeemed by engagement.
You were redeemed by Christ.
You do not need strangers to validate what the cross has already declared about the astonishing mercy of God toward those who belong to Jesus.
That freedom changes how you influence.
Now you can tell the truth even when truth performs badly.
You can refuse clickbait that distorts Scripture.
You can admit when you were wrong.
You can delete something misleading.
You can refuse to exploit tragedy.
You can celebrate another ministry's fruit without secretly resenting it.
You can serve people who can do absolutely nothing for your platform.
You can disappear for prayer without panicking that the algorithm will forget you.
You can lose followers for refusing to compromise.
You can become less impressive and more faithful.
You can mean it when you say:
If they remember anything, let them remember Jesus.
That is Christian influence redeemed.
Not celebrity baptized in religious vocabulary.
Not personal branding with Bible verses sprinkled over it.
Not turning the Gospel into a ladder toward fame.
It is stewardship.
It is carrying light into dark places while remembering that you are not the source of the light.
It is standing where people can see you while continually pointing beyond yourself.
And perhaps that is why John the Baptist remains such a powerful picture for anyone with an audience.
People were coming to him.
People were listening.
His ministry had attention.
Yet when Christ came into view, John's instinct was not to protect his market share.
“He must increase, but I must decrease.” — John 3:30.
What a terrifying prayer for an influencer.
Jesus, increase even if I decrease.
Could you pray it?
Jesus, increase even if people stop mentioning my name.
Jesus, increase even if someone else gets the opportunity.
Jesus, increase even if my numbers fall because I refuse to compromise.
Jesus, increase even if the truth costs me popularity.
Jesus, increase even if everything I built becomes merely a road someone traveled to find You.
That is surrender.
And surrender is where influence becomes ministry.
This is also why supporting Christian work must never be presented as purchasing God's favor.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Christ has already paid the price sinners could never pay.
But grace creates generosity.

When believers freely support faithful Gospel work, they can help Scripture-centered teaching travel farther, resources reach more people, and ministry continue. Paul himself describes believers participating in Gospel ministry through giving and partnership, while the New Testament repeatedly insists that giving must not be coerced.
But there is something you can do without spending anything.
Not because sharing a post earns glory for God automatically. It doesn't.
Someone you know may be building an image while their soul is starving.
Someone may be comparing their tiny ministry with somebody else's enormous platform.
Someone may believe they are useless because only twenty people listen to them.
Someone may secretly be addicted to applause.
Someone may have walked away from Christianity after watching Christian personalities fall.
Someone may need to discover that Christianity was never ultimately about the personality holding the microphone.
It was always about Jesus.
If sharing this can put that truth in front of one person who needs it, then use your influence for that.
If this exposed something uncomfortable in you, don't manufacture a polished spiritual answer.
Your honesty may give another believer permission to stop pretending.
Because success has a strange way of making yesterday's convictions easy to forget.
Come back when the numbers start climbing.
Come back when they collapse.
Come back when someone praises you.
Come back when someone criticizes you.
Come back when another Christian passes you.
Come back when you're tempted to compromise truth for reach.
And remember:
The goal was never to make your name impossible to ignore. The goal was to live so faithfully that your life makes Jesus harder to ignore.
Maybe Christians should become influencers.
But only if we are willing to redefine influence at the cross.
Influence is not how many people know your name.
It is what happens in someone's life because you were faithful with what God placed in your hands.
Maybe your audience is five people.
Love them.
Maybe it is fifty.
Serve them.
Maybe it is fifty thousand.
Tremble a little.
Stay humble.
Stay teachable.
Stay accountable.
Open your Bible more than you open your analytics.
Pray when nobody can photograph it.
Repent when nobody can monetize it.
Tell the truth when lies would travel faster.
Refuse to turn wounds into branding.
Never confuse followers with disciples.
Never confuse visibility with anointing.
Never confuse virality with faithfulness.
And never forget that the greatest thing your platform can ever accomplish is not making people say,
“What an incredible Christian.”
It is making someone whisper,
“I need Jesus.”
Because one day the screen will go dark.
The notifications will stop.
The audience will move on.
Your name will eventually disappear from timelines.
But Christ will still be King.
So build accordingly.
Speak accordingly.
Post accordingly.
Live accordingly.
And if God gives you influence, hold it with an open hand.
Because perhaps the holiest thing an influencer can finally become is a signpost nobody worships, pointing toward a Savior nobody can afford to miss.
Let your name become smaller if necessary. Let your reach become smaller if necessary. But never make Jesus smaller so your platform can become bigger.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Is Tithing Still Required Today? The Answer May Expose What Really Owns Your Heart
paragraphs: Is Tithing Still Required Today? The Answer May Expose What Really Owns Your Heart

Christians have argued over the ten percent for generations. But Jesus may be asking a far more uncomfortable question: not “How little must I give?” but “After the cross, how much of me still belongs to me?”
Imagine this.
Sunday morning. Worship has ended. The offering moment arrives.
You already know what is sitting in your bank account.
You know the electricity bill is coming.
You know what groceries cost now.
You know there is something your child needs.
You also remember the sermon somebody preached years ago: “If you don't give God ten percent, you're robbing Him.”
And suddenly something that was supposed to be worship feels like fear.
So your hand reaches for your wallet while your heart quietly asks a question you almost feel guilty for asking:
Does God really require Christians to tithe today?
Maybe you have been told that if you do not give exactly ten percent, you are disobedient.
Maybe you have heard Malachi 3 used like a spiritual invoice.
Maybe you were promised that if you tithed, God would make you financially prosperous.
Maybe you gave faithfully and then watched the medical bill arrive anyway.
The job still disappeared.
The business still struggled.
The prayer still seemed unanswered.
And somewhere inside you, a dangerous thought began forming:
Did God fail me?
Or perhaps you are standing on the opposite side.
You discovered that Christians live under the new covenant, concluded that tithing is “Old Testament,” and quietly turned Christian freedom into permission to give almost nothing.
That is why this question matters.
Because underneath the argument about ten percent is something much bigger.
Who owns your heart?
And Scripture's answer is more beautiful—and more demanding—than either legalism or selfishness.
The English word tithe simply means a tenth. In Hebrew, the important word is מַעֲשֵׂר — maʿaser, meaning “a tenth” or “tithe.”
Tithing appears before the Mosaic Law. Abraham gave Melchizedek a tenth of the spoils after battle in Genesis 14:18–20. Jacob later vowed to give God a tenth in Genesis 28:20–22.

But neither passage establishes a universal command requiring every believer in every age to surrender exactly ten percent of every form of income. They show that giving a tenth existed before Sinai, but description must not automatically be turned into command.
Then came Israel's covenant law.
And this is where modern conversations often become too simplistic.

Biblical Israel's tithing system was woven into the religious, agricultural, social, and covenant life of the nation. Numbers 18 describes support for the Levites. Deuteronomy 14 describes tithes connected with worship and also provision for Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows. The Old Testament picture is therefore richer than the modern slogan, “God always requires ten percent of your paycheck.”
Then we arrive at the verse almost everyone knows.
Malachi 3:10 begins:
הָבִיאוּ אֶת־כָּל־הַמַּעֲשֵׂר אֶל־בֵּית הָאוֹצָר
Havi'u et-kol-hamma'aser el-beit ha'otzar...
“Bring the full tithe into the storehouse...”
That is genuinely what the Hebrew says. Ha-maʿaser is “the tithe,” and beit ha'otzar is the storehouse. Malachi speaks of food being present in God's house and of God's covenant blessing.
So Malachi 3 should not be erased.
But neither should it be ripped from its covenant setting and transformed into a Christian get-rich formula.

Malachi was confronting covenant unfaithfulness among God's people. This was not God handing the modern church a heavenly investment scheme in which ten percent deposited guarantees a larger financial withdrawal.
The God of Scripture is not a slot machine.
Giving is not a lever by which we force His hand.
And Jesus is not for sale.
Then someone will immediately say, “But Jesus Himself taught tithing.”
There is truth there that requires context.

In Matthew 23:23, Jesus rebuked scribes and Pharisees who carefully tithed even their herbs while neglecting “the weightier matters of the law”—justice, mercy, and faithfulness. He told them that they should have practiced the latter without neglecting the former.
Jesus was not condemning their tithe.
He was condemning the grotesque contradiction of being meticulous about religious percentages while becoming spiritually blind to the heart of God's law.
Picture it.
A man carefully measures his mint.
His dill.
His cumin.
Everything mathematically correct.
Everything outwardly religious.
And standing in front of him is the Son of God saying, in effect:
You counted the leaves and missed the heart.
That should terrify religious people more than any argument about percentages.
Because it is possible to give ten percent and still worship money.
It is possible to tithe and remain greedy.
It is possible to put money into an offering while refusing mercy to somebody who desperately needs it.
It is possible to calculate exactly what “belongs to God” because, secretly, we want permission to call the remaining ninety percent ours.
Then Jesus goes to the cross.
A new covenant is inaugurated through His blood.
And when we turn to the New Testament instructions given to the churches, something striking happens.
The apostles repeatedly teach Christians to give.
Generously.
Sacrificially.
Intentionally.
Regularly.
Willingly.
According to their means.
For the poor.
For fellow believers.
For Gospel ministry.
For those laboring in the proclamation of the Gospel.
But the New Testament epistles do not plainly impose the Mosaic tithe as a universal ten-percent legal requirement upon Christians.
Paul's language in 2 Corinthians 9:7 is particularly important:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ, μὴ ἐκ λύπης ἢ ἐξ ἀνάγκης· ἱλαρὸν γὰρ δότην ἀγαπᾷ ὁ θεός.
Hekastos kathōs proērētai tē kardia, mē ek lypēs ē ex anankēs; hilaron gar dotēn agapa ho Theos.
The sense is:

Each person should give according to what he has determined in his heart, not from grief or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver. The Greek ἀνάγκη — anankē carries the idea of necessity, constraint, or compulsion, while ἱλαρός — hilaros describes the cheerful or willing character of the giver.
Read that again.
Not under compulsion.
That destroys one distortion of Christian giving.
But don't stop reading there.

Because the same chapter speaks about sowing generously, God's provision enabling good works, generosity toward others, meeting the needs of God's people, thanksgiving rising to God, and generosity resulting in God's glory.
That destroys the opposite distortion too.
Grace does not say:
“Great. I don't have to tithe, so I can keep everything.”
Grace asks:
“If Jesus gave Himself for me, how can generosity not transform me?”
This is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Under legalism, you ask:
What percentage do I have to surrender?
Under grace, you begin asking:
Lord, what have You entrusted to me, and how can I use it for Your glory?
Those are very different questions.
One searches for the minimum.
The other has seen Calvary.
Jesus did not purchase you with ten percent of His blood.
He gave Himself.

That does not mean Christians must donate everything they possess to a church or ministry. Scripture recognizes legitimate responsibilities toward family and personal needs. Paul strongly teaches responsibility for one's household in 1 Timothy 5:8. Biblical generosity is not financial recklessness, manipulation, neglect of dependents, or giving money you do not actually possess.
But the cross destroys the illusion that Jesus can be Lord of your eternity while money remains lord of your present life.
This is why ten percent can still be useful.
For many Christians, a tithe can function as a wise starting discipline—a practical benchmark for intentional generosity.
But a benchmark is not the Savior.
And ten percent must never become a weapon for condemnation where the New Testament does not explicitly impose it as the covenant law of Christ.
Some believers may prayerfully give ten percent.
Some may presently be able to give less while growing in generosity and faithfully caring for genuine obligations.
Others whom God has prospered may discover that ten percent is far below what they can joyfully give.
Think about that last possibility.
What if the danger for some Christians isn't that ten percent is too high?
What if it is too low?
Suppose God entrusts someone with extraordinary resources, yet that person says, “I gave my ten percent. The rest is mine.”
Has the Gospel really taught us to think that way?
The New Testament pushes deeper.
In 1 Corinthians 16:2, believers are instructed to set something aside in keeping with their prosperity.

In 2 Corinthians 8, Paul points to believers whose generosity emerged even amid affliction and poverty, and then reaches the Christ-centered foundation of Christian generosity: Jesus Christ, though rich, became poor for our sake so that through His poverty we might become rich—not a promise of luxury, but the staggering grace of Christ's self-giving work.
In Acts, generosity sometimes became radically sacrificial.

And yet Acts 5:4 shows that property remained under the owner's control before it was voluntarily given. The early church's generosity was remarkable precisely because it was genuine generosity—not confiscation disguised as worship.

Paul also teaches that Gospel ministry may legitimately receive material support. In 1 Corinthians 9:14, he says that the Lord directed that those proclaiming the Gospel should receive their living from the Gospel.
So yes, supporting faithful Gospel work is biblical.
Helping the poor is biblical.
Supporting those who labor in teaching and ministry is biblical.
Generous Christian giving is biblical.
But manipulating frightened Christians with promises that sending money guarantees health, wealth, or supernatural financial multiplication is another matter entirely.
Please hear this carefully.
You cannot buy God's love.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
You cannot donate enough money to erase your sin.
Your offering cannot reconcile you to God.
Only Jesus can.
The scandal at the center of Christianity is that bankrupt sinners cannot pay their debt.
Christ paid it.
We did not climb to God with offerings.
God came down to us in Christ.
Jesus lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose.
Forgiveness is received through faith in Christ, not purchased through religious transactions.
And once grace captures a person...
something happens to the hands.
They begin opening.
Not because a preacher frightened them.
Not because an algorithm pressured them.
Not because somebody promised them a mansion if they sent money.
Because the heart has encountered a Savior who gave everything necessary to rescue sinners.
That changes giving.
Perhaps that is the question you needed more than, “Do I still have to tithe?”
Maybe the deeper question is:
Has Jesus reached my wallet because Jesus has reached my heart?
Be honest.
If your giving disappeared tomorrow, would anything in the Kingdom of God notice?
Do you instinctively spend on yourself and give God whatever survives?
Do you call yourself generous because you occasionally give what you never would have missed?
Or perhaps your wound is completely different.
Maybe churches have hurt you.
Maybe someone used Malachi to frighten you.
Maybe you were pressured to give money you needed for food or medicine.
Maybe spiritual authority became financial manipulation, and now every conversation about giving makes something inside you tense.
If that is your story, do not confuse Jesus with people who misused His name.
Christ does not need manipulation to produce generosity.
The Gospel creates something stronger than coercion.
Love.
Repentance.
Gratitude.
Freedom.
So, is tithing still required today?

If by “tithing” we mean that every Christian under the new covenant is explicitly commanded to give exactly ten percent under the Mosaic tithing legislation, the New Testament does not clearly establish such a universal command.
But if someone uses that conclusion to argue that Christians therefore have little responsibility to give, that conclusion runs headfirst into the New Testament.
Christian giving is not less serious under grace.
It goes deeper.
The New Testament moves the conversation from merely calculating a percentage toward a transformed heart characterized by willing, proportionate, sacrificial, cheerful generosity.
Ten percent may be a healthy beginning.
It makes a terrible finish line if God has enabled you to do far more.
And this is where Gospel Warrior must also practice what this article teaches.

If you genuinely want to glorify God with what He has entrusted to you, prayerfully consider whether supporting and sharing sound Christian teaching should become part of your generosity. Scripture connects generosity with thanksgiving and glory to God, but that must remain willing worship rather than spiritual pressure.
But don't stop at money.
Sometimes the offering God places in your hand is influence.
Not to make us famous.
Make Jesus known.
And don't disappear silently after reading this.
And if God has taught you a testimony about generosity that could strengthen someone else, tell it. Someone reading the comments may need your testimony more than you realize.
Because maybe the greatest danger was never giving nine percent instead of ten.
Maybe the greatest danger was spending your whole life asking how much Jesus requires while forgetting how much Jesus gave.
At the cross, grace did not calculate the minimum.
Grace poured itself out.
So don't give because you're terrified God will stop loving you.
Give because in Christ you have discovered a love money could never purchase.
Don't give to purchase blessing.
Give because Christ Himself is your treasure.
Don't give to become redeemed.
Give because the redeemed heart is learning to hold earthly things with open hands.
And when you fail—even here—return to Jesus.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
Get up.
Begin again.
Because the Gospel has never been the story of perfect people paying God enough to keep Him happy.
It is the story of sinners who could never pay their debt being rescued by a Savior who paid it completely.
And when that truth finally travels from your theology into your heart, the question begins changing.
Not merely:
“How much do I have to give?”
But:
“Jesus... after everything You have given for me, how can everything I am become worship?”
The Gospel does not merely change what leaves your hand—it changes who sits on the throne of your heart.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS DEPRESSION A SIN? The Answer Many Hurting Christians Are Afraid to Hear
paragraphs:
IS DEPRESSION A SIN? The Answer Many Hurting Christians Are Afraid to Hear
When your prayers feel empty, your Bible stays closed, and getting out of bed feels like a battle, has God become disappointed in you—or could Jesus be nearer to your darkness than you realize?
There is a particular kind of pain that becomes even heavier inside a Christian.
It is not only the sadness.
It is the shame about being sad.
You love Jesus—or at least you desperately want to.
You know the verses.
You have heard the sermons.
You have told other people that God is faithful.
And yet there are mornings when opening your eyes feels like discovering that the battle survived the night.
Your body gets out of bed, but something inside you does not.
People ask, “How are you?”
“Good.”
You smile.
You go to church.
You worship.
Maybe you even raise your hands.
But somewhere behind the worship song is a thought you are terrified to say aloud:
Why am I still like this if I really trust God?
Then another thought comes.
Maybe depression is a sin.
And suddenly you are carrying two burdens instead of one.
The pain itself...
and the fear that God is angry with you for feeling it.
So we need to answer this carefully, because careless theology can put chains around people Jesus came to set free.
Is depression a sin?
Not simply by virtue of being depression.

The Bible never gives us a commandment saying, “You shall not be depressed.” Scripture does condemn unbelief, sinful anxiety, bitterness, hopeless rebellion, drunkenness, self-destruction, and many other responses into which suffering can sometimes tempt us. Those things should not be renamed merely “depression” when repentance is actually needed.
But neither should every experience of profound sadness, exhaustion, emotional numbness, anguish, or psychological suffering be renamed “sin.”
Those are not the same claim.
And Scripture gives us remarkably honest pictures of suffering people.
Listen to the language of Psalm 42.
“Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me?”
The Hebrew behind “cast down” uses the verb שׁוּחַ (shuaḥ), carrying the sense of being bowed down or sunk low.
And “my soul” is נַפְשִׁי (nafshi)—my nephesh, my life, my inner self.
The psalmist is essentially staring into his own collapsing interior world.
Why are you bowed down, my soul?
Why are you in turmoil within me?
He does not pretend the turmoil is absent.
He names it.
And then, while still speaking from inside the struggle, he tells his soul:
“Hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him.”
Notice the word yet.
That may be one of the most beautiful words ever spoken from darkness.
Not, “Everything already feels better.”
Not, “I finally understand why this happened.”
Not, “I prayed once and all the heaviness disappeared.”
Yet.
I cannot see clearly right now...
yet I will hope.
I cannot feel what I once felt...
yet God has not ceased being God.
My emotions are speaking loudly...
yet they do not get the final word.
That is biblical faith.
Faith is not always smiling.
Sometimes faith is whispering the name of Jesus while your emotions are screaming that nothing will ever change.
And if you think a servant of God could never become emotionally overwhelmed enough to want life itself to end, you need to sit underneath a broom tree with Elijah.
This is the prophet who had witnessed astonishing demonstrations of God's power.
Then 1 Kings 19 shows us another scene.
Elijah runs into the wilderness, sits beneath a broom tree, and says:
“I have had enough, Lord... Take my life.”
Think about that.
A prophet.
A man used mightily by God.
Exhausted.
Afraid.
Alone.
Wanting to die.
And look carefully at what God does next.
God does not begin by humiliating Elijah.
He does not say, “What kind of prophet are you?”
He does not revoke Elijah's calling because Elijah reached the edge of himself.
Elijah sleeps.
An angel touches him.
There is food.
There is water.
He sleeps again.
And the angel returns, telling him to eat because the journey is too much for him.
There is something profoundly tender here.
Sometimes Christians become so eager to spiritualize suffering that we forget God created human beings with bodies.
Sometimes the exhausted person needs prayer.
Sometimes the exhausted person needs repentance.
Sometimes the exhausted person needs sleep.
Sometimes the exhausted person needs food.
Sometimes the exhausted person needs companionship.
Sometimes the exhausted person needs qualified medical or mental-health care.
And sometimes several of those things are true at once.

Seeking appropriate professional help is not automatically evidence that you have abandoned faith in Christ. God's common grace can work through physicians, counselors, medicine, wise pastors, supportive families, sleep, nutrition, community, and countless ordinary means.
We should never force a false choice between “trust Jesus” and “receive appropriate care.”
But there is an even deeper reason Christians must stop treating sorrow itself as proof of spiritual failure.
Go to Gethsemane.
Listen to Jesus.
Matthew 26:38 records Him saying:
“My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death.”
The Greek is breathtaking:
περίλυπός ἐστιν ἡ ψυχή μου ἕως θανάτου
Perilypos estin hē psychē mou heōs thanatou.
“My soul is deeply sorrowful... to the point of death.”
The word περίλυπος (perilypos) describes profound, encompassing sorrow or grief.
We must be precise here.
The Bible does not say that Jesus suffered clinical depression, and we should not diagnose Him across two thousand years from one passage.
But Gethsemane destroys the shallow idea that intense sorrow is inherently sinful.
Jesus experienced crushing sorrow.
And Jesus was without sin.
That matters.
Deep emotional pain and moral rebellion cannot simply be treated as synonyms.
Jesus did not hide His anguish behind religious performance.
He prayed.
He asked His friends to remain near Him.
He poured Himself before the Father.
And ultimately He surrendered:
“Not as I will, but as thou wilt.”
There is the difference we desperately need.
Pain is not necessarily rebellion.
Tears are not necessarily unbelief.
Emotional exhaustion is not necessarily apostasy.
But suffering can become a battlefield where temptation speaks.
Depression may whisper:
God has abandoned you.
Scripture answers:
He has promised never to leave His people.
Depression may whisper:
You are worthless.
The Gospel answers:

Your worth is not determined by your productivity, appearance, emotional stability, income, popularity, or ability to impress people. Human beings bear God's image, and for everyone who belongs to Christ, your deepest identity is found in Him.
Depression may whisper:
Hide.
The Gospel invites you into the light.
Depression may whisper:
Nobody should know.
James tells believers to pray for one another.
Depression may whisper:
There is no future.
And Scripture keeps answering with resurrection.
That does not mean quoting a verse will instantly remove a medical condition.
It means depression does not possess authority to rewrite what God has declared eternally true.
Your feelings are real.
But they are not God.
Your thoughts can be powerful.
But they are not Scripture.
Your darkest night can feel endless.
But it cannot cancel resurrection morning.
And perhaps this is where somebody reading needs to stop pretending.
Maybe you have been calling yourself “lazy” when you are deeply exhausted.
Maybe you have been calling yourself “faithless” because prayer feels difficult.
Maybe everybody thinks you are strong because you learned how to suffer quietly.
Maybe you encourage everyone else and then go home wondering who would notice if you disappeared.
Please hear this carefully.
Do not turn your suffering into a secret altar where you slowly sacrifice yourself.
Tell somebody.
A trusted Christian.
A mature pastor.
A family member.
A qualified counselor or physician.

And if your depression has reached the point where you are thinking about harming yourself or ending your life, do not remain alone with those thoughts. Tell someone immediately and seek urgent professional or emergency help where you live.
You do not have to prove your faith by suffering in silence.
Elijah needed somebody to touch him awake.
The psalmist talked to his own collapsing soul.
Paul openly described being burdened beyond his strength.
Jesus asked His disciples to remain near Him in Gethsemane.
Why have we created a Christianity where wounded people think holiness means pretending not to bleed?
Maybe because pretending is easier than confession.
And that is where depression and sin must be carefully distinguished.
Depression itself should not automatically be condemned as sin.
But none of us should use suffering as a shield against God's loving conviction either.
Pain can tempt us toward sinful responses.
We can become bitter.
We can deliberately isolate ourselves.
We can medicate pain through destructive habits.
We can feed resentment.
We can surrender to lies.
We can neglect responsibilities that we genuinely remain capable of fulfilling.
We can begin accusing God instead of bringing our questions honestly to God.
Where sin exists, Jesus does not call us to rename it.
He calls us to repent.
But repentance is not God kicking a wounded person while they are down.
Repentance is Christ calling us away from death and back toward Himself.
That is the scandal of grace.
Christianity does not say, “Get yourself together and then Jesus will accept you.”
The Gospel says something infinitely more shocking.
While we were sinners, Christ died for us.
Jesus did not wait until humanity became emotionally stable, morally respectable, spiritually impressive, and sufficiently religious.
He came into our ruin.
He carried our sin.
He endured the cross.
He shed His blood.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Grace walked directly into the scandal.
Maybe your scandal is not something everyone knows.
Maybe it happened inside your own mind.
The breakdown nobody saw.
The nights you cried without making noise.
The medication hidden in your drawer because you were afraid Christians would judge you.
The counseling appointment you almost canceled because someone told you that “real Christians just need more faith.”
The Bible you wanted to open but could not concentrate long enough to read.
The prayer that became only two words:
“Jesus... help.”
Do you know something?
That is still a prayer.
Peter sinking beneath the water did not deliver a theological lecture.
“Lord, save me.”
And Jesus reached for him.
Maybe today your prayer is not impressive.
Maybe it is:
“Jesus, I don't want to feel this anymore.”
“Jesus, I don't understand myself.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, keep me alive.”
“Jesus, I believe; help my unbelief.”
Bring Him the truth.
Not the church version.
Not the social-media version.
Not the cleaned-up testimony you think Christians want to hear.
The truth.
Because Christ already knows what is inside the room you keep locked.
And He is not frightened by darkness.
He walked into a tomb and walked back out.
That is why Christianity offers something deeper than positive thinking.
Our hope is not:
“Tomorrow will definitely be easier.”
Our hope is:
Jesus Christ is Lord.
Our hope is not:
“I will never experience another depressive episode.”
Our hope is:
Nothing can separate God's people from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
Our hope is not:
“If I become spiritually mature enough, I will never hurt again.”
Our hope is:
One day Christ will make all things new.
Christian hope does not deny Friday.
It knows Sunday is coming.
And until then, sometimes faith looks like worship.
Sometimes faith looks like repentance.
Sometimes faith looks like opening Scripture.
Sometimes faith looks like calling your pastor.
Sometimes faith looks like swallowing the medicine your doctor appropriately prescribed.
Sometimes faith looks like attending the counseling session.
Sometimes faith looks like finally telling your spouse, “I haven't been okay.”
Sometimes faith looks like eating something, drinking water, and sleeping—just as Elijah's story reminds us that human weakness is not always solved by a lecture.
And sometimes faith looks like surviving tonight because you believe Jesus deserves to write tomorrow.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to explain your entire life publicly. But you can take one small step out of isolation.
Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer needed tonight.
Not because every dark day can be solved by rereading a post, but because dark days can make us forget things we knew clearly in the light.
Send this to the person who has become unusually quiet.
Not as proof that you are a better Christian.
Not because sharing a Gospel article earns favor with God.

Financial support does not buy God's blessing or make anyone more righteous; salvation is God's gift through Christ. But believers have always been called to generosity and to participate willingly in Gospel work.
Jesus is.
And if you want to help sustain and expand this work:
But before you leave this page, remember the person we met at the beginning.
The Christian who woke up tired.
The Christian who wondered whether God was disappointed.
Maybe that person was you.
Then hear this one more time.
Depression is not automatically evidence that you have rejected God.
Your suffering should be taken seriously.
Your sin, wherever it exists, should be brought honestly to Christ in repentance.
Your wounds should not become hiding places.
Your darkest thoughts should not be faced alone.
And your salvation does not rest upon whether you managed to feel happy today.
It rests upon Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Reigning.
Coming again.
So when your soul asks, “Why are you cast down?” you do not have to manufacture an emotion you cannot feel.
You can answer with the psalmist:
I will yet praise Him.
Maybe not because the night has ended.
Maybe because you finally remembered that the night does not own you.
Jesus does.
And the hands holding your story still bear scars.
The chapter where you thought your story ended may become the page where people discover Who was holding you in the dark.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SOLOMON RECEIVED ABOUT $3.2 BILLION IN GOLD IN ONE YEAR—BUT THE MOST TERRIFYING PART OF HIS STORY WASN’T HOW RICH HE BECAME
paragraphs: SOLOMON RECEIVED ABOUT $3.2 BILLION IN GOLD IN ONE YEAR—BUT THE MOST TERRIFYING PART OF HIS STORY WASN’T HOW RICH HE BECAME

The Bible records a fortune so enormous that silver became practically ordinary in Solomon’s Jerusalem. But buried beneath the gold is a warning for every person who has ever whispered, “If I just had a little more, then I would finally be okay.”
Imagine waking tomorrow morning and discovering that, over the next twelve months, roughly $3.2 billion worth of gold would flow into your hands.
Not your lifetime earnings.
Not the estimated value of everything you own.
One year.
And even that would not include all your other streams of income.
What would that kind of money do to you?
Would it make you more generous?
More grateful?
More faithful?
Would you finally stop worrying?
Would you finally feel secure?
Or would it simply give the desires already living inside your heart enough power to become your masters?
That is where Solomon’s story stops being ancient history.
Because the frightening question is not, “How much would Solomon be worth today?”
The frightening question is...
What happened to the heart of a man who had almost everything money could buy?
First, we need to be careful with the numbers.
First Kings 10:14 records:
“Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was 666 talents of gold...”
The Hebrew is even more striking:
וַיְהִי מִשְׁקַל הַזָּהָב אֲשֶׁר־בָּא לִשְׁלֹמֹה בְּשָׁנָה אֶחָת שֵׁשׁ מֵאוֹת שִׁשִּׁים וָשֵׁשׁ כִּכַּר זָהָב
Vayehi mishqal hazzahav asher-ba lishlomoh beshanah echat... kikkar zahav.
In context: the weight of the gold that came to Solomon “in one year” was 666 kikkar—talents—of gold. The Hebrew itself emphasizes weight, gold, Solomon, and a single year.
The NIV footnote estimates those 666 talents at approximately 25 tons, or about 23 metric tonnes, of gold.
Now bring that ancient quantity into August 2026.
Gold futures closed August 7, 2026 at approximately $4,340.70 per troy ounce. Using the biblical estimate of roughly 23 metric tonnes, that amount contains about 739,000 troy ounces.
That puts the gold mentioned in 1 Kings 10:14 at approximately...
$3.2 BILLION.
In one year.
And please notice something people often miss.
The Bible immediately says this was besides income associated with merchants, traders, kings, and governors.
So $3.2 billion is not a responsible estimate of Solomon’s entire net worth.
It is not even necessarily his entire annual income.
It is simply a modern commodity-value estimate for the staggering quantity of gold specifically recorded in that verse.
And Scripture keeps going.
There were enormous gold shields.
An ivory throne overlaid with gold.
Gold drinking vessels.
Gold vessels throughout the House of the Forest of Lebanon.
Then comes one almost unbelievable sentence:
Silver was considered practically insignificant during Solomon’s reign because of the abundance surrounding him.
Try to picture it.
You walk through the palace doors.
Gold catches the light.
Gold on shields.
Gold on vessels.
Gold around the throne.
Foreign dignitaries arrive carrying treasures.
Merchants move through the kingdom.
Kings recognize Solomon’s greatness.
The Queen of Sheba has already witnessed his wisdom and prosperity and been overwhelmed by what she saw.
This was not merely a wealthy man.
This was a man standing at the summit of earthly achievement.
Power.
Prestige.
Wisdom.
Influence.
Luxury.
Recognition.
Security.
A kingdom people traveled enormous distances just to see.
And if the Bible ended Solomon’s story there, prosperity preachers would have material for centuries.
But the Bible does not end at 1 Kings 10.
There is a chapter 11.
And sometimes the most dangerous chapter of your life begins immediately after everybody else thinks you have finally made it.
Because Solomon’s greatest tragedy was never that he possessed gold.
It was that a heart once famous for wisdom became divided.
The man who had almost everything eventually wanted what God had forbidden.
And that should frighten every one of us who secretly believes that getting “more” will finally cure what is happening inside us.
More money.
More followers.
More recognition.
A bigger house.
A better business.
A better body.
A bigger ministry.
More applause.
More influence.
More security.
Just a little more.
Then I’ll be happy.
Then I’ll relax.
Then I’ll become generous.
Then I’ll serve God seriously.
Then I’ll stop being afraid.
But “more” is a terrible savior.
Because whatever number you reach, there is always another number waiting above it.
Solomon’s wealth became astonishing, but Scripture had already given Israel’s kings a warning.
Deuteronomy 17 warned that Israel’s king was not to multiply horses, wives, silver, and gold for himself.
Why?
Because God understood something about human beings that our consumer culture desperately wants us to forget.
You can possess something until eventually...
it possesses you.
Money itself is not presented in Scripture as inherently evil. Wealthy people such as Abraham appear in Scripture, and material provision can clearly be received with gratitude and used generously.
The problem is not that gold exists.
The problem is when gold becomes god.
The problem is when blessing replaces the Blesser.
When provision becomes identity.
When abundance produces independence from God instead of gratitude toward God.
When the gift quietly climbs onto the throne that belongs only to the Giver.
And before judging Solomon too quickly, look at your own heart.
Maybe you do not have 23 metric tonnes of gold.
Maybe you are reading this while wondering how you will pay next month’s bills.
Maybe your bank account is almost empty.
Maybe your business is struggling.
Maybe you have been praying for financial breakthrough for years.
But idolatry does not require billions.
A poor person can worship money they desperately want.
A rich person can worship money they desperately fear losing.
And either person can be enslaved by it.
That is why Jesus goes deeper than your wallet.
He goes after your heart.
In Matthew 6:19, the Greek begins:
Μὴ θησαυρίζετε ὑμῖν θησαυροὺς ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς...
Mē thēsaurizete hymin thēsaurous epi tēs gēs...
The language uses the related words thēsaurizete and thēsaurous—storing up treasures, accumulating treasure—before Jesus redirects His disciples toward treasure in heaven.
And then Jesus exposes the issue beneath the issue:
Where your treasure is, your heart will follow.
Think about that.
We usually assume our money follows our heart.
Jesus warns us that our heart can follow our treasure.
What you continually invest yourself in begins pulling something out of you.
Attention.
Affection.
Fear.
Hope.
Identity.
Time.
Energy.
Devotion.
Your treasure leaves fingerprints on your soul.
So perhaps the most important question this article can ask you is not whether Solomon would be a billionaire today.
It is:
What owns your heart today?
What are you terrified of losing?
What do you believe you absolutely must obtain before your life can finally mean something?
What disappointment makes you question God’s goodness?
What success would make you feel important?
What possession secretly makes you feel superior?
What number in your bank account would finally make you say, “Now I am safe”?
Be careful.
You can post Bible verses while craving applause.
You can attend church while worshiping success.

You can sing, “Jesus is enough,” while quietly living as though Jesus plus money, Jesus plus recognition, Jesus plus romance, Jesus plus comfort, Jesus plus influence is what would actually satisfy you.
That is where Solomon’s story becomes painful.
He knew God.
He had received extraordinary wisdom.
He had experienced extraordinary blessing.
He built the temple.
People traveled from distant nations to hear him.
And still...
his heart could wander.
That should destroy one of Christianity’s most dangerous illusions:
“If God blesses me enough, I could never drift away.”
You can.
Blessing does not eliminate your need for dependence.
Success does not eliminate your need for repentance.
Knowledge does not eliminate your need for obedience.
Yesterday’s encounter with God does not excuse today’s compromise.
And knowing Scripture is not the same thing as surrendering to the God who spoke it.
Solomon could explain wisdom while eventually behaving foolishly.
And some of us know exactly what that feels like.
You knew better.
You did it anyway.
You knew that relationship was pulling you away from Christ.
You stayed.
You knew that habit was becoming your master.
You hid it.
You knew bitterness was poisoning you.
You fed it.
You knew pride was growing.
You protected it.
You knew God was calling you back.
You kept saying...
Tomorrow.
And perhaps that is why Solomon’s story hurts.
Because somewhere beneath his royal robes, we recognize ourselves.
Different palace.
Same human heart.
Different idols.
Same temptation.
Different century.
Same desperate need for grace.
But Solomon is not the final King in the Bible.
Another King came.
And He looked nothing like the kings humanity expected.
Jesus Christ did not arrive surrounded by Solomon’s gold.
He was born into humility.
He walked dusty roads.
He touched people society avoided.
He ate with sinners.
He welcomed the broken.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He had no earthly palace from which He ruled.
And when humanity finally crowned Him...
we used thorns.
Solomon sat upon an extraordinary throne.
Jesus was nailed to a cross.
Solomon accumulated treasures.
Jesus gave Himself.
Solomon’s glory made rulers travel to see him.
Jesus’ glory was veiled beneath suffering while people mocked Him.
Solomon’s kingdom eventually fractured.
Jesus Christ rose from the grave and established a Kingdom death itself cannot destroy.
That is the Gospel.
Not poor people becoming rich.
Not unsuccessful people learning secrets for success.
Not God becoming a tool for building the life you always wanted.
The Gospel is something infinitely better.
Sinners being reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
The guilty forgiven.
The rebellious brought home.
The spiritually dead made alive.
The ashamed clothed in grace.
The captive liberated.
The wandering heart called back.
The scandal rewritten.
Not because we earned another chance.
Because Christ paid for sinners with something more precious than Solomon’s gold.
His own blood.
Maybe you have wasted years chasing things you thought would complete you.
Maybe you finally got some of them...
and discovered you were still empty.
Maybe everybody thinks you are doing well.
But tonight, when the room becomes quiet and there is nobody left to impress, you know something is wrong.
Come back to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
Repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yourself.
It is turning.
Turning from sin.
Turning from false gods.
Turning from self-rule.
Turning toward the crucified and risen Christ in faith.
You do not need Solomon’s fortune to become rich toward God.
And you could possess Solomon’s fortune and still be spiritually bankrupt.
Jesus asked what it profits a person to gain the whole world and lose his soul.
Solomon’s gold makes that question feel terrifyingly concrete.
Suppose somebody deposited $3.2 billion into your account tonight.
Would you trade Christ for it?
Most Christians would immediately say no.
So let me make the question harder.
Would you compromise Christ for $100 million?
One million?
Ten thousand?
A promotion?
A relationship?
Acceptance?
A few minutes of secret pleasure?
Enough likes to finally feel noticed?
That is where theology becomes personal.
Because almost nobody sells his soul in one dramatic transaction.
Usually we trade pieces of obedience away slowly.
One compromise.
One excuse.
One hidden thing.
One rationalization.
One more night.
Until the person who once said, “I could never walk away from God,” looks around and realizes he has traveled frighteningly far.
But listen carefully.
If that is you...
the story does not have to end there.
Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Grace is still grace.
The cross is still enough.
The tomb is still empty.
Christ is still saving.
Christ is still restoring.
Christ is still breaking chains.
Christ is still calling prodigals home.
Christ is still rewriting stories that human beings would have thrown away.
That is why we keep saying it:
Be honest.
Someone reading your three words may realize they are not the only believer still fighting.

Not because Solomon’s billions make interesting trivia, but because there may come a day when success, money, fear, comparison, temptation, or disappointment begins whispering that Jesus is not enough.
Come back and read it again.
Not as a superstition. Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God. Salvation cannot be purchased, and God is not impressed by social-media metrics.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that they are spiritually exhausted.
Supporting Gospel ministry does not purchase God’s blessing and does not make someone more loved by Christ.
But generosity, sharing truth, encouraging believers, and helping sound Christian resources reach people can certainly be ways believers use what God has entrusted to them for His glory.
But before you leave this article, remember the number that brought you here.
666 talents.
Roughly 23 metric tonnes.
Approximately $3.2 billion at the referenced August 2026 gold price.
An almost unimaginable river of gold.
Yet Solomon’s life reminds us that possessing extraordinary treasure cannot guarantee an undivided heart.
And Jesus offers something Solomon’s treasury never could.
Forgiveness.
Reconciliation.
A new heart.
Eternal life.
Christ Himself.
So if God gives you much, steward it for His glory.
If God gives you little, remain faithful with what is in your hands.
Work.
Give.
Build.
Create.
Provide for your family.
Be generous.
But never ask money to do what only Jesus can do.
Gold can purchase a magnificent house.
It cannot make it a home.
Gold can hire security.
It cannot give peace with God.
Gold can buy medicine.
It cannot defeat death.
Gold can surround a throne.
It cannot cleanse a conscience.
Gold can make people notice your name.
It cannot write your name in the Book of Life.
And if you ever have to choose between possessing everything this world can place into your hands and belonging completely to Jesus Christ...
let the gold fall from your hands before you ever let Christ disappear from your heart.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE HARVEST ISN’T WAITING: The Terrifying Reason Jesus Said the Workers Are Few
paragraphs: THE HARVEST ISN’T WAITING: The Terrifying Reason Jesus Said the Workers Are Few

Jesus did not say there were too few hurting people. He said there were too few workers willing to go to them—and perhaps the most uncomfortable part of Matthew 9:37–38 is realizing that the worker you have been praying for may be you.
There are verses we love because they comfort us.
And then there are verses that refuse to leave us comfortable.
“The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few.”
We have printed those words on missionary banners. Preached them at conferences. Quoted them during evangelism campaigns. Turned them into prayer themes.
But imagine hearing them for the first time.
Not inside a church.
Not surrounded by worship music.
Not while holding a Bible with highlighted pages.
Imagine standing beside Jesus and watching His eyes move across a crowd of exhausted human beings.

Matthew tells us that Jesus had been moving through cities and villages, teaching, proclaiming the Gospel of the Kingdom, and healing sickness. Then something happened before He ever mentioned a harvest.
He saw them.
And what He saw moved Him.
Matthew describes the crowds as distressed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd. Then Jesus turned to His disciples and spoke about the harvest.
That order matters.
Before there was a command...
there was compassion.
Before Jesus spoke about workers...
He looked at wounded people.
And perhaps that is where this passage begins confronting us.
Because it is possible to see crowds without seeing souls.
The angry person.
The alcoholic.
The successful businessman who cannot sleep.
The teenager quietly wondering whether life is worth continuing.
The woman smiling in photographs while crying when nobody is watching.
The man who hasn't prayed in years.
The Christian who still attends church but has slowly stopped loving Christ.
The unbeliever who mocks Christianity because the Christians he encountered wounded him.
The person sitting beside you at work.
The relative you stopped praying for.
The friend whose jokes hide a collapsing marriage.
The stranger reading these words right now.
Jesus sees people differently.
Matthew 9:36 says that when Christ saw the crowds, He was moved with compassion.

The Greek expression behind that compassion is extraordinarily vivid. The verb ἐσπλαγχνίσθη — esplagchnisthē describes compassion felt deeply within a person. This was not detached sympathy. Jesus was not studying humanity as a problem to solve.
Their condition moved Him.
Then came the sentence.
Ὁ μὲν θερισμὸς πολύς, οἱ δὲ ἐργάται ὀλίγοι.
Ho men therismos polys, hoi de ergatai oligoi.
“The harvest is plentiful, but the workers are few.”
The Greek text of Matthew preserves precisely this contrast: a great harvest against a small number of workers.
θερισμός — therismos means harvest.
ἐργάται — ergatai means workers or laborers.
ὀλίγοι — oligoi means few.
Jesus was looking at enormous spiritual need and saying, in effect:
There is no shortage of people who need shepherding.
There is no shortage of brokenness.
There is no shortage of people who need the Gospel.
There is a shortage of workers.
And suddenly this ancient sentence becomes painfully modern.
Because perhaps we have spent years asking why the world is becoming darker while rarely asking whether we have carried the Light into it.
We complain about what people post.
We complain about culture.
We complain about declining morality.
We complain about lukewarm Christianity.
We complain about churches.
We complain about younger generations.
We complain about families abandoning biblical truth.
And Jesus looks across the field and says:
Where are the workers?
That question is difficult because Christianity was never designed to make spectators comfortable.
Jesus did not rescue us merely so we could spend the rest of our lives celebrating our rescue while drowning people remain around us.
Grace makes rescued people into rescuers.
Not saviors.
There is only one Savior.
Jesus Christ.
We cannot regenerate a heart. We cannot forgive another person's sins before God. We cannot produce repentance. We cannot manipulate somebody into the Kingdom.
Salvation belongs to the Lord.
The field belongs to Him too.
Notice what Jesus calls God:
“the Lord of the harvest.”
The harvest is His.
The workers are His.
The mission is His.
The power is His.
The Gospel is His.
And the glory must remain His.
That protects this passage from becoming a guilt-driven demand for religious busyness.
Jesus does not tell His disciples to manufacture a harvest.
He tells them to pray.
Matthew 9:38 continues:
“Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.”
That command is fascinating because the Greek verb translated “send forth” is ἐκβάλῃ — ekbalē, from ekballō. In this context it carries the force of sending or thrusting workers out.
Jesus is not describing casual Christianity.
“Maybe I'll serve someday.”
“Maybe I'll tell somebody about Christ when life gets less busy.”
“Maybe I'll start using what God gave me after everything becomes convenient.”
The harvest does not operate according to our convenience.
Harvests have urgency.
There is a window.
And perhaps someone reading this has been waiting for a sign from God while repeatedly ignoring the people God has already placed around you.
You keep asking:
“Lord, what is my calling?”
And perhaps heaven keeps pointing toward your family.
Your children.
Your workplace.
Your classmates.
Your neighborhood.
Your Facebook friends.
Your wounded friend.
Your unbelieving brother.
Your exhausted spouse.
Your church.
Your phone.
That last one may sting.
Because generations before us crossed oceans carrying the Gospel.
Many believers today can cross continents with one click.
You may never preach before ten thousand people.
But you can send one person a Scripture tonight.
You can share a testimony.
You can pray with somebody.
You can tell a friend what Jesus has done for you.
You can share an article about Christ instead of another argument.
You can stop being ashamed of the Name that saved you.
And somebody might encounter the Gospel because you finally decided that obedience mattered more than embarrassment.
But there is something even deeper happening in Matthew.

Immediately after Jesus tells His disciples to pray for workers in Matthew 9, Matthew 10 begins with Jesus summoning the Twelve and sending them into ministry. The people praying about the shortage become part of God's answer to the shortage.
Read that again slowly.
They prayed for workers.
Then Jesus sent them.
That changes the prayer.
“Lord, send somebody.”
Perhaps.
But sometimes the answer is:
I am sending you.
That does not mean every Christian becomes a missionary overseas, a pastor, an evangelist, or a public preacher. Scripture describes different gifts and callings within Christ's body.
But there is no category of Christian called “permanent spectator.”
Every believer bears witness to Christ.
Every believer can pray.
Every believer can love.
Every believer can serve.
Every believer can speak truth.
Every believer can point somebody toward Jesus.
Every believer can participate in making disciples according to the opportunities and gifts God provides.
And maybe this is where the article stops being about “workers” somewhere else.
Maybe it becomes about you.
Because somebody once carried the Gospel far enough for it to reach you.
Think about that.
Somebody prayed.
Somebody preached.
Somebody translated Scripture.
Somebody taught.
Somebody sacrificed.
Somebody invited.
Somebody gave.
Somebody shared.
Somebody refused to remain silent.

Across generations, languages, nations, persecution, poverty, oceans, prisons, revivals, churches, kitchen tables, hospital rooms, missionary graves, handwritten Bibles, printed pages, radio signals, phone screens...
the message traveled.
Until one day it reached you.
Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again.
The holy Son of God entered our rebellion.
He bore sin.
He endured the cross.
He conquered death.
And sinners who repent and trust in Christ are not merely improved.
They are forgiven.
Reconciled.
Redeemed.
Given new life.
That is why the harvest matters.
Christian mission is not about building an audience for Christianity.
It is about announcing Christ to people who desperately need Him.
And none of us enters that field as someone morally superior to those still lost.
We enter as former wanderers carrying directions to the Shepherd.
We enter as forgiven sinners telling other sinners where mercy found us.
That is Gospel Warrior's heartbeat:
Because Scripture is filled with people whose stories should have ended differently.
Peter denied Jesus.
Grace did not call denial good.
Grace restored the denier.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Grace did not pretend his violence was righteousness.
Christ confronted him, transformed him, and sent him.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to build a religious résumé.
He had only a guilty past, a dying breath, and a crucified King beside him.
Yet grace reached him there.
This is what Jesus does.
He does not rewrite everything by pretending the scandal never happened.
He rewrites everything by bringing redemption into places sin tried to destroy.
Maybe your scandal has a name.
Addiction.
Adultery.
Pride.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Greed.
Hypocrisy.
Abortion.
A broken marriage.
Years wasted.
Faith abandoned.
Secret sin.
A reputation ruined.
A child you failed.
A parent you never forgave.
A season when you knew what God said and deliberately walked the opposite direction.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say your sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more terribly than we like admitting.
But the cross also proves something else.
Your sin is not greater than the grace of the crucified and risen Christ.
Repentance is not God demanding that you clean yourself before coming home.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can make you clean.
And perhaps the first harvest field God wants to confront tonight is not your neighborhood.
Perhaps it is your own heart.
Because you can talk about reaching the lost while slowly becoming lost in religious performance yourself.
You can share Christian content while hiding sin.
You can quote Jesus without obeying Jesus.
You can defend Christianity online while neglecting Christ privately.
You can look like a worker while your soul is starving.
Jesus does not merely want your activity.
He wants you.
Come back.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you feel worthy.
Not after you repair your image.
Come back now.
If something hidden was exposed while reading this, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly.
And mean it.
Sometimes one honest sentence beneath an article becomes the moment another believer realizes, I'm not the only one struggling.
That is part of the harvest too.
People need truth.
But people also need to see what grace looks like when truth reaches a real human life.
So do not only ask, “Who needs the Gospel?”
Ask:
“Lord, where have You already placed me?”
There may be a name entering your mind right now.
Do not ignore it.
Pray for that person.
And when wisdom allows, reach out.
Not with superiority.
Not with a theological hammer.
Not to win an argument.
With truth and compassion.
Remember the order.
Jesus saw the crowds.
Jesus had compassion.
