Jesus spoke about the harvest.
Compassion without truth can leave people comfortably lost.
Truth without compassion can make wounded people feel like projects.
Jesus gives us neither distortion.
He is full of grace and truth.
And His workers must learn His heart.
That is also why sharing Gospel-centered truth matters.
If this article convicted you, do not share it merely because someone told you sharing increases reach.
I thought about you.
Because there will be mornings when the harvest feels distant.
There will be days when you feel spiritually useless.
There will be moments when fear whispers, “Let somebody else do it.”
Come back and remember:
The field belongs to God.
You only have to remain faithful to the part He gives you.
It does not.
Not because supporting a Christian ministry proves your salvation.
It does not.
And certainly not because money can purchase spiritual blessing.
It cannot.
We support Gospel work because grace has already been freely given to us in Christ, and because we want biblical truth to continue reaching people.
If these messages have become part of your spiritual nourishment, stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who has drifted.
Invite the struggling Christian.
Invite the person who does not yet believe.
Invite the believer who is hungry for Scripture.
Jesus is calling workers into His harvest.
And this is bigger than Gospel Warrior.
Bigger than one ministry.
Bigger than one church.
Bigger than one Facebook page.
The Kingdom belongs to Christ.
The harvest belongs to Christ.
The Church belongs to Christ.
The glory belongs to Christ.
And one day our opportunity to labor will end.
There will be a final conversation.
A final message.
A final Sunday.
A final opportunity to forgive.
A final opportunity to share Christ.
A final opportunity to tell somebody what Jesus did for you.
We rarely know when a “next time” is actually the last time.
So pray.
Then listen.
Then go where Christ sends you.
Maybe across an ocean.
Maybe across the street.
Maybe across the hallway.
Maybe across the dinner table.
Maybe into the comment section beneath this article.
Not because those words make you heroic.
Because they make you available.
Invite believers, seekers, struggling Christians, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow along.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is tired.
Somebody is ashamed.
Somebody thinks God could never forgive what they have done.
Somebody believes their scandal has written the final chapter.

And perhaps God will use an ordinary worker—a praying mother, a quiet student, a repentant father, a recovering sinner, a faithful friend, a trembling believer with a phone in their hand—to tell them the news that changed eternity:
Jesus still saves.
The harvest is plentiful.
The workers are few.
And perhaps after reading this, there will be one more worker in the field.
Never forget: somebody else's road from scandal to grace may begin when one forgiven sinner refuses to stay silent about Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “SLEEP WITH ME”: One of the Bible’s Bluntest Sexual Propositions—and the Man Who Ran
paragraphs: “SLEEP WITH ME”: One of the Bible’s Bluntest Sexual Propositions—and the Man Who Ran

She wanted his body. He chose his God. He lost his coat, his reputation, and his freedom—but not his soul. And thousands of years later, Joseph’s decision in a locked room still asks what you will do when temptation knows your name.
“Sleep with me.”
No poetry.
No romance.
No careful euphemism.
No long seduction speech.
Just a married woman looking at a young man who belonged to her husband’s household and giving him one of the bluntest sexual propositions recorded in Scripture.
The Hebrew of Genesis 39:7 is almost startling in its brevity:
שִׁכְבָה עִמִּי — shikhvah ‘immi
“Lie with me.”

That is essentially what the Hebrew says. The biblical text does not need embellishment to make the moment uncomfortable. Potiphar’s wife “cast her eyes upon Joseph” and issued the command. Genesis 39:12 records her saying it again.
And Joseph said no.
But if that is all we take from this story—“Joseph resisted sexual temptation”—we may miss the wound underneath the victory.
Because Joseph was not standing there as a sheltered man who had never experienced loneliness.
He was a betrayed son.
A hated brother.
A young man ripped away from his father.
A foreigner.
A slave.
A man living far from home, far from the people who knew his name before Egypt gave him a price.
His own brothers had thrown him into a pit.
They had sold him.
His father was somewhere far away believing him gone.
And now, in Egypt, someone wanted him.
Think about that.
Sometimes temptation does not knock on the door wearing horns.
Sometimes it arrives offering the exact thing your wounds have been begging to feel.
Wanted.
Desired.
Seen.
Comforted.
Validated.
Touched.
Joseph could have constructed a hundred excuses.
Nobody will know.
My family abandoned me anyway.
After everything that happened to me, don't I deserve something for myself?
I'm lonely.
I'm young.
She came after me.
I didn't start this.
God allowed me to become a slave, so why should I keep obeying Him?
Scripture records none of those excuses.
Instead, there is a small Hebrew expression that changes the atmosphere of the entire scene:
וַיְמָאֵן — vayema'en
“But he refused.”
Genesis 39:8.
Before Joseph gives his explanation, Scripture gives us his decision.
He refused.
Then comes the reason.
Joseph tells her that Potiphar has entrusted virtually everything in the household to him and withheld only her because she is Potiphar’s wife. Then Joseph asks:
“How then could I do this most wicked thing, and sin before God?”
There it is.
Joseph understood something our culture desperately needs to recover.
Sin against another human being is ultimately also rebellion against God.
Sexual sin is not merely about chemistry.
Not merely attraction.
Not merely consenting adults.
Not merely whether somebody gets caught.
Joseph sees covenant, trust, morality, and God.
He does not say, “What if your husband discovers us?”
He essentially asks, “How can I do this before God?”
That changes everything.
Because secrecy disappears when you believe God is in the room.
And perhaps somebody reading this needs that sentence more than they expected.
God is in the room.
The hotel room.
The bedroom.
The office.
The private chat.
The deleted conversation.
The browser history.
The relationship nobody knows about.
The emotional affair you keep calling friendship.
The messages you would panic to see projected on a church wall.
The pornography hidden behind passwords.
The fantasy nobody else can hear.
The compromise you have renamed because calling it sin would require repentance.
God is in the room.
Not because He is waiting gleefully to destroy you.
But because there has never been a darkness deep enough to make Him absent.
And that truth is terrifying when we want to sin.
It becomes breathtaking when we want to come home.
Joseph's temptation also did not disappear after one heroic refusal.
Genesis says she spoke to him “day after day.”
Day after day.
That matters.
Some battles are not won because temptation stops calling.
They are won because grace keeps teaching you not to answer.
Joseph's holiness was not one dramatic Instagram-worthy moment.
It was repeated resistance.
Monday.
No.
Tuesday.
No.
Wednesday.
Still no.
Again.
Again.
Again.
Scripture says he refused “to lie beside her, to be with her.”
Notice the wisdom.
Joseph was not asking how close he could get without technically crossing the line.
He was creating distance.
Some of us keep praying, “God, give me strength,” while keeping the person's number.
We pray for freedom while protecting access to bondage.
We ask Jesus to rescue us from the fire while carrying matches in our pocket.
There are moments when spiritual maturity does not look like standing there proving how strong you are.
It looks like running.
And eventually Joseph ran.
Genesis 39:12 says she grabbed his garment and again demanded, “Lie with me!”
Joseph left the garment in her hand and fled outside.
He did not stay to negotiate.
He did not explain himself for another twenty minutes.
He did not test his self-control.
He ran.
Sometimes the holiest thing your feet can do is leave.
Run from the conversation.
Run from the secret meeting.
Run from the screen.
Run from the relationship that keeps pulling you away from Christ.
Run from the environment where you repeatedly become somebody you promised God you did not want to be anymore.
Paul would later tell believers, “Flee sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18).
Not study it.
Not flirt with it.
Not see how near you can stand.
Flee.
But here is where Joseph's story becomes painful.
He did the right thing...
and his life got worse.
Potiphar's wife took the garment Joseph had left behind and turned the evidence of his escape into evidence against him.
The coat of integrity became the weapon of accusation.
Joseph refused to sleep with her, and she accused him.
Potiphar became angry.
Joseph was thrown into prison.
Sit with that for a moment.
Joseph obeyed God...
and went to jail.
That does not fit neatly into the version of Christianity that says obedience always produces immediate comfort.
Sometimes doing right costs you.
Sometimes purity loses the relationship.
Sometimes integrity loses the opportunity.
Sometimes telling the truth costs money.
Sometimes refusing compromise makes people hate you.
Sometimes you can obey God and still cry yourself to sleep wondering why obedience hurt so much.
Joseph had already been betrayed by his brothers.
Now he was falsely accused by the woman whose advances he rejected.
Pit.
Slavery.
Temptation.
False accusation.
Prison.
And yet Genesis 39 contains a sentence stronger than all of them.
“The LORD was with Joseph.”
That truth appears before the temptation, and Scripture returns to it in the prison.
God was with him.
Do not confuse painful circumstances with divine abandonment.
Joseph's prison did not mean God had disappeared.
And your darkest chapter does not automatically mean God has left you either.
But now we need to be careful.
Because Joseph's story can inspire us while simultaneously crushing us if we turn him into the ultimate hero.
Joseph resisted.
Maybe you didn't.
Joseph ran.
Maybe you stayed.
Joseph left the garment.
Maybe you went back.
Maybe the phrase “sexual temptation” does not make you think of victory.
Maybe it brings back memories.
Maybe you crossed lines.
Maybe you betrayed someone.
Maybe somebody betrayed you.
Maybe your marriage carries scars nobody at church knows about.
Maybe pornography became your anesthetic.
Maybe loneliness turned into compromise.
Maybe you have confessed the same sin so many times that saying “I'm sorry, Jesus” now feels embarrassing.
Maybe you are reading about Joseph and thinking:
I wish I had run.
Then hear the Gospel.
Christianity is not ultimately the announcement that Joseph was strong enough.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
Joseph points us toward faithfulness.
Jesus brings us redemption.
And where Joseph's story makes us confront temptation, Christ forces us to confront something even deeper: none of us has lived with perfect purity before God.
Jesus did.
The Son of God entered our broken world and remained without sin.
He was tempted, yet without sin.
He was rejected.
Falsely accused.
Condemned though innocent.
Stripped.
Mocked.
And led toward a punishment He did not deserve.
At the cross, however, something infinitely greater than Joseph's unjust suffering was happening.
Jesus willingly gave Himself for sinners.
The innocent One died for the guilty.
Not because sin did not matter.
Because sin mattered so much that redemption required a Savior.
This is why grace is not God shrugging at your sexual sin.
Grace is God dealing with sin through the cross and opening the door for sinners to be forgiven, cleansed, reconciled, and transformed through Jesus Christ.
Repentance therefore is not merely feeling disgusting about what you did.
Repentance turns.
It comes into the light.
It stops defending what God calls sin.
It stops negotiating.
It stops hiding.
And it runs toward Christ.
Maybe you cannot rewrite what happened last night.
Maybe you cannot unsend the message.
Maybe you cannot recover the years.
Maybe you cannot undo the affair.
Maybe you cannot erase what you watched.
Maybe you cannot return to yourself the innocence you threw away.
But you can come to Jesus.
That is the scandal of grace.
The Gospel does not say your sin never happened.
The Gospel says your sin does not have to have the final word.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).
That promise does not belong to people who successfully convinced God they were never guilty.
It belongs to those who are in Christ Jesus.
Forgiven people are not people with spotless histories.
They are people with a spotless Savior.
And perhaps this is where Joseph's garment becomes strangely unforgettable.
Joseph left his garment behind to escape temptation.
Years earlier, his brothers had used another garment—his special robe—to help deceive their father after selling Joseph.
Now another garment was being used to tell another lie about him.
His story seems surrounded by clothing other people keep turning into evidence.
But God was writing something nobody in that Egyptian house could yet see.
The prison was not the end.
The accusation was not the end.
The pit was not the end.
The betrayal was not the end.
God would raise Joseph.
He would eventually stand before Pharaoh.
The forgotten prisoner would become a ruler.
The betrayed brother would become an instrument through whom lives were preserved during famine.
And eventually the brothers who sold him would stand before the brother they could not destroy.
Joseph would later look back upon the evil done against him and recognize the sovereign hand of God bringing good through what others intended for evil (Genesis 50:20).
That does not make evil good.
It means evil does not get sovereignty.
God does.
And maybe that is what you needed tonight.
Your worst chapter is not necessarily your last chapter.
Your temptation is not your identity.
Your failure is not your name.
Your wound is not your destiny.
Your accusation is not your Judge.
Your past is not your Savior.
Jesus is.
So when temptation whispers, “Sleep with me,” “Click me,” “Message me,” “Nobody will know,” “You deserve this,” “Just once,” remember Joseph.
But when your conscience whispers, “You already failed, so God could never want you again,” remember Jesus.
Run from sin.
Run to Christ.
Those two movements belong together.
And if something hidden was exposed while you were reading this, do not turn this article into another emotional moment that disappears when you scroll.
Be honest before God.
No performance.
No pretending.
Bring it into the light.
Not as a badge that says, “Look how holy I am,” but because somebody scrolling silently tonight may be fighting a battle they have told absolutely no one about.
Sometimes running is worship.
The Gospel cannot be bought. Salvation is God's gift in Christ.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of helping biblical truth reach more people.

If you want your resources to glorify God, consider putting some of them behind work that points people toward Jesus. Sharing this article publicly costs nothing, yet it may place the Gospel in front of someone who would never walk into a church.
But whether you ever spend a cent or not, do not miss the greater invitation.
Come to Christ.
If you are standing in Joseph's room right now, run.
If you already fell, repent and run to Jesus.
If you have been forgiven, stop crawling back into the grave Christ called you out of.

If someone else's sexual sin wounded you, know that this story does not excuse coercion, harassment, assault, manipulation, or abuse. Joseph himself was subjected to persistent unwanted sexual pressure and was physically grabbed before he escaped. Scripture does not portray him as responsible for another person's predatory behavior.

And if you are the one who sinned, grace does not mean avoiding responsibility. Biblical repentance can require confession, ending sinful access, accepting consequences, making restitution where appropriate, seeking wise pastoral or professional help, and establishing boundaries strong enough to protect others and yourself.
Jesus did not shed His blood so we could become comfortable hiding.
He died and rose again to make sinners new.
So share this with the person whose battle is happening behind a smile.
Because one of the Bible's bluntest propositions was answered by one of its simplest acts of courage:
He refused.
Then he ran.
And if you failed to run when you should have, the story is still not over—because there is a Savior whose grace reaches farther than the room where you fell.
Sometimes the garment you leave behind while running from sin will cost you something—but nothing you surrender for Christ is worth more than the soul you refuse to leave behind.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ESAU TRADED SOMETHING PRICELESS FOR ONE MEAL — SOME DECISIONS COST MORE THAN THEY FEEL
paragraphs: ESAU TRADED SOMETHING PRICELESS FOR ONE MEAL — SOME DECISIONS COST MORE THAN THEY FEEL

The most dangerous decisions are often not made when we hate God. They are made when we are tired, hungry, lonely, angry, tempted, wounded—and desperate for something that promises to make the pain stop right now.
There was nothing obviously terrifying about the bowl.
That is what makes the story terrifying.
No serpent appears in Genesis 25. No idol is erected. No army approaches. No thunder rolls from heaven.
There is only a tired man.
A hungry stomach.
The smell of food.
A brother who sees an opportunity.
And one decision that probably felt reasonable for a few minutes.
Esau came home from the field exhausted. Jacob was cooking lentil stew. The Hebrew text describes Esau as עָיֵף — ʿayef, weary, exhausted, faint.
He was depleted.
And depleted people can become dangerously vulnerable to immediate relief.
Esau looked at what was steaming in front of him and wanted it now. Jacob responded with a shocking price:
Sell me your birthright.
Esau answered, essentially, “I am going to die anyway. What good is this birthright to me?”
So he swore an oath.
He traded it.
Jacob gave him bread and lentil stew.
Then Scripture records the aftermath with almost brutal simplicity:
“he ate and drank and rose and went his way.”
And then comes God's assessment of what had actually happened:
וַיִּבֶז עֵשָׂו אֶת־הַבְּכֹרָה — vayyivez ʿEsav et-habekhorah.
“Thus Esau despised his birthright.”
That final word changes everything.
The Hebrew verb behind “despised” is בָּזָה — bazah: to treat with contempt, to regard lightly, to consider something of little worth.
Esau's tragedy was bigger than hunger.
The bowl exposed his valuation system.

He treated something weighty as though it were worthless because something immediate felt more urgent. Genesis deliberately ends the episode not merely by saying that Esau sold the birthright, but that he despised it.
And suddenly this ancient story becomes painfully modern.
Because we still do this.
Not with lentil stew.
With screens.
With bodies.
With secret conversations.
With pornography.
With bitterness.
With revenge.
With another drink.
With applause.
With money.
With relationships we know are pulling us away from Christ.
With compromises nobody else knows about.
With the desperate need to feel wanted.
With the need to win an argument.
With the temptation to become somebody online that we would be ashamed to become before Jesus.
The bowl changes.
The transaction does not.
Something temporary whispers:
“Give me something valuable, and I will make you feel better right now.”
That is how temptation frequently works.
It exaggerates the urgency of the appetite while hiding the value of what obedience protects.
Read that again.
Temptation makes the bowl look enormous and the birthright look small.
When you are lonely, one forbidden relationship can feel enormous.
When you are sexually tempted, a few minutes of gratification can feel enormous.
When you are furious, sending that message can feel enormous.
When you are wounded, revenge can feel enormous.
When you are financially desperate, dishonest money can feel enormous.
When you are exhausted spiritually, walking away from prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and obedience can feel almost reasonable.
That is the frightening thing about Esau.
His decision did not necessarily feel catastrophic while he was making it.
He was hungry.
There was food.
He wanted relief.
And there was something in his possession whose value could not satisfy his stomach in that particular moment.
So he measured eternal significance using temporary appetite.
And lost.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You did not wake up planning to destroy anything.
You were just lonely.
Just angry.
Just curious.
Just exhausted.
Just hurting.
Just desperate to feel something.
Just desperate to stop feeling something.
And somewhere between the wound and the relief, you made a trade.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe the consequences are sitting beside you right now.
Maybe your marriage changed because of it.
Maybe trust disappeared.
Maybe years were lost.
Maybe your children saw something you wish they had never seen.
Maybe your private compromise became a public scandal.
Maybe your faith grew cold so gradually that you cannot remember the exact day Jesus stopped being the center.
And now you keep replaying the decision.
“If only I hadn't…”
“If only I had walked away…”
“If only I had waited…”
“If only I had prayed…”
“If only I could go back.”
This is where Esau's story becomes even heavier.
Centuries later, Hebrews reaches back into Genesis and warns Christians:
μή τις… βέβηλος ὡς Ἠσαῦ — mē tis… bebēlos hōs Ēsau.
The key description is βέβηλος — bebēlos, commonly rendered “profane,” “unholy,” or “godless”—someone treating sacred things as common.
Hebrews says Esau, “for one meal sold his birthright.”
The Greek is devastatingly precise:
ἀντὶ βρώσεως μιᾶς — anti brōseōs mias.
“For one meal.”
One.
That is the biblical emphasis.
Something enduring was exchanged for something consumed almost immediately.
Think about that.
The stew disappeared.
The decision remained.
His stomach became full.
The transaction did not disappear with his hunger.
And there are people reading this who understand that sentence more deeply than they wish they did.
The pleasure ended.
The screenshot remained.
The affair ended.
The wound remained.
The high ended.
The consequences remained.
The applause ended.
The compromise remained.
The money disappeared.
The dishonesty remained.
The argument ended.
The words remained.
The night ended.
But morning remembered.
That is why some decisions cost more than they feel.
Sin almost never shows you the invoice before you purchase the experience.
It advertises pleasure and conceals slavery.
It advertises relief and conceals regret.
It advertises freedom and conceals chains.
James explains the progression: desire conceives and gives birth to sin, and sin, when fully grown, brings forth death.
Jesus asks the question that destroys the mathematics of every sinful bargain:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
What profit?
That is the question Esau should have asked before eating.
And it is the question we must ask before clicking, sleeping with, buying, saying, hiding, taking, leaving, betraying, retaliating, or surrendering to whatever our bowl happens to be.
What am I receiving?
And what am I trading?
But there is something extremely important we must not distort.
The Bible does not teach that every bad decision places a genuinely repentant sinner beyond the mercy of Jesus Christ.
That would mutilate the Gospel.

Hebrews 12:17 speaks solemnly of Esau later wanting the blessing and encountering an irreversible consequence. We should not twist that warning into the claim that a repentant sinner who comes to Christ can somehow exhaust the saving mercy of God. Hebrews itself repeatedly calls believers to draw near to God through Christ. The New Testament announces forgiveness to sinners who repent and believe.
There is a difference between forgiveness and the removal of every earthly consequence.
David was forgiven, yet consequences entered his household.
Peter denied Jesus, yet Jesus restored him.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left with which to repair his reputation, yet Jesus promised him paradise.
Paul carried memories of persecuting the church, yet grace transformed the persecutor into a preacher of the Christ he once opposed.
The Gospel does not say your choices never mattered.
The Gospel says your failures do not possess greater saving power than the blood of Jesus.
That distinction matters.
Because maybe you already ate the stew.
Maybe this article reached you after the decision.
After the compromise.
After the divorce.
After the relapse.
After the betrayal.
After the secret.
After the scandal.
And Satan has changed his strategy.
Before the sin, he whispered:
“It isn't that serious.”
After the sin, he whispers:
“You are beyond forgiveness.”
He lies both times.
Before sin, he minimizes sin.
After sin, he minimizes grace.
But the cross exposes both lies.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to Calvary.
Grace is so astonishing that the Son of God willingly went to Calvary for sinners.
Jesus did not die because our rebellion was insignificant.
He died because our condition was desperate.
And He rose because death could not hold Him.
This is where Esau's bowl forces us to look beyond Esau—to Jesus Christ.
Esau was hungry and surrendered something precious to satisfy himself.
Jesus was hungry in the wilderness after fasting forty days, and when the tempter urged Him to turn stones into bread, Christ refused to abandon obedience to His Father for immediate satisfaction.
Where humanity repeatedly says, “Give me the bowl,” Jesus remained faithful.
Where we have surrendered to temptation, Christ overcame.
Where we have sinned, Christ remained sinless.
And the sinless Christ eventually went to a cross for sinful people.
Jesus did something radically opposite to Esau's transaction.
Esau surrendered something valuable to satisfy himself.
Christ surrendered Himself to rescue people who had nothing worthy enough to purchase salvation.
You cannot buy that grace.
You cannot earn it.
You cannot clean yourself enough to deserve it.
You come empty-handed.
You repent.
You believe.
You surrender to Christ.
And the One who knows the worst chapter of your story is still capable of writing redemption into the pages that remain.
That does not mean pretending consequences do not exist.
Grace is not denial.
Grace tells the truth.
Grace confesses.
Grace repents.
Grace makes restitution where possible.
Grace walks away from sin.
Grace accepts accountability.
Grace stops calling bondage “freedom.”
Grace stops decorating the bowl.
Grace looks at Jesus and finally realizes:
He is better.
Better than the affair.
Better than the addiction.
Better than the applause.
Better than the money.
Better than revenge.
Better than pornography.
Better than being desired.
Better than being right.
Better than the temporary relief you have been purchasing with pieces of your soul.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe somewhere inside these words, your bowl got a name.
Do not hide from that conviction.
Bring it into the light.
Not because public humiliation saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But repentance stops defending what grace came to deliver us from.
Tell Christ the truth.
If necessary, tell a mature, trustworthy believer who can walk with you.
Confess what Scripture calls sin.
Receive God's mercy through faith in Jesus.
Then begin walking differently.
You may not be able to undo yesterday.
But through Christ, yesterday does not have to become the god of tomorrow.
And please hear this carefully: the answer to Esau's story is not “try harder so God will love you.”
The answer is Jesus.
Christianity is not starving yourself beside a forbidden bowl while secretly wishing you could eat it.
Christianity is discovering a Savior so infinitely worthy that the bowl begins losing its authority over you.
You were made for more than appetites.
More than impulses.
More than five-minute pleasures.
More than secret addictions.
More than validation.
More than the approval of people who will eventually forget your name.
You were made to know God.
And in Christ, sinners are invited into something no earthly appetite can manufacture: reconciliation with God, forgiveness, adoption, holiness, hope, and eternal life.
So before your next decision, remember Esau.
When you are tired, remember Esau.
When you are lonely at 2:00 in the morning, remember Esau.
When the message appears, remember Esau.
When nobody would know, remember Esau.
When your anger tells you to speak immediately, remember Esau.
When your flesh says, “I need this,” ask another question:
What will this cost me after the hunger passes?
Then look at Jesus.
Because sometimes the holiest thing you can do is refuse to make a permanent decision under the dictatorship of a temporary appetite.
Wait.
Pray.
Leave the room.
Close the screen.
Call someone.
Open Scripture.
Go home.
Confess.
Ask for help.
Run from temptation.
Run toward Christ.
There is no bowl worth exchanging fellowship with God, obedience to Christ, integrity, family, testimony, purity, peace, or a clear conscience to possess.
And if you already made the trade?
Come home.
Not casually.
Not pretending sin does not matter.
Come repentant.
Come broken.
Come trusting Jesus.
The father in Christ's parable of the prodigal son did not celebrate the far country. He celebrated the return of his son.
That is grace.
Grace does not rename the pigpen.
Grace brings prodigals home.
Maybe your most important decision today is not regretting yesterday harder.
Maybe it is finally surrendering today to Jesus.
Your testimony may become the evidence another wounded person needs that failure does not have to be the final chapter.
Then send this to the person who is standing near a bowl right now.
You know who they are.
The friend growing cold toward God.
The husband secretly struggling.
The wife carrying silent pain.
The teenager learning how seductive instant gratification can be.
The believer who thinks one compromise will not matter.
The person who already failed and believes Jesus no longer wants them.
Not because you need it while you feel strong.
But before you leave, remember the scene.
A tired man.
A steaming bowl.
A priceless inheritance.
A moment of appetite.
Then the meal was over.
That is the part I cannot forget.
The bowl became empty long before the consequences did.
So when temptation puts something temporary in front of you and demands something precious in exchange, remember Esau.
And when shame tells you that what you traded can never be redeemed, remember Jesus.
The warning is real.
The consequences can be real.
But so is the cross.
So is the empty tomb.
So is repentance.
So is forgiveness.
So is transforming grace.
Your scandal may explain part of your story.
It does not have the authority to write the ending when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
The bowl may have had your yesterday. Do not let it have your tomorrow. Give tomorrow to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID GOD TELL JEREMIAH NOT TO MARRY?
paragraphs:
WHY DID GOD TELL JEREMIAH NOT TO MARRY?
The Terrifying Mercy Hidden in One of the Bible’s Strangest Commands—and What It Reveals About Judgment, Obedience, and the God Who Still Offers Grace
There are commands in Scripture that comfort you.
There are commands that correct you.
And then there are commands that make you stop reading.
This is one of them.
God looked at Jeremiah—a man already carrying the crushing weight of speaking truth to a nation that did not want to hear it—and told him something deeply personal:
Do not marry.
Not because marriage was sinful.
Not because love was evil.
Not because Jeremiah was somehow too spiritual for a wife and children.
The reason was far more disturbing.
God knew what was coming.
And once you understand what was coming, this strange command stops looking like God denying Jeremiah something beautiful.
It begins to look like severe mercy.
The Hebrew text of Jeremiah 16:2 reads:
לֹא־תִקַּח לְךָ אִשָּׁה וְלֹא־יִהְיוּ לְךָ בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת בַּמָּקוֹם הַזֶּה
Lo-tiqqach lekha ishshah, velo-yihyu lekha banim uvanot, bammaqom hazzeh.
In straightforward English:
“You shall not take a wife, nor shall you have sons or daughters in this place.”
Notice those final words.
“In this place.”
They matter.

The Hebrew text does not present a universal command forbidding God's servants to marry. God was giving Jeremiah a specific prophetic command in a specific historical setting. Jeremiah's unmarried life itself would become part of his message.
His life was going to preach.
And what it preached was terrifying.
God immediately explained why:

“For thus says the LORD concerning the sons and daughters who are born in this place, and concerning their mothers who bore them and their fathers who fathered them in this land: They shall die of deadly diseases. They shall not be lamented, nor shall they be buried.”
Then come the words nobody wants embroidered on a pillow.
Sword.
Famine.
Death.
Unburied bodies.

Jeremiah was announcing catastrophe to Judah. The judgment he warned about would eventually be bound up with Babylon's devastation of Jerusalem. Elsewhere Jeremiah repeatedly warns of death by sword, famine, and pestilence.
God was not telling Jeremiah that marriage was bad.
God was telling Jeremiah that disaster was coming.
That distinction changes everything.
Imagine Jeremiah hearing it.
Perhaps he had imagined having a home one day.
Perhaps he had wondered what it would feel like to come home after being mocked for preaching and find someone waiting for him.
Perhaps he had imagined children running toward him.
Scripture never tells us that he did, so we must not pretend that we know.
But we do know something about being human.
And Jeremiah was human.
Marriage was an honorable and ordinary part of covenant life. Yet God required this prophet to surrender even that possibility as part of his calling.
His empty house would become a sermon.
His absence from the wedding celebration would become a warning.
His lack of children would become a living prophecy.
Because sometimes God did not merely give His prophets messages.
He made their lives part of the message.
Hosea's marriage became prophetic symbolism.
Isaiah's children carried prophetic names.
Ezekiel endured devastating personal loss while serving as a sign to Israel.
And Jeremiah's singleness became a visible warning that normal life was about to be violently interrupted.
Think about how unsettling that would have been.
Someone could have asked Jeremiah:
“Why aren't you married?”
And Jeremiah's life itself answered:
Because you are living as though tomorrow is guaranteed, and God says judgment is approaching.
That is where this ancient passage suddenly becomes uncomfortable for modern readers.
Because we are very good at building permanent lives in temporary worlds.
We plan.
We purchase.
We upgrade.
We decorate.
We scroll.
We accumulate.
We tell ourselves there will always be another year.
Another birthday.
Another Christmas.
Another opportunity to apologize.
Another Sunday to return to God.
Another chance to forgive.
Another chance to repent.
Another chance to finally surrender the secret sin.
Another chance to tell somebody about Jesus.
Another chance to become the person we keep promising God we will become.
Jeremiah walked into a society carrying the unbearable message that “later” is not something human beings own.
His unmarried life confronted an entire culture with that reality.
But there is something else we must understand.
Jeremiah 16 is not permission for Christians to look at every unmarried believer and say, “God must be keeping you single because something terrible is coming.”
No.
That abuses the passage.
Neither should someone use Jeremiah 16 to claim that marriage is spiritually inferior to singleness.
Scripture will not allow that conclusion either.

Marriage is honored in Scripture, and Jesus Himself affirmed God's creation design for marriage. The New Testament also recognizes that some believers serve God unmarried and that singleness can provide particular freedom for undivided devotion to the Lord.
Jeremiah's situation was extraordinary.
This was prophetic obedience under extraordinary circumstances.
And perhaps that is where the passage reaches deeper than marriage.
Because the real question eventually becomes:
What happens when obeying God costs you something you genuinely wanted?
That question hurts.
It is easy to sing about surrender when surrender remains theoretical.
It is different when obedience walks into your plans.
When the relationship disappears.
When the door closes.
When the future you imagined never arrives.
When faithfulness costs reputation.
When telling the truth costs friendships.
When refusing compromise costs money.
When following Christ separates you from something your flesh desperately wants.
Jeremiah knew something about costly obedience.
And here is where we must be careful.
Not every disappointment in your life is God “taking something away.”
Not every closed door is a mysterious divine command.
Not every heartbreak should be spiritualized.
Scripture does not give us permission to manufacture revelation around our pain.
But Scripture does teach us something far more dependable:
God is worthy of obedience even when obedience is costly.
Jeremiah could not see everything God saw.
God could.
And sometimes the command of God makes more sense when you finally understand what God knows that you do not.
A child may think a father's hand pulling him backward is preventing him from getting somewhere.
Then the speeding vehicle passes.
Suddenly the same hand feels different.
The restriction was protection.
Jeremiah 16 contains something like that—but on a devastating national scale.
God knew what Jeremiah would have been bringing a wife and children into.
He knew the sword that was coming.
He knew the famine that was coming.
He knew the grief that was coming.
He knew what the people refused to believe.
And so the command that initially sounds harsh begins to reveal another dimension.
Jeremiah would still suffer enormously.
He would be rejected.
Mocked.
Threatened.
Beaten.
Imprisoned.
Misunderstood.
His obedience did not produce a painless life.
Christianity never promises that.
But God did spare him from one particular category of agony: watching his own wife and children face the catastrophe described in this prophecy.
That is sobering.
Because sometimes mercy does not look like receiving what you prayed for.
Sometimes mercy may involve being kept from something whose consequences you cannot yet see.
We should never use that sentence to pretend we know God's secret explanation for every disappointment. We don't.
But we can trust the character of the God who does know.
And then Jeremiah 16 does something remarkable.
After judgment comes another promise.

God speaks of a future restoration so astonishing that the coming return of His people would become a defining testimony of divine deliverance. The same chapter that contains death, exile, and judgment also looks toward gathering.
That matters.
Because biblical judgment is never evidence that God has stopped being holy.
And restoration is never evidence that God has stopped caring about sin.
God is both holy and merciful.
The Bible does not give us a sentimental God who shrugs at rebellion.
It gives us something infinitely better.
A holy God who confronts sin—and a merciful God who makes redemption possible.
And ultimately, the story carries us beyond Jeremiah.
To Jesus Christ.
Jeremiah stood before a rebellious people and announced judgment.
Jesus came to rebellious humanity and did something astonishing.
He bore judgment for sinners.
At the cross, God did not pretend sin was harmless.
He demonstrated how serious it truly is.
Christ was crucified.
The innocent One stood in the place of the guilty.
The sinless Son of God bore our sins so that sinners could be forgiven, reconciled, and made new.
This is why grace should never be confused with God lowering His standards.
Grace is infinitely more costly than that.
At Calvary, justice and mercy meet.
The scandal is not merely that humanity sinned against its Creator.
The greater scandal is that the Creator came seeking sinners.
Jesus touched people religious society avoided.
He ate with sinners.
He called the compromised.
He forgave the guilty.
He restored the disgraced.
He welcomed the repentant.
And finally He went to a cross where He carried what sinners could never carry for themselves.
Then He rose.
That is the Gospel.
Not “become good enough and perhaps God will accept you.”
Not “hide your past until religious people approve of you.”
Not “repair yourself and then come to Jesus.”
The Gospel says Christ came for sinners.
Repent.
Believe.
Come into the light.
Receive the mercy purchased by Jesus Christ.
And let Him transform you.
Maybe that is why Jeremiah's strange command still reaches into our lives thousands of years later.
Because somewhere beneath the question “Why couldn't Jeremiah marry?” is another question:
Do I trust God when I don't understand what He is doing?
And beneath that question may be an even more dangerous one:
Have I actually surrendered my life to Christ—or have I only surrendered the parts that never cost me anything?
That one can become painfully personal.
Maybe you love Jesus publicly but protect a secret compromise privately.
Maybe everyone thinks you are spiritually strong while you are exhausted from pretending.
Maybe you keep telling God, “Everything is Yours,” while quietly adding, “except this.”
This relationship.
This habit.
This resentment.
This ambition.
This hidden browser history.
This bitterness.
This pride.
This need to be admired.
This refusal to forgive.
This version of your future.
And perhaps God is not asking you to understand everything tonight.
Perhaps His Word is confronting you with something more basic.
Will you trust Christ enough to obey Him?
Jeremiah's generation learned painfully that ignoring God's warnings does not make them disappear.
We need to remember that.
Because Jesus is not merely an accessory for the life we already planned.
He is Lord.
Yet the Lord before whom we surrender is also the Savior whose hands were pierced for us.
So if this article exposed something hidden in you, do not run deeper into hiding.
Run toward Christ.
If you need forgiveness, ask Him.
If you have wandered, return.
If there is sin to confess, bring it into the light.
If there is someone you need to forgive, begin surrendering that wound to God.
If you have spent years performing Christianity without truly yielding your heart to Jesus, stop performing.
Come home.
And if these words found you in a season where God's path makes absolutely no sense, remember Jeremiah.
You may not know what tomorrow contains.
You may not understand the closed door.
You may not understand why one prayer seemed unanswered while someone else's was answered.
You may not understand why obedience became so expensive.
Do not invent explanations God has not given you.
But do not confuse unanswered questions with an absent God.
The cross has already shown you His heart.
And the empty tomb has already shown you that the darkest chapter is not necessarily the final chapter.
Jesus Christ is still in the business of taking stories that look finished and writing redemption where everyone else expected an ending.
And please don't keep this message trapped on your screen.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't. We are saved by grace through faith, and even that is God's gift.
But if biblical truth has strengthened you, sharing it can become one simple way of helping put that truth in front of someone else.
Someone angry with God.
Someone hiding sin.
Someone considering walking away from the faith.
Someone convinced his scandal is greater than Christ's grace.
Someone who will never search for a Christian article—but might read the one you shared.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedient lives, and financial support can be one voluntary expression of generosity—not a spiritual transaction.
Jeremiah surrendered the future he might have imagined because the Word of God mattered more than the life he might have planned.
Jesus surrendered infinitely more.
He gave Himself.
For sinners.
For rebels.
For failures.
For hypocrites who finally stop pretending.
For prodigals coming home.
For people whose stories became scandals.
For people who thought they had gone too far.
For you.
So perhaps the question you will remember tomorrow will no longer be:
“Why did God tell Jeremiah not to marry?”
Perhaps it will be:
“What am I still refusing to surrender to the Christ who surrendered Himself for me?”
Bring it to Him.
The shame.
The secret.
The disappointment.
The future.
The unanswered question.
The thing you cannot control.
Bring it all.
Because the God who warned through Jeremiah is the God who ultimately revealed His saving mercy in Jesus Christ.
Judgment is real.
Sin is serious.
Repentance matters.
Grace is costly.
Forgiveness is possible.
And Jesus still saves.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is asking God why the story did not go according to plan.
And perhaps what they desperately need to discover is this:
The chapter that broke your expectations does not have authority to write the ending when your life belongs to Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU DID IT AGAIN. DID SOMETHING JUST DIE INSIDE YOU?
paragraphs: YOU DID IT AGAIN. DID SOMETHING JUST DIE INSIDE YOU?

What really happens spiritually when a man or woman masturbates—and does it mean you are going to hell? The biblical answer is more serious than cheap reassurance, but far more hopeful than shame ever told you.
The room is quiet again.
The screen is dark.
Your breathing has slowed.
And suddenly the thing that promised relief has left you with a question you were trying not to ask.
What did I just do to my soul?
Maybe you're a man who has fought this since adolescence.
Maybe you're a woman who has never told anyone because people talk about sexual temptation as though women don't experience it.
Maybe pornography was involved.
Maybe it wasn't.
Maybe there was a fantasy you knew you shouldn't entertain.
Maybe you promised God the last time would actually be the last time.
Then stress came.
Loneliness came.
The late-night scrolling came.
The memories came.
The temptation came.
And now you're sitting in the aftermath wondering whether God is disgusted with you.
You may even be afraid to pray.
"How can I talk to God after doing that?"
And underneath that question is an even more terrifying one:
"If I die tonight, am I going to hell?"
We need to answer that carefully, because Christians can make two opposite mistakes here.
One says, "It's masturbation. Everybody does it. Stop making a big deal about it."
The other practically tells the struggling believer, "You failed sexually again, so God must have abandoned you."
Neither response handles Scripture faithfully.
So before fear becomes your theologian, hear this:
The Bible never directly says, "A person who masturbates is automatically condemned to hell."
There is no verse that says those words.
That matters.
We should never claim God explicitly said something Scripture does not explicitly say.
But don't close this article yet, because that doesn't mean Scripture has nothing serious to say about what may be happening in your heart, imagination, body, habits, and relationship with Christ.
Jesus takes sexual holiness extraordinarily seriously.
And He also takes grace extraordinarily seriously.
That combination is where freedom begins.
Jesus said in Matthew 5:28 that whoever looks at another person lustfully has already committed adultery in the heart.
The key Greek expression includes πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι — pros to epithymēsai, expressing looking directed toward lustful desire.
Jesus moves the conversation beneath external behavior.
Into desire.
Into intention.
Into the hidden room nobody else sees.
That means the biblical question cannot simply be:
"Did my body experience sexual release?"
The deeper questions are:
What was I desiring? What was I imagining? What was I feeding? What was ruling me?
Was pornography involved?
Was another person's body turned into material for fantasy?
Was someone who bears God's image reduced in your imagination to an object for your gratification?
Have you become dependent upon the behavior for comfort, escape, sleep, emotional regulation, or relief?
Do you repeatedly tell yourself you can stop whenever you want—only to discover that your desires seem increasingly capable of commanding you?
Then the issue has become much larger than a momentary physical sensation.
Paul writes:
πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν, ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος
The heart of 1 Corinthians 6:12 is staggering:
"I will not be dominated by anything."
That word ἐξουσιασθήσομαι — exousiasthēsomai carries the idea of being mastered or brought under another's authority.
Now ask yourself something uncomfortable.
Can you say no?
Not theoretically.
Actually.
When loneliness tells you to do it, can you say no?
When your body demands it, can you say no?
When the pornography tab is one touch away, can you say no?
When nobody would ever know, can you still say no because Jesus is enough reason?
That question reaches deeper than masturbation.
It reaches lordship.
Because Christianity is not merely about asking, "How close can I get to sin without technically crossing a line?"
Christianity asks:
"Jesus, how completely can I belong to You?"
Paul's instruction becomes even stronger a few verses later:
φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν — pheugete tēn porneian.
"Flee sexual immorality."
Not negotiate with it.
Not keep it bookmarked.
Not see how long you can stare before technically sinning.
Flee.

Then Paul gives the reason that changes everything: the believer's body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, the believer is not his or her own, and has been "bought with a price." Therefore, glorify God in your body. See 1 Corinthians 6:18–20.
Notice what Christianity does here.
It does not tell you your body is filthy.
It tells you your body is valuable.
Christian sexual holiness is not based on hatred of the body.
It is based on the astonishing dignity of the body.
Your body matters to God.
Your sexuality matters to God.
Your imagination matters to God.
What you repeatedly teach your desires to crave matters to God.
You were made for something greater than being controlled by an appetite.
But now we have to address the frightening question.
What happens to your spirit when you masturbate?
Scripture does not teach that masturbation causes some identifiable spiritual substance to leave your body.
It does not say that semen contains spiritual power.
It does not teach that orgasm removes part of your soul.
It does not say masturbation automatically makes the Holy Spirit depart from a Christian.
Those claims should not be presented as biblical doctrine because Scripture does not teach them.
What Scripture does teach is that sin affects fellowship with God, forms habits of desire, can harden the heart when persistently embraced, and must never be treated casually.
Sexual sin matters.
Paul explicitly commands Christians to flee sexual immorality and reminds them that their bodies belong to God.
But here is an important distinction.
Temptation is not identical to sin.
Sexual desire itself is not proof that you are filthy.
Having a body that experiences sexual arousal is not evidence that God made a mistake.
The question is what you do with desire.
James describes desire conceiving and giving birth to sin, and sin eventually producing death. That is a process worth noticing.
Desire.
Consent.
Sin.
Death.
So don't confuse the knock at the door with opening the door.
But don't invite temptation inside for dinner and then pretend nothing happened either.
Jesus does not call you to fear your sexuality.
He calls you to surrender it.
And this is where someone reading this may be trembling.
Because you're thinking:
"But I didn't just struggle once."
"I've done this hundreds of times."
"I've prayed for forgiveness and returned to it."
"What if my repentance isn't real?"
"What if God is finished with me?"
Listen carefully.
The gospel is not the announcement that sexually disciplined people can save themselves.
The gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ saves sinners.
At the cross, Jesus did not die for the imaginary polished version of you.
He knew.
He knew every hidden browser window.
Every fantasy.
Every compromise.
Every promise you would break.
Every night you would feel too ashamed to pray.
Every secret you hoped nobody would discover.
And Christ went to the cross knowing the complete truth.
That does not make your sin insignificant.
It makes His grace astonishing.
Romans 8:1 begins with one of the greatest declarations ever given to guilty people:
Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα τοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.
Ouden ara nyn katakrima tois en Christō Iēsou.
"There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus."
Read that again.
No condemnation.
The Greek word κατάκριμα — katakrima refers to condemnation, a judicial sentence against someone.
Paul doesn't say there is no conviction.
Conviction and condemnation are not the same thing.
Conviction says:
"This is sin. Bring it into the light. Come back to Christ."
Condemnation says:
"You are hopeless. Hide from Christ."
One draws the sinner toward repentance.
The other whispers that there is no point returning.
And the devil would love nothing more than for your shame to accomplish what temptation couldn't.
Perhaps temptation got you to fall.
Now shame wants you to stay down.
But Jesus Christ is not standing over the repentant sinner saying, "I can't believe you came back again."
The entire Christian life exists because sinners need grace again.
So are people who masturbate automatically bound for hell?
No biblical text gives us authority to pronounce that sentence merely because someone has masturbated.
Salvation is not achieved by maintaining a flawless record of sexual behavior.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
But neither should anyone use grace as permission to cherish sin.
Scripture repeatedly warns against lives characterized by unrepentant sexual immorality. The Christian response therefore isn't, "It doesn't matter because Jesus forgives me."
It is:
"Because Jesus has forgiven me, I don't want anything else sitting on His throne."
There is an enormous difference between fighting sin and making peace with sin.
A believer may stumble terribly while still hating the sin and running repeatedly toward Christ.
Another person may deliberately cherish sin, defend it, refuse repentance, and want Jesus only as insurance against judgment.
Those are spiritually different postures.
The evidence of grace is not necessarily that you have never fallen.
Sometimes it is that something inside you refuses to call darkness light.
You fall.
You grieve.
You confess.
You get up.
You remove access.
You seek accountability.
You learn your triggers.
You stop protecting the environment in which your sin keeps surviving.
You run toward Christ again.
And again.
And again.
Not because sin doesn't matter.
Because Christ matters more.
If pornography is part of your masturbation pattern, stop treating pornography as harmless entertainment.
You are training your imagination.
You are teaching your brain and heart what to seek when lonely, stressed, angry, rejected, or bored.
And behind the pixels are human beings made in the image of God.
They are not products for your imagination.
They are people Christ commands you to see with dignity.
If fantasy is involved, bring the fantasy itself before God.
If loneliness drives the behavior, deal with the loneliness.
If anxiety drives it, deal with the anxiety.
If boredom drives it, change your rhythms.
If your phone repeatedly becomes the doorway, stop congratulating yourself for spiritual determination while carrying unrestricted temptation into bed every night.
Sometimes repentance looks very spiritual.
Sometimes repentance looks like charging your phone in another room.
Sometimes it looks like deleting an app.
Sometimes it looks like finally telling a mature Christian friend:
"I need help."
You don't defeat secrecy by becoming stronger at hiding.
You defeat secrecy by bringing darkness into the light.
And maybe this is the moment where somebody finally needs to stop pretending.
You love Jesus.
But you're exhausted.
You worship on Sunday and struggle at midnight.
People think you're spiritually strong.
Nobody knows this battle has been eating you alive.
Then let today become the day you stop confusing secrecy with safety.
You don't need to publish graphic details.
You don't need to expose private information.
Just step out of the illusion that you're the only Christian who has ever fought a sexual battle.
Someone scrolling silently may desperately need to know that freedom is possible.
Your testimony may become somebody else's reason not to give up tonight.
Not because an article can rescue you.
It cannot.
Jesus can.

Save it so when shame returns and tells you that one failure means God wants nothing more to do with you, you can remember the difference between conviction that leads you home and condemnation that tells you to run away.
Not to announce your private struggles.
A husband.
A wife.
A teenager.
A pastor.
A new Christian.
Someone who thinks sexual temptation means God could never love them.
Someone who has fallen so many times that tonight they are considering simply surrendering to the addiction.
You may never know whose midnight prayer begins because you were willing to put truth on their screen.
Protect people's dignity. But share the truth widely.
It doesn't.
Not because giving money proves that you glorify God.
It doesn't.
Jesus purchased salvation. We cannot purchase His approval.
But believers can glorify God by generously supporting faithful Gospel work, helping biblical teaching reach people who desperately need it, and sharing truth with others.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody is sitting in the same silence described at the beginning of this article.
The screen just went dark.
The pleasure disappeared.
The shame arrived.
And they are wondering:
"Does Jesus still want me?"
If they belong to Christ, the answer is not found in pretending their sin doesn't matter.
The answer is found at a blood-stained cross proving that their sin mattered enough for Jesus to die—and His love was great enough for Him to do it willingly.
So if you fell tonight, don't make another dramatic promise that you'll become worthy enough for God tomorrow.
Come to Christ tonight.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive mercy.
Get practical.
Bring the battle into the light.
Cut off what keeps feeding it.
Ask another mature believer for help.
And when temptation returns, don't merely tell yourself:
"I can't do this."
Remember something greater.
"I was bought with a price."
Your body is not garbage.
Your sexuality is not your master.
Your worst secret is not your identity.
Your failure does not get to rename you.
Jesus does.
The scandal may be what you did in darkness.
Grace is what Christ did publicly on a cross.
And resurrection means your story does not have to end where your shame says it should.
Because the goal was never merely to stop touching your body.
The goal is far greater.
To belong—body, mind, imagination, sexuality, wounds, desires, failures, future and all—to Jesus Christ.
And remember this when shame whispers your name tonight:
The hands pierced for your sin are still the hands reaching for the repentant sinner.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Job Lost Almost Everything in Days — Yet Heaven Knew Something Job Couldn’t See
paragraphs: Job Lost Almost Everything in Days — Yet Heaven Knew Something Job Couldn’t See
The most terrifying chapter of Job’s life began with silence from heaven—but the silence was never proof that God had abandoned him.
There are days when one terrible phone call would be enough.
Job had several.
One messenger came running.
Then another.
Then another.
Then another.
Before Job had time to absorb one catastrophe, the next one was already standing at his door.
His oxen and donkeys were taken. Servants were killed. Fire fell and consumed sheep and servants. Raiders swept away his camels. Then came the message no father should ever have to hear.
His sons and daughters were dead.
All of them.
The story is recorded with almost unbearable speed in Job 1:13–19. Scripture does not give Job time to recover between sentences because Job himself barely had time to recover between disasters.
“While he was yet speaking…”
Again.
“While he was yet speaking…”
Again.
“While he was yet speaking…”
Sometimes suffering does not knock politely.
It kicks the door down.
And maybe that is why Job still reaches people thousands of years later.
You may never have owned thousands of sheep or camels, but you know what it feels like when life divides itself into before and after.
Before the diagnosis.
Before the funeral.
Before the betrayal.
Before the marriage collapsed.
Before the business failed.
Before your child stopped calling.
Before you discovered what had been hidden from you.
Before the person you trusted became the reason you could not sleep.
Before you found yourself sitting alone, wondering how the life you thanked God for became the life you could barely survive.
Job understood that kind of “after.”
But there was something Job did not know.
And this changes how we read everything.
Before catastrophe entered Job’s world, heaven had already spoken about Job.
The suffering man on earth could see ashes.
He could not see the conversation in heaven.
Job 1:8 records the LORD saying concerning him:
“Have you considered my servant Job…?”
The Hebrew is striking:
הֲשַׂמְתָּ לִבְּךָ עַל־עַבְדִּי אִיּוֹב
Ha-samta libbekha ‘al-avdi Iyyov?
The expression שִׂים לֵב — sim lev, literally involving the idea of “setting” or directing the heart toward something, carries the sense of giving careful attention or consideration.
And notice what God calls Job:
עַבְדִּי — avdi
“My servant.”
Before Job lost his property, God knew his name.
Before Job buried his children, God knew his faith.
Before Job sat among the ashes, God called him “My servant.”
Before Job questioned what was happening, heaven was not questioning who Job belonged to.
That matters.
Because suffering has a cruel way of changing the questions inside us.
“Does God still see me?”
“Did I do something wrong?”
“Has God rejected me?”
“Why am I praying when nothing seems to change?”
“Why does heaven feel silent?”
Maybe you have whispered something even more frightening:
“God… where are You?”
Job eventually asked questions like that too.
This is important because the Bible does not portray Job as a smiling religious machine pretending tragedy did not hurt.
He tore his robe.
He shaved his head.
He fell to the ground.
Later, he lamented the day of his birth.
He argued.
He grieved.
He desperately wanted answers.
Job was faithful, but Job was wounded.
Biblical faith is not pretending that pain does not hurt.
Sometimes faith looks like worship.
Sometimes faith looks like crying while refusing to walk away from God.
Sometimes faith is nothing more impressive than waking up tomorrow and whispering the name “Jesus” because you have no strength left for a longer prayer.
But Job’s first response after the death of his children remains staggering:
“Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.” — Job 1:21
The Hebrew ending is:
יְהִי שֵׁם יְהוָה מְבֹרָךְ
Yehi shem YHWH mevorakh.
“May the name of the LORD be blessed.”
Job did not call the tragedy good.
He called God worthy.
There is a difference.
And we must be careful here.
The book of Job should never be weaponized against suffering people.
It does not teach that every tragedy happens because someone secretly sinned.

In fact, one of the great tensions of the book is that Job’s friends repeatedly try to squeeze his suffering into simplistic explanations. They assume extraordinary suffering must mean extraordinary guilt.
God ultimately rebukes them.
Job 42:7 records the LORD telling Eliphaz:
“You have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has.”
So when somebody is suffering, Christianity does not give us permission to stand over their wounds and invent reasons God has not revealed.
Sometimes we simply do not know why.
Job did not.
And that may be the most unsettling part of the entire story.
We, the readers, are shown something Job was not shown.
Job knew what was happening to him.
He did not know what had happened before it.
He experienced the earthly chapter without receiving the heavenly prologue.
Think about that.
Job worshiped while missing information.
Job prayed while missing information.
Job remained in relationship with God while missing information.
And perhaps you are living inside a chapter where you are missing information too.
You see what left.
God sees what you cannot.
You see the closed door.
God sees beyond it.
You see the prayer that appears unanswered.
God sees the entire story at once.

That does not mean every loss will be replaced exactly as we want it. It does not mean every tragedy will suddenly make sense during this lifetime. And Job’s later restoration must never be interpreted as though new children somehow erased the children he buried.
They did not.
People are not replaceable.
The ending of Job is restoration, not erasure.
The scars remain part of the story.
And this is where Job begins pointing beyond himself toward something even greater.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of human beings learning how to suffer bravely.
Christianity is the story of Jesus Christ entering human suffering Himself.
Job longed for someone who could stand between humanity and God.
In Job 9:33 he cries:
“There is no arbiter between us, who might lay his hand on us both.”
Centuries later, the New Testament announces something breathtaking:
“For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.” — 1 Timothy 2:5
The Greek word translated “mediator” is:
μεσίτης — mesitēs
One who stands between parties as mediator.
Job longed for someone who could bridge the distance.
The Gospel reveals His name.
Jesus.
And Jesus did not save us by observing suffering from a safe distance.
He entered it.
He was rejected.
Betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Abandoned by friends.
Nailed to a cross.
And there, darkness covered the land.
The innocent One suffered.
The sinless Son was crucified.
Yet even when the disciples could see nothing but catastrophe, heaven knew something they could not yet see.
Friday looked like defeat.
Sunday revealed victory.
The cross looked like scandal.
God was accomplishing redemption.
The tomb looked final.
Jesus walked out.
That does not make Job and Jesus identical. Job was a righteous man in the sense described by the book; Jesus is the sinless Son of God and the Redeemer Job needed just as we do.
But Job’s story trains our hearts to understand something the cross displays perfectly:
What human eyes can see in the middle of suffering is not always the whole story.
And maybe that is exactly where this reaches you.
Because perhaps your faith has become difficult lately.
You still believe in God.
You are just tired.
You still love Jesus.
You just do not understand what He is allowing.
You still pray.
But some nights your prayers sound less like sermons and more like:
“Lord, please.”
Maybe nobody knows how exhausted you really are because you have become very good at saying, “I’m okay.”
You serve.
You smile.
You post encouraging Scriptures.
You help everybody else.
Then the room becomes quiet.
And suddenly you are alone with the question you are afraid to say publicly:
“God, have You forgotten me?”
Job whispers across thousands of years:
No.
Silence is not the same thing as absence.
And the cross shouts something even greater:
God has not remained distant from human suffering.
Jesus Christ stepped directly into it.
There is another line in Job that feels almost prophetic in its longing.
Job says:
וַאֲנִי יָדַעְתִּי גֹּאֲלִי חָי
Va’ani yadati go’ali chai.
“For I know that my Redeemer lives.” — Job 19:25
The Hebrew word גֹּאֵל — go’el refers to a redeemer or kinsman-redeemer, someone who acts on behalf of another.
Christians should read Job 19 carefully and responsibly within its ancient context rather than pretending Job possessed the entire later New Testament revelation.
But standing on this side of the resurrection, Christians cannot hear the language of a living Redeemer without remembering where the biblical story ultimately takes us.
Jesus Christ lives.
Your hope is not an idea.
Your hope has a name.
And if you have sinned, your greatest need is not merely for circumstances to improve.
You need reconciliation with God.
So do I.
So did Job.
The Gospel does not say, “Become strong enough and God will accept you.”
It says Christ did what sinners could never do for themselves.
He lived without sin.
He died for sinners.
He rose again.
And Scripture calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
Grace does not mean sin never mattered.
Grace means Jesus paid what sinners could never pay.
Forgiveness is not God pretending your rebellion never happened.
At the cross, sin was taken with terrifying seriousness.
And mercy was offered with astonishing generosity.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
This is where the ashamed come out of hiding.
This is where the guilty can be forgiven.
This is where prodigals can come home.
This is where broken people discover that their worst chapter does not have authority to write the final sentence.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your current chapter is Job 1.
Everything feels as though it is disappearing at once.
Maybe it is Job 3.
You are asking questions you are embarrassed to admit.
Maybe you are surrounded by your own version of Job’s friends—people with easy explanations for wounds they have never carried.
Or maybe the problem is not what happened to you.
Maybe the Holy Spirit is exposing what has been happening inside you.
Pride.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Adultery.
Envy.
Secret compromise.
Religious performance.
An addiction nobody knows about.
A resentment you have fed for years.
A double life.
Do not use suffering as an excuse to run from God.
And do not use shame as an excuse to hide from Christ.
Run toward Him.
Repentance is not the doorway into humiliation.
In Christ, it is the doorway out of hiding.
Confess.
Turn.
Come home.
There is grace at the feet of Jesus.
Not cheap grace that tells you sin does not matter.
Transforming grace that forgives you and begins changing you.
Pray for them.
There is a human being behind that comment.
This is what Christian community should look like.
Not spectators watching wounded people bleed.
Brothers and sisters carrying one another toward Jesus.
There may come a night when your own faith is shaking and you need to remember what Job could not see:
The chapter visible from earth is not necessarily the entire story.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
But if Christ has given you something worth proclaiming, sharing biblical truth can be one simple way of putting that truth where someone else may encounter it.
Someone may be grieving privately.
Someone may be thinking about abandoning the faith.
Someone may be drowning in shame.
Someone may never enter a church building this week—but they may read something you share.
So if this article points faithfully toward Christ, share it freely.
But before you leave, remember Job.
He sat in ashes without knowing about the conversation that preceded his suffering.
He could not see what the reader could see.
And there will be moments in your life when you cannot see either.
That is why our hope cannot finally rest in explanations.
Our hope rests in God.
More specifically, for the Christian, our hope rests in Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
You may not receive every answer you want.
Job did not.
When God finally spoke from the whirlwind, He did not hand Job a neat explanation for every tragedy. He revealed Himself.
And sometimes the answer our hearts desperately demand is “Why?”
while the deeper answer God gives is:
“Know Me.”
Not because questions are sinful.
Not because grief is weakness.
But because there comes a boundary beyond which human understanding cannot carry us.
Christ can.
The God who held Job when Job could not understand his story is the God revealed supremely to us in Jesus Christ.
So cry if you need to cry.
Grieve what you have lost.
Ask the difficult questions.
Refuse shallow explanations.
But do not confuse a chapter you cannot understand with a God who has ceased to be faithful.
Job could not see heaven.
The disciples could not see resurrection while Jesus lay in the tomb.
And perhaps right now, you cannot see what God is doing either.
But the Gospel gives you something stronger than optimism.
It gives you a crucified and risen Savior.
A living Redeemer.
Jesus Christ.
So when you cannot understand the chapter, cling to the One who already holds the ending.
And remember this when the room goes dark:
The ashes in your hands are not proof that Jesus has dropped the pen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Thought You Never Arrested May Be the One Quietly Ruining Your Life
paragraphs:
The Thought You Never Arrested May Be the One Quietly Ruining Your Life
What Paul Really Meant by “Take Every Thought Captive”—and Why the Battle in Your Mind Is Ultimately a Battle Over Who Gets to Rule You
There is a thought you have believed for so long that you no longer recognize it as a thought.
It feels like truth.
Maybe it says, You will never change.
Maybe it whispers, God has forgiven other people, but what you did was different.
Maybe it keeps replaying somebody’s rejection until their voice has become louder in your mind than the voice of Scripture.
Maybe it sounds religious.
God must be disappointed with me.
If I were really saved, I wouldn’t struggle like this.
I have already failed too many times.
Or maybe your thoughts move in another direction.
I deserve this.
I don’t need anyone correcting me.
I know what Scripture says, but God understands why my situation is different.
And somewhere between the first whisper and the thousandth repetition, you stopped interrogating the thought.
You gave it a room.
Then a key.
Then authority.
And eventually you began living as though the thought were telling you the truth.
This is why one sentence written by the apostle Paul nearly two thousand years ago remains terrifyingly relevant:
“...we take every thought captive to make it obey Christ.” — 2 Corinthians 10:5
Read that again.
Not admire every thought.
Not believe every thought.
Not identify yourself by every thought.
Not obey every thought.
Take it captive.
But there is something important Christians sometimes miss when quoting this verse.
Paul was not originally giving the Corinthians a modern self-help technique for stopping negative thinking.
The context is bigger.
Far bigger.
Paul writes:

Although we walk “in the flesh”—living ordinary human lives—Paul says that the warfare being waged is not conducted according to merely human methods. He speaks of weapons powerful through God for demolishing strongholds, destroying arguments, and confronting everything raised against the knowledge of God. Then comes the famous statement about taking every thought captive.
Listen to the Greek:
λογισμοὺς καθαιροῦντες... καὶ αἰχμαλωτίζοντες πᾶν νόημα εἰς τὴν ὑπακοὴν τοῦ Χριστοῦ
logismous kathairountes... kai aichmalōtizontes pan noēma eis tēn hypakoēn tou Christou.
The language is aggressive because the picture is warfare.
λογισμούς — logismous refers to reasonings, calculations, arguments, or ways of thinking.
καθαιροῦντες — kathairountes carries the idea of pulling down or demolishing.
Then Paul uses αἰχμαλωτίζοντες — aichmalōtizontes.
Taking captive.
Leading away as a prisoner.
And νόημα — noēma can refer to a thought, purpose, intention, or that which occupies the mind.
Then comes the destination of the captive:
εἰς τὴν ὑπακοὴν τοῦ Χριστοῦ
Into obedience to Christ.
That final phrase changes everything.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about teaching your thoughts to obey you.
It is about bringing the entire life—including the intellect, imagination, arguments, desires, assumptions, fears, pride, and inner narratives—under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
The NET translators even note that the Greek construction here is best understood in the sense of making the thought obey Christ.
So when a thought enters your mind, the Christian question is not merely:
Does this make me feel good?
It is not:
Does this feel authentic to me?
It is not even:
Have I thought this for a long time?
The question becomes:
Does this thought bow to Jesus Christ?
Imagine what would happen if you began asking that.
Your shame says:
God could never want someone like you.
Stop.
Bring it before Christ.
Does it bow?
Scripture says that “while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).
The thought does not survive.
Your pride says:
I don’t need to repent.
Bring it before Christ.
Does it bow?
Jesus began His public proclamation with a call to repentance and faith in the Gospel (Mark 1:15).
The thought does not survive.
Your temptation says:
Just once. Nobody will know.
Bring it before Christ.
Does it bow?
Jesus said that what is hidden is not ultimately hidden from God.
The thought does not survive.
Your despair says:
Your failure is the final chapter.
Bring it before Christ.
Does it bow?
Peter denied Jesus.
Three times.
Not privately in his imagination, but publicly when loyalty became costly.
And after the resurrection, Jesus did not pretend Peter's failure had never happened.
He went directly into the wound.
“Do you love me?”
Then He restored him to service.
“Feed my sheep.”
That is what Jesus does.
He does not call darkness light.
He does not rename rebellion as authenticity.
He does not excuse sin because confronting it might hurt our feelings.
He exposes.
He calls to repentance.
He forgives.
He restores.
And then He rewrites what we thought had already reached its ending.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But perhaps your most dangerous thought is not lust.
Not anger.
Not envy.
Not fear.
Perhaps it is the thought you have wrapped around your identity:
This is simply who I am.
Be careful.
There is a difference between experiencing a thought and surrendering your identity to it.
A temptation is not automatically a command.
A feeling is not automatically a prophecy.
A memory is not automatically your identity.
An accusation is not automatically God's verdict.
And a thought appearing in your mind does not mean Christ has authorized it to sit on the throne.
Some people have spent years condemning themselves simply because disturbing, unwanted, fearful, angry, or tempting thoughts appeared in their minds.
But Paul does not say that the existence of a thought makes it your master.
He says thoughts are to be taken captive.
