A prophetic-sounding declaration.
And sometimes the most dangerous deception is not the thing that looks completely evil.
It is the thing that looks almost Christian.
Almost biblical.
Almost true.
Because nobody needs discernment to recognize a message saying, “Reject Jesus and worship Satan.”
The frightening deception is the message that mentions Jesus while quietly changing who Jesus is.
The message that quotes Scripture while twisting what Scripture means.
The message that promises blessing while removing repentance.
The message that talks constantly about destiny but rarely about holiness.
The message that offers crowns without crosses, breakthrough without obedience, forgiveness without repentance, Christianity without Christ as Lord.
That is where discernment becomes costly.
Because biblical discernment sometimes requires you to question something you desperately wanted to believe.
And perhaps that is where this becomes personal.
Maybe you have prayed desperately for an answer.
Maybe someone approached you and said, “God showed me something about you.”
Your heart jumped.
Finally.
Direction.
Confirmation.
An answer.
Maybe what they said sounded exactly like what you hoped God would say.
And because you wanted it to be true...
you never tested it.
That is one of the vulnerabilities of the human heart.
We often scrutinize words we dislike while eagerly accepting words that confirm what we already desire.
But Scripture does not say:
“Test only the spirits you disagree with.”
It says:
“Test the spirits.”
Even the comforting ones.
Even the exciting ones.
Even the ones spoken by people you admire.
Even mine.
Yes.
Even this article.
Do not believe something merely because Gospel Warrior published it.
Open your Bible.
Read the passage.
Look at its context.
Ask whether what you are reading faithfully represents what God has actually revealed.
Because biblical ministry should never be afraid of an open Bible.
Truth does not need you to switch off your mind.
Jesus said the greatest commandment includes loving God with all your mind.
The Bereans were commended because they received apostolic preaching eagerly while examining the Scriptures daily to determine whether what they were hearing was true.
Think about that.
They listened.
Then they checked.
That is not rebellion.
That is wisdom.
And this is where 1 John becomes even more Christ-centered.
John does not leave “testing the spirits” as some vague mystical exercise where Christians attempt to identify invisible entities through feelings.
He immediately brings the test toward Jesus Christ:
πᾶν πνεῦμα ὃ ὁμολογεῖ Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν ἐν σαρκὶ ἐληλυθότα ἐκ τοῦ θεοῦ ἐστιν
“Every spirit that confesses Jesus Christ having come in the flesh is from God.”
—1 John 4:2
There it is.
Jesus Christ.
Not your intuition at the center.
Not the prophet at the center.
Not the experience at the center.
Not manifestations at the center.
Christ.
John's immediate concern includes the true confession of Jesus Christ coming in the flesh.
Christian discernment therefore cannot be reduced to asking, “Did this make me feel peaceful?”
Feelings matter, but feelings are not infallible.
You can feel peaceful while making a terrible decision.
You can feel frightened while obeying God.
Jesus experienced anguish in Gethsemane while perfectly obeying His Father.
The biblical question is deeper:
Is it true?
Does it agree with God's revealed Word?
What does it say about Jesus?
Does it lead toward the Christ revealed in Scripture?
Does it produce obedience to Him?
Does it call sin what God calls sin?
Does it magnify grace without redefining repentance?
Does it honor the Gospel?
Does it survive examination?
Paul gives a remarkably similar command:
“Test everything; hold fast what is good.”
—1 Thessalonians 5:21
Notice the balance.
Christian discernment is neither gullibility nor cynicism.
The gullible Christian believes everything.
The cynical Christian believes nothing.
The discerning Christian tests everything and holds tightly to what is good.
There is a difference.
Discernment is not becoming the suspicious person in church who believes everyone except himself is deceived.
It is not watching sermons solely to catch mistakes.
It is not calling every theological disagreement demonic.
It is not declaring everyone outside your favorite denomination a false teacher.
It is not becoming spiritually paranoid.
And it certainly is not pretending that you personally possess an infallible ability to identify deception.
In fact, genuine discernment begins with enough humility to admit:
I can be deceived too.
That sentence is harder to say than it looks.
Because pride does something strange to discernment.
Eventually, a person can become so obsessed with identifying false teachers that he stops testing himself.
He detects pride everywhere...
except in the mirror.
He condemns manipulation...
while manipulating people.
He exposes harshness...
with cruelty.
He fights error...
without love.
And suddenly the person who wanted to defend truth has forgotten something John says only a few verses later:
“Beloved, let us love one another, for love is from God.”
Truth and love are not enemies.
The same apostle who commands Christians to test the spirits commands Christians to love one another.
So if your “discernment” makes you proud, cruel, unteachable, obsessed with accusation, or delighted by another person's downfall...
something has gone terribly wrong.
Biblical discernment should make you cling more tightly to Jesus, not become more impressed with yourself.
And perhaps the spirit most desperately needing examination today is not the one operating through somebody else's social-media feed.
Perhaps you need to examine what has been shaping you.
The voice saying:
“You don't need to forgive them.”
Test it.
The voice saying:
“Everybody does this. Your sin isn't serious.”
Test it.
The voice saying:
“You can follow Jesus without surrendering that part of your life.”
Test it.
The voice saying:
“You have sinned too badly. Jesus will never receive you again.”
Test that one too.
Because deception does not always tempt you toward arrogance.
Sometimes it drives you toward despair.
The enemy does not care whether he pushes you into self-righteousness or hopeless condemnation if either one keeps your eyes away from Christ.
One voice says:
“You don't need a Savior. You're good enough.”
Another says:
“You're too filthy for the Savior.”
The Gospel destroys both lies.
You are more sinful than your pride wants to admit.
And in Christ there is more grace than your shame dares to believe.
That is the scandal.
That is the grace.
At the cross, God does not pretend sin is insignificant.
Look at Jesus.
Nails.
Blood.
Mockery.
Darkness.
The innocent Son of God bearing what sinners deserved.
The cross tells you sin is so serious that redemption required the sacrifice of Christ.
But the cross simultaneously announces something breathtaking:
God loved sinners enough to give His Son.
Christ died for sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the risen Jesus still receives repentant sinners.
Your darkest chapter does not have to become the title of your entire life.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Corinthian church carried an embarrassing past.
The Gospel did not pretend their histories never happened.
Grace rewrote what those histories meant.
That is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to this truth:
But understand what “Jesus rewrites everything” means.
It does not mean Jesus calls evil good.
It means Jesus takes guilty people, forgives them through His finished work, gives them new life, and begins transforming them by grace.
He does not merely improve the old story.
He makes sinners new.
And that means one of the most dangerous counterfeit spirits is any message that offers you transformation without Jesus.
Spirituality without Jesus.
Healing without Jesus.
Manifestation without Jesus.
Purpose without Jesus.
Prosperity without Jesus.
Self-discovery without Jesus.
Even “Christianity” without the biblical Jesus.
John will not permit it.
Jesus Christ stands in the middle of the test.
And notice something else.
John does not say believers should live terrified.
Immediately after warning them about deception, he writes:
—1 John 4:4
What a sentence.
Test every spirit...
but do not live afraid of every shadow.
Be discerning...
but not terrified.
Be watchful...
but remember Who lives in you.
The answer to deception is not obsession with darkness.
It is deeper allegiance to Christ.
Know Scripture so well that distortion becomes recognizable.
Know the Gospel so deeply that counterfeit gospels taste strange.
Know the character of Jesus revealed in Scripture so intimately that a distorted Christ cannot easily replace Him.
And when you fail?
Come back.
When you realize you believed something false?
Come back.
When pride fooled you?
Come back.
When you followed the wrong voice?
Come back.
When you defended something you now realize Scripture does not support?
Come back.
You do not have to defend yesterday's error simply because admitting you were wrong feels embarrassing.
Repentance is not humiliation before God.
It is liberation.
You can say:
“Lord, I was wrong.”
And grace will meet you there.
Maybe this article is exposing something uncomfortable.
Maybe you have been calling your desire “God's voice.”
Maybe you have been following personalities more carefully than Scripture.
Maybe someone has been controlling you through repeated claims that “God told me” while making you afraid to question them.
Maybe you have been consuming endless prophetic content while barely opening your Bible.
Maybe you have been so frightened of false teaching that suspicion has slowly replaced love.
Or maybe you have spent years believing the accusing voice saying God is finished with you.
Then hear this clearly:
Run to Jesus.
Not to hype.
Not to another personality.
Not to spiritual spectacle.
To Jesus.
Confess your sin.
Trust His mercy.
Return to His Word.
Ask God for wisdom.
Walk with mature believers who are willing to open Scripture with you.
Test what you hear.
Hold fast to what is good.
And above everything...
hold fast to Christ.
Not because every sentence I wrote should be treated as unquestionable.
Exactly the opposite.
Save it so you can return with your Bible open and test what you have read.
Send it privately to the believer who has been confused, wounded, manipulated, or afraid.

Sharing biblical truth can be one way we serve others and glorify God—but never confuse supporting a ministry with earning God's favor. If this ministry genuinely helps you know Christ, understand Scripture, and encourage others, then supporting the work is one practical way you may freely choose to help it reach more people.
Your support helps strengthen the work behind the articles, discipleship material, Gospel resources, and content being shared with believers and seekers.
“Test every spirit.”
Then remember the Person standing at the center of the test.
Jesus Christ.
Because the safest Christian is not the Christian who believes every supernatural claim.
And it is not the Christian who is terrified of everything supernatural.

It is the Christian whose eyes keep returning to Christ, whose Bible stays open, whose heart remains humble, whose sins are brought into the light, whose confidence rests in the Gospel, and whose deepest prayer remains:

“Jesus, whatever is false in me, expose it. Whatever is sinful in me, forgive it. Whatever is wounded in me, heal it. Whatever competes with You in me, tear it down. Teach me Your truth, and keep me close to You.”
Because one day every viral voice will become silent.
Every platform will disappear.
Every famous preacher will leave the stage.
Every algorithm will stop recommending.
Every human opinion will lose its applause.
But Jesus Christ will still be Lord.
So test the voices.
Test the teaching.
Test the claims.
Test even the things you desperately want to hear.
And when everything counterfeit has fallen away...
may the voice you refused to trade for all the others be the voice of the Shepherd who knew your name all along.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She Had Been Bleeding for 12 Years—Then One Touch Changed Everything
paragraphs: She Had Been Bleeding for 12 Years—Then One Touch Changed Everything
Everyone saw a woman touching Jesus. Jesus saw twelve years of suffering reaching for her last hope.
She had been bleeding for twelve years.
Read that again slowly.
Twelve years.
Long enough for people to forget when it started.
Long enough for pain to stop feeling temporary and start feeling like identity.
Long enough to wake up some mornings wondering whether this was simply what the rest of her life would be.
The Gospel of Mark does not give us her name.
Maybe that is one reason her story has survived so powerfully.
Because somewhere inside this unnamed woman, almost anyone who has suffered secretly can recognize something of themselves.
Mark tells us:
“And there was a woman who had had a discharge of blood for twelve years, and who had suffered much under many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was no better but rather grew worse.”
That sentence is devastating.
She suffered.
She sought help.
She spent everything.
And she got worse.
There is a particular kind of exhaustion that comes from suffering.
Then there is another kind entirely—the exhaustion of trying everything you know to do and discovering that nothing has fixed what is hurting you.
Maybe you know that feeling.
You prayed.
You promised God you would change.
You deleted it.
Then downloaded it again.
You walked away.
Then went back.
You told everybody you were doing better because explaining the truth felt exhausting.
You smiled in church while something inside you was collapsing.
You encouraged other people with verses you were struggling to believe for yourself.
And somewhere beneath the Christian vocabulary, the worship songs, the Sunday clothes, and the carefully chosen Facebook posts, there may be a sentence you are afraid to say aloud:
“Jesus, I am tired.”
That is where this woman enters the story.
But to understand how scandalous her approach to Jesus was, we have to understand what twelve years of bleeding meant in her world.
Leviticus 15:25 addresses prolonged bleeding in a woman. The Hebrew language speaks of a flow of blood beyond the ordinary period of menstruation. The text includes the phrase:
זֹוב דָּמָהּ — zov damah
A “flow” or “discharge of her blood.”
Under Israel's ritual purity laws, such a condition rendered a woman ritually unclean while the discharge continued.
That needs to be understood carefully.
Biblical ritual uncleanness was not identical to personal sinfulness.
Her bleeding did not mean she was morally corrupt, secretly wicked, or being punished because she was somehow worse than everyone else.
The distinction matters.
Scripture gives us no permission to accuse this woman of causing her condition through personal sin.
But her condition nevertheless had enormous religious and social consequences within the purity system described in the Torah.
Twelve years of blood meant twelve years of living with a condition that affected ordinary human contact and participation in community life.
Imagine what twelve years can do to a person.
Twelve years of managing embarrassment.
Twelve years of explanations.
Twelve years of people knowing.
Twelve years of wondering whether somebody will pull away.
Twelve years of hoping the next treatment might finally work.
Then Mark adds four brutal words:
ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον εἰς τὸ χεῖρον ἐλθοῦσα
The sense is unmistakable:
She had become worse.
Not better.
Worse.
And then she heard about Jesus.
That changes the temperature of the entire story.
Because somewhere between desperation and faith, this exhausted woman made a decision.
Mark 5:27–28 says:
“She had heard the reports about Jesus and came up behind him in the crowd and touched his garment. For she said, ‘If I touch even his garments, I will be made well.’”
The Greek preserves the intensity beautifully:
ἐὰν ἅψωμαι κἂν τῶν ἱματίων αὐτοῦ σωθήσομαι
“If I touch even His garments, I will be saved/made well.”
That final word is important:
σωθήσομαι — sōthēsomai
It comes from σῴζω — sōzō, a word whose range can include saving, rescuing, delivering, and making well.
She was not reaching for magic fabric.
The garment was not the Savior.
Jesus was.
And this is where her story gets uncomfortable.
Because desperate faith does not always look dignified.
Sometimes faith walks confidently.
Sometimes faith crawls.
Sometimes faith sings.
Sometimes faith can barely whisper.
Sometimes faith sounds like:
“If I can just get to Jesus.”
There was a crowd around Him.
People pressing against Him from every direction.
Yet somehow this suffering woman moved through them.
Perhaps shoulders blocked her.
Perhaps people recognized her.
Perhaps shame screamed at her to go home.
But after twelve years of bleeding, she had reached the place where desperation became stronger than embarrassment.
She stretched out her hand.
And touched Him.
Then—
everything changed.
Mark says:
“And immediately the flow of blood dried up, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease.”
—Mark 5:29
Immediately.
Twelve years of suffering met one moment in the presence and power of Christ.
But something happened next that makes this account far deeper than a physical healing story.
Jesus stopped.
He asked:
“Who touched my garments?”
The disciples were almost bewildered.
Everybody was touching Him.
There was a crowd pressing against Him.
But Jesus knew something had happened.
Many people were near Jesus.
One woman had reached toward Him in faith.
There is a difference between being surrounded by Christian things and personally trusting Christ.
You can know worship lyrics and still need Jesus.
You can quote Scripture and still need Jesus.
and still desperately need Jesus.
Proximity to Christianity is not the same thing as faith in Christ.
Then comes the moment that breaks me every time.
The woman realizes she cannot remain hidden.
Mark says she came:
φοβηθεῖσα καὶ τρέμουσα
“fearing and trembling.”
She fell before Jesus.
And told Him—
πᾶσαν τὴν ἀλήθειαν
“the whole truth.”
The whole truth.
Not the cleaned-up truth.
Not the church-friendly version.
Not the version designed to preserve her reputation.
The whole truth.
Somebody reading this has been giving Jesus edited versions of the story.
You confess enough to quiet your conscience but keep the darkest room locked.
You tell people, “I'm struggling,” when the truth is you feel trapped.
You say, “Keep me in prayer,” because saying what is actually happening feels terrifying.
You have learned how to appear spiritually alive while privately bleeding.
But Jesus already knows the whole truth.
And still He calls you closer.
The woman may have expected embarrassment.
Maybe rebuke.
Maybe rejection.
Instead, Jesus looked at someone who had lived for twelve years beneath the weight of suffering and addressed her with astonishing tenderness:
Θυγάτηρ
“Daughter.”
Do not rush past that word.
Daughter.
In Mark's Gospel, this is the only recorded occasion where Jesus directly addresses someone with this particular term.
The crowd knew her condition.
Jesus spoke to her identity.
The crowd could have reduced her to “the bleeding woman.”
Jesus called her “Daughter.”
Her suffering described something she had experienced.
Jesus refused to let suffering have the final word over who she was.
Then He said:
“Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace, and be healed of your disease.”
—Mark 5:34
ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε
“Your faith has saved/made you well.”
Again we encounter the language of sōzō.
But we must be biblically careful here.
The lesson is not that faith is a supernatural force by which Christians can demand whatever healing they desire.
The New Testament never gives us permission to turn faith into a technique for controlling God.
The power was Christ's.
The woman did not heal herself by believing hard enough.
She reached toward the One who could save.
That distinction protects hurting people from one of the cruelest distortions of Christianity—the accusation that continued suffering automatically means somebody simply “didn't have enough faith.”
Jesus Christ is sovereign.
God can heal miraculously.
God can also sustain His people through suffering.

Paul himself pleaded repeatedly concerning his “thorn in the flesh,” yet instead of removing it, the Lord answered, “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9).
So this story is not a formula.
It is a revelation.
A revelation of who Jesus is.
He is not contaminated by the unclean.
His holiness overcomes uncleanness.
He is not frightened by broken bodies.
He is not repulsed by desperate people.
He does not lose sight of an individual because a crowd is demanding His attention.
And He is not too busy for the person trembling at His feet.
That is where her story becomes ours.
Because perhaps your bleeding isn't blood.
Maybe yours has a different name.
Pornography.
Bitterness.
Secret debt.
Grief.
Envy.
A marriage quietly collapsing.
A child you cannot stop worrying about.
A prayer that seems unanswered.
An addiction nobody knows about.
A private compromise you keep promising will be “the last time.”
A wound from somebody who was supposed to protect you.
A religious mask you are exhausted from wearing.
Maybe you have been bleeding emotionally for years while making sure nobody sees the stain.
And you have gotten incredibly good at hiding it.
But there is something the Gospel keeps confronting us with:
Jesus does not save the version of you that you successfully manufacture for everybody else.
He calls the real you.
The sinner.
The ashamed.
The exhausted.
The guilty.
The frightened.
The one who cannot repair himself.
This is why the Gospel is bigger than inspirational self-improvement.
Our deepest problem is not merely that life has wounded us.
Scripture teaches that all of us have sinned and fallen short of God's glory (Romans 3:23).
We do not merely need encouragement.
We need reconciliation with God.
We need forgiveness.
We need redemption.
We need a Savior.
And Jesus did something infinitely greater than allowing a suffering woman to touch His garment.
He went to a cross.
There, the sinless Son of God bore sin, willingly laying down His life.
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose.
The woman in Mark 5 reached toward Jesus because she believed He could rescue her from what she could not overcome.
That posture still confronts us today.
Stop pretending you can save yourself.
Come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Bring Him the whole truth.
Not because confession earns His mercy, but because there is no reason to keep hiding from the One who already sees you completely.
Jesus knew the woman's story before she ever fell trembling before Him.
And He did not walk away.
Maybe that is the sentence you needed tonight.
He did not walk away.
When your past is exposed, He does not discover something He didn't know.
When you confess your sin, Christ is not shocked.
When you finally admit how far you wandered, heaven is not receiving breaking news.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace tells the truth about sin—and then points us toward the Savior who paid for sinners.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is turning from sin toward the One who can actually save you.
So perhaps your moment is not about touching a garment.
Perhaps your moment is simply this:
“No more hiding, Jesus.
Here is the whole truth.”
Not because typing words saves you.
Only Christ saves.
But sometimes bringing darkness into the light begins with refusing to pretend anymore.

There are believers reading beside you who know what it means to keep walking while hurting. Let the comment section become more than numbers beneath a post. Let it become a place where people pray, encourage, testify, and remind one another that Jesus is still worthy.
And if Christ has already carried you through a season you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what He did.
Your testimony may become the reason another exhausted person reaches toward hope instead of surrendering to despair.
Not because every emotional moment needs to become content, but because there are days when truth must be remembered twice.
Send it to the family member who stopped talking about God.
Send it to the believer who is tired.
Send it to the seeker who thinks Jesus only welcomes people who already have themselves together.
Even send it to the person who does not yet believe.
You never know where somebody's twelve-year road has brought them.
More importantly, the goal is deeper discipleship.
But before you leave, remember the woman.
Twelve years.
Thousands of mornings waking up with the same problem.
Money gone.
Treatments failed.
Body exhausted.
Hope battered.
Yet her story did not end with the sentence:
“She grew worse.”
Because Jesus entered the story.
And when Jesus enters a story, the darkest chapter does not get the authority to name the ending.
Maybe people remember what you did.
Maybe you remember it even more painfully than they do.
Maybe shame has been calling you by the name of your worst chapter.
Maybe suffering has convinced you that nothing will ever change.
But the Gospel declares that Jesus Christ receives repentant sinners, forgives the guilty, restores the broken, and gives eternal life to those who trust in Him.
The woman came trembling.
She left hearing:
“Daughter.”
That is the scandal of grace.
The unclean reaches toward the Holy One—and instead of Jesus becoming unclean, His power makes her clean.
The broken comes near.
The Savior does not recoil.
The truth comes out.
Grace speaks.
So bring Him the whole truth.
And remember this when shame whispers your old name:
Your wound may explain the chapter—but Jesus Christ still has authority over the ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Jesus Knew Why She Was Crying—So Why Did He Ask, “Why Are You Weeping?”
paragraphs: Jesus Knew Why She Was Crying—So Why Did He Ask, “Why Are You Weeping?”

Mary thought she was standing beside a grave. She did not yet realize she was standing only seconds away from hearing the risen Jesus speak her name—and discovering that the place she thought proved everything was over had become the place where God was beginning something no tomb could contain.
There are questions Jesus asks in Scripture that seem almost unnecessary.
“Why are you afraid?”
“Do you want to be healed?”
“Who do you say that I am?”
And then, outside a borrowed tomb on the morning that changed human history, Jesus asks a devastated woman a question that almost feels painfully obvious:
“Woman, why are you weeping?”
Why ask?
Jesus knew.
He knew exactly why Mary Magdalene was crying.
He knew what had happened on Golgotha.
He knew what she had watched.
He knew whose body she believed had disappeared.
He knew the grief underneath her words before she ever spoke them.
And most importantly, Jesus knew something Mary did not know yet.
The Man she was crying over was standing in front of her alive.
That changes everything about the question.
John 20 places us inside one of the most emotionally breathtaking scenes in all of Scripture.

Mary Magdalene comes to the tomb while it is still dark. She discovers that the stone has been removed. She runs to Simon Peter and the disciple whom Jesus loved. They come, see the empty tomb, and eventually return home.
But Mary stays.
That detail matters.
She stays near the place where her heart has been shattered.
John writes:
The Greek is striking:
Μαρία δὲ εἱστήκει πρὸς τῷ μνημείῳ ἔξω κλαίουσα
Maria de heistēkei pros tō mnēmeiō exō klaiousa.
Mary was standing outside the tomb, weeping.
The word translated “weeping” comes from κλαίω — klaiō, a word used for crying, lamenting, mourning.
This is not the picture of a detached theological observer examining evidence.
This is grief.
This is a woman standing where hope appears to have died.
And maybe that is why this scene reaches so deeply into us.
Because most of us eventually stand outside some kind of tomb.
Not necessarily one made of stone.
Sometimes the tomb is a marriage you thought would survive.
Sometimes it is the phone call that changed your family forever.
Sometimes it is a child who walked away from God.
Sometimes it is the prayer you prayed for years that seemed to receive silence.
Sometimes it is the person you used to be before addiction, betrayal, pride, lust, anger, compromise, or secret sin hollowed something out inside you.
Sometimes nobody around you even knows you are grieving.
You still smile.
You still work.
You still attend church.
You still answer, “I’m fine.”
But somewhere inside your soul, you are standing beside something you buried.
Mary understands that place.
She looks into the tomb and sees two angels.
They ask her:
“Woman, why are you weeping?”
She answers:
“They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.”
Notice her words.
“My Lord.”
Her theology may not yet understand the resurrection unfolding around her, but her heart is still attached to Jesus.
Then Mary turns.
And there He is.
Jesus.
Alive.
Standing close enough to speak to her.
Yet John tells us something astonishing:
She did not know that it was Jesus.
Think about the unbearable beauty of that moment.
Mary is crying because she cannot find Jesus...
while looking at Jesus.
She believes death has won...
while Resurrection Himself is standing in front of her.
She thinks someone has taken His body...
while His resurrected body is speaking to her.
Her conclusion makes perfect sense according to what she can presently see.
And it is completely wrong according to what God has already done.
That is where this story stops being merely Mary's story.
Because there are moments when sorrow interprets reality for us.
We see the empty place.
We see the unanswered prayer.
We see the broken relationship.
We see what disappeared.
We see what failed.
We see what we lost.
And then grief whispers:
This is the whole story.
But grief is not omniscient.
Pain is real, but pain does not know everything.
Your tears may be telling the truth about what hurts while still being unable to tell you everything God is doing.
That does not mean Christians should pretend suffering does not hurt.
Jesus never teaches that.
The same Christ who conquered death also wept at Lazarus's tomb.
Christian hope is not emotional denial.
The Gospel does not say, “Nothing terrible happened.”
The Gospel says something infinitely stronger:
Terrible things happened—and Jesus Christ entered the darkness, bore sin, defeated death, rose bodily from the grave, and darkness did not get the final word.
So Jesus looks at Mary and asks:
“Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?”
In Greek:
Γύναι, τί κλαίεις; τίνα ζητεῖς;
Gynai, ti klaieis? tina zēteis?
“Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?”
Notice that second question.
Not merely:
“What happened?”
But:
“Whom are you seeking?”
Jesus brings the conversation back to a Person.
That is Christianity.
At the center of our faith is not merely a philosophy, morality system, political identity, self-improvement program, or collection of inspirational sayings.
At the center is Jesus Christ.
Mary is seeking Jesus.
She simply does not yet recognize that the Jesus she seeks has already found her.
She assumes He is the gardener.
And through tears she says:
“Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.”
There is something heartbreaking about her devotion.
She is willing to carry away the One who is about to carry her grief into an entirely new reality.
Then Jesus does something astonishingly simple.
He says one word.
Her name.
Μαριάμ — Mariam.
“Mary.”
That is the turning point.
No long argument.
No rebuke for failing to recognize Him.
No theological lecture before comfort.
Jesus calls her by name.
And suddenly the supposed gardener becomes her risen Lord.
Mary turns toward Him and cries:
Ῥαββουνί — Rabbouni!
John explains that this means “Teacher.”

The term is Semitic in origin, preserved in Greek letters by John. Behind the Greek text stands the linguistic world Jesus and Mary inhabited, where Aramaic was commonly spoken. John intentionally lets us hear something of the intimacy of the encounter rather than flattening the moment into abstraction.
“Mary.”
“Rabbouni!”
The resurrection becomes personal.
And maybe that is what somebody reading this desperately needs to understand.
Jesus did not rise merely so Christians could win theological arguments about Him.
Christ rose because sin and death had to be defeated.
He rose because the Scriptures had to be fulfilled.
He rose because salvation is found in Him.
He rose so guilty sinners could be forgiven, enemies reconciled to God, captives liberated, and people spiritually dead in sin could receive life.
The empty tomb is not positive thinking.
It is an announcement:
Jesus Christ is alive.
And because He lives, your sin does not have to write the final chapter of your life.
Your worst night does not have to become your permanent identity.
Your scandal does not have to be your conclusion.
Your shame does not have to become your name.
Your failure does not possess the authority to decide who you will always be.
But there is something important we cannot sentimentalize.
Grace is not Jesus telling us our sin does not matter.
Grace cost Him the cross.
The biblical Gospel calls us to repentance and faith.
Jesus did not die to make peace with the sins destroying us. He died to save sinners, forgive sinners, reconcile sinners to God, and transform those who belong to Him.
That means some tears need more than comfort.
Some tears need repentance.
Maybe you are grieving consequences from choices nobody forced you to make.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you once promised God you would never cross.
Maybe pornography has become your hidden room.
Maybe bitterness has become your daily bread.
Maybe you know exactly how to look spiritual while your private life is collapsing.
Maybe your Bible gathers dust while your screen gets hours of your attention.
Maybe you have learned Christian language without surrendering the throne of your heart.
Maybe everybody thinks you are close to Jesus...
and you know you have been hiding.
Listen carefully.
The risen Christ is not exposed by your darkness.
He already sees it.
And still the Gospel invitation stands:
Repent. Come to Christ.
Not because your sin is small.
Because His grace is greater.
Not because holiness does not matter.
Because He loves us too much to leave us chained to what He died to deliver us from.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples scattered.
Mary wept.
And Jesus rose.
Christianity does not present heroes who saved themselves.
It presents sinners and sufferers encountering a Savior.
That is why our theme is more than a beautiful phrase:
But understand what “rewrites” means.
Jesus does not rewrite history by pretending your past never happened.
He does something far more glorious.
He redeems.
The scars of crucifixion remained visible on His resurrected body.
The wounds were real.
The resurrection did not make Good Friday imaginary.
It revealed that Good Friday was not the ending.
And perhaps that is the deeper beauty behind Jesus asking Mary:
“Why are you weeping?”
It was not ignorance.
It was invitation.
Jesus was drawing Mary from what she believed had happened into the reality of what God had actually done.
Mary's tears belonged to a story whose ending she had misunderstood.
She thought she needed information about where a corpse had been placed.
What she actually needed was revelation that Christ was alive.
And when she recognized Him, Jesus eventually gave her something to do.
He sent her.
Mary went to the disciples announcing:
“I have seen the Lord.”
Do you see the movement?
She came grieving.
She encountered Jesus.
She left witnessing.
The woman standing outside the tomb becomes a messenger of resurrection.
That is what encounters with Christ do.
Grace does not merely give you something to feel.
Grace gives you Someone to proclaim.
Maybe that is why you cannot keep everything God has done in you private.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be standing beside their own invisible tomb tonight.
Someone you work with is exhausted from pretending.
Someone in your family is one secret away from collapsing.
Someone who used to pray no longer believes God wants to hear them.
They need the Gospel.
Not manufactured hype.
Not promises God never made.
Not shallow religious clichés.
They need Jesus.
So if this article reminded you that Christ is alive, do not treat sharing it merely as helping a page grow.
Send it privately to the friend who stopped talking about what hurts.
Somebody else's faith may be strengthened by discovering they are not the only person who has cried outside a tomb.
There is another reason Gospel Warrior keeps publishing messages like this.
Discipleship cannot survive on occasional inspiration.
We need Scripture when emotions change.
Truth when culture shifts.
Conviction when compromise feels convenient.
Grace when shame tells us to run from God.
Brothers and sisters who remind us to look again toward Christ.
Christ alone saves.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way to help biblical encouragement and discipleship resources continue reaching people.
Because somewhere, somebody is still crying.
Somebody still thinks the stone means the story is finished.
Somebody still believes Friday gets the last word.
Somebody still thinks their failure has buried them too deeply for redemption.
And Christians have been entrusted with news too magnificent to keep to ourselves:
The tomb is empty.
Jesus Christ is risen.
Sin can be forgiven.
The wandering can come home.
The ashamed can repent.
The broken can be restored.
The spiritually dead can receive life.
And those who belong to Christ can grieve with genuine hope because death itself will not have the final word.
Mary entered that garden searching for a dead Jesus.
She left announcing a living Lord.
Maybe today Jesus' question reaches beyond that ancient garden and enters the place you have been afraid to let anyone see:
“Why are you weeping?”
Tell Him.
Tell Him what hurts.
Tell Him what you lost.
Tell Him what you regret.
Confess what needs confessing.
Repent of what needs abandoning.
Stop hiding what He already sees.
And then remember that the Christian answer to despair is not that everything in this life will happen the way you want.
It is better than that.
Jesus Christ has risen from the dead.
Your hope ultimately rests not in circumstances changing, but in the crucified and risen Savior who does not change.
Perhaps you came to this page staring at what was taken from you.
Perhaps Christ is calling you to look again at what the empty tomb means.
Because sometimes the tears are real...
the grave is real...
the scars are real...
but the ending you feared is not.
And comment before you leave—not for an algorithm alone, but because confession, testimony, prayer, and encouragement can remind another human being that they are not walking alone.
If you can only find three words today, let them be:
“Pray for me.”
Someone may answer.
Someone may understand.
And more importantly, Christ is still the risen Lord.
Never mistake the tears in your eyes for proof that Jesus is absent; Mary was crying because she could not find Him while the risen Christ was already standing beside her.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY EZEKIEL PACKED HIS BAGS THROUGH A WALL
paragraphs: WHY EZEKIEL PACKED HIS BAGS THROUGH A WALL
The prophet who turned his own life into a warning—and the terrifying reason his strange midnight escape still speaks to anyone who keeps postponing surrender to God.
Imagine looking out your window and seeing your pastor packing a bag.
Not for vacation.
Not for a conference.
Not because he is moving.
He walks outside carrying what looks like the bare necessities of someone being driven from his home. People begin watching. Neighbors whisper. Children stare.
Then evening comes.
And instead of walking through the door...
he starts digging through a wall.
With his hands.
Then he lifts his belongings onto his shoulder, covers his face, and disappears into the darkness.
You would probably ask exactly what Ezekiel's neighbors asked:
“What are you doing?”
And that question is precisely what God wanted them to ask.
Because Ezekiel was not having a breakdown.
He was preaching.
Without a pulpit.
Without a microphone.
Without a sermon manuscript.
His body was the sermon.
His baggage was the sermon.
The hole in the wall was the sermon.
The darkness was the sermon.
And what God was saying through him was terrifying:
You have ignored My words so long that I am going to let you watch what those words look like when they become reality.
Ezekiel 12 opens with one of the saddest diagnoses God can give a people:
They had eyes...
but would not truly see.
They had ears...
but would not truly hear.
The Hebrew calls them בֵּית־הַמֶּרִי — beit ha-meri, a “house of rebellion.”
That matters.
Their problem was not lack of information.
It was resistance to revelation.
They could see the prophet.
They could hear the warnings.
They could possess religious identity and still refuse the God who was confronting them.
And that is where this ancient scene becomes uncomfortable.
Because sometimes the most spiritually dangerous person is not the person who has never heard truth.
It is the person who has heard truth so many times that it no longer disturbs them.
You can hear sermons about repentance and keep scrolling.
You can read Scripture and immediately return to the secret thing Scripture just exposed.
You can sing about surrender while privately negotiating which parts of your life Jesus is actually allowed to touch.
You can know the vocabulary of Christianity without living beneath the lordship of Christ.
You can become familiar with conviction.
And familiarity with conviction can become deadly when conviction never becomes repentance.
So God tells Ezekiel to do something unforgettable.
The Hebrew of Ezekiel 12:3 says:
עֲשֵׂה לְךָ כְּלֵי גוֹלָה — aseh lekha kelei golah
Prepare for yourself the belongings—the gear—of exile.

The expression כְּלֵי גוֹלָה — kelei golah refers to the things associated with going into exile. Ezekiel is effectively told to pack like a displaced person. Then he is to move those belongings publicly, where everybody can see him.
Notice how repeatedly the passage emphasizes visibility.
Before their eyes.
Before their eyes.
Before their eyes.
God was making rebellion watch its own destination.
Then comes the command that makes the scene impossible to forget:
לְעֵינֵיהֶם חֲתָר־לְךָ בַקִּיר
“Before their eyes, break through the wall...”
Ezekiel later says:
וּבָעֶרֶב חָתַרְתִּי־לִי בַקִּיר בְּיָד
“In the evening I broke through the wall with my own hands.”
Picture it.
Scrape.
Pull.
Break.
Dust falling.
Another piece loosening.
People watching.
Nobody understanding.
And Ezekiel keeps digging.
He does not give them a polished speech first.
He gives them an image they will not be able to erase from their minds.
A man leaving home through a hole in a wall.
Then he puts the baggage on his shoulder.
Darkness falls.
He covers his face.
And he goes out.
Why?
God explains it:
כִּי־מוֹפֵת נְתַתִּיךָ לְבֵית יִשְׂרָאֵל
“For I have set you as a sign to the house of Israel.”
The Hebrew word מוֹפֵת — mofet carries the idea of a sign, portent, or extraordinary demonstration.
Ezekiel was becoming a living prophecy.
And then morning came.
God asked Ezekiel whether the rebellious house had asked him:
“What are you doing?”
They had.
The hook had worked.
Now came the explanation.
Ezekiel was acting out what was coming upon Jerusalem and its ruler.
“As I have done,” Ezekiel was to tell them, “so shall it be done to them.”
Exile.
Captivity.
Flight in darkness.
A ruler attempting to leave through a breach in the wall.
And then one of the strangest prophetic statements in the chapter:
God says He will bring that ruler to Babylon...
yet the ruler will not see it.
He will die there.
This is not merely dramatic religious symbolism.
It is judgment.
And Scripture does not allow us to turn judgment into something sentimental.
God is patient.
God is merciful.
God repeatedly warns.
But biblical grace never means that rebellion is harmless.
The God who forgives sinners is also the holy God against whom sin is committed.
That is why Ezekiel's strange little bag matters.
Every item he carried was announcing:
The life you assume will always be here can disappear.
The wall mattered too.
Walls represented protection.
Security.
Normality.
The illusion that tomorrow would resemble yesterday.
Yet Ezekiel was commanded to tear through the very thing people expected to remain standing.
There is something hauntingly contemporary about that.
We build walls too.
Not necessarily from mudbrick or stone.
Money can become a wall.
Reputation can become a wall.
Religious activity can become a wall.
A relationship can become a wall.
Success can become a wall.
Our carefully curated Christian image can become a wall.
We tell ourselves:
“I attend church.”
“I believe in God.”
“I post Bible verses.”
“I've always been Christian.”
“I'll deal with this eventually.”
“God understands.”
And sometimes what we mean is:
I want enough Jesus to calm my conscience, but not enough Jesus to crucify my idols.
That is not discipleship.
Jesus did not call people merely to admire Him.
He said:
“If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me.”
The Gospel does not invite us to decorate our old life with Christian language.
Christ calls us to die and live again.
And perhaps somebody reading this has been carrying something for years.
Nobody knows.
The browser history gets deleted.
The messages disappear.
The addiction has a respectable name.
The bitterness has been justified so many times that it feels righteous.
The affair exists only emotionally—for now.
The pride hides behind ministry.
The jealousy hides behind criticism.
The greed hides behind ambition.
The loneliness hides behind jokes.
The wounds hide behind “I'm fine.”
And every time conviction comes, another brick goes into the wall.
Not tonight.
Not yet.
Later.
Later.
Later.
But Ezekiel standing beside that broken wall reminds us that later is not a covenant God has made with us.
Today is the day to hear His voice.
Today is the day to stop defending what Christ is asking you to surrender.
Today is the day to stop confusing God's patience with God's approval.
Be honest.
Did that hit harder than you expected?
If there is something you need to bring into the light before Jesus, you do not need to describe your private sin publicly. But you can mark this moment of surrender.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
It doesn't.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes an honest confession is the first crack in a wall we have spent years protecting.
And here is where Ezekiel's story becomes even more astonishing.
Because judgment is not the final chapter of the Bible.
The exile was real.
Jerusalem's fall was real.
Israel's rebellion was real.
Sin's consequences were real.
But God was not finished writing.
The same broad prophetic story that exposes human rebellion eventually carries us toward God's promises of cleansing, a new heart, a new spirit, restoration, and God's presence among His people.
And ultimately the whole biblical story brings us to Jesus Christ.
Not because Ezekiel's hole in the wall is some secret prediction that should be artificially turned into an allegory of the cross.
We do not need to force Scripture to make Christ glorious.
The actual biblical story is already enough.
Human beings rebel.
God is holy.
Judgment is deserved.
We cannot rescue ourselves.
And then...
Christ comes.
The innocent One stands where the guilty should stand.
The Son of God enters our human darkness.
Jesus lives the righteousness we have failed to live.
At the cross, He bears sin.
Not His sin.
Ours.
The scandal is not that God pretended rebellion did not matter.
The scandal is that grace was so costly that the Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.”
That is 2 Corinthians 5:21.
The cross does not minimize God's judgment.
It reveals how serious sin truly is—and how breathtaking God's mercy truly is.
Then the stone is rolled away.
Christ rises.
Death does not get the last word.
Shame does not get the last word.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending.
Jesus does.
That is why repentance is not God screaming, “Clean yourself up before you come near Me.”
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Christ who receives sinners, forgives sinners, cleanses sinners, and transforms sinners.
Maybe your scandal is something everybody knows.
Maybe your scandal is something nobody knows.
Maybe your greatest shame happened ten years ago.
Maybe it happened last night.
Maybe you have spent years trying to compensate for it by becoming useful, successful, religious, funny, generous, busy...
anything except honest.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not permission to continue hiding.
It is permission to come out.
You can confess.
You can repent.
You can return.
You can ask forgiveness.
You can make things right where repentance requires making things right.
You can seek accountability.
You can stop feeding what is destroying you.
Not because you are strong enough to rewrite yourself.
But because Jesus Christ specializes in resurrecting what sin convinced us was beyond redemption.
From scandal...
to grace.
That does not mean every earthly consequence disappears.
Grace is not an eraser that makes history imaginary.
Grace does something better.
It gives sinners a Savior.
It gives the condemned forgiveness in Christ.
It gives the spiritually dead new life.
It gives the ashamed a new identity.
It gives the runaway somewhere to return.
And it gives broken stories an Author greater than their worst chapter.
Maybe that is why Ezekiel's bags still speak.
They ask us a question:
What are you carrying because you refused to surrender it when God first spoke?
Some baggage belongs at the foot of the cross.
Some secrets belong in the light.
Some grudges need to die.
Some compromises need to end.
Some relationships need boundaries.
Some apologies need to be made.
Some believers need to stop performing Christianity and finally surrender to Christ.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person fighting to come home.
That matters.
And if this article brought somebody to your mind, do not just think about them.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to announce that you think they are sinful.
God still calls rebels home.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
But if biblical truth helped you, sharing it can be one simple way of putting that truth where another wounded person may encounter it.

Glorifying God is bigger than clicking a button. It means living for Him with the whole life He has given us. And part of that life can include generously supporting and spreading faithful Gospel work so more people can hear about Jesus.
It is not a shortcut to spiritual maturity.

It is simply a practical way to help Gospel-centered content continue reaching people while keeping yourself connected to biblical nourishment, conviction, encouragement, discipleship, and spiritual sharpening.
And there is more available without charge.
Because there may come a night when the wall starts going back up.
A night when shame tells you to hide again.
A night when compromise begins sounding reasonable again.
A night when you need to remember an old prophet standing in the darkness with dust on his hands and baggage on his shoulder, silently warning an entire generation:
Do not wait until consequences become the sermon you refused to hear in words.
Send it privately to someone fighting in silence.
And comment something real.
Not something impressive.
Something real.
“Jesus forgive me.”
“No more hiding.”
“Pray for me.”
“Christ is still healing me.”
Because Ezekiel's neighbors eventually asked the question God wanted them to ask:
“What are you doing?”
Maybe tonight the question has changed.
Maybe now it is Jesus asking you:
What are you still carrying that I have been calling you to surrender?
The wall does not have to become your grave.
The baggage does not have to become your identity.
Your sin does not have to become your master.
Your shame does not have to become your name.
There is grace for repentant sinners because there is a crucified and risen Savior.
Come to Christ.
While you can hear Him.
Come into the light.
While grace is calling.
Come home.
Because perhaps the most frightening thing about Ezekiel's broken wall was never that a man had to crawl through it.
It was that an entire people had heard God's voice for so long that they almost stopped realizing He was speaking.
Do not become so comfortable carrying your baggage that you forget Jesus died and rose again to give you a new life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Rachel Gave Jacob Another Woman: The Surrogacy Crisis Nobody Talks About
paragraphs:
Rachel Gave Jacob Another Woman: The Surrogacy Crisis Nobody Talks About
She thought another woman’s womb could end her pain. Instead, Genesis exposes what happens when a wounded heart tries to force what only God can give—and why Jesus is still rewriting stories born in jealousy, desperation, rivalry, and shame.
There is a sentence in Genesis that sounds almost too explosive to read slowly.
Rachel looked at the man who loved her and essentially said:
Give me children—or I die.
Not someday.
Not, “I’m struggling.”
Not even, “Please pray for me.”
Children.
Or death.
And what happens next is one of those biblical stories we can read so quickly that we miss the human wreckage hiding between the verses.
Rachel gives Jacob another woman.
Her servant.
Bilhah.
And tells him to sleep with her.
If that sounds scandalous, uncomfortable, ethically complicated, and painfully human, that is because it is.
But before anyone turns this into gossip about a dysfunctional Bible family, look closer.
Because Rachel's crisis did not begin with Bilhah.
It began with pain.
And pain, when it is allowed to become an idol, can make us reach for things we once thought we never would.
Genesis 30 opens with Rachel watching her sister Leah bear children while her own womb remains empty. The Hebrew refuses to sanitize what happens inside her:
וַתְּקַנֵּא רָחֵל בַּאֲחֹתָהּ
Vatteqanne Rachel ba'achotah.
“Rachel envied her sister.”
There it is.
Envy.
Not the Instagram version where someone says, “I'm so jealous!” while smiling.
The kind that hurts.
The kind that makes another person's blessing feel like evidence that God has forgotten you.
Rachel had Jacob's love.
Leah had children.
And somehow neither woman seemed able to enjoy what she had because she was staring at what the other woman possessed.
Leah wanted to be loved.
Rachel wanted to be a mother.
Two sisters.
Two wounds.
One household slowly becoming a battlefield.
Maybe that is why this ancient story still feels disturbingly modern.
You can love God and still look across the room at someone else's life and whisper inside yourself:
Why her?
Why him?
Why not me?
Why did their prayer get answered?
Why did they get married?
Why did their ministry grow?
Why did their business succeed?
Why did they get healed?
Why did they have the baby?
Why did their children come back to God?
Why does everyone celebrate them while I am trying not to fall apart?
Comparison rarely announces itself as spiritual warfare.
Sometimes it just feels like scrolling.
Sometimes it sounds like congratulations spoken through clenched teeth.
Sometimes it looks like smiling at somebody's testimony and crying after you get home.
Rachel finally breaks.
הָבָה־לִּי בָנִים וְאִם־אַיִן מֵתָה אָנֹכִי
Havah-li vanim, ve'im-ayin, metah anokhi.
“Give me children, or I shall die.”
Those words matter because Scripture does not turn Rachel into a cardboard saint.
The Bible lets us hear her desperation.
Jacob responds angrily:
הֲתַחַת אֱלֹהִים אָנֹכִי
Hatachat Elohim anokhi?
“Am I in the place of God?”
Jacob understood at least this much: he was not sovereign over Rachel's womb.
But desperation rarely disappears merely because someone tells us a theological truth.
Rachel already knew Jacob was not God.
Her heart still hurt.
So she created a solution.
And her solution had a name.
Bilhah.
Rachel says:
הִנֵּה אֲמָתִי בִלְהָה
Hinneh amati Bilhah.
“Here is my maid Bilhah.”
Then comes the line that makes this story so difficult:
בֹּא אֵלֶיהָ וְתֵלֵד עַל־בִּרְכַּי וְאִבָּנֶה גַם־אָנֹכִי מִמֶּנָּה

In context, Rachel tells Jacob to go to Bilhah so that Bilhah might bear a child in connection with Rachel, allowing Rachel to be “built up” through her. Genesis then says Rachel gave Bilhah to Jacob “as a wife,” and Bilhah conceived.
We need to be careful here.

Calling this “surrogacy” can help a modern reader recognize the reproductive arrangement, but it can also mislead if we imagine a twenty-first-century fertility clinic, contract, IVF procedure, or modern gestational carrier.
Genesis describes an ancient household arrangement involving a female servant, sexual intercourse with Jacob, pregnancy, and Rachel's attempt to obtain children through Bilhah.
The Bible describes it.
That does not mean the Bible presents every feature of the arrangement as God's ideal.
That distinction matters.
Scripture often tells the truth about what broken human beings did without commanding us to imitate everything they did.
Abraham had already entered a similarly painful arrangement involving Hagar in Genesis 16.
Now another generation reaches for another human solution to unbearable waiting.
And there is something haunting here.
Rachel wanted a child so badly that another woman's body became part of her strategy.
We should not erase Bilhah.
She was not merely a plot device.
She was a woman.

Genesis identifies her repeatedly as Rachel's servant, and whatever assumptions we bring to the ancient institution behind that status, there was plainly an enormous difference in household power between Rachel and Bilhah. The text does not record Bilhah initiating the arrangement. Rachel gives her to Jacob.
That should make us read slowly.
Not arrogantly.
Not as people standing above these ancient sinners.
As people capable of doing our own versions of the same thing.
Because desperation has a frightening ability to turn people into instruments.
When I need you to make me feel valuable, you become an instrument.
When I need a relationship to prove I am lovable, another human being becomes an instrument.
When I need ministry numbers to prove God is using me, people become statistics.
When I need money to prove God has blessed me, everything becomes transactional.
When I need applause to silence insecurity, even “serving God” can secretly become about serving myself.
That is where Rachel's story stops being ancient history.
We may never give a servant to a spouse.
But we know what it means to say:
God is taking too long.
So I will make something happen.
And sometimes the most dangerous decisions are made immediately after that sentence.
Bilhah conceives.
A son is born.
Rachel names him Dan and declares that God has heard her.
Then Bilhah conceives again.
Another son.
And Rachel gives him one of the saddest victory names in Genesis.
Naphtali.
The Hebrew of Genesis 30:8 is intense:
נַפְתּוּלֵי אֱלֹהִים נִפְתַּלְתִּי עִם־אֲחֹתִי גַּם־יָכֹלְתִּי
The wording is difficult to capture with a single English phrase, but it describes an extraordinary struggle or contest with her sister. The name Naphtali is deliberately connected to that wrestling.
Listen to what has happened.
A baby has been born...
and Rachel is still talking about Leah.
That is the tragedy of comparison.
You can finally receive something you desperately wanted and still be unable to enjoy it because your real goal was never merely receiving the blessing.
It was beating somebody else.
Rachel says, in effect:
I wrestled with my sister.
And I prevailed.
But did she?
Because if your peace requires somebody else's defeat, you are not free.
If another person's blessing ruins your gratitude, you are not free.

If you need to be prettier, richer, more successful, more followed, more admired, more married, more fertile, more influential, more “anointed,” more noticed, or more celebrated than somebody else before you can rest...
you are not living.
You are competing.
And the finish line keeps moving.
This is where Genesis becomes brutally compassionate.
God does not abandon Rachel.
Later, Genesis 30:22 says:
וַיִּזְכֹּר אֱלֹהִים אֶת־רָחֵל
Vayyizkor Elohim et-Rachel.
“God remembered Rachel.”
In biblical language, God's “remembering” does not mean He had temporarily forgotten she existed. It signals God's turning toward someone in covenantal action.
And Rachel conceives.
Joseph is born.
Notice what Scripture did not say.
Rachel manipulated God successfully.
No.
God remembered Rachel.
Grace arrived not because Rachel had engineered herself into deserving it, but because God remained God in the middle of a deeply fractured family.
And that is where this scandal begins pointing beyond Rachel.
Because the Bible is full of people whose families are too complicated for religious public relations.
Jacob.
Leah.
Rachel.
Bilhah.
Zilpah.
Jealousy.
Favoritism.
Manipulation.
Sexual arrangements far removed from Eden's simple picture of husband and wife becoming one flesh.
Competition between sisters.
Children born into adult conflict.
And somehow...
God keeps moving His redemptive purpose forward.
Not because dysfunction is holy.
Because grace is powerful.
And then the story becomes even more astonishing.
The Messiah does not enter history through a spotless human family tree.
Jesus comes into a world already drenched in scandal.
The Bible's genealogies do not airbrush humanity before presenting Christ.
They lead us through broken people toward the only truly righteous Savior.
And here is one of the most beautiful ironies in Rachel and Leah's story:
Jesus does not descend biologically from Rachel.
He comes through Leah's son Judah.
Leah—the woman who knew what it was like to feel unloved.
Genesis says that after bearing sons while aching for Jacob's affection, Leah eventually gives birth again and says:
הַפַּעַם אוֹדֶה אֶת־יְהוָה
Happa'am odeh et-YHWH.
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
And she calls him Judah.
From Judah would eventually come David.
And from David's royal line...
Jesus Christ.
Do you see it?
The household that looked like a scandal became part of the history through which God brought the Savior into the world.
That does not make the sin good.
It makes the grace breathtaking.
God does not need your past to be beautiful in order to redeem your future.
He does not call evil good.
He does something greater.
He defeats evil with His purposes.
He forgives sinners.
He restores the ruined.
He takes what human beings have twisted and demonstrates that our failures cannot outmaneuver His sovereign plan.
That is why the Gospel is not self-improvement.
Jesus did not come merely to make dysfunctional people slightly more functional.
He came to save sinners.
At the cross, Christ bears sin.
Our envy.
Our lust.
Our manipulation.
Our bitterness.
Our attempts to control outcomes.
Our secret competitions.
Our desperation.
Our shame.
Our religious pretending.
The Gospel does not say, “Rachel was messy, so being messy doesn't matter.”
The Gospel says sin matters so much that the Son of God went to the cross—and grace is so astonishing that everyone who turns to Christ in repentance and faith can be forgiven.
That includes the person reading this who has made decisions from desperation.
Maybe you forced a relationship because loneliness terrified you.
Maybe you compromised because waiting on God became unbearable.
Maybe jealousy has been eating you alive while everybody thinks you are doing fine.
Maybe you secretly resent your sibling.
Your friend.
Your coworker.
Another ministry.
Another mother.
Another father.
Another Christian.
Maybe somebody else's blessing feels like your rejection.
And you hate admitting that.
Hear this carefully:
You do not have to become Rachel's judge.
You need to recognize Rachel's God.
The God who sees wounded people.
The God who refuses to call sin righteousness.
The God who nevertheless works through shattered families.
The God who eventually stepped into our human catastrophe in the Person of Jesus Christ.
You cannot manipulate your way into peace.
You cannot compete your way into identity.
You cannot outperform your insecurity.
You cannot use another human being to heal what only God can heal.
And you cannot save yourself.
But Christ can save you.
Maybe the prayer tonight is not complicated.
Jesus, forgive me.
Forgive me for comparing.
Forgive me for forcing doors.
Forgive me for resenting people You blessed.
Forgive me for turning people into tools for my happiness.
Forgive me for pretending my desperation justified my disobedience.
I repent.
Teach me to trust You when waiting hurts.
Teach me to rejoice when somebody else receives what I still desire.
Teach me to believe that another person's blessing is not proof of Your absence from my life.
And above everything else...
give me Christ.
Be honest.
There are moments when confession becomes the first crack through which light enters.

One meaningful way to glorify God is to steward what He has given you in service of Gospel work; supporting and sharing Christ-centered teaching can be part of that stewardship. Salvation and grace cannot be bought. But voluntary support can help Gospel-centered resources continue reaching people who desperately need biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, and hope.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting the Savior.
Jesus does not need your money.
You need His mercy.
The cross cannot be purchased.
Forgiveness cannot be merchandised.
Grace cannot be earned.
The Gospel is received by faith in Christ.
So share because someone needs truth.
Save because tomorrow you may need to remember what God showed you today.
Follow because your soul needs more than endless noise in its feed.
But above all...
follow Jesus.
Rachel thought she needed to win against her sister.
What she really needed was God.
And perhaps that is the sentence some of us have spent years avoiding:
The thing you are desperately trying to obtain may not be the deepest thing your heart needs.
You can get the relationship and still ache.
Get the money and still fear.
Get the platform and still compare.
Get the recognition and still feel invisible.
Get what you begged for...
and discover that no created thing was ever designed to carry the weight of being your god.
Only Jesus can meet you at the bottom of that hunger.
Only Jesus can forgive the things desperation made you do.
Only Jesus can give an identity comparison cannot steal.
Only Jesus can take a story you are ashamed to tell and make it testimony to a grace you could never manufacture.
Your worst chapter does not get the final sentence when the Author of redemption has taken hold of the story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Could the Antichrist Be Alive Today?
paragraphs: Could the Antichrist Be Alive Today?
The Bible never tells us to guess his name. It tells us to recognize his spirit, refuse his deception, endure in truth, and belong completely to Jesus Christ.
Maybe he is already alive.
Maybe he isn't.

Maybe somewhere tonight, an ordinary-looking man is eating dinner, answering a phone, walking through an airport, building influence, or living completely unknown to the world—unaware, perhaps, of what history will eventually call him.
Or maybe the person Scripture describes has not yet been born.
The Bible does not tell us.
And that silence matters.
Because while millions of people are asking, “Could the Antichrist be alive today?” Scripture presses a far more uncomfortable question into the human heart:
If the spirit of antichrist is already in the world, how much of its deception are you already willing to tolerate?
That question changes everything.
Suddenly this is not merely prophecy.
It is personal.
John wrote words almost two thousand years ago that sound startlingly immediate:
“Παιδία, ἐσχάτη ὥρα ἐστίν… καὶ νῦν ἀντίχριστοι πολλοὶ γεγόνασιν.”
Paidia, eschatē hōra estin… kai nyn antichristoi polloi gegonasin.
“Children, it is the last hour… and now many antichrists have come.” — 1 John 2:18
The Greek word is ἀντίχριστος — antichristos.

It combines anti with Christos—Christ, the Anointed One. The idea carries opposition to Christ and, in its wider lexical sense, hostility toward the Messiah. John is the New Testament writer who actually uses the word antichrist.
And notice something many sensational discussions miss.
John did not merely say that an antichrist will come.
He said:
“…even now many antichrists have come.”
Already.
In John's lifetime.

That means biblical teaching about antichrist cannot responsibly be reduced to frantic attempts to identify one politician, billionaire, religious leader, military figure, technological innovator, pope, president, king, or celebrity.
Christians have repeatedly been tempted to do exactly that.
But speculation is not revelation.
If Scripture does not name the final individual for us, we should not pretend God whispered the missing name into our favorite headline.
John gives us something much more useful than a guessing game.
He gives us a test.
“Who is the liar but he who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist…” — 1 John 2:22.

Later he writes that the spirit refusing the truth about Jesus Christ “is the spirit of the antichrist,” which his readers had heard was coming and which was already in the world (1 John 4:3). He also warns in 2 John 7 about deceivers who do not confess Jesus Christ coming in the flesh.
That is the battlefield.
Jesus.
Who He is.
What He has done.
Whether He is truly Lord.
Whether He is truly the Christ.
Whether He really came in the flesh.
Whether humanity needs His cross.
Whether His resurrection changes everything.
Whether His Word deserves obedience.
Whether we belong to Him—or merely use His name while remaining lord of our own lives.
The spirit of antichrist does not ultimately need you to wear a satanic symbol.
It only needs you to reject the true Christ.
And sometimes rejection does not sound like hatred.
Sometimes it sounds like:
“I believe in Jesus, but I don't think He gets to tell me how to live.”
“I love God, but repentance seems extreme.”
“I believe the Bible when it agrees with me.”
“I want grace without surrender.”
“I want heaven without holiness.”
“I want a Savior who forgives me, but not a Lord who commands me.”
And suddenly the prophecy stops being something happening somewhere “out there.”
It walks into the room.
It sits beside us.
It reaches for our hearts.
This is why the question “Could the Antichrist be alive today?” deserves a careful answer.
Yes, it is possible.
There is nothing in Scripture requiring us to conclude that a future climactic opponent of Christ could not presently be alive.
But we cannot biblically claim that he definitely is.
Scripture has not given us his birth certificate.
It has not given us his photograph.
It has not authorized Christians to turn every geopolitical crisis into a certainty that “this person is definitely the Antichrist.”

There are also legitimate differences among faithful Christians regarding how the relevant prophetic passages fit together and how Revelation, Daniel, Matthew 24, 1–2 John, and 2 Thessalonians should be interpreted.
We should therefore distinguish what Scripture plainly says from conclusions produced by a particular end-times system.
That distinction is not weakness.
It is humility before the Word of God.
Paul describes a terrifying figure in 2 Thessalonians 2 commonly associated in Christian interpretation with the final Antichrist, although Paul himself calls him the “man of lawlessness.”
The Greek expression is:
ὁ ἄνθρωπος τῆς ἀνομίας
ho anthrōpos tēs anomias—
the man of lawlessness.
Paul says this figure opposes and exalts himself above what is called god or worshiped and presents himself as God. Paul also says something chilling:
“τὸ γὰρ μυστήριον ἤδη ἐνεργεῖται τῆς ἀνομίας.”
to gar mystērion ēdē energeitai tēs anomias.
“For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work.” — 2 Thessalonians 2:7.
Read that again.
Already at work.
John says many antichrists had already appeared.
Paul says the mystery of lawlessness was already operating.
The final manifestation may be future.
But rebellion against Christ is not waiting for the future.
It is here.
It has been here.
And this is where prophecy becomes painfully intimate.
Imagine a man obsessively studying every theory about the Antichrist while pornography quietly destroys his marriage.
Imagine a woman watching hours of prophecy videos while refusing to forgive the person she hates.
Imagine a church arguing about the identity of the Beast while gossip, pride, greed, sexual immorality, cruelty, and spiritual apathy move through its hallways untouched.
Imagine someone recognizing every supposed “sign of the times” while never recognizing the sin hardening his own heart.
What good is identifying every possible counterfeit if you barely know the real Christ?
What good is calculating timelines if you would not obey Jesus tonight?
What good is knowing the Greek word antichristos if Christ Himself remains outside the locked rooms of your life?
That is the danger.
We can become fascinated with darkness while neglecting the Light.
And Jesus did not command His disciples to become professional conspiracy hunters.
When Christ spoke about the end, He repeatedly warned about deception.
“See that no one leads you astray.”
False christs.
False prophets.
Wars.
Rumors of wars.
Tribulation.
Lawlessness.
Yet the heartbeat of biblical readiness is not panic.
It is faithfulness.
Jesus is preparing disciples, not detectives.
The Christian response to prophecy is not supposed to be:
“I figured out who he is!”
It is supposed to be:
“Whatever comes, I belong to Jesus.”
That difference is enormous.
Because the Antichrist—however one understands all the details surrounding his final appearance—is not the central character of biblical prophecy.
Jesus Christ is.
The Beast does not get the last word.
Satan does not get the last word.
Lawlessness does not get the last word.
Empire does not get the last word.
Death does not get the last word.
Jesus does.
Paul's description of the lawless one does not climax with Satan winning.
It climaxes with Christ destroying the lawless one at His coming.
The frightening figure whom human beings may someday consider unstoppable is, before the risen Christ, temporary.
That should change how Christians read prophecy.
We are not waiting to discover whether Jesus wins.
The Lamb has already been slain, the tomb is already empty, Christ is already risen, and His final victory is certain.
The cross looked like scandal.
A mocked Messiah.
A crown made from thorns.
Blood running down a beaten face.
Nails.
Darkness.
A borrowed tomb.
If you had stood outside Jerusalem that Friday without knowing Sunday was coming, you might have mistaken apparent defeat for the end of the story.
But God was writing redemption through what looked like catastrophe.
The greatest scandal became the doorway to grace.
Jesus took sin's accusation and answered it with His blood.
He took death's apparent victory and walked out of the grave.
He took guilty people who deserved judgment and offered them forgiveness they could never purchase.
That is the Gospel.
And that is why Christians should never allow fascination with the Antichrist to eclipse adoration of Christ.
The most important question is not whether the Antichrist is alive tonight.
The most important question is whether Christ is Lord of you tonight.
Because you can correctly predict nothing about tomorrow and still be ready for eternity.
And you can correctly predict a thousand things about tomorrow and still be lost.
Maybe you know Bible prophecy.
Maybe you know Daniel's seventy weeks.
Maybe you have studied Revelation 13.
Maybe you have opinions about the Beast, Babylon, the false prophet, the mark, Israel, the temple, the tribulation, the millennium, and the timing of Christ's return.
But when nobody is watching…
Who owns you?
What secret sin keeps getting your yes?
What has Jesus told you to surrender that you keep renegotiating?
What bitterness have you baptized as “discernment”?
What compromise have you renamed “freedom”?
What idol would hurt to lose more than Christ would hurt to dishonor?
Because deception rarely begins by announcing:
“I am deception.”
It offers another lord.
Another truth.
Another identity.
Another salvation.
Another gospel.
Another way to live without surrendering completely to Jesus.
That is why the safest place in the last days is not possession of a secret prophetic chart.
It is at the feet of Christ.
Knowing His voice.
Loving His truth.
Living in His Word.
Walking in repentance.
Depending upon His Spirit.
Refusing counterfeit gospels.
Remaining faithful when obedience becomes costly.
And getting back up when you fall because your confidence is not in your flawless performance but in the mercy of the crucified and risen Son of God.
Maybe that is why you are reading this.
Not because God wanted to satisfy your curiosity about the Antichrist.
Maybe He wanted to expose something in you.
A heart that has become cold.
A secret compromise.
A prayer life that disappeared.
A Bible gathering dust.
A private addiction nobody knows about.
A wound that turned into bitterness.
A faith that looks alive online but feels almost dead when the screen goes dark.
Then hear this carefully:
Jesus is not calling you into panic. He is calling you home.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the mercy of God refusing to leave you chained to what is killing you.
The Greek New Testament uses μετάνοια — metanoia for repentance, carrying the sense of a change of mind that turns a person toward God.
Not cosmetic Christianity.
Not “I'll try harder.”
Not fear for forty-eight hours because another prophecy video scared you.
Turn.
Come back.
Confess the sin.
End the secret arrangement with darkness.
Bring the hidden thing into the light.
Trust Christ.
Because the blood shed at Calvary is sufficient for sinners who come to Him.
The person reading this with tears forming behind tired eyes needs to understand something:
Your scandal does not have to become your final chapter.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
The disciples ran.
Paul once persecuted the church.
A criminal dying beside Christ had nothing left to offer Him but faith.
And again and again, Scripture tells the story of human ruin colliding with divine mercy.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending sin never mattered.
By paying for it.
Not by calling evil good.
By bearing judgment and offering sinners reconciliation with God.
Not by helping us decorate our chains.
By setting captives free.
So could the Antichrist be alive today?
Yes.
Possibly.
But Scripture does not permit us to declare that as a certainty, much less confidently identify some contemporary person without biblical warrant.
What Scripture allows us to say with far greater confidence is this:
