The spirit of antichrist was already operating in the apostolic age.
Deception is real.
Lawlessness is real.
A climactic rebellion against God is presented in Scripture.
Christ will return.
Jesus will triumph.
And every human being must decide what he or she will do with the Son of God.
That is enough truth to keep us awake.
Not terrified.
Awake.
Talk to Jesus.
Right there.
No performance.
No religious vocabulary required.
Confess what is true.
Ask Him for mercy.
Trust the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need evidence that grace still reaches ruined places.
Not because clicking “Share” earns God's favor. It does not.
It cannot.
The Gospel cannot be bought. Salvation is by God's grace through faith, not a commercial transaction.

But if biblical truth has strengthened you, supporting Gospel Warrior can help that truth reach another exhausted believer, another wandering son, another skeptical friend, another person awake at 2:00 a.m. wondering whether God could possibly still want them.
There may come a day when the headlines are louder, fear is heavier, and you need to remember that prophecy was never given to make Jesus smaller and darkness bigger.
You cannot.
Grace is free because Jesus paid what we never could.
And before you leave, remember the question with which we began.
Could the Antichrist be alive today?
Perhaps.
But there is something infinitely more important.
Jesus Christ is alive today.
The tomb is empty.
The King is coming.
Grace is still being offered.
And while the world keeps trying to guess the identity of the man of lawlessness, make absolutely certain that when Christ comes, He finds your heart already belonging to Him.
Do not become so fascinated trying to recognize the Antichrist that you fail to recognize how desperately you need Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE MAN WHO DIED TRYING TO TELL DAVID GOOD NEWS
paragraphs: THE MAN WHO DIED TRYING TO TELL DAVID GOOD NEWS

Everyone thought the battle was over. David had won. His throne was safe. A messenger was running toward him with “good news.” But the king was waiting for the answer to only one question—and when the truth finally reached him, victory sounded like a funeral.
There is something you need to know before we go any further.
The title is supposed to make you stop.
But Scripture makes us correct something immediately.
The messenger did not die.
Ahimaaz did not die trying to tell David the news. The Cushite messenger is not recorded as dying either.
Someone else died.
And once you realize who it was, this story becomes far more painful than the title.
Because the dead man was the king’s son.
His name was Absalom.
And somewhere between a battlefield covered with the aftermath of rebellion and a father sitting anxiously between the city gates, a man started running.
He thought he was carrying good news.
That is where this story becomes frighteningly personal.
Because sometimes what looks like victory from the battlefield feels completely different when it reaches the heart.
Second Samuel 18 is not a neat story about heroes and villains.
It is a family tragedy.
It is rebellion.
Betrayal.
Judgment.
Political upheaval.
A father’s failure.
A son’s pride.
A kingdom bleeding from wounds that began long before anyone picked up a sword.
And behind all of it stands David—a man who knew both scandal and grace.
David had defeated Goliath.
David had written songs of worship.
David had been called and anointed by God.
And David had also committed terrible sin.
He committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged the death of Uriah. When Nathan confronted him, David finally stopped hiding:
“I have sinned against the LORD.”
Forgiveness came.
But forgiveness did not mean that every earthly consequence disappeared.
That distinction matters.
Grace is not God pretending sin never mattered.
Grace is God refusing to abandon the repentant sinner to the condemnation that sin deserves.
And now David was living inside a house fractured by consequences.
His son Absalom had rebelled against him.
The son wanted the father’s throne.
The father had been forced from Jerusalem.
Israel descended into conflict.
Yet before the battle, David gave his commanders an astonishing order concerning the very son attempting to overthrow him:
“Deal gently for my sake with the young man Absalom.”
For my sake.
Listen to the father inside the king.
David knew Absalom was a rebel.
David knew soldiers might die because of Absalom.
David knew his kingdom was being torn apart.
But Absalom was still his son.
Somebody reading this understands that kind of love.
The child who broke your heart is still your child.
The person who betrayed you is still someone whose name can make your chest tighten.
You can know someone is wrong and still grieve what is happening to them.
You can establish boundaries and still cry.
You can hate what sin has done without ceasing to love the person trapped inside its consequences.
That is the emotional landscape of 2 Samuel 18.
Then Absalom dies.
The rebellion collapses.
David’s forces win.
And Ahimaaz, son of Zadok, sees something every messenger longs to see:
news worth running with.
He tells Joab:
“Let me now run, and bear the king tidings…”
The Hebrew vocabulary underneath this scene is powerful.
The biblical root is בָּשַׂר — basar, carrying the idea of announcing or bringing news, often good news.
The related noun is בְּשׂוֹרָה — besorah, news or good tidings.
Ahimaaz looks at the battlefield and sees victory.
The king’s enemies have been defeated.
The throne has survived.
The rebellion is finished.
Surely this is good news.
But Joab knows something Ahimaaz has not emotionally processed.
The king’s son is dead.
Joab essentially tells him:
Not today.
This is not the day for you to carry these tidings.
Then Joab sends a Cushite who had witnessed what happened.
But Ahimaaz cannot let it go.
“Let me run.”
Joab questions him.
Ahimaaz insists.
Let me run.
Finally Joab says:
Run.
And Ahimaaz runs so hard that he overtakes the Cushite.
Picture it.
Dust rising beneath his feet.
Heart pounding.
Lungs burning.
One messenger behind him.
A city ahead.
A king waiting between the gates.
Ahimaaz runs faster.
Faster.
Faster.
Until the watchman sees him in the distance.
One man running alone.
David hears about him and assumes:
There is news in his mouth.
Then the watchman recognizes the runner’s movement.
It looks like Ahimaaz.
David responds that he is a good man and must be bringing good news.
The runner finally arrives.
Breathless.
Exhausted.
And the first word out of his mouth is extraordinary:
שָׁלוֹם — shalom.
“Peace.”
“All is well.”
Shalom carries a rich range of meaning involving peace, welfare, well-being, wholeness and safety.
Ahimaaz bows before David.
He praises the LORD.
God has delivered the king from those who rose against him.
Everything he is saying sounds victorious.
The rebellion is broken.
The kingdom is preserved.
The king is alive.
God has given deliverance.
And David responds with one question.
Not:
“How many enemies died?”
Not:
“Is my throne secure?”
Not:
“Did we win?”
Not:
“Will Jerusalem receive me again?”
David asks:
“Is the young man Absalom safe?”
In Hebrew:
הֲשָׁלוֹם לַנַּעַר לְאַבְשָׁלוֹם
Ha-shalom la-na'ar le-Avshalom?
In sense:
“Is there shalom for the young man Absalom?”
Is my boy all right?
Suddenly Ahimaaz has a problem.
He has run faster than the man carrying the complete answer.
He has reached the king with victory...
but he cannot bring himself to say what the king most desperately needs to know.
He speaks about seeing confusion.
A commotion.
He says he does not know what happened.
And David tells him to stand aside.
Imagine that moment.
All that running.
All that urgency.
All that speed.
And now...
stand aside.
That may be one of the most haunting pictures of modern Christianity.
We can become very good at running.
Posting.
Talking.
Debating.
Building platforms.
Making videos.
Quoting verses.
Winning arguments.
Defending doctrines.
Creating Christian content.
Being seen.
Being heard.
Being first.
And still arrive without the answer wounded people desperately need.
You can outrun everyone and still not be ready to carry the message.
You can have speed without courage.
Reach without compassion.
A Bible verse without biblical character.
Religious vocabulary without the Gospel.
You can shout “peace” while avoiding the wound sitting directly in front of you.
Then the second runner arrives.
The Cushite.
He announces the victory.
The LORD has delivered David.
And David asks him exactly what he asked Ahimaaz:
Is Absalom safe?
This time the answer comes.
Carefully.
Painfully.
The king understands.
Absalom is dead.
And suddenly the military victory disappears behind the sound of a father breaking.
David goes up to the chamber above the gate.
He weeps.
And then Scripture gives us one of the most agonizing cries in the Old Testament:
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom!”
Then David says words that should stop every Christian who knows where the biblical story eventually leads:
“Would God I had died for thee…”
I wish I could have died instead of you.
Do you see it?
David wants substitution.
The father wishes he could die in the place of his rebellious son.
But David cannot rewrite what has happened.
He cannot climb backward through history.
He cannot take Absalom’s place after death has already claimed him.
He cannot trade graves with his son.
He can only weep.
But centuries later...
another King would come.
Another Son of David.
Jesus Christ.
And where David could only cry, “Would I had died instead of you,” Jesus actually gave His life for sinners.
We must be careful here.
David is not Jesus, and every detail of Absalom’s story should not be forced into an allegory.
But Scripture unmistakably brings us eventually to the greater Son of David, Jesus Christ, whose substitutionary death accomplishes what human grief could never accomplish.
Christ did not merely stand over humanity’s rebellion and wish He could rescue us.
He came for us.
“The Son of man came…to give his life a ransom for many.”
We rebelled against the King.
And the King came looking for rebels.
That is the scandal of grace.
We sinned.
Christ was sinless.
We deserved judgment.
Christ willingly bore judgment for His people.
We accumulated guilt.
Christ brought forgiveness.
We ran away.
Christ came near.
The cross does not say your sin was insignificant.
The cross says your sin was so serious that redemption required the blood of the spotless Lamb of God—and that the love of God was so astonishing that Christ willingly gave Himself to save sinners.
That is why Christianity is not self-improvement dressed in religious language.
The Gospel is not:
Become impressive enough for God.
Clean yourself up.
Hide the addiction.
Hide the bitterness.
Hide the pornography.
Hide the affair.
Hide the envy.
Hide the pride.
Hide the secret messages.
Hide the unbelief.
Hide what happened last night.
Walk into church.
Smile.
Sing.
Pretend.
No.
Jesus did not die to make you better at hiding.
He died and rose again to reconcile sinners to God.
Repentance means the hiding can end.
Grace means you can finally tell the truth.
Maybe that is why this story hurts.
Because perhaps you have been Ahimaaz.
Running hard.
Looking faithful.
Saying the correct things.
People recognize your running.
People call you good.
People expect good news from your mouth.
But underneath everything...
you are terrified someone will ask the one question you do not want to answer.
“How is your marriage?”
“I don't know.”
“How is your prayer life?”
“I don't know.”
“Are you still secretly going back to that sin?”
“I don't know.”
“Have you forgiven them?”
“I don't know.”
“Are you actually following Jesus—or just maintaining the appearance that you are?”
Silence.
And maybe Jesus is touching the place you have spent years protecting.
Not to humiliate you.
To bring you into the light.
Because there are questions we can avoid with people that we cannot avoid before God.
You can outrun another messenger.
You cannot outrun God.
You can fool followers.
You cannot fool the One who sees the heart.
You can delete browser history.
You cannot delete guilt.
You can curate an image.
You cannot curate your soul before an omniscient God.
And that sounds terrifying until you remember who is calling you out of hiding.
Jesus.
The One who already knows.
The One who died for sinners.
The One who welcomed the broken.
The One who confronted hypocrisy.
The One who called people to repentance.
The One who forgave.
The One who went to the cross.
The One who walked out of the grave.
The One who still saves.
So stop running merely to be seen running.
Run to Christ.
Stop trying to arrive first.
Arrive surrendered.
Stop confusing religious activity with spiritual life.
You do not need to impress Jesus with your speed.
You need Jesus to save you.
If something hidden has been exposed while reading this, do not turn conviction into another five minutes of scrolling.
Talk to God.
Confess honestly.
Repent.
Ask for mercy.
Trust Christ.
And if you already belong to Him but have wandered, come home.
Grace is not permission to keep rebelling.
Grace is the open door through which repentant sinners return.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Do not underestimate what sharing biblical truth can do.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list smiling publicly while privately collapsing.
Someone grieving.
Someone trapped in secret sin.
Someone angry with God.
Someone who has not prayed honestly in months.
Someone who thinks they have gone too far.
Someone who needs to discover that the Gospel is not about pretending the scandal never happened.
It is about what Jesus Christ can do with a surrendered life after the scandal.
But hear this clearly because biblical truth matters more than conversion numbers:
Your standing before God cannot be purchased by supporting a ministry.
Buying Christian merchandise cannot make God love you more.
Sharing this article does not earn righteousness.
Jesus Christ saves.
Jesus Christ receives the glory.

Yet if this ministry is bearing good spiritual fruit in your life, voluntarily supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of helping that work continue and helping biblical resources reach more people.
Come to Jesus.
Because Ahimaaz could run quickly, but speed could not heal David.
David could win a kingdom, but victory could not resurrect Absalom.
David could wish to die for his rebellious son, but wishing could not exchange their places.
Then came Jesus.
The greater Son of David.
The crucified King.
The risen Savior.
And He did not merely wish He could die for sinners.
He gave Himself.
That is our hope.
Not that our past was clean.
Not that our families were never broken.
Not that our choices produced no consequences.
Not that our stories contain no scandal.
Our hope is that Jesus Christ still saves sinners who come to Him in repentance and faith.
So when your past whispers your name...
when shame opens an old file...
when the enemy reminds you what you did...
when consequences still hurt...
when someone remembers the version of you that you desperately wish you could erase...
remember the cross.
Remember the empty tomb.
Remember that Christianity is built around a Savior who specializes in resurrection.
And remember this:
Some messengers run carrying news of a victory. Jesus came carrying the scars that made our victory possible.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE MOMENT YOU THINK YOU’RE BETTER THAN EVERYONE ELSE, YOU MAY BE FARTHER FROM JESUS THAN YOU THINK
paragraphs: THE MOMENT YOU THINK YOU’RE BETTER THAN EVERYONE ELSE, YOU MAY BE FARTHER FROM JESUS THAN YOU THINK
The frightening story Jesus told about a religious man who looked righteous, prayed correctly, lived morally—and still walked away unjustified.
There is a kind of sin that rarely feels like sin.
It does not stumble into church smelling like alcohol.
It does not arrive with scandal written across its face.
It knows the songs.
It carries a Bible.
It can quote Scripture.
It may serve, give, fast, pray, preach, correct theology, defend Christian morality, and warn everybody else about compromise.
And that is exactly why it can be so dangerous.
Because some sins make you ashamed enough to run toward Jesus.
This one can make you feel righteous enough to believe you no longer desperately need Him.
Read that again.

There may come a moment in your Christian life when you look at somebody else's marriage, addiction, failure, clothing, parenting, theology, finances, past, church attendance, political opinions, sexual sin, temper, weakness, or reputation—and something almost invisible happens inside you.
You do not necessarily say anything.
You just think...
“At least I’m not like them.”
And somewhere in that sentence, a throne is being built.
Jesus once told a story about two men who walked into the same place to pray.
One looked respectable.
The other carried a reputation people despised.
One could present an impressive spiritual résumé.
The other could barely present himself.
And Jesus deliberately made the ending uncomfortable.
Luke tells us that Jesus spoke the parable specifically to people who “trusted in themselves that they were righteous, and treated others with contempt” (Luke 18:9).
That description matters.
Their problem was not merely confidence.
Their confidence had found the wrong foundation.
They trusted in themselves.
Then self-righteousness produced its predictable offspring:
contempt.
Jesus continues:
“Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector” (Luke 18:10).
To modern ears, “Pharisee” can immediately sound like “villain.”
That can cause us to miss the shock.
The Pharisee was the visibly religious man.
The tax collector belonged to a profession widely despised in Jewish society under Roman rule and associated with exploitation and collaboration.
If you had been standing nearby judging the two men by reputation alone, you might have expected the Pharisee to be the spiritual success story.
Then he began praying.
In the Greek text of Luke 18:11 we encounter these devastating words:
“ὁ θεὸς, εὐχαριστῶ σοι ὅτι οὐκ εἰμὶ ὥσπερ οἱ λοιποὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων...”
“God, I thank You that I am not like the rest of mankind...”
At first, it almost sounds like gratitude.
“God, I thank You...”
But listen to what his gratitude becomes.
A comparison.
He begins talking to God while measuring himself against people.
He mentions extortioners, unjust people, adulterers.
Then his eyes land on the man standing nearby.
“...or even like this tax collector.”
This is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because you do not have to say those exact words to pray the Pharisee’s prayer.
“Thank God my children didn't turn out like theirs.”
“Thank God I understand Scripture better than those people.”
“Thank God I would never fall into that sin.”
“Thank God I’m not one of those lukewarm Christians.”
“Thank God my church actually teaches truth.”
“Thank God I’m not like him.”
“Thank God I’m not like her.”
And perhaps the most dangerous version:
“Thank God I’m not like that Pharisee.”
There it is.
Pride is so deceptive that we can become proud of recognizing pride in somebody else.
The Pharisee continues by listing his spiritual achievements.
He fasts.
He tithes.
Those actions themselves were not the problem.
Fasting can honor God.
Giving can honor God.
Obedience matters.
Holiness matters.
Jesus was not condemning faithfulness.
He was exposing what happens when obedience stops producing gratitude and starts producing superiority.
There is an enormous difference between saying:
“Jesus has been merciful to me.”
and quietly believing:
“Jesus must be impressed with me.”
Then Jesus moves our attention toward the other man.
The tax collector stands at a distance.
He will not even lift his eyes toward heaven.
He beats his breast.
And his prayer is painfully short.
Luke 18:13 records:
“ὁ θεός, ἱλάσθητί μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ.”
“God, be merciful to me, the sinner.”
No résumé.
No comparison.
No excuses.
No explanation of childhood trauma.
No list of people worse than him.
No bargaining.
No attempt to impress heaven.
Just a sinner who finally understands that his greatest hope is not that somebody else is worse.
His hope is mercy.
And this is where Jesus overturns the room.
“I tell you, this man went down to his house justified, rather than the other...” (Luke 18:14).
The scandalous man goes home justified.
The respectable man does not.
Why?
Not because sin suddenly became irrelevant.
Not because repentance does not matter.
Not because righteousness does not matter.
The tax collector understood something the Pharisee had forgotten:
You cannot rescue yourself.
The Gospel does not begin with how much better you are becoming than everybody else.
It begins with how desperately you need a Savior.
That is why Christianity leaves no room for spiritual boasting.
Paul asks one of the most pride-destroying questions in the New Testament:
“τί δὲ ἔχεις ὃ οὐκ ἔλαβες;”
“What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).
Think about that.
Your breath?
Received.
Your intelligence?
Received.
Your opportunities?
Received.
Your ability to read Scripture?
Received.
The people who discipled you?
Grace.
The conviction that brought you to repentance?
Grace.
The strength that helped you resist temptation yesterday?
Grace.
The forgiveness covering sins you would be horrified to see projected publicly?
Grace.
The cross?
Grace.
The empty tomb?
Grace.
The promise of eternal life?
Grace upon grace.
So what exactly are we boasting about?
The Gospel does not tell you that you are superior.
It tells you that you were helpless enough to need the blood of the Son of God.
That should destroy both despair and arrogance at the same time.
You cannot say, “I am too filthy for Jesus,” because His grace is greater than your sin.
But you also cannot stand at Calvary and say, “I am better than those people,” because the cross announces that you needed saving too.
At the foot of the cross, nobody has an impressive résumé.
We arrive as sinners.
We survive by mercy.
We stand by grace.
This is why Paul writes in Romans 12:3 not to think of ourselves “more highly” than we ought to think.
And Philippians 2:3 presses even deeper:
“μηδὲν κατὰ ἐριθείαν μηδὲ κατὰ κενοδοξίαν...”
“Do nothing from selfish ambition or empty conceit...”
The Greek word κενοδοξία carries the idea of empty or vain glory.
Empty glory.
That is such an accurate picture of pride.
We spend years constructing trophies heaven never asked us to win.
Better Christian.
Better parent.
Better theologian.
Better church member.
Better husband.
Better wife.
Better preacher.
Better denomination.
Better testimony.
Better morality.
Better understanding.
Better than them.
Then Jesus walks into our carefully constructed ranking system and asks a question that makes every trophy suddenly feel hollow:
Who gave you what you have?
That does not mean Christians should pretend truth and error are identical.
They are not.
Jesus confronted sin.
The apostles confronted false teaching.
Scripture commands discernment.
Biblical humility is not moral confusion.
You can call sin what God calls sin without treating the sinner as though you never needed mercy yourself.
You can defend truth without worshiping your own correctness.
You can confront someone without enjoying their humiliation.
You can disagree without despising.
You can pursue holiness without turning holiness into a ladder from which you look down on everyone underneath you.
And perhaps this is where it hurts.
Sometimes we do not actually want restoration for the person who fell.
We want confirmation that we were better than them all along.
Someone's marriage collapses, and secretly we feel validated.
A pastor falls publicly, and somewhere beneath our righteous anger is a whisper:
“I knew something was wrong with him.”
Someone who criticized us fails, and their pain almost tastes like vindication.
A struggling believer confesses the same sin again, and compassion slowly becomes irritation.
We forget how patient Jesus has been with us.
We remember people's worst chapters while asking God to remember ours no more.
We demand justice for their sins and mercy for our own.
That is not the heart of Christ.
Imagine if Jesus treated you according to the standard you sometimes use on everyone else.
Imagine if every secret thought were exposed.
Every jealous impulse.
Every lustful glance.
Every dishonest motive.
Every prayer performed for appearances.
Every moment you wanted recognition.
Every private bitterness.
Every act of obedience secretly hoping somebody would notice.
Every time you judged another person's visible battle while protecting your invisible one.
Would you still feel superior?
This is why grace is so offensive to human pride.
Grace means the person you judged can be forgiven.
Grace means the addict can become your brother.
The prostitute can become your sister.
The prisoner can become a preacher.
The prodigal can come home.
The religious hypocrite can repent.
The person whose life became a public scandal can kneel before Jesus and rise covered by a righteousness they could never manufacture.
And so can you.
That is the Gospel.
Not good people proving themselves worthy.
Not bad people learning to behave impressively.
Sinners reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Christ bore sin.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ saves.
Christ forgives.
Christ transforms.
And because salvation is rooted in Him, there is no room left for boasting as though we accomplished our own resurrection.
Maybe your scandal was public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your greatest scandal is the pride you have hidden beneath religious respectability.
Jesus is still calling you away from self-righteousness and toward grace.
Repentance does not mean pretending sin is small.
Repentance means finally agreeing with God about it and turning toward the One who can forgive and transform you.
Maybe tonight your prayer does not need to be impressive.
Maybe it only needs to be honest.
“God, be merciful to me, a sinner.”
That prayer is not weakness.
It is the collapse of an illusion.
You were never saved because you were better.
You were saved because Jesus is merciful.
And when you truly understand that, something changes in the way you see people.
The broken person stops being merely disgusting and becomes someone who needs the Savior you needed.
The struggling Christian stops being merely frustrating and becomes someone who needs the patience Christ repeatedly gives you.
The unbeliever stops being your enemy to defeat and becomes a soul for whom Christ calls His people to bear witness.
The fallen believer becomes someone who may need correction, repentance, accountability—and restoration.
And you?
You stop needing everybody beneath you in order to feel secure.
Your identity is no longer built on being better than them.
It is built on belonging to Him.
That is freedom.
Who have I been looking down on?
Do not answer for your spouse.
Do not answer for your pastor.
Do not answer for the person whose hypocrisy irritates you.
Answer for yourself.
Whose name came into your mind?
That person may be exactly where Jesus wants to expose something in your heart.
Not so He can destroy you.
So He can free you.
You can simply write, “Jesus, humble me.”
If you have been fighting pride and you are tired of measuring your life against everyone else's, comment, “Grace, not pride.”
If you need prayer because your heart has grown hard toward somebody, comment, “pray for me.”

And if Christ has already rescued you from a season when you thought you were beyond restoration, tell somebody what His grace did. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person needed before giving up.
Not because you need another saved post buried in a folder, but because pride has a remarkable ability to return after conviction fades.
Come back when you are tempted to believe somebody else's failure makes you righteous.
But if Gospel Warrior is genuinely helping you follow Christ, supporting and sharing this work can be one practical way to help these messages reach people who may never walk through a church door.
Not to make Gospel Warrior famous.
Not to make yourself look spiritual.
a tax collector who desperately needs mercy...
a wounded Christian who thinks the church has no place left for them...
or a sinner who has never understood that Jesus receives people who come to Him empty-handed.
And before you judge which one of them needs this most...
remember the story.
Two men entered the temple.
One carried an impressive record.
One carried nothing but repentance.
Only one went home justified.
The most dangerous distance from Jesus may not begin when you realize how sinful you are.
It may begin when you become convinced that everybody else's sin has made you righteous.
So come down from the pedestal.
There is room at the foot of the cross.
There always was.
Because when everything we used to prove that we were better finally falls from our hands, we discover something infinitely better waiting there:
Jesus.
Mercy for the guilty.
Grace for the proud.
Forgiveness for the repentant.
A new heart for the surrendered.
And a completely rewritten ending for anyone who comes to Christ.
Never forget this:
The moment you stop needing grace because you think you are better than everyone else may be the very moment you need grace to open your eyes again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Proverbs Describes a Young Man Being Sexually Seduced—and It Sounds Shockingly Modern
paragraphs: Proverbs Describes a Young Man Being Sexually Seduced—and It Sounds Shockingly Modern

He had no smartphone. No private browser. No dating app. No disappearing messages. Yet almost three thousand years ago, Scripture described the anatomy of sexual temptation with a precision that feels frighteningly familiar.
He was walking at night.
That is how the scene begins.
Not in a brothel. Not in a bedroom. Not even in the act itself.
He was simply walking.
And that may be the most terrifying part of Proverbs 7.
Because long before the young man falls sexually, Scripture shows us something happening inside him.
The ancient Hebrew describes him this way:
נַעַר חֲסַר־לֵב — naʿar ḥasar-lēv.
A young man “lacking heart.”

Many English translations understandably render the phrase “lacking sense,” “lacking judgment,” or “void of understanding.” But the Hebrew wording is unusually vivid. Lēv, “heart,” in biblical Hebrew can reach beyond emotion into the inner person—the place of thought, intention, discernment, and will.
So Solomon is not merely showing us a stupid young man.
He is showing us a young man whose inner defenses are missing.
And then he starts walking toward the wrong corner.
That should make some of us uncomfortable.
Because perhaps your downfall did not begin when you clicked the image.
Perhaps it began when you decided you could handle the temptation.
Perhaps the affair did not begin with the kiss.
Perhaps it began with the conversation you knew you should have ended.
Perhaps pornography did not conquer you the first night you watched it.
Perhaps it slowly trained you through a thousand moments when conviction whispered, “Leave,” and desire answered, “Just a little longer.”
Perhaps you never planned to betray your spouse.
You only enjoyed being noticed by someone who was not your spouse.
Perhaps you never intended to become sexually trapped.
You were lonely.
Curious.
Rejected.
Bored.
Angry.
Tired.
Wanting to feel wanted.
And somewhere between loneliness and secrecy, you started walking toward a corner you should never have approached.
That is Proverbs 7.
And that is why it sounds so modern.
The ancient text says the young man was:
עֹבֵר בַּשּׁוּק אֵצֶל פִּנָּהּ
Passing through the street near her corner.
Then comes the detail that should stop us:
וְדֶרֶךְ בֵּיתָהּ יִצְעָד
He was walking in the direction of her house.
Notice the progression.
He has not committed adultery yet.
But his feet are already cooperating with his appetite.
This is one of Scripture's most uncomfortable truths about temptation:
Sometimes we pray for God to deliver us from places we keep deliberately walking toward.
We ask Jesus for freedom while keeping the number.
We ask for purity while preserving the secret account.
We ask God to protect our marriage while continuing the private conversation.
We pray against lust and then feed ourselves images designed to awaken it.
We say, “I would never cross that line.”
Then quietly move the line.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Until one night we discover we are no longer standing where we thought we were.
Proverbs places the young man there:
בְּנֶשֶׁף־בְּעֶרֶב יוֹם... לַיְלָה וַאֲפֵלָה
In the twilight. In the evening. In the darkness of night.
There is something almost cinematic about it.
A street.
A young man.
A corner.
Darkness.
Then she appears.
Proverbs does not sanitize what happens next.

The woman approaches him aggressively. She kisses him. She speaks boldly. She tells him her husband is away. She has prepared her bed. She invites him to spend the night satisfying themselves with love.
This is not merely attraction.
This is temptation with a sales pitch.
And that is where Proverbs becomes painfully contemporary.
Because temptation still knows how to advertise.
It rarely introduces itself by saying:
“I am here to destroy your marriage.”
It says:
“You deserve affection.”
It does not say:
“I want to enslave your mind.”
It says:
“Everybody watches this.”
It does not say:
“I am going to teach you to objectify human beings made in God's image.”
It says:
“It is only fantasy.”
It does not say:
“This secret relationship may eventually devastate your children.”
It says:
“You two just understand each other.”
It does not say:
“I want to make you hide from God.”
It whispers:
“No one will know.”
That last lie is ancient.
Proverbs 7 emphasizes that the husband is away on a long journey.
In other words:
There appears to be opportunity without immediate accountability.
Nobody is watching.
Nobody is coming home.
Nobody needs to know.
And suddenly an ancient bedroom sounds remarkably like the glow of a locked smartphone at 1:17 in the morning.
Different technology.
Same human heart.
Different century.
Same serpent-shaped logic.
Different screen.
Same lie.
“You can have this without consequences.”
But Scripture refuses to end the camera shot at pleasure.
That is what makes Proverbs 7 merciful.
Yes—merciful.
Because God loves us enough to show us where the road actually ends.
The woman persuades the young man with seductive speech, and then Proverbs says he follows her.
Suddenly the imagery changes.
He thought he was walking toward pleasure.
God shows us an ox walking toward slaughter.
He thought he was entering a bedroom.
God shows us a bird flying toward a trap.
He thought he was about to become more alive.
Scripture reveals that he is walking toward death.
This is what sin does.
It advertises the entrance and hides the exit.
It shows you the bed but not the broken home.
The body but not the bondage.
The excitement but not the shame.
The fantasy but not the neurological habit.
The secret messages but not the spouse crying.
The thrill but not the spiritual numbness.
The moment but not the morning afterward.
And before anyone uses Proverbs 7 as ammunition to blame women for male sexual sin, we need to be biblically serious.
The villain of Scripture is not womanhood.
Proverbs itself personifies divine Wisdom as a woman calling people toward life. Immediately after this warning, Proverbs 8 opens with Wisdom raising her voice and calling humanity to understanding.
The contrast is not “women are dangerous.”
The contrast is folly versus wisdom.
Unfaithfulness versus covenant faithfulness.
Death versus life.
And the young man is morally responsible for where his own feet take him.
Men cannot blame women for their lust.
Women cannot blame men for theirs.
A seductive culture cannot remove our responsibility before God.
And temptation itself is not identical with sin. Jesus Christ was tempted and remained without sin.
The issue is what we do when temptation knocks.
Some of you reading this know exactly why this article found you.
There is something you need to delete.
Someone you need to stop messaging.
Somewhere you need to stop going.
Something you need to confess.
A browser history that has become a graveyard of promises you made to God.
A relationship you keep calling “complicated” because calling it sinful would require a decision.
A secret that has survived because you have carefully protected it from the light.
And perhaps nobody knows.
Your spouse does not know.
Your parents do not know.
Your pastor does not know.
Your friends at church would never imagine it.
You worship on Sunday.
You smile.
You serve.
You post Bible verses.
And somewhere underneath the Christian vocabulary is a terrified human being thinking:
“If people knew what I have done, would anyone still believe I belong to Jesus?”
Listen carefully.
Proverbs 7 is a warning.
But Proverbs 7 is not the whole Gospel.
Because the Bible does not merely reveal the road into sexual sin.
Ultimately, Scripture leads sinners to the Savior.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
Jesus did not come for people who successfully maintained an impressive religious appearance.
He came for sinners.
For adulterers.
For sexually broken people.
For porn addicts.
For hypocrites.
For people carrying histories they wish they could erase.
For the ashamed.
For the guilty.
For the person reading this with tears beginning to form because this stopped being an article several paragraphs ago.
It became a mirror.
The Gospel does not say your sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more terribly than we usually understand.
Christ bore sin in His body.
The innocent Son of God suffered for the guilty.
Jesus was crucified, buried, and raised from the dead.
Grace is not God pretending rebellion is harmless.
Grace is God providing in Christ what guilty sinners could never provide for themselves.
Forgiveness.
Cleansing.
Reconciliation.
A new heart.
A new direction.
A new life.
That means repentance is not merely feeling terrible after you fall.
Repentance turns.
Maybe that is the word somebody desperately needs tonight.
Turn.
Before the meeting.
Before the hotel room.
Before the photograph.
Before the next message.
Before another night staring at images you promised yourself you would never watch again.
Turn.
And if you already crossed the line?
Turn now.
If you crossed it a hundred times?
Turn now.
If your secret has lasted years?
Bring it into the light now.
Not because repentance purchases God's mercy, but because genuine faith does not make peace with the darkness Christ came to save us from.
There is a profound contrast hiding in this story.
The young man of Proverbs 7 walks toward her house.
Jesus calls sinners to follow Him.
Two directions.
Two voices.
Two destinations.
One voice says, “Come, let us take our fill of love.”
The other says, “Follow Me.”
One promises immediate pleasure while concealing destruction.
Christ calls us to deny ourselves, take up our cross, and follow Him—and leads us into life.
The question is not whether voices are calling you.
The question is:
Which voice is determining where your feet go?
Maybe you have fallen sexually and believed the scandal became your permanent name.
Adulterer.
Addict.
Unclean.
Damaged.
Hypocrite.
Disqualified.
But the Gospel announces something scandalously beautiful:
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
There may still be consequences.
Trust may require years to rebuild.
A wounded spouse may need time.
Confession may cost you comfort.
Repentance may require radical boundaries, pastoral help, accountability, counseling, broken relationships, deleted accounts, surrendered devices, and humiliating honesty.
Grace does not eliminate every earthly consequence.
But grace means your sin does not have to become your final identity.
Christ does not merely offer better behavior.
He offers redemption.
That is why our message will always be:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming sin as self-expression.
Not by teaching people to feel comfortable while destruction consumes them.
Jesus rewrites everything by meeting guilty people with truth and grace, calling them to repentance, forgiving those who come to Him, and transforming people who thought their story was already over.
So be honest for a moment.
What corner have you been walking toward?
You do not have to tell the whole internet your private sin. Wisdom matters. Some confessions belong in safe, accountable, pastoral or professional settings rather than a public comment section.
But you can stop pretending.

And if Christ has already brought you out of sexual bondage, shame, adultery, pornography, or another hidden prison, consider sharing your testimony without graphic details. Someone reading the comments may believe freedom is impossible until they discover that Jesus has already begun writing resurrection stories in people like them.
Not because saving a post makes anyone holy.
Not as a religious performance. Not to prove that you are righteous. And not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
Send it privately to the husband who is struggling.
The wife carrying secret shame.
The teenager being discipled more aggressively by sexualized media than by godly wisdom.
The believer who fell and thinks Jesus could never want them again.
The person who does not yet know Christ but desperately needs to discover that Christianity is not merely God shouting “stop” at sinners—it is God offering sinners reconciliation through His Son.
But understand the order clearly:
You glorify God by loving Him, obeying Him, serving others, stewarding what He has entrusted to you, and seeking first His kingdom.

If this ministry genuinely feeds your faith, however, supporting it financially can become one voluntary expression of that stewardship—helping Gospel-centered teaching reach people who may never walk through the doors of a church.
Because sometimes sharing one article is not “just social media.”
Sometimes it places truth in front of someone at exactly the moment they are standing at the corner.
Thousands of years ago, an old man looked through a window and saw a young man walking through the darkness.
He could see something the young man could not.
He could see where the road ended.
Today Scripture has opened that window for us.
You can see the corner.
You can hear the invitation.
You can see the trap.
And if you are already farther down that road than you ever intended to go, hear this before shame convinces you to keep walking:
Jesus Christ is still calling sinners out of darkness.
Turn around.
Come into the light.
Confess what needs confessing.
Cut off what keeps dragging you backward.
Receive the mercy of Christ rather than making another promise in your own strength.
Walk with wise believers.
Guard your heart.
Guard your marriage.
Guard your eyes.
Guard your private life.
And when temptation whispers that nobody is watching and nothing will happen, remember the young man walking through the darkness of Proverbs 7.
He thought he was approaching pleasure.
God could already see the trap.
The darkest corner of your story does not have to become your final destination when Jesus is still calling you home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “DO NOT WORRY ABOUT TOMORROW” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MANY CHRISTIANS THINK IT MEANS
paragraphs:
“DO NOT WORRY ABOUT TOMORROW” DOESN’T MEAN WHAT MANY CHRISTIANS THINK IT MEANS
Jesus Was Never Teaching You to Sit Still and Call It Faith. He Was Teaching You How to Work, Prepare, Obey, and Walk Into an Uncertain Tomorrow Without Letting Tomorrow Become Your Master.
Maybe the sentence that has been quietly stealing your peace begins with two words:
“What if...?”
What if the money does not come?
What if the doctor calls?
What if the business fails?
What if my child walks away from God?
What if I lose this job?
What if the marriage does not survive?
What if I make the wrong decision?
What if everything I have been building suddenly collapses?
You are lying in bed, but your mind has already traveled three months into the future.
Your body is under the blanket.
Your heart is somewhere inside a catastrophe that has not happened.
You are answering imaginary phone calls. Fighting imaginary battles. Paying imaginary bills. Mourning imaginary losses. Rehearsing conversations that may never take place.
And because you are thinking so intensely about tomorrow, it feels responsible.
It feels like preparation.
Sometimes it even feels spiritual.
But there is a difference between preparing for tomorrow and trying to emotionally survive tomorrow before God has even allowed tomorrow to arrive.
Jesus knew that difference.
And in the Sermon on the Mount, He spoke words that have comforted frightened believers for generations:
“Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.”
Matthew 6:34.
But those words have sometimes been misunderstood.
Jesus was not saying, “Never plan.”
He was not saying, “Ignore your responsibilities.”
He was not saying, “Do nothing and expect God to clean up the consequences.”
He was not turning laziness into a spiritual virtue.
He was confronting something far deeper.
The original Greek brings us close to the force of His words:
“Μὴ οὖν μεριμνήσητε εἰς τὴν αὔριον...”
Mē oun merimnēsēte eis tēn aurion...
“Therefore, do not be anxious about tomorrow...”
The word translated “worry” comes from μεριμνάω — merimnaō — a word used for being anxious, concerned, or consumed with care.
Jesus was not forbidding foresight.
He was forbidding tomorrow from possessing your heart today.
And that changes everything.
Because biblical faith is not passive.
Faith does not sit on the couch while the electricity bill remains unopened and say, “God will provide.”
Faith opens the bill.
Faith makes the call.
Faith creates the budget.
Faith goes to work.
Faith asks for help when help is needed.
Faith apologizes when repentance is required.
Faith prepares.
Faith plants.
Faith builds.
Faith obeys.
And after doing what obedience requires, faith refuses to pretend that it has become God.
That is where worry begins to lose its grip.
Look carefully at the context surrounding Jesus’ command.
Before Jesus says not to worry about tomorrow, He speaks about food, drink, clothing, birds, flowers, and the Father who knows what His children need.
Then comes the command that gives the entire passage its center:
“But seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness...”
Matthew 6:33.
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not say, “Seek first a trouble-free life.”
He does not say, “Seek first financial certainty.”
He does not say, “Seek first an explanation for everything that frightens you.”
He points His disciples toward the kingdom of God.
That means Matthew 6:34 is not primarily a motivational slogan about positive thinking.
It is a kingdom command.
Jesus is teaching His disciples where their allegiance belongs when circumstances become uncertain.
Your responsibility is faithfulness.
God's responsibility is sovereignty.
And we become exhausted when we try to perform both jobs.
Maybe that is where you are right now.
You have called it “thinking ahead.”
But deep down, you know you are afraid.
You keep checking.
Checking your account.
Checking your messages.
Checking the results.
Checking whether they replied.
Checking whether something changed.
Checking whether the thing you fear has finally happened.
You pray about it...
then pick it back up five minutes later.
You surrender it at night...
then reclaim it before breakfast.
And somewhere along the way, worry starts disguising itself as wisdom.
But worry makes promises it cannot keep.
Worry says, “If you think about this long enough, you will eventually control it.”
You won't.
Worry says, “If you imagine every possible disaster, nothing will surprise you.”
It still might.
Worry says, “If you carry tomorrow today, tomorrow will hurt less.”
Jesus says something radically different.
Tomorrow already has enough belonging to tomorrow.
Today has enough belonging to today.
“ἀρκετὸν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἡ κακία αὐτῆς.”
Arketon tē hēmera hē kakia autēs.
“Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.”
The word ἀρκετόν — arketon — carries the sense of sufficient or enough.
Enough.
There is something almost painfully compassionate about that word.
Jesus does not pretend life is easy.
He actually acknowledges trouble.
That matters.
Christian faith does not require pretending that cancer is pleasant, unemployment is harmless, betrayal does not hurt, grief is easy, or financial pressure is imaginary.
Jesus does not say there will be no trouble.
He says today already has enough of its own.
In other words, do not drag tomorrow's burden backward into today.
You were never given grace to live tomorrow today.
You were given grace for obedience now.
And maybe this is the sentence someone desperately needs to hear:
God is already present in the tomorrow you are afraid of entering.
You cannot see Him there yet because you are still standing here.
But He is not pacing heaven wondering what He will do if your worst fear happens.
God does not discover tomorrow when you do.
That does not mean your preferred outcome is guaranteed.
Biblical trust is deeper than believing God will make everything happen exactly as we want.
Sometimes the answer is no.
Sometimes the door closes.
Sometimes the relationship ends.
Sometimes the diagnosis is devastating.
Sometimes faithful Christians suffer.
Sometimes obedience costs enormously.
The cross itself destroys the shallow idea that faithfulness always produces immediate comfort.
Christian confidence rests somewhere stronger:
Whatever tomorrow contains, Jesus Christ remains Lord.
And suddenly “do not worry about tomorrow” becomes much stronger than “everything will be okay.”
It becomes:
Even when everything is not okay, Christ will still be Christ.
That is faith.
Faith is not confidence that nothing painful will happen.
Faith is confidence that nothing can dethrone Jesus.
And that kind of faith moves.
Consider Noah.
God warned him about something coming.
Noah did not respond, “I refuse to think about the future because worrying about tomorrow is sinful.”
He built an ark.
Consider Joseph.
When God revealed years of abundance followed by famine, Joseph did not refuse to store grain because “God will provide.”
His preparation became part of God's provision.
Consider the wisdom literature of Scripture, which praises diligence and prudent preparation.
Biblical trust and biblical planning are not enemies.
The difference lies in what rules the heart.
Planning says, “Tomorrow may come, so I will faithfully prepare.”
Worry says, “Tomorrow may come, so I must control it.”
Planning can finish its work and sleep.
Worry keeps rewriting the future at 2:17 in the morning.
Planning holds a calendar.
Worry wants the throne.
And there is another detail we cannot miss.
Jesus points to birds.
Birds do not sit motionless in nests waiting for worms to fly into their mouths.
They move.
They search.
They gather.
Yet Jesus directs our attention beyond their activity to the Father's provision.
That is the tension mature faith learns to live inside:
Work without worshiping your work.
Prepare without worshiping your preparation.
Save without worshiping your savings.
Go to the doctor without worshiping medicine.
Build without worshiping the building.
Apply for the job without making the job your savior.
Love people deeply without demanding that people become your god.
Do what faithfulness requires...
and leave the throne occupied by the One who belongs there.
Jesus.
Because eventually every anxious heart arrives at the same uncomfortable question:
“Can I trust God if He does not give me the tomorrow I want?”
That is where Christianity stops being inspirational language and becomes surrender.
Anyone can praise God when the numbers are rising.
Anyone can say “God is good” when the test comes back clear.
Anyone can post Jeremiah 29:11 when the promotion arrives.
But what happens when God remains good while your circumstances remain painful?
Look at Jesus.
On the night before His crucifixion, He knew suffering was coming.
He did not deny reality.
He did not pretend pain was an illusion.
He prayed in Gethsemane.
He felt the terrible weight of what lay ahead.
And still He surrendered Himself to the Father's will.
Christian peace, therefore, is not emotional numbness.
It is surrendered trust.
And the gospel goes even deeper.
Because the greatest tomorrow humanity ever needed to fear was not financial collapse, sickness, rejection, unemployment, or death.
It was standing guilty before a holy God.
Sin had written a future for us.
Judgment.
Separation.
Death.
We could not budget our way out of it.
Could not hustle our way out.
Could not become religious enough to erase our guilt.
Could not perform enough good deeds to make the scandal disappear.
And then Jesus stepped into our story.
The sinless Son of God carried sin to the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And suddenly people whose stories appeared destined for condemnation could receive forgiveness, reconciliation, and eternal life through Him.
That is the scandal of grace.
Peter could fail and still be restored.
The persecutor Saul could become Paul.
The thief beside Christ could discover that grace was closer than his final breath.
And sinners like us can repent, believe, and discover that our worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So perhaps your deepest problem is not that tomorrow feels uncertain.
Perhaps you have forgotten who holds you when tomorrow arrives.
Jesus never promised you control.
He offered something infinitely better.
Himself.
So make the plan.
Set the alarm.
Prepare the presentation.
Study for the examination.
Send the application.
Schedule the appointment.
Create the budget.
Have the difficult conversation.
Save wisely.
Work diligently.
Seek counsel.
Take responsibility.
Repent where you have sinned.
Repair what you can repair.
But after you have done what faithfulness requires, stop demanding from yourself something God never asked you to possess:
omniscience.
You do not need to know everything that happens next in order to obey God now.
Read that again.
You do not need to know everything that happens next in order to obey God now.
Maybe you only need enough light for today's step.
Maybe faith today looks like getting out of bed.
Maybe it looks like sending one application.
Maybe it looks like finally opening the envelope you have been afraid to open.
Maybe it looks like telling somebody, “I need help.”
Maybe it looks like praying again after months of silence.
Maybe it looks like confessing the hidden sin that has been eating you alive.
Maybe it looks like forgiving someone.
Maybe it looks like walking away from something God has already told you to leave.
Maybe it looks like saying:
“Jesus, I don't know what happens tomorrow. But today belongs to You.”
That is not passive faith.
That is surrendered obedience.
And if something inside you has been exposed while reading this, do not rush past it.
Be honest.
What tomorrow have you been trying to live today?
What future have you mentally rehearsed so many times that fear has started feeling like reality?
What are you terrified God will not handle the way you want Him to?
Bring that specific fear into the light.
There is no shame in admitting that the battle is real.
Sometimes another believer needs to see that they are not the only person learning how to trust Christ one frightened day at a time.
And think of one person whose mind has been living inside tomorrow lately.
You know who they are.
The friend waiting for medical results.
The father wondering how he will provide.
The mother losing sleep over her children.
The believer whose faith has been battered.
The person smiling publicly while privately imagining everything falling apart.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor. It does not.
It cannot.
But if Christ has used this truth to strengthen you, helping biblical encouragement reach another frightened person can be one practical act of love.

If you want to glorify God through supporting Gospel work, do it from gratitude rather than guilt—share truth, encourage people, pray, serve, give where God leads, and help sound biblical discipleship reach people who desperately need Jesus.
Because there may come a night when tomorrow starts shouting again.
It means doing today's obedience without demanding tomorrow's control.
Because tomorrow will come carrying whatever tomorrow carries.
There may be laughter.
There may be tears.
There may be an answered prayer.
There may be a closed door.
There may be something you never expected.
But if you belong to Christ, you will not enter tomorrow alone.
The same Jesus who meets you in today's trouble will not suddenly disappear at midnight.
So tonight...
make the plan if a plan needs making.
Do the work that needs doing.
Say the prayer that needs praying.
Repent of what needs repenting.
Then release the future from your clenched hands.
Tomorrow was never asking you to become its savior.
You already have One.
His name is Jesus.
And when tomorrow finally becomes today, Christ will already be there.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY GRACE DOESN’T EXCUSE SIN
paragraphs: WHY GRACE DOESN’T EXCUSE SIN
The grace that refuses to condemn the repentant sinner is the very grace that refuses to leave that sinner enslaved.
There is a sentence Christians sometimes whisper after doing what they already knew was wrong.
“God understands.”
And there is truth buried inside those words.
God does understand.

He understands your weakness more completely than you do. He knows the wound behind the habit, the loneliness behind the compromise, the fear behind the lie, the hunger beneath the addiction, the anger underneath the bitterness, and every secret battle you have never had enough courage to tell another human being.
He knows.
But sometimes “God understands” slowly becomes something God never said:
“Therefore, it doesn’t matter.”
That is where grace gets dangerously misunderstood.
Because the same Jesus who receives sinners does not make peace with the sin destroying them.
Maybe nobody knows about yours.
Maybe you can worship on Sunday while feeding it on Monday.
Maybe you know exactly how to clear the browser history.
How to delete the conversation.
How to smile beside your spouse.
How to raise your hands during worship while resentment is eating you alive.
How to post Scripture while privately living somewhere you know Jesus is asking you to leave.
Maybe your struggle is less visible.
Pride.
Jealousy.
Gossip.
Greed.
Unforgiveness.
The need to be admired.
The secret pleasure you feel when somebody you envy fails.
And somewhere along the way, perhaps you learned enough Christian vocabulary to silence conviction without actually surrendering.
“Everybody sins.”
“I’m under grace.”
“God knows my heart.”
“He’ll forgive me.”
Yes.
We are saved by grace.
Yes.
Christ receives sinners.
Yes.
There is forgiveness for the guilty.
But listen carefully, because eternity is too important for comforting lies:
Grace is not God's permission to remain comfortably in the very bondage from which Jesus died to redeem you.
Paul anticipated the distortion nearly two thousand years ago.
After proclaiming the breathtaking abundance of God's grace, he asked the question someone was inevitably going to ask:
“Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν; ἐπιμένωμεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, ἵνα ἡ χάρις πλεονάσῃ;”
Ti oun eroumen? Epimenōmen tē hamartia, hina hē charis pleonasē?
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?” — Romans 6:1.
The Greek matters.
Paul uses χάρις — charis, grace, favor, gift.
But notice another word:
ἐπιμένωμεν — epimenōmen.
It carries the idea of remaining, continuing, persisting.
Paul is not asking whether Christians will ever stumble.
He is confronting the horrifying idea that because grace is abundant, we might deliberately make sin our home.
And his answer is explosive:
“μὴ γένοιτο.”
Mē genoito.
“By no means.”
“Absolutely not.”
The thought is rejected with force.
Then Paul asks:
“How can we who died to sin still live in it?” — Romans 6:2.
That changes everything.
Christianity is not the story of bad people learning how to behave well enough for God to tolerate them.
It is the story of spiritually dead sinners being united to a crucified and risen Savior and receiving a new life they could never manufacture themselves.
That is why grace and repentance are not enemies.
Grace makes repentance possible.
Grace does not stand at the doorway of your prison saying, “Stay inside. I forgive you.”
Grace opens the door and says:
“Come out.”
Because you have been asking Jesus to forgive something you have quietly decided to protect.
There is a difference between fighting sin and making peace with sin.
A believer may fall terribly.
A believer may struggle repeatedly.
A believer may sometimes leave a battle ashamed, wounded, and wondering how they could have failed again.

Scripture does not teach sinless perfection in this present life. John writes to believers precisely because Christians still need the promise that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us (1 John 1:9), and that when anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1).
So this is not an article telling the struggling Christian:
“You sinned again. Jesus wants nothing to do with you.”
No.
Look at the cross.
Jesus knew what He was purchasing.
Romans declares that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory and are justified freely by God's grace through the redemption found in Christ Jesus (Romans 3:23–24).
You were never saved because your record became impressive.
You are saved through Christ.
The danger begins when we turn that astonishing mercy into permission.
There is a difference between someone crawling toward Jesus saying,
“Lord, I hate what this is doing to me. Help me.”
and someone turning away from Jesus saying,
“I know what You said, but I intend to keep this.”
One is warfare.
The other is surrender to the enemy.
And some of us have mislabeled surrender as grace.
Paul destroys that counterfeit understanding again in Titus:
“For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people…”
Beautiful.
But keep reading.

That same grace is “training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions” and to live godly lives while awaiting Jesus Christ, who gave Himself to redeem and purify a people for Himself (Titus 2:11–14).
Grace saves.
And grace trains.
Grace forgives.
And grace transforms.
Grace receives you filthy.
And then grace begins washing what sin covered in mud.
Grace finds you in chains.
But grace loves you too much to decorate your chains and call them freedom.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
God did not look at humanity's rebellion and pretend sin wasn't serious.
He demonstrated just how serious it was at a Roman cross.
The cross simultaneously destroys two lies.
The first lie says:
“My sin is too terrible for God to forgive.”
Look at Jesus.
There is grace.
The second says:
“My sin isn't serious enough for me to repent.”
Look at Jesus again.
There is the cross.
If sin were trivial, Calvary makes no sense.
If sinners were hopeless, Calvary makes no sense.
At the cross, justice and mercy meet.
Jesus does not save us by pretending we are innocent.
He saves guilty people through His own sacrificial death and victorious resurrection.
That means Christianity offers something infinitely better than self-improvement.
Redemption.
Maybe you have wasted years.
Redemption.
Maybe pornography has hollowed out your soul.
Redemption.
Maybe adultery shattered your marriage.
Redemption.
Maybe alcohol became the place you run when life hurts.
Redemption.
Maybe pride has made you unbearable to the people who love you.
Redemption.
Maybe bitterness has occupied your heart so long that you no longer remember who you were before the wound.
Redemption.
Maybe everybody thinks you're spiritually strong while you know exactly what happens when the door closes.
Redemption.
Not because sin is small.
Because Christ is mighty to save.
And this is why repentance is beautiful.
Biblical repentance is not payment for forgiveness.
You cannot purchase the blood of Jesus with tears.
You cannot earn justification by feeling guilty enough.
You cannot punish yourself into salvation.
Christ paid.
Christ died.
Christ rose.
Christ saves.
Repentance is the sinner finally dropping the weapon and turning toward the King who was willing to die for His enemies.
It is saying:
“Jesus, I don't want to defend what nailed You to the cross anymore.”
Somebody reading this has been hiding.
You love Jesus.
But you're exhausted.
You keep falling.
You confess.
You promise.
You cry.
Then three days later, three weeks later, maybe three hours later…
again.
And shame tells you:
“See? You're fake.”
Listen carefully.
The answer is not to rename your sin.
And the answer is not to run from Jesus.
Run to Him.
Bring the whole ugly thing into His light.
Confess it.
Cut off access to what repeatedly drags you back.
Seek mature Christian accountability.
Open Scripture when temptation tells you to isolate.
Pray before the battle, not only after losing it.
And when you fall, do not lie on the battlefield worshiping your failure.
Get up and run again toward Christ.
The Christian life is not sustained by pretending temptation disappeared.
It is sustained by dependence upon the Savior.
Jesus is not merely interested in making your guilt disappear.
He is making you His.
That is why holiness matters.
Not because holiness purchases salvation.
Because salvation produces a new direction.
We do not obey so Christ will finally love us.
In Christ, we learn obedience because He first loved us.
We do not flee sin because we are trying to become our own saviors.
We flee sin because we already have one.
And suddenly grace becomes far more magnificent than permission.
Imagine a prisoner sitting inside an unlocked cell.
The ransom has been paid.
The door has been opened.
His chains have fallen.
Someone stands outside calling his name.
But the prisoner remains seated.
“Why won't you come out?”
And he answers:
“Because the door is open, I suppose staying imprisoned doesn't matter anymore.”
That would be madness.
Yet spiritually, we sometimes do exactly that.
Christ did not break your chains so you could carry them around as souvenirs.
He did not call you from darkness so you could negotiate visitation rights with the darkness.
Grace doesn't tell the prodigal son that the pigpen is actually a perfectly acceptable permanent address.
Grace brings him home.
And perhaps the most frightening thing about cherished sin is that eventually we stop feeling frightened by it.
What once convicted us becomes normal.
What once made us pray becomes entertainment.
What once made us blush becomes something we defend.
That is why conviction can itself be mercy.
When Scripture exposes you, God is not being cruel.
When the Holy Spirit presses something upon your conscience through God's Word, the loving response is not to harden yourself.
Come into the light.
You do not have to clean yourself before approaching Jesus.
But do not demand that Jesus call your darkness light.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the affair.
Bring Him the rage.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the greed.
Bring Him the secret account.
Bring Him the unforgiveness.
Bring Him the hypocrisy.
Bring Him the version of you nobody else knows exists.
Bring Him the thing you hoped this article would never mention.
And say:
“Jesus Christ, have mercy on me.”
Because the Gospel is not:
“Become worthy, then come.”
The Gospel announces that Christ came for sinners.
But when Christ takes hold of a life, He does not merely change its eternal destination.
He begins changing the person.
Slowly sometimes.
Painfully sometimes.
With battles and tears and failures and getting back up.
But truly.
That is sanctifying grace.
Be honest.
If you need repentance, repent before God first.

And if Christ has already brought you out of something you once believed would own you forever, tell that testimony. Somebody hiding in the same darkness may need evidence that Jesus still transforms lives.
Not because clicking “Share” earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
Not because supporting a Christian ministry purchases blessing.
It cannot.
But if this message faithfully communicates biblical truth, sharing it can become one small act of helping truth travel farther.
Send it to the person you immediately thought about while reading.
Send it to the believer drifting toward compromise.
Send it even to the skeptic who thinks Christianity is merely religious people pretending to be morally superior.
Let them discover what the Gospel actually says:
We are not the heroes.
Jesus is.
There may come a night when temptation starts negotiating with you again and you need to remember:
Grace did not set you free so you could return willingly to the chains.
Your support simply helps us keep putting biblical truth in front of people who may desperately need it.
What are you going to do with Jesus?
Not the polished church version of you.
You.
The person behind the screen.
The person carrying memories nobody knows.
The person who has failed.
The person who promised God, “Never again,” and then did it again.
The person who sometimes wonders whether grace could possibly still reach this far.
It can.
But grace is not calling you deeper into hiding.
Grace is calling you home.
You do not need another excuse.
You need Jesus.
And the astonishing news of Christianity is that Jesus is not standing at the end of your transformation waiting for you to finally become worthy enough to approach Him.
He is where transformation begins.
Come guilty.
Come exhausted.
Come ashamed.
Come with trembling hands.
Come with the confession you have avoided.
Come with the chains you cannot break yourself.
But come.
Because the blood of Christ is not permission to cherish the disease.
It is the price paid to redeem the diseased.
The resurrection is not permission to remain inside the tomb.
It is the announcement that death does not get the final word.
And grace is not Jesus looking at your chains and saying they do not matter.
Grace is Jesus calling you by name and leading you into freedom.
So share this with somebody whose secret battle is becoming a secret prison.
And comment.
Not for an algorithm alone.
For honesty.
For testimony.
For the believer reading silently at 2:00 in the morning wondering whether anyone else is still fighting.
Tell them.
“Christ is still healing me.”
Because maybe somebody needs to discover tonight that the Gospel was never about pretending the scandal didn't happen.
It was about discovering that the scandal doesn't have to write the ending.
Grace does not excuse the chains that held you. Grace introduces you to the Savior who can finally teach you how to walk free.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN HORMONES BE AN EXCUSE FOR SIN? THE ANSWER MAY CONVICT YOU—BUT IT MAY ALSO SET YOU FREE
paragraphs: CAN HORMONES BE AN EXCUSE FOR SIN? THE ANSWER MAY CONVICT YOU—BUT IT MAY ALSO SET YOU FREE

Your body can explain why the battle feels harder. It cannot turn darkness into light. And somewhere between your hormones, your wounds, your desires, and your choices stands a Savior who understands human weakness without ever calling sin holy.
There are days when you barely recognize yourself.
You wake up irritated.
Something small happens and suddenly your emotions feel ten times larger than the moment deserves.
Your patience disappears.
Your thoughts become darker.
Your desires become louder.
Your body feels restless, exhausted, sexually charged, emotionally raw, anxious, angry, or overwhelmed.
Then you say something you regret.
You lash out at your spouse.
You entertain the fantasy.
You click what you promised God you would never click again.
You explode at your children.
You become cruel.
You feed lust.
You surrender to bitterness.
You justify jealousy.
You let your emotions drive the car while wisdom sits gagged in the back seat.
And afterward comes the sentence that sounds almost reasonable:
“Maybe it was just my hormones.”
Maybe they were involved.
But here is the question that reaches much deeper:
Can hormones explain part of the battle without excusing the sin?
Yes.
And understanding that distinction may rescue you from two equally dangerous lies.
The first lie says, “If my body influenced me, I am not responsible for anything I did.”
The second says, “If I struggled this badly, I must be a hopeless Christian.”
Neither is the Gospel.
Jesus gives us something far more truthful—and far more merciful.
On the darkest night before His crucifixion, Jesus found His disciples unable to remain awake with Him. He told them:
“Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”
Matthew 26:41, KJV
The Greek is piercing:
“γρηγορεῖτε καὶ προσεύχεσθε, ἵνα μὴ εἰσέλθητε εἰς πειρασμόν· τὸ μὲν πνεῦμα πρόθυμον ἡ δὲ σὰρξ ἀσθενής.”
Grēgoreite kai proseuchesthe… to men pneuma prothymon, hē de sarx asthenēs.
Watch.
Pray.
Do not enter into temptation.
The spirit is willing.
The flesh is weak.
Notice what Jesus does not do.
He does not pretend human weakness is imaginary.
He acknowledges it.
“ἡ δὲ σὰρξ ἀσθενής.”
The flesh is weak.

Jesus knows what it means to inhabit a human body. Scripture tells us that He was tempted, yet without sin. He understands exhaustion, hunger, grief, anguish, pain, pressure, rejection, and physical weakness.
Christianity does not require you to pretend biology does not exist.
Hormones are real.
Bodies are real.
Sleep deprivation is real.
Physical illness is real.
Stress is real.
Trauma can affect people profoundly.

Menstrual cycles, pregnancy, postpartum changes, menopause, puberty, aging, medications, endocrine disorders, and countless other physical realities can affect mood, energy, sexual desire, irritability, concentration, and emotional intensity.
Sometimes what feels like a purely “spiritual” problem deserves medical attention too.
Seeking appropriate medical or mental-health care is not necessarily evidence of weak faith. A wise Christian does not have to choose between prayer and responsible care.
But acknowledging influence is not the same thing as erasing responsibility.
That distinction matters enormously.
Imagine standing beside a fire.
The wind suddenly becomes violent.
The wind did not create the fire, but it can intensify it.
It can push flames toward places they might not otherwise have reached.
Hormonal fluctuations and other bodily conditions can sometimes function similarly in human experience: they may intensify emotions, appetites, fatigue, agitation, or vulnerability.
But Scripture directs our attention beyond the intensity of desire to what happens when desire is welcomed, cultivated, and acted upon.
James writes:
James 1:14
The crucial word is ἐπιθυμία—epithymia—desire, craving, longing.
James continues:
“εἶτα ἡ ἐπιθυμία συλλαβοῦσα τίκτει ἁμαρτίαν…”
“Then, after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin…”
James 1:15
Read that carefully.
Desire.
Then conception.
Then sin.
Then death.
There is movement.
There is progression.
This means temptation must not simply be equated with sin.
Jesus Himself “was in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin” according to Hebrews 4:15.
Feeling temptation does not mean you have already lost.
Experiencing an unwanted impulse is not identical to deliberately embracing it.
Feeling anger is not identical to murdering someone with your tongue.
Experiencing sexual temptation is not identical to choosing lust.
Feeling emotionally unstable is not identical to deliberately destroying the people around you.
Being exhausted is not identical to cruelty.
Being hormonally affected is not identical to being morally condemned for every involuntary feeling that passes through your body.
Someone reading this desperately needed that distinction.
Because perhaps you have been repenting for temptation itself.
You have been ashamed because the thought appeared.
Ashamed because the desire became loud.
Ashamed because your body reacted.
Ashamed because you felt anger rising.
Ashamed because temptation came back after you thought you had defeated it.
Listen carefully:
Temptation is not proof that Christ abandoned you.
The battlefield is not the same thing as defeat.
But neither should we turn the battlefield into an excuse for surrender.
Paul describes an actual conflict in Galatians 5:
“ἡ γὰρ σὰρξ ἐπιθυμεῖ κατὰ τοῦ πνεύματος, τὸ δὲ πνεῦμα κατὰ τῆς σαρκός…”
“For the flesh desires what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh.”
There is conflict.
War.
Resistance.
And then Paul says something astonishing:
“πνεύματι περιπατεῖτε…”
Pneumati peripateite.
Walk by the Spirit.
Not merely believe certain truths about the Spirit.
Walk.
Live.
Move.
Order your life under His rule.
Paul eventually names the fruit produced by the Spirit:
Love.
Joy.
Peace.
Patience.
Kindness.
Goodness.
Faithfulness.
Gentleness.
And then comes the word that destroys one of our favorite excuses:
“ἐγκράτεια.”
Enkrateia.
Self-control.
Galatians 5:22–23.
That means biblical Christianity never promises that faithful obedience will always feel easy.
Sometimes obedience happens while every emotion inside you is screaming in the opposite direction.
Sometimes holiness sounds like:
“I desperately want to say this, but I will remain silent.”
“I feel sexually overwhelmed, but my body belongs to Christ.”
“I am furious, but I will not punish my family for what I am feeling.”
“I feel rejected, but I will not seek validation through adultery, pornography, revenge, manipulation, or attention from someone who is not my spouse.”
“I am emotionally exhausted, so I need rest, prayer, help, wise boundaries, perhaps professional care—and repentance where I have sinned.”
That last sentence matters.
Because Christianity does not tell suffering people merely to “try harder.”
The Gospel is not behavior modification with Bible verses taped over the cracks.
Jesus did not come merely to make badly behaved people slightly more respectable.
He came to save sinners.
Maybe your hormones contributed to the intensity.
Maybe exhaustion lowered your resistance.
Maybe old wounds made the situation especially painful.
Maybe your body was screaming.
Maybe another person genuinely hurt you.
Those realities may help explain why the temptation became so fierce.
But if you sinned, freedom begins when you stop needing the explanation to become an acquittal.
There is something strangely beautiful about finally saying:
“Lord, there were factors involved. There were pressures. There was weakness. But what I did was wrong. I sinned. Please forgive me.”
That is not self-hatred.
That is repentance.
And repentance is not God dragging you into a courtroom so He can enjoy humiliating you.
For the person who comes to Christ, repentance is the doorway home.
Think about Peter.
He was confident.
Loud.
Certain.
He told Jesus that even if everyone else fell away, he would remain faithful.
Then pressure arrived.
Fear arrived.
The courtyard grew dangerous.
And Peter denied Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Imagine that sound.
