But that does not mean the Bible leaves Christians without an answer.

Scripture regularly gives principles broad enough to govern circumstances its original human authors never encountered. Christians do this constantly. The Bible does not name every modern technology, substance, entertainment platform, financial practice, or medical development. Yet its commands concerning holiness, wisdom, stewardship, love, self-control, conscience, freedom, and the glory of God remain astonishingly relevant.
And one passage cuts frighteningly close to the heart of this question.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:12:
Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν, ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντα συμφέρει... ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος.
The last expression is especially important.
ἐξουσιασθήσομαι — exousiasthēsomai.
It carries the idea of being brought under another's authority or being mastered.
Paul's principle is essentially this: something being permissible does not automatically make it beneficial—and he refuses to be mastered by anything.
Read that again, slowly.
I will not be mastered by anything.
Suddenly the question changes.
Not merely:
“Is vaping technically forbidden?”
But:
“Is this mastering me?”
Can you leave it alone?
Not for ten minutes while you are distracted.
Could you genuinely walk away from it?
If the thought of giving it up immediately creates panic, irritation, bargaining, excuses, or the desperate thought, I need this...
then perhaps the deepest spiritual issue is no longer sitting inside the vape.
It is sitting on a throne.
Because Christianity is not ultimately about constructing a giant catalog of forbidden objects.
Christianity is about lordship.
Jesus Christ is Lord.
That means the Christian does not merely ask, “How close can I get to sin without technically crossing the line?”
We ask something radically different.
Does this belong beneath the lordship of Jesus?

There is another text people often bring into this conversation. Paul tells believers that their bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit and that they were bought with a price, concluding, “glorify God in your body” (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).
That passage deserves careful handling.
Its immediate context concerns sexual immorality. We should not rip it from that context and pretend Paul was secretly writing about nicotine two thousand years before modern vaping existed.
Yet the theological reality underneath the passage remains breathtaking.
Your body belongs to God.
For the Christian, your body is not disposable property.
It is not an enemy.
It is not an idol either.
It belongs to the One who redeemed you.
Jesus did not purchase some invisible spiritual portion of you while leaving the rest untouched.
He redeemed you.
And that means the Christian question about the body cannot simply be:
“Can I get away with this?”
It becomes:
“How do I honor Christ with the body He has given me?”

That does not mean every unhealthy choice automatically carries identical moral weight. Christians eat desserts. Some drink too much coffee. Some sleep too little. Some sit too much. Some train obsessively. Others neglect exercise altogether.
We should therefore be careful about creating simplistic equations such as:
“Unhealthy = automatically sinful in exactly the same way.”
Scripture demands more careful thinking than that.
But neither should we use everyone else's imperfect habits as camouflage for the habit God may be confronting in us.
That is one of the easiest tricks of the human heart.
What about coffee?
What about sugar?
What about fast food?
What about people who never exercise?
Perhaps those questions deserve answers too.
But sometimes “What about them?” is simply another way of avoiding “What about me?”
And Jesus has an uncomfortable habit of bringing conversations back to the heart.
There is another question.
Can you do it for God's glory?
Paul writes:
Εἴτε οὖν ἐσθίετε εἴτε πίνετε εἴτε τι ποιεῖτε, πάντα εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ ποιεῖτε.
“Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.” — 1 Corinthians 10:31.
Notice the breathtaking scope.
εἴτε τι ποιεῖτε — eite ti poieite
“whatever you do.”
Paul reaches into ordinary life—eating, drinking, mundane actions—and places all of it beneath one enormous purpose:
εἰς δόξαν θεοῦ — eis doxan Theou
toward the glory of God.
So perhaps one of the most revealing questions a Christian who vapes can ask is not simply, “Where does the Bible prohibit this?”
Ask instead:
Can I sincerely receive this habit beneath the lordship of Jesus and practice it to the glory of God?
Not sarcastically.
Not defensively.
Before Christ.
With an open Bible and an open heart.
That question reaches places rules sometimes cannot.
And then there is conscience.

Romans 14 deals with disputed matters among believers, particularly questions involving food and observance of days. Paul does not teach that our personal feelings magically determine morality. God's truth remains God's truth.
But he does teach something deeply sobering about acting against faith and conscience.
Romans 14:23 concludes:
πᾶν δὲ ὃ οὐκ ἐκ πίστεως ἁμαρτία ἐστίν.
pan de ho ouk ek pisteōs hamartia estin
“whatever is not from faith is sin.”
That does not mean every anxious thought is God's voice.
Our consciences must be formed by Scripture.

But if you cannot vape with a clear conscience before Christ—if every inhale is accompanied by the quiet knowledge that you are resisting what you believe God is asking you to surrender—then stop searching for an internet stranger to give you permission to violate your conscience.
Sometimes we ask, “Is it a sin?” when what we actually mean is:
“Can somebody please tell me I don't have to surrender this yet?”
That sentence may hurt.
But stay here.
Because this is where Christianity becomes radically different from mere religious condemnation.
Jesus did not come for people who had already conquered everything controlling them.
He came for sinners.
He came for captives.
He came for ashamed people.
He came for people with secret battles.
People who promised, This is the last time, and returned again.
People who prayed sincerely on Sunday and stumbled desperately on Monday.
People who love God and still have places inside themselves that desperately need transformation.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself perfectly, then perhaps Christ will receive you.”
The Gospel announces that while we were sinners, Christ died for us.
At the cross, Jesus bore sin.
He endured judgment.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And He rose again.
Forgiveness is not purchased by your ability to stop vaping.
Salvation is not earned by nicotine abstinence.
You are not justified before God because you successfully defeated every habit.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
But grace is not permission to make peace with slavery.
The Christ who forgives also transforms.
The Savior who says, in effect, Come as you are, loves us far too deeply to leave us untouched.
Maybe that is where this article has found you.
Perhaps vaping is not even the deepest issue.
Maybe underneath the nicotine there is anxiety.
Pain.
Stress.
Loneliness.
Trauma.
Boredom.
A need to belong.
A desperate craving for a few seconds of relief.
Maybe you are not simply craving vapor.
Maybe you are craving peace.
And perhaps that is why quitting has felt like losing a friend.
The vape was there after the breakup.
There after the argument.
There during the night shift.
There when nobody texted.
There when your thoughts would not stop.
There when you felt pressure building inside your chest and needed something.
And suddenly surrender feels frightening because God is not merely touching a habit.
He is touching the place where you learned to hide.
Please understand this carefully:
Jesus is not standing over the struggling believer with disgust.
He is calling you out of slavery.
There is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Conviction says, Bring this into the light.
Condemnation whispers, Hide from God until you become worthy of Him.
The Gospel destroys that lie.
You do not run away from Jesus because you are struggling.
You run to Jesus with the struggle.
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need impressive theology.
Maybe it sounds like:

“Jesus, I don't know whether I can let this go. Part of me doesn't even want to. But I don't want anything controlling me more than You. Show me what is true. Forgive what is sinful. Break what has mastered me. Heal whatever I have been medicating instead of surrendering. I belong to You.”
That is not weakness.
That is honesty.
And repentance begins in honesty.

If dependence is involved, do not confuse spiritual surrender with pretending withdrawal or addiction does not exist. Seeking appropriate medical help, evidence-based cessation support, accountability, and practical assistance is not evidence that you lack faith. God's ordinary providence can include doctors, counselors, pastors, mature believers, treatment, community, and wise plans.
You do not have to manufacture a dramatic overnight testimony to prove Jesus is working.
Sometimes freedom arrives like a prison door exploding open.
Sometimes freedom looks like getting up again tomorrow.
And again.
And again.
Grace does not make surrender unnecessary.
Grace makes surrender possible.
So—is vaping a sin?
Scripture does not explicitly name vaping, so Christians should resist claiming a direct biblical prohibition that is not there.
But Scripture gives us penetrating questions that refuse to let the issue remain superficial.
Is it mastering you?
Is it beneficial?
Can you do it with a clear conscience before Christ?
Can you genuinely do it for the glory of God?
Are you stewarding your body faithfully?
Is your use connected to dependence?
Are you using it as a refuge that has begun occupying territory in your heart that belongs to God?
And perhaps most personally:
If Jesus put His finger on this today and said, Give it to Me...
would you?
There it is.
Maybe that was the question beneath the question all along.
Not:
“How much am I allowed to keep?”
But:
“Jesus, is there anything I refuse to give You?”
Because Christianity eventually leads every disciple to an altar.
Pride goes there.
Lust goes there.
Bitterness goes there.
Secret addictions go there.
Our need for approval goes there.
Our excuses go there.
Our bodies go there.
Our future goes there.
And sometimes something as small as a vape sits in our hand while exposing something enormous inside our heart.
Be honest.
Someone reading your words may discover that they are not the only Christian fighting a battle nobody sees.

Invite your family, your Christian friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the unbeliever who has questions about Jesus to follow too. We want this community to remain a place of daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Christ.
Supporting Gospel work can be a meaningful way to glorify God when it is done freely, cheerfully, wisely, and from love—not from guilt or spiritual pressure.
You cannot buy grace.
You cannot purchase forgiveness.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
Support ministry because you love Christ and want truth to travel—not because anyone told you God would love you more if you did.
And tonight, when everything becomes quiet and there is nobody left to impress, perhaps place that familiar thing in your hand and ask one final question:
“Jesus... does this have me, or do You?”
Then listen.
Open His Word.
Tell Him the truth.
And if conviction comes, don't run from the Savior because of what He exposed.
Run toward Him.
Because the most unforgettable part of your story may not be the thing that once controlled you.
It may be the moment you finally opened your hand.
What you are afraid to surrender may be the very place where Christ is preparing to teach you what freedom feels like.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Did God Approve Polygamy—or Did He Regulate the Damage?
paragraphs: Did God Approve Polygamy—or Did He Regulate the Damage?

The Old Testament contains men with multiple wives—and even laws governing households where more than one wife existed. But describing a broken reality is not the same as calling it God's design. When Jesus was questioned about marriage, He did something breathtaking: He reached behind Moses, behind Israel's failures, behind centuries of human compromise, and took us back to Eden.
There is a question hiding in some of the most uncomfortable pages of the Bible.
If God opposed polygamy, why didn't He simply say, "No man shall ever have more than one wife"?
Why do Abraham, Jacob, David, Solomon, and other Old Testament men appear in stories involving multiple women?
Why does the Law of Moses contain instructions that seem to assume a man might have more than one wife?
And here is the question that can quietly shake someone's confidence in Scripture:
If God regulated polygamy, doesn't that mean He approved it?
Stay with that question.
Because the answer reveals something much bigger than an ancient marriage controversy.
It reveals how God deals with human hardness without surrendering His holiness.
It reveals the difference between what Scripture records, what biblical law regulates, and what God originally designed.
And eventually, Jesus Himself steps into the argument.
When He does, He takes us somewhere many people forget to look.
Back before Abraham.
Before Jacob.
Before David.
Before Solomon.
Before Moses.
Before Israel had accumulated centuries of complicated marriages and broken households.
Jesus takes us back to a garden.
But first, we have to walk through the uncomfortable text.
Deuteronomy 21:15 begins:
כִּֽי־תִהְיֶ֨יןָ לְאִ֜ישׁ שְׁתֵּ֣י נָשִׁ֗ים
Ki tihyena le'ish shtei nashim...
Literally, the sentence begins with a circumstance: "If a man has two wives..."
The Hebrew does not say, "A man should take two wives."
It does not command polygamy.
It addresses a situation in which two wives already exist.
The passage continues by imagining one wife being loved and the other being hated or unloved—אַהוּבָה, ahuvah, and שְׂנוּאָה, senu'ah—and then deals with the inheritance rights of the firstborn son.
The father is forbidden to manipulate the inheritance simply because he prefers one woman over another. The actual firstborn retains his legal right.
That distinction matters enormously.
The command is not:
"Take multiple wives."
The command is effectively:
"When this situation exists, you do not get to use favoritism to rob the vulnerable."
The law steps into an already fractured household and places a boundary around what the powerful man may do.
That is regulation.
It is not necessarily endorsement.
We understand this distinction instinctively elsewhere.
A government can regulate divorce without believing divorce is desirable.
A hospital can establish procedures for drug overdoses without approving drug abuse.
A nation can establish laws governing prisoners of war without endorsing war itself.
Rules governing what happens inside a broken circumstance do not automatically establish that circumstance as the ideal.
And that becomes especially important when we allow Scripture to interpret Scripture.
Exodus contains another uncomfortable example:
אִם־אַחֶרֶת יִֽקַּֽח־לוֹ שְׁאֵרָהּ כְּסוּתָהּ וְעֹנָתָהּ לֹא יִגְרָע
Im acheret yiqqach-lo, she'erah kesutah ve'onatah lo yigra.
"If he takes another..." he must not diminish the first woman's provisions, clothing, or marital rights.

Whatever questions modern readers have about the social world surrounding Exodus 21—and there are important questions—the direction of this particular command is unmistakable: the man is restrained from neglecting the woman already under his responsibility.
Again, notice where the pressure of the law falls.
On the powerful.
He does not get to say, "I found someone else, so you no longer matter."
He does not get to erase one woman's needs because another woman has captured his affection.
The legislation confronts human behavior as it exists and limits injustice within it.
And suddenly Deuteronomy 21 becomes painfully human.
One loved.
One unloved.
Children caught between them.
A father tempted to turn affection into favoritism.
An inheritance about to become another weapon in a wounded family.
Does that sound like a celebration of polygamy?
Or does it sound disturbingly like the consequences of it?
Look at the stories.
Abraham's household becomes torn by conflict involving Sarah and Hagar.
Jacob loves Rachel more than Leah, and the home becomes a battlefield of longing, jealousy, competition, children, barrenness, and desperation.
Hannah is provoked by Peninnah.
David's family becomes catastrophically fractured.
Then Solomon takes the multiplication of wives to an almost grotesque extreme, and Scripture does not present the result as spiritual flourishing.
Long before Solomon, Israel's king had already been warned:
וְלֹא יַרְבֶּה־לּוֹ נָשִׁים וְלֹא יָסוּר לְבָבוֹ
Velo yarbeh-lo nashim, velo yasur levavo.
He must not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away.
Then Solomon's life becomes almost a living commentary on that warning.
This is where we must learn one of the most important rules for reading the Bible:
Biblical biography is not automatically biblical endorsement.
Scripture tells the truth about its heroes.
Sometimes brutally.
Noah gets drunk.
Abraham lies about Sarah.
Jacob deceives.
Moses disobeys.
David commits adultery and arranges a man's death.
Peter denies Jesus.
Their presence in the Bible does not turn their failures into commandments.
In fact, one reason Scripture feels so painfully authentic is that it refuses to airbrush its people.
The Bible does not need its heroes to look clean because its ultimate Hero is not Abraham.
Not Jacob.
Not Moses.
Not David.
Not Solomon.
Jesus Christ is the Hero.
That changes everything.
Because if you ask only, "What did some Old Testament patriarchs do?" you can construct a very strange theology.
The better question is:
What pattern did God establish, what accommodations did fallen human society require, and where does the biblical story ultimately point?
And that trail leads straight back to Genesis.
Before there were two wives competing for one husband's affection, there was one man and one woman.
Genesis 2:24 describes the foundational union: a man leaves his father and mother, clings to his wife, and they become one flesh.
The Hebrew expression is unforgettable:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
Vehayu levasar echad.
"And they shall become one flesh."
Echad.
One.
A union.
A covenantal joining.
A new human kinship.
Genesis does not introduce marriage by presenting Adam surrounded by wives.

God creates the woman and brings her to the man, and the narrative moves toward the two becoming one flesh. Later Jewish interpretation likewise recognized Genesis 2:24 as describing an extraordinarily intimate union between husband and wife.
But perhaps someone could still say:
"That's Genesis. What does Jesus say?"
This is where the entire question turns.
When Jesus is confronted in Matthew 19 about divorce, He could have begun with the later legal regulations.
Instead, He reaches behind them.
He asks whether His hearers have read what the Creator did "from the beginning."
Then Jesus quotes Genesis.
And the surviving Greek text preserves something extremely significant:
καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
kai esontai hoi duo eis sarka mian
"And the two shall become one flesh."
Hoi duo.
The two.
Sarka mian.
One flesh.
Then comes Christ's conclusion: what God has joined together, human beings must not separate.
Jesus' argument is profound because He distinguishes between God's creational intention and legislation given in response to fallen human conditions.
Regarding divorce, He explicitly explains that Moses permitted something because of the hardness of human hearts, "but from the beginning it was not so."
That principle matters here.

We should be careful: Matthew 19 is directly answering a question about divorce, not giving a standalone lecture about every Old Testament instance of polygamy. We should not make Jesus say words He did not say.
But neither should we ignore the marriage pattern to which Jesus deliberately appeals.
When defining marriage's creational foundation, Christ does not point to Jacob's household.
He does not point to David's marriages.
He does not point to Solomon.
He points to creation.
Male and female.
The man joined to his wife.
The two becoming one flesh.
This is why the strongest biblical conclusion is not the simplistic statement that "God approved polygamy in the Old Testament."
A more careful conclusion is this:

The Old Testament recognizes polygamy as a real practice within the fallen societies it addresses and regulates injustices arising within such households, while the canonical trajectory—beginning with creation and clarified by Jesus—points us back toward the one-flesh marriage union established in Genesis.
Regulation is not identical to celebration.
Tolerance within fallen history is not identical to creation's ideal.
And description is not prescription.
That matters far beyond polygamy.
Because maybe you have been reading your own life the same way.
Maybe something has existed in your story for so long that you have started calling it normal.
A compromise.
A secret relationship.
Pornography nobody knows about.
Bitterness you have learned to live with.
A marriage that looks alive online but is dying behind closed doors.
An emotional affair you keep insisting isn't technically adultery.
A private addiction surrounded by Christian vocabulary.
A wound you have converted into permission to wound other people.
Maybe you have become very skilled at asking:
"How much will God tolerate?"
When the deeper question is:
"What did God create me for?"
That is where this ancient discussion suddenly becomes frighteningly personal.
We love loopholes.
Jesus loves truth.
We ask where the boundary is.
Jesus asks for the heart.
We ask whether our behavior can technically be defended.
Jesus keeps bringing us back to what God intended.
And if that exposes you, do not run.
Because Christianity does not end with exposure.
It begins there.
The same Jesus who speaks with uncompromising holiness moves toward sinners with astonishing mercy.
He does not redefine darkness as light so that we can feel comfortable.
He enters our darkness and calls us out of it.
That is the Gospel.
Repentance is not God standing over you saying, "Clean yourself up enough and perhaps I will love you."
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Christ who came for sinners.
The cross destroys two lies at once.
The first says:
"My sin isn't serious."
Look at Calvary.
It is.
The second says:
"My sin is too serious for grace."
Look at Calvary again.
It isn't.
Jesus Christ was crucified for sinners and rose again.
Forgiveness is not pretending sin never mattered.
Forgiveness cost blood.
Grace is not God's permission to remain unchanged.
Grace brings us home to the King who changes us.
That is why the scandalous families of Scripture do not embarrass the Gospel.
In a strange way, they prepare us to understand it.
God works through broken people without calling their brokenness good.
He keeps His promises through families full of jealousy, deception, sexual failure, favoritism, rivalry, grief, and sin.
Then from that bruised human history comes the Messiah.
Jesus.
The spotless One entering a bloodline full of people who desperately needed mercy.
That is our story too.
Not because scandal becomes righteousness.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He does not rewrite God's definition of holiness.
He rewrites the sinner's ending.
And perhaps that is the sentence someone reading this needs more than the debate itself.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
But you cannot receive transformation while clutching the very thing Christ is calling you to surrender.
Grace says, "Come."
Repentance says, "I'm coming."
Faith says, "Jesus, I cannot save myself."
And the Gospel says, "He already knew that. That is why He came."
You don't have to tell strangers every detail of your private life. But you can simply write "Jesus, bring me back to Your design" if that is genuinely your prayer.
And read the other comments too.
Sometimes the person confessing beneath you needs to discover that Christians are not a museum of people who never fell.
We are people who need a Savior.
Come back to the distinction between description, regulation, concession in a fallen world, creation, and Christ's appeal to "the beginning."
Salvation cannot be purchased, and God's grace is not merchandise.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical way of helping that work reach more people.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer who nearly gave up.
Invite the Christian who has been living on spiritual crumbs.
Invite the skeptic with difficult questions.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity is merely a collection of rules.
Let them encounter Christ.
Because ultimately the question is bigger than whether an ancient Israelite could have two wives.
The question is whether we will allow the failures Scripture records to become excuses for our own compromises—or whether we will follow Jesus all the way back to the heart of God.
The Law can meet human beings in the wreckage and restrain the damage.
The stories can show us what human sin actually does.
The prophets can warn us.
But Jesus does something more.
Jesus calls us home.
Home to truth.
Home to holiness.
Home to mercy.
Home to the God whose standards are higher than our excuses and whose grace reaches deeper than our shame.
And maybe that is why this ancient question still matters.
Because somewhere between what humanity normalized and what God originally intended, every one of us eventually has to decide which voice will define our lives.
God may meet you in the wreckage, but He loves you too much to call the wreckage Eden.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOUR PASTOR IS NOT YOUR MEDIATOR—JESUS IS
paragraphs: YOUR PASTOR IS NOT YOUR MEDIATOR—JESUS IS

The person behind the pulpit may shepherd you, teach you, correct you, pray with you, and point you toward God—but there is only One who can stand between a guilty sinner and a holy God. And His name is Jesus.
There is a dangerous moment that can happen inside a church without anyone noticing.
The music is beautiful.
The sermon is powerful.
The pastor is gifted.

You trust him. You respect him. Maybe his preaching helped pull you out of one of the darkest seasons of your life. Maybe he prayed for your marriage when it was collapsing. Maybe his words confronted an addiction nobody else knew about. Maybe God used his ministry to bring you back after years of wandering.
And slowly—almost invisibly—something shifts.
You stop merely appreciating the shepherd.
You begin depending on him for what only the Savior can give.
You feel close to God when your pastor notices you.
You feel forgotten by God when your pastor does not.
You need his approval before you feel spiritually secure.
You assume his prayers somehow reach heaven more effectively than yours.
When your conscience is crushed, your first instinct is not always to run to Christ but to find a spiritual person who can somehow make things right between you and God.
And perhaps the most revealing question is this:
If your pastor disappeared tomorrow, would your relationship with Jesus collapse with him?
That question may sting.
But sometimes the questions that hurt are the ones that expose where our trust has quietly moved.
Scripture gives us a sentence so simple that it destroys every attempt to place another human being in the position belonging exclusively to Christ:
“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.” — 1 Timothy 2:5, KJV
The Greek is even more striking:
εἷς γὰρ Θεός, εἷς καὶ μεσίτης Θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων, ἄνθρωπος Χριστὸς Ἰησοῦς
heis gar Theos, heis kai mesitēs Theou kai anthrōpōn, anthrōpos Christos Iēsous.
One God.
One Mediator.
The Greek word μεσίτης — mesitēs refers to a mediator, an intermediary, one who stands between parties in order to bring about reconciliation or establish a covenant relationship.
And Paul does not leave the identity of that Mediator open for speculation.
Χριστὸς Ἰησοῦς.
Christ Jesus.
Not your pastor.
Not your favorite preacher.
Not the Christian influencer whose videos you watch every morning.
Not the evangelist whose sermons make you cry.
Not the theologian whose books transformed your thinking.
Not the person who baptized you.
Not the person who discipled you.
Not even the most faithful spiritual leader you have ever known.
Jesus.
This does not dishonor faithful pastors.
It actually honors the biblical purpose of pastoral ministry.
Because a faithful pastor does not want to become the destination of your faith.
He wants to point beyond himself.
Paul described Christ as giving leaders—including pastors and teachers—“for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ” in Ephesians 4:11–12.
Pastors matter.
Teachers matter.
Elders matter.
Discipleship matters.
Spiritual accountability matters.
Hebrews 13:17 takes spiritual leadership seriously enough to command believers to respond appropriately to those who watch over their souls.
So this is not an article about despising pastors.
It is about refusing to make pastors carry a weight that Jesus never asked them to carry.
Your pastor can preach the cross.
He cannot become the cross.
Your pastor can tell you about the blood of Christ.
He cannot shed blood that removes your guilt.
Your pastor can remind you that forgiveness is available.
He cannot purchase your forgiveness.
Your pastor can pray beside your hospital bed.
He cannot conquer death for you.
Your pastor can counsel you after your failure.
He cannot bear the wrath your sin deserved.
Your pastor can shepherd you toward the throne.
But only Jesus opened the way to it.
That distinction changes everything.
Because some people have quietly built their entire Christianity around access to another Christian.
They know how to ask the pastor to pray.
They know how to request counseling.
They know how to sit in a service.
They know when to say amen.
They know how to appear spiritually healthy.
But alone at 2:13 in the morning, when there is no worship team, no microphone, no pastor, no church crowd, and no one left to impress…
they do not know how to come trembling to Jesus.
Maybe that is you.
Maybe there is something you have been hiding.
Something you did.
Something you keep doing.
Something you promised God you would never do again.
And then you did it again.
You know the cycle.
Temptation.
Compromise.
Guilt.
Promises.
A few good days.
Then another fall.
Eventually you begin wondering whether God is tired of hearing your apologies.
So you search for somebody “more spiritual” to pray for you because somewhere inside you is the fear that Jesus may listen to them more willingly than He listens to you.
But hear what Hebrews says about Christ:
“Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.” — Hebrews 7:25, KJV
Read that again.
He ever liveth to make intercession for them.
The Greek uses the verb ἐντυγχάνειν — entynchanein, carrying the sense here of interceding or appealing on behalf of another.
Your hope does not ultimately rest in finding a human being holy enough to convince Jesus to care about you.
Jesus Himself intercedes.
The crucified and risen Christ is not reluctant to receive repentant sinners.
He is their Mediator.
And this is where the Gospel becomes almost unbearably beautiful.
Because Jesus does not mediate between God and humanity as a detached negotiator.
He gave Himself.
The very next verse after Paul identifies the “one mediator” says Christ Jesus “gave himself a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:6).
The Mediator became the sacrifice.
The One standing between holy God and sinful humanity did not merely deliver a message.
He delivered Himself.
This is why Christianity is not fundamentally about finding the right religious professional who can get you closer to God.
It is about God coming near to sinners in Jesus Christ.
Think about what happened when Christ died.
Matthew records that the veil of the temple was torn “in twain from the top to the bottom” (Matthew 27:51).
That direction matters.
From top to bottom.
God was not waiting for humanity to climb high enough.
Christ had opened the way.
Hebrews 10:19–22 therefore speaks of believers having boldness to enter through the blood of Jesus and urges them to “draw near.”
Draw near.
Not because you finally became impressive.
Not because your pastor knows your name.
Not because you belong to the perfect church.
Not because you accumulated enough good behavior to cancel the things you regret.
Draw near because of Jesus.
Maybe religion taught you to hide when you were dirty.
The Gospel tells repentant sinners where to run when they are dirty.
To Christ.
Maybe shame told you, “Stay away until you fix yourself.”
Jesus says the sick need a physician.
Maybe your failures have been whispering, “There is no way back after what you did.”
The cross answers, “It is finished.”
The Gospel does not say your sin is insignificant.
It says your sin was so serious that Christ died—and His grace is so astonishing that the Son of God willingly came to save sinners.
That is the scandal.
Holy God.
Guilty humanity.
And between them stands not our résumé, our church attendance, our pastor, our religious performance, or our reputation.
There stands a crucified Savior.
Jesus Christ.
This is why placing a pastor in the role of mediator is dangerous even when the pastor himself never asks for it.
Eventually, every human shepherd will disappoint you.
Some will misunderstand you.
Some will make mistakes.
Some will preach a sermon you disagree with.
Some will fail to notice your pain.
Some may leave a ministry.
Some may fall seriously into sin and require biblical accountability and discipline.
And when people have confused their pastor with their Mediator, a pastor's failure can feel like God's failure.
But Jesus is not your pastor's character flaw.
Jesus is not your pastor's bad decision.
Jesus is not your church hurt.
Jesus is not the hypocrisy somebody committed while carrying His name.
Human shepherds can fail.
The Good Shepherd remains faithful.
This matters deeply for people carrying church wounds.
You may have been hurt by somebody who preached Scripture.
You may have trusted someone who abused that trust.
You may have watched religious hypocrisy destroy something inside you.
And perhaps you walked away thinking:
“If that is Christianity, I want nothing to do with it.”
But before you walk away from Jesus because somebody representing Him represented Him badly, look at Jesus Himself.
Do not measure Christ by the worst behavior of someone who claimed His name.
Measure Christians by Christ.
The answer to pastoral idolatry is not pastoral hatred.
The answer to spiritual abuse is not pretending biblical spiritual authority does not exist.
The answer is putting every human authority underneath the authority of Jesus Christ and His Word.
A faithful pastor should be able to say, in the spirit of Paul's words in 1 Corinthians 11:1, follow me as I follow Christ.
Christ remains the standard.
Christ remains the center.
Christ remains the Head of His church.
Christ remains the Savior.
Christ remains the Mediator.
That also means you do not need celebrity access to have heavenly access.
Perhaps nobody important knows your name.
Maybe you will never sit at the table with a famous preacher.
Maybe your comment will never receive a response.
Maybe nobody will invite you onto a stage.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, obscurity on earth does not mean obscurity in heaven.
You can pray.
You can repent.
You can confess your sins to God.
You can open Scripture.
You can cry before Christ when nobody else knows you are crying.
You can whisper His name from a hospital room.
From a prison cell.
From a broken marriage.
From a bedroom where addiction has beaten you again.
From a car parked outside your house because you are afraid to walk inside and face what your choices have done.
You can come to Jesus.
Not casually.
Not arrogantly.
Not because sin does not matter.
But because the blood of Christ does.
And maybe that is what somebody reading this needs tonight.
Not another performance.
Not another religious mask.
Not another week pretending everything is fine.
Jesus.
If there is hidden sin, bring it into His light.
If repentance is necessary, repent.
If you have harmed someone, pursue biblical reconciliation where appropriate.
If you need wise pastoral counsel, seek it.
If you need mature believers around you, do not isolate yourself.
Christianity was never designed as solitary spirituality.
But understand the difference:
Christian community accompanies you to Christ.
It does not replace Christ.
Pastors shepherd you toward Christ.
They do not replace Christ.
Teachers explain the Word of Christ.
They do not replace Christ.
Brothers and sisters pray with you.
They do not replace Christ.
There is one Mediator.
And if this exposed the uncomfortable possibility that you have depended more on spiritual personalities than on the Savior Himself, do not hide behind embarrassment.
Bring even that to Jesus.
Somebody else may need evidence tonight that losing confidence in a person does not require losing confidence in Jesus.
Then think of one person who needs this truth.
Not fifty random people.
One.
The friend who stopped attending church because a leader wounded them.
The believer who has become spiritually dependent on a personality.
The exhausted pastor who secretly feels pressured to become everything for everyone.
The person who thinks they are too filthy to approach God.
Send this privately if that would be wiser.
Because there may come a day when someone you admire disappoints you, and on that day you may need this reminder again:
Your pastor was never your foundation.
Jesus is.
Your pastor was never your Savior.
Jesus is.
Your pastor was never your Mediator.
Jesus is.
The purpose is not to build devotion to a personality. It is to keep pointing people toward biblical truth, repentance, grace, healing, discipleship, and the Lord Jesus Christ.
We will never put a price tag on access to Jesus.
Leave thinking about Jesus.
The One who knew your scandal before anyone else knew.
The One who saw the chapter you desperately wanted erased.
The One who did not excuse your sin but carried sin's judgment at Calvary.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who still receives repentant sinners.
The One who intercedes.
The One who saves.
The One who remains when heroes fall, crowds disappear, churches disappoint, feelings fade, and your own strength finally runs out.
Your pastor may point you toward the door.
But Jesus is the reason the door is open.
And perhaps that is the sentence you should carry with you tonight:
When every human voice goes silent, the blood of Jesus is still speaking a better word over every sinner who comes to God through Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Can Christians Joke About Sex? The Laugh That May Be Revealing More Than You Think
paragraphs: Can Christians Joke About Sex? The Laugh That May Be Revealing More Than You Think
Some jokes disappear in seconds. Others quietly teach your heart to laugh at what Jesus died to redeem.
Everybody laughed.
You did too.
Maybe it happened at work. Maybe inside a group chat. Maybe around friends who knew exactly how far they could push the conversation before somebody said, “Okay, okay… that’s too much.”
Someone made the joke.
There was a pause.
Then the room exploded.
And you laughed.
Not because you had planned to dishonor God. Not because you woke up that morning thinking, Today I want to become sexually impure.
It was just funny.
At least, that is what you told yourself.
“It’s only a joke.”
Four words.
Four incredibly convenient words.
Because once something becomes “just a joke,” we sometimes act as though morality has temporarily left the room.
But has it?
Can Christians joke about sex?
The answer requires more care than either extreme usually gives it.
Because one Christian may respond, “Absolutely not. Christians shouldn’t joke about anything sexual.”
Another may shrug and say, “God has a sense of humor. Stop being so religious.”
Neither statement, by itself, settles the biblical question.
Scripture never commands Christians to become humorless people.

The Bible contains irony, satire, wordplay, celebration, joy, feasting, marriage, romance, and laughter. Ecclesiastes says there is “a time to laugh.” Proverbs even describes a joyful heart as good medicine.
And sex itself is not dirty.
That needs to be said clearly.
God created human sexuality.

Before pornography existed, before adultery existed, before lust corrupted desire, before humanity learned to exploit bodies for pleasure, God created male and female and established marriage. Genesis presents marital union without embarrassment. Song of Songs celebrates marital desire with remarkable tenderness and intensity.
Christian holiness is not the belief that bodies are disgusting or that sexuality is shameful.
The biblical story is far more beautiful than that.
Sex is not dirty because God designed it.
Sin is what distorts it.
And that distinction changes the entire conversation.
The real question is therefore not simply, “Did the joke mention sex?”
The deeper question is:
What did the joke make of sex, another person, and the holiness of God?
Paul gives us language for answering that question.

Writing to believers in Ephesus, he places sexual conduct and speech remarkably close together. He warns against sexual immorality, impurity, and greed, and then turns almost immediately toward what comes out of the mouth:
“Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks.”
That is Ephesians 5:4 in the public-domain King James Version.
But underneath the English translation sits something revealing.
Paul writes:
αἰσχρότης … μωρολογία … εὐτραπελία
aischrotēs … mōrologia … eutrapelia.

The terms point toward shameful or obscene speech, foolish talk, and inappropriate jesting. The last word, εὐτραπελία — eutrapelia, is especially important because it could carry the idea of quick, clever wit, yet in this context takes the negative sense of low, vulgar, or ribald joking.
Paul is not issuing a divine prohibition against being funny.
He is confronting humor that has been bent toward impurity.
That difference matters.
Because you can be hilarious without being filthy.
You can make people laugh without turning someone’s body into entertainment.
You can enjoy marriage without mocking its intimacy.
You can acknowledge sexuality without sexualizing every conversation.
You can possess wit without allowing lust to borrow your microphone.
And perhaps that is where this gets uncomfortable.
Because sometimes we call something humor when humor is only the delivery system.
The real content is lust.
Or objectification.
Or humiliation.
Or fantasy.
Or rebellion.
Or curiosity about darkness.
And because everybody laughed, nobody examined it.
Imagine someone placing poison inside candy.
The sweetness would not change what was inside.
Humor can work similarly. A laugh can lower defenses. Something we would immediately reject if stated seriously can enter our imagination when delivered as a punchline.
That does not mean every questionable joke permanently corrupts somebody. Scripture does not give us permission to manufacture exaggerated claims.
But Scripture repeatedly treats speech as spiritually significant.
Jesus taught that words reveal something about the abundance of the heart.
Paul told believers that corrupting speech should give way to words that build others up.
James compared the tongue to a small fire capable of enormous consequences.
Words matter because hearts matter.
And sometimes what repeatedly makes us laugh reveals what we have slowly stopped grieving.
That sentence may sting.
Stay with it.
There was probably a time when something bothered your conscience more than it does now.
The first explicit joke felt uncomfortable.
Then another came.
Then another.
Eventually you learned when to laugh.
Then you learned how to contribute.
Then you became the person who could make everybody else laugh.
And somewhere between discomfort and applause, the boundary moved.
Not necessarily overnight.
Usually holiness does not disappear that dramatically.
Sometimes compromise arrives laughing.
That is why Scripture's treatment of sexual sin is so radically different from our culture's casual treatment of it.
In 1 Corinthians 6:18, Paul writes:
φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Φεύγετε — pheugete is an imperative: flee.
Run.
Do not negotiate with it.
Do not see how close you can stand to the edge while technically remaining innocent.
Paul's concern is not that sexuality itself is evil. His argument is precisely the opposite: the believer's body belongs to the Lord and is a temple of the Holy Spirit.
Your body has dignity.
The bodies of other people have dignity.
Sex has dignity within God's design.
And therefore reducing something God gave profound covenantal meaning into disposable entertainment deserves more serious thought than, “Relax. It was funny.”
Here is a question worth sitting with:
Could I tell this joke if Jesus were visibly sitting beside me?
Before you answer too quickly, remember something.
For the Christian, Christ does not need to become visibly present before His presence matters.
That changes the room.
That changes the group chat.
That changes the comment section.
That changes what you send privately.
That changes what you watch when nobody knows.
And it changes the joke you are about to tell.
But now we need to protect this conversation from another mistake.
Someone may read this and conclude that Christians can never make playful references to marital intimacy.
That goes beyond what Scripture says.

A husband and wife can enjoy playful affection. Mature believers can discuss sexuality appropriately. Parents can teach children about bodies without shame. Pastors can preach biblical sexual ethics without pretending sex does not exist. Married couples can laugh together about the awkward, ordinary realities of marriage.
Context matters.
Intent matters.
Content matters.
The people listening matter.
What Scripture does not permit us to do is baptize obscenity simply because we found it funny.
There is a difference between humor about the human experience of sexuality and humor that feeds sexual impurity.
There is a difference between marital playfulness and public vulgarity.
There is a difference between acknowledging sex and exploiting it.
There is a difference between laughing about an awkward married-life moment and making someone's breasts, genitals, sexual performance, sexual history, or private intimacy the entertainment.
There is a difference between laughter that strengthens affection and laughter that trains people to objectify.
Wisdom asks more than:
“Is this technically allowed?”
Wisdom asks:
“What is this doing to my heart?”
And perhaps even more importantly:
“What is this doing to theirs?”
Because the person laughing beside you has a story you cannot see.
Maybe he is fighting pornography.
Maybe she survived sexual exploitation.
Maybe that teenager is quietly learning what adults believe sex is supposed to be.
Maybe the married person across the table is already tempted toward adultery.
Maybe the single Christian in the group is desperately trying to rebuild boundaries after years of sexual compromise.
You do not know every battle sitting around the table.
Christian liberty never means Christian indifference.
Love notices people.
Love does not merely ask, “Can I say it?”
Love asks, “Will saying it help me love this person as someone made in the image of God?”
And then Paul does something beautiful in Ephesians 5:4.
He does not merely say what should disappear from Christian speech.
He tells us what should replace it.
εὐχαριστία — eucharistia.
Thanksgiving.
Think about that contrast.
Crude joking reduces.
Thanksgiving recognizes.
Lust looks at another person and says, “What pleasure could I get from you?”
Gratitude looks at God's creation and says, “What dignity has God placed here?”
Pornography consumes.
Gratitude receives.
Objectification takes.
Gratitude honors.
The Gospel does not merely tell the filthy mouth to shut up.
Jesus gives the heart a new song.
And this is where the story becomes much bigger than dirty jokes.
Because perhaps your jokes are not really your deepest problem.
Perhaps they are smoke.
And somewhere beneath the smoke there is a fire.
Maybe nobody knows what you watch.
Maybe nobody knows what you imagine.
Maybe nobody knows the conversations you delete.
Maybe nobody knows how different your private humor is from your Sunday worship.
You know the worship songs.
You know when to raise your hands.
You know the Bible verses.
You know how to say, “God is good.”
But your hidden life feels like another person.
And now shame whispers:
If people really knew you, they would never look at you the same way.
Maybe they would not.
But Jesus already knows.
Every search.
Every fantasy.
Every joke.
Every message.
Every compromise.
Every time conviction came and you pushed it down.
He knows.
And He still calls sinners to come.
This is where Christianity becomes scandalous in the most beautiful way.
Jesus did not come because respectable people had successfully cleaned themselves.
He came for sinners.
At the cross, Christ carried sin's judgment. He rose from the dead. And now the Gospel does not say, “Hide better.”
It says:
Repent and come home.
Repentance is not pretending the joke was never funny.
Repentance is recognizing that something can make your flesh laugh while grieving the God who loves you.
Repentance says:
“Jesus, I have normalized what You call unclean.”
“I have used humor to excuse lust.”
“I have laughed when I should have walked away.”
“I have treated bodies made in Your image as punchlines.”
“I have hidden behind everybody does it.”
“Forgive me.”
And grace answers the repentant sinner not with permission to remain enslaved, but with power to become new.
That is why Romans 8:1 is so precious: there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
No condemnation does not mean no transformation.
Grace does not tell you that sin does not matter.
Grace tells you sin does not get the final word.
Jesus does.
Maybe you have told hundreds of jokes you wish you could take back.
Jesus is still able to redeem your tongue.
Maybe pornography shaped your sense of humor for years.
Jesus is still able to renew your mind.
Maybe vulgarity became part of your personality because being funny made people accept you.
Jesus is still able to show you an identity deeper than applause.
Maybe you crossed sexual boundaries far beyond joking.
Hear this carefully:
Your story does not have to end where your sin took you.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is cleansing in Christ.
There is a new life through the Spirit.
There is repentance.
There is restoration.
There is grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So the next time somebody makes that joke and everyone looks at you waiting for the laugh, you do not need to become self-righteous.
You do not need to lecture the room.
You do not need to act spiritually superior.
Maybe you simply refuse to feed it.
Maybe you redirect the conversation.
Maybe you become the person who proves Christians can possess extraordinary joy without borrowing vulgarity to manufacture laughter.
And when you fail?
Do not hide.
Run toward Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive mercy.
Get back up.
Follow Him again.
Holiness is not a performance by people who never struggled.
It is the fruit of belonging to a Savior who refuses to leave His people unchanged.
So, can Christians joke about sex?
Scripture gives us something wiser than a simplistic slogan.

Sex itself is God's creation and is not inherently shameful. Appropriate humor is not forbidden. But obscenity, foolish speech, sexually degrading humor, vulgar innuendo, and joking that turns impurity into entertainment do not fit the life to which Christ calls His people.
The question is not merely whether somebody laughed.
The question is whether Christ was honored.
Be honest.
There is no prize here for pretending.
We need Christian communities where confession leads people toward Christ rather than deeper into hiding.
But whatever you do after reading this, remember the deeper invitation.
Do not merely clean up your jokes.
Give Jesus your heart.
Because one day you may discover that the joke you stopped laughing at was not evidence that you had lost your sense of humor.
It was evidence that Christ was teaching your heart to love what is holy again.
Somewhere between the laughter and the silence, Jesus may be asking for the part of your heart you thought nobody could see.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN EXERCISE REDUCE SEXUAL TEMPTATION? THE ANSWER IS MORE SPIRITUAL THAN YOU THINK
paragraphs: CAN EXERCISE REDUCE SEXUAL TEMPTATION? THE ANSWER IS MORE SPIRITUAL THAN YOU THINK
You can exhaust your body and still carry lust into bed. But what happens when physical discipline becomes part of a much deeper surrender to Christ?
It is 11:47 at night.
You already know what is about to happen.
Not because anyone else is in the room.
Because no one is.
The house is quiet. The lights are low. Your phone is close enough to reach without getting out of bed.
And suddenly that familiar battle begins.
Maybe for you it is pornography.
Maybe it is fantasizing about someone who is not your spouse.
Maybe it is scrolling through images you know awaken something you should not feed.
Maybe it is a conversation that became flirtation, and flirtation became secrecy.
Maybe nobody knows.
You pray.
You promise God this is the last time.
You delete something.
Then reinstall it.
You resist for several days.
Then loneliness comes.
Stress comes.
Boredom comes.
Rejection comes.
Exhaustion comes.
And the temptation that seemed dead suddenly starts breathing again.
So someone gives you practical advice:
“Go exercise.”
And strangely enough, sometimes it helps.
You run.
You lift.
You walk until your breathing changes.
You come home physically tired, mentally clearer, and the temptation that felt enormous an hour earlier seems quieter.
So you begin wondering:
Can exercise actually reduce sexual temptation?
The answer is more complicated—and more spiritually important—than a simple yes.

Exercise may help you manage some of the circumstances in which temptation becomes powerful. It can provide structure, redirect restless energy, interrupt an unhealthy routine, improve mood, and remove you physically from an environment where you normally fall.
But exercise cannot crucify lust.
A treadmill cannot regenerate a heart.
A barbell cannot forgive sin.
Sweat cannot wash a conscience clean.
And there is another important truth Christians need to hear: exercise should not be marketed as though science has proven that working out simply switches off sexual desire.

In fact, research examining physical activity and sexual health frequently associates exercise with better sexual function, not the destruction of sexuality. Reviews have reported beneficial relationships between physical activity and aspects of sexual function in both men and women.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because Christianity does not teach that sexual desire itself is dirty.
God created sexuality.
Sin distorts it.
There is a difference.
The goal of Christian purity is not becoming incapable of sexual desire. The goal is learning, through the grace and power of God, to bring our desires under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
And Jesus takes that battle far deeper than behavior.
He says in Matthew 5:28:
ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν…
A central word is ἐπιθυμῆσαι — epithymēsai, from epithymeō.
It carries the sense of setting one's desire upon something, longing for it, coveting it, lusting after it.
Jesus continues that the person who looks at a woman πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν—with the purpose of lusting after her—has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
Jesus takes the battle into the hidden room.
The heart.
That place nobody sees when you smile at church.
That place nobody sees when you post the Bible verse.
That place nobody sees when you tell everyone, “I'm doing fine.”
Jesus sees it.
And remarkably, He does not expose it because He enjoys humiliating you.
He exposes what enslaves you because He intends to free you.
That is where exercise finds its proper place.
Not as Savior.
As stewardship.
Your body matters to God.
Paul tells Timothy that bodily training has value, while godliness has value in every way.
Notice that Scripture does not say physical training is worthless.
It simply refuses to make it ultimate.
And that means going for a run instead of lying alone with your phone may sometimes be an excellent decision.
Taking a long walk when your mind begins spiraling may be wise.
Going to the gym after work instead of returning immediately to the environment where you habitually fall may interrupt a destructive pattern.
Joining a sports community may reduce isolation.
Developing disciplined sleeping, eating, working, praying, and exercising rhythms may make your life less vulnerable to the chaos in which old habits often flourish.
There is nothing unspiritual about using your legs to get away from temptation.
In fact, Paul uses remarkably physical language concerning sexual immorality.
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
That first word matters.
Φεύγετε — pheugete.
Flee.
Run away.
Escape.
Shun.
Paul does not say:
“Stand there and prove how spiritually strong you are.”
He says:
Run.
Sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do is leave.
Close the laptop.
Put the phone outside the bedroom.
Get out of the apartment.
Walk around the block.
Call somebody.
Go somewhere public.
Start doing something constructive.
Remove yourself from the opportunity.
Run if necessary.
Not because running saves you.
Because wisdom does not negotiate with what God told you to flee.
Joseph understood that long before Paul wrote Corinthians.
Potiphar's wife repeatedly attempted to seduce him.
Joseph did not remain in the room conducting an extended theological debate with temptation.
When she grabbed his garment and demanded that he lie with her, Genesis 39 tells us that Joseph left the garment and fled outside.
Sometimes victory looks remarkably undignified.
Sometimes victory is leaving your coat behind.
Sometimes victory is blocking the number.
Sometimes victory is deleting the secret account.
Sometimes victory is handing someone else the password.
Sometimes victory is getting out of bed and walking.
Sometimes victory is saying:
“I know where this thought goes, and I'm not following it tonight.”
But here is where things become uncomfortable.
You can run five kilometers and still love lust.
You can build an impressive body while secretly feeding an undisciplined heart.
You can become physically exhausted and remain spiritually hungry for the wrong things.
Because sexual temptation is not merely stored energy waiting to be burned off.
Human desire is more complicated than that.
Sometimes lust is connected to loneliness.
Sometimes pornography becomes anesthesia for anxiety.
Sometimes fantasy becomes an escape from disappointment.
Sometimes sexual attention becomes proof that you still feel desirable.
Sometimes masturbation becomes an automatic response to stress or boredom.
Sometimes temptation arrives after conflict with your spouse.
Sometimes it comes when you feel rejected.
Sometimes it comes when you feel successful and entitled.
Sometimes it comes because you have trained your brain through repetition to expect sexual stimulation whenever you feel uncomfortable.
And sometimes temptation comes simply because fallen human beings still battle sinful desires.
Exercise may change the environment.
But only Christ can transform the person living inside it.
That is why Christianity offers something far greater than behavior modification.
The Gospel does not merely say:
“Try harder.”
It says:
You need a new heart.
And this is precisely why some Christians remain trapped for years.
They keep making promises to God from the strength of the flesh.
“I'll never do it again.”
Then they fall.
Then shame arrives.
Then they hide.
Then they pray.
Then they make another promise.
Then they fall again.
Eventually they begin believing something terrifying:
“Maybe this is just who I am.”
No.
Your sin may describe something you have done repeatedly.
It does not have the authority to define who Jesus can make you.
Paul wrote to believers in Corinth about people whose histories included serious sexual sin and then said something breathtaking:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Past tense.
Then:
“You were washed.”
“You were sanctified.”
“You were justified.”
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God.
Do you see the Gospel?
Not:
“Clean yourself so Jesus might accept you.”
But:
“Come to Jesus because you cannot clean yourself.”
The cross is where pretending ends.
Christ did not die for the polished version of you.
He died for sinners.
The version with browser history.
The version with secrets.
The version who promised God twenty times.
The version who feels disgusting afterward.
The version afraid someone will discover everything.
Jesus already knows.
And still the invitation of the Gospel remains:
Repent.
Come into the light.
Receive mercy.
Follow Him.
Repentance is not merely feeling horrible after sin.
It is a turning.
A change of direction.
And sometimes genuine repentance becomes extremely practical.
If your phone repeatedly becomes the doorway, change how you use your phone.
If midnight is when you fall, stop treating midnight like neutral territory.
If loneliness is your trigger, build Christian community before loneliness becomes desperation.
If certain social-media accounts awaken lust, unfollow them.
If private browsing is where your integrity dies, remove the secrecy.
If you keep falling alone, tell a mature, trustworthy Christian.
Bring darkness into light.
And yes—
exercise.
Train your body.
Walk.
Run.
Lift.
Swim.
Play basketball.
Move.
Build discipline.
Sleep properly.
Use the body God gave you in healthy ways.
But while you train your body, train your soul toward godliness.
Pray while walking.
Memorize Scripture.
Fill your mind with what is true, honorable, just, pure, lovely, commendable, excellent, and worthy of praise.
Learn to recognize the first five seconds of temptation instead of waiting until minute twenty-five.
And stop asking only:
“How close can I get without technically sinning?”
Ask instead:
“How can I honor Christ with my body today?”
That question changes everything.
Because Christian purity is not ultimately about becoming terrified of sexuality.
It is about discovering that Jesus is worthy of every room in your life—including the room you have kept locked.
Your sexuality belongs under His lordship.
Your imagination belongs under His lordship.
Your eyes belong under His lordship.
Your phone belongs under His lordship.
Your gym routine belongs under His lordship.
Your loneliness belongs under His lordship.
Your wounds belong under His lordship.
Your body belongs under His lordship.
And when you fail?
Do not turn failure into permission to continue.
Run toward Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Get back into the fight.
Grace is not God's permission to remain enslaved.
Grace is God's undeserved kindness toward sinners, and the same grace that forgives also teaches us to renounce ungodliness.
Maybe somebody reading this fell last night.
Maybe ten minutes ago.
Maybe you opened this article because the title sounded practical, but somewhere along the way God put His finger on something much deeper.
You thought you needed a better workout.
Maybe you need surrender.
You thought your greatest problem was sexual tension.
Maybe your deeper problem is the secret agreement you have made with temptation:
“I'll resist you publicly, but I'll keep a small doorway open privately.”
Close it.
Not tomorrow.
Now.
You do not need to punish yourself before coming to Jesus.
You need to repent and come.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is cleansing at the cross.
There is no sin you can make respectable enough to avoid needing the cross, and no repentant sinner so filthy that the blood of Christ is insufficient.
Exercise can become one weapon in a wise strategy.
Accountability can become another.
Boundaries can become another.
Removing access can become another.
Prayer.
Scripture.
Christian fellowship.
Confession.
Fasting.
Service.
Healthy sleep.
Purposeful work.
All of these can have their place.
But never confuse the weapons with the Warrior who saves you.
Jesus Christ is not another technique in your purity plan.
He is Lord.
And freedom begins when the goal stops being merely, “How do I stop feeling tempted?”
and becomes:
“Jesus, how do I belong completely to You?”
Because temptation may still knock.
There may be difficult nights.
There may be moments when your body screams one thing while obedience requires another.
But every act of obedience says something.
Jesus is better.
Better than the image.
Better than the fantasy.
Better than the secret conversation.
Better than those few minutes of pleasure followed by emptiness.
Better than hiding.
Better than pretending.
Better than slavery.
And perhaps tonight, when temptation comes, you should put on your shoes and run.
But don't merely run from something.
Run to Someone.
Run from secrecy toward light.
Run from isolation toward Christian community.
Run from fantasy toward truth.
Run from self-condemnation toward repentance.
Run from slavery toward Christ.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to describe your private sin publicly. But you can take one small step out of isolation.
Someone reading your comment may realize they are not fighting alone.
Send this privately to the person you know is struggling.
We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives surrendered to Him.
Because perhaps the person who shares this article will never know whose midnight battle it interrupted.
Perhaps you will never know whose browser closed.
Whose secret conversation ended.
Whose knees finally touched the floor.
Whose confession finally came out.
Whose shame finally met the Gospel.
But heaven has always been able to do extraordinary things with ordinary acts of obedience.
So yes.
Put on your running shoes.
Train your body.
Build discipline.
Flee what Scripture tells you to flee.
But never believe sweat can accomplish what only blood could accomplish.
You can outrun an opportunity to sin for an evening—but only Jesus can lead your heart out of slavery and teach it where home really is.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HOW HEAVY WAS GOLIATH’S ARMOR? THE ANSWER MAKES DAVID’S FAITH EVEN MORE TERRIFYING
paragraphs: HOW HEAVY WAS GOLIATH’S ARMOR? THE ANSWER MAKES DAVID’S FAITH EVEN MORE TERRIFYING
He walked into the valley covered in thousands of shekels of bronze. David walked in carrying something Goliath could never manufacture, wear, or intimidate—the name of the living God.
Before David ever picked up a stone, Israel had already lost the battle in their minds.
For forty days, a man walked into the valley and talked.
That was all it took.
He talked…and warriors trembled.
He shouted…and an army backed away.
He appeared…and men who had swords, shields, military training, and a king suddenly remembered every reason they could lose.
His name was Goliath.
And when Scripture introduces him, it does something fascinating.
It doesn't immediately rush to David.
It makes you look at the giant.
Look at his helmet.
Look at his armor.
Look at his weapons.
Feel the weight of what is coming against Israel.
Because if you don't understand how terrifying Goliath looked, you may never appreciate how outrageous David's faith sounded.
First Samuel 17:5 preserves this extraordinary description in Hebrew:
“וְכוֹבַע נְחֹשֶׁת עַל־רֹאשׁוֹ וְשִׁרְיוֹן קַשְׂקַשִּׂים הוּא לָבוּשׁ וּמִשְׁקַל הַשִּׁרְיוֹן חֲמֵשֶׁת־אֲלָפִים שְׁקָלִים נְחֹשֶׁת”
Ve-khova nechoshet al-rosho, ve-shiryon qasqassim hu lavush; u-mishqal ha-shiryon, chameshet-alafim sheqalim nechoshet.
In context, the verse says that Goliath wore a bronze helmet and a shiryon qasqassim—armor described with a word connected with “scales”—and that the armor weighed five thousand shekels of bronze.
Five thousand.
Don't race past that number.

An ancient shekel was a unit of weight, not merely the modern currency that the word may bring to mind today. The precise conversion should be stated with humility because ancient weight standards were not perfectly uniform across every period and place. Archaeological discussions of the royal Hebrew shekel place it around 11.3 grams.
Using approximately 11.3 grams as a reasonable comparison, five thousand shekels would be about 56.5 kilograms—roughly 125 pounds.
And that is the stated weight of the armor in verse 5, not a biblical statement of the combined weight of every piece of equipment Goliath carried.
Around 125 pounds.
Imagine it.
Before this man even swings his spear, before he says a word, before he takes a step toward David…
he is carrying roughly the weight of another human being on his torso.
Then Scripture keeps going.

Bronze greaves covered his legs. A bronze weapon was carried between or upon his shoulders. The shaft of his spear was compared to a weaver's beam. And the iron head of that spear alone weighed six hundred shekels.
Using the same approximate standard merely for perspective, that spearhead could have been around 6.8 kilograms—approximately 15 pounds.
The spearhead.
Not necessarily the whole spear.
This was not the Bible describing a slightly larger-than-average bully.
The narrator is constructing an image of overwhelming military power.
Bronze.
Iron.
Armor.
Weapons.
A shield-bearer.
Experience.
Size.
Reputation.
Everything visible said the same thing:
You cannot beat this man.
And maybe that is where this story stops being ancient history and starts walking into your life.
Because some giants don't stand in valleys.
Some sit beside you at 2:13 in the morning.
Some live inside memories you cannot erase.
Some appear when the house becomes quiet.
Some wear the face of debt.
Some sound like a doctor's report.
Some have the voice of addiction.
Some carry the name of shame.
Some are buried underneath church clothes, smiling photographs, worship songs, and the answer, “I'm doing fine.”
And some giants have been talking to you for years.
“You'll never change.”
“God is tired of you.”
“You've failed too many times.”
“You'll go back to the same sin.”
“Your marriage is finished.”
“Your children are too far gone.”
“You ruined everything.”
“You're too dirty for God.”
“You prayed before. Nothing happened.”
“You call yourself a Christian after what you did?”
And every day you listen, the giant seems to get heavier.
That is what fear does.
Fear measures the armor.
Faith remembers the God standing behind the promise.
But we need to be careful here, because David and Goliath is often reduced to a motivational slogan Scripture never intended to teach.
“You are David. Your problems are Goliath. Believe in yourself and kill your giants.”
That is too small.
David did not walk into the valley believing in David.
David walked into the valley believing in YHWH.
That changes everything.
Listen to David's own words in 1 Samuel 17:45:
“You come to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a javelin; but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts…”
There is the center of the story.
Not the sling.
Not the stone.
Not David's confidence.
God.
Goliath's confidence was wrapped around his body.
David's confidence was anchored beyond himself.
Goliath could point to what he carried.
David could point to the One who carried him.
And there is a devastating spiritual lesson hiding there.
You can have armor and still be exposed.
You can have strength and still be helpless.
You can have reputation and still be defeated.
You can look invincible in front of people while standing completely powerless before God.
Goliath's armor may have weighed approximately 125 pounds, but there was something infinitely heavier resting upon that valley:
the glory of God.
David understood what Saul's frightened army had forgotten.
Goliath had not merely challenged Israel.
He had defied the living God.
That is why David's language is so God-centered. In verse 46, David says that the outcome will cause the earth to know that there is a God in Israel. Then verse 47 drives the truth home:
“The battle is the LORD's.”
There it is.
Not “David is amazing.”
Not “Believe hard enough and you'll always win.”
Not “Christians never lose earthly battles.”
Not “Faith guarantees the outcome you want.”
The battle belongs to the Lord.
Biblical faith is not confidence that God must obey our preferred outcome.
Biblical faith is confidence that God remains God regardless of the outcome.
And Christians can see something even greater when we read David's story within the whole storyline of Scripture.
David was the anointed king who stepped forward when Israel's warriors could not save themselves.
He fought a representative battle.
One man stood for the Philistines.
One man stood for Israel.
When the champion fell, the people who had been terrified moments earlier shared in a victory they had not personally accomplished.
That should make the Christian heart beat faster.
Because David's victory ultimately points beyond David—not because every detail must be forced into an allegory, but because Scripture's story moves toward David's greater Son.
Jesus Christ.
And Jesus did not come carrying Saul's armor.
He came carrying a cross.
The world looked at Golgotha and saw weakness.
Heaven was accomplishing redemption.
The soldiers saw a condemned man.
Faith sees the Lamb of God.
The crowd saw humiliation.
God was dealing with sin.
Satan's apparent hour of triumph became the stage upon which Christ would accomplish the work of redemption and rise victorious from the grave.
This is where the Gospel becomes more than a David-and-Goliath motivational speech.
Your deepest enemy is not your difficult coworker.
Not your bank account.
Not the person who betrayed you.
Not even the circumstances keeping you awake tonight.
Our deepest crisis is sin and our alienation from the holy God.
And you cannot sling a stone hard enough to fix that.
You cannot become disciplined enough to erase your guilt.
You cannot donate enough.
Serve enough.
Cry enough.
Promise enough.
Hide enough.
Pretend enough.
You need a Savior.
And this is the scandal of grace:
the victory you desperately needed was won by Someone else.

Jesus lived the righteousness we could not produce, gave Himself for sinners, and rose from the dead. Forgiveness is not God pretending sin never mattered. The cross tells us sin mattered so terribly that the Son of God gave Himself for our redemption.
Grace is free to the sinner.
But grace was not cheap.
Maybe you have spent years building armor.
Achievement became armor.
Money became armor.
Humor became armor.
Pornography became anesthesia.
Alcohol became escape.
Anger became protection.
Relationships became validation.
Ministry became camouflage.
You learned how to say “God is good” while quietly wondering whether God could still want you.
You learned when to lift your hands during worship.
You learned Christian vocabulary.
You learned which Bible verses to post.
But underneath all of it…
you're tired.
So tired.
And perhaps the most exhausting armor you have ever carried is the version of yourself you created so nobody would discover how badly you need grace.
Jesus already knows.
That secret?
He knows.
That relapse?
He knows.
That bitterness?
He knows.
That browser history?
He knows.
That pride?
He knows.
That thing you hope nobody ever asks about?
He knows.
And the Gospel does not say, “Hide it better.”
The Gospel calls you into the light.
Repent.
Come to Christ.
Confess your sin.
Stop negotiating with what Jesus died to save sinners from.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace is God's undeserved mercy that brings sinners home and begins transforming them.
This is why David's battlefield still speaks.
Israel saw five thousand shekels of bronze.
David saw a mortal man standing against the living God.
Israel asked, in effect, “How can we defeat him?”
David's faith asked another question:
“How can he possibly stand against God?”
Maybe the giant in front of you really is enormous.
Christianity does not require you to lie about that.
Cancer is frightening.
Grief hurts.
Betrayal devastates.
Addiction destroys.
Financial collapse has consequences.
Depression can make a room feel unbearably dark.
Broken families leave scars.
Persecution is real.
Death itself is an enemy.
Faith does not call darkness light.
Faith simply refuses to call darkness God.
Your situation can be enormous without being sovereign.
Your pain can be real without being lord.
Your past can explain scars without owning your future.
Your sin can be horrific without being stronger than Christ's blood when you truly turn to Him.
Goliath's armor was heavy.
But it couldn't save him.
And some of us need to hear that because we have spent our lives envying other people's armor.
Their money.
Their followers.
Their appearance.
Their marriage.
Their ministry.
Their intelligence.
Their platform.
Their success.
Their confidence.
Their possessions.
We look across the valley and think, “If I had what they have, I wouldn't be afraid.”
David shows us something better.
You don't need Goliath's armor.
You need Goliath's God?
No.
That is exactly the point.
Goliath's gods could not save him.
You need David's God—the living God—and ultimately David's greater Son, Jesus Christ.
That is the difference between inspirational Christianity and the Gospel.
The Gospel is not primarily about discovering the warrior inside you.
It is about surrendering to the King above you.
It is not “You are enough.”
It is “Christ is enough.”
It is not “Save yourself.”
It is “You need the Savior.”
It is not “Try harder until God loves you.”
It is that in Christ, sinners are summoned to repent and believe the good news of a crucified and risen Lord.
And maybe right now, while reading an article about the weight of an ancient warrior's armor, you have realized something uncomfortable.
Goliath's armor isn't the heaviest thing in this story.
Your heart is carrying something too.
Guilt.
Fear.
Secret sin.
Regret.
A prayer you stopped praying because disappointment hurt too much.
A child you cannot rescue.
A marriage you cannot repair by yourself.
A wound nobody knows exists.
A version of Christianity that looks alive online but feels dead when the screen goes dark.
What if today you stopped pretending it wasn't heavy?
What if you stopped confusing hiding with healing?
What if your next prayer wasn't impressive at all?
“Jesus, have mercy on me.”
There are prayers heaven does not need decorated.
Come honestly.
Come repentantly.
Come believing.
The Savior who welcomed broken sinners has not changed.
Someone reading silently may desperately need to know that God's grace still reaches people in valleys.
