That dishonest business practice.
That addiction to human approval.
That pride.
That envy.
That habit of appearing holy while your private world collapses.
That apology you refuse to make.
That forgiveness you refuse to extend.
That truth you refuse to obey because obedience may cost you something.
Please understand this carefully:
You do not earn Christ's love by cleaning yourself up.
But when Christ saves us, His grace does not teach us to make peace with the sin that nailed Him to the cross.
So stop calling partial surrender complete surrender.
Stop decorating the cage.
Stop giving holy names to things God has already confronted.
Stop saying, “But look at everything else I obeyed.”
Saul could point toward an entire battlefield of obedience.
Samuel could still hear one sheep.
And perhaps that is the sentence somebody reading this needed today:
The thing you keep defending may be the very thing Jesus is asking you to finally bring into the light.
Not so He can destroy you.
So He can free you.
There is grace for the person who finally stops pretending.
There is forgiveness for the person who confesses.
There is restoration for the believer who has wandered.
There is cleansing for the ashamed.
There is mercy for the hypocrite who finally removes the mask.
There is a cross for sinners.
There is an empty tomb for people who thought their story was finished.
And there is a Savior whose blood speaks a better word than your worst failure.
His name is Jesus.
Maybe this article exposed something you have been protecting.
Don't perform for us.
Don't manufacture emotion.
Let those words become more than engagement.
Let them become confession.
Somebody scrolling silently may need to discover that Christians are not people who never needed rescuing.
We are people who know the Rescuer.
Not because every sentence deserves remembering, but because there may come a day when your heart begins negotiating again and you need to hear the sheep.
Sharing biblical truth should never become a substitute for living it.
But sharing it can become an act of love when the motive is genuinely to point someone toward Christ.
Christ alone saves, by grace.
But if you sincerely want to glorify God with your resources, one legitimate way to do that is voluntarily supporting faithful Gospel work that helps spread His Word.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that good people managed to obey enough.
It is the announcement that the perfect King came to rescue rebels.
Saul's story warns us what happens when we keep rewriting God's commands.
Jesus' story reveals what happens when God rewrites ours.
And maybe tonight, after the scrolling stops and the room becomes quiet, you will finally hear it...
that one thing still bleating in the background.
Don't hide it.
Don't rename it.
Don't sacrifice around it.
Bring it to Jesus.
Because the most dangerous sheep is not the one Samuel could hear—it is the one we have learned to stop hearing.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Can Christians Drink Alcohol Without Sinning? The Biblical Answer May Expose a Deeper Question
paragraphs: Can Christians Drink Alcohol Without Sinning? The Biblical Answer May Expose a Deeper Question

The Bible does not simply ask what is in your glass. It asks who has your heart, what controls you, whom your freedom affects, and whether you are willing to surrender even a permitted thing for the glory of Christ.
There is a glass sitting on the table.
Maybe it is wine at a wedding.
Maybe it is beer after work.
Maybe it is champagne at a celebration.
Maybe nobody around you thinks twice about it.
And maybe you have quietly wondered something you were almost afraid to ask in church:
Can a Christian drink alcohol without sinning?
Some believers will answer before you finish the sentence.
“Absolutely not.”
Others will laugh.
“Of course. Jesus drank wine.”
And somewhere between those two reactions sits the Christian who genuinely wants to please God—not looking for an excuse to sin, not interested in religious pride, but honestly asking:
Jesus, what do You want from me?
That question changes everything.
Because perhaps the most dangerous question is not, “How much can I drink before it becomes sinful?”
Perhaps the better question is:
“How much of my life can Jesus have?”
Stay with that question.
It may take us somewhere uncomfortable.
Scripture does not teach that every consumption of wine is inherently sinful. Paul even instructed Timothy, “use a little wine” because of his stomach and frequent illnesses (1 Timothy 5:23).
Notice the wording.
The Greek phrase contains οἴνῳ ὀλίγῳ — oinō oligō.
Wine.
A little.
Paul did not need to write that sentence if the mere consumption of wine were automatically sinful.
That matters because Christians should never make Scripture say more than Scripture says.
But we must also refuse to make Scripture say less than Scripture says.
Because the same New Testament gives a command so clear that no honest reading can dismiss it:
“Do not get drunk on wine... Instead, be filled with the Spirit.” — Ephesians 5:18
The Greek begins:
καὶ μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ — kai mē methyskesthe oinō
“Do not become drunk with wine.”
Then comes the breathtaking contrast:
ἀλλὰ πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι — alla plērousthe en pneumati
“But be filled with the Spirit.”
Do you see what Paul does?
He doesn't merely move from alcohol to prohibition.
He moves from intoxication to filling.
From one influence to another.
From surrendering yourself to something in a cup to surrendering yourself to the Spirit of God.
And suddenly the conversation becomes much bigger than alcohol.
What is controlling you?
What do you run toward when your heart hurts?
What do you need before you can relax?
What do you reach for when anxiety crawls into your chest?
What do you use to become somebody different for a few hours?
What do you tell yourself you can quit anytime—but strangely never seem willing to surrender?
Because a person can spend years arguing, “The Bible never says I can't drink this,” while completely avoiding the more frightening question:
“Why is it so important to me that nobody tells me I shouldn't?”
That question can hurt.
Especially if alcohol has become more than a beverage.
Maybe nobody knows.
You still go to church.
You still post Scripture.
You still pray before meals.
You still know the worship songs.
But there are nights when one drink becomes another.
And another.
The room gets softer.
The memories get quieter.
The loneliness becomes easier to ignore.
The anger loses its edges.
For a little while, you don't have to feel everything.
Then morning comes.
And whatever you were escaping is still waiting.
Perhaps with shame sitting beside it.
Listen carefully: the Gospel does not begin with Jesus standing over ashamed sinners asking, “How could you?”
The Gospel shows us Jesus coming for sinners precisely because we could never rescue ourselves.
Christ did not come merely to improve your behavior.
He came to redeem you.
The cross is not God's decoration for respectable people.
It is God's rescue mission for guilty people.
That means there is an enormous difference between enjoying something with thanksgiving and needing something because your heart has quietly learned to depend upon it.

The Bible's concern with alcohol repeatedly includes intoxication, loss of self-control, foolishness, destructive behavior, and harm to others. Ephesians 5:18 explicitly forbids drunkenness and contrasts it with being filled by the Spirit.
So can Christians drink alcohol without sinning?
Biblically, drinking alcohol is not presented as inherently sinful in every circumstance. Drunkenness is sinful.
But please don't close the article yet.
Because answering only that question can leave us with a technically correct answer and a spiritually dangerous heart.
Christian freedom was never designed to become:
“How close can I walk to the edge without falling?”
The mature Christian begins asking:
“How can my freedom make Jesus visible?”
That is where Romans 14 becomes uncomfortable.
Paul writes that it is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything that causes a brother or sister to stumble.
Think about that.
Something may be permissible for you...
and love may still lead you to put it down.
Imagine sitting across from someone Jesus rescued from alcoholism.
They have fought battles you never saw.
They remember waking up in places they don't remember entering.
They remember promises broken.
Children disappointed.
Money disappearing.
Marriage collapsing.
Maybe alcohol almost killed them.
And now they are trying to rebuild their life around Christ.
You could sit there defending your freedom.
“I have the right.”
Maybe you do.
But love sometimes asks a different question:
“Is exercising my right worth endangering my brother?”
That is Christian maturity.
The world says freedom means, “Nobody gets to tell me no.”
Jesus-shaped freedom says,
“I am so free that I can willingly say no.”
That distinction is enormous.
Sometimes abstinence isn't legalism.
Sometimes abstinence is love.
Sometimes pouring the drink away isn't admitting that every Christian who drinks is sinning.
Sometimes it simply means:
“Jesus, this isn't worth somebody's soul, somebody's recovery, my witness, my self-control, or my intimacy with You.”
And there is another uncomfortable truth.
For some Christians, the safest and wisest amount of alcohol really is none.
Not because they are more holy than everyone else.
Not because wine itself magically becomes sinful when it crosses their lips.
But because they know their history.
They know their weaknesses.
They know what happened last time.
They know that “just one” has repeatedly become five.
They know the family history.
They know the cravings.
They know how quickly celebration becomes dependence.
They know the voice that whispers:
You deserve another.
And wisdom doesn't prove strength by repeatedly walking toward the cliff.
Sometimes wisdom builds a fence.
If that is you, surrender is not defeat.
It may be one of the bravest acts of worship you have ever offered Christ.
There is no trophy in heaven for discovering exactly how close you could get to bondage without technically calling yourself enslaved.
Jesus did not shed His blood so you could negotiate with chains.
He came to make captives free.
And perhaps alcohol isn't your issue at all.
Perhaps you've never been drunk.
But something else controls you.
Pornography.
Approval.
Food.
Money.
Anger.
Shopping.
Attention.
Work.
Entertainment.
Social media.
A relationship you know is pulling you from Christ.
We are incredibly talented at condemning another person's bottle while protecting our own idol.
That is why this conversation cannot end with alcohol.
The deeper question is always worship.
Who owns me?
Paul's contrast in Ephesians is extraordinary because Christianity is not merely a religion of subtraction.
Don't get drunk...
be filled with the Spirit.
Don't simply empty the glass.
Be filled with Someone better.
That is the difference between behavior modification and transformation.
Jesus does not merely walk into the wreckage of our lives and say:
“Stop.”
He says:
“Follow Me.”
Something greater has arrived.
Forgiveness greater than your shame.
Grace stronger than your addiction.
A kingdom greater than your appetite.
A Savior more satisfying than whatever you have been using to numb yourself.
Maybe you crossed the line long ago.
Maybe alcohol stopped being recreational and became medicinal—not medicine for your body, but anesthesia for your soul.
You drink because you don't want to remember.
You drink because somebody left.
You drink because somebody died.
You drink because the marriage feels empty.
You drink because silence is unbearable.
You drink because sober you has to feel things intoxicated you can temporarily escape.
And maybe this article suddenly stopped feeling theological.
Maybe it started feeling personal.
Then hear this carefully:
Jesus already knows.
He knows about the hidden bottles.
The deleted messages.
The embarrassing nights.
The promises you made to God at 2:00 a.m.
The mornings when you whispered, Never again.
The relapse.
The shame.
The fear that somebody from church might discover the truth.
And still Christ calls sinners to Himself.
Not so we can remain enslaved.
So we can repent and become free.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who died and rose to reconcile sinners to God.
Grace doesn't say your bondage doesn't matter.
Grace says your bondage does not get the final word.
That is the scandal of Christianity.
Peter failed.
Thomas doubted.
Paul had persecuted the church.
The cross itself looked like catastrophic defeat.
And God kept writing redemption where human beings expected endings.
That is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe your story currently reads:
Addicted.
Jesus can write:
Redeemed.
Maybe it reads:
Ashamed.
Jesus can write:
Forgiven.
Maybe:
Enslaved.
Christ can write:
Free.
Maybe:
Too far gone.
The cross says:
Come home.
And if you can drink without drunkenness, without violating conscience, without being mastered, without placing someone else in spiritual danger, do not turn your liberty into arrogance.
Receive every legitimate gift with gratitude and keep Christ above the gift.
And if your conscience tells you not to drink, don't violate it merely because another Christian tells you that you are “free.”
You do not have to prove maturity by drinking.
And you do not prove maturity merely by abstaining.
Christlikeness is the goal.
Some people never touch alcohol and remain drunk on pride.
Others boast about Christian liberty while quietly becoming slaves to the very thing they insist they control.
Neither is freedom.
Freedom looks like belonging completely to Jesus.
So perhaps tonight the question isn't:
Can Christians drink alcohol without sinning?
Perhaps it is:
Can Jesus ask me to put mine down?
If the answer is no...
then the glass may have revealed something about your heart.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, don't turn the conviction into another reason for shame.
Bring it into the light.
Talk with a mature believer or pastor you trust. If alcohol has become difficult to control, seek appropriate professional help as well. Asking for help is not incompatible with faith.
Then pray without performing.

“Jesus, I belong to You. Show me anything mastering me. Forgive my sin. Give me wisdom where Scripture gives liberty, obedience where Scripture commands, love when my freedom could hurt another person, and courage to surrender anything standing between my heart and You.”
Maybe somebody reading this has been fighting alone.
You don't owe strangers your entire story.
Those three words are enough.

And if Christ has already delivered you from addiction or destructive drinking, consider commenting “Christ is still healing me.” Your testimony may become the reason another person finally believes that their story isn't finished.
Not because every paragraph was comfortable.
Because someday you may need to remember the difference between asking, “Am I allowed?” and asking, “Does this glorify Christ?”
Send it privately to the believer who has been quietly struggling.
It is simply a way to help Gospel Warrior continue creating and distributing biblical resources while receiving deeper discipleship content and spiritual encouragement.
Jesus is the treasure.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not merchandise.
Not Christian content.
Jesus Christ.
The One who was crucified for sinners.
The One who rose from the grave.
The One who forgives those who repent and believe.
The One who breaks chains.
The One who receives prodigals.
The One who can take the chapter you are ashamed to let anybody read and refuse to let it become the final chapter.
So look at the glass again.
Perhaps you can drink it without sinning.
Perhaps wisdom tells you not to.
Perhaps love asks you to surrender it for somebody else.
Perhaps your history tells you that touching it again would be walking willingly toward chains Christ has been breaking.
Whatever your situation, don't merely ask how much alcohol Christianity permits.
Ask something infinitely more important:
“Jesus, what would glorify You?”
Then be willing to obey the answer Scripture gives.
Because someday, the most important thing about that glass will not be whether you had permission to hold it.
It will be whether you were free enough in Christ to put it down.
The world calls freedom getting to have whatever you want. Jesus can make you so free that what once controlled you no longer gets a vote.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE KING WAS CHOSEN. THE CROWD WAS WAITING. BUT SAUL WAS HIDING IN THE BAGGAGE.
paragraphs: THE KING WAS CHOSEN. THE CROWD WAS WAITING. BUT SAUL WAS HIDING IN THE BAGGAGE.
The disturbing story of Saul’s coronation—and what happens when God’s calling finds a frightened man hiding where nobody thought to look.
Imagine hearing your name called in front of an entire nation.
Not for a punishment.
Not for an accusation.
For a crown.

Thousands of eyes are waiting to see the man who will become Israel’s first human king. The prophet Samuel is there. The tribes have assembled before the LORD. The selection has narrowed from Israel… to Benjamin… from Benjamin to a particular family… and finally to one man.
Saul son of Kish.
The moment has arrived.
The future king should step forward.
Except there is one problem.
Nobody can find him.
The man chosen to stand above the nation is nowhere to be seen.
People begin searching.
Samuel has already privately anointed him. Saul has already received extraordinary confirming signs. The Spirit of God has already come powerfully upon him. Saul has already prophesied.
And now, when the public moment finally comes…
he disappears.
So Israel does something almost unbelievable.
They ask God where their king is.
And God answers.
The ancient Hebrew preserves the scene with almost painful simplicity:
הִנֵּה־הוּא נֶחְבָּא אֶל־הַכֵּלִים
Hinnēh-hū neḥbāʾ el-ha-kēlîm.
“Behold, he is hiding among the baggage.”
—1 Samuel 10:22
There he is.
The king.
In the baggage.
Sit with that image for a moment.
A crown is waiting for him while he is hiding among supplies.
A nation is looking for him while he is trying not to be seen.
His name has been called, but fear—or perhaps overwhelming reluctance—has driven him into hiding.
And maybe that is why this ancient coronation suddenly feels painfully modern.
Because some of us know exactly what it means to hide.
We just have better baggage.
We hide behind work.
Behind humor.
Behind ministry.
Behind “I’m fine.”
Behind achievement.
Behind theological knowledge.
Behind the opinions of other people.
Behind old wounds.
Behind the memory of what we did.
Behind what somebody did to us.
Behind the fear that if people really knew us, they would walk away.
Some people even hide behind religion.
We can sing while hiding.
Serve while hiding.
Preach while hiding.
Post Bible verses while hiding.
Tell everyone else that God is faithful while privately wondering whether He could possibly still want anything to do with us.
The baggage has changed.
The hiding has not.
But to understand Saul’s moment correctly, we have to resist turning this passage into a shallow motivational slogan.
This is not merely, “Stop hiding because you are destined for greatness.”
The Bible is telling a far more sobering story.
Israel’s request for a king was itself spiritually complicated.
Before Saul was publicly selected, Samuel reminded Israel that God had delivered them from Egypt and rescued them from their oppressors, yet they had demanded, “Set a king over us.”
Israel already had a King.
The LORD.
And yet they wanted a king they could see.
A king like the nations around them.
Then comes Saul.
And from the human perspective, he looks spectacular.
When they finally drag him out from among the baggage and place him before the people, Scripture says he stands taller than everyone else.
Samuel announces:
“Do you see the one whom the LORD has chosen? There is no one like him among all the people.”
And the crowd erupts:
יְחִי הַמֶּלֶךְ
Yeḥi ha-melekh.
“Long live the king!”
What a scene.
The hidden man is suddenly standing above everybody.
The frightened man is surrounded by cheers.
The man behind the baggage is now at the center of the nation.
But if you know Saul’s story, those cheers hurt.
Because you know what comes later.
You know that Saul’s beginning will not guarantee his ending.
You know the man hiding from the crown will eventually become a man desperately clinging to the throne.
That is one of the tragedies of Saul.
At the beginning, he seems small in his own eyes.
Later, when obedience becomes costly, his relationship with power becomes something very different.
The man who once had to be pulled out of hiding will eventually fear losing what he once seemed afraid to possess.
And somewhere inside that transformation is a warning for every Christian.
Humility is not merely thinking little of yourself.
And insecurity is not automatically holiness.
Sometimes what looks like humility can coexist with a heart still governed by the opinions of people.
Saul’s later story exposes this painfully.
After his disobedience concerning Amalek, Saul eventually admits to Samuel:
“I have sinned. I violated the LORD’s command and your instructions. I was afraid of the people and obeyed their voice.”
—1 Samuel 15:24
There it is.
The crowd.
The same human eyes that once watched his coronation would become voices he feared disappointing.
And suddenly the baggage scene becomes even more haunting.
Because sometimes we come out of physical hiding without ever coming out of heart-level hiding.
You can stand in front of everyone and still be imprisoned by what everyone thinks.
You can wear the crown and still be afraid.
You can have the title and still need approval.
You can become successful and still be controlled by the terrified person you were before anybody knew your name.
Maybe that is where this story finds you.
Not behind literal baggage.
Behind emotional baggage.
The childhood that still whispers that you are not enough.
The father whose approval you never received.
The relationship that taught you not to trust.
The church wound you never processed.
The secret sin nobody knows about.
The addiction you keep promising will be the last time.
The prayer life that quietly disappeared.
The version of yourself you present publicly versus the person who lies awake at two in the morning.
You learned how to function.
But functioning and freedom are not the same thing.
And here is where we must be careful.
Saul’s story does not teach that every dream in your heart is a divine calling.
It does not promise everybody a throne.
It does not say that believing in yourself will produce your destiny.
Scripture gives us something infinitely better than self-esteem.
It gives us Christ.
Because Saul cannot carry the weight of Israel’s deepest hope.
Neither can David.
Neither can any human ruler.
The Bible keeps moving.
Through failed kings.
Broken kingdoms.
Exile.
Longing.
Prophecy.
Silence.
Until another King arrives.
Jesus Christ.
And the contrast is breathtaking.
Saul was physically impressive.
Jesus was not presented to Israel as the political spectacle many expected.
Saul would eventually disobey God to preserve what mattered to him.
Jesus says of His Father:
“Not my will, but yours, be done.”
Saul feared people.
Jesus walked toward the cross while crowds mocked Him.
Saul desperately tried to preserve his throne.
Jesus willingly surrendered Himself to death.
Saul’s kingship deteriorated beneath disobedience.
Jesus was “obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.”
And Saul was publicly acclaimed with:
“Long live the king!”
Jesus would eventually stand before another crowd.
Only this crowd would scream something far darker.
“Crucify him!”
Think about the scandal of that.
The true King came.
And humanity crowned Him with thorns.
The hands that formed humanity were pierced by human nails.
The One without sin was condemned among sinners.
The innocent Son of God carried a cross through streets filled with people He came to save.
And at Calvary, something happened infinitely greater than Saul emerging from the baggage.
Jesus carried ours.
Not suitcases.
Sin.
Guilt.
Condemnation.
Shame.
Our rebellion against God.
Our secret darkness.
Our religious hypocrisy.
Our lust.
Our bitterness.
Our pride.
Our lies.
Our self-righteousness.
Our attempts to become our own kings.
He carried what we could never remove from ourselves.
“For Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God.”
—1 Peter 3:18
That is the Gospel.
Not God discovering that you were secretly wonderful all along.
God loving sinners at unimaginable cost.
Not Jesus helping good people become slightly better.
Jesus dying for the guilty and rising victorious so sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
Grace does not pretend the baggage is empty.
Grace opens it.
Grace exposes what sin has done.
Grace calls sin what God calls it.
Then grace points trembling sinners toward a blood-stained cross and an empty tomb and says:
There is mercy here.
Maybe you have spent years hiding something.
You know exactly what it is.
Nobody reading this needs to know.
But God already does.
That sentence may terrify you.
It should also give you hope.
Because the God who knows where Saul is hiding knows where you are hiding too.
When Israel could not find Saul, God could.
“Behold, he is hiding among the baggage.”
There was no corner obscure enough to escape His sight.
And neither is yours.
Psalm 139 asks:
“Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence?”
The answer is nowhere.
But for the person who comes to Christ, that is not merely terrifying news.
It is beautiful news.
Because the One from whom you cannot hide is the very One who invites sinners to come into the light.
You do not need to clean every piece of baggage before approaching Jesus.
You come because you cannot cleanse yourself.
You repent.
You stop defending what God calls sin.
You stop negotiating.
You stop pretending.
You bring the truth into His light.
And you trust the crucified and risen Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
—1 John 1:9
Maybe your prayer tonight does not need to sound impressive.
Maybe it simply needs to be true.
“Jesus, I’m tired of hiding.”
There are people reading this who have been carrying something so long that it has started feeling like part of their identity.
It is not.
Your sin is serious.
Your wounds are real.
Your failures have consequences.
But none of them gets to be your Savior.
Jesus does.
And if you belong to Him, your worst chapter does not have authority to write the final sentence.
That belongs to Christ.
This is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is the mercy of God calling you away from destruction.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior.
Saul’s life warns us that a powerful beginning does not make obedience optional.
Anointing is not permission for rebellion.
Spiritual experiences are not substitutes for faithfulness.
Public applause is not evidence that everything is healthy inside.
And yesterday’s encounter with God cannot become an excuse for today’s disobedience.
The question is not merely whether God has used you.
The question is whether your heart belongs to Him.
Because there is something more frightening than being found hiding among baggage.
It is eventually standing before everyone while your heart remains hidden from surrender.
So be honest.
What are you hiding behind?
What are you protecting that Jesus is asking you to surrender?
What opinion matters so much that you have started compromising obedience?
What secret would collapse the image you have spent years constructing?
What baggage has become comfortable enough that you almost forgot it was hiding you?
You might forget this article.
Do not forget that question.
And if the Holy Spirit is exposing something in you through Scripture, do not bury it beneath another distraction.
Bring it to Christ.
Today.
Not after you become worthy.
You cannot make yourself worthy.
Come because Jesus is worthy.
Come because His blood is sufficient.
Come because the tomb is empty.
Come because grace is still grace.
Come because the King you actually need is not Saul.
His name is Jesus.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by financial support, social-media engagement, or religious works.

But if this ministry is faithfully helping people encounter Scripture and hear the Gospel, supporting and sharing that work can be one practical way to participate in putting biblical truth in front of people who may never walk into a church.
It does not buy His favor.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
But supporting Gospel-centered work can be a voluntary act of generosity that helps more Scripture-centered content and discipleship resources reach people who desperately need them.
But whether you ever give a cent or not, hear this clearly:
Do not hide from Jesus.
The baggage cannot forgive you.
The applause cannot heal you.
The title cannot save you.
The image cannot cleanse you.
The crowd cannot tell you who you ultimately are.
Run to Christ.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Walk in the light.
And when grace pulls you out of hiding, do not crawl back into the baggage Jesus died to free you from.
Because sometimes the most dangerous hiding place is not where nobody can see you—it is where everybody can see you, but nobody knows you are still hiding.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Woman Jericho Called a Prostitute—But God Wrote Her Into the Bloodline of Jesus
paragraphs: The Woman Jericho Called a Prostitute—But God Wrote Her Into the Bloodline of Jesus
How Rahab went from a condemned city and a scandalous past to the genealogy of Christ—and why her scarlet cord still whispers to every person who thinks their past has disqualified them from grace.
There is a woman in the genealogy of Jesus Christ whom many respectable people would probably have edited out.
Her name was Rahab.
And Scripture does not sanitize her story.

Before she became associated with Israel, before Hebrews remembered her for faith, before James pointed to the evidence of that faith, and centuries before Matthew placed her name in the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ, Joshua introduced her with words that would have followed a woman like a scarlet letter:
רָחָב הַזּוֹנָה — Rāḥāḇ ha-zônāh.
Rahab the prostitute.
The Hebrew word זֹנָה (zônāh) refers to a prostitute. The New Testament remembers her similarly with the Greek expression Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη — Rhaab hē pornē, “Rahab the prostitute.”
God did not need the Bible to lie about Rahab's past in order to tell the truth about His grace.
And maybe that is where this story finds you.
Because some of us know exactly what it feels like to believe that one chapter has become our entire identity.
Divorced.
Addicted.
Unfaithful.
Abandoned.
Promiscuous.
Angry.
Ashamed.
Lukewarm.
Hypocrite.
Failure.
Maybe nobody else knows the word you secretly use for yourself.
But you do.
You remember what you did.
You remember who you were.

You remember the night you wish you could erase, the relationship you should never have entered, the compromise nobody discovered, the prayer you stopped praying, the promise you broke, the person you wounded, the years you wasted.
And sometimes the cruelest voice in the room is not another person's.
It is your own.
But Rahab's story forces us to confront a breathtaking truth:
God can tell the complete truth about your past without allowing your past to have the final word about your future.
Rahab lived in Jericho, a Canaanite city standing under divine judgment. When Joshua sent two men secretly to spy out the land, they entered Rahab's house.
Then something extraordinary happened.
Rahab hid them.
Why?
Not merely because she suddenly liked Israelites.
She had heard.

She told them that the inhabitants of the land had heard what the LORD had done—how He dried up the Red Sea and defeated Israel's enemies. Jericho had heard about Israel's God, and fear had fallen over the city.
But Rahab did something with what she heard.
She believed.
Her confession in Joshua 2:11 is astonishing:
“The LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath.”
Behind the English word LORD stands God's covenant name in the Hebrew text:
יְהוָה — YHWH.
Rahab was confessing the supremacy of Israel's God while living inside a culture destined for judgment.
Think about that.
She had no respectable Israelite pedigree.
No childhood memories of Moses.
No wilderness testimony.
No ancestry descending from Abraham.
She was a Canaanite.
A woman.
A prostitute.
A resident of Jericho.
From a human perspective, she appeared to be standing on the wrong side of almost every boundary.
Yet faith crossed the boundary.
That does not mean Rahab earned salvation by becoming morally impressive overnight. Scripture refuses to turn her story into salvation by human merit.
Hebrews 11:31 places the emphasis exactly where it belongs:
“By faith…”
The Greek begins:
Πίστει Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη… — Pistei Rhaab hē pornē…
“By faith, Rahab the prostitute…”
That first word matters.
Πίστει — pistei — “by faith.”
Rahab's actions mattered because they revealed that her confession was more than frightened religious language.
She trusted the God she confessed.

James later points to Rahab when explaining that genuine faith does not remain sterile and invisible. She received the messengers and sent them out another way. Her works did not function as a price with which she purchased God's grace; they demonstrated the reality of a faith that acted. James explicitly remembers what she did.
This distinction matters enormously.
Christianity does not teach, “Clean yourself up enough and perhaps God will finally love you.”
The Gospel announces something infinitely better.
God saves sinners by grace through faith, and the faith that truly encounters Him begins producing a changed life.
Rahab believed.
And because she believed, she acted.
There comes a moment when faith stops being something you merely say and becomes something you stake your life upon.
Rahab reached that moment.
Imagine the scene.
Jericho's authorities are searching.
Two Israelite spies are hidden.
Rahab knows discovery could cost her everything.
She has to choose.
The city she can see…
or the God she has only heard about.
The old allegiance…
or a terrifying new faith.
Safety as she understood it…
or surrender to the God of Israel.
And somewhere in that decision, Rahab crossed an invisible line.
Her address was still Jericho.
Her history was still real.
Her past had not magically disappeared.
But her allegiance had changed.
That may be the word someone reading this needs.
Repentance is not pretending yesterday never happened.
It is turning toward God today.
The Gospel does not require you to manufacture a cleaner history before coming to Jesus.
It calls you to come to Jesus with the history you actually have.
Rahab then pleaded for mercy not only for herself but for her family.
The spies agreed. A scarlet cord was to hang from her window, identifying the house whose occupants would be spared when judgment came upon Jericho.
A scarlet cord.
It is difficult for a Christian reader not to feel the theological resonance.
But we should be careful here.
Scripture itself does not explicitly say that Rahab's scarlet cord was a prophecy of the blood of Christ. We should not claim more than the Bible claims.

Yet within the Bible's larger story, the imagery can certainly remind Christians of a greater rescue: judgment is real, refuge is necessary, and ultimately sinners are saved not by their moral record but through God's provision, fulfilled supremely in Jesus Christ and His atoning death.
Rahab's cord was not Jesus' blood.
But Rahab's rescue belongs to the same unfolding biblical story that eventually leads us to the cross.
And when Jericho fell, Rahab lived.
Hebrews remembers the reason: “By faith.” She did not perish with the disobedient because she welcomed the spies in peace.
But surviving Jericho was not the most astonishing thing God would do with Rahab's story.
Because generations later, Matthew opens his Gospel.
And genealogies begin.
Names.
Fathers.
Sons.
Generations.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
Then suddenly…
Rahab.
Matthew 1:5 identifies Salmon as the father of Boaz by Rahab, and Boaz becomes the father of Obed, Obed the father of Jesse, and Jesse the father of David.
Follow that line forward through the generations and Matthew brings us to Jesus Christ.
Do you understand what that means?
The woman once identified with Jericho's prostitution became part of the family line through which the Messiah entered history.
Rahab was connected to Jesus through the genealogy Matthew records.
She was an ancestor in the Messianic line.
The scandal was not erased from Scripture.
Grace simply wrote beyond it.
And this is where Rahab stops being merely an ancient character and begins standing uncomfortably close to us.
Because perhaps you have secretly assumed that Jesus wants people with cleaner biographies.
People who did not sleep with that person.
People who did not destroy that marriage.
People who did not waste those years.
People who did not relapse.
People who did not walk away from church.
People who do not carry your memories.
You look at Christians whose lives appear polished and think, Maybe God can use them.
Then you look at yourself and think, But He knows me.
Yes.
He does.
That is precisely what makes grace grace.
Jesus did not come because humanity needed minor improvement.
He came because sinners needed rescue.
The cross destroys both despair and pride.
It destroys despair because no repentant sinner is beyond the reach of Christ.
And it destroys pride because nobody enters God's kingdom because his résumé was impressive enough.
At Calvary, respectable sinners and publicly scandalous sinners have the same need.
Mercy.
This does not mean sin is insignificant.
Grace never required God to rename evil as good.
Jesus' mercy is precious precisely because sin is serious.
The Gospel does not say, “Your sin doesn't matter.”
The Gospel says something far more costly:
Your sin mattered enough that Christ went to the cross, and His grace is powerful enough that your sin does not have to remain your master.
That is the difference between cheap reassurance and biblical redemption.
Jesus does not merely improve reputations.
He raises the spiritually dead.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
He reconciles.
He transforms.
And He gives sinners a new identity in Himself.
Maybe you have spent years trying to hide your Jericho.
Rahab's story says you can stop pretending.
Bring it into the light.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Run to Christ.
Not because Rahab saved herself.
Not because you can save yourself.
But because the Savior who eventually came through Rahab's family line came specifically to save sinners.
That baby Matthew introduces after recording generations of complicated human history eventually walked toward a Roman cross.
There He carried sin.
There He endured judgment.
There He shed His blood.
There He died.
And on the third day, He rose.
That is why your worst chapter does not need to become your final chapter.
Not because positive thinking can rewrite you.
Not because religion can rewrite you.
Not because a motivational article can rewrite you.
Because Jesus Christ can.
Rahab was once part of a condemned city.
Then she became part of God's people.
Her story appeared among the heroes of faith.
Her actions became an apostolic illustration of living faith.
And her name appeared in the genealogy leading to Christ.
The Bible remembered what she had been.
But heaven's story revealed what grace could do.
That is from scandal to grace.
And perhaps the most beautiful part is that Rahab's story never becomes mainly about Rahab.
It points beyond her.
Toward Jesus.
Every redeemed sinner's testimony eventually must.
Maybe your testimony begins with addiction.
Maybe betrayal.
Maybe sexual sin.
Maybe pride.
Maybe religion without Christ.
Maybe years of pretending.
Maybe nobody would call your history scandalous, but you know how far your heart has wandered from God.
Whatever the beginning, redemption has one center:
Jesus Christ.
So do not turn Rahab into permission to remain where sin left you.
Rahab did not stay aligned with Jericho.
Faith changed her allegiance.
Grace calls us out.
Jesus receives sinners, but He does not call us to make peace with the chains from which He came to free us.
Repent.
Believe.
Follow Him.
And if you have already trusted Christ but shame keeps dragging old photographs from your past into your mind, remember Rahab.
God was not embarrassed to put her name in Matthew 1.
Perhaps you are still introducing yourself by a name Christ died to free you from.
“Dirty.”
“Ruined.”
“Unworthy.”
“Too far gone.”
But for everyone who is truly in Christ, Scripture gives language stronger than shame: forgiven, reconciled, redeemed, adopted, made new.
Your scars may remain part of your testimony.
They do not have to remain your identity.
And somebody on your Facebook friends list needs to hear this tonight.
Not eventually.
Now.
Someone is smiling publicly while privately wondering whether God could possibly want them after what they have done.
Your comment may become the courage someone else needs to stop pretending.

Gospel Warrior exists because biblical truth should not merely fill a feed. It should reach wounded people, confront sin, announce grace, strengthen disciples, and keep pointing hearts back to Jesus Christ.

We glorify God through lives of faith, obedience, worship, love, generosity, and faithful witness. But when you freely support Gospel work that genuinely serves Christ, that support can help biblical encouragement reach people who desperately need it.
Not because a share saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sharing can put the message of Jesus in front of someone you may never realize was quietly searching for hope.
Invite your family.
Send it to the friend who thinks Christianity is only for people who already have their lives together.
Let the seeker read it.
Let the lukewarm Christian wrestle with it.
Let the person drowning in shame discover Rahab standing in Matthew's genealogy.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody believes their scandal is stronger than God's grace.
Rahab's name says otherwise.
The cross says otherwise.
The empty tomb says otherwise.
Your past may explain some of your scars.
It may explain some of your fears.
It may explain why certain nights still hurt.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your past does not possess the authority to write the ending.
Christ does.
Jericho knew Rahab by her scandal; Scripture remembers her by faith—and generations later, her name stood in the earthly family line leading to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CALLING OUT FALSE TEACHING ISN’T AUTOMATICALLY SLANDER
paragraphs:
CALLING OUT FALSE TEACHING ISN’T AUTOMATICALLY SLANDER
Sometimes Silence Looks Like Love—Until Someone You Love Swallows the Lie
There is a sentence Christians are increasingly afraid to say.
“That teaching is false.”
Not, “I hate that preacher.”
Not, “Destroy that ministry.”
Not, “Everyone who listens to them is stupid.”
Simply...
“That teaching is not faithful to Scripture.”
And almost immediately, somebody reaches for a frightening word.
Slander.
“Stop attacking people.”
“Touch not the Lord’s anointed.”
“Why are you judging?”
“Why can’t Christians just love each other?”
And because sincere believers do not want to sin with their mouths, many retreat into silence.
But there is a question we desperately need to ask before silence becomes our definition of love:
What if refusing to identify spiritual poison allows someone you love to keep drinking it?
That question matters because the Bible condemns slander—and the same Bible commands Christians to confront destructive teaching.
Both truths must remain standing.
If we erase the first, discernment can become cruelty.
If we erase the second, kindness can become cowardice.
And somewhere between those two cliffs stands Jesus Christ, who was infinitely full of grace and infinitely committed to truth.
This is where the conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because calling something “slander” does not automatically make it slander.
And calling something “discernment” does not automatically make it righteous.
God cares about the truth you speak.
He also cares about why you speak it, how you speak it, whether you have represented someone accurately, and what you secretly hope happens to them after you speak.
That last one hurts.
Because sometimes the doctrine really is wrong...
but our heart is wrong too.
The New Testament gives us language for both dangers. James warns believers:
Μὴ καταλαλεῖτε ἀλλήλων, ἀδελφοί.
Mē katalaleite allēlōn, adelphoi.
“Do not speak against one another, brothers.”
That opening command in James 4:11 uses καταλαλεῖτε, from katalaleō—language associated with speaking against or speaking evil of another.
Scripture does not give Christians permission to turn theological disagreement into character assassination.
We do not get to invent motives.
We do not get to edit clips dishonestly.
We do not get to repeat accusations we have never verified.
We do not get to exaggerate someone’s words because the exaggerated version is easier to destroy.
We do not get to enjoy another Christian's humiliation and then baptize that enjoyment with the word “discernment.”

And there is another sobering Greek word worth knowing: διαβάλλω — diaballō, a word associated with accusing, defaming, or slandering. Its related noun διάβολος — diabolos can mean “slanderer” or “false accuser” and is famously used as a designation for the devil.
Think about that.
A Christian defending truth must never begin imitating the character of the Accuser in order to defend the God of truth.
You can win the argument and wound the body.
You can expose theological error while secretly feeding pride.
You can quote the correct verse with the wrong spirit.
You can be factually accurate and still weaponize facts maliciously.
That is why biblical discernment requires more than discovering who is wrong.
It requires examining yourself.
Before you press “post,” ask yourself something painful:
If this person publicly repented tomorrow, would I rejoice...
or would I be disappointed because I lost my enemy?
If that question makes your stomach tighten, stay there for a moment.
Jesus may be exposing something deeper than somebody else's doctrine.
But now we must face the other side.
Because Scripture's prohibition against sinful speech cannot honestly be interpreted as a prohibition against identifying false teaching.
Paul told Titus that an overseer must hold firmly to the trustworthy message so that he can both encourage others with sound doctrine and refute those who contradict it (Titus 1:9).
That is not slander.
That is pastoral responsibility.
Paul warned Timothy about people who taught different doctrine and instructed him to confront the problem (1 Timothy 1:3–7).
That is not slander.
Paul warned the Galatians about anyone preaching a gospel contrary to the one they had received (Galatians 1:6–9).
That is not slander.
Jude urged believers to “contend for the faith” entrusted to God's people (Jude 3).
That is not slander.
John warned believers not to believe every spirit but to test the spirits because false prophets had gone out into the world (1 John 4:1).
That is not slander.
And Jesus Himself warned:
“Beware of false prophets.” (Matthew 7:15)
Notice something painfully obvious.
You cannot beware of false prophets while simultaneously believing it is sinful even to recognize that false prophets exist.
Discernment requires distinctions.
Truth necessarily distinguishes truth from error.
The issue, then, is not simply, “Did you call something false?”
The deeper questions are:
Was it actually false?
Did Scripture establish that conclusion?
Did you represent the teaching accurately?
Were you correcting doctrine or assassinating character?
Were you protecting people or building an audience through outrage?
Were you grieving over deception...
or enjoying destruction?
Those questions separate biblical discernment from religious blood sport.
And Scripture gives us an astonishing example.
Peter.
Yes...
Peter.
The apostle.
The eyewitness.
The man who confessed Jesus as the Christ.
The man Jesus restored after his devastating denial.
Peter behaved in a way that compromised the truth of the Gospel.
And Paul did not shrug.
He did not say, “Peter has a huge ministry, so we should stay quiet.”
He did not say, “Who am I to judge?”
He did not hide behind a distorted version of unity.
Paul writes in Galatians 2:11:
Ὅτε δὲ ἦλθεν Κηφᾶς εἰς Ἀντιόχειαν, κατὰ πρόσωπον αὐτῷ ἀντέστην...
Hote de ēlthen Kēphas eis Antiocheian, kata prosōpon autō antestēn...
“But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face...”
To his face.
That matters.
Paul was not spreading anonymous rumors in the shadows.
He confronted a real, observable problem because Gospel truth was at stake.
And here is the beautiful part that modern outrage culture often forgets:
Peter was not Paul's disposable enemy.
Peter was his brother.
Correction was not cancellation.
Confrontation was not a declaration that grace had run out.
Peter's failure did not become the final chapter of Peter's story.
And maybe that is exactly what Christian discernment desperately needs to recover.
We expose error because we believe Jesus can still redeem people trapped in it.
Read that again.
The goal is not merely to prove someone wrong.
The goal is truth...
repentance...
restoration...
protection of Christ's sheep...
and ultimately the glory of Jesus Christ.
There is an enormous difference between saying:
“This person taught X. Scripture teaches Y. Here is the context and evidence, and here is why the distinction matters.”
and saying:
“This person is obviously a wicked fraud who never loved God and is probably doing everything for money.”
The first may be legitimate biblical criticism.
The second may involve claims about motives and hearts that you cannot possibly know.
You are not omniscient.
Neither am I.
Only God sees the heart perfectly.
That should make every discernment ministry tremble.
Because the moment exposing error becomes entertainment, something sacred has been corrupted.
Real people are involved.
Real families.
Real congregations.
Real souls.
Real wounds.
Real eternities.
This is not Christian celebrity gossip with Bible verses sprinkled over it.
Doctrine matters because people matter.

Paul told Timothy that a servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome but kind, able to teach, patiently enduring evil, and correcting opponents with gentleness, because God may grant them repentance leading to knowledge of the truth (2 Timothy 2:24–26).
There it is.
The heartbeat.
Repentance.
Not humiliation.
Not clicks.
Not “I destroyed him.”
Repentance.
The Christian does not expose darkness because he enjoys watching people burn.
He shines light because he desperately wants people to come home.
And suddenly this article is no longer about that preacher.
It is about us.
About me.
About you.
Because falsehood does not only live behind pulpits.
Sometimes it lives quietly inside our hearts.
“I can keep this sin hidden.”
“God understands, so repentance isn't necessary.”
“I am too dirty for Jesus to forgive.”
“If God loved me, I wouldn't suffer.”
“I can follow Christ without surrendering this part of my life.”
“My good works will make God accept me.”
“I don't really need Scripture; I know what feels right.”
Those are teachings too.
Some came from pulpits.
Some came from culture.
Some came from trauma.
Some came from pride.
Some came from shame.
Some were whispered so many times inside your own head that they began sounding like your voice.
And perhaps the false teacher you most urgently need to confront tonight is the voice inside you telling you something Jesus never said.
Maybe it keeps saying:
“You're too far gone.”
Look at the cross.
That is false teaching.
Maybe it says:
“Your scandal is stronger than His grace.”
Look at the empty tomb.
False.
Maybe it says:
“If people knew what you did, Jesus wouldn't want you.”
Look at Peter.
Look at the thief beside Christ.
Look at Paul.
Look at sinners eating at Jesus' table.
The Gospel does not say your sin was insignificant.
The Gospel says your sin was so serious that Christ died—and His grace is so magnificent that His blood can cleanse the repentant sinner.
Christianity is not God pretending scandal never happened.
It is God doing something human beings could never do with scandal.
Redeeming it.
This is why our message remains:
Not scandal to self-righteousness.
Not scandal to internet execution.
Not scandal to permanent exile.
Scandal...
to repentance...
to the cross...
to forgiveness...
to restoration...
to transformation...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
And this is precisely why false teaching matters.
False doctrine eventually gives you a false picture of Christ.
A false picture of sin.
A false picture of grace.
A false picture of salvation.
A false picture of holiness.
A false picture of God.
So yes—when Scripture requires it, Christians must lovingly identify dangerous teaching.
But we must do it with trembling hands.
Tell the truth.
Show the evidence.
Open the Bible.
Represent people fairly.
Distinguish essential Gospel truth from secondary disagreements.
Never fabricate.
Never manipulate.
Never weaponize private pain.
Never pretend to know someone's hidden motives.
Never confuse disagreement with heresy.
Never confuse cruelty with courage.
Never confuse cowardice with love.
And always remember that the person you are correcting is a human being for whom repentance and mercy remain things we should desire.
Because maybe tomorrow...
you will be the one who needs correction.
That sentence changes everything.
Imagine discovering that something you confidently believed for fifteen years was wrong.
Would you want someone to mock you?
Would you want thousands celebrating your embarrassment?
Would you want your worst sentence preserved forever as if Jesus could never transform you?
Or would you want a brother or sister courageous enough to tell you the truth...
and gracious enough to leave the door open for repentance?
That is Christian correction.
Truth without love becomes a hammer.
Love without truth becomes abandonment.
But truth spoken in love can become an instrument in the hands of the Great Physician.

And if this exposed something uncomfortable in you—maybe your fear of speaking when truth matters, or perhaps the secret pleasure you have felt watching someone else fall—don't run from that conviction.
Run to Christ.
Someone reading may desperately need proof that correction does not have to end in condemnation.
And if somebody came to your mind while reading this, don't immediately send it as a weapon.
Pray first.
Then, if sharing it would genuinely serve them, send it as an invitation toward truth.

Supporting Gospel ministry should never be presented as a biblical requirement for glorifying God—Scripture does not give us permission to make that claim. But voluntary generosity, sharing sound teaching, and helping worthwhile Gospel work reach others can certainly be sincere expressions of stewardship and love for Christ.
Because we do not need more people addicted to outrage.
We need disciples who love Jesus enough to defend truth...
and love people enough to defend it without becoming cruel.
We need Christians courageous enough to say, “That teaching is false,” when Scripture clearly demands it...
humble enough to say, “I was wrong,” when Scripture corrects them...
and broken enough to say, “Jesus, have mercy on me,” when the light exposes something darker inside their own hearts.
Calling out false teaching isn't automatically slander.
But calling out false teaching does not automatically make us righteous either.
The cross leaves no room for cowardice.
And it leaves no room for pride.
At Calvary, Truth Himself was crucified for liars, slanderers, hypocrites, cowards, false accusers, religious sinners, rebellious sinners...
people like us.
And the risen Christ still transforms them.
So contend for the faith.
Guard the sheep.
Test what you hear.
Open your Bible.
Correct error.
Reject slander.
Refuse cruelty.
Welcome repentance.
Extend grace.
And never forget the person standing on the other side of your correction may yet become another breathtaking testimony that Jesus was not finished writing.
Because when Jesus holds the pen, even the chapter called “I Was Wrong” can become the beginning of somebody's restoration.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE LAST TIME JESUS ENTERED THE TEMPLE
paragraphs: THE LAST TIME JESUS ENTERED THE TEMPLE

They welcomed Him like a King. He walked into His Father’s house. He looked at everything. And what He did next should terrify comfortable religion—and give extraordinary hope to every sinner who still thinks grace cannot reach them.
There is a detail in the final week of Jesus’ earthly ministry that is easy to read too quickly.
Jesus entered Jerusalem.
Crowds had celebrated Him.
Branches had been spread before Him.
“Hosanna” had filled the road.
Expectations were burning.
And then Jesus went somewhere very specific.
The Temple.
But Mark records something almost unsettling in its simplicity:
“And Jesus entered into Jerusalem, and into the temple: and when he had looked round about upon all things…” — Mark 11:11, KJV.
He looked around.
That is all Mark tells us He did that evening.
No overturned tables yet.
No confrontation yet.
No whip-crack drama.
No public rebuke.
Jesus simply entered the Temple…
and looked.
The Greek behind Mark’s description is even more vivid:
περιβλεψάμενος πάντα — periblepsamenos panta
“Having looked around at everything.”
Not some things.
Everything.

The verb carries the sense of looking around, surveying what surrounds you. Jesus was not wandering through the Temple distractedly. Mark deliberately tells us that He looked around at πάντα—panta—everything.
Imagine standing there.
Priests moving.
Pilgrims arriving.
Animals being brought for sacrifice.
Money changing hands.
Religious activity everywhere.
The Temple was alive with motion.
And somewhere in the middle of all that religious noise stood the Son of God…
watching.
That thought should make us uncomfortable.
Because we are very good at noticing what other people can see.
Jesus notices what they cannot.
People see attendance.
Jesus sees affection.
People hear worship.
Jesus knows whether the heart singing it belongs to Him.
People see the Bible highlighted on the table.
Jesus knows whether its words are obeyed when nobody is watching.
People see ministry.
Jesus sees motive.
People see reputation.
Jesus sees reality.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility in Christianity is not that a person might look obviously rebellious.
It is that someone can look spiritually alive while producing very little spiritual fruit.
Mark places something strange between Jesus surveying the Temple and Jesus cleansing it.
A fig tree.
The next morning Jesus was hungry. From a distance He saw a fig tree covered with leaves. He approached it looking for fruit.
There was plenty to see.
Leaves.
Appearance.
Promise.
But when Jesus came close, Mark says He found “nothing but leaves.”
Then Jesus returned to Jerusalem.
Back to the Temple.
Suddenly the placement of the fig-tree account becomes difficult to ignore.
A tree full of leaves.
A Temple full of activity.
Appearance without the fruit God desired.

This is not permission to flatten every detail into an allegory, but Mark’s arrangement strongly invites the reader to see the connection: Jesus inspects the fig tree, then enters and judges the corruption of the Temple, and afterward the disciples discover the tree withered.
Leaves can fool people.
They never fool Jesus.
And maybe that is where this story stops being ancient history.
Because you can have leaves too.
You can know Christian vocabulary and still be hiding bitterness.
You can repost Scripture and secretly be feeding an addiction.
You can sing about surrender while protecting the one area of your life you refuse to surrender.
You can say, “God knows my heart,” forgetting that this is precisely why repentance is necessary.
He does know.
He knows the wound beneath the anger.
He knows the fear beneath the control.
He knows the loneliness beneath the temptation.
He knows why you keep returning to the thing you promised Him you would leave.
He knows the prayer you stopped praying.
He knows the apology you still owe.
He knows the secret browser history.
He knows the jealousy you disguise as discernment.
He knows the unforgiveness you renamed “boundaries” because admitting hatred would hurt too much.
He knows how exhausted you are from maintaining the version of yourself everyone else believes.
Jesus looks around at everything.
And yet…
He came back.
Do not miss that.
The One who saw everything did not simply walk away.

The following day Jesus entered the Temple courts and began driving out those buying and selling. He overturned the tables of the money changers and the seats of those selling doves. He even prevented people from carrying merchandise through the courts.
This was not Jesus losing control.
This was Jesus exercising authority.
And then He explained why.
He reached backward into Israel’s Scriptures and joined two prophetic warnings into one devastating indictment.
“My house will be called a house of prayer for all nations”…
and then:
“you have made it ‘a den of robbers.’”
The first comes from Isaiah 56:7.
The second echoes Jeremiah 7:11.
That context matters.
Jesus was not merely angry because commerce existed.
The issue was deeper than “Jesus disliked people selling things near church.”
He was confronting corruption and the distortion of the purpose of God’s house.
God had declared through Isaiah that His house would be a house of prayer for all nations. Jesus deliberately invokes that vision while confronting what the Temple courts had become.
Think about the tragedy.
The place intended to testify to the holiness and mercy of God had become associated with exploitation and obstruction.
Religion had become busy…
while missing the heart of God.
And Jesus overturned the tables.
There are moments when grace comforts you.
There are also moments when grace flips the table you keep hiding behind.
We usually want Jesus to enter our lives as Comforter.
We want Him near our anxiety.
Near our grief.
Near our financial struggle.
Near our broken relationships.
Near our sickness.
Near the prayers that seem unanswered.
And He is compassionate beyond what we understand.
But the Jesus who comforts wounded sinners is the same Jesus who confronts cherished sin.
We cannot invite Him into the Temple and then tell Him which tables He is allowed to touch.
That secret relationship?
He sees it.
That dishonest business practice?
He sees it.
That pornography nobody knows about?
He sees it.
That obsession with approval?
He sees it.
That resentment you keep rehearsing?
He sees it.
That pride hiding underneath your theology?
He sees it.
That public Christianity masking a private collapse?
He sees it.
And maybe you are reading this thinking, Then I am finished.
No.
This is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Jesus did not enter Jerusalem merely to expose corrupted worship.
He entered Jerusalem knowing He was walking toward a cross.
Within days, the hands that overturned tables would be pierced.
The voice that confronted hypocrisy would cry out from Golgotha.
The One examining the Temple would Himself become the sacrifice.
Jesus did not come merely to identify sinners.
He came to save them.
He did not expose darkness because He enjoyed humiliation.
He brought darkness into the light because darkness destroys the people He loves.
This is the difference between condemnation and Gospel conviction.
Condemnation whispers:
“Hide from God.”
The Gospel says:
“Run to Christ.”
Condemnation says:
“You have sinned, therefore there is no hope.”
The Gospel says:
“You have sinned, therefore you desperately need the Savior who died for sinners.”
Repentance is not paying Jesus back.
You cannot.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the One whose mercy you could never purchase.
Christianity is not Jesus helping good people become slightly better.
Christianity announces that sinners can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
The scandal is that we were guilty.
The grace is that Christ came for the guilty.
The scandal is that our leaves could not save us.
The grace is that His blood can.
The scandal is that God sees everything.
The grace is that the God who sees everything still calls sinners to come.
And there is another chilling moment after Jesus’ confrontations in Jerusalem.
Later, as He was leaving the Temple, one of His disciples drew attention to its magnificent stones and buildings.
The Greek text of Mark 13 begins:
Καὶ ἐκπορευομένου αὐτοῦ ἐκ τοῦ ἱεροῦ…
Kai ekporeuomenou autou ek tou hierou…
“And as He was going out of the temple…”
A disciple effectively says, Teacher, look at these stones. Look at these buildings.
Jesus responds with a prophecy of devastating judgment: these great buildings would be brought down; not one stone would be left upon another.
Imagine the weight of that departure.
The disciples saw magnificent stones.
Jesus saw approaching judgment.
They were impressed by the building.
Jesus was concerned with faithfulness to God.
And this is where you and I have to stop reading about “those religious people” and allow the text to interrogate us.
What if Jesus walked through your Christianity tonight?
Not your church building.
Your Christianity.
What would He find?
If He looked around at everything…
your thoughts,
your spending,
your private conversations,
your ambitions,
your entertainment,
your relationships,
your resentment,
your generosity,
your prayer life,
your treatment of people who cannot benefit you,
your hidden compromises,
your Sunday worship,
your Monday decisions…
what would He find?
Fruit?
Or leaves?
Do not answer quickly.
Some questions deserve silence.
Because one day every performance ends.
Every carefully managed reputation disappears.
Every title becomes irrelevant.
Every follower count becomes meaningless.
Every excuse collapses.
And you stand before the One who has always known the truth.
But if you belong to Christ, that truth does not need to drive you into hopelessness.
It should drive you into repentance.
Because the Jesus who overturns tables is also the Jesus who went to the cross.
He knows the worst thing about you more completely than you know it yourself.
And the invitation of the Gospel remains:
Come.
Repent.
Believe.
Stop hiding.
Stop decorating the leaves.
Stop defending the table.
Let Christ overturn whatever must be overturned.
Maybe the table is lust.
Maybe it is pride.
Maybe money has become your functional god.
Maybe it is bitterness toward someone who wounded you.
Maybe it is a secret habit you have repeatedly promised to quit.
Maybe you have spent years looking Christian while slowly becoming numb to Christ.
Then do not merely feel something while reading this.
Turn to Him.
Confess honestly.
Ask for mercy.
Trust Jesus Christ—not your religious record, not your goodness, not your ability to fix yourself.
And if you have fallen again after promising God you never would, hear this carefully:
Your answer is not better camouflage.
Your answer is Christ.
You do not need better leaves.
You need life.
Maybe that is why you encountered these words today.
Not so you could say, “Powerful article.”
Not so you could feel emotional for sixty seconds and continue exactly as before.
Maybe Jesus is putting His finger on something.
Pray:

Jesus Christ, You see everything. You know what I have hidden, defended, excused, and feared admitting. I cannot cleanse myself. Forgive me. Have mercy on me. Expose what must be exposed. Remove what must be removed. Teach me genuine repentance. Make my life fruitful for Your glory. I trust not in my performance, but in Your death and resurrection. Make me Yours completely. Amen.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, be honest enough to say it.
Do not keep this article trapped on your screen.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not. We are saved by grace, not social-media activity.
But if this message faithfully points people toward Jesus, then sharing it can become one small act of witness.
You may never know.
Share it anyway.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly.
Not to purchase God's blessing.
Not to prove your faith.
Not because God needs your money.
But because Gospel ministry in the digital world still requires people willing to support the work that places biblical truth in front of another exhausted soul at two in the morning.

If glorifying God is truly your desire, one practical way to participate is to use what He has entrusted to you—your voice, your influence, your sharing, your generosity—to help sound biblical teaching reach others. Scripture never permits us to turn financial support into a test of salvation, but it does repeatedly call believers toward willing generosity and partnership in Gospel work.
while tables desperately need overturning inside.
And remember the scene.
Jesus enters.
Jesus looks.
Jesus sees everything.
Yet the story does not end with Him looking.
He walks toward the cross.
That is the wonder at the center of Christianity.
The One who knew exactly what was inside us was the One who willingly gave Himself for sinners.
So when Jesus comes near the tables you have spent years protecting, do not run from Him.
Let them fall.
Because sometimes the sound of a table crashing is the sound of grace finally reaching the room you kept locked.
You do not have to spend the rest of your life protecting what Jesus died to redeem.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Sentence We Don’t Want to Hear: The Shocking Truth Hidden in Ecclesiastes 7:29
paragraphs: The Sentence We Don’t Want to Hear: The Shocking Truth Hidden in Ecclesiastes 7:29
God made humanity upright. We became experts at finding another way. And hidden inside that uncomfortable sentence is the reason the Gospel is such astonishingly good news.
There is something frightening about realizing that the thing ruining your life may not always be the thing that happened to you.
Sometimes it is the thing growing inside you.
The excuse you keep protecting.
The desire you keep feeding.
The resentment you keep rehearsing.
The compromise you renamed “freedom.”
The secret you promised yourself would happen only once.
The version of yourself you constructed so carefully that eventually even you forgot it was a mask.
Ecclesiastes contains a sentence that strips away our favorite explanations with almost surgical precision:

“Lo, this only have I found, that God hath made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions.”
—Ecclesiastes 7:29, KJV
Read that slowly.
God made man upright.
But they sought out many inventions.
That word “inventions” can sound strangely harmless to modern ears. It can make the verse sound as though Solomon is criticizing human creativity.
He is not.
The Hebrew is far more penetrating.
The key words are:
הָאֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת־הָאָדָם יָשָׁר
ha’Elohim ‘asah et-ha’adam yashar
“God made humankind upright.”
Then comes the devastating contrast:
וְהֵמָּה בִקְשׁוּ חִשְּׁבֹנוֹת רַבִּים
vehemmah viqshu chishvonot rabbim
“But they have sought many schemes.”
The Hebrew word יָשָׁר — yashar carries the sense of being straight, right, upright.
Then Solomon deliberately places that straightness against humanity's חִשְּׁבֹנוֹת — chishvonot: calculations, devices, reasonings, schemes, contrivances.
That changes the way you hear the verse.
God did not create evil humanity and then become disappointed that evil humanity acted evil.
The biblical story is far more tragic.
God's creation was good.
Humanity rebelled.
And we have been devising crooked alternatives to God's good order ever since.
Ecclesiastes 7:29 is not an isolated philosophical thought. It echoes the opening chapters of Genesis.
God creates humanity in His image.

“So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them.”
—Genesis 1:27, KJV
Then Genesis says:

“And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good.”
—Genesis 1:31, KJV
Very good.
That matters.
Because Christianity does not teach that sin exists because God designed humanity morally corrupt and then punished us for functioning according to His design.
Scripture places responsibility for rebellion where it belongs.
Human beings distrusted God.
Human beings reached for what God had forbidden.
Human beings wanted wisdom apart from submission to the One who is Wisdom.
And something shattered.
The serpent's ancient temptation was not merely about fruit.
It was about authority.
“Did God really say?”
Behind countless sins is essentially the same question.
Does God really get to decide what is good?
We still ask it.
We simply learned how to make it sound sophisticated.
God says forgive.
We calculate why bitterness is justified.
God says flee sexual immorality.
We construct explanations for why our circumstances make compromise understandable.
God says tell the truth.
We discover seventeen different names for lying.
God says love your enemy.
We build entire identities around despising ours.
God says repent.
We call repentance shame.
God says surrender.
We call surrender oppression.
God says holiness.
We say, “But this is who I am.”
חִשְּׁבֹנוֹת רַבִּים.
Chishvonot rabbim.
Many schemes.
Many calculations.
Many human attempts to make crookedness appear straight.
And perhaps the most dangerous scheme is the one in which we manage to convince ourselves that everybody is responsible for our sin except us.
Yes, people can wound us terribly.
Some wounds were never invited.
Some betrayals were never deserved.
Some people carry memories they would erase in a heartbeat if they could.
The Bible never requires us to pretend evil done against us was acceptable.
But Scripture also refuses to let another person's sin become permission for ours.
That distinction can hurt.
Because eventually the Gospel brings us to a mirror.
And there are moments when the Holy Spirit does not allow us to keep pointing through the glass at everyone else.
Eventually the finger turns around.
Maybe they really did betray you.
But what has bitterness been turning you into?
Maybe they abandoned you.
But what have you begun worshiping because you desperately need never to feel abandoned again?
Maybe someone shattered your trust.
But have you now made self-protection your god?
Maybe you were humiliated.
But how many people have you wounded trying to prove you are no longer weak?
Maybe you were rejected.
But how much compromise have you accepted because you became terrified of being unwanted?
This is where Ecclesiastes stops being an ancient book and walks straight into the room.
God made humanity upright.
We sought many schemes.
And eventually our schemes become prisons.
That secret relationship.
That hidden browser history.
That quiet envy.
That carefully curated Christian image.
That addiction nobody knows about.
That private arrogance hidden beneath public ministry.
That unforgiveness you have rehearsed so many times it now feels like personality.
That hunger for applause.
That obsession with money.
That need to be noticed.
That spiritual exhaustion caused by trying to appear spiritually alive.
We are extraordinarily talented at hiding.
Adam was too.
After humanity's rebellion, one of the first things fallen people did was cover themselves.
Then they hid.
Then came blame.
The pattern is ancient.
Sin.
Shame.
Covering.
Hiding.
Blaming.
And we are still doing it.
Different century.
Different clothing.
Different technology.
Same human heart.
But there is another movement in Genesis that we often rush past.
God came looking.
“Where art thou?”
Not because the omniscient God had misplaced Adam.
The question exposed Adam.
Where are you?
Maybe that question has traveled thousands of years to reach you.
Where are you?
Not where does everybody think you are.
Not what does your church attendance communicate.
Not what does your family believe about you.
Where are you?
When the room becomes quiet...
when the phone is down...
when nobody is applauding...
when nobody is watching...
where are you with God?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
And perhaps your instinct is to hide.
But please understand something before shame tells you to run.
Conviction is not Christ telling you to disappear.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners who deserve judgment can be reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Ecclesiastes tells us humanity wandered into schemes.
The Gospel tells us God entered human history to rescue schemers.
Jesus did not come merely to improve our calculations.
He came to save us.
The One through whom all things were made stepped into the wreckage of what sin had done.
Jesus lived the righteous life we have not lived.
He obeyed where Adam rebelled.
He remained faithful where we wander.
He resisted temptation where we rationalize it.
He loved perfectly where we love selectively.
He obeyed the Father even unto death.
Then He went to the cross.
And suddenly the scandal becomes grace.
At Calvary, humanity's rebellion and God's mercy collide.
Christ was not crucified because human beings needed motivational improvement.
The cross tells us our condition was far worse than that.
We needed reconciliation.
Forgiveness.
Atonement.
Redemption.
New life.
Paul writes:
—Romans 5:19, KJV
Do you see the breathtaking reversal?
Adam's disobedience.
Christ's obedience.
Humanity running.
Christ coming.
Humanity hiding.
Christ seeking.
Humanity scheming.
Christ redeeming.
Humanity accumulating guilt.
Christ bearing sin.
Humanity reaching for fig leaves.
Christ stretching His hands upon a cross.
And when Jesus died, He was not pretending sin was insignificant.
Grace is not God shrugging at evil.
Grace cost blood.
The sin we excuse was serious enough that the Son of God went to Calvary.
And the sinner we think may be beyond redemption was loved enough that Christ willingly went there.
That is why Christianity cannot end with “be a better person.”
The Gospel is not cosmetic surgery for respectable sinners.
It is resurrection for the spiritually dead.
Paul writes:
—2 Corinthians 5:17, KJV
In Christ.
Those two words change everything.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Your sin is real.
Judgment is real.
Repentance is necessary.
But mercy is real too.
Forgiveness is real.
The cross is sufficient.
The tomb is empty.
Jesus Christ is alive.
And the person who turns to Christ in repentant faith does not merely receive religious advice.
He receives Christ.
Maybe you have spent years creating chishvonot—schemes for surviving without surrendering.
Perhaps you have calculated exactly how Christian you can appear while still protecting the one thing Jesus keeps touching.
Maybe nobody knows.
But you know.
And God knows.
You can keep constructing explanations.
Or you can finally come home.
You do not have to clean yourself before coming to Christ as though your righteousness could purchase His attention.
Come confessing.
Come repenting.
