Come believing.
Come empty-handed.
Come without the performance.
Come without the Christian vocabulary designed to disguise the condition of your heart.
Come saying, “Jesus, I have sinned. Have mercy on me.”
Because the Savior who exposes sin is also the Savior who receives repentant sinners.
Remember the woman caught in adultery.
Scandal surrounded her.
Accusation surrounded her.
Her sin was not called righteousness.
Yet neither was her story allowed to end beneath the stones of her accusers.
Jesus showed mercy and called her away from sin.
That is grace.
Not permission to remain chained.
Power to walk away from the chain.
Christ does not redeem your scandal so you can decorate it.
He redeems you so that your life can belong to Him.
Maybe that is what somebody reading this needs more than another comfortable devotional.
Not another spiritual sedative.
Not another sentence telling you that everything you desire must automatically be God's desire.
Maybe you need the terrifying mercy of being told the truth:
You cannot save yourself.
Neither can your intelligence.
Neither can your morality.
Neither can your religious reputation.
Neither can your trauma become righteousness.
Neither can your excuses erase guilt.
Neither can your schemes straighten the human heart.
But Jesus saves sinners.
That sentence has rescued murderers.
Adulterers.
Liars.
Religious hypocrites.
The proud.
The broken.
The ashamed.
The addicted.
The self-righteous.
People who destroyed things they loved and wondered afterward whether God could possibly want them.
The answer of the Gospel is not that their sins never mattered.
The answer is that Jesus Christ is a greater Savior than repentant sinners imagined.
So perhaps Ecclesiastes 7:29 is not merely telling us what went wrong.
Perhaps it is preparing us to understand why redemption is necessary.
God made humanity upright.
Humanity sought many schemes.
And Scripture's great story moves toward the One who can make sinners right with God.
That is why the message of Gospel Warrior will always return here.
Not to us.
Not to a personality.
Not to merchandise.
Not to an algorithm.
To Jesus Christ.
And if this exposed something you have kept hidden, do not merely scroll into the next distraction.
Talk to God.
Confess it.
Repent.
Ask Christ for mercy.
Then tell somebody you trust who will help you walk faithfully.
Maybe your confession is different.
There is no shame in admitting you need prayer.
Someone else reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person fighting to come back to God.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
It cannot.
Jesus cannot be bought.
Grace cannot be purchased.
Salvation is God's gift, received through faith in Christ.
But if Christ has given you truth worth carrying, you can help carry it.
Return to Ecclesiastes 7:29 the next time your heart becomes exceptionally skilled at explaining away what God is asking you to surrender.

Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelieving friends to follow as well. Sometimes one shared truth becomes the doorway to a conversation you never expected to have.
Do it to support the work—not to purchase God's approval.
The Gospel is Jesus.
Christ crucified for sinners.
Christ risen from the dead.
Christ calling sinners to repent and believe.
Christ forgiving.
Christ restoring.
Christ transforming.
Christ making all things new.
Ecclesiastes 7:29 begins with the tragedy of humanity searching for countless crooked ways.
But your story does not have to end inside one of them.
You can stop hiding.
You can stop defending what God is asking you to confess.
You can stop trying to calculate a life where you get Jesus as Savior while remaining your own lord.
Turn around.
Come home.
There is grace at the cross for sinners who finally stop pretending they do not need it.
And perhaps this is the sentence worth carrying with you after everything else fades:
You may have spent years inventing ways to run from God, but one blood-stained cross still stands on the road home.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DID JESUS DIE TO SET YOU FREE—OR TO PUT YOU UNDER ANOTHER RELIGIOUS SYSTEM?
paragraphs: DID JESUS DIE TO SET YOU FREE—OR TO PUT YOU UNDER ANOTHER RELIGIOUS SYSTEM?

What if some of what you have called “Christian obedience” is actually fear wearing church clothes—and what if the freedom Jesus purchased is far more radical, holy, and beautiful than simply replacing one prison with another?
There is a kind of Christianity that can leave a person exhausted.
You know the language.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know which verses to post.
You know how to smile when somebody asks how you are doing.
You know how to raise your hands while your heart is quietly collapsing.
And somewhere along the way, without deliberately choosing it, your relationship with Jesus can begin to feel less like being rescued and more like being monitored.
Read enough.
Pray enough.
Serve enough.
Give enough.
Look spiritual enough.
Never admit too much.
Never struggle too publicly.
Never ask the question everybody else seems afraid to ask.
Because what if they discover you still have battles?

What if they discover that underneath the worship songs, Bible verses, church attendance, and Christian vocabulary, there are wounds you have not understood, temptations you have not completely conquered, questions you are frightened to voice, and nights when God feels painfully silent?
So you try harder.
And harder.
And harder.
Until one day a terrifying question rises from somewhere deep inside you:
Did Jesus really die to set me free… or did He simply transfer me into another religious system?
Stay with that question.
Because answering it carelessly can lead to two opposite disasters.
One person hears “freedom” and decides Christianity must mean freedom from commandments, repentance, holiness, accountability, and obedience.

Another hears “obedience” and builds a Christianity dominated by fear, human rules, spiritual performance, comparison, condemnation, and the desperate attempt to earn what Christ said could only be received by grace.
Both miss something breathtaking about the Gospel.
Jesus did not die to make sin comfortable.
But neither did He die to make religious slavery respectable.
He came to rescue sinners and make them His.
Paul wrote words so explosive that Christians have been wrestling with their implications for centuries:
Τῇ ἐλευθερίᾳ ἡμᾶς Χριστὸς ἠλευθέρωσεν.
“For freedom Christ has set us free.”
That is Galatians 5:1.

The Greek word ἐλευθερίᾳ — eleutheria speaks of freedom or liberty. Paul then uses ἠλευθέρωσεν — ēleutherōsen, from eleutheroō: to liberate, to set free. The sentence practically reverberates with freedom: Christ liberated us for freedom.
But Paul does not stop there.
στήκετε… καὶ μὴ πάλιν ζυγῷ δουλείας ἐνέχεσθε
Stand firm… and do not become entangled again in a yoke of slavery.
The word ζυγῷ — zygō means a yoke.
Picture it.
Something placed across the neck.
Something under which you are compelled to labor.

Paul was writing in a specific controversy. False teachers were pressuring Gentile believers toward circumcision and reliance upon observance of the Mosaic law in a way that compromised justification through Christ. Paul becomes astonishingly severe because the sufficiency of Christ is at stake. Galatians 5 continues by warning that the person seeking justification through law places himself under an obligation to keep the whole law.
So we need to be careful here.
Paul is not saying, “Jesus freed you, therefore holiness no longer matters.”
He is saying something far more powerful:
Stop trying to make yourself right with God through a system of achievement when God has provided righteousness through Christ.
There is a difference between obeying God because you are terrified that He will stop loving you…
…and obeying God because, in Christ, you have been loved beyond anything you deserved.
One produces slavery.
The other produces worship.
And perhaps this is where the Gospel becomes painfully personal.
Some of us learned how to fear failure before we learned how to understand grace.
Maybe somebody made you believe God was perpetually disappointed in you.
Maybe Christianity was presented almost entirely as a list of things you were forbidden to do.
Maybe you learned to hide your struggles because everyone around you seemed victorious.
Maybe you secretly believed that mature Christians never wrestled with doubt, temptation, loneliness, anger, sexual brokenness, shame, anxiety, resentment, or spiritual exhaustion.
So when those things appeared in you, you did not run toward Jesus.
You hid from Him.
Exactly as Adam hid.
And religion can become remarkably useful for hiding.
You can hide behind ministry.
Hide behind theology.
Hide behind Christian posts.
Hide behind arguments.
Hide behind perfect church attendance.
Hide behind serving everybody while refusing to admit that your own soul is bleeding.
You can even hide behind holiness language while privately wondering whether God could possibly love the person underneath the performance.
But then Jesus walks straight into the hiding place.
And He does not say sin does not matter.
The cross proves that sin matters more terribly than we often comprehend.
Christ does something infinitely better than pretending sin is harmless.
He bears it.
The Gospel is not God lowering His holiness until sinners become acceptable.
It is God accomplishing in Christ what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
Jesus lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He went willingly toward the cross.
He bore judgment.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
The scandal of grace is not that God suddenly stopped caring about righteousness.
The scandal is that the righteous Son of God stood where guilty people deserved to stand so guilty people could receive what they could never earn.
That is why Christian freedom can never mean, “Now I can sin however I want.”
Paul destroys that interpretation in Romans 6.
He asks whether grace means believers should continue in sin.
His answer is emphatic: absolutely not.
And then comes another statement that initially sounds almost contradictory:
ἐλευθερωθέντες δὲ ἀπὸ τῆς ἁμαρτίας ἐδουλώθητε τῇ δικαιοσύνῃ
“Having been set free from sin, you became slaves of righteousness.”
Notice the movement.
ἐλευθερωθέντες — eleutherōthentes: having been set free.
Then:
ἐδουλώθητε — edoulōthēte: you became enslaved.
Freedom…and slavery?
Yes.
Because biblical freedom is not ultimately the freedom to belong to nobody.
It is liberation from the tyrant who was destroying you so that you may belong to the King who gives you life.

Romans 6 says believers have been liberated from sin and become servants of righteousness, leading toward holiness; the chapter culminates by contrasting sin's wages—death—with God's gift of eternal life in Christ Jesus.
That changes everything.
Jesus did not free the alcoholic so alcohol could remain his master.
He did not free the sexually broken so lust could remain king.
He did not free the bitter so resentment could keep occupying the throne.
He did not free the greedy so money could become god.
He did not free the proud so self could remain sovereign.
He did not free us for sin.
He freed us from sin.
And that means grace is far more radical than permission.
Grace does not look at your chains and say, “Those chains are fine.”
Grace breaks them.
Sometimes immediately.
Sometimes through a long, painful process of sanctification in which you stumble, confess, rise, learn, surrender, and discover again and again that Jesus is more faithful than you imagined.
But grace never makes peace with the prison.
And here is where some believers desperately need to hear the other half.
Your obedience does not purchase God's acceptance.
Jesus already paid a price you could never pay.
You do not pray enough to make the Father finally love you.
You do not read enough chapters to purchase adoption.
You do not serve enough ministries to erase yesterday.
You do not give enough money to buy forgiveness.
You do not manufacture justification through religious exhaustion.
Salvation is not Christ doing ninety-nine percent while you desperately accomplish the final one.
Christ is not an assistant to your self-salvation project.
Christ is the Savior.
And when that finally moves from theological vocabulary into the terrified chambers of the human heart, something begins to change.
You start praying differently.
Not, “God, maybe if I pray long enough You will finally tolerate me.”
But, “Father, because of Christ, I can come.”
You read Scripture differently.
Not, “Maybe these chapters will make me worthy today.”
But, “Speak, Lord. I belong to You.”
You repent differently.
Not, “I must hide this before God discovers who I really am.”
But, “Jesus already knows. I am done running.”
That is freedom.
Not sinlessness overnight.
Not independence from God.
Not Christianity without truth.
Not spirituality without doctrine.
Not grace without repentance.
Freedom is discovering that the door of the prison has been opened by Someone whose hands still carry scars.
And maybe you have spent years standing inside an unlocked cell.
Maybe Jesus has already declared freedom while shame keeps whispering:
Stay inside.
Maybe people remember your scandal.
Jesus remembers your surrender.
People may know what you did.
Jesus knows what He is making you.
People may introduce you by your worst chapter.
Jesus is still writing the book.
That is why our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior remains:
Not because consequences magically disappear.
Not because repentance becomes unnecessary.
Not because every broken relationship instantly repairs itself.
But because your worst chapter does not possess greater authority than the blood of Jesus Christ.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Corinthian church was filled with people whose former lives included devastating patterns of sin.
Yet Scripture's story is repeatedly the story of God taking people who should have been finished and writing grace where everyone expected a grave.
And perhaps that is exactly why you are still reading.
Maybe nobody knows how tired you are.
Maybe you love Jesus, but religion has exhausted you.
Maybe you have confused conviction with condemnation.
Conviction says, “Come out of that darkness.”
Condemnation whispers, “Stay there. God doesn't want someone like you.”
Conviction leads you toward Christ.
Condemnation makes you hide from Him.
The Holy Spirit exposes sin not because God delights in humiliating His children, but because God loves us too deeply to leave us chained to what is killing us.
So stop running.
Not from church attendance.
Not from Christian community.
Not from biblical teaching.
Not from obedience.
Run from the idea that any of those things can replace Jesus.
A church cannot die for you.
A denomination cannot justify you.
A pastor cannot carry your sins.
A religious reputation cannot resurrect you.
A ministry title cannot cleanse your conscience.
Your theological knowledge cannot substitute for knowing Christ.
There is only one Savior.
Jesus.
And if Christianity has become nothing more than managing appearances, perhaps today is the day the performance ends.
Tell Him the truth.
“Jesus, I have been hiding.”
“Jesus, I have been performing.”
“Jesus, I have been trying to earn what You offered through grace.”
Or perhaps your confession is different:
“Jesus, I have used grace as an excuse to protect a sin I do not want to surrender.”
Whatever it is…
bring the real thing.
Christ did not die for the fictional version of you that you present to religious people.
He came for sinners.
Real ones.
And real grace produces real transformation.
So no—Jesus did not die merely to move you from one meaningless religious cage into another.
But neither did He die so you could crown yourself king.
He freed you from sin, condemnation, and futile attempts at self-justification so that you could belong completely, joyfully, eternally to Him.
Christianity is not freedom from Jesus.
Christianity is freedom in Jesus.
And when you understand that, obedience stops being an entrance fee into God's family.
It becomes the response of someone who has already been welcomed home.
You begin wanting holiness not because holiness purchases heaven, but because you have encountered the Holy One.
You forgive because you were forgiven.
You love because He loved you first.
You give because you received freely.
You serve because the King served you.
You repent because darkness no longer feels like home.
And slowly, sometimes painfully, the chains begin falling.
One lie at a time.
One confession at a time.
One surrender at a time.
One morning when you choose Christ instead of the old addiction.
One night when you forgive the person whose name still hurts.
One prayer whispered through tears.
One Scripture opened when you wanted to quit.
One more step toward Jesus.
That is discipleship.
Be honest.
Someone reading silently may desperately need evidence that Jesus is still restoring lives.
Not as a superstition. Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
There may come a night when shame returns with an old accusation, and you will need to remember what Scripture actually says:
Christ set us free.
Because perhaps the question was never merely whether Jesus came to remove your chains.
Perhaps the deeper question is whether you will finally stop picking them back up.
The hands that broke your chains are scarred because your freedom was never cheap.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DID GOD CALL JEREMIAH SO YOUNG?
paragraphs:
WHY DID GOD CALL JEREMIAH SO YOUNG?
He Said, “I Am Only a Youth.” God’s Answer Still Confronts Every Person Who Thinks They’re Too Young, Too Weak, Too Broken, or Too Unqualified to Be Used.
There is something frightening about being called by God before you feel ready.
Not frightening because God is cruel.
Frightening because sometimes God speaks into your life while you are still staring at everything you think disqualifies you.
You see your age.
Your weakness.
Your past.
Your lack of experience.
Your trembling voice.
Your secret failures.
God sees something else.
And Jeremiah discovered this in one of the most unsettling call narratives in Scripture.
He did not introduce himself as fearless.
He did not tell God, “I have been waiting for this.”
He did not respond like someone who believed he was destined for greatness.
He basically said:
You have the wrong person.
And perhaps that is why his story reaches so deeply into ours.
Because some of us know exactly what it feels like to believe God could use somebody...
just not us.
Then Jeremiah 1 takes us into a conversation that destroys that excuse.
God tells Jeremiah:
“Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you.”
The Hebrew is breathtaking:
בְּטֶרֶם אֶצָּרְךָ בַבֶּטֶן יְדַעְתִּיךָ
Beterem etzorkha va-beten yeda'tikha.
“Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you.”
Then:
וּבְטֶרֶם תֵּצֵא מֵרֶחֶם הִקְדַּשְׁתִּיךָ
U-veterem tetze me-rechem hiqdash'tikha.
“Before you came out from the womb, I consecrated you.”
And then comes the assignment:
נָבִיא לַגּוֹיִם נְתַתִּיךָ
Navi la-goyim netattikha.
“I appointed you a prophet to the nations.”
Jeremiah's calling did not begin with Jeremiah's confidence.
It began with God's purpose.
That distinction changes everything.
Jeremiah responds:
אֲהָהּ אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה הִנֵּה לֹא־יָדַעְתִּי דַּבֵּר כִּי־נַעַר אָנֹכִי
Ahah, Adonai YHWH... lo-yada'ti dabber, ki-na'ar anokhi.
“Ah, Lord GOD! Look, I do not know how to speak, because I am a na'ar.”
That Hebrew word matters.
נַעַר — na'ar.

It can describe a boy, youth, young man, or young servant depending on context. Jeremiah certainly presents his youth as a reason he feels inadequate, but Scripture does not give us his exact numerical age here.
That matters because Christians sometimes confidently say Jeremiah was seventeen, eighteen, twenty, or another specific age.
The biblical text does not tell us.
We should not pretend God said something He did not say.
What Scripture does tell us is more powerful anyway.
Jeremiah considered himself young enough that his youth seemed like a legitimate objection to the assignment God had just placed before him.
And God did not respond by giving Jeremiah an inspirational speech about believing in himself.
That is one of the most beautiful details in the entire passage.
God never says:
“Jeremiah, believe in yourself.”
He says, in effect:
Stop making your inadequacy the final authority over My command.
The Hebrew begins:
אַל־תֹּאמַר נַעַר אָנֹכִי
Al-tomar na'ar anokhi.
“Do not say, ‘I am a youth.’”
Why?
Because:
“To everyone I send you, you shall go, and whatever I command you, you shall speak.”
Then comes the sentence every frightened servant of God eventually has to learn:
אַל־תִּירָא מִפְּנֵיהֶם כִּי־אִתְּךָ אֲנִי
Al-tira mipneihem, ki-itkha ani.
“Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you.”
There it is.
The secret was never Jeremiah.
It was the presence of God.
God did not call Jeremiah because youth automatically makes someone spiritually superior.
He did not call him because young people are somehow more important than older believers.
And this passage should never be twisted into the idea that every ambition we have was secretly ordained before birth.
Jeremiah 1 describes Jeremiah's prophetic commission.
But the principle revealed through his calling reaches far beyond him:
God's ability to accomplish His purposes is not limited by the weakness of the people He chooses to obey Him.
Think about what God was actually asking this young prophet to do.
Jeremiah would not become a celebrity preacher surrounded by applause.
He was being sent into national rebellion.
He would speak during the final decades of Judah before Jerusalem's catastrophic fall.
He would confront kings.
Priests.
False prophets.
Leaders.
An entire culture desperately resistant to the truth.
He would announce judgment when people wanted reassurance.
He would weep when others refused to repent.
He would be mocked.
Threatened.
Beaten.
Imprisoned.
Thrown into a cistern.
Accused of betrayal.
His prophetic ministry would stretch across decades of political upheaval and eventually into the catastrophe of Jerusalem's destruction.
So why call someone who already felt too young?
Perhaps the better question is:
Why do we assume God waits until His servants feel sufficient?
Moses said he was not eloquent.
Gideon pointed toward his weakness.
Isaiah became painfully aware of his uncleanness.
Jeremiah pointed toward his youth.
Peter eventually collapsed beneath the shame of denying Jesus.
Paul never forgot that he had persecuted the church.
Again and again, Scripture refuses to build God's kingdom around human self-sufficiency.
Because when God works through weakness, the weakness cannot take the glory.
And this is where Jeremiah's story stops being ancient history and starts becoming uncomfortable.
Maybe your sentence is not:
“I am too young.”
Maybe yours is:
“I have already wasted too many years.”
“I don't know enough Scripture.”
“My family knows who I used to be.”
“I failed God too many times.”
“I am ashamed of what I did.”
“I am too ordinary.”
“I don't speak well.”
“I am scared people will laugh.”
“I am still fighting sins nobody knows about.”
“I don't think God could possibly want me anymore.”
Different sentence.
Same hiding place.
We become experts at explaining to God why obedience should wait.
Until we are stronger.
Until the fear disappears.
Until our finances improve.
Until people approve.
Until the addiction is forgotten.
Until our reputation is repaired.
Until we know more.
Until life becomes convenient.
But what if the question has never been whether you feel ready?
What if the question is whether Christ is worthy of your yes?
There is another reason Jeremiah matters so profoundly to Christians.
Jeremiah's story ultimately belongs inside the larger story of redemption that reaches its fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
Jeremiah warned of judgment, exposed sin, confronted false religion, and called a rebellious people back toward God.
But Jeremiah also announced hope.
Through him God promised something astonishing:
a new covenant.
Jeremiah 31:31 declares:
הִנֵּה יָמִים בָּאִים ... וְכָרַתִּי ... בְּרִית חֲדָשָׁה
Hineh yamim ba'im... ve-kharatti... berit chadashah.
“Behold, days are coming... when I will make... a new covenant.”
בְּרִית חֲדָשָׁה — berit chadashah.
A new covenant.
God promised His law written upon hearts.
He promised relationship.
He promised forgiveness.
And centuries later, on the night before His crucifixion, Jesus lifted the cup and identified His coming sacrificial death with the new covenant.
Jeremiah stood in the ruins announcing a promise.
Jesus came to accomplish redemption through His blood.
And suddenly Jeremiah's story becomes even bigger.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of frightened people learning how amazing they secretly are.
It is the story of sinners discovering how sufficient Christ truly is.
You do not need a motivational version of Jesus who exists to improve your self-esteem.
You need the crucified and risen Son of God.
The Christ who carried sin.
The Christ who calls sinners to repentance.
The Christ who forgives.
The Christ who restores.
The Christ who transforms.
The Christ who walked out of the grave.
Maybe you have spent years believing your scandal disqualified you.
Look at the Gospel.
Peter denied Jesus.
Grace restored him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Grace transformed him into a preacher of the faith he once tried to destroy.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Yet he turned toward Jesus.
And Christ gave him hope beyond the grave.
This is why our message will always be:
Not because sin does not matter.
Because sin matters so much that Christ went to the cross.
Grace is not God pretending rebellion is harmless.
Grace is God doing for guilty sinners what guilty sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by pretending your wounds never happened.
Not by deleting repentance.
But by taking sinners who turn to Him and giving them something scandal could never manufacture:
forgiveness.
A new identity.
A new direction.
A new Master.
A new hope.
A new life.
Maybe the deepest reason Jeremiah's youth bothers us is because it removes one of our favorite excuses.
God knew Jeremiah's limitations when He called him.
Jeremiah's weakness was not information God had somehow overlooked.
And neither is yours.
Christ knows exactly what He is rescuing when He rescues you.
He knows the chapter you never tell anyone.
He knows the browser history.
The resentment.
The relapse.
The secret pride.
The private tears.
The prayer life that has almost disappeared.
The compromise everyone else thinks you defeated years ago.
He knows.
And the Gospel does not tell you to hide it better.
It tells you to bring your sin into the light, repent, and run toward Christ.
Maybe somebody reading this right now has been pretending for months.
You post Christian things.
You know Christian vocabulary.
You smile at church.
People ask how you are doing.
“I'm good.”
But you know you are drifting.
You know prayer has become rare.
You know compromise has become normal.
You know something inside you is getting colder.
And perhaps underneath all of it sits one terrifying thought:
Maybe I have gone too far.
Listen carefully.
Do not confuse conviction with a command to run away from Jesus.
Run toward Him.
Confess.
Repent.
Come back.
The cross exists precisely because sinners need mercy.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9
You do not clean yourself before coming to the One who cleanses sinners.
Come.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, don't manufacture a polished religious response.
Be honest.
No performance.
Sometimes three words are enough to stop suffering alone.
And maybe you know someone who needs this.
Not “someone” in the abstract.
You can see their face right now.
The teenager convinced they are useless.
The young believer terrified of their calling.
The father ashamed of his failures.
The mother quietly exhausted.
The friend who stopped going to church.
The person who thinks their scandal became the final chapter.
Send this to them.
Not because an algorithm deserves your loyalty.
Because somebody scrolling at 1:17 in the morning may desperately need to discover that failure does not have to be the last sentence when Jesus Christ enters the story.
There may come a night when you are the person who needs to read it again.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, consider staying close to this work.
Supporting Christian ministry should never be treated as purchasing God's favor. Grace cannot be bought, salvation cannot be purchased, and sharing a post does not make someone righteous before God.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedient lives of worship, generosity, love, truth, and service.
If God has used this ministry to feed you, and you are able to support it, consider becoming part of the people who help us keep feeding others.
Not as a transaction with God.
Not to prove you are spiritual.
Do it because truth worth receiving is truth worth carrying.
Because somewhere beyond your screen may be another Jeremiah whispering:
“I can't.”
And maybe God will use what you share to remind them:
The question was never whether they were impressive enough.
The question was whether God would be with them.
Jeremiah was young.
Jeremiah was afraid.
Jeremiah felt inadequate.
And God knew all of that before Jeremiah ever opened his mouth.
That is the part I hope follows you after you close this article.
Your weakness may explain why you are afraid.
It does not determine what God is capable of doing through surrendered obedience.
So repent where repentance is needed.
Return where you have wandered.
Forgive where bitterness has hardened you.
Confess what darkness has been feeding.
Obey what Christ has already made clear.
And stop waiting to become impressive enough to need Jesus less.
You never will.
That was never the goal.
The goal is Christ.
His glory.
His Gospel.
His grace.
His transforming power.
And perhaps the young prophet's trembling sentence has survived for more than two and a half millennia because God knew people like us would eventually need to hear His answer.
“I am only...”
Too young.
Too old.
Too damaged.
Too ashamed.
Too inexperienced.
Too weak.
Too late.
God heard Jeremiah's version.
And He sent him anyway.
Never let the chapter that made you feel disqualified become louder than the Christ who died and rose to redeem sinners.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Is Masturbation a Habit… or a Heart Issue?
paragraphs:
Is Masturbation a Habit… or a Heart Issue?
The Bible Never Uses the Word “Masturbation.” But What Jesus Says About Lust, Mastery, the Body, and the Secret Life May Be Far More Uncomfortable—and Far More Hopeful—Than a Simple Rule.
There is a moment after the screen goes dark.
After the fantasy ends.
After the body settles.
After whatever promised relief has given you exactly what it promised for a few seconds—and then quietly left the room.
And there you are.
Alone again.
Maybe you whisper, “God, I’m sorry.”
Maybe you promise Him this was the last time.
Maybe you don't pray at all anymore because you are exhausted from apologizing for something you keep returning to.
Maybe masturbation isn't even something you feel guilty about. Perhaps you have heard Christians argue both sides so many times that you genuinely don't know what Scripture requires.
So let's begin somewhere unusually honest.
The Bible does not explicitly mention masturbation by name.
There is no verse that says, “You shall not masturbate.”
And Christians should be careful not to pretend Scripture says something explicitly when it does not.

The story of Onan in Genesis 38 is sometimes presented as a direct prohibition of masturbation, but that is not what the passage is about. Onan's judgment occurs in the context of his refusal to fulfill his obligation to Tamar while exploiting the sexual relationship for himself. Turning that passage into a simple proof text about masturbation misses its immediate context.
But that does not mean Scripture has nothing meaningful to say about the issue.
Because Christianity is not merely about finding a verse containing the exact modern word for something.
Jesus goes deeper.
He goes after the heart.
And that is where this conversation becomes uncomfortable.
Because perhaps the most revealing question isn't merely:
“Is masturbation technically a sin?”
Perhaps the question is:
“What is happening inside my heart when I do it—and who is becoming master of me?”
Paul gives us a startling category for answering that question:
“I will not be mastered by anything.” — 1 Corinthians 6:12
The Greek underneath that statement is striking:
ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος
all’ ouk egō exousiasthēsomai hypo tinos
In context, Paul is addressing Christian freedom and the body. His point is not simply, “Can I do this?”
He introduces another question:
“Will this rule me?”
That changes everything.
Because something can begin as something you do and quietly become something you need.
You tell yourself you can stop whenever you want.
Then stress comes.
Loneliness comes.
The argument comes.
The rejection comes.
The insomnia comes.
The memory comes.
The temptation comes.
And almost automatically, your hand reaches for the same escape.
Suddenly this isn't merely a discussion about sexuality.
It is about mastery.
What do you run to when your soul hurts?
What has trained you to believe, I need this before I can feel okay again?
What do you repeatedly reach for instead of bringing your loneliness, anxiety, disappointment, desire, and wounds before Christ?

That doesn't mean every sexual sensation is sinful. Sexual desire itself is not dirty. God created human beings as embodied, sexual creatures, and biblical Christianity does not teach that the body is evil.
In fact, Paul argues almost exactly the opposite.
He writes:
τὸ δὲ σῶμα οὐ τῇ πορνείᾳ ἀλλὰ τῷ κυρίῳ
to de sōma ou tē porneia alla tō kyriō
In essence:
“The body is not for sexual immorality, but for the Lord.”
Read those last words again.
For the Lord.
Your body isn't disgusting.
Your sexuality isn't an embarrassing mistake God wishes He hadn't designed.
Your body matters precisely because it belongs to Christ.
And this is where the conversation about masturbation cannot honestly be separated from what frequently accompanies it:
lust.
Pornography.
Fantasy.
Mental possession of another person's body.
Jesus takes us straight there.
In Matthew 5:28, He says that the person who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.
The Greek contains the expression:
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν
pros to epithymēsai autēn
The issue Jesus exposes isn't merely that a human being noticed someone was attractive.
Temptation itself is not identical to surrender.
Rather, Jesus penetrates beneath outward respectability and exposes deliberately cultivated lust within the heart.
That matters enormously.
Because someone can appear sexually “pure” publicly while living an entirely different sexual life privately.
Nobody touched anybody.
Nobody knows.
Browser history erased.
Door locked.
Phone turned facedown.
Church on Sunday.
Worship music playing.
Bible verse shared online.
And an entire hidden world alive behind the eyes.
Jesus says the heart matters.
Not because He enjoys catching people.
Because He wants all of you.
This is why reducing the question to “Did my body perform a forbidden mechanical action?” can miss the deeper spiritual examination.
Ask instead:
What am I imagining?
Whom am I mentally using?
Do I need pornography or sexually explicit material to sustain this?
Am I deliberately feeding lust?
Has this become compulsive?
Can I surrender it without becoming restless, angry, or desperate?
Do I repeatedly hide it?
Is it training me to experience sexuality as self-focused consumption rather than covenantal self-giving?
Does it make prayer harder because I know what I am intentionally cultivating?
And perhaps the hardest question:
Can I sincerely do this while saying, “Jesus, I am doing this for Your glory”?
Paul eventually brings the Corinthian argument to an astonishing conclusion:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς· δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν
ēgorasthēte gar timēs; doxasate dē ton theon en tō sōmati hymōn
“You were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body.”
There it is.
Christian sexual ethics ultimately aren't built around disgust.
They're built around ownership and redemption.
You were bought.
At a price.
And the price was not silver.
Not religious performance.
Not promises that you'll never fail again.
The price points us toward the crucified Christ.
Jesus gave Himself for sinners.
So Christianity doesn't merely ask:
“How close can I get to sin without technically crossing the line?”
Love asks something different:
“Jesus, how can this body glorify You?”

And if pornography is involved, the biblical issue becomes clearer still. Lust is not something Jesus tells His disciples to cultivate privately. Sexual immorality and impurity are repeatedly treated seriously in the New Testament, and Paul commands believers to flee sexual immorality rather than negotiate with it.
The Greek command in 1 Corinthians 6:18 is wonderfully uncomplicated:
φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν
pheugete tēn porneian
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not manage it.
Not flirt with it.
Not see how close you can stand to the edge.
Flee.
But somebody reading this just felt the old shame rising.
Because you've tried.
You deleted everything.
Then downloaded it again.
You installed the blocker.
Then discovered how to bypass it.
You prayed.
You cried.
You made vows at 1:13 in the morning.
“This is the last time, God.”
Three days later…
again.
And perhaps the worst part isn't even the failure anymore.
It is what you have started believing about yourself.
God must be disgusted with me.
I'm fake.
Real Christians don't struggle like this.
Maybe I'm beyond changing.
Listen carefully.
That voice telling you to hide from Jesus after you sin is not preaching the Gospel.
The Gospel does not say your sin doesn't matter.
It says your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and His grace is so astonishing that sinners who come to Him do not have to remain what sin made them.
This is the difference between conviction and hopeless shame.
Conviction says:
Come into the light.
Hopeless shame says:
Hide.
Conviction says:
Confess it.
Hopeless shame says:
You are it.
Conviction points toward Christ.
Hopeless shame keeps your eyes permanently fixed on yourself.
The Gospel says something infinitely better than either indulgence or self-hatred.
It says there is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is a new Master.
There is a new identity.
There is a cross stained with the blood of Jesus Christ where guilty people discover that repentance isn't crawling toward a reluctant Savior.
It is returning to the One who already knows.
Think about that.
Jesus already knows the thing you are terrified someone might discover.
He knows what you've watched.
He knows what you've imagined.
He knows the nights.
He knows the promises.
He knows the relapses.
He knows whether masturbation became anesthesia for loneliness, rejection, stress, trauma, boredom, anger, or the desperate need to feel something.
And still the Gospel invitation is:
Come.
Not “clean yourself first.”
Come.
Repentance is not merely feeling horrible afterward.
Repentance means turning.
Bringing darkness into light.
Removing access where necessary.
Refusing to feed fantasies.
Seeking accountability.
Learning your triggers.
Replacing secrecy with truth.

And, when the pattern has become deeply compulsive or connected to significant emotional distress, seeking wise pastoral care and qualified professional help can be part of walking honestly toward freedom.
Because sometimes you are not merely fighting the behavior.
You are fighting what the behavior has been medicating.
Maybe you weren't actually craving pornography.
You were craving comfort.
Maybe you weren't merely craving orgasm.
You were craving relief.
Maybe beneath the habit was loneliness.
Beneath the loneliness was rejection.
Beneath the rejection was the terrifying belief:
“Nobody really wants me.”
And every night you found a counterfeit intimacy that asked nothing from you, risked no rejection, required no covenant, and disappeared when the screen went black.
But Jesus doesn't merely want to take your coping mechanism away and leave an empty room behind.
He wants you.
That is why biblical holiness is so much bigger than behavior modification.
Christianity isn't Jesus standing outside your bedroom screaming:
“Stop touching yourself.”
It is Christ calling:
“Give Me your heart.”
Give Him the fantasy.
Give Him the loneliness.
Give Him the browser.
Give Him the memories.
Give Him the hormones.
Give Him the shame.
Give Him the desire to be loved.
Give Him the part of yourself you've been hiding even while singing worship songs.
All of it.
Because freedom isn't simply reaching Day 30, Day 100, or Day 1,000 without falling.
Freedom is reaching the place where Jesus becomes more precious than the thing you were using to survive without Him.
And if you fall again?
Don't turn grace into permission.
But don't turn failure into a reason to run from Christ either.
Get up.
Confess.
Repent.
Bring it into the light.
Identify what opened the door.
Cut off what needs cutting off.
Return to Christ.
Again.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Because Jesus is greater.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
The scandal is that people who know better still fall.
The scandal is that religious-looking people have secret rooms.
The scandal is that we can raise our hands in worship while hiding battles nobody around us knows exist.
But grace walks straight into the scandal.
Not to decorate the chains.
To break them.
And maybe that's why you're reading this right now.
Not because God wanted another opportunity to humiliate you.
Perhaps this became the moment you finally stopped asking:
“How much can I get away with?”
and started praying:
“Jesus, what part of my heart have I still refused to give You?”
That prayer can change a life.
So is masturbation merely a habit…
or a heart issue?
Biblically, masturbation itself is not explicitly named, so Christians should resist inventing a verse that directly settles every conceivable circumstance.
But Scripture gives us categories that refuse to let us dismiss the matter casually.
Lust.
Sexual purity.
Self-control.
Mastery.
The purpose of the body.
The secret intentions of the heart.
And whether our bodies are being offered for the glory of God.
Those categories can make the answer uncomfortable.
But they also make it hopeful.
Because Jesus didn't come merely to control your hands.
He came to redeem your heart.
And perhaps someone on your Facebook friends list is fighting this tonight while everyone assumes they're fine.
Not to advertise your righteousness.
Not to embarrass anybody.
And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, consider going deeper with us.

Supporting Gospel-centered work can itself be an act of stewardship when it is done freely, prayerfully, and for God's glory—not as a way of purchasing His favor. You never have to buy God's blessing, earn grace, or pay for spiritual acceptance. Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
Jesus Christ is the treasure.
Not Gospel Warrior.
Not merchandise.
Not streaks of perfect behavior.
Jesus.
If this article leads you anywhere, let it lead you to Him.
Follow because your soul needs truth more often than your algorithm naturally gives it to you.
And tonight, when the room becomes quiet…
when nobody is watching…
when the old urge whispers your name again…
remember:
The secret place where you thought your story was ruined may become the very place where Jesus begins rewriting it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Your Spirit Said Yes. Your Body Said Not Tonight.
paragraphs: Your Spirit Said Yes. Your Body Said Not Tonight.
Why “The Spirit Is Willing but the Flesh Is Weak” is not an excuse for your failure—but one of Jesus’ most piercing warnings about the battle inside every believer.
There are nights when you love Jesus sincerely… and still lose the battle.
You meant to pray.
You meant to close the app.
You meant to forgive them.
You meant to stop going back to that secret thing.
You meant to open your Bible instead of disappearing into another hour of scrolling.
You meant it when you told God, “This time will be different.”
And perhaps that is what makes the failure hurt so much.
Because somewhere underneath the shame is a frightening question:
If I really love Jesus, why do I keep struggling to do what I know is right?
Jesus once spoke directly into that contradiction.
But He did not say those words from a comfortable hillside while the disciples quietly took notes.
He said them in a garden.
At night.
Under crushing sorrow.
Only hours before nails would tear through His hands.
And one of His closest disciples was about to discover that sincere love for Jesus does not automatically make a person spiritually ready for temptation.
Peter had been confident.
Dangerously confident.
When Jesus warned His disciples that they would fall away, Peter essentially insisted that everyone else might fail—but he would not.
“Though they all fall away because of you, I will never fall away” (Matthew 26:33).
Peter loved Jesus.
That part matters.
His confidence was not necessarily fake.
His devotion was not entirely theatrical.
He really believed he was prepared to stand.
Jesus knew otherwise.

Soon they entered Gethsemane, and Christ began experiencing extraordinary anguish. Matthew tells us that Jesus became “sorrowful and troubled” and said, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death” (Matthew 26:37–38).
Jesus asked Peter, James, and John to remain and watch with Him.
Then He went farther into the darkness.
And prayed.
“Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” (Matthew 26:39).
This is holy ground.
The eternal Son was not running from obedience. He was moving toward the cross in perfect submission to His Father, fully conscious of the horror before Him.
Then Jesus returned to His disciples.
They were sleeping.
Imagine that scene.
Jesus is approaching the hour in which He will be betrayed, arrested, mocked, scourged, condemned, and crucified.
Peter had just declared that he was prepared to remain faithful even if everyone else abandoned Christ.
And now Peter cannot remain awake.
Jesus says:
“Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”
Matthew 26:41.
The Greek is painfully beautiful:
τὸ μὲν πνεῦμα πρόθυμον, ἡ δὲ σὰρξ ἀσθενής
to men pneuma prothymon, hē de sarx asthenēs
“The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”
The word πνεῦμα — pneuma can mean “spirit.” In this immediate context, Jesus is describing the disciples’ inward willingness—their sincere intention and readiness of heart.
πρόθυμον — prothymon carries the idea of being willing, eager, ready, or disposed toward something.
Peter wanted to be faithful.
That desire was real.
But then comes the devastating contrast:
σὰρξ — sarx.
“Flesh.”
And ἀσθενής — asthenēs:
“Weak.”
Without strength.
Frail.
Jesus was exposing something Peter had not yet learned about himself.
Wanting to obey God is not the same thing as being prepared to resist temptation.
Read that again.
Because some of our greatest spiritual collapses begin with the assumption that good intentions will be enough.
“I would never do that.”
“I can handle this.”
“I don't need boundaries.”
“I'll stop whenever I want.”
“My faith is strong.”
“I love Jesus too much to fall that far.”
Peter probably would have understood those sentences.
He had already effectively said his version of them.
Then Gethsemane happened.
Jesus did not tell Peter, “Your spirit is willing, so don't worry about your weakness.”
He said:
“Watch and pray.”
That changes everything.
“The flesh is weak” is not permission to surrender to sin.
It is a warning not to trust yourself.
There is a massive difference.
Sometimes this verse gets used almost jokingly.
Someone reaches for another piece of cake.
“The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.”
Someone gives in to something they knew they should resist.
“Well, you know what Jesus said…”
But in its biblical context, these words are anything but casual.
Judas is approaching.
Soldiers are coming.
Temptation is near.
The cross is hours away.
Peter's self-confidence is about to collapse.
And Jesus is telling him to pray.
The verse is not an excuse whispered after surrender.
It is an alarm sounded before temptation arrives.
Watch.
Pray.
Know your weakness.
Depend upon God.
Because there are battles you can lose while sincerely intending to win.
And perhaps that explains something you have been unable to understand about yourself.
You love Christ…
yet sometimes your eyes wander.
You believe Scripture…
yet resentment keeps returning.
You know God forgives…
yet shame keeps dragging yesterday into today.
You want purity…
yet temptation seems to know exactly when you are lonely.
You want to pray…
yet your phone somehow becomes easier to reach than God.
You want to forgive…
yet another part of you keeps replaying the injury.
You want to trust…
yet fear keeps constructing futures God never promised would happen.
You want to worship…
but exhaustion has hollowed you out.
You want to follow Jesus faithfully.
And sometimes you are shocked by how weak you can still be.
Jesus is not shocked.
That is part of what makes this passage so beautiful.
He knew Peter's weakness before Peter discovered it.
He knew Peter would sleep.
He knew Peter would panic.
He knew Peter would pull a sword.
He knew Peter would eventually stand near a charcoal fire and deny Him.
Three times.
“I do not know the man” (Matthew 26:72).
Think about the distance between Peter's confidence and Peter's collapse.
“I will never fall away.”
“I do not know the man.”
That distance can be shorter than we imagine.
Which is why spiritual maturity does not teach you to become increasingly impressed with yourself.
It teaches you to become increasingly dependent upon Christ.
Paul would later express another dimension of the believer's inner conflict when he wrote:
“For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing” (Romans 7:19).
He does not end there.
He cries:
“Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?”
And then:
“Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (Romans 7:24–25).
Christianity is not the story of human beings finally becoming strong enough to save themselves.
It is the story of sinners discovering that they desperately need a Savior.
That Savior has a name.
Jesus Christ.
And this is where Gethsemane becomes even more breathtaking.
While the disciples repeatedly failed to watch…
Jesus continued praying.
While their weakness was being exposed…
His obedience remained steadfast.
While Peter's promises were beginning to unravel…
Jesus was moving toward the fulfillment of His.
Peter would fail Jesus before sunrise.
Jesus would still go to the cross for Peter.
That is grace.
Not grace that calls Peter's denial harmless.
Not grace that pretends sin does not matter.
Not grace that tells us to remain exactly as we are.
Grace that confronts.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that restores.
Grace that transforms.
After the resurrection, Jesus did not discard Peter as damaged merchandise.
John 21 records another scene beside another charcoal fire.
The man who denied Jesus three times is questioned by Jesus three times.
“Do you love me?”
Peter is no longer boasting about being more faithful than everybody else.
Something in him has been broken.
Something healthier is beginning to grow.
“Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you” (John 21:17).
There is a world of difference between the Peter who says, essentially, I know what I am capable of…
and the Peter who says,
Lord, You know.
Failure had shattered his illusion of self-sufficiency.
But failure did not get the final word.
Jesus did.
That is the Gospel.
Maybe your failure has been whispering that your story is finished.
Maybe there is something you have never told anyone.
A relapse.
A secret habit.
An affair of the heart nobody can see.
Pornography you keep returning to.
Bitterness you have learned to disguise as discernment.
Pride dressed in religious language.
A prayer life that has almost disappeared.
A Bible gathering dust while your screen tells you what to desire.
A compromise that started small enough to justify and has now become strong enough to frighten you.
Do not use “the flesh is weak” to make peace with what Christ is calling you to bring into the light.
But do not use your weakness to conclude that Christ wants nothing more to do with you either.
Come to Him.
Confess.
Repent.
Receive His mercy.
Then watch and pray.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling terrible about yesterday.
It is a turning of the heart toward God.
First John 1:9 gives believers this astonishing assurance: if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Romans 8:1 declares that there is “no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
And Romans 8 does not leave the Christian helpless before the flesh. Those who belong to Christ are called to live by the Spirit, putting sin to death rather than making excuses for it.
Grace is not God's permission slip for your chains.
Grace is God meeting guilty people in Christ and leading them into freedom.
So perhaps the prayer tonight should not be:
“God, make me strong enough that I never need You.”
Perhaps it should be:
“Jesus, I finally understand how much I need You.”
That is a prayer pride hates.
But heaven has always done extraordinary things with surrendered people.
The flesh is weak.
Yes.
Your determination can fail.
Your emotions can change.
Your confidence can betray you.
Your body can become exhausted.
Your attention can wander.
Your courage can evaporate when the cost suddenly becomes real.
So watch.
Pray.
Run from what needs to be fled.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Forgive whom Christ is calling you to forgive.
Seek help where secrecy has kept you imprisoned.
Fill your mind with Scripture.
Stay close to believers who will tell you the truth.
And stop treating temptation as harmless simply because you have not fallen yet.
Jesus' warning came before Peter's denial.
Maybe this article reached you before yours.
If something hidden was exposed while you read this, you do not need to tell strangers every detail. But you also do not have to pretend.
Sometimes three honest words are more meaningful than a paragraph designed to make everybody think you have everything together.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this, send this article to them.
Save it too.
Because temptation has a strange way of making us forget in the moment what seemed painfully obvious in the light.
The Gospel cannot be bought. Salvation is God's gift through Jesus Christ.

But supporting Gospel-centered work can be one voluntary way to help biblical encouragement continue reaching people who may never walk into a church but will stop long enough to read something shared by a friend.
Not so we can build an audience around ourselves.
So we can keep pointing an audience beyond ourselves.
To Jesus.
Because Peter's story was never ultimately about how badly Peter failed.
It was about how completely Christ remained faithful.
The disciple who slept in the garden would later stand publicly and proclaim the risen Christ.
The mouth that denied Jesus would preach Jesus.
The frightened man warming himself beside a fire would become a witness of the resurrection.
His scandal was real.
His failure was real.
His repentance was real.
But grace was greater.
And maybe that is what you needed to hear tonight.
Your weakness should humble you.
Your temptation should sober you.
Your sin should lead you to repentance.
But none of those things should convince you that Jesus is incapable of rewriting a surrendered life.
The Spirit is willing.
The flesh is weak.
So do not trust the flesh.
Do not worship your willpower.
Do not sleep through the warning.
Watch.
Pray.
Repent when you fall.
Get back up by grace.
Keep your eyes on Christ.
Because the same Jesus who knew Peter would fail also knew what grace would make of him afterward.
Your weakest chapter does not have to become your final chapter when the Author of redemption is still writing.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DOES THE NEW TESTAMENT END THE DEBATE ON POLYGAMY?
paragraphs:
DOES THE NEW TESTAMENT END THE DEBATE ON POLYGAMY?
Jesus Never Said the Word “Polygamy”—But What He Said About Marriage May Be Far More Difficult to Escape
There is a question Christians sometimes ask in a whisper because saying it aloud can feel dangerous:
“If God allowed men like Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon to have multiple wives… where does the New Testament actually say a Christian man can have only one?”
It sounds like a devastating question.
At first.
Because there is something uncomfortable that serious Bible readers have to admit.
You can search the New Testament looking for a verse that reads, word for word, “Thou shalt not practice polygamy,” and you will not find one.
And that is precisely where some people stop.
They assume silence means permission.
But then Jesus speaks.
And suddenly the question is no longer merely, “Where is polygamy prohibited?”
The deeper question becomes:
“What did God intend marriage to be?”
That changes everything.
Because when Jesus was confronted with controversy surrounding marriage, He did something remarkable.
He did not begin with Abraham.
He did not begin with Jacob.
He did not begin with David.
He did not begin with Solomon.
He went farther back.
Past Israel’s kings.
Past Moses.
Past human failure.
Past cultural accommodation.
All the way back to creation.
“Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female…”
Then Jesus reaches into Genesis 2:24:
ἕνεκεν τούτου καταλείψει ἄνθρωπος τὸν πατέρα καὶ τὴν μητέρα καὶ κολληθήσεται τῇ γυναικὶ αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν.
The heart of the sentence is difficult to miss:
καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν.
“And the two shall become one flesh.”
Then Jesus says:
ὥστε οὐκέτι εἰσὶν δύο ἀλλὰ σὰρξ μία.
“So they are no longer two, but one flesh.”
Matthew 19:4–6.
Read those words slowly.
The two.
Not because the Greek word δύο—“two”—is somehow a secret technical prohibition of every possible marital arrangement. We should never force a word to prove more than it actually proves.
The power is in the whole argument.
Jesus is describing marriage by returning His listeners to the Creator’s design.
One man leaves father and mother.
He is joined to his wife.
The two become one flesh.
And God joins them.
Jesus does not appeal to every marital arrangement recorded after humanity’s fall.
He appeals to the beginning.
That distinction matters because the Bible sometimes records what human beings did without presenting what they did as God’s ideal.
Scripture is brutally honest about its heroes.
Abraham could act from fear.
Jacob could deceive.
David could commit horrifying sexual sin and murder.
Solomon could fill his house with wives until those relationships helped turn his heart away from the LORD.
The Bible does not airbrush its saints.
That is one of the reasons you can trust it.
It lets you see the scandal.
Then it lets you see what grace can do with broken people.
But description is not automatically prescription.
The fact that Scripture tells you something happened does not necessarily mean Scripture tells you to imitate it.
And nowhere is that more important than in discussions about marriage.
Look closely at the Hebrew foundation Jesus was quoting.
Genesis 2:24 says:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
Transliterated:
ʿal-kēn yaʿăzāb-ʾîš ʾet-ʾābîw wəʾet-ʾimmô, wədābaq bəʾištô, wəhāyû ləbāśār ʾeḥād.
In plain English:
A man leaves his father and mother, holds fast to his wife, and they become “one flesh.”
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד.
Basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Marriage, at creation, is therefore more than legalized sexual access.
More than reproduction.
More than economics.
More than a household arrangement.
More than a man accumulating women under his authority.
It is covenantal union.
A joining so profound that Jesus can speak of the two as no longer two but one flesh.
And then the New Testament goes somewhere even deeper.
Paul takes that creation text and connects marriage to Jesus Christ Himself.
In Ephesians 5 he writes of husband and wife, quotes Genesis 2:24, and then declares:
τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν.
“This mystery is great.”
And what is Paul ultimately talking about?
Christ and the Church.
That should stop every Christian marriage debate in its tracks.
Because suddenly marriage is not merely about what arrangements human beings can justify.
Marriage becomes a living picture pointing beyond itself.
Christ.
And His Bride.
Jesus is not portrayed as collecting competing covenant brides.
He loves His Church.
He gives Himself for her.
He sanctifies her.
He cleanses her.
He presents her to Himself.
The earthly marriage covenant is called to echo that astonishing Gospel reality.
This is why Christian marriage cannot finally be understood by asking only:
“What was tolerated?”
We have to ask:
“What points faithfully to Christ?”
There is another New Testament passage frequently brought into this debate.
Paul says an overseer must be:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα.
Mias gynaikos andra.
Traditionally rendered, “the husband of one wife.”
The expression appears in the pastoral qualifications for church leadership, and Christians have debated its precise force.
Does it specifically mean “not polygamous”?
Does it mean “faithful to his wife”?
Does it describe a “one-woman man”—a man characterized by sexual and marital faithfulness?
Responsible interpretation should acknowledge that discussion rather than pretending three Greek words settle every question by themselves.
But notice something important.
Whichever of those closely related readings you take, the phrase hardly provides positive support for polygamy.
Paul’s picture of exemplary Christian masculinity is marital fidelity, integrity, self-control, and an ordered household.
Then look beyond church leadership.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 7:
διὰ δὲ τὰς πορνείας ἕκαστος τὴν ἑαυτοῦ γυναῖκα ἐχέτω, καὶ ἑκάστη τὸν ἴδιον ἄνδρα ἐχέτω.
Because of sexual immorality, “each man” is to have his own wife and “each woman” her own husband.
Notice the reciprocity.
The wife is not presented merely as one member of a male collection.
Husband and wife possess genuine marital obligations toward one another.
Paul immediately continues with startling mutuality: the husband owes his wife marital affection, and the wife owes the same to her husband. Neither spouse is portrayed as sexually autonomous.
That would have sounded radical in parts of the ancient world.
Christian marriage was being pulled toward something beautiful.
Faithfulness.
Mutual belonging.
Holiness.
Self-giving love.
Christ.
Which brings us back to the question.
Does the New Testament end the debate on polygamy?
If by “end the debate” we mean, “Does Jesus utter a sentence containing the Greek equivalent of ‘Polygamy is forbidden’?” then no.
That sentence does not exist.
We should be honest enough to say so.

But if the question is whether the New Testament gives Christians a normative theology of marriage that points toward the exclusive covenantal union of one man and one woman, the cumulative case is powerful.
Creation gives us the pattern.
Jesus deliberately returns us to that creation pattern.
Paul repeats it.
Christian sexual ethics reinforce marital exclusivity and fidelity.
Church leadership embodies exemplary marital faithfulness.
And Ephesians lifts marriage beyond mere social convention until husband and wife become a signpost toward Christ and His Church.
The case is cumulative.
And perhaps that is exactly why this subject reaches farther into the heart than polygamy.
Because most people reading this are probably not trying to acquire another spouse.
But many of us are doing something spiritually similar.
We want Jesus…
and something else.
Jesus and the secret relationship.
Jesus and pornography.
Jesus and the affair nobody knows about.
Jesus and bitterness.
Jesus and money.
Jesus and reputation.
Jesus and the addiction.
Jesus and the person whose approval has become more important than obedience.
Jesus and the private life we would panic to see projected onto the church wall.
We want covenant without exclusivity.
We want Christ without surrender.
We want grace without repentance.
And somewhere underneath a theological argument about marriage, another question begins breathing.
Has your heart become divided?
That one hurts.
Because you can defend biblical marriage publicly while betraying Christ privately.
You can condemn somebody else’s sexual sin while feeding your own.
You can quote Greek words and still have a hidden browser history.
You can argue about Solomon while quietly becoming him.
That is where this stops being somebody else’s debate.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your wife does not know.
Maybe your husband does not know.
Maybe your pastor does not know.
Maybe your children think you are stronger than you really are.
Maybe everyone sees the Bible in your hand but nobody sees the war inside your heart.
Jesus does.
And somehow that is both terrifying…
and breathtakingly hopeful.
Because the Christ who exposes sin is also the Christ who died for sinners.
The Gospel is not God pretending your sin does not matter.
The Gospel is God demonstrating just how much sin matters by placing its judgment upon the crucified Son.
Jesus did not bleed so we could rename rebellion.
He bled to redeem rebels.
He did not rise from the grave so we could become better at hiding.
He rose so dead people could live.
Repentance therefore is not God standing at the door saying, “Clean yourself up before you come home.”
Repentance is the sinner finally dropping the weapons and running toward the Father through Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have wrecked a marriage.
Maybe you committed adultery.
Maybe sexual sin has owned years of your life.
Maybe you have wounded people you once promised to protect.
Maybe you have spent years defending something Scripture has been asking you to surrender.
Do not confuse consequences with hopelessness.
Some consequences remain.
Some relationships require difficult truth, wise pastoral care, patient restoration, and sometimes professional counsel.
Following Jesus does not mean pretending complicated family situations can be repaired with careless slogans.
Especially where existing spouses and children are involved, Christians must not manufacture additional injustice while claiming to correct previous wrongs.
But hear this clearly:
Your history does not possess greater redemptive authority than the blood of Jesus Christ.
The Cross has seen worse sinners than you.
And the tomb is still empty.
That is why our message will always be:
Not because scandal is harmless.
Because Jesus is greater.
Grace does not call evil good.
Grace looks evil directly in the face, calls it what God calls it, leads us through repentance…
and then refuses to let confessed and forgiven sin write the final sentence of our lives.
Jesus writes that sentence.
Maybe this article exposed something completely unrelated to polygamy.
Maybe while reading about divided marriages, God showed you a divided heart.
Talk to Christ.
Confess honestly.
Come into the light.
Not because typing three words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
And if Christ has already begun restoring something you thought could never be restored, tell somebody what He has done.
Your testimony may become the sentence God uses to keep another wounded believer from giving up tonight.
Not merely because sharing helps a page grow.
Someone may be compromising.
Someone may be hiding.
Someone may be convinced his scandal has disqualified him permanently from grace.
Put truth where wounded people can find it.
You may need to return to these Scriptures when emotion is louder than truth.
Invite struggling believers.
Invite lukewarm Christians.
Invite seekers.
Invite people who do not believe yet.
Let them encounter Christianity that is not afraid of difficult passages because biblical faith does not require us to manipulate Scripture to protect Jesus.
Truth can survive examination.
Not as a payment for God's favor. Never.
The Gospel cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be bought.
We are saved by grace through faith in Jesus Christ.
But Christians can glorify God by willingly supporting faithful Gospel work and helping biblical truth reach people who desperately need it.
And there is something else we want believers to know.
Belong to Christ.
Completely.
Because the deepest lesson hidden beneath this entire debate was never merely about how many wives a man can justify having.
It was about covenant.
Faithfulness.
Undivided love.
And a Bridegroom who did not abandon His Bride when she was stained.
He came for her.
He paid for her.
He shed His blood for her.
He rose for her.
And He is coming again for her.
Maybe that is the sentence you needed tonight.
You may have brought Jesus a story full of chapters you wish had never been written.
Adultery.
Addiction.
Failure.
Shame.
Compromise.
A broken home.
A divided heart.
A secret nobody knows.
Bring Him the pages.
Bring Him the truth.
Bring Him the scandal.
Because the hands holding the pen still bear nail scars.
And when Jesus takes hold of a surrendered story, your worst chapter does not get to decide how the book ends.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: LOT’S WIFE ESCAPED SODOM — BUT HER HEART WAS STILL LOOKING BACK
paragraphs:
LOT’S WIFE ESCAPED SODOM — BUT HER HEART WAS STILL LOOKING BACK
She was already outside the city when she turned around. That may be the most terrifying part of her story—because sometimes God can bring a person out of something before that person has fully stopped longing for what He told them to leave behind.
There are Bible stories we remember because they comfort us.
And then there are Bible stories Jesus Himself tells us not to forget.
Lot’s wife belongs to the second kind.
Jesus reduced her entire story to three haunting words in many English translations:
“Remember Lot’s wife.” — Luke 17:32
In Greek, the warning is just as stark:

Μνημονεύετε τῆς γυναικὸς Λώτ.
Mnēmoneúete tēs gynaikòs Lṓt.
“Remember the wife of Lot.”
The verb μνημονεύετε — mnēmoneúete carries the sense of remembering, keeping something in mind, calling it to remembrance.
Jesus did not tell His hearers to admire her.
He did not tell them merely to study her.
He said, in effect:
Remember her.
Because apparently it is possible to be close enough to deliverance to feel the angels pulling you away from destruction...
and still have something inside you turning backward.
That should make every one of us uncomfortable.
Not because Scripture gives us permission to invent motives for Lot’s wife that the text never states. It does not.
Genesis never tells us exactly what flashed through her mind in that fatal moment.
Was she thinking about possessions?
Friends?
Her home?
The life she had known?
Fear?
Regret?
Disbelief?
We are not told.
And if we want to handle the Bible faithfully, we must not pretend God revealed details He did not reveal.
But Scripture tells us something we cannot escape.
She was warned.
She was being rescued.
And she looked back.
Genesis 19:17 records the urgent command given as Lot and his family were brought out:
“Escape for your life. Do not look behind you…”
Then comes Genesis 19:26.
The Hebrew is chillingly brief:
וַתַּבֵּט אִשְׁתּוֹ מֵאַחֲרָיו וַתְּהִי נְצִיב מֶלַח
Vattabbēṭ ishtō mē’aḥarāv vattehī netziv melaḥ.
A careful sense of the line is:
“But his wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar of salt.”
There is no long speech.
No dramatic confession.
No paragraph explaining what she felt.
Just a look.
And judgment.
That is what makes the passage so unsettling.
Because some of the most dangerous movements of the human heart begin with something that appears small.
One glance.
One secret longing.
One reopened door.
One message you know you should not send.
One relationship God has repeatedly shown you is pulling you away from Him.
One private habit you keep romanticizing.
One version of yourself Jesus is calling you to bury, while you keep visiting its grave.
You walked away...
but sometimes you still miss it.
You deleted it...
but sometimes you still search for it.
You surrendered it...
but secretly you keep imagining what life would be like if you took it back.
You asked God to free you...
and then found yourself remembering the chains as though they were jewelry.
That is where Lot’s wife stops feeling like an ancient character standing somewhere near the ruins of Sodom.
Suddenly, she feels uncomfortably close.
Because there are things we can leave physically while still being tempted to return to them inwardly.
You can leave the toxic relationship while continuing to hunger for the validation it gave you.
You can stop the sinful behavior while secretly mourning the pleasure attached to it.
You can walk into church while mentally replaying the life Christ is calling you to surrender.
You can raise your hands during worship while protecting a hidden room of your heart from Jesus.
You can say, “God delivered me,” while part of you is still asking whether Egypt really was that bad.
And Scripture repeatedly exposes this strange tendency of fallen humanity.
God delivers...
and we remember bondage selectively.
Israel experienced it.
God shattered Pharaoh’s grip.
The sea opened.
Their oppressors were behind them.
God was leading them toward His promise.
Yet hardship came, and suddenly slavery began to look strangely attractive in their memories.
That is what sin does.
It edits the footage.
It removes the screams and keeps the pleasure.
It deletes the consequences and preserves the excitement.
It hides the shame and replays the sensation.
It makes chains look familiar enough to call home.
And maybe somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
You know Jesus has been calling you forward.
But lately...
you have been looking back.
Not necessarily with your eyes.
With your imagination.
With your browser history.
With your conversations.
With your fantasies.
With your resentment.
With that secret account.
With that person you keep checking on.
With that compromise nobody knows about.
With the bitterness you keep feeding because forgiving them feels like letting them win.
With the old identity Christ died to free you from.
And perhaps the frightening part is that everyone around you thinks you have moved on.
You learned the Christian vocabulary.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You share verses.
You encourage people.
You know the worship songs.
You know how to appear strong.
But God sees where your heart keeps wandering when nobody else is watching.
Lot’s wife had left Sodom.
But Jesus still said:
Remember her.
And the context in Luke makes His warning even sharper.

Jesus was teaching about the coming of the Son of Man. He spoke about Noah. He spoke about Lot. He described ordinary life continuing—eating, drinking, buying, selling, planting, building—until judgment arrived.
Then Jesus said:
“On that day, let the one who is on the housetop, with his goods in the house, not come down to take them away, and likewise let the one who is in the field not turn back.” — Luke 17:31
Then:
“Remember Lot’s wife.” — Luke 17:32
And immediately afterward:
“Whoever seeks to preserve his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life will keep it.” — Luke 17:33
Now the warning becomes clearer.
This is bigger than curiosity.
This is about what we cling to when God calls us to abandon everything and trust Him.
What is so precious to you that when Christ says, “Come,” your heart says, “But what about that?”
What are you trying to carry into the new life Jesus is calling you into?
What part of Sodom are you hoping Christianity will allow you to keep?
That question hurts.
But grace sometimes wounds before it heals.
Jesus does not call us out of darkness because He wants to make our lives empty.
He calls us out because the house is burning.
The command to flee is mercy.
The warning not to return is mercy.
Conviction is mercy.
The uncomfortable Scripture you wish you had not read tonight may itself be mercy.
Because God loves people enough to warn them before destruction.
And this is where the Gospel changes everything.
Christianity is not merely the command:
“Stop looking back.”
If that were the whole message, we would all eventually fail.
The Gospel is that there is Someone worth looking toward.
Jesus Christ.
The One who did not merely stand at a safe distance shouting instructions to sinners.
He entered our broken world.
He touched the unclean.
He welcomed repentant sinners.
He confronted hypocrites.
He carried our grief.
And then He walked toward a cross carrying a burden that belonged to us.
Our sin.
Our guilt.
Our rebellion.
Our shame.
The scandal of the Gospel is not that decent people can improve themselves enough for God to accept them.
The scandal is that guilty sinners can be forgiven because the sinless Son of God gave Himself for them.
Jesus did not die because your sin was small.
He died because your sin was deadly.
And He did not rise again merely to make you more religious.
He rose so that those who belong to Him might have new life.
That means repentance is not God trying to ruin your happiness.
Repentance is turning from death toward Life Himself.

The New Testament word often translated “repent” is μετανοέω — metanoeō, carrying the idea of changing one’s mind, turning in response to truth. Biblical repentance is deeper than feeling bad because consequences arrived. It is a turning of the heart toward God that bears fruit in a changed life.
And grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Grace makes repentance possible without despair.
You do not have to pretend you never looked back.
You need to turn again toward Christ.
Maybe you have been hiding.
Come into the light.
Maybe you fell again.
Confess it.
Maybe your prayer life has collapsed.
Call His name.
Maybe you became spiritually numb.
Open His Word again.
Maybe you wandered farther than you ever thought you would.
Do not make the mistake of believing distance has somehow made Jesus powerless to save.
Scripture says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9
And Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Read that carefully.
Not “less condemnation.”
No condemnation.
For whom?
Those who are in Christ Jesus.
Grace is not permission to run back into Sodom.
Grace is the miracle that sinners who deserve judgment can be washed, forgiven, reconciled, transformed, and brought home through Jesus Christ.
That is why the Gospel Warrior theme means so much:
