Because Jesus rewrites everything.
He rewrites the adulterer’s story through forgiveness and repentance.
He rewrites the addict’s story through freedom and truth.
He rewrites the bitter heart through mercy.
He rewrites the ashamed through the cross.
He rewrites the prodigal through restoration.
He rewrites the self-righteous through brokenness.
He rewrites the hopeless through resurrection.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by renaming sin so nobody feels uncomfortable.
He confronts sin...
pays for sin...
forgives repentant sinners...
and transforms people who could never rescue themselves.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe somewhere between Sodom and this sentence, the story stopped being about Lot’s wife.
It became about you.
There is something behind you that still knows your name.
Something Jesus has been telling you to leave.
Something you keep dressing up in nostalgia.
Something you keep calling “my weakness” when perhaps God has been calling it something much more serious.
Sin.
And maybe today you finally need to stop negotiating with what Jesus died to free you from.
Not tomorrow.
Not when life becomes easier.
Not after one final visit.
Not after one final conversation.
Not after one final secret indulgence.
Now.
Turn toward Christ.
Not toward religion.
Not toward Gospel Warrior.
Not toward a personality, page, ministry, denomination, or brand.
Toward Jesus Christ.
Only Christ saves.
Only His blood atones for sin.
Only His resurrection defeats death.
Only His grace can reconcile sinners to God.
And if this exposed something you have been hiding, do not manufacture a polished Christian response.
Be honest.
Somebody reading silently may desperately need to know that Jesus still restores people.
And send this to the person who has been drifting.
You never know whose midnight prayer may begin with something you were willing to share.
Because there may come a night when the old life starts whispering again.
And on that night, you may need to remember:
God did not bring you this far so you could romanticize the prison He was leading you away from.

We glorify God through faith in Christ and lives surrendered to Him. But generosity, sharing biblical truth, and helping Gospel-centered work reach others can certainly become practical ways of serving and honoring Him when they are done freely, prayerfully, and with the right heart.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who is struggling.
Invite the lukewarm believer who knows something has gone cold.
Invite the seeker with more questions than answers.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks their story is too scandalous for God.
Because the Gospel was never about pretending we have spotless histories.
It is about a spotless Savior who receives repentant sinners.
If Jesus is calling you forward... what are you still turning around to see?
Lot’s wife reminds us that there are moments when looking backward is far more serious than nostalgia.
So remember her.
Remember the warning.
Remember the mercy that pulled Lot from destruction.
Remember the Savior who calls sinners out of darkness.
And above everything else...
remember that whatever Christ asks you to leave behind can never compare with the One calling you forward.
Do not spend your life staring at what Jesus died to rescue you from.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Delilah Asked the Same Dangerous Question Until Samson Finally Broke
paragraphs: Delilah Asked the Same Dangerous Question Until Samson Finally Broke

He could tear apart a lion. He could carry away the gates of a city. He could defeat armies. But the enemy discovered something terrifying about Samson: if strength would not break him, repetition might.
There is a kind of temptation that does not arrive looking like temptation.
It sounds like a question.
It feels like affection.
It waits beside you.
It speaks softly enough that you stop recognizing it as dangerous.
And then it asks again.
And again.
And again.
Until one day, you surrender something you once swore you would never surrender.
That is what makes the story of Samson and Delilah so disturbing.
Samson did not lose everything because Delilah asked one brilliant question.
She kept pressing the same vulnerable place until the man who had survived battles became exhausted by words.
The Hebrew text makes the moment painfully vivid.
Delilah says:
אֵיךְ תֹּאמַר אֲהַבְתִּיךְ וְלִבְּךָ אֵין אִתִּי
’Eikh tomar, ahavtikh, velibbeka ein itti?
“How can you say, ‘I love you,’ when your heart is not with me?” — Judges 16:15.
Read that carefully.
She connected his love with his willingness to surrender what should not have been surrendered.
“If you really love me…”
Those words have destroyed more boundaries than many threats ever could.
“If you really cared about me…”
“If you trusted me…”
“Everybody else does it…”
“Just this once…”
“God will forgive you…”
“You’re taking your faith too seriously…”
The words change.
The strategy does not.
And Scripture says Delilah continued.
Day after day.
The Hebrew of Judges 16:16 describes her pressing him continually with her words. Then comes the devastating expression:
וַתִּקְצַר נַפְשׁוֹ לָמוּת
Vattiqtsar nafsho lamut.

His נֶפֶשׁ — nephesh, his life, his inner self, his very person, became so worn down that the text describes him as being pressed toward death. English translations render the force in different ways: his soul was “vexed to death,” he was “sick to death,” or “annoyed to death.”
And then Samson broke.
Not on a battlefield.
Not surrounded by thousands of soldiers.
Not while staring at a sword.
In a conversation.
That should frighten us in the right way.
Because some of the most dangerous battles of your Christian life will never look dramatic enough for anybody else to notice.
Nobody sees the private message.
Nobody hears the conversation.
Nobody knows about the website.
Nobody sees what happens after midnight.
Nobody hears the thought that has been returning for six months.
Nobody knows about the compromise you keep approaching, retreating from, then approaching again.
You have resisted it before.
Maybe dozens of times.
And because you resisted yesterday, you have started assuming you will always resist tomorrow.
Samson's story says: do not confuse yesterday's victory with tomorrow's immunity.
The enemy does not always need you to say yes immediately.
Sometimes he only needs you to become tired of saying no.
That is the terrifying power of repeated temptation.
The first time, your conscience screams.
The tenth time, it speaks.
The fiftieth time, it whispers.
Eventually you can begin negotiating with something you once fled from.

Samson had already given Delilah false answers about the source of his strength. She tested those answers, and each time the Philistines were waiting. The warning signs were not subtle. Yet he remained in the situation. Judges 16 portrays not one isolated mistake but a disastrous progression toward disclosure.
Think about that.
He kept waking up in the presence of evidence that something was terribly wrong.
And he stayed.
Somebody reading this knows exactly what that feels like.
God has already shown you.
The relationship keeps pulling you away from Christ.
The secret habit keeps hollowing you out.
The conversation keeps crossing boundaries.
The bitterness keeps poisoning you.
The pornography keeps promising relief and leaving shame.
The attention you receive from someone who is not your spouse keeps feeling more intoxicating.
The compromise at work keeps becoming easier.
The approval you desperately want keeps costing you pieces of your convictions.
You keep surviving the consequences and interpreting survival as permission.
But mercy is not permission.
Sometimes the fact that you survived your last compromise is not proof that the compromise was harmless.
It is proof that God was merciful.
Samson's strength also needs to be understood correctly.
His hair was not magic.

Scripture had already identified Samson as a Nazirite set apart to God from the womb, and Samson himself tells Delilah that no razor had come upon his head because of that consecration. When he finally reveals his heart, he connects shaving his head with losing his strength and becoming like another man.
The tragedy, therefore, is deeper than a haircut.
The outward sign represented a life that belonged to God.
Samson was treating holy things casually long before the barber arrived.
And that may be where this story finds us.
You can still look strong while becoming spiritually careless.
You can preach and be drifting.
You can worship and be hiding.
You can quote Scripture and secretly feed an addiction.
You can serve at church while starving your private relationship with Jesus.
You can have Christian language, Christian friends, Christian music, Christian posts, and a Christian reputation while repeatedly putting your consecration on Delilah's lap.
That is why this story is not merely about sexual temptation.
It is about misplaced surrender.
Your “Delilah” may not be a woman.
It may not be a man.
It could be anything you repeatedly allow close enough to negotiate with what belongs to God.
Approval.
Money.
Lust.
Resentment.
Ambition.
Loneliness.
Entertainment.
Pride.
Secret attention.
The desperate need to be wanted.
The hunger to prove somebody wrong.
Anything can become spiritually catastrophic when you repeatedly give it access to the places where obedience to God should have the final word.
Then came the sentence Samson should never have spoken.
Scripture says:
וַיַּגֶּד־לָהּ אֶת־כָּל־לִבּוֹ
He “told her all his heart.” — Judges 16:17.
There it is.
The surrender.
Delilah did not suddenly become dangerous at that moment.
Samson finally stopped guarding what should never have been handed to her.
And somebody needs to hear this before your own breaking point:
You do not have to answer every question temptation keeps asking you.
You do not have to prove how close you can stand to the edge without falling.
You do not have to keep revisiting the conversation.
You do not have to keep the number.
You do not have to keep opening the app.
You do not have to maintain access to the thing that repeatedly awakens what you are trying to crucify.
There are moments when holiness looks less like standing there heroically resisting temptation and more like running away.
Joseph ran from Potiphar's wife.
Paul told Timothy to flee youthful passions.
Jesus taught His disciples to pray, “Lead us not into temptation.”
Biblical maturity is not proving that you can sit comfortably beside destruction.
Sometimes maturity shuts the door.
Blocks the number.
Confesses the secret.
Calls the pastor.
Tells the spouse.
Installs the accountability software.
Leaves the room.
Cancels the meeting.
Stops explaining.
Runs.
Because there are things you cannot cuddle and crucify at the same time.
And then Samson falls asleep.
Delilah has his hair shaved.
His strength leaves him.
The Philistines seize him.
His eyes are gouged out.
He is taken to Gaza in chains and forced to grind in prison.
The mighty Samson becomes entertainment for his enemies.
Sin has always been a terrible employer.
It advertises freedom and manufactures chains.
It promises pleasure and eventually demands payment.
It tells you that surrender will finally quiet the pressure.
Then, once you surrender, it asks for more.
But if Samson's story ended in that prison, it would merely be a tragedy.
Scripture gives us another sentence.
A quiet sentence.
One that almost feels too small for everything that has happened.
Judges 16:22 says that the hair of Samson's head began to grow again after it had been shaved.
His hair began to grow again.
Slowly.
Quietly.
While he was blind.
While he was imprisoned.
While the consequences remained.
Something was growing.
Grace does not always remove consequences.
But failure does not put a repentant sinner beyond the reach of God.

Samson eventually calls upon the LORD again. His final prayer is not a model of flawless spiritual maturity—his motives still contain personal vengeance—but it is unmistakably a cry of dependence: he asks the Lord GOD to remember him and strengthen him once more. The strength he needs is acknowledged as coming from God.
And God hears him.
That does not make Samson's choices good.
Grace never needs us to rename evil as good.
Grace is greater than that.
Grace can look directly at the wreckage, call sin what it is, and still say:
God is not finished.
The New Testament does something astonishing with Samson.
Centuries later, Hebrews 11 includes Samson among people remembered in the discussion of faith.
Samson.
The compromised judge.
The reckless man.
The prisoner with empty eye sockets.
His scandal was real.
His failure was real.
His consequences were real.
But failure was not the final sentence written over his name.
And now we arrive at Jesus.
Because Samson can only take us so far.
Samson was a deeply flawed deliverer who needed grace himself.
Jesus Christ is the sinless Deliverer.
Samson repeatedly moved toward temptation.
Jesus was tempted and did not sin.
Samson's disobedience led him into bondage.
Jesus willingly entered suffering in obedience to the Father.
Samson stretched out his arms between pillars and died while bringing judgment upon God's enemies.
But Jesus stretched out His arms upon a cross and bore judgment for His enemies so that His enemies could become sons and daughters of God.
That is the greater story.
Not Samson's strength.
Christ's salvation.
Not Samson's hair growing back.
Christ walking out of the grave.
Not human willpower.
Resurrection power.
The Gospel does not say, “Try harder so God might love you again.”
The Gospel says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Jesus does not excuse the sin that destroyed you.
He paid for sin with His blood.
He calls you to repent—to turn from it and come to Him.
Forgiveness is not pretending nothing happened.
Forgiveness was purchased at a cross.
Maybe you have already told Delilah everything.
Maybe the secret has already been exposed.
Maybe the marriage is wounded.
Maybe trust has been broken.
Maybe you returned to the addiction after promising God you never would.
Maybe everybody thinks you are spiritually strong while you know how exhausted you have become.
Maybe you are reading this after doing something last night that you begged God months ago to deliver you from.
Listen carefully.
Do not turn Samson's restoration into permission to keep sinning.
And do not turn Samson's failure into permission to stop seeking God.
Run to Christ.
Confess.
Repent.
Bring the darkness into the light.
Receive the mercy Christ purchased.
Then start walking again.
One obedient decision.
Then another.
Then another.
Perhaps your spiritual hair is beginning to grow again.
Nobody notices yet.
That's okay.
Prayer is returning.
Conviction is returning.
You opened your Bible again.
You finally confessed.
You deleted the thing.
You apologized.
You asked for help.
You cried during worship for the first time in years.
You whispered the name “Jesus” when you had no impressive prayer left.
Something is growing.
Do not despise it.
Be truthful.
And if God has already brought you out of something that once controlled you, tell part of your testimony. Somebody reading the comments may desperately need evidence that chains really can break.
Then think of one person who has been getting spiritually tired.
Not someone you want to embarrass.
Someone you love.
Because Delilah rarely asks only once.
There may be a night when the question returns.
Read this again before you answer it.
Samson's story warns us that repeated compromise can wear down even someone who appears extraordinarily strong.
But the Gospel tells us something greater.
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write your final one.
Jesus does.
So guard your heart before Delilah gets the answer.
Run when temptation tells you to stay.
Repent when sin tells you to hide.
Come into the light when shame tells you that darkness is safer.
And when you find yourself sitting among the ruins of choices you cannot undo, remember the prisoner in Gaza.
His eyes were gone.
His reputation was shattered.
His enemies were celebrating.
But quietly…
his hair began to grow again.
The enemy may have celebrated the night you fell, but he does not get to write the ending of the person who turns back to God.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Did God Really Command Polygamy? The Verse People Keep Combining That the Bible Never Combined
paragraphs: Did God Really Command Polygamy? The Verse People Keep Combining That the Bible Never Combined

“Go into all the world.” “Be fruitful and multiply.” Two biblical commands. One dangerous conclusion when they are stitched together carelessly. What if the controversy disappears the moment we let Scripture speak in its own words?
There is a sentence floating around Christian conversations that sounds biblical enough to make people stop and wonder:
“Didn’t God tell us to go into the world and multiply?”
And sometimes the question underneath it is much sharper.
“If God commanded humanity to multiply, wouldn’t having several wives help a man obey that command faster? Could polygamy actually be biblical?”
It sounds provocative.
Maybe even logical.
More wives. More children. More multiplication.
Case closed?
Not even close.
Because before we debate whether God commanded polygamy, we need to notice something surprisingly important:
“Go into the world and multiply” is not actually a sentence found in the Bible.
It is a fusion of different biblical passages spoken in different contexts.
That changes everything.
In Genesis, God tells humanity to be fruitful and multiply. In the Gospel commission, Christ sends His followers into the world with the Gospel.
Those are both biblical ideas.

But joining them together and then building a sexual ethic from the resulting sentence is not careful interpretation. We cannot manufacture a new command by taking pieces of separate commands and welding them together.
And this matters far beyond polygamy.
Because some of the most dangerous distortions of Scripture are not complete lies.
They are pieces of truth rearranged until they say something God never said.
Go back to the beginning.
Before Abraham.
Before Jacob.
Before David.
Before Solomon.
Before human kingdoms complicated marriage.
Before sin fractured Eden.
Genesis 1:28 records God's blessing and commission to the first humans. The Hebrew contains the famous words:
פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ — peru urevu
“Be fruitful and multiply.”
The underlying verbs carry the ideas of bearing fruit and becoming numerous. The command continues with filling the earth.
Notice what is absent.
God does not say:
“Adam, acquire additional wives so that you can multiply more efficiently.”
He does not establish a household containing one husband and several wives.
He does not create Adam, Eve, Rachel, Leah, Bilhah, and Zilpah in Eden.
He creates the man and the woman.
And then Genesis moves from humanity's commission to humanity's foundational description of marriage:
A man leaves his father and mother, is joined to his wife, and the two become one flesh.
That word two becomes extraordinarily important later.
Because Jesus Himself reaches back past the patriarchs, past Israel's kings, past centuries of broken human relationships, and points His hearers back toward creation.

When questioned about marriage in Matthew 19, Christ quotes the creation account and emphasizes that the two become one flesh, concluding that what God has joined together human beings must not separate.
Jesus does something beautiful there.
When people bring Him the complications created by fallen humanity, He takes them back to the Creator's intention.
Back before the excuses.
Back before the loopholes.
Back before everybody started asking how much brokenness God would tolerate.
Back to Eden.
And suddenly the question is no longer merely, “Did important men in the Bible have several wives?”
Of course some did.
The real question becomes:
Does the Bible recording polygamy mean God was commanding polygamy?
Those are not remotely the same thing.
This is one of the most important principles for understanding Scripture.
The Bible often describes human behavior without prescribing human behavior.
Scripture tells the truth about its heroes.
Sometimes brutally.
Abraham's failures remain on the page.
Jacob's dysfunctional household remains on the page.
David's sins remain on the page.
Solomon's excess remains on the page.
The Bible does not airbrush its people because its ultimate Hero is not Abraham.
Not Jacob.
Not David.
Not Solomon.
It is Jesus Christ.
And when you actually read the Old Testament's polygamous households as stories instead of merely counting wives, something sobering happens.
The supposed advertisement for polygamy begins looking remarkably like a warning about human brokenness.
Jealousy.
Competition.
Favoritism.
Humiliation.
Children caught inside adult rivalry.
Inheritance conflict.
Political disaster.
Heartbreak.
The biblical text is startlingly honest about what happens when sinful human desires enter the home.
Think about Jacob's household.
Rachel wanted children.
Leah wanted to be loved.
Handmaids became involved in the rivalry.
Children entered a family already fractured by competition and favoritism.
You can count Jacob's sons and call it “multiplication.”
But Scripture forces you to look at the tears too.
That is the danger of reading the Bible merely to justify what we already want.
We count the children.
God makes us notice the wounded hearts.
We notice what biblical characters were permitted to do.
God keeps pointing us toward what He designed them to become.
And perhaps someone reading this has done the same thing in another area of life.
Maybe not polygamy.
Maybe you found a verse that sounded close enough to what you wanted that you stopped reading.
Maybe you wanted the relationship.
The money.
The revenge.
The sexual compromise.
The divorce.
The secret.
The habit.
The bitterness.
The excuse.
And instead of allowing Scripture to confront your desire, you quietly recruited Scripture to defend it.
That is when the Bible becomes dangerous in our hands—not because God's Word is dangerous, but because a human heart determined to justify itself can turn fragments of truth into camouflage.
The serpent did not approach Jesus in the wilderness without Scripture.
He quoted Scripture.
The problem was never merely whether words from the Bible were being used.
The question was whether the Word of God was being handled faithfully.
And now we arrive at the other half of the sentence people sometimes combine with Genesis.
Jesus' missionary command in Mark 16:15 appears in Greek as:
Πορευθέντες εἰς τὸν κόσμον ἅπαντα κηρύξατε τὸ εὐαγγέλιον πάσῃ τῇ κτίσει.
The central idea is unmistakable: go into all the world and proclaim the Gospel to all creation.
Notice what Jesus commands His disciples to spread.
Not their DNA.
The Gospel.
Christ's worldwide mission is not a command for Christian men to travel across nations producing biological descendants with multiple women.
It is a commission to carry the good news of Jesus Christ.
That difference is enormous.
Genesis says, in its creation setting, “Be fruitful and multiply.”
Christ commissions His followers to take the Gospel into the world.
Do not merge them into a command God never spoke.
There is another passage that deserves careful treatment because it frequently enters discussions about polygamy.
In 1 Timothy 3:2, Paul describes an overseer with the Greek expression:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα — mias gynaikos andra.

Literally, the expression is along the lines of a “man/husband of one woman/wife.” The Greek text is clear, although interpreters have debated the precise force of the idiom—whether Paul is especially stressing marital fidelity, excluding particular marital situations, or addressing more than one concern simultaneously. We should not pretend an interpretive debate does not exist merely because certainty sounds stronger in a social-media post.
But the larger New Testament sexual ethic is not difficult to recognize.
Marriage is treated as covenant fidelity.
Jesus appeals to the creation pattern.
The two become one flesh.
And marriage eventually becomes something even more breathtaking than an argument about how many spouses somebody can justify.
Paul takes us to Christ and His Church.
That is where Christian marriage reaches its deepest theological meaning.
The husband is called toward sacrificial love patterned after Christ's love for His people.
Suddenly marriage is not about maximizing a man's reproductive capacity.
It is about covenant.
Faithfulness.
Self-giving.
Holiness.
Love willing to bleed for another.
That is Christianity's revolution.
The question stops being:
“How many women can I biblically possess?”
And becomes:
“How faithfully can my life resemble Jesus?”
That question reaches much deeper.
Because the Gospel does not exist to help us discover the maximum amount of our desires we can keep while technically remaining religious.
Jesus does not stand at the edge of our appetites holding a measuring tape while we ask, “How close can I get?”
He calls us to Himself.
“Follow Me.”
And following Christ means sometimes discovering that the Bible was never affirming the thing we hoped it was affirming.
That hurts.
Especially when our desires are involved.
Especially when our identity is involved.
Especially when admitting we were wrong means changing something expensive.
There are people who do not want interpretation.
They want permission.
There are people who do not open Scripture asking, “Lord, what are You saying?”
They open it asking, “How can I make You agree with me?”
And if that sentence stung, don't run from it.
Stay here.
Because Christianity is not the story of people who interpreted everything correctly on their first attempt.
Christianity is the story of sinners rescued by a Savior.
Peter misunderstood.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The disciples argued about greatness while walking beside Greatness Himself.
And still Jesus transformed them.
That is why biblical correction does not have to end in humiliation.
It can end in grace.
Maybe you have misused Scripture before.
Maybe you defended something you now know was wrong.
Maybe you stayed in sin because you found someone online who gave you a theological excuse.
Maybe you are carrying sexual failure that makes an article about marriage feel less like theology and more like somebody pressing a finger against an old wound.
Listen carefully.
The answer is not hiding.
The answer is Jesus.
Repentance is not God screaming, “Stay away from Me.”
Repentance is the mercy of God calling a sinner home.
Christ did not die for the polished version of you.
He died for sinners.
At the cross, our self-justification collapses because there is nothing left to pretend.
Sin is serious enough that the Son of God went to Calvary.
Grace is powerful enough that He willingly did.
And the resurrection announces that sin does not get the final sentence over anyone who belongs to Christ.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Not because Jesus calls scandal righteousness.
Not because grace changes God's standards until our desires become holy.
Grace is greater than that.
Jesus meets sinners in the wreckage, forgives those who repent and believe, and begins rewriting what sin tried to destroy.
That is the Gospel.
And perhaps that is the question underneath the question you started reading.
Not merely:
“Does ‘go into the world and multiply’ command polygamy?”
No.

The phrase itself combines separate biblical commands, and the creation account does not present multiplying as an instruction to collect wives. Jesus' own appeal to Genesis reinforces the “two becoming one flesh” pattern, while His worldwide commission concerns proclaiming the Gospel.
But perhaps your deeper question is:
“Can I really trust Scripture when it confronts something I want?”
Yes.
Because the God who tells you “no” to sin is the same God who said “yes” to the cross.
His boundaries are not evidence that He hates you.
His Son is evidence that He loves sinners enough to rescue them from what destroys them.
So do not merely ask whether something can be defended with a verse.
Ask whether your interpretation survives the whole counsel of Scripture.
Ask whether you are reading a command in context.
Ask whether you have confused description with prescription.
Ask whether Jesus confirms your interpretation.
Ask whether you are submitting your desires to Scripture—or submitting Scripture to your desires.
And then ask the most dangerous question of all:
“Jesus, what in me are You trying to change?”
Be honest.
Someone reading the comments may discover they are not the only believer fighting that battle.
And somebody on your Facebook friends list may currently be building an entire belief around a verse they have never examined in context.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It doesn't.
It cannot.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedience, love, truth, generosity, witness, and service—not through a transaction with a page.
Send this to the friend who has heard “the Bible supports polygamy” and never knew how to answer.
It is practical support for creating more Christ-centered teaching, biblical nourishment, discipleship, encouragement, and resources.

If this ministry is feeding your faith, helping you understand Scripture, or giving you something worth placing into another person's hands, supporting it allows that work to reach farther. Share the article publicly. And above everything else, glorify God by taking the truth you receive and actually living it.
Because someday the question will not be how cleverly we defended what we wanted.
The question will be whether, when Jesus confronted our hearts, we loved Him enough to surrender.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Matthew Was Probably Making Good Money—So Why Did He Walk Away?
paragraphs: Matthew Was Probably Making Good Money—So Why Did He Walk Away?

We cannot honestly calculate Matthew’s salary from Scripture. But what the Bible does tell us about his occupation makes the moment Jesus called him far more costly—and far more beautiful—than many readers realize.
There is a dangerous way to read Matthew 9:9.
We can read it too quickly.
Jesus walks by. Matthew is sitting there. Jesus says, “Follow Me.” Matthew gets up. End of story.
A few seconds on the page.
But imagine refusing to turn the page.
Stay at the booth.
Look at the money.
Look at the ledgers.
Look at the merchandise passing through.
Look at the man everyone knows.
Then listen to the footsteps of Jesus getting closer.
Because Matthew was not sitting beside a fishing net when Christ called him.
He was sitting at a place where money changed hands.
And that changes the emotional weight of everything.
The Greek text of Matthew 9:9 says:
Καὶ παράγων ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐκεῖθεν εἶδεν ἄνθρωπον καθήμενον ἐπὶ τὸ τελώνιον, Μαθθαῖον λεγόμενον... Ἀκολούθει μοι.
At the heart of the scene is one revealing word:
τελώνιον — telōnion.

It means a tax or toll booth, a place where customs were collected. The NET translators specifically note that we should not imagine a comfortable modern government office. Such booths could be situated where goods entered or passed through a town or port so customs duties and tolls could be collected.
Matthew was sitting where commerce met taxation.
Then Jesus arrived.
And before we ask how much Matthew made, we need to admit something Scripture never tells us.
The Bible gives us no salary figure for Matthew.
No annual income.
No commission percentage.
No surviving payslip.
No verse tells us Matthew earned the ancient equivalent of $50,000, $100,000, or any other modern amount.
So when someone confidently announces an exact salary for Matthew, they have moved beyond what the biblical text can establish.
We should not manufacture numbers to make Scripture dramatic.
Scripture is already dramatic enough.
What we can say is that Matthew was a τελώνης — telōnēs, a tax collector. Matthew 10:3 even preserves the designation beside his name: Matthew “the tax collector.”
That occupation mattered.
Matthew was not merely a man with a job.
He was a man associated with a profession that carried enormous social and moral baggage in the Gospel world.
And the story immediately shows us the company in which tax collectors were commonly placed.

After Matthew's call, Jesus eats with tax collectors and people publicly regarded as sinners. The Pharisees object to precisely that company, asking why Jesus eats with them. Christ responds with the language of sickness, mercy, and sinners needing His call.
Think about what that means emotionally.
Matthew may have known how to count money while wondering whether anybody still counted him worthy of love.
He could collect from other people while carrying something inside himself nobody could collect away.
He could sit at a booth surrounded by transactions and still have a bankrupt soul.
And maybe that is where this stops being an article about Matthew.
Maybe this is where it becomes an article about us.
Because you do not need to be a first-century tax collector to understand what it means to build a life that looks profitable from the outside and becomes expensive on the inside.
Some people make good money and cannot sleep.
Some have the career but lost the marriage.
Some built the reputation but buried the secret.
Some gained followers and lost themselves.
Some sit in church every Sunday while quietly wondering whether Jesus could possibly want the version of them nobody else knows exists.
Some have become so good at surviving that nobody realizes they are bleeding.
Matthew's booth had money in it.
But money could not say what Jesus was about to say.
Ἀκολούθει μοι — Akolouthei moi.
“Follow Me.”
The verb ἀκολούθει carries the sense of following, accompanying, going in the same way with someone. In Matthew 9:9 it appears as a command addressed directly to Matthew.
Not:
“Clean yourself up and perhaps I will reconsider you.”
Not:
“Pay back enough first and then approach Me.”
Not:
“Convince these religious people that you deserve another chance.”
Jesus saw him.
Jesus called him.
And Matthew got up.
καὶ ἀναστὰς ἠκολούθησεν αὐτῷ
He rose and followed Him.
Do not miss the violence hidden inside that quiet sentence.
Matthew stood up from the place where his old life worked.
Fishermen who followed Jesus could conceivably return to fishing. Boats still floated. Nets could be repaired.

But Matthew's occupation involved a position at a revenue point. The text does not tell us whether his particular post could ever have been reclaimed, so we should not romanticize details we cannot prove.
Yet the scene unquestionably presents a decisive movement.
He was sitting.
Christ called.
Matthew rose.
He followed.
Whatever Matthew's precise income had been, the point of the Gospel is not that Jesus offered him a better compensation package.
Jesus offered him Jesus.
That is the scandal.
And that is the grace.
We live in a world obsessed with asking, “How much does it pay?”
Matthew's story forces another question:
What is it costing your soul?
What if the thing paying you is possessing you?
What if the relationship you refuse to surrender is slowly teaching you to live without obedience?
What if the applause has become your master?
What if your hidden sin gives you five minutes of pleasure and steals another piece of your peace every night?
What if you have spent years building the booth Jesus is asking you to leave?
That is where Christianity becomes uncomfortable.
Because Jesus did not come merely to become an accessory to the life we already designed.
He is Lord.
Grace is free, but following Christ rearranges allegiances.
Jesus later asks the terrifying question: what does it profit someone to gain the whole world and forfeit his soul?
Matthew's booth makes that question visible.
Coins on one side.
Christ on the other.
And perhaps the most astonishing part is that Jesus knew exactly who was sitting there.
Matthew did not surprise Him.
His profession did not surprise Him.
His reputation did not surprise Him.
His past did not make Jesus hesitate.
εἶδεν ἄνθρωπον
He saw a man.
Before the crowd saw a category, Jesus saw a person.
Before people could reduce him to “tax collector,” Christ saw the human being sitting behind the title.
And somebody reading this desperately needs that truth.
Jesus sees you behind what happened.
Behind what you did.
Behind what was done to you.
Behind the addiction you keep renaming.
Behind the browser history.
Behind the private messages.
Behind the bitterness.
Behind the religious performance.
Behind the smile you put on before entering church.
Behind the sentence, “I'm fine.”
He sees.
But biblical grace never means Jesus looks at our sin and says it does not matter.
Grace means the sinner can be called out of the old life because mercy has come near.
This becomes unmistakable in what happens next.
Jesus is at the table with tax collectors and sinners, and religious observers are offended.
Then Christ says that healthy people do not need a physician, but sick people do. He tells His hearers to learn the meaning of, “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,” and says He came to call sinners.
The Physician does not deny the disease.
He comes for the diseased.
That is the Gospel.
Jesus does not save us by pretending sin is harmless.
He saves sinners.
He forgives sinners.
He transforms sinners.
Ultimately He goes to the cross for sinners, bears sin, dies, and rises again victorious.
The Gospel is not God saying, “Your old life was fine.”
It is Christ saying, in effect:
Leave the booth. Follow Me.
And suddenly Matthew's income is not the most interesting thing about Matthew anymore.
That may be the answer you did not expect when you clicked this article.
How much did Matthew make?
We do not know.
Perhaps his work gave him a financially advantageous life compared with many around him; the text simply does not give us enough information to calculate it responsibly.
But we know something infinitely more important.
When Jesus called, Matthew discovered Someone worth more than whatever was sitting on that table.
That is the wealth of the story.
Not Matthew's coins.
Matthew's Christ.
And then grace does something beautiful.
The man at the tax booth becomes part of the apostolic company. Matthew 10:2–4 names Matthew among the Twelve and uniquely remembers him there as “the tax collector.”
Think about that.
His past was not erased from the vocabulary.
It was reinterpreted by grace.
“The tax collector” became a disciple of Jesus.
A scandalous history became part of a testimony.
That does not mean the past became good.
It means the past no longer got the final word.
This is what Jesus does.
He does not merely improve résumés.
He resurrects lives.
He takes people with histories.
People with regrets.
People who chose money over integrity.
People who compromised.
People who lied.
People who wasted years.
People who feel spiritually disqualified.
People everybody else has already categorized.
And He calls sinners to Himself.
Repentance means we do not remain comfortably seated at the booth while claiming to follow Jesus.
There comes a moment when grace demands a response.
Matthew rose.
Maybe your “booth” is not money.
Maybe it is pornography.
Maybe unforgiveness.
Maybe pride.
Maybe adultery.
Maybe greed.
Maybe the need to impress everyone.
Maybe secret dishonesty.
Maybe a relationship you know is dragging you away from Christ.
Maybe religious hypocrisy.
Maybe you have become extremely successful at looking Christian without actually surrendering to Christ.
You know the booth.
And worse...
you may already know what Jesus has been telling you about it.
There is something terrifying about staying seated when Christ says, “Follow Me.”
But there is something unimaginably beautiful about standing up.
You may lose something.
Matthew's story never promises otherwise.
Following Jesus has always been more serious than adding inspirational Bible verses to an unchanged life.
But whatever obedience costs, Christ is greater.
Your sin cannot offer what His blood offers.
Your money cannot purchase what His grace gives.
Your reputation cannot provide what His forgiveness provides.
Your secret addiction cannot love you.
Your success cannot resurrect you.
Your possessions cannot die for you.
Jesus did.
And Jesus rose.
So perhaps the question was never merely:
“What was Matthew's income like?”
Perhaps the question hiding underneath it was:
“What could make a man get up from a profitable table and follow Jesus?”
The answer is not poverty.
The answer is not adventure.
The answer is not self-improvement.
The answer is a Person.
Jesus Christ.
If this exposed a booth in your own heart that you have been afraid to leave, do not hide behind religious language.
Be honest before God.
Repent.
Come to Christ.
Somebody reading underneath this article may need to discover that Jesus still transforms real people with real histories.
And do not keep this story trapped on your screen.
Not as a transaction with God. Not because clicking “share” earns divine favor. We are saved by God's grace through faith, and genuine good works flow from that grace.
But if this ministry is helping proclaim Christ, supporting and sharing it can be one practical way of participating in that work.

If you want your online presence to glorify God, let it carry something greater than entertainment. Share truth. Share Scripture. Share the Gospel. Send this article to the person whose “successful” life may secretly be crushing them.
One day the booth may start looking attractive again.
One day obedience may feel expensive.
Come back and remember Matthew standing up.
Jesus cannot be bought.
It is simply a tangible way to support the continued creation and distribution of Christ-centered teaching, discipleship resources, and Gospel content so more people can encounter biblical truth.
Matthew left his booth because Jesus was worth following.
The Gospel still confronts every generation with the same Christ.
You can accumulate money and still be poor toward God.
You can lose the world's applause and discover eternal treasure.
You can carry a scandalous past and still encounter astonishing grace.
Because when Jesus becomes the center of the story, your worst chapter does not have to write your ending.
Follow so we can keep walking through Scripture together.
But above everything else...
follow Jesus.
Because the greatest thing Matthew ever received was not whatever income passed through his hands.
It was the moment Christ passed by his booth...
and Matthew finally discovered something worth getting up for.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE DAY JESUS OPENED THE SCROLL: The Detail in Luke 4 That Changes How You Hear the Voice of Christ
paragraphs: THE DAY JESUS OPENED THE SCROLL: The Detail in Luke 4 That Changes How You Hear the Voice of Christ
How do we know Jesus could read the sacred Scriptures—and can we really say He read Hebrew? The answer is more powerful, more historically grounded, and more personal than many Christians realize.
There is a moment in the Gospel of Luke that is so familiar we can read straight through it without feeling the weight of what just happened.
Jesus walks into a synagogue.
Not in Jerusalem.
Not before Caesar.
Not before an audience that already considers Him extraordinary.
He goes home.
Nazareth.
The little town where people knew His family.
The place where somebody probably remembered Him as a boy.
The place where people could look at the Messiah standing in front of them and still think they already knew everything worth knowing about Him.
Then something happens.
A scroll is placed into His hands.
And Jesus reads.
Luke records:
“Καὶ ἀνέστη ἀναγνῶναι.”
Kai anestē anagnōnai.
“And He stood up to read.”
That final Greek word matters.
ἀναγνῶναι — anagnōnai — “to read.”

Luke does not merely say Jesus recited something He had memorized. He describes Jesus standing to read. Then Luke says the scroll of the prophet Isaiah was given to Him, Jesus opened it, and “found the place where it was written.”
The Greek is striking:
“εὗρεν τὸν τόπον οὗ ἦν γεγραμμένον”
He found the place where it was written.
That is Luke 4:16–17.
Picture it.
Hands that would one day be pierced are holding Scripture.
Eyes that would look upon Peter after his denial are moving across the sacred text.
The voice that commanded storms to be still is about to read the words of Isaiah.
And somewhere in that synagogue sits an ordinary crowd that does not yet understand who is standing before them.
But here we need to be careful, because loving Scripture means refusing to make Scripture say more than it actually says.
Can we prove from Luke 4 alone that the physical scroll Jesus held in Nazareth was written in Hebrew?
No.
Luke wrote his Gospel in Greek, and he does not explicitly identify the language of that particular synagogue scroll.
That distinction matters.
There is a difference between defending the Bible and exaggerating our evidence.
Christian faith does not need exaggerated evidence.
Truth can survive careful questions.

What Luke gives us explicitly is already remarkable: Jesus stood to read, received the Isaiah scroll, opened it, located the passage, read it, returned the scroll, sat down, and interpreted its fulfillment.
And the historical world surrounding that scene makes Hebrew literacy entirely plausible.

The Dead Sea Scrolls give us an extraordinary window into the Jewish world surrounding the time of Jesus. The Israel Antiquities Authority notes that the majority of the Dead Sea Scrolls are written in Hebrew, although Aramaic and Greek are also represented. The collection demonstrates that Hebrew was very much alive as a literary and religious language in Second Temple Judaism.
Even more directly relevant, surviving manuscripts of Isaiah itself from Qumran are written in Hebrew.
So we should avoid two opposite mistakes.
We should not claim Luke explicitly says, “Jesus read this particular Hebrew manuscript,” because Luke does not say that.
But neither should we imagine Hebrew had disappeared and therefore Jesus could not possibly have read it. The manuscript evidence simply does not permit such an easy dismissal.
Hebrew Scripture existed.
Hebrew Isaiah manuscripts existed.
Hebrew remained an important language of Jewish religious literature.
Aramaic was also enormously important and was likely a major spoken language of Jewish Palestine.
Greek was present too.
Jesus lived in a multilingual world.
And then Luke deliberately shows us Jesus standing before His hometown congregation and reading Scripture for Himself.
That should make us stop.
Because the greater question is not merely, “What languages could Jesus read?”
The greater question is:
What did Jesus believe the Scriptures were saying about Him?
The scroll opens to Isaiah.
Behind Luke’s Greek stands the prophetic world of Isaiah 61.
The Hebrew begins:
רוּחַ אֲדֹנָי יְהוִה עָלָי
Ruach Adonai YHWH ‘alay.
“The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me.”
Then comes the language of anointing and good news:
יַעַן מָשַׁח יְהוָה אֹתִי לְבַשֵּׂר עֲנָוִים
Because the LORD has anointed me to bring good news to the afflicted, humble, or poor.
Luke presents Jesus reading this prophetic mission in Greek:
“Πνεῦμα κυρίου ἐπ᾽ ἐμέ…”
“The Spirit of the Lord is upon Me…”
Good news to the poor.
Liberty for captives.
Sight for the blind.
Freedom for the oppressed.
The acceptable year of the Lord.
Then Jesus stops.
Rolls up the scroll.
Hands it back.
Sits down.
And suddenly every eye in that synagogue is fixed on Him.
Imagine the silence.
No worship music underneath the moment.
No stage lights.
No dramatic editing.
Just Jesus.
The scroll.
And a room full of people waiting for Him to speak.
Then comes the sentence that changes everything:
“Σήμερον πεπλήρωται ἡ γραφὴ αὕτη…”
Sēmeron peplērōtai hē graphē hautē…
“Today this Scripture has been fulfilled…”
Today.
Not someday.
Not eventually.
Not when Israel finally gets everything together.
Today.
Jesus was not simply giving His hometown a lesson about Isaiah.
He was placing Himself inside Isaiah’s promise.
The One Isaiah anticipated was standing in the room.
That is where this stops being merely an interesting question about ancient literacy.
Because you can know that Jesus read Scripture and still refuse the Jesus revealed by Scripture.
The people of Nazareth heard Him.
They watched Him.
They knew His family.
They were astonished by His words.
And yet familiarity became a veil.
“Is this not Joseph’s son?”
Think about the tragedy of that question.
God's promised Christ could be standing close enough to touch, yet they could reduce Him to the category they had already assigned Him.
And perhaps that is closer to our problem than we want to admit.
Some of us have become familiar with Jesus too.
We know Christmas Jesus.
Sunday Jesus.
Cross-necklace Jesus.
Bible-verse-on-the-wall Jesus.
Jesus in the bio.
Jesus in the caption.
Jesus when life is collapsing.
But the Jesus holding Isaiah’s scroll in Nazareth does not permit us to keep Him as decoration.
He announces good news.
He confronts captivity.
He exposes blindness.
He brings freedom.
And eventually the same hometown crowd that marvels at His gracious words becomes furious enough to drive Him toward the edge of a hill.
That is how quickly admiration can turn into rejection when Jesus refuses to become the Messiah we invented.
Maybe that is where this story finds you.
You know Scripture.
But does Scripture know you?
You can pronounce “grace.”
But have you surrendered the sin you keep asking grace to excuse?
You can defend the Bible online.
But are you obeying it when nobody is watching?
You can argue that Jesus read Hebrew.
But are you listening to what Jesus is saying?
That question hurts because it should.
The demons could recognize Jesus.
Religious leaders could quote Scripture.
Crowds could admire miracles.
Judas could walk beside Christ.
None of those things by themselves were saving faith.
Christianity is not merely agreeing that Jesus existed, that the manuscripts are ancient, that the historical evidence is impressive, or that the Bible deserves respect.
The Gospel comes closer than that.
It comes after the hidden room.
The private addiction.
The resentment you have learned to justify.
The pride disguised as discernment.
The secret messages.
The unforgiveness.
The religious performance.
The version of yourself everyone else sees.
And the version only God sees.
Then Jesus announces liberty to captives.
Do you understand what that means?
He does not announce liberty because nobody is captive.
He announces liberty because we are.
Sin is not merely a collection of embarrassing mistakes. Scripture presents sin as rebellion against God, something that leaves humanity guilty and unable to rescue itself.
Yet the Christ who read Isaiah in Nazareth continued walking toward Jerusalem.
Toward betrayal.
Toward mockery.
Toward nails.
Toward a cross.
And there the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
The hands that held the scroll would be stretched across wood.
The eyes that read Isaiah would be bruised and bloodied.
The One announcing freedom to captives would allow Himself to be bound.
Not because Rome defeated Him.
Not because His mission failed.
Because this was the mission.
Christ died for our sins.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And forgiveness is not God's reward for people who successfully repair themselves.
It is grace purchased by Jesus Christ.
That is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is finally dropping the weapons.
It is coming into the light.
It is saying, “Jesus, I cannot save myself.”
Maybe your story has pages you would burn if you could.
Maybe there are chapters you hope nobody ever reads.
Maybe your marriage is wounded.
Maybe your children have watched you become someone you never intended to become.
Maybe pornography has hollowed out your private life.
Maybe bitterness has lived inside you so long that it feels like personality.
Maybe you walked away from God and now feel too ashamed to walk back.
Maybe you still sit in church while your soul feels miles away.
Listen to the Christ of Luke 4.
Good news is being announced to the poor.
Freedom to captives.
Sight to the blind.
Release to the crushed.
Jesus did not come merely to improve the public image of respectable sinners.
He came to save sinners.
That is why our message remains:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by lowering God's holiness until our sin becomes harmless.
Jesus rewrites everything by entering the guilty person's story with a cross, an empty tomb, forgiveness, reconciliation, and a call to follow Him.
Grace does not edit sin into innocence.
Grace brings the sinner to Christ.
And Christ makes all things new.
So perhaps the most dangerous person in Nazareth that Sabbath was not the openly broken person.
Perhaps it was the person who knew the scroll but could not recognize the Savior standing beside it.
Please do not let that become your story.
Do not spend your life studying evidence about Jesus while refusing Jesus.
Do not become an expert on biblical languages while remaining spiritually deaf to the voice speaking through Scripture.
Do not win an argument about whether Jesus could read Hebrew and lose your soul because you would not hear what He said.
If something hidden has been exposed while reading this, do not hide behind religious language.
Be honest.

And if Christ has already brought you out of something you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what He has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needed to read tonight.
Not because an algorithm deserves your attention.
Because someone you know may be quietly losing a battle nobody knows they are fighting.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but desperately needs to know Christ still receives repentant sinners.
Save it too.
Come back when familiarity starts making Jesus seem ordinary again.
But understand the heart behind that invitation.
Supporting Christian ministry should never be presented as purchasing God's favor.
We are saved by grace.
Jesus purchased redemption.
Not us.
And this is bigger than merchandise.
The greatest response this article could ever produce is not a purchase.
It is repentance.
Faith.
A sinner coming home.
A Bible opening again.
A marriage choosing forgiveness.
A secret being dragged into the light.
A prodigal whispering the name of Jesus after years of running.
A believer deciding that Christ will no longer be an accessory to life but Lord over all of it.
Because nearly two thousand years ago, Jesus stood in a synagogue, opened the prophet Isaiah, found the place where it was written, and announced that God's promised rescue had arrived.
The people stared at Him.
Some marveled.
Some questioned.
Some eventually rejected Him.
The scroll was closed.
But the question it opened has never closed.
What will you do with Jesus?
Not the Jesus your culture created.
Not the Jesus social media markets.
Not the Jesus reconstructed to approve everything we already wanted.
Jesus Christ as Scripture reveals Him.
Crucified.
Risen.
Holy.
Merciful.
Calling sinners to repent.
Offering forgiveness.
Breaking chains.
Receiving prodigals.
Making dead hearts alive.
Because somewhere tonight, somebody believes the worst page of their story has already written the ending.
But when that ruined page is placed into the scarred hands of Jesus, the scandal does not get the final word—grace does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WOMAN JERICHO CALLED A PROSTITUTE—BUT GOD WROTE HER INTO THE FAMILY LINE OF JESUS
paragraphs: THE WOMAN JERICHO CALLED A PROSTITUTE—BUT GOD WROTE HER INTO THE FAMILY LINE OF JESUS

Rahab lived behind a wall marked for destruction, carrying a name stained by her past. Then faith entered her house—and centuries later, when Matthew opened the story of Jesus Christ, her name was still there.
Imagine hearing that your city is going to die.
Not metaphorically.
Not someday.
Soon.
The walls that made everyone feel untouchable would fall. The streets you knew would become ruins. The world you had built your survival around was already under judgment.
And you are Rahab.
A woman with a past.
A woman Scripture does not sanitize.
Joshua 2:1 identifies her with the Hebrew expression אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה — ’ishah zonah: a woman who was a prostitute.
That matters.

Some have tried through the centuries to soften Rahab's occupation into something more respectable, such as an innkeeper. But the biblical witness does not need that rescue. The New Testament remembers her with equally unmistakable Greek: Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη — Rhaab hē pornē, “Rahab the prostitute.”
Hebrews remembers her that way.
James remembers her that way.
And remarkably, God was not embarrassed to preserve that description while simultaneously preserving something greater:
her faith.
The scandal is not that the Bible tells us what Rahab had been.
The scandal is what grace did with her afterward.
Maybe that is why her story can feel uncomfortable.
Because most of us know what it is like to have some word we fear could summarize us.
Addict.
Adulterer.
Divorced.
Abandoned.
Liar.
Failure.
Hypocrite.
Unwanted.
Dirty.
Lukewarm.
Backslider.
The thing nobody at church knows.
The thing your family still remembers.
The thing you wish you could remove from your history.
Rahab's story begins with a label too.
But it does not end there.
And neither must yours.
Two Israelite spies entered Jericho and came to Rahab's house. The king discovered that spies were in the city and demanded that she surrender them.
Suddenly this woman stood at the dividing line between the kingdom she had always known and the God she had only heard about.
And something extraordinary came out of her mouth.
Rahab told the spies that she knew the LORD had given Israel the land. She spoke about the Red Sea. She knew what God had done to Israel's enemies. Jericho had heard the reports.
Then came her confession.
יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם הוּא אֱלֹהִים בַּשָּׁמַיִם מִמַּעַל וְעַל־הָאָרֶץ מִתָּחַת
YHWH Eloheikhem hu Elohim bashamayim mimma‘al ve‘al-ha’aretz mittachat.

“The LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath.”
—Joshua 2:11, KJV
Read that again.
A Canaanite prostitute living in a condemned pagan city had come to believe that Israel's God was not merely another tribal deity.
He is God.
Above.
Below.
Everywhere.
Rahab had heard enough about the LORD to realize that the gods surrounding her were not gods at all.
This is where her story becomes painfully personal.
Rahab had not seen the Red Sea divide.
She heard about it.
She had not walked through the wilderness with Israel.
She heard what God had done.
And what she heard produced a decision.
The New Testament later interprets that moment for us: “By faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace.” —Hebrews 11:31, KJV.
By faith.
In Greek:
Πίστει Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη...
Pistei Rhaab hē pornē...
“By faith, Rahab the prostitute...”
Notice what Scripture does not say.
By perfection, Rahab...
By an immaculate history, Rahab...
By religious pedigree, Rahab...
By having everything together, Rahab...
No.
By faith.
And biblical faith is not merely agreeing that God exists.
Rahab's faith moved.
It risked.
It chose allegiance.

James deliberately points to Rahab when teaching that genuine faith produces action. He says she received the messengers and sent them out another way. James is not teaching that sinners purchase salvation by accumulating good deeds. He is showing that living faith does not remain a lifeless claim. Rahab's actions revealed the reality of the allegiance she professed.
She believed enough to act.
That distinction matters because Christianity is not salvation through moral self-repair.
The Gospel is not:
Clean yourself enough and perhaps Jesus will accept you.

The Gospel is that sinners who cannot rescue themselves are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ. Salvation is by grace through faith, not our works; yet the faith that receives grace begins producing a changed life.
Rahab could not rewrite yesterday.
But she could entrust tomorrow to the true God.
Then came the scarlet cord.
The spies promised that when judgment came, Rahab was to gather her family inside her house and tie a scarlet cord in the window.
So picture it.
A red cord hanging against Jericho's wall.
Inside that house were people waiting for mercy while an entire city remained under judgment.

The text does not explicitly call the scarlet cord a symbol of Christ's blood, so we should be careful not to claim something Scripture itself does not directly state. Yet Christians cannot read Rahab's rescue without recognizing the greater biblical reality toward which all salvation ultimately leads: sinners escape final judgment only through God's saving mercy, fulfilled supremely in Jesus Christ.
The cord was not magic.
Rahab's past did not save her.
Her ethnicity did not save her.
Jericho's walls certainly could not save her.
Her hope rested in the promise attached to the refuge God had provided.
And then the day came.
Trumpets.
Marching.
Waiting.
Another circuit around Jericho.
Then the shout.
And walls that generations probably assumed could never fall...
fell.
Think about Rahab in that moment.
Dust.
Noise.
Terror.
Everything familiar collapsing.
The city that had defined her was disappearing.
Yet Joshua 6 records an astonishing exception.
Rahab lived.
Her father lived.
Her mother lived.
Her brothers and those belonging to her household were brought out.
Joshua 6:25 says that Rahab and her family were spared and that she came to live among Israel.
Do not rush past that.
She went from a condemned city...
into the covenant community of Israel.
From the woman inside Jericho...
to the woman living among God's people.
But God still was not finished writing.
Turn the pages.
Joshua becomes Judges.
Judges becomes Ruth.
Kings rise.
Kings fall.
Prophets speak.
Centuries pass.
Then Matthew begins his Gospel.
And before Matthew tells us about Bethlehem...
before the wise men...
before the Sermon on the Mount...
before Calvary...
before the empty tomb...
Matthew gives us a genealogy.
Most people skim genealogies.
Do not skim this one.
Because there, in Matthew 1:5, is the name Jericho could never have predicted:
Rahab.
“Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab...”
Rahab became the mother of Boaz.
Boaz fathered Obed.
Obed fathered Jesse.
Jesse fathered David.
And Matthew's genealogy eventually arrives at Jesus Christ.
The prostitute of Jericho appears in the Messiah's family line.
Let that land.
The woman whose city was scheduled for destruction became an ancestor in the line through which the promised Messiah came.
God did not merely pull Rahab from the rubble.
He gave her a future she could never have manufactured.
She entered Israel.
She entered the biblical story.
She entered the genealogy Matthew records on the opening page of the New Testament.
And Hebrews later placed her among examples of faith. James used her as an example of faith demonstrated through action.
Jericho knew her profession.
Scripture remembered her faith.
Grace gave her story another ending.
That does not mean sin is insignificant.
Quite the opposite.
Grace is breathtaking precisely because sin is deadly.
Jesus did not come to convince us that rebellion against God does not matter. He came because it matters so profoundly that reconciliation required something we could never provide for ourselves.
At the cross, Jesus Christ bore sin.
The sinless Son of God died for sinners.
He rose again.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not “pretend your past never happened.”
It is:
Repent and come to Christ.
Bring the real history.
Bring the shame.
Bring the addiction.
Bring the sexual sin.
Bring the secret messages.
Bring the bitterness.
Bring the years you wasted.
Bring the compromises.
Bring the double life.
Bring the part of your testimony you desperately wish belonged to somebody else.
You do not need to make sin beautiful.
You need a Savior powerful enough to redeem sinners.
Rahab's story does not teach that everybody automatically receives a happy earthly ending.
It teaches something better.
Your past does not possess greater authority than God's grace.
Maybe somebody reading this has spent years assuming, “God could forgive someone like me, but He could never really use someone like me.”
Why not?
Look at Rahab.
Perhaps people still remember who you were.
They may even be correct about what you did.
Grace does not require us to rewrite history dishonestly.
Rahab really was a prostitute.
David really did commit terrible sin.
Peter really did deny Jesus.
Paul really did persecute Christians.
The Gospel does not require fake biographies.
It produces redeemed ones.
There is an enormous difference.
Repentance says, “Yes, that was sin.”
Grace says, “And Christ is greater.”
Repentance does not rename darkness as light.
Grace brings people out of darkness.
That is why your worst chapter does not need to become your final chapter.
Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
Still forgives.
Still restores.
Still receives the repentant.
Still transforms lives.
Still turns testimonies once whispered in shame into evidence that His mercy is stronger than our ruin.
Maybe your Jericho is collapsing right now.
Something you trusted is falling apart.
A relationship.
A reputation.
A secret.
A career.
The carefully constructed version of yourself everyone else believed.
And perhaps beneath all the fear is a realization you have avoided for years:
I need God.
Then learn from Rahab.
Do not cling to the wall when God is offering mercy.
Turn to Him.
Rahab heard.
Rahab believed.
Rahab acted.
And when judgment reached Jericho, she discovered that trusting the true God had changed the trajectory of her life.
If you have never surrendered to Jesus Christ, this is bigger than an inspirational story about overcoming your past.
You need reconciliation with God.
You need forgiveness.
You need Christ.
Confess your sin. Turn from it. Place your trust in Jesus Christ—His death for sinners, His resurrection, His lordship, His mercy.
You do not earn the cross.
You run to the One who died upon it.
And if you already belong to Jesus but shame keeps dragging you back into rooms God has called you out of, remember Rahab.
Not to excuse what happened.
Not to glorify what happened.
But to remember who gets the final word over a surrendered life.
Christ does.
Perhaps that is why somebody else needs this article today.
Not because sharing a Facebook post earns favor with God—it does not.
But if Christ has given us good news, love should make us want other people to hear it.
Let someone who believes they are too dirty for God discover Rahab. Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly how exhausted they are from hiding.
Somebody may be reading silently who desperately needs evidence that Jesus still changes people.
There will be days when old accusations return.
Days when the enemy points backward.
Days when you need to remember a prostitute from Jericho whose name somehow appears in Matthew 1.
If you want to glorify God through generosity, one meaningful way is to help Gospel-centered truth travel farther.
And there is much more waiting for those serious about growing deeper in Jesus Christ.
Not because sharing saves you.
Jesus saves.
Someone living inside their own Jericho.
Someone convinced their reputation is permanent.
Someone certain heaven could never want their name.
Someone smiling publicly while privately believing they have gone too far.
Let them encounter the truth.
Rahab's name did not disappear when Jericho's walls disappeared.
God carried her story forward.
Through faith.
Through rescue.
Through a new people.
Through generations.
Until one day Matthew dipped his pen, began recording the genealogy of Jesus Christ, and wrote a name that should make every ashamed sinner stop breathing for a second:
Rahab.
The prostitute.
The outsider.
The woman from the condemned city.
The woman who believed.
The woman who was rescued.
The woman remembered among the faithful.
The woman whose name appears in the family line Matthew traces to Christ.
So when your past whispers, Look what you were...
look toward Jesus and remember what grace can do.
Jericho remembered what Rahab had been; grace carried her name all the way to Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Can Occasional Porn Still Damage Your Soul?
paragraphs: Can Occasional Porn Still Damage Your Soul?
The Sin You Call “Occasional” May Be Training Your Heart Every Time You Return—and Jesus Loves You Too Much to Leave You There
Maybe you do not think you have an addiction.
That is what makes this conversation uncomfortable.
You can go days without it.
Maybe weeks.
Maybe even months.
You work. You pray. You go to church. You love your family. You read Scripture. You worship. You may genuinely love Jesus.
And every once in a while...
you go back.
Late at night.
After an argument.
After rejection.
When loneliness becomes louder than conviction.
When stress has drained you.
When curiosity gets the better of you.
When nobody is watching.
You tell yourself, It isn't controlling me.
I don't do this every day.
At least I'm not addicted.
This is only occasional.
Then the screen goes dark.
The room becomes quiet again.
And somewhere beneath all the explanations is a question you would rather not ask:
If it really means so little to me, why do I keep returning to it?
Stay with that question.
Not because I want to crush you with shame.
Because Jesus did not shed His blood merely to make your public life look Christian while a private room in your heart remains locked.
The question is not merely whether occasional pornography can become an addiction.
The deeper question is whether something must become an addiction before a follower of Christ should take it seriously.
And Scripture gives us an uncomfortable answer.
Jesus did not begin His warning about sexual sin with frequency.
He began with the heart.
In Matthew 5:28, the Greek text reads in part:
πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν... ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ
pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn... en tē kardia autou.
Jesus says that the one who looks at a woman “to lust after her” has already committed adultery with her “in his heart.”

That word translated “to lust,” ἐπιθυμῆσαι — epithymēsai, comes from a verb meaning to desire, long for, covet, or set one's desire upon something. The construction matters. Jesus is addressing more than merely noticing that another human being is attractive. He takes His listeners beneath outward behavior and confronts intentional desire cultivated in the heart.
That distinction matters enormously.
Christian purity is not pretending you have no sexuality.
Temptation itself is not identical to sin.
Accidentally seeing something sexual is not the same thing as deliberately seeking it.
Recognizing beauty is not the same thing as mentally consuming another person.
But pornography is built around something radically different from an accidental glance.
It invites you to stay.
To search.
To choose.
To imagine.
To consume.
To turn a person made in the image of God into material for private gratification.
And suddenly the question, “How often can I watch porn before it becomes spiritually dangerous?” begins to sound like the wrong question.
Imagine someone asking:
“How much poison can I drink occasionally without calling myself a poison drinker?”
You would not begin by debating the label.
You would ask why they are drinking poison.
That is what pornography does spiritually. The greatest danger is not simply that someday you might watch more.
The danger is what you are practicing now.
Every return says something to the heart.
When I am lonely, I can escape here.
When I am stressed, I can medicate here.
When I feel unwanted, I can manufacture intimacy here.
When desire becomes uncomfortable, I can satisfy it without covenant, sacrifice, patience, vulnerability, or love.
Pornography offers the sensation of intimacy while requiring none of intimacy's holiness.
No covenant.
No responsibility.
No self-giving love.
No being truly known.
Just bodies without biographies.
Pleasure without covenant.
Desire without responsibility.
And afterward...
silence.
That is why Job's ancient words feel startlingly modern.
Long before smartphones, private browsing, streaming video, or social media existed, Job said:
בְּרִית כָּרַתִּי לְעֵינָי
Berit karatti le'enai.
Literally, the Hebrew speaks of making—or “cutting”—a covenant with my eyes.
Job 31:1 continues by asking how he could then gaze upon a young woman. The Hebrew begins with בְּרִית — berit, “covenant,” and connects that covenant directly with his eyes.
Notice the seriousness.
Job did not say, “I made a suggestion to my eyes.”
He did not say, “I'll try to behave when temptation becomes intense.”
He used covenant language.
Why?
Because what enters through your eyes does not always remain in your eyes.
Some images become memories.
Some memories become fantasies.
Some fantasies become refuges.
And some refuges quietly become masters.
You may close the browser in seconds.
But the heart does not have a “clear history” button.
This is where someone may whisper:
But I only watch occasionally.
Then hear this carefully.
The Bible does not give us a numerical threshold at which pornography suddenly becomes sinful.
There is no verse saying that pornography becomes spiritually dangerous after the fifth viewing in thirty days.
Scripture gives us something much more searching.
It asks what you are doing with desire.
It asks where your eyes are going.
It asks what your heart is cultivating.
It asks whether something is mastering you.
It asks whether your body is being offered to God.
Paul's words to Corinth are startling:
φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not negotiate with it.
Not see how close you can stand to it.
Not calculate how infrequently you can return to it and still feel respectable.
Flee.

And only moments later Paul writes that the believer's body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, that believers are not their own, that they were “bought at a price,” and therefore are to glorify God in their bodies.
There is the center of Christian sexual ethics.
Not merely:
“Porn is bad.”
But:
“You were bought with a price.”
The Gospel changes the entire conversation.
Your body matters because Christ purchased you.
Your sexuality matters because Christ is Lord.
Your imagination matters because Jesus is not interested in renting the religious portion of your existence.
He is Lord of the whole person.
Your Sunday.
Your Monday.
Your marriage.
Your singleness.
Your bedroom.
Your loneliness.
Your browser history.
Your eyes.
Your imagination.
Your body.
Your secret places.
Everything.
And perhaps this is where the article stops being theoretical.
Because maybe you have already promised God you would stop.
More than once.
You deleted something.
Then reinstalled it.
You prayed afterward.
You cried afterward.
You felt disgusted afterward.
You told Jesus, “Never again.”
Then enough time passed for the pain to fade.
And one night...
again.
Now you do not only hate the pornography.
You hate what you think it says about you.
You wonder whether your repentance was real.
You wonder whether God is tired of hearing the same confession.
You wonder whether you have exhausted grace.
You wonder whether a real Christian could struggle like this.
And that is precisely where Satan loves to turn conviction into condemnation.
Conviction says:
“Come into the light.”
Condemnation whispers:
“Hide from God until you become worthy of Him again.”
But you cannot clean yourself enough to earn your way back to the cross.
The cross is where dirty people come to be washed.
The Gospel is not that good people successfully avoided every scandal.
The Gospel is that sinners were so hopelessly unable to save themselves that the Son of God came for them.
Jesus did not die for the edited version of you.
He knew.
The lust.
The searches.
The deleted history.
The relapse.
The hypocrisy.
The promises you broke.
The things nobody else knows.
And He went to the cross knowing the full weight of human sin.
That does not make pornography less serious.
It makes grace more astonishing.
Because biblical grace never says:
“Your sin doesn't matter.”
Grace says:
“Your sin mattered enough for Christ to die—and His mercy is powerful enough to transform you.”
This is the difference between cheap reassurance and the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely want you to feel less guilty after pornography.
He wants freedom to invade the place pornography occupied.
He wants to teach you to see people as people again.
He wants to teach your heart that loneliness does not have to become lust.
That rejection does not have to become fantasy.
That stress does not have to become escape.
That sexual desire does not have to become your master.
That shame does not get the final word.
And that you are not fighting merely to stop looking at something.
You are fighting to recover your ability to see.
To see women and men as image-bearers rather than objects.
To see sexuality as God's gift rather than consumer entertainment.
To see your body as belonging to Christ.
To see temptation as something that can be resisted rather than obeyed.
To see confession as a doorway into light rather than humiliation.
To see Jesus not standing at the end of your struggle with folded arms, but as the Savior without whom none of us could stand at all.
This also means repentance needs to become practical.
If pornography reaches you through a particular app, account, device, time of night, or private routine, do not baptize passivity and call it faith.

Jesus' language immediately after His teaching on lust is intentionally severe: if your eye causes you to sin, tear it out; if your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. This is not a command for bodily mutilation. It is shocking language communicating the radical seriousness with which sin should be treated.
So remove access.
Change routines.
Stop protecting the doorway through which the thing destroying you keeps entering.
Put the phone outside the bedroom if necessary.
Use filtering and accountability tools.
Tell a mature believer who will love you enough not to flatter you.
If you are married, stop pretending secret sexual habits cannot wound covenant intimacy.
If the struggle feels compulsive or deeply entrenched, seek wise pastoral care and qualified professional help rather than assuming secrecy will eventually cure secrecy.
And when temptation comes, do not merely stare at the command “DON'T.”
Run toward something greater.
Pray.
Open Scripture.
Leave the room.
Call someone.
Walk.
Worship.
Serve.
Bring your body and mind into the light.
The Christian life is not sustained merely by saying no to lesser desires.
We learn to say yes to Someone infinitely better.
Jesus Christ.
Maybe you fell yesterday.
Maybe you fell an hour ago.
Then this next sentence is for you.
Do not let shame convince you to spend another night hiding from the only One who can actually heal you.
Confess.
Repent.
Come into the light.
Get help.
Then get up.
Not because pornography is harmless.
Not because holiness does not matter.
But because Jesus Christ is still a Savior.
There are believers reading those words who understand the battle more than you realize.
Your testimony may become someone else's reason to believe freedom is possible.
