Not as a badge announcing that you have everything together.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the person who does not yet believe to follow too. We want to keep putting Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment in places where darkness normally gets the loudest voice.

We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ. But one practical way you can help this ministry continue sharing Gospel-centered resources is by supporting the work and sharing these articles with others.
Come back to Jesus.
Because the deepest question was never merely:
“Can occasional porn still damage my soul?”
Yes, deliberately cultivating lust is spiritually serious even when it is occasional. Jesus locates sexual sin deeper than outward frequency; He reaches into the desires of the heart.
But there is another question.
A better question.
Can Jesus redeem the person who keeps returning to Him broken?
Look at the cross.
That is your answer.
The scandal may be real.
The consequences may be real.
The battle may be longer than you wanted.
Repentance may cost you privacy, convenience, habits, access, pride, and excuses.
But the scandal does not have to become the final chapter.
Grace can write another sentence.
Jesus can write another chapter.
And perhaps tonight, instead of deleting your history and pretending nothing happened...
you finally bring your history to Christ.
Because the most dangerous secret is not the one Jesus discovers.
It is the one you keep hiding from the Savior who already knows—and still calls you into the light.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: YOU THOUGHT GOD FORGOT YOU—BUT ISAIAH 40:31 SAYS SOMETHING FAR MORE POWERFUL THAN “JUST WAIT”
paragraphs: YOU THOUGHT GOD FORGOT YOU—BUT ISAIAH 40:31 SAYS SOMETHING FAR MORE POWERFUL THAN “JUST WAIT”
What “Wait Upon the Lord” Really Means When You’re Tired of Praying, Tired of Hoping, and Starting to Wonder Whether God Still Sees You
There is a kind of tiredness sleep cannot fix.
You can sleep eight hours and wake up carrying it.
You can smile in church with it.
You can worship while carrying it.
You can answer, “I’m okay,” while something inside you quietly whispers…
No, I’m not.
Maybe you have been praying about the same thing for months.
Maybe years.
You prayed when you were hopeful.
You prayed when you were terrified.
You prayed with faith.
You prayed through tears.
Then eventually your prayers became shorter because disappointment had exhausted your vocabulary.
“Lord… please.”
And still, nothing seems to move.
The door remains closed.
The relationship remains broken.
The answer remains unclear.
The grief still hurts.
The temptation keeps returning.
The person you love still has not come back to God.
The breakthrough you thought was coming never arrived.
And somewhere between your first confident prayer and your hundredth exhausted one, a frightening question entered your mind:
God, have You forgotten me?
That question is exactly why Isaiah 40:31 is far more powerful than the inspirational quote we sometimes make it.
Because Isaiah was not speaking to comfortable people who needed a motivational boost.
He was speaking into despair.
And before we reach verse 31, we hear the wounded heart behind the promise:
“Why sayest thou, O Jacob, and speakest, O Israel, My way is hid from the LORD, and my judgment is passed over from my God?” — Isaiah 40:27, KJV
In other words:
God doesn’t see what is happening to me.
God has overlooked my situation.
Maybe heaven has forgotten my name.
Sound familiar?
Then God answers.
Not first by explaining their circumstances.
By revealing Himself.
“Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?” — Isaiah 40:28, KJV
Read that again slowly.
You are tired.
God is not.
You are confused.
God is not.
You cannot see tomorrow.
God is already Lord over it.
Your strength has limits.
His does not.
And then comes one of Scripture’s most beloved promises:
“But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint.” — Isaiah 40:31, KJV
But what does “wait” actually mean?
Because this is where we can misunderstand the verse.
The Hebrew behind the opening phrase is:
וְקוֹיֵי יְהוָה
weqōwê YHWH
Often rendered, “those who wait for the LORD.”
The key idea comes from the Hebrew verb קָוָה — qāvâ.
Depending on context, it carries the sense of waiting, looking for, expecting, or hoping.
That matters.
Biblical waiting is not spiritual laziness.
It is not sitting motionless while refusing responsibility.
It is not pretending pain does not hurt.
It is not manufacturing positive thoughts until God gives you what you ordered.
And it certainly does not mean that if you wait long enough, God is obligated to give you the exact relationship, promotion, healing, opportunity, money, or earthly outcome you requested.
Waiting upon the Lord means your expectation becomes anchored in God Himself.
There is an enormous difference between saying…
“I trust God because I know He will give me what I want”
…and saying…
“I trust God because He is God, even when I do not yet understand what He is doing.”
The first trusts an outcome.
The second trusts the Lord.
And sometimes God allows the outcome to remain uncertain until we discover which one we were actually worshiping.
That hurts.
Because some of us do not merely want God.
We want God plus the answer.
God plus the marriage.
God plus the healing.
God plus the restored relationship.
God plus the successful ministry.
God plus financial security.
God plus the apology.
God plus vindication.
And if God does not give us the thing after His name, our hearts begin wondering whether He is still good.
Isaiah 40 confronts that theology.
The promise is not that those who wait upon God will always receive their preferred circumstances.
The promise is that God Himself supplies strength to people who have reached the end of theirs.
Verse 29 says:
“He giveth power to the faint; and to them that have no might he increaseth strength.”
Notice who qualifies.
The faint.
The powerless.
The exhausted.
Not merely the impressive believer.
Not the person who never struggles.
Not the Christian who always knows exactly what God is doing.
The exhausted person.
That means your weakness is not automatically evidence that God has abandoned you.
Sometimes weakness is the very place where you finally stop pretending you can carry yourself.
Even young people grow exhausted, Isaiah says. Even the naturally strong eventually stumble.
Human strength always reaches a boundary.
God’s does not.
And then Isaiah says those who wait for YHWH will “renew” their strength.
The Hebrew expression is:
יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ
yaḥălîp̄û kōaḥ
They will renew strength.
The verb can carry the idea of changing or renewing. The picture is not that believers suddenly become self-sufficient superheroes.
The source remains God.
You arrive depleted.
He remains inexhaustible.
You arrive saying, “I cannot.”
And sometimes God does not immediately remove the road.
He gives you strength for the next step.
That may be the part of Isaiah 40:31 we overlook.
Everybody loves the eagle.
“They shall mount up with wings as eagles…”
That belongs on posters.
Then comes:
“They shall run, and not be weary…”
Still inspiring.
But finally:
“They shall walk, and not faint.”
Walk?
After flying?
After running?
Why end there?
Perhaps because much of faithful Christianity does not feel like flying.
It feels like walking.
One ordinary obedient step after another.
Getting out of bed when grief says stay there.
Opening Scripture when your emotions feel numb.
Praying when heaven feels silent.
Refusing the pornography again.
Forgiving again.
Repenting again.
Showing up again.
Choosing integrity when compromise would be easier.
Worshiping Christ when nobody applauds.
Trusting God on Tuesday afternoon when there is no dramatic music, no miracle in sight, and no explanation for why the road became this difficult.
Walking.
And not fainting.
Maybe that is the miracle you have been overlooking.
You wanted God to make you fly.
But God has been keeping you walking.
You thought nothing supernatural was happening because the mountain was still there.
Yet somehow, after everything that should have destroyed you…
you are still here.
Still praying.
Still searching.
Still reading this.
Still whispering the name of Jesus.
Maybe with trembling faith.
Maybe with questions.
Maybe with scars.
But still here.
Do not despise that.
Sometimes grace looks less like escaping the fire and more like discovering that Christ did not abandon you inside it.
And this is where Isaiah 40 ultimately directs Christian hearts beyond ourselves.
The Gospel does not tell us that faithful people never suffer.
It gives us Jesus Christ.
Jesus entered suffering.
He knew rejection.
He knew betrayal.
He knew exhaustion.
He knew sorrow.
He knew what it was to be abandoned by friends.
And at Calvary, the sinless Son of God bore the judgment sinners deserve.
Christian hope therefore rests on something infinitely stronger than “things will eventually work out the way I want.”
Our hope rests on a crucified and risen Savior.
Jesus died for our sins.
Jesus was buried.
Jesus rose again.
And because Christ lives, waiting is never ultimately waiting upon an uncertain God.
We know His character most clearly at the cross.
The cross tells the guilty sinner:
God's grace is greater than your scandal.
The resurrection tells the despairing believer:
The darkest chapter does not get to write the ending.
Maybe your greatest waiting problem is not even your circumstances.
Maybe you have been running from God.
Maybe there is secret sin nobody knows about.
Maybe everyone thinks you are spiritually strong, but you know what happens when the door closes and the screen lights up.
Maybe resentment has hardened you.
Maybe pride has quietly replaced prayer.
Maybe you have learned Christian vocabulary without actually surrendering your life to Christ.
Maybe you have been asking God to change your circumstances while He has been confronting your heart.
Then waiting upon the Lord cannot mean merely waiting for God to improve your life.
It means turning toward Him.
Repentance is not paying God back for your sins.
You cannot.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior who paid what you could never pay.
You do not clean yourself enough to become worthy of Jesus.
You come to Jesus because you are not.
That is grace.
Peter failed spectacularly.
Thomas doubted.
Paul once persecuted Christ’s church.
The thief beside Jesus had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
Yet the Gospel repeatedly shows us a Savior who meets sinners in places respectable religion would rather hide.
That does not make sin insignificant.
It makes grace astonishing.
Jesus does not merely decorate broken lives.
He redeems sinners.
He forgives.
He restores.
He transforms.
He calls us out of darkness and teaches us to walk with Him.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
So perhaps tonight your prayer does not need to be impressive.
Maybe it simply needs to be true.
“Jesus, I am tired.”
“Jesus, I don't understand.”
“Jesus, forgive me.”
“Jesus, I have been trying to control everything.”
“Jesus, I have been trusting the answer more than I have been trusting You.”
“Jesus, teach me to wait.”
That is not weak faith.
Sometimes that is where genuine faith begins.
Waiting upon the Lord means I may cry while I wait.
I may ask questions while I wait.
I may seek wise counsel while I wait.
I may work responsibly while I wait.
I may go to the doctor while I wait.
I may apply for the job while I wait.
I may apologize while I wait.
I may establish necessary boundaries while I wait.
I may lament while I wait.
But underneath all of it remains one stubborn confession:
My hope is in the Lord.
Not because I know exactly what He will do.
Because I know who He is.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not manufacture a polished testimony. Be honest.

And if Christ has already carried you through a season you once thought would destroy you, tell someone what He did. Your testimony may become the encouragement another exhausted believer desperately needs tonight.
Not because every day will feel inspiring.
The friend who keeps saying, “I’m fine.”
The believer who is tired.
The person who stopped attending church.
The one wrestling with doubt.
Even the person who does not yet believe in Jesus.
Not to pressure them.
To remind them that there is still hope in Christ.
Supporting Christian ministry financially is not what makes someone faithful, saved, or pleasing to God.
But believers are called to use what God entrusts to them for His glory, and voluntary generosity has always had a place in advancing Gospel work.
If God has used this ministry to strengthen you, and you are able and willing to help us keep placing Christ-centered truth before more people, you can support Gospel Warrior here:
And comment.
Tell us where you are in the waiting.
You do not need to reveal private details.
Just write:
Because somewhere beneath this article, another exhausted believer may see your comment and realize…
I’m not the only one.
And perhaps that is what you needed to hear too.
You are not commanded to understand everything before trusting God.
You are invited to know the One who never grows weary.
So when you cannot fly…
walk.
When you cannot run…
walk.
When yesterday's strength is gone…
wait upon the Lord.
When your prayers seem unanswered…
wait upon the Lord.
When tears keep coming…
wait upon the Lord.
When you cannot see what God is doing…
look again at Jesus Christ.
Look at the cross.
Look at the empty tomb.
Your circumstances may still contain unanswered questions.
But the cross has already answered the greatest question:
Does God love sinners enough to come for them?
Yes.
With nail-pierced hands.
And maybe the sentence you need to carry into tomorrow is simply this:
The God you are waiting for has not grown tired of carrying you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN A CHRISTIAN BE POSSESSED BY A DEMON?
paragraphs: CAN A CHRISTIAN BE POSSESSED BY A DEMON?
The question is frightening. The biblical answer is more hopeful—and more sobering—than many Christians have been told.
There are questions Christians ask loudly.
And then there are questions we whisper.
Usually late at night.
Usually after another battle we thought we had already won.
“Why do these thoughts keep coming back?”
“Why am I still tempted like this after giving my life to Christ?”
“Why does fear sometimes feel stronger than my faith?”
“Why does this darkness feel so close?”
And then comes the question many believers are almost afraid to say:
Can a Christian be possessed by a demon?
Maybe you clicked this because the question is theological.
Maybe you clicked because it is personal.
Maybe something has been happening in your life that you cannot explain.
Before we go any further, hear this carefully:
Not every struggle is a demon.
Not every intrusive thought is demonic.
Not every illness is spiritual oppression.
Not every addiction proves possession.
Not every nightmare is an attack from Satan.
Not every emotional or psychological struggle should be “cast out.”

Christians can suffer trauma. Christians can experience mental illness. Christians can have neurological and physical conditions requiring competent medical care. Christians can also sin because the flesh is still at war with the Spirit.
Scripture gives us no permission to turn Satan into an explanation for everything that hurts.
But Scripture gives us equally little permission to pretend Satan does not exist.
Jesus believed demons were real.
The apostles believed demons were real.
The New Testament repeatedly describes spiritual conflict as real.
So we must refuse two equally dangerous mistakes: seeing a demon behind everything, and seeing a demon behind nothing.
And once we do that, we can finally ask the real question.
Can someone who genuinely belongs to Jesus Christ be possessed by a demon?
The first complication is that our English word “possessed” can communicate more than the Greek text itself says.

One important New Testament term is δαιμονίζομαι — daimonizomai, commonly translated in English versions with expressions such as being demon-possessed or demonized. The word describes someone suffering demonic activity or control, but we should be cautious about constructing an entire theology from the English concept of “possession,” as though the Greek term automatically defines precise degrees of ownership, influence, indwelling, oppression, and control.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because the Bible clearly teaches that Christians can experience spiritual warfare.
But that is not the same thing as saying Satan owns them.
And this is where the Gospel becomes breathtaking.
Paul tells believers something extraordinary about their bodies:
“ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς τοῦ ἐν ὑμῖν ἁγίου πνεύματός ἐστιν…”
The heart of 1 Corinthians 6:19 is this:
Your body is a ναός — naos, a temple or sanctuary, of the Holy Spirit who is in you.
Not merely near you.
Not merely advising you.
In you.
Paul continues by telling Christians that they are not their own because they were bought with a price.
Think about what that means.
The believer belongs to Christ.
The believer has been purchased by Christ.
The believer is indwelt by the Spirit of Christ.

This is why the strongest biblical case is that a genuinely regenerated, Spirit-indwelt Christian should not be described as demon-possessed in the sense of a demon owning or indwelling that believer as its property. Paul explicitly describes the believer's body as the temple of the Holy Spirit and says the Christian has been bought by God.
But please do not stop reading there.
Because saying, “A Christian belongs to Christ” does not mean saying, “A Christian cannot be attacked.”
Those are radically different statements.
Jesus belonged perfectly to the Father, yet Satan tempted Him.
Peter belonged to Jesus, yet Jesus warned him:
“Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat.”
Paul was Christ's apostle, yet he described Christian existence as warfare.
And Peter later warned believers that their adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour.
Notice whom the apostles warn.
Believers.
You do not warn people about an enemy who cannot affect them.
But neither do you tell soldiers that being shot at means the enemy owns them.
That may be the distinction someone reading this desperately needs tonight.
Attack is not ownership.
Temptation is not ownership.
Oppression is not ownership.
Spiritual warfare is not ownership.
The presence of a battle does not prove the absence of Christ.
Sometimes the battle is fierce precisely because you have begun resisting what once ruled you without resistance.
Before Christ, sin may have felt normal.
After Christ, it becomes war.
Before Christ, pornography may have been entertainment.
Now your conscience grieves.
Before Christ, bitterness felt justified.
Now the Spirit confronts it.
Before Christ, pride felt like strength.
Now God exposes it.
Before Christ, darkness could sit comfortably in rooms of your heart because you never turned on the light.
Then Jesus came.
And suddenly you could see.
That does not mean darkness owns the house.
It means the Light has exposed what was hiding there.
This is where some Christians become confused.
They think, “If I were really saved, I wouldn't be fighting this.”
But Scripture does not say salvation eliminates warfare.
Salvation changes whose side you are on.
Paul writes in Ephesians 4:27:
μηδὲ δίδοτε τόπον τῷ διαβόλῳ
A close rendering is:
“And do not give a place/opportunity to the devil.”
The important Greek word is τόπος — topos: place, room, location, opportunity.
English translations variously render the idea as giving the devil a “foothold,” an “opportunity,” or “place.”
And Paul is writing to Christians.
That should sober us.
Because apparently it is possible to belong to Jesus while foolishly giving the enemy opportunities to work against us.
Not ownership.
Opportunity.
There is a difference.
Imagine a house legally owned by a king.
An enemy does not own that house simply because someone leaves a window open.
But an open window can still create devastation.

That is why Scripture repeatedly calls Christians to resist the devil, flee sin, forgive others, put away bitterness, remain sober-minded, pray, wear the armor of God, take thoughts captive, walk by the Spirit, confess sin, and submit themselves to God.
If Christians were completely untouchable by demonic influence, much of that language would become strangely unnecessary.
Yet if demons owned Christians, the New Testament's language about belonging to Christ would become equally difficult to explain.
The biblical picture is stronger and more nuanced:
Christ owns His people, yet His people must still fight.
And perhaps now we have reached the uncomfortable part.
Because sometimes we would rather blame a demon than repent.
It is easier to say, “The devil made me angry,” than admit that I have been feeding bitterness for six years.
It is easier to say, “A spirit of lust attacked me,” than admit that I keep returning to the same secret website.
It is easier to rebuke Satan than delete the number.
Easier to scream at darkness than confess the lie.
Easier to seek deliverance than forgive the person whose name still makes your blood boil.
Easier to blame a demon than surrender the idol.
And biblical spiritual warfare never removes personal responsibility.
Look at the context surrounding Paul's warning not to give the devil an opportunity.
He talks about anger.
Stealing.
Corrupt speech.
Bitterness.
Wrath.
Malice.
Then he calls believers toward kindness, compassion, forgiveness, and holiness.
The warfare is spiritual, but the obedience is painfully practical.
Sometimes victory looks dramatic.
Sometimes victory looks like closing your laptop.
Sometimes it looks like confessing to your spouse.
Sometimes it looks like calling a mature pastor and finally telling the truth.
Sometimes it looks like forgiving someone you promised yourself you would hate forever.
Sometimes it looks like making an appointment with a qualified mental-health professional instead of assuming every symptom is demonic.
Sometimes it looks like getting on your knees and whispering:
“Jesus... I cannot keep living like this.”
And maybe that is where grace has been waiting for you.
Not at the place where you finally become impressive.
At the place where you finally stop hiding.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that strong people defeated their demons.
The Gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ defeated the powers of darkness for helpless sinners.
At the cross, Satan did not watch humanity demonstrate its strength.
He watched the Son of God give His life.
Jesus carried our sin.
Jesus bore our judgment.
Jesus shed His blood.
Jesus died.
And what looked like history's greatest defeat became history's greatest victory.
Paul describes Christ as disarming rulers and authorities and triumphing over them through the cross.
Then the tomb opened.
Death lost its claim.
Christ rose.
That is why Christianity's answer to darkness is ultimately not a technique.
It is not a magic sentence.
It is not screaming louder than a demon.
It is not obsessing over Satan.
It is Jesus Christ.
The Christian's confidence is never, “I am too spiritually powerful for the devil.”
Our confidence is:
I belong to Jesus.
There is a massive difference.
Jesus said concerning His sheep that He gives them eternal life and that no one will snatch them out of His hand.
Your security is not ultimately the strength of your grip on Christ.
It is the strength of Christ's grip on you.
So can Christians face demonic temptation?
Yes.
Can Christians experience spiritual attack?
Scripture clearly expects spiritual warfare.
Can believers foolishly give Satan an opportunity through persistent sin, unforgiveness, deception, anger, or disobedience?
Paul's warning in Ephesians 4:27 demonstrates that Christians must take such danger seriously.
Should every difficult experience be labeled demonic?
Absolutely not.
And can a genuinely regenerated believer, indwelt by the Holy Spirit and purchased by Christ, properly be described as a demon's possession—as though Satan owns what Christ purchased?
The biblical evidence gives us strong reason to say no.
Your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit.
You were bought with a price.
But perhaps you have been reading this entire article thinking:
Then why am I struggling so badly?
Listen carefully.
Your struggle does not automatically mean you are possessed.
Your temptation does not automatically mean Christ abandoned you.
The thoughts frightening you do not automatically define you.
And if you have genuinely trusted Christ, your worst night does not rewrite the ownership established by His blood.
But neither should grace become an excuse for leaving doors open.
If there is sin, confess it.
If there is bitterness, surrender it.
If you have harmed someone, seek to make it right.
If you are trapped in addiction, bring it into the light and seek wise pastoral, professional, and community support.

If you are experiencing disturbing voices, hallucinations, severe paranoia, self-harm thoughts, seizures, or dramatic behavioral changes, do not assume the cause is demonic. Seek appropriate medical or mental-health evaluation while also asking trustworthy Christian leaders to pray with you. Seeking professional care is not a betrayal of faith.
And if you have never truly surrendered yourself to Jesus Christ, the deepest question tonight is not:
“Do I have a demon?”
It is:
“Do I belong to Christ?”
Because you can spend your entire life terrified of demons while remaining separated from the One demons themselves fear.
You can learn every deliverance vocabulary imaginable and still never repent.
You can know everything about darkness and know nothing of the Savior.
Jesus did not come merely to make frightening experiences disappear.
He came to save sinners.
He calls you to repent and believe the Gospel.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the hatred.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the occult past.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the version of yourself you desperately hope nobody discovers.
You do not clean yourself before coming to the cross.
You come because you cannot clean yourself.
And there—
at the foot of a blood-stained cross—
scandal meets grace.
Your scandal.
His grace.
Your rebellion.
His mercy.
Your chains.
His authority.
Your death.
His resurrection.
This is why Jesus changes everything.
Be honest.
Your comment might become the courage another frightened believer needs to admit, “Me too.”
But whatever you do after reading this, remember the sentence the enemy would rather you forget:
The darkness fighting around you does not get to rename the person Jesus purchased with His blood.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: JESUS KNEW PETER WOULD DENY HIM—AND STILL WASHED HIS FEET
paragraphs: JESUS KNEW PETER WOULD DENY HIM—AND STILL WASHED HIS FEET
He already knew the sound of Peter’s denial before Peter ever heard the rooster crow. He knew the fear, the failure, the shame, and the bitter tears that were coming. And still… Jesus knelt.
There is something important we need to correct before we go any further.
Peter did not betray Jesus in the same specific sense that Judas betrayed Him. Judas deliberately handed Jesus over to His enemies. Peter denied knowing Him.
And that distinction matters.
But perhaps what makes Peter’s story so devastating is that his failure feels painfully familiar.
Peter loved Jesus.
Peter meant what he said.
Peter believed he would remain faithful.
And Peter still collapsed.
Maybe that is why this story gets so close to the heart.
Because some of our worst failures did not happen because we stopped believing in Jesus.
They happened while we still loved Him.
We just discovered that our courage was weaker than we thought.
Our flesh was weaker than we admitted.
Our fear was stronger than our promises.
And Jesus knew.
Before Peter failed publicly, Jesus knew privately.
Before the courtyard.
Before the servant girl.
Before the questions.
Before the third denial.
Before the rooster.
Before Peter walked away weeping.
Jesus knew.
And still…
He washed Peter’s feet.
Do not rush past that.
Imagine the room.
The meal is underway. The shadow of the cross is already stretching across the evening. Jesus knows where He is going. He knows what Judas is preparing to do. He knows His disciples will scatter.
John writes:
—John 13:1, KJV
The Greek is breathtaking:

εἰς τέλος ἠγάπησεν αὐτούς
eis telos ēgapēsen autous
“He loved them to the end.”
The expression εἰς τέλος — eis telos carries the sense of love reaching its end, its completion, its full extent.
Jesus was not running out of love as His disciples were running out of courage.
Then something happens that should make every proud heart uncomfortable.
Jesus gets up.
He lays aside His outer garments.
He takes a towel.
He pours water into a basin.
And the hands that would soon be pierced begin washing dirty feet.
John 13:5 says:
“After that he poureth water into a bason, and began to wash the disciples’ feet…”
Peter watches Jesus move closer.
Maybe he sees another disciple’s feet enter the basin.
Then another.
Then another.
Until Jesus comes to him.
Peter cannot accept it.
“Lord, dost thou wash my feet?”
Jesus answers him:

“What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt know hereafter.”
—John 13:7
Peter protests.
“Thou shalt never wash my feet.”
The Greek is even more forceful:
Οὐ μὴ νίψῃς μου τοὺς πόδας εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα.
Ou mē nipsēs mou tous podas eis ton aiōna.
In effect: You will certainly never wash my feet.
Peter still thinks discipleship is partly about proving how devoted he is to Jesus.
Jesus is about to teach him that salvation begins somewhere far more humbling:
letting Jesus do for you what you cannot do for yourself.
“Jesus answered him, If I wash thee not, thou hast no part with me.”
Peter immediately swings to the other extreme.
“Lord, not my feet only, but also my hands and my head.”
That sounds like Peter.
Passionate.
Impulsive.
Sincere.
And still not fully understanding.
But here is what should stop us.
Jesus is washing the feet of a man whose future failure He already knows.
Those feet will soon carry Peter into a courtyard where fear will expose him.
Jesus knows it.
Peter does not.
Peter still believes his loyalty is stronger than it really is.
Later he will declare:

“Though all men shall be offended because of thee, yet will I never be offended.”
—Matthew 26:33
Peter essentially looks at the possibility of everyone else falling and says:
Maybe them.
Not me.
And there it is.
The dangerous confidence of a believer who has not yet discovered how desperately he needs grace.
Jesus answers:

“Verily I say unto thee, That this night, before the cock crow, thou shalt deny me thrice.”
—Matthew 26:34
Peter pushes harder.
“Though I should die with thee, yet will I not deny thee.”
He meant it.
That is what makes this hurt.
Peter was not necessarily lying when he promised loyalty.
He simply did not know Peter as well as Jesus knew Peter.
And maybe you know what that feels like.
“I'll never go back.”
Then you went back.
“I'll never look at that again.”
Then you did.
“I'll never become that person.”
Then one day you looked in the mirror and hardly recognized yourself.
“I'll pray more.”
“I'll forgive.”
“I'll stop hiding.”
“I'll surrender this.”
“I'll never deny Him.”
And then came the courtyard.
Not Peter’s courtyard.
Yours.
The relationship where you compromised.
The browser history nobody knows about.
The bitterness you keep feeding.
The secret addiction.
The conversation where you were embarrassed to admit you follow Christ.
The money you knew was becoming your master.
The applause you wanted more than obedience.
The prayer life that slowly disappeared.
The private sin living behind a public Christian image.
The resentment dressed up as discernment.
The pride disguised as strength.
The version of yourself everybody sees…
and the version God sees when nobody else is looking.
Then someone recognizes Peter.
“Aren’t you one of His disciples?”
Peter says no.
Another accusation comes.
Again, no.
Then another.
And Peter denies Jesus a third time.
Luke records one of the most haunting details in the entire Passion narrative:

“And the Lord turned, and looked upon Peter.”
—Luke 22:61
Jesus looked at him.
Imagine that moment.
Peter has barely finished denying Him.
Then their eyes meet.
The Greek verb Luke uses is ἐνέβλεψεν — eneblepsen, from emblepō, describing a direct, intent look.
Jesus looked at Peter.
And suddenly Peter remembered.
The warning.
The confidence.
The promise.
The rooster.
Everything.

“And Peter went out, and wept bitterly.”
—Luke 22:62
The Greek says:

ἔκλαυσεν πικρῶς
eklausen pikrōs
He wept bitterly.
Some tears come from pain.
Others come from finally seeing yourself clearly.
Peter had just discovered something terrifying:
He was capable of doing the very thing he was certain he would never do.
Maybe you have had your rooster-crow moment.
That moment when the excuses stopped working.
When Scripture exposed you.
When consequences arrived.
When somebody found out.
When nobody found out—but the Holy Spirit would not let you pretend anymore.
When you finally admitted:
“I did it.”
“I became it.”
“I chose it.”
“I denied Him with my life even when my lips still called Him Lord.”
And this is where shame begins whispering its favorite theology.
God is finished with you.
You ruined everything.
You knew better.
Real Christians don't fail like this.
Hide.
Pretend.
Run.
But shame has forgotten something.
Jesus knew about the courtyard…
when He picked up the towel.
Read that again.
Jesus knew about the courtyard when He picked up the towel.
Peter’s failure surprised Peter.
It did not surprise Jesus.
This does not make Peter’s sin insignificant.
Grace never requires us to rename sin.
Peter really denied Christ.
He really failed.
He really needed repentance.
Biblical grace is not Jesus saying sin does not matter.
The cross proves precisely the opposite.
Sin is so serious that the Son of God went to Calvary.
But grace declares something equally astonishing:
your sin does not have to write the final chapter when Christ becomes the Author of your redemption.
Jesus had already told Peter something remarkable before Peter fell.
Luke records Jesus saying:

“Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.”
—Luke 22:31–32
Do you see it?
Jesus does not say, “If you return.”
He says, “when thou art converted”—in context, when you turn back.
The Greek expression is:
καὶ σύ ποτε ἐπιστρέψας στήρισον τοὺς ἀδελφούς σου
kai sy pote epistrepsas stērison tous adelphous sou
“When you have turned back, strengthen your brothers.”
Before Peter falls, Jesus speaks beyond Peter’s fall.
Before Peter breaks, Jesus sees restoration.
Before Peter denies Him, Jesus sees a restored disciple strengthening others.
That is grace.
Not permission to fall.
Power to return.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Redeeming the person inside the scandal.
And this is where Peter’s story becomes our story.
The Gospel is not the announcement that good people managed to become good enough for God.
The Gospel is the announcement that sinners who could never rescue themselves were pursued by a Savior who could.
Jesus Christ lived without sin.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
Forgiveness is not God lowering His standard until our sin becomes acceptable.
Forgiveness was purchased at terrible cost.
Peter could not wash away Peter’s denial.
You cannot wash away yours either.
But Jesus can make sinners clean.
That basin in the upper room points our eyes toward something infinitely greater than water.
Toward the blood of Christ.
Toward the cross.
Toward the Savior who does not merely improve guilty people but reconciles sinners to God.
And after the resurrection, Jesus goes looking for Peter.
John 21 brings us to another fire.
That detail matters.
Peter denied Jesus near a charcoal fire.
John 18:18 uses the Greek word ἀνθρακιά — anthrakia, a charcoal fire.
Then, after the resurrection, John 21:9 uses that same unusual word.
ἀνθρακιά.
Another charcoal fire.
Another morning.
Another encounter with Jesus.
You can almost smell Peter’s memory burning.
Jesus does not restore Peter by pretending nothing happened.
He brings him close.
“Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me?”
Again.
“Lovest thou me?”
Again.
“Lovest thou me?”
Three questions.
After three denials.
Not public humiliation.
Restoration.
And each time, Jesus redirects Peter outward.
“Feed my lambs.”
“Feed my sheep.”
“Feed my sheep.”
Peter’s failure would not become his final identity.
The mouth that denied Jesus would proclaim Him.
The frightened disciple would become a witness.
The broken man would strengthen his brothers.
Grace did not merely comfort Peter.
Grace transformed him.
That is why this message cannot end with, “Don't worry about your sin because Jesus understands.”
That is not the Gospel.
Jesus calls sinners to repent.
Jesus forgives.
Jesus restores.
Jesus transforms.
Grace does not make peace with the darkness destroying you.
Grace brings you out of it.
Maybe the question is not whether Jesus knows your worst moment.
He does.
The question is what you will do now that you know He already knows.
Will you keep hiding?
Or will you come into the light?
Will you keep defending the thing Christ is calling you to surrender?
Or will you finally say:
“Jesus, forgive me.”
There is no secret confession you need to type publicly to earn forgiveness.
It is by grace.
Through faith.
In Christ.

“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God.”
—Ephesians 2:8
But if this story exposed something you have been hiding, do not waste that conviction.
Talk to Jesus.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Trust Him.
Then think of one Peter in your life.
Someone ashamed of what they have done.
Someone who believes failure has disqualified them forever.
Someone slowly disappearing from church.
Someone pretending to be okay.
Someone who thinks Jesus could never want them after what happened.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is Jesus.
It is truth.
It is discipleship.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even unbelievers to follow too.
But before you leave, remember the scene.
Peter does not yet hear the rooster.
Peter does not yet feel the terror of that courtyard.
Peter does not yet taste the bitterness of those tears.
Peter does not yet know how badly Peter is going to fail.
Jesus does.
And Jesus is already on His knees.
Towel around His waist.
Water in the basin.
Love moving toward a man who will soon swear that he does not know Him.
That is not cheap grace.
That is the terrifying beauty of a Savior who knows the truth about us before we finally admit it ourselves—and still calls us to repent, come home, be cleansed, and follow Him.
The rooster may expose your failure.
But it does not get to write your ending.
Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Your Body Is Asking for Release. But Is It Really a Need?
paragraphs: Your Body Is Asking for Release. But Is It Really a Need?
What biology actually says about sexual release, what Scripture really says about desire, and why the Gospel offers something far deeper than either shame or surrender.
There is a particular kind of battle almost nobody wants to describe honestly.
It usually happens when nobody is watching.
The room is quiet. The phone is close. The mind begins wandering. The body responds before you have finished deciding what you are going to do.
And then comes the argument.
I need this.
Not necessarily because you want rebellion.
Not necessarily because you stopped loving Jesus.
Sometimes you are simply tired of fighting.

Maybe you have resisted for days. Maybe weeks. Maybe you are single and wondering how long God expects you to live with sexual desire without sexual expression. Maybe you are married but lonely. Maybe your spouse is unavailable, distant, sick, exhausted, or emotionally disconnected. Maybe pornography became intertwined with sexual release years ago, and now you cannot tell where ordinary physical desire ends and compulsive behavior begins.
Or perhaps you have heard the biological argument so many times that it sounds unquestionable:
The body needs sexual release.
It's natural.
Holding it in is unhealthy.
God created these hormones, didn't He?
And underneath all those questions sits one question that can change the way you understand your body:
Is sexual release actually a biological need?
The answer requires more honesty than slogans from either side.
Sexual desire is biologically real.
Sexual arousal is biologically real.
Hormones are real. Genital responses are real. Attraction is real. Sexual tension can feel extraordinarily powerful. Orgasm involves genuine physiological processes.
But something can be biologically normal without being biologically necessary for survival or health.
That distinction matters.
People sometimes use the word need when they really mean strong desire, drive, urge, pleasurable release, or something that helps me relax.
Those are not identical categories.

Contemporary sexual-health information recognizes masturbation as common and generally physically safe, while also acknowledging that some people do not masturbate at all. In other words, the existence of sexual desire does not establish a medical requirement for intentional sexual release.
That means Christians should not manufacture medical horror stories to defend biblical holiness.
We do not need bad science to defend good theology.
Scripture is strong enough.
And this is where the conversation becomes much deeper than the question, "Can my body survive without an orgasm?"
Because Christianity asks another question:
Who is Lord of my body?
Paul writes something startling in 1 Corinthians 6:12:
Πάντα μοι ἔξεστιν· ἀλλ’ οὐ πάντα συμφέρει... ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἐγὼ ἐξουσιασθήσομαι ὑπό τινος.
A careful sense of the Greek is:
"All things are lawful for me, but not all things are beneficial... I will not be mastered by anything."
Read that last thought again.
I will not be mastered by anything.
That word cuts deeper than a thousand arguments about technical permission.
Because perhaps the most revealing question is not merely:
"Is this allowed?"
Perhaps it is:
"What happens inside me when I cannot have it?"
If you become furious without it...
If you cannot sleep because you believe you must have it...
If stress automatically sends you toward sexual stimulation...
If loneliness sends you toward pornography...
If anxiety sends your hand toward your body before your heart turns toward God...
If you repeatedly promise Jesus, "Never again," and hours later feel powerless...
then whatever theological label you eventually place on the behavior, another issue deserves attention:
Something may be mastering you.
And Paul refuses to surrender that territory.
But notice what Christianity does not teach.
Christianity does not teach that the human body is filthy.
Your body is not God's embarrassing mistake.
Sexuality did not originate with pornography.
Satan did not invent sexual desire.

God created human beings embodied and sexual. Genesis presents the one-flesh union of husband and wife as part of God's created design, and Paul himself reaches back to Genesis when discussing sexual union in 1 Corinthians 6.
The problem is not that you possess sexual desire.
The question is what that desire becomes, what feeds it, where it leads, and whether it remains under the lordship of Christ.
That distinction is crucial because some Christians have been crushed beneath unnecessary shame simply for experiencing temptation.
Listen carefully:
Temptation is not identical to surrender.
Feeling sexual arousal does not automatically mean you have sinned.
Experiencing an unwanted sexual thought is not identical to choosing to cultivate it.
Having a body that responds sexually does not make you spiritually defective.
Jesus does not save us by turning human beings into disembodied creatures who never experience desire.
He teaches us how desire itself comes under His kingship.
And that is harder.
Because sometimes the real struggle isn't happening below your waist.
It is happening behind your eyes.
Jesus went directly there.

In Matthew 5:27–28, He moves beyond merely external adultery into the intentional lust of the heart. The issue is not simply that another human body exists or that attraction occurs. Christ confronts the inward cultivation of sexual desire toward someone who is not yours to possess.
That changes the masturbation conversation considerably.
Because the Bible never gives us a verse saying, in those exact words, "Thou shalt not masturbate."
We should be honest about that.
Christians damage biblical credibility when we pretend Scripture says something explicitly when it does not.
But the absence of an explicit sentence does not mean Scripture has nothing to say.
The Christian question must examine the whole event.
What are you imagining?
What are you watching?
Whom are you mentally using?
What desire are you deliberately feeding?
Does the practice require pornography?
Does it train you to reduce another image-bearer to material for gratification?
Is it increasingly compulsive?
Does it strengthen self-control—or repeatedly bypass it?
Can you bring the entire practice before Jesus without hiding portions of it?
And perhaps most piercingly:
Can you thank God while doing it?
Because Paul eventually brings the body somewhere astonishing.
Not into disgust.
Not into denial.
Into worship.
He writes:
ἠγοράσθητε γὰρ τιμῆς· δοξάσατε δὴ τὸν Θεὸν ἐν τῷ σώματι ὑμῶν.
"You were bought with a price; therefore glorify God in your body."
The Greek verb δοξάσατε — doxasate carries the command to glorify, honor, magnify God.
And σώματι — sōmati means body.
Not merely your church attendance.
Not merely your theology.
Not merely the worship songs coming from your mouth.
Your body.
Your sexuality belongs inside discipleship.
Your browser history belongs inside discipleship.
Your fantasies belong inside discipleship.
Your loneliness belongs inside discipleship.
Your hormones belong inside discipleship.
Your bedroom belongs inside discipleship.
Even the parts of yourself you have been too ashamed to discuss with anyone belong beneath the mercy and authority of Jesus Christ.
And suddenly the question changes.
Instead of asking:
"How much can I get away with before God calls it sin?"
you begin asking:
"Jesus, how can this body glorify You?"
That is an entirely different kind of Christianity.
And maybe that scares you.
Because you have failed.
Again.
You deleted it and downloaded it again.
You prayed and returned to it.
You made promises after midnight that disappeared by the following night.
Maybe pornography entered your life when you were young, and what began as curiosity eventually became a hiding place.
Stress.
Click.
Loneliness.
Click.
Rejection.
Click.
Boredom.
Click.
Shame.
Click.
Release.
Regret.
Repent.
Repeat.
Eventually you stopped believing you were fighting lust.
You started believing lust was simply who you were.
And this is where the Gospel interrupts the story.
Because immediately before Paul's teaching about the body, he speaks to people whose histories were anything but spotless.
Then comes one of the most beautiful turns in the chapter:
καὶ ταῦτά τινες ἦτε
"And such were some of you."
Then three thunderous statements:
ἀλλὰ ἀπελούσασθε... ἀλλὰ ἡγιάσθητε... ἀλλὰ ἐδικαιώθητε
"But you were washed... but you were sanctified... but you were justified..."
And how?
ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ
"In the name of the Lord Jesus."
Did you see it?
Paul does not say:
"And such are you forever."
He says:
Such were some of you.
That is Gospel language.
Your history can be real without becoming your identity.
Your sin can be serious without being stronger than Christ.
Your temptation can be persistent without becoming your master.
Your shame can scream your old name while Jesus calls you by a new one.
This is why biblical sexual holiness cannot merely become "Stop touching yourself."
That is far too small.
Jesus did not shed His blood merely to produce people who behave better in dark bedrooms.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
He came to forgive.
To cleanse.
To redeem.
To transform.
To teach enslaved hearts freedom.
To turn hiding places into places of surrender.
The Christian message isn't:
"Control yourself so Jesus will love you."
It is:
"Because Christ loved you and purchased you at immeasurable cost, bring even your sexuality beneath the freedom of His lordship."
That is a radically different motivation.
Fear says, "If I fail again, God won't want me."
Grace says, "Because I belong to Christ, I don't have to make peace with what masters me."
And grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace teaches us to come out of hiding.
Maybe tonight the victory will not feel dramatic.
Maybe victory looks like putting your phone outside the bedroom.
Maybe it means confessing pornography use to a mature, trustworthy Christian instead of protecting your secret.
Maybe it means installing accountability safeguards.

Maybe it means discovering that what you have been calling sexual hunger is sometimes loneliness, anxiety, exhaustion, rejection, or the desperate desire to feel something comforting for five minutes.
Maybe it means refusing pornography even when your body screams.
Maybe it means admitting that you cannot keep fighting alone.
Maybe it means praying one embarrassingly honest sentence:
"Jesus, I want this right now more than I want obedience. Please change what I want."
That prayer is not polished.
It is not impressive.
But it is honest.
And Jesus already knows.
There is no browser history hidden from Him.
No fantasy surprises Him.
No relapse makes heaven suddenly discover what kind of sinner you are.
The cross already tells us God knows the catastrophe of human sin.
And the resurrection tells us catastrophe does not get the final word.
So, is sexual release a biological need?

Sexual desire is a genuine biological drive, and sexual release can be pleasurable and may have ordinary physiological or stress-relieving effects. Mainstream health sources describe masturbation as common and generally safe, while also recognizing that some people simply do not masturbate. That does not support the stronger claim that intentional sexual release is universally required for health.
But for the follower of Jesus, there is an even greater truth.
Not every strong appetite is a command.
Your body can communicate desire without possessing ultimate authority.
Hunger speaks.
Fatigue speaks.
Anger speaks.
Fear speaks.
Sexual desire speaks.
But none of them gets to sit on the throne.
Jesus does.
And perhaps this is what somebody desperately needed to hear:
You do not need to hate your sexuality to surrender it to Christ.
You do not need to pretend you have no desires.
You do not need fake holiness.
You need Jesus in the room where you keep losing.
Jesus in the loneliness.
Jesus in the arousal.
Jesus in the memory.
Jesus in the temptation.
Jesus after the failure.
Jesus during repentance.
Jesus while new habits are painfully being formed.
Jesus when you are victorious.
Jesus when you are ashamed to lift your head.
Jesus.
Not shame.
Not secrecy.
Not pornography.
Not compulsive release.
Not religious pretending.
Jesus.
Not because typing words earns forgiveness.
It doesn't.
Christ alone saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending there is no battle.
Send it privately to the person who would never admit publicly that this battle is destroying them.
We will not manipulate your love for Jesus that way. Glorifying God includes faithful obedience, generosity, worship, service, love, witness, and honoring Him with your body and your life.
If you want to go deeper and help sustain the work:
Because maybe the greatest freedom isn't finally reaching the day when your body never feels the pull again.
Maybe freedom is reaching the day when the pull is still speaking...
but it no longer gets the final word.
Jesus does.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: SOLOMON RECEIVED 666 TALENTS OF GOLD EVERY YEAR—BUT THE MOST TERRIFYING PART OF THE STORY IS WHAT HAPPENED TO HIS HEART
paragraphs: SOLOMON RECEIVED 666 TALENTS OF GOLD EVERY YEAR—BUT THE MOST TERRIFYING PART OF THE STORY IS WHAT HAPPENED TO HIS HEART

The Bible records a staggering amount of gold flowing into Solomon’s kingdom every year. But buried beneath the glitter of Israel’s richest king is a warning every Christian living in a world obsessed with money, success, influence, and comfort desperately needs to hear.
There is a number sitting quietly in the Old Testament that can stop you in your tracks.

Long before John wrote Revelation, long before generations of Christians debated the number of the beast, Scripture recorded this number in connection with one of the wealthiest kings who ever sat on Israel’s throne.
King Solomon.
And gold.
An almost unimaginable amount of gold.
First Kings 10:14 records:
“Now the weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was six hundred threescore and six talents of gold.”
The Hebrew is equally striking:
וַיְהִי מִשְׁקַל הַזָּהָב אֲשֶׁר־בָּא לִשְׁלֹמֹה בְּשָׁנָה אֶחָת שֵׁשׁ מֵאוֹת שִׁשִּׁים וָשֵׁשׁ כִּכַּר זָהָב
Wayhi mishqal hazzahav asher-ba liShlomoh beshanah echat, shesh me'ot shishim washesh kikkar zahav.
In straightforward English:
The weight of the gold that came to Solomon in one year was six hundred sixty-six talents of gold.
Read that again.
Not over his entire reign.
In one year.
And Scripture immediately tells us that this figure did not even include every source of revenue flowing toward Solomon.
Imagine standing inside his kingdom.
Gold everywhere.
Gold shields.
Gold vessels.
Gold surrounding the throne.
Foreign rulers arriving to hear Solomon's wisdom.
Merchants bringing wealth.
Ships returning with treasures.
Kings paying tribute.
The reputation of Solomon spreading across nations.
People looking at Jerusalem and seeing what appeared to be the ultimate picture of divine blessing.
And perhaps that is exactly where this story becomes dangerous.
Because you can be surrounded by evidence of success...
while something inside your heart is slowly moving away from God.

A biblical “talent” here is not a coin. The Hebrew word is כִּכָּר — kikkār, a substantial unit of weight. Ancient weight standards varied, so modern conversions should be treated as approximations rather than mathematical certainty. Using a commonly cited estimate of roughly 34 kilograms, or about 75 pounds, per talent, Solomon’s 666 talents would represent approximately 22.6 metric tons—nearly 50,000 pounds—of gold in a single year.
Let that image settle into your mind.
Tons of gold.
Year after year.
Enough wealth to make modern readers struggle to comprehend the scale.
But here is what makes First Kings 10 so much more than an ancient financial report.
God had already given Israel instructions concerning its kings.

Long before Solomon accumulated this staggering wealth, Deuteronomy 17 warned that Israel’s king was not to multiply horses for himself, was not to multiply wives for himself so that his heart would turn away, and was not to accumulate excessive silver and gold for himself.
Then read Solomon’s story.
Horses multiply.
Gold multiplies.
Wives multiply.
And eventually...
his gods multiply.
That progression should frighten anyone who thinks spiritual collapse always begins dramatically.
It usually doesn't.
Sometimes apostasy begins quietly.
Another compromise.
Another appetite justified.
Another blessing turned into an idol.
Another thing we once received with gratitude becoming something we believe we cannot live without.
Another prayer skipped because life is busy.
Another conviction ignored.
Another desire entertained.
Another small corner of the heart surrendered to something other than God.
And one day the person who once desperately sought the Lord realizes he has built an entire life in which he barely needs Him.
Solomon knew God.
That is what makes his story hurt.
When Solomon was young and God invited him to ask for what he desired, Solomon did not initially ask for riches.
He asked for wisdom.
He understood the enormous responsibility placed upon him.
God blessed him extraordinarily.
Wisdom.
Honor.
Influence.
Wealth.
A kingdom whose glory became legendary.
Solomon built the Temple.
Solomon prayed.
Solomon worshiped.
Solomon spoke wisdom that people traveled enormous distances to hear.
The Queen of Sheba came and was overwhelmed by what she witnessed.
Yet Scripture refuses to end Solomon’s story at the height of his success.
It takes us behind the palace walls.
Behind the gold.
Behind the reputation.
Behind the accomplishments.
Behind everything that would have made people say:
“Look how blessed he is.”
And then Scripture shows us his heart.
First Kings 11 tells us that Solomon loved many foreign women, contrary to God's command concerning the nations that would turn Israel toward their gods.
Then comes one of the saddest sentences ever written about a man who once walked closely with God:
“For it came to pass, when Solomon was old, that his wives turned away his heart after other gods.”
His kingdom was still magnificent.
But his heart was divided.
His palace still glittered.
But something inside him had become dark.
People could still see gold.
God could see the heart.
And maybe that is where Solomon’s story stops being merely about Solomon.
Maybe now it becomes about us.
Because most of us will never receive 666 talents of gold.
But every one of us knows what it feels like to want something badly enough that it begins negotiating with our obedience.
Money.
Recognition.
A relationship.
Sex.
Status.
Success.
Comfort.
Approval.
A career.
A ministry.
Followers.
Possessions.
Control.
Even something originally given by God can become dangerous when the gift occupies the throne belonging to the Giver.
That is the trap.
The Bible does not teach that money itself is evil.
It warns that the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.
Abraham possessed wealth.
Job possessed wealth.
David possessed wealth.
God is not threatened by possessions.
The issue has always been possession in the deeper sense:
Do you possess what God has given you, or has what God gave you begun possessing you?
Solomon had gold.
Eventually, the deeper tragedy was that Solomon’s desires had his heart.
And there is something painfully modern about that.
We live in a generation trained to measure life numerically.
Bank balances.
Followers.
Views.
Square footage.
Salary.
Sales.
Engagement.
Promotions.
Net worth.
We count almost everything.
And sometimes we become so obsessed with counting what we have gained that we stop noticing what our souls have lost.
You can gain money and lose peace.
Gain followers and lose integrity.
Gain influence and lose humility.
Gain a relationship and lose obedience.
Gain comfort and lose hunger for God.
Gain the whole world...
and lose your soul.
Jesus asked exactly that question:
“For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?”
Solomon’s mountains of gold suddenly feel much smaller beside those words.
Because Jesus Christ offers something Solomon’s treasury could never purchase.
Forgiveness.
A cleansed conscience.
Peace with God.
A new heart.
Eternal life.
Grace.
Redemption.
You cannot purchase those things with 666 talents of gold.
You cannot purchase them with 6,666 talents.
You cannot purchase them with every ounce of gold on earth.
The Gospel destroys the illusion that enough wealth, achievement, religion, or human goodness can rescue us.
We are sinners.
We have wandered.
We have loved created things more than the Creator.
We have built private idols.
Some of them sit inside bank accounts.
Others sit inside bedrooms.
Some sit inside careers.
Some live inside our phones.
Some are hidden so deeply inside our hearts that nobody knows they are there.
But God knows.
And still...
Jesus came.
That is where scandal becomes grace.
The eternal Son of God did not come because humanity had finally become worthy.
He came because we weren't.
Christ lived the righteousness we failed to live.
He carried sin to the cross.
He suffered.
He bled.
He died.
And He rose again.
The King of kings did something Solomon could never do.
Solomon accumulated gold.
Jesus gave Himself.
Solomon sat upon an extraordinary throne.
Jesus left heavenly glory and took the form of a servant.
Solomon became famous because nations came to see his splendor.
Jesus was mocked, stripped, beaten, crucified, and crowned with thorns.
Solomon’s kingdom eventually fractured.
Christ's Kingdom will never end.
And perhaps you needed to read this because your heart has been drifting.
Nobody knows.
Your church friends don't know.
Your spouse may not know.
Your family may not know.
People scrolling through your photographs certainly don't know.
Everything still looks normal.
You still say “God bless.”
You still know Christian language.
You may still attend church.
You may still worship.
You may even serve in ministry.
But somewhere beneath the surface, Jesus is no longer where He once was.
Something else has been slowly taking His place.
If that is you, do not hide behind religious appearances.
Come home.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is God calling you out of the thing that is destroying you.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the compromise.
Bring Him the greed.
Bring Him the pornography.
Bring Him the bitterness.
Bring Him the affair.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the obsession.
Bring Him the money.
Bring Him the ambition.
Bring Him the addiction to human approval.
Bring Him the heart that has wandered.
You do not need another layer of pretending.
You need Jesus.
And the astonishing message of the Gospel is that the sinner who genuinely turns toward Christ does not encounter a Savior reluctantly holding forgiveness behind His back.
We encounter the crucified and risen Christ who calls sinners to repent and believe.
Grace does not tell us our sin doesn't matter.
The cross proves how much it matters.
Grace tells us that sin does not get the final word over everyone who belongs to Jesus Christ.
Maybe your life has become scandalous.
Maybe nobody knows yet.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe you destroyed something precious.
Maybe you walked away.
Maybe you became someone you once promised God you would never become.
Hear this carefully:
Your worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
We want to keep placing Scripture in front of exhausted believers, wandering Christians, curious seekers, wounded people, and sinners who desperately need to remember that Jesus Christ still saves.
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes publicly acknowledging the battle is the first crack in the wall we have spent years building around our hearts.
Someone may be considering walking away from God.
Someone may be drowning in secret sin.
Someone may believe money will heal the emptiness.
Someone may think they have wandered too far for Jesus to receive them.
We will never pretend otherwise.
Your support helps us keep creating and sharing Christ-centered material designed to reach people who might never walk through a church door but will stop for a story on their phone.
But the greatest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
It is discipleship.
Because someday the danger may not be poverty.
It may be prosperity.
Someday you may finally receive the thing you have been praying for, and when you do, you will need to remember Solomon.
Remember the gold.
Remember the palace.
Remember the wisdom.
Remember the warning.
Remember that a person can have astonishing blessings surrounding them while their heart quietly wanders from the One who gave them everything.
And remember something greater still.
There is a King better than Solomon.
Jesus Christ.
Solomon received mountains of gold.
Jesus received nails.
Solomon wore royal garments.
Jesus was stripped.
Solomon sat upon an ivory throne covered with gold.
Jesus hung upon a wooden cross covered with blood.
Solomon’s glory made nations marvel.
Christ's humiliation made sinners righteous before God through faith in Him.
And the grave could not hold Him.
He rose.
He reigns.
He saves.
So when the world asks you what you are worth, don't point toward your possessions.
Point toward the cross.
When the world tells you to accumulate everything you can, remember the King who emptied Himself.
When success begins whispering that you no longer desperately need God, remember Solomon.
And when shame whispers that you have wandered too far to come home...
remember Jesus.

Because the greatest tragedy is not having too little gold—it is having everything the world can give you and discovering that somewhere along the way, you traded away the treasure of an undivided heart.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Asked God for Wisdom Instead of Wealth. What Happened Next Made Him Legendary.
paragraphs: He Asked God for Wisdom Instead of Wealth. What Happened Next Made Him Legendary.

Solomon could have asked for money, power, revenge, or a longer life. Instead, one young king asked God for something almost nobody asks for when given the chance—and what God gave him shook nations. But the most haunting part of Solomon’s story is not how wisely he began. It is what happened to his heart afterward… and why Jesus is the answer to the tragedy even the wisest man could not escape.
Imagine God appearing to you tonight.
Not metaphorically.
Not through a motivational quote.
Not through somebody telling you, “God has something for you.”
Imagine the living God confronting you with an invitation so staggering that it would expose almost instantly what your heart truly loves.
“Ask what I shall give thee.”
That is essentially what happened to Solomon at Gibeon.

The young king was standing beneath the enormous shadow of his father David. A kingdom rested on his shoulders. Enemies existed. Political pressures were real. Wealth could secure influence. Military strength could protect borders. Long life could preserve his reign.
He could have asked for any of it.
And this is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because if God placed a blank check in your hands tonight, what would you write?
More money?
A healed relationship?
Recognition?
A successful business?
Freedom from debt?
A bigger ministry?
Justice against somebody who wounded you?
Would you ask God to change your circumstances…
or would you ask Him to change you?
Solomon's answer in 1 Kings 3 is one of the most extraordinary prayers ever prayed by a ruler.
The Hebrew is even more revealing.
וְנָתַתָּ לְעַבְדְּךָ לֵב שֹׁמֵעַ
Ve'natatta le'avdekha lev shomea…
At the center are two unforgettable words:
לֵב שֹׁמֵעַ — lev shomea.
A listening heart.
Often translated as an “understanding heart,” the Hebrew expression carries the idea of a heart that hears—one capable of listening, discerning, and therefore judging rightly.
Solomon was not merely saying, “God, make me smart.”
He was asking, in effect:
Give Your servant a heart that can hear.
That changes everything.
Because biblical wisdom is not merely possessing more information.
You can know Bible verses and still destroy your marriage.
You can recognize theology and still worship your ego.
You can win arguments and lose tenderness.
You can know exactly what Scripture says while quietly refusing to obey what God has already made clear.
Solomon did not initially ask God to make him impressive.
He asked God to make him able to discern.
He confessed that he needed help governing God's people, distinguishing between good and evil.
And God was pleased.

Scripture says that because Solomon had not asked for long life, riches, or the death of his enemies, God granted him exceptional wisdom and discernment—and also gave him riches and honor he had not requested.
Then the evidence began appearing.
Two women eventually stood before the king with a horrifying dispute.
They lived together. Both had given birth. One infant had died during the night.
And now both women claimed the surviving baby.
No DNA testing.
No security cameras.
No eyewitness capable of settling the dispute.
Just two grieving women…
one living child…
and two contradictory stories.
Solomon called for a sword.
Then came the terrifying command: divide the living child and give half to each woman.
One woman accepted.
The other broke.
She begged the king to give the baby to the other woman rather than kill him.
And Solomon knew.
The true mother's love would rather surrender possession than watch her child die.
“Give her the living child.”
The kingdom heard about the judgment, and the people recognized that God's wisdom was operating through their king.
But that was only the beginning.

First Kings later describes Solomon's wisdom as extraordinary in scope. His fame crossed borders. He spoke thousands of proverbs and more than a thousand songs. He discoursed about plant life and animals. People came from nations to hear him, and rulers heard about his wisdom.
Eventually, even the Queen of Sheba came to test him with difficult questions.
The young man who could have asked God for wealth had become so renowned that wealth came looking for him.
Pause there.
Because somebody reading this has been begging God to give them what they think will make their life successful.
Maybe your prayer has been:
“Lord, give me the opportunity.”
“Give me the money.”
“Give me the platform.”
“Give me the relationship.”
“Give me the breakthrough.”
But perhaps a deeper prayer is waiting beneath all of those:
“Lord, give me the wisdom to know what to do if You actually give it to me.”
Money without wisdom can magnify foolishness.
Influence without wisdom can magnify pride.
Relationships without wisdom can magnify wounds.
A platform without wisdom can magnify ego.
Success without wisdom can accelerate destruction.
Maybe you don't merely need another open door.
Maybe you need a lev shomea before you walk through it.
A listening heart.
James later tells believers who lack wisdom to ask God, who gives generously and without reproach.
So ask.
But Solomon's story contains a warning that makes this article much more than a success story.
Because if we stop while Solomon is famous, wealthy, respected, and brilliant, we turn Scripture into motivational content.
The Bible refuses to do that.
It shows us the uncomfortable ending too.
And this is where Solomon's story becomes painfully human.
The man who asked for a listening heart eventually stopped listening.
Let that sink in.
The man renowned for wisdom was not immune to foolishness.
The man who could discern what was happening in other people's lives failed catastrophically to guard what was happening inside his own heart.

Solomon accumulated wives and concubines, and Scripture says that as he grew older, his wives turned his heart toward other gods. His heart was no longer wholly devoted to the LORD. He built high places associated with pagan worship, and the Lord confronted his unfaithfulness.
The tragedy was not that Solomon lacked information.
He had wisdom.
He had revelation.
He had experienced God's generosity.
God had even appeared to him.
Yet knowledge did not make rebellion impossible.
That should frighten every comfortable Christian just a little.
Because knowing truth is not the same thing as surrendering to truth.
You can know what God says about forgiveness and remain bitter.
You can know what Jesus says about lust and keep feeding it privately.
You can know what Scripture says about pride while secretly craving applause.
You can sing worship songs while building hidden altars.
You can give biblical advice to everybody around you while your own heart slowly wanders from God.
There are people who can tell everyone else what they should do…
and cannot admit what they themselves have become.
Solomon's downfall did not erase the wisdom God genuinely gave him. But it exposed something terrifying about the human heart:
Wisdom is a gift, but wisdom is not a substitute for faithfulness to God.
And now the story turns toward Jesus.
Because Solomon was never supposed to be the final destination.
Centuries later, Someone greater arrived.
Jesus spoke about the Queen of the South coming from far away to hear Solomon's wisdom, and then made an astonishing declaration:
“Something greater than Solomon is here.”
Think about that.
Greater than the king whose wisdom drew nations.
Greater than the ruler whose fame crossed borders.
Greater than the man associated with Proverbs, splendor, riches, judgment, and intellectual brilliance.
Jesus Christ.
Solomon received wisdom.
Jesus is greater than Solomon.
The New Testament goes even further and speaks of Christ as the wisdom of God, and says that Christ has become wisdom for those who belong to Him.
This is where Christianity violently disrupts the self-improvement story.
The Gospel is not:
“Become wise enough and maybe God will accept you.”
It is not:
“Make fewer mistakes than Solomon.”
It is not:
“Get your life together.”
The Gospel begins with the devastating confession that no amount of intelligence can cure the deepest disease of the human heart.
Sin.
Solomon's tragedy demonstrates it.
The wisest king could still wander.
The wealthiest king could still hunger for forbidden things.
The man capable of judging others could still need judgment and mercy himself.
And so do we.
Maybe your scandal has never reached a newspaper.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your family thinks you're fine.
Maybe your church sees the version of you that knows when to smile.
But behind the screen…
behind the locked door…
behind the deleted messages…
behind the resentment…
behind the secret habit…
behind the spiritual exhaustion…
there is something you know is not right.
And perhaps you have become skilled at explaining it.
That's another danger of intelligence.
Sometimes we become smart enough to manufacture sophisticated excuses for simple disobedience.
But Jesus did not come merely to make sinners more intelligent.
He came to save sinners.
He lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He obeyed where we rebelled.
He remained faithful where human hearts wander.
Then He went to the cross, bearing sin and judgment, and rose from the grave.
The answer to Solomon's broken story—and yours—is not simply more Solomon.
It is Jesus.
Repentance is therefore not God humiliating you for being imperfect.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who receives sinners by grace.
Maybe the wisest prayer you could pray tonight isn't complicated at all.
“Jesus, I have wandered.”
“I've been pretending.”
“I've known better and still chosen wrong.”
“Forgive me.”
“Give me a heart that hears You again.”
“Teach me to obey.”
“Change what I cannot change by myself.”
There is grace for the person who finally stops hiding.
There is forgiveness at the cross.
There is cleansing for sinners.
There is restoration for the broken.
There is wisdom for those humble enough to ask.
And there is a King infinitely greater than Solomon whose kingdom will never collapse because His heart will never turn away from righteousness.
His name is Jesus.
If this exposed something you've been hiding, don't manufacture a religious answer.
Be honest.
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing a struggle into the light is the first crack in the wall we've spent years building around ourselves.
And somebody else reading your words may realize they aren't the only one fighting.
Not because every sentence needs to be remembered, but because sooner or later you will face another decision where what you want and what is wise before God are not the same thing.
When that moment comes, remember Solomon.
Remember לֵב שֹׁמֵעַ — lev shomea.
A listening heart.
We glorify God through faith, love, obedience, and lives surrendered to Christ—not through transactions or algorithms.
But if Gospel-centered teaching is helping you, supporting its continued spread can be one practical way to participate in putting biblical encouragement in front of more people.
And there is something else worth knowing.
Because the goal isn't merely to create readers.
It's to point people toward Christ.
And perhaps that is the final irony in Solomon's story.
He became legendary because he asked for wisdom instead of riches.
But his life became a warning because even extraordinary wisdom could not replace an obedient heart.
So don't merely ask God to make you successful.
Don't merely ask Him to make you knowledgeable.
Don't merely ask Him to give you enough wisdom to impress people.
Ask Him for the kind of heart that still listens when obedience costs you something.
Ask Him for wisdom that kneels.
Wisdom that repents.
Wisdom that chooses holiness when nobody is watching.
Wisdom that recognizes that the greatest treasure isn't a throne, a fortune, a platform, a relationship, or a reputation.
The greatest treasure is Christ Himself.
Solomon possessed treasures kings dreamed about.
Yet Jesus said Someone greater than Solomon had arrived.
So when you are standing before the thousand things this world tells you to chase, remember the young king at Gibeon.
Then remember the greater King at Calvary.
One asked God for wisdom.
The Other came as God's answer to sinners who could never become wise enough to save themselves.
And when your own story reaches the chapter you're ashamed for anyone to read, remember this:
Your worst chapter does not have to get the final sentence when your life is surrendered to Jesus Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: DAVID AND GOLIATH: WHEN EVERYONE ELSE SEES A GIANT BUT YOU SEE A GOD
paragraphs: DAVID AND GOLIATH: WHEN EVERYONE ELSE SEES A GIANT BUT YOU SEE A GOD
The giant was real. The fear was real. The danger was real. But David walked into the valley knowing something fear had made everyone else forget: the battle belonged to God.
There are moments when everybody around you can see exactly why you should be afraid.
They can calculate the odds.
They can explain the danger.
They can remind you how small you are.
And the frightening part is… they may not even be wrong.
The diagnosis may really be serious.
The marriage may really be collapsing.
The bills may really be overdue.
The addiction may really have followed you for years.
The betrayal really happened.
The person you loved really left.
The opportunity really disappeared.
Your child really wandered.
You really failed.
You really sinned.
You really are tired.
And that thing standing in front of you may actually be bigger than you.
That is what makes the story of David and Goliath so powerful.
David did not walk into the Valley of Elah because Goliath was imaginary.
Goliath was terrifyingly real.
