And if your exhaustion has become thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, please do not romanticize Elijah's words. Tell someone trustworthy now and seek immediate professional or emergency help where you live. Elijah's request to die was not God's verdict over Elijah's life.
God did not agree with Elijah's despair.
That may be the most important sentence in this entire article.
Elijah said, in effect, “Enough.”
God's actions said, “I am not finished.”
Elijah saw an ending.
God saw a journey.
Elijah thought his usefulness had collapsed.
God still had work for him to do.
Elijah believed he was alone.
God would reveal that he was not.
And perhaps you should not make a permanent conclusion about your life from inside a temporary wilderness.
Because exhaustion can speak with tremendous authority.
It whispers:
“You will always feel like this.”
“You ruined everything.”
“Nobody understands.”
“God cannot use you anymore.”
“You should disappear.”
But exhaustion is not omniscient.
Your pain does not know the future.
Your fear does not know the future.
Your shame does not know the future.
Only God does.
And Elijah's God was already standing in the future Elijah could not see.
There were still conversations ahead.
There were still assignments ahead.
There was still Elisha ahead.
There was still restoration of perspective ahead.
There was still a legacy ahead.
The broom tree was real.
But it was not the final page.
And this is where Elijah's story begins pointing beyond Elijah.
Because as powerful as Elijah was, he was never meant to be our ultimate Savior.
Jesus is.
Elijah fled when death threatened him.
Jesus knowingly walked toward the cross.
Elijah sat beneath a tree overwhelmed by the thought of dying.
Jesus was nailed to a tree and willingly gave His life for sinners.
Elijah asked for death because his strength was spent.
Christ accepted death because redemption required a spotless sacrifice.
At Calvary, the sinless Son of God bore what sinners deserved.
The cross looked like scandal.
The Messiah rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified between criminals.
His disciples scattered.
His body placed inside a tomb.
If you stopped reading there, it would look like defeat had won.
But Jesus rewrites endings.
The stone was rolled away.
Christ rose.
Death did not have the final word.
Sin did not have the final word.
Shame did not have the final word.
The grave did not have the final word.
And if you belong to Christ, neither does your worst night.

This is not a promise that Christians will never experience depression, grief, trauma, burnout, fear, or profound emotional exhaustion. Scripture itself will not permit us to preach something so shallow.
The Gospel promises something infinitely stronger:
Your salvation rests finally on Christ's finished work, not on your ability to feel strong every day.
Jesus did not die for the polished version of you.
He died for sinners.
People with shame.
People with secrets.
People who failed.
People who ran.
People who reached the end of themselves.
And He calls us not to manufacture strength, but to repent and believe the Gospel.
Maybe your greatest need today is not another motivational sentence.
Maybe it is surrender.
Maybe beneath the exhaustion there is sin you have been protecting.
Bitterness.
Pornography.
Pride.
An affair.
Dishonesty.
An addiction.
Secret compromise.
Unforgiveness.
A double life nobody knows about.
If the Holy Spirit is exposing something, do not use Elijah's exhaustion as permission to excuse sin.
Bring it into the light.
Repent.
Run to Christ.
The same Jesus who exposes sin is the Savior whose blood cleanses sinners who come to Him in faith.
Grace is not God pretending your sin does not matter.
Grace is God providing in Christ what you could never provide for yourself.
The cross proves sin is more serious than we wanted to believe.
The cross also proves God's mercy is greater than repentant sinners dared to hope.
That is the Gospel.
Not “be stronger.”
Not “try harder until God accepts you.”
Christ died for our sins.
Christ was buried.
Christ rose again.
Turn from sin.
Trust Him.
Follow Him.
And when you fall exhausted beneath your own broom tree, remember whose hands are holding the story.
Perhaps that is why this story hurts so beautifully.
Because Elijah's collapse did not erase Carmel.
And Carmel did not make Elijah incapable of collapsing.
Both belonged to the same man's story.
Fire and fatigue.
Courage and fear.
Prayer and despair.
Victory and wilderness.
And through all of it…
God remained God.
So if you have been hiding because you thought Christians were not allowed to admit they were tired, stop performing.
Tell someone.
Pray honestly.
Ask for help.
Return to Scripture.
Rest when rest is needed.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive help where help is needed.
And keep your eyes on Jesus.
You may be underneath the tree right now.
But you do not know what God has written on the next page.
And if someone came into your mind while reading this, do not merely think about them.
Not to embarrass them.
To remind them they are seen.
They are helping support a mission that exists to tell more people about the One who already paid the price.
Because there may come a night when you remember the fire but can only feel the exhaustion.
Follow because your soul needs more than an algorithm can accidentally place in front of you.
But above everything else…
follow Jesus.
Because Elijah's story was never ultimately about the greatness of Elijah.
It was about the faithfulness of Elijah's God.
And your story will never finally be about how perfectly you held yourself together.
It will be about the Savior who holds His people when their strength is gone.
The tree where Elijah wanted his story to end became only a resting place on the road to what God had not yet shown him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE GUNSHOTS STOPPED IN ZAMBOANGA—BUT THERE IS A QUESTION STILL ECHOING THROUGH EVERY HOME
paragraphs: THE GUNSHOTS STOPPED IN ZAMBOANGA—BUT THERE IS A QUESTION STILL ECHOING THROUGH EVERY HOME

After the Ateneo de Zamboanga school shooting, perhaps the question Christians must ask is not merely, “How could this happen?” but something far more uncomfortable: “Who around us is silently falling apart while everybody assumes they are okay?”
A child went to school.
Another child went to school.
Parents expected classrooms, notebooks, conversations, assignments, ordinary complaints about an ordinary day.
Then gunfire shattered the ordinary.

On August 18, 2026, violence erupted at the Junior High School campus of Ateneo de Zamboanga University in Zamboanga City. Two minors died, including the student authorities identified as responsible for the attack, and others were injured. Authorities say portions of the violence were livestreamed. Investigators have been examining how the firearms were obtained and brought onto the campus, what may have contributed to the attack, and what safeguards could prevent another tragedy.

Some details reported during the first days have conflicted, as often happens during rapidly developing investigations involving minors. So we should resist the temptation to turn uncertain details into certainty.
But one fact requires no speculation.
Two children are dead.
Families are grieving.
Students heard sounds no child should have to hear at school.
And somewhere tonight, there are parents looking at their children differently.
Maybe holding them a little longer.
Maybe wondering what happens inside their minds after the bedroom door closes.
Maybe asking a question they never thought they would have to ask:
Do I really know what my child is carrying inside?
Because some wounds do not bleed where anyone can see them.
Some children laugh while hurting.
Some adults do too.
Some people sit beside us in classrooms, churches, offices, jeepneys, dinner tables and Sunday services carrying wars nobody else knows are happening.
And this is where the tragedy in Zamboanga must become more than another headline we consume before scrolling to something else.
We must not sensationalize the dead.
We must not endlessly circulate graphic footage.
We must not turn traumatized children into entertainment.
We must not pretend to know motives investigators themselves are still trying to establish.
And Christians especially must resist another temptation:
giving a simple spiritual explanation to a complicated human tragedy.
Jesus never taught us to look at suffering from a comfortable distance and congratulate ourselves for having an explanation.
He taught us to come near.
There is a tiny Greek word in the New Testament that reveals something breathtaking about the heart of Christ.
ἐσπλαγχνίσθη — esplanchnisthē.
It comes from σπλαγχνίζομαι — splagchnizomai.
Our English Bibles often translate it, “He had compassion.”
But the word is visceral.
It speaks of being moved in the deepest inward parts of a person.
When Jesus saw suffering, He was not merely intellectually concerned.
He was moved.
When Matthew 9:36 says Jesus saw the crowds and had compassion on them, the Greek text says:
ἰδὼν δὲ τοὺς ὄχλους ἐσπλαγχνίσθη περὶ αὐτῶν
Seeing the crowds, He was moved with compassion for them.
Why?
Because they were harassed and helpless, like sheep without a shepherd.
That is where Christians should stand after Zamboanga.
Not above the grieving.
Beside them.
Not diagnosing people we never knew.
Weeping with people whose worlds have changed.
Not asking first, “Whose side am I supposed to take?”
But:
“Jesus, teach us to see people before their hidden pain becomes catastrophe.”
Because there was a victim whose life mattered.
There are wounded people whose lives matter.
There are classmates and teachers whose trauma matters.
There are parents whose grief matters.
And even when someone commits terrible violence, Christians cannot abandon the biblical truth that human beings are more than content, statistics, villains or headlines.
Human beings bear the image of God.
Genesis 1:27 says:
בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים — b’tselem Elohim.
“In the image of God.”
That does not excuse evil.
Christian compassion never requires pretending evil is good.
Murder is evil.
Violence is evil.
Taking innocent life violates the sacred dignity God gives human beings.
But Scripture forces us to hold another uncomfortable truth beside that one.
Every human heart needs redemption.
Including ours.
Perhaps that is why this story is so frightening.
We desperately want evil to belong exclusively to “those people.”
The dangerous people.
The disturbed people.
The people somewhere outside our homes and churches.
Then Jesus says something devastating:

“For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts…”
—Mark 7:21
Jesus locates humanity's deepest crisis somewhere security cameras cannot reach.
The human heart.
That does not mean security is unnecessary.
It does not mean firearm safeguards are unnecessary.
It does not mean schools, parents, authorities and communities should ignore warning signs, online influences, bullying, isolation, threats or emotional distress.
Quite the opposite.
Love pays attention.
Love protects.
Love intervenes.
Love asks difficult questions before funerals force us to ask them.
But Christianity says something even deeper.
Humanity does not merely need better circumstances.
Humanity needs reconciliation with God.
We need Christ.
And perhaps someone reading this has been hiding something too.
Not a weapon.
Pain.
Rage.
Shame.
A secret addiction.
Bitterness.
Thoughts you are terrified to tell anyone about.
A wound you keep disguising with jokes.
Maybe everyone thinks you are okay.
You know you aren't.
Please hear this:
Do not wait until your pain chooses your next action for you.
Tell someone.
Tell your parents.
Tell someone trustworthy.
Tell a pastor who will actually listen.
Tell a counselor.
Tell someone who can help keep you and other people safe.
And tell Jesus the truth.
Not the religious version.
The truth.
“I am angry.”
“I am jealous.”
“I hate what happened to me.”
“I don't know what I'm becoming.”
“Lord, help me.”
Christianity was never built upon pretending broken people were already whole.
It was built around a cross where sinners could finally stop pretending.
The Greek word translated “repent” is μετανοεῖτε — metanoeite, from μετανοέω — metanoeō.
It carries the sense of changing one's mind, turning, reconsidering one's direction.
Jesus begins His public proclamation in Mark 1:15 with a summons:
μετανοεῖτε καὶ πιστεύετε ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
“Repent and believe in the gospel.”
Repentance is not God standing over shattered people shouting, “Become respectable.”
It is the King calling rebels home.
Turn around.
Come back.
Put down what is destroying you.
Stop feeding the darkness.
Stop rehearsing revenge.
Stop hiding.
Come into the light.
And there, standing in the light, is not a Savior shocked by what He discovers.
There is Jesus Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Still calling sinners.
The Gospel does not say your darkest chapter never happened.
It says your darkest chapter does not have to write your final sentence.
That is why the cross remains the greatest scandal of grace history has ever witnessed.
Jesus did not die because humanity was basically fine.
He died because sin is devastatingly real.
Yet the same cross declaring the horror of sin declares something else:
mercy is real too.
χάρις — charis.
Grace.
Undeserved favor.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The ashamed can come home.
The spiritually dead can live.
The violent heart can be transformed.
The bitter heart can become tender.
The addicted can seek freedom.
The proud can kneel.
The hiding can step into light.
Not because Christianity offers motivational language.
Because Jesus Christ lives.
Maybe that is the word somebody desperately needs tonight.
Come into the light before darkness convinces you there is nowhere left to go.
And parents...
please look up from your phones.
Children...
please look up from yours.
Families...
talk.
Not only when something goes wrong.
Ask the uncomfortable question.
“How are you really?”
Then survive the silence long enough to hear the answer.
Churches, become places where struggling young people can tell the truth without immediately becoming gossip.
Pastors, preach holiness without making wounded people terrified to admit they are wounded.
Christians, stop assuming the quiet person is okay because they smiled during worship.
Teachers, keep noticing.
Friends, keep checking.
And if someone tells you they may harm themselves or somebody else, do not keep that information secret merely because they asked you to.
Get responsible adults and emergency professionals involved immediately.
Sometimes love sounds like prayer.
Sometimes love sounds like listening.
And sometimes love sounds like:
“I care about you too much to leave you alone with this.”
There is another Greek sentence Christians should carry into moments like this.
Romans 12:15:
κλαίειν μετὰ κλαιόντων
“Weep with those who weep.”
Notice what Paul does not say.
Exploit those who weep.
Photograph those who weep.
Turn those who weep into arguments.
He says:
Weep.
So before you share footage from Zamboanga, ask whether sharing it protects dignity or feeds curiosity.
Before repeating an allegation, ask whether it has actually been established.
Before turning minors into permanent internet identities attached to the worst day imaginable, remember that families are grieving behind these headlines.
Share truth.
Share compassion.
Share resources that may help someone.
But don't make another person's trauma your entertainment.
And maybe this article should not end with Zamboanga at all.
Maybe it should end in your house.
With one bedroom door.
One conversation.
One apology.
One phone call.
One prayer.
One father finally saying, “Son, talk to me.”
One mother finally saying, “You don't have to hide this from me.”
One teenager finally whispering, “I need help.”
One Christian finally confessing, “Jesus, I have been feeding something inside me that needs to die.”
One sinner discovering that the door of grace is still open.
Not because comments save anybody.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession breaks isolation, testimony reminds another person that they are not alone, and one honest sentence gives someone else permission to finally speak.
Come back to it when anger tells you revenge is strength.
Come back when shame tells you hiding is safer.
Come back when despair tells you your story is finished.
We want this community to remain a place for daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
It is not purchasing God's favor.
It does not make you more loved by God.
You do not buy blessing, salvation or spiritual status.
The Gospel cannot be bought.

But voluntary generosity can help Gospel-centered teaching travel farther. Your sharing can put biblical truth in front of someone we may never meet. Your support can help us keep creating resources intended to point wounded, wandering and searching people toward Jesus.
whether you buy anything or never do...
do something infinitely more important.
Go to Jesus.
Then go check on somebody.
Listen before judging.
Protect before posting.
Pray before speculating.
Repent where the Holy Spirit exposes you.
Forgive where Christ commands you.
Seek help where darkness has become dangerous.
And remember the families in Zamboanga who now have to live beyond a morning they would give anything to undo.
A headline will eventually disappear from our feeds.
Their grief will not.
May the Church still be there when everybody else has scrolled away.
May we become people who notice suffering before it becomes spectacle.
May parents listen.
May children speak.
May churches become safe places for truth.
May responsible authorities pursue truth and meaningful protection.
May wounded minds find compassionate help.
May those harboring hatred surrender it before hatred demands a price that can never be refunded.
And above everything...
may sinners discover that there is still a blood-stained cross, an empty tomb, and a Savior whose invitation remains open.
Because perhaps the most terrifying lie darkness whispers is:
“It is too late for you.”
The Gospel answers:
Jesus is still calling you home.
Because after the screaming stops...
after the cameras leave...
after the hashtags disappear...
there will still be human hearts needing somebody to notice them.
And sometimes the person standing one conversation away from the edge looks completely ordinary.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE TAX COLLECTOR WHO WALKED AWAY FROM MONEY: How Do We Know Matthew Was Wealthy?
paragraphs:
THE TAX COLLECTOR WHO WALKED AWAY FROM MONEY: How Do We Know Matthew Was Wealthy?
The Bible never tells us Matthew’s bank balance. But one dinner, one Greek word, one abandoned booth, and two words from Jesus reveal something far more important than how much money he had: what happened when a man who had learned how to profit from this world finally discovered Someone worth losing everything for.
There was money on the table.
Maybe a lot of it.
Coins changing hands. Goods passing through. Merchants waiting. Travelers calculating what they owed.
And sitting in the middle of that machinery was a man named Matthew.
Then Jesus walked by.
No lengthy negotiation.
No carefully prepared discipleship contract.
No promise that Matthew would become famous.
No guarantee of comfort.
Just a command:
“Follow Me.”
And Matthew stood up.
That sounds simple until you understand what he was standing up from.
Because when Jesus called fishermen, they could conceivably return to their boats.
Matthew was sitting at something very different.
The Greek text of Matthew 9:9 describes him as:
“ἐπὶ τὸ τελώνιον”
epi to telōnion — at the tax booth, the toll or customs office.
The word τελώνιον (telōnion) refers to the place where tolls, customs, or taxes were collected.
Matthew was not introduced to us begging beside the road.
He was not introduced as a fisherman repairing torn nets.
He was sitting at a revenue station.
And that matters.
But we need to be careful here, because Christians should never make Scripture say more than Scripture says.
The Bible never gives Matthew’s net worth.
It never says, “Matthew was a rich man.”
It never tells us how many coins he owned, how large his property was, or how much money he earned in a year.
So saying with absolute certainty that Matthew was extraordinarily wealthy would go beyond the biblical evidence.
But Scripture does give us clues that Matthew—also identified with Levi in the parallel Gospel accounts—possessed meaningful financial resources.
And one of the strongest clues appears almost immediately after Jesus calls him.
Luke records the moment this way:
“Καὶ καταλιπὼν πάντα ἀναστὰς ἠκολούθει αὐτῷ.”
Leaving everything, he rose and followed Him.
Everything.
Luke does not merely tell us Matthew changed careers.
He tells us something was left behind.
Then comes a fascinating detail.
Matthew throws a banquet.
Not merely a private meal.
Not bread for Jesus and a few friends.
Luke describes it as:
“δοχὴν μεγάλην”
dochēn megalēn.
A great banquet.
And it happened in Matthew’s own house.
A large crowd was there, including many tax collectors and others.
Think about that scene.
Tables.
Food.
Guests.
A house capable of receiving them.
A host capable of providing for them.
Matthew had apparently accumulated enough resources to host a significant gathering, and enough social influence within his former world that many people came.
That does not allow us to calculate his wealth.
But it certainly suggests that Matthew was not destitute.
There is another clue hidden in his occupation.

Tax collectors occupied a deeply controversial place in first-century Jewish society. They handled revenue within a political and economic system hated by many of their fellow Jews. Tax collection could provide opportunities for profit and abuse, which helps explain why “tax collectors and sinners” appear together so frequently in the Gospel narratives.
But we should also resist turning Matthew into a criminal when Scripture never explicitly tells us that he personally cheated anyone.
Zacchaeus speaks about restoring anything obtained through fraud.
Matthew does not.
The Gospel calls Matthew a tax collector.
That alone carried enormous social stigma.
But Scripture does not give us permission to invent sins for him.
And this is where Matthew's story becomes more uncomfortable than a simplistic tale about a greedy rich man.
Because perhaps the deepest scandal was not merely what Matthew had done.
It was who Jesus was willing to call.
Imagine Matthew sitting behind that booth.
People knew him.
People had opinions about him.
Some probably despised him before he ever opened his mouth.
Maybe he had money...
but money cannot make people love you.
Maybe he had influence...
but influence cannot silence shame.
Maybe his house could hold a crowd...
but a crowded house does not guarantee an unlonely heart.
You can own things and still feel owned by them.
You can make money and quietly wonder what your life is worth.
You can smile in photographs, pay your bills, build your career, buy another thing you once prayed to afford...
and still lie awake wondering:
Is this really all there is?
That is where Matthew's story stops being ancient history.
Because somewhere inside many of us sits a tax booth.
Not literally.
But there is something we are afraid Jesus might ask us to leave.
A relationship.
An addiction.
A secret.
An image.
A career that has become an idol.
Money.
Pornography.
Pride.
Bitterness.
The approval of people.
A hidden compromise nobody at church knows about.
We want Jesus...
but we would prefer Him not to touch the booth.
We want salvation without surrender.
Grace without repentance.
A Savior who forgives us, but preferably not a Lord who tells us to get up.
Then Jesus walks straight toward the place we thought He would avoid.
And He says:
Follow Me.
Notice what He did not say.
“Matthew, clean yourself up first.”
“Matthew, repair your reputation.”
“Matthew, prove you deserve another chance.”
“Matthew, explain every mistake you have ever made.”
Jesus called him.
And Matthew got up.
That is grace.
But do not confuse grace with permission to remain unchanged.
The grace that found Matthew at the booth called Matthew away from the booth.
That distinction matters desperately in a generation that sometimes wants Jesus as Savior while resisting Jesus as Lord.
Biblical grace does not say your sin does not matter.
Biblical grace says your sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross for it—and His mercy is so powerful that your sin no longer has to own you.
Jesus would later explain why He was sitting with people like Matthew:
“I came not to call the righteous, but sinners.”
This is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Jesus does not wait at a distance for sinners to become respectable enough to approach Him.
He enters their world.
He calls them.
He eats with them.
And ultimately He goes to a cross for them.
But there is something beautiful about Matthew's first response that we can easily miss.
What does this former tax collector do with his resources after encountering Jesus?
He opens his home.
He fills his table.
And he brings people from his old world close enough to encounter Christ.
Read that again.
The house that could have represented Matthew's success became a place where sinners encountered Jesus.
The resources that could have served Matthew's status became instruments of hospitality.
The relationships attached to his former life became a mission field.
Matthew did not merely walk away from something.
He began using what remained for Someone.
And perhaps that is the question this story has been moving toward all along.
Not:
How wealthy was Matthew?
But:
Who owns what you have?
Your house.
Your money.
Your business.
Your audience.
Your influence.
Your phone.
Your voice.
Your gifts.
Your time.
Your story.
If Jesus has rewritten your life, what would happen if the things that once existed primarily for you became places where other people encountered Him?
That is why sharing the Gospel should never merely be an algorithmic exercise.
It can be worship.
Salvation cannot be purchased.
Grace cannot be purchased.
God's approval cannot be purchased.
“For by grace are ye saved through faith.”
We support Gospel work not to earn salvation, but because salvation has already produced gratitude.
So if you genuinely want to glorify God through the resources and influence He has entrusted to you, consider helping Gospel truth travel farther.
Send it privately to someone sitting at their own invisible tax booth.
Maybe their story is one encounter with Jesus away from being rewritten.
Be honest.
There is no shame in needing prayer.
Matthew's story exists because Jesus specializes in calling people nobody expected Him to call.
There may come a day when the thing you are tempted to return to starts calling your name again.
Come back and remember the tax booth.
Remember the banquet.
Remember the command.
Follow Me.

We want this community to remain a place for daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, spiritual nourishment, repentance, grace, and the relentless announcement that Jesus Christ still saves sinners.
It is not a payment to God.
It is not a shortcut to blessing.
It is not proof that you are a better Christian.
Christ alone saves.
But financial support can help Gospel ministry continue reaching people, just as believers throughout Scripture willingly used material resources to serve the work of God.
But before you leave, return to Matthew.
The coins are still on the table.
The booth is still standing.
People are still passing by.
And the man who used to sit there is walking away.
Can you see him?
He does not know everything that following Jesus will cost.
He does not know every road ahead.
He does not know every argument, every miracle, every storm, every failure among the disciples, every bewildering moment still waiting for them.
He only knows who called him.
And somehow...
that is enough.
This is what makes Matthew's possible prosperity interesting but ultimately secondary.
The miracle is not that a man may have possessed significant resources.
The miracle is that when Jesus became more precious than what he possessed, he got up.
The scandal was the tax collector.
The grace was Jesus walking toward him.
The transformation was Matthew walking away with Jesus.
And eventually the story of a despised tax collector would become inseparable from the proclamation of a King whose kingdom cannot be bought.
Maybe you have spent years building your booth.
Maybe yours has a different name.
Success.
Pleasure.
Reputation.
Control.
Religion.
Comfort.
Secret sin.
Maybe nobody else recognizes it.
Jesus does.
And still...
He comes near.
Not because your sin is small.
Not because holiness does not matter.
Not because repentance is optional.
He comes because sinners are exactly the people He came to save.
At the cross, Jesus Christ bore sin.
He died.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And the same Christ who called Matthew still calls sinners today—not merely toward improved behavior, but toward Himself.
So the greatest question is no longer:
Was Matthew wealthy?
The evidence suggests he had meaningful means, but Scripture does not give us enough information to calculate his wealth with certainty.
The greater question is:
What could Matthew possibly have possessed that was worth more than Jesus?
Nothing.
Neither do we.
So share this if somebody needs to hear that their past does not have the authority to write their final chapter.
And comment—not for an algorithm, but as an act of spiritual honesty:
“Jesus, I will follow You.”
Because somewhere right now, another Matthew is still sitting behind another booth...
and Jesus is still calling sinners to get up.
The world may remember where you were sitting. Jesus is writing the story of where you go after you stand.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Can You Lose Your Salvation?
paragraphs:
Can You Lose Your Salvation?
The Question That Has Kept Millions Awake at Night... and the Truth That Might Change How You See Jesus Forever
There are questions people ask out loud.
Then there are the questions whispered only in the silence.
The ones that arrive after another failure.
After another hidden sin.
After another promise to God that was broken before sunset.
Questions like...
"Did I just lose my salvation?"
"Has God finally given up on me?"
"What if I crossed the line?"
"What if Jesus doesn't want me anymore?"
Maybe you smiled in church this Sunday.
Maybe you lifted your hands during worship.
Maybe everyone believes your faith is strong.
Yet deep inside, you wonder if God is quietly preparing to abandon you.
That fear has haunted Christians for centuries.
It has stolen peace from sincere believers.
It has imprisoned tender consciences.
It has caused many to spend more time fearing hell than loving Christ.
But here's the question we must answer—not with emotions, traditions, or popular opinions—but with Scripture.
Can a person truly lose salvation?
The answer is far deeper than a simple yes or no.
Because before asking whether salvation can be lost, we must first understand what salvation actually is.
The Bible never describes salvation as a temporary religious membership.
It is not probation.
It is not a spiritual paycheck.
It is not a reward earned by consistent performance.
Salvation is God's supernatural work from beginning to end.
Paul writes,
"For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so that no one may boast." (Ephesians 2:8–9)
The Greek word translated "grace" is χάρις (charis).
It means unearned favor.
Undeserved kindness.
A gift flowing entirely from God's generosity.
If grace is earned, it is no longer grace.
Paul makes that unmistakably clear.
The Greek word for "saved" is σεσῳσμένοι (sesōsmenoi), a perfect passive participle from σῴζω (sōzō).
The perfect tense carries profound meaning.
It describes an action completed in the past whose results continue into the present.
In other words...
God saves.
And His saving work continues.
Not because we maintain it.
But because He completed it.
This is why Jesus did not cry from the cross,
"I am almost finished."
He declared,
"Τετέλεσται (Tetelestai)." (John 19:30)
One word.
Yet one of the most powerful words ever spoken.
Tetelestai means:
"It is finished."
"It has been accomplished."
"It has been paid in full."
Ancient receipts were stamped with this exact word after debts had been completely satisfied.
Jesus was announcing that the debt of sin had been fully paid.
Nothing remained.
Nothing needed to be added.
Nothing could improve what Christ had already accomplished.
That does not mean sin suddenly becomes acceptable.
Far from it.
Grace never encourages rebellion.
Grace transforms rebels into worshipers.
This is where many misunderstand salvation.
Some believe Christians must continually earn God's acceptance through perfect obedience.
Others wrongly assume grace gives permission to live however they desire.
Both errors miss the Gospel.
The Gospel never says,
"Try harder so God will love you."
Nor does it say,
"Since God loves you, sin doesn't matter."
Instead, Scripture says,
"You are loved in Christ, therefore you are being transformed into His image."
Real salvation changes people.
Not instantly into perfection.
But progressively into Christlikeness.
The Bible calls this sanctification.
The Greek word is ἁγιασμός (hagiasmos).
It means being made holy.
Growing.
Being shaped.
Being refined.
Notice something important.
Growth implies process.
Children fall while learning to walk.
That does not mean they stop being children.
Likewise, genuine believers stumble.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
David committed adultery and murder.
Jonah ran from God's calling.
Thomas doubted.
Yet God did not erase their names.
He restored them.
Because God's grace is stronger than our worst failures.
Jesus Himself gives one of the clearest promises in all Scripture.
"My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of my hand." (John 10:27–28)
The Greek phrase οὐ μὴ ἀπόλωνται (ou mē apolōntai) is one of the strongest possible negatives in Greek grammar.
It could be rendered,
"They shall certainly never perish."
Not maybe.
Not probably.
Certainly never.
Jesus continues,
"My Father... is greater than all, and no one is able to snatch them out of the Father's hand." (John 10:29)
Think about that.
Your security is not based upon how tightly you hold Jesus.
It rests upon how tightly Jesus holds you.
If salvation ultimately depended on human strength...
No one would remain saved for a single day.
Because every believer still battles weakness.
Every believer still fights temptation.
Every believer still needs grace.
John writes,
"If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves." (1 John 1:8)
Notice he says "we."
Even the apostle includes himself.
Christians continue battling sin.
But they no longer make peace with sin.
There is an enormous difference.
Romans 8 begins with one of Scripture's greatest declarations.
"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus."
The Greek word κατάκριμα (katakrima) means judicial condemnation.
A courtroom verdict.
For those united to Christ...
That verdict has already been settled.
Not guilty.
Not because we were innocent.
But because Jesus took our guilt.
Isaiah foresaw this seven centuries before Calvary.
The Hebrew prophet wrote,
"But He was pierced for our transgressions; He was crushed for our iniquities... and with His wounds we are healed." (Isaiah 53:5)
The Hebrew word מְחֹלָל (mecholal) means pierced or wounded through.
The Messiah would bear what belonged to us.
So we could receive what belonged to Him.
That exchange is the heart of Christianity.
Our sin.
His righteousness.
Our shame.
His honor.
Our death.
His life.
Still, some readers may ask,
"What about the warning passages?"

Scripture contains serious warnings against falling away, hardening the heart, and abandoning the faith. These warnings must never be ignored or explained away. They function as real exhortations that God uses to keep His people persevering. Passages such as Hebrews 6, Hebrews 10, and others have been understood differently by faithful Christians throughout church history. Some traditions conclude that a true believer can finally fall away through persistent unbelief; others understand these passages as describing those who have experienced the blessings of the Christian community without ever possessing genuine saving faith, or as warnings that God uses to preserve believers. What all orthodox Christians agree on is this: salvation is found only in Christ, and no one should presume upon grace while living in deliberate, unrepentant rebellion.
Jesus said,
"By their fruits you will know them." (Matthew 7:20)
Fruit does not create the tree.
It reveals the tree.
Good works never create salvation.
They reveal a transformed heart.
James writes,
"Faith without works is dead."
James is not saying works save us.
He is saying genuine faith inevitably produces evidence.
Not perfection.
Evidence.
The Apostle Paul himself wrestled with sin.
Listen carefully.
"For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing." (Romans 7:19)
Does that sound like someone who lost salvation?
No.
It sounds like someone engaged in spiritual warfare.
Every genuine Christian knows that battle.
The old flesh resists.
The Holy Spirit convicts.
Grace continues transforming.
This is why Philippians 1:6 gives incredible hope.
"He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ."
Notice who begins the work.
God.
Notice who finishes the work.
God.
Salvation begins with Him.
It continues through Him.
It is completed by Him.

This does not eliminate human responsibility. The New Testament repeatedly calls believers to repent, endure, obey, watch, pray, and continue in the faith. Those commands are not contradictions to grace; they are the ordinary means through which God matures and preserves His people. Assurance is never an excuse for spiritual complacency. Genuine assurance produces humility, gratitude, holiness, and perseverance—not careless living.
Perhaps the deepest question is not,
"Can I lose my salvation?"
Perhaps it is,
"Do I truly know the Savior?"
Because salvation is not merely believing facts about Jesus.
It is trusting Jesus.
Following Jesus.
Loving Jesus.
Repenting when you fail.
Running toward Him instead of away from Him.
The enemy whispers,
"You've failed too many times."
Jesus says,
"Whoever comes to me I will never cast out." (John 6:37)
The Greek phrase οὐ μὴ ἐκβάλω ἔξω (ou mē ekbalō exō) is another emphatic promise.
"I will certainly never cast out."
Never.
Not after your worst day.
Not after your greatest regret.
Not after your deepest shame.

If you belong to Christ, your confidence rests not in your flawless record but in His perfect righteousness. If you have wandered, the call of the Gospel is the same today as it has always been: repent and return to the Savior whose arms remain open. If you have never truly trusted Him, today is the day to turn from sin and believe the Good News.
The Gospel has never been about pretending perfect people deserve heaven.
It has always been about a perfect Savior rescuing broken people.
That is why our theme is more than a slogan.
It is the heartbeat of Scripture.
From scandal...
to grace...
because Jesus rewrites everything.

If this article strengthened your faith, don't let it stop with you. Whether it's "Jesus is holding me," "Pray for me," or simply "From scandal to grace," your testimony may become the encouragement another believer desperately needs today.
Because someone else's eternity may begin with one share... and your obedience today may become the answer to someone else's prayer.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Cup in Joseph’s Sack Was Never About Theft—It Was About the Heart God Was Trying to Reveal
paragraphs:
The Cup in Joseph’s Sack Was Never About Theft—It Was About the Heart God Was Trying to Reveal
The Forgotten Test That Exposed Hidden Guilt, Proved True Repentance, and Revealed How Jesus Still Turns Every Scandal Into Grace
There are moments in Scripture that seem strange until you realize they are mirrors.
Joseph's silver cup was one of them.
At first glance, it appears to be a story about a missing object, a false accusation, and a family in crisis. But if you read carefully, you discover the cup was never the real issue.
The cup simply revealed what was already inside people's hearts.
And perhaps that is exactly what God is still doing today.
We spend so much of our lives trying to prove our innocence before people while God is trying to expose our hearts before Him.
That is why this ancient story still feels painfully modern.
Because most of us have carried a "cup in our sack" without realizing it.
Some carry hidden shame.
Some carry secret sin.
Some carry bitterness.
Some carry pride disguised as righteousness.
Some carry wounds they have buried for decades.
Others carry guilt that Jesus has already paid for but refuse to surrender.

Genesis chapters 42 through 45 tell one of the most emotionally brilliant narratives ever written. Years after being sold into slavery by his own brothers, falsely accused, imprisoned, and finally exalted by God to become ruler under Pharaoh in Egypt, Joseph stands face to face with the very men who destroyed his life.
They do not recognize him.
But Joseph recognizes every one of them.
He remembers the pit.
The chains.
The tears.
The betrayal.
The silence.
He remembers everything.
Yet instead of immediate revenge, Joseph creates a series of tests.
Not because he wants to destroy them.
Because he wants to discover whether they have truly changed.
The climax arrives in Genesis 44.
Joseph secretly commands his steward to place his personal silver cup inside Benjamin's sack before the brothers begin their journey home.

The Hebrew text calls it גָּבִיעַ (gāḇîaʿ)—a cup or goblet, often associated with royalty, honor, and authority. This was no ordinary drinking vessel. It represented Joseph's position, discernment, and authority in Egypt. The narrative also speaks of silver, כֶּסֶף (keseph), a word frequently associated throughout Scripture with redemption, value, and even the price of betrayal in later biblical themes.
The brothers leave believing everything is finally behind them.
Until soldiers appear.
"Why have you repaid good with evil?" (Genesis 44:4)
The bags are searched.
One by one.
Beginning with the oldest.
Ending with the youngest.
Then Scripture records the devastating moment:
"And he searched, beginning with the eldest and ending with the youngest: and the cup was found in Benjamin's sack." (Genesis 44:12, KJV)
The Hebrew is strikingly simple:

וַיִּמָּצֵא הַגָּבִיעַ בְּאַמְתַּחַת בִּנְיָמִין
"Vayyimmāṣē' haggāḇîaʿ be'amtachat Binyāmīn."
"The cup was found in Benjamin's sack."
Notice the wording.
The cup was found.
It does not say Benjamin stole it.
The narrative intentionally distinguishes discovery from guilt.
Benjamin is innocent.
Yet he appears guilty.
That alone should stop every believer.
How many people have been judged by appearances?
How many have carried accusations they never deserved?
How many have been condemned before the facts were known?
Isaiah foresaw Someone who would experience this perfectly:
"He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He opened not His mouth..." (Isaiah 53:7)
Jesus Himself stood silent while false witnesses surrounded Him.
The Innocent One looked guilty so the guilty could become righteous.
Paul later writes:
Joseph's test quietly whispers toward the Gospel.
An innocent brother appears condemned.
A substitute will soon be offered.
Grace is preparing to interrupt judgment.
But before restoration comes revelation.
Joseph was not interested in Benjamin's innocence.
He already knew Benjamin had done nothing.
Joseph wanted to know something far deeper.
Would the brothers abandon Benjamin the way they abandoned Joseph?
Years earlier they sacrificed one brother to protect themselves.
Would they repeat history?
Or had repentance transformed them?
That is the true purpose of the cup.
Not evidence.
Exposure.
God often allows circumstances that reveal what years of religious activity have managed to hide.
Our trials frequently expose us more than they punish us.
James writes:
The Greek word translated "testing" is δοκίμιον (dokimion), referring to proving something genuine after examination.
Not creating faith.
Revealing authentic faith.
That is exactly what Joseph was doing.
The cup exposed what already existed.
Then something extraordinary happens.
Judah steps forward.
The same Judah who once suggested selling Joseph into slavery now offers himself as Benjamin's substitute.
His words remain among the most moving in Scripture:
"Now therefore, please let your servant remain instead of the boy as a servant to my lord, and let the boy go back with his brothers." (Genesis 44:33, ESV)
This is no longer the same man.
Years earlier he protected himself.
Now he offers himself.
The Hebrew verb behind his plea reflects approaching with humility rather than demanding justice.
Repentance is no longer merely spoken.
It has become visible.
True repentance always changes what we are willing to sacrifice.
The New Testament word is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It literally means "a change of mind."
But biblically it always results in a changed life.
Not perfection.
Transformation.
Not merely feeling guilty.
Living differently.
Joseph has now seen everything he needed.
The brothers have changed.
The scandal no longer defines them.
Grace can finally speak.
Genesis 45 records one of the greatest moments of reconciliation ever written.
Joseph can no longer control himself.
He sends everyone else away.
Then he weeps so loudly that all Egypt hears him.
"I am Joseph."
Imagine the silence.
Every heartbeat frozen.
Every memory returning.
Every lie exposed.
Every regret alive again.
Surely judgment has come.
Instead Joseph says words that echo across eternity:
"Do not be distressed or angry with yourselves because you sold me here, for God sent me before you to preserve life." (Genesis 45:5)
Notice the theology.
Joseph never minimizes evil.
His brothers truly sinned.
They truly betrayed him.
They truly caused unimaginable suffering.
Yet Joseph also sees something greater.
God never surrendered His sovereignty.
Human evil never overruled divine purpose.
The scandal became the pathway for salvation.
Peter preaches the same mystery after the resurrection of Christ.
Jesus was crucified by wicked hands.
Yet it happened according to "the definite plan and foreknowledge of God" (Acts 2:23).
People meant evil.
God accomplished redemption.
Joseph's story ultimately points beyond Egypt.
It points to Jesus.
Joseph was rejected by his brothers.
Jesus came to His own, and His own received Him not (John 1:11).
Joseph was sold for silver.
Jesus was betrayed for silver.
Joseph suffered though innocent.
Jesus suffered though sinless.
Joseph became the source of bread for starving nations.
Jesus declared:
"I am the bread of life." (John 6:35)
Joseph forgave those who wounded him.
Jesus prayed:
"Father, forgive them..." (Luke 23:34)
Joseph preserved physical life.
Jesus grants eternal life.
The cup in Benjamin's sack ultimately prepares us to understand another cup.
On the night before the cross, Jesus took the cup and said:
"This cup is the new covenant in My blood..." (Luke 22:20)
The Greek word is ποτήριον (potērion).
Throughout Scripture, the cup often symbolizes destiny, judgment, blessing, or suffering.
Jesus willingly drank the cup of divine wrath so believers could receive the cup of salvation.
Psalm 116:13 beautifully anticipates this:
"I will lift up the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the LORD."
The innocent Brother accepted the cup of judgment.
The guilty brothers received the cup of grace.
That is the Gospel.
Perhaps today you feel like Benjamin.
Accused.
Misunderstood.
Burdened by something you did not choose.
Or perhaps you feel like Judah.
Ashamed of your past.
Wishing you could rewrite decisions that still haunt you.
Maybe you resemble Joseph.
Carrying wounds inflicted by people you loved.
Wondering whether forgiveness is even possible.
Or maybe you recognize yourself among the other brothers—religious on the outside, but secretly hoping old sins never come to light.
Whoever you are, hear this carefully.
Jesus does not expose hearts to destroy them.
He exposes them so He can heal them.
Conviction is not condemnation.
The Holy Spirit reveals sin so that grace may replace it with forgiveness and transformation.
Romans 8:1 declares:
"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus."

The Greek word κατάκριμα (katakrima) means judicial condemnation—a guilty verdict carrying punishment. In Christ, that verdict has been removed. This does not excuse sin; it announces that those who repent and trust in Jesus stand justified because He bore the penalty in their place.

The cup in Benjamin's sack reminds us that appearances can deceive, hidden motives can be exposed, repentance can be genuine, forgiveness can be real, and God can redeem what human beings intended for evil.
That is why the Gospel is never merely about escaping judgment.
It is about becoming new.
Bring it to Jesus. He already knows what is in your sack, and He is inviting you to lay it before Him. His grace is greater than your scandal, and His mercy is stronger than your shame.
You never know who is quietly carrying guilt, grief, or the weight of a hidden past and needs to discover that Jesus still rewrites lives today.

Because every shared testimony, every prayer, every faithful act of generosity, and every soul pointed toward Christ becomes another reminder that God's grace is still writing stories the world thought were finished.
The cup exposed the past—but the cross rewrote the future.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: How Do I Know If I'm Really Saved?
paragraphs:
How Do I Know If I'm Really Saved?
The Question That Keeps Millions Awake at Night... and the Gospel Answer That Can Finally Set Your Soul Free
Some questions haunt the human heart more than death itself.
Not because they are difficult.
But because they are eternal.
"What if I'm deceiving myself?"
"What if I only think I'm a Christian?"
"What if I stand before Jesus one day... and He says, 'I never knew you'?"
Maybe you've prayed that prayer a hundred times.
Maybe you've cried yourself to sleep wondering if you really belong to Christ.
Maybe you feel like everyone else has assurance except you.
Or maybe you've convinced yourself you're safe because you walked an aisle years ago, raised a hand at a crusade, repeated a prayer, were baptized, or grew up in church.
But deep inside...
You're not sure.
And if we're honest, that uncertainty can become either crushing fear or dangerous complacency.
The Bible refuses to comfort false assurance.
Yet it also refuses to leave true believers living in constant terror.
The Gospel does something far better.
It exposes false hope.
Then it gives unshakable hope.
Not hope built on your performance.
Not hope built on your feelings.
But hope built on Jesus Christ Himself.
This is where the greatest scandal becomes the greatest grace.
Because Jesus doesn't merely improve sinners.
He saves them.
And when He saves...
He rewrites everything.
The first thing Scripture teaches is that salvation begins with God—not with us.
The apostle Paul writes:
The Greek word translated "grace" is χάρις (charis).
It means undeserved favor.
Unearned kindness.
A gift freely given.
The word translated "saved" is σεσῳσμένοι (sesōsmenoi), a perfect passive participle.
The grammar matters.
It describes a completed action with continuing results.
God saves.
And the effects continue.
Salvation is not something you manufacture.
It is something God accomplishes.
That means your assurance cannot ultimately rest in how strongly you hold onto Christ.
It rests in how perfectly Christ holds onto you.
Jesus declared:
"My sheep hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me. I give them eternal life, and they will never perish, and no one will snatch them out of My hand." (John 10:27–28)
The Greek expression οὐ μὴ ἀπόλωνται (ou mē apolōntai) is one of the strongest negations in the New Testament.
It could be expressed as:
"They shall certainly never perish."
Never.
Not because believers are strong.
Because Christ is.
Yet the Bible also warns against empty professions of faith.
Jesus said:
"Not everyone who says to Me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of My Father who is in heaven." (Matthew 7:21)
These people knew religious language.
They performed miracles.
They served.
They preached.
But Jesus says:
"I never knew you."
Notice carefully.
He does not say:
"I knew you once."
He says:
"I never knew you."
Biblically, the issue is not losing salvation.
It is possessing counterfeit faith.
This should humble every believer.
Not drive us into panic.
But drive us to Christ.
The apostle John writes one of the clearest purposes of his letter:
"I write these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God that you may know that you have eternal life." (1 John 5:13)
Notice that word:
Know.
The Greek is εἰδῆτε (eidēte).
It means settled knowledge.
Confidence.
Assurance.
Not wishful thinking.
God does not want His children endlessly guessing.
He wants them anchored in Christ.
So...
How do we know?
Not by counting emotional experiences.
Not by comparing ourselves with others.
Not by remembering one emotional church service twenty years ago.
The New Testament repeatedly points to several evidences.
Do you trust Christ alone—not yourself?
Have you repented?
The Greek word is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It means a change of mind that results in a changed direction.
Biblical repentance is not perfection.
It is a heart turning toward Christ instead of remaining comfortable in sin.
Do you love Jesus?
Peter failed spectacularly.
He denied Christ three times.
Yet Jesus restored him with one question repeated three times:
"Do you love Me?"
Not:
"Were you flawless?"
Not:
"Did you never fail?"
But:
"Do you love Me?"
True believers stumble.
They grieve.
They repent.
They return.
Because the Shepherd keeps pursuing His sheep.
One of the greatest evidences of salvation is not sinlessness.
It is your relationship with sin.
Before salvation, many love their sin.
After salvation, believers may still battle sin—but they no longer make peace with it.
Paul described this painful battle:
"For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing." (Romans 7:19)
Many frightened Christians read this and think:
"That's me."
Exactly.
The struggle itself often reveals spiritual life.
Dead people do not fight.
A spiritually dead heart feels little grief over offending God.
A regenerated heart does.
That sorrow does not save you.
It reveals the work of the Holy Spirit within you.
The prophet Ezekiel foretold the miracle God would perform:
"I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you." (Ezekiel 36:26)
In Hebrew:
לֵב חָדָשׁ (lev chadash)
A new heart.
Not repaired.
Not patched.
New.
God does not simply polish the old sinner.
He creates a new creation.
Paul later echoes this:
"Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation." (2 Corinthians 5:17)
Notice carefully.
The Bible never teaches that believers become instantly mature.
It teaches they become genuinely new.
Growth takes time.
Trees do not mature overnight.
Neither do disciples.
Perhaps your greatest fear is this:
"I still sin."
Every genuine believer does.
John writes:
Notice.
Not "if unbelievers."
If we.
Even the apostle includes himself.
The Christian life is not marked by sinless perfection.
It is marked by ongoing confession and growing dependence upon Christ.
Immediately afterward John comforts believers:
"If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness." (1 John 1:9)
The foundation is God's faithfulness.
Not ours.
What about James?
He famously wrote:
"Faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead." (James 2:17)
James is not contradicting Paul.
Paul teaches that works never earn salvation.
James teaches that genuine salvation produces fruit.
Fruit does not create life.
Life creates fruit.
An apple tree bears apples because it is alive.
It does not become alive by producing apples.
Likewise, Christians obey because Christ has already given them life.
Some people ask,
"What if my faith is weak?"
Jesus answered that question long ago.
He compared faith to a mustard seed.
Saving faith is not measured by size.
It is measured by its object.
A weak faith resting in a perfect Savior saves.
A strong faith resting in yourself cannot.
Perhaps you feel disqualified by your past.
Your failures.
Your addictions.
Your hidden shame.
Remember the thief on the cross.
He had no opportunity to earn anything.
No religious résumé.
No years of faithful service.
No baptism.
No ministry.
No chance to fix his life.
He simply entrusted himself to Jesus.
And Christ answered:
"Today you will be with Me in Paradise." (Luke 23:43)
Grace has always scandalized religious people.
Because it means nobody earns heaven.
Everyone receives it through Christ alone.

The earliest followers of Jesus often spoke Aramaic. One of the most intimate words preserved in the New Testament is אַבָּא (Abba), meaning "Father" (Mark 14:36; Romans 8:15; Galatians 4:6). It is not childish sentimentality but a relational expression of trust and belonging. Through Christ, those who are justified are adopted into God's family. Assurance grows not from staring inward endlessly but from looking to the finished work of Christ and crying, by the Spirit, "Abba, Father."
So...
How do you know if you're really saved?
Not because you never struggle.
Not because you've never doubted.
Not because you've never fallen.
But because your confidence rests in Christ alone.
You trust His finished work.
You hate the sin you once embraced.
You continue returning to Him.
You love Him.
You desire to obey Him.
You persevere because He preserves you.
As Jesus cried from the cross:
Τετέλεσται (Tetelestai) — "It is finished." (John 19:30)
This was not a cry of defeat.
It was the declaration that the debt of sin had been paid in full.
Your assurance ultimately rests there.
Not in your changing emotions.
But in Christ's unchanging accomplishment.

If today you realize you've been trusting religion instead of Christ, don't harden your heart. Turn to Him in repentance and faith. If you belong to Him and have been tormented by fear, let His promises speak louder than your doubts. Keep examining yourself (2 Corinthians 13:5), but do so with the Scriptures open and your eyes fixed on Jesus, "the founder and perfecter of our faith" (Hebrews 12:2).

If this article strengthened your confidence in Christ or lovingly challenged false confidence, don't let it stop with you. Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else has been praying for.
More importantly, your partnership helps proclaim the Gospel to more people who desperately need to hear it.
The greatest evidence that Jesus has rewritten your story is not that your past disappeared—but that your future now belongs to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What Happens One Second After You Die?
paragraphs:
What Happens One Second After You Die?
The Moment Every Human Will Face—The Truth That Can Change the Rest of Your Life Before It Is Too Late
There is a question that has silenced kings, terrified atheists, humbled scholars, comforted saints, and haunted every human heart since the beginning of time.
What happens... one second after you die?
Not a hundred years later.
Not after history ends.
Not after your funeral.
One second.

In that instant, every opinion disappears. Every argument ends. Every excuse loses its voice. Every achievement, every title, every possession, every follower count, every bank account, every secret, every hidden sin, every silent prayer suddenly becomes insignificant compared to one reality:
You are standing before the God who has always been there.
Death is the one appointment every human being will keep.
Scripture declares,

"And just as it is appointed for man to die once, and after that comes judgment."
— Hebrews 9:27 (ESV)
The Greek word translated "appointed" is ἀπόκειται (apokeitai)—something laid away, reserved, fixed beforehand. Death is not random. It is an appointment already waiting.
No one escapes it.
Not the wealthy.
Not the powerful.
Not the religious.
Not the famous.
Not the forgotten.
Not you.
Not me.
And perhaps that is why we spend so much of our lives trying not to think about it.
We distract ourselves.
We scroll.
We laugh.
We build careers.
We chase relationships.
We collect experiences.
We fill calendars.
We buy more things.
Anything to avoid asking the one question that waits patiently behind every heartbeat.
Where will I be... one second after I die?
Jesus never avoided that question.
In fact, He answered it more directly than anyone else.
In Luke 16, Jesus tells the account of a rich man and a poor beggar named Lazarus.
Notice something remarkable.
Jesus gives Lazarus a name.
Parables normally do not name their characters.

Many faithful scholars throughout church history have observed that this account bears unique characteristics unlike Jesus' other parables, leading some to believe He was describing an actual historical event. Whether understood as a parable or an account rooted in reality, the theological truth remains the same: conscious existence continues immediately after death.
Jesus says,

"The poor man died and was carried by the angels to Abraham's side. The rich man also died and was buried, and in Hades, being in torment..."
— Luke 16:22–23 (ESV)
The Greek word is ᾅδης (Hádēs).
It refers to the realm of the dead—not yet the final Lake of Fire described in Revelation 20, but an intermediate state where the unrighteous await final judgment.
Lazarus immediately experiences comfort.
The rich man immediately experiences torment.
Neither sleeps.
Neither ceases to exist.
Both remain conscious.
Both remember.
Both recognize.
Both understand.
Death did not erase identity.
It revealed reality.
One second after death...
everything becomes perfectly clear.
Jesus' words dismantle one of humanity's favorite illusions—that somehow death ends accountability.
Instead, death begins eternity.
The Apostle Paul describes another side of this hope.
He writes,

"To be absent from the body is to be at home with the Lord."
— 2 Corinthians 5:8
The Greek phrase ἐνδημῆσαι πρὸς τὸν κύριον (endēmēsai pros ton Kyrion) literally expresses being "at home with the Lord."
For believers, death is not annihilation.
It is arrival.
Not because Christians earned heaven.
Not because they were good enough.
Not because they deserved it.
Because Jesus deserved it on their behalf.
That changes everything.
When Jesus hung on the cross beside the repentant criminal, He did not promise,
"You'll sleep until someday."
He said,

"Truly, I say to you, today you will be with me in Paradise."
— Luke 23:43
The Greek word Παράδεισος (Paradeisos) comes from an ancient Persian term for a royal garden, later used in Scripture to describe the blessed presence of God.
Notice the word "today."
Not centuries later.
Not after soul sleep.
Today.
Immediate.
Personal.
Certain.
Yet Scripture also speaks of a future bodily resurrection.

At Christ's return, believers will receive glorified bodies (1 Corinthians 15:42–57; 1 Thessalonians 4:13–18), and unbelievers will also be raised for final judgment (John 5:28–29; Revelation 20:11–15). The intermediate state described after death is therefore not the end of God's redemptive plan but part of His unfolding justice and restoration.
Many people assume that if God is loving, everyone eventually reaches heaven.
Jesus never taught that.
He spoke more often about hell than anyone else recorded in Scripture.
Not because He delighted in judgment.
Because He loved sinners enough to warn them.
The Hebrew prophets had already spoken about the seriousness of rejecting God.
Isaiah writes,

"All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned—every one—to his own way; and the LORD has laid on Him the iniquity of us all."
— Isaiah 53:6
The Hebrew word for iniquity is עָוֹן (ʿāwōn).
It means more than isolated sins.
It describes guilt, moral crookedness, corruption carried within us.
That corruption is humanity's scandal.
It is not merely that we commit sinful acts.
We are born with hearts bent away from God.
The Apostle Paul echoes this truth:

"For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God."
— Romans 3:23
The Greek word ἥμαρτον (hēmarton) literally means "missed the mark."
Every one of us.
Every culture.
Every nation.
Every generation.
No exceptions.
Our greatest scandal is not what others know about us.
It is what God already knows.
The hidden bitterness.
The secret lust.
The selfish ambition.
The unforgiven wounds.
The pride disguised as morality.
The envy hidden behind smiles.
The hypocrisy covered by religion.
God sees it all.
Yet this is where Christianity becomes unlike every other religion.
God did not merely expose humanity's scandal.
He entered it.
John writes,

"And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us."
— John 1:14
The Greek says,
ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο (ho Logos sarx egeneto).
"The Word became flesh."
Not an illusion.
Not an appearance.
God Himself stepped into human suffering.
Into betrayal.
Into rejection.
Into exhaustion.
Into poverty.
Into temptation without sin.
Into injustice.
Into crucifixion.
Why?
Because scandal was never God's final chapter.
Grace was.
Romans 5:8 declares,
"But God demonstrates His own love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
Notice.
Not after we improved.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after religion fixed us.
While we were still sinners.
That is grace.
The Greek word χάρις (charis) means undeserved favor, freely given kindness from God toward those who could never earn it.
This is why the cross changes everything.
Jesus absorbed the judgment sinners deserved so repentant believers could receive the righteousness they never earned.
At the cross, scandal met grace.
And grace won.
When Jesus cried,
"It is finished."
He used one Greek word.
Τετέλεσται (Tetelestai).
A perfect tense verb meaning "It has been fully accomplished."
Paid in full.
Completed forever.
Nothing left unpaid.
Nothing left unfinished.
Nothing left for sinners to purchase through religious effort.
Salvation is received through repentance and faith in Christ alone (Ephesians 2:8–9). Good works are the fruit of genuine faith, not the cause of salvation (James 2:17; Titus 3:5–8).
One second after death, nobody wishes they had accumulated more wealth.
Nobody wishes they had won more arguments online.
Nobody wishes they had gained more applause.
Many would wish they had responded to Christ while there was still time.
Jesus Himself asked,

"For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul?"
— Mark 8:36
The Greek word for soul, ψυχή (psychē), refers to the whole person—the enduring life that continues beyond physical death.
Your soul will outlive every possession you own.
It will outlive civilizations.
It will outlive stars.
It will outlive history itself.
The question is not whether you will live forever.
The question is where.
Perhaps as you've read this article, memories have surfaced.
Moments you regret.
Words you cannot take back.
People you hurt.
Years wasted.
Faith abandoned.
Dreams buried.
Secrets hidden.
Failures repeated.
Hear the Gospel clearly.
If you are breathing, grace is still being offered.
Peter writes,

"The Lord is not slow to fulfill His promise... but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance."
— 2 Peter 3:9
Repentance is not merely feeling guilty.

The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) means a change of mind that leads to a changed direction—a turning away from sin and a turning toward God in faith. It is God's gracious invitation to surrender your life to Christ.
No sin is too dark for Christ's blood.
No scandal is beyond His redemption.
No failure is beyond His forgiveness for those who truly come to Him.
That is why our mission has always been simple:

If this message stirred your heart, don't let it end here. Someone in your family, a friend carrying silent grief, or even a stranger scrolling late at night may be only one message away from hearing the Gospel that leads to life. In God's providence, your simple act of sharing could become the instrument He uses to awaken another soul.
One second after death, nothing will matter more than what you did with Jesus Christ.
May that truth shape every second you still have.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “If Masturbation Isn't Mentioned in the Bible, Why Do Christians Call It Sin?”
paragraphs:
“If Masturbation Isn't Mentioned in the Bible, Why Do Christians Call It Sin?”
The Question Millions Secretly Ask—And the Gospel Answer That Can Set You Free
What if the question you've been asking all along is actually the wrong question?
Not because your question is foolish.
But because it isn't deep enough.
"If masturbation isn't mentioned anywhere in the Bible, why do Christians keep calling it sin?"
For many, this isn't an intellectual debate.
It's deeply personal.
It's the question whispered after another night of shame.
The question searched in private browser tabs.
The question hidden behind silence because no one wants to admit they're struggling.
Some have almost walked away from Christianity because they were told, "It's obviously sinful," without anyone opening the Scriptures.
Others have convinced themselves, "Since the Bible never explicitly says it, God must not care."
Neither response truly satisfies.
Because neither one begins where the Bible begins.
The Bible isn't merely a list of forbidden actions.
It is God's revelation of His holy character, His design for humanity, and His redeeming love through Jesus Christ.
The issue isn't whether a specific English word appears.
The issue is whether an action reflects the heart God created us to have.
That changes everything.
The Bible never uses the English word "masturbation."
Just as it never mentions smartphones, internet pornography, recreational drug abuse by modern names, social media addiction, artificial intelligence, or many modern issues.
Yet Scripture gives timeless principles powerful enough to judge every generation.
The Bible consistently asks a deeper question:
"What is happening inside the heart?"
Jesus Himself shifted the conversation away from merely external actions.
In Matthew 5:27–28 He said,
"You have heard that it was said, 'You shall not commit adultery.' But I tell you that everyone who looks at a woman with lust has already committed adultery with her in his heart."
The Greek word translated "lust" is ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō).
It means far more than noticing beauty.
It describes setting one's desire upon someone in order to possess them—cultivating inward sinful craving.
Jesus was revealing something revolutionary.
Sin begins long before physical behavior.
It begins inside.
Most masturbation is inseparably connected with intentional sexual fantasy, pornography, imagined encounters, or lustful indulgence.
Even when pornography is absent, the heart is often feeding desires disconnected from God's design for covenant marriage.

This is why many Christian theologians throughout history have understood masturbation not as an isolated physical movement but as part of a deeper issue involving lust, self-gratification, and distorted sexual desire.
That distinction matters enormously.
Scripture repeatedly teaches that God designed sexuality with purpose.
Genesis declares,
"Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh."
The Hebrew phrase is בָּשָׂר אֶחָד (basar echad)—"one flesh."
This is not merely physical intimacy.
It describes covenant union.
Body.
Soul.
Commitment.
Faithfulness.
Self-giving love.
Sex was never designed as merely a mechanism for pleasure.
It was created as an expression of covenantal love that reflects God's faithful relationship with His people.
When sexuality becomes detached from self-giving love and redirected inward merely for self-consumption, something sacred becomes diminished.
Not because pleasure itself is evil.
God created pleasure.
But because God's gifts flourish only within God's design.
Some people immediately raise another objection.
"What about Onan?"
Genesis 38 is frequently quoted.
Onan "spilled his seed on the ground."
Many assume God killed him because he masturbated.
But careful biblical interpretation says otherwise.
The Hebrew narrative makes the issue clear.
Onan refused to fulfill his covenant responsibility to provide offspring for his deceased brother according to levirate marriage customs.
His sin was deliberate rebellion, greed, and covenant unfaithfulness—not simply the physical act of emission itself.
Using Onan as the primary proof-text against masturbation stretches the passage beyond its intended meaning.
Good theology refuses to force Scripture to say what it does not say.
Truth does not need exaggeration.
But neither should silence be mistaken for approval.
Throughout Scripture, God consistently calls His people toward purity.
Paul writes in 1 Thessalonians 4:3–5,
"For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality."
The Greek word translated "sexual immorality" is πορνεία (porneia).
This word carries broad meaning.
It encompasses every form of sexual behavior outside God's intended design.
It is intentionally comprehensive rather than narrowly defined.
Paul continues by calling believers to learn self-control rather than living in "passionate lust."
Again, the emphasis is not merely behavior.
It is mastery of desires through the Holy Spirit.
The Bible repeatedly presents self-control as evidence of spiritual maturity.
Galatians 5 lists ἐγκράτεια (enkrateia)—self-control—as fruit of the Holy Spirit.
Notice something remarkable.
Paul does not merely say Christians should avoid wrong actions.
He says God's Spirit actually transforms desires.
Christianity is not behavior modification.
It is heart transformation.
This is why many believers who sincerely love Jesus continue struggling.
They try to fight behavior while leaving the heart untouched.
Rules alone cannot heal desire.
Only Christ can.
Perhaps that's why so many feel trapped.
They promise God,
"Never again."
Then fail.
Then apologize.
Then fail again.
Eventually shame whispers,
"You're a hypocrite."
"You'll never change."
"God is tired of you."
But shame has always been one of Satan's favorite languages.
The Gospel speaks differently.
Romans 8:1 declares,
"There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus."
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not say there is no sin.
He says there is no condemnation for those united with Christ.
Jesus never minimizes sin.
He destroys its power.
This is where many articles stop.
"Just don't do it."
But the Gospel goes deeper.
Why are you turning to it?
Loneliness?
Stress?
Trauma?
Anxiety?
Rejection?
Depression?
Boredom?
Unresolved wounds?
Sometimes masturbation is less about sexuality and more about medicating pain.
The body seeks relief because the soul is exhausted.
Jesus never ignored wounded souls.
Neither should His Church.
That does not make sinful responses righteous.
But it reminds us that behind many habits stands a hurting person whom Christ deeply loves.
The answer is not merely stronger willpower.
It is deeper surrender.
Psalm 51 records David's cry after devastating sexual sin.
He did not merely ask God to improve his behavior.
He prayed,
"Create in me a clean heart, O God."
The Hebrew word לֵב (lev) means the inner person—the center of desire, will, and affection.
David knew external restraint would never be enough.
He needed a new heart.
And that is exactly what God promises.
Ezekiel 36:26 declares,
"I will give you a new heart."
Not a patched heart.
Not an improved heart.
A new one.
This is the miracle of the Gospel.
Jesus does not merely forgive failures.
He recreates people.
That is why our ministry exists under one unchanging message:
Perhaps your scandal isn't public.
Perhaps nobody knows.
Perhaps your browser history knows.
Perhaps your imagination knows.
Perhaps only you and God know.
But hidden sins are not beyond hidden grace.
The cross is large enough for secret struggles.
The resurrection is powerful enough for lasting transformation.
If you belong to Christ, your identity is no longer "the one who struggles."
Your identity is beloved, redeemed, forgiven, adopted, and being sanctified.
Sanctification is often a process.
Sometimes victory comes suddenly.
Sometimes it comes one surrendered day at a time.
When you fall, run toward Christ, not away from Him.
Repentance is not merely feeling guilty.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia) means a change of mind that results in a changed direction of life.
Real repentance keeps returning to Jesus because He alone changes hearts.
So...
Is masturbation explicitly named in the Bible?
No.
Does Scripture provide principles that lead many faithful Christians to conclude that lust-driven masturbation falls outside God's design for holy sexuality?
Yes.
Can sincere believers wrestle with difficult questions while remaining committed to biblical authority?
Absolutely.
Should Christians avoid creating laws where Scripture is silent?
Yes.
Should Christians also avoid ignoring the clear biblical principles concerning holiness, lust, purity, self-control, and God's design for sexuality?
Also yes.
The Gospel refuses both legalism and license.
It calls us into something far more beautiful.
Holiness born from love.
Purity flowing from grace.
Obedience empowered by the Holy Spirit.
Not because we are trying to earn God's love.
But because in Christ, we have already received it.
Maybe this article didn't give you the simple yes-or-no answer you expected.
Because Jesus rarely settles for surface answers.
He always reaches the heart.
And perhaps that's exactly where He is speaking today.
Sometimes God uses one shared message to begin a lifelong journey from bondage to freedom.
Let it remind you that Christ's grace speaks louder than your failures.
Someone's eternity may be impacted by one invitation.
They also gain access to exclusive discipleship content while supporting the continued expansion of this ministry.
One surrendered heart has always been worth more to Heaven than a thousand hidden victories no one ever needed to fight alone.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Every Time You Replay That Memory, Something Is Worshiping: What the Bible Really Says About Sexual Memories—and the Grace That Can Rewrite Them
paragraphs:
Every Time You Replay That Memory, Something Is Worshiping: What the Bible Really Says About Sexual Memories—and the Grace That Can Rewrite Them
