"Wide is the gate and broad is the road that leads to destruction." (Matthew 7:13)
The broad road is attractive.
Popular.
Easy.
Crowded.
That has never made it right.
Sin often looks rewarding because Satan advertises the beginning...
never the ending.
He markets pleasure.
God reveals consequences.
Hebrews reminds us Moses chose differently.
"He considered the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt..." (Hebrews 11:26)
Imagine that.
The richest empire in the world.
Unlimited luxury.
Power.
Influence.
Prestige.
Yet Moses walked away.
Why?
Because he believed eternity outweighed temporary comfort.
Faith always sees farther than envy can.
The Apostle Paul reached the same conclusion.
"For our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison." (2 Corinthians 4:17)
Notice Paul's language.
Light?
Momentary?
Paul endured imprisonment.
Beatings.
Shipwrecks.
Hunger.
Persecution.
Yet compared with eternity...
he called them light.
That perspective cannot be manufactured.
It comes from seeing Jesus.
The greatest answer to envy is not trying harder.
It is looking longer at Christ.
Because Jesus also appeared to lose.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
To the watching world...
He looked defeated.
Yet what appeared to be history's greatest scandal became history's greatest victory.
The cross is proof that appearances cannot be trusted.
What looked like failure became redemption.
What looked like shame became glory.
What looked like death became eternal life.
That is our story too.
This is why our theme is more than a slogan.
From Scandal to Grace. Because Jesus Rewrites Everything.
The Gospel never promises believers the easiest life.
It promises the truest one.
Not the richest life.
The redeemed one.
Not temporary applause.
Everlasting joy.
Peter writes:
The Greek phrase ἀνεκλαλήτῳ χαρᾷ (aneklalētō charā) means a joy too wonderful for words.
The world cannot manufacture that.
Money cannot purchase it.
Success cannot imitate it.
Sin cannot sustain it.
Only Christ gives it.
Perhaps today you have secretly envied someone living apart from God.
Perhaps you have wondered why obedience sometimes feels costly.
You are not the first.
Neither was Asaph.
Neither was David.
Neither was Jeremiah.
God did not reject them for their honesty.
He restored them through truth.
Bring your envy into God's presence before it grows into unbelief.
Tell Him exactly where your heart has wandered.
He already knows.
And His grace is greater than your hidden struggle.
Jesus did not come for people pretending they have perfect faith.
He came for people willing to confess they need Him.
Maybe this article exposed something you have never admitted before.
That is not condemnation.
That is grace inviting you home.
If this spoke to your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
There will be days when scrolling through success, wealth, and worldly pleasure will tempt your heart again. Return to these truths before envy gains a foothold.
One faithful act of obedience is worth more than a lifetime of applauded rebellion.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Thought It Was Harmless… Until This Scripture Exposed It
paragraphs:
You Thought It Was Harmless… Until This Scripture Exposed It
What the Bible Actually Says About Sexual Fantasies (And Why It’s Deeper Than You Think)
It never starts loud.
No warning. No alarm. Just a thought.

A glance that lingers a second too long.
A memory replayed when no one’s watching.
A “what if” that quietly drifts into your mind when you’re tired… alone… vulnerable.
And you tell yourself it’s not that serious.
Because you didn’t act on it.
Because nobody saw it.
Because it’s “just in your head.”
But somewhere deep inside… you already know something feels off.
And that tension? That quiet conviction you keep brushing away?
Jesus didn’t ignore it.
He walked straight into it.
In Matthew 5:28, He said something that shattered every excuse people like us have ever made:
“But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman to lust for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
The Greek doesn’t soften it. It actually intensifies it.
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων… πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι” (pas ho blepōn… pros to epithymēsai)

It doesn’t just mean noticing beauty.
It means looking with the intention to desire.
To internally pursue. To mentally engage.
This isn’t about accidental attraction.
This is about intentional imagination.
The kind that creates a private world where sin feels safe… because it’s hidden.
And Jesus says… that world is not hidden.
Because the battlefield was never just your body.
It’s your heart.
The word He uses for “heart” is καρδία (kardia). Not just emotions. Not just feelings.
It means the center of your will, your thoughts, your desires… the place where decisions are born.
So when fantasies live there unchecked… they’re not harmless.
They’re forming something.
Shaping something.
Becoming something.
Long before action ever shows up.
And suddenly this isn’t just about “thinking wrong.”
It’s about who you are becoming when no one is watching.
David understood this tension in a way that should make you uncomfortable.
This is the same David who wrote worship songs… who danced before the Lord… who was called “a man after God’s own heart.”
And yet one night… a glance turned into a thought… and a thought turned into a decision… and a decision turned into destruction.
Before Bathsheba was ever touched… she was imagined.
Before the sin was physical… it was internal.
And Psalm 51 exposes the aftermath like a wound left open on purpose:
“Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity… and in sin did my mother conceive me… Behold, You desire truth in the inward being…”
In Hebrew, “inward being” is:
“בַּטֻּחוֹת” (batuchot)
It means the hidden places. The concealed parts. The private inner chambers.
The places no one sees.
Except God.
David didn’t just confess what he did.
He confessed what lived inside him before he ever did it.
That’s where this gets real.
Because sexual fantasies aren’t just random thoughts.
They are invitations.
Invitations to dwell… to replay… to build a reality that slowly rewires your desires.
James 1:14–15 explains the process with unsettling clarity:
“But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire (ἐπιθυμία, epithymia). Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin…”
Do you see it?
Conception happens before birth.
Which means sin doesn’t start when it’s visible.
It starts when it’s entertained.
When you feed it.
When you protect it.
When you return to it because it feels easier than facing the emptiness you’re trying to escape.
And that’s the part most people don’t want to admit.
Sometimes it’s not even about lust.
Sometimes it’s loneliness dressed as desire.
Sometimes it’s pain trying to feel control.
Sometimes it’s a wounded heart searching for comfort in a counterfeit version of intimacy.
And the enemy doesn’t need you to act…
If he can keep you imagining.
Because what you repeatedly imagine… you slowly normalize.
And what you normalize… you eventually justify.
And what you justify… you become.
But here’s where the story shifts.
Because this is not where Jesus leaves you.
Not in shame.
Not in condemnation.
Not in hiding.
He goes deeper than exposure.
He goes to restoration.
In John 8, when a woman caught in sexual sin was dragged before Him, everyone expected judgment.
Stones were already in hands.
Accusations already formed.
But Jesus didn’t mirror their reaction.
He bent down.
Paused.
Then spoke words that still echo into places like yours:
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.”
In Greek:
“οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω” (oude egō se katakrinō)
“I do not condemn you.”
But notice… He didn’t excuse the sin.
He didn’t redefine it.
He didn’t say it was harmless.
He offered something far more powerful.
Freedom.
Not just from consequences.
But from the pattern itself.
Because grace is not permission to stay the same.
It is power to become new.
This is why Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 10:5:
The Greek word for “captive” is:
“αἰχμαλωτίζοντες” (aichmalōtizontes)
It means to take prisoner. To seize control.
Not ignore. Not tolerate.
But confront.
Which means you are not powerless against your thoughts.
But you are responsible for what you allow to stay.
And maybe that’s the moment this stops being theoretical.
Because if you’re honest…
There are thoughts you’ve been entertaining.
Places your mind goes when it shouldn’t.
Moments you’ve justified because “at least I didn’t act on it.”
But right now… something in you knows…
God is not just calling out behavior.
He’s calling you back to purity in the place no one sees.
Not to shame you.
But to free you.
Because the version of you that keeps returning to those fantasies…
Is not the version of you that Christ died to create.
And this is where you have a choice.
Or you can finally be honest.
Don’t stay silent.
Silence is where these things grow.
Bring it into the light.
And if you’re serious about going deeper—about real transformation, not surface-level change—step into what we’re building.
They are people choosing discipleship over distraction.
People choosing truth over comfort.
If you want your life to glorify God… then don’t just consume truth.
Support it. Spread it. Stand with it.
Because someone else is where you were yesterday…
And your share might be the moment they wake up.
Your tag might be the interruption they needed.
Your obedience might be someone else’s rescue.
And maybe… just maybe…
God didn’t expose this to shame you…
But to finally set you free.
Because the thoughts you hide today… shape the person you become tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: When Love Multiplies but Peace Divides: The Hidden War Between Monogamy and Polygamy in Scripture
paragraphs: When Love Multiplies but Peace Divides: The Hidden War Between Monogamy and Polygamy in Scripture
There is a quiet question buried beneath the surface of Scripture… one that most people never dare to sit with long enough.
What actually caused more damage in the Bible… monogamy… or polygamy?
Not what culture says. Not what tradition softened. Not what modern opinion reshaped.
But what the lives… the tears… the broken homes… and the whispered prayers inside Scripture actually reveal.
Because if you read slowly enough… if you feel it instead of just scanning it… you’ll notice something unsettling.
The Bible never hides the consequences of multiplied love.
It exposes them.
And it hurts.
The first time God defines marriage, it is not complicated. It is not layered. It is not plural.
In Genesis 2:24, the Hebrew speaks with a clarity that cuts through centuries of debate:
“וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד” (ve’hayu le’basar echad)
“And they shall become one flesh.”
Not many… becoming many.
But two… becoming one.
There is unity in the design. There is peace in the limit. There is protection in the boundary.
And yet… humanity didn’t stay there long.
The first recorded polygamist in Scripture is not a hero.
He is a descendant of Cain.
Lamech.
And his introduction isn’t gentle. It’s violent.
“I have killed a man…” (Genesis 4:23)
And almost as a side note… “he took two wives.”
Polygamy enters the story not through covenant… but through corruption.
And from that moment forward… something begins to fracture.
You see it in Abraham’s house.
God gave a promise. A son would come through Sarah.
But waiting felt too long.
So human logic stepped in.
Hagar.
A second relationship. A second womb. A second plan.
And suddenly… jealousy was born.
Genesis 16 doesn’t read like a blessing. It reads like tension tightening its grip.
Sarah despises Hagar.
Hagar flees.
Abraham is caught between them.
And a child grows up in the middle of conflict that should have never existed.
This wasn’t expansion.
This was complication.
Then comes Jacob.
Two sisters.
Leah… and Rachel.
And if you read the Hebrew closely, the pain becomes almost unbearable.
In Genesis 29:31, it says:
“וַיַּרְא יְהוָה כִּי שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה” (Vayar Adonai ki senu’ah Leah)
“And the LORD saw that Leah was hated.”
Hated.
Not unloved in a mild sense.
The word carries weight. Rejection. Emotional abandonment.
And what follows?
Competition.
Wombs competing for worth.
Children becoming proof of validation.
Rachel envies. Leah aches. Servants are given as extensions of rivalry.
This is not romance.
This is war… inside a family.
And the ripple doesn’t stop there.
Those children grow into tribes.
The tension multiplies across generations.
All because love was divided.
Then David.
A man after God’s own heart… yet not untouched by the pattern.
Multiple wives.
Multiple households.
And eventually… chaos within his own sons.
Amnon violates Tamar.
Absalom murders Amnon.
Absalom rebels against David.
A kingdom fractures… from inside the family.
And then Solomon.
Seven hundred wives.
Three hundred concubines.
At that point… it’s no longer about relationship.
It’s accumulation.
And Scripture doesn’t celebrate it.
It warns us.
1 Kings 11:3 says plainly:
“his wives turned away his heart.”
The Hebrew word “וַיַּטּוּ” (vayattu) means to stretch, to bend, to incline away.
Not instantly… but gradually.
Quietly.
Until devotion is no longer singular.
Until God is no longer first.
And the wisest man on earth… becomes spiritually divided.
This is the pattern Scripture refuses to hide.
Polygamy didn’t just add people.
It multiplied problems.
Jealousy.
Comparison.
Division.
Spiritual drift.
Broken children.
Fractured leadership.
And yet… monogamy is not presented as perfect either.
Because the issue was never just structure.
It was the human heart.
Even in one-on-one covenant… there can be betrayal, neglect, hardness.
But here’s the difference.
Monogamy reflects the original design.
Polygamy reflects human deviation.
One aligns with unity.
The other introduces division by nature.
And then… everything shifts.
Because the Bible is not just about broken patterns.
It is about redemption.
When Jesus speaks about marriage, He doesn’t expand it.
He restores it.
In Matthew 19:5, He echoes Genesis:
“καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν” (kai esontai hoi duo eis sarka mian)
“And the two shall become one flesh.”
Two.
Not many.
Jesus pulls us back… not forward into complexity.
Back to design.
Back to intention.
Back to something sacred that cannot be multiplied without being diluted.
And then Paul… writing in Ephesians 5… takes it even deeper.
Marriage becomes a picture.
A living metaphor.
Christ… and the Church.
Not Christ and churches.
Not divided affection.
Not scattered devotion.
But one Bride.
One covenant.
One love.
“οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν· τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν” (Ephesians 5:31-32)
“This mystery is great…”
Because it was never just about marriage.
It was about God’s heart.
And His love… has never been divided.
So which caused more problems in the Bible?
The answer isn’t hidden.
Polygamy consistently multiplied pain.
Not because God endorsed it… but because He allowed human freedom to expose its consequences.
Scripture doesn’t need to condemn it loudly.
It simply shows you what happens.
And if you’re honest… you feel it.
The tension.
The tears.
The silent suffering between verses.
This isn’t just ancient history.
This is a mirror.
Because even today… hearts are divided.
Not always between people…
But between God and everything else competing for attention.
And that’s where the real battle lives.
Be honest.
How many “loves” are pulling on your heart right now?
How many priorities are quietly bending your devotion?
How many things have slowly taken the place that only Jesus should hold?
This is where it gets personal.
This is where it stops being theology…
And starts becoming conviction.
Because Jesus didn’t come to manage divided hearts.
He came to restore them.
Fully.
Completely.
Back to one.
If something in you felt exposed reading this…
Sit with it.
Let it speak.
Let it heal.
Someone else reading your honesty might finally find the courage to be honest too.
And if this stirred something deeper in you… if you feel that pull toward real discipleship, real growth, real surrender…
you can take it further.
If your heart is saying yes… don’t ignore it.
Because glorifying God was never meant to stay private.
It moves.
It shares.
It reaches.
And it costs something.
But it’s always worth it.
Here’s the echo you won’t shake tonight:
A divided heart doesn’t collapse in a moment… it drifts one quiet compromise at a time.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Thought It Was Just a Memory… But It Became a Battlefield: Is It Sinful to Think About Your Ex Sexually?
paragraphs: You Thought It Was Just a Memory… But It Became a Battlefield: Is It Sinful to Think About Your Ex Sexually?
You didn’t plan for it to happen.
It just slipped in—quiet, uninvited, almost familiar.

A memory.
A moment.
A body you once knew too well.
And suddenly your mind isn’t just remembering… it’s reliving.

You feel the weight of it after. That strange mixture of comfort and conviction. Desire and disgust. You tell yourself, “It’s just a thought.” But deep down, something inside you whispers, This isn’t harmless.
So now you’re here, asking the question most people are too afraid to say out loud:
Is this sin?
Not just the act… but the thought.
Not just what you did before… but what you’re still doing in your mind.
Jesus didn’t avoid this question. He went straight into it—deeper than behavior, deeper than appearances, deeper than what anyone else could see.
He said in Matthew 5:28:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.”
Pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn ēdē emoicheusen autēn en tē kardia autou.
Translation: “Everyone who looks at a woman with the intent to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Did you catch that?

“πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι” — pros to epithymēsai
It doesn’t just mean noticing. It means aiming your desire toward her. Feeding it. Entertaining it. Choosing to stay there.
This isn’t about accidental thoughts.
This is about what you do when the thought arrives.
Because thoughts will come. You’re human. You have memory. You have history. You have scars and attachments that don’t just disappear overnight.
But sin doesn’t begin with the first flicker of a thought.
It begins when you welcome it, sit with it, replay it, and let it become something your heart agrees with.
James 1:14-15 explains it with painful clarity:
“ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος· εἶτα ἡ ἐπιθυμία συλλαβοῦσα τίκτει ἁμαρτίαν…”
He is dragged away by his own desire and enticed. Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin…
Did you see the progression?
Desire → entertained → conceived → sin.
That means the moment you start feeding that sexual memory of your ex… letting it linger… replaying their body in your mind… imagining what you once had or wish you still had…
That’s where the line is crossed.
Not because God is trying to shame you…
But because He knows something you’re still learning:
You cannot heal from what you keep revisiting.
You cannot be made new while emotionally and mentally undressing your past.
That person is no longer your covenant.
And your mind was never meant to be a graveyard where old intimacy keeps getting resurrected.
In Hebrew, the word for heart—לֵב (lev)—doesn’t just mean emotion.
It means the control center of your will, your desires, your decisions.
So when Jesus says sin happens in the heart…
He’s saying it happens in the place where you choose what to keep.
And maybe that’s what this is really about.
Not just lust.
But attachment.
Not just desire.
But longing for something that once made you feel seen, wanted, alive.
And now that it’s gone… your mind keeps trying to bring it back.
But listen carefully:
God is not asking you to pretend you never felt anything.
He’s asking you to surrender what you’re still holding onto.
Because every time you go back there in your mind… you reopen something Jesus is trying to close.
Every time you entertain that thought… you reinforce a connection God is trying to break.
Every time you linger… you delay your healing.
But here’s the part most people miss:
Conviction is not rejection.
The fact that you feel this tension… this discomfort… this internal pull…
That’s not God pushing you away.
That’s God calling you back.
Romans 8:1 says:
“Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα τοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.”
There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
No condemnation.
But also—no compromise.
Grace doesn’t excuse the struggle.
It gives you the power to fight it.
So what do you do when the thought comes?
You don’t panic.
You don’t pretend.
You don’t indulge.
You interrupt it.
You bring it into the light.
You replace it.
You fight it with truth.
You say, “That’s not who I am anymore.”
You say, “That part of my life is under the blood of Jesus.”
You say, “I will not turn memory into sin.”
And you keep choosing that… again and again… even when it’s hard.
Especially when it’s hard.
Because sanctification isn’t instant.
It’s a daily death to what still feels familiar.
And maybe that’s where you are right now.
Tired of the cycle.
Tired of pretending you’re okay.
Tired of fighting thoughts that feel stronger at night… when no one’s watching… when it’s just you and your memories.
Be honest.
This hit deeper than you expected, didn’t it?
You’re not alone in this battle.
But silence is where it grows.
Bring it into the light.
And if you know someone who is struggling with hidden thoughts, with secret cycles, with a past they can’t seem to let go of…
Not to expose them… but to free them.
Because someone you love is losing this fight in silence.
And maybe this is the moment God uses to reach them.
Save this too.
Because the next time that thought comes… you’ll need truth stronger than your memory.
Follow closely if you’re serious about growing in Christ.
Not just surface-level faith… but real transformation. The kind that confronts, heals, and rebuilds from the inside out.
And if you truly want to glorify God with your life… support the mission.
Not out of pressure… but out of purpose.
You’re helping spread the Gospel to people who are still trapped in darkness, silence, and shame.
Respond.
Engage.
Take a step.
Because the battle in your mind is real…
But so is the freedom in Christ.
And the cross didn’t just forgive your past…
It gave you power over it.
You don’t have to live replaying what God already redeemed.
You don’t have to keep revisiting what Jesus already buried.
You don’t have to be owned by memories that no longer have authority over your identity.
You are not who you were with them.
You are who Christ says you are now.
And that changes everything.
The thought may come…
…but it doesn’t get to stay.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He didn’t hear God that day.
paragraphs: He didn’t hear God that day.
No whisper. No vision. No dream.
Just silence… and a torn piece of fabric soaked in blood.

Jacob held Joseph’s coat in trembling hands, the one he had once given with pride, now returned with a lie stitched into every thread. The colors that once reflected favor now screamed loss. And in that moment, something inside him collapsed.
The Scripture says it plainly, but the weight of it is unbearable if you really sit in it:

“וַיַּכִּרָהּ וַיֹּאמֶר כְּתֹנֶת בְּנִי חַיָּה רָעָה אֲכָלָתְהוּ טָרֹף טֹרַף יוֹסֵף”
Vayyakkirah vayomer: ketonet beni; chayyah ra’ah achalathu; tarof toraf Yosef
“Then he recognized it and said, ‘It is my son’s robe. A wild animal has devoured him. Joseph is without doubt torn to pieces.’” — Genesis 37:33
He believed it.
Not because it was true… but because it felt true.
And sometimes that’s the most dangerous kind of lie.
The kind that aligns perfectly with your worst fear.
The kind that requires no evidence because your heart is already breaking.
Jacob tore his garments. He put on sackcloth. He mourned for days that turned into years. And when people tried to comfort him, he refused.
“I will go down to Sheol to my son, mourning.” — Genesis 37:35

The Hebrew word used there for mourning, “אֵבֶל” (evel), isn’t casual grief. It’s deep, consuming sorrow. The kind that reshapes your identity. The kind that convinces you life will never feel whole again.
Jacob didn’t just lose Joseph…
He buried the future he thought God had promised.
Because Joseph had dreams.
God-given dreams.
Dreams where his brothers bowed… where his life had purpose… where something bigger was unfolding.
But now?
All Jacob could see was blood.
And maybe that’s where this hits harder than expected…
Because you’ve held your own “bloody coat” before.
Something you thought God gave you… something that felt sacred… something full of promise… now lying in pieces in your hands.
A relationship that died.
A prayer that went unanswered.
A future that never happened.
And the silence of God felt louder than the pain itself.
Be honest.
This hit deeper than you expected.
Because what hurts most isn’t just loss…
It’s the feeling that God allowed it.
Jacob didn’t know what heaven knew.
He didn’t see Joseph in the pit.
He didn’t see the Ishmaelites passing by.
He didn’t see the Midianite traders.
He didn’t see Egypt.
He didn’t see Potiphar.
He didn’t see the prison.
He didn’t see the palace.
He didn’t see the famine.
He didn’t see the reunion.
He didn’t see the tears that would one day wash away this grief.
He only saw the coat.
And he built his entire belief around incomplete evidence.
And this is where everything shifts.
Because heaven never confirmed Joseph was dead.
It only allowed Jacob to believe it.
And that changes everything.
Because sometimes God will allow a narrative to unfold that looks like loss… feels like death… and sounds like silence… but is actually positioning something far greater than you can comprehend.
Joseph wasn’t dead.
He was being developed.
The Hebrew root behind Joseph’s name, “יָסַף” (yasaf), means “to add,” “to increase,” “to continue doing again.”
Jacob thought God had taken something away.
But God was actually multiplying something unseen.
And maybe… just maybe…
That’s what’s happening in your life right now.
You’re grieving something God is still growing.
You’re burying something heaven is still building.
You’re calling it over… while God is calling it forward.
Because God doesn’t move through fake strength.
He meets you in honest surrender.
Years later, when Joseph finally revealed himself, the truth shattered the lie Jacob had lived with for so long.
Joseph said:

“וְעַתָּה לֹא אַתֶּם שְׁלַחְתֶּם אֹתִי הֵנָּה כִּי הָאֱלֹהִים”
Ve’atah lo atem shelachtem oti henah, ki ha’Elohim
“And now it was not you who sent me here, but God.” — Genesis 45:8
And then again:
“You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.” — Genesis 50:20
The Hebrew word for “meant” there is “חָשַׁב” (chashav) — to weave, to plan, to think, to account.
God was weaving… while Jacob was weeping.
God was planning… while Jacob was mourning.
God was writing… while Jacob thought the story had ended.
And this is the truth most people don’t want to hear…
Just because it looks dead doesn’t mean God is done.
Just because you don’t understand it doesn’t mean He’s not in it.
Just because it hurts doesn’t mean it’s not holy.
Because healing isn’t always loud.
Sometimes it looks like survival.
Sometimes it looks like getting up when you don’t want to.
Sometimes it looks like holding on to God when everything in you wants to let go.
And if you’ve read this far, this isn’t random.
This is a moment.
A turning point.
A quiet invitation to stop believing the version of your story that pain has been telling you.
Because Jesus didn’t come just to comfort you…
He came to rewrite you.
The same God who allowed Jacob to sit in grief…
Is the same God who restored him with overwhelming joy.
The same God who allowed Joseph to be betrayed…
Is the same God who elevated him beyond imagination.
This is the Gospel.
Scandal to grace.
Brokenness to redemption.
Death to life.
And it all points to Jesus.
Because on a hill called Golgotha, it looked like another story had ended.
Blood was spilled.
Hope looked buried.
Silence filled the sky.
But heaven wasn’t finished.
The Greek word Jesus cried, “Τετέλεσται” (Tetelestai) — “It is finished” (John 19:30) — wasn’t defeat.
It was fulfillment.
It meant the debt was paid.
The story was complete.
The victory was secured.
And three days later… the stone rolled away.
Because what looks final on earth… is often just the beginning in heaven.
So before you walk away…
Sit with it.
Respond to it.
Because there are more people reading your comment than you realize… and your honesty might be the lifeline someone else needed.
And if you truly want to glorify God through your life, not just your words…
Support what is feeding your spirit.
This isn’t just content.
This is calling.
This is alignment.
This is choosing truth over comfort.
Because staying close to truth is how you survive seasons that try to break you.
And maybe the coat in your hands isn’t proof that it’s over…
Maybe it’s proof that you’re in the middle of a story God hasn’t finished yet.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE CHAINS THAT SHOOK HEAVEN: Why Paul Was Imprisoned… And Why It Still Exposes Us Today
paragraphs: THE CHAINS THAT SHOOK HEAVEN: Why Paul Was Imprisoned… And Why It Still Exposes Us Today
Subtitle: The scandal wasn’t his chains… it was the Gospel he refused to dilute.
There is something unsettling about a man who keeps preaching even when it costs him everything.
Not comfort. Not reputation. Everything.
Paul was not imprisoned because he failed.
He was imprisoned because he refused to change the message.
And if we’re honest… that’s where this starts to get uncomfortable.
Because deep down, many of us have learned how to soften truth just enough to stay accepted.
Paul didn’t.
And it cost him his freedom.
In the book of Acts, we see the turning point. The moment where obedience collided with consequence.
In Acts 21:13, Paul says something that doesn’t sound like modern Christianity at all:
“I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus.”
The Greek phrase carries weight that gets lost in translation. “ἑτοίμως ἔχω” (hetoimōs echō) — I am fully prepared, resolved, already decided.
This was not emotional hype.
This was settled conviction.
He wasn’t walking into prison blindly.
He walked into it willingly.
Because truth, to him, was not negotiable.
But what truth?
Why did they hate him so much?
Why did religious leaders, crowds, and even political authorities all turn against him?
It wasn’t just preaching Jesus.
It was what he said about Jesus.
Paul declared that righteousness does not come from the law.
That shattered entire systems of control.
In Romans 3:28, he writes:
The Greek word “δικαιοῦσθαι” (dikaiousthai) means to be declared righteous, acquitted, made right before God.
Not earned.
Declared.
That message was dangerous.
Because it removed human pride from salvation.
And pride does not surrender quietly.
In Hebrew thinking, righteousness was tied deeply to covenant obedience. The word “צֶדֶק” (tsedeq) carried legal and moral weight.
Paul comes in and says: You cannot achieve this on your own.
That was the scandal.
Not sin.
Grace.
And grace offends people who still want credit.
This is why in Acts 22, when Paul shares his testimony, the crowd listens… until he mentions that God sent him to the Gentiles.
Then everything explodes.
Because now it wasn’t just about theology.
It was about inclusion.
Acts 22:21–22 reveals the breaking point:
“Go, for I will send you far from here to the Gentiles.”
They listened to him until this word, and then they raised their voices and said, “Away with such a fellow from the earth!”
Why?
Because grace was crossing boundaries they wanted to keep.
The Gospel was no longer controlled.
It was being offered.
Freely.
To outsiders.
To sinners.
To people who didn’t earn it.
To people like us.
And that’s when Paul became dangerous.
Because when grace becomes real, systems built on performance begin to crumble.
That’s why he was beaten.
That’s why he was falsely accused.
That’s why he was imprisoned.
Not because he was wrong.
But because he was faithful.
In Philippians 1:12–13, written while imprisoned, Paul says:
“What has happened to me has actually served to advance the gospel…”
The Greek word “προκοπή” (prokopē) means to cut forward, like clearing a path through resistance.
His chains weren’t stopping the Gospel.
They were carving its way deeper into the world.
Even into places it couldn’t have reached otherwise.
Even into hearts that needed to see that faith was worth suffering for.
Because here’s the truth we don’t say out loud often enough:
A Gospel that costs nothing changes nothing.
Paul understood something we are still trying to avoid.
Following Jesus is not about comfort.
It is about surrender.
And surrender always looks like loss before it looks like transformation.
He writes in 2 Corinthians 12:9:
The word “ἀσθενείᾳ” (astheneia) means fragility, limitation, inability.
That’s where God chooses to show His strength.
Not in polished lives.
Not in perfect reputations.
But in broken people who refuse to let go of Jesus.
Paul in chains is not a tragedy.
It is a revelation.
Because it forces a question most of us try to avoid:
Would you still follow Jesus if it cost you your image… your comfort… your acceptance?
Or do you only follow Him when it’s safe?
Be honest.
This hits deeper than expected.
Paul’s imprisonment was not just a historical event.
It was a mirror.
And what it reflects is uncomfortable.
Because many of us want the power of the Gospel without the cost of obedience.
We want resurrection without crucifixion.
We want grace without surrender.
But Jesus never offered that version.
In fact, Jesus Himself said in Luke 9:23:
“If anyone would come after Me, let him deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me.”
The Greek word “ἀπαρνησάσθω” (aparnēsasthō) means to completely disown oneself.
Not improve yourself.
Not upgrade your life.
Deny yourself.
That’s the invitation.
And that’s what Paul said yes to.
That’s why he was imprisoned.
Not because God abandoned him.
But because God trusted him.
Trusted him to carry a message that would offend pride, break chains, and rescue souls.
And now here we are.
Reading his story from the comfort he never had.
Hearing his words without the risk he faced.
And the question quietly lingers…
What are we doing with the freedom he suffered to protect?
If this stirred something in you… don’t ignore it.
Be honest.
Your honesty might be the breakthrough someone else needs to see.
Someone who looks strong on the outside but is fighting battles you can’t see.
Because there will be a day you feel tired… and you’ll need to remember that chains don’t mean God has left you.
Sometimes they mean you’re exactly where obedience led you.
And if you truly want to glorify God—not just in words, but in impact—then support what is feeding your spirit.
You’re stepping into deeper discipleship.
Daily truth.
Conviction.
Healing.
Growth.
Accountability.
You’re helping this message reach more people who are lost, tired, and searching for something real.
If you’ve been coasting, this is your moment to go deeper.
If you’ve been silent, this is your moment to stand.
If you’ve been comfortable, this is your moment to surrender.
Because the truth is…
Paul didn’t just carry chains.
He carried a Gospel that refused to bow.
And now that Gospel is in your hands.
What will you do with it?
The chains didn’t silence him… they revealed who he truly belonged to.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Stayed Faithful While She Slowly Broke Him — But What God Revealed Next Will Shake You
paragraphs: He Stayed Faithful While She Slowly Broke Him — But What God Revealed Next Will Shake You
When love turns into silence… when effort is met with indifference… when respect becomes a memory instead of a reality… it does something to a man that no one sees.
He doesn’t always cry out loud.
He just starts fading quietly.

You wake up every day choosing her, choosing the marriage, choosing to fight for something that feels like it stopped fighting for you a long time ago. You try to lead, but your voice feels ignored. You try to love, but it feels rejected. You try to correct, but it turns into conflict. You try to hold it together, but it feels like you’re the only one holding anything at all.
And somewhere deep inside, a question starts forming that you’re almost afraid to admit:
“God… what do I do when I’m giving everything… and it still isn’t enough?”
This isn’t just about marriage.
This is about identity… authority… love… pain… and the quiet war between obedience to God and the breaking of your own heart.
Because Scripture never ignores this.
But it also never simplifies it.
In Ephesians 5:25, the Greek says, “ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας” (agapate tas gynaikas) — “love your wives,” but not just casually… this is agape — sacrificial, self-denying, relentless love.
“καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν” — “as Christ loved the Church.”
That’s not romantic love.
That’s crucified love.
That’s the kind of love that bleeds… stays… forgives… endures… even when it is not returned the way it should be.
But here is what many men silently carry:

“Does that mean I just accept disrespect?
Does that mean I let her dishonor me publicly?
Does that mean I lead someone who refuses to follow?”
Now the truth gets uncomfortable.
Because Scripture doesn’t only speak to husbands.
It speaks to wives too.
Ephesians 5:33 continues:
“ἡ δὲ γυνὴ ἵνα φοβῆται τὸν ἄνδρα” — “the wife must respect (phobeitai — deeply honor, revere) her husband.”
Respect is not optional in God’s design.
It is not cultural.
It is covenantal.
So what happens when one obeys… and the other resists?
This is where many men either break… or become something dangerous.
They either collapse into silence…
Or they rise in anger, control, bitterness, even dominance.
But neither is Christ.
Neither reflects Jesus.
And that’s where the real battle is.
Because you are not just called to save your marriage.
You are called to reflect Christ inside your marriage.
And that means something deeper than just “trying harder.”
It means understanding this painful truth:
You cannot force transformation in someone who is resisting God.
Even Jesus, in His perfection, was rejected.
Isaiah 53:3 says, “He was despised and rejected by men…”
The Hebrew word “נִבְזֶה” (nivzeh) — despised — means treated as worthless.
Even Christ experienced what you are feeling.
Giving everything… and receiving rejection.
So what do you do?
You do not enable sin.
You do not normalize disrespect.
But you also do not abandon your calling.
You stand in truth… not in pride.
You lead in righteousness… not in control.
You correct in love… not in anger.
Matthew 18:15 gives a principle:
“If your brother sins against you, go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone…”
That applies here too.
Not public arguments.
Not silent resentment.
But honest, direct, Spirit-led confrontation.
And if she still refuses?
Then you begin shifting your focus from “changing her” to “remaining faithful to God.”
Because at the end of this… your obedience is what God will measure.
Not her response.
And this is where many don’t want to hear the truth:
Sometimes God allows a broken dynamic… to refine one heart before restoring two.
Sometimes the marriage struggle is exposing deeper wounds, pride, rebellion, or spiritual immaturity — not just in her… but in both.
And sometimes… it’s revealing that what you thought was leadership… still needs surrender.
Because leadership in God’s kingdom is not control.
It is Christlikeness.
And Christ did not force submission.
He invited it… through sacrifice.
But hear this clearly…
You are not called to be disrespected without boundaries.
You are not called to tolerate dishonor as if it pleases God.
Even Jesus flipped tables when holiness was violated.
There is a place for firm, godly boundaries.
A place where you say, calmly but clearly:
“This is not acceptable. Not because of my ego… but because of God’s design.”
And then you stand on that.
Without rage.
Without fear.
Without compromise.
But also without hatred.
Because if your heart becomes bitter… you lose something far more important than the marriage.
You lose your reflection of Christ.
And maybe that’s where this hits the deepest.
Because this isn’t just about what she’s doing to you.
It’s about what this situation is trying to turn you into.
Angry.
Cold.
Detached.
Or worse… spiritually numb.
Don’t let it.
Guard your spirit.
Stay in the Word.
Pray even when it feels pointless.
Because God is not blind to what you’re carrying.
Galatians 6:9 reminds us:
“μὴ ἐγκακῶμεν” — do not grow weary.
God sees the effort.
God sees the restraint.
God sees the nights you stayed silent just to keep peace.
God sees the moments you chose patience over reaction.
Nothing is wasted.
Nothing.
But now let me speak to your heart directly…
Be honest.
Because you are not the only one in this.
There are others reading this… feeling the exact same weight… and your honesty might be the thing that reminds them they’re not alone.
And if you’re serious about growing deeper in Christ, understanding His design for marriage, healing your spirit, and becoming the man God called you to be…
Stay close.
Because this is not surface-level encouragement.
This is discipleship.
If this message spoke to you… don’t keep it to yourself.
Support what God is doing here.
Because sometimes God uses your share… to save someone else’s story.
Because honoring God is not just what you believe…
It’s what you choose to support.
And maybe… just maybe… this isn’t the end of your story.
Maybe this is the part where God is rewriting everything.
And the pain you thought would destroy you…
Becomes the place where grace finally breaks through.
The marriage may feel like it’s dying… but God specializes in resurrection.
And resurrection never starts with comfort.
It starts with surrender.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What If You Miss Your Old Sexual Lifestyle?
paragraphs:
What If You Miss Your Old Sexual Lifestyle?
The Secret Grief Nobody Talks About After Choosing Jesus
There are nights you don’t talk about.

Nights where your room is quiet, but your mind isn’t. Nights where your body remembers what your spirit has already renounced. Nights where you stare at the ceiling and wonder if something is wrong with you… because a part of you still misses what God told you to leave behind.
And you hate that you miss it.
No one warned you about this part.
They told you about freedom. They told you about deliverance. They told you about being made new.
But they didn’t tell you that sometimes, freedom still aches.
They didn’t tell you that leaving your old sexual life behind can feel like grieving a relationship that once felt alive… even if it was destroying you.
So here you are.
Saved… but still remembering.
Free… but still tempted.
Changed… but not numb.
And the enemy whispers, “If you miss it, maybe you never really changed.”
But that’s not the voice of God.
Because Scripture never promised you wouldn’t feel the pull.
It promised you power over it.
In Galatians 5:17, Paul writes something brutally honest:
In the original Greek, “σὰρξ” (sarx) means the flesh, the human nature inclined toward sin. And “ἐπιθυμεῖ” (epithumei) means to crave, to long for, to desire intensely.
That means the struggle you feel isn’t proof of failure.
It’s evidence of war.
And war only exists where two sides are alive.
Before Christ, there was no war. You didn’t fight it—you followed it. You didn’t resist—you indulged it. You didn’t question—you justified.
But now?
Now something inside you resists what you used to run toward.
That’s not weakness.
That’s transformation beginning to breathe.
But let’s be honest.
There were moments in that old life that felt good.
Moments of closeness.
Moments where you felt wanted.
Moments where loneliness disappeared, even if only temporarily.
And your flesh doesn’t remember the consequences first.
It remembers the pleasure.
James 1:14-15 says:
“Each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire…”
The Greek word for “lured” is “ἐξελκόμενος” (exelkomenos), like a fish being drawn out by bait.
Temptation doesn’t show you the hook.
It shows you what glitters.
It shows you the memory without the regret.
The feeling without the emptiness.
The connection without the confusion.
And for a moment… you almost forget why you left.
But you did leave.
Not because it never felt good.
But because it was never truly good for you.
There’s a difference.
Hebrews 11:25 speaks of “the fleeting pleasures of sin.”
Fleeting.
Temporary.
Passing.
In Hebrew thought, the idea of temporary pleasure is often tied to what fades like vapor—here for a moment, gone the next, leaving you emptier than before.
And if you’re honest…
It did leave you empty.
After the texts stopped.
After the bodies separated.
After the moment passed.
You were still searching.
Still restless.
Still wanting something deeper.
Because what your soul was craving was never just physical.
It was spiritual.
Connection.
Covenant.
To be fully known without shame.
And that kind of intimacy doesn’t come from lust.
It comes from God.
In Genesis 2:24, the Hebrew word for “one flesh” is “בָּשָׂר אֶחָד” (basar echad).
Not just physical union.
Total unity.
Body, soul, and spirit aligned under God’s design.
What you were tasting before wasn’t that.
It was a counterfeit.
A shadow of something sacred, stripped of its covering.
So yes…
You might miss it.
But what you miss isn’t always what you think.
You don’t just miss the act.
You miss the feeling of being wanted.
You miss the illusion of closeness.
You miss the temporary silence of your loneliness.
But Jesus doesn’t offer illusions.
He offers truth.
And truth sometimes hurts before it heals.
In John 8:36, Jesus says:
“So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.”
The Greek word for “free indeed” is “ὄντως ἐλεύθεροι” (ontos eleutheroi).
Truly free.
Genuinely free.
Not just behavior modification… but heart transformation.
And real freedom doesn’t mean you never feel tempted.
It means you’re no longer controlled.
So when you miss your old sexual lifestyle…
Don’t panic.
Don’t spiral.
Don’t assume you’ve gone backward.
Instead, recognize what’s happening.
Your flesh is remembering.
But your spirit is choosing.
And every time you choose Christ over craving…
Something eternal is being built inside you.
Even if it doesn’t feel like it.
Especially when it doesn’t feel like it.
This is where most people quit.
Not because they don’t love God…
But because they’re tired of fighting feelings they thought would disappear.
But following Jesus was never about feelings disappearing.
It was about truth becoming stronger than feelings.
And sometimes that truth whispers, not shouts.
“Stay.”
“Hold on.”
“Don’t go back.”
Because what’s ahead of you is holier than what’s behind you.
You’re not losing something.
You’re being prepared for something sacred.
A love that doesn’t leave you confused.
A connection that doesn’t make you question your worth.
A future where intimacy is covered by covenant, not chaos.
But you have to walk through this tension to get there.
So if you’re in that place right now…
Missing it.
Fighting it.
Trying not to go back…
Be honest.
Not as a performance.
But as a confession.
Because you’re not the only one.
And your honesty might give someone else the courage to stay too.
And if you’re serious about walking deeper with Jesus—not just in moments like this, but daily—stay close.
Follow.
Because you weren’t meant to fight this alone.
And if God is using this to speak to you… support what is feeding your spirit.
Not out of pressure.
But out of purpose.
You’re fueling discipleship.
You’re helping truth reach people who are drowning silently.
More than that…
If you want to go deeper, stay rooted, and grow in Christ, this is where it begins:
Because this isn’t just about resisting sin.
It’s about becoming someone new.
And that process?
It’s messy.
It’s painful.
It’s holy.
So don’t run from the tension.
Let it transform you.
Because one day, you won’t just look back and say, “I survived that.”
You’ll say, “God used that to change me.”
And that old life you miss?
It won’t even recognize who you’ve become.
You don’t actually miss your past… you’re just learning how to live without chains.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Know the Bible… But Why Do You Still Break People?
paragraphs:
You Know the Bible… But Why Do You Still Break People?
The terrifying truth about spiritual maturity without emotional transformation—and why Jesus refuses to leave you that way.
You can quote Scripture and still wound the people closest to you.
You can fast, pray, serve in ministry, lead worship… and still carry reactions that look nothing like Christ when someone challenges you, corrects you, or simply doesn’t meet your expectations.
And if that stung a little, stay here.

Because this is not an attack.
This is an exposure… the kind that leads to healing.
There is a dangerous illusion many believers live inside.

It sounds like this:
“If I know more about God, I must be growing in God.”
But Scripture never said knowledge alone transforms you.

Paul warned about this directly in 1 Corinthians 8:1:
“Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.”
The Greek word he used for “puffs up” is φυσιόω (physioō)—to inflate, to swell, to become proud. It paints a picture of something that looks bigger than it really is… something hollow inside.
So yes… you can grow in information and still be emotionally stunted.
You can look spiritually mature… and still respond like a wounded child.
And this is where the tension becomes uncomfortable.
Because Jesus never separated spiritual maturity from emotional transformation.
When He spoke about fruit in John 15, He wasn’t talking about how much Scripture you can memorize.
He was talking about what grows out of your life when pressure hits.

Galatians 5:22–23 says:
“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control…”
The original Greek word for patience is μακροθυμία (makrothymia)—long-suffering, the ability to endure difficult people without reacting in anger.
Self-control is ἐγκράτεια (enkrateia)—mastery over your internal world.
Not just your behavior in public… but your reactions in private.
So let’s ask the question honestly.
If someone criticizes you… what comes out?
If someone disappoints you… what rises up?
If someone wounds you… what do you release back into the world?
Because that… is your real level of maturity.
Not your Bible app streak.
Not your ministry title.
Not how many people think you’re “on fire for God.”
Your reactions reveal your formation.
And Jesus cares deeply about that.

In Luke 6:45, He said:
“Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks.”
The Greek word for “abundance” is περίσσευμα (perisseuma)—overflow, surplus, what spills out when something is full.
Meaning… you don’t accidentally lash out.
You overflow what’s stored inside.
And this is where many believers wrestle silently.
Because they love God… but they haven’t allowed God into the places that shaped their emotional patterns.

The rejection.
The abandonment.
The betrayal.
The years of learning to survive instead of trust.
So they build spiritual habits… without surrendering emotional wounds.
They learn how to worship… but not how to process pain.
They learn how to preach truth… but not how to sit with their own brokenness.
And slowly… something dangerous forms.

A version of Christianity that looks strong… but reacts harshly.
A version of faith that speaks truth… but lacks tenderness.
A version of maturity that teaches others… but cannot be corrected.
And Jesus never modeled that.
Look at Him closely.
When He was betrayed, He didn’t explode.
When He was falsely accused, He didn’t defend His ego.
When He was crucified, He didn’t curse His enemies.

He said in Luke 23:34:
“Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”
The Aramaic root behind this expression carries the sense of releasing a debt… letting go of rightful offense.
That is not emotional suppression.
That is transformed emotion.
That is what it looks like when the Spirit of God doesn’t just inform your mind… but heals your heart.
And this is the invitation many are avoiding.
Because healing requires honesty.
And honesty feels like vulnerability.
And vulnerability feels like losing control.
But the truth?
You’re not losing control.
You’re finally surrendering it to the One who can actually transform you.

This is why David cried out in Psalm 51:10:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God…”
The Hebrew word for “create” is בָּרָא (bara)—the same word used in Genesis when God created the heavens and the earth.
David wasn’t asking for adjustment.
He was asking for recreation.
Because he understood something many still resist:
You don’t need behavior modification.
You need heart transformation.
And that includes your emotional life.

Your triggers.
Your tone.
Your reactions.
Your defensiveness.
Your silence when you should speak… and your harshness when you should listen.
Jesus is not just after your Sunday life.
He’s after your internal world.
And here’s the part many don’t want to hear…
If your spiritual growth is not making you more patient, more gentle, more forgiving, more self-controlled…
Then something is being built… but it’s not Christlikeness.
And deep down, you know it.
You’ve felt the tension.

The moments after you react and think,
“That wasn’t who I want to be.”
The silence after a harsh word.
The regret after an emotional outburst.
The distance it creates with people you actually love.
This is not condemnation.
This is invitation.
Because Jesus doesn’t expose to shame you.
He exposes to heal you.
And this is where everything shifts.
You don’t have to keep performing spirituality while hiding emotional immaturity.
You can bring both to the cross.
You can let Him rebuild you from the inside out.
You can become the kind of person whose presence feels like peace… not pressure.
Whose words heal… not cut.
Whose reactions reflect Christ… not past wounds.
But you have to be honest.
So be honest right here.
Let it be real.
Because someone else reading your comment might realize they’re not alone.
And if you feel something shifting inside you right now… don’t walk away from it.
Follow closely.
Stay near truth that refines you, not just comforts you.
Because this is deeper than information.
This is transformation.
And if you truly want to glorify God—not just in what you say, but in who you are becoming—then support what is feeding your spirit.
Because this journey is not about looking mature.
It’s about becoming like Him.
And He is not finished with you.
Not even close.

You don’t need to pretend you’re healed…
You just need to let Him touch the places you’ve been hiding.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Lord Is My Shepherd… But Not the Way You’ve Been Told
paragraphs:
The Lord Is My Shepherd… But Not the Way You’ve Been Told
The Psalm that comforts millions—yet confronts the parts of you still hiding from God
You’ve heard it at funerals. Whispered in hospital rooms. Quoted in captions when life feels heavy.
“The Lord is my shepherd…”
It sounds soft. Peaceful. Almost like a lullaby for anxious souls.
But if you really understood what David meant when he wrote it, it wouldn’t just comfort you…
…it would expose you.
Because the truth is, most people love the promise of Psalm 23—but resist the reality of having a Shepherd.
David didn’t write poetry from comfort. He wrote from collision. From failure. From scandal. From nights where guilt didn’t let him sleep and mornings where mercy somehow still found him.

And when he said, in Hebrew,
יְהוָה רֹעִי לֹא אֶחְסָר (Adonai ro’i lo echsar)
“The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not lack”…
he wasn’t saying, “God gives me everything I want.”
He was saying, “I belong to Someone who won’t let me destroy myself anymore.”
That word ro’i—“my shepherd”—is not gentle in the way modern culture imagines.
A shepherd doesn’t just cuddle sheep.

He leads them… even when they resist.
He corrects them… even when they wander.
He disciplines them… when their wandering could cost them their life.
And sheep?
They are not strong. Not independent. Not self-sufficient.
They are dependent.
Completely.
That’s where this hits harder than you expected.

Because many people want God as a provider… but not as an authority.
They want comfort… but not correction.
They want green pastures… but not the rod and the staff.
But David continues:
“He makes me lie down in green pastures…”
That word “makes” in Hebrew carries weight. It implies force, intervention, even interruption.
Because sheep don’t lie down peacefully unless everything is right—no fear, no hunger, no tension.
And sometimes, God has to remove what you keep chasing… just so your soul can finally rest.
You called it loss.
He called it rescue.
“He restores my soul…”
The Hebrew word here, יְשׁוֹבֵב (yeshovev), means “to bring back,” “to return,” “to restore what has wandered.”
This is not maintenance.
This is recovery.
This is God going after the version of you that got lost in sin, in compromise, in exhaustion, in pretending you were okay when you weren’t.
This is not a distant God.
This is a pursuing Shepherd.
And here’s where it gets uncomfortable again:
“He leads me in paths of righteousness for His name’s sake.”
Not for your reputation.
Not for your image.
For His name.
Which means sometimes the path He leads you on will cost you things you were trying to hold onto.
Relationships.
Habits.
Secrets.
Versions of yourself you’ve been protecting.
And then David says something that most people skip over too quickly:
“Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death…”
Notice—through, not around.
The Shepherd doesn’t always remove the valley.
He walks you through it.
The Hebrew phrase גֵּיא צַלְמָוֶת (gei tsalmavet) implies deep darkness, a place where death casts a shadow so real it feels alive.
You’ve been there.

Where anxiety feels louder than truth.
Where guilt whispers your past like it’s your identity.
Where silence feels like abandonment.
But David doesn’t say, “I fear no evil because I’m strong.”
He says, “I fear no evil because You are with me.”
Not explanations.
Presence.
Not answers.
Presence.
Not instant escape.
Presence.
That’s what changes everything.
“Your rod and your staff, they comfort me.”
That sounds strange, doesn’t it?
Because the rod corrects.
The staff guides.
And yet both bring comfort.
Why?
Because they mean you’re not alone.
Because they mean you’re not left to wander into destruction.
Because they mean someone is actually watching over your soul.
And here’s the part most people misunderstand completely:
“You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies…”
This is not about flexing on people who doubted you.
This is about peace that exists even when the battle isn’t over.
It’s about sitting in grace while everything around you still looks unresolved.
It’s about God saying, “You don’t have to win every fight… you just have to stay with Me.”
Then David says:
“My cup overflows.”
Not because life is perfect.
But because God is present.
Because grace is real.
Because mercy didn’t run out when you messed up again.
Because the Shepherd didn’t leave when you thought He should.
And then the final line…
“Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life…”
The Hebrew word for “follow,” יִרְדְּפוּנִי (yirdefuni), doesn’t mean gently trail behind.
It means pursue.
Chase.
Run after.
God’s goodness and mercy are not passive.
They are relentless.
They are chasing you… even when you’ve been running the other way.
And this is where everything shifts.
Because “The Lord is my Shepherd” is not a cute verse to memorize.
It is a surrender to live.
It is saying:
“I am no longer leading myself.”
“I am no longer trusting my own broken instincts.”
“I am no longer pretending I don’t need help.”
It is laying down your pride… your control… your illusion of independence…
…and finally letting Jesus lead.
The same Shepherd David wrote about is revealed fully in Christ.
Jesus said in Greek:

ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ποιμὴν ὁ καλός (egō eimi ho poimēn ho kalos)
“I am the good shepherd.” (John 10:11)
And then He proved it.
“The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.”
This is where Psalm 23 stops being poetry…
…and becomes personal.
Because the Shepherd didn’t just guide you.
He died for you.
He stepped into your valley.
He carried your sin.
He took your punishment.
And then He rose—so you could finally come home.
Be honest.
Let someone see your honesty. Let someone stand with you.
And if you feel something pulling you deeper—don’t ignore it.
Following isn’t just clicking a button.
It’s choosing to stay close to truth when everything else feels loud.
If this message reached you, imagine how many more it needs to reach through you.
Because glorifying God isn’t passive.
It’s participation.
It’s obedience.
It’s letting your life—and even your share button—be used for His purpose.
The Shepherd is not just comforting you…
He’s calling you.
And deep down, you know it.
You were never meant to lead your own life.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: There are questions people whisper in the dark… the kind they don’t bring to church, the kind they don’t type publicly, the kind they carry like a secret weight pressing against their chest.
paragraphs: There are questions people whisper in the dark… the kind they don’t bring to church, the kind they don’t type publicly, the kind they carry like a secret weight pressing against their chest.
“Does God care about my sexual preferences?”
Not the polished version. Not the theological version. The real one.

Does He look at me differently?
Does He feel disappointed?
Does He still want me… or just a version of me that doesn’t exist yet?
You don’t ask that question unless something inside you is already trembling.
And maybe that’s where this needs to start—not with answers, but with honesty.
Because the Bible never pretends humans are clean before they come to God. It shows the opposite.

David wasn’t clean.
The woman at the well wasn’t clean.
The woman caught in adultery wasn’t clean.
And yet… Jesus didn’t walk away.
He walked closer.

In John 8:7, when everyone was ready to stone her, Jesus said in Greek,
“Ὁ ἀναμάρτητος ὑμῶν πρῶτος ἐπ’ αὐτὴν βαλέτω λίθον”
“He who is without sin among you, let him throw the first stone.”
And one by one… they dropped their stones.
But don’t miss what happens next.
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.” (John 8:11)
There it is.
Grace… and truth.
Not one without the other.
Because God absolutely cares about your sexual life… but not the way most people think.

He doesn’t care so He can shame you.
He cares because He made you.

In Genesis 1:27, the Hebrew says,
“וַיִּבְרָא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הָאָדָם בְּצַלְמוֹ”
“Vayyivra Elohim et-ha’adam b’tzalmo”
“So God created man in His image.”

That means your body isn’t random.
Your desires aren’t meaningless.
Your identity isn’t self-invented.
You were designed.
And anything designed… has intention.
So when people ask, “Does God care about my sexual preferences?” what they’re really asking is:
“Does God care about what I do with the parts of me that feel the most personal… the most powerful… the most defining?”
Yes.
Deeply.
Because sexuality isn’t just behavior in Scripture—it’s covenant language. It’s tied to faithfulness, to union, to reflection of something divine.
Ephesians 5:31–32 reveals something shocking:
“This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.”
Marriage… intimacy… union… it was never just physical.
It was always pointing to Jesus.
Which means when sexuality is pulled outside of God’s design, it doesn’t just break a rule… it distorts a reflection.
And yet—this is where most people get it wrong—
God’s response to distortion is not abandonment.
It’s redemption.
Look at the Samaritan woman in John 4.

Five husbands.
Living with a man who wasn’t her husband.
If anyone had a complicated sexual history… it was her.
And Jesus meets her alone at a well.

No audience.
No performance.
No condemnation.
He speaks directly into her reality:
“You have had five husbands, and the one you now have is not your husband.” (John 4:18)
He doesn’t ignore truth.
But He doesn’t leave her there either.
He offers her something deeper than validation… and something more powerful than rejection.
“Living water.”
And that moment… that one encounter… turns her from someone hiding at a well into someone running back to a city, saying:
“Come, see a man who told me everything I ever did.”
She wasn’t canceled.
She was called.
So let’s answer it clearly now.
Does God care about your sexual preferences?
Yes.
But not because He’s obsessed with controlling you.
Because He’s committed to restoring you.
Because sin—any sin, not just sexual—separates us from the life we were created for.

Romans 3:23 says in Greek:
“πάντες γὰρ ἥμαρτον”
“For all have sinned.”

Not some.
Not a category.
Not a group you can point at to feel better about yourself.
All.
Which means this isn’t about “your sin vs their sin.”
It’s about all of us standing in need of the same Savior.
Jesus didn’t come to rank sins.
He came to carry them.

1 Peter 2:24 says,
“He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree.”

Every hidden struggle.
Every identity confusion.
Every moment you felt divided inside yourself.
He carried it.
So the real question isn’t, “Does God care about your sexual preferences?”
The real question is:
Will you trust Him enough to let Him define what’s good for your soul?
Because the hardest part isn’t admitting struggle.
It’s surrendering authority.
And that’s where transformation begins.
Not when you pretend you’re fine.
But when you stop hiding.
Maybe you’ve been trying to reconcile two voices inside you.
One that says, “This is who I am.”
And another whispering, “But is this who God created me to be?”
That tension… that discomfort… that quiet unrest…
That’s not rejection.
That’s invitation.
An invitation to come closer, not run further.
To wrestle honestly, not silence conviction.
To let Jesus—not culture, not feelings, not fear—be the One who defines truth.
Because the Gospel doesn’t say, “Stay as you are.”
It says, “Come as you are… and be made new.”

2 Corinthians 5:17 in Greek:
“καινὴ κτίσις”
“a new creation.”

Not adjusted.
Not slightly improved.
New.
And that kind of transformation… it doesn’t happen through arguments.
It happens through encounter.
Through relationship.
Through surrender.
Sit with it.
Be honest.
Because this isn’t about being perfect.
It’s about being real before a God who already sees everything… and still chooses to love you.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
And don’t keep this to yourself.
You might be the reason they finally feel seen.
You’re going to need this reminder again when the questions come back.
And if you feel God pulling you deeper… not just into inspiration, but into real discipleship, accountability, and transformation…
Because supporting this mission isn’t just about content.
It’s about helping more people encounter Jesus without filters.
It’s about making sure the Gospel reaches the ones who feel too far gone.
If this message stirred something in you… don’t ignore it.
God isn’t pushing you away.
He’s calling you closer.
And the part of you you’re most afraid to bring to Him…
is the exact place He wants to redeem.
You don’t need to fix yourself before you come.
You need to come… so He can fix what you never could.
The place you thought disqualified you… might be the very place grace begins.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHY DOES GOD FEEL SO FAR WHEN YOU NEED HIM MOST?
paragraphs:
WHY DOES GOD FEEL SO FAR WHEN YOU NEED HIM MOST?
The silence that breaks you might be the place where He is closest

There are moments you don’t post about.
Moments where your prayers don’t sound holy… they sound desperate.
Where your voice shakes, your chest feels heavy, and heaven feels… closed.

You whispered, “God, where are You?”
And the silence answered back.

Not a whisper.
Not a sign.
Not even a feeling.
Just… nothing.
And that nothing can feel louder than any storm.

The truth most people are afraid to admit is this: sometimes God feels distant not when life is easy—but when life is collapsing. When you needed Him most. When the diagnosis came. When the relationship shattered. When the anxiety wouldn’t let you sleep. When your faith felt like it was slipping through your fingers.
And in that silence, something dangerous begins to grow.
Doubt.

Not the loud kind.
The quiet kind.
The kind that whispers, “Maybe He left.”
But Scripture does not ignore this feeling. It walks straight into it.
David cried out in Psalm 22:1:

“אֵלִי אֵלִי לָמָה עֲזַבְתָּנִי”
Eli, Eli, lama azavtani
“My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?”

This wasn’t rebellion.
This was raw honesty.
And centuries later… hanging on a cross, bleeding, suffocating, carrying the weight of every sin ever committed… Jesus Himself echoed those exact words:

“Ἐλωΐ Ἐλωΐ λιμὰ σαβαχθανί” (Mark 15:34)
Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani
“My God, my God, why have You forsaken me?”
Let that settle into your spirit.
Jesus—the Son of God—felt the silence too.

So if you’ve ever felt abandoned… you are not outside of faith.
You are standing in a place even Christ stepped into.
But here is what most people miss.

Jesus was not quoting despair without purpose.
He was pointing back to Psalm 22—a chapter that begins in agony but ends in victory. A psalm that starts with distance… but ends with deliverance.
God didn’t leave Him.
And God hasn’t left you either.
The silence is not absence.

The Hebrew word often used for God’s presence is “עִמָּנוּ” (Immanu), meaning “with us.” As in “Immanuel”—God with us. Not God near us when things are good. Not God visiting us occasionally. But God with us—even when we don’t feel Him.
Feelings are real… but they are not always true.
There are moments when heaven feels quiet not because God is distant—but because He is doing something deeper than your emotions can perceive.
In Isaiah 45:15, it says:

“אָכֵן אַתָּה אֵל מִסְתַּתֵּר”
Indeed, You are a God who hides Himself

Not absent.
Hidden.
There is a difference.

Hidden does not mean gone.
Hidden means working in ways you cannot yet see.
Think about Joseph—betrayed, sold, falsely accused, imprisoned. Years of silence. Years where God felt nowhere to be found. Yet in Genesis 50:20, the truth breaks through:
“What you meant for evil, God meant for good.”

The silence was not punishment.
It was positioning.

The distance was not rejection.
It was redirection.
But in the middle of it… it doesn’t feel like that.
It feels like abandonment.
And this is where many people walk away—not because God failed them, but because they expected Him to move in ways that match their timeline, their emotions, their understanding.
But God is not bound by your timing.
2 Peter 3:8 reminds us:

“μία ἡμέρα παρὰ Κυρίῳ ὡς χίλια ἔτη”
With the Lord one day is like a thousand years

He is not late.
He is eternal.
And sometimes what feels like silence… is actually protection.
Sometimes the door didn’t open because it would have destroyed you.
Sometimes the relationship ended because it was pulling you away from Him.
Sometimes the waiting is not God ignoring you—it’s God preserving you.
But let’s be honest.
That doesn’t always comfort you in the moment.
Because what you really want is not theology.
You want Him.
You want to feel Him again.
You want to know He’s still there.
And here is the truth that changes everything:
God’s presence is not proven by your feelings… it is proven by the cross.
Romans 5:8 says:
“But God demonstrates His love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”

Not when you felt Him.
Not when you deserved it.
Not when life made sense.
But while you were broken.
That means even in your darkest, most silent moment… His love is still active.
Still present.
Still pursuing you.
So why does God feel far when you need Him most?
Because in those moments, He is doing heart work, not surface work.
He is breaking dependence on feelings and building trust in truth.
He is teaching you to walk by faith—not by sight.
And that kind of faith… feels like darkness before it feels like strength.
If you’ve been in that place lately… where your prayers feel like they hit the ceiling… where your heart feels numb… where your faith feels tired…
You are not alone.
And you are not abandoned.
You are in a sacred place.
A painful place.
But a powerful one.
Because this is where shallow faith dies… and real faith is born.
So don’t run.
Don’t shut down.
Don’t give up.
Lean in.
Even if all you can whisper is, “God… I don’t feel You.”
That’s enough.
Because He hears even what your soul struggles to say.
And maybe… just maybe… this silence you’re in is not the end of your story.
It’s the turning point.
The moment where everything shifts from performance… to surrender.
Be honest.
Your voice matters. Your struggle matters. And your honesty might be the thing that helps someone else breathe again.
And if you want to stay rooted in truth like this daily—real, raw, Scripture-centered, life-changing truth—follow closely.
Because this is not just content.
This is discipleship.
This is transformation.
And if you truly want to glorify God—not just privately, but boldly—then support what is feeding your spirit. Share it. Stand behind it. Help it reach the people who are one step away from giving up.
If you’re ready for that kind of growth, step into it here:
Because staying close to truth in a world full of noise is not accidental… it’s intentional.
And this is your invitation.
You thought God left… but He was closer than your breaking point.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They don’t tell you this part when you first decide to fight sin.
paragraphs: They don’t tell you this part when you first decide to fight sin.
No one warns you that the moment you finally say “enough”… it feels like everything inside you screams louder.
The thoughts don’t disappear.
They multiply.
The images don’t fade.
They sharpen.
The desire doesn’t weaken.
It surges.
And somewhere in that storm, a quiet fear begins to whisper, “Maybe this is who you really are.”
That’s where many people give up.
Not because they don’t love God.
But because they don’t understand what’s happening inside their own soul.
This is the part no one explains clearly.
And if you don’t understand it, you’ll keep thinking you’re losing… when you’re actually in the middle of breaking something that has ruled you for years.
The Apostle Paul felt this exact war, and he didn’t hide it behind polished language. He exposed it raw, almost uncomfortably honest.
In Romans 7:19 he says, “For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.”
In the original Greek, the phrase “I keep on doing” comes from “πράσσω” (prassō), meaning repeated, habitual action… not a one-time failure, but a pattern that feels like it owns you.
Paul wasn’t describing weakness.
He was describing war.
And war always gets louder when resistance begins.
Before you resisted, sin felt quiet because it was unchallenged.
But the moment you push back, something awakens.
James 1:14 explains it with terrifying clarity: “But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire.”
The Greek word for “desire” is “ἐπιθυμία” (epithymia), a deep craving, a pulling force… not just a surface thought, but something rooted in the heart.
This is why resisting sexual temptation feels like fighting yourself.
Because in a sense… it is.
But that’s not the whole truth.
There is another voice in you now.
Another presence.
Another nature.
And that’s why the tension feels unbearable.
Galatians 5:17 says, “For the flesh desires what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh.”
The word “flesh” here is “σάρξ” (sarx)… not just your body, but your fallen human nature, shaped by sin.
And “Spirit” is “πνεῦμα” (pneuma)… the very breath of God alive inside you.
Two forces.
One body.
Opposing directions.
No compromise.
So when temptation gets stronger, it’s not proof that you’re failing.
It’s evidence that something inside you has changed.
Before Christ, there was no war.
Now there is conflict.
And conflict means something holy is alive in you.
But here’s where it gets dangerous.
Because many people misinterpret the intensity of temptation as defeat.
They think, “If I was really changed, I wouldn’t feel this.”
But Jesus Himself was tempted.
Matthew 4 describes it, and the Greek word used is “πειρασθῆναι” (peirasthēnai)… to be tested, to be tried under pressure.
Temptation is not sin.
Agreement is.
That distinction will either free you… or keep you in chains.
Even Jesus, in His humanity, felt the weight of temptation, yet remained without sin (Hebrews 4:15).
So what you’re feeling doesn’t disqualify you.
It reveals the battlefield.
And if you’ve ever noticed that temptation feels strongest right after you decide to get serious with God… that’s not coincidence.
It’s exposure.
Light always agitates what darkness was hiding.
John 3:20 says, “Everyone who does evil hates the light… lest his works should be exposed.”
When you step toward God, you don’t just feel peace.
You also feel everything that was buried.
That’s why resisting feels harder at first.
Because you’re no longer numbing it.
You’re facing it.
And facing it hurts.
It’s like detox.
Like tearing something out of your system that once felt like comfort.
Sexual sin, especially, is not just physical.
It’s emotional.
It’s spiritual.
It promises intimacy but delivers emptiness.
It offers escape but leaves deeper bondage.
That’s why Scripture doesn’t say “fight” sexual immorality.
It says “flee.”
1 Corinthians 6:18 uses the Greek “φεύγετε” (pheugete)… run, escape immediately, don’t negotiate.
Because this battle is not won by willpower alone.
It’s won by direction.
By what you run from… and Who you run to.
And here’s the part that changes everything.
You’re not just resisting sin.
You’re being transformed.
The word “repentance” in the New Testament is “μετάνοια” (metanoia)… a change of mind, yes, but deeper than that… a reorientation of your entire inner world.
Your desires don’t disappear overnight.
They get rewired over time.
But that process feels messy.
It feels like losing control before gaining freedom.
Like breaking before healing.
And that’s why so many quit too early.
They mistake the breaking for failure.
But it’s actually the beginning of freedom.
Be honest.
Because silence is where sin grows strongest.
You’re not alone in this.
But you do have to choose.
Because what you feed will grow.
And what you starve will weaken.
Not instantly.
But undeniably.
If you know someone silently fighting this… don’t leave them alone in it.
Sometimes one message can interrupt a cycle someone thought they could never escape.
Save this too.
Because the next time temptation hits… and it will… you’ll need truth, not just feelings.
And if you’ve been quietly reading these without really committing… maybe it’s time to stop consuming and start walking.
Following Gospel Warrior isn’t about content.
It’s about staying close to truth when your emotions try to lie to you.
