Because maybe as you’re reading this… something feels exposed.
Not publicly.
But internally.

You know the patterns.
You know the triggers.
You know the quiet compromises no one else sees.
And maybe you’ve tried to stop.

Maybe you’ve promised God before.
Maybe you’ve felt the guilt… the shame… the exhaustion.
But here’s the truth you need to hear:
Jesus didn’t come to shame you out of lust.
He came to heal you out of it.

The same eyes that wandered…
the same heart that compared…
the same soul that craved…
He died for that.
Not the cleaned-up version of you.
The real you.
The struggling you.
The tired you.
The version of you that’s still fighting in secret.
“While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
He didn’t wait for your purity.
He moved in your brokenness.
And now He invites you into something deeper than behavior control.
He invites you into transformation.
Not just changing what you look at…
But healing why you look.
Because when Christ becomes your satisfaction… comparison loses its voice.
When His presence fills you… counterfeit desire loses its power.
When you truly see Him… everything else loses its grip.
But that requires surrender.

Not partial.
Not occasional.
Not when it’s convenient.
Real surrender.
So be honest.
What have you been comparing lately?
What has been quietly fueling your desires?
What have you been telling yourself you “need” that God hasn’t given you?
Because that’s where the battle is.
And that’s where Jesus wants to meet you.
Right there.
Not after you fix yourself.
But while you’re still in it.
Be honest. This hit deeper than you expected.
And don’t keep this to yourself.
And if you feel something shifting in your spirit right now… don’t walk away from it.
Stay close.
This isn’t just content.
This is transformation.
If you truly want to glorify God, don’t just consume truth.
Help carry it.
Support it.
Spread it.
Because someone else is still where you used to be.
And maybe this isn’t just about lust.
Maybe this is about finally seeing what’s been controlling you… and choosing Jesus instead.

Because the moment you stop comparing…
is the moment your healing finally begins.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Was Never King There… The Lie That Made Hell Look Like a Throne Room
paragraphs: He Was Never King There… The Lie That Made Hell Look Like a Throne Room
The Bible Never Says Satan Rules Hell — And That Changes Everything You Thought You Knew About Judgment, Power, and the Cross
You grew up hearing it.
In jokes. In movies. In quiet warnings whispered by people who meant well but never opened the text deeply enough.
“Satan is the ruler of hell.”
But pause… just for a second.
If that were true… then why does the Bible never say it?
Not once.
Not in Hebrew. Not in Greek. Not in Aramaic. Not in any faithful translation.
And what if that misunderstanding has quietly distorted how you see evil… judgment… and even Jesus Himself?
Because if Satan rules hell… then hell is his kingdom.
But if he doesn’t… then hell is something far more terrifying.
It means Satan isn’t a king there.
He’s a prisoner.
And suddenly… the story changes.
You feel it, don’t you?
Something just shifted inside you.
Because now this isn’t about mythology anymore.
This is about truth.
And truth has weight.
The Scriptures don’t play games with this.

In the Greek of the New Testament, Jesus uses the word γέεννα (Gehenna) when speaking of final judgment—a term rooted in the Valley of Hinnom, a place of fire, judgment, and destruction. Not a throne room. Not a kingdom. A place of divine judgment.
And when we look at the clearest description of Satan’s future, it’s not him ruling anything.
It’s him being judged.
Revelation 20:10 doesn’t leave space for imagination:
“And the devil who deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur… and they will be tormented day and night forever and ever.”
The Greek word used for “tormented” is βασανισθήσονται (basanisthēsontai) — it means to be tested, tortured, or punished under authority.
Not ruling.
Not commanding.
Not reigning.
Suffering.
Under judgment.
Under God.
Let that sit in your chest for a moment.
Satan doesn’t own hell.
God does.
And that’s the part most people don’t want to face.
Because it means hell isn’t a chaotic playground of demons doing whatever they want.
It is a place of justice.
Holy justice.
Righteous judgment.
Prepared, as Jesus Himself said in Matthew 25:41:
“Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.”
Prepared for them.
Not ruled by them.
That changes everything.
Because the enemy you thought was powerful enough to rule hell… is actually powerless before the One who created justice itself.
Even the Hebrew understanding of the realm of the dead—שְׁאוֹל (Sheol)—was never a kingdom of Satan. It was a place under God’s dominion, where all souls went before final judgment.
Satan has never had ownership over death.
Only influence over sin.
And even that influence was crushed.
You remember the moment.
The cross.
That wasn’t just suffering.
That was victory.
Colossians 2:15 says:
“He disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them in Him.”
The Greek word for “disarmed” is ἀπεκδυσάμενος (apekdysamenos) — stripped bare… completely exposed… humiliated.
That’s what Jesus did to the powers of darkness.
Not negotiated with them.
Not shared territory.
He triumphed.
Publicly.
Completely.
So why do people still imagine Satan sitting on a throne in hell?
Because it’s easier.
It makes evil look organized… almost powerful.
But the truth?
Evil is defeated.
Condemned.
Awaiting judgment.
And that truth… is both terrifying and freeing.
Terrifying because hell is real.
And no one escapes God’s authority.
But freeing because Satan is not equal to God.
Not even close.
There is no dual kingdom.
No balance of power.
There is only one throne.
One Judge.
One Savior.
Jesus Christ.
And this is where it turns personal.
Because if Satan doesn’t rule hell… then no one escapes judgment by aligning with him.
There is no “other side” to run to.
There is only separation from God… or restoration through Christ.
That’s it.
No middle ground.
No loopholes.
No alternate kingdom.
Just truth.
And grace.
You feel the tension, don’t you?
Because deep down… this isn’t just theology.
This is about where you stand.
About whether you’ve been playing with sin thinking it leads somewhere powerful… when in reality it leads somewhere broken.
Condemned.
Empty.
But here’s the part that changes everything…
Grace.
Because the same God who prepared judgment… also made a way of escape.
Through Jesus.
Through the cross.
Through forgiveness that doesn’t make sense but changes everything.
Romans 5:8 reminds us:
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not when we were clean.
Not when we figured it out.
While we were still broken.
That’s the Gospel.
That’s the rewrite.
From scandal… to grace.
And maybe this hit you harder than you expected.
Maybe you’ve believed things about God… about hell… about Satan… that were never actually true.
Maybe you’ve been closer to truth than you realized… but still holding onto pieces that kept you distant.
Be honest.
This stirred something.
Sit with it.
Wrestle with it.
And if this exposed something in you…
If you’ve been tired, struggling, questioning…
If you know Jesus is still working on you…
Your honesty might be the thing that helps someone else step out of darkness too.
Not because it’s content… but because someone you love is believing the wrong story about eternity.
Yes, even the one who avoids these conversations.
Especially them.
Because you’ll need to come back to truth when confusion tries to creep back in.
And follow closely… not for a personality… but for daily reminders of what is real, what is eternal, and what actually saves.
Because the truth is…
You were never meant to just consume truth.
You were meant to carry it.
And someone is waiting on the other side of your obedience.
Satan was never king there… and he never will be.
Only Jesus holds the keys.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: It Never Says “Enough”: The Sin That Whispers Softly While Destroying Loudly
paragraphs:
It Never Says “Enough”: The Sin That Whispers Softly While Destroying Loudly
Why Lust Keeps Taking, Keeps Emptying, and Still Leaves You Wanting More
It never announces itself as destruction.

It doesn’t knock on your door like violence or scream like chaos. It enters quietly… almost respectfully. A glance. A thought. A scroll that lasts a little longer than it should. A curiosity you promise yourself you’ll control.
But you don’t realize—you’re not controlling it anymore.
It’s controlling you.
Scripture doesn’t soften this reality. It exposes it with unsettling clarity. In the original Hebrew of Proverbs 27:20, it says:

“שְׁאוֹל וַאֲבַדּוֹן לֹא תִשְׂבַּעְנָה וְעֵינֵי הָאָדָם לֹא תִשְׂבַּעְנָה”
(Sheol va’avadon lo tisba‘nah, ve’einei ha’adam lo tisba‘nah)
Translation: “Death and destruction are never satisfied, and neither are the eyes of man.”
The eyes… never satisfied.
That word “תִשְׂבַּעְנָה” (tisba‘nah) means to be filled, to be full, to reach a point where you say, “This is enough.”
But lust?
It never reaches that point.
You told yourself it was just once. Then twice. Then only when you’re stressed. Then only when no one’s around. Then suddenly… it’s part of you.
And still, it doesn’t say “enough.”
Jesus didn’t ignore this. He went straight to the root. In Matthew 5:28, the Greek hits harder than most translations capture:

“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν”
(pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn)
It doesn’t just say “looks.” It says “looking with intent to desire.”
The word ἐπιθυμῆσαι (epithymēsai) isn’t casual attraction. It’s craving. Hunger. A deep, internal pull that says, “I need this.”
And that’s the lie.
Because lust doesn’t satisfy hunger.
It feeds it.
It promises fullness but engineers emptiness. It convinces you that one more glance, one more video, one more secret moment will finally quiet the noise inside you…
But it only makes the silence louder afterward.
You feel it, don’t you?
That moment after.
When the screen goes dark. When the fantasy fades. When reality rushes back in like cold water.
You don’t feel fulfilled.
You feel exposed.
And maybe you’ve learned how to hide it so well that no one else knows. You still smile. You still show up. You still worship. You still say the right things.
But inside… something feels off.
Because sin never just stays external. It rewires the inside.
James 1:14–15 doesn’t romanticize the process:

“ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας… εἶτα ἡ ἐπιθυμία συλλαβοῦσα τίκτει ἁμαρτίαν”
(hekastos de peirazetai hypo tēs idias epithymias… eita hē epithymia syllabousa tiktei hamartian)
Translation: “Each person is tempted when they are dragged away by their own desire… then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin.”
Did you catch that?
Desire… conceives.
Sin… is born.
This isn’t just behavior. This is something growing inside you.
And if it’s left unchecked, it matures into something heavier. Something darker. Something harder to break.
That’s why lust never says “enough.”
Because it’s not designed to stop.
It’s designed to consume.
But here’s the part no one tells you clearly enough:
Your struggle doesn’t mean you’re too far gone.
It means there’s still a war happening inside you.
And that war… is evidence that your soul hasn’t surrendered completely.
Because if you were truly numb, you wouldn’t feel conviction at all.
That ache you feel? That discomfort? That quiet voice telling you, “This isn’t who you are”?
That’s not shame.
That’s God calling you back.

In Aramaic, when Jesus speaks of the heart, He uses a concept deeply tied to the inner core—the unseen place where decisions are made, where desires are formed, where truth either takes root or gets choked out.
And He doesn’t just expose sin.
He offers rescue.
John 8:36 in Greek says:

“ἐὰν οὖν ὁ υἱὸς ὑμᾶς ἐλευθερώσῃ, ὄντως ἐλεύθεροι ἔσεσθε”
(ean oun ho huios hymas eleutherōsē, ontōs eleutheroi esesthe)
Translation: “So if the Son sets you free, you will be free indeed.”
Not partially free.
Not temporarily free.
Truly free.
But freedom requires honesty.
Not the kind you show people.
The kind you admit to God.
So be honest for a moment…
Is this something you’ve been hiding?
Is this something that keeps pulling you back?
Is this something you’ve tried to quit but keep returning to when no one’s watching?
If it is…
You’re not alone.
But you also don’t have to stay here.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
And if you know someone who’s silently battling this—someone who looks strong on the outside but is struggling in secret—share this with them. Not to expose them… but to reach them.
Or send it privately.
Because silence is where this sin grows.
Light is where it dies.
And if this spoke to something real inside you, don’t just move on like this was another post.
You’re going to need this reminder again when the temptation comes back.
Because it will try again.
But next time… you won’t be unarmed.
And if you want to go deeper—not just surface-level motivation, but real discipleship, real accountability, real spiritual growth—you need to stay close to truth daily.
Not for content.
For transformation.
For truth that confronts and heals.
For reminders that don’t let you drift.
For a community that refuses to pretend.
Not because we’re selling something empty.
But because building a space that consistently reaches souls, restores hearts, and spreads the Gospel requires support.
If you want to glorify God not just in what you feel, but in what you sustain—this is one way to do it.
But more than that…
You’re investing in something eternal.
You’re helping truth reach someone who might be one post away from surrendering to Jesus.
You don’t have to walk this alone.
You were never meant to.
Because the sin that never says “enough” doesn’t get the final word.
Jesus does.
And He’s still rewriting your story… even now.
The thing you thought would stay hidden is the very place God wants to bring healing.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “The Silence That Speaks: Why the Bible Didn’t Call Polygamy a Sin… Yet Still Points You to Something Greater”
paragraphs:
“The Silence That Speaks: Why the Bible Didn’t Call Polygamy a Sin… Yet Still Points You to Something Greater”
What looks like permission may actually be exposure… and what feels like acceptance may be God patiently leading us back to His original design.
You probably noticed it.
You were reading the Bible… maybe Genesis, maybe Kings… and something didn’t sit right.

Abraham had more than one woman.
Jacob had multiple wives and concubines.
David, “a man after God’s own heart,” had many.
Even Solomon—wisest of all—had hundreds.
And nowhere… nowhere did you find a verse that clearly says, “Polygamy is a sin.”
So the question quietly forms in your mind, maybe even your spirit:
Why didn’t God just say it plainly?
And if you’ve ever wrestled with that… you’re not alone.

But what if the Bible isn’t silent because it approves…
What if it’s silent because it’s exposing something deeper?

Because sometimes God doesn’t shout condemnation…
He lets the consequences speak louder than words.
Go back to the beginning.
Before kings, before covenants, before chaos.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
In Hebrew, it reads:

וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
“Ve’davaq b’ishto v’hayu l’basar echad”
“And he shall cling to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”

Not wives.
Not many.
Not divided.
One.
From the very first page, God reveals a design—not just a rule, but a reflection. A union so intimate, so whole, it mirrors something eternal.
But then sin enters.
And everything fractures.
What was once unity becomes multiplication without harmony.
The first polygamist mentioned? Not a righteous man. It was Lamech in Genesis 4:19—a descendant of Cain, marked by violence and rebellion.
That’s not random.
That’s a pattern.
From there, polygamy appears again and again… but never without pain.

Abraham takes Hagar, and suddenly there’s tension, jealousy, and division.
Jacob marries Leah and Rachel, and his household becomes a battlefield of comparison and insecurity.
David’s family is filled with betrayal and tragedy.
Solomon’s many wives eventually turn his heart away from God.
The Bible doesn’t need to label it “sin” in every instance…
Because it shows you what sin does.
And maybe that’s the point.
God’s Word is not just a list of forbidden actions. It’s a revelation of what leads to life… and what leads to fracture.
By the time we reach the New Testament, the picture sharpens.
Jesus is questioned about marriage, and He doesn’t introduce something new—He goes back to the beginning.
Matthew 19:4–6:
“Have you not read that He who created them from the beginning made them male and female… and the two shall become one flesh? So they are no longer two but one flesh.”
In Greek:

καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
“kai esontai hoi duo eis sarka mian”
“And the two shall become one flesh.”
Two.
Not three. Not many.
Two becoming one.
And then Paul, writing to the church, gives even clearer direction.
1 Timothy 3:2:
“An overseer must be above reproach, the husband of one wife…”
In Greek:

μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα
“mias gynaikos andra”
“A one-woman man.”
Because by now, God isn’t just revealing history…
He’s restoring design.
But don’t miss this…
The Bible is brutally honest about human failure, not because God approves of it—but because He refuses to hide it.
Polygamy is recorded, not endorsed.
It’s described, not prescribed.
And through every broken story, God is whispering something:
“This is not what I intended… but I will still redeem it.”
Because the real story of Scripture is not about perfect people making perfect choices.
It’s about a perfect Savior stepping into imperfect lives.
And here’s where it gets deeply personal…
Some of you reading this aren’t wrestling with polygamy.
You’re wrestling with compromise.
With divided hearts.
With loving God… but also holding onto things you know pull you away.
And maybe you’ve been waiting for God to shout, “That’s sin!”
But instead… He’s been showing you the consequences.

The unrest.
The confusion.
The quiet conviction you can’t shake.
Because sometimes God doesn’t need to label it…
Your soul already knows.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected, didn’t it?
You’re not alone in this.
And you’re not too far gone either.
Because the same Bible that shows broken marriages… also shows redeeming grace.
Jesus didn’t come for people who got it right.
He came for people who got it wrong and were willing to surrender.
2 Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
In Greek:

καινὴ κτίσις
“kainē ktisis”
“A completely new creation… not a repaired version of the old.”
That means your past doesn’t define your future.
Your mistakes don’t cancel your calling.
And your story—no matter how messy—can still glorify God.
If this spoke to you, don’t keep it to yourself.
And if you feel something shifting in your spirit right now… don’t ignore it.
We’re building something deeper than content—we’re building conviction, healing, and real discipleship in Christ.
And if you’re serious about growing, about going beyond surface-level faith, about actually transforming your life through the Word of God…
Then take the next step.
This isn’t just content.
This is transformation.
This is coming back to what God originally designed… and letting Jesus rewrite everything sin tried to distort.
Because in the end…
God didn’t ignore polygamy.

He exposed it through broken stories…
and then pointed us back to a love that is whole, faithful, and undivided.
A love that looks like Christ.
And maybe the real question isn’t “Why didn’t God call it sin?”
Maybe the real question is…
“Why do I keep holding onto things He’s already shown me aren’t His best for me?”
Because He isn’t.
And He never will be.
The things God doesn’t immediately condemn… He often patiently reveals—until your heart is ready to surrender them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “God Knows Your Heart”… And That Should Terrify You Before It Comforts You
paragraphs:
“God Knows Your Heart”… And That Should Terrify You Before It Comforts You
The hidden warning behind the phrase we use to excuse what God is trying to expose
You whispered it to yourself again… didn’t you?
“God knows my heart.”
Not out loud. Not in front of people. Just quietly… when conviction started knocking and you didn’t feel like opening the door.

You said it when you stayed in that relationship you knew God warned you about.
You said it when you entertained that sin just a little longer than you should have.
You said it when you smiled in church but felt completely distant from God inside.
“God knows my heart.”
And you meant it as comfort.
But what if… it was never meant to comfort you in that moment?
What if it was a warning?

Because Scripture doesn’t treat that phrase lightly. It doesn’t use it as a blanket of reassurance for hidden compromise. It uses it like a spotlight… exposing what we desperately try to keep in the dark.
In Jeremiah 17:9, the Hebrew cuts deeper than most translations let us feel:

“עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וְאָנֻשׁ הוּא; מִי יֵדָעֶנּוּ”
“The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can know it?”
That word “עָקֹב” (aqov) doesn’t just mean deceitful… it carries the sense of being twisted, crooked, manipulative. Not just broken… but actively misleading.
Your heart isn’t just weak. It lies to you.
And yet we say… “God knows my heart” as if that’s supposed to defend us.
But look at the very next verse:

“אֲנִי יְהוָה חֹקֵר לֵב בֹּחֵן כְּלָיוֹת”
“I, the LORD, search the heart and test the mind…” (Jeremiah 17:10)
He doesn’t just know your heart.
He searches it.
That word “חֹקֵר” (ḥōqēr) means to examine, to dig, to investigate deeply… like someone uncovering something buried on purpose.
Let that sit for a second.

God isn’t just aware of what’s in you.
He is actively uncovering it.
So when you say “God knows my heart”… you are not appealing to His ignorance.
You are standing fully exposed before His investigation.
And suddenly… that phrase doesn’t feel so comfortable anymore.
Because in 1 Samuel 16:7, when God rejected what humans approved, He said:

“כִּי הָאָדָם יִרְאֶה לַעֵינַיִם וַיהוָה יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב”
“Man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.”
We quote that like a badge of honor.
But it was spoken in a moment of rejection.
God was saying… “You see what looks right. I see what actually is.”

That means you can fool people.
You can even fool yourself.
But you cannot fool the God who sees the intentions beneath your intentions.
Hebrews 4:12-13 takes it even further, in Greek so precise it almost feels surgical:

“κριτικὸς ἐνθυμήσεων καὶ ἐννοιῶν καρδίας”
“a discerner of the thoughts and intentions of the heart”

“κριτικὸς” (kritikos)… where we get “critical” or “judge.”
God’s Word doesn’t just observe your heart… it judges the motives inside it.
And then it says:

“πάντα δὲ γυμνὰ καὶ τετραχηλισμένα”
“All are naked and exposed…”

Not partially seen.
Not mostly understood.
Fully exposed.
So why do we keep using “God knows my heart” as a shield… when Scripture uses it like a mirror?
Because if we’re honest… we don’t always want transformation.
We want permission.

We want God to understand why we haven’t let go.
We want Him to validate what we’re still holding onto.
We want grace without surrender.
But grace has never been permission to stay the same.
It has always been power to change.
And here’s where everything shifts…
Because yes, God knows your heart.

He knows the hidden sin… but He also knows the hidden wounds.
He sees the compromise… but He also sees the pain that led you there.
He sees the excuses… but He also sees the battles you’ve been quietly losing.
In Psalm 51:6, David, after one of the worst moral failures in Scripture, finally stopped hiding and said:

“הֵן־אֱמֶת חָפַצְתָּ בַטֻּחוֹת”
“Behold, You desire truth in the inward being…”
Not perfection.
Truth.
Not image.
Honesty.
Not performance.
Surrender.
That’s when “God knows my heart” stops being dangerous… and starts becoming healing.
When it’s no longer used to excuse sin… but to confess it.
Because in the same broken prayer, David cries:

“לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים”
“Create in me a clean heart, O God…” (Psalm 51:10)
That word “בְּרָא” (bara) is the same word used in Genesis 1.
Create… from nothing.
David wasn’t asking God to fix his heart.
He was asking for a new one.
And that’s the Gospel.
Not behavior modification.
Heart transformation.
Ezekiel 36:26 promised it long before Jesus came:

“וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב חָדָשׁ”
“I will give you a new heart…”
And Jesus fulfilled it.
Because the cross was never about making bad people slightly better.
It was about giving dead hearts life.
So yes… God knows your heart.

He knows the version of you you show people.
He knows the version of you you hide from people.
And He knows the version of you you’re afraid to admit even exists.
And still… He chose the cross.
Still… He offers forgiveness.
Still… He calls you out of hiding.
But don’t twist that into comfort without conviction.
Because the same truth that heals you… will first expose you.
So be honest.

Are you saying “God knows my heart” because you trust Him…
or because you’re avoiding Him?
This isn’t about shame.
It’s about surrender.

Because the moment you stop defending your heart…
is the moment God begins to transform it.
And if you’re serious about glorifying God—not just in words but in action—then support what is feeding your spirit.
Because one day… you won’t be able to say “God knows my heart” as an excuse.
Only as a testimony.
And here’s the part that stays with you…
The God who sees everything in you… is the same God who still chose to die for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “Is It Sin to Enjoy Sex… or Only to Abuse It?”
paragraphs:
“Is It Sin to Enjoy Sex… or Only to Abuse It?”
The question nobody says out loud… but everyone is silently wrestling with.
It usually doesn’t start with rebellion.
It starts with confusion.
A quiet question sitting in the back of your mind while you scroll, while you remember, while you feel something you don’t know how to categorize anymore…
“Why do I feel guilty… for something God created?”
And you don’t say it out loud, because in church circles, even asking the question can feel dangerous.
But let’s be honest for a second—really honest.
Somewhere along the way, many believers were taught to associate desire with shame… intimacy with suspicion… and pleasure with sin.
So now you’re stuck in this silent tension—wanting to honor God, but also wondering why something that feels so natural feels so condemned.
And if you’ve ever asked yourself that question… you’re not alone.
But more importantly—Scripture actually answers it.
Not with cultural opinions… not with fear-based control… but with truth.
Raw, unfiltered, and deeply freeing truth.
Because when God first designed intimacy, He didn’t whisper it in shame.
He spoke it boldly in blessing.
In the beginning, before sin ever entered the world, before guilt distorted what was pure, there was this moment in Genesis that most people rush past without realizing how profound it is:

“וַיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עֲרוּמִּים הָאָדָם וְאִשְׁתּוֹ וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ”
(Vayihyu sheneihem arummim ha’adam ve’ishto velo yitboshashu)
“And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.” (Genesis 2:25)
No shame.
No guilt.
No confusion.
Just purity.
Just design.
Just union exactly the way God intended it.
Let that settle for a moment.
Before sin corrupted the human heart, intimacy was not hidden… it was holy.
So what changed?
Not the design.
The distortion.
Sin didn’t create sex—it corrupted it.
Which means the issue was never enjoyment.
The issue was always misuse.
That’s why Scripture never condemns intimacy within God’s design—it celebrates it.
Read this slowly, without rushing past it:

“דּוֹדִי לִי וַאֲנִי לוֹ”
(Dodi li va’ani lo)
“My beloved is mine, and I am his.” (Song of Songs 2:16)
That entire book—often avoided—is a poetic, God-preserved expression of desire, affection, longing, and physical attraction within covenant love.
Not tolerated.
Celebrated.
Even in the New Testament, Paul doesn’t command distance in marriage—he commands connection:

“μὴ ἀποστερεῖτε ἀλλήλους…”
(Mē apostereite allēlous)
“Do not deprive one another…” (1 Corinthians 7:5)
That’s not restriction.
That’s protection.
That’s God saying: intimacy, when kept inside covenant, is not something to fear—it’s something to steward.
So no… enjoying intimacy itself is not sin.
But abusing it?
Twisting it?
Removing it from God’s design?
That’s where the fracture begins.
Because outside of God’s order, what was meant to unite begins to wound.
What was meant to give life begins to take it.
What was meant to reflect covenant becomes driven by consumption.
And that’s the part no one tells you plainly.
The problem isn’t that you feel desire.
The problem is when desire becomes detached from truth.
Jesus didn’t come to erase desire—He came to restore it.
Because even the word “lust” in Scripture carries a deeper meaning than just attraction.
“ἐπιθυμέω” (epithumeō)—to crave, to set your heart upon, to long for something in a way that takes rather than gives.
That’s the difference.
Holy desire gives.
Sinful desire consumes.
One reflects love.
The other reflects hunger without covenant.
And if we’re being real… a lot of people aren’t struggling because they enjoy intimacy.
They’re struggling because they’ve been taught to feel ashamed of something God created, while simultaneously being surrounded by a world that abuses it in every direction.
That confusion creates silence.
That silence creates hidden battles.
And hidden battles grow into quiet shame.
But Jesus never approached brokenness with shame.
He approached it with truth and restoration.
Think about the woman caught in adultery.
Exposed.
Condemned.
Ready to be destroyed.
And yet Jesus didn’t say, “Your desire is the problem.”
He said, “Go and sin no more.”
He addressed the misuse… not the existence of longing.
Because He knew something we often forget—
The goal isn’t suppression.
It’s transformation.
And that changes everything.
Because suddenly, you realize…
God isn’t trying to take something from you.
He’s trying to protect something sacred.
He’s not anti-pleasure.
He’s anti-destruction.
Sit in it.
Because some of you have been carrying shame that God never placed on you.
And others of you know… you’ve crossed lines that you can’t pretend didn’t happen.
Both need the same thing.
Grace.
Real grace.
The kind that doesn’t ignore truth—but meets you inside it.
Because the Gospel was never about pretending we’re clean.
It was about Jesus making us clean.
And this is where everything shifts.
From scandal… to grace.
If this exposed something hidden in you, don’t brush it off.
Be honest.
Let it be real.
Let it be seen.
Because healing grows where honesty lives.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this… someone struggling, confused, or silently battling—don’t keep this to yourself.
Not to expose them—but to reach them.
You never know who’s been waiting for truth like this.
Save this too.
Because there will be moments when your mind gets loud again… and you’ll need to come back to what God actually said.
Stay close to truth.
Because drifting is subtle… but so is growth.
And for those who want to go deeper—not just reading but truly growing—there’s something waiting for you.
Not surface-level content.
Real spiritual nourishment.
If your heart is in this… if you want to glorify God not just in words but in action… then stand with us.
Not out of pressure.
But out of purpose.
Because when truth reaches you… it’s meant to reach others through you.
And maybe this is the moment where something changes.
Not just what you believe…
But how you live.
Because what God made holy was never meant to feel dirty—only restored.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “You Feel It… But Is It Sin? The Question No One Dares to Answer Out Loud”
paragraphs:
“You Feel It… But Is It Sin? The Question No One Dares to Answer Out Loud”
When Desire Doesn’t Match Your Faith—And You’re Terrified to Ask God About It
There are thoughts you never say out loud.
Not in church. Not with your family. Not even in prayer.
Because the moment you admit it, even to yourself, it feels like something inside you might break.
What if… I’m attracted to the same sex?
And suddenly your entire identity feels like it’s standing in front of a courtroom—with no lawyer, no defense, just silence and fear.
You don’t choose the moment it starts. It just… happens.
A glance that lingers too long. A connection that feels deeper than it should. A quiet pull that doesn’t go away no matter how many worship songs you play or how many verses you try to memorize.
And then the question comes like a whisper you wish you could silence:
“Is this… sin?”
Not what you do. Not your actions.
But what you feel.
Because if even your feelings are sin… then where does that leave you?
And if they aren’t… then why does it feel so heavy?
Let’s not rush this.
Let’s sit in the tension for a moment.
Because Scripture doesn’t run from hard questions—and neither should we.
In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus says something that shifts everything we thought we understood about sin:
“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν” (Matthew 5:28)
Translated carefully from the Greek, it means:
“Everyone who looks at a woman with the intent to desire her has already committed adultery in his heart.”
Notice what Jesus is doing.
He’s not condemning the existence of attraction.
He’s confronting the cultivation of desire.
There is a difference between a moment you experience… and a direction you choose.
The Greek word “ἐπιθυμῆσαι” (epithymēsai) is not passive—it’s intentional, nurtured longing.
So the question isn’t:
“Did you feel something?”
The deeper question is:
“What are you doing with what you felt?”
Because temptation itself is not sin.
Even Jesus was tempted.
Hebrews 4:15 says:
“πειρασθέντα κατὰ πάντα καθ᾽ ὁμοιότητα χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας”
“He was tempted in every way as we are—yet without sin.”
Temptation came.
It knocked.
But it never took residence.
That means attraction—whether toward the same sex or the opposite sex—is not, by itself, the final verdict of your soul.
It is a moment.
A signal.
A crossroad.
But not your identity.
Not your condemnation.
And definitely not beyond the reach of grace.
Now here’s where it gets real.
Because Scripture does not stay silent about sexual behavior.
Romans 1:26–27 speaks plainly about same-sex acts within the context of humanity turning away from God.
The Greek word used—“πάθη ἀτιμίας” (pathē atimias)—means “dishonorable passions,” pointing to desires that are acted upon in ways outside God’s design.
But don’t miss this.
The passage is not isolating one group of people as uniquely broken.
It is describing all humanity apart from God.
Because just a few verses later, Paul levels the ground:
“οὐκ ἔστιν δίκαιος, οὐδὲ εἷς” (Romans 3:10)
“There is no one righteous, not even one.”
So if you’re reading this thinking, “Does this mean I’m worse?”
No.
It means you’re human.
And humanity—every version of it—needs a Savior.
The enemy wants to trap you in one of two lies:
Either your attraction defines you completely…
Or your attraction disqualifies you completely.
But the Gospel destroys both.
Because in Christ, you are not your urges.
And you are not your shame.
You are someone being called.
Someone being pursued.
Someone being rewritten.
The Hebrew heart of Scripture echoes this truth in Psalm 51:10:
“לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים”
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Not “reward me for already being clean.”
Not “accept me as I am and leave me unchanged.”
But “create.”
Because transformation is not self-made.
It is God-breathed.
So is it sin to be attracted to the same sex?
No.
But like every human desire, it becomes spiritually dangerous when it is embraced, nurtured, and acted upon outside the will of God.
And here’s the part most people won’t tell you:
Following Jesus has never been about which desires you have.
It has always been about which desires you surrender.
Luke 9:23—straight from the Greek:
“ἀπαρνησάσθω ἑαυτὸν… καὶ ἀκολουθείτω μοι”
“Deny yourself… and follow Me.”
Not deny your existence.
Not deny your humanity.
But deny the version of yourself that tries to live without God’s authority.
And that applies to everyone.
Every craving.
Every longing.
Every hidden thought.
This is not a message of rejection.
It’s a call to something deeper.
Because Jesus never looked at someone trapped in sin and said, “Stay there.”
But He also never said, “You’re too far gone.”
He said, “Follow Me.”
And following Him means walking through tension.
It means nights where you wrestle.
Moments where you don’t understand yourself.
Days where obedience feels heavier than comfort.
But it also means something else.
Freedom.
Real freedom.
Not the kind that tells you to do whatever you feel.
But the kind that frees you from being controlled by what you feel.
Sit with it.
Let it speak.
And be honest…
When you read this, did something inside you quietly whisper, “That’s me”?
If it did, don’t hide.
You’re not the only one fighting.
And you were never meant to fight alone.
Someone who won’t judge but will walk with you.
Because supporting this mission isn’t about money.
It’s about multiplying truth.
It’s about making sure messages like this reach the next person before shame convinces them to give up.
Because this isn’t about labeling you.
It’s about leading you.
To the One who sees everything you’re afraid to admit…
And still chose the cross.
You are not the question you’re asking.
You are the person Jesus is still calling.
And He’s not finished with you yet.
Somewhere between your struggle and your surrender… grace is already rewriting your story.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Said “I Do”… So Why Do You Still Want Them?
paragraphs:
You Said “I Do”… So Why Do You Still Want Them?
The Quiet Battle No One Talks About in Marriage… and the Grace That Still Chases You
It doesn’t start loud.
It never does.

It’s a glance that lingers just a second too long.
A conversation that feels… easier than it should.
A thought you didn’t invite… but didn’t exactly fight either.

And suddenly you’re sitting there, married… committed… wearing a ring that once felt like fire on your finger…
wondering why your heart is wandering where your body never promised to go.
No one prepared you for this part.

No one told you that you could love your spouse… and still feel temptation toward someone else.
No one warned you that desire doesn’t die at the altar—it just gets redirected… or neglected.
And now you’re asking the question you’re too ashamed to say out loud:
“What’s wrong with me?”
Let this hit you gently… but truthfully:
Nothing is “wrong” with you… but something is at war inside you.
The Apostle Paul didn’t hide this tension. He exposed it brutally:

“For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate…”
(Romans 7:15)

In the original Greek, he says:
“ὃ γὰρ κατεργάζομαι οὐ γινώσκω” (ho gar katergazomai ou ginōskō)
—“What I am working out in my life… I don’t even fully understand.”
You feel that?

Because this isn’t just about attraction.
This is about the battlefield of the heart.
James doesn’t sugarcoat it either:

“But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire.”
(James 1:14)
The Greek word used there is “ἐπιθυμία” (epithymia) — a deep, overreaching desire… not always sinful at its root… but dangerous when it goes ungoverned.
So let’s be honest for a moment.

You didn’t wake up one day and decide to betray your marriage.
But maybe… just maybe… you stopped guarding it.

Maybe you got comfortable.
Maybe the conversations got shallow.
Maybe the intimacy faded into routine.
Maybe the appreciation dried up.
And in that quiet dryness… something else started to feel like rain.
That’s how the enemy works.
Not always through destruction… but through substitution.
Not always through obvious sin… but through emotional drift.
Jesus didn’t ignore this either. He went deeper than behavior… straight to the root:

“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’
But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
(Matthew 5:27–28)
The Greek phrase “πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι” (pros to epithymēsai) means “to deliberately desire… to cultivate longing.”
This isn’t about accidental attraction.
This is about what you choose to feed.

Because attraction may knock…
but lust is when you open the door, pull up a chair, and serve it dinner.
Let this sit with you:

You are not condemned for being tempted.
But you are responsible for what you do with that temptation.
Even Jesus was tempted.

“In every respect has been tempted as we are, yet without sin.”
(Hebrews 4:15)
The difference?
He didn’t entertain what He refused to become.
So what now?

Do you suppress it?
Ignore it?
Pretend it’s not there?
No.
You bring it into the light before it destroys you in the dark.
The Hebrew word for truth is “אֱמֶת” (emet) — meaning firmness, faithfulness, reality.
Real healing starts with real honesty.

Not polished prayers.
Not religious performance.
But raw confession.

“Search me, O God, and know my heart… test me and know my anxious thoughts.”
(Psalm 139:23)
Because what you refuse to confront… you will eventually become controlled by.
But here’s the part no one tells you:
This struggle doesn’t disqualify you from love… it reveals your need for deeper transformation.
Marriage was never meant to replace your need for Christ.
Your spouse can’t carry what only Jesus was designed to hold.

If you’re looking for someone else to complete what only God can restore…
you’ll keep chasing shadows.
And shadows never satisfy.
So maybe this isn’t just about temptation.
Maybe this is about disconnection… from God first.
Because when your soul starts starving… it will reach for anything that feels like food.
Even if it poisons you slowly.
Jesus said:

“I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger…”
(John 6:35)

Not your coworker.
Not that person in your DMs.
Not the one who “understands you better.”
Only Him.
And here’s the scandal no one expects:
Even if you’ve already entertained it… even if you’ve crossed lines emotionally… even if your thoughts have gone further than you admit…
Grace is still reaching for you.
Right now.

Not after you fix yourself.
Not after you clean it up.
Now.

“Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more.”
(Romans 5:20)

The Greek says: “ὑπερεπερίσσευσεν ἡ χάρις” (hyper eperisseusen hē charis)
—Grace didn’t just match your failure… it overflowed beyond it.
So you’re not stuck.
You’re being invited back.

Back to integrity.
Back to truth.
Back to the kind of love that doesn’t wander because it’s rooted.
But this is where you decide:

Will you keep feeding what’s pulling you away…
or start fighting for what you once vowed to protect?
Because love isn’t just a feeling you fell into.
It’s a covenant you fight to keep.
Sit in it.
Be honest.
Someone reading your honesty might finally feel less alone.
And if you want to go deeper—if you’re serious about honoring God not just publicly but privately—stay close.
If this message mattered to you… supporting it helps it reach someone who might be one decision away from breaking something sacred.

Because glorifying God isn’t just about what you believe…
it’s also about what you help spread.
And here’s the truth that won’t leave you:
Temptation may knock on your door… but grace is still standing inside your house, asking you who you really belong to.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Are Soul Ties Real… or Just Emotional Attachment?
paragraphs: Are Soul Ties Real… or Just Emotional Attachment?
The night you said you were finally over them… why did their name still echo in your chest like something unfinished?

You deleted the messages. You stopped checking their profile. You told your friends you were done. But somehow, in quiet moments, your spirit still drifts back… like there’s an invisible thread pulling you toward a memory that refuses to die.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Because what if it’s not just “feelings”? What if something deeper is happening—something Scripture has been whispering about long before modern psychology tried to explain it away?

In Genesis 2:24, the Word says, “Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” The Hebrew word for “cleave” is דָּבַק (dabaq), which means to cling, to stick, to be glued together. This is not casual language. This is covenant language. This is spiritual bonding.

And then Paul echoes this in 1 Corinthians 6:16: “Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, as it is written, ‘The two will become one flesh.’” The Greek word used here is κολλάω (kollaō), meaning to join, to glue, to bind together inseparably.
Let that sink in.

Scripture never uses the phrase “soul ties,” but it absolutely reveals the reality of deep, binding connections—spiritual, emotional, and even physical unions that leave an imprint far beyond the moment.
So no… you’re not crazy.
That pull you feel? That unexplained heaviness? That lingering attachment even after everything ended?
It may not just be emotional attachment.
It might be something your soul hasn’t let go of yet.
But here’s where it gets dangerous.
Because the world will tell you, “Just move on. Time heals everything.” But Jesus never said time heals. He said truth sets free.
In John 8:32, “And you shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.” The Greek word for “free” is ἐλευθερόω (eleutheroō), meaning to liberate, to release from bondage.
Bondage.
Not just memory. Not just emotion. Bondage.
Some connections don’t just break with distance… they have to be broken with truth, repentance, and the authority of Christ.
But don’t misunderstand this.

Not every attachment is a “soul tie” in some mystical, uncontrollable sense. Some are simply wounds. Some are habits. Some are patterns of the heart seeking validation in the wrong places. And some are deep emotional imprints formed through intimacy, vulnerability, and shared experiences.
Yet Scripture shows us that intimacy—especially sexual intimacy—carries a weight that goes beyond the physical. It’s not just bodies meeting. It’s souls intertwining.
And that’s why some people leave your life… but something of them stays behind.
Their voice becomes your inner critic.
Their approval becomes your hidden addiction.
Their absence becomes your quiet ache.
But here’s the truth most people don’t tell you:
What was formed outside of God’s design can feel powerful… but it is not permanent.
Because there is a stronger bond than any soul tie.
There is a deeper connection than any past attachment.
There is a greater union than any human relationship.
It’s the one you were created for.
1 Corinthians 6:17 says, “But he who is joined to the Lord becomes one spirit with Him.” The Greek word again—κολλάω (kollaō). The same word. The same binding.
Do you see it?
The same intensity of connection… but this time, it’s holy.
This time, it heals instead of wounds.
This time, it restores instead of drains.
This time, it sets you free instead of keeping you stuck.
Jesus doesn’t just ask you to “move on.” He offers to reconnect your soul to its rightful source.
Because some of you are not just missing a person…
You’re missing the version of yourself you became when you were connected to them.
And you’ve been trying to get that back… without realizing that only Christ can restore what was lost.
This is where scandal turns into grace.
Because maybe the relationship you regret… the one you wish you never entered… the one that still lingers in your thoughts…
Maybe that wasn’t the end of your story.
Maybe it was the place where God began to show you that your soul was never meant to be held together by human hands.
Maybe it exposed your hunger for connection… so you could finally find it in Him.
So no… you are not stuck forever.
You are not bound beyond redemption.
You are not defined by who you gave yourself to.
Because Jesus specializes in breaking what feels unbreakable… and restoring what feels permanently lost.
But healing doesn’t happen by accident.
It happens when you bring everything into the light.
It happens when you stop romanticizing what God is trying to deliver you from.
It happens when you surrender—not just the person—but the attachment, the memory, the identity you built around them.
Because freedom starts with honesty.
And someone reading this right now… you’ve been calling it love, but deep down, you know it was attachment, dependency, maybe even idolatry.
And Jesus is not exposing you to shame you.
He’s exposing you to free you.
If this spoke directly into your situation, don’t keep it to yourself.
Not to call them out… but to call them out of bondage.
Because there will be a moment—late at night, when memories come back—and you’ll need to remember this truth again.
Because discipleship is not a moment—it’s a daily surrender.
Because this is not the end of your story.
The same God who allowed you to feel the weight of that attachment… is the same God who can completely set you free from it.
And one day, you won’t just remember what broke you…
You’ll testify about what healed you.
You were never meant to stay bound to what Jesus already paid to release.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: What If You Enjoy the Sin You’re Trying to Quit?
paragraphs:
What If You Enjoy the Sin You’re Trying to Quit?
The secret battle nobody admits… and the grace nobody expects
You didn’t expect to like it this much.
That’s the part that scares you.
Because it’s not just that you keep falling… it’s that somewhere inside, there’s a part of you that doesn’t want to stop.
And you hate that part.
You pray, you cry, you promise God, “This is the last time,” but when the moment comes… your heart doesn’t run away. It leans in.
You don’t just sin.
You enjoy it.
And now you’re stuck in the most silent kind of guilt—the kind that whispers, “If I really loved God… why does this feel good?”
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because deep down, you’ve asked the question you were too afraid to say out loud:
“What if I don’t actually want to change?”
The apostle Paul asked something dangerously similar, and he didn’t hide it.
In Romans 7:15, he writes:
“For what I am doing, I do not understand; for what I want, this I do not practice, but what I hate, this I do.”
He goes further in verse 22–23:
“συνήδομαι γὰρ τῷ νόμῳ τοῦ Θεοῦ… βλέπω δὲ ἕτερον νόμον ἐν τοῖς μέλεσίν μου…”
“For I delight (συνήδομαι — I rejoice with) in the law of God in my inner being, but I see another law in my members…”
Did you catch that?
There are two desires inside one person.
One that loves God.
One that loves sin.
And they don’t take turns… they fight at the same time.
So if you feel like you’re living a double life inside your own chest… you’re not alone.
You’re human.
Even deeper, the Hebrew understanding of the heart—לֵב (lev)—was never just emotions. It was the seat of will, desire, intention.
Meaning… your “heart” can want God and want sin at the same time.
That tension doesn’t make you fake.
It reveals the war.
But here’s where most people get it wrong…
They think the problem is that sin feels good.
But Scripture never denies that.
Hebrews 11:25 calls it exactly what it is:
“ἀπόλαυσιν ἁμαρτίας” — the fleeting pleasure of sin.
Not imaginary pleasure.
Real pleasure.
Temporary.
Deceptive.
But real.
And that’s why it’s so powerful.
Sin doesn’t show up ugly.
It shows up desirable.
From the very beginning, Genesis 3:6 says:
“וַתֵּרֶא הָאִשָּׁה כִּי־טוֹב הָעֵץ לְמַאֲכָל…”
“And the woman saw that the tree was good for food…”
Sin was seen as good before it was known as deadly.
So if you’re waiting for sin to feel disgusting before you leave it… you will stay stuck longer than you think.
Because the trap isn’t just in the act.
It’s in the desire.
And desire doesn’t disappear just because you hate the consequences.
This is where Jesus goes deeper than behavior.
In Matthew 26:41, He says:
“τὸ μὲν πνεῦμα πρόθυμον, ἡ δὲ σὰρξ ἀσθενής.”
“The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.”
The word σὰρξ (sarx)—flesh—is not just your body.
It’s the part of you still wired toward rebellion.
The part that can enjoy what is destroying you.
So what if you enjoy the sin you’re trying to quit?
Then the battle is not fake.
It’s real.
And real battles require more than guilt.
They require surrender.
Because here’s the truth nobody told you clearly enough:
You don’t defeat sin by pretending it’s not enjoyable.
You defeat it by discovering something better.
Psalm 16:11 says in Hebrew:
“שֹׂבַע שְׂמָחוֹת אֶת־פָּנֶיךָ… נְעִמוֹת בִּימִינְךָ נֶצַח”
“In Your presence is fullness of joy… at Your right hand are pleasures forevermore.”
Not weaker pleasure.
Stronger.
Deeper.
Lasting.
Sin offers a spark.
God offers a fire that doesn’t burn out.
But here’s where it gets personal…
Because some of you aren’t struggling because you don’t know God.
You’re struggling because you haven’t stayed close long enough to taste Him fully.
So sin still feels louder.
More immediate.
More satisfying.
And you’re trying to fight it with willpower instead of intimacy.
That’s why you keep going back.
Because whatever you feed grows.
And whatever you starve weakens.
So if you feed your flesh all week and only visit God occasionally… don’t be surprised which voice feels stronger.
This isn’t condemnation.
This is clarity.
Because grace doesn’t just forgive you.
It teaches you.
Titus 2:11–12 says:
“ἡ γὰρ χάρις τοῦ Θεοῦ… παιδεύουσα ἡμᾶς…”
“For the grace of God… is training us…”
Grace is not permission to stay stuck.
It’s power to walk free.
But freedom doesn’t always feel immediate.
Sometimes it feels like war.
Sometimes it feels like loss.
Sometimes it feels like letting go of something you still crave.
And that’s the part nobody posts about.
But that’s also the place where transformation begins.
So if you’re in that place right now…
Where you hate your sin but still crave it…
Where you love God but still fall…
Where you’re tired of pretending you’re okay…
Because healing starts where honesty begins.
And listen carefully…
Your struggle does not disqualify you.
Your surrender is what God is looking for.
Not perfection.
Not performance.
Surrender.
Because the same Paul who cried out in Romans 7 didn’t end there.
He said in Romans 7:24–25:
“ταλαίπωρος ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπος… τίς με ῥύσεται…; χάρις δὲ τῷ Θεῷ διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ…”
“O wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me…? Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ…”
The answer was never “try harder.”
The answer was always Jesus.
And Jesus doesn’t just forgive your sin.
He breaks its power.
But you have to come out of hiding.
You’re not just supporting content… you’re helping reach souls who are drowning in silence right now.
Because this isn’t just content.
This is a call.
And the part of you that still enjoys sin…
Is not the end of your story.
It’s the battlefield where Jesus is about to rewrite everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why You Can’t Outpray a Lifestyle You Won’t Change
paragraphs:
Why You Can’t Outpray a Lifestyle You Won’t Change
The Night Heaven Stayed Silent While Your Lips Kept Moving
There was a night you prayed until your voice cracked.

Not the soft, polite kind of prayer you learned in church, but the kind that spills out of a tired soul—half whisper, half desperation. You said all the right things. You called on God’s name. You even cried.
And yet… nothing changed.
Same habits. Same secret sins. Same cycle you promised God you’d break “this time.”
And deep down, a question you’re almost afraid to say out loud began to form—
“Why isn’t God listening?”
But what if Heaven wasn’t silent?
What if Heaven was answering… and you just didn’t like the answer?
Because somewhere between your prayers and your patterns, there’s a tension most people refuse to confront.
You cannot outpray a lifestyle you refuse to surrender.
Scripture doesn’t whisper this truth—it declares it, even when it hurts.

In Psalm 66:18, the Hebrew is painfully direct:
"אִם־רָאִיתִי אָוֶן בְּלִבִּי לֹא יִשְׁמַע אֲדֹנָי"
(Im ra’iti aven belibi, lo yishma Adonai)
“If I had cherished iniquity in my heart, the Lord would not have listened.”
Not “struggled.” Not “fought.” Cherished.
Held onto.
Protected.
Entertained.
That thing you keep going back to after you say “Amen.”
That compromise you’ve learned to justify so well it doesn’t even feel like sin anymore.
That version of you that only exists when no one else is watching.
You’re not confused about what needs to change.
You’re just not ready to let it go.
And so you pray harder.
Longer.
Louder.
Hoping intensity will replace obedience.
But God is not moved by volume.
He is moved by surrender.

Isaiah 1:15 doesn’t soften it either.
“Even though you make many prayers, I will not listen; your hands are full of blood.”
The Hebrew word for “many prayers” is תְּפִלּוֹת (tefillot), meaning repeated, multiplied petitions.
In other words, it’s possible to pray often… and still be ignored.
Not because God is cruel.
But because God is holy.
And holiness refuses to partner with what you’re unwilling to put to death.
You keep asking God to remove the consequences while holding onto the cause.
You want peace without repentance.
Breakthrough without transformation.
Freedom without crucifixion.
But Jesus didn’t die so you could manage sin more comfortably.
He died so you could be free from it completely.

Listen closely to what Jesus says in Luke 6:46.
In Greek, it cuts deeper than the English translation:
“Τί δέ με καλεῖτε· Κύριε, Κύριε, καὶ οὐ ποιεῖτε ἃ λέγω;”
(Ti de me kaleite, Kyrie, Kyrie, kai ou poieite ha lego?)
“Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I say?”
Why do you keep saying “Lord” with your lips… but refuse His authority in your life?
That’s not a prayer problem.
That’s a surrender problem.
And this is where it gets uncomfortable.
Because you don’t need another prayer strategy.
You need a funeral.

Galatians 5:24 says,
“Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.”
Crucified.
Not negotiated.
Not reduced.
Not slowly phased out.
Killed.
That habit you keep defending? It needs a cross.
That relationship God told you to walk away from? It needs a cross.
That hidden addiction you keep renaming so it sounds less serious? It needs a cross.
And here’s the part no one tells you—
Crucifixion is painful.
Because it costs you something.
It costs comfort.
It costs identity.
It costs the version of you that feels familiar… even if it’s destroying you.
But on the other side of that cross is something you’ve been praying for this whole time.
Freedom.
Real freedom.
Not the temporary relief you get after a good prayer session.
But the kind that rewires your desires, renews your mind, and restores your soul.

Romans 12:2 says,
“Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind.”
The Greek word for “transformed” is μεταμορφοῦσθε (metamorphousthe).
It’s where we get the word metamorphosis.
A complete change.
Not behavior modification.
Not spiritual performance.
Transformation.
And transformation doesn’t happen through prayer alone.
It happens when prayer leads to obedience.
When conviction leads to repentance.
When surrender becomes a daily decision, not a one-time emotional moment.
You don’t need to pray more about what God already told you to change.
You need to obey what He already revealed.
And maybe that’s why this is hitting you harder than you expected.
Because you recognize yourself in this.
You’ve been praying… but not changing.
Asking… but not surrendering.
Crying… but not crucifying.
Be honest.
What is it in your life right now that God has already told you to let go of?
Not what you’re “working on.”
Not what you’re “thinking about.”
What you know.
What you feel every time conviction hits.
What you silence with distraction, excuses, or delay.
This is the moment where everything can change.
Not because you pray another emotional prayer.
But because you finally say, “No more.”
No more hiding.
No more negotiating with sin.
No more trying to outpray what God is calling you to put to death.
This isn’t about guilt.
This is about freedom.
And freedom begins where excuses end.
Not because we’re selling something cheap.
But because discipleship costs something, and growth requires commitment.
This is bigger than content.
This is about your soul.
If you truly want to glorify God, then don’t just consume truth—help spread it.
Let your page become a place where someone else encounters Jesus.
Because someone is watching your life, even now.
And they don’t need to see a perfect Christian.
They need to see a surrendered one.
Here’s the truth you can’t escape—
God hears your prayers.
But He honors your obedience.
And the life you refuse to change will always be louder than the prayers you keep repeating.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Can You Truly Love More Than One Person at the Same Time?
paragraphs:
Can You Truly Love More Than One Person at the Same Time?
The Question That Exposes the Heart—and the Grace That Rewrites It
You didn’t expect it to feel this complicated.

At first, it was just a thought you tried to ignore. Then it became a quiet tension. Then a secret you couldn’t fully confess. You found yourself caring… deeply… for more than one person at the same time—and now your heart feels like a courtroom with no clear verdict.
You keep asking yourself, “Is this love… or am I just deceiving myself?”

And somewhere beneath the noise, there’s a heavier question pressing in—
“What does God say about this?”
Not what culture normalizes. Not what emotions justify. Not what loneliness whispers at night.
But truth.
The kind that doesn’t flatter you… but frees you.
Because Scripture doesn’t ignore complicated hearts—it confronts them.
In the ancient language of the Bible, love is not a single emotion. It is layered, weighty, and revealing.
In Greek, the New Testament speaks of ἀγάπη (agápē)—a sacrificial, self-giving love that reflects God Himself. Not driven by desire, but by devotion. Not ruled by feeling, but by truth.
There is also φιλία (philia)—brotherly affection, connection, warmth.
And ἔρως (eros)—romantic desire, longing, passion.
So yes… it is possible to feel multiple forms of affection toward more than one person. Your heart can pull in different directions. Your emotions can overlap.
But Scripture never asks, “What do you feel?”
It asks, “Who do you belong to?”
Because love, in its truest form, is not measured by how many people you can feel something for… but by how faithfully you reflect Christ in what you choose.
Jesus didn’t say, “Follow your heart.”
He said, “If anyone would come after Me, let him deny himself…” (Matthew 16:24)
That word “deny” carries weight. In Greek, it’s ἀπαρνησάσθω (aparnēsasthō)—to utterly disown, to refuse alignment with self-driven desires.
That means sometimes, what feels like “love” must be surrendered… because it competes with obedience.
And that’s where it gets uncomfortable.
Because if you’re honest, some of what you’re calling love… is actually attachment. Or loneliness. Or the fear of letting go.
You’re not just holding onto people.
You’re holding onto what they make you feel.
But Scripture cuts through illusion with piercing clarity.
In Hebrew, the word for love is אַהֲבָה (ahavah)—not just emotion, but covenantal commitment. A binding, intentional giving of oneself that mirrors God’s faithfulness.
That kind of love doesn’t divide itself to satisfy desire.
It anchors itself in truth.
James 1:8 says, “A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways.”
The phrase “double-minded” in Greek is δίψυχος (dipsychos)—literally “two-souled.”
Trying to live in two emotional allegiances at once.
Trying to give your heart in multiple directions without tearing something sacred.
And maybe that’s why you feel restless.
Not because you’re incapable of love…
But because your heart wasn’t created to be split between competing devotions.
Jesus didn’t die to make you emotionally satisfied.
He died to make you whole.
And wholeness requires alignment.
Not just of actions… but of affections.
There’s a reason Scripture consistently reflects covenant love as singular and faithful. Not because God is restrictive—but because He is protective.
Love that reflects Christ doesn’t multiply itself to avoid loss.
It chooses… and then it commits.
Ephesians 5:25 says, “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.”
Not “them.”
Her.
Singular. Focused. Sacrificial.
Because Christ’s love for His people is not divided.
It is complete.
And here’s the part many avoid…
If you’re trying to love more than one person in a way that creates confusion, secrecy, or compromise—then it’s not just about love anymore.
It’s about surrender.
About whether you’re willing to let God redefine what love actually looks like in your life.
Because real love doesn’t ask, “How much can I hold onto?”
It asks, “What must I release to remain faithful to God?”
And that’s where grace enters.
Because maybe as you read this, conviction is rising.
Not condemnation.
Conviction.
There’s a difference.
Condemnation says, “You’ve failed. Hide.”
Conviction says, “You’ve wandered. Come back.”
And Jesus is not standing at a distance waiting to shame you.
He’s calling you closer—into truth that heals.
Into clarity that restores.
Into a love that doesn’t leave you fragmented.
1 John 4:8 says, “ὁ Θεὸς ἀγάπη ἐστίν (ho Theos agapē estin)” — God is love.
Not confusion.
Not divided desire.
Not emotional chaos.
God is love.
Which means if what you’re experiencing is pulling you away from truth, from peace, from holiness—it’s not leading you closer to Him.
And anything that doesn’t lead you closer to Him… no matter how good it feels… will eventually leave you empty.
So what do you do?
You bring it into the light.
You stop justifying what God is gently exposing.
You choose obedience over emotional comfort.
And you trust that losing something outside of God’s will… is not loss.
It’s protection.
Because Jesus doesn’t just forgive your past.
He rewrites your direction.
And maybe that’s why this question found you.
Not to give you permission to stay divided…
But to call you into something deeper.
Something purer.
Something that actually satisfies.
So be honest…
Have you been calling something love… that God is asking you to release?
Sit with it.
Pray through it.
And be bold enough to respond.
Someone else reading your honesty might finally feel less alone.
It’s not just support… it’s partnership in spreading truth that reaches hearts still trapped in silence.
Because glorifying God isn’t just about what you believe…
It’s about what you support, what you share, and who you help reach.
And someone out there is one honest post away from encountering Jesus.
Don’t keep this to yourself.
The love you’re searching for will never be found in divided hearts—but in a surrendered one.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Didn’t Kill Desire… He Exposed It
paragraphs:
He Didn’t Kill Desire… He Exposed It
The words of Jesus that didn’t just confront sin—they uncovered the war inside your heart
There are sins people see… and then there are desires people hide.

And if you’re honest, it’s not always the visible sin that scares you the most. It’s the quiet pull inside you. The thoughts you don’t say out loud. The cravings that show up uninvited. The moments where you look composed on the outside but feel divided on the inside.
Jesus didn’t ignore that part of you.
He went straight for it.
Not the behavior first… the desire behind it.
And when He spoke about it, He didn’t soften the truth to make it easier to hear.
He made it impossible to ignore.

“Ἠκούσατε ὅτι ἐρρέθη· Οὐ μοιχεύσεις.
ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα
πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.”
(Matthew 5:27–28, Greek)
“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I tell you that anyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
He didn’t just address the act.
He addressed the gaze.
The intention.
The internal agreement with desire.
That word “ἐπιθυμῆσαι” (epithymēsai)… it’s not casual attraction. It means a deep craving, a consuming desire, a longing that pulls the will toward something.
Jesus was saying something radical:

Sin doesn’t begin when you act.
It begins when you entertain.
And suddenly, the conversation shifts.

Because now it’s not about “Did I do it?”
It’s about “Did I desire it?”
That hits deeper.
Uncomfortably deeper.
Because you can hide actions… but desire exposes you.
And that’s exactly where Jesus wanted to meet you.
Not at the surface where you perform righteousness.
But in the hidden place where you wrestle.
Because if desire is left untouched, behavior will eventually follow.
James would later echo this truth with unsettling clarity:

“ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται
ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας
ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος·
εἶτα ἡ ἐπιθυμία συλλαβοῦσα
τίκτει ἁμαρτίαν…”
(James 1:14–15, Greek)
“Each person is tempted when they are dragged away by their own desire and enticed. Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin…”
Desire is not harmless.
It’s formative.
It’s reproductive.
It grows into something.
And if it’s not surrendered, it will eventually become something you regret.
But here’s where most people misunderstand Jesus…
He wasn’t condemning you for feeling desire.
He was confronting what you do with it.
Because desire itself isn’t always evil.
God created desire.

The Hebrew word often used in Scripture, “תַּאֲוָה” (ta’avah), simply means longing or craving. In some contexts, it’s neutral—even good. “Delight yourself in the Lord, and He will give you the desires (מִשְׁאֲלוֹת) of your heart” (Psalm 37:4).
So the issue isn’t that you feel.
The issue is what your desire is aimed at… and what you allow it to become.
Jesus didn’t come to erase your humanity.
He came to redeem it.
To redirect desire from self-centered consumption to God-centered transformation.
That’s why He goes further, and it almost sounds extreme:
“If your right eye causes you to stumble, gouge it out…” (Matthew 5:29)
Not because He wanted mutilation…
But because He was revealing something urgent:
Whatever feeds your destructive desire… has to go.
Not halfway.
Not negotiated.
Removed.
Because your soul is worth more than your habits.
And this is where it becomes painfully personal.
Because deep down, you already know what feeds it.
You know what you scroll.
What you revisit.
What you entertain when no one is watching.
You know the conversations that blur lines.
The fantasies that replay.
The compromises you justify.
And Jesus is not speaking to shame you.
He’s speaking to free you.
Because desire unmanaged becomes chains.
But desire surrendered becomes transformation.
This is the part religion often misses.
It tells you to suppress desire.
Jesus tells you to bring it into the light.
To confess it.
To confront it.
To let Him reshape it.
Because He doesn’t just forgive sin.
He restores the heart that produced it.
And that’s the scandal of grace.
That He sees everything in you… and still moves toward you.
Not away.
The woman caught in adultery expected stones.
Instead, she met eyes full of truth and mercy.
“Neither do I condemn you… go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11)
That wasn’t permission.
That was transformation.
He acknowledged the sin.
But He also released her from its identity.
Because in Christ, your desire does not define you.
It can be healed.
It can be retrained.
It can be made new.

“καὶ δώσω ὑμῖν καρδίαν καινήν…”
(Ezekiel 36:26, Septuagint Greek)
“I will give you a new heart…”
Not a slightly improved one.
A new one.
Because the goal was never behavior modification.
It was heart resurrection.
And if you’ve been fighting desires that feel stronger than your will…
If you’ve been hiding things you’re ashamed to admit…
If you’ve been exhausted trying to look okay while feeling broken…
This is your moment to stop pretending.
And start surrendering.
Be honest.
This hit deeper than you expected.
Your honesty could be the permission someone else needs to come into the light.
Stay close.
Because truth isn’t something you visit once.
It’s something you live in daily.
And if you genuinely want to glorify God with your life—not just in words but in surrender—then support what is feeding your spirit.
You’re stepping into deeper discipleship, accountability, and spiritual growth.
You don’t have to fight this alone.
You were never meant to.
Because the battle for your desires… is really the battle for your heart.
And Jesus is still winning hearts.
From the darkest places.
From the most hidden struggles.
From the things no one else sees.
From scandal…
to grace.
Because He never just exposes…
He restores.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Wife He Never Wanted… But God Chose Anyway
paragraphs:
The Wife He Never Wanted… But God Chose Anyway
When love feels forced, when obedience feels like loss, when your story feels like a mistake… heaven might be writing something eternal.
He never prayed for her.
Not like that.

There were other dreams, cleaner dreams, simpler futures where love came easy and didn’t carry whispers behind closed doors. He had plans that didn’t involve explaining himself to neighbors, didn’t involve the quiet weight of shame pressing against his chest every time someone looked too long.
And then God spoke.
Not loudly. Not in a crowd. Not in a way that could be proven to anyone else.
Just enough to ruin his original life.
In the silence of that moment, everything changed.

“יוֹסֵף… יִרְאֶה אַל־תִּירָא לָקַחַת אֶת־מִרְיָם לְאִשָּׁה”
Yosef… yir’eh al-tira laqachat et-Miryam le’ishah
“Joseph… do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife.” (Matthew 1:20, Hebrew reconstruction)
Do not be afraid.
But fear was exactly what this felt like.
Because she carried something he didn’t understand. Something he didn’t ask for. Something that, by every human standard, looked like betrayal.
And yet heaven called it purpose.

We love the idea of God’s will until it costs us our comfort. We worship the idea of obedience until it threatens our reputation. We say we trust Him… until the story He writes doesn’t match the one we planned.
Joseph didn’t want this.
Let’s stop pretending he did.
The text doesn’t romanticize it. It reveals it.

“ἐβουλήθη λάθρᾳ ἀπολῦσαι αὐτήν”
eboulēthē lathra apolysai autēn
“He intended to divorce her quietly.” (Matthew 1:19, Greek)
Quietly.
Because even in his pain, he still loved her enough not to destroy her.
That’s where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because Joseph wasn’t a villain. He was a good man… trying to do the right thing… with incomplete understanding.
And sometimes, that’s exactly where God interrupts.
What if the life you’re trying to walk away from… is the very place God is asking you to stay?
What if the relationship you’re questioning… the responsibility you never wanted… the situation that feels unfair… is actually sacred?
Joseph could have walked away.
No lightning would have struck him.
No crowd would have stopped him.
But heaven had already chosen.
Not because Joseph was ready.
But because God is sovereign.

“כִּי מִן־רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ הָרָה”
ki min-ruach ha’qodesh harah
“For that which is conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.” (Matthew 1:20, Hebrew reconstruction)
From the Spirit.
Not from scandal.
Not from betrayal.
Not from sin.
But Joseph couldn’t see that yet.
And that’s the tension that will break you open if you let it…
God often calls you to commit… before He explains.
Sit with that.
Because some of you are carrying silent questions right now.
Some of you are living in a chapter you never would have chosen.
Some of you are loving people you don’t fully understand.
And deep down, there’s a whisper…
“This isn’t what I signed up for.”
Joseph felt that.
And still… he stayed.

“ἐποίησεν ὡς προσέταξεν αὐτῷ ὁ ἄγγελος Κυρίου”
epoiēsen hōs prosetaxen autō ho angelos Kyriou
“He did as the angel of the Lord commanded him.” (Matthew 1:24, Greek)
No argument recorded.
No delay mentioned.
Just obedience.
Not because it was easy.
But because it was God.
There is something holy about staying when leaving would be easier.
There is something powerful about choosing obedience over understanding.
There is something eternal about saying yes… when your emotions are screaming no.
Joseph took her as his wife.
The wife he never wanted.
The life he never planned.
The story that looked like scandal.
And in doing so… he stepped into the greatest redemption story humanity would ever witness.
Because inside that “inconvenience”…
Was Jesus.
Let that land.
The thing you’re resisting… might be carrying something sacred.
The season you’re questioning… might be protecting something eternal.
The person you don’t understand… might be part of God’s redemptive plan in your life.
We want clean stories.
God writes transformative ones.
We want clarity.
God asks for trust.
We want control.
God invites surrender.
And somewhere between your disappointment and your obedience…
Grace begins to rewrite everything.
Be honest.
How many times have you judged a situation too quickly?
How many times have you labeled something “wrong” because it felt uncomfortable?
How many times have you tried to walk away from something God was still working through?
This is where the Gospel confronts us.
Because Jesus Himself would grow up under the shadow of that decision.
People would talk.
Questions would linger.
But Joseph’s obedience protected the very Savior who would later carry the sins of the world.

“καλέσεις τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ Ἰησοῦν… αὐτὸς γὰρ σώσει τὸν λαὸν αὐτοῦ”
kalesēis to onoma autou Iēsoun… autos gar sōsei ton laon autou
“You shall call His name Jesus… for He will save His people.” (Matthew 1:21, Greek)
Saved.
Because one man chose obedience over pride.
Because one man trusted God over appearances.
Because one man stayed… when walking away would have been justified.
And now here you are.
Reading this.
Feeling something stir inside you that you can’t fully explain.
That tension… that discomfort… that quiet conviction…
That’s not random.
That’s God knocking.
Be honest.
This hit deeper than you expected.
And someone you know needs this too.
Because this is what we do here…
We don’t just inspire.
We disciple.
And if you feel called to go deeper, to truly grow, to stop surviving your faith and start living it…
Then step into deeper discipleship.
You don’t have to stay where you are spiritually.
You don’t have to keep guessing your way through your faith.
You can grow.
You can heal.
You can be transformed.
Because sometimes…
The life you didn’t want…
Is the very place God chose to reveal His glory.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Silence That Breaks You Before God Rebuilds You
paragraphs:
The Silence That Breaks You Before God Rebuilds You
Why Heaven Goes Quiet Right Before Everything Changes
It always starts the same way.
