Not with thunder. Not with a voice. Not with clarity.
But with silence so heavy it feels like God has stepped out of the room… and forgot to come back.

You pray, but the words fall flat. You open Scripture, but nothing moves you the way it used to. You worship, but it feels like you're singing into a ceiling instead of heaven. And somewhere deep inside, a quiet fear begins to whisper:
“Did God leave me?”
But what if that silence… isn’t abandonment?
What if it’s positioning?
Because Scripture doesn’t hide this pattern—it repeats it.

Right before Abraham saw the promise fulfilled, there were years of silence. Right before Joseph stepped into authority, there were nights in a prison where heaven said nothing. Right before David wore a crown, he hid in caves where even his closest allies couldn’t find him.
And right before Jesus changed everything… heaven went quiet for 400 years.
Four. Hundred. Years.
No prophets. No fresh word. No divine interruption.
Just silence.
But silence has never meant absence.
In Hebrew, the word often associated with stillness or silence is “דּוּמִיָּה” (dumiyyah)—a quietness that isn’t empty, but full… waiting… intentional. In Psalm 62:1, it says:

“My soul waits in silence for God only…”
אַךְ אֶל־אֱלֹהִים דּוּמִיָּה נַפְשִׁי (akh el-Elohim dumiyyah nafshi)
That word “dumiyyah” isn’t passive silence. It’s the kind of silence where something is happening beneath the surface… something you can’t see yet.
And that’s where most people quit.
Because we’ve been taught to associate God’s voice with His presence. So when the voice fades, we assume the presence has too.
But Scripture flips that assumption.
Think about Gethsemane.
Jesus is sweating blood. His soul is overwhelmed. He prays:
“Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me…”
And heaven?
Says nothing.
No angelic choir. No audible reassurance. No interruption.
Just silence.
And yet… that silence wasn’t rejection.
It was alignment.
Because what followed wasn’t abandonment—it was the cross… and then resurrection.
You don’t get resurrection without the silence of the grave.
In Greek, when Jesus cried from the cross, “My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” the word used is “ἐγκατέλιπες” (egkatelipes)—to abandon, to leave behind.
But here’s the mystery.
He felt abandoned… but He wasn’t.
Because three days later proved that silence never had the final word.
And maybe that’s where you are right now.
Not in rebellion. Not in sin. Not in failure.
Just… silence.
And it’s messing with your faith more than any storm ever could.
Because storms at least remind you God is doing something.
Silence makes you question if He’s doing anything at all.
But what if God goes quiet… not because He’s distant…
…but because He’s doing the deepest work?
There are things God will say to you in silence that words could never carry.
He strips away the noise.
The dependence.
The emotional crutches.
The constant need for confirmation.
Until all that’s left is raw, uncomfortable trust.
Not “God, I feel You.”
But “God, even if I don’t… I’m still not leaving.”
That’s where transformation happens.
That’s where shallow faith dies… and real faith is born.
Because anyone can follow God when He’s speaking.
But silence reveals who trusts Him when He doesn’t.
And here’s the part no one tells you:
Silence is often the space between who you were… and who you’re about to become.
God is not ignoring you.
He is transitioning you.
From dependence on feelings… to dependence on truth.
From needing signs… to standing on His Word.
From comfort… to calling.
And calling always costs something.
Ask Peter.
The same man who denied Jesus in fear… stood boldly in Acts after a season of confusion and waiting.
Ask Paul.
Years of hidden preparation before public impact.
Ask anyone God has ever used deeply…
There was always a season where heaven felt quiet.
Because God does His deepest construction underground.
Roots grow in silence.
Seeds break in darkness.
And both look like death before they become life.
So if God feels silent right now…
You’re not being forgotten.
You’re being formed.
And I need you to hear this carefully—
Don’t walk away in the silence and then blame God for missing the shift.
Because the shift doesn’t start when God speaks again.
It starts when you decide to stay… even when He doesn’t.
Be honest.
This hit deeper than you expected, didn’t it?
And if you know someone who’s been quietly struggling—send this to them. Don’t let them fight silence alone.
Save this too.
Because the next time God feels quiet… you’ll need to remember this moment.
And if this stirred something real in you—something deeper than emotion, something that feels like conviction—then stay close.
Because truth is… it will.
But next time, you’ll recognize it differently.
Not as abandonment.
But as preparation.

And if you truly want to glorify God—not just in words, but in action—then help this message reach more souls who are on the edge of giving up. Let it breathe where someone else might be silently breaking.
There are people on your timeline who are losing faith quietly.
This might be the interruption they’ve been praying for.
And if you want to go deeper—if you’re tired of surface-level faith and you’re ready for real discipleship, healing, and growth in Jesus Christ—then become part of what God is building here.
This isn’t about content.
This is about transformation.
Because silence isn’t the end of your story.
It’s where Jesus starts rewriting it.
And one day, you’ll look back at this quiet season and realize…
It wasn’t where God left you.
It was where He changed you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “They Said God Hates Divorce… But No One Told Me What He Does With the Broken After”
paragraphs:
“They Said God Hates Divorce… But No One Told Me What He Does With the Broken After”
When love shatters, vows echo, and grace rewrites what shame tried to finish
You didn’t plan for this.

No one stands at an altar, heart trembling, whispering “I do” while secretly preparing for the day they’ll whisper “I’m done.” You believed it would last. You believed the prayers, the promises, the late-night tears would be enough to hold it together.
And now here you are… holding pieces.
Some people are watching you, waiting to see if you’ll fall apart. Others are whispering Scripture at you like stones instead of lifelines.
“God hates divorce.”
You’ve heard it. Maybe it pierced deeper than anything your spouse ever said.
But no one sat you down and told you what God does with the ones who didn’t want the breaking… but are now living in it.
No one told you what happens after.
So let’s not rush this. Let’s walk slowly… honestly… biblically.
Because truth—real truth—doesn’t condemn the wounded. It heals them.

In the Hebrew Scriptures, Malachi 2:16 is often quoted with sharp edges:
כִּ֣י שָׂנֵ֤א שַׁלַּח֙ אָמַ֣ר יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֵ֔י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל
“Ki sane shalach, amar Adonai Elohei Yisrael…”
It’s often translated, “For I hate divorce, says the Lord.”

But the deeper context… the heartbeat behind the words… is God confronting treachery. Not broken people seeking mercy—but hardened hearts discarding covenant like it meant nothing. The word “shalach” implies a violent sending away, a betrayal wrapped in convenience.
God isn’t standing against the wounded.
He’s standing against the cruelty that wounds.
And suddenly… that changes everything.
Because maybe you didn’t walk away lightly.
Maybe you fought. Stayed. Prayed. Forgave… again and again until your soul felt like it was bleeding through your silence.
So the question isn’t just “Does God hate divorce?”
The real question is… does He see you?
Jesus answered this tension in Matthew 19, when religious voices tried to trap Him with legalism.

He said:
ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς δὲ οὐ γέγονεν οὕτως
“ap’ archēs de ou gegonen houtōs”
“From the beginning, it was not so.”
God’s design was never division. Never betrayal. Never abandonment.
But then Jesus said something that still shakes hearts:
“Whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality (πορνεία, porneia), and marries another, commits adultery.”
And people stop there… trembling.
But they miss something.
Jesus wasn’t building a cage.
He was exposing how seriously God takes covenant—and how deeply sin fractures it.
Porneia is not just a single mistake. It’s a pattern of sexual brokenness that violates the covenant itself. A tearing… not just a slipping.
And then Paul, writing in 1 Corinthians 7, adds another layer of mercy:
“If the unbelieving partner separates, let it be so. In such cases the brother or sister is not enslaved.”
Not enslaved.
Do you hear that?
God does not chain you to abandonment.
He does not bind you to destruction in the name of holiness.
He sees covenant… but He also sees when covenant has already been shattered.
This is where it gets painfully real.
Because some of you are asking the question you’re afraid to say out loud:
“Can I remarry… and still be right with God?”
And I won’t give you a shallow answer.
Because your life is not a theology debate. It’s a battlefield of memory, regret, hope, and fear.
The truth?
Scripture shows that remarriage after divorce can be permissible… but it is never casual. It flows through the lens of what broke the covenant.
Infidelity. Abandonment. A marriage already spiritually destroyed.
But here’s what many never say—and you need to hear this carefully:
God’s grace is not limited to perfect timelines.
Even where mistakes were made… even where decisions were rushed… even where you look back and say, “I didn’t fully understand then”…
Grace still speaks.
Because the Gospel was never built on your flawless history.
It was built on Christ’s finished work.
The same Jesus who met the Samaritan woman—five husbands deep, living with a man who wasn’t hers—did not open with condemnation.
He offered her living water.
He saw her story.
He didn’t deny her past… but He didn’t reduce her to it either.
That’s where many have been lied to.
You were told your story disqualified you.
But Jesus keeps rewriting stories that religion tries to end.
So can a Christian divorce?
Sometimes, yes… in the presence of real covenant-breaking.
Can a Christian remarry?
Sometimes, yes… with discernment, repentance where needed, and alignment with God—not human pressure.
But here’s the deeper truth most people avoid:
This is not just about permission.
It’s about transformation.
Because you can remarry… and still carry the same wounds, patterns, and unhealed places that broke the first.
Or…
You can surrender everything—your past, your pain, your decisions, your regrets—and let Jesus rebuild you from the inside out.
And that… is where grace becomes real.
Not as an excuse.
But as a resurrection.
So if you’re reading this with tears you didn’t expect…
If something in your chest feels exposed…
Be honest.
You are not alone in this.
There are thousands walking through the same quiet questions… the same silent guilt… the same longing to be right with God again.
And if this message brought clarity where confusion once lived… if it gave you peace where fear used to control you…
Then stay close.
And if you want to go deeper… not just emotionally, but biblically, spiritually, and personally…
Because this isn’t about content.
It’s about transformation.
And maybe… just maybe…
This wasn’t the end of your story.
Maybe this was the chapter where Jesus stepped in and said…
“I’m not done with you yet.”
And that truth should shake something loose inside you.
Because grace doesn’t erase your past…
It rewrites your future.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Laughed at Eight Words… Until an Entire City Fell to Its Knees
paragraphs: They Laughed at Eight Words… Until an Entire City Fell to Its Knees
How a Reluctant Prophet, a Dying Message, and a Holy God Turned Judgment into Mercy in a Way You Didn’t See Coming

You would think it would take eloquence.
You would expect a sermon layered with persuasion, emotion, strategy, and time.
But it didn’t.
It took eight words.
Eight.

Not a conference.
Not a worship set.
Not a carefully crafted message with transitions and storytelling arcs.
Just eight words… spoken by a man who didn’t even want to be there.
And yet an entire city collapsed into repentance.
The kind of repentance we beg for today but rarely see.
The kind that shakes heaven.
The kind that exposes everything.

And if you’re honest…
this might disturb you more than inspire you.
Because it forces a question most people don’t want to face:

What if it was never about how well we speak…
but how deeply God is still willing to move?
The text is simple, almost offensively so.
In Jonah 3:4, the Hebrew reads:

"וַיִּקְרָא וַיֹּאמַר עוֹד אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם וְנִינְוֵה נֶהְפָּכֶת"
(Vayyiqra vayomer, ‘od arba’im yom, v’Nineveh nehpachet.)
“Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.”
Eight words.

No invitation.
No worship music swelling in the background.
No altar call.
Just a declaration of judgment.
And what’s even more unsettling…
Jonah didn’t even want them to be saved.
He ran from God first.
He resisted the assignment.
He knew who Nineveh was.
Violent. Corrupt. Brutal.
The kind of people we quietly decide don’t deserve mercy.
If we’re being honest, some of us have our own “Nineveh.”

People we’ve already written off.
People we secretly hope God deals with instead of saves.
Jonah wasn’t confused.
He was angry.
Because he knew something about God that many of us forget.
He says it himself in Jonah 4:2:

“כִּי־יָדַעְתִּי כִּי אַתָּה אֵל־חַנּוּן וְרַחוּם אֶרֶךְ אַפַּיִם וְרַב־חֶסֶד”
(Ki yadati ki attah El channun v’rachum, erekh appayim v’rav chesed.)
“I knew that You are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abundant in lovingkindness…”
Jonah wasn’t afraid Nineveh would be destroyed.
He was afraid they wouldn’t be.
And that’s where this story starts to feel personal.

Because deep down…
we don’t just struggle with obedience.
We struggle with God’s mercy when it reaches people we didn’t think deserved it.
But here’s where everything shifts.
Jonah walks into Nineveh.
A massive city.
Scripture says it took three days to go through it.
And he doesn’t deliver a series.
He doesn’t build rapport.
He doesn’t soften the message.
He speaks eight words.
And something supernatural happens.
The people believe God.
Not Jonah.
God.
The Hebrew makes it clear:

"וַיַּאֲמִינוּ אַנְשֵׁי נִינְוֵה בֵּאלֹהִים"
(Vaya’aminu anshei Nineveh b’Elohim.)
“The men of Nineveh believed in God.”
Not because Jonah was convincing.
But because God was moving.

From the greatest to the least…
they fasted.
They wept.
Even the king stepped down from his throne, removed his robe, and sat in ashes.
Let that sink in.
A king humbled by eight words.

No one argued.
No one debated theology.
No one asked for proof.
They responded.
Immediately.
Urgently.
Desperately.

Because when God’s voice pierces the soul…
you don’t negotiate.
You surrender.
And maybe that’s what’s been missing.
Not better messaging.
Not better delivery.
But a heart that trembles again at God’s Word.
Because somewhere along the way, we learned how to hear without responding.
We listen… but we don’t change.
We nod… but we don’t repent.
We agree… but we don’t surrender.
Nineveh didn’t do that.
They moved.
They turned.
The Hebrew word used is “שׁוּב” (shuv) — to return, to turn back.
Not partial.
Not symbolic.
Total.
And God saw it.
Jonah 3:10 says:

“וַיַּרְא הָאֱלֹהִים אֶת־מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם כִּי־שָׁבוּ מִדַּרְכָּם הָרָעָה”
(Vayar ha’Elohim et ma’aseihem ki shavu midarkam hara’ah.)
“Then God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way…”
And God relented.
Judgment was coming.
But grace interrupted it.
This is where the story breaks you if you let it.
Because this wasn’t just about Nineveh.
This was always about us.
We are the city that deserved judgment.
We are the ones who ran, resisted, rebelled.
And yet God didn’t send eight words to us.
He sent His Son.
“Ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο” (Ho Logos sarx egeneto) — “The Word became flesh.” (John 1:14)
Jesus didn’t just warn.
He took the judgment.
He absorbed the wrath.
He became what we deserved… so we could receive what we never earned.
Grace.
Real grace.
The kind Jonah struggled to accept.
The kind that still offends pride.
Because it means salvation isn’t about deserving.
It’s about surrendering.

If eight words could shake a city…
what is God already saying to you right now?
And why haven’t you responded?
Be honest.
Not for me.
For your soul.
Or just write what you’ve been too afraid to say out loud.
There are others reading this who need to know they’re not alone.
Don’t stay silent.
Because silence is where conviction dies.
And this message isn’t something you just read.
It’s something you carry.
Yes, that one.
Saving this might matter more than you think.
Because you’ll need this reminder again when your heart tries to harden.
And if you want to go deeper… not just feel something for a moment but actually grow, heal, and be discipled in truth…
Stay close to messages that don’t entertain your comfort but challenge your soul.
And if you truly want to glorify God with your life, support what spreads His truth.
It’s alignment.
It’s saying, “I want more of what brings me closer to Christ.”
If that’s you…
Don’t delay.
Because here’s the truth that lingers long after you stop reading this…
God is still speaking… but not everyone is still listening.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Sleeping Beside a Stranger Who Calls You by Another Name
paragraphs:
Sleeping Beside a Stranger Who Calls You by Another Name
When Love Feels Like Rejection but God Is Whispering Redemption

There is a silence that screams louder than words. It lives in the space between two bodies lying side by side… where warmth exists, but connection has already died. You feel it when they touch you, but it doesn’t feel like they’re touching you. It feels like they’re reaching for someone else through you.
You don’t say it out loud, but your soul already knows the truth: you are being loved as a substitute.
And somehow, that hurts deeper than being alone.
Because rejection in absence is one thing… but rejection in proximity? That breaks something sacred.
You start asking questions you’re too afraid to finish.

“Why am I not enough?”
“Who are they thinking about when they look at me?”
“Why does it feel like I’m competing with a ghost?”
And slowly, quietly, your identity begins to erode.
Scripture doesn’t ignore this kind of pain. It walks straight into it.
In Genesis 29, Leah is given to Jacob, but not chosen. Not desired. Not loved the way she longs to be loved. And the Bible doesn’t hide it. It says plainly:

“וַיַּרְא יְהוָה כִּי שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה”
(Vayar YHWH ki senu’ah Leah)
“The LORD saw that Leah was hated…” (Genesis 29:31)
Not overlooked. Not misunderstood. Hated.
That word “שְׂנוּאָה” (senu’ah) carries the weight of rejection, of being unwanted, of being second when your heart was ready to be first.
Leah knew what it felt like to lie beside someone who wished she were someone else.
And yet… God saw her.
Not the version she tried to become to earn love. Not the performance. Not the striving.
He saw her.
And everything changed from that moment forward.
Because when man rejects you, God doesn’t step back… He steps closer.

Leah spent years trying to earn Jacob’s love through children, through proving her worth, through becoming what she thought he wanted. Every time she gave birth, she named her sons with hope that “now my husband will love me.”
But it never worked.
Because you cannot compete with an idol someone refuses to let go of.
And some of you are living there right now.
Giving more. Trying harder. Changing yourself. Silencing your needs. Lowering your standards.
All just to be chosen by someone who already made their decision.
And it’s exhausting.
Be honest… this hit harder than you expected.
But here’s where the story shifts.
There comes a moment when Leah stops chasing Jacob’s love… and turns her eyes toward God.
When she gives birth to Judah, she says:

“הַפַּעַם אוֹדֶה אֶת־יְהוָה”
(Ha-pa’am odeh et-YHWH)
“This time I will praise the LORD.” (Genesis 29:35)

Not “this time he will love me.”
Not “this time I will be enough.”
“This time… I will praise the LORD.”
Something broke. Something healed. Something awakened.
And from that moment, Leah stopped living for someone else’s approval… and started living in God’s presence.
Do you understand what that means?
The woman who felt unwanted became the vessel through which the lineage of Jesus Christ would come.
Judah… the son she bore in surrender… became the tribe of the Messiah.
Jesus came through the womb of the woman who was never chosen.
Let that sit with you.
God didn’t rewrite her story by changing Jacob’s feelings.
He rewrote her story by changing her identity.
And that’s what He’s trying to do with you.
Because some of you are sleeping in places where your spirit is suffocating.
You’re staying in relationships where your worth is being negotiated.
You’re giving your body where your soul is not being honored.
And deep down… you know.
Scripture doesn’t stay silent about this either.
In 1 Corinthians 6:18, the Greek says:

“φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν”
(Pheúgete tēn porneían)
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not manage it. Not justify it. Not tolerate it.
Flee.
Because your body is not just flesh. It is sacred.

“ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς τοῦ Ἁγίου Πνεύματός ἐστιν;”
“Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit?” (1 Corinthians 6:19)
You were never created to be someone’s replacement.
You were never designed to carry the weight of someone else’s unresolved desires.
You were never meant to be touched without being treasured.
And yet… here you are.
Still hoping they’ll change.
Still believing one more chance will fix everything.
Still lying beside someone who wishes you were someone else.
But what if God is not trying to fix them?
What if He’s trying to free you?
Because healing begins when honesty finally speaks.
Jesus doesn’t enter your life to help you survive broken love.
He enters your life to redefine love completely.

“ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς σεαυτόν”
“Love your neighbor as yourself.” (Mark 12:31)
But how can you love rightly… when you’ve accepted being loved wrongly?
Christ doesn’t call you to endure emotional starvation.
He calls you into fullness.
Into truth.
Into freedom.
Into a love that does not compare you, replace you, or reduce you.
And yes… walking away might feel like losing everything.
But staying where your soul is slowly dying is not love.
It’s bondage.
And Jesus came to break chains, not decorate them.
Not out of shame… but out of surrender.
Because grace is not permission to stay broken.
Grace is the power to be made new.
If you truly want to glorify God, don’t just receive truth… support the mission that spreads it.
Because this is bigger than content.
This is about souls.
This is about freedom.
This is about Jesus rewriting stories people thought were finished.
You were never meant to be someone’s second choice… when Heaven already called you chosen.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Laughed Until the Sky Broke: The Untold Weight of Why Noah Built Before It Ever Rained
paragraphs: They Laughed Until the Sky Broke: The Untold Weight of Why Noah Built Before It Ever Rained
Before a single drop fell… before thunder ever introduced itself to human fear… before the sky had ever betrayed the illusion of stability… there was a man building something no one understood.
Noah.
Not a preacher on a stage. Not a king. Not a warrior. Just a man who heard something from God that sounded impossible… and chose obedience over explanation.

Genesis 6:13 records the moment everything shifted: “And God said unto Noah…” — in Hebrew, “וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים לְנֹחַ” (Vayomer Elohim l’Noach). It wasn’t a suggestion. It wasn’t a motivational speech. It was a divine interruption into normal life.
Because everything looked normal.
People were still laughing. Still building. Still marrying. Still chasing pleasure. Still ignoring the quiet decay of their own souls.

Genesis 6:5 says, “every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.” The Hebrew word for imagination here is “יֵצֶר” (yetzer), meaning the shaping, the forming, the internal architecture of desire. Humanity didn’t just sin occasionally… they were designing sin into their identity.
And in the middle of that corruption… God chose one man to build something that made no sense in a world that had never seen rain.

Hebrews 11:7 gives us the deeper lens: “By faith Noah, being warned of God of things not seen as yet…” — in Greek, “χρηματισθεὶς περὶ τῶν μηδέπω βλεπομένων” (chrēmatistheis peri tōn mēdepō blepomenōn). Things not yet visible. Not yet experienced. Not yet proven.
Noah was asked to act on a reality that didn’t exist yet.
Let that sit in your chest for a moment.
He was building for a future no one believed in.
Imagine the sound of wood being cut day after day… year after year… while people walked by shaking their heads.
“Where’s the water, Noah?”
“Why are you wasting your life?”
“Who told you this?”
They didn’t realize… obedience often looks like insanity to people who only believe what they can see.

God gave exact instructions in Genesis 6:14 — “Make thee an ark of gopher wood…” The Hebrew says “עֲשֵׂה לְךָ תֵּבַת” (aseh lecha tevat) — build for yourself a vessel. This wasn’t just about survival. It was about alignment. Noah wasn’t just constructing a boat… he was constructing trust.
Every measurement. Every nail. Every silent moment of doubt he had to crush beneath obedience.
Because building the ark wasn’t about rain.
It was about faith that moves before evidence appears.
And maybe that’s where this hits deeper than expected.
Because some of you have been feeling God whisper something that doesn’t make sense yet.
To walk away from something.
To start something.
To forgive someone.
To surrender something you’ve been hiding.
And it feels like building an ark under a clear sky.
No confirmation. No applause. No visible reason.
Just obedience… and the weight of being misunderstood.
But Noah didn’t need the crowd to agree. He only needed God to speak.
2 Peter 2:5 calls him a “preacher of righteousness” — not because he stood on platforms… but because his life itself was the message. Every swing of the hammer was a sermon.
And then… one day… the sky changed.

Genesis 7:11 says, “all the fountains of the great deep were broken up, and the windows of heaven were opened.” The Hebrew phrase “נִבְקְעוּ כָּל־מַעְיְנֹת תְּהוֹם רַבָּה” (nivke’u kol ma’yanot tehom rabbah) paints a violent bursting — not just rain from above, but chaos from beneath.
Judgment didn’t trickle in… it erupted.
And suddenly… the thing they mocked… became the only thing that could save them.
The ark wasn’t ridiculous anymore.
It was mercy in physical form.
And here’s where it becomes impossible to ignore the deeper truth.
The ark was never just about Noah.
It was a shadow.
A foreshadowing.
A living prophecy pointing to Jesus Christ.
Because just like the ark… Jesus is the only refuge when judgment comes.

Acts 4:12 says, “Neither is there salvation in any other…” In Greek, “οὐκ ἔστιν ἐν ἄλλῳ οὐδενὶ ἡ σωτηρία” (ouk estin en allō oudeni hē sōtēria). There is no other escape. No alternative vessel. No backup plan.
The ark had one door.
Jesus said in John 10:9, “I am the door…”
One entrance. One way. One salvation.
And just like in Noah’s time… people are still laughing under clear skies.
Still delaying repentance.
Still calling obedience “extreme.”
Still waiting for visible proof before they move.
But the rain always comes.
Not because God desires destruction… but because He is just.
Yet even in judgment… He provided a way.
That’s grace.
That’s the scandal.
That God would warn a broken world… and still make room for them to be saved.
And maybe the real question isn’t why Noah built before it rained.
Maybe the real question is… why are we still waiting when the warning has already been given?
Be honest.
This hit something deeper, didn’t it?
You’re not alone in this.
But you also don’t have forever.

And if you’ve been searching for truth that doesn’t water down the Gospel… follow closely. Not because of me… but because staying close to truth might be the very thing that keeps you anchored when everything else starts to collapse.
And if your heart is serious about going deeper… about understanding Scripture, healing, discipleship, and real transformation in Christ… you can step further into that journey here:
This isn’t about religion.
This is about rescue.
Because one day… what you built your life on will be tested.
And only what was built in obedience to God will stand.
So build now.
Even if no one understands yet.
Because the rain doesn’t ask for your permission before it falls.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Pattern You Didn’t Notice… Until It Was You
paragraphs: The Pattern You Didn’t Notice… Until It Was You
Why do people keep walking away from God… even after everything He has done for them?
It never starts loud.
It never starts with rebellion.
It starts quietly… almost unnoticeably… like a slow fading light you don’t realize is dimming until the room is already dark.
The Scriptures never hid this pattern.
In fact, they recorded it with painful honesty.
From the very beginning, humanity has lived inside a repeating cycle—one that feels uncomfortably familiar if you’re willing to be honest with yourself.
In Judges 2:12, it says, “They forsook the LORD… and followed other gods.”
The Hebrew word used for “forsook” is עָזַב (ʿazav)—it doesn’t mean sudden abandonment. It means to loosen your grip… to gradually let go.
That’s how it happens.
Not in one decision… but in a series of small compromises that feel harmless in the moment.
You stop praying like you used to.
You stop reading the Word with hunger.
You stop feeling convicted… and start feeling comfortable.
And then one day, without announcing it, your heart has drifted.
The pattern repeats again in Hosea 4:6, “My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge.”
The word “knowledge” here is דַּעַת (daʿat)—not information, but intimate knowing… relational closeness.
People don’t walk away from God because they suddenly hate Him.
They walk away because they slowly stop knowing Him.
And that’s where it gets dangerous.
Because distance makes deception feel like truth.
What once felt wrong… now feels normal.
What once convicted you… now entertains you.
What once brought you to your knees… now barely crosses your mind.
And yet, God keeps speaking.
Even when ignored.
Even when forgotten.
Even when replaced.
In Jeremiah 2:13, God says something that should shake you to your core:
“My people have committed two evils: they have forsaken Me, the fountain of living waters, and hewed out cisterns for themselves… broken cisterns that can hold no water.”
The Hebrew phrase “fountain of living waters” is מְקוֹר מַיִם חַיִּים (meqor mayim chayyim)—a source that never runs dry.
And yet people leave it.
For what?
Temporary satisfaction.
Empty distractions.
False fulfillment.
Broken systems that were never meant to sustain the soul.
Be honest…
How many times have you tried to drink from something that left you emptier than before?
How many times have you convinced yourself that you were “fine”… while your spirit was quietly starving?
This is the pattern.
And it didn’t stop in the Old Testament.
In the New Testament, the same warning echoes.
In Revelation 2:4, Jesus says, “You have abandoned the love you had at first.”
The Greek word for “abandoned” is ἀφῆκας (aphēkas)—again, not an explosion… but a release.
You didn’t wake up one day deciding to leave Jesus.
You just stopped holding on.
And that’s what makes this so dangerous.
Because it feels normal.
It feels gradual.
It feels justifiable.
Until one day… you look up and realize you’re not where you used to be.
But here’s where everything shifts.
Because the story doesn’t end with people walking away.
It never has.
The Gospel is not about people holding onto God perfectly.
It’s about God refusing to let go of people completely.
Romans 5:8 says, “But God demonstrates His love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
The Greek word for “demonstrates” is συνίστησιν (synistēsin)—to prove, to establish beyond doubt.
God didn’t wait for you to come back.
He moved toward you… even when you were drifting away.
Even when you were distracted.
Even when you were numb.
Even when you were pretending everything was okay.
This is where the pattern breaks.
Not because people suddenly become faithful…
But because Jesus is.
In Luke 15, the story of the prodigal son reveals something most people miss.
When the son returns, the father runs.
In the culture of that time, men of honor did not run.
But the father did.
Because love breaks protocol.
Because grace doesn’t wait for perfection.
Because God would rather restore you than prove a point.
The Aramaic tone behind this moment carries something deeper than words—it’s urgency, compassion, restoration.
Not hesitation.
Not condemnation.
Not delay.
So if you’re reading this and something inside you feels exposed…
That’s not guilt trying to crush you.
That’s truth trying to wake you up.
Because the same pattern that leads people away from God…
Can be reversed in a single moment of surrender.
You don’t need to clean yourself up first.
You don’t need to fix everything overnight.
You don’t need to pretend anymore.
You just need to come back.
Really come back.
Not halfway.
Not casually.
Not temporarily.
But honestly.
Because God isn’t looking for performance.
He’s looking for your heart.
and start returning.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
And if someone came to your mind while reading this… someone who’s slowly drifting, quietly struggling, silently walking away…
Don’t ignore that.
It might be the interruption their soul needs before it’s too late.
Save this too… because there will be moments when you feel yourself slipping again, and you’ll need to remember what God showed you here.
Because this isn’t just content.
This is discipleship.
This is accountability.
This is spiritual survival in a world designed to pull you away from God.
Because glorifying God isn’t just about believing…
It’s about committing to grow.
And sometimes, support isn’t just financial…
It’s obedience.
It’s choosing to stand with truth.
It’s choosing to help others find their way back too.
Don’t just read this and move on.
Respond.
Return.
Rebuild.
Because the pattern only continues… if you let it.
And tonight, something shifted.
You felt it.
You know it.
And you can’t unhear it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “The Lie We’ve Been Quoting: ‘Cleanliness Is Next to Godliness’… But God Never Said That”
paragraphs:
“The Lie We’ve Been Quoting: ‘Cleanliness Is Next to Godliness’… But God Never Said That”
The hidden truth about dirt, shame, and the kind of purity Jesus actually died for
You’ve probably said it before without even thinking.
“Cleanliness is next to godliness.”

Maybe your parents said it when your room was a mess. Maybe a teacher, a pastor, or even your own voice echoed it while you were trying to fix yourself… clean yourself… make yourself presentable enough for God.
But here’s the uncomfortable truth that hits harder the deeper you sit with it…
God never said that.
Not once.
Not in Hebrew. Not in Greek. Not in Aramaic.
Search the Torah. Search the Prophets. Search the Gospels. Search the letters of Paul. You will not find that phrase anywhere in Scripture.
And yet somehow… we built a whole version of Christianity around it.
A version where you have to clean yourself up before you come close to God.
A version where your mess disqualifies you.
A version where your dirt makes God step back.
But if that were true… Jesus would have never touched lepers.
He would have never sat with sinners.
He would have never let a broken, bleeding woman reach for His garment.
He would have never allowed Himself to be crucified between criminals.
So where did we get this idea?
Because when you go back to the original text… it tells a completely different story.
In Mark 2:17, Jesus says something that destroys that false belief at its root:
“οὐ χρείαν ἔχουσιν οἱ ἰσχύοντες ἰατροῦ ἀλλ’ οἱ κακῶς ἔχοντες… οὐκ ἦλθον καλέσαι δικαίους ἀλλὰ ἁμαρτωλούς.”
Translation:
“It is not the healthy who need a physician, but the sick… I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”
Read that again slowly.
Jesus didn’t come for the clean.
He came for the contaminated.
He didn’t come for the polished.
He came for the broken, the stained, the ones hiding things they don’t want anyone to see.
That means… if you’ve been waiting to “get your life together” before coming to God…
You’ve been waiting for something God never required.
Because Scripture doesn’t say cleanliness leads to godliness.
It says something far more dangerous… and far more freeing.
In Romans 5:8, written in Greek:
“συνίστησιν δὲ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀγάπην εἰς ἡμᾶς ὁ Θεός… ὅτι ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν Χριστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀπέθανεν.”
“But God demonstrates His own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.”
Not after you fixed yourself.
Not after you cleaned your habits.
Not after you hid your secrets better.
While you were still in it.
Still messy.
Still struggling.
Still failing in ways you don’t even talk about.
That’s when He chose you.
That’s when He died.
That’s when grace stepped into your scandal.
And maybe that’s the part we don’t like.
Because if we’re honest… we’d rather believe we earned it.
We’d rather believe we became worthy.
We’d rather believe our effort made God proud.
But the Gospel doesn’t flatter your effort.
It exposes your need.
In Hebrew, the word often translated as “clean” is “טָהוֹר” (tahor)… and yes, the Old Testament speaks about ritual cleanliness. But even those laws were never about moral perfection.
They were shadows.
Pointing forward.
Pointing to the One who would make people clean… not by their effort… but by His sacrifice.
That’s why in Isaiah 1:18, God says:
“Come now, let us reason together… though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow.”
Scarlet doesn’t fade easily.
It stains deep.
It marks you.
It lingers.
And yet God doesn’t say, “Wash yourself first, then come.”
He says, “Come… and I will make you clean.”
Do you see the difference?
Religion says: clean yourself, then approach.
Jesus says: approach… and I will clean you.
That’s why in Aramaic, when Jesus healed, there was authority in His words.
“ܐܬܕܟܐ” (ethdaka) — “Be cleansed.”
Not “clean yourself.”
Be cleansed.
Passive.
Received.
Given.
Not earned.
And that changes everything.
Because some of you reading this… you’ve been exhausted trying to fix yourself.
You’ve been scrubbing your life, hiding your past, managing your image… trying to look “holy” enough to belong.
But deep down, you know…
You’re tired.
Tired of pretending.
Tired of carrying things you haven’t surrendered.
Tired of being “clean” on the outside while something inside still feels broken.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because this is where everything shifts.
God is not waiting for a polished version of you.
He’s calling the real version of you.
The one you hide.
The one you edit out.
The one you think disqualifies you.
That’s the one Jesus died for.
And if you’re still here reading this… that’s not an accident.
That’s invitation.
Not to clean yourself.
But to come as you are… and let Him do what you can’t.
And listen… this is bigger than you.
Because someone you know right now believes the same lie you used to believe.
Someone is still hiding.
Still thinking they’re too far gone.
Still thinking they need to fix themselves first.
Not for attention… but because someone’s silence might break when they read this.
Stay close to truth.
And if you’re serious about going deeper… not just emotionally moved but spiritually changed…
There’s more waiting for you.
Because supporting truth isn’t about money.
It’s about mission.
If this message reached you… imagine who else it could reach through you.
If you want to glorify God, don’t just agree with truth… advance it.
Because at the end of all this…
It was never about how clean you looked.
It was about who made you clean.
And He’s still not done with you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE HABIT THAT INVITED WISDOM
paragraphs:
THE HABIT THAT INVITED WISDOM
The Quiet Discipline That Changed Everything… and Might Be Missing in You
There are moments in life where everything looks fine on the outside… but inside, something is quietly collapsing.
You’re still smiling. Still posting. Still showing up.
But your decisions have been off. Your peace feels distant. Your discernment is blurred. And deep down, you know… something sacred has been neglected.
Not something loud.
Not something obvious.
Something quiet.
A habit.
A habit that, when ignored, doesn’t scream at you—it slowly starves you.
And when it’s restored… everything begins to realign.
Scripture doesn’t introduce wisdom as something you chase with intelligence, status, or experience.
It introduces wisdom as something that visits… something that comes near… something that responds.
But only when it is invited.
Not casually.
Not occasionally.
But habitually.
In the Hebrew Scriptures, wisdom is not abstract. It is alive, almost personified.
In Proverbs 8:34, the original Hebrew says:
“אַשְׁרֵי אָדָם שֹׁמֵעַ לִי, לִשְׁקֹד עַל-דַּלְתוֹתַי יוֹם יוֹם, לִשְׁמֹר מְזוּזוֹת פְּתָחָי”
Ashrei adam shomea li, lishqod al-daltotai yom yom, lishmor mezuzot petachai.
“Blessed is the one who listens to me, watching daily at my doors, waiting at my doorway.”
Did you catch it?
Watching.
Daily.
Waiting.
Not rushing. Not visiting occasionally. Not checking in when life gets hard.
But building a rhythm of presence.
A habit of positioning.
Wisdom doesn’t shout over chaos.
It meets consistency.
There is something deeply uncomfortable about this truth… because it exposes why many of us feel lost even while being spiritually “active.”
We pray when we panic.
We read when we feel guilty.
We seek when we’re desperate.
But wisdom is not built on emotional spikes.
It’s built on daily surrender.
And that’s the habit most people quietly abandon.
In the Greek New Testament, James 1:5 says:
“Εἴ δέ τις ὑμῶν λείπεται σοφίας, αἰτείτω παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ…”
Ei de tis hymōn leipetai sophias, aiteitō para tou Theou…
“If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask of God…”
But the word “ask” here—aiteitō—is not a one-time request.
It carries the sense of ongoing, continuous asking.
A posture. A pattern. A habit.
Because wisdom is not information.
Wisdom is alignment with God.
And alignment doesn’t happen randomly.
It happens relationally.
Daily.
There was a time when you felt closer to God.
You heard Him clearer.
You discerned faster.
You resisted better.
But then life got louder.
Schedules filled up.
Distractions multiplied.
And the habit quietly faded.
Not overnight.
But slowly.
Almost unnoticeably.
Until one day, you realized… you’re still believing in God, but you’re no longer walking with Him.
That gap?
That distance?
It didn’t come from rebellion.
It came from neglect.
And neglect is dangerous because it feels harmless.
But Scripture never treats it lightly.
In Luke 5:16, speaking of Jesus Himself, the Greek reveals something powerful:
“αὐτὸς δὲ ἦν ὑποχωρῶν ἐν ταῖς ἐρήμοις καὶ προσευχόμενος”
autos de ēn hypochōrōn en tais erēmois kai proseuchomenos
“But He would withdraw to desolate places and pray.”
Not once.
Not occasionally.
“But He would withdraw…”
Repeated action.
Habit.
Even Jesus—perfect, sinless, divine—guarded a rhythm of withdrawal to be with the Father.
So what makes us think we can function without it?
This is where everything shifts.
Because the habit that invites wisdom is not just reading Scripture.
It’s not just praying.
It’s choosing daily nearness over occasional desperation.
It’s showing up at the “doorway” even when you don’t feel anything.
It’s waiting… even when nothing seems to happen.
Because something is happening.
You’re being aligned.
You’re being shaped.
You’re being guarded in ways you don’t even realize yet.
And one day, you’ll face a decision… and respond with clarity you didn’t know you had.
That’s wisdom.
Not sudden.
But cultivated.
But here’s the part most people don’t want to hear.
You can’t expect God’s voice to guide you… if His presence is not a place you regularly return to.
That’s not condemnation.
That’s reality.
And maybe this is hitting deeper than expected.
Because you know.
You remember when the habit was alive.
When mornings felt sacred.
When Scripture wasn’t a task—it was a lifeline.
When prayer wasn’t rushed—it was real.
And now?
You’ve been surviving on fragments.
Quick verses.
Half-focused prayers.
Spiritual leftovers.
And your soul feels it.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because here’s the truth that changes everything.
God is not waiting to punish your inconsistency.
He’s waiting to restore your intimacy.
The Gospel is not about how disciplined you’ve been.
It’s about how faithful Jesus remains.
Even when you stopped showing up…
He didn’t stop loving you.
Romans 5:8 reminds us in the Greek:
“συνίστησιν δὲ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀγάπην… ὅτι ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν…”
synistēsin de tēn heautou agapēn… hoti eti hamartōlōn ontōn hēmōn
“But God demonstrates His own love… while we were still sinners…”
Not after you fixed your habits.
Not after you became consistent again.
While you were still drifting.
Still distracted.
Still inconsistent.
That’s grace.
But grace is not permission to stay distant.
It’s an invitation to come back.
And rebuild the habit that changes everything.
Not perfectly.
But faithfully.
Day by day.
Moment by moment.
Because wisdom is waiting at the doorway.
The question is… will you return?
If this spoke to you, don’t keep it to yourself.
If you truly want to glorify God, support what feeds your spirit.
Because this isn’t about content.
It’s about transformation.
And someone you love might need this more than you think.
Respond.
Return.
Rebuild.
Because the habit you’ve been neglecting… might be the doorway God has been waiting at all along.
And here’s what will stay with you long after this moment fades:
You didn’t lose wisdom… you just stopped meeting it daily.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE TRUTH ABOUT HIDDEN OBEDIENCE
paragraphs:
THE TRUTH ABOUT HIDDEN OBEDIENCE
The quiet place where no one sees… but Heaven records everything
There is a kind of obedience no one claps for.

No spotlight.
No recognition.
No reposts.
No applause echoing your name.

Just you…
and God…
and the moment you decide whether you will still obey when it costs you everything.
Most people don’t talk about that place.

Because that place is where reputations don’t matter… but souls do.
Where influence disappears… but integrity is tested.
Where the crowd is gone… and all that’s left is truth.

And if we’re being honest…
this is where many quietly fall apart.

Not in public sin.
Not in visible rebellion.
But in hidden compromise.

The message you almost sent.
The lie you almost justified.
The habit you keep excusing.
The obedience you keep delaying.
And you tell yourself…

“It’s not that serious.”
“No one will know.”
“I’ll fix it later.”
But Heaven sees what the world ignores.
Scripture doesn’t hide this reality. It confronts it.
In Luke 16:10, Jesus says:
“Whoever is faithful in very little is faithful also in much…”
But the original Greek cuts deeper than the surface translation.
“ὁ πιστὸς ἐν ἐλαχίστῳ καὶ ἐν πολλῷ πιστός ἐστιν”
ho pistos en elachistō kai en pollō pistos estin
Faithful in the smallest… faithful in the great.

This isn’t about size.
It’s about consistency of the soul.
Hidden obedience is not preparation for something greater.
It is the test.

And some of you are asking God for open doors…
while quietly failing Him behind closed ones.
That’s the tension no one wants to admit.

We pray for elevation…
but resist surrender.

We ask for purpose…
but avoid obedience.

We want God to trust us publicly…
while we betray Him privately.

And yet…
this is where grace enters the story.
Because hidden obedience is not just about what you do right…
It’s about what you do when you realize you’ve been doing it wrong.
David understood this kind of exposure.

Not the kind that comes from people…
but the kind that comes from God.
In Psalm 51:6, he writes:
The Hebrew says:
“הֵן־אֱמֶת חָפַצְתָּ בַטֻּחוֹת”
hen emet chafatzta batuchot
Truth… in the hidden parts.

Not the polished version of you.
Not the curated image.
Not the version that gets likes.
The hidden you.
The one you think no one sees.
That’s the version God is after.
And here’s what breaks people…
God already sees it.

Every motive.
Every struggle.
Every compromise.
Every silent battle you thought was invisible.
Nothing is hidden from Him.
Hebrews 4:13 says:
“And no creature is hidden from His sight, but all are naked and exposed…”
Greek:
“πάντα δὲ γυμνὰ καὶ τετραχηλισμένα”
panta de gymna kai tetrachēlismena
Completely uncovered.
Completely seen.
And yet…
He still calls you.
That’s the scandal of grace.
Because if we’re honest, some of us aren’t struggling with sin…
We’re hiding from surrender.
We’re not confused about what God wants.
We just don’t want to let go of what He’s asking us to release.

That relationship.
That secret.
That pride.
That control.
And hidden obedience feels like loss… until you realize it’s actually rescue.
Jesus Himself lived this.

Not just on the cross…
but long before it.

There were years no one recorded.
Moments no one documented.
Obedience no crowd ever witnessed.
And yet, heaven was watching.
Philippians 2:8 says:
“He humbled Himself by becoming obedient to the point of death…”
Greek:
“ἐταπείνωσεν ἑαυτὸν γενόμενος ὑπήκοος μέχρι θανάτου”
etapeinōsen heauton genomenos hypēkoos mechri thanatou
Obedient… even when it led to suffering.
That’s the part we skip.

We celebrate resurrection…
but avoid obedience that leads to dying.

Dying to self.
Dying to ego.
Dying to secret sin.
But that’s where transformation happens.
Not in what people see…
But in what you surrender when no one is looking.
And this is where everything shifts.
Because hidden obedience is not about perfection.
It’s about direction.

It’s about choosing God again…
even after you failed Him yesterday.

It’s about turning back…
even when shame tells you to stay away.

It’s about whispering “yes” to God…
when every part of your flesh wants to say no.
And maybe that’s you right now.

Tired.
Convicted.
Exposed in a way you didn’t expect.

This didn’t just hit your mind…
it hit your soul.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because something powerful happens when you stop hiding and start confessing.

The enemy thrives in secrecy.
But healing begins in honesty.

Not tomorrow.
Not someday.
Right now.

Not to expose them…
but to remind them they’re not alone.
And if this spoke to you in a way you can’t explain…
You’re going to need this reminder again.
Because hidden obedience is not a one-time decision…
It’s a daily surrender.
And if you want to stay rooted in truth, conviction, healing, and real discipleship…
Follow closely.
Because this is more than content.
This is spiritual survival.
And for those who are ready to go deeper—truly deeper, not surface-level faith…
There’s a place for you.
It’s participation in spreading the Gospel.
It’s helping truth reach someone who’s about to give up.
It’s choosing to glorify God not just in words… but in action.
If your heart is stirring right now… don’t ignore it.
Because He’s not.

Not in your hidden places.
Not in your struggle.
Not in your story.
The places you thought disqualified you…
Are the very places Jesus is rewriting.
And one day, what was hidden obedience…
Will become visible testimony.
The quiet “yes” no one heard…
Will echo in eternity.
Because God never wastes obedience… even when no one else sees it.
The secret battles you win today… are shaping the soul you’ll stand with tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Thought You Had to Control It… But What If You’ve Been Fighting the Wrong Battle?
paragraphs:
You Thought You Had to Control It… But What If You’ve Been Fighting the Wrong Battle?
Can You Control Sexual Thoughts… or Are You Meant to Surrender Them?

It didn’t start with action.
It started with a thought you didn’t invite.

A flash.
A memory.
A curiosity that lingered just a little too long.
And before you even realized it, your mind had already traveled somewhere your spirit didn’t want to go.

You sat there after, quiet… maybe even ashamed. Wondering why it keeps happening. Wondering if something is wrong with you. Wondering if God is tired of watching you fight the same invisible battle over and over again.
Because no one really talks about this part.
Not the part where you didn’t do anything… but your mind did.
Not the part where your body feels one thing, but your spirit is crying out for something completely different.
So the question lingers, heavy and uncomfortable:

Can you actually control sexual thoughts…
or are you just meant to manage them?

Because if you’re honest… it doesn’t feel like control.
It feels like war.
And Scripture never pretended this battle was easy.
In fact, the Bible goes deeper than behavior. It goes straight to the battlefield you’re actually standing in—your mind.

“πᾶς δὲ ὁ πειραζόμενος ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος” (James 1:14)
“Each person is tempted when he is dragged away and enticed by his own desire.”

That word “ἐπιθυμία” (epithymia)… it doesn’t just mean desire.
It means a deep craving, a pull, something that reaches inside you and tries to take control from within.

This isn’t just about what you see.
It’s about what is already stirring inside you.
And that’s why controlling thoughts feels impossible sometimes—because temptation doesn’t begin outside. It begins within.
But here’s what most people misunderstand:
The thought itself is not the sin.
Jesus made that distinction painfully clear.

“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν” (Matthew 5:28)
“Whoever looks at a woman to lust after her…”
Notice that phrase: “πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι” — with the intent to dwell, to cultivate, to entertain the desire.

The first glance isn’t the fall.
The lingering… the feeding… the agreement—that’s where the line gets crossed.
And suddenly, this isn’t just about control anymore.
It’s about surrender.
Because the truth is… you were never designed to win this battle through willpower alone.
If control was enough, you wouldn’t still be fighting.
If discipline alone could purify the mind, Jesus wouldn’t have gone to the cross.

This is deeper than behavior modification.
This is transformation.

“καὶ μὴ συσχηματίζεσθε τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ, ἀλλὰ μεταμορφοῦσθε” (Romans 12:2)
“Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind.”
That word “μεταμορφοῦσθε” (metamorphousthe)… it’s where we get “metamorphosis.”

God is not asking you to manage sinful thoughts better.
He’s calling you into a complete renewal of the way your mind functions.
But let’s be real…
That process is messy.

There are days you feel strong.
And there are nights you feel like you’re losing ground again.

Moments where you avoid it…
And moments where it comes back stronger than you expected.
And this is where shame tries to step in and whisper:
“You’ll never be free.”
But shame is a liar that thrives in silence.
Because Scripture never says you won’t be tempted.
It says you won’t be abandoned in it.

“נִסָּיוֹן לֹא-בָא עֲלֵיכֶם כִּי אִם-כְּמוֹ שֶׁבְּנֵי אָדָם יְכוֹלִים לָשֵׂאת” (1 Corinthians 10:13, Hebrew rendering)
“No temptation has overtaken you except what is common to mankind… and God is faithful.”
Common.
That means you’re not alone in this fight.

Not broken beyond repair.
Not secretly disqualified.
Just human… in need of grace.
And that’s where everything changes.
Because the goal is not perfect control.
The goal is daily surrender.
It’s catching the thought before it becomes a dwelling place.
It’s redirecting your mind when it starts to wander.
It’s choosing, again and again, not what feels natural—but what leads to life.

“αἰχμαλωτίζοντες πᾶν νόημα εἰς τὴν ὑπακοὴν τοῦ Χριστοῦ” (2 Corinthians 10:5)
“Taking every thought captive to the obedience of Christ.”
Captive.

That means you don’t let the thought lead you.
You confront it.
You hand it over.
You refuse to build a home for it in your mind.
But that doesn’t mean the battle disappears overnight.
It means you stop fighting it alone.
Because the truth most people don’t tell you is this:

Freedom from sexual thoughts doesn’t come from controlling your mind harder…
it comes from loving Jesus deeper.

Because the more your heart is filled with Him…
the less space there is for everything else.
And slowly… quietly… something begins to change.
The thoughts don’t control you the same way anymore.

Not because you became stronger—
but because you became surrendered.
So be honest…
How long have you been trying to fight this battle by yourself?
How long have you been carrying shame for something God is actually inviting you to bring into the light?
Someone else needs to see your honesty… because they’re fighting the same battle in silence.
And if you’ve been searching for deeper truth, real discipleship, and daily reminders that actually strengthen your walk with Christ… stay close.
Because this isn’t just content… this is spiritual survival in a world that constantly pulls your mind away from God.
And if you truly want to glorify God with your life… support what feeds your spirit.
If you’re ready to stop walking in circles and start walking in transformation…
Because your mind is not meant to be a battlefield forever.
It’s meant to become a dwelling place for God.

And the moment you stop hiding…
is the moment healing actually begins.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Does Healing Take So Long for You?
paragraphs:
Why Does Healing Take So Long for You?
The silent war between your pain and God’s timing… and the grace you almost missed
You prayed for it to end.

You cried when no one was watching. You lifted your hands in worship while your heart was still breaking underneath. You told God you believed… but deep down, something in you whispered, “Why is this taking so long?”
And maybe you’ve been too afraid to say it out loud… but you’ve thought it.
“If God can heal instantly… why hasn’t He healed me yet?”
There’s a moment in Scripture that feels almost uncomfortable when you really slow down and sit inside it.
In Mark 8:23–25, Jesus heals a blind man—but not instantly.
The text says:

“Καὶ ἐπιλαβόμενος τῆς χειρὸς τοῦ τυφλοῦ… ἐπηρώτα αὐτόν, Εἴ τι βλέπεις;”
(“Taking the blind man by the hand… He asked him, ‘Do you see anything?’”)
The man responds:

“Βλέπω τοὺς ἀνθρώπους, ὅτι ὡς δένδρα ὁρῶ περιπατοῦντας.”
(“I see people, but they look like trees walking.”)
He wasn’t fully healed.
Not yet.
Jesus touches him again… and then his sight is restored.
Fully.
Clearly.
Completely.
But don’t rush past that moment.
Jesus—the same Jesus who spoke and storms obeyed… the same Jesus who said “Lazarus, come out” and a dead man walked out of a grave—chose to heal this man in stages.
Why?
Because sometimes your healing is not delayed… it’s being developed.
You want instant clarity, but God is working through process.
You want relief, but God is building something deeper than relief—He’s building transformation.
The Hebrew word often used for healing is “רָפָא” (rapha)—not just meaning to cure, but to restore, to make whole, to mend what has been broken over time.
God is not just interested in stopping your pain.
He’s interested in restoring your soul.
And restoration takes time.
You didn’t break overnight.
You won’t be rebuilt overnight.
But somewhere along the journey, the enemy starts whispering lies.
“If God loved you, this would be over by now.”
“If you had more faith, you’d already be healed.”
“If you were truly changed, you wouldn’t still struggle with this.”
But Scripture answers those lies with something deeper than emotion… it answers with truth.
In Psalm 147:3:
“He heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds.”
The Hebrew paints a picture that feels almost too tender to ignore.

“הָרֹפֵא לִשְׁבוּרֵי־לֵב” (ha-rofe lishvurei-lev)
He is the healer of shattered hearts.
Not rushed hearts.
Not surface wounds.
Shattered.
Fragmented.
The kind of broken that takes time to piece back together.
And then it says He “binds up” their wounds.
That’s not instant.
That’s careful.
Intentional.
Close.
Personal.
Healing that takes time doesn’t mean God is distant.
It means He is involved.
Closer than you think.
Working deeper than you can see.
And maybe this is the part you didn’t expect to hear…
Some of you don’t actually want healing.
You want relief.
Because healing will require you to let go of things you’ve grown comfortable holding onto.
Old identities.
Hidden sins.
Bitterness you’ve learned to justify.
The Greek word for repentance is “μετάνοια” (metanoia)—a complete change of mind, direction, and inner life.
Not behavior management.
Transformation.
And transformation is uncomfortable.
That’s why healing feels slow.
Because God isn’t just removing pain…
He’s removing what caused it.
And that process touches everything.
Your habits.
Your relationships.
Your thoughts.
Your identity.
Even the version of yourself you’ve been clinging to.
So when you ask, “Why is this taking so long?”…
He answers, “Because I love you too much to heal you halfway.”
You saw it in Mark.
Half-healing wasn’t the end of the story.
It was part of it.
And maybe that’s where you are right now.
Not blind anymore…
But not fully clear yet either.
You’re seeing… but it’s blurry.
You’re walking… but it still hurts.
You’re believing… but you’re tired.
Listen carefully…
God didn’t abandon the process.
And He hasn’t abandoned you.
Philippians 1:6 says:
“He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion…”
The Greek word “ἐπιτελέσει” (epitelesei) means to finish, to bring to full completion, to perfect over time.
Not rush.
Not skip.
Complete.
So no, your healing is not late.
It’s unfolding.
And yes… it hurts.
But even Jesus, in the middle of suffering, cried out:

“Ἐλωΐ, Ἐλωΐ, λιμὰ σαβαχθανί?”
(“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”)
He understands what it feels like to be in the middle of pain that doesn’t immediately end.
But here’s what changed everything…
The cross looked like delay.
The resurrection proved it was divine timing.
From scandal… to grace.
From suffering… to salvation.
From what looked like the end… to eternal life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Even your timeline.
Even your pain.
Even your story.
So if your healing is taking longer than you expected…
Maybe it’s because God is writing something deeper than you imagined.
Something real.
Something lasting.
Something that won’t just change your circumstances…
But transform your entire life.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Your honesty might be the permission someone else needs to finally open up too.
And if you want to glorify God not just with words but with action… support what spreads His truth.
Follow closely if you’re done with shallow faith and ready for real transformation.
You can join here:
Because healing doesn’t just happen in moments.
It happens in what you choose daily.
Stay close.
Stay surrendered.
Stay hungry for truth.
Because the same God who started your healing…
Has already decided how your story ends.
And it doesn’t end in brokenness.
It ends in redemption.
Your delay is not denial… it’s where God is rewriting you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: WHEN SIN STOPS FEELING LIKE SIN
paragraphs:
WHEN SIN STOPS FEELING LIKE SIN
The Most Dangerous Judgment May Not Be God's Lightning… But God's Silence.
There is something more terrifying than being caught in sin.
It is waking up one morning and no longer feeling guilty about it.
The first lie never comes wearing horns.
It comes dressed as relief.
"It isn't that bad."
"Everyone does it."
"God understands."
"I'll repent later."

Little by little, what once made your conscience tremble becomes ordinary. What once drove you to your knees no longer interrupts your sleep. Your Bible remains closed. Your prayers become shorter. Worship becomes routine. Conviction fades into comfort.
And perhaps the most frightening part is this:
You may not even realize it happened.
Scripture never portrays the hardening of the heart as an overnight catastrophe. It is almost always gradual. Quiet. Invisible. Like rust eating steel from the inside.
The Bible repeatedly warns that the greatest spiritual danger is not merely committing sin—it is becoming comfortable living with it.
David understood this.

After his adultery with Bathsheba and the arranged death of Uriah, there was no immediate public collapse. Days passed. Weeks passed. Life appeared to continue. Outwardly, everything looked successful.
Until God sent Nathan.
Only then did David finally see what he had become.
His prayer in Psalm 51 was not simply asking for forgiveness.
It was the desperate cry of a man terrified that his heart had grown numb.
In Hebrew he pleaded:

לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים
Lev tahor bera li Elohim.
"Create in me a clean heart, O God." (Psalm 51:10)
The word בָּרָא (bara') is remarkable.
It is the same Hebrew verb used in Genesis 1:1 when God created the heavens and the earth from nothing.
David wasn't asking God for self-improvement.
He knew his heart needed recreation.
Only God could perform that miracle.
That is still true today.
Our culture has become remarkably skilled at renaming sin.
Pride becomes confidence.
Greed becomes ambition.
Lust becomes freedom.
Envy becomes motivation.
Bitterness becomes boundaries.
Covetousness becomes manifesting success.
Rebellion becomes authenticity.
But changing the label never changes reality.
Isaiah warned generations ago:
"Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil." (Isaiah 5:20)
Truth does not evolve because society becomes uncomfortable with it.
God's holiness has never depended upon cultural approval.
The Apostle Paul describes an even darker condition in Romans.
"They became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened."
Later he writes that God "gave them over."
The Greek phrase is:

παρέδωκεν αὐτοὺς ὁ Θεός
paredōken autous ho Theos.
The verb παραδίδωμι (paradidōmi) means "to hand over," "to deliver," or "to surrender into another's power."
This is one of the most sobering realities in Scripture.
Sometimes God's judgment is not immediate destruction.
Sometimes His judgment is allowing people to continue chasing the very sins they refuse to surrender.
That is terrifying.
Not because God stops loving.
But because persistent rejection eventually produces spiritual blindness.
The conscience slowly loses sensitivity.
Paul describes people whose consciences have become "seared."
The Greek word is:
καυστηριάζω (kaustēriazō)
It literally refers to flesh burned with a hot iron until it loses feeling.
That is exactly what repeated, unrepented sin does.
At first, conviction hurts.
Later, conviction whispers.
Eventually…
Silence.
Yet this article is not ultimately about judgment.
It is about hope.
Because every scandal in Scripture points toward grace.
The woman caught in adultery expected stones.
She encountered Jesus.
The tax collector expected rejection.
He received a calling.
Peter denied Christ three times.
Jesus restored him three times.
The thief expected death.
He entered Paradise.
Saul expected victory over Christians.
Instead, he met Christ and became Paul.
That is the Gospel.
Scandal does not surprise Jesus.
Sin is serious because it separates humanity from God, but God's answer was never denial, excuses, or self-justification.
His answer was the Cross.
John opens his Gospel with breathtaking words.
"In the beginning was the Word..."
The Greek reads:

Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἦν ὁ Λόγος
En archē ēn ho Logos.
The word Λόγος (Logos) means far more than "word."
It carries the idea of God's eternal self-expression, His divine wisdom, His perfect revelation.
Jesus is not merely someone who speaks truth.
He is Truth.
The eternal Logos entered history, took on flesh, carried our guilt, bore our shame, and defeated death through His resurrection.
That is why grace is not permission to continue sinning.
Grace is God's power to leave sin behind.
Paul asks in Romans 6:1:
"Shall we continue in sin that grace may abound?"
His answer could not be stronger.
μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito).
"Absolutely not."
"May it never be."
The Gospel never minimizes sin.
It magnifies the mercy of Christ that is greater than sin.
Perhaps today your greatest fear is not what you've done.
Perhaps it is that you no longer feel anything.
If so, hear this carefully.
The very fact that your heart is still wrestling, still questioning, still longing for God is itself evidence that His Spirit is still calling you.
Do not ignore that invitation.
Run toward Christ while conviction still speaks.
Do not wait until tomorrow.
The enemy whispers that tomorrow is guaranteed.
Scripture never does.
Hebrews reminds us:
"Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts."
The Greek word for "today" is σήμερον (sēmeron).
Not someday.
Not eventually.
Today.
Jesus never promised easy transformation.
He promised new life.
He does not merely improve sinners.
He makes them new.
If this article stirred your soul, don't let it end here.
One day, the sins that stopped bothering you will either become the chains that keep you from Christ—or the scars that forever remind you how completely He set you free.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Is Sexual Compatibility a Biblical Concept?
paragraphs:
Is Sexual Compatibility a Biblical Concept?
The Truth That Might Shake What You Thought You Knew About Love, Lust, and Covenant
It started with a whisper most people don’t question anymore.
“What if we’re just not sexually compatible?”

That sentence has quietly become one of the most powerful deal-breakers in modern relationships. It sounds logical. Honest. Even wise. People say it to justify walking away, delaying commitment, or testing intimacy before marriage as if God somehow forgot to include that part in His design.
But somewhere between desire and devotion, something got distorted.
Because Scripture never once commands you to test compatibility. It calls you to something far deeper… and far more terrifying.
Covenant.
In Genesis 2:24, the first blueprint of human intimacy is written in Hebrew with a weight most people never pause to feel:

“וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד”
“Ve’davaq b’ishto, vehayu lebasar echad.”
“And he shall cling to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”

That word “דָּבַק” (davaq) does not mean casual attachment. It means to cling, to cleave, to bind yourself so tightly that separation feels like tearing flesh. And “בָּשָׂר אֶחָד” (basar echad)… one flesh… is not just physical union. It is spiritual, emotional, covenantal fusion.
God did not design sex as a compatibility test.
He designed it as a covenant seal.
So when the world asks, “Are we sexually compatible?” the Kingdom asks something different:
“Are you willing to become one?”
And that question exposes something most people are not ready to admit.
Because compatibility is about preference. Covenant is about sacrifice.

Compatibility says, “Do you satisfy me?”
Covenant says, “I give myself to you.”
One is consumer-driven. The other is cross-shaped.
The Apostle Paul confronts this head-on in 1 Corinthians 6:16, written in Greek:

“ἢ οὐκ οἴδατε ὅτι ὁ κολλώμενος τῇ πόρνῃ ἓν σῶμά ἐστιν;”
“Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her?”

The word “κολλώμενος” (kollōmenos) means glued, bonded, fused together. Even outside covenant, sex still creates a form of “one flesh.” That means every time intimacy is treated casually, something sacred is being formed in a place where it was never meant to remain.
That’s why people feel broken after giving themselves away.
That’s why comparison creeps into marriages.
That’s why dissatisfaction grows even when “compatibility” was supposedly tested.
Because the problem was never compatibility.
It was disconnection from God’s design.
Let this sit with you for a moment…
If sexual compatibility was truly the foundation of lasting love, then the most sexually “compatible” couples would have the strongest marriages.
But we know that’s not true.
People who once said, “We’re perfect together,” now sleep in separate rooms, emotionally distant, spiritually dry, and silently aching.
Because compatibility can ignite desire…
But only covenant sustains it.
Hebrews 13:4 says:

“τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος”
“Let marriage be held in honor among all, and let the marriage bed be undefiled.”
The “bed” (κοίτη, koitē) is not dishonored by lack of experience. It is dishonored when intimacy is separated from covenant.
God never commands you to perfect sexual chemistry before marriage.
He calls you to purity before it… and faithfulness within it.
And here’s the part most people are afraid to say out loud:
Real intimacy is learned, not pre-tested.
It grows through trust, communication, patience, vulnerability, and selflessness. It matures as two people submit to Christ, not just to each other.
Ephesians 5:25 shifts the entire framework:

“ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν”
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church…”
Christ did not evaluate compatibility before going to the cross.
He committed.
He sacrificed.
He gave Himself completely.
And that is the model.
So no… sexual compatibility is not a biblical concept in the way the world defines it.
But something far more powerful is.
Sanctified intimacy.
A love that is shaped, refined, and deepened through surrender to Christ.
A union where two imperfect people grow into oneness—not because they matched perfectly at the start, but because they chose each other daily under God.
And maybe this is where it gets personal.
Maybe you’ve already crossed boundaries you can’t undo.
Maybe you’re carrying memories that still whisper comparisons into your present.
Maybe you’ve believed the lie that you’ve “ruined” your future.
But hear this clearly…
Jesus does not restore you back to a lesser version of yourself.
He redeems you completely.
In John 8, when the woman caught in adultery stood exposed, ashamed, and condemned, Jesus did not ask about her compatibility.
He said:

“οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω· πορεύου, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε.”
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.”
That is grace.
Not permission to continue… but power to change.
So if something in you is stirring right now…
If you feel conviction instead of comfort…
If this exposed something you’ve been avoiding…
Be honest. This hit deeper than you expected, didn’t it?
Someone you love is believing the same lie you once believed. Share this with them, not to shame them, but to wake them up.
Stay close to what calls you higher.
Because this is bigger than one article.
This is about discipleship.
If you truly desire to glorify God, don’t just consume truth—help spread it.
Because the truth is…
Sexual compatibility might feel like the question.
But surrender to Christ is the answer.
And the moment you stop asking, “Does this satisfy me?” and start asking, “Does this glorify Him?”… everything begins to change.
The love you’re looking for was never meant to be tested first… it was meant to be transformed.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Lived for Centuries… But What If We’ve Been Asking the Wrong Question?
paragraphs:
They Lived for Centuries… But What If We’ve Been Asking the Wrong Question?
Could the Bible’s Long Lifespans Be Explained… or Are They Trying to Explain Us?
There’s a moment most people quietly skip past.
You’re reading Genesis. The creation story feels poetic, powerful… then suddenly, the numbers start sounding impossible.
Nine hundred years. Eight hundred years. Seven hundred years.
And something in you hesitates.

Because part of you wants to believe…
and another part of you whispers, “That can’t be literal.”
But what if the question isn’t whether it’s literal or symbolic?
What if the deeper question is this:
Why did God want you to wrestle with it in the first place?
Because Scripture doesn’t just inform—it confronts.
And these long lifespans… they aren’t just numbers. They are signals. Echoes. Warnings. Invitations.
The Hebrew text in Genesis doesn’t soften it. It doesn’t apologize.

“וַיִּחְיוּ כָּל־יְמֵי מְתוּשֶׁלַח תֵּשַׁע וְשִׁשִּׁים וּתְשַׁע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה”
“All the days of Methuselah were nine hundred sixty-nine years.” (Genesis 5:27)
Nine hundred sixty-nine.
Not poetic language. Not metaphorical phrasing. A precise number in a genealogical record rooted in ancient Hebrew culture that valued lineage, history, and covenant continuity.
So what do we do with that?

Some try to explain it scientifically. Maybe the pre-flood world had a different atmosphere. A vapor canopy. Less radiation. Stronger genetics. Others suggest symbolic frameworks—numerical theology, dynastic naming, or ancient literary conventions.
And those discussions have their place.
But if you stay there… you’ll miss the weight of what’s actually happening.
Because Genesis 5 doesn’t climax with how long they lived.
It climaxes with how they all died.
“And he died… and he died… and he died…”
Over and over again, like a drumbeat.
Longevity didn’t save them.
Time didn’t heal them.
Years didn’t redeem them.
Even nine hundred years couldn’t outrun what entered the world in Genesis 3.
Sin.
Death.
Separation.
The Hebrew word for life—“חַיִּים” (chayyim)—is rich, layered, overflowing. It doesn’t just mean existence. It means vitality, wholeness, divine connection.
But something fractured that.
And suddenly, even centuries of breathing weren’t the same as truly living.
That’s why this question about long lifespans starts to feel uncomfortable the longer you sit with it.
Because it quietly exposes something about us.

We are obsessed with extending life…
but we rarely ask if we are actually alive.
Jesus later confronts this same tension in the New Testament, but now in Greek, the language sharpens differently:

“ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ζωή”
“I am the life.” (John 14:6)
Not a life. Not longer life.
The life.
“ζωή” (zoē) — divine, eternal, God-originated life. Not measured in years… but in relationship.
So suddenly, those long lifespans in Genesis start to shift in meaning.
They aren’t proof that humans were once “better.”
They are proof that even when humans had more time, they still needed a Savior.
Let that sit for a second.

If Adam lived 930 years and still fell…
If Methuselah lived 969 years and still died…
If Noah lived through the flood and still carried human brokenness…
Then your problem was never time.
It was always sin.
And that’s where the story stops being historical curiosity… and starts becoming personal confrontation.
Because right now, you’re living your life measuring things the same way we all do.
More time. More chances. More years. More control.

“I’ll change later.”
“I’ll get serious with God eventually.”
“I just need more time.”
But Genesis quietly dismantles that illusion.
They had more time than you could ever imagine.
And it still wasn’t enough.
Because transformation doesn’t come from time.
It comes from surrender.
There’s a moment in the genealogy that almost gets overlooked—but it changes everything.

“וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ חֲנוֹךְ אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים”
“Enoch walked with God.” (Genesis 5:24)
He didn’t just live long.
He walked closely.
And then…

“וְאֵינֶנּוּ כִּי־לָקַח אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים”
