Be honest… this hit deeper than you expected.
Not because it’s easy… but because you’re choosing faith anyway.
And listen carefully…
Delay is where many people walk away from God.
But it’s also where the deepest believers are formed.
Because in delay, motives are exposed.
Are you following God for what He gives… or for who He is?
That question changes everything.
Because when the miracle finally comes — and it will — you won’t just celebrate the outcome.
You’ll understand the process.
And you’ll realize something that changes your entire walk with Christ:
God wasn’t late.
He was intentional.
And that realization will anchor your faith in a way instant answers never could.
If this message stirred something in you, don’t keep it to yourself.
You know exactly who came to mind.
If you truly want to glorify God, don’t just consume truth.
Help it reach others.
Support the mission. Share the message. Stay planted in truth.
Because someone else’s breakthrough might be waiting on your obedience to share.
And never forget this—
The silence you fear might be the very place where God is building something you couldn’t survive without.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You’re Praying for a Spouse… But God Is Preparing a Covenant You Might Not Be Ready to Carry
paragraphs: You’re Praying for a Spouse… But God Is Preparing a Covenant You Might Not Be Ready to Carry
The hidden work of God before love arrives… and why your future marriage is being shaped long before you meet them.
You think you’re waiting.
But heaven knows—you’re being built.
There’s a silence in this season that feels almost offensive. No text. No confirmation. No “this is the one.” Just long nights, quiet prayers, and questions that echo louder than answers.
“God, where are they?”
But the deeper question—one most people never ask—is this:
“God… who am I becoming before they arrive?”
Because Scripture never presents marriage as a moment.
It presents it as a covenant.
And covenants… they crush unprepared hearts.
In the beginning, before there was romance, before there were vows, before there were wedding songs, there was formation.

Genesis 2:18 says in Hebrew:
לֹא־טוֹב הֱיוֹת הָאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ
Lo-tov heyot ha’adam levado — “It is not good that the man should be alone.”
But what’s often missed is this:
God didn’t immediately bring Eve.
He let Adam feel alone first.
He let him name, work, tend, steward, and walk with God before he ever touched companionship.
Because loneliness wasn’t punishment…
It was preparation.
Some of you are rushing to be found, but you haven’t learned how to stand.
You want someone to love you deeply, but you haven’t let God heal you honestly.
And that’s where things break.
Because marriage doesn’t fix what you refuse to confront.
It reveals it.
That insecurity you ignore? It will speak louder in intimacy.
That hidden sin you manage? It will bleed into covenant.
That unhealed wound? It will ask your spouse to carry what only Christ can heal.
And suddenly, what you thought was “love” becomes pressure.
What you thought was “destiny” becomes damage.
What you thought was “the one” becomes a mirror you weren’t ready to face.
Scripture speaks this truth with surgical clarity.

In Matthew 7:5, Jesus says:
ὑποκριτά, ἔκβαλε πρῶτον τὴν δοκὸν
Hypokrita, ekbale prōton tēn dokon — “Hypocrite, first remove the beam…”
First.
Before you look at them.
Before you evaluate them.
Before you blame them.
God says: deal with you.
Because the greatest threat to your future marriage isn’t a bad partner…
It’s an unprepared heart.
And this is where the Gospel interrupts everything.
Because preparation isn’t self-improvement.
It’s surrender.
You don’t become “ready” by becoming perfect.
You become ready by becoming submitted.
There’s a difference.

Paul writes in Ephesians 5:25:
καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν
Kathōs kai ho Christos ēgapēsen tēn ekklēsian — “As Christ loved the church…”
That’s the standard.
Not feelings.
Not compatibility.
Not convenience.
Christ.
And how did Christ love?
He died.
So before you ask, “Who will love me like that?”
Ask:
“Am I becoming someone who can love like that?”
Because marriage is not about being chosen.
It’s about being crucified.
Your pride.
Your control.
Your selfishness.
Your need to always be right.
Your fear of vulnerability.
All of it gets exposed under covenant.
And if you haven’t learned to lay those things down at the feet of Jesus…
You will lay them on the heart of your spouse.
That’s why this season matters more than you think.
This hidden, stretching, uncomfortable, sometimes lonely season…
It’s not empty.
It’s sacred.
God is teaching you how to forgive before you’re offended.
How to communicate before conflict.
How to pray before panic.
How to stand before you lean.
Because the goal isn’t just marriage.
It’s a marriage that reflects Christ.
And Christ was not reactive.
He was rooted.
He was not driven by emotion.
He was anchored in obedience.
He didn’t love based on how He felt.
He loved based on who He was.
And that’s what God is forming in you.
Right now.
Even if no one sees it.
Even if no one applauds it.
Even if you feel forgotten.
You are not being skipped.
You are being prepared.
But here’s the part most people don’t want to hear.
You can delay your own answered prayer.
Not because God is withholding…
But because you are resisting.
Resisting correction.
Resisting growth.
Resisting accountability.
Resisting truth.
You keep asking God to send someone…
While ignoring the things He’s asking you to release.
And heaven will not send a covenant into chaos.
Not because God is cruel…
But because He is holy.
And He cares more about your transformation than your timeline.
So tonight, stop asking “when.”
Start asking “what.”
“What are You trying to build in me, God?”
“What needs to die in me before I say ‘I do’?”
“What am I carrying that cannot follow me into covenant?”
Be honest.
Because pretending now becomes pain later.
And God loves you too much to let you walk into something holy unprepared.
If this exposed something in you…
Sit in it.
Pray through it.
Be real with God.
And be real with yourself.
Someone you know is rushing into something they’re not spiritually ready for.
Not to judge them.
But to protect them.
And if you feel like this kind of truth is rare…
That’s because it is.
Not for us… but because truth like this needs to reach souls before they make irreversible decisions without Christ.
Because preparation isn’t about waiting for love…
It’s about becoming someone who won’t destroy it when it arrives.
And some of you are closer than you think…
But God is making sure you don’t carry old wounds into a new covenant.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Waited for Marriage… So Why Does It Hurt Now?
paragraphs:
They Waited for Marriage… So Why Does It Hurt Now?
The Quiet Crisis of Christian Intimacy—and the Gospel That Heals What No One Talks About
No one warned them that the silence would follow them into the bedroom.

They were faithful. They resisted. They prayed. They said no when everything in them wanted to say yes. They honored God in the dark when nobody was watching. They built their love on Scripture, not on impulse.
And then… the wedding came.
The vows were spoken. The covenant sealed. The ring slipped onto trembling fingers. The room erupted with celebration. Heaven smiled.
And that night—the night they were told would finally be free, holy, beautiful, unrestrained—it felt… confusing.
Awkward.
Heavy.
Sometimes even painful.
They didn’t say it out loud. Not to friends. Not to church. Not even to each other at first.
But something wasn’t right.
And now they’re lying side by side in the dark, wondering…
“Why does this feel harder than it’s supposed to?”
This is the quiet crisis so many Christian couples carry behind closed doors.
Because we taught them how to say no.
But we never taught them how to say yes.
And the truth is… Scripture never shamed intimacy. We did.

From the beginning, God did not whisper sexuality into existence—He declared it. In the Hebrew, Genesis 2:24 says:
“וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ” (ve’davaq b’ishto)—“and he shall cling, cleave, be joined to his wife.”
That word davaq is not passive. It is fierce attachment. It is pursuit. It is intimacy that binds soul and body together.
And then comes the line that most churches read quickly and never sit in long enough:

“וַיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עֲרוּמִּים… וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ”
“They were both naked… and not ashamed.” (Genesis 2:25)
No shame.
No hiding.
No performance.
No fear.
Just presence.
Just union.
Just God in the middle of it.
But somewhere along the way, many believers didn’t just flee sin…
They learned to fear their own bodies.
They learned that desire was dangerous.
That arousal was suspicious.
That sexuality was something to suppress, manage, control, survive.
So they built years—sometimes decades—of internal resistance.
And then one day, they stood at an altar and expected that switch to flip instantly.
But trauma doesn’t disappear with a wedding ring.
Conditioning doesn’t dissolve with vows.
Fear doesn’t vanish just because something became “allowed.”
So now intimacy feels like pressure instead of freedom.
Like obligation instead of connection.
Like performance instead of presence.
And nobody talks about it.
Because they’re supposed to be the “godly couple.”
But listen carefully… because this is where everything begins to change.
God never designed sex as a test of performance.
He designed it as a language of covenant.

In the Greek, 1 Corinthians 7:3 says:
“ὁ ἀνὴρ τῇ γυναικὶ τὴν ὀφειλὴν ἀποδιδότω” (ho anēr tē gynaiki tēn opheilēn apodidotō)
“The husband should give to his wife her due…”
But this is not a cold transaction.
It is mutual giving.
Mutual surrender.
Mutual honoring.
The passage continues by saying their bodies belong to each other—not as ownership, but as entrusted care.
And here’s what many miss…
Intimacy is not just physical access.
It is emotional safety.
It is spiritual vulnerability.
It is the removal of masks.
And if shame is still present, intimacy will struggle—no matter how “biblical” the marriage looks from the outside.
Some couples are fighting battles they don’t even realize have names.
Purity culture wounds.
Past sexual trauma.
Comparison.
Unrealistic expectations.
Pornography history.
Silence.
Fear of rejection.
Fear of failure.
And underneath it all… a quiet question:
“Am I enough?”
But the Gospel doesn’t ignore this.
It enters it.
Jesus never flinches at broken places.
He moves toward them.

The same Christ who restored Peter after denial…
who defended the woman caught in adultery…
who touched the untouchable…
is not uncomfortable with your marriage bed.
He is not distant from your struggle.
He is not ashamed of your questions.
Because redemption does not stop at salvation.
It flows into every hidden corner of your life—including your intimacy.
Song of Songs was never meant to be skipped.
It was meant to be felt.

“דּוֹדִי לִי וַאֲנִי לוֹ” (dodi li va’ani lo)
“My beloved is mine, and I am his.” (Song of Songs 2:16)
This is not lust.
This is covenant desire—redeemed, pure, alive.
And if your marriage feels distant right now…
You are not broken beyond repair.
You are not disqualified.
You are not alone.
Healing often begins with something simple but terrifying:
Honesty.
Real conversations.
Slow rebuilding.
Unlearning shame.
Inviting God into the space instead of leaving Him outside the door.
Because intimacy was never meant to be hidden from Him.
It was designed in His presence.
So if this exposed something you’ve been silently carrying…
Let that be your first step out of isolation.
And if you’re still fighting to believe your marriage can be restored…
Because that matters more than perfection ever will.
And if you want to grow deeper—not just in marriage, but in Christ Himself—stay close.
Because supporting this mission isn’t about money…
It’s about multiplying truth.
It’s about helping more marriages heal.
It’s about bringing light into places the church has been too quiet about.
The Gospel was never meant to stay comfortable.
It was meant to restore what shame tried to bury.
And maybe… just maybe…
your story isn’t falling apart.
Maybe Jesus is rewriting it—slowly, intimately, beautifully.
And one day you’ll look back at this struggle…
and realize it was the place grace found you both.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Said God Allowed It… But God Never Blessed It: The Hidden Lies of Polygamy That Are Breaking Souls
paragraphs: He Said God Allowed It… But God Never Blessed It: The Hidden Lies of Polygamy That Are Breaking Souls
You’ve probably heard it before… whispered in debates, justified in conversations, even defended with Scripture that feels half-true and dangerously convincing.
“God allowed polygamy in the Bible.”
And just like that, something sacred gets twisted.
Something holy becomes tolerated.
Something that wounds quietly gets labeled as acceptable.
But deep down… something doesn’t sit right.
Because if you’ve ever watched relationships fracture, hearts divide, or love turn into competition instead of covenant—you already feel it.
This isn’t God’s design.
This is humanity trying to survive outside of it.
From the very beginning, before culture complicated things and before sin distorted desire, God spoke something so clear it almost feels uncomfortable to read it now in a world full of compromise.
In Genesis 2:24, the Hebrew says:
“עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד”
“Al-ken ya'azov ish et aviv ve’et imo, ve’davaq be’ishto, ve’hayu le’basar echad.”
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
Not many.
One.
Not divided.
One flesh.
There is no Hebrew word here that suggests “wives.”
No hint of multiplicity.
No allowance for divided intimacy.
Just one man… one woman… one covenant… one union.
So where did the confusion begin?
It began where compromise always begins.
Sin.
The first recorded polygamist in Scripture isn’t a hero of faith.
It’s Lamech.
A descendant of Cain.
A man whose life reflected rebellion, not righteousness.
Genesis 4:19 says:
“וַיִּקַּח־לוֹ לֶמֶךְ שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים”
“Vayikach-lo Lemech shtei nashim.”
“Lamech took two wives for himself.”
Not God gave.
Not God blessed.
He took.
And everything that follows his story is violence, pride, and distortion.
That’s not coincidence.
That’s consequence.
And yet, as generations pass, people point to men like Abraham, Jacob, David, and Solomon and say, “See? God allowed it.”
But allowance is not approval.
God also allowed Israel to demand a king, and it led to cycles of rebellion.
God allowed divorce because of hardness of heart, but Jesus clarified in Matthew 19:8:
“πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν ἐπέτρεψεν ὑμῖν”
“Pros tēn sklērokardian hymōn epetrepsen hymin.”
“Because of your hardness of heart, He permitted you…”
Permitted.
Not designed.
Not blessed.
Permitted because humanity refused to fully surrender.
And if we’re honest… that’s still happening today.
Polygamy doesn’t multiply love.
It divides it.
It creates silent comparisons.
Unspoken insecurity.
Hidden competition.
A love that was meant to be whole becomes fragmented.
Even in the lives of biblical figures, the fruit is undeniable.
Abraham’s household fractured through Hagar and Sarah.
Jacob’s marriages turned into rivalry between Leah and Rachel.
David’s family collapsed into betrayal and bloodshed.
Solomon… the wisest man… was led into idolatry because of his many wives.
These aren’t success stories.
They’re warnings.
And yet people still try to dress wounds as blessings.
Still try to call broken systems “biblical.”
Still try to justify what God never designed.
Because sometimes it’s easier to defend a lifestyle than to surrender it.
But here’s where everything changes.
Jesus.
Because Jesus didn’t come to adjust broken systems.
He came to restore God’s original design.
In Ephesians 5:31–32, Paul echoes Genesis, but then reveals something deeper:
“ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν… τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν· ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω εἰς Χριστὸν καὶ εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν.”
“The two shall become one flesh… this mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the Church.”
One Bride.
One Groom.
Jesus is not coming back for multiple brides.
He is coming back for one Church.
Faithful.
Undivided.
Set apart.
Polygamy doesn’t just distort relationships.
It distorts the Gospel itself.
Because marriage was never just about companionship.
It was always meant to reflect Christ.
And Christ does not share His Bride.
Let that sit with you.
Let it challenge you.
Let it expose anything in you that has accepted what God never ordained.
Because this isn’t about condemnation.
This is about clarity.
This is about truth breaking through generations of confusion.
This is about healing what culture normalized but God never sanctified.
And maybe as you’re reading this… something inside you feels unsettled.
Not because you’re being attacked.
But because truth has a way of reaching places we tried to hide.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
You’re not alone in this.
There are people reading this right now who are wrestling with the same convictions, the same questions, the same quiet discomfort they’ve been ignoring for years.
Someone who’s been confused.
Someone who deserves clarity rooted in Scripture, not culture.
Because truth doesn’t spread unless someone is willing to carry it.
And maybe that someone is you.
Not just as a post.
But as a reminder of what God actually said… not what people reshaped it to be.
And if this message stirred something deeper in you—if you’re hungry for truth that convicts, restores, and transforms—then stay close.
Because this isn’t about information.
This is about transformation.
For those who are ready to go deeper, there is something waiting for you.
It’s partnership in the Gospel.
If you truly want to glorify God, don’t just agree silently.
Stand publicly.
Support boldly.
Spread truth intentionally.
Because someone out there is still believing a lie… and your share might be the moment God uses to set them free.
The lie was never harmless… it was just slowly destroying what God meant to be whole.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Leah Kept Naming Sons
paragraphs:
Why Leah Kept Naming Sons
The woman who was never chosen… but never stopped hoping
They never told her she was the consolation prize.

No one said it out loud when her father led her into that tent in the dark, when the veil covered more than her face, when deception sealed a marriage that was never supposed to be hers. But Leah felt it the moment morning came and love did not follow.
Scripture doesn’t soften it. It doesn’t try to protect her dignity from the rawness of truth.

“וַיַּרְא יְהוָה כִּי־שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה”
“Vayar YHWH ki senu’ah Leah”
“And the LORD saw that Leah was hated.” (Genesis 29:31)

Not unloved in a mild way. Not overlooked politely. The Hebrew word שְׂנוּאָה (senu’ah) carries the weight of rejection, emotional abandonment, being set aside. Leah wasn’t just second… she was unwanted.
And yet, God saw her.
That’s where the story begins. Not with Jacob. Not with rivalry. But with divine attention falling on a woman nobody chose.
So God opened her womb.
And Leah did something that feels strange until you realize it’s exactly what we do too… she started naming her pain.
Her first son, she called Reuben.

“כִּי־רָאָה יְהוָה בְּעָנְיִי”
“Ki ra’ah YHWH b’onyi”
“Because the LORD has seen my affliction.” (Genesis 29:32)
Reuben… “See, a son.”
Can you hear it? She wasn’t just naming a child. She was speaking to the ache inside her chest.
Maybe now my husband will see me.
Maybe now I’ll be enough.
Maybe now I won’t feel invisible.
But Jacob didn’t change.
So she had another son.
Simeon.

“כִּי־שָׁמַע יְהוָה”
“Ki shama YHWH”
“Because the LORD has heard.” (Genesis 29:33)
If seeing didn’t fix it, maybe being heard will.
God hears me… but does he?
Does anyone?

Some of you reading this… you’ve been there. You’ve prayed, you’ve cried, you’ve tried to prove your worth in ways nobody ever asked you to. You keep hoping something will finally make you feel chosen.
But the silence keeps answering.
Leah wasn’t done.
She had a third son.
Levi.

“הַפַּעַם יִלָּוֶה אִישִׁי אֵלַי”
“Hapa’am yilaveh ishi elai”
“Now this time my husband will be attached to me.” (Genesis 29:34)
Do you feel the shift?
She’s no longer just naming what God did. She’s pleading through her naming.
This time…
This time he’ll stay.
This time I’ll matter.
This time I won’t feel alone.
But nothing changed.
And that’s the part we skip too quickly when we read her story. Because it’s uncomfortable to sit in a place where prayers seem unanswered and effort feels wasted. But Leah lived there.
Child after child.
Hope after disappointment.
Effort after silence.
Until something broke inside her… or maybe something finally healed.
Her fourth son.
Judah.

“הַפַּעַם אוֹדֶה אֶת־יְהוָה”
“Hapa’am odeh et YHWH”
“Now I will praise the LORD.” (Genesis 29:35)
No mention of Jacob.
No more bargaining.
No more “maybe now he will love me.”
Just… praise.
That word אוֹדֶה (odeh) comes from the root ידה (yadah), meaning to give thanks, to confess, to surrender acknowledgment. This wasn’t surface-level gratitude. This was a deep, soul-level release.
Leah stopped naming her pain based on what she hoped people would give her… and started naming her life based on what God already had.
And everything changed.
Not her circumstances.
Not Jacob’s affection.
Not her position.
But her center.
Because the moment she stopped chasing validation horizontally… she found identity vertically.
And here’s the part that should shake you.
Judah… the son born from surrender… becomes the lineage of Jesus Christ.

“βίβλος γενέσεως Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ… Ἰούδας”
“Biblos geneseos Iēsou Christou… Ioudas”
“The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ… Judah.” (Matthew 1:1–2)
Not Rachel.
Not the loved one.
Leah.
The rejected woman.
The overlooked wife.
The one who kept naming sons in the middle of heartbreak.
God didn’t just see her.
He wrote Himself into her story.
And maybe that’s why this hits harder than expected.
Because some of you are still in your “Reuben” season… trying to be seen.
Some of you are in your “Simeon” season… crying out to be heard.
Some of you are in your “Levi” season… hoping someone will finally stay.
But God is calling you into your “Judah” season.
Where praise isn’t dependent on people.
Where identity isn’t tied to approval.
Where your worth isn’t negotiated through performance.
Leah kept naming sons because she was searching for something every human soul craves… to be chosen.
And she found it… not in Jacob… but in God.
Be honest… this exposed something deeper than you expected, didn’t it?

Someone you love is still stuck in a cycle of trying to be enough for people who will never choose them. Share this with them… not casually, but intentionally. This could be the moment God uses to shift their entire life.
Follow closely if you’re serious about growing deeper in Christ… not surface faith, but real transformation, real surrender, real healing.

And if you truly want to glorify God through what you consume and support… stand with this mission. This isn’t just content… this is discipleship, this is restoration, this is souls being called back to Jesus.
Because at the end of everything… Leah’s story wasn’t about being unwanted.
It was about being chosen by the only One who truly matters.
And He is still choosing people like her… like you… like me.
The love you keep begging for from people was never meant to replace the love God already gave you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: When Intimacy Becomes a Transaction, Not a Connection
paragraphs:
When Intimacy Becomes a Transaction, Not a Connection
The night your soul stopped feeling—and the moment Jesus called you back
You didn’t notice the exact moment it changed.
There was no loud warning. No breaking sound. No visible fracture.

Just a slow shift…
where something sacred quietly became something traded.

Where touch lost its meaning.
Where closeness became currency.
Where “I love you” started sounding like a negotiation instead of a surrender.
And maybe you’re reading this because deep down, you felt it.

That uncomfortable silence after connection that didn’t feel real.
That emptiness that followed something that was supposed to make you feel whole.
That haunting thought you tried to suppress:
“Was that intimacy… or was I just being used… or using someone?”
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.

Because somewhere along the way, intimacy stopped being about union…
and started becoming about exchange.

Give me this… I’ll give you that.
Meet my need… I’ll stay a little longer.
Make me feel wanted… and I’ll call it love.
But heaven never defined intimacy that way.
From the beginning, God’s design was never transactional.

In Genesis 2:24, the Hebrew says:
“וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד” (ve-hayu lebasar echad)
“and they shall become one flesh.”

Not two people negotiating terms.
Not two people extracting value.
One.
A union so deep it dissolves self-centered agendas.
But sin doesn’t just break morality… it distorts meaning.

What was once covenant became consumption.
What was once giving became taking.
What was once sacred became strategic.
And suddenly intimacy became something you perform to get something back.

Affection became leverage.
Presence became a tool.
Bodies became bargaining chips.

And the soul…
the soul quietly started starving.
Because your spirit was never designed to survive on transactions.
It was created for communion.

That’s why even after moments of physical closeness, there’s still a void.
Because connection without covenant leaves residue, not restoration.

In the Greek, 1 Corinthians 6:16 says:
“κολλώμενος τῇ πόρνῃ ἓν σῶμά ἐστιν” (kollōmenos tē pornē hen sōma estin)
“He who joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her.”
The word “κολλώμενος” (kollōmenos) means to glue, to cling, to fuse.

Even when it’s transactional…
your soul still bonds.

That’s why it hurts more than you admit.
That’s why you feel fragmented after.
That’s why something in you whispers, “This isn’t what I was made for.”

Because even in broken intimacy…
your soul still remembers Eden.
And maybe no one ever told you this clearly:

You were never created to be consumed.
And you were never created to consume others.
You were created to reflect Christ.
And Christ never loved transactionally.

Romans 5:8 reminds us in the original Greek:
“συνίστησιν… τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀγάπην” (synistēsin… tēn heautou agapēn)
“God demonstrates His own love…”

Not negotiates it.
Not withholds it until conditions are met.
He gives it.

Fully.
Sacrificially.
Unconditionally.
While we were still sinners.
That’s the love your soul is craving.

Not the kind that asks, “What do I get?”
But the kind that says, “I give because I am yours.”
And here’s where it gets uncomfortable…
Some of you didn’t just experience transactional intimacy.
You became fluent in it.

You learned how to perform.
How to give just enough.
How to keep people attached without ever fully opening your heart.
You mastered the art of appearing close… while staying guarded.
And now it’s hard to even recognize real connection.
Because real intimacy requires something transactions never will:

Vulnerability.
Surrender.
Truth.

Jesus said in John 8:32:
“καὶ γνώσεσθε τὴν ἀλήθειαν” (kai gnōsesthe tēn alētheian)
“and you will know the truth…”

Not avoid it.
Not numb it.
Know it.
And the truth is this:
Some of us are tired.

Tired of pretending we’re okay with empty connections.
Tired of calling it “casual” when it’s actually costing our souls.
Tired of feeling used… or realizing we’ve been using others.
So here it is.
The moment of honesty.
Because healing begins where honesty shows up.
Jesus doesn’t shame you for where intimacy got distorted.
He restores what was broken.

The woman at the well had five husbands… and was with a man who wasn’t hers.
A life full of relational transactions.
And yet Jesus met her there.

Not with condemnation…
but with revelation.

In John 4:14, He says:
“ὕδωρ ἁλλομένου εἰς ζωὴν αἰώνιον” (hydōr hallomenou eis zōēn aiōnion)
“a spring of water welling up to eternal life.”
He wasn’t offering another transaction.
He was offering transformation.
That’s what He’s offering you right now.

Not better transactions.
Not more controlled intimacy.
A new heart.

A restored understanding of love.
A redeemed identity that no longer needs to trade itself to feel valued.
And if you’ve been searching for deeper healing, real discipleship, and truth that doesn’t dilute the Gospel…
Because staying close to truth is how transformation becomes a lifestyle, not a moment.
If you want to go deeper, there’s something more waiting for you.
This isn’t about buying something.
It’s about building something in your spirit.

Not out of pressure…
but out of purpose.
Because when you support what spreads the Gospel, you’re not just consuming content…
You’re participating in someone else’s rescue story.

Let this be the moment you stop settling for transactions…
and start stepping into transformation.
Because intimacy was never meant to cost your soul.
It was meant to reveal it… healed, whole, and anchored in Christ.

And the most dangerous lie you ever believed…
was that empty connection was better than holy loneliness.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Lie That Dresses Like Scripture: How Lust Twists God’s Word to Justify Polygamy
paragraphs: The Lie That Dresses Like Scripture: How Lust Twists God’s Word to Justify Polygamy
There are sins that shout, and there are sins that whisper… and the most dangerous ones are the ones that learn how to quote Scripture while they’re whispering.

You’ve probably heard it before. Maybe you’ve even wrestled with it in silence. Someone opens the Bible, points to Abraham, David, Solomon… and suddenly what God tolerated in broken men is being preached as something He designed for holy living. And if we’re honest, sometimes the argument doesn’t come from a pulpit. It comes from a place deeper. Quieter. A place inside the human heart that doesn’t want to surrender desire… it wants to baptize it.
That’s where lust becomes a theologian.
Not a loud one. Not an obvious one. But a clever one.
The kind that doesn’t deny God’s Word… it twists it.

In the beginning, before kings, before kingdoms, before culture complicated everything, God already spoke clearly. In Genesis 2:24, the Hebrew is painfully simple, almost offensively direct to human desire: “וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד” (ve’hayu le’basar echad) — “and they shall become one flesh.”
Not one man and many women. Not divided flesh. Not shared covenant.
One.

There’s something sacred about that word in Hebrew — “אֶחָד” (echad). It doesn’t just mean one as a number. It means unity. Wholeness. Undivided existence. God wasn’t just defining marriage… He was revealing His own nature through it. A covenant that reflects divine faithfulness, not human appetite.
But lust doesn’t like “one.”
Lust wants more.
And when desire grows louder than devotion, people don’t usually abandon Scripture… they reinterpret it.

They point to Abraham and say, “But he had Hagar.”
They point to David and say, “But he had many wives.”
They point to Solomon and say, “But God still used him.”
What they don’t say… is what those choices cost.

Abraham’s house was torn by jealousy and exile.
David’s family was fractured by violence, betrayal, and grief.
Solomon’s heart was turned away from God, exactly as warned.
The Bible never hides the consequences. It records them in painful detail. Because Scripture is not endorsing their choices… it is exposing them.
There’s a difference between description and prescription. And lust depends on people confusing the two.
Jesus doesn’t leave room for confusion.

When questioned about marriage, He didn’t point to David or Solomon. He went all the way back. Back before sin complicated relationships. Back before culture normalized compromise. Back to the original design.
In Matthew 19:4–6, He says, “ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς” (ap’ archēs) — “from the beginning.”
Not from tradition. Not from cultural practice. Not from what people got away with.
From the beginning.
And then He repeats it: “the two shall become one flesh.”
Two.
Not three. Not many.
Two.
And then He says something that should shake every argument built on convenience: “What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.”
Lust hears that… and still tries to negotiate.
Because lust isn’t just about desire for bodies. It’s about control. It’s about refusing to die to self. It’s about reshaping truth until it no longer confronts us.

Even the New Testament closes the door firmly. When describing church leadership in 1 Timothy 3:2, Paul writes that an overseer must be “μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα” (mias gynaikos andra) — literally, “a one-woman man.”
Not because faithfulness is optional for others… but because leadership must reflect what God already established as holy.
So why do people still argue for polygamy?
Because the heart is capable of reading truth… and still choosing desire.
And that’s the part no one likes to admit.
This isn’t just about ancient cultures or theological debates. This is about something personal. Something uncomfortable. Something that might be sitting quietly in your own thoughts.
Are there areas where you’re not rejecting God’s Word… you’re just reshaping it to fit what you want?
Be honest.
Because this is where the Gospel becomes more than information… it becomes confrontation.
Jesus didn’t come just to forgive sin. He came to destroy its authority.
Lust doesn’t get healed by justification. It gets healed by surrender.
And surrender feels like loss… until you realize what you’re actually gaining.
Freedom.
Clarity.
Wholeness.
The kind of love that isn’t divided, negotiated, or secretly compromised.
This is what grace does. It doesn’t adjust truth to fit your life… it transforms your life to align with truth.
And that transformation always starts the same way.
Honesty.
Sit with it.
Let it expose something if it needs to.
There’s no shame in admitting the struggle… but there is danger in pretending it’s not there.
And if this spoke to something real in you, don’t keep it to yourself. Someone close to you is quietly believing a lie that sounds biblical. Not to shame them… but to wake them up.
You’re going to need this reminder again when your feelings try to rewrite truth.
And follow closely, because truth like this isn’t something you hear once… it’s something you stay anchored to.
Not because truth is for sale… but because building something that reaches souls requires people who are willing to stand behind it.
If you truly want to glorify God, don’t just consume truth… help carry it.
Because someone out there is still believing a lie… and your share might be the moment it breaks.
The most dangerous deception isn’t rejecting God’s Word… it’s reshaping it until it no longer requires you to change.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Told You Purity Would Save You… So Why Did It Leave Some People Bleeding?
paragraphs:
They Told You Purity Would Save You… So Why Did It Leave Some People Bleeding?
When holiness was preached, but hearts were sometimes mishandled—and how Jesus still rewrites every story from scandal to grace

You remember the moment. The room was quiet, maybe too quiet. The message was clear, maybe too clear. Don’t touch. Don’t look. Don’t feel. Don’t cross the line. Because if you do… you lose something you can never get back.

For some, that message became a shield. It guarded their steps, protected their decisions, gave them language for holiness in a world that was unraveling. It taught them that their bodies mattered, that intimacy was sacred, that God was not silent about desire. And in that, purity culture did something good. It reminded a generation that holiness was not outdated, that God still says, “Be holy, for I am holy” — קְדֹשִׁים תִּהְיוּ (qedoshim tihyu) from Leviticus 19:2.
But for others… it didn’t feel like a shield.
It felt like a cage.

Because somewhere along the way, the message shifted. Not always intentionally, but powerfully. Holiness became fear. Conviction became shame. Boundaries became identity. And instead of pointing people to Jesus… it sometimes pointed them to themselves.

To their failure.
To their mistakes.
To their “lost worth.”
And that’s where the wound began.
Because Scripture never said your value could be stolen by a moment.

In fact, when Jesus encountered the woman caught in adultery, dragged publicly, exposed, humiliated, ready to be destroyed—He didn’t echo the shame culture around her. He disrupted it. In John 8:11, He says, “Neither do I condemn you; go, and sin no more.” The Greek there—οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω (oude egō se katakrinō)—is not passive. It’s deeply intentional. “I do not sentence you to destruction.”
He didn’t deny her sin. But He refused to define her by it.
That’s where purity culture helped some… and hurt others.
Because when purity is taught without grace, it becomes a scoreboard. And no one wins forever.
When purity is taught without the cross, it becomes pressure. And pressure eventually breaks people.
When purity is taught without Jesus at the center, it becomes performance. And performance creates either pride… or despair.

Some walked away thinking, “I stayed pure. I did everything right.”
Others walked away thinking, “I messed up. I’m disqualified.”
But both missed the deeper truth.
Because purity was never meant to be your savior.
Jesus is.

Even the word “pure” in Scripture carries a deeper weight than we often realize. In Matthew 5:8, “Blessed are the pure in heart,” the Greek word is καθαροὶ (katharoi)—not meaning flawless behavior, but a heart that has been cleansed, made whole, undivided. This is not something you manufacture. It is something God does in you.

David understood this after his own moral failure. Not theory. Not culture. Real failure. And what did he cry out in Psalm 51:10?
“Create in me a clean heart, O God”—לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים (lev tahor bera-li Elohim).
Create.
Because he knew he couldn’t fix himself.
That’s the difference.

Purity culture sometimes told you to maintain something.
The Gospel tells you to receive something.

A new heart.
A new identity.
A new story.

Some people were protected by purity teaching. And that matters. It saved them from pain they didn’t have to experience. That is not something to dismiss. God’s design for sexuality is still holy, still good, still worth honoring.
But others… were crushed under expectations they couldn’t carry alone.
And maybe that’s you.
Maybe you’re reading this and thinking, “I tried. I really tried. But I failed.”
Or maybe you’re thinking, “I did everything right… but I still feel empty.”
Both are invitations.
Because the goal was never just behavioral purity.
It was intimacy with Christ.
It was transformation from the inside out.
It was becoming someone who doesn’t just avoid sin… but actually loves God deeply.

That’s why 2 Corinthians 5:17 doesn’t say “If anyone performs well…”
It says, “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation”—καινὴ κτίσις (kainē ktisis). Completely new.
Not repaired. Not patched. New.
So if purity culture helped you… thank God for the protection.
If it hurt you… bring that pain to Jesus.
Because He is not intimidated by your past. He is not confused by your story. He is not standing at a distance waiting for you to clean yourself up.
He is already reaching for you.
And maybe this is the moment you stop measuring your worth by what you did… or didn’t do… and start receiving who He says you are.
Be honest.
This hit something, didn’t it?
Your honesty might be the permission someone else needs to come out of silence.
Not because it’s just another post… but because there will be a day when the lies come back, and you’ll need to remember what is true.
Follow and stay close if you want daily truth that doesn’t just inform you… but transforms you.
Because supporting this mission isn’t just about content.
It’s about souls.
It’s about truth.
It’s about making sure no one believes the lie that they are too far gone.
Because here’s the truth that refuses to let you go:
You were never saved by your purity… and you are not disqualified by your past.
You are saved by a Savior who still calls broken people “redeemed.”
And that changes everything.
You thought your story ended in failure… but heaven is still writing.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE DAY HE CHOSE TO DIE: Why the Cross Stood on Passover and Why That Changes Everything
paragraphs: THE DAY HE CHOSE TO DIE: Why the Cross Stood on Passover and Why That Changes Everything
He didn’t just die… He chose the exact day history could never forget.
There is a moment in every honest life when the question stops being casual and starts becoming personal.

Not “Did Jesus die?”
But “Why that day?”
Because if the cross happened randomly, then maybe grace is accidental.

But if it happened on Passover…
then nothing about your life is coincidence anymore.

The streets of Jerusalem were swollen with pilgrims. Lambs were being led, inspected, chosen. Families were whispering ancient words passed down from trembling generations. The smell of sacrifice hung in the air like memory itself.
And somewhere in that same city, another Lamb was walking… but no one realized He had already been chosen before the foundations of the world.
The Gospel writers don’t leave this vague. They anchor it in time, in ritual, in covenant reality.
John writes with surgical precision:
The Greek reads: ἦν δὲ παρασκευὴ τοῦ πάσχα (ēn de paraskeuē tou pascha) — not just preparation, but the exact day everything is made ready for sacrifice.
This is not poetic coincidence.
This is divine timing.
Because centuries earlier, in the trembling night of Egypt, God spoke through Moses:
“Your lamb shall be without blemish… and the whole assembly… shall kill it at twilight.” (Exodus 12:5–6)
In Hebrew: שֶׂה תָמִים זָכָר (seh tamim zakhar) — a spotless, male lamb.
No defect. No flaw. No corruption.
And then the blood.
“The blood shall be a sign for you… when I see the blood, I will pass over you.” (Exodus 12:13)
וְרָאִיתִי אֶת־הַדָּם וּפָסַחְתִּי עֲלֵכֶם (ve-ra’iti et-ha-dam u’fasachti alechem)
“I will see the blood… and I will pass over you.”
That word פָּסַח (pasach) — “pass over” — is where Passover is born.
Not because Israel was perfect.
But because the blood spoke louder than their failures.
Now come closer… because this is where it stops being history and starts becoming you.
When John the Baptist sees Jesus, he doesn’t introduce Him as teacher, prophet, or revolutionary.
He says:
“Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29)
Greek: Ἴδε ὁ ἀμνὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ (Ide ho amnos tou Theou)
Not a lamb.
The Lamb.
The fulfillment of every trembling hand that ever placed blood on a doorpost.
The Gospels reveal something staggering: Jesus enters Jerusalem days before Passover… the exact time lambs were being inspected for sacrifice.
He is questioned. Examined. Challenged.
And yet, no one finds fault.
Pilate says it plainly:
“I find no guilt in Him.” (John 19:6)
The Lamb passes inspection.
Perfect. Blameless. Untouched by sin.
And then… the timing tightens like a heartbeat.
Mark tells us:
“And it was the third hour when they crucified Him.” (Mark 15:25)

While lambs were being prepared…
while priests were moving in ritual obedience…
the true Lamb was being lifted onto wood.
And John adds another layer that most people miss:
“These things took place that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘Not one of His bones will be broken.’” (John 19:36)
This echoes Exodus 12:46:
“You shall not break any of its bones.”

The Lamb in Egypt…
and the Lamb on the cross…
both untouched in their bones.
This is not symbolic coincidence.
This is precision.
This is God writing a story no human author could fabricate.
Even the timing of His death aligns with the slaughter of the Passover lambs in the Temple.

While priests were offering sacrifices that could only cover sin temporarily…
Jesus was offering Himself once and for all.
Hebrews declares:
“Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.” (1 Corinthians 5:7)
Greek: τὸ πάσχα ἡμῶν ἐτύθη Χριστός (to pascha hēmōn etythē Christos)
He didn’t just die during Passover.
He became Passover.
Now pause… because this is where it cuts deep.
The Israelites in Egypt had to apply the blood.
It wasn’t enough that the lamb died.
The blood had to be placed… personally.
On their doorposts.
Visible. Intentional. Costly.
Because God said, “When I see the blood…”

Not when I see your effort.
Not when I see your morality.
Not when I see your potential.
When I see the blood.
So what about you?
You’ve heard about Jesus.
You’ve maybe even believed parts of the story.
But has the blood been applied?
Or are you still standing inside a house marked by fear, pretending judgment won’t come?
This is why Passover matters.
Because the cross wasn’t random suffering.
It was a scheduled rescue.
Jesus wasn’t a victim of history.
He was the author of redemption.
He chose the exact day when every Jewish heart would already be thinking about deliverance… and then He rewrote the meaning forever.

From Egypt’s chains…
to sin’s chains.

From temporary covering…
to eternal cleansing.

From animal blood…
to divine sacrifice.
This is why the Gospel doesn’t ask for admiration.
It demands surrender.

Because if He is the Passover Lamb…
then your life is either covered… or it isn’t.
There is no middle ground.
Be honest.
This hit something deeper than information, didn’t it?
If you truly want to glorify God, don’t just consume truth—support the spreading of it.
You don’t have to stay where you are.

Because the same blood that marked doorposts…
is still marking lives.

And the same God who passed over judgment…
is still offering mercy.
He didn’t miss His moment then.
He’s not missing you now.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: HE PREPARED A GALLOWS… BUT ENDED UP PARADING HIS ENEMY
paragraphs:
HE PREPARED A GALLOWS… BUT ENDED UP PARADING HIS ENEMY
When Pride Forces You to Honor the One God Chose
There is a kind of hatred that doesn’t shout… it waits.
It smiles in public, but sharpens knives in private. It builds plans, drafts speeches, rehearses victory… all while pretending everything is fine.
Haman knew that kind of hatred intimately.
He wasn’t just offended by Mordecai. He was consumed by him.
Every time Mordecai refused to bow, something inside Haman cracked a little more. Not because Mordecai attacked him… but because Mordecai would not worship him.

Scripture says in Esther 3:2 that all the king’s servants bowed to Haman, “כִּי־כֵן צִוָּה־לוֹ הַמֶּלֶךְ” (ki-khen tzivah-lo ha-melekh) — “for so the king had commanded.”
But Mordecai didn’t move.
No applause. No protest. Just quiet defiance.
And that silence exposed Haman’s soul.
Because pride doesn’t just want recognition… it demands worship.
Haman went home burning. Not satisfied with power, wealth, or influence. One man’s refusal outweighed everything he had.
Be honest… have you ever felt that?
Everything is going right… but one person, one moment, one insult… and suddenly peace disappears.
That’s not a small issue. That’s a heart issue.
And Haman’s heart was already rotting.
So he did what pride always does when it feels threatened… it escalates.
He didn’t just want Mordecai humbled.
He wanted him erased.
Not just him… his entire people.
In Esther 3:6, it says Haman sought “לְהַשְׁמִיד” (lehashmid) — to destroy, annihilate completely.
That’s what unchecked hatred becomes.
It doesn’t stay small.
It spreads.
But here’s where heaven quietly steps in.
Because while Haman was building gallows…
God was building a reversal.
There’s a moment in the story that feels almost accidental, but it’s anything but.
The king couldn’t sleep.
No war. No crisis. Just… restlessness.
So he calls for the chronicles to be read, and suddenly… Mordecai’s forgotten act of loyalty surfaces.
Years earlier, Mordecai had saved the king’s life.
And no one had rewarded him.
Until now.
Right before Haman walks in… ready to ask for Mordecai’s execution.
Timing like that doesn’t belong to coincidence.
It belongs to sovereignty.
The king asks, “What should be done for the man the king delights to honor?”
And Haman… oh Haman…
He thinks it’s about him.
Of course he does.
Pride always assumes it’s the center of the story.
So he paints a picture of glory. Royal robes. A king’s horse. A public parade.
He describes honor with such detail… because that’s what he secretly craves.
Then the words fall like thunder.
“Go at once… and do so for Mordecai.”
You can almost hear his soul collapse.
The man he hates.
The man he plotted against.
The man he refused to tolerate.
Now he has to lift him up.
Scripture records it simply in Esther 6:11:

“וַיִּקַּח הָמָן אֶת־הַלְּבוּשׁ וְאֶת־הַסּוּס… וַיַּלְבֵּשׁ אֶת־מָרְדֳּכַי”
(Vayikach Haman et-halevush ve’et-hasus… vayalbes et-Mordechai)
“So Haman took the robe and the horse… and he clothed Mordecai.”
The hands that built destruction… now dress honor.
The voice that plotted death… now proclaims dignity.
This is what God does.
He doesn’t just stop evil.
He flips it.
Completely.
And maybe this is where it gets uncomfortable…
Because this isn’t just Haman’s story.
It’s ours.
We don’t build gallows out of wood…
But we build them in our hearts.
Resentment.
Jealousy.
Comparison.
Silent bitterness.
Moments where we can’t stand to see someone else lifted because something in us feels overlooked.
Moments where we’d rather see someone fall than face what’s broken inside us.
But God sees it.
Not to shame you…
To save you.
Because pride leads to destruction, but surrender leads to transformation.
The Greek word for repentance in the New Testament is “μετάνοια” (metanoia) — a change of mind, a turning.
Not just feeling bad… but becoming different.
Haman never turned.
That’s the tragedy.
He experienced the humiliation… but not the transformation.
And it cost him everything.
But you… you’re still here.
Which means your story isn’t finished.
Jesus steps into stories like Haman’s… and rewrites them before they end the same way.
Where pride once ruled… grace can take over.
Where hatred once lived… healing can begin.
Where you once resisted… you can now surrender.
Because the cross is the ultimate reversal.
The One who was mocked… is now exalted.
The One who was crucified… is now King.
Philippians 2:9 says, “ὁ Θεὸς αὐτὸν ὑπερύψωσεν” (ho Theos auton hyperypsōsen) — “God highly exalted Him.”
That’s what God does.
He lifts what the world tries to crush.
And He humbles what pride tries to elevate.
So the question isn’t just about Haman…
It’s about you.
What are you building in your heart right now?
And what would it look like to surrender it before God has to tear it down?
Sit with it.
Feel it.
Let it expose what needs to be healed.
Be honest. This hit deeper than expected, didn’t it?
Follow closely if you want daily reminders that don’t entertain your flesh but strengthen your spirit.
And if you truly want to glorify God with your life… don’t just consume truth, support it being spread.
Join the mission.
This isn’t just content.
This is discipleship.
This is transformation.
This is war for souls.
And you’re invited to be part of it.
Because in the end…
The gallows you build in pride may become the stage where God humbles you… or the place where He begins to change you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Are You Fighting Lust… or Feeding It Quietly?
paragraphs:
Are You Fighting Lust… or Feeding It Quietly?
The Sin You Pray Against at Night but Entertain in Secret by Day
You closed the app… but not before looking one last time.

You told yourself it wasn’t that bad.
“It’s just a scroll.”
“It’s just curiosity.”
“It’s not like I acted on it.”

But something inside you went quiet afterward. Not peaceful… just quieter.
Like conviction got suffocated under justification.
And now here you are again… asking God for strength… while secretly keeping the door unlocked.
Be honest.
Are you really fighting lust… or just managing it well enough to keep your conscience calm?
Because Scripture doesn’t treat lust like a harmless thought—it exposes it like a fire already burning.
Jesus didn’t soften it. He intensified it.
In Matthew 5:28, He says:
“But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”

The Greek word used here for “lustful intent” is ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō)—it doesn’t mean accidental attraction. It means a deep, consuming desire… a craving that lingers… a willful gaze that feeds the imagination.

This isn’t about noticing beauty.
This is about choosing to dwell on it… to replay it… to mentally possess what God never gave you.
And the part that should shake you is this:
Jesus says the sin isn’t waiting for the act.
It already happened in your heart.

That late-night scrolling?
That saved content?
That “just five seconds” look that turned into minutes?
That wasn’t harmless.
That was participation.
James writes it plainly in James 1:14–15:

Lust is not neutral.
It’s pregnant.
It doesn’t stay contained—it grows, it matures, it demands more.
And what started as a glance slowly becomes a grip.

You don’t fall into lust overnight.
You feed it… quietly… consistently… until it feels normal.
That’s the deception.

You can still pray.
Still worship.
Still show up at church.
But inside… something is dividing.
David knew this war intimately. A man after God’s own heart… yet still capable of falling hard.
In Psalm 51:10, after his sin with Bathsheba, he cries out:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me.”
The Hebrew word for “create” here is בָּרָא (bara)—the same word used in Genesis when God created the heavens and the earth.
David wasn’t asking for a small adjustment.
He was asking for a complete re-creation.
Because he understood something most people ignore:

You can’t manage lust.
You need God to remake your heart.
And yet… we try to control it instead of crucify it.

We negotiate with it.
We rename it.
We excuse it because “everyone struggles.”
But Scripture doesn’t say “cope with your flesh.”
It says in Galatians 5:24:
“And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.”
Crucified.

Not hidden.
Not reduced.
Not scheduled around your spiritual life.
Killed.
So ask yourself again… and don’t rush past it this time:
Are you starving your flesh… or feeding it just enough to keep it alive?
Because what you feed… grows.
And what you starve… dies.
This is where it gets uncomfortable.

Because you already know the places you go that weaken you.
You already know the triggers you refuse to cut off.
You already know the moments where you choose compromise instead of obedience.
Jesus said in Matthew 5:29:
“If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away.”
That’s not about self-harm—it’s about radical separation from sin.
It means if something leads you there… it has to go.

Not later.
Not when you feel stronger.
Now.
Because delayed obedience is still disobedience.
And the truth most people won’t say out loud is this:
Some of you aren’t trapped.
You’re tolerating it.
You don’t hate the sin… you just hate the guilt.
But there is still grace.
Not cheap grace that excuses… but powerful grace that transforms.
1 Corinthians 10:13 says:
“No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and He will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation He will also provide the way of escape…”
The Greek word for “escape” is ἔκβασις (ekbasis)—it means a way out… an exit route already prepared.
Which means every time you said “I couldn’t help it”… wasn’t fully true.
There was a door.
But you didn’t take it.
And this isn’t written to condemn you—it’s written to wake you up.
Because Jesus didn’t die so you could stay stuck in cycles you secretly protect.
He died to break them.
To cleanse you.
To restore what lust has been draining out of your soul.
Pause.
Let it sit.
Let it expose what you’ve been hiding—even from yourself.
And be honest… not polished, not religious… just real.
Your honesty could be the moment someone else realizes they’re not alone.
You’ll need to come back to it the next time temptation whispers louder than truth.
And if you truly want to glorify God—not just in words but in action—support what is feeding your spirit instead of what’s feeding your flesh.
You don’t overcome lust by trying harder.
You overcome it by surrendering deeper.
Because the same Jesus who saw your secret sin… still chose the cross for you.
And He’s not done rewriting your story.
The battle isn’t proof you’ve lost… it’s proof you’re still being pursued.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “Is It Sin to Enjoy Flirting Even If It Goes Nowhere?”
paragraphs:
“Is It Sin to Enjoy Flirting Even If It Goes Nowhere?”
When a Smile Becomes a Secret Door Your Heart Quietly Walks Through
There are moments no one else sees.

A glance that lingers half a second too long. A message typed, deleted, then sent anyway. A joke that feels just a little too personal. A warmth in your chest that you pretend is harmless because “it’s not like anything is happening.”
You tell yourself it’s nothing.
No touching. No commitment. No betrayal… at least not the kind people can point to.
But something inside you knows this isn’t as innocent as it looks.
And that’s where the question starts to whisper louder than you want it to…
Is this sin?
Not the loud kind. Not the obvious kind. But the quiet kind that grows roots in hidden places.
Jesus once said something that dismantled the idea that sin is only what people can see. In Matthew 5:28, He spoke words that cut deeper than behavior and exposed the heart itself:
“But I say unto you, That whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart.”
The Greek doesn’t soften it. “πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν” (pros to epithymēsai autēn) means to desire, to long for, to set the heart upon.
This wasn’t about physical action. It was about direction.
Because the heart doesn’t stay neutral. It moves.
And flirting… even when it “goes nowhere”… is rarely standing still.
It’s leaning.
It’s opening.
It’s inviting something to grow in a place where God may not have permission to lead.
And that’s what makes this uncomfortable.
Because flirting feels light. Playful. Harmless. It gives attention without responsibility. Validation without accountability. Connection without covenant.
But the heart was never designed to play with intimacy like it’s disposable.
In Hebrew, the word for heart is “לֵב” (lev). It doesn’t just mean emotions. It means the core of your will, your desires, your identity. Your whole inner life.
So when Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life,” the Hebrew literally carries the sense of guarding it like a fortress.
Because everything flows from there.
Everything.
And flirting, when it stirs desire, begins to unlock doors in that fortress.
You might say, “But I don’t mean anything by it.”
And that might even be true… at first.
But intention doesn’t cancel influence.
A spark doesn’t ask permission before it becomes a fire.
James 1:14–15 breaks it down with unsettling clarity:
“But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin…”
The Greek word “ἐξελκόμενος” (exelkomenos) means being dragged away. Slowly. Subtly. Not forced… but pulled.
That’s how this works.
It doesn’t start with sin.
It starts with enjoyment.
Enjoying being noticed.
Enjoying the chemistry.
Enjoying the attention.
Enjoying the possibility.
And before you realize it, your heart is no longer where your body is.
You’re somewhere else… emotionally invested in something you told yourself didn’t matter.
That’s why this hits deeper than just a yes-or-no answer.
Because flirting isn’t always sin in the surface sense.
But it becomes sin the moment it begins to cultivate desire outside of God’s design, stir emotional attachment that leads away from purity, or invite intimacy that isn’t covered by commitment.
God isn’t against connection.
He created attraction. He designed desire. He authored love.
But He never intended for those things to be treated casually.
Because what feels light to you can leave weight in your soul.
And some of you already feel that weight.
You replay conversations in your head.
You check your phone more than you admit.
You feel a pull you didn’t expect.
And now you’re here… wondering if this is something you should walk away from.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because deep down, you know the difference between innocent and intentional.
You know when your heart is starting to lean.
And maybe this isn’t about condemnation.
Maybe this is about invitation.
Because Jesus doesn’t just expose what’s wrong… He restores what’s broken.
Even the hidden things.
Even the quiet compromises.
Even the moments no one else knows about.
In 1 Corinthians 6:19–20, Paul writes:
The word “ναός” (naos) refers to the inner sanctuary. The sacred place where God dwells.
That means your life isn’t casual.
Your heart isn’t disposable.
Your emotions aren’t a playground.
You carry something holy.
So the question isn’t just “Is flirting sin?”
The real question is…
Is this drawing me closer to Christ… or slowly pulling my heart somewhere He is not leading?
And only you can answer that honestly.
Let this not just be something you read.
Let it be something you respond to.
Because someone else needs to see your honesty and realize they’re not alone.
Follow closely if you’re tired of surface-level faith and want truth that actually confronts and heals.
And if you feel God stirring something deeper in you… a hunger to grow, to be sharpened, to be discipled, to stop living casually with your faith… then step into it.
If you truly want to glorify God, don’t just consume truth… support the mission that spreads it.
Because what you feed… grows.
And what you starve… dies.
And your heart deserves more than casual attention—it was created for covenant with Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Night Love Bled and Marriage Was Rewritten Forever
paragraphs: The Night Love Bled and Marriage Was Rewritten Forever
Somewhere between “I do” and “I’m tired,” something begins to fracture.
Not loudly. Not all at once.

It’s in the silence after an argument that never got resolved…
In the cold distance on the same bed meant to hold warmth…
In the quiet question no one dares to say out loud:
“Is this still what love is supposed to look like?”
And if we’re honest… many marriages aren’t collapsing because of one great betrayal… but because of a thousand small crucifixions no one understood.
Because we forgot what the Cross was actually teaching us.
Not religion. Not performance. Not who’s right.
Love.
But not the kind we post.
The kind that bleeds.
The kind that stays.
The kind that dies… so something greater can live.
When the apostle Paul wrote to husbands, he didn’t give advice. He gave a command that sounds almost impossible:
“ἀγαπᾶτε (agapate) τὰς γυναῖκας…” — “Love your wives…” (Ephesians 5:25)
But he didn’t stop there.

“…καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν…”
“…as Christ loved the church…”
And then he goes further.

“…καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.”
“…and gave Himself up for her.”
This is not poetic. This is violent.
“παρέδωκεν” (paredōken) — He handed Himself over. Surrendered. Yielded. Gave Himself to suffering voluntarily.
Husbands… this means your love is not proven in provision alone… not in authority… not in being “right”…
But in your willingness to die to yourself daily.

To your pride.
To your ego.
To your need to win every argument.
Because the Cross didn’t win arguments.
It absorbed them.
And wives… when Scripture calls you to respect and respond, it is not asking you to shrink… it is inviting you into something sacred.

“וְהָאִשָּׁה תִּירָא אֶת־בַּעְלָהּ” (Ephesians 5:33 Hebrew rendering conceptually)
“Let the wife revere her husband.”
But this reverence is not fear of harm… it is honor born from trust.
And trust cannot grow where love is unsafe.
Which is why the Cross stands in the center of marriage like a mirror no one can escape.
Because Jesus didn’t wait for the Church to be perfect before loving her.
Romans 5:8 says:

“Συνίστησιν δὲ τὴν ἑαυτοῦ ἀγάπην…”
“But God demonstrates His own love…”

“…ὅτι ἔτι ἁμαρτωλῶν ὄντων ἡμῶν…”
“…while we were still sinners…”

“…Χριστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀπέθανεν.”
“…Christ died for us.”
Still sinners.

Not when we fixed ourselves.
Not when we became easy to love.
Not when we deserved it.
So what does that mean for marriage?
It means love doesn’t wait for perfection.
It moves first.
It forgives first.
It softens first.
It chooses grace when everything inside you wants justice.
And this is where most marriages break…
Because we start keeping score instead of carrying crosses.

“Why should I apologize first?”
“Why should I always be the one adjusting?”
“Why do I have to keep forgiving?”
And quietly… pride builds a throne where the Cross was supposed to stand.
But Jesus never asked, “Why should I go first?”
He already knew what it would cost Him.
And He went anyway.
There are husbands reading this who feel disrespected, unheard, unseen.
There are wives reading this who feel unloved, exhausted, emotionally abandoned.
And both are silently waiting for the other to change first.
But the Cross interrupts that waiting.
Because love that waits to be deserved is not the love that saved you.
And maybe… just maybe… your marriage isn’t dying.
Maybe it’s being invited to die to the version of love that was never strong enough to sustain it.
Because resurrection never comes without crucifixion.
And no… this doesn’t mean tolerating abuse, sin, or harm.
Jesus confronted sin. He didn’t enable it.
But He also didn’t weaponize love to control.
He gave Himself… not to manipulate… but to redeem.
So imagine this…

A husband who listens even when he’s misunderstood…
A wife who honors even when she feels unseen…
Both kneeling before God instead of standing against each other…
Not perfect.
But surrendered.
Not flawless.
But fighting for each other instead of against each other.
That kind of marriage doesn’t just survive.
It preaches.
It becomes living evidence that Jesus is still rewriting stories.
And someone reading this right now… you felt something shift.
Not because this was comfortable.
But because it was true.
Be honest.
This hit deeper than you expected.
Someone you love needs to see this.

Your spouse.
A friend struggling silently.
A couple on the edge.
Even someone who doesn’t believe yet.
Because the Cross is not just theology.
It’s the blueprint for love that doesn’t collapse under pressure.
You will need to come back to this on a hard day… when emotions are loud and grace feels far.
And if this spoke to your spirit… if you want to go deeper into real discipleship, real healing, real understanding of Scripture…
Support the mission.
Not out of pressure… but out of purpose.
You’re helping spread the Gospel to people who are still lost, still hurting, still searching.
You don’t have to do this alone.
Walk with us.
Grow with us.
Fight for what God ordained… not with your strength… but with His.
Because at the end of it all… marriage was never meant to be sustained by feelings alone…
It was meant to be anchored to a Cross that already proved love doesn’t walk away.
The kind of love that dies… and still chooses you again.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Pray Loud… But Whisper About This: Why Christians Don’t Talk Honestly About Sexual Desire
paragraphs: They Pray Loud… But Whisper About This: Why Christians Don’t Talk Honestly About Sexual Desire
There’s a silence in the Church that feels holy on the outside… but hollow underneath.

You can hear it in the pauses.
In the way conversations change direction.
In the way certain struggles are dressed up in vague language—“temptation,” “weakness,” “fleshly battles”—but never named out loud.
Sexual desire.
Not the perversion. Not the scandal. Not the fall.
Just the desire itself.
And somehow, that alone has become something Christians are afraid to speak about honestly.
But the silence is not coming from Scripture.
It’s coming from shame.
Because deep down, many believers are carrying a quiet question they’ve never said out loud:
“If God made me this way… why do I feel so guilty for feeling it?”
And that question—left unanswered—has driven people into hiding, into cycles, into secret battles that never see the light where healing actually happens.
The truth is, the Bible never treats desire as the enemy.
It treats distortion as the enemy.
In the beginning, before sin fractured everything, desire existed without shame.
In Genesis 2:25, it says:

“וַיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עֲרוּמִּים… וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ”
Vayihyu sheneihem arummim… velo yitboshashu
“They were both naked… and they were not ashamed.”

No hiding.
No confusion.
No internal war.
Desire wasn’t dirty. It was aligned.
But something broke.
And when sin entered, the first thing humanity did was not just disobey…
They hid.

“וַיִּתְחַבֵּא הָאָדָם”
Vayitchabe ha’adam
“The man hid himself…” (Genesis 3:8)
That’s where the silence began.
Not in God.
In us.
Because after the fall, desire didn’t disappear—it became disordered.
And instead of learning how to bring it to God, we learned how to bury it from people.
That pattern still lives today.
We preach purity, but we don’t teach honesty.
We call for holiness, but we don’t create space for confession.

So people sit in church, lifting their hands on Sunday…
while carrying private battles Monday through Saturday.
And some of those battles are not even rebellion.
They’re confusion.
Because Scripture never commands the absence of desire.
It commands its transformation.
In James 1:14-15, the Greek says:

“ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος”
hekastos de peirazetai hypo tēs idias epithymias exelkomenos kai deleazomenos
“But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire…”
Notice that.
Temptation doesn’t come from desire existing.
It comes from desire leading.
Unsubmitted desire becomes distortion.
But submitted desire becomes worship.
And this is where everything changes.
Because the problem is not that Christians feel sexual desire.
The problem is that many have never been taught what to do with it.
So they either suppress it… or surrender to it.
And both lead to bondage.
Suppression creates shame.
Indulgence creates chains.
But surrender to Christ creates transformation.
This is what Paul was talking about in Romans 12:2:

“μεταμορφοῦσθε τῇ ἀνακαινώσει τοῦ νοός”
metamorphousthe tē anakainōsei tou noos
“Be transformed by the renewing of your mind.”
Not erased.
Transformed.
God doesn’t call you to become less human.
He calls you to become rightly aligned.
Even David—yes, that David—was not silent about his inner struggles.
After falling into sexual sin, he didn’t pretend.
He didn’t hide behind religious language.
He cried out in Psalm 51:10:

“לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים”
Lev tahor bera-li Elohim
“Create in me a clean heart, O God…”
He brought it into the light.
And that’s the part we’ve lost.
We want clean hearts without honest prayers.
We want purity without exposure.
We want freedom… without confession.
But healing doesn’t happen in silence.
It happens in truth.
And the Gospel was never about pretending you don’t struggle.
It was about bringing your struggle to the only One who can redeem it.
Jesus didn’t come for people who have no desires.
He came for people whose desires are broken, misdirected, wounded… and in need of restoration.
And this is where the scandal turns into grace.
Because the same Savior who met the woman caught in adultery didn’t start with condemnation.
He started with exposure… then compassion… then transformation.
“Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.” (John 8:11)
Grace didn’t ignore the issue.
It rewrote the ending.
That’s what He still does.
Even now.
Even with you.
So maybe the real question isn’t why Christians don’t talk about sexual desire honestly.
Maybe the question is…
What would happen if we finally did?
What would change in your life if you stopped hiding what God already sees?
What freedom might begin the moment you stop pretending you’re okay?
Be honest.
This hit deeper than you expected.
Your honesty might be the permission someone else needs to stop hiding too.
And if you want to go deeper—if you’re serious about real transformation, not surface-level religion—stay close.
Because this is not about perfection.
This is about becoming honest enough for God to rebuild you from the inside out.
And if this message fed something in your spirit… if it challenged you, convicted you, or brought clarity you’ve been missing… then don’t just consume it.
Support it.
If you want that kind of depth… that kind of accountability… that kind of transformation…
Because silence is where shame grows.
But truth is where freedom begins.
And the moment you stop hiding might be the moment God finally starts rewriting everything.
You were never meant to fight this in the dark.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They mocked him before the battle even began.
paragraphs: They mocked him before the battle even began.

Not out loud—no, this wasn’t the kind of mockery you hear. This was quieter. Heavier. The kind that settles in the air when numbers don’t add up, when logic screams defeat, when everything visible says, “You don’t stand a chance.”
King Abijah stood facing an army twice his size.
Four hundred thousand against eight hundred thousand. Steel against overwhelming steel. Breathing men staring at death, knowing the odds had already chosen a winner.
But heaven hadn’t.
And that’s the part most people miss.
Because this wasn’t just a war between two kingdoms.
This was a collision between trust and pride… between covenant and rebellion… between God’s promise and human confidence.
And somewhere in the tension of that battlefield, a truth was about to be written so loud it would echo for generations.
A truth you might need right now more than you realize.
The Scriptures say in 2 Chronicles 13:3–5 that Abijah faced Jeroboam with half the army. Jeroboam, the king of Israel, had strength, numbers, strategy—and confidence rooted in what he could see.
But Abijah had something else.
He stood on Mount Zemaraim and cried out—not to his soldiers first, but to the truth.

“הֲלֹא לָכֶם לָדַעַת כִּי יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל נָתַן מַמְלָכָה לְדָוִיד עַל־יִשְׂרָאֵל לְעוֹלָם לּוֹ וּלְבָנָיו בְּרִית מֶלַח”
(Hălō lāḵem lāḏa‘aṯ kî YHWH ’ĕlōhê Yiśrā’ēl nāṯan mamlāḵāh ləḏāwîḏ ‘al-Yiśrā’ēl lə‘ōlām lō ûləḇānāw bə·rîṯ melaḥ)
“Do you not know that the LORD God of Israel gave the kingship over Israel forever to David and his sons by a covenant of salt?”
A covenant of salt.
Not temporary. Not fragile. Not negotiable.
Salt in ancient times symbolized permanence—preservation that could not be undone.
Abijah wasn’t trusting his army.
He was standing on a promise.
And that’s where everything shifts.
Because Jeroboam had numbers, but he had abandoned the altar.
He had replaced priests. Created false worship. Built a system that looked religious but was disconnected from God’s presence.
And this is where the danger still lives today.
You can look strong… and still be spiritually empty.
You can build something impressive… and still be standing outside the will of God.
You can win in the eyes of people… and still be losing where it actually matters.
Jeroboam set an ambush behind Abijah. Strategically brilliant. Completely devastating.

From the front, an army.
From the back, a trap.
It was over.
At least, that’s what logic would say.
But Scripture says something different happened next.

“וַיִּצְעֲקוּ אֶל־יְהוָה”
(Vayyits‘ăqū ’el-YHWH)
“They cried out to the LORD.” — 2 Chronicles 13:14
Not strategized.
Not negotiated.
Not panicked.
They cried out.
Because when you run out of options, you finally discover where your strength was supposed to come from all along.
And God answered.
The text says God struck Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah.
Not Abijah’s skill.
Not Abijah’s numbers.
God.
That’s the part that humbles every prideful heart.
Because victory didn’t come from superiority.
It came from surrender.
And maybe that’s the part of your story you’ve been resisting.

You’ve been trying to outwork what only God can overcome.
Trying to fix what only grace can heal.
Trying to win battles God never asked you to fight alone.
But here’s what Abijah understood…
God doesn’t need favorable odds.
He needs faithful hearts.
The Greek word often used in the New Testament for victory—“νίκη” (níkē)—doesn’t just mean winning. It carries the idea of overcoming, prevailing despite resistance.
And that kind of victory never starts in your hands.
It starts in your surrender.
Because Jesus Himself became the ultimate picture of this.
He didn’t conquer Rome with armies.
He walked into death.

Publicly shamed.
Beaten.
Mocked.
A scandal.
The Greek word “σκάνδαλον” (skándalon) means a stumbling block… something offensive… something that doesn’t make sense.
That’s what the cross looked like.
And yet, that scandal became salvation.
That defeat became redemption.
That ending became everything.
From scandal… to grace.
Just like Abijah’s battlefield.
Just like your story.
You might feel surrounded right now.

By mistakes.
By fear.
By consequences.
By voices telling you it’s already over.
But the same God who answered a cry on a battlefield is still listening.
And He hasn’t forgotten His covenant.
He hasn’t changed His nature.
He hasn’t lost His power.
The question is not whether God can win your battle.
The question is whether you’ll finally stop fighting it your way.
Be honest…
How many times have you tried to handle things on your own first… and only cried out when everything collapsed?
How many hidden battles are you still pretending you can manage?
How many wounds are you covering instead of surrendering?
Because healing begins where honesty starts.
And someone else reading your comment might realize they’re not alone.
And if you’re serious about growing deeper in your walk with Christ… if you’re tired of surface-level faith and ready for real transformation…
Stay close to truth.
Because discipleship isn’t built in moments—it’s built in daily surrender.
And for those who want to go deeper…
There’s something waiting for you.
If this message moved you… if it stirred something deeper… don’t ignore that.
Step into it.
Because supporting what spreads the Gospel isn’t just generosity…
It’s obedience.
And it helps more souls encounter the same truth that just reached you.
Because one day, you’ll realize…
The battle that looked impossible was actually the place God was waiting for your surrender.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: When Attraction Overrides Calling: Jacob’s Obsession With Rachel
paragraphs:
When Attraction Overrides Calling: Jacob’s Obsession With Rachel
The love that looked pure… but quietly pulled him off God’s original path
It didn’t start as rebellion.
It rarely does.
It started with a glance… a moment… a feeling that felt too strong to question.
