Jacob wasn’t looking for trouble. He was running from his past, carrying the weight of deception, trying to outrun consequences that clung to his soul like dust. And then he saw her.
Rachel.
Scripture doesn’t rush past that moment. It slows down… almost like God wants you to feel it the way Jacob did.

“וְרָחֵל הָיְתָה יְפַת־תֹּאַר וִיפַת מַרְאֶה”
“And Rachel was beautiful of form and appearance.” (Genesis 29:17)
Not just beautiful.
Striking.
The kind of beauty that interrupts your thoughts… rearranges your priorities… and whispers, “This is what you’ve been missing.”
And just like that, something shifted inside Jacob.
Because attraction, when left unchecked, doesn’t stay in its lane.
It begins to rewrite your focus.
It begins to negotiate with your calling.
It begins to convince you that what you want must be what God wants too.
Jacob fell fast.
So fast that he offered seven years of his life—seven years of labor—for the chance to have Rachel. And the Bible says something that feels almost poetic… almost dangerous if you read it too quickly:

“וַיַּעֲבֹד יַעֲקֹב בְּרָחֵל שֶׁבַע שָׁנִים וַיִּהְיוּ בְעֵינָיו כְּיָמִים אֲחָדִים בְּאַהֲבָתוֹ אֹתָהּ”
“So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him but a few days because of his love for her.” (Genesis 29:20)
That sounds beautiful… until you realize what it cost him.
Because when attraction overrides calling, sacrifice starts to feel normal… even when it’s misaligned.
And here’s where it gets uncomfortable.
Because many people read this story and celebrate Jacob’s love.
But Scripture never says Rachel was God’s chosen vessel for covenant fulfillment.
Leah was.
Not the one Jacob wanted.
Not the one he cried for.
Not the one he worked for.
But the one God used to bring forth Judah…
And from Judah…
Jesus.
Let that sit with you.
The line of Christ did not come through the woman Jacob was obsessed with.
It came through the one he overlooked.

“וַיַּרְא יְהוָה כִּי שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה וַיִּפְתַּח אֶת־רַחְמָהּ”
“And the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, and He opened her womb…” (Genesis 29:31)
God saw what Jacob refused to see.
And while Jacob chased what looked right…
God moved through what felt wrong.
Because calling is not always wrapped in attraction.
Sometimes it’s hidden in discomfort… in rejection… in the places you didn’t choose.
Jacob’s obsession didn’t just cost him time.
It cost him clarity.
It delayed alignment.
It complicated his life with rivalry, tension, jealousy, and emotional chaos between two sisters… all because he followed what he felt instead of what God was doing.
And if you’re honest…
This isn’t just Jacob’s story.
It’s yours too.
How many times have you prayed for God’s will… but secretly hoped it looked like what you already wanted?
How many times have you labeled something “from God” simply because it felt right?
Be honest.
Because some of you are still holding onto a “Rachel” that God never called you to build your life around.
And it’s draining you.
Distracting you.
Pulling you further from the quiet, overlooked “Leah” spaces where God is actually trying to birth purpose.
This is where it gets real.
Because Jesus didn’t come through perfection.
He came through a messy lineage.
Through broken choices.
Through misaligned desires.
Through scandal.
And still…
God rewrote everything.
That’s grace.
Not approval of the mistake…
But redemption beyond it.

“χάρις δὲ τοῦ Θεοῦ εἰμι ὅ εἰμι”
“But by the grace of God I am what I am.” (1 Corinthians 15:10)
Grace doesn’t erase your past.
It repositions it.
Jacob’s story didn’t end in obsession.
It ended in transformation.
But only after wrestling… surrendering… and finally letting God rename him.
Israel.
And maybe that’s where you are right now.
In the tension.
Between what you want… and what God is doing.
Between attraction… and calling.
Between illusion… and truth.
So here’s the question that won’t leave you alone tonight:
What are you chasing… that God never asked you to carry?
And what are you ignoring… that God is actually trying to use?
Sit with it.
Because your answer might expose more than you expected.
If this stirred something deep in you, don’t keep it silent.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Someone you love is silently battling this same struggle.
And if you felt conviction while reading this, don’t just move on like nothing happened.
You’re going to need to come back to it when emotions start getting louder than God’s voice again.
And if you’re serious about going deeper…
There’s something waiting for you.
New resources are being added almost every day for believers who refuse to stay stagnant.
They grow.
They heal.
They get accountability, deeper teaching, and spiritual nourishment that goes beyond what you see here.
If you truly desire to glorify God, support the mission that spreads His truth.
Not out of pressure…
But out of purpose.
Because some messages aren’t just meant to be read…
They’re meant to be carried, shared, and lived.
And the life you’re called to live might be waiting on the other side of the thing you finally release.
You don’t need another sign.
You need surrender.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Didn’t Fall Overnight: The Quiet Line Between Attraction and Temptation (And Why Most People Cross It Without Noticing)
paragraphs: You Didn’t Fall Overnight: The Quiet Line Between Attraction and Temptation (And Why Most People Cross It Without Noticing)
It never starts with a decision.

It starts with a glance that lingers just a little too long… a conversation that feels too easy… a message you reread at midnight even though you know you shouldn’t. Nothing dramatic. Nothing loud. Just a quiet shift in your heart that nobody else can see.
And that’s exactly why it’s dangerous.
Because attraction feels innocent.
It feels human.
It feels like something you shouldn’t have to fight.
But somewhere in that space between noticing and nurturing… between feeling and feeding… a line exists. And most people don’t even realize when they’ve crossed it.
Jesus didn’t leave this vague.
He went straight for the heart.
In Matthew 5:28, the original Greek says, “πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν” — pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn — “everyone who looks at a woman in order to desire her…”
Not just looking.
Not just noticing.
But looking with intention… feeding the desire… letting it grow roots.
That word ἐπιθυμέω (epithymeō) doesn’t just mean attraction. It means craving. Longing. Setting your heart toward something that was never meant to belong to you.
That’s the line.
Attraction happens.
Temptation whispers.
But sin begins when you agree with it.
When you stop resisting and start entertaining.
When you replay the moment instead of rejecting it.
When your heart quietly says, “This feels good… I want more.”
And suddenly, what once felt harmless becomes something you hide.
You start guarding your phone.
You start justifying your thoughts.
You start creating little private worlds where your emotions can wander without consequences.
But there are always consequences.

James 1:14–15 breaks it down with unsettling clarity: “ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος” — each person is tempted when they are dragged away and enticed by their own desire. Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin.
Dragged.
Enticed.
Conceived.
It’s not instant.
It’s a process.
And most people don’t fall because they wanted to destroy their life.
They fall because they didn’t take the early stages seriously.
They played with something that was already pulling them.
Maybe that’s you right now.
You’re not “doing anything wrong”… at least not outwardly.
But inside, something is shifting.
Your thoughts are getting harder to control.
Your emotions are getting harder to silence.
Your boundaries are getting weaker.
And you keep telling yourself, “I still have control.”
That’s the most dangerous lie.
Because temptation doesn’t need your permission to show up.
But it does need your cooperation to stay.
Even David — a man after God’s own heart — didn’t fall when he saw Bathsheba.
He fell when he kept looking.
2 Samuel 11 doesn’t describe a man who instantly collapsed.
It describes a man who lingered… who sent… who inquired… who acted.
Step by step.
Moment by moment.
Until what started as attraction became destruction.
Sin rarely announces itself.
It disguises itself as curiosity.
As connection.
As something that “just happened.”
But nothing just happens in the heart.
Jesus sees deeper than behavior.
He sees intention.
That’s why in the Hebrew understanding of the heart — לֵב (lev) — it’s not just emotions. It’s will, desire, decision. The control center of your entire life.
So when your heart leans toward something… it’s already moving your life in that direction.
The real question isn’t “Did I sin yet?”
The real question is “Where is my heart going?”
Because if your heart is drifting… your life will follow.
And yet… this isn’t where the story ends.
Because you’re not reading this by accident.
Conviction is not condemnation.
It’s an invitation.
An interruption of grace.
A moment where God steps into your quiet compromise and says, “Come back before this goes further.”
Even now… there is mercy.
Even now… there is a way out.
1 Corinthians 10:13 reminds us that no temptation is beyond what is common to man, and God always provides a way of escape.
Not later.
Not after you fall.
But in the moment.
The exit is always there.
But you have to choose it.
You have to close the door.
You have to stop feeding what’s been growing in the dark.
You have to be honest… with yourself and with God.
So be honest right now.
Not with me.
With Him.
Have you been entertaining something you should have been resisting?
Have you been calling it “harmless” when deep down you know it’s not?
Have you been standing too close to a line you were never meant to flirt with?
Sit in it.
Let it confront you.
Let it cleanse you.
And if you feel that tension in your chest right now… that pull between conviction and resistance…
You’re not the only one fighting this.
And your honesty might be the thing that helps someone else finally break their silence too.
You’ll need to come back to truth when the feelings return.
Because growing in Christ isn’t a one-time decision… it’s a daily fight for your heart.
And if you truly want to glorify God with your life… then support what is feeding your spirit.
You don’t have to walk this alone.
Stay close to truth.
Stay close to Him.
Because the line you keep flirting with today… could become the regret you carry tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Counted the Fish… But Missed the Moment That Changed Everything Forever
paragraphs: They Counted the Fish… But Missed the Moment That Changed Everything Forever

There are moments in Scripture that feel almost… unnecessary at first glance. Details that seem too specific, too random, almost like they slipped into the story unnoticed. But then you look again. And you realize—nothing God records is accidental.
John 21 doesn’t just tell us that the disciples caught fish. It tells us they caught exactly 153.
Not 150. Not “a lot.” Not “more than they expected.”
One hundred fifty-three.
And suddenly, the question won’t leave you alone…
Why did the Holy Spirit preserve that number?
Because buried in that number is a story about failure, restoration, calling, and a grace so scandalous it rewrites everything.
The night before that miracle, the disciples were not walking in victory. They were not preaching boldly. They were not healing the sick or casting out demons.
They went back to fishing.
Back to what felt safe.
Back to what they knew before Jesus changed everything.
Simon Peter, the same man who said, “Even if all fall away, I will not,” had already denied Jesus three times. The weight of that failure didn’t just disappear. It followed him. It whispered to him.
“You blew it.”
And so he said, “I’m going fishing.”

In the Greek text, John records it as:
“Ὑπάγω ἁλιεύειν” (Hypagō halieuein)
“I am going away to fish.”
Not just a casual activity. A retreat. A quiet resignation.
The others followed him.
Isn’t that how it happens?
When one person loses fire, others drift too.
They fished all night. And caught nothing.
Nothing.
The emptiness wasn’t just in their nets. It was in their hearts.
Then morning came.
And Jesus stood on the shore.
But they didn’t recognize Him.
How many times has He stood close… and we didn’t realize?
He called out to them, “Children, do you have any fish?”

In Greek:
“Παιδία, μή τι προσφάγιον ἔχετε;” (Paidia, mē ti prosphagion echete?)
“Little ones… do you have anything to eat?”
They answered Him with a single word.
“No.”
Then He said something that must have felt almost insulting.
“Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.”
And somehow… they obeyed.
They cast the net.
And suddenly—everything changed.

John records:
“They were not able to haul it in, because of the quantity of fish.”
And then, when they finally pulled it in, the Holy Spirit slows the moment down and says:
“There were 153 fish.”

In Greek:
“ἑκατὸν πεντήκοντα τριῶν” (hekaton pentēkonta triōn)
Why?
Because this was not just a miracle of provision.
This was a moment of restoration.

Some early church scholars believed 153 symbolized the known number of fish species at the time—meaning the Gospel would reach every kind of person. Others saw numerical patterns tied to divine completeness.
But beyond theories, there is something deeper, something personal.
Jesus didn’t just give them fish.
He recreated the moment where it all began.
In Luke 5, the first time He called Peter, there was also a miraculous catch of fish.
And now, after Peter’s greatest failure… Jesus brings him back to the same place.
Not to shame him.
But to restore him.
Because Jesus doesn’t erase your past by ignoring it.
He redeems it by rewriting it.
And then comes the moment that breaks everything open.
Jesus sits with Peter.
Three times He asks him, “Do you love Me?”

In Greek:
“ἀγαπᾷς με;” (agapas me?)

And Peter responds:
“φιλῶ σε” (philo se)
“I love You… as a friend.”
Three denials.
Three restorations.
Grace meeting failure face-to-face.
And here’s where the 153 fish becomes more than a number.
It becomes proof that even after failure, even after shame, even after running back to your old life…
Jesus still fills your empty nets.
Not because you earned it.
But because He is faithful to who He is.
Be honest…
How many times have you gone back to what God already called you out of?
How many nights have you labored, trying to fix your life without Him… and caught nothing?
This is not just Peter’s story.
This is yours.
This is mine.
And this is why this moment matters so much.
Because Jesus didn’t wait for Peter to come back perfect.
He met him in his failure.
He stood on the shore of his regret.
And He called him forward again.
153 fish.
Not random.
Not meaningless.
Every fish counted… just like every moment of your life is seen.
Every failure.
Every silent tear.
Every hidden struggle.
Counted.
Known.
And still… He calls you.
Be honest.
You’re not the only one here.
There are people reading this who feel exactly what you feel.
Because there will be a day you feel empty again… and you’ll need to remember that empty nets are not the end of your story.
Follow closely.
Not just casually.
Because truth like this is not something you visit… it’s something you stay near.
And if you truly want to glorify God through what you receive, then support what feeds your spirit.
If something in your spirit is telling you this is where you need to grow, don’t ignore it.
Step in.
Because at the end of everything… it was never just about the fish.
It was about the Savior who still calls you after you fail.
And the truth that refuses to let you stay where you broke.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They told you it was just a number.
paragraphs: They told you it was just a number.
Four hundred thirty years.

A statistic buried in ancient text… easy to skim, easy to forget… until you realize that number carries the weight of suffering, silence, broken promises, and a God who seemed quiet—but was never absent.
And suddenly it’s not just about Israel anymore.
It’s about you.
Because there are seasons in your life that feel just like Egypt… long, suffocating, and unanswered.
So how do we know Israel really spent 430 years connected to Egypt?
And more importantly… what does that mean for your story?
The answer doesn’t begin with archaeology. It begins with a promise that sounded impossible when it was first spoken.
In Genesis 15:13, God speaks to Abram in a moment that feels almost unsettling. The Hebrew text says:
"וַיֹּאמֶר לְאַבְרָם יָדֹעַ תֵּדַע כִּי־גֵר יִהְיֶה זַרְעֲךָ בְּאֶרֶץ לֹא לָהֶם… וַעֲבָדוּם וְעִנּוּ אֹתָם אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה"
“Know for certain that your offspring will be strangers in a land not their own… and they will be enslaved and oppressed four hundred years.”
Did you catch that?
Before Israel ever stepped foot in Egypt… before Joseph was sold… before Pharaoh hardened his heart… God already saw the suffering.
Nothing caught Him off guard.

Not the chains.
Not the waiting.
Not the silence.
And yet… He allowed it.
That’s the part we don’t like to talk about.
Because it sounds too familiar.

You’ve prayed.
You’ve waited.
You’ve cried out.
And it feels like heaven is watching… but not intervening.
Then comes Exodus 12:40–41, where the timeline sharpens with precision:
"וּמוֹשַׁב בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר יָשְׁבוּ בְּמִצְרָיִם שְׁלֹשִׁים שָׁנָה וְאַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שָׁנָה"
“Now the dwelling of the sons of Israel who lived in Egypt was four hundred and thirty years.”
Four hundred. Thirty.
Not symbolic. Not exaggerated.
Measured.
Counted.
Felt.
Every year of labor. Every cry in the night. Every generation wondering if God had forgotten.
But here’s where it gets deeper… and where many people misunderstand.

The Greek translation in the Septuagint (LXX) and Paul’s explanation in Galatians 3:17 expand the timeline to include the entire period from Abraham to the Exodus—not just the years physically in Egypt.
Paul writes:
“The law… came 430 years later.”
So what does that mean?
It means the 430 years represents the full span of God’s covenant journey—from promise to fulfillment.
From calling… to captivity… to deliverance.
This wasn’t just about geography.
It was about transformation.
Israel didn’t just leave Egypt.
They were forged in it.
And that changes everything.
Because maybe your “Egypt” isn’t punishment.
Maybe it’s preparation.
Maybe the delay… the struggle… the unanswered questions… aren’t signs that God has abandoned you.
Maybe they are evidence that He is writing something deeper than you can see.
Acts 7:6 echoes the same truth in Greek:
"ἔσται τὸ σπέρμα αὐτοῦ πάροικον… καὶ δουλώσουσιν αὐτὸ καὶ κακώσουσιν ἔτη τετρακόσια"
“His descendants will be strangers… enslaved and mistreated four hundred years.”
This wasn’t hidden.
This wasn’t accidental.
This was part of a divine narrative that moved from scandal… to grace.
Because let’s be honest.
Israel’s story isn’t clean.
It’s messy. It’s painful. It’s filled with doubt, rebellion, fear, and moments where they questioned God openly.
Just like you.
Just like me.
And yet… God still fulfilled His promise.
Exactly.
To the year.
Exodus 12:41 says it happened “on that very day.”
Not late.
Not early.
Not forgotten.
Exact.
And that should shake something inside you.
Because if God was that precise with Israel…
What makes you think He’s careless with your life?
You might feel like you’re stuck in year 3… or year 30… or year 300 of your own wilderness.
But heaven doesn’t lose track of time.
God doesn’t misplace promises.
He doesn’t abandon stories halfway through.
He finishes them.
But here’s the truth most people avoid…
Deliverance came, yes.
But it came through blood.
Through the Passover lamb.
Through judgment.
Through surrender.
And this is where everything shifts to Jesus.
Because the same God who counted 430 years to deliver Israel…
Counted every moment leading to the cross.
Where another Lamb would be sacrificed.
Not just to free a nation…
But to free your soul.
This is not just history.
This is a mirror.
Because some of you are still in Egypt spiritually.
Still bound.
Still pretending you're free while carrying chains nobody sees.
And you know it.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because freedom begins where honesty starts.
And someone you know needs this truth too.
And if you’ve been fighting quietly…
Because your story isn’t over.
Not even close.
And if something inside you is waking up… if you feel that pull to go deeper… to stop playing surface-level faith…
Not for me.
For your growth.
For your healing.
For your relationship with Jesus.
Because the truth is… staying close to truth changes everything.
If you truly want to glorify God… don’t just consume truth.
Carry it.
Support it.
Because what feeds your spirit should also be sustained.
Because at the end of the day…
This was never just about 430 years.
It was about a God who never breaks His word.
A God who walks through generations of pain just to fulfill a promise.
A God who turns slavery into freedom…
And sinners into sons.
And maybe… just maybe…
Your Egypt is the beginning of your exodus.
The clock isn’t against you.
It’s working for you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Thought He Escaped Death… But What If Enoch Was Showing Us Something Far More Terrifying—and Beautiful?
paragraphs: They Thought He Escaped Death… But What If Enoch Was Showing Us Something Far More Terrifying—and Beautiful?
The Man Who Walked So Close to God… He Never Came Back
Nobody saw it coming.
One moment, Enoch was here—breathing the same dust as everyone else, walking the same broken ground, surrounded by the same corruption that was swallowing the world whole.
And then… he wasn’t.

No funeral.
No grave.
No body to mourn.
Just a sentence that has haunted readers for generations:
“Enoch walked with God; then he was no more, because God took him.” (Genesis 5:24)

In Hebrew, it reads:
וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ חֲנוֹךְ אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים וְאֵינֶנּוּ כִּי־לָקַח אֹתוֹ אֱלֹהִים
Vayyithalekh Chanokh et-ha’Elohim ve’einenû ki-lakaḥ oto Elohim
He walked… and then he wasn’t… because God took him.
That word “took”—לָקַח (laqach)—is not casual. It is intimate. Deliberate. Personal. It’s the same kind of taking used when God receives something into His own possession.
God didn’t just remove Enoch.
God claimed him.
And if you read too fast, you’ll miss it.
Because the real question isn’t just why Enoch never died.
It’s why everyone else did.
Because Genesis 5 reads like a funeral drumbeat.
“And he died… and he died… and he died…”
Over and over again.
Except for one man.
Enoch breaks the pattern like a crack in a coffin.
And suddenly, Scripture whispers something that should unsettle you if you’re really paying attention—
Death was never supposed to be normal.
Hebrews 11:5 pulls the veil back even further:
“By faith Enoch was taken (μετετέθη – metetethē) so that he did not see death; and he was not found, because God had taken him. For before he was taken, he was commended as having pleased God.”
Metetethē.
Transferred. Relocated. Moved from one place to another.
Not escaped.
Moved.
Let that sit in your chest for a second.
Enoch didn’t cheat death.
He walked so deeply with God that death itself lost its grip on him.
And here’s where it gets uncomfortable.
Because Enoch lived in one of the darkest periods in human history—before the flood, when corruption, violence, and rebellion saturated the earth.
And yet, in the middle of that chaos, he walked with God.
The Hebrew phrase “walked with God” — וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ אֶת־הָאֱלֹהִים (vayyithalekh et-ha’Elohim) — implies ongoing, habitual, intimate movement.
Not occasional prayer.
Not Sunday religion.
A life aligned. Step for step.
Breath for breath.
He didn’t visit God.
He lived with Him.
So why didn’t Enoch die?
Because death is the consequence of separation from God.
“For the wages of sin is death…” (Romans 6:23)
But Enoch’s life was marked by something rare—continuous fellowship.
He wasn’t sinless. Scripture never says that.
But he was surrendered.
And surrender changes everything.
And maybe this is the part no one tells you plainly—
Enoch is not just a mystery.
He’s a mirror.
Because every one of us is walking somewhere.

Some are walking with culture.
Some are walking with hidden sin.
Some are walking with pain they refuse to release.
Some are walking with God… but only when it’s convenient.
But Enoch walked with God until there was no distance left between them.
Until heaven felt closer than earth.
Until God simply said…
“Come home.”
And suddenly this ancient story stops being distant.
It becomes personal.
Because deep down, you know the tension.
You know what it feels like to live divided.
To smile publicly but wrestle privately.
To carry things you’ve never confessed.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because Enoch’s story is not about escaping death.
It’s about exposing distance.
Distance between you and God.
Distance that Jesus came to close.
Because thousands of years after Enoch walked into eternity, another man would walk this earth perfectly.
Jesus Christ.
And unlike Enoch, Jesus did not avoid death.
He walked straight into it.
Willingly.
Publicly.
Brutally.

“Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?” (Matthew 27:46)
Ἠλί Ἠλί λεμὰ σαβαχθανί
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
He experienced the separation we deserved…
So we could experience the closeness Enoch had.
That’s the Gospel.
Not that we escape death like Enoch.
But that through Christ, death no longer owns us.
“He who believes in Me, though he die, yet shall he live.” (John 11:25)
So the real question is not:
Why didn’t Enoch die?
The real question is:
Why are you still living far from the God who is calling you closer?
Because one day, every one of us will be “taken.”
Not all like Enoch.
Some through death.
Some when Christ returns.
But every soul will stand before God.
And only one thing will matter—
Did you walk with Him?
Or did you just know about Him?
And if something inside you is stirring… don’t ignore it.
That’s not emotion.
That’s conviction.
Because this is what we’re building here—daily truth, daily conviction, daily reminders that Jesus is still rewriting lives.
And if you’re ready to go deeper, to be sharpened, to grow, to be held accountable, to be fed with real biblical truth—not watered-down motivation—then step into it.
Because this isn’t about content.
It’s about transformation.
And if Enoch’s life teaches us anything, it’s this—
God is still looking for people who will walk so closely with Him… that everything else fades.
And maybe tonight, instead of running from Him…
You take one step closer.
Because the distance you feel…
Was never created by Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: She Was Chosen… But Never Wanted
paragraphs:
She Was Chosen… But Never Wanted
Leah Didn’t Lack Value… She Lacked His Desire—and That Changed Everything
She heard the footsteps again.
Every night felt the same.

Not because she didn’t belong there…
but because she knew, deep in the quiet places of her soul,
that she was not the one he longed for.
Leah was chosen.
But she was not desired.

And if you’ve ever been in a place where you were present but not preferred… where you gave your best but felt unseen… where you were committed but not cherished… then her story isn’t ancient history.
It’s painfully familiar.
Scripture does not hide her reality.
In Genesis 29:31, it says, “When the LORD saw that Leah was hated…”
The Hebrew word used there is שְׂנוּאָה (senu’ah) — often translated “hated,” but more accurately meaning rejected, unloved, set aside in affection.
Leah wasn’t worthless.
She wasn’t broken.
She wasn’t lacking.
She was simply not the one he desired.
And that kind of pain cuts deeper than rejection itself.
Because it whispers, “You’re good… just not good enough.”
Jacob loved Rachel.
Everyone knew it.
The text makes it clear.
In Genesis 29:30, “He loved Rachel more than Leah.”
Not instead of.
More than.
That word “more” becomes a dagger when you live on the lesser side of love.
Leah lived in comparison.
In competition she never signed up for.
In a marriage that felt like proximity without intimacy.
And yet… God saw her.
Not the version others tolerated.
Not the version Jacob overlooked.
But her.
Fully.
Completely.
Deeply.
Genesis 29:31 continues, “...He opened her womb, but Rachel was barren.”
The God who sees does something radical.
He doesn’t erase Leah’s pain immediately.
He enters it.
He works through it.
Leah begins to bear children.
And every child carries a cry.
A longing.
A wound trying to heal.
Her first son: Reuben.
She says in Genesis 29:32, “Because the LORD has seen my affliction; surely now my husband will love me.”
The Hebrew word for “seen” is רָאָה (ra’ah) — not just noticing, but perceiving deeply, understanding fully.
God saw her.
But she still longed for Jacob to see her too.
Her second son: Simeon.
Genesis 29:33, “Because the LORD has heard that I am hated…”
The word “heard” is שָׁמַע (shama’) — to listen with attention, to respond.
God wasn’t ignoring her cries.
But she still hoped Jacob would.
Her third son: Levi.
Genesis 29:34, “Now this time my husband will become attached to me…”
The word “attached” is לָוָה (lavah) — to join, to cling, to be bound.
She was still chasing affection.
Still trying to earn love through performance.
Through giving.
Through proving.
Maybe if I do more…
Maybe if I give him more sons…
Maybe if I become more…
Then finally… I’ll be enough.
But something shifts.
Not in Jacob.
In Leah.
Her fourth son is born.
Judah.
And for the first time, her words change.
Genesis 29:35, “This time I will praise the LORD.”
The Hebrew word for praise is יָדָה (yadah) — to surrender, to throw out the hands in worship.
She stops striving for Jacob’s love.
And starts resting in God’s presence.
That moment… changes everything.
Because Judah becomes the line of kings.
Judah becomes the tribe of David.
Judah becomes the lineage of Jesus Christ.
Let that sink in.

The woman who felt unwanted…
becomes the vessel through which the Savior enters the world.
She lacked his desire…
But she was chosen by God for something eternal.
And this is where the Gospel explodes into the story.
Because centuries later, another Man would come.
Jesus.
Rejected.
Despised.
Isaiah 53:3 says, “He was despised and rejected by men…”
The Hebrew says נִבְזֶה וַחֲדַל אִישִׁים (nivzeh va-chadal ishím) — despised, forsaken, abandoned.
He knows what it feels like to not be desired.
He understands Leah.
He understands you.
On the cross, Jesus carries every moment you felt overlooked, unloved, replaced, forgotten.
And instead of demanding your perfection…
He offers you His love.
Not partial.
Not conditional.
Not “less than.”
But complete.
In the Greek, when Jesus says “It is finished” in John 19:30, the word is τετέλεσται (tetelestai) — paid in full, accomplished, nothing lacking.
You don’t have to compete anymore.
You don’t have to perform anymore.
You don’t have to beg for love anymore.
Because in Christ, you are fully seen, fully known, and fully loved.
Leah didn’t lack value.
She lacked his desire.
But God rewrote her story.
And He’s rewriting yours too.
So be honest.
Did this hit something you’ve been trying to ignore?
Someone you love is living Leah’s story right now.
Because sometimes healing starts with being seen.
And sometimes God uses your share to reach the one who feels forgotten.
Not for inspiration.
For survival.
For the nights when you question your worth.
For the moments when comparison suffocates your peace.
And if this message stirred something deeper in you…
Follow.
Stay close.
Because truth like this isn’t meant to be heard once.
It’s meant to reshape you daily.
If you truly want to glorify God with your life… then don’t just consume truth.
Help it reach others.
Partner with this mission.
And beyond that…
You don’t have to walk this journey alone.
Because the truth is…
The love you were begging for from people… was already secured for you at the cross.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: CAN PRAYER ALONE DEFEAT SEXUAL TEMPTATION?
paragraphs:
CAN PRAYER ALONE DEFEAT SEXUAL TEMPTATION?
The silent battle no one talks about… and the truth that will either free you or expose you.
You prayed again last night.

Not the polished kind. Not the “church voice.”
The desperate kind. The kind that sounds more like breaking than believing.
“God… please take this away from me.”
And for a moment, it felt real. Clean. Lighter. Like maybe this time… it worked.
But then the silence came back.
And so did the thoughts.

And suddenly you weren’t just fighting temptation anymore…
you were fighting disappointment. Shame. Confusion. Even doubt.
Because no one told you what to do when prayer doesn’t feel like enough.
So now you're asking the question quietly, maybe even afraid to say it out loud:
Can prayer alone actually defeat sexual temptation… or am I missing something?
And if you’ve ever asked that… you’re not weak.
You’re finally being honest.
Because Scripture never lied to you. We just didn’t always understand it fully.
When Jesus said in Matthew 26:41, He didn’t whisper comfort—He issued a warning:
“Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.”
In the original Greek, “watch” is γρηγορεῖτε (grēgoreite) — stay awake, be vigilant, be alert like your life depends on it.
And “pray” is προσεύχεσθε (proseuchesthe) — continuous, active, ongoing communion with God.
Not one or the other.
Both.
Because prayer alone was never meant to replace vigilance… it was meant to fuel it.
And this is where many believers quietly lose the battle.
You prayed… but you didn’t guard your eyes.
You asked God for strength… but kept feeding the same doorway that weakness walks through.
You cried out for deliverance… but didn’t flee.
And Scripture is painfully clear about that part.
“Flee sexual immorality.” — 1 Corinthians 6:18
The word “flee” in Greek is φεύγετε (pheugete) — run away, escape, avoid at all costs.
Not negotiate. Not manage. Not tolerate.
Run.
Joseph didn’t pray when Potiphar’s wife grabbed him.
He ran.
He left his cloak behind if it meant keeping his soul intact.
Because sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do… is leave.
And that truth stings because it removes our favorite excuse:
“I already prayed about it.”
Prayer is not permission to stay in the environment that’s killing you.
Prayer is power… but obedience is the response that activates it.
Even Jesus, in the wilderness, didn’t just pray.
He responded with the Word.
“It is written…” — Matthew 4:4
In Greek, γέγραπται (gegraptai) — it stands written, permanently established truth.
That means victory wasn’t just emotional… it was anchored in truth.

So when temptation whispers,
you don’t just feel your way through it…
you confront it with what God has already said.
David learned this the hard way.
He didn’t fall into sin because he lacked prayer.
He fell because he stayed where he shouldn’t have stayed.
“At the time when kings go out to battle… David remained at Jerusalem.” — 2 Samuel 11:1
That one decision… led to Bathsheba, adultery, deception, and blood.
And yet, even there… grace stepped in.
In Psalm 51, David cries:
“Create in me a clean heart, O God…”
In Hebrew, “create” is בְּרָא (bara) — the same word used in Genesis when God created the world out of nothing.
Meaning David wasn’t asking for improvement.
He was asking for a miracle.
Because once you realize the depth of your struggle… you stop pretending you can fix it yourself.
And that’s where this becomes real.
Because maybe you’re not just dealing with temptation.
Maybe you’re tired of pretending you’re okay.
Maybe you’re exhausted from fighting something that keeps coming back stronger than your last prayer.
Maybe you love God… but you don’t love who you are when no one’s watching.
And that tension is suffocating.
So hear this clearly:
Prayer alone is powerful… but it was never designed to stand alone.
God calls you to pray…
and to fight…
and to flee…
and to renew your mind…
and to crucify the flesh.
“Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh.” — Galatians 5:16
“Walk” in Greek is περιπατεῖτε (peripateite) — to live daily, consistently, step by step.
This is not a one-time victory.
It’s a lifestyle of surrender.
And yes… it’s hard.
But it’s also possible.
Because this isn’t about your willpower.
It’s about the power of the One who already overcame.
You are not fighting for victory.
You are fighting from it.
And if that truth is hitting somewhere deeper than you expected…
be honest.
You’re not alone in this battle.
But isolation will convince you that you are.
And if you’re serious about walking in freedom, not just visiting it…
Because staying close to truth is how you stay anchored when temptation hits again.
And if you want to go deeper—real discipleship, real growth, real transformation—
This isn’t about selling you something.
It’s about strengthening you for a battle that’s already trying to destroy you.
Because glorifying God isn’t passive.
It costs something.
And supporting what feeds your spirit… is part of that obedience.
Here’s the truth you can’t ignore:
You don’t lose the battle in the moment of temptation.
You lose it in the moments you thought didn’t matter.
And maybe tonight… is the moment everything changes.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Told You Hell Was Fire… But What If the Most Terrifying Part Isn’t the Flames?
paragraphs: They Told You Hell Was Fire… But What If the Most Terrifying Part Isn’t the Flames?
There is a silence no one prepares you for.

Not the kind you enjoy when the world finally stops talking… but the kind that feels like something sacred has been taken away forever. The kind of silence where your soul realizes it has been cut off from the very voice that once called your name.
We’ve been taught to fear the fire.
The flames. The torment. The imagery of burning.
But what if the fire isn’t the deepest horror of hell?
What if the true terror… is the absence?
Jesus didn’t just describe hell with fire. He described something far more unsettling. Something that doesn’t scream… it empties.
In Matthew 8:12, He said people would be cast into “outer darkness.”
The Greek phrase is σκότος τὸ ἐξώτερον (skotos to exoteron) — not just darkness, but a darkness that exists outside… separated… cut off. Not just a place, but a condition of being removed.
Removed from light.
Removed from presence.
Removed from God.
And that’s where most people misunderstand everything.
Because fire burns the body… but separation destroys the soul.
In 2 Thessalonians 1:9, Paul writes that those who reject God will suffer “everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord.”
The Greek says: ἀπὸ προσώπου τοῦ Κυρίου (apo prosopou tou Kyriou) — literally, “away from the face of the Lord.”
Not just punishment.
Distance.
Not just pain.
Separation.
You were never designed to exist apart from Him.
In Genesis, when Adam sinned, the first consequence wasn’t fire. It was hiding.
He lost presence before he lost anything else.
That’s always been the pattern.
Hell is not just where God sends people.
It is where His presence is no longer felt.
And if you’ve ever had a moment in your life where you felt spiritually numb… where prayer felt empty… where worship felt distant… where everything felt hollow…
You’ve tasted a shadow of it.
Just a shadow.
Now imagine that… without end.
Jesus also spoke of fire — yes. In Mark 9:48, He says, “where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched.”
The Greek word for fire is πῦρ (pyr), meaning literal fire, but often used symbolically to describe judgment, purification, or consuming reality.
Fire reveals.
Fire consumes.
Fire exposes.
But fire is not the whole picture.
Because Revelation 20:14 calls hell “the second death.”
Death in Scripture isn’t just about physical ending.
It’s separation.
James 2:26 says the body without the spirit is dead.
So what is the second death?
The soul… without God.
And suddenly, the fire makes more sense.
Because the flames are not random punishment.
They are the external expression of an internal reality — a soul cut off from the only source of life.
No peace.
No love.
No hope.
No presence.
Just existence… without Him.
And that is what makes hell unbearable.
Not just what is there…
But Who isn’t.
Now pause.
Be honest.
Have you ever chased things that pulled you away from God?
Have you ever chosen sin knowing it would create distance?
Have you ever felt that quiet emptiness afterward?
That wasn’t just guilt.
That was a glimpse.
A warning.
Because sin doesn’t just break rules.
It breaks connection.
Isaiah 59:2 says, “your iniquities have separated you from your God.”
The Hebrew word for separated is בָּדַל (badal) — to divide, to sever, to cut off.
Sin is not just rebellion.
It is disconnection.
And if left unrepented… it leads to permanent separation.
That is hell.
But this is where everything changes.
Because the Gospel is not just about escaping fire.
It’s about restoring presence.
When Jesus hung on the cross, something happened that most people read past too quickly.
In Matthew 27:46, He cried out:
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”
In Aramaic, He said:
“Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?”
Sabachthani means “to abandon, to leave, to forsake completely.”
For the first time… the Son felt separation.
Not because He sinned.
But because He took yours.
He stepped into the absence… so you wouldn’t have to stay there.
He absorbed the separation.
He carried the distance.
He endured the silence.
So you could be brought back into the presence of God.
That’s the real rescue.
Not just from flames…
But from being forever without Him.
And maybe this is hitting deeper than you expected.
Maybe you’ve been focused on avoiding punishment…
But not realizing you’ve been drifting from presence.
Maybe you look okay on the outside…
But inside, something feels distant.
Cold.
Disconnected.
Be honest.
This isn’t about fear anymore.
This is about reality.
Because He already sees you.
And He’s still calling you back.
Right now.
Not later.
Not when you feel ready.
Now.
And if this stirred something in you — don’t keep it to yourself.
And if you feel God moving in your heart right now… don’t ignore it.
There is something deeper waiting for you.
Because supporting this isn’t just about content.
It’s about reaching the lost.
It’s about pulling people back from the edge of separation.
If you want to be part of that… if you want your life to help point others back to Christ…
Because the greatest tragedy isn’t the fire you fear…
It’s the presence you might lose.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “IS IT WRONG TO WANT SEX BEFORE MARRIAGE THIS BADLY?”
paragraphs:
“IS IT WRONG TO WANT SEX BEFORE MARRIAGE THIS BADLY?”
When your body is loud… but your soul is whispering something deeper
It doesn’t start as rebellion.
It starts as longing.

A glance that lingers a second too long. A conversation that feels a little too good. A touch that awakens something you didn’t expect to feel this intensely. And suddenly… it’s not just attraction anymore. It’s hunger. It’s curiosity. It’s pressure building quietly beneath your self-control.
You love God. That’s what makes this harder.

Because no one talks about the nights when you’re lying awake, fighting thoughts you didn’t invite. No one talks about how your body can crave something your spirit is trying to surrender. No one talks about how exhausting it is to keep saying “no” when everything inside you is screaming “yes.”
So you ask the question you’re almost afraid to say out loud…
“Is it wrong to want sex this badly before marriage?”
Let’s be honest.
The desire itself isn’t the sin.
God never created your body to be numb. He created it with fire. With desire. With the capacity to bond, to feel, to crave intimacy. From the beginning, it was never evil.
In Genesis, the Hebrew reveals something raw and unashamed:

“וַיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עֲרוּמִּים… וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ”
(Vayihyu sheneihem arummim… v’lo yitboshashu)
“They were both naked… and they felt no shame.” (Genesis 2:25)
No shame. No guilt. No confusion.
Desire existed before sin ever entered the story.
But then something shifted.
Sin didn’t just corrupt actions—it distorted desires.

Now what was once pure became tangled. What was once holy became urgent, impulsive, sometimes overwhelming. That’s why the battle you’re feeling is so intense. You’re not just dealing with desire… you’re dealing with desire living in a fallen world.
And Paul understood this tension more than most.
In Romans 7, the Greek carries the weight of internal conflict:

“ὃ γὰρ θέλω τοῦτο οὐ πράσσω… ἀλλ’ ὃ μισῶ τοῦτο ποιῶ”
(Ho gar thelō touto ou prassō… all’ ho misō touto poiō)
“For what I want to do, I do not do… but what I hate, I do.”
That’s the war.
Not just behavior… but desire versus identity.
So no… you’re not broken for wanting.
But here’s where truth gets uncomfortable.
Desire becomes dangerous when it starts leading instead of submitting.
Because God didn’t design sex as just physical release… He designed it as covenant expression.

“Marriage should be honored by all, and the marriage bed kept pure…”
(Hebrews 13:4)
Not because God is trying to restrict joy… but because He’s protecting something sacred.
Sex isn’t just about bodies.
It’s about bonding. It’s about spiritual imprinting. It’s about giving pieces of yourself you can’t easily take back.
That’s why 1 Corinthians 6:18 doesn’t whisper—it warns:
“Flee from sexual immorality…”
Not manage it. Not negotiate with it. Not slowly walk away from it.
Run.
Because this isn’t just about rules.
It’s about your soul.
And maybe that’s what you’re really feeling right now.
Not just desire…
But a deeper ache to be known. To be held. To be chosen. To feel close to someone without walls.
And the enemy is subtle. He takes a real need and offers a counterfeit shortcut.

He tells you:
“It’s just physical.”
“It’s natural.”
“You can handle it.”
“It won’t affect your relationship with God.”
But deep down… you already feel it.
The tension.
The quiet conviction.
The sense that giving in might satisfy something temporarily… but cost something eternally deeper.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because maybe you’ve already crossed lines you said you wouldn’t.
Maybe you’ve justified things you once prayed against.
Maybe you’re tired of the cycle—desire, compromise, guilt, repeat.
So what now?
This is where the story changes.
Not with shame…
But with grace.
Because Jesus didn’t come for people who never struggled.
He came for people caught in the middle of it.
In John 8, when the woman was dragged in scandal, exposed in sin, ready to be condemned… Jesus didn’t deny her sin.
But He also didn’t define her by it.
“Neither do I condemn you… go, and sin no more.”
Grace didn’t excuse her behavior.
Grace gave her a new direction.
That’s what Jesus does.
He doesn’t erase your desire…
He redeems it.
He teaches you that waiting isn’t punishment.
It’s preparation.
That self-control isn’t suppression…
It’s strength.
That holiness isn’t restriction…
It’s freedom from regret.
So if you’re asking, “Is it wrong to want this badly?”
No.
But it is dangerous to let that desire lead you somewhere God never intended you to go.
And right now… you have a choice.
Not between desire and numbness.
But between surrender and control.
You’re not alone in this.
And you’re not too far gone.
But don’t keep this to yourself.
Not to expose them… but to remind them they’re not alone either.
Because there will be nights when your emotions are louder than your convictions… and you’ll need to come back to truth.
Because supporting this mission isn’t about money—it’s about multiplying truth in a world drowning in confusion.
Because glorifying God isn’t passive.
It’s lived, shared, defended, and multiplied.
And sometimes the most powerful thing you can do…
is refuse to give your body what your soul isn’t ready to carry.
You felt something reading this… don’t ignore it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Didn’t Just Write Psalms… They Sang Them While Bleeding
paragraphs: They Didn’t Just Write Psalms… They Sang Them While Bleeding
Why the Psalms Were Sung—and why your soul still aches to sing them even when you don’t have the strength to speak
There’s something unsettling about the Psalms if you really slow down and listen.
Not read… listen.
Because they were never meant to stay trapped on paper.
They were sung.
Not in perfect churches with polished voices and controlled emotions—but in caves, in exile, in betrayal, in guilt, in war, in tears that wouldn’t stop falling.
The Psalms were sung when words alone were not enough to carry the weight of a breaking soul.
And maybe that’s why something in you feels exposed when you read them.
Because deep down, you recognize the sound of someone crying out to God without pretending.
In Psalm 51, after David’s scandal—his sin with Bathsheba, the deception, the blood on his hands—he doesn’t write a quiet apology. He sings a broken confession:

“חָנֵּנִי אֱלֹהִים כְּחַסְדֶּךָ”
Channēnī Elohim kechasdecha
“Have mercy on me, O God, according to Your steadfast love.”
That word חָנֵּנִי (Channēnī) isn’t polite.
It’s desperate.
It’s the cry of someone who knows he has nothing left to offer God but his need.
And he didn’t whisper it.
He sang it.
Can you imagine that?
A king… exposed… undone… singing his repentance out loud.
Because singing forces honesty.
You can fake a prayer.
You can hide behind religious words.
But when you sing something, your soul gets involved whether you want it to or not.
That’s why the Psalms were sung.
Because God never wanted performance.
He wanted your heart to stop hiding.
In Psalm 13, David doesn’t sound like a man of unshakable faith. He sounds like someone on the edge:

“עַד־אָנָה יְהוָה תִּשְׁכָּחֵנִי נֶצַח”
Ad-anah YHWH tishkacheni netzach
“How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?”
That question feels dangerous.
Almost disrespectful.
But it’s sung.
Because God would rather hear your honest confusion than your fake strength.
Some of you haven’t prayed in a long time… but you’ve been feeling things you don’t know how to say.
That ache?
That frustration?
That quiet anger?
That exhaustion?
That’s exactly where the Psalms live.
And that’s exactly why they were sung.
Because when the heart is overwhelmed, melody carries what language cannot.
Even Jesus, hanging on the cross, didn’t choose random words in His final moments.
He reached for a Psalm.

“Ἐλωΐ, Ἐλωΐ, λιμὰ σαβαχθανί;”
Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?
“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?” (Psalm 22:1)
That wasn’t just a cry.
It was a song.
A suffering Messiah singing the ancient words of David—entering fully into human pain while fulfilling divine redemption.
This is where it shifts.
Because the Psalms are not just about human emotion.
They are prophetic.
They are Christ-centered.
They are echoes of Jesus long before He walked the earth.
Psalm 22 continues with details that feel impossible to ignore:

“They pierced my hands and my feet…”
“They divide my garments among them…”
David sang it.
But Jesus fulfilled it.
Which means the Psalms are not just songs of sorrow.
They are songs of transformation.
From scandal… to grace.
From guilt… to forgiveness.
From abandonment… to redemption.
From death… to resurrection.
And maybe that’s why you’re still here reading this.
Because something in your life feels like a scandal right now.
Something hidden.
Something heavy.
Something you don’t talk about.
Something you think disqualifies you.
But the Psalms say otherwise.
Because the same David who sang in guilt also sang in restoration:

“אָשִׁירָה לַיהוָה כִּי גָמַל עָלָי”
Ashirah laYHWH ki gamal alai
“I will sing to the LORD, for He has been good to me.” (Psalm 13:6)
Wait.
The same man who asked “How long?” ends up singing about God’s goodness.
Nothing changed overnight.
But something changed within him.
That’s what singing does.
It realigns the soul with truth—even before circumstances change.
That’s why the early church didn’t just teach doctrine.
They sang it.

“ψαλμοῖς καὶ ὕμνοις καὶ ᾠδαῖς πνευματικαῖς”
psalmois kai hymnois kai ōdais pneumatikais
“with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs…” (Ephesians 5:19)
Because singing makes truth unforgettable.
It sinks deeper.
It stays longer.
It transforms slower—but stronger.
And now the question is no longer just “Why were Psalms sung?”
The question is…
Why have you been silent?
Why have you been carrying things alone that were meant to be poured out before God?
Why have you been trying to stay strong when your soul is clearly asking for surrender?
Be honest.
This didn’t just inform you.
It confronted you.
Because silence is where shame survives.
But confession is where grace begins.
And someone you know needs this too.
Because there will be a night when your words fail—and you’ll need to come back to this reminder that God still listens when all you have left is a song.
And if you truly want to glorify God—not just in words but in action—support what is feeding your soul.
They step into deeper discipleship.
Because this isn’t just about reading.
It’s about transformation.
About choosing growth.
About refusing to stay where you are.
If this spoke to you… don’t ignore it.
Something holy just brushed against your heart.
And you know it.
Because even now… there’s a quiet song rising inside you that you’ve been trying to silence.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “FORGIVE THEM” WAS NOT SOFT — IT WAS WAR: The Hidden Meaning That Confronts Your Pride and Exposes Your Heart
paragraphs: “FORGIVE THEM” WAS NOT SOFT — IT WAS WAR: The Hidden Meaning That Confronts Your Pride and Exposes Your Heart
There is a moment on the cross that most people read too quickly.
It’s not loud. It doesn’t shake the earth like the veil tearing. It doesn’t draw the same attention as “It is finished.”
But if you slow down… if you really sit inside it… it will confront something in you that you’ve been protecting.
Jesus, bleeding, suffocating, mocked, abandoned, betrayed…
And then He says it.
“Father, forgive them…”

In the original Greek, it’s written:
“Πάτερ, ἄφες αὐτοῖς· οὐ γὰρ οἴδασιν τί ποιοῦσιν.” (Pater, aphes autois; ou gar oidasin ti poiousin.) — Luke 23:34
“Aphes.” Forgive.
But this word isn’t passive. It isn’t gentle in the way we imagine forgiveness to be.
It comes from aphiēmi — which means to release, to send away, to let go of a debt, to cancel what is owed.
Not pretend it didn’t happen.
Not excuse it.
Cancel it.
Erase the claim.
Let it go even when justice feels deserved.
And that’s where it starts to hurt.
Because most of us don’t struggle with the idea of forgiveness…
We struggle with giving up our right to hold someone accountable in the way we think they deserve.
We want healing, but we also want them to feel what they did.
We want peace, but we still replay the offense like a courtroom in our mind.
We say we’ve “moved on”… but we haven’t released.
And Jesus, in the middle of the worst injustice in human history, didn’t just model forgiveness…
He chose it when it cost Him everything.
This wasn’t theory.
This was blood-soaked obedience.
And what makes it even more unsettling is this:
He wasn’t forgiving people who said sorry.
They weren’t repenting.
They weren’t even aware.
“οὐ γὰρ οἴδασιν” — “for they do not know.”
Not ignorance as an excuse…
But blindness as a condition.
They were spiritually blind, acting out evil they didn’t fully comprehend.
And Jesus responds not with condemnation…
But intercession.
He speaks to the Father for them.
Pause there.
Because if we’re honest, some of us aren’t even praying for the people who hurt us.
We’re replaying what they did.
We’re building silent arguments.
We’re holding emotional evidence.
But Jesus?
He becomes their advocate while they’re still harming Him.
That’s not normal.
That’s divine.
And it reveals something uncomfortable:
Forgiveness is not about the other person being worthy.
It’s about you being free.
But pride hates that.
Pride whispers, “If you forgive, you’re letting them win.”
Pride says, “They don’t deserve it.”
Pride keeps the wound open because it feels like justice.
But Scripture dismantles that thinking.

In Hebrew, forgiveness is often tied to the word:
“סָלַח” (salach) — to pardon, to spare, to release from consequence.
It’s something only God fully embodies.
And yet… He calls us into it.
Not because it’s easy.
But because it’s necessary for transformation.
Because unforgiveness doesn’t punish them…
It imprisons you.
And here’s the deeper layer most people miss:
When Jesus said “forgive them,” He wasn’t just speaking about them.
He was speaking over you.
Because at some point in your life…
You were the one who didn’t know what you were doing.
You were the one blind.
The one rebelling.
The one choosing sin over surrender.
And still…
He said “aphiēmi” over your life.
He canceled your debt.
The cross is not just where forgiveness was demonstrated.
It’s where it was paid for.
Fully.
Completely.
Without negotiation.
That’s why this message is so confronting.
Because we love receiving grace…
But we hesitate extending it.
We celebrate being forgiven…
But resist forgiving.
And somewhere in that tension, pride quietly builds a throne in our hearts.
But Jesus didn’t die so pride could stay alive.
He died to break it.
To humble us.
To remind us that we are not the judge.
We are the forgiven.
So the real question isn’t “Do they deserve forgiveness?”
The real question is…
Are you willing to look like Christ when it costs you something?
Because real forgiveness will cost you your ego.
Your right to revenge.
Your need to be right.
Your desire to see them pay.
But what you gain…
Is freedom.
Peace that isn’t dependent on apology.
Healing that doesn’t wait for closure.
And a heart that starts to look like Jesus.
Be honest.
There’s someone that came to your mind while reading this.
Someone you’ve been holding in that quiet place.
Someone whose name still stings.
This isn’t random.
This is invitation.
Not to excuse what happened…
But to release what’s been controlling you.
Sit in it.
Let it search you.
Because healing starts where honesty begins.
And if you want to go deeper…
If you’re serious about growing in Christ, healing what’s hidden, and walking in truth instead of cycles…
Not for hype.
But for transformation.
If this message reached you, don’t keep it to yourself.
If it challenged you, don’t ignore it.
If it exposed something… don’t bury it again.
Step into it.
Grow through it.
Let Jesus rewrite what pain tried to define.
Because following Christ isn’t about comfort…
It’s about transformation.
And transformation begins where pride ends.
Some wounds stay open because pride refuses to let grace touch them.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Temptation Feels Personal
paragraphs:
Why Temptation Feels Personal
When the Battle Knows Your Name and Still Calls You Anyway

It didn’t feel random the first time you noticed it. The way the thought came—not loud, not violent, just familiar. Too familiar. Like it knew where to sit inside your mind without asking permission. Like it had been there before.
And maybe that’s why it scares you.
Because temptation doesn’t feel like an outside attack. It feels like something that belongs to you.
Like it came from you.
Like it is you.
But Scripture whispers something deeper than your fear.

In James 1:14, the Greek doesn’t soften it—it exposes it: “ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας” (hekastos de peirazetai hypo tēs idias epithymias) — “each one is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire.”
Your own desire. Not imported. Not injected. Not foreign.
And that’s where it starts to feel personal.
Because the battlefield isn’t just around you—it’s within you.

But don’t miss what Scripture is actually saying. It’s not condemning you for being tempted. It’s revealing why the pull feels so intimate. Temptation studies your wounds. It memorizes your loneliness. It watches where your guard drops. It doesn’t need to break in—it waits for the door you already struggle to close.
Even Jesus stepped into that same arena.
In Matthew 4:1, the Greek says, “τότε ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἀνήχθη… πειρασθῆναι ὑπὸ τοῦ διαβόλου” (tote ho Iēsous anēchthē… peirasthēnai hypo tou diabolou) — “Then Jesus was led… to be tempted by the devil.”
Tempted.
The sinless Son of God stood where you stand.
Hungry. Weak. Alone in the wilderness.
And the enemy didn’t come with something irrelevant. He came with something that made sense.
“If you are the Son of God…”
That’s not just a challenge. That’s personal.
Because temptation doesn’t just target your behavior—it questions your identity.
It whispers, “If you really were who God says you are, you wouldn’t feel this.”
So you start fighting two battles at once. The temptation itself… and the shame of being tempted.
And somewhere in that tension, you begin to believe a lie.
That because it feels personal, it must mean you’re failing God.

But Hebrews 4:15 breaks that lie open: “πειρασθέντα κατὰ πάντα καθ’ ὁμοιότητα χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας” (peirasthenta kata panta kath’ homoiotēta chōris hamartias) — “tempted in every way as we are, yet without sin.”
Jesus didn’t distance Himself from your struggle.
He stepped into it.
Fully.
So when temptation feels personal, it’s not proof that you’re too far gone.
It’s proof that you’re human in a fallen world… and still being pursued by grace.
But here’s where it shifts.
Because temptation doesn’t just expose desire—it reveals direction.
Romans 7:15 echoes the tension in Paul’s own voice: “ὃ γὰρ κατεργάζομαι οὐ γινώσκω” — “For I do not understand what I do.”
Have you ever felt that?
Doing the very thing you prayed you wouldn’t do.
Thinking the very thought you said you were done with.
And wondering why it still has access to you.
This is where many people quit quietly. Not publicly. Not dramatically. Just internally.
They stop believing transformation is possible.
They keep attending, keep posting, keep smiling… but inside, they’ve already accepted defeat.
But the Gospel doesn’t agree with that conclusion.
Not even close.
Because temptation may feel personal… but your identity is not anchored in your impulses.
It’s anchored in Christ.
In 2 Corinthians 5:17, the Greek says, “εἴ τις ἐν Χριστῷ, καινὴ κτίσις” (ei tis en Christō, kainē ktisis) — “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
Not partially new.
Not conditionally new.
New.
That means the voice tempting you is not the voice defining you.
And the struggle inside you is not the author of your story.
Jesus is.
And He specializes in rewriting what felt permanent.
From scandal… to grace.
From failure… to redemption.
From shame… to restoration.
But here’s the part people don’t say out loud.
You don’t defeat temptation by pretending it’s not personal.
You defeat it by bringing it into the light personally with God.
Honest. Unfiltered. Unpolished.
“Lord, this is where I’m weak.”
“Lord, this is what still pulls me.”
“Lord, this doesn’t feel like it’s leaving.”
Because healing doesn’t start where you hide.
It starts where you finally tell the truth.
Psalm 51 in Hebrew carries that cry: “לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים” (Lev tahor bera-li Elohim) — “Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
Not fix.
Create.
Because some battles aren’t about behavior modification.
They’re about heart transformation.
And that only happens when you stop performing… and start surrendering.
Temptation feels personal because it knows where you’ve been empty.
But grace is even more personal.
It knows where God is about to fill.
Be honest.
Let this become a moment, not just another post.

And if you truly want to glorify God—not just with words but with obedience and action—then support what is feeding your spirit. This isn’t about pressure. It’s about partnership in spreading truth that pulls people out of darkness.
If God used this to reach you, don’t keep it to yourself.
Because someone else is waiting for the exact moment you decide to share.
The thing that feels like it knows you best… is the very thing Jesus came to break completely.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Is Sexual Attraction a Gift… or a Test?
paragraphs:
Is Sexual Attraction a Gift… or a Test?
The Desire That Feels Holy… Until It Doesn’t
You didn’t expect it to feel this confusing.
One moment, it feels beautiful. Natural. Even sacred. Your heart beats faster, your mind drifts, your body responds—and somewhere deep inside, you wonder… did God put this here?
And then the next moment… it feels like war.
Because the same attraction that made you feel alive… now makes you feel guilty. Torn. Exposed. Like something inside you is pulling in two directions at once.
And no one really talks about that part.
They tell you “just resist temptation,” but they don’t explain why the desire itself feels so powerful… so human… so close to something good.
So you sit there, quietly asking the question most people are too afraid to say out loud:
Is sexual attraction a gift… or a test?
The truth is… it’s both.
But not in the way you think.
In the beginning, before shame ever entered the human story, before hiding became instinct, before guilt wrapped itself around desire—God created something good.
The Hebrew language doesn’t hide this.
In Genesis 1:27–28, it says:
“וַיִּבְרָא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־הָאָדָם… זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה בָּרָא אֹתָם… וַיְבָרֶךְ אֹתָם אֱלֹהִים… וַיֹּאמֶר לָהֶם פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ”
“Vayivra Elohim et-ha’adam… zakhar u’neqevah bara otam… vayevarekh otam Elohim… vayomer lahem, ‘peru u’revu.’”
God created man… male and female… and He blessed them… and said, “Be fruitful and multiply.”
Do you see it?

Before sin ever existed, attraction had a purpose. It was part of blessing, not brokenness. It wasn’t dirty. It wasn’t shameful. It was sacred… designed to draw two people into covenant, into unity, into something that reflects God’s own creative power.
Even in Genesis 2:25, it says:
“וַיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עֲרוּמִּים… וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ”
“They were both naked… and were not ashamed.”
No hiding. No confusion. No inner war.
Just purity.
So what happened?
Sin didn’t remove desire.
It distorted it.
Now the same attraction that once pointed toward covenant… can pull toward compromise. The same desire meant to unite… can now divide your soul.
James 1:14–15 reveals this tension clearly:
“ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας… εἶτα ἡ ἐπιθυμία συλλαβοῦσα τίκτει ἁμαρτίαν”
“Each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire… then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin.”
Notice that.
Desire itself is not immediately called sin.
It’s what happens next.
It’s what you do with it.
It’s where you allow it to go.
That’s where the test begins.
Sexual attraction is a gift when it draws you toward God’s design.
It becomes a test when it tries to pull you outside of it.
And this is where most people break… not because they’re evil, but because they’re exhausted.
Exhausted from fighting something that feels natural.
Exhausted from hiding struggles no one sees.
Exhausted from pretending they’re stronger than they really are.
But here’s what you need to hear… and feel deep in your bones:
Jesus did not come to shame your struggle.
He came to redeem it.
Even the word for temptation in Greek, “πειρασμός” (peirasmos), carries a deeper meaning—it can mean testing… proving… refining.
Not destroying you.
Refining you.
Because God isn’t trying to expose you as weak.
He’s trying to transform you into someone free.
1 Corinthians 10:13 says:
“No temptation (πειρασμός) has overtaken you except what is common to mankind. And God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear…”
Do you understand what that means?
You are not uniquely broken.
You are not alone in this war.
You are not disqualified because you feel desire.
You are being invited into a deeper kind of strength… the kind that doesn’t come from pretending you don’t feel… but from surrendering what you feel to Christ.
Because the real question isn’t “why do I feel this?”
The real question is… “who will I become through this?”
Will you let attraction lead you… or will you let Christ lead you through it?
That’s the difference between bondage… and transformation.
And maybe right now, if you’re honest… there’s something this is exposing.
Something you’ve been hiding.
Something you’ve been justifying.
Something you’ve been quietly losing to.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because this isn’t just content.
This is confrontation… wrapped in grace.
And if this spoke to something real inside you… don’t keep it to yourself.
And if you want to stay close to truth like this… follow.
Not for me.
But because your soul needs consistent light in a world that keeps normalizing darkness.
And if you’re serious about growing deeper in Jesus Christ—not surface-level faith, but real transformation—then take the next step.
Because discipleship isn’t accidental.
It’s intentional.
Not to promote a brand…
But to strengthen a life that refuses to stay lukewarm.
Because glorifying God isn’t just about what you feel.
It’s about what you choose… even when it’s hard.
And maybe that’s what this really is.
Not just a struggle.
Not just a question.
But an invitation.
To let Jesus rewrite the part of your story you thought would always control you.
Because the desire didn’t come to destroy you…
It came to reveal what still needs to be surrendered.
And Jesus is still willing to take it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Heard the Rooster… and Everything Broke Inside Him
paragraphs:
He Heard the Rooster… and Everything Broke Inside Him
When Peter Realized What He Had Done—and the Moment Grace Began to Chase Him
It wasn’t loud at first.
Not the courtyard. Not the accusations. Not even the fear clawing at Peter’s chest.
It was just a question.
“You also were with Him.”
Simple. Direct. Dangerous.

The fire cracked beside him, shadows dancing across faces that didn’t care about truth—only suspicion. And in that moment, Peter—the same Peter who swore loyalty, who walked on water, who said, “Even if all fall away, I never will”—felt something unfamiliar tighten around his soul.
Fear.
Raw. Human. Paralyzing fear.
And so he answered.
“I do not know Him.”
In Greek, the words cut deeper than they sound in English: οὐκ οἶδα αὐτόν (ouk oida auton). Not just “I don’t know Him,” but “I have no understanding of Him. No connection. No association.”
He didn’t just distance himself.
He erased Jesus with his mouth.
And the night wasn’t finished.
Another voice pressed in. Another accusation. Another chance to stand.
Again, Peter denied.
And then a third time—this time with oaths, curses, desperation leaking through every syllable—he severed himself completely.
“I do not know the man!”
Not “Rabbi.” Not “Lord.” Not “Teacher.”
Just… the man.
And then it happened.
The sound split the night.
A rooster crowed.
But it wasn’t just a sound.
It was a mirror.
Because in that exact moment, the Gospel of Luke records something that should make your chest tighten:
“The Lord turned and looked at Peter.” (Luke 22:61)
Turned.
Looked.
No words.
No shouting.
No condemnation.
Just eyes.
Eyes that had called him.
Eyes that had believed in him.
Eyes that had just been denied by the one who once said, “You are the Christ.”

In Aramaic—the language Jesus spoke—there’s no surviving direct manuscript of this exact sentence, but the emotional weight aligns with expressions like ḥazāh (to see, to behold deeply). This wasn’t a glance.
It was a knowing.
A piercing.
A moment where heaven and failure collided in silence.
And suddenly, Peter remembered.
“Before the rooster crows today, you will deny Me three times.”
Memory is a strange thing.
It doesn’t always come gently.
Sometimes it crashes in like a wave, dragging truth with it.
And when it did, Peter didn’t argue.
He didn’t justify.
He didn’t defend himself.
He broke.
Scripture says, “He went out and wept bitterly.” (Matthew 26:75)
The Greek says: καὶ ἐξελθὼν ἔξω ἔκλαυσεν πικρῶς (kai exelthōn exō eklausen pikrōs).
Pikrōs.
Bitterly. Violently. Deep, gut-wrenching sorrow.
Not polite tears.
Not quiet regret.
This was the kind of crying that empties you.
The kind that exposes everything you tried to hide—even from yourself.
Because Peter didn’t just fail.
He failed Him.
And if you’re honest… you know this feeling.
Maybe not in a courtyard.
Maybe not beside a fire.

But in the quiet compromises… the moments you stayed silent when you should have stood… the times you chose comfort over conviction… the nights you said with your life, “I don’t know Him,” even if your lips never formed the words.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because Peter’s story isn’t distant.
It’s disturbingly familiar.
But here’s what makes this moment unforgettable.
This is not where Peter’s story ends.
Because while Peter was outside weeping… Jesus was inside being condemned.
While Peter was drowning in guilt… Jesus was moving toward the cross.
For him.
For the man who denied Him.
For the man who said, “I don’t know Him.”
For you.
For every hidden failure.
For every whispered denial.
For every moment you thought you disqualified yourself.
The Hebrew idea of covenant love—חֶסֶד (chesed)—is not based on your consistency.
It’s based on God’s.
And Jesus was about to prove that in blood.
Because days later, after the cross, after the grave, after death itself had been defeated, Jesus didn’t avoid Peter.
He pursued him.
On a quiet shore, with a charcoal fire—almost like the one where Peter denied Him—Jesus asked a question.
“Do you love Me?”
Three times.
Not to shame him.
But to restore him.
The same number as the denials.
Grace meeting failure, point for point.
The Greek word Jesus uses shifts between ἀγαπᾷς (agapas – sacrificial love) and φιλεῖς (phileis – brotherly love), meeting Peter exactly where he is—not where he pretended to be.
Jesus wasn’t exposing Peter.
He was rebuilding him.
This is the scandal.
This is the beauty.
This is the Gospel.
That your worst moment does not cancel God’s calling on your life.
That your denial does not disqualify you from His grace.
That the same eyes that saw Peter fail… also saw who he would become.
A rock.
A preacher.
A man who would one day stand boldly and proclaim Jesus without fear.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Your voice matters. Your honesty matters. Your confession might be the thing that helps someone else stop hiding too.
If you truly want to glorify God, support what feeds your spirit. This isn’t about a page—it’s about a mission.
Because this isn’t just content.
It’s a lifeline.
And maybe… just maybe…
You’re not the only one who needed this tonight.
The rooster didn’t expose Peter to destroy him… it exposed him so grace could find him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Did Men in the Bible Have Multiple Wives?
paragraphs:
Why Did Men in the Bible Have Multiple Wives?
The Truth That Feels Uncomfortable… But Might Set You Free
There are questions people whisper but rarely ask out loud.
This is one of them.
Why did men in the Bible have multiple wives… and God didn’t immediately stop it?
Be honest… that tension has crossed your mind before.

Maybe you felt confused.
Maybe it made the Bible feel inconsistent.
Maybe it even shook your trust a little.
And if you’ve ever felt that… you’re not alone.
Because when you read about Abraham, Jacob, David, Solomon… it almost feels like God allowed something that doesn’t match what we now understand as His will.
But here’s where everything changes…

The Bible never hides human brokenness.
It exposes it.
From the very beginning, before sin fractured everything, God already revealed His design.

In Genesis 2:24, the Hebrew text says:
“וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד” (ve-hayu lebasar echad)
“…and they shall become one flesh.”

Not multiple.
Not divided.
One.

This wasn’t just about physical union.
It was covenant, identity, and spiritual oneness.
One man. One woman. One covenant before God.
So what happened?
Sin happened.
Not just the obvious sins we think about… but the slow drift of the human heart.

By the time you reach Genesis 4:19, you meet Lamech—the first recorded polygamist:
“וַיִּקַּח־לוֹ לֶמֶךְ שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים” (vayikach-lo Lemech shtei nashim)
“And Lamech took two wives.”

Notice something…
God didn’t command it.
God didn’t celebrate it.
It simply records it.
Because Scripture often shows what people did… not what God approved.
And from that moment forward, polygamy spreads not as God’s design… but as a symptom of human distortion.
When you look closely at every polygamous relationship in the Bible, something else always appears.
Conflict.
Jealousy.
Division.
Pain.

Sarah and Hagar… tension so deep it drove people into the wilderness.
Jacob, Leah, and Rachel… a household filled with rivalry and heartbreak.
David… power mixed with moral compromise.
Solomon… wisdom overshadowed by divided devotion.
The pattern is undeniable.
Polygamy was never portrayed as peaceful or ideal.
It was tolerated… but never blessed as the standard.
Even in the Law, God begins to regulate what He never originally designed, because human hearts were already entangled.

In Deuteronomy 17:17, speaking about kings:
“וְלֹא־יַרְבֶּה־לוֹ נָשִׁים” (velo yarbeh-lo nashim)
“He shall not multiply wives for himself…”
Why?
Because God knew what it would do to the heart.
Divide it.
And a divided heart cannot fully belong to Him.
This is where many people misunderstand God.
They think permission equals approval.
But sometimes… God allows what He does not desire, because He is working through broken people to bring about redemption.
That’s the scandal.
God’s story has always included messy people… not because He agrees with their mess, but because He refuses to abandon them in it.
And then Jesus steps into history… and everything becomes clear again.
In Matthew 19:4–6, Jesus brings us back, not forward, not adjusted… back.

“ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς” (ap’ archēs)
“from the beginning…”

He says:
“So they are no longer two, but one flesh.”
Jesus didn’t redefine marriage.
He restored it.
He stripped away centuries of compromise and pointed directly to God’s original intention.
One.
Undivided.
Faithful.
Whole.
And suddenly… the confusion fades.
Polygamy in the Bible isn’t God’s endorsement.
It’s evidence of how far humanity drifted from His design.
But here’s where it becomes personal.
Because this isn’t just about ancient marriages.
It’s about us.
We may not have multiple spouses… but how many divided loves do we carry?
How many things compete for our devotion?
How often is our heart split between God… and everything else?
This is why the greatest commandment isn’t about behavior first… it’s about love.

“ἀγαπήσεις Κύριον τὸν Θεόν σου…” (agapēseis Kyrion ton Theon sou)
“You shall love the Lord your God…”
With all your heart.

Not half.
Not divided.
All.
Because God has never wanted to share you.
Not in a controlling way… but in a covenant way.
The same way marriage was designed to reflect.
One.
And this is where grace steps in.
Because even when people got it wrong… God kept writing their story.
Even David… even Solomon… even broken families and fractured hearts…
God didn’t stop the story.
He redeemed it.
That’s the Gospel.
Not perfection… but restoration.
Not flawless people… but a faithful God.
And maybe that’s what you needed to hear more than anything else.
Because your life might feel messy right now.

Your past might feel complicated.
Your decisions might not reflect God’s design.
But neither did theirs.
And still…
