God rewrote everything.
If this stirred something in you… don’t ignore it.
Be honest.
Someone else needs to see your honesty… because your testimony might be the permission they need to come back to God.
And if you feel something deeper pulling on your spirit right now… don’t stay at the surface.
If you truly desire to glorify God, then support the mission that is helping bring truth, conviction, and healing to thousands of souls daily.
You don’t need more noise.
You need truth that transforms.

Because following casually won’t change your life…
but walking closely with Christ will.
And here’s the echo you won’t forget—

God never needed perfect people…
He only needed willing hearts.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You’re Smiling in Church… But Breaking in Private
paragraphs:
You’re Smiling in Church… But Breaking in Private
The hidden fracture no one claps for… and the grace that still finds you there
You lifted your hands today.

You sang the words. You knew when to say “Amen.” You smiled at people who think you’re doing better than you really are. You even encouraged someone else… while quietly wondering why you feel so empty inside.
No one saw it.
Because you’ve learned how to survive in public… while slowly unraveling in private.
And maybe that’s the part that hurts the most.
Not the struggle itself—but the silence around it.
You sit in rows of worshippers, surrounded by voices declaring victory, while inside your own soul whispers something different:

“Why am I still like this?”
“Why hasn’t God fixed me yet?”
“Why do I feel so far… when I’m trying so hard?”
You smile… but something in you is breaking.
And you don’t know how much longer you can keep pretending.
But listen carefully—because what you’re feeling right now is not new to heaven.
David felt it.
The same David who killed Goliath… who was called a man after God’s own heart… wrote words that feel almost too raw to say out loud:

“כִּי אֵין שָׁלוֹם בַּעֲצָמָי מִפְּנֵי חַטָּאתִי”
“There is no peace in my bones because of my sin.” (Psalm 38:3)
No peace… in his bones.
Not just on the surface. Not just in passing emotions.
Deep. Internal. Hidden.
David knew how to worship publicly… while bleeding privately.
And yet… God didn’t abandon him there.
Because the Gospel was never about perfect people holding it together.
It’s about broken people being held together by Christ.
You don’t have to fake strength to be accepted by God.
You don’t have to perform healing to stay in His presence.
Because Jesus did not come for the version of you that smiles in church…
He came for the version of you that cries when no one is watching.
The one who replays mistakes at night.
The one who feels like a hypocrite.
The one who wonders if their faith is even real.
The one who is tired… but still shows up.
That version of you… is the one He is after.
Scripture doesn’t hide this truth—it confronts it.

“Ἐλθέτε πρός με πάντες οἱ κοπιῶντες καὶ πεφορτισμένοι…”
“Come to Me, all who are weary and burdened…” (Matthew 11:28)
Not the strong.
Not the polished.
Not the ones who have it all together.
The weary.
The burdened.
The ones who are smiling outside… but collapsing inside.
And here’s what makes this so powerful—Jesus didn’t say “fix yourself, then come.”
He said come… as you are.
That means your hidden anxiety… your quiet addictions… your secret doubts… your emotional exhaustion…
None of it disqualifies you.
In fact, it’s the very reason He’s calling you closer.
But here’s the tension we don’t talk about enough:
You can sit in church every week… and still hide from God.
Not physically.
But emotionally. Spiritually. honestly.
You can sing songs about surrender… without ever actually surrendering.
You can look alive… while parts of your soul are still dying in silence.
And that’s where this becomes dangerous.
Because hidden pain, when left unaddressed, slowly turns into distance from God.
Not because He leaves you…
But because you stop letting Him see the real you.
But the Gospel doesn’t work in hiding.
It works in honesty.

“ἐὰν ὁμολογῶμεν τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν…”
“If we confess our sins…” (1 John 1:9)
Confession is not about condemnation.
It’s about connection.
It’s the moment you stop pretending… and start being known.
Fully.
And still loved.
That’s where grace begins to feel real.
Not when you act healed.
But when you admit you’re not.
So if you’re reading this… and something inside you feels exposed…
Good.
Not because shame is good.
But because truth is breaking through.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because deep down… you know this is you.
The smile.
The mask.
The quiet breaking.
Respond to it.
You are not the only one fighting this battle.
And you were never meant to fight it alone.
And if you’ve been watching from a distance, unsure where you stand with God…
Not for content.
But for daily truth, conviction, healing, and reminders that Jesus hasn’t given up on you.
And if you’re ready to go deeper—not just emotionally, but spiritually…
Not out of pressure… but out of purpose.
Because if you truly desire to glorify God with your life, you don’t just consume truth—you support what spreads it.
Because this isn’t about building a platform.
It’s about building people.
Broken people.
Honest people.
People who are done pretending… and ready to be transformed.
And hear this before you go—
The version of you that feels the most unworthy right now… is the exact version Jesus died to save.
He saw the private breaking…
And still chose the cross.
You are not too far gone.
You are not too fake.
You are not too late.
You are exactly the kind of story Jesus rewrites.
And maybe… just maybe…
Your healing doesn’t start the next time you smile in church—
It starts the moment you stop hiding from God.
The mask is heavy… but grace is stronger.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: ARE YOU DATING… OR JUST ENTERTAINING LONELINESS?
paragraphs: ARE YOU DATING… OR JUST ENTERTAINING LONELINESS?
The question doesn’t sound dangerous at first.
It feels casual. Harmless.
But sit with it long enough… and it starts to expose things you’ve been avoiding.
Because some relationships aren’t built on love.
They’re built on silence.
On the fear of eating alone.
On nights that feel too long.
On the quiet panic that maybe… just maybe… no one else is coming.
And so you text back.
Even when you know they don’t lead you closer to God.
Even when your spirit feels heavier after every conversation.
Even when deep down, something inside you whispers, “This isn’t it.”
But loneliness has a way of making almost anything feel like provision.
And suddenly, you’re not dating for purpose…
You’re dating to escape emptiness.
Scripture doesn’t ignore this kind of struggle.
In Genesis 2:18, God says:

“לֹא־טוֹב הֱיוֹת הָאָדָם לְבַדּוֹ”
Lo tov heyot ha’adam levado
“It is not good for man to be alone.”
But notice what God does next.
He doesn’t rush Adam into the nearest available connection.
He doesn’t give him distraction.
He gives him alignment.
He brings someone suitable.

“עֵזֶר כְּנֶגְדּוֹ”
Ezer kenegdo — a helper fit, corresponding, aligned.
Not someone to numb loneliness.
Someone to walk in purpose.
And this is where many hearts quietly break.
Because what we often call “connection”…
God might call “misalignment.”
You can be talking every day…
Laughing…
Sharing secrets…
Even praying together…
And still be completely outside God’s design.
Because proximity is not purpose.
Chemistry is not covenant.
Attention is not love.
And loneliness will lie to you if you let it.
It will whisper things like:
“At least they’re here.”
“At least someone cares.”
“At least you’re not alone tonight.”
But Scripture speaks differently.
In Psalm 34:18:

“קָרוֹב יְהוָה לְנִשְׁבְּרֵי־לֵב”
Karov Adonai lenishberei-lev
“The Lord is near to the brokenhearted.”
Not “the next relationship.”
Not “the next distraction.”
God Himself.
Close.
Present.
Enough.
And yet we still run.
We run into conversations we shouldn’t entertain.
We run into situationships we know won’t last.
We run into emotional attachments that slowly pull us away from obedience.
Why?
Because silence scares us.
But what if the silence you’re trying to escape…
Is actually where God is trying to speak?
In the Greek of Matthew 6:33, Jesus says:

“ζητεῖτε δὲ πρῶτον τὴν βασιλείαν”
zēteite de prōton tēn basileian
“Seek first the kingdom…”
Not second.
Not after you feel secure.
Not after someone validates you.
First.
Because anything you place before God…
Even love…
Becomes an idol.
And idols don’t heal loneliness.
They deepen it.
You start needing more texts.
More reassurance.
More presence.
More emotional fixes.
Until one day you realize…
You’re not being loved.
You’re being temporarily distracted.
And it’s exhausting.
Be honest.
Some of you aren’t in love.
You’re in withdrawal.
You’re addicted to feeling wanted.
To hearing your phone light up.
To knowing someone is thinking about you.
Even if they’re not leading you to Christ.
Even if they’re slowly pulling you away.
Even if your spirit feels quieter… weaker… more compromised.
That’s not love.
That’s emotional survival.
And Jesus didn’t die so you could survive emotionally.
He died so you could be transformed completely.
In 2 Corinthians 5:17:

“ὥστε εἴ τις ἐν Χριστῷ, καινὴ κτίσις”
hōste ei tis en Christō, kainē ktisis
“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.”
Not half-healed.
Not partially free.
New.
But new things require letting go of old patterns.
Old dependencies.
Old fears.
Even old relationships.
Yes… even the ones that feel good.
Because not everything that feels good is sent by God.
Some things feel good because they temporarily numb what God is trying to heal.
And healing… is rarely comfortable.
But it’s always worth it.
So let me ask you again…
Are you dating…
Or just entertaining loneliness?
Because one leads to purpose.
The other leads to slow spiritual compromise.
And you already know which one you’re in.
You felt it while reading this.
That quiet conviction.
That subtle discomfort.
That moment where you paused and thought…
“This is me.”
Don’t ignore that.
That’s not guilt.
That’s grace interrupting your pattern.
Jesus doesn’t expose you to shame you.
He exposes you to free you.
And freedom sometimes starts with a hard decision:
Letting go of what’s easy…
To receive what’s eternal.
Sit in it.
Be honest.
Let your voice be heard. Someone else needs to see they’re not alone in this.
And if you know someone who’s been stuck in this cycle…
Not to expose them…
But to reach them.
Follow closely if you want daily truth that doesn’t just comfort you—but transforms you.
And if you’re serious about growing deeper in Christ, about healing the parts of you that keep running back to what breaks you…
If you truly desire to glorify God, supporting what spreads His truth matters more than you think.
Not out of pressure…
But out of purpose.
Because the same God who is calling you out of loneliness…
Is calling you into something far greater.
And this moment…
This exact moment you’re reading this…
Might be where everything begins to change.
You were never meant to be completed by attention…
You were meant to be transformed by Christ.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Walked Away With a Limp and a New Name… Then God Said It Again
paragraphs:
He Walked Away With a Limp and a New Name… Then God Said It Again
Why God Didn’t Just Rename Jacob Once—and What That Means for the Parts of You Still Wrestling in Silence
There are moments in life when you think God has already changed you… and yet something inside you still feels unfinished.
Jacob knew that feeling.

He had spent years running from his past—deception clinging to his name like a shadow he couldn’t outrun. His very identity was a scandal. “Jacob” (יַעֲקֹב, Yaʿaqōḇ)—from the Hebrew root ʿaqab, meaning “to supplant,” “to deceive,” “to grasp the heel.” His story began with him gripping his brother’s heel in the womb (Genesis 25:26), as if even then, he was trying to take something that wasn’t his.
And if you’re honest… you’ve had moments like that too. Not necessarily stealing a birthright—but grasping, manipulating, trying to control outcomes because trusting God felt too slow.
But then came that night.
That night when Jacob stopped running.
Genesis 32:24 says, “וַיִּוָּתֵר יַעֲקֹב לְבַדּוֹ… וַיֵּאָבֵק אִישׁ עִמּוֹ” (Vayyivater Yaʿaqōḇ levado… vayyēʾāvēq ish ʿimmō) — “And Jacob was left alone… and a man wrestled with him.”
Alone.
No audience. No excuses. No masks.
Just him… and God.

The Hebrew word “וַיֵּאָבֵק” (vayyēʾāvēq)—“wrestled”—comes from a root that carries the sense of dust being stirred up, like a desperate, gritty struggle in the dirt. This wasn’t a clean, composed prayer. This was messy. Emotional. Raw.
Some of you haven’t had that moment yet. Not fully.
You’ve prayed—but you haven’t wrestled.
Jacob clung to God until his strength gave out. Until his hip was dislocated. Until he physically could not stand the same way again.
And then… God asked him a question that sounds almost strange:
“What is your name?” (Genesis 32:27)
God knew his name.
But Jacob needed to say it.
“Jacob.”
Deceiver.
Supplanter.
Manipulator.
That was his confession.
And then everything changed.
Genesis 32:28: “לֹא יַעֲקֹב יֵאָמֵר עוֹד שִׁמְךָ כִּי אִם־יִשְׂרָאֵל” (Lo Yaʿaqōḇ yeʾamer ʿōd shimkha ki im-Yisraʾel) — “Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but Israel.”
“Israel” (יִשְׂרָאֵל, Yisraʾel)—“one who strives with God” or “God prevails.”
Not deceiver.
Wrestler.
Chosen.
Transformed.
And yet… years later… God says it again.
Genesis 35:10: “שִׁמְךָ יַעֲקֹב… לֹא־יִקָּרֵא שִׁמְךָ עוֹד יַעֲקֹב כִּי אִם־יִשְׂרָאֵל” — “Your name is Jacob… no longer shall your name be called Jacob, but Israel shall be your name.”
Wait… why repeat it?
Did God forget?
No.
Jacob did.
Because transformation in a moment doesn’t always mean transformation in memory.
God had already renamed him in Genesis 32… but Jacob kept living like Jacob.
He went back to old patterns. Old fears. Old compromises. The name changed—but the habits lagged behind.
And if that doesn’t expose something in us…
How many times has God spoken identity over you—and you still answer to your past?
How many times has grace renamed you—and you still introduce yourself by your failures?
God wasn’t correcting Himself in Genesis 35.
He was reinforcing Jacob.
Because sometimes one encounter with God changes your direction… but repeated reminders are what change your identity.
God met him again at Bethel—the place of promise. Not in crisis this time, but in confirmation.
And this matters more than most people realize.
Because Jacob’s first renaming happened in pain.
The second happened in purpose.
The first was survival.
The second was establishment.
God wasn’t just changing what Jacob had been.
He was anchoring who Jacob would become.
This is where the Gospel begins to breathe into the story.
Because what happened to Jacob didn’t end with Jacob.
Centuries later, another name would be spoken in a quiet, scandal-filled place.
“Jesus.”
In Hebrew, יֵשׁוּעַ (Yeshua)—“Yahweh saves.”
And unlike Jacob, Jesus didn’t wrestle because of sin.
He wrestled for ours.
Luke 22:44 describes Him in Gethsemane: “being in agony, He prayed more earnestly, and His sweat became like great drops of blood.”
The Greek word ἀγωνία (agōnia)—agony—carries the sense of intense struggle, like an athlete fighting to the limit.
Jesus entered the dust… not because He was a deceiver—but because we were.
He took the identity of Jacob… so we could receive the identity of Israel.
He was treated as the sinner… so we could be called sons.
This is the part that changes everything.
Jacob walked away from that night with a limp.
Jesus walked to the cross knowing it would cost Him everything.
And because of that…
Your name doesn’t have to stay what your past called you.
But here’s the truth most people avoid:
God may have already renamed you… but are you still responding to your old name?
Are you still living like “Jacob” when heaven calls you “Israel”?
Are you still hiding when grace already exposed and covered you?
Be honest.
This isn’t about information.
This is about identity.
Because someone reading your honesty might finally stop pretending too.
If this message stirred something deeper in you… not just inspiration but conviction… then step into something more intentional.
Help carry it.
Because someone is still trapped in a name Jesus already died to change.
And never forget this—
God didn’t repeat the name change because He forgot who Jacob was…
He repeated it because Jacob kept forgetting who he had become.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Storm Didn’t Want Him… The Fish Didn’t Want Him… But God Wouldn’t Let Him Go
paragraphs:
The Storm Didn’t Want Him… The Fish Didn’t Want Him… But God Wouldn’t Let Him Go
Why Jonah Had to Be Swallowed — The Scandal That Became Grace
There are moments when you know… you’ve run too far.
Not just physically. Not geographically. But spiritually.

You didn’t just make a mistake—you resisted God. You heard His voice, felt His conviction, and still chose the opposite direction. And now you’re somewhere you never planned to be… wondering how everything spiraled so fast.
That’s where Jonah was.
And if you’re honest… that’s where some of you are right now.

The story begins quietly, almost deceptively simple. “וַיְהִי דְּבַר־יְהוָה אֶל־יוֹנָה” (Vayehi devar-YHWH el-Yonah) — “Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah” (Jonah 1:1). The call was clear. No confusion. No distortion. God told him to go to Nineveh.
And Jonah ran.
Not because he didn’t understand… but because he understood too well.

Nineveh wasn’t just a city. It was an enemy. Violent. Corrupt. Brutal. Jonah didn’t want them saved. He wanted them judged. And here is where the scandal begins—God was offering mercy to people Jonah believed deserved destruction.
So Jonah boarded a ship to Tarshish, the opposite direction.
And some of you have done the same thing.

God said forgive… you chose resentment.
God said stay… you walked away.
God said speak… you stayed silent.
You didn’t mishear Him.
You just didn’t want to obey.
But here’s the part we often misunderstand: the storm wasn’t punishment… it was pursuit.
“וַיהוָה הֵטִיל רוּחַ גְּדוֹלָה אֶל־הַיָּם” (VaYHWH hetil ruach gedolah el-hayam) — “But the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea” (Jonah 1:4).
God sent the storm.
Not to destroy Jonah… but to interrupt his rebellion.
The sailors were terrified. They cried out to their gods. They threw cargo overboard. They did everything they could to survive. Meanwhile Jonah was asleep—disconnected, numb, avoiding reality.
That’s what disobedience does. It numbs you while chaos builds around you.
Eventually Jonah is exposed. The lot falls on him. He confesses.
“I know that this great storm is because of me.”
And then he says something shocking:
“Take me and throw me into the sea.”
Not repentance… resignation.
Some of you haven’t truly repented either.
You’ve just accepted the consequences without surrendering your heart.
But God wasn’t finished.
“וַיְמַן יְהוָה דָּג גָּדוֹל לִבְלֹעַ אֶת־יוֹנָה” (Va-yeman YHWH dag gadol livloa et-Yonah) — “And the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah” (Jonah 1:17).
Read that again.
God appointed the fish.
This wasn’t random.
This wasn’t coincidence.
This wasn’t judgment in the way you think.
It was mercy in disguise.
Because the sea would have killed him.
The fish saved him.
The thing that looked like death… was actually rescue.
Some of you have been calling something “ruin” that God calls “intervention.”
That relationship ending… that door closing… that failure… that breaking point…
What if it wasn’t God abandoning you?
What if it was Him refusing to let you destroy yourself?
Inside the fish, Jonah finally prays.
Not casually. Not religiously. Desperately.
“מִבֶּטֶן שְׁאוֹל שִׁוַּעְתִּי” (Mi-beten Sheol shivvati) — “From the belly of Sheol I cried out” (Jonah 2:2).
Sheol. The place of the dead.
That’s how it felt.
And maybe that’s how it feels for you right now.
Dark. Suffocating. Silent. Alone.
But here’s what changes everything—God hears from the belly.
Not just from churches. Not just from clean lives. Not just from people who have it all together.
From the lowest place… God listens.
Jonah continues:
“When my life was fainting away, I remembered the LORD” (Jonah 2:7).
That’s it.
That’s the turning point.
Not perfection.
Not performance.
Just remembrance.
Some of you don’t need a new strategy.
You need to remember God again.
Remember who He is.
Remember what He’s done.
Remember that you’re not too far gone.
Because you’re not.
After three days and three nights, the fish releases Jonah.
And here’s where it gets even deeper.
Jesus Himself connects to this moment.
“ὥσπερ γὰρ ἦν Ἰωνᾶς… τρεῖς ἡμέρας καὶ τρεῖς νύκτας… οὕτως ἔσται ὁ Υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου…” (Matthew 12:40)
“For just as Jonah was three days and three nights… so will the Son of Man be…”
Jonah’s story wasn’t just about Jonah.
It was a shadow of Jesus.
Jesus would also go into the depths.
Not because He ran from God… but because He obeyed perfectly.
He entered death so you could be pulled out of yours.
Jonah was swallowed because he ran.
Jesus was crucified because He stayed.
And now… grace is offered to both the rebellious and the broken.
That’s the scandal.
That’s the beauty.
That’s the Gospel.
So why was Jonah swallowed?
Not to destroy him.
To stop him.
To humble him.
To realign him.
To save him from himself.
And maybe… that’s exactly what God is doing in your life right now.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Your honesty might be the beginning of someone else’s healing too.
You’re going to need this reminder again.
If you truly desire to glorify God, don’t just consume truth… help spread it.
You’re not stuck.
You’re being redirected.
Even in the belly… God is still writing your story.
And He’s not done with you yet.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Bible Never Said Money Is Evil… But What It Reveals Will Expose Your Heart
paragraphs: The Bible Never Said Money Is Evil… But What It Reveals Will Expose Your Heart
You’ve probably heard it your whole life… whispered in sermons, thrown around in conversations, even used to shame success…
“Money is the root of all evil.”
But something about that never sat right, did it?
Because deep down, you’ve seen good people with money… and broken people without it.
So what if I told you the Bible never actually said that?
Not once.
The verse everyone quotes comes from 1 Timothy 6:10, and in the original Greek, it reads:

“ῥίζα γὰρ πάντων τῶν κακῶν ἐστιν ἡ φιλαργυρία”
(rhiza gar pantōn tōn kakōn estin hē philargyria)
Which translates accurately to:
“For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil.”
Not money.
The love of it.
“φιλαργυρία” (philargyria) literally means an obsessive affection, a deep craving, a devotion to wealth that begins to replace God.
And that’s where everything shifts.
Because now the question isn’t “Is money evil?”
The real question is…
What does your heart do when money enters the room?
Because money doesn’t create your character.
It reveals it.
Jesus Himself said in Luke 16:13:
“No servant can serve two masters… You cannot serve God and mammon.”
That word “mammon” comes from Aramaic — מָמוֹנָא (mamona) — meaning wealth, yes… but more deeply, it carries the idea of that which you trust in.
So this was never just about currency.
It was always about worship.
What do you rely on when life starts shaking?
What do you run to when you feel empty?
What makes you feel safe?
Be honest…
Because if it’s not God, then it’s already become your master.
And here’s where it gets uncomfortable.
Money can bless.
Money can build.
Money can feed the hungry, fund ministries, rescue lives, support families, spread the Gospel to places your feet will never touch.
But money can also quietly corrupt… without making a sound.
Judas didn’t betray Jesus for power.
He did it for thirty pieces of silver.
Not because money was evil…
But because his heart loved it more than Christ.
That’s the scandal we don’t talk about enough.
You can walk with Jesus… and still be secretly attached to something else.
You can serve… preach… show up… smile…
And still have something sitting on the throne that doesn’t belong there.
That’s why Scripture goes deeper than behavior.
It goes straight to the heart.
In Matthew 6:21, Jesus says:
“For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.”
The original Greek word for “treasure” is “θησαυρός” (thēsauros) — not just money, but anything you store up, protect, prioritize, and give value to.
So let’s not pretend this is just about finances.
This is about devotion.
This is about identity.
This is about what owns you when no one is watching.
Because the truth is…
Some people don’t have money, but money still has them.
And others have wealth, but it doesn’t have their heart.
That’s the difference.
Abraham was rich.
David had wealth.
Solomon had unimaginable riches.
Yet when their hearts were aligned with God, their resources became instruments of purpose, not idols of destruction.
But when Solomon’s heart drifted…
The same wealth that once reflected God’s blessing became entangled with idolatry.
So again… it’s not the money.
It’s the heart holding it.
And if you’re reading this right now, something in you probably stirred.
Maybe conviction.
Maybe recognition.
Maybe a quiet discomfort you can’t ignore.
Be honest…
Have you ever trusted money more than God?
Have you ever felt safer with a full bank account than with a full prayer life?
Have you ever delayed obedience because of financial fear?
Because this isn’t about shame.
This is about freedom.
Jesus never came to take from you.
He came to free you.
Free you from the silent chains that don’t look like sin on the outside… but slowly pull your heart away from Him.
He came to rewrite your story.
Even the parts you thought were too entangled.
Even the parts where money became your security, your identity, your escape.
Because grace doesn’t just forgive…
It transforms.
Zacchaeus was a wealthy tax collector, known for corruption.
But one encounter with Jesus…
And everything changed.
He didn’t just say sorry.
He gave back what he stole.
He surrendered his wealth’s control over him.
That’s what real transformation looks like.
Not just belief.
But release.
So the question isn’t “Do you have money?”
The question is…
Does money have you?
And if it does…
Jesus is still inviting you out of that prison.
Not with condemnation.
But with grace.
If this message spoke to you, don’t keep it to yourself.
Because this is more than content.
This is discipleship.
If you want to glorify God not just with words but with action…
Support what feeds your spirit.
Stay connected to truth.
Commit to growth.
Because following Jesus isn’t about avoiding evil…
It’s about surrendering everything that quietly replaces Him.
And maybe the most dangerous idols…
Are the ones we’ve learned to justify.
Let this be the moment you stop pretending and start surrendering.
Because what you cling to…
Might be the very thing keeping you from freedom.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: There are numbers… and then there are moments where numbers stop being numbers.
paragraphs: There are numbers… and then there are moments where numbers stop being numbers.
Seven is one of those moments.

Not because of math. Not because of superstition. But because somewhere between the first breath of creation and the final whisper of redemption, God chose seven to carry a weight that most people feel… but never fully understand.
And maybe that’s where this begins—with you feeling like something in your life is unfinished.
Something unresolved.
Something that keeps repeating like a cycle you can’t break.
Because deep down, every human soul is searching for completion.
And Scripture doesn’t ignore that longing… it answers it.
The very first time we encounter seven, it isn’t casual. It’s deliberate. It’s sacred.

“וַיְכַל אֱלֹהִים בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי”
Vay’chal Elohim bayom hashvi’i
“Thus God completed on the seventh day…” (Genesis 2:2)
The Hebrew word “וַיְכַל” (vay’chal) doesn’t just mean “finished” in the sense of stopping work. It carries the deeper meaning of bringing something to its intended fullness… its perfect state.
God didn’t stop because He was tired.
He stopped because it was complete.
Seven wasn’t an ending.
Seven was fulfillment.
And if you’ve ever felt like your life is stuck somewhere between day six and day seven… this is for you.
Because we live in a world addicted to six.
Six days of striving.
Six days of proving.
Six days of trying to fix what feels broken inside.
Six days of pretending we’re okay when we’re not.
But God never designed us to live in six.
He designed us to enter seven.
Completion.
Rest.
Wholeness.
Not earned… but given.
And yet, somewhere along the way, we learned to chase completion in everything except God.
Relationships.
Achievements.
Approval.
Even religion.
But none of those can carry the weight of what seven was meant to hold.
That’s why the pattern keeps showing up across Scripture like a heartbeat you can’t ignore.
Seven days of creation.
Seven lamps on the menorah.
Seven feasts of Israel.
Seven times Naaman washed in the Jordan before healing came.
Seven times the walls of Jericho were circled before they collapsed.
Seven statements from Jesus on the cross.
Seven churches in Revelation.
Seven seals.
Seven trumpets.
Seven bowls.
It’s not repetition.
It’s revelation.
God is saying something.
Completion doesn’t come from your effort… it comes from His design.
And the most powerful moment where seven reaches its deepest meaning isn’t in Genesis.
It’s at the cross.
When Jesus cried out:
“Τετέλεσται” (Tetelestai) — “It is finished.” (John 19:30)
That word… tetelestai… wasn’t just a statement of death.
It was a declaration of completion.
In the Greek, it carries the meaning of a debt fully paid, a mission fully accomplished, nothing left undone.
Jesus didn’t say, “I tried.”
He didn’t say, “I did my part.”
He said, “It is finished.”
Seven… fulfilled in flesh and blood.
And this is where everything shifts.
Because the same humanity that lives in cycles of six—failure, sin, shame, repetition—is invited into the completion of Christ.
Not because we deserve it.
But because He finished it.
That’s the scandal.
That’s the grace.
That’s the Gospel.
You were never meant to complete yourself.
You were meant to surrender into the One who already did.
But surrender is uncomfortable.
Because it means admitting something most people spend their entire lives avoiding:
You can’t fix you.
And maybe that’s what this is exposing right now.
The hidden exhaustion.
The silent battles.
The moments where you smile in public but wrestle in private.
The prayers you stopped praying because you thought nothing was changing.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because deep down, you don’t just want progress.
You want completion.
And Scripture isn’t vague about where that comes from.

“ὁ Θεὸς… ὁ ἐναρξάμενος ἐν ὑμῖν ἔργον ἀγαθὸν ἐπιτελέσει”
“He who began a good work in you will complete it.” (Philippians 1:6)
The Greek word “ἐπιτελέσει” (epitelesei) means to bring something to full completion, to perfect it, to carry it through to its intended end.
God doesn’t start things He doesn’t finish.
Including you.
Even the parts of you you’ve given up on.
Even the habits you’re ashamed of.
Even the faith that feels weak.
Seven is not just a number in Scripture.
Seven is a promise.
Completion is coming.
But it doesn’t come through control.
It comes through surrender.
So here’s the question that isn’t easy to ignore:
What are you still trying to complete on your own… that Jesus already finished?
Your honesty might be the very thing someone else needs to see tonight.
Follow closely if you’re done with surface-level faith and ready for truth that actually transforms.

And if this message stirred something deeper in you… if you truly desire to glorify God not just in belief but in action… then support the mission that is bringing truth like this into the lives of people who are drowning in silence.
You don’t have to stay where you are.
But you do have to choose where you’re going.
Because following Jesus isn’t about trying harder.
It’s about surrendering deeper.
And maybe… just maybe…
this is the moment you stop living in six… and finally step into seven.
The place where striving ends… and grace begins.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Thought It Was Love… But Was It Lust? The Truth About Desiring Your Future Spouse Will Confront You
paragraphs: You Thought It Was Love… But Was It Lust? The Truth About Desiring Your Future Spouse Will Confront You
There are moments no one talks about.

Late at night.
Alone.
Scrolling, thinking, imagining…
Not about random people.
But about them.

The person you believe God has for you.
Your future husband.
Your future wife.
And in that quiet space, something rises.
Desire.
Not just emotional. Not just spiritual.
Sexual.
And then comes the question that lingers like a whisper you can’t silence…
“Is this wrong?”
Because no one prepared you for this part of waiting.

No one told you that purity wouldn’t just be about avoiding people…
It would be about confronting your own heart.
Jesus didn’t avoid this conversation.
He walked straight into it.
In Matthew 5:28, He says something that still shakes people who try to water it down:
“But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
The original Greek hits even harder.
“πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν” (pros to epithymēsai autēn) — not just noticing, not just attraction… but intentional desire that seeks to possess.
This isn’t about recognizing beauty.
This is about crossing a line internally where a person—real or imagined—becomes something to consume rather than someone to honor.
And that’s where things get uncomfortable.
Because you’re not thinking about a stranger.
You’re thinking about someone you hope to marry.
So your mind starts justifying it.

“It’s okay… they’re going to be mine anyway.”
“It’s not like I’m acting on it.”
“At least I’m not sinning physically.”
But Scripture doesn’t let us hide behind technicalities.
Because the issue has never been proximity.
It’s been purity of the heart.
The Hebrew understanding of desire in passages like Proverbs 6:25 uses the word “תַּחְמֹד” (tachmod) — to covet, to set your heart upon in a way that pulls you toward taking.
It’s not neutral.
It’s directional.
It moves you somewhere.
And if we’re honest… it rarely moves us toward God.
It moves us deeper into imagination, into fantasy, into a version of love that’s more about gratification than covenant.
And that’s the danger.
Because what you rehearse in secret… you normalize in your spirit.
You start relating to your “future spouse” as a body before you ever learn to honor them as a soul.
You train your heart to consume before it ever learns to sacrifice.
And suddenly, what you call “waiting on God” becomes quietly shaped by desires that God never designed to lead you.
But here’s where grace interrupts the shame.
Desire itself is not the enemy.
God created it.
In Genesis, when God formed man and woman, He didn’t create a cold, emotionless bond.
He created something powerful.
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.” (Genesis 2:24)
“One flesh” in Hebrew is “בָּשָׂר אֶחָד” (basar echad) — a union so deep it’s physical, emotional, spiritual.
Sex wasn’t an accident.
It was intentional.
Holy.
Designed.
So the feeling you have?
The longing?
The anticipation?
That’s not something to hate.
But it is something to steward.
Because outside of covenant, desire tends to turn inward.
Self-focused.
Possessive.
Impatient.
Inside covenant, it becomes something entirely different.

Giving.
Honoring.
Sacrificial.
Holy.
So the real question isn’t, “Is it wrong to desire your future spouse sexually?”
The deeper question is…
“What is that desire doing inside you right now?”
Is it drawing you closer to purity… or slowly training you to justify compromise?
Is it teaching you patience… or feeding a quiet entitlement?
Is it rooted in love… or controlled by fantasy?
Be honest.
This isn’t about condemnation.
This is about alignment.
Because some of you are fighting battles no one sees.
You’re trying to stay pure physically, but mentally you feel like you’re losing.
And it’s exhausting.
That tension you feel?
That conviction?
That discomfort?
That’s not God pushing you away.
That’s God inviting you deeper.
Not just to control your actions…
But to surrender your imagination.
To let Him reshape what love looks like before you ever step into it.
To learn how to see someone not as a future outlet…
But as a future responsibility.
And maybe this hit harder than you expected.
Maybe you didn’t think something “private” mattered this much.
But your heart matters.
Your thought life matters.
Your hidden life matters.
Because who you are in secret is who you bring into marriage.
Let this be the moment you stop managing sin… and start surrendering it.
And don’t keep this to yourself.
Someone you know is silently battling this exact thing.
And if you feel God stirring something deeper in you… don’t ignore it.
Not out of pressure.
But out of purpose.
Because supporting what feeds your spirit is part of honoring God.
Because glorifying God isn’t just about what you avoid…
It’s also about what you choose to build.
And what you choose to support.
And what you choose to become.
Here’s the truth that will stay with you long after you close this:
What you entertain in secret today… is shaping the love you will live tomorrow.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “Can God Restore You After Sexual Sin… Completely?”
paragraphs:
“Can God Restore You After Sexual Sin… Completely?”
The question you’re almost afraid to ask out loud… but your soul has been whispering it for a long time.
There are moments you remember too clearly.

Not just what happened…
but how it felt after.

The silence.
The guilt.
The way you couldn’t look at yourself the same anymore.

You told yourself it was just one mistake.
But something inside you knew it wasn’t just physical…
it touched something deeper.
Something sacred.
And now the question won’t leave you alone—

“Did I ruin what God had for me?”
“Can I ever be clean again… or just forgiven but still damaged?”

You won’t say it publicly.
But be honest…
This hit harder than you expected.

Because deep down, you’re not just asking if God forgives.
You’re asking if God restores.
Completely.

Not halfway.
Not patched together.
Not “you’re saved but permanently stained.”
But truly, fully… restored.

The Bible doesn’t run from your question.
It walks straight into it.

King David didn’t whisper his failure.
He recorded it for generations.

Adultery.
Deception.
Broken trust.
And when the weight of it crushed him, he didn’t ask for a second chance at behavior…
He cried out for something deeper.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God…” (Psalm 51:10)
In Hebrew, he used the word “בְּרָא” (bara) — the same word used in Genesis 1:1.
Creation out of nothing.

David wasn’t asking God to fix him.
He was asking God to recreate him.
That’s not repair.
That’s resurrection.

Because sexual sin doesn’t just touch the body.
Scripture says in 1 Corinthians 6:18 that it is sin “εἰς τὸ ἴδιον σῶμα” (eis to idion soma) — against one’s own body.

It wounds identity.
It distorts intimacy.
It rewires what was meant to be holy.
That’s why it feels different.
That’s why it lingers.
That’s why you still feel it even after you’ve said “I’m sorry.”
But here is where everything shifts—
God doesn’t minimize the weight of sexual sin…
but He also doesn’t limit the power of His restoration.
The same David who fell… was called a man after God’s own heart.
The same woman caught in adultery, dragged publicly in shame, waiting for stones to crush her life…
stood face to face with Jesus.
And He said, “Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.” (John 8:11)
In the Greek, “οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω” (oude ego se katakrino) — “Neither do I condemn you.”

Not “I tolerate you.”
Not “I’ll deal with you later.”
No condemnation.
But He didn’t leave her there either.
Grace didn’t excuse her sin.
Grace rewrote her future.
Because Jesus doesn’t just forgive…
He restores.
Completely.

Not the version of you that pretends nothing happened—
but the version of you that has been transformed through surrender.
This is where many people miss it.

They want forgiveness without transformation…
or they accept forgiveness but reject restoration.
They live like they’ve been spiritually pardoned but emotionally disqualified.

Still ashamed.
Still hiding.
Still believing they’re “less than.”
But Scripture says:
“If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation…” (2 Corinthians 5:17)
The Greek word for new is “καινὴ” (kainē) — not just new in time, but new in nature.
Different.
Rewritten.

You are not a repaired version of your past.
You are a recreated reality in Christ.
So no—
your story didn’t end in that moment of weakness.
That wasn’t your final chapter.
That was the place where grace began to rewrite everything.
But restoration isn’t passive.
It requires honesty.
Repentance.
Surrender.

Not just saying “I messed up”…
but allowing God to transform the desires, the patterns, the wounds that led you there.
And yes… healing takes time.
But restoration is not partial.
God doesn’t restore halfway.
When He heals, He heals deeply.
When He cleanses, He cleanses fully.
“Though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be white as snow…” (Isaiah 1:18)
Scarlet was permanent dye in ancient times.
Impossible to remove by human effort.
But God says what you cannot erase…
He can completely remove.
So why are you still holding onto what God is offering to cleanse?
Why are you still carrying what Jesus already carried to the cross?
This is the moment you stop negotiating with shame.
This is the moment you stop calling yourself what God has already forgiven.
This is the moment you stop living like your sin has more authority than His grace.
There are people reading this who feel disqualified from love, from purpose, from calling…
and this is your reminder:
Jesus specializes in restoring what people think is ruined.
And if you feel something awakening in your spirit right now…
don’t walk away unchanged.
Because this isn’t about emotional moments…
this is about lifelong transformation in Christ.
And if you want to go deeper—
If this message stirred something real in you…
support it.

Not for us—
but because spreading the Gospel matters.
Because someone else is where you were…
and your share might be the moment their story changes too.
And here’s the truth you can’t un-hear now—
You were never too broken… just waiting to be rebuilt by grace.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “God Is Love”… But Not the Love You Were Told About
paragraphs:
“God Is Love”… But Not the Love You Were Told About
The dangerous misunderstanding that comforts people straight into spiritual silence—and the truth that will either break you or bring you back to life
You’ve heard it your whole life.
“God is love.”
It’s printed on mugs. Whispered at funerals. Posted under filtered sunsets. Used to excuse compromise. Used to avoid conviction. Used to silence truth.

But somewhere along the way…
we stopped asking what that actually means.
And that silence has cost more souls than we realize.

Because the world didn’t reject “God is love.”
It redefined it.
And the version it created… doesn’t save.
It numbs.
It comforts people on the edge of eternity while they slowly drift away from the very God they claim to believe in.

I remember sitting in a room full of people who said they loved God… but no one trembled at His Word anymore. No one repented. No one wept. No one wrestled. Everyone just… existed in a version of faith that felt good but required nothing.
That’s when it hit me.
We weren’t worshiping God as He revealed Himself.
We were worshiping a version of love that never existed.
Scripture doesn’t leave “God is love” open to interpretation.
It says it clearly:
“Ὁ Θεὸς ἀγάπη ἐστίν” (Ho Theos agapē estin) — 1 John 4:8
God is agapē.
Not preference. Not tolerance. Not emotional approval.
Agapē is a love that gives… but also a love that purifies.
A love that embraces… but also confronts.
A love that saves… but also demands surrender.
The Hebrew Scriptures echo this tension in a way modern ears struggle to accept:

“יְהוָה יְהוָה אֵל רַחוּם וְחַנּוּן… וְנַקֵּה לֹא יְנַקֶּה”
(YHWH, YHWH, El rachum ve’chanun… ve’nakkeh lo yenakkeh) — Exodus 34:6–7

The LORD is compassionate and gracious…
but He will by no means clear the guilty.
That doesn’t fit the version of love we were taught.
Because the world says love means acceptance without transformation.
God says love means transformation because of truth.
And that’s where most people quietly walk away.
Not loudly. Not dramatically.
Just slowly.
Because real love… the kind God embodies… exposes things we’d rather keep hidden.

It reveals pride we’ve learned to dress up as confidence.
It confronts sin we’ve learned to rename as personality.
It dismantles identities we’ve built outside of Him.

And if we’re honest…
that kind of love feels uncomfortable.
So we soften it.
We reshape it.
We turn “God is love” into something manageable.

Something that won’t interrupt our habits.
Something that won’t challenge our desires.
Something that won’t call us to die to ourselves.
But Jesus never did that.
Not once.
He looked at people with love… and then He said things that changed everything.

To the woman caught in sin:
“Neither do I condemn you… go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11)

To His disciples:
“If anyone would come after Me, let him deny himself…” (Matthew 16:24)
To the rich young ruler… He loved him… and then told him to give up everything.
That’s agapē.
Not approval.
Not comfort.
Not silence.
Sacrificial, truth-filled, soul-awakening love.

The kind that doesn’t just meet you where you are…
but refuses to leave you there.
And maybe that’s what you’ve been running from.
Not God.
But the version of Him you were never shown.
Because deep down… you know something isn’t right.

You feel it in quiet moments.
In the middle of the night.
When the noise fades and your thoughts get louder.

You know a love that never corrects…
isn’t really love.

You know a God who never confronts…
isn’t the God of Scripture.
And maybe that realization stings a little.
Or a lot.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected, didn’t it?
Because this isn’t about shame.
It’s about awakening.

It’s about realizing that the same love that convicts you…
is the same love that was nailed to a cross for you.

“Ἀγάπη… Χριστὸς ἀπέθανεν ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν”
(Agapē… Christos apethanen hyper hēmōn) — Romans 5:8
Love… is that Christ died for us.
Not when we were perfect.
But while we were still sinners.
That’s the part people love to quote.
But they stop there.

Because if you keep reading Scripture…
that love doesn’t just forgive.
It transforms.
It calls.
It rebuilds.
It rewrites everything.
From scandal… to grace.

And if you’ve been living in a version of love that never changed you…
then maybe you’ve never truly encountered Him.
Not fully.
Not deeply.
Not yet.
But you can.
Right now.
Not by pretending you’re okay.
Not by hiding behind “God understands.”
But by surrendering.
By coming honestly.
By letting His love do what it was always meant to do.

Heal you…
and change you.
Someone you love is living in a false version of love right now.
And if you’re serious about going deeper—about not just hearing truth but living it—then stay close.
Because this isn’t about content.
It’s about transformation.
Not out of pressure… but purpose. Because reaching more souls requires obedience, not silence.

Because “God is love”…
but not the kind that leaves you unchanged.
The kind that breaks chains… and calls you by a new name.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Call It Grace… But Heaven Calls It Something Else
paragraphs:
They Call It Grace… But Heaven Calls It Something Else
Why Some People Use “Grace” to Excuse Sexual Sin—and the Truth That Shatters the Illusion
It never starts with rebellion.
It starts with a whisper.

A quiet justification in the dark when no one is watching…
“It’s okay. God will forgive me anyway.”
And suddenly, grace—the most sacred, blood-bought gift in all of eternity—gets twisted into permission.
Not transformation.
Not surrender.
Permission.
You can feel it, can’t you?
That tension between what you know is right… and what your flesh keeps negotiating.
Because somewhere along the way, grace stopped being something that rescues… and started being something people use to hide behind.
But that’s not the grace Jesus died for.
The Apostle Paul saw this coming long before we ever scrolled through temptation on our screens.
In Romans 6:1–2, he writes:
(Ti oun eroumen? Epimenoumen tē hamartia hina hē charis pleonasē? Mē genoito.)
“What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin that grace may abound? God forbid.”
That phrase—μὴ γένοιτο (mē genoito)—is not a soft correction.
It is a violent rejection.
It means: May it never be. Absolutely not. This must not even be considered.
Yet here we are… in a generation where people don’t just consider it—they live by it.
Sex outside of covenant is normalized.
Lust is entertained.
Pornography is excused.
Casual relationships are rebranded as “freedom.”
And grace… is blamed.
But grace never told you to stay in chains.
Grace is what breaks them.

The word Paul uses for sin—ἁμαρτία (hamartia)—means “to miss the mark.”
But sexual sin isn’t just missing the mark… it’s redefining the target so you never feel like you missed.
And that’s where deception lives.
Because real grace doesn’t lower the standard.
It lifts you into a new identity.
In 1 Corinthians 6:18–20, Paul doesn’t negotiate:
“φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν…” (pheugete tēn porneian) — “Flee sexual immorality.”
Not manage it.
Not justify it.
Flee it.
Why?
Because your body is not casual.
It’s sacred.
“Your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit… you are not your own.”
That word πορνεία (porneia)—sexual immorality—isn’t vague.
It includes every form of sexual activity outside of God’s design.
And yet people still say, “God understands.”
Yes… He understands so deeply that He sent His Son to bleed for it.
This is where everything changes.
Because grace is not God pretending your sin isn’t serious.
Grace is God proving just how serious it is—by paying for it Himself.
In Hebrew, the word for grace is חֵן (chen)—favor you didn’t earn.
But favor was never meant to make you comfortable in sin.
It was meant to draw you out of it.
Titus 2:11–12 says:
“For the grace of God has appeared… teaching us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts.”
Teaching.
Grace teaches.
Grace corrects.
Grace disciplines.
Grace transforms.
If what you’re calling “grace” is not changing you… it’s not biblical grace.
It’s something else wearing its name.
And deep down… you already know it.
That quiet conviction you keep pushing away?
That’s not shame.
That’s the Holy Spirit refusing to let you settle for less than who you were created to be.
Because Jesus didn’t die so you could stay comfortable in sin.
He died so you could become someone new.

“εἴ τις ἐν Χριστῷ, καινὴ κτίσις”
(ei tis en Christō, kainē ktisis) — “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)
Not a slightly improved version.
A new creation.
Which means the version of you that keeps justifying sexual sin… is not the version Jesus is forming.
And this is where it gets uncomfortable.
Because this isn’t about condemnation.
It’s about honesty.
Some people don’t want freedom.
They want forgiveness without transformation.
They want heaven… without surrender.
They want grace… without repentance.
But grace and repentance are not enemies.
They are inseparable.
In Aramaic, repentance carries the idea of turning back fully—not partially, not temporarily, not emotionally—but completely.
And that’s the invitation.
Not “try harder.”
Not “be perfect.”
But “come back.”
Fully.
Honestly.
Without excuses.
So be honest for a moment…
Have you been calling something “grace” that God calls compromise?
Have you been leaning on forgiveness instead of walking in freedom?
Have you been hiding in what sounds spiritual… but feels empty?
This isn’t about shame.
This is about awakening.
Because someone you love is walking the same road you are.
There is a reason you felt this.
There is a reason you didn’t skip it.
There is a reason your spirit feels unsettled right now.
And if you truly want to glorify God—not just in words but in your life—then stand with truth.
Support what feeds your spirit.
This is not about selling something.
This is about building something inside you that sin tried to destroy.
If you’re ready to go deeper—not just inspired, but transformed—step in:
Because grace was never meant to excuse your sin.
It was meant to end your slavery to it.
And the moment you stop using grace as a shield for sin… is the moment grace finally becomes your freedom.
You were never meant to survive sin—you were meant to walk away from it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The One Thing Sex Can Never Replace
paragraphs:
The One Thing Sex Can Never Replace
The hunger beneath your skin was never physical… it was always spiritual
You can turn off the lights, silence your conscience, and convince your body that what you feel is love.
But deep down… you already know.

Because even after the touch fades, even after the pleasure peaks and collapses into silence, there’s something still awake inside you… something unsettled, something unfilled, something quietly asking, “Why do I still feel empty?”

You tried to ignore it.
You tried to drown it.
You tried to rename it.
But it never left.
Because sex was never designed to carry the weight of your soul.

The world told you it could.
Culture preached it like a gospel.
Your own desires whispered, “This will fix it.”
But now you’re here… still searching.
And if you’re honest… still aching.
Scripture never shied away from desire. It never denied that longing exists. But it always told the truth about where that longing belongs.
In the beginning, when God created intimacy, He didn’t create it as an escape… He created it as a covenant.
“וַיִּהְיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד” (vayyihyu lebasar echad) — “and they shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24)

Not just bodies touching… but lives intertwining.
Not just pleasure… but purpose.
Not just sensation… but sacred union.
And yet somewhere along the way, we reduced something holy into something consumable.
We took what was meant to reflect God’s covenant… and turned it into a momentary transaction.
And now we’re surprised it doesn’t satisfy us.
Because here’s the truth that hits harder than most are willing to admit:
Sex can touch your body… but it can never heal your soul.
That emptiness you feel after? That quiet disconnect? That subtle guilt that creeps in when the moment is over?
That’s not weakness.
That’s your soul recognizing it was never meant to be fed that way.
Jesus didn’t come just to forgive sin. He came to restore what sin distorted.
When He met the woman at the well in John 4, He wasn’t just speaking to her history… He was speaking to her hunger.
She had been with five men. Searching. Reaching. Hoping the next one would finally satisfy the ache she couldn’t explain.
And Jesus said to her:

“πᾶς ὁ πίνων ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος τούτου διψήσει πάλιν”
(pas ho pinōn ek tou hydatos toutou dipsēsei palin)
“Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again…”
But then He looked deeper than her past… deeper than her shame… deeper than her patterns…

“ὃς δ’ ἂν πίῃ ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος οὗ ἐγὼ δώσω αὐτῷ οὐ μὴ διψήσει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα”
(hos d’ an piē ek tou hydatos hou egō dōsō autō ou mē dipsēsei eis ton aiōna)
“But whoever drinks of the water that I will give him will never thirst again.”
That’s it.
That’s the thing sex can never replace.
Living water.
Real fulfillment.
A soul finally at rest.
Because the truth is… you weren’t chasing a body.
You were chasing relief.

You were chasing connection.
Validation.
Escape.
Belonging.
But none of those things were ever meant to be found in someone else’s arms outside of God’s design.
And now maybe you’re starting to see it clearly.
Maybe the patterns are making sense.
Maybe the regret is finally speaking louder than the desire.
Maybe God is opening your eyes right now.
So be honest.
Because this isn’t about shame.
This is about awakening.
The Gospel doesn’t expose you to condemn you… it exposes you to free you.

“וְיָדַעְתֶּם אֶת־הָאֱמֶת וְהָאֱמֶת תְּשַׁחְרֵר אֶתְכֶם” (John 8:32 in Hebrew rendering)
“And you shall know the truth, and the truth shall set you free.”
Freedom doesn’t come from suppressing desire.
It comes from surrendering it.
And yes… that’s hard.

Because your flesh will fight you.
Your habits will call you back.
Your loneliness will try to convince you that anything is better than nothing.
But God is not calling you to emptiness.
He is calling you to fullness.

To something deeper than pleasure.
To something stronger than impulse.
To something eternal.
“φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν” (pheugete tēn porneian) — “Flee sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18)
Not because God wants to restrict you… but because He refuses to let you settle for something that will never satisfy you.
You were not created for temporary highs.
You were created for eternal union with Christ.
And when that truth finally lands… everything changes.
Desire doesn’t disappear… it gets redirected.
Your identity stops being shaped by what you crave… and starts being anchored in who you belong to.
Jesus.
The One who doesn’t just touch your body… but heals your soul.
The One who doesn’t leave you emptier after… but fills you completely.
The One who doesn’t use you… but redeems you.
So if this is hitting you deeper than expected…
And if you truly want to glorify God… not just in words, but in action… help this message reach more people.
Stay close. Keep growing. Keep fighting.
Because the hunger you feel was never meant to be silenced… it was meant to be satisfied in Him.
And until you find that…
Nothing else will ever be enough.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Can Great Sex Build a Great Marriage… Or Is That the Lie We’ve Been Sold?
paragraphs:
Can Great Sex Build a Great Marriage… Or Is That the Lie We’ve Been Sold?
The truth about intimacy, covenant, and the kind of love that survives when passion fades and souls are exposed
There are nights no one posts about.

Nights where the lights are off, not because it’s romantic… but because something feels distant. Forced. Empty. Nights where two people who once couldn’t keep their hands off each other now lie inches apart… but feel miles away.
And nobody warned you that this could happen—even if the sex was once incredible.
So you start asking the question quietly, almost afraid to say it out loud:
“If our sex life was so good… why does our marriage feel like it’s falling apart?”
We were taught—through movies, culture, even casual conversations—that great sex is the glue. The proof. The engine. The sign that everything is “right.”
But Scripture tells a deeper story. A more uncomfortable one.
In the beginning, before sin ever entered the world, intimacy was never just physical.
Genesis 2:24 says:

“וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד”
“Ve’davaq b’ishto v’hayu l’basar echad”
“And he shall cling to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
That word davaq—cling—means to stick, to pursue, to hold fast with loyalty, not just desire. It’s covenant language, not chemistry language.
And “one flesh” (basar echad) was never meant to be reduced to bodies touching—it’s souls aligning, lives intertwining, identities surrendering into something sacred.
So no… great sex alone cannot build a great marriage.
Because marriage was never built on performance. It was built on covenant.
And covenant demands something deeper than attraction.
It demands dying.
That’s where it gets quiet.
Because most people want intimacy without crucifixion. Passion without sacrifice. Connection without confession.
But the Gospel never works that way.
Ephesians 5:25 doesn’t say, “Husbands, satisfy your wives.”
It says:

“ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας” (agapate tas gynaikas) —
“Love your wives…”
“…καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν”
“…just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her.”
That word agapē is not emotional. It’s sacrificial. It bleeds. It chooses even when it doesn’t feel like it.
So when a marriage begins to crumble, it’s rarely because the sex wasn’t good enough.
It’s because something deeper was never surrendered.
Pride.
Secrets.
Unhealed wounds.
Unspoken disappointments.
The kind of things that don’t get fixed in the bedroom… because they were born in the heart.
You can have passion without purity.
You can have chemistry without covenant.
You can even have frequency without faithfulness.
But you cannot build something eternal on something temporary.
And this is where Jesus changes everything.
Because He doesn’t enter perfect marriages.
He redeems broken ones.
The woman at the well had multiple relationships. Emotional baggage. A past full of complicated intimacy.
And yet Jesus didn’t shame her story.
He exposed her thirst.

“πᾶς ὁ πίνων ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος τούτου διψήσει πάλιν…”
“Everyone who drinks of this water will thirst again…”
“…but whoever drinks of the water that I will give him shall never thirst.”
She wasn’t just looking for love.
She was looking for something that sex, relationships, and validation could never satisfy.
And maybe… so are you.
Maybe what feels like a “marriage problem” is actually a soul problem.
Maybe what feels like a lack of intimacy is actually a lack of surrender.
Because when Christ becomes the center, intimacy stops being about taking… and becomes about giving.
It becomes safe again.
Real again.
Holy again.
1 Corinthians 13 doesn’t describe a feeling.
It describes a decision.

“ἡ ἀγάπη μακροθυμεῖ… χρηστεύεται…”
“Love is patient… love is kind…”
Not “love is exciting.”
Not “love always feels good.”
But love endures.
And that’s the kind of love that builds marriages that don’t collapse when the feelings fluctuate.
So no… great sex doesn’t build a great marriage.
But a Christ-centered marriage will transform even your intimacy into something deeper than pleasure—into connection, healing, and unity that the world cannot counterfeit.
This isn’t about lowering the importance of intimacy.
It’s about restoring its purpose.
Because when sex becomes the foundation, it eventually cracks.
But when Christ becomes the foundation… even broken pieces can be rebuilt into something stronger than before.
And maybe this is hitting closer than you expected.
Maybe you’ve been silently wondering why things feel off.
Why the connection faded.
Why the excitement doesn’t fix the emptiness anymore.
Be honest.
This isn’t about shame.
This is about truth.
Someone else reading your words might realize they’re not alone.
And if this stirred something in you… don’t keep it to yourself.
Come back to it when emotions get confusing again.
And if you want to go deeper—not just emotionally, but spiritually… stay close.
Because real transformation doesn’t happen in one moment.
It happens through daily surrender.
If you truly want to glorify God in your relationships, your marriage, and even your private life… then don’t just consume truth—support it, spread it, stand with it.
If you feel that pull… don’t ignore it.
Because the truth is…
The greatest intimacy you’ll ever experience won’t begin in a bedroom.
It will begin at the feet of Jesus.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Felt It… But Did You Sin? The Hidden Battle Between Temptation and Guilt That Most Christians Misunderstand
paragraphs: You Felt It… But Did You Sin? The Hidden Battle Between Temptation and Guilt That Most Christians Misunderstand
What if the war in your mind isn’t proof you’re failing… but evidence you’re still fighting?
It didn’t start with action.
It started with a thought you didn’t invite.
A flash. A whisper. A pull.
And before you could even process it, guilt already wrapped itself around your chest like chains.
You didn’t act on it… but it was there.
So now you’re asking the question most believers are too afraid to say out loud:
“Did I just sin… or was I just tempted?”
Because if we’re honest, some of the deepest shame we carry isn’t from what we’ve done…
…it’s from what crossed our mind.
And that’s where everything changes.
Scripture doesn’t leave us guessing.
It takes us straight into the wilderness.
Straight into hunger. Weakness. Silence.
Straight into the moment where even Jesus Himself was tempted.

“τότε ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἀνήχθη… πειρασθῆναι ὑπὸ τοῦ διαβόλου”
(τότε ὁ Ἰησοῦς… peirasthēnai hypo tou diabolou)
“Then Jesus was led… to be tempted by the devil.”
— Matthew 4:1 (Greek)
Read that slowly.
Not accused.
Not fallen.
Tempted.
The Greek word πειρασθῆναι (peirasthēnai) means to be tested, tried, enticed… not yet to sin.
Jesus stood in the tension every believer knows.
The pull was real.
The hunger was real.
The opportunity was real.
But sin?
That required something else.
Because temptation knocks…
…but sin opens the door.
James makes it painfully clear, and yet incredibly freeing:

“ἀλλ’ ἕκαστος πειράζεται… εἶτα ἡ ἐπιθυμία συλλαβοῦσα τίκτει ἁμαρτίαν”
(“But each person is tempted… then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin.”)
— James 1:14–15 (Greek)
Did you catch that?
Temptation is not the birth of sin.
It’s the moment before the decision.
The battlefield… not the defeat.
Even in Hebrew thought, the idea of temptation carries the sense of testing, not immediate guilt. In Genesis, when Abraham was “tested,” the Hebrew says:

“וְהָאֱלֹהִים נִסָּה אֶת־אַבְרָהָם”
(veha’Elohim nissah et-Avraham)
“God tested Abraham.”
— Genesis 22:1 (Hebrew)
The word נִסָּה (nissah) means to prove, to examine, to reveal what’s inside.
Not to condemn.
To expose.
And maybe that’s what’s happening inside you right now.
That thought that scared you…
That urge you didn’t ask for…
That pull you resisted…
What if it wasn’t proof you’re dirty…
…but proof your heart is still alive?
Because dead things don’t fight.
And numb souls don’t wrestle.
But you did.
You paused.
You questioned.
You felt conviction rise up like a warning siren.
That’s not guilt…
that’s the Holy Spirit still speaking.
Hebrews brings it home with something so powerful it almost feels unbelievable:

“πειρασθέντα κατὰ πάντα καθ’ ὁμοιότητα χωρὶς ἁμαρτίας”
(“Tempted in every way, just as we are—yet without sin.”)
— Hebrews 4:15 (Greek)
Every way.
That means Jesus knows what it feels like to be pulled, pressed, and provoked.
But He never crossed into agreement.
Because temptation is an invitation…
sin is an agreement.
And some of you have been condemning yourselves for invitations you never accepted.
Let that sink in.
You’ve been apologizing for battles you actually won.
You’ve been carrying shame for thoughts you rejected.
You’ve been calling yourself guilty…
when heaven saw you resist.
This is where the enemy works overtime.
If he can’t make you sin…
he’ll try to make you feel like you already did.
Because shame isolates.
Shame silences.
Shame convinces you to hide from the very grace that’s trying to heal you.
But Jesus didn’t come for people who never felt temptation.
He came for people who felt it…
and needed strength to overcome it.
So no…
being tempted doesn’t make you guilty.
But what you do next…
that’s where your story is written.
And here’s the part nobody tells you:
Every resisted temptation becomes worship.
Every “no” whispered in weakness echoes loudly in heaven.
Every moment you choose Christ over compromise…
rewrites your identity.
This is not about pretending you’re strong.
It’s about knowing where your strength comes from.
Because even Jesus answered temptation with truth:

“γέγραπται”
(gegraptai)
“It is written.”
He didn’t argue feelings.
He stood on Word.
And that same Word is available to you right now.
Not to shame you…
but to anchor you.
So if you’ve been fighting quietly…
if your mind has been a battlefield lately…
if you’ve been exhausted from resisting things nobody else sees…
be honest.
This hit deeper than you expected, didn’t it?
There are people reading your comment who need to know they’re not alone.
And if you truly want to glorify God—not just privately, but boldly—then stand with what is building His Kingdom. Support what feeds truth, exposes lies, and brings people back to Jesus.
Follow closely, because drifting is easier than you think.
This isn’t just content.
It’s formation.
It’s sharpening.
It’s coming back to the Cross again and again until your life reflects it.
Because temptation may knock…
but grace still holds the door.
And Jesus is still standing there, reminding you who you really are.
You are not what tried to pull you…
you are who you chose to follow.
And that changes everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Nights He Touched One Woman But Longed for Another
paragraphs:
The Nights He Touched One Woman But Longed for Another
When Love Was Confused, When Desire Was Divided, When God Was Still Writing
There are nights the Bible does not soften.
Nights it does not clean up.
Nights where love is not pure, not clear, not even honest.
And somehow… God still shows up there.

Jacob thought he knew what love looked like. He had already seen her once and the world stopped. Rachel. The one his heart ran toward before his feet could follow. Scripture doesn’t hide it. In the Hebrew it says, “וַיֶּאֱהַב יַעֲקֹב אֶת־רָחֵל” (Vaye’ehav Ya‘aqov et-Rachel) — “Jacob loved Rachel” (Genesis 29:18). Not admired. Not preferred. Loved. Deep, consuming, undeniable.
Seven years felt like days to him.
That’s what real desire does. It bends time. It makes sacrifice feel small.
But then came a night that rewrote everything.
No warning. No clarity. No consent to the truth.
Just darkness.
Just deception.
Just a father’s scheme and a daughter’s silence.

“And it came to pass in the evening, that he took Leah his daughter, and brought her to him; and he went in unto her” (Genesis 29:23). In Hebrew, the phrasing is stark, almost unsettling in its simplicity: “וַיְהִי בָעֶרֶב… וַיָּבֹא אֵלֶיהָ” (Vayehi ba‘erev… vayyavo eleha). No romance. No buildup. Just a moment that would echo for generations.
Jacob woke up… and reality hit him like a blow to the chest.
“And behold, it was Leah” (Genesis 29:25).
Behold.
Look.
Face it.
It was never who you thought.
And suddenly, Jacob’s nights became divided.
His body with Leah.
His heart with Rachel.
His covenant confused.
His desires tangled.
And Leah… she wasn’t blind to it.

Scripture gives her one of the most quietly devastating lines in all of Genesis: “וַיַּרְא יְהוָה כִּי־שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה” (Vayar YHWH ki-senu’ah Leah) — “The LORD saw that Leah was hated” (Genesis 29:31).
Not ignored.
Not overlooked.
Hated.
Or more precisely in Hebrew context — rejected, unloved, set aside.
God saw it.
God always sees what people pretend isn’t happening.
Leah knew the truth every night Jacob closed his eyes.
She knew he was touching her…
…but dreaming of someone else.
And maybe that’s where this stops being Jacob’s story.
Maybe this is yours.
The relationship where you were chosen… but not really wanted.
The marriage where presence replaced passion.
The silent comparison you could feel but never prove.
The nights where someone held you… but their heart wasn’t there.
Leah didn’t scream.
She didn’t expose.
She didn’t fight for attention.
She turned somewhere deeper.
With every child she bore, she spoke not just names… but wounds.
“Reuben” — “רְאוּבֵן” (Re’uven): “Because the LORD has looked upon my affliction” (Genesis 29:32). See me, God. Because he doesn’t.
“Simeon” — “שִׁמְעוֹן” (Shim‘on): “Because the LORD has heard that I am hated” (Genesis 29:33). Hear me, God. Because he won’t.
“Levi” — “לֵוִי” (Levi): “Now this time my husband will be joined unto me” (Genesis 29:34). Stay with me. Please.
But then something shifts.
Something breaks.
Or maybe something heals.
When Judah is born, she says something different.
“הַפַּעַם אוֹדֶה אֶת־יְהוָה” (Hapa‘am odeh et-YHWH) — “Now I will praise the LORD” (Genesis 29:35).
Not “now he will love me.”
Not “now I am enough.”
Not “now I’ve earned it.”
Just… “Now I will praise.”
That’s the moment everything changes.
Because Leah stops trying to win a love that keeps choosing someone else…
…and starts anchoring herself in a God who already chose her.
And here’s the part that will shake you if you really let it.
Jesus didn’t come through Rachel.
The Messiah didn’t trace His bloodline through the woman Jacob adored.
He came through Leah.
Through the unloved.
Through the overlooked.
Through the one who cried herself to sleep while someone else was being desired.
Matthew 1:2–3 traces it clearly. Judah. Born from Leah. The line continues… all the way to Christ.
God didn’t just see Leah.
He wrote eternity through her.
Sit with that.
The nights Jacob spent with Leah but dreamed of Rachel…
were not wasted nights.
They were uncomfortable, messy, broken pages in a story God refused to abandon.
Because God specializes in rewriting what people ruin.
Some of you have been living in Leah’s place.
Feeling like the substitute.
Feeling like the second choice.
Feeling like you’re tolerated but not treasured.
And it’s been eating at you quietly.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because here’s the truth that will either confront you or free you…
God is not waiting for you to become Rachel.
He is meeting you as Leah.
Right there in the ache.
Right there in the rejection.
Right there in the nights no one applauds.
And He is writing something eternal through it.
This isn’t about buying something.
It’s about building something eternal in your walk with Him.
If you feel led to stand with this mission and glorify God through it, step into it here:
Because the same God who saw Leah…
sees you.
And He is not finished writing.
The nights that broke you may become the very pages that reveal Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Drenched the Fire Before It Fell — The Scandalous Faith of Elijah That Still Confronts Your Doubt
paragraphs: They Drenched the Fire Before It Fell — The Scandalous Faith of Elijah That Still Confronts Your Doubt
You would think if you were asking God to send fire from heaven… you wouldn’t make it harder.
But Elijah did.
Not just harder… impossible.

The prophet stood on Mount Carmel, facing 450 prophets of Baal, surrounded by a nation that had already started forgetting what truth felt like. The air was thick with compromise. People who once whispered the name of Yahweh now spoke it like a distant memory.
And Elijah didn’t begin with fire.
He began with exposure.

“עַד־מָתַי אַתֶּם פֹּסְחִים עַל־שְׁתֵּי הַסְּעִפִּים” (ʿad-mātay atem poschim al-shtei ha-seʿippim)
“How long will you limp between two opinions?” (1 Kings 18:21)
That word “פֹּסְחִים” (poschim)… it doesn’t just mean hesitate. It means to limp, to stagger, to dance awkwardly between loyalties. That’s not just Israel’s condition.
That’s ours.
We don’t fully walk away from God… we just don’t fully stay either.
And then comes the moment that should shake you.
Elijah builds the altar, lays the wood, cuts the sacrifice. Everything is ready for fire… but instead of asking God immediately, he commands something that makes no sense.
“Fill four jars with water, and pour it on the offering.”
Once.
Twice.
Three times.
Until everything is soaked.
The wood… soaked.
The sacrifice… soaked.
Even the trench… overflowing.
This wasn’t just water.
It was a confrontation.

Water, in Hebrew, “מַיִם” (mayim), often symbolizes life, cleansing, provision… but here it becomes an obstacle. A barrier. A visible declaration that what’s about to happen cannot be explained by human effort.
Elijah wasn’t making the miracle harder for God.
He was removing every excuse for man.
Because if the fire came now… no one could say it was coincidence.
No one could say it was manipulation.
No one could say it was emotional hype.
It would have to be God.
And maybe that’s why this story feels uncomfortable.
Because we spend most of our lives doing the opposite.
We try to make things easier for God.
We control outcomes.
We reduce risk.
We leave just enough room for ourselves to take credit if something works.
But Elijah drenched the altar.
He drowned his backup plan.
He buried human possibility so divine power would be undeniable.
And then he prayed.
Not a long prayer.
Not a dramatic performance.
Just a simple, surrendered call:

“יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵי אַבְרָהָם יִצְחָק וְיִשְׂרָאֵל הַיּוֹם יִוָּדַע כִּי־אַתָּה אֱלֹהִים”
“YHWH, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, let it be known today that You are God…” (1 Kings 18:36)
And heaven answered.

“וַתִּפֹּל אֵשׁ־יְהוָה” (vattippol esh-YHWH)
“The fire of the LORD fell…” (1 Kings 18:38)
Not just on the sacrifice.
It consumed everything.
The wood.
The stones.
The dust.
Even the water.
Because when God moves… He doesn’t just prove a point.
He overwhelms doubt.
And suddenly, the same people who were limping between opinions fell on their faces and cried:

“יְהוָה הוּא הָאֱלֹהִים”
“The LORD—He is God!” (1 Kings 18:39)
But here’s the part no one says out loud.
The fire didn’t come until the altar was soaked.
And maybe that’s why some prayers feel unanswered.
Because we’re still protecting something.
Still holding back.
Still leaving parts of our lives dry enough to control.
But Elijah shows us something dangerous and beautiful at the same time…
God’s glory is most undeniable when your situation looks most impossible.
The deeper truth runs even further.
This moment on Mount Carmel wasn’t just about fire.
It was pointing forward.
To another “altar.”
Another sacrifice.
Another moment where everything looked finished… soaked… impossible.
At the cross, Jesus cried:

“τετέλεσται” (tetelestai)
“It is finished.” (John 19:30)
And it looked like defeat.
Like everything had been extinguished.
Like hope itself had been drowned.
But just like Carmel…
The impossibility was intentional.
Because three days later, the fire of resurrection would fall… not consuming a sacrifice, but raising it.
Not proving power… but revealing grace.
That’s the scandal.
That God doesn’t wait for perfect conditions.
He steps into impossible ones.
And rewrites them.
So when Elijah poured water, he wasn’t just preparing an altar.
He was exposing a truth we still struggle to accept:
If God is going to move in your life… it won’t be because you made it easy for Him.
It will be because you finally surrendered what you were trying to control.
Be honest.
What are you still keeping dry?
Your pride?
Your hidden sin?
Your fear of fully committing?
Your reputation?
Your comfort?
Because fire doesn’t fall on partial surrender.
It falls where everything has been laid down.
Be honest. This hit deeper than you expected.
And don’t keep this to yourself.
You’re going to need to come back when your faith feels dry again.
And if you truly want to glorify God… support what is feeding your spirit.
Not out of pressure… but out of purpose.
Because at some point… you have to decide.
Will you keep limping between two opinions…
Or will you drench the altar and trust God to send the fire?
The fire only falls where nothing is left to protect.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: IS POLYGAMY BIBLICAL… OR HAVE WE MISREAD GOD ALL ALONG?
paragraphs: IS POLYGAMY BIBLICAL… OR HAVE WE MISREAD GOD ALL ALONG?
The question doesn’t whisper… it disturbs.
