Because somewhere between ancient pages and modern confusion, people have seen men in Scripture with multiple wives and quietly wondered… “Did God allow this… or did He just tolerate it?”
And if we’re honest… some are not asking out of curiosity.
They’re asking because they’re trying to justify something already growing in their heart.
So don’t rush this.
Sit with it.
Because this isn’t just about marriage.
This is about how we read God… how we interpret silence… and how easily we can mistake permission for approval.
The first time marriage is ever spoken into existence, it wasn’t complicated.
It wasn’t layered.
It wasn’t culturally adjusted.
It was pure.
Genesis 2:24 doesn’t leave room for confusion:
“עַל־כֵּן֙ יַעֲזָב־אִ֔ישׁ אֶת־אָבִ֖יו וְאֶת־אִמּ֑וֹ וְדָבַ֣ק בְּאִשְׁתּ֔וֹ וְהָי֖וּ לְבָשָׂ֥ר אֶחָֽד׃”
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
One man.
One woman.
One flesh.
Not multiple unions.
Not divided covenant.
The Hebrew word “אֶחָד” (echad) — one — speaks of unity, not fragmentation.
Before culture ever complicated it… God made it simple.
But then something happens.
Sin enters.
And with sin comes distortion.
The first recorded polygamist in Scripture is not a hero.
It’s Lamech.
Genesis 4:19:
“וַיִּקַּ֥ח ל֖וֹ לֶ֣מֶךְ שְׁתֵּ֣י נָשִׁ֑ים”
“Lamech took two wives.”
And if you keep reading… you don’t find peace.
You find violence.
Boasting.
Pride.
Distortion.
Polygamy didn’t begin in righteousness.
It appeared in rebellion.
And yet… the tension deepens.
Because later, we see Abraham… Jacob… David… Solomon.
Men chosen by God.
Men who had multiple wives.
So what does that mean?
Did God change His mind?
Or are we missing something deeper?
Look closer.
Every time polygamy appears in their lives… peace disappears.
Abraham and Hagar lead to jealousy and division.
Genesis 16 is not a love story… it’s a fracture.
Sarah’s pain. Hagar’s rejection. Ishmael’s separation.
Jacob’s household becomes a battlefield between Leah and Rachel.
Genesis 30 is filled with competition, bitterness, and aching hearts.
David’s multiple wives lead to chaos within his own house… betrayal among his sons… deep wounds that never fully heal.
And Solomon…
The wisest man who ever lived…
1 Kings 11:3:
“He had seven hundred wives… and three hundred concubines, and his wives turned away his heart.”
Turned.
Away.
His heart.
Polygamy didn’t strengthen devotion.
It diluted it.
So was God endorsing it?
Or was He allowing broken people to live with the consequences of their choices?
Because Scripture never celebrates polygamy.
It records it.
There’s a difference.
And if you read carefully… God is often working in spite of it, not because of it.
Then Jesus speaks.
And everything comes back into focus.
Matthew 19:4-6:
“οὐκ ἀνέγνωτε ὅτι ὁ κτίσας… ἄρσεν καὶ θῆλυ ἐποίησεν αὐτούς… καὶ ἔσονται οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν”
“Have you not read that He who created them from the beginning made them male and female… and the two shall become one flesh?”
The two.
Not the many.
Jesus doesn’t adjust the design to match culture.
He restores the design to match truth.
Because the standard was never rewritten.
Humanity just drifted from it.
Even church leadership reflects this clarity.
1 Timothy 3:2:
“δεῖ… μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα”
“An overseer must be the husband of one wife.”
Not because it’s a random rule…
But because it reflects the heart of covenant.
Singular.
Faithful.
Whole.
And then… the deepest layer.
Marriage was never just about people.
It was always about pointing to Christ.
Ephesians 5:25:
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church…”
One Christ.
One Church.
Not divided.
Not multiplied.
Undivided love.
Undivided devotion.
So now the question changes.
It’s no longer…
“Was polygamy ever practiced?”
We already know it was.
The real question is…
“Does it reflect the heart of God?”
And the answer is written not just in law… but in pain, in consequence, in restoration, and in redemption.
Because from the beginning… through the fall… through broken families… through divided hearts…
God has been telling one consistent story.
Not of multiple loves…
But of one faithful love pursuing an unfaithful people.
And maybe that’s why this hits deeper than expected.
Because this isn’t just about ancient marriages.
It’s about divided hearts today.
Loving God… but also holding onto things we don’t want to let go of.
Calling Him Lord… but keeping other “loves” hidden in the shadows.
Be honest.
Has your heart been fully His?
Or has it been shared?
Because God is not after part of you.
He’s after all of you.
Undivided.
Whole.
Faithful.
This is a moment.
And if you feel something pulling you deeper… that’s not pressure.
That’s invitation.
Because staying close to truth matters.
Following matters.
Growing matters.
And if you truly want to glorify God with your life… support what spreads His truth.
You’re stepping into deeper discipleship, accountability, and daily spiritual nourishment.
Stay where truth lives.
Stay where conviction leads to healing.
Stay where Jesus is not diluted.
Because partial surrender still leaves room for idols.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Night David Lost His Son
paragraphs:
The Night David Lost His Son
When a King Learned That Sin Echoes… But So Does Mercy
There are nights that never end.

Not because the sun refuses to rise…
but because the soul refuses to forget.
That was the night David entered.

Not as a king.
Not as a warrior.
Not as the man who killed Goliath.
But as a father… waiting for his child to die.
And the silence in that room was louder than any battlefield he had ever survived.

Because this time, the enemy wasn’t outside the gates.
It was inside his own choices.

It started with a glance that turned into a desire…
a desire that became a decision…
a decision that became a scandal.

Bathsheba.
Uriah.
Blood.
Deception.
David thought he had buried it.
But heaven does not forget what earth tries to hide.

When the prophet Nathan stood before him, he didn’t raise a sword.
He told a story.
And David, the king who judged others with precision, condemned the man in the story… not realizing he was condemning himself.
“אַתָּה הָאִישׁ” (Attah ha’ish) — “You are the man.” (2 Samuel 12:7)
Everything collapsed in that moment.

The crown suddenly felt heavy.
The throne felt cold.
And the God he loved felt… distant.

David didn’t defend himself.
He didn’t argue.
He didn’t justify.
He broke.
“חָטָאתִי לַיהוָה” (Chatati la’Adonai) — “I have sinned against the LORD.” (2 Samuel 12:13)

No excuses.
No performance.
Just truth.
And here is where the story should have ended… if God operated like we do.
But God didn’t strike him dead.
Instead, He pronounced something far more terrifying:

“The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die.”
And then—
“the child that is born to you shall die.” (2 Samuel 12:13–14)
Forgiveness… but consequences.
Grace… but scars.
That night, David entered a different kind of battle.

Not with swords.
But with surrender.

He fell to the ground.
He fasted.
He wept.
He refused comfort.
For seven days, the palace watched their king unravel.

He didn’t eat.
He didn’t sleep.
He didn’t speak like a king anymore.
He spoke like a desperate father.

Because when sin finally catches up to you…
you realize it never just affects you.
It spreads.
It reaches.
It breaks things you never meant to break.
And now, the life of his son hung in the balance.
David prayed like a man who had nothing left to lose.
And maybe you’ve been there too…

When the prayer isn’t polished anymore.
When it’s not theological.
When it’s just raw, trembling words between sobs.
“Please, God… not this.”
But heaven stayed quiet.
And on the seventh day…
the child died.

No thunder.
No warning.
No miracle.
Just silence.
The servants were afraid to tell him.
Because if David was like this while the child lived… what would he do now?
But when David saw their faces… he knew.
And this is the moment that doesn’t make sense.
David stood up.

He washed himself.
He anointed himself.
He changed his clothes.
And then he did something no one expected—
He went into the house of the LORD and worshiped.
Worshiped.
After losing the son born out of his failure.
After facing the consequences of his sin.
After praying with everything he had… and still hearing “no.”
Why?
Because somewhere between the scandal and the sorrow… David understood something deeper than his pain.
God had not abandoned him.
“לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא־לִי אֱלֹהִים” (Lev tahor bera-li Elohim) — “Create in me a clean heart, O God.” (Psalm 51:10)

He didn’t ask for his reputation back.
He didn’t ask for his image restored.
He asked for a clean heart.
Because David realized something we often resist:

The greatest tragedy is not losing something we love…
it’s losing the presence of God and pretending we’re fine.

And even in discipline…
even in loss…
even in consequences…
God was still near.
The child was gone.
But grace remained.
And years later… God would give David another son.
Solomon.

Not born from perfection…
but from redemption.

Because God doesn’t just forgive—
He restores.

Not the way we expect…
but in a way that proves His mercy is stronger than our worst decisions.
And maybe this is where this story stops being about David…
and starts being about you.
Because some of you are carrying a night like this.

A mistake you can’t undo.
A consequence you can’t escape.
A regret that keeps replaying when everything gets quiet.

You’ve asked God to fix it.
To reverse it.
To take it away.
And maybe… He didn’t.
And now you don’t know what to do with the silence.
But David is whispering across time:

Get up.
Wash your face.
Go back into the presence of God.
Not because everything is okay…
but because He still is.
Be honest… this hit deeper than you expected.
You’re not alone in this.
If you truly want to glorify God with your life… support what is feeding your spirit.

Because the night you thought ended you…
might be the place where God begins rewriting you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: When God Says “Be Still” But Your World Is Falling Apart: The Command That Feels Impossible in Chaos
paragraphs: When God Says “Be Still” But Your World Is Falling Apart: The Command That Feels Impossible in Chaos
There are moments when everything inside you is screaming… and yet heaven answers with silence.

Not because God is absent.
Not because He doesn’t care.
But because He is saying something your panic cannot hear.
“Be still.”
And if you’re honest… that command almost feels offensive when your life is breaking.
Because how do you “be still” when your heart is racing, your prayers feel unanswered, your fears feel louder than your faith, and your world is unraveling in ways you didn’t see coming?

Psalm 46:10 says, “Be still, and know that I am God.”
But the original Hebrew reveals something deeper, something far more confrontational than the soft, peaceful version we often imagine.

The phrase “be still” comes from the Hebrew word רָפָה (raphah) — which doesn’t mean “relax” or “calm down.”
It means: to let go, to release, to drop your grip, to surrender.

God isn’t whispering comfort first.
He is commanding surrender.
“Let go… and know that I am God.”
Because the truth is, chaos exposes what we’re still trying to control.
And that’s where this verse stops being poetic… and starts becoming personal.
Because some of us aren’t just overwhelmed — we’re gripping things God never asked us to carry.
We’re holding onto outcomes, timelines, people, control, fear, and even pain… as if our survival depends on it.
But heaven is not asking you to figure everything out.
Heaven is asking you to release.
The second part of the verse says, “and know that I am God.”
The word “know” here is from the Hebrew יָדַע (yadaʿ) — not intellectual knowledge, but intimate, experiential knowing.

God is not inviting you into information.
He’s inviting you into encounter.
Because you don’t truly know God when life is easy.
You know Him when everything falls apart… and He still holds.
You know Him when your plans fail… and His sovereignty doesn’t.
You know Him when your strength runs out… and His presence doesn’t.
This is the tension of the Gospel — surrender feels like loss, but it is actually the doorway to revelation.
Even Jesus modeled this.
In the Garden of Gethsemane, in the crushing weight before the cross, He prayed:
“Abba, Father… remove this cup from Me. Yet not what I will, but what You will.” (Mark 14:36)
The word “Abba” in Aramaic — אבא (Abba) — is deeply intimate. It means “Father,” but carries the vulnerability of “Daddy.”

Even in agony… Jesus didn’t hold control.
He surrendered into relationship.
And that’s the heartbeat of “be still.”

It is not passive.
It is not weak.
It is not giving up.
It is the fiercest act of trust a human soul can make.
Because to “be still” in chaos means you are choosing to believe that God is still God… even when life doesn’t make sense.
And maybe that’s where this is hitting you right now.
Because something in your life feels out of control.
Something didn’t go the way you prayed.
Something broke. Something ended. Something shifted.
And you’ve been trying to fix it… hold it… understand it… carry it…
But God is not asking you to carry it anymore.
He’s asking you to let go.
Be honest…
What are you still gripping that God is asking you to release?
What fear have you been feeding instead of surrendering?
What situation have you been trying to control instead of trusting Him with?
This is where it gets real.
Because surrender is not just spiritual language.
It is a decision that costs your pride, your control, your timeline, your comfort.
But it gives you something you cannot manufacture:

Peace that doesn’t make sense.
Strength that doesn’t come from you.
Clarity that rises from trust, not understanding.
The kind of peace Paul described in Greek as:
εἰρήνη (eirēnē) — not just absence of conflict, but wholeness, restoration, completeness.
That peace only comes when surrender replaces striving.
So when God says “be still,” He is not ignoring your chaos.
He is inviting you into a deeper reality where chaos does not have the final word.
Because the truth is…
God has never lost control — even when you feel like you have.
And maybe this is the moment you stop fighting to hold everything together…
…and start trusting the One who already is.
Let it sit.
Let it confront you.
Let it change you.
Be honest. This hit deeper than you expected.
And if you feel God stirring something deeper in you — not just emotion, but transformation — then step into it.
Those who truly desire to glorify God don’t just consume truth… they support and spread it.
If you’re ready to stop living on the surface… and start walking in truth:
Because this isn’t just about reading.
It’s about becoming.
And if you’ve read this far… something in you already knows.

You don’t need more control.
You need more surrender.

And the moment you finally let go…
you’ll realize God never lost hold of you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Told You It Was “Just a Little”… But No One Told You What It Would Cost
paragraphs: They Told You It Was “Just a Little”… But No One Told You What It Would Cost
Is it really sin… if you only go a little further than you planned?

That question doesn’t usually show up in a church pew. It shows up in the quiet. In the car after a date. In a dim room where your convictions feel softer than your emotions. It whispers, not shouts. It negotiates, not commands.
“Just a little.”
That’s how it always begins.

No one wakes up planning to fall. No one says, “Tonight, I will distance myself from God.” It’s always smaller than that. Softer. Almost harmless. A hand held longer than necessary. A boundary pushed just slightly. A kiss that lingers into something heavier. A moment where your spirit hesitates… but your body keeps moving.
And somewhere deep inside, you feel it.
Not shame at first. Not guilt. Just… a tension.
Because your soul remembers something your flesh is trying to forget.

In the ancient Greek of Scripture, the word for sexual immorality is “πορνεία” (porneía). It is not a narrow word. It is not limited to extreme acts. It is expansive, encompassing every form of sexual expression outside God’s covenant design. Not because God is restrictive, but because He is protective.

When Paul wrote in 1 Corinthians 6:18, “Flee from sexual immorality,” the Greek says, “φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν” (pheúgete tēn porneían). Flee. Not manage. Not flirt with. Not gradually approach and then retreat.
Run.
Why would God use such urgent language if “just a little” wasn’t dangerous?
Because “a little” is never just a little.

In Hebrew thought, sin isn’t merely about the act. It’s about the direction of the heart. The word “חָטָא” (chata’) means “to miss the mark.” Not to rebel violently… but to drift. To aim slightly off-center. To convince yourself that a small deviation won’t change the outcome.
But it always does.
You don’t fall into sin. You drift into it… one “just this once” at a time.
And yet, here’s the part no one says out loud…
You didn’t push that boundary because you hate God.
You pushed it because you wanted to feel something.
To feel loved. Desired. Seen. Close. Safe. Alive.
There is a human ache behind every compromise.
But the tragedy is this: we keep trying to satisfy a spiritual hunger with physical permission.
And it never fills.
James 1:14–15 explains it with surgical honesty. Desire conceives. Then it gives birth to sin. And sin, when fully grown, brings forth death.
Not always physical death.
But something dies.
Your sensitivity. Your peace. Your clarity. Your boldness before God.
And suddenly, prayer feels heavier. Worship feels distant. Conviction feels louder… but obedience feels harder.
Not because God moved away.
But because you slowly stepped out of alignment.

Even in Aramaic—the language Jesus likely spoke—there’s a weight to purity that goes beyond behavior. The heart was never meant to be divided. God wasn’t asking for restriction… He was asking for wholeness.
And every time we test the boundary, we fracture that wholeness just a little more.
Be honest…
You’ve felt that moment after.
When everything goes quiet.
When the excitement fades faster than expected.
When your soul whispers, “This isn’t who you are.”
That whisper is not condemnation.
That is mercy.
Because God doesn’t expose to shame you. He exposes to bring you back.
And here is where everything shifts.
Because this isn’t just a story about temptation.
This is a story about redemption.
There was a woman once, caught in sexual sin. Dragged publicly. Shamed brutally. The law was clear about what she deserved.
Death.
But Jesus did something scandalous.
He knelt.
He wrote in the dust.
And then He said, “Let him who is without sin cast the first stone.”
One by one, they walked away.
And Jesus looked at her—not as a case, not as a failure, not as a warning—but as someone still worth restoring.
“Neither do I condemn you. Go… and sin no more.”
Notice that.
He didn’t say her sin didn’t matter.
He said it didn’t define her anymore.
That is the Gospel.
You may have tested the boundary.
You may have crossed it.
You may be sitting in the quiet aftermath right now.
But you are not disqualified.
You are being called back.
And maybe this is the moment where you stop asking, “How far can I go without sinning?”
And start asking, “How close can I live to Jesus?”
Because holiness isn’t about the edge.
It’s about proximity.
The closer you walk with Christ, the less appealing the edge becomes.
Not out of fear…
But out of love.
So be honest right now.
Not with me.
With God.
Because it did.
And someone you know needs this too.
If you truly want to glorify God, then don’t just consume truth… support the mission that spreads it.
Because this isn’t about behavior management.
This is about transformation.
And Jesus is still rewriting stories that looked too far gone.
You’re not one mistake away from rejection… you’re one surrender away from restoration.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why You Keep Falling Into the Same Sexual Sin
paragraphs:
Why You Keep Falling Into the Same Sexual Sin
And the Truth About the Battle You Thought You Already Lost
You told yourself this was the last time.
You said it with conviction. With tears. Maybe even on your knees.
But somehow… you ended up back there again.

The same screen.
The same thoughts.
The same hidden place no one sees.
And now the silence feels louder than ever.

Not because God left…
…but because you don’t know how to face Him again.
You’re not just tired of the sin.
You’re tired of yourself.
Be honest… this hit deeper than you expected.
Because this isn’t just about lust, pornography, secret relationships, or fantasies that won’t leave you alone. This is about a war happening inside you that you don’t fully understand yet.
The apostle Paul described this exact struggle in Romans 7:19:
“For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.”

In the original Greek, he uses the phrase:
“ὃ γὰρ θέλω τοῦτο οὐ πράσσω, ἀλλ᾽ ὃ μισῶ τοῦτο ποιῶ”
It literally carries the tension of a man trapped between desire and action… wanting holiness but practicing what he hates.
This is not weakness.
This is war.
And the reason you keep falling isn’t just because you lack discipline.
It’s because you’re fighting a spiritual battle with flesh-only weapons.
Galatians 5:17 says:
“For the flesh desires what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh.”
The word “flesh” here is “σάρξ” (sarx) — not just your body, but your fallen nature… the part of you that still craves what destroys you.

So every time you say, “Why do I keep going back?”
The deeper truth is…
There is something in you that still wants to.
That’s the part no one wants to admit.
And until you confront that honestly… you will keep repeating the cycle.
James 1:14 explains it without softening the blow:
“But each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire.”
The Greek word for “lured” is “ἐξελκόμενος” — like a fish being dragged out by bait.
You’re not just falling.
You’re being drawn.
Hooked.
Pulled.
Because something inside you hasn’t died yet.
And this is where most people get it wrong.
They try to manage sin instead of killing it.
Jesus didn’t say “control your sin.”
He said in Matthew 5:29:
“If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away.”
This isn’t about literal self-harm.
It’s about radical separation.
Because partial surrender will never produce full freedom.
But here’s where the story changes… and where grace interrupts the scandal.
Because even in your repeated failure…
God has not walked away.
In the Hebrew of Lamentations 3:22–23:
“חַסְדֵי יְהוָה כִּי לֹא־תָמְנוּ… חֲדָשִׁים לַבְּקָרִים”

His mercies… never end.
They are new every morning.
Not every “perfect streak.”
Not every “successful attempt.”
Every morning.
Even the morning after you failed again.
Let that sit with you.

God knew how many times you would fall…
and still chose to love you completely.
But grace is not permission to stay stuck.
Grace is the power to get up differently.
Titus 2:11–12 says grace “teaches us to say no to ungodliness.”
Grace trains you.
It transforms you.
It doesn’t just forgive you.
So why do you keep falling?
Because you’ve been trying to fight sin without fully surrendering your heart.
Because you’ve been hiding instead of confessing.
Because you’ve been managing symptoms instead of crucifying the root.
Galatians 2:20 says:
“I have been crucified with Christ…”
The Greek: “Χριστῷ συνεσταύρωμαι”
It’s not partial death.
It’s complete identification with His cross.
Your old desires don’t get cleaned up.
They get nailed down.
And that’s where real freedom begins.
Not when temptation disappears…
…but when your identity changes.
You are not your urges.
You are not your past.
You are not your last failure.
You are who Christ says you are.
And He didn’t die so you could stay chained to something that’s already been defeated.
So hear this clearly…
You are not too far gone.
You are not too addicted.
You are not too broken.
But you do need to stop pretending this isn’t serious.
Because sin always takes more than it promises.
And it never stops on its own.
Your honesty might be the beginning of someone else’s freedom too.
And if you feel something shifting in your spirit right now…
don’t ignore it.
That’s conviction.
That’s God pulling you closer, not pushing you away.
If you truly want to glorify God with your life… then don’t just receive truth.
Support the mission that’s helping bring it to others.
You don’t need more willpower.
You need deeper surrender.

Because the same place you fell…
can become the place where God rebuilds you stronger than before.
The shame you carry is not the end of your story.
It’s the beginning of your transformation… if you bring it into the light.
You were never meant to fight this alone.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Loved Rachel More… And Leah Had to Sleep With That Reality
paragraphs: He Loved Rachel More… And Leah Had to Sleep With That Reality
The Night God Saw the Woman Nobody Chose
It doesn’t start with romance. It starts with a quiet betrayal… the kind that doesn’t scream, but settles into the bones and stays there.
Leah knew.
She knew the way Jacob’s eyes softened when Rachel walked into the room. She knew the silence that followed when he looked at her. She knew the difference between being chosen… and being tolerated.
Scripture doesn’t hide it. It doesn’t soften it. It doesn’t try to protect your feelings from the truth.

In Genesis 29:30, the Hebrew says it plainly:
“וַיֶּאֱהַב גַּם־אֶת־רָחֵל מִלֵּאָה”
“Vaye’ehav gam et-Rachel miLe’ah”
“He loved Rachel also more than Leah.”
More than.
Not equal. Not growing into love. Not learning her heart over time.
More than.
And Leah had to sleep next to that reality.

Imagine that kind of pain… not for a moment, but every single day. Waking up next to a man who fulfills his duty but withholds his affection. Hearing laughter meant for someone else. Feeling invisible in your own story.
Some of you don’t have to imagine it.
You’ve lived it.
Being overlooked. Being second. Being the one people settle for but never celebrate. Being present, but never pursued.
And here’s the part that breaks you open…
God saw her.

Genesis 29:31 says:
“וַיַּרְא יְהוָה כִּי־שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה”
“Vayar YHWH ki-senu’ah Le’ah”
“And the LORD saw that Leah was hated.”
That word “שְׂנוּאָה” (senu’ah) doesn’t always mean active hatred—it means rejected, unloved, pushed aside.
God didn’t ignore it.
He didn’t say, “Just be patient.”
He saw.
Really saw.
The tears she hid. The prayers she whispered into the night. The ache of never being enough for the person she longed for.
And then something unexpected happened.
God opened her womb.
Not as a reward for her pain… but as a reminder that heaven was still writing her story.
Her first son—Reuben.

“כִּי־רָאָה יְהוָה בְּעָנְיִי”
“Ki-ra’ah YHWH be’onyi”
“Because the LORD has seen my affliction.” (Genesis 29:32)
Seen.
Leah wasn’t invisible to God, even if she was invisible to Jacob.
But pain doesn’t disappear overnight.
She kept hoping.
“This time my husband will love me…”
You can hear it in every name she gave her sons.

Simeon: “The LORD has heard.”
Levi: “Now my husband will become attached to me…”
Still reaching. Still longing. Still trying to earn what should have been freely given.
And maybe this is where it hits you hardest.
Because you’ve done the same.
Trying harder. Giving more. Becoming less of yourself just to be loved by someone who already decided you weren’t their first choice.
Then comes Judah.
And everything shifts.

Genesis 29:35:
“הַפַּעַם אוֹדֶה אֶת־יְהוָה”
“Hapa’am odeh et-YHWH”
“This time I will praise the LORD.”
Did you catch it?
Not, “This time he will love me.”
Not, “This time I’ll finally be enough.”
This time… I will praise.
Something broke inside Leah… and something holy replaced it.
She stopped chasing Jacob’s approval… and started anchoring herself in God’s presence.
And from Judah…
Came Jesus.
Let that sit with you.
The Messiah—the Savior of the world—did not come through the woman who was loved more.
He came through the one who was overlooked.
The one who cried herself to sleep.
The one who knew rejection intimately.
The one who had to wrestle her worth out of the hands of disappointment and place it into the hands of God.
If that doesn’t shake you… you’re not listening.
Because this isn’t just Leah’s story.
This is yours.
This is every hidden wound… every silent prayer… every moment you questioned if you were enough.
God is not building your story based on who rejected you.
He’s building it based on what He sees in you.
And He sees more than they ever did.
Be honest…
This hit deeper than you expected, didn’t it?
There are people in your life who need to hear this truth but don’t even know how to say it out loud.
And if you feel something stirring inside you right now… that pull toward something deeper, something real…
Follow closely.
Because this isn’t just content.
This is discipleship.
This is truth that cuts… and then heals.
And yes… there’s a deeper level of support.
If this message reached you… if it convicted you… if it reminded you that God sees what others overlook… then supporting this mission is one way to glorify Him.
But more than that…
You’re helping more Leahs find their way back to God.
You’re helping more hidden stories be seen.
You’re helping more broken hearts encounter Jesus.
If you’re ready for that step, go here:
Because this isn’t about a transaction.
It’s about transformation.
And someone out there is still waiting for a message like this to reach them.
Don’t let it stop with you.
Because the same God who saw Leah…
Sees you too.
And He’s not done writing your story.
Even if they loved someone else more… God chose to bring glory through you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They thought it was the end of him.
paragraphs: They thought it was the end of him.

The pit was too deep.
The betrayal was too personal.
The silence from heaven was too loud.
And if we’re honest… some of us have stood in that same darkness, wondering if God forgot our name.
Before God ever promoted Joseph, He allowed him to be stripped, sold, lied about, and forgotten.
That part doesn’t get preached enough.
Because we love the palace, but we don’t talk about the pit.

Genesis tells it plainly, without softening the blow. “וַיִּפְשִׁיטוּ אֶת־יוֹסֵף אֶת־כֻּתָּנְתּוֹ” (Vayafshitu et-Yosef et-kuttoneto) — “And they stripped Joseph of his robe” (Genesis 37:23). That robe wasn’t just clothing. It was identity. Favor. Promise.
And God let it be taken.
Sit with that.

God didn’t stop the brothers.
God didn’t block the betrayal.
God didn’t interrupt the injustice.
Because sometimes the very thing you think is destroying your calling… is actually preparing it.

Joseph didn’t go from dream to destiny.
He went from dream to devastation.
Thrown into a pit. “הַבּוֹר רֵק אֵין בּוֹ מָיִם” (habbor req, ein bo mayim) — “The pit was empty; there was no water in it” (Genesis 37:24). No water. No life. No comfort.
Just silence.
Have you ever prayed and felt that kind of silence?
Like your words hit the ceiling and fell back on your chest?
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Because some of you are there right now. Not in a literal pit, but in a season that feels empty. Dry. Confusing.
And you’re asking, “God, what did I do wrong?”
Joseph did nothing wrong.
Let that break something inside you that needed to be broken.
He was faithful. Obedient. Pure-hearted.
And still… he was sold.
“וַיִּמְכְּרוּ אֶת־יוֹסֵף” (vayimkeru et-Yosef) — “They sold Joseph” (Genesis 37:28).
Thirty pieces of silver would later echo in another betrayal. Another innocent man. Another story where it looked like evil was winning.
But heaven was writing something deeper.

Joseph’s life was not falling apart.
It was falling into place.
But you don’t see that when you’re in chains.
In Potiphar’s house, Joseph served. In prison, Joseph interpreted dreams. And the Scripture whispers something that changes everything:
“וַיהוָה הָיָה עִם־יוֹסֵף” (Adonai hayah im-Yosef) — “The LORD was with Joseph” (Genesis 39:2).

With him… in slavery.
With him… in false accusation.
With him… in prison.

God’s presence is not proven by comfort.
It’s proven by purpose.
Even in the Greek Septuagint, the idea holds: “Κύριος ἦν μετὰ Ἰωσήφ” (Kyrios ēn meta Iōsēph) — “The Lord was with Joseph.”
Not occasionally. Not when things improved.
With him.
Right there in the injustice.
Right there in the waiting.
Right there in the silence you thought meant abandonment.
If that doesn’t wake something up in your spirit… read it again.
Because we’ve been taught a dangerous lie — that God’s favor means ease.
Joseph’s life proves the opposite.
Favor will put you in places where your character is tested, your faith is stretched, and your trust in God is refined like fire.
Before the throne… there was a prison.
Before authority… there was accusation.
Before elevation… there was humiliation.
And some of you want what Joseph had… but you’re resisting what Joseph endured.

Because the truth is, God is not ignoring you.
He is developing you.
There’s a Hebrew weight to the word “tested” — “נָסָה” (nasah). It means to prove, to try, to refine.
God wasn’t punishing Joseph.
He was proving him.
There is a difference.
And when the moment finally came… it happened suddenly.
One day he was forgotten in prison.
The next day, Pharaoh was calling his name.
That’s how God moves.
Quiet for a long time… then everything shifts in a moment.
“וַיְרִיצֻהוּ מִן־הַבּוֹר” (vayeritzuhu min-habor) — “They quickly brought him out of the pit” (Genesis 41:14).
Quickly.
After years of waiting… suddenly.
That’s the part people don’t understand.
God is never late. He is precise.
And when Joseph stood before Pharaoh, he didn’t take credit.
“It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace” (Genesis 41:16).
That’s the man the pit produced.
Not arrogant. Not bitter. Not broken beyond repair.
Refined.
And that’s when God trusted him with influence.
Promotion is not about gifting.
It’s about character.
And God will never elevate what hasn’t been tested.

So if you’re in a season where nothing makes sense…
where people walked away…
where doors closed…
where your prayers feel unanswered…
You are not buried.
You are planted.
And planted things don’t look like they’re growing… until they break through.
Not for today, but for the day when your faith feels weak and you need to remember what God is doing behind the scenes.
Not because we’re selling something cheap, but because we’re building something eternal.
If you truly want to glorify God… don’t just consume truth. Help carry it.
Because this isn’t just content.
This is calling.
This is rescue.
This is the moment someone decides not to give up.
The pit didn’t cancel Joseph.
It revealed him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE GUILTY ALWAYS SPEAK FIRST… AND THEY SPEAK FAST
paragraphs:
THE GUILTY ALWAYS SPEAK FIRST… AND THEY SPEAK FAST
Why excuses rush out of a heart that already knows the truth—and how Jesus still rewrites the ending
You can hear it before you even see it.

The quick explanation.
The sudden defense.
The words that come out too fast… too polished… too ready.
Almost like they were waiting.

Not for the truth…
but for the moment they’d have to hide it.
Because deep down, guilt doesn’t walk… it runs.
It doesn’t whisper… it panics.
And if you’re honest—painfully honest—you’ve felt it too.
That moment when something inside you knew you were wrong… and before anyone even accused you, you were already building your defense.

Already explaining.
Already shifting blame.
Already trying to control the narrative.
Not because you were innocent…
…but because you were exposed.
It started in a garden.

Not a courtroom.
Not a battlefield.
A garden.
Where everything was perfect… until it wasn’t.
Genesis 3:12 doesn’t read like a confession. It reads like a defense attorney speaking under pressure:

“הָאִשָּׁה אֲשֶׁר נָתַתָּה עִמָּדִי”
Ha’ishah asher natatah immadi
“The woman whom You gave to be with me…”
Do you hear it?

Not just blame…
but layered blame.
Adam didn’t just point at Eve.
He pointed at God.
“The woman YOU gave me.”

Translation:
“This is not fully my fault.”

And just like that…
the first human response to guilt was born.
Excuse.
Deflection.
Distance from responsibility.
And Eve?
She followed the same rhythm.
“The serpent deceived me…”

Not a lie…
but not the whole truth either.

Because guilt doesn’t always deny facts…
it rearranges them.
It edits the story just enough to survive it.
And we’ve been doing the same thing ever since.
You said you’d stop… but you didn’t.
You promised you’d change… but nothing moved.
You told yourself “this is the last time”… and here you are again.

And when conviction came…
you didn’t fall on your knees.
You explained it.
You justified it.
You softened it.
You made it sound less serious than it really was.
Because guilt is uncomfortable…
…but surrender feels like death.
And yet, Scripture cuts deeper than our excuses.
In the Greek, when Jesus confronts truth and exposure, He doesn’t argue with surface words—He goes straight to the heart.
John 3:19 says:

“ἡ δὲ κρίσις ἐστίν…”
Hē de krisis estin
“This is the judgment…”
“…that light has come into the world, and people loved darkness rather than light…”
Why?
“…because their deeds were evil.”
Not misunderstood.
Not miscommunicated.
Evil.
And instead of running to the light…
we run from it.
Fast.
With excuses in our mouths.
But here’s the part no one expects…
Jesus doesn’t chase you with condemnation.
He meets you with truth.
There’s a moment in John 8 where a woman is dragged in—publicly exposed, undeniably guilty, no room for excuses left.
Caught.
Shamed.
Cornered.
If anyone had the right to speak fast… it was her.
But she didn’t.
Because when guilt is fully exposed… excuses run out.
And Jesus steps into the silence.
“Neither do I condemn you…”
Not because she was innocent…
…but because He was about to take her place.
This is where everything shifts.
Because the Gospel is not about how well you explain your sin…
it’s about how fully Jesus paid for it.
Isaiah 53:5 in the original Hebrew says:

“וְהוּא מְחֹלָל מִפְּשָׁעֵנוּ”
Vehu mecholal mipesha’einu
“But He was pierced for our transgressions…”
Not your polished excuses.
Not your edited version of events.
Your transgressions.
Fully known.
Fully seen.
Fully carried.
So the question isn’t…
“Can you explain what you did?”
The question is…
“Will you stop explaining… and finally surrender it?”
Because excuses keep you hiding.
But confession brings you home.
1 John 1:9 doesn’t say “if you explain…”
It says:
“If we confess…”
The Greek word is “ὁμολογῶμεν” (homologōmen)—to agree with God.
Not argue.
Not defend.
Agree.
Say what He says about it.
Call it what He calls it.
And then watch what happens:
“He is faithful and just to forgive…”
Not hesitant.
Not reluctant.
Faithful.
Meaning He already decided.
Before you even opened your mouth.
So why are you still running?
Why are you still explaining?
Why are you still exhausting yourself trying to manage an image…
when Jesus is offering you freedom?
Be honest.
This hit something.
Not on the surface…
but deeper.
That place you don’t let people see.
That habit you keep renaming.
That struggle you keep minimizing.
That guilt you keep outrunning.
You don’t need another excuse.
You need a Savior.
And His name is Jesus.
Because silence can be another form of hiding.
Let your honesty breathe.
Let your confession live.
And let someone else see that they’re not alone in this fight.
If you truly want to glorify God… don’t just consume truth.
Carry it.
Support what spreads it.
Because someone else is still hiding… and your share might be the moment they finally come into the light.
You don’t need a better excuse… you need a surrendered heart.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Light That Hunts You in the Dark: The Hidden War Inside Your Soul (And Why Jesus Still Wins)
paragraphs: Light That Hunts You in the Dark: The Hidden War Inside Your Soul (And Why Jesus Still Wins)

There are nights your body lies still, but your soul is loud.
Not the kind of loud people hear… the kind that echoes in the hidden places.
The kind that remembers things you’ve buried. The kind that whispers, “You’re not who they think you are.”
And if you’re honest… you’ve learned how to survive in that space between light and darkness.
The Bible doesn’t pretend that tension doesn’t exist. It exposes it. Names it. Walks straight into it.
From the very beginning, before there was breath in your lungs or guilt in your memory, Scripture opens with a collision:
“וַיֹּאמֶר אֱלֹהִים יְהִי אוֹר” (Vayomer Elohim, yehi or) — “And God said, ‘Let there be light.’” (Genesis 1:3)

Light wasn’t discovered.
Light was spoken.

Darkness didn’t argue.
It retreated.

But here’s what most people miss…
darkness wasn’t destroyed. It was separated.
“And God separated the light from the darkness.” (Genesis 1:4)
That separation still lives inside you.

Because this isn’t just about the sky turning blue or the sun rising over oceans.
This is about the battlefield inside the human heart.
Jesus later steps into that same narrative and doesn’t soften it. He intensifies it.
“ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου” (egō eimi to phōs tou kosmou) — “I am the light of the world.” (John 8:12)

Not a light.
Not one option among many.
The Light.
And then He says something that feels comforting… until it feels terrifying:
“Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness…”
Which means without Him… you are.
No middle ground. No neutral zone. No safe gray.
That’s where it gets personal.

Because darkness in Scripture is never just absence of light.
It’s presence of separation.
The Hebrew word often used is “חֹשֶׁךְ” (choshekh) — not just physical darkness, but moral obscurity, hiddenness, confusion, exile from clarity.

It’s the place where truth feels optional.
Where sin feels manageable.
Where conviction feels inconvenient.

And if you’ve ever said, “I know it’s wrong, but…”
You’ve felt it.
The New Testament sharpens it even more:

“καὶ τὸ φῶς ἐν τῇ σκοτίᾳ φαίνει, καὶ ἡ σκοτία αὐτὸ οὐ κατέλαβεν”
“The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it.” (John 1:5)
That word “κατέλαβεν” (katalaben)… it means to overpower, to grasp, to extinguish.

Darkness has been trying to choke out your light for a long time.
Through shame.
Through addiction.
Through secrets.
Through the quiet lies you’ve made peace with.
But it has never succeeded.
Not once.
That’s why you’re still reading this.
Because something in you refuses to fully go dark.
Even now… there’s a flicker.
And it bothers you, doesn’t it?
Because light doesn’t just comfort… it exposes.

“πᾶς γὰρ ὁ φαῦλα πράσσων μισεῖ τὸ φῶς”
“For everyone who does wicked things hates the light…” (John 3:20)

Not dislikes.
Hates.
Because light forces honesty.

It drags hidden things into visibility.
It dismantles the version of you that people applaud but God doesn’t recognize.
And yet… the same light that exposes you is the only thing that can heal you.
That’s the paradox of the Gospel.

You don’t clean yourself up and then come to the light.
You come broken… and the light does the work.

“ὁ δὲ ποιῶν τὴν ἀλήθειαν ἔρχεται πρὸς τὸ φῶς”
“But whoever lives by the truth comes into the light…” (John 3:21)

Not perfection.
Truth.
Raw. Unfiltered. Uncomfortable truth.
So here’s the question you’ve been avoiding:
What part of your life only survives in the dark?
Because that’s the exact place Jesus is coming for.

Not to shame you.
To free you.
This is where scandal meets grace.
Because the same Bible that exposes darkness also tells the story of people who lived in it… and were rewritten by light.

David — a king with blood on his hands and secrets in his bed.
Paul — a man who hunted Christians before becoming one.
Peter — who swore loyalty and then denied Jesus three times in one night.
Their stories weren’t canceled.
They were transformed.

Because light didn’t just reveal who they were…
it rewrote who they became.
And it’s still doing that.
Right now.
In you.
But there’s a cost people don’t like to talk about.
Stepping into the light means losing your right to hide.
It means surrendering the version of yourself that thrives in secrecy.
It means choosing conviction over comfort… truth over image… Jesus over control.

And that decision?
It changes everything.
Not overnight perfection… but irreversible direction.
Be honest.
Your honesty could be the light someone else is waiting for.
And if you feel something shifting in you… don’t stay at the surface.
Because going deeper isn’t optional if you’re serious about transformation.
Because at some point… you have to decide.

Do you want to visit the light…
or live in it?
And here’s the truth you can’t escape:

The darkness knows your name…
but the Light knows your future.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Thought It Was Over… Until God Said, “I Will Restore What the Locusts Have Eaten”
paragraphs: They Thought It Was Over… Until God Said, “I Will Restore What the Locusts Have Eaten”
When everything feels stolen, wasted, or beyond repair—God speaks a promise that refuses to let your story end in loss.
There are seasons that don’t just hurt… they erase.
Not slowly. Not gently. But violently.

Dreams you nurtured—gone.
Years you invested—wasted.
Faith you tried to hold onto—shaken until it barely whispered your name back.
And the worst part?
No one really sees what was taken from you.
They only see what’s left.

Joel spoke into a moment like that—when an entire nation stood in the ruins of what once was. Crops devoured. Land stripped bare. Hope reduced to dust. The devastation wasn’t symbolic—it was real, visible, humiliating loss.
But what makes it even heavier is this: the locusts didn’t just take food… they took time.
And time is the one thing you can’t get back.
Yet right there, in the middle of devastation, God didn’t offer a coping mechanism.
He made a promise.

“וְשִׁלַּמְתִּי לָכֶם אֶת־הַשָּׁנִים אֲשֶׁר אָכַל הָאַרְבֶּה…”
“Veshillamti lakhem et-hashanim asher akhal ha’arbeh…”
“I will restore to you the years that the locust has eaten…” (Joel 2:25)

Not days.
Not moments.
Years.
Read that again.
God didn’t say, “I’ll help you move on.”
He said, “I will restore.”
The Hebrew word “שִׁלַּמְתִּי” (shillamti) carries the weight of repayment, compensation, making something whole again—as if the loss never had the final say.
Let that sink into the places you don’t talk about.
Because some of you aren’t just dealing with pain…
You’re grieving stolen years.

Years lost to addiction.
Years buried in sin.
Years wasted chasing things that left you empty.
Years spent in relationships that broke you instead of building you.
Years where you knew God… but ran anyway.
And now, quietly, you wonder…
“Did I miss my chance?”
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
But here’s the part that will shake you in the best way:
God’s restoration doesn’t follow human math.
He doesn’t need equal time to restore what was lost.
He compresses redemption into moments that rewrite entire timelines.
Look at Joseph—years of betrayal, slavery, prison… and suddenly, one moment before Pharaoh changed everything.
Look at David—from failure and scandal to being called “a man after God’s own heart.”
Look at Peter—denied Christ three times, then restored with three questions: “Do you love Me?”
God doesn’t erase your past.
He redeems it so deeply that it becomes part of your testimony.
The enemy wanted your story to end in shame.
God rewrites it into grace.

Even in the Greek, the heartbeat of restoration echoes in the New Testament. In Acts 3:21, the phrase “ἀποκαταστάσεως πάντων” (apokatastaseōs pantōn) speaks of the “restoration of all things”—a divine resetting, a putting-back-into-order what was broken, scattered, and lost.
This is not partial healing.
This is divine restoration.
But there’s something most people skip over.
Before Joel 2:25 comes Joel 2:12:

“שׁוּבוּ עָדַי בְּכָל־לְבַבְכֶם”
“Shuvu adai b’khol levavkhem”
“Return to Me with all your heart…”
Restoration is promised…
But it is tied to returning.

Not halfway.
Not casually.
Not when it’s convenient.
With all your heart.
That means the hidden parts too.
The parts you’ve been pretending don’t matter.
The habits you’ve been defending.
The compromises you’ve been justifying.
God isn’t asking for perfection.
He’s asking for surrender.
Because the moment you truly return…
Restoration begins.
Not always instantly visible.
But undeniably real.
And suddenly, things start shifting.

Peace where anxiety lived.
Clarity where confusion ruled.
Purpose where emptiness echoed.
God starts rebuilding what you thought was permanently lost.
And not just restoring…
But multiplying.
Joel 2:24 says the threshing floors will overflow.
Overflow.
That means what’s coming isn’t just recovery.
It’s abundance.
This is where it gets uncomfortable for some people.
Because if God is restoring you…
Then your story isn’t just about you anymore.
It becomes a testimony.
And testimonies are meant to be shared.
Someone you know is silently grieving their “lost years.”
Someone scrolling right now is convinced it’s too late for them.
Someone close to you is carrying shame they’ve never spoken out loud.
Don’t keep this to yourself.
Because restoration spreads.
Hope multiplies when it’s shared.
And if this spoke to something deep in you…
Don’t just feel it.
Stay rooted in it.
Because supporting this mission isn’t about a transaction…
It’s about participation in spreading the Gospel.
If you truly want to glorify God…
Don’t just receive the message.
Help carry it.
Be honest…
Because the same God who spoke through Joel…
Is still speaking over your life.
And He is not done restoring you.
Not even close.
Even the years you’re ashamed to talk about are still within His reach.
And somehow, in a way only He can do…
He will make it beautiful again.
He doesn’t just give you back what you lost… He gives you a version of yourself that never could have existed without the breaking.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: GOD OPENED LEAH’S WOMB… BUT NOT JACOB’S HEART
paragraphs:
GOD OPENED LEAH’S WOMB… BUT NOT JACOB’S HEART
When Heaven Sees You… But the One You Love Doesn’t
There is a kind of pain that doesn’t scream… it whispers.
It shows up in the quiet moments—when you’ve done everything right, loved deeply, given fully… and still, you are not chosen.
Leah knew that pain.
Not the surface kind. Not the kind people post about.
The kind that sits in your chest and asks questions you’re afraid to answer out loud.
Why am I not enough?
Why am I always second?
Why does God bless me… but not fix the one thing I ache for most?
Genesis doesn’t hide her story. It exposes it with a kind of honesty that feels almost uncomfortable.

“וַיַּ֧רְא יְהוָ֛ה כִּֽי־שְׂנוּאָ֥ה לֵאָ֖ה וַיִּפְתַּ֣ח אֶת־רַחְמָ֑הּ”
Vayar Adonai ki senu’ah Leah vayiftach et-rachmah
“And the LORD saw that Leah was hated, and He opened her womb…” (Genesis 29:31)
God saw.
Not overlooked. Not ignored. Not forgotten.
Seen.
The Hebrew word there—שְׂנוּאָה (senu’ah)—doesn’t just mean “less loved.” It carries the weight of rejection, emotional neglect, being unwanted in the place you longed to belong.
Leah was married… but unloved. Chosen by circumstance… but not by heart.
And God responded.
But not the way she probably prayed for.
He didn’t change Jacob’s heart.
He didn’t rewrite the love story.
He opened her womb.
Let that sit with you.
Because sometimes God will bless your life… without fixing your heartbreak.
Sometimes He will move in one area… while leaving another untouched.
And that tension? That’s where faith either deepens… or quietly dies.
Leah starts naming her sons like journal entries written in tears.

“רְאוּבֵן (Re’uven)” — “See, a son!”
“כִּֽי־רָאָ֤ה יְהוָה֙ בְּעָנְיִ֔י כִּ֥י עַתָּ֖ה יֶאֱהָבַ֥נִי אִישִֽׁי”
“For the LORD has looked upon my affliction; now my husband will love me.” (Genesis 29:32)
Did you catch that?
She believed this blessing would finally earn her love.
If I give enough… maybe I’ll be enough.
If I produce enough… maybe I’ll be seen.
If I become what they want… maybe they’ll choose me.
But Jacob didn’t change.
So she tried again.

“שִׁמְעוֹן (Shim’on)” — “Heard.”
“כִּֽי־שָׁמַ֤ע יְהוָה֙ כִּֽי־שְׂנוּאָ֣ה אָנֹ֔כִי”
“Because the LORD has heard that I am hated…” (Genesis 29:33)
God heard her.
But Jacob still didn’t.
Again.

“לֵוִי (Levi)” — “Attached.”
“עַתָּ֤ה הַפַּ֙עַם֙ יִלָּוֶ֣ה אִישִׁ֔י אֵלַ֖י”
“Now this time my husband will become attached to me…” (Genesis 29:34)
Three sons deep… still reaching for a love that wouldn’t come.
Be honest.
How many of us are living that same cycle?
Trying harder. Giving more. Becoming less of ourselves… just to be chosen by someone who already decided we weren’t their first choice.
This is where the story shifts.
Not because Jacob changed.
But because Leah did.

“וַתַּ֙הַר֙ ע֔וֹד וַתֵּ֥לֶד בֵּ֖ן וַתֹּ֣אמֶר הַפַּ֗עַם אוֹדֶ֤ה אֶת־יְהוָה֙”
“And she conceived again and bore a son and said, ‘This time I will praise the LORD.’” (Genesis 29:35)
This time.
Not “maybe he’ll love me now.”
Not “maybe I’ll finally be enough.”
Just… praise.
“יְהוּדָה (Yehudah)” — Judah.
Praise.
Something broke inside her… and something holy replaced it.
She stopped chasing Jacob’s heart…
…and turned fully toward God’s.
That’s the moment everything changed.
Not externally.
Internally.
Because when your identity stops depending on who rejects you…
…and starts resting in the God who sees you…
you become unshakeable.
And here’s the part that will wreck you in the best way.
Judah… the son born out of surrender instead of striving…
becomes the lineage of Jesus Christ.

“Ἰούδας δὲ ἐγέννησεν…”
“Judah begot…” (Matthew 1:2)
The Messiah didn’t come through the loved wife.
He came through the rejected one.
Let that settle deep.
God didn’t need Jacob’s affection to fulfill His plan.
He used Leah’s pain.
He rewrote her story.
From overlooked…
to chosen.
From rejected…
to redeemed.
From scandal…
to grace.
If you’ve ever felt like Leah…
unseen in a relationship, overlooked in your family, unnoticed in your efforts, or quietly breaking while everyone else celebrates…
this is not the end of your story.
God still sees.
God still hears.
God still writes.
But you have to stop asking, “Why won’t they love me?”
…and start asking, “What is God building through this?”
Because sometimes the greatest thing God gives you…
is not what you begged for…
but what you become when He doesn’t.
Be honest.
Did this expose something you’ve been carrying silently?
Someone you know is living Leah’s story right now.
And if you feel something shifting inside you right now… don’t ignore it.
Follow closely. Stay near truth. Walk this out daily.
If you truly want to glorify God with your life, don’t just consume truth… support what spreads it.
Because healing doesn’t happen by accident.
Growth doesn’t happen casually.
Transformation requires staying connected.
And you were never meant to walk this alone.
Here’s the echo you won’t shake tonight:
God may not change who refused to love you… but He will change who you become because of it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Sex Was Never Just Physical… And Why Your Soul Still Remembers
paragraphs:
Why Sex Was Never Just Physical… And Why Your Soul Still Remembers
The Hidden Covenant Your Body Makes That Your Heart Can’t Undo
Nobody told you that your body would remember what your mind tries to forget.
You thought it was just a moment. Just chemistry. Just curiosity. Just love. Or something that looked close enough to it.
But days later… weeks later… sometimes even years later… there’s still something there. A pull. A memory. A connection that doesn’t fully break, even when the relationship does.
And you don’t always understand why.
Because the world taught you that sex is casual.
Scripture never did.
Long before modern psychology tried to explain attachment, the Word of God revealed something deeper, something spiritual, something binding that goes beyond flesh.
In Genesis, when God established union, He didn’t describe it as an experience. He described it as a transformation.
“וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד” (ve-hayu lebasar echad) — “and they shall become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24).
Not act like one.
Not feel like one.
Become one.
That Hebrew word “אֶחָד” (echad) doesn’t mean temporary closeness. It means unity… fused identity… something joined in a way that carries continuity.
Something that doesn’t just disappear when you walk away.
And that’s where most people were never warned.
Because sex is not just physical connection.
It is covenant language written into your body.
Even Paul, speaking to a culture drowning in sexual freedom, didn’t soften this truth. He intensified it.
“Or do you not know that he who is joined to a prostitute becomes one body with her? For, as it is written, ‘The two will become one flesh.’” (1 Corinthians 6:16)
The Greek word used here is “κολλώμενος” (kollōmenos).
It means to glue… to cling… to bind together in a way that is not easily separated.
This is not poetic exaggeration.
This is spiritual reality.
Every time you give your body, something deeper is happening whether you acknowledge it or not.
And maybe that explains why some names still echo in your heart.
Why some memories still carry weight.
Why some separations felt like tearing instead of parting.
Because part of you was never designed to treat that union as casual.
You weren’t weak for feeling attached.
You were created for covenant.
Be honest… this hit deeper than you expected.
Because this is where things get real.
The enemy didn’t invent sex.
God did.
But what God created for covenant, the world reduced to consumption.
What was meant to bind in love became something that fragments the soul when misused.
And yet… this is not where the story ends.
Because if sex can bind…
Jesus can restore.
If your body remembers…
your Savior redeems.
There is a moment in Scripture where a woman, known more for her sin than her name, walks into a room filled with judgment. Her past was not hidden. Her reputation was not clean.
And yet she draws near to Jesus.
No defense.
No excuse.
Just brokenness.
And Jesus doesn’t expose her.
He restores her.
“ἀφέωνταί σου αἱ ἁμαρτίαι” (apheōntai sou hai hamartiai) — “Your sins are forgiven.” (Luke 7:48)
That word “ἀφέωνταί” (apheōntai) means released… sent away… dismissed.
Not managed.
Not tolerated.
Removed.
Which means every misplaced attachment, every bond formed outside God’s design, every moment you wish you could undo…
Jesus didn’t come to shame you for it.
He came to free you from it.
And this is the part nobody talks about enough.
Healing doesn’t mean your past never happened.
It means your past no longer owns you.
It means the bonds that were formed outside of covenant can be broken through a greater covenant… the blood of Christ.
“καὶ ἡ ἀλήθεια ἐλευθερώσει ὑμᾶς” (kai hē alētheia eleutherōsei hymas) — “and the truth will set you free.” (John 8:32)
Freedom is not pretending it didn’t matter.
Freedom is finally understanding why it did… and letting Jesus rewrite what it did to you.
If you’ve ever wondered why it was so hard to let go…
now you know.
If you’ve ever felt like pieces of you were left behind…
now you understand.
But if you’re still here reading this… that means God is not finished with your story.
And don’t keep this to yourself.
Because this isn’t about condemnation.
It’s about awakening.
And if this spoke to you, if this opened your eyes, if this helped you understand something you’ve carried for years…
then support what God is doing here.
Not out of pressure… but out of purpose.
You’re helping spread truth, healing, and the Gospel to people who are still lost in silence.
Because glorifying God isn’t just about what you believe…
it’s also about what you choose to support and share.
And somewhere… someone is one post away from finally understanding why they feel the way they feel.
Don’t let them miss it.
You weren’t broken by love… you were misaligned from covenant—but Jesus is still restoring what you thought was lost.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Hate Waiting… But Heaven Is Doing Its Deepest Work There
paragraphs: You Hate Waiting… But Heaven Is Doing Its Deepest Work There
Why the silence, the delay, the unanswered prayers… might be the most dangerous and beautiful place your soul will ever stand
There’s a kind of pain no one prepares you for.

Not the loud kind.
Not the breaking kind.
But the quiet, suffocating kind.
The kind where nothing is happening.

You prayed… and heaven felt still.
You cried… and the door didn’t open.
You believed… but the timeline didn’t move.

And somewhere in that silence, a question starts whispering:
“God… did You forget me?”

But what if waiting isn’t where God abandons you…
What if it’s where He hides you… to rebuild you?
In the ancient Hebrew text, the word often translated as “wait” is קָוָה (qavah). It doesn’t just mean to sit still. It means to bind together, to twist, to stretch like a cord under tension.

Isaiah 40:31 says:
“But those who wait on the Lord shall renew their strength…”
But the original language breathes deeper:
“וְקֹוֵי יְהוָה (ve-qovey YHWH) יַחֲלִיפוּ כֹחַ (yachalifu koach)”
Those who are being stretched… those being pulled… those under holy tension… they are the ones being renewed.

So what you call delay…
God calls strengthening.
And that changes everything.
Because maybe you’re not stuck.
Maybe you’re being stretched beyond your current capacity… so you don’t break under the weight of what you prayed for.
Think about it.

Joseph waited in a prison for a promise he didn’t see fulfilled for years.
David was anointed king… then sent back to sheep.
Abraham was given a son in promise… but decades passed before Isaac’s cry filled the tent.
Waiting has always been God’s workshop for warriors.

But let’s be honest…
Waiting doesn’t feel holy.

It feels like rejection.
It feels like confusion.
It feels like being forgotten.
Even in the New Testament, the Greek word used for endurance is ὑπομονή (hypomonē) — it means to remain under, to stay beneath the weight without escaping.

Not running.
Not quitting.
Not numbing out.
Remaining.
That’s what you’ve been doing.
And you didn’t even realize it was worship.

Because staying when it hurts…
Trusting when it’s quiet…
Holding on when nothing makes sense…
That’s not weakness.
That’s a battlefield most people walk away from.
But you stayed.
And heaven noticed.
There’s a moment in Scripture that most people read too quickly.

Lamentations 3:25 says:
“The Lord is good to those who wait for Him…”
But the Hebrew reveals something deeper again:
“טוֹב יְהוָה לְקֹוָיו (tov YHWH le-qovav)”

God is good not just to those who wait…
But to those who are being tightly wound into Him.
So waiting isn’t distance.
It’s intimacy under pressure.
You thought God stepped away…
But He was actually pulling you closer than ever before.
And yes… it hurts.

Because every day you wake up and the answer still hasn’t come.
Every night you lie down with questions that haven’t been resolved.
But listen carefully…
Jesus Himself waited.

Thirty years of hidden life before three years of ministry.
Silence before impact.
Obscurity before revelation.

And in Gethsemane, He prayed:
“Father… if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me…”
But heaven didn’t remove the moment.
He had to wait through it.
And that waiting became salvation for the entire world.
So don’t tell me waiting is meaningless.
Waiting is where eternity shifts.
Some of you reading this… you’re exhausted.

You’ve been strong for too long.
You’ve smiled when you wanted to break.
You’ve kept believing when it would’ve been easier to quit.
Be honest…
This hit deeper than you expected.
Because you’re not alone in this.
There are thousands of people right now silently fighting battles no one sees… waiting for answers only God can give.
And something about your honesty might help someone else breathe again.
Don’t keep this to yourself.
And if something in your spirit knows… I need more of this kind of truth daily…
Then follow and stay close.
Because this isn’t just content…
This is discipleship in real time.
There’s something powerful you need to understand:

When you support what spreads the Gospel…
you become part of every life it reaches.
It’s participation in kingdom impact.
But more than that…
It’s about standing for something eternal.

Not out of pressure…
But out of purpose.
Because some messages shouldn’t stay contained.
They should multiply.
And maybe… just maybe… your waiting season is the very thing God will use to bring someone else into freedom.
So don’t despise it.
Don’t rush it.
Don’t numb it.
Let Him finish it.

Because the same God who feels silent…
is the same God who never wastes a single second of your waiting.
And when it finally unfolds…
You’ll realize…
He wasn’t late.
He was precise.
And you weren’t forgotten.
You were being formed.
God is not delaying your life… He is developing your soul in places no one else can see.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Thought It Was Love… But It Slowly Tore Everything Apart
paragraphs: They Thought It Was Love… But It Slowly Tore Everything Apart
The first time he said it, it didn’t sound wrong.
“God allowed it in the Old Testament.”
It sounded spiritual. Justified. Almost holy.
But what started as a quiet compromise didn’t stay quiet.
It never does.

Because some things don’t explode immediately… they unravel slowly—through tension at the dinner table, silent comparisons, divided affection, children who don’t understand why love feels unequal, and a heart that used to belong fully to God but is now pulled in too many directions.
Polygamy doesn’t just multiply relationships.
It multiplies wounds.
And Scripture never hides that truth.
From the very beginning, God’s design was never unclear.
In Genesis 2:24, the Hebrew text says:
עַל־כֵּן יַעֲזָב־אִישׁ אֶת־אָבִיו וְאֶת־אִמּוֹ וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
“Al-ken ya’azov ish et-aviv ve’et-immo, vedavaq be’ishto, vehayu lebasar echad.”
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
Not two.
Not three.
One.
The Hebrew word “דָבַק” (davaq) means to cling, to cleave, to be glued together with deep, covenantal attachment. It speaks of exclusivity, intimacy, and total union.
God didn’t design love to be divided.
He designed it to be whole.
But humanity… chose otherwise.
And the Bible doesn’t sanitize what happened next.
Abraham took Hagar—and what followed was jealousy, conflict, and generational division.
Jacob loved Rachel but married Leah—and the house became a battlefield of comparison, insecurity, and rivalry.
David had many wives—and his family was marked by betrayal, rebellion, and tragedy.
Solomon multiplied wives beyond measure—and Scripture records his downfall with devastating clarity.
In 1 Kings 11:3–4, the Hebrew reveals something haunting:
וַיְהִי לָעֵת זִקְנַת שְׁלֹמֹה נָשָׁיו הִטּוּ אֶת־לְבָבוֹ אַחֲרֵי אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים
“Vayehi le’et ziknat Shlomo, nashav hittu et-levavo acharei elohim acherim.”
“As Solomon grew old, his wives turned his heart after other gods.”
Not just distracted.
Turned.
His heart—“לְבָבוֹ” (levavo)—the very center of his devotion—was divided until it was no longer fully God’s.
That’s the quiet danger no one talks about.
Polygamy doesn’t just affect your relationships.
It affects your worship.
Because whatever divides your love… eventually divides your loyalty.
Jesus Himself restored the original standard when He spoke in Matthew 19:4–6, echoing Genesis:
In Greek, it reads:
οἱ δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν
“hoi duo eis sarka mian”
“The two shall become one flesh.”
Two.
Defined. Clear. Restored.
Not because culture demanded it—but because truth never changed.
And maybe this is where it gets uncomfortable.
Because some people don’t pursue polygamy out of rebellion… but out of desire, loneliness, control, fear of commitment, or even a misreading of Scripture.
But the fruit tells the truth.
It always does.
And deep down, some already know.
The tension.
The imbalance.
The silent competition.
The emotional exhaustion.
The spiritual dryness.
The way prayer feels different when your life is built on something God never designed.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because conviction is not condemnation.
It’s an invitation.
An invitation back to alignment.
Back to truth.
Back to a love that doesn’t fracture the soul.
Because here’s what most people miss…
The Bible includes polygamy stories—but it never celebrates them.
It records them honestly… so you can see the consequences clearly.
That’s not permission.
That’s warning.
And yet… this is where grace enters.
Because even in the middle of broken structures, divided homes, and compromised hearts…
God still pursued people.
He didn’t wait for perfect families.
He stepped into messy ones.
That’s the Gospel.
In Romans 5:8, the Greek says:
Χριστὸς ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν ἀπέθανεν
“Christos hyper hēmōn apethanen”
“Christ died for us.”
Not when we got everything right.
But while we were still broken.
Still confused.
Still choosing things that slowly destroyed us.
Jesus didn’t come to shame you.
He came to restore what sin distorted.
To rewrite what culture normalized.
To heal what compromise damaged.
To bring you back to a kind of love that reflects Him—faithful, undivided, covenantal.
So if something in your life doesn’t align…
You don’t have to defend it.
You can surrender it.
There is no freedom in trying to bend God’s design to fit your desires.
But there is healing in letting Him reshape your life according to truth.
And if this message opened your eyes, stirred your spirit, or exposed something you’ve been avoiding…
Don’t keep it to yourself.
Save this so you don’t forget what God showed you here.
Because supporting this mission isn’t just about content.
It’s about advancing truth in a world full of confusion.
If God is feeding you here…
Be part of what helps feed others.
Because truth like this needs to reach more hearts before compromise destroys more homes.
And maybe the reason this message found you…
Is because God is calling you back before it’s too late.
The love you’re chasing was never meant to divide you.
It was meant to lead you back to Him.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They told you it was just a habit.
paragraphs: They told you it was just a habit.
Just stress. Just curiosity. Just loneliness wearing a different face.
But deep down, you knew it wasn’t just that.

Because every time it ended, something inside you felt… hollow. Not just physically tired—but spiritually exposed. Like something sacred had been traded for something temporary. And no one saw it… except God.
So you start asking the question most people are too afraid to say out loud:
Can fasting actually break this?
Or is that just another religious idea that sounds powerful but doesn’t really touch the chains?
Because what you’re dealing with doesn’t feel surface-level.
It feels like a war inside your body.
A war inside your mind.
A war inside your soul.
And Scripture doesn’t ignore that war.
It walks straight into it.

When Jesus said in Matthew 26:41, “Watch and pray, that you enter not into temptation,” the Greek behind “watch” is γρηγορεῖτε (grēgoreite)—it means to stay awake, to be alert, to be vigilant like someone guarding something valuable. And the word for temptation, πειρασμόν (peirasmon), isn’t just a casual urge. It’s a testing. A pressure. A pulling toward something that can either refine you… or ruin you.
That’s the tension you feel.
And fasting—real biblical fasting—is not starvation. It’s not punishment. It’s not you trying to impress God.
It’s you choosing hunger… on purpose… to remind your soul that your body is not your master.

In Hebrew, when David speaks about humbling himself with fasting in Psalm 35:13, the word used is עָנָה (anah)—to afflict, to bow low, to bring oneself into submission. Not self-hatred. Not shame. But alignment.
Because the truth most people won’t say is this:
Sexual addiction isn’t just about sex.
It’s about control.
It’s about comfort.
It’s about escape.
And fasting confronts all three at once.
When you fast, your body screams.
It demands.
It negotiates.
It reminds you how loud your flesh really is.
And that’s exactly why it works—not as a magic fix, but as a spiritual weapon.
Because suddenly, the same voice that says “I need this right now” when you’re tempted… is the same voice you’ve already been saying “no” to when you deny food.
You start recognizing it.
You start resisting it.
You start weakening its authority.

Jesus said in Matthew 17:21 (in manuscripts that include it), “This kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting.” The Greek phrase ἐν προσευχῇ καὶ νηστείᾳ (en proseuchē kai nēsteia) ties prayer and fasting together—not as rituals, but as force multipliers in spiritual warfare.
Because some chains don’t break with casual faith.
They break with surrendered hunger.
But hear this clearly—fasting doesn’t earn your freedom.
Jesus already paid for that.

In the Aramaic heart of the Gospel message, the cry “Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?”—“My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?”—wasn’t weakness. It was the moment Jesus carried every hidden sin, every secret addiction, every private shame… including yours.
You’re not trying to deserve freedom.
You’re learning to walk in it.
Fasting simply helps you detach from what’s been controlling you long enough to remember who actually owns you.
And who owns you is not your urges.
Not your past.
Not your browser history.
But Christ.
And the more you fast, the more you start noticing something strange.
The cravings don’t disappear instantly…
But they lose their authority.
The impulses still come…
But they don’t feel as powerful.
Because something deeper is growing.
Hunger for God.
Real hunger.
The kind David described in Psalm 42:1, “As the deer pants for streams of water…” The Hebrew word תַּעֲרֹג (ta’arog) means to long for deeply, to crave with intensity.
That same intensity that once pulled you toward sin…
God begins to redirect toward Himself.
That’s where transformation happens.
Not when temptation vanishes.
But when your desire shifts.
And maybe that’s why this is hitting you harder than you expected.
Because you’ve tried willpower.
You’ve tried hiding.
You’ve tried promising “this is the last time.”
But you haven’t fully surrendered the battlefield.
Fasting is where surrender becomes physical.
Visible.
Undeniable.
And listen… you don’t have to do this perfectly.
You just have to start.
Even one meal.
Even one day.
Even one moment where you choose God over the urge.
That moment matters more than you think.
Be honest. This isn’t about perfection—it’s about truth.
And someone else reading your comment might realize they’re not alone for the first time.
Not because it sounded good—but because you’ll need this reminder the next time temptation whispers louder than truth.
And if you’re serious about glorifying God—not just in public, but in private where no one sees—then support what feeds your spirit.
Because freedom isn’t just something you pray for.
It’s something you walk into… one surrendered hunger at a time.
And the version of you you thought was too far gone… is exactly the one Jesus came to redeem.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “No Hands, No Sin? The Lie We Scroll Through at Night”
paragraphs:
“No Hands, No Sin? The Lie We Scroll Through at Night”
When your body stays still but your heart runs wild—what heaven actually sees in the dark.
It usually starts quietly.

No loud rebellion. No dramatic fall. Just a screen glowing in the dark, a message that lingers a little too long, a photo that says more than words ever could. You tell yourself, “I’m not touching anyone… I’m not doing anything physical… this isn’t the same.”
But deep down, something unsettles you.
Because even in silence, your spirit knows when it’s drifting.
Jesus didn’t leave this gray. He didn’t leave loopholes for modern technology or hidden corners of desire. He spoke straight into the heart, into the unseen, into the places nobody else can monitor.

He said in Matthew 5:28,
“Everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
The original Greek cuts deeper than most translations let us feel.

“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων… πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτήν”
(Pas ho blepōn… pros to epithymēsai autēn)

It doesn’t just mean a passing glance. It means looking with purpose. Intentionally feeding desire. Choosing to engage, to dwell, to stir something that God never designed to be consumed outside of covenant.
Sexting isn’t just “texting.” It’s intentional looking. Intentional stirring. Intentional participation.
Even without touch… something is happening.
Because sin was never limited to skin. It begins in the καρδία (kardia)—the heart, the inner seat of desire, will, and imagination.
And that’s where this battle actually lives.
You can keep your hands clean and still let your heart burn with something that slowly rewrites your convictions.
You can stay physically distant and still be spiritually entangled.
That’s why what feels “private” often becomes powerful enough to shape your identity.
And this is where many people get it wrong.
They reduce sin to action… while Jesus raises the standard to intention.
They measure boundaries by bodies… while heaven measures by the heart.

Even in the Hebrew understanding of desire, the word “חָמַד” (chamad) — to covet — isn’t just about possession. It’s about longing in a way that leads the soul away from God’s design. It’s inward, invisible, and deeply spiritual.
So no, sexting isn’t “safe” just because there’s no physical contact.
Because what it awakens… what it feeds… what it normalizes… is shaping your heart in real time.
But here’s where the story doesn’t end.
Because if this exposed something in you… if you felt that quiet conviction rising while reading this… that is not condemnation.
That is mercy.
That is God interrupting your drift before it becomes your direction.
There was a woman once, caught in the middle of scandal. Exposed. Guilty. No excuses left. The kind of moment where shame feels final.
And yet Jesus didn’t erase truth.
He fulfilled it with grace.
He told her, “Neither do I condemn you… go, and sin no more.”

In the original Greek:
“οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω· πορεύου καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε”
He didn’t say it didn’t matter.
He didn’t say it wasn’t sin.
He said… it doesn’t have to define you anymore.
That’s the difference.
Sexting may begin as curiosity… loneliness… validation… or even what feels like connection.
But it often leaves behind something heavier: comparison, dissatisfaction, secrecy, and a quiet distance from God that grows over time.
And if you’re honest… you’ve felt that distance.
The question isn’t just “Is this a sin?”
The deeper question is…
What is this doing to your soul?
What is it teaching your heart to crave?
What version of you is being formed in the dark?
Because Jesus didn’t come just to regulate behavior.
He came to transform desire.
To take what has been twisted and restore it to something holy, something whole, something rooted in covenant instead of consumption.
And you don’t have to clean yourself up first.
You just have to stop pretending this doesn’t matter.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Let this not stay private.
Because healing rarely happens in silence.
