You’re going to need this reminder again on a night when your guard is down.
And if this spoke to something real inside you, follow closely. Stay near truth. Stay near the voice that calls you higher than your impulses.
If you genuinely want to glorify God—not just in public, but in private—then support what is feeding your spirit. Help keep this message alive, reaching people who are quietly losing this battle.
This isn’t about control.
It’s about freedom.
Because what you entertain in secret eventually shapes what you become in public.
And Jesus didn’t die just to forgive your past…
He died to transform your desires.
You’re not too far gone.
You’re not stuck.
You’re being called back.
And this moment right here… might be where everything begins to change.
The screen can go dark… but your soul doesn’t have to.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: 40 Days Before the Fire Falls: The Pattern You Didn’t Notice Until It Found You
paragraphs: 40 Days Before the Fire Falls: The Pattern You Didn’t Notice Until It Found You
When Heaven Goes Silent Before It Moves Loudest, You’re Probably Standing Inside a “Forty”

You thought it was delay. You called it abandonment. Some days it felt like punishment. But what if the silence, the waiting, the stretching… was actually a pattern God has always used before He breaks something open?
There’s a number that keeps showing up in Scripture like a quiet drumbeat before the explosion of purpose.
Forty.
Not randomly. Not symbolically alone. Intentionally.

Forty days of rain before the earth was reset. Forty years before a promise was entered. Forty days in the wilderness before public ministry ignited. Forty nights on a mountain before glory was revealed.
And somehow… you’re in your own version of forty right now.
You don’t call it that. You call it confusion.
But Heaven calls it preparation.

In Genesis, when the flood began, the Hebrew text says, “וַיְהִי הַגֶּשֶׁם עַל־הָאָרֶץ אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם וְאַרְבָּעִים לָיְלָה” (vayehi hageshem al-ha’aretz arba’im yom ve’arba’im laylah) — “And the rain was upon the earth forty days and forty nights” (Genesis 7:12). It wasn’t just destruction. It was a cleansing. A reset. Something had to be washed before something new could breathe.
And that’s where it gets uncomfortable.
Because forty doesn’t feel like breakthrough when you’re inside it. It feels like drowning.

Moses didn’t come down glowing the first hour he was on the mountain. He waited. Alone. No applause. No validation. Just presence. The Hebrew says he was there “אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם וְאַרְבָּעִים לָיְלָה” again — forty days and nights (Exodus 34:28). Not because God forgot him… but because transformation takes time when it’s real.
Jesus Himself didn’t skip this pattern.

The Gospel of Matthew records, “καὶ νηστεύσας ἡμέρας τεσσεράκοντα καὶ νύκτας τεσσεράκοντα” (kai nēsteusas hēmeras tesserakonta kai nyktas tesserakonta) — “and having fasted forty days and forty nights…” (Matthew 4:2). Before the miracles. Before the crowds. Before the authority.
He was alone.
Hungry.
Tested.
Forty always comes before manifestation.
Which means what you’re in right now might not be failure… it might be alignment.
You keep asking why nothing is changing, but what if everything is being rearranged in ways you can’t yet recognize?
Israel wandered for forty years, not because God couldn’t bring them in faster, but because Egypt had to come out of them before they could step into promise. The land was ready. They weren’t.
That’s the part we don’t like.
We want breakthrough without becoming the person who can carry it.
We want promise without purification.
We want glory without wilderness.
But Scripture refuses to support that version of faith.
Even Jonah, running from God, spent what felt like death inside a fish before obedience came alive. It wasn’t comfortable. It wasn’t pretty. But it was necessary.
Forty is where God confronts what you’ve been avoiding.
Forty is where excuses die.
Forty is where identity is rebuilt.
And maybe that’s why this season has been so intense for you.
Because something in you is being undone… so something eternal can be established.
Be honest.
You’ve been asking God to change your situation.
But deep down, you know He’s been trying to change you.
And that’s harder.
Because it means surrender.
It means repentance.
It means facing things you buried under distractions, habits, or silence.
The Greek word for repentance is μετάνοια (metanoia) — not just feeling sorry, but a complete transformation of mind. A turning. A rewiring of how you see, think, and live.
That doesn’t happen overnight.
It happens in the “forty.”
So when you feel like giving up… understand this:
Breakthrough is often closer than it feels, but it’s hidden behind obedience.

Jesus didn’t leave the wilderness empty. Luke says, “καὶ ὑπέστρεψεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἐν τῇ δυνάμει τοῦ πνεύματος” (kai hypestrepsen ho Iēsous en tē dynamei tou pneumatos) — “And Jesus returned in the power of the Spirit” (Luke 4:14).
Power didn’t come before the wilderness.
It came after.
And that changes everything.
Because it means your struggle is not wasted.
Your waiting is not pointless.
Your silence is not empty.
It’s forming something.
Sit with it.
Because this might be the moment God is trying to wake something up inside you.
Be honest. This isn’t about performance. It’s about truth.
And someone else needs to see your honesty too.
Follow closely if you don’t want watered-down faith but real, Scripture-rooted truth that confronts, heals, and restores.
And if you truly desire to glorify God, not just in words but in action, support what is feeding your spirit.
Because this isn’t just content.
This is discipleship.
This is formation.
This is your turning point if you let it be.
And here’s the truth that will stay with you long after this moment fades:
Your “forty” is not where God left you… it’s where He’s been preparing to reveal you.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Waiting Until Marriage Feels Impossible for This Generation
paragraphs:
Why Waiting Until Marriage Feels Impossible for This Generation
And Why That Struggle Might Be the Loudest Cry Your Soul Has Ever Made
It doesn’t start with rebellion.
It starts with exhaustion.

Late nights scrolling, bodies on display, intimacy turned into entertainment, love reduced to chemistry, and commitment treated like a joke. You didn’t wake up one day and decide to compromise your convictions… you just slowly got tired of feeling like the only one trying to hold the line.
And somewhere between loneliness and longing, something inside you whispered, “Maybe it’s not that serious.”
But deep down, you knew it was.
Because every time you crossed a line you once swore you wouldn’t, it didn’t feel like freedom… it felt like something sacred slipping through your fingers.
And that ache? That quiet, almost unexplainable grief?
Scripture already gave it a name.

In Hebrew, the word for covenant is “בְּרִית” (berith). It’s not just an agreement—it’s a binding of souls, a sacred union witnessed by God Himself. Waiting until marriage was never about restriction. It was about protecting something holy that the world keeps trying to make casual.
And now you’re here… trying to survive in a generation that laughs at purity but secretly craves real love.
That tension is tearing people apart.
Jesus never ignored that tension.
When He spoke about lust, He didn’t just address the act—He went deeper, straight into the heart:

“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν”
(Pas ho blepōn gynaika pros to epithymēsai autēn ēdē emoicheusen)
“Everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery…” (Matthew 5:28)
Not to shame you.
But to reveal something devastatingly honest:
This battle isn’t just physical. It’s spiritual.
And that’s why it feels impossible.
Because you’re not just fighting desire… you’re fighting a culture that feeds it, normalizes it, celebrates it, and then leaves you empty afterward.
Let’s be real.
You’ve tried to stop.
You’ve made promises.
You’ve deleted things, avoided people, prayed desperate prayers.
But temptation didn’t disappear.
It adapted.
It followed you into your quiet moments… your weak nights… your loneliness.
And suddenly, waiting doesn’t just feel hard.
It feels unrealistic.
Almost unfair.
But here’s what no one tells you…
The struggle itself is not proof that you’re failing.
It’s proof that something inside you still belongs to God.
Paul wrote something that hits differently when you’ve actually wrestled with this:

“φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν… τὸ σῶμα ὑμῶν ναὸς τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματός ἐστιν”
(Pheugēte tēn porneian… to sōma hymōn naos tou hagiou pneumatos estin)
“Flee from sexual immorality… your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:18–19)
A temple.
Not a playground.
Not a tool for validation.
Not something disposable.
You weren’t created to be consumed.
You were created to be consecrated.
And that changes everything.
But let’s not pretend this is easy.
Waiting until marriage in this generation feels like trying to breathe underwater.
Everyone around you is diving deeper into things you’re trying to escape.
Even some believers have quietly given up.
They stopped talking about it.
Stopped fighting it.
Stopped believing it was even possible.
But Jesus never lowered the standard to match human weakness.
He raised people up to meet it through grace.
And that’s the part many forget.
Grace is not permission to stay stuck.
It’s power to be transformed.
The Greek word for grace—“χάρις” (charis)—means divine empowerment. Not just forgiveness, but the ability to become someone new.
So when you fall… and you will have moments where you do…
That’s not the end of your story.
That’s where grace rewrites it.
Because the Gospel has never been about perfect people maintaining purity flawlessly.
It’s about broken people being restored completely.
There are people reading this right now who feel disqualified.
Because of what you’ve done.
Because of who you’ve been with.
Because of how far you’ve gone.
But listen carefully…
Jesus didn’t die for a version of you that never struggled.
He died for the real you.
The one who tried.
The one who failed.
The one who still feels something when truth hits.
And that means your story is not over.
It’s being rewritten.
From scandal…
to grace.
If this stirred something in you—don’t ignore it.
Be honest.
Your honesty might be the breakthrough someone else needs to see.
And if you’re serious about growing in Christ—not just emotionally moved for a moment but actually transformed—stay close.
Support the mission.
If you truly want to glorify God… don’t just agree with truth.
Help carry it.
Because someone else is waiting to hear what just reached you.
And maybe your share is the moment their life changes.
You’re not crazy for wanting something real.
You’re not weak for struggling.
You’re not alone in this fight.
And you are not beyond redemption.
The battle you hate might be the place God is making you holy.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They Whisper “Don’t Judge Me”… But That’s Not What Jesus Meant
paragraphs: They Whisper “Don’t Judge Me”… But That’s Not What Jesus Meant

The most misused sentence in modern Christianity isn’t hidden in some obscure verse. It’s shouted, reposted, defended, and weaponized almost daily—often by people who haven’t even read the full passage.
“Judge not.”

Three words. That’s all it takes to silence conviction, avoid accountability, and escape truth. Three words that have been stretched so far from their original meaning that they now protect the very sin Jesus came to expose and heal.
But if you slow down… if you sit with the actual words of Christ… if you listen carefully… something uncomfortable begins to rise in your chest.
Because Jesus never told us to stop discerning.
He told us to stop pretending.

In Matthew 7:1, the original Greek reads:
“Μὴ κρίνετε, ἵνα μὴ κριθῆτε” (Mē krinete, hina mē krithēte)
“Krinete” doesn’t simply mean “don’t ever judge anything.” It carries the sense of condemning, passing final judgment, placing yourself in the position of ultimate authority over someone’s soul.
Jesus wasn’t abolishing moral clarity.
He was confronting hypocrisy.
And then He goes further… much further than most people quoting that verse are willing to read.
“Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3)
The imagery is almost uncomfortable. A man with a massive beam stuck in his eye… trying to perform delicate eye surgery on someone else.
It’s not just ironic.
It’s tragic.
Because that’s exactly what happens when people use “judge not” as a shield instead of a mirror.
Jesus never said ignore sin.
He said deal with yours first.
Then He says something that gets conveniently skipped:
“First remove the log from your own eye, and then you will see clearly to remove the speck from your brother’s eye.” (Matthew 7:5)
Read that again slowly.
“Then you will see clearly…”
He fully expects you to help your brother.
But now it comes from humility, not superiority.
From brokenness, not pride.
From love, not ego.
That changes everything.

The Hebrew mindset behind judgment wasn’t just about punishment—it was about restoration. In the Old Testament, the word “שָׁפַט” (shaphat) often meant to govern, to bring things back into right order.
Not destroy.
Restore.
That’s the heart of God.
And when Jesus spoke, He wasn’t introducing something new. He was revealing what had always been true: God’s justice and mercy were never meant to be separated.
But somewhere along the way, we flipped it.
We created two extremes.
One group condemns harshly without mercy.
Another refuses to confront anything at all.
Both miss Jesus.
Because Jesus looked at sin directly… and still chose the cross.
Think about the woman caught in adultery in John 8.
The crowd was ready. Stones in hand. Laws memorized. Judgment justified.
And Jesus says:
“He who is without sin among you, let him be the first to throw a stone.”
One by one, they leave.
Then He turns to her.
And this is where everything shifts.
“Neither do I condemn you… go, and from now on sin no more.”
No condemnation.
But also no permission to stay the same.
That’s the balance we’ve lost.
We want grace without transformation.
Acceptance without repentance.
Comfort without truth.
But real love doesn’t ignore what’s killing you.
Real love calls you out… because it wants to call you back.
Be honest.
How many times have you said “don’t judge me” when deep down… you already knew something wasn’t right?
How many times have you used those words not for protection… but for escape?
This isn’t about shame.
This is about clarity.
Because the moment we twist Jesus’ words, we don’t just misunderstand Scripture…
we delay our healing.
And maybe that’s why this hits so deeply.
Because you’re not just reading an article.
You’re recognizing something.
Something you’ve said.
Something you’ve felt.
Something you’ve avoided.
Sit in it for a second.
Let it search you.
Because the truth is… Jesus wasn’t trying to silence correction.
He was purifying it.
He was calling us to a kind of honesty that starts with ourselves and then extends outward in love.
Not to shame people.
But to bring them back to life.
If this exposed something in you… don’t ignore it.
Be real. Someone reading your comment might finally feel less alone.
You’ll need to come back to it the next time conviction feels like offense.
And if you feel something shifting in your spirit right now… don’t ignore it.
Lean into it.
If you’ve ever said you want to glorify God… this is one of those moments where that decision becomes real.
You can step in.
You can help truth reach someone else.
You can be part of what God is doing.
Because sometimes the words we use to protect ourselves… are the very chains Jesus is trying to break.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Is It Wrong to Dress Attractively Sexy as a Christian?
paragraphs:
Is It Wrong to Dress Attractively Sexy as a Christian?
When Beauty Becomes a Battlefield Between Identity and Intention
It didn’t start with rebellion.
It started quietly… almost innocently. A mirror. A glance. A thought that lingered a little longer than it should have.
“Do I look good… or am I trying to be seen?”
That question doesn’t shout. It whispers. And for many believers, it’s one of the most uncomfortable conversations we avoid having with God.
Because deep down, this isn’t really about clothes.
It’s about the heart.
And Scripture has never been silent about the heart.

In 1 Samuel 16:7, the Hebrew reveals something piercing:
“כִּי הָאָדָם יִרְאֶה לַעֵינַיִם וַיהוָה יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב”
(Ki ha’adam yir’eh la’einayim, va’Adonai yir’eh la’levav)
Man looks at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart.
Not the outfit. Not the style. Not even the body.
The heart.
So now the question shifts.
Not “Is this too sexy?”
But “What is my heart trying to say through this?”
Because there is a difference between beauty that reflects God… and beauty that competes for attention God should receive.
Genesis tells us something profound. When God created humanity, He didn’t hide beauty. He authored it.

“וַיַּרְא אֱלֹהִים אֶת־כָּל־אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה וְהִנֵּה־טוֹב מְאֹד”
(Vayar Elohim et kol asher asah, vehineh tov me’od)
God saw everything He made, and it was very good.
Your body was never the problem.
Your beauty was never a mistake.
But sin has a way of twisting what was meant to reflect God… into something that replaces Him.
And this is where it gets uncomfortable.
Because modesty in Scripture was never about hiding beauty out of shame.
It was about guarding intention.

In 1 Timothy 2:9, Paul writes in Greek:
(kosmein heautas en katastolē kosmiō meta aidous kai sōphrosynēs)
Adorn yourselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control.
The word “αἰδοῦς” (aidous) doesn’t simply mean covering up.
It means a sense of reverence… a holy awareness… a humility that says, “My body is not for performance. It is for purpose.”
And “σωφροσύνης” (sōphrosynēs)… self-control… a mind that is governed, not driven by impulse, attention, or validation.
So let’s be honest.
Because this is where conviction begins to breathe.
Are you dressing to honor God… or to be noticed by people?
Are you expressing confidence… or feeding a deeper hunger for validation?
Are you celebrating what God created… or subtly inviting attention that pulls eyes away from Him?
This is not about legalism.
This is about alignment.
Because Jesus never came to control your wardrobe.
He came to transform your identity.
And identity changes everything.

Peter echoes this in 1 Peter 3:3-4:
“μὴ ἔστω ὁ ἔξωθεν ἐμπλοκῆς τριχῶν… ἀλλ’ ὁ κρυπτὸς τῆς καρδίας ἄνθρωπος”
(Do not let your adorning be external… but the hidden person of the heart)
God is not anti-beauty.
He is anti-distraction from what matters most.
Because when beauty becomes the loudest thing about you… something sacred has gone quiet.
And maybe that’s why this hits deeper than expected.
Because some of us didn’t realize we were slowly trading spiritual intimacy… for external affirmation.
We didn’t mean to.
We just wanted to feel seen.
Wanted.
Valued.
But Jesus never asked you to compete for attention.
He already chose you.
Fully.
Completely.
Without performance.
Without exposure.
Without proving anything.
And here’s where grace enters the story.
Because maybe you’re reading this and feeling that tension in your chest.
Not condemnation.
But conviction.
That quiet realization that something needs to shift.
That’s not shame.
That’s the Holy Spirit calling you back to alignment.
Back to identity.
Back to Him.
So is it wrong to dress attractively?
No.
But it becomes dangerous when attraction becomes the mission.
When your body becomes a message your spirit never intended to send.
When the desire to be seen outweighs the desire to reflect Christ.
That’s where the shift happens.
That’s where beauty becomes a battlefield.
And that’s where Jesus meets you… not to shame you… but to restore you.
Because this has never been about fabric.
It has always been about formation.
Christ being formed in you.
So if this stirred something in you…
Sit with it.
Let God speak.
And be honest…
Your honesty might be the breakthrough someone else needs to see.
It’s a daily surrender.
And if you’ve been quietly searching for deeper truth, stronger conviction, and real spiritual growth…
Stay close to truth that doesn’t bend with culture.
Because this journey is not meant to be walked alone.
And if you feel called to go deeper… to grow stronger… to be sharpened daily in Christ…
This isn’t just content.
It’s calling.
It’s sharpening.
It’s transformation.
Because supporting what feeds your spirit… is one way you glorify God with your life.
And here’s the truth that lingers long after this ends:
The world taught you to be seen… but Jesus died so you could be known.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Promised God You’d Never Go Back… So Why Are You Here Again?
paragraphs:
You Promised God You’d Never Go Back… So Why Are You Here Again?
When repentance feels real—but the fall still happens, what does grace actually do now?
You remember the moment.

The tears weren’t fake. Your chest felt like it was splitting open as you whispered, “God, I’m done. I don’t want this anymore.” You meant it. You weren’t playing games. You weren’t trying to manipulate heaven. You were desperate.
You repented.
Not casually. Not half-heartedly. You turned. You deleted things. You avoided people. You prayed longer than usual. You even felt… clean for a while.
And then it happened again.

Not because you planned it. Not because you woke up wanting to betray God. But because something inside you cracked at the wrong moment. Loneliness. Temptation. Memory. Flesh. Weakness. And suddenly you were there again—doing the very thing you swore you had buried.
Now you’re sitting in the aftermath.
And the silence feels louder than the sin.
Because the real question isn’t “Did I sin?”
It’s “Did I just lose God?”
There’s a verse that many people quote but few actually understand in its original weight. In 1 John 1:9, the Greek says:

“ἐὰν ὁμολογῶμεν τὰς ἁμαρτίας ἡμῶν, πιστός ἐστιν καὶ δίκαιος…”
“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just…”
The word “ὁμολογῶμεν” (homologōmen) doesn’t just mean to admit. It means to agree fully, to come into alignment with God about your sin—without hiding, without softening, without pretending.
And you did that.
So what changed?
Nothing about God.
Everything about the battlefield.
Because repentance is not the removal of your flesh—it’s the reorientation of your heart. And your flesh doesn’t surrender quietly.
Paul didn’t whisper this struggle—he cried it out in Romans 7:15:

“ὃ γὰρ κατεργάζομαι οὐ γινώσκω…”
“For what I am doing, I do not understand…”
He goes further:

“οὐ γὰρ ὃ θέλω τοῦτο πράσσω, ἀλλ’ ὃ μισῶ τοῦτο ποιῶ.”
“For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate.”
Let that sit with you.
The man who wrote half the New Testament understood what it felt like to hate sin… and still fall into it.
So if you fell again, it doesn’t automatically mean your repentance was fake.
It means the war is real.
But here’s where most people collapse.
Not in the sin—but in the shame after.
Because the enemy doesn’t just want you to fall. He wants you to stay down. He wants you to believe that one failure erased every prayer, every tear, every moment of surrender.
He whispers, “You’re a hypocrite.”
But Scripture doesn’t agree.
In Hebrew, Proverbs 24:16 says:

“כִּי שֶׁבַע יִפּוֹל צַדִּיק וָקָם”
“For a righteous man falls seven times and rises again…”
Notice that.
He is still called righteous… even while falling.
Because righteousness was never built on your consistency.
It was anchored in Christ.
The enemy wants you to confuse conviction with rejection.
Conviction says, “Come back.”
Condemnation says, “Stay away.”
And Romans 8:1 settles this tension with brutal clarity:

“Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα…”
“There is therefore now no condemnation…”
Not less condemnation.
Not delayed condemnation.
No condemnation.
For those in Christ Jesus.
So what do you do now?
You don’t run from God.
You run into Him—while still feeling dirty, ashamed, exposed, and undeserving.
Because grace was never designed for your best moments.
It was built for this exact moment.
David didn’t clean himself up before crying out in Psalm 51. He said:

“חָנֵּנִי אֱלֹהִים כְּחַסְדֶּךָ”
“Have mercy on me, O God, according to Your steadfast love…”
Not according to his performance.
Not according to how many times he failed.
According to God’s hesed—His covenant love that refuses to let go even when you let go of Him.
So if you fell again…
Don’t hide again.
Don’t disappear again.
Don’t pretend again.
Come back—honestly this time, not perfectly.
Because the cross was not a one-time rescue.
It’s a daily covering.
And maybe this is where it gets uncomfortable.
If this spoke to you… if this exposed something you’ve been hiding…
Be honest.
Not for attention.
But for freedom.
Because silence is where shame grows.
But confession is where healing starts.
Someone scrolling right now is exactly where you were five minutes ago—and your honesty might be the thing that pulls them back before they go deeper.
Not to shame them.
But to remind them they’re not alone in the fight.
And you’ll need truth ready, not emotions.
Not because we’re perfect—but because we refuse to dilute the Gospel.
Because discipleship requires proximity.
If you truly want to glorify God… don’t just feel convicted.
Respond.
Stay connected.
Grow intentionally.
Because falling again doesn’t mean your story is over.
It means God is still writing it.
And He has never been afraid of messy chapters.
You thought your failure disqualified you…
But grace just pulled you closer than you’ve ever been.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Said “I Trust God”… But Your Heart Is Tired
paragraphs:
You Said “I Trust God”… But Your Heart Is Tired
The quiet exhaustion no one sees—and the grace that still carries you when your faith feels like it’s breaking
You said it out loud.
“I trust God.”

You meant it.
You weren’t lying.
You weren’t pretending.
But somewhere between the prayers you whispered and the silence that followed… something inside you started to wear down.

Not your belief.
Not your theology.
Your heart.

Because trusting God sounds strong when you say it.
But it feels different when you’re living it.

It feels like waiting longer than you thought you would.
Like praying harder but hearing less.
Like holding on while everything inside you quietly asks, “How much longer, Lord?”
And now here you are.

Still showing up.
Still trying.
Still saying the right things.
But if you’re honest…
You’re tired.
Not physically.
Soul tired.
The kind of tired David wrote about when he said:

“עַד־אָנָה יְהוָה תִּשְׁכָּחֵנִי נֶצַח”
Ad-anah YHWH tishkacheni netsach
“How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1)
That wasn’t a man without faith.
That was a man with deep faith… who felt forgotten.
And maybe that’s where this hits you.
Because no one talks about this part.

The part where trust doesn’t feel victorious.
The part where faith doesn’t feel strong.
The part where you still believe in God… but your emotions feel like they’re collapsing underneath that belief.
You didn’t walk away from God.
But you’ve wondered why it feels like He’s distant.
And that question alone has made you feel guilty.

Like maybe you’re doing something wrong.
Like maybe your faith isn’t enough.
Like maybe you’re failing God quietly while everyone else seems to be thriving.
But listen carefully…
Jesus never rejected tired hearts.
He moved toward them.

“Δεῦτε πρός με πάντες οἱ κοπιῶντες καὶ πεφορτισμένοι”
Deute pros me pantes hoi kopiōntes kai pephortismenoi
“Come to Me, all who are weary and burdened…” (Matthew 11:28)

Not the strong.
Not the ones who have it all together.
The weary.
That word “κοπιῶντες” (kopiōntes) means exhausted from labor… drained from carrying something too heavy for too long.
That’s you, isn’t it?
You trusted God.

But you carried pain longer than you expected.
You held onto hope longer than you thought you’d have to.
You kept believing while silently breaking.
And here’s the part no one told you…
Trusting God doesn’t mean your heart won’t get tired.
It means your tired heart still has somewhere to go.
Because even Jesus, in His humanity, felt the crushing weight of surrender.
In Gethsemane, He prayed:

“πάτερ μου… παρελθέτω ἀπ’ ἐμοῦ τὸ ποτήριον τοῦτο”
Pater mou… parelthetō ap’ emou to potērion touto
“My Father… if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me…” (Matthew 26:39)
That wasn’t weakness.
That was real trust.

Trust that doesn’t hide pain.
Trust that speaks honestly.
Trust that still surrenders… even when it hurts.
And that’s where everything changes.
Because maybe your story isn’t about losing faith.
Maybe it’s about discovering a deeper one.

The kind that doesn’t rely on feelings.
The kind that survives silence.
The kind that holds on… even when it doesn’t understand.
Because God was never asking you to feel strong.
He was asking you to stay.
And you did.
Even tired… you stayed.
Even confused… you stayed.
Even hurting… you stayed.
And that matters more than you think.
Because Scripture never says God is close to the perfect.
It says:

“קָרוֹב יְהוָה לְנִשְׁבְּרֵי־לֵב”
Qarov YHWH lenishbere-lev
“The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18)
Not distant.
Near.
Even now.
Especially now.

So if your heart feels tired…
if your prayers feel heavy…
if your trust feels like it’s barely holding on…
You’re not failing.
You’re being carried.
And maybe this moment—this quiet, exhausted, fragile place—is where God is rewriting your story the most.
Not through strength.
Through surrender.
Not through perfection.
Through dependence.
Not through loud victories.
Through quiet endurance.
This is what grace looks like when it meets a tired soul.
Not condemnation.
Not disappointment.
Compassion.
Because Jesus didn’t come for the ones who had it all together.
He came for the ones barely holding on.
And if that’s you…
You’re exactly where grace can reach you.
So don’t hide this part of your story.
Don’t pretend you’re okay if you’re not.
Bring your real heart to God.
He can handle it.
He always could.
And if this spoke directly into something you’ve been carrying silently…
And be honest…
You’re not alone in this.
Not here.
Not anymore.
Not out of pressure.
But out of purpose.
Because when you support what feeds your spirit, you’re not just consuming truth—you’re helping spread it.
If you feel God pulling you closer… don’t ignore that.
Take the step.
Because sometimes the most powerful faith isn’t loud…
…it’s the one that whispers, “I’m tired… but I’m still trusting.”
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE WHISPER THAT DESTROYED ME
paragraphs:
THE WHISPER THAT DESTROYED ME
How Small Compromises Quietly Build the Fall You Never Saw Coming
It didn’t start with rebellion.
It started with something small… almost harmless.

A thought you didn’t fight.
A conviction you delayed.
A line you told yourself you wouldn’t cross… but stepped closer to anyway.
You didn’t wake up one day deciding to fall.
You drifted.
And the terrifying part?
You barely noticed.
Because sin rarely announces itself with noise. It whispers.

In Hebrew, the word for sin, חַטָּאת (chatta’ah), carries the idea of “missing the mark.” Not always a violent rebellion… sometimes just a slight misalignment. Just enough to be off. Just enough to miss.
And that’s how it begins.
A small compromise.
Then another.
Then another.
Until one day… you look back and realize you are standing somewhere you swore you would never be.
James didn’t describe sin as an explosion. He described it as a process:
“Each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire. Then desire when it has conceived gives birth to sin, and sin when it is fully grown brings forth death.” (James 1:14–15)

In the original Greek, “lured” is ἐξελκόμενος (exelkomenos)—dragged out slowly.
“Enticed” is δελεαζόμενος (deleazomenos)—baited like a fish.
You weren’t pushed.
You were pulled.
Little by little.
Moment by moment.

Until desire became permission…
and permission became action…
and action became a pattern…
and the pattern became a fall.
Be honest.
This didn’t hit you randomly.
You felt that.
Because deep down, you remember where it started.
That one decision you justified.
That one boundary you softened.
That one time you said, “It’s not that serious.”
But Scripture never treats small compromises lightly.
In Song of Songs 2:15, it says:
“Catch the foxes for us, the little foxes that spoil the vineyards…”
Not the big ones.
The little ones.
The quiet ones.
The ones that seem harmless while they’re destroying everything beneath the surface.
That’s what you’ve been dealing with.
Not just sin… but tolerated sin.
Hidden sin.
Managed sin.
And it’s exhausting you.
Because you were never designed to carry what you’re hiding.
David knew this weight. He tried to bury his compromise. He tried to manage it. But listen to what he said:
“When I kept silent, my bones wasted away through my groaning all day long.” (Psalm 32:3)
The Hebrew word for “wasted away” is בָּלָה (balah)—to decay, to wear out, to fall apart from the inside.
That’s what compromise does.
It doesn’t just affect your behavior.
It corrodes your soul.
And maybe you’re reading this right now, and something inside you is breaking a little… because you know.

You know the habit.
You know the secret.
You know the compromise you’ve been feeding.
But here’s where everything changes.
Because this is not just a story about falling.
This is a story about rescue.
Peter didn’t fall overnight either.
He followed Jesus. He loved Jesus. He swore loyalty.
And still… in one night, under pressure, through fear and small moments of compromise… he denied Him three times.
Three.
Not because he hated Jesus.
But because compromise had weakened his courage.
In Luke 22:61, after the third denial, it says:
“And the Lord turned and looked at Peter.”
That look…
It wasn’t hatred.
It wasn’t rejection.
It was recognition.
Grace looking straight into failure.
And Peter broke.
Not because he was condemned…
but because he was loved even there.
That’s the part many people miss.
Yes, small compromises lead to big falls.
But your fall does not disqualify you from grace.
In fact… it’s often where grace meets you most powerfully.
Because Jesus doesn’t just expose sin.
He restores sinners.
The same Peter who denied Christ became the one who boldly preached Him.
The same mouth that said, “I don’t know Him,” later declared, “There is salvation in no one else.”
That’s what Jesus does.
He rewrites everything.
Your compromise is not the end of your story.
But it cannot stay hidden.
It must be surrendered.
The Greek word for repentance, μετάνοια (metanoia), doesn’t just mean feeling sorry.
It means a complete change of mind… a turning… a transformation.
Not managing sin.
Killing it.
Not hiding.
Healing.
And maybe this is your moment.
Not to ignore the conviction.
But to respond.
Be honest.
This hit deeper than you expected.
And someone you know is silently drifting the same way you were.
If you truly want to glorify God… don’t just consume truth.
Support it.
Spread it.
Live it.
Because the enemy works in whispers…
but God restores in truth.
And right now… you’re being called back.
You’re not too far gone.
You’re not too compromised.
You’re not beyond restoration.
You’re one surrender away from everything changing.
The fall may have started small…
but so can your return.
And this time…
don’t ignore it.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: The Secret Prison No One Talks About: Why So Many Can’t Escape Masturbation—And the Grace That Still Reaches Them
paragraphs: The Secret Prison No One Talks About: Why So Many Can’t Escape Masturbation—And the Grace That Still Reaches Them
There are battles people fight in silence… the kind that never make it into prayer meetings, never get posted, never get confessed out loud.
But they’re real.
And they’re exhausting.

You close the tab, wipe the guilt off your face, and promise God—“This is the last time.”
Then somehow… it isn’t.
Again.
And again.
And again.
What keeps a person trapped here isn’t just the act itself. It’s something deeper. Something older. Something spiritual.
Because sin doesn’t just want your behavior—it wants your agreement.

The Scripture says in James 1:14–15, “each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire.” The Greek word used there is ἐπιθυμία (epithymia)—a longing, a craving, a pull that feels almost like it belongs to you.
That’s the trap.

It doesn’t feel like an enemy.
It feels like you.
So when you fall, you don’t just feel guilty… you feel like you are the problem.
But that’s not where the story starts.
And it’s definitely not where it ends.

From the beginning, the enemy has always worked through distortion. In Genesis, the Hebrew word for nakedness, עָרוּם (‘arum), carries a dual meaning—innocence… and vulnerability. What was once pure became exposed, twisted, and exploited after sin entered.
That same distortion still lives today.
Sex was created holy. Intimacy was designed by God. Desire itself is not evil.
But when desire is disconnected from covenant, from truth, from God’s design—it becomes a counterfeit comfort.
And counterfeit comforts are addictive.
Not because they satisfy… but because they almost do.
That’s why people stay trapped.

Not just because of lust.
But because of loneliness.

Not just because of temptation.
But because of pain.

Not just because of habit.
But because it becomes a hiding place.

A place where no one sees.
Where no one judges.
Where control feels possible… even if just for a moment.
And that moment becomes a cycle.

The Apostle Paul understood this internal war. In Romans 7:19, he writes in Greek, “οὐ γὰρ ὃ θέλω ποιῶ ἀγαθόν, ἀλλ’ ὃ οὐ θέλω κακὸν τοῦτο πράσσω”—“For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing.”
That’s not weakness talking.
That’s humanity… without surrender.
Because willpower alone cannot break what the soul is using as medicine.
And that’s the truth most people don’t want to face.
Masturbation, for many, isn’t just about lust.
It’s about escape.

Escape from rejection.
Escape from stress.
Escape from emptiness.
Escape from wounds that were never healed.
So even when you hate it… part of you still runs back to it.
And then the shame comes.
Heavy. Loud. Suffocating.
The enemy whispers in Hebrew accusation, just like the name “Satan”—שָׂטָן (satan)—the accuser.

“You’re fake.”
“You’ll never change.”
“God is tired of you.”
But that’s not God’s voice.
Because when Jesus encountered broken people… He didn’t trap them in their sin.
He rewrote their story.
In John 8, the woman caught in adultery stood exposed, condemned, waiting to be destroyed.
And Jesus said, “Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.”
In Greek, “οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω”—“Neither do I condemn you.”
Notice what He didn’t say.
He didn’t say, “Stay as you are.”
He didn’t say, “It’s okay.”
He removed condemnation… and then called her higher.
That’s grace.
Not permission to stay broken… but power to become whole.
So what keeps people trapped?

Silence.
Shame.
Isolation.
Unhealed wounds.
Misunderstood identity.
But what sets them free?

Truth.
Light.
Surrender.
And a Savior who doesn’t flinch at your mess.
Because Jesus didn’t come for the version of you that has it all together.
He came for the version of you that’s still fighting… still failing… still reaching.
If that’s you… be honest.
You don’t need another promise you’ll break.
You need a deeper encounter with the One who never breaks His.
This isn’t about behavior modification.
It’s about transformation.
The Greek word for repentance, μετάνοια (metanoia), means a change of mind… a turning… a complete reorientation of the soul.
Not just stopping sin… but seeing differently.
Seeing yourself not as a slave… but as someone already fought for.
Already pursued.
Already loved.
And slowly… the chains begin to loosen.
Not overnight.
But truly.
Come back to it when the urge hits.
And if you’ve been consuming content that feeds your struggle… maybe it’s time to start feeding your spirit instead.
If this message reached you… it wasn’t random.
It was mercy.
Because God is not finished with you.
Not even close.
Be honest.
This hit deeper than you expected, didn’t it?
You were never meant to win this battle alone… and maybe the turning point starts right here.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: They mocked Him while He was still breathing.
paragraphs: They mocked Him while He was still breathing.
Blood in His mouth. Skin torn open. Heaven watching in silence.
And then… He said it.
Not a whisper of defeat. Not the surrender of a broken man.
But a declaration that shook eternity:
“Τετέλεσται.” (Tetelestai.)
“It is finished.” — John 19:30
If you’ve ever heard that line and thought it meant “it’s over,” you missed the weight of what just happened on that cross.
Because Jesus wasn’t saying He lost.
He was announcing that everything broken in you finally had a way back.

The Greek word “τετέλεσται” (tetelestai) comes from “τελέω” (teleō), meaning to complete, to accomplish, to fulfill a mission in full. In the first century, it was stamped on receipts—“paid in full.” No balance left. No debt remaining. Nothing owed.
So when Jesus said it, He wasn’t describing His condition.
He was declaring your freedom.
Long before that moment, the Hebrew Scriptures had already whispered what this would look like. Isaiah wrote it in a language soaked with sorrow and prophecy:
“נִגַּשׂ וְהוּא נַעֲנֶה” (niggas ve-hu na’aneh) — “He was oppressed and afflicted…” (Isaiah 53:7)
“וַיהוָה הִפְגִּיעַ בּוֹ אֵת עֲוֹן כֻּלָּנוּ” — “And the Lord laid on Him the iniquity of us all.” (Isaiah 53:6)
Not some of us.
All of us.
Every hidden habit. Every quiet addiction. Every lie you rehearsed until it felt like truth. Every night you said, “God, I’ll do better,” and didn’t.
All of it… placed on Him.
So when Jesus cried out “Tetelestai,” He wasn’t escaping pain—He was finishing payment.
The kind of payment you could never afford.
The kind religion keeps trying to invoice you for.
The kind shame keeps reminding you you haven’t paid.
But heaven stamped your record with one word:
Finished.
And yet… why do you still feel like you owe something?
Why do you still wake up carrying guilt like it’s your responsibility to fix what God already resolved?
Somewhere along the way, you believed the lie that Jesus started your salvation—but you have to maintain it.
That grace got you in… but performance keeps you there.
That God saved you… but now He’s watching, arms crossed, waiting for you to mess up again.
But that’s not what “Tetelestai” means.
It doesn’t mean “partially complete.”
It doesn’t mean “to be continued.”
It doesn’t mean “almost enough.”
It means fully accomplished. Entirely settled. Eternally secured.
Even in Aramaic, the language Jesus likely spoke on that cross, the sense carries the same finality—completion with nothing left undone.
This is where the scandal begins.
Because grace like that offends people who built their identity on earning.
Grace like that disrupts systems that thrive on control.
Grace like that exposes the truth:
You didn’t save yourself.
You couldn’t.
And you never will.
That’s why the cross is offensive.
Because it strips you of the illusion that you’re the hero.
And introduces you to the One who already finished the story.
But here’s the part that hits deeper than theology…
If it’s truly finished… then why are you still hiding?
Why are you still pretending God is surprised by your struggle?
Why are you still performing like your worth depends on your consistency?
You don’t clean yourself up to come to Jesus.
You come to Jesus because you can’t clean yourself up.
And the moment you stop running, you realize—
He already knew.
And He stayed anyway.
Be honest.
Don’t keep that inside. There’s freedom in bringing it into the light.
Because the cross wasn’t a performance.
It was a rescue.
And the resurrection wasn’t a plot twist.
It was proof.
Proof that sin doesn’t get the last word.
Proof that shame doesn’t get to define you.
Proof that your worst chapter doesn’t get to be your final identity.
From scandal… to grace.
That’s the story Jesus finished.
And if you’ve ever felt like your life is too messy, too complicated, too far gone…
You’re exactly the kind of story He rewrites.
And if you’re serious about growing deeper in Christ—not surface-level faith, but real transformation, real healing, real discipleship—stay close.
Because this isn’t about motivation.
This is about resurrection.
And if this message stirred something in you… if it helped you see Jesus more clearly, love Him more deeply, or understand the cross more truthfully—then support what God is doing here.
Not out of pressure.
But out of purpose.
Because when you support, you help push the Gospel further.
If you want to be part of something that glorifies God beyond a single moment… step in.
Because someone out there is still waiting to hear what you almost kept to yourself.
And this message might be the one that brings them back.
It wasn’t the nails that held Him there—it was His decision to finish what you never could.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Is Flirting Cheating… Even If Nothing Physical Happened?
paragraphs:
Is Flirting Cheating… Even If Nothing Physical Happened?
When Your Heart Crossed the Line Before Your Body Ever Did
It never starts with a bed. It starts with a glance you didn’t look away from. A message you reread a little too slowly. A laugh that felt a little too good coming from someone who isn’t yours.
And you tell yourself, “Nothing happened.”
But something did.
Somewhere deep in the quiet spaces of your heart, a line was crossed so softly that no one else heard it… but God did.

Jesus once said something that still unsettles people who think sin only counts when it becomes visible. In Matthew 5:28, the Greek text records His words as, “πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν” — “everyone who looks at a woman to desire her.” Not just looking… but looking with intention. Not just noticing… but feeding something inside.

He didn’t say, “when you touch.”
He didn’t say, “when you act.”
He said, “when you desire.”
Because Jesus wasn’t just exposing behavior. He was exposing the hidden negotiations of the heart.
And that’s where flirting lives.

Flirting is rarely about the other person. It’s about what wakes up inside you when they notice you. It’s about the validation, the attention, the feeling of being wanted again. It’s about feeding something that was supposed to be surrendered.

The Hebrew word for heart, “לֵב” (lev), doesn’t just mean emotions. It means the center of will, desire, intention — the control room of your life. So when Proverbs 4:23 says, “Guard your heart,” the Hebrew reads “מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ” — guard your lev above all guarding. Why? Because everything flows from there.

Not just actions.
Affections.
Attachments.
Allegiances.
So no, flirting isn’t “nothing.”
It’s often the beginning of something.

The enemy doesn’t need you to fall overnight. He just needs you to entertain what you should have shut down. A little conversation. A little secrecy. A little emotional intimacy that doesn’t belong to you.
And suddenly, your heart is divided.

James 1:14–15 explains the progression with uncomfortable clarity. In Greek, “ἐπιθυμία” (epithymia) — desire — gives birth. Not instantly. But slowly. It conceives. Then it grows. Then it brings forth sin.

Not when it becomes physical.
When it becomes internal agreement.
You didn’t plan to cheat. But you also didn’t stop the moment you should have.
And here’s the part most people don’t want to admit: sometimes flirting feels harmless because it hasn’t cost you anything yet.
But spiritually, it already has.

It costs intimacy with God.
It costs purity of mind.
It costs honesty within your own soul.
And if you’re in a relationship… it costs trust, even if they don’t know yet.
Be honest. This hit harder than you expected.
Maybe you’re thinking about that one person right now. The one you “just talk to.” The one who “gets you.” The one you would never cross the line with… but you’ve already crossed something deeper.
Because conviction isn’t condemnation. It’s God calling you back before you go further than you ever intended.
The beauty of the Gospel is this: Jesus doesn’t just confront the sin we can see. He heals the places we hide.
The same Savior who said those piercing words in Matthew 5 is the same One who sat with the woman caught in adultery and said, “Neither do I condemn you… go, and sin no more.”
Grace doesn’t ignore the truth. It restores you through it.
In Aramaic, the language Jesus spoke daily, forgiveness carries a sense of release… of being untied. What you’ve been binding yourself to in secret, He’s ready to break.
But you have to let go.
Not later. Not when it gets worse. Now.
Because the longer you feed something, the harder it is to starve it.
And maybe this isn’t just about flirting. Maybe this is about loneliness. About unmet needs. About wounds you’ve been trying to soothe with attention that was never meant to heal you.
Jesus sees that too.
He’s not just asking you to stop. He’s inviting you to be whole.
And if you want to glorify God not just in words but in action, support what is feeding your spirit. You’re helping spread the Gospel to people who are still trapped in silence.
If your heart is serious about transformation, don’t stay at the surface.
Follow if you want truth that doesn’t water things down. Stay close if you’re done playing with sin and ready to walk in freedom.
Because the war isn’t always visible. But it’s always real.
And Jesus is still rewriting stories that looked like they were headed for destruction.

You’re not too far gone.
You’re not too compromised.
You’re not beyond redemption.
You’re one surrendered decision away from grace rewriting everything.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: Why Does the Bible Guard Sex Like a Sacred Fire?
paragraphs:
Why Does the Bible Guard Sex Like a Sacred Fire?
Because what feels like freedom can either crown your soul… or quietly burn it.

It didn’t start with rules.
It started with breath.

Before there were boundaries, before commandments were carved into stone, before shame ever whispered its name into the human story—there was God, leaning into dust, breathing life into a man who didn’t yet know what it meant to be alive.
And then something holy happened.
“זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה בָּרָא אֹתָם” (Zakar u’neqevah bara otam) — “Male and female He created them.” (Genesis 1:27)

Not accident. Not evolution of desire. Not experimentation.
Design.
There is something about sex that heaven never treated casually. Not because it’s dirty… but because it’s dangerously powerful when disconnected from the One who created it.
We were never taught that properly.
Some of you learned about sex through screens. Some through silence. Some through trauma. Some through curiosity that turned into chains you didn’t expect to wear this long.
And now you’re trying to figure out why something that felt so right at first… left something so broken afterward.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.

The Bible doesn’t protect sex because God is trying to restrict joy.
He protects it because He understands what it does to the soul.
When Paul writes in Greek, “φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν” (pheugete tēn porneian) — “Flee sexual immorality” (1 Corinthians 6:18), he doesn’t say manage it… control it… or minimize it.
He says run.
Why?
Because sexual sin is not like other sin.

“πᾶν ἁμάρτημα… ἐκτὸς τοῦ σώματος ἐστιν… ὁ δὲ πορνεύων εἰς τὸ ἴδιον σῶμα ἁμαρτάνει”
(Pan hamartēma… ektos tou sōmatos estin… ho de porneuōn eis to idion sōma hamartanei)
— “Every other sin a person commits is outside the body, but the sexually immoral person sins against his own body.” (1 Corinthians 6:18)

There’s a reason your memories don’t let go.
There’s a reason certain attachments still linger.
There’s a reason some nights feel heavier than others.
Sex was never just physical.
It was covenant language.
“וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד” (Ve’hayu levasar echad) — “And they shall become one flesh.” (Genesis 2:24)

Not one night.
Not one moment.
One flesh.
Do you understand what that means?

God designed sex to unite souls in a way that echoes eternity.
That’s why it feels so deep.
That’s why it hurts when it’s broken.
That’s why it lingers even when the person is gone.
Because something real happened.
Something spiritual.
And we’ve been trying to treat it like it’s disposable.
That’s the scandal.
But here’s where everything shifts.
Because the Bible doesn’t just expose the damage.
It reveals a Redeemer who steps into it.
There was a woman once. Dragged. Accused. Exposed. No defense left. No dignity left. No future left.
You know her story.
They wanted to stone her.
Jesus bent down and wrote in the dust.
No shouting. No condemnation. No performance.
Just silence… and authority.

“ὁ ἀναμάρτητος… πρῶτος τὸν λίθον βαλέτω”
(Ho anamartētos… prōtos ton lithon baletō)
— “Let him who is without sin cast the first stone.” (John 8:7)
One by one… they left.
And then Jesus looked at her.

Not with lust.
Not with disgust.
Not with indifference.
With truth… and mercy.

“οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω· πορεύου καὶ μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε”
(Oude egō se katakrinō; poreuou kai mēketi hamartane)
— “Neither do I condemn you. Go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11)
Did you catch that?

He didn’t excuse her sin.
But He didn’t define her by it either.
That’s the Gospel.

Not permission to continue…
But power to become new.
If sex was only physical, Jesus wouldn’t have needed to die for what we’ve done with it.
But because it touches the soul… He went to the cross to redeem the soul.
“καὶνὴ κτίσις” (kainē ktisis) — “a new creation.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)
That means your past doesn’t get the final word.

Not the addiction.
Not the regret.
Not the secret.
Not the thing you hope nobody ever finds out.
Jesus rewrites everything.
So why does the Bible guard sex so carefully?
Because it’s not trying to control you.
It’s trying to protect what’s sacred inside you.
And maybe… just maybe… the reason you’ve felt so conflicted isn’t because God is distant…
…but because your soul remembers what it was created for.
This isn’t about shame.
This is about restoration.
And if this reached you at the exact moment you needed it, don’t keep it to yourself.
Not out of obligation… but out of alignment. Because supporting what spreads the Gospel is part of glorifying God too.
Because healing doesn’t happen by accident.
It happens when you stay close to truth.
And the truth is…

What God protects isn’t to limit your life…
…it’s to preserve your soul.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: “You Didn’t Touch Them… But Your Heart Did.”
paragraphs:
“You Didn’t Touch Them… But Your Heart Did.”
Is It Sin to Watch Romantic Movies That Stir Desire? Or Is Something Deeper Already Being Touched?
You told yourself it was harmless.

Just a movie.
Just a love story.
Just two people finding each other in a broken world.
But somewhere between the glances… the tension… the slow-burning moments that linger just a little too long… something shifted inside you.
Your heart didn’t stay neutral.
Your thoughts didn’t stay clean.
And now you’re wondering… not out loud, but deep inside:
“God… did I just sin?”

Not because you touched someone.
Not because you acted on anything.
But because something in you responded.
And that response… felt real.
Scripture doesn’t ignore moments like this. It exposes them.
Jesus said something that still unsettles even the most disciplined believers:

“πᾶς ὁ βλέπων γυναῖκα πρὸς τὸ ἐπιθυμῆσαι αὐτὴν
ἤδη ἐμοίχευσεν αὐτὴν ἐν τῇ καρδίᾳ αὐτοῦ.”
(Matthew 5:28, Greek)
“Everyone who looks at a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.”
Notice what He did there.
He didn’t wait for the act.
He went straight to the desire.
Because sin doesn’t begin in behavior.
It begins in the heart.
The Greek word “ἐπιθυμῆσαι” (epithymēsai) means more than just noticing beauty. It means a craving… a pulling… a desire that wants to possess.
That’s where things become dangerous.
Because romantic movies are not always about love.
Many of them are carefully crafted to awaken longing.
Not covenant. Not commitment. Not Christ-centered love.
But emotional intoxication.
And your heart… responds.
James writes it with uncomfortable clarity:

ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος.”
(James 1:14, Greek)
“But each person is tempted when he is drawn away by his own desire and enticed.”
Drawn away.
Not forced.
Not attacked.
Drawn.
Because something inside us answers the call.
That’s why this question isn’t really about movies.
It’s about alignment.
It’s about what your heart is learning to love.
There are romantic stories that reflect God’s design—sacrificial love, covenant, purity, patience.
And then there are stories that glorify emotional lust, fantasy intimacy, and connections built on desire rather than devotion.
One feeds your spirit.
The other feeds your flesh.
Paul doesn’t soften this when he writes:
(1 Corinthians 6:18)
The Greek word “φεύγετε” (pheugete) means run. Escape. Get away fast.
Not manage it.
Not flirt with it.
Not sit in it and hope your heart stays untouched.
Because the truth is…
You don’t just watch content.
Content shapes what you desire.
And desire, when entertained, doesn’t stay quiet.
It grows.

“כִּי כָל־לֵב אָדָם רַע מִנְּעֻרָיו”
(Genesis 8:21, Hebrew)
“For the inclination of the human heart is evil from youth.”
That’s not condemnation.
That’s diagnosis.
Your heart is not neutral territory.
So when you sit in front of something designed to stir desire… you are not observing.
You are participating.
Even if it’s only in your thoughts.
And thoughts matter to God.
Deeply.
Because God isn’t just after your actions.
He’s after your heart.
But here’s where grace enters the story.
Because if you’re reading this and feeling convicted… that’s not God pushing you away.
That’s Him calling you closer.
Romans 8:1 says:

“Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα
τοῖς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ.”
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
Conviction is not rejection.
It’s invitation.
An invitation to realign.
To ask yourself honestly:
“What is this feeding in me?”
“Is this drawing me closer to Christ… or quietly reshaping what I crave?”
And maybe the hardest question:
“Would I watch this if Jesus was sitting beside me?”
Not the version of Jesus we imagine.
But the holy, pure, heart-searching Savior who sees everything… including what we feel.
Be honest.
This hit differently, didn’t it?
Sit in it.
Because this is where transformation begins.
And if you know someone who casually consumes things that are slowly shaping their desires… share this with them.
Not to judge them.
But to wake them up.
Because you’ll need this reminder again.
Following Christ isn’t just about avoiding obvious sin.
It’s about guarding the invisible places.
And if you want to go deeper—not just surface-level faith but real transformation—stay close.
Follow for daily truth that challenges, heals, and realigns your heart with Jesus.
And if you’re serious about growing, about being sharpened, about stepping out of lukewarm faith and into something real…
If your heart is being stirred right now… don’t ignore that.
Step into it.
Support what feeds your spirit.
Because if we truly want to glorify God…
We don’t just consume content.
We invest in truth.
We spread truth.
We live truth.
And sometimes the most spiritual thing you can do…
is walk away from what your flesh secretly wants.
You didn’t touch them…
but your heart knows where it went.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: THE 3-DAY PATTERN YOU KEEP IGNORING… AND WHY IT’S QUIETLY DEFINING YOUR LIFE
paragraphs: THE 3-DAY PATTERN YOU KEEP IGNORING… AND WHY IT’S QUIETLY DEFINING YOUR LIFE
What if the darkest season you’re in right now is not the end… but the middle?
There’s something hidden in Scripture that most people read past.

Not because it isn’t there…
but because it’s uncomfortable to sit in.

Because it forces you to stay in the silence.
The waiting.
The in-between.
The third day.

You’ve probably prayed for instant answers.
Immediate healing.
Quick rescue.
But God keeps writing stories in three days.
And you keep trying to escape day two.
Sit with this for a second…
In Genesis 22, Abraham walks with Isaac up the mountain. God had asked for everything. The promise. The son. The future. For three days, Abraham carried that weight.
The Hebrew text says: “בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי” (bayyom hashlishi) — “on the third day.”

Not the first.
Not immediately.
God let him walk… feel… wrestle… trust.
And then—provision appeared.
But only after the third day.
You don’t see God move because you keep trying to leave before He finishes the pattern.
Jonah?
Three days in the belly of the fish.
The Hebrew says: “שְׁלֹשָׁה יָמִים וּשְׁלֹשָׁה לֵילוֹת” (sheloshah yamim usheloshah leilot) — “three days and three nights.”
Not symbolic.
Not poetic exaggeration.

A real darkness.
A real confinement.
A real confrontation with himself.
Jonah wasn’t just being punished.
He was being reshaped.
And maybe that’s what your situation is too.
Not destruction…
But interruption.
Not abandonment…
But recalibration.
Hosea writes something that feels almost like a whisper from God to the broken:

“After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up.”
(Hosea 6:2)

In Hebrew:
“יְחַיֵּנוּ מִיֹּמָיִם בַּיּוֹם הַשְּׁלִישִׁי יְקִימֵנוּ” (yechayyenu miyomayim bayyom hashlishi yeqimenu)
Do you see it?

Day one: loss.
Day two: silence.
Day three: resurrection.
But you’re panicking on day two…
thinking God has already decided your ending.
And then Jesus…
This is where it stops being a pattern…
and becomes a promise.
Jesus Himself said in Greek:

“τῇ τρίτῃ ἡμέρᾳ ἐγερθήσεται” (tē tritē hēmera egerthēsetai) —
“on the third day He will be raised.” (Matthew 16:21)
The cross wasn’t the end.
But it looked like it.
The tomb wasn’t the conclusion.
But it felt like it.
Imagine the disciples.
Everything shattered.
Every hope buried.
Every prayer seemingly unanswered.

He said He was the Messiah…
but now He’s gone.

Day one: shock.
Day two: silence.

No miracles.
No voice.
No explanation.
Just… stillness.
Have you ever been there?
Where heaven feels quiet…
and your heart starts writing conclusions God never said?
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because some of you are living in that exact space right now.

You prayed… and nothing moved.
You believed… and nothing changed.
You trusted… and everything still fell apart.
But what if you’re not abandoned…
What if you’re just in day two?
Because day three…
is where God reveals what He was doing all along.

The stone didn’t move on day one.
It didn’t move on day two.
But when it moved…
it changed everything.
Resurrection is God’s signature move.
And He never signs too early.
He waits until it looks impossible.
Until you stop relying on yourself.
Until the only explanation left…
is Him.
So maybe your situation isn’t dead.
Maybe it’s just waiting for its third day.
And here’s where it gets personal…
You’ve been trying to rush God.
Skip the process.
Avoid the discomfort.
But God is not just interested in your outcome.
He’s after your transformation.

Day one breaks you.
Day two empties you.
Day three reveals Him.
And if you leave too early…
you miss the miracle.
You miss the encounter.
You miss the version of yourself that only exists after surrender.
Let this become real.
Let this become honest.
Because faith isn’t pretending everything is okay…
it’s trusting that God is still working when it’s not.
And if this spoke to something deep in you…
don’t keep it to yourself.
Because there will be a moment when you feel like quitting again…
and you’ll need this reminder.
And if you truly want to glorify God through your life…
then support what spreads His truth.
But more than that…
you become part of something eternal.
A movement of people who refuse to stay silent about what Jesus has done.
If you’re ready for deeper discipleship, daily conviction, and spiritual growth…
And don’t forget…
You’re not just reading content…
you’re stepping into transformation.
Because the same God who waited three days…
is still writing stories today.
And yours…
is not finished.
Even if it feels buried right now.
Even if it feels silent right now.
Even if it feels impossible right now.
The stone hasn’t moved yet…
but that doesn’t mean God isn’t about to.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: He Was Just a Shepherd… Until God Spoke His Name
paragraphs:
He Was Just a Shepherd… Until God Spoke His Name
The Scandal of Being Unqualified and the Grace That Turns Nobodies into Prophets
There are callings that make sense… and then there are the kind that feel almost offensive.

Because if we’re honest, when we picture a prophet, we imagine someone trained, polished, chosen early, prepared for the spotlight. Someone who looks the part. Sounds the part. Lives somewhere close to power, influence, and religious prestige.
But Amos?

Amos was dirt under the fingernails.
Amos smelled like sheep.
Amos was unnoticed… until heaven interrupted his ordinary.
And maybe that’s why this story hits harder than most.
Because it exposes something we don’t like to admit—God doesn’t need our qualifications… He looks for our surrender.
Amos himself didn’t pretend otherwise. He said it plainly in Amos 7:14:
“I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet’s son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit…”
In Hebrew, the word he uses for shepherd is “בּוֹקֵר” (bōqēr)—not a royal shepherd, not a poetic figure, but a simple cattle herder. A laborer. A nobody in the eyes of society.
And yet… that’s exactly where God went.

Not to the palace.
Not to the academy.
Not to the religious elite.
God walked into the fields… and called a man who didn’t even think he belonged in the conversation.
Let that settle in you.
Because some of you have already disqualified yourselves from what God is trying to do in your life.

You think your past is too messy.
Your voice too small.
Your knowledge too limited.
Your life too ordinary.
But Amos didn’t upgrade himself into a prophet.
God rewrote him into one.
And when God calls, He doesn’t ask for permission from your insecurity.
The calling of Amos wasn’t comfortable either. God didn’t lift him up just to celebrate him. He sent him into confrontation.
Into a nation that had grown spiritually numb. Into a people who performed religion but abandoned righteousness.
The message was heavy. Unpopular. Dangerous.
In Amos 5:24, God speaks through him:
“But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.”
In Hebrew, “justice” is “מִשְׁפָּט” (mishpat)—not just fairness, but divine order restored. And “righteousness,” “צְדָקָה” (tsedaqah)—a life aligned with God’s heart, not just outward behavior.
God wasn’t impressed with their rituals.
He wanted their hearts back.
And Amos… the shepherd… became the voice.
This is where it gets uncomfortable.
Because we love the idea of being chosen… but we hesitate when we realize what that calling might demand.

Amos had no platform.
No following.
No safety net.
Just obedience.
And obedience will cost you something.

It might cost your comfort.
Your reputation.
Your relationships.
Your plans.
But here’s the truth most people avoid:
The life you’re trying to protect might be the very thing keeping you from becoming who God called you to be.
And that’s the scandal.
God doesn’t just call the prepared… He prepares the called.
Even when they’re standing in a field, holding nothing but a shepherd’s staff.
Even when they feel like imposters.
Even when they don’t see it yet.
If you’ve ever felt like you’re too far behind, too broken, too unseen, too unqualified…
You are standing exactly where Amos stood.
And that means this might be your moment.

Not because you’re ready…
But because God is.
Be honest for a second…
Have you been running from something you know God is asking you to step into?
Have you been hiding behind “I’m not ready” when deep down, you know it’s really fear?
Let that be your first step out of silence.
And if you feel like your faith has been weak, inconsistent, or tired lately…
There’s something powerful about saying it out loud.
Remind them that heaven still calls shepherds.
And if you want to stay rooted in truth like this daily—real Scripture, real conviction, real transformation—follow closely.
Not for content… but for alignment.
Because following truth keeps you from drifting back into comfortable lies.
And if you’re serious about growing deeper in Jesus Christ—not surface-level faith, but real discipleship, healing, accountability—there’s more waiting for you.
If God is using this to stir something in you… don’t ignore it.
Support what is feeding your spirit.
Because when you help spread truth, you’re not just supporting content—you’re participating in someone else’s encounter with God.
Because glorifying God isn’t passive… it moves, it shares, it multiplies.
And maybe… just maybe…
The next “Amos” is someone reading this right now, thinking they’re still just a shepherd.
But heaven has already said your name.
And once God speaks… ordinary is no longer your identity.
You were never just what you did… you are who He calls you to become.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: When Desire Turns Into Desperation
paragraphs:
When Desire Turns Into Desperation
The quiet moment where the heart stops asking God… and starts reaching without Him.
It didn’t happen all at once.
That’s the part nobody warns you about.

Desperation rarely kicks the door down. It whispers. It lingers. It slowly reshapes what you once called conviction into something you start calling “understanding.” You tell yourself it’s just a season. Just a need. Just this once.
And suddenly… desire is no longer something you surrender.
It’s something you serve.
Scripture doesn’t hide this progression. It exposes it with uncomfortable clarity:

In James 1:14–15, the original Greek says, “ἕκαστος δὲ πειράζεται ὑπὸ τῆς ἰδίας ἐπιθυμίας ἐξελκόμενος καὶ δελεαζόμενος” — each person is tempted when they are dragged away and enticed by their own desire.
Dragged away.
Not pushed. Not forced.
Dragged.
Something inside you begins to pull harder than your obedience.
And then comes the shift: “εἶτα ἡ ἐπιθυμία συλλαβοῦσα τίκτει ἁμαρτίαν” — then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin.
Desire… conceives.
That means it stays. It grows. It becomes something living inside you.
And by the time it gives birth, you’re already too attached to let it die quietly.
Be honest.
There was a moment you knew better.
There was a moment when God’s voice was still clear, still interrupting, still convicting… and you felt that internal tension. That hesitation. That holy resistance.
But you stayed.
You entertained it.
You fed it.
You told yourself, “I just need this.”
That’s when desire crossed the line.
That’s when it became desperation.
The Hebrew language in Genesis 3:6 paints this vividly: “וַתֵּרֶא הָאִשָּׁה כִּי־טוֹב הָעֵץ לְמַאֲכָל” — the woman saw that the tree was good for food.
Saw.
Desired.
Reached.
Eve didn’t fall because she was ignorant. She fell because something looked “good” enough to override obedience.
That’s the danger.
Desperation doesn’t always look evil.
Sometimes it looks reasonable.
It looks like loneliness that just wants comfort.
It looks like exhaustion that just wants relief.
It looks like silence from God that makes you think you have to act for yourself.
So you take matters into your own hands.
You grasp.
You settle.
You compromise.
And afterward… there’s that silence.
That heavy, suffocating silence.
Not because God left you.
But because deep down, you know you stepped away from Him first.
David knew that silence.
After everything… the power, the calling, the victories… he found himself staring at Bathsheba, letting desire become something darker.
And when it was done, when the moment passed and reality settled in, his words in Psalm 51:3–4 cut deep:
“כִּי־פְשָׁעַי אֲנִי אֵדָע” — for I know my transgressions.
Not “I made a mistake.”
Not “it just happened.”
I know.
There is something terrifying about knowing exactly where you crossed the line.
And yet…
There is something even more powerful about what comes next.
Because the story doesn’t end in desperation.
It never does with Jesus.
In the Aramaic heart of the Gospel, Jesus doesn’t run from the desperate. He moves toward them.
The woman caught in sin.
The man possessed.
The thief on the cross.
People whose desires led them to broken places… and yet grace still found them.
In John 8:11, Jesus says, “οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω· πορεύου, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ νῦν μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε” — neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.
Did you catch that?
No condemnation… but also no permission to stay the same.
Grace doesn’t excuse desperation.
It transforms it.
That’s the turning point.
That’s where everything shifts.
You don’t have to keep feeding what’s destroying you.
You don’t have to keep calling it “need” when it’s actually pulling you away from God.
You don’t have to stay trapped in the cycle.
But you do have to be honest.
Because healing begins where pretending ends.
What have you been calling “need” that is actually desperation?
What have you been justifying… even though you know it’s slowly separating you from God?
What have you been holding onto… that God has been asking you to release?
Be honest.
This is where everything changes.
There are people reading your honesty who need to know they’re not alone.
And if this spoke to something real in you, don’t stay distant.
Because the truth is… you were never meant to fight this alone.
And if your heart is serious about glorifying God, then don’t just consume truth—help carry it.
If your soul is hungry… don’t ignore it.
Feed it.
Grow it.
Guard it.
Because one honest decision today can break a cycle that’s been controlling you for years.
And here’s the truth you can’t afford to forget:
Desperation may have written your last chapter… but it doesn’t get to write your ending.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Knew It Was Wrong… So Why Did You Still Do It?
paragraphs:
You Knew It Was Wrong… So Why Did You Still Do It?
The quiet war between conviction and compromise—and the mercy that still comes for you anyway
You didn’t wake up planning to cross the line.
It was smaller than that. Softer. Almost invisible.

A thought you entertained longer than you should have.
A message you didn’t delete.
A habit you renamed so it didn’t sound like sin anymore.
And somewhere between knowing and doing… you built a defense for something your spirit already rejected.
That tension you feel? That restless weight that doesn’t go away even when no one else knows?
Scripture already described it long before you lived it.
Paul said it in a way that almost feels like he was reading your private thoughts:

“ὃ γὰρ κατεργάζομαι οὐ γινώσκω· οὐ γὰρ ὃ θέλω τοῦτο πράσσω, ἀλλ’ ὃ μισῶ τοῦτο ποιῶ.”
(ho gar katergazomai ou ginōskō; ou gar ho thelō touto prassō, all’ ho misō touto poiō)
“For what I am doing, I do not understand. For what I will to do, that I do not practice; but what I hate, that I do.” (Romans 7:15)
You don’t just sin. You argue your way into it.
That’s the part nobody talks about.
You don’t wake up and say, “I want to rebel against God today.”
You say things like:

“It’s not that serious.”
“I deserve this.”
“God understands my situation.”
“I’ll fix it later.”
And just like that… truth gets negotiated.
But the Hebrew word for truth—אֱמֶת (’emet)—doesn’t bend to comfort. It stands.
So why do you keep justifying what you already know is wrong?
Because sin doesn’t always look like rebellion.
Sometimes it looks like reasoning.
In Genesis, the first lie didn’t begin with disobedience. It began with distortion.
“אַף כִּי אָמַר אֱלֹהִים” (aph ki amar Elohim) — “Did God really say…?” (Genesis 3:1)
That’s where it starts.
Not with breaking God’s Word… but questioning it just enough to make room for yourself.
And once doubt enters, desire starts negotiating.
“וַתֵּרֶא הָאִשָּׁה” (vatere ha’ishah) — “And the woman saw…” (Genesis 3:6)
She saw what she wanted to see.
That’s what you’re doing too.
You’re not blind.
You’re selective.
You highlight the parts that support your choice and ignore the parts that expose it.
You call it understanding yourself… but deep down, it’s avoidance.
And here’s what makes it heavier…
You feel the Holy Spirit warning you.

“καὶ μὴ λυπεῖτε τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ Ἅγιον”
(kai mē lupeite to Pneuma to Hagion)
“And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God.” (Ephesians 4:30)
That uneasiness? That interruption in your peace?
That’s not anxiety.
That’s conviction.
But instead of surrendering, you explain it away.
You rename conviction as overthinking.
You call discipline “too extreme.”
You call obedience “unrealistic.”
And slowly… your heart gets quieter.
Not because God stopped speaking.
But because you got better at not listening.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Because this isn’t about one mistake.
It’s about a pattern.
A cycle.
Conviction… justification… compromise… guilt… repeat.
And every time you justify what you know is wrong, you train your heart to trust your feelings over God’s voice.
But here’s the part you weren’t expecting.
God is not waiting to expose you.
He’s waiting to restore you.
Even Paul, in the middle of that internal war, cried out:

“ταλαίπωρος ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπος!”
(talaipōros egō anthrōpos)
“O wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me…?” (Romans 7:24)
And the answer wasn’t self-discipline.
It wasn’t trying harder.
It was a Person.

“χάρις δὲ τῷ Θεῷ διὰ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ”
(charis de tō Theō dia Iēsou Christou)
“Thanks be to God—through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (Romans 7:25)
This is where everything changes.
Not when you finally get it right…
…but when you finally stop pretending you already are.
Jesus didn’t come for the version of you that has everything under control.
He came for the version of you that keeps making excuses and doesn’t know how to stop.
And that’s the scandal.
That grace meets you in the middle of your rationalized sin… not after you’ve cleaned it up.
But grace doesn’t leave you there.
It rewrites you.
This is your moment.
There are people reading your honesty who feel the same weight but don’t know how to say it yet.
Let them see you.
Not to expose them… but to remind them they’re not alone.
Not for content.
For accountability.
For growth.
For truth that doesn’t bend.
If you truly want to glorify God, don’t just consume truth—help spread it.
Because someone you know is currently justifying something that’s quietly destroying them.
And this might be the interruption that saves them.
You don’t need a better excuse… you need a surrendered heart.
author: Gospel Warrior (John Domino Sanchez Asis)

title: You Didn’t Cheat… But Your Heart Did: The Quiet Betrayal That Starts With a “Like”
paragraphs: You Didn’t Cheat… But Your Heart Did: The Quiet Betrayal That Starts With a “Like”

There are affairs that begin in hotel rooms… and then there are the ones that begin in silence—on glowing screens, in lingering glances, in conversations that feel “harmless” until your spirit starts to feel distant from God and strangely alive in all the wrong places.
You told yourself it was nothing.

Just a reply.
